## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

# COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY

Or a universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, corrected with the greatest care; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions that have appeared during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or each author of some importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; enlarged by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; an edition so accurate, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, uniform and consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price—and especially this collection, a single, methodical, and chronological work, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.

## First Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# The Complete Works of Saint Leo the Great

Roman Pontiff,

Revised, corrected, and enlarged after the recension of Paschasius Quesnellus, by means of numerous and highly distinguished manuscript codices that he had not consulted; illustrated with prefaces, admonitions, and annotations. Also included are all the materials found in the Quesnellian edition, restored to critical examination. Edited by Peter and Jerome Ballerini, brothers, Veronese priests; with the final hand supplied by J.-P. Migne, who additionally contributed studies on the entire work.

## Saint Leo the Great

By Peter Thomas Cacciari.

Containing the authentic works of the holy pontiff, namely, the sermons and letters together with the appendices. Three volumes. Price: 24 francs.

## Sermons and Letters

[Col. 0009]

# Dedication of the Ballerini Brothers to Benedict XIV, Supreme Pontiff

Peter and Jerome Ballerini, brothers, Veronese priests.

[Col. 0009]

To whom could we more appropriately dedicate these works of the most holy, learned, and supreme pontiff Leo the Great, now issued in a more exact, corrected, and enlarged form according especially to the finest Roman codices, than to you, most blessed Father? You are the successor of so great a pontiff in that same Roman see; following in the footsteps of his zeal and learning, you appear to be the same Leo the Great restored to life.

He, indeed, because of the many distinguished achievements of his long pontificate—during which he was terrified by no change or difficulty of times and circumstances, but most vigorously defended the dogmas of the Catholic Church against stubborn and treacherous enemies of the faith; opposed the novel and rash undertakings of certain persons; courageously vindicated the privileges of the Churches and the rights of the apostolic see; and strove to detect, rebuke, correct, and eradicate the corruptions and abuses creeping into the custody and observance of ecclesiastical discipline—he, I say, so great a pontiff deserved the title “Great” by right on account of such outstanding deeds. His distinguished works, by which he advanced and accomplished so many matters of such great importance, have been handed down to us for the perpetual memory of posterity and commended with the highest praises not only by the Latins but also by the Greeks, both ancient and modern. They demonstrate the worthiness and justice of that same title.

But what shall we say of you, most blessed Father? From the very beginning of your pontificate, how many and how complicated were the causes that converged in accordance with the circumstances of these times, by which now the integrity of the faith, now pontifical rights, now ecclesiastical discipline and sound moral teaching were attacked? Yet you spared no labor or reflection, and provided timely care for all. Your constant care and vigilance are known to everyone: content with the sparingest food and brief sleep, you devote yourself tirelessly day and night to pastoral duties and public affairs, and devote whatever remains of your leisure to composing, as circumstances require, learned and deeply scholarly Institutions and Constitutions.

Your own works, which have so far appeared arranged in several volumes and which continue to appear repeatedly day by day—works that provide not merely for the present but also for the future in every ecclesiastical matter—are read by all with pleasure and profit. Everyone admires in them not their bulk, but their learning, variety of subject, method, clarity, and doctrine; and they do not hesitate to compare you with the more distinguished pontiffs of antiquity and to acknowledge you as truly Great, or rather Greatest. The works, therefore, of the ancient Roman bishop Leo the Great had most justly to be dedicated above all to you, his successor and rival in greatness.

To this most appropriate reason another, weightier and stronger, must be added. A few years ago, when one of us was residing in Rome and repeatedly presenting himself before your feet, mention was made during the conversations that, in your supreme kindness, you were accustomed to have with him—conversations in which you usually discussed many matters concerning excellent studies and ecclesiastical disciplines—of that edition of Saint Leo by which Paschasius Quesnellus had endeavored not so much to correct and illustrate the works of the holy pontiff as to refute, pervert, and deform them in many places by means of several harmful little notes, observations, and numerous dissertations.

You then mentioned the need for a new edition, to be prepared especially according to the Vatican manuscript codices that he had not consulted, and to blunt and break the force of his audacious efforts. Although this same plan had occurred to certain of your predecessors, it had never been completed by those to whom the task was entrusted, nor was it thought likely to be completed, and you could not tolerate the postponement of so necessary an edition any longer. You therefore judged that it ought to be imposed upon us.

At first, not only the magnitude of the work and the learning and genius of a great adversary, but also—and much more—our own weakness, of which we are conscious in ourselves, kept us hesitant and anxious in mind. [Col. 0011] Yet your will and authority had to be obeyed. To raise and restore our spirits, you used not words alone but also contributed your assistance to the same edition.

Since, in preparing such editions, the support of superior codices is of the greatest importance, you immediately ordered that the Vatican exemplars be made available. Moreover, to make collation easier and more convenient, you granted us the rare privilege of having the books we needed brought to our home and retained there for as long as necessary. You also arranged, with your customary kindness, that accurate collations should be made from other cities where rare and unconsulted codices were found. Indeed, you sent to our city, accompanied by your most gracious letters, the variant readings of certain ancient books, which, because of the distance of the places, reached you only later.

In the judgment of fair-minded evaluators, this is so significant that this edition, of which you were the originator and helper, should in some sense be regarded as yours. Consequently, when we dedicate it to your name, we are not offering something wholly our own; rather, we are returning what we received through your benefaction. We therefore trust that you will kindly receive and protect the edition as your own work. All who understand that it was undertaken at your command and completed with your assistance will commend your distinguished care and singular favor; and if they find that anything has been carried out less suitably by us, we hope that, out of regard for your name and patronage, they will forgive it.

Before we bring this letter to an end, however, permit us, we ask, most blessed Father, to submit to your wisest judgment what we believe to be especially fitting and glorious for Saint Leo. We wish to propose to you, as we trust not unpleasantly, a few matters concerning the granting to that holy pontiff of the title and veneration of “Doctor.”

We have no doubt that he who obtained the name “Great” also deserves the title “Doctor.” For if those are worthy of the title and veneration of “Doctor” who, joining eminent holiness with distinguished learning, both taught the universal Church while they were alive and continue to teach it after death through works left behind that will be useful for the faith and discipline of the Church at all times, surely Saint Leo—whose holiness is beyond question, and who taught, teaches, and will always teach the universal Church—must be counted among them.

He published numerous sermons and letters especially suited both to forming Christian conduct, preserving the true faith, and refuting the errors of the heterodox. These works have been received and celebrated with the greatest honor not only in the Churches of the West but also in those of the East, and are very frequently cited with the greatest weight of authority, just as the works of the more renowned Doctors are customarily cited.

Accordingly, Cassiodorus once not undeservedly bestowed upon him the name “Doctor” [Note: [Col. 0011] On Psalm LXV], as did two supreme pontiffs—Vigilius [Note: [Col. 0011] Constitution no. 22, vol. VI of the Councils, Venetian edition, col. 305] and Hadrian I [Note: [Col. 0011] Letter 97, Codex Carolinus]—who must be held in the highest esteem. Subsequently others did the same, among them Usuard and Wandelbert, who inserted the same title into the Martyrology.

Several Doctors of the Gallican Church also did not hesitate to honor him under this title in the public offices, as we learn from their liturgical books. We shall mention here only a few testimonies by way of example. The most eminent Cardinal Philip de Montibus, who strongly favored our plan, communicated them to us from his exceptionally select library shortly before his death.

From the Langres Breviary of 1731, on October 30: “Leo I, pope and Doctor of the Church.”

From the Châlons Breviary of 1736, on October 20: “Leo the Great, pope and Doctor of the Church.”

The same words are found in the Breviaries of Cluny of 1726, Rouen of 1728, and Clermont of 1733, on April 11; in that of Narbonne of 1709, on January 28; in those of Sens of 1726 and Orléans of 1731, on October 30; in that of Paris of 1736, on November 10; and in that of Bourges of 1734, on November 30.

Whether the time has now come for the Roman Church also—which cherishes no less love for this most holy and learned pontiff of hers, by whom she is especially adorned—to solemnly confer this same title and veneration upon him and extend it by general decree throughout the Christian world, we leave to you, most blessed Father, to judge and determine.

In your celebrated work On Beatification and Canonization, filled with sacred learning of every kind and destined to become a solemn and most secure rule for such rites in the future, you designated three conditions necessary for establishing a Doctor of the Church [Col. 0013] [Note: [Col. 0013] Book IV, part II, chapter 11, no. 13]: eminent learning, distinguished holiness of life, and, in addition, a declaration by the supreme pontiff or by a legitimately convened general council.

The Roman Church has sufficiently testified, both in other public records and in the Martyrology, that the first two conditions—in which the basis and merit of conferring this title consist—are found in our Leo. It remains that the third condition, by which the same title and veneration are established for him throughout the universal Church by legitimate authority, should be added by you. Considering his merits, you may perhaps pronounce concerning him what you wrote concerning Saint Bernard in the same work [Note: [Col. 0013] There, chapter 12, no. 9]:

> “It seems regrettable that until now no thought has been given to honoring in the universal Church with the title of Doctor a saint so distinguished in merits and so richly endowed with heavenly doctrine.”

Perhaps this praise has been reserved for you, whose greatest pleasure is promoting the veneration of the saints and who demonstrated your particular devotion to Saint Leo, while you were Canon Archivist of the Basilica of Saint Peter, especially in the most recent discovery of his body [Note: [Col. 0013] On this matter, see more in vol. II, in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 1 concerning the year 461]. You, I say, who are the great successor and rival of the great Leo, may adorn so great a pontiff with the title of Doctor on the occasion of this edition—which, being prepared according to purer codices and illustrated at your command and with your assistance, and published under your name, will repeatedly confirm the merit of this great Doctor.

But let this remain your judgment. Meanwhile, as we offer you this volume, we humbly kiss your holy feet and beg your apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0013]

# General Preface of the Ballerini Brothers to the Complete Edition of the Works of Saint Leo

## I

When the supreme pontiff Benedict XIV, while one of us was in Rome, assigned him the task of preparing a new edition of the works of Pope Saint Leo—an edition that could be set against and preferred to the already condemned Quesnellian edition—many serious and weighty considerations initially filled us with alarm.

For only those who are unfamiliar with Quesnellus’s edition can be unaware of what sort of edition it is and how important it is—the edition that Paschasius Quesnellus prepared with the greatest zeal. If one examines the text, which must be considered first and foremost in evaluating ancient editions, and in which the question is whether it has been corrected and enlarged by unpublished minor works, Quesnellus obtained numerous and highly distinguished codices. With their assistance he successfully corrected many passages that had been corrupted in earlier editions, and from a single Grimanic manuscript he was able to enlarge the pontiff’s Letters—which, among his works, are especially useful for sacred history—with twenty-eight previously unpublished letters.

He also added certain other unpublished materials, among which the most celebrated is that very ancient collection of Canons and Letters of the Roman pontiffs. It yields nothing to the Dionysian collection and is of the greatest assistance to students of the most ancient canon law.

But if one considers the editor’s own studies inserted into the text or intended to illustrate the subject matter—for this is the second thing sought in editions—what edition of the Fathers will be found enriched by so many observations, admonitions, notes, and dissertations by one editor as the edition of Leo printed by Quesnellus?

The works of that same pontiff, which in ancient editions had been contained in a small volume in what is called octavo or quarto format, fill two substantial folio volumes because of Quesnellus’s additions.

Who, moreover, would not be moved by such zeal for editing Leo, undertaken and energetically pursued by a man endowed with outstanding talent and extensive learning, who was capable of accomplishing so much, and who, after twenty-five years, reprinted his earlier edition, revised with new care and enlarged? It ought therefore to be judged as polished and perfected as far as he was able to make it.

[Col. 0015]

This edition received magnificent praises from very many learned men. For that reason, having been not merely first printed but reprinted, it was immediately dispersed and received throughout the world, and is still desired by many. Although it suffered no small loss of standing among Catholics because of the censures of certain persons, especially the Roman Inquisition in 1676, Johann Albert Fabricius nevertheless did not hesitate to affirm that it was approved by learned men everywhere.

This praise from a heterodox man—although it is altogether wrongly set against the Roman censure—nevertheless shows that the widespread opinion concerning the edition was confirmed by the testimonies of other Catholics as well.

## II

Set against these considerations, which caused apprehension, was the need for yet another edition after the Quesnellian one.

First, it was judged highly important to bring the works of the holy pontiff especially into conformity with Roman codices. Although these ought to be presumed superior and purer in the works of the Roman bishop, Quesnellus nevertheless sought them without success, as he himself testifies in his preface, and therefore had to pass them over in the first edition. In the second edition he received only the variant readings of the Barberini manuscripts, and even from these he used very few, and only in the Letters.

This examination of Roman exemplars appeared all the more necessary because, on the one hand, Quesnellus was accused by certain persons—especially Baluze and Coustant, who were highly skilled in the study of ancient books—of negligence in using codices; while, on the other hand, his known freedom in repeatedly correcting the text without citing any manuscript had aroused suspicion in some.

Moreover, many things had been inserted too freely into his studies, by which he favored false doctrines and attacked, sometimes openly and sometimes covertly, not so much Leo as the prerogatives of the Roman see. Thus this edition, which rather deforms than illustrates Leo, deserved the most just prohibition.

## III

For these reasons, we believe it can be inferred that as soon as the same edition appeared in 1675, plans were immediately begun for preparing a new edition in Rome. This may be gathered from an Italian letter written by Lorenzo Mari to Francesco Grisendo on March 30, 1677. He states that the instruction of the illustrious Brancaccio concerning a new edition of the works of Saint Leo had been communicated to him:

> “I have received the commands of the most illustrious Monsignor Brancaccio, my lord, concerning the new edition of Saint Leo.”

He adds that an inquiry was made into whatever his brother Giovanni Battista Maro had prepared from Roman manuscripts.

We found this letter in the Barberini codex. More extensive information about it will be given in the preface placed before Leo’s sermons, section 7.

The same idea of a new edition was revived in 1716, with the support of Pope Clement XI. A reliable testimony of the Trivulzian Fathers is included in the *Mémoires* for April 1716, page 722, where the following is transmitted from a letter written in Rome:

> “The plan for a new edition of Saint Leo has been formed. His Holiness, who has a particular devotion to this holy Doctor, favors the undertaking.”

Under Clement XII the same plan not only revived but was also entrusted to two distinguished men. When their studies were combined and many materials had been prepared on both sides, expectation of this Roman edition grew so great that the most eminent Cardinal Quirini wrote on this subject in 1740, in the appendix attached to the Life of Paul II, page 161, that not only did the prayers of the devout and learned demand it, but that they also hoped for a sounder and more faithful edition, based especially on the Vatican codices.

## IV

When one of us went to Rome in 1748 for another reason, he asked several people about this new edition. Some replied that they had heard nothing about it for a long time; others that all hope had vanished.

When the matter was discussed in the presence of the supreme pontiff Benedict XIV, one of the two men to whom the edition had been entrusted under Clement XII confirmed this complete hopelessness. The pope then imposed this scholarly task upon us.

Although, in addition to the matters mentioned at the beginning, the weakness of our own abilities also deterred us, we could not resist such great authority for long. When word of the undertaking had spread through the City, several cardinals, prelates, and friends came forward with encouragement and also offered their assistance.

Since the work had to begin with the codices, the praised supreme pontiff, in order to make collation easier and more efficient, granted us the special privilege of having the manuscript books of the Vatican Library that would be most useful brought to our home.

The other Roman libraries also opened their collections to us: the Barberini, Chigi, Casanatense, Vallicellian, Angelica, and that of the Basilica of Saint Peter.

Since there were many codices to be examined, and one person was not enough, assistants were hired for payment, while others contributed their voluntary and unpaid labor. Among these, Father Bruno Toma deserves particular praise. At that time a lecturer and now prior of the Dominican Fathers of Santa Sabina, he joined several of his fellow religious to himself in the collations. [Col. 0017]

He spent all the time during which one of us was staying in Rome—that is, a full year and a half—unceasingly among the codices in this labor.

When he left the City, leaving several matters still to be collated, several friends very courteously supplied assistance: Father Master Schiara, a Dominican and prefect of the Casanatense Library; Count Joseph Garampi, canon of the Basilica of Saint Peter and custodian of the Vatican Archive; our fellow citizen Father Francesco dal Pozzo, priest of the Oratory at the Vallicella; Simon Ballarini of the Barberini Library; and several others. They sent to Verona the variant readings of the manuscripts that we desired, carefully copied out by themselves.

## V

We also extended our diligence to other Italian libraries untouched by Quesnellus and especially renowned for their manuscript exemplars. We arranged, either ourselves or through friends, for all the Leonine codices of any value known to us to be collated.

Besides several highly distinguished exemplars of the cathedral chapter of Verona—which, because of their remarkable antiquity, yield to none of the others—we were able to find in Venice, in the Library of Saint Mark, which is exceptionally well supplied with Greek and Latin codices, quite a few materials useful for the present undertaking. We also experienced the greatest courtesy from Antonio Zanetti, its custodian, who is favorably disposed toward all students and was especially helpful in examining Greek books.

At Padua, in the library of the Hermit Fathers, Father Master Antonio Manentius supplied codices and assistance; in the monastery of the Benedictine monks of Saint Justina, Father D. Spiridion Peristianus did likewise; and at Saint Anthony’s, in the house of the Conventual Fathers of Saint Francis, Father Master Reginald Fischer provided codices and labor.

From the distinguished Benedictine monastery of Polirone in the Mantuan territory, Father D. John Augustine Gradonicus sent variant readings of codices collected with no small labor.

At Florence, both in the Library of Saint Mark and in the Laurentian Medicean Library, we owe much to Father Lecturer Philip Maria Sereno, who collated some materials and also copied others.

At Fiesole, Father Alexander Chiappinus, recently deceased, the general abbot of the Lateran Canons, procured what was needed.

With regard to the manuscripts of Monte Cassino, we found a great patron in the most eminent Cardinal Tamburini. His extraordinary favor will be mentioned more fully in the preface to the sermons, no. 16.

Father John Dominic Mansi, highly experienced in ancient manuscripts and known through numerous published documents and volumes, spontaneously offered to collate the codices of Lucca.

At Bergamo our dearest friend Father Hyacinth Sala, of the Dominican order and public professor of theology at the University of Turin, provided assistance.

Other forms of help were available through others at Milan, Trent, Turin, and elsewhere.

## VI

We extended our diligence beyond Italy as well, specifically to the Imperial Library of Vienna and to the Library of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg.

From the Imperial Library—which the French editor had unsuccessfully sought to consult—we obtained, sparing no expense, the most diligent possible collation of two exceptionally fine exemplars of the Spanish and Quesnellian collections.

In the Regensburg library, Father Bernard Pez had reported in the introductory dissertation prefixed to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, no. 65, that an altogether outstanding and unique codex of the Letters of Saint Leo was preserved there. It had been given to that library as a gift by Bishop Tuto at the end of the ninth century or the beginning of the tenth.

Desiring this codex, the one of us who was in Rome approached Father Master Thomas Ricchini, a Dominican and secretary of the Congregation of the Index. With his cooperation, Father Master Emeric Langenuaeter, of the same order, provincial of Dacia and associate of the master general, immediately wrote to Father Master Antoninus Veichtner.

As soon as Father Antoninus recognized, in keeping with his exceptional expertise in these studies, the excellence and usefulness of the codex, he decided—not merely to collate it, but to transcribe it word for word with the greatest possible accuracy, displaying a favor no less remarkable than his labor.

To make this possible for him more conveniently, the most reverend abbot of Saint Emmeram, prince of the Holy Roman Empire and a man highly cultivated in every branch of letters and sciences, with the greatest kindness granted permission for the same codex to be transported to Landshut, to the convent of the aforementioned Father Antoninus.

The extraordinary diligence of one man in copying and the kindness of the other in lending so distinguished a codex—of which more will be said in the preface to the Letters—ought to be proclaimed to the whole world and commended to perpetual memory.

Through these resources we discovered that the text of Saint Leo could still be corrected to a considerable extent after Quesnellus and enlarged by new unpublished documents.

## VII

Roman manuscript exemplars contributed most of all to the correction of the sermons. Among these, since some certainly belonged to the basilicas of the City, they are certainly Roman and preserved purer readings for us.

Although Quesnellus corrected many passages, because he did not use these codices [Col. 0019] he left some things uncorrected and changed others either not suitably enough or incorrectly. We were able to restore approximately three hundred passages by certain correction or to bring them back to a better reading.

Moreover, after collating simultaneously so many and such great codices of different origins—of which we shall provide a distinct account in the preface to the Sermons—we discovered that the order of certain sermons had been disturbed and needed correction; that two sermons which had merged into one had to be divided; that a sermon wrongly attributed to Leo by everyone had to be removed; that another sermon which Quesnellus had fabricated for Leo from his own codex had likewise to be removed; and that still another, which he had taken away from Leo, had to be restored.

We accomplished many other things with the aid of the manuscripts, as will be evident from the admonitions and annotations.

## VIII

Similar discoveries will be made even more frequently in the Letters. Numerous and important corrections will repeatedly occur; among them, the chronology of several Letters has been restored, and the order of all of them had to be changed.

With the assistance especially of the manuscript books, we were able to defend certain Letters that Quesnellus had called into question and to restore several passages that he had deleted.

## IX

In both the Sermons and the Letters, Quesnellus changed many passages without citing any manuscript or even indicating the ancient reading. This led some people to suspect arbitrary correction or corruption.

To forestall this criticism, in the general preface, no. 7, he did not hesitate to acknowledge the fact openly and offered the following twofold explanation:

> “I have often omitted citing these codices when the correction is of indubitable certainty and all the codices agree with it.”

Neither reason, however, appeared sufficiently adequate.

For when the issue is not an obvious error of a copyist or printer—as is generally not the case in the passages corrected by Quesnellus—the readings substituted for previously published readings that conveyed a not-bad sense cannot be called of indubitable certainty.

Moreover, if Quesnellus’s general assertion about the agreement of all the codices has sometimes proved deceptive when he wrote concerning this or that reading that he himself had introduced, “Thus all the codices,” what credibility does it deserve in passages whose correction he mentions without citing any codex?

Nor should one therefore assert that whenever he cites nothing, he changed or corrupted the published text arbitrarily. This may appear so to those who collated only the codices of the later collections from which the published editions arose.

We, however, having obtained more ancient and superior exemplars, were able, through careful collation of them, to distinguish and judge which passages he corrected neither arbitrarily nor incorrectly. We shall therefore retain the corrections themselves and support them by citing the manuscripts.

But readings that we found supported either by no ancient book or only by manuscripts of inferior quality we rightly judged ought to be removed, restoring the ancient reading or introducing another new reading on the authority of better codices.

In this matter, we would sometimes gladly have retained a reading introduced by him without mention of any ancient book, if he had produced the authority of some excellent codex.

## X

Since in our edition it was necessary not to omit the works that Quesnellus attributed to Leo or judged worthy of inclusion in his edition, we also found many things in these works that needed correction when examined according to the authority of the manuscripts, and some that needed to be supplied.

This will become especially clear in the books *On the Calling of All Nations* and in the *Code of Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*. In editing the latter, Quesnellus generally followed a more recent and faulty codex.

## XI

With regard to unpublished materials, we found in our manuscript exemplars not only nearly all those Letters that Quesnellus published from the Grimanic codex, and found them corrected in many passages, but we shall also bring to light three additional new Letters of Leo from the distinguished Regensburg codex.

From the Vatican we shall publish one Greek letter of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, to our Leo; it contributes greatly to the illumination of the history of Eutyches.

We also drew from the same Vatican codex several Letters in an ancient Greek translation. The importance of making them public will be shown in the preface to the Letters, no. 51.

The complete proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon, held on behalf of Leo’s Letter 93 and not yet published, were supplied to us by two Greek codices of Saint Mark’s in Venice. With their assistance, and with the help of Antonio Zanetti, we also collated, with great usefulness for correcting many passages, the Greek edition of numerous Letters. Although these are translations, they nevertheless had to be inserted into our edition.

Another proceeding of the same council, concerning Domnus of Antioch and commending Leo’s pontifical authority, will be published from an ancient manuscript formerly in Verona and now in the Vatican [Col. 0021], and will be placed in its proper setting in volume II.

We excerpted several unpublished sermons attributed to Leo in manuscript exemplars; they appeared to us not to be omitted from the appendix.

## XII

Father Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, of the Society of Jesus, had raised hopes of finding several previously unknown Letters of our pontiff contained in an ancient Vercelli book, in a letter inserted in volume XLI of the *Opuscula* published at Venice by Father Angelo Calogerà.

He mentions one of the codices of the distinguished capitular library of Vercelli, which he calls an incomparable and unpublished collection of the most ancient councils. On the authority of the celebrated editor of the Eusebian Evangeliary, he testifies that it is:

> “richly adorned with several previously unseen letters of Saint Leo and of other pontiffs.”

To ensure that such distinguished documents might more certainly be added to our edition, we sought the authority of the supreme pontiff himself, who had ordered the edition.

Accordingly, the codices of the aforementioned chapter were examined with the greatest care. But no such collection could be found that produced even a single unpublished letter of Leo.

As for the codex that seemed to contain some unpublished material, we learned with complete certainty—from the transcribed documents sent to the pontiff together with a collation of the other published codices, from other information subsequently received, and from the same editor of the Eusebian Evangeliary—that it was entirely similar to three other manuscript books that we were able to find and collate in Rome.

It contains the Dionysian-Hadrianic collection with particular additions. These will be indicated in the preface to the Letters and described more fully in volume III, in the treatise on ancient collections.

These matters had especially to be noted, lest we appear to have neglected any diligence in seeking unpublished materials.

We think that it has been made clear from what has been said that, as regards the text of Leo, this edition will be more corrected and more enlarged than the Quesnellian edition. Add also that, as regards the works of Leo themselves, it will be more authentic, since it separates his genuine works from the spurious ones, which Quesnellus, in a completely arbitrary and altogether erroneous manner, passed off as Leonine.

### XIII.

Now concerning Quesnel’s scholarly labors, which make his edition especially famous. If at first the man’s outstanding intellect and learning had inspired apprehension, once we had subjected his actual works to a more exact reckoning and detected in most of them a great abuse of intellect and learning, our spirits were raised and strengthened. For although he gathers together many things subtly and learnedly—things that carried not a few men, and not men of the lowest rank, over to his opinions—nevertheless, upon a careful examination of each item, we found that this exceedingly acute man, indulgent toward his own ingenuity and toward novelty, and carried away by zeal for certain parties, had run intemperately into conjectures that were for the most part utterly false. By weaving these together with great acumen and skill, and disguising them with great learning, he gave many new and false claims a certain appearance of probability. Lest we be thought to have made any harsher assertions under the influence of opposition to his party, or of what are called Italian prejudices, before proceeding further we must first offer the testimony of several distinguished foreigners who cannot be accused of such partiality or prejudice.

### XIV.

Father Coustantius sufficiently exposed the enormous abuse of conjecturing in that dissertation in which Quesnel, intending to defend the Collection of Canons published by himself as belonging to the Roman Church, strove to support it by a great mass of conjectures. Coustantius wrote this in the preface to volume I of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 79:

> “While this most distinguished man indulges such conjectures beyond measure, he himself increasingly reveals the emptiness of his opinion.”

And more openly, in no. 87, noting the fallacies added to his conjectures:

> “To follow one by one the arguments of the learned man and subject them to examination would take too long. It is enough to refute the principal ones. If these are judged according to truth, they are nothing other than either conjectures—indeed, as they say, cleverly and elegantly devised, but nevertheless mere conjectures—or testimonies forcibly twisted, which, when restored to their proper place and understood in their proper sense, lose their strength—or finally proofs drawn from passages that he wrongly considered peculiar to the Roman codex.”

For this reason, in nos. 43 and 63 he called the opinion which Quesnel defended with so much effort “a mere hypothesis and indeed an ingenious, but less than solid, system.” He expressed astonishment that the same system could have been asserted—or, he would not say asserted, but even conceived in the mind—by a man of such exceptionally keen judgment.

Stephen Baluzius likewise noticed and censured a similar weakness in conjecturing in his observations on Quesnel’s dissertation concerning the Council of Telepte, where Quesnel strove at length to brand that council as spurious. After carefully discussing the matter, Baluzius wrote:

> “I am fully persuaded that Quesnel’s opinions may indeed dazzle the eyes, but that there is nothing certain, solid, or firm in them.”

These observations of Baluzius are printed in the Paris edition of Peter de Marca’s *Concordia*, published in 1704, p. 1341. There also, on p. 1347, he testifies that Quesnel was not sufficiently sincere or diligent in this edition, and reproaches him for following, at a certain point, the faulty reading of the Oxford codex, whereas the Thuaneum exemplar was preferable to it in every respect. In the preface to the ancient Latin version of the Council of Chalcedon, no. 22, accusing him of the same negligence in another matter, Baluzius writes:

> “If he had consulted the ancient codices carefully, as we did, he would not have conceived this opinion in his mind.”

In the same no. 22, concerning one of Quesnel’s conjectures, he says:

> “It is mere divination, if I may say so without offending him, and it is not supported by reason.”

Father Bernard de Montfaucon, or rather the Benedictine monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, declare the following about Quesnel in their dissertation on the *Quicumque* Creed, in volume II of the works of Saint Athanasius, p. 724. Quesnel had attributed that creed to Vigilius of Thapsus:

> “Yet, although he possesses considerable acumen and learning, he speaks only by conjecturing.”

William Cave, under the year 440, p. 279, likewise wrote of Quesnel’s dissertation in which he undertook to assign the books *On the Calling of All Nations* to Leo:

> “He endeavors to claim them for Leo, and does so by a long train of conjectures rather than arguments.”

After briefly reviewing these conjectures, Cave adds:

> “The learned man says many things of this kind which, since they usually vary according to each person’s ingenuity and may be found to a greater or lesser extent in other writers, do not seem to provide a sufficiently firm foundation for this opinion.”

And Father William Cuper, in the *Acts of the Saints* under 25 August, p. 133, says of one argument by which Quesnel rejected the account of the miracle of Saint Genesius:

> “This slight little argument, or Quesnel’s rash conjecture, seems to collapse in the face of the chronology.”

We pass over many other testimonies of the same kind; these seem sufficient for our purpose.

### XV.

Thus far these men have spoken about Quesnel’s particular discussions and arguments, since they subjected only particular matters to examination. We, however, who have undertaken by design to examine and cut back to the quick all his scholarly labors inserted into the Leonine edition, can make the same assertion about most of them, not to say all: scarcely any dissertation of his will remain that does not have to be either refuted in its principal subject by the observations placed below, or corrected in many respects.

The same happened to very many of his notes, which he either appended with a more expansive pen to Leo’s sermons or relegated, after the dissertations, to his letters. Lest these words be thought boastful, or lest it be suspected that, while attacking Quesnel, we have plucked from his work certain passages which, once detached from their context, could easily be twisted into hatred and reproach, we have decided to insert his own scholarly labors in full into our edition and to place beside each of them its corresponding observations. These will attack or correct whatever deserves refutation.

We are so confident in our cause that we do not shrink from confronting the adversary face to face. This will also make Quesnel’s edition no longer necessary, since it will be found incorporated in its entirety into ours; and everyone will be able to read in this edition the scholarly labors that have been prohibited in his editions, and compare them with our observations and censures. From this we hope that the truth will become more readily known and that everyone will be able to see whether we have dared too much.

### XVI.

It is proper to acknowledge here that this method of disputing with an adversary present and fighting us face to face has made the undertaking more difficult. Richard Simon, drawing on Élie Dupin, noted two things about Quesnel’s edition: namely, that Quesnel’s dissertations were excessively long and that some of them bore only a remote relation to Leo’s works. Dupin wrote:

> “The dissertations are nevertheless too long, and some have only a remote connection with the works of Saint Leo.”  
> [Note: *Critique de la Bibliothèque . . . par M. Dupin*, book II, chapter 16.]

These two matters caused the greatest difficulty. To speak first of the latter point: since it is the editor’s task to examine and unfold carefully whatever concerns his author and his works, it would have been necessary to consider and scrutinize in Quesnel only those few matters that properly belong to Leo or to his works. We would not have been compelled to wander into the subjects on which he ran further and more freely, and thus we could have passed over many of the more difficult matters.

But since we were inserting all Quesnel’s dissertations, admonitions, and annotations, each item had to be subjected to examination, whether it concerned Leo or his works, or whether it had been introduced incidentally and led very far afield. Nothing could be concealed or passed over, however difficult and involved it might be—especially since even in such discussions, very remote from an edition of Leo, there are many things that appeared to deserve substantial censure. Since the variety and difficulty of the matters into which Quesnel wandered required longer reflection and more numerous observations, this, I say, was chiefly why the edition could be sent to press later than had initially been expected.

### XVII.

As for the excessive length of Quesnel’s dissertations noted by Dupin, it was usually necessary for Quesnel himself to prolong them in many places. For since, in very many of his theses, he lacked established reasons and documentation—where such things are present, only a few suffice to conclude the matter—he was forced to take refuge in conjectures, and weak ones at that.

Moreover, because this acute man understood that such conjectures, if few in number and stated briefly, could accomplish very little, he took pains to heap many of them together at once, linking them to one another and repeatedly fortifying them with learned information, rhetorical skill, and subtle reasoning, so that he might gradually and more easily entice his readers and draw them over to his opinion.

At first it seemed that we too would have to follow the same path and refute everything, item by item, that demanded censure. But by this method we would have fallen under the same charge of excessive prolixity. Lest this be thought an excuse for avoiding labor or difficulty, we observe that those who defend the truth need only overthrow the central and stronger arguments. Once these have been removed, the remaining weaker arguments, which depend upon them, collapse of themselves, so that it would be the mark of an excessively tedious person to detain readers longer in refuting them.

Yet even in this apparent reduction of labor, it was sometimes extremely difficult to separate, among the many conjectures, those that were central and especially in need of refutation. For Quesnel joins and mixes so many things with astonishing skill that it is scarcely possible to discover what is doing the work. When he has proposed some weaker points, to which the response would be easy, he suddenly slips away like a snake and runs on to other matters which, even if perhaps equally weak, nevertheless appear more serious because of what precedes them.

Now he conjectures by asking questions rather than by affirming; now he inserts other questions into a question, or at least scatters certain doubts, by which—when they are drawn out at length, eloquently, and subtly—the deception is not easily discerned. Adding conjecture to conjecture, he trusts that what he could not obtain with a few, he will accomplish by their multitude.

Anyone experienced in these matters will understand how much attention and diligence were required to examine all this exactly and reduce it to a few certain and more important points, lest the refutation become too long and produce weariness and even confusion in readers through its multiplicity. If, in refuting these more important points, our observations sometimes seem too long to someone, let him consider that more is often required to overthrow an error than to propose it.

We shall also use such an easy division and method that the reader will immediately understand what is being done and why a longer discussion was necessary in certain sections on which the others depend. We hope that by this method it will become clear that, while taking account of brevity as far as possible, we have omitted nothing of central importance, but have rightly neglected only the smaller points, which collapse once the more important arguments supporting them have been torn away.

If some matters inserted by Quesnel into his dissertations require particular censure but find no suitable place in the course of our observations on the individual dissertations, we shall briefly indicate such censures in the annotations attached to those same places, so that nothing necessary may be lacking.

### XVIII.

Richard Simon, whom we mentioned shortly before, gives the following testimony concerning Quesnel’s edition of Saint Leo, which we think must not be omitted here. After quoting the praise with which Dupin had commended Quesnel’s dissertations, he adds:

> “The edition of the works of Saint Leo published under the name of Father Quesnel certainly deserves this praise; but the librarian did not know that this work came from several hands. Father Quesnel gathered its materials over a period of several years; some of them were supplied to him by several learned persons in Paris. But since this Father did not know Latin sufficiently to compose his work in that language, he first composed it in French, and had it translated into Latin by a learned Irishman who had formerly belonged to the Oratory and who at that time taught rhetoric at the College of Beauvais. He also composed the Life of Saint Leo in French, and it was translated into Latin by Father Gérard du Bois, who was then living with Father Quesnel in the house of the Fathers of the Oratory on the Rue Saint-Honoré. Father du Bois altered several passages in this Life that seemed to him too harsh against Rome—alterations which Father Quesnel could not approve. But if he had profited from the good advice given him by his confrère, he might perhaps have been spared the displeasure of seeing his work stigmatized at Rome. For the rest, I state nothing here of which I have not been well informed; so that one may say of the author of the edition of Saint Leo published under the name of Father Quesnel: *We are Legion*.”  
> [Note: *Critique de la Bibliothèque . . . par M. Dupin*, book II, chapter 16.]

Thus far Richard Simon, who lived for a long time in the Congregation of the Oratory together with Quesnel, down to approximately the time of the Leonine edition.

In this testimony, it is especially important to observe that Quesnel was so bitter and hostile toward the Roman See that even one of his own confrères disliked certain passages and therefore thought they should be softened in the Latin translation. Since Quesnel rejected this, it cannot be said that anything was added or exaggerated in this respect by the translators; rather, whatever is read as especially harsh in that edition must be acknowledged to have proceeded entirely from Quesnel’s own mind and judgment.

### XIX.

There were two principal prejudices from which he suffered: one concerning grace, and the other against certain prerogatives of the Roman See. How badly he thought on the subject of grace is made clear by what he later published and what was condemned by a solemn Constitution. He inserted some of these ideas into Leo’s edition, but covertly and sparingly. They will be discussed to some extent in several observations on Leo’s sermons and on the second dissertation concerning the books *On the Calling of All Nations*.

Against the prerogatives of the pontiffs, however, he wandered more openly and extensively. Although ill-disposed toward them, and wishing to conceal all passion and prejudice, he repeatedly set forth, in magnificent language, certain declarations of observance, devotion, and reverence toward the Apostolic See. In practice, however, he tried by every means available to weaken and diminish its authority.

Quesnel showed himself to have gone far beyond the other men of his party in this matter by striving, through utterly empty conjectures, to represent as spurious, or at least doubtful, documents that appeared to favor Roman prerogatives, even though they were entirely certain. For this reason, it seems, he judged that the Council of Telepte should be expunged, together with the letter of Pope Siricius; likewise the Chalcedonian act concerning Domnus, and the Life of Saint Romanus—or at least the text which he imagines to have been inserted and intruded into it.

Many other passages revealing the man’s poor disposition toward the Roman pontiffs will repeatedly occur in our observations and also in some of our annotations. Anyone who reads them with an impartial mind will admit, if we are not mistaken, that it was necessary to oppose Quesnel’s edition with another edition in which all his scholarly labors would be individually subjected to examination and marked at the proper time with just censures.

The only regrettable point is that this task fell to men less well equipped in learning and knowledge. Yet this will make the truth increasingly manifest. For if we, who possess only modest abilities, demonstrate how wrongly Quesnel wrote in many places, it will be evident that this was accomplished not by ingenuity, skill, or any special assistance, but by truth itself making the matter clear.

### XX.

It remains now to explain the arrangement of our edition. Quesnel’s edition is contained in two volumes. The first includes Leo’s works, not so much genuine as spurious. The genuine works are the Sermons and Letters. But the two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, the *Capitula* on grace, and the *Letter to Demetrias*, or book *On Humility*, which Quesnel wrongly attributed to Leo, we classify among the spurious works.

At the end of the same volume he added the Life of Saint Hilary of Arles and some of that author’s short works.

In the second volume he published from manuscripts the most ancient and distinguished Collection of Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See, which he thought should be entitled the *Code of the Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church*. He did not do this because the codices bore that title, but because he believed the Collection to have belonged specifically to the Roman Church, to have been in force in Leo’s time, and to have been enlarged in several places by Leo himself.

He then appended sixteen dissertations on Leo’s works and on the aforementioned ancient Collection of Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See. Finally, he printed various readings, notes, and observations on the Letters of the Holy Pontiff.

It should be noted, however, that in the second, Lyons edition of 1700, Quesnel added a considerable number of things that were absent from the first, Paris edition of 1675. He inserted certain documents that had been brought to light after the first edition, namely two Greek letters of Marcian to Leo, edited by Arnold; one of Eutyches to the same pontiff, published by Father Lupus; a fragment of a letter of Anatolius of Constantinople; and the Greek text of Flavian’s letter, which Cotelerius printed; as well as John Ciampini’s dissertation on the correction of a word in Sermon VII of Saint Leo, *On the Nativity of the Lord*.

Moreover, he sometimes used in his notes or postils variants from three Barberini manuscripts of the Letters, which he later obtained. He also added a considerable amount to his dissertations and notes, in which he made every effort to defend and confirm his earlier opinions after they had been attacked by Lupus, Baluzius, and other critics.

### XXI.

We shall divide our edition into three volumes. The first volume will present all Leo’s genuine works, that is, his authentic Sermons and Letters. In reviewing and correcting these, we have used our manuscripts in such a way that we also examined Quesnel’s variants. Thus both our copies and Quesnel’s contributed to the completion of this edition.

We have placed prefaces and admonitions at the beginning wherever necessary. The annotations attached to the Sermons and Letters will explain the grounds of the corrections, accurately identify the variant readings of both our manuscripts and Quesnel’s, and illuminate the pontiff’s text wherever it appeared to require it.

These annotations will also include those notes which Quesnel occasionally attached to the Sermons or the Letters themselves, so that nothing belonging to him may be lacking. Since he attached to some Sermons certain annotations or postils that require a longer discussion, we shall, for their sake, publish after the Sermons our observations on particular passages of those same Sermons. These will contain the aforementioned annotations or postils of Quesnel, as well as the celebrated dissertation of Ciampini, which serves to elucidate a single sermon.

We have relegated doubtful Sermons, or those wrongly attributed to Leo, some of which have been published but most of which are unpublished, to an appendix of Sermons. In the preface to that appendix, among other matters, information is given about other Sermons wrongly attributed to Leo in certain manuscript copies and assigned to various other authors in various other codices. Since they appeared among the works of other Fathers, they did not need to be reprinted; we have indicated in which books they were published.

Leo’s Letters will be followed by a dissertation on lost letters—both those of Saint Leo to others and those of others to Saint Leo—and on other documents relating to the letters, arranged in chronological order. The surviving Leonine fragments will be inserted there.

Next will come an account of the decrees attributed to Leo in the *Pontifical Book*. Finally, an appendix of the letters of Saint Leo the Great will contain several spurious letters and other documents relating to the Letters that ought not to have been placed among his Letters.

### XXII.

The second volume will present an appendix of the longer works that were attributed to Leo. First will be published the most ancient Sacramentary, commonly called the Leonine Sacramentary because it is attributed to Leo.

It could not be classified among the certain works of this pontiff, since not everything contained in it belongs to Leo, nor can the same pontiff certainly be called its compiler. But because certain Leonine materials are read in it, and because on their basis it was attributed to Leo in printed editions, it ought not to be omitted from the appendix in which other works attributed to Leo are to be published—works that contain nothing certainly Leonine.

It was all the more necessary to do this because Quesnel published three prefaces as though they were Leonine at the end of the Sermons. Two of them are found in the surviving part of that Sacramentary, while we reasonably believe that the third existed in the portion that has perished.

Second, we shall publish the two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, the *Capitula* or *Authorities on Grace and Free Will*, and the *Letter to the Virgin Demetrias*, or treatise *On Humility*. Quesnel prefixed Leo’s name to all of them.

We have reviewed these works against manuscript codices. With their assistance we corrected many passages and also supplied certain things that were missing in some copies.

There will follow the *Brief Against Heretics*, otherwise called the *Brief of the Faith Against the Arians*, which Father Sirmond published without the author’s name. We found it attributed to Leo in two ancient codices, the Padua and Milan manuscripts, which supplied several corrections. The reason why we have listed it among the spurious rather than among Leo’s works will be clear from the admonition already given.

After these works, so that nothing Quesnel inserted into his edition might be lacking, the Life of Saint Hilary of Arles and his short works—two of them added by us—will be published after comparison with and correction from several manuscript copies. Here the appendix ends.

Furthermore, so that Quesnel’s scholarly labors might be inserted into our edition as we promised, eleven of his sixteen dissertations will be reprinted in this volume, since they concern either Leo or the works mentioned above. The remaining five are reserved for the third volume because they concern the *Code of the Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*, which we have postponed to the third volume.

Whenever the principal subject proposed by Quesnel in a dissertation has to be refuted, observations serving in place of a critical review will be appended to each dissertation. Where only certain points in the dissertations require correction or confirmation, annotations placed at the foot of the pages will be sufficient.

This was especially necessary with respect to the first dissertation, which describes the Life of Saint Leo. Although not a few things there will require correction and some additions will also be necessary, many more matters are sufficiently established.

This volume will conclude with Quesnel’s observations and notes on Leo’s Letters, which Quesnel himself published after the dissertations because they were more extensive. Where necessary, we shall correct them with other annotations of our own, presented distinctly.

### XXIII.

The occasion for publishing the third volume separately and assembling it in its proper size was provided by the most ancient Collection of Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See, which Quesnel brought to light at the beginning of the second volume under the arbitrary and false title *Code of the Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church*.

He published it from a more recent and very corrupt Oxford manuscript. He made only limited and unsuitable use of the older and excellent Thuaneum exemplar, which he came to know only later. We obtained much more from this codex by other means.

A very large amount was also supplied from another previously unknown but extremely ancient book of the same Collection in the Imperial Library. With these aids we were able to correct many errors and restore the Collection itself to a better and more original form.

Since, while seeking assistance from other Collections for correcting or elucidating this one, we examined at Rome and elsewhere all the manuscript copies of other ancient Collections that we could find, and since it proved useful to discover and review in them all or nearly all the documents of the aforementioned Collection, even though scattered throughout them, we derived from this study another and much more valuable benefit.

For in these codices we found many exceedingly rare, and even entirely unknown, monuments of the most ancient canon law. We believe it will be welcome and useful to publish them after the aforementioned Collection, either in more correct form or for the first time.

What these documents are, and what their use and importance may be, will be understood from what will be said in the preface to the third volume.

This diligent examination of very many manuscript Collections also enabled us not only to discover several unknown and unpublished Collections of Canons, but to acquire much information concerning published Collections that had escaped even the most recent and learned writers on these subjects, and by which the history of ancient canon law can be greatly illuminated.

For this reason we shall place before Quesnel’s Collection a treatise on both the published and unpublished ancient Collections and collectors of Canons down to Gratian. All these matters will be explained fully there.

Finally, after the ancient documents, we shall publish the five dissertations of Quesnel which concern the Collection of Canons published by him and which we have therefore reserved for this volume, together with our observations. In accordance with our undertaking, these will be necessary for refuting them wherever he formed erroneous opinions.

### XXIV.

We have omitted a separate account of the individual editions, which would have had a suitable place in the general preface. Such an account is provided in Quesnel’s preface, which, so that nothing belonging to Quesnel’s edition might be lacking in accordance with our plan, we shall immediately append with a few annotations.

At the end we mention this point: since at Rome and elsewhere we had heard complaints from learned men about modern editions, which, being printed in large folio for magnificence, are difficult to handle and read, especially at night, we thought it best to choose the format of a small folio that could be conveniently opened and read.

---

# GENERAL PREFACE OF FATHER QUESNEL TO HIS EDITION OF THE WORKS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT

### 1.

The foundation of the holy Catholic Church, laid by Christ, is one: divine faith. The sole source of faith is the word of God, whether that which is read expressed in the sacred writings, or that which we have received as having been entrusted orally to the apostles and transmitted down to us through the tradition of the holy Fathers.

For this reason, this labor and this work must above all be judged worthy of an ecclesiastical man: that the two channels of the Catholic faith may always become purer, cleansed of foreign pollution, lest the minds of the faithful, when those living and heavenly waters of divine truth have been muddied with the mire of alien doctrines, be contaminated rather than refreshed.

The learned sons of the Catholic Church have labored with such careful attention and such happy success to separate and cleanse the errors with which the sacred page had been sprinkled either through ignorance of times or through the malice of heretics, that everyone may now draw the knowledge of salvation from that perfectly clear fountain without any fear of error.

But the writings of the holy Fathers, through which truth is conveyed from Christ the Head down to us as through a second channel, rolling onward through the centuries, have not yet been sufficiently cleansed of the dregs of errors and interpolations, nor fully restored to their purity. Nevertheless, for a hundred and fifty years and more, men of outstanding learning have begun to work toward this end with no ordinary vigilance, so that the holy Fathers might be, as it were, reborn for us in their entirety.

The palm of this achievement seems to have been reserved for our age. In it, accurate editions of the works of the principal Fathers, illuminated by the splendid commentaries of learned men, have either appeared not long ago or are soon to appear.

In proportion to the smallness of my abilities, I have received this small share in so extensive a labor: to undertake the purification and, if possible, restoration to their former brilliance of the works of Pope Saint Leo—Leo, I say, the least in the bulk of his writings but the Great in surname; greatest in the holiness of his life and in both his deeds and his writings; whose writings possess all the greater weight in sacred tradition because the apostles to whom he succeeded were greater, and because the Roman Church which he governed, more ancient than the other Western Churches and preeminent among them all, has always been regarded as possessing a more powerful “principality,” as Irenaeus calls it.

In the work we have undertaken, we have had so many predecessors that scarcely one of the holy Fathers can be found whose writings have received the healing hand of more editors; yet no other writings were more in need of such care.

Before, therefore, we explain the plan and method of our undertaking and labor in this edition, it is worthwhile briefly to set out here what others have accomplished in their editions—not only so that the praise owed to each may not be lost, but also so that everyone may more easily understand what our small work has added to theirs.

### II.

John Andrew of Aleria, bishop on the island of Corsica, prepared the first edition of the works of Saint Leo I at Venice in 1485, printed by Andrew of Parma, associate in the printing craft.

This first edition contains very few Letters appended to the Sermons.

[Note: It should be said that it was printed at Rome before the year 1472, as will become clear from what will be said in the preface to the Sermons of Saint Leo, no. 22. Another reissue of the same edition at Venice in 1482 must also be added; it preceded the Venetian edition of 1485. Mention should likewise be made here of an Italian translation of the Sermons of Saint Leo based on Aleria’s same Latin edition, so that both five letters of the same pontiff and Aleria’s own dedicatory letter were rendered into Italian. The title of this extremely rare folio edition, which I was able to inspect in the possession of the distinguished man Apostolo Zeno, is: *Corsini di Bartolomeo Fiorentino. Sermoni del Beato Leone papa di lingua Latina in lingua Toscana da lui tradotti adi 21 di Maggio 1485*—“Sermons of Blessed Pope Leo, translated by him from the Latin language into the Tuscan language, on 21 May 1485.”]

The same edition was reprinted there in 1505, in the printing house of Bartholomew de Zanis de Portesio, highly skilled in the book trade, at the expense of the heirs of the noble late Lord Octavianus Scotus.

Another edition appeared at Paris in 1511, in which the treatise *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* is included.

James Merlin, doctor of theology at Paris, published at Paris in 1524 the Isidorian Collection of Councils and Papal Letters. It contains ninety-four Letters of Leo, certainly faulty in many places, but in turn more accurately corrected in some places than in much later editions. This work was again printed at Cologne in 1530 and at Paris in 1535.

Peter Crabbe, a Franciscan and native of Mechelen, prepared a more extensive edition of the Councils in 1538 and had it printed at Cologne. In it, as he notes, there is “a more proper and suitable arrangement of the Letters of Pope Leo I.” For, as he adds, “those which had previously been written in confusion are now arranged according to the proper order of consuls—where these can be known—and months; where these are lacking, the order of the remaining Letters that appeared more suitable has been preserved.”

Thus the first praise for attempting an arrangement of these Letters belongs to Crabbe. His edition was reprinted in 1551.

Peter Canisius of Nijmegen, then a cleric of the diocese of Cologne, who later joined the Society of Jesus and was distinguished for piety and learning, published a fuller collection of the works of Saint Leo at Cologne in 1546 and 1547. He wrote that he had been assisted by “very ancient and most accurate exemplars,” although not without great labor.

The diligence of the man, who was still young at the time, deserves praise; his success does not deserve praise everywhere. For while wishing to produce a fuller Leo, he inserted among Leo’s writings that little book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which the mere mention of the Rule of Saint Benedict ought to have convinced him was not the work of our Leo.

It also contains many errors and several grandiose titles for Letters, which are found neither in the earlier Canisian editions nor in manuscript codices, as we shall note in their proper places.

Laurentius Surius, the Carthusian, famous throughout the Church, devoted his efforts to an edition of Leo in 1561. He professes to have spent much time and labor correcting Leo’s works, although, as he says, they had already appeared corrected several years earlier through the efforts of learned men.

He nevertheless admits that he did not everywhere restore the whole of Leo so completely to its integrity that nothing remained deserving correction:

> “Nor is this surprising,” he says, “since Leo himself admits that even while he was still alive, that letter of his which is addressed to Flavian had been corrupted.”

He also inserted Leo’s Letters into his Collection of Councils, which appeared at Cologne in 1567, and reprinted there in 1569 his earlier edition of all Leo’s works.

John Sichard collected the works of Clement of Rome and appended to them the pseudo-letters of ancient pontiffs. After several editions had been issued in Germany,

[Note: Concerning Sichard’s authentic Basel edition of 1536, see the preface to the Letters of Saint Leo, no. 28.]

the work also appeared at Paris in 1568, with the addition of several papal letters, especially those of our Leo. The anonymous editor responsible for this edition testifies that these had been restored according to the authority of ancient Victorine exemplars.

This is the edition which we have designated under Sichard’s name in our notes and variant readings.

JOANNES ULIMMERIUS, prior of St. Martin’s at Leuven, together with the other regular canons of that monastery, compared Leo’s works with manuscript codices in the year 1575. Among these, Ulimmerius praises an ancient codex of the Letters belonging to Joannes Vuamesius, doctor of both laws. This edition was published at Leuven in the years 1575 and 1577, and at Antwerp in 1583.

Leo’s Letters are also included in the edition of the Councils issued at Venice in 1585 by Dominicus Nicolinus, who especially commends the work undertaken in revising them by DOMINICUS BOLANUS of the Order of Preachers.

After all these came that celebrated Collection of the Decretal Letters of the supreme pontiffs, which was published at Rome from the Press of the Roman People in 1591, prepared by the most learned Cardinal ANTONIUS CARAFA, so well known for his editions of the sacred Scriptures and of the holy Fathers, with the aid of the most ancient codices of the Vatican Library and of others diligently sought out from every quarter and from diverse distant regions. ANTONIUS DE AQUINO left this attested in his dedicatory letter to Innocent IX. When Carafa was carried off by a premature death—the cardinal whom he had assisted while he was engaged upon the work—De Aquino undertook the task of bringing it to light.

[Col. 0035C] SEVERINUS BINIUS, at the beginning of the present century, published at Cologne in 1606 his Latin edition of the Councils. Nearly twelve years later, in 1618, it was followed by a second, Greek-Latin edition. This latter was printed at Paris by the Morellian press in 1638. In these editions we have the collection of the Letters of St. Leo.

I know of no complete works of Leo having been published at Paris before the years 1614 and 1618. They were published together with the homilies of Maximus of Turin and Peter Chrysologus, enlarged by three sermons from an ancient manuscript codex of Nicolaus Faber, which is now preserved in the celebrated Parisian library of the Thuani. It is written in a character resembling the Saxon. Afterwards these works were printed again and again, both at Lyons and at Paris, in the years 1623, 1633, 1651, 1661, 1671, and 1672. Finally, the latest Parisian compilation of all the Councils provided a place for the Letters of Pope St. Leo in volume IV.

The most learned Cardinal Baronius also rendered outstanding service to our Leo: he inserted several letters of the holy pontiff into his Annals, copied from a codex of the Church of Arles. So too did Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, who published in his notes some letters from manuscript codices belonging to Cardinal Sirletus, a man of great reputation among scholars, and furnished them with annotations. Indeed, Vossius himself had promised to publish all the works of St. Leo, revised, augmented, and illustrated in many places through his own study and labor. He declared this at the end of his edition of the Works of St. Ephrem; but, forestalled by death, he was unable, as I suppose, to fulfill his pledge.

Equal praise on this account is owed to the most learned Jacobus Sirmond of the Society of Jesus, because he corrected the Letters of Leo concerning the Gallican Church against ancient manuscript codices, enlarged them by the addition of one letter, and also adorned them with his own notes, which are reproduced at greater length in the appendix to volume IV of Labbe’s edition of the Councils.

Finally, Josias Simlerus, in his Collection of Writings on the Two Natures in Christ, published at Zurich in 1571, and Joannes Leunclavius in 1578—both of them outside the camp of the Church—devoted their efforts to correcting and illustrating Leo’s principal Letter to Flavian, and published it partly in Latin and partly in Greek-Latin form. Two Catholic and learned men did likewise: Gerard Vossius, already mentioned, and Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius of the Society of Jesus, at the end of the Works of Vigilius of Thapsus.

## III

After the care and diligence of so many distinguished men had been devoted to correcting and illustrating Leo, no one will easily believe that any labor remained for us, unless he has either already examined with his own eyes what we have accomplished, or reads here what we are obliged to set forth in advance in order to explain the rationale of our undertaking.

We have divided the entire Work into two volumes. The first contains everything that belongs to Leo; in the second we have placed what is associated with Leo, whether in the form of an appendix or for the purpose of illustrating our author, not without benefit to the reader.

Two little books, truly golden, ON THE CALLING OF ALL NATIONS, come before the rest of Leo’s works, because they appear to have been written by him while he was still serving as archdeacon in the Roman Church. They had long since been published, first among the Works of St. Ambrose and later among those of Prosper, everywhere with very numerous and serious errors. We removed these errors with the aid of an excellent manuscript codex of the Thuani Library, also collating the ancient editions, which sometimes provided assistance in doubtful places. We scattered shorter Notes wherever the more obscure text seemed to require illumination; from fuller notes, however, where the subject was famous and had been troubled by lengthy controversies, we deliberately abstained, lest we appear more eager to promote contention than to shed light upon the author.

[Note: These little books and the two following ones, since they were wrongly attributed to Leo, will be relegated to the second volume among the spurious works. There, too, the arguments and dissertations of Quesnellus composed in defense of attributing them to Leo will be refuted.]

The AUTHORITIES ON GRACE AND FREE CHOICE follow. We have expended less labor in revising these, because they had already long ago been corrected by all editors of the Councils and Papal Letters, and because manuscript codices of them are abundant in the libraries.

The LETTER, OR LITTLE BOOK, TO THE VIRGIN DEMETRIAS follows both of those treatises. There is such a scarcity of manuscript codices containing it that we were unable to obtain even one that could assist in restoring obscure and corrupt passages. Only ancient printed copies proved useful, together with the very brief scholia of Petrus Nannius of Alkmaar, printed with the Works of St. Ambrose at Basel in 1551. Where these were lacking, conjecture had to be indulged. Whether with unfortunate success, each reader will judge.

There will perhaps be not a few who accuse me of rashness and of failing to await the judgment of more learned men, because I have unhesitatingly counted the three treatises just mentioned among Leo’s works, although not a single printed or manuscript codex raises its voice in Leo’s favor, while the testimony of more than eight hundred years from councils and numerous writers stands against it. At present I ask only this of those who think so: that they suspend all prejudice for a little while, until they have read Dissertations 2, 3, and 4, which contain the grounds of our decision. Meanwhile, I beg that the charge of rashness be withheld from me on the example of the most learned men, who have not hesitated to claim for celebrated authors certain treatises on the sole authority of their style and to publish them under their names.

The SERMONS of our Pontiff follow the treatises just mentioned.

[Note: See our preface placed before the Sermons.]

This part of Leo’s Works, because it has been more generally used and more frequently handled by everyone, has also been more exposed to variation of readings, interpolations, and errors. As regards them, two kinds of manuscript codices are found in libraries. Some contain all Leo’s sermons collected into a single body and arranged according to the order of the solemnities of the year, approximately as they appear in printed editions.
