Others are Lectionaries copied for the use of churches, containing sermons and homilies of various Fathers, especially of Leo, to be recited at the nocturnal offices.

The former have the advantage that they comprise all our author’s sermons at a single glance; their disadvantage is that they are generally more recent and, because they stand farther from the source, less suitable for correcting errors. The latter unquestionably excel the others in antiquity, but they suffer from more than one disadvantage. First, they do not all contain the sermons: some contain certain ones, others different ones, according to the varying customs of the churches for whose use they were copied. Thus, in order to collate a few sermons against these codices, you will generally have to go through an immense and countless number of volumes. Secondly, since they have been adapted to the various particular solemnities of different places, they are very often enlarged by certain foreign additions wholly alien to the author’s mind, so that sometimes you can scarcely distinguish them. A striking example of this kind is found in Sermon 41, which is the fourth on Lent. Thirdly, because the monks devoted to copying these sermons are very often less educated and insufficiently skilled in the Latin language, such books frequently appear blemished and teeming with errors. We have therefore used both kinds with equal judgment and fairness, placing confidence in none of them until the matter had been examined with the greatest care.

We arranged all the sermons in a single numerical sequence, without abandoning the customary earlier method of numbering. None has been moved from its proper place, with only three exceptions: the fourth, On the Anniversary of His Assumption; the sixth, On Collections and Almsgiving; and the ninth, On the Fast of the Tenth Month. These had formerly been added at the end of the others from the manuscript codex of the distinguished Nicolaus Faber; now they lie in their proper places, at columns 19, 37, and 61. We have not increased the number of sermons; indeed, we have reduced it by relegating one or two to the appendix. We counted among the others the single Sermon 96, On the Chair of St. Peter, transcribed from the Royal Codex, and we do not regret having done so.

[Note: This sermon, supplied in full, will be published as Sermon 14 in the appendix of spurious sermons. The admonition prefixed to it must be read.]

For although, at this very point in the preface, we had corrected our own criticism of it from the first edition, after reexamining the matter and carefully weighing the style, we returned to our earlier judgment and did not dare to attribute this sermon to Leo.

What we have appended to the Sermons from the Roman Pontifical, and for what reason, as well as what the appendices to those works contain, is sufficiently and more than sufficiently explained in the admonitions prefixed to each in its proper place.

## IV. LETTERS

[Note: See the preface placed before the Letters.]

The LETTERS, which occupy the final part of the first volume, by everyone’s judgment rightly hold the first place among all Leo’s works, because they contain very many decrees that contribute to an understanding of the whole of ecclesiastical discipline, both general and sacramental, and especially penitential discipline, into which Pacianus long ago warned that the discipline of the whole Church was, as it were, to be compressed like a clasp.

The Letters do not teach discipline alone. Whatever events of greater importance took place in the Church from the year 440 over a period of more than twenty years is almost entirely either contained in these Letters or illuminated by them.

But we have also accomplished the following with regard to them:

1. Spurious and forged letters have been rejected.

2. Genuine letters have been cleansed of the blemishes of errors and interpolations.

3. The order has been changed and, insofar as possible, restored to its authentic form.

4. The number has been increased by the addition of several letters.

5. We have prefixed a synopsis to each, as we have not omitted to do for the Sermons.

6. Whatever letters written by others to St. Leo were encountered, we inserted among the corresponding letters of his own, since they are often necessary for understanding them and generally are not readily available to a reader of Leo.

We entirely rejected one letter, that to the bishops of Germany and Gaul concerning chorepiscopi, because there can be no doubt that it is spurious; we have explained the reasons for its rejection in Dissertation 11, which is contained in volume II.

We judged that the seventh, which is read as having been written to Septimius, and the seventeenth, which is addressed to all the bishops of Sicily, should be removed in the notes from the number of the Letters of our Leo. Nevertheless, we retained their places, lest we appear to prejudge the judgment of more learned men, to whom we submit our reasons.

We have given an ample account of the corrections of the genuine letters in the notes, to which we refer the reader.

Someone may criticize the unchanged order of the Letters, both because it seems vexatious to impose a new arrangement upon those accustomed to the old numbering, and because it will be difficult to find passages cited by writers under the former number when the letters have been assigned new numbers and placed in an order now unfamiliar. Yet the indices that will follow this preface will remove every fear of inconvenience. They will reproduce not only the order of later editions but also that of the earlier ones—a feature found in no other edition.

Everyone will readily understand how necessary a new arrangement of the Letters was, if he compares our recent edition with the old one and considers how greatly the chronological order of the historical letters assists memory, contributes to a clear knowledge of events, and habitually helps to unravel difficulties that are often of the greatest importance.

The need to innovate the order was increased both by the addition of those letters that we are publishing for the first time and by the confusion of the old ones. For just as the letters, when placed according to the order of the years, form a single historical sequence, so, if thirty newly added letters and thirty from the old editions—previously published without preserving any chronological order—were placed indiscriminately together, they would produce a wholly shapeless and disordered body of letters.

It matters so greatly that the letters be examined after their genuine sequence has been restored that Pelagius II, or Gregory the Great under his name, in his letter to Elias and the other bishops of Istria, censures them for having taken certain testimonies from the letters and encyclicals of St. Leo for purposes of deception, mixing them together in a confused and disordered fashion.

Immediately afterward, when he himself reviews the testimonies produced by the Istrian bishops from the letter to Leo Augustus—formerly numbered 78 but now 132 in our edition—

[Note: For us it is Letter 162.]

he calls this the last letter of Leo. Without doubt he means the last letter in the codex of letters that was handled at Rome by the hands of the pontiffs, of a kind that, I believe, had not emerged from darkness until this day.

In the manuscript copy of the Roman Codex belonging to the Thuani, the following is added: “A collection of thirty-three letters of our Leo,” which is extremely ancient and scarcely separable from the very Codex of Canons and other Constitutions. Nevertheless, I would not dare to affirm that it is the same collection that Pelagius II and Gregory I had before them. For although the last letter called such by him is the last of those addressed to Leo Augustus in the Codex mentioned, it is not the final letter of all. For two letters to Anatolius, a third to the bishops who had taken part in the Council of Chalcedon, a fourth to Dorus of Beneventum, and, after some intervening material, a fifth to Theodoret are found in that manuscript copy. Whether they were added to it afterward, I do not think anyone can assert or deny except by guesswork.

[Note: We were fortunate enough to find the outstanding collection of Regensburg. In it, the last letter of Leo is the one indicated by Pelagius II. We shall show in the preface to the Letters, no. 42, that this is the collection compiled by Pope Vigilius and identified by the same Pelagius. Hence Quesnellus’s inquiry whether this collection is represented in the Thuaneus Codex is entirely superfluous and also empty for another reason. For in this codex there is Collection 5, which we shall prove in volume III to be not Roman but Gallican. Moreover, the thirty-two letters of Leo initially transcribed in Collection 5 end not with the letter to Leo Augustus but with the letter to Dorus. Consequently, only those matters appended to this letter in the Thuaneus Codex are additions, which are absent from the pure manuscripts of the same collection and are not indicated in the table of the Thuaneus Codex itself, where the monuments of its original formation are listed.]

Now we must discuss somewhat more fully the enlargement of the number of Letters. We received two from the Roman Collection of the most learned Lucas Holstenius; a third, which had not previously been published, we possess in a more carefully corrected form from the Grimanic Codex. One, transcribed from the Bona Vallis Codex, was supplied by volume I of J. Sirmond’s Ancient Councils of Gaul. We also transcribed a single letter from the Library of Fleury, but its reliability is very doubtful.

## V

But the Church owes twenty-eight distinguished letters to the Codex of Cardinal Dominicus Grimani, which the library of the House of the Institution of the Oratory of Jesus in the Parisian suburb of St. Michael now possesses, having received it as a gift from the Reverend Father Andrea de Berziau, a priest of the Oratory and a worthy member of that house.

This Codex came to him as a not insignificant part of his paternal inheritance from his noble relative, Theodorus de Berziau, president of the Inquisitorial Chambers at the Paris court, a man renowned not only for inherited nobility but also for his own excellence, because of his outstanding natural gifts and singular devotion to literary studies.

He had received the Leonine Codex, together with other books of the highest quality, from his illustrious stepfather, Andrea Huralto Messaeo, privy counselor to the Most Christian Kings Charles IX, Henry III, and Henry IV. Huralto was a man of no ordinary prudence and skill in the conduct of public affairs. The celebrated Hurault de Cheverny, chancellor of France, had greatly desired that he be chosen, even during his lifetime, as keeper of the royal seal. Finally, he was made famous by the successful completion of two embassies to the Venetian Republic in the most difficult circumstances.

When he was staying at Venice on that occasion, being, as he was, passionately devoted to letters, he diligently sought out and purchased with his own money numerous volumes of selected books, partly printed and partly manuscript, transported them to Gaul, and added them to his library.

From this store, seventy-five years ago, some Greek treatises of Synesius were published through the efforts of Fredericus Morellus, then royal professor at the Academy, with the aid of a Greek manuscript codex containing several Letters and Treatises. The most learned Petavius also used this codex, lent to him by Morellus, in his edition of all the Works of Synesius, published in 1612 and reprinted in 1631 and 1640. This codex is now preserved in the same Oratorian library in the suburb of Saint-Michel.

Thus the manuscript Codex of the Letters of St. Leo, which had once belonged to the celebrated Cardinal Dominicus Grimani, was transported from Venice to our Gaul. For the codex numbered 1124 had been inscribed, apparently in his own hand, as follows: “The Book of DOMINICUS GRIMANI, CARDINAL OF ST. MARK.”

He was the son of Antonio, Duke of Venice, and was celebrated in the writings of Sabellicus, Niphus, Erasmus, Pico della Mirandola, and others. He was Bishop of Porto and Patriarch of Aquileia, a man of blameless life, of rare devotion to his father, and supremely learned in every branch of knowledge. He left behind an extremely well-equipped library of eight thousand volumes, filled, as Erasmus says of it, with books in every language.

I do not know whether I should correctly believe that this was the same library that Cardinal Dominicus Grimani built in the monastery of St. Anthony at Venice and furnished, for the public benefit and at enormous expense, with marble statues and books of the highest distinction. Joannes Dominicus Trajanus testifies to this in the preface to the Works of William of Auvergne, Bishop of Paris, whose edition he supervised at Venice in 1591, relying especially upon a codex from this Grimanic library.

One of these books was the manuscript we are praising. A certain Antonius Bellonus of Udine, a notary, had presented it to the cardinal as a codex of exceptional quality.

[Note: Concerning this excellent man, see Muratori, *Rerum Italicarum*, volume XVI, pages 23 and 68. We append here other letters of the same Bellonus, written in 1515 and therefore earlier than those which Quesnellus inserted into this preface. Among other things, we learn from them that this excellent Leonine codex, before it came into Bellonus’s and Cardinal Grimani’s possession, had belonged to Petrus Passerinus, a celebrated antiquary of his native Friuli. Bellonus wrote of him in a letter sent in the same year to Jacobus Purlilianus, Count: “There is nothing throughout the whole homeland of ancient books, nothing of ancient sculpture, that he has not carefully examined and collected with exact precision,” and so forth.

“Antonius Bellonus sends greetings to Petrus Passerinus. Although the book of the most holy Pope Leo was once given to me by you as a gift, I have reverently preserved it, not as mine but as still yours. For I did not wish to receive and keep it in such a way that you would have no more right to dispose of Leo than of me myself. I now desire, with your permission, to honor Angelus Gabriel in imitation of you by giving him the book. For, being both a patrician in the Venetian Republic and an eminent man of letters, he will be able to restore Leo to his proper dignity and to benefit us greatly. As for the book, you will no longer be able to dispose of it; but you will always be able to dispose of me. Farewell.”

The Count Franciscus Florius, first canon of the cathedral of Udine, who has rendered distinguished service to sound studies and to ancient documents in many matters, shared with us out of his kindness this letter of Bellonus, as well as the excerpt quoted from another letter.]

The letter or little book of Donation prefixed to the codex attests this. We reproduce it so that posterity may know from what first source, insofar as we have been able to determine it, so many excellent letters of Leo the Great proceeded.

“Antonius Bellonus of Udine, notary, sends greetings to the Most Reverend Lord Dominicus Grimani, Cardinal of St. Mark.

“I hear that you are erecting a library at Venice, a most beautiful monument to Grimani virtue and munificence, and I am exceedingly glad. For the liberal arts, from which illustrious honor proceeds, will be cultivated for all time. Scholars too will owe you much, since you will have sought to make all future generations wise through their participation in many volumes. Nor is this surprising: you are a man in whom wisdom contends with liberality, and liberality with wisdom, for supremacy.

“But so that I may enlarge this library of yours by whatever small gift I can offer—for a library is adorned by the antiquity, abundance, and selection of its books—I give you this codex of the divine Leo, venerable for its antiquity. You will examine it, and, if it seems worthy, you will place it among your chosen books.

“For the rest, I hope that, if Fortune deigns to favor virtue, you will one day restore Leo himself, just as in knowledge and holiness, so also in rank and seat—the thing most desired by all good men—to the tenth place, if it is not permissible to call it higher, certainly inferior to none.

“Farewell.”

Opposite this letter there is still found a dedicatory epigram for the same codex by Germanus Bellonus, apparently a kinsman of Antonius. I reproduce it for the reader:

> Behold, Grimani, Leo, who, written in the ancient Book,  
> Flies to you from the heavenly watchtower.  
> His holy right hand gives you the little book auspiciously  
> And announces an old man blessed with a new voice;  
> It promises you, at last, everlasting honor,  
> While Jupiter thunders swiftly from the left-hand axis.  
> Therefore receive him, and among sacred volumes let Pallas  
> Conceal him, and grant that he be in his proper place.  
> But the hand that gave him will restore you to your proper seat,  
> And Jupiter will always make you blessed.

This Leonine Grimanic codex is nearly nine hundred years old. It contains one hundred and seven letters of Leo, twenty-eight of which had never previously been published. That they are authentic and genuine is demonstrated most clearly by their style, subject matter, the antiquity of the codex, and everything else that can support the integrity of a text of the highest quality.

Moreover, several of them are confirmed as unquestionably genuine by highly reliable witnesses summoned from various regions of the Christian world—from Africa, Italy, Gaul, and England—namely, the pontiffs of the Apostolic See, Pope Vigilius and Pelagius II; Facundus, Bishop of Hermiane; Prudentius, Bishop of Troyes; and Bede the priest, who produced fragments of some of them in the places where they must be noted. Leo himself refers to several of them in other letters on the same subject, as the reader will find observed in our notes.

Nor is this all that we owe to the Grimanic Codex: it has not only enriched Leo’s writings with numerous letters of great importance, but has also made them far more accurate than they had previously been. For no codex has appeared from which we have drawn a greater number of more significant corrections.

After the Letters, you will find fragments of several other writings, including the memorandum given to the legates departing for the Council of Chalcedon. To these is added the one surviving letter of Julian, Bishop of Cos, to Leo Augustus. If so many letters of this Julian to our Leo, written in the course of his legation, had not been lost through the injury of time, both the Letters of our Leo and the memory of the events then taking place in the Church would have received immense illumination from them.

The Life of St. Hilary, Bishop of Arles, written by St. Honoratus, Bishop of Marseille and his disciple, nearly closes the first volume. We requested that this be placed among Leo’s Works because we had undertaken to compose an Apology for Hilary. Since, on that occasion, we extracted much from his Life in the fifth dissertation, it will be convenient for the reader who wishes to consult the source itself to find it before his eyes.

Nor was it right to separate from this Life the Life of Honoratus, Hilary’s relative, teacher, and predecessor in the episcopate of Arles, written by Hilary himself. This was so both because of the close connection between the two works and so that anyone wishing to compare the remaining little works of Hilary with his Life and Apology might have them readily available—and in more carefully corrected form than the ancient copies, which are also rare.

In the same place you will find the poem *On Genesis*, addressed to Pope St. Leo, which circulates under Hilary’s name, and a very brief letter of his written to Eucherius, Bishop of Lyons.

## VI

THE SECOND VOLUME of this work contains an Appendix, or Codex of the Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See, now published for the first time from the manuscript codices of the Thuani and Oxford libraries; then dissertations both on this Codex itself and on our Leo; and finally notes, variant readings, and several observations.

I have titled that Codex the most extensive and most ancient of all those that have so far been published, and I am confident that no one will contradict me.

[Note: No one can deny that this codex is ancient and exceptional. Yet it will become clear from what will be discussed at length in volume III concerning this codex and other unknown collections of the canons and constitutions of the Apostolic See that it is neither the most extensive of all collections nor a representation of the Roman collection. There we shall also refute what Paschasius Quesnellus, proceeding from the same prejudice of his, repeatedly draws from it.]

Certainly, if we wish to speak of the codices of the canons and constitutions of the Roman Church, I dare to say something more. For I ought to have called it not merely the oldest and most extensive, but the only one.

Our twelfth dissertation explains what should be thought of the ancient codex of Justellus. Neither of the two codices of Dionysius Exiguus—the one of synodal canons and the other of papal Letters—was ever composed for the use of the Roman Church or of the Roman bishops, whether by their command or by their advice. The former was produced at the urging of Stephanus, Bishop of Salona; the latter through the pious study and diligence, as he himself says, of Julian, priest of St. Anastasia. The Roman Church afterward embraced them in her highly celebrated use.

Thus, on the authority of Cassiodorus (*Divine Readings*, chapter 3), writers on canon law commonly assert the matter, although Cassiodorus says this only of the codex of ecclesiastical canons prepared at the request of Stephanus, not of the other. Let this be so concerning both. There is nevertheless this one distinction in favor of the Dionysian Codex: although it was produced by the industry of a private individual, it deserved to be adopted by the Roman Church and assigned to her uses when the sixth century was already half spent.

But our codex is precisely the one that the Roman Church prepared for herself as soon as she herself began to be governed by written law and to rule the churches subject to her order.

Indeed, before the canons of Nicaea and Sardica had been established, what was called ecclesiastical law in the Roman Church seems to have consisted solely of ecclesiastical custom and of rules received partly from the princes of the apostles and partly from their immediate successors through actual practice and living tradition. After the Synod of Sardica, however, thought began to be given to composing a codex of canons. Formed from the Nicene and Sardican canons gathered under a single numerical sequence, this codex alone for some time established the law by which ecclesiastical affairs were governed; then, enlarged by various additions over succeeding ages, it assumed the form that you now have before your eyes, and that genuinely represents the discipline of two hundred years of that more blessed age.

From this one fact alone anyone whose taste is formed by ecclesiastical antiquity and ancient canonical discipline can understand how highly this outstanding treasure (*κειμήλιον*) of both is to be valued. I do not know whether anything better or more suited to ecclesiastical affairs has been rescued from darkness in the present age.

There are nevertheless further features that commend the codex. What of the fact that it presents that ancient version of the Eastern canons which was in use among several Western churches before the Dionysian version? We possess part of this in the Isidorian Collection. Yet no one could confidently pronounce it to be this ancient version before its identity became apparent through comparison with ours; nor is it preserved wholly intact in Isidore, but is corrupted by errors, interpolations, and other deformations.

Moreover, the ancient discipline of the Roman Church becomes known from this version, since it shows that the Roman Church rejected certain Eastern canons and altered others, adapting them to her own use. This remains obscure in Dionysius’s version, since he translated the canons according to the Greek text without regard to the discipline received by the Roman Church.

I pass over the fact that the codex contains the ancient and original translations of several works of holy Fathers who were famous at the beginning of the fifth century and whose writings were consecrated by the use of Roman pontiffs and councils; that it makes the connection between Roman and African discipline clearer; that it contains several statements of faith, some previously published and some not previously published; that it restores certain African decrees omitted from printed editions; that it restores several letters of Roman pontiffs and other documents that had been seriously interpolated to their genuine form; and that it contains not only what pertains to ecclesiastical discipline, but almost everything that was done or written in defense of the faith during those times, whether by the Apostolic See or by other bishops.

In this respect it surpasses both the Dionysian Codex and the other codices of canons and constitutions, which touch nothing concerning matters of faith, except for the chapters on grace and free choice appended to the letter of Coelestine, which are found in Dionysius and are lacking in ours, and the anathemas of Gangra.

[Col. 0045A] These and other features of the same kind, which will appear in their proper places, are indeed outstanding. Yet, in addition to them, there are two matters that will especially affect those devoted to the Roman Church—and who, if he is Catholic, is not devoted to it?—and lovers of ecclesiastical antiquity.

The first is that, with the aid of this codex, it can be determined which Eastern synods were received for use in the Roman Church and at what time—namely, the Antiochene, Constantinopolitan, African, and any others that are called into question.

The second is that from this same codex the shameless calumny is driven back and utterly overturned which those notorious Magdeburg Centuriators wickedly constructed against the most holy Roman pontiffs Zosimus, Boniface, and Coelestine. They openly and publicly denounce them as adulterators, falsifiers, and corruptors of the Nicene canons, as though through monstrous crime and impiety, and through frenzied ambition, the Sardican canons had been substituted for the Nicene canons by Pope Zosimus knowingly and willingly, when he presented them under the name of the Nicene canons to the Council of Carthage through his legates in that celebrated case of the presbyter Apiarius.

They say that Boniface, an ambitious and impious man, persisted obstinately in this criminal adulteration of the Nicene decrees, and that Coelestine persisted in it with equal obstinacy, although he supposedly knew perfectly well that the African synod had received more accurate copies of the Nicene canons from Constantinople and Alexandria, and that the wicked fraud of the falsifiers of the canons had been exposed.

From now on, inspection of the codex will make certain—not merely among Catholics but also among any persons whose conscience is not beyond hope—both the criminal perversity of men whose minds are corrupted and the sincerity and candor of the Roman bishops, who in good faith put forward what they read in their own codex as having been received from their predecessors. For that reason you cannot accuse them of ignorance without likewise implicating the African, Eastern, and most Western bishops, to whom the Sardican canons and the number of the Nicene canons were either wholly unknown or known only very obscurely. Concerning that number, scholarly controversy has continued down to our own age.

## VII

“This is all very well,” someone may say, “and the usefulness and integrity of the codex remain established. But why was it appended to the Works of Leo, so that they might be published together? Surely he, together with his own dissertations, was sufficient for a volume to be printed separately.”

[Col. 0045D] Certainly, more than one consideration persuaded me to adopt this plan. I shall not mention merely that, while I was laboring to publish Leo, I discovered the codex and from it conceived the idea of issuing both works together in a single publication; nor that our Leo used this same codex; nor that it sheds some light on Leo’s works, especially in the passage where he cites the Sardican canons as Nicene; nor that much was added to the codex in his time, and a large part inserted into it by Leo himself; nor that most of it concerns the condemned doctrines of Eutyches and his followers, which constitute both Leo’s particular victory and the subject matter of his writings.

[Col. 0046A] But the more important reason was that Leo’s Letters, which form the most distinguished part of his works, are as it were a necessary supplement to the codex. If they are removed, the codex will be diminished and mutilated in its nobler part; if they are added, it becomes complete and presents the entire library of the old Roman canon law, from which the laws of ecclesiastical administration were drawn for so many centuries by the prelates of the Apostolic See.

I called Leo’s Letters a necessary supplement to the codex because we have nothing at all by Leo inserted into the codex [Note: [Col. 0045D] We indicated in annotation 8 that thirty-two letters of Leo had been inserted into this collection. We shall explain the origin of Quesnel’s prejudice in the observations [Col. 0046D] to his twelfth dissertation, which will be published in the third volume.], although it contains the principal letters of all the Roman prelates from Pope Siricius to Anastasius II, with the exceptions of Anastasius I, of whom nothing survives; Sixtus III, who wrote scarcely two letters; and Pope Hilary, who wrote several. Yet whose letters ought rather to have had their place in the codex than Leo’s—Leo, who wrote more than the others concerning the observance of ecclesiastical discipline, who played a major role in condemning the Pelagian and Eutychian heresies—which occupy almost the whole of the remaining codex—and who played the leading role in the latter controversy as well?

No one would say that this omission occurred by chance or forgetfulness, much less that it arose from contempt. It was therefore done deliberately by those who thought it preferable, after the codex’s chapters 41 and 42—which contain the proceedings against Eutyches and appear to have been inserted by Leo—to append in a single sequence the proceedings conducted against the same heretics under the Roman pontiffs Simplicius, Felix, and Gelasius, rather than interrupt the chain of the proceedings with Leo’s lengthy letters on many different subjects. Had they inserted only some portion of those letters into the codex, they would have produced something less useful and convenient than when, as I suspect was done, they collected most of Leo’s letters into a single body and placed them at the end of the codex.

Our conjecture is supported by both manuscript copies of the codex, the Thuaneus and the Oxoniensis, at whose end Leo’s letters are transcribed as a supplement, as we stated in the twelfth dissertation; anyone can also see this in the complete index of the Thuaneus, which we prefixed to the codex.

Of the remaining parts of this volume, there is scarcely anything that needs to be prefaced here. The index of the dissertations, which follows shortly, sets out their subject matter. The notes, observations, and variant readings are clear in themselves. I have generally identified the manuscripts from which these materials derive, or by which the genuine readings [Col. 0046D] are restored. I have often omitted listing them when the correction is plainly certain and all the manuscripts agree with it. Some of these notes may perhaps seem too lengthy and somewhat extraneous. In this I have followed the example of many learned writers, who preferred clarity to brevity and considered it wrong not to illuminate, even in an unsuitable place, matters that happened to arise on any occasion and required clarification.

In these matters we sometimes depart from the opinions of the most learned men, and at times even attack them—not led by anything other than the desire to bring the truth to light. While sincerely seeking it, if we have occasionally strayed from it—as I rightly fear has often happened to me—I shall regard it as praise and a benefit if anyone, whether in friendship or hostility, warns me of my error; I shall count it a victory to acknowledge and correct it.

VIII. I shall cease prefacing only after first ensuring that the literary world does not remain unaware whose assistance advanced and supported our work of purging Leo, when they made manuscript codices available and generously provided every form of help.

The illustrious D. Carcavi, the most vigilant director of this treasury, most willingly allowed us access to the royal collection of manuscripts. Whatever could be useful to us from the celebrated library of the monastery of Saint-Germain, whether printed or manuscript, was all most generously placed at our disposal by the Reverend Father Dom Lucas Dacheri, whose learning and piety I admire with everyone, and whose friendship I boast of possessing with few others.

The most learned custodian of the very rich library of Saint-Victor, D. le Tonnellier, most courteously shared with me a manuscript codex of Leo. I cannot express how much I owe to the most learned Edward Bernard, Savilian Professor of Astronomy at the University of Oxford. For he not only sent me, copied through his care, a manuscript reproduction of the Roman codex whose value is beyond estimation, but also himself searched the Oxford libraries with the greatest diligence. He examined the Laudian, Bodleian, Oriel, Balliol, and Pembroke archives, and others; compared the printed works with the manuscript codices; and transcribed the variant readings with his own hand, with such care, dedication, and courtesy that one would scarcely find, if indeed one could find, his equal.

Nor was it enough for this most generous man to expend his own resources: he also enlisted the study and labor of his friends, whose eyes he sent through the Cambridge libraries and manuscript codices, from which he extracted and sent us variant readings. When Bernard indicates that I owe this assistance to the most courteous D. Thomas Gale, I would be ungrateful if I concealed the man’s name here.

Nor can I pass over your name in silence, my dear Joseph Quesnel, my most beloved kinsman, nor mention you without expressing my gratitude. From that rich literary storehouse of the illustrious Thuaneus, of which you are the faithful keeper and steward, you supplied both a manuscript copy of the Roman codex and so many manuscript codices of Leo, moved by an extraordinary love not only for me but also for literature.

If I fail to praise the most illustrious D. Vion d’Herouval for the assistance he gave in collating the codices, I shall be the only one among all who labor either to recover or to illuminate antiquity who could do so; nor, even if they wished, could they withdraw themselves from his most generous devotion to literature and to literary men.

The other persons to whom we owe any courteous assistance will have their own praise, to be recorded in the appropriate places.

[Col. 0048B] If I do not praise either the Imperial Library at Vienna [Note: [Col. 0047C] We touched upon the Vindobonensis and Roman library codices that were useful to us in the general preface; but we say more about them in the special prefaces to the Sermons and Letters. We found in the Barberini Library the codex that belonged to John Baptist Mari, canon of Saint Angelo, and that contains only the variant readings of the Sermons of Saint Leo. See the preface to the Sermons, no. 27.], or the Roman libraries, someone may be indignant, as though I had neglected to visit those most richly furnished archives (ἀρχεῖα). I certainly spared neither effort nor friends in seeking access to those sanctuaries of learning, but my attempt was unsuccessful.

Above all, I would have wished to gain access to the codex of the Works of Saint Leo, which I had learned from the most learned Emeric Bigot of Rouen, a man universally renowned for his learning, had once been collated by the most learned Francisco Pegna with the manuscript codices of the Roman libraries. After Francisco Pegna’s death, that codex had come into the possession of Marius, canon of Saint Angelo; Bigot found it in Marius’s library and had it before him. After Marius’s death, Bigot inquired about the codex by letter, but received no answer other than that it was not known what had become of it.

Perhaps what was unavailable for this first edition may be supplied for the preparation of a second, should that ever take place. We earnestly exhort all learned men, with fervent prayers, to make this assistance readily available, out of their reverence for the most holy pontiff of the Apostolic See and teacher of the Church, and out of their devotion to the Church herself.

[Col. 0047]

## The Dedication of the Same Quesnel Prefixed to His Edition

[Col. 0047]

[Col. 0047D] To Saint Leo the Great, bishop of the Roman Church, not unequal to so great a see, an apostolic man [Note: [Col. 0047D] Hincmar of Reims, *On Predestination*, chapter 33.], the light of the Church [Note: [Col. 0047D] Facundus, book V, chapter 5.], the pillar of the orthodox faith [Note: [Col. 0047D] The petition of the Eastern bishops to Pope Agapetus.], interpreter of Peter’s voice [Note: [Col. 0047D] Book II of the Syrians’ letter to the emperor Justinian.], defender of the apostolic doctrines [Note: [Col. 0047D] The report of the Council of Chalcedon to Pope Leo.], equal to the apostles [Note: [Col. 0047D] The Synodical Petition, chapter 89.], equal to the angels [Note: [Col. 0047D] The same, chapter 94.];

whose judgment everything that is Catholic everywhere admires, celebrates, and venerates as a heavenly oracle [Note: [Col. 0048D] *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 149.];

an assertor of Catholic truth [Note: [Col. 0048D] Pope Adrian II at the Fourth Council of Constantinople.], yet peaceful;

a lover of ecclesiastical peace, yet fearless [Note: [Col. 0048D] Letter 20, now 23, of Saint Leo to Flavian, chapter 2; letters 69 and 89, now 89 and 115, etc.];

an interpreter of the evangelical law, yet not on his own authority [Note: [Col. 0048D] Letters 78, 79, 80, and 81, now 104, 105, 106, and 107, etc.];

a herald of priestly holiness, yet not idle [Note: [Col. 0049B] In the Sermons and elsewhere throughout.];

a teacher of the Catholic Church, yet a disciple of tradition [Note: [Col. 0049B] See Dissertation 1, *On His Life and Deeds*.];

a most wise restorer of canonical discipline [Note: [Col. 0049B] Leo, letters 134 and 135, now 165 and 166, etc.; and Pope Simplicius’s letter to the emperor Zeno.];

a most devout executor [Note: [Col. 0049B] Facundus, book II, chapter 6.], and its most valiant defender [Note: [Col. 0049B] The Decretal Letter 1, 2, etc.; Pope Gelasius’s letter to Dardanus and to the emperor Marcian, in the same place.];

a faithful and confident champion of the Church [Note: [Col. 0049B] Facundus, book V, p. 213, and Dissertation 1, *On His Life*.];

a sincere and undaunted opponent of heretics [Note: [Col. 0049B] Facundus, book II, chapter 5.];

whose concern and diligence, labor and zeal, freedom and steadfastness on behalf of the Catholic faith the whole Church never ceases to proclaim [Note: [Col. 0049B] The same, in the same place.];

who explained, asserted, and defended, against the Priscillianists the mystery of the most holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0049B] The same, book V, chapter 4.];

against the Jews the necessity of the incarnation of Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0049B] Letter 15 to Turibius, and the Sermon on Pentecost.];

against the Arians the identity of substance with the Father [Note: [Col. 0049B] The Sermon on the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord.];

against Eutyches the properties of the human nature [Note: [Col. 0049B] The same, and in the Letters.];

against Nestorius the singularity of the person [Note: [Col. 0049B] Letter 24, now 28, to Flavian, etc.];

against the Novatians the rights and power of the Church [Note: [Col. 0049B] Letters 27, 46, 64, 77, 92, 96, and 97, now 31, 59, [Col. 0049C] 84, 102, 119, 123, and 124; and in the Sermon of Eulogius, letter of the Alexandrian bishop [Col. 0050B] in defense of Pope Saint Leo.];

against the Donatists the unity of the mystical body [Note: [Col. 0050B] Letter 14, now 18, to Januarius of Aquileia, and letter 1, now 12, to the Africans.];

against the Pelagians and the remnants of the Pelagians the absolute necessity, gratuitous bestowal, and unconquerable power of grace won by the blood of the Mediator [Note: [Col. 0050B] *On the Calling of the Nations*; letter to Demetrias; chapters on Grace and Free Will; letter 6 to the bishops of Aquileia, etc.];

against the Manichaeans the truth, dignity, and holiness of all the mysteries [Note: [Col. 0050B] Letter 8, now 7, to the bishops of Italy; letter 15 to Turibius; Sermons 8, 15, 23, and 74, now 9, 16, 24, and 76, etc.];

against the impious and the pseudo-Christians the sincere worship of religion [Note: [Col. 0050B] Throughout the Sermons, etc.];

and he explained, asserted, and defended all these things through heavenly doctrine, singular piety, an unconquered spirit, example, sermons, and writings proceeding from the very heart of the apostles [Note: [Col. 0050B] Pope Hormisdas’s letter to the clergy and archimandrites of Syria II.].

To a pontiff of such holiness, such faith, and such learning [Note: [Col. 0050B] Letter 44 of the bishops of Gaul to Leo, chapter 5, now letter 99.], divinely prepared for the Church’s victory [Note: [Col. 0050B] Address of the Council of Chalcedon to the emperor Marcian.], his most devoted client Paschasius Quesnel of Paris, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of Jesus, offers, dedicates, and consecrates himself and this small work of his, whatever its worth, consisting in the collection, purification, and elucidation of Leo’s writings, from the bosom of the Gallican Church, from which he was once sought for the Chair of Peter [Note: [Col. 0050B] Prosper, in his *Chronicle*.].

On the fourth day before the Kalends of July, sacred to the memory of Leo the Great.

In the year of salvation 1675 [Note: [Col. 0050B] See volume II, Dissertation 1, on the year 461, no. 8 [Col. 0050C] and following.]

[Col. 0049]

## Schoenemann’s Historical-Literary Notice on Saint Leo the Great

*(From Schoenemann,* Historical-Literary Library of the Latin Fathers, *Leipzig, 1794, volume II.)*

[Col. 0049]

## Chapter One. On the Life of Saint Leo the Great

[Col. 0049C]

Leo, surnamed the Great, was a Roman by birth. We have received no information from the ancient records of the Church concerning the year of his birth, nor can anything certain be conjectured from what survives to us of his life [Col. 0049D] or from the age at which he died. His father was named Quintianus, a man of uncertain, but undoubtedly not low, social standing; for a son of such mature character must have been educated by him in no ordinary manner. Unless one prefers to suppose that Leo acquired the qualities in which he later excelled, and by which he deserved to be distinguished among the Roman pontiffs by the name “the Great,” only among the priests, by whom, as was customary in the ancient Church, he was trained as a young man for the duties of the Church, together with the natural gifts of his own intelligence: namely, an intellect thoroughly prepared to administer aptly and honorably not only every kind of ecclesiastical business but also other affairs that had no connection either with faith or discipline [Col. 0050D].

Certainly, he must already at an early age have given evidence of natural virtue and devotion to duty, since, while still an acolyte under Pope Zosimus in the year 418, he was sent to Carthage to convey to Aurelius and the other bishops of Africa the pontiff’s judgment concerning Caelestius [Note: [Col. 0049D] This is established by the testimony of Augustine’s letter 104 to Sixtus, then a presbyter of the Roman Church and later Coelestine’s successor in the episcopate; Sixtus had used the same occasion to send letters to Augustine [Col. 0050D]. It is especially probable from the chronological agreement that the acolyte mentioned there was this Leo and no other.].

During the time of Pope Coelestine he served as a deacon [Col. 0051A]. But the matters concerning the administration of ecclesiastical affairs that Quesnel argues were entrusted to him by Coelestine require arguments other than those on which Quesnel relies [Note: [Col. 0051D] Quesnel, *Life of Leo*, for the years 430–432, no. 3, in the Ballerini edition, volume II, p. 406. But compare the Ballerinis’ notes on Leo’s Letter to Maximus of Antioch, 119, volume I, p. 1216, n. 24.].

Nevertheless, the esteem in which Leo was then held at Rome is most clearly attested by Cassian’s letter, in which, in the year 431, he presented Leo with the books *On the Incarnation against Nestorius*, written at Leo’s urging. Other evidence no less worthy of this esteem also exists, showing the authority and influence that Leo enjoyed not only at Rome with the pontiff but also at the courts of princes.

For if we believe Prosper, it was chiefly through Leo’s vigilance and urging that Pope Sixtus resisted the devices of Julian of Eclanum, by which Julian was attempting to insinuate himself into communion with the Church. The embassy that Leo undertook in 440, at the emperor’s command, to reconcile the hostile minds of Aetius and Albinus, commanders of the Roman forces in Gaul, whose dissension was feared throughout the empire, became still better known through Leo’s subsequent election to the Roman episcopate. While Leo was still occupied with this mission, Pope Sixtus died, and immediately all the votes of the Roman clergy and people named the deacon Leo as bishop.

Thus summoned from his honorable embassy and ordained, he inaugurated his new office with a solemn act of thanksgiving, and every year celebrated the day of his ordination in a sermon.

His episcopate fell during the disastrous period of the Roman Empire in the West. For, while the rulers displayed extreme negligence and stupefaction, bands of barbarians were everywhere either assailing the borders of the empire or flooding the provinces with incursions, devastating and depopulating them, or, after expelling or subduing the inhabitants, making those provinces their own settlements [Col. 0051C].

It was impossible to witness the calamity that the whole Church necessarily suffered from the affliction of its individual provinces without the fear arising that a similar fate might befall Italy and Rome herself. If Rome’s oppression were to continue, the gravest damage to the dignity of the Apostolic See, which at that time held its present position, was to be expected. Added to this was the hatred of the barbarians, imbued with Arianism, toward the adherents of the Catholic Church, together with the severe persecutions inflicted in many places.

Amid these gathering clouds of a rising storm, a bishop assuming the helm of the Church certainly needed strength of spirit. Nevertheless, the Church’s internal condition was not equally desperate; indeed, it was not without encouraging signs, if it was to be judged by the interests of the Roman pontiff. The movements of heretics, so frequent in those centuries, could not alarm a new bishop who was intent on advancing the authority of his see and was not wholly ignorant of ancient precedents. He had to know how much authority and power the Roman See had gained from nearly every such controversy, even through bishops who were less learned and not very firm in spirit, and how much opportunity for further expansion had been created by the recent conflicts in the East [Col. 0052A] [Note: [Col. 0051D] To make the beginning of Leo’s episcopate appear more difficult, Quesnel portrays not only the empire as afflicted but also the Church as miserably harassed and almost torn apart by internal enemies—namely, heretics springing up everywhere [Col. 0052D]. This is correct if affairs are to be assessed in general; but not so, in my judgment, if they are considered from the standpoint of the Roman bishop, and especially of Leo.].

How much greater, then, were the hopes Leo was entitled to entertain, since, in addition to his other qualities of mind and intellect, he brought to this dignity the authority of learning and eloquence, and in defining the most serious and subtle questions of faith could regard himself as not merely equal but even superior to the Greeks.

Events confirmed that Leo held such views, or views of this kind. However sincere and vigorous his devotion to governing ecclesiastical discipline and defending the faith received from antiquity—a devotion that he displayed immediately from the beginning of his office and never ceased to display throughout his episcopate, and which was greatly strengthened by his own natural energy and firmness—he nevertheless used these same qualities no less to increase the dignity and authority of his see [Col. 0052B]. In these efforts, the innate force of his intellect often degenerated into an arrogance and obstinacy that were intolerable and even irrational.

His conflict with Hilary of Arles is evidence of this: it was full of pride and passions unworthy of so great a bishop, although we emphatically do not agree with Quesnel in excusing and defending Hilary. The history of the Eutychian controversy supplies further evidence of the same disposition. Indeed, the evidence is such that, while we may readily grant that Leo’s predecessors in the Roman See had sought to advance their authority and power only as circumstances required, I believe that Leo was the first to attempt, by deliberate design, to subject all the other bishops to his rule. Indeed, I believe that he did not first conceive this plan only after becoming bishop, but brought it with him to the episcopate.

I believe that his concern should above all be referred to this: he strove to establish the doctrine of the dignity and power of the Roman See, founded upon Peter and transmitted by him to his successors, and to implant it in the minds of everyone throughout the West and East.

This doctrine began with Innocent, and was thereafter never neglected by his successors; but Leo explained and consolidated it in such a way that it became, not for him alone but for all Roman bishops after him, the foundation for contriving, elevating, and enlarging their domination, nor could any doctrine be found more fertile in monstrous opinions favoring it. Nor did he use it only when he wished to accomplish something by his authority; before the people he was also accustomed to treat of it with particular zeal, often on other occasions and especially on the anniversary of his ordination.

First, indeed, he so extols and embellishes the gifts and privileges granted by Christ to Peter above the other apostles [Col. 0052D] that he already dared to profess that divine condescension had granted this man a share in its own power, and that, if Christ had wished the other princes to have anything in common with Peter, he had never given it except through Peter—whatever he had not denied to the others [Note: [Col. 0052D] Sermon 4 in Ballerini, p. 16, no. 12. If one surveys it from the beginning, one will understand that the word “princes” is not free from deceit.].

Then, while affirming that he himself holds Peter’s place, he devotes all his efforts to persuading his hearers [Col. 0053A] that he had transmitted to his own heirs that solidity which he himself had received from Christ, having also become a Rock; that Peter did not cease to preside over his see, presiding over it with salutary counsels and equitable judgments; and that Leo presided over Peter’s see less than he served it, so that whatever was now rightly done and arranged by the Roman pontiff was to be attributed to Peter’s works and Peter’s governance.

Moreover, he maintained that the sublimity of the Church had to arise from Peter’s firmness; and for this reason, special care for Peter had been assumed by the Lord and prayer had been offered specifically for Peter’s faith, as though the condition of the others would be more secure if the mind of their prince had not been overcome.

With this purpose and in this spirit Leo began to handle the case of Eutyches. Eutyches, an archimandrite of Constantinople, while pursuing the remnants of Nestorianism [Col. 0053B] with excessive vigor and burdening certain Eastern bishops with the unjust suspicion of heresy, fell into the opposite error and did not hesitate to maintain that the two natures in Christ had, after the union, coalesced into one.

He was a diligent student both of the Holy Scriptures and of the expositions of the holy Fathers, and openly confessed that he regarded these as superior and as the only certain and reliable authorities. Yet, from this same solitary study and fear of Nestorianism, he seems to have taken excessive care over his words and to have fallen into error more because of his excessive avoidance of ambiguous expressions than for any other reason [Note: [Col. 0053D] S. V. Griesbach, in *Theological Passages Collected from Leo II*, section 3, § 18, pp. 40–41.].

Nor was he obstinate, nor did he reject the corrections of wiser and more learned men. But at the Constantinopolitan synod (*ἐνδημούσῃ*, the resident synod), at which his case was first heard before Flavian in 448 [Col. 0053C], he willingly embraced Flavian’s judgment; only, when ordered to anathematize those who thought otherwise, he was afraid and openly refused.

For this sole reason he was anathematized by the synod and at the same time removed both from office and from communion with the Church. Then Eutyches, perceiving that his own ardent zeal against Nestorianism had brought about his downfall, began to approach the emperor and to implore the assistance of other bishops, especially the bishops of the Alexandrian and Roman sees.

Nor was this in vain. The emperor, who considered the Nestorian heresy more deadly than any plague, took up his patronage both by his own inclination and perhaps also through the efforts of certain friends—Chrysaphius the eunuch is mentioned in the records of this affair—who either themselves favored Flavian less or were genuinely distressed by the wrong which Eutyches had suffered from him [Col. 0053D].

As for the Alexandrian bishop, unless a perpetual hatred of the bishops of Constantinople existed—or, even apart from that, unless the memory of Cyril alone made a man of Eutyches’ disposition seem worthy of his protection, Dioscorus could have had no more welcome opportunity for gratifying his resentment against a rival.

Finally, Leo’s disposition to plead Eutyches’ cause was already by no means obscure. Eutyches had long before commended himself to Leo by letters addressed to him on account of his zeal against the Nestorians. Now not only had Eutyches himself complained to Leo of the wrong done to him, but Theodosius had also written that a great uproar had been raised by Flavian [Col. 0054A] and had asked Leo to come to the aid of the distressed Eutyches. Leo therefore began vehemently to remonstrate with Flavian, expressing his astonishment that Flavian could have kept that scandal silent from him and had not rather arranged that Leo should first be informed through a report from Flavian himself; and he demanded that as soon as possible the grounds of Flavian’s judgment and everything that had taken place should be conveyed to him fully and clearly.

But when, through Flavian’s letter, he had been informed about Eutyches’ heresy, the depravity of his opinion seemed to him so detestable, the offspring of errors springing from it so extensive and manifold, and the danger threatening the purity of the faith from it so great, that he immediately declared his agreement to Flavian in a brief letter, while at the same time promising a fuller letter in which he would instruct Bishop Flavian what ought to be decided concerning the whole case.

This was that famous letter to Flavian in which he examined and defined the entire doctrine of the Incarnation. Having proscribed the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches, he strove to set forth Catholic doctrine so accurately, both in its propositions and in its language, that everything written in it could be shown to have been taken from apostolic and evangelical teaching.

He had decided to send it to Constantinople through the same cleric who had brought Flavian’s earlier letters. But in the meantime the emperor had summoned a general synod at Ephesus for the Kalends of August 449, and Leo gave the legates sent there instructions to have the letter read publicly at the synod.

The outcome of that synod, however, is well known. It is infamous under the name of the Robber Synod; Dioscorus alone exercised authority; the Roman legates were prevented from reading Leo’s letter to Flavian; and after the fury of the faction had thrown everything into confusion, they were placed under guard, with only Hilary escaping by flight [Col. 0054C].

The cries of the oppressed were useless; useless was the indignation of all good men; useless were Leo’s complaints to Theodosius and Pulcheria, to the clergy and people, and to the archimandrites of Constantinople. In vain did the Roman synod condemn the proceedings of that synod; in vain did Valentinian, together with the Augustae Placidia and Pulcheria, strive to obtain from Theodosius a council in the West. Then suddenly, upon the death of Theodosius on 28 July 450, the gloomy aspect of affairs was changed into a more favorable one—indeed, one most auspicious for the authority of the Roman pontiff.

For the new emperor Marcian, aided by his wife Pulcheria, devoted all his care and thought from the beginning of his reign [Col. 0054D] to repairing the damage inflicted upon the faith by Eutyches, and by letter he declared to Leo his intention of convening a council as soon as possible [Note: [Col. 0053D] Letter 73 in Ballerini.].

Meanwhile Eutyches was ordered to leave the City, and a synod was convened at Constantinople in the presence of the Roman legates. There Leo’s doctrinal letter to Flavian was read, and the new bishop of Constantinople, Anatolius, subscribed it together with the other bishops, archimandrites, presbyters, and deacons [Note: [Col. 0054D] See Leo’s Letter to Anatolius, 80, in Ballerini.]. They sent it for subscription also to all the metropolitans everywhere [Note: [Col. 0054D] Council of Chalcedon, session 4.].

With affairs therefore moving in this direction [Col. 0055A], Leo, thinking that an opportunity had arisen to extend the authority of his judgment more widely, took fresh courage and, as though the entire decision belonged to him alone, dared with his arrogance to mock the moderation of others.

The letter just mentioned to Anatolius is full of this disdain. In it Leo indicates that he rejoices because Anatolius had assented to his letter to Flavian—or, to use Leo’s own words, he boasts that Anatolius had shown himself a follower of evangelical learning—and he congratulates him on the peace of the apostolic see as confirmed in him.

But he gave still more numerous and clearer proofs of his attitude through his legates at the Council of Chalcedon. First, he tried with all possible insistence to bring about the postponement of the entire synod, presenting it as more suitable to await a time when many bishops from the more distant provinces could also be summoned [Col. 0055B]. Perhaps, however, he did so for no other reason than that he hoped the heresy would be considered refuted by his letter alone, to which all the bishops of the whole world had subscribed their names together with an anathematization of Nestorius, Eutyches, and their errors—and to which they were still going to subscribe—especially since the restoration of the bishops unjustly expelled from their sees at the Ephesian synod, and the exclusion of Dioscorus and his associates from communion, had already been addressed at the Constantinopolitan synod in accordance with the instructions of Leo’s own legates [Note: [Col. 0055D] Letter 80, to Anatolius.].

It is also not difficult to understand that Leo feared that the bishop of Constantinople, whose see at Flavian’s time had been subjected by Dioscorus to severe disgrace, might, elated by the sudden humiliation of his Alexandrian adversary and by the prevailing mood, use this opportunity to enlarge the prerogatives of his own see.

Nor was this fear unfounded, as what follows will show. Since Leo could obtain neither this postponement nor that the synod be held in Italy, he sent Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, and the presbyter Boniface as legates to Nicaea, where the synod had first been summoned and from which it was later transferred to Chalcedon.

The synod began at Chalcedon on 8 October and was concluded on 1 November in sixteen sessions [Note: [Col. 0055D] Sixteen, that is, according to the number found in the acts. Others count ninety-three, while still others count fifteen.]. In them the legates of the Roman bishop omitted absolutely nothing that could raise his authority above that of the synod.

So little reverence was shown them, whether by the bishops present or by the officials who attended with authority, that they repeatedly shouted that Leo so wished and so commanded, that this was contained in their instructions, and they even threatened to withdraw unless it was done [Col. 0055D].

In most matters, indeed, because the desire for peace and the pressing necessity of debating the cases demanded it, and because of their respect for the emperor, the synod complied with them to such an extent that it might appear to have depended on Leo’s nod and direction.

As for the heresy of Eutyches itself, which had originally been the cause of so great a dispute, and likewise that of Nestorius, the assembled Fathers were far from decreeing anything new. Rather, in three sessions in which this question was debated partly through the efforts of the Roman legates and partly through those of the other bishops [Note: [Col. 0056D] Sessions 2, 4, and 5.], Leo’s letter to Flavian was again and again impressed upon them as the firmest defense against these corruptions and was approved by everyone, together with the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds and Cyril’s two letters to Nestorius from the Council of Ephesus, as the one and perpetual norm of the faith [Col. 0056A].

Thus, for the first time, the definition of the Roman bishop constituted the rule of faith for the universal Church, and was, as it were, dictated by him to the universal Church.

Yet Leo did not wish to appear to have gained this triumph as something new. Instead, composing his expression and language to solemn dignity, he pretended that he had done nothing except what belonged to the order and custom of the Roman see.

But the more joyful this success was, the greater the distress it brought him on account of what he habitually called Bishop Anatolius’ ambition—or, as Anatolius represented it, the zeal of his clergy, without fault on his own part, for the see of Constantinople.

When all matters that seemed to belong to the synod’s primary business had been completed, the clergy of Constantinople and the bishops began, in session 16, to demand that the synod should establish something in honor of the Constantinopolitan see [Col. 0056B].

This was by no means unforeseen or unexpected by Leo. For he had instructed his legates that if any bishops, trusting in the splendor of their cities, should attempt to appropriate something for themselves, they were to repel it with the firmness it deserved.

Accordingly, they resisted these innovations with the utmost determination. Nevertheless, they could not prevent the decree that the bishop of Constantinople, as bishop of New Rome, should enjoy the first honor after the Roman bishop, should possess right and authority over the dioceses of Thrace, Pontus, and Asia and their metropolitans, and should ordain the bishops of the barbarian peoples.

The Roman legates had left the synod when discussion began concerning the canons to be enacted on this matter. But when they nevertheless learned that the canons had been enacted, they returned the next day and complained gravely and deviously about proceedings conducted in their absence. Finally, in order at least partly to fulfill their instructions, they solemnly opposed the canons and engaged in other conduct foreign to courtesy and moderation, about which Anatolius complains with restraint in his letter to Leo [Note: [Col. 0056D] Letter 101 in Ballerini, p. 1134.].

Leo, however, was far more intemperate. Disregarding the emperors’ most gracious expression of their will and disregarding the pleas of the Eastern bishops, he immediately began to rage against Anatolius, reproaching him for refusing to obey his legates, charging him with wicked ambition and a desire harmful to the universal Church, judging him to possess nothing honorable and nothing trustworthy, even criticizing the circumstances of his ordination and already threatening to deprive him of communion.

As long as he still retained some hope in Pulcheria and in the exceedingly pliable emperor Marcian, he left no stratagem or argument untried by which he might win them over and induce them to withhold their assent from Anatolius and to rescind the canons he disliked.

For he argued not only that the decrees of the Nicene synod were violated by these acts, but also that the prerogatives of the Alexandrian and Antiochene sees were being offended and the rights of many metropolitans diminished [Col. 0057A]. He predicted still greater evils for the Church from this bishop’s immoderate pursuit of honors [Note: [Col. 0057B] The Ballerini show remarkable acumen in arguing that the Roman legates did not oppose canon 28, nor did Leo reject it, because the honor of the Constantinopolitan bishop immediately after the Roman bishop had been decreed—“equal privileges of honor after the bishop of Rome” (*τὰ ἴσα πρεσβεῖα τῆς τιμῆς μετὰ τὸν Ῥώμης ἐπίσκοπον*)—or because jurisdiction over the three new dioceses of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace had been granted to him. In neither case, they say, was anything detracted either from the dignity or from the jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff’s primacy. Rather, the opposition arose solely because the Fathers had said that the privileges of the Roman Church had been granted on account of the empire, and because they had dared to confer equal privileges upon the bishop of Constantinople on account of the dignity of New Rome. Yet the Roman see had received its primacy not from the Fathers, nor on account of the dignity attached to the imperial city, but from God himself through the apostle Peter; consequently, the see of Constantinople could not be compared with it either by divine institution or by jurisdiction. See the notes to Quesnel’s dissertation *On the Life of Leo*, vol. II, pp. 514–515. But of this grievance, which could easily have been removed, the angry Leo made not the slightest mention.].

Meanwhile he sent no reply to the letters addressed to him by the bishops of the Council of Chalcedon, in which they had reported everything that had been done. As a result, some people began to suspect the council’s decrees, and doubts arose concerning their orthodoxy, since the Roman bishop opposed them.

But when Leo saw that his efforts had failed in this respect, and when the emperors rather pressed him not to delay any longer in confirming the Chalcedonian decrees, he yielded so far to their authority that he did not regret his compliance and confirmed by his assent everything that concerned the matter of the faith. The canons concerning the honor of the see of Constantinople, however, he rejected completely [Col. 0057B].

Furthermore, he abstained from all correspondence with Anatolius and, in an entirely unprecedented act, as though Anatolius were insufficiently devoted to the Catholic faith, appointed one of his own men as guardian and observer of his actions: Julian, bishop of Cos [Note: [Col. 0057D] It is commonly held that Julian’s office provided the first example of the apostolic *apocrisiarius* at the courts of rulers. But the Ballerini, who everywhere display the utmost concern for the honor of the Roman see, have observed that when Leo entrusted Julian with his place in the emperor’s entourage, he did not do so with the intention of following the example of the Alexandrian bishop or of other prominent Eastern bishops. He did so solely so that Julian, watching over the integrity of the faith with apostolic zeal, might ensure that the Catholic faith suffered no harm from the Nestorians or Eutychians, and, whenever necessary, might seek the emperor’s protection and assistance in this matter. They further observe that at that time the city of Rome was not subject to the Eastern emperor in the same way as the Eastern cities were, so that it needed some representative for the conduct of various causes and affairs; and that the entire institution of the representatives and *apocrisiarii* of the Roman Church began only under Justinian, who ruled Italy no less than the East [Col. 0058B]. They hold that Leo was moved to this action because he had perceived in Anatolius none of the Catholic vigor that circumstances required. These points are indeed consistent both with the history and with Leo’s own words.

For he wrote to Marcian (Letter 111):

“I also ask your Clemency’s benevolence to hold your worshipful brother, Bishop Julian, in your affection, as you are accustomed to do; through his services, may an image of my presence be rendered to you. For, confident in the sincerity of his faith, I have delegated to him my office against the heretics of our time, and I have required him not to be absent from your entourage for the sake of guarding the Churches and peace. May you deign to hear his suggestions, offered for the concord of Catholic unity, as though they were mine, pleasing God, who may grant you, in addition to the royal crown, the palm of priestly victory.”

To Julian he gave this instruction (Letter 113):

“Let your Charity, dearest brother, devote pious and necessary care to the solicitude of the apostolic see. Since you were nurtured within it as a Catholic, that see entrusts to you by maternal right its action against the heretics Nestorians and Eutychians [Col. 0058D], so that, supported by divine aid, you may not cease to watch over the circumstances of the city of Constantinople, lest the impious upheaval of the doctrines mentioned above arise anywhere. And since the faith of the glorious rulers is so great that you can confidently bring to their attention matters that ought to be reported, make use of their piety for the benefit of the universal Church. If your Charity consults me about matters concerning which you think there may be uncertainty, my reply will not be lacking to inform your reports. Setting aside those actions in cases which ought to be settled by the knowledge of the bishops in their respective Churches, assume this special care on my behalf, so that neither the Nestorian nor the Eutychian heresy may revive in any part. For there is no Catholic vigor in the bishop of Constantinople, nor is he greatly concerned either for the mystery of human salvation or for his own reputation. If he possessed any spiritual diligence, he ought to consider both by whom he was ordained and whose successor he became, so that he might follow blessed Flavian rather than the authors of his own honor.”

Although later, at Marcian’s insistence and also at Anatolius’ request, Leo pretended to return to friendly relations with him, the very declaration of his peace was nevertheless directed so plainly toward the disgrace and injury of the bishop of Constantinople, and was so crafty and equivocal, that it is not surprising that from this time onward the chief bishop of the Eastern Church became estranged from the Roman see.

After his victory over Eutyches and the triumph of his formula, Leo was distinguished by no event more celebrated than his embassy to Attila, undertaken in the same year in which the Council of Chalcedon was completed.

Attila, having restored his strength after suffering defeat in the Catalaunian Fields, had invaded Italy through the Pannonias; Italy had been left without even the slightest defense through the supreme negligence of the emperor and the general Aetius. Indeed, the indolence of both was so great that they preferred to withdraw from all Italy rather than undertake anything for its defense.

The noblest provinces therefore lay open to every fury of hostile rapacity and lust. At the first assault the royal cities—Aquileia, Ticinum, and Mediolanum—were captured and plundered; and now the Hun, elated by this unexpected success, was hastening toward Rome.

Then, amid the extreme terror of all, no counsel seemed more salutary to the emperor, senate, and Roman people than to seek peace through an embassy from the most savage king. The task of negotiating was entrusted to Leo, with two men of consular and prefectural rank, Avienus and Trigetius, added to him.

But history is silent about their roles, as well as about the conditions they were to offer, being concerned here almost exclusively with celebrating Leo’s memory. What they did and how they did it we likewise do not know. But Leo alone is said to have brought Attila to desist from his hostile purpose and to prepare a sudden withdrawal.

Prosper relates that the king received the entire embassy with dignity and was so pleased by the presence of the high priest that he abstained from war and withdrew beyond the Danube. Prosper seems to imply [Col. 0059A] that what broke Attila’s spirit proceeded from the more august appearance of Leo’s face and bodily presence.

Others preferred to attribute this power to Leo’s eloquence. Although it can readily be observed that stronger causes must have existed for moving the Hun’s mind, and although the history of his expedition contains circumstances that may be called sufficiently plausible [Note: [Col. 0059] See the distinguished Heyne, “On Leo the Great’s Making Attila and Genseric Suppliants,” in vol. III of the *Academic Opuscula*, pp. 127 ff.], there were nevertheless those to whom the whole affair seemed not unrelated to a miracle. Through their inventions they caused Leo’s name to become illustrious even among those whose view of his virtues was obscured either by distance or by duller judgment.

By contrast, another encounter of his with Genseric the Vandal, although much more beneficial, received little renown. For when, in 455, after the emperor Valentinian had been killed, Maximus seized the Western empire and married his wife Eudoxia [Col. 0059B], who was unaware of the murder, she soon learned of Maximus’ crime against her husband and resolved to avenge his death. In the excess of her anger, she devoted the whole City to destruction and summoned Genseric, king of the Vandals, from Africa.

The Vandal immediately crossed into Italy with a huge army, attacked the City, which was entirely without defense, and occupied it. He would already have surrendered wholly to slaughter and fires had Leo not gone out to meet him beyond the gates and, by his supplication, obtained that Genseric should be content with plunder and abstain from killing and burning.

Certainly, whatever this was, it was entirely due to Leo’s miserable assistance. For Attila had not been superstitiously tormented by terrors, wavering as he went and returned, nor had he feared a hostile encounter because his forces had been worn down by disease and want. This was an enemy who already held everything in his power [Col. 0059C], and to whom, in addition to his innate ferocity, religion itself added spurs to anger; his savagery could be broken or softened by no power except prayer.

Leo’s final concern was caused by the disturbances raised in the Alexandrian Church by Timothy the Cat in 457, through which the authority of the Council of Chalcedon appeared to be placed in no slight danger.

The whole matter was settled under the new Eastern emperor Leo and through the bishop of Constantinople, but it was greatly assisted by the efforts and prudence of the Roman bishop. After Leo had once again seen his cause victorious, and after Timothy the Cat had been expelled and another Timothy, called Solophaciolus, had properly taken possession of the Alexandrian see, he did not remain long among mortals. He left as the final memorial of his care for the Church [Col. 0059D] a congratulatory letter to the new bishop, to his ordainers, and to the Alexandrian clergy; less than a full year later, on 10 November 461, he departed to heaven.

# CHAPTER II. The Writings of Saint Leo

The writings of Leo the Great consist of Sermons and Letters. We shall enumerate both classes according to the edition of the Ballerini, adding the order of Quesnel and of the earlier editions.

## I. SERMONS

[Col. 0060A]

I–V. On the anniversary of his ordination, delivered on the day of that ordination and on its anniversary. In Quesnel, I–IV, since the first was divided by the Ballerini into two, of which the former consists of chapter 1 and the latter of chapters 2 and 3.

VI–XI. On the Collections. In Quesnel, V–X.

XII–XX. On the fast of the tenth month. In Quesnel, XI–XIX.

XXI–XXX. On the Nativity of the Lord. In Quesnel, XX–XXXVII.

XXXI–XXXVIII. On the Epiphany of the Lord. In Quesnel, XXX–XXXVII.

XXXIX–L. On Lent. In Quesnel, XXXVIII–XLIX.

[Col. 0060B]

LI. Homily delivered before the Second Sunday of Lent, on the Gospel according to Matthew: “At that time Jesus took Peter,” etc. In Quesnel, XCIV, entitled “On the Transfiguration of the Lord.”

LII–LXX. On the Passion of the Lord. In Quesnel, L–LXVIII.

LXXI–LXXII. On the Resurrection of the Lord. In Quesnel, LXIX–LXX.

LXXIII–LXXIV. On the Ascension of the Lord. In Quesnel, LXXI–LXXII.

LXXV–LXXVII. On Pentecost. In Quesnel, LXXIII–LXXV.

LXXVIII–LXXXI. On the Fast of Pentecost. In Quesnel, LXXVI–LXXIX.

LXXXII. On the Feast of the apostles Peter and Paul. In Quesnel [Col. 0060C], LXXX.

LXXXIII. On the Feast of Saint Peter the Apostle. In Quesnel’s Appendix, Sermon IV.

LXXXIV. On the Octave of the apostles Peter and Paul. In Quesnel, LXXXI.

LXXXV. On the Feast of Saint Lawrence the Martyr. In Quesnel, LXXXIII.

LXXXVI–XCIV. On the Fast of the seventh month. In Quesnel, LXXXIV–XCII.

XCV. On the steps of ascent to blessedness. In Quesnel, XCV.

XCVI. Treatise against the heresy of Eutyches. In Quesnel, XCIII.

The following have been separated from these and relegated to the Appendix as falsely attributed to Leo.

[Col. 0060D]

I. Treatise against the errors of Eutyches and the other heretics. In Quesnel’s Appendix, V.

II. On the Nativity of the Lord. In the same Appendix, II.

III–IV. On Lent.

V–VI. On the Passion of the Lord.

VII. On Palm Sunday.
