VIII–X. On the Resurrection of the Lord.

XI. On the Ascension of the Lord. In the same Appendix, III.

XII. On the Most Holy Trinity.

XIII. On the Feast of Saint Vincent the Martyr. In the same Appendix, I.

[Col. 0061A]

XIV. On the Chair of Saint Peter. First published by Quesnel among the genuine works as number XCVI, but later removed by his own judgment. The Ballerini supplied it from Vatican manuscripts.

XV. On the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

XVI. On the Feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

XVII. On the Feast of the Blessed Apostle Paul.

XVIII. On Saint Peter, how he was led out of prison.

XIX. On the Feast of the holy seven Maccabean brothers, now placed in the Appendix for the first time and restored to Saint Augustine. In Quesnel, Sermon LXXXII.

XX. On the Transfiguration of the Lord.

To Neon of Ravenna (Q. 135, A. 37). CLXVII. To Rusticus of Narbonne (Q. 2, A. 92). CLXVIII. To the bishops established throughout Campania, Samnium, and Tuscany (Q. 136, A. 80). CLXIX. To Leo Augustus (Q. 137, A. 99). CLXX. To Gennadius of Constantinople (Q. 138, A. 100). CLXXI. To Timothy of Alexandria (Q. 139, A. 101). CLXXII. To the priests and deacons of Alexandria (Q. 140, A. 102). CLXXIII. To Theophilus and the other Egyptian bishops (Q. 141, A. 103).

They were all written between the years 442 and 460, according to the Ballerini brothers’ reckoning, in the following sequence: I, II, III, in 442. IV, in 443. V, VI, VII, in 444. VIII–XI, [Col. 0064B] in 445. XII–XIV, in 446. XV–XVIII, in 447. XIX–XXI, in 448. XXII, at the end of that year or the beginning of 449. XXIII–LIV, in 449. LV–LXXVII, in 450. LXXVIII–CI, in 451. CII–CIX, in 452. CX–CXXV, in 453. CXXVI–CXL, in 454. CXLI–CXLIII, in 455. CXLIV–CLVIII, in 457. CLIX–CLXVI, in 458. CLXVII, in that year or the following; CLXVIII, in 459. CLXIX–CLXXIII, in 460.

For Leo’s works that have been lost, both sermons and letters, one must consult the Ballerini brothers. In a novel instance, Quesnellus dared to attribute to Leo the four books *On the Calling of All Nations*, as well as the letter to Demetriades and the *Authorities of the Bishops of the Apostolic See of Former Times concerning Grace*, which are also commonly attributed to Prosper, not to mention others; but he found few supporters for this opinion. Concerning Antelmius’s view, see what is reported under Prosper.

## CHAPTER III

### § I. Editions

Among the Roman pontiffs of the most celebrated name, there is none whose writings, however distinguished, have enjoyed such renown, and have been received with such veneration and zeal throughout every age, as those of Leo. This is attested not only by the multitude of printed copies that have appeared in various regions during the past three centuries, but much more clearly by the immense number and variety of manuscript books through which so many of his sermons and letters have been transmitted to us from the beginning. Indeed, only through the careful examination and classification of these manuscripts has the work of the most recent editors achieved the point at which the history of Leo’s Works can almost be reconstructed without interruption from the author himself. Since this earlier history of the writings is of such great importance—indeed, absolutely necessary—for understanding the principles of the printed editions and assessing the merits of the editors, especially in the case of an author whose distinction depends less upon his own genius than upon the resources of those engaged in polishing his work, we would gladly have inserted here, drawn from the Ballerini brothers, an account of the vicissitudes of Leo’s manuscript sermons and letters insofar as they would help illuminate the history of the editions, if the learning that they acquired through prolonged labor and tireless study could have been encompassed so easily and in so few words without loss of the whole; and if it had not seemed more advisable to append a summary of all their observations on this matter, in as concise a style as possible, to this commentary on Leo’s writings and editions. That, however, will be done more suitably below, where discussion must be made of the manuscripts consulted by the principal editors. We therefore refer readers who wish to be informed to that place and proceed, in our customary manner, to recount the fortunes of this pontiff’s Works from the time they began to be committed to type [Col. 0065B].

The first initiative toward publishing Leo’s writings was given by John, bishop of Aléria, in the *Sermons* printed at Rome by Conrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz in 1470. These were reprinted there in the same or the following year by Ulrich Han, but without mention of place or year; shortly afterward by Venetian printers in 1482, 1485, and 1505; and by Jean Petit at Paris in 1515, as well as by others who preferred to remain concealed rather than disclose their names. Nevertheless, of the anonymous editions, those which we designate in the following catalogue as 1475 and II depart somewhat from the Alérian archetype, while the one marked III (IV) appears to be entirely different. During the same period various sermons of Leo customarily appeared in different editions of the *Homiliary of the Doctors*. [Col. 0065C]

The *Letters* were first published by Jacques Merlin, doctor of theology at Paris, in the *Collection of Councils and Pontifical Letters*, at Paris in 1524, and reprinted there in 1530 and 1535. He was soon followed by Sichard, who published another collection of fifty letters at the end of Clement of Rome in 1536; it was reprinted at Paris in 1568. Peter Crabbe of Mechelen then took responsibility for arranging the letters, and inserted Merlin’s letters, arranged in the proper order of consuls and months, into his *Collection of Councils*, published at Cologne in 1538 and prepared and reprinted in 1551. Peter Canisius of Nijmegen, then a cleric of the diocese of Cologne and later a member of the Society of Jesus, first attempted to unite both kinds of writings, arranging for the letters [Col. 0065D] and sermons to be printed in two volumes at Cologne in 1546 and 1547.

He was followed by Laurentius Surius, later more celebrated for his edition of the *Lives of the Saints*, who published the same Works of Leo, corrected and revised from manuscript copies, at Cologne in 1561 and again in 1569. He also inserted Leo’s letters into the councils that he edited, and reproduced several sermons anew together with his enlarged *Homiliary of the Doctors*. Proceeding at an equal pace with these was the edition of the Canons Regular of Saint Martin of Leuven, likewise corrected from manuscript codices, published at Leuven in 1575–77 and again at Antwerp in 1583. Meanwhile Leo’s Letters received some additions from the *Collection of Decretal Letters* of Cardinal Antonio Carafa, which appeared at Rome in 1591 under the care of Antonio de Aquino with great ceremony, as well as from Caesar Baronius’s *Annals* of 1566 and the *Miscellanies of the Fathers* by Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, appended to the Works of Gregory Thaumaturgus [Col. 0066B] at Mainz in 1604. Almost all of these, arranged in proper order, are included in the *Collection of Councils* of Severinus Binius, published in 1606 and subsequently issued again, a second and a third time, at Cologne and Paris.

Jacques Sirmond also gave the letters pertaining to the Gallican Church, corrected from manuscript codices and increased by the addition of one, in his *Councils of Gaul* of 1629. That Vossius, who in the work just mentioned published letters from Vatican manuscript codices and from those of Cardinal Sirlet, was planning a complete edition of Leo’s Works, drawn from manuscripts and elucidated, to be issued by the Parisian bookseller Michel Sonnius, and who mentioned and promised it more than once in other writings, [Note: [Col. 0065D] at the end of the Works of Saint Ephrem, and also in the notes to Leo’s treatise against Eutyches published in the aforementioned *Miscellanies*, where he recalls his observations in reviewing Leo and his annotations in the margins of the Letters. Add Nicolas Fabri’s letter to the same man (in Fabri’s *Opuscula*, pp. 113–114), in which he testifies that he had heard that Michel Sonnius, the Parisian printer, was awaiting as soon as possible an edition of the Works of Saint Leo by him. In fact, Jean-Baptiste Marus had obtained an edition of Leo’s *Sermons* in whose margins Gerard Vossius had noted variant readings, which Marus himself also used; and the Ballerini brothers (in the preface to Leo’s *Sermons*, p. 81) suspect that the codex of Leo’s Works collated by Franciscus Pegna with manuscript codices from Roman libraries—the codex which Quesnellus writes, at the end of his general preface, that he once saw after Pegna’s death in the possession of Marius, canon of Sant’Angelo—was Vossian. For they show that the Marius mentioned was none other than Jean-Baptiste Marus, whom Quesnellus elsewhere expressly calls canon of Sant’Angelo in the Fish Market, and who is said to have possessed the codex of Leo annotated by Vossius with various readings from manuscript books. They therefore hold that the attribution to Pegna of what ought to have been assigned to Vossius resulted from Bigotius’s error, because Vossius’s codex had come into Pegna’s hands before passing into Marius’s library.] But this expectation was frustrated by the man’s death in 1609 and forced those interested in Leo to begin hoping for something else—though that hope too subsequently collapsed.

For when certain Parisian booksellers had undertaken, by private agreement, to print the Works of Leo the Great together with those of Maximus of Turin, Peter Chrysologus, and others, especially authors of homilies, whose number gradually increased, and after several editions of these had appeared in 1614, 1618, and 1623—in which the Leuven edition was almost simply reprinted but enlarged by three sermons from an old manuscript belonging to Nicolas Fabri—the undertaking finally came into the hands of Théophile Raynaud, a theologian of great reputation. He completed a heptad of these authors, in which he strove above all to restore Leo’s Works to their genuine meaning. This edition appeared at Paris in 1633 and was put through the press again in 1651, 1661, and 1671. But since he relied less upon the variety of printed editions and the authority of ancient manuscripts than upon his own ingenuity and learning, the undertaking he had begun was taken up by Jean-Baptiste Marus, a Roman canon, known for having published in 1644 certain sermons of Augustine from Vatican and Barberini manuscripts, again from a Vatican codex of Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, later Victor III’s *Dialogues*, and, in 1633, Peter the Deacon’s little work *On the Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*.

He completed the sermons, supported by manuscript codices from the Vatican and Saint Peter’s Basilica, as well as by others and by Vossius’s variants; but sudden death snatched the entire work from his hands. The volume of sermons restored according to the evidence of numerous manuscripts, which had been handed through his brother to Cardinal Michael Angelo Ricci, was entirely buried in oblivion, except for the preface.

Thus far had the efforts of learned men in restoring Leo the Great advanced. In this general survey of editions it is unnecessary to mention the various printings of the *Letter to Flavian* made during this and the preceding century in works of differing purpose, or the sermons inserted into the *Libraries of the Fathers* and collections of sermons, or the letters copied anew from earlier editions in collections of councils. Looking back over these works, we must admit that, from the first edition of the *Sermons*, Leo’s Works received substantial additions on various occasions; but as far as the correction and explanation of the text are concerned, the efforts and ingenuity of learned men were, as we have seen, greatly wanting—not indeed through the fault of all of them. But what had been awaited in vain for two entire centuries—when at times ingenuity lacked the resources with which an editor of Leo necessarily had to be equipped, and at other times the resources lacked ingenuity—was suddenly accomplished by one man, without any grand announcement: PASCHASIUS QUESNELLUS, with whom the entire history of Leo’s editions takes on a new beginning.

For with his remarkable abundance of manuscript codices, especially Gallican ones, which—with a few exceptions—no one before him had used, Quesnellus corrected both the *Sermons* and the *Letters* in countless places; enlarged them with new material; arranged and organized them according to a new method; and so enriched them with an abundant apparatus of variant readings, notes, extensive observations, learned dissertations, and treatments of various matters sometimes only indirectly connected with Leo’s actions, that an author who had previously been treated so meagerly now became the instigator and cause of a new scholarship and of many, indeed then most serious, questions and controversies.

The Quesnellian edition appeared at Paris in 1675, in quarto, in two splendid volumes. Yet it aroused the severe censure of the Roman pontiff no less quickly than the admiration and acclaim of everyone. For since the new editor had discussed rather freely certain matters both of faith and of the discipline of the ancient Church, and had especially dared to show that the authority of the Roman pontiff had been assumed in many matters and to demonstrate this through the testimony and agreement both of Leo’s views and of other writers, he could not escape the vengeance of the Holy Inquisition, but was struck with an anathema in a decree issued on 29 April 1676. All the sons of the Catholic Church were also forbidden, under the same penalty of anathema, to imbibe new, foreign, and poisonous doctrines [Note: [Col. 0067D] These are the words of Cacciarius, from the preface to volume I, p. 3, where he says that the Apostolic See, guided by the divine Spirit and taking precautions for the piety and salvation of its children, enacted this sanction. But if he was correct in making that determination, then the censure of the theological faculty of Paris (14 June 1670) could not have proceeded from anything but an evil spirit. Those theologians declare that they found nothing in this edition contrary to revealed dogmas, opposed to Christian morals, or alien to the discipline of the universal Church; on the contrary, they approved the editor’s courage, by which, when occasion arose, he had vigorously defended the splendor of the Gallican Church, the innocence of the Gallican bishops, and the true liberties of the Gallican Church.]; the reading of Leo’s Works, corrupted by Quesnellus, was forbidden under the same penalty of anathema, and all his annotations and disputations concerning Leo were entered into the Index of Prohibited Books [Note: [Col. 0068D] Of the year 1682, p. 277.].

But since it was clearly understood in the Roman Curia that all human nature is inclined toward what is forbidden, and they readily perceived that by this barricade they could not keep the contagion of such pernicious opinions from everyone’s minds or protect them against it, they desired a remedy for those already infected—one that would immediately blunt and completely extinguish the power of the poison swallowed either unwittingly or through depraved appetite: an anti-Quesnellian edition.

Nor was this concern unfounded. The new edition found so many readers and admirers that it could be committed to the press again in the final year of that century; this was done at Lyons in the largest format. Quesnellus showed so little repentance, however, that he removed or retracted nothing in the Lyons edition of all that he had learned had so greatly displeased the Roman See.

The desire for this new Leonine edition, by contrast, was satisfied only slowly. There were indeed learned men who allowed this burden to be imposed upon them or voluntarily undertook it; and there was certainly enough to add weight to the undertaking and attract those eager for honor: the correction—or even the candor—desired by some learned men in Quesnellus’s emendations, and, on the other hand, the display of Roman codices and quasi-archetypes from which Leo seemed capable of emerging in purer form. But whether because others had measured the task inadequately against their own powers, or because they were overwhelmed by the difficulties of the work and abandoned it, or because of some other impediment, the most certain hopes repeatedly vanished.

Meanwhile, through the private enterprise of several Venetian booksellers, the Works of Leo were reprinted according to the Quesnellian edition—by Augustinus Savioli in 1741 and by Andrea Poletti in 1748—with more or less material added from Quesnellus’s notes and dissertations; they sold quickly. After them, Peter Thomas Cacciarius, a Carmelite and lecturer in polemical theology at the Roman College of the Propaganda Fide, brought forth at Rome a new edition, chiefly based on Roman manuscript codices and opposed to Quesnellus, in three folio volumes: the first containing *Exercises on Leo*, the other two the Works themselves. These appeared in 1751, 1753, and 1755.

But although he possessed as much abundance of manuscripts as could have been desired, he could not accomplish what he had proposed—and, indeed, promised with excessive confidence—through mere will or reliance upon powers that he had not sufficiently tested. Thus it happened that, when at almost the same time the outstanding work of the BALLERINI brothers appeared at Venice in 1753, 1756, and 1757, all his labor began to be obscured and punished with oblivion. Even in what he had recently produced from Vatican and Regensburg manuscripts he could not win the favor of scholars, since all the same material, and considerably more, was also found among the Ballerini brothers.

For through their abundance and knowledge of the best manuscript codices, their critical practice, their precise learning and its convenient arrangement, and the method of the whole undertaking, the Ballerini brothers produced such an edition of Leo’s Works as no Latin ecclesiastical writer had enjoyed after Coustant’s *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*—not to mention that the wishes of the Roman Curia were fully satisfied, and that Benedict XIV had no reason to regret his commission, by which he sought men of such quality for this task, men in whom one might hesitate whether learning and skill, or devotion and zeal toward the Roman See, were greater. Nevertheless, those who are differently disposed will rightly disagree with them on quite a few points.

Thus the entire sequence of the fortunes of Leo’s writings, from the time they began to be committed to the press, consists of two transformations: one beginning with Quesnellus, the other proceeding from the Ballerini brothers. The latter surpasses the former by a very long way in everything relating to the treatment of the author, provided that one does not forget [Col. 0069C] that Quesnellus, by his own example, preceded the Ballerini brothers—and everyone who came after him to revise editions of ecclesiastical writings—with an example of surpassing distinction.

The annals of Leo’s individual editions follow.

## FIFTEENTH CENTURY

### 1470

At Rome, by Conrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz, folio. *Sermons and Letters of Saint Leo the Pope*, from the recension and with the preface of John Andrew to Paul II. At the end: “You behold the illustrious …,” etc. M. CCCC. LXX.

This volume contains ninety-two sermons and five letters. The first of these, to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, is inserted among the sermons after the sixteenth; the remaining four—namely, first, to Maximus, bishop of Antioch; second, to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople; third and fourth, to Leo Augustus—are added after the sermons have been completed, together with the same author’s treatise against the heresy of Eutyches, which he delivered at Rome in the basilica of Saint Anastasia and which immediately follows the sermons. The work concludes with the Nicene Creed and testimonies excerpted from the books of Catholic Fathers, collected by Pope Leo and addressed to the emperor Leo, concerning the fact that our Lord Jesus Christ is true God and true man. All this material appended to the sermons, including the treatise against Eutyches, occupies fourteen leaves. At the beginning are three leaves containing John of Aléria’s preface to Paul II and the rubrics of the entire work in order.

Audiffredus gave roughly this account of Leo’s first edition in the book so often cited by us, p. 47. We have found that the description agrees for the most part with the appearance of another edition copied from this one, which we shall mention immediately. Before Audiffredus, however, P. Xavier Laire had already mentioned it in his *Historical Specimen of Roman Typography*, etc., p. 153; Laire was severely censured by him, according to his usual practice and the purpose of his book, for a few comparatively minor [Greek: παροράματα]—errors or oversights. It is listed in the catalogues of the Smith Library, p. 265; of the Duke de La Vallière, vol. I, p. 178; of Nicolas Rossi, p. 47; and of Crevenna’s most recent catalogue, octavo, vol. I, p. [Col. 0070B] 112. Audiffredus examined several copies in Italy, so that it is remarkable that Cardinal Quirini failed to notice it, since in his appendix to the *Life of Paul II*, on the best Roman editions, while arranging for John of Aléria’s preface to be reprinted from the Florentine edition, he called Maettairus’s testimony concerning this edition into doubt.

The situation is different with the Cologne edition of 1470, folio, which the same Maettarius, vol. I, part I, p. 298, cites, adding the testimony of Saubert’s *Catalogue of the Nuremberg Library*, p. 118. I know of no bibliographer who has ever seen it.

### Without year, place, or printer — Rome, by Ulrich Han

Folio. *The Sermons of Blessed Leo*, etc., with a description entirely similar to the preceding one. The type reveals Ulrich Han and is exactly like that which he used in printing Quintilian. We have found P. Laire’s assertion true by comparing the two copies. In both books the pages contain thirty-five lines; but they differ in this respect: in Leo, the titles of the sermons are for the most part [Note: [Col. 0069] Audiffredus counted those that were lacking, evidently in order to accuse Laire of negligence, since Laire had said generally that the titles were printed in larger type.] printed in uncial letters, whereas in Quintilian they are entirely absent.

If, therefore, this type is correctly attributed to Ulrich Han, it is highly probable that it was produced either in the same year or immediately at the beginning of the following year, since we know that these Roman printers were so closely associated that whenever one produced something new, the other immediately put the same thing to press. Besides Laire, Audiffredus, and Quirini, all of whom examined this edition with their own eyes, it is also cited by the *Catalogue of the Bunau Library*, p. 162; the Duke de La Vallière, p. 179; Nicolas Rossi, p. 47; and Pinelli, vol. I, p. 103.

Our copy had already been made known by Hamberger in *Reliable News*, vol. III, p. 203, though he considered it the first edition, as Morellus recently did in the Pinelli Catalogue. I do not know on what grounds.

### (1475)

Without place or printer, folio. *The Sermons of Saint Leo*. At the beginning: “Here happily begins the Book of the Sermons of Saint Leo the First, pope, most splendid and most eloquent teacher”; then, on the same line: “The first sermon, on his ordination as pope”; at the end: “Here end the sermons of Pope Leo.”

[Col. 0071A] The volume consists of 124 leaves, printed in a shorter and heavier Gothic type, but clear, in two columns, with 38 lines to a page. The paper is thick, quite white, though somewhat coarse; the margins and the spaces between the columns are broad. The punctuation consists of the colon and the full stop. Initial letters, folio numbers, catchwords, and signatures are absent. The titles of the sermons, however, are all printed in the same type.

The text is preceded by three leaves containing John of Aleria’s preface and the rubrics of the sermons; but the rubrics extend only to line 13 of the first page of the third leaf, across both columns. Although, because of the praised preface of the bishop of Aleria, this type might seem to reproduce exactly the Roman edition, in fact it does not, since together with the treatise against the heresy of Eutyches, which is last, it numbers 95 sermons and is entirely without the letters that appeared earlier, as well as those that had been added to the letters as an appendix, the Nicene Creed, and the testimonies collected by Leo from the writings of the Fathers.

It would therefore be desirable for someone interested in such matters to examine it more carefully, to determine whether it perhaps differs from the Roman editions even in individual readings. But I already hear readers asking me where, finally, I obtained the year given above, if this volume of Leo’s sermons lacks a fuller colophon. It is, of course, that edition mentioned in the Maettarian catalogues, vol. I, part I, p. 351, of which, apart from that reference, no bibliographer has remembered it. For this reason we have thought that a concise and reliable account of it should no longer be withheld from readers.

The Homilies of Gregory the Great and of Origen were printed at the same time, in one and the same type and format, as Leo’s Sermons, in such a way that each author’s work could conveniently be separated from the other’s; nevertheless, the latter two works were included under one and the same colophon at the end of Origen’s Homilies [Note: [Col. 0071D] It reads: “Here end the homilies of blessed Pope Gregory and of the presbyter Origen.” The year is added, but not the place. A fuller description will be found among the Gregorian editions [Col. 0072D] in the following volume.]. As a result, they have often been separated from one another, and it is now very rare to find them together. Thus the Homilies of Gregory and Origen, with Leo removed, appear in the Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de la Vallière, vol. I, p. 180, no. 499; and one might say that Vallarsi handled the same edition—unless perhaps only Origen’s Homilies—when, in his *Hieronymian Subsidia*, he praises a Basel edition of several homilies of Origen dated 1475, which I admitted above that I did not know [Note: [Col. 0072D] See vol. I, p. 475.].

I nevertheless judge it to be different from this one. Certainly, if it was the very edition that he perhaps, led by conjecture, called Basel, he does not have me as an adherent. For, unless everything deceives me, this volume was printed in Italy. But lest anyone think that our argument produces the opposite of what we intend, and suppose that we could be compelled to assign this edition of Leo to any other date, without a note of place or year, merely because it has been dated 1475 on the ground that it was bound together with a similar work printed in that year, we shall reply, first, that—leaving aside entirely the question of assigning a year—we wished to ensure that it could be identified with the greatest possible certainty by everyone. I thought this would be achieved if I did not voluntarily increase the number of editions issued without a year and did not point more emphatically to the Maettarian edition, otherwise unknown [Note: [Col. 0072D] See Denis, *Garellian Library*, p. 195.]. Moreover, I do not think that I have been greatly mistaken, since those three little works are connected with one another by similarity of subject and are very similar in the execution of their printing; nor is it far removed from the practice of the early printers to mark only the last year and place of printing among several works that they had printed together.

**1482.** Venice, by Lucas the Venetian, son of Dominic. 7 August, in folio. *The Sermons and Letters of Pope Saint Leo*, with a preface by John of Aleria. Maittaire, vol. I, [Col. 0072B] part II, p. 429. It occurs in the *Catalogue of the Library of the Duke de la Vallière*, vol. I, p. 180, no. 495.

**1482.** Speyer, by Peter Drach, in folio. Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, commonly called that of Charlemagne. There are 21 sermons. We discussed this extremely rare edition above on the occasion of Augustine’s Sermons. Compare Ballerini’s preface to Leo’s Sermons, § 6, no. 26. They did not use this edition perfunctorily, but carefully compared it with the Basel edition of Nicholas Kessler, 1496, in order to ascertain the genuine readings of Paul the Deacon.

**1485.** Venice, by Andrew of Parma, in small folio. *The Homilies of the Divine Leo* (Sermons and Letters). Maittaire, vol. I, part II, p. 470. It was in the Crevenna Library. See the *Newest Catalogue* (in octavo), vol. I, p. 112, no. 498.

[Col. 0072C] **1493.** Basel, by Nicholas Kessler, in folio. Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, printed according to the most ancient arrangement of the library of the Church of Basel. Compare the Augustinian material.

**1494.** Nuremberg, by Anthony Koburger, in quarto. Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the same collection.

**1496.** Basel, by Nicholas Kessler, in folio. Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the second edition of the *Homiliary of the Doctors*.

**1498.** Basel . . . in folio. Leo’s Sermons, in the same collection, which Maittaire praises, vol. I, part II, p. 675.

**Without year or place, in folio (two, or perhaps even three, of this kind).** *The Sermons of Pope Saint Leo I.*

It begins with Aleria’s preface, which is entitled, just as in the edition of 1475: “John Andrew, bishop of Aleria, to the supreme pontiff Paul II, the Venetian, in praise of that holy Pope Leo.” It is printed on the verso of the first leaf and ends at line 28; immediately afterward come the rubrics, which end at line 35 of the first page of the third leaf, whose verso is left blank. The text begins with the same heading as the 1475 edition. At the end likewise: “Here end the Sermons of Pope Leo.”

The little work consists of 152 leaves, printed in large Gothic type on clean white paper, with 34 lines on a full page. Signatures, numbers, catchwords, and initials are absent. The only punctuation used is the full stop. P. Placidus Braun gives me almost this description of the edition, unknown to me, in *Historical and Literary Notes*, I, p. 56, and remarks that it had already been recorded by Baverus in *Universal Library*, vol. II, p. 275.

It appears, however, to be quite different from the one I described under the year 1475, although from the titles one might conclude that one had been copied from the other, and therefore that they contain points in which they differ from the Roman archetypes. I could wish that the very diligent scholar had thought fit to state its contents explicitly.

For some time I wondered why Braun and other bibliographers, when estimating the date of anonymous editions, followed almost a single standard, the year 1475. Braun has now added that another edition, without the printer’s name or place, was issued in 1475. But do not suppose that he recognized the one described above by us. Another cause lies behind this: Debure’s assertion that a Roman edition without a year, by Ulrich Gallus, was printed in 1475. Hence that year became widely accepted. P. Xavier Laire, however, criticized this error of Debure in *Specimen*, p. 153.

**Without year, place, or printer, in folio (third, or, if preferred, fourth).** *The Sermons of Pope Saint Leo.* It begins: “Here begins the book of the Sermons of blessed Pope Leo, and the first sermon on his ordination follows.” At the end: “Jesus Christ, Mary.” It contains 94 sermons, of which the penultimate is the treatise against the heresy of Eutyches, while the last, the sermon on Absalom, is spurious.

This is the third—or, if one prefers, the fourth—of Leo’s editions that bears neither place nor year, and by far the rarest of all the ancient editions. Our knowledge of it is due to Denis the Younger in the illustrious *Memorabilia of the Garellian Library*, p. 194; no one apart from him has so far discussed a copy of it.

He reports that the leaves of this volume, numbered by himself, amount to 133, with 37 lines per page; that the letters are Gothic, but of an entirely new kind—large, wavering, and rough, appearing almost to have been carved with a chisel. He says that rounded letters *a*, *st*, and *ct* are often visible in the middle of words, and that the uncial forms C, O, S, and T also frequently resemble the Roman form. Abbreviations of letters are rare. The punctuation consists of the full stop and colon. Catchwords, signatures, numbers, and initials are absent. Each sermon has its own title; at the end of each is added the word “Amen,” with the letters widely spaced.

The Garellian copy had the year 1461 written on it in purple ink, but Denis suspects that this was done fraudulently. Forced to offer a conjecture of his own, he states that either Anthony Sorg of Augsburg or Conrad Finer of Esslingen seems to him to have been the printer. It is clear from the contents, however, that this edition was copied not from the Roman editions, nor from their Venetian repetitions, but from one of the others listed above, with some material omitted and other material added.

**Without year, Cologne, by Conrad of Homborch, in folio.** Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, in the edition described above among the Augustinian editions.

## THE SIXTEENTH CENTURY

[Col. 0074A]

**1505.** Venice, in the printing house of Bartholomew de Zanis de Portesio, highly skilled in the book trade, at the expense of the heirs of the nobleman Quintus Octavianus Scotus, in folio. *The Sermons of Saint Leo.* According to the Parma edition. Quesnellus mentions it in his General Preface.

**1511.** Paris, by John Badius Ascensius, in quarto. *The Catholic Letters of Pope Saint Leo, full of holy learning.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris; also the catalogues of Bunaventure and the Bodleian Library. A little book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* is inserted, wrongly attributed to Leo, as to many other Fathers.

**1515.** Paris, in quarto. *The Sermons of Leo, supreme pontiff, most diligently and recently corrected and happily printed to the utmost extent permitted by the art.* They are sold in Paris (so printed), in the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the Golden Lily, by John Parvus (Jean Petit).

The copy from which they were described was the Roman edition. It therefore contains the five letters, all in the same order, together with the appendices. At the end, after the rest of the work had been completely finished, following a blank page of the last leaf—that is, the 108th—so that it could be separated, a little book of Pope Leo *On the Conflict of Vices* was added.

Immediately below the title, which appears at the top of the page, is this note: “The little work that follows is also attributed to Leo. We have therefore added it, since that seemed useful. Whatever it may be, therefore, dearest and most good-natured reader, examine it as you see fit.” It occupies eight leaves, which are not numbered. At the end is this clause: “Here ends the splendid and distinguished treatise of Pope Leo on the conflict of vices and virtues, together with his sermons. Printed at Paris, at the Golden Sun in the Rue Saint-Jacques, by Master Berthold Rembolt, in the year of the Lord 1515, on 2 March.” The type is small Gothic; the words are shortened by frequent abbreviations; the more notable passages of Leo are marked in the margin by lemma, and biblical numbers are added.

**1516.** Lyons, by John Clein, in folio. Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, under Augustine.

**1524.** Paris . . . in folio. The Letters of Pope Leo, in the collection of councils, both general and provincial, and of pontifical decrees, by Jacobus Merlinus.

Quesnellus is witness to this: he writes that it contains ninety-four letters of Leo, defective in many places, but in turn much more accurately corrected in some passages than in much more recent editions.

**1525.** Lyons, by John Crespin, in folio. Several of Leo’s Sermons, among the Homilies of the ecclesiastical doctors, etc.

**1525.** Mainz, at the establishment of John Schaeffer, in folio. . . . Forty-nine decrees of Pope Leo, in the first edition of the Collection of Councils and Canons of Dionysius Exiguus, whom we have often cited above.

**1530.** Cologne, from the office of Peter Quentel, in folio. The Letters of Pope Leo, in the repeated edition of the same Merlin collection of general councils, etc. In vol. II, from folio 188 to 228, ninety-seven letters are numbered.

**1530.** Cologne, from the office of Eucharius Cervicornus, in folio. [Col. 0075A] Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the *Homilies of the Most Distinguished Doctors of the Church*.

**1535.** Paris, at the establishment of Francis Regnault, in octavo. The Letters of Pope Leo, in the same councils, reprinted in the same year and place, from folio 202 to 447.

**1536.** Basel, in folio. Fifty letters of Pope Leo, together with other letters of the Roman pontiffs, added to the *Recognitions of Clement of Rome*, edited by John Sichard, from p. 306 to the end (that is, p. 374).

To the first edition of Clement’s *Recognitions*, which appeared in Basel in 1526 at the establishment of John Bebelius, in folio, Sichard had already added several letters of Roman pontiffs, most of them spurious. This edition brought a much fuller addition, including a considerable portion of Leo as well. The Ballerini brothers consulted it carefully.

**1538.** Cologne, at the establishment of Peter Quentel, in folio. *The Letters and Decrees of Pope Leo I*, in the *Collection of All Councils* by Peter Crabbe of Mechelen, vol. I, folios 343–392.

The editor promises a more proper and suitable arrangement of Leo’s letters. “For whereas,” he says, “they were previously written in confusion, they have now been arranged according to the proper order of the consulates, where these can be known, and of the months; when these are lacking, the order of the remaining letters that seemed more suitable is retained.” A table of contents is prefixed to each letter. Biblical passages are marked in the margin, and variant readings have been added here and there.

**1546–47.** Cologne, in octavo, two volumes. *The Decretal and Familiar Letters of the Lord Leo, etc., Pope; and his Sermons and Homilies*, edited by Peter Canisius of Nijmegen. Quesnellus writes that Canisius professed to have been assisted by very ancient and carefully corrected copies. See the reissue of this edition in 1566. Quesnellus criticizes him for adding the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* as though it were Leo’s.

**1551.** Cologne, at the establishment of Peter Quentel, in folio. The Letters and Decrees of Pope Leo I, in a reissued edition of Peter Crabbe’s Councils.

**1551.** In the same place, in folio. *The Sermons of Saint Leo.* John Ciampinus praises this edition—indeed, he writes that he handled it—in a letter to Erasmus Gattola of Gaeta. Yet even this declaration does not remove all our doubts, since in other editions that he also appears to claim to have examined, we have clearly caught him in error: he praises the editions of Louvain, 1566, and Antwerp, 1583, as though they had been printed in quarto. Nor did he greatly commend his learning to us, since, although he was himself a Roman and lived in Rome, he could call the Cologne edition of this year the oldest edition of the sermons.

**1553.** Venice, in folio. *The Sermons of Saint Leo*, according to the same Ciampinus. Let us therefore leave it uncertain whether they were published separately or in some collection.

**1555.** Basel, by Henry Petri, in folio. Pope Leo I’s Letter to Flavian against Eutyches, in John Herold’s *Orthodoxographia*, no. 37.

[Col. 0076A] **1561. (Cologne.)** *The Works of Saint Leo*, edited by Laurentius Surius.

“Laurentius Surius, a Carthusian, professes to have devoted much time and effort in the 1561 edition to correcting Leo’s works, although, as he says, they had been published several years earlier after being corrected through the efforts of learned men. He nevertheless admits that he did not restore the whole of Leo to such integrity that nothing remained worthy of correction; nor is this surprising, he says, since Leo himself admits that, even while he was still alive, that letter of his to Flavian had been corrupted.” This is Quesnellus’s account, though he gives no indication of the place where this edition was printed, which nevertheless can scarcely be anywhere other than Cologne. I myself doubt whether an edition of this year exists at all. Harzheim, certainly, in his *Cologne Library* (Cologne, 1747, in folio), p. 220, knows of none except that of 1568.

**1566.** Louvain, at the establishment of Jerome Wellaeus, under the sign of the Diamond, in octavo, two volumes. Volume I is entitled: *The Sermons and Homilies of the Lord Leo, Pope of this name the First, who long ago rightly possesses the surname “the Great,” all that are extant. Now corrected and enlarged for the second time with the greatest care according to all the most ancient copies. With a twofold index.* The second volume bears the title: *The Decretal and Familiar Letters of the Lord Leo, Pope, all that could so far be found. Corrected for the second time with the greatest care according to the most ancient copies.*

[Col. 0076C] The title does not indicate which volume is first and which second. In the copy supplied to us by the Royal Library, they were bound in the reverse order from that in which we have presented them. But it seemed preferable to place first the volume to which the editor’s preface and Leo’s life are added (from the first edition of 1546–47), and which, if one considers the time when the Sermons or Letters were first published, properly claims the first place—the place it thereafter always held in all subsequent editions.

Canisius’s preface is addressed to John of Lippia, bishop of Cyrene, auxiliary bishop and principal ecclesiastic of Cologne. He attacks the madness of the age and its cause, the monstrous fury of self-love, from which arise perverse studies producing new books, an ambitious display of learning, and a certain headstrong presumption of wisdom; likewise an unrestrained desire to devise new doctrines, by which people begin both to disdain ancient things and to let the old documents become obsolete, as though these tendencies sprang from a fountain. “Through these stages, or rather steps,” he says, “of all impiety, it has now reached . . .” He predicts that Leo will not enjoy a more favorable reception among such despisers of laws and ancestral institutions worthy of all reverence; yet he hopes that, provided they are willing to read, they will all be compelled to admire the man’s spirit and to embrace the doctrines that they have rejected with reckless presumption.

The order of the Letters has been reproduced, as seemed appropriate to us, from Peter Crabbe’s edition. In both parts, following the practice of the earlier editions, biblical texts and certain variants have been added in the margins.

**1567.** Cologne, from the office of John Quentel, in folio. The Letters and Decretals of Pope Leo I, in Surian’s Collection of Councils.

**1568.** Paris, at the establishment of Michael Sonnius, in folio. The Letters of Pope Leo, together with the Works of Clement of Rome, edited by John Sichard.

Quesnellus used this edition and made the following observation about it in his General Preface:

“John Sichard collected the works of Clement of Rome, to which he added the pseudo-letters of the ancient pontiffs. After several editions had been issued in Germany, these too appeared in Paris in 1568, with an addition of several pontifical letters, especially those of our Leo, which the anonymous editor responsible for this edition testifies to have been restored according to the authority of ancient Victorine copies.”

I would judge that these words of his should not be understood as meaning that this Paris edition alone was enriched with those letters, but that what he says about the addition should be extended also to the German editions. The extent to which this is true was explained above under the year 1536. Indeed, perhaps this edition cannot even claim to have been the first to benefit from corrections based on Victorine manuscripts. An earlier Paris edition appeared at the establishment of the widow of Charles Guillard in 1544, in folio; I do not know whether it was the source of this one. Certainly its title declares that Clement’s Letters were corrected from Victorine manuscripts; we shall give it in the third volume among the Additions to Rufinus (at vol. I, p. 635).

[Col. 0077C] **1569.** Cologne, by Martin Cholimnus, in folio. Several of Leo’s Sermons (21), in the *Homiliary of Catholic Doctors*, enlarged with selected homilies and edited by Laurentius Surius. John Ciampinus praises Leo’s Sermons as published in this year, place, and format, without mentioning the collection in which they were inserted. One might therefore think that he intended to indicate a complete edition published separately, especially since he asserts that he not only held it in his hands but read it with careful attention. But this, like the other promises of that man, is empty, since, occupied with the care of a single word, he attends to everything else only in a desultory fashion.

**1569.** Basel, by Henry Petri, in folio. Pope Leo I’s Letter to Flavian against Eutyches, in Jacobus Grynaeus’s *Orthodox Monuments*, p. 41.

[Col. 0077D] **1572.** Zurich, in folio. Two letters of Leo, bishop of Rome: one to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, against Eutyches; the other to the emperor Leo Augustus against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches; in *The Ancient Latin Writings on the One Person and Two Natures of the Lord*, etc., edited by Joshua Simler, p. 74.

**1573.** Venice, in folio. *The Sermons of Saint Leo.* Ciampinus is the authority, but he does not say whether they appeared separately or in some collection.

**1575–77.** Louvain, at the establishment of Jerome Wellaeus under the sign of the Diamond, printed by John Masius, in octavo, two volumes. *The Decretal and Familiar Letters of the Lord Leo, Pope of this name the First (Sermons and Homilies), now more carefully purged of various errors and blemishes, by the Augustinian canons regular of Saint Martin of the town and the University of Louvain.*

The Letters appeared in 1575, the Sermons in 1577. Only the former volume is at hand, externally very similar to Peter Canisius’s edition. The preface is absent. Whether it was added to the other volume, I do not know. It is certainly entirely missing from the second edition. Nevertheless, John Ulimmerius, prior of Saint Martin’s, dedicated it to Arnold Ganthois, abbot of the monastery of Marcen, in a letter dated Louvain, 1 August 1575, praising “the manuscript book of Letters by John Wamesius, doctor of both laws and professor of pontifical law at the University of Louvain.”

**1578.** Basel, from the office of Henry Petri, in octavo. *The Greek-Latin Letter of Leo the Great to Flavian, pillar of the true faith; together with the Embassy of the emperor Manuel Comnenus to the Armenians*, edited by Leunclavius, pp. 169–227.

**1583.** Antwerp, at the establishment of Philip Nutius, in octavo, two volumes. *The Works of the Lord Leo the Great*, by the canons regular of Saint Martin, etc., corrected from manuscript copies, with new indexes.

This is the title of the first volume, that is, of the Sermons; the Letters are entitled as in the first edition. The paper and type, however, are clearer than in that edition.

**1585.** Venice, at the establishment of Dominic Nicolinus, in folio. Leo’s Decretal Letters, in the *Collection of All Councils* by certain Catholic theologians, chiefly Dominic Polanus of Venice, of the Order of Preachers.

[Col. 0078C] **1588.** Lyons, from the office of the Junta family, in folio. Several of Leo’s Sermons, in the *Library of Ancient Fathers’ Homilies and Sermons* by Laurentius Cumdius, edited and completed by George Mosanus.

**1591.** Rome, from the Roman Printing House, printed by George Ferrarius, in folio. The Decretal Letters of Saint Leo I, in the *Collection of the Decretal Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*, prepared by Cardinal Antonio Carafa and published by Antonio de Aquino.

I greatly regret that we lack access to a copy of this splendid work, completed from the oldest manuscripts of the Vatican Library and many others. But see below what is said in reference to Cocquelin’s *Collection of Bulls*.

**1569.** Rome, from the press of the Congregation of the Oratory, in folio. Several previously unpublished letters of Leo, in Baronius’s *Annals*, vol. VI. Namely:

1. To the bishops established throughout the Gallic province of Arles, in the subsequent edition, no. 106, under the year 449, no. 16, from an ancient manuscript of the Church of Arles.

2. To Ravennius, bishop of Arles, under the year 449, no. 62, from the same manuscript, no. 207.

3. The letter of the bishops of the province of the metropolitan see of Arles, under the year 450, no. 52, from the same source, no. 108.

4. Leo’s letter to the bishops of the province of the metropolitan see of Arles, under the year 450, no. 57, no. 109.

5. To Ravennius, archbishop of Arles, no. 210, both letters likewise from the same manuscript.

## THE SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

**1604.** Mainz, at the establishment of Balthasar Lippius, at the expense of Anthony Heirat, in quarto. *Several Letters of Pope Saint Leo and certain other works*, collected and first published as an appendix to the works of Gregory of Neocaesarea, by the learned Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren.

From p. 144 to p. 238 are included the following:

1. The Letter to Flavian, Greek and Latin, with an argument and appended notes by Vossius.

2. The Letter to Leo the emperor Augustus, Greek and Latin, with an argument and notes.

3. Testimonies of the Holy Fathers, etc., not only in Latin, as they had previously been published, but also in Greek, as the editor testifies that he found them in ancient manuscripts.

4. The Letter of Peter, bishop of Ravenna, to the presbyter Eutyches against his errors, in support of Leo, Greek and Latin, from the Vatican manuscripts and those of Cardinal Sirletus.

5. A treatise of Saint Leo against the errors of Eutyches and other heretics, beginning “For instructing the sons of the Church, etc.” (from Vatican manuscript no. 2346), which the editor more fully attributes to Leo in the appended notes on the basis of the similarity of style and sentences.

6. The Edict of Saint Leo to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.

7. The Letter to Julian, bishop of Coena. He transcribed both of these previously unpublished works from a manuscript of Cardinal Sirletus and attempts to demonstrate from their diction and historical testimony that they truly belong to Leo.

But he denied to Leo the following works that were also added:

8. *On the Martyrs*.

9. *On Absalom, when he was pursuing his father David*.

These had been sold as Leo’s in ancient as well as in previously printed copies. Vossius illustrated all these matters with notes.

**1606.** Cologne, at the establishments of John Gymnicus and Anthony Hierat, in folio. *The Letters and Decrees of Pope Leo I*, preceded by his Life, in Severinus Binius’s *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, pp. 935–1009. It contains 110 letters, including those recently published by Baronius and Vossius.

**1614.** Hamburg, from the press of Paul Langius, in octavo. *The Greek-Latin Letter of Leo the Great to Flavian*, taken from an anonymous Greek manuscript, rescued from the sack of the Byzantine city; published first in Greek and separately in Latin in Leo’s own words, with a preface by M. Nicholas Glaser. After the preface is added, from the same manuscript, Gregory Thaumaturgus’s *Doctrine of the Holy Trinity*.

The editor, then rector of the school at Verden, had obtained from the library of Philip Sigismund, Duke of Brunswick and Lüneburg and bishop of Osnabrück and Verden, a manuscript in which the Greek version of this letter was presented together with certain other works. It had, as he writes, been rescued from the fire of Byzantium, carried by a certain Hebrew to Egypt, thence to the island of Malta, and from there transported to Germany by a Rhodian knight; finally it was added to the episcopal library by Henry Schradaeus, doctor of law and burgomaster of Osnabrück. But when he thought he was about to bring it to light, and the printing work was already nearly complete, he learned at last that Leunclavius had taken this honor from him. He therefore contented himself with adding at the end several variant readings excerpted from Leunclavius’s edition.

**1614.** Paris, at the establishment of Claudius Morellus, in folio. *The Complete Works that Could Be Found of the Holy Fathers Leo the Great, Roman pontiff of this name the First; Maximus, bishop of Turin; and Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna.* See the reissue of this edition immediately below.

**1618.** Paris, at the expense of Sebastian Cramoisy, in folio. *The Complete Works of the Holy Fathers Leo the Great, etc. A new, enlarged, and revised edition.* So runs the title; in fact, this edition is no more revised than the first, but both are copied word for word from the Louvain edition. Nor did the booksellers hesitate—since this alone was their concern—to reprint Ulimmerius’s letter at the front of the work.

It is surprising that Quesnellus could write that he did not know of a complete edition of Leo’s works published before 1614, although he was well acquainted with Ulimmerius’s undertaking. They could have been called more complete, if what he writes is true, because they were enlarged by three sermons from the old manuscript of Nicholas Fabri, then preserved in the Thuanus Library; but, because of the lack of an index, we were unable to compare it with the preceding editions. It contains 110 letters and the treatise against the errors of Eutyches edited by Vossius.

**1618.** Carouge near Geneva, at the expense of Anthony Hierat, in folio. Leo’s Letters and Decrees (110), in the reissued Binius edition of the Councils.

**1618.** In the same place, by the same printer, in folio. *Sermons of Leo the Great, pontiff, on the principal solemnities of the Lord and the saints; Decretal and Familiar Letters*, from the Louvain edition, in the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. V, part II.

**1622.** Cologne, at the expense of Anthony Hierat, in folio. *The Treatise of Pope Saint Leo I against the Errors of Eutyches and Other Heretics; his Edict on the Non-alienation of Church Property; and also his Letter on the Authority of the Nicene Council and on Not Seeking Several Churches*, from the edition of Gerard Vossius and with his notes, in the *Supplement to the Cologne Library of the Fathers*, p. 157.

**1623.** Lyons, at the expense of Claudius Landry, in folio. *The Complete Works That Could Be Found of the Holy Fathers Leo the Great, Pope of This Name the First; Maximus of Turin; Peter Chrysologus of Ravenna; Fulgentius of Ruspe; Valerian of Cemele; and Asterius of Amasea. An edition revised and enlarged beyond the others, with the notes of Gerard Vossius on Saint Leo, etc.*

The volume is quite conveniently printed; the bookseller dedicated it to Dionysius Simon de Marquemont, then archbishop of Lyons. An index of the Sermons is prefixed, but not one of the Letters. Leo shares an index of biblical passages with Maximus. Quesnellus is mistaken, however, when he describes this as a reissue of the 1618 edition. In respect of the text, all belong to the same family; but in respect of the bookseller’s undertaking they differ greatly.

**1633.** Lyons . . . in folio. *The Septad of the Most Distinguished Bishops in Christian Wisdom and Eloquence: Leo the Great, Maximus of Turin, etc.*, edited by Theophilus Raynaudus of the Society of Jesus.

The editor formed this septad of writings by inserting into the collection published there ten years earlier, at the same bookseller’s establishment, as I believe, Amedeus of Lausanne, who immediately precedes Asterius. It was therefore not modeled on the edition of 1618, as Quesnellus suggests.

**1638.** Paris, from the Morellian press, in folio. *The Life, Letters, and Decrees of Saint Leo*, in the Binius edition of the Councils, its final reissue.

**1642.** Paris, at the expense of Claudius Sonnius and D. Bechet, in folio. The Letter of Saint Leo to Theodoret, in Latin, at the end of Theodoret’s Works, vol. VI, p. 724.

**1644.** Paris, from the Royal Printing House, in folio. *The Life, Letters, and Decrees of Leo the Great*, in the Royal Collection of Councils, vol. VII, pp. 49–272, and in vol. VIII.

**1651.** Paris . . . in folio. *The Works of Leo.* Quesnellus praises it as a repetition of the 1618 edition; but, if it exists at all, the entire Raynaudian collection was doubtless reprinted in it.

**1661.** Paris, at the establishment of Simeon Piget, sworn bookseller in the Rue Jacob, under the sign of Prudence, in folio. *Leo the Great, Roman pontiff; Maximus of Turin; Peter Chrysologus of Ravenna; Fulgentius of Ruspe; Valerian of Cemele; Amedeus of Lausanne; and Asterius of Amasea: the septad of bishops most distinguished for Christian wisdom and eloquence.*

The theologian Theophilus Raynaudus of the Society of Jesus enlarged his earlier edition with various additions to Saint Leo and Fulgentius, and with eighty sermons of Fulgentius from a manuscript. He appended a refutation of the unfair criticism of the book *On Predestination and Grace*, attributed to Saint Fulgentius. He defended Valerian of Cemele in detail against the accuser of scant charity. He added the highly accomplished homilies of Amedeus on the Mother of God.

In this final edition, the third book of Fulgentius, *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*, previously mutilated, appears for the first time complete in all its chapters. The same is true of the Homilies of Asterius, to which twenty sermons by the same author, altogether exceptionally elegant, have been added.

I preferred to give the full title here, so that in what follows readers would not have to search for it piecemeal under each author.

**1662.** Paris, at the expense of Anthony Bertier, in folio. Leo’s Sermon for the Nativity of the Lord, in Combefis’s *Library of Sermons*, p. 241.

**1662.** Rome, from the press of Jacob Dragondelli, in octavo. Nine letters of Leo and of others to Leo, published from the Barberini manuscript among the Acts of the Roman Synod under Boniface II, in Luke Holstenius’s two-part *Roman Collection*, pp. 103–163.

The letters are as follows:

1. Valentinian and Marcian Augustus to Leo (in the Ballerini edition, no. 100).
2. Leo to Marcian (there, no. 104).
3. To Anatolius (there, no. 106).
4. To Marcian (there, no. 136).
5. Anatolius to Leo (there, no. 132).
6. Leo to Anatolius (no. 135).
7. To Anastasius (there, no. 6).
8. To the metropolitans of Illyricum (there, no. 5).
9. To the metropolitans of Achaia (there, no. 13).

Of these, six—namely the first, fourth, fifth, seventh, and ninth [the enumeration in the source is retained]—were previously unpublished and occur almost nowhere in other manuscripts, except for the first and fourth. Quesnellus found the fourth in the Grimani manuscript, while the Ballerini brothers found it in the manuscript of Regensburg. Arnold found the first, written in Greek, in a Bodleian codex, just as the Ballerini brothers found it in Vatican Greek manuscript 1455. Compare the Ballerini brothers’ observations on the collections of Leo’s Letters, excerpts from which we give below, at collection 16.

**1670.** Zwickau, printed and financed by Samuel Ebel, in octavo. *The Sermons of Saint Leo the Great, Roman pontiff, Leo I, on the solemnity of the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, sermons 2, 7, and 9, in *Homilies and Meditations for the Feast of the Nativity of Jesus Christ*, collected from various works of several holy Fathers and ancient Doctors of the Church who wrote in prose, and published separately by Christian Daumius, pp. 103–121.

### 1671

Paris, at the expense of Pierre Variquet, on Jacob Street, under the sign of the Gridiron, near the church of Saint Benedict, in folio. The works of Saint Leo the Great, etc., edited by Theophilus Raynaud. Added to this latest edition are the works of Prosper of Aquitaine, etc.

### 1675

Paris, at the expense of Jean-Baptiste Coignard, on Jacob Street, under the sign of the Golden Bibles, in quarto. Two volumes. The complete works of Saint Leo the Great, pope, now enlarged for the first time by thirty letters and three treatises on the grace of Christ, carefully arranged according to the exact sequence of the years, purged of spurious works, interpolations, and countless errors, and supplied with appendices, dissertations, notes, and observations. Added are the minor works, Life, and Apology of Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles. A double codex of the canons and constitutions of the Roman Church emerges from darkness.

The order of the contents is as follows. Leading the procession are the books which, as we saw above, were finally vindicated for Leo by Quesnel: the two books *On the Calling of All Nations*; the *Authorities on Grace and Free Choice*; and the *Booklet to the Virgin Demetrias*. These are followed by the Sermons, arranged under a single numerical sequence, though the previously customary method of numbering has not been omitted.

He admits, however, that nothing has been moved from its proper place except three items: the fourth, *On the Anniversary of His Assumption*; the sixth, *On Collections and Almsgiving*; and the ninth, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*. These had formerly been appended at the end of the others from the manuscript of Nicolas Fabri, but Quesnel has assigned them to their proper places, on pages 110, 121, and 140.

“I have added,” he says, “the single Sermon 96, *On the Chair of Saint Peter*, transcribed from the royal manuscript, to the others—and I regret having added it—because, although more than one consideration recommended this at that time, nevertheless, now that it has again been weighed by its style, both on its own and on another’s scales, we correct our earlier judgment and deny it to Leo.”

Indeed, in a later edition he revised this judgment as well and admitted that he stood by his first opinion.

The series of ninety-six Sermons is brought to an end by the prefaces from the Roman Pontifical, placed here because of their similarity of diction to the other works of Leo, and by an appendix of sermons which, in his view, bore Leo’s name falsely in the manuscript codices: namely, first, *On the Feast of Saint Vincent the Martyr*; second, *On the Nativity of the Lord*; third, *On the Ascension of the Lord*; fourth, *On the Nativity of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul*; and fifth, the *Treatise Against the Errors of Eutyches*. This appendix is printed in smaller type than the rest.

The other, as it were, part of the first volume consists of 141 Letters. He himself summarizes what he has done in six headings:

1. He rejected spurious and substituted letters.
2. He removed the stains of errors and interpolations from the genuine letters.
3. He changed the order and restored it to its authentic form.
4. He increased the number by adding more than thirty-three letters.
5. As with the Sermons, he prefixed to each letter its own synopsis.
6. He inserted in their proper places all the letters sent to Leo by others, which are often necessary for understanding his replies, so that they may easily be distinguished from Leo’s letters by their smaller type.

He acted conveniently, however, in not assigning numbers to them. Nearly all the more distinguished editors of the Fathers, and especially the Benedictines, have erred in this respect by presenting letters sent to their author by others continuously together with the number of the author’s own letters. This is often very troublesome for anyone consulting these volumes, especially when, in the prefixed indexes in which the orders of different editions are compared, one sees that this inconvenience has not been addressed.

He entirely rejected as spurious one previously edited letter, addressed to the bishops of Germany and Gaul concerning chorepiscopi. He also judged that the seventh letter to Septimius and the seventeenth to all the bishops of Sicily should be removed from the number of the others; nevertheless, he retained their place, lest he seem to prejudge the judgment of learned men.

Some fragments of letters have been added, along with the sole surviving letter of Julian, bishop of Cos. Finally, this volume closes with the Life of Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, written by Saint Honoratus, bishop of Marseille and Hilary’s disciple, added for the sake of the *Apology of Hilary*. This is followed by Hilary’s poem on Genesis and his Letter to Eucherius, bishop of Lyon.

In the preface—preceded by the dedicatory letter of John Cassian to Saint Leo, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, which served as the dedication of his books *On the Incarnation of Christ Against Nestorius*, and by certain testimonies concerning Leo—he speaks at length about earlier editions of Leo, and about his own work and the resources with which he undertook it.

To the preface he appended indexes: first, a general index of the contents of both volumes; second, a chronological index of the letters; third, an index comparing the earlier editions of the letters with the new one; and fourth, an alphabetical index of the letters. A very extensive subject index to Leo’s writings appears at the end.

The second volume is entitled: *Appendix to the Works of Saint Leo the Great, or the Code of the Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See. Dissertations, Various Readings, Notes, Observations, and Indexes. Volume II.*

The individual sections follow one another in the very order in which they are listed in the title, except that the various readings, notes, and observations are presented intermingled with one another. The Code of Canons will be discussed elsewhere.

There are sixteen dissertations. Five of the later ones concern the Code of Canons; the rest bear more directly on Leo, and we shall enumerate them.

The first discusses the life and deeds of Leo. The second concerns the books *On the Calling of All Nations*, which are vindicated as Leo’s. The third concerns the *Authorities on the Grace of God and Free Choice*, which are likewise to be attributed to him. The fourth argues that the booklet to Demetrias belongs to Leo himself, not to Prosper. The fifth is an apologetic work on behalf of Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles. The sixth discusses the Saturday fast in the Roman Church during the time of Saint Leo. The seventh sets out the case of Eutyches, archimandrite of Constantinople, appealing from the judgment of the Council of Constantinople under Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. The eighth concerns the case of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, appealing from the judgment of the false synod of Ephesus. The ninth concerns the case of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, deposed at that same false synod, and the ordination of Maximus in his place. The tenth treats the case of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, appealing from the judgment of the same false synod. The eleventh maintains that the Letter on the Privileges of Chorepiscopi, addressed in Leo’s name to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, was fabricated.

After the dissertations and notes, certain additions to both volumes follow, together with information about several letters of Saint Leo and other monuments that have perished.

The presentation of the entire work is exceedingly elegant. The paper is of the largest format, thick yet translucent, and the type is exceptionally clear. The convenience of readers has been considered everywhere, especially in the Letters, where a chronology has been placed at the top of each page and statements of greater importance—those commonly regarded as such by advocates of the papacy—have been marked throughout in the margins; among them one frequently finds various readings and biblical passages interspersed.

The dedication of the work is a singular example. It is consecrated to Leo the Great himself, and all the praises of Leo—collected from his life, deeds, and writings, as well as from the judgments of his contemporaries, of posterity, and of Quesnel himself—are reduced to the form of a stone inscription with truly rare acumen. It occupies the equivalent of four pages, with the sources of each item added in the margins.

Quesnel, clearly unable not to feel how great a cloud of odium and how many adversaries he would stir up against himself by his freedom of judgment and his audacity in attacking long-established errors, seems to have wished by this quasi-formula of faith to defend himself against the charge of having injured the pontifical dignity.

From what we have so far related about the contents and arrangement of this edition, it is easy to see, even without a guide, how far it leaves all earlier editions behind it, indeed how greatly it surpasses in intellectual and scholarly resources and in the expenditure of labor all editions of all the Fathers, Greek as well as Latin, that have appeared down to the present year.

We therefore do not think it necessary to produce an impressive array of witnesses to prove how honorably the learned men of both Churches thought and judged of it. Nor should Catholic writers feel any scruple about assigning it its due praise, even though it has been marked with a black mark in the Roman Curia, following the example of the most recent editors, who, in commending Quesnel’s merits as they deserved, assumed the role of impartial and fair judges, and taught that victory must be expected only from a just assessment of an adversary’s strength and from a consciousness of one’s own superiority.

As something that may stand for all the rest, it is not unwelcome to set down here the Ballerinis’ judgment of Quesnel:

> “What and how great is the edition of Leo which Paschasius Quesnel took the greatest pains to prepare,” they say in the general preface, p. 13, “can be unknown only to those who do not know his edition. If one examines the text—which, in evaluating ancient editions, must be considered first and above all, and in which the question is whether it has been corrected and enlarged by previously unpublished minor works—he obtained a number of excellent manuscripts. With their help he successfully corrected many passages corrupted in earlier editions, and from a single Grimanic manuscript he was able to enlarge the letters of the pontiff, which are among the more useful sources of sacred history in his works, by twenty-eight letters previously unpublished.
>
> “He also added several other unpublished materials, among which the most celebrated is that very ancient collection of the canons and letters of the Roman pontiffs. It yields nothing to the Dionysian collection and is of the greatest assistance to students of ancient canon law.

**[Note: Col. 0085D–0086D]** Thus the Ballerinis had not read—or, if they had read, had dismissed as a fable—the account which Richard Simon, in his *Critique of Dupin’s Library*, s.v. Leo, vol. I, pp. 190 ff., apparently reports in all seriousness concerning Quesnel and this work: namely, that not Quesnel alone but several persons, to whom the phrase “We are a legion” would apply, were the authors of this edition; that Quesnel merely collected over many years what he had received from several learned men in Paris; that, because he did not know how to write Latin, he composed it in the vernacular and then had it translated into Latin by a learned Irishman, formerly his fellow Oratorian and then a teacher of rhetoric at the Collège de Beauvais; and that Fr. Gérard Dubois, then a member of the same society, translated the Life of Leo and, against Quesnel’s wishes, softened in translating certain harsher statements made in it against the Roman See.]
>
> “If, moreover, you consider the editor’s own labors, inserted for the illustration of the text or of the matters treated—for this is the second thing sought in editions, namely, what edition of the Fathers will be found enriched with so many observations, admonitions, notes, and dissertations by a single editor—what other edition of Leo compares with the one Quesnel printed? For the works of that pontiff which in ancient editions were contained in a small volume, in what is called octavo or quarto format, because of Quesnel’s additions fill two substantial volumes in folio.
>
> “Who would not be moved by the great care he undertook and devoted energetically to editing Leo? He was endowed with outstanding intelligence and much learning, and possessed very great ability. After twenty-five years he reprinted his earlier edition, revised with new care and enlarged, so that it must be judged as polished and perfected as far as he could make it.”

The criticisms usually directed against him fall into three main categories. First, he is accused of negligence in using manuscripts, particularly by the eminent scholars Baluze and Coustant, who were highly experienced in the study of ancient books. Next, he is accused of excessive freedom, since he sometimes emends the text without citing any manuscript.

The gravest criticism of all, however, is that he did not hesitate to acknowledge himself in these labors as a patron of false doctrines, and that he attacked not so much Leo as the prerogatives of the Roman See, sometimes openly and sometimes covertly.

This was all the more offensive in a man who had already given unmistakable signs of his hatred for the members of the Society of Jesus and appeared to possess a mind scarcely free from partisan zeal. Indeed, even the members of our own Church, who have almost always embraced with willing enthusiasm every most vehement opponent of the rights of the Roman pontiff, ought not to have denied that Quesnel sometimes indulged his temperament and, carried away at times by the force of argument or pursuing with excessive zeal opinions contrary to those commonly held, wrote things that possess more appearance than solidity.

As for the first points, there is no doubt that he was justly criticized by the eminent scholars Baluze and Coustant; even the argumentative method we have just noted—more heated than sober—does not indicate a critic everywhere as painstaking as he should have been.

But let us take care not immediately to turn whatever occurred through his fault into a suspicion of fraud and malice. For in identifying and distinguishing so many printed editions, examining and comparing manuscript codices, judging in so difficult a matter between genuine and spurious writings, establishing the chronology in so complicated a task, and attending to the manifold interconnections of the numerous details that had to be considered, who will be surprised that he could have made mistakes, and who will deny pardon to a man worn out or at times excessively acute?

Finally, we shall not conceal that Quesnel’s dissertations are generally rather long and lead the reader through each individual fact; they also often linger over matters that touch Leo only more remotely.

### 1677

Paris, at François Muguet’s, in quarto. Certain letters of Pope Leo and of others to him, almost all previously unpublished, drawn from a royal manuscript by Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, in *Monuments of the Greek Church*, vol. I, pp. 50–65.

They contain:

1. The Letter of Flavian of Constantinople to Leo of Rome, from Royal manuscripts 1026 and 2614.
2. The Letter of Pope Leo and the Roman Synod to the Augusta Pulcheria, from Royal manuscript 1026.
3. Leo’s Synodical Letter to the Constantinopolitans, from the same codex.
4. The Letter of Hilarion, or Hilary the Deacon, to Pulcheria, from the same manuscript.
5. The Letter of Galla Placidia to Aelia Pulcheria, from the same manuscript.
6. The Letter of Leo of Rome to the archimandrites of Constantinople, from the same codex.
7. A fragment of the Letter of Anatolius of Constantinople to Leo, Roman pontiff, from Royal manuscript 940.

### 1677

Lyons, at the house of the Anissons, in folio. The Sermons of Leo the Great on the principal solemnities of the Lord and of the saints; his decretal and familiar letters to various persons; and also the *Treatise Against the Errors of Eutyches* and of other heretics, in *Bibliotheca Patrum Maxima*, vol. VII.

### 1687

Paris, at the Royal Printing House, in folio. Forty-nine decrees of Pope Leo, reprinted in the collection of Dionysius Exiguus from the ancient codex of the Canons of the Roman Church, in the new edition of François Pithou, pp. 228–249.

### 1700

Lyons, at the bookshop of Jean Certe, in the Market Street, under the sign of the Trinity, in folio. Volume II. The complete works of Saint Leo the Great, pope, now enlarged for the first time by thirty-three letters and three treatises on the grace of Christ, etc.

A repetition of the Quesnelian recension. The editor changed his opinion on certain minor matters, but not on those in which he was accused of having raged with impious fury against the Apostolic See.

From pages 195 to 202 of the first volume there is inserted a *Little Work on the Correction of a Word in Sermon 7 of Saint Leo the Great on the Nativity of the Lord*, **Γραμματίου Δωρημάτιον** (as printed), that is, “a little gift of a little letter,” which John Clampinus of Rome, Master of Briefs of Grace and Referendary in both Signatures, gives and offers to the most reverend Father Erasmo Gattola of Gaeta, monk of the illustrious monastery of Monte Cassino, dean, vicar general, and librarian, in Rome, 1693, from the printing house of Johann Jakob Komarek of Bohemia at Saint Angelo Custode.

In it the author maintains that the word *ara* in the celebrated sermon is corrupt and demonstrates from manuscript codices that *areae* should be read, referring to the spaces by which the rows of the stairs leading up into the basilica of Saint Peter are distinguished. The emendation is certainly beyond doubt; consequently, Quesnel accepted it without hesitation into the text on page 81, adding a commendatory notice of the author.

From this letter, moreover, we derived information about certain editions of Leo’s Sermons which I do not recall having learned of elsewhere. I must not, however, conceal from readers that, as I have also noted in the individual places where I present them, I have not found the man’s reliability in this matter sufficiently established.

As for the other merits of this reprint, it received somewhat fuller indexes, including a new index of the books and their chapters, the sermons, the letters and their synopses, and all the other titles of the first volume—an index which the earlier edition rather sorely lacked.
