It is displeasing, however, that these same indexes, although for the most part repeated from the earlier edition, are displayed with great pomp in the titles of both volumes. Finally, the work is printed in clear type, in two columns per page, on paper of no contemptible quality.

## EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

### 1739

Rome, from the press of Saint Michael at the Ripetta, at the expense of Girolamo Mainardi, in folio. The decretal letters of Saint Leo, in the *Very Extensive Collection of the Bulls of the Roman Pontiffs*, edited by Carlo Cocquelines, vol. I, pp. 25–47.

The number of items is nineteen. According to Quesnel’s order, they are: I, II, III, V, VIII, XII, XV, XVI, XVII, XIV, XCVII, XXIX, XLVII, L, CXXXV, LXXVII, LXXXVII, CXXIX, and CXXXVI.

At the very beginning, in a note appended to the first letter, the editor states that he took them all from the first volume of Cardinal Antonio Carafa’s *Decretal Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*. He adds that, owing to the work of this cardinal, who had been assisted by the Vatican codices, they have been rendered quite different from the versions published by canonists and by the collectors of Saint Leo’s works.

### 1741

Venice, at the house of Augustino Savioli, in folio. The complete works of Saint Leo the Great, pontiff, corrected according to the authority of manuscript codices. Added are the works of Maximus of Turin.

This edition is little known, and scarcely a single copy crossed the Alps. It deservedly has that fate if our booksellers have detected the trickery of the publisher, who advertised manuscripts in the title in order frequently to attract buyers. In reality, he reprinted Leo’s works as they appeared in Quesnel, adding Quesnel’s dissertations on the three minor works which he had first vindicated as Leo’s; and, if Cacciari is to be trusted—and we do not think his testimony should be rejected—he disfigured the work with countless typographical errors.

Nor should one suppose that he openly acknowledged Quesnel’s diligence. On the contrary, despising the judgment of his readers, he assumed Quesnel’s persona and presented what Quesnel had written and finally vindicated for Leo as though it had now been vindicated for the first time through his own work—that is, through the bookseller’s work—and corrected anew according to manuscript codices.

By this very shamelessness he finally provided readers with a joke. In the commendatory inscription to Leo composed by Quesnel, which he likewise reprinted with the same pomp, he substituted for Quesnel’s name the words:

> “Augustino Savioli, the most devoted and obedient client.”

For the rest, readers should remember that the same bookseller reprinted the works of Peter Chrysologus according to an old edition; they will learn below that the same thing happened to Fulgentius.

### 1748

Venice, at the house of Andrea Poletti, in folio. Two volumes. The works of Saint Leo. Added are the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church* and the Sermons and Homilies of Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, corrected anew and enlarged according to manuscript codices.

The curator of this edition was Andrea Poletti, likewise a Venetian printer. From him we first learn that the earlier edition of Augustino Savioli, although miserably patched together, had nevertheless been sold through such a frequent influx of buyers that copies were already unavailable.

Accordingly, since he judged that it would be profitable to commit Leo’s works to the press again, he nevertheless considered it wrong rashly to copy Savioli’s exemplar. He claims that, guided by the advice of learned men, he arranged for another exemplar of better quality and enriched with additions to be reproduced. This was nothing other than Quesnel’s Paris edition, although certain items were removed and others added in their place, as the title indicates.

You should know, however, that he called it not “Quesnel’s edition” but merely “the Paris edition.” Whether he did this out of a justifiable fear, or in order by this deception to mislead men of modest learning but all the more religiously scrupulous, I shall not decide.

The first volume, like Quesnel’s editions, contains Sermons divided into various sections, each prefaced by a synopsis, with which the Paris editor had first supplied them. It then contains the same number of Letters, in the same order and arrangement, with Quesnel’s words indicating the sources from which the new letters had been drawn.

Nor did he reject the three minor works which were first attributed to Leo in the Paris edition. He departed from it only in placing them not at the beginning of the other works but rather at the end, immediately followed by the three dissertations concerning them.

Conversely, the items added to the first volume in the Paris edition—the Life of Hilary by Honoratus and the rest—are presented here in the second volume after the Code of Canons. At the end of the volume, since Quesnel’s remaining dissertations have been omitted, come the Sermons of Maximus.

If one asks what name and value should be assigned to Poletti’s work, one may properly call it a purged or mutilated edition of Quesnel. For not only have the items just mentioned been removed from the Paris edition, but one will also look in vain here for much of Quesnel’s own commentary and admonition.

This is the principal feature which Petrus Thomas Cacciari, the author of the following work, praises in it; to him alone we owe our knowledge of both this Venetian edition and the preceding one.

He considers, in general, that Poletti’s attempt to appropriate anything from Quesnel deserves the harshest criticism—indeed, almost detestation. He thinks Poletti even more blameworthy because he paid no attention to the reputation that had begun to spread concerning Cacciari’s own undertaking of a new edition. He places among Poletti’s merits only those features by which he departed from the Paris edition.

> “Above all,” he says, “we cannot conceal that the printer Poletti acquired some praise for himself by not copying the preceding edition of Savioli, which both he himself and all who examined it rightly and deservedly complained was filled with countless typographical errors.
>
> “A further praise which Poletti acquired for himself is that he inserted into his Venetian edition as few as possible of Quesnel’s observations, and cut out the admonitions which for the most part either conflict with Leo’s meaning, with the rites of the Church, with the structures of ecclesiastical hierarchy, or finally even with the rules of the Catholic faith. Observations and admonitions of this kind, which one encounters throughout both of Quesnel’s French editions, are entirely absent from the one published by Poletti.
>
> “Attending in his new printing only to Quesnel’s synopses and to the text of Leo as it appeared in France, he flattered himself that he was displaying such purity that the work could scarcely emerge more carefully corrected or polished.”

Cacciari then turns his pen against Poletti still more sharply by disseminating a refutation of Quesnel at greater length, though he does this more in accordance with his own plan; we shall discuss that later.

His judgment of Poletti seems to us more imprudent in the following respect: he criticizes him for not hesitating to include the three celebrated dissertations of Quesnel, while making no mention of those writers who had opposed Quesnel with all their strength in order to refute his prejudiced opinions. He also criticizes Poletti for saying that the authority of the Code of Canons, which other writers had diminished, was highly valued by Peter Coustant in the preface to his *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, and for claiming that he had satisfied the wishes of readers by ensuring that they would not be forced to seek that work elsewhere.

The bookseller would, of course, have served his own interests admirably if mentioning these controversies had instilled scruples into superstitious people.

There is undoubtedly a more serious criticism: Poletti’s work suffers from numerous typographical errors and displays clear evidence of excessive haste. A particularly disgraceful example reveals this: the *Treatise of Saint Leo Against the Errors of Eutyches and Other Heretics* was printed twice, in the same words and with the same heading, once on page 102 and again on page 309.

### 1751

Bologna, at the house of Girolamo Corciolani and the brothers Colli, in quarto. The Sermon of Saint Leo on Lent, beginning, “Beloved, our faith admonishes us,” with annotations by Giovanni Crisostomo Trombelli, together with three other sermons on the Resurrection of the Lord and on the feast of Saint Paul, falsely attributed to the same author, and one on the son of Abraham by an uncertain author, perhaps Leo himself, from a Bolognese codex; in *Minor Works of the Ancient Latin Fathers, or Anecdotes*, published by the Canons Regular of Saint Savior at Bologna, vol. II, part I, pp. 233–253.

None of these sermons, nor even the earlier one on Lent, as Trombelli entitled it, belongs to Leo, as the Ballerinis demonstrate in their dissertation *On Sermons Falsely Attributed to Leo the Great*.

### 1751

Rome, from the printing house of Antonio Fulgoni at Saint Eustace, in folio. *Studies Pertaining to the Whole of the Works of Saint Leo the Great, Concerning the Histories of the Heresies of the Manichaeans, Priscillianists, Pelagians, and Eutychians, Which the Holy Pontiff Overthrew and Condemned with the Greatest Zeal and Labor*, dedicated to the most holy Father Benedict XIV, supreme pontiff, by Brother Petrus Thomas Cacciari, Carmelite, lecturer in polemical theology at the Urban College of the Propagation of the Faith and apostolic examiner of the Roman clergy.

Cacciari had long been turning over in his mind an anti-Quesnelian edition of Leo’s works; he had even caused it to be awaited for some time. Since, however, it appeared to be delayed too long—a delay which he attributed to just causes, namely, the demands of his office and the gravity of the undertaking itself—and since he had begun to be assailed by taunts from those who considered him unequal to the task or disliked the entire plan, he finally sought, by publishing these dissertations, both to dispel hostile rumors and to secure a path for himself among fairer judges.

For this reason, above all, it is necessary to show what attitude he adopted toward Quesnel. He complained especially of three things that Quesnel had seriously done wrong: first, that he had introduced numerous passages contrary to the genuine text; second, that he had mixed in much that was less compatible with ecclesiastical order and practice, and, more seriously, plainly alien to Catholic doctrine, so that he seemed not to have applied a remedy to the pontifical writings but to have grievously wounded them; and finally, that he had not collected all the monuments, but had deliberately omitted some and rejected or mutilated others as entirely spurious—or at least as full of interpolations—because they opposed the purpose he may have set for himself.

Such, in summary, are Cacciari’s criticisms of Quesnel. He pursues them more distinctly as follows:

> “Quesnel, endowed with an exceedingly sharp intellect, very ready to provoke disputes and quarrels, and altogether prompt in constructing equivocations and fallacies, set himself a goal different from that which all Catholics, and especially men of his own nation, have pursued in preparing and correcting the volumes of the ancient Fathers.
>
> “For at times he disfigured clearer passages of the holy pontiff with obscure, equivocal, and false annotations; he twisted others toward entirely violent interpretations; he concealed and suppressed the truth by fallacies; and, under the perpetual pretext of investigating and illuminating antiquity, he gradually and everywhere labored to establish systems favorable to the parties of the heretics and destructive of the governance of the sacred ecclesiastical hierarchy.
>
> “At times he almost abolished, or at least diminished, the true and legitimate jurisdiction of the Roman pontiffs over all the other Churches, including those of the East.
>
> “Meanwhile, he pretended to be someone else. For in writing his works and preparing Leo’s writings, he employed much artifice, affecting reverence, piety, and devotion toward the Roman pontiffs and the Apostolic See in order to deceive the unwary. Acting very often as a hidden enemy, after a splendid display of words he spewed forth propositions sprinkled with poison, which he imagined could clothe his erroneous and wholly fictitious systems in some false appearance of truth.”

**[Note:]** In the preface prefixed to the works themselves he expresses the same complaint as follows:

> “Far from having conferred these benefits upon the ecclesiastical and literary commonwealth—as though he had restored to Leo’s writings the original integrity and brilliance which he professed to restore—Quesnel instead gravely wounded the text itself in several passages, twisted it in others toward entirely violent interpretations, and finally explained it in certain places in a manner insufficiently Catholic. Thus his studies and labors have redounded only to the injury of Saint Leo, the ruin of the Catholic Church, and the protection and favor of those outside the Catholic faith.”

In these circumstances, therefore, believing that an immense burden of labor had been laid upon his shoulders—both in purging the text of false and corrupt readings and restoring it to its original integrity, which he asserts that even the synopses, deliberately tampered with by Quesnellus, demand, and in enlarging it by the addition of certain genuine works while eliminating those which Quesnellus had inserted into the Leonine corpus only with a perverse and deceptive intention (he means the books *On the Calling of the Nations*, the authorities of the apostolic see *On Grace*, and the *Letter to Demetrias*, as well as the *Code of Canons of the Roman Church*)—yet not hoping that he would fully attain what he desired, namely, to blunt all Quesnellus’s poisoned barbs, many of which, and the most serious, he was convinced still remained in his dissertation *On the Life and Deeds of Leo the Great*, he resolved to direct his most select forces of learning especially to this task and to engage him with the utmost exertion of his intellect on this field of exercises.

But let us hear him himself:

> Among those dissertations composed by Paschasius Quesnellus under the guise of illustrating ecclesiastical tradition and Leonine doctrine, the foremost place belongs to the one entitled *On the Life and Deeds of St. Leo the Great*. I could scarcely have understood how filled this entire dissertation and the others that follow it are with frauds and fictions, had I not, while going through them, continually appealed to the Leonine text itself in order to examine the truth of the matters. But since he is accustomed to employ such great artifice that he can gradually draw even upright and excellent readers into his perverse opinions and imbue them with many prejudices, the present work will show how much labor I have had to expend. I can scarcely describe the effort he has devoted to exaggerating his devotion and pious feeling toward St. Leo and the apostolic see—devotion which he pretends to attest by an embellished style, either by digressing into praise of him, or by comparing Leo’s deeds and statutes with the works of other bishops renowned for their teaching, piety, and religion, or by bringing forward meanwhile the regulations of certain particular synods which had prevailed somewhere before Leo’s time, and which he asserts that the supreme pontiff ought to have obeyed and followed. What else can one say? At times he has constructed so vast and elaborate a display of learning to delight his readers that, little by little, he turns ancient ecclesiastical affairs upside down, disturbs and confuses them, so that scarcely even appear the lures he used to insinuate and establish his perverse systems; perhaps flattering himself that, in treating sacred and ecclesiastical matters, human minds can be persuaded more by verbal artistry and philosophical conjectures than by the truth of things and the weight of arguments. No one can easily understand what diligence and attention of mind I had to employ, lest I be deceived, in going through this and other dissertations of Quesnellus—unless perhaps those who preceded me in composing highly learned commentaries relating to ecclesiastical affairs can do so. Those who have assessed the six volumes *On the Power of the Church* by the distinguished Giovanni Antonio Bianchini know that he most recently did this. In conversations we held privately, he more than once testified that he had never read another writer who employed so many disguises and artifices, apart from Quesnellus. For whenever the latter sensed that he could easily be seized and strangled, he immediately slips away like a snake, and, proceeding from one question to another or to several others, mixes true things with uncertain and ambiguous ones; and again inserts and entangles false and erroneous claims with doubtful and probable ones, so as to reach the goal he has set for himself.

It was therefore not enough merely to remove from Leo’s works so many fictions, deceptions, and trifles, and to assert the apostolic see’s legitimate rights, by presenting Leo’s text naked and sincere, purged everywhere of all corruptions, ambiguities, and false interpretations. It was also necessary to compose, in an ordered method, certain exercises by which considerable light could be brought to Leo’s deeds, to the rights of the apostolic see, and to the form and order of ecclesiastical government.

[Col. 0092D] In particular, he undertook to narrate the history of those heresies—or at least of the principal ones—which, during the period from St. Leo’s elevation to the supreme pontificate until the end of his life, attacked the Catholic religion and ravaged both West and East. “For this reason,” he says, “in order to fulfill the duties of his office and safeguard the Christian faith, he had to devote every effort and labor to calming the most savage storms which, while the devil raged furiously, were promoting the destruction of the faith and harassing the dominion of Christ and the Roman Church. From all these conflicts the supreme pontiff himself carried away those victories which the Lord Christ had promised in the Scriptures to the blessed Peter and his successors.”

He therefore composed an extensive treatment in two books of the Manichaeans, one book of the Priscillianists, one of the Pelagian heresy, and likewise two books on the Eutychian heresy and its history. He began to weave the history of Manichaeism from its very origins, perhaps not according to his original plan. For he writes that this task had already been completed when, warned by a friend, he took Belsobrius’s little book into his hands and realized that he had to revise anew the fabric already woven. Hence in these books he combats Belsobrius more than Quesnellus.

[Col. 0093B] In the history of Pelagianism, by contrast, he considered only what touched Leo, and in each matter he places in a conspicuous position everything in which Leo’s role was involved, whether through his writings or through his deeds. Now, since I believe that the man’s talent and design have been sufficiently revealed by these specimens, let us proceed to the actual edition of Leo’s works.

**1753–55. Rome, at the press of Joseph Collini, folio, vol. II.** *All the Works of St. Leo the Great, first pope, corrected according to manuscript codices, enlarged with new monuments, and furnished with notes and observations, through the labors of F. Peter Thomas Cacciari, Carmelite.*

Indeed, the three things which, according to the words of the Ballerini brothers quoted above, editors require in order for an edition to be presented as purged of defects, enlarged with new writings, and illustrated, Cacciari likewise believed and promised that he had accomplished in these volumes. He produced an edition purged of defects and enriched chiefly from Vatican codices, and for that reason wishes it to be called Roman; he illustrated it not only through the preliminary exercises, but also through the notes now placed beneath the text. Since nearly all these notes are directed against Quesnellus’s opinions and assertions, he consequently proclaims that his edition may rightly be called anti-Quesnellian.

Having therefore excised the books which Quesnellus had attempted to vindicate for Leo by a new argument, and likewise excised the *Code of Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*, he included in the first volume the *Sermons*, together with certain other monuments concerning liturgical matters drawn from the *Missal*, the *Roman Order*, and the *Sacramentary Code*, and in the second volume the *Letters alone*.

In the *Sermons*, certainly, he departed from Quesnellus in more than one respect: he restored not only the order of the earlier editors—which he had observed to have been preserved by the ancient Collectors in handwritten archetypes—and the synopses which they had composed, but also altered the text in various places according to the authority of the manuscripts and, as he himself believed, corrected it. As for the variant readings discovered in printed and manuscript books, he asserts that he nowhere removed readings published by other editors and introduced new ones, except when the complete agreement of the codices themselves and the character of Leo’s discourse appeared to demand it, or when, after recognizing an obvious ancient error, he judged that the readings could and ought to be corrected with the aid of at least two codices.

“In this matter,” he says, “while paying particular attention also to the customary and sufficiently familiar formulas of speech of the holy pontiff expressed elsewhere, we supplied certain corrupt passages from repetitions found in other places, while informing our readers of the reasons which taught us that certain obscure and more difficult meanings of Leo ought to be interpreted by means of others that were clearer and more certain.”

He indicates that all this had to be done not only for the sake of truth, but also so that he might as often as possible counter the devices of his adversary Quesnellus, who either accused Leo or turned him into a support for his own assertions. For this same reason, he writes that he was compelled to adorn the text thus restored with the aid of manuscript codices with notes, observations, and preliminary notices, lest all the usefulness that might arise from this correction either perish entirely or at least remain concealed, and thus the opinion of some concerning the superiority of Quesnellus’s edition over all others continue, or his notes and observations appear to have such weight that no one could mark them as erroneous or convict them of falsehood.

> “It was therefore necessary,” he says, “to oppose these Quesnellian notes and observations with new, truer, and more sincere ones, and not to reserve them for the end of our volume, as otherwise very learned men have sometimes done, but to distribute them in suitable and appropriate places, so that the reader would undergo no labor at all in turning the pages of the book in order to understand what we have written in this Roman edition against Quesnellus’s. Since, finally, as we have said, he is accustomed to cite the Leonine text, wrongly and violently interpreted, in support of his false propositions, we have taken pains to have those passages printed in larger type which are especially suitable for exposing the falsehood of this adversary of ours and overthrowing so many assertions that are less Catholic or that he has pronounced with the greatest impudence.”

As for the final feature of this edition, namely, the additions made in this volume, he found in so many different manuscript codices as he examined a number of sermons inscribed with Leo’s name. Some appeared more genuine, others less so; others plainly showed that they falsely bore this name and had been sewn together from six hundred scraps of other works. He lost no small amount of labor and more than a little time in properly and suitably distinguishing all of them, and he complains that this was one of the obstacles that prevented him from publishing the edition as early as he had expected.

He added to Leo’s genuine *Sermons* five new ones drawn from Vatican and Vallicellian codices, as well as the final part of the sermon on the feast of the Chair of St. Peter, which Quesnellus had first published mutilated and incomplete. They are as follows:

1. *On the Sunday of the Resurrection*, the same sermon which Trombellus had published, whose doubts concerning its authenticity our editor endeavored to overturn in an extensive preliminary notice.

2. *On the Feast of the Lord’s Ascension*.

3–4. *For the feast of the holy brothers the Maccabees*, customarily celebrated at Rome on the Kalends of August in the Church of St. Peter at the Chains.

The latter two he encountered in ancient codices either anonymously or under Augustine’s name; but, after an examination conducted according to his own judgment and that of other learned men, he assigned them to Leo.

5. *On the Birthday of the Holy Apostle Paul*, likewise published by Trombellus as another work of Pope Leo, but now reproduced from the very ancient Vatican codex no. 3835 and asserted to be by Leo the Great.

He then separated the doubtful and spurious works, as well as those pieced together from various fragments of Leo, following the example of Quesnellus and of the Maurist Fathers who edited Augustine’s sermons. In the first appendix he gathered only those contained in Quesnellus’s appendix; in the second, which he entitled the *New Appendix*, he presented nine mutilated and incomplete, doubtful and apocryphal sermons which bore Leo’s name in various manuscripts. Finally, he placed there the *Breviary against Heretics and Schismatics*, previously published by Sirmond and in the *Library of the Fathers*, but recently discovered under Leo’s name in a seventh-century manuscript codex in the library of the Augustinian Hermits at Padua.

Thus far concerning the first volume of this edition.

The second volume contains the *Letters*. In preparing it he was assisted by no less abundant a supply of manuscript codices, especially Vatican ones, and he believed that he had gathered such a harvest from them that he ventured freely to declare this edition entirely new and drawn exclusively from manuscript authority.

Since the Vatican library was as rich in Greek as in Latin manuscript codices, he happened upon certain new Greek monuments. Some of these, already published in the *Collection of Councils*, appeared to require a corrective hand; others, published nowhere in Greek but only in Latin, he resolved to add for the sake of a fuller fidelity to ecclesiastical history; and still others, previously known neither in Greek nor in Latin, he decided to add as ornaments of his edition.

In this work, since he himself was insufficiently conversant with Greek authors and even less able to read the abbreviated annotations of handwritten books, he employed the services of a certain learned Greek, Raphael Vernazza, born on Chios and a Roman priest. Vernazza copied forty-seven Greek letters and reread them against other exemplars, or carefully compared them with printed editions wherever such editions were available.

It is unnecessary to enumerate them individually here; it will be enough to indicate four entirely new letters, by which he enlarged the number of the Quesnellian letters from 141 to 145. They are:

1. **No. 27:** Leo’s letter to the emperors Theodosius concerning the Incarnation of the divine Word—or rather, a fragment of a letter, Greek and Latin, extracted from Vatican codex no. 720, p. 74.

2. **No. 85:** To Julian, bishop, concerning the monks who adhered to Eutyches.

3. **No. 117:** To the same, concerning his efforts against the Eutychians.

4. **No. 126:** To Anatolius, bishop, concerning Atticus, bishop of Constantinople.

All are from a manuscript codex of the monastery of St. Emmeram at Regensburg, of which there will be occasion to speak below.

He inserted these letters in the places indicated; in the remaining letters he followed Quesnellus’s order, and, following Quesnellus’s practice, assigned no numbers to the letters addressed to Leo by others.

He also retained Quesnellus’s synopses, with the liberty of correcting, supplementing, or entirely composing new ones wherever he judged that they did not fully correspond to Leo’s meaning. At the end of nearly every letter he noted the difference between Quesnellus’s wording and his own.

Finally, he added notes, admonitions, and marginalia, partly to explain his reasons for the variants and corrections, and partly—and most frequently—to brandish a sword against Quesnellus. For when he had observed that Quesnellus’s annotations, which Quesnellus had relegated to the end of the volume, much to the reader’s inconvenience, did not always contain true or sound doctrine, and when he had gradually detected fraud, deception, and bad faith in them very often, he recalled all of them, to use his own words, to the scales of truth in their appropriate places, and, relying on the gravest arguments, demonstrated that Quesnellus had either failed through hallucination or sought to deceive unwary readers.

“In carrying out this task,” he says, “we did not always strive for brevity, since at times many matters, widely disparate from one another, were brought forward, matters which it seemed utterly impossible to indicate, remove, and refute in a few words.”

It now remains for us to add a few remarks concerning the description, appearance, and arrangement of the entire work.

In each volume, after the dedication—the first is inscribed to Cardinal Nerio Corsini, the second to Benedict XV, P. S.—there follows a preface in which he discusses, usually at considerable length, the purpose of the edition, earlier editions, especially Quesnellus’s edition and its method and bad practices, and finally his own efforts and resources. Each preface concludes with a list of the manuscript books he used.

In the second volume, before turning to these subjects, he began an extensive discourse on certain matters, especially the doctrines of the Catholic Church, which Quesnellus had attempted to undermine; he brings it to an end only after forty and more pages.

There follow indexes of the contents of the *Sermons* and *Letters*, together with the synopses, which are printed twice, and finally the text itself, printed in two columns, with notes beneath it at the bottom of the page, written across the full width. At the beginning of each sermon or letter, the editions and manuscript codices from which it was taken and corrected are indicated in small letters in the margin, just as the subjects and principal statements are indicated in the other marginal annotations.

Admonitions or notices are sometimes placed before the text, sometimes appended at the end, and sometimes inserted between the two writings to which they pertain. Finally, a sufficiently extensive index of noteworthy matters and names is added to each volume.

The type is for the most part rounded and fairly large, but the characters are well suited to one another according to their position and are clear; typographical errors are rare.

If you ask my opinion of the editor and his merits, I think it would have been better for him to weigh his powers more carefully before undertaking such a work on the Leonine writings, and especially an edition of the *Letters* after Quesnellus, let alone against Quesnellus. In fact, without any hesitation he plunged into so vast an ocean, although he ought to have recognized that he lacked many of the qualities necessary in an editor, much less those that constitute an ornament.

For apart from some knowledge of polemical theology—not elegant knowledge, but such as might perhaps suffice for the office of examiner of the Roman clergy—his entire learning, especially in ecclesiastical history and law, was not acquired through prolonged reading and study, but was hastily assembled according to the immediate needs of the matter. Thus, whatever he has just learned from others through immense labor, unless it is too far removed from his own sense and understanding, he immediately dares to present as his own, as though it had arisen within his mind, and to teach it to others.

This is evident not only from his *Exercises*, but especially from his opinions concerning Quesnellus. He scarcely acknowledges that Quesnellus ever performed any laudable service in Leo’s edition.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] Preface to vol. I, p. 21, where, concerning the order of the letters established by Quesnellus, against which he did not dare to undertake anything for the most just reasons, he says that the author thereby deserved no small praise.]

He never admits that Quesnellus was learned; instead, like a cowardly man, he loudly proclaims that the adversary whom he rashly took upon himself to provoke was to be feared not for his own virtue but for fraud and cunning.

Certainly, if the many amusing exclamations and complaints about Quesnellus’s devices, deceptions, false disguises, and ambiguous interpretations, repeated on nearly every page, demonstrate anything else, they show how great a burden the learning of a most ingenious man imposed upon the impoverished Cacciari—especially while Cacciari, always looking around lest a snake be hidden in the grass, frequently calls out to his readers not to consider him timid or to believe that Quesnellus cannot be defeated.

Hence, plainly unequal to this contest, he must approach it uncertain whether to attack his opponent in the open field or merely to nip at him when an opportunity presents itself. He neither attacks the whole system of false doctrines with the combined strength of argument, nor always opposes each point with whatever is most appropriate. Instead, he generally employs declamation and not infrequently offers, as a refutation, the objection that he does not understand him.

Nevertheless, anyone who has had the opportunity to handle Cacciari’s edition and is not disinclined to undertake the labor will discover that this criticism is true and just.

But even before the success of this undertaking revealed the man’s ability, we are taught once again by his own testimony that no one was more aware than he himself of the weakness of his powers. This is the direction of those complaints of his concerning the envious and detractors, whose mockery and hostile zeal against him he experienced daily, not without hindering the edition—complaints already mentioned in connection with his *Exercises* and repeated in the prefaces to both volumes.

Those who observed matters more closely could recognize that work which he might have devoted successfully to any other ecclesiastical writer would be wasted on Leo. From this they could disapprove of his plan either openly or secretly and, when it was prolonged for an excessive length of time, suppose that he had collapsed in the middle of the work.

**1755–57. Venice, at the press of Simon Occhi, folio, three volumes.** *The Works of St. Leo the Great, Roman pontiff, revised after the recension of Paschasius Quesnellus according to numerous and most excellent manuscript codices not consulted by him, corrected and enlarged with unpublished materials; illustrated with prefaces, annotations, and admonitions. Everything also found in Quesnellus’s edition is added, and is subjected to critical review; under the care of the brothers Peter and Jerome Ballerini, Veronese priests.*

**Volume I**, containing the genuine works of the holy pontiff, namely, the *Sermons* and *Letters*, with their appendices.

**Volume II**, containing the works attributed to St. Leo which do not belong either to the *Sermons* or to the *Letters*. Also included are the minor works of St. Hilary, bishop of Arles, corrected and enlarged according to manuscript codices. Eleven dissertations of Quesnellus on the works of the holy pontiff are appended, together with his notes on the *Letters*, accompanied by critical observations.

**Volume III**, or the *Appendix to the Works of St. Leo the Great*, or the very ancient *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons and Constitutions of the Holy Apostolic See*, added by Quesnellus to the works of that pontiff, but now revised according to the most excellent manuscript exemplars and restored to a much better form. Other extremely rare materials are appended, together with five dissertations of Quesnellus on the same Code of Canons, subjected to critical review. A treatise on ancient collections and collectors of canons, both published and unpublished, down to Gratian, is placed first.

Thus is the edition entitled—an edition which, apart from Coustant’s distinguished work on the letters of the Roman pontiffs, can scarcely be compared with any other in the whole of ecclesiastical literature, and which rightly assigns its editors the third place among the leading figures of this field of study—I mean Baluze and Coustant.

They surpass Quesnellus not only in the abundance and excellence of their resources, that is, of their manuscript books, but much more in their knowledge and careful use of them, as well as in their ready and exact learning. They possessed not only numerous and outstanding manuscripts from the Vatican library, but also manuscripts from many other libraries within and outside Rome and throughout almost the whole of Italy; in Germany as well, they had highly distinguished materials from Vienna, the Imperial Library, and the library of St. Emmeram at Regensburg.

The Roman exemplars were especially useful for correcting the *Sermons*. They learned that some of them had belonged to the basilicas of the City and were certainly Roman, and they frequently substituted their readings as purer for those commonly printed, which Quesnellus had either not corrected or had altered inadequately or incorrectly.

They assert that they restored about three hundred passages either through certain correction or by bringing them back to a better reading. Moreover, by collating so many codices of different origins at once, they discovered and corrected the fact that the order had been disturbed in certain places; they divided two sermons which had coalesced into one; they removed one sermon wrongly attributed to Leo and another which Quesnellus had fabricated for him from his own codex; finally, they restored another sermon which Quesnellus had taken away from Leo; and they accomplished many other things of this kind, about which they give notice throughout their annotations.

Likewise, in the *Letters* they introduced neither few nor insignificant corrections, restored the chronology in certain places, and altered the entire order. With the aid of manuscript books they also vindicated certain letters which Quesnellus had called into doubt and several which he had expunged.

As for unpublished materials, they added to this edition three new letters of Leo from the Regensburg codex—

[Note: [Col. 0099] The same letters which Cacciari published at almost exactly this time.]

—and one Greek letter of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, to Leo; also several letters in an ancient Greek translation from the same Vatican codex; furthermore, from the Venetian codex of St. Mark, the complete proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon held in support of Leo’s Letter 93, as well as another proceeding of that council in the case of Domnus of Antioch, in which Leo’s papal authority is commended, from a manuscript formerly at Verona and now in the Vatican, in the second volume; and finally several sermons attributed to Leo in manuscripts, in the appendix.

The first labor of the editors was therefore to ensure that the text should appear more corrected and more enlarged than in Quesnellus’s edition. Their second concern was to make the Leonine works themselves more genuine by separating the authentic from the spurious, especially those which Quesnellus had arbitrarily attributed to Leo. They did not think that everything once collected there by him should be omitted; rather, they preferred to separate it and, wherever the opportunity was available, apply the remedy of manuscript books.

There remained a third task: understanding the text and providing a proper explanation of the deeds performed by Leo or relating to him. This could not be done without a severe examination of all Quesnellus’s annotations and dissertations. Although the matters in which he gave offense chiefly concern two headings—divine grace, on the one hand, and certain prerogatives of the Roman see, on the other—they nevertheless understood that it would not be possible to confront him on these points in general in such a way that all his errors would be exposed and convicted. Instead, they had to follow him step by step and dissect each and every one of his assertions and inventions.

They therefore decided to insert his own works in full into their edition and to append to each their own observations, by which they would attack or correct whatever seemed to deserve refutation. At the same time, they hoped to achieve the result that Quesnellus’s edition, which would be found inserted in its entirety into theirs, would no longer be necessary, and that his writings—which had been forbidden in his editions—could be read in this one together with their remarks and censures.

When the plan of the work had thus been described, the following order and arrangement emerged.

Volume I presents all Leo’s genuine works, that is, his authentic *Sermons* and *Letters*, in correcting which they used both their own manuscript codices and Quesnellus’s variants. This volume therefore consists of two parts. Before each part there is a special preface, exceptionally useful for a general critical treatment of the sources and manuscripts from which both the *Sermons* and the *Letters* altogether have emerged.

They prefixed prefaces and admonitions to the *Sermons* and *Letters* wherever necessary. The annotations appended to both partly explain the reasons for their corrections and indicate the variant readings of both their own codices and Quesnellus’s, and partly illustrate the pontiff’s text wherever it appeared to require explanation.

Among these annotations of the Ballerini brothers there is also room for the notes which Quesnellus sometimes attached to the *Sermons* or *Letters* themselves, so that nothing of his might be lacking. Since he had affixed to the *Sermons* certain notes or postils which required a longer discussion, they therefore published, after the *Sermons*, observations on certain particular passages in them, inserting into those observations Quesnellus’s notes or postils, as well as Ciampini’s dissertation on the correction of the word *area* in Sermon 27.

I could wish, however, that following the same practice they had added immediately after the *Letters* Quesnellus’s longer observations on them, so that everything relating to the elucidation of the *Sermons* and *Letters* might have been more neatly contained in one volume. They reserved these observations for the second volume, to be published in the same order as in Quesnellus, after the dissertations—doubtless for no other reason than to make the volumes equal in size.

Immediately after the genuine *Sermons* follows an appendix of doubtful works or works wrongly attributed to Leo, for the most part unpublished. A notice is prefixed concerning others which, in some manuscript exemplars, were wrongly ascribed to Leo but in other codices were attributed to other authors and, because they had already been printed among the works of other Fathers, did not appear to require repetition.

The *Letters* are followed by a dissertation on the lost letters, both those of St. Leo to others and those of others to St. Leo, as well as on other monuments relating to the *Letters*, arranged in chronological order. The Leonine fragments that survive are inserted at the same time. This is followed by a notice of the decrees attributed to Leo in the *Pontifical Book*, and finally by an appendix of St. Leo’s letters, containing several spurious letters and other documents relating to the *Letters* which ought not to have been placed among the *Letters* themselves.

Volume II presents a more extensive appendix of works attributed to Leo.

First, the most ancient *Sacramentary*, commonly called Leonine and believed to be Leo’s, is published. Since, however, not everything contained in it belongs to Leo, nor can the same pontiff certainly be called its compiler, yet certain Leonine materials are found in it, and these appeared to demand their rightful place in the appendix, since they had been attributed to Leo in printed editions.

The editors note that this had to be done all the more because Quesnellus had published three prefaces as Leonine at the end of the *Sermons*. Two of these are found in the surviving part of that same *Sacramentary*, while it is probable that the third existed in the portion that has perished.

The *Sacramentary* is followed by the two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, the *Chapters*, or authorities, *On Grace and Free Will*, and the *Letter to the Virgin Demetrias*, or treatise *On Humility*. Quesnellus had published all these under Leo’s name; the Ballerini brothers corrected them from manuscript codices and supplied them in several places.

Next is appended the *Breviary against Heretics*, or, as it is entitled elsewhere, the *Breviary of the Faith against the Arians*, which Sirmondus once published without the author’s name. They found it attributed to Leo in two ancient codices, one from Padua and the other from Milan, which also supplied several corrections.

Although it had been inserted among the works of that pontiff in two other codices discovered by Sirmondus, it nevertheless could not be attributed to the pontiff himself because of the manifest difference in authorship. They judged that it may perhaps have been connected with him as something that has not come to our knowledge, and therefore not unworthy of an appendix.

After this, so that nothing might be lacking which Quesnellus had inserted into his edition, they reproduced the *Life and Minor Works of Hilary of Arles*, enlarged by two pieces—namely, the *Sermon on the Miracle of Genesius, Martyr of Arles*, and the *Poem on the Maccabees*—and corrected from several manuscript exemplars.

Thus far the appendix.

After this, eleven of Quesnellus’s dissertations relating either to Leo or to the works mentioned above were reprinted in this volume. Observations are appended to each dissertation which, as the editors say, may serve in place of a censorial review and are intended to refute each of the principal themes proposed by Quesnellus.

Where only certain passages in the dissertations needed correction or confirmation, notes were added at the foot of the pages. This procedure had to be followed especially in the first dissertation, which describes Leo’s life. Although not a few things in it required correction and some additions were also necessary, they admit that many more matters are sufficiently established.

This volume concludes with Quesnellus’s observations and notes on Leo’s *Letters*, which Quesnellus himself published at length after the dissertations, together with the editors’ annotations appended at the bottom of the page.

The third volume, containing the most ancient Collection of Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See, together with other monuments of the most ancient canon law, is wholly the editors’ own and distinctive contribution; it is also of the greatest utility and lends the utmost distinction to this edition. For although the celebrated collection had first been published by Quesnel from two manuscript copies—one from Oxford, more recent and very corrupt, the other from Thuaneus, older and of excellent quality, but received too late for him to use it with sufficient care—and had been elucidated by five dissertations, which are likewise appended here [Col. 0101D], the Ballerini brothers, having obtained from it not only much more material from the Thuaneus manuscript than was available elsewhere, but also very much from another hitherto unknown yet extremely ancient book of the same collection belonging to the Imperial Library [Col. 0102A], were able to correct very many errors and restore the collection itself to a better, almost original form.

Nor were they satisfied with this. For they sought out every resource that could contribute something to the correction and elucidation of this collection, especially manuscript copies of other ancient collections, in which all, or nearly all, of the documents of this collection could be found and examined, although inserted there only in scattered form. From this research they derived another and much greater benefit. In those same codices they discovered not a few exceedingly rare monuments of the most ancient canon law, which, after the celebrated Collection, they were able either to publish in more accurate form [Col. 0102B] or to publish for the first time altogether.

> **Note:** These are:  
> 1. The ancient Latin edition of the Canons, containing the canons of the Councils of Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Nicaea, Sardica, Antioch, Constantinople I, and Chalcedon. It first came to light from the most ancient manuscript of Christopher Justellus; the Ballerini brothers present it complete and more accurately, collated with other ancient manuscript collections.  
> 2. The most ancient Latin translation of the Nicene Canons, now published for the first time from Vat. Regina Suecorum 1997.  
> 3. An old Latin translation of the Canons of Nicaea, Sardica, and Chalcedon, together with other documents relating to the Nicene and Sardican synods, now published for the first time from the very ancient manuscript codex 55 of the Chapter of Verona.  
> 4. Documents of ancient canon law:  
>    1. The canons of the Council of Carthage held in 419, as they are read in the most ancient Italian collections;  
>    2. The Council of Carthage of 421, under Aurelius XVIII, now published for the first time from manuscript codex 55 of the Chapter of Verona;  
>    3. The ancient Statutes of the Church, published from the finest manuscript collections;  
>    4. A canonical epistle: “What presbyters, deacons, or subdeacons must fulfill”;  
>    5. The precepts of Saint Peter concerning the preservation of the sacraments;  
>    6. The edict of the Emperor Glycerius against simoniacal ordinations, now recovered from Vat. Reg. 1997.

At the same time, this careful examination of manuscript books resulted not only in their detecting several unknown and unpublished collections of Canons, but also in their gathering, concerning the collections already in circulation, information that had escaped the notice of the most recent and learned writers on these subjects, and by which the history of ancient canon law has been extraordinarily illuminated. From this arose the treatise on ancient collections and collectors of Canons, both published and unpublished, down to Gratian, prefixed to the Quesnellian collection; after it, whatever others had previously debated on the same subject immediately began to seem diminished and almost worthless.

That treatise is divided into four parts. The first deals with Greek collections of Canons; the second with the older Latin collections, whether earlier than Dionysius or derived from sources earlier than Dionysius; the third with the Dionysian collections and the others that developed from Dionysius; and the fourth, finally, with ancient abridgments of the Canons and other Latin collections arranged by titles and commonplaces, down to Gratian.

Five dissertations by Quesnel, the five remaining from the sixteen relating to the Code of Canons, conclude this volume, together with the Ballerini brothers’ lengthy and highly useful annotations and corrections.

Indeed, so far are we from thinking that this general description of the edition adequately declares how much ingenuity, learning, and labor have been devoted to it, that we rather think that anyone wishing properly to explain all its merits would have to recount the treatment of each individual Sermon and Epistle [Col. 0102D]. There are in fact so many and such remarkable examples of these men’s skill and acumen that, whereas in the works of authors who are not ordinarily insignificant it often happens that a long familiarity and continued use diminish the opinion first formed of them, or even gradually expose the author’s faults and errors to the eye, the opposite is true of this work: the more assiduously one studies it, the more intensely one must admire it.

Let the first and second admonitions prefixed to the Epistle to the Bishop of Aquileia and to Septimius of Altinum serve as examples—together with the eighteenth Epistle to Januarius of Aquileia, which is joined to them—as well as the admonition prefixed to Epistle XXVIII to Flavian.

Nor, lest I pass over another important aspect of this work so highly praised—an aspect in which, both because of the long-standing desire for such an edition, fostered by the stricter defenders of the Roman See’s bishops and their rights and authority, and because of the special mandate of Benedict XIV [Col. 0103B], the editors’ labor ought to have had its most glorious part—I mean the refutation of Quesnel. We readily admit that the learning and method with which they knew how to confront each of their adversary’s assertions and arguments, sometimes openly and sometimes indirectly, and to charge them in innumerable places, indeed almost on every page, with carelessness, obvious error, or, more importantly, deceit and fraud, are so closely joined to the whole glory of their intellect and erudition that they cannot be separated from it. Nor can it often happen that, while praising their critical ability and their art of exposition, one criticizes their criticism of Quesnel’s arguments.

As for the resolution of the entire question concerning the force and authority of the papal primacy, we do not think that it is for us here to pass judgment on these men’s heterodoxy, which, as I believe, is unknown to few [Col. 0103C], since even someone wholly free from party spirit might be put at risk by the authors’ skill.

> **Note:** One of the brothers is well known among the opponents of Febronius through a work published at Verona in 1768 in quarto, entitled *A Book on the Power of the Supreme Pontiffs and of General Councils, together with Vindications of Papal Authority against the Work of Justin Febronius*, by Peter Ballerini, priest of Verona. An appendix on the infallibility of those same pontiffs in definitions of faith is added.

A detailed review of this edition appears in the *Theological Library*—written in the vernacular—of Johann August Ernesti, vol. IV, fascicle VII (1763), pp. 579–614.

### 1761

Florence, at the expense of Antonio Zatta of Venice, folio. *The Life, Epistles, and Decrees of Pope Leo I*, in Jo. Dominicus Mansi’s *New and Most Extensive Collection of the Sacred Councils*, vol. V, cols. 1203–1430; vol. VI, cols. 1–432.

Although this title bears the flavor of the Labbean and Bini editions, and Mansi almost never—and not even, for Coustant’s sake, in his reproduction of Labbe’s Venetian edition—dared depart from the example of his predecessors, here he nevertheless abandoned their model and took care to reproduce the Ballerini edition, not so much because of the outstanding excellence of that work as because the task seemed easier to complete in this way.

For he understood that, after the editions of Quesnel, Cacciari, and the Ballerini brothers, much would have to be repaired and supplied in Labbe; and because he feared that, when inserting these additions in their proper places, some error might occasionally creep in through his own carelessness or that something might be transposed—an evil that, at such a distance from the place where the edition was being produced, Venice, could scarcely have been remedied—or that the printers might be deceived into taking one leaf for another and assigning certain items to the wrong place, he decided to use the Ballerini edition in place of the Labbean.

“Yet,” he says, “as though fearing that he had not sufficiently displayed his own ingenuity, I judged this edition preferable to the others—not because I considered it superior to that which Father Cacciari, a Carmelite, prepared and produced in Roman type at almost the same time as the Ballerini brothers prepared theirs, but because a work printed at Venice was more readily available and accessible to a Venetian printer.”

Thus this compilation by a man undeservedly praised displays not even the slightest appearance of generosity. From the Ballerini brothers’ observations he retained those which they had placed immediately after the text, chiefly critical and shorter ones; but he removed the more extensive pieces, such as admonitions and dissertations, because their purpose differed from the conclusion reached by the Ballerini brothers, or occasionally compressed them into fewer words. He also inserted Cacciari’s additions that he missed in the Ballerini edition, as well as Sirmond’s rarer notes from his appendix to the Councils, just as they had been presented in Colet’s edition of the Councils.

Of his own he added an ancient synopsis of certain Epistles of Leo from the Lucca codex 190, which was not unknown to the Ballerini brothers; and, so that nothing from the earlier material should be lost, he prefixed Leo’s life from the *Liber Pontificalis*, together with Bini’s notes.

Someone may object to me that this ought to have been done for the sake of greater agreement with the other parts. I grant the point, and do not greatly criticize that particular decision; but I condemn the entire undertaking and consider it unworthy of this man’s reputation [Col. 0104C]. For what purpose was there in repeating, with such pomp, material that had been written quite creditably more than a hundred years earlier, and in stitching together, with such anxious care, the annotations and corrections of learned men one after another, when he could have devoted his own efforts to such a work with far greater profit?

It is unnecessary to point out, moreover, that the Epistles relating to the Council of Chalcedon were not reproduced again in that council’s acts, but that readers are referred to this complete collection.

### 1780

Helmstedt, printed by the widow Schnorr, quarto. *The Epistle of Leo the Great, Bishop of Rome, against Eutyches, on the True Incarnation of the Lord, to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople*. From the recension of the Ballerini brothers, with the principal textual variants, notes [Col. 0104D], and a historical admonition. Presented to the citizens of the Julia Carolina Academy for the solemn religious service dedicated to Christ incarnate in 1780, by Heinrich Philipp Conrad Hencke, theologian of Helmstedt.

The celebrated editor made excellent use of this solemn occasion to place in the hands of young men diligently studying theology a booklet dealing with so distinguished a subject. Accordingly, in the historical admonition prefixed to the Epistle itself, he first demonstrated how important it is in the history of the doctrine concerning Christ; then he discussed its author, occasion, purpose, authority, and reputation, which it possessed from the very beginning and subsequently acquired in ever greater measure [Col. 0105A].

To help establish the genuine text of the Epistle itself, he also brought forward the ancient Greek version, using it likewise to explain certain more difficult Latin phrases. See the *Helmstedt Commentaries on Recent Literary Matters*, 1781, fascicle I, section 5, p. 38 ff.

### 1789

Paris, at the expense of Pierre Didot the eldest son, folio. *Twelve Epistles of Saint Leo I, Pope, to the Bishops of Gaul, and the Epistle to Flavian (Dogmatic Epistle XXVIII), together with one sent to Ravennius, newly elucidated with Notes, Observations, and Annotations by the Monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur*, in the *Collection of the Councils of Gaul*, recently begun by them, vol. I, pp. 442–568.

Sirmond’s edition served as the foundation. In their corrections, however, they followed Quesnel so closely that they did not neglect to inspect the manuscripts anew. They also had Coustant’s papers available, from which they incorporated quite a few items into their observations.

## § II. Versions

We know that Leo’s Sermons were once held in such high esteem that they were translated into Italian more than once. I have been able to find only one French version, as the following catalogue shows.

### 1485

Florence, folio. *The Sermons of Saint Leo, translated by Filippo di Bartolomeo Corsini*, at the end: “In Florence, on 21 May 1485.”

It reproduces Andrea of Aléria’s edition and also translates his Epistle to Paul II, Supreme Pontiff; this is followed by a brief commendation of the translator attributed to Marsilio Ficino, and thereafter by the work’s rubric. The Ballerini brothers mention this edition in vol. I, preface, p. 30; it is included in the *Library of Vernacular Authors* in *Collection of Scientific and Philological Opuscula*, vol. XXXIV, p. 261; and in Argelati’s *Library of Vernacular Translations* (Milan, 1767), vol. II, p. 300 ff.

### 1547

Venice, “at the sign of Hope,” octavo. *The Divine Sermons of Saint Leo I, Pope, newly translated from Latin into the vernacular by Gabriel Foresto of Brescia.* See the collection cited above and Argelati, p. 301 ff., where the translator’s complete epistle and a table of contents are reproduced and described at considerable length.

From this, however, it appears that there are two versions of Leo’s Sermons from the same year, place, and printer, yet differing considerably in content.

### 1564

Venice, printed by Girolamo Scotto, quarto. Three sermons of Saint Leo I, Pope: Sermon V, *On the Fast of the Seventh Month*; Sermon XI, *On the Fast of the Four Ember Days*; and a sermon for the Feast of All Saints, in *Sermons of Saints Augustine, Chrysostom, Bernard, and Basil*, Part Two. See Argelati, cited above, and p. 158; also vol. I, p. 14. The translator was Galeazzo Florimonzio, bishop.

### 1698

Paris, chez André Pralard, octavo. *Sermons of Saint Leo, Pope, surnamed the Great, translated from Father Quesnel’s Latin edition by Nicolas Fontaine.* Catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, vol. I, p. 385, no. 811.

## § III. Codices

We do not think it worthwhile to examine with particular care the manuscript copies of Leo that were called upon by the editors before Quesnel. After Quesnel, Cacciari collated several codices that Quesnel had not seen; but the Ballerini brothers examined far more of them, and with much greater skill. They devoted such outstanding labor to examining, arranging, and describing these manuscripts that the information obtained here concerning Leo’s manuscript codices may also yield considerable benefit for the works of other ecclesiastical writers, especially those of the Roman pontiffs. We have therefore judged it not unworthy of special attention here.

## I. Quesnel’s Codices

### A) Sermons

1. **Corbeiensis.** Three manuscript codices formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Peter of Corbie, now in the monastic Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, containing sixty or more Sermons.

2. **Navarraeus**, that is, a codex of the Library of the Royal College of Navarre in the University of Paris, containing various Sermons, among them several by Leo.

3. **Regii.** Two lectionaries containing several Sermons of Leo.

4. **Sammaglorianus**, a manuscript lectionary for the use of the Abbey of Saint-Magloire in Paris, in the Sammaglorian Library of the archiepiscopal seminary of the priests of the Oratory of Jesus at the Paris walls.

5. **Thuanei:**  
   1. a manuscript codex formerly belonging to Nicolas Fabri, containing several Sermons of Leo;  
   2. a lectionary for the use of the distinguished Church of Lyon;  
   3. a lectionary codex of Saint-Pierre-du-Fossé, containing several Sermons, written in 1057.

### B) Epistles

1. **Barberiniani.** Three manuscript codices of the Library of Cardinal Francesco Barberini, from which he sent Quesnel, by his own order, after the publication of the first edition, various readings of many Epistles of Saint Leo. They were numbered 57, 77, and 2888. The third also contained the Code of Canons that Quesnel calls Roman.

2. **Bellovacensis**, that is, a manuscript codex of Canons and Papal Decrees belonging to the Library of the Church of Beauvais, containing several items from Leo.

3. **S. Germanensis.** A codex of the Dionysian Collection of Canons and Decrees from the monastic Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

4. **Grimanicus.** A manuscript codex of Cardinal Grimani of Saint Mark’s, approximately nine hundred years old, containing 107 Epistles of Leo, twenty-eight of which had not been published before Quesnel, as well as several others that were almost new. He had received it from the Library of the House of the Oratory of Jesus at the Paris walls. Quesnel discusses this codex at length in the preface, § 5. See the Ballerini brothers’ *Observations*.

5. **Corbeiensis.** A most ancient codex of Canons, whose collection the Ballerini brothers described at great length in their dissertation on ancient collections of Canons, included in vol. III of Leo’s Works. From the monastic Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

6. **Herovallianus.** A manuscript codex of the Isidorian Collection, followed also by Liberatus’s *Breviary* and certain other works. Since he had received it through the good offices of Monsieur Vion d’Heronval, Quesnel called it Herovallianus before learning that it came from the Library of Antoine Faure, doctor of theology, canon of the metropolitan Church of Reims, and vicar general of the bishop of Reims.

7. **Oxoniensis.** A manuscript codex containing the book that Quesnel calls the *Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See*, together with various works of Leo appended to it. E. Bernard, then professor of astronomy at Oxford, sent Quesnel both its contents list and a copy of the codex. It was preserved in the Library of Christ Church College at Oxford, no. 91, B.

8. **Remigianus.** A manuscript codex of Epistles, information about which and various readings from it were supplied from the Library of Saint-Remi at Reims by Dom François Delfau, Benedictine of Saint-Germain.

9. **Thuanei:**  
   1. a manuscript codex of the Canons and Constitutions of the Apostolic See, with thirty-three Epistles of Leo, no. 129;  
   2. a manuscript codex containing several Epistles relating to the Council of Chalcedon and to the privileges of the Church of Arles, as well as a previously unpublished version of Flavian’s Epistle to Saint Leo and other material first brought out of darkness, no. 780;  
   3. a manuscript codex of books *On the Calling of All Nations* and several Epistles of Saint Leo, no. 729;  
   4. a manuscript codex containing many Epistles of Saint Leo, no. 432;  
   5. a manuscript codex of the Canons and Decrees of the Roman Fathers, compiled by Dionysius Exiguus;  
   6, 7, 8. three manuscript codices of the Isidorian Collection of Councils and Papal Epistles;  
   9. a manuscript codex of the Canons and Decrees of the Roman pontiffs, as published at Mainz in 1525, formerly belonging to Claude Fauchet;  
   10. a manuscript codex containing part of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

10. **Treco-Pithoeanus.** A manuscript codex containing many Councils, Papal Epistles—especially those of Leo—and other ecclesiastical monuments. It formerly belonged to the celebrated Pithou and came from the Library of the Troyes-Pithou College of the priests of the Oratory of Jesus.

### C) Sermons and Epistles

1. **Cisterciensis**, that is, the Library of the Cistercian Abbey in Paris: a manuscript codex whose contents list and several passages had been communicated by Dom Jacques de Lannoy, subprior of that abbey.

2. **Claromaricensis**, that is, the Library of the Monastery of Clairmarais near Saint-Omer: a manuscript codex whose contents list Quesnel had received through Jean Mabillon.

3. **S. Mariani et Regniacensis**, that is, the Library of the Premonstratensian Monastery of Saint-Marien at Auxerre: two manuscript codices whose collated readings, together with the contents list of the other, formerly belonging to the monastery of Régny, were excerpted and sent to Quesnel by Dom Chrestien, canon of the Church of Auxerre and doctor of theology in Paris.

4. **Victorinus**, that is, the Library of Saint-Victor in Paris: a manuscript codex containing nearly all the Sermons and Epistles of Saint Leo.

## II. Cacciari’s Codices

### A) Sermons

#### I. Vatican Codices

1. Codex no. 3835. The first part of an ancient parchment lectionary, containing a considerable number of homilies to be recited at the night offices for the Nativity of Saint Leo, the Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension of the Lord, Pentecost, and the solemnities of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Written during the eighth century in Roman characters arranged in two columns. Cacciari reproduced specimens of the script of this and the following codex in copper engraving in the preface to volume I of this review, p. 29.

2. Codex no. 3836, the second part of the preceding lectionary, containing Sermons for the feast of the holy seven brothers, the Maccabees, for Saint Lawrence, on the Fast of the Seventh Month, and other homilies to be recited up to the Nativity of the Lord, among them the celebrated Epistle XXIV to Flavian on the Incarnation of the Word.

3. Codex no. 3828, parchment, written in the tenth century, containing several Sermons of Leo for various solemnities of the year.

4. Codex no. 1195, parchment folio, containing, besides certain homilies of the saints, several also by Leo. In Cacciari’s judgment, written around the eleventh century.

5. Codex no. 1267, like the preceding but larger in format, written in two columns around the eleventh century. Among Sermons of several ancient Fathers, it contains some by Leo the Great on the Nativity, Epiphany, and Saint Stephen.

6. Codex no. 1268, the other part of the preceding lectionary, containing numerous Sermons to be read from Septuagesima Sunday through the Nativity of the Lord.

7. Codex no. 1269, the final part of the same, containing, besides Sermons for the Temporal cycle, prayers for the Nativity of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, for the Nativity of Saint Lawrence, and for the Assumption of Saint Leo to the pontificate.

8. Codex no. 1270, a large parchment folio containing various Sermons of Leo. Cacciari testifies that with its assistance he restored to its original completeness the Sermon on the Feast of the Chair of Peter, which Quesnel had first published, but mutilated and incomplete.

9. Codex no. 1271, parchment folio, presenting various Sermons of Leo.

10. Codex no. 1272, parchment quarto, of the tenth century, containing Sermons and Homilies formerly read on the individual feasts of the apostles. Besides certain prayers of Leo, it also contained an ancient Canon of the Mass, attached to the Homily on the Eight Beatitudes, which Cacciari arranged to have printed in full, together with a specimen of its script, immediately below it, pp. 297–304 of vol. I.

11. Codex no. 4222, large folio, written in Lombard characters in the ninth century, containing certain Sermons of Leo to be read according to the feast days of the year.

12. Codex no. 5451, written in Roman characters in the twelfth century, containing Sermons of Leo on the solemnity of Easter, Pentecost, and the feasts of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

13. Codex no. 6450, parchment, of the twelfth century, containing homilies to be recited at the night offices, among them several by Leo and also the one for the Feast of the Chair of Peter, which was likewise mutilated in Quesnel’s codices.

14. Codex no. 6451, resembling the preceding, written in the same century and character, containing the third Sermon on Easter, with which Cacciari first honored Leo.

15. Codex no. 6452, very similar to the preceding two in format, appearance, century, and script, containing Leo’s Sermons for Lent, together with several others relating to the Passion of the Lord.

16. Codex no. 6454, similar to the preceding three. Besides other Sermons of the Fathers, it contained, under Leo’s name, several from the published collection and several others, which he rejected into an appendix as doubtful [Col. 0109B].

#### II. Vatican-Palatine Codices nos. 442 and 443

Two paper books of Readings and Homilies of the Holy Fathers, containing numerous Sermons of Leo, some of them mutilated and incomplete, adapted for the use of a particular church. The script was German, divided into two columns and filled with extremely difficult abbreviated signs; Cacciari admits that he himself was unable to read it.

#### III. Old Vallicellian Codex

An ancient book containing various Sermons of Leo, which Cacciari himself did not see. Father Joseph Blanchini, however, carefully collated it with the printed editions, and certain Sermons were copied from it; Cacciari refers to them in their proper places.

#### IV. Chisian Codex

A codex formerly copied from the Vatican archives, containing various Sermons of Leo, among them three of those which Chrysostomus Trombetti was the first of all to prepare in vol. II, part I, of the *Anecdota*.

### B) Epistles

#### a) Latin

##### 1. Vatican Codices

1. Codex no. 541, large parchment folio, carefully decorated around the thirteenth century with various paintings in gold and vermilion, and used by Pope Nicholas V. It contains all the Epistles of Leo found in editions published before the Quesnellian edition.

2. Codex no. 542, parchment quarto, of the thirteenth century, containing the same Epistles.

3, 4, 5, 6, 7. Codices nos. 543–547, all similar to the preceding in script, collection of Epistles, and age. None was written before the twelfth century [Col. 0109D]. They nevertheless differed from one another in their readings.

8. Codex no. 630, large parchment folio, approximately of the thirteenth century, containing Isidore Mercator’s collection of Canons and Epistles of the Roman pontiffs, among them thirty-nine by Leo.

9. Codex no. 631, presenting a collection similar to the preceding, copied toward the end of the twelfth century, but containing only five Epistles of Leo.

10. Codex no. 1319, quarto, of the twelfth century, containing the acts of the Council of Chalcedon together with various Epistles of Leo written concerning the case of Eutyches and the Eutychians.

11. Codex no. 1321, small folio, approximately of the twelfth century, containing Facundus of Hermiane’s books *For the Council of Chalcedon*. Among them are not only various fragments of Leo’s Epistles [Col. 0110A], but also those Epistles that Leo composed in confirmation of that general council.

12. Codex no. 1322, manifestly most ancient, as appears from the specimen of its script that Cacciari had engraved in the preface to volume II, p. 65. It contains all the individual acts of the Council of Chalcedon. Among them Cacciari notes the act concerning the case of Domnus, bishop of Antioch, which Quesnel judged should be rejected as spurious and fabricated by a Latin impostor: first, because, as he claimed, it is not read in the Greek copies; and second, because it was said to have emerged from a single paper codex of no authority or antiquity, produced by unknown scholars. This codex also contains various Epistles relating to the same council.

13. Codex no. 1342, parchment, written at the end of the ninth or beginning of the tenth century. Cacciari had its script and marks copied in the same place as those of the preceding codex. It contains an ancient Collection of Canons with sixteen Epistles of Leo, the first of them to Rusticus of Narbonne.

14. Codex no. 1328, parchment folio, approximately of the twelfth century, containing the acts of the Sixth General Council and, besides fragments of Epistles occurring in those acts, certain other Epistles of Leo together with some acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

15. Codex no. 1337, parchment, written before the eleventh century, containing the Canons of various councils and the decretal Epistles of several supreme pontiffs. The Collection begins with the Nicene Canons and presents all the titles of Leo’s decretal Epistles together with the Epistles themselves.

16. Codex no. 1338, containing a collection similar to the preceding but copied later, in the thirteenth century. Among the Leonine Canons it also lists the Epistle to the Africans of the province of Mauretania, written concerning the case of Bishop Lupicinus, which Quesnel dared to call spurious.

17. Codex no. 1340, parchment, of the thirteenth century, containing Isidore’s Collection, including all the Epistles of Leo found in the editions of Surius, the Louvain scholars, and Raynaldus. Cacciari testifies that he used this Collection very frequently, since he found it more accurately corrected than the more recent copies.

18. Codex no. 1341, of the eleventh century, written by a careful and skilled scribe, containing, besides the Canons of various councils and the Epistles of several Roman pontiffs, forty-one Epistles of Leo.

19. Codex no. 1343, of the eleventh century, containing a collection exactly similar to the preceding.

20. Codex no. 1344, entirely similar to the preceding two in format and script, containing the acts of the Council of Chalcedon together with Leo’s Epistles relating to it.

21. Codex no. 1345, of the eleventh century, entitled *The Collection of Cresconius*, formerly belonging to the celebrated monastery of Saint Columbanus at Bobbio, containing several Epistles of Leo.

22. Codex no. 1353, of the twelfth century, very well written, containing several Epistles of Leo.

23. Codex no. 3791, of the twelfth century and excellent quality, containing fifty Epistles of Leo.

24. Codex no. 3836, the lectionary mentioned above under the Sermons, containing only the Epistle to Flavian, which in the eighth and ninth centuries they customarily read in the divine offices before the feast of the Nativity.

25. Codex no. 3787, parchment folio, of the twelfth century, containing six Epistles concerning the case of the Church of Alexandria and Timothy the Cat.

26. Codex no. 4661, corresponding to the preceding, containing the same number of Epistles.

27. Codex no. 5748, containing Cresconius’s Harmony of the Canons together with several decretal Epistles of Leo.

28. Codex no. 5750, written before the ninth century. It formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint Columbanus at Bobbio. It contains thirty-one Epistles of Leo together with the first act of the Council of Chalcedon. Cacciari reproduced its format and script in copper engraving on p. 65.

29. Codex no. 5845, extremely ancient and usually called by Cacciari Lombardic, containing a Collection of Canons and Epistles of the Roman pontiffs, among them twenty-four by Leo.

#### II. Vatican-Palatine Codex
