Codex no. 579, of the tenth century, containing only four Epistles of Leo.

#### III. Vatican-Urbinate Codices

1. Codex no. 65, parchment, excellently written in the fifteenth century, containing all the Epistles published in editions before Quesnel.

2. Codex no. 179, recent and therefore of little use, containing Isidore Mercator’s Collection.

#### IV. Vatican-Alexandrian Codices

That is, Vatican codices formerly belonging to Queen Christina Alexandra of Sweden.

1. Codex no. 586, parchment quarto, of the twelfth century, containing, among other things, Paschasinus of Lilybaeum’s Epistle to Leo.

2. Codex no. 755, small parchment folio, of the thirteenth century, containing the same author’s Epistle on the observance of Easter.

3. Codex no. 849, parchment, of the twelfth century, containing a Collection of Canons, chiefly from the councils of Africa, certain acts of the Council of Chalcedon, and Leo’s Epistle to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

4. Codex no. 1038, parchment folio, of the twelfth century, containing the Decrees of the Roman pontiffs from Isidore’s Collection, as well as Bede’s book *On the Computation* and other works.

5. Codex no. 1039, parchment folio, of the fourteenth century, containing Cresconius’s *Harmony of Discordant Canons*.

6. Codex no. 1040, folio, of the eleventh century, containing the Sixth General Council.

7. Codex no. 1044, parchment folio, of the thirteenth century, containing the Epistles of the Roman pontiffs from Clement to Leo.

8. Codex no. 1043, parchment folio, of the thirteenth century, containing a Collection of Canons—“perhaps Dionysian,” Cacciari says—with the added Decrees of Symmachus and Hormisdas.

9. Codex no. 1127, parchment folio, of the tenth century, containing various works of the Fathers and a codex of Canons comprising the Decrees of the apostles and councils and the Epistles of the Roman pontiffs.

10. Codex no. 1997, parchment folio, of the tenth century, containing the Dionysian Collection, in which there are only five Epistles of Leo.

#### V. Turin Codex

Codex no. 29, D. IV, of the Royal Library, parchment folio, excellently written around the thirteenth century, containing fifty-two Epistles of Leo and several by others. It was collated for Cacciari in 1739 by Father Cyril Gubernatis, a Carmelite of Turin.

#### VI. Florentine Codex

A parchment folio of the Medicean Library, of the thirteenth century, containing all the Epistles of Leo published in editions before Quesnel.

#### VII. Grimani Codex

Cacciari had a copy of this celebrated codex transcribed on paper in Paris in order to test Quesnel’s accuracy, and from there deposited it in the Vatican Library.

#### VIII. Regensburg Codex

Codex no. 113, DDAA, of the Library of the Monastery of Saint Emmeram, parchment quarto, consisting of 157 folios and containing seventy-two Epistles of Leo. Cacciari had the form of its script, taken from a drawing by Frobenius Forster, then prior and librarian at Saint Emmeram, who had copied the same Epistles most carefully for the use of the Roman editor, engraved in copper on p. 62 of the preface.

On the basis of Forster’s testimony concerning its age, Bernard Pez estimated it at nearly a thousand years in vol. I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, p. 11. More about it may be found in Forster’s letter, dated at Saint Emmeram on 21 August 1752 and printed on pp. 61 ff.

#### b) Greek

##### I. Vatican Codices

1. Codex no. 451, paper folio, of the fourteenth century, containing among the writings of various Greek Fathers a fragment of Flavian’s Epistle to Leo on the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ.

2. Codex no. 730, paper folio, approximately of the fifteenth century, containing the Epistles of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus.

3. Codex no. 720, parchment folio, of the tenth century, containing among the works of various Fathers several Epistles of Leo.

4. Codex no. 712, octavo, of the fourteenth century, containing Epistles of various Fathers, especially those that Flavian wrote to Leo concerning the case of Eutyches, together with Leo’s replies.

5. Codex no. 1178, paper folio, of the fifteenth century, containing all the acts of the Council of Chalcedon together with the Epistles of Leo relating to it.

6. Codex no. 1431, parchment folio, of the twelfth century, containing, among various works and Epistles, also Epistles of Leo together with collections relating to the Council of Chalcedon.

7. Codex no. 1455, cotton paper, of the thirteenth century, excellently written, containing Epistles of the Roman pontiffs and the holy Fathers. Among them are the Epistles of Flavian, Theodoret, Anatolius, and Marcian to Leo, together with Leo’s replies.

##### II. Royal-Vatican Codices

1. Codex no. 44, paper quarto, of the sixteenth century, containing Homilies and works of several holy Fathers and other authors, relating both to Scripture and to ecclesiastical matters, among them several Epistles of Leo.

2. Codex no. 57, paper folio, of the fourteenth century, containing the Canons of general and particular councils and other works of the ancient Fathers, among them the Epistles of Flavian and Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, to Leo.

[Col. 0113A] 3. Codex no. 67, paper, fifteenth century, containing only one letter of Leo.

III. Vatican–Ottobonian, codex no. 29, not unlike Vatican codex no. 1178, containing all the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, together with various letters of Leo contained therein.

## C) Sermons and Letters

### I. Vatican Codices

1. Codex no. 541, parchment, ornamented with gold and various colors at the command of Nicholas V, containing only the Sermons and Letters of Leo—specifically, those published in editions issued before Quesnel.

2. Codex no. 542, parchment in quarto, from the end of the twelfth century. A similar collection.

3. Codex no. 644, parchment in folio, approximately from the thirteenth century. A collection not unlike the preceding one.

[Col. 0113B] 4. Codex no. 545, parchment in quarto, written around the end of the twelfth century. It contains an equal number of sermons and letters.

5. Codex no. 546, parchment in folio, twelfth century. A collection similar to the preceding one.

6. Codex no. 547, parchment in quarto, of the same age and condition.

7. Codex no. 548, parchment in quarto. Besides the sermons contained in the preceding codices, it also presented a sermon on Absalom, but Cacciarius judged that it did not belong to Leo and therefore omitted it.

8. Codex no. 549, parchment in quarto, similar to the preceding one and likewise containing the sermon on Absalom at the end.

9. Codex no. 550, parchment in quarto, in every respect similar to the preceding codices.

[Col. 0113C] II. Regio-Vatican, codex no. 139 of the Alexandrian Library, parchment in quarto, very finely written, from the twelfth century, containing only a collection of Leo’s Sermons, Homilies, and Letters.

III. Urbino. Codex no. 65, parchment in small folio, from the end of the fourteenth century, containing the same collection.

## III. BALLERINI CODICES

### A) Sermons

#### a) Lectionaries

I. Bergamo: two codices, approximately from the twelfth century, from the archives of the Lords of the Consortium of the Church of Saint Alexander in Colonna, in the possession of the Bergamese patrician Joseph de Salvaneis de Roteriis, containing twelve sermons of Leo.

[Col. 0113D] II. Chigi: two codices of the Chigi Library, nos. 3 and 5, from the twelfth century, containing four sermons of Leo.

III. Padilirone: three codices of the monastery of Padilirone of Saint Benedict in the Mantuan territory, containing nine sermons of Leo and the Letter to Flavian.

IV. Padua: codex no. 408 of the Conventual Fathers of Saint Anthony, from the thirteenth century, containing thirty sermons.

V. Hermits of Padua: three codices of the Hermit Fathers of Saints Philip and James, nos. 111, 110, and 113, containing sixteen sermons together with the Letter to Flavian.

VI. Padua, Saint Justina: two codices of the Cassinese monks of Saint Justina, from the fifteenth century, containing fourteen sermons together with the aforementioned letter.

[Col. 0114A] VII. Basilica of Saint Peter in the Vatican: three codices, nos. 107, 105, and 106. The first two, however, were far superior to the third. Although the third was written in the twelfth century, it contained no more than six authentic sermons of Leo, along with others falsely attributed to him.

VIII. Trent: a manuscript codex of the chapter of Trent, from the fourteenth century, containing four sermons of Leo.

IX. Vallicella—that is, codices of the Library of Saint Mary in Vallicella belonging to the Fathers of the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri in Rome. This library placed several codices from the eleventh and twelfth centuries at the disposal of the Ballerini. Among these they listed codices 25 and 26, which, besides Letter 165, read to Leo Augustus during Advent (in place of which [Col. 0114B] other lectionaries contain Letter 28, to Flavian), contained twenty-five sermons; codex 2, containing the Letter to Flavian and twenty-four sermons; codex A. 6, containing seven sermons; codex A. 7, containing thirteen sermons; codex A. 9, which had belonged to the monastery of Saint Eutychius, containing ten sermons; codex A. 10, containing seven sermons; and codices 7, 20, 23, and A. 16, containing five, four, or three sermons.

[Col. 0114B] X. Vatican codices: the oldest of all the lectionaries, among which nos. 3835 and 3836 especially stood out as truly Roman; these they examined with the greatest care. They also inspected several other lectionary codices, though not throughout, but wherever necessary.

XI. Venice: two codices of the Venetian Library of Saint Mark, lectionaries designated nos. 153 and 154, approximately from the [Col. 0114C] thirteenth century, containing fifty-one sermons of Leo.

XII. Vercelli. From the lectionaries of the Eusebian Library of the chapter of Vercelli, they obtained collated readings of eleven sermons of Leo.

XIII. Verona, Chapter—that is, of the Library of the Chapter of Verona: two lectionary codices that supplied fifteen sermons of Leo; in addition, codex 74, older than the preceding ones, containing eight sermons; and a more recent manuscript book, no. 214, containing one sermon.

XIV. Verona, Saint Firmus—that is, a codex of the Conventual Fathers of Saint Firmus Major. A lectionary from approximately the thirteenth century, containing one sermon of Leo.

#### b) Collections

[Col. 0114D]

They distinguished five manuscript types of these collections. Only the most important codices of each type are indicated: from Collection I, the manuscript book of Monte Cassino, no. 126; from Collection II, Barberinian codex no. 88 and Casanatensian codex C. III, 7; from Collection III, the copies of the first edition, which they judged to have been taken from a manuscript of this collection; from Collection IV, Vatican codex no. 546, and codex 541, which was used on occasion; and finally, from Collection V, Vatican codex no. 544.

### B) Letters

These matters have been discussed so clearly and fully in the observations of the Ballerini that an enumeration of each codex seemed superfluous.

[Note: [Col. 0113D] Under the title *Observations of the Ballerini*, Schoenemann presents fragments of the prefaces that the editorial brothers prefixed to the Sermons and Letters of Saint Leo. [Col. 0114D] We shall present these prefaces in their proper place and therefore refer the reader there. EDIT.]

[Col. 0115]

# TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENT FATHERS CONCERNING SAINT LEO

## The Dedication Letter of John Cassian, Presbyter, for His Books on the Incarnation of Christ against Nestorius

[Col. 0115A]

Having long ago completed the little books of the *Spiritual Conferences*, distinguished more by their meaning than by their language—for the language of our incompetence was unequal to the profound understanding of holy men—I had considered, and had almost resolved, after that shame of publicly revealed ignorance, to establish myself in the harbor of silence, so that, as far as lay within me, I might excuse through the modesty of silence the boldness of speech.

But you have overcome my purpose and decision by your praiseworthy zeal and your most commanding affection, my Leo, my venerable and admirable beloved [Alternative: “my venerable Leo”], the glory of the Roman Church and of the divine ministry. You draw me from that retreat of premeditated silence into the [Col. 0115B] public arena and its fearful judgment, and you compel me, still ashamed of the past, to undertake new trials. Although I was unequal even to lesser tasks, you force me to be equal to greater ones.

For I would not even have attempted to undertake or appropriate anything in those little works by which, through the small offering of our feeble talent, we sacrificed to the Lord, had I not been compelled by episcopal authority. Thus, through you, the dignity of our mouth and pen has increased. Formerly we were ordered to speak about the Lord’s concerns; now you demand that we speak about the Lord’s Incarnation itself and his majesty. Thus, having previously been introduced into the holy temple, as it were by a priestly hand, under your guidance and with your assistance we now penetrate, as it were, into the Holy of Holies.

Great is the honor, but dangerous the advance [Alternative: “the undertaking”], [Col. 0115C] because the prize of gaining access to the sacred inner sanctuary and the divine reward cannot be obtained unless the enemy is overcome. You therefore demand and command that our weak hands engage the recent heresy and the new enemy of the faith, and that we stand with open mouth, as they say, against the deadly serpent’s deep jaws. You wish the prophetic power and divine force of evangelical speech, as though I were an enchanter, to burst in upon the dragon rising against the Churches of God in its winding coils.

I obey your entreaty; I obey your command. For I would rather trust you concerning myself than trust myself concerning me, especially since the love of Jesus Christ my Lord commands this together with you—and commands the same thing in you. It remains for you to ask from the one through whom you commanded that the task you imposed may be brought to completion. For here it is now more your cause than mine that is at stake; your [Col. 0115D] judgment, rather than my service, is in danger.

Whether I am equal to your command or not, the very reason of obedience and humility excuses me to some extent—except that my obedience has greater merit if my ability is smaller. We easily satisfy anyone’s command from an abundance of resources; but great and admirable is the service of one who has in his desire even what he does not have in his strength.

This, then, is your affair, your task, the work of your responsibility. Pray and entreat that your choice may not be endangered by my incompetence; and if we do not measure up to the great opinion [Col. 0116A] held of us, then, although I may rightly obey through the pardon granted by obedience, you may nevertheless appear to have commanded wrongly through lack of careful judgment.

## Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, in a Letter to Bishop Abundius, in Baronius, under the year 450, no. 33

We have read what he [Saint Leo] wrote to Flavian, of holy and blessed memory, and we gave thanks to our most humane Lord God because we had found an advocate and defender of the truth. I too agreed with this letter . . . . I also subscribed to it; and from this I proved that I follow the apostolic rules—that is, the true doctrines.

## At the Council of Chalcedon, Act 2, after Leo’s second Letter to Flavian had been read, the Fathers cried out:

“Peter has spoken through Leo . . . . Leo has taught piously and [Col. 0116B] truly.”

## The Same Council in Its Report to Pulcheria, Published in the Fourth Volume of the Venetian Edition of the Councils, p. 1354

“They have brought their ships back onto their course, with Christ favorably guiding them toward understanding. He has shown the truth in the remarkable person of Leo; just as he used wise Peter, so he uses this man as its defender.”

## The Same Council in Its Address to the Emperor Marcian, vol. IV of the Councils, p. 1758

“God has provided us with an impenetrable defender against every error and has prepared the pope of the Roman Church for victory, binding him in every respect to the teachings of the truth, so that, just as Peter did, this man too, contending with still more fervent devotion, may lead every perception and understanding toward God.”

## Leontius, Bishop of Arles, in a Letter to Pope Hilary, Leo’s Successor, vol. V of the Councils, p. 63

[Col. 0116D]

“We grieve that death has taken away Leo, your most holy predecessor, who kept watch against heresies and, alas, was uprooting the tares that were flourishing all too abundantly in the Lord’s field.”

## Pope Simplicius in a Letter to the Emperor Leo, vol. V, p. 98

“Pope Leo explained the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation so fully and clearly that no one who does not plainly recognize there [that is, in Leo’s letters] the causes of his redemption can now be called not only a Catholic, but even a Christian.”

## Pope Gelasius at the Roman Synod of Seventy Bishops, in the Decree on Apocryphal Books, vol. V, p. 387

[Col. 0116D] “We accept the letter of the blessed Pope Leo addressed to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople. If anyone disputes even one iota of its text and does not accept it in every respect with reverence, let him be anathema.”

## The Eastern Bishops in a Letter to Pope Symmachus, vol. V, p. 436

“Leo, the archbishop who preceded Your Beatitude and who has been numbered among the saints, did not consider it unworthy to go in person to Attila, then a wandering barbarian, [Col. 0117A] in order to redress bodily captivity.” And below, p. 437: “The true confession of the right faith handed down to us by Pope Leo, who has been numbered among the saints.”

## Cassiodorus in His Commentary on Psalm 65

“Pope Leo, the apostolic teacher, writing to Flavian, says . . . .”

## Facundus of Hermiane, Book XII, chapter 2

“Who would not praise the dignity of this Roman bishop [Leo]? Who would not honor such steadfastness? Could secular power in any way move him from his decision not to retract what had been divinely established at the Council of Chalcedon, when it could not physically move him from his place?”

## Pope Vigilius in the *Constitutum* of 24 February 554, vol. VI of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 305, no. 22

[Col. 0117B] “The letter of so distinguished a pontiff and teacher—that is, of the blessed Leo—plainly containing pious doctrines, and so forth.”

## Saint Pope Gregory, Letter 52 of Book IX

“The most holy Churches of the East hold the faith of Leo, of blessed memory, with one understanding and one doctrine.”

## Saint Maximus the Greek Theologian in the Spiritual and Dogmatic Tome against the *Ecthesis* of the Emperor Heraclius

“The most holy Leo, bishop of the great Roman Church, a man of the most courageous spirit.”

## Hadrian I to the Bishops throughout Spain, Letter 97 of the *Codex Carolinus*

“But blessed Leo, that distinguished pope and eminent [Col. 0118A] teacher, also taught us in his sermon on the holy Epiphany as follows . . . .”

## Pope Nicholas I in a Letter to the Emperor Michael

“When all the bishops, and even the patriarchs themselves, were collapsing in the Ephesian Robbery, unless Leo the Great—an imitator, of course, of that Leo of whom it is written, ‘The Lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered’—had been divinely raised up, opened his mouth, shaken the whole world and the emperors themselves, and moved them to piety, the Christian religion would have utterly collapsed.”

## Photius of Constantinople in a Letter to Michael, Prince of Bulgaria

“There was great glory and great zeal and devotion for piety and religion in the most holy Pope Leo of Rome.”

## The Greek Menologion Compiled at the Command of the Emperor Basil

[Col. 0118B]

“Leo, bishop of the Roman Church, endowed with admirable strength of spirit, wisdom, and holiness, left behind most distinguished monuments attesting to his virtue, and especially to his right faith.”

## Ado, Bishop of Vienne, in His Chronicle

“Leo, the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome, is regarded as illustrious for his teaching of the faith.”

## The Synodical Booklet, chapter 94

“Leo, pope of Rome, equal to the apostles.”

Other ancient testimonies are found partly in letters written to Leo and partly in admonitions, especially those inserted in connection with Letter 28.

# THE FIRST PART OF THE AUTHENTIC WORKS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF, CONTAINING THE SERMONS OF THE HOLY FATHER

[Col. 0117]

## PREFACE: The Manuscript Sources from Which the Sermons of Saint Leo Were Produced and from Which They Must Especially Be Corrected

1. There are, in general, two manuscript sources from which the sermons of the holy Fathers may be consulted or corrected: namely, the lectionaries compiled from the sermons of various saints, and the separate collections of the sermons of an individual saint.

# CHAPTER ONE

## On Manuscript Lectionaries, the First Source of the Sermons of Saint Leo

[Col. 0119]

### § I. On the Antiquity and Excellence of the Lectionaries, and How Carefully We Sought These Codices

2. Lectionaries are ordinarily of older origin. For it has happened to only a few saints, such as Saints Zeno, Gaudentius, and Peter Chrysologus, that collections of their sermons, equal or nearly equal in age to their authors, have come down to us. This perhaps happened because, if their sermons had not been preserved in separate collections, those whose sermons were not transferred into lectionaries would have perished.

But when, not long after an author’s death, his sermons possessed such authority and renown that they were entered into the lectionaries of almost all the Churches and read during public services, then either no collections were made, or, if some were made, they gradually perished. Since all, or nearly all, the sermons were preserved in the books of the Churches, it seemed unnecessary to copy a separate collection of them.

Thus Possidius suggests that Augustine’s sermons—or, as they were called, his treatises—had existed in some arrangement in the library of the Church of Hippo. In the eighteenth chapter of Augustine’s *Life*, speaking of the treatises just as he speaks of the other works of the holy teacher, which were certainly contained in separate codices, he states that he appended a list of them all, so that each person might choose what he wished to read and learn, and might seek it for copying either from the library of the Church of Hippo, where more accurate copies might perhaps be found, or from wherever else he wished, and copy what he found.

Nevertheless, the oldest copies of this kind are lacking. For, as the most learned Maurist Fathers observed in the preface to volume V, the three oldest surviving collections of the sermons of Saint Augustine—*On the Words of the Lord*, *On the Words of the Apostle*, and the collection of fifty homilies—although they are found in manuscripts eight hundred years old or more, cannot be considered equal in age to Augustine. This is so not only because Possidius does not mention them, but especially because they are not free from spurious material.

In other words, Augustine’s sermons were transmitted piecemeal in lectionaries, thereby eliminating the need to undertake the labor of copying collections. The three collections mentioned above were later compiled from lectionaries, and subsequently other sermons were copied from other lectionaries and added to Augustine’s works in editions that appeared from time to time. Nor will there be lacking those who may derive other sermons of the same teacher from these same sources, just as we intend at some point to publish more than twenty authentic sermons in the *Miscellaneous Anecdota*.

3. We think that something similar happened with the sermons of Saint Leo. That this holy pontiff labored over his sermons with great care and retained accurate copies of them is shown by the fact that, in his dogmatic letters—which, because of the sublime and difficult exposition of the doctrines discussed in them, demanded the greatest care and selectiveness not so much in thought as in wording—he inserted considerable fragments from certain sermons.

There can be no doubt that these autograph copies of the sermons were preserved for a long time in the apostolic archive. But because of the author’s authority and renown, and the special care he devoted to composing his sermons, they were copied shortly after Leo’s death into the lectionaries of the Roman Churches among the sermons of other saints. From there they passed into similar codices of other Churches throughout the West.

As a result, in ancient times there was no concern to gather these same sermons into a separate volume. Therefore it is not surprising that Gennadius, who mentions the sermons of Saint Maximus of Turin, makes no mention of Leo’s sermons in chapter 70. He found some very ancient collection of Maximus’s sermons, but none of Leo’s; nor did he direct his eyes and mind toward the lectionaries into which Leo’s sermons had been transferred.

4. The oldest sources, therefore, from which Leo’s sermons have come down to us are the ancient lectionaries. Ninth-century writers certainly cited them: Hincmar of Reims, Remigius of Lyons, Prudentius of Troyes, and especially Florus.

Florus compiled from Leo’s testimonies an entire book of sixty-two large columns, written in abbreviated notation, preserved in manuscript collections on Paul’s letters at the Grande Chartreuse. He very plainly excerpted fragments of sermons from lectionaries, for he uses the same order and titles that we find in the lectionaries of the Basilica of Saint Peter.

Before all these writers, Paul the Deacon used the same lectionaries in his *Homiliary*, in which he copied several sermons of Leo according to the requirements of the feasts.

5. We were able to see and consult many codices of this kind, and among them some of the highest quality, which derive from different sources, in the Roman libraries: the Vatican, the Basilica of Saint Peter, the Vallicellana, and the Chigiana; in Venice, at Saint Mark’s and Saint Gregory the Great; in Padua, those of the monks of Saint Justina, the Conventual Fathers of Saint Anthony, and the Hermits of Saints Philip and James; in the Eusebian Library of the chapter of the cathedral of Vercelli; in the Royal Library of Turin; in the Cassinese monastery of Saint Benedict at Padilirone; in Saint Alexander in Colonna at Bergamo; and finally in our own chapter library at Verona.

Readings, or corrections of readings, must be taken chiefly from these manuscripts, since they are the older sources of the sermons. Quesnel, who recognized that these codices were more excellent and of earlier origin than the manuscript collections—as is clear from his general preface, before its midpoint—acknowledged that the lectionaries deserved the greatest consideration when revising the sermons. The principal corrections he introduced into the text owe their origin to these manuscripts.

But he encountered this disadvantage in such books: they do not all contain the sermons, and some contain certain sermons while others contain different ones, according to the diverse customs of the Churches for whose use they were copied. Thus one generally has to examine immense and countless volumes in order to compare a few sermons with those codices.

Having encountered this [Col. 0121] difficulty, I say, he examined only a limited number of lectionaries, and in those he used he did not find all of Leo’s sermons. Deprived of this assistance, he was forced to compare many sermons only with the later collections, which are less accurate.

We, however, having understood that the lectionaries deserved primary consideration, spared no labor and diligently sought out as many as we could. With fortunate success, we were able to find and collate all the sermons that could usefully be found in lectionaries, except for the four sermons mentioned under no. 9, which we sought in vain amid such a multitude of lectionaries.

Here we must acknowledge that we were neither able nor did we think it necessary to reread each sermon against every manuscript of this kind, since we found them copied in very many of them. We considered it sufficient to collate them with the more excellent lectionaries, while examining the other codices of this kind wherever certain passages presenting variant readings here and there created greater difficulty.

### § II. On Manuscript Lectionaries Certainly Roman

6. To say something particular about these lectionaries: we value not so much their number as the excellence of certain ones. Quesnel saw none of these Roman codices, although they were always carefully preserved in the Roman Church and transmitted to later generations. Since they derive their origin from Leo’s original and autograph writings, they possess the greatest authority.

We found four manuscript books that we can confidently call Roman, because they were formerly used in the public services of the Roman Churches. First are two Vatican parchment codices in folio, nos. 3835 and 3836. Written in Roman, or—as they say—uncial letters around the eighth century, they belonged to the Basilica of Saints Philip and James, as the following antiquarian note at the end of codex 3835 indicates:

“You who read, I beg you to pray for the scribe, that through the prince of the apostles [read: ‘through the prince,’ singular] the bonds of Agimundus, the sinful presbyter, may be loosed, as of an unworthy scribe. Thanks be to the God of heaven. Basilica of the Apostles Philip and James.”

The remarkable antiquity of the first scribe is confirmed by these words appended to the sermons on the Ascension, in which Leo, not yet numbered among the saints, is honored with the title “lord”:

“The sermons of Lord Leo, pope, on the Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ, two in number, are completed. Thanks be to God.”

In this manuscript, Vatican 3835, accurately described by Father Joseph Blanchini with a specimen of its script in volume II of the *Evangelia Quadruplicia*, p. 602, there are Leo’s first ten sermons on the Passion, two on the Ascension, three on Pentecost, and two on Saint Peter.

Vatican 3836 contains three sermons on the fast of the tenth month—nos. 1, 7, and 8 in the editions—as well as three on his own feast, that is, on Leo’s accession to the pontificate: nos. 1, with no. 2 attached to it, 3, and 4 in the editions; nine on the fast of the seventh month; and a sermon on Saint Laurence.

7. There are also two lectionary books of the Basilica of Saint Peter. The first, designated no. 107, although written in a later script, is nevertheless to be valued more highly. For it was copied not only from an older lectionary of the same basilica, worn down or almost destroyed by long use, whose origin derived from the autographs that Leo had left to the Roman Church; it is also much more accurate than the others. Accordingly, we excerpted from it very many important corrections that we found in no other books, or in only a few.

That it was intended for the use of the basilica itself is made certain by the careful account, read at the end, of the revenues paid to that basilica from the entire Christian world.

It contains sermons from Advent to the Lord’s Passion. It presents all the sermons inscribed with Leo’s name as authentic and none as spurious. Moreover, none of Leo’s sermons from that period is missing from this codex, except for four: no. 20, on the fast of the tenth month; no. 51, on Lent; and nos. 56 and 60, on the Passion. Other lectionary books of other Churches omit many sermons and frequently attribute to Leo some that have other authors.

The other codex of the same basilica, no. 105, is completely similar to this one, except that in copying the final sermons of certain solemnities the scribe sometimes stopped short. Nevertheless, it derives from the same exemplar, since it presents the sermons it contains in the same order and with nearly the same readings.

If copies of the other part, extending from Easter to Advent, still existed in the same basilica, we have no doubt that we would likewise find all, or nearly all, of Leo’s other sermons copied there. Thus corrections could have been sought more securely from this one library. But since this part is missing there—the most exact of all—we have been deprived of a great and especially valuable aid.

### § III. On the Manuscript Lectionaries of Other Churches and How Much They Contributed; Three Sermons of Saint Leo Published from a Single Codex of Nicolas Faber Vindicated; On the Disadvantages and Usefulness of Lectionaries

8. When we examined the lectionaries of the other Churches already mentioned, although none of them is as accurate throughout as the praised codices of the Vatican basilica, they nevertheless either confirmed or supplied quite a few excellent readings and provided considerable assistance for sermons that were missing from them.

We also succeeded, through the multiplicity of codices that we searched everywhere, in finding copies of certain sermons that no one else had found. Four sermons on the offerings and one on the octave of the Apostles, which, for a particular reason, we had despaired of finding inserted in Leo’s other lectionaries, we found in the Vallicellana manuscript lectionary A. 6.

His distinctive sermons on his own feast, which Quesnel was unable to find in any lectionary, were found in Vatican 3836 and also in Vallicellana A. 7, except for the fifth, which was published from Faber’s unique codex.

9. There remain four sermons that we were unable to find in any lectionary: namely, the fifth sermon on the pope’s feast, the sixth on the offerings, the ninth on the fast of the tenth month, and the ninety-sixth, entitled:

[Col. 0123] “Treatise against the Eutychians, delivered in the Church of Saint Anastasia.”

Since this sermon against the Eutychians was preserved in the manuscript collections of Saint Leo—which, as we shall see, derive from the lectionaries—we have no doubt that it is contained in some lectionary book that we have not yet been able to find.

10. We do not believe that the same can be said of the other three sermons: the fifth on the pope’s feast, the sixth on the offerings, and the ninth on the fast of the tenth month, which were published from the manuscript of Nicolas Faber.

Just as they are absent from the collections of Saint Leo’s sermons that derived from lectionaries, so we judge that they were neither found nor can be found in any lectionaries. We therefore think that these three sermons are contained in a single codex of Nicolas Faber, unless perhaps another similar one should someday emerge.

This codex of Faber, which in Quesnel’s time had passed into the library of the House of Thou, from which it is called “Thuaneus” by the same author, later moved into the Colbertine Library and finally into the Royal Library of Paris. It contains various short works of the Fathers.

Joseph Antelmius discusses it at length in dissertation 6, *On the True Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, no. 4 and following, and he states, on the judgment of Mabillon, Baluze, and other experts, that it was written more than nine hundred years ago.

Among the short works of various Fathers, three sermons of Leo are copied. The first is erroneously attributed to Prosper under this title: “Here begins Prosper’s sermon on the pope’s feast.” The other two sermons are entitled: “Here begins [the sermon] on the day of the offerings,” and “Here begins [the sermon] on the fast of the tenth month.”

That all these sermons belong to Leo is decisively demonstrated by their style and by the agreement of their subject matter and ideas with the other sermons bearing the same titles that are unquestionably Leonine.

Nicolas Faber, who owned the codex itself, recognized this in a letter to Vossius, provost of Tongeren, inserted among his short works. Concerning the first sermon, which bears Prosper’s name, he says:

“As for the one attributed to Prosper, its being by the same author as the others is indicated to me by its similarity and by the fact that its author speaks of himself as if he were the Roman pontiff. For although they say that blessed Leo made use of Prosper’s works, no one will persuade me that the most eloquent pontiff begged words from another and proclaimed them to the people as his own.”

Antelmius himself, who in the aforementioned dissertation had seemed to attribute not merely these three but all of Leo’s sermons to Prosper in some sense, and who had introduced the inscription of this codex, explained his thought more clearly in a second letter written in French on 4 November 1689, nos. 35 and 40. There he added his own vote to the common judgment by which the sermons are attributed to Leo.

But who can determine why these three sermons of Leo are found in this one codex, which contains nothing else by Leo, or why at least the first bears Prosper’s name?

Perhaps Prosper, who was very close to Leo and is called his notary by Ado, copied these sermons separately in his own hand and sent them to Gaul, where they were preserved for us. Then perhaps the first copyist who inserted them into the codex, recognizing the scribe from his familiar handwriting, made him out to be the author.

Something similar happened with letters. Five letters of Leo have been preserved for us among the works of others solely in the manuscript copies of the Avellana collection, which will be discussed more fully in the preface to Leo’s letters. Those five letters alone, among all the Leonine letters, are found in that collection.

Just as it is unknown how these letters, which are absent from all other collections, came separately into that collection, so it remains hidden by what means those three sermons came into Faber’s codex.

11. To return to the lectionary codices: when Quesnel reviewed their disadvantages in his preface, he especially emphasized foreign additions. “Since,” he says, “they have been adapted to the various particular solemnities of different places, they are very often enlarged by certain foreign additions, entirely alien to the author’s intention, which sometimes can scarcely be distinguished.”

You have a notable example of this in sermon 41—our sermon 42—which is the fourth on Lent. Some additions occur in certain lectionaries, as do occasional omissions and mutilations.

But that this happens very often, at least in Leo’s case, is completely false, although we have collated many books of this kind. Indeed, we successfully detected and corrected from the lectionaries precisely such defects as we found more frequently in the later collections. Quesnel himself, on the authority of five lectionaries, removed an addition to sermon 4 on Lent that had entered the editions from the later Leonine collections.

Moreover, Quesnel’s complaint concerning the frequent stains and errors with which the carelessness or ignorance of scribes corrupts such books applies to all manuscript codices. But some are corrected by others, and certain codices of excellent quality—especially the manuscripts of the Basilica of Saint Peter—were of the greatest assistance to us. With their help, we were able to restore or correct approximately five hundred passages to a sounder reading.

12. Before we pass from the lectionaries to the collections, it should be noted that there is a principal difference among lectionary books. Not only do some present more and others fewer sermons of Leo belonging to the same solemnity, and do some omit the sermons of one feast while others omit those of another; the order of the same sermons also differs in different lectionaries.

The more notable Roman lectionaries of the Basilicas of Saint Peter and of Saints Philip and James may serve as an example. In the lectionaries of Saint Peter, for instance, the sermons on the Passion have a different order from that in Vatican 3835, from the Basilica of Saints Philip and James. Since one book was not derived from the other, it is most probable that these very ancient Roman lectionary codices originated from Leo’s autograph sermons, which were first copied in different orders.

The varying order found in the other lectionaries of other Churches may have arisen from the discretion of the scribes.

We shall say quite a few things in the preface to the appendix about the spurious sermons that are scattered through the lectionaries—not, however, the Roman lectionaries praised above—and are attributed to Leo.

# CHAPTER TWO

## On the Manuscript Collections, the Second Source of the Sermons of Saint Leo, and on Their Classification and Use

[Col. 0125]

### § I. Manuscript Collections of the Sermons of Saint Leo Do Not Extend Beyond the Eleventh Century; They Must Be Distinguished from One Another, and Caution Must Be Used with Their Codices
### 13

Let us now turn to the collections of the sermons of St. Leo. The earliest mention of these collections that we encounter among authors is not earlier than the eleventh century. Micrologus, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 25, not only implies that Leo’s sermons had been collected in a codex which he calls the “Book of Sermons,” but, when proving that the fast of the fourth month was celebrated only during the week of Pentecost, he refers readers to the same book, adding:

> Nor is this found only in one sermon, but in several, which he is read to have composed concerning Pentecost in different years; and whoever carefully reads that same book will not be able to overlook it.

Among the codices which Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino and later Roman pontiff Victor III, added to the library of his monastery, one bearing the title *Sermons of Pope Leo* is mentioned by Leo of Ostia in *The Cassinese Chronicle*, book III, chapter 63. The first among writers on illustrious men, or on ecclesiastical writers, to mention Leo’s sermons is the anonymous Mellicensis author of the eleventh century, first published by P. Pez and later by Albert Fabricius. He writes as follows, chapter 7:

> Leo the Great was an outstanding apostolic preacher, who greatly benefited the Christian religion by word and example. Moreover, the number of his sermons is uncertain, although many are held to concern the Advent of the Lord, the Nativity, the Epiphany, fasting, the Passion, and holy Pentecost. Some are also found among the celebrations of the saints’ birthdays.

While he appears to be reviewing approximately the same sequence of sermons that exists in the collections, by declaring their number uncertain he may instead be understood to have had in mind the Lectionaries, which contain different numbers of sermons. These are the more ancient testimonies that can be brought forward for the collections of Leo’s sermons, and this indicates that collections of this kind were not considerably older.

### 14

Indeed, among the very many manuscript books of Leo’s sermons which we have seen in various libraries, we have been unable to find any that exceeds the eleventh century, although we have discovered quite a number of Lectionaries containing Leo’s sermons that belong to an earlier period. We believe this happened because the sermons of the holy pontiff began to be collected around the eleventh century. Certainly, we have found five collections of different origin, the oldest of which belong to that same century.

They were taken from Lectionaries, not only because no older collection has been found from which they could have been copied, but also because they differ in the number and order of the sermons, or at least in their titles, and furthermore in various readings, according as they derive from Lectionaries that likewise differ from one another.

### 15

It is of the greatest importance to note the distinctions among the individual collections as carefully as possible. For from this it will become clear not only that their origins are different, but also that caution must be exercised in the use of manuscripts of this kind.

Whenever several codices of the same collection are found, since they derive from the same original exemplar, nearly the same readings will occur in all of them, apart from errors or arbitrary corrections by scribes. Thus, whoever has collated one codex of a collection will generally have collated them all. From this it follows that one must especially observe how futile it usually is to cite twelve or twenty codices if all of them belong to one and the same collection. For two or three exemplars from different collections usually provide greater evidence for establishing a reading than a hundred from one collection.

## § II. On the First Collection

### 16

We believe that the first collection is the one found in a parchment codex of the eleventh century, now numbered 126 in the Cassinese library, with the title: *The First Part of Pope Leo I: Sermons*. This appears to be the very codex which, as we indicated from the testimony of Leo of Ostia, was assembled in the eleventh century at the command of Abbot Desiderius. Since Leo of Ostia also records that another book of letters, or, as he calls it, the *Register of Leo*, was placed by the same abbot in the same library, he sufficiently indicates what the second part, now missing, contained.

In this codex ninety-one sermons are read. Among them one is copied twice, another is doubtful, and ten are spurious; consequently seventy-nine sermons remain genuine and certain. It will be useful to append the sequence of the sermons themselves, so that the distinction of the other collections may more easily become clear.

[Col. 0127]

This sequence of sermons, together with other information and collations from the same codex, was obtained from the abbot of Monte Cassino by the eminent Cardinal Tamburini. He not only shows favor toward all lovers of sacred studies, in which he is especially distinguished, but, while I was in Rome preparing the materials for this edition entrusted to me by the supreme pontiff, he never ceased to provide me with every assistance in his power.

When, after returning to my homeland, I desired several additional things from the same Cassinese codex for the preparation of the edition—things that required greater labor and diligence—the cardinal, so as not to burden any of the Cassinese monks, arranged for the codex to be sent to Rome. He himself wished to collate it, and to mark and transcribe its variants. In a man of such dignity, occupied with so many weighty concerns, this is truly remarkable; it shows his notable inclination toward these studies and his singular kindness toward us.

### 17

That this collection was compiled from Lectionaries is indicated not only by the spurious sermons, which frequently occur in Lectionaries, but also by the actual sequence of certain sermons which we were able to observe in those same books, as we indicated above.

Nor should it seem surprising that, when several spurious sermons have been inserted, several genuine ones are missing. This derives from the Lectionary books used by the compiler. In them, sermons belonging to another author are repeatedly assigned to one author, and not all genuine sermons are included.

The same thing happened in the case of Augustine. His sermons, once collected from Lectionaries, contain many wrongly attributed pieces while omitting many genuine ones.

## § III. On the Second Collection

### 18

We call the second collection the one which we found in three manuscript books: Casanatense G. III 7, St. Peter’s Basilica 210, and Barberini 88. The first two belong approximately to the twelfth century. The Casanatense is mutilated in several leaves and contains variants added in the margin by some scholar from later collections, sometimes also inserted into the text.

This collection contains one hundred sermons. It begins with Leo’s letter to Flavian, which we have seen inserted in several ancient Lectionaries. Seven sermons on the fast of the tenth month follow, in the same order as in the first collection, with Sermons XIV and XV likewise joined into one. Ten sermons on the Nativity of the Lord and eight on the Epiphany follow; these are found in the first collection, but their slightly altered order indicates a different origin.

Between the eighth and ninth sermons on the Nativity, sermon 16 is inserted: a sermon on Absalom wrongly attributed to Leo. It is also added at the end in some manuscripts of the later collections, but is absent from the first collection. Conversely, sermon 18 of the first collection does not appear; St. Maximus is its author.

The sermons on the fast of Lent and on the Passion, which are read in the first collection, also occur in this second collection in a considerably different order. The same two sermons which we identified as spurious are included as well. Moreover, in place of sermon 41 of the first collection, which is uselessly repeated, this second collection adds, as no. 56, one genuine sermon of Leo on the Passion of the Lord, *Exigit fides* (“Faith requires”), Sermon LIII in our edition, which is missing from the Cassinese collection.

A doubtful sermon on the Resurrection, *Licet omnes solemnitates* (“Although all solemnities…”), follows; it is no. 62 in both collections. Then come the two genuine sermons on the Ascension, nos. 63 and 64, in the same order. The entirely spurious sermon 65 of the first collection is omitted.

Seven sermons on Pentecost are added; they are found in the first collection, but here they are placed together in a different order. In the first collection only six are presented at this point, while one was added separately at the end. Up to this point, with three sermons inserted into the second collection and three omitted from it, the number of sermons in the two collections finally coincides. For both contain seventy-one sermons.

The greater difference in what follows made it necessary to append a catalogue of the remaining sermons, especially since distinctive titles occur, which we excerpted from the table at the end of the Casanatense manuscript.

The final five sermons, which are absent from the first collection, have been placed outside their proper position. The first ought to have been placed among the sermons on Lent, as it is found in the Lectionaries and later collections. The second, on the Maccabees, ought to have been placed before the sermons on St. Lawrence. The remaining three on the fast of the seventh month ought to have been added to the other six sermons with the same title, nos. 72–77, which were described above in their proper place.

This makes it clear that the collection was first laboriously compiled from those Lectionary books which lacked these sermons. Later, however, other books came into the compiler’s hands which contained them, and he therefore thought that they should be added at the end.

### 19

This collection contains all the genuine sermons of Leo that occur in the first collection, except Sermon 2, on the pope’s nativity, which begins *Honorabilem* (“Honorable”). On the other hand, it includes twelve other genuine sermons that are absent from the Cassinese collection.

Although more sermons by other authors are attributed to Leo in these two collections—sermons not found in the three following collections, so that the two should be ranked below those collections in this respect—nevertheless, since they generally preserve better readings, they are much more useful to editors in themselves and should be valued more highly.

In manuscript 210 of the Basilica of St. Peter, after the one hundred sermons listed above, certain works of St. Cyprian are found. These are followed by St. Leo’s letter 165 to the Emperor Leo Augustus, which is inserted in Vallicelliana Lectionary 26. Then fourteen other sermons follow without any author’s name; these are generally listed in the Augustinian appendix.

In Barberini codex 88, this addition of sermons is appended to the one hundred sermons mentioned above, so that it might appear to belong to the same Leo. It is entirely absent, however, from Casanatense manuscript G. III 7. Thus it is evident that it is neither the work of the first compiler nor part of this collection.

Peter Mallius, a twelfth-century author, in his *History of the Basilica of St. Peter*, published by the Bollandists in volume VI, part II, of the *Acta Sanctorum*, chapter 3, no. 37, mentions a certain collection of the sermons of St. Leo which also contained the letter to Flavian. Then, in chapter 7, no. 131, he cites a sermon from the aforementioned appendix, saying:

> There is also a fortress which was the memorial of the Emperor Hadrian, as is read in a sermon of Pope St. Leo on the feast of St. Peter.

He is reporting testimony from Sermon 13 included in the aforementioned appendix, which we shall publish in our appendix. He appears to be referring to a copy of the collection mentioned above, preserved in the archive of the Basilica of St. Peter.

## § IV. On Three Other Collections

### 20

We call the third collection the one that existed in the manuscript from which the first Roman edition was taken by Giovanni Andrea, Bishop of Aleria. We found it in Vatican manuscript 545, which contains only Leo’s sermons.

We believe that the Bolognese codex belongs to this same collection. We found its variants marked in Barberini manuscript 3520, and these generally agree with the readings of the first edition.

This collection contains ninety-three sermons of Leo, all genuine and none spurious, except for one on the Maccabees, which we shall assign to Augustine in the appendix.

Before the sermons on the Nativity of the Lord it places the letter to Flavian, which also indicates that this collection derives from Lectionaries. Only three genuine sermons are missing; these were published from the manuscript of Nicolas Fabri.

The order of the ninety-three sermons is the same as in the more common printed editions, which lack these three sermons, with one exception: Sermon 51, on Matthew 17, is copied among the sermons on Lent, as it is placed in all Lectionaries on the Saturday of the Ember Days of Lent; the editors, however, transferred it to another location.

### 21

Apart from its order, which differs greatly from that of the preceding collections, this collection contains two sermons omitted in them: one on the collects, beginning *Notum vobis* (“Known to you”), Sermon VII in our edition; and another against the heresy of Eutyches, beginning *Sicut peritorum* (“As [is the case] with experts”), Sermon XCVI in our edition.

It has distinctive titles for the sermons, by which it differs most notably both from the printed editions and from the other collections. Together with its often very dissimilar readings, this clearly reveals an entirely different source.

It will suffice to indicate the different titles. The twelve sermons on Lent have the following special division and titles:

The first four are entitled *On Lent*. The fifth is entitled *On the Lenten Fast, Sermon V*. The sixth, seventh, and eighth are entitled *On the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord, Sermons I, II, and III*. The ninth, tenth, and eleventh are entitled *On the Paschal Feast, Sermons I, II, and III*. The twelfth is entitled *On the Passion of the Lord, Sermon IV*.

Then, after the sermon on Matthew 17 has been inserted, the nineteen printed sermons on the Passion and the two following sermons on the Resurrection are presented in a continuous numerical series as follows:

The first: *On the Lord’s Parasceve, on the Passion, Sermon I*. The next five: *On the Passion of the Lord, II, III, IV, V, and VI*. The seventh: *On the Lord’s Pascha, Sermon VII*. The next four: *On the Passion, VIII, IX, X, and XI*.

The remaining eight printed sermons on the Passion and the first on the Resurrection are prefaced by the title: *On the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord, XII, XIII, XIV, XV, XVI, XVII, XVIII, XIX, and XX*.

Finally, the last sermon is entitled *On the Resurrection of the Lord, Sermon XXI*.

### 22

Since we have very frequently used, for this collection, the exemplar of the first Roman edition—which is extremely rare and was unknown to Quesnel—it seems necessary to say something about it.

In his general preface, no. 2, Quesnel presented the Venetian edition of 1485 as the first edition of the sermons. It bears Giovanni Andrea, Bishop of Aleria, as its author, and Quesnel also used it occasionally, though very rarely, in his list of variants.

But, apart from the fact that another Venetian edition exists, by Luca Venetus, from the year 1482, both of these editions were reprints made from the Roman edition which the aforementioned bishop had published in Rome from a Vatican codex and dedicated to Pope Paul II.

Those who have compiled typographical annals assign this Roman edition to the year 1470 and testify that at its end one reads the verses *Aspicis illustres* (“You behold the illustrious [men]”), etc., which give the names of the printers working in the house of the Maxima family. On what basis they have made these claims is unknown.

For not only do the two copies of this edition seen by the eminent Cardinal Quirinus lack every indication of time and place, as well as the verses just mentioned, but so do the three which we ourselves had the opportunity to see: one in Rome, in the possession of the eminent Passionei; another at Verona, in the Muselli Library; and a third in the Veronese suburb, among the Lateran canons of St. Leonard. The latter had been purchased in Rome in 1472 by the celebrated Celsus Maffei, as is recorded in a handwritten note by Maffei himself.

In the catalogue of books printed by the German printers Conrad Sweynheim and Arnold Pannartz in the house of the Maximi up to 20 March 1472, and reviewed by the aforementioned Bishop of Aleria at the beginning of volume V of the works of Nicholas of Lyra, the *Sermons of the Divine Pope Leo* are listed. The catalogue records 275 copies as having been printed. This is why the first edition is so rare: so few copies were printed.

It is clear from the Bishop of Aleria’s letter to Paul II that the edition had been put into type before the year 1472. Paul II died on 21 July 1471.

[Note: [Col. 0133] After this had been written in the first edition, Ballerini were informed by Father Montius, librarian of the Dominican Fathers of St. Mary of Grace in Milan, that a copy of the Roman edition of 1470 was found in the library of that church. At its end, in addition to the year, the verses *Aspicis illustres* (“You behold the illustrious [men]”), etc., were printed, as they appear in the typographical annals.

This edition, the rarest of all, differs from the other Roman edition, of which we reviewed five copies. For not only does the latter lack the verses mentioned and the indication of the year, but it also differs in its lines and individual pages. Moreover, the former lacks the four letters of Leo with which the second edition was enriched.

Since the latter edition which we examined was entirely printed from the first edition, and represents the codex which the Bishop of Aleria used in his earlier edition, the references to the first edition which we gave in the notes do not need to be corrected. — EDITOR.]

### 23

A fourth collection occurs more frequently in manuscripts. It presents exactly the same sermons in the same order as we saw in the preceding collection. It differs from that collection, however, in its titles, which are the same as those in the printed editions, and also in numerous and substantial variants which cannot be attributed to scribal error or discretion, but must be assigned to a different origin.

Most of the codices have a collection of letters attached to them. For this reason they omit the letter to Flavian among the sermons, since it is placed in its proper position among the letters.

The following manuscripts belong to this type: Vatican manuscripts 541, 546, and 547; the Vatican Urbinas 65; one manuscript of the Augustinian Hermits in the Angelica Library; another Venetian manuscript, St. Mark’s 79; and the Fiesolan manuscript of the Lateran canons.

We found this same collection with the letter to Flavian, but without the collection of letters, in the manuscripts of St. Justina at Padua belonging to the Cassinese monks, and also in another Venetian manuscript of the monks of San Giorgio Maggiore.

We were unable to find any exemplar older than the fourteenth century; from this we conclude that the collection is quite recent.

It is certainly the most corrupt of all. Since the printed editions of the sermons appear to have been derived from a codex of this collection by those who were ignorant of the Alerian edition, it is not surprising that they abound in numerous errors and corrupt readings.

### 24

We found a fifth collection of the sermons separated from the collection of letters in no manuscript. Just as the collection of letters attached to it differs from the collection of letters joined to the fourth collection of sermons, so the collection of sermons is likewise distinguishable by several, though few, clear characteristics, and reveals a different origin.

I pass over the divergent readings. Although this recension is better in its readings than the two preceding recensions, it easily yields to the first and second collections.

Its principal distinction lies in the two sermons *Exsultemus* (“Let us rejoice”), on Saints Peter and Paul, and *Gratias, dilectissimi* (“Let us give thanks, most beloved”), on the Maccabees, which are not found in this collection. The first is read in the four collections preceding it, while the second occurs in the second, third, and fourth.

The order of the remaining sermons is the same as in the third and fourth collections, with this one difference: after the sermons on the fast of Pentecost, the order is reversed. First comes *In octavis apostolorum* (“On the octave of the apostles”), *Religiosam* (“Religious”), Sermon LXXXIV; then *In natali apostolorum Petri et Pauli* (“On the nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul”), *Omnium quidem* (“Indeed, of all”), Sermon LXXXII. This is the order of these sermons in the second collection.

But in the third and fourth collections, where *Exsultemus* is inserted more correctly, they are presented as follows: *On the Nativity of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, Sermon I*; *Omnium quidem* (“Indeed, of all”), Sermon II; *Exsultemus* (“Let us rejoice”); and *On the Octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul, Religiosam* (“Religious”).

This collection, the purest of all because it contains nothing spurious, is found in Vatican manuscript 544, approximately from the twelfth century; in Vatican Regina Sueciae 139, from the thirteenth or fourteenth century; in one manuscript of the Conventual Franciscans of St. Francis at Cesena, from the fifteenth century; and also in the Victorine manuscript used by Quesnel.

## § V. On Another Oxford Manuscript Collection Cited by Quesnel

### 25

These are the collections which we have seen. Quesnel, however, cites in Dissertation 12, chapter 2, an Oxford codex from the eleventh or twelfth century, containing a certain collection of Leo’s sermons together with his letters. At first sight, it might be thought to be one or the other of the two last collections, which join the pontiff’s sermons and letters.

But Quesnel’s indication demonstrates that it is entirely different from all those which we have so far been able to find. He says:

> Inserted among the letters are the constitutions of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian against the Manichaeans and against Hilary of Arles. Two letters follow the sermons, those of Proterius of Alexandria and Paschasinus of Lilybaeum to our Leo, together with several other things relating to the life of the holy pontiff.

Just as we have nowhere found the collection of letters with these additions, so the collection of sermons, on account of the additions indicated, differs from all those we have seen.

It is unfortunate that Quesnel did not provide more precise information about this collection. From the order and number of the sermons we could form a particular judgment about it.

From the same codex he quotes only the following distinctive title, which we inserted in the observation on the first sermon included in the admonition mentioned above:

> In the name of the Most High God. Here begin the treatises which the most blessed Pope Leo delivered to the people from the day of his ordination throughout a continuous period of five years.

From these words Quesnel thought it possible to conclude that this collection of sermons derived from a copy of a collection written in Leo’s own age. He says:

> This title breathes antiquity throughout and indicates that the sermons, or treatises—for this was a word familiar in Leo’s age—were copied from a codex written in the pontiff’s lifetime.

Since the sermons themselves provide no indications by which the year in which each was delivered can be determined, the first exemplar of this codex must have been copied immediately after that five-year period.

The use of the word “treatises” for sermons does indeed suggest antiquity. But if the codex contains the printed sermons, the title that assigns them to the first five years of Leo’s pontificate—that is, between the years 440 and 445—reveals an obvious error.

For nine sermons on the fast of the tenth month, ten on the Nativity of the Lord, eight on the Epiphany, and twenty-one—or at least nineteen—on the Passion of the Lord exceed a five-year period simply by calculating from the sermons themselves, which were delivered in different years. The same is true of several sermons on the collects, as is clear from the chronological indications given in them.

The eighth sermon on the Nativity and the sixth on the fast of the seventh month explicitly name Eutyches as a heretic. This could not have happened before the year 449, or more probably somewhat later. In that year Leo condemned his error, but, since he hoped that Eutyches would be corrected, he appears to have spared the man himself.

The sermon on the octave of the apostles, which was delivered after the sack of Rome, must be placed after the year 445. The treatise against the heresy of Eutyches—Sermon XCVI in our edition—was delivered in the Basilica of St. Anastasia after the death of Proterius, which occurred in the year 457.

These considerations therefore confirm what we established at the outset: no codex survives containing a collection written in Leo’s own age.

## § VI. On the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon

### 26

It remains for us to say something about the *Homiliary of the Doctors*, since this too will have to be used as a kind of codex.

The author of this Homiliary is Paul the Deacon, who, at the command of Charlemagne, collected various homilies of the Fathers according to the requirements of the feasts at the end of the eighth century. This is clear from the preface of Charlemagne prefixed to the extremely rare Speyer edition of 1482, and reprinted by Mabillon in volume I of the *Analecta*, page 25.

Twenty sermons of Leo inserted there are read in that work. Since this collection derives from manuscript books older than the ninth century which Paul the Deacon used, it must be considered highly important.

Several editions of the same Homiliary were later published. When Quesnel cited it, he sometimes used a much later edition in which others had altered a considerable number of the printed Leonine sermons.

To learn the genuine readings of Paul the Deacon, we collated the Basel edition of Nicholas Kessler from the year 1496, taken from a very ancient codex of the Church of Basel. Although, like the Speyer edition, it includes some additional sermons by later authors, it nevertheless reproduces Paul the Deacon’s genuine edition with respect to the remaining sermons, including Leo’s.

These Leonine sermons are indeed found without the additions in two manuscripts of Reichenau, as Mabillon himself reports in volume IV of the *Analecta*, pages 631–632.

## § VII. On the Barberini Manuscript Containing Various Readings of the Sermons of St. Leo
27. Before I withdraw my hand from this preface, I should first mention that, while I was staying in Rome, I discovered in the Barberini Library a more recent codex, no. 3320, which contains quite a few variant readings of the sermons of St. Leo prepared for publication. It is preceded by an Italian letter written by Lorenzo Mari on 30 March 1677. When the most eminent Cardinals Francesco Barberini and Brancaccio had asked him, in their own name and that of a prelate, what his brother Giovanni Battista Marus had left toward an edition of Leo, he replied that several years earlier an edition of Leo’s sermons had come into the hands of that same brother, in the margins of which Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, had noted variant readings. Giovanni Battista had then excerpted these and added other variants from different codices and editions, with the intention of publishing a new edition of the sermons under the title *Sermons of St. Leo the Great, restored on the authority of several manuscript codices*. He concludes by saying that he had entrusted the aforementioned edition, together with Vossius’s variants and his brother’s labors, to Michelangelo Ricci, later a cardinal, from whom anyone who wished could obtain them. What follows is the preface of Giovanni Battista Marus, intended to precede the edition, which we reproduce here.

## TO THE READER  
### GIOVANNI BATTISTA MARUS

[Col. 0135]

“Once again the holy Leo, great in every respect, comes forth into the light, restored by a final hand and with greater accuracy than before. So great is the dignity of the author, the majesty of his eloquence, the holiness of his life, and so great the glory of the heresies he conquered, of Attila whom he restrained, and of Rome which he saved, that work devoted to restoring his writings to their authentic meaning cannot be undertaken without the richest benefit to the Church and without the greatest pleasure to learned men.

This labor was undertaken a few years ago by Father Theophilus Raynaudus of the Society of Jesus, a theologian whose manifold learning is abundantly attested by the distinguished works he published in print. But since the undertaking depended not so much on ingenuity and learning as on the variety of printed editions and the reliability of ancient manuscripts, although he labored over it not without praise and usefulness, nevertheless, because he lacked very many examples of both kinds, he could not, as he wished, restore the writings of so great a pontiff to their native brilliance. Consequently, the work lacked the desired completion, and not a few errors remained in the readings of the sacred office which Holy Church customarily borrows from the divine eloquence of the great Leo on the chief solemnities of the year, since, when types are renewed, it is customary to fall back upon the latest edition as though it were the more corrected one.

Therefore, since we had obtained several printed editions and not a few trustworthy ancient manuscripts which Theophilus Raynaudus had lacked, we considered that the light which could abundantly be drawn from them ought to be applied to the honor of so great a pontiff, to the desired restoration of his writings, to the benefit of the Church, and to the pleasure of learned men. Farewell, friendly reader; and while you welcome the fruit of our labor, favor it, and, if you know anything better, bring it forth.”

This Giovanni Battista Marus, who took pleasure in such studies, had published at Rome in 1644, from Vatican and Barberini manuscripts, certain sermons of Augustine; from Vatican codex 1203, the dialogues of Desiderius, abbot of Cassino and later Victor III; and finally, in 1655, from a Barberini manuscript, Peter the Deacon’s *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*. We observe, however, that the preface mentioned above makes no reference to the variants of Vossius which Lorenzo Marus reported. In the Barberini codex, several variants of the sermons are appended, sometimes in a disordered sequence. Most are taken from codices of the Basilica of St. Peter; others from the Vatican manuscripts; and some from codex Bon., that is, the Bolognese codex. They are more frequent in those sermons contained in the lectionaries of the Basilica of St. Peter. Where these lectionaries were lacking, variants are indicated very rarely and sometimes not at all.

It is impossible to distinguish which variants were taken from Vossius and which were added by Marus. It can indeed be inferred, from the *Miscellanies of the Holy Fathers* appended to the Mainz edition of 1604 of the works of St. Gregory Thaumaturgus, that Vossius, who at one time studied in Rome, collated Roman codices with respect to Leo; there he published some of Leo’s material from Roman manuscripts. That he prepared more than is suggested in Lorenzo Marus’s letter is proved by what Vossius himself states at the end of the works of St. Ephrem, where he promises that he will publish all the works of the holy pontiff, not merely the sermons, after revising and illustrating them. In his note on St. Leo’s treatise *Against Eutyches*, published in the aforementioned Mainz edition, he likewise testifies:

“Of the many things observed by us in our Leonine revision and noted in the margin of the letters …”

There he shows that, besides the sermons, he had also revised the letters himself and noted their variants in the margins of the edition of the letters.

For this reason Nicolaus Faber, in a letter to Vossius, printed among Faber’s *Opuscula*, pp. 113–114, testifies that he had heard the Parisian printer Michel Sonnius was awaiting the edition of the works of St. Leo, which he expected to receive as soon as possible.

At the end of his general preface Quesnellus mentions a codex of the works of St. Leo which Emeric Bigotius had once seen, after the death of Pegna, in the possession of Marius of Sant’Angelo, a canon, after the codex had been collated by the very learned Francisco Pegna with manuscripts from Roman libraries. Since the Giovanni Battista Marus mentioned shortly before is called in his published works a canon of Sant’Angelo in the fish market, there is no doubt that the Marius praised by Quesnellus is the same person as Giovanni Battista Marus.

Which codex Bigotius found in his possession becomes known from the Barberini manuscript; and perhaps through Bigotius’s error, what ought to have been attributed to Vossius was attributed to Pegna, because Vossius’s codex had come into Pegna’s hands before it passed into the library of Marus.

We did not find the codex itself, or Leo’s edition collated by Vossius with the manuscripts, but we obtained Marus’s work in the Barberini codex, which includes the variants of both Vossius and Marus. We collated many passages of this Barberini manuscript with the lectionaries of the Basilica of St. Peter. Since we found them accurately recorded, we were relieved of the need for a fuller collation of those lectionaries; thus we were able more conveniently to devote ourselves to examining many other manuscript copies, both of that same basilica, of the Vatican, and of other Roman libraries.

[Col. 0137]

# SERMONS OF ST. LEO THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF, DELIVERED TO THE ROMAN PEOPLE ON THE PRINCIPAL FESTIVITIES OF THE ENTIRE YEAR

[Col. 0137]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE TWO FOLLOWING SERMONS

These sermons were improperly joined into one in earlier editions, as also in quite a few manuscript copies.

In earlier editions there was one sermon which we now publish divided into two. So that you, reader, may understand the reason for this, some preliminary explanation is necessary. In the editions published before Quesnellus, the first sermon, composed from the two that follow, was prefaced by this title:

“On the anniversary of the day of his elevation to the summit and burden of the Roman pontificate.”

But Quesnellus, who had retained the same title in his first edition, judged in the second that it should be changed as follows:

“On the octave of his consecration.”

He endeavored to prove this at length, and we reproduce his argument here in full.

“I left this first sermon of St. Leo in my first edition under the same title which all the older editions had long given it, as though it had been delivered on the anniversary of the day of his elevation, although some scruple continued to trouble me. The new considerations of two learned men of the Society of Jesus, John Garnerius and Daniel Papebrochius, induced me to subject the matter to a second examination.

Garnerius writes on page 33 of the *Liber Diurnus of the Roman Pontiffs*:

‘On the very day of his elevation St. Leo delivered a sermon similar to this address—which he says was inserted as the second profession of faith of Pope Gregory II—except that he did not append the profession of faith to the sermon in the same way. Perhaps it had not yet become customary to issue a second profession of faith other than the one made at the body of St. Peter. Or perhaps, and this is what I rather think, the profession was omitted by the compiler of Leo’s sermons because it was a common formula and did not differ from the Roman Apostles’ Creed.’

In the appendix, p. 172, he writes that the word ‘anniversary’ had slipped into the title, because, as he says, the sermon itself teaches and clearly shows that it was delivered on the very day of his elevation … Again, on p. 174 he says:

‘If an anniversary day, and not the actual day of his elevation, is meant, why is it said: “The service of the consecrated pontiff is beginning”? Why is mention made of his return from a long journey? Why are thanks given for the election? Why does the verb “raises” stand in the present tense, if he had already spent at least one full year in the pontifical seat?’

Accordingly, he thinks that the sermon was delivered when the day of the election recurred, so that the man who had been elected on a Friday—which was 29 March—might be ordained on the same weekday, which was 10 May.

Daniel Papebrochius embraced his colleague’s opinion in his attempt at a chronology of the supreme pontiffs, insofar as it assigned the sermon to the day of the consecration itself. But with respect to the other part, which claimed that the consecration had been celebrated on a Friday, the very learned man recognized how monstrous the error was. For Leo himself, on the basis of the teaching and institution of the apostles, asserts the authority of the custom by which it was always observed that those who were to be consecrated by priestly or levitical ordination should receive the blessing only on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, that is, on Sunday.

I am likewise certain that this first sermon cannot be assigned to the anniversary day. But that it should not be assigned to the very day of the consecration is made clear by these words of Leo alone:

‘When therefore the day returned in its proper order on which the Lord willed me to have the beginning of episcopal office, etc.’

Everyone can see that the beginning of episcopal office is the ordination.
