But the day of this beginning or ordination returning in its proper order must be understood as the second Sunday, immediately following the ordination—that is, the eighth day after the ordination—if Leo is to agree with Leo. I therefore think that this first sermon of St. Leo was delivered during the solemnity of the ordination itself, or on the eighth day, which was part and conclusion of that solemnity: the day of consecration returning in its proper order, that is, after seven days of the week had elapsed, on the first day, Sunday, returning in the order of the days. This cannot be understood in any other sense once it has been established that the sermon cannot be explained as referring to the anniversary day, as is in fact established by the entire sequence of the sermon itself.

This new opinion is confirmed by an old codex of the Bodleian Library at Oxford, with which the very learned Edmund Bernard, Savilian Professor of Astronomy at that university, had collated several of our Leo’s sermons and letters, and from which he had formerly sent me the collected variant readings. The antiquity of the codex is commended by this conspicuous inscription at its beginning:

‘In the name of the Most High God begin the treatises which the most blessed Pope Leo delivered to the people continuously for five years from the day of his ordination.’

This title breathes antiquity throughout and indicates that the sermons or treatises—a word familiar in Leo’s age—were copied from a codex written during that pontiff’s lifetime. Since the sermons themselves provide no indications by which it might appear in what year each was delivered, the first exemplar of this codex must have been copied almost immediately after those five years. In that codex the title of the first sermon is not ‘On the anniversary,’ as it appears in the heading of the later sermon, but ‘Sermon I on his ordination.’ This sermon alone could have been delivered on the day of the ordination, as the earlier title indicates, namely, on the day when it returned, as Leo himself said, or on the eighth day.

Furthermore, he rightly says that the service of the consecrated pontiff began after the solemnity of the ordination had been completed. The day of the ordination itself was indeed the beginning of episcopal office, as Leo explicitly states; but it was not the beginning of the service, or the exercise of the office undertaken, since the length of that solemn day, occupied by prolonged prayers and extended ceremonies, did not allow it.

Once this has been established, the custom of celebrating the solemnity of consecrated pontiffs on the eighth day becomes known, although I do not remember that it is attested elsewhere. Yet the practice is readily supported by the annual religious celebration of consecration festivals, by the similar custom of celebrating the eighth day after the baptismal consecration of the faithful, and even by the dedication of sacred basilicas. The latter practice still continues today, although the dedication of churches is far inferior in rank to pontifical ordination.

Thus far Quesnellus.

Accordingly, he saw that the anniversary day could not be assigned to the first sermon as it had been published, because, as Garnerius observed, the first part of the sermon says that the service of the consecrated pontiff is beginning and mentions a return from a long journey, neither of which is at all compatible with an anniversary day. Hence the day of the ordination itself seemed to have to be accepted.

But since the words ‘When therefore the day returned in its proper order,’ and so forth, do not fit the day of the ordination itself, Quesnellus thought that the eighth day should be assigned to this sermon. Yet the solemnity of the eighth day, at which a gathering of bishops would take place, as the words of the sermon require, is unknown to all antiquity.

That a gathering of bishops was accustomed to take place not so much on the day of the ordination as on its anniversary is clear from Paulinus’s Letter 16 to Delphinus, from Sixtus III’s Letter to Cyril, and from the letter of Pope Hilary, Leo’s successor, to Ascanus. Hence Tillemont, in his note on the article on Leo in volume XV, p. 417, suspected that two sermons had been improperly joined.

This difficulty, however, has been resolved by six codices. In three manuscripts of the second collection—namely, Barberini 88, Basilica of St. Peter 210, and Casanatense G, III, 7—as well as in the Vallicellian lectionary 26, the sermon beginning ‘The praise of the Lord’ is presented, concluding with the words ‘you have given testimony,’ and ending with the final clause ‘Through Christ our Lord.’

The Casinensis codex 126 of the first collection, which at no. 75 contains the same sermon with the same ending, had prefixed at no. 72, as a distinct sermon, one beginning:

‘The divine favor has made today honorable to me, beloved …’

Elsewhere this had been improperly attached to the first sermon by inserting the particle *igitur* (‘therefore’) after the word *Honorabilem* (‘honorable’), and it thereby formed the second and third chapters.

In the Vallicellian lectionary manuscript A, 7, the same distinction between the two sermons is also found, and in the same order: first comes the sermon ‘The divine favor,’ on p. 185, and then the sermon ‘The praise of the Lord,’ on p. 189.

All matters are best reconciled by these witnesses. For the first sermon, ‘The praise of the Lord,’ which contains formulas proper to the day of the ordination, was delivered on the very day of his elevation or ordination; and perhaps the prolonged solemnity of that day did not permit a longer sermon.

The second sermon, ‘Honorable to me,’ was recited on the anniversary day, when there returned, as Leo says, ‘the day in its proper order on which the Lord willed me to have the beginning of episcopal office.’

The difficulty which Garnerius raises from the verb *provehit* (‘raises’) in our second sermon, if St. Leo had already spent at least one year in the pontifical seat, is slight and can easily be removed by correcting one letter and reading *provexit* (‘raised’). It could have arisen from the carelessness of copyists.

Perhaps *provexit* was also read in some of the more accurate codices. But when this sermon was joined to the preceding one, which concerns the very day of the ordination, the reading was transferred into the present tense so that coherence with what preceded might be preserved.

For the same reason *ipse mihi fiet* (‘he will become for me’) seems to have been written, which suits the beginning of the pontificate, in place of *ipse est* (‘he is’), which is preserved in some manuscript copies and which we have restored as more suitable to the anniversary day.

No one should be surprised that two sermons were joined into one, for in Leo’s own codices we find other examples of the same kind. Thus, in the manuscript books of the first and second collections, two sermons on the fast of the tenth month—the third and fourth—are joined into one.

Perhaps when the first sermon seemed shorter than the customary readings of the divine office required, it was decided in some lectionaries, even ancient ones, to join two together; from these the same combination passed into most collections.”

Thus far Quesnellus.

## 7. FIRST SERMON

[Note: [Col. 0141B] This is the title found in several excellent codices, especially in the very ancient Vatican codex 3836, as well as in another very ancient Vatican codex written in what are called Lombard letters. This title also agrees with the ancient designation of the day of ordination, which St. Leo himself calls a natal day in Sermon 4, chapter 4. Similarly, Sixtus III, in his Letter to Cyril, no. 3, and in Letter 2 to John of Antioch; Paulinus of Nola, in Letter 20 to Delphinus, no. 2; and Pope Hilary, in Letter 2 to Ascanus, chapter 2, likewise call it a natal day.

In ancient sacramentaries also, especially in the very ancient Veronese manuscript 80, which was Roman and reflects Leo’s age, the Mass of the anniversary day of the pontiffs’ consecration bears this title: ‘On the natal day of bishops.’

In later codices, the title of this and the following sermons is ‘On his ordination’ or ‘On his elevation’; in the commonly published editions, ‘On the anniversary of the day of his elevation.’

A distinctive title is found in the manuscripts of the third collection, from which the first edition originated, namely: ‘Sermon I of thanksgiving for his elevation to the pontificate.’

In the table of the Casanatense manuscript of the second collection: ‘Sermon of Pope Leo delivered on the day of his ordination.’

Finally, in codex Vallicellian A, 7: ‘On the praises of the apostles’; the following sermon, however, is entitled ‘On the natal day of St. Peter the apostle.’]

### On the Natal Day of St. Leo I Himself; Delivered on the Day of His Ordination

[Col. 0141A]

### SYNOPSIS

St. Leo, elected in his absence, returns thanks for the favor and earnestly asks for the prayers of his Church.

Let my mouth speak the praise of the Lord (Ps. 144:21), and let my soul, spirit, flesh, and tongue bless his holy name. For it is a sign not of a modest but of an ungrateful mind to be silent about divine benefits; and it is entirely fitting that the service of the consecrated pontiff should begin with sacrifices of the Lord’s praise.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] The Lombard Vatican codex has *vitium* (‘fault’) instead of the reading implied here.]

Because the Lord remembered us in our lowliness (Ps. 135:24) and blessed us; because he alone has done great wonders for me (ibid., 4), so that the devotion of your holiness might believe me present,

[Col. 0141B]

[Note: [Col. 0141D] The printed editions, together with several codices, had *cerneret* (‘might see’). We have substituted *crederet* (‘might believe’) from other manuscripts, especially the Lombard Vatican codex and the very ancient Vatican 3836, since this reading seemed more appropriate. A little later, some codices have *fecit* (‘has done’) in place of *fecerat* (‘had made’).]

the necessity of a long journey had made me absent. Therefore I give thanks to our God, and I shall always give thanks for all that he has repaid me.

[Note: [Col. 0141D] Most of the ancient Roman codices read this way. The printed editions have *tribuit* (‘has granted’).]

I also celebrate with due thanksgiving the judgment of your favor, clearly understanding how much the devotion of your affection can contribute to me in reverence, love, and faith, since I desire the salvation of your souls with pastoral solicitude, and you have passed so holy a judgment concerning me, although I have scarcely any preceding merits.

Therefore I beseech you, through the mercies of the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0142C] Elsewhere: ‘through mercy.’]

help by your prayers the one whom you sought with your desires, so that the Spirit of grace may remain in me and your judgments may not waver.

May he grant us all together the blessing of peace,

[Note: [Col. 0142C] The printed editions had: ‘He who infused into us the devotion to unanimity.’ Vatican 3836 places the word *unanimitatis* (‘of unanimity’) after *studia* (‘devotion’), in a syntax thoroughly characteristic of Leo. We have emended *vobis* (‘to you’) not so much on the basis of the first edition as of the Lombard codex and three other Vatican codices, because Leo seems to be referring to the unanimity of those who elected him.

In these codices, however, *vobis* also occurs in the preceding clause: ‘May he grant you all together the blessing of peace.’ We think Leo is praying for peace shared both by himself and by his hearers. The same manuscripts, together with the first edition, prefer *humanitatis* (‘of humanity’) to *unanimitatis*. Our reading is confirmed by Vallicellian codex 26.]

he who has infused in you the devotion to unanimity; so that throughout all the days of my life, ready for the service of almighty God and for your service, I may confidently beseech the Lord:

“Holy Father, preserve in your name those whom you have given me” (John 17:11);

and, as you continually advance toward salvation, may my soul magnify the Lord, and may the account of my priesthood stand before the just Judge at the recompense of the future judgment in such a way (1 Thess. 2:19) that through your good works you may be my joy and my crown—you who by your good will have given sincere testimony to the present life.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] We have added this conclusion from those codices which end the sermon at this point, as we stated in the preceding notice.]

Through Christ our Lord.

[Col. 0142B]

## SERMON II

### On the Natal Day of the Same, II; Delivered on the Anniversary of His Ordination

### SYNOPSIS

I. No one should presume on his own righteousness or despair of God’s mercy.  
II. The assembly of bishops on the anniversary of the consecration of the Roman pontiff, whom the Church receives as Peter because he is Peter’s heir.

[Note: [Col. 0142D] This sermon was joined to the preceding one, with the particle *igitur* (‘therefore’) inserted at this point. The reason why we separated it was stated in the notice prefixed to the preceding sermon.]

[Col. 0143C]

[Note: [Col. 0142D] The first edition has *facit* (‘makes’) in place of *fecit* (‘made’).]

### CHAPTER I

The divine favor has made today honorable to me, beloved, for, by raising my lowliness to the highest rank,

[Col. 0143A]

[Note: [Col. 0143C] The reading was *provehit* (‘raises’). Although no codices support it, we were obliged, even against our inclination, to make the correction of one letter necessary for the reasons set out in the notice.]

it has shown that it despises none of its own. Hence, although it is necessary to tremble concerning one’s merit, it is nevertheless religious to rejoice in the gift, because he who is the author of the burden is himself the helper in its administration; and, lest the weak man succumb beneath the greatness of grace, he will give strength who has bestowed the dignity.

Therefore, when the day returned in its proper order on which the Lord willed me to have the beginning of episcopal office,

[Note: [Col. 0143D] The Lombard Vatican codex has *episcopatus* (‘of the episcopate’). Later, Massonus in his Life of Leo read *principatum* (‘rule’) instead of *principium* (‘beginning’), but we have found this reading in none of the editions or even in our codices.]

I have true reason for rejoicing to the glory of God: he who forgave me much so that I might love him greatly, and who, in order to make his grace wonderful, bestowed his gifts upon one in whom he found no support from merits.

Through this work of his, what does the Lord impress upon our hearts and commend to us, except that no one should presume upon his own righteousness and no one despair of his mercy, which is most clearly exalted when a sinner is sanctified and an outcast is raised up?

For the measure of heavenly gifts does not depend upon the quality of our works; nor, in this world, in which the whole of life is a trial (Job 7:1), is each person repaid what he deserves. If the Lord were to observe iniquities, no one would withstand his judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0143D] Vatican 3836 has *evidenter prominet* (‘stands forth clearly’). A little later, the Vallicellian codex has *meritorum nostrorum* (‘of our merits’) in place of *nostrorum operum* (‘of our works’).]

[Note: [Col. 0143D] This reading is taken from the Vallicellian lectionary, the Lombard manuscript, and another Vatican codex, which add *suum* (‘his’) after *judicium*.]

### CHAPTER II

Magnify the Lord with me, beloved, and let us exalt his name together (Ps. 33:4), so that the entire meaning of today’s celebration may be referred to the praise of its author.

For my own feelings, I confess that I rejoice greatly in the devotion of all of you. And when I see this most splendid gathering of my venerable fellow priests,

[Note: [Col. 0143D] The codices Regius and Victor, Quesnellus’s codices, and one of our Vatican codices have *frequentationem* (‘attendance’) here. At this point Quesnellus had noted, both in the synopsis of this chapter and in a marginal postscript to his second edition, ‘the assembly of bishops on the octave of the consecration of the Roman pontiff,’ because he believed that this sermon had been delivered on that octave. But in the notice we have shown that both this sermon and the assembly of bishops took place on the anniversary of the consecration.]

I sense that an angelic assembly is present among us in so many holy men. Nor do I doubt that today we are visited by a more abundant grace of the divine presence, when so many most beautiful dwelling places of God are present together and so many outstanding members of Christ’s body shine with a single light.

Nor, as I trust, is the gracious favor and faithful affection of the most blessed apostle Peter absent from this gathering; nor has he abandoned your devotion, since reverence for him has assembled you.

[Col. 0144A]

[Note: [Col. 0144D] We have corrected this on the basis of the oldest Vatican manuscript, the Vallicellian manuscript, and two other Vatican codices, since most printed editions had previously read *nos* (‘us’), which was less suitable. A little later, the Lombard codex has *in consortiis* (‘among the fellowships’) in place of *in consortibus* (‘among the companions’).]

He rejoices in your affection, and in those who share his honor he embraces the observance of the Lord’s institution, approving the perfectly ordered charity of the whole Church, which receives Peter in the seat of Peter and does not grow lukewarm in love for so great a shepherd even toward an heir so unequal to him in person.

Therefore, beloved, so that this devotion which you unanimously display toward my lowliness may obtain the fruit of its earnestness, earnestly beseech the most merciful clemency of our God,

[Note: [Col. 0144D] The first edition has *misericordem* (‘merciful’). The Vallicellian codex has *Domini nostri* (‘of our Lord’). A little later, three Vatican codices have *exorate* (‘implore’) in place of *obsecrate* (‘beseech’).]

that in our days he may defeat those who attack us, strengthen our faith,

[Note: [Col. 0144D] This is the reading of the superior codices Vatican 3836 and the Lombard codex, whereas the printed editions read: ‘Strengthen your faith, increase devotion and love, and enlarge peace.’ The Vallicellian and Casinensis codices, as well as Vatican 541 of the fourth collection, prefer our reading, with this one exception: ‘increase love.’]

increase our love, increase our peace, and deem me, his servant, whom he has willed to preside over the governance of the Church in order to display the riches of his grace, sufficient for so great a work and useful for your edification,

[Note: [Col. 0144D] This is found in all nine of our codices and in Quesnellus’s two codices, Regius and Gaudiivallensis. The printed editions have *defensioni* (‘defense’).]

and extend the time of our service, so that what he grants to our age may advance our devotion, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## SERMON III [Alternatively II]

### On the Natal Day of Leo Himself, III; Delivered on the Anniversary of His Elevation to the Office of Supreme Pontiff

### SYNOPSIS

I. The honor of the priesthood must be referred to God. Its figure was foreshadowed in Melchizedek; the distinction between the two.  
II. How unequal human weakness is to so great a burden. Christ always governs the Church. The firmness of Peter’s faith remains.  
III. The praises of Peter, who even now does not abandon the care of the Church. In what sense he is the rock and foundation.  
IV. Peter is to be honored in his successors: first among all bishops. The progress of the flock is the praise of the shepherd.

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0144C]

Whenever God’s mercy deigns to renew the days of his gifts for us, there is, beloved, a just and reasonable cause for rejoicing, if the beginning of the office we have undertaken is referred to the praise of its author.

For I recognize that this observance is appropriate to all priests, but especially necessary to me, who, looking upon the smallness of my insignificance and the greatness of the office I have undertaken,

[Note: [Col. 0144D] Alternatively: *quoniam* (‘because’). QUESNELLUS.—Our three Vatican codices likewise have this reading.]

and considering them, must also proclaim that prophetic utterance:

“Lord, I heard your report, and I was afraid; I considered your works, and I was terrified.”

For what is so unusual, so dreadful, as labor imposed upon the fragile, sublimity upon the lowly, dignity upon one who has not deserved it?

[Col. 0145A]

[Note: [Col. 0145D] The Bodleian codices and Gaudiivallensis, in the margin, have *sollicitum* (‘anxious’). QUESNELLUS.—The very ancient Vatican 3836 likewise has this reading.]

And yet we neither despair nor fail, because we place our confidence not in ourselves but in him who works in us.

Therefore, beloved, we sang the Davidic psalm with harmonious voice, not for our own exaltation but for the glory of Christ the Lord. For he is the one of whom it is prophetically written:

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 7:11).

That is, not according to the order of Aaron, whose priesthood, proceeding through the succession of his descendants, belonged to a temporal ministry and ceased with the law of the Old Testament; but according to the order of Melchizedek, in whom the form of the eternal Pontiff went before.

And since it is not reported from which parents he was born, he is understood to be the one whose generation cannot be recounted.

Finally, when the mystery of this divine priesthood also reached human functions, it was not entered upon through a succession of generations,

[Note: [Col. 0145D] Alternatively: *currit* (‘runs’). QUESNELLUS.]

nor is what flesh and blood has created chosen; but, the privilege of fathers ceasing and the order of families being set aside, the Church receives as its rulers those whom the Holy Spirit has prepared.

Thus, in the people adopted by God, whose whole body is both priestly and royal, it is not the prerogative of earthly origin

[Note: [Col. 0145D] It seems clear to me from this passage that material anointing was already in use at that time in episcopal ordination, at least in the Roman Church. For in Leo, obtaining anointing and becoming a bishop are the same thing; if this were understood only of spiritual anointing, the meaning would be highly ambiguous.

There is a somewhat similar, though more obscure, reference to material anointing in the following sermon, chapter 1. See also Sermon 8 on the Passion of the Lord, chapter 7: ‘Now,’ he says, ‘the order of the Levites is more distinguished, the dignity of the elders greater, and the anointing of priests more sacred.’

He also clearly alludes to the outward anointing of priests in the subsequent sermon, when he speaks in chapter 1 of the spiritual anointing of all the baptized, that is, of the faithful: ‘The anointing of the Holy Spirit consecrates as priests all who have been reborn in Christ.’ And below: ‘When the oil of blessing has been poured out,’ etc. QUESNELLUS.]

that obtains the anointing, but the favor of heavenly grace that gives birth to a bishop.

### CHAPTER II
Although, therefore, dearly beloved, we are found both weak and sluggish in fulfilling the service of our office, since, whenever we wish to do anything devoutly and energetically, the frailty of our condition delays us, nevertheless, because we possess the unceasing propitiation of the almighty and eternal Priest, who, being like us and equal to the Father, humbled his divinity even to human things and raised his humanity even to divine things, we rightly and devoutly rejoice in his constitution. For although he entrusted the care of their sheep to many shepherds, he himself did not abandon the guardianship of his beloved flock. From his sovereign and eternal protection we have also received a defense of apostolic assistance, which certainly does not cease from its work; and the firmness of the foundation on which the height of the whole Church is built is not troubled by the mass of the temple resting upon it [Perhaps read *lassescit* (“grows weary”).] [Note: Earlier editions before Quesnellus read “of apostolic work.” He preferred the reading of the Vict. and Gaudiival manuscripts. Four of our Vatican manuscripts support it. Moreover, we read *accipimus* (“we receive”) rather than *accepimus* (“we received”), as in the most ancient Vatican manuscript.]. For the solidity of that faith which was praised in the prince of the apostles is perpetual [Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads *perpetuat* (“makes perpetual”). We have deferred Quesnellus’s annotation on this passage to the observations to be published after the Sermons; there we shall explain Leo’s meaning.]; and just as what Peter believed in Christ remains, so what Christ established in Peter remains.

For when, as the Gospel reading has disclosed, the Lord had asked the disciples whom they believed him to be, while many held various opinions, and blessed Peter had replied, saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” the Lord said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:16–19) [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts add *apostolus* (“apostle”) after “blessed.”] [Note: Vatican manuscript 3836 reads: “Whatever you bind … will be bound; and whatever you loose … will be loosed.” A similar reading occurs in the following sermon, chapter 3.]

## CHAPTER III

The arrangement of truth therefore remains, and blessed Peter, persevering in the strength he received [Note: In the same manuscript and in another Vatican manuscript, the word “rock” is absent. A little later these manuscripts read “does not abandon.”], has not abandoned the governance of the Church that he undertook. For he was ordained above the others in such a way that, when he is called “Rock,” when he is declared the foundation, when he is appointed doorkeeper of the kingdom of heaven, and when he is constituted judge of what is to be bound and loosed, we might recognize, through the very mysteries of his titles, what sort of fellowship he has with Christ: he is placed in authority over the definition of his judgments, which will remain even in heaven [Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript reads “is determined by the definition of judgments”; another Vatican manuscript reads “is brought to completion.”].

Now he carries out more fully and powerfully what was entrusted to him, and performs in him and with him, through whom he was glorified, every part of his offices and responsibilities. If, therefore, anything is rightly done or rightly discerned by us; if anything is obtained from God’s mercy through our daily supplications, it is the work and merit of him whose power lives in his see and whose authority excels. For this was achieved, dearly beloved, by that confession which, inspired by God the Father in the apostolic heart, transcended all the uncertainties of human opinion and received the firmness of a rock that no assaults could shake. Throughout the universal Church, Peter says each day, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and every tongue that confesses the Lord is instructed by the teaching of this utterance. This faith conquers the devil and releases the bonds of his captives. It brings those rescued from the world into heaven, and the gates of hell cannot prevail against it. For it has been fortified by such divine solidity that neither heretical perversity has ever been able to corrupt it [Note: Quesnellus printed “break through,” although he noted that the printed editions and the Gaudiival manuscript read “corrupt.” We have restored the reading of the editions, since it is supported by the older manuscripts.], nor pagan unbelief overcome it.

## CHAPTER IV

By these means, dearly beloved, today’s festival is celebrated with rational devotion: in the person of my humility, he is understood and honored in whom the solicitude of all shepherds, together with the guardianship of the sheep entrusted to them, continues, and whose dignity does not fail even in an unworthy heir [Note: We have restored this from the most ancient Vatican manuscript, since other editions had “whose dignity also belongs to the unworthy one.” In the first edition and in several manuscripts, *etiam* (“also”) is absent.]. Hence the desired and honored presence of my venerable brothers and fellow priests is all the more sacred and devout, if they principally offer to him the piety of this service in which they have deigned to be present [Note: Vatican manuscript 544 reads “they refer,” perhaps more aptly, since the honor shown to the pontiffs is understood to be referred to Peter.], whom they know to be not only the bishop of this see but also the primate of all bishops.

Therefore, when we address our exhortations to the ears of your holiness, believe that it is he, whose place we occupy, who speaks to you [Note: To “act in someone’s place,” and *vicarii*, are ancient expressions also used of successors, who exercise no lesser dignity and power than their predecessor. We could demonstrate this with many ancient witnesses. The Roman pontiffs, however, are said in a special way to act in Peter’s place, or to be Peter’s vicars, so that they are understood not to possess a dignity and authority proper to themselves, but to have received Peter’s own dignity and authority, transmitted to all his successors. As Leo says in this very sermon, chapter 3, Peter’s power “lives in his see,” that is, in his successors, and his authority excels; and in chapter 4, “whose dignity does not fail even in an unworthy heir.” We have noted this because of the marginal note Quesnellus placed here: “The primacy of Peter, whose vicars the Roman pontiffs are.”]. For we admonish you with his affection, and preach to you nothing other than what he taught: namely, that you gird the loins of your mind and lead a chaste and sober life in the fear of God, and that your mind, forgetful of its sovereignty, not consent to the desires of the flesh. The joys of earthly pleasures are brief and passing; they try to turn those called to eternity away from the paths of life [Note: Vatican manuscript 3836 reads “try to turn them away from the heavenly life.”]. Let a faithful and devout spirit therefore desire the things of heaven, and, eager for the divine promises, raise itself toward love of the incorruptible good and hope of the true light.

Be certain, dearly beloved, that your labor, by which you resist vices and oppose carnal desires, is pleasing and precious in God’s sight, and will be useful not only to you but also to me before God’s mercy. For the shepherd’s care glories in the progress of the Lord’s flock [Note: The Vict. manuscript deletes *Dominici* (“of the Lord”). Quesnellus.]. For, as the Apostle says, “You are my crown and my joy” (1 Thessalonians 2:19), if your faith, which has been proclaimed throughout the whole world from the beginning of the Gospel (Romans 1:8), remains in love and holiness.

Although it is necessary that the whole Church, which exists throughout the world, flourish in every virtue, it is especially fitting that you surpass other peoples in the merits of devotion, since you are founded upon the very stronghold of the apostolic rock, and our Lord Jesus Christ redeemed you together with all others, while blessed Peter the apostle instructed you above all others. Through the same Christ our Lord. Amen.

# SERMON IV [Alternatively III]

On the fourth feast of his nativity, on the anniversary of his elevation [Note: In Casinensis manuscript 39, which after other works by various Fathers contains only two sermons of Saint Leo, this sermon appears on page 588 under the title: “Here begins the sermon on the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle, which is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.” Indeed, the readings of the third nocturn, which are still read on this day in the Roman Breviary, are taken from this sermon. In the table of the Casanatensis manuscript it is entitled: “On the feast of blessed Peter the apostle.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. This festival is common to all Christians, who are both kings and priests.  
II. How much was bestowed upon Peter above the others: the Church was founded upon Peter and upon his faith.  
III. The power of the keys, which Peter received, passed to the other apostles. Peter’s special privilege: the Lord assumes a special care of him and prays particularly for Peter’s faith, so that the firmness granted by Christ to Peter may be conferred through Peter upon the apostles.  
IV. Whatever good is done by Peter’s successors is owed to Peter’s prayers and solicitude. [Col. 0148B]

## CHAPTER I

I rejoice, dearly beloved, in the devout affection of your devotion, and I give thanks to God that I recognize in you the piety of Christian unity. For, as your very great attendance testifies, you understand that the return of this day belongs to a common joy, and that the honor of the whole flock’s shepherd is celebrated by annual festivals. Although the whole Church of God has been ordered in distinct ranks, so that the integrity of the sacred body may subsist from diverse members, nevertheless, as the Apostle says, we are all one in Christ (1 Corinthians 12:13). No one is so separated from another’s office that the humility of any part does not belong to the connection of the head [Note: Vatican manuscript 3836 reads “into unity.”].

Thus, in the unity of faith and baptism, we possess, dearly beloved, an undivided fellowship and a common dignity, in accordance with that most sacred utterance of blessed Peter the apostle, who says: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built up into spiritual houses, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ”; and below: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Peter 2:5, 9) [Note: All editions and our manuscripts—including the most ancient Vatican manuscript and the cited Casinensis manuscript—have “in accordance with the Gospel,” rather than “in accordance with that saying.” Quesnellus, however, deleted the words *sacratissima voce dicentis* (“in his most sacred voice saying”), on the authority of an unspecified manuscript, and substituted another form: “In accordance with that saying of blessed Peter the apostle, to which this sermon ought to be subordinate: ‘And you, as stones,’” etc.].

For all who have been reborn in Christ, the sign of the cross makes kings, while the anointing of the Holy Spirit consecrates priests [Note: The particle *vero* (“while,” “indeed”) is absent in the most ancient Vatican manuscript and in the Casinensis manuscript, which later reads *efficit* (“makes”) instead of *consecrat* (“consecrates”). A little later, *nostri* (“of our”) is absent in the cited Vatican manuscript.]. Thus, apart from the particular service of our ministry, all spiritual and rational Christians should recognize that they share in royal descent and priestly office [Note: Three of our best manuscripts and the first edition read “spiritual and rational.” Other editions before Quesnellus, and other manuscripts together with the Gaudiival manuscript, read “spiritual and reasonable”; Quesnellus deleted these words and placed them in the margin.].

For what is as royal as to have a mind subject to God and ruling its own body? And what is as priestly as devoting a pure conscience to the Lord and offering spotless sacrifices of devotion upon the altar of the heart? Although this has become common to all through God’s grace, it is nevertheless devout and praiseworthy for you to rejoice in the day of our advancement as though it were your own honor [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and one Bolognese manuscript, together with the first edition, read “for you”; this is indeed better, since Saint Leo praises his hearers, who rejoiced in his advancement or ordination as though in their own honor. Other editions and some manuscripts read “for us,” while in certain manuscripts *tamen* (“nevertheless”) is absent.]. Thus the sacrament of the pontificate may be celebrated as one thing throughout the whole body of the Church: when the oil of blessing is poured out, it flows more abundantly upon the higher members, but it also descends without stint upon the lower [Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript omits what follows through the end of the chapter. Shortly afterward, the Casinensis manuscript reads “of the poured-out” or “of the outpoured.”].

## CHAPTER II

Since, therefore, dearly beloved, our sharing in this office provides great material for common joys, our reason for rejoicing will nevertheless be truer and more excellent if you do not linger in consideration of our humility. It is far more useful and worthy to raise the eye of the mind to contemplate the glory of blessed Peter the apostle and to celebrate this day chiefly in his veneration. From the very source of all gifts he was flooded with such abundant streams that, although he alone received many things, nothing passed to anyone without his participation [Note: We have preferred the reading of the better Vatican and Casinensis manuscripts. Some manuscripts of the fourth collection, together with the editions, read “of himself” rather than “of his own.” Others read “of him.”].

“The Word had already become flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and Christ had given himself entirely for the restoration of the human race [Note: The editions formerly read: “For the Word had become flesh and already dwelt among us, so that Christ might give himself entirely for the restoration of the human race.” The reading of the most ancient Vatican and Casinensis manuscripts seemed preferable; the manuscripts of the fourth and fifth collections also confirm the final portion, including “for the restoration … he had given himself.”]. Nothing was beyond the ordering of wisdom; nothing was difficult for power. The elements served; spirits ministered; angels obeyed [Note: All editions and manuscripts except the Casinensis read *ministrabant* (“ministered”), while the Casinensis has *adorabant* (“adored”). Quesnellus noted that this reading occurs not only in the editions but also in the Gaudiival manuscripts. Yet he did not state what manuscript authority led him to exclude it and print: “The elements served, the angelic spirits ministered.”].

And yet, from the whole world Peter alone is chosen, to be placed over the calling of all nations, over all the apostles, and over all the Fathers of the Church. Thus, although there are many priests and many shepherds in the people of God [Note: Quesnellus deleted “and many shepherds,” which appeared in the editions, citing four manuscripts lacking these words. We have restored them, supported not merely by all editions but by Roman and the best Italian manuscripts.], Peter alone properly rules all those whom Christ also principally rules.

Divine condescension granted this man a great and marvelous share in its own power; and if it wished other leaders to have anything in common with him, it never gave anything that it did not grant through him. Finally, the Lord asks all the apostles what people think about him; and the speech of those answering remains common only so long as the uncertainty of human ignorance is being clarified [Note: This is the reading of the most ancient Vatican and Casinensis manuscripts. Other Vatican manuscripts and the editions read *intelligentiae* (“of understanding”) rather than *ignorantiae* (“of ignorance”), but consistently have *explicatur* (“is clarified”). Quesnellus printed, on the basis of four manuscripts, “the ambiguity of human understanding persisted,” and noted that *explicatur* is likewise read in the Gaudiival manuscript and the editions. Had he found *ignorantiae* in the ancient manuscripts, he would readily have preferred our reading.].

But when the sense of the disciples is demanded, he is first in the Lord’s confession who is first in apostolic dignity. When he had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” Jesus answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:16–17). That is: You are blessed because my Father taught you, and earthly opinion did not deceive you, but heavenly inspiration instructed you [Note: We followed the best Vatican and Casinensis manuscripts. The editions and some manuscripts read: “because my Father taught you … but heavenly inspiration instructed you”; another form has “because my Father taught you … but heavenly inspiration instructed you, and not flesh and blood,” etc.].

And not flesh and blood, but he revealed me to you, whose only-begotten Son I am. “And I say to you,” he says: just as my Father revealed my divinity to you, so I make your excellence known to you: “For you are Peter.” That is: although I am the inviolable rock, I am the cornerstone that makes both one, I am the foundation besides which no one can lay another (Ephesians 2:14, 20), nevertheless you too are rock, because you are made firm by my power, so that what belongs properly to me by power may be common to you with me by participation.

“And upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). Upon this strength, he says, I will construct an eternal temple, and the exalted height of my Church, destined to be carried into heaven, will rise upon the firmness of this faith.

## CHAPTER III

The gates of hell will not hold this confession; the bonds of death will not bind it, for this utterance is the voice of life. Just as it raises its confessors into heavenly things, so it plunges its deniers into the depths below. Therefore it is said to blessed Peter: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. And whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

The right of this power did indeed pass also to the other apostles [Note: Quesnellus’s note reads: “So the manuscript copies. Hincmarus of Reims, *Opusculum* 55, against Hincmarus of Laon, chapter 20, and in the letter in the name of Charles the Bald to Pope Hadrian, *Opusculum* 43; also in the letter in the name of Emperor Charles II and Cardinal Jacobatius to Pope John VIII, in the treatise *On the Council*. The editions read *vis* (“power”).” Thus far Quesnellus. The Roman manuscripts and the Casinensis manuscript, which we collated, also read *jus* (“right”). It would have been easy to read *vis* for *jus*. In Sermon 83, chapter 2, which was taken from this passage, *jus* is likewise read.], and the decree of this ordinance came to all the leaders of the Church; yet it is not without reason that what is announced to all is entrusted specially to one [Note: Vatican manuscript 544 reads “he commended.”]. For this is entrusted uniquely to Peter because Peter’s form is set before all the leaders of the Church [Note: The Casinensis manuscript reads “is proposed.”]. Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is issued according to his equity [Note: We shall include Quesnellus’s lengthy annotation on this passage among the observations to be published after the Sermons, and, subjecting it to examination, explain the genuine meaning of the holy pontiff from the context. A little later, the most ancient Vatican manuscript reads *refertur* (“is referred”) instead of *fertur* (“is issued”).].

There is neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency where nothing will be bound or loosed except what blessed Peter has bound or loosed. As his passion approached—a passion that was to disturb the disciples’ steadfastness—the Lord said: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers, so that you may not enter into temptation” (Luke 22:31–32) [Note: Hincmarus, citing this passage in *Opusculum* 33, reads it thus with the manuscripts. The editions have *cribraret* (“might sift”), Quesnellus says. The first edition, however, has *cerneret* (“might behold”), as likewise do three Vatican and two Casinensis manuscripts; these have only *velut* (“as”) for *sicut* (“like”). Manuscripts of collection 4 have *cribraret*, as does Sermon 83, chapter 3. A little later the editions and some less authoritative manuscripts read *ut non deficiat* (“that it may not fail”). We have preferred Vatican manuscript 3836 and two Casinensis manuscripts, whose reading agrees with Sermon 83, chapter 3, another most ancient Vatican manuscript 3835, and the Casinensis manuscript. The first three manuscripts soon omit *aliquando* (“once”); we have nevertheless not deleted it, because it is retained in Sermon 83 from the best manuscripts.] [Note: Sermon 83, chapter 3, reads “so that you may not enter into temptation.” These words are absent from the Greek and the common Latin text of Luke 22:32, and are found only somewhat later, at verse 40. Yet that they were formerly read in the same context at verse 32 is clear not only from this passage of Leo and from the similar passage in Sermon 83, but also from the author of *On the Calling of All Nations*, book 1, chapter 24, and book 2, chapter 28, and from Prosper in his letter to Rufinus, chapter 10. Those two writers, however, precede the words “so that you may not enter” with “and pray” or “and pray that.” In four very ancient manuscripts of the Gospels recently edited by our Father Joseph Blanchini—the Vercelli, Verona, Corbie, and Vienna manuscripts, which preserve the ancient reading—the addition likewise appears: “And pray that you may not enter into temptation.” Hence the words “and pray” seem perhaps to be added to Leo’s text; nevertheless, we have not inserted them without the authority of any Leonine edition or manuscript. Indeed, since these words are consistently absent from not merely one sermon but two, in every edition and manuscript we have collated, especially in two very ancient and certainly Roman Vatican manuscripts written in uncial script—one containing this sermon and the other the other sermon—we believe it highly probable that Leo read this Gospel passage in his books without those words.].

The danger of fearful temptation was common to all the apostles, and all equally needed the help of divine protection, since the devil desired to harass and overthrow them all. Yet the Lord assumes a special care for Peter and prays particularly for Peter’s faith, as though the condition of the others would be more secure if the mind of their leader were not overcome. In Peter, therefore, the strength of all is fortified, and the help of divine grace is so ordered that the firmness granted by Christ to Peter may be conferred through Peter upon the apostles.

## CHAPTER IV

Since, therefore, dearly beloved, we see that such a defense has been divinely established for us, we rightly and justly rejoice in the merits and dignity of our leader, giving thanks to the eternal King, our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ [Note: This is the reading of the Vatican and Casinensis manuscripts. The same occurs in Sermon 83, chapter 4, into which Saint Leo transferred this passage. Other manuscripts read “who.”], because he gave such power to the one whom he made the leader of the whole Church, so that, if anything is rightly done or rightly ordered by us even in our own times, it should be attributed to his works and to his governance, to whom it was said: “And you, once converted, strengthen your brothers”; and to whom, after his resurrection, the Lord said three times, through the mystery of a threefold profession of eternal love: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17) [Note: Some manuscripts read “threefold”; two of Quesnellus’s manuscripts do so.].

This he undoubtedly does even now, and the devoted shepherd carries out the Lord’s command, strengthening us by his exhortations and never ceasing to pray for us, so that we may not be overcome by any temptation. If, as we must believe, he everywhere displays this care of his devotion toward all God’s people, how much more will he deign to extend his assistance to us, his foster children, among whom he rests in the sacred bed of his blessed dormition, in the same flesh in which he presided [Note: Four manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus read “deigns.”]?

To him, therefore, let us ascribe this anniversary of our service; to him let us assign this festival, through whose patronage we have deserved to share in his see [Note: Casinensis manuscript 39 reads “we have deserved to have a share.”], while the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ assists us in all things. He lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON V [Alternatively IV]

On the fifth feast of his nativity, on the anniversary of his elevation to the pontificate [Note: This sermon was published several years ago from a manuscript of Nicholas Fabri, later belonging to D. Thuani and now preserved in the Colbert Library. Thus Quesnellus. Antelmius, however, in dissertation 6, *On the Genuine Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, no. 4, p. 348, observed that in that manuscript Prosper’s name had been prefixed by the first hand under the title: “Here begins Prosper’s sermon on the feast of the pope.” In a later hand, however, after the erased parchment, Leo’s name had been written. Since the context of the sermon indicates a Roman pontiff as its author, while its style plainly agrees with the style of Leo’s other sermons and differs greatly from Prosper’s style, there is no reason to doubt that it is genuinely Leo’s work. On Prosper’s name in the title, compare what we conjectured in the preface, no. 10.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. Everything must be referred to God.  
II. The higher a person’s position in the Church, the more he must fear.  
III. Christ is truly a priest according to the order of Melchizedek and is always present to his Church.  
IV. Peter continually cares for the Roman see.  
V. Honor must be offered chiefly to the one whose see his successors serve.

## CHAPTER I

Just as the dignity of fathers is the honor of their children, dearly beloved, so the joy of the people is the gladness of the priest. Since this comes from a divine gift—for, as it is written, “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17)—we ought to give thanks to the author of all good things, because whether in natural growth or in moral formation, he made us, and not we ourselves (Psalm 99:3). When we devoutly and faithfully confess this, and glory not in ourselves but in the Lord, our vows are fruitfully renewed with the passage of time, and religious festivals are rightly occasions of joy: in them we are neither ungrateful by keeping silent about gifts nor proud by presuming upon merits.

Let us therefore, dearly beloved, carry the whole cause and meaning of today’s solemnity back to its origin and source, and praise with due thanksgiving him in whose hand are both the stages of offices and the moments of time. For if we look to ourselves and to what belongs to us, we scarcely find anything in which we can rightly rejoice. Clothed in mortal flesh and subject to the frailty of corruption, we are never so free that we are not struck by some assault; nor is victory in this contest ever so secure that renewed struggles do not arise even after triumphs. Hence no pontiff is so perfect, no bishop so spotless, that he ought to offer sacrifices of reconciliation only for the sins of the people and not also for his own sins.

## CHAPTER II

If this condition generally applies to all priests, how much more does it burden and bind us, for whom the very greatness of the work undertaken is a frequent occasion of offense. Although each shepherd presides over his own flock with particular solicitude and knows that he must render an account for the sheep entrusted to him, our care is nevertheless shared with all; and no one’s administration is unrelated to a portion of our labor. Thus, while people come from the whole world to the see of blessed Peter the apostle, and the love of the universal Church, entrusted by the Lord to him, is also demanded through our administration, we feel the burden pressing upon us all the more because we owe more to everyone.

In this matter of trembling, what confidence could we have for the service we must discharge, if he who guards Israel neither slumbered nor slept, and who says to his disciples, “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20), did not deign to be not only the guardian of the sheep but also the shepherd of shepherds? He is not seen by bodily sight, but is perceived by the spiritual heart: absent in the flesh, through which he could be visible, yet present in divinity, through which he is always wholly everywhere.

Because “the just man lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4), and because this is the justice of the believer—to receive in the mind what he does not see with the eyes—the Lord, ascending on high, led captivity captive and gave gifts to men (Psalm 67:19): namely, faith, hope, and charity. They are great, strong, and precious because what cannot be grasped by the eyes of the flesh is nevertheless believed, hoped for, and loved through the mind’s wondrous affection.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, dearly beloved, the Lord Jesus Christ is present in the midst of believers, as we confess not rashly but faithfully. Although he sits at the right hand of God the Father until he places his enemies beneath his feet (Psalm 109:3), the supreme Pontiff is nevertheless not absent from the assembly of his pontiffs; and deservedly the whole Church and all priests sing to him with one voice: “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid., 6).

He is the true and eternal Bishop, whose administration can undergo neither change nor end. He is the one whose form the priest Melchizedek prefigured, offering not Jewish sacrifices to God, but sacrificing that sacrament which our Redeemer consecrated in his body and blood. He is the one whose priesthood the Father established—not according to the order of Aaron, which was to pass away with the time of the Law, but according to the order of Melchizedek, to be celebrated perpetually with the confirmation of an unbreakable oath.

For just as an oath among human beings is employed in matters established by perpetual agreements, so the testimony of the divine oath is found in promises fixed by unchangeable decrees. And because repentance indicates a change of will, God does not repent in the case of one concerning whom, according to his eternal purpose, he cannot will anything other than what he has willed.

## CHAPTER IV

It is not therefore, dearly beloved, a presumptuous festival by which we honor the day of our priesthood, mindful that it is a divine gift, since we devoutly and truthfully confess that Christ performs the work of our ministry in everything we rightly do. We glory not in ourselves, who can do nothing without him, but in him, who is our ability.

The dignity of blessed Peter, not only apostolic but also episcopal, is added to the rationale of our solemnity. He does not cease to preside over his see and maintains an unfailing fellowship with the eternal Priest. For that solidity which he received from Christ the Rock, having himself also been made rock, has passed into his heirs as well; and wherever any firmness is displayed, the strength of the shepherd plainly appears.

For if nearly all martyrs everywhere have been granted this power, in manifestation of their merits and in proportion to the sufferings they endured, so that they can bring help to those in danger, drive away diseases, expel unclean spirits, and cure countless illnesses, who could be so ignorant or so grudging in estimating the glory of blessed Peter as to believe that any part of the Church is not ruled by his care or increased by his help?

That love of God and humanity which neither prison bars, nor chains, nor popular assaults, nor royal threats terrified remains fully vigorous and alive in the prince of the apostles; and so does that unconquerable faith which did not yield in battle and did not grow lukewarm in victory.

## CHAPTER V
Therefore, since in our days sorrows are turned into joy, labors into rest, and discord into peace, we recognize that we are aided by the merits and prayers of our bishop, and by frequent proofs we experience that he presides over us with salutary counsels and equitable judgments. Thus, while the authority of binding and loosing remains among us, through the governance of the most blessed Peter both the condemned person is led to repentance and the reconciled person is brought to pardon. And so, whatever service you have rendered us today, whether out of the condescension of brothers or the devotion of sons [Note: [Col. 0155B] The service which St. Leo says the brothers rendered one another out of condescension concerns only the assembly of bishops to which these men had gathered after being invited to celebrate the anniversary of his ordination. See Sermon 2, chapter 2. These and similar services [Col. 0156B], to which no law and no precept compelled them, were rendered no less through the devotion of sons than through the condescension of brothers. There was therefore no reason for Quesnellus to append to this passage, in a marginal note, the general proposition: “Bishops, out of condescension, render services to the Roman pontiff.”], know that you have offered it more reverently and truly to him whose see we rejoice not so much to preside over as to serve. We hope through his prayers to obtain that the merciful God may graciously regard the period of our ministry and may always deign to guard and feed the shepherd of his sheep.

## ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING SERMONS CONCERNING THE COLLECTIONS

[Col. 0155]

The sermons of Saint Leo concerning the Collections are especially famous. They evidently refer to certain particular collections, which, although many people mention them as belonging to Leo, I have not been able to find explained by anyone. Quesnellus, in his note on the first sermon concerning the Collections, added only this: “To assemble here much material about the use and antiquity of the collections would be to do what has already been done. Let anyone who wishes consult the eminent Cardinal Baronius under the years of Christ 44, no. 30–31, and 58, no. 35.” That they were not customarily held only on Sunday in Leo’s time is clear from Sermons 2 and 3, where Monday and Tuesday are mentioned. We nevertheless believe that in these sermons Saint Leo is not speaking of the ordinary collections that were formerly held in all churches, but of an extraordinary and particularly important collection of alms: one announced and begun at a definite time of year and on a definite first day, and completed on the following days.

The appointment of a definite day is clear from each sermon. In the first sermon the collection is announced for Sunday, in the second for Monday, in the third for Tuesday, in the fourth for Wednesday—or rather Thursday—in the fifth again for Sunday, and in the sixth for Saturday. Since these sermons were delivered in different years, this variation of days undoubtedly indicates a particular day of some month, which fell on Sunday in one year, Monday in another, Tuesday in another, and so forth, and in the course of the years again fell on Sunday. But the day mentioned in these sermons is called not the sole day but the first day of the collections in Sermon 2; and Sermon 5, chapter 4, says: “On Sunday the first collection is to take place.” Thus other collections took place on the other days, and these collections consequently extended over several days.

On these days the Romans were to assemble through the churches of their districts for the distribution of alms, as means and devotion advised, as is related in Sermons 3 and 4, chapter 3, and Sermon 6, chapter 2. In Leo’s time there were seven ecclesiastical districts in the City, each of which had its own deaconry, where there were hospitals and lodgings for the poor, in which widows and other needy persons were supported from church funds. See Mabillon, *Commentary on the Roman Order*, in volume II of the *Museum Italicum*, p. 17. The alms were therefore to be brought to these deaconries; through the care of their administrators they supplied the expenses required, since, as Leo says in Sermon 6, chapter 2, people chiefly hasten to the Church whenever anyone seeks assistance.

We must now determine, if possible, the institution of these collections, the month in which they fell, the day of the month on which they began, and the number of days over which they continued. Saint Leo gives an indication of their institution in Sermons 3, 4, and 5, where he declares that such collections were formerly introduced by the Fathers so that, on the day when pagans served the devil through their superstitions, Christians might offer their own offerings to God with greater sanctity. Thus Sermon 2 says:

“To destroy the snares of the ancient enemy, on the day when the impious served the devil under the name of their idols, the first collection was most prudently instituted in the holy Church.”

And more explicitly Sermon 4, chapter 3:

“The day of apostolic institution summons us, on which the first collection of holy contributions was wisely and beneficially ordered by the Fathers, so that, because at this season the former pagan people served the demons with exceptional superstition, the most sacred offering of our alms might be celebrated in opposition to the profane sacrifices of the impious. Since this proved exceedingly fruitful for the growth of the Church, it was decided that it should be perpetual.”

And Sermon 5, chapter 1, testifies that this institution had formerly served to destroy vanities. Two conclusions follow from this. First, the ancient Fathers of the Church—who converted several other days polluted by superstitions to pious worship—transformed some celebrated pagan superstition, on which profane sacrifices or certain offerings were brought on a particular solemn day for the impious worship of idols, into collections of this kind for pious purposes. Second, this institution was so solemn and useful to the Church that those same Fathers wished it to be perpetual; and therefore, although that ancient superstition had been abolished, it still flourished in Leo’s time.

What this superstition was, then, from where such collections derived their origin, and in what month and on what day they fell—by which the month and day of the collections are to be determined—must be gathered from elsewhere, since Saint Leo reveals nothing. For this purpose the order of these sermons, which we have found in several manuscripts, is useful. Four of these sermons are contained in the Vallicellan Lectionary A, 6. They are written after the sermons for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul and before Leo’s Sermon 84, which in manuscript collections is attached to the third, fourth, and fifth days of the octave of those same apostles. The same order is found in the manuscripts of the second collection. It therefore appears that both the superstitions already mentioned and collections of this sort fell at the beginning of July.

At the beginning of July, the day that had been superstitious was the day before the Nones, on which the pagans celebrated the Apollinarian Games with particular solemnity and also contributed money toward their celebration. These games had been instituted after the disaster at Cannae, on the basis of a poem by the famous seer Marcius, which Livy reproduces in book XXV, chapter 12, as follows:

“Romans, if you wish to drive out the enemy . . . I advise that games be vowed to Apollo, to be celebrated every year in honor of Apollo, when the people shall have contributed a portion from public funds and private individuals shall contribute for themselves and their families; the praetor shall preside over the celebration of these games.”

When this poem had been found and brought before the Senate, the Fathers decided that games should be vowed to Apollo and celebrated by the urban praetor. When the praetor was about to hold them in the Circus Maximus, he announced that during those games the people should contribute to Apollo whatever amount they could conveniently afford.

At first these games were held without a fixed day. But in A.U.C. 546, Publius Varus, urban praetor, was ordered by a law passed before the people to establish a definite day. “Accordingly,” Livy says in book XXVII, “he first vowed and celebrated them on the day before the third day of the Nones of Quintilis.” This date was thereafter preserved as solemn. The text of Livy must be corrected on the basis of two ancient calendars, the Maffeian and the Blanchinian; instead of “the third day of the Nones,” we should read “the day before the Nones of Quintilis.” This is likewise confirmed by a third calendar, engraved on marble and found at Amiternum, published by Muratori in volume I of the *Thesaurus of Inscriptions*, p. 101. The only calendar that places them on the third day of the Nones—the calendar published by Lambecius from a manuscript of the Caesarean collection—is not to be preferred to the three calendars mentioned above, since it is also later in date. The error could easily have arisen through a scribal mistake. In volume VI, part II of the June *Acta Sanctorum*, the Bollandists placed opposite this calendar, first published by Lambecius, another previously unpublished calendar written by Polemius Silvius in the age of our Leo. In it, as in the marble calendars, the games are assigned to the day before the Nones. The fact that one day was initially established for these games, and that they were later repeated or continued over several days, was inferred from the testimony of several ancient writers who mention different days by Norisius in *Pisan Cenotaphs*, dissertation 2, chapter 6; before him, by Manutius in *On the Laws of the Romans* and in his commentary on Letter 1 of book XVI to Atticus.

From the Roman calendar engraved in the first century of the Church and preserved in the Capitoline Museum, published by Francesco Blanchini in volume II of Anastasius, p. 305, plate C, and also from the frequently reprinted Maffeian calendar, we learn that the Apollinarian Games began on the day before the Nones of July and continued until the fourth day before the Ides, that is, until the twelfth day of the same month. In the Lambecian calendar the same Apollinarian Games are also recorded on the third day before the Ides of that month, that is, on the thirteenth. This is explained by Cicero, Letter 4 of book XVI to Atticus, where he mentions a hunt on the day after the Apollinarian Games, which was regarded as an appendix to the Apollinarian Games. Hence the Blanchinian calendar has “In the Circus” on the third day before the Ides, while the Maffeian and Amiternian calendars have “Games in the Circus” on that same day.

Since this superstition was thus converted by the ancient Fathers to pious use, the first day of the collections appears to have been the day before the Nones of July, which is the day of the octave of Saints Peter and Paul. It had to be announced somewhat earlier, so that the people could prepare themselves for the collection at the proper time. It is therefore most likely that these sermons were delivered between the feast day and the octave of the holy apostles.

If three of these sermons are found in the use of the divine offices, assigned in the Vallicellan Lectionary mentioned above to Sundays 2, 3, and 4 after the apostles’ feast day, this occurred at a later period, when a Sunday was assigned to each of them. Similarly, Sermon 84, which belongs to the apostles’ octave, is described in the same Lectionary as being read on the sixth Sunday after their feast day.

From what we have established thus far, it is easy to identify the year of each sermon. Since the holy pontiff presided over the Roman Church from A.D. 440 to 461, the first and fifth sermons, delivered in different years in which the first collection is announced for Sunday, must be assigned to A.D. 441, 447, 452, or 458; in those years the sixth day of July, according to the Dominical Letter E, fell on Sunday. The second sermon, which announces the first collection for Monday, must be assigned to A.D. 442, 453, or 459, in which years the day before the Nones of July was Monday. Similarly, the third sermon, which designates Tuesday, must be assigned to A.D. 443, 448, or 454, in which the same day was Tuesday. The sixth sermon, which specifies Saturday, was delivered in A.D. 446 or 457, when the sixth day of July fell on Saturday.

The Wednesday specified in the fourth sermon does not seem to agree with another indication in that same sermon. For this sermon was clearly delivered when, at the beginning of the exposure of the error, proceedings were being undertaken at Rome against the Manichaeans; in chapter 4 the holy pontiff urges his hearers to report them to the presbyters. This fits the month of July only in the year 444, since in 443 the Manichaeans had not yet been exposed in that month. But the beginnings of the exposure of Manichaeism at Rome absolutely do not permit us to place this sermon later, in 449, 455, or 460, when the sixth day of July fell on the Wednesday designated by the sermon.

This difficulty had aroused suspicion that Leo was referring to another superstitious solemnity, whose first day, and with it the first collection associated with it, fell on Wednesday in 444. But since we have found no other pagan solemnity that would fit equally well, and since all the other indications in these sermons correspond more closely to the Apollinarian Games, which began on the sixth day of July, we believe that an error entered the notation of Wednesday in the fourth sermon. It would have been very easy, through the scribes’ confusion, to read or write “Wednesday” instead of “Thursday”; and Thursday indeed coincided with the day before the Nones of July in A.D. 444.

## 27. SERMON VI [Alternatively V]. Concerning the Collections I

[Col. 0157A]

### SYNOPSIS

After first commending almsgiving, he announces that the Sunday of the collections has arrived.

We are taught by many testimonies of the divine Scriptures how great is the merit of almsgiving and how great its power. For it is certain that each of us benefits his own soul whenever, through his mercy, he comes to the aid of another’s need. Therefore, dearly beloved, generosity among us ought to be ready and easy, if we believe that each person provides for himself what he gives to the needy. He stores his treasure in heaven who feeds Christ in the poor. Recognize, then, in this the kindness and administration of divine mercy. For this reason he wished you to abound, so that through you another might not be in need, and so that through the ministry of your action he might free the poor from the labor of poverty and you from the multitude of sins.

O wonderful providence [Note: The words “and goodness” are absent from the first edition.] and goodness of the Creator, who wished two persons to be helped by one action! The coming Sunday, therefore, is to be the day of the collections. I exhort and admonish your holiness: let each and every one of you remember both the poor and yourselves, and according to the capacity of your strength understand Christ in the needy. He commended the poor to us so strongly that he testified that he himself is clothed and received in them and fed in them—Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: The Vallicellan manuscript has “testifies.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript omits the words “with the Father and the Holy Spirit.”]

## SERMON VII [Alternatively VI]. Concerning the Collections II

[Col. 0159A]

### SYNOPSIS

Almsgiving is another washing away of sins and a work of the greatest charity.

Dearly beloved, we proclaim to you, with pastoral exhortation, a familiar command known to you: devote yourselves to works of mercy. Although this is never neglected by your holiness, it must now be carried out with greater readiness and zeal, because the first day of the collections, most salutarily instituted by the holy Fathers, requires that each person, according to what is vowed and possible, contribute from his resources for the use and sustenance [Note: The first edition reads “almsgiving.”] of the poor. You should know that, besides the washing of regeneration in which the stains of all sins have been cleansed, this remedy has been divinely granted to human weakness: if any fault is contracted in this earthly dwelling, it may be wiped away by almsgiving.

For the works of almsgiving are works of charity, and we know that “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8; Proverbs 10:12). Therefore, dearly beloved, diligently prepare your voluntary collections for Monday [Note: Alternatively, “collections.” The same reading is found in the Gaudivallian manuscript cited by Quesnellus and in three of our Vatican manuscripts; another Vatican manuscript incorrectly has “contributions.”], so that whatever you take from your temporal possessions, you may receive back multiplied in eternal recompense.

## SERMON VIII [Alternatively VII]. Concerning the Collections III

### SYNOPSIS

The collections were instituted on the occasion of pagan superstitions, from which not even the poor are excluded; almsgiving torments demons; the poor are not excluded from the fruit of the collections.

It belongs to Christian devotion, dearly beloved, that what has been instituted through apostolic traditions should be preserved with persevering dedication. For those most blessed disciples of truth commended this teaching, divinely inspired, so that whenever the blindness of the pagans was more intent upon their superstitions [Note: The Vulgate editions add the preposition “in,” which we have more correctly removed on the basis of the Vallicellan manuscript. Some manuscripts and the Vulgate editions add in the margin: “upon their institutions.” The first edition reads “in their superstitions.”], then especially the people of God should persist in prayers and works of devotion. For insofar as unclean spirits rejoice in the error of the pagans, they are beaten down by the observance of true religion, and the growth of righteousness burns the author of impiety [Note: The fifth collection of Vatican manuscripts has “they revere observance.” The Vallicellan manuscript has “are crushed” instead of “are worn down.”].

The blessed teacher of the nations guarded against his impious and profane inventions bringing any pollution to hearts consecrated to the true God when he said with apostolic voice: “Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers. For what participation is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14). Then he added the voice of the prophetic Spirit, saying: “Go out, go out from their midst, and be separated, says the Lord, and do not touch what is unclean” (ibid., 17; Isaiah 52:11). Therefore, because on the day when the impious served the devil under the name of their idols the first collection was most prudently instituted in the holy Church to destroy the snares of the ancient enemy, we wish your charity to assemble on Tuesday in all the churches of your districts with voluntary offerings of alms.

Although not everyone possesses equal means for this work, devotion ought to be equal, since the generosity of the faithful is measured not by the weight of the gift but by the extent of their goodwill. Let the poor, then, also gain something in this exchange of mercy, and let them set aside from whatever possessions they have something that does not distress them, for the support of the needy. Let the rich be more abundant in their gift, while the poor are not inferior in spirit. Although a greater return is expected from a greater sowing, much fruit of righteousness can nevertheless arise even from a small sowing [Note: We have also inserted “even” from the same manuscripts and from the Antwerp edition of 1583.]. For our judge is just and truthful, and he defrauds no one of the reward of merit. Therefore he wishes us to care for the poor, so that at the examination of the future recompense Christ our God may bestow on the merciful the mercy he promised—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: We have added “therefore,” which was missing, from two Vatican manuscripts and the Vallicellan Lectionary.]

## SERMON IX [Alternatively VIII]. Concerning the Collections IV

### SYNOPSIS

I. By the light of the Gospel, the darkness of pagan superstition is driven away, from which all crimes proceed.  
II. Therefore the coming judgment is proclaimed by Christ, so that sins may be redeemed through the generosity of mercy.  
III. The collections are an apostolic institution; they were arranged on the occasion of pagan superstition; the especially bashful poor are to be assisted.  
IV. Denouncing heretics is especially pleasing to God. The doctrines of the Manichaeans.

### CHAPTER I

Mercy and the justice of God, dearly beloved, have disclosed to us with most gracious explanation, through the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ, the form of his retributions established from the foundation of the world, so that, having received indications of events, we might already know as though accomplished what we believe is to come. For our Redeemer and Savior knew how many errors the devil’s deceit had scattered throughout the world and how many superstitions had subjected the greater part of the human race to himself.

But lest the creature formed in the image of God should, through ignorance of the truth, be driven any longer toward the precipices of perpetual death, he inserted in the Gospel pages a description of his judgment [Note: Latinus Latinius, in *Sacred and Profane Library*, p. 74, thought that *equity* or *equality* should be read. The Bonn manuscript has *equality*.] that would recall every human being from the snares of the most cunning enemy, since no one could now be unaware what rewards were to be hoped for by the good and what punishments were to be feared by the wicked [Note: The Vulgate editions, with most manuscripts, read “to be inflicted.” The reading of the Vallicellan manuscript seemed better, since the word “to be feared” is opposed to “to be hoped for” in Leo’s manner.].
