For that instigator and author of sin, first proud so that he might fall, then envious so that he might do harm, because he did not stand in the truth (John 8:44), placed all his power in falsehood and produced every kind of deception from this most poisonous source of his craft, so that he might exclude human devotion from the good which he himself had lost through his own pride and draw into fellowship with his condemnation those whose reconciliation he could not share.

Therefore, whoever among human beings has offended God through any kind of impiety has been led astray by his fraud and corrupted by his wickedness [Note: We have corrected this from the Vallicellan manuscript. In our other manuscripts and in all printed editions it read: “Whatever of human beings has offended God through any kind of impiety has been led astray through his fraud and corrupted by this wickedness.”]. For he easily drove into every crime those whom he deceived in religion [Note: Two manuscripts of the fourth collection, another of the fifth collection, and the Antwerp edition add “in religion”; the Vallicellan manuscript reads “he received them into religion.”]. Knowing that God is denied not only in words but also in deeds, he took charity away from many from whom he could not take faith; and when the field of their hearts had been seized by the roots of avarice, he deprived of the fruit of works those whom he had not deprived of confession with their lips.

### CHAPTER II

Because of these devices of the ancient enemy, therefore, dearly beloved, the ineffable kindness of Christ wished us to know what would be decreed concerning the whole human race on the day of recompense. Thus, while in the present time the medicine of lawful remedies is offered, while restoration is not denied to those who have fallen, and those who have long been barren can at last become fruitful, the judgment of justice already ordained may be forestalled, and the image of divine discernment may never depart from the eyes of the heart [Note: The Bonn manuscript, with the first edition, reads “severity,” not inappropriately.].

For the Lord will come in the glory of his majesty, as he himself foretold (Matthew 25:31), and with him there will be an innumerable multitude of angelic armies, radiant in their splendors. The peoples of all nations will be gathered before the throne of his power; and whatever human beings have been born throughout all the ages and throughout the whole world will stand before the one who judges.

The righteous will be separated from the unjust, the innocent from the guilty. When the children of devotion have received the kingdom prepared for them, after the works of mercy have been reviewed, the hardness of sterility will be reproached to the unjust. Having nothing in common with those on the right, they will be sent by the condemnation of the almighty Judge into the fire prepared for the torments of the devil and his angels, to share punishment with the one whose will they chose to do.

Who, then, would not dread this lot of eternal torments? Who would not fear evils that will never end? But since severity has been announced for the purpose of seeking mercy, we must live in the present days with generous mercy, so that after perilous negligence a person returning to works of devotion may be able to escape this sentence. This is what the power of the Judge and the grace of the Savior accomplish [Note: The Vallicellan manuscript reads “of the Savior”]: that the impious person may abandon his ways and the sinner withdraw from the habit of his iniquity.

Let those who wish Christ to spare them have mercy on the poor. Let those who desire to reach the fellowship of the blessed be ready to provide food for the wretched [Note: We substituted “of the blessed,” opposed to “of the wretched,” for “of the faithful,” on the weak authority of four manuscripts and the Antwerp edition. Some manuscripts read “to belong” instead of “to reach.”]. Let no human being be worthless to another, and let no one despise that nature which the Creator of all things made his own. For to which of the suffering may one deny what Christ declares is offered to him? A fellow servant is helped, and the Lord gives thanks in return. The food of the needy is the price of the heavenly kingdom; and the giver of temporal things becomes heir of eternal things.

How, then, did these small expenditures deserve to be valued so highly, unless the weights of charitable works are measured on the scales, and when a person loves what God loves, one rightly ascends into the kingdom of the one whose affection one shares?

### CHAPTER III

For the pious care of these works, dearly beloved, the day of apostolic institution summons us. On it the first collection of holy contributions was wisely and beneficially ordered by the Fathers [Note: The printed editions, with most manuscripts, read “of collections.” The Vallicellan reading is better, since “contributions” corresponds perfectly to the offering of alms mentioned shortly afterward. The first edition has “the first contribution of holy collections”; this is not unacceptable.]. Because at this season the former pagan people served the demons with exceptional superstition, the most sacred offering of our alms was to be celebrated in opposition to the profane sacrifices of the impious [Note: We have followed the reading of the first edition, confirmed by manuscripts of the third collection and the Vallicellan Lectionary. Other editions read “our most sacred [offering],” and Quesnellus “most sacredly.”]. Since this proved exceedingly fruitful for the growth of the Church, it was decided that it should be perpetual.

Therefore we exhort your holiness to contribute from your resources on Wednesday [Note: “Thursday” should be read, as we stated in the admonition; but since no manuscript supports the correction, we have not altered the text], through the churches of your districts, as ability and willingness advise, toward the expenses of mercy. Thus you may be able to merit that blessedness in which the person who understands the needy and poor will rejoice without end (Psalm 40:1).

To understand him, dearly beloved, we must watch with solicitous kindness so that we may find the person whom modesty conceals and shame hinders [Note: The first edition reads “prevents.”]. There are people who are ashamed to ask openly for what they need and prefer to be afflicted by the misery of silent poverty rather than be embarrassed by a public request [Note: The Vallicellan manuscript reads “distress.”]. Such persons must therefore be understood and relieved from hidden need [Note: Manuscripts of the fourth and fifth collections read “revealed”], so that they may rejoice all the more when provision has been made both for their poverty and for their modesty.

Rightly, in the needy and poor person, the person of Jesus Christ our Lord himself is perceived. Although he was rich, as the blessed Apostle says, he became poor in order to enrich us through his poverty (2 Corinthians 8:9) [Note: This is the reading of the Vallicellan manuscript and of manuscripts of the fourth and fifth collections. Other copies read, “as the Apostle says, he became without means.”]. And lest he seem to be absent from us, he so tempered the mystery of his humility and glory that, while we adore him as King and Lord in the majesty of the Father, we should feed that same one in his poor. Through this we shall be delivered on the evil day from eternal condemnation and, through care for the poor person whom we have understood, be admitted into fellowship with the heavenly kingdom [Note: Alternatively, “by his presence.”].

### CHAPTER IV

But so that your devotion may please the Lord in every respect, dearly beloved, we also exhort you to this diligence: report the Manichaeans, wherever they may be hiding, to your presbyters. For it is a great act of devotion to expose the hiding places of the impious and to conquer in them the devil himself whom they serve.

Against these people, dearly beloved, the whole world and the entire Church everywhere ought indeed to take up the weapons of faith [Note: The Antwerp edition has “shield” in the margin. The Vallicellan manuscript has “to seize.”]. But your devotion in this work ought to excel, since in your forefathers you learned the Gospel of the cross of Christ from the very mouths of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

People who do not believe that the law given through Moses is to be received—a law in which God is shown to be the Creator of all things—must not be allowed to remain hidden. They contradict the prophets and the Holy Spirit; they dare, with damnable impiety, to reject David’s psalms, which are sung throughout the universal Church with complete devotion; they deny the birth of Christ the Lord according to the flesh; they say that his passion and resurrection were simulated, not real; and they strip the baptism of regeneration of the power of every grace.

Among them nothing is holy, nothing whole, nothing true. They must be guarded against, lest they harm anyone; they must be reported, lest they establish themselves in any part of our city [Note: We have restored the preposition “in,” omitted by Rainaudus and Quesnellus, from the other editions and all our manuscripts.]. Before the tribunal of the Lord, dearly beloved, it will benefit you that we proclaim this and that we ask it of you.

For it is fitting that the crown of this work also be joined to the sacrifice of almsgiving [Note: The printed editions read “and of this work,” followed by “for us on your behalf.” We preferred the reading of the Vallicellan manuscript, with which manuscripts of the fifth collection agree in the word “for you.”], with the Lord Jesus Christ assisting you in all things—he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## 34. SERMON X [Alternatively IX]

### Concerning the Collections V

### SYNOPSIS

I. The faithful are assisted by the custom of collections handed down by the apostles. Wealth has been entrusted by God not so much to be possessed as to be administered.  
II. How wretched are those who spend their wealth only for their own use and not on the poor.  
III. Without mercy toward the poor, the other virtues are of no benefit.  
IV. Faith without works is dead; it is brought to life through charity. What are the benefits of almsgiving and temperance?

### CHAPTER I

Keeping the institutions of apostolic tradition, dearly beloved, we exhort you with pastoral concern to celebrate with the devotion of religious custom the day which the apostles purified from impious superstition and consecrated to works of mercy. In this way we show that the authority of the Fathers lives among us and that their teaching endures in our obedience.

For the holy benefit of so great an institution looked forward not only to the past but also to our own age, so that what served them for the destruction of vanities might serve us for the growth of virtues [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “the great benefit of so holy an act.”]. What is so suited to faith, what so agreeable to devotion, as to assist the poverty of the needy [Note: This is the reading of the Vallicellan manuscript. Other copies read “the poor in their poverty,”], to assume responsibility for the sick, to help the needs of our brothers, and to remember, in the labor of others, the condition proper to oneself?

In this work, how much each person can do, and how much he cannot, is discerned truthfully by the one who knows what he has bestowed on each [Note: The words “and how much he cannot” are absent from the manuscript of Victorinus cited by Quesnellus and from other manuscripts of our fifth collection.]. For not only spiritual riches and heavenly gifts are received through God’s generosity; earthly and bodily resources also come from his bounty, so that he will rightly demand an account of them [Note: The Vallicellan manuscript reads: “who entrusted them not so much to be distributed as he committed them to be administered.” The word “their” should have been written earlier in this reading, as the Antwerp edition has it; otherwise it follows the common reading of the other editions.], since he entrusted them not so much to be possessed as to be administered.

The gifts of God must therefore be used justly and wisely, lest the material for a good work become the cause of sin [Note: Thus, together with Quesnellus, our manuscripts. Earlier editions read: “For riches, insofar as they are considered in their forms,” and so forth.]. For riches, insofar as their forms and substance are concerned, are good and greatly benefit human society when they are held by benevolent and generous people; but neither should the luxurious squander them nor the miser hoard them [Note: The Vallicellan manuscript reads “blocks them.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript has “so that they may be dissipated when spent.”], so that they perish as much through being badly stored as through being foolishly spent.

### CHAPTER II
Although it is praiseworthy to flee intemperance and avoid the losses caused by shameful pleasures, and although many distinguished men disdain to conceal their resources and, flourishing in abundance, shrink from a mean and shabby frugality [Note: [Col. 0164D] The Vallicellian manuscript and one Vatican manuscript, together with the first edition, read *inter copias* (“amid riches”).], nevertheless such abundance is neither fortunate nor such frugality commendable [Note: [Col. 0164D] Codex Victorinus in Quesnellus and our collection 5: *blanda frugalitas* (“an indulgent frugality”).] if their wealth serves only themselves; if none of the poor are helped by their goods, none of the weak are supported; if, from the abundance of their great resources, no captive feels his redemption, no traveler comfort, no exile assistance.

Such rich men are poorer than all the poor. For they lose those revenues which they could possess forever [Note: [Col. 0164D] Thus from the Vallicellian manuscript. Elsewhere, *possunt* (“they can”). Shortly afterward, instead of *incubant* [Col. 0165C], editions after the first and before Quesnellus read *incumbunt* [Col. 0165D].], and while they cling to a brief and not always free use of them, they are nourished by no food of justice [Note: [Col. 0165D] In the Vallicellian manuscript: “by no mercy.”.] and refreshed by no sweetness of mercy; splendid outwardly, dark within; rich in temporal things [Note: [Col. 0165D] The same manuscript: “abounding in temporal things, destitute of eternal ones.”.], poor in eternal things: because they themselves afflict their souls with hunger and dishonor them with nakedness [Note: [Col. 0165D] The same Vallicellian manuscript adds: “who have committed nothing from what they entrusted to earthly storehouses to the heavenly treasuries.”.], since they have transferred nothing to the heavenly treasuries from what they entrusted to earthly storehouses.

But perhaps there are some rich people who, although they are not accustomed to help the poor of the Church with any gifts, nevertheless keep other commandments of God and, amid various merits of faith and uprightness, consider that one virtue is permissibly lacking in them. Yet this virtue is so great [Note: [Col. 0165D] The aforementioned Vallicellian manuscript adds, in a second hand, after *est* (“is”): “the virtue of mercy.” This is an addition by some zealous student, absent from the other manuscripts. Immediately afterward, the same manuscript reads *etiamsi* (“even if”) instead of *etsi*.] that without it the others, even if they exist, cannot be beneficial. For although someone may be faithful, chaste, sober, and adorned with other great distinctions [Col. 0165B], yet if he is not merciful, he does not merit mercy [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “he will not merit mercy”; for the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them.”.]. For the Lord says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V, 7).

But when the Son of Man comes in his majesty, sits upon his throne of glory, and, with all the nations gathered together, the distinction between good and evil has been made (Matt. XXV, 33), for what will those who stand at his right hand be praised, except for works of benevolence and acts of charity, which Jesus Christ will regard as rendered to himself? For he who made human nature his own in no respect separated himself from human humility [Note: [Col. 0165D] The same manuscript: “did not separate himself from humanity.”.]. And what will be charged against those on the left, except neglect of love, the hardness of inhumanity, and mercy denied to the poor?—as though those on the right had no other virtues, or those on the left no other offenses [Col. 0165C]. But in that great and supreme judgment the kindness of generosity and the impiety of stinginess will be valued so highly that, in place of the fullness of all virtues and the sum of all offenses, these will be brought into the kingdom by one good deed, and those will be sent into eternal fire by one evil deed.

Therefore, beloved, let no one flatter himself about any merits of a good life if works of charity are lacking in him; nor let anyone be secure because of the purity of his body [Note: [Col. 0165D] Thus from three manuscripts—the Vallicellian, Vatican, and Bononian—and the first edition. Elsewhere, *qualitate* (“quality”).], if he is not cleansed by any purification through almsgiving. For almsgiving wipes away sins (Eccli. III, 33), destroys death, and extinguishes the punishment of everlasting fire. But whoever is empty of its fruit [Col. 0166A] will be excluded from the pardon of the one who rewards, as Solomon says: “He who stops his ears so as not to hear the weak will himself call upon the Lord, and there will be no one to hear him” [Note: [Col. 0165D] The Antwerp edition, together with the Vallicellian manuscript, reads “he will call upon the Lord.”.].

Hence Tobias, instructing his son in precepts of piety, says: “From your substance give alms, and do not turn your face away from the poor man; thus it will happen that the face of God will not be turned away from you” (Tob. IV, 7). This virtue makes all virtues useful; by its participation it even gives life to faith itself, by which the righteous person lives (Hab. II, 4; Rom. I, 17; Gal. III, 11), and which is called dead without works (Jas. II, 26): for just as the account of works is found in faith, so the strength of faith is found in works.

Therefore, while we have time, as the Apostle says, “let us do what is good toward all, but especially toward those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. VI, 10). “And in doing good, let us not grow weary, for in due season we shall reap” (ibid., 9) [Col. 0166B]. The present life, then, is the time of sowing, and the day of repayment is the time of harvest, when each person will receive the fruit of his seeds according to the measure of his sowing. No one will be deceived about the yield of this crop, because there the measure of souls rather than of expenditures will be assessed; and small things from small things will return as much as great things from great things.

And therefore, beloved, let the apostolic ordinances be fulfilled. Since the first collection will take place on the Lord’s Day [Note: [Col. 0166D] Codex Victorinus of Quesnellus and our collection 5, together with the Vallicellian manuscript, read *die illo* (“on that day”) instead of *die Dominica* (“on the Lord’s Day”). This expression, frequent in formularies, indicates the day on which the first day of the collections was to be announced, according to the varying years, as falling on the day before the Nones of July. We have retained *die Dominica*, as the other manuscripts and all editions have it, because Leo is presumed to have announced this day when he delivered this sermon in a particular year.], prepare yourselves wholly for the voluntary offering of devotion, so that each person, according to his means, may have a share in the most sacred offering. The alms themselves, and those who will be helped by your gifts, will intercede for you, so that you may always be able to perform every good work, in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XI [elsewhere X]

[Note: [Col. 0166D] It was first published at Paris in 1614 from an old manuscript of Nicolas Fabri, later known as the Thuaneus and then the Colbertinus, and now preserved in the Royal Library. In that manuscript it is entitled “On the Day of the Collections.” Antelmius noted in dissertation 6, *On the True Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, no. 4, p. 350, that Leo’s name had been added to this sermon in the same manuscript by a later hand, whereas it was absent from the first hand. We have shown in the preface to the Sermons, no. 10, that it should rightly be attributed to Leo.]

### On Collections VI

### Synopsis

I. How greatly the final sentence of our Judge commends works of mercy.  
II. From where the custom of collections originated in the Church.

### Chapter I

From both the divine commandments, beloved, and the apostolic ordinances we have learned that every person placed amid the dangers of this life must seek the mercy of God by showing mercy. For what hope would raise up the fallen, what medicine would heal the wounded, unless almsgiving released sins and the needs of the poor became remedies for offenses?

Therefore, because the Lord had said, “Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matt. V, 7), he showed that the whole judgment by which, in his present majesty, he will judge the entire world is to be weighed according to this equity: once the quality of works toward the needy has been examined, the impious will be destined to burn with the devil, and the kindly to reign with Christ.

What will not then be brought into the midst? What hidden things will not be disclosed? What consciences will not be laid open? It will be a time when no one will truly boast that he has a clean heart or is pure from sin (Prov. XX, 9). But because mercy will be exalted above judgment, and the gifts of clemency will surpass every recompense of justice [Col. 0167B], the whole life of mortals and the varied character of all their actions will be assessed according to the condition of a single rule. There will be no need there to recall anyone’s crime where works of piety have been found through confession of the Creator.

Therefore those on the left will not be condemned only for what will be reproached in them, nor, because they will be shown to be strangers to humanity, will they be found free from other sins; rather, they will be condemned for many things, and especially because they did not redeem their crimes through almsgiving. For since it is the mark of an extremely hard heart not to be moved by the misery of people in distress, and since one who has the ability to help but does not aid the afflicted is as unjust as one who oppresses the weak, what hope remains for the sinner who does not show mercy even in order to obtain mercy?

First, therefore, beloved, the person who is not good to another is bad to himself, and harms his own soul if he does not come to the aid of another as far as he can. The rich and the poor have one nature [Note: [Col. 0167D] In the Paris edition of 1671, which is a reprint of the first edition of this sermon, the passage reads: “And among the other evils of human frailty, no security of health is safe, because what can happen to one person is something no one ought not to fear.” Although this reading is better, we have retained Quesnellus’s reading, since, having consulted the manuscript itself, he seems to have given its reading and relegated to the margin the variant readings of the editions, which appear to have been introduced into the text by someone’s arbitrary judgment to bring out the meaning more suitably. Yet, so as not to alter the manuscript reading in the text, he preferred to note in the margin that *inter caetera* (“among other things”) should be read as *inter incerta* (“among uncertain things”), and *sanitatis* (“of health”) perhaps as *divitis* (“of the rich”).], and amid the other frailties of human nature there is no secure happiness in health, because no one ought not to fear what can befall another.

Let mortal, changeable, and perishable humanity recognize itself in every human being, and, according to the common condition, return affection to its own kind; let it weep with those who weep and groan with the groans of those who suffer; let it share its resources with the needy; while the service of his body is sound, let him bend toward the sick person who lies ill [Note: [Col. 0167D] The same Paris edition: “while the ministry of a healthy body is available, let him bend toward the sick person lying in a worse condition.”.]; let it count among its own food the portion of the hungry, and in the pale, trembling nakedness of others let it believe that it too is cold.

FOR THE ONE WHO relieves the temporal misery of a suffering person escapes the eternal punishment of the sinner [Col. 0168A].

### Chapter II

Therefore, beloved, the holy Fathers wisely and piously arranged that at various times there should be certain days to summon the devotion of the faithful people to a public contribution. Since everyone seeking aid hastens especially to the church, a voluntary and holy collection was to be made from the means of many, which, through the care of those presiding, would meet necessary expenses.

The approaching day invites you, as we believe, to the desired fruit of this work; together with our admonitions, it calls you to bring gifts of mercy to the churches of your districts on the coming Saturday [Note: [Col. 0167D] The reference is to the deaconal churches, as we observed in the admonition prefixed to Sermon 6. Hence Quesnellus wrongly added in a marginal note to this passage “parish churches,” over which titular priests, not deacons, presided.].

And because God loves a cheerful giver (II Cor. IX, 7), let no one declare himself more generous than his substance permits [Col. 0168B]. Let each person be a fair judge between himself and the poor. Let joyful and confident compassion remove distrust; and let the one who helps the needy understand that he is offering to God what he gives.

From whatever resources one gives—for their measure is certainly not the same—the merit can be equal, if, amid the differing amounts contributed, no one’s piety is less than his means. For God, with whom there is no partiality, receives the gift of the rich and of the poor alike, because he knows what he has given to each and what he has not given; and ON THE DAY of repayment it is not the size of one’s wealth that will be judged, but the quality of one’s intentions. Through Christ our Lord.

## SERMON XII [elsewhere XI]

[Note: [Col. 0168D] In the first edition and in manuscripts of collection 3, this sermon is entitled “Sermon VI on Collections,” and “I on the Fast of the Tenth Month.” The title “On Collections” is likewise added to the following sermon, and from there passed into the other editions. But wrongly: neither this sermon nor the following mentions collections, as do the six preceding sermons, which truly concern collections. The manuscripts of all the other collections lack this title “On Collections”; like the lectionary manuscripts, they all entitle these sermons “On the Fast of the Tenth Month.”.]

### On the Fast of the Tenth Month I

### Synopsis

[Col. 0168C]

I. Human beings were created in order to imitate their creator; this too is God’s gift.  
II. Charity embraces not only God but also one’s neighbor, even one’s enemies; such is the breadth of Christian charity.  
III. Everyone must be subject to all God’s judgments and give thanks no less for poverty than for abundance.  
IV. All virtues are comprised in fasting, prayer, and almsgiving.

### Chapter I

If we understand faithfully and wisely the beginning of our creation [Note: [Col. 0168D] The Casinensian manuscript of collection 1 reads, “we understand.”], we shall find that human beings were created in the image of God so that they might be imitators of their creator; and that this is the natural dignity of our race: that the form of divine kindness should shine within us as in a certain mirror.

To this condition the grace of the Savior restores us daily [Note: [Col. 0168D] Two lectionary manuscripts of the Basilica of St. Peter and Vatican manuscript 541, collection 4, read: “so that what fell in the first Adam may be raised up in the second.” In the most ancient Vatican lectionary, manuscript 3836, *et* (“and”) appears instead of *dum* (“while”).], while what fell in the first Adam is raised up in the second [Col. 0169A]. The cause of our restoration is nothing other than the mercy of God: whom we would not love unless he himself first loved us [Note: [Col. 0169C] Most printed editions before Quesnellus: “unless he first loved us himself.”.], and scattered the darkness of our ignorance by the light of his truth.

Foretelling this through the holy Isaiah, the Lord says [Note: [Col. 0169C] Thus two manuscripts of St. Peter, the most ancient Vatican manuscript, and the edition of Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary* published at Basel in 1496. In editions before Quesnellus it was *denuntians* (“announcing”); in Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of collections 4 and 5, *pronuntians* (“proclaiming”). [Col. 0169D] Correctly conjecturing the reading, he noted in the margin that perhaps *praenuntians* (“foretelling”) should be read.]: “I will lead the blind by a way that they did not know, and I will make them tread paths that they did not know. I will turn darkness into light before them, and crooked things into straight. I will do these things for them, and I will not abandon them” (Isa. XLII, 16) [Note: [Col. 0169D] Vatican manuscript 3836: “and I will not forsake them.”.].

And again he says: “I have been found by those who did not seek me, and I appeared openly to those who did not ask about me” (Isa. LXV, 1). The apostle John teaches how this was fulfilled, saying: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true one and may be in his true Son” (I John V, 20) [Note: [Col. 0169D] In Paul the Deacon: “the Son of God has already come.”.]. And again: “Therefore let us love God, because he first loved us” (I John IV, 19).

By loving us, therefore, God restores us to his image; and, so that he may find in us the form of his goodness, he gives us the means to perform in our turn what he himself does, kindling the lamps of our minds and inflaming us with the fire of his charity [Note: [Col. 0169D] The most ancient Vatican manuscript and one of St. Peter’s manuscripts read “inflames us.”.], so that we may love not only him but also whatever he loves.

For if among human beings that friendship is ultimately firm which likeness of character has joined together, although similarity of desires often tends toward reprehensible affections, how greatly ought we to desire and strive not to differ in anything from what is pleasing to God! Of this the prophet says: “For there is anger in his indignation, and life in his goodwill” (Ps. XXIX, 6), because the dignity of divine majesty will exist in us only if there has been imitation of his will [Col. 0169C].

### Chapter II

Since the Lord says, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. XXII, 37), let the faithful soul receive the unfading charity of its creator and ruler, and subject itself wholly to his will, in whose works and judgments nothing is empty of the truth of justice and nothing of the compassion of mercy.

For even if someone is wearied by great labors and exhausted by many hardships, the cause for enduring them is good if he understands that through adversity he is either corrected or tested [Note: [Col. 0169D] The first edition and the Bononian manuscript read: “that is a good reason for enduring them, by which he understands himself either to be corrected or tested through adversity.”.].

But the piety of this charity cannot be perfect unless one’s neighbor is loved as well. By “neighbor” we are not to understand only those joined to us by friendship or kinship, but absolutely all human beings with whom we share a common nature [Note: [Col. 0169D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter: “a common measure and nature.”.], whether they are enemies or allies, free or enslaved.

For one Creator fashioned us all, one Creator gave us all life; we all enjoy the same heaven and air, the same days and nights [Col. 0170A]; and although some are good and others evil, some just and others unjust, God is nevertheless the giver and benefactor of all. Thus Paul and the apostle Barnabas say to the people of Lycaonia concerning God’s providence: “In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. Yet he did not leave himself without witness, doing good, giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, and filling our hearts with food [Note: [Col. 0169D] We have preferred this reading, which agrees with the Greek text and the Vulgate, from the most ancient Vatican lectionary, an ancient copy of Paul the Deacon, and manuscripts of collection 4. Elsewhere: “justice.” Immediately afterward three of our manuscripts read “your hearts.”.] and gladness” (Acts XIV, 15–16) [Col. 0170B] [Note: [Col. 0169D] So it appears in Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary*.].

The breadth of Christian grace, extending through every part of the whole world, has given us still greater reasons for loving our neighbor [Note: [Col. 0170C] We consider this reading of the first edition and manuscripts of collection 3 more suitable. In the other printed editions: “it despises no one while it teaches.” Manuscripts Victorinus, Corbey, Thuaneus, and Gaudiival in Quesnellus, and our Vatican manuscript 541, collection 4: “it despairs of no one while it teaches.” Another Vatican manuscript, 546, collection 4, Vatican manuscript 544, collection 5, two manuscripts of St. Peter, and Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary*: “it despairs of no human being while it teaches.” Finally, Vatican manuscript 3836: “it despairs of no human beings while it teaches.”.], teaching, while it despises no one, that no one is to be neglected.

And rightly he also commands that enemies be loved and that prayer be offered for persecutors (Matt. V, 44), since, inserting a shoot of the wild olive into the sacred branches of his olive tree [Note: [Col. 0170D] In both the printed editions and most manuscripts *fractis* (“broken”) was read instead of *sacris* (“sacred”); this seemed to correspond to Paul’s testimony in Rom. XI, 17 and 19, where broken branches are mentioned. But we have preferred the reading of three Roman lectionaries—Vatican manuscript 3836 and two of the Basilica of St. Peter—especially since grafting takes place not into broken and cut-off branches but into branches from which those others have been cut off. The Apostle calls these branches of the olive tree holy in verse 16, no less than the root. Shortly afterward, in Paul’s testimony, the first edition and two manuscripts of St. Peter omit the word “Christ.”.], he reconciles enemies, adopts strangers, and makes the impious just; “so that every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 10).

### Chapter III

Since God wants us to be good because he is good, nothing in his judgments ought to displease us. For what else is it than to reproach him in some respect if we do not give him thanks for everything? Human foolishness often dares to murmur against its Creator not only because of poverty but also because of abundance: it complains when something is lacking and is ungrateful when certain things overflow.

The owner of a rich harvest grew weary of the fullness of his storehouses [Col. 0171A] (Luke XII, 16), and groaned at the abundance of his overflowing vintage; he did not rejoice in the size of his crops but complained of their low price. But if the earth is more sparing in the seeds entrusted to it, and vines and olive trees yield a more restrained harvest [Note: [Col. 0171D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the first edition: “the year is accused.”.], the years are accused, the elements are arraigned, and neither air nor sky is spared.

Yet nothing commends and strengthens faithful and pious disciples of truth more than perseverance in God and tireless praise [Note: [Col. 0171D] The most ancient Vatican manuscript reads: “disciples of peace.” Two manuscripts of St. Peter have: “And since the faithful disciple of peace and truth commends and urges nothing more than perseverance in God and tireless praise,” followed by “Rejoice always,” etc.]. The Apostle says: “Rejoice always; pray without ceasing; give thanks in everything. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (I Thess. V, 16) [Note: [Col. 0171D] Thus from our manuscripts, the first edition, and Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary*. Likewise in St. Paul. Other editions and Quesnellus read “for us.”.].

But how can we share in this devotion unless the variety of circumstances exercises the constancy of the mind, so that love directed toward God neither grows proud amid prosperity nor fails amid adversity? Let what pleases God please us also [Note: [Col. 0171D] Thus our manuscripts. The printed editions: “and all things please us.”.]. Let us rejoice in every measure of his gifts. Whoever has used great things well, let him use small things well also. We are cared for by abundance no less than by scarcity.

Nor will we be weighed down by a narrow yield in spiritual gains [Note: [Col. 0171D] Vatican manuscript 3836: “we shall not be burdened by a meager harvest.”.], if the fruitfulness of our souls does not wither. Let what the earth has not produced arise from the field of the heart [Note: [Col. 0171D] Thus the three Roman lectionaries mentioned above. Elsewhere: “what he has not given.”.]. There is always something for one to give whose goodwill does not fail.

Therefore, beloved, let the character of every season assist us in every work of piety, and let no temporal difficulty hinder Christian benevolence. The Lord knows how to fill the vessels of the hospitable widow, emptied for the work of his piety [Note: [Col. 0171D] Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary*: “emptied of the resources of his piety.” One Vatican manuscript omits “of his.” The first edition omits “for the work of his piety.”.] (IV Kings IV, 5); he knows how to turn water into wine (John II, 9); he knows how to satisfy five thousand hungry people from a few loaves (John VI, 9) [Col. 0171C]. And he who is fed in his poor [Note: [Col. 0171D] We have added “in the poor” from the three lectionaries mentioned above.] can, by receiving, multiply what he was able to increase by giving.

### Chapter IV

There are three things above all that pertain to religious practice: prayer, fasting, and almsgiving. Every time is suitable for exercising them [Note: [Col. 0172D] Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary*: “ready.”], but that time is to be observed with greater diligence which we have received as consecrated by apostolic traditions. Thus this tenth month also recalls the custom of the ancient institution, so that we may carry out more diligently the three practices of which I have spoken.

By prayer we seek God’s propitiation; by fasting the lust of the flesh is extinguished; by almsgiving sins are redeemed (Dan. IV, 24). At the same time the image of God is renewed in us in every respect, if we are always ready to praise him, unceasingly concerned with our purification, and continually attentive to the support of our neighbor [Note: [Col. 0172D] Thus most manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus; in Quesnellus, “we are attentive.”.].

This threefold observance, beloved, embraces the effect of all virtues. It reaches the image and likeness of God and makes us inseparable from the Holy Spirit. For right faith remains in prayers [Note: [Col. 0172D] This is better read in the plural from Paul the Deacon’s *Homiliary*, as do all the editions and manuscripts shortly afterward in the plural, “in almsgiving”; hence shortly afterward the holy pontiff repeats “fasts.” Elsewhere, singular: “in fasting.”.], an innocent life in fasts, and a kindly mind in almsgiving.

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the most blessed apostle Peter, who will deign to assist our prayers, fasts, and almsgiving by his prayers [Note: [Col. 0172D] After “to assist,” one Vatican manuscript adds: “so that we may keep watch more diligently.”.]. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIII [elsewhere XII]

### On the Fast of the Tenth Month II

[Col. 0172B]

### Synopsis

The reason why the fast of the tenth month was instituted; praise of that fast and of Christian mercy toward the poor.

What the season and the custom of our devotion admonish us of, beloved, we proclaim to you with pastoral concern: the fast of the tenth month is to be celebrated, during which, in grateful acknowledgment of the completion of all the fruits, a most worthy offering of abstinence is presented to their giver, God [Note: [Col. 0172D] The books, both printed and manuscript, vary here. Some, followed by Quesnellus, read *diligentissime* (“most diligently”); others, *dignissimo* (“to the most worthy”). The reading of the first edition and Rainaudus seemed better, and is confirmed by other manuscripts.].

For what can be more effective than fasting? Through its observance we draw near to God, and, resisting the devil, overcome alluring vices. Fasting has always been food for virtue [Note: [Col. 0172D] We have added *semper* (“always”) from our manuscripts.]. From abstinence proceed chaste thoughts, rational [Col. 0172C] wills, and healthier counsels [Note: [Col. 0172D] Two manuscripts: “Finally, from abstinence.”.]. Through voluntary afflictions the flesh dies to its desires, and the spirit is renewed in virtues.

But because the salvation of our souls is not acquired by fasting alone [Note: [Col. 0172D] One manuscript of St. Peter: “by fasting alone.”], let us supplement our fast with mercies toward the poor. Let us devote to virtue what we withdraw from pleasure. Let the abstinence of the one who fasts become the nourishment of the poor. Let us be diligent in defending widows, assisting orphans, consoling mourners, and bringing peace to those who disagree. Let the traveler be welcomed, the oppressed helped, the naked clothed [Col. 0172C], and the sick comforted, so that whoever among us offers to the author of all good, God, the sacrifice of this piety from his just labors may deserve to receive from him the reward of the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0172D] The same manuscript: “to receive.”.].

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday [Col. 0173A]; on Saturday let us keep vigil together at the blessed apostle Peter, so that, with his merits interceding, we may obtain what we ask, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIV [elsewhere XIII]

[Note: [Col. 0173D] In editions based on manuscripts of collection 3, the title of this and the following sermons is “On the Fast of the Tenth Month and Its Almsgiving.” We have removed the addition, since it is absent from the other manuscripts.]

### On the Fast of the Tenth Month III

### Synopsis

I. By what means the field of the heart is cultivated and made fruitful.  
II. That the devil rages more fiercely against the faithful when good works are either commanded or practiced.

### Chapter I

In the Lord’s field, beloved, whose laborers we are, we must exercise spiritual cultivation wisely and vigilantly, so that by persevering diligence, attending to what must be carried out at the proper times, we may rejoice in the fruit of holy works.

If these things are neglected through sluggish idleness and inert laziness, our land will produce no noble shoot; covered with thorns and thistles [Note: [Col. 0173D] Thus from the lectionary of St. Peter. Elsewhere: “subject to.”], it will produce not what is to be stored in barns but what is to be burned in flames.

This field, beloved, watered from above by the dew of God’s grace, is fortified by faith, cultivated by fasts [Note: [Col. 0173D] The same manuscript: “is marked out.”.], sown with almsgiving, and made fruitful by prayers, so that amid our plantings and waterings no root of bitterness may sprout, nor may the growth of any harmful shoot raise itself up. But when the seed of every vice has been destroyed [Note: [Col. 0173D] Thus two Vatican manuscripts and one of St. Peter. Elsewhere, “every.” From these manuscripts and another Bononian manuscript we have restored *coalescat* (“may grow together”) instead of *convalescat* (“may recover”).], let the joyful harvest of virtues grow together.

Piety urges us to this diligence at every time [Note: [Col. 0173D] Elsewhere: “the teacher of piety.” Quesnellus. Shortly afterward two manuscripts and the first edition read *instituti* (“of the institution”) instead of *praestituti* (“appointed”).], but in these days, which have been appointed especially for this work, greater courage and more fervent care must be stirred up, lest it be impious to neglect what, once commanded and proclaimed, it is pious to do.

### Chapter II

We know that your charity has been prepared with religious purpose for the fast of the tenth month. Therefore, with one accord, aided by Christ, we exhort you to celebrate it [Note: [Col. 0173D] Thus the Bononian manuscript and the first edition. Elsewhere, “celebrating.” In the manuscript of St. Peter: “we exhort you to celebrate it with one accord, aided by Christ.” Shortly afterward, the manuscript of St. Peter reads “in our sanctification.”.], admonishing each person to shine in good works according to the measure of ability he has received from God.

For our enemies, who are tormented by our sanctification, know that these days have been appointed for us for more diligent observance, and so they rage more fiercely and lie in wait with subtler cunning. They seek to draw very many away from sharing in this devotion: some by instilling fear of poverty because of the expense of generosity [Col. 0174A], others by imposing sadness because of the labor of fasting [Note: [Col. 0173D] Thus from the lectionary of St. Peter and two other Vatican manuscripts. Elsewhere: “by instilling.”.].

Against these temptations, beloved, let the intention of a pious heart keep watch within us, and let thoughts of distrust be driven from Christian minds. For little is needed by the poor person [Note: [Col. 0173D] Some manuscripts: “is enough for the poor person.”.]. Neither his food nor his clothing is burdensome. What he hungers for is cheap; what he thirsts for is cheap; and the nakedness that needs to be covered asks not for adornment [Note: [Col. 0173D] This is better in the manuscript of St. Peter. Elsewhere: “which needs to be covered does not ask to be adorned.”.].

And yet our Lord, so pious an arbiter of our works and so generous an assessor, will reward even a cup of cold water. Since he is a just examiner of souls, he will reward not only the expenditure of the work but also the affection of the one who performs it, through Christ our Lord.

## SERMON XV [elsewhere XIV]

[Note: [Col. 0174D] In manuscripts of collections 1 and 2, and also in the lectionary manuscript of the Basilica of St. Peter, this sermon is joined to the preceding one; but wrongly, since the distinction is sufficiently clear from the context and is confirmed by other manuscripts. Perhaps, because the preceding sermon seemed somewhat shorter than the reading for the divine offices once required, this other sermon was added—as we have likewise seen happen with the first and second sermons on the Lord’s Nativity, which, perhaps for the same reason, were combined into one despite the opposing evidence of the context. Compare the admonition prefixed to the first sermon.]

### On the Fast of the Tenth Month IV

[Col. 0174B]

### Synopsis

I. The threefold remedy of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving against the temptations of the devil and the wounds of sin.  
II. The commandment of fasting, like the commandment of love, has not been abolished by the grace of the new law; works of mercy must be joined to it.

### Chapter I
We confidently exhort you, beloved, to works of piety, because experience has taught us that you willingly accept what we urge. For you know—and, with God as your teacher, understand—that observance of the divine commandments will benefit you for eternal joy. Since human weakness often grows weary in carrying them out and stumbles in many things through the slipperiness of its infirmity, the merciful and gracious Lord has given us remedies and aids [Note: Some copies read: “has given us remedies for victory.” Codex Corbeiensis of Quesnel.] by which we may obtain pardon. For who could escape so many allurements of the world, so many snares of the devil, and, finally, so many dangers arising from his own mutability, unless the clemency of the eternal King preferred to restore us rather than destroy us? Even those who have already been redeemed, regenerated, and made children of light [Note: Three manuscripts read: “already children.”], nevertheless remain as long as they are in this world, which lies wholly in the power of the Evil One (1 John 5:19) [Note: The Bonn manuscript and the first edition read *retinentur*, “are held fast.” Below, two manuscripts together with the first edition read *sine trepidatione*, “without trembling,” instead of “without temptation.”]; and as long as corruptible and temporal things flatter the weakness of the flesh, they cannot pass these days without temptation. Nor does anyone easily achieve so bloodless a victory that, amid many enemies and frequent conflicts, even if free from death, he is also unharmed by wounds [Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter reads: “amid many and frequent conflicts.”].

To heal the injuries often suffered by those who engage in combat with the invisible enemy, the medicine of three remedies above all must be applied: perseverance in prayer, the discipline of fasting, and generosity in almsgiving. When these are practiced together, God is appeased, guilt is erased, and the tempter is struck down. The faithful soul ought always to be equipped with these defenses, but it should prepare itself with greater earnestness when those days arrive that have been specially appointed for such duties of piety.

## CHAPTER II

Among these is also the solemn fast of this tenth month. It must not therefore be neglected because it was adopted from the observance of the old law, as though it belonged among those practices that, amid distinctions of foods, differences of baptisms, and sacrifices of birds and cattle, have ceased [Note: Quesnel deleted the word *esse*, “to be,” as did the Padua manuscript; we have restored it from all the other printed editions and our manuscripts. A little later the Bonn manuscript reads “of bodies and soul.”]. For when those things that bore figures of future realities had been fulfilled, the things they signified came to an end. The usefulness of fasts, however, was not abolished by the grace of the New Testament; rather, it piously embraced abstinence, which is always beneficial to body and soul. For just as, according to Christian understanding, these words remain: “You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone” (Matthew 4:10); and, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (Matthew 22:37); and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (ibid., 39); and the other commandments of this kind—so the commandment given in those same books concerning the sanctification and healing effected by fasts is not emptied of meaning by any interpretation [Note: We have restored “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” from manuscripts of Collection 5, the Padua manuscript, and the Lectionary book of Saint Peter. The latter reads below “of the other commandments” instead of “of such commandments,” and *evacuatur*, “is emptied,” instead of *vacuatur*, “is voided.”].

At every season and throughout all the days of this present life, fasts make us stronger against sins; fasts conquer desires, drive away temptations, bend down pride, calm anger, and nourish every inclination of good will toward the maturity of complete virtue—provided that they take benevolence in charity into their company and wisely exercise themselves in works of mercy [Note: Some copies read “their own benevolence.” Quesnel.].

For fasting without almsgiving is not so much purification of the soul as affliction of the flesh; and it should be attributed more to avarice than to self-restraint when someone abstains from food in such a way that he also fasts from piety [Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter and Padua read “withdraws himself from piety.” Quesnel. Other printed editions, together with manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5, read “abstains from piety.”]. Therefore, beloved, let our fasts abound in the fruits of generosity, and let them be fruitful toward Christ’s poor in kindly gifts.

Nor should those of modest means be held back in this work because they think they can remove only a little from their resources. The Lord knows the strength of everyone, and the just examiner knows from what measure each person gives what he gives. Unequal resources cannot have equal distributions; yet what differs in expense is often made equal in merit, because the intention can be equal even where the wealth is unequal.

Therefore, with God’s help, let these things be carried out with devout dedication: let us fast on Wednesday and Friday, but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the blessed Apostle Peter, so that, aided by his prayers, we may in all things obtain God’s mercy.

# SERMON XVI [Elsewhere XV]

## On the Fast of the Tenth Month V

### SYNOPSIS

I. Let the rich also give thanks to God, who bestows wealth upon them, and let them share it with the poor.  
II. Why the fast of the tenth month was instituted. Effective prayer, supported by almsgiving.  
III. Heretics serve the devil in corrupting the faithful under the Christian name.  
IV. The heresy of the Manichaeans, a cesspool of every impurity. What Leo did against them at Rome.  
V. They must both be avoided and exposed.  
VI. Through zeal against heretics, prayers, fasts, and almsgiving become more pleasing to God.

## CHAPTER I

The sublimity of God’s grace works this daily in Christian hearts, beloved: that all our desire may be transferred from earthly things to heavenly ones. Yet the present life too is guided by the Creator’s aid and sustained by his providence, because the one who gives temporal things is also the promiser of eternal things.

Therefore, just as we ought to give thanks to God in hope of the future happiness toward which we hasten by faith, because we are being raised up for the attainment of so great a preparation [Note: *Enim*, “for,” stood in place of *ergo*, “therefore,” in editions before Quesnel.], so also, for those benefits that we obtain through the yearly cycle, God must be honored and praised by us. He gave such fertility to the earth from the beginning and established such laws for the production of fruits in every shoot and seed that he never abandoned his ordinances, but the benevolent administration of the Creator continued within created things.

Whatever the fields, vineyards, and olive groves have produced for human use has flowed entirely from the generosity of divine goodness. Varying the qualities of the elements, it mercifully assisted the uncertain labors of farmers, so that winds and rains, cold and heat, days and nights might serve our needs. Human reasoning would not suffice by itself for the results of its work, unless God supplied the customary increase to plantings and irrigations.

It is therefore full of piety and justice that, from the things which the heavenly Father has mercifully bestowed upon us, we too should assist others. There are many who possess no share in fields, no share in vineyards, and no share in olive groves; their poverty must be relieved from the abundance that the Lord has given, so that they too may bless God with us for the fruitfulness of the earth and rejoice that what was given to its possessors has also been made common to the poor and to strangers.

Blessed is that granary, and most worthy of the multiplication of all fruits, from which the hunger of the needy and weak is satisfied, from which the need of the stranger is relieved, and from which the desire of the sick is nourished [Note: Thus read all our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnel, who has: “from which the need of strangers is relieved, from which the desire of the sick is fostered.”]. For this reason the justice of God has permitted them to labor under various afflictions, so that both the wretched for their patience and the merciful for their benevolence might be crowned.

## CHAPTER II

Although every season is suitable for this work, beloved, the present time is especially fitting and appropriate. In it, our holy fathers, inspired by God, established the fast of the tenth month, so that, when the gathering of all the fruits had been completed, reasonable abstinence might be dedicated to God, and each person might remember to use abundance in such a way that he would be more restrained toward himself and more generous toward the poor.

For supplication for sins is most effective when joined with almsgiving and fasting, and prayer raised by such assistance swiftly ascends to the divine ears. As it is written, “The merciful person does good to his own soul” (Proverbs 12:17), and nothing belongs so properly to each person as what he spends on his neighbor. The portion of bodily resources that is supplied to the needy passes into eternal riches; from such generosity are born those riches that can be diminished by no use and violated by no corruption.

“Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them” (Matthew 5:7) [Note: Editions before Quesnel read *autem*, “but,” instead of *namque*, “for.”]. He himself will be the fullness of their reward, he who is the model of the commandment.

## CHAPTER III

Amid these works of piety, beloved, by which we commend ourselves more and more to God, there is no doubt that our enemy, eager for and skilled in doing harm, is stirred by sharper goads of envy. Those whom he is not permitted to attack through open and bloody persecutions, he corrupts under the false profession of the Christian name. He has heretics serving this purpose: people who have deviated from the Catholic faith and whom he has made his subjects, serving in his camp under various errors.

Just as he assumed the serpent’s ministry to deceive the first human beings (Genesis 3:1), so he armed their tongues with the poison of his falsehood to seduce the minds of the upright. But, beloved, we meet these snares with pastoral concern, insofar as the Lord assists us. Taking precautions so that nothing may perish from the holy flock, we warn you with paternal admonitions to avoid lying lips and a deceitful tongue, from which the prophet asks that his soul be delivered (Psalm 119:2), because, as the blessed Apostle says, “their speech spreads like gangrene” (2 Timothy 2:17).

They creep in humbly, seize gently, bind softly, and kill secretly. They come, as the Savior foretold, “in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7:15), because they could not deceive true and simple sheep unless they covered their bestial rage with the name of Christ.

In all these people that one operates who, although he is the enemy of true illumination, transforms himself into an angel of light [Note: We have added the word *ille*, “that one,” from the manuscript of Saint Peter.]. By his art Basilides operates; by his skill Marcion knows how to act; under his guidance Sabellius proceeds; under his direction Photinus is brought down; Arius serves his power; Eunomius serves his spirit. Finally, the whole company of such beasts has departed from the unity of the Church under his presidency and has fallen away from the truth under his instruction [Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter reads: “the cohort of such plagues.”].

## CHAPTER IV

Although he holds chief place in every kind of perversity, he nevertheless built his citadel in the madness of the Manichaeans and found in them a very spacious hall in which to display himself more exultantly. There he possessed not merely one form of depravity, but, in general, a mixture of all errors and impieties at once.

Whatever is profane among pagans, whatever is blind and carnal among Jews, whatever is illicit in the secret practices of magic, and, finally, whatever is sacrilegious and blasphemous in all heresies—this has flowed together into these people, as into a kind of cesspool, with a confluence of every impurity.

To recount all their impieties and obscenities would therefore take far too long; the multitude of crimes exceeds the capacity of words. A few examples suffice to indicate the rest, so that from what you hear you may also judge those matters that we discreetly pass over [Note: The editions of Rainaud and Quesnel read *et*, “and,” in place of *ex*, “from,” here; we have corrected it from our manuscripts and the other printed editions. Shortly afterward, some copies read *manifestari*, “to be revealed,” instead of *manifestare*, “to reveal.”].

We will not, however, be silent about their sacred rites, which among them are as obscene as they are abominable, because the Lord has willed to disclose them to our investigation. No one should think that we have believed in obscure rumors and uncertain opinions concerning this matter.

When bishops and presbyters were seated with me, and Christian men and nobles had been gathered into the same assembly [Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter reads “meeting.” Concerning this assembly and judgment, see the holy pontiff’s Letters 7 and 15.], we ordered their Elect and Elect women to be brought before us. After they had disclosed many things about the perversity of their doctrine and the customs of their festivals [Note: We have corrected this from the same manuscript of Saint Peter, which reads *reserarent*, “might disclose,” instead of the transmitted form.], they also revealed that crime which it is shameful to mention. It had been investigated with such care that nothing remained for the incredulous to doubt and nothing ambiguous for detractors [Note: The same manuscript reads “nothing for the unbelieving.”].

All the persons through whom the unspeakable deed had been perpetrated were present: a girl of approximately ten years of age, two women who had raised her and prepared her for this crime, a young man who had violated the girl, and their bishop, who had organized the detestable offense [Note: Thus, according to the syntax of Leo found in the manuscript of Saint Peter. Other copies read: “All these were equal in this, and there was one confession by all, and the accursed deed was disclosed,” and so forth.].

The confession of all these people was alike and one, and an abomination was disclosed that our ears could scarcely endure. To avoid offending chaste ears by speaking more openly, the documentary evidence is sufficient. It proves completely that no modesty, no decency, and absolutely no chastity can be found in this sect, in which law is falsehood, the devil is religion, and sacrifice is depravity.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, beloved, wholly reject from your friendship these utterly detestable and pestilential people [Note: The word *homines*, “people,” is absent from the Bonn manuscript and the first edition, which also reads *ideo*, “therefore,” in place of *itaque*.], whom the disturbances of other regions have brought to us in greater numbers [Note: It is clear from Augustine’s *Confessions* 5.10 that Manichaeans had long before this secretly been present at Rome; but disturbances in other regions, especially the troubles in Africa under Gaiseric, who occupied Carthage in 439, brought them in greater numbers.]. And especially you women, keep away from acquaintance and conversation with such people, lest, while an unwary ear delights in their fabulous stories, you fall into the devil’s snares.

Knowing that he first deceived the man through the woman’s mouth and through feminine credulity cast all human beings down from the happiness of paradise [Note: The Bonn manuscript and the first edition read: “and that through the female [sex].”], he now attacks your sex with even more secure cunning, so that those whom he can entice through the agents of his falsehood he may strip both of faith and of modesty [Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter reads: “He attacks our sex, yours and ours, with more secure cunning, so that those whom he can deceive through the ministers of his falsehood he may strip both of faith and of modesty.” Since the preceding words especially address women, the context seems to require that the statement refer particularly to women.].

I also urge you, beloved, with an earnest plea: if any one of you learns where these people live, where they teach, whom they visit, and in whose company they spend their time, faithfully report it to our vigilance [Note: The Bonn manuscript and the first edition omit “where they live” and “where they frequent,” reading only “where they teach.”]. For it is of little benefit to anyone that, while the Holy Spirit protects him, he himself is not captured by these people if, when he realizes that others are being captured, he remains unmoved [Note: The same manuscript reads “the Spirit of God”; below, “is not shaken,” and shortly afterward, with the first edition and the same manuscript, “against all enemies.”].

Against common enemies, there must be one vigilance on the part of all for the common salvation, lest, from the wound of one member, other members also be corrupted, and those who think that such people should not be exposed be found guilty before Christ’s judgment because of their silence, even if they are not contaminated by consent [Note: The preposition *de*, “by,” is omitted in the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Bonn and in the first edition. At the beginning of chapter 6 below, the manuscript of Saint Peter reads *itaque*, “therefore,” instead of *igitur*, “therefore.”].

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore take up the pious zeal of religious vigilance, and let the concern of all the faithful rise against the fiercest enemies of souls. For this reason the merciful God disclosed to us a certain portion of the harmful people: so that, once the danger had been revealed, the diligence of precaution might be aroused [Note: Printed editions read *ideoque*, “and therefore.” We have deleted *que* in accordance with our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Bonn and the first edition read *manifesto*, “with the danger revealed,” instead of *manifestato*, “after the danger had been revealed.”].

Let what has been done not be sufficient; let the same investigation continue. With God’s help, it will achieve this: not only that those who are upright may remain safe, but also that many who have been deceived by the devil’s seduction may be recalled from error [Note: Thus according to our manuscripts and the first edition. Other copies read *consequitur*, “it follows.”].

Your prayers, almsgiving, and fasts will be offered to the merciful God with greater sanctity through this very devotion when this work of faith has been added to all duties of piety.

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the blessed Apostle Peter who, as we experience and believe, continually extends pastoral watch over the sheep entrusted to him by the Lord. By his prayers he will entreat that the Church of God, established through his preaching, may be free from every error. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

# SERMON XVII [Elsewhere XVI]

## On the Fast of the Tenth Month VI

### SYNOPSIS

I. Fasting transferred from the old law into the new is owed to God in a spirit of grateful acknowledgment and makes prayer more effective.  
II. A pious loan is to be practiced with God; how unjustly and impiously human beings demand interest.  
III. Whatever outcome follows, the practice of lending at interest is always evil.  
IV. The abundance of some and the poverty of others have been arranged for this purpose: that the rich may imitate God’s goodness.

## CHAPTER I

The teachings of the Gospel give much authority to the teaching of the Law when certain matters are transferred from the old commandment to the new observance. Ecclesiastical devotion itself demonstrates that the Lord Jesus Christ did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5:17).

For the signs by which the coming of our Savior was announced have ceased, and the figures that his very presence removed have been completed. Yet those things that the reasoning of piety established either as rules of conduct or for the simple worship of God continue among us in the same form in which they were established; and what was appropriate to both Testaments has not been altered by any change.

Among these things is also the solemn fast of the tenth month, which we are now to celebrate each year as a customary observance [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and one of Saint Peter’s, together with the first edition, read “because it is full of justice.”]. It is full of justice and piety to give thanks to divine generosity for the fruits that the earth has produced for human use according to the ordering of supreme providence.

To show that we do this with a willing spirit [Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter reads “to demonstrate.”], we must undertake not only the restraint of fasting but also care for almsgiving, so that from the soil of our heart there may arise a shoot of justice and a fruit of charity, and so that by showing mercy to God’s poor we may deserve God’s mercy.

For the petition to God that is supported by works of piety is most effective in obtaining an answer. Whoever does not turn his heart away from the poor quickly turns the Lord’s hearing toward himself, as the Lord says: “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful; forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:36–37).

What is kinder than this justice? What is more merciful than this recompense, in which the judgment of the one who will judge is placed in the power of those being judged? “Give,” he says, “and it will be given to you” (ibid., 38). How quickly the anxious hesitation of distrust and avarice is cut off, so that humanity may confidently spend what Truth promises it will return [Note: The same manuscript reads “humility.”].

## CHAPTER II

Be steadfast, Christian giver: give what you may receive, sow what you may reap, scatter what you may gather. Do not fear loss; do not sigh over uncertain profit. When your substance is well distributed, it increases.

Desire the righteous profit of mercy and pursue the commerce of eternal gain. Your benefactor wants you to be generous, and he who gives so that you may possess commands you to give, saying: “Give, and it will be given to you.” You should embrace and welcome the condition of this promise. Although you have nothing except what you have received, you cannot fail to possess what you have given.

Therefore, if someone loves money and desires to multiply his wealth by excessive increases, let him practice this holy lending instead and grow rich by this art of interest. Let him not prey upon the necessities of laboring people or, through deceitful benefits, cast them into the snares of insoluble debts [Note: We have emended this from three Vatican manuscripts. Other copies read: “lest through deceitful services he fall into snares.”]. Let him be the creditor and lender of the one who says: “Give, and it will be given to you; and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

But he who does not wish to possess permanently what he judges worthy of love is faithless and unjust even to himself—even if he adds, stores, and heaps up as much as possible [Note: *Quantalibet adjiciat*, “however much he may add,” was missing in Quesnel’s edition. We have restored it from other editions and all our manuscripts.]—will depart from this world poor and needy, as the prophet David says: “For when he dies, he will not receive everything, nor will his glory descend with him” (Psalm 48:18) [Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter reads “he will not take.” Below, “the glory of his house,” instead of “his glory,” in Vatican manuscript 544, Collection 5. Then, in the first edition, “For if,” instead of “If he.”].

If he were kind to his own soul, he would entrust his possessions to the one who is both an able guarantor for the poor and a most generous payer of interest. But unjust and shameless avarice, which says that it is conferring a benefit when it deceives, does not believe God when he truthfully promises, but anxiously believes a human being who makes a pact [Note: Some copies read “lukewarmly.” Quesnel in the margin.]. While it regards present things as more certain than future ones, it deservedly and often falls into this: that the desire for unjust profit becomes for it the cause of just loss.

## CHAPTER III

Whatever outcome follows, the practice of lending at interest is always evil. For the lender, it is a sin both when his money decreases and when it increases: he is either wretched in losing what he gave or more wretched in receiving what he did not give.

The wickedness of interest must be avoided altogether, and profit devoid of all humanity must be shunned. Wealth is indeed multiplied by unjust and sorrowful increases, but the substance of the mind wastes away, because interest on money is the death of the soul.

What God thinks of such people is revealed by the most sacred prophet David. When he asks, “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm 15:1), he is instructed by the answer of the divine voice and learns that the person belongs to eternal rest who, among the other rules of pious conduct, has not lent his money at interest.

The person who seeks deceitful profit from the interest on his money is shown to be alien to God’s tabernacle and a stranger to his holy mountain; while he desires to grow rich through another’s losses, he is judged worthy of being punished with eternal poverty.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, beloved, you who have believed with your whole heart in the Lord’s promises, flee the most filthy leprosy of avarice and use God’s gifts piously and wisely. Since you rightly rejoice in his generosity [Note: We have added the adverb “rightly” from the Lectionary of Saint Peter.], take care that you may have others as companions in your joys.

Many lack what is available to you, and in the need of some you have been given the opportunity to imitate divine goodness: so that through you God’s benefits may also pass to others, and, by administering temporal things well, you may acquire eternal ones.

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; on Saturday let us keep vigil at the blessed Apostle Peter [Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter and Collection 5 read “at the most blessed [Peter].”], through whose prayers may divine protection be obtained for us in all things. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

# SERMON XVIII [Elsewhere XVII]

## On the Fast of the Tenth Month VII

### SYNOPSIS

I. Although regenerated, the soul is inclined by its own nature toward worse things, yet by God’s goodness it is fortified with many defenses.  
II. A common abstinence is proclaimed for the whole Church, so that the devil may be overcome both in part and in the whole.  
III. Christ condemned the barren tree in order to commend works of mercy. How the Christian is constantly attacked, and what weapons the devout possess against invisible enemies.

## CHAPTER I

The defenses divinely established for the sanctification of our minds and bodies, beloved, are continually renewed as the courses of days and seasons pass without interruption, so that the medicine itself may remind us of our weaknesses [Note: All printed copies and some manuscripts add “of the Christian warfare.” These words are absent from three Royal manuscripts, the Corbeiensis, and the Victorinus; I mention this so that no one may attribute their omission to the printers. Quesnel. The same words are likewise absent from the most ancient Vatican Lectionary 3836, another old Vatican manuscript, 1267, two Vallicellian manuscripts, the Augustinian Hermits’ Padua manuscript, the Veronese, the Venetian Saint Mark’s manuscript, and other Lectionaries, as well as from Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary. They are also absent from manuscripts of Collections 1, 2, and 5. But they are found in Collections 3 and 4 and in the collection of the very ancient Veronese Sacramentary edited by P. Blanchini, where the Leonine wording seems to be: “The defenses of the Christian warfare are to be begun with holy fasts.”].

For our nature is mutable and mortal through the stain of sin; although it has already been redeemed and reborn through holy baptism, insofar as it is capable of suffering, it is equally inclined toward worse things [Note: This is better supported by the very ancient Vatican 3836, the Augustinian Hermits’ Padua 117, the Veronese 74, and other Lectionaries of excellent quality, as well as by the Cassinese manuscript of Collection 1. The editions, based on manuscripts of Collections 3, 4, and 5, read: “Although it has already been redeemed and reborn through holy baptism, insofar as it is capable of suffering, so far is it inclined toward worse things; and it would be corrupted by carnal desire,” and so forth. One Vallicellian manuscript reads: “For it would be corrupted by carnal desire,” and so forth.].

It would be corrupted by carnal desire unless it were fortified by spiritual aid. For just as it never lacks a means by which it may fall, so a means of support is always at hand, as the Apostle says: “For God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will bring about an outcome so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Although the Lord protects his warriors, and the one who is mighty in battle (Psalm 24:8) encourages his soldiers and says, “Do not be afraid, because I have overcome the world” (John 16:33), it must nevertheless be understood, beloved [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “through these encouragements.”], that this encouragement has removed fear, not combat. Once the sting of fear has been blunted, the cause of the struggle remains.

The struggle is set in motion by a crafty enemy with terrifying fury when persecution rages, but it is brought more harmfully under the appearance of peace [Note: Printed editions and most manuscripts read “against the innocent.” Some manuscripts, indicating an error in this word, read “against those who warn.” We believe *nocentius*, “more harmfully,” should be read, together with the Veronese manuscript.
