As an adverb opposed to the preceding *terribiliter*, “terrifyingly,” it indicates that the struggle in a time of peace is more destructive, although not as terrifying as when persecution is raging.].

Where battles are open, crowns too are manifest. This itself nourishes and kindles the strength of endurance: just as tribulation is near, so too is the promise near. But when public attacks by the impious cease, and the devil restrains himself from the slaughter and punishments of the faithful lest the persistence of his cruelties make the increase of our number a multiplication of triumphs [Note: The pronoun *se*, “himself,” which Quesnel supplied, is found in most and best of our manuscripts.], the raging adversary turns bloody hostility into peaceful ambushes.

Those whom he could not overcome by hunger, cold, fire, and the sword, he warms into complacency through idleness, ensnares through desires, inflates through ambition, and corrupts through pleasure [Note: We have restored the word *flammis*, “by flames,” omitted by Quesnel, from all the other printed editions and all our manuscripts. Only Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, together with two Vatican manuscripts, reads “by the sword and flames.” Shortly afterward, the verb *tepefaceret*, “he might warm,” accepted by Quesnel, is supported by two Lectionaries of Saint Peter, the most ancient Vatican manuscript, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary. Other printed editions and some manuscripts, especially those of the later collections, read *tabefaceret*, “he might melt away.” Both readings occur in Quesnel’s Gaudiival manuscript.].

## CHAPTER II
But against these [Note: [Col. 0183D] Editions before Quesnell add *malis* (“evils”), as we find it in the inferior manuscripts of Collections 3 and 4.] and all other things to be destroyed, the Christian army possesses powerful fortifications and victorious weapons, while, as the Spirit of truth equips his soldiers, gentleness extinguishes anger, generosity greed, [Col. 0184A] and kindness envy. [Note: [Col. 0183D] Editions before Quesnell and the Vatican manuscripts of Collections 3, 4, and 5 read: “with God, indeed, equipping his soldiers, so that, by the Spirit of truth, gentleness may extinguish anger [lacuna] and kindness extinguish envy.” But the very oldest Vatican manuscript, two of St. Peter, one Veronese manuscript, and the copy of Paul the Deacon read as in the text.] For, as the right hand of the Most High changes the hearts of many, old age returns to newness, and from servants of iniquity there have emerged ministers of justice. Continence subdued lust; humility drove back arrogance; and those who had been stained by immodesty were made radiant by chastity. [Note: [Col. 0184C] Thus in all our manuscripts and in editions before Quesnell, who, with the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, preferred *ergo* (“therefore”) to *enim* (“for”).]

Through these conversions, beloved, [Note: [Col. 0184C] Editions before Quesnell, with manuscripts of the three later Collections, read “by the providence of God’s grace.” The further addition concerning certain fasts, which on particular days would require from the whole Church the devotion of general observance, is understood by some as though the fasts of the four seasons—including the fast of the tenth month—were at this time observed by the whole Church. Here, however, as also in another similar sermon, Sermon 89, or the fourth on the fast of the seventh month, chapter 2 (which is likewise cited as evidence for the same opinion), St. Leo establishes only the general principle that public fasts and other pious works performed by the whole Church, or by all its members, are more effective than private ones. This is true even if a particular Church assigns certain days to fasting or other pious works by general observance. That the fast of the tenth or seventh month, which the Roman Church certainly observed at this time, was not kept equally by all other Churches is demonstrated at length by Ludovicus Muratorius in his investigation “On the Fasts of the Four Seasons,” *Anecdota Latina*, vol. II, pp. 248 ff. See note 4 on Sermon 79.] through the providence of God’s grace, holy fasts have also been added, which on certain days would require from the whole Church the devotion of general observance. For although it is beautiful and praiseworthy that each member of Christ’s body should be adorned with its own functions, it is nevertheless an action of greater excellence and a virtue of greater holiness when the hearts of the godly people converge upon one purpose: so that he for whom our sanctification is punishment may be overcome not merely in part but also in our united strength. [Note: [Col. 0184D] The editions after the first wrongly read *illi*. We have corrected it from the oldest Vatican manuscript, the two manuscripts of St. Peter, and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon.]

For this work, beloved, the tenth month is now offered, in a way admonishing us, according to the character of its season, that no one should grow numb through the cold of unbelief, but rather should grow strong through the spirit of charity. [Note: [Col. 0184D] This reading was preferred on the authority of two manuscripts of St. Peter and the Veronese Lectionary, as well as the first edition and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon. Other copies read *concalescat* (“grow warm”). Shortly afterward, two manuscripts of St. Peter, one of Bologna, and the first edition read *accepimus* (“we have received”) instead of *accipimus* (“we receive”).] For through the very elements of the world, as through public pages, we receive an indication of the divine will; nor does heavenly instruction ever cease, since even from those things that serve us we are taught.

## CHAPTER III

Besides that apostolic pronouncement by which people lacking the fruit of piety are compared with barren trees, we must also beware of that fig tree whose example of fruitlessness the Lord Jesus, as the Gospel relates, condemned to perpetual sterility because he found nothing on it for the hungry man to take. [Note: [Col. 0184D] The Veronese manuscript reads “the Evangelist.” Below, after the words “does not refresh,” several manuscripts and editions before Quesnell add “the needy.”] Thus we might understand that whoever does not refresh the hungry denies him the food which, he said, had been given to the poor as though it had been given to himself. And trees of this curse will be those to whom the Judge will say:

> Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared by my Father for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; and so forth.

(Matthew 25:41–42.)

These things are recalled one by one for this reason: that we may understand that no one who has performed even part of these works will be excluded from mercy. But the soul that helps no one will be a tree without fruit, when it is found to be alien to all piety. [Note: [Col. 0185C] The Vulgate copies before Quesnell, with the Gaudiival manuscript and other manuscripts of our more recent collections, insert the word *fructu* (“fruit”), which we have found absent from our best Lectionaries and from the copy of Paul the Deacon. Some of these alone read *invenitur* (“is found”) instead of *invenietur* (“will be found”).]

The fast of the tenth month, therefore, since it belongs to the winter season, calls us to a mystical cultivation, by which the strength of grainfields, vines, and trees—through which human weakness is sustained—may be cultivated by spiritual pursuits. Thus the Lord’s field may be enriched by its own expenditures, [Note: [Col. 0185D] The copy of Paul the Deacon reads “by riches.”] and that which is never expedient to leave without fruit may become more fruitful through its own abundance.

Your Holiness certainly understands that this must be referred to the advancement of the whole Church, [Note: [Col. 0185D] Thus from our Vatican, St. Peter’s, and Veronese Lectionaries, and better than in the Vulgate, as is clear from the following relative clause, “whose.”] whose germ is in faith, whose growth is in hope, and whose maturity is in charity. For chastisement of the body and perseverance in prayer then attain true purity when they rest upon the sanctification of almsgiving, as the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). [Note: [Col. 0185D] So according to those same Lectionaries. Another copy reads “they shine.”]

Let us therefore fast on Wednesday and Friday. [Note: [Col. 0185D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter, two Vatican manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5, and the copy of Paul the Deacon read “Friday.”] On Saturday, however, let us celebrate vigils at the most blessed Apostle Peter, [Note: [Col. 0185D] In Vatican manuscript 3836, what follows is absent to the end. In the two manuscripts of St. Peter, after “let us celebrate,” there is: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father, etc.”] with him granting and helping us who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XIX [Elsewhere XVIII]

## On the Fast of the Tenth Month VIII

### SUMMARY

I. Abstinence prepares the way for the Lord and raises the mind to heavenly things.  
II. Why the fasts of the Four Seasons were instituted, and why fasting from vices must be added to them.  
III. On the worship of God and the use of temporal goods. On the twofold fast.

## CHAPTER I

When the Savior was instructing his disciples concerning the coming of the kingdom of God and the end of the world, and through the Apostles was teaching his whole Church, he said:

> Take heed lest perhaps your hearts become weighed down with gluttony, drunkenness, and worldly cares.

(Luke 21:43.) [Note: [Col. 0185D] We preferred the older and better Lectionaries—Vatican manuscript 3836, the two of the basilica of St. Peter, and the Veronese 74. Another reading is: “and concerning the end of the world and the ages.”]

We recognize, beloved, that this command applies especially to us, since the day announced to us, even if it is hidden, is undoubtedly near. Everyone must be prepared for its coming, [Note: [Col. 0186C] Several Vatican manuscripts, the Veronese manuscript with the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, and the first edition read “so that it may find no one.”] lest it find anyone devoted to the belly or entangled in worldly cares.

For daily experience proves, beloved, [Note: [Col. 0186C] Thus the oldest Vatican, St. Peter’s, and Veronese Lectionaries, as well as the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon. Another reading: [Col. 0186D] “by satiety of drink.” Shortly afterward the Veronese manuscript has “of the body” instead of “of the bodies.”] that the mind’s keenness is blunted by satiety of the flesh, and that the vigor of the heart is dulled by an excess of food, so that the pleasure of eating is even harmful to the health of the body unless the discipline of moderation resists the enticement and withdraws from pleasure what will later become a burden.

Although the flesh desires nothing without the soul and receives sensation from the same source from which it receives movement, it nevertheless belongs to that same soul to deny certain things to the substance subject to it and, by inward judgment, to restrain external things from what is unsuitable. [Note: [Col. 0186D] In some Vatican manuscripts *animae* (“of the soul”) is absent. Below, two manuscripts of St. Peter and two Vatican manuscripts read “from things entering” instead of “from unsuitable things,” and the manuscripts of St. Peter read *refrenare* (“restrain”) instead of *frenare*.] Thus, freed more often from bodily desires, the soul may devote itself to divine wisdom in the hall of the mind, where, when all the noise of earthly cares has fallen silent, it may rejoice in holy meditations and eternal delights.

Although it is difficult to continue this uninterruptedly in the present life, it can nevertheless be undertaken frequently, so that we may be occupied more often and longer with spiritual rather than bodily matters; and when we devote more time to better concerns, even temporal actions may pass over into incorruptible riches. [Note: [Col. 0186D] We wrote *etsi* (“although”) rather than *si* (“if”), which appeared in the editions, on the authority of the very oldest Vatican manuscript, two manuscripts of St. Peter, and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon. A little later, the Veronese manuscript and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon omit the adverb *potius* (“rather”). One Vatican manuscript and another Veronese read “into incorruptible things.” Shortly afterward, two Vatican manuscripts and the first edition read “they pass over” instead of “they cross over.”]

## CHAPTER II

The usefulness of this observance is chiefly established in the fasts of the Church, which, according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit, have been distributed throughout the circuit of the whole year, so that the law of abstinence is assigned to every season. Thus we celebrate the spring fast in Lent, the summer fast at Pentecost, the autumn fast in the seventh month, and the winter fast in this, the tenth month. We understand that nothing in the divine commands is empty and that all the elements serve the word of God for our instruction. Through the four hinges of the world, as through the four Gospels, [Note: [Col. 0186D] The Veronese manuscript, the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, and the first edition read “with an unceasing trumpet.”] we continually learn what we should proclaim and do.

For when the prophet says:

> The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands. Day pours forth the word to day, and night announces knowledge to night.

(Psalm 18:1–2.) What is there through which the truth does not speak to us? [Note: [Col. 0187D] One manuscript of St. Peter, another Vatican manuscript, and the first edition read “does not speak.”] His voices are heard in the day, his voices are heard in the night, and the beauty of things created by the workmanship of the one God never ceases to insinuate the teaching of reason into the ears of the heart, so that God’s invisible attributes may be perceived through understanding the things that have been made (Romans 1:20). [Note: [Col. 0187D] The Homiliary of Paul the Deacon reads “may be seen through understanding.”] Thus we serve not creatures but the Creator of all.

Since, therefore, all vices are destroyed by continence, and whatever greed thirsts for, whatever pride seeks, and whatever lust desires is overcome by the firmness of this virtue, who does not understand how much protection fasting provides us? [Note: [Col. 0187D] We supplied the word *praesidii* (“protection”) from four Lectionaries: the oldest Vatican, the two of St. Peter, and the Veronese. Shortly afterward the same Vatican and Veronese manuscripts, as well as the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, read “is learned” wrongly instead of “is enjoined.”] Through fasting we are commanded to abstain not only from food but also from all carnal desires.

Otherwise it is pointless to undertake hunger and not lay aside an evil will; to cut off food and not recoil from the sin conceived within. [Note: [Col. 0187D] We followed the first edition and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon. The other editions read “not to cease,” which none of our manuscripts supports; they all have the corrupt reading “not to be silent.” “To be silent” could easily have entered through a scribal error from *resilire* (“to recoil”), but not from *desinere* (“to cease”).] It is a carnal, not a spiritual, fast when the body alone is denied, while one remains in those things more harmful than every luxury. What does it profit the soul to act outwardly as mistress and inwardly to serve as a captive, to command its own limbs and lose the right of its own freedom? [Note: [Col. 0187D] The Veronese manuscript reads: “so that it rightly often suffers.”] And rightly the rebellious servant often suffers, when she does not render to the Lord the service owed to him. [Note: [Col. 0187D] The first edition reads: “Let the body therefore fast from foods.” Later editions read: “The body therefore fasting from foods.” Quesnell’s emendation is confirmed by our manuscripts. The Veronese manuscript alone reads “fasting from foods in the body”; but with this reading, *mente* (“in the mind”) should follow, not *mens* (“the mind”).]

When the body therefore fasts from food, let the mind fast from vices, and let it judge earthly cares and desires by the law of its king.

## CHAPTER III

Let him remember that the first love is owed to God and the second to his neighbor, [Note: [Col. 0188D] The Veronese manuscript reads “that he owes.”] and that all his affections must be directed by this rule, so that he neither withdraws from the worship of the Lord nor from the usefulness of his fellow servant.

How is God worshiped, unless what pleases him also pleases us, and our affection never rebels against his command? For if we desire what he desires, our weakness will receive virtue from him, from whom we received the desire itself. For God is the one who, as the Apostle says, works in us both to will and to accomplish [Note: [Col. 0188D] Vatican manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5 read “according to the good will.”] according to his good pleasure (Philippians 2:13).

Therefore a person will neither be inflated by pride nor broken by despair if he uses the good things divinely given for the glory of the giver and withdraws his desires from those things he knows will harm him. [Note: [Col. 0188D] We preferred *itaque* (“therefore”) to *denique* (“finally”) on the authority of several of our more numerous and better manuscripts and of the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon.]

By abstaining from the malignity of envy, from the dissipation of lust, from the disturbance of anger, and from the desire for revenge, he will be purified by the sanctification of true fasting and nourished by the pleasure of incorruptible delights. Thus, through spiritual use, he will learn to transfer even earthly resources into heavenly substance, not hoarding for himself what he has received but multiplying more and more what he has given.

Therefore, with the affection of paternal charity, we admonish your love to make the fast of the tenth month fruitful for yourselves through generous almsgiving, rejoicing that through you the Lord feeds and clothes his poor. He could, of course, have granted those resources to the poor which he has bestowed upon you, unless in his ineffable mercy he wished to justify them through the endurance of labor [Note: [Col. 0188D] The oldest Vatican manuscript and two others read “to justify them through patience.”] and you through the work of charity.

Let us therefore fast on Wednesday and Friday; [Note: [Col. 0188D] The same oldest Vatican manuscript and the Veronese read “Friday.”] on Saturday, however, let us celebrate vigils at the most blessed Apostle Peter, who will deign through his prayers to assist our prayers, fasts, and almsgiving, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. [Note: [Col. 0188D] In the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon: “since he will also assist our prayers”; after “to help,” it adds: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.”] Amen.

# SERMON XX [Elsewhere XIX]

## On the Fast of the Tenth Month IX

[Note: [Col. 0188D] Edited from the sole manuscript of this sermon, belonging to Nicholas Fabri; concerning it, see what we said in the preface to the Sermons, no. 10.]

### SUMMARY

I. Some observances were instituted in the Law for a particular time, while others were to remain also under the New Law. The nature of fasting and of all moral commands.  
II. The fast of the tenth month prescribed by the Church’s regulations as thanksgiving to God for the fruits received from the earth. Let the earth’s fertility be emulated by the abundance of souls, so that God’s human being may be an imitator.  
III. Charity contains all the commandments; through it human beings are distinguished from beasts. We should love our neighbor as God loves us. Not even the poor are excluded from works of mercy.

## CHAPTER I

The dispensations of God’s mercy, which our Savior undertook for the restoration of the human race, were divinely ordered, beloved, in such a way that the Gospel of grace would remove the veil of the Law, not destroy its institutions. Therefore we must observe that saying of the Lord in which he said that he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it, so that we too may serve this rule as far as we can with God’s gift. We must know that nothing in the ordinances of the Old Testament is to be neglected if we diligently strive to recognize what there was established under the veil of a passing shadow and what was established as an action destined to remain.

For the distinction of foods and sacrifices, circumcision of the flesh, the distinction of baptisms, and the observance of washings are no longer to be performed under figurative meanings, since the realities they signified have themselves been fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 0188D] Editions before Quesnell, from the same manuscript, read *districtio* (“separation”). Quesnell recorded this reading in the margin; whether he corrected it from the manuscript or by conjecture, we do not know.] But the commandments and moral precepts remain as they were issued, because they signify nothing other than what they say; and among Christian believers they increase through growth rather than decline through cessation.

To love God and one’s neighbor, to honor father and mother, not to worship foreign gods, and all the rest—whether they are solemnly prohibited or salutarily commanded—we venerate no differently in the legal institutions than in the evangelical decrees. Thus, although many things have been added through the newness of grace, nothing has been diminished from the antiquity of justice.

Therefore the apostolic decrees rightly determined that the usefulness of the ancient fasts should remain. Although the custom of the Church had learned to exercise itself through longer disciplines, it nevertheless embraced the sanctification of continence that comes from the Law; for those to whom it had been granted to do what is greater, it was unfitting not to celebrate what is lesser.

## CHAPTER II

Instructed, then, by this reasoning, beloved, we add the fast of the tenth month to the Church’s regulations and, as is customary, announce it to your devotion. For it is full of piety and full of justice that, once the receiving of the earth’s fruits has been completed, thanksgiving should be offered to God and a sacrifice of mercy paid to him together with the offering of fasting.

Let each person rejoice in his abundance and be glad that he has brought much into his storehouses, but in such a way that the poor also rejoice in his abundance. Let the fruitfulness of the grainfields, the flow of the vines, and the produce of the trees be emulated by the abundance of souls. Let hearts give what the earth has given, so that we may say with the prophet: “Our earth has given its fruit” (Psalm 66:6).

For the true and supreme farmer, God, is the author not only of bodily but also of spiritual fruits, and he knows how to cultivate both kinds of seed and both kinds of plantation with a twofold cultivation: giving the fields the growth of shoots and giving souls the increase of virtues. Just as both have received their beginning from one providence, so both call us to the effect of one work.

Human beings, made in the image and likeness of God, possess nothing so proper to the honor of their nature as imitating the goodness of their creator. As he is a merciful giver of his gifts, so he is also their just demander, wishing us to be partners in his works. Although we cannot create any nature, we can nevertheless exercise the material received through God’s grace, because earthly goods have not been bestowed for our use merely to serve the pleasure and satiety of bodily senses. [Note: [Col. 0189D] Another reading: “to serve.”] Otherwise we would differ in nothing from cattle or beasts, which do not know how to attend to the needs of others and know only to care for themselves and their offspring.

## CHAPTER III

Animals, therefore, lacking understanding, have been taught by no commandment and have received no law, because they have received no reason. But where there is the illumination of reason, there is also the discipline of piety, which owes love both to God and to one’s neighbor.

A person cannot otherwise be shown to be a lover of himself unless he is seen to love, above himself, the author of his nature, and, beside himself, the companion of his nature. Rightly does the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon these two commandments; rightly has the breadth of all discussion been explained in a most complete summary under a few words: let God be loved, and let one’s neighbor also be loved, so that we take the pattern for loving our neighbor from the love with which God loves us. He is good even to the wicked, and by the gifts of his kindness he cherishes not only his worshipers but also those who deny him.

Let relatives be loved; let strangers be loved; and let what is owed to friends be given beyond obligation to enemies. Although the malignity of some cannot be softened by any human kindness, works of piety are nevertheless not fruitless, and benevolence never loses what it bestows upon the ungrateful.

Let no one, beloved, make himself a stranger to good work; let no one plead his poverty, as though one who scarcely suffices for himself could not help another. It is a great thing when someone brings forth something from little, and on the scale of divine justice the weight is measured not by the quantity of gifts but by the disposition of the hearts.

The Gospel widow put two small coins into the treasury (Mark 12:42), and surpassed the gifts of all the rich. No piety is worthless before God; no compassion is fruitless. He has given people different resources, but he seeks dispositions that are not different. Let everyone assess his possessions, and let those who have received more give more.

Let the abstinence of the faithful become food for the poor, and let what each person withdraws from himself benefit the needy. For although remedies of frugality contribute much both to souls and to bodies, fasts themselves are of little use unless they are sanctified by the effect of mercy.

In almsgiving a certain form of baptism has been established, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. And through the same [Note: [Col. 0190D] The word *Christum* (“Christ”) seems superfluous, or the word *spiritum* (“spirit”) should be substituted in its place. Quesnell.] Christ it is said, “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1:16); and through him it is said, “Give alms, and everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Thus no one should doubt or distrust that the brightness of regeneration can be restored even after many sins, if he strives to be cleansed through the purification of almsgiving.

# SERMON XXI [Elsewhere XX]

## On the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ I

### SUMMARY

I. No one is excluded from the joy of the Lord’s Nativity, which alone is without the stain of sin.  
II. The dispensation of this mystery is wondrous.  
III. Whoever wishes to put on the new person must lay aside the old.

## CHAPTER I

Our Savior was born today, beloved; let us rejoice. For there is no place for sadness where the birthday of life is celebrated, which, having consumed the fear of mortality, brings us the joy of promised eternity. [Note: [Col. 0190D] In several manuscripts, in editions before Quesnell, and in the copy of Paul the Deacon, *ibi* (“there”) is absent.] No one is excluded from sharing in this gladness; the reason for joy is common to all, because our Lord, destroyer of sin and death, came to free everyone, just as he found no one free from guilt. [Note: [Col. 0191C] The Vercellese manuscript and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, together with the first edition, read “for those to be freed” instead of “to free everyone.”]

Let the holy person rejoice, because he draws near to the palm. Let the sinner be glad, because he is invited to forgiveness. Let the gentile be encouraged, because he is called to life. For the Son of God, in the fullness of time arranged by the inscrutable depth of the divine plan, assumed the nature of the human race in order to reconcile it to its creator, so that the inventor of death, the devil, might be conquered by the very nature that he had conquered. [Note: [Col. 0191C] One manuscript of St. Peter and another of Bologna, together with the first edition, read “might be conquered by the very nature by which he had conquered.” Veronese manuscript 74 reads “might be conquered by the very nature by which he had conquered,” omitting the second verb.]

In this conflict undertaken for us, the contest was conducted according to the great and wondrous law of justice: the omnipotent Lord confronted the most savage enemy not in his own majesty but in our humility, setting before him the same form and the same nature—sharing indeed in our mortality, but wholly free from sin.

For what is read concerning everyone is foreign to this birth:

> No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day.

(Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint.) [Note: [Col. 0191C] According to Quesnell, the Corbie manuscript has this passage as follows: “No one is clean from defilement, not even an infant of one day, if his life is upon the earth.” In the manuscript of St. Peter: “not even an infant whose life upon the earth is one day.” In the first edition: “not even an infant of one day whose life is upon the earth.” Shortly afterward the Vercellese manuscripts, the two Veronese manuscripts, and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon omit *ergo* (“therefore”).]

Nothing, therefore, from the desire of the flesh passed into this singular birth; nothing from the law of sin proceeded from it. A virgin of David’s royal lineage is chosen, who, destined to be made pregnant with a sacred offspring, would first conceive the divine and human child in her mind before conceiving him in her body. [Note: [Col. 0191D] The manuscript of St. Peter and the first edition read “conceived.”]

And so that, being ignorant of the heavenly plan, she might not fear the unusual effect that was to be worked in her by the Holy Spirit, she learned it through an angelic conversation. [Note: [Col. 0191D] Three manuscripts and most editions read *effectus* (“effect”) as in the text; two other Royal manuscripts have *affectus* (“emotion”), through a copyist’s error. The sense also requires that, if this reading is retained, *alta* (“lofty,” found in earlier editions) be rejected in place of *affatus* (“address”); for the passage is not speaking of the angelic conversation, whose intervention, as is immediately stated, removed Mary’s fear—the fear she would have experienced from the unusual effect of the conception of the Word. Quesnell. The reading of the text is also confirmed by the manuscript of St. Peter, one Veronese manuscript, and the copy of Paul the Deacon.] Nor did she, soon to become the Mother of God, regard the novelty of the conception as a loss to her modesty. For why should she despair of the novelty of conception, when she was promised that it would be accomplished through the power of the Most High? [Note: [Col. 0192C] The Vatican, St. Peter’s, and Bologna manuscripts, as well as the first edition, read “whose.”]

The faith of the believer is also confirmed by the testimony of a preceding miracle, [Note: [Col. 0192D] Some printed copies, through a scribal error, read “above all.”] and an unexpected fertility is granted to Elizabeth, so that he who had granted conception to a barren woman would not be doubted to grant it also to a virgin.

## CHAPTER II

The Word of God, God, the Son of God, who in the beginning was with God, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:1–3), became human in order to free humanity from eternal death. He thus bent himself to assume our lowliness without diminishing his majesty, so that, remaining what he was and assuming what he was not, he might unite the true form of a servant to the form in which he is equal to God the Father (Philippians 2:6). He joined the two natures in so firm a bond that glorification did not consume the lower, nor did assumption diminish the higher. [Note: [Col. 0192D] The same wording occurs in Letter 28, chapter 3.]

With the proper character of both substances preserved and the two united in one person, lowliness is received by majesty, weakness by power, and mortality by eternity. And, in order to discharge the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, and true God and true human being were joined into the unity of the Lord. Thus what suited our restoration, the one and same mediator between God and human beings (1 Timothy 2:5), could both die in virtue of one nature and rise again in virtue of the other.

Rightly, therefore, the birth of salvation brought no corruption to virginal integrity, because it was the preservation of modesty and the bringing forth of truth. Such a birth, beloved, suited the power and wisdom of God, Christ, since it corresponded to us in humanity and surpassed us in divinity. [Note: [Col. 0192D] Thus the seven manuscripts of Quesnell and all ours read; formerly *humilitate* (“in humility”) was read, even in the copy of the first edition of Collection 3.] Unless he were true God, he would not bring the remedy; unless he were true human being, he would not provide the example.

Therefore, when the Lord was born, the rejoicing angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest,” and peace on earth was announced to people of good will (Luke 2:14). For they saw the heavenly Jerusalem being built from all the nations of the world. In this indescribable work of divine mercy, how greatly ought the lowliness of human beings to rejoice, since the sublimity of angels rejoices so greatly?

## CHAPTER III

Let us therefore give thanks, beloved, to God the Father, through his Son, in the Holy Spirit, who, because of his great mercy, with which he loved us, had mercy upon us; and when we were dead in sins, he made us alive together with Christ (Ephesians 2:5), so that in him we might be a new creation and a new work. [Note: [Col. 0192D] Thus the five manuscripts of Quesnell read. Most of ours, however, and Quesnell’s Gaudiival manuscript, together with the earlier editions, read *charitatem suam* (“his love”).]

Let us therefore lay aside the old person with his deeds (Ephesians 4:22; Colossians 3:9), and, having received a share in Christ’s generation, let us renounce the works of the flesh. Recognize, O Christian, your dignity, and, having become a participant in the divine nature, do not return to your former baseness through a degenerate way of life.

Remember whose head and whose body you are a member of. Remember that, having been snatched from the power of darkness, you have been transferred into God’s light and kingdom. Through the sacrament of baptism you have become a temple of the Holy Spirit. Do not drive away so great an inhabitant from you through evil deeds and subject yourself again to the devil’s slavery. For your price is the blood of Christ; for he will judge you in truth, [Note: [Col. 0193B] Another reading: “who mercifully [judges].” The Vercellese manuscript reads: “who will judge you in truth, who redeemed you in mercy.” One manuscript of St. Peter reads: “because Christ our Lord redeemed you in mercy, who lives, etc.” The Padiliron manuscript similarly prefers this reading and closes only with: “who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, God, forever and ever.” [Col. 0193C] Amen.] he who redeemed you in mercy, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXII [in other editions XXI]

*On the Nativity of the Lord II*

> **Editorial note** [Col. 0193C]. In Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, and likewise in an ancient manuscript Lectionary of the Church of Vercelli, this sermon appears in a form different from that found in the printed editions and other manuscripts. It seemed appropriate to indicate the difference carefully here. The first chapter agrees with the printed editions, and the variation begins at the opening of the second chapter. For, with the words “When, therefore, the appointed times had come, beloved, which had been ordained for the redemption of humanity” omitted, the chapter begins: “The Son of God enters these lowly things of the world,” and so forth, through the words “to be subject to the laws of death.” Then follows: “But by a new birth he was begotten, because inviolate virginity knew no desire and supplied the substance. Nature, not guilt, was assumed from the mother of the Lord,” together with the rest read at the end of chapter 3, through the words “would exclude the defect of antiquity.” From this point, however, Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary and the Vercelli manuscript contain the same reading that appears continuously in Letter 28 of Saint Leo to Flavian, from the end of chapter 3 to the middle of chapter 4—that is, from the words “For because the devil gloried,” and so forth (which are read near the end of chapter 1 of the present sermon), through “Nature, not guilt, was assumed from the mother of the Lord”; these words are recited in the same context and in the same form in the letter to Flavian.

> After the words “would exclude the defect of antiquity,” the aforesaid Homiliaries do not immediately continue, as the printed editions do, with chapter 4 of the sermon: “Since, therefore, the merciful and almighty Savior”; instead, three omitted paragraphs from chapter 3 are inserted. For immediately after “would exclude the defect of antiquity,” they read: “For the Lord’s true mercy, when he had many resources ineffably available for restoring the human race,” and so forth, through “unless he were conquered by that which he had subjected.” Then chapter 4 is added: “Since, therefore, the merciful and almighty,” together with the rest through the words “by grace you might obtain what you did not possess by nature.” Then, with the remainder of chapter 5 omitted, chapter 6 follows: “Since, therefore, we possess confidence in so great a hope,” and so forth, through the end of the paragraph beginning “with this reading, which, as they say, seems honorable because of the rising of a new sun.” The intervening words are omitted, and the text proceeds to “and although they possess wondrous beauty,” through the end of the sermon.

> So great a variation in one and the same sermon, found in two manuscripts of such antiquity and differing from all the other manuscripts and editions, raises the suspicion that Leo may have published this sermon in a different form, and that the complete testimony preserved in continuous sequence in these two manuscripts was inserted into Letter 28. It is enough to have pointed this out; judgment may be left to others.

## Synopsis

1. In the incarnation of the Word, God’s original purpose toward humanity is fulfilled, but through a more hidden mystery.
2. Through a new order and a new birth, the Son of God was begotten.
3. Why Christ chose to be born of a Virgin.
4. The devil was deceived through the incarnation from a Virgin.
5. Christ was therefore born in the flesh so that we might be reborn from the Spirit.
6. The Manichaeans worship not the rising of the God-Man, but, as they say, that of a new sun.

## Chapter I

Let us exult in the Lord, beloved, and rejoice with spiritual gladness, because there has dawned for us the day of new redemption, ancient preparation, and eternal happiness.  

> **Note** [Col. 0194C]. The manuscript of Saint Peter and, in the margin of the Cologne edition of 1547, that of Peter Canisius, read “of our redemption.” The other manuscripts require “of the new,” in opposition to “ancient.” The printed editions before Quesnellus had “of restoration,” as we have found in several manuscripts. It should have been written “of preparation,” not only on the basis of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, but also of our more accurate Lectionaries and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, especially since the sense demands it. In the times before Christ’s coming, many prophecies and figures could be called the preparation of redemption or restoration, but not restoration itself.

For the mystery of our salvation is renewed for us by the annual cycle: promised from the beginning, bestowed at the end, and destined to remain without end. In this mystery it is fitting that, with our hearts lifted upward, we should adore the divine mystery, so that what is accomplished by the great gift of God may be celebrated with the Church’s great joys.

> **Note** [Col. 0194D]. The manuscript of Saint Peter reads: “For God’s kindness toward us, whose nature is goodness,” and so forth.

For almighty and merciful God—whose nature is goodness, whose will is power, and whose work is mercy—immediately after the devil’s wickedness had killed us with the poison of its envy, marked out, from the very beginnings of the world, the remedies of his compassion prepared for the renewal of mortals. He declared to the serpent that the woman’s future offspring would crush by his power the pride of its harmful head (Genesis 3:2)—namely, Christ, God and man, who would come in the flesh and, born of a Virgin, would condemn the violator of the human race by an incorrupt birth.

> **Note** [Col. 0194D]. Quesnellus and our manuscripts read “signifying.” The earlier printed editions read “marking out.”

> **Note** [Col. 0194D]. The words enclosed in brackets appear exactly in Letter 28 to Flavian, chapters 3 and 4.

> [For because the devil gloried that the man deceived by his fraud had been deprived of the divine gifts, stripped of the endowment of immortality, and subjected to the harsh sentence of death—  
>   
> **Note** [Col. 0194D]. The manuscripts of Saint Peter read “dreadful.”  
>   
> —and because he had found a certain consolation in his own evils through the companionship of the transgressor, and because he thought that God too, with the demand of just severity, had changed his former judgment toward the man whom he had created in such great honor, it was necessary, beloved, by a secret dispensation of counsel, that the unchangeable God—whose will cannot be deprived of its goodness—should fulfill the first disposition of his mercy through a more hidden mystery, and that the man driven into guilt by the devil’s wicked cunning should not perish contrary to God’s purpose.]  

> **Note** [Col. 0194D]. The printed editions before Quesnellus, together with Gaudiival and our two Vatican manuscripts, collections 4 and 5, read “predestined.” The Lectionary manuscripts and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary read “prepared.”

> **Note** [Col. 0194D]. The earlier editions have “justly,” without the diphthong and with a comma, so that the adverb referred to the verb “changed.” We have corrected the text from our manuscripts; the reading of Letter 28, chapter 3, “with the demand of justice,” confirms the correction.

> **Note** [Col. 0194D]. The Vercelli manuscript reads “by a secret dispensation.”

> **Note** [Col. 0195C]. The first edition and the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Bologna read “driven into guilt.”

## Chapter II

When, therefore, the appointed times had come, beloved, which had been ordained for the redemption of humanity,

> **Note** [Col. 0195C]. The printed editions read “these lowest things.” We have inserted “of the world” on the authority of the manuscripts of Saint Peter, Vercelli, Padua, Saint Anthony, Venice, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary. In Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 4, from which Leo transferred this passage, all the manuscripts prefer “of the world.” Some manuscripts of this sermon, as also in that letter, have “weak” instead of “lowest.” Immediately afterward, the editions before Quesnellus, together with some manuscripts, have “our Lord” or “our God” in place of “the Son of God.”

the Son of God, Jesus Christ, enters these lowly things of the world, descending from his heavenly throne yet not departing from the Father’s glory, begotten in a new order and by a new birth. In a new order, because he who was invisible in his own nature became visible in ours; the incomprehensible willed to be comprehended; remaining before the ages, he began to exist in time; the Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, with the dignity of his majesty veiled; and God, incapable of suffering, did not disdain to become man capable of suffering and to be subject to the laws of death.

But by a new birth he was begotten, conceived of a Virgin and born of a Virgin, without the desire of a father’s flesh and without injury to his mother’s integrity. Such a birth befitted the future Savior of humanity: one who would possess in himself the nature of human substance yet know nothing of the defilement of human flesh.

> **Note** [Col. 0195D]. Two Vatican manuscripts and the Bologna manuscript, together with the first edition, read: “begotten, because conceived of a Virgin.” Two manuscripts of Saint Peter read: “was begotten, because conceived from a Virgin.”

For God is the author of the God born in the flesh, as the archangel testified to the blessed Virgin Mary:

> **Note** [Col. 0195D]. In the editions before Quesnellus and in manuscripts of the later collections, the word “God” is absent. “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

The origin is unlike, but the nature alike. It is without human custom or ordinary process, yet is supported by divine power: that a virgin should conceive, that a virgin should give birth, and that she should remain a virgin.

> **Note** [Col. 0195D]. The printed editions insert “as we believe,” words which we have rightly removed as unnecessary with the help of the better manuscripts of Saint Peter and the first edition. Then one manuscript of Saint Peter and another of Venice read: “that the virgin should conceive and the virgin should give birth,” and so forth. In one Vatican manuscript the second occurrence of “that” is absent.

Here one must not consider the condition of the woman giving birth, but the will of the one being born, who was born man as he willed and as he was able.

> **Note** [Col. 0195D]. Three Vatican manuscripts, one of Saint Peter, and the first edition read “he became.” The others have the reading retained in the text.

If you seek the truth of his nature, acknowledge the human material; if you examine the reason for his origin, confess the divine power.

> **Note** [Col. 0195D]. Quesnellus printed this reading, supported by the manuscripts of Saint Peter. The printed editions and some manuscripts had “the material of human nature.”

For the Lord Jesus Christ came to remove our contagions, not to suffer them; not to succumb to vices, but to heal them. He came to cure every disease of corruption and all the ulcers of defiled souls.

> **Note** [Col. 0196C]. The editions before Quesnellus, together with some manuscripts of the later collections, read “wounds.” Three Vatican manuscripts and the first edition read “vices.” We have retained “ulcers” on the authority of the manuscripts of Saint Peter. Shortly afterward, instead of “inflicted,” Quesnellus read “inserted” in the Corbie manuscript.

For this reason it was necessary that he should be born in a new manner, since he brought to human bodies the new grace of unstained purity. For it was necessary that the incorruptibility of the one being born should preserve the first virginity of the mother, and that the power of the divine Spirit, poured into her, should preserve the enclosure of modesty and the dwelling place of holiness that had pleased him.

> **Note** [Col. 0196C]. We have corrected the text from two manuscripts of Saint Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, and the first edition. The printed editions read: “so that the incorruption of the birth might preserve the mother’s first integrity.”

He had determined to raise up what had fallen, to strengthen what had been broken, and to grant multiplied power of chastity for overcoming the enticements of the flesh.

> **Note** [Col. 0196D]. This is the reading of two manuscripts of Saint Peter, one of Bologna, and the first edition. Others read “which had determined.” Thus virginity, which in others could not remain safe through childbearing, might become in others an object of imitation through rebirth.

> **Note** [Col. 0196D]. This correction was supplied by two copies of Saint Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, and the first edition. Other copies read “so that it might become in others capable of imitation, both by confessing and by being reborn.”

## Chapter III

But, beloved, does it not appear that there was the deepest reason why Christ chose to be born of a Virgin? It was so that the devil might not know the salvation born for the human race and, while the conception remained spiritually hidden, might see him as no different from others and believe that he had been born in the same manner as the rest.

> **Note** [Col. 0196D]. We have adopted the reading of our manuscripts, which is also that of the editions before Quesnellus. Quesnellus reads “the salvation of the human race.”

For when he perceived that his nature was like that of everyone else, he assumed that the cause was the same as for all; he did not understand that the one whom he found not exempt from mortal weakness was free from the bonds of transgression.

For the true mercy of God, although he possessed many ineffable means for restoring the human race, chose above all this method of intervention: in destroying the devil’s work, he would use not the power of might but the reasoning of justice. For the pride of the ancient enemy rightly claimed tyrannical authority over all human beings, and he oppressed under an authority that was not unjust those whom he had enticed away from God’s command into obedience to his own will.

> **Note** [Col. 0196D]. The Vercelli manuscript reads “from God’s command.”

He would not justly have lost his original servitude over the human race unless he had been conquered by the one whom he had subjected.

> **Note** [Col. 0196D]. Four of Quesnellus’s manuscripts and several of ours, together with Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, read “servitude.” Earlier editions, with the manuscripts of Victorinus and Gaudiival, Quesnellus’s Vatican collection 5, and others, read “those delivered into slavery.” Another Vatican manuscript, collection 4, reads “of the debt,” in place of “of the human race.”

To accomplish this, Christ was conceived of a virgin without male seed; she was fertilized not by human intercourse but by the Holy Spirit.

> **Note** [Col. 0196D]. We have corrected “was conceived” from the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Bologna. Others read “was brought forth.” And while in all other mothers conception does not occur without the stain of sin, this conception drew purification from the source of its conception. For where the transmission of paternal seed did not reach, there the origin of sin did not mingle.

“Inviolate virginity knew no desire; it supplied the substance.”

> **Note** [Col. 0196D]. “Nature, not guilt, was assumed from the mother of the Lord.” The Corbie, Gaudiival, Victorinus, and Regius manuscripts do not read “from the mother,” but “human nature,” as formerly. Quesnellus—The first edition nevertheless reads “of the Lord,” as do most of our manuscripts and Paul the Deacon’s copy; and, more importantly, the same reading occurs in every manuscript of Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 4. Only Vatican manuscript 544, collection 5, reads “of man” in this sermon; in the letter to Flavian it reads “of the Lord.”

The form of a servant was created without servile condition, because the new man was so joined with the old that he received the truth of the race while excluding the defect of antiquity.

> **Note** [Col. 0197D]. Four manuscripts and Gaudiival read this way. The printed editions have “without a man’s condition.” Quesnellus—Our manuscripts, together with the first edition, likewise read “servile.” Immediately afterward, the Vercelli manuscript has “and new” instead of “because new.”

## Chapter IV

Since, therefore, the merciful and almighty Savior so governed the beginnings of his assumption of humanity that, beneath the veil of our weakness, he concealed the power of the inseparable Godhead united with his manhood, the cunning of the unsuspecting enemy was deceived. He thought that the birth of the child brought forth for the salvation of the human race was subject to him in the same way as the birth of all others.

For he saw him crying and weeping; he saw him wrapped in swaddling clothes (Luke 2:12),

> **Note** [Col. 0197D]. Three Vatican manuscripts and the manuscripts of Saint Peter read “wrapped.”

subjected to circumcision and having undergone the offering of the legal sacrifice. Then he recognized the customary stages of childhood and did not doubt that he had advanced to manhood through natural growth.

> **Note** [Col. 0197D]. Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary reads “to mature years.”

During all this he inflicted insults, multiplied injuries, applied curses, reproaches, blasphemies, and abuse; finally, he poured out against him every force of his fury and ran through every kind of temptation.

> **Note** [Col. 0197D]. The same Homiliary reads “and everything.” Then three Vatican manuscripts, the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Bologna, and the first edition read “he traversed,” instead of “he ran through”; the former, however, indicates a past action corresponding to what precedes. Immediately afterward, these same manuscripts and the first edition read “knowing that.”

And, knowing with what poison he had infected human nature, he in no way believed him exempt from the first transgression, whom he had learned from so many proofs to be mortal.

Thus the wicked robber and grasping exactor persisted in attacking one who possessed nothing of his, and, while pursuing the general prejudice of a corrupted origin, he exceeded the written bond on which he relied, demanding from the one in whom he found no guilt the punishment of iniquity.

> **Note** [Col. 0197D]. Two Vatican manuscripts read “by which he was held”; the first edition reads “which he used.” Then, for “exceeds,” the printed editions before Quesnellus and some manuscripts read “fell away”; others of ours, and those used by Quesnellus, have the reading retained in the text.

Thus the harmful written contract of the deadly pact is dissolved, and by the injustice of demanding more, the entirety of the debt is cancelled.

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary and the first edition read “the ill-advised contract.”

That mighty one is bound in his own chains, and every scheme of the wicked one is turned back upon his own head. When the prince of the world has been bound, the vessels of captivity are seized. Nature, cleansed from its ancient contagions, returns to its honor; death is destroyed by death; birth is restored by birth. For at once redemption removes slavery, regeneration changes origin, and faith justifies the sinner.

## Chapter V

Whoever, therefore, piously and faithfully glories in the Christian name, weigh with a just judgment the grace of this reconciliation.

For you—once rejected; you, cast out from the dwellings of paradise; you, dying through long exiles;

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary reads “remaining.”

you, dissolved into dust and ashes, for whom no hope of living remained—you have been given, through the incarnation of the Word, the power to return from afar to your creator, to recognize your parent, to be made free from a slave, to be advanced from a stranger into a son.

Thus, although you were born from corruptible flesh, you may be reborn from God’s Spirit and obtain by grace what you did not possess by nature.

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. Two Vatican manuscripts, the Bologna manuscript, and the first edition read this way. Other copies read: “and, if you.”

And if through the spirit of adoption you recognize yourself as a son of God, you may now dare to call God your Father. Freed from the guilt of an evil conscience, aspire to the heavenly kingdoms; do God’s will, strengthened by divine assistance; imitate the angels on earth; feed upon the power of an immortal substance; fight confidently against hostile temptations on behalf of piety; and, if you preserve the sacred vows of the heavenly army, do not doubt that you are to be crowned for victory in the triumphant camp of the eternal King, when the resurrection prepared for the godly receives you and advances you into fellowship with the heavenly kingdom.

## Chapter VI

Having, therefore, beloved, confidence in so great a hope, remain steadfast in the faith in which you have been founded, lest that same tempter, from whom Christ has now removed dominion over you, deceive you again by some snares and corrupt, by the artifice of his deceit, the very joys of this present day. He deceives simpler minds by the pernicious persuasion of certain people, for whom this day of our solemnity seems worthy of honor not so much because of Christ’s nativity as because of the rising, as they say, of a new sun.

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. The Vercelli and Bologna manuscripts, and the first edition, read “from us”; then, again, “us.” Some Vatican manuscripts of the later collections read “condemnation” instead of “dominion.”

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. Others read “presumption.”

Their hearts are wrapped in deep darkness and estranged from every increase of the true light. For they are still drawn along by the most foolish errors of paganism; and because they cannot raise the gaze of their mind above what they behold with bodily sight, they venerate the ministering lights of the world with divine honor.

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. The first edition omits “and.”

Far be such impious superstition and monstrous falsehood from Christian minds. Temporal things differ beyond all measure from the eternal, bodily things from the incorporeal, and things subject to rule from their ruler; for, although they possess a wondrous beauty, they do not possess a Godhead worthy of worship.

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. In the same edition, “which” appears instead of “because.”

That power, that wisdom, that majesty is to be worshipped which created the universe from nothing and, by almighty reason, brought forth earthly and heavenly substance into whatever forms and measures it willed.

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary reads “majesty alone is to be worshipped.”

Let the sun, moon, and stars be useful to those who employ them and beautiful to those who behold them, but let thanks for them be given to their Creator, and let God be worshipped, who made them, not the creature that serves.

> **Note** [Col. 0198D]. The same Homiliary reads “who created these things.” Shortly afterward, the first edition and the Bologna manuscript read “Praise, therefore, the Lord.”

Praise God, therefore, beloved, in all his works and judgments. Let your belief in virginal integrity and childbirth be unwavering. Honor with holy and sincere service the sacred and divine mystery of humanity’s restoration. Embrace Christ as born in our flesh, so that we may deserve to see that same God of glory reigning in his majesty, who remains with the Father and the Holy Spirit in the unity of the Godhead for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII [in other editions XXII]

*On the Nativity of the Lord III*

## Synopsis

1. Both generations of Christ are ineffable, and both natures were brought forth from Mary.
2. Whence Arius’s error arose; the mystery of the incarnation is explained.
3. The necessity of the incarnation, so that the errors and sins of humanity might be removed.
4. The faith and power of the incarnation have always been one and the same as they are today.
5. The Nativity of the Lord is to be celebrated not with carnal but with spiritual joy. Christ became our flesh by being born; we become his flesh by being reborn.

## Chapter I

The matters pertaining to the mystery of today’s solemnity are indeed known to you, beloved, and frequently heard. But just as this visible light gives pleasure to sound eyes, so the Savior’s birth gives eternal joy to healthy hearts. It must never be passed over in silence by us, even though it cannot be explained as fully as it deserves.

> **Note** [Col. 0199C]. We have corrected “known to you” from most of our manuscripts; others read “known to us.” Shortly afterward, we have written “pertaining to the mystery” from four Vatican manuscripts; others read “pertaining to the mysteries.”

> **Note** [Col. 0199C]. We have supplied the following seven words from the manuscript of Saint Peter, since they seem required by Leo’s argument below. From that manuscript we have also written “not to be passed over in silence,” instead of “not to be kept silent,” which appeared in the printed editions and some other manuscripts.

For we believe that the saying, “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8), pertains not only to that mystery by which the Son of God is coeternal with the Father, but also to this birth by which the Word became flesh (John 1:14).

God, therefore, the Son of God, equal and of the same nature as the Father and with the Father, Creator and Lord of the universe, wholly present everywhere and wholly surpassing all things, derived from the Father and of the same nature with the Father,

> **Note** [Col. 0199C]. We judged that the reading of the cited manuscript of Saint Peter should be adopted. Others read “surpassing the universe.” Immediately afterward, the Bologna manuscript and the first edition read “pass through” instead of “run their course.” Then the word “Mary,” supplied from the manuscripts of Saint Peter, has been added.

chose for himself, within the order of time—which proceeds according to his own disposition—this day on which he would be born from the blessed Virgin Mary for the salvation of the world, with the modesty of the one giving birth unimpaired in every respect. As her virginity was not violated by giving birth, so it had not been violated by conception.

> **Note** [Col. 0199C]. This is more correctly taken from the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Bologna and the first edition. Others read: “Just as she was not violated by childbirth, so she had not been.”

Thus was fulfilled, as the Evangelist says, what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14).

For this miraculous birth of the holy Virgin truly brought forth, in one offspring, one person who was truly human and truly divine.

> **Note** [Col. 0199D]. The printed editions read “truly divine nature,” and one edition has “in one offspring.” We preferred the reading of the Lectionary of the Basilica of Saint Peter, especially since Saint Peter Damian proves that this reading was formerly current: in his work 1.9 he seems likewise to have read it in his Roman manuscript, except that, instead of “offspring,” he has “in the offspring.” Moreover, the context itself seems to require this reading. For Leo’s reasoning, since it is directed toward excluding two persons, presupposes one person in the proposition. As for the meaning of the passage, when the holy pontiff professes one person, he did not call this person truly human and truly divine with the intention of signifying two persons, one human and the other divine—for shortly afterward he explicitly excludes a distinction of persons, that is, two distinct persons. Rather, he intended to signify the one person he acknowledges as truly human and truly divine in different respects: truly divine in himself, because he is truly the divine person of the Word; but truly human, if one may speak in this way, by function, because that divine person of the Word, united to human nature, is the true hypostasis of that nature, insofar as Christ’s human nature truly subsists in the person of the Word and receives the ultimate completion proper to a true person. This appears to have been said against the Nestorians, who admitted two persons in Christ, or two sons.

For the two substances did not retain their own properties in such a way that there could be a distinction of persons in them; nor was the creature assumed into fellowship with its Creator so that he would be the indweller and it the dwelling place; rather, one nature was so joined to the other.

> **Note** [Col. 0200D]. The manuscript of Saint Peter reads “was united,” perhaps “was inserted” or “was joined,” as below in chapter 2, where “is joined” occurs. Regarding the word “mixed,” we shall give Quesnellus’s lengthy annotation in the observations, where we shall see that “mixed” is used for “united.”

And although one is what is assumed and the other what assumes, the diversity of both came together in such great unity that there is one and the same Son, who, insofar as he is truly man, says that he is less than the Father (John 14:28), and, insofar as he is truly God, declares himself equal to the Father (John 10:30).

> **Note** [Col. 0200D]. The manuscript of Saint Peter reads: “that he is the one and same Son of God.”

## Chapter II

Arian blindness could not perceive with the eyes of understanding this unity by which the creature is joined to the Creator. It did not believe that God’s Only-Begotten was of the same glory and substance as the Father; it declared the Son’s divinity to be inferior, drawing its arguments from those things that must be referred to the form of a servant. Yet the same Son of God, in order to show that this form in him is neither separate nor that of another person, says one thing together with the other:

> **Note** [Col. 0200D]. We have supplied the words “the same Son of God,” from the manuscript of Saint Peter and Cassinese collection 1, as the context also requires. In the printed editions and other manuscripts, the words were absent because of a scribal leap: “The Father is greater than I,” which he says together with, “The Father and I are one.”

“The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), just as he says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

In the form of a servant, which he assumed at the end of the ages for the sake of our restoration, he is less than the Father; but in the form of God, in which he existed before the ages, he is equal to the Father. In human lowliness he was made from a woman, made under the Law (Galatians 4:4); in divine majesty he remained the Word of God, through whom all things were made (John 1:3).

> **Note** [Col. 0200D]. The same words occur in Letter 28, chapter 3.

Therefore, he who in the form of God made man became man in the form of a servant; yet in both respects he is God, because of the power of the one who assumes, and in both respects he is man, because of the lowliness of what is assumed.

> **Note** [Col. 0201C]. The Bologna manuscript and the first edition read “because of the majesty.”

Each nature retains its own property without defect.

> **Note** [Col. 0201C]. Two manuscripts of Saint Peter, one Vatican manuscript, and another of Bologna read: “And just as the form of a servant does not take away the form of God, so the form of God does not diminish the form of a servant.” But the printed text agrees with the reading of Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 3. A similar formula occurs in Letter 35, chapter 2: “What belongs to the Godhead, the flesh does not diminish; what belongs to the flesh, the Godhead does not destroy.”

And just as the form of God does not take away the form of a servant, so the form of a servant does not diminish the form of God (Philippians 2:6).

The mystery of power united with weakness, on account of the same human nature, allows the Son to be called less than the Father. But the Godhead, which is one in the Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, excludes every notion of inequality. For there is nothing temporal in its eternity, nothing unlike in its nature; there is one will, the same substance, equal power, and not three gods but one God. For the unity is true and inseparable where no diversity can exist.

> **Note** [Col. 0201D]. The same words are read in Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 3.

In the complete and perfect nature of a true man, therefore, the true God was born: wholly in what was his own, wholly in what was ours. By “ours” we mean those things that the Creator established in us from the beginning and assumed in order to restore them. But those things that the deceiver introduced and deceived humanity admitted had no trace in the Savior. Nor, because he shared in the weaknesses of humanity, was he therefore a participant in our sins.

He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, elevating what was human without diminishing what was divine. For that self-emptying by which the invisible made himself visible was an inclination of compassion, not a diminution of power.

## Chapter III

Therefore, so that we might be recalled to eternal blessedness from our original bonds and worldly errors, he himself descended to us, to whom we could not ascend. For although many possessed love of the truth, they were deceived by the cunning of misleading demons amid the variety of uncertain opinions, and human ignorance was dragged into diverse and conflicting doctrines by a knowledge falsely so called.

To remove this mockery, through which captive minds served the proud devil, legal instruction was not sufficient, nor could our nature be restored through prophetic exhortations alone. The truth of redemption had to be added to moral teachings, and our origin, corrupted from the beginning, had to be reborn through new beginnings.

> **Note** [Col. 0201D]. Some manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus read “for mortals,” incorrectly.

An offering had to be presented for reconciliation, one that would both share our race and be free from our contamination. Thus the purpose of God—that the sin of the world should be destroyed through the birth and passion of Jesus Christ—would extend through all the ages of generations.

> **Note** [Col. 0201D]. The manuscript of Saint Peter reads this way. Others read “to destroy.”

The mysteries, varied according to the course of the ages, should not trouble us but rather strengthen us, since the faith by which we live has never been different in any age.

## Chapter IV

Let the complaints of those who, with impious murmuring, speak against the divine dispensations therefore cease. They complain about the lateness of the Lord’s Nativity, as though what was accomplished in the final age of the world had not been bestowed in former times.

> **Note** [Col. 0201D]. The printed editions read “has been accomplished.” We preferred the manuscripts of Saint Peter and two Vatican copies. Then the editions before Quesnellus, omitting the particle “for,” had: “The incarnation of the Word brought about what was to be done, which was done.” Quesnellus, without citing any authority, corrected this to: “For the incarnation of the Word brought about what was to be done, which was done.” We found this reading in collections 1 and 5. We preferred the reading of the manuscripts of Saint Peter and collection 2, from which three other manuscripts differ little; in them, through scribal error, it was written: “For the incarnation of the Word brought about what was to be done, which was done.” Immediately afterward, on the basis of the same manuscripts of Saint Peter, we removed the preposition “in” that had preceded “any antiquity,” since it is never found in the ancient witnesses.

For the incarnation of the Word brought about what was to be done, which was done; and the mystery of human salvation has never ceased in any antiquity. What the apostles preached, the prophets announced; what was always believed was not fulfilled late.

The wisdom and kindness of God, through this delay in the saving work, made us more capable of his calling, so that what had been foretold through so many ages by many signs, many words, and many mysteries would not be uncertain in the days of the Gospel. And the Savior’s birth, which was destined to exceed every miracle and every measure of human understanding, would generate a more steadfast faith in us because its proclamation had preceded it both earlier and more frequently.

> **Note** [Col. 0202D]. This is better taken from the more excellent manuscripts of Saint Peter. Others read: “the birth, which surpassed every miracle and every measure of understanding.”

God did not therefore provide for human affairs by a new plan or with belated mercy; rather, from the foundation of the world he established one and the same cause of salvation for all.

For the grace of God, by which the whole community of the saints has always been justified, was increased when Christ was born, not begun. And this great mystery of compassion, by which the whole world has now been filled, was so powerful even in its signs that those who believed it when promised obtained no less than those who received it when given.

> **Note** [Col. 0202D]. The editions before Quesnellus read “however.” Our manuscripts read “for.”

## Chapter V
Therefore, beloved, since such great riches of divine goodness have been poured out upon us—[Note: [Col. 0202D] In editions before Quesnell and in some manuscripts there was *tantae in nobis divinae bonitatis effusae sint gratiae, quibus ad aeternitatem vocandis non solum praecedentium exemplorum utilitas*, etc. We found Quesnell’s emendation in the manuscript of St. Peter, from which we supplied *divinae*, omitted by Quesnell.] riches by which, as we are called to eternity, we have been served not only by the usefulness of preceding examples but also by the very truth appearing visibly and bodily—we ought to celebrate the day of the Lord’s Nativity with manifest devotion and with joy that is neither sluggish nor carnal. [Col. 0203A] This will be done worthily and diligently by each person if everyone remembers whose bodily member he is and to which head he has been joined, lest a discordant structure fail to adhere to the sacred edifice. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Thus according to the manuscripts of St. Peter and the first edition. Others have *intelligenter*, “intelligently.”]

Consider, beloved, and prudently observe, in accordance with the illumination of the Holy Spirit, who has received us into himself and whom we have received into ourselves. For just as the Lord Jesus, by being born, became our flesh, so we have become his body by being reborn. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Thus in the manuscripts of St. Peter, which agree with manuscript collections 1 and 2. They alone omit *nostra*, “our,” which other manuscripts preserve and which the following word *ipsius* seems to require, in Leo’s manner. Earlier editions and some manuscripts read: “Just as the Lord became our flesh by being born, so we too have become his by being reborn.” A little later, some manuscripts have “the Spirit of God” instead of “the Holy Spirit.”]

Therefore we are both members of Christ and a temple of the Holy Spirit. For this reason the blessed Apostle says: “Glorify God and carry him in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). By setting before us the form of his gentleness and humility, he imbued us with the virtue by which he redeemed us, the Lord himself promising: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29).

Let us therefore accept the yoke of the Truth who rules us—a yoke that is neither heavy nor harsh—and let us become like his humility, whose glory we desire to share. May he himself assist us and lead us to his promises: Jesus Christ our Lord, who according to his great mercy is able to blot out our sins and perfect his gifts in us. [Note: [Col. 0203D] The manuscript of St. Peter reads: “and to wipe away our sins and perfect his gifts in us.” Some manuscripts add afterward: “through endless ages of ages.”] He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXIV [Alternatively XXIII]  
## On the Nativity of the Lord IV

### Synopsis

I. Through the incarnation of the Word, figures and promises have been fulfilled.  
II. Unless God became human, no remedy would remain for humanity’s wounds.  
III. Christ is true God and true human, free from original sin; the image of whose Nativity is found in baptism.  
IV. The Manichaeans, who deny that Christ was born bodily, are alien to this.  
V. Other heretics possess something sound in some respect; the Manichaeans possess nothing that is not impious.  
VI. One must beware their feigned piety and adhere to the unity of faith, without which nothing is true.

## CHAPTER I

Always, beloved, divine goodness has cared for the human race in various ways and by many measures, and throughout all past ages it has mercifully bestowed very many gifts of its providence. But in the final times it surpassed all the abundance of its accustomed kindness, when in Christ there descended mercy itself toward sinners, truth itself toward those who had gone astray, and life itself toward the dead. Thus the Word, coeternal and coequal with the Father, assumed within the unity of his divinity the substance of our lowliness, so that he who was born God from God might also be born human from a human being. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Some Vatican manuscripts, the manuscript of Boulogne, and the first edition have *materiam*, “material substance.”]

This had indeed been promised from the foundation of the world and had always been foretold through many signs in events and words. [Note: [Col. 0203D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter and one Vatican manuscript have *signationibus*, “signs” or “significations.”] But how large a portion of humanity would those figures and veiled mysteries have saved, unless Christ by his coming had fulfilled the long-hidden promises, so that what at that time benefited a few believers as something yet to be done would, once accomplished, benefit countless faithful people? [Note: [Col. 0204D] One manuscript of St. Peter and the first edition have *ut quod*, “so that what.”]

Now, therefore, we are led to faith not by signs or images, but the Gospel history confirms what we believe to have happened and adore. The prophetic writings are added to our instruction, so that we may have no uncertainty about what we know was foretold by such numerous oracles.

For this reason the Lord said to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). For this reason David sings the promise of God by the prophetic Spirit, saying: “The Lord swore to David, and he will not frustrate him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon your throne’” (Ps. 131:11). [Note: [Col. 0204D] We supplied *dicens*, “saying,” from several manuscripts and editions. The first edition then reads: “The Lord swore truth to David.” The manuscript of St. Peter reads: “The Lord swore, and he will not repent: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will set upon my throne.’”]
