For this reason the same Lord says through Isaiah: “Behold, a virgin shall receive in the womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14). And again: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. 11:1). In this rod, without doubt, the blessed Virgin Mary was foretold. Born from the stock of Jesse and David and made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, she brought forth a new flower of human flesh: truly from a mother’s womb, but by a virginal birth.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore let the righteous rejoice in the Lord, let the hearts of believers rise in praise of God, and let the children of humanity confess his wonders, because in this work of God above all our lowliness recognizes how highly its Creator valued it. [Note: [Col. 0204D] We retained the reading of the first edition, supported by the manuscripts of the Lectionary of St. Peter and manuscript collection 3. The other editions and manuscripts omit *justi in Domino*, “the righteous in the Lord,” and.] Though he had already bestowed much upon human origins by making us in his image, he bestowed far more upon our restoration when the Lord himself joined himself to the form of a servant. Whatever the Creator gives to the creature proceeds from one and the same goodness; nevertheless, it is less astonishing for a human being to advance toward divine things than for God to descend toward human things.

But unless almighty God had deigned to do this, no appearance of righteousness and no form of wisdom could have rescued anyone from the captivity of the devil and the depths of eternal death. [Note: [Col. 0205D] The word *Deus*, “God,” has been added from the manuscripts of St. Peter, Vatican and Boulogne manuscripts, and the first edition. Shortly afterward, the manuscript of St. Peter has *specie* rather than *species*.] For condemnation, passing from one person to all along with sin, would have remained, and nature, weakened by a deadly wound, would have found no remedy, since it could not change its condition by its own strength. [Note: [Col. 0205D] Two Vatican manuscripts, one manuscript of Boulogne, and the first edition have *labefacta*, “shaken”; the manuscript of St. Peter has *labefactata*, “weakened.”]

For the first human being received the substance of flesh from the earth and was animated by a rational spirit through the breathing of the Creator (Gen. 2:7), so that, living according to the image and likeness of his author, he might preserve the form of God’s goodness and righteousness in the splendor of imitation, as in the brightness of a mirror. [Note: [Col. 0205D] *Dei*, “of God,” is absent from the first edition.] If he had cultivated this supremely beautiful dignity of his nature perseveringly through observance of the law that had been given, his incorrupt mind would have led that very earthly quality of the body to heavenly glory.

But because he rashly and unhappily believed the envious deceiver (Gen. 3:6), and, yielding to the counsels of pride, preferred to seize the reserved increase of honor rather than earn it, not only that human being but also all his posterity in him heard: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). “As was the earthly one, so also are the earthly” (1 Cor. 15:49); and no one is immortal, because no one is heavenly.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Several manuscripts and the first edition have *Ad hujus*, “For the undoing of this.”]

For the undoing of this bond of sin and death, the almighty Son of God—filling all things, containing all things, equal in every respect to the Father, and coeternal with him and from him in one essence—assumed human nature into himself. The Creator and Lord of all things deigned to become one of mortal beings, choosing for himself the mother whom he had made. Without compromising her virginal integrity, she served only as the minister of bodily substance, so that, with the contagion of human seed excluded, both purity and reality might belong to the new human being. [Note: [Col. 0205D] Four manuscripts, including two of St. Peter and the first edition, have *generis*, “of the race”; and “For it is not,” rather than “Therefore it is not.”]

Therefore, because the birth of Christ, born from a virgin’s womb, is miraculous, it does not follow that our nature is unlike his. For he who is true God is also true human, and there is no falsehood in either substance. The Word became flesh through the elevation of flesh, not through the diminution of divinity. His power thus moderated its goodness that, by assuming what is ours, it might elevate it, and by sharing what is his, it might not lose it. [Note: [Col. 0206D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, one manuscript of Boulogne, and the first edition have *non proderet*, “would not benefit,” in place of *non perderet*, “would not lose it.”]

In this Nativity of Christ, according to the prophecy of David, “truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12). In this Nativity also the words of Isaiah were fulfilled: “Let the earth bring forth and germinate a Savior, and let righteousness arise likewise” (Isa. 45:8). For the earth of human flesh, which had been cursed in the first transgressor, in this sole birth of the blessed Virgin produced a blessed shoot, alien from the fault of its stock. Everyone attains its spiritual origin in rebirth. For every person who is reborn, the water of baptism is like a virginal womb: the same Holy Spirit fills the font who filled the Virgin, so that the sacred conception removed sin there, while here the mystical washing removes it.

## CHAPTER IV

Beloved, the insane error of the Manichaeans is alien to this sacrament, and those who deny that Christ was born bodily from the Virgin Mary have no share in his rebirth. Since they do not believe in his true birth, they do not receive a true passion; and since they do not confess that he was truly buried, they reject his genuine resurrection. Having entered upon the precipitous path of an accursed doctrine—a path in which nothing is not dark and nothing is not slippery—they plunge into the depths of death through the precipices of falsehood. They find nothing solid on which to lean, since, in addition to all the devil’s shameful contrivances, as was revealed by their recent confession, they rejoice in pollution both of mind and of body on the very principal feast of their observance, preserving neither the integrity of faith nor modesty, so that they are found impious in their doctrines and obscene in their sacred rites. [Note: [Col. 0206D] Thus Quesnell, with the first edition and three of our manuscripts. Others have *propter*, “because of.” A little later, the manuscripts of St. Peter have “both of mind and body.”] [Note: [Col. 0206D] We emended this from the manuscript of St. Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, and one manuscript of Boulogne. Others read: “preserving neither integrity in faith nor modesty.” The first edition and another manuscript of Boulogne read: “preserving neither modesty nor integrity in faith.”]

## CHAPTER V

Other heresies, beloved, although all rightly deserve condemnation in their distinct forms, nevertheless each possesses in some part of itself something that is true. [Note: [Col. 0206D] The editions have *in sua perversitate*, “in their perversity.” We corrected this from the manuscripts of St. Peter, since the holy pontiff notes the distinction of each one. A little later, the same manuscripts of St. Peter and the manuscript of Boulogne have *verum sit*, “may be true.”]

Arius, defining the Son of God as lesser than the Father and as a creature, and supposing that the Holy Spirit too was created by him among all other things, destroyed himself through great impiety. Yet he did not deny in the Father’s essence the eternal and unchangeable divinity that he failed to recognize in the unity of the Trinity.

Macedonius, alienated from the light of truth, did not accept the divinity of the Holy Spirit, but confessed that the Father and the Son possess one power and the same nature.

Sabellius, confused by an inexplicable error, understood the unity of substance in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as inseparable, but assigned to singularity what he ought to have attributed to equality. Unable to understand the true Trinity, he believed that one and the same person existed under a threefold designation. [Note: [Col. 0206D] Thus from the manuscript of St. Peter. Another source has *inexplanabili*, “inexplicable.”]

Photinus, deceived by blindness of mind, confessed Christ to be truly human and of our substance, but did not believe that he was the same God born from God before all ages.

Apollinaris, deprived of the solidity of faith, believed that the Son of God had assumed the true nature of human flesh in such a way that he said there was no soul in that flesh, because divinity itself had fulfilled its role.

If, in this way, the errors of all whom the catholic faith has anathematized are reviewed, something can be found in one or another of them that may be separated from what is condemnable. But in the utterly criminal doctrine of the Manichaeans there is absolutely nothing that can be judged tolerable in any respect.

## CHAPTER VI

But you, beloved, whom I address in no words more worthy than those of the blessed Apostle Peter—“a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession” (1 Pet. 2:9)—built upon Christ, the inviolable rock, and incorporated into the Lord and our Savior himself through the true assumption of our flesh, remain steadfast in the faith that you confessed before many witnesses and in which, reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, you received the chrism of salvation and the seal of eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0207D] The editions have *charisma*, “gift.” Quesnell writes: “We have found this reading in none of the editions we used.” A little later, the manuscripts of St. Peter and the first edition have *aliquid annuntiaverit*, “announced anything,” rather than *aliud annuntiaverit*, “announced something else.”]

But if anyone announces to you anything other than what you learned, let him be accursed. Do not place impious fables before the clearest truth, and whatever you happen to read or hear contrary to the rule of the catholic and apostolic creed, judge that altogether deadly and diabolical.

Let not feigned and simulated fasts deceive you by their deceptive arts. They promote not purification but the destruction of souls. [Note: [Col. 0207D] One Vatican manuscript has *proficient*, “they will advance.”] They assume for themselves an appearance of piety and chastity, but by this trick they conceal the obscenities of their deeds and shoot forth, from the inner chambers of a profane heart, arrows by which the simple may be wounded, so that, as the prophet says, “they shoot in the darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. 10:3). [Note: [Col. 0207D] The manuscripts of St. Peter, Boulogne, and the first edition have *de profani*, “from the profane.”]

Unimpaired faith, true faith, is a great protection. Nothing can be added to it or taken away from it by anyone, because if it is not one, it is not faith. The Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in us all” (Eph. 4:5–6). Beloved, cling to this unity with unshaken minds, and in it pursue all holiness (Heb. 12:14); in it serve the Lord’s commandments, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), and without it nothing is holy, nothing chaste, nothing living. “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4). Whoever loses it through the devil’s deception is dead while alive, because just as righteousness is obtained through faith, so eternal life is obtained through true faith. The Lord and Savior says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). [Note: [Col. 0207D] The same manuscript of Boulogne and the first edition have *nos*, “us.”]

May he cause you to advance and persevere to the end, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXV [Alternatively XXIV]  
[Note: [Col. 0207D] In one manuscript of St. Peter this sermon is entitled: “On the Nativity of the Lord, against heretics”; in another: “Against Jews and heretics.”]  
## On the Nativity of the Lord V

### Synopsis

I. Leo acknowledges himself a debtor to the inexperienced children of the Church. The way is narrow not only in observing the commandments but also on the path of faith.  
II. The Word, equal and consubstantial with the Father, became less than the Father through the incarnation with respect to human nature.  
III. The profound mystery of the incarnation is examined.  
IV. Christ, foretold in the Old Law and sent in the New, can be known only through the Spirit of God.  
V. Unless the Word became flesh, death would reign from Adam onward. The Son of God became human so that human beings might become children of God. The power of baptism.  
VI. The incarnation is both a mystery and an example.

## CHAPTER I

Although the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ is ineffable, by which he clothed himself with the flesh of our nature, I nevertheless dare to rely not on my own ability [Note: [Col. 0208D] *Fidere*, “to rely,” is absent from editions before Quesnell and from some manuscripts; we found the word especially in the manuscripts of St. Peter and the Casinensis manuscript.] but upon his inspiration, so that on the day chosen for the sacrament of human restoration something may be brought forth by us that can edify those who hear it. [Note: [Col. 0208D] One manuscript of St. Peter has “in the sacrament of human restoration”; another manuscript of St. Peter and four Vatican manuscripts have “in the sacrament of human renewal.”]

It is not because the greater part of God’s Church understands what it believes that it is therefore unnecessary to say again what has been said. Since we owe the service of our mouths to the many who are now first coming to faith, it is better to burden the learned with things already known than to defraud beginners of what they must learn.

The Son of God, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit is not one person but one essence, deigned to become a participant in our lowliness and to be one among those subject to suffering and one among mortals. This is so sacred and so marvelous that the reason for the divine plan cannot be clear to the wise of this world unless the true light has dispelled the darkness of human ignorance. [Note: [Col. 0208D] Thus two manuscripts of St. Peter and six Vatican manuscripts; the same reading occurs in chapter 3. Others have *humanitatis*, “of humanity.” Leo uses *humilitas* and *humanitas* somewhat interchangeably.]

For the way that leads to life is narrow and difficult not only in the work of virtues or in the observance of commandments, but also on the path of faith (Matt. 7:14). It is a task of great labor and great danger to walk with unhindered steps along the one path of sound doctrine amid the doubtful opinions of the unlearned and plausible falsehoods, and, when snares of error confront us from every side, to escape every danger of deception. [Note: [Col. 0208D] The manuscript of St. Peter has *sanam*, “sound.”]

But who is suited for these things except one who is taught and guided by the Spirit of God? The Apostle says: “We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12). David also sings: “Blessed is the person whom you instruct, Lord, and teach from your law” (Ps. 93:12). [Note: [Col. 0209D] The first edition omits *homo*, “person.”]

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, beloved, possessing safeguards of truth amid the dangers of error and instructed not by words of human wisdom but by the teaching of the Holy Spirit, we believe what we have learned and proclaim what we believe: that the Son of God was begotten from the Father before the ages, coeternal with the Father in eternal and consubstantial equality. [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts of St. Peter and one Vatican manuscript read: “We believe and proclaim the Son of God, God begotten from the Father before the ages.” The first edition adds *Deum*, “God,” and omits *a Patre*, “from the Father.”]

He came into this world through the womb of the Virgin, chosen for this sacrament of divine goodness. In her and from her, Wisdom built himself a house (Prov. 9:1), and the immutable divinity of the Word joined to himself the form of a servant in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3). [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts of St. Peter have *in hoc sacramento*, “in this sacrament.”]

In no respect was his glory less in himself, or in relation to the Father and the Holy Spirit, because the nature of the supreme and eternal essence admits neither diminution nor variation. Yet for the sake of our weakness he diminished himself to those incapable of receiving him and concealed beneath the veil of the body the splendor of his majesty, which human eyes could not bear. [Note: [Col. 0209D] The manuscripts of St. Peter, one Vatican manuscript, and the Venetian edition of 1485 have *et sui velamine*, “and beneath the veil of his own [body].”]

For this reason he is also said to have emptied himself (Phil. 2:7), as though he had emptied himself by his own power, since in the humility by which he cared for us he became lower not only than the Father but also than himself. Yet nothing was diminished in him, for with the Father and the Holy Spirit he shares the very fact of being. Thus we understand that this itself belongs to omnipotence: that he who is lower according to what is ours is not lower according to what is his own. [Note: [Col. 0209D] Thus the manuscripts of Quesnell and most of ours; in earlier editions *in* was absent before *esse*.]

Because light looked upon the blind, power upon the weak, and mercy upon the wretched, it was accomplished by great power that the Son of God assumed human substance and the human cause—he who would both restore our nature, which he had created, and abolish the death, which he had not made. [Note: [Col. 0209D] One Vatican manuscript has *pietate*, “goodness.” Shortly afterward, two Vatican manuscripts have *substantiam*, “substance,” and *humanamque causam susciperet*, “would assume human substance and condition.” The manuscript of St. Peter likewise reads *susciperet*. In those same Vatican manuscripts *nostram*, “our,” is absent.]

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, with all the opinions of the impious rejected and cast far away—opinions for which Christ is either foolishness or a stumbling block—let the faith of upright minds rejoice and understand that the true and one Son of God is not only Son according to his divinity, by which he was begotten from the Father, but also according to his humanity, by which he was born from a virgin mother. [Note: [Col. 0209D] Editions before Quesnell and several of our manuscripts have *Crux Christi*, “the cross of Christ.” But the manuscript of St. Peter has *Christus*, “Christ.” A little later, we have retained *in humilitate*, “in lowliness,” rather than *in humanitate*, “in humanity,” with Quesnell, on the authority of several of our better manuscripts.]

He is the one who is in our lowliness and in divine majesty, true human and true God; eternal in what is his, temporal in what is ours; one with the Father in substance, which was never less than the Father; one with his mother in the body that he created.

In assuming our nature, he became for us the step by which we can ascend to him through him. For that essence which is always wholly everywhere had no need of a local descent; and it was as proper to him to be wholly joined to humanity as it is proper to him to remain wholly undivided from the Father.

Therefore “the Word remains, which was in the beginning” (John 1:1), and it is not accidental to him that what he is once was not at some time. For eternally the Son is Son, and eternally the Father is Father.

Since the Son himself says, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9), your impiety, heretic, has blinded you, so that, because you did not see the majesty of the Son, you did not see the glory of the Father. By saying that the one who did not exist was begotten, you assert that the Son is temporal; and by asserting that the Son is temporal, you believe that the Father is changeable. [Note: [Col. 0210D] Thus more correctly from the manuscripts of St. Peter. Editions with other manuscripts have *credidisti*, “you have believed.”]

For not only what is diminished is changeable, but also whatever is increased. If the Begotten is therefore unequal to the Father because, as you suppose, the Father begot him who did not exist, then the essence of the one who begot was also imperfect, since by begetting he advanced toward possessing what he had not possessed. [Note: [Col. 0210D] Later editions and those before Quesnell have: “by begetting he perfected what he did not have, by acquiring it.” The better manuscripts support the reading inserted in the text.]

But catholic faith abhors and condemns this impious perversity of yours. In true divinity it recognizes nothing temporal; rather, it confesses both Father and Son as belonging to one eternity. The radiance arising from light is not later than the light, and true light never lacks its own radiance, always possessing the power to shine substantially just as it always possesses the power to exist substantially.

The manifestation of this radiance is called a sending, by which Christ appeared to the world. Although he always filled all things with his invisible majesty, he nevertheless came to those who did not know him as though from the most distant and highest secret place, when he removed the blindness of ignorance and, as it is written, “light arose for those sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Isa. 9:2). [Note: [Col. 0210D] The manuscripts of two Vatican collections and the first edition have *et cum omnia*, “and although he filled all things.” Some of our manuscripts have *abstulit*, “removed,” rather than *sustulit*, and they also preserve the conjunction *et*, omitted in editions before Quesnell.]

## CHAPTER IV

Although in earlier ages too the light of truth was sent forth for the illumination of the holy fathers and prophets—for David says, “Send forth your light and your truth” (Ps. 42:3)—and although the divinity of the Son declared the works of his presence in various ways and through many signs, all those signs and all those miracles were testimonies to this sending of which the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4). [Note: [Col. 0210D] The editions have *natum*, “born.” We accepted the reading of the cited manuscripts, which agrees with the Vulgate.]

What is this, then, except that the Word became flesh, the Creator of the world was born through a virgin’s womb, the Lord of majesty joined himself to human beginnings, and, although no contamination of earthly seed was mingled with the spiritual conception, he nevertheless took from his mother alone the nature needed for true flesh? [Note: [Col. 0211D] The first edition has *sumpsit*, “took.”]

Through this sending, by which God was united to humanity, the Son is less than the Father—not in what he is from the Father, but in what he became from a human being. Humanity did not corrupt the equality that divinity possesses inviolate; and the Creator’s descent toward the creature is the believers’ advancement toward eternal things. [Note: [Col. 0211D] Thus from the manuscripts of St. Peter and the first edition. Others have *subvectio*, “conveyance upward.” One Vatican manuscript has *subvectio: quia*, “conveyance upward, because,” as the Apostle says, “the world through its wisdom did not know God.”]

For, as the Apostle says, “since the world through its wisdom did not know God, God was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:21). To the world—that is, to the wise of the world—its own wisdom became blindness, and through it they were unable to know God, whose knowledge is approached only in his wisdom. Therefore, because the world was proud of the vanity of its doctrines, the Lord established the faith of those to be saved in that which seemed both unworthy and foolish, so that, when every presumption of human opinions failed, the grace of God alone might reveal what human understanding could not comprehend. [Note: [Col. 0211D] We deleted the conjunction *et*, inserted in editions before *deficientibus*, on the authority of the manuscript of St. Peter and Vatican manuscript collections 4 and 5.]

## CHAPTER V

Therefore let catholic faith recognize its glory in the Lord’s lowliness, and let the Church, which is Christ’s body, rejoice in the mysteries of its salvation. For unless the Word of God became flesh and dwelt among us, unless the Creator himself descended into communion with the creature and by his birth recalled the old human condition to a new beginning, death would reign from Adam (Rom. 5:14) to the end, and an unbreakable condemnation would remain over all human beings, since there would be one common cause of destruction arising solely from the condition of birth.

Therefore the Lord Jesus alone among the children of humanity was born innocent, because he alone was conceived without the pollution of carnal desire. He became human from our race so that we might become participants in the divine nature. The origin that he took in the Virgin’s womb he placed in the baptismal font; he gave the water what he had given his mother. For the power of the Most High and the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:35), which caused Mary to bear the Savior, likewise causes the water to regenerate the believer.

What was more suitable for healing the sick, enlightening the blind, and giving life to the dead than that the wounds of pride should be cured by remedies of humility? Adam, neglecting God’s commandment, introduced the condemnation of sin; Jesus, made subject to the law, restored freedom to righteousness. The former, obeying the devil even to transgression, deserved that all should die in him; the latter, obeying the Father even to the cross, brought it about that all should be made alive in him. The former, desiring angelic honor, lost the dignity of his nature; the latter, assuming the condition of our weakness, placed in the heavenly realms those for whose sake he descended to the depths. Finally, to the one who fell through arrogance it was said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19); to the one exalted through submission it was said, “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1).

## CHAPTER VI

Beloved, these works of our Lord are useful to us not only as a sacrament but also as an example for imitation, if the remedies themselves are transferred into our conduct, so that what has been bestowed in the mysteries may also benefit our morals. [Note: [Col. 0211D] The manuscripts of St. Peter have *mysterium*, “mystery.”] Let us remember that we must live in the humility and gentleness of our Redeemer, because, as the Apostle says, “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8:17).

For we are called Christians in vain if we are not imitators of Christ. He therefore said that he was the way (John 14:6), so that the conduct of the Master might be the model for his disciples, and so that the servant might choose the humility that the Lord followed. [Note: [Col. 0211D] Thus from the manuscripts of St. Peter. The Vatican manuscript collection 5 likewise has *discipulis*, “for the disciples.” Editions had: “so that he might be the form of the disciple, and that servant might choose that humility.” The manuscripts of St. Peter continue: “who lives and reigns with God the Father almighty and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.” Vatican manuscript collection 4 has: “who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever.”]

He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXVI [Alternatively XXV]  
[Note: [Col. 0212D] The manuscript of St. Peter: “Sermon of St. Leo the Pope against heretics, on the Nativity of the Lord.”]  
## On the Nativity of the Lord VI

### Synopsis

I. The mysteries of Christ’s Nativity and infancy must always be recalled.  
II. While venerating Christ’s birth, the Church celebrates its own.  
III. What kind of peace Christ bestows by being born without human seed.  
IV. Whoever is a son of God should imitate God and serve God’s grace and will.  
V. The Lord’s birthday is the birthday of peace. What the peace of the world and of the elect is like.

## CHAPTER I
All days and seasons, beloved, present to the minds of the faithful who meditate on divine things the birth of our Lord and Savior from a Virgin mother, so that the mind, raised up to confess its Author, whether it is engaged in the groaning of supplication, the exultation of praise, or the offering of sacrifice, encounters nothing more frequently—and nothing more confidently with spiritual vision—than this: that God the Son of God, begotten from the coeternal Father, was also born through a human birth.

[Note: The same manuscript of Saint Peter reads “in exaltation.”]

[Note: Thus the manuscripts of Saint Peter agree with Quesnell. Earlier editions read: “and nothing more confidently.”]

Yet no day impresses this birth, to be adored in heaven and on earth, upon us more than today; and, as a new light also shines through the elements, it brings before our senses the splendor of this wondrous mystery. For Gabriel’s conversation with the astonished Mary returns not merely to our memory but, in a certain sense, before our eyes, as does the conception from the Holy Spirit, so wondrously promised and believed.

[Note: Quesnell emended this without indicating any manuscript. We find the reading “and the conception” in the manuscripts of Saint Peter and other codices; the addition “For today” occurs in manuscripts of Collection 5. The printed editions, with certain manuscripts, read: “and the conception from the Holy Spirit, so wondrously promised as believed, the Author of the world was brought forth.”]

Today the Author of the world was born from a virgin womb, and he who created every nature became the Son of the nature he had created. Today the Word of God appeared clothed in flesh, and what had never been visible to human eyes began also to be handled by human hands. Today the shepherds learned through angelic voices of the Savior born in the substance of our flesh and soul; and today the pattern of proclaiming the Gospel was established among the shepherds of the Lord’s flocks, so that we too may say with the army of the heavenly host: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:4).

[Note: The word “begotten” is absent from Vatican Collection Manuscript 5.]

## Chapter II

Although that infancy, which the majesty of the Son of God did not disdain, advanced by the increase of age into perfect manhood, and although, after the triumph of his Passion and Resurrection, all the actions of humility that he had undertaken for us had passed away, today’s feast nevertheless renews for us the sacred beginnings of Jesus’ birth from the Virgin Mary. While we adore the birth of our Savior, we discover that we are celebrating our own beginning.

For Christ’s generation is the origin of the Christian people, and the birth of the Head is the birth of the Body. Although each of the called may have his own order, and all the children of the Church may be distinguished by the succession of time, the entire fullness of the faithful, born from the font of baptism, has been born together with Christ in this birth, just as it was crucified with Christ in his Passion, raised with him in his Resurrection, and placed at the right hand of the Father in his Ascension.

[Note: The printed editions read “we are.” We have judged the reading of two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and one Vatican manuscript preferable: “they are.”]

For whoever among believing people, in whatever part of the world, is regenerated in Christ, cutting across the path of original antiquity, passes into the new human being by being reborn. He is no longer counted in the descent of a carnal father but in the offspring of the Savior, who for this reason became the Son of Man so that we might be sons of God. For unless he had descended to us in this humility, no one could have reached him by any merit of his own.

Let no earthly wisdom bring darkness upon the hearts of the called, and let not the dust of earthly thoughts—soon to return to the depths—raise itself against the height of God’s grace. What had been arranged before eternal times has been fulfilled at the end of the ages; and, when realities were present and the signs of figures had ceased, the Law and prophecy became truth. Thus Abraham was made the father of all nations, and in his seed the blessing promised to the world was given. Nor were only those Israelites whom blood and flesh had produced to enter into possession of the inheritance prepared for the children of faith; rather, the whole company of adoption was to enter it.

[Note: The common texts read “Israel.” We have corrected this on the basis of the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s.]

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “Let them not object.”]

Let the calumnies of foolish questions not clamor against this, and let human reasoning not scrutinize the effect of a divine work. With Abraham we believe God, and we do not hesitate through disbelief (Romans 4:20); rather, we know with complete certainty that what the Lord promised, he is able also to accomplish.

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter’s read “God.”]

## Chapter III

The Savior, then, is born not from the seed of flesh but from the Holy Spirit, so that the condemnation of the first transgression might not hold him. Hence the greatness of the gift bestowed itself demands from us a reverence worthy of its splendor. For, as the blessed Apostle teaches, “we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:12): he is not worshiped piously unless what he himself bestows is offered to him.

[Note: In the same manuscripts of Saint Peter, “teaches.”]

[Note: We have supplied “however” for “for,” on the basis of the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and certain Vatican manuscripts.]

What, then, can we find in the treasury of the Lord’s generosity so fitting for the honor of the present feast as peace, which was first proclaimed at the Lord’s birth in an angelic chorus? For peace is what gives birth to the children of God, the nurse of love and the mother of unity; the rest of the blessed and the dwelling place of eternity. Its proper and distinctive work is to join to God those whom it separates from the world.

Therefore the Apostle urges us toward this good, saying: “Therefore, justified by faith, let us have peace with God” (Romans 5:1). In the brevity of this statement the effect of almost all the commandments is contained, because where the truth of peace is present, nothing of virtue can be lacking.

What, then, beloved, does it mean to have peace with God except to will what he commands and not to will what he forbids? For if human friendships seek equal minds and similar wills, and if a difference of character can never arrive at firm harmony, how will someone share in divine peace if he takes pleasure in things displeasing to God and desires to delight in what he knows offends him?

This is not the disposition of the children of God, nor does adoptive nobility receive such wisdom. Let the chosen and royal race answer to the dignity of its regeneration: let it love what the Father loves and disagree with its Author in nothing, lest the Lord again say: “I have begotten and exalted children, but they have despised me. The ox knows its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood” (Isaiah 1:2).

## Chapter IV

Great, beloved, is the mystery of this gift, and this gift surpasses all gifts: that God calls a human being his child, and that a human being calls God his Father. Through these names one perceives and learns what kind of affection rises to such a height.

For if, in carnal descent and earthly lineage, the faults of a bad way of life obscure those born of distinguished parents, and offspring unworthy of the light of their ancestors are themselves disgraced, what will become of those who, because of their love of the world, do not fear to renounce their membership in Christ’s generation?

But if it belongs to human praise that the glory of fathers should shine in their offspring, how much more glorious it is for those born from God to reflect the image of their Author and to display within themselves the one who generated them. The Lord says: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

[Note: Another reading is “those born.” We have written “those born from God” on the basis of the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and the Vatican manuscripts. Other witnesses read “them” or “those.”]

[Note: Some ancient editions read “your light.” From the manuscript of Saint Peter’s and one Vatican manuscript we have written “may glorify,” instead of “may magnify.” The same reading occurs in Sermon 38, chapter 3, and Sermon 43, chapter 4.]

We know, as the Apostle John says, that “the whole world lies in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19). While the devil and his angels lie in wait, countless temptations afflict us, so that they may either terrify the human being striving toward heavenly things through adversity or corrupt him through prosperity. But greater is he who is in us than he who is against us; and for those who have peace with God and continually say to the Father with their whole heart, “Your will be done” (Matthew 6:10), no trial can prevail and no conflict can harm them.

By accusing ourselves through our confessions and denying the consent of our mind to the desires of the flesh, we indeed provoke against us the hostility of the one who is the author of sin; but by serving God’s grace we make firm an unconquerable peace with God, so that we are subject to our King not only in obedience but are also joined with him in judgment.

For if we are of the same mind, if we will what he wills and disapprove what he rejects, he himself will already finish all the battles for us. He who gave the will will also grant the power, so that we may be fellow workers in his works and, with the exultation of faith, say the prophetic words: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Psalm 26:1).

[Note: In Vatican Collection Manuscript 5, “of faith” is absent.]

## Chapter V

Therefore those who have been born “not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1:13), should offer the Father the harmony of peaceful children.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter reads: “nor from the pleasure of the flesh, nor from the pleasure of a man.” Hilary, *On the Trinity* I.10, has the same reading in a very ancient manuscript of the same basilica of Saint Peter.] Let all the members of adoption come together in the firstborn of the new creation, who came not to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him.

[Note: In the Bologna manuscript, the Vatican manuscript, and the first edition, the text reads “also in the firstborn.”]

For the Father’s grace adopted as heirs not those who are discordant or unlike one another, but those who think and love as one. The soul must be conformed to the one image into which it has been restored.

The Lord’s birth is the birth of peace. Thus the Apostle says: “He himself is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2:14), because “whether Jew or Gentile, through him we have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18). Before the day of his Passion, by a voluntary arrangement already determined, he instructed his disciples chiefly in this teaching, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:17).

[Note: The printed editions and several manuscripts add “his own,” which we have deleted on the basis of the manuscript of Saint Peter’s and the first edition.]

And lest the character of his peace remain hidden under the general name of peace, he added: “I do not give to you as the world gives.”

[Note: Quesnell inserted “for” in place of “he says”; we do not know on what authority, for all our manuscripts and the printed editions read “he says.” However, without “not” and with the word “its” we found the reading in two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and in the Casinensis. Earlier editions and manuscripts of the three later collections read: “The world, he says, does not have true friendships, and it makes many…” In one Vatican manuscript, “because it makes many” occurs instead of “and it makes many.”]

The world, he says, has its friendships and makes many people harmonious through perverse love. There are also minds equal in vice, and similarity of desires produces equality of affections.

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and the Vatican manuscripts read “but if”; the first edition reads “and if.”]

And if some perhaps are found who do not approve of wicked and dishonorable things and who exclude unlawful agreements from the covenant of their love, nevertheless such people too—whether they are Jews, heretics, or pagans—belong not to the friendship of God but to the peace of the world.

But the peace of spiritual and catholic people, coming from above and leading to what is above, does not wish us to mingle in any fellowship with lovers of the world. It wishes us to resist every obstacle and to flee from destructive pleasures toward true joys.

[Note: In the manuscript of Saint Peter’s, the reading is: “is coming … which, with lovers…”]

The Lord says: “Where your treasure is, there also will your heart be” (Matthew 6:22). That is: if the things you love are below, you will descend to the depths; if the things you love are above, you will reach the heights. May the Spirit of peace guide us and lead us there, as we will and think as one and are united in faith, hope, and charity. For “all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God” (Romans 8:14), who reigns with the Son and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon XXVII [Elsewhere XXVI]

[Note: One manuscript of Saint Peter’s reads: “Sermon of Saint Leo, pope, against heretics, on the Incarnation of the Lord.”]

On the Nativity of the Lord VII

### Synopsis

I. To deny either nature in Christ is equally dangerous.  
II. How is “the Word became flesh” to be understood? What were its effects?  
III. The devil tempts people in various ways according to their affections and pursuits.  
IV. The inclination of certain Christians toward the rising sun derives from superstition.  
V. The heavenly bodies serve human benefit.  
VI. The proper use of creatures. The human being born for present things is reborn for future things.

## Chapter I

Beloved, the true worshiper and devout celebrant of today’s feast is one who thinks nothing false about the Lord’s Incarnation and nothing unworthy about his Deity. For the danger is equal if either the truth of our nature is denied to him or equality with the glory of the Father is denied.

When we approach the mystery of Christ’s Nativity, by which he was born from a Virgin mother, let the darkness of earthly reasoning be driven far away, and let the smoke of worldly wisdom depart from the eyes enlightened by faith. The authority to which we believe is divine; the teaching we follow is divine.

[Note: Thus the manuscript of Saint Peter. Another reading is “eye.” The first edition reads: “and let the eye of faith be enlightened.”]

For whether we apply our inward hearing to the testimony of the Law, the oracles of the prophets, or the trumpet of the Gospel, it is true what the blessed John, filled with the Holy Spirit, proclaimed aloud:

[Note: We have added “blessed” from the lectionaries of Saint Peter and Verona.] “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

It is equally true what the same preacher added: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father” (John 1:14).

[Note: The first edition adds “full of grace and truth.” Subsequently: “In both natures” occurs in two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s, in a Vatican manuscript, and in the first edition.]

In both natures the same Son of God takes what is ours without losing what is his own. In the human being he renews humanity while remaining unchanged in himself. For the Deity that he shares with the Father suffered no diminution of omnipotence, nor did the form of a servant violate the form of God. The supreme and eternal essence, which inclined itself toward the salvation of the human race, transferred us into its glory, but did not cease to be what it was.

Therefore, when the Only-Begotten Son of God confesses himself less than the Father (John 14:28), while declaring himself equal to him (John 10:30), he demonstrates in himself the truth of both forms: the inequality proves his humanity, and the equality declares his divinity.

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter’s read “he himself, remaining unchangeable.” Later, the Verona manuscript reads “did not cease,” instead of “did not desist.”]

## Chapter II

The bodily birth took nothing away from the majesty of the Son of God and added nothing to it, because an unchangeable substance could neither be diminished nor increased.

The statement “the Word became flesh” does not mean that God’s nature was changed into flesh. It means that flesh was assumed by the Word into the unity of person. In this designation the whole human being is understood: within the Virgin’s womb, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and never destined to lose its virginity, the Son of God was joined to it so inseparably that the one who was timelessly begotten from the substance of the Father was himself temporally born from the Virgin’s womb.

[Note: Thus according to our manuscripts and the first edition. Other printed editions read “is united.”]

For otherwise we could not be released from the bonds of eternal death unless the one who remained omnipotent in his own nature became humble in ours.

[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s add “and exalted.” Shortly before this, the Verona manuscript reads “we could not,” instead of “we could not have.”]

Thus, in being born, our Lord Jesus Christ, true human being who never ceased to be true God, established in himself the beginning of a new creation. In the form of his birth he gave the human race a spiritual beginning, so that, for the abolition of the defilements of carnal generation, he might be the origin without the seed of sin for those who were to be reborn. Of them it is said: “They were born not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1:13).

[Note: The first edition lacks the preposition “in.”]

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter’s reads “from desire,” as also in the preceding sermon, chapter 5.]

What mind can comprehend this mystery? What tongue can tell of this grace? Iniquity returns to innocence, antiquity to newness; strangers enter into adoption, and outsiders enter into the inheritance. The impious begin to be just, the greedy kind, the incontinent chaste, and the earthly heavenly.

What is this change except the right hand of the Most High? For the Son of God came to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8), and he so united himself to us and us to himself that God’s descent to human things became humanity’s advancement to divine things.

[Note: The Bologna manuscript and the first edition read “inserted.”]

## Chapter III

In this mercy of God, beloved, whose greatness toward us we cannot explain, Christians must take great care lest they again be caught by the devil’s snares and become entangled once more in the errors they renounced.

[Note: Thus according to the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Verona. Another reading is “we cannot.”]

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and Verona read “which they had renounced.”]

The ancient enemy never ceases, transforming himself into an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), to spread everywhere the snares of deception and to persist in corrupting the faith of believers by whatever means he can.

He knows to whom he should bring the heat of desire, into whom he should inject the allurements of gluttony, to whom he should present the incentives of lust, and into whom he should pour the poison of envy. He knows whom to disturb with sorrow, whom to deceive with joy, whom to oppress with fear, and whom to seduce with admiration. He examines everyone’s habits, weighs their concerns, and scrutinizes their affections; and he seeks the causes of doing harm precisely where he sees each person occupied most zealously.

For he has many among those whom he has bound most tightly who are suited to his arts, and he uses both their ingenuity and their tongues to deceive others. Through them remedies for illnesses, indications of future events, appeasement of demons, and the driving away of shadows are promised.

[Note: Earlier editions, before Quesnell, and certain manuscripts read, “And they are added.” The correction is confirmed by the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s, Verona, and the Casinensis. Shortly afterward we have restored “by effects” from editions before Quesnell and from our better manuscripts. Quesnell, following Vatican Collection Manuscript 5, read “by affections”; in the margin: “Another reading: by effects.”]

Those who falsely claim that the whole condition of human life depends upon the effects of the stars also join them, saying that whatever belongs either to the divine will or to ours is determined by unalterable fates. Yet, to make their harm more complete, they promise that these things can be changed if one supplicates the stars that oppose them.

Thus the impious fiction destroys itself by its own reasoning: if the predictions do not remain fixed, the fates are not to be feared; if they remain fixed, the stars are not to be venerated.

[Note: Another reading is “by this”; Quesnell, in the margin.]

## Chapter IV

From such practices also arises the impiety that, at the beginning of the daylight, when the sun rises, certain more foolish people worship it from elevated places.

[Note: We have restored the preposition “in” from the manuscripts of Saint Peter, three Vatican manuscripts, and the first edition.] Some Christians even think that they are performing this religiously, so that before reaching the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, which is dedicated to the one living and true God, they climb the steps by which one ascends to the platform of the upper courtyard, turn their bodies toward the rising sun, and, bowing their necks, incline themselves in honor of the shining orb.

[Note: Quesnell attached the following annotation in his second edition: “Previously the reading was ‘of the altar,’ also in our first edition. The error was first detected by the most distinguished Roman scholar Giovanni Ciampini, Master of Briefs of Grace and referendary in both chancelleries, who vindicated the true reading in a work printed at Rome in 1693 under the title: On the Correction of a Word in Sermon 7 of Saint Leo the Great on the Nativity of the Lord, etc. We extract nothing here from the learned man’s dissertation, because we reproduce it in full at the end of these sermons. I note only that this passage was corrected on the authority of Vatican Manuscript 1277, written approximately six hundred years ago.” Thus far Quesnell.

An error entered the number of the Vatican manuscript 1277, which Ciampini obtained with the excellent reading. The manuscript bearing that number contains nothing relating to Leo. After careful investigation, however, we found the reading in the very ancient Vatican Lectionary 1267, and we believe that this is the manuscript Ciampini cited. To it we add two other manuscripts of the basilica of Saint Peter, numbered 105 and 107, and one Vallicellian manuscript, A 10, which likewise prefer the reading “of the courtyard.” In another manuscript of the same basilica, number 106, which is not of such ancient origin, “of the fortress” is found instead of “of the courtyard,” as also in the Verona manuscript. Perhaps an ancient scribe found “of the chest” written and thought that “of the fortress” ought rather to be written. In another Vallicellian manuscript, XXVI, “of bronze” is found instead of “of the courtyard.”]

We are deeply troubled and grieved that this is done, partly through the fault of ignorance and partly through the spirit of paganism. For even if some perhaps worship the Creator rather than the beautiful light itself—which is a creature—it is nevertheless necessary to abstain from the very appearance of such a religious act. When the one who has abandoned the worship of the gods finds this practice among us, will he not retain with himself, as something plausible, this part of his former belief, which he sees shared by Christians and pagans?

[Note: The reading is taken from the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and Verona. Another reading is “from the very appearance of this kind of service.”]

[Note: The author says that this custom arose partly from ignorance and partly from the spirit of paganism, and that it originated from the wrongheaded veneration of the stars practiced either by the Manichaeans or by the Priscillianists. Since he suggests that some may perhaps have worshiped the Creator of the beautiful light rather than the light itself, it is highly probable that the practice arose from the ancient Christian custom of praying turned toward the rising sun. This was especially so when people were being baptized: turned toward the west, they renounced Satan; then, turning toward the east, they saluted and worshiped Christ.

But why did this occur at the entrance of the basilica of Saint Peter rather than at other churches? At that time Christian churches were accustomed to face the rising sun, which those entering them would have before them; consequently, those entering did not need to turn their bodies toward the rising sun. Since the basilica of Saint Peter, like certain other ancient basilicas of the City, faced the setting sun from its entrance, Christians who were accustomed to pray toward the east retained this ancient custom received from their fathers and used even in baptism, so that it would not be entirely erased. They retained it specifically at the entrance of that basilica, where formerly there had been a baptismal font in which the faithful, having been washed, were accustomed to give themselves to Christ under the hand of the Roman pontiff.

Quesnell. Compare the excellent explanation arranged by Ciampini for this passage in the place cited in the preceding annotation. Among other things, he shows that the entrance or façade of the basilica of Saint Peter faced east, so that those wishing to venerate the rising sun had to turn their bodies on the platform of the upper courtyard. This was done by certain Christians partly through ignorance and partly through the spirit of paganism. They adopted the ancient Christian custom of praying with their faces turned toward the east, but, ignorant of the reason for the custom—that it was God, not the sun, who was worshiped—transferred it in a pagan spirit to the worship of the rising sun.

Thus the holy pontiff indicates that this perverse custom among these Christians arose not from the Manichaeans or Priscillianists but from an ancient Christian practice ignorantly transferred to the sun in a pagan spirit. He does not, however, condemn the practice of praying toward the east itself, but its abuse, by which either the sun was worshiped or, even if God rather than the sun was worshiped, scandal could arise from the circumstances.]

## Chapter V

Therefore let the condemned perversity be cast out of the custom of the faithful, and let the honor owed to the one God not be mingled with the rites of those who serve creatures. For divine Scripture says: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10).

And blessed Job, a blameless man, as the Lord says, and one who restrained himself from every evil thing (Job 1:8), says: “Have I looked upon the sun when it shone, and the moon moving brightly, and has my heart rejoiced in secret, and have I kissed my hand? This is the greatest iniquity and a denial against the Most High God” (Job 31:26–28).

What, then, are the sun and the moon except the elements of visible creation and bodily light? One possesses greater brightness, and the other a lesser light. Just as some periods belong to the day and others to the night, so the Creator established different qualities in the heavenly lights. Yet before these were made, days had already existed without the service of the sun and nights without the ministry of the moon.

[Note: Perhaps “visible.” Quesnell, in the margin.]

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “different qualities among the luminaries.” The Bologna manuscript and the first edition read “in the lights.”]

These things were created for the usefulness of human beings, so that the rational animal would not be deceived in the division of months, the recurrence of years, or the counting of times. By the unequal durations of unequal hours and the clear signs of differing risings, the sun marked off the years and the moon renewed the months.

[Note: The first edition and one Vatican manuscript read “they were granted.” Other editions before Quesnell read “they were created.” We found Quesnell’s correction in seven of our manuscripts, to which the Casinensis adds “they were owed.” Shortly afterward we have restored “for making” from the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s, the Vatican, Vallicella, and the Casinensis, as well as from the first edition, in place of “for being made.”]

For, as we read, on the fourth day God said: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them shine upon the earth, and let them divide between day and night, and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and for years, and let them be in the firmament of heaven, to shine upon the earth” (Genesis 1:14–15).

[Note: The manuscripts of Corbie, Gaudival, and Victor, as well as Quesnell’s edition, read “of equal.” The same occurs in our manuscripts and certain editions. Another reading is “of equal length.”]

[Note: Another reading in the manuscript of Corbie is “determine.”]

## Chapter VI

Awake, human being, and recognize the dignity of your nature. Remember that you were made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26). Although that image was corrupted in Adam, it has nevertheless been restored in Christ.

Use visible creatures as they are meant to be used, just as you use the earth, the sea, the sky, the air, springs, and rivers. Whatever is beautiful and wondrous in them, refer to the praise and glory of the Creator.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “so that you may refer whatever…”]

Do not be devoted to that light in which birds and serpents, beasts and cattle, flies and worms delight. Touch bodily light with bodily sense, but embrace with the whole affection of your mind that true light which enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9), and of which the prophet says: “Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm 33:6).

[Note: This is the reading of all our manuscripts and of the editions before Quesnell, who testifies that it is also found in the manuscripts of Gaudival. He himself printed “incorporeal,” and later “with incorporeal sense,” without identifying any manuscript that supports it. Nor does Leo’s context require it. For he does not forbid bodily light to be touched by bodily sense, since he had prefaced the statement with “Use visible things as they are meant to be used”; only the bodily senses are to touch it, while with the mind we are to embrace the true light.]

For if we are God’s temple and the Spirit of God dwells in us (1 Corinthians 3:16), there is more in the soul of each faithful person than in what he admires in heaven.

[Note: This is taken from the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and the Casinensis. Another reading is “has in his own soul.” Shortly afterward the first edition reads “certainly,” instead of “therefore.”]

Therefore, beloved, we neither announce nor persuade you to despise God’s works or to judge anything contrary to your faith among the things that the good God created as good. Rather, we urge you to use every form of creature and the entire adornment of this world rationally and temperately. For, as the Apostle says, “the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

[Note: Since we have been born for present things and reborn for future things, this is found in the Bologna manuscript and the first edition.]

Therefore, since we have been born for present things but reborn for future things, let us not be devoted to temporal goods but intent upon eternal ones. And so that we may contemplate our hope more closely, let us consider in the very mystery of the Lord’s Nativity what divine grace has conferred upon our nature.

Let us hear the Apostle saying: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3–4), who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## Sermon XXVIII [Elsewhere XXVII]

[Note: One manuscript of Saint Peter’s reads: “On the Nativity of the Lord, against heretics.” In another manuscript of the same basilica: “Against Nestorius and other heretics, on the Incarnation of the Lord.”]

On the Nativity of the Lord VIII

### Synopsis

I. With what great joy the mystery of the newborn Christ should be received.  
II. That the Word was absent from Christ’s human flesh and soul at no moment.  
III. That justice was preserved in the voluntary destruction of Adam’s sin.  
IV. Various errors concerning the Lord’s Incarnation.  
V. The impious doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches.  
VI. The truth of both natures in Christ coming together in the unity of person.  
VII. How the fullness of Deity dwells bodily in Christ, and in the Church.

## Chapter I

Although all the divine utterances exhort us always to rejoice in the Lord, beloved, today we are undoubtedly urged more abundantly toward spiritual joy, as the mystery of the Lord’s Nativity shines more brightly upon us. Let us return to that unspeakable condescension of divine mercy by which the Creator of human beings deigned to become human, so that we may be found in the nature of the one whom we adore in ours.

For God, the Son of God, the Only-Begotten from the eternal and unbegotten Father, while remaining eternal in the form of God and possessing immutably and timelessly the very being that the Father has, took the form of a servant without diminishing his majesty, so that he might raise us up in himself and not lower himself into our condition.

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Peter’s and Vatican Manuscript 1267 read “the human being.”]

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and Bologna read “being nothing other than what the Father is.” We have added one word to the common reading from these manuscripts and from the ancient Vatican Lectionary 1267.]

[Note: The printed editions read “so that he himself would not fail in our condition.” The reading in the manuscript of Saint Peter’s is better. Shortly afterward this manuscript and Vatican Lectionary 1267 read “not separated from the human being,” and “whatever belongs to the human being.”]

Thus, while each nature remains in its own properties, such a communion of unity has been effected that whatever is there of God is not separated from humanity, and whatever is there of the human being is not divided from Deity.

## Chapter II
Celebrating, therefore, beloved, the birthday of the Lord and Savior, let us contemplate in its entirety the childbirth of the blessed Virgin, so that we may believe that the power of the Word was absent from neither the conceived flesh nor the conceived soul at any moment of time. Let us not suppose that the temple of Christ’s body was first formed and animated and that, subsequently arriving, the inhabitant claimed it for himself; rather, let us believe that its beginning was given through him and in him as the new man, so that in the one Son of God and man there might be both Deity without a mother and humanity without a father. For at the same time, virginity, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit, without any trace of corruption brought forth both offspring of its own kind and the author of its own lineage. Hence the same Lord, as the Evangelist records, asked the Jews whose son they had learned from the authority of Scripture that Christ was; and when they replied that he was to come from David’s seed, he said: “How, then, does David in the Spirit call him his Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’?” (Matt. 22:43–44; Ps. 109:1). The Jews could not resolve the question put to them, because they did not understand that in the one Christ there were both Davidic descent and the divine nature foretold by the prophets.

## CHAPTER III

The majesty of the Son of God, equal to the Father, clothing itself in the humility of a servant, neither feared diminution nor needed increase. By the sole power of his Deity he could accomplish the work of his mercy, which he was devoting to the restoration of humanity, so that he might rescue the creature formed in the image of God (Gen. 1:26) from the yoke of a cruel ruler.

[Note: The printed editions read “from the yoke of harsh domination.” Quesnell, in the margin, proposed “of a harsh ruler”; this reading has been preferred on the authority of two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and of Cassino, etc. In Vaticanus 1267 the reading is “of a severe ruler.” Shortly afterward, the Bonon. manuscript reads *exueret* (“might strip off”) instead of *erueret* (“might rescue”); and in the same manuscript and the first edition, *factam* (“made”) appears shortly before instead of *conditam* (“formed”).]

But since the devil had not acted violently against the first man in such a way as to transfer him to his own side without the consent of free will, the voluntary and hostile design had to be destroyed, so that the rule of justice would not be rendered ineffective by the gift of grace.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and one of St. Peter’s read *fuit* (“was”) instead. Vaticanus 1267 reads: “Thus the voluntary and hostile design had to be destroyed.”]

Thus, amid the common ruin of the entire human race, there was one remedy, hidden within the divine plan, that could aid the fallen: if one of Adam’s sons were born free from original transgression and innocent, so that he might benefit the rest both by example and by merit. But because natural generation did not permit this, and the offspring of a corrupted root could not be without the seed from which Scripture says, “Who can make clean what has been conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you, who alone are?” (Job 14:4), the Lord became the son of David; and from the fruit of the promised shoot there arose offspring without sin, with two natures united in one person. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ was begotten by the same conception and the same birth, possessing true Deity for the performance of miraculous works and true humanity for enduring sufferings.

[Note: In editions before Quesnell and in some manuscripts, the reading is “of the lineage.” The reading “of the shoot,” found in other Vatican and St. Peter’s manuscripts, agrees better with the text of Jeremiah 23:5, “I will raise up for David a righteous shoot,” and Isaiah 11:1, “A shoot from his root.”]

[Note: We have supplied the conjunction “and” from five manuscripts and the first edition.]

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, beloved, let the catholic faith reject the errors of the barking heretics. Deceived by the vanity of worldly wisdom, they have withdrawn from the Gospel of truth; unable to understand the incarnation of the Word, they have made the cause of illumination an occasion of blindness. When the opinions of nearly all who believe falsely have been reconsidered—opinions that even rush into denial of the Holy Spirit—we recognize that scarcely anyone has gone astray except one who has not believed, under the confession of one person, the truth of the two natures in Christ.

For some attributed to the Lord only humanity, others only Deity. Some acknowledged true divinity in him but said that his flesh was an illusion. Others professed that he had assumed true flesh but did not possess the nature of God the Father; and, assigning to his Deity what belonged to human substance, they imagined for themselves a greater God and a lesser one, although there can be no degrees within true Deity, since whatever is less than God is not God.

[Note: The Cassino manuscript, two Vatican manuscripts, and the first edition read “there cannot be.”]

Others, recognizing that there was no distinction between the Father and the Son, but unable to understand the unity of Deity except as unity of person, asserted that the Father and the Son were the same person. Thus birth and nurture, suffering and death, burial and resurrection would all belong to the same one, who in every respect would fulfill both the person of a human being and that of the Word.

[Note: Four manuscripts and the first edition read “the truth.” We have retained “unity,” because in Sermon 24, chapter 5, the same pontiff, speaking of this Sabellian heresy, likewise calls it “unity of substance.” Shortly afterward, our manuscripts and the first edition prefer “so that birth … might pertain,” with Quesnell, rather than “so that birth … might pertain” in the alternative arrangement found in other editions.]

Some thought that the Lord Jesus Christ did not possess a body of our substance, but one taken from higher and more subtle elements. Others, however, judged that a human soul had not been present in Christ’s flesh, but that the Deity of the Word had filled the functions of the soul. Their folly went so far that they did indeed admit that the Lord had a soul, but said that it lacked a mind, since Deity alone would suffice for all the activities of reason.

[Note: Several manuscripts and editions before Quesnell read “had not dwelt there, nor existed.” Shortly afterward, the first edition reads “the folly of some” instead of “their folly”; this may be preferable, since certain Apollinarists, mentioned in the preceding period, had inclined toward this error.]

Finally, these same people dared to assert that some part of the Word had been changed into flesh, so that, amid the multiplicity of variations within a single doctrine, they dissolved not only the nature of flesh and soul but also the very essence of the Word.

[Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts and of editions before Quesnell, which, without identifying any manuscript or noting a variant, printed: “They dissolved not only the nature but also the essence of the Word itself.” In one Vallicellian manuscript, A 10, with only a slight difference from the printed reading, it is: “So that, amid the multiplicity of variations in this doctrine, not only the nature of flesh and soul but also the essence of the Word itself might be dissolved.” At the beginning of the following chapter, Vaticanus 1267 reads: “There are many other things.”]

## CHAPTER V

There are also many other monstrous falsehoods, whose enumeration would weary the ears of your charity. But after the various impieties, which are linked to one another by the kinship of manifold blasphemies, I chiefly admonish your devotion to be vigilant in avoiding these errors: one of them, formerly under the leadership of Nestorius, attempted to arise with impunity; the other, recently erupting under the advocacy of Eutyches, must be condemned with equal abhorrence.

For Nestorius dared to proclaim the blessed Virgin Mary merely the mother of a human being, so that no union of the Word and flesh would be believed to have taken place in her conception and childbirth, because the Son of God himself had not become the son of a human being, but had joined himself to the created man only by an act of condescension.

[Note: Some manuscripts read: “he was made [the son of man], and afterward joined himself.”]

Catholic ears could never tolerate this, for they have been so imbued with the Gospel of truth that they know with complete certainty that there is no hope of salvation for the human race unless he himself was the son of the Virgin who is the Creator of his mother.

But this profane advocate of the more recent sacrilege confessed indeed that there were two natures united in Christ; yet he said that the result of this very union was that one nature remained from the two, with the substance of the other in no way existing—something that could end only either by destruction or by separation.

[Note: This is the reading of Quesnell and the first edition, together with the manuscripts of St. Peter’s and other Vatican manuscripts. In other printed editions and in some manuscripts of later collections, the reading is incorrectly *fieri* (“to come about”) instead of *finiri* (“to come to an end”).]

These things are so hostile to sound faith that they cannot be accepted without the destruction of the Christian name. For if the incarnation of the Word is not the union of divine and human nature, but by that very joining what was two became one, then only Deity was born from the Virgin’s womb; only Deity, under the deceptive appearance of flesh, underwent bodily nourishment and growth; and, to omit all the other changes of human condition, only Deity was crucified, only Deity died, only Deity was buried. According to the views of such people, there would then be no reason to hope for a resurrection, nor would Christ be “the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18), because there would have been no one who ought to be raised, if there had been no one who could be killed.

[Note: The word “not” was present in the printed editions and in several manuscripts, but it was rightly inserted here: Eutyches, whose error St. Leo is attacking, did not deny the union of the two natures; rather, he confessed it in such a way that he said that after the union one nature remained from the two. This particle is absent from two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, from the Vallicellian manuscript, from the Cassino manuscript, and others. In the first edition and the Bonon. manuscript, not only is “not” absent, but also the word “union,” so that the sentence reads: “For if the incarnation of the Word is divine and human nature.” Shortly afterward, with the more authoritative manuscripts, we have inserted the preposition “from” before “womb,” which is omitted in some editions and by Quesnell.]

## CHAPTER VI

Let the poisonous falsehoods of diabolical inspirations be far from your hearts, beloved. Knowing that the eternal Deity of the Son grew by no increase in relation to the Father, understand wisely that what was said to the nature in Adam, “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19), is said to the same nature in Christ: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

According to the nature by which Christ is equal to the Father, the Only-Begotten was never lower in dignity than the Father who begot him, nor is his glory with the Father temporal. He is at the Father’s right hand, of which Exodus says: “Your right hand, Lord, is glorified in strength” (Exod. 15:6); and Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1; Rom. 10:17).

[Note: We emended the text on the basis of two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, the Vallicellian and Cassino manuscripts. Previously it read: “which is itself the Father’s right hand.” One Vatican manuscript, Collection 5, reads: “which is itself the Father’s right hand”; another Vatican manuscript reads: “because he himself is the Father’s right hand.” The emendation agrees with Psalm 109:1, “Sit at my right hand.” Shortly afterward, one manuscript of St. Peter’s and the Vallicellian manuscript read “in Exodus it is sung.”]

The man assumed into the Son of God was received into the unity of Christ’s person from the very beginnings of his bodily existence, so that he was conceived neither without Deity, nor born without Deity, nor nourished without Deity. The same one was present in miracles and in insults; through human weakness he was crucified, died, and was buried; through divine power he was raised on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of God the Father. In the nature of man he received from the Father what, in the nature of Deity, he himself also gave.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts of St. Peter’s and of the ancient Vaticanus 1267. Others read “he sits.” At the beginning of the following chapter, the Bonon. manuscript and the first edition read “This, beloved” instead of “These things, beloved.”]

## CHAPTER VII

Meditating on these things with devout hearts, beloved, always remember the apostolic command, which warns everyone, saying: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition and not according to Christ, because in him dwells all the fullness of Deity bodily, and you have been filled in him” (Col. 2:8, 10).

[Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts, the first edition, and Quesnell’s edition. Other printed editions read “let him deceive you.” Shortly afterward, we have written “dwells within” instead of “dwells,” on the basis of a manuscript of St. Peter’s; this reading better agrees with what follows, “the bodily indwelling of Deity,” and also with the reading of the cited Sermon 30, chapter 3.]

He did not say “spiritually,” but “bodily,” so that we might understand the true substance of the flesh, in which the fullness of Deity dwells bodily (Eph. 1:23). The whole Church, too, is filled by this fullness, for, clinging to the head, it is the body of Christ (Col. 1:21). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXIX [Alternative numbering: XXVIII]

On the Nativity of the Lord IX.

[Note: One manuscript of St. Peter’s has the title “On the Nativity of the Lord, against the heretics.” Another manuscript of the same basilica has “Against the Jews and heretics, on the Incarnation of the Lord.”]

### SYNOPSIS

I. What peace is announced by the angels at Christ’s birth.  
II. That the mysteries have passed away only with respect to their bodily dispensation. The saying “The Lord said to my Lord” is explained.
