III. We should glory in the mercy of the one who adopts us. Christ’s infancy is to be honored.

## CHAPTER I

The greatness of the divine work exceeds and rises far above the capacity of human speech, beloved; and difficulty in speaking arises precisely where there is reason not to remain silent. For in Christ Jesus, the Son of God, what was said through the prophet pertains not only to the divine essence but also to the human nature: “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

Unless faith believes that both substances have come together in one person, speech cannot explain it. Therefore the subject of praise never runs out, because the resources of the one who praises are never sufficient. Let us rejoice, then, that we are unequal to expressing so great a sacrament of mercy and, since we cannot explain the height of our salvation, let us recognize that it is good for us to be overcome.

[Note: This reading is drawn from two manuscripts of St. Peter’s. The Bonon. manuscript and the first edition read “we cannot express such a great [mercy].” Shortly afterward, from the same manuscripts of St. Peter’s and from the Padiliron. manuscript, we have preferred “we are unable to explain,” rather than the common reading. In the Veronese manuscript: “we are unable to express.” Shortly afterward, the cited Padiliron. manuscript reads “comes closer.”]

For no one comes nearer to the knowledge of truth than one who understands that in divine matters, even if he makes great progress, there always remains for him something to seek. For one who presumes to have reached the goal toward which he is striving does not find what he sought; rather, he has failed in the act of seeking.

[Note: The manuscripts of St. Peter’s, the Bonon. manuscript, and the first edition read “if he”; shortly afterward, those same manuscripts and the Veronese manuscript read *deficit* (“fails”) instead of *defecit* (“has failed”). The Vatican Collection 5 manuscript reads “toward which it tends.” Shortly afterward, the Padiliron. manuscript reads “not sought.”]

But lest we be troubled by the narrowness of our weakness, the evangelical and prophetic voices assist us. Through them we are so kindled and instructed that, when the Word became flesh (John 1:14), we seem not so much to recall the Lord’s Nativity as to behold it present before us.

What the angel of the Lord announced to the shepherds keeping watch over their flocks has also filled our ears. And therefore we preside over the Lord’s sheep, because we preserve in the ear of our hearts words divinely uttered, as though it were being said at today’s festival as well: “Behold, I announce to you good news of great joy, which will be for all the people: for today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10).

[Note: We supplied “of the Lord” from two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and from the Veronese and Padiliron. manuscripts.]

To the summit of this proclamation is added the rejoicing of innumerable angels, so that the testimony might be made more excellent, with the multitude of the heavenly host singing together in God’s honor with one blessing: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

[Note: The manuscripts of St. Peter’s, the Bonon. manuscript, and the first edition read “with one voice.” Shortly afterward, those same manuscripts, together with the Veronese and Padiliron. manuscripts, read “glory in the highest.”]

The infancy of Christ, born from the Virgin Mother, is therefore the glory of God, and the restoration of the human race is rightly referred in praise to its author. For the angel Gabriel, sent by God to the blessed Mary, had himself said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

[Note: The common editions read “he himself.” We have emended this with the first edition, on the basis of the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, the Veronese and Bonon. manuscripts, and the Padiliron. manuscript. Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscripts of later Collections 4 and 5 read *conditur* (“is established”) instead of *conceditur* (“is granted”).]

On earth, however, that peace is granted which makes people of good will. For by the same Spirit through whom Christ is born from the inward parts of the undefiled mother, the Christian is reborn from the womb of holy Church. The Christian possesses true peace when he is not separated from God’s will and delights only in those things that God loves.

[Note: In the first edition, a period is placed after the word “Christian,” and the following sentence is read: “Let no one doubt that his true peace consists in not being separated from God’s will and in delighting only in those things that God loves.” In the Padiliron. manuscript: “whose true peace consists in God’s will, if he does not doubt that it consists in those things alone which …”]

## CHAPTER II

Celebrating, therefore, beloved, the Lord’s birthday, which has been chosen from all the days of past ages, although the dispensation of bodily actions has passed, just as it had been ordained by the eternal plan, and the whole humility of the Redeemer has been raised into the glory of the Father’s majesty, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2:10–11), nevertheless we continually adore the saving Virgin’s childbirth. We revere the inseparable union of the Word and flesh lying in the manger no less than when it sits on the throne of the Father’s sublimity.

[Note: Three manuscripts and the first edition read “of eternal majesty.” But the scriptural text quoted below has “in the glory of God the Father”; shortly afterward it reads “of the Father’s exaltedness.”]

[Note: The Veronese and Padiliron. manuscripts add “Christ,” as in St. Paul.]

For the unchangeable Deity, although it contained within itself both its own splendor and its power, was nevertheless not absent from the one being born merely because it was not visible to human eyes. Thus, through the unprecedented beginnings of a true human being, the one who was both Lord and son of King David might be recognized. For he himself sings through the prophetic Spirit, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

By this testimony, as the Gospel reports, the impiety of the Jews was refuted. For when Jesus asked the Jews whose son they said Christ was, and they answered, “David’s,” the Lord immediately exposed their blindness and said: “How, then, does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying: ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’?” (Matt. 22:43).

You have closed the way of understanding against yourselves, O Jews. While you look only upon the nature of flesh, you have deprived yourselves of the whole light of truth. Expecting, according to the fabulous inventions of your belief, a son of David from bodily descent alone, and placing your hope in a mere human being, you rejected God the Son of God, so that what it is glorious for us to confess could not benefit you.

For when we are asked whose son Christ is, we confess with the Apostle’s voice that he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:2); and from the very beginning of the Gospel proclamation we are instructed by reading: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David” (Matt. 1:1).

[Note: Two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, another Padiliron. manuscript, and the Cassino manuscript read “to confess” instead of “for us to profess.”]

But we are distinguished from your impiety because the one whom we know to have been born as a human being from David’s line, we believe to be, insofar as the Word became flesh (John 1:14), coeternal God with God the Father.

[Note: We have restored the syntax found in editions before Quesnell, as well as in our manuscripts. Quesnell deleted *eumdem* (“the same one”) here and moved it before the word “God.” Shortly afterward, the Padiliron. manuscript reads “if you were to hear with ears that are not deaf.”]

Therefore, if you understood the dignity of your name, O Israel, and did not pass through the prophetic pronouncements with a blinded heart, Isaiah would disclose the evangelical truth to you, and you would hear, not deafly, him speaking by divine inspiration: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23).

[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “will conceive”; editions before Quesnell and some manuscripts read “he will be called” instead of “they will call.”]

If you did not see him in so precise a meaning of the sacred name, you would at least have learned from David’s words not to deny, contrary to the testimony of the New and Old Testaments, that Jesus Christ is the son of David—him whom you do not confess as David’s Lord.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript likewise reads “whom you would confess.”]

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, beloved, since through the ineffable grace of God the Church of the faithful among the Gentiles has obtained what the synagogue of the carnal Jews did not deserve, as David says: “The Lord has made his salvation known; in the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. 97:2); and as Isaiah likewise proclaims: “The people who sat in darkness have seen a great light; light has risen for those who dwelt in the region and shadow of death” (Isa. 9:2); and again: “Nations that did not know you shall call upon you, and peoples who did not know you shall flee to you” (Isa. 55:5):

[Note: The manuscripts of St. Peter’s, the Bonon. manuscript, and the first edition read “who do not know you.”]

let us rejoice in the day of our salvation. Through the New Testament we have been taken into fellowship with the one to whom the Father says through the prophet: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:7). Let us glory in the mercy of the one who adopts us, because, as the Apostle says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

[Note: The manuscripts of St. Peter’s read “that the will of so great a Father may be fulfilled by adopted sons.”]

For it is worthy and fitting that the will of the Father who bears witness should be fulfilled by sons of adoption. And since the Apostle says, “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him” (Rom. 8:3), let those who are to be heirs of future glory be fellow participants in Christ’s humility.

[Note: Quesnell, with Rainaud, read “of future glory.” We have emended the text on the basis of the other editions and our manuscripts; among them, only the manuscripts of the later Collections 4 and 5 prefer both forms, “of the future” and “of future glory.”]

Let the Lord be honored in his infancy. Let his bodily beginnings and growth not be reckoned an injury to his Deity, because our nature neither added anything to nor diminished anything from the unchangeable nature. Rather, he who deigned to become like human beings in the likeness of sinful flesh remains equal to the Father in the unity of Deity.

[Note: The Padiliron. manuscript supports this reading. The common text reads “in the likeness.”]

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXX [Alternative numbering: XXXI]

On the Nativity of the Lord X.

### SYNOPSIS

I. Both generations of Christ are ineffable.  
II. The various errors concerning the incarnation of the Word.  
III. Christ dwelt bodily with the fullness of Deity.  
IV. Christ’s conception is unique among all conceptions.  
V. The properties of both natures in Christ are examined.  
VI. Christ, consubstantial with the Father and with his mother, saves us through both.  
VII. The one faith of Christ saves the faithful of every age. Why Christ’s genealogy differs in Matthew and Luke.

## CHAPTER I

Often, as you know, beloved, we have devoted to you a salutary discourse on the excellence of today’s festival solemnity; and we do not doubt that the power of divine goodness has so shone in your hearts that what has been implanted in you by faith has also been grasped by understanding.

[Note: Two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and the first edition read “concerning the excellence of today’s most exalted festival solemnity.”]

But because the birth of our Lord and Savior, not only according to his Deity from the Father but also according to the flesh from his mother, so exceeds the capacity of human speech that the saying “Who shall recount his generation?” (Isa. 53:8) is rightly referred to both, the very fact that it cannot be adequately explained always supplies material for discourse—not because it is permissible to hold differing opinions, but because no language can suffice for the dignity of the subject.

Therefore, the greatness of the sacrament, arranged before the eternal ages for the salvation of the human race and disclosed at the end of the ages, allows nothing to be taken away from its integrity and nothing to be added to it.

[Note: Editions before Quesnell, together with some of our manuscripts, read “nor to be increased.” Quesnell’s reading is supported by two manuscripts of St. Peter’s.]

Just as it does not lose what belongs to it, so it does not take on what belongs to another. But many, following their own opinions and being readier to teach what they had not yet understood than to learn it, “have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith,” as the Apostle says (1 Tim. 1:19). I shall briefly touch upon their perverse and mutually conflicting views, so that, once the darkness of error has been distinguished from the light of truth, the divine benefits may both be honored religiously and human falsehoods avoided knowingly.

[Note: We have emended the text on the basis of five manuscripts and the first edition. Others read “worldly.”]

## CHAPTER II

Some people, relying upon those details of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ that demonstrated him to be truly the son of a human being, believed him to be nothing more than a human being’s son. They did not think Deity should be attributed to him, since his infant beginnings, bodily growth, and the condition of his sufferings even unto death on the cross had shown him to be no different from other mortals.

[Note: One manuscript of St. Peter’s reads “than a human being they believed.” The Bonon. manuscript and the first edition read “they believed.” Shortly afterward, we have substituted “they themselves” for “they,” on the basis of three of our manuscripts and the first edition. Quesnell noted that some editions read “dignity” instead of “Deity”; the first edition and our manuscripts likewise read “Deity.”]

Others, however, moved by wonder at his powers and recognizing that the novelty of his origin and the power of his words and deeds belonged to the divine nature, thought that there was nothing of our substance in him. They held that everything pertaining to bodily action and form had either arisen from matter of a higher kind or possessed an assumed appearance of flesh, so that the senses of those who saw and touched him would be deceived by an illusory image.

Among some who went astray there was also the belief that they could assert that something from the very substance of the Word had been changed into flesh, and that Jesus, born from the Virgin Mary, possessed nothing of his mother’s nature. Rather, both what was God and what was human would have belonged to what is the Word, so that in Christ humanity would be false through diversity of substance, and divinity would not be true because it lacked mutability.

[Note: Some editions before Quesnell, together with Vatican Collection 5, read: “and that Jesus, born from Mary the Virgin, possessed nothing of his mother’s nature.” Other manuscripts and the first edition have the reading found in the text.]

## CHAPTER III

The catholic faith long ago crushed these and other impieties, conceived through diabolical inspiration and poured out through vessels of destruction to the harm of many. God is both its teacher and its helper. The Holy Spirit exhorts and instructs us through the testimony of the Law, the prophecies of the prophets, the evangelical trumpet, and apostolic teaching, so that we may believe firmly and intelligently that, as blessed John says, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

[Note: We have emended the text on the basis of two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, another Bonon. manuscript, and the first edition. Others read “to whom God belongs.” Shortly afterward, on the basis of the same manuscripts, another Vatican manuscript, and the first edition, we have added “we” after the word “instructing.”]

He dwelt among us, certainly among those whom the divinity of the Word joined to itself, whose flesh, taken from the Virgin’s womb, is our flesh. If that flesh were not from our nature—that is, truly human—the Word made flesh would not have dwelt among us. But he dwelt among us because he made the nature of our body his own, with Wisdom building a house for himself (Prov. 9:1), not from just any material, but from a substance properly our own. Its assumption was made manifest when it was said: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

[Note: The first edition reads “to this most sacred assertion.”]

The teaching of blessed Paul the Apostle also agrees with this most sacred proclamation. He says: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ, because in him dwells all the fullness of Deity bodily, and you have been filled in him” (Col. 2:8–10).

[Note: We have emended the text on the basis of two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and two Vatican manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5; it agrees with the reading of Sermon 28, chapter 7. The printed editions read “in Christ dwells.”]

The whole Deity therefore fills the whole body. Just as nothing is lacking from that majesty by whose indwelling the dwelling-place is filled, so nothing is lacking from the body that is not filled by its inhabitant.

[Note: Two manuscripts of St. Peter’s read “from that majesty,” and shortly afterward “from the body.”]

But when it is said, “You have been filled in him,” our nature is certainly signified: we are the ones to whom that fullness would not pertain unless the Word of God had united to himself both a soul and a body of our race.

## CHAPTER IV
It must certainly be acknowledged, beloved, and confessed with all our heart, that this generation by which both the Word and flesh—that is, God and man—become one Son of God and one Christ, surpasses every origin of human creation. For neither Adam’s formation from the clay of the earth, nor Eve’s fashioning from the man’s flesh (Gen. II, 22), nor the creation of the rest of humanity through the union of the two sexes can be compared with the birth of Jesus Christ.

Abraham, though old, fathered the heir of the divine promise, and Sarah, barren beyond the years of fertility, conceived (Gen. XXI, 2). Jacob was loved by God before he was born, and, by preceding grace, was distinguished in his voluntary actions from the shaggy roughness of his twin brother (Gen. XXV, 25; Malach. I, 3; Rom. IX, 13). To Jeremiah it is said: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. I, 5). Anna, long deprived of fertility, gave birth to the prophet Samuel, whom she was to offer to God (I Reg. I, 20), so that she might be renowned both for her childbirth and for her vow. The priest Zechariah received from the barren Elizabeth a holy offspring (Luke I, 24), and John, who was destined to be Christ’s forerunner, received the prophetic spirit within his mother’s womb; while still unborn, he revealed the Lord’s mother by the sign of a hidden exultation (ibid., 44).

> [Note: [Col. 0232D] We restored *received* from four manuscripts and the first edition in place of *had received*, which was read in the other printed editions and in manuscript Collection 5; the former better agrees with the preceding verbs, “conceived,” “gave birth,” and “received.” For the same reason, from two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and the first edition we soon restored *revealed* in place of *had revealed*.]

All these things are great and filled with the miracles of divine works; but their very multitude makes them more restrained in their wonder.

> [Note: [Col. 0232D] Printed editions before Quesnell read “more immoderately.”]

The birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, however, surpasses all understanding and transcends every example. Nor can anything equal it, since it is unique among all things.

> [Note: [Col. 0232D] In the Vatican manuscripts of the later collections and in the editions before Quesnell, *any* is read. On the authority of two manuscripts of St. Peter’s we placed *anything*, and thereafter, on their authority, as well as that of two other Vatican manuscripts and the first edition, we wrote *among all*, that is, among all examples, in place of *among everyone*.]

> [Note: [Col. 0232D] The printed editions read: “For to the chosen Virgin from the seed,” etc. We judged the reading of the manuscripts of St. Peter’s better; the Casinensis codex seems to approach it: “To the chosen Virgin, and now from the seed.”]

To the chosen Virgin, formerly promised through prophetic utterances and mystical signs as descended from the seed of Abraham and from the root of Jesse, the archangel announces blessed fertility without injury to her modesty—a sacred virginity that would be violated neither by conception nor by childbirth. For when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke I, 35), the immutable Word of God assumed human flesh from her undefiled body and made it his own dwelling. This flesh would draw no contamination from carnal desire, yet would possess nothing lacking from all that belongs to the nature of soul and body.

## CHAPTER V

> [Note: [Col. 0232D] Accordingly, we restored the adverb *therefore* from some manuscripts and the first edition. Immediately afterward, two manuscripts of St. Peter’s repeat *withdraw* in place of *go*.]

Let the monstrous forms of heretical opinions withdraw far away and go into their own darkness, together with the sacrileges of deranged falsehoods. Let us adore both the Word in Christ the man and Christ the man in the Word, as the multitude of heaven exulting in the praise of God and the shepherds instructed by angels have taught us, having learned the realities of both natures.

For if, as the Apostle says, “the one who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17), how much more is the Word made flesh one Christ? In him there is nothing belonging to one nature that is not also possessed by both.

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] This is the reading of our manuscripts and Quesnellus. Other printed editions have *in counsels*. Shortly afterward, where the printed editions read *manifestly*, Quesnellus wrote *manifest*, which we also found in our manuscripts and have retained.]

Let us not therefore grow weak in the plan of God’s mercy, which both reforms us to innocence and restores us to life. Nor, because in our Savior we clearly recognize signs of a twofold nature, should we doubt either the truth of the flesh in the glory of God or the majesty of the Godhead in the humility of man.

The same one is in the form of God who took the form of a servant.

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter’s read: “The same man is in the form of God who received the form of a servant.” *Received* is also found in two Vatican manuscripts.]

The same one remains incorporeal while assuming a body. The same one is inviolable in his own power and subject to suffering in our weakness. The same one is not separated from the Father’s throne and was crucified on the wood by the ungodly. The same one ascended above the heights of heaven as victor over death and does not abandon the universal Church until the consummation of the age. Finally, the same one will come in the very flesh in which he ascended; just as he endured the judgment of the ungodly, so he will judge the deeds of all mortals.

Therefore, not to linger over many testimonies, one passage from the Gospel of blessed John is sufficient, in which our Lord himself says:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming—and now is—when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself; and he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John V, 25).

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] Three manuscripts add *these*; the first edition, together with the manuscript of Bon., has *this*.]

Thus, in a single statement, he showed that the same one is both the Son of God and the Son of Man.

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] Quesnellus inserted the word *the same*, which we found in the first edition and in some manuscripts.]

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] We restored *who* in place of *because* from the first edition and two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, as well as from one Vatican manuscript and the Bononian manuscript.]

From this it is evident how we ought to believe in Christ the Lord in the unity of his person: he who, although he is the Son of God through whom we were made, also became the Son of Man through the assumption of flesh, so that he might die, as the Apostle says, “for our sins,” and rise “for our justification” (Rom. IV, 25).

## CHAPTER VI

This confession, beloved, fears no contradictions and yields to no errors.

> [Note: [Col. 0233D] In four manuscripts and the first edition, *found*. We have retained the commonly received reading, which we also found in other, even ancient, manuscripts, because the confession of faith concerning Christ did indeed encounter many contradictions, but feared none.]

For we recognize the mercy of God promised from the beginning and prepared before the ages, through which alone the chains of human captivity could be broken—chains with which the evil counselor, the author of sin, had bound the first man and all his posterity, claiming the enslaved offspring for himself by the prior claim of original guilt.

> [Note: [Col. 0234D] Quesnellus added the word *alone* from the manuscripts of Corb. and Gaudiival. We found the same reading in four of our manuscripts and in the first edition. Later, Quesnellus accepted *evil counselor*, which we found in some manuscripts and in the first edition. Other printed editions and the manuscript of St. Peter’s read *evil persuader*.]

Since this chiefly benefits the justification of human beings—that the Only-Begotten of God also deigned to be the Son of Man, so that, as God, he might be *homoousios* with the Father, that is, “of one substance,” and, as true man, might also be consubstantial according to the flesh with his mother—we rejoice in both, because we are saved by both and by neither one separately. We divide neither the visible from the invisible, nor the corporeal from the incorporeal, nor the passible from the impassible, nor the tangible from the intangible, nor the form of a servant from the form of God.

> [Note: [Col. 0234D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s reads *of man*.]

For although one remains from eternity and the other began in time, they nevertheless came together into one unity and can have neither separation nor an end. The exalting and exalted, the glorifying and glorified, adhered so closely to one another that

> [Note: [Col. 0234D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter’s read *inhaerent* (“adhere”).]

that, whether in omnipotence or in humiliation, the divine in Christ is not without the human, nor the human without the divine.

## CHAPTER VII

> [Note: [Col. 0234D] We inserted the adjective *true* from manuscripts of St. Peter’s, one Bononian manuscript, and the first edition.]

Believing this, beloved, we are true Christians, true Israelites, and truly adopted into fellowship with the children of God. For all the saints who preceded the time of our Savior were justified by this faith and, through this mystery, became the body of Christ, awaiting the universal redemption of believers in the seed of Abraham, concerning whom the Apostle says:

> “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “And to your seed,” which is Christ (Gal. III, 16).

> [Note: [Col. 0234D] Three manuscripts and the first edition read *which is*. Shortly afterward, *percucurrit* (“ran through”) in place of *percurrit* (“runs through”) is found in two of our manuscripts and in the first edition.]

For this reason the evangelist Matthew, in order to show that the promise made to Abraham had been fulfilled in Christ, traverses the order of the generations and demonstrates in whom the blessing appointed for all nations had been established. The evangelist Luke likewise traced the sequence of his lineage upward from the Lord’s birth itself (Luke III, 23), so that he might teach that even the ages preceding the Flood were connected with this mystery and that all the stages of succession from the beginning had stretched toward him in whom alone the salvation of all was found.

> [Note: [Col. 0234D] Thus in two manuscripts of St. Peter’s. Others read *praevenerunt* (“preceded”) in place of *praevenerant* (“had preceded”). Later, in two manuscripts and the first edition, *salvation might be* is found.]

Therefore it must not be doubted that, apart from Christ, there is no other name given under heaven among human beings by which we must be saved (Acts IV, 5). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXI [Another numbering: XXX]

## On the Solemnity of the Epiphany of Our Lord Jesus Christ I

### Summary

I. Christ, born, desires to be acknowledged by all; he gives the sign of the star and at the same time the gift of understanding and seeking.

II. Herod rages against Christ in vain. The Magi profess their faith through gifts.

III. Christ turns Herod’s wickedness toward the good of the infants. What virtues we ought to imitate in the infant God.

## CHAPTER I

On the day immediately following the day on which undefiled virginity gave birth to the Savior of the human race,

> [Note: [Col. 0235C] Printed editions have *on the next day*, as do some manuscripts. Two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and manuscripts 1 and 2 of the collections have *immediately*. We judged this reading preferable. The feast of the Lord’s Nativity, which is twelve days distant from the Epiphany, could apparently be called “celebrated immediately,” but not “celebrated on the next day.” In the following sermon Leo says, in chapter 1: “After a brief interval of time following the solemnity of Christ’s Nativity, the feast of his manifestation has dawned.” The correction is confirmed by the old edition of Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, which has “On the day immediately following the feast,” or, in Surius’s edition, “Immediately after the day was celebrated.” In this Homiliary one also finds shortly afterward “Mary’s undefiled virginity,” as in the canon of the Mass of the Lord’s Nativity, discussed in the following note.]

the venerable feast of the Epiphany gives us, beloved, a continuation of our joys, so that amid the neighboring mysteries of kindred solemnities the vigor of our exultation and the fervor of our faith may not grow cold.

> [Note: [Col. 0235C] In the canon of the Mass of the Lord’s Nativity: “Celebrating the most sacred day on which the undefiled virginity of blessed Mary gave the Savior to this world.” Nearly the same words occur, and in addition the word *most sacred*, which is especially familiar to Leo. In chapter 4 of the following sermon this very day is called “most sacred.” It therefore appears probable—and this is confirmed elsewhere—that many things in ecclesiastical offices and rites, especially in the prefaces and the canon, were either composed or improved by our Leo. Quesnellus.]

For what had already been revealed to the whole world, while the Mediator between God and humanity was still confined to a little town, concerns the salvation of all human beings.

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] The Vercelli manuscript reads *concerned*. Shortly afterward, the first edition has *the infancy of the Savior and Mediator*.]

Although he had chosen the Israelite people, and within that people a single family, from which he would assume the nature of universal humanity, he nevertheless did not wish the beginnings of his birth to remain hidden within the narrow confines of his mother’s dwelling. Rather, he immediately desired to be acknowledged by all—he who had deigned to be born for all.

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] We added the preposition *for* from the manuscripts of St. Peter’s and Vercelli.]

Therefore, in the region of the East, a star of new brightness appeared to three Magi. More radiant than the other stars and more beautiful than they, it easily turned the eyes and minds of those who looked upon it toward itself, so that it might immediately be understood that something was intended by what appeared so unusual.

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] Others read *seemed*. Later, in place of *sought out*, which corresponds to the preceding verb “to seek,” we preferred the reading from manuscripts of St. Peter’s and the first edition: *inquired after*. Others have *requested*.]

Thus the sign gave understanding to those who observed it, and what caused itself to be understood caused itself to be sought; once sought, it offered itself to be found.

## CHAPTER II

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] The Vercelli manuscript adds *therefore*.]

The three men followed the guidance of the heavenly light, accompanying with attentive contemplation the indication of the preceding radiance. They were led by the splendor of grace to recognition of the truth, and by human reasoning judged that the birth of the king signified to them should be sought in a royal city.

But the one who had assumed the form of a servant and had come not to judge but to be judged chose Bethlehem for his birth and Jerusalem for his passion.

Herod, hearing that the ruler of the Jews had been born, was terrified, suspecting a successor; and, plotting the death of the author of salvation, he falsely promised obedience.

> [Note: [Col. 0235D] Quesnellus has *promises*, in agreement with manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5. We retained the reading of the earlier editions, which is preferred by the lectionaries of St. Peter’s, the Vercelli manuscript, and the older collections.]

How happy he would have been if he had imitated the faith of the Magi and had turned to religion what he was preparing as a fraud!

O blind wickedness of foolish rivalry, which thinks that the divine plan can be disturbed by your frenzy!

> [Note: [Col. 0236C] Four Vatican manuscripts, the Bononian manuscript, and the first edition give *what?* as a question. We retained the reading of the older codices and editions.]

The Lord of the world does not seek a temporal kingdom, for he grants an eternal one. Why do you attempt to overturn the unchangeable order of appointed events and anticipate another person’s crime?

Christ’s death does not belong to your time. The Gospel must first be established, the kingdom of God must first be preached, healings must first be granted, and miracles must first be performed. Why do you wish what will belong to another’s work to become your crime? Why, when your crime will achieve no result, do you rush headlong into the guilt of mere intention?

You accomplish nothing by this plot; you achieve nothing. He who was born by his own will will die by the power of his own choice.

The Magi therefore fulfill their desire and, with the same star leading them, arrive at the child Lord Jesus Christ. They adore the Word in the flesh, wisdom in infancy, power in weakness, and the Lord of majesty in the reality of humanity. And, so that they might manifest the mystery of their faith and understanding, they profess through gifts what they believe in their hearts.

They offer frankincense to God, myrrh to the man, and gold to the king, knowingly venerating the divine and human nature in unity. For although each nature possessed its own properties, what was proper to the substances was not different in authority.

> [Note: [Col. 0236C–D] We compared four lectionaries, two of St. Peter’s, one Vercelli manuscript, another Venetian manuscript, Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, and copies of all five collections. Specifically, the first edition, together with manuscripts of Collections 3 and 4, has *knowingly*. The readings *knowing* and *venerable* are found without difficulty in the Venetian manuscript, Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, and Quesnellus’s first edition. The Vercelli manuscript incorrectly has *knowing and venerating*. We retained *knowingly and venerating* with the other editions and manuscripts. Later, in place of *in unity*, two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and manuscripts of Collection 2 have *in the man*. We judged that the reading of all the other manuscripts and editions should not be abandoned, since the meaning, soon to be explained by the words *in unity*, agrees perfectly with it. Finally, the printed editions, together with only the manuscripts of Collection 5, had *in person* in place of *in power*. We inserted *in power* from all the lectionaries and the other collections, as well as Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary; this is also approved by the sense of the entire context, which is as follows: When the Magi offered frankincense to God, they venerated the divine nature; when they offered myrrh to the man, the human nature; but when they offered gold to the king, they venerated both natures together in unity. For although each nature has its own properties, royal dignity, or authority, belonged to Christ both as God and as man. Therefore, what was proper to the substances—that is, the natures—was not different in authority. Other testimonies of Leo explain this understanding. Thus, in Sermon 21, chapter 2: “The true God and the true man are joined into one Lord”; and in Sermon 46, chapter 1: “The Son of God and likewise the Son of Man is one Lord.”]

## CHAPTER III

When the Magi had returned to their own region and Jesus had been transferred to Egypt at the divine warning, Herod’s madness flared up in vain in his schemes.

> [Note: [Col. 0237D] The printed editions, together with manuscripts of the later collections, have *frustrated*. The reading of the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, Vercelli, and Venice appeared better.]

He orders all the boys in Bethlehem to be killed, and, because he does not know which infant he fears, he directs a general sentence against the entire suspected age.

> [Note: [Col. 0237D] Thus from two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, the first edition, and codices of Collections 2, 3, and 4. The printed editions, together with manuscripts of Collections 1 and 5 and the Vercelli and Venetian lectionaries, read *cruelty*. Shortly afterward, *removed* in place of *removes* occurs in the Bononian manuscript and the first edition. Later, the Vercelli manuscript has *bestowed* in place of *bestows*.]

But what the impious king removes from the world, Christ inserts into heaven; and to those for whom he had not yet granted redemption through his blood, he already bestows the dignity of martyrdom.

Therefore, beloved, raise your faithful spirits toward the flashing grace of everlasting light, and, venerating the mysteries bestowed for human salvation, submit your devotion to the things accomplished for you.

> [Note: [Col. 0237D] Printed editions read “venerating the mysteries of grace bestowed for human salvation.” The Vatican manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5, together with the Venetian lectionary, omit *grace*. We followed the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, Vercelli, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary.]

Love the purity of chastity, because Christ is the son of virginity.

> [Note: [Col. 0238D] Quesnellus noted in the margin: “Others: *of the Virgin*,” and this is indeed found in the Venetian manuscript of St. Mark’s.]

Abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul (I Peter II, 11), just as the blessed Apostle who is present among us exhorts us in his own words, as we read.

Be children in malice (I Cor. XIV, 20), because the Lord of glory conformed himself to the infancy of mortals. Pursue the humility which the Son of God deigned to teach his disciples (Matt. XI, 29). Clothe yourselves with the virtue of patience, by which you may gain your souls; for he who is the redemption of all is himself the strength of all.

Set your minds on the things above, not on the things upon the earth (Col. III, 2). Walk steadfastly along the way of truth and life. Let not earthly things hinder you, since heavenly things have been prepared for you, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXII [Another numbering: XXXI]

## On the Solemnity of the Epiphany II

### Summary

I. Herod announces Christ, born for the world, while attempting to remove him from the world. Christ, exiled in Egypt, prepares Egypt for salvation.

II. How much we owe God is demonstrated by the blindness of the Jews, who did not recognize Christ in order to crucify him.

III. The ignorance of the infants is more blessed than the knowledge of the Jewish priests. Christ consecrates the infancy of little children through his own infancy.

VI. The calling of the Magi is the beginning of our own calling. Everyone ought to imitate their gifts, so that we may cooperate with Christ as he works our salvation.

## CHAPTER I

“Rejoice in the Lord, beloved; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV, 1), for after a brief interval of time following the solemnity of Christ’s birth, the feast of his manifestation has dawned; and the one whom the Virgin bore on that day was acknowledged by the world on this day.

> [Note: [Col. 0238D] The printed editions insert the particle *also*, which we deleted with the aid of the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, Bon., and Verona, and of the first edition.]

For the Word made flesh (John I, 14) so ordered the beginnings of his assumption of our nature that Jesus, once born, would be manifest to believers and hidden from persecutors.

Even then, therefore, “the heavens declared the glory of God” (Ps. XVIII, 1), and “the sound of the truth went out into all the earth” (Rom. X, 18), when an army of angels appeared to the shepherds as the herald of the Savior’s birth (Luke II, 13), and a preceding star led the Magi to adore him (Matt. II, 2). Thus, from the rising of the sun to its setting, the birth of the true king shone forth: the kingdoms of the East learned the truth of the event through the Magi, and the Roman Empire did not remain unaware of it.

For even Herod’s savagery, which desired to extinguish the beginning of the king he suspected, unknowingly served this dispensation. While intent upon a brutal crime and pursuing an unknown child through the indiscriminate slaughter of infants, he caused the birth of the heavenly Ruler, announced from heaven, to be proclaimed everywhere by a more famous report—one made more readily and diligently repeated both by the novelty of the heavenly sign and by the impiety of the bloodiest persecutor.

> [Note: [Col. 0238D] The manuscripts of St. Peter’s and the first edition have *of the sign*.]

Then the Savior was brought into Egypt, so that a people devoted to ancient errors might already be called, through hidden grace, to salvation that was near; and the people that had not yet expelled superstition from its mind might already receive the truth as a guest.

> [Note: [Col. 0238D] Thus in five of Quesnellus’s manuscripts and in our more excellent manuscripts of St. Peter’s, as well as in the manuscripts of Casin., Veron., Casanat., and Barber. Others in the editions before Quesnellus and in certain manuscripts read *might be marked*. The first edition has, in place of “already to salvation that was near,” “already near to salvation”; likewise in a manuscript of St. Peter’s, where only *already* is omitted. Shortly afterward, a manuscript of St. Peter’s has *might receive* in place of *might recover*.]

## CHAPTER II

With good reason, therefore, beloved, this day consecrated by the Lord’s manifestation has obtained a special dignity throughout the world. It ought to shine in our hearts with a worthy splendor, so that we may venerate the order of events not only by believing but also by understanding.

For how great a thanksgiving we owe the Lord for the illumination of the nations is proved by the blindness of the Jews.

> [Note: [Col. 0238D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s reads *blindness*, and likewise in chapter 4.]

What indeed was so blind, what so estranged from the light, as those Israelite priests and scribes? When the Magi asked, and Herod inquired where Christ was to be born according to the testimony of the Scriptures (Matt. II, 4), they answered from the prophetic utterance what the star from heaven had indicated.

The star could certainly have led the Magi by its sign directly to the child’s cradle, bypassing Jerusalem, as it later did, unless this had served to refute the Jews’ stubbornness, so that the Savior’s birth might become known not only through the guidance of the star but also through the Jews’ own declaration.

> [Note: [Col. 0238D] In the same manuscript, *their stubbornness*. Shortly before, the Veronese manuscript has *to confound* in place of *to refute*.]

Thus the prophetic word was already passing over to instruct the nations, and the hearts of foreigners were learning of Christ, foretold by ancient oracles, while the unbelief of the Jews proclaimed the truth with its mouth and retained falsehood in its heart.

For they were unwilling to recognize with their eyes the one whom they had identified from the sacred books:

> [Note: [Col. 0239D] Thus from the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, to which the Vatican manuscript of Collection 5 also agrees, where *they indicated* is read. Others have *they were indicating*.]

so that the one whom they did not adore in the humility of infancy they might later crucify, shining in the sublimity of his powers.

## CHAPTER III

What sort of knowledge is this in you, Jews—so uninstructed and so unlearned a doctrine?

When asked where Christ was to be born (Matt. II, 4), you truthfully and accurately say what you have read: “In Bethlehem of Judea” (ibid., 5). For it is written through the prophet:

> “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah. For from you will go forth a ruler who will govern my people Israel” (Micah V, 2).

> [Note: [Col. 0239D] The first edition and the Veronese manuscript have *among the rulers*. Shortly afterward, that edition, together with the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, Vercelli, and Bon., has *a ruler will go forth* in place of *a prince will go forth*.]

The angels announced this ruler’s birth to the shepherds (Luke II, 13), and the shepherds announced it to you (Matt. II, 2). The distant nations of the Eastern peoples learned of this ruler’s birth through the extraordinary brightness of the new star. And, lest they doubt the birthplace of the king who had been born, your learning revealed what the star did not teach.

Why do you obstruct the way that you open to others? Why does doubt remain in your unbelief regarding what becomes clear through your own answer? You point out the place of the birth from the testimony of the Scriptures; you recognize the time of his presence from the witness of heaven and earth; and yet, where Herod’s spirit flared up to persecute him, there your understanding hardened against belief.

More blessed, then, was the ignorance of the infants whom the persecutor killed (Matt. II, 16) than your knowledge, which he consulted in his own disturbance.

You were unwilling to receive the kingdom of the one whose town you were able to point out. They were able to die for the one whom they were not yet able to confess.

> [Note: [Col. 0239D] Two manuscripts and the first edition have *were not able*. Shortly afterward, from ten of our manuscripts and the first edition we restored *Thus Christ* in place of *Therefore Christ*. Moreover, two Vatican manuscripts and the first edition have *so that no* in place of *lest any*. Finally, *exercised* rather than *exerted* is found in the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, Bon., Vercelli, and the first edition.]

Thus Christ, so that no period of his life might be without a miracle, silently exercised the power of the Word before the use of speech. As though he were already saying, “Let the little children come to me, for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 14), he crowned infants with a new glory and consecrated the beginnings of little children from his own beginnings, so that it might be learned that no human being is incapable of the divine mystery, since even that age was suited to the glory of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER IV

Let us therefore recognize in the Magi, worshipers of Christ, the first fruits of our calling and faith, and let us celebrate with exultant hearts the beginnings of blessed hope.

> [Note: [Col. 0239D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s reads *adoring Christ*.]

From that time onward we began to enter into an eternal inheritance; from that time the Scriptures’ secrets, speaking of Christ, were opened to us; and the truth, which the blindness of the Jews does not receive, brought its light to all nations.

Therefore let us honor the most sacred day on which the author of our salvation appeared. The one whom the Magi venerated as an infant in the cradle, let us adore as almighty in heaven.

And just as they offered the Lord mystical kinds of gifts from their treasures, so let us bring forth from our hearts what is worthy of God. For although he himself is the giver of all good things, he nevertheless seeks the fruit of our own diligence. The kingdom of heaven does not come to those who sleep, but to those who labor and keep watch in God’s commandments, so that, if we do not render his gifts ineffective, through the things he has given we may deserve to receive what he promised.

> [Note: [Col. 0239D–0240D] Thus in seven of our manuscripts. The printed editions have *his gift, ineffective*. Shortly afterward, the manuscript of St. Peter’s and one Vatican manuscript have *which he promised* in place of *what he promised*.]

Therefore we exhort your charity to abstain from every evil work and pursue the things that are chaste and just (Rom. XIII, 22). For the children of light must cast away the works of darkness. Accordingly, avoid hatred, cast away lies, destroy pride through humility, cast off avarice, and love generosity.

> [Note: [Col. 0240D] The editions before Quesnellus have “destroy avarice through generosity.” Our manuscripts of Collections 3, 4, and 5 likewise have that reading. Yet we found the reading inserted by Quesnellus in two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, in the Patavine lectionary of the Hermit Fathers, in the Veronese manuscript, and in the manuscripts of Collections 1 and 2. Later, *of blessings* rather than *of beatitudes* is found in four of our manuscripts and in the first edition. The manuscript of St. Peter’s has *may they deserve* in place of *may we deserve*.]

For it is fitting that the members agree with their head, so that we may deserve to share in the promised blessedness, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXIII [Another numbering: XXXII]

## On the Solemnity of the Epiphany III

### Summary

I. Christ came to free the world when all were shut up under sin, so that no one might glory in his own merits.

II. Why was he born under Herod, and why was he shown by a star? Grace was working inwardly so that the sign might be understood and Christ sought.

III. How great was the blindness of the Jews at Christ’s birth. The calling of the nations fulfills the promise made to Abraham.

IV. Why did the Magi return by another road after adoring Christ? Why did Christ wish to be transferred into Egypt?

V. This feast must be celebrated with thanksgiving, since it contains the first fruits of the calling of the nations. How shall we imitate the star?

## CHAPTER I

Although I know, beloved, that the reason for today’s feast is not hidden from your holiness and that the Gospel discourse has disclosed it to you according to custom, nevertheless, so that you may lack none of the service I owe you, I shall dare to speak about the same matter as the Lord grants me.

Thus, in our common joy, the devotion of all may be more religious in proportion as the solemnity has been more fully understood by everyone.

> [Note: [Col. 0240D] Thus from the manuscript of St. Peter’s. Elsewhere: “so that nothing of our duty may be lacking.”]

For the providence of God’s mercy, having determined to come to the aid of the perishing world in the final times, preordained the salvation of all nations in Christ, so that, since impious error had long turned all nations away from the worship of the true God and Israel itself, the particular people of God, had almost entirely fallen away from the institutions of the Law, he might have mercy on all, all having been shut up under sin (Rom. XI, 32).

For with justice failing everywhere and the whole world sinking into vanity and wickedness, unless divine power delayed its judgment, the whole human race would have received the sentence of condemnation. But wrath was transferred into pardon; and, so that the greatness of the grace to be brought forth might become more conspicuous, it pleased God to bring the mystery of remission to human beings for the abolition of sins at a time when no one could glory in his own merits.

> [Note: [Col. 0241C] Others have *to be exercised*. Quesnellus has *to be brought forth*, together with some of our manuscripts. Later, the lectionaries of St. Peter’s have *from his own merit*.]

## CHAPTER II
But the manifestation of this ineffable mercy, [Note: [Col. 0241C] Quesnellus added the word *dilectissimi* (“beloved”) here; we found it in the manuscript of St. Peter.] beloved, took place when Herod held royal authority among the Jews, at a time when the legitimate succession of kings had ceased and the power of the high priests had been destroyed, and a foreigner had obtained the principate: so that the birth of the true King might be confirmed by the voice of that prophecy which had said: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved, and he himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:10). Of these, an innumerable succession had once been promised to the most blessed patriarch Abraham, to be generated not by the seed of the flesh but by the fertility of faith; and therefore it was compared with the multitude of the stars, so that from the father of all nations a progeny might be expected not earthly but heavenly.

[Note: [Col. 0241C] Two manuscripts of St. Peter read *Petri Abrahae* (probably *patri Abrahae*, “to father Abraham”). A little earlier, the Lectionary of St. Antony of Padua reads *jam* (“already”) instead of *quondam* (“once”).]

Therefore, to bring forth the promised offspring, heirs designated in the stars are aroused by the rising of a new star, so that where the testimony of heaven had been employed, the service of heaven might attend.

[Note: [Col. 0241D] We have emended this from all our manuscripts and certain printed editions. The first edition and Quesnellus read *ab omni* (“from every [nation]”). A little later, the Padua manuscript reads *ut cui coeli* (“so that [one] to whom heaven …”; the fragmentary reading is uncertain).]

[Note: [Col. 0241D] The first edition, together with the manuscripts of St. Peter, reads *commonet* (“admonishes”). The cited Padua manuscript reads *commovit … et in mirandi luminis claritate* (“moved … and in the brightness of wondrous light”). A little later, the same edition and the manuscripts of Bologna and three Vatican manuscripts read *magnitudinem sanctificationis* (“greatness of sanctification”).]

A star brighter than the other stars moves the Magi, inhabitants of the more distant East, and men who were not ignorant of observing such things understand, from the splendor of its wondrous light, the greatness of the sign: unquestionably, divine inspiration was at work in their hearts, so that the mystery of so great a vision would not remain hidden from them and what was shown to their eyes as extraordinary would not be obscure to their minds. Finally, they arrange their duty with religious devotion and prepare themselves with these gifts, so that by adoring one person they might show that they believed in three things together: honoring with gold the royal person, with myrrh the human, and with incense the divine.

[Note: [Col. 0241D] Beware of suspecting anything akin to Nestorian doctrine in these words, since our Leo acknowledges in Christ both a human and a divine person. For just as no one would say that he imagined a third *suppositum* in Christ, when he seems to call the royal person distinct from both, so Leo should not be thought to have imagined a human *suppositum* distinct from the Word in Christ. He therefore understands one person of Christ, found through the incarnation of the Word to possess at once royal dignity, human nature, and divine essence. Quesnellus: We have shown by several examples that the ancients sometimes used the word *persona* in the sense of “as,” in note 71 on tractate 16, book I, of St. Zeno, p. 133. Thus here, “honoring the royal, human, and divine person” is equivalent to “honoring Christ with gold as king, with myrrh as man, and with incense as God”; and the following sermon, chapter 3, expresses this very interpretation: “To him were due royal honor in gold, divine worship in incense, and confession of mortality in myrrh.” Compare also sermon 36, chapter 1. Moreover, in many passages he openly professes the unity of the person of Christ in his two natures.]

## CHAPTER III

And so the Magi enter the principal city of the Jewish kingdom, and in the royal city ask that the one whom they had learned had been born to reign be shown to them.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] Some manuscripts of the later collections add *puerum* (“the child”). The first edition reads: *puerum quem ad regendum sibi didicerant procreatum* (“the child whom they had learned had been born to rule them”). A little later, the manuscripts of St. Peter, Bologna, and the first edition read: “Where is your glory, O Jew?”]

Herod is troubled; he fears for his safety and dreads for his power. He asks the priests and teachers of the Law what Scripture had foretold concerning Christ’s birth, and what had been prophesied comes to his knowledge. Truth enlightens the Magi; unbelief blinds the teachers. Carnal Israel does not understand what it reads, nor see what it displays; it uses pages whose utterances it does not believe.

Where is your glory, O Jew (Rom. 3:27)? Where is the nobility derived from Abraham your father? Has not your circumcision become uncircumcision (Rom. 2:25)? Behold, the greater is subject to the lesser (Gen. 25:23), and, while foreigners enter into the portion of your inheritance, you serve by reciting that covenant which you hold only in the letter. Let the fullness of the nations enter—let it enter—into the family of the patriarchs, and let the children of promise receive the blessing in the offspring of Abraham from which the children of the flesh disown themselves. In the three Magi let all the peoples adore the author of the universe; and let God be known not only in Judea but throughout the whole world, so that his name may be great everywhere in Israel (Ps. 75:2). For just as unbelief proves this dignity of the chosen race degenerate in its descendants, so faith makes it common to all.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter, one of Vallicella, and one of Padua read: “He chose this dignity of the race, so that just as unbelief in its descendants made it degenerate” (the Padua manuscript reads *convinci*, the Vallicella manuscript *convincit*), “so faith made it common to all” (the Padua and Vallicella manuscripts more correctly read *faciat*, “makes it”).]

## CHAPTER IV

After the Lord had been adored, and every act of devotion had been completed, the Magi, in accordance with the warning given in a dream, did not return by the same road on which they had come. For it was necessary that, having now believed in Christ, they should no longer walk along the paths of their former way of life, but, entering upon a new road, should abstain from their abandoned errors.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] The first edition reads *antiquas* (“old”) instead of *antiquae*. A little later, the same edition and the manuscripts of St. Peter and Bologna read *furiam* (“fury”) instead of *furorem* (“rage”).]

This also enabled them to elude the plots of Herod, who was contriving, under the pretense of official duty, the impiety of deceit against the child Jesus. Therefore, because the hope of this fabrication had been frustrated, the king’s anger flares into even greater fury. For, recalling the time which the Magi had indicated, he pours the rage of his cruelty upon all the children of Bethlehem,

[Note: [Col. 0243C] Quesnellus, relegating this reading—which was found in the earlier editions—to the notes, inserted another from three manuscripts, namely two of Thuanus and one of Corbie, to which our Padua, Venetian, and Cassinese manuscripts agree: “And by a general slaughter he raged against the blessed infancy of that city.” We, however, thought that the reading of the earlier editors should be restored, since it is found not only in manuscripts of collections 3, 4, and 5, but also in the Lectionaries of St. Peter, which seemed preferable to the manuscripts just mentioned; especially since the same reading is found in the manuscripts of the Casanatense and Barberini collections 2, where we read: “And by a general slaughter he raged against the infancy of the whole city, which was destined to pass into eternal glory.” The Vallicella Lectionary also agrees, reading *trucidavit* (“he slaughtered”) instead of *trucidat* (“he slaughters”). A little later, the Padua manuscript reads: *At ille, quia sanguinem* (“But he, because the blood …”).]

and by a general slaughter he cuts down the infancy of the whole city, which was destined to pass into eternal glory, thinking that, if no little child there remained alive, Christ too would be killed.

But he, whose blood was to be poured out for the redemption of the world at another age, had been carried into Egypt by the service of his parents. He was returning, so to speak, to the ancient cradle of the Hebrew people and arranging the principate of the true Joseph by the power of a greater providence, so that, coming from heaven as the bread of life (John 6:59) and food of reason, he might remove that famine more dreadful than every other famine, by which the minds of the Egyptians were suffering from the lack of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0243D] One manuscript of St. Peter and another Vatican manuscript read *duriorem* (“more harsh”) instead of *diriorem* (“more dreadful”).]

Nor was the sacrament of the singular sacrifice prepared without that region, in which, through the first slaughter of the lamb, the saving sign of the cross and the Lord’s Passover had been prefigured.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, beloved, instructed by these mysteries of divine grace, let us celebrate with rational joy the day of our first beginnings and the commencement of the calling of the nations. Let us give thanks to the merciful God, who, as the Apostle says, has made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints in light; who has rescued us from the power of darkness

[Note: [Col. 0243D] The manuscript of St. Peter reads: “from darkness and from the power of darkness.”]

and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son (Col. 1:12–13). For, as Isaiah prophesied, “The people of the nations who sat in darkness have seen a great light, and upon those who dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, light has dawned” (Isa. 9:2). Concerning them he likewise says to the Lord: “The nations that did not know you will call upon you, and the peoples who did not know you will take refuge in you” (Isa. 55:5).

[Note: [Col. 0243D] The Cassinese manuscript reads *non cognoverunt* (“did not know”). Shortly afterward we have written *qui te nescierunt* (“who did not know you”) from the same manuscript, since the same reading occurs in sermon 29, chapter 3. Others read *nesciebant* (“did not know”); the Padua manuscript reads *nesciunt* (“do not know”).]

[Note: [Col. 0243D] The Cassinese manuscript reads *quas fecisti* (“which you made”) and *honorificabunt nomen* (“they will honor the name”). The Padua manuscript likewise has *honorificabunt* instead of *glorificabunt* (“they will glorify”), and later reads *in conspectu* (“in the sight of”) instead of *ante conspectum* (“before the sight of”).]

Abraham saw this day and rejoiced (John 8:56), when he recognized that the children of his faith were to be blessed in his offspring, which is Christ, and foresaw by believing that he would become the father of all nations (Rom. 4:18), giving glory to God and knowing with complete certainty that he is able also to do what he promised (ibid., 21).

David sang of this day in the Psalms, saying: “All the nations that you made will come and adore before you, O Lord, and they will glorify your name” (Ps. 85:9); and again: “The Lord has made his salvation known; before the sight of the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. 97:2).

We know that this certainly began to take place from the time when a star led three Magi, drawn forth from the remoteness of their own region, to recognize and adore the King of heaven and earth.

[Note: [Col. 0244C] In the printed editions and some manuscripts, *excitatos* (“roused”) is read. Quesnellus suggested in the margin, perhaps, *excitōs* (“drawn forth”); since we found this reading in two manuscripts of St. Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, and one Padua manuscript, we did not hesitate to insert it into the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0244C] After the word *perduxit*, the following additional words are found in printed manuscripts: “And it does not cease to appear daily to those who look carefully. And if it could make Christ known while hidden in infancy, how much more can it reveal that same Christ reigning in majesty!” Since these words are absent from all the better manuscripts I have seen—namely, two Thuanus manuscripts and one of Corbie—there is no doubt, in my view, that they eventually slipped into the text from the marginal note of someone excessively devoted to astrology. The sequence of the text itself clearly demonstrates that these words should be removed. Quesnellus: These words are likewise absent from manuscripts of collections 1 and 2 and from certain of our Lectionaries, Padua, Venice, and others. If they are found in the manuscripts of St. Peter, this should cause no concern, for after the words “reigning in majesty” they contain “with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen,” and immediately afterward add: “Whose service, in any case …” That clause, “with the Father, etc.,” inserted before the end of the sermon, confirms still more strongly the intrusion of those words.]

Its service, in any case, urges us to imitate its obedience, so that we may serve, as far as we can, this grace which invites everyone to Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0244D] The first edition reads: “by which all are invited to Christ.”]

For whoever lives piously and chastely in the Church, whoever sets his mind on the things above (Col. 3:1), not on those of earth, is in a certain sense like a heavenly light; and while he preserves the splendor of a holy life, he shows many the way to the Lord, as though he were a star. In this endeavor, beloved, you ought all to benefit one another, so that in the kingdom of God, to which one reaches by right faith and good works, you may shine as children of light: through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXIV [also XXXIII]

[Note: [Col. 0244D] The manuscript of St. Peter: “On the Epiphany, against the Manichaeans.”]

On the Fourth Celebration of the Solemnity of the Epiphany

## SYNOPSIS

I. The Magi were called from a distant region so that the Christian faith might be strengthened—the faith that believes Christ to be God and man.

II. The Magi were instructed by the prophecy of Balaam and confirmed by the answer of the Jews. The latter were deceived by hope of a temporal leader; Herod was troubled by fear of a rival.

III. The journey of the Magi and their choice of gifts were the work of grace teaching inwardly. Their diligence served our faith.

IV. The impiety of the Manichaeans overturns the faith and truth of the incarnation.

V. The Manichaeans must be avoided; their sacrileges have been exposed. It is the practice of the Church to pour forth prayers for them and for other heretics.

## CHAPTER I

It is just and reasonable, beloved, that on days which proclaim the works of divine mercy we should rejoice with our whole heart and honorably celebrate the deeds accomplished for our salvation. The very law of the returning seasons calls us to this devotion: after the day on which the Son of God, coeternal with the Father, was born of a Virgin, it introduced, after a brief interval, the feast of the Epiphany, consecrated by the manifestation of the Lord.

In this feast divine providence established a great support for our faith, so that, while the infancy of the Savior, adored at its beginning, is commemorated with solemn veneration, the true nature of his humanity might be proved by the very evidences of his origin.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Quesnellus added *istum* (“this one”) here; it is absent both from the other printed editions and from our manuscripts, and ought to be removed because the sense itself requires this.]

[Note: [Col. 0245D] We restored this reading from our manuscripts and editions preceding Quesnellus, in whose edition the reading is *colitur* (“is worshiped”).]

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Thus read two manuscripts of St. Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, and one of Verona, together with Quesnellus. Other printed editions read: *veri hominis in Christo orta natura* (“the nature of the true man arising in Christ”).]

For this is what justifies the ungodly; this is what makes saints out of sinners: that in one and the same Lord Jesus Christ both true divinity and true humanity are believed—divinity, by which before all ages he is equal to the Father in the form of God; humanity, by which in the last days he was united to man in the form of a servant.

Therefore, to strengthen this faith, which was being fortified against every error,

[Note: [Col. 0245D] The editions before Quesnellus read *pronuntiabatur* (“was proclaimed”), as do manuscripts of collections 3 and 4. We followed Quesnellus’s reading, confirmed by the manuscripts of St. Peter and two Vatican manuscripts. The Verona manuscript reads *muniebatur* (“was fortified”). A little later, one Vatican manuscript reads *factum est* (“it came to pass”) instead of *gestum est* (“was accomplished”).]

it was accomplished by a great act of divine kindness and providence that a people dwelling in a distant region of the eastern land, skilled in the art of observing the stars, should receive a sign of the child who was born to reign over all Israel. For a new brightness appeared among the Magi, a star more brilliant than the others, and it filled the minds of those who observed it with such admiration for its splendor that they could in no way believe that what was announced by so great a sign should be neglected.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] Three of our manuscripts and the first edition read *judicio* (“judgment”) here. A little later, two manuscripts of St. Peter read *dicere* (“to say”) instead of *disseri* (“to be expressed”). The Verona manuscript reads *discere* (“to learn”).]

As events showed, the grace of God presided over this miracle; and although not even all Bethlehem yet knew of Christ’s birth, it was already bringing that birth to the nations who would believe. What could not yet be expressed in human speech, heaven caused to be known by proclaiming the Gospel.

## CHAPTER II

Although it was a gift of divine condescension that the Savior’s birth should become known to the nations, the Magi could nevertheless have been reminded of the miracle of the sign by the ancient predictions of Balaam, knowing that it had long ago been foretold and widely circulated in memory: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel, and he shall rule the nations” (Num. 24:17).

Thus three men, divinely stirred by the unusual brilliance of the star, follow the course of the flashing light before them, thinking that they would find in Jerusalem, the royal city, the child who had been indicated.

[Note: [Col. 0245D] The first edition and one Vatican manuscript read *signatum* (“designated”); another Vatican manuscript reads *significatum sibi puerum* (“the child signified to them”).]

But when this expectation had deceived them, they learned through the Jewish scribes and teachers what sacred Scripture had foretold concerning Christ’s birth, so that, confirmed by a twofold testimony, they might seek with more ardent faith the one whom both the brightness of the star and the authority of prophecy revealed.

When the divine oracle had been brought forth through the responses of the high priests, and the voice of the Spirit had declared: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are not the least among the rulers of Judah; for from you will go forth a leader who will govern my people Israel” (Mic. 5:2; Matt. 2:6),

[Note: [Col. 0246D] Thus read four Vatican manuscripts and one of Verona, together with Quesnellus, and similarly sermon 32, chapter 3. Other printed editions read *nequaquam minima es* (“you are by no means the least”). Two manuscripts of St. Peter read *non eris minima* (“you will not be the least”).]

how easy, and how fitting, it would have been for the leaders of the Hebrews to believe what they were teaching. But it is apparent that they thought carnally with Herod and judged Christ’s kingdom to be like the powers of this world: they hoped for a temporal leader, while Herod feared an earthly rival.

In vain you are troubled by fear, Herod, and uselessly strive in your suspicion to rage against the child. Your kingdom cannot contain Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0246D] The first edition, together with the Verona manuscript, reads *regia tua* (“your royal power”).]

nor is the Lord of the world confined within the narrow limits of your power. The one whom you do not wish to reign in Judea reigns everywhere; and you yourself would reign more happily if you submitted to his rule. Why do you not sincerely perform what you falsely promise? Go with the Magi and, by humbly adoring the true King, honor him.

But, following more closely the blindness of the Jews, you do not imitate the faith of the nations. Instead, you turn your perverse heart toward cruel plots, neither intending to kill the one whom you fear nor succeeding in harming those whom you destroy.

## CHAPTER III

And so, beloved, the Magi, led to Bethlehem by the service of the star that went before them, rejoiced with exceedingly great joy, as the Evangelist related. Entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother; and falling down, they adored him; and opening their treasures, they offered him gifts—gold, frankincense, and myrrh (Matt. 2:10–11).

O wondrous faith of perfect knowledge, taught not by earthly wisdom but instituted by the Holy Spirit! For when these men set out from their homeland, having not yet seen Jesus,

[Note: [Col. 0246D] The first edition, together with the Venetian manuscript and manuscripts of Vatican collections 3, 4, and 5, reads *nec aliquo contuitu ejus, quod eum tam ordinate venerarentur* (“nor by any sight of him [had they perceived] that they should honor him so appropriately”). The Verona manuscript is similar, but omits only *eum*. The edition of Rainaudus has *quo* instead of *quod*. The Casanatense manuscript, collection 2, reads *nec aliquod contuitu, quo tam ordinate venerarentur*. Although Quesnellus gives no indication, he seems to have assembled from these variant readings one reading that we have found nowhere: *Nec aliquid contuitu ejus, quo eum tam ordinate venerarentur*. We have presented the reading of the two manuscripts of St. Peter and the Cassinese manuscript. A little later, the first edition reads *signari sibi* instead of *sibi significari*.]

nor had they perceived anything by sight of him that would lead them to honor him so appropriately, how did they preserve this arrangement in bringing their gifts? It was because, beyond the appearance of the star that stirred their bodily sight, a brighter ray of truth instructed their hearts, so that before beginning the labors of the journey they understood that the one was being signified to them to whom royal honor was due in gold, divine worship in incense, and confession of mortality in myrrh.

As far as the illumination of faith was concerned, this could have been sufficient for them—what they had believed and understood—so that they would not seek by bodily sight what they had perceived with the fullest vision of the mind. But the diligence of their discerning service, persevering until they saw the child, served the peoples of future times and the people of our age. Just as what benefited us was that, after the Lord’s resurrection, the hand of the apostle Thomas examined the traces of the wounds in his flesh,

[Note: [Col. 0247D] The first edition omits *nobis* (“for us”).]

so it benefited us that the sight of the Magi confirmed his infancy.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] Thus read nearly all our manuscripts, especially the better ones, together with the editions preceding Quesnellus, and more suitably: for the word *quod* in this second member is not relative, just as it is not in the first, as it would have to be if one read, with Quesnellus, the manuscripts of collection 5, and the Verona Lectionary, *in infantia ipsius* (“in his infancy”).]

The Magi therefore saw and adored the child from the tribe of Judah, from the seed of David according to the flesh (Rom. 1:3), made from a woman, made under the Law (Gal. 4:4), which he had come not to abolish but to fulfill (Matt. 5:17). They saw and adored the child, small in stature, in need of another’s assistance, unable to speak, and in no respect unlike the general condition of human infancy.

[Note: [Col. 0247D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter read *parvum* (“small”) instead of *parvulum* (“a little child”), and *discretum* (“distinct”) instead of *dissimilem* (“unlike”). The Verona manuscript likewise has *discretum*.]
