For just as the testimonies that asserted in him the majesty of invisible divinity were trustworthy, so it had to be fully established that the Word made flesh had assumed a true human nature and that the eternal essence of the Son of God had assumed the true nature of man,

[Note: [Col. 0247D] We wrote *debebat* (“had to be”) instead of *decebat* (“was fitting”) on the basis of the manuscripts of St. Peter, three other better manuscripts, and the first edition. The article in question is especially necessary, since the matter concerns what “had to be” fully established. From the same manuscripts of St. Peter and the first edition we restored *suscipiendarum* (“to be undergone”) instead of *excipiendarum* (“to be received”).]

lest either the miracles of the ineffable works that would follow or the sufferings of the passions to be endured should disturb the mystery of faith through the apparent diversity of events; for they could in no way be justified unless they believed the Lord Jesus to be both true God and true man.

## CHAPTER IV

Against this singular faith, beloved, and the truth proclaimed throughout all the ages, the diabolical impiety of the Manichaeans resists. To destroy the souls of the deceived, they have woven for themselves the deadly fiction of an impious doctrine from sacrilegious and fabulous lies. Through the ruins of these insane opinions they have plunged headlong so far that they imagined for themselves a Christ with a false body, who presented nothing solid, nothing real, to human eyes or in human actions,

[Note: [Col. 0247D] We printed this reading on the authority of the manuscripts of St. Peter, Venice, Verona, and manuscripts of collections 1 and 2. The printed editions, together with the manuscripts of the three later collections, read *actibusque* (“deeds”); following this reading, Quesnellus noted in the margin that perhaps *tactibusque* (“touch”) should be read. But the better manuscripts exclude this correction.]

but displayed an empty image of simulated flesh.

For they wish it to appear unworthy of belief that God, the Son of God, entered a woman’s womb and subjected his majesty to this dishonor, so that, mingled with the nature of flesh, he might be born in a true body of human substance.

[Note: [Col. 0248D] See our observations, which will be noted at a similar passage in sermon 23. A little later, the Corbie manuscript reads *hoc corpus* (“this body”) instead of *hoc opus* (“this work”); and for *credenda* (“to be believed”), the same manuscript reads *ridenda* (“to be mocked”). Quesnellus suspected in the margin that *pudenda* (“to be considered shameful”) should be read, but none of our manuscripts supports this.]

But the whole of this work is not an injury to him but an exercise of his power; it is not pollution to be believed but glorious condescension. For if this visible light is not violated by any impurities over which it is poured, and if no filthy or muddy places contaminate the radiance of the sun’s rays—which are unquestionably a bodily creation—what could have polluted the essence of that eternal and incorporeal light by any quality of its own? By joining itself to the creature that it had made in its own image, it brought purification to the creature without receiving a stain; and it healed the wounds of weakness without suffering any loss of power.

Because this great and ineffable sacrament of divine mercy was announced by all the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, these men of whom we speak, adversaries of the truth, rejected the Law given through Moses and the divinely inspired oracles of the prophets. They violated the Gospel and apostolic writings themselves, removing some things and inserting others.

They fabricated for themselves, under the names of the apostles and under the words of the Savior himself, many volumes of falsehood, by which they might reinforce the fictions of their error and pour deadly poison into the minds of those whom they sought to deceive. For they saw that everything opposed them, that everything protested against them, and that the sacrilegious madness of their impiety was refuted not only by the New but also by the Old Testament.

[Note: [Col. 0248D] The printed editions read *sacrilegae* (“sacrilegious”), but we preferred the reading of the manuscripts of St. Peter. A little later, three manuscripts read *in furoris mendaciis* (“in the lies of fury”).]

Yet, persisting in their frenzied lies, they do not cease to trouble the Church of God with their deceptions. They persuade those wretched people whom they are able to ensnare to deny that the Lord Jesus Christ truly assumed human nature; to deny that he was truly crucified for the salvation of the world; to deny that blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side pierced by the lance; to deny that he was buried and raised on the third day; to deny that in the sight of his disciples he was lifted up to sit at the right hand of the Father, above all the heights of heaven; and, once the whole truth of the apostolic Creed has been removed, so that no fear may terrify the impious and no hope inspire the saints, to deny that the living and the dead will be judged by Christ. Thus, after depriving those whom they have corrupted of the power of so many sacraments, they teach them to worship Christ in the sun and moon and, under the name of the Holy Spirit, to adore Manichaeus himself as the teacher of such impieties.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, beloved, for the strengthening of your hearts in faith and truth, may today’s feast benefit all. May the Catholic confession be fortified by the testimony of the Savior’s manifested infancy, and may the impiety of those who deny that Christ assumed the flesh of our nature be anathematized.

[Note: [Col. 0248D] Thus read the same manuscripts of St. Peter. Others read *nostra* (“our”).]

The blessed apostle John warned us of this in unmistakable language, saying: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the Antichrist” (1 John 4:2–3).

Let no Christian have anything in common with such people; let there be no fellowship or association with them. May it benefit the whole Church that many of them have been exposed, by the Lord’s mercy, and that their own confession has revealed the sacrileges in which they were living. Let no one be deceived by their distinctions among foods, the filthiness of their garments, or the pallor of their faces. Their fasts are not chaste when they arise not from the discipline of self-restraint but from the art of deceit.

[Note: [Col. 0249D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Verona manuscript read *nocuerint* (“they have harmed”) and *illuserint* (“they have deceived”). A little later, one manuscript of St. Peter and the Verona manuscript read *nullus* (“no one”) instead of *nullius* (“of no one”).]

Until now they may have harmed the unwary and deceived the inexperienced; after this, no one’s fall will be excusable. He must no longer be regarded as simple but as thoroughly wicked and perverse who is henceforth found bound by this abominable error.

We certainly do not prohibit, but rather encourage, the ecclesiastical and divinely instituted devotion that you pray with us to the Lord even for such people. For we too, with tears and sorrow, pity the ruins of deceived souls, following the example of apostolic compassion, so that “with those who are weak we may be weak” (2 Cor. 11:29), and “with those who weep we may weep” (Rom. 12:15).

For we hope that the mercy of God may be entreated by the many tears and legitimate penitence of those who have fallen. Since we live in this body, the restoration of no one is to be despaired of, but the correction of all is to be desired, with the help of the Lord, “who raises up those who are bowed down, releases those who are bound, and gives light to the blind” (Ps. 145:8). To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXV [also XXXIV]

On the Fifth Celebration of the Solemnity of the Epiphany

## SYNOPSIS

I. What the star signifies: the star that powerfully moved the Magi and drew them onward with perseverance.

II. Herod, in the person of the devil, still rages against the children of the Church; and the Jews, blinded and deprived of every form of religion, serve Herod. The nations take their place.

III. We must pray for the Jews. We must cooperate vigorously with God’s grace. Grace provides assistance; obedience softens command.

IV. God invites everyone through his benefits. If a person does not obey him, his hard and ungrateful heart itself becomes his punishment. Earthly things must be abandoned and heavenly things sought, so that we may be joined to the fellowship of the saints.

## CHAPTER I

As you know, beloved, today’s feast is illumined by the manifestation of our Lord and Savior,

[Note: [Col. 0249D] The first edition reads *incessanter* (“unceasingly”).]

and this is the day on which a guiding star led the three Magi to recognize and adore the Son of God. It was rightly decided that the memory of this event should be celebrated with annual honor, so that, while the Gospel narrative is continually reviewed, its saving mystery might always present itself to the minds of those who understand it through this remarkable miracle.

Many proofs had indeed preceded it, clearly declaring the Lord’s bodily birth: when the blessed Virgin Mary heard and believed that she would be made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and would give birth to the Son of God; when, at her greeting, John, not yet born, was moved to prophetic exultation in Elizabeth’s womb (Luke 1:24), as though even within his mother’s womb he were already crying out: “Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who takes away

[Note: [Col. 0249D] One manuscript of St. Peter reads *peccatum* (“sin”). A little later, two manuscripts of St. Peter read *cum in ortu Domini* (“when, at the Lord’s birth”).]

the sins of the world” (John 1:29); or when, at the angel’s announcement of the Lord’s birth, the shepherds were surrounded by the radiance of the heavenly host (Luke 2:13), so that they would not doubt the majesty of the child whom they were about to see in the manger,

[Note: [Col. 0249D] The first edition and the Bologna manuscript read *de potestate* (“concerning the power”).]

nor think that he had been born merely in the nature of a man, since the attendance of the heavenly army served him.

But these and similar signs seem at that time to have become known to only a few persons, either related to the Virgin Mary or belonging to the household of Saint Joseph. This sign, however, which both powerfully moved the Magi while they were far away and persistently drew them to the Lord Jesus, was unquestionably the sacrament of that grace and the beginning of that calling by which the Gospel of Christ was to be preached not only in Judea but also throughout the world. Thus, through that star which shone before the eyes of the Magi but did not shine before the eyes of the Israelites, both the illumination of the nations and the blindness of the Jews were signified.

[Note: [Col. 0249D] The first edition reads: “The blindness of the Jews was declared.”]

## CHAPTER II
The form of the events symbolized therefore remains, beloved, as is clearly evident, and what was begun in image is completed in reality. [Note: [Col. 0249D] The printed editions, together with certain manuscripts, read: “For a star shines from heaven through grace, and three magi,” etc. We preferred the reading of the best manuscripts—namely, two of Saint Peter’s, the Venetian, the Vallicellian, Casinese Collection 1, and Casanatense Collection 2—in which the preposition *e* (“from”) alone is omitted before *coelo* (“heaven”), because of the similar letter with which the preceding word *Radiante* (“shining”) ends, a practice familiar to scribes. Then three Vatican manuscripts and the first edition read: “they hasten to adore the infancy of the supreme King.”] As a star shines from heaven through grace, three magi, summoned by the radiance of the Gospel’s splendor, hasten daily from all nations to adore the power of the supreme King. Herod too rages in the devil (Matt. II, 3), and groans that the kingdom of his wickedness is being taken from him in those who pass over to Christ. Hence, if he kills little children, he thinks that he is killing Jesus. This he constantly attempts to do, while he tries to snatch the Holy Spirit from those newly reborn and to extinguish, as it were, the infancy of tender faith.

But the Jews, who have chosen to remain outside Christ’s kingdom, are still, in a certain sense, under Herod’s rule; while the enemy of the Savior dominates them, they serve an alien power, as though they did not know what was prophesied when Jacob said: “The ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes for whom it has been reserved” [Note: [Col. 0250D] Above, Sermon 23, chapter 2, where it is restored as “the kingdom”; the first edition there also adds “the kingdom.”] “and he is the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

Yet they do not understand what they cannot deny, and they do not grasp intellectually what they know from the narrative of Scripture: for truth is a stumbling block to mad teachers, and what is light becomes darkness to blind instructors. When questioned, they answer that Christ is born in Bethlehem; yet they do not follow the knowledge with which they instruct others. They have therefore lost the succession of kings, the appeasement of sacrifices, the place of prayers, and the order of priests; and although they find that everything is closed to them and everything has come to an end, they do not see that these things have been transferred to Christ.

Therefore, what those three men, representing all the nations, obtained after adoring the Lord, the whole world attains among its peoples through faith, which justifies the ungodly. The adopted receive the inheritance of the Lord prepared before the ages, while those who seemed legitimate lose it.

Come to your senses at last, Jew; come to your senses, and turn even you, having laid aside unbelief, to your Redeemer. Do not be terrified by the enormity of your crime: Christ calls not the righteous but sinners (Matt. IX, 13); nor does he reject your impiety, who prayed for you when he was crucified (Luke XXIII, 34). Break the implacable sentence of your cruel fathers, and do not allow yourself to be bound by the curse of those who, crying out concerning Christ, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25), transferred the guilt of their crime onto you. Return to the merciful one; make use of the clemency of him who forgives. For the savagery of your wickedness has been turned into the cause of salvation. He lives whom you wished to perish. Confess the one you denied; adore the one you sold, so that his goodness may benefit you, whom your malice could not harm.

## CHAPTER III

As regards true charity, beloved, which we also owe to our enemies from the Lord’s prayer (Matt. V, 44) [Note: [Col. 0251D] The printed editions, with certain manuscripts, read *eruditione* (“instruction”). We judged that the reading found by Quesnellus in the Corbie manuscript should be adopted, since it is preferred in our better codices—namely, two of Saint Peter’s, the Venetian, and Manuscript Collections 1 and 2. The holy pontiff alludes not so much to the fifth petition of the Lord’s Prayer as to Christ’s prayer while hanging on the cross, who, as he had said a little earlier, prayed for you when he was crucified.], we must desire and strive for this: that this people too, which has fallen away from the spiritual nobility of its fathers, may be grafted into the branches of its own tree. For this benevolence greatly commends us to God, because their transgression has made room for our mercy precisely so that our faith might call them back to a rivalry in receiving salvation.

For the life of the devout ought to be useful not only to themselves but also to others, so that what cannot be accomplished among them by words may be achieved by examples. Therefore, beloved, considering the ineffable generosity of the divine gifts toward us, let us be fellow workers with the grace of God working within us.

The kingdom of heaven does not come to those who sleep, nor is the blessedness of eternity bestowed upon those who languish in idleness and sloth. Rather, since, as the Apostle says, “if we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him” (Rom. VIII, 17; II Tim. II, 12), we must run along that way which the Lord himself testified that he is (John XIV, 6). Without any merits of works to support us, he provided us with both a sacrament and an example: through the former to advance those called into adoption toward salvation, through the latter to train them for labor.

This labor, beloved, is not merely neither harsh nor burdensome to devout children and good servants; it is also pleasant and light [Note: [Col. 0251D] Thus according to our manuscripts and the first edition, instead of the reading *lenis* (“gentle”). The correction is required by the testimony of Scripture cited by Leo himself.], as the Lord says:

“Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is pleasant and my burden is light” (Matt. XI, 28–30).

Nothing, therefore, beloved, is difficult for the humble, nothing harsh for the gentle, and all the commandments easily come into effect when grace offers assistance and obedience makes the command mild. [Note: [Col. 0251D] This is the reading of the older and more carefully corrected exemplars of Saint Peter’s, the Venetian, the Vallicellian, the Casanatense, and the Barberinian. Other printed editions and some manuscripts read: “For the utterance of God sounds daily in our ears, and every person,” etc. [Col. 0252D] A little later, the first edition reads “according to what he has done.”] For God’s words resound daily in our ears, and every person is convicted of knowing what pleases divine justice.

But because that judgment in which each person will receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil (I Cor. V, 10), is deferred in the patience and goodness of the Judge, unbelieving hearts promise themselves impunity for their wickedness and think that the quality of human actions does not fall under the scrutiny of divine providence—as though evil deeds were not often punished by the clearest penalties, or as though the terror of heavenly threats were not frequently displayed [Note: [Col. 0252D] One Vatican manuscript reads: “the terror of heavenly threats displays.” The first edition, another Vatican manuscript, the Venetian, and the Casinese read: “the terror of heavenly threats is displayed.” The same reading was in the first hand of the Casanatense manuscript and was corrected only in the margin by adding the pronoun *se* before *coelestium*.]—by which faith is warned and unbelief rebuked.

## CHAPTER IV

Meanwhile, the goodness of God remains above all things and denies his mercy to no one, since he lavishly bestows many good things upon all alike and prefers to invite by benefits those whom he might justly subject to punishments.

The delay of vengeance gives room for repentance. Yet it cannot be said [Note: [Col. 0252D] One Vatican manuscript, the Bononian edition, and the first edition read: “There is no vengeance there.” Immediately afterward, these same codices and editions read “in conscience itself” instead of “in its own conscience.”] that there is no vengeance where there is no conversion, because a hard and ungrateful mind is already punishment for itself and suffers in its own conscience whatever is deferred by God’s goodness. Let sinners therefore not take such delight in their sins that the end of this life finds them still engaged in their deeds; for in hell there is no correction, nor is there any remedy of satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0252D] The first edition reads: “if action of the will no longer remains.”] where no exercise of the will remains, as the prophet David says: “For in death there is no one who remembers you; but in hell, who will confess you?” (Ps. VI, 6).

Let harmful [Note: [Col. 0252D] Quesnellus’s manuscript of Gaudiaval reads *voluntates* (“wills”); so too do two Vatican manuscripts and one Bononian manuscript, which additionally give the passage as: “Let harmful wills be driven away.” One manuscript of Saint Peter reads: “Let harmful pleasures therefore flee.”] pleasures, hostile joys, and desires that are already on the point of perishing be shunned. What fruit or benefit is there in continually desiring things which, even if they do not abandon us, must nevertheless be abandoned? Let the love of perishing things be transferred to incorruptible things, and let the soul called to higher things take delight in heavenly realities.

Strengthen your friendships with the holy angels; enter the city of God, whose dwelling is promised to us [Note: [Col. 0253D] Thus the better manuscripts; others read “whose habitation.” A little later, “seek their support,” occurs in Saint Peter’s manuscripts and in Vatican Collection 5.], and join yourselves to the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs. Rejoice in what makes them rejoice. Desire their riches, and through a good rivalry seek their support. For with those with whom we share devotion, we shall also share dignity [Note: [Col. 0253D] The editions before Quesnellus read *vobis* (“with you”). The reading we have retained is approved by Saint Peter’s manuscripts.].

While time is granted to you for carrying out God’s commandments, glorify God in your body (I Cor. VI, 20), and shine, beloved, like lights in this world (Phil. II, 15). Let the lamps of your minds always burn, and let nothing dark remain in your hearts (Luke XI, 35), because, as the Apostle says, “you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” [Note: [Col. 0253D] The words “walk as children of light” are absent from two Vatican manuscripts and the first edition.] (Eph. V, 8). Let what was foreshadowed in the figure of the three magi be fulfilled in you, and let your light so shine before men that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. V, 16).

For just as it is a great sin when the Lord’s name is blasphemed among the nations because of bad Christians, so it is a great merit of piety when he is blessed in the holy conduct of his servants. To him belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXVI [Alternatively XXXV]

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Saint Peter’s manuscripts: “On the octave of Epiphany.”]

## On the Solemnity of the Epiphany VI

### SYNOPSIS

I. The mysteries must always be honored; they remain effective by their power and are still fulfilled in the Church. Grace inwardly accomplishes what the star signifies outwardly. How the same gifts are offered by the faithful.

II. The devil still assumes the role of Herod, exercising envy in the Jews, deceit in heretics, and savagery in pagans. Yet Christ triumphs through charity in his members.

III. The Church grew through persecutions. The glory of rulers is to serve Christ. In the Church’s peace, the persecution of desires must be feared; by these the devil is worshiped no less than by sacrifices.

IV. One must repent while the opportunity for repentance remains; one must not yield to difficulty, but pray to God, who gives both the means of asking and what is asked.

## CHAPTER I

The day on which Christ, the Savior of the world, first appeared to the nations is to be venerated by us with sacred honor, beloved; and today we ought to conceive in our hearts those joys which were in the breasts of the three magi when, stirred by the sign and guidance of the new star, they adored the visible King of heaven and earth whom they had believed to be promised [Note: [Col. 0253D] One manuscript of Saint Peter, another Vatican manuscript, and the first edition read: “and those joys are to be conceived by us today which were in the minds of the three magi.” Several other manuscripts likewise read “in their minds.” Then, instead of “by the sign and guidance,” one Vatican manuscript reads “with the sign led forth.”].

For that day did not pass in such a way that the power of the deed revealed then has disappeared and nothing has reached us except the report of what happened, which faith would receive and memory celebrate [Note: [Col. 0253D] Saint Peter’s manuscripts read: “which faith received and memory celebrated.”]. Rather, through the multiplication of God’s gifts, our own times experience daily whatever those beginnings contained.

Although the Gospel narrative specifically records those days on which the three men—whom neither prophetic preaching had taught nor the testimony of the Law instructed—came from the most distant part of the East to know God, we nevertheless see this same event taking place now more openly and more abundantly in the illumination of all who are called. For the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled: “The Lord has revealed his holy arm in the sight of all the nations” (Isa. LII, 10); and, “All the nations of the earth have seen the salvation that is from the Lord our God” [Note: [Col. 0253D] “They will see” is found in the same two manuscripts of Saint Peter, the Padilirian manuscript, and another Veronese manuscript; the latter reads “the ends” instead of “the nations.”] (ibid.); and again: “Those to whom he was not announced will see, and those who have not heard will understand” (ibid., 15).

Therefore, when we see people devoted to worldly wisdom and distant from confessing Jesus Christ being led out of the depth of their error and called to the knowledge of the true light [Note: [Col. 0253D] In the printed editions the word *cernimus* (“we see”) was inserted here. On the authority of Saint Peter’s, Padilirian, and Veronese manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts, we have more appropriately moved it before *advocari* (“to be called”). Quesnellus found *educi* (“to be led out”) instead of *reduci* (“to be brought back”) in those same manuscripts.], the splendor of divine grace is unquestionably at work; and whatever of new light appears in darkened hearts flashes from the rays of that same star, so that those whom it touches with its radiance it both moves by its wonder and leads ahead to adore God.

If we wish to consider attentively how that threefold kind of gifts is offered by all who come to Christ with the step of faith, is not the same offering celebrated in the hearts of those who rightly believe? The one who acknowledges Christ as King of the universe brings forth gold from the treasure of his soul; the one who believes that the Only-Begotten of God has united a true human nature to himself offers myrrh; and the one who confesses that he is in no respect inferior to the Father’s majesty venerates him with a kind of incense [Note: [Col. 0254D] Five manuscripts read *majestatis* (“of majesty”).].

## CHAPTER II

When these comparisons have been carefully examined, beloved [Note: [Col. 0254D] The Bononian manuscript and the first edition read “carefully.”], we find that Herod’s role is not absent either. The devil himself, just as he was then the hidden instigator, is now also his tireless imitator.

He is tormented by the calling of all the nations [Note: [Col. 0254D] We have added the word “all” on the authority of Saint Peter’s, Padilirian, and Veronese manuscripts, as well as the better collections. Books written around this period are likewise entitled *On the Calling of All Nations*, regardless of whom they are thought to belong to.], and he is tortured by the daily destruction of his power, grieving that he is everywhere abandoned and that the true King is adored in every place. He prepares deceits, fabricates friendly agreements [Note: [Col. 0254D] The printed editions and several inferior manuscripts read *dissensiones* (“dissensions”); but the more suitable reading is *consensiones* (“agreements”), found in one manuscript of Saint Peter, another Vatican manuscript, the Veronese, the Padilirian, and the Casinese. A related but otherwise corrupt reading in another manuscript of Saint Peter, another Vatican manuscript, and Collection 2 is *confessiones* (“confessions”). Deceit fabricates not dissensions or enmities but friendly agreements, so that slaughter may break out. A little later, instead of *reliquiis eorum, quos* (“the remnants of those whom”), two manuscripts of Saint Peter and the first edition read *reliquis, quos* (“the others whom”); one Vatican manuscript reads *reliquiis quos*.], bursts into slaughter, and, so that he may make use of the remnants of those whom he still deceives, burns with envy among the Jews, lies in wait through pretence among heretics, and is inflamed by savagery among pagans.

For he sees that the power of the eternal King is unconquerable, whose death has extinguished the force of death itself [Note: [Col. 0255D] One manuscript of Saint Peter reads “had extinguished.”]. Therefore he has armed his entire art of harming against those who serve the true King: hardening some through the conceit of legal knowledge, corrupting others through the fabrications of false faith, and inciting still others to the frenzy of persecution [Note: [Col. 0255D] The manuscripts of Victor and Corbie used by Quesnellus, and two of our own—one of Saint Peter and another Vatican manuscript—read “through inflaming.” The printed editions had the order reversed: “inciting some to the fury of persecution, corrupting others through the fabrications of false faith.” We have restored the order found in several of our manuscripts, which corresponds to what precedes: the first clause to the Jews, the second to the heretics, and the third to the pagans, mentioned earlier in that order.].

But the one who crowned even little children with the glory of martyrdom [Note: [Col. 0255D] Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Another reading: ‘with the palm.’”] conquers and destroys this frenzy of that Herod. He has given his faithful such unconquerable charity that they dare to say in the Apostle’s words:

“Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or hunger? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us” (Rom. VIII, 35; Ps. XLIII, 22).

## CHAPTER III

We do not believe, beloved, that this courage was necessary only in those times when the kings of the world and all the powers of the age raged against God’s people with bloody impiety, considering it the height of their glory if they could remove the Christian name from the earth, unaware that the Church of God was increased by the fury of their cruelty. For in the sufferings and deaths of the blessed martyrs, whom they thought were being diminished in number, those martyrs were multiplied by their example.

Indeed, the assault of the persecutors contributed so much to our faith that nothing adorns royal power more than that the rulers of the world are members of Christ. They do not glory so much in having been born to imperial authority as they rejoice in having been reborn in baptism.

But because the storm of the earlier whirlwinds has subsided and, since battles ceased long ago, a certain tranquility seems to smile upon us, those dangers must be guarded against vigilantly which arise from the leisure of peace itself. For the adversary, who was ineffective in open persecutions, rages through a concealed art of harming, so that those whom he did not strike down by the blow of affliction he may overthrow by the fall of pleasure [Note: [Col. 0255D] Quesnellus likewise notes in the margin, as do two manuscripts of Saint Peter, the Padilirian, and the Veronese: “by the assault.”].

Seeing, therefore, that the faith of the rulers resists him and that the inseparable Trinity of the one God is worshiped no less in palaces than in churches, he grieves that the shedding of Christian blood has been forbidden. Those whose death he cannot obtain, he attacks in their morals [Note: [Col. 0255D] We preferred *mortem* (“death”) to *mortes* (“deaths”), and *terrorem* (“terror”) to *terrores* (“terrors”), on the authority of two manuscripts of Saint Peter, one Vatican manuscript, and another Veronese manuscript.].

He changes the terror of proscriptions into the fire of avarice, and those whom he has not broken by losses he corrupts through desire. For malice, long steeped in its own wickedness, has not laid aside its hatred but has changed its method, by which it may subject the minds of the faithful to its flatteries. It inflames with desires those whom it cannot harass with torments [Note: [Col. 0256D] The printed editions read *blandius* (“more gently”). We preferred the Saint Peter manuscripts; from them, and also from one Padilirian and another Vatican manuscript, we removed the particle *enim* (“for”), which appeared after *inflammat* (“it inflames”) and had been inserted into the preceding sentence in all manuscripts and editions, where its repetition seemed unnecessary. A little later, “let the hearts of captives return” occurs in the cited Padilirian manuscript.]; it sows disagreements, kindles anger, stirs tongues, and, so that more cautious hearts may not withdraw from unlawful deceits, it thrusts opportunities for completing crimes upon them. For this is the fruit of all its deceit: that the one who is not worshiped by the sacrifice of cattle, rams, and the burning of incense [Note: [Col. 0256D] We supplied the words “and rams” from the same manuscripts of Saint Peter. The Veronese and Padilirian manuscripts read “at the burning of the altar” instead of “and the burning of incense.”] should nevertheless be served by every kind of crime.

## CHAPTER IV

Our peace, therefore, has its dangers, beloved; and those who do not resist the desires of their vices are secure in vain concerning the freedom of faith. The heart of human beings is shown by the quality of their deeds, and the appearance of their actions reveals the form of their minds. For there are some who, as the Apostle says, “profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus I, 16).

The guilt of denial is truly incurred when the good that is heard in the sound of the voice is not possessed in the conscience. Human weakness readily slips into offenses, and because no sin exists without pleasure, one quickly yields to deceptive delight. But let one turn back from carnal desires to spiritual protection, and let the mind that possesses knowledge of its God turn away from the counsels of the enemy who gives evil advice [Note: [Col. 0256D] One Vatican manuscript and the first edition, together with the Veronese manuscript, read *malesuadi* (“of the one giving evil advice”); another Vatican manuscript reads *male suasi* (“ill-advised”). A little earlier, the Veronese and Padilirian manuscripts read: “the mind that possesses knowledge of the Lord.”].

May God’s patience benefit such a person, and may the delay of vengeance not nourish a stubbornness in sinning. Let the sinner not be secure because of impunity, since if he loses the time of repentance, he will have no place for pardon, as the prophet says: “For in death there is no one who remembers you; but in hell, who will confess you?” (Ps. VI, 6).

But whoever finds the restoration of correction difficult for himself should flee to the clemency of the assisting God and ask him to break the bonds of evil habit—him who lifts up all who fall and raises up all who are crushed (Ps. CXLV, 8). The prayer of one who confesses will not be empty, for the merciful God will fulfill the desire of those who fear him; and he will give what is asked, who has given the means by which it may be asked.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, living and reigning [Note: [Col. 0256D] We have added the words “with the Father and the Holy Spirit” from two Vatican manuscripts, one manuscript of Saint Peter, and another Padilirian manuscript.] with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXVII [Alternatively XXXVI]

## On the Solemnity of the Epiphany VII

[Col. 0257A]

### SYNOPSIS

I. What is believed by faith must be imitated in action. The mysteries of Christ are both sacraments and examples.

II. The infancy of Christ, which is the law of living, proclaims nothing except the cross and humility.

III. Christ’s entire strength is humility, which constitutes the whole discipline of Christian wisdom and whose teacher is infancy.

IV. In what Christian infancy consists, to which Christ’s infancy invites us.

## CHAPTER I

The remembrance of the deeds performed by the Savior of the human race confers great benefit upon us, beloved, if we accept for imitation what we venerate as something believed [Note: [Col. 0257D] One Vatican manuscript, another Bononian manuscript, and the first edition read “what has been established.”]. For in the dispensations of Christ’s sacraments there are both virtues of grace and incentives to teaching, so that we may follow by the example of our works the one whom we confess in the spirit of faith.

For even the very beginnings which the Son of God undertook by being born through the Virgin Mother instruct us toward progress in piety [Note: [Col. 0257D] Three Vatican manuscripts and the first edition read “toward advancement.”]. At once human humility and divine majesty appear in one and the same person to right-believing hearts. The one whom the cradle testifies to be an infant, heaven and the heavenly beings proclaim as their creator. A child small in body is Lord and Ruler of the world [Note: [Col. 0257D] Thus all our manuscripts agree with Quesnellus and the first edition. Others read: “A child small in body, the Ruler and Lord of the world.”]; he is held in his mother’s lap who is contained by no limit.

But in these things lies the healing of our wounds and the raising up of our humiliation: for unless such great diversity were united in one, human nature could not be reconciled to God.

## CHAPTER II

Our remedies have therefore prescribed for us a law of living, and from the source from which medicine was bestowed on the dead, a pattern for conduct was given. It was not without reason that, when the brilliance of the new star had led the three magi to adore Jesus, they did not see him commanding demons, raising the dead, restoring sight to the blind, walking to the lame, or speech to the mute, nor engaged in any action of divine power [Note: [Col. 0257D] We substituted *nec* (“nor”) for *vel* (“or”), which appeared in the more common editions and certain manuscripts, on the authority of two manuscripts of Saint Peter and the first edition.].

Rather, they saw a silent and tranquil child placed under his mother’s care; in him no sign of power appeared, but a great miracle of humility was displayed [Note: [Col. 0257D] The editions read “appeared and was displayed.” We corrected this on the authority of the first edition, two manuscripts of Saint Peter, and one Bononian manuscript, especially since the context strongly requires this reading.].

The very appearance of the sacred infancy, to which the Son of God had adapted himself, presented to the eyes a preaching that was to be impressed upon the ears [Note: [Col. 0257D] The editions before Quesnellus and one Vatican manuscript corruptly read “and he bore before his eyes.” We found Quesnellus’s correction in the rest of our manuscripts and in the first edition. One Vatican manuscript and two manuscripts of Saint Peter have *inferebat* (“brought in”) instead of *ingerebat* (“impressed”). After *ingerebat*, all the editions and most manuscripts read: “and what the sound of his voice did not yet utter, the effect of his vision already taught.” Quesnellus corrected the passage without indicating anything; we found the same reading in the manuscripts of Saint Peter.], so that what the sound of his voice did not yet utter, the effect of his appearance already taught.

For the whole victory of the Savior, which overcame both the devil and the world, began in humility and was completed in humility [Note: [Col. 0258D] The editions and certain manuscripts had: “was conceived in humility, was completed in humility,” a syntax that seems foreign to Leo. The correction was suggested by two manuscripts of Saint Peter, another Venetian manuscript, the Vallicellian, and the Casinese, differing in that one manuscript of Saint Peter reads *concepta* (“conceived”) instead of *coepta* (“begun”), while the Venetian reads *de humilitate* (“from humility”). In the Casanatense manuscript the words *humilitate confecta* (“completed in humility”) are absent from the first hand but were supplied later; the same later hand corrected *coepta* to *concepta*.]. He began the appointed days under persecution and ended them under persecution; the endurance of suffering was not lacking to the child, nor childlike gentleness to the one who was to suffer, because the only-begotten Son of God, under one inclination of his majesty, accepted both that he should be born as a human being and that he could be killed by human beings [Note: [Col. 0258D] The word “Son” has been added from the manuscripts of Saint Peter.].

## CHAPTER III

If, then, almighty God made our very bad cause good through the privilege of humility, and destroyed death and the author of death because he did not refuse all that his persecutors inflicted but, obedient to the Father, endured the cruelties of those raging against him with the gentlest meekness, how humble and how patient ought we to be, who, whenever we encounter any hardship, endure it only by our own merit?

“For who will boast that he has a pure heart or that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. XX, 9). And since blessed John says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8), who will be found so free from guilt that in him justice has nothing to reproach or mercy anything to forgive?

Therefore, beloved, the whole discipline of Christian wisdom consists not in abundance of speech, nor in cleverness of disputation, nor in the pursuit of praise and glory, but in true and voluntary humility, which the Lord Jesus Christ both chose and taught as his entire strength, from his mother’s womb even to the punishment of the cross.

For when his disciples, as the Evangelist says, were asking among themselves [Note: [Col. 0258D] The printed editions and some manuscripts read “among themselves.” The sounder reading was supplied by the cited manuscripts of Saint Peter and another Vatican manuscript.] which of them was greater in the kingdom of heaven, he called a little child and placed him in their midst [Note: [Col. 0258D] The first edition reads: “and said: Amen, amen, I say to you.” The same edition and two manuscripts of Saint Peter read: “like this little child, he is greater.”], and said:

“Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever therefore humbles himself like this child will be greater in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVIII, 1–6; Luke IX, 46–48).

Christ loves infancy, which he first assumed in mind and body [Note: [Col. 0258D] “Which he first” is found in two Vatican manuscripts.]. Christ loves infancy, the teacher of humility, the rule of innocence, the pattern of gentleness. Christ loves infancy, toward which he directs the conduct of the mature, toward which he brings back the age of the old [Note: [Col. 0258D] The editions before Quesnellus, as well as Gaudiaval’s manuscript and one of our Vatican manuscripts, read “which,” whereas the first edition and the other manuscripts have the reading retained in the text.], and to whose example he bends those whom he raises to the eternal kingdom.

## CHAPTER IV

But so that we may fully recognize how such a remarkable transformation may be embraced, and by what change we must return to a childlike condition, blessed Paul teaches and says:

“Do not become children in understanding, but be infants in wickedness” (I Cor. XIV, 20).

We must not therefore return to the frivolous and imperfect beginnings of infancy [Note: [Col. 0259C] The editions before Quesnellus and Gaudiaval’s manuscript, as well as several of our manuscripts, read *lubrica* (“unstable”). Latinus Latinius, in the *Sacred and Profane Library*, conjectured that *ludicra* (“frivolous”) should be read. We found this reading accepted by Quesnellus and approved by a manuscript of Saint Peter and another manuscript; these same manuscripts also approve *revertendum est* (“we must return”) instead of *redeundum est* (“we must go back”), which appears in the editions and other manuscripts.], but must take from them something that also suits mature years [Note: [Col. 0259D] Several editions and certain manuscripts read “from there it must be taken.” “A swift passage to anger” follows. Casanatense Collection 2 reads: “From there a swift passage of emotions must be taken”; Quesnellus and the Antwerp edition of 1583 likewise. Three Vatican manuscripts, Collections 4 and 5, read: “From there a swift passage of emotions must be taken.” The reading of the first edition and the Bononian manuscript, which we have inserted into the text, seemed sounder: namely, that we shall be childlike in wickedness if, as happens with children, fits of anger pass quickly, the return to peace is swift, and there is no memory of offense, etc. Casinese Collection 1 approaches this reading, with: “From there it must be taken. Let the passage of emotions be swift.” That reading would be preferable if Leo did not seem to avoid the superfluous and harsher repetition of *est* (“is”) after the participial phrase *revertendum est* (“we must return”).], so that the passage of emotions may be swift and the return to peace quick; let there be no memory of offense, no desire for rank; let there be love of shared fellowship [Note: [Col. 0259D] The editions read *dilectionis* (“of affection”). The reading of the best manuscripts of Saint Peter and one Vallicellian manuscript is more appropriate.], and natural equality.

For it is a great good not to know how to harm and not to understand evil [Note: [Col. 0260C] The editions read “and toward evil.” We removed *ad* (“toward”) on the authority of the same manuscripts.], because to inflict and return injury is the wisdom of this world; but to repay no one evil for evil is the childlike quality of Christian evenness [Note: [Col. 0260C] Thus all our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus, who, without indicating any manuscript, wrote “the equanimity of infancy.” A little later, the first edition and the Bononian manuscript read “to this we,” and below “to us” instead of “to you.”].

The mystery of today’s festival invites you, beloved, to this likeness of little children, and the Savior, a child adored by the magi, suggests to you this form of humility. To show his imitators what glory he was preparing for them, he consecrated to martyrdom those born at the time of his birth, so that those born in Bethlehem, where Christ was born, might by sharing the same age become partners in his suffering [Note: [Col. 0260C] Two manuscripts of Saint Peter read: “Within Bethlehem.”].

Let humility therefore be loved, and let all pride be avoided by the faithful. Let each person prefer the other to himself, and let no one seek what is his own but what belongs to another, so that when the affection of benevolence has abounded in all, the poison of envy may be found in no one. For “whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11), as our Lord Jesus Christ himself testifies, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XXXVIII [Alternatively XXXVII]

[Note: [Col. 0260C] This sermon appears in its entirety among the sermons formerly attributed to Augustine, formerly Sermon 33 *On the Seasons*, now in the appendix as Sermon 133, where the Benedictine editors note that it is Pope Leo’s and is attributed to him in all the manuscripts. Several variants will be excerpted from this appendix.]

## On the Solemnity of the Epiphany VIII

[Col. 0260A]

### SYNOPSIS

I.

Stella represents grace, the Magi all the nations, Herod the pagans, and the slaughtered infants the martyrs. The present festival belongs to all times.—II. The mystery of Christ, God and man, necessary for the restoration of humanity, can be approached only by the light of faith.—III. The necessity of grace. In doing good, a human being receives from God both the accomplishment of the deed and the beginning of the will. The saints must fear lest, exalted by the very works of piety, they be abandoned by the help of grace. By what signs can each person test whether God dwells within him?—IV. We recognize God as the inhabitant of the heart chiefly through charity. How earnestly one must labor for charity.

## CHAPTER I

The cause and meaning of today’s solemnity have often been made clear to you both by the Gospel narrative and by the custom of observance. Nor is it necessary now to repeat in such a way the events belonging to the human beginnings of our Savior that we should discuss the brilliance of the new star, the Magi and their gifts, the savagery of Herod, and the slaughter of the infants. For, as you know, the grace of God was prefigured in the radiance of the star, the calling of the nations in the three men, the cruelty of the pagans in the impious king, and the form of all the martyrs in the killing of the infants.

But because, on this most sacred day, the duty of priestly speech must answer your expectation, let us strive, with the help of God’s Spirit as far as we can, to reach through the paths of understanding the point at which we may recognize that the mystery of the present feast belongs to the times of all the faithful; and let it by no means be considered strange that, in the order of God’s dispensations, an ancient reality is worshiped.

## CHAPTER II

Although, therefore, every Christian soul ought to think nothing unworthy of the majesty of the Son of God, and although each person, having passed beyond the first rudiments of faith, ought to advance toward higher things, nevertheless it is not necessary, when Christ has accepted true humanity, for the weakness of the human mind to tremble at the very sharing of our nature, or to approach with difficulty, through bodily beginnings or growth, the recognition of the one Godhead that he shares with the Father.

But when a ray of heavenly light has shone through minds obscured by darkness, let the splendor of truth break through the delays of hesitant faith, so that the heart, set free and released from visible things, may follow the light of understanding as its guiding star. For, as the Apostle says, “The Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 11), so that it may worship without hesitation, reigning with the Father, the very one it reverently worshiped lying humbly in the cradle.

This manifestation, beloved, which dissolves the clouds of hesitant souls and makes the Son of God known in such a way that his being also the Son of Man causes no obstacle, belongs to the dignity of the present feast. The Savior’s true infancy is a declaration of his Godhead, when the perception of the flesh is transferred from human things to divine ones, so that the signs of his powers may raise up those whom the experiences of weakness depress. For our nature and our cause required such assistance: that, in restoring the human race, humility should not be without majesty, nor majesty without humility.

## CHAPTER III

Now, when the observance of the divine commandments shines forth in the progress of individual believers and what was said is fulfilled—“Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16)—who would not understand that the Godhead is present wherever he sees true virtue appearing? Virtue certainly does not exist without God, nor does it possess the character of divinity unless it is enlivened by the Spirit of its author.

For when the Lord says to his disciples, “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5), there can be no doubt that a person doing good receives from God both the accomplishment of the deed and the beginning of the will.

Hence the Apostle, the most abundant exhorter of the faithful, says: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 12).

And this is a reason for the saints to tremble and fear: lest, exalted by the very works of piety, they be abandoned by the help of grace and remain in the weakness of nature.

But whoever wishes to test whether God dwells within him—of whom it is said, “God is wonderful in his saints” (Ps. LXVII, 36)—should examine the inner recesses of his heart with sincere scrutiny and carefully ask with what humility he resists pride, with what goodwill he struggles against envy, how he is not ensnared by flattering tongues, and how much he rejoices in the good of others; whether he does not wish to return evil for evil, and prefers to forget injuries without retaliation rather than lose the image and likeness of his Creator, who, summoning all people to knowledge of himself by universal gifts, “rains on the just and the unjust, and makes his sun rise on the good and the wicked” (Matt. V, 45).

## CHAPTER IV

And so that this careful examination of discernment may not labor over many things, let it seek in the hidden places of its mind charity itself, the mother of all virtues. If it finds that charity is wholly intent upon the love of God and neighbor, so that it wishes even its enemies to receive what it desires to be granted to itself, let anyone who is such a person have no doubt that God is both the ruler and the inhabitant of him. He receives God all the more magnificently the more he glories not in himself but in the Lord (I Cor. I, 31).

For those to whom it is said, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII, 21), do everything by the Spirit of him whose authority governs them.

Knowing, therefore, beloved, that “God is charity” (I John IV, 16), who works all things in all people (I Cor. XII, 6), pursue charity, so that the hearts of all the faithful may come together in one chaste affection of love.

Let passing and empty things not occupy us; with constant desire let us strive toward those things that will always remain. For the mystery of the present feast ought to be perpetual within us. It will indeed be celebrated without end if the Lord Jesus Christ appears in all our actions—he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

### Notes

- **[Col. 0260D]** Codex Bononiensis and the first edition read *nobis* (“to us”).
- **[Col. 0260D]** Thus, with Quesnellus and the first edition, all our codices except the Veronese, which, like the other printed editions, has *habeat*. Then, instead of *transcensis* (“having crossed over”), one codex of St. Peter has *transgressis* (“having passed beyond”), another *transcursis* (“having traversed”).
- **[Col. 0260D]** The printed editions omit *non* (“not”), a particle that we have added from the codices of St. Peter as more suitable. From the fact that a Christian soul ought to think nothing unworthy of the majesty of the Son of God, etc., it might seem to follow that the weakness of the human mind should tremble at the sharing of our very nature, as though it were unworthy of the Son of God, etc. Leo, however, asserts that although the first point is true, the second is nevertheless not necessary. Similarly, from the same codices of St. Peter we have written *accepit Christus* (“Christ accepted”) instead of the reading found elsewhere, *accipit Christum* (“accepts Christ”). The Venetian and Vallicellian codices have *accepit Christum*. Soon afterward, the Veronese codex omits *corporea* (“bodily”).
- **[Col. 0261C]** In the Augustinian appendix: *cunctantis fidei moras* (“the delays of hesitant faith”).
- **[Col. 0261C]** Thus our codices, together with the first edition and the Augustinian appendix. Other printed editions have *quem ut* (“whom as”).
- **[Col. 0261C]** We have written this from the same codices and from editions preceding Quesnellus, which, together with the Augustinian appendix, placed *sine differentia* (“without distinction”). Since the sermon concerns fearfulness regarding faith, *sine diffidentia* (“without doubt”) was certainly to be preferred.
- **[Col. 0261C]** The first edition and the Augustinian appendix, together with some codices, have *lux vestra* (“your light”). Other manuscripts have *lumen vestrum* (“your lamp/light”), as is also found in Sermon 26, chapter 4. Then, instead of *magnificent* (“magnify”), the Bononiensis manuscript and the first edition have *glorificent* (“glorify”).
- **[Col. 0261D]** Thus Quesnellus, with the Augustinian appendix and likewise the codices of St. Peter. Others have *majestatem* (“majesty”). Shortly afterward, six of our codices, together with the first edition, the Quesnellian edition, and the Augustinian appendix, have *Deitatis* (“of the Godhead”); other editions have *dignitatis* (“of dignity”).
- **[Col. 0261D]** Five of our reliable codices, together with the first edition and the Augustinian appendix, have this reading. Others have *a Deo* (“from God”). Then, in the first edition and the Bononiensis manuscript, *initium bonae voluntatis* (“the beginning of good will”).
- **[Col. 0261D]** One Vatican codex, another Bononiensis codex, and the first edition have *in nobis* (“in us”).
- **[Col. 0261D]** The manuscript of St. Peter and the Veronese and Padiliron codices have *repugnet* (“resist”).
- **[Col. 0262D]** The Bononiensis manuscript and the first edition have *in nobis* (“in us”).
- **[Col. 0262D]** Our ten codices and the editions preceding Quesnellus have this reading. Quesnellus inserted into the text from a single Corbey manuscript: “Let human things pass away from us, lest they occupy us.” He noted that the common reading is found in the Gaudiival manuscript, and that instead of *vana* (“empty things”) some read *ima* (“lowly things”). In the Augustinian appendix: “Let empty things pass away from us, and lest they occupy us”; *constanti* (“with constant …”).
- **[Col. 0261D]** This is the preferable reading, found in the first edition, the Antwerp edition of 1583, the Augustinian appendix, and several of our codices, rather than *solitae* (“customary”) in other editions. The Benedictine editors add another notable variant in their annotation: the Navarrese and Corbey manuscripts have, “And so that it may not labor in vain over many things, let it examine discernment carefully.”
- **[Col. 0262C]** Thus Quesnellus, with our Padiliron manuscript and the Augustinian appendix. The other editions, together with some of our codices, have: “and if in it he finds the love of God and neighbor earnestly with his whole heart.” The manuscript of St. Peter has: “with an earnest heart.”
- **[Col. 0262C]** Others have *inhabitatorem* (“inhabitant”).
- **[Col. 0262C]** The Bononiensis codex and the first edition have *intra nos* (“within us”).
- **[Col. 0262C]** This passage varies remarkably among the codices and editions. The first edition, together with the Victor manuscript, Quesnellus’s copy, and two of our Vatican and Bononiensis codices, reads: *hi nimirum illius aguntur spiritu* (“these, plainly, are moved by his Spirit”). Quesnellus, from the Corbey manuscript, preferred *non nisi illius aguntur spiritu* (“are moved only by his Spirit”), which is likewise read in the Augustinian appendix. The Barberinian, Padiliron, and Venetian codices have *nihilominus illius aguntur spiritu* (“nevertheless are moved by his Spirit”); and somewhat differently the Casinensis, Vallicellian, and Casanatensian codices have *nihil non illius aguntur spiritu* (“all things are moved by his Spirit”). We have preferred the reading of the editions preceding Quesnellus, since it is confirmed by two Lectionaries of St. Peter, another Veronese manuscript, and Vatican manuscript Collection 5, and since it also gives the best sense: among the most reliable authors, *nihil non* signifies “everything” or “all things.”

## SERMON XXXIX [formerly XXXVIII]

### On Lent I

In one manuscript of St. Peter, a general title is prefixed to this first sermon on Lent: “Here begin the sermons of Saint Leo the Pope on the fast of Lent.” In another codex of St. Peter: “Sermon of Pope Leo on the fast of Lent.” The omission of the title “saint” seems there to indicate the manuscript’s ancient origin. The same codices generally give the following sermons the title “On the fast of Lent.”

### Synopsis

I. Fasting according to the example of the Hebrews, especially against invisible enemies.—II. The devil prepares snares especially during Lent.—III. Why Christ wished to be tempted, and how great are the struggles of human beings in this life.—IV. How great the devil’s envy is. What are the weapons of Christians?—V. What virtues ought especially to accompany fasting?—VI. True fasting consists chiefly in works of mercy.

## CHAPTER I

Once, when the people of the Hebrews and all the tribes of Israel were oppressed by the harsh domination of the Philistines because of the offenses caused by their sins, they restored the strength of mind and body for the purpose of overcoming their enemies by imposing a fast upon themselves, as sacred history makes clear. For they understood that they had deserved that harsh and wretched subjection by neglecting God’s commandments and corrupting their conduct, and that they would fight with weapons in vain unless they had first fought against their vices.

Therefore, abstaining from food and drink, they imposed upon themselves the discipline of severe chastisement; and, in order to conquer their enemies, they first conquered the enticement of the appetite within themselves. In this way it came about that savage adversaries and harsh masters yielded to the hungry, whom they had subjugated when they were well fed.

And so we too, beloved, placed amid many adversities and battles, if we wish to use similar remedies, should be healed by a similar observance. For our cause is almost the same as theirs: just as they were chiefly attacked by fleshly adversaries, so we are attacked chiefly by spiritual enemies. If these are conquered through the correction of conduct granted to us by God’s grace, the strength of our bodily enemies will also yield; and those whom not their own merits but our sins made harsh toward us will be weakened by our amendment.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, beloved, so that we may be able to overcome all our enemies, let us seek divine assistance through observance of the heavenly commandments, knowing that we cannot prevail over our adversaries unless we have also prevailed over ourselves.

For there are many conflicts within us: “The flesh desires one thing against the spirit, and the spirit another against the flesh” (Gal. V, 17). If, in this dissension, bodily desires are stronger, the mind will shamefully lose its proper dignity, and it will be most destructive for the one who ought to rule to become a servant. But if the mind, subject to its ruler and delighting in heavenly gifts, tramples down the impulses of earthly pleasure and does not allow sin to reign in its mortal body (Rom. VI, 12), reason will hold the principate in perfect order, and no illusion of spiritual wickedness will shake its defenses. For there is true peace and true freedom for a human being when the flesh is governed by the judgment of the mind, and the mind is directed under God’s rule.

This preparation, beloved, although it is salutarily undertaken at all times so that vigilant enemies may be overcome by unceasing diligence, must now be sought with greater concern and built with greater care, when the enemies themselves, subtle as they are, lie in wait with sharper cunning.

For, knowing that the most sacred days of Lent have arrived, during whose observance all past sluggishness is chastised and all negligence washed away, they direct the whole force of their wickedness toward this one goal: that when we are about to celebrate the holy Pasch of the Lord, we may be found unclean in some respect; and that from the very source from which forgiveness ought to be obtained, offense may instead be incurred.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, beloved, as we approach the beginning of Lent—that is, a more diligent service of the Lord—because we are entering, as it were, an arena of holy work, let us prepare our souls for the battles of temptation; and let us understand that the more earnestly we labor for our salvation, the more fiercely we will be attacked by our adversaries.

But he who is in us is stronger than he who is against us, and through him we are powerful, in whose strength we trust. For this reason the Lord allowed himself to be tempted by the tempter: so that we might be instructed by the example of the one whose help protects us.

For, as you have heard, he conquered his adversary by the testimonies of the Law, not by the power of his might, so that by this very act he might both honor humanity more and punish the adversary more, since the enemy of the human race was conquered not now as though by God, but as though by a human being.

He fought then so that we might afterward fight; he conquered so that we too might likewise conquer. For there are no works of virtue, beloved, without the testing of temptations; no faith without trials; no battle without an enemy; no victory without a struggle.

This life of ours exists amid snares and amid battles. If we do not wish to be deceived, we must keep watch; if we wish to overcome, we must fight. And therefore the wisest Solomon says: “My son, as you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Sir. II, 1).

That man, full of the wisdom of God, knowing that the pursuit of religion involves the labor of combat, foresaw the danger of battle and warned the one who was about to fight in advance, lest, if the tempter approached someone unprepared and unaware, he might quickly wound him.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, beloved, since we have been instructed by divine teachings and approach knowingly the contest of the present struggle, let us hear the Apostle saying: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI, 12).

And let us not be unaware that these enemies of ours perceive that everything we attempt to do for our salvation is done against them; and that by this very fact—that we desire something good—we provoke our adversaries.

For there is an ancient dissension between us and them, nourished by diabolical envy, so that, because they fell away from those goods toward which we are advancing with God’s help, they are tormented by our justification. If we rise, they fall; if we grow strong, they grow weak. Our remedies are their wounds, because they are wounded by the healing of our wounds.

Stand firm, therefore, beloved, as the Apostle says, “with the loins of your mind girded in truth, and with your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace; taking above all the shield of faith, with which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the evil one; and take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI, 14).

See, beloved, with what powerful weapons and what impregnable defenses the leader distinguished by many triumphs, the unconquered commander of the Christian army, has armed us. He girded the loins with the belt of chastity and shod the feet with the bonds of peace: for the unbelted soldier is quickly conquered by the instigator of impurity, and the unshod person is easily bitten by the serpent.

He gave the shield of faith for the protection of the whole body; he placed the helmet of salvation upon the head; he armed the right hand with the sword—that is, with the word of truth—so that the spiritual warrior might not only be safe from wounds but also be able to wound the one who resists.

## CHAPTER V

Relying, therefore, on these weapons, beloved, let us enter eagerly and fearlessly upon the contest set before us, so that in this arena of fasting we may not be content merely to think that abstinence from food alone is what must be pursued.

For it is little if the substance of the flesh is weakened while the strength of the soul is not nourished. Let the outer person be afflicted for a little while, but let the inner person be restored; and, when bodily fullness has been withdrawn from the flesh, let the mind be strengthened by spiritual delights.

Let every Christian soul examine itself and scrutinize the inner recesses of its heart with severe investigation. Let it see whether any discord has remained there, whether any desire has settled there. Let chastity drive away incontinence; let the light of truth dispel the darkness of dissimulation. Let pride subside, let anger recover its senses, let the darts of harmful deeds be shattered, and let slanderous speech be restrained.

Let acts of vengeance cease, and let injuries be consigned to oblivion. Finally, let every plant that the heavenly Father has not planted be uprooted (Matt. XV, 13). For the seeds of virtue are then well nourished within us when every foreign shoot is torn from the field of our heart.

If anyone has burned with such a desire for vengeance against another that he has handed him over to prison or bound him in chains, let him hasten to release not only the innocent person but also the one who appears deserving of punishment, so that he may confidently use the rule of the Lord’s Prayer, saying: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI, 12).

The Lord commends this part of the petitions with such particular emphasis that the entire effect of the prayer seems to depend upon this condition: “For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins” (ibid., 14).

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore, beloved, mindful of our weakness, since we easily slip into any kind of wrongdoing, let us in no way neglect this especially effective remedy and this most powerful cure for our wounds.

Let us forgive, so that we may be forgiven; let us grant the pardon for which we ask; and let us not strive to take revenge when we pray to be forgiven.

Let us not pass by the groans of the poor with deaf ears, but let us offer mercy to those in need with ready kindness, so that we may deserve to find mercy in judgment.

Whoever, aided by God’s grace, directs his efforts toward this perfection will faithfully observe the holy fast (I Cor. V, 8). Free from the leaven of former malice, he will reach the blessed Pasch in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and through the newness of life he will worthily rejoice in the mystery of the restoration of humanity, through Christ our Lord, who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XL [formerly XXXIX]

### On Lent II

### Synopsis

I. One must always make progress in this life.—II. During Lent one must strive especially toward this, since the devil rages more fiercely.—III. Why Christ did not change stones into bread when he was hungry.—IV. The fasting of Lent must not be fruitless.—V. During Lent the mercy and clemency of rulers should be imitated.

## CHAPTER I

Although the approaching Paschal festival and the return of the proper season itself indicate to us the Lenten fast, an exhortation from our sermon must nevertheless also be added—one which, with the Lord’s help, will be neither useless to the sluggish nor burdensome to the devout.

For since the reason of these days demands that all our observance be increased, there is, as I trust, no one among you who does not gladly welcome encouragement toward good work.

Our nature, still subject to mortality, is changeable; and even if it advances toward the highest pursuits of virtue, just as it can always have somewhere to fall, so it can always have somewhere to grow.

And this is the true righteousness of the perfect: that they never presume themselves to be perfect, lest, ceasing their pursuit along a road not yet completed, they fall into the danger of failing precisely where they have abandoned the desire to advance.

Therefore, beloved, since none of us is so perfect and holy that he cannot be more perfect and holier still, let us all together, without distinction of rank or discrimination of merits, run with devout eagerness from the things we have reached toward those we have not yet attained, and let us add some necessary increase to the measure of our customary practice.

For a person is shown to be scarcely religious at another time if he is not found more religious during these days.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, appropriately, the reading of the Apostle’s preaching has sounded in our ears, saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2).

For what is more acceptable than this time, what more beneficial than these days, in which war is declared against vices and progress in all virtues is increased?

Certainly, Christian soul, you have always had to keep watch against the adversary of your salvation, lest any opening be left for the tempter’s snares. But now greater caution and more attentive prudence must be exercised, since your same enemy rages with sharper envy.

For now, throughout the whole world, the power of his ancient domination is being taken away from him, and countless vessels of captivity are being snatched from him. From peoples of every nation and every language, the most savage robber is renounced; and no kind of human being is now found that does not resist his tyrannical laws, while throughout all the regions of the earth countless thousands are being prepared for rebirth in Christ. As the birth of the new creation approaches, spiritual wickedness is driven out from those whom it possessed.

Therefore the impious fury of the dispossessed enemy rages and seeks a new gain, because he has lost his former right. Tireless and ever watchful, he looks for any sheep that he may find wandering carelessly from the sacred flocks, so that he may lead them through the slopes of pleasure and the descents of luxury into the lodging places of death.

Thus he inflames anger, nurtures hatred, sharpens desires, mocks continence, and incites gluttony.

## CHAPTER III

### Notes

- **[Col. 0263D]** The first edition has *non possent* (“could not”). This would have to be written in that form if the sentence referred to the preceding part and to the verb *premerentur* (“were oppressed”). But with the punctuation changed, this clause refers to what follows; therefore the common reading, which is also found in the better codices, has not been changed.
- **[Col. 0263D]** Two manuscripts of St. Peter have *et* (“and”) instead of *etiam* (“also”), as was read in the editions preceding Quesnellus and also occurs in some codices.
- **[Col. 0263D]** Thus from our codices and the editions preceding Quesnellus, who, without indicating any authority, wrote *corporeae* (“bodily”). Shortly afterward, in the two praised codices of St. Peter, we find *perniciosissimum* (“most destructive”), which he preferred instead of *perniciosum* (“destructive”).
- **[Col. 0264C]** Thus in the codices of St. Peter mentioned above. Others have *hominis* (“of a human being”). Shortly afterward, the same codices omit *autem* (“however”).
- **[Col. 0264C]** Most codices and all editions before Quesnellus have *instruenda* (“to be built”), while he has *struenda*. In the manuscripts of St. Peter, *fruenda* (“to be enjoyed”).
- **[Col. 0264C]** The editions preceding Quesnellus, as well as the later manuscript collections, had: “For, knowing that we are carrying out the most sacred …” But he wrote *adesse* (“to be present”) instead of *agere nos* (“that we are carrying out”), and we found the same reading in two Lectionaries of St. Peter. It is required by the following chapter: “Therefore, approaching, beloved, the beginning of Lent.”
- **[Col. 0264D]** Thus the Thuan and Corbey manuscripts, better than *inveniamur indigni* (“we may be found unworthy”), which is read in the common editions. For our author alludes to the command concerning legal purity, which in the Old Testament was necessary for celebrating the Pasch. Quesnellus: “It is likewise written in the codices of St. Peter and in manuscript Collection 2.” From these we have coherently added *eis* (“for them”) instead of *nobis* (“for us”), which Quesnellus retained, but improperly, since it refers to *celebraturi* (“we who are about to celebrate”): Leo says that they “may be found,” whereas *nobis* is found in those codices that read *agere nos* and *inveniamur indigni*.
- **[Col. 0264D]** The two manuscripts of St. Peter have *animos* (“souls”) instead of *animas* (“souls”); the difference is grammatical rather than substantive.

- **[Col. 0265C]** Before Quesnellus the reading was: “not only as by God but also as by a human being he was attacked and conquered.” He corrected it from three codices, Victor, Thuan, and Corbey; the correction is confirmed by two Lectionaries of St. Peter, the Bononiensis codex, and manuscript Collection 2.
- **[Col. 0265C]** Thus in the Thuan and Corbey manuscripts. Others have *sine perturbationibus* (“without disturbances”), which is plainly corrupt and devoid of good sense, whereas the present reading agrees with Paul’s teaching and words. Quesnellus: “Likewise in our codices of St. Peter and Collection 2.”
- **[Col. 0265C]** Others have *insidiatorum* (“of those lying in wait”). The correction of Quesnellus is approved by the manuscripts of St. Peter.
- **[Col. 0265D]** Earlier editions had *divinis institutionibus eruditi* (“instructed by divine institutions”). We preferred the reading of the manuscripts of St. Peter and Collection 2, also confirmed by the Corbey and Thuan exemplars cited by Quesnellus. One Vatican manuscript of Collection 4 has *divinis instructionibus eruditi* (“instructed by divine teachings”).
- **[Col. 0265D]** The two codices praised by Quesnellus, Corbey and Thuan, have *adversus mundi rectores, mundi hujus tenebrarum harum* (“against the rulers of the world, of this world’s darkness”). Two manuscripts of St. Peter and two Vatican manuscripts have *adversus rectores mundi hujus tenebrarum*, omitting *harum* (“of these”). The codices of Collection 2 have the text as here and as in the common Scripture.
- **[Col. 0265D]** One manuscript of St. Peter has *quo* (“by which”).
- **[Col. 0265D]** The first edition has *tela nequitiae ignea* (“the fiery darts of wickedness”). *Ignita* (“fiery”) for *ignea* (“fiery”) occurs in the Corbey and Thuan manuscripts, as Quesnellus notes. Shortly afterward, one manuscript of St. Peter has *assumere* (“to take”) instead of *assumite* (“take”).
