- **[Col. 0266C]** Thus all our codices and the editions preceding Quesnellus, who, for reasons unknown, wrote *ab impudentiae incentore* (“by the instigator of shamelessness”), although the clause refers to “he girded the loins with the belt of chastity.”
- **[Col. 0266C]** Some editions, together with certain codices, had: “Let the light of truth drive away the darkness of falsehood, for the mouth that lies kills the soul of the liar. Let pride subside, let humility be assumed, let anger recover its senses.” Quesnellus substituted *simulationis* (“of dissimulation”) for *mendacii* (“of falsehood”) and retained the common text in the rest, deleting “let humility be assumed,” because, he says, it is absent from the manuscripts and breaks the thread of the prayer. He also noted in the margin that the words “for the mouth that lies kills the soul of the liar” are absent from the Corbey and Thuan manuscripts. We too have excluded them, because they are additionally absent from the ancient and more reliable Lectionaries of St. Peter and from the manuscripts of the better collections, which present the reading inserted into the text. Then, instead of *noxarum* (“of harmful deeds”), which is found in the ancient Lectionaries and older manuscript collections, the exemplar of the first edition has *noxiarum* (“harmful”). Since this scribal error was not detected, the substantive *cogitationum* (“thoughts”) was added in later manuscript collections to complete the sense.
- **[Col. 0267C]** Thus, more correctly, from a manuscript of St. Peter, rather than *traderet et illigaret* (“handed over and bound”), as was found in the editions.
- **[Col. 0267C]** We have substituted *ut* (“so that”) as the better reading from the Lectionaries of St. Peter.
- **[Col. 0267C]** Quesnellus noted in the margin that the following sentence is absent from the Corbey and Thuan manuscripts.

- **[Col. 0267C]** *Potissimum* (“especially effective”) seemed preferable to *potentissimum* (“most powerful”), from the same codices of St. Peter and one Vatican manuscript. A little earlier, instead of *quia facile* (“since easily”), some codices have *qua facile* (“by which easily”). Shortly afterward, *ut remittat* (“so that he may forgive”) occurs instead of *ut remittatur* (“so that it may be forgiven”); and then the manuscripts of St. Peter have *optamus* (“we desire”) instead of *precamur* (“we pray”).
- **[Col. 0267D]** The codices of St. Peter have *peragit* (“observes/fulfills”).

- **[Col. 0267D]** Thus, together with the first edition and another Cologne edition of 1547, several of our codices; and better than Quesnellus’s reading with other common editions and manuscripts, *ad opus horum* (“for the work of these”). In the following sentence the Padiliron codex has *potest habere quo recedat* (“can have somewhere to withdraw”).
- **[Col. 0267D]** Most codices, together with the editions preceding Quesnellus, have *necessarii aliquid addamus augmenti* (“let us add some necessary increase”). We have retained Quesnellus’s reading, which is approved by the manuscripts of St. Peter and Padiliron.
- **[Col. 0267D]** This is indeed the same reading of Paul’s Epistle that today resounds throughout the Church in the first nocturn and at Mass. It therefore proves the antiquity of the ecclesiastical office and refutes the error of Theodemar, abbot of Monte Cassino, or of Paul the Deacon, writing in his name to the emperor Charlemagne. He says that, at the time when Saint Benedict was writing his Rule, it was not customary in the Roman Church, as it is now, to read the sacred Scriptures. From Gelasius and others, the learned Mabillon proves this opinion false in his inquiry into the Gallican Course, p. 385. Leo, older than Gelasius by many years, also supports this, both here and in many other places: for example, at the beginning of Sermon 41 (now 42), or Sermon 4 on Lent: “About to preach … what more suitable beginning could I use than to begin with the words of the Apostle … and say what has been read: Behold, now is the acceptable time, etc.” Sermon 50 (now 52), the first on the Passion of the Lord, indicates that on that day the Passion narrative had been read from the Gospel. The same is indicated by the closing words of Sermon 3 on the Passion, and by the opening of Sermon 13 (now 15), which attributes this custom to the whole Church. See also Sermon 18, chapter 2, and Sermon 19, chapter 1, where he observes that the Gospel reading on the Passion had been carried out according to custom; and Sermon 2 on the Resurrection, or rather on Holy Saturday; and Sermon 94 (now 51), on the Gospel of the Transfiguration of the Lord. Quesnellus: shortly afterward, instead of *acceptum* (“accepted”), the first edition, together with some manuscripts, has *acceptabile* (“acceptable”), as is also read in Sermon 42, chapter 1.
- **[Col. 0269C]** The printed editions have *assumenda prudentia est* (“prudence must be adopted”). We preferred the manuscripts of St. Peter, from which we have also shortly afterward written *terrarum* (“of the lands”) instead of *terrae* (“of the earth”); the Padiliron codex confirms this.
- **[Col. 0269C]** Thus from the same codices of St. Peter and one Vatican manuscript. Others, together with the editions, have *excluditur* (“is excluded”). Shortly afterward, instead of *perdidit* (“he lost”), two Vatican manuscripts have *perdit* (“he loses”).
- **[Col. 0269C]** One manuscript of St. Peter and another Vatican manuscript, together with some printed editions, have *per proclivia* (“through the slopes”). Shortly afterward, one Vatican manuscript has *acuit cupiditates* (“sharpens desires”) instead of *movet cupiditates* (“moves desires”).

For who would he not dare to tempt, when he did not refrain from attempting his fraud even against our Lord Jesus Christ? [Note: [Col. 0269D] Thus, with Quesnellus, one manuscript of St. Peter’s and another of Padiliron. Others have *conatum* (“attempt”), as does the printed text.] For, as the Gospel narrative disclosed, when our Savior, who was true God, wished also to demonstrate himself truly human and to exclude the impious opinions of every error, after fasting forty days [Note: [Col. 0269D] Paul the Deacon’s copy omits “and nights.”] and nights, he had taken upon himself the hunger of our weakness. The devil rejoiced, thinking that he had found in him a sign of a suffering and mortal nature, and wished to test the power which he feared: “If you are the Son of God,” he said, “command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matt. 4:2).

The Almighty certainly could do this, [Note: [Col. 0269D] Thus, with Quesnellus, two manuscripts of St. Peter’s and one Vatican manuscript; others have *itaque* (“therefore”).] and it would have been easy, at the Creator’s command, for any creature to change into whatever form it was ordered to assume, [Note: [Col. 0269D] Others have *natura* (“nature”) in the margin of the editions, as well as in Paul the Deacon’s Homily and the Padiliron manuscript.] just as, when he wished, he changed water into wine at the wedding feast (John 2:9). [Note: [Col. 0269D] Thus our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus, which have *apud quem* (“with whom”); one Padiliron manuscript supports *nuptiarum* (“of the wedding”).] But it accorded more closely with the dispositions that bring salvation [Note: [Col. 0269D] Others have *dispensationibus* (“dispensations”), as in Paul the Deacon’s Homily and two Vatican manuscripts. The manuscripts of St. Peter’s have the reading in the text. They also prefer *superbissimi* (“most proud”), which was read in the printed editions as *nequissimi* (“most wicked”), in accordance with Quesnellus’s emendation. This reading seemed preferable because the Roman pontiff sets the mystery of humility against the demon’s pride.] that the cunning of the most proud enemy should be overcome by the Lord, not through the power of the Godhead [Note: [Col. 0270C] We have added “by the Lord” from two Lectionaries of St. Peter’s, in which there follows immediately: “and the tempter, frustrated in all his arts,” as we have printed after Quesnellus. In the other editions, in several manuscripts, and in Paul the Deacon’s Homily, the reading is: “and all the arts of the crafty tempter having been shattered.”] but through the mystery of humility.

Finally, when the devil had been put to flight and the tempter frustrated in all his arts, [Col. 0270A] angels came to the Lord and ministered to him. Thus, in the true man and true God, his humanity remained inviolate amid the deceitful questions, while his divinity was made manifest through the holy ministrations. Therefore let the sons and disciples of the devil be confounded [Note: [Col. 0270D] Three manuscripts have *igitur* (“therefore”).]—those who, filled with viperous inspiration, deceive the simple by denying that both natures are truly present in Christ, stripping either the Godhead from the man or the man from the Godhead, although both falsehoods were destroyed by a twofold demonstration at the same moment: for perfect humanity was shown through the hunger of the body, [Note: [Col. 0270D] The Bonn manuscript and the first edition have “true humanity.” Thereafter, in that edition and three other manuscripts, “manifest divinity.”] and perfect divinity through the angels who ministered to him.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, beloved, since we have been taught by the instruction of our Redeemer that “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Matt. 4:4; Deut. 8:3), it is fitting that the Christian people, however great their abstinence, should desire more to satisfy themselves with God’s word than with bodily food. Let us therefore undertake the solemn fast with ready devotion and joyful faith—not as a barren deprivation, which bodily weakness and the disease of greed often impose [Note: [Col. 0270D] The first edition has *inducit* (“induces”). In some manuscripts, *scilicet* (“namely”) is absent.]—but as something to be celebrated in generous benevolence, so that we may belong to those of whom Truth itself says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

Let works of mercy, then, be our delights, and let us be filled with those foods that nourish us for eternity. [Note: [Col. 0270D] Paul the Deacon’s copy has “that nourish us.”] Let us rejoice in the refreshment of the poor, whom our expenditures have satisfied. Let us take pleasure in clothing those whose nakedness we have covered with necessary garments. Let the sick who lie bedridden, the weakness of the feeble, the hardships of exiles, the abandonment of orphans, and the sorrow of widows feel our humanity; [Note: [Col. 0270D] Thus in Quesnellus and in the manuscripts of St. Peter’s. Others have *lamenta* (“lamentations”). Shortly afterward, one manuscript of St. Peter’s has *non aliquam habere possit* (“may be unable to have any”), in place of *non aliquam possit exsequi* (“is unable to perform some”).] [Col. 0270C] in helping them, no one is unable to perform some share of benevolence.

For no one has scant resources if he has a generous spirit; nor does the measure of compassion or piety depend only upon one’s household means. [Note: [Col. 0270D] We have restored, on the authority of the editions before Quesnellus and of the better manuscripts, the reading of the editors. Only the first edition prefers “and of piety.” Quesnellus has “the measure of piety depends upon [one’s means],” and the Venetian manuscript has a somewhat different wording, “the measure of piety depends upon [one’s means].”] Even in limited means, the abundance of a good will is never without reward. The expenditures of the rich are indeed greater and those of people of moderate means smaller; but the fruit of their works does not differ when the affection of those who act is the same. [Note: [Col. 0271C] Two manuscripts of St. Peter’s have “does not differ.” Paul the Deacon’s copy has “does not disagree,” and one Vatican manuscript has “is not lacking.”]

## CHAPTER V

In this opportunity, beloved, for exercising the virtues, there are also distinguished crowns [Note: [Col. 0271C] The editions before Quesnellus have “distinguished works of crowns”; one Vatican manuscript and Padiliron have “distinguished works of virtues.”] that can be won without loss from the granaries or diminution of money: if wantonness is driven away, if drunkenness is renounced, and carnal desire is subdued by the laws of chastity; if hatreds pass into love, if enmities are changed into peace, if tranquility extinguishes anger, if gentleness forgives injury; and finally, if the conduct of masters and servants is so ordered that the authority of the former is milder and the discipline of the latter more dutiful.

By this observance, beloved, the mercy of God will be obtained, and with the guilt of sins abolished, Easter, which must be religiously venerated, will be celebrated. The most devout emperors of the Roman world also preserve the ancient sacred institutions by their observance; [Note: [Col. 0271C] Although “of the Roman City” occurs in two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, supported by the Venetian manuscript in its use of *Urbis*, we have not wished to remove the common reading, which is preferred by the Casinense manuscript of Collection 1 and by manuscripts of Collections 3, 4, and 5. For emperors are usually called “of the Roman world,” not “of the Roman City.” The Venetian manuscript, which has *Romani*, indicates that *Urbis* was erroneously written for *Orbis*. Manuscripts of Collection 2 read differently: “which both the Roman City and the most devout emperors preserve.” Yet what follows applies only to the emperors. Then the Venetian manuscript, the Casinense manuscript of Collection 1, and other manuscripts of Collection 2 have “preserve the sacred institutions established long ago.” Since the preceding accusative *quod* does not admit another accusative, *sancta instituta* was corrected by a later hand in the Casinense manuscript to *institutione*. A related common reading is “preserve by the sacred observance established in antiquity.” We have inserted into the text the reading of two manuscripts of St. Peter’s as the better one, and from them have also written “in honor of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection.” The editions before Quesnellus lacked “and Resurrection”; Quesnellus has “in honor of the Passion and Resurrection of Christ,” as does the Venetian manuscript.] they bow the height of their power in honor of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, and, with the severity of their laws softened, they order many guilty persons to be released. [Note: [Col. 0272C] The editions, together with some manuscripts, have “they order them to be released.” We judged that the two Lectionaries of St. Peter’s should not be abandoned. On this matter, compare the observation in Sermon 45, to be placed among the observations after the appendix.] Thus, during the days when the world is saved by divine mercy, their clemency too may be imitated as a reflection of heavenly goodness. [Note: [Col. 0272C] In the same manuscripts of St. Peter’s and in the Venetian manuscript: “that even their clemency may be honored.” “Let them imitate, therefore” follows. The common reading, found also in very many manuscripts, accords better with what follows.]

Let Christian peoples imitate their rulers and be encouraged to domestic forgiveness by royal examples. For private laws must not rightly be more severe than public ones. Let offenses be forgiven, bonds loosed, injuries erased, and vengeance abolished, so that the sacred festival, through divine and human [Col. 0271C] grace, may have all rejoicing and all innocent: through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen. [Note: [Col. 0272C] Thus from the manuscripts of St. Peter’s. Quesnellus has “through mercy,” a reading found in Vatican manuscript Collection 5. The other editions and several manuscripts have “through benevolence”; one Vatican manuscript has “through clemency.”]

# SERMON XLI [Elsewhere XL]  
## On Lent III

[Col. 0272A]

### Synopsis

I. With what purity of conscience the fast ought to be celebrated, and how each person should examine himself.  
II. The devil’s boldness in tempting Christ ought to make us more cautious, especially at this season.  
III. The fast is sanctified by mercy.

## CHAPTER I

It is always fitting, beloved, for us to live wisely and holily [Note: [Col. 0272D] On the authority of the majority and better manuscripts, we have restored the adverb *sancte* (“holily”), in place of which Quesnellus substituted *juste* (“justly”), as it is found in some other manuscripts. After “the heart,” manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5 delete “our.”] and to direct our wills and actions toward what we know is pleasing to divine justice. But when those days approach that have been made brighter for us by the mysteries of our salvation, our hearts must be cleansed with more diligent care, and the discipline of virtue must be exercised more earnestly. Thus, just as the mysteries themselves are greater in a certain respect, so our observance may surpass its customary measure in some way; and whoever has a more exalted festival to celebrate may also be found more adorned for it.

For if it seems reasonable and in some sense religious to go out on a feast day in brighter clothing [Note: [Col. 0272D] Two manuscripts and Paul the Deacon’s copy add “and in bodily appearance.”] and to display the joy of the mind through the body’s attire; if at that time we also adorn, as far as we can, the very house of prayer with more attentive care and greater dignity, is it not fitting that the Christian soul, which is the true and living temple of God, should wisely adorn its appearance and, as it prepares to celebrate the mystery of its redemption, take every precaution lest any stain of iniquity darken it or a wrinkle of a divided heart disfigure it?

For what benefit is there in outward dress that displays the form of decency if the inner parts of a person are soiled by the contamination of some vices? [Note: [Col. 0272D] Others have *contagione* (“contagion”), as Quesnellus notes in the margin. Shortly afterward, three Thuanus manuscripts cited by him have *eliminatione* (“elimination”) in place of *elimatione* (“polishing”).] [Col. 0272C] Everything, therefore, that clouds the purity of the soul and the mirror of the mind must be diligently wiped away and made clearer through a kind of polishing. [Note: [Col. 0272D] The editions have “must be scraped away.” “Let each person examine himself,” and so forth. We preferred the reading of the St. Peter’s manuscript. Paul the Deacon’s Homily has “and set before him the judgment of his own conscience.”] examination.

Let each person scrutinize his conscience and place himself before himself under the scrutiny of his own judgment. Let him see whether, in the secrecy of his heart, he finds that peace which Christ gives (John 14:27); whether the desire of the spirit is attacked by no lust of the flesh; whether he does not despise what is humble; whether he does not seek what is exalted; whether he takes pleasure in unjust profit; whether he rejoices excessively in the increase of his possessions; and finally, whether he burns with envy at another’s happiness or rejoices at an enemy’s misery.

And if, upon sincere examination, he perhaps finds none of these disturbances in himself, let him investigate what kinds of thoughts habitually occupy him; whether he yields to no images of vanities, or how quickly he withdraws his mind from those things that flatter it harmfully. [Note: [Col. 0273D] Paul the Deacon’s manuscript adds “of the heart,” and for *disquirat* (“investigate”) that manuscript, another Bonn manuscript, and the first edition have *discutiat* (“examine”).]

For to be moved by no allurements and tickled by no desires is not a condition of this life, which is entirely temptation (Job 7:1); and the one who does not fear being conquered by it is surely conquered by it. It is arrogant to presume that one can easily avoid sin, since this very presumption is itself sin, as the blessed apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). [Note: [Col. 0273D] In the same copy of Paul the Deacon, *tentationibus* (“temptations”) stands in place of *illecebris* (“allurements”). One Vatican manuscript has *nimium* (“excessively”) for *nimirum* (“surely”); later, Paul the Deacon has *peccasse sit* (“it should be to have sinned”) for *peccatum sit* (“it is sin”).]

## CHAPTER II

Let no one, therefore, beloved, deceive himself; let no one mislead himself. [Note: [Col. 0273D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s inserts *ita* (“so”). Shortly afterward, the first edition has *videt* (“he sees”) for *viderit* (“he has seen”).] Let no one so trust in the purity of his heart as to think himself subject to no dangers of temptation, since that ever-watchful tempter attacks with more violent snares those whom he sees most abstaining from sins.

For from whom would he restrain his deceit, when he dared to tempt even the Lord of majesty by the fraud of his cunning? [Note: [Col. 0272D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s has: “who by his deceit tempted the Lord of majesty himself.”] He had seen his own pride trampled beneath the humility of the baptized Lord Jesus. He had understood that every desire of the flesh had been excluded by a fast of forty days [Note: [Col. 0274D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s has “that every desire of the flesh had been excluded during the space of forty days.” Paul the Deacon’s copy likewise has “desire of the flesh.”] and yet the spiritual wickedness of his malice did not despair of its devices. He presumed so much upon the mutability of our nature that, having found him to be truly human, he supposed that he could become a sinner.

If, then, the devil did not withdraw the snares of his deceptions from our Lord and Savior himself, how much more boldly will he attack our weakness, [Note: [Col. 0274D] This reading of the first edition and several manuscripts is better than the common reading, *praesumit* (“he presumes”).] whom he has pursued with more vehement hatred and fiercer envy ever since we renounced him in baptism and passed by divine rebirth from the origin over which he ruled into a new creation!

Therefore, since, while we are clothed in mortal flesh, our ancient enemy never ceases to spread the snares of sin everywhere before us, and rages most fiercely against Christ’s members when they are about to celebrate the holier mysteries, the teaching of the Holy Spirit rightly instructs the Christian people through this discipline, so that they may prepare themselves for the Easter festival by forty days of self-restraint.

The purpose of this purification now invites us to observe its salutary practice and imposes upon us diligence in the chastisement we have undertaken. [Note: [Col. 0274D] Three of our manuscripts have “of a more disciplined purpose.”] For the holier each person is found to have spent these days, the more religiously he will be proved to have honored the Lord’s Pascha.

## CHAPTER III

During these days of the holy fasts, then, let us perform more abundantly the works of piety to which we ought always to devote ourselves: “Let us be merciful to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10). Thus, even in the distribution of alms, let us imitate the goodness of our heavenly Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45).

Although the poverty of the faithful should especially be assisted, nevertheless even those who have not yet received the Gospel should be pitied in their labor. For the fellowship of nature is to be cherished in all human beings [Note: [Col. 0274D] The word “human beings” has been added from our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus.], and it ought to make us kind even toward those who are subject to us in any condition—especially if they have already been reborn by the same grace and redeemed by the price of Christ’s blood.

For we have in common with them that we were created in the image of God. They are not separated from us by bodily origin or spiritual birth. We are sanctified by the same Spirit, we live by the same faith, and we hasten to the same sacraments. Let this unity not be despised, nor let so great a fellowship be cheap in our eyes. Rather, let the very fact that we exercise authority over them make us gentler in all things, since with them we are subject in the same service to one Lord.

If, therefore, any of these have offended their masters by more serious offenses, let them receive pardon now, during these days of reconciliation. Let compassion remove severity, and forgiveness erase vengeance. Let no one be held in custody; let no one be confined in prison, because our God has promised his mercy on this condition: that the person who has forgiven another’s sins should know that his own sins will be forgiven (Matt. 18:33).

Let the causes of dissension and the barbs of enmity be crushed, beloved. Let hatreds cease and quarrels come to an end. Let all the members of Christ come together in the unity of love. For “blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9)—not sons only, but also heirs, and fellow heirs with Christ (Rom. 8:17), [Note: [Col. 0274D] The manuscript of St. Peter’s adds “our Lord,”] who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XLII [Elsewhere XLI]  
## On Lent IV

### Synopsis

I. Lent was salutarily instituted for cleansing the stains of souls.  
II. One should pursue every virtue during this season; virtues are measured according to the will.  
III. The devil lies in wait even through piety; the order and method of his temptations against Christ are explained.  
IV. The perverse abstinence of the Manichaeans.  
V. That the same people fast in honor of the sun and moon on Sunday and Monday, abstain from participation in Christ’s blood, and so forth.  
VI. How Lent may be sanctified through works of virtue.

## CHAPTER I

As I am about to preach to you, beloved, of this most holy and greatest fast, [Note: [Col. 0275C] One manuscript of St. Peter’s has “the most sacred fast of Lent.”] what opening could I use more suitably than to begin with the words of the Apostle, in whom Christ was speaking, and say what has been read: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now are the days of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2)?

Although there are no times that are not filled with divine gifts, and access to God’s mercy is always granted to us through his grace, nevertheless now all minds ought to be moved with greater zeal toward spiritual progress and animated with greater confidence, since the return of the day on which we were redeemed invites us to every work of piety. Thus, with both bodies and souls purified, we may celebrate the surpassing mystery of the Lord’s Passion.

Indeed, unceasing devotion and continuous reverence were owed to such great mysteries, so that we might remain before God such as it is fitting for us to be found at the Easter festival itself. But because this strength belongs to few, and stricter observance is relaxed on account of the weakness of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0275C] This reading is better in the manuscripts of St. Peter’s and four other manuscripts than the reading in the printed editions, “the weakness of the flesh.”], while the concerns of this life stretch us through various activities, it is necessary that even devout hearts become soiled by the dust of the world.

In the great healing provision of divine instruction, therefore, it was arranged that a forty-day exercise should remedy us by restoring the purity of our minds, so that during these days pious works might redeem the sins of other times [Col. 0275C] and chaste fasts purge them.

## CHAPTER II

As we enter, beloved, these mystical days consecrated by the remedies of fasting, let us take care to obey the apostolic commands and cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit (2 Cor. 7:1). [Note: [Col. 0275C] Thus in two very ancient manuscripts, from Corbie and the Royal Library, as will be discussed below. In place of these words, the common editions read: “And instituted more sacredly for the purification of souls and bodies.” I think these words were substituted by those who adapted this sermon to another solemnity, one not consecrated by the same number of days of fasting. —Quesnellus. This correction is also confirmed by the Lectionaries of St. Peter’s and Padiliron, and by that of St. Anthony at Padua, as well as by manuscripts of the older collections. The rejected reading, found in manuscripts of the later collections and in Paul the Deacon’s Homily, is foreign to this passage, as is evident from the fact that almost the same sentence, expressed in nearly the same words, belongs to Sermon 78, on the fast of Pentecost, chapter 1. There it more appropriately concerns the fast itself rather than the mystical days: “The solemn fast, salutarily instituted for the healing of souls and bodies,” and so forth. The same wording is also found in a collect of the ancient Veronese Sacramentary, where it is assigned to the fast of the fourth month, namely the Pentecost fast. Since it is clear from many documents that, from the time of Charlemagne onward, Lent began on Ash Wednesday, this collect was perhaps transferred at that time from the Pentecost fast to the Lenten fast. Just as it is now read on the Saturday before the First Sunday of Lent, so it was also read on that Saturday in those days; hence, in the common Gelasian Sacramentary, which received certain additions, it is placed on the seventh day of Quinquagesima. Perhaps for this reason the reading of this collect was inserted into the Leonine sermon, which was formerly read on the First Sunday of Lent, just as it is still recited with the same reading at the second nocturn. Immediately afterward, in place of “the commands of the Apostle,” we restored “the apostolic commands” from all our manuscripts, from Paul the Deacon’s Homily, and from several editions.]

Thus, after disciplining the struggles between the two substances, let the mind—established under God’s guidance and rightly appointed ruler of its body—obtain the dignity of its dominion, so that, giving offense to no one, we may not be liable to the reproaches of slanderers.

For we shall rightly be censured by unbelievers, and by our fault impious tongues will arm themselves against religion, if the conduct of those who fast differs from the purity of perfect self-restraint. For the essence of our fast does not consist solely in abstaining from food, nor is food profitably withdrawn from the body [Note: [Col. 0276D] Three manuscript Lectionaries have “unless the mind.”] unless the mind is recalled from iniquity and the tongue restrained from slander.

Let our freedom in eating [Note: [Col. 0276D] Thus two of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, two of ours from St. Peter’s, and others of better authority. The printed editions and manuscripts of the later collections have *moderanda* (“to be moderated”). The old and true reading is retained in the Padua Lectionary, though it was recognized as corrupt and the new reading adopted. It reads: “The freedom of eating and chastising is to be moderated.”] therefore be disciplined in such a way that other desires too may be restrained by the same rule. This is a time for gentleness and patience, for peace and tranquility; during it, with every contamination of vice excluded, we must acquire an enduring possession of virtue. [Note: [Col. 0276D] We preferred this reading from the Lectionaries of St. Peter’s, Padiliron, Padua, and others. The printed editions have “to be obtained.” One Vatican manuscript and the first edition have “to be observed.”]

Now let the strength of devout minds become accustomed to forgive offenses, disregard insults, and forget injuries. Now let the faithful soul exercise itself through the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left (2 Cor. 6:7), so that through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute, neither praise may inflate nor reproach weary a secure conscience and steadfast integrity.

The modesty of the devout must not be gloomy but holy. No murmurs of complaint should be found in them, since the consolations of holy joys are never lacking to them. Let no reduction of earthly resources be feared in works of mercy. Christian poverty is always rich, because it possesses more than it lacks. [Note: [Col. 0276D] The Padua manuscript has “nor will it be able”; Padiliron has “nor could it.”]

It does not fear laboring in need in this world, since it has been granted to possess all things in the Lord of all things. Therefore, when people perform what is good, they need not fear at all that they will lack the means to act. The devotion of that Gospel widow was magnified even through two small coins [Note: [Col. 0276D] Paul the Deacon’s Homily has “small coins.” Immediately afterward, for *magnificata* (“magnified”), the editions before Quesnellus have “praised.” Padiliron alone has “more greatly praised.”] (Luke 21:2), and a free gift has its reward for a cup of cold water (Matt. 10:42). [Col. 0276C]

For the measure of benevolence is assessed according to the dispositions of the devout, and the effectiveness of compassion never abandons the person in whom compassion itself does not fail. [Note: [Col. 0277C] The first edition has “did not fail.” Thereafter, the editions before Quesnellus and some manuscripts, together with Paul the Deacon’s Homily, have “that widow,” instead of “the holy widow,” which we find in the same Lectionaries.]

The holy widow of Zarephath experienced this: during a time of famine, she set before blessed Elijah the food for one day, which was all she had (1 Kings 17:12), and, preferring the prophet’s hunger to her own necessity, she unhesitatingly spent her small amount of flour and little oil. Yet what she had faithfully distributed did not fail her. In the vessels emptied by her pious outpouring, a fountain of new abundance sprang up, [Note: [Col. 0277C] The reading of five of our better manuscripts seemed preferable; it is also found in two of Quesnellus’s manuscripts. Among the Latins, *facultas* means abundance and plenty. Perhaps some scribes did not fully understand it and substituted *ubertatis* (“of abundance”), which is found in other manuscripts and editions.] so that the fullness of her substance was not diminished for holy uses, since its depletion had not been feared.

## CHAPTER III

With regard to these practices, beloved, for which we trust that you have willingly prepared yourselves, do not doubt that the devil, who is the adversary of every virtue, envies them [Note: [Col. 0277C] Some editions before Quesnellus have “we do not doubt.” The Padua manuscript has “you do not doubt.” Immediately afterward, “the devil is the adversary of every virtue” occurs in Vatican manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5.] and arms the force of his malice for this purpose: to set snares for piety through piety itself, and, when he cannot overthrow people through distrust, to try to conquer them through glory.

The evil of pride is close to upright actions, and exaltation always lies in wait for virtues from nearby, because it is difficult for human praise not to captivate one who lives laudably, unless, as it is written, “the one who boasts should boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

Whose resolve would that most wicked enemy not dare to attack? Whose fast would he not seek to violate, when, as the Gospel reading has revealed, he did not restrain his deceptions even from the Savior of the world himself?

Alarmed by his fast of forty days and nights, he wished to investigate with great cunning whether Christ had this self-restraint as something granted or as something proper to himself, so that he would not fear that the works of his deceptions might be undone if Christ were of the same condition as his body. [Note: [Col. 0277D] Thus from the manuscripts of St. Peter’s, Padiliron, and Padua. Others have “craftily.” Immediately afterward, the editions before Quesnellus have “to be dissolved,” instead of “to be undone,” which our manuscripts support.]

First, therefore, by deception he examined whether Christ himself was the creator of substantial things [Note: [Col. 0277D] The Padua manuscript has “the creator of substantial things,”] who could change bodily things into whatever natures he wished; second, whether, beneath the appearance of human flesh, the Godhead was concealed, for whom it would be easy to make the air passable to him and to float earthly limbs through the void. [Note: [Col. 0277D] The first edition and the Bonn manuscript have *in quo vellet* (“into which he wished”); other editions have *in quae vellet* (“into which he wished”); two Vatican manuscripts have *in quod* (“into which”); Padua has *in quid* (“into what”). The reading of two manuscripts of St. Peter’s, the Padiliron manuscript, and Paul the Deacon’s copy seemed more congruent. Immediately afterward, three Lectionaries have “and to float earthly limbs through the void.”]

But when the Lord chose to set against him the righteousness of a true man rather than reveal the power of his divinity, he turned the ingenuity of his third deception to tempting the one in whom the signs of divine power had ceased, through the desire to rule, and by promising him the kingdoms of the world, to lead him into worship of himself.

But the wisdom of God made the devil’s prudence foolish: so that the proud enemy might be bound by the one whom he had once bound, and might not fear to persecute the one who had to be killed for the world. [Note: [Col. 0277D] The editions before Quesnellus, Paul the Deacon’s Homily, and several manuscripts have: “so that the proud enemy, seeing the man whom he had once overcome, would not fear to pursue the one who had to be killed for all.” We have retained the reading introduced by Quesnellus on the authority of the two excellent manuscripts from Corbie and the Royal Library, since it is also confirmed by the better manuscripts of St. Peter’s, Padiliron, Padua, and manuscripts of Collection 2. From all these we have written “for the world”; Quesnellus has “for all.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Let us therefore beware of the deceits of this adversary not only in the allurements of gluttony but also in the purpose of abstinence. For he who knew how to inflict death upon the human race through food also knows how to harm it through fasting itself. [Note: [Col. 0278C] Some manuscripts of the later collections, together with the editions before Quesnellus, have: “and, employing the Manichaeans as servants of the opposite deception, just as through the serpent he brought about the taking of what was forbidden, so through hunger he persuades people to avoid what is permitted.” We preferred the reading that Quesnellus substituted from his manuscripts, since we found it coherent with our manuscripts cited in the preceding note. With that reading, “through the serpent” should have been removed, and likewise “through hunger,” which Quesnellus nevertheless retained. It is absent from our manuscripts and seems to be excluded by the sense itself.]

By employing the Manichaeans as servants of the contrary fraud, he persuades people to avoid what is permitted just as he once prompted them to take what was forbidden.

Observance is indeed useful when, accustomed to a sparing diet, it restrains the appetite for luxuries. [Note: [Col. 0278D] The editions have “abstinence.” We preferred *observantia* (“observance”) from our best Lectionaries, especially since Leo frequently uses this word for fasting, as Jacobus Acamius notes in *On the Antiquity of the Veronese Sacramentary*, p. 89, citing Sermon 41, chapter 1; Sermon 49, chapter 3; Sermon 71, chapter 1; Sermon 75, chapter 1; and Sermon 86, chapter 3. In this sermon itself, chapter 5, the Manichaeans are said to be “polluted by their own observance.” Immediately afterward, the Padua manuscript has “small” instead of “sparing.”] But woe to the doctrine of those among whom even fasting becomes sin!

They condemn the natures of created things, to the injury of the Creator, and assert that those who eat are defiled by things whose creator, they maintain, is not God but the devil. Yet there is absolutely no evil substance, nor is there any nature belonging to evil itself. [Col. 0278C] For the good Author established all things good, and there is one Creator of all things, who made heaven and earth, the sea and everything in them (Ps. 145:6).

Whatever among these things has been granted to human beings for food and drink is holy and clean according to the quality of its kind. If it is consumed with immoderate greed, excess disgraces those who eat and drink; it is not the nature of the food or drink that contaminates them. For, as the Apostle says, “all things are clean to the clean.” But “to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean; rather, their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus 1:15).

## CHAPTER V
But you, beloved, holy offspring of the Catholic mother, whom the Spirit of God has instructed in the school of truth [Note: [Col. 0279C] Thus, with Quesnellus, the manuscripts of St. Peter, Patav., Padiliron., and Casin. Al.: “the Holy Spirit.” Then, following the appropriate reading in the example of Paul the Deacon, “with appropriate devotion,” instead of “with appropriate reason.”], regulate your freedom with fitting judgment, knowing that it is good even to abstain from what is lawful, and, when one must live more austerely, to distinguish foods in such a way that their use is set aside, but [Col. 0279B] their nature is not condemned. [Note: [Col. 0279C] The Vulgate edition reads: “Therefore let no impiety of this contagion besprinkle you.” Quesnellus’s reading is confirmed by six of our better manuscripts. Only Padilir., Patav., and Casin. have “because of their own” instead of “who by their own.”]

Therefore let no contagion of their error touch you—those who are polluted above all by their own observance, serving the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1:25), and devoting themselves to a foolish abstinence from the heavenly luminaries: [Note: [Col. 0279C] The printed editions had: “whom no one doubts to be Manichaeans, who were discovered to fast on Sunday and on the second day in honor of the sun and moon; by one act of their perversity they are twice impious and twice profane, since they instituted their fast both for the worship of the stars and for contempt of Christ’s Resurrection.” Quesnellus alone, following the common reading, noted regarding the words “whom no one doubts to be Manichaeans”: “I suspect that these words entered the text from a marginal note, since they seem both superfluous and are missing in the manuscript codices Corb. and Reg.; in their place those codices read: ‘Since they chose to fast in honor of the sun and moon on Sunday and the second day.’” Thus far Quesnellus. From extensive examination of the codices, we have discovered that the common reading occurs in the manuscripts of the three later collections from which the editions derive. The reading inserted by us into the text occurs in the Lectionaries of St. Peter, Padiliron., and Patav., as well as in the manuscripts Casin. collection 1 and Barber. collection 2. Two Lectionaries cited by Quesnellus agree with them, except for the words “first” and “second” of the Sabbath.]

since they chose to fast in honor of the sun and moon on the first and second days of the Sabbath, twice impious and twice profane by one work of their perversity, instituting their fast both for the worship of the stars and for contempt of the Lord’s Resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0279D] The editions before Quesnellus read: “For they reject the sacrament of human salvation and, just as they deny that Christ our Lord was born in the truth of our flesh, so they do not believe that he truly died and rose again.” So also the codices of the later collections. We found the reading restored by Quesnellus from the manuscripts Reg. and Corb. in the more excellent manuscript Lectionaries and collections mentioned in the preceding note.]

For they recoil from the sacrament of human salvation, and do not believe that Christ our Lord, truly born in the true flesh of our nature, truly suffered, was truly buried, and was truly raised. And for this reason they condemn the day [Note: [Col. 0280C] Thus our better codices, indeed also the manuscripts of collections 4 and 5. The editions read: “the day of our salvation and joy by the sorrow of their fast.”] of our joy by the sorrow of their fast. Although, to conceal their unbelief, they dare to attend our assemblies, they so restrain themselves in communion of the sacraments [Col. 0279C] [Col. 0280A] [Note: [Col. 0280C] Thus the same manuscripts of excellent quality. The editions read “mysteries.”] that sometimes, lest they be wholly unable to remain hidden, they receive Christ’s body with an unworthy mouth, but altogether refuse to drink the blood of our redemption. [Note: [Col. 0280C] The editions before Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of the later collections, read: “so that they may sometimes hide more safely, they receive Christ’s body with an unworthy mouth, but altogether decline to drink the blood of our redemption. We wish your holiness to know this for the following reason.” The correction introduced by Quesnellus and retained by us is supported by our better manuscripts. Only Patav., Padilir., and Casin. omit “altogether.”] We make this known to your holiness so that such people may be exposed to you by these indications, and that those whose sacrilegious hypocrisy has been detected [Note: [Col. 0280C] Some codices read “even to these.” The manuscripts of St. Peter, Patav., Padiliron., and Casin. read “even among their own.”] may be expelled from the fellowship of the holy by priestly authority. [Note: [Col. 0280C] The editions before Quesnellus, together with the codices not only of collections 3, 4, and 5 but also the Lectionaries of St. Peter and Padilir., add “marked and exposed” after “whose sacrilegious hypocrisy.”]

For concerning such people the blessed Apostle Paul gives the Church of God this careful warning, saying: [Note: [Col. 0280D] The codices Patav. and Padilir. read “We beg.” Then, “which you have heard” instead of “which you have learned,” in the first edition and manuscript Bon., where immediately afterward “from them” occurs instead of “from those.” Two codices of St. Peter, two Vatican codices, one Patav., and another Padilir. read “from these.”]

“But we beg you, brothers, to watch those who create dissensions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching that you have learned, and avoid them. For such people do not serve Christ the Lord but their own belly; and by smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. 16:17–18).

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0280B]

Therefore, beloved, sufficiently instructed by these admonitions of ours, which we have repeatedly impressed upon your ears against the detestable error [Note: [Col. 0280D] Quesnellus and our better manuscripts read “against the detestable sect.” Other printed editions read “against the detestable error.”], receive the holy days of Lent with devout observance, and prepare yourselves by works of mercy to obtain God’s mercy. Extinguish anger, [Note: [Col. 0280D] Quesnellus reads: “avoid hatreds, love unity, and anticipate one another with the honor of sincere humility.” He cites no manuscript and merely notes in the margin the reading of other editions: “lay aside hatreds, love unanimity, and anticipate one another with the sincere duties of humility.” We have followed the two manuscripts of St. Peter, Patav., Padilir., and Casin.] destroy hatreds, love unity, and anticipate one another with sincere acts of humility. Rule servants and those subject to you with equity; let none of them be tormented by confinement or chains. Let vengeance cease, let offenses be forgiven; let severity be changed into gentleness, indignation into meekness, discord into peace. Let everyone find us restrained, everyone peaceful, everyone kind, so that our fasts may be acceptable to God. To him we offer the sacrifice of true abstinence and true devotion only if we restrain ourselves from every evil: [Col. 0281A] [Note: [Col. 0281C] After the words “if we restrain ourselves from every evil,” other editions contain approximately twenty lines, including the following: “Therefore let us fast on the second, fourth, and sixth days,” and so forth. These lines have supplied ecclesiastical writers with abundant material for debate. We have judged that they should be removed from the context, relying both on the authority of five manuscripts and on several other arguments, which are considered at length in the dissertation on the Sabbath fast. Quesnellus. — We found these lines only in the manuscripts of later collections 3, 4, and 5, not in the manuscripts of collections 1 and 2, nor in the Lectionaries of St. Peter, Venet., Patav., Vallicell., Padiliron., etc. [Col. 0281D] The omitted words are: “Let us have no agreement, then, with the enemies of the cross of Christ, lest the holiness of the faithful be polluted by the company of the impious. Let light be separated from darkness, and let the sons of truth flee the sons of the devil. Nothing contaminated should be brought into the temple of the Lord, which is the Church of Christ, and nothing profane should be admitted, so that, with every impurity excluded from the inner chambers of the heart, our fast may be sanctified and we may be the eternal dwelling of the Holy Spirit, who may deign both always to possess and to govern us once cleansed from the filth of sins. Therefore let us fast on the second, fourth, and sixth days; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the blessed Apostle Peter, who, never ceasing to care for the flock entrusted to him, will obtain protection for us through his prayers. With God assisting us in all things,” and so forth.] with God almighty assisting us in all things [Note: [Col. 0281D] Codex Venet. adds “the Father.”], to whom, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, belong one Godhead and one majesty forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIII [formerly XLI]

[Note: [Col. 0281D] This sermon is found inserted in the appendix of the sermons of St. Augustine, to whom it is wrongly attributed in some manuscripts. There it is Sermon 148, formerly 36, formerly On Time 73.]

### On Lent V

### Synopsis

I. How a person cooperates with grace so as to be renewed inwardly, something necessary for everyone.

II. Few are unshaken by adversity or not inflated by prosperity.

III. Everyone is obliged to repent.

IV. Sins are especially erased by works of mercy.

## CHAPTER I

The apostolic teaching, beloved, [Note: [Col. 0282C] The exemplar of Paul the Deacon reads “statement.” Then the first edition: “that we may put off . . . and from day to day . . . be renewed.”] admonishes us that, putting off the old person with his deeds (Eph. 4:22; Col. 3:9), we should be renewed from day to day by holy conduct. For if we are God’s temple and the Holy Spirit dwells in our minds, since the Apostle says, “You are the temple of the living God” (1 Cor. 6:16), we must labor with great vigilance so that the receptacle of our heart may not be unworthy of so great a guest. And just as in buildings made by human hands careful provision is commendably taken so that, if anything has been damaged by the infiltration of rain, the violence of storms, or even age itself, prompt attention may restore it to wholeness [Note: [Col. 0282C] We have added “promptly” from the Homily of Paul the Deacon and the appendix of Augustine.], so we must constantly take care lest anything disordered, lest anything unclean, be found in our souls. For although our building cannot stand without the work of its craftsman [Note: [Col. 0282C] Thus, with Quesnellus and the first edition, two codices of St. Peter, another Vatican codex, the exemplar of Paul the Deacon, and the appendix of Augustine, with some others: “without its own work.”], and our structure cannot remain sound unless the protection of its creator is present, nevertheless, because we are rational stones and living material, the hand of our creator built us in such a way [Note: [Col. 0282C] This is better supported by Codex Venet. and the first edition than the reading of other editions, “builds.” Quesnellus’s note on the following words will be given in the observations on this sermon.], that the one who is being restored may work together with his builder. Therefore let human obedience not withdraw from God’s grace, nor fall away from that good without which it cannot itself be good. And if it encounters anything impossible or difficult in carrying out the commandments, let it not remain within itself, but return to the one who commands—who gives the command in order to awaken desire and provide assistance—as the prophet says: “Cast your thought upon God, and he himself will nourish you” (Ps. 54:23). [Note: [Col. 0282D] Some codices read “your concern.”]

[Note: [Col. 0282D] We restored the particle “and” from the first edition and the appendix of Augustine.]

Or does anyone presumptuously exalt himself so greatly, and presume himself to be so unharmed and so undefiled, that he now needs no renewal? Such confidence is wholly mistaken, and whoever believes himself immune from every wound amid the temptations of this life grows old through excessive vanity. Everything is full of dangers; everything is full of snares. Desires incite, enticements lie in wait, profits flatter, losses deter, the tongues of those who revile are bitter, and the mouths of those who praise are not always truthful [Note: [Col. 0282D] Codex Bon. and the first edition read “of those who flatter.”]. From one side hatred rages, from the other deceptive service misleads [Note: [Col. 0282D] The adjective “lying,” found in the editions, was relegated by Quesnellus to the margin. We have restored it from our manuscripts, the Homily of Paul the Deacon, the appendix of Augustine, and the context itself.], so that it is easier to avoid one who is quarrelsome than to evade one who is deceitful.

## CHAPTER II

Even in attaining the virtues there is such an uncertain measure and such an unreliable discernment [Note: [Col. 0282D] We restored the verb “is” from the first edition, two Vatican manuscripts, the Homily of Paul the Deacon, and the appendix of Augustine.], that if anyone can preserve the measures of the most subtle distinction between the boundaries of good and evil, it is difficult for integrity conscious of its own rectitude not to be bitten by the tongue of slanderers, and for one to escape the reproaches of the wicked when justice is his friend. When human thought turns to the very variations of temporal affairs, how many shadows confront it, how many errors of perverse opinions arise, so that complaints draw their material from the clash of opposites. For although [Note: [Col. 0282D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter read “all.”] the hearts of all the faithful do not doubt that divine providence is absent from no part or time of this world, nor that the outcomes of worldly affairs depend upon the power of the stars—which has no power—but that everything is arranged by the most just and merciful judgment of the highest King, since, as it is written, “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10), nevertheless, when certain things do not proceed according to our desires, and under the error of human judgment the cause of the wicked is often stronger than that of the just, it is very near and almost immediate that these things should shake even great minds [Note: [Col. 0283D] The exemplar of Paul the Deacon reads “stir up.”] and drive them into some unlawful complaint.

Indeed, through these very variations the most eminent prophet David admits that he was shaken almost to the point of danger, and says: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps nearly slipped, because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72:2–3). Since few possess such solid strength that they are shaken by no disturbance of inequalities, and since many of the faithful are corrupted not only by adversity but also by prosperity, careful treatment must be applied to heal the wounds by which human weakness is injured. For this reason I have briefly passed through some of the dangers with which this world is full, so that, when Scripture says, “Who can boast that he has a chaste heart, or that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:9), all may understand that they need both forgiveness of sins and the medicine of restoration.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: [Col. 0283D] The editions before Quesnellus read “we have recourse.”]

When, beloved, should we have recourse to divine remedies more appropriately than when the very sacraments of our redemption are presented to us according to the appointed course of time? In order to celebrate them more worthily, let us most beneficially prepare ourselves by a forty-day fast. For not only those who, through the mystery of Christ’s death and resurrection, are about to be regenerated into new life by baptism [Note: [Col. 0283D] Thus all our manuscripts and the editions of Leo before Quesnellus, as well as the exemplar of Paul the Deacon. Only the manuscripts of St. Peter read “about to be regenerated,” where a scribal error appears to have written “to be regenerated” instead of “regenerating.” From this perhaps it happened that other copyists transcribed only the word “to be regenerated,” omitting the other word “about to be,” as did the appendix of Augustine and Quesnellus.], but also all the peoples of the reborn, usefully and necessarily take up the protection of this sanctification: the former so that they may receive what they do not yet possess; the latter so that they may preserve what they have received. Since the Apostle says, “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Cor. 10:12), no one is supported by such firmness that he ought to be secure about his stability.

Let us therefore use, beloved, the venerable practices of this most healthful season, and with more watchful care wipe clean the mirrors of our hearts [Note: [Col. 0283D] The Vulgate editions have “purifications,” incorrectly. The better manuscripts and the appendix of Augustine, as in the first edition and Quesnellus, read “mirrors,” and rightly so: the holy pontiff is speaking of the conscience of the just, free from grave sins, which, like a mirror, must be carefully wiped even of the dust of lesser faults, lest they fall into more serious ones.]. For however chastely and soberly this mortal life may be led, it is nevertheless sprinkled with a certain dust of earthly conduct, and the brightness of minds created in the image of God is not so free from the smoke of all vanity that it cannot be darkened by any stain and does not always need polishing. If this is necessary even for the most cautious minds, how much more should it be desired by those who have passed through nearly the whole span of the year either more securely or perhaps more carelessly [Note: [Col. 0283D] Quesnellus, together with the exemplar of Paul the Deacon, the appendix of Augustine, Codex Venet., and the manuscripts of collections 4 and 5, has “perhaps” instead of “nearly”; he deletes it before “more carelessly.” The first edition has “perhaps” in both places. The reading inserted in the text, found in the other editions, is more suitable, and the manuscripts of St. Peter agree with it. The appendix of Augustine reads “they have passed through” instead of “they have passed.”]? We admonish them with due charity not to flatter themselves on the ground that the consciences of individuals cannot be open to us, since neither hidden places nor the barriers of walls exclude the eyes of God, who sees everything at once; and not only deeds and thoughts but also deeds yet to be done and thoughts yet to be conceived are known to him.

This, then, is the knowledge of the highest Judge; this is his terrifying gaze, to which every solid thing is passable and every secret is open; before which dark things shine, the mute answer, silence confesses, and the mind speaks without a voice. Let no one contemptuously regard God’s patience (Rom. 2:4) as impunity for his sins; nor, because he has not yet experienced God’s anger, let him suppose that he has not offended him. The reprieves of mortal life are not long, nor is the license of foolish desires lasting [Note: [Col. 0284D] Thus we have emended the text from two manuscripts of St. Peter and the Homily of Paul the Deacon. Some have “the license of pleasures.” Codex Vat. collection 4 reads “the license of foolish desires or the sweetness of pleasures.”] before it passes into the pain of eternal punishments, if, while the sentence of justice is suspended, the medicine of repentance is not sought.

## CHAPTER IV

Let us therefore flee to God’s mercy, which is present everywhere, and, so that the holy Pasch of the Lord may be celebrated with worthy observance, let the hearts of all the faithful sanctify themselves [Note: [Col. 0284D] We restored this reading from all our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus, which preferred the reading common to the appendix of Augustine: “the hearts of all the faithful may be sanctified.”]. Let cruelty grow mild, let anger become gentle, let everyone forgive one another’s faults, and let no one who asks forgiveness be an exactor of vengeance. For when we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), we bind ourselves with the harshest chains unless we fulfill what we profess. Therefore, if the most sacred covenant of this prayer has not been kept in all its conditions, at least now let each person examine his conscience and, by forgiving the offenses of others, obtain the abolition of his own sins.

For the Lord says: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses” (Matt. 6:14; 18:35; Luke 6:37). What one asks is not far from anyone, since the sentence of the judge depends upon the kindness of the petitioner: he is a merciful and just hearer of human prayers, and according to his own equity he has prescribed, by our gentleness, that he should have no right to exercise severity against those whom he finds not eager for revenge. Generosity is also fitting for merciful and gentle spirits. Nothing is more worthy than that a human being should imitate his creator and, according to the measure of his own resources, carry out the work of God.

For when the hungry are fed, the naked clothed, and the sick comforted, does not the hand of God, through the minister, complete his assistance [Note: [Col. 0284D] The Lectionary of St. Mark at Venice reads: “the gift of God’s assistance” (perhaps “hand”) “is fulfilled by the minister.”], and is not the kindness of the servant the gift of the Lord? Although he needs no helper for the effects of his mercy, he so tempered his omnipotence that he would aid human beings through human beings. And rightly thanks are returned to God for deeds of devotion, whose work is seen in his servants.

For this reason the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). [Note: [Col. 0285C] The first edition and the codices of collections 4 and 5 read “your light”; afterward, “glorify” instead of “magnify” occurs in one manuscript of St. Peter and another Vatican manuscript. All the editions read “so that, seeing your good works, they may magnify.” We preferred the reading of Codex Venet. St. Mark, since it agrees with the similar reading in Sermon 26, chapter 4, and Sermon 45, chapter 3.] He, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV [formerly XLIII]

[Note: [Col. 0285D] In the first edition and in the manuscripts of collection 3, this title reads: “On the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord, Sermon I,” and similarly in the following two sermons, which are entitled Sermons II and III. In the manuscripts of St. Peter the title continues: “On the Fast of Lent”; in others: “On Lent.”]

### On Lent VI

### Synopsis

I. Especially during Lent, the vices of the old self must be cleansed; no one is free from them.

II. Fasting must be joined with integrity of heart, unity of peace, and generosity in almsgiving, from which no one is excluded.

III. The spirit of pride and the desire for vengeance must be driven away by humility and gentleness.

## CHAPTER I

Indeed, beloved, “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Ps. 132:5), and for every believer the very nature of things is a lesson in worshiping God, since heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, proclaim the goodness and omnipotence of their creator, while the wondrous beauty of the elements that serve him [Note: [Col. 0285D] Codex Vat. reads “of the stars and elements”; another Vatican manuscript reads “of the stars and,” with the remainder supplied in the margin.] demands a fitting offering of thanks from the rational creature.

But when we return to these days that have been marked out more especially by the mysteries of human restoration, and that immediately precede the festival of Pasch, we are instructed to prepare ourselves more diligently through religious purification. For although at every time many live innocent lives, and the habit of good works commends very many to God [Note: [Col. 0285D] We restored “to God” from the editions before Quesnellus and from our manuscripts.], we must not trust so much in the integrity of our conscience that we suppose human frailty, living amid scandals and temptations [Note: [Col. 0285D] The editions after the first and before that of Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of collection 5, read: “so that human frailty, living amid scandals and temptations.” The first edition omits this phrase.], could not have stumbled into anything that wounded it. The most eminent prophet says: “Who can boast that he has a chaste heart, or that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:9). And again: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 19:13).

If, as experience proves, such is the condition of those who resist desires, struggle against the impulses of anger, and discipline even the secrets of their thoughts, that they can never fail to find in their hearts something to condemn and are often either deceived by hidden faults or burdened by those of others [Note: [Col. 0286C] The conjunction “and” is absent in several manuscripts of good quality.], then [Note: [Col. 0286C] The editions before Quesnellus and almost all our manuscripts omit the words “at this season we must consider more attentively,” and after “or burdened by those of others” continue: “What vices,” etc., so that Leo seems here to argue from the lesser to the greater, or from those who resist desires to others who do not struggle in the same way. But on that interpretation one would have to read “how great will they be,” to produce the force of a question. Since all editions and manuscripts read “are,” Quesnellus’s reading had to be retained, although we found it in only one otherwise excellent Casin. manuscript of collection 1.] at this season we must consider more attentively what vices, what illnesses, and how great the wounds are that require a more severe medicine, lest anyone be found alien to that sacrament by which the works of the devil are dissolved. For the distinctive character of the Paschal festival is that the whole Church rejoices in the remission of sins—not only those who are reborn through holy baptism, but also those who have long been counted among the adopted.

Although the washing of regeneration principally makes new people, nevertheless, because daily renewal against the rust of mortality remains necessary for everyone [Note: [Col. 0286D] The editions had “is always necessary for all.” Vatican collection 4 reads “is always from all,” corruptly. We corrected the text from two manuscripts of St. Peter and Patav., with which the codices of collections 2 and 5 agree. Shortly afterward, we read “progress” instead of “perfection,” from all our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus. The Paris edition of 1671 alone has “degrees between the perfect and imperfect.”], and there is no one among the stages of progress who ought not always to become better [Note: [Col. 0286D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter read “ought to be better.” Then, “on the day of regeneration and redemption” occurs in two Vatican manuscripts of collection 4. Quesnellus’s annotation on this passage will be found among the observations.], we must strive generally so that, on the day of redemption, no one may be found in the vices of the old self.

## CHAPTER II

What, then, beloved, it is fitting for each Christian to do at every time must now be carried out with greater care [Note: [Col. 0286D] Codex Vat. collection 4 adds “and more diligently.”] and devotion, so that the apostolic institution may be fulfilled by the forty-day fast—not merely by moderation in food, but above all by deprivation of vices. Since [Note: [Col. 0286D] Thus, with Quesnellus, two manuscripts of St. Peter. Others read “for this purpose.”] this discipline is undertaken for the purpose of removing the fuel of carnal desires, no form of self-restraint should be pursued more earnestly than that we should always be sober from unjust desire and fasting from dishonorable action.

This devotion does not exclude the sick or separate the weak, because integrity of spirit can be found even in a feeble and useless body, if the foundations of virtue are strengthened where the seat of depravity had been. And therefore the weakness of the flesh is sufficient as this affliction, which often exceeds the measure of voluntary hardship, provided only that the mind fulfills its duty, and that the person who does not indulge in bodily feasting is not nourished by iniquity.

To rational and holy fasts nothing is more usefully joined than the work of almsgiving, which under the single name of mercy contains many laudable acts of devotion, so that all the faithful may be equal in spirit even though unequal in resources. For the love owed simultaneously to God and to human beings is never so [Note: [Col. 0287D] We added “so” from two manuscripts of St. Peter and Vatican manuscripts of collections 4 and 5; the context itself requires it.] obstructed that it is not always free to wish another well. When the angels said, “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14), whoever compassionately shares the suffering of others afflicted by any misery is made blessed not only by the virtue of goodwill but also by the blessing of peace. [Note: [Col. 0287D] The manuscripts of collection 4 read “is joined and sympathizes.”]

The works of devotion are exceedingly broad, and by their very variety they grant true Christians this opportunity: in the distribution of alms, not only the rich and prosperous but also those of moderate means and the poor may have their portions, and those unequal in the power to give may nevertheless be alike in affection of mind.

For when, before the eyes of the Lord, many were contributing much from their abundance in the treasury, a certain widow put in two coins (Luke 21:2; Mark 12:42), and by such a testimony of Jesus Christ deserved to be crowned, so that, although her gift was so small, it was judged worthy to be preferred to the contribution of all [Note: [Col. 0287D] Thus from the manuscripts of St. Peter. Others read “equally deserving.”], because among the great gifts of those who possessed much, what belonged to her, though little, was her whole possession.

But if someone is constrained by such straitness of poverty that he is unable even to contribute two copper coins to a poor person [Col. 0287C], he has in the Lord’s commandments something by which he may fulfill the duty of good will. For whoever gives a thirsty poor person a cup of cold water will receive the reward of his deed (Matt. 10:42). So many opportunities has the Lord prepared for his servants to obtain his kingdom that even the giving of water, whose use is free and common, would not be without reward. And so that no difficulty might shut anyone out, the example of devotion is set in the form of cold water, lest someone think he would lose his reward because he lacked the expense of fuel for heating the drink.

Nevertheless, the Lord does not warn us without reason that this cup is to be given in his name, because faith makes precious what is in itself cheap, whereas what unbelievers give, even if it is costly, is nevertheless empty of all justification.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, beloved, as we prepare to celebrate the Lord’s Pasch, exercise yourselves in holy fasts so that you may come to the most sacred festivals free from every disturbance. Let the spirit of pride, from which all sins arose, be driven away by love of humility; and let those who had swollen with arrogance be calmed by gentleness. Those whose minds some offense has embittered should, once reconciled, strive to return to unity and harmony with one another [Note: [Col. 0287D] Thus, with Quesnellus, two manuscripts of St. Peter. Others read “through reconciliation.”].

Returning no evil for evil and forgiving one another as Christ forgave us (Rom. 12:17), erase human enmities through peace. And if any of your subjects have deserved confinement or chains [Note: [Col. 0288D] The first edition reads “have deserved it.”], let them be released mercifully, so that we, who need the remedies of daily forgiveness, may not find it difficult to forgive the sins of others.

For when we say to the Lord, our Father, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), it is certain that when we grant forgiveness for the offenses of others, we prepare divine clemency for ourselves. [Note: [Col. 0288D] Thus two Lectionaries of St. Peter and other codices. The editions read “through Christ our Lord. Amen.”]

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLV [formerly XLIV]

### On Lent VII

[Col. 0288B]

### Synopsis

I. Everyone—whether just, sinful, or a catechumen—must prepare the way for the Lord during Lent.

II. During Lent one must devote oneself to mercy and truth, in imitation of God, and to faith and charity.

III. What is provided for Christ is expended for Christ.

IV. During this season one must devote oneself to the practice of every virtue.

## CHAPTER I
Virtue, beloved, and the wisdom of Christian faith are love of God and love of neighbor; nor does anyone lack any duty of piety who is devoted to honoring the Lord and assisting a fellow servant. The twofold unity of these affections must indeed be practiced at every time and increased progressively, but now it must be broadened through greater increases, so that the forty-day fast, [Col. 0288C] which precedes the paschal feast, [Note: [Col. 0288D] The manuscripts of Saint Peter: “by the inner hearing of the heart.”] may stir the inner hearing of the heart like that voice in which John the Baptist, using the words of the prophet Isaiah, said: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight” (Isa. 40:3; Matt. 3:3).

Whether we consider that part of the people which, having long ago entered the contests of the gospel struggle, continually presses toward the palm of victory along the course of the spiritual arena; or that part which, conscious of deadly sins, hastens toward pardon through the help of reconciliation; or that part which, destined to be regenerated by the baptism of the Holy Spirit, desires to strip off the oldness of Adam and be clothed in the newness of Christ—the saying is aptly and profitably addressed to all: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

Let us learn, moreover, what the ways of the Lord and his paths are from the exhortation of the same preacher. While promising the works and gifts of divine grace, he disclosed the effects of future transformations, adding the words of the prophetic sermon and saying: “Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; and crooked places shall become straight, and rough ways shall become level” (Isa. 40:4). The valley therefore signifies the gentleness of the humble, while the mountain and hill signify the exaltation of the proud. But because, as the Truth says, “whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11; 18:14), rightly there is both a filling of the valleys [Note: [Col. 0289D] This is the reading of our manuscripts and of editions before Quesnellus; in Quesnellus: “both the filling of the valley and of the mountain.”] and a proclaimed lowering of the mountains: so that the level places may have nothing causing offense, and the straight places nothing crooked.

Although the way that leads to life is narrow and difficult (Matt. 7:14), the one whom truth strengthens and piety guides does not walk in it with difficulty; nor is there no delight in walking where the journey is made firm by the rock of virtues, rather than undermined by the sand of vices.

## CHAPTER II

But so that we may know more fully by what sort of ways we must advance toward God’s promises, let us hear what the prophet David teaches: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). The pattern of the faithful’s conduct therefore comes from the example of God’s works; and rightly God requires those whom he made in his image and likeness to imitate him. We shall possess the dignity of that glory in no other way than if both mercy and truth are found in us.

For by the means through which the Savior came to save us, [Note: [Col. 0289D] Quesnellus, with Rainaudus, added “and.” We have removed it on the authority of the other editions and our manuscripts. Shortly afterward the first edition reads *saving* instead of *saved*.] those who have been saved must hasten toward the one who saves, so that the mercy of God may make us merciful and the truth of God may make us truthful. Just as a righteous mind walks along the way of truth, so a kindly mind walks along the way of mercy. Yet these paths have never been divided, [Note: [Col. 0289D] Thus, with Quesnellus, two manuscripts of Saint Peter and four Vatican manuscripts; others read “are distinct.”] as though each of these goods were sought by different routes, and growing in mercy were one thing, [Note: [Col. 0289D] Printed editions here repeat “and.” We have removed it on the authority of two Vatican manuscripts.] while advancing in truth were another.

A person is not merciful if alien to truth; nor is one capable of justice if a stranger to piety. [Note: [Col. 0289D] Thus five of our manuscripts agree with Quesnellus; others read “of truth.” Earlier editions, with most manuscripts, incorrectly read “nor by either virtue”; Quesnellus, perhaps compelled by the sense, altered this to “nor by either one,” though we find it in no manuscript. The manuscript lectionary of Saint Justina at Padua alone supplied the true reading, “neither.”] Whoever does not grow rich in both virtues practices neither virtue.
