Love is the strength of faith, and faith is the fortitude of love. The true name and true fruit of both appear when the connection between them remains unbreakable. For wherever they are not together, both are absent, since they are mutually each other’s help and light, until the reward of vision fulfills the desire of belief, and what is now neither loved without faith nor believed without love is seen and loved unchangeably. [Note: [Col. 0289D] From our observations you may gather the sense of this proposition—“it is not believed without love”—as it is intended in Leo’s own thought; there we shall also reproduce and examine the annotation appended here by Quesnellus.]

Therefore, as the Apostle says, “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. 5:6), let us devote ourselves simultaneously and conjointly to love and to faith. This is the most effective flight of two wings, by which purity of mind is lifted up to merit and behold God, so that it is not weighed down by the burden of bodily cares.

For the one who says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6), [Note: [Col. 0290D] The particle “so that,” absent from editions before Quesnellus but prefixed by him to the word *ligno* (“wood”), has here been inserted from two manuscripts of Saint Peter.] also says: “If I have all faith, so that I can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing” (1 Cor. 13:2). Therefore, so that the divine mysteries of the paschal sacraments may be received with worthy devotion, let these two things—within which the teaching of all the commandments converges—be pursued with particular zeal. Through them each of the faithful may become both a sacrifice to God and a temple.

Let faith persist in hoping for what it believes; let love persist in making favorable the one whom it loves: both belong to the one who loves, and both to the one who believes. And let us join ourselves by an imitation of piety to the same understanding to which we submit by concession. [Note: [Col. 0290D] Quesnellus reads “by agreement,” contrary not only to the earlier editions but also to all our manuscripts. “Concession of understanding,” not “agreement,” which belongs to the will, is rightly assigned the meaning of yielding, as in the Apostle: “taking every thought captive in obedience to faith.”]

It is the voice of God: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 19:2; 20:7); and it is the voice of the Lord: “Be merciful, just as your Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36).

## CHAPTER III

And so that we may not doubt that what is expended on the needy is offered to God, let us hear what transactions the distributors of alms enter into, when the Lord declares what the form of his judgment will be. He will say to those placed at his right hand [Note: [Col. 0290D] Printed editions read “to be placed”; the better reading, from manuscripts of Saint Peter and another Vatican manuscript of collection 5, is “placed.”]: “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food. I was thirsty, and you gave me drink. I was a stranger, and you welcomed me. I was naked, and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me” (Matt. 25:34–36). But when the righteous ask when [Note: [Col. 0290D] “Or” in place of “and” seemed preferable on the authority of three of our manuscripts.] or how they could have rendered these services, the King will answer them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: insofar as you did these things for one of the least of my brothers, you did them for me” (ibid., 40). [Note: [Col. 0290D] We added “these things” from the manuscripts of Saint Peter.]

What work is more fruitful than this? What humanity is happier? [Note: [Col. 0290D] Certain editions before Quesnellus read “more easily.”] It certainly would not be deprived of its praise if, because of the commonality of nature itself, one human being rendered assistance to another. [Note: [Col. 0290D] Thus from two manuscripts of Saint Peter; others read “were afforded.”] But because what does not proceed from the fountain of faith does not attain eternal rewards, the condition of heavenly works is one thing, and that of earthly works another.

Worldly benevolence comes to an end in those whom it helps; Christian piety passes over to its author, since we are said to be kind toward the one whom we confess to be working in us. The Lord says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). [Note: [Col. 0290D] Some manuscripts read “we may be said”; then, instead of “we confess,” others read “we acknowledge.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Rejoice, therefore, mind of the faithful, and, recognizing your glory in the glory of him who works in you, burn with zeal for the paschal feast. [Note: [Col. 0291D] Others read “solemnity.” Shortly afterward printed editions read “be prepared”; we prefer “be prepared” in the feminine, not only from several manuscripts but also because it appears to refer to the feminine noun *mens* (“mind”).] For it is your duty to be prepared to suffer with the one who suffered for all, since the devout life of the saints is never estranged from the cross of Christ: by the nails of self-restraint it fastens the desires of the flesh, and by the power of the Spirit dwelling within it puts bodily cravings to death.

It is difficult for anyone not to have within himself something to destroy. Anger must be extinguished, pride mortified, lust overthrown, and the root of greed pursued more deeply, so that the seed of every evil may be cut off if its source can be torn out.

Although the mind must be cultivated unceasingly with such diligence, and the body must be used in such a way that the lower nature offers necessary service to its ruler, now above all the flesh must be governed by the reins of self-restraint, and whatever obstructs higher desires must be cut away.

While both substances—soul and body—are prepared through appropriate purifications for the celebration of the Lord’s Passover, a practice profitable for all time is being nourished. Let harsh commands toward subordinates subside; let punishment for sin cease; and let those guilty of crimes rejoice that they have reached these days in which, under holy and pious rulers, even the severity of public penalties is relaxed. [Note: [Col. 0291D] Manuscripts of collection 4 read: “Let commands not be harsh.”] Let hatred be abolished, hostilities cease, let the affection of peace and goodwill increase, [Note: [Col. 0291D] Three of our manuscripts and the first edition read “the effects.”] and let whoever could be stained by malice strive to be cleansed by kindness. [Note: [Col. 0291D] See our observations, where Quesnellus’s annotation will be described.]

For God’s judgment will be as severe toward the merciless as it will be gentle toward the merciful; and while those placed on the left are thrust into the fire of Gehenna because of their inhumanity, those on the right, praised for their merciful almsgiving, will be received into the eternal blessedness of the heavenly kingdom (Matt. 25:34, 42). [Note: [Col. 0291D] We restored the preposition “under” in place of “for,” from the manuscripts of Saint Peter.]

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XLVI [Alternative numbering: XLV]  
## On Lent VIII

## SYNOPSIS

I. Not only vices but errors must be rejected; the twofold nature in Christ must be acknowledged.  
II. In all Christ’s actions, varied testimonies of both natures shine forth.  
III. What must be believed concerning Christ incarnate.  
IV. Fasting and prayer are made fruitful not only by almsgiving but also by the remission of offenses.

## CHAPTER I

We know, beloved, that this is the fervor of your devotion: in the fasts that precede the Lord’s Passover, many of you anticipate our exhortations. [Note: [Col. 0291D] We added “in” from two manuscripts of Saint Peter.] But since the benefit of self-restraint is necessary not only for the chastisement of the flesh but also for the purity of the mind, we desire your observance to be so complete that, just as you cut back the pleasures arising from the desires of the flesh, so you exclude errors from the mind’s perceptions. [Note: [Col. 0291D] Editions before Quesnellus read: “just as you cut off the pleasures of the flesh from desire,” or “from desires.” The present reading is found in the manuscripts of Saint Peter and in Vatican collection 5.]

For in the paschal feast, [Note: [Col. 0291D–0292D] Thus two manuscripts of Saint Peter read “in which”; printed editions and certain manuscripts read “in what,” while Quesnellus reads “by which.”] in which all the sacraments of our religion converge, the person who prepares himself through true and rational purification is the one whose heart is polluted by no unbelief. For since the Apostle says, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), the fasts of those whom the father of lies deceives with his illusions will be useless and empty, and the true flesh of Christ will not nourish them. [Note: [Col. 0291D] One manuscript of Saint Peter and Vatican collection 4 read “deceived.”]

Therefore, just as we must serve the divine commandments and sound teaching with our whole heart, so we must abstain with complete prudence from impious opinions. [Note: [Col. 0292D] We restored the word “mind,” absent in Quesnellus, from the other editions and our manuscripts.] The mind then practices a holy and spiritual fast when it rejects the food of error and the poisons of falsehood—things which the deceitful and crafty enemy introduces more insidiously when, at the very recurrence of the venerable feast, the whole Church is generally summoned to understand the mysteries of its salvation. [Note: [Col. 0292D] Quesnellus, together with the Antwerp edition of 1583 and most of our manuscripts, reads “is stirred.” Others read “is moved.”]

The true confessor and worshiper of Christ’s resurrection is the one who is neither ashamed of his passion nor deceived concerning his bodily birth. For certain people, ashamed of the gospel of Christ’s cross, sought more boldly to nullify the punishment undertaken for the redemption of the world and denied that the Lord possessed the nature of true flesh. They did not understand that the impassible and unchangeable divinity of the Word inclined itself toward human salvation in such a way that it both powerfully did not lose what was properly its own and mercifully assumed what was ours. [Note: [Col. 0292D] The first edition reads “thus inclined toward human nature and its salvation.” Other editions before Quesnellus read “thus inclining itself toward human nature and its salvation.” Quesnellus reads “thus inclined toward human nature,” omitting “and its salvation”; yet the mention of salvation is especially required by the preceding words, “the punishment undertaken for the redemption of the world,” to which this passage refers. We have followed the Saint Peter exemplars and two Vatican manuscripts.]

Thus one person is constituted from the twofold form in Christ: the Son of God and likewise the son of man is one Lord. He accepted the condition of a servant through a purpose of compassion, [Note: [Col. 0292D] Thus Quesnellus with one manuscript of Saint Peter; others read “nor by law.”] not through the compulsion of necessity; for he became humble, capable of suffering, and mortal by his own power, so that, in destroying the dominion of sin and death, the substance of weakness might be capable of punishment while the nature of power lost nothing of its glory.

## CHAPTER II

When, beloved, you read or hear the Gospel and recognize that certain things in our Lord Jesus Christ were subjected to insults while others were illumined by miracles, so that in the same person human things appear at one time and divine things shine forth at another, do not ascribe any of these matters to falsehood, as though Christ possessed either humanity alone or divinity alone. Rather, believe both faithfully and worship both humbly. Thus, in the unity of the Word and flesh, there is no division, nor, because divine signs were manifest in Jesus, should the bodily realities be considered false testimonies.

The testimonies of both natures are true and abundant in him, converging there through the height of the divine plan, so that, without the inviolable Word being separated from passible flesh, the divinity may be understood to share fully in flesh and the flesh in divinity. [Note: [Col. 0293D] Editions before Quesnellus and not a few manuscripts read “in Christ.”]

Therefore, Christian mind, fleeing falsehood and a disciple of truth, use the evangelical history confidently. [Note: [Col. 0293D] Thus, with Quesnellus, certain of our manuscripts. Earlier editions read “which faithfully and visibly”; the Antwerp edition of 1583 reads “which faithfully and universally,” with “visibly” in the margin.] As though joined to the apostles themselves, distinguish by spiritual understanding and bodily perception what was visibly accomplished by the Lord.

Give to the human being the fact that a child was born from a woman; [Note: [Col. 0293D] In two manuscripts of Saint Peter: “Give to the Word.”] give to God the fact that neither at conception nor at birth was the mother’s virginity harmed. Recognize the form of a servant wrapped in cloths and lying in a manger; but confess as the form of the Lord the one announced by angels, declared by the elements, and worshiped by the magi.

Understand as human the fact that he did not avoid a wedding banquet; approve as divine the fact that he changed water into wine (John 2:9). Let our human affection be made known to you when tears are offered for a dead friend; let divine power be perceived when that same man, already foul after four days in the tomb, is raised to life by the command of a voice alone (John 11:39).

That clay was made from spittle and earth belonged to bodily action (John 9:6); but that the blind man’s eyes, smeared with it, were illumined was unquestionably the work of that power which had reserved for the manifestation of its glory what it had not granted at the beginnings of nature.

It belongs to true humanity to relieve bodily weariness through the rest of sleep (Mark 4:38); but it belongs to true divinity to restrain the violence of raging storms by a rebuke of command.

To set food before the hungry (John 6:38) belongs to human kindness and to a spirit of fellowship; [Note: [Col. 0293D–0294D] The word *est* (“is”), as superfluous, is omitted in certain manuscripts. Then the first edition has “working” instead of “cooperating.”] but who would dare deny that it was the work of divinity to satisfy five thousand men, apart from women and children, with five loaves and two fish? Through the cooperation of the functions of true flesh, divinity was showing both that it dwelt in the human being and that the human being dwelt in it. For the wounds of the original state of decay could not otherwise be healed in human nature unless, with the Word of God assuming flesh for himself from the Virgin’s womb, in one and the same person flesh and the Word were born together.

## CHAPTER III

Keeping this faith of the Lord’s incarnation, beloved—the faith through which the whole Church is the body of Christ—with an unwavering heart, fast from all the lies of heretics. Believe that works of mercy will profit you, and that the purity of self-restraint will be fruitful, only if your minds have not been defiled by any contamination of depraved opinions.

Reject the arguments of worldly wisdom, hateful to the Lord, [Note: [Col. 0294D] Editions before Quesnellus and several manuscripts read “arguments of worldly wisdom.”] through which no one has been able to arrive at knowledge of the truth. Hold firmly in your mind what you profess in the Creed.

Believe that the Son of God is coeternal with the Father, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3), and that according to the flesh he was also generated at the end of time.

Believe that he was crucified bodily, died, was raised, and lifted above the heights of the heavenly dominions; that he was established at the Father’s right hand; and that he will come to judge the living and the dead in the same flesh in which he ascended.

The Apostle proclaims this to all the faithful, saying: “If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on those that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:1–4).

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, beloved, possessing the confidence of so great a promise, be heavenly not only in hope but also in conduct. Although at every time one must strive for the sanctification of both mind and body, during these forty-day fasts especially cultivate yourselves through more attentive works of piety—not only by distributing alms, which have a great effect in bringing amendment, [Note: [Col. 0294D] Some manuscripts of the later collections read “purification.”] but also by forgiving offenses and releasing the guilt of sins, so that the condition God established between himself and humanity may not resist those who pray.

For when we say, according to the Lord’s teaching, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), we must fulfill with our whole heart what we say. Then what we ask in what follows will certainly come about: that we may not be led into temptation and may be delivered from every evil.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XLVII [Alternative numbering: XLVI]  
## On Lent IX

[Note: [Col. 0294D] In the first edition and in manuscripts of collection 3, this inscription is prefixed: “Sermon I on the Paschal Feast”; the following two sermons are similarly called Sermons II and III.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. During the time of the greater, that is, Lenten fasts, Christians are prepared for the paschal feast through endurance of the cross.  
II. Not only moral integrity but also faith must be preserved, especially faith in Christ’s divinity and humanity.  
III. God is especially appeased by mercy and by the remission of offenses.

## CHAPTER I

In all Christian solemnities, beloved, we know that the paschal mystery is preeminent. The observances of the entire year certainly prepare us to receive it worthily and appropriately; [Note: [Col. 0295C] Thus, with Quesnellus, seven of our manuscripts; others read “restore.”] but above all our devotion is demanded by these present days, which we know are especially suited to that sublime sacrament of divine mercy. During them the holy apostles, through the teaching of the Holy Spirit, rightly ordained greater fasts, so that through a common participation in the cross of Christ we too might do something in that which he accomplished for us, as the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him” (Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:12).

The expectation of the promised blessedness is certain and secure wherever there is participation in the Lord’s passion. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Thus in two manuscripts of Saint Peter. Editions before Quesnellus, with some manuscripts, read “There is no one”; this text instead has “For there is no one,” as do one Venetian manuscript and two Patavine manuscripts of Saint Anthony and Saint Justina, where “for” seems less fitting and may perhaps have been changed into “for indeed.” Among Latin authors of good standing, “no one” is joined with negative particles, which do not weaken but rather intensify the force of the statement, so that “no one does not” signifies more strongly than “no one.”]

There is no one at all, beloved, to whom the fellowship of this glory is denied by the circumstances of time, as though the tranquility of peace were deprived of the opportunity for virtue. For the Apostle proclaims: “All who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). Therefore persecution never fails if the practice of piety never fails.

The Lord himself says in his exhortations: [Note: [Col. 0295D] Editions before Quesnellus incorrectly read “For the Lord says in his exhortations.” Quesnellus’s correction is supported by five of our manuscripts.] “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:38). Nor should we doubt that this saying applies not only to Christ’s disciples but to all the faithful and to the whole Church, which was hearing its saving instruction universally in those who were present.

Just as it belongs to the whole of time to live piously, so it belongs to the whole of time to bear the cross. It is rightly called each person’s own, [Note: [Col. 0295D] Editions before Quesnellus read “it is rightly urged that each person bear it.” The better reading of Quesnellus is found in the Saint Peter exemplars.] because it is borne by each according to individual ways and measures. [Note: [Col. 0295D] Quesnellus and some of our manuscripts read “the body”; the first edition also has “the cross of the body” in the second clause.] Persecution is one name, but the cause of the struggle is not one; and more danger is often found in a hidden assailant than in an open enemy.

Blessed Job, instructed by the alternating fortunes and misfortunes of this world, said piously and truly: “Is not human life a temptation upon the earth?” (Job 7:1). For the faithful soul is attacked not only by bodily pains and punishments; even when the limbs remain unharmed, it is pressed by severe disease if it is softened by the pleasure of the flesh.

But when the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, the rational mind is equipped by the protection of Christ’s cross. It does not consent when enticed by harmful desires, because it is pierced by the nail of self-restraint and by fear of God. [Note: [Col. 0295D] We followed all earlier editions and our manuscripts. Quesnellus reads “and the spirit against the flesh,” and shortly afterward deleted “of Christ.”]

Thus, among those established in a good purpose, hostilities against people of dissimilar character do not fail, with the devil inciting them. [Note: [Col. 0296D] That is, those dissimilar in conduct. In what follows we have not departed from the reading of editions before Quesnellus, confirmed by all our manuscripts, among which are five lectionaries of excellent authority. Quesnellus, perhaps intending to explain Leo’s meaning more clearly, without citing any manuscript printed “so that they easily burst into hatreds,” and later “the righteous” instead of “the upright.”] Their wicked behavior becomes more detestable by comparison with the upright, and they easily erupt into hatred. Iniquity has no peace with justice; drunkenness hates sobriety; falsehood has no harmony with truth; pride does not love gentleness, insolence modesty, or greed generosity.

This difference has conflicts so persistent that even if it becomes outwardly quiet, it nevertheless does not cease disturbing the inner chambers of pious hearts. Thus it is true that those who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:12), and true that this entire life is a temptation (Job 7:1).

Each believer, instructed by personal experience, must arm himself with Christ’s cross, so that he may be regarded as worthy of Christ. [Note: [Col. 0296D] Certain editions and Vatican collection 3 read “more worthy.”]

## CHAPTER II

As those striving through this contest toward eternal rewards advance, beloved, the devil’s cunning lies in this above all: when he cannot corrupt their moral integrity, he overthrows their faith. For whoever is led away from the confession of truth is transferred to another road, and his entire course is a departure; he will be nearer to death in proportion as he is farther from the Catholic light. [Note: [Col. 0296D] Thus Quesnellus with four of our manuscripts; others read “faith.” Certain manuscripts shortly before have “darkness” instead of “death,” perhaps better.]

This is also suffered in our own days by those who, through their own negligence, have conceived the ancient madness from a spirit of error long ago destroyed and condemned. They dare to deny the twofold nature in Christ, either by refusing to acknowledge the truth of the flesh he assumed or by converting divinity into flesh. Thus, according to Manichaeus, there would be no resurrection because there was no passion; or, according to Apollinaris, the very divinity of the Word would itself have become changeable and passible. [Note: [Col. 0296D] Two manuscripts of Saint Peter and one Venetian manuscript read “by which the twofold nature.”]

To think this, and to thrust it into the ears of the Christian people, what else is it than to tear out the very foundations of our religion [Note: [Col. 0296D] We restored “our,” omitted by Quesnellus, from all the other editions and all our manuscripts.] and to deny that the true Son of God is truly the son of man? In him alone the restoration of the human race was testified through the Law, promised through the Prophets, and announced through all the symbols of the Old Testament. Thus that great sacrament of divine mercy, destined to benefit all ages and frequently and long signified beforehand, was not to be doubted when fulfilled at the appointed time. [Note: [Col. 0296D] The manuscripts of Saint Peter read “mysteries.”]

Therefore, although from the time when “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14) there is one person in Christ, of God and of man, so that none of his actions involves a division of the two natures, [Note: [Col. 0297D] The same manuscripts and the first edition, with the Bonn manuscript, read “is.” We have retained Quesnellus’s “profess” instead of “confess,” on the authority of two manuscripts of Saint Peter.] nevertheless the evangelical truth very often strives to identify the one whom it proclaims the Son of God as the son of man. Thus, although the things discussed are some matters of humanity and others of divinity, both are nevertheless mentioned under the name “son of man,” lest faith—which believes the Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin Mary, to be simultaneously God and man—hesitate to confess either humanity in God or divinity in man.

Thus, in the Word of the assumed human being there is true human humility, and in the flesh of the assuming God there is true divine majesty. [Note: [Col. 0297D] Printed editions read “humanity.” The manuscripts of Saint Peter furnish the correction, which cannot be rejected, since in Leo’s frequent usage the true humility of man is contrasted with the true majesty of God.]

## CHAPTER III

Beloved, it is enough on this occasion of the paschal feast—which we must prepare for through purity of heart—to have briefly touched upon the incarnation of the Word, since you remember having been instructed about it several times.

Now I admonish your devotion concerning what the season demands: adorn the holy and health-giving fast with works of piety. And because we must labor especially for the forgiveness of offenses, promise yourselves an unquestionable divine mercy if you too have transferred every offense against your subordinates to pardon. [Note: [Col. 0297D] Quesnellus reads “toward your subordinates.” We restored “concerning” from the other editions and most manuscripts. So also Sermon 50, chapter 3: “Whether concerning subordinates or equals.”]

It is fitting for God’s people to come together for so great a feast in peace and harmony, so that the severity of punishments—which is now also relaxed in public judgments—may be softened much more in the hearts of Christians. For the care of the saints ought to be directed especially toward this: that no one be cold, no one hungry, no one fail from want, no one waste away in sorrow, no one have anyone bound in chains, and no one have anyone confined in prison.

However great the causes of offense may be between one person and another, one must consider not so much the magnitude of the offense as the commonality of nature, so that from the judgment by which one judges another one may obtain the mercy of God, who judges. For “blessed are the merciful, because God will have mercy on them” (Matt. 5:7).

He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XLVIII [Alternative numbering: XLVII]  
## On Lent X

## SYNOPSIS

I. Everyone must prepare himself for the paschal mystery—which consecrates all other things—through the forty-day fast. The operation of grace and human cooperation.  
II. Envy of one’s neighbor’s good, which is peculiar to the devil, must be especially avoided.  
III. Without love, virtues are bare and fruitless; there must be no limit to that virtue.  
IV. Each person must merit mercy through showing mercy.  
V. Alms must be distributed abundantly during this season.

## CHAPTER I
Among all the days that Christian devotion honors in many ways, dearly beloved, none is more excellent than the paschal feast, through which the dignity of all solemnities is consecrated in the Church of God. [Col. 0298D] Indeed, even the Lord’s birth from his mother was undertaken for the sake of this sacrament; nor was there any other reason for the Son of God to be born than that he might be fastened to the cross.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus and most manuscripts read “was” (fuit).] In the Virgin’s womb mortal flesh was assumed; in mortal flesh the plan of the Passion was completed; and through the ineffable counsel of God’s mercy it was brought about that this should be for us the sacrifice of redemption, the abolition of sin, and the beginning of rising again to eternal life. [Col. 0298B]

[Note: Some codices read, “Nothing is more excellent.”]

Considering what the whole world has obtained through the Lord’s cross, we recognize that we rightly prepare ourselves to celebrate the day of Easter by a forty-day fast, so that we may be worthy to participate in the divine mysteries.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “whatever” (quidquid).]

For not only the chief bishops, or priests of the second order, or merely the ministers of the sacraments, but the entire body of the Church and the whole number of the faithful must be cleansed from every defilement, so that the temple of God—whose founder is God himself—may be beautiful in all its stones and radiant throughout every part of itself. [Col. 0298C]

[Note: The word “founder” is absent from the Corbie manuscript and from Quesnellus. Shortly afterward, Vatican manuscripts of Collection 5 read “precious” instead of “beautiful.”]

For if the palaces of kings and the praetoria of exalted authorities are reasonably adorned with every decoration, so that the dwellings of those whose merits are greater may be more distinguished, how much more ought the dwelling of the Deity itself to be built, and with what honor ought it to be adorned! [Col. 0298C]

Although this dwelling cannot be begun and completed without its author, it has nevertheless been granted by its builder that it may also seek increase through its own labor. Living and rational material is taken up for the construction of this temple, and by the Spirit of grace it is moved so that it may voluntarily fit together into one structure.

[Note: We restore the reading of all editions before Quesnellus, which is also found in our manuscripts. Quesnellus, without citing any manuscript, reads instead: “And through the Spirit of grace it is suitably urged into one structure as something voluntary.”]

It was loved and sought for this reason: that it might itself become one that seeks, though previously it did not seek, and one that loves, though previously it did not love, as the blessed apostle John says: “Let us therefore love one another, because God first loved us” (1 John 4:19). [Col. 0298D]

Since all the faithful together, and each one individually, are one and the same temple of God, just as this temple must be perfect in all of them, so it must be perfect in each individual. For although all the members do not possess the same beauty, and equality of merits cannot exist amid such a variety of parts, the connection of charity nevertheless secures a shared beauty.

[Note: Three of our manuscripts read “throughout the whole” instead of “in all its parts.”]

Those who share in holy love, even if they do not enjoy the same gifts of grace, nevertheless rejoice in one another’s goods. What they love cannot be foreign to them, because those who rejoice in another’s progress grow rich through their own. [Col. 0299A]

## CHAPTER II

In this unity of the saints, where the same thing is loved, cherished, and understood, there is no place for the proud, the envious, or the greedy. Whatever it may be by which vanity boasts, anger rages, or lust revels, is judged to belong not to the covenant of Christ but to the devil’s side, and is excluded far from the dwellings of godliness.

The adversary of innocence and enemy of peace therefore rages. Because he himself did not stand in the truth (John 8:44), and through his pride lost all the glory of his nature, he grieves that humanity is restored by God’s mercy and brought into the good things that he himself lost. [Col. 0299B]

It is no wonder that the author of sin is tortured by the upright conduct of those who act well and tormented by the steadfastness of those whom he cannot overthrow, since even among human beings there are found people who imitate this wickedness.

Many—for this is grievous—are consumed by the progress of others; and because they know that vices are displeasing to virtue, they arm themselves in hatred against those whose example they do not follow.

[Note: The printed editions read, “and because they know themselves to be empty of virtues and despised.” Several manuscripts read similarly: one omits “themselves,” and another reads “and those who know themselves.” This reading, which suggests that the good are despised by the wicked, appears contrary to the author’s following words, in which he says that the good are hostile not to wicked people but to vices. We have therefore preferred the reading of two manuscripts of Saint Peter and one Vatican manuscript.]

But God’s servants and disciples of truth love even those unlike themselves. They declare war on vices rather than on human beings, returning evil to no one for evil (Romans 12:17), but always desiring the correction of sinners.

It is very beautiful and worthy of divine benevolence for each person to recognize himself in another, and to love his own nature even in an enemy. For we know that many have passed from the worst ways of life to the best: drunkards have become sober, the cruel compassionate, the rapacious generous, the incontinent chaste, and the savage peaceful. [Col. 0299C]

[Note: Quesnellus reads “we have known.”]

Since the Lord says, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:13), no Christian is permitted to hate anyone, because no one is saved except through the forgiveness of sins; and those whom worldly wisdom has made contemptible, we do not know how precious spiritual grace may make them.

[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter add, “while the Pharisees and scribes were maligning him.” Then the first edition and the manuscript of Bonn read, “how beautiful and precious are spiritual [things],” etc.]

## CHAPTER III

Let God’s people therefore be holy; let them be kind. Holy, so that they avoid what is forbidden; kind, so that they do what is commanded.

Although it is a great thing to possess right faith and sound doctrine, and although restraint of the appetite, gentleness of temper, and purity of chastity deserve much praise, all the virtues are nevertheless naked without charity. Nothing can be called fruitful in any excellence of conduct [Col. 0299D] unless it has been produced by love.

Thus the Lord says in John’s Gospel: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). And in the Epistle of the same apostle we read: “Beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves is born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love” (1 John 4:7–8). [Col. 0300A]

[Note: Vatican manuscripts of Collections 1 and 5 read “if you have” in the plural. Shortly afterward, the first edition reads, “Therefore in the Epistle of the same Gospel”—that is, “of the evangelist.” After the words “whoever loves,” two Vatican manuscripts add “his brother.”]

Let the minds of the faithful therefore examine themselves, and let them judge the deepest affections of their hearts by a true scrutiny.

[Note: The first edition reads “as if” (ut si).]

If they find within their consciences something stored up from the fruits of charity, let them not doubt that God dwells within them; and, so that they may become ever more capable of so great a guest, let them grow continually richer in works of mercy.

[Note: The same edition, as well as the Antwerp edition of 1583, reads “let them become continually more abundant in works of mercy.”]

For if love is God, charity ought to have no limit, because the Divinity cannot be enclosed by any boundary.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0300B]

Therefore, dearly beloved, although every season is suitable for practicing the good of charity, these present days especially exhort us to do so. Those who desire to receive the Lord’s Pascha with sanctification of soul and body should strive above all to acquire this grace, in which the fullness of every virtue is contained and the multitude of sins is covered.

Since we are about to celebrate that supreme sacrament above all others, through which the blood of Jesus Christ abolished our iniquities, let us first prepare offerings of mercy, so that we too may grant to those who have sinned against us what God’s goodness has granted to us.

[Note: Thus according to two manuscripts of Saint Peter. Another reads “and that.”]

Let injuries be forgotten; let offenses no longer know punishment; and let all the offenses of those under our authority be released from fear of vengeance. [Col. 0300C]

[Note: We have restored the word “those under authority,” which Quesnellus had relegated to the margin, from earlier editions and our manuscripts. It is customary for the holy pontiff to exhort people to transfer every offense against those under their authority into forgiveness, as in the preceding sermon, chapter 3, and similarly elsewhere. Quesnellus later reads, “If anyone holds such people.”]

Let no one be held in punitive confinement, and let the sad groans of the guilty not persist in dark prisons.

If anyone holds people bound for some offense, let him not doubt that he himself is a sinner. And in order that he may himself receive forgiveness, let him rejoice that he has found someone whom he may pardon. Thus, when according to God’s teaching we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), let us be confident that through the pattern of our prayer we obtain divine clemency.

## CHAPTER V

Let generous giving now be exercised more abundantly toward the poor and those hindered by various infirmities, so that thanks may be offered to God by the voices of many, and the nourishment of the needy may support our fasts.

The Lord is pleased by no devotion of the faithful more than by that which is offered to his poor; and wherever he finds the care of mercy, there he recognizes the image of his own compassion. [Col. 0300D]

Let there be no fear that these expenditures will exhaust one’s resources, because generosity itself is great wealth. The material for giving cannot be lacking where Christ feeds and is fed. [Col. 0301A]

[Note: The first edition and the manuscripts of Collection 5 read, “both feeds and is fed.”]

In all this work that hand is present which increases bread by breaking it and multiplies it by distributing it. [Col. 0301A]

Let the distributor of alms be confident and cheerful, because he will have the greatest profit when he has kept the least for himself. As the blessed apostle Paul says: “He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness” (2 Corinthians 9:10).

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLIX [Al. XLVIII]. On Lent XI

### SYNOPSIS

I. The Lenten fast, the greatest and most sacred fast, has been imposed upon everyone without exception, because it is necessary for everyone, since no one is free from guilt.—II. How few enter the way of salvation, and how many are occupied with temporal things.—III. Just as the devil lies in wait and rages more fiercely during Lent, so Christians ought to devote themselves more fully to God and to their salvation.—IV. To prepare ourselves for the paschal feast, we must carry out God’s commands, which are given so that God’s grace may be sought and one’s own life may be seen as in a mirror.—V. The first effect of mercy, namely forgetfulness of offenses, must be sought from God and granted to one’s neighbor.—VI. Whoever wishes to be regarded as a son must cherish his brother and give alms, so as to be a minister of divine mercy.

## CHAPTER I

On all days and at all times, dearly beloved, certain signs of divine goodness have been appointed for us, and no part of the year is separated from the sacred mysteries. Thus, while the aids to our salvation meet us everywhere, we should seek with greater eagerness the mercy of God, which is always inviting us. [Col. 0301C]

[Note: With Quesnellus, the manuscripts of Saint Peter and several Vatican manuscripts read “seek” (expetamus); other editions, with other manuscripts, read “await” (exspectemus). Shortly afterward, some copies read “for restoration” (ad reparationem) instead of “for the restoration” (reparationi).]

But whatever is bestowed in the various works and gifts of grace for the restoration of human souls is now presented to us more clearly and abundantly, when not certain things separately but everything together must be celebrated.

For as the paschal feast approaches, the greatest and most sacred fast is present, announcing its observance to all the faithful without exception: no one is so holy that he need not become holier, and no one is so devoted that he ought not to become more devoted.

[Note: From five of our manuscripts we have substituted “for” (enim) for the “but” (autem) found in the printed editions, since it better suits the context.]

For who, established in the uncertainty of this life, can be found free from temptation or free from guilt? Who is there who does not wish some virtue to be added to himself, or some vice to be taken away? Both adversity causes harm and prosperity corrupts, and it is no less dangerous to lack what one desires than to possess what has been granted.

There are snares in the abundance of wealth and snares in the constraints of poverty. The former lift people toward pride; the latter incite them to complaint. Health is a temptation, and sickness is a temptation, since the one provides an occasion for negligence and the other a cause for sadness.

There is a trap in security and a trap in fear. It makes no difference whether the mind, held by an earthly attachment, is occupied by joys or by cares, since it is the same disease either to languish under empty pleasure or to labor under anxious concern. [Col. 0302A]

[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter and another manuscript of Bonn read, “since it is part of the same disease.”]

## CHAPTER II

The saying of Truth is therefore fulfilled in every respect, by which we learn that the way leading to life is narrow and difficult (Matthew 7:14).

[Note: Thus our manuscripts and the editions published before Quesnellus; in his edition, “it is said” (dicitur).]

While the broad road leading to death is crowded by great multitudes, the paths of salvation bear the rare footprints of the few who enter them. [Col. 0302B]

Why is the left-hand road more populous than the right, unless because the multitude is inclined toward worldly joys and bodily goods?

[Note: Quesnellus inserted “more devastated” (populatior) into the text and noted: “Thus all manuscripts, not ‘more populous’ (populosior), as the printed editions.” We judge that the printed reading, found in most and in the better of our manuscripts, should be restored: for populatior, derived from populatus, pertains to ravaging and is foreign to Leo’s sense.]

Although what is desired is fleeting and uncertain, people more readily undertake labor for the sake of pleasure than for love of virtue. Thus, although countless people desire visible things, scarcely any are found who place eternal things before temporal ones.

Therefore, as the blessed apostle Paul says, “The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18), the way of virtue is, as it were, hidden and concealed, because “we were saved in hope” (Romans 8:24), and true faith loves above all what no bodily sense can grasp.

It is therefore a great work and labor to restrain the mobility of the heart from every sin and, while countless enticements to pleasure flatter us from every side, not to relax the strength of the mind toward any defilement.

[Col. 0302C] “Who touches pitch and is not stained by it?” (Sirach 13:1). Who is not weakened in the flesh? Who is not soiled in the dust? Finally, who possesses such purity that he is not polluted by the things without which life cannot be lived?

Divine teaching commands through the Apostle that those who have wives should be as though they did not have them; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they possessed nothing; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For “the form of this world is passing away” (1 Corinthians 7:29–31).

Blessed, therefore, is the mind that passes through the time of its pilgrimage in chaste sobriety and does not remain in the things through which it must necessarily travel, so that, as a guest rather than a master of earthly things, it does not lack human affections but rests upon divine promises. [Col. 0303A]

[Note: Thus the Corbie, Victor, and Thuane manuscripts, as the sense requires. Through the error of an unskilled scribe, these words were wrongly replaced in the printed editions: “Let it neither rest upon human affections nor fail in divine promises.” Quesnellus.]

[Note: The textual reading is also supported by our manuscripts of Saint Peter, the Barberini manuscript, and several Vatican manuscripts. The first edition reads similarly: “Let it neither fail in human affections nor be unsupported by divine promises.”]

## CHAPTER III

No days demand and confer this strength more than the present ones, dearly beloved. Through them, while a special observance is practiced, a habit of perseverance is acquired.

[Note: We have corrected “spiritual” (spiritalis) to “special” (specialis) from two manuscripts of Saint Peter, two Vatican manuscripts, and the first edition; the other printed editions read “spiritual.”]

You know that this is the time when, throughout the world, while the devil rages, the Christian battle line ought to engage. If any people have been made sluggish by indolence or occupied by anxiety, it is now necessary for them to be equipped with spiritual weapons and stirred by the heavenly trumpet to enter the same contest.

[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter and Collections 4 and 5 read “ought” (debeat), and shortly afterward “it is necessary” (oporteat). The same manuscripts read “to enter the same contest” (ad idem certamen) instead of “to enter the contest” (ad ineundum certamen).]

For he through whose envy death entered the world (Wisdom 2:24) is now consumed by an especially intense hatred and tormented by the greatest anguish. He sees new peoples from every human race being brought into the adoption of the sons of God, and the births of regeneration increasing through the virginal fruitfulness of the Church. [Col. 0303B]

He sees himself deprived of the right of his dominion and expelled from the hearts of those whom he possessed. Thousands of old men, thousands of young men, and thousands of children of both sexes are snatched from him. Neither personal nor original sin is an obstacle to anyone where justification is not repaid according to merits but bestowed solely through the generosity of grace.

He also sees those who have fallen and been deceived by the fraud of his snares washed clean by the tears of repentance and, as the apostolic key unlocks the gates of mercy, admitted to the remedies of reconciliation.

Moreover, he feels that the day of the Lord’s Passion is near and that he is to be crushed by the power of that cross which, in Christ, was the redemption of the world from every debt of death—not the punishment of sin.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, so that the malignity of the raging enemy may produce no effects of its envy, we must undertake our devotion to the execution of the Lord’s commands with greater diligence. [Col. 0303C]

[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter read “the effects of his labor” (sui laboris), perhaps better.]

We must receive this season, in which all the mysteries of divine mercy converge, with preparation of both soul and body, imploring God’s guidance and assistance, so that through him, without whom we can do nothing, we may be able to accomplish everything. [Col. 0303D]

[Note: Between “guidance” and “assistance,” most editions before Quesnellus add “and mercy”; it is absent from Quesnellus’s manuscripts, from most of ours, and from the editions of Surius and Antwerp (1583).]

The command is given for this very reason: so that the help of the one who commands may be sought.

Let no one excuse himself on the pretext of weakness, since he who granted the will also grants the ability, as the blessed apostle James says: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5).

[Note: Editions before Quesnellus read, “because he who granted the will will also grant the ability.” The first edition and the manuscript of Saint Justina at Padua read “grants” instead of “will grant.” Quesnellus’s emendation is confirmed by our manuscripts of Collections 1 and 5. The lectionary manuscript of Saint Peter agrees, reading “to make progress,” or more suitably “to complete,” instead of “ability.” Compare a similar statement in Sermon 94, chapter 2. Leo repeatedly uses “ability” for effective power. Thus in Sermon 76, chapter 5, he writes: “After the apostles had been filled with a new abundance of the Holy Spirit, they began to will more ardently and to be able more effectively, progressing from knowledge of the commands to endurance of sufferings, so that, now trembling under no storm, they might tread upon the waves of the world and its arrogance, as faith rose above them,” and so forth.]

What believer does not know which virtues he ought to pursue and which vices he ought to resist? Who is so favorable or so ignorant a judge of his conscience that he does not know what ought to be taken away from him or what ought to be increased within him? [Col. 0304A]

No one is so estranged from reason that he does not understand the quality of his conduct or know the secrets of his heart. Let no one therefore approve himself in every respect, or judge himself according to the pleasures of the flesh. Rather, let him place his whole way of life upon the scale of the divine commands.

When some things are commanded to be done and others forbidden so that they may not be done, the person who has weighed the conduct of his life by comparing the two weights will examine himself by a just judgment. [Col. 0304B]

For God, the craftsman of mercy, has placed in his commands a most splendid mirror, in which a person may look upon the face of his mind and recognize how closely conformed—or how unlike—it is to the image of God.

[Note: The manuscripts of Collection 5 read “conformed to the image of God”; others read “of the image of God.” The first edition reads “to the image,” omitting “of God.”]

This is especially so that, setting aside for a little while bodily cares and restless occupations, at least during the days of our redemption and restoration, we may turn from earthly things to heavenly ones.

## CHAPTER V

Since, as it is written, “we all offend in many things” (James 3:2), let the first impulse of mercy be conceived: that the offenses of others against us may be forgotten. Let us not violate, through any desire for vengeance, that most devout covenant to which we have bound ourselves in the Lord’s Prayer.

[Note: Quesnellus’s Corbie manuscript reads “let the effect of mercy be desired” (concipiatur effectus). Shortly afterward, we have corrected aliorum (“of others”) to alienorum (“of others’/strangers’”) from two manuscripts of Saint Peter.]

When we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12), let us not be difficult in granting forgiveness. For either the desire for revenge or the indulgence of gentleness returns upon us.

For a person always exposed to the dangers of temptation ought rather to desire that his own offenses remain unpunished than that he punish the offenses of others. [Col. 0304C]

[Note: Our manuscript reading, omitted in Quesnellus, has been restored from the editions and manuscripts.]

[Note: Thus, with Quesnellus, two manuscripts of Saint Peter, one Vatican manuscript, and the first edition. The other editions read “punished,” incorrectly, since the passage indicates that it is preferable and desirable for one’s own sins to be forgiven by God rather than for the sins of others to be punished through vengeance.]

What could be more consistent with Christian faith than that forgiveness of sins should take place not only in the Church but also in every household?

Let threats be laid aside; let the bonds be loosened by which the person who does not release them will bind himself far more dangerously. For whatever someone decrees against another, by his own law he decides against himself. [Col. 0305A]

“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy” (Matthew 5:7). God is both just and kind in his judgments. For this reason he permits some people to be under the authority of others, so that under equitable moderation both the usefulness of discipline and the gentleness of clemency may be preserved.

Let no one dare to deny another the forgiveness that he hopes to receive for his own offenses.

## CHAPTER VI

Since the Lord says, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9), let the conflicts of every disagreement and hatred be laid aside. Let no one think that he will share in the paschal feast if he has neglected to restore fraternal peace.

For before the supreme Father, whoever is not in charity with his brothers will not be counted among his sons. [Col. 0305B]

Let Christian fasts also grow rich through the distribution of alms and care for the poor. Whatever each person takes away from his own pleasures, let him devote to the weak and needy.

Let care be taken that everyone may bless God with one voice. Whoever gives some portion of his property should understand that he is a minister of divine mercy, since God has placed the poor person’s portion in the hand of the giver.

Thus sins that are washed away either by the waters of baptism or by the tears of repentance may also be erased by almsgiving, as Scripture says: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Sirach 3:33). [Col. 0305C]

[Note: We have added the word “or” from a manuscript of Saint Peter. Shortly afterward, Vatican manuscripts of Collections 4 and 5 read, “so that they may also be erased by almsgiving.”]

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON L [Al. XLIX]. On Lent XII

### SYNOPSIS

I. Each person ought to prepare for the paschal banquet through examination of conscience and correction of life.—II. Mercy must be practiced; one must fast from vices and cling to heavenly things.—III. Each person is prepared for the paschal sacrament, which was established for the remission of sins, when he imitates it by forgiving offenses.

## CHAPTER I

As the paschal solemnity approaches, dearly beloved, the customary fast that precedes it is present; by the number of forty days it trains us in the sanctification of body and mind. [Col. 0305C]

[Note: Thus two manuscript lectionaries, the Paduan manuscript, one of the Eremitani, another of Saint Justina, the Cassinese manuscript, Collection 1, and manuscripts of Collection 2. The preceding sermon, chapter 1, has something similar: “For as the paschal feast approaches, the greatest and most sacred fast is present.” Before Quesnellus, the printed editions and some manuscripts read: “The practice of fasting must therefore be anticipated in such a way that the number of forty days may exercise us for the sanctification of body and mind.” Quesnellus rejected this reading and noted that it had led Catholic writers unfamiliar with the matter to an interpretation foreign to Leo’s meaning, since they understood it of the four days of fasting now placed before the first Sunday of Lent, in order to complete the number forty. From two manuscripts, those of Thuane and Corbie, he inserted this other reading into the text: “Let us anticipate it with the customary fast, which trains us …” But our reading is also confirmed by those manuscripts in which, in place of the reading found in the printed editions, “it is present” is read instead of “it is thus.”]

As we are about to receive the greatest of all feasts, we must prepare ourselves with such observance that, in whose resurrection [Col. 0306A] we have been raised together, we may also be found to have died together in his Passion.

[Note: The first edition and the Bonn manuscript read “death” (morte). The editions before Quesnellus and some manuscripts read “For when Christ” (Cum enim Christus). Shortly afterward, several manuscripts do not have the word “death” (mortis) inserted by Quesnellus.]

The blessed apostle Paul says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3).

What is participation in death with Christ except that we cease to be what we were? And what is likeness to the resurrection except the laying aside of our former state?

Therefore, whoever understands the sacrament of his restoration must strip himself of the vices of the flesh and cast away every stain of sin, so that, as he enters the wedding banquet, he may shine in the garment of virtues.

[Note: The Paduan manuscript of Saint Anthony reads “as he is about to enter.”]

Although the bridegroom’s kindness invites everyone to share in the royal banquet, all who have been invited must nevertheless strive not to be found unworthy of the gift of the sacred food (Matthew 22:11).

Some abuse God’s patience. Although they are not free in conscience, they become secure through the long postponement of punishment, even though punishment is delayed so that correction may have time.

Let no one therefore delay embracing the mercy of our God, who does not desire the death of the sinner but only that he turn and live (Ezekiel 18:32; 33:11), merely because he has not received what he deserved.

[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter read, “because he does not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn and live.”]

For whatever is delayed is not taken away, nor has the person who has not sought forgiveness escaped condemnation.

There is not, however, one reason for everyone to implore forgiveness, since sin differs from sin and crime from crime in many ways and by many degrees.

But since the whole body of the faithful ought to strive toward perfect innocence and complete purity, so that it may deserve to be counted among those of whom it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8), we must strive with every effort and strength to erase through the most careful cleansings whatever stains the secret conscience and whatever darkens the mind’s vision. [Col. 0306C]

[Note: The first edition reads “through corrections.”]

Although it is written, “Who can boast that he has a pure heart, or that he is clean from sin?” (Proverbs 20:9), the attainment of purity must not nevertheless be despaired of. For when it is continually sought, it is continually received, and what has been cleansed by confession does not remain subject to condemnation in judgment.

[Note: Thus the Corbie manuscript. Leo alludes to the Lord’s saying, “Everyone who asks receives.” Accordingly, the printed editions are wrong to read: “Which, although it is always desired, is not always received.” Quesnellus. His emendation is also approved by two lectionaries of Saint Peter and by manuscripts of Collections 2 and 5, which we have found suitable at this point.]

## CHAPTER II

This is what all the sons of the Church say alike when they pray according to the Lord’s teaching: “Forgive us our debts, as we also [Col. 0307A] forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

No one is so holy, no one so righteous, that in the time of this life—which is wholly a time of trial—he does not need forgiveness of some sin.

Countless dangers of offenses surround us on every side (Job 7:1). Through legitimate uses we pass into immoderate excesses, as the pleasure of sensuality insinuates itself through concern for health, and what may be sufficient for nature is not sufficient for desire.

From this arises a love of possessing that can never be satisfied. From this arises the desire to excel, which, whether it is attached to one’s lineage or to one’s offspring, now has pride as its child and now as its parent.

[Note: Quesnellus notes the alternative “to be loved” (amandus). We have corrected “attached” (innexa) from two manuscripts of Saint Peter and two Vatican manuscripts.]

Against these and other temptations, whose interconnection is manifold and endless, what virtue is more appropriately opposed than self-restraint? It both nourishes and preserves the goods of soul and body, and [Col. 0307B] gives them increase and strength.

Therefore, in the heavenly disciplines of the Church, divinely instituted fasts bring great benefit. While bodily appetite is subjected to the laws of self-restraint, the inner impulses are also moderated, so that just as the body fasts from food, the mind may fast from iniquity.

For the Lord says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

The people of God therefore possess spiritual banquets and chaste delights, which they healthfully seek and laudably desire, since the prophet praises and says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9).

Whoever has touched with the taste of his heart the sweetness of God’s justice and mercy, by which all his providence is administered, and has drawn from the experience of heavenly joys that must never be diminished by satiety, will look down upon corruptible and temporal goods in admiration of eternal things.

He will grow warm in that fire which God’s charity kindles, so that, with coldness transformed into fervor and night changed into light, the Holy Spirit may in one work drive away darkness and consume sins in the minds of the faithful. [Col. 0307C]

[Note: One Vatican lectionary reads “which he may seek and laudably desire.”]

## CHAPTER III

Since self-restraint, the mother of virtues, produces such fruits and leads those who fast from vices to ineffable delights, let us now, dearly beloved, carry out the heavenly commands with more earnest effort.

Since the whole paschal sacrament was established for the remission of sins, let us imitate what we desire to celebrate. [Col. 0308A]

For the merciful and just Lord promises his forgiveness in such a way that he also points it out to those whom he spares. Explaining the rule according to which he wished us to pray to God the Father, he says:

“If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. But if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your sins” (Matthew 6:14–15).

[Note: Quesnellus, together with the first edition and certain of our manuscripts, reads “which he indicates to those whom he spares.” Another reading, “which he investigates,” is incorrect. Shortly afterward, one Vatican manuscript reads “he wished” instead of “he may have wished.”]

It is an entirely just and kind condition by which a human being becomes a participant in divine power: he weighs God’s sentence by his own judgment and binds the Lord to himself by the judgment with which he has judged his fellow servant.

[Note: Manuscripts of Saint Peter read “by that judgment.”]

Whether toward those under authority or toward equals, therefore, let [Col. 0308B] equality of nature be loved. Since no one is without sin, let no one fail to forgive. Let us readily grant what we have gratefully received, so that whether through the generosity of alms or through the forgiveness of sins, the more merciful we have been, the more perfectly innocent we may be.

[Note: One manuscript of Saint Peter reads “which we receive.”]

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0307D] In the more widely circulated editions this sermon was relegated among the final sermons, after the treatise against the heresy of Eutyches. In all the manuscript collections, however, except the second, it is placed after Sermon 12 on Lent and before the sermons on the Passion, and likewise in the first edition. In Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary it is also listed among the Lenten sermons, as well as in the manuscript Lectionaries Vallicellianus A. 16 and 26, Venetian 153, Chigianus S. Basil., Vatican 106, Veronese, and Tridentine. In the manuscripts of Collection 2 alone it is placed outside this order, because the final sermons were discovered and added after the collection had been completed and could not be inserted in their proper places. For the same reason, three sermons *On the Fast of the Seventh Month* are found at the end of that collection outside their proper place, although six others with the same title had previously been placed where they belonged. Indeed, in the table of contents of the Casanatensian manuscript, which belongs to this second collection, this sermon is entitled *On the Fast of the Sabbath of the First Month*, which pertains to the season of Lent. Moreover, that this sermon was delivered on the Saturday before the Second Sunday of Lent is indicated not only by the title prefixed to it in Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary and in the Lectionaries of St. Peter’s Basilica 106, the Vallicellian A. 16, the Tridentine, and the Veronese, as well as in the manuscripts of Collection 2, but is also demonstrated by the Gospel capitularies, in which the Gospel of the Lord’s Transfiguration is shown to have been read only on that Saturday.]

## SERMON LI [Elsewhere XCIV]

Or, a homily delivered on the Saturday before the Second Sunday of Lent, on the Gospel according to Matthew: [Note: [Col. 0308D] Quesnellus noted this wording in the margin: “There can scarcely be any doubt that this beginning of the Gospel reading was copied from a recent breviary manuscript.” He is mistaken: the same beginning is read not only in the manuscripts of Collections 2, 3, 4, and 5, but also in Lectionaries of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, which derive from older copies. Rather, the title is more recent, the one Quesnellus accepted with the other editors, entitling this sermon *On the Lord’s Transfiguration*. This title is absent from all the Lectionaries, as well as from the manuscripts of Collections 2, 4, and 5. We have adopted the heading *On the Gospel according to Matthew*, as more suitable, from the manuscripts of Collection 5.] “At that time: Jesus took Peter, and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain apart, and so forth” (Matthew 17).

## SYNOPSIS

I. True faith confesses Christ as both God and man; this faith was rewarded with great authority in Peter.  
II. Christ was transfigured chiefly to establish the truth and power of his flesh.  
III. He was transfigured also to remove the scandal of the cross and strengthen the hope of his Church.  
IV. The harmony of the Old and New Testaments concerning Christ is signified through the appearance of Moses and Elijah.  
V. Peter’s desire was not wrong, but disordered.  
VI. “This is my beloved Son,” etc., is explained.  
VII. “Hear him” is examined.  
VIII. By this testimony of the Father the weakness of all is strengthened.

## CHAPTER I

The Gospel reading, dearly beloved, which through the ears of the body has struck the inner hearing of our minds, calls us to understand a great mystery. We shall attain it more easily with the grace of God assisting us if we direct our consideration to what was related shortly before. [Note: [Col. 0309D] In the Venetian Lectionary 153, *paulo* is absent. Then, instead of *Jesus Christ*, that same manuscript has *the Lord Christ*, and some Vatican manuscripts have *God Christ*.]

For Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, establishing that faith which calls both the ungodly to righteousness and the dead back to life, was instructing his disciples by the admonitions of his teaching and the miracles of his works so that the same Christ might be believed both the only-begotten Son of God and the Son of man. For either one without the other brought no benefit for salvation, and it was equally dangerous to believe the Lord Jesus Christ to be either God alone without man or man alone without God, since both had to be confessed alike: for just as true humanity was in God, so true divinity was in man.

To confirm, therefore, the most wholesome knowledge of this faith, [Note: [Col. 0309D] Two manuscript Lectionaries, Vatican 1268 and the Venetian, have “its saving character”; and instead of *cognitionem*, Quesnellus proposed *conditionem* in the margin.] the Lord had asked his disciples, amid the various opinions of others, what they themselves believed and thought about him. There the apostle Peter, by a revelation of the supreme Father, rising above bodily things and transcending human matters, saw with the eyes of his mind the Son of the living God and confessed the glory of his divinity, [Note: [Col. 0309D] One manuscript has *who did not*.] because he did not regard merely the substance of flesh and blood.

And he so pleased him by the sublimity of this faith that, endowed with the blessedness of beatitude, he received the sacred firmness of the inviolable rock. Upon that rock the Church, founded, would prevail against the gates of hell and the laws of death; nor, in the matters of releasing or binding anyone, would anything be ratified in heaven except what had been settled by Peter’s judgment.

## CHAPTER II

This height of praised understanding, dearly beloved, [Note: [Col. 0309D] The Venetian manuscript has “strength.”] had to be instructed concerning the mystery of the lower substance, lest the apostolic faith, raised up to confess the glory of Christ’s divinity, should judge the assumption of our weakness unworthy and incompatible with the impassible God, and should thus believe that human nature had already been glorified in him [Note: [Col. 0309D] The editions read “in Christ.”] in such a way that it could neither suffer punishment nor be dissolved by death. [Note: [Col. 0309D] The first edition and the Bonner manuscript have “redemption.”]

And therefore, when the Lord said that he had to go to Jerusalem, suffer many things from the elders, scribes, and chief priests, be killed, and rise again on the third day (Matthew 16:21; 20:17–19), blessed Peter—illumined by heavenly light and burning with the most ardent confession of the Son of God—had rejected the insults of mockery and the disgrace of a most savage death with what he thought was religious and free disdain. He was corrected by Jesus with a kindly rebuke and was then stirred to desire participation in his passion.

For the exhortation that followed [Note: [Col. 0309D] The Venetian manuscript omits “for.”] inspired and taught this: those who wished to follow him were to deny themselves and consider temporal losses exceedingly slight in hope of eternal things, because only the one who was not afraid to lose his soul for Christ would save it (Matthew 16:25). Therefore, so that they might conceive this strength of blessed steadfastness with all the heart of the apostle, and tremble at nothing in taking up the harshness of the cross, and not be ashamed of Christ’s punishment, [Note: [Col. 0309D] The same manuscript has “and should not blush at the Cross.”] nor regard as disgraceful to themselves the endurance that was to undergo the violence of passion without losing the glory of power, “Jesus took Peter, and James, and his brother John” (Matthew 17:1).

And after climbing with them a lofty mountain apart, he showed them the splendor of his glory [Note: [Col. 0309D–0310D] Quesnellus supplied the word “to them” (*illis*), absent from earlier editions, as it is found in our manuscripts. Shortly afterward Paul the Deacon’s exemplar has “although they had understood.”]: for although they understood the majesty of God in him, they did not know the power of that very body by which the divinity was veiled. Therefore he had expressly and distinctly promised that some of the disciples standing there would not taste death before they saw the Son of man coming in his kingdom (Matthew 16:28)—that is, in royal splendor—which he wished to be specially visible to these three men as belonging to the nature of the man he had assumed. [Note: [Col. 0310D] The common editions have *spiritually* here. The grammarian Latinus Latinius indicated that it should be read *specially* in his *Bibliotheca sacra*. We have therefore restored *specially* from the first edition, as well as from the Venetian Lectionary and other manuscripts of ours; some of them, by abbreviation, have *spaliter*, which the editors took for *spiritally*.]

For they could in no way, while still enclosed in mortal flesh, behold and see that ineffable and inaccessible vision of his divinity which is reserved for the pure in heart unto eternal life. [Note: [Col. 0310D] Another manuscript has “imperishable,” as Quesnellus noted in the margin.]

## CHAPTER III

The Lord therefore reveals his glory before chosen witnesses and brightens that bodily form which he shared with the others with such splendor that his face became like the radiance of the sun and his clothing equal to the whiteness of snow (Matthew 17:2).

In this transfiguration the principal purpose was that the scandal of the cross might be removed from the hearts of the disciples [Note: [Col. 0310D] The Venetian manuscript has “of the apostles”]; and that the voluntary humility of the passion might not disturb the faith of those to whom the excellence of his hidden dignity had been revealed. But with no less providence the hope of the holy Church was founded, so that the whole body of Christ might recognize the transformation with which it was to be endowed, [Note: [Col. 0310D] Instead of *ut*, which occurs in the earlier editions, but is needlessly repeated here from the preceding *ut*, we have written *at*, following some Vatican manuscripts and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary.] and that its members might promise themselves a share in the honor that had shone forth in the head.

The same Lord had spoken of this when he was describing the majesty of his coming: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43). [Note: [Col. 0310D] The Venetian manuscript reads “of my Father.”] Blessed Paul the apostle bears witness to the same thing when he says: “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18); and again: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:3–4). [Note: [Col. 0311D] The same manuscript omits the words “in God.”]

## CHAPTER IV

For the apostles to be strengthened and advanced toward complete knowledge, another instruction was also added to that miracle. Moses and Elijah—that is, the Law and the Prophets—appeared speaking with the Lord, so that in the presence of those five men there might most truly be fulfilled what was said: “Every word stands on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16; John 8:17; 2 Corinthians 13:1; Hebrews 10:28). [Note: [Col. 0311D] Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary has “and prophecy”; shortly afterward, with the Vatican Lectionary and two other manuscripts, it reads “every word will stand.”]

What is more stable or firmer than a word at whose proclamation the trumpet of the Old and New Testaments resounds in harmony, and with the teaching of the Gospel the instruments of ancient testimonies converge? The pages of both covenants mutually support one another. The one whom the earlier signs had promised beneath the veil of mysteries is shown openly and clearly by the splendor of his present glory. For, as blessed John says, “The law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). In him the promise of the prophetic figures and the purpose of the legal commandments were fulfilled: by his presence he teaches true prophecy, and by grace he makes the commandments possible.

## CHAPTER V

Stirred, therefore, by these revelations of the mysteries, the apostle Peter, scorning worldly and despising earthly things, was carried away by a kind of mental ecstasy into desire for eternal things. Filled with joy at the whole vision, he wished to dwell there with Jesus, where he rejoiced in the manifestation of his glory; and therefore he said: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here, one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4). [Note: [Col. 0311D] One Vatican manuscript has “he hoped.” Shortly afterward, some editions have “where they were manifest.”]

But the Lord did not answer this suggestion, signifying that what he desired was not indeed wrong, but disordered. [Note: [Col. 0311D] One Vatican manuscript adds “what he was asking.”] Since the world could not be saved except by Christ’s death, and the faith of believers was called to this by the Lord’s example, we were to understand that, although there should be no doubt concerning the promises of blessedness, [Note: [Col. 0311D] One Vatican manuscript has “concerning future promises”; the Venetian manuscript, “concerning the promise of blessedness.”] we must nevertheless first ask for endurance amid the trials of this life rather than glory: for the happiness of reigning cannot precede the times of suffering.

## CHAPTER VI
