While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and behold, a voice from the cloud said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (ibid., 5). [Note: [Col. 0311D] Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary has “from heaven.” Shortly afterward, following that Homiliary and all our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus, we have restored the word “beloved,” which had been removed here.]

The Father was indeed present in the Son, and in that glory of the Lord which he had moderated for the disciples’ sight, the essence of the Begetter was not separated from the Only-Begotten. But to commend the distinctiveness of the two persons, just as the splendor from the body indicated the Son to the sight, so the voice from the cloud announced the Father to the hearing. [Note: [Col. 0312D] One Vatican manuscript has “signified.”]

When the voice was received, the disciples fell on their faces and were very afraid. [Note: [Col. 0312D] The Venetian manuscript has “indeed.” Shortly afterward, Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary reads, “They were afraid of the majesty of the Son.”] They trembled not only before the majesty of the Father but also before that of the Son, for in a deeper understanding they recognized the one divinity of both; and because there was no hesitation in their faith, there was no distinction in their fear. [Note: [Col. 0312D] The Venetian manuscript has “joyful.”]

That testimony, therefore, was broad and manifold, and more was heard in the power of the words than in the sound of the voice. [Note: [Col. 0312D] Some Vatican manuscripts omit the preposition *in*.] For when the Father said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him,” was this not plainly heard: “This is my Son, whose being from me and with me is without time”? For neither is the Begetter prior to the Begotten, nor is the Begotten later than the Begetter.

“This is my Son, whom divinity does not separate from me, power does not divide, and eternity does not distinguish. This is my Son, not adopted but proper; not created from elsewhere but begotten from me; not made comparable to me from another nature, but born equal to me from my essence.” [Note: [Col. 0312D] The Venetian manuscript adds *est* (“is”) and later deletes *mihi* (“to me”).]

“This is my Son, through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made” (John 1:3), because everything that I do he likewise does, and whatever I accomplish, he accomplishes inseparably and without distinction with me. For the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son (John 5:19), and our unity is never divided.

And although I, who begot him, am one, and he, whom I begot, is another, you are nevertheless permitted to think of him as nothing other than what it is possible to believe concerning me. This is my Son, who did not seek the equality that he possesses with me as a prize to be seized, nor claim it by usurpation (Philippians 2:6), but, while remaining in the form of my glory, in order to carry out the common plan for restoring the human race, humbled his unchangeable divinity even to the form of a servant.

## CHAPTER VII

Hear without hesitation, therefore, this one in whom I am well pleased in every respect, and by whose proclamation I am manifested and by whose humility I am glorified. [Note: [Col. 0312D] Thus, together with all our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus, who has *mihi bene per omnia placeo* (“I am well pleasing to myself in every respect”). Shortly afterward, the Venetian manuscript, deleting the conjunction *et*, has “in whose proclamation.”]

For he himself is truth and life, he himself my power and wisdom. Hear him whom the mysteries of the Law foretold and the mouths of the prophets sang. Hear him who redeems the world by his blood, who binds the devil and seizes his vessels, who tears up the record of sin and the agreements of transgression. [Note: [Col. 0313C] The same Venetian manuscript has “the covenant.”]

Hear him who opens the way to heaven and, through the punishment of the cross, prepares for you the steps of ascent to the kingdom. Why do you tremble at being redeemed? Why, though wounded, are you afraid to be freed? [Note: [Col. 0313C] The cited manuscript has “Let what Christ wills be done according to my will.”] Let what Christ wills, with me willing it, be done. Cast away fleshly fear and arm yourselves with faithful steadfastness. For it is unworthy that you should fear in the passion of the Savior what, by his gift, you will not fear even at your own end.

## CHAPTER VIII

These things, dearly beloved, were spoken not only for the benefit of those who heard them with their own ears. In those three apostles the universal Church learned whatever their eyes saw and their ears received. Let the faith of all, therefore, be strengthened according to the preaching of the most holy Gospel, and let no one be ashamed of Christ’s cross, through which the world was redeemed.

Nor should anyone fear to suffer for righteousness or distrust the repayment of what was promised, since through labor we pass to rest and through death to life, while he assumed the whole weakness of our humility. If we remain in confession and love of him, then what he conquered we conquer, and what he promised we receive. [Note: [Col. 0313C] Several Vatican manuscripts omit the preposition *in* in the second occurrence. The Venetian manuscript omits *et in dilectione* (“and in love”). Shortly afterward, one Vatican manuscript has “what we conquered, we conquered,” and “what he promised, we received.”]

For whether we are to carry out commandments or endure adversities, the Father’s preceding voice should always resound in our ears [Note: [Col. 0313D] Quesnellus alone reads “ring out” (*intonare*).], saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.” [Note: [Col. 0313D] The first edition has: “Who lives and reigns, blessed forever.”] He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## 198 SERMON LII [Elsewhere L]

[Note: [Col. 0313D] In one ancient Vatican manuscript and in the first edition this sermon is entitled: “The First Sermon of the Same Leo on the Lord’s Good Friday.” Since, near the end of the sermon, the holy pontiff promises that he will discuss other matters, which he now omits, on Wednesday, Quesnellus rightly noted in a marginal postscript: “It appears to have been delivered on Palm Sunday, and not before the discovery of Eutyches’ error, as is evident from various passages.”]

## On the Passion of the Lord I

Delivered on Sunday.

## SYNOPSIS

I. Salvation comes to man solely through the incarnation of the Word; faith in this was necessary even in the Old Testament and before the Law.  
II. Salvation is achieved through the power of the Word and the humility of the flesh.  
III. The cross and abasement of the one who, by a single word during his passion, struck down the soldiers must not be despised.  
IV. Christ willingly handed himself over to death; he restrained Peter’s zeal and restored the servant’s ear.  
V. Christ’s death frees us and accuses the Jews and Judas, although they too could have been redeemed by it.

## CHAPTER I

The sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, dearly beloved, which the Lord Jesus, the Son of God, undertook for the salvation of the human race, and which, as he promised, drew all things to himself when he was exalted, has been so plainly and lucidly disclosed by the Gospel sermon that for religious and devout hearts to hear what has been read is no different from seeing what was done. [Note: [Col. 0313D] In the common editions and also in some manuscripts this sermon begins: “The most sacred day of the Lord’s Passion, which …” We have preferred the reading of the most ancient Vatican Lectionary 3835, a manuscript certainly Roman and belonging to the Basilica of the holy apostles Philip and James, especially since the manuscripts of the more authoritative Collections 1 and 2 agree with it. The context also fits better: for the Gospel sermon itself is said to have disclosed the mystery of the Lord’s Passion, rather than the most sacred day.]

Since the sacred narrative possesses unquestionable authority, we must strive, with the Lord’s help, to ensure that understanding makes clear what history has made known. [Note: [Col. 0314D] The manuscripts of Collection 2 have “that it may have clear understanding.”]

For after the first and universal ruin of human transgression, through which sin entered this world by one man, and through sin death, and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12), no one [Note: [Col. 0314D] We have added “dreadful” (*tetram*) from the most ancient Vatican manuscript and the manuscripts of the ancient collections.] could escape the dreadful domination of the devil or the bonds of terrible captivity. No one would have access either to reconciliation for pardon or to a return to life unless the Son of God, coeternal and coequal with God the Father, [Note: [Col. 0314D] The same Vatican manuscript reads “the Son, God.”] deigned also to become the Son of man, coming to seek and save what had been lost (Luke 19:10), so that just as death came through Adam, so through our Lord Jesus Christ there might be a resurrection of the dead (1 Corinthians 15:22).

For although, according to the inscrutable purpose of God’s wisdom, in the last days the Word became flesh (John 1:14), it does not follow that the birth of the saving Virgin benefited only the generations of the final age and did not extend itself also into earlier ages. All antiquity that worshiped the true God, every multitude of saints in the ages before us, lived and found favor in this faith. Neither for the patriarchs, nor for the prophets, nor for any of the saints was there salvation and justification except in the redemption of our Lord Jesus Christ. This redemption, as it was awaited and promised through many prophetic oracles and signs, was likewise presented in the gift itself and in the deed. [Note: [Col. 0314D] The editions have “in sacred faith.” The reading of the manuscripts of Collection 2 seemed preferable, as being especially suited to the context.] [Note: [Col. 0314D] The Casanatensian manuscript adds “by human beings.” Shortly afterward, the Barberini manuscript has “in the gift of Christ” instead of “for the gift”; the Bonner manuscript has “carried out” instead of “presented,” and another manuscript has “represented.”]

## CHAPTER II

Therefore now, dearly beloved, throughout the whole course of the Lord’s Passion, let us not consider human weakness in such a way as to suppose that divine power was absent there; nor let us imagine the form of the Only-Begotten, coeternal and equal with the Father, in such a way as to think that the things which appear unworthy of God were not real. [Note: [Col. 0314D] Two of our manuscripts have “coequal.” The most ancient Vatican manuscript has “nor let us imagine that form equal and coeternal with the Father.”]

The two natures are wholly one Christ [Note: [Col. 0314D] We have added the word “is” from the same Vatican manuscript and the Casanatensian manuscript.]: the Word was not separated there from the man, nor was the man dissociated from the Word. Humility was not disdained, because majesty was not diminished. [Note: [Col. 0314D] The Casanatensian manuscript has “nor did it harm.”] Nothing harmful happened to the inviolable nature that had to be inflicted upon the passible nature; and the entire mystery, which humanity and divinity together brought to completion, was an administration of mercy and an act of loving-kindness.

For we were held by such bonds [Note: [Col. 0315D] Thus the most ancient Vatican manuscript; others have “constrained” or “bound”] that we could not be released except through this aid. The humility of divinity, therefore, is our advancement. We are redeemed at so great a price; we are healed at so great an expenditure. For what return would there be from ungodliness to righteousness, from misery to blessedness, unless the righteous stooped toward the ungodly and the blessed toward the miserable?

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, dearly beloved, [Note: [Col. 0315D] We have inserted “for us” from the same Vatican manuscript and three other manuscripts.] Christ’s cross is not something of which we should be ashamed. It derives from the power of the divine plan, not from the condition of sin. Although the Lord Jesus truly suffered from our weakness and truly died, he did not so withdraw from his glory that, amid the insults of his passion, he exercised none of the works of divinity.

For when the ungodly Judas, no longer concealed beneath a sheep’s skin but revealed in wolfish fury, began the force of his crime under the appearance of peace and offered the sign of betrayal with a kiss more savage than any weapon, and when the frenzied crowd that had gathered with an armed cohort of soldiers to seize the Lord, amid torches and lanterns, failed to see the true light because it was blinded by its own darkness, [Note: [Col. 0315D] Here and in several other places in this sermon we have adjusted the arrangement of certain words, differing from the editions, in accordance with the more reliable manuscripts.] the Lord—who, as the evangelist John testifies, chose to await the crowd rather than avoid it (John 18:4)—asked those who had not yet found him whom they sought. When they said that they were looking for Jesus, he replied: “I am he” (ibid., 5).

That word struck and overwhelmed the group assembled from the fiercest men as if by a kind of lightning bolt, so that all those fierce, threatening, and terrifying men were driven backward and fell. Where was the conspiracy of savagery? Where the heat of anger? Where the array of weapons? The Lord says, “I am he,” and at his voice the crowd of ungodly men is overthrown. What will his majesty be able to do when he comes as judge, whose humility was able to do this when he himself was being judged?

## CHAPTER IV

Nevertheless, the Lord, knowing what was more fitting to the mystery he had undertaken, [Note: [Col. 0315D] The Barberini manuscript has “he did not wish to use this power.”] did not remain in the exercise of this power, but allowed his persecutors to return to the opportunity of carrying out the crime that had been arranged. For if he had not wished to be held, he would certainly not have been held.

But who among human beings could have been saved if he had not allowed himself to be seized? Blessed Peter, too, who clung to the Lord with more spirited steadfastness and burned with the ardor of holy love against the attacks of the violent, used a sword against the servant of the high priest and more fiercely cut off the ear of the man who was pressing forward (Matthew 26:51; Mark 14:47; Luke 22:50; John 18:10).

But the Lord does not allow the devout impulse of the zealous apostle to proceed further. He orders the sword to be put away and does not permit himself to be defended against the ungodly by hand and steel. For it was contrary to the mystery of our redemption that the one who had come to die for all should refuse to be captured; otherwise, by delaying the glorious triumph of the cross, the devil’s domination and human captivity would both have been prolonged. [Note: [Col. 0315D] The first edition and the Vatican manuscripts of Collections 3 and 5 have: “For if … had been delayed.” Shortly afterward, another Vatican manuscript has “the glorious triumph of the cross.”]

He therefore gives those raging against him permission to inflict violence, yet does not disdain even in such circumstances to reveal his divinity. Christ’s hand restores the servant’s ear—already dead through the severing itself and separated from the framework of the living body—to the seat of the dishonored head. [Note: [Col. 0315D] The first edition has “He reforms what he himself had formed,” together with the Bonner manuscript.] He reforms what he himself had formed; and the flesh is not slow to obey the command of the one whose handiwork it was.

## CHAPTER V

These works, therefore, possess divine power. But the fact that the Lord restrains the power of his majesty and allows the persecutor’s violence against him proceeds from that will by which he loved us and handed himself over for us (Ephesians 5:25), with the Father himself cooperating in this—he who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all (Romans 8:32). [Note: [Col. 0315D] The editions before Quesnellus have “the Father himself.” Our manuscripts read as in the text, which we have retained with Quesnellus.]

For the will of the Father and of the Son is one, just as their divinity is one. Concerning the effect of this disposition, we owe you nothing of grace, Jews, nor do we owe you anything, Judas. Your ungodliness served our salvation, though you did not will it; and through you everything came about that the hand and plan of God had decreed should happen (Acts 4:28).

Christ’s death therefore frees us and accuses you. Rightly, you alone do not possess what you wished everyone to lose. Yet the goodness of our Redeemer is so great that you too could obtain pardon if, by confessing Christ as the Son of God, you abandoned that murderous wickedness. For the Lord did not pray on the cross in vain when he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

That remedy would not have passed you by, Judas, if you had fled to the repentance that would have recalled you to Christ, rather than to that which drove you to the noose. For by saying, “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matthew 27:4), you persisted in the obstinacy of your ungodliness, because in the extreme peril of your death you believed Jesus to be not God, the Son of God, but merely a man of our condition. [Note: [Col. 0316D] Thus from the most ancient Vatican manuscript. Two Vatican manuscripts have “even in the extreme peril of your death.”] You would have bent his mercy toward you if you had not denied his omnipotence.

These things, dearly beloved, which have been imparted to your devout ears today, are sufficient, lest weariness creep in through excessive length. What is lacking for completeness we promise to supply on Wednesday, with the Lord’s help, since he who gave us what we have spoken will, as we believe, give us what we shall speak: [Note: [Col. 0316D] Thus from the same most ancient Vatican manuscript. The first edition has: “Through Christ our Lord. Amen.” Other editions before Quesnellus have: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.” Several manuscripts likewise have this form, omitting only “your Son.” Quesnellus has: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who with God and the Holy Spirit …” The Antwerp edition of 1583 has the same as Quesnellus, but reads *eo* (“him”) instead of *Deo* (“God”).] through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON LIII [Elsewhere LI]

## On the Passion of the Lord II

Delivered on Wednesday.

## SYNOPSIS

I. The conversion of the thief, who remained guilty up to the cross but suddenly became a confessor of Christ, was the work of grace.  
II. All creatures, when they bore witness to Christ on the cross, pronounced judgment against the Jews.  
III. Christians must be conformed to Christ’s humility and patience; there is no other way to eternal things.

## CHAPTER I

Faith requires, dearly beloved, that we now deliver, with the Lord’s help, the portion of the sermon on the Lord’s Passion that we promised. We do not doubt that we are assisted in this by your prayers. For it contributes to the common benefit if you are able to have me devoted to the task, because whatever is granted to my ability is expended for your edification.

After that impious and detestable transaction with Judas, by which the Redeemer of the world was handed over by him to the persecuting Jews; after those sacrilegious mockeries amid which his gentleness was led even to the place of punishment, two thieves were crucified with him, with crosses set up on either side. One of them, until that moment equal and similar to his companion, a highway robber and always hostile to human safety, guilty even to the cross, suddenly becomes a confessor of Christ.

Amid those most severe torments of body and soul, which both their persistence and the difficulty of death intensified, he was changed by a marvelous conversion and said: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

What exhortation persuaded him to this faith? What teaching instructed him? What preacher kindled it? He had not previously seen the miracles that had been performed. At that time the healing of the sick, the illumination of the blind, and the raising of the dead had ceased; even those things that were soon to be done were not present. Yet he confesses as Lord and King the one whom he sees sharing his punishment.

From there, therefore, arose this gift—from the place where faith itself received its answer. For Jesus said to him: [Note: [Col. 0317D] The same edition repeats “Amen, amen.” Later, toward the end of the chapter, some manuscripts retain *servant* instead of *saved*, and after the phrase “and the unity” the first edition, Collection 3, and one Vatican manuscript of Collection 4 delete *suam* (“its own”).] “Amen, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise” (ibid., 43).

This promise surpasses human condition; it is issued not so much from the wood of the cross as from the throne of power. From that height the reward of faith is given at which the record of human transgression is erased. For the form of God does not separate itself from the form of a servant, while amid the punishments themselves the inviolable divinity and the passible nature preserved their distinctiveness and unity.

## CHAPTER II

The testimony of all creation is added to confirm our entire hope. When Christ gave up his spirit, all the elements trembled. The splendor of the sun was covered by dense darkness and extraordinarily subjected the day to night. The earth, shaken by deep convulsions, did not retain its stability, and the solidity of the rocks, broken apart, split open. The veil of the Temple, which no longer needed to conceal the mysteries of former times, was torn; and when the bodies of many saints were raised, the tombs were opened to strengthen faith in the resurrection (Matthew 27:51–53; Mark 15:38; Luke 23:45–46).

Against you, therefore, Jews, heaven and earth pronounced judgment. For you the sun withdrew its service and the day; for you the ranks of the elements denied their ministry. As creation’s service departed from its laws, your blindness and your confusion were signified. For since you said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25), it was justly repaid that what the ungodly portion of your race lost should be attained by the faithful fullness of the nations. [Note: [Col. 0318D] Another edition has “its power.” Quesnellus.]

## CHAPTER III
We, therefore, dearly beloved, for whom our Lord Jesus Christ crucified is not a stumbling-block or foolishness, but the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:23)—we, I say, the spiritual seed of Abraham, born not in the offspring of slavery but reborn into the household of freedom, for whom, after we were brought out of the oppression of Egyptian rule with a strong hand and an outstretched arm [Note: Col. 0318D. Thus from the manuscript of St. Peter. Others read, “with an exalted arm.”], Christ, the true and spotless Lamb, was sacrificed (1 Cor. 5:7)—let us embrace the wonderful sacrament of the saving Passover, and let us be reformed into the likeness of him who was made conformable to our deformity. Let us rise toward him who made the dust of our lowliness the body of his glory [Col. 0318C]; and, so that we may deserve to share in his resurrection, let us in every respect conform ourselves to his humility and patience.

We have undertaken the discipline of the service of a great name and of a great profession. Those who follow Christ may not depart from the royal way; rather, as we press toward eternal things, it is fitting that we not be occupied with temporal matters. And because we have been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, let us glorify and bear God in our body (1 Cor. 6:20), so that we may deserve to attain what has been prepared for the faithful, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen. [Note: Col. 0318D. Thus the very ancient Vatican manuscript 3835. The manuscript of St. Peter reads: “Through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever.”]

# SERMON LIV [Others: LII]

On the Passion of the Lord III. Delivered on the Lord’s Day.

## SYNOPSIS

[Col. 0318D]

I. The mystery of the cross and redemption, prefigured in ancient times, requires two natures in Christ.  
II. The properties of each nature are distinct, and the human passions were voluntarily assumed.  
III. How unjustly Judas distrusted the Lord’s goodness, although the Lord had not excluded him from communion in his body and blood.  
IV. That our sadness and fear were voluntarily assumed by Christ [Col. 0319A].  
V. That Peter’s conversion was the work of Christ’s inward gaze.  
VI. The magnitude of the evils whose origin was the Jews’ outcry by which they handed Christ over to death.

## CHAPTER I

Among all the works of God’s mercy that, from the beginning, have been bestowed for the salvation of mortals, dearly beloved, nothing is more wonderful, nothing more sublime, than that Christ was crucified for the world. For all the mysteries of the preceding ages served this sacrament, and whatever was varied through the sacred dispensation in the different kinds of sacrifices, in prophetic signs, and in legal institutions [Note: Col. 0319D. The preposition “in” has been added from Vatican manuscript 3835.], foretold this as arranged and promised this as destined to be fulfilled: so that now, when images and figures have ceased, it benefits us to believe that what formerly benefited us to believe would be accomplished has already been accomplished.

In everything, therefore, dearly beloved, that pertains to the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Catholic faith transmits and requires this: that we recognize two natures as having come together in our Redeemer. Their properties remaining intact, such unity of both substances was accomplished that, from the time when, as the condition of the human race required, the Word became flesh in the womb of the blessed Virgin [Note: Col. 0319D. The manuscript of St. Peter reads, “within the womb of the blessed Virgin.”] (John 1:14), it is not permissible to think of him as God without what he is as man, or as man without what he is as God. [Note: The first edition and the Bonn manuscript read, “under different and distinct actions.”]

Each nature certainly expresses its truth through distinct actions, but neither separates itself from the connection with the other. Nothing there is absent from the other; humility is wholly in majesty, and majesty wholly in humility. Unity does not introduce confusion, nor does distinction divide unity [Col. 0319C]. One is capable of suffering, the other inviolable; yet the insult belongs to the same one to whom the glory belongs. He himself is in weakness who is also in power; he is both capable of death and victorious over death. God therefore assumed the whole human being and so joined himself to humanity, and humanity to himself, through mercy and power, that each nature should exist in the other [Note: Col. 0319D. The same edition and manuscript read, “nature”], while neither passed over from its own property into the other.

## CHAPTER II

But because the dispensation of the sacrament, arranged before the eternal ages for our restoration, was to be completed neither without human weakness nor without divine power [Note: Col. 0319D. The same in Epistle 28 to Flavian, chapter 4.], each form acts in communion with the other according to what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines forth in miracles [Col. 0319D]; the other submits to injuries. [Note: We corrected “that one” on the authority of the oldest Vatican manuscript. Others read, “the other.”] The former does not withdraw from equality with the Father’s glory; the latter does not abandon the nature of our race.

Yet even the reception of sufferings was not so exposed to the humility of our condition [Note: The printed editions had “to our affection.” We placed “of our humility” after “affection,” on the authority of the aforementioned oldest Vatican manuscript. In one manuscript of St. Peter, “affliction” occurs instead of “affection.”] that it was separated from the power of divinity. Whatever mockery and insult, whatever harassment and punishment, the fury of the impious inflicted upon the Lord was endured not by necessity but assumed by will. For the Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished (Luke 10:10); and he used the malice of his persecutors for the redemption of all in such a way that, in the sacrament of his death and resurrection, even his killers [Note: Col. 0319D. The cited Vatican manuscript reads “of him” in place of “his own.”] could be saved if they believed.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, Judas, you proved more wicked than all and more wretched: repentance did not call you back to the Lord, but despair dragged you to the noose. You should have awaited the completion of your crime and postponed the hideous suspension of death until the blood of Christ had been poured out for all sinners. And when so many miracles of the Lord and so many gifts were tormenting your conscience, at least those sacraments should have called you back from your plunge—those which you had received at the paschal supper, after your treachery had been disclosed by the sign of divine knowledge [Note: We restored “sacraments” from the oldest Vatican manuscript and from editions prior to Quesnell. Immediately afterward, the manuscript of St. Peter reads “in your treachery.”].

Why do you distrust his goodness, who did not exclude you from communion in his body and blood, who did not deny you the kiss of peace when you came with the crowds and a cohort of armed men to seize him (John 18:5)? But, a man incapable of conversion, a spirit that goes away and does not return (Ps. 77:39) [Note: Col. 0320D. Some editions read “incorruptible” or “corruptible.” Subsequently one manuscript of St. Peter reads “while you stood” in place of “and while [the devil] stood.”], you followed the fury of your heart; and while the devil stood at your right hand (Ps. 108:6), you turned back upon your own head the wickedness that you had armed against the head of all the saints. Since your crime had exceeded every measure of vengeance, your own impiety made itself your judge, and your own punishment became your executioner. [Note: The same manuscript of St. Peter and the first edition read, “your impiety.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Since God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself (1 Cor. 5:19), and since the Creator himself bore the creature in order to restore it according to the image of its creator [Note: Col. 0320D. Thus from the oldest Vatican manuscript, as well as from the manuscript of St. Peter and other codices. Others read, “of the Creator.” Immediately afterward, the first edition and the Bonn manuscript read “maker” (conditor) in place of “Creator” (creator).], after the miracles of divine works had been completed—works that the prophetic Spirit had once foretold would be performed:

“Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened,  
and the ears of the deaf shall hear;  
then the lame man shall leap like a stag,  
and the tongue of the mute shall be clear” [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript reads “clear.” At this passage of Isaiah, both “clear” and “plain” are found among the Fathers, as Father Sabbatier shows.] (Isa. 35:5)—

Jesus, knowing that the time had already come for the glorious Passion to be fulfilled, said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38); and again: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid., v. 39). By these words, which express a certain fear, he cared for the emotions of our weakness by sharing them, and by undergoing the fear of painful experience he underwent it. [Note: The manuscript of St. Peter reads, “He trembled with our pallor and had clothed himself in the assumption of our weakness, so that he might bear ours,” and so forth.]

The Lord therefore trembled in our fear, so that he might put on the assumption of our weakness and clothe our inconstancy with the firmness of his power. For a rich and merciful merchant had come into this world from heaven [Note: The printed editions read “of the sky.” We corrected this from the oldest Vatican manuscript and the manuscript of St. Peter. The first edition reads, “and by the exchange of heaven.” After a little we have written “giving what was his” with the older editions and the two cited manuscripts. Quesnell has “restoring what was his.”], and by a marvelous exchange had entered into a saving commerce, receiving what was ours and giving what was his: honor in place of insults [Note: The same oldest Vatican manuscript reads “honors,” and afterward “healing” instead of “salvation.”], salvation in place of sufferings, life in place of death. And although more than twelve thousand legions of angels could have served him for the destruction of his persecutors (Matt. 26:53) [Note: Reference is made to Matthew 26:53, where “thousands” is not now read, but was formerly read in some copies, as can be seen in the oldest Gospels of Verona, Brescia, and Friuli edited by Father Blanchini. Hence Augustine likewise read it in his copies, in On the Spirit and the Letter, chapters 1 and 35, and Hilary in Psalm 53, no. 1; Psalm 54, no. 6; and Book X of On the Trinity, no. 42.], he preferred to receive our fear rather than exercise his own power.

## CHAPTER V

How much this humility bestowed upon all the faithful was first experienced by the most blessed apostle Peter (ibid.) [Note: Thus read our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnell, who has, “The Apostle experienced this, to whom, when….” The oldest Vatican manuscript inserts the word “Peter” but deletes “Apostle.”]. When a violent storm of impending savagery had shaken him, he turned quickly toward the restoration of his strength, taking a remedy from the example, so that the suddenly trembling member might return to the firmness of its head.

For a servant could not be greater than his lord, nor a disciple than his master (Matt. 10:24; John 15:20), nor could he overcome the trembling of human weakness unless the victor over death had first been afraid. The Lord therefore looked upon Peter (Luke 22:61), and while he stood amid the priests’ accusations [Note: Col. 0321D. The manuscript of St. Peter reads, “amid the slanders of the elders.”], the witnesses’ falsehoods, and the insults of those who struck and spat, he met the troubled disciple with the eyes by which he had foreseen that he would be troubled. The scrutiny of truth entered him [Note: Col. 0322C. Thus the oldest Vatican manuscript, the manuscripts of St. Peter and two other Vatican manuscripts, together with the Victorine manuscript cited by Quesnell in the margin. The first edition reads, “went out”; other editions, with manuscripts of collection 4, read, “was converted.”], where correction of the heart was required; as though a certain voice of the Lord sounded there [Note: Col. 0322C. The printed editions read “to him.” We corrected this from the very ancient Vatican manuscript and the manuscript of St. Peter.] and said:

“Where are you going, Peter? Why are you withdrawing into yourself? Turn back to me, trust in me, follow me. This is the time of my Passion; the hour of your punishment has not yet come. Why are you afraid of what you yourself will also overcome? Let not the weakness that I have assumed confuse you. I was trembling because of you; you must be secure because of me.” [Note: Col. 0322C. We preferred the reading of the oldest Vatican manuscript. Others read: “What do you have, Peter? Why do you withdraw into your conscience?” The manuscript of St. Peter reads, “Why do you withdraw within?” where “within” appears to be a scribal error for “into your.” Immediately afterward, some Vatican manuscripts read “return” instead of “turn.” Another Vatican manuscript reads “turn back again.”]

When morning came, all the chief priests and the elders of the people took counsel against Jesus in order to hand him over to death (Matt. 27:1). This morning, Jews, brought you not the rising of light but its setting; the customary day did not rise for your eyes, but night of grim blindness settled upon your impious minds. This morning destroyed your temple and altars, took away the law and the prophets, removed the kingdom and priesthood, and turned all your festivals into eternal mourning [Note: We have added “for you” from the oldest Vatican manuscript and the manuscript of St. Peter].

For you entered into a mad and bloody plot—you fattened bulls, numerous calves, roaring beasts, rabid dogs—in order to hand over to death the author of life and the Lord of glory. And as though the enormity of your fury would be diminished if you used the judgment of the man who governed your province, you led bound Jesus to Pilate’s tribunal, so that, after overcoming the frightened governor with your wicked cries, you might choose a murderer for release and demand the Savior of the world for punishment. [Note: Thus read certain of our Vatican manuscripts, as Quesnell conjectured in a marginal note, though he did not dare alter the customary reading, “a man.”]

After this condemnation of Christ, which was carried out more by the cowardice than by the authority of Pilate the governor [Note: We have corrected this from the manuscripts of St. Peter and another Vatican lectionary. The oldest Vatican manuscript likewise reads “which,” whereas others have “by which”; the former better excuses the cowardice of Pilate the governor rather than his authority.], who, after washing his hands and polluting his mouth, sent Jesus to the cross with the same lips with which he had pronounced him innocent [Note: Some manuscripts and the first edition read, “had foretold him.”], the people’s license, serving the priests’ eyes, inflicted many insults upon the Lord; and the frenzied crowd raged against his gentleness, although he willingly endured these things.

But because it is too much, dearly beloved, for today’s sermon to traverse everything, let the remaining matters be postponed until Wednesday, when the reading of the Lord’s Passion will be repeated. The Lord will grant, when you pray, that by his gift we may fulfill what we promise: through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen. [Note: Col. 0322D. The oldest Vatican manuscript reads: “Through the same our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.”]

# SERMON LV [Others: LIII]

On the Passion of the Lord IV. On Wednesday.

## SYNOPSIS

[Col. 0322C]

I. The crucifixion of Christ, in which the distinction between the elect and the rejected is prefigured through the robbers.  
II. The ignorance of the Jews’ blasphemies against Christ, since it had been foretold that he would not descend from the cross but would reign from the tree.  
III. On the cross, which is the sacrament of the true altar, the record of sin was erased by Christ’s blood, and the robber was marvelously converted.  
IV. On the vinegar that he tasted, the words “It is finished,” the inclination of Christ’s head, and his death.  
V. The preparation of hearts through charity and purity for celebrating the paschal feast.

## CHAPTER I

What is owed to your expectation, dearly beloved, must be paid back by the Lord’s generosity, your prayers making us worthy, so that he may make us capable [Note: Col. 0323D. The first edition reads “makes.”] of discharging what he has made you eager to receive. Recently speaking about the Lord’s Passion, we came as far as the place in the Gospel narrative where Pilate is said to have yielded to the wicked cries of the Jews [Note: Col. 0323D. Laurentius Latinius conjectured that “wicked” (improbis) should perhaps be read.] that Jesus should be crucified. Therefore, after everything had been completed that divinity, tempered by the veil of flesh, permitted to be done, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was fastened to the cross which he himself had also carried [Note: The first edition reads “had carried.”], and two robbers were likewise crucified, one at his right and the other at his left. Thus, even in the appearance of the gibbet itself, that distinction which must be made in his judgment among all human beings was displayed: the faith of the believing robber expressed the figure of those who would be saved, while the impiety of the blasphemer marked beforehand the form of those who would be condemned. [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript 3835 omits “of the robber.”]

The Passion of Christ therefore contains the sacrament of our salvation. From the instrument that the wickedness of the Jews had prepared for punishment, the power of the Redeemer made a step for us toward glory [Note: Although Quesnell substituted “joy” for “step,” and this is confirmed by several and better manuscripts, we have restored the earlier editors’ reading, “step,” which is approved by the exemplar of the first edition, collection 3, both because it is more suitable and because the same reading occurs in Sermon 51, chapter 7: “Through the punishment of the cross he prepares for you a step of ascent to the kingdom.”]. The Lord Jesus undertook it for the salvation of all human beings in such a way that, amid the nails by which he was fastened to the wood, he pleaded the Father’s mercy for his executioners [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript reads “the mercy of the Father”] and said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

## CHAPTER II

But the chief priests, for whom the Savior was asking pardon, sharpened the punishment of the cross with the goads of mockery [Note: Thus the manuscript of St. Peter. Others read “assailed.”]. Against the one whom they could no longer attack with their hands, they hurled the weapons of their tongues, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” [Note: Col. 0323D. The adverb “now” is lacking in the very ancient Vatican manuscript.] (Matt. 27:42).

From what source of error [Note: Perhaps “of fury,” as Laurentius Latinius conjectured in the Bibliotheca], Jews, from what lake of envy, did you drink the poisons of such blasphemies? What teacher handed these things down to you? What teaching persuaded you that you ought to believe that he was the king of Israel and the Son of God, who would either not allow himself to be crucified or would shake his body free from the fastening of the nails? [Note: Col. 0324D. We added “or” from the manuscripts of St. Peter and the very ancient Vatican manuscript, which adds “body” after “free.” In some Vatican manuscripts, “the utterances of the prophets proclaimed” follows shortly afterward.] The mysteries of the law did not proclaim this to you; neither did the sacraments of the paschal observance, nor at any time the mouth of any prophet. But you read abundantly and truly what pertains both to the detestable impiety of your crime and to the Lord’s voluntary Passion.

For he himself speaks through Isaiah: “I gave my back to scourging, my cheeks to those who struck them; I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. 50:6). [Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads, “but my cheeks,” and immediately afterward, “in my food.”] He himself says through David: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. Many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me. They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves watched and looked upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. 68:22; 21:17). [Note: We corrected this from the same Vatican manuscript. Others read “plan.” Afterward, instead of “they looked upon,” we have written “they gazed upon,” from the same manuscript and another Vatican manuscript, collection 5. The first edition reads, “they gazed upon me.”]

And lest it seem that only the order of your crime had been foretold, while no power of the crucified one had been announced, you did not indeed read, “The Lord will descend from the cross” [Note: The first edition and three manuscripts read “will descend.”]; rather, you read: “The Lord reigned from the tree” (Ps. 95:10).

## CHAPTER III

The cross of Christ therefore possesses the sacrament of the true and foretold altar, where the offering of human nature would be celebrated through a saving sacrifice. There the blood of the spotless Lamb erased the covenants of the ancient transgression; there the whole opposition of the devil’s domination was crushed, and victorious humility triumphed over the arrogance of pride [Note: The manuscript of St. Peter reads, “over the casting down of pride”]. The effect of faith was so swift that, among the robbers crucified with Christ, the one who believed in Christ the Son of God entered Paradise justified.

Who could explain the sacrament of so great a gift? Who could recount the power of so marvelous an exchange? In a brief moment, the guilt of long crimes is abolished. Amid the harsh torments of a struggling soul, he clings to the gibbet and passes over to Christ; and the one to whom his own impiety brought punishment receives a crown through Christ’s grace.

## CHAPTER IV

Then, after tasting the vinegar supplied by that vineyard which, degenerating from the planting of its author, had been turned into the bitterness of a foreign vine, the Lord said, “It is finished” (Matt. 21:38; John 19:30)—that is, “The Scriptures have been fulfilled. There is nothing more that I should expect from the madness of the raging people; I have suffered nothing less than I foretold that I would suffer.” [Note: Col. 0324D. Thus corrected from the manuscript of St. Peter. In the manuscript of St. Antony of Padua, through a scribe’s error, “from the madman” stands where “from madness” should have been written. Other manuscripts and printed editions read “madness”; the first edition reads, “There is nothing else by which I should expect the madness of the people.”] The mysteries of weakness have been completed; let the proofs of power be brought forth.

Therefore, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit; and, for the body that would be raised on the third day, he accepted the rest of peaceful sleep. As the author of life offered himself for this sacrament, and as the structure of the whole world was shaken by so great an inclination of divine majesty, the whole creation condemned the impious deed by its own confusion [Note: The manuscript of St. Peter reads “by its own confusion.” One Vatican manuscript reads “confession” instead of “confusion”; the first edition reads “nature” instead of “creation.”], and the elements of the world themselves brought forth a manifest sentence against the guilty. What kind of spirit, Jews, did you have? What conscience was yours, when the judgment of the whole universe pressed upon you, and your impiety could not recall itself from the crime it had completed? What confusion covered you? What punishment seized your heart?

## CHAPTER V

Since, therefore, dearly beloved, God’s mercy is so great that he has deigned to justify many even from such a people through faith, and since he adopted us, perishing once beneath the deep darkness of ancient ignorance [Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads, “beneath the ancient night of ignorance.” The first edition reads, “beneath the ancient deep night of ignorance.”], into the fellowship of the patriarchs and into the lot of the chosen race, let us run toward the height of our hope neither sluggishly nor with torpor [Note: Another marginal reading in the editions is “with time,” and our manuscript, collection 5, has the same.], but thinking wisely and faithfully about from what captivity and how wretched a slavery we have been redeemed, at what price, and by what arm we have been brought out, let us glorify God in our body, so that by the integrity of our conduct we may show that he dwells in us. [Note: One Vatican manuscript and another of St. Peter read “so that, because.” The first edition has “and of charity” instead of “so that of charity.”]

And because nothing among all the excellences of the virtues is more outstanding than merciful devotion and purity of chastity, let us equip ourselves especially with these defenses, so that, raised as though on two wings by works of charity and the splendor of purity, we may deserve to become heavenly beings from earthly ones. Whoever, aided by God’s grace, is filled with this desire and glories in his progress not in himself but in the Lord, properly honors the paschal sacrament.

The destroying angel does not enter the thresholds marked beforehand with the blood of the Lamb and the sign of the cross. [Note: In the manuscript of St. Peter, “the very wounds.” Immediately afterward we have added “his enemies” from the oldest Vatican manuscript.] He does not fear the Egyptian plagues, and in the same waters by which he himself was saved he leaves his enemies dead. Let us therefore embrace, dearly beloved, with purified minds and bodies, the wonderful sacrament of our salvation; cleansed from every leaven of the old malice (1 Cor. 5:7), let us celebrate the Lord’s Passover with worthy observance [Note: Thus Quesnell reads with our manuscripts. Earlier editions have “observance” instead of “fasting.” Moreover, “observance” for “fasting” occurs frequently in Leo.], so that, with the Holy Spirit guiding us, we may not be separated by any temptation from the charity of Christ. In his blood he has made all things peaceful, has withdrawn into the height of the Father’s glory, and has not abandoned the humility of those who serve him. To him are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LVI [Others: LIV]

On the Passion of the Lord V. Delivered on the Lord’s Day.

## SYNOPSIS

I. Our salvation is placed in the cross, in which Christ contended with justice and power, divinity and humanity [Col. 0326A].  
II. On Christ’s prayer and the conflict of the two wills, ordered for our instruction.  
III. On Christ’s gentleness toward Judas, Judas’s criminal repentance, and humanity’s redemption through Christ.

## CHAPTER I

Christ, the Creator and Lord of all things, after the extraordinary birth from the sacred Virgin, after the magi’s confession had adored the cradle, and after the many teachings of heavenly speech and the cures of various illnesses accomplished by the command of his powerful word, completes the dispensation of all the sacraments and all the virtues through his saving Passion.

The true reason and principal cause of Christian hope, dearly beloved, is the cross of Christ. Although it is a stumbling-block to the Jews and foolishness to the nations, it is nevertheless the power of God and the wisdom of God for us (1 Cor. 1:23). Therefore this supreme and most powerful sacrament of divine mercy must always be retained in our hearts with all its dignity; but now it demands a more lively feeling of the soul and a purer gaze of the mind, since the whole work of our salvation is presented to us not only by the return of the season but also by the text of the Gospel reading.

Let no room, therefore, be given among us to the thoughts of the impious; let neither Jewish offense nor Gentile mockery corrupt the integrity of sound understanding, so that what was accomplished for us not only humbly but also sublimely may not appear impossible according to humanity or unworthy according to God. Both must be accepted, and both must be believed, because no human being can be saved unless in both.

For the just and merciful God did not use the right of his will in such a way that, for our restoration, he would exercise only the power of goodness [Note: Since this passage was corrupt, Quesnell published “not thus by gift,” noting in the margin: “Corrected by the Venetian edition of 1505, which was reproduced from the older edition of 1485; all printed copies and manuscripts I have seen read ‘not thus by injustice.’” The first edition, from which the Venetian edition of 1485 was taken, together with collection 3 of the manuscripts, reads “by gift,” but this is not entirely satisfactory. The true reading, “not thus by right,” is supplied by the oldest Vatican manuscript. Immediately afterward, the first edition reads “he exercised” instead of “he extended.”]. Rather, since it followed that the human being who commits sin should be sin’s slave (John 8:34), medicine was supplied to the sick, reconciliation to the guilty, and redemption to the captives in such a way that the just sentence of condemnation was dissolved by the just work of the liberator [Note: Thus more correctly from the same manuscript. Others read “of just condemnation.”].

For if divinity alone interposed itself on behalf of sinners, it would not be reason but power that conquered the devil. And again, if the cause of the fallen were undertaken by the nature of mortals alone, it would not be freed from its condition, since that nature would not be free from its origin. Therefore it was necessary that divine and human substance should come together in our one Lord Jesus Christ, so that, through the Word made flesh, both the origin of the new human being and his suffering might come to the aid of our mortality.

## CHAPTER II

Since in Christ Jesus the blindness of the Jews does not see the things that are divine, while the wisdom of the nations despises the things that are human [Note: The printed editions had: “Let the stubbornness of the Jews despise the divine things, and the blindness of the nations the human things.” Two Vatican manuscripts, collection 4 and 5, and the Patavine Lectionary of St. Antony read: “Let the blindness of the Jews despise the human things,” where blindness is attributed to the Jews, and the scribes passed over from “the divine things” to “the human things.” The oldest Vatican manuscript suggested the correction.], with the former bringing accusations against the Lord’s glory and the latter displaying arrogance against his humility, we adore the Son of God both in his own powers and in our weaknesses. We are not ashamed of Christ’s cross, and amid the tongues of those who contradict us we doubt neither his death nor his resurrection.

For what draws the proud toward unbelief directs us toward faith; and what among them is a cause of shame is among us a cause of devotion. Therefore, after instructing the disciples to contend against the force of the impending temptation through watchful prayer, the Lord himself, pleading with the Father, said: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26:39).

The first request belongs to weakness, the second to power. The former he desired from what was ours; the latter he chose from what was his own [Note: Thus from the oldest Vatican manuscript. Others read “from what was proper.”]. For the Son, equal to the Father, did not fail to know that all things are possible for God, nor had he descended into this world to undertake the cross without his own will, so that he might suffer this conflict of differing emotions as though with a disturbed reason. Rather, so that the distinction between the nature assuming and the nature assumed might be made clear, he desired divine power as what belonged to humanity, and as what belonged to God he regarded the human cause.

The lower will therefore yielded to the higher will, and it was quickly demonstrated what may be prayed for by one who trembles and what must not be granted by one who heals. Since we do not know what we ought to pray for (Rom. 8:26), and since it is often beneficial for us that what we want should not happen, the just and good God shows mercy by refusing what is harmful when it is requested.

After the Lord had strengthened the correction of our will through a threefold prayer, while the disciples were still weighed down with sorrow he said: “Sleep now and rest. Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go. Behold, the one who will betray me has drawn near” (Matt. 26:45–46). [Note: The first edition reads, “Let us go from here.”]

## CHAPTER III
Amid the very words of the Lord, those who had been foretold rushed in, and a crowd carrying swords and clubs [Col. 0327D] gathered to seize Christ, following Judas Iscariot as its leader. By the privilege of treachery he had obtained [Col. 0328A] the chief position in the crime. So that no offense might provide him with a pretext for his crime, no favor was denied him; but, inflamed by the spirit to which he had willingly offered himself as a servant [Note: [Col. 0327D] The oldest Vatican manuscript adds *se*; the reading seems to be: “to which he willingly offered himself as a servant.”], he burned with rage, and he found a ruler corresponding to the mind he himself possessed. Rightly, as the prophet also had foretold [Note: [Col. 0327D] In the same Vatican manuscript, *et* (“also”) is missing.], his prayer became sin (Ps. 108:7): for, when his crime was completed, his conversion was so perverse that he sinned even in repenting [Note: [Col. 0327D] We corrected this from the same oldest Vatican manuscript. Another reading: “so perverse was the conversion of the wicked.”].

Thus the Son of God admits impious hands upon himself, and what is carried out by the fury of those who rage is completed by the power of the one who suffers [Note: [Col. 0328D] Thus according to the same manuscript, where the printed editions had: “he completed it by the patient power.”]. For this was the mystery of that great piety which Christ pursued amid insults [Note: [Col. 0328D] The first edition and one Vatican manuscript read: “Christ was consecrated by insults.”]: if he had driven them back by open power and manifest might, he would have exercised only what was divine and would not have cared for what was human.

But in all the insults and wanton outrages that popular and priestly madness inflicted upon him [Note: [Col. 0328D] Corrected from the oldest Vatican manuscript. Another reading: *illa* (“those things”).], our stains were washed away and our offenses expiated. For the nature which in us had always been guilty and captive [Note: [Col. 0328D] Thus in the same manuscript, rightly, since the guilty and captive nature is contrasted with the innocent and free one. The printed editions and other manuscripts read *victa* (“conquered”); the first edition with the Bologna manuscript reads *vincta* (“bound”).] suffered in him innocent and free, so that, to take away the sin of the world, he might offer himself as the Lamb, the sacrifice whom bodily substance joined to all bodily things and spiritual origin distinguished from all spiritual things [Note: [Col. 0328D] The first edition reads: “whom substance joined to all bodily things, and origin distinguished from all spiritual things.” Two Vatican manuscripts, collections 4 and 5, read simply *corporalibus* (“bodily things”).].

Let these words, beloved, suffice for your ears today [Note: [Col. 0328D] The oldest Vatican manuscript reads *suffecerint* (“may suffice”).]. Let the rest be postponed until Wednesday, with the Lord’s help and your prayers; may he deign to grant that we fulfill what we promise [Note: [Col. 0328D] We added this conclusion, which was absent, from the oldest Vatican manuscript. Another Vatican manuscript reads *implere valeamus* (“may we be able to fulfill”) instead of *impleamus*:]: through the same Lord of ours, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LVII [Elsewhere LV]

## On the Passion of the Lord VI. Delivered on Wednesday

[Col. 0328C]

## Synopsis

I. That Christ, willingly seized, did not wish to be defended.

II. That Christ, by the same words, struck the consciences of unbelievers and strengthened the hearts of believers; and that Caiaphas, when he tore his garment, stripped himself of priestly honor.

III. What blindness possessed the priests, who crucified Christ with their tongues while wishing to appear to hold back their hands from the killing. Their similarly blind superstition concerning Judas’s money.

IV. That Christ, exalted upon the cross, drew all creatures into communion with his Passion.

V. That Christians, redeemed at so great a price, must beware the snares of the devil, who deceives human beings by a vain knowledge of the stars.

## CHAPTER I

Mindful of our pledge, beloved, we render to your holiness what we owe, hoping that God’s grace will be present, so that devotion may arise in us from the source where our promise was stirred up. When the Lord Christ was seized [Col. 0328D] by the crowds whom the chief priests and teachers of the law had armed, in order to fulfill the dispensation, he restrained his power [Note: [Col. 0329D] The printed editions read *cohibet*. We have corrected this from the oldest Vatican manuscript, 3835, and from the Lectionary of St. Peter, which has *dispositionem* instead of *dispensationem*.]; and he commanded the blessed apostle Peter, moved by human aggressiveness against those rushing upon them, to abstain from the sword (Matt. 26:53).

For it was superfluous that one who did not wish to be aided by the protection of angelic legions should wish to be defended by the resistance of a single disciple. Though the savage crowd carried out what it wished and exulted in the accomplishment of its crime [Note: [Col. 0329D] The printed editions read *affectu*. The correction is supplied by the two manuscripts just mentioned.], the strength of the one seized was nevertheless greater than that of those who seized him. For the blindness of the Jews achieved nothing except that, by their impiety, they should destroy themselves; but Christ’s patience achieved this, that he should save all by his Passion.

## CHAPTER II

When Jesus had been brought to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the whole priestly order had assembled (Matt. 26:57), false testimonies against the Lord were being sought [Col. 0329B]. But amid the confused and discordant voices Jesus wonderfully chose to remain silent [Note: [Col. 0329D] In the manuscript of St. Peter: “so that by remaining silent he might conquer.”].

Yet when Caiaphas said, “I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God” (ibid., 63), he answered with such truthful and provident authority that, in the very words of his reply, he both blinded the consciences of unbelievers [Note: [Col. 0329D] The printed editions and some manuscripts read *caederet*, “might strike.” We have corrected this from the two manuscripts mentioned: *caecaret*, “might blind,” which refers to Isaiah 6:10: “Blind the heart of this people.”] and strengthened the hearts of believers. To every part of Caiaphas’s question he replied, “You have said so,” adding what follows: “Nevertheless I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the power [Note: [Col. 0329D] In the printed editions before Quesnellus, *virtutis* was absent.] of God and coming on the clouds of heaven” (ibid., 64).

But Caiaphas, to heighten the hatred aroused by the words he had heard, tore his garments; and, not knowing what this madness signified, he deprived himself of priestly honor. Where is, Caiaphas, the breastplate of judgment upon your chest? Where is the belt of self-restraint? [Col. 0329C] Where is the shoulder-piece of virtues? You yourself strip yourself of that mystical and sacred vestment, and with your own hands tear apart the pontifical garments, forgetting the commandment you had read concerning the high priest: “He shall not remove the turban from his head, nor tear his garments” (Lev. 21:10) [Note: [Col. 0329D] The manuscript of St. Peter reads: “nor shall he tear them.”].

But you, from whom this dignity was already being alienated, are yourself the executor of your disgrace; and, to make manifest the end of the ancient institution, the same rending removes the priestly adornment that soon afterward also tears the veil of the temple [Note: [Col. 0329D] We supplied the following from the Lectionaries of St. Peter and the oldest Vatican manuscript. In the latter, one manuscript alone reads *auferret* instead of *aufert*, while another has *discindit* instead of *discidit*. The printed editions and other manuscripts we examined had: “the same rending of the priesthood pertains to the end of the ancient institution.” Hence the continuation, beginning “now,” etc.].

## CHAPTER III

From this point, beloved, after the night had passed amid multiplied mockeries, they handed Jesus, bound, over to Pilate the governor [216]. For the chief priests and elders of the people were conducting the affair with this plan: to appear free from responsibility for their crime [Note: [Col. 0330D] The editions of Rainaldus and Quesnellus delete *sui*; we have restored it from earlier editions and our manuscripts.], withdrawing the work of their hands and thrusting forward the weapons of their tongues [Col. 0329D], unwilling to kill him themselves yet crying, “Crucify, crucify” [Col. 0330A].

What is more unjust than this appearance of religion? What is more cruel than this simulation of clemency? By what law, Jews, is it lawful for you to desire what it is not lawful for you to do? By what reasoning does what pollutes bodies not wound hearts? You fear being contaminated by the killing of one whose blood you demanded should be poured out upon you and upon your children (John 18:28).

If your impiety does not carry out so great a crime, allow the governor to judge according to his own conviction. But you, even against him, severe and violent, do not allow him to incline toward the decision from which you yourselves falsely abstain. Pilate may have sinned by doing what he did not wish to do; nevertheless, whatever your fury extorted flows together into your conscience.

The same was your observance there also, when you refused to put into the treasury the price which the seller of Christ brought back to you [Col. 0330B], taking care, clearly, lest bloody money pollute the sacred coffers. What sort of heart possesses this simulation? The conscience of the priests accepts what the treasury of the temple does not receive (Matt. 27:6). The valuation of that blood is rejected, although its shedding is not feared. However many little shadows of deceit you use to cover yourselves, a transaction with the betrayer was entered into: just as it was not lawful for you to purchase righteous blood, so it should not have been lawful for you to shed it [Note: [Col. 0330D] This reading seemed preferable from the manuscript of St. Peter. Another has: “so it ought not to have been shed.”].

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, when Pilate yielded to the seditious clamors of the Jews [Note: [Col. 0330D] Quesnellus corrected this very well, as our manuscripts also read. The other printed editions have *sedente*, “while Pilate was seated.”], Christ was crucified at the place called Golgotha (Matt. 27:24). [Note: [Col. 0330D] The manuscript of Bologna: “Therefore, deservedly, through the wood.”]

Through the wood he who fell by the wood is raised up, and by the taste of gall and vinegar the food of sin is dissolved. Deservedly, before he was handed over, the Lord had said, “When I am lifted up, I will draw everything to myself” (John 12:32): that is, “I will take up the whole cause of the human race and restore the nature once lost to wholeness. In me every weakness will be abolished; in me every wound will be healed.”

But that the exalted Jesus had drawn all things to himself was shown not only by the Passion of our substance but also by the convulsion of the whole world [Note: [Col. 0330D] Thus from the oldest Vatican manuscript and the manuscript of St. Peter. Another has, incorrectly, *commutatione*, “by a change.”]. For while the Creator hung upon the gallows, all creation groaned together, and all the elements at once felt the nails of the Cross. Nothing was free from that punishment.

Through it he drew earth and heaven into communion with himself, broke rocks, opened tombs [Note: [Col. 0330D] The oldest Vatican manuscript has “its own,” and then: “and opened the monuments.”], unbarred the underworld, and concealed the rays of the sun beneath the horror of dense darkness [217]. The world owed this testimony to its Creator, that at the setting of its Maker all things should wish to come to an end. But the patience of God preserves its proper order for things and times [Col. 0330D], and instead invites us to an affection for him [Col. 0331A] by which we seek the salvation of those whose crime we shudder at [Note: [Col. 0331C] Thus the oldest Vatican manuscript. Another has *vocat*, “calls.”].

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, beloved, delivered from the power of darkness and released from the bonds of our ancient captivity at so great a price [Note: [Col. 0331C] Thus the same Vatican manuscript. Another has *tanto* without *que*], and by so great a sacrament, take care that the devil corrupt the integrity of your minds by no artifice.

Whatever is thrust upon you against the Christian faith, whatever is urged against God’s commandments, comes from the deceptions of the one who tries by innumerable tricks to turn you away from eternal life [Note: [Col. 0331C] From our three better manuscripts we have restored *vobis* (“you”) for *nobis* (“us”), and shortly afterward *qui vos* (“who [turns] you”) for *qui nos* (“who [turns] us”).], seeking out certain opportunities in human weakness through which he may lead heedless and negligent souls again into the snares of his own death [Note: [Col. 0331C] The manuscript of Bologna and the first edition read *tandem*, “at last,” instead of *iterum*, “again.” The manuscript of St. Peter omits both.].

Therefore, all who have been reborn through water and the Holy Spirit, let them remember to whom they have renounced and by what profession they have shaken off from themselves the yoke of tyrannical domination [Col. 0331B]. Let no one, whether in prosperity or adversity, run to the devil’s deadly aid.

For he is a liar from the beginning (John 8:44), and thrives only in the art of deception, so that by displaying false knowledge he may deceive human ignorance and become now the malicious instigator of those whose wicked accuser he will afterward be.

The years of our life and the qualities of our temporal actions rest neither in the nature of the elements nor in the effects of the stars, but in the power of the highest and true God. We ought to implore his help and mercy in all things that we rightly desire [Note: [Col. 0331D] The printed editions and some manuscripts read: “which we desire to obtain.” The reading of the manuscripts mentioned seemed preferable.].

For just as, if—God forbid—he is offended, there is nothing apart from him that can avail to support us [Note: [Col. 0331D] We added *praeter ipsum*, “apart from him,” from the same two manuscripts. Another Vatican manuscript has *praeter*, incorrectly omitting *ipsum*]; so, when he is favorable, no adversity will harm us. For if God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also, together with him, grant us all things? (Rom. 8:31–32) [Note: [Col. 0331D] Our better manuscripts and some printed editions read *donabit*, “will grant.” Another has *donavit*, “granted.”]

He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LVIII [Elsewhere LVI]

[Note: [Col. 0331D] The first edition and manuscripts of collection 3: “On the Lord’s Passover.”]

## On the Passion of the Lord VII. Delivered on Sunday

## Synopsis

I. Why Christ chose to suffer during the paschal solemnity.

II. That the Jews, intent upon crime, neglected the things that belonged to the law [Col. 0332A].

III. That Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood at the very time when a plot concerning his death was being formed; his kindness toward Judas and Judas’s obstinacy.

IV. That Judas was present bodily at the supper but intent upon crime in his mind. Christ’s discourse after the supper, his prayer in the garden, and the common counsel of the Father and the Son concerning his death.

V. That through Christ’s prayer and trembling our fear is driven away.

## CHAPTER I

I know indeed, beloved, that the paschal feast is a mystery of such sublime importance that it surpasses not only the feeble understanding of my humility but also the capacity of great minds. Yet the greatness of the divine work must not be considered by me in such a way that I either distrust myself or blush at the service I owe, since the sacrament of human salvation may not be kept silent, even if it cannot be explained [Note: [Col. 0331D] Thus, with Quesnellus, the first edition, and our manuscripts. Another has “be silent.”].

With your prayers assisting us, we believe that God’s grace will be present, sprinkling the barrenness of our heart with the dew of its inspiration [Col. 0332B] [Note: [Col. 0331D] Thus in the same Quesnellian manuscript of St. Peter, one Vatican manuscript, and the Vercelli manuscript. The other editions, with the oldest Vatican manuscript and another manuscript of collection 5, read *abstergat*, “wipe away.”], so that through the ministry of the pastoral tongue those things may be brought forth which are useful to the ears of the holy flock.

For when the Lord, the giver of all good things, says, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11), we dare to say to him in the prophetic words: “Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50:17) [Note: [Col. 0331D] The first edition and the Vercelli manuscript have *eisdem*, “with the same,” instead of *eidem*, “to him.”].

Beginning, therefore, beloved, to review the Gospel history of the Lord’s Passion, we understand that it was arranged by divine counsel that the sacrilegious leaders and impious priests of the Jews, who had often sought opportunities to rage against Christ, should receive the power to exercise their fury only during the paschal solemnity [Note: [Col. 0332C] The same Vercelli manuscript omits *impii*, “impious,” and shortly afterward *sui*, “their own.”].

For it was necessary that the things which had long been promised through a figurative mystery should be fulfilled in a manifest event [Col. 0332C] [219] [Note: [Col. 0332C] The oldest Vatican manuscript reads: “which had long been promised in prophetic mystery, so that the true sheep might remove the figurative sheep.” The Vercelli manuscript has *ovemque*, “and the sheep,” instead of *ut ovem*. The manuscripts of the basilica of St. Peter, with many others, present the common reading.]: that the true sheep should remove the symbolic sheep [Note: [Col. 0332C] The copy of Paul the Deacon and one manuscript omit the particle *ut*, which seems superfluous and almost nauseatingly repeated. [Col. 0332D] In Vatican manuscript 544, collection 5, the passage is expressed differently: “and so that, once the sacrifice had been completed, the distinction among the various victims might cease.” This agrees with chapter 7 of the following sermon: “Now also, with the variety of carnal sacrifices having ceased, your one offering of body and blood fulfills all the differences among sacrifices.” But since this sermon shortly afterward reads, “the images should cease in the presence of the truth,” we judged that the common reading, found in more and better manuscripts, should not be changed.], and so that the diversity of various victims might be fulfilled in one sacrifice.

For all those things which had been divinely prescribed through Moses concerning the immolation of the lamb had prophesied Christ and specifically announced Christ’s killing [Note: [Col. 0332D] In two manuscripts of St. Peter and in the Vercelli manuscript: “had been instituted.” Shortly afterward, “they prophesied and announced,” appears in Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary and in the first edition.].

Therefore, so that the shadow might yield to the body and the images cease in the presence of the truth, the ancient observance is removed by a new sacrament: victim passes into victim, blood is taken away by blood, and, while the legal feast is changed, it is fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0332D] The oldest Vatican manuscript was preferred; the editions before Quesnellus and most of our manuscripts, especially those of St. Peter, agree with it. Quesnellus, with the Vercelli manuscript, Vatican manuscript collection 4, and Paul the Deacon’s copy, has *novo excluditur*, “is excluded by the new.” Shortly afterward, with Quesnellus we retained *aufertur*, “is taken away,” as read in the manuscripts of St. Peter, the Vercelli manuscript, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary. The oldest Vatican manuscript has *excluditur*, “is excluded,” while the other editions, with manuscripts of collections 3, 4, and 5, read *sanguinem sanguis excludit*, “blood excludes blood.”].

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, when the scribes and elders of the people [Note: [Col. 0333C] Thus from the oldest Vatican manuscript. The same interpretation is supported by two manuscripts of St. Peter and Paul the Deacon’s copy, and it refers to Matthew 26:4: “And they took counsel to seize Jesus by deceit,” etc. The editions, with other manuscripts, read “to the council of impiety.” Although Quesnellus noted in the margin, “Another reading: to the impious,” he found this reading, which no edition prefers, in some of his manuscripts. Shortly before, Vatican manuscript 544 has *scribae et seniores*, “the scribes and elders,” so that these words govern the verb *congregarent*, “should assemble.”] assembled the high priests for an impious council, and concern for admitting the crime against Jesus had seized the minds of all the priests, they themselves deprived themselves of the law as teachers of the law and, by a voluntary falling away, removed from themselves their ancestral rites [Note: [Col. 0333D] Thus Quesnellus and our better manuscripts. Other manuscripts, with the earlier editions, have *abstulerunt*, “took away.” Later, the oldest Vatican manuscript reads “to arrange the temple,” while two manuscripts of St. Peter and another Vatican manuscript have “more careful diligence.”].

For when the paschal feast began, those who ought to have adorned the temple, cleansed the vessels, provided the victims, and applied the most sacred diligence to the lawful purifications, having conceived the fury of murderous hatred, devoted themselves to one task and conspired with equal cruelty in one crime [Note: [Col. 0333D] The editions and many manuscripts had: “what they would accomplish.” The reading inserted into the text from two manuscripts of St. Peter seemed more fitting.], destined to achieve nothing by the punishment of innocence [Note: [Col. 0333D] The editions omit the conjunction *et*, “and,” which we more suitably added from the oldest Vatican manuscript.
