We retained the words “by the condemnation of justice,” although they are absent from the manuscripts of St. Peter and Vercelli. The same Vatican manuscript has in what follows: “except that they should neither apprehend our Passover nor violate their own feasts.”].

They intended, therefore, not that the new mysteries should be grasped, but that the ancient ones should be violated. Since the leaders were taking care that no disturbance should arise on the holy day [Note: [Col. 0333D] The editions before Quesnellus had *festo*, “festive,” instead of *sancto*, “holy,” and *devotioni*, “devotion,” instead of *festivitati*, “festivity.” This reading is preferred not only in manuscripts of the later collections but also in the oldest Vatican manuscript. We preferred the reading of the manuscripts of St. Peter, with which the Vercelli manuscript and Paul the Deacon’s copy agree. Quesnellus likewise inserted *sancto* into the text from his manuscripts and noted in the margin: “Another reading: festive,” but retained *devotioni*.], they were concerned not with the festivity but with the crime; nor did this care serve religion, but guilt [Note: [Col. 0334C] The Vercelli manuscript reads: “this care was not serving religion.”].

For the high priests, diligent and anxious priests, feared that disturbances of the crowds would occur during the chief solemnity, not so that the people would not sin, but lest Christ escape [220].

## CHAPTER III

But Jesus, certain of his purpose and undaunted in carrying out the Father’s disposition [Note: [Col. 0334C] Paul the Deacon’s copy has *dispensationis*, “dispensation,” instead of *dispositionis*, “disposition.”], was bringing the Old Testament to completion and founding the new Passover.

While the disciples reclined with him to eat the mystical supper [Note: [Col. 0334C] The word *secum*, “with him,” was added from the oldest Vatican and Vercelli manuscripts and the first edition. Shortly afterward, the Vercelli manuscript reads “might be killed.”], while in the courtyard of Caiaphas it was being discussed how Christ might be killed, he, arranging the sacrament of his body and blood, was teaching what sort of victim ought to be offered to God. He did not even remove the betrayer from this mystery, so that it might be shown that one whose voluntary wickedness was foreknown [Note: [Col. 0334D] Thus Quesnellus from four of his manuscripts—Regius, Victorinus, Thuaneus, and Corbeiensis—with which most of ours agree. The first edition has *praestitutus*; others, *perstiturus*.] had not been provoked to anger by any injury.

For he himself was the material of his ruin and the cause of his treachery, following the devil as his leader and refusing to have Christ as his ruler.

Thus, when the Lord said, “Amen, I tell you, one of you is going to betray me” (Matt. 26:21), he displayed his awareness of the betrayer’s conscience—not exposing the impious man with harsh or open rebuke, but addressing him with a gentle and silent warning, so that repentance might more easily correct one whom no public humiliation had disfigured.

Why, unhappy Judas, do you not make use of such great kindness? Behold, the Lord spares your boldness [Note: [Col. 0334D] One Vatican manuscript: “your ears.”], and Christ identifies you to no one but yourself. Neither your name nor your person is exposed; only the secrets of your heart are touched by a word of truth and mercy. The honor of the apostolic order is not denied you, nor is communion in the sacraments. Return to wholeness, and recover your senses by laying aside your fury. Mercy invites you; salvation knocks; life calls you back to life [Note: [Col. 0334D] Two Vatican manuscripts omit “to life.” The Vercelli manuscript omits *te*, “you.”].

Behold, your blameless and innocent fellow disciples [Note: [Col. 0334D] The Vercelli manuscript adds “conscious of themselves,” that is, conscious of their present innocence, as is explained below. Shortly afterward it reads: “uncertain because of the failure of human mutability.”] tremble at the indication of the crime, and, since the author of the impiety has not been named, each fears for himself. They were saddened not by guilt of conscience, but by uncertainty concerning human mutability, fearing that what each knew within himself might be less true than what Truth itself foresaw.

But amid this trembling of the saints you abuse the Lord’s patience and think that your audacity conceals you. You add shamelessness to your crime and are not terrified by a clearer sign. While the others held back from the food in which the Lord had placed the indication [Note: [Col. 0334D] The editions read *judicium*, “judgment.” Quesnellus noted in the margin: “Perhaps *indicium*, ‘indication.’” We found this in two manuscripts of St. Peter and one Vatican manuscript and inserted it into the text. Shortly afterward, we restored *animum*, “mind,” instead of *animam*, “soul,” from our better manuscripts, the first edition, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary.], you do not withdraw your hand from the dish, because you do not turn your mind away from the crime.

## CHAPTER IV

It followed, beloved, as the Evangelist John narrated [Note: [Col. 0334D] The oldest Vatican manuscript: “had narrated.”], that, when the Lord had more clearly identified his betrayer by offering him the dipped morsel [Col. 0334C], the devil wholly seized Judas (John 13:26); and the one whom he had bound by wicked thoughts he now possessed through the very work of his impiety.

For bodily he reclined with those who were eating, but in mind he was arming the envy of the priests, the falsehood of the witnesses, and the fury of the ignorant crowd [Col. 0335A]. Finally, when the Lord saw what outrage Judas was intent upon, he said, “What you are doing, do more quickly” (John 13:27) [Note: [Col. 0335C] The oldest Vatican manuscript, two others of collections 4 and 5, and the Vercelli manuscript together with Paul the Deacon’s copy present this more rapidly.].

This is not the voice of one giving orders, but of one remaining silent; not of one trembling, but of one prepared. Possessing power over all times, he showed that he neither delayed for the betrayer nor, in this way, carried out the Father’s will for the redemption of the world so as either to provoke or fear the crime being prepared by the persecutors [Note: [Col. 0335C] Many manuscripts, with the editions before Quesnellus, delete the conjunction *et*, which nevertheless appears in the Vercelli Lectionary and Paul the Deacon’s copy. Shortly afterward, for *et sic*, the same Vercelli manuscript has *et se*. Then Paul the Deacon has “from the persecutors” instead of “from those pursuing.”].

Therefore, after Judas, persuaded by the devil, departed from Christ and cut himself off from the body of apostolic unity, the Lord was disturbed by no fear but was concerned only for the salvation of those to be redeemed. He devoted all the time that was free from the attack of the persecutors to mystical discourse and sacred teaching, as the Gospel of John makes clear [Note: [Col. 0335C] The Vercelli manuscript reads “as the Evangelist John declares”; afterward, omitting the words “the Father to the Son,” it has “and was going to give,” so that the clauses would be joined.].

He lifted his eyes to heaven [Col. 0335B] and prayed to the Father for the whole Church, that all whom the Father had given and would give to the Son might be one (John 17:11) and remain in the glory of the undivided Redeemer [Note: [Col. 0335C] Two Vatican manuscripts read “in the glory of redemption.”]. Finally he added the prayer in which he says, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39).

We must not suppose that the Lord Jesus wished to avoid the Passion and death whose sacramental meaning he had already entrusted to his disciples [Note: [Col. 0335D] Three of Quesnellus’s manuscripts have “whose knowledge he had entrusted to his disciples.” Paul the Deacon’s copy and the Vercelli manuscript have “had already given his disciples an understanding of.”], since he himself forbade the blessed apostle Peter, burning with devoted faith and love, to use the sword against the persecutors, saying, “The cup which the Father has given me, shall I not drink it?” (John 18:11).

And it is certain that, according to the Gospel of John, the Lord said, “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him [Note: [Col. 0335D] The Vercelli manuscript reads “in him.”] should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16) [Col. 0335C]; and that the apostle Paul said of him, “Christ loved us and handed himself over for us as an offering and sacrifice to God, for a fragrant aroma” (Eph. 5:2) [Note: [Col. 0335D] The editions before Quesnellus and the Apostle’s own text have “as a victim for us.” He deleted these words because, as he noted in the margin, they were absent from his manuscripts. We have restored them because they are found in all our manuscripts and also in Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary.].

For in the salvation of all through the cross of Christ, the will of the Father and the Son was shared, and their counsel was one [Note: [Col. 0336C] This reading of the oldest Vatican manuscript is more characteristically Leonine. Another has: “the common will of the Father and the Son was one common counsel.”]. Nor could what had been mercifully arranged and unchangeably determined before the eternal ages be disturbed in any way.

Therefore, beloved, since he assumed the whole human being in truth [Note: [Col. 0336C] We added “beloved” from two manuscripts of St. Peter, the Vercelli manuscript, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary; the latter also reads: “and assumed the whole human being … and received the experiences of the soul.” The Vercelli manuscript has “and received the effects of the soul.”], he received the true sensations of the body and the true experiences of the soul. Nor, because everything in him was full of sacraments and full of miracles, did he weep false tears, take food from a feigned hunger, or sleep in simulated slumber.

He was despised in our humiliation, saddened in our sadness [Note: [Col. 0336D] Paul the Deacon’s copy: “troubled.”], and crucified in our pain. He underwent the sufferings of our mortality in his mercy in order to heal; in his power he received them in order to conquer.

Isaiah prophesied this most openly, saying: “He bears our sins and suffers for us; and we thought him to be in pain, in a wound, and in affliction. But he was wounded because of our sins [Note: [Col. 0336D] The oldest Vatican manuscript and another manuscript have *facinora*, “crimes”; afterward, *peccata*, “sins.”], and he was weakened because of our crimes, and by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. 53:4–5) [223].

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, beloved, when the Son of God says, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39), he uses the voice of our nature and pleads the case of human weakness and trembling, so that in the things that must be endured both endurance may be strengthened and fear driven away.

Finally, ceasing to ask this very thing and, as it were, excusing the fear of our weakness—a fear in which it is not profitable for us to remain—he passes to another disposition and says, “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (ibid.); and again: “If this cup cannot pass from me unless I drink it, let your will be done” (ibid., 42).

This voice of the Head is the salvation of the whole body; this voice instructed all the faithful, kindled all confessors [Col. 0336C], and crowned all martyrs. For who could overcome the world’s hatred, who could overcome the storms of temptation, who could overcome the terrors of persecutors [Note: [Col. 0336D] Two manuscripts of St. Peter and Paul the Deacon’s copy: “of persecutions.”], unless Christ, in all and for all [Note: [Col. 0336D] The editions before Quesnellus added *patiens*, “being patient”; he deleted it because he found it absent from the Corbeiensis, Victorinus, and Thuaneus manuscripts. It is also absent from our manuscripts. Only two manuscripts of St. Peter read *Pater*, “Father,” instead of *Patri*, “to the Father.”], said to the Father, “Your will be done”? [Note: [Col. 0336D] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the Corbeiensis and Thuaneus manuscripts in Quesnellus, and from our Vercelli manuscript and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary. They occur, however, in all the other manuscripts, including the better ones.]

Let all learn this voice: the children of the Church, redeemed at a great price and justified freely. And when the adversity of some violent temptation presses upon them [Note: [Col. 0337C] The oldest Vatican manuscript reads “rests upon them.” Shortly afterward, it has *rationis*, “of reason,” instead of *orationis*, “of prayer,” as in the editions before Quesnellus and in most manuscripts. One Vatican manuscript has the reading popularized by Quesnellus, *orationis*, which better suits the context.], let them use the protection of the most powerful prayer, so that, once the trembling of fear has been overcome, they may receive endurance for suffering.

From this point, beloved, the sermon must turn to review the sequence of the Lord’s Passion. But, lest we burden you with the weight of excessive length, let us divide the common labor and defer it until Wednesday [Note: [Col. 0337C] The Regius, Corbeiensis, and two Thuaneus manuscripts cited by Quesnellus, as well as one of ours together with Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, have “until Friday.” We have retained the common reading, since it is confirmed by other better manuscripts and agrees with Leo’s other sermons on the Passion of the Lord delivered on Sunday, which likewise defer the remaining discussion of the same subject until Wednesday, not Friday. In some of our manuscripts, “on Wednesday” appears instead of “on the fourth day of the week.” The oldest Vatican manuscript omits “common” and prefers “we defer.”].

God’s grace will be present as you pray, granting me the ability to discharge my debt. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, living and reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen [Note: [Col. 0337D] We took this conclusion from two Lectionaries of St. Peter. The printed editions had: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.” The oldest Vatican manuscript has: “Through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.”].

# SERMON LIX [Elsewhere LVII]

## On the Passion of the Lord VIII. Delivered on Wednesday

## Synopsis
I. Christ, having cast off the trembling of weakness, willingly allowed himself to be led and suffered for all. — II. By how many prejudices the Jews drove Pilate to condemn Christ, and how cowardly he yielded to their clamors. — III. Pilate’s cruelty toward Christ proceeded from a certain clemency; the Jews are burdened with the whole crime. — IV. While Christ carried the wood of punishment, he transformed it into a scepter. — V. In Simon of Cyrene the nations were represented, nations that were to be called to faith in Christ’s cross and sanctified by a new sacrifice. — VI. Christ’s cross must be contemplated especially with the inward gaze. — VII. How does Christ, exalted, draw everything to himself? What is the excellence of the Christian religion? How great is the power of the cross? — VIII. We are not to live for ourselves, but for Christ who died for us.

## CHAPTER I

Having completed in the previous sermon, beloved, the matters that preceded the Lord’s arrest, it now remains, with the help of God’s grace, that we discuss, as we promised, the course of the Passion itself. For when the Lord had declared in the words of his sacred prayer that he possessed most truly and completely both a human and a divine nature, showing from what source came his unwillingness to suffer and from what source his willingness; having cast off the trembling of weakness and strengthened the greatness of his courage, he returned to the resolve of his eternal purpose and presented to the raging devil, acting through the agencies of the Jews, the form of a servant who possessed no sin, so that through him the cause of all might be accomplished, in whom alone the nature of all was without guilt.

*[Note: In the most ancient Vatican manuscript, the passage reads: “having cast off human trembling and strengthened by divine power, he returned.” In Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, instead of “greatness of courage” there is “greatness.”]*

*[Note: We have restored the word “his,” which Quesnel deleted and which is also omitted in some of our manuscripts, on the authority of the manuscripts of Saint Peter and many others.]*

Then the children of darkness rushed upon the true light, and, using torches and lanterns, they did not escape the night of their unbelief, because they did not understand the author of light. They seize one who is ready to be held and drag one who is willing to be dragged. If he had wished to resist, their impious hands could indeed have done him no harm, but the redemption of the world would have been delayed, and no one would have been saved unharmed—he who was destined to die for the salvation of all.

*[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary read: “who possessed no sin.” Then, in one Vatican manuscript, collection 5, the reading is “in which alone there was”; in the first edition, “in which there alone was.”]*

*[Note: Our manuscripts agree here with Quesnel. The other editions read “would be delayed.”]*

## CHAPTER II

Allowing himself, therefore, to be subjected to whatever the popular fury, aroused by the instigations of the priests, dared to inflict, he is led to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas, and then, through Annas’s transfer, to Caiaphas. After the mad accusations of his accusers and the fabricated falsehoods of suborned witnesses, he is transferred, by delegation of the chief priests, for a hearing before Pilate.

*[Note: This reading is taken from two manuscripts of Saint Peter and from Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary. The common reading has “incited.” Immediately after the word “dared,” the most ancient Vatican manuscript, omitting the intervening words, continues: “after the insane voices of those making accusations in the house of Caiaphas, after the fictitious falsehoods of the witnesses, to Pilate’s examination.”]*

*[Note: Editions before Quesnel, together with manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 and the very ancient Vatican manuscript, read “voices.” The manuscripts of Saint Peter, Vatican collection 4, and Paul the Deacon’s copy, preferred with Quesnel, read “accusations.”]*

*[Note: The editions before Quesnel read “for examination.” On the authority of the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, “for a hearing” seemed preferable.]*

They, disregarding divine law, cried out that they had no king except Caesar (John 19:15). As though devoted to Roman laws, they reserved every judgment to the governor’s authority and sought an executor of savagery rather than an arbiter of the case.

*[Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript and another manuscript of collection 5 read “Caesar’s authority.”]*

For they presented Jesus bound in harsh chains, beaten repeatedly with blows and slaps, smeared with spittle, and condemned in advance by their shouts, so that amid so many prejudgments Pilate would not dare to acquit the one whom they all wanted destroyed. Indeed, the very proceedings show that he neither found guilt in the accused nor maintained firmness in his judgment: the judge pronounces him innocent, yet condemns him, assigning the blood of the righteous to the unjust people—a blood from which he had recognized through his own understanding that he ought to abstain and which he had learned through his wife’s dream.

*[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter and one Vatican manuscript read: “and that he found no cause in him.” The first edition and the Bologna manuscript read: “and that he found no cause in the accused.”]*

*[Note: The first edition reads “the righteous.” Later, the most ancient Vatican manuscript and another manuscript of collection 5 read “he had recognized.”]*

*[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary read “impious hands”; shortly afterward, they read “they had hurled” instead of “they were casting.”]*

Washed hands do not cleanse a polluted soul, nor is what is committed with an impious mind serving as accomplice expiated by fingers sprinkled with water. The crime of the Jews certainly exceeded Pilate’s guilt: they frightened him by invoking Caesar’s name and drove him to the execution of their crime by their envious cries. Yet he himself did not escape guilt, for he cooperated with the seditious, abandoned his own judgment, and entered into another’s crime.

*[Note: Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary and the manuscripts of Saint Peter read “by the seditions.” The most ancient Vatican manuscript reads “overcome by the seditions.”]*

## CHAPTER III

Since Pilate, beloved, overcome by the madness of an implacable people, allowed Jesus to be dishonored by many mockeries and harassed by excessive insults, and displayed him—beaten with scourges, crowned with thorns, and clothed in a garment of derision—to the sight of the scribes and priests, he doubtless thought that the minds of his enemies would thereby be appeased: once their hatred born of envy had been sated, they would no longer believe that the one whom they saw afflicted in so many ways should be pursued further.

*[Note: The first edition and the Bologna manuscript read “in many ways.” Shortly afterward, instead of “of the scribes and priests,” which the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary prefer with Quesnel, the other editions and the remaining manuscripts, including the most ancient Vatican manuscript, read “of the persecutors.”]*

But when the anger of those shouting grew hot, demanding that Barabbas be released as a favor and that Jesus receive the punishment of the cross; when the crowds cried out with one accord, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25), the wicked obtained, to their own condemnation, what they obstinately demanded. Their teeth, as the prophet testified, were weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword (Psalm 56:5).

For in vain did they restrain their own hands from crucifying the Lord of majesty, against whom they hurled the deadly darts of their voices and the poisoned weapons of their words. Upon you, upon you, false Jews and sacrilegious leaders of the people, rests the entire weight of this crime. Although the enormity of the offense implicated both the governor and the soldiers, the whole deed nevertheless condemns you. Whatever in Christ’s punishment was sinful in Pilate’s judgment or in the cohort’s obedience makes you more deserving of the hatred of the human race, because at the impulse of your fury even those whom your wickedness displeased were not permitted to remain innocent.

*[Note: Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary adds: “although they would have preferred to see you become gentler.”]*

## CHAPTER IV

*[Note: The beginning of this chapter is presented with a notable variation in the most ancient Vatican manuscript and in Casinensis collection 1: “Since, therefore, the blindness of the unhappy Jews denied that their king was the Lord of the universe, the Lord Jesus was handed over to the will of those raging against him and, for the mockery of royal dignity, was ordered to be the bearer of his own cross, since he was plainly worthy of this disgrace, whose glory would be turned into dishonor. This was indeed a great mockery in the eyes of the impious,” and so forth. In manuscripts of collection 2 it appears differently: “Therefore, beloved, the Lord was handed over by the will of those raging against him, for the mockery of royal dignity,” followed by the rest as in the text. The reading printed here is confirmed by the manuscripts of Saint Peter and other codices.]*

Thus the Lord, handed over to the will of those raging against him, was ordered, for the mockery of royal dignity, to be the bearer of his own punishment, so that what the prophet Isaiah had foreseen might be fulfilled when he said: “Behold, a child is born, and a son is given to us, whose government is upon his shoulders” (Isaiah 9:6).

When the Lord carried the wood of the cross, which he was to transform into a scepter of power, this was indeed a great mockery in the eyes of the impious, but a great mystery was revealed to the faithful. For the most glorious victor over the devil and the most powerful conqueror of hostile forces carried, in the beautiful form of his triumph, the trophy of his victory; and upon the shoulders of unconquered patience he brought before all kingdoms the sign of salvation, to be adored. It was as though even then, through the very image of his deed, he strengthened all his imitators and said: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:38).

*[Note: In the same most ancient Vatican manuscript, “of hostile spirits.”]*

## CHAPTER V

*[Note: In the same Vatican manuscript and in Casinensis collection 1, the words from the beginning of the chapter through “the fullness passed over” are absent. Thus, after “is not worthy of me,” the text continues: “Our Passover, therefore, as the Apostle says,” and so forth. Shortly afterward we restored the older reading “the wood of the cross,” supported by our manuscripts, instead of Quesnel’s “the wood of punishment.”]*

As the crowds went with Jesus to the place of punishment, a certain Simon of Cyrene was found, upon whom the Lord’s crossbeam was transferred (Matthew 27:32), so that even by this act the faith of the nations might be prefigured—nations for whom Christ’s cross would be not confusion but glory. It was therefore not accidental but figurative and mystical that, while the Jews raged against Christ, a foreigner came forward to suffer with him, as the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Romans 8:17). Thus, for the most sacred disgrace of the Savior, no Hebrew or Israelite, but a foreigner, was subjected.

Through this transfer, from circumcision to uncircumcision, from carnal children to spiritual children, the propitiation of the spotless Lamb and the fullness of all the mysteries passed over. For “our Passover,” as the Apostle says, “Christ has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). Offering himself to the Father as the new and true sacrifice of reconciliation, he was crucified not in the temple, whose veneration had already come to an end, nor within the boundaries of the city, which were destined to be destroyed because of its guilt, but outside and beyond the camp.

*[Note: In the Casinensis manuscript the conjunction “and” is omitted.]*

Thus, with the mystery of the ancient victims brought to an end, a new victim was placed upon a new altar, and Christ’s cross was not the altar of the temple but of the world (Hebrews 13:11).

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore, beloved, with Christ exalted by the cross, let not only that appearance present itself to the mind’s sight which was before the eyes of the impious, to whom it was said through Moses: “And your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall fear day and night, and you shall not trust in your life” (Deuteronomy 28:66). For they could think of nothing in the crucified Lord except their own crime, possessing not the fear by which true faith is justified, but the fear by which an evil conscience is tormented.

Let our understanding, however, which the Spirit of truth illuminates, receive with a pure and free heart the glory of the cross shining throughout heaven and earth, and let it see with its inward gaze what it means that the Lord, when speaking of the imminence of his Passion, said: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John 12:23). And later: “Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I have come to this hour. Father, glorify your Son” (John 12:27–28). When the Father’s voice came from heaven, saying, “I have glorified him, and I will glorify him again” (ibid., 28), Jesus answered those standing around him: “This voice came not for me but for you. Now is the judgment of the world; now the prince of this world will be cast out. And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (ibid., 30).

*[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “the present imminence.”]*

*[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary read “will be dismissed” or “will be sent downward.” Shortly afterward, we have written “to myself” with most and the better manuscripts and editions. Quesnel reads “to me”; the first edition reads “with me.”]*

## CHAPTER VII

O marvelous power of the cross! O ineffable glory of the Passion! In it are both the Lord’s tribunal and the judgment of the world and the power of the crucified one. For you drew everything to yourself, Lord, and when you stretched out your hands all day toward a people that did not believe and contradicted you, the whole world received the understanding that it must confess your majesty (Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21).

*[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter read “toward the people.”]*

You drew everything to yourself, Lord, when all the elements pronounced one sentence against the curse of Jewish crime, when the heavenly lights were darkened, the day was turned into night, the earth was shaken by unaccustomed movements, and the whole creation refused itself for the use of the impious.

*[Note: This is the reading of the better and most of our manuscripts and of the editions before Quesnel, who has “swayed.” In one manuscript of Saint Peter, “announced” seems to have been written instead of “swayed.”]*

You drew everything to yourself, Lord, because when the veil of the temple was torn, the Holy of Holies withdrew from unworthy priests, so that the figure might be turned into reality, prophecy into manifestation, and the law into the Gospel.

You drew everything to yourself, Lord, so that what had been performed in the single temple of Judea under the shadow of veiled signs might be celebrated everywhere by the devotion of all nations, in a full and open sacrament.

*[Note: In two manuscripts of Saint Peter, “of the Jews.” Then we corrected “was being performed” from two manuscripts of Saint Peter, instead of the “might be performed” written in the oldest Vatican manuscript. Another reading is “was covered.”]*

Now, indeed, the order of the Levites is more illustrious, the dignity of the elders greater, and the anointing of priests more sacred, because your cross is the source of all blessings and the cause of all graces. Through it believers receive strength from weakness, glory from disgrace, and life from death.

This final sentence is absent from Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary.

Now also, with the variety of carnal sacrifices having ceased, your one offering of body and blood fulfills all the distinctions among sacrifices, because you are the true Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John 1:29). Thus you complete all the mysteries in yourself: just as there is one sacrifice in place of every victim, so there is one kingdom from every nation.

*[Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript reads “the sin.”]*

## CHAPTER VIII

Let us therefore confess, beloved, what the blessed Apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations, confessed in a glorious voice, saying: “The saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15). For in this the mercy of God toward us is more marvelous: Christ died not for the righteous or the holy, but for the wicked and the impious (Romans 5:6). And although the divine nature could not receive the sting of death, by being born from us it nevertheless assumed what it could offer for us.

For long ago he threatened our death with the power of his death, saying through the prophet Hosea: “O death, I shall be your death; O underworld, I shall be your sting” (Hosea 13:14).

*[Note: In Vatican manuscripts of collection 4 and 5: “O death, I shall be your death; O underworld, I shall be your sting.”]*

He submitted to the laws of the underworld by dying, but by rising he dissolved them. Thus he cut short the perpetuity of death, making it temporal rather than eternal. For “as all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:22).

*[Note: In the most ancient Vatican manuscript: “As all die in Adam, so also shall all be made alive in Christ.”]*

Let what the Apostle Paul says therefore be fulfilled, beloved: “Those who live should no longer live for themselves, but for him who died for all and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:15). Since the old things have passed away and everything has become new, let no one remain in the oldness of carnal life, but let us all be renewed from day to day, advancing through growth in devotion.

*[Note: In one Vatican manuscript, “advancing” is absent. In two manuscripts of Saint Peter, the words “through growth in devotion” are omitted. Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary reads “be renewed” instead of “let us be renewed.”]*

However justified someone may be, while he remains in this life he still has room to become more approved and better.

*[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary read “while he is in this body.”]*

Whoever does not advance falls back; whoever gains nothing loses something.

*[Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript reads “does not lose a little.”]*

We must therefore run with the steps of faith, works of mercy, and love of righteousness, so that, spiritually celebrating the day of our redemption, we may deserve to share in Christ’s resurrection—not in the old leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5:8). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

*[Note: In the same manuscript: “celebrating with holy works, we may deserve to share in Christ’s resurrection,” with Paul’s intervening text omitted. On the basis of two manuscripts of Saint Peter, we have written “old leaven” (veteri) instead of “of old [leaven]” (veteris).]*

# SERMON LX [Also LVIII]. On the Passion of the Lord IX

## SYNOPSIS

I. The mysteries of the new law were foretold in the ancient law and narrated in the Gospel. — II. The Paschal feasts, which brought us true redemption, are not to be celebrated sorrowfully. — III. The figures are shown to have been fulfilled in Christ’s death, in which the devil was caught by his own deceit. — IV. How greatly avarice must be avoided, as shown by Judas’s fall; Peter, stumbling through fear, rose through love by means of Christ’s inward gaze.

## CHAPTER I

The mystery of the Lord’s Passion, appointed from eternity for the salvation of the human race and announced throughout all past ages by many signs, is no longer something we await to be revealed, but something already fulfilled that we adore.

*[Note: This wording is taken from two manuscripts of Saint Peter. Elsewhere the preceding sentence continues, omitting “therefore.”]*

Since both new and ancient testimonies converge for our instruction—while what the prophetic trumpet sang is unfolded by evangelical history—and as it is written, “Deep calls to deep at the sound of your cataracts” (Psalm 42), because the heights of both Testaments answer one another with equal voices in proclaiming the glory of God’s grace, what had been profound beneath the veil of figures becomes clear in the light once revealed.

*[Note: This is the reading of all our manuscripts and of the editions before Quesnel, who has “of your own.”]*

Yet if, amid those miracles of the Savior that were performed before the eyes of the peoples, few perceived the presence of Truth, and if the disciples themselves, shaken by the Lord’s voluntary Passion, did not escape the scandal of the cross without the fear of temptation, from where would our faith take understanding, from where would our conscience receive strength, unless we read beforehand what we recognize to have happened?

*[Note: Quesnel reads “amid those dangers.” We have retained the earlier common reading, approved by all our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, the most ancient Vatican manuscript prefers “But if” for “Yet if.” The Vercelli manuscript and Paul the Deacon’s copy read “Nevertheless.”]*

*[Note: In two manuscripts of Saint Peter: “so that the disciples themselves also did not escape …”]*

*[Note: This is Quesnel’s reading from four of his manuscripts, and it is also found in several of ours, especially the most ancient Vatican manuscript and Paul the Deacon’s copy. Earlier editions, with other manuscripts, read “steadfastness.” Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of Saint Peter read “proclaimed” instead of “foretold.”]*

## CHAPTER II

Now that the Savior’s triumph has been accomplished and the dispensations announced by all the words of the Old Testament have been brought to completion, let the carnal Jew mourn, but let the spiritual Christian rejoice. Let the festival that was turned into night for them shine upon us as light, because Christ’s cross is both the glory of believers and the punishment of unbelievers.

Although the fury of the persecutors accomplished nothing against the Lord of majesty except savage cruelty and merciless punishment, those redeemed by this Passion of the Lord have a truer and more just reason for rejoicing than for sorrow.

*[Note: The Vercelli manuscript and Paul the Deacon’s copy read “It had been,” and shortly afterward, “had fallen into.”]*

*[Note: In the oldest Vatican manuscript and in the first edition, “by this” is absent.]*

*[Note: The first edition and two manuscripts of Saint Peter read “to be observed.”]*

Even if the disciples’ fear was then excusable, and apostolic sorrow did not incur the guilt of unbelief, when Jews and the leaders of the Jews converged upon one crime, when the proud swelling of fattened bulls and the insolent wantonness of calves raged, when beneath the eyes of the sheep the rage of roaring beasts demanded the blood of the righteous shepherd, and when finally he himself, who had come to suffer, said in sharing our nature: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38).

*[Note: The Corbey manuscript of Quesnel reads “of the raging beasts.”]*

But now, after power has been glorified through the assumption of weakness, no faithful person’s sorrow should darken the Paschal solemnity, nor should the sequence of events be recalled by us with sadness, since the Lord used the wickedness of the Jews in such a way that from the intention of the crime the will of the merciful one was fulfilled.

*[Note: In two manuscripts of Saint Peter, “through the assumption,” so that “power” is expressed in the ablative. The editions before Quesnel, together with the manuscripts of later collections, read “by the assumption.” The oldest Vatican manuscript and other manuscripts of ours prefer the reading in the text.]*

*[Note: The first edition and two manuscripts of Saint Peter read “to be observed.”]*

*[Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript reads “was to be fulfilled.”]*

If, at the exodus of Israel from Egypt, the blood of a lamb was the restoration of freedom, and a most sacred festival was instituted because the victim of an animal turned away the destroyer’s wrath, how great a joy ought the Christian peoples to conceive, for whom the almighty Father did not spare his only-begotten Son, but handed him over for us all (Romans 8:32), so that in Christ’s slaughter there might be a true Passover and a unique sacrifice by which not one people from Pharaoh’s domination but the whole world from the devil’s captivity might be delivered?

*[Note: In the same manuscript, “had turned away.” Shortly afterward, the Vercelli manuscript reads “how much more the people” instead of “how great for the peoples.”]*

## CHAPTER III

This, beloved, is that mystery to which all mysteries have served from the beginning.

*[Note: In Paul the Deacon’s copy: “For the blood …” Shortly afterward, the Vercelli manuscript reads “by death” instead of “death.”]*

Now the blood of the righteous Abel speaks of the death of the supreme Shepherd, and in the fratricide of the Jews Cain, the slayer of his brother, is recognized (Genesis 4:8). Now the Flood and Noah’s ark (ibid., 7:17) reveal what renewal there is in baptism and what salvation there is in the wood. Now Abraham, the father of the nations, acquires the heirs who were promised; and in his seed, not a bodily shoot but an offspring of faith is blessed (Genesis 22:18; Romans 4:11).

Now the sacred month of new things has shone forth for the feast foretold by all festivals, so that in the month in which the world received its beginning, the Christian creation might have its origin.

*[Note: Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary and another manuscript read “has burst forth.”]*

Although the raging Jews therefore did against the Lord Jesus whatever they wished, and although divine power did not remove the reality of the humanity he had assumed through any of their assaults, the Lord’s patience nevertheless fulfilled the purpose of his plan, and the obstinacy of sacrilegious cruelty furthered the Savior’s work. The scribes, the Pharisees, and the chief priests did not understand this: “For if they had understood it, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty” (1 Corinthians 2:8).

*[Note: In the most ancient Vatican manuscript: “For if they had understood it.” Shortly afterward, the editions before Quesnel and the manuscripts of later collections, as well as Paul the Deacon’s copy, had “glory” instead of “majesty.” Our better and more ancient manuscripts prefer “majesty.”]*

The devil himself, therefore, did not understand that by raging against Christ he would destroy his own dominion, because he would not have lost the rights of his ancient deceit if he had kept himself from the blood of the Lord Jesus. But malice, greedy to do harm, while it rushed upon him fell; while it seized, it was seized; while it persecuted a mortal, it encountered the Savior.

*[Note: The Vercelli manuscript deletes “therefore.” Later, most editions and that manuscript read “who” instead of “because.”]*

*[Note: Editions before Quesnel, together with certain manuscripts, read “greedy,” so that the adjective refers to the devil; they likewise read “he was seized” instead of “she was seized.” Later, Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary reads “and while he persecuted.”]*

In that undertaking of rash audacity he found a fitting accomplice and companion, since the impious Judas preferred to be the devil’s servant rather than Christ’s apostle. He did not abandon Christ through the agitation of fear, but sold him through greed for money.

*[Note: The first edition and the Bologna manuscript read “of shamelessness,” and later “a disciple” instead of “a servant.”]*

## CHAPTER IV

See, beloved, and examine carefully what shoots and what fruits arise from the root of avarice, which the Apostle rightly defined as the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10), because no sin is committed without covetousness, and every illicit desire is a disease of this greed.

Every affection is cheap to the love of money, and a soul greedy for profit does not fear to perish even for a small gain. There is no trace of righteousness in the heart in which avarice has made its dwelling.

*[Note: The Vercelli manuscript reads “watchful.” Then, instead of “made its dwelling,” the first edition reads “makes its dwelling.”]*

The treacherous Judas, intoxicated by this poison, while thirsting for profit, reached the noose. He was so foolishly wicked that for thirty pieces of silver he sold both the Lord and the Teacher.

When the Son of God had offered himself to receive the judgment of iniquity, the blessed apostle Peter—whose faith burned with such devotion that he was ready both to suffer with the Lord and to die with him—was frightened by the priest’s maidservant as she accused him and, through weakness, incurred the danger of denial.

*[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter, the Vercelli manuscript, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary read “incurred the weakness of denial.”]*

For this reason, as is evident, he was permitted to hesitate, so that in the chief of the Church a remedy of repentance might be established, and no one would dare to trust in his own strength when even the blessed Peter could not escape the danger of changeability.

The Lord Jesus, who within the high priest’s council was held there only in body, saw with divine insight the trembling of his disciple who stood outside. As soon as he looked upon the fearful man, he raised him up and moved him to tears of repentance.

*[Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript reads “of the one trembling.”]*

Blessed are your tears, holy apostle, which possessed the power of sacred baptism for washing away the guilt of denial. For the right hand of the Lord Jesus Christ was present, and it caught you as you were falling before you were cast down; and in the very danger of falling you received the strength to stand.

*[Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter read “before you fell.” Shortly afterward, Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary reads “and by which firmness …”]*

The Lord saw in you not a faith defeated, nor a love turned away, but steadfastness disturbed.

*[Note: The editions before Quesnel read “a feigned faith,” together with manuscripts of collections 3 and 4. Our better manuscripts, especially the Lectionaries of Saint Peter, read “a defeated faith.”]*

Tears abounded where affection did not fail, and the fountain of love washed away the words of fear. The remedy of obliteration was not delayed where there had been no deliberate judgment. Thus the rock quickly returned to its firmness, receiving such strength that what he had feared then in Christ’s Passion he did not fear afterward in his own punishment.

*[Note: All our manuscripts, together with Paul the Deacon’s copy and all editions before Quesnel, read this way. We do not know by what authority he inserted “Peter,” indicating no variant.]*

*[Note: We have added the closing sentence from the most ancient Vatican manuscript.]*

Through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXI [Also LIX]. On the Passion of the Lord X

## SYNOPSIS

I. How falsely Christ was accused of aspiring to kingship. — II. Whatever Christ did belonged to divine power, not to an earthly king. — III. Why Christ restrained the tears of the women. — IV. How Christ turned punishments back upon his enemy. — V. All creation condemns the Jews who blasphemed against Christ; and the torn veil demonstrates that they had been deprived of all the mysteries of religion.

## CHAPTER I

Since Jewish impiety was striving in many ways, beloved, to find some cause for committing a crime against the Lord Jesus, and the lies that false witnesses had produced in the service of unjust priests offered nothing deserving death, they found what seemed insuperable: to press the Lord of the world with the charge of aspiring to kingship.

*[Note: With Quesnel, our better manuscripts read “some opportunity.” The other editions read “a cause.”]*

When Pilate wished to release Jesus, whom he saw accused without justification, they cried out deceitfully and threateningly: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend; everyone who makes himself a king contradicts Caesar” (John 19:12).

*[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “with foolish accusation.”]*

You feared this foolish accusation imprudently, Pilate. But let the royal name have been so fearsome that a new attempt at power ought to have been suppressed for Caesar’s authority, if a tyrannical display revealed to you a plan of domination, if preparations of weapons and a gathering of wealth and military defenses had been discovered.

*[Note: The particle “but” is omitted in Vatican manuscript 3835. The first edition reads “if it was frightening.” Shortly afterward, that edition and the same ancient Vatican manuscript read “and” instead of “for authority.”]*

Why do you allow him to be burdened with aspiring to power when his distinctive teaching concerned humility? He did not contradict Roman laws; he paid the census tax, paid the didrachma, did not forbid tribute, and established that what belongs to God must be given to God and what belongs to Caesar to Caesar. He chose poverty, taught obedience, and preached gentleness. This is truly not to oppose Caesar but to assist him.

## CHAPTER II

Nevertheless, lest the Jews’ objection seem entirely empty, examine more carefully, governor, what is known about the works of the Lord Jesus and what has been discovered about his power. He gave sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, speech to the mute; he drove away fevers, relieved pains, expelled demons, brought the dead to life, and commanded the sea and winds to be still (Matthew 8:27). These works plainly demonstrate a great king, one who excels not by human power but by divine strength.

*[Note: The Vercelli manuscript reads “who excels.”]*

Let the Jews therefore bring forward this power, let them change their charge, and let them say with their mouths what they hold in their hearts. Why do they make accusations about earthly matters when they persecute heavenly ones?

*[Note: That is, “their accusation,” with “charge” being a word transferred from the language of the courtroom, as Quesnel noted in his annotation. The first edition gives “he presents his accusation,” and the margin of the Verona manuscript 214 has the same reading.]*

Although Pilate felt it burdensome and provoking that the Jews attacked him for neglecting Caesar’s friendship, he nevertheless tried for some time to calm their fury. Therefore he either permitted or ordered the Lord Jesus to be subjected to various insults, so that, once their wickedness had been sated by injuries inflicted on the innocent, they would not rage further.

But obstinate malice grew through its own increases, and against the one over whom it had obtained the right of mockery it demanded also the right of death. Thus, when the chief priests, the leaders of the Jews, and the entire crowd loudly shouted again and again, “Crucify him, crucify him,” he handed Jesus over to the will of his persecutors, releasing Barabbas the robber to them, so that, while they were killing the author of life on the feast day, impunity might be granted to the murderer.

## CHAPTER III
As the Lord was proceeding, beloved, to the place of his glorification, and as mercy was going forth from the tents of the ungodly, so that what is written might be fulfilled, “Salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155), a multitude of the people followed him, together with women who were beating their breasts and lamenting over him (Luke 23:27). For the weaker sex is accustomed to be moved to tears even on behalf of those deserving death, and, in consideration of our common nature, to pity the end of the condemned. But the Lord Jesus disdains to have this lamentation offered for him, because mourning was not fitting for a triumph, nor lamentation for a victory.

Finally, turning to them, he said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children. For the days are coming in which they will say: ‘Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that have not borne, and the breasts that have not nursed.’” Where is the sorrow of one being crucified? Where is the fear of one about to die? The hour of punishment does not terrify the mind of him who is about to suffer; and, teaching that there is no reason to weep for him, he commands repentance by announcing vengeance. “There is no reason,” he says, “for you, daughters of Jerusalem, to grieve over me; weep for yourselves and wail for your children. This lamentation is directed against those whom your wombs have brought forth in such a condition.”

You must plainly mourn—not for the Savior of believers, but for the impiety of those who are perishing. I willingly endure the cross, and accept death in myself, though I am destined to destroy it. Do not weep for him who is dying for the redemption of the world, whom you will see judging in the majesty of the Father.

## CHAPTER IV

Christ Jesus, therefore, exalted upon the wood, turned death back upon the author of death, and, by the exposure of passible flesh, shattered all principalities and hostile powers, admitting into himself the audacity of the ancient enemy. That enemy, raging against the nature subject to him, dared to be an exactor of the debt even there where he could find no trace of sin.

Thus that general and deadly bond of our sale was cancelled, and the contract of captivity passed into the jurisdiction of the Redeemer. Those nails that had pierced the Lord’s hands and feet fastened the devil with perpetual wounds, and the punishment of the holy limbs became the destruction of the hostile powers. Thus Christ completed his victory, so that in him and with him all who believed in him might triumph.

## CHAPTER V

When, therefore, the Lord, exalted by the elevation of his crucified body, was accomplishing the reconciliation of the world upon a kind of summit of punishment, and was summoning the converted thief to the dwelling-place of paradise, you, rulers of the Jews and teachers of the Law, neither pierced by the impiety of your conscience nor softened by the effect of your crime, were adding the weapons of your tongues to the wounds of the nails, saying: “He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the king of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe in him” (Matt. 27:42).

But all the elements answer these foolish and blasphemous words of yours, and heaven, earth, the sun, and the stars together pronounce a single sentence against you. By a terrible convulsion they declare you unworthy of their service, and by an extraordinary eclipse they display darkness to the world, corresponding to your blindness (ibid.). And if neither heavenly nor infernal things are sufficient to rebuke you, and if rocks and tombs were able to sense Christ’s cross more than your hearts, at least observe knowingly what took place in the Temple.

The veil whose barrier enclosed the Holy of Holies was torn from top to bottom, and that sacred and mystical secret which only the high priest had been commanded to enter was opened, so that there was no longer any distinction where no holiness remained. You ought therefore to have recognized that you had been rejected and had lost the entire right of the priesthood, because what the Truth had said to you was true: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also” (John 5:46).

Rightly, therefore, both Testaments condemn you: you have been emptied of grace and deprived of the Law, because you resist the new precisely because you did not believe the old. But we, beloved, who have been freed from the darkness of ignorance, have received the light of faith, and have entered by our adoption into the inheritance of the New Testament, let us rejoice in the festival that carnal Israel lost. For “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). Through his ineffable grace we are enriched with the blessing of every spiritual gift, and are transferred from oldness into newness, so that we are restored not only to the dwelling-place of paradise but also prepared for the glory of the heavenly kingdom. This is granted by our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXII [also LX]

On the Passion of the Lord XI; delivered on the Lord’s Day.

## SUMMARY

I. How dull the human intellect is in contemplating the mysteries.

II. The faith of the Incarnation is taught through the Creed. The solidity of Peter’s faith, on account of which he was appointed the foundation-stone of the Church.

III. The devil was deceived by his own malice. Christ’s prayer for his enemies brought them to faith through Peter’s preaching.

IV. Since Christ died for all the ungodly, Judas too might have obtained a remedy if he had not hurried to the noose.

V. Christ’s death, cruel in the mind of the Jews, is wondrous in the power of the one who died.

## CHAPTER I

The long-desired festival of the Lord’s Passion, beloved, and one welcome to the whole world, has arrived; it does not permit us to remain silent amid the rejoicing of spiritual gladness. For although it is difficult to speak repeatedly about the same matter with sufficient dignity and appropriateness, it is nevertheless not permitted a priest to withhold from the ears of the faithful the duty of speech in so great a sacrament of divine mercy. The very subject, because it is ineffable, grants the ability to speak; nor can what is said about it ever fail, since what is said about it can never be enough.

Let human weakness therefore yield to the glory of God and always find itself unequal to explaining his works of mercy. Let us labor with our understanding, falter in our intelligence, and fail in eloquence. It is good that what we rightly think about the Lord’s majesty should still seem insufficient to us. For the prophet says: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:4). No one should presume that he has found everything he seeks, lest the one who ceases to draw near cease to approach.

Among all God’s works, in which human attention is wearied by wonder, what so delights and surpasses the contemplation of our mind as the Savior’s Passion? Whenever we contemplate, as we are able, his omnipotence—which he possesses with the Father in one and equal essence—his humility appears to us more wondrous in God than his power; and the self-emptying of divine majesty is more difficult to grasp than the supreme exaltation of servile form.

Yet this greatly assists our understanding: although the Creator is one thing and the creature another, the inviolable Godhead one thing and passible flesh another, the property of both substances nevertheless comes together in one person, so that whether in weaknesses or in powers, the dishonor belongs to the same one to whom the glory belongs.

## CHAPTER II

By this rule of faith, beloved, which at the very beginning of the Creed we received through the authority of apostolic institution, we confess our Lord Jesus Christ, whom we call the only Son of God the almighty Father, to have been likewise born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. Nor do we depart from his majesty when we believe that he himself was crucified and died, and was raised on the third day.

For everything that belongs to God and everything that belongs to humanity was fulfilled alike by the humanity and the Godhead: while the impassible one dwells in what is passible, neither can power be affected by weakness, nor weakness overcome by power.

The blessed apostle Peter is rightly praised for confessing this unity. When the Lord asked what the disciples understood about him, Peter was the first of all to anticipate their voices and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He did not see this through flesh or blood—things whose obstruction could hinder the inward eyes—but through the very Spirit of the Father working in the heart of the believer. Thus, prepared to govern the whole Church, he first learned what he was to teach, and, for the solidity of the faith he was to proclaim, he heard: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:16).

The strength, therefore, of Christian faith—which, built upon an unconquerable rock, does not fear the gates of death—confesses one Lord Jesus Christ, true God and true man. It believes him to be the Son of the Virgin, who is the author of his mother; the one born at the end of the ages, who is the Creator of time; the one Lord of all powers, and one sprung from mortal stock; the one who knew no sin, yet was sacrificed for sinners in the likeness of sinful flesh.

## CHAPTER III

In order to release the human race from the bonds of deadly transgression, he concealed from the raging devil the power of his majesty and presented the weakness of our humility. For if that cruel and proud enemy had been able to know God’s plan of mercy, he would have sought to moderate the minds of the Jews by gentleness rather than stir them up with unjust hatred, lest he lose the servitude of all his captives while persecuting the freedom of one who owed him nothing.

His own malice therefore deceived him. He inflicted upon the Son of God a punishment that would be turned into a remedy for all the children of humanity. He shed righteous blood, which would be both the price and the drink of the world’s reconciliation.

The Lord accepted what, according to the purpose of his will, he had chosen. He allowed the impious hands of the furious to act upon him; while those hands devoted themselves to their own crime, they served the Redeemer. His compassion toward his killers was so great that, pleading with the Father from the cross, he asked not that vengeance be taken upon himself but that they be forgiven, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).

The power of this prayer was such that the preaching of the apostle Peter converted to repentance the hearts of many of those who had said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25), and on a single day nearly three thousand Jews were baptized (Acts 2:41). Thus “there was one heart and one soul” among them all (ibid. 4:32), already prepared to die for the one whom they had demanded should be crucified.

## CHAPTER IV

The traitor Judas could not attain this forgiveness, because, as the son of perdition, with the devil standing at his right hand (Ps. 108), he passed into despair before Christ fulfilled the sacrament of universal redemption. For when the Lord had died for all the ungodly, Judas too might perhaps have obtained a remedy if he had not hurried to the noose.

But nothing of the Savior’s demonstrations of mercy had ever taken root in his evil heart—now given over to the frauds of theft, now occupied with murderous transactions. With impious ears he had received the Lord’s words: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:13); and, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 5:32). He had not understood Christ’s compassion: Christ not only healed bodily illnesses but also cured the wounds of weakened souls, saying to the paralytic: “Take courage, son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9:3); and saying to the adulterous woman who had been brought before him: “Neither will I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11). Through all his works he showed that in his coming he had come as the Savior of the world, not as its judge.

The impious traitor, alienated from this understanding, rose up against himself—not with the judgment of one who repents, but with the frenzy of one who perishes. He had sold the author of life to his executioners, and by dying he sinned further, increasing his condemnation.

## CHAPTER V

What the false witnesses, the bloodthirsty rulers, and the impious priests did against the Lord Jesus Christ through the ministry of a cowardly governor and the service of an ignorant cohort was both detestable to all ages and worthy of embrace. For the Lord’s cross, just as it was cruel in the mind of the Jews, is wondrous in the power of the Crucified.

The people rage against one, while Christ has mercy on all. What cruelty inflicts is received by will, so that the permission granted to the crime might accomplish the work of the eternal will.

Therefore the whole sequence of events, which the Gospel narrative recounts in full, must be received by the hearing of the faithful in such a way that, while the reality of the actions fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s Passion remains intact, we understand not only that the remission of sins was accomplished in Christ, but also that a pattern of righteousness was set forth.

But so that this may be discussed more carefully, with the Lord’s help, this portion of the sermon should be reserved for Wednesday. May the grace of God be present, as we hope, and, in answer to your prayers, enable us to fulfill what was promised; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## ADMONITION CONCERNING THE THREE SERMONS THAT FOLLOW

After the preceding sermon, the order of several subsequent sermons was confused in the printed editions, as also in quite a few manuscripts; for that reason it had to be completely rearranged by us.

The sermon beginning “All the times indeed” had been placed after the preceding sermon. At the end of the preceding sermon, however, another sermon is promised for Wednesday, in which Saint Leo undertakes to speak so that, while the reality of the actions fulfilled at the time of the Lord’s Passion remains intact, we may understand not only that the remission of sins was accomplished in Christ—which he had established in that sermon—but also that a pattern of righteousness was set forth; this he postpones for exposition on Wednesday.

Nothing of this appears in the printed sermon “All the times indeed” placed afterward. Indeed, that sermon itself promises another sermon, likewise to be delivered on Wednesday, which we shall identify below. In the following sermon, however, “Glory, beloved,” chapter 1, he both mentions the promise and adds: “This Passion of the Lord both redeemed us all and taught us, so that from the place where the price was given, righteousness might also be taken.” And in chapter 3: “He established both a sacrament and an example, so that they might grasp the one by being reborn and follow the other by imitation”—words that refer to the pattern of righteousness proposed above.

This sermon, therefore, as though it were a portion of the preceding sermon reserved for Wednesday, ought not to have been separated from it. After it we shall give the sermon “All the times indeed,” delivered on the Lord’s Day against the Eutychians. Since at its conclusion another sermon on the same subject is said to be added for Wednesday, and since it was not found immediately afterward in the printed editions, we have placed it there.

We discovered that this sermon is the one beginning: “The sermon, beloved, concerning the glorious Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, which was promised.” There the holy pontiff likewise discusses the error of Eutyches. Indeed, it is clear from Letters 124 and 165 that these two sermons are to be regarded as one on account of their continuity. In those letters, after Saint Leo had transcribed almost the entirety of chapters 3 and 4 from the sermon beginning “All the times indeed,” he immediately adds a fragment of the first chapter from another sermon beginning “The sermon, beloved.” Thus one is a portion of the other.

All this is confirmed by the order found in two ancient manuscript lectionaries of the Basilica of Saint Peter, numbers 105 and 107. There, among the sermons on the Passion, after the sermon “The long-desired,” comes “Glory, beloved”; then “All the times indeed”; and afterward “The sermon, beloved, concerning the glorious…” The same order is also found in three other manuscripts of the distinguished collection 2.

# SERMON LXIII

On the Passion of the Lord XII; delivered on Wednesday.

## SUMMARY

I. Christ did not fight by his own power alone, but from the humility of our condition, so that righteousness might be preserved.

II. Whatever we possess as fulfilled, the ancients possessed in shadow; there is one faith and one hope for all.

III. Christ’s union with both of his bodies, the natural and the mystical, is inseparable.

IV. The Christian must strive above all to imitate his Head.

V. Only the ceremonial precepts have been changed; grace has been given for moral observance.

VI. Through baptism Christ begets countless sons for himself, in which the likeness of his death and resurrection shines forth.

VII. Every merit of the Christian is Christ’s glory. Those whom he feeds with his flesh he also moves and governs by his Spirit.

## CHAPTER I

The glory of the Lord’s Passion, beloved, about which we promised to speak today also, is especially wondrous because of the mystery of humility. It both redeemed us all and taught us, so that from the place where the price was given, righteousness might also be taken.

The omnipotence of the Son of God—which, through the same essence, makes him equal to the Father—could have rescued the human race from the devil’s dominion by the sole command of his will, unless it had been most fitting to the divine works that the hostility of the enemy should be conquered by that which it had conquered, and that natural freedom should be restored through the very nature by which universal captivity had been inflicted.

When the Evangelist says, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), and the Apostle says, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19), it was shown that the Only-Begotten of the most high Father entered into such fellowship with human humility that, having assumed the substance of our flesh and soul, the one and same Son of God remained, increasing what was ours, not what was his own. For weakness had to be exalted, not power, so that when the creature was united to its Creator, nothing divine would be lacking in what was assumed, and nothing human would be lacking in the one who assumed it.

## CHAPTER II

This plan of God’s mercy and justice, although in past ages it was veiled beneath certain coverings, was not so hidden that it was denied to the understanding of the saints who proved worthy of praise from the beginning until the Lord’s coming. For salvation, which was destined to come in Christ, was promised both in prophetic words and through the signs of events that had occurred. It was obtained not only by those who proclaimed it but also by all who believed those who proclaimed it.

One faith justifies the saints of every age, and whatever we confess to have been accomplished through the mediator between God and humanity, Jesus Christ (1 Tim. 2:5), or whatever our fathers worshiped as destined to be accomplished, belongs to the same hope of the faithful.

There is no distinction between Jews and Gentiles. For, as the Apostle says, “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of the commandments of God” (Rom. 2:25; 1 Cor. 7:19). If these are observed with the integrity of faith, they make true children of Abraham—that is, perfect Christians. The same Apostle says:

“Whatever of you have been baptized in Christ Jesus have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female. For you are all one in Christ Jesus. And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:27–29).

## CHAPTER III

There is therefore no doubt, beloved, that human nature was assumed by the Son of God into so great a union that Christ is one and the same not only in that man who is the firstborn of all creation (Col. 1:18), but also in all his saints. Just as the head cannot be separated from the members, so the members cannot be separated from the head.

Although it belongs not to this life but to the eternal one that God should be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), even now he is the undivided inhabitant of his temple, which is the Church (Col. 1:18), in accordance with his own promise: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

In agreement with him the Apostle says: “He is the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold the first place in all things. For in him all fullness was pleased to dwell, and through him to reconcile all things to himself” (Col. 1:18–20).

## CHAPTER IV

What is suggested to our hearts by these and many other testimonies except that in all things we should be renewed according to the image of him who, while remaining in the form of God, deigned to become the form of sinful flesh (Phil. 2:6)?

He assumed all our weaknesses that arise from sin, without sharing in sin, so that he was not without the experiences of hunger and thirst, sleep and weariness, sorrow and weeping, and endured the fiercest pains even to the end of death. For no one could be released from the snares of mortality unless he in whom alone the nature of all humanity was innocent allowed himself to be killed by the hands of the ungodly.

Thus our Savior, the Son of God, established for all who believe in him both a sacrament and an example, so that they might grasp the one by being reborn and follow the other by imitation. The blessed apostle Peter teaches this, saying:

“Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges unjustly. He himself bore our sins in his body upon the wood, so that, having died to sins, we might live for righteousness” (1 Pet. 2:21–24).

## CHAPTER V

Just as there is no believer, beloved, to whom the gifts of grace should be denied, so there is no one who is not indebted to Christian discipline. For although the harshness of the mystical Law has been removed, the usefulness of willing observance has increased, as the Evangelist John says: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

Everything that preceded according to the Law—whether in the circumcision of the flesh, the various sacrifices, or the observance of the Sabbath—testified to Christ and anticipated Christ’s grace. And he is the end of the Law (Rom. 10:4), not by abolishing its signs but by fulfilling them.

Although he is the same author of the old things and the new, he changed the sacramental forms of the promises because he fulfilled what had been promised, and he brought the announcements to an end because the one announced had arrived. In the moral precepts, however, none of the decrees of the former Testament was rejected; rather, many were enlarged by evangelical instruction, so that those precepts that give salvation might be more perfect and clearer than those that promised the Savior.

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore we know all that the Son of God both did and taught for the reconciliation of the world not only as a history of past actions, but also experience it in the power of present works.

He is the one who, born from the Holy Spirit of the undefiled Virgin Mother, makes his Church fruitful through the same inspiration, so that through the birth of baptism an innumerable multitude of children of God may be generated. Of them it is said: “They were born not of bloods, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13).

He is the one in whom Abraham’s offspring is blessed by the adoption of the whole world, and he makes the patriarch the father of the nations (Gen. 22:18), while the children of the promise are born through faith, not through flesh.

He is the one who, making no exception for any nation, forms from every people under heaven one flock of holy sheep, and daily fulfills what he promised, saying: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; these also I must bring, and they will hear my voice; and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

Although he says principally to the blessed Peter, “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17), the care of all shepherds is nevertheless governed by one Lord. He feeds those who come to the rock in such joyful and well-watered pastures that countless sheep, strengthened by the richness of love, just as the good Shepherd deigned to lay down his life for his sheep (John 10:15), likewise do not hesitate to die for the name of the Shepherd.

He is the one with whom not only the glorious courage of the martyrs suffers together, but also the faith of all who are reborn suffers together in the very act of regeneration. When one renounces the devil and believes in God, when one passes from oldness into newness, when the image of the earthly human being is laid aside and the heavenly form is assumed, a certain kind of death and a certain likeness of resurrection intervene. Thus the one received by Christ, and receiving Christ, is not the same after the washing as before baptism, but the body of the reborn becomes the flesh of the Crucified.

## Editorial Notes and Variant Readings

- [Col. 0347C] The word *mercy* is absent from the Verona manuscript. A little later, *Salvation is far from sinners* occurs in the printed editions before Quesnel and in quite a few manuscripts.
- [Col. 0347D] The pronoun *him*, present in editions before Quesnel, has been restored from the very ancient Vatican manuscript and other manuscripts of established value. It is nevertheless absent from the Vercelli manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts.
- [Col. 0347D] The Verona manuscript reads: *days are coming upon you, in which it will be said*. Two St Peter manuscripts and one Vatican manuscript read: *you will say*. Later, editions before Quesnel and several manuscripts read *have not suckled*. The reading *have not nourished*, introduced by Quesnel from his manuscripts, is also supported by most of our books.
- [Col. 0347D] Some editions and several manuscripts read: *this lamentation is poured out*.
- [Col. 0347D] Thus, with Quesnel and the first edition, most and the better of our manuscripts read; others read: *concerning salvation*.
- [Col. 0347D] Editions before Quesnel and some manuscripts add: *and recklessness*; this is absent, however, from the very ancient Vatican manuscript, the Vercelli manuscript, and other manuscripts [Col. 0348C].
- [Col. 0348C] Some manuscripts, with editions preceding Quesnel, have *but* instead of *therefore*.
- [Col. 0348C] The very ancient Vatican manuscript reads: *by the abasement of passible flesh he mocked him*.
- [Col. 0348C–D] In the Vercelli manuscript the words from *admitting into himself* to the end of the period are omitted.
- [Col. 0348D] The Verona manuscript reads: *confirming*.
- [Col. 0348D] The same Verona manuscript reads: *pierced by piety*. A little later, the printed editions read *by the feeling of crime*. Better is *by the effect of crime*, from two St Peter manuscripts and three Vatican manuscripts.
- [Col. 0348D] We have inserted *together* from two St Peter manuscripts, the very ancient Vatican manuscript, Vercelli, Verona, and Vatican collection 5. One Vatican manuscript of collection 4 has *namely* instead of *together*, which confirms the omission in the editions.
- [Col. 0348D] The editions had *and the stars, declaring you unworthy of their service by a terrible convulsion*, etc. The reading of two St Peter manuscripts seemed preferable. A little later, editions before Quesnel, with some manuscripts, read *show* instead of *display*.
- [Col. 0348D] The Verona manuscript and another Vatican manuscript read: *to convict you*.
- [Col. 0348D] Editions before Quesnel read: *were enclosed*.
