- [Col. 0349D] This reading is from two St Peter manuscripts and the Verona manuscript, and also from John, deacon of the Lateran church, who seems likewise to have read it in the lectionaries of the Lateran basilica. It is found in vol. II of Mabillon’s *Museum Italicum*, p. 565. Elsewhere: *which the high priest alone*.
- [Col. 0349D] The Verona manuscript reads: *if you believe*. A little later, the Vercelli manuscript reads: *perhaps you would believe me also*.
- [Col. 0349D] The very ancient Vatican manuscript and our Verona manuscript read: *emptied*. Then *you resisted* instead of *you resist* occurs in the first edition and the Bonn manuscript.
- [Col. 0349D] The preposition *in* is omitted in the very ancient Vatican manuscript. One St Peter manuscript and another Bonn manuscript read: *let us rejoice that we have received the festival . . ., since*, etc.
- [Col. 0349D] We have emended this from two St Peter manuscripts and the Vercelli manuscript. Elsewhere: *concerning the same solemnity*.
- [Col. 0349D] Thus, with Quesnel, three previously cited manuscripts read, though he identifies no manuscript. Earlier editions and some manuscripts read: *to withhold the office of speech from faithful peoples*.
- [Col. 0349D–0350D] Printed editions and some manuscripts read *while never*. We preferred the authority of two St Peter manuscripts and one Vercelli manuscript, as well as the Bonn manuscript and the first edition, in which *about which* refers back to *subject matter*.
- [Col. 0350D] The Vercelli manuscript deletes *in*, so that the adjective *supreme* is joined to the noun *advancement*.
- [Col. 0350D] Some manuscripts read *comes together*. A little later the Vercelli manuscript reads *as is desired*.
- [Col. 0350D] In Vatican manuscript collection 5, *also* is absent, and *and Mary* is read instead of *from Mary*.
- [Col. 0350D] We supplied the preposition *in* here and before *power* from two St Peter manuscripts; the Vercelli manuscript agrees by placing it before *power*. It could have been omitted before *weakness*, as often happens with scribes because of the meeting of initial letters.
- [Col. 0350D] We have emended this from our better manuscripts and editions before Quesnel, whereas Quesnel reads *to whom*.
- [Col. 0350D] Two Vatican manuscripts and the first edition read: *or blood*. A little later some manuscripts read *might first learn*, perhaps better.
- [Col. 0350D–0351D] We discuss this passage and Quesnel’s note appended to it in the observations on the third sermon.
- [Col. 0351D] Thus two St Peter manuscripts and Remigius of Lyons, *On the Three Epistles*, ch. 19; elsewhere: *forgive*.
- [Col. 0351D] One Vatican manuscript and the Bonn manuscript read *his*; another Vatican manuscript and Remigius read *his* [a different Latin form, *eius* rather than *huius*].
- [Col. 0351D] The first edition lacks *perhaps*.
- [Col. 0351D] Thus we have emended from two St Peter manuscripts. Elsewhere: *now devoted to the thefts of frauds*.
- [Col. 0351D] This is better from the same manuscripts and another Vatican manuscript. In editions and some manuscripts, with different punctuation: *had taken root, nor had he accepted pious [words]*. In two Vatican manuscripts, *had received* stands for *had accepted*.

Later, editions before Quesnel read: *Take courage, son, your sins are forgiven you*. The reading introduced by Quesnel and retained by us is exhibited by two St Peter manuscripts and another Vercelli manuscript.

- [Col. 0353C] Thus Quesnel, two St Peter manuscripts, and one Vatican manuscript read. Earlier editions, with other manuscripts and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, read: *through the very matter*.
- [Col. 0353C] The Vercelli manuscript reads: *by assuming the substance of our flesh and soul*.
- [Col. 0353C–0354C] The same Vercelli manuscript adds *leaving [his own]*, wrongly, as is clear from what follows; for weakness, not power, had to be advanced. The addition would affirm the increase of our humanity but deny his proper divinity. A little later the same manuscript, with the first edition and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, incorrectly reads: *with its Creator*.
- [Col. 0354C] The Homiliary of Paul the Deacon reads: *from the beginning of the world*.
- [Col. 0354C] Thus all our manuscripts and editions before Quesnel, except the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, read. Quesnel substituted *hope and faith* without indicating any authority.
- [Col. 0354C] The editions read *adopted*. Quesnel notes in the margin: *but the first edition reads worshiped*.
- [Col. 0354C] Quesnel has *difference*, contrary to all our editions and manuscripts and to the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon. Paul’s text also has *distinction*.
- [Col. 0355D] The Homiliary of Paul the Deacon reads: *For you are all one in Christ Jesus*, as appears in Paul’s epistle.

- [Col. 0355D] Editions before Quesnel read: *to become a form*; our manuscripts do not support this.

- [Col. 0355D] The Vercelli manuscript and Paul the Deacon read: *that we might live*.
- [Col. 0355D–0356D] Thus Quesnel, with his Corbie, Victorius, Thouanus, Regius manuscripts and the marginal reading of Surius, reads. Most and the better of our manuscripts, with the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, read the same. Elsewhere: *the righteousness of the Law*.

- [Col. 0356D] Two St Peter manuscripts read: *in things present*.
- [Col. 0356D] In the same manuscripts: *from the desire of the flesh*.

The present tense is likewise read throughout what follows: *are born*, *makes*, *fulfills*. - [Col. 0357D] The word *his*, supplied by Quesnel, occurs in our manuscripts.
- [Col. 0357D] The editions add *for*. We have deleted it on the authority of the Vercelli manuscript and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, for the repeated construction *He is* continues.
- [Col. 0357D] The copy of Paul the Deacon reads: *may become a body*. In a similar sense the author of the Letter to Demetrias, ch. 1, attributes this to baptism: sinful flesh is transformed into Christ’s body.

## CHAPTER VII
This change, dearly beloved, is the right hand of the Most High (Ps. 67:21), who works all things in all (1 Cor. 12:6), so that in each of the faithful, through the quality of a good manner of life, we may recognize him as the author of holy works. Let us give thanks for the mercy of God, who adorns the whole body of the Church with innumerable gifts of grace in such a way that, through the many rays of one light, the same splendor appears everywhere, and that the merit of any Christian can be nothing other than the glory of Christ.

This is the true light that justifies and illumines every human being. This is what rescues us from the power of darkness and transfers us into the kingdom of the Son of God (Col. 1:13). This is what, through the newness of life, advances the desires of the soul and extinguishes the cravings of the flesh. This is by which the Lord’s Passover is lawfully celebrated in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5:8): when the leaven of the old wickedness has been cast away, the new creation is inebriated and nourished from the Lord himself.

For participation in the body and blood of Christ does nothing other than make us pass over into that which we receive; and in every way, both in spirit and in flesh, we bear him in whom we have died together, been buried together, and risen together. As the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXIV [Al. LXI]

On the Passion of the Lord XIII; delivered on Sunday

[Col. 0357D]

## SYNOPSIS

I. The Lord’s passion must be contemplated attentively, since its faith depends upon faith in the incarnation. — II. Why the Son, who is equal to the Father and alone without sin, became incarnate, and not another person. — III. Of what value are Christ’s death and sacrifice on the Cross? — IV. Each nature in Christ, while preserving its own properties, has distinct roles in the mysteries.

## CHAPTER I

All times, dearly beloved, exercise Christian minds through the mystery of the Lord’s passion and resurrection; and there is no religious observance of ours in which not only the reconciliation of the world but also the assumption of human nature in Christ is celebrated. But now the whole Church ought to be instructed with greater understanding and kindled with more fervent hope, since the very dignity of these events is expressed in the recurring cycle of the sacred days and in the pages of evangelical truth, so that the Lord’s Passover should not merely be recalled as past but honored as present.

Therefore, let our faith’s gaze wander in no respect from those things that pertain to the cross of Jesus Christ, and let us receive none of the events unfolded in the Gospel narrative with inattentive hearing. For there have been, and still are, those who attack the truth of the Lord’s incarnation and assert that the Word became flesh in the womb of the Virgin mother Mary (John 1:14), that the infant, born and progressing through bodily growth, advanced to the age of complete manhood, and that, having been crucified, dead, and buried, he rose on the third day—but that all this occurred in the form of our likeness, not in the nature of our flesh.

We, however, in no way departing from evangelical and apostolic testimonies, must strengthen ourselves through an understanding of those realities whose most certain evidence has instructed us, so that we may piously and steadfastly say: “For we too have been taught by those things; what they saw, we have seen; what they learned, we have learned; and what they handled, we have touched” (1 John 1:1). Therefore we are not disturbed by the Lord’s passion, because we are not deceived about his birth.

**Note:** The two manuscripts of St. Peter read *quam et humanam* (“as well as the human [nature]”).

## CHAPTER II

For we know, dearly beloved, and profess with our whole heart, that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one Deity, and that the essence of the eternal Trinity is consubstantial, divided from itself in nothing and different from itself in nothing, because it is simultaneously timeless, simultaneously unchangeable, and simultaneously never ceasing to be what it is.

Within this ineffable unity of the Trinity, whose works and judgments are common in all things, the person of the Son specifically undertook the restoration of the human race. Since he is the one through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made (John 1:3), and since he animated the human being formed from the clay of the earth with the breath of rational life, he likewise restored our nature, cast down from the citadel of eternity, to the dignity it had lost; and he whose creature it was became also its reformer.

Thus he directed his plan toward its fulfillment, so that, in destroying the devil’s dominion, he would make use more of the justice of reason than of the power of force. Since, therefore, the entire posterity of the first human being had fallen, wounded by one simultaneous blow, and none of the merits of the saints could overcome the condition of the death inflicted, a singular physician came from heaven. He had often been announced through many signs and had long been promised by prophetic prediction. Remaining in the form of God and losing nothing of his own majesty, he was to arise in the nature of our flesh and soul, without contamination by the ancient transgression.

For he alone, born as the son of the blessed Virgin, was without sin—not a stranger to the human race, but alien to crime [The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the Corbie manuscript: “in whom, formed in God’s image and likeness, both perfect innocence and true nature existed.”]. He alone existed from Adam’s lineage in whom the devil had no claim to call anything his own. When the devil raged against one whom he did not hold under the law of sin, he lost the right of his impious dominion.

## CHAPTER III

For the shedding of the blood of the just on behalf of the unjust was so powerful in conferring privilege and so rich in value that, if the whole company of captives believed in their Redeemer, no one would remain held by tyrannical bonds. For, as the Apostle says, “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5:20).

And since those born under the sentence of sin received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom became stronger than the debt of servitude. What hope, then, do those leave themselves in the protection of this mystery who deny the reality of human substance in the body of our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled, by what blood they were redeemed. Who is he “who gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor” (Eph. 5:2)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true Priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh?

Although the death of many saints was precious in the sight of the Lord (Ps. 116:15), the killing of no innocent person was the world’s propitiation. The righteous received crowns; they did not bestow them. From the courage of the faithful arose examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness. Their deaths were individual deaths, each for himself, and no one paid another’s debt by his own end, since among human beings there was only one Lord Jesus, in whom all have been crucified, all have died, all have been buried, and all have also been raised. Of them he himself said: “When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

**Note:** The two manuscripts of St. Peter, as well as the two letters mentioned above, read “nor did anyone pay another’s debt by his own death.” Other editions, with the later collections of manuscripts, read “by his own funeral.” In the printed editions and some manuscripts, the next phrase reads “there was one alone,” without *solus*; two manuscripts of St. Peter have *solus*. From the cited letters both terms have been joined. Some manuscripts add *Christus* after *Jesus*.

For true faith, which justifies the ungodly and makes the righteous, draws them into participation in its nature and obtains salvation in him [the passage was extremely corrupt in both printed editions and manuscripts. The name *homo* (“human being”), which governs the following verbs “finds” and “reaches,” was missing everywhere. We have emended and supplemented the passage from the two letters cited above; we have also added *solo* (“alone”) after *in quo*, as in the preceding sermon]. In him alone the human being finds himself innocent; and because “there is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5), through communion with his kind he reaches the peace of the Godhead, having the freedom, through God’s grace [added in the cited letters], to glory in the power of him who, having engaged the proud enemy in the weakness of our flesh, granted his victory to those in whose body he triumphed.

## CHAPTER IV

When, therefore, in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and human being, we confess the divine nature from the Father and the human substance from his mother, although the Word of God and the flesh are one person and both essences have common actions [the printed editions add “not one substance,” but this is absent from the manuscripts, including Quesnellus’s, and from the cited letters; in one of those letters the subsequent reading is altered to: “one person, who inseparably and indivisibly possesses common actions”], we must nevertheless understand the qualities of those actions. With the clear contemplation of faith we must discern toward what the humility of weakness is advanced and toward what the height of power bends: what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither conceive nor give birth; and without the reality of flesh, infancy would not lie wrapped in swaddling clothes (Matt. 2:11). Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not worship the child revealed by a new star; and without the reality of flesh, the child whom Herod desired to kill would not be ordered to be transferred into Egypt (ibid., 20).

**Note:** We have restored this reading from the Bologna manuscript and the first edition, although the Leonine text prefers *transferri* (“to be transferred”) earlier and *occidi* (“to be killed”) here. Other copies read *occidere* (“to kill”). In the cited letters the wording is slightly altered, but the passive construction is retained in both: “The child would not be ordered to be transferred into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution.”

Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not say, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17; Luke 3:22); and without the reality of flesh, John would not testify, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Without the power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the giving of life to the dead would not occur; and without the reality of flesh, food would not be necessary for one who was fasting, nor sleep for one who was weary.

Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father (John 10:30); and without the reality of flesh, the same one would not say that the Father was greater than he (John 14:28).

**Note:** The Vatican manuscript of collection 5 omits *se* (“himself”), as do the manuscripts of the treatise Against the Errors of Eutyches, chapter 11, which was taken from this sermon. The pronoun *se* is nevertheless found in the two letters mentioned above.

Since Catholic faith embraces and defends both, it believes, according to the proper character of the divine and human substance, that the one Son of God is both human being and Word.

There are many things, dearly beloved, that we could draw from the whole body of Scripture for the exposition of the faith we proclaim, since nothing is more frequently commended in the divine utterances than that the Son of God is eternal from the Father according to his Godhead, and the same one is temporal from his mother according to the flesh. But so that your loving attention may not grow weary, a limit must be placed upon today’s sermon, so that we may reserve for Wednesday what remains to be added, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXV [Al. LXIV]

On the Passion of the Lord XIV; delivered on Wednesday

## SYNOPSIS

I. When the Eutychians do not acknowledge true flesh in Christ, they must either believe that he was a false human being or that God was passible. — II. Christ restrained the power of his Godhead so that, by suffering, he might both save and strengthen. — III. Christ’s passion was real; the Jews deny him as God, the Eutychians as human being. — IV. All Christ’s mysteries prove that he had true flesh, without which he is not the firstfruits of those who sleep. — V. Unless Christ’s flesh is real, the Divinity cannot dwell bodily in him.

## CHAPTER I

The sermon on the glorious passion of our Lord Jesus Christ that was promised, dearly beloved, must, as I understand, be rendered to your expectation in such a way that the duty of exposition may serve the paschal feast and confront the assaults of impious error.

For those who deny that the Son of God assumed the true nature of our flesh are enemies of the Christian faith and attack evangelical preaching with excessive shamelessness. According to them, the cross of Christ was either the imitation of a phantom or the punishment of the Godhead. This must be banished far from the hearts of the faithful, because Catholic integrity can possess neither a stain of unbelief nor a wrinkle of falsehood. It confesses one Christ as both God and human being, without saying either that he was a false human being or that God was passible.

**Note:** The same appears in Letters 124, chapter 6, and 165, chapter 6.

Although, therefore, from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb (John 1:14), there was never any division between the divine and human substance, and although throughout all bodily growth the actions of the entire period belonged to one person, we do not confuse by any mixture the things that were done inseparably. Rather, from the character of the actions we discern what belongs to which nature. For the divine does not prejudice the human, nor the human the divine, since the two converge in such a way that neither the property of either is destroyed nor the person doubled.

## CHAPTER II

Having passed over the events that preceded the Lord’s passion, let us consider what instruction the paschal mystery contains. When the ferocity of the Jews was blazing toward the accomplishment of its crime, and “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19), no force could have been brought against the temple of his body unless he himself had permitted it.

That terrifying troop of soldiers and the multitude sent by the chief priests and Pharisees with swords and clubs were so struck down by the Lord’s single voice that, when the crowd said that it was seeking Jesus the Nazarene and he himself replied, “I am he” (John 18:3), none of them could remain standing. All at once, deprived of the use of their limbs, they were driven backward and fell prostrate.

**Note:** The first edition reads *percussa est* (“was struck”), and the Quesnellian edition *perculsa est* (“was overwhelmed”).

In this there was plainly a manifestation of divine power, which overthrew the efforts of the impious—not with opposing weapons, nor with the aid of any powerful creature, but solely by the power of the Word.

But because another course of action suited the salvation of the human race, and Christ’s blood could not become the price of believers unless the Redeemer allowed himself to be seized, he admitted the impious hands against himself; and the power of the Godhead was restrained within him [the same edition and the Bologna manuscript read: “the power of the Godhead was restrained within him, so that one might reach…”; earlier editions omit *in se*, while Quesnellus corrected *perveniret* to *perveniretur*, as do the better manuscripts], so that the glory of the passion might be reached.

Its appearance would certainly have been empty, and the image of endurance would have benefited no one, unless true Divinity had clothed itself in the true sensations of human flesh, so that the one Son of God and human being, impassible in one respect and passible in another, might renew our mortality through his immortality.

Therefore he was not without sorrow; therefore he was not without fear [one manuscript of St. Peter and another of Bologna, together with the first edition, read “strength”]. He did this so that, in overcoming disturbances of this kind, he might strengthen us not only through the mystery of his assumption but also through the example of his courage. For his exhortation to patience would have seemed unjust if he had no communion with our weakness.

## CHAPTER III

The prophet Isaiah foretells the Lord’s true sufferings in his own words, saying: “I gave my back to blows and my cheeks to the hands; I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting” (Isa. 50:6).

Therefore, what the Word made flesh suffered was not the punishment of the Word but of the flesh. Yet the insults and punishments of the flesh also overflowed upon the impassible one, so that they are rightly said to have been inflicted upon him, since they were admitted against his body. The Apostle says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

Blinded by their own wickedness, the Jews did not know into what crime they had rushed. Therefore the merciful Lord Jesus, who wished to save even his killers by his death, pleaded for the ignorance of those raging against him from the height of the cross, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

They did not perceive, either through the understanding of the heart, the hearing of the ear, or the sight of the eyes, whom they had attacked with false testimonies and whom they had compelled to be fastened to the cross, since they did not recognize the substance of the Godhead in the body of a human being.

They saw one who was humble, but did not worship the author of the universe; they did not understand the power of the one who would judge, despising the gentleness of the one judged. Thus one impiety joined together both the persecutors of the true God and the deniers of the true human being: the Jews judged Christ’s form of a servant to be the only reality, while the heretics assert that it was false.

## CHAPTER IV

Let these phantom-Christians, then, say what substance of the Savior was fastened to the wood, what substance lay in the tomb, and, when the stone of the monument had been rolled away, what flesh rose on the third day; or what sort of body Jesus brought before the eyes of his disciples when he entered to them although the doors were shut (John 20:19), since, to dispel the unbelief of those who saw him, he required that the still-open wounds of the nails and the fresh wound of his pierced side be examined with the eyes and handled with the fingers (Luke 24:39).

But if heretical obstinacy leaves its darkness amid so great a light of truth, let them show from where they promise themselves the hope of eternal life, from where they believe themselves to be sharers in Christ’s resurrection. For they cannot say with the Apostle, “Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. 15:20), because he is not the firstfruits of human beings if he is not from the stock of human nature.

For the one who first rose from the dead is a portion of the fullness that he preceded; and it is rightly believed that what was begun in the head must also be completed in the members: “For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (ibid., 22).

## CHAPTER V

Embracing, therefore, dearly beloved, the unique pledge of Christian hope [the first edition and the Bologna manuscript read “of human hope”; certain manuscripts and the marginal Vulgate read “of Christian faith”], let us not be torn away from the structure of Christ’s body. In him, as the Apostle says, “all the fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (Col. 2:9–10).

Since the substance of God is incorporeal, how does he dwell bodily in Christ unless it is because the flesh of our race became the flesh of the Godhead? And in him we have been filled with God—in him we were crucified, in him buried, and in him also raised—so that with the Apostle we may say: “Our citizenship is in heaven, from which we also await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humility to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21).

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXVI [Al. LXII]

On the Passion of the Lord XV

**Note:** Earlier printed editions placed this sermon as delivered on Wednesday because it followed Sermon 64, which begins *Omnia quidem tempora* (“All times indeed”) and promises another sermon for Wednesday at its conclusion. But in the preliminary notice to Sermon 63 we have shown that this sermon was improperly placed after it.

## SYNOPSIS

I. The grace of restoration is freely given; it could have been expected from no one except Christ, who alone was innocent and justified all who believed in him, even in the Old Testament. — II. The same mysteries exist in both Testaments: veiled in one, revealed in the other. — III. The Passover is not rightly celebrated except by believers. Each person must be instructed by the miracles that occurred at Christ’s death. The wondrous effects of Christ’s death. — IV. Everything Christ did was done for our sake; unbelief makes us strangers to him. — V. Christ’s enemies have been destroyed through his grace.

## CHAPTER I

The Gospel reading, dearly beloved, which has opened the most sacred history of the Lord’s passion, is so well known to the whole Church through frequent common hearing that each of you recalls the sequence of events as though it had been placed before your eyes.

Those who do not doubt what they have heard are not to be judged to have made little progress, even if they are not yet able clearly to grasp some mystery of the Scriptures. At least they firmly believe that there is no falsehood in the divine books [some manuscripts read “letters”].

Since the fullness of understanding has been promised to sincere faith, let the vigor of enlightened minds raise itself toward deserving the instruction of the Holy Spirit. Let no one be content merely to know the sequence of events unless he also examines the very reason for the devotion expended on his behalf, so that human nature may love its Creator more by knowing how greatly it has been loved by him.

God had no reason to take pity on us except his own goodness [the Vatican manuscript of collection 5 reads “his mercy”]. The second generation of human beings is more wondrous than the first condition [that is, creation, as is clear from what follows], because in the final ages God’s restoration of what had perished is greater than his creation, at the beginning, of what did not exist.

Therefore the freedom of natural innocence, which we lost through the transgression of our first parents, was recovered through no preceding merits of the saints. The sentence passed upon transgressors bound the whole offspring of captive posterity, and no one existed free from condemnation, because no one was free from crime.

But the Redeemer’s destruction of the devil’s work and breaking of the bonds of sin arranged the mystery of his great mercy in such a way that, although the predetermined fullness of generations would continue until the consummation of the world, the renewal of our origin through justification by undivided faith would extend to all the ages that had passed.

For the incarnation of the Word, and Christ’s killing and resurrection, became the salvation of all the faithful; and the blood of the one just man gave us this gift. We believe that it was poured out for the reconciliation of the world, and that it bestowed upon the fathers what they likewise believed would be poured out.

**Note:** We have emended this corrupt passage with the aid of two manuscripts of St. Peter and one of Bologna. The first edition and Quesnellus read: “the blood of the one just man, whom the Father gave us, whom we believe was poured out for the reconciliation of the world; this he bestowed upon the fathers,” and so on. Other editions have the same reading, except that they read *quia eum* (“because he…”) instead of *qui eum* (“who…”).

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, dearly beloved, nothing in the Christian religion is different from the ancient signs, nor was salvation ever hoped for by the earlier righteous from anyone except the Lord Jesus Christ. The arrangements varied according to the reason of the divine will, but the testimonies of the Law, the prophetic oracles, and the offerings of sacrifices all flashed toward the same reality.

For it was fitting that those peoples should be instructed in such a way that, since they could not grasp what had been revealed, they might receive it under a veil; and that the authority of the Gospel might be greater because the pages of the Old Testament had served it with so many signs and mysteries. Concerning these things the Lord declared that he had not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. 5:17).

Therefore let the Jew not imagine that it benefits him to linger carnally on the surface of the letter, while he is convicted of resisting those Scriptures that among us possess their true dignity, since we are instructed by what was foretold and enriched by what has been fulfilled.

For the Lord says: “When I am lifted up, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). Nothing of the legal institutions and nothing of the prophetic figures remained that did not wholly pass over into the mysteries of Christ.

With us is the seal of circumcision, the sanctification of anointings [some editions and manuscripts improperly read “of gifts of grace”], the consecration of priests; with us are the purity of sacrifice, the truth of baptism, and the honor of the temple. Properly, therefore, the messengers ceased when the things announced arrived; yet reverence for the promises is not emptied, because the fullness of grace has been revealed.

But because, as the Apostle says, “a partial blindness has happened to Israel,” and “not all who are children of the flesh are children of the promise” (Rom. 11:25; 9:8), the ineffable mercy of God made an Israelite people for himself from all nations. Having softened that stony hardness of the Gentiles’ hearts [the word “hearts” is absent from the first edition], he raised up true children for Abraham from stones (Matt. 3:9).

Thus, since all who were born according to the flesh were enclosed under sin (Rom. 11:32), they are reborn in spirit, and it makes no difference from what father each person was born, since through the undivided confession of one faith the baptismal font makes them innocent and the election of adoption confirms them as heirs.

## CHAPTER III

For what else does the cross of Christ do and accomplish than that, once hostilities have been destroyed, the world may be reconciled to God and all things may be restored to true peace through the sacrifice of the immolated Lamb?

But the person who dissents from the profession he made at his regeneration does not agree with God. Forgetful of the divine covenant, he is shown to cling to what he renounced and is found to recoil from what he believed.

In vain does he assume the Christian name, and he must not imagine that he celebrates the Lord’s Passover at all if he does not believe that Jesus Christ rose in the flesh in which he was born, suffered, died, and was buried, and if he does not confess that the firstfruits of our nature were raised in him [one Vatican manuscript of collection 5 reads “our firstfruits, raised in him”].

The true worshiper of the Lord’s passion should therefore look upon the crucified Jesus with the eyes of the heart in such a way as to recognize that his flesh is his own. Let earthly substance tremble at the punishment of its Redeemer; let the rocks of unbelieving minds be split; and let those who were weighed down by the tombs of mortality leap forth when the mass of their obstacles has been scattered.

Even now let the signs of the future resurrection appear in the holy city—that is, in the Church of God—and let what must be accomplished in bodies take place in hearts. No weak person has been denied the victory of the cross, nor is there anyone whom Christ’s prayer does not aid.

If that prayer benefited many who raged against him, how much more does it help those who turn toward him? Ignorance has been removed, difficulty has been moderated, and the sacred blood of Christ has extinguished the fiery sword by which the region of life was enclosed [possibly “shut off”; Quesnellus supplies this reading in the margin].

The darkness of the ancient night has yielded to the true light. The Christian people are invited to the riches of paradise, and for all who have been reborn the return to the lost homeland has been opened—provided that no one closes for himself the way that the faith of the thief was able to open.

## CHAPTER IV
Therefore, as we celebrate, dearly beloved, the ineffable mystery of the paschal feast, let us acknowledge—with the Spirit of God as our teacher—to what participation in glory we have been called and into what hope we have entered. Let not the activities of the present life occupy us, now anxiously and now arrogantly, in such a way that we do not strive with the whole affection of our heart to be conformed to our Redeemer through his examples. [Note: [Col. 0367D] In the same manuscript, perhaps better, *per ipsius* (“through his own”) instead of *per illius* (“through that one's”).] [Note: [Col. 0367D] In Vatican Manuscript Collection 5, the preposition *ad* is omitted here. Shortly afterward, the first edition has *sumus* (“we are”) instead of *simus* (“let us be”).]

For he did and endured everything for our salvation, so that the power which was in the Head might also be in the body. For, first of all, whom did that very assumption of our substance [Col. 0367B] into the Godhead—by which the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14)—leave outside the fellowship of his mercy, except one who was unbelieving? And who does not share a nature with Christ if he has received the one who assumed human nature, and has been regenerated by the Spirit by whom Christ was begotten? [Note: [Col. 0367D] Thus, better, from the Saint Peter manuscripts in the past tense, as the following words seem to require: *est regeneratus* (“has been regenerated”); this must be referred to the reception of Christ through faith, which indeed precedes regeneration through baptism. The Vulgate has *recipit* (“receives”).] [Note: [Col. 0367D] We shall examine the meaning of this passage and two marginal notes by Quesnellus in the observations.]

Next, who does not recognize his own weaknesses in him? Who does not see that the taking of food, the need for sleep, the anxiety of sorrow, and the tears of compassion belonged to the form of a servant? Since that nature had to be healed of ancient wounds and cleansed from the filth of sin, the Only-Begotten Son of God also became the son of man, in such a way that he lacked neither the whole truth of humanity nor the fullness of divinity. [Note: [Col. 0367D] We have restored *omni* (“the whole”), which Quesnellus omitted, from all our manuscripts and the earlier editions.]

Thus, just as what the mother’s virginity brought forth in union with the Godhead is ours [Note: [Col. 0368D] In certain editions and in Manuscript Collection 5, *unitione* (“union”)], so what Jewish impiety crucified is ours. [Col. 0367C] Ours is what lay lifeless in the tomb [Note: [Col. 0368D] We have added “in the tomb” from two manuscripts of Saint Peter], and what rose on the third day; ours is what ascended above all the heights of heaven to the right hand of the Father’s majesty. Thus, if we walk along the path of his commandments, and if we are not ashamed to confess what, in the humility of our bodily condition, contributes to our salvation, we too shall be raised to share in his glory; for plainly what he announced will be fulfilled:

“Everyone who acknowledges me before human beings, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32).

## CHAPTER V

The grace of God attends and assists this exhortation of ours. It has destroyed the enemies of Christ’s incarnation, death, and resurrection by the truth revealed throughout all the churches, so that the faithful [Col. 0367D] of the whole world, united with the authority of the apostolic faith, might rejoice with us in a single exultation. [Col. 0368A] Blessed Paul the Apostle says:

“Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death [Note: [Col. 0368D] The editions read: “with him through baptism into death.” We have followed the reading of two Saint Peter manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts.], so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also share in his resurrection. We know this: that our old self was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with him” (Romans 6:3–8)—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXVII [also LXV]

On the Passion of the Lord XVI; delivered on Sunday.

[Col. 0368B]

### SYNOPSIS

I. How greatly contemplation of God’s benefits profits us, whose prediction establishes faith.  
II. That Christ’s passion was decreed by God’s plan in such a way that neither God himself is the author of the crime nor the Jews are excusable.  
III. That even Christ’s executioners were not excluded from the gift of redemption.  
IV. How detestable was the crime of Judas, and how great the punishment of his crime.  
V. That Christ, through voluntary death, provided both a remedy and an example.  
VI. That Christ’s death removes every opportunity for both pride and negligence, and that the commandments cannot be fulfilled except through him.  
VII. That Christ, speaking in the person of his members, said: “Why have you forsaken me?”

## CHAPTER I

Always, dearly beloved, the minds of the faithful ought to dwell in admiration of God’s works, and rational hearts ought especially to cling to those thoughts through which they may attain an increase of faith. For when the attention of a devout heart is directed [Note: [Col. 0368D] Thus from two Saint Peter manuscripts. Elsewhere, *pia* (“devout”).] either toward general benefits or toward the particular gifts of grace itself, it drives many vanities away from itself [Note: [Col. 0368D] The Corbie manuscript of Quesnellus has *varietates* (“variations”)], and withdraws from bodily concerns into a kind of spiritual solitude.

But at this season of the Lord’s Passion this must be done with far greater eagerness and excellence, so that what has been recorded in the sacred readings may be received through the hearing with sound understanding, and what is great in words may appear greater still in its mysteries. The first reason for lifting our hearts upward is [Note: [Col. 0368D] The first edition has: “that even those things which…”] that what the evangelical truth has recounted, the prophetic voices sang not as things still to be done, but as things already done. What human ears did not yet know was to be done, the Holy Spirit was already proclaiming as accomplished. [Note: [Col. 0368D] We have added “Holy” from the first edition and several other editions preceding Rainaudus and Quesnellus, as well as from most of our manuscripts.]

For King David, whose descendant according to the flesh is Christ, preceded the day of the Lord’s cross [Note: [Col. 0368D] Here the pontiff follows the chronology of Eusebius. The authors of the Roman Martyrology also followed it, on 25 December. Whoever desires a more accurate computation should consult the more recent chronologists: Dionysius Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time* and *In the Rationarium*; James Ussher; and others, including an anonymous writer at the end of the Bibles published by Antonio Vitré, Paris, 1662. According to his calculation, only 1,050 years are counted from David’s death to the death of our Lord Jesus Christ, and 1,090 from the beginning of David’s reign. Quesnellus. — More probably, however, Leo used Prosper’s *Chronicle*, as we shall show in the observations on Sermon 76. Prosper expressly praises and follows Eusebius in the present matter. Shortly afterward, in some manuscripts, one reads: “the history of the Lord’s cross, who,” etc.], by an age of more than a thousand and one hundred years [Col. 0369A], and suffered none of the punishments which he records as inflicted upon himself. But because the One who was to assume passible flesh from his line was speaking through his mouth, the history of the cross is rightly prefaced in his person—he who bore in himself the bodily origin of the Savior. Truly, David suffered in Christ, because truly Jesus was crucified in the flesh in David.

## CHAPTER II

Since, then, everything that Jewish impiety committed against the Lord of majesty had been foretold so long beforehand [Note: [Col. 0369D] The first edition, together with Manuscript Collections 3 and 4, has *in Christo* (“in Christ”), rather than *in Dominum majestatis* (“against the Lord of majesty”); other editions before Quesnellus, together with Manuscript Collection 5, have *in Christum* (“against Christ”). The reading in the text, introduced by Quesnellus, is supported by the manuscript of Saint Peter. Shortly afterward, the first edition and a manuscript of Saint Peter have *praedicata* (“proclaimed”) instead of *praedicta* (“foretold”).], and the prophetic discourse is concerned not so much with future events as with past events [Note: [Col. 0369D] The editions had: “so that it concerns not so much future things as present ones.” The reading of the Saint Peter manuscript seemed preferable. From the context Leo appears to mean that the prophecies did not merely foretell certain things about Christ as future, but also spoke of certain things as past—for example, when David sang, “They pierced my hands and my feet,” etc. Although expressed in the past tense, these words do not fit David but Christ, as the author noted in the preceding chapter: David suffered none of the punishments which he records as inflicted upon himself. But … truly David suffered in Christ, because truly Jesus was crucified in the flesh in David. Moreover, in this chapter he adds: “It was rightly decided that those things be recalled as though they had happened” (note the past tense), which could in no way fail to happen.], what else is disclosed to us than the unchangeable order of God’s eternal purposes, before whom things that must be distinguished have already been judged, and things that will happen are already accomplished?

Since divine knowledge anticipates both the qualities of our actions and the effects of all our wills [Col. 0369B], how much more are God’s own works known to him? And it was rightly decided that those things be recalled as though they had happened, which could in no way fail to happen.

Therefore the Apostles, filled with the Spirit of God, when they were suffering the threats and fury of Christ’s enemies, said to God with one accord [Note: [Col. 0370D] Thus our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus; he has *unanimi* (“unanimous”).]:

“For truly, in this city, against your holy child Jesus, whom you anointed, Herod [Note: [Col. 0370D] The first edition and the Bologna manuscript have *viri* (“men”). The adjective *sanctum* (“holy”), introduced by Quesnellus, is supported by two Saint Peter lectionaries.] and Pontius Pilate, together with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered to do whatever your hand and your plan had decreed should happen” (Acts 4:27–28).

Did the wickedness of those persecuting Christ arise from God’s plan [Note: [Col. 0370D] Perhaps: “and armed them for the crime.” Quesnellus in the margin], and did divine preparation arm that deed which surpasses every crime? We certainly must not think this about supreme justice, because what was foreknown in the malignity of the Jews is very different and very contrary to what was ordained in Christ’s Passion. The will to kill did not proceed from the same source as the willingness to die; nor did the atrocity of the crime and the Redeemer’s endurance arise from one spirit. The Lord did not thrust the impious hands of the raging against himself, but he permitted them; and although he foreknew what had to be done, he did not compel it to happen, even though he had assumed flesh precisely so that it might happen.

## CHAPTER III

Finally, the causes of the crucified and of those crucifying are so different that what Christ undertook cannot be undone, whereas what they committed can be abolished. For he who came to save sinners (Matthew 9:13) did not deny mercy even to his own executioners, but changed the evil of the wicked into the good of believers. Thus the grace of God, mercifully prepared not according to human merits but according to the abundance of God’s wisdom and knowledge, became more wondrous, since the baptismal water received even those who had shed the Savior’s blood.

For, as the Scripture containing the Acts of the Apostles relates, when the preaching of blessed Peter the Apostle pierced the hearts of the Jews and, acknowledging the wickedness of their crime, they said, “What shall we do, brothers?”, the same Apostle replied:

“Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, everyone whom the Lord our God will call.”

Then the Scripture immediately adds and says:

“So those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand persons were added on that day” (Acts 2:37–41). [Note: [Col. 0370D] Quesnellus omitted *vobis* (“for you”), a word found both in the Greek and in the Vulgate text; we have restored it from our manuscripts and the other editions, which moreover add *facta* (“made”) after *enim* (“for”).]

Thus, although the Lord Jesus Christ willed to suffer the rage of those who raged against him, he was in no respect the author of their crimes. He did not cause them to wish these things, but yielded so that they might be able to do them. And he made use of the madness of the blinded crowd just as he did of the treachery of the betrayer, whom he graciously sought to recall from the monstrous crime he had conceived, both by benefits and by words: taking him as a disciple, advancing him as an apostle, admonishing him through signs, and consecrating him through mysteries [Col. 0370C] [Note: [Col. 0370D] The first edition has *movendo* (“moving”)]. Thus, nothing that could have encouraged correction was lacking for him, and nothing that could provide an occasion for crime remained.

## CHAPTER IV

But you, most impious man, seed of Canaan and not of Judah (Daniel 13:56), no longer a vessel of election but a son of perdition and death, believed the devil’s promptings more useful to you. [Note: [Col. 0370D] Two manuscripts of Saint Peter have: “so that, more easily inflamed by avarice…”] Inflamed by the torches of greed, you burned for the profit of thirty pieces of silver and did not see what riches you were losing. [Col. 0371A]

Even if you did not think the promises worthy of belief, what reason was there for preferring such a tiny sum of money to what you had already received? [Note: [Col. 0371D] Editions before Quesnellus and several later collection manuscripts omit *non* (“not”); it is read in two manuscripts of Saint Peter.] You commanded demons, healed the sick, were honored together with the Apostles, and, to satisfy the hunger of your greed, thefts from the purses lay open to you. But a soul greedy for what was forbidden was provoked still further by what was less permitted; and the magnitude of the sin pleased you more than the amount of the price. [Note: [Col. 0371D] Thus, with Quesnellus, the better manuscripts. Others have *admonitum* (“having been admonished”).]

Therefore your commercial crime is not detestable merely because you valued the Lord so cheaply, but because you sold even your own Redeemer, so that you would not spare yourself. And deservedly your punishment was entrusted to you, because no one more savage than yourself could be found for your torment.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, when Jesus Christ was crucified, died, and was buried at the appointed time according to the purpose of his will [Col. 0371B], this was not the necessity of his own condition but the redemption of our captivity. For this reason the Word became flesh: so that a passible nature might be taken from the Virgin’s womb, and what could not be inflicted upon the Son of God might be permitted against the son of man. [Note: [Col. 0371D] The Vulgate editions preceding Quesnellus have *non potuit* (“could not”) instead of *non poterat* (“could not” in the imperfect tense).]

For although signs of divinity shone in him from the very moment of his birth, and all the stages of bodily growth were filled with divine miracles, he had nevertheless assumed the reality of our weaknesses. Except for sharing in sin, he had excluded nothing of human weakness from himself, so that he might bring his own qualities to us [Note: [Col. 0371D] Thus from two manuscripts of Saint Peter. Others have *insereret* (“might insert”).], and heal ours in himself. For the almighty Physician prepared a twofold remedy for us wretched people: one part of it lies in the sacrament, the other in the example; through the one divine gifts are bestowed, through the other human duties are required [Col. 0371C]. [Note: [Col. 0372D] Thus Quesnellus, with his manuscripts and ours. Other editions have *erigantur* (“may be raised up”).] For just as God is the author of justification, so the human being is the debtor of devotion.

## CHAPTER VI

Through this ineffable restoration of our salvation, dearly beloved, no place is left for pride or negligence. For we have nothing except what we have received [Col. 0372A], and we are continually admonished not to hold the gifts of God’s grace carelessly (1 Timothy 4:14). Rightly does he press us with a command who goes before us with help, and kindly urges us to obedience who leads us to glory.

Therefore the Lord himself rightly became our way (John 14:6), because no one comes to Christ except through Christ. Through him, and toward him, advances the one who walks along the path of his patience and humility. On this road there is plainly neither a lack of the heat of toil, nor of the clouds of sorrow, nor of the storm of fear. There are the ambushes of the wicked, the persecutions of unbelievers, the threats of the powerful, and the insults of the proud. The Lord of hosts and King of glory (Psalm 23:10) passed through all these in the form of our weakness and in the likeness of sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript Collections 4 and 5 have *percurrit* (“he traversed”)], so that amid the dangers of the present life it should be less our desire to escape these by avoiding them than to overcome them by enduring them.

## CHAPTER VII

For this reason our Head, the Lord Jesus Christ, transforming all the members of his body into himself, cried out in the voice of his redeemed what he had formerly poured forth in the psalm during the suffering of the cross:

“God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:1)

This utterance, dearly beloved, is instruction, not complaint. For since Christ is one person of God and man, and could not be forsaken by the One from whom he could not be separated, he asks on behalf of us who are fearful and weak why the flesh, afraid to suffer, was not heard.

As his Passion drew near, in order to heal and correct our fear of weakness, he had said:

“Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.”

And again:

“Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done” (Matthew 26:39, 42).

Once the fear of the flesh had therefore been overcome, he had already passed into the Father’s will, and, having trampled down the whole terror of death, was completing the work ordained by him. Why, then, in the very triumph of such a victory, does he inquire into the cause and reason for which he was forsaken [Note: [Col. 0372D] Manuscript Collection 5 has: “why he was”], that is, not heard, unless to show that one was the feeling he assumed to excuse human fear, and another was the feeling he chose from the Father’s eternal purpose for the reconciliation of the world? [Note: [Col. 0372D] Quesnellus, without identifying any manuscript, printed “from the Father’s eternal plan.” We have restored the reading of the earlier editions, which all our manuscripts exhibit.]

Therefore the very voice of one not heard is a great exposition of the mystery [Note: [Col. 0372D] In one manuscript of Saint Peter: “great is the exposition of the mystery, because nothing…”]: the Redeemer’s power would have conferred nothing upon the human race if our weakness had obtained what it requested.

These things, dearly beloved, are sufficient for today, lest we burden you with the length of our sermon. Let us defer the rest until the fourth day of the week. The Lord will be present to your prayers, so that, by his giving, we may fulfill what we promise to expound, he who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXVIII [also LXVI]

On the Passion of the Lord XVII; delivered on Wednesday.

### SYNOPSIS

I. That the divinity inseparable from Christ could not have forsaken him.  
II. That Christ’s voluntary death for the salvation of the world is demonstrated by his cry, and could not be prevented by the voices of blasphemers.  
III. That Christ, disregarding blasphemies, offered his sacrifice, signifying it also by the tearing of the veil.  
IV. That the devil never ceases to lie in wait. The usefulness of the Lenten fast.

## CHAPTER I

The preceding sermon, dearly beloved, whose promised portion we desire to restore to you, had advanced in its argument to the point of discussing the voice of the crucified Lord crying out to the Father, so that a simple and inattentive hearer might not understand the words of the speaker—“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:1)—as though, when Jesus was fixed to the wood of the cross, the omnipotence of the Father’s divinity had withdrawn from him. The nature of God and man had come together in such unity that it could be divided neither by punishment nor separated by death.

For, while each substance remained in its own proper character, God did not abandon the suffering of his body, nor did flesh make God passible [Note: [Col. 0373D] The Vercelli manuscript has *a carne* (“by the flesh”).], because the divinity that was in the one who suffered was not itself in suffering. Therefore, according to the person of the Word and man, the same one is he who was made among all things and through whom all things were made. The same one is he who is seized by the hands of the impious and cannot be confined by any limit. The same one is he who is pierced by nails [Note: [Col. 0373D] Thus the same manuscript and two manuscripts of Saint Peter. Others have *configitur* (“is fastened”). Shortly afterward, where the text reads “wounded by no wound,” several of our better and more numerous manuscripts, as well as earlier editions, have “by no pain,” together with Manuscript Collection 5.] and who is wounded by no wound. Finally, the same one is he who underwent death and did not cease to be eternal, so that both truths might be made manifest by unmistakable signs: that there is true humility in Christ [Col. 0373B] [Note: [Col. 0373D] Quesnellus has *humanitas* (“humanity”), as does our Vercelli manuscript. We have restored the reading of the earlier editions on the authority of two manuscripts of Saint Peter and two Vatican manuscripts, not only because Leo frequently uses *humilitas* (“humility”) for *humanitas*, but also because here it is more suitably set against *majestas*, which signifies divinity.], and true majesty. For divine power joined itself to human weakness for this reason: that, while God made what is ours his own, he might make what is his ours. [Note: [Col. 0373D] The Vercelli manuscript has: “what are not his own.”]

The Son, therefore, was not absent from the Father, nor the Father from the Son; and that unchangeable divinity and inseparable Trinity could not have anything of itself separated from itself. Although the dispensation of the assumed incarnation properly belonged to the Only-Begotten Son of God, the Father was nevertheless not separated from the Son, just as flesh was not divided from the Word.

## CHAPTER II

For this reason Jesus cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Why have you forsaken me?”—so that he might make known to everyone [Note: [Col. 0373D] Thus, better, from two Saint Peter manuscripts, two Vatican manuscripts, and one Venetian manuscript. Elsewhere: “why it was necessary.”] why it was necessary for him not to be rescued or defended, but to be abandoned to the hands of those raging against him: namely, that he might become the Savior of the world and the Redeemer of all human beings—not through misery but through mercy, and not through the loss of assistance but through the determination to die.

What interruption of life [Note: [Col. 0373D] Perhaps *intercisio* (“cutting off”). Quesnellus in the margin.], however, can be understood there where the soul was both released by power and recalled by power? Blessed Paul the Apostle says that the Father “did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32) [Note: [Col. 0373D] The words *suo proprio* (“his own”) have been added from two manuscripts of Saint Peter and one Vercelli manuscript]. And again he says: “Christ loved the Church and handed himself over for her, to sanctify her” (Ephesians 5:2, 26).

Therefore to hand the Lord over to suffering was as much the Father’s will as his own, so that not only did the Father forsake him, but he himself in a certain sense abandoned himself—not through fearful departure, but through voluntary surrender. For the power of the Crucified restrained itself from the impious, and, in order to employ a hidden plan, did not use its manifest power. He who had come through his suffering to destroy death and the author of death—how could he save sinners if he resisted his persecutors?

It was therefore the Jews’ belief, dearly beloved, that Jesus had been forsaken by God, so that they could rage against him with such a great crime [Note: [Col. 0374D] *Quia* (“because”) was preferred to *qui* (“who”) on the authority of the Saint Peter manuscripts. Shortly afterward, instead of *patientiae* (“patience”), the first edition and one Vatican manuscript have *potentiae* (“power”).]. [Note: [Col. 0373D] Quesnellus has *fuerit* (“had been”); we restored the reading of the earlier editions, which is found in most of our manuscripts.] Ignorant of the mystery of wondrous patience, they said with sacrilegious mockery:

“He saved others; he cannot save himself. If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matthew 27:42).

It was not according to the judgment of your blindness, foolish scribes and impious priests, that the Savior’s power was to be displayed; nor according to the wicked tongues of blasphemers was the redemption of the human race to be interrupted [Note: [Col. 0374D] In many manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus: “nor according to the prayers of blaspheming tongues.” The reading inserted by him into the text is found in the Vercelli manuscript, from which we supplied the word *pravas* (“wicked”). From the same manuscript, instead of *omitti* (“be omitted”), which appeared in the editions, we supplied *intermitti* (“be interrupted”); for likewise in Sermon 52, chapter 4, “lest the triumph of the glorious cross, being delayed,” where the delay of this triumph corresponds to interruption. The Venetian manuscript has *peccatrices* (“sinful”) instead of *pravas*.].

If you had wished to acknowledge the Son’s divinity [Col. 0374B] [Note: [Col. 0374D] The word *Dei* (“of God”) has been restored from the first edition, two manuscripts of Saint Peter, and one of Bologna. Shortly afterward, the first edition has *confirmare debuerunt* (“ought to have confirmed”)], you would have seen his countless works, which ought to have confirmed you in that faith you falsely profess. But if, as you yourselves admit, it is true that “he saved others,” why did the many and great miracles performed in public view soften your hard hearts in no respect, unless because you have always resisted the Holy Spirit in such a way that you turned all God’s benefits to your destruction? For even if Christ had come down from the cross, you would nevertheless have remained in your crime.

## CHAPTER III

The insults of vain mockery were therefore disregarded, and no abuse or reproach could divert the Lord’s mercy, which was repairing what had been lost and fallen, from the path of its purpose. A unique sacrifice was being offered to God for the salvation of the world, and the slaying of Christ, the true Lamb, proclaimed through so many ages, was transferring the children of the promise into the freedom of faith. The New Testament was also being confirmed, and heirs of the eternal kingdom were being written in Christ’s blood.

The High Priest was entering the Holy of Holies, and the immaculate Priest was entering to make God favorable through the veil of his flesh (Hebrews 9:16 and following). Finally, the transfer from the Law to the Gospel, from the Synagogue to the Church, and from many sacrifices to one sacrifice [Note: [Col. 0374D] After “to one sacrifice,” the Vulgate adds “which is God.” Since these words are absent from the manuscript codices, we judged them to be an addition. Quesnellus. — They are also absent from many of our manuscripts.] was then so evident that, when the Lord released his Spirit, that mystical veil which by its obstruction enclosed the temple’s inner chambers and sacred mystery was suddenly torn by force from top to bottom. [Col. 0375A] For reality was removing the figures [Note: [Col. 0375D] We have restored the conjunction *et* (“and”), with the punctuation altered by Quesnellus, from our manuscripts and the earlier editions], and messengers were superfluous in the presence of the One who had been announced.

To these things was added the dreadful convulsion of all the elements (Matthew 27:51), and the very operations of nature withdrew from the authors of Christ’s crucifixion. When the centurion guarding the execution, terrified by what he had seen, said, “Truly this man was the Son of God” (ibid., 54), no compunction is reported to have softened the Jewish impiety, harder than all monuments and stones. Thus it appears that the Roman soldiers were then more ready to understand the Son of God than the Israelite priests.

## CHAPTER IV

Because the Jews, deprived of the sanctification of all the mysteries, turned their light into darkness and their festivals into mourning, let us, dearly beloved, adore the grace of God poured out over all the nations with bodies and souls prostrate [Note: [Col. 0375D] Editions before Quesnellus have *proclivibus* (“inclined”). In the margin of some copies is *prociduis* (“prostrate”)], entreating the merciful Father and the rich Redeemer that, aided by his help day after day, we may be able to escape all the dangers of this life.

For the crafty tempter is everywhere present and leaves nothing free from his snares. With the mercy of God assisting us—a mercy extended to us amid all adversities—we must always resist him with steadfast faith, so that, although he never ceases to attack, he may find no one whom he can overcome.

May the fasts celebrated with devotion, dearly beloved, benefit everyone, and may the usefulness of self-restraint, which we have found suitable both for souls and bodies, not be corrupted by any excesses. For practices belonging to sobriety and moderation have been observed more diligently during these days for this reason: that they might be transferred from a brief exercise into a lasting habit. Whether in works of mercy or in the practice of moderation, let the faithful have no time left empty, since, as the days advance and the seasons run their course, we ought to gain a profit in good works, not suffer a loss of merits. [Note: [Col. 0375D] Thus all our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus, who has *in occursu* (“at the approach”), found in none of our manuscripts. Earlier, instead of *utique*, some manuscripts have *ita* (“thus”).]

To devout practices and religious minds the mercy of God will be present, so that what he caused us to desire he may cause us to obtain—he who lives and reigns with our Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, and with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXIX [also LXVII]

On the Passion of the Lord XVIII.

### SYNOPSIS

I. That the height of the mystery of the cross is ineffable. That its faith is as unified as unbelief is varied and uncertain.  
II. That the figures ceased because the truth has shone forth, although its faith has always been the same.  
III. That Christ, God and man, died voluntarily, and that the devil was deceived by his own cunning.  
IV. That, by killing Christ, the devil gave human beings the opportunity to be liberated and to achieve complete victory over death and sin.  
V. That the devil’s snares must be carefully avoided, so that, having been crucified with Christ through mortification, we may be crowned in him.

## CHAPTER I

The greatness of the ineffable mystery, dearly beloved, surpasses the height of human understanding and the capacity of every form of eloquence, so that the triumph of the Lord’s Passion is loftier than even the most excellent intellects and the most eloquent tongues. We ought rather to rejoice than be ashamed that we are surpassed by the dignity of so great a subject; for no one has judged more humbly about it than the one who thought that what he said was sufficient [Note: [Col. 0375D] Thus Quesnellus, with the first edition and our manuscripts of the best quality. Others have *non suffecisse* (“had not been sufficient”). Shortly afterward, “what we have proclaimed,” supplied by Quesnellus, is found in the first edition and our manuscripts.].

Therefore we do not proclaim what we have proclaimed without purpose, nor should the distaste of bodily ears be feared by one speaking of divine matters, as though such things would be despised because they are often repeated. For this belongs especially to the solidity of Christian faith: that, according to apostolic teaching, we should all say the same thing and be perfect in the same understanding and in the same knowledge (1 Corinthians 1:10). [Note: [Col. 0375D] The first edition has *praedicemus* (“let us proclaim”). The Vercelli manuscript omits *omnes* (“all”). Shortly afterward, instead of *scientia* (“knowledge”), some have *sententia* (“understanding”).]

Unbelief, which is the mother of all errors, is divided among many opinions, which it must use the art of speech to color. [Note: [Col. 0376D] The Vercelli manuscript has *habet* (“has”) instead of *habeat* (“may have”).] But the testimony of truth never departs from its own light. If it shines less for some and more for others, this is caused not by a variation in the light but by weakness of contemplation.

According to the assistance of heavenly illumination, that light must also be served by my speech, so that, since you are God’s cultivation and God’s building (1 Corinthians 3:9), he himself may grant sufficiency both to the one administering and to the one receiving—the one who knows how to demand a just return on his gifts.

## CHAPTER II

Having completed, therefore, the text of the Gospel reading, which you heard with attentive ears concerning the glory of Christ’s cross, understand that all the mysteries of the divine utterances have been disclosed to you [Note: [Col. 0376D] The first edition, together with the Bologna manuscript and two manuscripts of Saint Peter, has “the words of the divine mysteries.” Earlier, in the same edition and the Vercelli manuscript, we find *nobis* (“to us”) instead of *vobis* (“to you”).], and rejoice that whatever the shadow of the Old Testament concealed beneath prophetic testimonies has been made manifest in the mystery of the Lord’s Passion.

For this reason the varieties of sacrifices [Note: [Col. 0376D] The same edition and the Vercelli manuscript have *varietas* (“variety”) in the singular] and the distinctions among purifications ceased; for this reason the commandment of circumcision, the distinction of foods, the rest of the Sabbath, and the slaughter of the paschal lamb ceased, because “the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).

The figures came beforehand so that the realities might follow, and when the announced events arrived, the duties of the messengers came to an end. Thus, through the reconciliation of the human race, salvation—which is in Christ—was ordered in such a way that it has been lacking in no age under the same justification. The delay itself served this purpose: that what had long been believed before it happened might be honored without hesitation. [Note: [Col. 0376D] We have restored the reading of all the editions before Quesnellus, supported by our better manuscripts. Quesnellus has: “might honor things unquestionably accomplished.” We could find the noun *facta* (“accomplished things”) in no manuscript.]

For since the power of faith is established in things not subject to sight (Hebrews 11:1), heavenly teaching dealt more gently with us, whom it postponed to these latter times of the world, so that, for ease of understanding, we might have the use of far more prophets and witnesses than those who came before us. [Note: [Col. 0377C] Before Quesnellus, the editions, together with the manuscripts of the later collections, had: “postponed us to the capacity of understanding, so that, with many more …” Quesnellus, without indicating this, emended the text to the reading found in the manuscripts of Saint Peter and Vercelli. Shortly afterward, instead of *uteremur* (“we might use”), the first edition and the Bologna manuscript have *urgeremur* (“we might be pressed”).]

## CHAPTER III
Therefore accept without a cloud of hesitation what the sacred Gospels, written by the finger of God, testify to us concerning the passion of the Lord Jesus Christ; and regard the sequence of events as clearly established as if you had touched everything bodily, with sight and touch. [Note: Col. 0377D, Codex Vercellensis: “as though you had touched everything . . .”] Let true divinity and true humanity be believed to exist in Christ. He is himself flesh who is the Word; and just as he is of one substance with the Father, so he is of one nature with his mother. [Note: Col. 0377D: Another reading, “not diminished.” Quesnellus placed it in the margin.] He is not two persons, nor is his essence confused; impassible in power, mortal in humility; but he employed both in such a way that power could glorify weakness, and weakness could not obscure power. [Note: Col. 0377D: We do not understand why Quesnellus rejected this quite satisfactory reading of all the earlier editions and of our manuscripts, and relegated it to the margin in order to substitute “but employing each in such a way”; no manuscript is indicated for the latter reading, which is not equally satisfactory.] He permits himself to be seized by persecutors, although he contains the world; he is bound by the hands of those whose hearts cannot contain him. [Note: Col. 0377D: This is the reading of most and better manuscripts, and of editions earlier than Quesnellus; Quesnellus preferred “by the persecutors.”] Justice does not resist the unjust, and truth yields to testimonies of falsehood, so that, while remaining in the form of God, he might fulfill the form of a servant and confirm the reality of bodily birth through the savagery of bodily suffering.

But for the Only-Begotten Son of God to undergo and endure this was not imposed by necessity; it was the plan of mercy: so that, by condemning sin through sin (Rom. 8:3), the work of the devil might be undone through the devil’s own work. For the enemy of the human race had inflicted at its very origin a deadly wound upon the whole race destined for death, and its captive offspring could not escape the iron law of a seed delivered into bondage. [Note: Col. 0377D: Thus two manuscripts of Saint Peter and Codex Vercellensis; the Vulgate reads “having been put to death.” Shortly afterward Codex Vercellensis has “condemned” for “delivered into bondage.”] When, therefore, among so many generations subject to the mortal law, he saw one among the sons of men whose virtues he marvelled to see surpassing all the saints of every age, he believed himself secure in the perpetuity of his own dominion, if no merits of righteousness could overcome the laws of death. [Note: Cols. 0377D–0378C: The preposition “in” is absent from three of our manuscripts of no slight authority. Two Saint Peter manuscripts read “of mortals” for “mortal,” and Codex Vercellensis “foresaw” for “saw.” Two Saint Peter manuscripts and Codex Vercellensis read “power” for “virtues.” Editions with manuscripts of Collections 3 and 4 read: “if no merits of fierce righteousness could overcome the power of death”; Vatican manuscript, Collection 5, omits “fierce”; Saint Peter lectionaries read: “if no merits of its own righteousness could by themselves overcome the power of death.” We judged the Vercelli reading more Leonine and therefore inserted it into the text.]

Accordingly, having violently incited his servants and hirelings, he raged to his own injury; and, while supposing that he had some claim upon one whom he had been able to kill, he did not recognize the freedom of unique innocence, because he pursued the likeness of nature. Yet he was not mistaken about the kind of being involved; he was deceived by the crime. [Note: Col. 0377D: The reading is based on two Saint Peter manuscripts and Codex Vercellensis. The Vulgate has “having been put to death”; shortly afterward Codex Vercellensis reads “condemned” for “delivered into bondage.”]

For the first Adam and the second Adam were one in flesh, but not in deed: “in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22). The former made his way to misery through the desire of pride; the latter prepared a way to glory through the strength of humility. Hence he himself says: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): the way, namely, in the form of righteous conduct; the truth, in expectation of a certain reality; the life, in the attainment of eternal happiness. [Note: Col. 0378D: Perhaps “of hope”; Quesnellus in the margin.]

## CHAPTER IV

Beloved, both Jewish impiety and diabolical pride were ignorant of this sacrament of great piety. For if they had known it, “they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). [Note: Col. 0378D: Earlier editions, with manuscripts of the three later collections, read “of glory.”] But because the plan of God’s mercy was hidden from the enemy of the human race, and God, reconciling the world to himself in Christ, was concealed beneath the opposing veil of flesh (2 Cor. 5:19), the enemy persisted in raging against the one in whom he could find nothing belonging to him. [Note: Col. 0378D: The homily of Paul the Deacon reads “of the dispensation” for “of the eternal disposition.”] Indeed, it would have benefited his wickedness more if he had spared him and refrained from shedding his blood, through which the captivity of all was to be dissolved and freedom restored. [Note: Col. 0378D: In the first edition and in Codex Bononiensis: “if he spared him, through whom,” with the intervening words omitted.]

But “the darkness did not comprehend the light” (John 1:5), and lying blindness could not behold the wisdom of truth. Meekness therefore maintained the patience it had prepared, and, restraining the power of the angelic legions serving him, he drank the cup of suffering and death, and transformed the whole punishment into triumph.
