[Note: Col. 0378D: Two Saint Peter manuscripts more correctly read “prepared”; another reading is “arranged.”] Errors were conquered, powers subdued, and the world received a new beginning, so that the condemned birth might not harm those whom rebirth would assist in saving. “The old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17). [Note: Col. 0378D: “Behold” is restored from all editions before Quesnellus and from the better manuscripts.] For all who believe in Christ and are reborn in the Holy Spirit have, through him and with him, a common participation in suffering and an eternity of resurrection, as the Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3).

## CHAPTER V

Established, then, in this hope, beloved, beware of all the devil’s cunning. He lies in wait not only through the desires of the flesh, nor merely through bodily enticements, but also by scattering weeds of falsehood among the very seeds of faith; he strives to violate the cultivation of truth, so that those whom he cannot corrupt through evil deeds he may overthrow through impious errors. [Note: Col. 0379D: This reading is found in all the manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus, who has “wiles.” Those same editions, together with many manuscripts, read “and he lies in wait only through bodily enticements.”]

Flee, therefore, the arguments of worldly teaching, and avoid the serpent-like conversations of heretics. Let nothing be shared between you and those who oppose the Catholic faith and are Christians in name only. They are neither the temple of the Spirit of God [Note: “Spirit” is absent in Codex Vercellensis] nor members of Christ; but, entangled in false opinions, they have as many forms of the devil as there are images of falsehood.

Freed from these evils by the Lord Jesus Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6), let us endure all the temptations and all the battles of this life with the exultation of faith. [Note: Col. 0379D: “All” has been added on the authority of Saint Peter manuscripts.] “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:12).

This reward is prepared not only for those who have been slain by the savagery of the ungodly for the name of the Lord. For the whole company of those who serve God and live for God, just as it has been crucified in Christ, so also is to be crowned in Christ: foremost in every glory are those who, by enduring dreadful deaths and savage torments to the point of breathing out their spirit, have overcome them; but following them are those who have conquered the desire for avarice, the exaltation of pride, and the cravings of lust by putting their own flesh to death.

Hence the Apostle rightly says that “all who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). No one is outside this persecution who is not estranged from piety. For he fittingly celebrates the Paschal solemnity who acts “not in the leaven of the old malice, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5:8). [Note: Col. 0379D: Codex Vercellensis reads “fittingly celebrates the solemnity.”] He no longer lives in the first Adam, but in the second Adam, having become a member of the body of Christ. Although Christ was in the form of God, he graciously became the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6), so that in the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), there might be both the fullness of divine majesty and the reality of human nature.

Unless the divinity of the Word had assumed it into the unity of his own person, there would be neither rebirth in the water of baptism nor redemption in the blood of the passion. [Note: Col. 0379D: Earlier editions, with some manuscripts, read: “unless the divinity of the Word had received it into the unity of its own person”; in the margin, for “received,” they note the alternative “had assumed.”] But because in the sacrament of Christ’s incarnation we have received nothing false and nothing figurative, we do not without reason believe that we have died with him who died and been raised with him who rose again, while he himself remains in us, working all things in all (1 Cor. 12:6), living and reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. [Note: Col. 0379D: Four of our manuscripts read “having died with” (*commortuos*) for “dead with.”] Amen.

# SERMON LXX [Another numbering: LXVIII]

## On the Passion of the Lord XIX

### SYNOPSIS

I. How true faith makes the passion of Christ present to us, although the mind of the Crucified and the deed of those who crucified him are utterly different.—II. How Christ made use of the Jews’ wickedness so that by his death he might offer the true Passover, through which even the killers themselves might be saved.—III. How the wisdom of the world is confounded in the mystery of the cross, in which both Christ’s power and his weakness save us.—IV. How the cross must continually be borne, so that what was accomplished sacramentally in baptism may be completed in action.—V. How the Lord’s passion is brought to completion until the end of the world through the mortification of his members. The devil’s hostility must be preferred to his friendship.—VI. How the mortification of our vices is Christ’s power and victory.

## CHAPTER I

Beloved, I think that the sacred history of the Lord’s passion, narrated in the customary Gospel reading, has so taken root in all your hearts that for each listener the reading itself became a kind of vision. True faith possesses this power: it is mentally present at those events in which bodily presence could not take part; and whether the heart of the believer returns to the past or extends itself into the future, knowledge of the truth feels no delay of time.

Thus an image of the events accomplished for our salvation is present to our senses, and whatever then touched the minds of the disciples also touches our affections. [Note: Cols. 0379D–0380D: Through faith, that is, we are mentally present at the events enacted in Christ’s passion, although we were not bodily present at them. Two manuscripts of Saint Peter read “your faith” instead of “true faith.”]

It is not that we are weighed down by sorrow or terrified by the savagery of the raging Jews, since the resurrection and ascension of the Lord raised even those whom the magnitude of that upheaval had shaken to unconquered steadfastness. But when we consider what the people of Jerusalem and what the priests were like at that time, let us receive the enormity of the ungodly deed with great trembling of mind.

[Note: Col. 0379D: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter read: “For the fact that we are either depressed by sadness or terrified by the fury of the raging Jews is somewhat lessened, since the resurrection and ascension of the Lord raised even those whom the magnitude of that storm had shaken to unconquered steadfastness. But because the thought arises of what the people of Jerusalem and the priests were like at that time, we receive with great trembling of mind so great a crime of the ungodly.” The copy of Paul the Deacon gives the reading of the text. It has only “the fury of the raging Jews” instead of “the savagery of the furious Jews.”]

Although the Savior’s passion belonged to the salvation of the human race, and the bonds of eternal death were broken by the Lord’s temporal death, the patience of the Crucified accomplished one thing and the madness of those who crucified him another; mercy and anger were not directed toward the same ends, even though Christ, by the shedding of the same blood, set the world free from captivity. [Note: Col. 0381D: The same copy of Paul the Deacon reads “and the Jews.”] The Jews killed the Redeemer of all.

## CHAPTER II

Their wickedness hardened carnal Israel, and neither the testimony of the Law, nor the images of its mysteries, nor the oracles of the prophets profited it, when John taught that the Passover of the Lord, celebrated throughout so many ages, had been fulfilled in the one of whom he publicly testified: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold, he who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). [Note: Col. 0381D: A Vatican manuscript of Collection 5 reads “sin.”]

Iniquity resists righteousness, blindness resists light, and falsehood resists truth. Yet from the savagery of those who opposed him and the crime of the cruel, Jesus obtained the result of the eternal plan; and he so provided for the human race by his death that he did not deny the sacrament of salvation even to his persecutors. [Note: Col. 0381D: Earlier editions read *enim* (“for”) instead of *igitur* (“therefore”); one Saint Peter manuscript and other Vatican manuscripts also read “therefore.”]

He who had come to forgive all sins to all believers did not wish to exclude the Jewish crime from the universal pardon. We detest their unbelief, but if they should convert, we embrace their faith. Imitating the Lord’s mercy—he prayed for those by whom he was crucified—we too join our prayers to those of the blessed Apostle Paul, and we desire that that people may obtain mercy, on account of whose offense we received the grace of reconciliation. For, as the same teacher of the nations says, “God has imprisoned all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32). [Note: Col. 0381D: The first edition reads, “we pray and desire.” The word “same” was added from the homily of Paul the Deacon.]

## CHAPTER III

What was it that robbed the Jews of understanding and disturbed the hearts of the world’s wise, if not the cross of the Son of God, which caused philosophical wisdom to vanish and made Israel’s teaching stumble? [Note: Col. 0381D: Earlier editions read: “and caused the philosophy of the wise to vanish,” together with some manuscripts. But the reading accepted by Quesnellus and by us from other manuscripts has a more Leonine character.]

The height of the divine plan exceeded every capacity of the human mind, when it pleased God “through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe” (1 Cor. 1:21), so that the steadfastness of faith might become more marvelous because of the difficulty of believing. It seemed inconsistent and irrational to accept in one’s mind that the undefiled Virgin had borne in the substance of true humanity the Creator of all natures; that the Son of God, equal to the Father, who fills all things and contains the universe, could be seized by the hands of the furious, condemned by the judgment of the wicked, and, after the disgrace of mockeries, permit himself to be fastened to a cross. [Note: Col. 0381D: The copy of Paul the Deacon reads “the Creator of all creatures.” The first edition soon afterward reads “he who fills all things and contains the universe”; and after “the disgrace of mockeries” it adds further words.]

Yet in all these things there are at once the humility of humanity and the height of divinity. The plan of mercy does not obscure the majesty of the one showing mercy, because it was accomplished through ineffable power: while the true human being is in the inviolable God, and the true God is in suffering flesh, glory was bestowed on humanity through dishonor, incorruption through punishment, and life through death. [Note: Cols. 0381D–0382D: This reading is taken from two manuscripts of Saint Peter and from the homily of Paul the Deacon. Other copies read, “so that, since the true human being is in God …”; but Quesnellus omits the word “is” here.]

Unless the Word became flesh, and the union in both natures were so solid that the short interval of death could not separate the one assumed from the one assuming him, mortality could never return to eternity. [Note: Col. 0382D: Saint Peter manuscripts and another Vatican manuscript read “existed” for “stood.”] But in Christ there was a unique protection for us: the condition of death did not remain in the passible nature that the impassible essence had received, and through what could not die, what had died could be raised.

## CHAPTER IV

Beloved, to conform inseparably to this sacrament, we must strive with great concentration of mind and body. For although it is a very grave offense to neglect the Paschal feast, it is more dangerous to join the ecclesiastical assemblies while not being included in the fellowship of the Lord’s passion. [Note: Col. 0382D: The first edition reads “of danger,” perhaps more correctly, since “more dangerously” follows shortly afterward.]

The Lord says: “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:38); and the Apostle says: “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:12). [Note: Col. 0382D: Two Saint Peter manuscripts read “we shall be glorified together.”] Who truly honors Christ who suffered, died, and was raised, except the one who suffers, dies, and rises with him? [Note: Col. 0382D: The conjunction “and” was added from an ancient Vatican manuscript. The first edition omits it both here and in the second clause.]

These things have already been begun in all the children of the Church through the mystery of rebirth itself: there the death of sin is the life of the one being reborn, and the threefold immersion imitates the Lord’s three-day death. As though the mound of a tomb had been removed, the waters of baptism bring forth as new those whom the font’s ancient hollow received. Nevertheless, what has been celebrated sacramentally must also be fulfilled in action; and whatever remains of the worldly bodily life of those born of the Holy Spirit must be lived not without taking up the cross. [Note: Col. 0382D: This reading is taken from two manuscripts of Saint Peter and another Vatican manuscript. The editions read “of worldly time.” The words refer to “body,” which occurs shortly afterward: “so that the dominion of the prince of the world may be cast out from the bodies of the redeemed.” It is therefore unnecessary to read “hearts” instead of “bodies,” as Quesnellus conjectured in a marginal note.]

Although through the power of Christ’s cross the vessels of the ancient plunder were snatched from the strong and cruel tyrant, and the dominion of the prince of the world was expelled from the bodies of the redeemed, that same wickedness nevertheless persists in lying in wait even for those who have been justified; and it attacks in many ways those over whom it does not reign. Thus, if it finds any souls careless and unwary, it entangles them again in more savage snares and, snatching them from the paradise of the Church, leads them into fellowship with its own condemnation.

Therefore, whenever anyone senses that he is exceeding the limits of Christian discipline [Note: Col. 0382D: Earlier editions read “the boundary,”] and directing his desires toward what makes him stray from the right path, [Note: Col. 0382D: This is the reading with Quesnellus in our manuscripts; another reading is “to turn aside.”] let him return to the cross of the Lord and fasten the movement of his harmful will to the tree of life; let him cry aloud to the Lord with the prophetic voice and say: “Pierce my flesh with nails from fear of you; for I have feared your judgments” (Ps. 118:120). [Note: Col. 0383C: This reading is found with Quesnellus in the manuscripts of Saint Peter and the copy of Paul the Deacon. Another reading is “with your fear.”]

## CHAPTER V

What does it mean to have the flesh fastened with the nails of the fear of God, except to restrain bodily senses from the enticement of unlawful desire under fear of divine judgment? Whoever resists sin and kills his desires so that he may do nothing worthy of death can dare to say with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14).

Let the Christian place himself where Christ took him with himself, and direct his whole way toward the place where he knows that human nature has been saved. [Note: Col. 0383C: Two Saint Peter manuscripts read “his whole life.”] For the Lord’s passion is prolonged until the end of the world. Just as he himself is honored in his saints, loved in them, fed and clothed in the poor, so he himself suffers with all who endure adversity for the sake of righteousness. [Note: Col. 0383C: The words “he himself is honored,” omitted by a typographical error, as we believe, in both of Quesnellus’s editions, are restored from all the other editions and all the manuscripts.]

Surely it must not be supposed that, as faith has multiplied throughout the world and the number of the ungodly has diminished, all persecutions and all the conflicts that raged against the blessed martyrs have ended, as though only those upon whom the most atrocious torments were inflicted to destroy their love of Christ had been required to take up the cross.

But those who serve God experience one thing, and the preaching of the Apostle also declares another: “All who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3:12). [Note: Col. 0383D: The copy of Paul the Deacon reads “will suffer.”] Certainly, no one who is not estranged from piety is exempt from this persecution. Anyone whom no persecution disturbs is shown by this saying to be exceedingly lukewarm and sluggish. For only lovers of the world can have peace with the world; never is there fellowship between iniquity and righteousness, concord between falsehood and truth, or agreement between darkness and light.

Even if the piety of the good desires that the wicked be corrected and, through the grace of the merciful God, obtains the conversion of many, the snares of malignant spirits against the saints do not cease. [Note: Col. 0383D: The first edition reads “of the wicked.”] Whether by hidden deceit or open battle, they assail the purpose of good will in all the faithful. Everything upright is their enemy, and everything holy. [Note: Col. 0383D: This reading has been corrected from two Saint Peter manuscripts and one Vatican manuscript; another reads “whatever is chaste.”]

Although they are permitted to do nothing against anyone beyond what divine justice allows—justice that deigns either to correct its own through discipline or to exercise them through endurance—they nevertheless act with the most cunning art of deception, so that by the arbitrary exercise of their own power they may seem either to harm or to spare. And, lamentably, they mock many through the wickedness of pretense in such a way that some fear having them hostile and desire to have them appeased. [Note: Col. 0383D: Earlier editions read “indeed, corruptly.”] Yet the benefits of demons are more harmful to everyone than wounds, because it is safer for a human being to have earned the devil’s enmity than his peace.

Thus wise souls, who have learned to fear one, love one, and hope in one Lord, with their desires put to death and the senses of their bodies crucified, bend neither to the fear of any enemy nor to any compliance. They place the will of God even before themselves, and love themselves more greatly in proportion as they love themselves less for God’s sake.

When they hear the divine command: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will” (Ecclus. 18:30), they divide their affections and distinguish the law of the mind from the law of the body. [Note: Col. 0384C: Another reading is “tear apart.” Shortly afterward the words “which they love carnally” occur in the homily of Paul the Deacon.] Thus they deny themselves to themselves in one respect, losing themselves in what they desire carnally and finding themselves in what they desire spiritually.

## CHAPTER VI

Beloved, Holy Pascha is rightly celebrated in such members of the body of Christ, and they lack none of the triumphs that the Savior’s passion obtained. For in those who, following the Apostle’s example, discipline their bodies and bring them into subjection (1 Cor. 9:27), the same enemies are crushed with the same courage, and now the world is conquered by Christ. [Note: Col. 0384C: Editions before Quesnellus read: “For even now the world is conquered by Christ, and when it is conquered by his servants.” Quesnellus and the first edition read: “for now indeed the world is conquered by Christ, and when it is conquered by his servants.” The copy of Paul the Deacon gives the sounder reading.]

Whenever the impulses of whatever vices are overcome by his servants, it is his power and his victory. [Note: Col. 0384D: Quesnellus reads “his own victory as well.” We have preferred the reading of our manuscripts and the other editions.]

Beloved, what has been said today has, I think, sufficiently brought to your ears those matters that concern participation in the cross, so that the Paschal sacrament may also be rightly celebrated in the members of the body of Christ. It remains for us to discuss obtaining fellowship in the resurrection. But lest a continuous discourse become burdensome both to me and to you, we shall postpone what was promised until the Sabbath day. [Note: Col. 0384D: One Saint Peter manuscript reads “we postpone what was promised until the fourth day of the week,” but this is erroneous, as the following admonition makes clear.] We trust that the grace of God will be present, so that with his help our obligation may be fulfilled—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

# ADMONITION CONCERNING THE TWO FOLLOWING SERMONS

## 1

We first present Quesnellus’s complete admonition. He says:

“The two sermons that follow are entitled ‘On the Resurrection of the Lord’ in all printed copies; but I am led by weighty considerations to regard it as certain that they were delivered not on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection but on Holy Saturday.

“First, since Easter Day was extremely occupied, it could scarcely have offered an opportunity for a sermon. The vigils, prolonged until late at night, comprised the entire service that is now performed throughout Holy Saturday morning. Then the catechumens were washed in the sacred font, anointed, and instructed in their proper teachings. Finally, the sacred mysteries were celebrated, occupying a large part of the morning hours.

“Second, this first sermon is the very one that he had promised in the preceding sermon in these words: ‘It remains for us to discuss obtaining fellowship in the resurrection; but lest a continuous discourse become burdensome both to me and to you, we shall postpone what was promised until the Sabbath day.’ It was therefore delivered on Holy Saturday. The observance of forty days had already elapsed, as is clear from the first chapter, and we are taught from the very beginning that it followed immediately upon the preceding sermon.

“Third, the sequence of both sermons makes it clear that the pontiff scarcely touches upon the mystery of the resurrection except with his lips, but devotes almost the whole discourse to explaining participation in the cross and death of Christ. Thus whatever it says about the resurrection appears to have been spoken beforehand, and because of the proximity of the feast.

“Fourth, it is clear from Sermon 2 that on the very day on which it was delivered the whole history of the Lord’s passion and resurrection was read in the Church from the Gospel accounts. This reading fits Holy Saturday extremely well, since that day, standing between the two mysteries as a kind of midpoint, belongs to both. The solemnity of the resurrection and the lengthy ceremonies of that day could scarcely have admitted such a reading, and still less could the priest’s exhortation have been added to the most sacred solemnity of the reading, as Saint Leo says.

“Fifth, Hincmar of Reims, in Book 1 of *On Predestination*, chapter 33, Sirmond’s edition, page 280, citing part of chapter 4 of the earlier sermon, quotes it in this manner: ‘Likewise, in the homily of Holy Saturday.’ And in Florus of Lyon, the same two sermons, which we later possessed under the titles 1 and 2 ‘On the Resurrection,’ are Sermons 10 and 11 ‘On the Passion of the Lord.’ He says this in the commentaries that he composed and arranged on all the Epistles of Saint Paul from excerpts from the writings of the holy Fathers, Augustine excepted, whom he excerpted in a volume of his own. That work, consisting of twelve books, Peter Francis Chifflet had once presented as a gift to the Reverend Father Dom Luca Acher, of blessed memory and very dear to me, and to me, having obtained it from a manuscript of the Grande Chartreuse; it was intended eventually to be published.

“Sixth, from Book 7, chapter 19, of Sozomen’s *History*, we learn that in the Roman Church neither the bishop nor anyone else delivered a sermon to the people on the first day of the Paschal solemnity. When I was preparing the first edition, I had not yet grasped the genuine meaning of this passage; the reader will find it explained according to the author’s intention, if I am not mistaken, in my first dissertation, chapter 12.

“Although these matters stand thus, we have thought that nothing should be altered in the titles or numbering of the sermons, lest this cause difficulty for readers accustomed to the earlier numbering.”

Thus far Paschasius Quesnellus. Although he judged the thesis he proposed very well, certain matters nevertheless require correction or addition.

## 2

If he had seen or examined the first edition of the sermons of Saint Leo, or the other editions subsequently reprinted from it, he would certainly not have written at the beginning of his admonition that these two sermons were entitled “On the Resurrection of the Lord” in all printed copies. For in the table prefixed to those editions, which gives the titles of the sermons, the first sermon, like the eight preceding ones, is given the title “Sermon 20: On the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord”; while the second is indeed entitled “On the Resurrection of the Lord,” but is included in the same numerical sequence as the sermons on the Passion and is called Sermon 21.

Moreover, both sermons are listed in the lectionaries of the Basilica of Saint Peter not only under the title “On the Passion of the Lord,” but are also found interspersed among the other sermons under that title, rather than placed at the end. Thus there can be no doubt that the title “On the Resurrection” was not perhaps omitted through the negligence of copyists.

They are likewise read in the manuscripts of Collection 2 mixed together with the sermons on the Passion. The same happens, though in a different order, in the manuscript of the Casinensian Collection 1, as well as in two manuscript lectionaries, Venetian 153 and Vallicellian II. In the former, only the first sermon is inserted among the sermons on the Passion; in the latter, only the second is so inserted. In the manuscripts of Collection 5, which follows another order, both sermons are similarly written under the title “On the Passion of the Lord.”

The copy used by Florus of Lyon, which cites our first and second sermons “On the Resurrection” as Sermons 10 and 11 “On the Passion of the Lord,” was similar to the lectionaries of the Basilica of Saint Peter, in which they are numbered among the sermons on the Passion with those same numbers.

## 3

We have no doubt, from the evidence proposed by Quesnellus in sections 2 and 5, that these sermons were delivered on Holy Saturday. If Hincmar of Reims, in *On Predestination*, chapter 33, cited the first sermon—which the holy pontiff in chapter 6 of the preceding sermon had postponed until the Sabbath—in this manner, “Likewise, in the homily of Holy Saturday,” then the second sermon is similarly entitled in the Vatican manuscript lectionary 4951: “Sermon of Blessed Pope Leo on Holy Saturday.” The same title is reported as having been found in another very ancient manuscript by the writer of the Barberini manuscript 3520.

That they were delivered during the Paschal vigils, when the office of the resurrection follows the commemoration of the Lord’s passion, is beyond doubt; for both mysteries are mentioned in these sermons.

## 3

Quesnellus asserts in section 4 that the history of the Lord’s passion and resurrection was read in the Church on this Saturday. He inferred this from Sermon 2 “On the Resurrection,” delivered on Holy Saturday, whose first chapter states that the text of the divinely inspired history clearly showed how the Lord Jesus Christ was handed over through impiety, condemned by judgment, crucified through savagery, and raised in glory.

These words do indeed indicate that both the history of the passion and the history of the resurrection were read from the Gospel. But they do not so clearly assign the reading of both mysteries to Holy Saturday itself that they cannot instead be understood as referring to the reading of the passion on the preceding day, that is, Good Friday, and the reading of the resurrection that followed on Holy Saturday night during the Paschal vigils.

Perhaps Quesnellus believed that the words of the cited chapter, which follow shortly afterward—“Let the office of exhortation follow the most sacred solemnity of the reading”—signified not so much that the resurrection reading as that the passion reading had preceded the sermon on that same Saturday. Yet this is not entirely certain.

No ancient orders and no capitula designate this Gospel reading for that day. But since these documents are later, it could have happened that this rite was in use in Leo’s time, just as it was in use among the Greeks, at least in the Church of Antioch, as is clear from Homily 87 on Matthew, delivered by Saint John Chrysostom at Antioch, where he states that the history of the passion was publicly read during the great Paschal evening.

Quesnellus’s argument in section 4 is therefore less decisive.

## 5

Likewise, the first argument—that Easter Day was so occupied—does not prove the point at all. Just as it cannot establish the exclusion from Easter Day of the sermons of Saints Augustine, Peter Chrysologus, Gregory the Great, and other bishops, which certainly were delivered at Easter, so it cannot be used to remove Leo’s sermons from that day.

Sozomen’s testimony cited by Quesnellus in section 6 is even less compelling, as will become clear from what we shall note about Sozomen’s meaning in the first dissertation of Quesnellus, chapter 12.

We have accepted and confirmed as sufficiently effective for establishing Holy Saturday only the evidence cited by Quesnellus in sections 2 and 5; yet it is clear that the following sermons were recited not during the day of Saturday itself but during the night of that day, when the office of the resurrection began at the Paschal vigils. Consequently, Quesnellus’s third argument is also undermined, since he maintains that the resurrection was mentioned beforehand.

# 281 SERMON LXXI [Another numbering: LXIX]

## On the Resurrection of the Lord I; delivered on Holy Saturday during the Paschal vigils

### SYNOPSIS

I.

I. Care must be taken lest the fruit of fasting be rendered void, so that those who have died with Christ may also rise with him. [Col. 0386A]

II. The day of the burial was shortened for the sake of the disciples.

III. Christ proved his resurrection by many arguments.

IV. What transformation took place in Christ’s flesh through the resurrection.

V. The Christian must despise earthly things and cling in mind to heavenly things.

VI. Care must be taken lest anyone return to the pleasure of sin after the Paschal feast.

## CHAPTER I

In my previous sermon, beloved, I believe that I appropriately suggested to you participation in Christ’s cross, so that the life of believers might itself contain the Paschal mystery, and so that what is honored by the feast might be celebrated in our conduct. [Note: The first edition reads *quantum autem* (“but how much”). Shortly afterward, that same edition, together with two Vatican manuscripts, reads: “you have learned from your own testing.”] You yourselves have proved how useful this is, and from your devotion you have learned how much longer fasts, more frequent prayers, and more generous almsgiving benefit both souls and bodies. For scarcely anyone has failed to make progress through this discipline or to store away, in the hidden chamber of conscience, something in which he may rightly rejoice.

But these gains must be guarded with persevering vigilance, lest, when labor has been relaxed into indolence, the envy of the devil steal away what the grace of God has bestowed. Since, therefore, by observing forty days we wished to accomplish this—that we might experience something of the cross during the time of the Lord’s Passion—we must strive also to be found sharers in Christ’s resurrection and, while we are in this body, to pass from death to life.

For every human being who is changed from one state into another by some transformation has as his end no longer to be what he was, and as his beginning to be what he was not. But it matters to whom one dies or for whom one lives, because there is a death that is the cause of life, and there is a life that is the cause of death. Neither is obtained anywhere except in this transitory world; [Note: This reading, found in two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s, is better than that of the printed editions and other manuscripts, which read *ut qualitate ... pendeant* (“so that they may depend upon quality”).] and the differences among eternal recompenses depend upon the character of temporal actions.

We must therefore die to the devil and live to God; we must cease from iniquity, so that we may rise again to righteousness. Let old things fall, so that new things may arise. And since, as the Truth says, “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24; Luke 16:13), let our master be not the one who struck down those who were standing into ruin, but the one who raised the fallen into glory.

## CHAPTER II

The Apostle says:

> “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so also are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so also are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:47, 49).

We ought to rejoice greatly over this transformation, by which, through the ineffable mercy of the one who descended into our condition in order to raise us into his own, we are transferred from earthly lowliness to heavenly dignity. He assumed not only the substance but also the condition of sinful nature, and divine impassibility allowed to be inflicted upon itself what human mortality experiences in utter misery.

Therefore, lest the disciples’ troubled minds be tortured by prolonged sorrow, he shortened the announced delay of three days with such wondrous speed that, while the last part of the first day and the first part of the third converged upon the whole of the second day, so that a certain amount of time fell short of the interval, nothing was lost from the number of days. [Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s read *spatium* (“a period” or “interval”).]

Thus the Savior’s resurrection neither left his soul long in the underworld nor his flesh long in the tomb; [Note: The Cologne edition of 1547 adds in the margin: “allowed [it] to remain.”] and the quickening of incorruptible flesh was so swift that there was more likeness to sleep than to death, because the Godhead, which did not withdraw from either substance of the humanity it had assumed, reunited by its power what it had divided by its power.

## CHAPTER III

Many proofs followed, by which the authority of the faith to be proclaimed throughout the whole world was established. Although the rolling away of the stone, the emptying of the tomb, the laying aside of the linen cloths, and the angels’ recounting of the entire event fully supported the truth of the Lord’s resurrection, he nevertheless appeared visibly to the women and frequently to the apostles (Acts 1:3): not only speaking with them, but also dwelling and eating with them, and allowing himself to be handled with careful and inquisitive touch by those whom doubt had troubled. [Note: We have supplied the particle *etiam* (“also”) from all our manuscripts.]

For this reason he entered to the disciples even when the doors were shut (John 20:19), gave them the Holy Spirit by his breath, and, having bestowed the light of understanding, opened the hidden meanings of the Holy Scriptures (Luke 24:27). Again he displayed the same wound in his side, the marks of the nails, and all the most recent signs of his Passion (John 20:27), so that it might be recognized that the individual identity of the divine and human nature remained undivided in him. Thus we might know that the Word is not the same as flesh, while confessing one Son of God, both Word and flesh.

## CHAPTER IV

The Apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations, does not disagree with this faith when he says: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16). For the Lord’s resurrection was not the end of the flesh but its transformation, nor was the substance consumed by an increase of power. Its condition changed; its nature did not fail. The body that could be crucified became impassible; what could be killed became immortal; what could be wounded became incorruptible.

And rightly is Christ’s flesh said to be unknown in the condition in which it had been known, because nothing passible, nothing weak, remained in it, so that it is itself in essence but is no longer itself in glory. But why should it be surprising if he makes this confession concerning Christ’s body, when he says concerning all spiritual Christians: “Therefore, from now on, we know no one according to the flesh” (2 Corinthians 5:16)? From this, he says, the beginning of our resurrection in Christ was made: from the time when, in the one who died for all, the pattern of all our hope went before us.

We do not hesitate through disbelief, nor are we suspended in uncertain expectation; but, having received the beginning of the promise, we already see with the eyes of faith what is to come, and, rejoicing in the advancement of nature, we already possess what we believe.

## CHAPTER V

Therefore, let not the appearances of temporal things occupy us, nor let earthly things turn our contemplation away from heavenly things. Let what has passed be regarded as already gone, for the greater part no longer exists; and let the mind intent upon what endures fix its desire there, where what is offered is eternal.

Although we have been saved in hope and still bear corruptible and mortal flesh, we are rightly said not to be in the flesh if carnal desires do not rule us; and rightly do we lay aside the designation of that whose will we do not follow. When the Apostle says, “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:14), we do not understand him to forbid those things that accord with health and that human weakness requires. But since we must not serve every desire, nor fulfill whatever the flesh covets, we recognize that we have been warned to apply the measure of temperance, so that we neither grant excesses to the flesh, which has been placed under the judgment of the mind, nor deny it necessities.

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “No one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Ephesians 5:29). It must, of course, be nourished and cherished not for vices or luxury, but for the service owed to it, so that renewed nature may preserve its proper order; neither may lower things perversely and shamefully prevail over higher things, nor higher things succumb to lower ones, so that, when vices have conquered the mind, servitude exists where mastery ought to be.

## CHAPTER VI

Let the people of God therefore recognize that they are a new creation in Christ, and let them vigilantly understand from whom they have been received and whom they have received. Let those things that have been made new not return to unstable oldness. Let the one who has put his hand to the plow not abandon his work (Luke 9:62), but attend to what he is sowing and not look back at what he has left behind.

Let no one fall back into the condition from which he arose. Even if, through bodily weakness, he still lies in certain ailments, let him earnestly desire to be healed and lifted up. This is the way of salvation and the imitation of the resurrection begun in Christ: since the slippery course of this life is full of various misfortunes and falls, the footsteps of those who walk must be transferred from unstable ground to solid ground. For, as it is written, “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he will delight in his way. When the righteous man falls, he will not be shattered, because the Lord will support his hand” (Psalm 36:23). [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, collections 4 and 5, read “will be directed.”]

This meditation, beloved, must be retained not merely for the Paschal solemnity but for the sanctification of the whole of life. The present discipline must be directed toward this end: that the things which, through the experience of a brief observance, have delighted the minds of the faithful may pass into habit and remain undefiled; and, if some fault has crept in, may be erased by swift repentance.

Since the treatment of old diseases is difficult and slow, remedies should be applied all the more quickly as the wounds are more recent. Thus, always rising again in wholeness from every offense, may we be worthy to attain, in Christ Jesus our Lord, that incorruptible resurrection in which the flesh is to be glorified. [Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and Quesnellus in the margin read *pertinere* (“to pertain”) instead of *pervenire* (“to attain”).] He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXII [Another numbering: LXX]  
## On the Resurrection of the Lord II

### SYNOPSIS

I. Christ’s cross is both a sacrament and an example for us.

II. Our nature was assumed by the Word in the Incarnation so that he might pay it as the price.

III. Having died and risen with Christ, we are strengthened by Christ’s remaining with us on earth and invited to glory by his reign in heaven.

IV. Everywhere the power of the cross and its example are present to us, so that we may be armed against desires.

V. We must strive toward heavenly things by despising earthly things, while preserving faith in both natures in Christ.

VI. Through Christ’s passage—which exists only in our nature—a passage to heavenly things is prepared for us.

VII. The Eutychians are excluded from the Paschal feast because they deny our nature in Christ.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0390B]

[Note: Editions before Quesnellus, with manuscripts of collections 2, 3, and 4, read *Notum* (“known”), and the margin has *Totum* (“the whole”). But the lectionaries we have seen and manuscripts of collections 1 and 5 prefer the reading inserted by Quesnellus and adopted by us.]

The entire Paschal mystery, beloved, has been presented to us by the Gospel narrative, and the hearing of the mind has been penetrated through the ear of the flesh, so that none of us has lacked an image of the events. The text of the divinely inspired history clearly showed with what impiety the Lord Jesus Christ was handed over, by what judgment he was condemned, with what cruelty he was crucified, and with what glory he was raised.

The ministry of our sermon must also be added, so that, just as I perceive that you demand the due of custom with pious expectation, [Note: Thus, with Quesnellus, the manuscripts of Saint Peter’s. Other editions read “to request.”] the priest’s exhortation may be joined to the reading of the most sacred solemnity.

Since, therefore, among the faithful there is no room for ears of ignorance, the seed of the word, which is contained in the preaching of the Gospel, must grow in the soil of your heart, so that, when the choking thorns and briars have been removed, the plantings of holy thoughts may freely bear their fruits and the shoots of upright wills may flourish. [Note: The manuscripts of Saint Peter’s read “the sharp points of thorns.”]

For Christ’s cross, which was expended for mortals who were to be saved, is both a sacrament and an example: a sacrament by which divine power is fulfilled, and an example by which human devotion is stirred. For redemption, having freed us from the yoke of captivity, grants this also: that imitation may follow it. [Note: One manuscript reads “provided this.”]

For if worldly wisdom so glories in its errors that each person follows the opinions, conduct, and every institution of the guide he has chosen for himself, what fellowship will the name of Christ have with us unless we are inseparably united to him who, as he himself taught, is “the Way, and the Truth, and the Life” (John 14:6)? The Way, that is, of holy conduct; the Truth, of divine doctrine; and the Life, of everlasting blessedness.

## CHAPTER II

When the fullness of the human race had fallen in our first parents, merciful God willed to assist the creature made in his image through his only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, so that the restoration of nature would not be outside nature, and so that the second condition might advance beyond the dignity of its original creation. Happy would he be if he did not fall away from what God made him; happier still if he remained in what God remade him. [Note: Manuscripts of collection 5 read “if he were not cast down.” Shortly afterward, some manuscripts together with the editions before Quesnellus read *maneret* (“might remain”) instead of *maneat* (“may remain”).]

It was a great thing to have received form from Christ, but it is greater to possess substance in Christ. That nature assumed us as its own—which bends itself into whatever measures of kindness it wishes, yet nowhere undergoes the alteration of mutability. That nature assumed us—which would consume neither its own nature in ours nor ours in its own; which made in itself one person of Godhead and humanity, so that, under the dispensation of weaknesses and powers, neither flesh could be inviolable through the Godhead nor the Godhead passible through the flesh. [Note: Manuscripts of collection 5 and the margins of the editions read *potestatem* (“power”) instead of *proprietatem* (“own possession”). The parenthetical words were absent from the editions before Quesnellus. He added them from the Thuane and Regius manuscripts, and we have found them in our eight manuscripts.]

That nature assumed us which neither severed the progeny of our race from the common course (*communi tramite*), [Note: One manuscript reads *a communi palmite*, “from the common vine.”] nor admitted the contagion of sin passing into all human beings. Weakness and mortality, which were not sin but the penalty of sin, were received by the Redeemer of the world for punishment, so that they might be offered as the price.

Therefore, what in all human beings was the transmission of condemnation is in Christ a sacrament of mercy. He presented himself to the most cruel exactor free from debt, and allowed the Jewish hands, the ministers of the devil, to inflict torture upon his spotless flesh.

For this reason he willed it to remain mortal until the resurrection, [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with quite a few manuscripts, add “the swiftest.”] so that for those who believe in him neither persecution might be insurmountable nor death terrifying, since there could be as little doubt about fellowship in glory as there was about communion in nature.

## CHAPTER III

If, therefore, beloved, we believe without hesitation in our heart what we confess with our mouth, we are crucified in Christ, we have died, we have been buried, and we have also been raised with him on the third day. Hence the Apostle says:

> “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Colossians 3:1–4).

So that the hearts of the faithful may know that they possess the means by which, after despising the desires of the world, they can rise to heavenly wisdom, [Note: The first edition reads “of sons” (*filiorum*) instead of “of the faithful” (*fidelium*).]  the Lord promises us his presence, saying:

> “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

For the Holy Spirit had not spoken through Isaiah without purpose:

> “Behold, a virgin shall receive in her womb and bear a son; and they shall call his name Emmanuel,”

which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 2:23). [Note: Thus, with Quesnellus, our better manuscripts. Others read “he shall be called.”]

Jesus therefore fulfills the meaning of his name. He who ascended into heaven does not abandon those whom he has adopted. He who sits at the right hand of the Father is himself the inhabitant of the whole body; and he who above invites us to glory himself strengthens us below for endurance. [Note: We have restored the word *idem* (“the same”) from our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus, which read *ipse* (“himself”). Only Vatican manuscript collection 5 has *is* (“he”). Shortly afterward, two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s read “toward repentance” instead of “toward endurance.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, we must neither lose our reason amid vanities nor tremble amid adversities. There, deceptions flatter; here, labors become heavy. But because “the earth is full of the mercy of the Lord” (Psalm 33:5), Christ’s victory is present to us everywhere, [Note: Six of our manuscripts of better quality, with Quesnellus, read *utique* (“indeed” or “certainly”).] so that what he says may be fulfilled: “Do not fear, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:33). Whether we fight against worldly ambition, the desires of the flesh, or the darts of heretics, let us always arm ourselves with the Lord’s cross. [Note: Vatican manuscript collection 5 reads “we are armed”; and “we never depart from the Paschal feast.” The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from Quesnellus’s manuscripts, from many of ours, and from the first edition; they are found, however, in several manuscripts of the best quality.]

For we never depart from the Paschal feast if we abstain from the leaven of former wickedness, in the sincerity of truth. [Note: The parenthetical phrase in the Latin text is editorially uncertain; it has been rendered according to the apparent sense.]

Amid all the variations of this life, which is full of different passions, we must remember the Apostle’s exhortation, by which he instructs us:

> “Have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus: who, although he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:5–11).

“If,” he says, “you understand the mystery of great godliness and perceive what the only-begotten Son of God accomplished for the salvation of the human race, have this mind among yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus.” His humility is to be despised by no wealthy person and is to be a source of shame to no noble person. For no human happiness can rise to such a height that it considers it shameful for itself that God, remaining in the form of God, did not regard it unworthy to assume the form of a servant. [Note: The editions, together with many manuscripts, had a corrupted and mutilated reading: “God, remaining God in the form of God, did not consider it unworthy.” The complete and correct reading was supplied by the manuscript Lectionary of Saint Peter’s. It refers to Saint Paul’s passage to the Philippians, chapter 2.]

## CHAPTER V

Imitate what he accomplished; love what he loved; and, finding God’s grace within yourselves, love your own nature anew in him. [Note: The editions, with different punctuation and wording, read: “and you will find God’s grace in yourselves. Love your nature anew in him, because …” We have followed our manuscripts.]

For just as he did not lose riches through poverty, did not diminish glory through humility, and did not lose eternity through death, so you too, by the same stages and in the same footsteps, must despise earthly things in order to grasp heavenly things. [Note: This is better supported by our manuscripts. The editions omit the conjunction in “by the same stages and footsteps.”]

Taking up the cross is the killing of desires, the slaying of vices, the avoidance of vanity, and the renunciation of every error. For although the Lord’s Pascha is not celebrated by an impure, lustful, or proud person, nor by a greedy person, no one is farther removed from this feast than heretics—especially those who think wrongly about the Incarnation of the Word, either diminishing what belongs to the Godhead or emptying what belongs to the flesh.

For the Son of God is true God, possessing entirely from the Father what the Father is: without any temporal beginning, unchangeable through any alteration; undivided from the One and not different from the Almighty; the eternal only-begotten Son of the eternal Begetter. Thus, when the faithful mind believes in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, it neither divides the unity of the one divine essence by degrees nor confounds the Trinity by singularity. [Note: Thus, with Quesnellus, two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s and two Vatican manuscripts. The other editions read “into the same essence of the one Godhead.”]

But it is not enough to know the Son of God only in the nature of the Father, unless we acknowledge him, without departing from what is proper to him, in what is ours. For that emptying which he devoted to the restoration of humanity was a dispensation of mercy, not a deprivation of power.

Since, according to the eternal counsel of God, no other name under heaven had been given to human beings by which they must be saved (Acts 4:12), he made his invisible substance visible, his timeless substance temporal, and his impassible substance passible—not so that power might fail in weakness, but so that weakness might pass into incorruptible power. [Note: The first edition omits “also.”]

## CHAPTER VI

For this reason the very feast which we call Pascha is called among the Hebrews *Phase*, that is, “passage,” as the Evangelist testifies when he says:

> “Before the feast of the Pascha, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, that he should pass from this world to the Father” (John 13:1).

[Note: The same edition reads “so that he might pass.”]

But of what nature was this passage to be, if not ours, since the Father was inseparably in the Son and the Son in the Father? But because the Word and the flesh are one person, the one who was assumed is not divided from the one who assumed him; and the honor of the one being raised is called an increase of the one who raises him.

The Apostle says, as we have already recalled:

> “Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

[Note: Thus, two Lectionaries of Saint Peter’s together with six other manuscripts. The editions read “and gave him.”]

In this, the exaltation of the assumed human being is clearly commended: he in whose sufferings the Godhead remains undivided is the same one who is coeternal in the glory of the Godhead.

The Lord himself was preparing this participation in an ineffable gift, this blessed passage, for his faithful when, already close to the imminent Passion, he prayed not only for his apostles and disciples but also for the whole Church, saying:

> “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us” (John 17:20–21).

[Note: Two manuscripts of Saint Peter’s read “when the approaching Passion was already imminent.”]

## CHAPTER VII

Those who deny that human nature remains in the Son of God, who is true God, can have no share in this unity. They are opponents of the sacrament that brings salvation and exiles from the Paschal feast. Since they dissent from the Gospel and contradict the Creed, they cannot celebrate with us.

Although they dare to assume the name Christian for themselves, they are nevertheless expelled from the whole creation of which Christ is the head. [Note: The same manuscripts and another Vatican manuscript, together with the first edition, read “yet from every nature to which Christ is head.”]

But you rightly rejoice and piously exult in this solemnity, because you receive no falsehood in the truth and do not doubt either Christ’s birth according to the flesh, his Passion and death, or his bodily resurrection. For without any separation of the Godhead, you acknowledge the true Christ from the Virgin’s womb, true on the wood of the cross, true in the tomb of the flesh, true in the glory of the resurrection, and true at the right hand of the Father’s majesty.

Therefore, as the Apostle says, “we await the Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform the body of our humiliation to be conformed to the body of his glory” (Philippians 3:20). He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXIII [Another numbering: LXXI]  
## On the Ascension of the Lord I

### SYNOPSIS

I. Christ’s delay on earth after the resurrection and the disciples’ doubt were arranged to strengthen faith.

II. How many things Christ accomplished during these days.

III. By allowing the disciples to touch his wounds, he strengthened their trembling hearts.

IV. Christ’s ascension brought joy to those whom his death had made fearful and his resurrection had left doubtful. Through Christ, greater things were bestowed than those taken away by the devil.

## CHAPTER I

After the blessed and glorious resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which divine power raised up in three days the true temple of God, destroyed by Jewish impiety, the number of forty sacred days has been completed today, beloved. This number was established by a most sacred ordering and devoted to the benefit of our instruction, so that, while the Lord extended the period of his bodily presence among us, the faith of the resurrection might be fortified by necessary proofs. [Note: Thus, with Quesnellus, the manuscripts of Verona and Vatican collection 5. Others read “during this interval.”]

For Christ’s death had greatly troubled the hearts of the disciples, and, while their minds were weighed down by sorrow over the punishment of the cross, the giving up of his spirit, and the burial of his lifeless body, a certain torpor of doubt had crept over them. [Note: The first edition, the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon, two Vatican manuscripts, and another manuscript of Verona read “had oppressed their burdened minds.” Quesnellus notes it in the margin. Shortly afterward, one manuscript reads *tepor* (“warmth”) instead of *torpor* (“numbness”).]

For when the holy women, as the Gospel narrative made known, announced that the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, that the tomb was empty of the body, and that angels were witnesses of the living Lord, their words seemed to the apostles and the other disciples like ravings. The Spirit of truth would never have allowed this hesitation, wavering through human weakness, to exist in the hearts of his preachers unless that trembling concern and our inquisitive hesitation had laid the foundations of our faith. [Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “wavering.” The old edition—that is, the first edition and the reprints derived from it—reads *contatio*, meaning “inquiry”; the common printed editions read *cunctatio*, “hesitation.” Quesnellus explains that *contatio* means the same as *cunctatio* and is not found with the meaning “inquiry.” In the first edition, *o* is frequently written for *u* in similar words. We have therefore restored *cunctatio* with all the manuscripts; it indicates hesitation joined with the curiosity of inquiry and the desire to know.]

Thus our disturbances and dangers were being addressed through the apostles. In those men we were being taught to resist the accusations of the impious and the arguments of earthly wisdom. Their sight instructed us; their hearing educated us; their touch confirmed us. Let us give thanks to the divine dispensation and to the necessary slowness of the holy Fathers. They doubted, so that we might not doubt.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, beloved, the days that passed between the Lord’s resurrection and his ascension did not pass in idle succession; rather, great sacraments were confirmed in them and great mysteries revealed. During them, the fear of dreadful death was removed, and the immortality not only of the soul but also of the flesh was declared.

During them, through the Lord’s breathing upon them, the Holy Spirit was infused into all the apostles; and to the blessed Apostle Peter, after the keys of the kingdom, care of the Lord’s sheepfold was entrusted. [Note: Paul the Deacon’s exemplar reads “was commended.”]

During those days, the Lord joins himself as a third companion on the road to two disciples (Luke 24:15), and, to clear away all the darkness of our uncertainty, the slowness of those who were afraid and trembling is rebuked. Hearts illuminated by faith conceive a flame; and what had been lukewarm, when the Lord opened the Scriptures, became [lacuna] ardent. [Note: An ancient Vatican manuscript, as Quesnellus conjectured should be restored in the margin, reads “ardent,” whereas the editions and other manuscripts read “trembling.”]

At the breaking of the bread, the eyes of those dining together are also opened. Much happier were the eyes of these men when the glorification of their nature was revealed to them than those of the founders of our race, to whom the confusion of their transgression was imposed. [Note: Thus, with Quesnellus, our better manuscripts. Others read “when their eyes were opened.”]

## CHAPTER III

Amid these and other miracles, while the disciples were agitated by fearful thoughts, the Lord appeared in their midst and said, “Peace be with you” (Luke 24:36; John 20:26). Lest what was turning over in their hearts remain in their minds—for they thought they were seeing a spirit, not flesh—he rebuked thoughts that disagreed with the truth. He placed before the eyes of those who doubted the enduring marks of the cross in his hands and feet and invited them to examine him more carefully.

For the traces of the nails and the spear had been preserved to heal the wounds of unbelieving hearts, so that the nature destined to sit upon the throne of God the Father might be held not by doubtful faith but by the most steadfast knowledge. [Note: The first edition and one Vatican manuscript read “might hold.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Throughout all this period, beloved, which elapsed between the Lord’s resurrection and his ascension, [Note: Editions before Quesnellus read “between the resurrection and ascension of the Lord”; we have retained Quesnellus’s reading, supported by our manuscripts.] God’s providence did this: it taught this and impressed it upon the eyes and hearts of his own [Note: One very old manuscript adds “disciples.”], so that the Lord Jesus Christ might truly be recognized as risen, he who had truly been born, suffered, and died. [Note: The word “Christ” has been added from the oldest Vatican manuscript and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon.]

Therefore the most blessed apostles and all the disciples, who had been fearful both of the outcome of the cross and uncertain about the faith of the resurrection, were strengthened by such clear truth that, when the Lord went exalted into the heavens, they were affected not by sadness but filled with great joy (Luke 24:52).

And truly the cause for rejoicing was great and ineffable, when, in the sight of the holy multitude, the nature of the human race ascended above the dignity of all heavenly creatures, was to surpass the angelic orders, and was to be raised beyond the heights of the archangels, without any limit to the extent of its advancement, except that, received into the presence of the eternal Father, it might share the glory of that throne with which, in the Son, its nature was joined.

Since Christ’s ascension is therefore our advancement, and where the glory of the Head has gone before, there the hope of the body is also called, let us rejoice, beloved, with worthy joy and exult in pious thanksgiving. Today we have not only been established as possessors of paradise; in Christ we have also entered the heavenly heights. Through Christ’s ineffable grace we have gained greater things than we lost through the devil’s envy.

For those whom the poisonous enemy cast down from the happiness of their first dwelling, the Son of God, having made them members of his own body, placed at the right hand of the Father. [Note: The same oldest Vatican manuscript and the Veronese manuscript read: “who lives and reigns with God the Father Almighty and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”]

He lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXIV [Another numbering: LXXII]  
## On the Ascension of the Lord II

### SYNOPSIS

I. Through the ascension, our joy is fulfilled and our faith and hope become more wondrous.

II. Christ ascended into heaven so that we might become capable of blessedness; he will remain there until the day of judgment.

III. Faith was strengthened by the ascension so that it could not be overcome by any torments, even in young girls.

IV. Through the ascension Christ became known in a more excellent way and was more present in his Godhead. What the angelic conversation signifies.

V. Christ’s ascension stirs us to despise earthly things as pilgrims and to love one another, without which no one goes to Christ.

## CHAPTER I
The sacrament of our salvation, beloved, which the Creator of the universe esteemed at the price of his blood, was accomplished from the day of his bodily birth until the end of his Passion through the dispensation of humility. [Note: In the margin of the Casinensis manuscript: “deigned to accomplish.”] Although many signs of divinity also shone forth in the form of a servant, properly speaking, the action of that period served to demonstrate the reality of the humanity he had assumed. But after the Passion, when the bonds of death had been broken—bonds which, by advancing against one who knew no sin, had displayed their power over him [Note: The Veronensis manuscript reads “in him”; shortly afterward, Rainaud’s edition has *incidendo* (“by striking”) instead of *incedendo* (“by advancing”); the first edition and one Vatican manuscript have *in endendo*.] [Note: The printed editions and several manuscripts read *perdiderat* (“had lost”). We preferred *pandiderat* (“had displayed”), on the authority of the oldest Vatican manuscript and another Vatican manuscript written in the so-called Lombardic script.]—weakness passed into power, mortality into eternity, and dishonor into glory. The Lord Jesus Christ made this known through many clear proofs (Acts 1:3), displaying it to the sight of many, until he carried into heaven the triumph of the victory he had won from the dead.

Therefore, just as the Lord’s resurrection was for us a cause of joy in the solemnity of Easter, so his ascension into heaven is now the subject of our rejoicing, as we recall and duly venerate that day on which the lowliness of our nature, in Christ, was raised above the entire heavenly host, above all the orders of angels, and beyond the height of all powers, to the throne of God the Father. [Note: The Vulgate reads “the lowliness of our nature.” We preferred to follow our three better manuscripts. Shortly afterward, the oldest Vatican manuscript and the Veronensis read *cunctarum* (“of all”) instead of *omnium* (“of all”).]

By this order of divine works we have been founded and built up, so that the grace of God might become more wonderful: when those things which deservedly seemed to command reverence for themselves were removed from human sight, faith would not falter, hope would not waver, and charity would not grow cold. [Note: We restored this from the first edition and seven of our manuscripts. The other editions read *non deficeret* (“would not fail”).] For here there is great strength of mind, and this is the light of truly faithful souls: to believe without hesitation what is not seen by bodily vision, and to fix one’s desire where one cannot direct one’s sight. [Note: We added *enim* (“for”) from six of our manuscripts and the first edition.] [Note: This was inserted from the same edition and from five of our more distinguished manuscripts.] But from where would this devotion arise in our hearts, or how would anyone be justified by faith, if our salvation consisted only in those things which lay before our eyes? [Note: The Lombard manuscript reads *subjacent* (“lie beneath” or “are present”).] Hence also that man who seemed to doubt Christ’s resurrection had to examine the marks of the Passion in Christ’s own flesh, both by sight and by touch: “Because you have seen me,” the Lord says, “you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

[Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript and the Veronensis manuscript read *possimus* (“we may be able”).]

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, beloved, so that we might become capable of this blessedness, when everything that corresponded to the preaching of the Gospel and the mysteries of the New Testament had been completed, our Lord Jesus Christ was raised into heaven in the presence of his disciples on the fortieth day after the resurrection (Luke 24:50; Matthew 16:19), [Note: *Corporali praesentiae* (“of bodily presence”) is found in Vatican manuscript collection 5 and also in the first edition, which adds *suae* (“his”).] bringing the mode of his bodily presence to an end. He will remain at the Father’s right hand until the divinely appointed times for multiplying the children of the Church have been completed, and he will come to judge the living and the dead in the same flesh in which he ascended.

Thus, what was visible in our Redeemer passed into sacramental reality; and, so that faith might be more excellent and firm, teaching succeeded sight, [Col. 0398B] and the hearts of believers, illumined by rays from above, would follow its authority.

## CHAPTER III

This faith, increased by the Lord’s ascension and strengthened by the gift of the Holy Spirit, was not terrified by chains, prisons, exile, hunger, fire, the tearing apart by wild beasts, or punishments devised with the refined cruelties of persecutors. [Note: Two older Vatican manuscripts read *crudelitatis* (“of cruelty”); perhaps the intended reading is *crudelitate* (“with cruelty”).] For this faith, throughout the whole world, not only men but also women, and not merely boys who had not reached puberty but also tender maidens, struggled even to the shedding of their blood.

This faith drove out demons, expelled illnesses, and raised the dead. Hence even the blessed apostles, who had been confirmed by so many miracles and instructed by so many discourses, although they had been terrified by the severity of the Lord’s Passion [Note: Thus restored from the oldest Vatican manuscript, the Bononiensis manuscript, and the first edition, which has *et atrocitate* (“and by the horror”), though it omits *tamen* (“nevertheless”). Other editions have *atrocitatem* (“the horror”).] and had accepted the truth of his resurrection not without hesitation, profited so greatly from the Lord’s ascension that whatever had previously brought them fear was turned into joy.

For they had raised the whole contemplation of their minds toward the Divinity seated at the Father’s right hand, and they were no longer hindered by the obstruction of bodily sight from directing the gaze of their minds toward him who, when descending from the Father, had not been absent from him, nor, when ascending from the disciples, had departed from them.

## CHAPTER IV

Then, beloved, the Son of Man, the Son of God, became known in a more excellent and sacred manner when he withdrew into the glory of the Father’s majesty and, in an ineffable way, began to be more present in his divinity, though he had become more distant in his humanity. Then faith, growing more learned, began to approach the Son, equal to the Father, by the step of the mind; and it no longer needed the handling of Christ’s bodily substance, [Note: We preferred *qua* (“by which”) to *quae* (“which”), although we found it in only one manuscript.] by which he is less than the Father (John 14:28): [Col. 0399A] for, while the nature of the glorified body remained, the faith of believers was called to that place where the Only-Begotten, equal to his Begetter, would be touched not by carnal hand but by spiritual understanding.

Hence comes what the Lord said after his resurrection [Note: The Vulgate reads: “The Lord, with Mary Magdalene representing the Church and hastening to approach him for the purpose of touching him, says to her: ‘Do not…’” We have followed the authority of four older manuscripts.] when Mary Magdalene, representing the Church, was hastening to approach him for the purpose of touching him: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:17). That is: “I do not want you to come to me bodily, nor to recognize me through the sense of the flesh; I am deferring you to higher things and preparing greater things for you.” When I have ascended to my Father, then you will touch me more perfectly and more truly, grasping what you do not touch and believing what you do not see.”

When the eyes of the disciples who followed the Lord as he ascended into heaven gazed upward with intense wonder, [Note: The first edition and the Bononiensis manuscript read *apostolorum* (“of the apostles”).] two angels stood before them, [Note: We supplied *coram* (“before”) on the authority of five better manuscripts and the first edition; from these and from all editions before Quesnellus we also restored *et* (“and”) before *dixerunt* (“they said”).] shining with wondrous whiteness of clothing, and they said: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11). By these words all the children of the Church were taught to believe that Jesus Christ would come visibly in the same flesh in which he had ascended. Nor could there be any doubt that all things were subject to him whom angelic service had attended from the very beginning of his bodily birth.

For just as an angel announced to the blessed Virgin that Christ would be conceived from the Holy Spirit, so, when he had been born of the Virgin, the voice of the heavenly host sang of him to the shepherds; just as the first testimonies of heavenly messengers proclaimed that he had risen from the dead, so the services of angels proclaimed that he would come in that same flesh to judge the world. [Note: The adjective *prima* (“first”) is absent from the oldest Vatican manuscript.] Thus we were to understand what great powers would be present with him when he came to judge, since such mighty powers had also ministered to him when he judged. [Note: The first edition and one manuscript remove the preposition *cum* (“with”).] [Note: Another reading is *declararunt* (“declared”) instead of *praedicarunt* (“proclaimed”).]

## CHAPTER V

Let us therefore, beloved, exult with spiritual joy and rejoice with thanksgiving worthy of God; let us raise the free eyes of our hearts to that height where Christ is. Let earthly desires not weigh down minds summoned above; let perishable things not occupy those chosen for eternal realities; let deceitful allurements not delay those who have entered the way of truth. And let the faithful pass through these temporal things in such a way that they recognize themselves as pilgrims in this valley of the world. Even if certain comforts flatter them there, they must not be wickedly embraced but bravely passed through.

The blessed apostle Peter urges us toward this devotion; and in accordance with that love which he conceived for feeding Christ’s sheep through his threefold profession of love for the Lord (John 21:15–17), he appeals to us, saying: “Beloved, I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Peter 2:11).

But against whom do fleshly pleasures wage war except the devil, who rejoices in binding souls striving toward heavenly things with the delights of corruptible goods and in leading them away from those dwelling places from which he himself fell? Against his snares every faithful person must wisely keep watch, so that he may strike down his enemy by means of that through which he is being tested. [Note: The first edition reads *hujus* (“of this”). Shortly afterward, two older manuscripts read *de eo potentatu possit elidere* (“may be able to strike him down from that power”).]

Nothing, beloved, is stronger against the devil’s deceptions than the kindness of mercy and the generosity of charity, through which every sin is either avoided or overcome. [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript reads “every sin is avoided, omitted, or conquered.” The Veronensis manuscript reads “every sin is either diminished or conquered.”] But the sublimity of this virtue is not grasped until what opposes it has been overthrown. And what is so hostile to mercy and works of charity as greed, from whose root the shoot of every evil emerges?

Unless greed is destroyed in its own fuel and tinder, it is inevitable that in the field of the heart where the plant of this evil has grown strong [Note: The Veronensis manuscript reads *hujusmodi planta* (“a plant of this kind”).] thorns and thistles of vices will arise rather than any seed of true virtue.

Let us therefore resist, beloved, this most deadly evil, and pursue charity, without which no virtue can shine (1 Corinthians 13), so that through this way of love by which Christ descended to us, we too may ascend to him. [Note: The same manuscript adds “and approach.”] To him, with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, belongs honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXV [Alternatively LXXIII]  
## On Pentecost I

### SYNOPSIS

I. Christian Pentecost corresponds to the Mosaic Pentecost.  
II. How swiftly and wonderfully the disciples were taught by the Holy Spirit.  
III. The perfect equality of the persons in the Holy Trinity is explained.  
IV. The error of the Macedonians concerning the Holy Spirit, who is the source and cause of every good thing.
