V. Everything in the Church is sanctified through the Holy Spirit; even the fasts were instituted by him.

## CHAPTER I

All Catholic hearts know that today’s solemnity is to be venerated among the principal feasts. [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript, no. 3835, reads *omnia* (“all things”).] Nor is there any doubt how much reverence is owed to this day, which the Holy Spirit consecrated by the most excellent miracle of his gift.

For from the day on which the Lord ascended above the whole height of the heavens to sit at the right hand of God the Father, this day, the tenth after his ascension and the fiftieth after his resurrection, has dawned for us in him from whom it began. [Note: The same manuscript omits *omnem* (“the whole”) and shortly afterward reads *in se* (“in itself”).] It contains within itself great mysteries both of the ancient sacraments and of the new, by which it is most clearly declared that grace was foretold through the Law and that the Law was fulfilled through grace.

For just as, once the Hebrew people had been liberated from the Egyptians, the Law was given on Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day after the sacrifice of the lamb (Exodus 19:17), so, after the Passion of Christ, through which the true Lamb of God was slain, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles and the community of believers on the fiftieth day after his resurrection (Acts 2:3). [Note: Thus restored from our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus, which read *Domini* (“of the Lord”) instead of *Christi* (“of Christ”). In the first edition both words are absent.] Thus the attentive Christian may easily recognize that the beginnings of the Old Testament served the beginnings of the Gospel, and that the second covenant was established by the same Spirit by whom the first had been instituted.

## CHAPTER II

For, as the apostolic history testifies, [Note: Another reading is *Cum* (“When”).] “When the days of Pentecost were being fulfilled and all the disciples were together in the same place, suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a violent, rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as though of fire, and one rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak in other tongues, as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance” (ibid., 1–4). [Note: The first edition reads *variis linguis* (“in various languages”).]

O how swift is the word of wisdom, and where God is the teacher, how quickly what is taught is learned! No interpretation was required for hearing, no practice for use, no period of study; but, when the Spirit of truth breathed where he willed (John 3:8), the proper voices of the individual nations became common in the mouth of the Church.

From this day, therefore, the trumpet of evangelical preaching resounded; from this day, showers of spiritual gifts and rivers of blessings watered every desert and the whole dry land. For the Spirit of God was borne over the waters in order to renew the face of the earth (Genesis 1:2), and, to drive away the ancient darkness, flashes of new light gleamed, as, amid the splendor of flashing tongues, the bright word of the Lord and fiery utterance were conceived—having both the efficacy to illuminate and the power to burn, in order to create understanding and consume sin. [Note: Quesnellus judged this reading should be retained, and the entire sequence of the passage supports it, although three of his Oxford manuscripts read *erudiendi* (“to instruct”) instead of *urendi* (“to burn”). We likewise retain it, although the oldest Vatican manuscript also has *erudiendi*; the Barberini manuscript 88, collection 2, gives the passage as: “And it possessed the power to illuminate and to instruct.”]

## CHAPTER III

Although, beloved, the form of the event itself was exceedingly wondrous, and although there is no doubt that the majesty of the Holy Spirit was present in that chorus of all human voices exulting together, [Note: Quesnellus, on the basis of his manuscripts, some of which are also among ours, printed *conventu* (“assembly”). The Paris edition of 1671 has *consensu* (“accord”). The reading of the earlier editions, supported by other manuscripts, seemed better, since it agrees more closely with what precedes, namely *humanarum vocum* (“of human voices”).] no one should suppose that his divine substance appeared in those things which were seen by bodily eyes. [Note: We restored the reading of editions before Quesnellus because we found it in the oldest Vatican manuscript and in others of ours, with which we wrote *aestimet* (“should suppose”) instead of the common *existimet* (“should suppose”). Quesnellus reads: “Yet no one should suppose that his divine substance appeared in those things …”] For his invisible nature, which he shares with the Father and the Son, displayed the quality of his gift and work by whatever sign he willed, but kept the proper character of his essence within his divinity. [Note: The words *atque operis* (“and of his work”) are absent from the oldest Vatican manuscript.] [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *substantiae* (“of the substance”).] For just as the human eye cannot reach the Father or the Son, so neither can it reach the Holy Spirit.

In the divine Trinity there is nothing unlike, nothing unequal; and everything that can be conceived concerning that substance differs neither in power, nor in glory, nor in eternity. Although, in the properties of the persons, the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another, there is nevertheless not another divinity or a different nature.

Indeed, although the Only-Begotten Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, he is not like any creature which belongs both to the Father and to the Son, but exists with both as living and powerful, eternal in his subsistence from what the Father and the Son are. [Note: Editions before Quesnellus read “and everlasting, and subsisting from what he is,” as do manuscript collections 4 and 5; in those manuscripts, however, the conjunction *et* before *ex eo* is omitted. The reading introduced by Quesnellus and confirmed by our oldest Vatican manuscript is sufficiently indicated.]

Therefore, when the Lord promised his disciples the coming of the Holy Spirit before the day of his Passion, he said: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:12–15). [Note: Editions before Quesnellus and the later manuscript collections read *audiet* (“he will hear”), though the oldest Vatican manuscript does not.]

Therefore the Father’s things are not one set of things, the Son’s another, and the Holy Spirit’s another; but whatever the Father has, the Son also has, and the Holy Spirit also has. Nor was this communion ever absent from that Trinity, because there “to have everything” is the same as always to exist. [Note: Thus restored from our manuscripts and the first edition. Other editions read *defuit* (“was absent”).]

Let no times, grades, or distinctions be imagined there. [Note: The first edition reads *ut si* (“so that if”); shortly afterward, it has *incommutabili* (“unchangeable”) instead of *ineffabili* (“ineffable”).] And if no one can explain what God is, let no one dare to affirm what he is not. For it is more excusable not to speak what is worthy concerning an ineffable nature than to define things contrary to it.

Whatever devout hearts can conceive concerning the Father’s eternal and unchangeable glory, let them understand the same simultaneously and inseparably, without distinction, of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. For this is why we confess the blessed Trinity as one God: because among these three persons there is no difference of substance, power, will, or operation.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, just as we detest the Arians, who want there to be some distance between the Father and the Son, so also we detest the Macedonians, who, although they attribute equality to the Father and the Son, nevertheless suppose that the Holy Spirit is of an inferior nature. [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript reads *eos* (“them”) instead of *Arianos* (“the Arians”); afterward, instead of *Macedonianos* (“the Macedonians”), omitting *ita etiam* (“so also”), it reads *illos pariter detestemur* (“let us likewise detest them”).]

They do not consider that they are falling into the blasphemy which, according to the Lord’s judgment, will not be forgiven either in the present age or in the age to come: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12:32).

Therefore, one who persists in this impiety remains without forgiveness, because he has excluded from himself the one through whom he could confess; and he will never reach the remedy of pardon if he does not have an advocate to plead for him. For from the Holy Spirit comes the invocation of the Father; from him come the tears of penitents; from him come the groans of those who plead; and no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3). [Note: The first edition reads *advocatio* (“advocacy” or “intercession”), as does the following sermon, chapter 4, without *Spiritus sancti* (“of the Holy Spirit”).]

The Apostle most clearly proclaims the Holy Spirit’s omnipotence, equal with that of the Father and the Son, and their one divinity, saying: “There are distinctions of gifts, but the same Spirit; there are distinctions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are distinctions of operations, but the same God, who works all things in all” (ibid., 4–6). [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript reads “the Apostle, proclaiming most clearly, says.”]

## CHAPTER V

By these and other testimonies, in which the authority of the divine utterances shines forth innumerably, let us be moved with one accord to venerate Pentecost, exulting in honor of the Holy Spirit, through whom the whole Catholic Church is sanctified and every rational soul is imbued; he is the inspirer of faith, the teacher of knowledge, the fountain of love, the seal of chastity, and the cause of every virtue.

Let the minds of the faithful rejoice that throughout the whole world one God—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is praised in the confession of every language; and that the sign which appeared in the form of fire persists both in its work and in its gift. For the Spirit of truth himself makes the house of his glory shine with the brightness of his light [Note: Another reading is *splendore* (“with splendor”). Quesnellus prints it in the margin.] and does not wish anything dark or tepid to be in his temple.

Through this work and teaching, the cleansing of fasts and almsgiving has also been given to us. For this venerable day is followed by the practice of a most salutary observance, which all the saints have always found most useful, and which we urge you diligently to celebrate with pastoral concern: if negligence and carelessness have contracted any stains in recent days, let the discipline of fasting chastise them and the devotion of piety correct them.

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; on Saturday, however, let us celebrate vigils with the customary devotion for the same purpose. [Note: The oldest manuscript reads “Friday of the week.”] [Note: We took this concluding formula from the same Roman manuscript. Another reading is: “Through Christ our Lord. Amen.”]

Through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit, one God, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXVI [Alternatively LXXIV]  
## On Pentecost II

### SYNOPSIS

I. The Holy Spirit must be discussed both for the spiritually mature and for the newly baptized.  
II. The persons of the Trinity are perfectly equal in all things, even though certain things are attributed to individual persons.  
III. The Holy Spirit was given in the Old Testament.  
IV. He was also given to the apostles before Pentecost; without him no one prays properly.  
V. What was it that the disciples were not yet able to bear?  
VI. How the foolishness of the Manichaeans is refuted from the Gospel, and at what time Mani lived.  
VII. How foolish it is to say that the Church lacked the Holy Spirit until Mani.  
VIII. It is necessary to deny that the Holy Spirit was given to the Church if one rejects true flesh in Christ.  
IX. Fasts are numbered among the gifts of the Holy Spirit and are prescribed according to apostolic tradition.

## CHAPTER I

The text of the divine utterances most fully sets before us the reason and meaning of today’s solemnity, by which we have learned that the Holy Spirit was poured out upon Christ’s disciples on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, the tenth day after his ascension, [Note: The Padiliron Lectionary reads *missum* (“sent”). Shortly afterward, Vatican manuscript no. 3385 reads *eloquium* (“utterance”) instead of *obsequium* (“service” or “attendance”).] just as he had been promised. But for the instruction of the Church’s new children, the service of our discourse must also be added.

For we do not fear that the spiritually mature and learned will find familiar things tedious, since it is to their benefit that they should wish what they themselves have learned, with great profit to themselves, to be communicated to as many as possible. [Note: Editions before Quesnellus and manuscripts of lesser quality read *ut spiritales* (“so that the spiritual”).] [Note: The Padiliron manuscript reads *quae ipsi* (“which they themselves”); two Lectionaries, Venetian no. 154 and Bergomensis, together with manuscript collection 5, read *cum magna humilitate* (“with great humility”). The first edition subsequently reads *per corda hominum* (“through the hearts of human beings”).] Let the distribution of divine gifts therefore pass through the hearts of all, and let the learned and unlearned alike not disdain the service of our speech: [Note: In the oldest Vatican manuscript, the following words are omitted up to *nesciunt* (“they do not know”).] the learned, so that they may show that they love what they know; the unlearned, so that they may show that they desire what they do not know.

For the generosity of the one whose majesty we are attempting to discuss will assist this preparation of yours, so that he may make you capable and us abundant for the advancement of the whole Church. [Note: The first edition has *etiam* (“also”) instead of *enim* (“for”). Shortly afterward, the better manuscripts have *vestrae* (“of yours”), while editions before Quesnellus prefer *nostrae* (“of ours”).] [Note: The same editions and some manuscripts read *gestimus* (“we eagerly desire”). Shortly afterward, the oldest Vatican manuscript has *Ecclesiae suae* (“of his Church”).]

## CHAPTER II

When, therefore, we direct the eyes of our minds toward understanding the dignity of the Holy Spirit, let us conceive of nothing different from the excellence of the Father and the Son, because the essence of the divine Trinity in no respect departs from its unity. [Note: Most manuscripts, though not the oldest Vatican, and editions before Quesnellus read *aciem* (“the gaze”). The reading we adopted, noted by Quesnellus in the margin as perhaps derived from a Lectionary, is supported by our Lectionaries. Subsequently, several manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus read *consempiterni* (“coeverlasting”) instead of *coaeterni* (“coeternal”).] It is eternal for the Father to be the begetter of his coeternal Son; it is eternal for the Son to have been begotten timelessly from the Father; it is likewise eternal for the Holy Spirit to be the Spirit of the Father and the Son. Thus the Father never existed without the Son, nor the Son without the Father, nor the Father and the Son without the Holy Spirit. Once all degrees of existence have been excluded, no person there is earlier and none later. [Note: Two Venetian and Bergomensis Lectionaries read *sibi* (“for itself”).]

For the unchangeable divinity of this blessed Trinity is one in substance, undivided in operation, harmonious in will, equal in power, and equal in glory. [Note: Editions before Quesnellus and some manuscripts read: “The one substance of the unchangeable divinity.” Shortly afterward, another reading is *in omnipotentia* (“in omnipotence”) instead of *in potentia* (“in power”).]

When Holy Scripture speaks of it in such a way that, whether in deeds or words, it assigns something that seems to belong to individual persons, [Note: Thus Quesnellus and the first edition read, together with our manuscript Lectionaries. Another reading is *convenisse* (“to have belonged”).] Catholic faith is not disturbed but instructed. Through the particularity of the word or work, the truth of the Trinity is made known to us, and understanding does not divide what hearing distinguishes.

For this reason certain things are expressed under the name of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, so that the confession of the faithful may not go astray in the Trinity. [Note: Another reading is *credentium* (“of believers”).] Since the Trinity is inseparable, it would never be understood as a Trinity if it were always spoken of inseparably.

The very difficulty of speaking therefore rightly draws our hearts toward understanding, and through our weakness heavenly teaching assists us. For because in the divinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit neither singularity nor diversity is to be imagined, true unity and true Trinity can to some extent be perceived together by the mind, but cannot be expressed together by the mouth. [Note: The first edition, together with two Bononiensis and Vatican manuscripts, reads: “so that it may be possible for true unity and true Trinity to be perceived together to some extent by the mind.” Other editions before Quesnellus read: “so that it may indeed be possible to perceive or be perceived to some extent by the mind.”]

## CHAPTER III

[Note: Editions before Quesnellus read *in cordibus nostris fide* (“with faith in our hearts”), omitting *hac* (“this”); our manuscripts do not support that omission.]

Therefore, beloved, once this faith has been established in our hearts, by which we salutarily believe that the whole Trinity together is one power, one majesty, and one substance—undivided in operation, inseparable in love, undifferentiated in authority, filling all things together and containing all things together—whatever the Father is, so also is the Son, and so also is the Holy Spirit. True divinity cannot be either greater or lesser in any respect; it must be confessed in three persons in such a way that the Trinity admits no solitude and equality preserves unity. [Note: Quesnellus reads: “the true divinity is in no respect either less or greater.” We restored the reading of the earlier editions, confirmed by our manuscripts.]

With this faith, beloved, firmly grasped, let us not doubt that when the Holy Spirit filled the Lord’s disciples on the day of Pentecost, it was not the beginning of the gift but an increase of generosity. [Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript reads *non fuerit* (“was not”).] For the patriarchs, prophets, priests, and all the saints who lived in earlier times were nourished by the sanctification of that same Spirit. [Note: The editions and several manuscripts add *sancti* (“saints”), a word we deleted on the authority of the oldest Vatican and Padiliron manuscripts, to avoid the cacophony caused by the following *sanctificatione*.] Without this grace no sacraments were ever instituted and no mysteries celebrated, so that the power of the spiritual gifts was always the same, although the measure of the gifts was not always the same.

## CHAPTER IV

Even the blessed apostles were not without the Holy Spirit before the Lord’s Passion, nor was the power of this Spirit absent from the Savior’s works. When he gave his disciples the healing of illnesses and the power to cast out demons, he was certainly granting the effects of that Spirit [Note: We corrected this from the oldest Vatican and Padiliron manuscripts. Another reading is *effectum* (“effect”).] in whom the impiety of the Jews denied that he commanded the unclean spirits and attributed divine benefits to the devil (Luke 10:19).

For this reason those who blasphemed in such a way rightly received that sentence of the Lord in which he said: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to human beings; but blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven to human beings. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12:31–32).

It is therefore clear that the remission of sins does not occur without the advocacy of the Holy Spirit, [Note: Another reading is *invocatione* (“invocation”), printed in the margin of the common editions but not found in our manuscripts.] and that no one without him can groan as is proper or pray as one ought, as the Apostle says: “For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8:26); and: “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3). To be emptied of him is exceedingly destructive and exceedingly deadly, because no one who is abandoned by his intercessor ever merits forgiveness. [Note: Quesnellus, in the margin and in the oldest Vatican manuscript, reads *perniciosum* (“destructive”); the first edition has *exitiale* (“fatal”). Shortly before this, the Padiliron manuscript has *vacare* (“to be without”) instead of *vacuari* (“to be emptied”).]

All, therefore, beloved, who had believed in the Lord Jesus possessed the Holy Spirit poured into them. The apostles had already received the power to forgive sins when, after his resurrection, the Lord breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). [Note: Editions before Quesnellus, together with the later manuscript collections, read *jam* (“already”) instead of *etiam* (“even then”).]

But a greater grace and a more abundant inspiration were reserved for that perfection which was to be conferred upon the disciples, through which they would receive what they had not yet received and possess more excellently what they had received. For this reason the Lord said: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce the things to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you” (John 16:12–14). [Note: In Vatican manuscript collection 5, *illa* (“them”) is absent. In the oldest Vatican manuscript the following Gospel text reads: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce the things to come; for he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.”]

### 304

What, then, is the meaning of the Lord’s promise to the disciples concerning the Holy Spirit, when he had already said, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you”? “I still have many things to say to you,” he says, “but you cannot bear them now. When that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:12–14). Did the Lord wish to be understood as possessing inferior knowledge, or as having learned something less from the Father than the Holy Spirit had—when he himself is the Truth, and when the Father can say nothing and the Spirit teach nothing without the Word? Hence it is said, “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14): for what the Spirit receives, with the Father giving it, the Son gives.

[Note: We have added *illa* (“them”) from Casinensis manuscript collection 1 and from the Venetian and Padiliron Lectionaries, since this word is likewise read in the preceding chapter.]

[Note: In the oldest Vatican manuscript: “that Spirit will guide you into all truth,” as the same codex also has in the text of the preceding chapter. See note 22.]

[Note: We supplied the word *Spiritus* (“Spirit”), which was absent from the printed editions but required by the context, from several of our manuscripts, especially the oldest Vatican manuscript and the Bergamo and Venetian Lectionaries. In Vatican manuscript collection 5: “the Father can say nothing, and the Spirit can say nothing without the Word.” Immediately afterward, instead of *quoniam quod accipit Spiritus* (“for what the Spirit receives”), the Casinensis manuscript has *et quia qui accipit donum Spiritus* (“and because the one who receives the gift of the Spirit”), where *donum* (“gift”) was added by a later hand. The Venetian manuscript likewise has *et quia* (“and because”) instead of *quoniam* (“for”).]

It was therefore not another truth that had to be imparted, nor another doctrine that had to be preached; rather, the capacity of those being taught had to be enlarged, and the steadfastness of that love had to be multiplied which would cast out all fear and would not fear the fury of persecutors.

[Note: The Casinensis manuscript has: “so that they would not fear the rage of their persecutors.”]

This is what the apostles began to desire more ardently and to be able to accomplish more effectively after they had been filled with the new abundance of the Holy Spirit, advancing from knowledge of the commandments to endurance of sufferings: so that, no longer trembling in any storm, they might trample underfoot the waves of the world and the world’s upheavals, with faith rising above them, and, scorning death, might bring the Gospel of truth to all nations.

[Note: In the same Casinensis manuscript and in the Padiliron codex: “advancing toward knowledge of the precepts and toward endurance of sufferings, so that, now fearing no storm,” and so forth. In one codex: “fearing no power.”]

## Chapter VI

Let us not, dearly beloved, receive what the Lord added when he said, “Whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you the things that are to come” (John 16:13), with sluggish understanding or passing attention. For, apart from the other sayings of truth by which the impiety of the Manichaeans is refuted, this statement most clearly overthrows the entire dogma of their sacrilegious falsehood.

[Note: In the oldest Vatican manuscript: “so that they might appear to follow a great and sublime author.” The same reading is found in the first edition, which omits only the particle *ut* (“so that”).]

For, in order that they might seem to follow some great and sublime author, they believed that the Holy Spirit had appeared in their teacher Mani, and that the Paraclete promised by the Lord had not come before this unhappy deceiver arose—so that the Spirit of God remained in him in such a way that Mani himself was nothing other than the spirit who, through the ministry of bodily voice and tongue, would lead his disciples into all truth and would at last disclose the secrets of past ages, which had never before been known.

[Note: Earlier printed editions, together with Vatican manuscript collection 5, have *Manichaeo* (“Manichaeus”). Another Vatican manuscript, one Vallicellian manuscript, and the Casinensis have *Mani*, and likewise below wherever *Manes* is mentioned. It should be noted that Latin Fathers frequently call Manes “Manichaeus,” as scholars have established. Quesnellus’s note on the name *Manes* follows: “Thus the manuscript codices read, and rightly so. For when this infamous heresiarch was originally called not Urbicus, as Augustine says in *On Heresies*, heresy 46, but Cubricus, as Epiphanius records, he adopted the name Manis for himself, deliberately taking a name signifying madness. When his disciples later noticed this in Greece, they called him Mannichaeus, doubling the letter *n*, as though he were pouring forth manna.” Thus far Quesnellus. In the first edition, the adverb *manifeste* (“plainly”) is placed before *apparuisse* (“had appeared”).]

[Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript omits the word *saeculorum* (“of the ages”).]

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and three Oxford manuscripts have the following form; hence it is surprising that the other reading entered the tradition, which earlier editions print: “It would be tedious to show how ridiculous and vain this is, unless some people were still unashamed to believe it.” The former reading is certainly preferable, because it immediately shows that, from the time when the Gospel was preached and consecrated by the blood of martyrs, during the eighth persecution and before Mani, the Holy Spirit had been given to the Church and poured into the hearts of the faithful. Quesnellus. The reading inserted in the text is also supported by our oldest Vatican manuscript and another excellent Venetian manuscript, in which only *ridiculum* (“ridiculous”) appears instead of *falsum* (“false”). The reading found in the other editions occurs in the manuscripts of all five collections, and also in two Vallicellian Lectionaries, the Padiliron, and the Bergamo Lectionary. It also has the character of Leo’s style and agrees with the historical fact that the Manichaeans were discovered at Rome.]

But the authority of the Gospel’s preaching itself declares how false and vain this is. Mani, therefore, a minister of diabolical falsehood and the founder of an obscene superstition, became known as deserving condemnation at the time when, after the Lord’s resurrection, the two hundred and sixtieth year had been completed, under the emperor Probus and the consul Paulinus, while the eighth persecution against the Christians was still raging; and countless thousands of martyrs, by their very victories, had shown that what the Lord had promised had been fulfilled, when he said:

“When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak. For it will be given to you in that hour what you are to speak. For it is not you who are speaking, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19–20).

[Note: Earlier printed editions, together with some codices, have *magister* (“teacher”). This reading, apparently more suitable, is supported by manuscripts of the first three collections and by two of our Vallicellian Lectionaries, the Bergamo Lectionary, and the Padiliron. Nevertheless, we did not remove the reading introduced by Quesnellus from his, as we believe, Lectionaries, since it is confirmed not only by Vatican manuscripts of collections 4 and 5 but also by two of our finest Lectionaries, the Venetian and especially the oldest Vatican.]

[Note: This does not mean that Mani was the first parent of the obscene Manichaean doctrine, but that its dissemination through many regions and parts of the world began from him. The first architect of those dreams was a certain Scythianus, originally from the region of the Saracens and raised in Arabia, near Palestine. When he was dying, he entrusted all his possessions to a certain Therbithus, the only disciple he had. Therbithus abandoned that name and wished to be called Buddas. After his infamous death, his ill-starred inheritance came into the hands of an old woman, who left it to Cubricus, or Mani, whom she had bought as a household slave. Mani thereafter disseminated his insane doctrines among the Persians, among whom he had been born and lived, to the ruin and destruction of many. See further Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6, “The Illuminating”; Philaster of Brescia; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, book II, volume II, heresy 60; and Augustine, heresy 46. Eusebius also treats him as the first author of this sect in *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 31. Quesnellus.]

[Note: All the manuscripts we have seen—and they are neither few nor insignificant, including six Lectionaries and manuscripts from all five collections—have this reading. One Oxford manuscript cited by Quesnellus gives in the margin the Roman numeral CCL. Concerning this year, indeed concerning the whole passage, which is entangled in various chronological and especially historical difficulties, more will be said in the observations on this sermon, where three rather lengthy notes by Quesnellus will also be reproduced. Immediately afterward, the editions before Quesnellus, together with some codices, have: “under the emperor Probus and the consul Paulinus.”]

[Note: The printed editions, together with manuscripts of the later collections, have *ebulliret* (“was boiling forth”). But *desaeviret* (“was raging”) is preferable, since it is read not only in manuscripts of the two more excellent collections, 1 and 2, and in the three Oxford manuscripts cited by Quesnellus, but also in all our Lectionaries, especially the oldest Vatican. Since the passage speaks of the persecution under Valerian, which had long since ended and had been extinguished under Gallienus, it ought, according to Father Ruinart’s observation in the preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs*, no. 54, to read *desaevisset* (“had raged”), so that the double *ss* may easily have been changed by scribal error into *r*. But, since no codex supports this, we have not altered the text. Immediately afterward, the words “countless thousands of martyrs” refer not only to the martyrs of the eighth persecution but to all who suffered death for Christ in the eight preceding persecutions.]

## Chapter VII

The Lord’s promise, therefore, could not be delayed through so many intervening ages, nor could that Spirit of truth, whom the world of the ungodly did not receive, have withheld the sevenfold abundance of his gifts in such a way as to deprive so many generations of the Church of his inspiration until that monstrous standard-bearer of shameful lies was born—

[Note: Earlier printed editions have *tanta per aetatum intervalla* (“through such long intervals of ages”). Two Vallicellian Lectionaries, one Padiliron manuscript, the Casinensis manuscript of collection 1, and Vatican manuscripts of collections 4 and 5 have *per tanta* (“through so many”). The oldest Vatican manuscript and manuscripts of collection 2 support the reading introduced by Quesnellus. Shortly afterward, the oldest Vatican manuscript and the Padiliron have *non accipit* (“does not receive”).]

—although not even this can be attributed to him, that he received any small portion of divine inspiration, since he too arose from that part of the world which cannot receive the Spirit of truth.

[Note: The parenthetical words are absent from the oldest Vatican manuscript, where perhaps more appropriately, after *nasceretur* (“was born”), there follows: “who, filled with the spirit of the devil, resisted the Spirit of Christ,” and so forth. One Vallicellian manuscript omits this. Shortly afterward, the Padiliron manuscript has *probationem* (“proof”) instead of *portionem* (“portion”).]

For, filled with the spirit of the devil, he resisted the Spirit of Christ; and while the Paraclete has bestowed on the saints this teaching, that they should foretell the future, he, lest the course of events itself expose his falsehoods, turned the shamelessness of his sacrilegious fables toward ages already past.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with most codices, have *ridendarum* (“to be mocked”). We have not removed that reading, because it is found in the oldest Vatican manuscript.]

And as though the holy Law and the divinely inspired prophecy had taught us nothing concerning the Creator’s eternity and nothing concerning the order of creation, he wove together, as an insult to God and an injury to all natures that were well created, monsters of contradictory falsehoods.

[Note: The printed editions here add *in universum mundum bene* (“well throughout the whole world”), as found in manuscripts of collections 3, 4, and 5. The Casinensis manuscript of collection 1 has: “throughout the whole world the good, holy, and divinely inspired law.” The Casanatensis manuscript of collection 2 and the Padiliron Lectionary remove *mundum* (“world”) and read: “throughout the whole world the good and holy law,” and so forth. Two Vallicellian Lectionaries have: “throughout the whole world the good, holy law,” and so forth. Given this variety, we preferred the reading of the oldest Roman Vatican Lectionary.]

[Note: Quesnellus has this reading, supported by one of his codices and by the oldest Vatican manuscript. Earlier editions, together with most manuscripts, have: “and he wove together, to the injury of all natures, inexplicable monsters of falsehood.” The first edition, with manuscripts of collections 3 and 4, adds *bene conditarum* (“well created”), as in the text, but the other editions have the same reading as the former.]

To whom, then, would he have been able to insinuate his insanities except to people who were very foolish and excessively turned away from the light of truth, who, whether through the blindness of ignorance or through the appetite for shamefulness, resort to those non-sacred but accursed things which, for the sake of common decency, should not be brought forth in our speech, since their confession has already revealed them in the fullest measure?

[Note: Earlier printed editions, together with manuscripts of the later collections, have *incestis* (“incestuous”). Two Vallicellian manuscripts, the Padiliron, and the Casinensis have *inertibus* (“sluggish”); this is sufficiently good. Nevertheless, we retained the word *insipientibus* (“foolish”), introduced by Quesnellus, on the authority of the oldest Vatican manuscript. Shortly afterward, “from the light of piety” is found in Vatican manuscript collection 5, another Bononian manuscript, and the Padiliron.]

[Note: The first edition, with manuscripts of collections 3 and 4, has “not sacred but accursed.” Quesnellus has “not sacraments but accursed sacraments,” a reading found in no codex. The printed reading is supported not only by the other editions together with manuscripts of collection 5, but also by our more important codices: the Casinensis, two Vallicellian manuscripts, the Padiliron, and the oldest Vatican.]

[Note: The two Vallicellian manuscripts and the Casinensis omit *jam* (“already”).]

## Chapter VIII

Let none of you, dearly beloved, be persuaded that the Holy Spirit deemed the author of such great impiety worthy in any respect. Absolutely none of that power reached him which Christ both promised and sent to his Church.

For the blessed apostle John says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). The Lord’s ascension was the reason for giving the Spirit; and the one who denies that the true man in Christ was raised to the session at the right hand of the Father must necessarily deny that the Spirit was given.

But we, dearly beloved, adopted through the regeneration of the Holy Spirit for blessed eternity both of soul and of body, let us celebrate this most sacred feast with rational devotion and chaste joy,

[Note: Earlier editions, together with manuscripts of the later collections, have “the day of this most sacred feast.” The Padiliron codex has “the day of the most sacred feast.” Immediately afterward, the words “and chaste joy” are absent from the oldest Vatican manuscript.]

confessing with the blessed apostle Paul that the Lord Jesus Christ, when he ascended on high, “led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19; Ephesians 4:8), so that God’s Gospel might be preached through every expression of human speech, and every tongue might confess that “the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:11).

[Note: From the oldest Vatican manuscript we added the words *beato apostolo* (“blessed apostle”). From the same manuscript and the first edition we have written *erat* (“was”) instead of *fuerat* (“had been”) in the phrase “because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”]

## Chapter IX

For the present solemnity, dearly beloved, we must also add this devotion: let us celebrate the fast that follows from apostolic tradition, because this too must be counted among the great gifts of the Holy Spirit. Through fasting, defenses have been granted to us against the allurements of the flesh and the snares of the devil, so that, with God’s help, we may conquer every temptation.

[Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript has *maxima* (“greatest”), which we preferred. The reading is also confirmed by two manuscripts mentioned by Quesnellus. Shortly afterward, the same Vatican manuscript has *concupiscentiam* (“desire”) instead of *illecebras* (“allurements”); Quesnellus perhaps has *concupiscentias* (“desires”) from one of his codices.]

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; on Saturday, let us celebrate vigils at the blessed apostle Peter’s basilica, with that same apostle interceding for our prayers, so that in all things we may deserve to obtain the mercy of God, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# Sermon LXXVII [formerly LXXV]  
## On Pentecost III

### Summary

I. The Holy Spirit did not begin his gifts at Pentecost but increased them, since the undivided Trinity acts.

II. It arose from sin that the persons of the Trinity should divide among themselves the work of our restoration, and how this occurred.

III. That division does not conflict in any way with the equality and consubstantiality of the persons.

IV. Nothing resembling created or visible things should be conceived concerning the Trinity, which is wholly equal.

V. Why Christ wishes the disciples to rejoice at his ascension.

VI. The three persons have one being and perform one work.

## Chapter I

This present feast, venerable throughout the whole world, dearly beloved, was consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, who, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, came upon the apostles and the people of believers, as had been expected (Acts 2:1).

[Note: In the oldest Vatican manuscript, 3835: “The Lord, on the fiftieth day after his resurrection, came upon the apostles and the people of believers, as had been hoped.”]

It was expected because the Lord Jesus had promised that he would come (Luke 24:47; Acts 1:4), not so that he would then first begin to dwell in the saints, but so that he might kindle more fervently the hearts consecrated to him and pour over them more abundantly—augmenting his gifts, not beginning them, and therefore not being new in his work because he was richer in generosity.

[Note: Earlier editions, together with manuscripts of the later collections, have *promiserat* (“had promised”).]

For the majesty of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit has never been separated from the omnipotence of the Father; and whatever divine governance does in the ordering of all things proceeds from the providence of the whole Trinity. There is one benevolence of mercy and one judgment of justice; nothing is divided in action where nothing is different in will.

[Note: The same edition and codex have: “Whom, then, does the Father illuminate?”]

The Father illuminates, the Son illuminates, and the Holy Spirit illuminates; and although the person who is sent is one, the person who sends another, and the person who promises another, unity and Trinity are simultaneously manifested to us: an essence possessing equality and not admitting solitude, of the same substance and yet understood not to be the same person.

## Chapter II

Therefore, while the cooperation of the inseparable Godhead remains intact, the fact that some things are carried out by the Father, some by the Son, and some properly by the Holy Spirit is the arrangement of our redemption and the means of our salvation.

For if the human being, made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 1:26), had remained in the honor of his nature and, deceived by the devil’s fraud, had not strayed through desire from the law imposed upon him,

[Note: One Vatican codex adds *post concupiscentias* (“after desires”).]

the Creator of the world would not have become a creature; nor would the eternal have undergone temporality, nor would the Son, God equal to God the Father, have assumed the form of a servant and the likeness of sinful flesh.

[Note: Three of our manuscripts and the first edition have *intravit* (“entered”) below instead of *introivit* (“entered”).]

But because, through the devil’s envy, death entered the world (Wisdom 2:24), and human captivity could not otherwise be released unless he undertook our cause who, without loss to his majesty, would both become truly human and alone remain free from the contagion of sin, the mercy of the Trinity divided among itself the work of our restoration: so that the Father might be appeased, the Son might appease, and the Holy Spirit might kindle.

For it was necessary that those who were to be saved should also do something on their own behalf, and, with their hearts turned toward the Redeemer, should withdraw from the enemy’s domination:

[Note: The first edition and the Bononian codex have *ab nimia damnatione discederent* (“should withdraw from excessive condemnation”). The other editions before Quesnellus have the reading in the text, with the single exception that they prefer *desciscerent* (“should break away”) instead of *discederent* (“should withdraw”). Our codices, however, agree with Quesnellus, and we have printed that reading.]

for, as the Apostle says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6).

[Note: The first edition and the Bononian manuscript have *in quo clamamus* (“in whom we cry out”).]

“Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17). And “no one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

## Chapter III

If, therefore, guided by grace, dearly beloved, we faithfully and wisely understand what is proper to the Father, what to the Son, and what to the Holy Spirit in our restoration, and what is common to them, we shall undoubtedly receive the things accomplished humbly and bodily for our sake in such a way that we shall think nothing unworthy of the one and same glory of the Trinity.

Although no mind is sufficient for thinking about God, and no tongue for speaking of him, nevertheless, whatever it is that is grasped by human understanding concerning the essence of the Father’s Godhead, unless it is one and the same when one thinks either of his Only-Begotten Son or of the Holy Spirit, one does not think piously but is blinded by excessive carnality, and even what seemed to have been appropriately understood concerning the Father is lost.

[Note: The Veronese codex has: “Whatever the human intellect reaches …”]

[Note: Thus all our codices and the editions before Quesnellus. Quesnellus, without citing any manuscript and perhaps to make the sentence clearer, printed *esse* (“to be”) with *cum de Unigenito* (“when concerning the Only-Begotten”). The reading we have printed is also confirmed by the manuscripts and edition of the treatise *Against Eutyches*, chapter 2, where this chapter is inserted. That treatise will be presented in the appendix.]

[Note: From the oldest Vatican manuscript and two Veronese manuscripts: *a tota* (“from the whole”).]

For one departs from the whole Trinity if unity is not maintained in it. And there is no true unity if something differs by any inequality.

## Chapter IV

Therefore, when we direct the mind’s attention toward confessing the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, let us drive far from our minds the forms of visible things and the temporal ages of created natures, the bodies of places and the places of bodies. Let whatever is extended through space, bounded by an end, or neither always everywhere nor wholly present depart from the heart.

Let thought formed concerning the Godhead of the Trinity understand nothing through distance and seek nothing through degrees;

[Note: Thus all our codices. The printed editions, after placing a full stop, have: “But if anything …”]

and if it has conceived anything worthy of God, let it not dare deny this to any person there, as though it should ascribe more honor to the Father by refusing to attribute it to the Son and the Spirit. It is not piety to prefer the Begetter to the Only-Begotten; an insult to the Son is an injury to the Father; whatever is taken from one is taken from both.

For since eternity and Godhead are common to them, the omnipotent Father would not be regarded as omnipotent, nor immutable as immutable, if either he begot one lesser than himself or advanced by possessing what he had not possessed.

## Chapter V

The Lord Jesus does indeed say to his disciples, as the Gospel reading has related: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). But those ears that have often heard, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and, “Whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14:9), receive these words without any difference in Godhead and do not understand them as referring to that essence which they know to be eternal with the Father and of the same nature.

[Note: The printed editions had *ejusdem naturae noverunt esse firma ratione* (“they know by firm reasoning that he is of the same nature”), while Quesnellus noted in the margin: “One Oxford manuscript omits these three words, *esse firma ratione*.” We followed the reading of the oldest Vatican manuscript and the Veronese Lectionary, which partly confirms this omission.]

Thus, in the incarnation of the Word, advancement in humanity is commended even to the holy apostles; and those who were troubled by the Lord’s announced departure are encouraged to eternal joys by an increase of their honor.

“If you loved me,” he says, “you would certainly rejoice, because I am going to the Father” (ibid., 28)—that is, if with perfect knowledge you saw what glory is bestowed upon you through this: that, begotten from God the Father, I was also born from a human mother; that I, Lord of eternal things, willed to be one of mortals; that I, invisible, presented myself as visible; that, eternal in the form of God, I received the form of a servant: “You would rejoice, because I am going to the Father.”

[Note: This is more correctly read from the same codices than in the printed editions: “This ascension is granted for you,” that is, this ascension takes place for your benefit; and therefore you should rejoice, because I am going to the Father.]

For this ascension is granted to you, and your lowliness in me is raised above all the heavens to be placed at the Father’s right hand. But I, who am with the Father what the Father is, remain indivisible with the Begetter; and, coming from him to you, I do not depart from him, just as, returning to him, I do not leave you.

Rejoice, therefore, because I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I. For I have united you to myself and have become the Son of Man, so that you might be sons of God. Thus, although I am one in both, insofar as I am conformed to you I am less than the Father; but insofar as I am not divided from the Father, I am greater even than myself.

[Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript has *quod vobis* (“that which is for you”); below, together with certain other codices and the editions before Quesnellus, it has *quod autem a Patre* (“but that which is from the Father”). We did not alter Quesnellus’s reading from the first edition, supported by collection 3, because we considered it better.]

Therefore let the nature that is lesser than the Father go to the Father, so that there the flesh may be where the Word always is; and let the one faith of the Catholic Church, which does not deny that he is lesser according to his humanity, believe him equal according to his Godhead.

[Note: Thus all our codices. Another reading has *vadit* (“goes”). Shortly afterward, the Veronese manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts have *et ibi sit caro* (“and there let the flesh be”); and then the oldest Vatican manuscript has *ut una Ecclesiae catholicae fides* (“so that there may be one faith of the Catholic Church”), without the conjunction *et*. That reading would be preferable if it were more pleasing to read earlier, “and there …”]

## Chapter VI

Let the vain and blind cunning of heretical impiety therefore be despised, dearly beloved, which flatters itself with a perverse interpretation of this statement. When the Lord says, “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15), it does not understand that it takes away from the Father whatever it dares deny to the Son, and it is so foolish in matters concerning Christ’s humanity that it thinks the Only-Begotten lacked the Father’s possessions because he assumed ours.

[Note: Earlier editions had *scientiae* (“of knowledge”) in the text and *sententiae* (“of interpretation”) in the margin; Quesnellus inserted the latter into the text, as it is also found in our manuscripts. He added to *scaeva* (“perverse”) the marginal note “that is, left-handed.”]

Mercy does not diminish God’s power, nor is the reconciliation of the beloved creature a defect in eternal glory.

[Note: The first edition has: “What the Father has, the Son also has, and the Holy Spirit has.”]

What the Father has, the Son has; and what the Father and the Son have, the Holy Spirit has, because the whole Trinity together is one God.

This faith was not discovered by earthly wisdom, nor persuaded by human opinion; the Only-Begotten Son himself taught it, and the Holy Spirit himself established it. Concerning him we must think nothing differently from what we think concerning the Father and the Son. For although he is not the Father and is not the Son, he is nevertheless not divided from the Father and the Son; and just as he has his own person within the Trinity, so he has one substance within the Godhead of the Father and the Son, filling all things, containing all things, and governing all things together with the Father and the Son. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Thus the oldest Vatican manuscript. The editions before Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of the later collections, have: “through infinite ages of ages. Amen.” Quesnellus has: “governing through the ages. Amen.”]

# Sermon LXXVIII [formerly LXXVI]

[Note: This title is found in manuscripts 2, 3, and 5 of the collections. In the first edition and in manuscript 3 of the collections, this sermon is entitled “Sermon IV on Pentecost”; its opening clearly shows that it was delivered on Pentecost itself. In the Casinensis manuscript of collection 1, all the following sermons—2, 3, and 4—on the Pentecost fast are included under the same title, “On Holy Pentecost.” A similar codex existed in the possession of Micrologus; for in chapter 25 of *On Ecclesiastical Observance*, when recalling a book of Saint Leo’s sermons, he says that Leo composed several sermons on Pentecost in different years. The word “several” shows that in that manuscript book all the sermons on the Pentecost fast were included under the title “On Pentecost.”

This fast, however, carried out within the octave of Pentecost, was formerly called “the fast of the fourth month,” just as in the oldest Sacramentary, edited from manuscripts of the chapter of Verona by Father Joseph Blanchini and attributed to Leo, the proper Mass of this fast—whose several sentences, and even words, agree exactly with the sentences and words of this first sermon, as we shall note below in their places—is presented under the title “In the fast of the fourth month.” The same title is preserved in Cardinal Thomasius’s Gelasian Sacramentary, book I, no. 83, and also in the Gregorian Sacramentary, which Muratori edited from two ancient and purer manuscripts.

Hence the title of the following sermons—if they are believed to have formerly been inscribed “On the Fast,” rather than “On Pentecost”—seems to have been “On the Fast of the Fourth Month,” just as the sermons of the other four seasons are entitled “On the Fast of the Seventh Month” or “of the Tenth Month.” Without any authority from the codices, however, we did not wish to alter anything.]

## On the Pentecost Fast I

### Summary

I. Fasts were instituted by the Holy Spirit so that Christians might fight more forcefully against their enemies.

II. Against one who is free from carnal desires, the devil is unarmed.

III. The fast was instituted after the feasts so that their fruit might remain and the negligent might not go unpunished.

IV. The fast accompanied by mercy has the greatest power.

## Chapter I
Today’s festival, dearly beloved, consecrated by the descent of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0416A], is followed, as you know, by the solemn fast, salutarily instituted for the healing of souls and bodies, which we are bound to celebrate with devout observance.

[Note: “Either,” says Quesnellus in his annotation, “the Church copied these words of Leo into the collect read on the first Saturday of Lent, or that collect was already then in use in the ecclesiastical offices, from which our author borrowed these words. From either alternative it may be inferred either how highly St. Leo is esteemed in the Church, or how ancient are the collects which the Church now uses in the divine offices.” More truly, St. Leo was the author of certain prayers read in the divine offices, as is clear from the very ancient Sacramentary mentioned above. Even if that Sacramentary is not entirely St. Leo’s, it nevertheless seems to contain no small number of compositions written by Leo and received into the use of the sacred offices, as will be shown in the notice concerning that Sacramentary in volume II. Among them is the prayer now read on the first Saturday of Lent; but in that Sacramentary it is placed under “The Fast of the Fourth Month,” that is, the fast of Pentecost, to which this sermon also belongs. The prayer in that same Sacramentary is as follows: “Be present, Lord, to your suppliants, so that we may celebrate with devoted service this solemn fast, salutarily instituted for the healing of souls and bodies.”]

For when the apostles had been filled with the promised power and the Spirit of truth had entered their hearts, we have no doubt that, among the other mysteries of heavenly teaching, this discipline of spiritual self-restraint was first conceived under the instruction of the Paraclete, so that minds sanctified by fasting might become more capable of receiving the charisms bestowed upon them. [Note: The printed editions read *quippe* (“indeed”), but *quidem* is better, from the Verona Lectionary, as the following context shows.]

Indeed, Christ’s disciples possessed the protection of almighty assistance, and the entire divinity of the Father and the Son presided over the leaders of the nascent Church in the presence of the Holy Spirit. But against the assaults of persecutors pressing upon them, against the threatening roars of the ungodly, the struggle was not to be waged by bodily strength [Col. 0416B] or by the fullness of flesh, since what delights the exterior chiefly corrupts the interior of a person; and the rational soul becomes purer in proportion as the substance of the flesh is more afflicted.

## Chapter II

These teachers, then, who instructed all the children of the Church by their examples and traditions, began the campaign of Christian warfare with holy fasts [Note: In the aforementioned Sacramentary, another prayer in a Mass for the Fast of the Fourth Month is recognized as derived from these words: “Grant us, Lord, to begin the defenses of Christian warfare with holy fasts, so that, as we are about to fight against spiritual wickedness, we may be fortified by the weapons of self-restraint.” This same prayer, transferred into the codex of Cardinal Thomasius’s Gelasian Sacramentary, is read in book I, no. 83. Shortly afterward, instead of *sanctis jejuniis inchoarunt* (“they began with holy fasts”), we have written *sanctis inchoavere jejuniis* (“they began with holy fasts”), which agrees better with the prayer just quoted, following the manuscript Lectionary of Verona; the printed editions had the former reading.], so that, about to fight against spiritual wickedness, they might take up the weapons of abstinence [Note: Manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 and editions before Quesnellus read *raperent* (“might seize”); manuscript collection 4 reads *reciperent* (“might receive”).], by which they might cut off the incitements of vices.

For invisible adversaries and incorporeal enemies will not be strong against us if we have not been immersed in any carnal desires. The tempter’s desire to do harm is perpetual, but he will be unarmed [Col. 0417A] and ineffective if he finds nothing in us with which to fight against us. Yet who, surrounded by this fragile flesh and established in this body of death—even one who has made great and vigorous progress—can already be so secure about his salvation that he believes himself free from every danger of enticement? [Note: The Verona codex and Vatican manuscript collection 5 read *valdeque* (“and very vigorously”).] Although divine grace may grant his saints daily victory, it does not remove the occasion for battle, since this too belongs to the mercy of the One who protects us: he wished something always to remain for mutable nature to conquer, lest it grow proud over a battle already finished. [Note: Thus from our manuscripts, *ab omni* (“from every”), rather than the reading “from all” in the printed editions.]

## Chapter III

Therefore, after the days of holy joy which we spent in honor of the Lord rising from the dead and then ascending into heaven, and after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, the practice of fasting has been salutarily and necessarily ordained [Note: The Verona manuscript reads “salutarily necessary.”]: so that, if during the very joys of the festivals careless freedom and disordered license have presumed upon anything, the discipline of religious abstinence may punish it. This discipline must also be observed with particular diligence so that those gifts divinely bestowed upon the Church on this day may remain in us. For having become a temple of the Holy Spirit and having been watered by the divine stream in greater abundance than ever, we must not be overcome by any desires or possessed by any vices, so that the dwelling-place of virtue may not be polluted by any contamination.

## Chapter IV

With the Lord governing and assisting us, everyone can certainly attain this, if through the purification of fasting and the generosity of mercy [Note: The Beneventan codex and the first edition read “through works of mercy.”] we strive both to be freed from the filth of sins and to be fruitful in the works of charity. Whatever is spent on the food of the poor, the treatment of the weak, the ransom of captives [Note: The conjunction *et* (“and”), omitted by Rainaudus and Quesnellus, has been restored from earlier editions and our manuscripts.], and any works of piety is not diminished but increased; nor can what faithful kindness has given ever perish with God, since whatever one gives for assistance, one stores up for oneself as a reward. For “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy from God” (Matt. 5:7); and there will be no remembrance of sins where testimony of piety has been present. Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the most blessed apostle Peter, trusting that by his prayers we shall be freed both from spiritual enemies and [Note: The first edition reads “from bodily enemies,” and then gives this conclusion to the sermon: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, who with you lives and reigns, God, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.”] from bodily foes.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. [Col. 0418B] Amen.

## Sermon LXXIX [alt. LXXVII]

[Note: In manuscript collection 3, which entitled the preceding sermon “The Fourth Sermon on Pentecost,” this sermon is prefaced by the title “The First Sermon on the Fast of Pentecost”; the same title appears in the table of contents of the first edition.]

### On the Fast of Pentecost II

### Synopsis

I. The fast of Pentecost derives from apostolic tradition and the institution of the Holy Spirit.

II. The difference between the fasts of the faithful and those of unbelievers.

III. What kind of fast does not proceed from the Holy Spirit and seeks human glory.

IV. The fast must be referred to God, because he is the author of every desire and every good work.

## Chapter I

There must be no doubt, dearly beloved, that every Christian observance is a matter of divine instruction [Note: Quesnellus’s edition omitted the adjective “Christian”; we restored it from the other editions, to which all our manuscripts except one agree.], and that whatever the Church has received into the custom of devotion [Note: The Bergamo Lectionary reads “into custom.”] has proceeded from apostolic tradition [Col. 0419A] and from the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: These statements seem consistent with Augustine’s teaching in *On Baptism*, book IV, chapter 24: “What the whole Church holds, and what has been instituted neither by councils but has always been retained, is most rightly believed to have been handed down only on apostolic authority.” Nevertheless, some disapprove that the Author attributed this prerogative of apostolic tradition also to the fast of the Four Seasons, which is under discussion here, since this fast was not always observed by the whole Church. But it seems to have become established by common usage and understanding that what was preserved by ancient observance in the Roman Church should be attributed to apostolic institution. Accordingly St. Jerome, in Epistle 71 to Lucinius, no. 6, although speaking of observances peculiar to certain churches, did not hesitate to write: “Let each province abound in its own understanding, and regard the commands of its elders as apostolic laws.”

We have further observed that Leo frequently attributes fasts and other works of Christian piety to apostolic institution for the reason that apostolic teaching commended fasting and other observances of the same kind, even though this or that particular specification of a fast or other pious work did not originate with the apostles but was instituted by the Fathers or elders from apostolic instruction. Thus he nonetheless attributes to apostolic institution certain collects peculiar to the Roman Church, which in Sermon 4 on the Collects, chapter 3, he acknowledges to have been prudently and usefully arranged by the Fathers. For, he says in Sermon 3, the most blessed disciples of truth—that is, the apostles—commended by divinely inspired teaching that whenever the blindness of the pagans was more intent upon its superstitions, then especially the people of God should persist in prayers and works of piety; yet he reports that those collects were instituted by the Fathers on the occasion of pagan superstition. Similarly, in Sermon 16, chapter 2, the holy pontiff expressly teaches that the fast of the Four Seasons in the tenth month was decreed by the Fathers, saying: “Our holy Fathers, divinely inspired, decreed the fast of the tenth month.” This can be reconciled with the apostolic tradition or institution to which he repeatedly ascribes the same fast only because, as he says in Sermon 81, chapter 1, “among all the institutions of apostolic teaching which have flowed from the fountain of divine instruction, there can be no doubt . . . that this observance was first conceived by them: that the saints should begin the rules of all the virtues with the holy observance of fasting.”] He now also presides over the hearts of the faithful through his institutions, so that all may preserve them obediently and understand them wisely.

For when, on Pentecost—the fiftieth day after the Lord’s Passover, as we celebrate it—the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord filled the minds of those awaiting him with greater abundance and with the clearer presence of his majesty [the supplied text has *qua . . . amquam*, evidently an OCR-distorted form of *quam umquam*, “than ever”], it is perfectly clear that, among the other gifts of God, the grace of fasting, which immediately and inseparably follows today’s festival, was also then bestowed: so that, just as desire was the beginning of sins, self-restraint might be the origin of virtues.

[Note: The preface of the aforementioned Mass has the same wording in the Verona Sacramentary, annotation 2: “It is truly worthy. After those days of holy joy which we spent in honor of the Lord rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, and after receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, these holy fasts were necessarily provided for us, so that, living with pure conduct, the things divinely bestowed upon the Church might remain. Through …” The close agreement of this Mass with the present sermon seems to demonstrate a common author. This preface is also read in the Gelasian Sacramentary.]

## Chapter II

In practicing this gift of God, we must not therefore be more sluggish because Jews and heretics often restrain themselves from freedom in eating, and because among the pagans also there are certain vain fasts [Note: The first edition and the Beneventan codex read *nova* (“new”), incorrectly. The reference is to fasts practiced by pagans for the sake of vainglory, which are consequently assigned to deception under falsehood. The author likewise recalls the fasts of the Pharisees, which he called idle in Sermon 89, chapter 1, and describes in Sermon 92, chapter 2, as undertaken to seek human praise. Three of our manuscripts shortly afterward read: “But one thing …”.]. For reason acts one way under truth, while deception acts another under falsehood. Among us, faith sanctifies even the one who eats; among them, unbelief pollutes the one who fasts [Note: The meaning of this passage will be explained in the observations.].

Therefore, since outside the Catholic Church nothing is whole and nothing is pure, as the Apostle says, “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), we are not compared with those separated from the unity of Christ’s body by any likeness, nor mingled with them by any communion. This is certainly for us the most salutary and greatest fast. For nothing belongs more essentially to the virtue of self-restraint than abstaining from errors, because one walks well only when one proceeds along the way of truth. Since those who turn aside from the narrow and difficult path and pursue the easy and broad one quickly arrive at destruction, a slower step along the straight road is better than swift speed along a crooked one.

## Chapter III

Let the Catholic Christian therefore recognize the fruit of his fast, which, even amid the greatest generosity, will be utterly barren unless it has proceeded from the watering of the Holy Spirit [Note: Quesnellus, following Rainaudus’s edition, reads “the holiness of his fast.” We preferred the reading of the earlier editions and our manuscripts, especially since the noun “fruit” agrees completely with the adjective “most barren” that follows.].

For since the Apostle says that no virtues benefit him without charity (1 Cor. 13:1), and likewise says that the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5), we must beware lest we lose through pride the good things which we cannot do without goodness. For he strips himself deservedly of all praise who glories more in himself than in the Lord concerning the efforts of his diligence (1 Cor. 1:31; 2 Cor. 10:17; Jer. 9:23). Blessed David teaches that God is to be praised in the works of the saints, saying: “Wonderful is God in his saints; the God of Israel himself will give strength and power to his people” (Ps. 67:36). And again: “Lord, they shall walk in the light of your countenance, and in your name they shall rejoice all the day, and in your righteousness they shall be exalted, for you are the glory of their strength” (Ps. 88:17).

## Chapter IV

Therefore, dearly beloved, in accordance with the instruction of the Holy Spirit, through whom all the gifts of the virtues have been bestowed upon the Church of God, let us undertake this solemn fast with eager faith. [Note: The Beneventan codex and the first edition read *ut in mandatis* (“as in the commandments”). Shortly afterward, Vatican manuscript collection 5 reads *potuerimus* (“we shall be able”) instead of *poterimus* (“we are able”).] In the commandments which we are able to fulfill, let us restrain ourselves from boastful self-inflation, referring everything to the glory of God, who both inspires good intentions and is the author of good actions. The Lord says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16). He lives and reigns [Note: Some manuscripts add “with the Son and the Holy Spirit.”] forever and ever. [Col. 0420B] Amen.

## Sermon LXXX [alt. LXXVIII]

[Note: It is clear that the two preceding sermons were delivered on the feast of Pentecost: the first mentions at its beginning “the present festival consecrated to the descent of the Holy Spirit,” and the second likewise calls it “the present festival” in chapter 1, which the grace of fasting immediately follows. The fact that this third sermon was delivered on the very day of the fast seems to be indicated by the words with which, at the beginning, it reports that the order of the holy solemnities has been celebrated and the devotion of spiritual joy completed.]

### On the Fast of Pentecost III

### Synopsis

One must fast in such a way that what is withdrawn from food is devoted to charity, which surpasses fasting.

After the order of the holy solemnities has been celebrated, dearly beloved, and the devotion of spiritual joy has been completed, we ought to return to the salutary practice of moderation and apply the remedy of fasting both to exercise our minds and to discipline our bodies. Divine admonitions and our own experience have taught us enough about this. First, through the return of these most sacred days [Note: Thus from the editions before Quesnellus, which read “after the passing of them.”], let us give thanks to divine mercy; then, desiring the holy delights of self-restraint, let us withdraw somewhat from the abundance of earthly foods [Col. 0420C], so that what is not spent on food may benefit almsgiving. [Note: Editions before Quesnellus, except the first, read “so that it may benefit …”.]

Only then does the medicine of fasting benefit the healing of the soul, when the abstinence of the one who fasts refreshes the hunger of the needy. Since we know, therefore, that with the merciful God the generosity of almsgiving surpasses fasting, the Lord himself saying, “Give alms, and everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41), if we desire to cleanse our souls from the filth of sins, let us not deny alms to the poor, so that on the day of recompense we may be assisted by works of mercy in obtaining God’s mercy, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## Sermon LXXXI [alt. LXXIX]

### On the Fast of Pentecost IV

[Col. 0420D]

### Synopsis

I. Since gluttony was the cause of sin, it must therefore be crushed by abstinence.

II. The inner person is wiser in proportion as the outer person restrains itself from the enticements of the senses.

III. After the times of indulgence, one must return to fasting so that negligence may either be corrected or not creep in.

IV. Through fasting and good works a person is cleansed from sins.

## Chapter I

Among all the institutions of apostolic teaching which have flowed from the fountain of divine instruction [Note: Thus in agreement with Quesnellus, our manuscripts likewise read, and similarly Sermon 79, chapter 1: “There must be no doubt that every Christian observance is a matter of divine instruction.” The other editions read “institution.”], there can be no doubt that, with the Holy Spirit influencing the leaders of the Church, this observance was first conceived by them: that the saints should begin the rules of all the virtues with the practice of fasting. For it would greatly aid the fulfillment of God’s commandments if the Christian army fortified itself by the sanctification of self-restraint against every incitement of vice. Since the first cause of sin entered through the enticement of food, what more salutary gift of God can redeemed freedom use than learning to abstain from what was permitted, when it had not known how to restrain itself from what was forbidden?

Every creature of God is indeed good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (1 Tim. 4:4). But we were not created for this purpose: to seek all the resources of the world with foul and shameless greed [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “imprudent greed,”] as though what may be consumed might not be left aside.

## Chapter II

Let God be praised, who has given so many things for human use. But let the rational mind recognize that greater delights have been given to the mind than to the flesh. And when it hears the Holy Spirit say to it, “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will” (Sirach 18:30) [Note: The same two manuscripts read “lest you follow them”; and afterward, instead of “to turn away,” one of them, collection 5, and the first edition of collection 3 read “to forbid.”], let it understand that, against all the things which flatter the bodily senses [Note: The same manuscripts read “bodily senses.”], it must pursue the virtue of temperance, through which, as the pleasure of the outer person diminishes, the wisdom of the inner person increases.

For the heart does not have the same vigor under the burden of food as under the lightness of fasting; nor can satiety produce the same perception as moderation. For when the flesh that desires is overcome by spiritual desire in opposition to the spirit (Gal. 5:17), sound health and healthy freedom are secured, so that the flesh is governed by the judgment of the mind and the mind by God’s assistance.

## Chapter III

The present time therefore invites us, dearly beloved, to this benefit: after fifty days have elapsed from the Lord’s resurrection to the coming of the Holy Spirit, days which we spent in the joy of the chief festival, let us return to the remedies of fasting [Note: The first edition and the Beneventan codex read “let us hasten together.”], lest, through the opportunity of a more flattering license, the enjoyment of pleasures should perhaps incur some faults of negligence.

For the soil of our flesh, unless it is broken up by constant cultivation, quickly produces thorns and thistles from sluggish idleness; and through degenerate growth it will yield a fruit fit not to be brought into barns [Col. 0422A] but to be burned in the fires.
