The Lord says: “Every planting which my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. 5:13). We must therefore guard the nobility of all the shoots and seeds which we have received from the planting of the supreme Farmer, and with vigilant care provide that no gifts of God be violated through the fraud of the envious enemy, and that a forest of vices not grow thick in the paradise of virtues.

## Chapter IV

To avoid this evil, nothing is more powerful than almsgiving and fasting: self-restraint kills carnal desires, while care for mercy multiplies the fruit of spiritual desires [Note: Thus our manuscripts and all editions except Quesnellus’s read “care”; Quesnellus’s edition, without indicating any manuscript, has “cultivation.”]. Therefore we solemnly exhort your charity: desiring to be cleansed from the filth of all sins through the discipline of the body and works of piety [Note: The first edition reads: “Let us take care to be cleansed from the filth of all sins. Therefore, on Wednesday and Friday, etc.”], let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the most blessed apostle Peter. By his merits and prayers, we believe that we shall be so assisted in every way that the mercy of God will be present both to our fasts and to our prayers, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

## Sermon LXXXII [alt. LXXX]

### On the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul

[Col. 0422D]

### Synopsis

I. How greatly Rome’s glory has increased through religion and the ministry of the apostles.

II. How the Roman Empire served the rule of Christ.

III. Why the principal see of the Church was established at Rome.

IV. The great courage and charity of Peter when he entered Rome.

V. Peter’s labors before he came to Rome.

VI. Peter and Paul, joined to Peter, are two splendid shoots of the divine seed.

VII. How greatly one should rejoice on their feast.

## Chapter I

Although the entire world shares in all the holy solemnities, dearly beloved, the piety of one faith requires that whatever has been done for the salvation of all and is commemorated should everywhere be celebrated with common rejoicing. Nevertheless, today’s festival, beyond the reverence it has earned throughout the world, must be honored with the special and distinctive exultation of our own city, so that where the end of the chief apostles was glorified, there, on the day of their martyrdom, joy may hold primacy. [Note: The Verona Lectionary of St. Firmus Major reads “we commemorate” instead of “is commemorated.” Quesnellus appended a lengthy annotation to these words; you will find it among the observations, where it has been illustrated by what we hope is a useful investigation.]

These are the men through whom the Gospel of Christ shone upon you, Rome; you who were once a teacher of error have become a disciple of truth. These are [Note: The word “holy” has been added from the very ancient Vatican manuscript 3835, the aforementioned Verona manuscript, and Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary.] your holy fathers and true shepherds, who established you for insertion into the heavenly kingdoms much more wisely and much more successfully than those whose efforts laid the first foundations of your walls—one of whom, the man who gave you your name, stained you with fraternal blood.

These are the men who raised you to such glory [Col. 0423A] that, as a holy nation, an elect people, a priestly and royal city, through the sacred see of blessed Peter you became the head of the world and presided more broadly through divine religion than through earthly domination. [Note: Here it should be observed that although Leo called Saints Peter and Paul the fathers and true shepherds of the city of Rome shortly before, he nevertheless assigns the episcopal see to Peter alone and teaches that through it Rome was made the head of the world. Because of this see it presides over the whole world, so that from that point it presides more widely through divine religion than through earthly rule. These words correspond to those of Prosper in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*:

> The see of Peter, Rome, which by pastoral honor  
> Has been made head of the world, whatever it does not possess by arms  
> It holds by religion.

Similar statements are found in the author of *On the Calling of All Nations*, book II, chapter 16. From this, however, the dignity and authority of primacy, which extends throughout the whole world, even beyond the boundaries of the Roman Empire, could not have originated from the imperial city to which Peter’s episcopate was attached, as certain heterodox thinkers have dreamed.]

For although you increased your power by many victories and extended your imperial authority by land and sea, what warlike labor subjected to you is nevertheless less than what Christian peace has made subject to you.

## Chapter II

For the good, just, and almighty God, who has never denied his mercy to the human race and has always instructed all mortals alike in knowledge of himself through his abundant benefits, [Note: The most ancient Vatican manuscript, likewise Roman, adds after “denied”: “he also placed for our protection in this city the blessed apostles and martyrs.” These words may perhaps have been omitted from other manuscript Lectionaries serving the use of other churches, and then from the collections, as being peculiar to the city of Rome.] took pity, through a more hidden plan and a deeper mercy, on the voluntary blindness of those who were in error and their inclination toward worse things, by sending his Word, equal and coeternal with himself. [Note: Editions before Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of collections 3 and 5, read: “Therefore the Word, having become flesh.” Quesnellus’s emendation is supported by our Lectionaries and by manuscripts of other collections.]

When this Word became flesh [Col. 0423B], he so united the divine nature with human nature that the descent of the former to the lowest things became for us an elevation to the highest. But in order that the effect of this ineffable grace might be spread throughout the world, divine providence prepared the Roman Empire, whose growth was brought to the boundaries where the whole neighboring and contiguous multitude of all nations was gathered. For the work divinely arranged it was especially fitting that many kingdoms should be confederated under one empire and that general preaching should quickly find peoples accessible—peoples whom the government of a single city held together. [Note: The Beneventan codex and the first edition read “continuous.”]

Yet this city, ignorant of the author of its advancement, while ruling almost all nations, served the errors of all nations; and it seemed to itself to have embraced a great religion because it had rejected no falsehood. [Note: Thus from the very ancient Vatican manuscript, the Verona manuscript, and Paul the Deacon; elsewhere, from the same manuscripts and from two other manuscripts of collections 4 and 5, *respuerat* (“had rejected”) is read, whereas the first edition has *respueret* (“would reject”) and the other editions *respuebat* (“was rejecting”).]

Therefore, to the extent that it had been more tightly bound by the devil, to that extent it was more wondrously freed by Christ. [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and the first edition read “by how much,” and afterward “by so much.” In the very ancient Vatican manuscript, instead of “more wondrously,” the reading is “more mercifully.”]

## Chapter III

For when the twelve apostles, having received through the Holy Spirit the speech of all languages, had undertaken the evangelization of the world, dividing the regions of the earth among themselves, the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostolic order [Note: From the most ancient Roman Sacramentary, which will be published in volume II, it is clear that certain sentences of this sermon, and even several distinctive words, were transferred into the preface for the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, no. 10, as comparison will show.], was sent to the citadel of the Roman Empire, so that the light of truth, which was being revealed for the salvation of all nations, might spread more effectively from the head itself throughout the body of the world.

What nation’s people were not then in this city? What peoples anywhere were ignorant of what Rome had learned? [Note: We have restored this reading not so much from editions before Quesnellus as from six of our manuscripts. To be sure, the remaining passages, similarly expressed as participles—*dissolvendae* (“to be dissolved”), *confutandus* (“to be refuted”), and *destruenda* (“to be destroyed”)—seem to require the participle *conculcandae* (“to be trampled down”). Quesnellus substituted *colluctantes* (“struggling”) from three of his manuscripts; but the reading *colluctandae* in the very ancient Vatican manuscript is better and more coherent.] Here the opinions of philosophy were to be trampled down; here the vanities of earthly wisdom were to be dissolved; here the worship of demons was to be refuted; here all the impiety of sacrifices [Col. 0424B] was to be destroyed, where whatever had anywhere been devised through various errors had been gathered with the most meticulous superstition. [Note: Editions before Quesnellus read “all sacrileges,” together with the very ancient Vatican manuscript and manuscripts of collections 3 and 4. In the margin they note “sacrifices.” Quesnellus inserted this word into the text from four of his manuscripts; we have not removed it, since we found it in the Verona Lectionary, in manuscripts of collection 5, and in the copy of Paul the Deacon. Shortly afterward, “through various errors” is preferred to “through vain errors” on the authority of three excellent Lectionaries.]

## Chapter IV

[Note: In Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary the reading is: “so that with Paul, your companion in glory, . . . you might enter more steadfastly than when walking on the sea.” Yet this is supported by no other manuscripts and moreover conflicts with Leo’s point: since he represents Paul as still occupied with arranging other churches, he could not have affirmed that Peter entered Rome with him. Moreover, this chapter indicates that Peter was in Rome under Claudius, while chapter 6 states that Paul was joined to him under Nero’s rule. These points also seem to derive from Prosper’s *Chronicle*, which we shall show Leo used in the observations on Sermon 77.]

Therefore, most blessed apostle Peter, you do not fear coming to this city, and, while your companion in glory, the apostle Paul, is still occupied with organizing other churches, you enter this forest of roaring beasts and this ocean of the most turbulent depths, more steadfast than when you were walking upon the sea (Matt. 14:30). Nor do you fear Rome, mistress of the world, although in the house of Caiaphas you had feared a priest’s maidservant (Matt. 26:70). Was either the power of Claudius or the cruelty of Nero less than the judgment of Pilate or the savagery of the Jews?

The force of love therefore overcame the matter of fear; [Note: Editions commonly read, together with the Verona Lectionary and later manuscript collections: “Nor did you think that one should yield to terror while you cared for the salvation of those whom you had undertaken to love.” Following this reading, Quesnellus, like Latinus Latinius, conjectured that instead of *diligendos* (“to be loved”), *dirigendos* (“to be directed”) might perhaps be read more suitably. But he says: “It was a matter of scruple to alter even a little letter without the authority of a manuscript,” and adds: “The editions of Canisius and Surius and the Victorine manuscript—and two of our Vatican manuscripts of collection 5—read *alendos* (‘to be nourished’),” which was also placed in the margin of the printed editions. The entire difficulty is removed by the reading inserted into the text on the authority of the very ancient Vatican manuscript and three Vallicellian Lectionaries, which also agrees well with the preceding words “fear” and “love.” Shortly afterward, the very ancient Vatican manuscript reads “ardor” instead of “affection.”] and you did not consider those whom you had undertaken to love objects of fear. You had certainly conceived this feeling of fearless charity already when the profession of your love for the Lord was confirmed by the mystery of the threefold questioning (John 21:15–17). Nor was anything else sought from this intention of your mind than that, by feeding the sheep of the one whom you loved [Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads “whom you love.”], you should provide them with the food with which you yourself had grown rich.

## Chapter V
The many signs of miracles, the many gifts of charisms, and the many proofs of spiritual powers also increased your confidence. [Note: [Col. 0425C] We have written *tot* (“so many”) instead of *atque* (“and”), which stood in the printed editions, from the most ancient Vatican manuscript, since it agrees better with the Leonine syntax.] You had already instructed the peoples who had come to believe from the circumcision; you had already founded the Church of Antioch, where the dignity of the Christian name first arose (Acts 11:26); you had already imbued Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia with the laws of evangelical preaching. [Note: [Col. 0426B–C] Thus better from the cited most ancient Vatican manuscript and two Vallicellan manuscripts. Others read *impleveras* (“you had filled”). This should not be referred to the Epistles that Peter sent to these provinces, since the holy pontiff here speaks from the context of events preceding Peter’s arrival at Rome under Claudius; moreover, at that time Peter’s two arrivals in the City were not distinguished, as may be inferred from Prosper’s *Chronicle*, used by the Romans of that age. Peter’s first Epistle to those provinces was written from Rome, after he had at least passed through them and preached the Gospel there; otherwise there was no reason for him to write to these provinces rather than others. Thus Quesnellus’s conjecture for excluding Asia from this sermon—that Leo could have thought Peter had not preached the Gospel to the Asians—falls away.] [Note: [Col. 0425C] The word *Asia* is absent from the manuscripts of Thuaneus, Corbeiensis, Oxoniensis, and Sammaglorianus. Hence we rightly suspect that it was added and transferred here from the beginning of the first Epistle of the blessed apostle Peter, where Asia is added to the four provinces enumerated here; or from Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Peter, from which our Leo seems to have borrowed this material. Whatever may be the case concerning the others, this could have been his opinion, perhaps drawn from the tradition of the Roman Church, that the Gospel had not been preached to the Asians by Peter. Indeed, the churches of Asia seem to owe the seeds of their faith to the apostle Paul, since on the one hand the Apostle testifies concerning himself: “Thus I preached this Gospel, not where Christ had already been named, lest I should build on another’s foundation; but as it is written: ‘Those to whom it was not announced concerning him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.’ For this reason I was very often hindered from coming to you, and until now I have been prevented.” On the other hand, Saint Irenaeus is a witness, in Book III, chapter 3, that the Church of Ephesus, the chief church of the entire province, was founded by that teacher of the nations and later cared for by John. The many churches founded there by the same apostle are readily demonstrated by what Saint Luke reports in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Paul’s journeys through the various provinces of Asia, and concerning his three-year stay and preaching there. Here it is pleasing to cite a passage from Gregory the Great, *Homily 17 on the Gospels*: “At that great judgment,” he says, “each person’s works will be revealed. There Peter will appear with the Judea that he drew after him. There Paul, leading, so to speak, the converted world. There Andrew, with Achaea following him. There John will lead Asia, and Thomas India, converted, into the sight of his Judge,” and so forth. QUESNELLUS. But to defend the reading *Asia*, we oppose to the four manuscripts cited by Quesnell not only all the codices of the five collections, but also four manuscript Lectionaries, three Vallicellan manuscripts, and the most ancient Vatican manuscript, which, being certainly Roman, must be regarded as highly authoritative. Nevertheless, we do not deny that the word is absent from the example of Paul the Deacon and from the Veronese Lectionary.]

You were bringing the triumph of Christ’s cross into the Roman citadels, neither uncertain about the outcome of the work nor ignorant of the span of your life. [Note: [Col. 0426C–D] Thus from several and better manuscripts and also from Paul the Deacon’s Homily; the printed editions read *provectu* (“advancement”). Peter could be said not to have been ignorant of the span of his life either because Christ foretold that he would reach old age (John 21:19), “When you are old,” or because Peter wrote in 2 Peter 1:14: “Knowing that the laying aside of my tent is swift, as our Lord Jesus Christ also indicated to me.”] In bringing it, you were preceded, by divine preordinations, by both the honor of authority and the glory of martyrdom.

## CHAPTER VI

At that time the blessed apostle who was your fellow apostle, Paul, the vessel of election (Acts 9:15) and the special teacher of the nations, came to meet you and was joined to you, when every innocence, every sense of shame, and every freedom was suffering under Nero’s rule. [Note: [Col. 0426D] This reading is to be preferred on the authority of the most ancient Vatican manuscript; another reading is *eodem* (“at the same time”).] His fury, inflamed by the excess of every vice, [Note: [Col. 0426D] Another reading: *excessus* (“excesses”).] drove him into such a torrent of madness that he was the first to inflict upon the Christian name the cruelty of a general persecution, as though God’s grace could be extinguished by the slaughter of the saints. Yet for them this itself was the greatest gain: that contempt for this passing life became the means of attaining eternal happiness. [Note: [Col. 0426D] The reading *quibus* (“for whom”), found in the first edition and two Vatican manuscripts, suits the context better than the printed reading *cujus* (“of which”).] “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” [Note: [Col. 0426D] We have added the word *est* (“is”) from the most ancient Vatican manuscript, the Veronese manuscript, Paul the Deacon’s Homily, and the first edition.] (Ps. 115:15); and the religion founded upon the mystery of Christ’s cross cannot be destroyed by any kind of cruelty. The Church is not diminished by persecutions but increased; and the Lord’s field is always clothed with a richer harvest, while the grains that fall singly are born multiplied. Thus these two glorious shoots of the divine seed have sprung into so great an offspring, as the thousands of blessed martyrs testify. [Note: [Col. 0426D] Thus the principal manuscripts agree with Quesnellus and the first edition. Others read *germinaverint* (“have germinated”); editions before Quesnellus and some manuscripts read *qui apostolicorum aemuli triumphorum* (“which emulate the apostles’ triumphs”); both readings are equally good.] Emulating the apostles’ triumphs, they surrounded our city with purple-clad peoples shining far and wide, and crowned it, as though with a single diadem composed of many precious gems.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0427A]

Concerning this protection, dearest brethren, divinely prepared for us as an example of patience and a strengthening of faith, we ought indeed to rejoice universally in the commemoration of all the saints; but in the excellence of these fathers we ought rightly to glory with greater exultation. [Note: [Col. 0427A] The same editions, with the Veronese codex and manuscripts of collections 3 and 5, read: “Concerning whose protection.”] God’s grace raised them to such a height among all the members of the Church that, in the body whose head is Christ (Ephesians 1:22), he established them as a kind of twin light of the eyes. [Note: [Col. 0427A–B] Thus with Quesnellus our manuscripts read. The other editions have *excellentius* (“more excellently”). Quesnellus printed *construeret* (“might construct”) from five manuscripts; none of our codices or editions prefers it, but they read either *constituerit* or *constitueret*. We prefer the former on the authority of several of our better manuscripts, especially the most ancient Vatican manuscript.]

Concerning their merits and virtues, which surpass every power of speech, we must think neither differently nor separately, because election made them peers, their labors were alike, and their end made them equal. [Note: [Col. 0427B] The words “and their election” are absent from the most ancient Vatican manuscript. The reference is to election to the apostolate, in which Peter and Paul were equals, since both were chosen by Christ as apostles; this in no way prejudices the primacy. As Leo says in Sermon 4, chapter 2: “One Peter is chosen, to be placed before all the apostles”; and in Epistle 10, chapter 1, speaking of the apostolate, to which all the apostles were called, he says: “The mystery of this office the Lord willed to belong to the function of all the apostles, yet he principally placed it in blessed Peter, supreme among all the apostles.” He later presented them as equal, not in the power of primacy, but in their end—that is, in death or martyrdom. These matters had to be noted because of a marginal note attached to this passage in Quesnell’s edition: “Peter and Paul, the twin eyes of the Church, each equal to the other.” Quesnell himself, in his work entitled *The Discipline of the Church*, volume I, page 96, after citing the Apostle’s words in 2 Corinthians 12:11, “I was in no way inferior to those who are super-apostles,” admits that this entire equality concerns only the apostolate, not the primacy of the apostolate: “In all this, equality concerns precisely only the apostolate, not the primacy of the apostolate.” Even the French theologians, together with the Catholic Church, acknowledge that this primacy is not merely one of honor but a primacy of special power and jurisdiction. Hence Leo, shortly before, in chapter 5, recognized that Peter had received from the divine preordinations not merely honor but the honor of authority.]

As we ourselves have experienced, and as our forefathers proved, we believe and are confident that, amid all the labors of this life, we are always aided in obtaining God’s mercy by the prayers of our special patrons: so that, to the extent that our own sins weigh us down, to that extent we may be raised up by the apostles’ merits. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belongs the same power and one divinity, for ever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0428B] With the words “made them equal,” this sermon ends in the manuscripts of Corbeiensis, Thuaneus, and Sammaglorianus; the words that follow to the end are absent. From this someone might conjecture either that these words were added for the use of some Church whose special patrons, as is stated there, were the apostles Peter and Paul—something very common, as those accustomed to examining ancient Lectionaries know—or, if they are Leo’s, that this part of the sermon was shortened in manuscripts written for the use of Churches that did not have these apostles as their special patrons. QUESNELLUS. We too found the subsequent words absent, not only in Paul the Deacon’s Homily, but also in manuscripts of collection 2, in three Vallicellan Lectionaries, in one Veronese manuscript, and especially in the most ancient Vatican manuscript, which was intended for the use of the Roman basilica of Saints Philip and James. In this manuscript and in two Vallicellan manuscripts, after the word “equal,” the following conclusion is added: “Through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.” Only the codices of the later collections 3, 4, and 5 contain the words that follow. Just as Quesnellus did not dare to delete them, neither do we, especially since they contain nothing contradictory and their style does not differ from Leo’s.]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SERMON

[Col. 0427]

Quesnellus placed the following notice in his editions to explain why he had removed the next sermon and relegated it to the appendix. These are his words:

“The following sermon, Sermon 2 on the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, appears in all the editions published up to the present. It begins, ‘Let us rejoice in the Lord,’ and so forth. We have therefore removed it from our edition because, apart from the opening, which is unquestionably not Leo’s, and about five lines taken from Sermon 2 (now 3) on the Anniversary of the Assumption, the remainder has been transcribed from Sermon 3 (now 4) on the Anniversary of the same event. We shall nevertheless give it a place in the appendix. We found this sermon in a single manuscript belonging to the Royal Library. It is clearly composed for the use of some particular Church, since in the opening, where we read, ‘He deigned to give blessed Peter precedence over this city,’ the manuscript reads, ‘He deigned to give him precedence over the city of Rome.’ This alteration indicates that it was not read at Rome.” Thus he.

For some time we were uncertain about this. But after considering that this sermon is consistently attributed to Leo not only in all the manuscripts of collections 1, 2, 3, and 4, which have four different origins, but also in very many Lectionaries of excellent quality, both Vatican and foreign, wherever we found it together with this sermon, we did not dare, with Quesnellus, to deny that it was Leo’s. Accordingly, we judged that it should be left in the place it occupied in the earlier editions. This seemed to be required above all by the authority of the outstanding Vatican Lectionary 3835, which is certainly Roman and attributes nothing inauthentic to Leo. Written a thousand years ago, it also clearly reveals an even more ancient origin through a particular annotation transcribed in the preface under number 6, where the nearly contemporary Roman pontiff is called not “holy” or “blessed,” but “lord.” This testimony must be valued above all others.

Although it was easy to make mistakes in recording the authors of other Churches concerning sermons received from elsewhere, it will not easily be found that anyone erred in the names of the authors of his own Church when older manuscripts—and, as in this codex, manuscripts close to Leo’s own time—were being copied. The authority of this Lectionary is all the greater because another part of the same Lectionary, marked number 3836, exposed as falsely attributed to Leo a sermon on the Maccabees, assigning it to Augustine rather than to Leo, as in the other codices and consequently in all the printed editions. Thus, in assigning authorship to Leo, these two most ancient Roman Lectionaries are found to be accurate. The style of this sermon is plainly Leonine; nor do we understand what in the opening offended Quesnellus, so that he asserted without adducing any reason that it was unquestionably not Leo’s.

[Col. 0429]

The one point that seems to create considerable difficulty is that, apart from the sermon’s opening, the rest is found to have been transcribed partly from the third sermon and partly from the fourth sermon on the Feast of Peter. Yet that it was customary for Leo to repeat and transcribe his own material is clear from the Epistles. In Epistle 28 to Flavian, chapters 3 and 4, several sentences are read that have been taken word for word from Sermons 21 and 22. Epistle 124 to the Palestinians contains seven chapters that are found, with the same wording apart from a few exceptions, in Epistle 165 to Leo Augustus; and in these two epistles there occurs a long passage from Sermon 65, comprising two complete chapters. Epistles 30 and 31 likewise contain numerous repetitions, while Epistle 18 repeats several passages from Epistles 1 and 2. Who, then, would wonder if the same thing occurred in this sermon?

If nothing of this kind is found in the other sermons of Leo that have been published, the reason seems to be that the material recited at one solemnity would not have suited another in the same way that it could be adapted to the Feast of Saint Peter, which had formerly spoken of Peter’s praises on his own feast. It was enough here to compose a new opening suited to the feast of Saint Peter; the remaining passages, excerpted here and there from Sermons 3 and 4, are connected so aptly and coherently that they reveal the same author and teacher, and they admit nothing incongruous anywhere. The same cannot be said of Sermon 1, which was inserted into the appendix: although composed from various fragments of Leo, it nevertheless reveals in places the careless compiler, as we shall note in its proper place.

Furthermore, we have plausibly conjectured in note 13 on Sermon 90 that Leo repeated some sermons with certain alterations, just as we know from Saints Zeno and Ambrose that other Fathers also employed repetitions of this kind. Why, then, should our holy pontiff not have excerpted and joined several passages from one or another sermon, prefixed a new opening proper to another feast, and thereby fashioned a new form and a new sermon?

Moreover, the words “He deigned to give blessed Peter precedence over this city,” which are retained in our codices, declare that the sermon was delivered at Rome and by the pontiff. There is no doubt that the alteration of the words in the codex seen by Quesnellus is to be attributed to the discretion of the scribe, who, writing a Lectionary for another particular Church, wished to indicate that Peter had been placed over not his own city but the city of Rome.

## 329 SERMON LXXXIII [Another numbering: LXXX]

[Note: [Col. 0429C] The printed editions had “On the Nativity of the Saints Peter and Paul,” which is incorrect, since Saint Paul is not mentioned. We have corrected it from the most ancient Vatican manuscript, which reads: “Likewise, a sermon of Saint Leo the pope on the Feast of Saint Peter the Apostle.”]

### On the Feast of Saint Peter the Apostle

[Col. 0429A]

### SYNOPSIS

I. Peter’s confession and excellence. — II. What Christ conferred upon him. — III. Christ prayed for Peter’s faith and granted firmness to that faith. He made him the head of the whole Church.

## CHAPTER I

Let us rejoice in the Lord, dearest brethren, and exult with spiritual gladness, because the only-begotten Son of God the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, in order to disclose to us the mysteries of his dispensation and divinity, deigned to give blessed Peter precedence over the apostolic order in this city. His solemnity today, recurring with the triumph of his martyrdom, has brought distinction and glory to the whole world. [Note: [Col. 0429C] The same appears in Sermon 3, chapter 3.]

This, dearest brethren, was achieved by that confession which, inspired by God the Father in the apostolic heart, transcended all the uncertainties of human opinions and received the firmness of a rock that no assaults could shake. [Note: [Col. 0429C] We have corrected this from the same Vatican manuscript; it also appears in Sermon 3, chapter 3, from which Leo took this passage. The printed editions have “of all.”] For when the Gospel narrative revealed the matter, [Note: [Col. 0429C] The printed editions read *referente* (“relating”); we have corrected this from the cited Vatican manuscript, in agreement with the words in chapter 2 of the mentioned sermon: “As has been disclosed by the Gospel reading.” This is from Sermon 4, chapters 2 and following.] the Lord asked all the apostles what people thought about him. [Note: [Col. 0429C] This sentence, up to the words “is explained,” is omitted in the first edition and also in the same Vatican manuscript.] The answer of those who responded remained common to all for as long as the uncertainty of human understanding was being explained. But when the disciples’ understanding was asked what it held, the one who was first in the Lord’s confession was also first in apostolic dignity.

When he had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” Jesus answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:16–17). [Note: [Col. 0430C] From the same codex we have added “that is,” as it likewise appears in Sermon 4, chapter 2.] That is: “You are blessed because my Father taught you; earthly opinion did not deceive you, but heavenly inspiration instructed you. It was not flesh [Note: [Col. 0430C] We have supplied the particle *nec* (“nor”) instead of the *et* (“and”) of the printed editions, from three Vatican manuscripts, among which is the most ancient.] nor blood, but he revealed me to you, whose only-begotten Son I am.”

“And I,” he says, “tell you this”: just as my Father revealed my divinity to you, so I make your excellence known to you. “Because you are Peter” (Ephesians 2:14)—that is, although I am the inviolable rock, the cornerstone who makes both one (ibid. 18), yet you too are a rock, because you are made firm by my power, so that what belongs properly to me by authority may be shared with you through participation with me.

## CHAPTER II

“Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” Upon this, he says, this strength, I will raise an eternal temple, and the exalted dignity of my Church, which is to be joined to heaven, shall rise upon the firmness of this faith. The gates of hell shall not hold this confession; the bonds of death shall not bind it. For this utterance is the utterance of life, and just as it lifts those who confess it into heavenly places, so it plunges those who deny it into the depths below.

Therefore it is said to the most blessed apostle Peter [Note: [Col. 0430C] Thus from the same most ancient manuscript, as also in Sermon 4, chapter 3; the printed editions read “to the blessed apostle Peter.”]: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.” This authority was indeed transferred also to the other apostles, [Note: [Col. 0430C] We have inserted *etiam* (“also”) from the cited manuscript and sermon.] but it was not without reason that what was entrusted to all was entrusted to one. [Note: [Col. 0430C] Thus from the same codices and sermon. The printed editions have: “For this is entrusted particularly to the blessed apostle Peter.”] For this was entrusted particularly to Peter because Peter’s pattern is set before all the rulers of the Church. Peter’s privilege therefore remains wherever judgment is pronounced according to his equity; and there is neither excessive severity nor excessive leniency wherever nothing will be bound and nothing loosed except what blessed Peter has either bound or loosed. [Note: [Col. 0430C] We have added the word “blessed,” omitted in the printed editions, from the same codices and sermon.]

## CHAPTER III

As his passion approached—a passion that was to disturb the steadfastness of his disciples—the Lord said: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers, lest you enter into temptation” (Luke 22:31–32). [Note: [Col. 0431B] Thus the most ancient Vatican manuscript and the Casinensis codex of collection 1. The printed editions have “so that it may not fail.” Shortly afterward, the common editions had “lest they enter.” We have corrected this from the cited codices and two other Vatican manuscripts, with which the reading of Sermon 4, chapter 3, agrees. See what we observed there in note 22 concerning this addition, which is found neither in the Greek text nor in the common Latin text.]

The danger of temptation and fear was common to all the apostles, and all alike needed the help of divine protection, since the devil wished to harass and overthrow them all. Yet the Lord undertakes a special care for Peter, and prayer is offered particularly for Peter’s faith, as though the condition of the others would be more secure if the mind of their leader were not overcome.

In Peter, therefore, the strength of all is fortified, and the help of divine grace is so ordered that the firmness granted to Peter through Christ may be conferred through Peter upon the apostles. [Note: [Col. 0431B] In what follows, some material is omitted, some transposed, and some borrowed from Sermon 4, chapter 4.]

For after his resurrection the Lord also said three times to the blessed apostle Peter, after giving him the keys of the kingdom and through a mystical utterance in response to his threefold profession of eternal love: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17). This he unquestionably does even now, and the devout shepherd carries out the Lord’s command, strengthening us with his exhortations and never ceasing to pray for us, so that we may not be overcome by any temptation.

If, as must be believed, he extends this care of his devotion everywhere to all God’s people, [Note: [Col. 0431B–0432B] Thus in the same most ancient Vatican manuscript and the cited sermon, chapter 4. The printed editions omit “to all” and then “to us,” and for *praetendit* (“extends”) read *protendit* (“stretches forth”).] how much more does he deign to offer his help to us, his foster-children, among whom he rests upon the sacred bed of his blessed repose in the same flesh in which he presided? [Note: [Col. 0432B] The word “blessed” has been added from the aforementioned Vatican manuscript; it likewise appears in the cited sermon.]

Since, then, dearest brethren, we see that such protection has been divinely established for us, we reasonably and justly rejoice in the merits and dignity of our leader, giving thanks to the eternal King, our Redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, [Note: [Col. 0432B] We have followed the reading of the most ancient Vatican manuscript, conforming to Sermon 4, chapter 3; the printed editions read: “and to our Redeemer Jesus Christ.”] because he gave such power to the one whom he made head of the whole Church, for the glory and praise of his name. [Note: [Col. 0432B] We have taken this conclusion, customary with Leo, from the same codex. The printed editions have: “Who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.”] To him be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SERMON

[Col. 0431]

Quesnellus prefixed the following lengthy annotation to the title of the next sermon:

“Cardinal Baronius believes that the events described in this sermon should be referred to the disaster caused by Attila, in the years 452 and 455. Certain words of the sermon rather suggest that some matters should be understood of the Vandal sack. For the sermon indicates that the people had formerly, in earlier years, been accustomed to gather in order to give thanks to God for the day of chastisement and deliverance. He laments that the Romans neither repent over their correction nor rejoice over their release. He applies to them the prophetic saying: ‘You struck them, and they did not grieve; you chastised them, and they refused to accept discipline.’ He attributes to God’s mercy the fact that he deigned to calm the hearts of the raging barbarians. All these details appear to suit more closely the devastation inflicted upon the city of Rome by the Vandals than Attila’s invasion, from which the city suffered no damage, since God calmed the barbarian before he invaded it.

“This becomes still clearer from the words of chapter 1: ‘Who,’ he says, ‘restored this city to safety? Who rescued it from captivity? Who defended it from slaughter?’ These words plainly indicate that Leo’s sermon must be understood of the city after its occupation by the Vandals. No one is restored to safety, no one is rescued from captivity, unless he has been in the power of enemies and his safety has been brought into the greatest danger.

“Finally, the fact that he recalls the city as having been defended from slaughter agrees entirely with the account in the *Miscella*, which reads: ‘Genseric immediately seized the city, left without a garrison, and, being calmed by the arrival of Pope Leo, preserved the city free from fire, slaughter, and punishments.’

“Moreover, only the title indicates that the sermon itself was delivered by our Leo on the eighth day of the apostles. Because of the scarcity of manuscript codices, it was not possible to investigate the truth of this title; only one manuscript, the quite recent Victorinus, was available to us. If one considers only Leo’s words, one point is clear: this sermon was delivered shortly after a public supplication had been appointed at Saint Peter’s as a thanksgiving for the city’s deliverance from a hostile army.

“That the sermon was delivered at a time other than the feast itself or the octave of the apostles seems to be shown by the fact that Circensian games were then being held in the city. Julius Caesar Bulengerus, in Book 1, chapter 1 of his work *On the Roman Circus and Circensian Games*, learned from Ovid’s *Fasti* II that these games were customarily given on the third day before the Kalends of March. Circensian games are also recorded on other days in the Roman Calendar published by Aldus and others from the Maffei marble; but not on the third day before the Kalends of July, on which the feast of the apostles occurs, nor on the day before the Nones of that same month, on which the octave occurs. For only the Apollinarian games are read as assigned to that day.”

Here Quesnellus noted three matters. First, it is entirely true that the events contained in this sermon are to be understood of the invasion of the Vandals.

As for the second, namely the title *On the Octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul*, it should be stated beforehand that this sermon, whose sole codex seen by Quesnellus was the Victorinus manuscript of collection 5, was found by us in manuscripts of collections 2, 3, 4, and 5, and also in Vallicellan Lectionary A, 6. Only the codices of collections 3, 4, and 5 bear that title.

Although another title is read in the table of the Casanatensis manuscript of collection 2 and in the Vallicellan Lectionary, the sermon should not for that reason be excluded from the day of the apostles’ octave. The table of the Casanatensis codex gives a title suited to the subject of the sermon, *On the Neglected Solemnity*, and this in no way conflicts with the day of the octave. As for the Vallicellan manuscript, it describes the same sermon as having been read on the sixth Sunday after the Feast of the Apostles, with the title “Sermon of Saint Leo the Pope to the People.” It should be observed that, at a later period, this sermon, which had been delivered on the octave, was transferred there to that sixth Sunday for use in the divine offices, just as three sermons on the Collects, certainly delivered within the octave of these same apostles, are found in the same codex under the second, third, and fourth Sundays after their feast, for the same reason. See the notice prefixed to Sermon 6. Hence there is no doubt that this sermon was recited on the octave of the apostles, that is, on the day before the Nones of July. We have retained both titles, “On the Octave” and “On the Neglected Solemnity.”

The third point is this: Quesnellus rightly acknowledges from Leo’s words that the sermon was delivered shortly after a public supplication had been appointed at Saint Peter’s as a thanksgiving for the city’s deliverance from a hostile army. But he raises a difficulty concerning the date, because the sermon mentions Circensian games, whereas the ancient Calendars do not record such games as having been held on the octave of the apostles, to which alone the Apollinarian games are assigned. To reconcile this third point properly, several matters must first be stated.

Since in the opening the holy pontiff complains about the small number of people gathering at Peter’s church, whereas formerly the whole people had assembled there to give thanks, he sufficiently indicates that the sermon was not delivered in the first year after Rome was captured and liberated by the Vandals, namely in 455—for at that beginning the gathering at the Church was greater—but several years later, when the former devotion had grown cold. Accordingly, this sermon belongs to the final years of Leo.

Thanksgiving seems to have been appointed at the church of Saint Peter, although it is not expressly named, because Rome was liberated on the very feast day of Saint Peter. For the emperor Maximus died on June 12, according to the anonymous author of the *Cuspinian Chronicle*, whom the Bollandists published in full from the imperial manuscript, volume VI of June, part II, page 187. Theophanes relates that Genseric and the Vandals occupied Rome three days after his death. They are said to have plundered it for fourteen days, according both to the aforementioned anonymous author and to Saint Prosper in his *Chronicle*, where he further clearly indicates that the same Vandals departed from Rome after those fourteen days, writing in one continuous passage: “For fourteen days, therefore, Rome was emptied of all its wealth by a secure and unrestrained search, and many thousands of captives were brought to Carthage.”

Now, if the calculation of three and fourteen days is made from the death of Maximus—from June 12 to the evacuation and liberation of Rome—you will find that this fell on June 29. Therefore, since Rome was liberated on Saint Peter’s day, thanksgiving was soon appointed to Saint Peter on some subsequent day within the octave of that apostle.

The Circensian games mentioned in this sermon should not be understood as games occurring on the very day to which this supplication was assigned. They may instead refer to the Apollinarian games, which began on the day of the octave and were held in the Circus at least on the thirteenth, as we explained from the ancient Calendars in the notice concerning the sermons on the Collects. The holy pontiff is simply drawing a comparison between the Circensian games and other spectacles, which were attended by large crowds, and the supplication just mentioned, which almost everyone had recently neglected. The word “recently” designates a day shortly preceding the day assigned to that supplication.

## 335 SERMON LXXXIV [Another numbering: LXXXI]

### On the Octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul

### ON THE NEGLECTED SOLEMNITY

[Col. 0433A]

### SYNOPSIS

I. The Romans, devoted to the Circensian games, have dangerously forgotten God’s benefits. — II. Rome’s deliverance from the barbarians is not the effect of the stars but God’s gift, which must be recalled with a grateful heart.

## CHAPTER I

The religious devotion by which, for the day of our chastisement and deliverance, the entire people of the faithful used to gather to give thanks to God had recently been almost universally neglected; the very small number of those who attended demonstrated this. It brought great sadness to my heart and caused me very great fear. [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Vallicellan Lectionary and the Barberinian codex of collection 2 have “dread.”]

For it is a great danger for human beings to be ungrateful to God and, through forgetfulness of his benefits, neither to grieve over their correction nor to rejoice over their deliverance. I fear, therefore, dearest brethren, that the prophetic voice may seem to have rebuked such people when it says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you chastised them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jeremiah 5:3).

For what correction is visible in those among whom such great aversion is found? I am ashamed to say it, but I must not remain silent: more attention is devoted to demons than to the apostles, and insane spectacles attract larger crowds than the blessed martyria. [Note: [Col. 0433C] Here *martyria* means churches dedicated in honor of the martyrs.]

Who restored this city to safety? Who rescued it from captivity? Who defended it from slaughter? Was it the Circus games, or the care of the saints? Through whose prayers, certainly, the sentence of divine judgment was turned aside, so that we, who deserved anger, might be preserved for pardon. [Note: [Col. 0433C] The Bonn manuscript and the first edition read: “so that he who deserved anger might be preserved for pardon.” The Vallicellan and Barberinian manuscripts have: “so that we, who had deserved it, might be preserved.”]

## CHAPTER II
Let that saying of the Savior, beloved, touch your hearts: when he had cleansed ten lepers by the power of his mercy, he said that only one of them returned to give thanks (Luke 17:15). He thereby signified, concerning the ungrateful, that even if they have attained bodily healing, they have nevertheless not been free from impiety of spirit. Therefore, beloved, lest this mark of ingratitude also be attributed to you, return to the Lord, recognizing the wonders he has deigned to work in us, and attributing our deliverance not—as the ungodly suppose—to the effects of the stars, but to the ineffable mercy of almighty God, who deigned to calm the hearts of the raging barbarians. Bring yourselves, with the full strength of faith, to grateful remembrance of so great a benefit.

A grave negligence must be remedied by greater penitence. Let us use the gentleness of the One who spares us for our amendment, so that blessed Peter and all the saints who have always stood by us amid many tribulations may deign to aid our supplications for you before the merciful God, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

**Textual notes:** [Col. 0433C] The Vallicellian codex reads, “cleansing, yet impiety of spirit had not been absent from them.” The Barberini manuscript agrees with the text, but has *solum defuerint* for *defuerunt*. The Barberini manuscript reads “return to God.” The Vallicellian codex reads “to gratitude for so great a benefit.” The same codex adds “the Apostle” after Peter; from it we have added “always,” for which the Barberini manuscript has “often.” Both words are absent from the editions. Shortly afterwards the Vallicellian manuscript reads “our supplication,” while the Barberini codex reads “your supplication for us.”

# SERMON LXXXV [Alternatively LXXXIII]

## On the Feast of Saint Lawrence the Martyr

### Synopsis

I. The difference between Christ’s death and the death of the martyrs.  
II. The efficacy of each.  
III. The courage with which Lawrence preserved both the resources and the faith of the Church.  
IV. How charity made Lawrence invincible.

### Chapter I

Since the whole summit of the virtues and the fullness of all righteousness arise from that love by which God and one’s neighbor are loved, this love is found nowhere to excel more sublimely or shine more clearly than in the blessed martyrs. By imitation of charity they are as close to our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for all human beings, as they are by the likeness of their suffering.

For although no kindness can equal that love by which the Lord redeemed us (Romans 5:8)—since it is one thing for a human being, who must die by necessity, to die for a just person, and another for one free from the debt of death to die for the ungodly—the martyrs nevertheless bestowed great benefit upon all humanity. The Lord, the giver of their courage, used it in such a way that he did not wish the punishment of death and the cruelty of the cross to be terrifying to any of his own, but made them imitable by many.

Therefore, if no good person is good only for himself, and no wise person’s wisdom is friendly only to himself—and if this is the nature of true virtues, that the one who is illumined by their light leads many away from dark error—then no example is more useful for instructing God’s people than that of the martyrs.

Let eloquence be ready for entreaty; let reasoning be effective for persuasion. Yet examples are stronger than words, and teaching by deeds is more powerful than teaching by speech.

**Editorial note:** Quesnellus appended the following gloss here: “No virtue and no righteousness exist except from charity.” But Saint Leo affirmed that the summit of all virtues and the fullness of all righteousness arise from charity. By this statement he does not deny that certain virtues—for example, faith and hope—can arise and persist without charity. See what we discuss in the notes on Sermons 45, 79, and 90.

**Textual note:** The first edition and Quesnellus’s edition, with manuscript collections 3 and 4, read: “Let eloquence be easy for exhortation.” The other editions, with manuscript collection 5, punctuate differently: “Let the eloquence of the martyrs be easy for exhortation; let reasoning be effective for persuasion,” and so forth. In the Homilies of Paul the Deacon the wording is somewhat different: “Let the eloquence of the martyrs be easy for prayer; let reasoning be effective for persuasion.” We preferred the reading of two Vatican lectionaries, the Lombard and the Veronese: “for entreaty” (*ad exorandum*), that is, for obtaining or securing something by prayer.

**Textual note:** This reading comes from the same two lectionaries of the highest authority and from the Homilies of Paul the Deacon. The first edition reads “more plainly”; the remaining editions, “more fully.”

### Chapter II

In this most excellent kind of instruction, the blessed martyr Lawrence—whose passion makes this day illustrious—possessed a glory so distinguished that even his persecutors were able to perceive it. That wondrous strength of spirit, conceived principally from love of Christ, not only did not yield, but also strengthened others by the example of his endurance.

For when the fury of the pagan authorities raged against the most chosen members of Christ, and especially attacked those of priestly rank, the impious persecutor erupted against Lawrence the levite. He excelled not only in the ministry of the sacraments but also in the administration of the Church’s wealth. The persecutor promised himself a double prize from the capture of one man: if he made him betray the sacred money, he would also make him an outcast from the true religion.

Thus the money-hungry enemy of truth armed himself with a double torch: greed, in order to seize the gold; impiety, in order to take away Christ. He demanded that the wealth of the Church, for which he lusted most avidly, be brought out to him by the immaculate guardian of the treasury. The most chaste levite, showing him where the wealth had been stored, presented the innumerable flocks of holy poor. In their food and clothing he had stored imperishable riches—riches all the safer because they were proved to have been expended in a holier manner.

**Textual note:** Three Vatican manuscripts read, “when he was with him.”

**Textual note:** The first edition reads *ipsis*, that is, “to the persecutors,” meaning that it did not yield to them.

**Textual note:** Two Vatican manuscripts read “against the choicest.” We preferred, on the evidence of editions before Quesnellus and of our manuscripts, to delete the particle *in*, which Quesnellus inserted from two Victor and Sammagallus manuscripts and from the old Basel edition of the homilies printed in 1513. In the margin of the editions appears: “Alternatively, in the mystery.”

**Textual note:** The first edition and the Bonaventure manuscript read “of sacred money.”

**Textual note:** The Homilies of Paul the Deacon read “guardian,” and shortly afterward omit “to be brought in.”

### Chapter III

The robber, frustrated, rages; and, inflamed with hatred toward the religion that had established such a use of wealth, he attacks the more valuable treasure, so that, finding no store of money there, he might carry away that deposit by which Lawrence was richer in holiness.

He orders Lawrence to renounce Christ and prepares to press that most unshakable strength of the levitical spirit with dreadful torments. When the first have achieved nothing, more severe ones follow. He orders the torn limbs, lacerated by many strokes of the scourge, to be roasted over a fire placed beneath them, so that, on an iron grate which had already acquired the power to burn through continuous heat, the alternating turning of the limbs would make the torment more severe and the punishment longer.

**Textual note:** The word “rages” is absent from the Lombard Vatican manuscript.

**Textual note:** This reading is better than the alternative *ardescens*, “burning,” because it is found in the Homilies of Paul the Deacon. Shortly afterward, the reading “the seizure of the treasure” is supported by the more accurate manuscripts, the first edition, and Quesnellus. Alternatively: “by seizure.”

**Textual note:** This reading seems preferable because it is found in the same homiliary, in the first edition, and in the Bonaventure manuscript. The two latter witnesses add *ei* after “deposit.” Elsewhere the particle *ut* is omitted, and the word *illud* is placed before “deposit.”

### Chapter IV

You achieve nothing; you make no progress, savage cruelty. The material for your inventions of death is withdrawn, and as Lawrence ascends to the heavens, you fail. The flame of Christ’s love could not be overcome by your flames; the fire that burned outwardly was weaker than the fire that had been kindled within.

You served the martyr, persecutor, when you raged; you increased his crown while piling on his punishment. For what device did your ingenuity not discover for the victor’s glory, when even the instruments of punishment were transformed into honors of triumph?

Let us therefore rejoice, beloved, with spiritual joy, and glory in the most blessed end of this illustrious man in the Lord, who is wonderful in his saints (Psalm 67:36). In them he has established for us both protection and example. He has so glorified his glory throughout the whole world that, from sunrise to sunset, with the radiance of levitical lights flashing forth, Jerusalem became as glorified by Stephen as Rome became illustrious through Lawrence.

We confidently believe that we are continually aided by Lawrence’s prayer and patronage, so that, since—as the Apostle says—“All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (1 Timothy 3:12), we may be strengthened by the spirit of charity and armed for overcoming every temptation with steadfast perseverance in faith.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

**Textual note:** Editions before Quesnellus read: “You fail in your flames. The flame of Christ’s love could not be overcome.” The second collection of the Barberini manuscript has a slightly different wording: “You fail in your flames. The love of Christ could not be overcome by your flame.” We have followed Quesnellus’s reading, taken from the Victor manuscript and the margins of the editions mentioned above, since it is confirmed by two of our lectionaries, three other Vatican manuscripts, and the text of Paul the Deacon. Another Vatican manuscript has a slightly different version: “You fail. The flame of Christ could not be overcome by your flames.”

**Textual note:** This reading, supported by the first edition, manuscript collection 3, two Vatican lectionaries, the Veronese lectionary, and the copy of Paul the Deacon, seemed better and more consonant with Leo’s syntax than the Vulgate reading: “You raged, persecutor, against the martyr; you raged and increased his palm, while you heaped up his punishment.” Paul the Deacon’s copy alone has “you exaggerate” for “you heap up”; one Vatican manuscript has “you increase.”

**Textual note:** Quesnellus read “for victory’s glory.” We have restored the reading of the other editions, which is better and is found in all our manuscripts as well as in the copy used by Paul the Deacon.

**Textual note:** The Homilies of Paul the Deacon read: “when the inventions of your tyranny passed into the honor of triumph, even amid the instruments of punishment.”

**Textual note:** The same homiliary reads “with the levitical number, the light of shining radiance, how glorified she was.” The first edition and the Bonaventure manuscript read “glorified”; the others agree with the text.

**Textual note:** The same edition and the Bonaventure manuscript read “of truth.”

**Textual note:** The copy of Paul the Deacon reads “the constancy of faith and perseverance.”

**Textual note:** The Lombard Vatican manuscript has: “Through him who lives and reigns forever and ever.” The first edition has: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.”

# SERMON LXXXVI [Alternatively LXXXIV]

## On the Fast of the Seventh Month I

### Synopsis

I. He proclaims the fast on the authority of Scripture and urges it out of charity, so that the body may be disciplined and the poor assisted.  
II. It is not enough to take nothing from another unless one also gives one’s own to the poor.

### Chapter I

We know, beloved, that your observance is so devout that you cultivate your souls not only through the fasts required by law but also through voluntary fasts. Nevertheless, the exhortation of our admonition must be added to this devotion, so that if any are slower in this exercise, they may at least on these days obediently join the common abstinence. On these days we ought to celebrate the most sacred custom with greater attentiveness, so that through the humility of fasting we may deserve divine help against all our enemies.

This is an undertaking of the highest importance, which we both prescribe on the authority of Scripture and recommend out of charity: by restraining somewhat the freedom to eat, we should devote ourselves to disciplining our bodies and nourishing the poor. Whoever refreshes them feeds his own soul and transforms temporal feasts into eternal delights.

**Textual note:** The Venetian lectionary of Saint Mark reads “exhortation.”

**Textual note:** The first edition reads “of the body.”

### Chapter II

Therefore let increases of holy desires succeed in the place of evil desires. Let wrongdoing cease, but let righteousness not be idle. Let someone who suffers no oppressor feel someone aiding him. For it is too little not to take another’s goods unless you also give your own. We are under the eyes of the just Judge, who knows how great an ability for doing good he has given to each person. He who distributed to his servants the measured talents of his mysteries in such a way that he increased what had been entrusted to the one who spent it generously, but took it away from the one who had kept it unproductively, does not wish his gifts to be idle (Matthew 25:28; Luke 19:26). Therefore, beloved, since we ought to observe the fast of the seventh month, we urge your holiness to fast on Wednesday and Friday, and on Saturday to keep vigil together at blessed Peter the Apostle, through whose interceding merits we may deserve to be delivered from all tribulations, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

**Textual notes:** [Col. 0438D] The same edition omits “together.” The final clause has been supplied from the Venetian codex.

# SERMON LXXXVII [Alternatively LXXXV]

## On the Fast of the Seventh Month II

### Synopsis

I. The devil must be resisted through self-restraint: he seeks in us, by the enticement of eating, the fruit of the seed sown in our first parents.  
II. Fasting greatly benefits both the salvation of others and one’s own.  
III. Those who cannot fast should give more abundant alms.  
IV. Wealth is placed securely and increased when it is distributed to the poor.

### Chapter I

God, the creator and redeemer of the human race, wishes us to walk toward the promises of eternal life along the paths of righteousness. Since temptations were not going to be lacking—temptations that would assail us on the journey of virtue with treacherous attacks—he equipped us, beloved, with many protections by which we might crush the devil’s snares. Among these he granted his servants this most salutary means: that they should arm themselves against all the enemy’s tricks with the strength of self-restraint and works of compassion.

For the one who from the beginning implanted in the first human beings an appetite for the forbidden food (Genesis 3:5), and who through the enticement of eating poured the poison of every desire into those who were easily led to believe, does not cease to repeat the same deceptions. In the nature which he knows to have been corrupted by his seeds, he seeks the germ of his sowing, so that he may kindle the desire for pleasure in order to weaken the pursuit of virtue.

For the Christian’s progress is his punishment, and he cannot in any way harm the souls of those who, with the Lord’s help, have learned to rule in their own flesh. Therefore rebellious desires must be restrained by reasonable moderation and holy purpose, and bodily lusts must not be allowed to resist chaste and spiritual desires.

Let the inner person recognize that he is the ruler of his outer self, so that the mind, governed by divine authority, may compel the earthly substance to obey the good will. Nor do we lack for preserving this order the help of the most merciful King, who has instructed us by the rule of a most salutary observance, appointing for us, as the seasons return, certain days of fasting on which the virtue of our spirits might be strengthened by discipline of the body.

### Chapter II

The gift of this remedy, beloved, has also been appointed for this seventh month, and we ought to receive it with ready eagerness. In addition to that abstinence by which each person individually and privately disciplines himself according to the measure of his ability, this fast, prescribed for everyone together, should be celebrated with greater courage.

For in every contest of Christian struggle, the usefulness of self-restraint is very great. Indeed, certain spirits of the fiercest demons, who are expelled from possessed bodies by no commands of exorcists, are driven out solely by the power of fasting and prayer, as the Lord says: “This kind of demon is expelled only by fasting and prayer” (Matthew 17:20; Mark 9:28).

The prayer of one who fasts is therefore pleasing to God and terrifying to the devil. Nor is it hidden how much it gains for its own salvation when it contributes so much to the salvation of another.

### Chapter III

In this observance, beloved, although all of us ought unanimously to be devoted, if there are nevertheless some whose will is hindered by weakness, let them redeem the bodily labor that exceeds their strength by the expenditure of their resources.

For there are many works of compassion that can rightly commend the necessity of eating more generously, if by their zeal for kindness they acquire the purification belonging to those who fast. Since those who omit nothing of the humiliation of fasting may sweat beneath a fruitless toil unless they sanctify themselves through whatever distribution of alms they can make, it is fitting that those whose strength for abstaining is less should be more generous in providing food for the poor.

Whatever one does not deny oneself in one’s own weakness, let one willingly spend on another’s poverty, making one’s own need a common one with the needy. The weak person who ends a fast is not blamed if a hungry poor person receives food from him; nor is the one who eats defiled, if he is cleansed by giving alms, as the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

**Editorial note:** This is understood from Sermon 18, on the Fast of the Seventh Month, chapter 3. There Leo urges almsgiving together with fasting, calling that fast sterile which lacks the fruits of compassion and almsgiving. These fruits are so necessary to Christians that, he says, the Lord Jesus condemned the barren fig tree—having nothing for him to take when he was hungry—to perpetual barrenness, because whoever does not refresh the hungry denies food to the One who said that what was given to the poor was given to himself. Such trees, he says, will hear from the Judge: “Depart from me,” and so forth: “I was hungry, and you did not give me food,” and so forth. A fast is therefore called sterile when those who fast do not join it with whatever almsgiving they are able to offer, because it lacks the fruit by which the one who is without that fruit will be condemned, since fasting does not assist him.

### Chapter IV

In this work, beloved, those too who restrain themselves from the pleasure of feasting ought to acquire for themselves the fruit of mercy, so that what they have sown more abundantly they may reap more abundantly.

This harvest never deceives its farmer, nor does the cultivation of compassion hold an uncertain hope of reward. Whatever is scattered in this way by the hand of the sower is not burned by heat, carried away by a torrent, or beaten down by hail. All expenditures of compassion remain forever safe; they not only remain intact, but are continually increased and changed in quality. Heavenly things arise from earthly ones, great things are generated from small ones, and a temporal gift passes into an eternal reward.

Therefore, whoever loves riches, whoever desires to multiply what he possesses, set your ardor upon these profits; sigh for these increases of your goods, from which no thief steals, no moth corrupts, and no rust consumes (Matthew 6:19).

Do not despair of interest; do not distrust the One who receives. Understand who it is that says, “Whatever you did for one of these, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40), and recognize with the discerning eyes of faith with whom you are safely placing your wealth.

Let the person to whom Christ is debtor have no doubt about receiving it. Let generosity not be anxious, and let fasting not be sorrowful, for God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9:7). He is faithful in his words and abundantly repays what he has graciously commanded to be given.

Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

**Textual note:** The first edition reads “who.” We have added the concluding words “Jesus Christ, our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen” from the Venetian manuscript. The first edition has a different conclusion: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen.”

# SERMON LXXXVIII [Alternatively LXXXVI]

## On the Fast of the Seventh Month III

### Synopsis

I. Fasts, without which God’s righteousness was not appeased for the ancients, are also necessary for us.  
II. They are much more powerful when celebrated by all the faithful together.  
III. Each person ought sometimes to withdraw from his concerns so that he may devote himself more attentively to his salvation. The power of united prayer.  
IV. The agreement of good people has great force before God. In almsgiving, the disposition of the soul, not the amount of wealth, is weighed.  
V. Each person ought to distribute alms according to his means, without distrust.

### Chapter I

We learn from the preaching of the holy prophets how powerful devout fasts are for entreating God’s mercy and renewing the condition of human weakness. They testify that the provocation of divine justice, which the people of Israel had frequently incurred through their wickedness, could be appeased only by fasting.

Therefore the prophet Joel also exhorts us, saying: “Thus says the Lord your God: Return to me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning; tear your hearts and not your garments, and return to the Lord your God, for he is merciful and patient, long-suffering and greatly merciful” (Joel 2:12–13). And again: “Sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing, gather the people, sanctify the Church” (Joel 2:15).

This exhortation, beloved, must also be embraced in our own times, because the remedies of this healing must also be proclaimed as necessary by us, so that, in the observance of ancient sanctification, what Jewish transgression lost may be acquired by Christian devotion.

### Chapter II

The reverence due to divine ordinances always possesses its own privilege among all exercises of voluntary observance: what is celebrated by public law is more sacred than what is undertaken by private decision.

The practice of self-restraint that each person imposes upon himself by his own choice benefits only a certain portion of the community. But the fast undertaken by the entire Church excludes no one from the common purification. The people of God then become most powerful, when the hearts of all the faithful come together in the unity of holy obedience, and when, in the camp of Christian warfare, preparation is alike in every respect and the same defense is everywhere established.

Let the vigilant fury of the bloodthirsty enemy rage and spread hidden snares everywhere: he will nevertheless be able neither to seize nor to wound anyone if he finds no one unarmed, no one idle, and no one deprived of the work of compassion.

### Chapter III

Beloved, this solemn fast of the seventh month also summons us to the power of this unconquerable unity, so that, freed from worldly cares and earthly activities, we may lift our souls to the Lord.

Because not all of us can always maintain this attention, which is perpetually necessary, and because through human weakness we repeatedly fall back from heavenly things to earthly ones, let us at least on these days, appointed for us as most salutary remedies, withdraw from worldly occupations and steal some time that may benefit eternal goods.

For, as it is written, “We all offend in many things” (James 3:2). And although God’s daily gift cleanses us from various contaminations, heavier stains often cling to unwary souls; these must be washed away by more diligent care and erased by greater expenditure.

The complete abolition of sins is obtained when the whole Church has one prayer and one confession. For if the Lord promises to grant everything requested by the holy and devout agreement of two or three (Matthew 18:20), what will he deny to a multitude of many thousands carrying out one observance together and petitioning harmoniously through one spirit?

### Chapter IV

Beloved, it is great and exceedingly precious in the sight of the Lord when the whole people of Christ engage together in the same duties, and when, among both sexes, all ranks and orders cooperate with the same disposition; when in turning away from evil and doing good there is one judgment and one purpose among all; when God is glorified in the works of his servants and, with abundant thanksgiving, blessing is offered to the author of all compassion.

The hungry are fed, the naked are clothed, the sick are visited, and no one seeks what is his own but what belongs to another (1 Corinthians 10:24). Each person’s measure is sufficient to relieve another’s misery, and it is easy to find a cheerful giver wherever the scale of the work is regulated by the measure of one’s means.

Through this grace of God, which works all things in all people (1 Corinthians 12:6), the fruit and merit of the faithful become common. For the disposition of those whose wealth is unequal can nevertheless be equal; and when one rejoices in another’s generosity, to which he could not equal the expense, he becomes equal in affection.

Nothing is disordered and nothing is divided in such a people, where all the members of the whole body agree with one another in a single strength of compassion. The person who rejoices in the wealth of others is not ashamed of his own poverty.

The excellence of one part is the ornament of the whole, and when we are all moved by God’s Spirit, not only are those things ours which we ourselves do, but also those in which we rejoice as others act.

### Chapter V

Let us therefore embrace, beloved, this blessed solidity of the most sacred unity, and let us undertake the solemn fast with a harmonious purpose of good will. Nothing difficult and nothing harsh is demanded from anyone; nor is anything imposed upon us that exceeds our strength, whether in the discipline of abstinence or in the generosity of almsgiving.

Each person knows what he can and cannot do. Let each weigh his own measure; let each assess himself by a just and reasonable reckoning, so that the sacrifice of mercy may not be offered with sadness or counted among losses.

Let that be spent on this devout work which justifies the heart, cleanses the conscience, and finally benefits both the recipient and the giver.

Blessed, indeed, and greatly admirable is the soul that does not fear the exhaustion of its resources because of its love of doing good, and that does not distrust the One who gave it what it is now to distribute. Yet because such greatness of soul belongs to few, and because it is also wholly charitable for each person not to abandon care of his own household, without prejudicing those who are more perfect, we exhort you all by this general rule: carry out God’s command according to the measure of your ability.

The generosity of a good will ought to be cheerful, regulating its giving in such a way that the poor rejoice in their nourishment and household sufficiency does not suffer.

“He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed and increase the fruits of your righteousness” (2 Corinthians 9:10).

Let us therefore fast on Wednesday and Friday, and on Saturday let us likewise celebrate vigils at the most blessed Apostle Peter. Through his merits and prayers we trust that the mercy of our God will be granted to us in all things.

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON LXXXIX [Alternatively LXXXVII]

## On the Fast of the Seventh Month IV

### Synopsis

I. How much the fast fulfilled by Christians through the grace of God surpasses the carnal observance of the Jews.  
II. The common and public fast is to be preferred to the private, as possessing greater merit and efficacy.  
III. The devil has innumerable weapons, which are avoided only by the person who loves God above all things.  
IV. Certain seasons are appointed so that we may breathe again toward divine things.  
V. Almsgiving must be joined to fasting, especially toward the faithful.  
VI. The poor are to be saved by patience, and the rich by mercy.

**Additional editorial and textual notes**

**Sermon LXXXVII, chapter I.** [Col. 0438D] The editions read “of the future temptation, which would oppose us . . .”; the Venetian codex’s reading, printed in the text, was preferred. The editions add “in which”; it has been deleted on the authority of our codices.
