Editions before Quesnellus add “and corrupted”; one Vatican manuscript reads “which it knows to have been stirred up and corrupted by its seeds,” and the first edition, “which it knows to have been stirred up by its seeds, to be corrupted.” The remaining manuscripts confirm Quesnellus’s reading. “And,” deleted by Quesnellus, has been restored from earlier editions; two Vatican manuscripts read “and.” For “preserving,” our manuscripts agree with Quesnellus; elsewhere is “to be observed.” Two manuscripts have “formed” for “instructed.”

**Sermon LXXXVII, chapter II.** The Venetian lectionary supplies “that” before “abstinence.” A Vatican manuscript omits “certain”; shortly afterwards the Venetian codex deletes *in* before “fasting” in Matthew’s text.

**Sermon LXXXVII, chapter III.** One Vatican codex reads “you”; shortly afterwards the Venetian lectionary has “hinders” for “may hinder.” All editions and codices have “commend,” though Quesnellus conjectures that “compensate” should be read. The explanation of “sterile toil” is as follows: this is clear from Sermon 18, On the Fast of the Seventh Month, chapter 3, where Leo, about to urge the joining of almsgiving with fasting, calls sterile that which lacks the fruits of piety and almsgiving. Such fruits are so necessary that the Lord Jesus, he says, condemned the barren fig tree, which had nothing for him to take when hungry, to perpetual barrenness; whoever does not sustain the hungry denies food to him who said that what is given to the poor is given to himself. Such trees will hear the Judge say, “Depart from me,” and so forth: “For I was hungry and you did not give me food,” and so forth. Thus a fast is called sterile when those fasting do not join to it such almsgiving as they can give; it lacks the fruit without which one will be condemned, fasting being of no assistance. The Venetian codex has “for abstinence” for “for abstaining.” “Anyone,” omitted in manuscript collection 5 and by Quesnellus, has been restored from earlier editions and the other ancient books.

**Sermon LXXXVII, chapter IV.** The Venetian codex reads “who,” rather than “which.” After a full stop, the first edition reads “Not only”; “but also now” has been adopted from most and the best manuscripts, rather than “but even now.” The first edition reads “loss” for “gift.” One Vatican codex reads “who says”; a Vatican codex suggested the correction “with discerning eyes,” conjectured in Quesnellus’s margin and earlier by Latinus Latinius in the *Bibliotheca Sacra*.

**Sermon LXXXVIII, chapter I.** The first edition and one Vatican codex read “of prosperity.” The Venetian manuscript has “with your whole heart”; the first edition and manuscript collections 3 and 4 have “rend” for “tear open.” The Venetian codex reads “must also be proclaimed by us as necessary.”

**Sermon LXXXVIII, chapter II.** “But” has been restored for “indeed” from the Venetian manuscript. The same Venetian codex reads “unity.” The word “piety,” deleted by Quesnellus, has been restored from all editions and our codices.

**Sermon LXXXVIII, chapter III.** Editions before Quesnellus, later manuscript collections, and the Venetian lectionary read “piety”; Quesnellus’s “unity” is better, since it refers to the unity of holy obedience mentioned in the preceding chapter and pursued at the opening of chapter V. Vatican manuscript collection 5 reads “we withdraw from heavenly things,” omitting “into earthly things”; another Vatican manuscript has “we fall” for “we fall back.” The particle “and,” deleted by Quesnellus, has been restored from all editions and our codices. The first edition and the Bonaventure manuscript read: “But the fullest abolition of sins is obtained.”

**Sermon LXXXVIII, chapter IV.** The reading “great in the sight of the Lord, beloved, and exceedingly precious” has been restored from editions before Quesnellus and from all our codices; Quesnellus, without notice, reads “and exceedingly precious in the sight of the Lord, beloved.” Our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus read “in turning away from evil and doing good”; Quesnellus reads “in turning away from evil, and doing good.” The Corbie and Victor manuscripts used by Quesnellus read “one substance.” “To the author” follows the Venetian lectionary; alternatively, “in much thanksgiving,” which also confirms the earlier printed reading *auctori* against Quesnellus’s *auctor*. Alternatively, “giver” for “generous giver.”

**Sermon LXXXVIII, chapter V.** “And” has been added from the Venetian manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts; “but indeed” has been restored from editions before Quesnellus and four codices. Earlier editions corruptly prefixed *cum* (“when”) to “this greatness of soul.”

### Chapter I
Our preaching, beloved, is aided by the familiar custom you share, and the season makes the priest’s duty appropriate, so that what both the commandment of the law requires and the devotion of the will moderates may seem neither burdensome nor difficult. When these come together, with God’s grace assisting, “it is not the letter that kills, but the Spirit that gives life” (I Cor. VIII, 1). “Where the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0443D] The Venetian manuscript has “of the Lord.”] of God is, there is liberty” (II Cor. III, 17), which fulfills the law not through fear but through love. Obedience softens authority; and where what is commanded is loved, service is not rendered under harsh compulsion.

Therefore, beloved, when we exhort you to certain practices instituted even in the Old Testament, we do not subject you to the yoke of Jewish observance [Col. 0444C], nor do we impose upon you the custom of a carnal people. Christian self-restraint surpasses their fasts; and although we and they may share certain seasons [Note: [Col. 0443D] Leo often mentions the fast of the tenth and seventh months as taken from the observance of the old law; in this respect he says here that Christians share the seasons with the Jews.], we do not share the same practices. Let them have their barefoot processions [Note: [Col. 0443D] He is doubtless criticizing a rite descending from Pharisaic superstition; for we read nowhere in Scripture that anything of this kind was prescribed for the Jews. It was also borrowed from pagan custom, which Tertullian mentions in On Fasting, at the end: “But the pagans too,” he says, “recognize every ταπεινοφροσύνην [humility or self-abasement]. When heaven is motionless and the year is dry, barefoot processions are proclaimed,” and so forth. Augustine mentions the heresy of men who always walked barefoot, because the Lord had commanded Moses, Joshua, and Isaiah to walk barefoot. Heresy 68. QUESNELLUS.], and display their idle fasts in gloomy faces [Note: [Col. 0444C] Thus from the Venetian Lectionary. Other copies have “let them display.” He is referring here to Matthew VI, 16, concerning hypocrites who fast: “They disfigure their faces, so that they may appear to men to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.” For this reason he calls such fasts fruitless, since they lack an eternal reward. Compare what is said in Sermon 92, chapter 2.]; we, without differing in anything from the propriety of our appearance [Note: [Col. 0444D] Quesnellus writes in the margin: “Perhaps, from the propriety of our appearance.”] and without refraining from just and necessary works, restrain the liberty of eating by simple moderation, so that moderation, not the creature, may be chosen in the use of food [Note: [Col. 0444D] The foods are meant which the Hebrews condemned as unclean, such as pork, blood, and so forth. Even in Leo’s time Christians abstained from these during the fast of the four seasons, because they did not eat meat in the interest of frugality and temperance—not because they rejected any food through Hebrew superstition.].

## CHAPTER II

Although each of us is free to afflict his own body by voluntary disciplines, and now more moderately, now more strictly, to tame the carnal desires that resist the spirit, nevertheless on certain days a general fast ought to be observed by all together. Devotion is then more effective and more sacred [Note: [Col. 0445D] Others have “more holy.”] when the whole Church is of one mind and one judgment in works of piety. Public practices must be preferred to private ones; and the chief principle of usefulness is to be recognized wherever common care is vigilant. [Note: [Col. 0445D] Thus with Quesnellus and the Venetian manuscript. The other editions, with the manuscripts of the later collections, have: “Let them maintain . . . observance.”]

Let each person therefore maintain his own diligence in observance, and, having implored the aid of divine protection against the ambushes of spiritual wickedness, let each seize the heavenly weapons [Note: [Col. 0445D] The common editions have “let him grasp.” We have preferred the reading of the Venetian manuscript.]. Even if the ecclesiastical soldier can fight bravely in individual battles, he will nevertheless fight more safely and successfully if he stands openly in line against the enemy. There he does not enter the struggle by his own strength alone, but, joined with his brothers’ ranks under the command of the unconquered King, completes the universal battle. For many engage the enemy with less danger than individuals; nor is one easily exposed to a wound when the strength not only of oneself but also of others defends one behind the opposing shield of faith, so that where the cause of all is one, the victory may also be one.

## CHAPTER III

Since our adversary does not cease to lie in wait for us by various arts of temptation, and since this is the one purpose of his cunning [Note: [Col. 0445D] The first edition omits “one.”]: to lead those redeemed by Christ’s blood away from the commandments of God, we must take every precaution lest we be wounded by any of the enemy’s arrows. His weapons are not harsh to the bodily senses; rather, they flatter the flesh excessively, so that they may harm the soul. They draw the eyes toward various desires [Note: [Col. 0445D] The same edition has “temptations.”], so that from the beauty of the world either the torches of desire may be kindled, or errors of superstition may arise [Note: [Col. 0445D] He seems to refer to the superstition of the pagan peoples who, captivated by the beauty of the stars, made gods of the stars; or to the Manichaeans, who, as Leo himself discovered, offered superstitious worship to the sun and moon, as is related in Sermon 42, chapter 5, and Letter 15 to Turibius, chapter 4. See also Sermon 27, chapter 4, concerning the particular superstition concerning the rising sun that was derived from the pagans.].

Through treacherous sounds, too, the hearing is struck by gentle blows, so that the solidity of the mind may be dissolved by seductive melody, and unwary and insufficiently sober hearts may be ensnared by the habit of deadly pleasures [Note: [Col. 0446D] Thus according to the Venetian manuscript. The first edition has: “For by treacherous sound and gentle actions.” Later editions not descended from the first have: “Also by treacherous sound and gentle blows.” Quesnellus has: “Also by treacherous sounds and gentle blows.”].

But divine grace and the precepts of evangelical teaching make these tricks of the devil ineffective and void. For those who have received the Holy Spirit, and in whom the fear of the Lord has arisen not from dread of punishment but from love of God, crush the snares of such entanglements with the foot of faith unharmed. Thus they use the beauty of all created things for the glory and praise of their Maker, and love him above all things, through whom all things were made (John I, 3).

## CHAPTER IV

Beloved, let the affection of all the faithful strive toward admiration of him. Let wise self-restraint seek from him pleasures not corruptible but eternal, and let undefiled chastity burn with love for that good without which no one is good [Note: [Col. 0446D] We supplied the word “his” from the aforementioned Venetian manuscript.]. For this purpose Christian disciplines have been given to us: so that, cutting away every illicit pleasure, we may burn with holy and spiritual delights.

Although we ought always to strive for virtue, certain days have nevertheless been consecrated to the discipline of common observance so that the soul, still entangled in earthly desires and hindered by worldly cares, may at least from time to time breathe toward divine things. And because it is a portion of the Lord’s field [Note: [Col. 0446D] The common editions have “of the divine field.” We have preferred “of the Lord,” from the Venetian manuscript, a wording customary with Leo.], it may bring forth fruits worthy of the heavenly granaries. For the hope of reaping is found wherever there has been diligence in sowing.

## CHAPTER V

Having briefly addressed these matters for your progress, beloved, as the season requires, we announce to you the fast of the seventh month. In it we remind you not only of abstinence from food but also of works of piety: whatever you withdraw from your own needs through religious frugality, transfer to the nourishment of the poor and to food for the weak. Show general benevolence toward all who are in need, but especially remember those who are members of Christ’s body and are joined to us by the unity of the Catholic faith. We owe more to our own people because of our fellowship in grace than to outsiders because of our common nature.

## CHAPTER VI

Therefore, beloved, let Christian kindness abound among you. Just as you desire the recurring seasons of the year to be full of fruits, so let your hearts be fruitful in nourishing the poor. God, to whom all things belong, could certainly have granted them the substance they require and bestowed such resources upon them that they would need none of your gifts. But both they and you would have been deprived of much material for virtue if poverty did not exercise them toward the crown of patience, and abundance did not summon you toward the glory of mercy.

Divine providence has wonderfully arranged that there should be in the Church both holy poor and good rich, who might benefit one another through this very difference, giving thanks to God when they receive and giving thanks to God when they distribute, so that they might earn eternal and incorruptible rewards. For, as it is written [Note: [Col. 0446D] We have restored the particle “and,” which was absent from Rainaudus and Quesnellus, from all our manuscripts and earlier editions. The Venetian manuscript has “of the poor man” instead of “of the poor.”], “the patience of the poor shall not perish forever” (Ps. IX, 19), and “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Cor. IX, 7).

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the most blessed Apostle Peter, hoping that through his prayers we shall be so assisted that the God of mercies may hear the sacrifice of our fast, having been reconciled [Note: [Col. 0447D] Thus according to our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus, who, without the support of any of our manuscripts, has “may receive the sacrifice, having been appeased.” We have expressed the closing clause from the Venetian manuscript. Others have: “Through Christ our Lord. Amen.”.] through Jesus Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XC [Otherwise LXXXVIII]  
## On the Fast of the Seventh Month V

### SYNOPSIS

I. Repentance is always necessary because of the continual snares of the enemy and the concupiscence of the flesh.  
II. Everything impossible through human weakness becomes possible through divine power.  
III. On love of God and of the world.  
IV. Love of God is nourished by good works. Why the fast of the seventh month.

## CHAPTER I

Beloved, we proclaim the sacred fast of the seventh month as an exercise of common devotion, confidently urging you with paternal exhortations to make what once belonged to the Jews your Christian observance [Note: [Col. 0447D] The fast of the seventh month was observed among the Hebrews on the Day of Atonement. Thus read the Venetian Lectionary and the editions before Rainaudus and Quesnellus; those editions have “may be.” Shortly afterward Vatican collected manuscript 5 has “for the season” instead of “as the season requires.”]. It is suitable for every season and accords with both Testaments that divine mercy should be sought through the discipline of both mind and body [Note: [Col. 0447D] We have added “and” from the aforementioned Venetian manuscript.]. Nothing is more effective in entreating God than for a person to judge himself, and never cease asking forgiveness, knowing that he is never without sin.

Human nature has this defect [Note: [Col. 0447D] The printed editions generally have “this defect.” The correction is supplied by the aforementioned Venetian manuscript.] within itself—not implanted by the Creator but contracted from the transgressor—and transmitted to posterity through the law of generation [Note: [Col. 0448D] Thus Quesnellus, the same Venetian manuscript, and Vatican collected manuscript 5; others have “by a general law.”], so that from a corruptible body there arises even that which can corrupt the soul. Hence the inward person, although already reborn in Christ and freed from the bonds of captivity, continually struggles with the flesh; and while restraining its desires, suffers its resistance [Note: [Col. 0448D] The common text before Quesnellus and several manuscripts have “if indeed.”].

[Note: [Col. 0448D] Thus, more correctly, from the first edition; Latinus Latinius likewise indicated that this should be corrected. Others have “in a person.”]

In this discord, victory is not easily so complete that even those things which ought to be broken do not entangle us, and those which ought to be slain do not wound us [Note: [Col. 0448D] We have added “those things” from the Venetian manuscript. The first edition has “let them bind” instead of “let them entangle.”]. However wisely and carefully the judging mind presides over the external senses [Note: [Col. 0448D] The common editions have “presides over its external things.” We have preferred the reading of the Venetian manuscript.], temptation is nevertheless always too near it amid the very cares and disciplines involved in governing and nourishing the flesh.

For who separates himself so completely either from bodily pleasure or from pain that what externally caresses or torments does not affect the mind itself? Joy is undivided, sorrow indistinguishable: there is nothing in a person that anger does not inflame, nothing that joy does not relax, nothing that grief does not affect. And what avoidance of sin can there be where there is one passion both of the ruler and of the subject? The Lord rightly declares that “the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. XXVI, 41).

## CHAPTER II

And lest we be driven by despair into sluggish inactivity, he promises that what is impossible for human beings through their own weakness is possible through divine power. “For narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII, 14); and no one would enter it, no one advance a step, unless Christ himself, making himself the way, opened the difficult approaches. Thus the possibility of the traveler comes from the author of the journey, since he both leads us into labor and brings us to rest.

In the same one in whom we have hope of eternal life, we also have the pattern of patience. “If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (II Tim. II, 12; Rom. VIII, 17). For, as the Apostle says, “whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (I John II, 6). Otherwise we use the appearance of a false profession if we do not follow the institutions of the one whose name we glory in. Those institutions would certainly not be burdensome to us and would free us from every danger if we loved nothing except what we are commanded to love.

## CHAPTER III

There are two loves, from which all wills proceed, differing in character as they are divided according to their authors. The rational mind, which cannot exist without love, is either a lover of God or a lover of the world [Note: [Col. 0448D] More will be said in the observations on this sermon concerning this celebrated text among the followers of Quesnellus and concerning the marginal note Quesnellus attached to it.]. In the love of God nothing is excessive; in the love of the world everything is harmful.

Therefore we must cling inseparably to eternal goods, but use temporal goods in passing, so that, as travelers hastening to return to our homeland, whatever of this world’s prosperity comes our way may be provisions for the journey, not an enticement to settle. For this reason the blessed Apostle proclaims: “The time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; those who weep as though they did not weep; those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 29–31).

But what attracts us by appearance, abundance, or variety is not easily avoided unless, amid the beauty of visible things, the Creator rather than the creature is loved. When he says, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength” (Matt. XXII, 37), he does not wish us to be released in any respect from the bonds of his love.

And when he joins to this commandment the love of our neighbor, he enjoins us to imitate his goodness, so that we may love what he loves and do what he does. Although we are God’s cultivation and God’s building (I Cor. III, 9), and “neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (ibid., 7), he nevertheless requires in everything the service of our ministry and wishes us to be stewards of his gifts, so that the one who bears the image of God may do the will of God.

For this reason, in the Lord’s Prayer, we most sacredly say: “Your kingdom come; your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth” (Matt. VI, 10). By these words what else do we ask than that God may subject to himself those whom he has not yet subjected to himself [Note: [Col. 0449C] The editions have “whom.” The Venetian manuscript more correctly has “those whom,” which is required by what follows, “people.”], and make people on earth ministers of his will just as he has made the angels in heaven? In making this request, we love God and we love our neighbor. Our love is not divided but one, since we desire both that the servant serve and that the master command.

## CHAPTER IV

This affection, beloved, by which earthly love is excluded, is strengthened by the practice of good works. For conscience must take delight in good actions [Note: [Col. 0449C] Others have “upright actions.”] and willingly do what it rejoices to have done.

Therefore fasting is undertaken, generosity multiplied, justice guarded, prayer practiced frequently, and the result is that the desire of each person becomes the one prayer of all. Labor nourishes patience, gentleness extinguishes anger, kindness tramples envy, unclean desires are put to death by holy longings, avarice is driven away by generosity, and the burdens of wealth become instruments of virtue.

[Note: [Col. 0449C] In the most ancient Vatican manuscript 3836, the end of this sermon is presented in a much different form, as follows:

“But because the snares of the devil do not rest even amid such devotions, let what was sung in the prophetic word be taken up as the prayerful disposition of those who pray, so that it may be said not only with the lips but also with the heart: ‘Guard me, Lord, as the apple of your eye; protect me under the shadow of your wings’ (Ps. XVI, 8). For we continually need divine help; and this is the unconquerable strength of human devotion: always to have him as our protector, without whom we cannot be strong.

“Therefore, so that this may benefit both the sanctification of bodies and the restoration of souls, let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us also celebrate vigils at the most blessed Apostle Peter, so that the prayer of the most glorious shepherd may protect us through the prayers of the pious sheep. Through our Lord, who reigns with the Father and with the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

Although the authority of this Roman Lectionary and its style suggest that this ending should be attributed to Leo, we nevertheless did not wish to abandon the common reading, which likewise breathes Leo’s spirit and is found in the other manuscripts and in the Venetian Lectionary. Since such great variation, reflecting Leo’s style, cannot be attributed to copyists, it seems possible to infer only this: that the holy pontiff recited this sermon twice, changing only the ending. Something similar most probably occurred in other sermons that display other substantial variations confirmed by excellent manuscript Lectionaries. Compare Sermon 22, in which the Vercelli Lectionary and the Homiliary of Paul the Deacon preserve considerable variation from the printed editions and other manuscripts, as we noted there in annotation 1. Likewise in Sermon 59, chapters 1 and 4, various readings and readings of another form were found in Vatican manuscript 3835 and in the Casinensis manuscript; these seem to have the same cause. After some words, the printed editions and the later manuscripts read: “the restoration of our strength has been undertaken.” The syntax of the Venetian Lectionary seems more Leonine.]

But because the snares of the devil do not rest even amid such devotions, the restoration of our strength has most appropriately been instituted at certain intervals of the seasons. When, amid the mildness of the heavens and the richness of the fields, the mind greedy for present goods can boast, and, after gathering fruits into spacious barns, say to its soul, “You have many good things; feast” (Luke XII, 19), there it should receive a certain rebuke from the divine voice and hear it say: “Fool, this night they are demanding your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (ibid., 20) [Note: [Col. 0450C] The first edition has “I shall reclaim.”].

This most careful meditation ought to belong to the wise person: since the days of this life are short and its duration uncertain, death should never be unforeseen for one who is going to die, nor should one who knows himself to be mortal meet an unregulated end [Note: [Col. 0450C] Perhaps “unexpected,” rather than “unregulated,” was formerly proposed as the reading. But I now detract somewhat from that conjecture, both because the word itself has a meaning suitable to this passage and because our teacher explains himself in Book II of On the Calling of the Gentiles, chapter 21, expressing the same thought in these words: “Therefore, whatever is mortal from the beginning, whenever it dies, does not perish contrary to the law of mortality, nor is it ever nearer to being able to live than to being able to cease. For whatever end he calls unregulated in the present sermon, there he calls it contrary to the law of mortality.” QUESNELLUS.—In this annotation Quesnellus thought that the books On the Calling of the Gentiles were Leo’s, although they belong to another author of uncertain identity, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere. All our manuscripts, however, prefer the common reading.].

Therefore, so that it may benefit both the sanctification of bodies and the restoration of souls, let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the most blessed Apostle Peter, being assisted by his prayers so that we may attain the fulfillment of holy desires [Note: [Col. 0450D] The Venetian manuscript has “at the most blessed one”; and shortly afterward, “being aided by his prayers.”], through Christ our Lord [Note: [Col. 0450D] We supplied what follows from the same manuscript.], who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XCI [Otherwise LXXXIX]  
## On the Fast of the Seventh Month VI

### SYNOPSIS

I. God’s will is taught even by the elements themselves, which command us to abstain both from foods and from worldly wisdom.  
II. The heresies both of Nestorius and of Eutyches must be detested.  
III. The truth of Christ’s flesh is proved by the Eucharistic sacrifice and by the commandment of almsgiving.

## CHAPTER I

Beloved, there is nothing in which divine providence does not assist the devotion of the faithful. For, in training minds and bodies toward holiness, the very elements of the world also serve [Note: [Col. 0450D] Quesnellus alone has “may serve.”], while the varied recurrence of days and months opens before us certain pages of instruction, so that what sacred institutions admonish, the seasons may in a certain way also proclaim.

Therefore, when the return of the year has brought us the seventh month, I am not unaware that your observance is spiritually stirred to celebrate the solemn fast. For experience has taught you how much this preparation purifies both the outward and the inward person, so that when one abstains from what is permitted, one more easily resists what is forbidden [Note: [Col. 0450D] Thus according to two manuscript Lectionaries, those of Bergamo and Saint Mark’s in Venice. Others have “by experience.” Shortly afterward these same manuscripts have “and when one abstains from permitted things.”].

The principle of self-restraint, beloved, is not found solely in disciplining the body, nor only in reducing food [Note: [Col. 0451C] Editions before Quesnellus have “is found.” The two Lectionaries mentioned above read as in the text.]. For the greater benefits of this virtue belong to that purity of soul which not only crushes the desires of the flesh but also rejects the vanities of worldly wisdom. The Apostle says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit according to human tradition” (Col. II, 8) [Note: [Col. 0451C] Quesnellus writes in the margin, and the Bergamo manuscript has: “For the greater virtue of this good … belongs.”].

## CHAPTER II

We must therefore abstain from foods, but much more must we fast from errors, so that the mind, devoted to no carnal pleasure, may be captive to no falsehood. For, both in former days and in our own, there are enemies of the truth who dare to stir up civil wars within the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0451C] The common editions have “among.” We have corrected it from the first edition and our manuscripts.], leading the inexperienced into agreement with impious doctrines and boasting that they have increased their own number by separating from Christ’s body as many as they can [Note: [Col. 0451C] The first edition and the Bonner manuscript have “certain people.” Shortly afterward the Bergamo manuscript has “to adhere” instead of “to increase.”].

For what is so opposed to the prophets, so contrary to the Gospels, and finally so rebellious against apostolic teachings as to proclaim one single and unique nature in the Lord Jesus Christ, born from Mary and eternally coeternal with the everlasting Father? [Note: [Col. 0451C] Thus with Quesnellus and the aforementioned Venetian manuscript. Earlier editions, together with other manuscripts, have “because,” and the same reading appears in the treatise Against the Eutychians, chapter 3, which will be printed in the appendix.]

If this is to be understood as belonging only to a human being, where is the divinity that saves? If it belongs only to God, where is the humanity that is saved? The Catholic faith, which resists every error, refutes these impieties together: condemning Nestorius, who divides the divine from the human, and detesting Eutyches, who empties human reality within the divine [Note: [Col. 0451C] Quesnellus has “the divine things.” We have restored the preposition “in” from earlier editions and the Bergamo and Venetian manuscripts. Since Eutyches denied not Christ’s divinity but his true humanity, he should be said not to have emptied the human from the divine but to have emptied the human in the divine. The treatise Against the Eutychians likewise has “in the divine.”].

For the true Son of God, true God, possessing unity and equality with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, also deigned to be true man. He was not separated from the flesh either by the conception of the Virgin Mother or by the birth [Note: [Col. 0451C] We added the verb “was” from editions preceding Quesnellus and from the Bergamo and Venetian manuscripts. Shortly afterward the Bergamo manuscript has: “nor by birth, thus joining humanity to himself so that God did not cease to remain unchangeable.”]. He united humanity to himself in such a way that he remained unchangeably God; he imparted divinity to the human being in such a way that he did not consume him through glorification but increased him.

For he who became the form of a servant did not cease to be the form of God; there are not two, one with the other, but one is in both. Thus, from the time when “the Word became flesh” (John I, 14), our faith is disturbed by no variation in the modes of salvation. Rather, whether in miracles of power or in the insults of the Passion, we believe both that he who is God is man and that he who is man is God.

## CHAPTER III

Beloved, professing this confession with your whole heart, reject the impious inventions of heretics, so that your fasts and almsgiving may not be stained by the contagion of any error [Note: [Col. 0451D] Quesnellus omits “your.” Other editions have “your fasts and almsgiving.” We have preferred the reading of the Venetian manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts. Shortly afterward the editions before Quesnellus have “by contagion”; our manuscripts have “by the contagion.”].

Then the offering of sacrifice is pure, and the distribution of mercy is holy, when those who make these offerings understand what they are doing [Note: [Col. 0451D] Others have “what they accomplish.”]. For since the Lord says, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John VI, 54), you ought to communicate at the sacred table in such a way that you doubt in no respect the reality of Christ’s body and blood [Note: [Col. 0451D] The holy pontiff is referring to the error of the Eutychians, who are said, after the union of the Word, to have denied the reality of Christ’s body and blood in the city of Rome itself. This is reported in Sermon 96, chapter 1, in these words:

“Our concern could not remain unaware that certain Egyptians, especially merchants, had come to the City and were defending those things wickedly committed by heretics at Alexandria, asserting that Christ had only the nature of divinity and had not at all possessed the reality of human flesh, which he took from the blessed Virgin Mary.”

This was the Eutychian understanding, which Leo therefore exposed in the preceding chapter of this sermon as emptying humanity in the divine; he expressed it even more clearly in Letter 35, chapter 1: “Whoever proclaims that the only-begotten Son of God was born from the womb of the blessed Virgin in such a way that he bore the appearance of a human body, but that the reality of human flesh was not united to the Word”; or, as it is related in Letter 31, “that the one who bore the form of a servant, who was like us and conformed to us, possessed something that was an image of our flesh, not its reality.”

The holy pontiff therefore wished to warn and fortify his hearers, lest anyone, because of this tares spread throughout the City, should doubt the reality of the true body and blood of Christ, which they confessed and approved in the Eucharist. For when they were about to receive the Eucharist, at the priest’s words, “The body of Christ and the blood of Christ,” they responded, “Amen.”

With the same purpose, he also used the doctrine and practice concerning the Eucharist to refute the Eutychian error in Letter 59, chapter 2: “They have lain so long in the sluggishness of time that they have learned neither by hearing nor by reading what is so consistently on everyone’s lips in the Church of God that even from the tongues of infants the truth of Christ’s body and blood is not silent amid the sacraments of communion.”

The Calvinists vainly attempt to evade these testimonies of Leo by replying that his meaning was that one must not doubt the reality of Christ’s body and blood in itself, but that he did not mean that one must not doubt their reality in the Eucharist. For the holy pontiff plainly affirmed: “What is believed by faith is received by the mouth.” Therefore, if faith requires belief that Christ possesses a true body and true blood, there can be no doubt that the same true body and true blood are received by the mouth.].

For “he who understands concerning the needy and the poor is blessed” (Ps. XL, 1). He is a praiseworthy distributor to the poor of clothing and food who knows how to clothe and feed Christ in the needy [Note: [Col. 0452D] The Venetian manuscript has “the needy.”], because Christ himself says: “As long as you did it to one of my brothers, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV, 40) [Note: [Col. 0452D] Editions before Quesnellus add the particle “to,” which is absent from most of our manuscripts. Shortly afterward the same editions read “to one of these, my brothers,” but this is absent from our Venetian Lectionary, which confirms the reading introduced by Quesnellus.].

Therefore the true God and true man is one Christ: rich in what belongs to him, poor in what belongs to us, receiving gifts and distributing gifts, sharing in mortality and bringing life to the dead [Note: [Col. 0453D] Rainaudus’s edition has “the giver of life.”]. Thus “in the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 10–11), living and reigning with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0453D] The Venetian manuscript has “with the Father and the Holy Spirit.”] forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XCII [Otherwise XC]  
## On the Fast of the Seventh Month VII

### SYNOPSIS

I. The moral commandments of the law have not been abolished; no one has ever been justified without love; the abundance of evangelical righteousness consists in the abundance of love.  
II. The fasts of the new law, taken from the old, must be performed in a different spirit.  
III. Everyone ought to please God alone; each person’s treasure is of the same character as that to which his heart clings.  
IV. The seventh month is consecrated by fasting, by good works, and by the number itself.

## CHAPTER I
The apostolic instruction, dearly beloved, which knew that the Lord Jesus Christ had come into this world for the purpose not of abolishing the law but of fulfilling it (Matt. 5:17), distinguished the decrees of the Old Testament [Note: The first edition has “sacraments.”] in such a way that it selected from them certain elements which, just as they had been established, would be useful for evangelical instruction, and that practices which had long belonged to Jewish custom would become Christian observances. For although the varieties of sacrifices, the differences among baptisms, the idleness of Sabbaths, and the circumcision of the flesh itself have ceased, nevertheless many moral precepts remain for us in those very books. And since it is said there, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:37, 39), we learn from Christ the Lord [Note: Vatican manuscript of Collection 5 has “teaching.” Shortly afterward the editions before Quesnellus read “we have come to know”; and because in the Venetian manuscript it says “on these two commandments.”] that “the whole law and the prophets depend on these two commandments” (ibid., 40). So great is the union of both Testaments under the commandment of this twofold love that without the connection of these virtues neither the law nor grace is found ever to have justified anyone.

Those portions also of the legal commandments in which some things are ordered to be done and others forbidden to be done retain the firmness of ancient authority. Nor should evangelical perfection therefore be thought opposed to them, since the pursuit of virtue is urged toward voluntary growth, and punishments for crimes are relaxed through the remedies of repentance. For the Lord says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20). [Note: The editions read “therefore.” But “however” is better, with the Venetian manuscript and three Vatican manuscripts.] But how will righteousness abound unless mercy greatly surpasses judgment (Jas. 2:13)? [Note: We supplied “judgment” from the Venetian codex. The word is also read in James 2:13 and is demanded by the sense of the passage itself. This passage refers to ecclesiastical judges, who, when they remit the crimes of penitents more mercifully, imitate God’s justice. Concerning this it is written in James at the place cited: “Mercy triumphs over judgment.” Shortly afterward, the first edition and the later Vatican manuscripts have “and what is so worthy,” instead of “and what is so fitting.”] And what is so fitting and so worthy as that a creature fashioned in the image and likeness of God should imitate its Creator, who established the restoration and sanctification of believers in the forgiveness of sins, so that, severity of vengeance having been removed and all punishment having ceased, the guilty person might be restored to innocence, and the end of crimes become the beginning of virtues?

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, dearly beloved, when we take up from the preaching of the ancient teaching the fast of the seventh month for the purification of our souls and bodies, we do not subject ourselves to legal burdens but embrace the usefulness of self-restraint [Note: The Venetian codex has “which serves Christ’s Gospel.”] that serves Christ’s Gospel. For in this also Christian righteousness can abound beyond that of the scribes and Pharisees, not by emptying the law but by rejecting a carnal understanding of it.

Our fasts ought not to be like those of the people to whom the prophet Isaiah spoke with the Holy Spirit speaking through him: “I cannot endure your new moons and Sabbaths and great day; your fast and festivals and feast days my soul hates” (Isa. 1:13). Thus also, when the Lord handed on to his disciples the manner of fasting, he said: [Note: The same codex adds “but”; shortly afterward it has “they have received” in place of “they received.”] “When you fast, do not become gloomy like the hypocrites. For they disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matt. 6:16). What reward, except human praise? Because of the desire for it, the appearance of righteousness is often put forward; and where there is no concern for conscience, the falsity of reputation is loved, so that iniquity, which is exposed by concealment, may rejoice in the opinion that it is truthful. [Note: Quesnellus and our Bergamo manuscript have “and iniquity, which is exposed by hidden action, rejoices in the opinion of falsehood.” We judged that the reading of all earlier editions and our other manuscripts, which is sufficiently appropriate, should not be abandoned. Nor is the word “concealment” objectionable, since it indicates the intention of vainglory, which is exposed precisely by the fact that iniquity is concealed.]

## CHAPTER III

Therefore let rational and holy fasting [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, with manuscripts of the three later collections and the Bergamo manuscript, read “with no boastfulness of praise and display”; three Vatican codices read “with no praise and boastfulness of display.” Quesnellus, without naming a manuscript and with no support from ours, reads “with no boastfulness of display.” We followed the Venetian manuscript; its word “display” is confirmed by the other editions and manuscripts and is used in place of “showing,” just as *ostento* is a frequentative verb for the simple *ostendo*.] not be polluted by any boastful display of ostentation, nor let any believer wish to make his goodness depend upon human judgments. For one who loves God is satisfied to please the one he loves: no greater reward should be sought than love itself, since love is from God in such a way that God himself is love.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with the later manuscripts of the collections, read: “The devout and chaste soul certainly rejoices to fulfill this in such a way that it seeks nothing outside him,” and so forth. One Vatican manuscript has “outside himself.” Quesnellus’s correction, confirmed by the Venetian Lectionary, is preferable on the basis of the context, since the relative “in whom,” not “which,” refers to God; to him, certainly, the following words “outside him” must refer. Shortly afterward the same Venetian codex reads: “It is therefore most true that the Lord says: ‘Where your treasure is, there will your heart also be.’” The same is likewise read in two Vatican collections, 4 and 5. The first edition has: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart.”]

In him, then, the devout and chaste soul rejoices to be filled in such a way that it desires to take pleasure in nothing outside him. For what the Lord says is entirely true: “Where your treasure is, there will your heart also be” (Matt. 6:21). But what is a person’s treasure except a certain gathering of his fruits and a collection of his labors? “Whatever one sows, that one will also reap” (Gal. 6:8), and whatever each person’s work is, such also is his gain; and wherever enjoyment is established, there the concern of the heart is bound. [Note: The Venetian manuscript has “is confined.”]

But since there are many kinds of riches [Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts and of editions earlier than Quesnellus, who, without indicating any authority, printed “as though they were dissimilar materials.”] and different kinds of material for rejoicing, each person’s treasure is the object of his desire. [Note: Quesnellus writes in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘effect’; but this could not be found either in the editions we consulted or in our manuscripts.] If that desire concerns earthly things, it does not make those who share in it blessed but wretched. But those who set their minds on the things above, not on those upon the earth (Col. 3:1), and who are devoted not to perishable things but to eternal ones, have incorruptible riches stored up in him of whom the prophet says: “Our treasure and salvation have come: wisdom, discipline, and piety are from the Lord; these are the treasures of righteousness” (Isa. 33:6, according to the Septuagint). Through these treasures, with God’s grace assisting, earthly goods also are transferred into heavenly ones, when many use riches—whether rightly left to them or acquired by other means—as an instrument of piety. [Note: Quesnellus, following Rainaudus’s edition and Collection 5, has “as an instrument of impiety,” and in the margin: “Perhaps it should read ‘piety.’” This is preferred by the three editions we examined—the first, the Cologne edition of 1547, and the Antwerp edition of 1583—as well as by two of our Lectionary manuscripts.]

When they distribute for the support of the poor whatever they are able to spare, they gather for themselves riches that cannot be lost, so that what they have stored up through almsgiving [Note: This is the reading of the editions before Quesnellus and of our manuscripts. Only the first edition and the Bergamo codex add “they have added.” Quesnellus reads “they have hidden away.”] can be subject to no losses; and fittingly they have their heart where they have their treasure (Matt. 6:21). For it is supremely blessed to exercise such riches so that they increase, and not to fear that they may perish. [Note: The editions before Quesnellus add “worthy”; most of our manuscripts do not.]

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, dearly beloved, while doing what is good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith (Gal. 6:10), let us assign the seventh month to the fruits of self-restraint. From its beginning it is mystical because of the sevenfold Spirit, and it is consecrated also by the number of its place in the sequence. Let us solemnly fast on the fourth and sixth days of the week; but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at blessed Peter’s. [Note: The same editions have “let us fast on the fourth and sixth days.” Our manuscripts have the reading in the text.] May his prayers and merits support us, [Note: The common editions read “so much as is bestowed on each of the faithful.” We preferred the reading of the very ancient Vatican Lectionary 3836, from which we also received the conclusion, “with his help,” whereas the text formerly read: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”] so that each believer may be granted as much power to desire what is good as he has been given the will to desire it, with the help of him who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCIII [Elsewhere XCI]  
### On the Fast of the Seventh Month VIII

## SYNOPSIS

I. The end of the law is the victory of right love over wrong love; concerning the evil and the good will.  
II. Righteousness should give far more delight than iniquity, whose law must be overcome by God’s law.  
III. The benefit of the fast of the seventh month, instituted by the law and the apostles.

## CHAPTER I

All instruction in the divine commandments, dearly beloved, aims above all at this in the hearts of believers: that wrong love be overcome by right love, and that the desire to sin be destroyed by delight in righteousness. Scripture says: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will” (Sir. 18:30). [Note: The same Venetian manuscript has “do not follow them”; one Vatican manuscript has “do not follow them, and turn away from your will.” The first edition has “and turn away from your evil will.”]

Since there are many good desires and praiseworthy wills in human souls, what is meant by the command that we should not consent to our own impulses, unless we are forbidden that desire and recalled from that will whose origin is from ourselves, and which is therefore declared evil because it is shown to be our own? Accordingly, for distinguishing desires that come from God, it was rightly said to a person: “Do not follow your desires,” so that, when he recognizes which desires are his own, he may know that they must be avoided.

Therefore the Lord, in the prayer that he gave us, did not wish us to say to God, “Our will be done,” but “Your will be done” (Matt. 6:10)—that is, not the will stirred up by the flesh, but the will inspired by the Holy Spirit. Those who know that they are children of Adam readily understand where this desire was conceived and why it must always be resisted; for when the father of the human race sinned, they do not doubt that what was corrupted in the root was corrupted also in the offspring.

Although through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ we have passed from the old creation into a new one, and the heavenly human being has stripped us of the image of the earthly human being, [Note: The first edition has “and the image of the earthly human being.” Other editions have “and the heavenly human being has stripped us of the image of the earthly human being.” Our manuscripts approve the reading adopted by Quesnellus.] nevertheless, as long as we bear a mortal body, we must fight against the desires of the flesh. It is good for the soul subject to God to fear falling [Note: Rainaudus’s edition has “lest it yield.” Shortly afterward the common editions before Quesnellus have “for self-restraint” instead of “to self-restraint.”] and to possess something with which to conquer, because power is brought to perfection in weakness; and what trains us toward self-restraint leads us to glory (2 Cor. 12:9).

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, dearly beloved, we must abstain from those things that flatter us to our harm, and the law of sin that is in our members (Rom. 7:23) must be overcome by God’s law. Thus, although many enticements lie in wait through all the bodily senses, the soul, for which God is the highest good and true joy, may dwell amid chaste and spiritual delights, in the breadth of wisdom and in the light of truth.

For if a rational person compares himself with himself and judges all the qualities of his actions by true examination, will he find in the depths [Note: The Bergamo manuscript has “in the lowest depths.”] of his conscience as much delight in committed iniquity as in preserved equity? Or will bodily pleasure produce as much joy for him as spiritual desire? Anyone who prefers to become filthy in things that are unclean rather than to shine in things that are holy has touched nothing of the goodness of virtues and tasted nothing of the sweetness of piety. [Note: The editions before Quesnellus have “he touches nothing of the splendor of virtues,” and afterward “he tastes.” Quesnellus has “he will touch nothing of the splendor of virtues, and will taste nothing,” but in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘of the benefits of virtues.’”]

Reason does not permit anger to delight hearts that are not entirely captive to it as much when it is satisfied as when vengeance is relinquished; nor can ill-gotten goods produce as much joy as goods rightly spent from one’s own resources. [Note: The editions before Quesnellus have “ill-gotten things” and afterward “goods spent.” Some manuscripts have only “goods spent.” The two Lectionaries we possess give the reading found in the text.]

Thrifty moderation is always happier than extravagant luxury; [Note: This agrees with Quesnellus and the Bergamo manuscript. The Venetian codex has something scarcely different: “greater repose.” Earlier editions, together with later collection manuscripts, have “and greater is the splendor of the humble.”] the humble have greater rest than the proud; and the mind that, amid what is forbidden and what is permitted, more surely hopes for heavenly things is nobler than one that loves earthly things.

But so that the religious spirit may excel in this progress and possess the right of its dominion, chastisement through fasting must be applied by subduing the body. [Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts and editions, except Quesnellus, who has “by subjecting.”] Although by the general name it may seem to concern every form of self-restraint, it properly refers to reducing food: so that it may now be beneficial voluntarily not to take what, at the beginning, harmed us when we seized it against the prohibition; so that, just as desire was then the cause of the wound, abstinence may here be the cause of salvation. [Note: Quesnellus adds “was,” as it is read in the Venetian codex.]

## CHAPTER III

Although every season is suitable for this medicine, dearly beloved, we have this one especially appropriate season, which we see to have been selected both by apostolic and by legal institutions: just as on the other days of the year, so in the seventh month we may cleanse ourselves through spiritual purification.

For when three practices are brought together for one purpose—namely, prayer, almsgiving, and fasting—the merciful God will grant us both restraint of desires, the hearing of prayers, [Note: From the Venetian manuscript and Vatican Collection 5 we supplied “with the Father and the Holy Spirit,” which was lacking.] and forgiveness of sins, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCIV [Elsewhere XCII]  
### On the Fast of the Seventh Month IX

## SYNOPSIS

I. Spiritual fasting must be cared for more than bodily fasting.  
II. In what spiritual fasting consists and by what assistance it must be fulfilled.  
III. Why the fast of the four seasons was instituted.  
IV. God is loved when one’s neighbor is loved and helped.

## CHAPTER I

I know, dearly beloved, that many of you are so devoted to the matters [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with Collections 3 and 4, have “that pertain to the observance of the Christian faith.” The other manuscripts we possess, as well as the Corbie and Victor manuscripts, prefer Quesnellus’s reading.] that pertain to Christian observance that you do not need to be admonished by our exhortations. For what tradition established long ago and custom confirmed is neither ignored by instruction nor neglected by piety.

But because it is the duty of the priestly office to have a common care for all the children of the Church, we encourage alike those whom we love together in what benefits both the unlearned and the learned: that we may celebrate with eager faith, through chastisement of soul and body, the fast announced to us by the return of the seventh month.

Although reducing food seems properly to affect the flesh, nevertheless nothing is either granted or denied to the bodily senses that does not concern the one who commands, just as it concerns the one who serves. Since each person therefore has within himself a twofold law of self-restraint, and since none of our actions should be referred to the body alone while many must be referred to the soul alone, we ought prudently to consider how improper and unjust it would be if what is commanded by the superior were neglected by the inferior.

But in order that the rational mind may healthfully chastise external things, it must also practice fasts of its own, since we must resist not only the desires of the flesh but also the cravings of the soul. Scripture says: “Do not follow your desires, and turn away from your will” (Sir. 18:30). [Note: The Venetian Lectionary has “forbid.”]

Therefore, while fasting from what the flesh desires, let the soul also fast from what the inner substance wickedly craves. For the worst food of the soul is to desire what is not permitted; and harmful to the heart is the delight that is nourished either by shameful profit, lifted up by pride, or rejoices in vengeance. [Note: This is Quesnellus’s reading, together with our Venetian Lectionary. Manuscripts of Collection 2 agree, having “vengeance.” Other editions have “flattery.”]

Although bodily movements also serve these emotions, everything nevertheless looks back to its origin, and the quality of an action is assessed where the beginning of the will is found. To recall the will from wicked desires is the best and greatest fast, because abstinence from food is fruitful when external frugality proceeds from inner self-restraint.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, dearly beloved, as we prepare to celebrate the true and spiritual fast that sanctifies both body and soul by its purity, let us examine the secrets of our hearts and investigate with just scrutiny the things by which they are either saddened or gladdened. If there is any love of vainglory, any root of greed, or any poison of envy within, let the soul take none of these as food; rather, intent upon the delights of virtue, let it prefer heavenly banquets to earthly pleasure.

Let a person recognize the dignity of his own nature and understand that he was made in the image and likeness of his Creator. Let him not be so terrified by the misery into which he fell through that great and common sin that he fails to raise himself toward the mercy of his Restorer. [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have “of his Creator”; another Vatican manuscript and the first edition have “of his Author.” Shortly afterward the Venetian manuscript has “because I am holy.” Shortly afterward the common editions have “love me.” We followed the reading of the majority and better of our copies. In some manuscripts “return to the one who commands” is read afterward.]

He himself says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 19:2)—that is, “Choose me, and abstain from what displeases me. Do what I love; love what I do.” And when what I command seems difficult, hasten to the one who commands, so that assistance may be supplied from the place where the command is given; I will not refuse help, since I have granted the will. [Note: The Venetian codex has “he will not refuse help, who has granted the will.”]

Fast from what is opposed; abstain from what is contrary. I am your food and drink: no one desires what belongs to me without effect; for whoever strives toward me seeks me through participation in me. [Note: The same Venetian manuscript has “desires.”]

## CHAPTER III

All the pages of the divine Scriptures are filled with these exhortations, dearly beloved, by which he invites us to unchangeable goods and eternal joys. The teaching of both Testaments works together with us so that we may cling to what is true and restrain ourselves from what is vain. For what is promised cannot be attained unless what is commanded has been guarded.

What, then, [Note: We inserted the particle “but” from five of our manuscripts.] could be more just than that a human being, who bears God’s image, should do his will and, through abstinence from food, fast from the law of sin? For this reason the observance of self-restraint has been assigned to the four seasons: so that, as the course of the entire year returns to the same point, we may recognize that we continually need purification and must always strive, while we are tossed about amid the changes of this life, [Note: From our Lectionaries we supplied the preposition “in.”] so that sin, contracted through the frailty of the flesh and the pollution of desires, may be wiped away by fasts and almsgiving.

## CHAPTER IV

Let us hunger a little, dearly beloved, and withdraw from our customary resources something that may benefit the poor who are to be helped. Let the conscience of the kind be delighted by the fruits of generosity; and, giving with joy, you will receive what will make you joyful. [Note: The Vulgate has “and joys.” The first edition, together with Collection 3, has “and with joy.” We corrected the text from Collection 2 manuscripts. Quesnellus removed the sentence beginning “Let the conscience” and ending “you will receive,” on the authority of the Corbie and Victor manuscripts. It is also absent from Vatican manuscript 544, Collection 5, which resembles Victor’s text; but it is read in other manuscripts, as well as in the Venetian Lectionary and Vatican 3836. Afterward, some manuscripts have “whatever he had contributed to a person.”]

Love of neighbor is love of God, who established the fullness of the law and the prophets in this unity of twofold love (Matt. 22:40), so that no one might doubt that what he had bestowed upon a human being he had offered to God. The Lord and Savior says this when speaking about feeding and helping the poor: “What you did for one of them, you did for me” (Matt. 25:40).

Therefore let us fast on Wednesday and Friday; [Note: The Venetian codex has “on Wednesday and Saturday.”] but on Saturday let us celebrate vigils at the church of the blessed apostle Peter. We believe that we shall be helped by his merits and prayers, so that we may please the merciful God through our fasting [Note: The same codex has “through our devotion to fasting.”] and devotion, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XCV, OR HOMILY ON THE STEPS OF ASCENT TO BLESSEDNESS

[Note: The first edition, three Vatican manuscripts, and the table of the Casanatense manuscript have this heading: “On the feast,” or “On the solemnity,” “of All Saints.” They then begin: “At that time, when Jesus saw the crowds,” and so forth. There is no doubt that the title “On the feast of All Saints”—a feast not yet introduced in Leo’s time—comes from later Lectionaries, in which this sermon is proposed for reading on that same solemnity. In the older Vatican Lectionary 1272, the heading reads: “Here begins a sermon of Saint Leo the pope on the nativity of the apostles concerning the eight beatitudes.” In the Casinensis manuscript of the first collection, only this heading is prefixed: “On the eight beatitudes”; but “eight” was written by mistake, since the author speaks of only seven beatitudes. Quesnellus explains the reason for this number in a note with these words: “The learned man John Cotelier observes in the notes to volume I of the Greek Monuments, p. 808, that our Leo recounts only seven beatitudes, because, as Augustine explains in his Sermon on the Mount, those seven are the steps perfecting a person, while the eighth beatitude belongs to the person who is already perfect.” Faustus the Manichaean, in Augustine’s fifth book Against Faustus, likewise lists only seven beatitudes mentioned by Leo, although in a different order. Augustine, in Sermon 53, elsewhere 14, among the sermons added by the Paris editors, discusses at length only six beatitudes. Moreover, in the editions this sermon is placed not only after the following sermon but also after another sermon on the Gospel passage “Jesus took Peter,” and so forth; because of considerations given there, we have judged that sermon 51 should be placed before the sermons on the Passion. We have followed the order of the first edition and Collections 3, 4, and 5, in which this sermon follows immediately upon the sermons on the fast of the seventh month.]

On the passage that is written: “When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up into the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him,” and so forth (Matt. 5:1 ff.).

## SYNOPSIS

I. Christ prepared souls for inward remedies through outward cures, which are accomplished by the gentleness of grace.  
II. Humility, which everyone can possess, is the first step toward blessedness.  
III. The poverty of the apostles, and especially of Peter, was exceedingly rich and powerful.  
IV. What kind of mourning is the way to blessedness?  
V. What land was promised to the meek?  
VI. Thirst for righteousness is nothing other than love of God.  
VII. Mercy makes a human being like God.  
VIII. The eye of the heart must be purified so that God may be seen.  
IX. What true peace is—the peace that makes a human being a child of God.

## CHAPTER I

When our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Three Lectionaries omit “our.”] was preaching the Gospel of the kingdom, dearly beloved, and healing various illnesses throughout Galilee, the fame of his powers had spread through all Syria; and many crowds from all Judea were gathering to the heavenly physician.

For human faith is slow to believe what it does not see and to hope for what it does not know. It was therefore necessary that people should be strengthened by divine instruction and stirred by bodily benefits and visible miracles, so that they would not doubt that his teaching was saving, since they experienced his power to be so benevolent.

Thus, in order to transfer outward cures to inward remedies, and after [Note: Two Lectionaries, Vatican 1272 and Padiliron, have “healing.”] working cures of bodies to perform healings of souls, the Lord withdrew from the surrounding crowds and ascended to a secluded place on a nearby mountain. Having summoned the apostles, he was to instruct them from that elevated and mystical seat in higher teachings. Through the character of the place and the work he signified that he was the one who had once deigned to speak with Moses: there, indeed, with more terrifying justice; here, with more sacred mercy. Thus was fulfilled what had been promised through the prophet Jeremiah: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. After those days, says the Lord, I will give my laws into their understanding, and I will write them on their hearts” (Jer. 31:31; Heb. 8:8). [Note: Three Lectionaries omit “the prophet Jeremiah, who says,” and instead read: “the prophet Jeremiah’s promise: ‘Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish the house of Israel.’” Two of these also delete the words “and over the house of Judah a new covenant,” and afterward have “in their understanding.” Later, three Vatican manuscripts have “apostles” instead of “disciples.”]

The one who had spoken to Moses therefore also spoke to the apostles; and in the hearts of the disciples the swift hand of the Word who writes was establishing the decrees of the New Testament. This was not, as formerly, amid a dense cloud spread around them, nor through terrifying sounds and flashes that kept the people away from access to the mountain, but in the calm openness of conversation that lay before the ears of those standing nearby. Thus, through the gentleness of grace, the harshness of the law might be removed and the spirit of adoption take away the fear of servitude.

## CHAPTER II

Christ’s sacred pronouncements themselves therefore declare what his teaching is, so that those who desire to reach eternal blessedness may recognize the steps of this most blessed ascent. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3). [Note: Paul the Deacon’s copy has “Concerning which poor the Lord was speaking.” The Padiliron codex likewise has “the Lord.”]

It might perhaps be unclear which poor the Truth was speaking about if, when he said “Blessed are the poor,” he had added nothing concerning the quality of the poor that was intended, and if the mere poverty that many endure under severe and harsh necessity seemed sufficient for deserving the kingdom of heaven. But when he says “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” he shows that the kingdom of heaven is to be granted to those whose souls are commended by humility rather than by lack of possessions.

There can be no doubt that the poor attain this good of humility more easily than the rich: gentleness is a friend to the poor in their poverty, while elevation is familiar to the rich amid their wealth. Nevertheless, in many rich people also there is found a spirit that uses its abundance not for the swelling of pride but for works of kindness, and counts among its greatest profits what it has spent to relieve the misery of another’s labor. [Note: Paul the Deacon has “may use,” then “may count,” and afterward “may have spent.”]

Every class and order of people is granted fellowship in this virtue, because they may be equal in purpose while unequal in wealth. It makes no difference how dissimilar they are in earthly resources if they are found equal in spiritual goods. Blessed, therefore, is that poverty which is not captivated by love of temporal things and does not desire to grow rich through the resources of the world, but longs to become rich in heavenly goods.

## CHAPTER III

[Note: This reading follows the Padiliron manuscript, three Vatican manuscripts, one Bonn manuscript, the first edition, and Paul the Deacon’s Homilies. Others read “the first.”]

The apostles, first after the Lord, gave us an example of this great-hearted poverty. Leaving all their possessions without distinction, at the voice of their heavenly teacher they were transformed with eager conversion from catchers of fish into fishers of human beings (Matt. 4:19), and through the imitation of their faith made many like themselves. At that beginning, the earliest sons of the Church were such that “the whole company of believers were of one heart and soul” (Acts 4:32). They sold all their goods and possessions and, through their most devoted poverty, became rich in eternal goods. From the apostolic preaching they rejoiced to have nothing of the world and to possess everything with Christ. [Note: The first edition has “in those first beginnings”; Paul the Deacon has “in those primitive beginnings.” We retained the common reading but inserted “sons,” which was lacking, on the authority of the ancient Vatican Lectionary 1272.]

Hence, when the blessed apostle Peter was ascending to the temple and a lame man asked him for alms, he said: “I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). [Note: The Vulgate has “with me.” We followed the Padiliron manuscript and the same copy of Paul the Deacon.]

What is more exalted than this humility? What is richer than this poverty? He has no defenses of money, but he has gifts of nature. The mother’s womb had brought forth the man weak, but Peter made him whole by a word; and he who did not give the image of Caesar on a coin restored the image of Christ in a human being.

The riches of this treasure aided not only the man whose ability to walk had been restored, but also the five thousand men who then believed at the Apostle’s exhortation because of the miracle of the same healing (Acts 4:4). That poor man, who had nothing to give the one asking, gave such an abundance of divine grace that, just as he had restored one man in his feet, so he healed so many thousands of believers in their hearts, making those who had been found limping in Jewish unbelief eager and joyful in Christ.

## CHAPTER IV
After the preaching of this most blessed poverty, the Lord added, saying:

> **Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted** (Matt. 5:5).

[Note: In the same exemplar of Paul the Deacon, the following beatitude, concerning the meek, is placed here together with the whole of the following chapter: “Blessed are the meek,” etc. Then the beatitude concerning those who mourn is appended, together with this entire chapter, as follows: “After this the Lord said and says: Blessed are those who mourn,” etc. Afterwards the sixth chapter continues with this beginning: “Then the Lord said: Blessed are those who hunger,” etc. Thus, in the ancient codex used by Paul the Deacon, the beatitude of the meek was placed before that of those who mourn, just as these two beatitudes are both listed in this order in the Vulgate Gospel and are explained by Hilary, Augustine, and other Fathers. Nevertheless, we judged that nothing should be changed, not only because all the codices of the collections that we have seen present the order printed here, but also because this same order is preserved in the Greek text and is used by the ancient author of the *Opus imperfectum on Matthew*, homily 9; hence it was also found by the same author in several Latin copies. Indeed, this order is presented in two very ancient Gospel books, the Veronese and the Brixian, which Father Joseph Blanchinius recently published in the work entitled *Evangelium quadruplex*, vol. I, p. 25.]

This mourning, dearly beloved, to which eternal consolation is promised, is not shared with the affliction of this world; nor do those lamentations make anyone blessed which pour forth amid the lamentation of the whole human race. The character of the saints’ groans is one thing, and the cause of blessed tears another. Religious sorrow mourns either another’s sin or its own; it does not grieve over what is carried out by divine justice, but laments what is committed by human wickedness. Here the one who does evil is more deserving of lamentation than the one who suffers, because malice plunges the unjust person into punishment, whereas endurance leads the just person to glory.

## CHAPTER V

Then the Lord said:

> **Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance** (Matt. 5:4).

The earth is promised to the meek and gentle, to the humble and restrained, and to those prepared to endure every injury. This inheritance should not be considered small or worthless, as though it were separated from the heavenly dwelling, since those who enter the kingdom of heaven are understood to be no others. The earth, therefore, promised to the meek and given into the possession of the gentle, is the flesh of the saints. On account of the merit of humility, it will be changed in a blessed resurrection and clothed with the glory of immortality; it will no longer be contrary to the spirit in anything, but will possess perfect unity and agreement with the will of the mind. Then the outward person will be the peaceful and undefiled possession of the inward person. Then the mind, intent upon seeing God, will be hindered by no obstacles of bodily weakness,

[Note: The same exemplar of Paul the Deacon has “of bodily mass.” Afterwards the Padiliron codex has “against the command of its ruler.”]

nor will it any longer be necessary to say:

> **The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks upon many things** (Wis. 9:15),

because the earth will not resist its inhabitant, nor will it dare to do anything immoderate against the command of its ruler. For the meek will possess it in perpetual peace, and nothing will ever be diminished from their right, when

[Note: In the same exemplar, “and when this mortal has assumed immortality.”]

> **this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality** (1 Cor. 15:53),

so that danger may be turned into reward, and what was a burden may become an honor.

## CHAPTER VI

After this the Lord adds and says:

> **Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied** (Matt. 5:6).

This hunger has nothing bodily about it, nor does this thirst seek anything earthly; rather, it desires to be filled with the good of righteousness and, having been introduced into the secret of all hidden things, longs to be fulfilled by the Lord himself. Happy is the mind that desires this food and burns with longing for such a drink; it would certainly not seek it if it had tasted nothing of its sweetness.

[Note: “While hearing the prophetic spirit say to him” in the same copy of Paul the Deacon. Likewise, “while hearing” in the Padiliron manuscript.]

When it heard the prophetic spirit saying to it:

> **Taste and see that the Lord is sweet** (Ps. 33:9),

it received a certain portion of heavenly sweetness

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts and the first edition read “a drink.” Shortly afterwards, that edition has “heavenly” instead of “most chaste.” A little later the Padiliron codex adds: “with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and with all your will; for,” etc.]

and was inflamed with love for the most chaste delight. Thus, spurning all temporal things, it was kindled with its whole affection to eat and drink righteousness, and grasped the truth of that first commandment which says:

> **You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, and with all your strength** (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37; Mark 12:30; Luke 10:27),

for loving God is nothing other than loving righteousness. Finally, just as care for one’s neighbor is joined to love of God,

[Note: We have adopted this reading from our manuscripts because it corresponds to that love with this desire. The printed editions have “in that love.” The first edition, however, which prefers “in that love,” then has more coherently “with this desire,” as does the Padiliron codex.]

so the virtue of mercy is joined to this desire for righteousness, and it is said:

## CHAPTER VII
