[Note: In Paul the Deacon: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” Recognize the dignity of Christian wisdom; understand to what kinds of disciplines and to what rewards you are called. In the Padiliron manuscript: “Recognize, Christian, the dignity of wisdom.”]

> **Blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy on them** (Matt. 5:7).

Recognize, Christian, the dignity of your wisdom, and understand by what kinds of disciplines you are called to what rewards. Mercy wishes you to be merciful, and righteousness wishes you to be just, so that the Creator may appear in his own creature

[Note: Quesnell omitted the word “own.” Since it is absent also from our Padiliron manuscript, we restored it from our other editions, our manuscripts, and the homily of Paul the Deacon.]

and the image of God, expressed through the lines of imitation, may shine back in the mirror of the human heart. The faith of those who act is secure; your desires will be granted, and you will enjoy without end the things you love. And because through almsgiving all things are clean for you, you will also attain that beatitude which is promised next,

[Note: We have likewise restored this particle, omitted in Quesnell’s edition, from the same printed editions and from all the manuscripts.]

as the Lord says:

## CHAPTER VIII

> **Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God** (Matt. 5:8).

Great is the happiness, dearly beloved, for which so great a reward is prepared. What, then, is it to have a pure heart except to pursue the virtues mentioned above? To see God—what blessedness this is, what mind can conceive it, what tongue can explain it? Yet this will be attained

[Note: The Padiliron codex has: “when human flesh will be transformed, so that,” etc.]

when human nature is transformed, so that it may see, not now through a mirror or in an enigma, but face to face (1 Cor. 13:12), the very Deity whom no human being has been able to see (John 1:18; 1 Tim. 6:16), as he is; and may possess, through the ineffable joy of eternal contemplation, what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered the human heart (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9). Properly, this beatitude is promised to purity of heart.

[Note: The first edition has: “His splendor, the true light.” Shortly afterwards, “a foul sight” appears in the homily of Paul the Deacon and in the Padiliron manuscript.]

For a dimmed sight will not be able to see the splendor of the true light; and what will be delight to pure minds will be punishment to the stained. Let the darkness of earthly vanities therefore be avoided, and let the inner eyes be wiped clean of every defilement of iniquity,

[Note: This is adopted from the Casinensis and Padiliron codices, supported by the exemplar of Paul the Deacon, which reads: “so that the gaze may be nourished by so great a vision.” The Vulgate editions have: “by so great a vision of God.”]

so that the serene gaze may be nourished by so great a vision of God. For this purpose, we understand the following to pertain:

## CHAPTER IX

> **Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God** (Matt. 5:9).

This beatitude, dearly beloved, is not that of just any agreement

[Note: Thus the exemplar of Paul the Deacon, the Padiliron codex, and two Vatican lectionaries, one of which has “of someone” instead of “of any kind.” The printed editions have “or of any kind.” A little later, the same Vatican manuscripts have “those who love your name.”]

nor of an arbitrary harmony, but of that peace concerning which the Apostle says:

> **Have peace with God** (Rom. 5:1; 2 Cor. 13:11),

and concerning which the prophet David says:

> **Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them** (Ps. 118:165).

Even the closest bonds of friendship and the undivided likenesses of minds cannot truly claim this peace for themselves if they do not agree with God’s will. Outside the dignity of this peace are the alliances of wicked desires, the covenants of crimes, and the agreements of vices. Love of the world does not accord with love of God, nor does the one who does not separate himself from carnal generation attain fellowship with the sons

[Note: The Padiliron codex deletes “of God,” and shortly afterwards has “in mind.”]

of God. But those who are always concerned in mind to preserve the unity of the spirit in the bond of peace (Eph. 4:3) never dissent from the eternal law, saying in faithful prayer:

> **Your will be done, as in heaven and on earth** (Matt. 6:10).

These are the peacemakers, these are rightly united and holy in concord; they are to be called by the eternal name “sons of God,” and coheirs of Christ (Rom. 8:17), because

[Note: We have restored the word “love” from three lectionaries and another Vatican codex.]

the love of God and the love of neighbor will merit this: that they no longer feel any adversities or fear any scandals, but, when the struggle of all temptations has ended, may rest in the most tranquil peace of God,

[Note: The first edition has: “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.”]

through our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XCVI [also XCIII]

Or, a Treatise Against the Heresy of Eutyches, Delivered at Rome in the Basilica of Saint Anastasia

[Note: We found this treatise only in manuscripts of collections 3, 4, and 5. In the codices of collections 4 and 5, “virgin” is added to the name of Saint Anastasia. It should also be observed that in all the manuscripts the title *treatise* is prefixed to this one sermon alone. This reveals its ancient origin. That sermons were called *treatises* by the ancients is clear from the examples of Zeno, Augustine, and other ancient Fathers.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He urges them, adhering to the Apostles’ Creed, to beware of Alexandrian merchants defending at Rome one nature in Christ.—II. Eutyches had formerly been condemned in other heretics. One must distinguish in Christ what belongs to his divinity and what to his humanity.—III. One must not communicate with condemned heretics. Praise of the Roman faith.

## CHAPTER I

Just as it belongs to experienced and prudent physicians to anticipate the sufferings of human illness with remedies and to show how things contrary to health may be avoided, so it belongs to pastoral duty to take care that heretical wickedness not harm the Lord’s flock and to demonstrate how the violence of wolves and robbers must be guarded against. For heretical impiety has never been able to lie so hidden that it was not both detected and rightly condemned by our holy fathers.

It could not escape our concern, which we devote to your affection, that certain Egyptians, especially merchants, have come to the City and are defending those deeds which were wickedly committed by heretics at Alexandria,

[Note: Quesnell rightly observed in a marginal annotation that this must be understood of the murder of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria. Although the Eutychians committed other wicked acts in various places, the only murder committed at Alexandria that could be indicated here, so far as we know, is that of Proterius.]

asserting that Christ had only the nature of deity and did not possess at all the reality of human flesh, which he assumed from the blessed Virgin Mary. This impiety says both that the man is false and that God is capable of suffering.

We cannot doubt with what spirit or purpose they dare this. For, having themselves departed from the truth of the Gospel and followed the devil’s lies, they wish to make others partners in their destruction as well. Therefore, with paternal and fraternal concern, we admonish you to receive no sentiment of agreement toward the enemies of the Catholic faith, the foes of the Church, the deniers of the Lord’s incarnation, and those who oppose the Creed instituted by the holy apostles. The Apostle says:

> **Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and sins, being condemned by his own judgment** (Tit. 3:10–11).

## CHAPTER II

For the one who pursues that impiety by which he knows that many before him have perished, perishes through his own obstinacy and in his madness departs from Christ. He considers it religious and catholic to hold what the judgment of the holy Fathers established as condemned in the perfidy of Photinus, the madness of Manichaeus, and the insanity of Apollinaris,

[Note: Leo explains these matters more fully in sermons 24 and 47, and elsewhere, as well as in letters 109 and 165. In the latter, however, it should be noted that the heresy of Photinus approaches Nestorianism, while that of Manichaeus and Apollinaris approaches Eutychianism.]

so that those who deny the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation may agree to a perversity that is supposedly new and not yet condemned, to the destruction of their own souls.

As though the entire Gospel reading taught us anything other than this one mystery of divine mercy: that the human race is saved in those who believe—that the only-begotten Son of God, equal in all things to the Father, by assuming our substance, while remaining what he was, deigned to become what he was not: true man, namely, and true God. Without any stain of sin, he united to himself our complete and perfect nature in the reality both of flesh and of soul; and, conceived within the womb of his blessed Virgin Mother by the power of the Holy Spirit, he did not disdain either the manner of birth or the beginnings of infancy. Thus the Word of God the Father might speak of a human substance present in him, both through the power of deity and through the weakness of flesh: possessing bodily actions from the body, and spiritual powers from the deity.

For it is human to hunger, thirst, and sleep; it is human to fear, weep, and grieve; finally, it is human to be crucified, to die, and to be buried. But it is divine to walk upon the sea, to turn water into wine, to raise the dead, to make the world tremble by his own death,

[Col. 0468A]

and to ascend with his vivified flesh above all the height of the heavens. Thus those who believe these things cannot doubt what they should attribute to humanity and what they should assign to deity, since in both there is one Christ, who neither lost the power of his deity nor, by being born, failed to assume the reality of a perfect human being.

## CHAPTER III

Flee, therefore, dearly beloved, from those of whom we speak as from deadly poison; curse them and avoid them. If, after being rebuked by you, they refuse to be corrected, abstain from their conversations, because, as it is written:

> **Their speech spreads like gangrene** (2 Tim. 2:17).

Those who have been rejected from the unity of the Church by a just judgment are to be granted no communion. They have lost it not through our hatred but through their own crimes.

You, therefore, beloved of God and approved by apostolic testimony—you to whom the blessed Apostle Paul, teacher of the nations, says:

> **Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world**—

preserve within yourselves what you recognize so great a preacher to have thought concerning you. Let none of you become alien to this praise, so that those whom, for so many ages, while the Holy Spirit taught, no heresy violated may not be stained even by the contagion of Eutychian impiety. We trust that God’s protection will guard your hearts and your faith, so that you may please him whom until now you have faithfully obeyed, by persevering forever in the observance of the Catholic faith, through Christ our Lord. Amen.

Quesnellus thought that two prefaces—one for the consecration of a bishop and the other for the ordination of a presbyter—and an address by an archdeacon to a bishop, which are presented in the Roman Pontifical, should be attributed to Saint Leo both because of the similarity of style and because they should be appended to his sermons. Although, as regards the author, we do not wholly disagree with Quesnellus’s opinion, we have not appended those prefaces and that address here because in the second volume we shall reprint the most ancient Roman Sacramentary from the Veronese manuscript, edited some years ago by Joseph Blanchinius and attributed by him to our author. That book contains the two prefaces. More will be discussed there concerning this matter, and we shall also add at its end the address, which is missing from that mutilated Sacramentary.

# APPENDIX TO THE FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT

## [SERMONS ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT LEO THE GREAT]

## PREFACE

1. In certain editions before Quesnellus, only the sermon on the Martyrs, which had previously been published as Leonine, was assigned to an unknown author as an appendix, in a different type. Quesnellus, omitting this sermon on the Martyrs, relegated five others to an appendix: three commonly attributed to Leo—one on Saint Vincent, another on the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and a third against the heresy of Eutyches—and two others that he transcribed from manuscripts, one on the Nativity and the other on the Ascension of the Lord. He prefaced these five sermons with the following notice, which we insert here:

2. “In the following appendix we have placed those sermons which are found marked with Leo’s name in manuscript codices, although both other considerations and, above all, the great difference of style prevent their being counted among his genuine sermons.

“First is the sermon on the feast of Saint Vincent the martyr, which I reread in the manuscript Lyon Lectionary preserved in the Thuanean Library and in the Corbie manuscript, now belonging to the Abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. In the Corbie manuscript it is attributed to Saint Augustine. The Lyon manuscript bears no author’s name. Most editions of Leo’s works testify that it is Leo’s. But style itself demonstrates that it should be attributed neither to Leo nor to Augustine. Certainly its author was neither African nor Italian; rather, he reveals himself to be Spanish, both at the very beginning of the sermon and especially in these words of chapter 1: ‘Let his own people therefore venerate him all the more, whom foreigners also admire.’ From this it is clear that the martyr Vincent was praised in this sermon where he had completed his struggle by the shedding of blood.

“Another argument is supplied by the custom of the Churches, especially the Roman Church. They were content to honor the memory of the martyrs of their own region with annual solemnity, while leaving foreigners to be honored by their own people with similar celebration. Indeed, if one excepts the Maccabees, who stand outside the usual order, our Leo praised no one in a public sermon except one whom the Roman Church had cherished in her own bosom; nor even Stephen the protomartyr, although he is to be venerated by the whole Church of Christ under so many titles. The sermon therefore has another author. One might plausibly conjecture Saint Leander, bishop of Seville. The similarity of the first syllables of the two names perhaps provided the opportunity for ‘Leo’ to be substituted for ‘Leander,’ while only the former remained in the manuscript, the other letters having been worn away by age.

“To this sermon we have added two others, one on the Nativity of the Lord and the other on the Ascension, both from the Corbie codex of the Library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. They bear Leo’s name at the beginning, but I have not been able to persuade myself that they are Leo’s. They seem to me more redolent of the style of Saint Fulgentius than of Leo; the author imitated Leo at the beginning of the first sermon, for similar passages occur in Leo in the first sermon on the Nativity.

“Finally, we have not excluded from our edition a pair of centos stitched together from the writings of our Leo. The first is the sermon that was formerly second in the sermon on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul; concerning it, see the notice prefixed to the first sermon for that feast. The other is a treatise of Saint Leo the Pope, as its title declares, against the errors of Eutyches and other heretics. Those who first inserted it into the works of Saint Leo are said to have transcribed it from an ancient manuscript of the Vatican Library. From the notes we have placed in the margin, the reader will easily recognize the source from which each piece was taken.”

3. Thus far Quesnellus. He is entirely correct concerning the first three sermons, and not wholly wrong concerning the fifth. But we cannot agree with him about the sermon on the feast of Saint Peter the Apostle, which begins “Let us rejoice in the Lord.” We proved it to be a genuine work of Leo in the notice prefixed to sermon 83, where we placed it. Rather, he should have counted among the apocrypha the sermon on the Chair of Saint Peter, which he published as genuine in sermon 96, whereas we shall reprint it in this appendix as certainly spurious, as sermon 14; more will be said about it there. We shall also demonstrate, by conclusive arguments, that another sermon on the Maccabees, which is included without hesitation in all editions of Leo, should be attributed to Augustine and not to Leo. This concerns the sermons hitherto published in editions of Leo.

4. We have also discovered several other sermons falsely attributed to our author in manuscript lectionaries and collections. The distinguished Father John Chrysostomus Trombellius recently published three of them in volume II, part I, of *Opuscula of the Ancient Latin Fathers*. Of these he considers two spurious and one genuine. We too had found these sermons, as well as several others, which we shall discuss shortly; but we do not regard even one of them as truly Leonine.

Without mentioning for the moment certain particular indications to be noted in their proper places—which deprive some of the sermons soon to be listed of Leo’s authorship and prove that others should be attributed to authors sometimes certain and sometimes uncertain—the following two characteristics are sufficient to distinguish the rest, which bear no special mark of this kind. The first is the obvious difference of style and syntax, which will immediately strike anyone familiar with Leo’s manner of writing. The second is the formula used in addressing the audience—“brothers,” “dearest sons,” and similar expressions—which is utterly foreign to Leo. He consistently uses only the adjective “dearly beloved,” as will be evident to anyone who works through all his sermons. Either characteristic is sufficient, especially when both are found in the sermons now to be mentioned.

5. In this appendix it was necessary not to omit the sermons that appeared in Quesnellus’s edition. Those that had not yet been included in this edition must be divided into two classes. Some were published among the works of other Fathers; others are entirely unpublished. As for those found among the works of other Fathers—except sermon 8, for a special reason to be indicated in its notice—it will be sufficient to insert their catalogue here and to identify the editions in which they appear. The sermons are as follows:

## ON ADVENT

**I.** “The holy and desirable, glorious and singular solemnity,” etc., as sermon 116 in the appendix to volume V of the latest edition of Saint Augustine’s sermons. It is attributed to Leo in the manuscripts of Saint Peter 106, Venice, Saint Mark 153, the Tridentine manuscript, and two Veronese manuscripts. But the Maurist Fathers observed in the cited appendix that Saint Caesarius is its author.

## ON THE NATIVITY

**II.** “Desiring to say something about the solemnity of this day,” etc. It is joined to a certain sermon of Leo’s in the Vallicellian manuscript 26, with the heading “From the foregoing,” indicating in the lectionaries that this sermon and the preceding one have the same author. It is a sermon of Saint Fulgentius, p. 525 of the Paris edition of 1671.

**III.** “Our Lord and Savior,” etc. It is prefixed with Leo’s name in the Paduan manuscript of the Hermits, 112. It is read in the appendix to Augustine, sermon 141, and is attributed to Saint Caesarius.

**IV.** “Most rightly, brothers, on the day of this present festival,” etc. It is listed among Leo’s sermons in the Casinensis collection 1, but it is Saint Maximus of Turin’s, and appears among his works as homily 2, *On the Nativity*.

**V.** “The Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh,” etc. It is wrongly attributed to Leo in Vallicellian manuscript 26. It is found in the appendix to Augustine, sermon 125.

**VI.** “The Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ [has filled] the whole world,” etc. In the same Vallicellian manuscript 26 it falsely bears Leo’s name. It was published in the appendix to Augustine, sermon 125.

## ON THE EPIPHANY

**VII.** “On this celebration, dearly beloved.” It is homily 1 of Saint Maximus on the Epiphany, but is wrongly attributed to Saint Leo in Vatican manuscript 1267.

**VIII.** “Most people on this holy Epiphany,” etc. It is attributed to Saint Leo in the Venetian manuscript 153. It appears in volume II of the latest edition of Ambrose, in the appendix as sermon 10, *On the Third Epiphany*.

## ON LENT

**IX.** “This remarkable conflict,” etc., falsely inscribed to Saint Leo in Vallicellian manuscript II and the Paduan manuscript of Saint Anthony 408, since it is homily 2 of Saint Maximus, *On Lent*.

**X.** “I ask and admonish you, dearest brothers,” etc., under Leo’s name in the Bergamo codex of Saint Alexander in Colonna. It is Caesarius’s and is read in the appendix to Augustine, sermon 142.

**XI.** “The seasons of fasting, according to the Scriptures,” etc., is listed among the sermons of Saint Leo in collections 1 and 2, but in the lectionaries of the Basilica of Saint Peter 105 and 107 it bears no author’s name. It was excerpted from book 1 of Saint Isidore of Seville’s *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapters 37–40.

**XII.** “These days of holy Lent,” etc., in the appendix to Augustine, sermon 145, under Leo’s name in the Paduan Hermit manuscript 112.

**XIII.** “It should not be considered surprising that a miracle was performed by God,” etc. The passage in John’s Gospel, “It was a feast day of the Jews,” which is read on the Friday of the Ember Days of Lent, is presented under Leo’s name in the Vatican Basilica manuscript of Saint Peter 106. It is actually Augustine’s *Tractate 17 on John*.

## ON THE DELIVERY OF THE CREED

**XIV.** “When among our fathers, as the Book of Judges relates,” etc., a sermon of Saint Leo in Vallicellian manuscript 2. It is actually Saint Maximus’s homily 1, *On Various Subjects*.

**XV.** “He who comes to today’s banquet in solemn assembly,” etc. It is attributed to Leo in the Paduan manuscript of Saint Anthony 408. It is found among the works of Chrysostom, volume III of the Nivellian edition, p. 743, but it is by an unknown Latin author.

## ON THE CROSS AND THE THIEF

**XVI.** “And when prayer proceeded from our cross,” etc., in the Casinensis manuscript of the first collection of Saint Leo’s sermons. It is by an unknown ancient Latin author and appears among the works of Chrysostom, volume III of the Basel Herwagen edition of 1539, p. 567.

## ON EASTER

**XVII.** “Your Holiness remembers,” etc., in the Vatican Basilica manuscript 106 and the Tridentine manuscript; it is read in the Augustinian appendix as sermon 162.

## ON THE ASCENSION

**XVIII.** “Dearest brothers, the renowned and royal mystery of the Lord’s Ascension,” etc., under Leo’s name in Vallicellian A, 7, and among Leo’s sermons in Casinensis collection 1. It is found in the appendix to Augustine as sermon 179.

**XIX.** “The glorification of our Lord Jesus Christ was completed by rising again and ascending,” etc. It is wrongly attributed to our author in Vallicellian manuscripts A, 9 and XXV, as well as in Chigian manuscript 5, since it is Saint Augustine’s sermon 263.

**XX.** “On this day we celebrate the Ascension into heaven,” etc. It is prefixed with Leo’s name in the Paduan manuscript of Saint Justina and in Vallicellian A, 7. The Maurists published it from the very ancient Remigius codex and attributed it to Saint Augustine at the end of his sermons, as sermon 395.

**XXI.** “Everything, dearly beloved, that the Lord Jesus Christ [did] in this world,” etc. It is read in Vallicellian manuscripts A, 9 and XXV, and in Chigian 5, with Leo’s name prefixed. It is found in the appendix to Augustine as sermon 176.

**XXII.** “Our Savior, dearly beloved, ascended into heaven,” etc. It likewise bears Leo’s name in the same three codices, but in the Augustinian appendix it is sermon 177.

## ON PENTECOST

**XXIII.** “As the Lord was about to depart from this world and ascend into heaven,” etc. It is a sermon in the appendix to Augustine, sermon 184. It is falsely attributed to Saint Leo not only in the Fossatensis and Germanensis manuscripts cited by the Maurists, but also in the Venetian codex 154. In the Veronese and Vallicellian A, 9 lectionaries it is read without any author’s name.

**XXIV.** “After that singular and remarkable victory,” etc. It is sermon 182 in the Augustinian appendix. In Vallicellian XXV and A, 9 it is prefixed with no name; but in the Chigian, Paduan Saint Justina, and Venetian 154 manuscripts it is wrongly attributed to Leo.

**XXV.** “Today the adornment of perpetual grace has shone forth,” etc. It bears Leo’s name in the Paduan, Bergamo Saint Alexander, and Venetian manuscripts, but no author’s name in Vallicellian XXV. It is read in the Augustinian appendix as sermon 186.

**XXVI.** “The festival of the vows should by now be known to Your Holiness, dearly beloved,” etc. It is sermon 185 in the Augustinian appendix; consult the observation prefixed there. In the Venetian codex 154 and Vallicellian XXV it falsely bears Leo’s name; in Vallicellian A, 9 it bears no author’s name.

## ON THE FAST OF THE TENTH MONTH

**XXVII.** “We read that Saint Moses gave commandments to the people of God,” etc. It is sermon 285 among those formerly attributed to Augustine, and in fact is listed among the works of that saint in Vatican manuscript Basel 170 under the title: “Likewise, on the Catholic faith, by Saint Augustine.” It is found under Leo’s name in Vallicellian manuscript II.

## ON THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER

**XXVIII.** “The institution of today’s solemnity by our elders,” etc., and

**XXIX.** “Although the solemnity of today’s festival,” etc. These are sermons 190 and 191 of the Augustinian appendix; consult there the learned observations of the Benedictines. They are attributed to Leo in Vallicellian XXVI and the Royal Turin manuscript 218.

## ON THE ANNUNCIATION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

**XXX.** “Today’s virginal solemnity calls our tongue, brothers, to proclamation.” In the Padiliron lectionary it is attributed to Pope Saint Leo. It is actually an ancient but extremely corrupt translation of the famous homily of Saint Proclus, at that time bishop of Cyzicus and later of Constantinople, in praise of the Mother of God. The Greek and Latin text is prefixed to the acts of the Council of Ephesus, volume III of the Venetian edition, p. 577, and it also appears among the prayers and homilies of the Greek Fathers published by Combefis, p. 301. In Latin it is found in the *Bibliotheca Concionatoria*, volume VI, p. 355. This same ancient version, inscribed to Saint Proclus, was published from Vatican codex 2836 [read: 3836] by Father Vincent Ricardius, p. 673 of the Roman edition of 1630 of all the works of Saint Proclus.

## ON THE FEAST OF SAINT JOHN THE BAPTIST

**XXXI.** “Today, dearly beloved brothers, he who went before the Lord’s coming,” etc. It is inscribed to Leo in Vallicellian manuscripts A, 9 and XXV. It is found in the Augustinian appendix as sermon 198.

**XXXII.** “After that most holy birthday of the Lord,” etc. It is sermon 196 in the Augustinian appendix and is falsely attributed to Leo in the Royal Turin manuscript 768.

## ON THE FEAST OF THE HOLY PETER AND PAUL

**XXXIII.** “With the joy of the apostolic feast, dearest brothers,” etc., and

**XXXIV.** “The passion of the most blessed apostles, whose feast we solemnly celebrate today,” etc., and also

**XXXV.** “The inseparable faith of the most blessed apostles Peter and Paul,” etc. These three sermons are found among those of Saint Leo in manuscript collections 1 and 2, and the last two bear Leo’s name prefixed in Vallicellian codex VII. They are read, however, among the works of Saint Maximus of Turin as homilies 2, 3, and 4, *On the Feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul*.

## ON SAINT PAUL

**XXXVI.** “My little children, hear us and free yourselves,” etc. It bears Leo’s name in the ancient Corbie manuscript, in the Paduan codex of the Hermits 3, and in the Veronese manuscript of Saint Firmus Major. See the Augustinian appendix, where it is sermon 204.

## ON SAINT LAWRENCE

**XXXVII.** “It is holy, brothers, and pleasing to God,” etc., and

**XXXVIII.** “As we have learned from the trustworthy report of our fathers, dearest brothers,” etc. These two sermons are wrongly attributed to Leo in manuscript collections 1 and 2, since they are homilies 1 and 2 of Saint Maximus, *On the Feast of Saint Lawrence*.

## ON SAINT STEPHEN

**XXXIX.** “Dearest brothers, yesterday we celebrated the feast on which the king of martyrs,” etc. It bears Leo’s name in Vatican manuscript 1267, although the style contradicts this attribution. It is read in the Augustinian appendix as sermon 215.

## ON ABSALOM, WHEN HE PERSECUTED HIS FATHER DAVID

**XL.** “The most wicked Absalom lost his mind, lost his understanding, and lost his counsel,” etc. It is found among Leo’s sermons in manuscript collection 2 and in some manuscripts of collections 3 and 4. Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, published this sermon from these codices among *Miscellanies of Several Greek and Latin Holy Fathers*, appended to the Mainz edition of the works of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus, 1604, p. 234. He judged, however, that the sermon should be attributed to an unknown Latin author, and noted that it is found in Latin editions of Saint John Chrysostom, for example in the Nivellian edition, volume I, p. 556.

## ON THE MARTYRS
XLI. Whenever, dearest brothers, we celebrate the solemnities of the holy martyrs, etc. It was published under Leo’s name in [Col. 0475] several ancient editions, and likewise in Paul the Deacon’s Homiliary, in the Basel edition of 1496. The Louvain editors, in the Antwerp edition of 1583, and Rainaudus attributed it to an uncertain author; similarly, Vossius of Tongeren, reprinting it in a more accurate form from manuscripts in the Miscellanies mentioned shortly before, denied that it was Leo’s. It is read, however, under Augustine’s name in the Roman Breviary and in the appendix to that same teacher, Sermon 225, where the editors consider it attributable to St. Caesarius.

6. We have not included here the sermons described in the appendix to the second collection, concerning which the preface to the sermons, no. 19, speaks, although they were published among the works of other writers to whom, for the most part, they must be attributed. They are found separated from Leo’s Sermons in manuscript Basilica of St. Peter 210, belonging to that same collection, and placed after certain intervening short works of Cyprian, without any author’s name; hence they cannot be called works attributed to Leo. For the same reason, we have not placed in this series the fragment of a sermon on Abraham’s son, edited from a manuscript of the library of S. Salvatore in Bologna by Abbot P. Trombellius, volume II of *Anecdota*, part I, p. 252. For not only does the codex lack the author’s name, but the editor himself, on the basis of a simple, vague, and uncertain conjecture, thought that it might be attributed either to Leo, or to Maximus of Turin, or to Peter Chrysologus.

7. What remain are sermons attributed to Leo in certain codices, which have appeared in no edition of the Fathers. When they seemed worthy of publication, you will find them in the appendix placed below. Those which had to be rejected from Leo for some particular reason will be preceded by a notice containing the appropriate observations. As for the others, which have nothing distinctive, since the two characteristics proposed in no. 3 sufficiently demonstrate that they cannot be attributed to Leo, it will be enough to indicate at the head of each sermon the codex from which we recovered it under Leo’s name.

8. We do not therefore believe that we have discovered all the sermons attributed to Leo in manuscripts. Indeed, since in nearly every lectionary and church book that we have compared we have encountered some new Leonine sermon, we have no doubt that others, as they examine other such codices, will likewise happen to find other sermons attributed to his name—that is, spurious sermons.

9. On this occasion, it will not be useless or unwelcome to readers to record here two more frequent sources of such attributions, which we detected while examining many lectionaries. Since sermons that were to be read during the divine offices according to the character of the feasts or weekdays were copied in the same codices, when several sermons belonging to the same solemnity had the same author, the author’s name was often prefixed only to the first sermon. In the others, which followed in continuous sequence, these words were written at the beginning: *Cujus supra* (“whose [name was given] above”) or *Unde supra* (“from the one mentioned above”). These indicated that the author of the following sermon was the same as that of the preceding one.

Later scribes, when copying such codices, repeatedly omitted some sermons or added others from different lectionaries, as each thought appropriate. It therefore often happened that, when they inserted a sermon by a particular author from a lectionary in which the heading *Cujus supra* or *Unde supra* appeared, they carelessly retained the same heading even though it was followed by a sermon or sermons of another author; readers consequently took the sermon to be by the same writer.

Thus, in the manuscript lectionary of the Conventual Fathers of St. Anthony at Padua, after two sermons of St. Maximus on the Epiphany, a sermon beginning, “Today’s feast, beloved, the manifestation of the Lord, etc.,” is copied under the title *Cujus supra*. From this title it appears attributable to St. Maximus, although its author is not St. Maximus but St. Leo, and it is the fifth sermon on that same solemnity—number 35 in our edition. Perhaps for this reason two sermons of Leo himself, 38 and 43, were attributed to Augustine and are found in Augustine’s appendix as Sermons 133 and 148. Similarly, Sermon 40 of that same pontiff, which was read under Leo’s name by the monks of Corbie, Dijon, Saint-Denis, and Compiègne, was inscribed under the name of St. Maximus among the monks of Cluny, as Ulderic reports in P. Martène, *De antiquis monachorum ritibus*, book III, chapter 11, no. 2.

10. Another source of spurious attribution, though less frequent, may also be mentioned. Sometimes scribes inserted in lectionaries, without any mention of an author, sermons by some writer unknown to us; these were later taken to be by the author under whose name the preceding sermons in the same codices were inscribed.

Thus, one of two sermons—one excerpted from the works of St. Isidore of Seville and mentioned shortly before in no. 11, the other beginning, “Beloved, our faith admonishes us,” and to be published in this appendix as no. 4—was inserted without any author’s name after Leo’s sermons on Lent in the lectionaries of the Basilica of St. Peter, 105 and 107. They are therefore counted as Leonine sermons in manuscript collections 1 and 2, which derive their origin from those or similar lectionaries.

Sermons of this kind appear to be those which, in different lectionaries, are attributed to different authors—for example, St. Augustine, St. John Chrysostom, St. Leo, and others. This very variation in the authors to whom they are assigned is evidence that their author is uncertain and unknown.

11. If to these causes one adds another proposed by the Maurist Fathers in the case of Ambrose—namely, the renown of an author, by which it was thought desirable to commend the works even of unknown or inferior writers—this too was a reason for attributing sermons to Leo, whose name was extremely celebrated.

The more sermons of a particular saint were inserted into lectionaries because of his renown, the more sermons belonging to others will be found attributed to him. This can be seen in Augustine, whose sermons, introduced everywhere into lectionaries, received an incredible abundance of additions, almost equaling the number of genuine sermons. Since, therefore, St. Leo’s sermons frequently occur in lectionaries, it was not difficult to find many that had been falsely attributed to him.

But now let us set before you the sermons themselves that are to be published in this appendix.

[Col. 0477]

SERMONS ATTRIBUTED TO ST. LEO THE GREAT. (G,S)*

NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING TREATISE.

This treatise was first edited from Vatican Codex 2346 by Gerard Vossius, Provost of Tongeren, and inserted among the *Miscellanies of Several Holy Fathers* appended to the Mainz edition of St. Gregory Thaumaturgus, in 1604. It subsequently found a place in other editions of St. Leo’s works.

Vossius noted that, in that manuscript, it was preceded by an unsuitable title: “Leo, pope and bishop of the first see, to Flavian, on the errors of Eutyches,” as though it were itself a letter addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

We found the same treatise in another codex, Vatican Regina Sueciae 139, dating from approximately the fourteenth century and containing Leo’s works. Its inscription on page 160 is as follows:

“The Faith of Pope Leo, which St. Gregory praises wonderfully in his letters, saying: ‘Whoever increases or diminishes the faith of Pope St. Leo, or does not fully embrace it down to the smallest atom, must in no way be called a bishop but must be punished with anathema.’”

St. Gregory, however, wrote this not about the present treatise but about the famous letter to Flavian. Similarly, after that treatise the following note is placed there:

“The canons prescribe that at the first synod the letters of Blessed Pope Leo, which he wrote to Flavian concerning the error of Eutyches, should be read.”

We also found the same treatise in Vatican manuscript 551. That it differs from Vossius’s codex will be evident from several variant readings, and especially from the final note. It is a codex dating from approximately the twelfth century and contains Jerome’s Letters. This treatise precedes them under the following title:

“Leo, pope and bishop of the first see, to”—with “Flavian” added by a later hand, where the writing of the first hand had been erased.

A note follows:

“This is that faith which St. Gregory [praises], etc.,”

and then:

“The canons prescribe, etc.,”

as in the Vatican Regina manuscript.

Quesnellus believed that this treatise should be rejected into the appendix as certainly spurious, on the grounds that it was a patchwork (*cento*) sewn together from Leo’s writings. Everything in it is taken word for word from various texts of the holy pontiff, now from the Sermons and now from the Letters, as indicated in the margin.

After identifying the sources from which this treatise was assembled, Vossius adds:

“We thought it appropriate to cite the passages we have compared here, if only to make it clear that this is the true teaching of St. Leo. Whether, however, the present treatise was composed by St. Leo himself in this form, or was compiled by others from his teaching, does not seem worth investigating here at length.”

From St. Leo’s Letters we know one thing for certain: the same statements are often repeated in different works. But the falsity of the inscription first arouses suspicion. In addition, certain passages create difficulty because they appear to provide the reasoning for what precedes, yet do not fit sufficiently with the preceding material; this will be especially clear from note 38.

We therefore believe that there can be no doubt that this is a patchwork which someone assembled with insufficient skill. Accordingly, we have decided to leave this treatise in the appendix into which Quesnellus had placed it.

We have given this patchwork the first place because works of this kind occupy a certain intermediate position between genuine and spurious writings. On the one hand, what consists of Leo’s own words and opinions is not entirely foreign to him; on the other hand, what was arranged by someone else is not wholly his own.

Although Vossius used only one codex in publishing this treatise, he nevertheless recorded certain variants in the margin, drawn from the reading of the Sermons or Letters; these alone are displayed by later editions. From the two manuscripts mentioned shortly before—the Vatican and the Regina—we shall provide other variants, or, where appropriate, transfer the older reading into the text after indicating it.

395 SERMON I, or TREATISE AGAINST THE ERRORS OF EUTYCHES AND OTHER HERETICS.

[Col. 0477A]

CHAPTER I.

[Note: [Col. 0477B] Transcribed almost in its entirety, word for word, from Sermon 2 on Pentecost, chapters 1–3.] To instruct the sons of the Church, the service of our sermon must be added. For we do not fear that the spiritual and learned will disdain what is familiar, since it belongs to their benefit to communicate to others what they themselves have learned with great advantage.

Therefore, let the distribution of divine gifts pass through the hearts of all, and let the learned and unlearned alike not disdain the service of our mouth.

[Note: [Col. 0477B] Thus our two codices and the editions preceding Quesnellus; Quesnellus has “to insinuate,” as in Sermon 2 on Pentecost, chapter 1.]

May there also be present the generosity of the faith about whose majesty we attempt to speak, so that, for the advancement of his whole Church, he may make you capable and us abundant.

[Note: [Col. 0477B] Another reading: “we desire.” VOSSIUS.]

When, therefore, we direct the eyes of our mind toward understanding the dignity of the Holy Spirit, let us think of nothing different from the excellence of the Father and the Son, because in no respect does the essence of the divine Trinity depart from its unity.

[Note: [Col. 0477B] Another reading: “the essence of the Divinity.” VOSSIUS.]

It is eternal for the Father to be the begetter of the Son, coeternal with himself. It is eternal for the Son to have been begotten timelessly by the Father. It is likewise eternal for the Holy Spirit to be the Spirit of the Father and the Son: so that the Father was never without the Son, the Son never without the Father, and the Father and Son never without the Holy Spirit. With every gradation of existence excluded, no person there is earlier or later.

[Note: [Col. 0478B] The Vatican Regina manuscript: “earlier”; the prior word *sit* (“is”) is deleted.]

For the immutable Divinity of this blessed Trinity is one in substance, undivided in operation, sharing one will, equal in omnipotence, equal in glory.

[Note: [Col. 0478B] Another reading: “and the one immutable Divinity has one substance.” VOSSIUS.]

When Holy Scripture speaks of it in such a way as to designate something, whether in deeds or words, as belonging to the individual persons, the Catholic faith is not confused but instructed. Thus, through the particularity of word or deed, the truth of the Trinity is made known to us, and understanding does not divide what hearing distinguishes.

For this reason certain things are expressed under the name either of the Father, or of the Son, or of the Holy Spirit, so that the confession of the faithful in the Trinity may not go astray.

[Note: [Col. 0478B] The same Vossius. Other manuscripts: “of believers.”]

Although the Trinity is inseparable, we would never understand it to be a Trinity if it were always described as inseparable.

[Note: [Col. 0478B] Our two codices: “inseparably.”]

The very difficulty of speaking therefore rightly draws our hearts toward understanding, and through our weakness heavenly teaching assists us. For because in the Divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit we must conceive neither singularity nor diversity, true unity and true Trinity can indeed be perceived simultaneously by the mind, but cannot be uttered simultaneously by the mouth.

With this faith, beloved, firmly established in our hearts, we rightly believe that the whole Trinity together is one power, one majesty, one substance, one undivided operation, one inseparable love, one undifferentiated power, filling all things together and containing all things together.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] The editions and the Vatican codex add “by which,” as is also found in the cited Sermon 2 on Pentecost, chapter 3. But it is absent from the Regina manuscript, and this is better. Otherwise the sentence would remain suspended in its context; that does not occur in the sermon, where the relative pronoun is rather required by what follows.]

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Another reading: “undivided in operation, inseparable in love, undifferentiated in power,” etc. VOSSIUS.]

For whatever the Father is, the Son also is, and the Holy Spirit also is; and the true Divinity can in no respect be less or greater.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Another reading: “is in no respect either less or greater in itself.” VOSSIUS. From this point the other editions reject this reading, although it is found in both our codices, and place it in the margin because it is faulty. They substituted the reading of the cited sermon, which is excellent.]

This must be confessed in the three persons in such a way that the Trinity admits no isolation, while equality preserves unity.

CHAPTER II.

[Note: [Col. 0479D] From Sermon 3 on Pentecost, chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4.]

The majesty of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is never separated from their omnipotence. Whatever divine governance does in the ordering of all things proceeds from the providence of the whole Trinity.

There is one benevolence of mercy and one standard of justice there; nor is anything divided in action where nothing differs in will. Therefore, what the Father illumines, the Son illumines, and the Holy Spirit illumines.

Since the person of the one sent is distinct from that of the one sending and that of the one promising, unity and Trinity are simultaneously manifested to us: the essence is understood to possess equality and to admit no isolation, while the persons are understood to be of the same substance but not the same person.

Whatever, therefore, while the cooperation of the inseparable Divinity remains intact, the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit performs specifically is the ordering of our redemption and the plan of our salvation.

For if the human being, made in the image and likeness of God (Genesis 2), had remained in the honor of his nature and, not deceived by the devil’s fraud, had not strayed through desire from the law imposed upon him, the Creator of the world would not have become a creature. The eternal would not have submitted to temporality, nor would the Son, equal to God the Father, God from God, have assumed the form of a servant and the likeness of sinful flesh.

But because through the devil’s envy death entered the world (Wisdom 2),

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Another reading: “of the earth.” VOSSIUS.]

and human captivity could not be released in any other way unless he took up our cause without loss to his majesty, became true man, and alone remained free from the contagion of sin,

[Col. 0479C]

the mercy of the Trinity divided the work of our restoration among its persons: the Father was to be propitiated, the Son was to make propitiation, and the Holy Spirit was to kindle the fire.

If, therefore, guided by grace, dearest brothers, we faithfully and wisely understand what is proper and what is common to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in our restoration, we shall doubtless receive the things accomplished for us humbly and bodily in such a way that we think nothing unworthy of the one and same glory of the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Both our codices lack the words “and bodily”; Vossius supplied them from Sermon 3 on Pentecost.]

Although no mind is sufficient to think of God and no tongue to speak of him, nevertheless, whatever it is that human understanding grasps concerning the essence of the Father’s Divinity, unless it is one and the same when thought is directed either to his Only-Begotten or to the Holy Spirit, it is not understood piously but is darkened in an excessively carnal manner, and what seemed to be rightly thought concerning the Father himself is lost. For one departs from the whole Trinity if unity is not maintained in it.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Our codices have this reading, which agrees with the reading of the cited sermon. Vossius and the other editions, however, print in the text: “when he is thought of as the Only-Begotten Son and as the Holy Spirit”; they display our reading in the margin.]

[Col. 0479D] Nothing, however, is truly one if it differs in any inequality.

When, therefore, we direct the attention of our mind toward confessing the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let us drive far from our soul the forms of visible things, the ages of temporal natures, the bodies of places, and the places of bodies. Let what is extended by space and bounded by an end depart from the heart—everything that is neither always everywhere nor wholly present.

When thought conceives of the Divinity of the Trinity, let it understand nothing through distance and seek nothing through degrees.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Another reading: “but if it has thought anything worthy of God.” VOSSIUS.]

Or, if it has thought anything worthy of God, let it dare to deny this to no person there.

CHAPTER III.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] From Sermon 3 on Pentecost, chapter 6, and Sermon 6 on the Fast of the Seventh Month, chapters 2 and 3.]

Earthly wisdom did not discover this faith, nor did human opinion persuade us of it; the Only-Begotten Son himself taught it, and the Holy Spirit himself instituted it. Concerning the Holy Spirit we must think no differently than concerning the Father and the Son. For although he is not the Father and is not the Son, he is nevertheless not divided from the Father and the Son.

Just as he has his own person in the Trinity, so he has one substance in the Divinity of the Father and the Son, filling all things, containing all things, and governing all things with the Father and the Son throughout the ages.

For what is so opposed to the prophets, so contrary to the Gospels, and finally so rebellious against the apostolic teachings as to proclaim one single nature in the Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary and timelessly coeternal with the eternal Father?

For if only his human nature is to be understood, where is the Divinity that saves? If only his divine nature, where is the humanity that is saved?

The Catholic faith, which resists all errors, also refutes these impieties together: it condemns Nestorius, who divides the divine nature from the human, and detests Eutyches, who eliminates the human element from the divine. For the true Son of God, true God, possessing unity and equality with the Father and the Holy Spirit, deigned to be the same true man. He was not separated from the flesh either by the conception or by the birth of the Virgin Mother. He united humanity to himself in such a way that he remained immutably God; he imparted Divinity to humanity in such a way that he did not consume it through glorification but increased it.

For he who was made in the form of a servant did not cease to be in the form of God; not one in the other, but one in both.

Let our faith not be disturbed by the varieties of his saving dispensations. Whether in miracles of power or in the insults of his passion, let us believe both that he who is God is man and that he who is man is God.

True God and true man, therefore, is one Christ: rich in what belongs to him, poor in what belongs to us; receiving gifts and distributing gifts; sharing in mortal life and giving life to the dead, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee may bow.

CHAPTER IV.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 2.]

Since Eutyches did not know what he ought to think concerning the incarnation of the Word of God, and did not wish to labor over the breadth of the holy Scriptures, he should at least have received with attentive hearing that common confession by which the entire body of the faithful professes that it believes in God the Father Almighty and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was conceived from the Holy Spirit

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Vossius. Another reading: “from Mary.”]

and the Virgin Mary.

By these three statements almost all the devices of the heretics are destroyed.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] Another reading: “For since God is believed to be both almighty and eternal, the Son is shown to be coeternal with him.” VOSS.]

For since God the Father is believed to be almighty,

[Col. 0480D]

the Son is shown to be eternal with him,

[Col. 0481A]

differing from the Father in no respect: for he is God from God, almighty from almighty, born from the eternal as coeternal—not later in time, not inferior in power, not unlike in glory, not divided in essence.

The same eternal Only-Begotten of the eternal Begetter was born from the Holy Spirit, from the Virgin Mary. This temporal birth neither diminished nor added anything to that divine and eternal birth. Rather, it devoted itself entirely to restoring the human being who had been deceived,

[Note: [Col. 0481D] Another reading: “so that he might also conquer death.” VOSSIUS.]

and to conquering death and destroying by his power the devil who held the authority of death.

CHAPTER V.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] From Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Lord, chapter 1.]

In the conflict undertaken for us, therefore, the struggle was fought under the great and marvelous law of justice: almighty God confronted the most savage enemy not in his own majesty but in our lowliness, setting against him

[Note: [Col. 0481D] We have supplied “to him” from our manuscripts and from Sermon 1 on the Nativity, chapter 1.]

the same form and the same nature, sharing in our mortality but entirely free from sin.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] From chapter 2 of Letter 28 to Flavian.]

For we could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he assumed our nature and made it his own—he whom neither sin could contaminate nor death hold.

He was conceived from the Holy Spirit within the womb of the Virgin Mother, who gave birth to him while preserving her virginity, just as she conceived him while preserving her virginity.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] From the end of the same chapter.]

Or did that heretic perhaps think that our Lord Jesus Christ was not of our nature because the angel sent to the Virgin said: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 2)? Did he therefore think that, because the Virgin’s conception was a divine work, the flesh conceived did not derive from the nature of the one conceiving?

But that uniquely marvelous and marvelously unique birth must not be understood in such a way that, through the novelty of creation, the property of the genus is removed. The Holy Spirit gave the Virgin fertility, but the reality of the body was taken from a body; and, as Wisdom built a house for itself (Proverbs 9), the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1)—that is, in the flesh which he took from a human being and which the spirit of rational life animated.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] From Sermon 1 on the Nativity, chapter 2.]

The Word of God, therefore, God, the Son of God, who in the beginning was with God, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, became man

[Note: [Col. 0481D] We supplied the necessary word “was” from Sermon 1 on the Nativity, chapter 2.]

in order to free humanity from eternal death. He inclined himself to assume our lowliness without diminishing his majesty, so that, while remaining what he was and assuming what he was not, he united the true form of a servant to the form in which he is equal to God the Father. He joined both natures in so great a bond that glorification did not consume the lower and assumption did not diminish the higher.

CHAPTER VI.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] From Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 3.]

With the property of each nature preserved, and with both coming together into one person, lowliness was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity. To settle the debt of our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that what suited our healing, the one and same mediator between God and human beings, Christ Jesus, could both die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] Another reading: “Therefore, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being.” VOSSIUS.]

In the complete perfection and perfect nature of a true human being, therefore, true God was born, wholly in what belongs to him and wholly in what belongs to us.

Our things are those which the Creator established in us from the beginning and which he assumed in order to restore. But those things which the deceiver introduced and the deceived human being admitted

[Note: [Col. 0481D] This had to be emended from Letter 28 to Flavian. Another reading: “lost.”]

left no trace in the Savior.

Nor, because he shared in the weaknesses of human beings, was he therefore a participant in our sins. He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, increasing what was human and diminishing nothing divine. For that emptying by which he, though invisible, made himself visible, and by which he, the Creator and Lord

[Note: [Col. 0481D] Another reading: “of all things.” VOSSIUS.]

of all things, chose to be one of mortals, was an inclination of compassion, not a loss of power.

Accordingly, he who, while remaining in the form of God, made humanity, became man in the form of a servant. Each nature retains its own property without defect.

[Note: [Col. 0481D] Another reading: “And just as the form of God does not take away the form of a servant, so the form of a servant does not diminish the form of God.” [Col. 0482D] Thus Vossius from the common text of Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 3, and from Sermon 3 on the Nativity, chapter 2. That sermon, however, in two Vatican codices of the Basilica, one Vatican codex, and another of Bologna, prefers the reading of the text.]

And just as the form of a servant does not take away the form of God, so the form of God does not diminish the form of a servant.

For the devil boasted that the human being, deceived by his fraud, had been deprived of divine gifts and stripped of the endowment of immortality, had undergone the harsh sentence of death, and that he himself had found a kind of consolation in his evils through sharing in the transgression of the transgressor.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Another reading: “of the transgression.” VOSSIUS.]

He also boasted that God, compelled by the requirements of justice, had changed his original decision regarding the human being whom he had created in such great honor.

It was therefore necessary to employ a secret dispensation of counsel, so that the immutable God—whose will cannot be deprived of its benevolence—might complete his first dispensation of mercy toward us through a more hidden mystery, and so that the human being, driven into guilt by the devil’s wicked cunning against God’s purpose, might not perish.

CHAPTER VII.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] From Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0482D] We have added the particle “therefore,” omitted by Quesnellus, from our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, for “weakness,” the editions have in the margin: “lowly things.”]

The Son of God therefore entered the lowly things of this world, descending from his heavenly seat but not departing from the Father’s glory, generated in a new order and by a new birth.

In a new order, because he who was invisible in what belonged to him was made visible in what belongs to us. Incomprehensible, he willed to be comprehended. Remaining before the ages, he began to exist in time. The Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, the immensity of his majesty being veiled.

God impassible did not disdain to be a passible human being and, though immortal, to submit to the laws of death.

Generated by a new birth, because inviolate virginity, knowing no desire, supplied the material of the flesh.

[Col. 0482D] Another reading: “Therefore, nature was assumed from the mother.” VOSSIUS.]

Nature, not guilt, was assumed from the Lord’s mother. Nor, in the Lord Jesus Christ born from the Virgin’s womb, does the fact that the birth is marvelous make our nature different.

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Another reading: “our nature is different.” VOSSIUS.]

For he who is true God is likewise true man. There is no falsehood in this unity, since in mutual relation there are both the humility of man and the exaltation of Divinity.

For just as God is not changed by compassion, so man is not consumed by dignity. Each form does what belongs to it in communion with the other: the Word performing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh.

One of these shines forth in miracles; the other submits to injuries. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the Father’s glory,

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Another reading: “did not depart.” VOSSIUS.]

so the flesh did not abandon the nature of our race.

For one and the same is, as must often be said, truly the Son of God and truly the Son of man. He is God by virtue of the fact that in the beginning the Word was, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; he is man by virtue of the fact that the Word became flesh and dwelt

[Col. 0482D]

among us (John 1).

[Note: [Col. 0482D] From Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 4, with a few omissions.]

As a human being, the devil’s cunning tests him; as God, angelic services minister to him. To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is plainly human.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Another reading: “But also concerning the five.”]

But to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves, to give the Samaritan woman living water, whose draught grants the drinker that she will never thirst again, to walk with feet that did not sink upon the back of the sea, and to still the rising waves by rebuking the storm is without doubt divine.

Therefore—as I pass over many things—it is not of the same nature to weep for Lazarus, a dead friend, out of compassionate affection, and to raise that same man alive at the command of his voice after removing the mound of his four-day burial; nor is it of the same nature to hang upon the cross and make all the elements tremble when daylight was changed into night; nor to be pierced by nails and to open the gate of paradise to the believing thief.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Another reading: “upon the wood.” VOSS.]

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Another reading: “the gates.” VOSS.]

In the same way, it is not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and to say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14).

Although in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and man, that from which humiliation is common to both is one thing, and that from which glory is common to both is another.

The humanity by which he is less than the Father is ours; the Divinity by which he is equal with the Father is from the Father.

CHAPTER VIII.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] From Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 5.]

Because of this unity of person, which must be understood in both natures, the Son of man is read to have descended from heaven, although the Son of God assumed flesh from that Virgin from whom he was born.

Again, the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he suffered these things not in the Divinity itself—in which, as the Only-Begotten, he is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father—but in the weakness of human nature.

Accordingly, we all confess in the Creed that the Only-Begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2).

For the Catholic Church lives by this faith and advances through it: in the Lord Jesus Christ, humanity is not believed without true Divinity, nor Divinity without true humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] From Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 6.]

When Eutyches, however, professed in the council that our Lord existed from two natures before the union but confessed one nature after the union, I am astonished that so absurd and perverse a profession was not rebuked by the judgment of those examining him, and that so foolish and blasphemous a statement was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard.

For it is just as impious to say that the Only-Begotten Son of God existed from two natures before the incarnation as it is sacrilegious to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there is in him a single nature.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] Another reading: “so that Eutyches might not.” VOSS.]

Eutyches should not therefore consider the statement either correct or tolerable merely because it was not refuted by any judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0483D] The editions add “your,” as it is read in Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 6. But the codices omit this word; and here it ought indeed to be omitted, since the author is not addressing Flavian in this passage as he does in the letter. For the same reason, the words from the letter quoted earlier—“When, in response to the examination of your questioning, Eutyches answered, saying: ‘I confess from two natures,’ etc.”—were expressed differently here: “When Eutyches professed in the council that he existed from two natures, etc.”]

[Note: [Col. 0484D] From Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 6, with many omissions.]

For then the true faith is defended most fruitfully when a false opinion is condemned even by its own adherents.

CHAPTER IX.

[Note: [Col. 0484D] From Letter 35, to Julian, bishop of Cos, chapters 1 and 2.]

Among these matters, therefore, just as Nestorius departed from the truth by separating the Divinity of the Word from the substance of the assumed man, so this man too departed from the straight path, declaring that the only-begotten Son of God was born from the womb of the blessed Virgin in such a way that he bore the appearance of a human body, but that the reality of human flesh was not united to the Word. Concerning this monstrous falsehood, who does not see what monstrous opinions arise from it? For one who denies the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, must be filled with many impieties; and either Apollinaris will claim him for himself, or Valentinus will usurp him, or Manichaeus will possess him—for none of these believed in Christ Jesus the reality of human flesh.

Once this reality is rejected, not only is it denied that the one who was in the form of God, remaining the same one in the form of a servant according to flesh and rational soul, was born a human being; it is also denied that he was crucified, died, and was buried; that on the third day he rose from the dead; and that, seated at the right hand of God the Father, he will come to judge the living and the dead in the same body in which he was judged. For the mysteries of our redemption are emptied of meaning if Christ is not believed to have assumed the true and complete nature of a true human being.

Or, because the divine signs were evident, are the bodily evidences to be called false? Will the testimonies of both natures be valid so that he may be understood as Creator, but not valid so that the creature may be saved? What belongs to the Divinity, flesh does not diminish; what belongs to flesh, the Divinity does not destroy. For he is at once eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother; inviolable in his own power, passible in our weakness; in the Divinity of the Trinity, of one and the same nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit; but in the assumption of humanity, not of one substance, yet of one and the same person. Thus the same one was rich in poverty, almighty in abasement, impassible in punishment, and immortal in death.

For the Word was not changed either into flesh or into a soul in any part of himself, since the simple and unchangeable nature of the Divinity always remains wholly in its own essence, receiving neither loss nor increase. Yet it so blessed the nature assumed that, glorified, it remained in the one who glorified it. Why should it seem inappropriate or impossible that the Word, flesh, and soul should be one Jesus Christ and one Son of God and of humanity, if flesh and soul—though they are of dissimilar natures—make one person even without the incarnation of the Word? It is much easier for power to establish this unity of the Divinity with the human being than for the weakness of humanity alone to maintain it in its substances.

The Word, therefore, was not changed into flesh, nor flesh into the Word; rather, both remain in the one, and the one is in both—not divided by difference, nor confused by mixture. It is not one from the Father and another from the mother, but the same one in one manner from the Father before all beginnings, and in another manner from his mother at the end of the ages. Thus he might be the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2), in whom the fullness of Divinity dwells bodily (Col. 2). For the exaltation of the one who was assumed, not of the one who assumed, is meant by the statement that God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name (Phil. 2).

## CHAPTER X

[Note: [Col. 0484D] From Letter 35, to Julian, bishop of Cos, chapter 3.]

The Lord’s birth according to the flesh, although it has certain features of its own by which it surpasses the beginnings of human condition—whether because he alone was conceived and born from an inviolate Virgin without the desire of the flesh, or because he was brought forth from his mother’s womb in such a way that fertility gave birth while virginity remained intact—nevertheless did not have flesh of a different nature from ours. Nor was a soul breathed into him from a different source than into other human beings, one that excelled not by difference of kind but by sublimity of virtue.

[Col. 0484D] Thus from two of our manuscripts; the common printed text has “our.”

For he had nothing hostile to his own flesh, nor did any discord of desires produce a conflict of wills.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Thus Quesnellus and our manuscripts. Another reading has “pleasures.”]

His bodily senses were vigorous without the law of sin, and the reality of his affections was under the governance of Divinity and mind. He was neither tempted by allurements nor overcome by injuries.

He was a true human being truly united to God; he was not brought down from heaven according to a soul that had existed beforehand, nor created from nothing according to the flesh. He bore the same person in the Divinity of the Word, while possessing with us the common nature of body and soul. For he would not be the mediator between God and humanity unless the same one were both God and human being, and unless he were one and true in both.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Thus the same manuscripts and Letter 35, to Julian, at the end of the letter. The printed editions erroneously read the same in both places.]

[Note: [Col. 0485D] From Letter 59, to the clergy and people of Constantinople.]

In addition, we do not call Christ God alone, like the heretical Manichaeans, nor human being alone, like the Photinian heretics. Nor do we call him human in such a way that he lacks anything certainly belonging to human nature—soul, rational mind, or flesh: not flesh taken from a woman, but flesh made from the Word after it had been converted and changed into flesh. The three various parties of the heretical Apollinarists advanced these three false and empty positions.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Another reading has: “three parts put them forward in various ways.” Vossius.]

Nor do we say that the blessed Virgin Mary conceived a human being without Divinity, who, created by the Holy Spirit, was afterward assumed by the Word, as Nestorius taught—a doctrine we rightly and justly condemned. Rather, we say that Christ the Son of God, true God, was born from God the Father without any beginning in time, and that the same one, true human being, was born from a human mother at the fullness of time. His humanity, by which the Father is greater than he, does not diminish anything in that nature by which he is equal to the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Another reading has: “by which he is less than the Father.”]

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Another reading has: “anything of his nature.”]

This one, however, is one Christ, who most truly said, according to his divinity, “I and the Father are one” (John 10), and according to his humanity, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14).

## CHAPTER XI

[Note: [Col. 0485D] From Sermon 13, chapter 4, On the Passion; Letter 124, to the Palestinians, chapter 5; and Letter 165, to Emperor Leo, chapter 6.]

Although, therefore, in our one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and of humanity, there is one person of the Word and flesh, and both essences have actions in common, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood. With the contemplation of sincere faith we must discern toward what the humility of weakness is raised and toward what the height of power bends: what flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without flesh.

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would not conceive or give birth; and without the reality of flesh, infancy would not lie wrapped in swaddling clothes. Without the power of the Word, there would be no restoration of the weak or giving of life to the dead; and without the reality of flesh, neither food would be necessary for one who was fasting nor sleep for one who was weary. Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father; and without the reality of flesh, the same one would not say that the Father is greater.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] The Vulgate editions insert “himself” here, contrary to both of our manuscripts.]

The Catholic faith accepts and defends both, believing, according to the proper character of the divine and human substance, that the one Son of God is both human being and Word.

Although, therefore, from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb (John 1), no division has ever existed between the divine and human substance, and although throughout all bodily growth the actions of the whole period belonged to one person, we nevertheless do not confuse those things that were inseparably done by any mixture. Rather, from the quality of the actions we discern what belongs to each form.

For the divine does not prejudice the human, nor the human the divine, since both converge so completely in unity that neither is its proper character taken away nor is the person doubled.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] From the aforementioned Letter 124, to the Palestinians, chapter 8.]

Although, therefore, the Lord Jesus Christ is one, and in him there is altogether one and the same person of true Divinity and true humanity, and although the solidity of this union cannot be separated by any division, nevertheless we understand the exaltation by which God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name as belonging to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification.

For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father; between the Begetter and the only-begotten there was no distinction in essence and no difference in majesty. Nor had anything departed from the Word through the mystery of the incarnation that needed to be restored to him by the gift of God the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0485D] Another reading has: “which belonged to him from the Father.”]

The form of a servant, through which the impassible Divinity fulfilled the mystery of great piety, is human humility. This was raised to such a unity by the glory of divine power—

[Note: [Col. 0485D] The Vulgate editions note in the margin “into glory,” from the reading of Letter 124, to the Palestinians, chapter 7. The Codex Vaticanus Reginensis reads: “the glory of divine power attained in such a unity, conceived by him, etc.” The Vatican Codex reads: “the glory of divine power was introduced in such a unity, etc.”]

—from the very conception of the Virgin, Divinity and humanity were joined together, so that neither the divine was done without the human nor the human without God.

For this reason, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so the one who is equal to God from eternity is said to have been exalted. Nor does it matter from which substance Christ is named, since, with the unity of person remaining inseparable, the same one is wholly the Son of humanity because of the flesh and wholly the Son of God because of his one Divinity with the Father.

Whatever Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which what it did not possess was conferred. For according to the power of the Word, the Son also possesses without distinction everything that the Father possesses; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of the Father.

## CHAPTER XII

[Note: [Col. 0486D] From Letter 124, to the Palestinians, chapter 1.]

When many heretics attacked this faith, Nestorius and Eutyches attempted to break into it with different assertions but similar impiety. Let Nestorius, therefore, be anathematized, for he believed that the blessed Virgin was only the mother of a human being, making one person of the flesh and another of the Divinity. Yet the Word became flesh within the Virgin’s womb in such a way that, through an ineffable mystery, in one conception and one birth, according to the truth and union of both natures, the same Virgin was both the handmaid of the Lord and his mother.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] From the same letter, chapter 3.]

Let Eutyches likewise be struck by the same anathema, for, denying the reality of human flesh and soul, he asserted that our entire Lord Jesus Christ was of one nature, as though the Divinity of the Word itself had changed into flesh and soul.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Another reading has: “the falsehoods of such impiety.”]

Such sacrilegious falsehoods have been condemned throughout the world by the judgments of the holy Fathers. But the singular and true Catholic faith, which justifies the impious and creates the righteous, when drawn to share in his humanity, obtains salvation in him in whom alone the human being finds himself innocent.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] This sense agrees with the end of Letter 165, chapter 6, but is expressed there in another manner; here is the better passage, in which the compiler of the cento added something.]
