This faith, according to the prophetic, evangelical, apostolic, and salutary teaching of the Creed, was established by the Council of Nicaea; the examination at Chalcedon confirmed it; the whole world celebrates and venerates it. Defend this same faith, most beloved, with devout and praiseworthy love—or rather, faithfully and firmly retain it,

[Note: [Col. 0486D] The words “and assert it steadfastly” are absent from both manuscripts. Since Vossius could not have taken them from Leo’s Letter 165, where the letter expresses the matter in different words, as we observed in the preceding note, it is clear that the Vatican Codex from which he copied this treatise was different from the two manuscripts with which we compared the treatise.]

and assert it steadfastly. For, as blessed Paul the Apostle says, great is the mystery of piety: “He was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16).

# SERMON II. On the Nativity of the Lord

Published in Quesnellus’s appendix from the Codex of Saint Peter of Corbie, in which it is attributed to Saint Leo.

## CHAPTER I

Our Savior, dearly beloved, was born today: let us rejoice. There ought to be no place for sadness where the birthday of joy is celebrated. This joy therefore belongs to everyone, because Christ came for everyone. Let no one, then, consider himself a stranger to the joy of this day. If anyone is holy, let him rejoice, because he will receive a reward. If anyone is a sinner, let him rejoice, because he is invited to forgiveness. If anyone is a Gentile, let him rejoice, because he is admitted to salvation.

God assumed the flesh of the human race for our sake. If we do not make ourselves strangers to Christ, we are already in Christ.

Let us therefore recognize our redemption; let us recognize our salvation. The one who denies that he is in the body of Christ makes himself a stranger to the fellowship of Christ.

But let us consider, dearly beloved, what we recognize today from the Scriptures that have been read: how the one who is the Creator of the ages was born at the end of the ages. For he himself spoke, and they came to be; he himself commanded, and they were created (Ps. 148:6).

## CHAPTER II

Christ, therefore, our Savior, dearly beloved, is believed to be human being and God: God from the Father, human being from his mother; God from Divinity, corporeal from flesh. Therefore he is God before the ages and human being after the ages; God before the beginnings and human being among the final things. He who in the beginning created through majesty came today to save through flesh.

The creation of human beings was the first display of power; salvation was the second act of mercy. Moved by an affection of kindness, the Lord willed that mercy should restore to us whatever offense had taken away. He descended so that we might ascend; he lowered the heavenly things so that he might raise up earthly things; he became a participant in humanity so that he might make humanity a participant in God; he was made, as you heard through the Apostle, “of a woman, made under the law” (Gal. 4:4).

But let no one be troubled when he hears “woman” spoken of as the mother of the Lord. The Virgin conceived from the Holy Spirit, but she is called a woman according to her sex. Thus the evangelist called her a virgin, while the Apostle called her a woman, so that all might recognize the omnipotence of Divinity in the Virgin’s childbirth, but hear the name of created condition in the designation “woman.”

## CHAPTER III

Our Lord was therefore born from flesh, but not from carnal corruption; born as a human being, but not generated as a human being. He assumed flesh in such a way as to preserve the honor of his majesty. Thus, separating the purity of his birth from the accumulation of human filth, he fully accomplished at his birth the dispensation of a human being, yet did not abandon the dignity of God.

For this reason, in this world he preserved the purity of his origin, which was such at his birth, also in the sincerity of his life. He alone is the one in whose mouth, as it is written, there was no deceit—so that the one who had not known human defilement in his creation would not know it in his manner of life either.

For, as the Apostle says, “Although he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant,” and so forth. All human beings, dearly beloved, were servants of sins. Therefore the Apostle rightly said that he assumed only the form of a servant, because he was indeed a true human being but was not stained by human vices. He had the form of a servant, but not the consciousness of a servant; for although he had the appearance of a human being, he did not have the consciousness of a sinner. As the Apostle says, “Although he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant and was found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. 2:6).

A human being in appearance, but God in power; like a servant in form, but Lord in nature; outwardly displaying the weakness of his mother, inwardly possessing the majesty of his Father; outwardly humble in body, inwardly powerful in Divinity.

## CHAPTER IV

Finally, his very life among human beings displayed both at once: a human being in his sufferings, God in his powers. For he was hungry, yet by multiplying loaves through blessing he fed those who were hungry. His hunger was from the flesh; his feeding was from God. His tears were from humanity; what he accomplished was from Divinity. He showed himself human by pouring out a prayer; he prayed and was heard.

In all things, therefore, he displayed a twofold nature in himself, and for this reason he is the mediator of both substances: while he humbled the heavenly things, he exalted the human. He made complete harmony out of diversity, so that both might become one in him—our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON III. On Lent I

Now published for the first time from three manuscripts: Venetian Saint Mark’s 153, Padua PP. Eremitani 113, and Verona 214, in which it is attributed to Saint Leo the pope. But from the characteristics set out in the preface, no. 4, another unknown ancient author is revealed. Aeneas of Paris, who quotes a considerable part of this sermon in his book Against the Greeks, volume I of the Spicilegium of Acher, attributes it to Saint Faustinus the bishop; the Benedictine Fathers likewise noted in the appendix to volume V of the Works of Saint Augustine that other sermons are attributed to him in certain manuscripts. In the Paduan Codex it is entitled “The Beginning of Lent Sunday.” That this sermon was delivered on the first Sunday of Lent is clear from the beginning of chapters 1 and 3.

## CHAPTER I

I believe, dearly beloved brothers, that you have been moved to ask why, from the preceding Sunday, we have been proceeding through Lent, and why, since today is its beginning, we began celebrating its observance one week earlier.

[Note: [Col. 0487D] Our manuscripts have “we traversed.” We preferred the reading of Aeneas of Paris. “We anticipated” would seem better. Saint Maximus, in a homily entitled “On Ash Wednesday,” testifies that in his time it was the custom of some people to anticipate the days of Lent by more devoted fasting. From this sermon we learn that the fast began one week earlier, namely on the Sunday of Quinquagesima, and indeed that it was to some extent imposed by the bishop, so that some were moved by this fact, while others, after understanding that the observance was uncertain—that is, not commanded but optional—neglected to fast.]

This observance cannot be criticized. For it is a sign of the very best devotion to carry out a law before you know the law’s regulations, and to obey commands before the commands compel obedience. The former is a matter of love; the latter, of fear. The one is demanded imperatively; the other is offered religiously. In the one case a debt is paid; in the other a gift is presented.

Thus we too offered God a religious gift by fasting more. An anticipated festival cannot be criticized.

For in celebrations of joy, vows always precede the solemnity, and devotion, by longing for future gladness, anticipates it. This was therefore done not merely without blame but also prudently. In uncertain matters one ought always to add something extra as a precaution, because what is more can be cut back, whereas what is less cannot be prolonged. This is what happened in the present observance.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] “Observance,” as also in Leo, is used here for fasting.]

For by fasting more on account of Lent, we did not diminish Lent; it remains complete for us. But if we had fasted fewer days, we could not have restored the number.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Thus the Venetian and Veronese manuscripts. The Paduan Codex has “prudently.”]

## CHAPTER II

But perhaps the reason is that the fast with which we have fasted does not benefit us with regard to Lent.

[Note: [Col. 0489C] We followed the reading of the Paduan and Veronese manuscripts. The Venetian Codex has: “There is another reason why.” Shortly afterward the Veronese manuscript has “will benefit” in both places.]

It certainly benefits us. For even if it does not benefit us with regard to Lent, it benefits us with regard to salvation. If it does not benefit the count, it benefits the merit. Whom has prayer, reading, or fasting ever failed to benefit? Whom have chastity, sobriety, or gentleness failed to benefit?

Except that I consider those more blameworthy who, although they had been ready to fast, neglected to fast after they heard that the solemn observances were uncertain.

[Note: [Col. 0489C] Another reading has “after they had heard,” and then “neglected.”]

They clearly showed that they did not wish to live religiously, but only under compulsion. They feared, I believe, that if the fast of five days were prolonged, their flesh and body would fail them, and they would be unable to endure the abstinence of Lent while weak and emaciated.

[Note: [Col. 0489D] The Paduan Codex has “four.” We preferred the reading of the Venetian Codex and Aeneas of Paris, “five,” which is also supported by the erroneous reading of the Veronese manuscript, “in no way”; for the double q occurs in the word *quinque* (“five”), but not in *quatuor* (“four”). The five days are understood as the days from Quinquagesima Sunday through Thursday inclusive, which otherwise were free from fasting and abstinence.]

## CHAPTER III

Let those who are well-fed and strong, as well as those who are thin and pale, hear: today is Lent. Let the former, I say, hear so that they may begin to fast; and the latter, so that they may not cease abstaining. Let all alike hasten to enter the ark of Christ.

Indeed, let those hasten more who began abstaining later, so that they may enter more disciplined and purer. For the ark of the Lord can sustain fasting amid dangers; it does not know how to sustain a drunken person.

[Note: [Col. 0489D] The Venetian and Paduan Codices have: “The one who cannot sustain the ark of the Lord in dangers through fasting.” The Veronese is similar, except that the negative particle has been deleted. The correct reading is supplied by the example of Aeneas of Paris.]

We therefore admonish you, as we have already said, people of our time, that amid the whirlwinds of this world each of you should hasten together to the house of God, just as righteous Noah admonished the people of his time.

[Note: [Col. 0490C] Apparently in a sermon delivered on Sexagesima Sunday, when the story of Noah from Genesis was read; from it the author took his example and urged that the fast be anticipated by one week.]

He warned them of the coming flood and did not cease preaching. Although the voice of his preaching was not heard, nevertheless, even if his tongue was silent, his works spoke; even if voices were silent, the construction resounded.

[Note: [Col. 0490C] Thus from the Venetian Codex. In the Paduan: “If his voice was silent, his appearance sounded.” The Veronese is similar but has “resounded.”]

For when he was building that enormous ark, the work itself testified to the reason for which it was being made. Its very arrangement testified that new shelters would be useful for new dangers.

Any wise person could understand that some kind of shipwreck was imminent when such a house was being built—one that would not cling to the earth but float in the depths; when such lodging was being prepared—one whose floor would not be fixed to the ground, yet which the waves would not overwhelm.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] The Veronese manuscript has “would cling.”]

What wise person, I ask, would not understand that the flood was at hand when he saw such a dwelling being built—one that would not so much enclose those received within it as carry them; one that would not so much repel showers of rain as ward off the storms of shipwreck?

[Note: [Col. 0490D] The Paduan and Veronese Codices have: “would not have turned away.”]

What person, I ask, failed to perceive the danger from that lodging? In that lodging one was not to live, but rather to dwell as an exile; in whatever part of the world it might be, it would be a foreign habitation with them.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] The Veronese Codex has: “Therefore, he himself.”]

Therefore holy Noah himself preached to the peoples through his work and said that evangelical saying of the Lord: “If you do not believe me, believe the works” (John 10:38).

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Although the Veronese manuscript contains the ending “Amen,” and the Venetian has “Who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit throughout all ages of ages, Amen,” the conclusion nevertheless seems to be lacking.]

# SERMON IV. On Lent II

Published by Father Abbot Giovanni Crisostomo Trombellius among the Short Works of the Ancient Latin Fathers, volume II, part I, page 291. He considers it to be Leo’s, as we likewise found it attributed to him in our collected manuscripts 1 and 2, as well as in the Venetian Lectionary 153 and Vatican Lectionary 6452. But in Lectionaries 105 and 107 of the Basilica of Saint Peter, which inscribe Leo’s name on his genuine sermons, it is placed after his sermons on Lent without Leo’s name, together with another sermon beginning “The time of fasting,” which we observed in the preface, no. 11, to have been taken from Isidore of Seville. It is likewise read as anonymous in Vatican Lectionary 1268. Similarity of doctrine, which is also found in Augustine and other Fathers, proves nothing; the same is true of a similar interpretation of an ecclesiastical text. The style is certainly more compressed and confined to shorter sentences, and differs markedly from Leo’s style.

## CHAPTER I

Your faith, dearly beloved, admonishes us to bring forth proofs of religious devotion. We exhort you to fasting, which for those who live rightly is an increase of devotion,

[Note: [Col. 0490D] One Vatican manuscript has “an indication.”]

a wall of faith, and a victory over wickedness. We also urge you not only to abstain from food but always to abstain from every vice.

“Do not be wasteful in feasting or arrogant in drunkenness,” for it is written in Solomon: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15). The Apostle also says: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13:14).

Abstain, therefore, during these days from worldly cares and carnal desires. Let the body be chastened so that the soul may be healed.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Some manuscripts have “may be satisfied.”]

For hope is strengthened when the flesh is weakened by frugality; and by the food of delights

[Note: [Col. 0490D] “Food” here means a manner of living.]

the present life is nourished, not the future one, because luxury accompanies abundance of possessions.

Remove from yourselves the hostility of envy,

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Thus Vatican Lectionary 1268. Another reading has “envies, rivalries.”]

despising evil speech and every seed of sin. Undo the snares of violent actions, and let the deceitful devices of slanders cease.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Thus from the aforementioned Vatican manuscript. Others have “knotted.”]

Offer lodging to the needy and to those of the household of faith. Tear up unjust bonds, so that you may celebrate a fast pleasing to God not only in body but also in spirit.

## CHAPTER II

We ought also to hope for the fruits of our own fasting from the seed of almsgiving.

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Manuscript collection 2 has “to look toward.”]

For it is written: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Eccl. 3:33). We must also act so that we are overcome not by zeal for greed but by care for mercy.

We ought to abstain from lavish preparations. Let us give temporal things to the poor, so that through their prayers perpetual gifts may be offered to us. For by the exchange of a little bread and bronze, impunity from sins is conferred upon us.

We should also know that just as the Lord made many rich, so he made many poor, so that there might be a necessity of begging the Lord; and that you, who have suffered none of these things, might fear lest you perhaps suffer them.

Feed the weak one, you who are healthy, as an example of calamity in the flesh. Feed the poor, you who are rich, for perhaps you received his portion from the Lord our God in order to feed him. Feed the fasting person, so that his portion, taken away from you, may be given to another who gives generously.

Feed the one dying of hunger. For whoever can save a human being by feeding him, if he does not feed him, has killed him.

The desires of beggars who are silent should also be anticipated, for we read: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Ps. 40:2).

Let us therefore give alms to the needy before they ask, lest, because of excessive necessity, by crying out they seem to compel us, who delay, to give. Let us offer them some portion of the heavenly gifts bestowed upon us, lest through negligence we return punitive interest to our creditor (Luke 16:2).

Let us think of that rich man who, because he had denied the poor even crumbs of bread,

[Note: The supplied text adds: “[supplying: denied to the poor].”]

asked for a drop of water and did not receive it. Let us recall that widow who, by putting two coins into the treasury (Luke 21:2), offered the Lord the whole means of sustenance that she possessed.

Let us also give to our brothers whatever we have in excess. And certainly we ought not to perform divine commands sadly, like hypocrites; rather, let us give thanks to God, the author of our generosity,

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Some manuscripts have: “so that, praying … and attaining life.”]

and, praying continually, let us provide the needy with the substance of temporal life, so that we may attain eternal life; through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON V. On the Passion of the Lord I

From the manuscript Lectionary of Bergamo, Saint Alexander in Colonna, where it is attributed to Saint Leo. But the author is later; at the beginning of the sermon he excerpted several things from Leo’s Sermon 52, On the Passion I, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER I

After that first and universal ruin caused by human transgression, through which sin entered this world through one human being, and through sin death (Rom. 5:12), no one would now escape the dominion of the devil, no one the bonds of dreadful captivity; nor would reconciliation to forgiveness or a return to life be open to anyone, unless the Son of God—God coeternal and entirely equal to the Father—deigned also to become the Son of humanity and were hung bodily upon the cross for the redemption and salvation of the whole human race.

[Note: Read: *appenderetur* (“were hung up”), or *penderet* (“were hanging”).]

[Note: [Col. 0491D] In Leo: “The Son of God, equal to God the Father, deigned also to be the Son of humanity.”]

For this was the cause of the redemption and salvation of the whole human race: that God himself truly suffered in a human being, truly died, and truly rose from the dead, so that he might truly open the gates of the heavenly kingdom to human beings who believed in him and died while remaining in his will,

[Note: “Forte manentibus”: perhaps “while remaining.”]

and might redeem us from eternal night and punishment.

For he endured many and varied injuries on our behalf—not because his own faults required them, since he never committed any sin, but solely because of our need. We had been bound with chains so harsh and cast into so deep an abyss of death that we could not be released except through his immense clemency and through his human passion and death; unless he by his death took eternal death away from us, unless he broke the devil’s strength, brought us with himself to the heavenly kingdom, and granted all of us who wished to remain in his will a smooth and easy path to the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, dearest brothers, what ought we to do for such great benefits of God except to die to the world and its desires? Let us put carnal desires to death within us through vigils, fasting, chastity, endurance of adversity, perseverance in goodness, and prayer. Let us continually commend ourselves to God by repenting, mourning, and confessing our sins, and by redeeming ourselves from eternal punishments through almsgiving, so that, supported by divine help, we may deserve to remain in eternal blessedness where our Lord God led us through his death; through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON VI. On the Passion of the Lord II

From the same Bergamo Lectionary, inscribed with Leo’s name. It appears to be by the same author as the preceding sermon, for several passages are similarly excerpted from Leo’s Sermon 56, On the Passion of the Lord V, chapter 1.

## CHAPTER I

The true foundation and principal cause of Christian hope is the cross of Christ. Although it is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles (1 Cor. 1:23), because it seemed unworthy to them that the Son of God should suffer such injuries for the salvation of the world, it is nevertheless for us the power of God, by which we believe that we have been liberated, and the wisdom of God, by which we believe, understand, and indeed recognize that we remain with God in the work of his commandments.

[Note: Perhaps *esse* (“to be”) is omitted after *manentes* (“remaining”).]

Hence this supreme and most important mystery of divine mercy must always be retained in our hearts with all due reverence, but especially when the commemoration of the Lord’s passion returns. Nor should anything that was humbly and sublimely accomplished for us in the Son of God seem either impossible according to humanity or unworthy according to himself.

Let us believe and venerate all this in truth. Let us not condemn it with the impious Jews as a stumbling block, nor with unbelieving Gentiles as foolishness.

For the just and merciful God, who created and redeemed us, when we were dead through sin, willed to exercise the power of his Divinity for our redemption. Yet he also willed that this should be accomplished through human suffering together with the power of dignity, so that the lost human being might be liberated through a human being.

## CHAPTER II
Thus the medicine for the sick, reconciliation for the guilty, and redemption for captives were provided in such a way that the just sentence of human condemnation might be annulled by the just work of liberation. For if the Godhead alone had opposed itself on behalf of sinners, it would have conquered the devil by power rather than by reason. Therefore the Son of God allowed impious hands to kill him in the flesh, so that he might destroy eternal death throughout the human race and bring the human race itself gloriously to eternal immortality, blessedness, and fellowship with the angels. In all that the madness of the Jews insultingly and shamelessly inflicted upon him, our sins were washed away and our offenses expiated: for human nature, which had been guilty and captive through sin, suffered innocently in Christ, freed from every fault, so that he might remove sins and grant forgiveness of offenses through repentance and confession to all who believe in him. [Col. 0492D]

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, brothers, let us continually remember at what glorious price we were redeemed and from what harsh condemnation of the devil we were liberated. Let us strive, as far as we can, with the Lord’s assistance, to imitate our glorious redemption by good works; and what during these days we have done sluggishly and slowly regarding our correction or amendment, let us at least during these few days undertake most diligently for our salvation. Let our fasts be fruitful, so that what is taken away from our body may be restored by the flesh of our needy neighbor. Let the offender receive forgiveness from us, so that we may deserve forgiveness of sins from God. Let our confession be pure, our penance severe, our prayer tearful, and our vigils constant, accompanied by works of mercy. Let the desire of the flesh be put to death, so that eternal salvation and glory may increase for our souls. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON VII  
## On Palm Sunday

Now published for the first time from four Lectionaries: Vaticanus 1276 of the Basilica of Saint Peter, 106; the Patavine Lectionary of the Hermits, 112; and another belonging to the chapter of Verona. Although it is attributed to Leo in them, its style nevertheless does not resemble Leo.

## CHAPTER I

Beloved brothers, you have heard the account of the Hebrew Exodus and the words of the mystery: how the lamb was sacrificed, how the people were saved, and how Pharaoh was struck through the mystery. Understand, beloved, how the paschal mystery is both new and old, temporal and eternal, corruptible and incorruptible, mortal and immortal. [Col. 0493B]

It is old according to the law, but new according to the Word; temporal in its example, eternal through grace; corruptible through the sacrifice of an animal, incorruptible because of the Lord’s life; mortal because of the burial, immortal because of the resurrection. The law is old, but the Word is new; the exemplar is temporal, but grace is everlasting; the sheep is corruptible, but the Lord is incorruptible. [Col. 0493B]

[Note: [Col. 0493D] Some manuscripts add *not*, but incorrectly, as is clear from the sense.]

He was broken like a lamb, but raised again like God. For just as a sheep was led to sacrifice, yet he was not a sheep; and just as a lamb was silent, yet he was not a lamb: the former things occurred in figure, whereas these are found in greater reality. As the lamb he is also God, and as the animal he was also made man. The human being, however, is Christ, in whom all things are contained.

For Isaiah says:

> Like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation judgment was taken away from him; who will recount his generation?  
> (Isaiah 53:7–8) [Col. 0493C]

## CHAPTER II

Many other things were also foretold by the prophets concerning the paschal mystery of Jesus Christ. He was led forth like a lamb, killed like a sheep; as though from Egypt, he redeemed us from the worship of the world and saved us from the hand of the devil as from the hand of Pharaoh. He marked our souls with his own Spirit and the members of our body with his precious blood.

This is he who brought death into confusion.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Alternatively, “he clothed death with confusion.”]

He is the one who placed the devil in mourning. He is the one who struck down iniquity and injustice, just as Moses condemned Egypt to barrenness. He is the one who rescued us from slavery into freedom, from darkness into light, from death into life, and from tyranny into an everlasting kingdom.

He is the one who endured many things in many persons. In Abel he was killed; in Isaac he was bound by the feet; in Jacob he lived as an exile; in Joseph he was sold; in Moses he was wrapped up and exposed on the river by his mother; in the lamb he was slaughtered; in David he was persecuted; in the prophets he was dishonored.

He is the one who was buried in the earth and, rising from the dead, ascended to the heights of heaven. He is the silent lamb; he is the one taken from the flock and sacrificed as an offering in the evening; he is the one buried at night.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] Some manuscripts end here.]

This is Jesus Christ our Lord, who rose from the dead and raised the human being from the lower tomb to life. [Col. 0493D]

## CHAPTER III

He, then, was killed in the midst of Jerusalem. By whom? By Israel. For what reason? Because he healed their lame, cleansed their lepers, gave sight to the blind, and raised the dead.

What have you done, O Israel, to commit so unprecedented an injustice? You dishonored the one who had made you noble. You disgraced the one who had glorified you. You rejected the one who had proclaimed you. You killed the one who had given you life. [Col. 0494A]

Is it not written: “You shall not shed innocent blood” (Deuteronomy 19:10), lest you die most miserably?

“I did this,” Israel says, “because it was necessary that he suffer.”

You are mistaken, O Israel, when you think in this way. It was necessary that he suffer, but not through you, O Israel. It was necessary that he be suspended upon the cross, but this should by no means have been done by your hand. With this voice, O Israel, you ought to have cried out to the Lord:

“O Lord, if your will has decreed that your Son should suffer, let him by no means suffer through me. Let him be judged by foreigners, by the uncircumcised; let any tyrant fasten him with nails. Far be it from me to perpetrate these impious deeds.”

You were unwilling to proclaim this, O Israel, and you did not spare your own hands from laying them upon the Lord. You do not belong among his works. Did he cause you no shame when the withered hand was restored unharmed to its own body? Nor when closed eyes were opened? Nor when dislocated limbs were strengthened by his word? Nor did you blush at that recent miracle by which a man already four days dead rose from the tomb at his command? [Col. 0494B]

O Israel, you saw so many miracles of Christ, and yet you remained always in unbelief? You passed over all these things and prepared the Lord for death. You prepared the sharpest nails, false witnesses, gall, and even a sword, as for a murderous robber. You also inflicted blows upon his little body, placed a crown of thorns upon his head, and bound his good hands—the hands that had formed you from the earth—with a chain. You gave his good mouth, through which you had been nourished with life, gall instead of nourishment.

On the great feast day you killed your Lord. You were enjoying banquets, while he suffered the hunger of famine. You drank wine and ate bread, while he received vinegar and gall. You were splendid in body, while he was worn down by sorrows. You rejoiced, while he was afflicted. You sang psalms, while he was judged. You led dances, while he was laid in the tomb. You lay upon a soft bed, while he lay in a grave and coffin. [Col. 0494C]

O most impious Israel, who perpetrated this unprecedented injustice: by subjecting your Lord to new sufferings, you killed your Ruler and your Creator, who honored you and gave you the name Israel. But you, Israel, were not found to be Israel at all.

## CHAPTER IV

You did not see the Lord, nor did you wish to understand God. Did you not know, O Israel, that this is the Firstborn of God, who was begotten before the morning star (Psalm 109:3)? He was the one who brought you into Egypt and, preserving you there, supplied you with food. He is the one who was sent to you, who healed your ancestors, who raised the dead. This is the one against whom you acted wickedly, whom you slaughtered. This is the one whom you sold.

Therefore, O Israel, because you did not tremble before the Lord, you trembled when attacked by enemies; you did not fear the Lord, you did not lament before the Lord, but you lamented over dead sons. Because you abandoned the Lord, you will not be found by him. You struck down the Lord, and you too will be struck down to the ground.

You lie upon the earth, while he, rising from the dead, has been carried to the height of heaven. [Col. 0494D]

Now, therefore, come, all families of humanity, who are mingled with sins, and receive remission of sins. I am your remission; I am the Passover of salvation; I am the Lamb slaughtered for you; I am your redemption; I am life; I am your salvation; I am your resurrection; I am your King. I shall raise you up by my right hand.

This is our Lord, who made heaven and earth, who was hung upon the wood, who was buried in the earth, who rose from the dead and ascended to the heights of heaven; who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.

# ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SERMON

[Col. 0495]

In the Latin editions of Saint John Chrysostom it was published as Homily 7, *On the Resurrection*, and even now it is read under Chrysostom’s name in the Breviary of the monks of the Cassinese Congregation. Since, however, it is manifestly the work not of a Greek but of an ancient Latin author—just as are other sermons in those editions wrongly attributed to Chrysostom—it is absent from the Greek editions of this teacher.

Moreover, in manuscripts of Collections 1 and 2, and in two more recent Lectionaries, Vaticanus 6451 and 6452, we found it inscribed with Leo’s name. Father Giovanni Battista Trombellius, who did not consult the Latin editions of Chrysostom, printed it under Leo’s name from the Bolognese manuscript of Collection 2 as though it were unpublished, in *Opuscula of the Ancient Fathers*, volume II, part I, page 231. There, however, he judged it to be falsely attributed to Leo. Its style does not differ greatly from Leo’s style; but the interpolated formula *Dilectissimi* (“Beloved”), repeated four times, seems perhaps to favor our Leo.

The author is certainly Latin and, indeed, a bishop of some Western church in which the practice prevailed of reading the opening chapter of Saint John’s Gospel—“In the beginning was the Word”—on Easter Day or during the Easter vigil. This is indicated by the words:

> The Evangelist who has been read says: “And the light shines in the darkness,” etc.

The same is indicated by the words added near the end:

> You have heard the Evangelist saying today that all who believe in God are children of God. For he gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.

These words, spoken to the neophytes baptized on Easter night, clearly suggest the reason for reading that chapter: namely, that from this reading they might understand the divine gift by which the Son of God, born as the Son of Man, raised human beings regenerated through baptism to the dignity of God’s children.

Since, however, none of the documents of the Roman Church published by Cassander, Hittorp, Mabillon, Fronto, Cardinal Thomasius, or Martène displays this practice, although those documents are later than Leo’s period, they nevertheless prevent anyone from affirming that Leo was the author of this sermon.

This practice, however, was celebrated in Africa, as we learn from Augustine’s Sermons 119 and 120, in which the same Gospel chapter is explained. The Maurist Fathers, in note 1 to Sermon 119, believe that these sermons were delivered not on Easter Day but on the night of Holy Saturday. Hence this sermon seems assignable to some African author.

To remove all doubt, two Vatican Lectionaries, 1270 and the very ancient 3835, attribute it to Augustine. The ancient interpretation of the verses of Psalms 117 and 125 likewise confirms that it suits Augustine; we find that interpretation expressed in the same words in Augustine.

Although this single sermon was formerly published among Chrysostom’s works, we have inserted it in the appendix because it is more worthy than any other of Leo and because, from our manuscripts, it was possible to correct several passages.

# SERMON VIII  
## On the Resurrection of the Lord I

[Col. 0495A]

## CHAPTER I

Although all the solemnities celebrated in the churches in honor of God are holy and venerable, beloved, nevertheless this present day of the Lord’s resurrection possesses a special festivity. This is because all other days contain within themselves the joy of the living alone, whereas this day contains also the joy of the dead.

This festivity is therefore shared alike by those below and those above.

[Note: [Col. 0495B] Alternatively, “the lower regions together with the upper.”]

For when the Lord rose from the dead, he gave a festival both there, where he conquered death, and here, where he returned victorious from death.

[Note: [Col. 0495B] Some manuscripts omit “from death.”]

Therefore the Psalmist rightly speaks particularly of this day:

[Note: [Col. 0495B] In the Latin edition of Chrysostom: “The Psalmist speaks well concerning this particular day, saying.” Codex Barberinianus: “particular.”]

> This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.  
> (Psalm 117:24)

For, announcing the Lord’s resurrection, he proclaimed a day of saving rejoicing not only for those above but also for those below.

[Note: [Col. 0495B] Chrysostom’s editions: “Foretelling the Lord’s resurrection.” Then some manuscripts read “not only above, but also below,” while others omit *also*; the printed Chrysostom editions have *and* for *also*.]

When the Lord descended into the dark gloom of the underworld, there too, without doubt, the most radiant day dawned, where the Savior shone.

[Note: [Col. 0495B] Alternatively, “introduced.” The Barberinianus omits “of the underworld”; the Casanatensis has “of the lower regions.”]

Hence the Evangelist who has been read beautifully says:

[Note: [Col. 0495C] Chrysostom’s editions add “now.”]

> The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.  
> (John 1:5)

For although the Lord descended into darkness, he did not experience the obscurity of darkness. In the horror of that night, the light of eternal nature preserved the inviolable splendor of his majesty. [Col. 0495C]

[Note: [Col. 0495C] Chrysostom’s editions: “The light shone with the splendor of eternal nature.”]

Thus it was not the light that was conquered by the night, but the night by the light.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0496A]

Let us therefore rejoice, beloved, and exult in the Lord. For today the Lord has given us the light of salvation, according to what the same Psalmist says later:

[Note: [Col. 0495C] Alternatively, “there.”]

> God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us.  
> (Psalm 117:27)

And what is added there—“Establish the solemn day with crowded assemblies up to the horns of the altar”—I see fulfilled today in the Church of God.

[Note: [Col. 0495C] Thus from codex Casanatensis, better than the alternative: “And what he still says: ‘Establish,’ he says, etc.” Chrysostom’s editions: “And what did he further add? ‘Establish,’ he says.”]

For since it is filled with devout assemblies up to the horns of the altar, the fullness of the holy Church has fulfilled that Scripture. [Col. 0496B]

[Note: [Col. 0496B] Thus from codex Barberinianus. Casanatensis: “It has been fulfilled today.” Chrysostom’s editions: “This too has been fulfilled today.” Thus from Casanatensis, and referring to the Church; elsewhere, “may be full,” for which Trombellius added “all,” a word found in Chrysostom’s editions before “devout.”]

This day, beloved, is therefore the day of resurrection and life.

[Note: [Col. 0496B] We have added *this* from Chrysostom’s editions.]

The more pleasing thanksgiving of faith makes it more joyful after Lent.

[Note: [Col. 0496B] The manuscripts read: “For he made Lent more pleasing.” We have preferred Chrysostom’s editions, from which we write *of the guilty* for the manuscript reading *of them*.]

Because days of forgiveness have been joined to the sorrow of the guilty, so that patience may immediately be followed by its reward,

[Note: [Col. 0496B–C] Codex Bononiensis reads *conquered*, for which Trombellius printed *added*; but our manuscripts, with Chrysostom’s editions, read *joined*.]

according to the saying:

> Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.  
> (Psalm 125:5)

Therefore, all you who have sown in tears, receive the rewards of exultation. Let each person know that the greater the seeds of tears he has sown, the greater the fruits of joy he will gather. [Col. 0496C]

The form of future blessedness is therefore already contained in the present.

[Note: [Col. 0496C] We have added the preposition *in* from the printed Chrysostom editions.]

For just as there is now release after discipline, so in the future there will be rest after labor.

[Note: [Col. 0496C] Codex Casanatensis reads *thus* here and then *as* for *thus*.]

## CHAPTER III

Therefore I entreat you, beloved—especially you who, regenerated into new salvation, have put on white garments, together with the whole Church—to keep pure and spotless the gift you have received, so that you may preserve the brightness of your clothing also in your manner of life, and so that your hearts may be as white as your garments. [Col. 0497A]

[Note: [Col. 0497D] The Leonine manuscripts read *victorem* (“conqueror”); Trombellius emended this to *candorem* (“whiteness”). We have restored *nitorem* (“brightness”) from Chrysostom’s editions and two Vatican manuscripts.]

Today you have heard the Evangelist saying that all who believe in God are children of God.

[Note: [Col. 0497D] Chrysostom’s editions: “For he gave,” he says, “power to become children of God to those who …” From codex Casanatensis we have then added: “who believe in his name.”]

For he gave power to become children of God to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God (John 1:12).

Therefore you too are now not born from the conception of the flesh, but generated by God the Father. It remains for you to preserve, through holy life and conduct, the dignity of your holy origin.

[Note: [Col. 0497D–0498D] Thus codex Casanatensis and two other Vatican manuscripts, as Trombellius most aptly emended it. Other manuscripts read either “through holy life, conduct, and the dignity of holy origin,” or “through the conduct of holy life, and the dignity of holy …”; Chrysostom’s editions read “through the conduct of holy life, the dignity of holy regeneration.”]

And truly, in accordance with what the Apostle says:

> Like newborn infants, long for the rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow into salvation.  
> (1 Peter 2:2)

And may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your hearts. [Col. 0498D]

[Note: [Col. 0498D] Chrysostom’s editions and the Vatican manuscripts add “and your bodies.”]

Through our Lord Jesus Christ,

[Note: [Col. 0498D] The same editions read: “who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”]

to whom are honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON IX  
## On the Resurrection of the Lord II

Now published from the Patavine Lectionary of Saint Anthony, where it incorrectly bears the name of Pope Leo. [Col. 0497B]

## CHAPTER I

On this holy day, beloved brothers; on this illustrious and excellent day; on this day of which the most sacred Psalm resounds:

> This is the day that the Lord has made.  
> (Psalm 117:24)

On this day sorrow was taken away from the hearts of the disciples, and confusion was placed before the eyes of the Jews.

On this day of the resurrection of the Lord Jesus Christ, the disciples, filled with sorrow, went wherever they could. There was no one to gather them, because what is written had already been fulfilled:

> I shall strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.  
> (Zechariah 13:7)

The tomb, however, had been sealed with the seal of the Jews and secured by a military guard. Within it there was a light that could not be bound at all. Whatever we seal, we can bind completely; light we cannot bind. Therefore eternal light, which in the beginning illumined the world, and which was, is, and will always be with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit—one in the Trinity and the Trinity in unity—he himself, God and man, deigned through his wondrous resurrection to touch the hearts of the faithful with the key of his truth, so that he might illumine what was obscure and open what was closed. [Col. 0497C]

He who, with an angel serving him, was joined to the Word was today, with an angel serving him, raised from the tomb. As though the sealing could harm him who had suffered no deception, guards were appointed to guard a man whom they already knew to perform miracles, cast out demons, cleanse lepers, and raise the dead. Could he not present himself from the tomb, when he could do all this?

## CHAPTER II

But the crowd of the Jews, blind in heart, who possessed the law but did not understand it, was singing the third Psalm but did not recognize the Lord’s Trinity. For the third Psalm says:

> I lay down and slept; I awoke, because the Lord sustained me.  
> (Psalm 3:6)

While they were intent and prepared to bring confusion upon the disciples, they deserved to find confusion in their own souls. [Col. 0497D]

For they say to Pilate:

> That deceiver said that he would rise on the third day. Let soldiers be stationed, they say, lest his disciples come and steal him.  
> (Matthew 27:63)

If the tomb was closed against the disciples, could it perhaps be closed against the holy angels? Or could he not rise from a sealed tomb who was able to come forth from a sealed Virgin?

The true Virgin was sealed, and the true burial was sealed. The true Virgin gave birth without a man, and a true sealed entrance was made in the tomb. [Col. 0498A]

While these guards were present, they were no longer guards but witnesses. They could guard, but God had determined to raise his Son. For the angel of the Lord had descended from heaven; when the guards saw him, they were terrified. They could not behold that exalted angel, because they were filled with Jewish falsehood. The women were permitted to see the angel, because they had come weeping to the tomb.

To them he spoke words of great joy:

> I know that you are seeking Jesus who was crucified. He is not here, but he has risen, as he said. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid.  
> (Matthew 28:5)

O joy not only for those women, but for all the faithful and believing who have been reborn! “He has risen,” he says.

## CHAPTER III

But, to say briefly what had long ago been foretold: that king David, filled with the Holy Spirit, truly sang in the Psalm:

> The Lord awoke as one sleeping.  
> (Psalm 77:65)

Why should I say more at length? Let faith now be satisfied with what speech cannot fully explain. Who can comprehend the heavy labor of the past night? Who can comprehend the splendor of this day? [Col. 0498B]

This day has brought immense joys to all Christians, since Christ has made it better for us than all other days. Let us therefore exult, beloved, and rejoice in it, because this is the day that the Lord has made.

I think, brothers, that this day alone should be called great, and the day in which the true Day was raised for us. This day shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.

By darkness I mean the Jews, who, when they denied Christ the Day, lost the light they had received. For when they cried, “Crucify, crucify,” darkness came in the middle of the day. Since the Jews therefore sought to seize Christ at night, they remained in darkness.

But the Gentiles and the nations’ inhabitants, who departed from the darkness of idols, deserved to become day, as the Apostle says:

> He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his majesty.  
> (Colossians 1:13)

And elsewhere he says:

> We are children of light and children of day; we are not of night or darkness. Let us walk honorably as in the day.  
> (1 Thessalonians 5:5; Romans 13:13) [Col. 0498C]

Let us therefore exult, beloved, all of us with all, because this is the day that the Lord has made.

## CHAPTER IV

What profit, I ask, did your iniquity bring you, O serpent, or what did your cruel persecution accomplish? Behold, he whom you Jews fastened to the wood has risen from the tomb. Today he has been seen alive who was thought to have been killed.

Guard carefully, Jew, the tomb of your cruelty. Add military guards. Order night watches and secret vigils, so that you may prove dead the one whom you refused to recognize as living.

You gave Judas the disciple the price of silver so that he might place the dead Christ in the tomb. Give the guards as much again, so that you may hear from the disciples the false story that he was stolen. Spend, spend silver on your crime. You keep watch at the tomb through the night in vain. [Col. 0498D]

He has already risen; he has already ascended to heaven; he has already been glorified for our sake, he who humbled himself for our sake. What will you do, having become the bitterest enemies from being friends? [Col. 0499A]

He whom you fastened to the wood with such zeal now sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven. He is the one who comes in the name of the Lord; God the Lord has shone upon us. He has shone upon us and subjected you beneath our feet.

For the Father has fulfilled for us what he promised to his Son. What did he fulfill for us, and what did he promise the Son? The Psalm says:

> The Lord said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool beneath your feet.”  
> (Psalm 109:1)

Behold, Christ sits at the right hand of the Father in heaven, and he has subjected you Jews beneath our feet on earth.

When, savage Judea, you purchased the one whom you would kill, you should have kept for yourself what you bought and not lost what you possessed. Behold, you have lost the silver, and you have not possessed the one whom you purchased.

# SERMON X  
## On the Resurrection of the Lord III

From the same Patavine codex of Saint Anthony, in which it is likewise attributed to Leo.

## CHAPTER I

The Gospel of Christ is most fully revealed when his resurrection is proclaimed. For the Gospel Scripture records that many miracles and signs had already been performed by the Lord. Yet he did none greater than when he rose with his body and lifted the earth into heaven. [Col. 0499B]

In Christ’s resurrection there is both a miracle and an example: a miracle, so that we may believe; an example, so that we may hope. For what he did at the beginning, he promised to us at the end.

The impious—who are called unbelievers and pagans—and the carnal Jews believe that Christ was killed. This, then, is the great thing to believe: that Christ died. For unbelievers share this with us; they too believe that Christ died.

But we believe in death because of the resurrection, since if death had not preceded it, there would have been no resurrection. Whoever denies that Christ died also denies the resurrection. Whoever professes that Christ died must still be dealt with, so that he may believe that Christ also rose. And so it will go well for us with the Lord God.

## CHAPTER II

Let us now endure present things and love future things. Let us not delight in the world’s flatteries, nor be broken by the world’s terrors. When God flatters us, he promises eternal life; when he terrifies us, he threatens us with Gehenna.

However much the world flatters you, take delight in that of which the Psalm says:

> Delights are at your right hand forever.  
> (Psalm 15:11)

There Christ now sits and protects us with his right hand. From there he shows himself to be our head. He sees his members laboring; he sees his body being harassed by great temptations. Do you think that the head does not care for its body? [Col. 0499C]

If your eyes could be unconcerned lest you stumble; if your ears could refuse to hear the remedies by which you might be healed; if your tongue did not wish to speak for your wound; or if your hands could refuse their labors rather than come to the aid of one of your suffering members—then perhaps our Lord Jesus Christ too could fail to care what we do or how we labor.

Why do we need to say more? Hear him crying out:

> Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?  
> (Acts 9:4)

In speaking thus for his members, he wished to make him his member. May the Lord Jesus Christ deign to make useful members of us also, to whom is glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON XI  
## On the Ascension of the Lord

Published by Quesnel from the codex of Saint Peter of Corbie, in which it is attributed to Saint Leo.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0499D]

Today, brothers, Christ’s victory has been completed; today his triumphal standards are raised. Tartarus, with its prince, grieves over the plundering of its possessions; the heavenly army rejoices over the restoration of its loss.

Today that flesh which was raised from the earth has been placed at the right hand of the Father, because all natures have been prostrated before it, and every principality and power has bowed before it.

Today the new way of which the Apostle speaks (Hebrews 10:20) has been opened for us. Through Christ’s flesh the entrance to heaven—through which no flesh had previously passed—has been opened. The same Apostle calls this way still living, because it has been prepared for Christ’s members, who in due time will enter through it.

Today the opening of the book has been completed, a book that no one could open except the Lamb who was slain. Its mysteries have been revealed, since the things found in the law and the prophets have today been completed through the consummated dispensation of his humanity.

Christ first descended in order to become a participant in our nature; finally he ascended in order to make us participants in his glory. In his descent, through temporal association and visible miracles, he nursed us like infants; in his ascent he gave gifts to human beings, by which they might be instructed [variant: nourished] and brought up, as it were, to mature strength, so that they would no longer desire his temporal vision but strive with complete desire to follow wherever he had gone before them. [Col. 0500A]

## CHAPTER II

Since, therefore, we have been deprived of his temporal presence, let us hasten with complete attention toward his eternal vision. Let us say to him in the words of the Psalmist:

> My heart has said to you: “I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek. Do not turn your face away from me.”  
> (Psalm 26:14)

For the entire dispensation of Christ’s humanity intended and accomplished nothing other than to direct our attention toward heavenly things and, when the period of our mortality had been completed, to lead us to the manifest vision of himself, and, once led there, to satisfy us with the eternal glory of his face.

For, as the Apostle testifies:

> We shall see him as he is.  
> (1 John 3:2)

Hence the Psalmist says:

> I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed.  
> (Psalm 16:15)

These are the good things, Jerusalem, that eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and the human heart has not conceived; things that God has prepared for those who love him (1 Corinthians 2:9). [Col. 0500B]

The Psalmist contemplated these good things as far as he could in a mystery when he said:

> For what is there for me in heaven, and what have I desired from you upon earth?  
> (Psalm 72:25)

He said this in wonder: “What is there for me in heaven?” For he was not sufficient either to express in words or to grasp in thought the greatness of heavenly glory.

## CHAPTER III

Let us therefore hunger for these things and thirst for them. For to this end the High Priest ascended before us into the true Holy of Holies, namely, to the right hand of the Father: to strengthen the hope of his members, so that the humility of the flock might follow wherever it believes its shepherd has gone before.

For the Lord himself promises his disciples:

> Where the body is, there also the eagles will be gathered.  
> (Luke 17:37)

He calls the saints eagles, those who desire to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23). For it is said that eagles by nature can sense corpses beyond the sea by their smell, and with swift flight hasten there to satisfy their hunger.

This hunger of the eagles signifies the desire of holy souls. Their head is placed in the highest peace, beyond the world’s disturbances; with the nostrils of faith they thirst [variant: perceive], and with the flight of hope they wish to stand before the presence of their Creator and rejoice endlessly in the satisfaction of his face. [Col. 0500C]

This, indeed, is the meaning of this solemnity: that we should believe Christ already reigning at the right hand of the Father and meanwhile follow him, as it were, on the two wings of the virtues—namely, charity and hope—so that when he has handed over the kingdom to God the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24), we may reign with him without end.

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, according to the Psalmist’s exhortation:

> Because the Lord has reigned, let the earth rejoice.  
> (Psalm 96:1)

That is, let the Church rejoice. Let it rejoice in faith, because:

> You, Lord, are most high over all the earth; you are greatly exalted above all gods.  
> (Psalm 96:9)

Let it rejoice in hope, because:

> We shall be filled with the good things of your house.

Let us cry out from the depths of our hearts with the Apostle:

> Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or the sword?  
> (Romans 8:35)

For when he has brought us from hope to vision, God will be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28). He himself will be food and drink, clothing, and everything that can honorably be conceived and desired by all. [Col. 0500D]

Let Christ’s soldiers desire this gift, and let them not desert their military service until, their struggle completed, they receive from their commander an unfading inheritance.

# SERMON XII  
## On the Most Holy Trinity

Now published for the first time from the Lectionary of the chapter of Verona, in which it is entitled: “Homily of Saint Leo, Pope, on chapter 15 of Saint John’s Gospel, verse 26.”

From many passages of the holy Gospel we find that the disciples, before the coming of the Holy Spirit, were less capable of understanding the mysteries of divine sublimity and less strong in enduring the adversities of human wickedness. But when the Holy Spirit came upon them, steadfastness was given them together with an increase in divine knowledge, so that they might withstand the burning hostility of this present world. Hence the Lord now says to them in his promise:

“When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father—the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father—he will bear witness concerning me, and you also will bear witness, because from the beginning you have been with me” (John 15:26).

It must first be noted that the Lord testifies both that the Spirit of truth is to be sent by him and that the same Spirit immediately proceeds from the Father—not because that Spirit proceeds from the Father in one way while being sent by the Son in another, but because the Son says that he is sent both by himself and proceeds from the Father in order to show that the Father is one person and he another, while declaring that, in this distinction of persons, his operation and will are one with the Father’s will and operation.

For when the grace of the same Spirit is given to human beings, the Spirit is certainly sent by the Father and sent by the Son; he proceeds from the Father and proceeds also from the Son, because his sending is itself that procession by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son. He comes by his own spontaneous will; for just as he is coequal with the Father and the Son, so he has the same will as the Father and the Son. For “the Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8); and, as the Apostle says after enumerating the heavenly gifts: “All these things are effected by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

When the Holy Spirit came, he bore witness concerning the Lord: breathing upon the hearts of the disciples, he revealed to them in clear light everything that mortals ought to understand concerning him—namely, that before the ages he was equal and consubstantial with the Father; that at the end of the ages he became consubstantial with us; and that, born of a Virgin, he lived in the world without sin.

*The ending appears to be missing.*

## 427. SERMON XIII. On the Birthday of Saint Vincent the Martyr

[Col. 0501C]

We found this sermon attributed to Leo in the Vallicellian manuscript XV, from which it was appended to Leo’s Sermons in some editions. Quesnellus first relegated it to the appendix and, having compared it with two manuscripts, presents it here; in the notice inserted in his preface he also conjectured, not implausibly, that the author was Spanish. The Maurist Fathers approve Quesnellus’s judgment; they reprinted this sermon in the appendix to volume V of Augustine’s works, sermon 188, since it is attributed to Augustine in most manuscripts.

### CHAPTER I

Although, dearly beloved, one faith makes all the glorious sufferings of the martyrs—

[Note: The Lectionary of the Church of Lyons in the Thuana Library has the word *whom* (*quos*). Quesnellus.]

whom different regions have deserved—worthy of veneration by all with undivided honor, those nevertheless claim for themselves a particular dignity in this service of veneration who, more than others, both raised up the Church of God by their teaching and assisted it by their patronage. Among these we rightly celebrate the blessed deacon Vincent, through whose confession and death we unquestionably recognize Christ preached to unbelievers.

[Note: Codex Vallicellianus reads “let us celebrate” (*celebremus*) instead of “we celebrate” (*celebramus*).]

He, in order to commend the devotion of the faithful more zealously to God, at last faithfully offered himself to death, burning with a loftier affection of charity, so that he might give his followers the strength of faith, founded upon Christ the most solid rock, to imitate; and so that the seed of apostolic preaching, scattered through him among many, might by the help of his intercession be kept safe and, filled with the fruit of perfect completion, finally be stored in the heavenly granaries.

Let those, therefore, venerate him more [reading uncertain: *amelius*] in his own land whom foreigners also admire, so that he may show himself more generous in benefits to those whom he recognizes as more beloved in joys, and so that, on his solemn feast, the scope of joy may become more abundant because the effect of faith has grown through him.

### CHAPTER II

[Note: Codex Vallicellianus: “Then the spirit of blessed Vincent”; and shortly afterward Codex Corbeiensis has *of the mystery* instead of *of the ministry*.]

The spirit of this man, finally, shone forth with so great a gift of virtues that, supported by the office of the sacred ministry, he who was destined to follow the Son of God, our Lord, in his passion first administered Christ’s cup to believers for their salvation.

Having been happily intoxicated in mind by drinking from it, he fearlessly approached the madness of the raging enemy who was persecuting Christ; with restraint he endured it, securely mocked it, knowing that he was prepared to resist, unaware that he was exalted by that whereby he conquered [Note: Codex Vallicellianus, Codex Corbeiensis, and the Appendix to Augustine read *quod* (“that”) for *quo* (“whereby”).]—because, strengthened by the love of the one whom he resisted with spiritual weapons, he overcame courageously by enduring whatever punishments the furious anger of the persecutor devised against him.

Therefore neither the fiery iron frying-pan, nor the rack, nor the claws and iron hands, nor the dreadful strength of those who beat him, nor the pain of his torn limbs, nor the roar of the fire and the pouring of sizzling salt into his open wounds could in any way subject him to Dacianus’s command.

But while the swelling of his madness grew so great that, rejoicing, he boasted that he had either conquered or killed one subdued by such sufferings, the hope he had embraced deceived him. From the place where he seemed to appear victorious, he was compelled to blush as the defeated; for the harsher the punishment with which the martyr of God was pressed, the more abundantly he exulted in the steadfastness of his confession.

[Note: Now “The Passion of Blessed Vincent” in the Vallicellian manuscript.]

Therefore, brothers, it is pleasing to consider or recall more clearly the final events of his passion, so that your holiness may observe by what deceptions the devil led his servant, and how Christ preserved his servant to the end.

[Note: Codex Corbeiensis reads *sui perduxerit doli ministrum* (“to what point he led the minister of his guile”) in place of *suum perduxerit dolis ministrum*.]

### CHAPTER III

What was truly wonderful was this: the more he was externally crushed and constricted by various kinds of punishment, the more he was inwardly enlarged as his inner man rejoiced; and the more the other was externally puffed up by the display of temporal power [Note: The Corbie and Lyons manuscripts read *inflammabatur* (“was inflamed”) for *inflabatur* (“was puffed up”).], the more, realizing inwardly that he was despised, he was choked and tormented by the inner man.

Seeing himself despised, he raged, but could no longer find anyone against whom to exact revenge. For he saw that the hands of the executioners who were raging against him found in Vincent more wound than body, and that only his vigorous spirit reproached him for his folly precisely because he challenged the standard of truth.

[Note: The same manuscripts, together with the Vallicellianus, read: “the spirit reproached him for his folly, because he challenged the standard of truth” (*spiritum ei stultitiam exprobrare suam, quod provocabat veritatis normam*).]

Therefore, believing that he would avert the cause of his disgrace if he removed from sight the person who had despised him, and that Dacianus would be less ashamed if the people did not see Vincent, he ordered him to be removed from public view. But even then he was not to be deprived of punishment: the broken pottery on which he lay was placed beneath him, so that the sharpness of its points might cut more deeply into the mass of the body above it, and so that the limbs restored to torment might receive the fragments that had been scattered before them.

[Note: Codex Corbeiensis reads, “the whole place in which he lay [was covered] with potsherd”; Codex Vallicellianus and the Appendix to Augustine read, “crushed potsherd.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts of Quesnellus, our Vallicellian manuscript, and the appendix to Augustine have *fragments*.]

### CHAPTER IV

Yet blind cruelty is deceived in its expectation of victory. For divine goodness, accompanying its beloved more fully in his confession, brings new light into the darkness and makes the gloomy prison a splendid dwelling.

The healing hand of God was soothing his torn limbs, and with a more beautiful increase of his former health it repaired the losses of his pierced side. The guards, struck by the unwonted brightness of this light, stood speechless; and the mind of the pale doorkeeper was terrified by a voice, while the angels sang a hymn to God.

[Note: Codex Vallicellianus: “He ran.”]

The servant ran, half-dead, to the governor. The report of the message was to strike him more heavily than a sword-blow. Unable, because of the greatness of what he had seen, to keep silent, the judge was seized by trembling, torn by grief, and inflamed by fury. And lest Vincent, victorious in his punishments, should obtain the glory of martyrdom, Dacianus said: “Let him be brought out of the prison at once, lest, while we persist in punishing the rebel, we appear rather to crown him with victory.”

He was therefore brought out of that gloomy prison-pit, more beautiful through heavenly grace and, if he still had to suffer, stronger. But when the envious mind understood that the desire tending toward the call to the kingdom could not be broken by any kind of punishment or death, it ordered the supports of a gentler bed to be substituted and arranged for him to be comforted by a softer rest—so that, if he quietly breathed out his soul after the executioner had been removed for a little while, it might be said that he had not been killed but had died; as though punishment had not destroyed him, when punishment itself had perished together with him.

### CHAPTER V

Meanwhile the heavenly court receives blessed Vincent and grants him the gift of blessed happiness. At his entrance the angelic spirits rejoice, and all the holy fellow citizens together offer congratulations.

And we give you thanks, Lord Jesus, because the soul worthy of fellowship with you, which endured stubborn punishment, fled deceitful service; and because she who had been content that the persecutor should rage was unwilling that he should spare her.

When the insane judge learned of his holy departure, Dacianus—who did not know that Christ had conquered in Vincent [Note: The Appendix to Augustine reads *nescius* (“ignorant”) for *nesciens* (“not knowing”).]—promised himself revenge through the exposure of that man’s corpse, whose victory through virtue made him groan. He ordered the lictors to throw it out to be consumed by wild beasts and dogs, so that he might fill the bellies of creatures whose mind he himself possessed.

But so that, as divine benefits increased, grace might grant Vincent a greater victory, a raven was sent—a bird friendly to corpses—to guard the exposed feast of the body while remaining unfed.

### CHAPTER VI

From this, dearly beloved brothers, observe the distinct services corresponding to distinct merits. Once, while cautiously avoiding the impious hands of Ahab and Jezebel (1 Kings 17), Elijah was fed in the desert by ravens serving him; but Vincent, defender of the truth, slain by Dacianus’s fury, was exposed to be consumed by wild beasts. Yet he was kept unharmed by the service of a raven.

Elijah therefore obtained, by divine command and through the provision of ravens, the means by which he might be fed; Vincent was granted, through the service of a raven, that he might not be eaten.

To show that it had been appointed from heaven as his guardian, the raven disturbed the other birds that approached from a distance with no sluggish force. Among them it also drove far away a huge wolf that came nearer, beating it with wings and feathers as though it presumed, with sacrilegious daring, to touch the treasure entrusted to it.

But the wolf, by a certain expression of its appearance, stupidly indicated that it had come not so much to inflict injury as to increase the splendor of the miracle.

O shameless fury and foolish madness! The raven serves, the wolf reverences, Dacianus persecutes, and, still fierce, he is not ashamed to wish to destroy one whom the tamed ferocity of beasts was striving to protect.

### CHAPTER VII

Therefore, to conceal the martyr’s glory, he chose not a secret place but the deep sea, believing that, for hiding his glory, not walls would preserve it but the sea—almost as though the same Lord of the elements were not the one through whom, shortly before, the hidden recesses of the prison had shone and sparkled with heavenly radiance.

The body was given to the waves to be drowned, so that the waters might at least contribute to the aid of one for whom the earth had failed as a means of overcoming Christ’s soldier. After most of the strait’s waters had been crossed, God’s almighty right hand overtook the body thrown among the swallowing waves; and the hand that had carried his spirit into heaven soon returned his body to the tomb.

Thus, dearest ones, the preacher of truth is neither conquered by the punishments of torture nor overcome by the narrowness of the dark prison. He is not torn apart by beasts, nor hidden in the deep [Note: The same appendix reads, “He is not cast to beasts and torn apart.”], but is returned to the shore and proclaimed abroad, so that he who had truly confessed the name of the Godhead might discover that the supports of divine goodness were present to him in truth.

The grace of his precious death so adorned the life he had gloriously lived by virtue that what he had taught by living he firmly established by dying [Note: Another reading has *astruxerit* instead of *astrueret*.]. It was fitting that through death he should attain the vision of the one to whom he had always borne witness by the conduct of a worthy life, knowing that from contempt for the present life arises the glory of eternal blessedness.

Through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever.

[Note: The appendix to Augustine adds “God.”]

Amen.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SERMON

[Col. 0503]

Quesnellus published the following sermon, attributed to Leo, from a Paris manuscript that was mutilated or lacked its ending. We present it complete from manuscripts Vatican 1271 and 6454, adding several chapters that agree with what precedes both in style and subject matter and complete the sermon.

Quesnellus prefaced this sermon with a notice in which he seemed to assert that it belonged to Saint Leo:

> “The following sermon on the Chair of Saint Peter, which we are publishing, was supplied to us by an old manuscript of the Royal Library, marked number 341, from which we made our transcription. It has Leo’s name prefixed in the manuscript in this form: ‘A sermon of Saint Leo, pope, on the Chair of Saint Peter the Apostle.’ There can be no doubt that it is ours, insofar as this can be discerned from its style, which seems to me entirely consonant with Leo’s; nor does anything occur that would require it to be withdrawn from our pontiff. It is certainly beyond doubt that this sermon was delivered at Rome and by some Roman pontiff, as can be argued from many passages; and many phrases and expressions familiar to Leo are found here.

> “This author says, ‘Peter was set over the people of God.’ That expression, rare in this sense, is found in Letter 12 (now 14), chapter 11: ‘Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over some people should not be distressed that someone has been placed over him.’ Here he praises the fiery companies of the heavenly spirits. Leo writes of Paul as fiery, of the heart being set aflame, and of the Holy Spirit setting aflame, in passages noted in Dissertation 2. ‘The abundance of divine grace,’ ‘the left-hand number of the goats,’ ‘careful provision,’ ‘careless severity,’ ‘the snares of roaring beasts,’ ‘from the mouth of truth,’ and several other modes of expression represent Leo speaking similarly in particular writings.

> “What is said in this sermon about ecclesiastical singing and the adornment of churches, I think no one will suggest as evidence of a later age. Saint Leo often mentions singing; and the use of church adornment on feast days is proved not to be foreign to Leo’s age by Sermon 40 (now 41) of Saint Leo alone, which is on Lent and is the third of that series, since it demonstrates this immediately from the beginning.

> “The antiquity of the feast of the Chair is asserted first from the very ancient calendar preserved by Aegidius Bucherius, in which we read: ‘The eighth day before the Kalends of February: the Birthday of Peter of the Chair’; and then, more certainly, from canon 22 of the Second Council of Tours. For if the feast was already celebrated at Tours at that time—that is, in the year of Christ 566—it must unquestionably have long been celebrated in the Roman Church. Indeed, the same canon proves that it was already ancient in the Gallican Church. The superstitions for whose removal the canon was enacted probably did not begin to creep in until a long period had passed since the institution of the feast.

> “Add that in the Church’s early centuries this custom prevailed: the consecration day of bishops who had been especially distinguished was celebrated every year, as is evident from the examples of Saints Gregory the Great, Ambrose, Basil, and others. With how much greater right, then, ought the pontificate of the prince of the apostles and primate of the Church to have been commemorated by an annual feast, at least in the Roman Church, where he had established his see?

> “Moreover, since two commemorations of the Chair of Saint Peter have now been established by a decree of Paul IV, Roman pontiff, in the year 1557—one on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February for the Roman chair, the other on the eighth day before the Kalends of March for the Antiochene—it is clear that formerly there was only one solemnity in the Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, when the memory—or rather, in general, the assumption of Saint Peter to the episcopate—was celebrated with due honor. It continued in the Roman Church until the decree of Paul IV, which was adopted by the Gallican Churches only very late, as the breviaries and missals show; nor is it accepted by some even today.

> “Furthermore, since the sermon on the Chair of Saint Peter circulated under the name of Saint Augustine has long ago been relegated by learned men to the appendices as a spurious offspring, there is no memorial of that feast that approaches the antiquity of this one. Hence the calendar of Sylvius, already partly published by John Bollandus, is either shown to be an interpolation or at least to have been corrupted in the place where, instead of the feast of the Chair on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, it records the deposition of both apostles.

> “More concerning this feast may be seen in the works of the eminent Cardinal Baronius, both in volume I of the *Annals* and in his notes on the *Martyrology*, as well as in the work of our most learned Charles Le Cointe, author of the *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, volume II, under the year of Christ 566, number 18 and following.”

After Quesnellus had stated these things in their proper place in the first edition, he later regretted attributing the sermon to Leo, after considering the matter more carefully in the general preface that he printed last. But in the preface to the second edition, number 3, he says:

> “After examining the matter again and weighing the style, we have returned to our first judgment and have not dared to withdraw this sermon from Leo.”

It is especially strange that a man experienced in reading Leo could have thought the style of the following sermon consonant with Leo’s. First, the formula in chapter 1, “Dearest brothers,” and that repeated twice in chapter 3, “Dearest brothers,” are wholly foreign to Leo’s sermons.
