Then there is the barbarous, grammatically discordant adjective in chapter 2; and, to say nothing of the entire syntax, the expression in chapter 3 by which Saint Peter, advising us, is called “the consul of the heavenly court”—these differ too greatly from Leo’s Latin and method.

Nor do expressions such as “fiery,” “giver of grace,” and others of this sort contribute anything, since they are found not so much in Leo as in other writers as well. Thus we read in Hilary’s *Life of Saint Honoratus*, number 3, “God, the giver of grace,” and in number 32, “with his fiery speech,” and so forth.

The chapters we have added are of the same kind. To pass over the allegorical expressions—“senators of the world,” “in the heavenly court,” “the starry kingdoms”—those words especially in chapter 5, “that we may return to you, my brothers who live in Christ, by the steps of our tongue,” are utterly foreign to the style of our Leo.

Moreover, what is said in the same chapter about the multitude of simoniacs living in luxury belongs to a later age. Thus, although several manuscripts agree in preferring Leo’s name alone, this offspring may perhaps be the work of some Leo, Roman pontiff, who flourished in a later and more corrupt age.

As for what Quesnellus observed concerning the recorded deposition of the apostles Peter and Paul on the eighth day before the Kalends of March in the calendar of Sylvius, this should be compared with what we shall establish concerning that calendar in the observations on Sermon 82, number 4.

## 433. SERMON XIV [Elsewhere among Leo’s Sermons XCVI]. On the Chair of Saint Peter

[Col. 0505A]

Edited by Quesnellus from a manuscript of the Royal Library and supplemented from Vatican manuscripts.

### CHAPTER I

The glorious solemnity of the blessed prince of the apostles is here, dearly beloved brothers; we ought to receive it with complete gladness of spirit and celebrate it with complete devotion of mind. For although the day of his martyrdom is rightly held to be most illustrious throughout the world, this day too must be celebrated with no lesser joy by the whole holy Church.

On that day, he was ineffably crowned amid the alternating hymn-singing choirs of the angels; on this day, amid the exultant throngs of the faithful everywhere, he has been elevated with great glory to the pontifical chair. On that day he ascended the heavenly throne to his own blessedness; on this day he attained the principate of the holy Church for our salvation.

On that day he was joined to the fiery companies of the blessed spirits, so that he himself might receive eternal rewards; on this day he was set over the people of God, so that he might call us all to eternal rewards.

That celebration, therefore, belongs especially to the angels; this one, however, belongs particularly to the faithful peoples. But through the grace of him who destroyed enmity in himself, making peace in one new man (Ephesians 2:16), what could have belonged separately to individuals has been made common to all—namely, to human beings and angels.

[Note: We have added “common” from our Vatican manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER II

Let us therefore, dearly beloved, celebrate this solemnity of ours, so to speak, with a twofold joy, as is fitting; and let us celebrate it not only outwardly but also inwardly, with the full desire of our spirit.

Let the symphonies of sweetly modulating voices resound on one side; on the other, let the harmonious movements of our minds alternate.

[Note: Quesnellus reads *concordent* (“be harmonious”) for *alternent* (“alternate”).]

Let the church be adorned with lamps; let the conscience shine with virtues. Let the pavement of the basilica be cleansed of filth; let the temple of the inner person be purified from vices, as Paul says: “The temple of God is holy, and that is what you are, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3:17).

Let nothing discordant be detected in our voices [Note: Quesnellus reads *comprehendatur* (“be comprehended” or “included”) for *deprehendatur* (“be detected”).]; let nothing grammatically discordant [or: “incompatible”] be found in our conduct. For the holy day has its dignity, and our mind also has its solemnity. The former means that we abstain from the laborious affairs of this world; the latter, that we abstain from the heat of earthly desire and from the allurements of every vice.

The former is so that it may shine with visible ornaments; the latter, so that it may gleam with virtues.

But since today, through the bounty of divine grace, we have received so excellent a shepherd [Note: The Vatican manuscripts have *quia* (“because”).], with what audacity do we dare, on our own part, to open our mouths to speak to you? Let us therefore behold with the eyes of faith our most blessed pontiff raised upon the episcopal seat, crowned with priestly bands, speaking to his people in person and preaching, as usual, in the assembly of the holy Church.

Let him—let him in person—say what he determines must be done by you and by us.

Behold, most blessed shepherd, we, your sheep, are all here together, and we humbly beseech you to grant us the nourishment of your teaching. Yet we cannot even be sheep from ourselves unless you instruct us how we ought to put on the fleece of innocence.

For you say: “Like newborn infants, long for the rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow toward salvation” (1 Peter 2:2).

### CHAPTER III

Now that we have heard how we ought to become sheep [Note: We have supplied *vero* (“indeed” or “now”) from our manuscripts.], it remains for him to show us also how we can escape the sinister number of wanton goats.

“I beseech you,” he says, “as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from carnal desires, which wage war against the soul” (1 Peter 2:11). And in order to confirm by a supreme example this mortification of the flesh, which he teaches by word, he says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you might follow his footsteps” (ibid., 21).

Now keepers of sheep are accustomed carefully to restrain their flock from harmful grasses and to move to distant pastures in search of wholesome grazing. When they prohibit some things to guard against destruction, they provide others to restore life. In one place they remove what is harmful; in another they permit what is beneficial, lest, while they carefully fast from poisonous nourishment, they should fail through careless severity because they are empty even of what brings salvation.

Therefore, because our shepherd restrains us by prohibiting the deadly pastures of carnal desires, he now opens the mouths of our hope toward the life-giving meadow.

[Note: Quesnellus reads *relaxet* (“may open”) for *relaxat* (“opens”).] For he says: “Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, by which he called us into a living hope, into an undefiled and unfading inheritance kept in heaven” (1 Peter 1:3).

Let us therefore, dearest brothers [Note: Another reading has “my brothers” (*fratres mei*).], listen with the ears of our hearts raised up to the words of our blessed guardian, the apostle Peter; and, keeping to the straight track of his footsteps, let us never stray from the pastures to which he calls us.

For if we willingly accept his counsel, we shall not fear the snares of roaring beasts. Does our guardian not diligently watch over his flock and cry out with anxious words that the attacks of wild beasts must be guarded against? “The devil,” he says, “like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour; resist him, firm in faith” (1 Peter 5:8).

It is therefore fitting, dearest brothers, that we listen with attentive hearts to the consul of the heavenly court advising us, and that we fear to disregard the most certain counsel of our salvation.

This is he who heard from the mouth of truth: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

### CHAPTER IV

A man therefore ought not to despise in his preaching the one who merited being honored by the Creator and Redeemer of humanity with the privilege of so great a dignity. It is terrible to disregard carelessly the counsel of one whose authority has subjected both heaven and earth to him—one who closes and opens heaven and binds and looses earthly things according to his will.

Thus the chair of ecclesiastical primacy was divinely handed over to him so that it might be founded upon perpetual stability. From the beginning of the world, we know that there were many chairs among the people of God, not only good but also evil—

[The words in parentheses are found in Codex Vaticanus 1271.]

—but in the chair of Peter Christ utterly overthrew the evil ones and strengthened the good ones with eternal stability.

Concerning the good chairs it is said: “Let them exalt him in the assembly of the people, and praise the Lord in the chair of the elders” (Psalm 106:32) [Note: Another reading has “praise *him*, the Lord.”]—those who preserve the teachings of the teachers of the holy Church by their works.

Moses held the chair among the Israelite people, concerning which Truth himself said [Note: Another reading has the present tense, *dicit* (“says”).]: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the chair of Moses” (Matthew 23:1).

But concerning the chair of the rejected, the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the chair of pestilence” (Psalm 1:1). For the one who teaches the people the pestilences of errors sits in the chair of pestilence.

### CHAPTER V

The Lord mystically overthrows such chairs when he drove the sellers and buyers alike from the temple. For it is written: “He poured out the bronze of the money-changers and overturned the chairs of those selling doves” (John 2:11).

That chair of pestilence Simon Magus tried to acquire when he desired to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit. But the hand of the apostolic tongue overthrew it before it was built and cut down the pestilential heresy at its very root, saying: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of sin. You have neither part nor lot in this matter” (Acts 8:23).

By the sword of this apostolic sentence all those have been struck down who either eagerly desire to purchase ecclesiastical honors or do not fear to sell them.

Their pitiable multitude is still seen today in the holy Church: people who are not afraid to possess the gift of God against the Lord for their own lust; who, although they may appear outwardly to be alive, already stink, buried in the perpetual death of damnation. They regard seeking profit from souls as nothing and nourish wretched flesh in delicacies and in the stench of luxury.

Against such people, I think it better to remain silent than to say a few words. For a few words are not sufficient to tear apart and rebuke their mortal danger—people against whom heaven and earth and all the elements bring testimony of condemnation.

Therefore we now cease speaking against dry bones, so that we may return by the steps of our tongue to you, my brothers who live in Christ.

### CHAPTER VI

Let us therefore, dearly beloved, establish the dwelling of our mind upon the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, so that it may remain unharmed against every assault of adversity.

Let us follow the example of the prudent man of whom the Lord says in the Gospel: “He built his house upon rock; the rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, because it had been founded upon rock” (Matthew 7:24–25).

[Note: The five preceding words, “because it had been founded upon rock,” are supplied by Codex Vaticanus 1271.]

Let us recall what is said through Paul: “We cannot rejoice here with the world and reign there with the Lord”; and again: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21).

Behold, the blessed apostle Peter, whose feast we celebrate today, who was so dear and familiar to our Lord Jesus Christ, who received from him the grant of such power not only on earth but also in heaven—through the martyrdom of the cross nevertheless entered the starry kingdoms.

### CHAPTER VII

Therefore, dearly beloved, let us constantly put our flesh to death with its vices and desires, and let us observe the apostolic commands with the greatest devotion, because we shall have to render an account of our actions to those very judges.

For it was said to them: “Amen, I say to you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19:23).

They are the senators of the world, concerning whom it is written: “Her husband is noble at the gates when he sits with the senators of the land” (Proverbs 31:23).

Founded, therefore, upon their faith and instructed by their teachings, let us strive, with divine assistance, to lead this mortal life temporally in such a way that we may deserve to rejoice with them without end in the heavenly court.

[Perhaps: “through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ.”]

To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XV. On the Annunciation of the Blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary

This sermon is wrongly attributed to Pope Leo in two Lectionaries of Saint Benedict of Padirion; in one manuscript it is appended to another sermon on the same feast, likewise attributed to Leo, which we mentioned in the preface to this appendix, number 30.

Just as we proved there that the other sermon is an ancient version of a sermon by Saint Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, so we not implausibly believe that this one too is an unpublished translation of another sermon by the same author, especially since it has been established that several of his homilies are missing.

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0508D]

The universal Church throughout this present age regularly celebrates the coming of our Lord and Savior, by which he deigned to visit us after clothing himself in humanity; and the annual return of this event makes her exceedingly joyful.

For what the world received, believing that it had once been accomplished for the redemption of its own salvation, it consecrated to posterity to be honored through eternal generations; and thus caused joy to be born from the old life in the newness of the mind.

Now, therefore, the miracle of the past is set before our eyes, while the divine readings solemnly present what was accomplished long ago and it is celebrated with the deepest devotion each year.

Behold, when the holy Gospel was read, we heard that the archangel Gabriel was sent by the Lord from the royal thrones to promise a Son to the Virgin Mary (Luke 1:26).

Entering to her, who modestly lay hidden in secret, away from human beings, he greeted her at the beginning of his message in this way:

“Hail, Mary,” he said, “hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you.”

[Note: One manuscript omits this second “Hail.”]

O wondrous announcement! O extraordinary greeting, bearing an abundance of fullness and illuminating the virgin breast!

The angel descended, sparkling in his fiery flight, illuminating both Mary’s dwelling and her mind with the radiance of his splendor. The herald, coming before the Judge, was so illustrious and gentle, so swift and hastening, that the Lord of majesty might be received in the palace of virginity, which remained hidden on earth.

“Hail,” he said, “Mary; hail, full of grace; the Lord is with you” (ibid., 28).

The one who created you has already chosen you in advance; the one whom you are to bear has already filled you.

### CHAPTER II
Troubled, then, as she was at his entrance, she was considering who had thus blessed her; while, preserving within herself the modest silence of her holy purpose and being unacquainted with masculine address, she was disturbed when the angel greeted her and was astonished that he blessed her in this manner—yet she did not dare to anticipate what he would say. Wondering inwardly for a long while [Note: One manuscript reads “with love”; another, “than with love.” The context required the emendation “with fear,” whence Gabriel said: “Do not fear.”], she weighed with a fearful heart why she was being blessed in such a way. As she hesitated, pondering at length, and more keenly perceived the angel’s presence—for in considering both the brilliance of his presence and the blessing she naturally hesitated—Gabriel, the illustrious archangel, envoy of the most holy Trinity and knower of heavenly secrets, looked upon her and said:

“Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father [Note: Another copy has “his own.”], and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:30–33).

Then Mary, listening to these angelic words with careful discernment and weighing them as a most prudent virgin in the balance of her mind, said: “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Ibid., 34). “Shall I have a son, who do not know a man? Shall I carry a fetus, who possess no maternal nourishment? From my dry breasts, whence shall I provide milk for the lips of an infant asking to suck, when neither inborn youthful love has possessed the bed [Note: The manuscripts read “throne.”] of my chamber nor any marital embrace has ever been granted?” And the angel said:

“Not so, Mary, not so. Do not be frightened; do not be anxious [Note: One manuscript has “about your own.”] about the integrity of your holiness. You will remain untouched, and you will rejoice in offspring, in a son. Without union with a mortal man you will become the daughter-in-law of the Most High, because you are to give birth to the Son of God. That chaste man Joseph, adorned with the name of righteousness, will not be your husband but your guardian; he will not approach you. Rather, the Holy Spirit will come upon you. You will not burn with carnal desire [Note: Another reading has “of the flesh.”], nor will a bridegroom cling to you; but the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Ibid., 35).

O dwelling worthy of God! Before the angel, by the most luminous testimony, had proved to her that what had been brought down from the hall of the Father’s palace was of such a nature as she was receiving with her own ears, she uttered no word with her modest mouth, no assent of response [Note: We believe that the word “no” must be supplied.]. But when Mary heard, confirmed by truthful assurance, that her virginity would remain unharmed, she immediately replied, composing with great adornment in her most holy breast the secret of the chamber that was to come:

“Behold,” she said, “the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word” (Ibid., 38).

As though she were saying: “My heart is ready, because my womb remains untouched. Let it happen to me, Gabriel the archangel, according to your word. Let him come to his dwelling who set his tent in the sun. Let the Sun of justice arise for me, who remain a virgin, in whose wings eternal health remains; he who, flourishing in perpetual chastity, has determined that integrity should endure in her [Note: Perhaps, “in me … integrity.”]. Let him go forth like righteous brightness, and let the Savior be kindled like a torch. The sun’s torch illumines everything, and penetrates inward into the private recesses that perhaps seem to obstruct its rays [Note: Perhaps, “inner chambers.”], destroying nothing at all. Let him now proceed, beautiful in appearance beyond the sons of men, into the eyes of humanity. Let the bridegroom proceed from his chamber, for I have been made secure concerning my purpose.”

## CHAPTER III

Who, my brothers, could narrate this birth in speech? What tongue or eloquence could explain it? The inviolability of virginity is preserved, [lacuna], and an infant grows within a virgin. When the time was fulfilled for her to give birth, the sacred child was brought forth, whose manner of conception the human father did not know [Note: One copy reads, “whose father had not known the woman who gave birth.”].

This is the ineffable nuptial union of the Word and flesh, of God and man. Thus Christ Jesus, man, was made mediator between God and humanity (1 Tim. 2:5). Therefore the womb of the virgin was chosen as the most precious bridal chamber, so that, since the world had become filthy and squalid through defiling sins, the Creator of the world, coming without the work of the world, poured forth [Note: The following six words are absent in one manuscript.] from pure entrails into the world, and, born in the world by a new miracle, might make the world pure.

For the Son of Man came, as the Son of God and man himself said, not to judge the world but to save the world (John 3:17).

Tell me now, I beg you, holy mother of holy things, who in the bosom of the Church brought forth the fragrance of the morning flower and the snowy lily of the valleys without the furrow of human descent and without the rain of carnal seed: tell me, I beg you, unique mother, by what hands or through what operation of Divinity he whose only father is God formed his son in your womb.

Tell me, I beseech you by God, who made you such that he himself might become in you; tell me, I say, what good you did, what reward you offered, by what powers you sought access, what patrons you had, what intercessions you promised, by what understanding or thought you attained this, so that the power and wisdom of the Father, which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1), remaining wholly everywhere and coming into your womb without any change in itself, might inhabit the narrow fortress of your belly in such a way that, entering, it would not injure it, and, departing, would preserve it unharmed.

Tell me, then, how you attained this. And she replied:

“You ask me what gift I offered in order to become the mother of my Savior? My offering is virginity; my promise is not given by me to myself, but granted to me by the author of every good. For every excellent gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (James 1:17).

“My ambition is my humility. Therefore my soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior, because he looked upon—not a tunic fastened with gold, not shining adornments with hidden gold for decorating my neck, nor precious stones and pearls hanging from my ears, nor the redness of my cheeks colored with deceptive cosmetics—but upon the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:46–48).

For he came to the humble, gentle, as he had been promised beforehand through the prophecy of the prophet, and said: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your King comes to you, gentle and mild, seated upon a cloud” (Zech. 9:9; Matt. 21:5)—upon Mary, that is, the virgin whom he himself presented to himself as mother, with no comparable star.

## CHAPTER IV

Thus the gentle one came, resting upon his mother’s humble and quiet spirit, trembling at his words. The gentle one came, filling the heavens, passing through the humble toward the proud, yet not abandoning the heavens. Like a gentle physician, he himself healed those swollen with the tumor of pride by applying the plaster of humility.

O profound humility! O height more excellent than the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways (Rom. 11:33)! The bread of angels is suckled at a mother’s breasts. The spring of water leaping up into eternal life (John 4:14) asks the Samaritan woman, prefiguring the Church, for a drink (Ibid., 7). He does not refuse to dine with sinners, though the dignity of the heavenly household serves him with trembling. The King of kings made the son of the royal official well (Ibid., 50), applying no poultice of various medicines, but carrying healing upon his tongue. He cures the Centurion’s servant, extinguished by fevers, whose faith was found praiseworthy (Matt. 8:10; Luke 7:9), because the Centurion believed that the Lord’s power would act just as he himself acted when commanding his soldiers subject to him.

Thus he took upon himself the sufferings of the paralytic (Matt. 9:2; Luke 5:20) [Note: This passage is very disordered.], so that as Lord, by mercifully visiting her, he healed the woman’s long-standing wound (Matt. 9:22), in whom the stagnant humor of disease had made her limbs wasting and diseased. The Savior himself, perceiving her silent faith, dried up the fountain of her persistent hemorrhage as it flowed from her bondage.

And when shall I go through everything [Note: Perhaps “how shall I recount everything”?]? Time fails in narration when one must tell with what magnificent power and profound goodness he accomplished all things—he who, great toward the small and humble toward the proud, descended full of compassion.

He did new things from the beginning of the ages, who came new into the age. In his wondrous form the evangelists display their figures: man, lion, calf, eagle. He was man, from a virgin mother without a man; as a strong lion he lay down in death; by his own power he was exalted upon the cross, like a young calf willingly slaughtered in his passion for the sins of the people; and like a powerful eagle, receiving his body from the tomb, he rose [Note: Perhaps “on a straight course,” or something must be supplied, such as “in flight”], cleaving the air with outstretched wings, trampling every fall, and ascending and flying above the Cherubim. He walks upon the wings of the winds and ascended into heaven. To him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

# SERMON XVI. On the Nativity of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul

Although this sermon belongs to Appendix 2, whose spurious sermons we demonstrated in the preface placed before the Sermons, no. 19—and for that reason it was also omitted from the Casanatense manuscript of the same collection—nevertheless, since it is cited as Leo’s, apparently from a manuscript of the basilica of Saint Peter, according to the testimony of Peter Mallius, which we quoted in the same preface and number, we thought it should be inserted in the appendix, lest anyone perhaps suspect that a genuine sermon had escaped our discovery. The author appears to have been some Roman pontiff.

## CHAPTER I

Today, dearest brothers, we celebrate the nativity of the two holy apostles Peter and Paul, whose sound and preaching have reached throughout the whole world. Their passion is celebrated from East to West, because they suffered for the King of heaven and earth.

The city of the Romans deserved to possess the places commemorating the apostles. For preachers of the heavenly kingdom ought to be there where the Roman kingdom was established, so that different peoples coming there might honor the memory of fishermen.

When people go to the blessed apostle Peter, who knows that there the memorial of the emperor Hadrian has been established, with a temple built of extraordinary size and beauty, can anyone say: “Let us enter the emperor’s memorial”? Therefore the emperor’s memorial is passed by, and people hasten to the fisherman’s memorial.

They became good fishermen, though they had been born fishermen. Fishermen of fish became fishers of men, when the Lord Christ said: “Come after me; I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19). I do not change your craft; I change the kind of fish. You were drawing living things from the sea toward death; now you will draw the dead from the world toward salvation.

## CHAPTER II

One was a fisherman and the other a persecutor. How greatly the persecutors and fishermen feared before they became preachers! Peter was chosen first in the order of the apostles; Paul was last in the order of the apostles, as he himself testifies, saying: “For I am the least of all the apostles” (Rom. 15:9). He who chose the first also chose the last, so that the first and the last might suffer together.

Good is the passion that now clings to praise. Good is the contest that completed martyrdom. The apostles knew toward what crown they were striving, the crown that Peter and Paul received in the city of Rome.

For the Lord had said in the Gospel: “Whoever leaves father or mother, wife or children, and all that he possesses, will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29); and, “Whoever loses his life for my sake in this world will preserve it for eternal life” (Matt. 10:39).

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, brothers, for the sake of life we ought not to love this life; for the sake of eternal life, temporal life must be despised. Good disciples, who held to the true teaching of the master, completed their course, kept the faith, loved the promises, despised temporal things, and possessed eternal life.

One was grafted in from a rustic stock; the other was made from a wolf into a lamb. Of the apostle Paul it was said: “A ravenous wolf; in the morning he will seize prey, and toward evening he will divide the spoils” (Gen. 49:27). Saul was a persecutor, but he was changed so that he might become the preacher Paul. Previously he had been a persecutor; afterward he became a magnificent preacher.

Christ, whom he had once blasphemed, he afterward preached publicly. For he himself testifies, saying: “I was formerly a blasphemer and a persecutor; but for this reason I received mercy, because I acted ignorantly in unbelief, so that God might reveal his Son in me” (1 Tim. 1:13; Gal. 1:16). This he granted to me, a persecutor.

But what did he grant to the fisherman, except the keys of the kingdom of heaven? The keys of the kingdom of heaven were merited by Peter’s faith, because he was the first to acknowledge the Son of God.

O glorious merit of the apostles! They were not chosen for glory on one day, but on one day they merited the palm. They were not chosen for apostleship on one day, but on one day they merited receiving consecrated martyrdom. They crossed beyond heaven and ran [Correct reading: “ran,” not “crowned”] to the Lord God.

# SERMON XVII. On the Nativity of the Blessed Apostle Paul

[Note: Thus in the Vallicellian manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts. Another version reads: “On Saint Paul,” or “On the Festival of Saint Paul.”]

This sermon was recently published from Collection 2 by Abbot Trombellius. Besides the manuscripts of Collection 2, we found it in the Cassinese manuscript of Collection 1, as well as in two Vallicellian lectionaries, VII and A, 6, everywhere bearing the name of Pope Leo.

In two Vatican manuscripts, 1272 and 3835, the following inscription is found without the certain name of any author: “Likewise, by the same author, on the Nativity of the Blessed Apostle Paul.” This generally indicates that the same person was the author of this and the preceding sermon. In both manuscripts, however, a sermon inscribed to Saint John Chrysostom precedes it.

Since the author of this sermon was certainly Roman, we here detect a clear instance of a copyist’s negligence of the kind mentioned in the preface, no. 9: namely, that he copied this sermon with the same heading from an older lectionary, even though he did not at all excerpt the preceding sermon, which in that manuscript had the name of its true author prefixed to it.

The Roman author lived after Gregory the Great. For in Gregory’s time, as the author of the *Micrologus* testifies, *On Ecclesiastical Observances*, chapter 42, the festival of Saint Paul began to be celebrated on the day after the feast of Saints Peter and Paul.

In the sacramentaries older than the Gregorian—namely, the Leonine, as it is called, and the Gelasian—the nativity of both apostles is assigned to the same day, and no other Mass proper to Saint Paul is described for the following day, as is first found in the Gregorian sacramentary.

We were able to find this sermon mutilated in most manuscript copies, but complete only in the oldest Vatican manuscript, 3835.

## CHAPTER I

The twin joys of today’s festival, dearest brothers, are renewed as we celebrate the annual nativity of the teacher of the world. Therefore, rejoicing in the Lord and offering immense praises to his ineffable majesty, let us give thanks with immense joy.

Indeed, we ought to rejoice with overflowing delight, because whenever the memory of the saints is celebrated, the minds of the faithful are filled with exceedingly great joy [Note: Vatican manuscript 3835 reads: “the minds of the faithful are raised by very great joy.”] and are greatly illumined by spiritual progress, since there is no doubt that the saints are present.

Therefore, as we gather, dearest ones, in this most holy hall [Note: Another version has “most sacred hall”], we believe that the same outstanding preacher stands among us and, in a spiritual and invisible manner, rejoices together with us at this celebrated solemnity of his.

For this reason, beloved, no bodily sluggishness should entangle any Christian and prevent him from coming to meet this venerable church, where his holy body rests. Above all, it is fitting that all who live in the city of Rome and the neighboring regions should hasten here as quickly as possible.

For if people from the farthest regions of the world, fearing neither the severity of the harshest journey nor the distances of the earth, eagerly desire to present themselves at the thresholds of the apostles at whatever time they can, what excuse can Roman citizens offer when, though they are present, they neglect even to attend their festival, while they are known to be protected by the prayers, defense, and assistance of these same apostles?

## CHAPTER II

Yesterday, on the day when these princes of the apostles were crowned with martyrdom [Note: In some copies “day” is absent; incorrectly], we hastened with the most devout affection to the church of the blessed apostle Peter and celebrated his solemnity [Note: Another version has “consecrated.”]. For it was fitting that the festival of him who deserved to attain the primacy of the apostleship should be celebrated first.

Today we celebrate the nativity of the teacher of the nations and illuminator of the whole world. Although both received the prize of martyrdom together, nevertheless, because of the crowd of people flowing together, there was reason for transferring the solemnity of the blessed apostle Paul to another day [Note: The Barberini manuscript reads: “There was reason for transferring the celebration of the blessed apostle Paul.” The Vallicellian manuscript reads: “There was reason for transferring the celebration of the blessed apostle Paul.” We have followed the Vatican manuscript.], so that, just as the whole multitude gathered in the hall of the blessed Peter, so the same congregation of people might gather together in the church of his fellow apostle, and everyone might possess an equal devotion of rejoicing [Note: Another version has “apostle.”].

But behold, many, either held back by desires or devoted to worldly care [Note: The word *cura* (“care”), absent in other manuscripts, is supplied by the best Vatican manuscript; on this basis the editor reads *desideria* (“desires”) rather than *desidia* (“laziness”), which other copies have.], delayed coming to this hall of the most distinguished blessed apostle Paul. Therefore, dearest brothers, every worldly concern must be cast aside, and desires for temporal gain must be rejected. With all the effort we can summon, let us hasten to celebrate the memory of the saints, especially the nativity of the blessed princes of the apostles Peter and Paul; gathered together with devotion in both their churches, let us assemble there, so that, just as divine favor honored them equally with the insignia of apostleship [Note: That is, “with the honor of apostleship”], human devotion may likewise regard them as equals in their solemnities [Note: Another version has “similarly.” The Vatican manuscript has “coequal.”].

## CHAPTER III

For this most blessed man, first Saul and afterward Paul—first, I say, a persecutor and afterward a preacher—infected with the savagery of Jewish credulity, burned with the madness of excessive ferocity against Christians.

For, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9:2), having received authority from the chief priests to bring bound to Jerusalem any of them belonging to the Christian religion whom he might find, he went trembling, seized by great fury. Suddenly illumined and terrified by the splendor of a heavenly ray, he heard a voice from heaven saying to him:

“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Ibid., 4).

Immediately he fell to the ground and lost the light of his eyes.

O great goodness of the compassion of our almighty God! O immeasurable mercy of his long-suffering! He terrified him briefly in order to console him abundantly. For he struck Paul so that he might heal him beyond measure [Note: These words occur only in the oldest Vatican manuscript; there, instead of “superfluously,” “from above” seems to be the reading.].

At once the Lord commanded Ananias to grant him the grace of rebirth through baptism and to restore the light he had lost from his eyes. The sheep was commanded to lead the wolf to the fold and make him a sheep like himself.

For Ananias is interpreted as “Sheep.” The sheep fears approaching the wolf, but, supported by the Lord’s command, he confidently approached the wolf. Seeing that he had been transformed into gentleness by the divine rebuke, he immediately bestowed upon him the gift of baptism, applied the standard of Christ, and placed him in the Lord’s fold.

O power of an operation worthy of wonder! The sheep made the wolf a sheep, because he received the strength of a good shepherd; and the one whom he had previously had as his most savage assailant, he afterward received as his gentlest fellow combatant.

The Lord, having predestined him before all ages, declares him to be a vessel of election and announces that he will carry his name among the nations.

## CHAPTER IV

O blessed Paul, outstanding preacher, how glorious and praiseworthy you shine among all the apostles and all the martyrs! Although you appear to have come last into the fellowship of the apostles, you are shown to have labored more than all in the Gospel of Christ.

Behold, your most radiant teaching shines throughout the whole world. With what praises could the human tongue worthily glorify you, most elegant prince of the apostles and most renowned preacher of truth? The Redeemer mercifully called you from heaven, established you as a worthy worshiper of himself, a most excellent vessel, and a most vigorous athlete.

Thus, having lawfully fought the good fight and completed the course of your ministry (2 Tim. 4:7), and for this reason having been caught up even to the third heaven, you merited hearing secret words. Thereafter, receiving from the just Judge, our Lord, the crown of righteousness laid up for you and the reward worthy of your labors, you rightly triumph forever with the angels in the heavenly kingdoms.

Therefore, as we venerate this most sacred solemnity of yours, glorious prince of the apostles and teacher of the nations, do not cease to commend us through constant intercessions to our Creator, for whose true name you confessed and for which you obtained the palm of martyrdom.

Thus, supported by the special assistance of your intercessions and strengthened by continual protection, may we deserve to be rescued from all the adversities of this flowing world. May we, with sincere hearts, carry out the joys of your most devout festival in security and attain the eternal kingdoms, through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom are honor and glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

# SERMON XVIII. On Saint Peter: How He Was Led Out of Prison

This is now published for the first time from the Cassinese manuscript.

## CHAPTER I

Your Belovedness has heard in due order how Saint Peter was bound in prison with two chains and handed over to four squads of soldiers, and how he was freed from there by the angel of the Lord (Acts 12).

Saint Peter was therefore sent into prison because of the name of Christ, but he could not dread the punishment of imprisonment, because he himself was the temple of God in prison. He was bound with two chains, but in that very prison he was drawing from believers the chains of their sins. He was guarded by four squads of soldiers, but under that very guard he was revealing the four Gospels to those coming to the faith.

It is certainly no wonder that he could not fear human custody, since he was protected by divine custody.

When Peter was therefore being carefully guarded in prison by four squads of soldiers and bound with two chains, the angel of the Lord came to him, as Your Belovedness has heard, opened the prison doors, and said to him:

“Rise, take your garment and cover yourself, put on your sandal, and come, follow me” (Ibid.).

He rose and followed him. When he had come with the angel to the iron gate, the gate immediately opened of its own accord before them.

It is certainly no wonder that the iron gate opened freely for Saint Peter, since he had already received the gates of hell into his power, when the Lord said to him:

“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:18).

He who opened the gates of hell opened the iron gate for Saint Peter. He who destroyed death itself rescued Peter from death.

## CHAPTER II

But what was then done to Saint Peter according to the letter, we recognize as also being done mystically among us, if we follow Peter’s faith.

For we too have been placed in this world as though in a prison. If, then, we deserve to be visited by the Lord, the angel of God is sent to us and says to each one of us:

“Gird yourself, put on your sandals, cover yourself with your garment, and follow me.”

We gird ourselves if we surround the loins of our body with the belt [Note: Perhaps “girdle”] of chastity, as Christ himself says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35) [Note: These words are spoken not by the Apostle but by Christ himself in the Gospel.], in chastity.

We put sandals on our feet if we fortify the steps of our life with the commandments of evangelical faith, so that, secure, we may trample underfoot the thorns of sin and the briars of iniquity.

We cover ourselves with a garment if we preserve within us that wedding garment, namely, the grace of baptism.

Let us faithfully fulfill these things. Immediately the chains will fall from our hands, that is, the chains of sins by which, bound and fettered in soul, we were held.

But we cannot otherwise escape from prison—that is, from the error of this world—unless we are visited by the Lord through an angel. The iron gate is opened for us also, that is, the gate of death and punishment, which the Son of God shattered by the power of his passion.

Then we will come to the house of Mary—that is, to the Church of Christ, where Mary the mother of the Lord dwells—and there a girl named Rhode will meet us.

The name Rhode itself appropriately signifies the mystery of our salvation. For *Rhode*, according to the Greek word, is called “rose.” When we come, therefore, to Mary’s house, a girl named Rhode meets us—that is, the congregation of the saints, which shines like a rose through the glorious blood of martyrdom.

# NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING SERMON

We are compelled to present the lengthy notice of Quesnell, in accordance with our established practice, by which we promised that all his material would be inserted into this edition.

“He says:

‘Whether this sermon was delivered on the feast of the seven martyr brothers, the Maccabees, or rather on the feast of the seven brothers who were sons of Saint Felicitas the martyr—namely Januarius, Felix, Philip, Silvanus, Alexander, Vitalis, and Martialis, who were crowned with martyrdom in the time of the emperor Antoninus—there may perhaps be someone who doubts, if he turns his eyes away for a little while from the title. Among learned people it is not wrong to call the reliability of this title, as also of other titles of this kind, into question.

‘Although the memory of these latter martyrs had long been celebrated at Rome, since they had made the City renowned by their contest, we nevertheless believe that this sermon was consecrated to the triumph of the former—that is, the Maccabees—first because it recalls their martyrdom as narrated from the sacred Scriptures: “You have learned,” he says, “the cause of today’s solemnity most fully from the reading of sacred history”; and also because it attributes such martyrdom not to the cruelty of an emperor or Roman prefect but to the impiety of a most savage king, namely Antiochus.

‘Moreover, Saint Leo indicates that another feast was joined to this solemnity of the martyrs, namely, as he says, the nativity or dedication of a church, whose consecration he later asserts doubled the ancient festival.

‘But he does not himself reveal whose church’s nativity and whose consecration this solemnity was, nor did anyone after him take pains to investigate it. Everyone apparently assumed, as I think, that this must certainly be understood as the dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter at the Chains, since even today the festival of that dedication and of the martyrdom of the Maccabees is attached to the Kalends of August.

‘We cannot in any way accept this opinion. The basilica of Saint Peter at the Chains was built by Eudoxia, the wife of the emperor Valentinian, on the Esquiline Hill; hence it was also called the title of Eudoxia. This does not at all agree with what Leo says about that place.

‘For it is clear that the basilica whose consecration was then being commemorated was built not by a woman but by a man. “The magnificent builder of walls,” he says, and so forth. Moreover, all the things Leo explains must apply to the person who erected the basilica in question:

‘First, he must have ordered the church to be built at his own expense and through his generosity: “The magnificent builder of walls,” and so forth, “dwelling in what he founded.”

‘Second, he must himself have consecrated or dedicated the church: “He who on this day doubled the ancient festival of this place by its consecration.”

‘Third, he must have cared for souls: “But a more magnificent builder of souls”; indeed, he must also have exercised the office of teaching in the city of Rome and therefore have served as bishop, “doing what he taught.”

‘Fourth, he must have been someone whose memory the Romans could venerate with fitting honor and join to the solemnity of the martyrs: “Honor with fitting reverence not only the martyrs and the mother of the martyrs, but also the memory of him who on this day doubled the ancient festival of this place by its consecration.”

‘Finally, he must have been contemporary with Leo and have displayed works of piety before the eyes of those whom Leo was addressing, so that they could be stirred to moral improvement by his memory no less than by the sight of the temple they saw. For the sense of these words is: “Therefore, dearest ones, take for the improvement of your edification all the things you see with your eyes and remember in your minds,” and so forth.

‘But none of these things can apply to Eudoxia. It is necessary, then, that the person be one of the Roman pontiffs, to whom alone it belonged to dedicate churches in the City and to act there as teachers and builders of souls.

‘These things can easily be said of Pope Celestine, who was conspicuous for holiness and is recorded to have built the basilica of Julius. Yet I am more inclined to refer them to Sixtus III, the last predecessor of our Leo.

‘First, it is clear that the church whose dedication was being celebrated on that feast day was one of the principal basilicas of the city of Rome. Its dedication was recalled by the whole Roman populace with such celebration, such magnificence of festivity, such united zeal and devout spirit, and such a gathering of the people. This was undoubtedly the basilica of Saint Mary Major, which is also called Saint Mary ad Nives, Saint Mary at the Crib, and the Basilica of Liberius.

‘That this basilica was rebuilt and consecrated anew by Pope Sixtus III is attested by the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs* and by Pope Hadrian in his letter to Charlemagne. “He made the basilica of Saint Mary, the mother of the Lord, which in ancient times was called that of Liberius,” says that book in its account of Sixtus III. Hadrian speaks of it thus: “Pope Sixtus, successor of Celestine, made the basilica of the holy mother of God Mary, called Major, which is also called at the Crib.”

‘Remarkable things are reported about this basilica by Peter of Cluny, Bede, and those authors who wrote about the seven churches of the City.

‘Furthermore, it is easy to believe that Leo broke forth into praise of Sixtus on the occasion of the solemnity, because he had been educated by him, had always remained attached to him as his deacon, and had succeeded him immediately, having rendered him excellent service in administering ecclesiastical affairs. Sixtus’ memory was also the most recent of all.

‘Finally, Sixtus himself, distinguished by the praise of holiness, is found inscribed among the blessed in the ecclesiastical calendars on the twenty-eighth day of March. Thus the holy pontiff could rightly have said that his memory should be venerated with fitting honor.’

‘One objection may be raised: the solemnity of the dedication of Saint Mary is celebrated on another day, namely the Nones of August, while, conversely, no dedication solemnity is assigned to the Kalends of August in the present Roman Martyrology except that of Saint Peter at the Chains.

‘But what wonder is it if, over the course of so many years, many things are found to have been changed in ecclesiastical calendars of this kind, whose reliability is not everywhere certain and indisputable?

‘Besides, since that most ancient basilica repeatedly needed to be restored and consecrated anew because of its age, just as custom required that the day of its final consecration should be counted among the festivals, so it was appropriate that the memory of its first construction and consecration should not perish, since it had become famous throughout the world through many notable miracles.

‘For this reason, as I think, the solemnity of that dedication, which had been carried out by Sixtus, was transferred from the first day of August to the fifth, so that the two solemnities might merge into one and the number of festival days might not increase to the detriment of public affairs.

‘It was especially fitting that this should be done because of the other dedication of Saint Peter at the Chains, whose solemnity happens to be celebrated on that same first day of August.’”

The foregoing was necessary on the hypothesis that the sermon was believed to be Leo’s sermon on the Maccabees. It will be recognized as superfluous and irrelevant, however, if we have demonstrated that the sermon is not Leo’s. For in the very ancient manuscript Lectionary Vatican 3836, which was undoubtedly Roman and intended for the use of the basilica of Saints Philip and James, where other genuine sermons of Leo are inscribed under his name, this sermon, on page 1, is attributed not to Leo but to Augustine under the following title: “Here begins the sermon of Saint Augustine on the holy Maccabees, August 1.” Who would dare to assert that a sermon belongs to Leo, when the Roman Church itself, by this most ancient testimony, removes it from him? It therefore happened through the error of later times that it was attributed to Leo in Collections 2, 3, and 4, which belong to a later age. This single document is for us utterly decisive.

Add that this sermon indicates that the solemnity of the Maccabees was celebrated in the city where the sermon was delivered. That it was celebrated in Africa is known both from the ancient Carthaginian Calendar, which Mabillon published in his *Analecta*, and from Augustine’s Sermons 300 and 301, delivered on the same feast; these too can confirm Augustine as the author of this sermon. But that no feast of the Maccabees was celebrated at Rome in Leo’s time may be inferred from the fact that no Mass for that feast is recorded on August 1, not only in the most ancient Sacramentary attributed to Leo, which will be reprinted in the second volume, but also in the earlier Gregorian Sacramentary, which Ludovicus Muratorius printed from two manuscripts in volume II of *Liturgia Romana vetus*. If this feast is asserted in the published Gelasian Sacramentary, it is certain that that book is not a pure Gelasian Sacramentary but has received several later additions. Among these the Mass of the Maccabees must be included; anyone will understand this from the absence of that Mass itself from the later Gregorian Sacramentary. This addition could have been introduced from some Church where the feast of the Maccabees was celebrated, just as it was celebrated in Gaul in Leo’s time. Hence their feast is marked in the Calendar of Polemius Silvius, whom we shall prove in the observations on Sermon 83, no. 4, to have been a Gallic writer who wrote in Gaul.

There is also a dedication inscription, published by several writers and most recently reprinted by Father Abbot Monsacratus in his work *On the Chains of Saint Peter*, p. 48. Among other things, it reads:

> This temple of the Lord was first dedicated to Peter;  
> The third bishop, Sixtus, once consecrated it;  
> Later it was itself destroyed in civil war.  
> Eudoxia then entirely renewed it here;  
> Pope Pelagius, the blessed, consecrated it again,  
> Placing there the bodies of the holy Maccabees.

If this inscription were ancient and conveyed genuine history, so that the celebration of the Maccabees at Rome had begun under Pelagius before Gregory, the sermon still could not be attributed to Leo. Finally, the expression “dearest” (*charissimi*), inserted at the beginning of chapter 3, is familiar to Augustine but entirely foreign to Leo’s usage; this indication more strongly confirms that the sermon was falsely attributed to Leo.

## 453 SERMON XIX  
[Alternatively, among the Leonine sermons, Sermon LXXXII]

### On the Feast of the Seven Holy Maccabean Brothers, Martyrs

[Note: Quesnellus added “and on the dedication of the Church,” because the sermon also discusses the dedication of a church. This addition is found in no manuscript.]

### [Column 0517A]

Now placed in the appendix for the first time, because it belongs not to Leo but to Augustine.

[Note: This Eudoxia, who renewed this church after it had been destroyed in civil war following Sixtus, and who is said to have brought Peter’s chains from Jerusalem to Rome, was not Eudoxia, the wife of Valentinian III, as Quesnellus supposed.]

### CHAPTER I

Let us give thanks, beloved, to our Lord God, for your assembly shows, even if I remain silent, how great is the solemnity of this day. You have gathered with such united zeal and devout spirit that, even if speech does not proclaim the magnificence of the feast, the congregation itself bears witness to it.

And rightly so: there is a twofold cause for rejoicing, since we celebrate the church’s birthday and rejoice in the passion of the martyrs. Nor does the Church rejoice in their martyrdom without reason, for she is adorned by their example.

You have therefore learned the cause of today’s solemnity, beloved, most fully from the reading of sacred history. You could not fail to recognize whom, amid so great an array of events, you had heard honored, when with joyful and outspoken affection you honored the glorious mother of seven martyrs—one who suffered in each of her sons but was crowned in them all.

She followed them to a blessed end, those whom by her unconquered exhortation she had sent ahead. Blessed mother, blessed offspring, memorable courage among those who went before! For when, in that succession of deaths and that arrangement of punishments, the impiety of the most savage king had contrived to promise itself victory both over the first, whom he would torture without the example of endurance, and over the last, whom he would torment with another’s punishment, the palms of the martyrs multiplied. While each conquered in all, they all gained, besides their individual crowns, seven crowns together.

[Textual notes: The later printed editions insert *agamus* (“let us give thanks”) after “Let us give thanks”; it was judged to be deleted on the authority of the first edition and of our manuscripts of Collections 2, 3, and 4. Codex Barberinianus, Collection 2, reads *solemnitatis* (“of the solemnity”) for “of the feast.” “The church’s birthday” is to be understood as the day of its dedication. Codex Casanatensis reads *quos munitos praemisit* (“whom she sent forth armed”); Codex Barberinianus has *ornatu* (“adornment”) for *hortatu* (“exhortation”). Codex Casanatensis alone reads *morientium* (“of those dying”) for “deaths.”]

### CHAPTER II

But these things must be recalled for the fruitful pleasure of hearing. “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1), unless obedience builds up. What is heard becomes burdensome unless it is received for imitation.

For although the persecutor and torturer have ceased, and although all the powers now serve God, Christians are not without sufferings to overcome. “My son,” he says, “when you come to the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1). And the Apostle says: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution for the sake of justice” (2 Tim. 3:12).

If, then, you think that persecution has ceased and that you have no conflict with enemies, examine the innermost secret of your heart. Enter carefully into all the recesses of your soul and see whether no adversity attacks you, whether no tyrant wishes to rule in the citadel of your mind.

Do not make peace with greed, and reject the increase of unjust profits. Refuse agreement with pride, and fear more to be received into glory than to be trampled down in humility. Separate yourself from anger, and do not let the desire for vengeance inflame grief through envy. Renounce pleasure, turn away from uncleanness, drive out lust, flee iniquity, oppose falsehood. And when you see that you have many battles, seek a numerous victory as an imitator of the martyrs.

For we die to sins as often as sins die within us. “Precious in the sight of the Lord is even this death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15), when a person is killed to the world—not by the destruction of the senses, but by the end of vices.

[Note: The later printed editions before Quesnellus read “not by the termination of the senses.” We have corrected this from two manuscripts of Collections 2.]

[Textual notes: Manuscripts Casanatensis and Barberinianus, Collection 2, read *ad infructuosam* (“for unfruitful”) rather than “for fruitful.” “All” is added from manuscripts of Collections 2 and 4. Editions before Quesnellus wrongly read *recursus* (“retreats”) for *recessus* (“recesses”). Codex Barberinianus reads *Dissocia te ab ira* (“Separate yourself from anger”). The reading “flee iniquity, oppose falsehood” follows the first edition and manuscripts of Collections 2 and 3; the common printed text reads *omitte falsitatem* (“omit falsehood”).]

### CHAPTER III

If, then, beloved, you do not bear the yoke with unbelievers (2 Cor. 6:14), if you cease to be sinners and yield to no temptations of bodily desires, you are celebrating this solemn day properly.

[Textual note: Quesnellus emended the text to *ceditis* (“yield”), as it is also read in our manuscripts; other witnesses read *creditis* (“believe”). The adverb *legitime* (“properly”) was added from the cited manuscripts of Collection 2.] You venerate not only the martyrs and the mother of the martyrs with due honor, but also the memory of the one who on this day doubled the ancient festival by consecrating this place: a magnificent builder of walls, but a more magnificent builder of souls, extending works of piety beyond the limits of his own age, so that devoted posterity might enjoy the benefits of his instruction even in his own work, both by inhabiting what he founded and by doing what he taught.

[Note: Since it was believed that this sermon was delivered by Leo in the church of Saint Peter in Chains, everyone had hitherto thought that Sixtus III, the consecrator of this church, was designated here; Quesnellus therefore appended to this passage a eulogy of Sixtus III. But since the author of this sermon is Augustine, as we have shown in the preface, every opinion concerning Sixtus III disappears. If Augustine delivered the sermon in the church at Hippo, he intended here to attach a eulogy of one of his predecessors. Moreover, since the same doctor, discussing the Maccabees in Sermon 300, mentions a basilica dedicated in their honor at Antioch, but not in the church where he was speaking, it appears that in the present sermon, delivered on the occasion of a church dedication that happened to fall on the day sacred to the Maccabees, he intended to speak about both subjects: the holy martyrs and the dedication.]

### CHAPTER IV

Therefore, beloved, take everything you see with your eyes and remember in your minds for the advancement of your edification. Let each of you use the dwelling prepared by his forebears in such a way that he remembers that the temple of God has been founded in himself.

Let him place nothing crooked in his structure, nothing weak beneath it. Rather, by fitting together with living and chosen stones, let him grow through an unbreakable bond into the unity of the Lord’s body, with the help of God and our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the cornerstone, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Textual notes: Quesnellus inserted *et* (“and”) before “for the advancement,” but this conjunction is absent from most of our manuscripts and from earlier editions. Vatican manuscript 3836 reads *superponat* (“place upon [it]”) for *supponat* (“place beneath [it]”); Codex Barberinianus reads: “by heaping up stones an indissoluble connection, let him grow into the unity of the Lord’s work.” The words “God and our Lord Jesus Christ himself, the cornerstone” were added from the most ancient Vatican manuscript 3836.]

## SERMON XX  
### On the Transfiguration of the Lord

Published here for the first time from the manuscript of Saint Anthony of Padua, incorrectly attributed to Leo.

### CHAPTER I

Today, dearest brothers, we solemnly celebrate the day of him who, governing all things with the Father, created every day—the Word, I mean, who in the beginning said, “Let there be light,” and light was made (Gen. 1:3).

Today his flesh was glorified on the mountain, as the Gospel narrative relates. The Lord was transfigured on the mountain before two prophets and three disciples, so that he might give us hope of his divinity; he wished to show them his face made whiter than snow.

If anyone wishes to know who these prophets were, let him hasten to the lofty words of the Evangelists. But if Luke seems to disagree with the other two because he reports that this glory of the Lord was shown not after six days but after eight (Luke 9:28), let him turn to the grammatical figure. Among grammarians there is a figure called *syllepsis*, in which many are included for one and one for many, and the whole is taken for the part and the part for the whole.

Let him understand that Luke likewise described the day when the promise was made figuratively, and included in his Gospel the day when it was fulfilled. For when the Lord made this promise, it was evening; and when he was transfigured, it was nevertheless morning. Matthew and Mark, omitting the days of the promise and of the Transfiguration, preferred to hand down for perpetual remembrance only the six complete intervening days.

### CHAPTER II

Nevertheless, if someone asks why he wished to be transfigured before two prophets and three disciples, let him recall that clear first sermon of the Lord. He himself says to the Jews: “It is written in your law that the testimony of two men is true” (John 8:17).

To show that he was the one who said to Moses, “I am who I am,” and, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14)—the one who had sent that same Moses to Pharaoh for the liberation of the children of Israel, had given him the law on Mount Sinai, and had carried the prophet Elijah into the heavenly realm in a chariot of fire—he brought these witnesses, by divine power, together with the disciples to contemplate the transfiguration of his glory. He was recalling one of them from the threshold of death and the other from his translation into paradise.

No one could know Moses’ tomb except the one who commanded him and brought him to himself; and no one knew where Elijah had been translated except the one who had called him to himself.

For this is the Father’s Only-Begotten, who, for the redemption of the human race, wished to become the firstborn of his mother. In today’s Transfiguration he wished to unite the harmony of both Scriptures. To show that he was the Lord of the Law and of the prophets, he wished to bring these men to bear witness to the Evangelists.

In this Transfiguration it pleased him, the steward of the Father, to show the steward of the Son: Peter to Moses. And he wished to show the chaste elder to the chaste younger: Elijah to John.

Today the disciples saw two suns on the mountain: one, which was observed by them all in the firmament; and another, more brilliantly shining than it, which was seen by the prophets and disciples—the face of Jesus. This Sun, which shone on the mountain, illuminated by its power the sun that is in the firmament. For this is the Sun of justice, burning and shining: by burning, he kindles the faithful within himself; by shining, he enlightens everyone.

Of this Sun John said: “He was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

### CHAPTER III

But so that his glory might be impressed upon us with absolute certainty, after the appearance of his face had been transfigured into another form, and after he had been overshadowed with the Apostles by a luminous cloud, he was truly glorified by the Father: “This,” he says, “is my beloved Son; listen to him” (Luke 9:35).

The disciples, unable to endure so great a voice, fell on their faces. When Moses and Elijah withdrew, the divine offspring alone remained. Raising them up, he said: “Do not be afraid”—which is to say: Let those who do not believe be afraid; let those whom phantoms deceive be afraid. You who obey the Father’s Son and take part in his hidden mysteries—why are you afraid?

Yet when the holy disciples looked around, they saw no one except Jesus alone, so that it might clearly be shown that the voice which had been sent belonged not to Moses or Elijah but solely to the Only-Begotten Son.

A most eloquent poet marvels at and praises the merit of these three apostles concerning this vision, saying:

> O sublime merit of the three, to whom it was granted  
> To see in the world what the world did not believe!  
> What more? They saw both Elijah and Moses,  
> Glorious in virtue, unknown to their eyes but seen by the light of the heart.  
> So that our faith might be greater, they saw that he is throughout the world  
> Its beginning and its end, Alpha, that is, and Omega,  
> Around whom such prophets shone. One still living, the other standing in the light of life:  
> And with a starry sound, saying, “This is my Son,”  
> The paternal voice showed by its word Christ, begotten.

When Moses, therefore, entreated and said, “Show me your glory,” the Lord replied: “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see me and live. Behold,” he said, “there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon the rock. When my glory passes by, I shall place you in a cleft of the rock and protect you with my right hand until I pass by. Then I shall remove my hand, and you shall see my back; but my face you cannot see” (Exod. 33:18, 20ff.).

What does this mean, beloved? What does it mean? Did no one ever see the Lord? Did one of these men lie who said, “No one has ever seen God, except the Only-Begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John 1:18)?

Is the almighty Father, incapable of being contained, immense, and invisible, believed to be corporeal, or are bodily members attributed to him so that he is said to have a back? This is great; this is profound. It is not easy for such little beings as we are to search out so profound a mystery. But it must be opened by him alone who, whenever he wills, opens the mouth of irrational animals for speech.

O Holy Spirit, reveal to us this supreme utterance of the Father. Pay close attention, beloved; pay more cautious attention, and prepare your minds here with me.

### CHAPTER IV

“When I have passed by,” says the Lord, “you shall see my back, but my face you cannot see” (Exod. 33:23).

The face of the Lord is his incomprehensible divinity; his back is to be understood as the humanity assumed by the Son. Through the face, which is the first part of the body, divinity is indicated as existing before all ages; the back, however, is Christ’s humanity, which in the final times came to us through the inviolate Mary.

On this day the Father faithfully fulfilled through the Son what he had promised to his servant Moses. Concerning the solemnity of this day David says: “You have put on praise and beauty, clothed in light as in a garment” (Ps. 103:1).

Christ put on praise and beauty when he was glorified by the glory of the Father’s voice. He was clothed in light as in a garment when he displayed to his disciples his face flashing with the splendor of the sun.

The prophet Habakkuk also marveled at the solemnity of this day when this passage was sung by him: “Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid; I considered your works and trembled” (Hab. 3:1).

Did he tremble in astonishment at the creation of the world? No. But at what did he tremble in astonishment? Hear what follows: “You shall be known,” he says, “in the midst of two animals.”

O dearest ones, what does “you shall be known in the midst of two animals” mean? Is it not either in the midst of the two Testaments, or in the midst of Moses and Elijah, who were speaking with him today on the mountain?

For this is the cornerstone in which both walls were joined: the Old Testament and the New. The Old was signified by Moses and Elijah, through whom the Law and the Prophets are represented. The New was signified by Peter, James, and John, through whom the holy and venerable Gospel is represented.

Or, through Moses and Elijah, the earlier Jewish people were signified; through Peter, James, and John, the Gentile people were represented.

This is the people walking in darkness who saw a great light. May the Father’s Only-Begotten lead us to contemplate that light in the homeland where the just will shine like the sun and God himself will be all in all. He lives and reigns and is glorified with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, throughout the ages of ages that shall never end. Amen.

## OBSERVATIONS ON THE SERMONS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT

### ON SERMON III  
#### In what sense Saint Leo understood the rock upon which Christ built the Church as solid faith

1. To these words of Leo in Sermon 3, chapter 2—“The solidity of that faith which was praised in the chief of the Apostles is perpetual”—Quesnellus appended the following annotation:

> “He explains the words of the Lord Christ that he subsequently sets out, and asserts that the solidity of the faith praised in Peter is that rock upon which Christ promises to build his Church, against which the gates of hell shall not prevail, because it is perpetual. As he says in chapter 3, Peter received the firmness of the rock, which could be shaken by no assaults, so that neither heretical perversity could ever break through it nor pagan unbelief overcome it. He explains the same words in the same sense in Sermon 3 [now 4], chapters 2 and 3, and in Sermon 60 [now 62], or Sermon on the Passion 11, chapter 2.”

Thus far Quesnellus. But lest this interpretation, which applies the name “rock” to the faith praised in Peter, be thought to favor those who, explaining Christ’s statement “Upon this rock I will build my Church” not of Peter but of faith, contend that it has no bearing whatsoever on establishing the prerogatives of Peter and his successors, Leo’s meaning must be explained more precisely.

2. When Saint Leo explained the rock upon which Christ promised to build his Church as faith, or as the solidity of that faith which Christ himself praised in Peter, we shall demonstrate with the utmost clarity that Leo understood not faith in general, nor Peter’s private faith, but the faith that Peter preached, whose deposit he left in the Roman See and transmitted to his successors with the same privilege of solidity.

It will therefore be clear how inaccurately Quesnellus wrote generally in the note appended to Sermon 62, chapter 2: “The rock upon which the Church is built, and against which hell does not prevail, is solid faith.”

3. That the faith preached by Peter must be understood according to Leo’s mind, the same pontiff openly declares in the cited Sermon 62, chapter 2. For he affirms that Peter, by God’s revelation, preceded all the Apostles in the profession of faith, so that, prepared for the governance of the whole Church, he might first learn what he was to teach. On account of the solidity of the faith “which he was to preach,” he heard: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.”

Here he attributes the solidity and the name of the rock upon which the Church was to be built, and against which the gates of hell would not prevail, to the faith that Peter was to preach and by preaching which he was to build the Church.

Yet lest the name “rock” be removed from Peter on this account, the Author himself testifies in Sermon 4, chapter 2, that Peter too was constituted a rock on account of the solidity of the faith he was to preach. For he introduces Christ as saying: “You too are a rock, because you are made solid by my power.” For this reason, in Letter 119 to Maximus of Antioch, chapter 2, he calls not so much Peter’s faith as Peter himself the rock of the Catholic faith.

4. Since Peter left and transmitted the deposit of this faith chiefly in the Roman Church and See to the Roman pontiffs who succeeded him, Leo clearly reveals that the same solidity of faith which existed in Peter continues, and will continue to the end of the world, in this Church and in Peter’s successors by a special privilege.

Thus in Sermon 3, chapter 2, he says: “For the solidity of that faith which was praised in the chief of the Apostles is perpetual; and as what Peter believed in Christ remains, so what Christ established in Peter remains.”

Christ established, namely, that his faith, upon which the Church was to be built, should be so solid that the gates of hell would never prevail against it. This requires that the solidity of the faith be perpetual.

But whoever likewise affirmed this solidity of faith to be perpetual clearly recognized that it did not cease in Peter but passed to his successors. Hence in Sermon 5, chapter 4, he says: “For that solidity which he himself, having become a rock, received from Christ the Rock, he also pours into his heirs.”

It was poured into those heirs in whom he indicates in many passages that Peter lives and continues to govern and teach the Church. Therefore, attributing the ever-enduring solidity of the rock to blessed Peter, he says in Sermon 3, chapter 3:

> “The arrangement of truth therefore remains, and blessed Peter, persevering in the strength of the rock he received, has not abandoned the government of the Church entrusted to him.”

We could bring forward corresponding testimonies from other Fathers, which we have collected in another treatise that, God willing, we shall publish one day. But our purpose here was to explain Leo’s single judgment. Everyone can see how greatly this judgment contributes to establishing the prerogatives of the Roman See.

### ON SERMON IV

#### What Leo understood by these words in chapter 3

> “The privilege of Peter remains wherever judgment is delivered according to his equity.”

Quesnellus’s annotation examined.

1. On the testimony just cited Quesnellus wrote the following:

> “Although this outstanding judgment has already been illuminated by the observations of many writers, the plan of our work does not permit us to pass over it untouched. After asserting at the beginning of the chapter that Saint Leo’s building rises upon the firmness of the faith affirmed through Peter, and after indicating that, in view of this confession, the power expressed in the words ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’ (Luke 22:23) was entrusted to him, he adds that the right of this power was not given to Peter alone but also passed to the Apostles. Nevertheless, it was intimated to Peter in a special way so that all the rulers of the Church might learn in one person what had been entrusted to them, and so that Peter’s pattern might be set before all. For just as the chief of the Apostles had made the profession of faith on behalf of all, and all had answered in him and through him, so he received the power of the keys on behalf of all, and all received it in him and through him.

> “Hence Leo again asserts that, just as the power was common to all, so the privilege was common to all, except for the honor of primacy [and jurisdiction; for the primacy that Christ bestowed on Peter and his successors was not merely one of honor, but especially one of jurisdiction and authority not shared with the other Apostles, as the Gallican Church itself teaches together with all Catholics; see note 29 on Sermon 82]. He asserts that Peter’s privilege remains wherever on earth judgment is delivered by bishops, the successors of the Apostles, according to Peter’s equity; and consequently that Peter’s privilege does not remain wherever judgment is not delivered according to his equity.

> “By this judgment, as King Charles the Bald says in a letter written in the style of Hincmar of Reims, it is established that Peter’s privilege does not remain where judgment is not delivered according to his equity. For when ‘wherever’ is said, just as no place is excepted, so no ruler of the Church is excepted who delivers judgment according to Peter’s equity, nor is anyone commended who delivers judgment contrary to that equity.
