> “And because Peter’s privilege does not remain without exception wherever judgment is not delivered according to his equity, shall we obey a command or receive a judgment that was not delivered according to Peter’s equity, and thus was deprived of Peter’s privilege?”

(*Letter of Charles the Bald to Pope Hadrian, among the Hincmarian letters in the latest edition.*)

The same Hincmarus, as well as other Gallican bishops, alludes to these words of Leo at the Council of Troyes in 878. In confirming, at the request of Pope John VIII, the condemnation of Lambert, an enemy of the Roman Church, they describe him as excommunicated “by the privilege of blessed Peter and the Apostolic See.” They appear to interpret this privilege and the equity of the Apostolic See as judgment delivered according to the sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world; and again, according to the course of Scripture and the decrees of the sacred canons.

See Peter de Marca, who treats these matters more fully in Book IV, chapters 6 and 8, of *The Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*.

Thus Quesnellus writes. Near the end, however, he gradually bends Saint Leo’s words toward his own meaning rather than that of the holy pontiff, implying that only those judgments of the Roman pontiffs enjoy and possess the privilege and equity of Peter which are delivered according to the standard of the canons.

Perhaps he prolonged this annotation for the purpose of making Leo himself, once this testimony had been interpreted accordingly, appear to favor what Quesnellus was preparing to establish in the case of Hilary of Arles in Dissertation 5. There he contends that Hilary was right to resist Leo, who was exercising judgment against him—as Quesnellus imagines—in violation of the canonical rules. He argues in Part III, chapter 1, of the same dissertation that the prerogative of the chief bishops toward lesser bishops would be inert and ineffective if they claimed nothing from them except according to the standard of the canons.

This is not the place to discuss Leo’s judgment in the case of Hilary of Arles. It will be demonstrated at length in the observations on that same Quesnellian dissertation that Leo’s judgment was undertaken and delivered at Rome both according to natural equity and according to the rules of the canons.

Here it is enough, lest the testimony of the holy pontiff be dragged into a meaning foreign to him that favors disobedience and attacks the prerogatives of the Roman See, to explain the genuine meaning of Leo’s proposition from Leo himself.

2. When, therefore, the holy pontiff declares that Peter’s privilege remains wherever judgment is delivered according to his equity, he is speaking of judgments concerning persons and especially concerning crimes. This is clear from what he immediately adds in the same sermon about excessive severity and excessive leniency, and also from Sermon 5, chapter 5, where he says:

> “Since the right of binding and loosing remains with us, through the moderation of blessed Peter the condemned person is led to penance, and the reconciled person is brought to forgiveness.”

Peter’s privilege is this: that whatever he looses or binds on earth is loosed or bound in heaven.

In those judgments, however, which the rulers of the Church pronounce concerning criminals, Leo teaches that Peter’s privilege remains if judgment is delivered according to Peter’s equity—that is, if it is equally right and just, as Peter’s judgments were right and just.

Here “equity” means actual justice, so that the person bound or condemned is truly a sinner, while the person absolved is truly penitent. Such persons, when they are bound or loosed on earth, are also bound or loosed in heaven.

But if through some error or fraud someone is bound or condemned who, though judged guilty in the external forum, is in fact innocent; or if someone is absolved who is believed to be penitent but is in fact deceitful and has not been converted before God—who would believe that in heaven a person was bound or loosed who was loosed or bound on earth in the same manner?

Nothing further can be drawn from the entire context of Leo. The whole passage concerns judgments made by the Church on earth in relation to the divine judgment in heaven.

3. Nothing here indicates anything about the canons or the method of the canons. Those who think that Peter’s equity must necessarily be derived from them should indicate which canons Peter followed in order to deliver judgments according to equity.

The canons certainly regarded natural equity when they prescribed certain rules for judgments. But the equity of Peter indicated here is to be referred to natural justice, or equity—the substance to which the canons are directed—not to the discipline or method of the canons, without which Peter could nevertheless bind or loose with complete equity.

4. As long as the judgments of the Roman pontiffs preserve this natural justice and equity, it makes no difference whether they are delivered according to the fixed method and discipline of the canons or otherwise, in accordance with that supreme authority by which they can sometimes, precisely through equity itself, dispense from or alter the method and discipline of the canons—not in the substance of natural equity, but in their method and discipline.

They will always enjoy Peter’s privilege, and whatever they loose or bind by Peter’s authority will be bound or loosed in heaven.

Conversely, if judgments were delivered by the same pontiffs even according to the rules and method of the canons, but lacked actual equity and justice—which can happen especially through an error of fact or through false witnesses or documents—the observance of the method and discipline of the canons would accomplish nothing.

Even if such judgments had to be regarded and observed as valid within the Church until the error was discovered and the judgment rescinded—as many theologians and canonists teach on the basis of the institutions of the Fathers and the rules of the canons—they would nevertheless not possess Peter’s privilege insofar as, before God in heaven, the person who was bound or absolved on earth through error and deception would not be bound or loosed.

This is the genuine and evident interpretation of Leo’s principle. From it, the use or abuse of that principle can easily be distinguished, so that there is no need to discuss further the testimony of Charles the Bald. That testimony would have to be examined in light of the entire context and its particular circumstances, and would require a longer discussion wholly unnecessary for the present subject.

### ON SERMON XVII

#### Leo’s judgment that usury is forbidden not only with the poor but also with the rich
## ON SERMON XVII  
### Quesnel’s longer annotation on usury, directed against the recent error

We have reserved for this place Quesnel’s longer annotation on usury, attached to Sermon 17 against the recent error.

> “So clearly,” he says, “is the recent dogma concerning the freedom to lend at interest to the wealthy overthrown in this passage—a dogma to which, sadly, some Catholics are being swept away—that it is worthwhile to consider Leo’s teaching more attentively [Col. 0526B].
>
> “It is therefore clear that he attacks not merely the lending practiced with the poor, but rejects every form of usury altogether. First, he adduces those passages of Scripture that condemn all usury and contain nothing peculiar concerning the poor. Secondly, he condemns the person who exploits the necessities of working people in order to multiply his wealth through excessive increases—something that scarcely occurs with a small sum received from the poor, but rather through the substantial profits obtained when someone exploits the necessities of working people, that is, merchants, and receives back the money lent, increased by excessive gains.
>
> “Thirdly, he refutes the reasoning of those who claim that they are conferring a benefit when they give their money to merchants at interest. For he calls such a benefit deceitful services, deceitful profit, unjust and shameless greed, which claims to confer a benefit while it deceives, and a desire for unjust gain, and so forth.
>
> “Fourthly, he declares in general that interest on money is the funeral of the soul; that the wickedness of interest must be altogether avoided [Col. 0526C]; and that the person who seeks deceitful profit from the interest on his money is a stranger to God’s holy mountain.
>
> “Fifthly, he says that the lender at interest is either wretched because he loses what he gave, or more wretched because he receives what he did not give. Here he shows that the injustice of usury properly consists in someone receiving what he did not give, contrary to God’s general judgment, which, as Saint Ambrose writes in his book *On Tobit*, excludes every increase of the principal. For usury, as Jerome defines it, is receiving more than one gives.
>
> “Finally, you may gather how weak are the little arguments with which usurers disguise their greed from these words: ‘Whatever the outcome may be, the calculation of the lender at interest is [467] always evil; for him it is a sin both to diminish and to increase the money.’ Thus, in Leo’s view, whether this lending appears to benefit the person who borrows, or to harm him, or to occur with danger and loss to the lender, or with profit, the lender’s calculation is always evil.
>
> “See also his Letter 3, alternatively 1 (now Letter 4), chapters 3 and 4, where, without any mention of the poor, he condemns in a general judgment [Col. 0526D] all who practice usury and wish to grow rich through interest; and he laments that this fault is found among those who wish to be called Christians.”

Thus Quesnel. More on this matter, argued against the same error, will be found in several works published most recently, and especially in the celebrated work of the reigning supreme pontiff Benedict XIV, *On the Diocesan Synod*, Book VII, chapter 47. He also condemned the same error by apostolic authority in the encyclical issued on 1 November 1745 and included in Volume I of that pontiff’s *Bullarium*.

## ON SERMON XX

### Quesnel’s censure of Alexander of Hales and Saint Thomas removed

1. Quesnel appended the following annotation to these words of Leo in Sermon 20, chapter 1:

> “The apostolic decrees rightly arranged that the usefulness of the ancient fasts should remain; and although the custom of the Church [Col. 0527A] had learned to exercise itself in longer disciplines, it nevertheless embraced the sanctification of abstinence that comes from the law,” and so forth:
>
> “Let later theologians see by what reasoning they can reconcile their teaching with the instructions of the holy Fathers—those theologians who, on the basis of the perfection of the law of grace, prefer the shorter disciplines of modern fasts to the longer ones.
>
> “Thus Alexander of Hales argues in Part IV, Question 28, *On Fasting*, Member 7, Article 2: ‘The more suitable hour for taking food during a fast,’ he says, ‘is the ninth hour rather than evening . . . . The Church ought to have kept the middle course, so that during the time of fasting we might eat at an intermediate time.’
>
> “His disciple Saint Thomas follows in his footsteps, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, Question 147, Article 7, Reply to Objection 1: ‘To the first objection, therefore,’ he says, ‘it must be replied that the state of the Old Testament is compared with night, while the state of the New Testament is compared with day, according to Romans 13: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near.” Therefore, in the Old Testament they fasted until night, but not in the New Testament.’
>
> “Our Leo philosophizes differently in the present [Col. 0527B] sermon: ‘The moral commandments and precepts,’ he says, ‘remain as they were issued, because they signify nothing other than what they say; and among Christian devotion they grow through increase, not decline through cessation.’ And below: ‘Although many things have been added through the newness of grace, nothing has nevertheless been diminished from the antiquity of righteousness.’
>
> “Consequently, he shows that the custom of the Church is to practice longer disciplines by this excellent reasoning: ‘For those to whom the power to do what is greater had been granted, it was unfitting not to celebrate what is less.’
>
> “In the same sense he writes in Sermon 14, *On the Passion*, chapter 5: ‘In the moral precepts no decrees of the former Testament were rejected, but many were increased by evangelical teaching, so that they might be more perfect and clearer—giving salvation rather than promising the Savior.’
>
> “See Sermon 6, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*, chapter 1.
>
> “But in order to compare with the two leading figures of scholastic theology two equal Fathers of the earlier theology, let us listen to Salvian, who sings in harmony with Leo, in Book II *To the Catholic Church* [Col. 0527C], where, before the middle, he says:
>
> “‘But perhaps someone asks what it is that God now requires more from Christians through the Gospel than he formerly required from the Jews through the law. The reason is clear. We now pay greater things to our Lord because we owe greater things. The Jews had, as it were, a shadow of realities; we have the truth,’ and so forth.
>
> “And a few lines earlier: ‘Then there was more indulgence and more license; then the eating of meat was prescribed, now abstinence; then, throughout the whole life, very few days of fasting, now life as a whole is, as it were, one fast,’ and so forth.”

2. We have shown in a few words how unnecessary, inappropriate, and even extravagant is this censure, which Quesnel composed at such length without any need to explain or defend Leo against such eminent theologians, and especially against Saint Thomas himself, the foremost of theologians.

They are reproached as though, on the basis of the perfection of the law of grace, they had preferred the shorter disciplines of modern fasts to the longer ones. Yet from the context itself it is clear that, considering the discipline of their own time [Col. 0527D], according to which the fast was broken at the ninth hour rather than in the evening, they sought a fitting explanation of that hour which would correspond to the law of grace in a mystical sense. Other ancient Fathers likewise offered mystical explanations for the institution of rites.

But nowhere will you find that they compared shorter disciplines of fasting with longer ones and preferred the former to the latter as more perfect on the basis of the perfection of the new law. Who in his right mind could think such a thing?

If they preferred the ninth hour to evening, they should not for that reason be said to have preferred a shorter discipline to a longer one. For approximately the same discipline could be maintained if someone, abstaining for a period of twenty-four hours, took a single meal either at the ninth hour or in the evening. The shorter abstinence of the person who broke the fast at the ninth hour could in a certain sense be compensated by the longer abstinence that followed.

Moreover, since those theologians were speaking chiefly about the Lenten fast, which was then broken at the ninth hour [Col. 0528A], they could regard the same abstinence and discipline as extending through twenty-four continuous hours both in the case of someone who fasted from the ninth hour after the meal on one day until the ninth hour of the following day, and in the case of someone who fasted from evening to evening. Thus, in the same twenty-four-hour abstinence, they considered the difference between eating at the ninth hour and eating in the evening to be of very little importance.

## ON SERMON XXI  
### On the formula used by Leo in chapter 3: “Thanks be to God the Father through his Son in the Holy Spirit”

> “This formula of prayer is above all Catholic—indeed, it is the sum and fullness of the Christian religion, since it is proper to Christianity to worship God through Christ, as Tertullian testifies in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 21, and Optatus in Book III:
>
> “‘Do you call him a pagan who, before the altar, has entreated God the Father through his Son?’
>
> “And, which is equivalent to the testimony of all witnesses, the Church uses this formula partly in her offices and partly in the public [Col. 0528B] prayer of the sacrifice. She concludes all her collects in this way: ‘Through Christ,’ and so forth—that is, through the mediator between God and human beings.
>
> “And so that prayer might always be directed to the Father at the altar, this was formerly decreed by the Council of Carthage called the Third, canon 23.
>
> “Formerly, however, while the Arian heresy was raging, this formula of speech used by Leo was not heard by all with equal acceptance. For the Arians concealed the impious meaning of their heresy beneath these words; they were accustomed to sing this doxology at the end of their hymns in the following form: ‘Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.’ Philostorgius is a witness to this in Book III of his *History*.
>
> “For this reason Eusebius Pamphili came under suspicion of Arian doctrine among certain people, as Socrates reports in Book II of his *History*, chapter 21, because he so frequently repeated these words in his writings: ‘Through Christ.’ Yet these words are familiar everywhere among ecclesiastical writers, and especially to the Apostle Paul. Nevertheless, says Socrates, he was never considered a teacher of perverse doctrine.”

Thus Quesnel.

## ON SERMON XXIII  
### On another expression of Leo, by which in chapter 1 he says that the divine and human natures in Christ were united so that one nature was mingled with the other

[Col. 0528C]

> “Similarly,” Quesnel says in his annotation, “in Sermon 4, *On the Epiphany*, the Son of God is said to have been mingled with the nature of the flesh.
>
> “The scholastic theologians avoided such ways of speaking more scrupulously than those fathers of the earlier theology, whose leader was Augustine. In Letter 3, to Volusianus, Augustine proposes this definition of the Lord’s incarnation, as full as it is brief: ‘A mingling of God and man.’
>
> “He immediately adds that the hearer must depart from the customary understanding of bodies, according to which two liquids are usually mingled in such a way that neither preserves its own integrity. Shortly afterward he is afraid that the name ‘mingling’ or ‘mixture’ might be admitted improperly for the union of God and man, indeed of soul and body.
>
> “Nevertheless, they spoke more confidently before the Eutychians began their disputes. The Eutychians, failing to depart from the customary understanding of bodies, as Augustine had warned, imagined that after the union the natures had coalesced into one.
>
> “After the rise of this heresy Leo spoke more cautiously and deliberately, lest, while warning Theodoret [Col. 0528D] against the Nestorians or the Eutychians, he should appear to turn his back on one of them, but so that he might avoid and condemn both enemies of Christ with equal balance (Letter 93, alternatively 63).
>
> “When, moreover, one nature is mingled with the other, it should be noted not only that, as our Leo frequently declares, neither nature was confused through the mingling, but also that this occurred in the following manner: when the Word of God, as Augustine says, was mingled with a soul possessing a body, he assumed both the soul and the body simultaneously (Saint Augustine, Letter 3).
>
> “But how was the Word mingled with the soul? Who could explain this, when Augustine himself did not dare to explain it? He says only that the Wisdom of God, which is his Word, present and hidden everywhere, confined nowhere, divided nowhere, swollen nowhere, but wholly present everywhere without bulk [Col. 0529A], assumed the human being in a manner altogether different from that in which it is present to other creatures, and made both itself and him one Jesus Christ, and so forth.
>
> “For, as he says elsewhere in the same letter, Wisdom joined to itself the rational soul, and through that soul also the human body, and the whole human being, who was altogether to be changed for the better, without itself in any way being changed for the worse; it graciously assumed from him the name of humanity, while generously bestowing on him that of divinity.
>
> “Finally, this union is nothing other than the intimate penetration of the soul and of the whole nature through it, into which God himself, wholly, infuses himself wholly in a manner that cannot belong to a creature—for no creature truly penetrates another.
>
> “But God,” says Augustine, “who is capable, not capable of being contained; penetrating, not penetrable; filling, not fillable; who is everywhere wholly at once and everywhere diffused, was mercifully mingled with human nature through the infusion of his power, not human nature with divine nature” (Augustine, in Leporius’s confession).

Thus far Quesnel. We have collected more on this subject in Dissertation 2, chapter 3, in the *Works of Saint Zeno*, page 91; anyone who wishes [Col. 0529B] may consult it.

## ON SERMON XXVII  
### On the correction of the word *AREAE*

[471]

Here we insert the short dissertation of John Ciampini on this subject, addressed to Erasmus Gattola and added by Quesnel to his second edition.

### To the Most Reverend Father Erasmus Gattola of Cajeta

John Ciampini of Rome, Master of Briefs of Grace and Referendary of both Signatures, sends greetings.

Your love of the liberal arts and of those devoted to them has long been known, as has your desire to serve them well—a desire that you have always displayed and continue to display without ceasing. You invite some to study, attract others, instruct still others through your most courteous and learned replies, and spare neither labor nor expense by which you may contribute, according to your ability, to the republic of letters [Col. 0529C].

I myself knew what was commonly said of you in this praise, not only by members of your most noble order but also by others generally. Yet I received a more certain and ample testimony of it, with great delight of mind, when not long ago, in the month of May, I went to visit the celebrated arch-monastery in which you live.

Without doubt I looked with wonder upon the holiness of the place, the beauty of God’s house in the church, and, so to speak, the renowned colony of every virtue that has given to the cities so many distinguished bishops, to the Vatican so many excellent cardinals, to the Church so many most holy pontiffs, and to heaven so many myriads of saints.

I admired the structure and magnificence of the monastery, entirely worthy both of its royal founders and of its monastic inhabitants. I gladly saw the most sumptuous gifts of emperors, kings, and princes, in which one could recognize both their Christian piety and the glory of your father Benedict.

It was also most delightful to me to experience the singular courtesy of all the monks, who received me on my arrival and, after most generously providing every service of religious hospitality, sent me away again [Col. 0529D].

But, to speak frankly—and this is most relevant to the present matter—I took extraordinary pleasure in seeing so many chests of ancient manuscripts in the library over which you yourself preside. I took, without doubt, even greater pleasure when I heard you read with the greatest ease the manuscripts themselves, written in so many different kinds of script.

I believe that this singular learning explains why, so often questioned by me about matters of doubt, you answered with the ease that we can expect only from a person occupied with these studies day and night for a long time.

Nor are you so devoted to manuscripts that you neglect books circulated through printing. Indeed, insofar as religious discipline permits, you have spent a considerable sum of money acquiring these as well. You carefully purchased them at Rome and transferred them to your noble museum, placing in them, like a wise man, your repose and your delight.

For this reason I believed that no more acceptable memorial of grateful affection could be offered to you by me than some literary work—especially one that, in a certain sense, proceeded from you and therefore seemed by a kind of right to be returned to you.

When I had already committed some of my studies, bearing the title *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by Constantine the Great*, to the press, and on that occasion [Col. 0530A] had described the Vatican basilica, famous throughout the whole world, I found among other things that the ancient faithful had been accustomed to ascend to it reverently on their knees, by way of the steps.

On this matter, while I happened to be conversing with our common friend, the Reverend Father Joseph Maria Tommasi, a priest of the Congregation of Clerics Regular and an outstanding investigator of ancient sacred rites, he told me that in Sermon 7 of Saint Leo the Great *On the Nativity of the Lord* he had noticed the word *ARAE*, which he thought had been placed there by mistake.

He therefore left the resolution of this doubt [Col. 0530B] to my care and investigation. I was most willing to comply with my friend’s request. Accordingly, I first turned to examining the printed editions.

If I recite all of them to you, I do not think I shall be burdensome, since you love letters. The most ancient printed edition of the sermons of Saint Leo is the one produced at Cologne in 1551, in folio, and issued in the same city and format in 1569. Then the sermons of the same Saint Leo were published at Venice in 1553 and reissued in the same format and city in 1573.

Next, in 1566, the same sermons were published at Louvain in quarto and afterward reprinted at Antwerp in 1583, likewise in quarto. In 1633 all the works of Saint Leo were published from the Lyon press; these were reprinted there in 1652 together with Saint Maximus and five other Fathers.

Finally, at Paris in 1675, they were published by the most learned Paschasius Quesnel, a priest of the Congregation of the Oratory, illustrated with appendices, dissertations, and observations [Col. 0530C].

I carefully read all these editions that came into my hands, and I found that all of them contained the word *ARAE*. I therefore immediately applied my mind to examining manuscripts.

For this reason I went to the Vatican Library, which is rich in manuscripts and which at that time I especially hoped would yield something because of the close relationship then existing with the late Emmanuel a Schelstrat, the first keeper of that library. But my hope failed me, since I found nothing [473].

Not discouraged by this, but rather made bolder, I turned to other libraries, both in the city and outside it, in order to visit them and examine them with the help of friends. I visited the celebrated Barberini, Ottoboni, and Angelica libraries. Although I found in them manuscripts containing the sermons of Saint Leo, they were not especially venerable because of their antiquity, and I observed in them nothing except the word *ARAE*.

Afterward I wrote to Milan to the Most Reverend Father Eustace [Col. 0530D] of Saint Ubaldo, a Discalced Augustinian and consultant to the Holy Inquisition in those regions, who had rendered outstanding service to the republic of letters. I asked him to investigate in the Ambrosian Library whether there was any manuscript containing the sermons of Saint Leo and showing the aforementioned word *ARAE*.

My friend replied that he had carefully searched the manuscripts and had read the word *ARAE* in them.

Soon afterward I also wrote to you and received your reply. You had found the sermon in question in the manuscript marked number 126, and in it the word *ARCAE* was written. You therefore thought it was a scribal error: the copyist had written *ARCAE* instead of *AREAE*, changing the letter *E* into *C*.

You also reported that this manuscript contained ninety-one sermons of Saint Leo, beginning:

> “Here begin the sermons of Saint Leo, pope. First, on the fast of the tenth month. If, beloved, we understand wisely and faithfully the beginning of our creation [Col. 0531A] . . .”

and ending:

> “If anyone, therefore, after rejecting the darkness of unbelief, wishes to obey his commands, orders, and efforts, he will safely enter the gates of heaven and paradise. Amen.”

You further reported that this manuscript had been written in Lombard letters more than six hundred years ago, because it had been written by order of Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, who afterward became Roman pontiff under the name Victor III, as is read in chapter 63 of Book III of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*. The characters of the manuscript also show this, since they resemble those of other manuscripts written at the order of the same Abbot Desiderius.

By communicating this information to me, you wished abundantly to testify to your kindness toward me. You also sent me the beginnings and endings [Col. 0531B] of sixteen other sermons found under the name of the same Saint Leo in other manuscript codices.

Of the nine that you identified, I already knew that they had been printed under the name of another saint; I do not know the authors of the rest. I found two of these in the Quesnel edition, but they are by no means complete, since they are portions of sermons. One, beginning “Honorabilem . . .,” is part of Sermon 1, *On the Anniversary of His Assumption*; the other is Sermon 48, *On Lent*.

Of the five remaining sermons that you transmitted, after comparing them, I found that they did not at all agree with Saint Leo’s polished and lucid style. I thought it appropriate in this matter also to follow the judgment of friends, who reached the same conclusion as I did.

I did not consider it right to rest content with these investigations. I therefore thought it proper to visit the Vatican Library again and undertake a new search. For this reason I asked the learned Laurent Zaccagna, second keeper of that library, to allow me to examine the indexes. He most courteously granted my request.

The new search was not fruitless. We found one manuscript marked number 1276, written two hundred years ago, on the reverse of page 39 of which is read the word *ARCE*, without the diphthong [Col. 0531C].

In another manuscript, marked number 1267, page 78, second column, on the reverse, written approximately six centuries ago in clear letters, I read the word *AREAE* that I had been seeking. This resolves the question of the doubt.

> **[Note: [Col. 0531] We found this same reading confirmed by three other manuscripts; see Note 17 on Sermon 27.]**

I thought I should inform you of the care I had taken, so that you might know that an error—*σφάλμα* (*sphálma*, “mistake” or “error”)—had entered this word and might observe how it ought to be read.

For a single letter, omitted through a copyist’s carelessness, entirely changes the meaning, as will become perfectly clear from what follows.

An *ara*, therefore, is the place in which sacred things are offered to God. An *area*, on the other hand, is the level space located at the top of a staircase, and sometimes in the middle or other parts of a staircase when it has many steps, so that those ascending it may pause there briefly because of the difficulty and labor of the climb.

The word *ARAE* is read [Col. 0531D] in chapter 4 of Sermon 7 of Saint Leo the pope *On the Nativity of the Lord*. The passage of the sermon runs as follows:

> “From such practices there also arises this impiety: that when the sun rises at the beginning of the daylight, certain more foolish people worship it from elevated places. Some Christians even think that they perform this act with such religious devotion that, before they reach the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, which is dedicated to the one living and true God, after climbing the steps by which one ascends to the upper platform of the *area*, they turn their bodies toward the rising sun and, bowing their necks, incline themselves in honor of the shining orb.
>
> “We greatly waste away and grieve that this is done partly through the fault of ignorance and partly through the spirit of paganism. For even if some perhaps worship the Creator of the beautiful light rather than the light itself, which is a creature, one must nevertheless abstain from this very form of observance. When someone who has abandoned the worship of the gods finds it practiced among our people, will he not retain with himself as something plausible this portion of his former belief, which he sees to be shared by Christians and impious people alike?
>
> “Therefore let the perverse practice condemned by the faithful be cast away from their custom, and let the honor due to the one God not be mingled with the rites of those who serve creatures.”

Here, I seem to see you rightly astonished that so obvious an error should have gone unnoticed by learned men who published the works of Saint Leo several times.

For this reason, do not disdain to interrupt your studies briefly and to read with a friendly spirit what I wrote for the sake of learning after the investigations reported above.

First, then, I turn [Col. 0532A] to the staircase of the Vatican basilica. I found that it had been extremely large: its thirty-five marble steps provided an ascent to the basilica’s upper *area*. They were divided into five flights, so that each flight consisted of seven steps.

For architects observe an odd number in the arrangement of steps. Nature always inclines us, when we ascend, to move the left foot first, and we generally come to rest on that same foot. Therefore, if the number of steps is even, the right foot comes to rest on the final step while the left remains suspended, as though it itself wished to terminate the ascent.

Thus the person ascending experiences a certain discomfort [Col. 0532B], because when nature wishes to find rest on the left foot, it cannot do so.

I display a drawing of this staircase as it formerly was on Plate 12 of my work *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by Constantine the Great*. There the five flights of steps, with the intervening platforms, can be distinctly seen; accordingly, each flight consisted of seven steps.

The purpose of the platforms placed between the flights of a staircase is to allow the person ascending, wearied by the climb, to find a little rest while walking about or standing still. At the top of the staircase there is another platform larger than all the others, because the person ascending must find greater rest there before entering the building.

On the staircase of Saint Peter’s there was a very large platform, which Saint Leo calls the upper platform of the *area*, in distinction from the other lower ones.

The ancient faithful ascended the steps of this staircase in fulfillment of a prayer-vow or as an act of thanksgiving, on their knees, as can be inferred [Col. 0532C] from the *Lives* of Gregory IV and Hadrian I preserved by the librarian.

Having therefore shown what the word *area* means and what it signifies in the sense of Saint Leo, it is worthwhile to examine the rebuke that the same pontiff directed at the faithful.

Some ancient Christians, before entering the Vatican basilica, would stop after climbing the staircase—namely, on the great platform of the staircase itself—on the day of the Nativity of the Lord and worship the rising sun. They adopted this practice from the Manichaeans, who observed this profane rite.

Thus the faithful, ignorant of their own rites, confused the rising Christ with the rising sun, worshiping the creature instead of the Creator.

I shall explain this more precisely. Almost all Gentiles, and especially those of the East, believed that the sun was the chief of the gods. This is taught by Gaspar Bartius, a man of remarkable learning and reading, in his *Commentaries on the Adversaria*, Book XLI, chapter 27.

The same is shown in many places by the man of wide-ranging learning and varied reading [Col. 0532D], Gaspar John Vossius, in his treatise *On Idolatry*, and likewise by Kircher in his *Egyptian Oedipus*.

Since the heresy of the Manichaeans originated in Mesopotamia, in the eastern region, as Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Constantia, or Salamis, in Cyprus, writes in *Against Heresies*, Heresy 46, or 66, it is not surprising that the Manichaeans worshiped the sun.

This is suggested by that great light of the Church, Saint Augustine, who writes of these same Manichaeans in his *Book on Heresies*, Heresy 46:

> “They pray to the sun during the day, wherever it travels around; at night, to the moon, if it appears in the northern region, where the sun, once it has set, returns to the east.”

Accordingly, they turned toward that region of the heavens in which they saw the sun at that hour, so that they might worship it there.

At the very beginning of the morning, therefore, the rising sun [Col. 0533A] faces the front of the Vatican basilica and illuminates it for many hours. Thus, if the Manichaeans wished to worship the sun while standing on the Vatican staircase, they turned their backs to the Vatican basilica.

Although this profane rite was observed by the Manichaeans every day and at every hour, nevertheless the day of 25 December, the Nativity of the Lord, was honored among the Manichaeans because of the sun’s rising. This is made entirely clear from the celebrated Saint Leo in Sermon 2 *On the Nativity of the Lord*, chapter 6, where he says:

> “Therefore, beloved, possessing the confidence of so great a hope, remain steadfast in the faith on which you have been founded, lest that same tempter, whose dominion Christ has already excluded from you, should again deceive you by some ambush and, through the artifice of his deceit, corrupt the joys of this present day.
>
> “He mocks the simpler minds through the destructive persuasion of certain people, to whom this day of our solemnity appears to be honored not so much because of Christ’s Nativity as because of the rising of the new sun, as they call it.
>
> “Their hearts are enveloped in vast darkness [Col. 0533B] and alienated from every increase of true light. They are still dragged along by the most foolish errors of paganism, because they cannot raise the eye of their mind above what they behold with bodily sight, and they worship the lights that serve the world with divine honor.
>
> “Far be impious superstition and monstrous falsehood from Christian minds. Temporal things are separated by an immeasurable distance from the eternal, corporeal things from the incorporeal, and subjects from the ruler. For although they possess wondrous beauty, they do not possess a deity worthy of worship.
>
> “That power, that wisdom, that majesty must be worshiped which created the whole universe from nothing and, by omnipotent reason, brought earthly and heavenly substance into whatever forms and measures it willed.
>
> “Let the sun, moon, and stars be useful to those who use them and beautiful to those who see them—but in such a way that thanks may be returned for them to their Author, and that God, who created them, may be worshiped, not the creature that serves.
>
> “Therefore, beloved, praise God in all his works and judgments. Let there be in you an unwavering belief in the virginity and childbearing. Honor with holy and sincere service the sacred and divine mystery of humanity’s restoration.”

The same Saint Leo again rebukes the faithful for this wicked practice of worship in the Sermon cited above, Sermon 7 *On the same Nativity*, chapter 4. I think it will not be inappropriate to repeat the passage here. Thus the saint speaks:

> “From such practices there also arises this impiety: that when the sun rises at the beginning of the daylight, certain more foolish people worship it from elevated places. Some Christians even think that they perform this act with such religious devotion that, before they reach the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, which is dedicated to the one living and true God, after climbing the steps by which one ascends to the upper platform of the *area*, they turn their bodies toward the rising sun and, bowing their necks, incline themselves in honor of the shining orb.
>
> “We greatly waste away and grieve that this is done partly through the fault of ignorance and partly through the spirit of paganism. For even if some perhaps worship the Creator of the beautiful light rather than the light itself, which is a creature, one must nevertheless abstain from this very form [Col. 0533D] of observance. When someone who has abandoned the worship of the gods finds it practiced among our people, will he not retain with himself as something plausible this portion of his former belief, which he sees to be shared by Christians and impious people alike?”

The truth derived from the sermons cited will become clearer if we examine the period of the same Saint Leo, especially with regard to the gathering of the people at the Vatican basilica.

For the ancient Roman pontiffs were accustomed, until the time of Gregory VII—that is, approximately until the end of the eleventh century—to celebrate the divine offices of the feast of the Nativity of the Lord in three distinct places and at distinct hours.

This is made entirely clear by the ancient books of the Roman Church’s Masses, namely the *Antiphonary of Saint Gregory the Pope*, recently published by the aforementioned Joseph Maria Tommasi. There, on page 15, the ancient books read [Col. 0534A]:

> “Seven days before the Kalends of January. The Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ. At midnight of the Nativity of the Lord. At Saint Mary’s: antiphon at the entrance, ‘The Lord said to me,’ etc.”

And on page 16:

> “Likewise, in the morning at the first hour. At Saint Anastasia’s: antiphon at the entrance, ‘Today light will shine upon us,’ etc.”

On page 17:

> “On the day of the Nativity of the Lord, at Mass. Station at Saint Peter’s. Antiphon at the entrance, ‘A child is born for us,’ etc.”

And in the *Comes* of Albinus, corrected by order of the Emperor Charles—that is, Charlemagne—after the *Antiphonary*, we read on page 1:

> “Here begin the titles of the lessons of the following book:
>
> “I. At the Vigil of the Lord.
>
> “II. At Saint Mary’s.
>
> “III. At Saint Mary’s.
>
> “IV. At Saint Peter’s.”

In the *Capitularies of the Gospels* for the yearly cycle [478], on page 141:

> “On the Nativity of the Lord. At Saint Mary Major’s, etc. Likewise at Saint Anastasia’s, etc. Likewise at Saint Peter’s, etc.”

What has been cited here is understood more clearly from Peter Mallius, who flourished in the twelfth century. He writes:

> “At the first Mass of that same night, at the Manger; in the morning, at Saint Anastasia’s. But in the Mass of the day, formerly—that is, until the time of Gregory VII—the station was at Saint Peter’s. Hence the canons still receive eight solidi for the night presbytery. But now the Mass of the day is celebrated [Col. 0534B] at Saint Mary Major’s, because the route is short and the days are brief.”

Mallius’s work was printed but is mutilated; the passages cited here occur at the beginning of the manuscript.

I therefore conclude that in Saint Leo’s time the station on the day of the Nativity of the Lord was at the Vatican basilica, that the people gathered there, and that Saint Leo delivered the homilies cited above there.

That most wise pontiff did not intend to prohibit prayer with the face turned toward the east. He knew very well the statements of the ancient Fathers; rather, he wished to abolish the wicked rite of the Manichaeans.

This is sufficient concerning the word *AREAE*.

I by no means think Casali’s opinion in *On the Ancient Sacred Rites of Christians*, chapter 3, should be passed over in silence. He thinks that this rite of turning toward the east was observed by the faithful in the atrium of Saint Peter; and therefore, in order to remove every suspicion of idolatry, in the year 1300 a mosaic work depicting a ship was made by Giotto of Florence, an outstanding painter, at the command of Cardinal Stefaneschi, nephew through the pope’s brother of Boniface VIII, the supreme pontiff. In it Saint Peter is seen with the other apostles, as well as our Lord Christ on the seashore calling Peter to himself. Since this painting was on the inner part of the portico, it was not placed there to abolish that rite of turning toward the east, but for a particular devotional or some other reason; for this rite was observed outside the portico, at the top of the steps, before the faithful entered the portico itself.

Accept, then, what I have said up to this point as a token of mutual affection; and I foretell to you that, just as you are flourishing in age and studies, so in that same age you will gather the richest fruits of your studies when you have reached maturity. Farewell.

## ON SERMON XLIII

### Several of Quesnel’s marginal notes examined. Saint Leo’s teaching opposed to propositions 1 and 3 of Jansen

**[Col. 0534D] 1.** Quesnel annotated two passages in chapter 1 of this sermon. First, to the words of the holy pontiff, “The hand of our Maker has so fashioned us that even the one who is being restored works together with his Maker,” he added the following note:

> “It is useful to explain these words by the words of blessed Bernard, *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 14: ‘Grace certainly comes beforehand for this purpose, so that free choice may thereafter cooperate with it. Yet what was begun by grace alone is brought to completion by both together, so that they work at each stage of advancement in combination, not separately; simultaneously, not alternately—not partly by grace and partly by free choice, but each accomplishes the whole by an undivided operation. The whole is accomplished by each, and the whole by the other; but just as the whole is in the one, so the whole is from the other.’”

This is sufficiently sound.

**2.** Moreover, to the Author’s words:

> “Therefore let human disobedience not withdraw itself from the grace of God, nor fall away from that good without which it cannot be good; and if it experiences anything impossible or difficult for itself in carrying out the commandments, let it not remain in itself, but return to the one who gives the command, who for this reason gives the commandment: that he may arouse desire and provide assistance,”

Quesnel added the following marginal note:

> “God’s commandments are impossible for a person who remains in himself.”

Yet the words of Leo, properly and generally understood, do not express this opinion. He does not make a general statement about all commandments—or rather, as he says, about the effects of the commandments. It is clear that the words “let it not remain in itself” were specifically intended to warn people not to trust themselves in matters they find impossible or difficult, but to return to God, who gives the command. Since the means of obtaining divine assistance is thereby indicated—and through that assistance even commandments concerning very difficult, or seemingly impossible, matters may be fulfilled—the impossibility of the commandments properly considered is excluded.

**3.** On this occasion it is useful to consider two other passages of the same Quesnel in Sermon 90, where his concern to introduce the impossibility of the commandments makes it even clearer how far he departs from Leo’s meaning.

**[Col. 0535B]** The holy pontiff wrote in Sermon 90, chapter 2:

> “And lest we be driven by despair into inert sluggishness, the Lord promises that what is impossible for human beings because of their own weakness is possible through divine power.”

Nothing could be sounder or truer. But Quesnel wrote in the margin:

> “The commandments are impossible without grace,”

and in the summary of chapter 2:

> “Nothing is possible without the grace of Christ, even for the regenerate.”

Do you see how broad the difference is between Leo’s words and Quesnel’s? Without the grace of God, Quesnel asserts a general impossibility and attributes it to the commandments themselves; and he asserts it in such a way that—if the proposition is not about the subject, which never happens—he seems to presume that this impossibility is at times found even in the regenerate. Leo, on the other hand, neither in the quoted words nor in the whole context suggests a general impossibility. Nor does he attribute the impossibility he asserts to the divine commandments, but to human weakness, in such a way that it can be overcome through divine assistance.

This impossibility of weakness, so to speak, does not signify absolute and genuine impossibility, but difficulty, which in ordinary usage is called impossibility. Hence, in the text cited from Sermon 43, the holy pontiff used “impossible” and “difficult” almost as synonyms; and in Sermon 94, chapter 2, when he says, “When what I command seems difficult,” he called “difficult” what elsewhere he had called “impossible.”

**4.** Elsewhere, however, Leo indicated that God’s commandments are possible in such a way that he attributed to them the power to move human beings to ask for assistance—which, if it is requested, will be obtained. If it is not requested and is absent, the impossibility will be voluntary; it will wrongly be attributed to the commandments and will provide no adequate excuse. Thus he wrote in Sermon 49, chapter 4:

> “For this reason the commandment is given, so that the assistance of the one who commands may be sought. Let no one excuse himself on the pretext of weakness, since the one who has granted the will also grants the ability.”

Accordingly, Saint Thomas rightly says in *Questions on Truth*, question 24, article 74, after teaching in his response to objection 1:

> “What God has commanded is not impossible for a human being to observe,”

and adds in his response to objection 2:

> “A person is rightly reproved when he does not fulfill the commandments, because it is through his negligence that he does not have the grace by which he can keep the commandments.”

**5.** We further observe that Leo, in Sermon 43, speaks of righteous people, to whom these words apply:

> “Nor let him fall away from that good without which he cannot be good.”

That he also speaks of the regenerate and the just can be gathered from chapter 1 of Sermon 90. Moreover, the Author plainly teaches in Sermon 18, chapter 1, that no commandments are impossible for a human being, especially for a righteous person. Speaking of human nature already redeemed and reborn through holy baptism, he writes:

> “He would be corrupted by carnal desire unless he were fortified by spiritual assistance; for just as there is never lacking for him an occasion by which he may fall, so there is always at hand an occasion by which he may stand, as the Apostle says: ‘God is faithful, and he will not let you be tested beyond what you can bear, but with the testing he will also provide a way out, so that you may be able to endure.’”

To this Quesnel added in a marginal note:

> “What is the soul, even when regenerated, without the assistance of God?”

He did not write “what it would be,” but “what it is,” as though, according to Leo’s view, some soul already regenerated, and therefore righteous, might at some point lack the assistance of God, although Leo testifies:

> “There is always at hand an occasion by which he may stand.”

Leo therefore could not have asserted in Sermon 43 that the divine commandments were impossible for such a person, since this impossibility is removed by that divine assistance which he teaches is always at hand.

Thus the holy pontiff plainly opposes Jansen’s first proposition, which declares that the divine commandments are impossible even for righteous people and that they lack the grace by which those commandments become possible. When Leo teaches that there is always at hand for them an occasion by which they may stand, he certainly recognized that some grace is always present for them, enabling them either to do what they can or to ask for what they cannot do, as the Council of Trent taught after Augustine (*On Nature and Grace*, chapter 43; Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 11). Hence, in more difficult cases, the holy pontiff frequently recommended the remedy of prayer, both in this Sermon 43 and elsewhere, as we have noted. See how beautifully this agrees with Catholic doctrine and how much it differs from the Jansenist position.

**[Col. 0536B] 6.** Quesnel, therefore, should have omitted the marginal note he attached to chapter 1 of Sermon 43 and substituted another more consistent with Leo’s meaning, namely, to the words of the testimony quoted:

> “Therefore let human obedience not withdraw itself from the grace of God,”

the following:

> “Let obedience not be withdrawn from the grace of God.”

This proposition presumes that obedience can be withdrawn and is in fact sometimes withdrawn. It therefore conflicts with the third Jansenist proposition and also with the fifteenth condemned Quesnellian proposition in the constitution *Unigenitus*, which openly implies that human obedience never withdraws itself from interior grace:

> “When God accompanies his commandment and his eternal utterance with the anointing of his Spirit and the interior power of grace, he works in the heart the obedience he demands.”

## ON SERMON XLIV  
### On the Christian justice that must always increase

**1.** To these words of Leo in chapter 1:

> “Among the stages of progress, there is none that should not always become better,”

Quesnel added the following note:

> “He says the same in Sermon 11 on Lent, chapter 1: ‘No one is so holy that he should not be holier; no one is so devoted that he should not be more devoted.’ Therefore he sins who does not always strive toward greater righteousness. For, as Augustine says, it is sin when either the love that ought to exist is absent or is less than it ought to be (*On the Perfection of Righteousness*, chapter 6 and following). Indeed, anyone who does not love God with his whole soul is guilty, since he is commanded to love him in this way; and anyone who desires what he is forbidden to desire is guilty. Yet he does not impute this to those who faithfully say to him: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’ Whoever thinks he ought not to pray this declares that he is not a Christian. For as long as we live here, there remains something of carnal desire that must be restrained by self-control, until perfect righteousness is achieved as complete health. Complete health comes when there is complete love; complete love comes when we shall see him as he is.”

So much for Quesnel.

**[Col. 0536D] 2.** Apart from the commandment of charity, which requires an increase in charity and righteousness—as Saint Thomas taught in *Sentences* III, distinction 29, question 1, article 8, question 2—Leo himself opens a more direct and easier path. In the present Sermon 6 on the Nativity of the Lord, and also in Sermon 11 cited by Quesnel, he joins this duty of increasing Christian righteousness with the temptations and desires that beset everyone, even the saints, on every side, as though one depended upon the other.

Indeed, it is certain that the commandment to love God requires not only that we avoid sins, even lesser ones, but also that we resist the desires and temptations that incite us to sin. In this daily resistance, which every person, even a saint, must exercise, many acts of virtue, and especially charity, must be practiced. Thus there is both an occasion and an obligation for Christian righteousness continually to increase.

Just as temptations and desires will never be entirely removed in this life, so we must never cease resisting them and consequently growing in righteousness from day to day, until we reach that eternal life in which there will be no temptations and no desires to resist. Therefore, in this life, among the stages of progress, as Leo says, “there is none that should not always become better.”

## ON SERMON XLV

### In what sense Saint Leo wrote in chapter 2: “Without love there is no believing.” Quesnel’s annotation examined

**1.** To the testimony of Saint Leo just mentioned, Quesnel appended this annotation:

> “A doctrine drawn from Augustine’s principles, indeed from the very principles of faith. For since no one can obey God’s commandments as he ought without charity, and since among God’s commandments the commandment to believe is not the least, it is clear that Leo wisely said that without love there is no believing. One passage from Augustine will suffice to make the identical meaning and doctrine of both understood. Thus, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 16: ‘Grace therefore comes before faith,’ he says, ‘for otherwise, if faith comes before it, surely the will comes before it as well, since faith cannot exist without the will. But if grace comes before faith, because it comes before the will, it certainly comes before every act of obedience; it also comes before charity, through which alone one obeys God truly and sweetly. And grace works all these things in the person to whom it is given, and whose every one of these things it precedes.’”

Thus far Quesnel.

**2.** The whole force of Quesnel’s annotation lies in this: Saint Leo supposedly asserted, “Without love there is no believing,” because, just as no one can obey the other commandments, so no one can obey the commandment of faith as he ought without charity. Through charity alone, as Augustine says, one obeys God truly and sweetly. For this reason Quesnel presents Leo’s doctrine as drawn from Augustine’s principles.

Care must be taken, however, lest this expression be understood in the sense conveyed by Quesnel’s condemned proposition 47 in the constitution *Unigenitus*, namely:

> “Obedience to the law must flow from its source, and that source is charity. When the love of God is its interior principle and the glory of God its end, then what appears externally is pure; otherwise it is nothing but hypocrisy or false righteousness.”

This agrees with proposition 17 condemned by Saint Pius V among the propositions of Baius:

> “The obedience to the law that is performed without charity is not true obedience.”

In defense of Quesnel’s proposition 47, we read in the Quesnellian *Hexapla* an excerpt from Augustine’s testimony in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 16, which is repeatedly invoked and wrongly explained—or rather twisted. For when the holy Doctor said that one obeys truly through charity alone, they inferred that without charity one does not obey truly, but deceitfully; and consequently that all such obedience is not true obedience to the law, but must be referred to hypocrisy and false righteousness.

**3.** If Quesnel appended this annotation with so perverse and condemned a meaning and intention, he would have wished to indicate that Leo’s words, “Without love there is no believing,” should be understood to mean that the faith found in sinners without charity is not true faith, by which the commandment of faith is truly obeyed. This opinion is akin to propositions 52 and 58 condemned in the same constitution, in which Quesnel asserted that true faith and religion cannot exist without love and charity.

The Council of Trent had long before explicitly condemned this monstrosity of doctrine with respect to faith, Session 6, chapter 28:

> “If anyone says … that the faith which remains in a sinner is not true faith, although it is not living faith; or that one who has faith without charity is not a Christian, let him be anathema.”

For this reason proposition 12 was also condemned by Alexander VIII:

> “When love fails in great sinners, faith also fails; and even if they appear to believe, it is not divine faith but human faith.”

**4.** But if Quesnel understood Leo’s words in his annotation in another sense—namely, as indicating that Leo was speaking not of faith in general but of living faith, and that Augustine likewise wrote that through charity alone one obeys truly, meaning the obedience required for true righteousness and the earning of eternal reward—then he would indeed have understood the matter correctly, but he would not have explained the opinion adequately, as it ought to have been explained and demonstrated in the annotation.

It is of the greatest importance for us to establish this clearly, so that it may be evident how far Leo’s words and opinion are from the condemned sense.

**5.** If the proposition “Without love there is no believing” is considered apart from its context, one might suspect that the holy pontiff took the word “love” in a broad sense—not merely for charity, but for love of every kind—so that it would include even the love by which anyone who believes at least loves truth and faith itself to some degree.

But just as the context, from which the genuine sense of words must always be gathered, makes it clear that by “love” Saint Leo understands that charity which produces eternal fruit, so by “faith” he understands living faith, which together with charity contributes to seeing and attaining God.

Indeed, at the beginning of the second chapter of that sermon, where the quoted words occur, he had already proposed to explain by what paths we must proceed toward God’s promises, namely, toward eternal glory. He immediately sets out two paths from sacred Scripture: mercy and truth. He warns that these are not to be separated, since both virtues must be joined if we are to strive toward that end.

He then turns to faith and charity and likewise declares the connection of these virtues necessary for the same end. Hence he adds:

> “Then the true name and the true fruit”—namely, the eternal fruit—“of both exist, when the indissoluble connection of the two remains.”

And, intending to explain that this connection is altogether necessary for that end, he immediately adds:

> “For where they are not together, they are both absent together, because they are mutually both assistance and light to one another: until the reward of vision fulfills the desire of belief, and what is now neither loved without faith nor believed without love is seen and loved unchangeably”—so that it may be believed profitably in order to obtain the reward of vision.

The connection and this end are more clearly indicated by what follows immediately:

> “For, as the Apostle says, in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value, but faith working through love. Let us therefore devote ourselves simultaneously and together to charity and to faith. For this is a most effective flight of two wings, by which purity of mind is lifted up to attain and behold God, lest it be weighed down by the burden of carnal concerns.”

For the one who says, “Without faith it is impossible to please God,” also says, “If I have all faith, so that I can move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing”—namely, before God, before whom nothing profits without charity, as the Apostle says in the same passage. Thus the holy pontiff explained it in Sermon 2 on the Fast of Pentecost, chapter 3:

> “When the Apostle says that no virtues profit him without charity.”

For this reason Leo again inserted the following principle in chapter 3 of Sermon 45:

> “What does not proceed from the source of faith does not reach eternal rewards.”

There he indicates that he is speaking of the faith by which we merit eternal reward, and which cannot exist without charity. You see, therefore, how properly everything is referred to the end of eternal blessedness.

**6.** It will finally become evident that this can be the only interpretation of Leo’s thought from Sermon 4 on almsgiving, chapter 1, where he sufficiently implies that faith exists in many without charity, but that such faith, separated from charity, contributes nothing to salvation or eternal reward.

Speaking of many Christians, he says:

> “From many of those whose faith the devil could not take away, he removed charity; and, after occupying the field of their hearts with the roots of avarice, he deprived them of the fruit of works, though he did not deprive them of the fruit of their lips.”

What could be clearer?

Likewise, in Sermon 10 on Lent, chapter 3, he openly acknowledges that correct faith—which sufficiently obeys the commandment of faith—can exist without charity, but that, if separated from charity, it is not fruitful for future glory:

> “Although it is a great thing to possess sound faith and correct doctrine, and although the circumcision of the appetite, gentleness of meekness, and purity of chastity are worthy of much praise, all virtues are nevertheless naked without charity; nor can anything be called fruitful in any excellence of conduct if it has not been brought forth by love.”

From this we can understand the words of Sermon 18, chapter 3, where, describing the various stages of Christian progress, he says:

> “In faith there is the germ, in hope the growth, in charity maturity.”

In these words he recognizes faith and hope as virtues, but not as fruitful for eternal life unless they attain maturity through charity.

Thus the teaching of the holy pontiff is drawn from the principles of faith established by Scripture and by the tradition of the Council of Trent, and is recognized as foreign to the condemned theses.

**7.** It is no less consistent with Augustine’s principles. In many passages Augustine expressly and repeatedly taught that faith exists without charity, as in Sermon 90, number 8:

> “You can have faith without love.”

He declares only that faith is empty—or useless for eternal reward—for the person who believes without charity. Thus he writes in the *Enchiridion*, number 117:

> “But whoever does not love believes in vain, even if what he believes is true.”

And in *On the Trinity*, book VIII, chapter 4:

> “Unless he is loved through faith, the heart cannot be cleansed so as to be fit and capable of seeing God.”

When, in *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 16, Augustine wrote of charity, through which alone one obeys God truly and sweetly, he understood “truly” as perfect obedience to the law, by which a person becomes fit and capable of seeing God, as those who discuss this doctrine of his at length demonstrate from his other testimonies.

For us, however, it is sufficient to have explained and established Leo’s opinion.

## ON THE SAME SERMON XLV

### On the words in chapter 4: “Let those guilty of crimes rejoice that they have reached these days [of Easter], during which even the severity of public punishments is relaxed by holy and devout rulers”

**[Col. 0539C]**

> “He says the same thing,” Quesnel writes in the annotation appended to the testimony just quoted, “above, in Sermon 2 on Lent, chapter 5: ‘The most devout emperors of the Roman world, observing an ancient holy custom, order many guilty of offenses to be released, in honor of Christ’s passion and resurrection, because the severity of their laws has been softened.’ And in Sermon 9, chapter 3: ‘So that the severity of punishments, which is now also relaxed in public judgments,’ and so forth.
>
> “I do not find it clearly defined how far this remission and relaxation extended: whether offenders who had merely been freed from chains remained in custody, or whether they were also released from prison. In the petition of the monks who were under Eutyches, inserted into act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon, we read: ‘The day of the saving Passion and the sacred night have arrived, and the feast of the Resurrection, on which condemnations are indeed released from very many sinners by our holy Fathers; but criminal bonds are also loosened by the emperors for the guilty. Just joy fills every household and every public square.’
>
> “From these words it seems that at least some offenders were restored to liberty at the Easter festival by imperial laws. Yet there is nothing in the Code that asserts this, although there are several laws that suspend all proceedings against offenders—some for the whole of Lent, others for the fifteen days of the Easter festival. In the Code, book III, title 12, *On Holidays*: ‘During the forty days which, by the institution of the ceremonies, anticipate the Easter season, every hearing of criminal cases is suspended.’ Emperors Valentinian, Valens, and Gratian, Augusti. ‘During the fifteen Easter days, the enforcement of the grain tax and the collection of all public and private debts shall be postponed.’ Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti.
>
> “Another constitution of the same emperors contains an exception that confirms rather than weakens the opinion of our Leo: ‘Nevertheless, during these days, let everyone have the freedom both to emancipate and to manumit.’ But Leo’s passage cited first, from Sermon 2 on Lent, seems to assert more clearly that the guilty of many offenses were released by imperial constitutions during the solemnity of the Easter days. For from Sermon 47 on the Passion, chapter 8, it is proved that ‘to release’ means nothing other than ‘to dismiss,’ where he writes that the people shouted so that Barabbas might be released by indulgence.”

Thus far Quesnel.

But if he had examined the title of Justinian’s Code, *On Episcopal Jurisdiction*, book I, title 4, he would have found law 3 of Valentinian II, recorded and issued in the year 385, in which the following appears:

> “Let the judges carry out what we are accustomed to grant. When the first day of Easter has arrived, let no prison hold anyone confined; let the bonds of all be dissolved.”

Exceptions concerning certain offenders and crimes are then added.

In the Theodosian Code, book IX, title 28, *On Indulgences for Crimes*, there are five such laws, two of Valentinian the Elder and three of Valentinian the Younger. The last is the one already cited. From these it may be gathered that this indulgence had formerly been introduced by custom, or even prescribed by annual letters from the emperors sent to all cities. As is clear from two testimonies of Chrysostom, this established custom produced doubts concerning certain offenders—whether they too were to be released by the same indulgence. Those laws were issued to resolve these doubts.

In the last law a general enactment was issued that included all the exceptions. See especially Jacobus Gothofredus’s commentary on law 3, where he quotes the passages of Chrysostom mentioned above.

## ON SERMON LXVI

### Quesnel’s note on Leo’s testimony in chapter 4 examined

“What human being did that very assumption of our substance in the Godhead, by which the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, leave excluded from its mercy, except an unbeliever?”

To these words of Leo Quesnel attached the following note:

> “The unbeliever is excluded from the grace of Christ.”

This indefinite proposition can be wrongly understood, so that it may seem to support proposition 26 condemned in the constitution *Unigenitus*, which states:

> “No graces are given except through faith.”

But the holy pontiff used the word “mercy,” not the word “grace.” To prevent the word “mercy” itself from deceiving anyone, the sense in which he called the unbeliever excluded from mercy must be explained from the context.

He therefore understands unbelievers to be excluded from that mercy of which he declares believers to be participants. The following words, immediately appended to the preceding testimony, pertain to believers:

> “And who does not share a common nature with Christ, if he has received the one who assumed him and has been regenerated by the same Spirit by whom Christ was begotten?”

Here he indicates the grace of faith and baptism, as we explained in note 24 on this passage.

Saint Leo is speaking of that mercy by which the Word, made flesh and dwelling among us, makes us, united to him through faith and baptism, sharers in the divine nature. Just as believers, who have received faith and baptism, are participants in this mercy, so unbelievers, who lack both faith and baptism, are rightly said to be excluded from this same mercy.

## ON SERMON LXXVI

### On the passage in chapter 6 concerning Manes: “He became known as one who was to be condemned at the time when two hundred and sixty years after the Lord’s resurrection had been completed, under the consulship of the emperor Probus and Paulinus, when the eighth persecution against the Christians was already raging”; three of Quesnel’s annotations and several of our observations are presented

**1.** Quesnel appended three annotations to this testimony, which we reproduce here.

First, on the words, “when two hundred and sixty years after the Lord’s resurrection had been completed,” he says:

> “Dionysius Petavius suspects that an error lies here in his annotations on Epiphanius, page 267, and wants CCLX to be read as CCXL, with one numeral transposed. His reason is that the consulship of Probus and Paulinus falls approximately in the year 277 of Christ according to the Dionysian era. ‘Subtracting thirty-one years from this number,’ he says, ‘there remain 246 years from the Lord’s ascension—exactly as many as Epiphanius gives on the authority of the other chronographers.
>
> “‘Our Leo therefore followed their opinion—if Petavius’s correction is sound—using the round number 240 instead of 246, something that especially tends to happen in preaching, when precise chronological details are not observed. Leo will come still closer to that date if he wrote CCL instead of CCLX; and one Oxford manuscript preserved in the Laudian archives does indeed have this reading.
>
> “‘Indeed, when types are being arranged for printing, it is easier for a single numeral, through the negligence of the workmen, to slip into the place of another, so that LX is printed instead of XL; likewise, in writing, it is easier for one numeral to be added to a total, so that X is added to L.’”

**[Col. 0541B] 2.** Second, on the words “under the consulship of the emperor Probus and Paulinus,” he says:

> “From this correct the consular Fasti of Cassiodorus, which place this consulship immediately after the consulship of Aurelian and Marcellinus. Correct also the ecclesiastical annals, which associate this consulship with the seventh year of the emperor Aurelian in the year 277 of Christ.
>
> “Since all the Fasti make it clear that Probus and Paulinus held the consulship together, and since our Leo calls Probus emperor, it is necessary that this consulship of Probus and Paulinus occurred after Aurelian’s death, indeed after the death of Tacitus, whom Probus succeeded.
>
> “The Chronology of Eusebius agrees with this, assigning the origin of the Manichaeans to the second year of the emperor Probus. Yet there is an easy way to reconcile the different authors who write about the beginnings of the Manichaean sect. Some are to be understood as speaking of Manes himself, others of his teachers Scythianus and Buddha, whom we discussed above; some of the very origin of that monstrosity; some of its various outbreaks into the Church, partly in the East and partly in the West; and finally others of the condemnation of its errors, which our Leo mentions.”

**3.** Third, on the words “when the eighth persecution against the Christians was already raging,” and so forth, he says:

> “If he is speaking of the persecution of the emperor Aurelian, as he seems certainly to be, this was not the eighth but the ninth, as Augustine numbers it in *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 3, and as is clear from the enumeration of the other persecutions.
>
> “If the acts of the martyr Chariton, which are read in Surius on September 24, deserve credence on this point, Tacitus, Probus’s predecessor, had already brought this persecution to an end. It is therefore helpful to interpret Leo’s words generously, since they seem also to signify the beginning of the persecution: ‘when it was already boiling over,’ and so forth, although three Oxford manuscript codices read *desaeviret* (‘was raging’) rather than *ebulliret*.”

These are all Quesnel’s remarks.

**4.** We have discovered that all the chronological notices in this passage were taken from the complete *Chronicle of Prosper*. Among the three—or rather four—editions of this Chronicle, which Father Jerome a Prato distinguishes and establishes with the greatest care in dissertation 3 on Sulpicius Severus, volume II, number 32 and following, one of the first two—or, if you prefer, the third—could have served Leo’s purpose in the present matter, which concerns the discovery of the Manichaeans at Rome.

The first edition was published by Prosper in the year 433; the second ends in the year 443 and can be confirmed from the ancient Veronese Saibante manuscript, which represents the complete Chronicle of Prosper ending in that year—that is, this very second edition. The third extends as far as the year 445.

Two certain indications demonstrate that Leo drew upon one of these editions in setting down the chronological notices mentioned above.

In one of Prosper’s Chronicles, the consulship of the emperor Probus and Paulinus is recorded. Prosper, who excerpted most of his material from the Chronicle of Eusebius as translated into Latin by Jerome, was the first of all to add consulships dating from the Passion—or resurrection—of Christ, and he assigned the beginnings of the Manichaean heresy to the consulship of the emperor Probus and Paulinus.

The notice of the eighth persecution must likewise be referred solely to Prosper’s Chronicle. For although Eusebius marked the persecutions at their proper places in his Chronicle, he did not state the number that we find in Prosper.

Accordingly, the notice of the year must also be said to have been calculated from the same Chronicle of Prosper.

**5.** If the calculation is believed to have been made correctly, the year that should have been written was rather 250 than 260. For if one calculates from the consulship of the Gemini, to which the Passion and resurrection of Christ are assigned in those same editions—since the change of opinion whereby Prosper assigned Christ’s manifestation or preaching to the consulship of the Gemini, but his Passion and resurrection three years later, must be attributed to the last edition, published in the year 455—if, I say, one calculates from that consulship of the Gemini to the consulship of Probus and Paulinus, to which the beginning of the Manichaean heresy is attached, one will find in the printed editions 247 years. This number could, as often happens, have been given approximately as the year 250, but not 260.

It must be observed, however, that in the commonly circulated *Chronicle of Prosper* some consulships were omitted through the negligence of copyists, while others were inserted incorrectly. This can be inferred from the Easter Canon of Victor of Aquitaine, who copied the consulships from Prosper more accurately, as well as from other arguments clearly set forth by Johannes Vander Haagen in his *Observations on the Chronicle of Prosper*, section 49 and following.

Moreover, from this same Canon of Victor and from other notices in Prosper’s Chronicle, it is clear that Prosper himself assigned the consulship of the Gemini, to which the Passion and resurrection of Christ are attributed, to the year corresponding to the twenty-eighth year of the common era.
