If you begin counting from this year of the common era up to the consulship of Probus and Paulinus, which coincides with the year 277 of the common era, you will find that, counting the endpoints, the two hundred and fiftieth year had elapsed. Leo calls it completed, though with less exactness.

### 6

It must indeed not be concealed that, if two consulships which certainly ought to be removed from Prosper’s *Chronicle* are expunged, and four which certainly ought to be added are inserted—as the aforementioned Vander Haagen proved—the consulship of Probus and Paulinus falls, counting from the consulship of the Gemini, in the year 249, just as it does in Victor’s account. But since the manuscripts of Prosper and Victor are evidently corrupt in their recording of the consulships, it does not seem worthwhile to dwell on this point at length.

Since, however, Prosper had already begun, somewhat before the consulship of Probus and Paulinus, and thereafter as well, to abandon the old anticipation by one year and to assign the consuls to each person’s proper year, it is more reasonable to believe that he likewise assigned the consulship of Probus and Paulinus to its proper year. Thus one consulship, which had been placed before it, is read incorrectly in the manuscripts as following it; and consequently their consulship truly coincided with the year 250 after the resurrection of Christ.

Since, therefore, Saint Leo took his other [Col. 0542D] chronological notices from Prosper’s *Chronicle*, it is credible that he likewise recorded the year 250 by calculation from the same source, and not 260. Yet only one Oxford manuscript, cited by Quesnellus, gives that year. Since, however, all the other manuscripts—both the numerous and ancient codices of the Collections and Lectionaries, which we carefully examined and compared, among them the very ancient Vatican manuscript 3835—have the year 260, and express it not with the Roman numerals CCLX, which scribes could easily have altered and corrupted, but in distinct words, *ducentesimus et sexagesimus* (“the two hundred and sixtieth”), which do not so readily admit of alteration, we have not dared to depart from the common reading.

Experience has shown how far from the primitive and original reading those men have departed who, although led by powerful conjectures, have arbitrarily attempted to correct certain numerical notices. Nor should the excess of a decade, which is evident in the year 260, trouble us. [Col. 0543A] For we have demonstrated by numerous examples that the ancient Fathers of the Church were not very exact in reckoning the years either from Christ’s birth or from his passion, and that they sometimes exceeded the correct figure by more than a decade; see Dissertation 1 prefixed to the edition of Saint Zeno, chapter 2, § 1.

This is sufficient concerning Quesnellus’s first annotation.

### 7

With regard to the second, it is enough to observe that Leo’s words concerning the time when Manes became known as deserving condemnation indicate the time when Archelaus, the first bishop of Caschara in Mesopotamia, held a public disputation with Manes; from that point onward Manes’s errors emerged in such a way that he was then recognized as one who ought to be condemned.

### 8

As for the third annotation, we shall now indicate that the mention of the eighth persecution was taken by the holy pontiff from Prosper’s *Chronicle*. Prosper, however, listed only nine persecutions. He did not think that the [Col. 0543B] persecution of Aurelian—which Augustine and Orosius call the ninth, and which is reported to have been initiated but immediately cut short by the lightning and death of that emperor—should be counted as a distinct persecution. Accordingly, he called Diocletian’s persecution—the one otherwise called the tenth—the ninth.

Hence, when Leo called it the eighth persecution, following Prosper’s usage, he meant not the persecution of Aurelian but that of Valerian, which is counted as the eighth both by Prosper and by Augustine and Orosius, as well as by Sulpicius and Jerome.

## 491 — ON SERMON LXXIX

### Whether Saint Leo taught that all works of the moral virtues performed by unbelievers are sins

### 1

In Sermon 79, the second sermon on the Pentecost fast, chapter 2, when speaking of the fasts of unbelievers, the holy pontiff not only called them vain but also asserted that they were defiled by unbelief:

> For reason acts in one way under truth, deception in another under falsehood. Among us, faith sanctifies even the one who eats; among them, unbelief pollutes the one who fasts.

Immediately afterward he adds this general proposition [Col. 0543C]:

> Outside the Catholic Church nothing is whole, nothing is pure, as the Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin.”

By these words he seems to imply that not merely fasts, but all acts of the other moral virtues, when defiled by unbelief, are sins. Quesnellus appended the following note to these words:

> Whether, and of what kind, the good works of unbelievers are.

### 2

So that no one may think that Saint Leo favored a doctrine proscribed by the Church, it must first be stated that elsewhere he openly professed that works of mercy and human kindness which do not proceed from faith are worthy of praise, provided that, being free from any corrupt purpose introduced from elsewhere, they arise from the motive proper to the virtues themselves.

For the following is found in Sermon 7 on Lent, chapter 3:

> What could be more blessed than this human kindness? It certainly ought not to be deprived of its praise if, because of the fellowship of nature—that is, the motive of natural virtue—one human being renders assistance to another.

But he adds:

> Since what does not proceed from the source of faith does not attain eternal rewards, the condition of heavenly works is one thing and that of earthly works another. [Col. 0543D] Worldly benevolence finds its end in those whom it helps; Christian devotion passes over to its author, since when we are said to be kind toward him, we confess that he works within us.

He who affirms that such human kindness ought not to be deprived of its praise, even though it does not proceed from the source of faith, provided that one human being assists another because of the fellowship of nature—which is the end of compassion and natural virtue—clearly regarded this kindness as good, not evil. For an evil that deserved only blame could not have been said not to be deprived of its praise.

He added only that such works lack the heavenly reward which God bestows, and that their entire reward ends among the human beings whom they benefit and in this present world. Therefore, if unbelievers perform works of mercy or of another moral virtue from the motive of virtue, although they do not perform them from faith, they are not, according to Leo’s judgment, to be accused of sin.

### 3

[Col. 0544A] If, then, in Sermon 79 he affirmed that their fasts were polluted by unbelief and that nothing whole or pure could be found among them, he must be understood to have asserted this in another sense, one that does not contradict his preceding statement: namely, insofar as he believed that fasts and other works of virtue among unbelievers generally arose not from the motive of virtue but from some vicious purpose.

In this connection it should be observed that the holy pontiff includes under the term “unbelievers” all who lack the Christian faith, whether they are pagans, Jews, or even heretics. He begins the second chapter as follows:

> In carrying out this service of God—that is, abstinence from food through fasting—we ought not to be more sluggish merely because Jews and heretics often restrain themselves from the freedom of eating, and because among the pagans also there are certain vain fasts.

Immediately afterward, speaking of all these people who fast, he adds:

> For reason acts in one way under truth, deception in another under falsehood. Among us, faith sanctifies even the one who eats; among them, unbelief pollutes the one who fasts.

Here “unbelief” extends not only to pagans but also to Hebrews and heretics.

[Col. 0544B] The abstinence of these people, and similarly their other acts of the moral virtues, could be polluted in various ways by some corrupt purpose. Everyone understands how the fasts of pagans—if, in Leo’s time, any such fasts were still practiced in the worship of empty gods, as was the fast instituted for Ceres which Livy records, and which is read as prescribed for the fourth day before the Nones of October in the ancient marble calendar excavated at Amiternum [see Muratori, *Thesaurus Inscriptionum*, p. 150]—could properly be called polluted by unbelief.

The same applies to the fasts of the Manichaeans in honor of the sun and moon, which Leo mentions in Sermon 4 on Lent, chapter 5, and in his letter to Turibius, chapter 4. Concerning them he accordingly says in the sermon cited above:

> They are polluted above all by their very observance.

He also briefly touched upon other fasts of these heretics in Sermon 4 on the Nativity, chapter 6:

> Let not the fabricated and counterfeit fasts of deceivers lead you astray. They advance not toward the purification but toward the destruction of souls. [Col. 0544C] They assume for themselves an appearance of piety and chastity; but under this deception they conceal the obscenities of their actions and send forth from the recesses of their profane hearts arrows by which the simple are wounded.

And again, concerning such fasts, in Sermon 4 on the Epiphany, chapter 5:

> Those fasts are not pure which arise not from the discipline of self-restraint but from the art of deceit. Let them have harmed the unwary only so far; let them have mocked the inexperienced only so far.

Since in these passages he attributes the vice of this kind of fasting to the purpose of deceiving, rather than to fasting itself, he thereby implies that fasts are pure when they arise from the discipline of self-restraint—that is, when, every corrupt purpose being excluded, they proceed from the sole motive of virtue.

The fasts of the Hebrews likewise may be understood as polluted either by the corrupt intention with which they thought obedience should be rendered to legal precepts that had already been abolished, or at least by empty glory, with which the Pharisees were puffed up when they fasted, as is reported in Matthew, chapter 6, verse 16. The holy pontiff noted this in Sermon 4 on the Fast of the Seventh Month, chapter 1, and especially in Sermon 7, chapter 2.

### 4

[Col. 0544D] That this vice of empty glory was particularly in Saint Leo’s mind in the sermon now under discussion may be inferred from the fact that in the third chapter he urges Christians to beware especially of boastfulness and pride in their fasts, lest the fast—which is good in itself—be corrupted by this vice.

He says:

> We must beware lest, through elation, we lose the good things which we cannot do without goodness. For he strips himself of all claim to praise who glories more in himself than in the Lord concerning the efforts of his diligence.

And in chapter 4:

> Let us restrain ourselves from the inflation of boastfulness, referring everything to the glory of God.

He seems to have inveighed especially against this vice when speaking of Christian fasts because, as he observes in Sermon 4 on Lent, chapter 3, among those who are not held by unbelief the devil chiefly lies in wait through this corrupt purpose:

> Those whom he could not overthrow through lack of faith, he attempts to overcome through glory.

[Col. 0545A] For the evil of pride is close to right actions, and elation always lies in wait near the virtues. It is difficult for human praise not to seize one who lives commendably, unless, as it is written, the one who boasts boasts in the Lord.

Since Saint Leo thought that among pagans, Jews, and heretics—who lack the true faith—fasts were infected either by this pride or by some other vice, and presumed that the other works of the moral virtues performed by them were similarly corrupted by some evil purpose, it is not surprising that he consequently affirmed that those works were polluted by unbelief and that among such people nothing whole and nothing pure could be found.

### 5

Nor should it therefore be concluded that he absolutely and generally condemned as sins all works of virtue performed by them outside the Church. For, as we have seen, he expressly taught that works worthy of praise and good in themselves, which do not proceed from the source of faith, are good if they are produced with every corrupt purpose excluded and from the motive of virtue.

He affirmed only that, among pagans and other unbelievers, when the true faith is lacking, some corrupt purpose—at least self-love or empty glory—very easily insinuates itself; and that the good works which we cannot perform without goodness are thereby corrupted and, in that respect, are neither whole nor pure. Augustine, Prosper, and other Fathers likewise taught this in the same sense.

[Col. 0545B] Hence, in Sermon 4 on the Nativity of the Lord, chapter 6, after criticizing the vicious fasts of the Manichaeans, he exhorted his hearers to maintain the true faith, especially for this reason: without it nothing is holy, nothing pure, nothing alive, for “the just person lives by faith.” The words “nothing pure” are to be understood in the sense indicated here.

### 6

This final text supplies another observation. When Leo teaches that without faith there is nothing holy and nothing living, he implies that the works of unbelievers, when not infected by any corrupt purpose, lack true sanctity and the merit of eternal life.

Thus, in Sermon 8 on Lent, chapter 1, when warning those who are about to fast not to be polluted by any unbelief, the holy pontiff gives the following reason:

> For since the Apostle says, “Whatever is not from faith is sin,” the fasts of those whom the father of lies deceives with his illusions and whom the true flesh of Christ does not nourish will be useless and vain.

[Col. 0545C] By these words he seems to interpret the term “sin,” used by the Apostle, as referring to works generally that are useless and vain—that is, lacking merit and eternal reward. He thereby includes even those works of mercy performed by unbelievers which, without any corrupt purpose, are undertaken to assist another human being because of the fellowship of nature, and which he had declared in Sermon 7 not to be deprived of their praise—that is, to be good.

Such works can therefore be called sins only in this broader sense: without living faith they contribute nothing to eternal reward. Hence in that same Sermon 7 he wrote:

> What does not proceed from the source of faith does not attain eternal rewards.

### 7

The holy pontiff therefore clearly distinguished two kinds of works of the moral virtues among unbelievers.

Some are good in their object but corrupted by a corrupt purpose, and thus evil. Others are not infected by any corrupt purpose; they are good not so much in their object as in the motive of virtue, yet they lack the merit of eternal life and are useless in that respect.

Of works of the first kind he affirmed absolutely and generally that among unbelievers nothing whole, nothing pure, and so forth, could be found, because in general all the good works of unbelievers are corrupted by some vicious purpose.

[Col. 0545D] Works of the second kind he admitted conditionally and, as it were, by way of exception, provided that they are performed from the motive of virtue. This suggests a possible but very rare case.

### 8

This is as far removed from the condemned propositions as Saint Augustine is from them. Augustine taught similarly concerning works of virtue among unbelievers.

In *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 26, he left the following written:

> Even among the number of impious people who do not truly worship the true God, we read, know, or hear of certain deeds which, according to the rule of justice, we can not only not censure but also rightly and deservedly praise.

This agrees with Leo’s statement that such works “are not to be deprived of their praise.”

Augustine immediately adds:

> Yet if you examine the purpose for which they are done, scarcely any will be found that deserve the praise and defense due to justice.

By implying that works of justice without some corrupt purpose would scarcely be found, he clearly believed that most of them were correspondingly corrupted among such people. Accordingly, elsewhere Augustine, just as Saint Leo did, generally condemned the works of virtue performed by unbelievers [Col. 0546A] solely because of the corrupt purpose with which they were infected, presuming that this was generally the case except in rare instances.

## ON SERMON LXXXII

### On the day of the martyrdom of the holy apostles Peter and Paul; the age and importance of the Bucherian calendar and the discovery of its author; concerning the calendar and the testimony of Polemius Silvius

### 1

To these words of Leo in Sermon 83 on the Feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, chapter 1—

> On the day of their martyrdom—

Quesnellus appended the following note:

> On what day and in what month the apostles Peter and Paul completed their contest, and on what day their martyrdom was likewise once commemorated in the Church by solemn celebration, there are some who do not wish to determine from the present ecclesiastical calendars and usage. For, they say, there is no sufficiently ancient witness who assigns that day to the third day before the Kalends of July. We do, however, possess a very ancient author, [Col. 0546B] contemporary with Leo himself, who records that the solemnity of the apostles’ deposition was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of March. He is Polemius Silvius. John Bollandus testifies in the general preface to the *Lives of the Saints*, chapter 4, § 3, that he had the whole of Silvius’s calendar, containing many sacred and secular festivals, in his possession. A specimen of that calendar, published in the same place, teaches us that the deposition of the apostles was celebrated in the Roman Church not on June 29, as it is now, but on February 22. It reads as follows: “VIII [before the Kalends of March]: Depositio SS. Petri et Pauli”—“The deposition of the holy Peter and Paul.”

If the manuscript may be trusted, that Silvius wrote it at Rome; and in the age of our Leo, under the emperors Theodosius the Younger and Valentinian, during the consulship of Postumianus and Zeno, illustrious men—that is, in the year of Christ 448—he completed his calendar in the following year, during the consulship of Asterius, namely in the year 449.

Yet it is difficult, on the authority of a single manuscript of uncertain reliability, to go against all the calendars, martyrologies, and other such monuments of the ancient Church [Col. 0546C] that have so far come to light. Among these are the sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Great, the *Roman Order*, and the very ancient *Lectionary of Saint Jerome*. In all of them the deposition or feast of Saints Peter and Paul is assigned to the third day before the Kalends of July.

Indeed, in a very ancient parchment or martyrology, which Bollandus himself, from the papers of Heribert Rosweyde, had presented to Aegidius Bucherius, and which Bucherius inserted in his commentary on Victor’s canon, the eighth day before the Kalends of March is expressly read not as the deposition of the apostles Peter and Paul but as the feast of Peter of the Chair. The day of the apostles’ martyrdom is assigned to the third day before the Kalends of July in these words:

> III Kal. Julii, Petri in Catacumbas, et Pauli Ostiense.  
> The third day before the Kalends of July: Peter at the Catacombs, and Paul at the Ostian Way.

Certainly, since these calendars compete with one another in antiquity, far greater confidence should be placed in the one supported by all the ancient monuments of the Church and by the consensus of all the authors than in the other, which alone supplies a novel opinion and in which an error could easily have crept in.

[Col. 0546D] So far Quesnellus, and quite properly. The only point that displeases us is that he wrote that the calendars of Polemius Silvius and Bucherius compete with one another in antiquity. For the calendar of Bucherius is almost an entire century earlier than that of Silvius.

### 2

To make the age and importance of the Bucherian calendar clearer, and to establish more securely the day of the martyrdom of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, it will be useful to examine more precisely certain facts concerning its author which, as far as we have seen, others have not yet noticed.

As far as we know, two manuscripts contain this calendar. The older one, though mutilated, is preserved among the Bollandists. From it Bucherius published the calendar and four other monuments: a catalogue of the prefects of the City, a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, a fragment of the consular fasti, and a Roman secular calendar lacking four months.

The other manuscript, more recent but complete, was found in the Imperial Library. Cuspinianus had used it [Col. 0547A] in his commentaries on Cassiodorus’s *Chronicle*, and from it, before Bucherius, had published the catalogue of the prefects of the City. From the same manuscript Lambecius published the complete calendar in volume 4 of the *Imperial Library*, and our cardinal Norisius published the complete fasti in his work *On the Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*.

Most recently, John George Eccard, in volume 1 of the *Corpus of the History of the Middle Ages*, accurately reprinted from the same manuscript the four remaining monuments, apart from the calendar, in the order in which they appear in the manuscript, including the same scribal errors.

From examination of these five documents it is clear that all were written during the reign of Constantius. In the Roman secular calendar no birthday of any emperor later than Constantius is recorded. Constantius is called not “divine,” as are the other emperors already dead, but “lord,” which indicates that he was still alive.

The consular fasti and the catalogue of the prefects of the City end in the year 354. The calendar commonly called Bucherian, entitled *The Deposition [Col. 0547B] of the Martyrs and Bishops*, records the day of death and place of burial of the Roman pontiffs and ends with Julius, who died in the year 352.

Finally, the catalogue of the supreme pontiffs concludes with Liberius, Julius’s successor, in such a way that it records the day of his ordination but not the day of his death, whereas the days of death had been given for his predecessors. This indicates that Liberius was still alive.

From these observations the one and same author of all these monuments is recognized as contemporary with Liberius and Constantius. The author’s name is derived from the secular calendar: Furius Dionysius Philocalus.

Since everything sacred and secular recorded in these monuments is Roman, and since they are filled with highly specific and minute information about the city of Rome and its Church, it now appears certain that Philocalus learned and wrote these notices at Rome. This greatly strengthens the credibility of the documents.

### 3

[Col. 0547C] It must further be acknowledged, for the purposes of the present discussion, that the complete text of the Bucherian calendar is expressed in these words:

> III Kal. Jul. Petri in Catacumbas, et Pauli Ostiense Tusco et Basso conss.  
> The third day before the Kalends of July: Peter at the Catacombs and Paul at the Ostian Way, during the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.

Because of the mention of the Catacombs and of the consulship, some have suspected that this calendar indicates the day of a translation rather than the day of death.

Philocalus himself resolves this difficulty through two other short works in which the day of the martyrdom of the holy apostles Peter and Paul is marked as the third day before the Kalends of July: first, in the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, in these words:

> Passus est [S. Petrus] cum Paulo d. III kal. Jul.  
> He [Saint Peter] suffered with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July.

This appears on page 26 of Eccard’s edition. Second, in the consular fasti, page 10:

> Nerone Caesare, Vetere. Hoc cons. passi sunt Petrus et Paulus III. kal. Jul.  
> Under Nero Caesar and Vetere. During this consulship Peter and Paul suffered on the third day before the Kalends of July.

The words “he suffered” and “they suffered” clearly indicate the day of death.

[Col. 0547D] Thus, if, when the Bucherian calendar is considered separately from the other works, one could doubt—especially because of the addition of the consulship—whether the author intended to designate the day of the translation rather than the day of death, certainly comparison of that calendar with the other two works by the same author leaves no doubt that in it, just as in those works, the author intended to indicate the day of the martyrdom. It may be that a translation or some other event unknown to us also coincided with that day and was indicated by the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.

This is sufficient concerning the author and meaning of the Bucherian calendar.

### 4

That Silvius, the author of the other secular calendar, was a Gallic writer is known not only from the fact that he dedicated his short work to Bishop Eucherius, who presided over the Church of Lyons, as may be seen in Bollandus, volume 1 of the January preface, chapter 4, § 3. It is also inferred from the *Life of Saint Hilary of Arles*, in which Silvius is listed among the writers who heard Hilary preach.

For this reason, the author of the *Chronicle* published under the name of Prosper Tiro—himself likewise a Gaul—mentions in the year 439 the same writer Silvius, who had been omitted by others because he was known to Prosper in Gaul.

[Col. 0548A] Silvius’s calendar is not sacred but secular. Bollandus demonstrates in the preface to volume 1 that Silvius had other calendars from which he made excerpts, expanding some matters in his own style, altering others, and adding still others.

Among the secular material only a very few sacred feasts are incidentally recorded, as may be seen in the Bollandists, volume 6, part 2 of June, where Silvius’s complete calendar was published. Among these festivals, the feast of Saint Vincent the Martyr on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February is noteworthy, since it was not then celebrated among the Romans. Likewise noteworthy is the feast of the Maccabees on the Kalends of August, which, as we demonstrated in the note prefixed to Sermon 18 of the Appendix, had not yet begun to be celebrated at Rome in the age contemporary with Leo.

Nor does it appear anywhere from the manuscript, as Quesnellus claims, that this calendar was written at Rome. Indeed, from the calendar’s own notation of the deposition of the holy apostles on the eighth day before the Kalends of March—a notation contradicted by the three monuments of Furius Philocalus and by all the other ecclesiastical documents—it is clear that the calendar could not have been written at Rome.

[Col. 0548B] This is shown even more clearly by the ancient Roman sacramentary published under the name of Leo and to be reprinted by us in volume 2. It bears the imprint of the age of Leo and of Silvius himself, as will be shown in that volume, and presents the day of the apostles’ martyrdom as celebrated in June, with its octave in July.

Indeed, the same conclusion may be drawn from Leo himself. In Sermon 85, delivered on their octave, chapter 1, he indicates that Rome was freed from the Vandals on the day of their festival. Since that liberation fell on June 29, as we established in the note to the same sermon, we understand that the festival, and consequently the day of the martyrdom, was assigned to that same day.

It is therefore more probable that Silvius, writing in Gaul and less familiar with Roman festivals, mistakenly noted on the eighth day before the Kalends of March the deposition of Saints Peter and Paul instead of the feast of Saint Peter of the Chair, which is assigned to that day in the Philocalian calendar.

[Col. 0548C] Perhaps, when he saw that the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter was celebrated among the Gauls on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, he supposed that the Romans celebrated the same festival on that date. Consequently, he may have thought that the festival recorded on the eighth day before the Kalends of March in certain documents resembling the Bucherian calendar was not the feast of the Chair but the day of the apostles’ deposition.

Silvius’s authority in this matter therefore seems to have been completely removed—the authority that alone had caused difficulty for all critics.

## ON SERMON XC

### What Saint Leo taught concerning the two loves, of God and of the world; Quesnellus’s note examined

### 1

Leo’s celebrated text concerning the two loves, of God and of the world, is expressed in these words in Sermon 5 on the Fast of the Seventh Month, chapter 3:

> For there are two loves from which all volitions proceed, differing in their qualities according as they are divided by their sources. The rational soul, which cannot exist without love, is either a lover of God or a lover of the world.

Quesnellus appended the following [Col. 0548D] note to these words:

> Whatever is not from the love of God is from the love of the world, and therefore is sin.

Since this statement could be referred to the condemned propositions of Baius and Quesnellus—and since this text of the holy pontiff is especially brought forward by the followers of Baius and Quesnellus—it is necessary to explain more carefully what was condemned in the proscribed theses and how far Leo’s words are removed from the condemned sense.

## § I. The condemned propositions concerning the two loves are set forth, and what was proscribed in them is explained

### 2

Among the propositions of Baius, proposition 38 is as follows:

> Every love of a creature is either the vicious desire by which the world is loved, a desire forbidden by John, or that praiseworthy charity by which God is loved through the Holy Spirit poured into the heart.

And proposition 40:

> In all his actions the sinner serves the ruling desire.

Among the Quesnellian propositions, proposition 44 reads:

> There are only two loves from which all our volitions and actions arise: the love of God, which does everything for God’s sake and which God rewards; and the love by which we love ourselves and the world, which does not refer to God what ought to be referred to him, and therefore becomes evil precisely for that reason.

[Col. 0549A] And proposition 45:

> Once the love of God no longer reigns in the sinner’s heart, carnal desire must reign in him and corrupt all his actions.

Here the subject is the love that reigns in the hearts of human beings. All acts are said to arise from the reigning love in such a way that even acts of virtue performed by sinners—in whom the love not of God but of the world reigns—must be sins infected by that love. Hence there is also Baius’s proposition 35:

> Everything a sinner or a slave of sin does is sin.

### 3

[Col. 0549B] Everyone can see how false and absurd these statements are. Just as the righteous, in whom the love of God reigns, can perform—and repeatedly do perform—some acts that are slightly evil, not indeed from the love of the world that dominates them, since that love cannot coexist with habitual charity, which reigns in the righteous, but from some lesser and incidental love of the world, such as empty glory or gluttony, by which desire neither dominates them nor expels their habitual love of God;

so sinners, in whom the love of the world reigns, can produce certain good acts from some love of virtue—for example, faith, hope, mercy, prayer, and so forth. Although this is not that love of God by which the reigning love of the world would be expelled, it is nevertheless not the love of the world and cannot be referred to the love of the world.

For this reason the Council of Trent, session 6, canon 7, struck with anathema the Lutheran doctrine that all works preceding justification are sins:

> If anyone says that all works performed before justification are truly sins … let him be anathema.

What is therefore condemned is the assertion that all works which do not proceed from the charity of God reigning in the hearts of human beings belong to the love and desire of the world and are consequently sins. Yet this is what the Quesnellian note described above indicates.

### 4

[Col. 0549C] If anyone attempts to soften some of the condemned theses by claiming that they do not concern the reigning love of God but rather the love of God understood in a broader sense, so that works are referred to God, it is likewise condemned to say that all acts of virtue, however good, are sins if they are not referred to God by this love, as the final part of Quesnellian proposition 44 suggests.

For, setting aside the celebrated question among theologians concerning the relation of works to God, it is certain, according to all Catholics, that works of the moral virtues performed not only by sinners but even by unbelievers, when carried out from the motive of virtue, are good in themselves—or at least good in the sense of duty, as they say—even if they are not referred to God.

For even those who defend more rigorously the obligation of referring works to God agree that this omission does not corrupt the good work in itself, but contaminates the person who omits the reference in some other respect.

### 5

[Col. 0549D] Certainly Saint Leo is very far removed from both corrupt senses. In Sermon 48 on the tenth day of Lent, chapter 3, he admits that among Christian sinners, in whom the love of the world dominates, both the true faith and other works of the moral virtues can be found. He testifies only that, because of the lack of charity, at least habitual charity, they are deprived of eternal fruit:

> Although it is a great thing to possess a sound and true faith, and although the curbing of the appetite, gentleness of meekness, and purity of chastity deserve much praise, all the virtues are nevertheless naked without charity, nor can what is not produced as the offspring of love be called fruitful in any excellence of character.

Moreover, in Sermon 44, the seventh sermon on Lent, chapter 3, speaking of works of mercy that do not proceed from the source of faith and are consequently performed even by unbelievers—who, since they do not know God, referred nothing to him—he asserted that such works are not to be deprived of their praise and are therefore good if they are produced from the motive of compassion without any corrupt purpose intermixed.

He taught only that they are almost sins because he presumed that unbelievers generally performed them not from the motive of virtue but from self-love, empty glory, or some other corrupt purpose. On this subject see the observation on Sermon 79.

[Col. 0550A] Thus we see how far Leo’s mind and teaching are removed from the senses of the condemned propositions. Unless one wishes to invent a contradiction between Leo and himself, it cannot be said that the testimony of the present Sermon 90 favors the proscribed theses.

## 501 — § II. What is the proper meaning of Leo’s text in Sermon 90

### 6

There are certainly some who think that by “the love of God” the holy pontiff meant, in a broad sense, any love of virtue, and by “the love of the world” any love of vice.

Just as every love of vice can properly be referred to the love of the world, insofar as the world loves and fosters vices, so, in a broad sense, the love of every virtue can be referred to the love of God, insofar as God loves and commands all virtues.

Indeed, since every virtue is justice and truth, as it is frequently called in Sacred Scripture, and since God is justice and truth, one may say in a broad sense that the person loves God who loves the virtues from the proper motive of those virtues, with no corrupt desire intermixed.

That the holy pontiff sometimes used “love of God” in this broad sense for the love of any virtue may be inferred from the words in Sermon 95, chapter 6:

> [Col. 0550B] To love God is nothing other than to love justice.

Accordingly, anyone who loves any virtue, since he loves justice, also loves God according to this principle of Leo’s.

Whoever performs an act of virtue from the motive of virtue must love the virtue itself. In this hypothesis of the twofold love, of God and of the world, to one or the other of which all acts of the will must be referred, it is undoubtedly preferable to refer acts of the moral virtues performed from the pure motive of virtue to the love of God understood broadly than to the love of the world.

[Col. 0550C] The way in which they can at least broadly be reduced to the love of God can be explained and understood from the reason just given. But if they are referred to the love of the world—which, being placed in the evil one, is a lover and promoter of vices, not virtues—and if they are referred to it in such a way that someone who loves and practices the virtues from the motive of virtue must be said to love and practice them from the love of the world, no sane person will understand such a claim.

7. But one thing is for this hypothesis to be absent from the condemned propositions, and another is for Leo’s words, which we are now examining, to be understood in this sense. You will readily perceive what meaning properly lies in those same words if you first make two observations.

First, the holy pontiff writes that there are two loves from which all wills proceed, not that all acts of the will proceed from them; and therefore he is speaking of the wills themselves, not of the individual acts of the will. Accordingly, when he declares that these wills differ in their qualities in the same way as they are divided according to their sources, or loves, he indicates that the wills are different—that is, good or evil—insofar as they differ from and are divided among themselves by different loves.

Second, it is clear that the two loves 502 mentioned here are not to be understood as every possible love of God or of the world, but as the love reigning in a person’s will, since only of such a love can it be affirmed that a person is constituted either a lover of God, that is, a just person, or a lover of the world, that is, a sinner. Hence, also, at the beginning of the following chapter [Col. 0550D] the Author said: “This affection”—that is, the affection of God—“by which earthly love is excluded”; and this is true of a dominant love of God. The point is confirmed much more clearly by what he immediately added: “And therefore one must cling inseparably to eternal goods”—which signifies a dominant love of the ultimate end—“but use temporal things in passing, neither enjoying nor clinging to them as to an ultimate end.”

8. With these points established, the Author’s clear and genuine meaning is as follows. There are two loves from which all wills proceed, differing in their qualities of goodness or wickedness in the same way as they are divided according to their sources. Those wills, of course, are affected by the love of God to such an extent that they love God above all things, and consequently a person is a lover of God, or is in the charity of God: these wills are good. Those, however, are evil in which love of the world so dominates that, with the charity of God excluded, the person is constituted a lover of the world.

Since the rational mind cannot exist without one side or the other [Col. 0551A] prevailing through love, a person is therefore either a lover of God or a lover of the world. All wills, accordingly, whether good or evil, differ in their qualities in the same way as they are divided according to their sources. The obvious sense of the words concerns all wills, good or evil according to their predominant love.

Who, then, does not see how improperly his words are dragged over to all acts of the will, individually and collectively—as though Leo had taught that each and every act proceeds from one or the other of those loves, so that whatever acts do not proceed from the love of God proceed from the love of the world and are therefore sins, as Quesnel’s Postilla suggests? On this interpretation, the very works of virtue that the holy pontiff professed to be not evil but good in sinners, and even in unbelievers, would have to be accused as sins.

§ III. Another passage of Quesnel’s Postilla on the same Sermon 90 examined

9. In this same sermon, chapter 3, St. Leo writes: “That which charms us by the appearance, abundance, and variety [of creatures] is not easily avoided unless, in that visible [Col. 0551B] beauty, the Creator is loved rather than the creature.” Quesnel noted in the margin against these words: “Only the love of God withdraws one from the love of the creature.”

Do you see, from the comparison, the less accurate interpreter? “It is not easily avoided,” says Leo. For those who stop at the love of creatures, and at their beauty, abundance, and variety [Col. 0552A], and do not love God rather than the creatures, do not easily turn away from their 503 perverse allurements and very easily fall into sin. This is the whole meaning of Leo’s statement.

But that the love of God, without which one does not easily withdraw from such charms and from an illicit love of creatures, is the sole force that draws one away from this forbidden affection—this is affirmed not by Leo but by Quesnel. Yet it is certain that people are restrained from sins, although not always so easily, also by fear—especially by fear of hell and of punishments, which produces sorrow for sins. That this fear, conceived through God’s gift and the impulse of the Holy Spirit, not only restrains the hand from an illicit act but also excludes the very will to sin, is sufficiently clearly gathered from the Council of Trent, session 14, 504 chapter 4. This fear of hell, into which one falls not so much through the act as through a depraved affection, must of itself impel and move a person to exclude both the act and every affection for sin, just as this is necessary in order to escape hell.

This must be pointed out lest, among Quesnel’s other propositions, proposition 61—condemned in the constitution *Unigenitus*—should perhaps insinuate itself: “Fear restrains only the hand, but the heart remains enslaved to sin for as long as it is not led by the love of righteousness.” But it is not our task to discuss this matter here; our sole purpose has been to show that Leo’s statement is alien to Quesnel’s interpretation. [Col. 0552B]

# THE SECOND PART OF THE GENUINE WORKS OF ST. LEO THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF, CONTAINING THE LETTERS OF THE HOLY FATHER

[Col. 0551]

## PREFACE

### On the Manuscript Codices Used in Correcting the Letters

## § I. The Classification of the Manuscript Collections Containing Leo’s Letters

1. Three kinds of codices in which Leo’s letters are contained must be distinguished. The first kind consists of general collections of canons and constitutions of the Roman pontiffs, in which several complete letters of Leo were copied. The second consists of particular collections, either of certain Churches or of Leo’s letters alone, which, having long ago been assembled from ancient or even original exemplars, display the most ancient origin. The third consists of particular collections of the letters of St. Leo, but more recent ones, which for the most part derive from collections of the first kind.

2. Just as there is no collection contemporary or nearly contemporary with Leo containing all his sermons, as we observed in the preface to the *Sermons*, so we are completely certain that no collection contemporary or nearly contemporary with him was made of all his letters. Consequently, in preparing an edition of Leo one may neither find nor hope for a codex containing all his letters. In former times they were not all gathered into a single body, or *register*, as it is called, in the way that the letters of St. Gregory the Great were.

At the beginning, indeed, ancient Roman custom suggests that all of them were placed and most carefully preserved in the chests, or archive, of the apostolic see among the other constitutions of the pontiffs. On this subject one may consult P. Coustant’s preface to the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 44 and following. The author of the *Roman Pontifical*, commonly known by the name of Anastasius the Librarian [Col. 0553], who wrote Leo’s life later in the eighth century, reports the following about his letters:

“The same most blessed Leo, archbishop, sent many letters concerning the faith, which are today kept deposited in the archive of the Roman Church. By his letters he frequently confirmed the Council of Chalcedon. He sent twelve letters to the Emperor Marcian, thirteen letters to the Emperor Leo, nine letters to Bishop Flavian, and eighteen letters to the bishops throughout the East, through which he confirmed the faith of the council.”

You see that even at this time the apostolic archive is cited, in which Leo’s letters were preserved. Although only the letters written for the Catholic faith against the Eutychian heresy are mentioned, we nevertheless know that more letters than those that have reached us then existed in that archive. For the extant letters to the Emperor Leo do not number thirteen, nor do those to Flavian number nine.

3. But when general collections of the canons and letters of the Roman pontiffs, composed long ago by private individuals for private use, began to spread and gain authority to such an extent that the same Roman bishops frequently took the letters of their predecessors not from the apostolic archives but from these collections, then it came about that the original copies of those letters, which had been in the apostolic archive, were gradually neglected and were lost through the changes of time.

Consequently, those ancient general collections are the oldest and most celebrated sources from which we have received the constitutions of the earlier pontiffs. Indeed, no letters of certain Roman bishops have reached us except those preserved in collections of this kind. These collections, and the manuscript codices that contain them, will be treated more fully in the treatise that you will find inserted in the third volume.

4. Since we are now going to deal only with Leo’s letters, we must examine only those things in the same collections that relate to those letters. For the present, we give this preliminary warning: it follows from what has been said that these ancient general collections must be regarded as original sources to which the edition of the letters must be referred.

Among the sources that are likewise to be regarded as original are certain ancient particular collections, either of particular Churches or of Leo’s letters. Since these were not taken from the aforesaid general collections, they arose from Leo’s original exemplars.

5. Collections that present only Leo’s letters, while clearly having taken at least the greater part of them from earlier collections, are recognized as later. To that extent they cannot be called original, nor are they to be preferred to the older collections from which they were derived.

It was nevertheless useful to collate their codices as well. For those that derived from more carefully corrected manuscripts of the ancient collections repeatedly supplied better readings and corrections not to be despised. Some of them also contain letters which, since they are not found in the ancient, known collections, must have been taken from other wholly unknown ancient collections. In this respect, therefore, they must be regarded as original.

This general classification of the collections had to be given first, so that not all those that will presently be listed might be valued equally, and so that the original and ancient might be distinguished from the more recent and derivative. We have found this knowledge especially necessary for the proper use of them in restoring the letters, as well as for many other matters that will be explained in their proper places.

6. The manuscript collections of the letters of St. Leo that are still known to us number twenty-four. Of these, thirteen belong to the ancient general collections, six to the ancient particular collections, and five are more recent particular collections of the same pontiff.

Just as these individual collections, differing among themselves in the number and order of their letters and in other characteristics, reveal different origins, so, in general, all the codices of each collection agree so closely in their readings that—as we observed concerning the same sermons in the preface to the *Sermons*—it is usually superfluous to consult several of them. Greater benefit is obtained by examining two or three manuscript books from different collections than by going through very many from a single collection.

We shall now discuss the individual collections, insofar as they concern Leo’s letters. For the other matters relating to a thorough knowledge of the general collections, we refer the reader to the treatise that we shall insert in the third volume.

## § II. On the Vatican Manuscript of the First Collection of the Queen of Sweden

7. The first general collection, which we believe to be the most ancient of all and hitherto unknown, is found in the Vatican Queen of Sweden codex 1997. It presents eight letters of Leo:

I. To Rusticus, letter 167 in our edition;  
II. To the bishops of Mauretania, letter 12;  
III. To Flavian, letter 28;  
IV. To Turibius, letter 15;  
V. To the Sicilians, letter 16;  
VI. To Nicetas, letter 159;  
VII. To the bishop of Aquileia, letter 1;  
VIII. To Septimus, letter 2.

## § III. On the Second Collection

8. To this Vatican Queen collection, in which the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs ends with Hormisdas, we append another collection whose catalogue ends with Vigilius. It is contained in a manuscript from Corbie, of venerable antiquity, in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés of the Benedictine Fathers of Paris; hence Coustant calls it the Corbie collection.

Although we have obtained no codex of this collection, since Quesnel used it and identifies the aforesaid codex whenever, either in the variants or in the notes, he cites the Corbie manuscript—as is clear from the *Catalogue of Manuscripts* that he himself described—we could not omit it, especially since we too shall repeatedly mention it on the basis of Quesnel.

Several letters of Leo are found in it. Since P. Coustant, who discusses this very important collection at greater length in the preface to the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 61, does not provide a distinct catalogue of these letters, we have been unable to ascertain their exact number and order [Col. 0555]. Nevertheless, from what are indicated both by Coustant and by Quesnel, it is certain that the following letters are contained in that manuscript. Since the order of the codex is lacking, we cite them according to the sequence of our edition:

I. To the Campanians, letter 4;  
II. To the Italians, letter 7;  
III. To the people of Vienne, letter 10;  
IV. To Anastasius, letter 14;  
V. To Turibius, letter 15;  
VI. Flavian’s letter to Leo, letter 22;  
VII. To Flavian, letter 28;  
VIII. To Theodosius, letter 29;  
IX. To Pulcheria, letter 31;  
X. To Julian, letter 35;  
XI. To the people of Constantinople, letter 59;  
XII. To Ravennius and the Gauls, letter 103;  
XIII. To Juvenal, letter 139;  
XIV. To the Emperor Leo, letter 165.

In the first note to letter X, *To the Bishops of the Province of Vienne*, Quesnel cites the Thuaneus codex, which appears to belong to this collection. Of it he says: “It is so similar to the Corbie manuscript that I believe it was copied from it.” He usually calls it the first Thuaneus in the *Postilla* and notes, and repeatedly cites it together with the Corbie manuscript, because the two have similar readings.

## § IV. On the Manuscripts of the Third Collection

9. In third place we put another unknown but very ancient and distinguished collection, which exists in two extremely old codices, Barberini 2888 and Vatican 1342. It comprises sixteen letters of Leo in the following order:

I. To Anastasius, letter 14;  
II. To Rusticus, letter 167;  
III. To the Sicilians, letter 16;  
IV. To the bishop of Aquileia, letter 1;  
V. To the Moors, letter 12;  
VI. To Nicetas, letter 159;  
VII. To Dioscorus, letter 9;  
VIII. To Juvenal, letter 139;  
IX. To the Emperor Leo, letter 145;  
X. To Maximus, letter 119;  
XI. To Flavian, letter 23;  
XII. Flavian’s letter to Leo, letter 22;  
XIII. To Eutyches, letter 20;  
XIV. To Flavian, letter 28;  
XV. To the Emperor Leo, letter 165;  
XVI. To Anatolius of Constantinople, letter 80.

## § V. On the Codices of the Fourth Collection

10. The fourth collection is found in an ancient codex of the chapter of Lucca. We owe its most accurate description to P. Giovanni Domenico Mansi, in a treatise written on the celebrated codex of the age of Charlemagne, which you will read published in volume XLV of P. Calogera’s *Opuscula*.

The same collection also exists in the manuscript formerly Colbertine 784, which is highly commended by Antelmius and Pagius, as well as by P. Coustant, who recognized this collection as Italian and described it more fully in the frequently cited preface, no. 89.

It provided only four letters of Leo, whose variants from the Lucca codex the aforementioned P. Mansi kindly sent to us. The letters are copied in the following order:

I. To Rusticus, letter 167;  
II. To the Moors, letter 12;  
III. To the bishop of Aquileia, letter 1;  
IV. To Septimus, letter 2.

## § VI. On the Fifth Collection, the Quesnellian Collection, and Its Codices

11. We call the fifth collection Quesnellian, for it is the one Quesnel published under the title improperly prefixed by him: *Book of Canons and Constitutions of the Roman Church*.

This collection closes with thirty-two letters of Leo, in the following order:

I. To the Emperor Leo, letter 165 of our edition;  
II. To Juvenal of Jerusalem, letter 139;  
III. To Flavian of Constantinople, letter 28;  
IV. To Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii in Gaul, letter 108;  
V. To Turbius (so), that is, Turibius of Asturia, letter 15;  
VI. To Rusticus of Narbonne, letter 167;  
VII. To Anastasius of Thessalonica, letter 14;  
VIII. To Nicetas of Aquileia, letter 159;  
IX. To Januarius of Aquileia, letter 18;  
X. To the bishops of Campania, Picenum, and Tuscia, letter 4;  
XI. To the bishops of Italy, letter 7;  
XII. To the bishops of Sicily, letter 16;  
XIII. To the Empress Pulcheria, letter 31;  
XIV. To the people of Constantinople, letter 59;  
XV. To the Palestinians, letter 124;  
XVI. To the bishop of Aquileia, letter 1;  
XVII. To Septimus, bishop of Altinum, letter 2;  
XVIII. To the bishops of Mauretania, letter 12;  
XIX. To the Council of Ephesus, letter 33;  
XX. To the Emperor Theodosius, letter 44;  
XXI. To the Empress Pulcheria, letter 45;  
XXII. To Julian, bishop of Cos, letter 25;  
XXIII. To the Emperor Theodosius, letter 29;  
XXIV. To the Emperor Marcian, letter 104;  
XXV. To Anatolius of Constantinople, letter 106;  
XXVI. To the Council of Chalcedon, letter 114;  
XXVII. To Anatolius of Constantinople, letter 155;  
XXVIII. To the Emperor Leo, letter 162;  
XXIX. To Anatolius, letter 163;  
XXX. To the same, letter 135;  
XXXI. To the Council of Chalcedon, letter 93;  
XXXII. To Dorus of Benevento, letter 19.

In several codices these are preceded by three other letters addressed to Leo, which will be published among Leo’s letters:

I. Of Eusebius and the Council of Milan, letter 97 in our edition;  
II. Of Ravennius and the other bishops of Gaul, letter 99;  
III. Finally, of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranius, bishops of Gaul, letter 68.

12. Several highly distinguished codices of this collection are sufficiently well known in the libraries of Gaul. Although Quesnel used an Oxford manuscript in publishing this collection, a much more recent and fairly corrupt one, in correcting Leo’s letters he chiefly employed two other notable Gallic codices of the same collection: namely, the Thuaneus, later Colbertine 932, which has most recently passed into the Royal Library, and the Trecopithoeanus, kept in the library of the Fathers of the Oratory at Troyes.

Thus, from Quesnel’s notes, the readings of this collection could have been collected with sufficient security. But in order that some special feature from a new and distinguished manuscript of this collection might be added to this edition, since we were unable to find any exemplar in Rome or elsewhere in Italy, we extended our diligence into Germany and discovered the most ancient exemplar of the Imperial Library of Vienna, no. 39. We procured a most careful collation of it, useful for correcting several passages.

Another ancient codex of the same Imperial Library, somewhat more recent than the preceding one, numbered 42, presents this same collection with certain inserted additions. For in Leo it includes twenty additional letters from the Hispanic, or Isidorian, collection, which will be discussed below in nos. 17 and 21.

Quesnel himself indicated in the general preface that the Thuaneus codex had also received several additions. Consult our note 9 in that preface. (Col. 41, n. a.)

13. Before proceeding further, it must be observed here that four of the five collections mentioned [Col. 0557], those that present Leo’s letter 167 to Rusticus, copy it together with Rusticus’s Questions, which are necessary for properly understanding the holy pontiff’s replies.

Accordingly, these collections are to be preferred in our edition to the collection of Dionysius, who, following his own method, supplied headings for the Questions and consequently published that letter neither in its entirety nor in the form in which it was written by Leo together with the Questions.

We also recognize from this that the origin of these collections cannot be traced to Dionysius, but must be sought in older and more authentic exemplars.

## § VII. On the Sixth Collection, That of Dionysius Exiguus, and on the Collection of Cresconius

14. The sixth collection is the Dionysian collection. In it—as it was compiled by Dionysius Exiguus around the time of Hormisdas—only seven letters of Leo are listed, namely:

I. To the Campanians, letter 4 of our edition;  
II. To the Italians, letter 7;  
III. To the Sicilians, letter 16;  
IV. To Januarius of Aquileia, letter 18;  
V. To Rusticus of Narbonne, letter 167;  
VI. To Anastasius of Thessalonica, letter 14;  
VII. To Nicetas of Aquileia, letter 159.

Another letter of Leo to the bishops of Mauretania, which is read in the commonly circulated copies of Dionysius, must be attributed to later additions, as we shall see in its proper place.

Manuscript books of this collection that are free from inserted additions are so rare that only two have so far been identified: the Vatican and the Royal Parisian. Of these, the Vatican 5845 is especially commended, and we have carefully collated it.

15. Since the African Cresconius used manuscripts of the pure Dionysian collection, and inserted the whole collection of Dionysius into his own work, distributed under specific headings, Cresconian codices may be regarded as pure Dionysian codices.

We have seen several in Rome: Vallicellian XVIII, Vatican 1347, Vatican Queen 849, and Vatican Palatine 579. But we chiefly collated manuscript 60 of the chapter of Verona, a book written in the eighth century in papyrus script.

## § VIII. On the Manuscripts of the Seventh, Hadrianic Collection

16. The same collection of Dionysius, with several additions inserted in their proper places, constitutes a seventh collection that must in no way be separated from the Dionysian. It is called Dionysio-Hadrianic, or Hadrianic, not because these additions were added to or inserted into Dionysius under Hadrian I, but because this pontiff sent the collection to King Charles.

Most manuscript codices commonly believed to be Dionysian, and even the printed editions, present this Dionysio-Hadrianic collection. We examined many manuscripts in Rome, among which the following older copies, written in the ninth or tenth century, deserve mention: Vatican 4969, Vatican Palatine 578, Vatican Queen 1021 and 1043, as well as Vatican 1337, which the Roman correctors call the *Book of Canons* in the edition of Gratian, and two Vallicellian codices, A. S. and XVIII.

Among the additions to this collection, only one was added to the seven letters of Leo copied by Dionysius, namely letter 12, to the bishops of Mauretania.

Among the editions, we mention the Paris edition of 1661 by Voellus and Justellus, which we shall repeatedly cite. Although they resolved to publish the pure Dionysian collection with the additions separated, since they had examined no Dionysian codex, they were unable to distinguish and separate all the additions, especially those concerning Leo.

## § IX. On the Eighth Collection

17. We found all these additions separated from the pure Dionysian collection and copied after Dionysius in the ancient Vatican manuscript 5845 mentioned above. To these, much larger additions are appended in the same codex. We found them attached to the Hadrianic collection in the Vallicellian A. S. codex, Vatican 1353, and in one codex of the chapter of Vercelli.

These additions may be regarded as a supplement to the Dionysian or Hadrianic collections. For a later author, gathering from other sources documents lacking in Dionysius, added them to the Dionysian collection.

Since these additions were never inserted into the collections of Dionysius or Hadrian, they are rightly regarded as a separate collection, which we shall call the eighth collection.

In these additions fifteen letters of Leo are presented:

I. To Dioscorus, letter 9 of our edition;  
II. To Turibius, letter 15;  
III. To the bishop of Aquileia, letter 1;  
IV. To Septimus, bishop of Altinum, letter 2;  
V. To Theodore, letter 108;  
VI. To the Sicilians, letter 17;  
VII. To Eutyches, letter 20;  
VIII. To Flavian, letter 23;  
IX. Flavian’s letter to Leo, letter 22;  
X. To Flavian, letter 28;  
XI. To Juvenal, letter 139;  
XII. To Maximus, letter 179;  
XIII. To Anatolius, letter 80;  
XIV. To the Emperor Leo, letter 145;  
XV. To the same emperor, letter 165.

## § X. On the Ninth, Hispanic Collection

18. We assign ninth place to the Hispanic collection, which before Coustant was not sufficiently well known. Its author took the letters recited by Dionysius, together with the same headings.

In one letter to Rusticus he added a heading and chapter that are absent from Dionysius, as will be said in its proper place. In addition to the seven letters of Leo taken from the Dionysian collection, he added thirty other letters of Leo, one of Peter Chrysologus to Eutyches, and another of Flavian to Leo; these will have to be included in the edition.

Thus, all the letters together number thirty-nine, arranged in this series:

I. To Eutyches, letter 20 of our edition;  
II. To Flavian, letter 23;  
III. Flavian’s letter to Leo, letter 22;  
IV. Leo’s letter to Flavian, letter 28;  
V. Peter of Ravenna’s letter to Eutyches, letter 25;  
VI. Leo’s letter to the Council of Ephesus, letter 33;  
VII. To Theodosius, letter 44;  
VIII. To Pulcheria, letter 45;  
IX. To the same, letter 60;  
X. To Martin and Faustus, letter 61;  
XI. To the Emperor Theodosius, letter 69;  
XII. To Pulcheria, letter 70;  
XIII. To Faustus, Martin, and the others, letter 71;  
XIV. To Pulcheria, letter 79;  
XV. To Anatolius, letter 80;  
XVI. To Marcian, letter 82;  
XVII. To the same emperor, letter 83;  
XVIII. To Anatolius [Col. 0559], letter 85;  
XIX. To Marcian, letter 90;  
XX. To the Council of Chalcedon, letter 93;  
XXI. To Marcian, letter 104;  
XXII. To Anatolius, letter 106;  
XXIII. To Marcian, letter 115;  
XXIV. To the same, letter 130;  
XXV. To the same, letter 134;  
XXVI. To the Emperor Leo, letter 165;  
XXVII. To Turibius of Asturia, letter 15;  
XXVIII. To the Italians, letter 7;  
XXIX. To the Sicilians, letter 16;  
XXX. To the bishops throughout Campania, etc., letter 4;  
XXXI. To Januarius, letter 18;  
XXXII. To Rusticus, letter 167;  
XXXIII. To Anastasius, letter 41;  
XXXIV. To Nicetas, letter 159;  
XXXV. To the Africans, letter 12;  
XXXVI. To Theodore, letter 108;  
XXXVII. To Leo—or Neon—of Ravenna, letter 166;  
XXXVIII. To Dioscorus, letter 9;  
XXXIX. To the Campanians, letter 168.

19. It must be noted here that in the catalogue of the decrees of the Roman pontiffs prefixed to this collection, both in the codices we have seen and in Coustant, three letters of Leo to Marcian are counted as numbers 51, 52, and 53, of which forty headings pertain to Leo.

But in the actual body of the collection, in all the manuscripts, and even in Isidore, who copied the entire Hispanic collection, only two letters to Marcian are found in that place. Consequently, there are only thirty-nine letters altogether.

It is also noteworthy that letter 12 to the African, or Moorish, bishops is presented in this collection in an abridged form and differs from the version read in the seventh, Hadrianic collection. This clearly shows that the author of the Hispanic collection possessed a pure Dionysian codex in which this letter was lacking. Otherwise he would have copied it, no less than the other seven letters of Leo, from his Dionysian codex into the same form in which it was added to Dionysius in the Hadrianic collection.

20. This collection presents a better order than the Dionysian collection. Just as its author, following Dionysius, retained Dionysius’s headings in the letters he took from him, so in the others that he added he prefixed headings according to the same method; we shall give these in their proper places.

The codices of this collection are very rare. We shall cite two that we carefully collated: Vatican 1341 and the Imperial Vienna codex 41, formerly 281, both dating approximately from the ninth century. The former derived from Gallic exemplars, while the latter derived from purer Hispanic exemplars. More will be said about it in the treatise on the ancient collections and collectors of canons in the third volume.

Here it is especially important to state in advance that the Vienna codex presents erroneous readings in a considerable number of places which, emended in the Vatican manuscript, generally yield a suitable sense. From the collation of other codices that agree in presenting Leo’s original reading, we have discovered that the error of the Vienna manuscript more often approaches that reading, while the reading of the Vatican manuscript departs from it to a much greater extent, so that an arbitrary correction becomes evident.

It is therefore clear that the first diligent copyist who transcribed this collection from some Hispanic but corrupt codex used considerable freedom in correcting its errors. Hence we could not place much confidence in these corrections, although they often present an excellent sense.

The exemplars of the Hispanic collection that we call Gallic are derived from a codex corrected in the same way, such as Vatican 1341 and others like it, which we shall cite in the aforementioned treatise.

Since the author of the collection called Isidorian took Leo’s letters from a Gallic exemplar of the Hispanic collection, and since the authors of later collections in turn derived the same letters from Isidore, as we shall note below, we consequently find in all of them nearly the same readings as in Vatican Hispanic 1341.

From this observation it is easy to infer how little value should be assigned to the readings of all these codices when they agree with the Hispanic Vatican manuscript but disagree with the Vienna manuscript.

For this reason it was not useless to record in the annotations, in several places, the corrupt readings of the Hispanic Vienna manuscript and to note the variants of the Vatican manuscript, so that the corrections might be exposed which, by comparison with the genuine text itself, are recognized as arbitrary. Other benefits of this diligence will become clear from the treatise mentioned above.

## § XI. On the Tenth, Isidorian Collection

21. After the Hispanic collection, the collection of Isidore Mercator would not, with respect to Leo’s letters, require separate mention. A pure Isidorian codex contains the same number of Leo’s letters, neither more nor fewer, and these were transferred into it from the Hispanic collection without any fabrication or addition. This is evident from Vatican 630, dating approximately from the ninth century, which we carefully collated, and from Vatican 631, dating approximately from the thirteenth century.

The other codices, because they admit additional material concerning Leo, although in most other respects they are Isidorian, do not represent a pure Isidore in Leo’s letters, as we shall see shortly. Thus the collection published by Merlin is improperly regarded as purely Isidorian.

We further discovered that nearly the same readings, generally with the same errors, are found in Vatican 1341 of the Hispanic collection and in Vatican 630 of the pure Isidorian collection, so that one appears to have been copied from the other; the two collections agree so closely in their treatment of Leo.

Since, however, the Hispanic collection is little known, whereas the Isidorian collection, as the better-known one, is regularly cited, and since Quesnel cites several codices of the Isidorian collection, it too must be designated separately by us. For this reason it is necessary to call it here the tenth collection.

## § XII. On the Eleventh Collection

22. Certain collections that derive from the Isidorian collection present, in their treatment of Leo, several letters that are absent from both Isidore and the Hispanic collection. They therefore reveal another origin and may accordingly be listed, with respect to Leo, as collections distinct from the Isidorian.

The eleventh collection is therefore found in two Isidorian manuscripts: namely, Vatican Ottobonianus 93, of the ninth or tenth century, which, although mutilated at the end, does not present all the letters [Col. 0561] proper to this collection; nevertheless, we gathered the complete number from another manuscript, Vatican 3791, of the eleventh century.

In addition to the thirty-nine letters copied from Isidore’s collection, with the order somewhat changed, another eighteen letters are added. Thus there are fifty-seven letters in all. In this number we include letter 28 to Flavian, which is recited twice in this collection from two sources.

The following sixteen letters precede the Isidorian letters:

I. To Theodoret, letter 120;  
II. Of Eusebius and the Council of Milan to Leo, letter 97;  
III. Of Ravennius and the other bishops of Gaul to Leo, letter 99;  
IV. Leo’s letter to Juvenal, letter 139;  
V. To Flavian of Constantinople, letter 28, taken from the reading that we found in the most ancient *Homiliaries*, and differing from the Isidorian reading, according to which this letter is listed again among the Isidorian letters;  
VI. To Pulcheria, letter 31;  
VII. To the clergy of Constantinople, letter 59;  
VIII. To the Palestinians, letter 124;  
IX. To the bishop of Aquileia, letter 1;  
X. To Julian, letter 35;  
XI. To Theodosius, letter 29;  
XII. To the Council of Chalcedon, letter 114;  
XIII. To Anatolius, letter 155;  
XIV. To the Emperor Leo, letter 162;  
XV. To Anatolius, letter 163;  
XVI. To the same, letter 135.

The thirty-nine letters of Isidore’s edition follow. Among them is inserted letter 19 of our edition, to Dorus of Benevento, which is absent from Isidore.

It is worthy of note that the letter to the African Moors, which is listed among the Isidorian letters, is not presented here from the abridged edition of Isidore, but from the Hadrianic collection. What is additionally read in Isidore is then appended to it as if it were an appendix. This method of editing appears to have passed from this source into several later collections.

Finally, a letter is presented that, so far as we know, is here attributed to Leo for the first time: a letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul. Thus the ancient origin of this attribution is recognized. Since the letter is absent from the pure Isidorian collection, Blondel and several others wrongly believed it to have been fabricated by Isidore.

23. The antiquity of this collection is proved not only by Vatican Ottobonianus 93, of the ninth or tenth century, as we have said, but much more by Hincmar, who, in *Opusculum* I, chapter 5, p. 23 of the Paris edition of Jean Cordes, mentions the letter to the Moors in summary form and reports in it, in order, the cases of Lupicinus, then Donatus, then Maximus, and finally Aggarus and Tiberianus.

Since this order is found in no other more ancient collection, Hincmar appears to have used this eleventh collection, and consequently it had already come into circulation in Hincmar’s time.

24. Two other manuscript books also seem to belong to this collection, although they have nothing to do with Isidore: namely, Barberini 57, cited by Quesnel in the *Catalogue of Manuscripts* prefixed to the second edition, and Vatican 4902.

Barberini 57, written approximately in the twelfth century, although mutilated at the end, nevertheless presents twenty-three letters of Leo in the order in which it breaks off, showing them to have been taken from the eleventh collection. Vatican 4902, much later in date but more complete, derives from a similar source.

## § XIII. On the Twelfth Collection, Published by Merlin; Also on the Sichardian Collection
### 25.

The additions appended to Isidore are fuller in the Vatican manuscript 1340; we found them copied as a separate volume in codex Venice, Biblioteca Marciana 169. These additions, which may be regarded as the twelfth collection, extend down to the Council of Reims in the year 1148. From this fact one may infer the age of the compiler, and perhaps even his nationality: for the other Gallican documents included in these additions, especially in the material concerning Leo, reveal the compiler as a Gaul. There are ninety-nine letters of Leo, or letters written to Leo; consequently this collection—if the eighteenth is excepted—is the richest of all. From it not only did several previously unknown letters first emerge, later to be found only in the rarest manuscripts, but some still survive that could be found in no manuscript of any other collection.

From this its compiler’s exceptional diligence, and the distinct origin of this collection from the others, become clear. The collection contains thirty-nine letters of Isidore’s tenth collection—including the abridged letter to the African bishops—and sixteen other letters added in the preceding collection, omitting Eusebius of Milan’s letter 97 and without repeating letter 28 to Flavian. The newly added letters are forty-four, whose catalogue we append here:

I, to Theodosius, letter 24;  
II, to the bishops of Gaul, letter 102;  
III, to Marcian, letter 121;  
IV, to Eudocia—read “Julian”—letter 122;  
V, to Septimus, bishop of Altinum, letter 2;  
VI, to the people of Vienne, letter 10;  
VII, to Ravennius, letter 41;  
VIII, to Pulcheria, letter 95;  
IX, to Marcian, letter 94;  
X, to Pulcheria, letter 105;  
XI, to Julian of Cos, letter 113;  
XII, to Marcian, letter 111;  
XIII, to Pulcheria, letter 112;  
XIV, to Julian, letter 118;  
XV, to Eudoxia, letter 123;  
XVI, to Julian, letter 125;  
XVII, to the same Julian, letter 127;  
XVIII, of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranius to Leo, letter 68;  
XIX, of Leo, Victorius, and Eustochius to the bishops and priests within the Third Province, to be published in the appendix;  
XX, of Pope Leo to Ravennius and the other bishops of Gaul, letter 103;  
XXI, to the Gauls and Spaniards, letter 138;  
XXII, to Theodosius, letter 54;  
XXIII, to Julian, letter 34;  
XXIV, to Flavian, letter 36;  
XXV, to Theodosius, letter 37;  
XXVI, to Flavian, letter 38;  
XXVII, to the same, letter 39;  
XXVIII, to the people of Constantinople, letter 50;  
XXIX, to Anastasius, letter 47;  
XXX, to Flavian, letter 49;  
XXXI, to Julian, letter 48;  
XXXII, to the Constantinopolitan archimandrites, letter 51;  
XXXIII, to Marcian, letter 74;  
XXXIV, to the same, letter 78;  
XXXV, to Julian, letter 81;  
XXXVI, to Pulcheria, letter 45;  
XXXVII, to Anatolius, letter 87;  
XXXVIII, to Marcian, letter 89;  
XXXIX, to Pulcheria, letter 116;  
XL, to Maximus, letter 119;  
XLI, to Leo Augustus, letter 145;  
XLII, to the same, letter 148;  
XLIII, to the same, letter 156;  
XLIV, to Pulcheria, letter 30.

### 26.

Most of these letters are found in none of the collections already described. Although some were later discovered in certain rare manuscripts, and others in manuscripts of collection 24, from which the author appears to have drawn, he nevertheless took five letters of Leo, not yet exhibited in any other collection, from some unknown manuscript [Col. 0563]: namely, letter 39 to Flavian, 47 to Anastasius, 48 to Julian, 74 to Marcian, and 138 to the Gauls and Spaniards.

Moreover, since this compiler added to his collection whatever he found in his manuscripts inscribed with Leo’s name, he incorrectly inserted the letter of Leo, Victorius, and Eustochius to the bishops and priests situated within the Third Province, failing to notice that this Leo was the bishop of Bourges. Accordingly, this letter will be relegated to the appendix.

### 27.

Merlin published this collection, since he printed an Isidorian manuscript similar to Vatican 1340. In his numbering of Leo’s letters there are only ninety-seven: in this series he omitted Peter of Ravenna’s letter 25 to Eutyches and the letter of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranius to Leo, letter 68, although these are inserted among the Leonine letters in the manuscripts of this collection. He also altered in some places the order of the letters found in the manuscript copies.

In collating Merlin’s example, we used his Cologne edition of 1530. The Isidorian manuscript repeatedly cited by Quesnellus, which he calls the Herovallian manuscript, belongs to this collection according to several indications. That a not very different collection is found in the Reims manuscript of Saint-Remigius, frequently praised by the same Quesnellus, we infer both from its many variant readings and from Coustant’s preface to *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, no. 163, where he testifies that the same Remigian manuscript is Isidorian and has been enlarged by several letters of Leo.

### 28.

The Isidorian manuscript from which Johannes Sichardus published the letters of the Roman pontiffs may likewise be assigned here. Most of the spurious letters of the earlier pontiffs are from Isidore’s workshop; but the fifty letters of Leo that close the edition, and which additionally contain Flavian’s letter 22 to Leo, are all genuine and are contained in the manuscripts of collection 12.

It is nevertheless clear from the different order and number of the letters that Sichard’s manuscript differed from ours.
