His readings, and especially the *pannus*—the textual patch—which Sichard’s manuscript exhibits in letter 1 to the bishop of Aquileia, sewn in at a different place, and in the reading of the present collection (since it is placed after the words after which it is read as inserted in the manuscripts of collection 24), as we shall note in annotation 26 to letter 1, show that the author of the Sichardian copy drew from the same source from which collection 24 originated.

When Quesnellus cites Sichard, he used the Paris edition of 1568, which had perhaps been corrected against Victorine manuscripts, probably Isidorian, but not against manuscripts similar to Sichard’s. We used the earlier Basel edition of 1536, which presents Sichard’s manuscript in its pure form.

## § XIV. On the thirteenth collection

### 29.

We call the thirteenth collection the one preserved in the Florentine manuscript, Biblioteca Marciana 182, of the twelfth century. It contains only letters of the Roman pontiffs. From the apocryphal letters, however, which it presents together with the genuine letters down to Sixtus III, Leo’s predecessor, it is recognized as Isidorian. In the material concerning Leo, however, it differs more than any other from the Isidorian manuscripts.

For it differs from Isidore—not merely in the order and character of the letters, but even from every other collection—and this one manuscript alone presents letter 12 to the Africans of Mauritania in a complete and exact form. This plainly demonstrates the collection’s distinctive and exceptionally valuable origin.

It contains twenty-three complete letters, while the twenty-fourth lacks its ending, for the manuscript is mutilated. We therefore do not know how many other letters this collection contained. We give the list of the individual letters:

I, to the bishops established throughout all the provinces, letter 4 of our edition;  
II, to the Italians, letter 7;  
III, to the Sicilians, letter 16;  
IV, to Januarius of Aquileia, letter 18;  
V, to Rusticus, letter 167;  
VI, to Anastasius, letter 14;  
VII, to Nicetas, letter 159;  
VIII, to the Moors, letter 12;  
IX, to the Palestinians, letter 124;  
X, to the people of Constantinople, letter 59;  
XI, to the Ephesian synod, letter 33;  
XII, to Theodosius, letter 44;  
XIII, to Pulcheria, letter 45;  
XIV, to Theodosius, letter 29;  
XV, to Julian, letter 35;  
XVI, to Pulcheria, letter 31;  
XVII, [lacuna], to the bishop of Aquileia, letter 1;  
XVIII, to Septimus, letter 2;  
XIX, to Anatolius, letter 163;  
XX, to the same, letter 135;  
XXI, to the Council of Chalcedon, letter 95;  
XXII, to Doro, letter 19;  
XXIII, to Flavian, letter 28;  
XXIV, it is incorrectly inscribed as being to Marcian; for letter 165 follows, beginning “I promised,” which was delivered to Leo Augustus.

The first eight letters follow the order of the Hadrianic collection. But the eighth, to the bishops of Mauritania, does not follow the Hadrianic edition, just as it does not follow the Isidorian one, as we noted shortly above.

## § XV. On the fourteenth collection, the Avellanian

### 30.

We now pass from the general collections to the particular ones, beginning with those that contain documents specific to certain churches. The principal collection of the Roman Church is the fourteenth, which we call the Avellanian. For its author, who apparently flourished at Rome in the time of Vigilius, gathered many special documents of the Roman pontiffs and of the Roman Church that are either entirely absent from the other collections or were transmitted there in a different form.

We called it Avellanian because the most celebrated and ancient manuscript of this collection, Vatican 4961, belonged to the monastery of Santa Croce at Fonte Avellana in Umbria. We also found other copies of the same collection: three at Rome, Vatican 3786, 3787, and 4903; one Corsinian; another in the Angelica Library; and two in Venice, Marciana 171 and 172. Among these, Vatican manuscript 3787, of the twelfth century, and the two Venetian manuscripts are in no way dependent on the Avellanian.

This collection, into which such distinctive documents of the Roman Church could have entered only from the apostolic archives, has supplied us with only five letters of Leo, first published by Surius, which one will search for in vain in other manuscripts or collections. They are:

I, to Leo Augustus, letter 169;  
II, to Gennadius of Constantinople, letter 170;  
III, to Timothy of Alexandria, letter 171;  
IV, to the Alexandrian priests and deacons, letter 172;  
V, to Theophilus and the other bishops of Egypt, letter 173 [Col. 0565].

## § XVI. On the fifteenth collection, the Arelatan

### 31.

The fifteenth collection, proper to the Church of Arles, contains letters of the Roman pontiffs to their own bishops, or of their bishops to the Roman pontiffs, by which their privileges or rights might be proved. To this collection we owe three letters of Leo and one to Leo, which would otherwise have perished, namely:

I, Leo’s letter to Constantius and the other bishops of Gaul, letter 40;  
II, to Ravennius of Arles, letter 42;  
III, the petition of the Gauls to Leo, letter 65;  
IV, the rescript of Saint Leo to the preceding letter, letter 66.

Two ancient manuscripts are cited, the Regius and the Colbertinus. We examined a more recent manuscript, Vallicellian G 99, but one copied with the greatest exactness from a very ancient Arelatan manuscript. Although Cardinal Baronius had published the letters mentioned above, it was nevertheless possible to correct several matters that had escaped the reader of the transcript because of the more difficult script of the exemplar.

## § XVII. On the sixteenth collection, that of the Church of Thessalonica

### 32.

The sixteenth collection is proper to the Church of Thessalonica. The Roman synod held under Boniface II in the year 531 must be regarded as belonging to this type: at it, not a few letters of the Roman pontiffs relating to that same church were produced and inserted.

Nicholas I gives authority to this collection. Since he frequently cites certain letters contained only in this collection, he thereby attests to the credibility of the whole collection. This collection, or Roman synod, is preserved in the Barberinian manuscript 3386, from which Holstenius’s edition was produced. Most of the documents recited there are unavailable elsewhere.

Leo Allatius had published several fragments from a Vatican manuscript in *The Concord of the Eastern and Western Churches*, pages 1370–1371; on page 1364 he describes it as extremely old, damaged, and corrupt in some places. The Barberinian manuscript, which besides the Roman synod contains several other items likewise printed by Holstenius, is more recent. It is recognized as having been copied from two older Vatican manuscripts, then numbered 5751, folio 55, and 6339, folio 12, which are indicated on its first page.

We believe Allatius used one of these when he recited those fragments. Yet however diligently I searched, I could not find either manuscript. For not only do the manuscripts now designated by those numbers contain nothing of the kind, but neither the Vatican catalogues nor inventories could provide any support.

If the Barberinian manuscript was copied under Holstenius’s direction—as may be inferred from the Vatican manuscript numbers written by his hand at the beginning—there is no reason to doubt that the copy was made accurately from the Vatican exemplar. Thus the errors in the Barberinian manuscript that he later corrected in his edition, as well as the few lacunae visible in it but supplied in Holstenius’s edition, must be attributed to the Vatican exemplar. Why the editor cited the Barberinian manuscript rather than the Vatican one remains unknown.

Holstenius corrected or supplied not a few passages in his edition from conjecture, without indicating what stood in the manuscript. We shall identify each such matter, whatever its nature, and have found it useful to consult the manuscript itself in restoring several passages.

It should also be noted that the Roman synod is not preserved complete in this manuscript. It ends with a letter wrongly attributed to Leo and addressed to Anastasius of Thessalonica, beginning: “We believed, after our letters …” From the context and the consular notation it is clear that the letter belongs to Boniface I and to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica. Holstenius therefore rightly printed it among the letters of Boniface, no. 7, under the heading: “Boniface to his beloved brother Rufus.” He should, however, have warned readers of the error that had entered the manuscript.

Since this Roman synod, as it appears in the manuscript, actually breaks off amid Leo’s letters—as is shown by the manuscript’s final words, written after those letters: “Likewise, it was recited …,” which indicate another letter following but missing from the manuscript—we do not know whether that letter concerned Leo, or whether one or several letters followed.

In the work mentioned, *The Concord*, page 1371, Allatius cites from the Vatican copy of this Roman synod a testimony from Leo’s letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica that is not read in the published Leonine letters. Lest anyone think it a fragment of another letter omitted near the end by the scribe of the Barberinian manuscript, it should be understood that the passage belongs to the aforementioned letter of Boniface to Rufus. Consequently, in both the Vatican and Barberinian manuscripts it was likewise wrongly inscribed as a letter of Leo to Anastasius. We thus recognize that the Barberinian manuscript was copied accurately from this same Vatican manuscript and that the copyist reproduced even its errors faithfully.

We now present the catalogue of the letters surviving in this collection:

I, Marcian’s letter to Leo, letter 100;  
II, Leo’s letter to Marcian, letter 104;  
III, to Anatolius, letter 106;  
IV, to Marcian, letter 136;  
V, Anatolius’s letter to Leo, letter 132;  
VI, Leo’s letter to Anatolius, letter 135;  
VII, to Anastasius, letter 6;  
VIII, to the metropolitans established throughout Illyricum, letter 5;  
IX, to Senecio and the other bishops of Achaea, letter 13.

Six of these, namely the first, fourth, fifth, seventh, eighth, and ninth, owe their first publication to this collection. We found the fourth in the Ratisponensian manuscript; Quesnellus found it in the Grimanian. Arnold later discovered the first, Marcian’s letter, written in Greek in the Blodeian manuscript; we found it in Vatican Greek 1455.

## § XVIII. On the seventeenth collection, the Chalcedonian

### 33.

Among the particular collections must be counted the one relating to the Council of Chalcedon. Since it contains numerous letters either of Leo or concerning Leo that will be printed in this edition, and since it is the oldest of all, it had to be placed before the other ancient collections of Leo, as it were as his special collection [Col. 0367].

This collection is divided into three parts. The first presents the documents that preceded the proceedings of the council; the second contains the council’s proceedings themselves; the third presents what was done after the synod.

In the first part, which Rusticus calls the *ante gesta*, the letters to be placed in our edition are twenty-seven. We append their sequence from the Latin manuscripts:

I, Leo’s letter to Eutyches, letter 20;  
II, Peter of Ravenna’s letter to Eutyches, letter 25;  
III, Leo’s letter to Flavian, letter 23;  
IV, Flavian’s letter to Leo, letter 22;  
V, Leo’s letter to Faustus, letter 72;  
VI, Flavian’s letter to Leo, letter 26;  
VII, Leo’s letter to Julian, letter 35;  
VIII, to Faustus and the other Constantinopolitans, letter 32;  
IX, to Theodosius, letter 29;  
X, to Pulcheria, letter 30;  
XI, to the Ephesian synod, letter 33;  
XII, to Theodosius, letter 43;  
XIII, to the same, letter 44;  
XIV, to Pulcheria, letter 45;  
XV, Hilary the deacon’s letter to Pulcheria, letter 46;  
XVI, Placidia’s letter to Pulcheria, letter 58;  
XVII, Valentinian’s letter to Theodosius, letter 55;  
XVIII, Placidia’s letter to the same, letter 56;  
XIX, Eudoxia’s letter to the same, letter 57;  
XX, Theodosius’s letter to Valentinian, letter 62;  
XXI, to Placidia, letter 63;  
XXII, to Eudoxia, letter 64;  
XXIII, Leo’s letter to the Constantinopolitans, letter 50;  
XXIV, to the Constantinopolitan archimandrites, letter 54;  
XXV, Marcian’s letter to Leo, letter 73;  
XXVI, to the same, letter 76;  
XXVII, Pulcheria’s letter to the same Leo, letter 77.

One letter is inserted into the action that is called the second in the published editions, namely Leo’s letter to Flavian, letter 28.

Finally, two letters belong to the third part, after the proceedings of the council: the letter of the Council of Chalcedon to Leo, letter 98, and Leo’s letter to that same council, letter 114.

The Greek manuscripts, however, which do not contain the latter, present another letter before the *ante gesta*, namely Leo’s letter to the Council of Nicaea, letter 93. The Greek manuscripts of Saint Mark’s Library in Venice not only place this same letter before the *ante gesta*, with the heading “to the synod at Nicaea,” where the council had first been summoned; they also repeat it in an unpublished action of the Council of Chalcedon, to be published in the appendix of public documents, where the reading of that letter occasioned its inclusion.

Here, however, instead of “at Nicaea,” we read “at Chalcedon,” perhaps because the legates altered the heading, since, owing to the change in the council’s indiction, the Fathers actually assembled at Chalcedon.

### 34.

This is the oldest of all the collections. For it appears to have been assembled in Greek while Leo himself was still alive, between the years 453 and 455. Since this fact will be useful for many matters that follow, it is of great importance to establish it clearly and retain it in memory.

Two epigraphs written by the compiler demonstrate it evidently. For although at least some of the letters of Latin origin contained in the Greek collection were not translated into Greek by the author of the Greek collection himself, but were merely gathered and arranged into one body after he found them already translated into Greek, nevertheless we are certain that the epigraphs prefixed to the letters—repeatedly in longer wording and with certain historical notes—belong to the same Greek compiler and were written at the time of the collection.

In the epigraph that the Greek compiler prefixed to the letters of Valentinian, Placidia, and Eudoxia to the emperor Theodosius, he calls Theodosius and Placidia, because they had died by the time of the collection, “of blessed memory”; but Valentinian, because he was still alive, he calls not “of blessed memory” but “lord.” We shall give the complete epigraph in the note prefixed to letter 55, no. 7.

Therefore this collection was arranged by a Greek author before Valentinian’s death. Moreover, in the epigraph prefixed by the same compiler to Pulcheria’s letter 77 to Leo—which in our edition will be given in place of a synopsis—she is called “of blessed memory,” a formula showing that she was already dead. Pulcheria died in the year 453, whereas Valentinian died in 455. Thus, in respect of its Greek origin, this collection must be placed between the years 453 and 455.

This may be confirmed by the omission of other otherwise notable but later letters of Leo, especially letter 165 to Leo Augustus. Since this letter was also extremely famous among the Greeks, as will be shown in the note to that letter, there is no doubt that the compiler of this collection would have inserted it above all others if he had composed the collection after those letters were sent to the East in the year 458. Since he assembled it shortly after the Council of Chalcedon and before 455, he could gather only the letters written before Chalcedon and those issued soon afterward in connection with that council.

When we say that this collection of letters was assembled among the Greeks during this period, we do not thereby believe that all the letters now inserted in the same collection were gathered at the same time. For some Greek copies contain more letters and others fewer. The entire difference concerns letters of Leo or letters relating to Leo.

In the Greek manuscript codices used by the Roman editors, and likewise in the two Venetian manuscripts, six letters are absent: letter 26, Flavian’s to Leo; letter 45, Leo’s to Pulcheria; letter 46, Hilary’s to the same; letter 50, Leo’s to the Constantinopolitans; letter 51, his to the archimandrites; and letter 58, Placidia’s to Pulcheria.

Cotelerius found and published these in two Parisian manuscripts. Since they are absent from the first collection, they are recognized as later additions. Nevertheless, the addition is extremely ancient, for Rusticus obtained manuscripts similar to the Parisian ones when he revised this collection around the middle of the sixth century. Since such manuscripts were already in circulation then, the six letters must have been added long before that and perhaps not long after the first collection.

The letters bearing the epigraphs mentioned above, however, belong to the first collection, which we have shown was made between the years 453 and 455.

### 35.

This Greek collection was subsequently translated into Latin before Pope Vigilius, as Baluzius proves in the preface to the ancient translation of the Council of Chalcedon, no. 3.

The translator rendered into Latin only those documents that had originally been written in Greek or whose Latin original he could not find. Whenever he found the Latin original, he inserted it into the Latin manuscripts.

Thus most of Leo’s letters, which had been translated into Greek and compiled by the Greek collector, are not translations from the Greek in the Latin copies of this same collection, but the original Latin itself. This is evident not only from Leo’s syntax, which shines through in most of the Latin letters of this collection, but much more from those letters whose Latin copies—of unquestionably Latin origin, contained in other Latin collections and manuscripts not derived from the Greek—reproduce the same wording that is read in the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection. This will be clear especially to those who compare letters 23, 28, 29, 30, 32, 50, and 51.

The same point is wonderfully confirmed by Leo’s letter 35 to Julian. In the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, this letter is not mutilated in the same three places as it is in all the Greek manuscripts; moreover, it lacks certain additions that are read only in the Greek text. It is therefore recognized that, in the Latin manuscripts of this collection, the letter was not translated from Greek but taken from the Latin original.

For this reason, the Latin manuscripts of this collection will be of the greatest use to our edition [Col. 0569].

### 36.

Since, however, in some letters the Latin translator inserted in his manuscripts a translation from the Greek in place of the Latin original, which he was unable to find, the translations of the letters can readily be distinguished from the originals by the following indication. This concerns only letters written by their authors in Latin.

Those that bear a chronological notation in the Latin manuscripts were taken from Latin originals in which the chronological notation was recorded. Those that lack this notation are translations from the Greek, in which the Greek translator omitted the chronological notations.

This observation supplies a new confirmation, further strengthening what we established shortly above: Latin letters whose chronological notation could not have been taken from the Greek were transferred into the Latin manuscripts of the Council of Chalcedon from Latin copies that certainly retained such notation.

It should not be omitted, however, that Leo’s letter 93 to the Council of Nicaea, which is placed before the *ante gesta* in the Greek text, gives a day and a month. But this letter is absent from the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection and was not in the ancient Greek collection; otherwise the Latin translator would not have omitted it from the Latin copies. Thus what is now read in the Greek manuscripts must be attributed to a later addition. Indeed, it is placed as an addition in the Greek Venetian manuscripts at the very end of the material before the *ante gesta*, whereas the Greek compiler would, according to his custom, have prefixed it to the other documents.

### 37.

We must now mention the manuscripts we shall use. Here we need speak only of the Latin manuscripts, since most of the letters required for this collection were written in Latin and, as we have proved, taken from the Latin original. We shall discuss the Greek manuscripts separately below.

Quesnellus at times used two Thuanean manuscript copies. We, however, benefited not only from the three manuscripts of Corbie, Dijon, and Colbert, whose variants the most diligent Baluzius published in his recension of the entire Chalcedonian collection, but also collated exactly four others: Chigianus 483, Vatican 1323, another Vatican manuscript, 4166, and one exceptionally fine manuscript belonging to the chapter of Verona, no. 57. The latter, written in a larger format tending toward a square, with the script divided into two columns, belongs approximately to the seventh century.

Nor should the equally ancient Vatican manuscript 1322 be omitted. Among the Chalcedonian proceedings it presents letter 28 to Flavian and the report of the synod to Saint Leo from the ancient version, together with the bishops’ subscriptions.

## § XIX. On the eighteenth collection

### 38.

We now turn to the ancient particular collections of the letters of Saint Leo. In the old catalogue of the manuscripts of the library of the monastery of Bobbio, which Muratorius published from an Ambrosian manuscript of the ninth or tenth century, volume III of *Antiquitates Italicae*, dissertation 49, page 819, we read:

“Likewise, concerning the canons, among the major and minor books there are fifteen books of canons, and two books of the letters of Leo.”

This was undoubtedly a particular collection of Leo’s letters, of which two copies are indicated by the designation “two books.” If the catalogue belongs to the ninth or tenth century, who would doubt the antiquity of the collections themselves, or of the manuscripts praised in it?

Leo of Ostia relates, book III, chapter 63, that Desiderius of Monte Cassino—later Pope Victor III—among the other manuscripts he acquired for the Cassinese library, purchased not only a book of Saint Leo’s sermons but also a collection of his letters; there he calls it the “register of Pope Leo.” The book of sermons is still preserved in that library, but the register of letters is missing.

This collection of letters, however, was probably of a later age, namely the eleventh century, just as we noted in the preface to the sermons that the surviving collection of sermons is also more recent.

### 39.

Since we are now speaking of ancient collections, into which everything, or at least most things, was once transferred from the archives, the Grimanian manuscript first presents itself. Quesnellus used it above all to illuminate his edition. Since Quesnellus has provided much information about this distinguished collection, to which we assign the eighteenth place, in the general preface that we likewise appended to our general preface, we refer the reader to it; there is no need to repeat the same material.

We note only that Father Coustant, in the preface to *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, no. 166, judged that this manuscript had been copied seven hundred years ago, that is, around the tenth century. He also thought that the collection itself had been derived from the archives of the Roman Church, since it presents so many particular letters that it would be difficult to suppose that they could have been found elsewhere.

Of Leo’s 107 letters contained in this manuscript, twenty-eight previously unpublished letters first emerged from it, namely:

one to Flavian, letter 27;  
one to Faustus, letter 75;  
eight to Julian, letters 86, 92, 117, 131, 140, 141, 147, and 152;  
one to Paschasinus, letter 88;  
four to Anatolius, letters 91, 143, 146, and 157 [Col. 0571];  
four to Marcian, letters 126, 128, 137, and 142;  
one to Proterius of Alexandria, letter 129;  
one to Aetius, letter 153;  
one to Basil of Antioch, letter 149;  
one to Euxitheus of Thessalonica, letter 150;  
three to the Egyptians, letters 154, 158, and 160;  
one to the Constantinopolitan clergy, letter 161;  
and one to Leo Augustus, letter 164.

### 40.

Not all the letters of this collection, however, can be said to have been taken from the Roman archives or from any other archive. Since Dionysian headings are prefixed to the letters to Rusticus, it cannot be denied that the compiler took something from Dionysius. He could likewise have derived other material from other ancient collections, especially from the seventeenth, the Chalcedonian collection, from which alone he could certainly have drawn letter 43 to Theodosius. For some of its principal readings, its lacuna, and its errors depend on the Greek text of that same collection, as we shall show more fully in the note to that letter.

Perhaps something was also added later by some copyist; and it seems more probably attributable to a later addition that the single letter of Symmachus is read at the end of this manuscript.

### 41.

The letters concerning the Eutychian heresy, which are found in greater number and with greater rarity in this collection than elsewhere, seem to derive—if they were not requested from the Roman archive itself—from some certainly older collection taken from that same archive. We have seen in no. 2 that the author of the *Roman Pontifical* testified that letters concerning the faith had been preserved there in their own time.

In his letter 4 to the emperor Zeno, Simplicius writes that he sent Acacius copies of Leo’s letters concerning the faith; but he mentions only the letters to Marcian, to Leo Augustus, and to the Council of Chalcedon.

Pope Vigilius sent Justinian a fuller collection on the same subject. For in letter 4 to that same emperor he says:

> “So that all things may inform Your Piety … we have added, from the enactments of our predecessor Pope Leo of blessed memory, which were directed to the East at various times, as many as we judge necessary at present, asking … that Your Piety may deign to read them all, lest anything remain entirely unread.”

That some such collection of Leo’s letters concerning the faith against the Eutychians was once circulated among the Latins seems to be proved by the ancient formula of profession, which is also read in volume X of the Councils, page 1388, Venetian edition, expressed in these words:

> “I profess that I will preserve inviolate in every respect and in all things, and will always freely proclaim, the letter of Leo, of blessed memory, bishop of the apostolic see, given to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, as well as all his letters written concerning the firmness of the faith.”

We shall show with sufficient probability in the following section that this collection of Vigilius was preserved for us in the Ratisponensian manuscript. The author of the Grimanian collection did not use it; for he did not copy all the letters contained in it and therefore drew from other unknown sources.

## § XX. On the outstanding nineteenth collection, the Ratisponensian, whose author appears to have been Pope Vigilius
42. We believe the Ratisponensian collection to be older than the Grimanic and somewhat more outstanding as well. We found it in a manuscript of the library of St. Emmeram. This codex, which has hitherto been of no use to any edition, not only presented sixteen letters formerly unpublished, before they appeared from the Grimanic manuscript, and eight which are read only in manuscripts of Collection 12, and one which exists in the very rare Collection 16, as well as another found only in Collection 23; it also supplied us with three others previously unknown, especially useful for illuminating the history of Eutyches: namely, two letters to Julian, Letters 109 and 144, and another to Anatolius, Letter 151.

Moreover, this codex is much more accurate. With its assistance, therefore, we were able securely to confirm certain readings and to correct and restore many passages that had previously been corrupted. This collection contains only letters pertaining to the Eutychian heresy, though not all of them; for some letters on the same subject are found only in certain other specialized collections. From this we infer that such a collection cannot have been contemporary with the age of Leo. For if it had been compiled in Leo’s time, all the letters pertaining to the Eutychians would have been collected and found in it.

Perhaps this is the collection which we saw, in the preceding section, that Pope Vigilius sent to Justinian. For Pelagius II, in Letter 3 to Elias of Aquileia, chapter 3, volume VI of the Councils, Venetian edition, page 261, apparently referring to this collection of his predecessor Vigilius, writes:

> “From Your Dilection, therefore, the first testimony of our holy predecessor Leo is set forth, which is contained in his LAST letter.”

This testimony is from Letter 162. Since that letter is indeed the last one in the Ratisponensian manuscript, this codex may be believed to contain Vigilius’s collection. In it, Vigilius testifies that he had collected not all, but only certain of Leo’s more important letters, from among the many letters concerning the Eutychian heresy; and this agrees very well with the Ratisponensian collection.

The compiler collected only Leo’s letters, not letters of others addressed to Leo. He followed chronological order, except for six letters which are found outside their proper places. The letters transcribed in this collection number seventy-two, with the qualification that at number 71, instead of a letter, copies of testimonies are transcribed—namely, those testimonies of the Fathers which are appended to the letter of St. Leo to the emperor Leo in our edition as Letter 165. The final letter is mutilated because the codex lacks its last page.

The antiquity of this codex is revealed by the inscription on its first page, in these words:

> “Luog gave this book to Saint Emmeram for Bishop Tuto and for the salvation of his soul.”

This Tuto presided over the Church of Ratisbon from the year 891 until the year 930. The script is of the ninth or tenth century and resembles the specimen published by P. Mabillon in *De Re Diplomatica*, plate 57.

[Col. 0573] 43. To avoid providing a lengthy catalogue of all the letters, it will be sufficient, for recognizing and distinguishing the order of this collection, to indicate its first four and its last four letters:

I. Leo’s Letter 24 to Theodosius;  
II. Letter 23 to Flavian;  
III. Letter 29 to Theodosius;  
IV. Letter 30 to Pulcheria.

It is noteworthy that after Letter 36 of this collection, to Pulcheria—which is Letter 95 in our edition—the following special notation is appended:

> “Here end the letters of the most holy Pope Leo which were sent before the holy Council of Chalcedon.”

Then, beginning afresh:

> “Here begin those which followed after the proceedings.”

Letter 37 follows, our Letter 104, written to Marcian after the council.

We now indicate the final four:

LXIX. Letter 164 to the emperor Leo;  
LXX. Letter 165 to the same;  
LXXI. Copies of the testimonies which are customarily appended to the preceding letter;  
LXXII. Letter 162 to the same emperor Leo.

In the general preface, number 6, we gratefully acknowledged how much we owe to those who provided us with the most accurate possible transcript of this outstanding codex and collection.

§ XXI. On the Twentieth Collection

44. We found this collection in Roman manuscript 237 of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, dating from approximately the eleventh century. The book, however, lacks both its beginning and its end; consequently, it contains only twenty-seven letters, of which the first and last are mutilated.

The order of the final eleven letters is frequent in other collections. The first sixteen letters, however, follow an order so different from that of all the collections that for this reason we thought a distinct collection should be assigned to this codex. Thus, for example, after Letter 28 of our edition, to Flavian, it places Letter 35 to Julian, then Letter 31 to Pulcheria, Letter 59 to the Constantinopolitans, Letter 124 to the Palestinians, Letter 1 to the bishop of Aquileia, Letter 163 to Anatolius, Letter 165 to the emperor Leo, and so forth. This disordered sequence is found in this one collection alone.

In the surviving letters, however, there is none that does not also appear in the following collection. This codex contains Letter 12 to the Moors with its appendix. Among Leo’s letters it includes the spurious letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, and it entitles the letter to Dorus of Beneventum “To Theodore.” There is no need to say more about this collection.

§ XXII. On the Twenty-First Collection

45. This collection, more frequently found in manuscripts, contains the same fifty-six letters that we listed in Collection 11, but in an order and with readings so different that it seems to reveal a different origin. It begins with Leo’s letter to Eutyches, our Letter 20, and ends with the letter to the bishops of Campania, our Letter 168.

The oldest example of this collection that we have seen is manuscript 170 of the Venetian library of St. Mark, dating from approximately the twelfth century. It contains letters alone, as do two other codices, Vatican manuscripts 542 and 543, of the fourteenth century.

The letters together with the sermons of Collection 4 are found in Vatican manuscripts 546 and 347; Vatican Urbinus 65; one manuscript of the Augustinian Fathers’ Angelica Library in Rome, number 5, 10; two Florentine Medicean manuscripts, numbers 11 and 23, shelf 21; and one manuscript of the Lateran canons at Fiesole, numbered 7, shelf 3.

This same collection, together with the sermons, is also read in Vatican manuscript 541, which was presented to Nicholas V in the year 1452. After the fifty-six letters proper to this collection, this codex contains an addition of twelve other letters, eleven of which are included in Collection 24. But since this codex does not transmit all the Leonine letters of Collection 24, and since the twelfth—or final—letter, to Maximus of Antioch, is absent from that Twenty-Fourth Collection, the author of the addition seems to have drawn from another source.

Since the variant readings of these twelve letters generally agree with those of the manuscripts of Collection 12, it is credible that the compilers of both collections drew them from the same source.

46. Two manuscripts, Vatican 3137 and Vatican Ottobonianus 332, may be assigned to this collection. They contain the same fifty-six letters. Although eleven letters removed from the end of this collection are inserted in these codices after Letter 26, and the remaining letters from 27 through 45 then continue, since all the letters nevertheless preserve among themselves the same order found in this collection and generally agree in their readings, this alteration of the order seems attributable to the discretion of some scribe rather than to a different origin.

§ XXIII. On the Twenty-Second Collection

47. Venetian manuscript St. Mark 79, besides the sermons of Collection 4, provides a distinct collection of letters. It contains letters from Collections 17 and 21 in the following order: first, the first twenty-six letters of Collection 21, in the same sequence; then all the letters of the Chalcedonian Collection 17, likewise in the same order, except for two which had already been transcribed among the preceding twenty-six; finally, the remaining letters of Collection 21, but with three omitted and the order altered to a considerable degree. Its readings are also repeatedly very different, clearly revealing another origin.

The omitted letters are: Eusebius of Milan’s letter to Leo, our Letter 97; Ravennius’s letter to the same, our Letter 99; and Leo’s letter to the bishops of Campania, Letter 168.

§ XXIV. On the Twenty-Third Collection

48. A peculiar collection exists in Vatican Ottobonianus manuscript 297, of the twelfth century. At the beginning it provides the fifteen letters of Leo previously listed in Collection 8, the fifteenth of which is Letter 165, to the emperor Leo.

After this letter, and before the testimonies of the Fathers appended to it, the letters of Innocent I to Decentius, Boniface I to the emperor Honorius, the reply of Honorius, and Celestine’s letter to Venerius are inserted. Then the testimonies of the Fathers pertaining to the aforementioned Letter 165 follow.

Next come the fifty-six letters of Collection 21, except those that had been transcribed among the first fifteen letters, with the order altered in some places. Finally, at the end, four extremely rare letters are added [Col. 0575]: to Julian, Letter 107; to the Constantinopolitans, Letter 50; to Flavian, Letter 49; and to Martin and Faustus, Letter 51.

Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, published two letters then unpublished from a manuscript of this collection that had belonged to Cardinal Sirleto: one to the Sicilians, Letter 17 in our edition, and the other to Julian, Letter 107. This may be seen in the appendix of short works appended to the Mainz edition of the works of St. Gregory Thaumaturgus, published in 1604.

§ XXV. On the Twenty-Fourth Collection

49. We assign the final place to a collection of letters that we found together with the sermons of Collection 5. It contains seventy-one letters: namely, fifty-four letters of Collection 21—omitting two, Peter Chrysologus’s letter to Eutyches and Eusebius of Milan’s letter to Leo—and, in addition, seventeen other rare letters found in Collection 12, namely Letters 2, 10, 24, 41, 94, 95, 102, 105, 111, 112, 113, 118, 121, 122, 123, 125, and 127 of our edition.

The fifty-four letters might be thought to have been taken from Collection 21 or 11. The reason not to believe this is Letter 12 to the Moors. Although it is counted among the fifty-four, in this collection it is abridged, whereas in Collections 11 and 21 it carries an appended addition. Similarly, the seventeen letters cannot be said to have been taken from Collection 12; for if the compiler had drawn from that collection, he would have copied other letters from it as well, not these seventeen alone.

Add to this an observation we made when speaking of Sichard’s collection, number 28. Moreover, the order of all these seventy-one letters differs from the order of both Collections 12 and 21, and their readings likewise differ, demonstrating another unknown source. Accordingly, when collating certain letters, we found this collection to function as an original distinct from the others, to such an extent that in these letters it does not derive from the Hispanic Collection, from which they flowed into the other later collections.

The codices of this collection are Vatican 544, of the twelfth century; Vatican Regius 139, of the thirteenth century; the Cesena manuscript of the Friars Minor Conventual of St. Francis; and Florentine Laurentianus 14, shelf 21, which adds two further letters, namely Letters 119 and 145.

Quesnellus knew of three manuscripts of this collection: the Victorinus, the Regniacensis, and that of Saint-Martin of Auxerre, as is clear from the *Admonitio* on Letter 12, number 2. He generally used only the Victorinus manuscript.

In Fiesolan manuscript 10, shelf 3, only twenty-five letters of this collection were transcribed, most of them among the seventeen indicated above; the letter to the Moors is in an abridged form.

Thus far concerning the collections. We do not, however, believe that others cannot be found. For the author of Collection 12 undoubtedly derived five distinctive letters from collections still unknown, as we observed above, number 26.

§ XXVI. On Certain Manuscripts Used in Addition to the Collections Mentioned

50. We must now briefly discuss those codices which, although they are not collections of letters, nevertheless supplied some letters of Leo.

Three very ancient manuscripts, approximately a thousand years old, deserve mention first. Veronese manuscript 8, after the Catholic Epistles of the New Testament, gives Leo’s Letter 28 to Flavian. Another Veronese manuscript, number 58, containing various documents of the two synods of Ephesus and Chalcedon, supplies the same letter to Flavian and another to Rusticus of Narbonne, together with the *Inquisitiones*. Another Veronese manuscript, now Vatican 1322, presents five letters of Leo before the acts of Chalcedon, namely Letters 87, 89, 93, 94, and 114.

In Vatican Regina manuscript 293, of the twelfth century, four letters of St. Leo—31, 35, 139, and 165—are transcribed after the books *On the Calling of All Nations*. Quesnellus seems to have possessed a similar Thuanus codex, as may be inferred from the information concerning his manuscripts.

In Vallicellian manuscript 18, of the eleventh century, which contains various short works, two letters of Leo are inserted in short work 73: namely, title 398, Letter 106, and title 399, Letter 93.

In Vatican 1343, of the tenth century, formerly belonging to the Church of Pavia and containing a miscellany of the Dionysian and Isidorian collections, four letters of Leo are placed first. They seem to have been taken from the Dionysian additions, or from Collection 8, namely Letters 9, 17, 20, and 108.

Vatican 1347, of the tenth century, and similar manuscripts—Vatican Palatine 579 and Vatican Regina 849—supplied Letter 14 to Anastasius.

The Barberini codex 77, which Quesnellus mentions in his second edition, supplied only an abridged version of Letter 12 to the bishops of Mauritania.

The copy of the first edition of the sermons of St. Leo, published by Joannes Andreas, bishop of Aleria, supplied, besides Letter 28 to Flavian, four others appended to the sermons: namely Letters 80, 119, 145, and 165.

Other manuscripts of the same kind, which assisted in correcting the particular letters of Paschasinus and Proterius to Leo, will be indicated in their proper places, as will those which contributed something toward the inclusion of certain laws in this edition.

§ XXVII. On the Greek Manuscripts

51. We proved above, number 34, that the letters of Leo prefixed to Chalcedonian Collection 17 were soon translated and compiled in Greek, between the years 453 and 455. There can be no doubt that the same was subsequently done with his other letters which he sent to the East on the same matter. Hence Letter 175, to the emperor Leo, was long famous among the Greeks; its Greek version is the most accurate of all.

We called it the most accurate of all because the other Greek translations are generally found to be obscure and involved. Nor should this be considered foreign to that earlier period. Just as at that time there were few Latins who knew Greek thoroughly and could produce an exact translation from Greek, so among the Greeks there were few who possessed Latin perfectly and could produce an accurate translation from Latin.

As for the Latins, sufficient evidence is provided by Celestine’s Letter 13 to Nestorius, number 2, where he says that he replied to his letters only later for this reason:

> “For the discourse had to be translated into Latin.”

This suggests how difficult it was to find a translator promptly in Rome.

Cyril seems to have known this so well that, when he intended to send certain Greek documents to the same Celestine, he arranged for them to be translated into Latin, as far as possible, by those who were living in Alexandria, for easier and more immediate use, as he himself testifies in Letter 8 to Celestine, number 9.

[Note: [Col. 0577] “As far as possible,” he says; for Proterius did not readily expect the Greek writings of the Alexandrians of his time to be carefully rendered into Latin, as may be seen in Letter 131, chapter 9.]

Likewise, St. Leo, in Letter 113, chapter 4, after affirming that the record of the proceedings of Chalcedon had been insufficiently clear among the Romans because of the difference of the Greek language in which they had been written, and despairing of finding a skilled translator in Rome, earnestly asked Julian of Cos to arrange for them to be translated from Constantinople into Latin.

Those ancient Latin versions of certain documents, produced before Dionysius Exiguus, are so involved that they amply confirm this same difficulty.

The same thing occurred among the Greeks when Latin documents had to be rendered into Greek. The ancient Greek versions which were read either at the Council of Ephesus or at the Council of Chalcedon provide the fullest testimony to this. In those times, too, what St. Gregory wrote in his own age could be said:

> “For today in the city of Constantinople there are none who can properly translate dictated material from Latin into Greek; for while they preserve the words and pay no attention to the meaning, they neither make the words intelligible nor preserve the meaning.”

Thus it is no surprise if the Greek versions of Leo’s letters do not correspond exactly to the Latin original, whose sense the Greek translator is sometimes recognized to have grasped less fully.

52. Nevertheless, these versions are not for that reason to be valued less. For under Hormisdas, when the Easterners were reconciled with the Western Church, they customarily professed not only St. Leo’s letter to Flavian but all his letters on the same subject.

The aforementioned pontiff had instructed his legates sent to Constantinople to require this, as is clear from the memorandum delivered to them, which is read in volume V of the Councils, Venetian edition, page 567.

Thus John, bishop of Nicopolis, says in his letter to the same pontiff, page 578a:

> “Following in all things the synodical and apostolic letters written by the true bishop of the Roman Church, Leo.”

In the profession of the Easterners, published and sent to the same pontiff in the year 517, page 583a, we read:

> “We receive and approve all the letters of Pope Leo, all those which he wrote concerning the Christian religion.”

John of Constantinople, in his letter to the same pontiff, page 622d:

> “We approve and embrace all the letters of Blessed Pope Leo of the city of Rome, which he wrote concerning the true faith.”

To omit other testimonies of this kind, the emperor Justinian himself, in his letter to Pope Agapetus, page 947e, says:

> “Approving in every respect and embracing all the letters of Blessed Leo, which he wrote concerning the Christian faith.”

The letters which these men approved and embraced were in the Greek translation. Therefore, the Greek text of these letters must not be regarded as a private writing, but as a public monument of the Eastern Church, approved and received by it for establishing the Catholic faith against the Eutychians. From this everyone can see how great the authority of these translations is and how important their publication must be.

Furthermore, other letters written by Greek authors to Leo, and to be included among the Leonine letters, were written in Greek; hence the original Greek exemplar could not be omitted.

Likewise, Leo’s Letters 43 and 72, one letter of Hilary, deacon of the Roman Church, to Pulcheria, Letter 46, and part of Peter of Ravenna’s Letter 25 to Eutyches, although written by their authors in Latin, must be regarded as having the Greek ancient version in place of the original text, since their Latin originals are lost and the Greek version was later rendered into Latin by others.

The same applies to the four imperial letters, 55, 56, 57, and 58, sent from the West to the East: their Latin originals having perished, the only ancient Greek version, later translated into Latin, must be regarded as standing in place of the original.

53. In his first edition Quesnellus published the Greek text of only twelve letters—namely, those which he believed either to have been written in Greek from the beginning or to be regarded as originals: Letters 22, 52, 55, 56, 57, 62, 63, 64, 73, 76, 77, and 98.

In his second edition he added two other Greek letters, 26 and 53, which had been printed by Cotelerius, and likewise 100 and 110, which had been printed by Arnold after the earlier edition. Thus he extracted sixteen Greek letters from published sources.

We, however, whose purpose is to produce the Greek text of all the letters, will, for the reasons explained above, add the Greek text of twenty-five other letters, so that there will be forty-one Greek letters in our edition.

Among these, Letter 101 of Anatolius to Leo will now appear for the first time from Greek Vatican manuscript 1455. From the same codex will also be added five ancient Greek translations that have not yet seen the light: Letters 104, 106, 114, 115, and 139.

We shall also add from Vossius the exceedingly accurate Greek translation of Letter 165, Leo’s letter to the emperor Leo, which is not read in the published editions of the Councils.

For all the remaining letters, we shall not merely reprint published texts, as has hitherto been done. We investigated the Greek codices and found some with which it was possible to collate nearly all the Greek letters, including those rarest letters published by Arnold.

Cotelerius found in the Royal Library at Paris a complete Greek exemplar of the Chalcedonian collection, entirely similar to that which the ancient Latin translator of the same collection used. He printed from this Royal manuscript six Greek letters which are read before the proceedings in the Latin translator but are absent from the codices used by the Roman editors in publishing the Greek text.

For the other Greek letters, no one had yet been found who had reviewed and corrected the Greek text against any manuscript. We, however, with the assistance of the distinguished Antonio Zanetto, keeper of the library, were able in the Greek manuscripts of the Venetian library of St. Mark to reread the letters published by the Romans against two Greek exemplars of the same collection, numbers 555, of the eleventh or twelfth century, and 164, of a more recent period. These are of a different origin and of better quality than those used by the Roman editors.

In Greek manuscript 165 of the same library, which contains some documents of the same collection, we found one of the six letters published by Cotelerius: namely, Flavian’s Letter 26, together with the translation of Leo’s Letter 28 to the same Flavian.

We likewise found these two letters in the ancient Roman manuscript 19 of the Basilian Fathers and collated both letters with both codices.

With the assistance of these codices we were able to heal many passages of the Greek text. In this matter we acknowledge that we owe very much to Father Julian Ferrario, a priest of the Oratory congregation at Verona, who, among his other accomplishments in letters and the liberal disciplines, shines with particular expertise in the Greek language.

Moreover, from the two aforementioned Venetian manuscripts, 164 and 555, we shall publish in the appendix an unpublished act of the Council of Chalcedon, in which Leo’s Letter 93 was read to the synod.

[Note: [Col. 0579] In the additions placed at the end of volume II, the Roman editors further insert the following passage, which should be read here: “But since, after the first volume had been published, the Roman edition of Father Pietro Tommaso Cacciari appeared, other Greek Vatican codices which we were able to collate were useful to us both for correcting certain passages and for including in the appendix three previously unpublished Greek fragments.”]

54. One final point must be noted here. Some Greek readings affixed to the margin of the Roman edition of the Councils, and from there transmitted into other editions and also added by Quesnellus to the Greek letters which he included in Leo’s edition, are not variant readings taken from any Greek codex. Rather, they were partly constructed by the Roman editors from the Latin text, from which the Greek version differed, and partly devised from their own judgment where the text seemed difficult or corrupt.

From this you will understand what those Greek readings are which we shall occasionally cite from the Roman editors.

§ XXVIII. Particular Features of This Edition

55. From the examination of so many collections, and of so many distinctive and outstanding codices as well, everyone will understand how much assistance we have had in preparing a more perfect edition of the letters of St. Leo than any previous one. No one has hitherto had the use of more numerous, older, or more distinctive codices than we have.

At the beginning of each letter we shall indicate the collections in which it is found with this or a similar formula:

> “It exists in the manuscripts of Collections 1, 2, 3, etc.”

We shall expressly cite the Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian collections by their proper names, since they are better known.

It should be observed here that under the name Dionysian or Hadrianic, the codices of Collection 8 are also to be understood, in which the Hadrianic collection is preceded by Dionysian additions. The name Isidorian Collection likewise includes the manuscripts of Collections 11 and 12, which repeat the Isidorian collection.

These collections will be called separately only when the discussion concerns letters that do not belong to the Hadrianic or Isidorian collection and that entered those collections from another source.

By the same reasoning, the collection of Isidore should not have been named, since, as far as Leo’s letters are concerned, it is merely a repetition of the Hispanic Collection. Why, nevertheless, it was not possible to refrain from citing it has been explained in number 21.

56. Quesnellus generally omitted the ancient titles of the letters found in the codices, preferring to place before them new synopses that he himself had constructed and considered more suitable.

We, however, retaining Quesnellus’s titles—or correcting them where necessary—shall accurately present all the ancient ones in the annotations, namely those found in the Dionysian and Hispanic collections, or in Isidore’s, and in the Fifth Quesnellian Collection.

57. The order of the letters will necessarily be changed. First, the chronological notation of not a few letters will have to be corrected from our codices. Other letters lacking chronological notes will likewise be transferred to another period on the basis of substantial evidence, and the sequence itself will consequently have to be arranged differently.

Next, one letter accepted by Quesnellus will be removed, while other previously unpublished letters will be added.

Finally, although Quesnellus quite properly published among Leo’s letters various letters of others written to Leo or concerning him, he inserted them without any number by which they could easily be cited and located. In addition to adding several more, we shall follow the example of the most approved editors and assign each its own number. This will disrupt the order of numbers proposed by Quesnellus considerably further.

58. In correcting the text, we shall not neglect Quesnellian variants, whether designated in the margin or in the notes. You will also find in the second volume of this edition the more extensive notes and observations of Quesnellus, which he himself placed in the second volume after the dissertations, repeatedly either elucidated or corrected by us.

An appendix will follow Leo’s letters. Besides spurious works, it will contain various other documents pertaining to Leo’s letters, including several previously unpublished items.

59. We do not append here a list of the codices of the individual collections which we used in correcting the letters. Since we have named them distinctly above in their proper places, and since in most collections there is only one or only a few, it will be easy to determine which codex from each collection we shall cite.

Only because we found several manuscript exemplars in Collection 21 should it be noted that two were especially useful: Vatican manuscripts 543 and 546. You will understand these to be intended whenever you encounter citations of the Vatican manuscripts of Collection 21.

If other codices seemed worth consulting for certain readings, we shall cite them by their proper names.

[Col. 0581] 60. Finally, we note here that Cassian’s letter to Leo was omitted from the sequence of letters because it was addressed to Leo when he was not yet pontiff but archdeacon of the Roman Church, and is transcribed among the testimonies at the beginning.

The supplications of the deacons Theodore and Ischirion, the presbyter Athanasius, and the layman Stephen of the Alexandrian Church, which were addressed to Leo, bishop of Rome, and to the holy and universal Council of Chalcedon, and presented at that council, are inserted in the third act of the council itself. Since they do not concern a particular matter involving our Leo and were not sent to him, they did not seem able to occupy a proper place among the letters of this pontiff.

Rather, among Leo’s letters should have been counted the encyclical letter of Gennadius of Constantinople and the seventy-three bishops against the simoniacs. In volume V of the Councils, Venetian edition, page 45, it is transmitted as addressed to all the metropolitans, καὶ πρὸς τὸν πάπαν Ῥώμης, “and to the pope of Rome.”

Since this encyclical was written around the year 459, it would have to be said to have been sent to our Leo. But although the words καὶ πρὸς τὸν πάπαν Ῥώμης, “and to the pope of Rome,” are indeed read in the printed editions and in Colbertine manuscript 4262, they are omitted in two older manuscripts, the Caesarean and another Colbertine manuscript, 924, in which the subscriptions published by Baluzius are found.

We are therefore especially uncertain about this part of the superscription, insofar as it would refer to Leo; for this reason we have thought it sufficient to mention this letter only here.

[Col. 0551]

LETTERS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT, ROMAN PONTIFF. (G)*

[Col. 0581]

ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING TWO LETTERS, I AND II, INCLUDING ALSO LETTER XVIII. (G)

1. The two letters—1, to the bishop of Aquileia, and 2, to Septimus of Altinum—which should be joined together because of their subject matter, cannot be discussed without also saying something about Letter 18 to Januarius, which, because of the controversies it provoked, seems to have a considerable connection with them. Thus this first admonition will illuminate three letters.

2. After Cardinal Noris, in Book II, chapter 12 of his *Pelagian History*, published in parallel columns two letters of Leo, one to Septimus and the other to Januarius, and made it clear that both were of the same exemplar, doubts began to arise about one or the other of them.

Quesnellus, in an extended observation, accused the letter to Septimus of being spurious and believed Isidore Mercator to have been the author of the forgery.

Joseph Antelmius, on the contrary, in Dissertation 4, *On the Genuine Works of St. Leo the Great*, defended this letter as genuine and argued that the one to Januarius was spurious.

Several letters were subsequently published by both men, each attempting to defend his own position. Pagi followed the opinion of his friend and fellow countryman Antelmius in his *Critica* for the year 447, number 8. P. Bernard de Rubeis, in *Monuments of the Church of Aquileia*, chapter 15, page 140, favored Quesnellus.

Tillemont, volume XV, note 3 on the *Life of Leo*, page 890, soundly refutes Quesnellus’s arguments by which he attempted to reject the letter to Septimus. But he does not dare to approve Antelmius’s opinion, by which the letter to Januarius is rejected.

At the end he merely declares that, if this letter did not rest upon considerable authority and it were necessary to reject either the letter to Januarius or the letter to Septimus as spurious, the former would seem rather than the latter to deserve rejection. Nevertheless, he admits that in the work itself, article 7, page 431, nothing sufficiently forceful or convincing has been brought forward for disallowing either one.

§ I. On the Codices of the Various Collections in Which the Letters Mentioned Are Contained

3. Before stating our own judgment, by which we believe all these letters should be defended, we must first mention the manuscript codices and collections in which one, or two, or all three of the letters in question are found. From these, above all, the argument for their authenticity will be drawn.

The first letter alone, to the bishop of Aquileia, about which no one has any doubt, is found in the codices of the Third Collection, Barberinianus 2888 and Vatican 1342, as well as in Sichard’s exemplar.

4. Only Letter 18 to Januarius is found in the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, and through Dionysius in the Hispanic, Hadrianic, and pure Isidorian collections. Here, however, it must first be noted that the latter collection of Isidore, insofar as Leo’s letters are concerned, contains not a single one beyond those copied in the Hispanic collection, from which Isidore took them. In the Hadrianic collection, which derives from Dionysius, one letter, Letter 12 to Maurus, is read in addition to the Dionysian letters, as will be shown in the Admonition to that same letter.

The first point concerning Isidore had to be noted against Quesnellus, who affirms that the supposedly spurious letter to Septimus was derived from the Isidorian collection, thereby confusing the pure collection of Isidore, which contains no letter to Septimus, with the collection edited by Merlin, which, being an expanded Isidorian collection and called by us Collection 12, did receive that letter to Septimus.

The second point concerning the collection of Dionysius had to be prefaced against Antelmius, who, in the first letters he wrote in French concerning this controversy, seeking to evade the authority of Dionysius—which is especially weighty in favor of Letter 18 to Januarius—reports that this letter was not inserted by Dionysius but added by someone later, just as the letter to Maurus was added. But this comparison is entirely futile.

For two manuscripts of the pure Dionysius are available: Vaticanus 5845 and another preserved in the library of the King of France. In the manuscript of the King of France, the letter to Januarius appears in its proper place; but the letter to Maurus, although it too is genuine, as we shall see elsewhere, appears nowhere, since it was not inserted by Dionysius. In the Vatican manuscript 5845, the additions made to Dionysius at a later time can be clearly distinguished. None of these is inserted in its proper place, as happened in the Hadrianic collection; rather, they are found added at the end, after the pure collection of Dionysius has been copied. Among them is the letter to Maurus, as will be explained more fully in the admonition to that letter.

Indeed, the heading of Leo’s titles prefixed to the table, no. 48, requires the letter to [Col. 0583] Januarius, to which exactly that many titles—and no more—correspond in the body of the manuscript; but it excludes the letter to Maurus, which is numbered 49 in the Hadrianic editions. Hence Cresconius, who arranged his collection from the pure Dionysius, nowhere cites anything from the letter to Maurus, but gave the entire letter to Januarius as title 61.

The author of the Hispanic collection, who transferred into his own work whatever he found in Dionysius, with the same Dionysian titles, does indeed possess the letter to Januarius, with Dionysius’s title and text. But since he did not find the letter to Maurus there, he produced it from another abridged edition, which differs from the edition in which it was subsequently added to Dionysius.

Finally, the letter to Januarius is not placed by Dionysius at the end of Leo’s letters but in the middle: it is the fourth among the seven letters placed there by Dionysius. The letter to Maurus, however, since it is an addition, is located at the end of the Hadrianic collection, which received the Dionysian additions. The same would have happened to the letter to Januarius if it had been among the additions.

5. The earliest manuscripts—Vaticanus Reginae 1997 of Collection 1 of Lucca, and a similar Colbertine manuscript of Collection 4—present Letter 1 to the Aquileian bishop together with Letter 2 to Septimus, immediately following it. The same is true of another manuscript of the Paris Jesuits, cited by Antelmius in Letter 1 and by Pagi under the year 447, although its more recent document belongs to the year 615. Finally, the same arrangement is found in four exceptionally ancient manuscripts of Collection 8: Vaticanus 5845, the Vallicellian manuscript marked A. 5, the Vercelli manuscript of the ninth century, and Vaticanus 1353, which was transcribed from another Bergamo manuscript of the ninth century.

6. We find the same Letter 1 to the Aquileian bishop together with Letter 18 to Januarius—not as a single unit, but separated by other Leonine letters—in the manuscripts of Collections 11, 20, 21, and 22.

7. Finally, all three of these letters—Letter 1 to the Aquileian bishop, Letter 2 to Septimus joined immediately to it, and Letter 18 to Januarius copied separately—are contained in the manuscripts of the very ancient Collection 5, in a special Florentine manuscript of Collection 13 at San Marco, and in the manuscripts of Collections 12, 23, and 24, which we mentioned more fully in the preface.

## II. Evidence from the Manuscripts for Establishing the Authenticity of the Letters to Septimus of Altinum and Januarius of Aquileia, Which Alone Are Suspected by Some

8. From this information concerning the manuscripts we learn that the letters to Septimus and Januarius, which are disputed, are found in different collections: the letter to Septimus in nine collections, and the letter to Januarius in thirteen collections.

9. Since no one calls Letter 1 to the Aquileian bishop into question, it will be sufficient if we establish the authenticity of Letters 2 to Septimus and 18 to Januarius from the collections just mentioned. Although both are copied in several collections, we shall insist only upon the ancient collections, which were compiled around the sixth century, possess greater authority, and from which the others originated.

10. The letter to Septimus is read in Vaticanus Reginae, the first collection, compiled at the beginning of the sixth century, which contains nothing apocryphal; in the very ancient Collection 4 of the Lucca and Colbertine manuscripts; in the old Collection 5 and Collection 8; and finally in the manuscript of the Paris Jesuits. Although that manuscript extends, in its councils, to the year 615, since it presents a catalogue of the popes ending with Felix, the successor of Hormisdas, this collection may be regarded as having been compiled at its origin around that time, with later documents subsequently added to it.

It is strange that Quesnellus rejected this letter of Leo as spurious without taking into account at least the manuscripts of Collection 5, which he published under the name of the manuscript of the Roman Church. He can indeed withdraw from this objection by claiming that he did not regard this manuscript as having been compiled all at once, but assigned Leo’s letters to additions of a later period. Yet this is a fabricated escape, supported by neither reason nor authority.

All the ancient manuscripts of that collection mentioned either by Pithoeus or by Coustant, as well as our Vindobonese manuscripts, contain Leo’s letters; Quesnellus himself observes the same. In his note 1 on the letter to Maurus, no. 1, while discussing the Thuaneus manuscript, he commended the antiquity and care of this same collection.

Although this collection was formed neither under Leo nor by Romans, but outside Italy at the end of the fifth or beginning of the sixth century, as we shall show in Volume III, its antiquity and the care of its compiler are nevertheless so great that from this collection alone very substantial testimony accrues in defense of the second letter.

We may add another significant point. The letter to Septimus is read in all the oldest collections together with the letter to the Aquileian bishop, and conversely the letter to the Aquileian bishop is not found without the letter to Septimus, with the exception of Collection 3, which contains only the letter to the Aquileian bishop. In these collections, the letter about which there is no doubt is always presented with the other letter immediately following and joined to it.

This indicates that both letters were found together in the exemplars from which the ancient compilers copied them. Thus one cannot be doubted without doubting the other; and if there is no reason to doubt the first letter, neither can the second be doubted.

11. Letter 18 to Januarius can be defended most decisively by the authority of Dionysius alone. It is absolutely certain that shortly after Leo, Dionysius compiled his collection at Rome from authentic exemplars, and that he introduced nothing spurious. Who, without evident arguments—which plainly do not exist—would dare accuse him of having inserted this letter, as we have seen?

To the authority of the Dionysian collection is added another collection of equal antiquity, namely Quesnellian Collection 5, which derives from a different source, as Father Coustant rightly observed in the preface to the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, no. 87, p. 78. Another compiler, collecting Leo’s letters in a different region, obtained genuine exemplars in every other case; therefore, even regarding the exemplar of this letter—which, although it did not derive from Dionysius, nevertheless agrees with the Dionysian text—there can be no reasonable doubt.

Moreover, this one letter is dated in both collections by day, month, and consulship, chronological markers that suit Leo’s age. This strongly confirms its authenticity, since spurious letters generally conflict with such indications.

Nor should Antelmius’s objection cause concern. In Letter 1, no. 6, he listed manuscripts of ancient collections which, while presenting the genuine and indisputable letter to the Aquileian bishop, do contain the letter to Septimus but omit the letter to Januarius; he advanced this as an argument for spuriousness.

Among the oldest collections, however, is certainly Quesnellian Collection 5, of which he possessed insufficiently accurate knowledge. In that collection, together with those two letters, there is also the letter to Januarius, just as it is found in the Florentine manuscript of Collection 13 and in the manuscripts of Collection 24, which acknowledge an origin different from that of the Quesnellian collection.

Therefore, even in those very ancient times, when Collection 5 was composed not long after Leo, exemplars of all three letters existed. If this antiquity, where no certain objection is brought forward, is insufficient to prove the authenticity of this letter, then nothing in collections of this kind could be exempt from doubt.

12. The authority of the manuscripts and collections—especially the ancient ones—which we have considered thus far both for the letter to Septimus and for the letter to Januarius ought therefore to be sufficient to refute the conjectures set against them, so that no response would be necessary.

At this point, however, what Quesnellus himself replied to [Col. 0585] Antelmius in this very controversy, in his letter to a friend of 15 August 1689, is especially effective against both Quesnellus and Antelmius: namely, that manuscripts of such ancient collections are sufficient to demonstrate that the conjectures proclaimed in triumph must be counted among delusions, and that from this example many others of the same kind, put forward in the name of demonstrations, are rendered suspect.

Nevertheless, we do not wish to pass over the principal objections without some answer.

## III. Objections against the Letter to Septimus Answered

13. Quesnellus objects, in his notes on the letter to Septimus, that the Aquileian bishop is there called “Metropolitan of the province of Venetia,” whereas formerly this was called the province of Istria, as he attempts to show from Pelagius, Gregory, and other later documents.

But on what basis does he determine that before Pelagius this province was called Istria rather than Venetia? Certainly Saint Ambrose, in his letter to the people of Vercelli, calls it the territory of Liguria, Aemilia, and Venetia; and at the Roman council of the year 501, volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 457, the bishops of Liguria, Aemilia, and Venetia are likewise named.

Saint Leo flourished between the time of Ambrose and that council. If he said “of Venetia” rather than “of the Venetias,” this makes no difference, since in inscriptions and in the consular register of the empire one finds “Venetia,” “province of Venetia,” and so forth, in the singular number.

14. Much less weight should be given to what the same Quesnellus asserts: that the same letter contains threats of deposition. For those who examine the matter carefully will see that the words of the letter to the Aquileian bishop, which is entirely genuine, imply precisely the same thing.

Moreover, Leo himself, in Letter 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne, chapter 7, indicates clearly enough that, out of consideration for the Apostolic See, he refrained from deposing Hilary, the Gallican metropolitan; Valentinian confirms this in Novel 11.

In the case of the Pelagians, who are the subject of the letter to Septimus, there is the additional fact that the law of Honorius against Pelagius and Coelestius had decreed the loss of episcopal office not only for those infected by this heresy but also against those who, by dissembling and conniving, or by failing to condemn it, had shown harmful favor toward it. The letter to Septimus, however, speaks of rulers who, by acting too negligently toward the Pelagians, were conniving at the spreading heresy.

## IV. Objections against the Letter to Januarius Dispelled

15. Antelmius (Letter 1, nos. 13 ff.) objects to the letter to Januarius that what is decreed there from the canons was foreign to the discipline of that age: namely, that clerics returning from heresy or schism were granted, by way of indulgence, permission to remain in the same rank, but were not to be promoted to higher offices.

“Concerning these persons,” Saint Leo says, “we likewise command that the canonical decree be observed, so that they may regard it as a great benefit if, after every hope of promotion has been taken from them, they remain in perpetual stability in the order in which they are found, provided that they have not been defiled by a repeated baptism.”

Antelmius maintains that no such general canonical decree concerning all heretics and schismatics existed in Leo’s age. When Quesnellus asserted in his notes, no. 3, that the reference was to Nicene Canon 8, Antelmius replies that this canon, which concerns only the Cathari—that is, the Novatians—could not have been understood or cited by Leo as a general rule concerning all heretics and schismatics.

He further attempts to show that neither this Nicene canon nor any other prohibited those received into their former rank from being promoted to a higher order; indeed, he tries to demonstrate by several examples that precisely because they were received into their former rank, they could also be advanced to a higher one.

16. To refute this objection, it must first be stated that the primitive discipline of the Church was that no one—whether cleric or layperson—returning from heresy was to be received into the clerical order.

In the West, witnesses to this discipline are Saint Cyprian, Letter 72 to Stephen; Innocent I, Letter 17, no. 8, and Letter 24, no. 4; and the council of Italy, among the canons of the African Church, chapter 56. Although the African bishops acknowledged the equity of this law, they nevertheless sent a delegation to Pope Anastasius asking that, because of the scarcity of clerics, the severity of the law might be somewhat relaxed.

Indeed, other African bishops, in their letter to John II, speaking of Arian priests returning to the Church, declared: “From the silent feelings of all our colleagues, we have perceived that no one approves their being received with their honors” (Councils, vol. V, p. 901).

That the same principle prevailed in the East is clear from Athanasius’s letter to Rufinianus. There, recalling a decree by which certain persons, less culpably deceived by the Arians, had been admitted to the clergy, he affirms that this had been done by a certain dispensation. A dispensation presupposes a contrary law.

Augustine indicates the same dispensation in Letter 185, no. 44. When the Donatists objected: “If, then, we ought to repent that we were outside the Church and against the Church, how is it that after this repentance we remain among you as clerics or even bishops?” he replies: “This would not happen—because, in truth, as must be admitted, it ought not to happen—unless it were healed by the compensation of peace itself.”

It ought not to have happened because, as persons unworthy of the honors of the clergy, they were excluded by the discipline of the Church; but for the sake of peace it was necessary to employ a dispensation. Hence our Leo rightly wrote that receiving heretics and schismatics into their former rank was to be considered a great benefit.

For the same reason, Nicene Canon 8 must likewise be attributed to a dispensation: by it the clerics of the Cathari were restored to their former rank for the sake of peace. The same must be understood of the other heretics and schismatics who were similarly received.

But whether those whose former rank was granted by dispensation were also permitted to rise to a higher one, the Nicene canon seems sufficiently to indicate: “Let them remain in the clergy, and thereafter let them remain in the same order.” Certainly those who rise to a higher order do not remain in the same order.

Let us, however, set aside this canon as not entirely clear. Since the other testimonies likewise speak of persons received into their former rank, there is no reason to infer from one dispensation another and broader one.

17. That this discipline prevailed in the West—or at least in Italy and in the Roman Church—so that those received into their former rank did not rise to a higher one is clear from the decree by which Saint Ambrose, in the case of Dictinius, who had returned from the Priscillianists to the Catholics, determined that, for the sake of peace, he should retain his place among the presbyters but should not receive an increase of honor.
