This is attested by the Fathers of the Council of Toledo in the year 400. They consequently complained that he had nevertheless been promoted by Symphosius to the episcopate. The matter was excused, however, on the grounds that this had been forced by the multitude of the people.

It is quite probable that this judgment of Ambrose was approved by Pope Siricius, who wrote a letter in the same case, since the same Fathers praise Siricius’s letter in the same passage.

Zosimus also seems to confirm the same discipline in Letter 4 to Aurelius and the other bishops, where the case of Tuetius, who had been improperly ordained a bishop, is discussed. Among his other faults, no. 3, he charges him with the following: although he had been a Priscillianist, and had been carefully healed by the Apostolic See, the humanity and mercy of that same See had formerly provided for him, so that it had granted him a benefit almost without precedent; but, failing to observe this benefit—that is, not content with it—he had hastened headlong to the priesthood and had not considered that he should remain in the rank proper to him.

It could not have been called a benefit almost without precedent for a repentant and healed heretic to be received into the unity of the Church, unless this meant that he was restored to his former rank or presbyterate. If he was blameworthy because, failing to observe this benefit and rank, he did not abstain from a position improper to him, then it is undoubtedly to be presumed that those received from heresy were not permitted to rise to a further rank.

Our Leo approves this discipline still more clearly in Letter 135. Antelmius brings it forward [Col. 0587] by way of objection because there Saint Leo ordered Andrew and Euphratas, formerly supporters of Eutyches, to be promoted to the presbyterate.

But the context makes clear that this was granted on account of a particular circumstance and by a certain dispensation. Leo was disturbed that the archdeaconate of the Church of Constantinople, after Aetius, the defender of Flavian, had been removed under the pretext of promotion, had been conferred upon Andrew, who had formerly adhered to the Eutychian heresy and had accused Saint Flavian. It seemed unworthy that the ministry of so important an office should be taken away from one who had always held the Catholic faith in order to entrust it to one who had once been tainted by heretical defilement.

Hence, after vehemently complaining about Andrew’s promotion, Leo affirmed in Letter 112 that his conversion from heresy and his satisfaction—which Antelmius cites—could have merited only this one indulgence: that he be received into the rank of deacon, not that he be preferred to the others:

“Even if,” he says, “he could have merited indulgence through great satisfaction, he ought by no means to have been preferred to those who had remained in the faith.” Similarly, in Letter 111, chapter 3: “Even if he had been cleansed through great satisfaction, nevertheless, after returning from his doubtful error, he ought to have been placed after the Catholic deacons, not before them.”

When Anatolius, in order to satisfy Leo, removed Andrew from the archdeaconate and reserved to the pontiff’s judgment what should be done with him, this pleased Leo so much that he ordered Andrew himself and his associate Euphratas—who had likewise accused Flavian—to be promoted to the presbyterate, once they had demonstrated through explicit professions that they had corrected their error. Perhaps this was done so that they might never be able to insinuate themselves into the archdeaconate.

That this was granted by a special dispensation is suggested by the decree immediately following concerning the others who were involved in an equal guilt. If these should seek pardon with a similar profession and satisfaction, Leo decrees that they are not to be promoted but merely restored to their former orders, with the further condition that only those whose freedom from every error has been established may be admitted to the primacy of offices.

Does not this prohibition—that no one received from heresy within the same order may be promoted to the primacy of that order, a rule clearly still in force under Saint Gregory, as is evident from Book I, Letter 77—presuppose an expressly stated constitution in Letter 18 to Januarius, forbidding clerics of the same kind, once restored to their orders, to rise to a higher order?

A special dispensation in an exceptional case does not derogate from a general constitution. If other similar examples were brought forward, they too would have to be referred to a dispensation.

The examples produced by Antelmius concern persons received into the same order, not those promoted to a higher one. Such are the two cases of the bishops Maximus and Donatus, mentioned by Leo in Letter 12, no. 12, chapter 6, as well as the other case of the Donatists in Augustine, Letter 43, no. 16.

As for what he introduces concerning the Meletians from the letter of the Council of Nicaea in Theodoretus, Book I, chapters 8 and 9, it proves only that clerics ordained by Meletius, who had been received into their former rank in such a way that they occupied the lowest place after the clerics ordained by the legitimate bishop, with all authority reserved to the latter, could after their death be substituted in their place and authority if certain circumstances required it. This promotion concerns the same order endowed with authority, not a higher order.

But whatever one may think of this case, neither it nor any other exceptional case—which must be attributed to a dispensation—can call into doubt the constitution and discipline which we have shown to be sufficiently certain from the testimony of Ambrose, Zosimus, and Leo himself.

Therefore, there is no reason on this account to reject the letter to Januarius as though it presented a discipline unknown in that period.

18. As for which canons Leo understood when he invoked a canonical constitution in this matter: since the existence of the discipline is established by what has been said, the inability to produce a certain canon or constitution, given the great scarcity of ancient records, is of no consequence.

Perhaps Saint Leo thought that Nicene Canon 8, which legislates concerning the Cathari or Novatians, should, in accordance with the discipline of his own time, be understood and presented as encompassing all heretics and schismatics.

Even if Innocent I, in Letter 17 to the Macedonians, chapter 3, affirms that this canon speaks only of the Novatians and does not apply to clerics of other heresies, that same pontiff nevertheless does not deny in the same letter that this benefit, decreed for the Novatians alone, could be extended not only to other schismatics but also to heretics whenever the good of peace and necessity required such indulgence.

Accordingly, he judged the decision of Anysius and his colleagues worthy of approval: they had received into their former ranks those ordained by Bonosus the heretic. Likewise, in Letter 3 to the Council of Toledo, with the same intention he not only approved the moderation of that council, which had decreed that converted Priscillianists should be received into their former ranks, but also reproved those who opposed this indulgence as contrary to the canons.

From this example such indulgence seems gradually to have gained strength, so that in Leo’s time the good and necessity of the Church required that the same rule be understood of all schismatics and heretics, provided they had not been defiled by a repeated baptism. For all the canons and the constant discipline of the Church excluded such persons from orders and from the clergy.

It should not be thought that this practice gained force in any other way, or was approved by Innocent in any other sense, than as belonging to the discipline which, as we have shown from Ambrose, prevailed before Innocent. Leo could therefore cite this canon as incorporated into that discipline.

Whatever one may wish to think about this canon, if Innocent’s Letter 3 to the Council of Toledo is not to be rejected merely because it attributes to the Nicene regulations certain sanctions that are not found in the Nicene canon, then Leo’s letter to Januarius, preserved by the authority of Dionysius Exiguus and confirmed by the authority of the fifth collection, should be rejected even less. If it commends a canonical constitution, it does not call it Nicene; nevertheless, it agrees sufficiently with Nicene Canon 8, understood and extended more broadly according to the discipline of the Church.

19. Antelmius’s more serious objection is based on the fact that the letter to Januarius is copied, in almost exactly the same words, partly from the letter to Septimus and partly from the letter to the Aquileian bishop.

Since the words of the letter to Septimus are found repeated in the letter to Januarius, it is presumed that one or the other must certainly be false. Quesnellus accused the letter to Septimus of falsity.

Antelmius, however, argues even more readily that the letter to Januarius should be rejected on the basis of this repetition, because in it not only the entire letter to Septimus is repeated, but even that final sentence, which is left suspended at its conclusion, is taken from the letter to the Aquileian bishop. It is incredible, he maintains, that two letters sent at the same time to the same Aquileian bishop should end with the same sentence, especially since that sentence is not found in the letter to Septimus.

20. This objection, although it possesses some force, does not exceed the limits of conjecture. No conjecture can prevail against the certain authority of Dionysius, who compiled his collection at Rome shortly after Leo’s time, nor against the authority of the earlier—or at least contemporary—Quesnellian Collection 5, by which the letter to Januarius is vindicated.

Moreover, for this objection to have any force against Leo, it must presuppose two hypotheses: first, that Letter 1 to the Aquileian bishop was delivered to the same Januarius to whom Letter 18 is addressed; and second, that it was delivered at the same time.

For if these two letters were sent to two different Aquileian bishops, or if they were written to the same bishop but not at the same time, the entire difficulty concerning Leo disappears.

It is established that when writing to different persons this pontiff sometimes transmitted letters in the same form, with only a few changes or additions, as happened in Letters 150 to Basil and 151 to Euxitheus. At other times he copied certain passages word for word from one letter into another. Thus he inserted seven complete chapters in Letter 166 to the Emperor Leo, which are found excerpted from Letter 126 to the Palestinians.

Moreover, it will become clear from the following section that Letters 1 and 18 were probably sent to different Aquileian bishops, and certainly that a considerable period—several years—elapsed between them. There we shall show that the first letter was written [Col. 0589] not to Januarius but, more probably, to his predecessor.

Or, at the very least, whoever received it, it was written at the beginning of Leo’s pontificate, around the year 442—that is, approximately five years before Letter 18, which was delivered to Januarius at the end of the year 447.

Thus, when Leo wrote to the latter in that year, he first copied the letter to Septimus with certain alterations; then, from Letter 1, probably written long before to his predecessor, he took only the final sentence and closed the letter. This final sentence may be regarded as a kind of formula or concluding clause of decrees, as Father Bernard of Rubeis seems to have thought, so that it is not surprising to find the same sentence in different letters to the same person.

But whatever may be thought of these replies, the testimony of the Quesnellian and Dionysian collections, as we have said, most certainly outweighs every conjecture and objection.

## V. Which Aquileian Bishop Received the First Letter Written by Leo: From This the Date of the First and Second Letters Is Also Established

21. Now that both the letter to Septimus, against Quesnellus, and the other letter to Januarius, against Antelmius—both of which had been called into question—have been vindicated, we must ask to whom Letter 1 to the Aquileian bishop was delivered. On the same occasion, the date at which both this letter and the other letter to Septimus, which lack chronological indications, were written will be established.

The assumption that the first letter was delivered to Januarius, the Aquileian bishop, rests on no sufficiently certain foundation. For the manuscripts give it without the bishop’s name, either as “to the Aquileian bishop,” as in Vaticanus Reginae of Collection 1, Barberinus and Vaticanus of Collection 3, the Lucca manuscript with the Colbertine manuscript of Collection 4, the Vindobonese manuscript of Collection 5, and Vaticanus 5845, among the Dionysian additions of Collection 8; or as “to Aquileius,” as in Vaticanus and Ottobonianus of Collection 11, the manuscript of Santa Croce in Jerusalem of Collection 20, and the manuscripts of Collections 21 and 22.

Quesnellus makes the same statement concerning his manuscripts, merely noting that the two later manuscripts, Cisterciensis and Isidorianus, have “To the metropolitan bishop of Venetia.”

The Louvain editors, followed thereafter by others, were perhaps the first to add, without—so far as we know—the testimony of any manuscript, the title: “To Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.”

In the manuscripts of Collections 12 and 24, Letter 2 to Septimus is copied first, and Letter 1 is then placed immediately after it, with the heading “To the same,” as though it had been delivered to the same Septimus. For this reason, in one manuscript from Fiesole and another Florentine manuscript of San Lorenzo, marked no. 14, shelf 21, which contain several letters from manuscripts of Collection 24, the following inscription is prefixed to the first letter: “Leo to Septimus, bishop.”

This is undoubtedly erroneous, since Septimus, who was not bishop of Aquileia but of Altinum, is named at the very beginning of Letter 1 as the person on whose account Leo wrote to the Aquileian bishop. Yet neither do these manuscripts support the attribution to Januarius.

22. Only Vaticanus Ottobonianus 297 of Collection 23 and certain manuscripts of Collection 8, such as the Vercelli manuscript and Vaticanus 1353, give the name Januarius.

But it is clear that this name was inserted later into the manuscripts of Collection 8, since it had previously been absent from that collection. This is evident from the Vallicellian manuscript A. 5, and still more clearly from Vaticanus 5845, which also belongs to Collection 8.

For in the Vallicellian manuscript the text reads, on page 278, “to the Aquileian bishop,” while the name Januarius is visibly added above. In the oldest Vatican manuscript, 5845, in whose additions pertaining to Collection 8 this letter is found, no trace of Januarius appears.

We therefore learn that in the manuscripts of this collection the name Januarius was originally entirely absent, as in Vaticanus 5845; that it was then added above the line, as in the Vallicellian manuscript; and finally that it entered the text, as in the Vercelli manuscript and Vaticanus 1353.

Since the author of Collection 23, contained in Ottobonianus 297, copied the first fifteen letters word for word and in the same order from manuscripts of Collection 8, when he inserted the name Januarius he was using a manuscript of that collection in which the name had been inserted or added above the line. Thus the entire authority of this name is reduced to Collection 8 alone; yet we have shown that this collection originally lacked the name, just as the other manuscripts—and especially the oldest manuscripts of all the collections—also lack it.

Hence the Florentine manuscript of San Marco, Collection 13, which is distinguished by other features concerning Leo’s letters, as we shall see in the Admonition to Letter 12, gives this heading to the letter under discussion:

“Leo, bishop of the city of Rome . . . . . to the Aquileian bishop.”

The blank interval signifies that the name of the bishop was unknown.

Once, therefore, the authority of the manuscripts that give Januarius has been removed, nothing remains in the manuscripts that compels us to affirm that Letter 1 was delivered to the same Januarius to whom Letter 18 was plainly written.

23. That it was addressed to some predecessor of Januarius, and indeed at the very beginning of Leo’s pontificate, may be gathered from other evidence. Photius, in describing an ancient codex composed at the beginning of the sixth century, containing a most exact history of Pelagian affairs derived from particular documents, reports the following concerning the deeds of the Pelagians under Leo’s pontificate (Bibliotheca, cod. 54):

> As time then passed, after the members of this sect had been restored to the Church through their renunciation of their heresy, the evil was renewed by them. But Septimus, the bishop, checked the course of the resurgent plague by sending a letter to Leo, who at that time held the apostolic see at Rome; and Leo fought against the impious with fervent zeal. Not long afterward, however, when the bitter root showed no shame at sprouting again, certain people in Rome were speaking openly in favor of the heresy. But a certain Prosper, truly a man of God, by delivering written accusations against them made them disappear, while the aforementioned Leo was still governing the Roman see.

Two actions against the Pelagians under Leo are indicated: the first, in which Septimus and Leo jointly exerted themselves, and to which the two following letters certainly correspond; the second, later in time, in which Saint Prosper presented written accusations at Rome, as we shall explain more fully in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 2, chapter 1, final section.

The author of the work *On the Promises*, a contemporary of Leo, writes in part IV, chapter 6:

> In Italy also, while we were staying in Campania, when the venerable Pope Leo, who must be named with apostolic honor, was overthrowing the Manichaeans and crushing the Pelagians, and especially Julian, a certain Florus, as it happened, etc.

This context assigns both of Leo’s undertakings, against the Manichaeans and against the Pelagians, to the same period. Prosper dates the overthrow of the Manichaeans in his *Chronicle* to the year 443; and it may be inferred that this belongs to the end of that year from Leo’s Letter 4, dated 10 October, in which, writing to the bishops of Campania, he said nothing about avoiding the Manichaeans, as he later warned in Letter 7, written on 30 January of the following year, 444.

In the fifth sermon *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*, delivered on Sunday, 12 December 443, when he was about to announce the fast of the four seasons, he declared to the people what had been done against the Manichaeans; he repeats the same point in Sermon 4 *On the Nativity of the Lord*, which is clearly shown to have been delivered on the Nativity of that same year. Thus, at the same time when the holy pontiff overthrew the Manichaeans, he also crushed the Pelagians.

Of the two actions against the Pelagians mentioned in Photius’s ancient codex, the first, in which Leo is said to have acted together with Septimus of Altinum, seems less well suited to the words of the book *On the Promises*, “he was crushing the Pelagians, and especially Julian.” For in the case of Septimus the Pelagians of the province of Aquileia are concerned, among whom Julian or the other Campanian heretics had no part; nor can Leo properly be said to have crushed them merely because of the letter in which he prescribed a cautious procedure for receiving them.

Therefore, the words “he was crushing the Pelagians, and especially Julian” fit the second event more aptly. From it we learn that the audacity of the Pelagians had advanced so far that even in Rome there were people who spoke openly. Julian may have contributed something to these Pelagian efforts. When Prosper delivered his written accusations, and the Pelagians soon disappeared, it is certain that Pope Leo—who, as is clear from other evidence, was especially hostile to them—devoted all his efforts against them; we understand that he crushed them.

This event, together with the action against the Manichaeans, joined together in the book *On the Promises*, belongs to the end of the year 443. The event in the province of Aquileia, in which Septimus and Leo acted together against the Pelagians, had occurred somewhat earlier, as the words with which Photius introduces the second event indicate: “Not long afterward, however, again …” (*μεν` ού πολὺ δὲ πάλιν*: “not much later, however, again”). Therefore, this event in the province of Aquileia must be assigned to the beginning of 443, or to 442.

Accordingly, Letter 1 to the bishop of Aquileia, which concerns this event, cannot be attributed to any successor of Januarius, but to Adelphus, whom we believe Saint Peter Chrysologus praises in Sermon 136, or rather to Maximus, who is reported in the Aquileian catalogues and chronicles to have been the immediate predecessor of Januarius after Adelphus. This may be affirmed with greater probability if the beginning of Januarius’s episcopate is to be placed in the year 443, as Dandulus noted in his *Chronicle*.

24. This may be confirmed especially by the text of Letter 18 to Januarius himself:

> Lest the serpentine deceit be able to prevail, we have judged that your Dilection should be admonished, indicating that it pertains to the danger of the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics or schismatics and has in some way stained himself with the contagion of heretical communion, after coming to his senses, should be held in Catholic communion without a legitimate profession of satisfaction.

The words “we have judged that your Dilection should be admonished” do not refer to an earlier Letter 1 addressed to the same Januarius, in which a similar position is explained at greater length. It is plainly evident from what precedes that the discussion concerns a letter written in reply after Januarius’s letter had been read. Thus, just as at the beginning of Letter 18 it says, “Having read the letter of your Brotherhood, we recognized the vigor of your faith, congratulating you, etc.,” so it later adds, “we have judged that you should be admonished, indicating, etc.” Both the congratulation and the indication are made in the same Letter 18 after Leo had read Januarius’s own letter.

This is also demanded by the preceding word *possit* (“may be able”) and the following *habeatur* (“should be held”). If the discussion concerned an earlier letter and a matter indicated long ago, the force of the expression *duximus commonendam* (“we have judged that [you] should be admonished”) would require *posset* and *haberet* for the syntax to be correct. If this is judged evident, it follows that the first letter was not addressed to Januarius.

For Leo thereby indicates that he has now decided to admonish him, as though he had never previously admonished him concerning the same matter. Therefore, Letter 1, in which the same admonition is delivered at greater length, must be said to have been addressed not to Januarius but to one of his predecessors.

25. From these considerations the date of the two following letters can also be established, and it will become clear why we began with them. The year 444, to which Quesnellus assigned these letters on the authority of the book *On the Promises*, is sufficiently disproved once the same testimony and the authority of Photius have been explained. The opinion of Antelmius is rejected still more decisively, for he assigns the same letters to the year 447.

At first sight, the chief point on which Antelmius insists may not seem insignificant. In Letter 1, no. 11, page 7, he maintains that chapter 1 of the letter to the bishop of Aquileia mentions “our decrees,” and that chapter 5 says: “It was formerly decreed by the holy Fathers and by us many times,” in a discussion of the prohibition against the transfer of clerics from one church to another. By these words, he believes that other decrees of Leo issued before this letter are indicated.

Yet it is not necessary, with Antelmius, to understand this as referring to Letters 13 to the metropolitans of Illyricum and Letter 14 to Anastasius, written in 446, in which a similar decree is found. Since it appears established from what has been said that Letter 1 to the bishop of Aquileia was written around the year 442, and since it is certain that several of Leo’s letters have perished, as will be noted in many places, it is sufficiently probable that before the year 442, at the very beginning of his pontificate, the same pontiff had occasion to renew an ancient constitution.

That constitution, formerly issued by the Fathers—that is, by the Nicene and Sardican canons, which the Roman Church had then received—and repeatedly renewed by Damasus and his other successors, and finally renewed by Leo himself, could rightly be called something “often decreed.” Moreover, in annotation 27 on Letter 9 to Dioscorus we shall show that the words “to us” there refer not so much to Leo as to his predecessors. Thus here also the expressions “by us” and “our decrees” may be understood of the decrees of Leo’s predecessors.

Since the authority of predecessors and successors is one and the same, and since papal decrees derive all their force from this authority, decrees issued by predecessors through an authority shared with their successors could be called “our decrees.” To call them “our decrees,” therefore, is equivalent to saying that they were issued by papal authority, which is one and the same in predecessors and successors alike.

Gelasius also used a similar manner of speaking, as we shall show in the annotations on chapter 50 of the codex edited by Quesnellus.

26. That the two following letters were written at the beginning of Leo’s pontificate and around the year 442 will also be confirmed by a certain historical observation, which was first brought forward by Cardinal Norisius, volume III, page 1177, and volume IV, page 752; afterward by Pagi, under the year 418, no. 57; and finally by P. Bernardus de Rubeis, *Aquileian Monuments*, chapter 14, page 120.

Sirmondus transcribed from a manuscript at Verona a profession of faith issued by the Pelagians. From Sirmondus’s copy, Garnerius published this profession in his edition of Marius Mercator, and afterward the Benedictines of Saint Maur published it in the appendix to volume X of Augustine, page 110.

This profession of Pelagian faith concludes as follows:

> Here ends the profession of faith of S. I. C.

Garnerius wrongly interpreted these initials as *Siculorum* (“of the Sicilians”), whereas Tillemont and the Benedictines believe they should more properly be explained as *Sacerdotum Jesu Christi* (“of the priests of Jesus Christ”).

This profession is known to have been addressed to Augustine from the word *Augustine*, which is inserted in the document. From the context it can be understood that he was the metropolitan, primate, or superior of the very Pelagians who presented the profession.

Garnerius and the Benedictines, recognizing that this could not apply to Saint Augustine, bishop of Hippo, suspected an error on the part of the copyists and thought that *Zosimo* (“to Zosimus”) should be read instead of *Augustine*. They consequently believed that this was one or the other of the two professions which Julian of Eclanum and the other Pelagians are known to have presented to Pope Zosimus.

Although the profession transcribed by Sirmondus contains some matters similar in substance to the two aforementioned professions, the words that survive from those professions in Augustine and Marius Mercator are not found in this document. It therefore cannot be identified with either of the two presented to Zosimus.

Consequently, it must be recognized as another profession, presented after Zosimus’s *Tractoria*—the decree issued throughout the whole world against the Pelagians, which required subscriptions—to some metropolitan named Augustine, who had issued a letter requesting subscriptions to the *Tractoria*.

Chromatius of Aquileia, famous at the beginning of the fifth century, was succeeded by Augustine, who flourished under Pope Zosimus. Norisius was the first of all to note that this profession had rightly been presented to him by the Pelagians.

It is therefore evident that the Pelagian heresy had already entered the province of Aquileia from the beginning. It had become so powerful there while Augustine held the Aquileian see that the authors of the aforementioned profession not only refused to subscribe to Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, but even dared to appeal to a plenary synod.

There is consequently nothing surprising in the fact that under Pope Leo—that is, about twenty years later—some remnants of the Pelagians still remained among the presbyters and clerics of that province. When Septimus of Altinum reported these to the same pontiff, Leo, in addition to Letter 2, by which he replied to Septimus, sent another letter to the metropolitan of Aquileia, so that an effective remedy might be applied to these remnants.

This event is more reasonably assigned to approximately 442 than to later years. For it is probable that the Pelagians of this province, having been harassed from the time of Augustine after Zosimus’s *Tractoria*, were not long afterward received into the unity of the Church. Yet when Septimus discovered that some had been imprudently admitted without the condemnation of their error and of its authors and without the required subscriptions, Leo ordered that the remedy of explicit condemnation and subscription be applied to them.

This most probably occurred at the beginning of Leo’s pontificate, especially if Letter 1 is believed to have been addressed not to Januarius but to one of his predecessors. When this predecessor soon died, Januarius energetically and successfully carried out the same undertaking, which required a considerable period of time. In the year 447, therefore, Saint Leo received a letter from him in which Januarius, displaying his zeal and diligence, seems to have reported not only that Pelagians had been cautiously restored to their rank, but also that some had been promoted to a higher rank.

Leo first commended his zeal, then impressed upon him the old admonition that no one coming from heresy should be received without the required guarantees. He then judged that the canonical constitution should also be brought forward: those who had been admitted to their own rank should not likewise be promoted to a higher one. From the same letter of Januarius he had discovered that this was the one remaining matter requiring correction.

589. LETTER I  
[Note: [Col. 0593B] Formerly no. 6; what was previously no. 1 is now no. 12. Written around the year 442.]

[Note: [Col. 0593B] We presented the variant readings of this title in the preceding introduction, no. 21. See also Quesnellus’s note 1 [Col. 0593C]. The letter itself is found in thirteen collections of different origin, which we listed there under nos. 3, 5, 6, and 7, and also in Sichardus.]

TO THE BISHOP OF AQUILEIA.

[Col. 0593A]

[Note: [Col. 0593C] In the table of Quesnellus’s collection 5, this title appears as chapter 82: “To the bishop of Aquileia, concerning the careless reception of Pelagianists, so that no one of the ecclesiastical order may be transferred from one church to another.”]

SYNOPSIS

I. The Pelagians are wrongly received into communion without renunciation of their error and profession of the faith.  
II. He orders a synod to be convened so that a profession of faith may be required from them.  
III. What should be believed concerning the grace of Christ?  
IV. Anyone who does not submit to the Church’s decrees concerning grace must be expelled from it.  
V. Everyone must remain where he was ordained.

CHAPTER I

From the report of our holy brother and fellow bishop Septimus [Note: [Col. 0593C] The printed editions read *Septimii*. We have followed the testimony of our manuscripts, especially the older ones, which prefer *Septimus* not only here but also in the following letter. Photius, codex 54, agrees with them in the passage cited in the introduction, no. 23. In place of *in subditis*, Sichardus’s copy, together with certain later manuscripts, reads *in scriptis*. But the expression *in subditis* (“in what follows”) indicates that Leo has appended Septimus’s report to this letter.], which is contained in what follows, we have learned that certain presbyters [Note: [Col. 0593C] On the authority of six more authoritative manuscripts, we have added the conjunction “and.”] and deacons and clerics of various orders, whom the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy had entangled, have come to Catholic communion in your province in such a way that no condemnation of their own error was required from them [Note: [Col. 0593C] Codex Vaticanus 5845 reads “by the same persons.”];

and that, while pastoral watchmen were sleeping too deeply [Col. 0593B] [Note: [Col. 0593D] The editions preceding Quesnellus and the manuscripts of collections 4 and 24, together with Sichardus’s copy, read: “a wolf covered with sheep’s feet … should enter.”], wolves clothed in sheep’s skins entered the Lord’s sheepfold (Matthew 7:15) without laying aside their bestial dispositions;

and that they usurped what, by the authority of the canons and our decrees, is not granted even to the innocent [Note: [Col. 0593D] Another reading: “to claim”];

so that, abandoning the churches in which they had either received or regained the clerical office, they might carry their instability about in different places [Note: [Col. 0593D] The Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with only the manuscripts of collection 24 [Col. 0594B] and Sichardus, reads: “that in their instability they may be carried about through various places.”], always loving to wander and never to remain upon the apostolic foundation.

For those who have not been examined by any investigation and have not been bound by any prior judgment concerning their profession seek this fruit above all: that under the cover of communion they may enter many houses and corrupt the hearts of many through knowledge falsely so called [Note: [Col. 0594B] Two manuscripts read “through ignorance.”].

They could certainly not accomplish this if the bishops of the churches had maintained the necessary diligence in receiving such persons [Note: [Col. 0594C] Another reading, found with the manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus: “if they had maintained it.” The words “so that no one of them would have been permitted to wander into different places” are absent from the Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1. Sichardus omits “into different places.”]. Thus no one of them would have been permitted to wander into different places.

CHAPTER II

Therefore, lest this be dared any longer [Note: [Col. 0594C] We have restored the word *audeatur* (“be dared”), which Quesnellus excluded on the authority of his manuscripts, on the authority of six of our manuscripts belonging to five collections of different origin and particular importance. Among these, four especially ancient manuscripts deserve mention: the Vatican Regius, collection 1; Vatican 1342, collection 3; Lucca, collection 4; and Vallicellian A. 5, collection 8. It is also found in Sichardus’s copy. The editions of Canisius and Nicolinus have *audiatur* (“be heard”) instead of *audeatur*.], and lest the destruction introduced through the negligence of certain persons extend to the overthrow of many souls, by the authority of this command of ours we charge your Brotherhood’s diligence that, once a synod of the provincial priests has been convened among you, all—whether presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any order—[Note: [Col. 0594C] The words “who have been received from the company of the Pelagians and Coelestians” are absent from the Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1.] who have been received from the company of the Pelagians and Coelestians into Catholic communion with such recklessness that they were not first compelled to condemn their error, must now, at least after their hypocrisy has been partly exposed [Col. 0594B], be compelled to true correction, which can benefit them and harm no one.

Let them openly condemn, in formal professions of their own, the authors of their proud error [Note: [Col. 0594C] See Quesnellus’s note 2 and our observation on that note.], and let them detest whatever the universal Church has abhorred in their teaching. Let them declare, in full, open, and personally signed statements, that they embrace and approve in every respect all the synodal decrees which the authority of the Apostolic See has confirmed for the destruction of this heresy [Note: [Col. 0594C] Our observation on Quesnellus’s note 3 should be read.].

Let nothing obscure or ambiguous be found in their words [Note: [Col. 0594C] Codex Vaticanus, collection 11, deletes “nothing obscure.” In the manuscripts of collection 21: “Let nothing obscure, nothing ambiguous in meaning, be found in their words.”]. For we know this to be their characteristic trickery: in whatever small part of the accursed doctrine they have distinguished themselves from the solidity of what must be condemned [Note: [Col. 0594D] Most and the better of our manuscripts confirm Quesnellus’s emendation, especially Vatican Regius, collection 1; Vatican, collection 3; Lucca, collection 4; Vienna, collection 5; and three manuscripts of collection 8. Three copies of the later collections 11 and 21 read: “in which they have distinguished themselves from the solidity of our [or: their] people.” The editions before Quesnellus, together with Sichardus, read: “in which they have distinguished themselves from the company of the condemned.” We found this reading in Vatican manuscript 544, collection 24, which alone omits *qua*. Antelmius, in his first letter, written in French and appended to his dissertations *On the True Works of Saints Leo and Prosper*, no. 26, angrily reproached Quesnellus for changing the editors’ reading on the authority of his manuscripts, which Antelmius claimed were less exact. Yet not only the manuscripts cited by Quesnellus but also our own, which we have identified, belong to diverse and very ancient collections and ought to be preferred to the manuscripts of a single later collection. Nor is the meaning obscure if the force of the words is correctly understood. Indeed, although the words arrive at the same meaning by a different route, they signify the customary trickery of heretics, who strive to devise some other interpretation in whatever part of the accursed doctrine they can, so that they may appear to depart and differ from the solidity of the doctrines to be condemned—that is, from the whole mass of meanings to be condemned. The reading “of what must be condemned” also agrees better with the preceding “accursed doctrine” than does “of the condemned.”], they consider none of their meanings secure [Note: [Col. 0595D] Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “not saved.”].

CHAPTER III

And although they pretend to disapprove and abandon all their definitions as though these made it easy to creep in [Note: [Col. 0595D] See Quesnellus’s note 5, whose emendation is supported by our more authoritative manuscripts. Only the manuscripts of collection 21 read “to the ease of the one creeping in.” Earlier editions and Sichardus, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, read “to such great ease”; these manuscripts soon read incorrectly, together with the Louvain editions, “this by the whole art.” Other editions read, much worse, “this for you by the whole art.”], they reserve this, with all the artifice of deception, unless it is understood [Note: [Col. 0595D] The Lucca codex reads “unless it is understood”; shortly afterward, “unless it is given freely.”], so that grace is thought to be given by God according to the merits of those who receive it [Note: [Col. 0595D] 1, question 1, “If grace is not,” chapter 1.].

But if it is not given freely, it is not grace, but payment and recompense of merits, as the blessed Apostle says:

> By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves [Note: [Col. 0595D] The Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 and another manuscript of collection 11 read: “You have been saved freely.”], but it is God’s gift, not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them (Ephesians 2:8).

[Note: [Col. 0595D] We have added “but it is God’s gift” on the authority of four very ancient manuscripts of collections 1, 3, and 4, and of the Vallicellian collection 8, as well as Sichardus. The editions before Quesnellus read: “for it is God’s gift.”]

[Note: [Col. 0595D] All our manuscripts agree with those cited by Quesnellus in note 6 in this reading, except those of collection 24, among which is the Victorinus mentioned by him. There, with the earlier editions and Sichardus, it reads: “Every devotion to good works is divine preparation; nor is anyone justified by his own virtue, since grace for each person is the beginning of righteousness and the fountain and source of merits.”]

Therefore every gift of good works is God’s preparation, because no one is justified by his own power before he is justified by grace, which is for each person the beginning of righteousness and the fountain and source of merits.

But these people say that grace is preceded by natural effort so that what is already clear through their own exertion before grace may appear not to have been wounded by original sin [Note: [Col. 0596B] The Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with one Vatican manuscript, reads: “may have been given.”]; and so that what the Truth says may be false:

> For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost (Luke 19:10).

[Note: [Col. 0596C] In all editions before Quesnellus, several passages excerpted almost verbatim from Augustine’s *Enchiridion* were inserted here, forming chapter 4. Quesnellus removed them on the authority of his manuscripts, which our manuscripts also support, and relegated them to his note 7, where they may be read in volume II of this edition, but in volume I of ours. We found the same words inserted only in the manuscripts of the later collections 12 and 24 and in Sichardus’s copy, with this difference: in the manuscripts of collection 12, the passage beginning “a patch is sewn on” follows the words “what was lost”; in the manuscripts of collection 24 and in Sichardus’s copy, it follows the preceding words “wounded by original sin,” with everything through the end of the chapter omitted.]

CHAPTER IV [Another numbering: V]

Therefore your Dilection must take care, and provide with great diligence [Col. 0596A] [Note: [Col. 0596C] The Vercelli codex, collection 8, reads “lest scandals be raised,” omitting the intervening words. In the Lucca codex, the words “through such people” are absent.], lest through such people scandals long since extinguished be stirred up again, and from the doctrine once cut off some shoot of the same evil arise in your province, which may not only grow from its roots but also infect the offspring of the holy Church with the poison of its mouth [Note: [Col. 0596C] Quesnellus and other editions, together with certain manuscripts, read “with the poison of its odor.” The Cambridge manuscript cited by Quesnellus and the edition of Canisius, together with our manuscripts of collections 21, read “with the odor of its poison.” We have preferred the reading of five most authoritative copies: the Vatican Regius, Vatican 1342, Lucca, Vallicellian, and Vercelli. Shortly before this, the same Vercelli manuscript reads “the offspring of the holy Church.”].

Let those who wish to appear corrected purge themselves of every suspicion; and by obeying us let them prove themselves to be ours. If any one of them refuses to satisfy these salutary commands, whether he is a cleric or a layman, let him be expelled from the fellowship of the Church, lest, being the destroyer of his own soul, he lie in wait for another’s salvation [Note: [Col. 0596D] Three of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, three of ours, and Canisius’s edition read “lest, through the destruction of his own soul, he lie in wait for another’s salvation.” Hadrian I, Letter 97, to the Spanish bishops, reads “traitor.”].

CHAPTER V [Another numbering: VI]

Restore also that part of ecclesiastical discipline by which it was formerly decreed by the holy Fathers and by us many times [Note: [Col. 0596D] The Vatican manuscript 5845 reads “and formerly.” Four other manuscripts read “which was formerly decreed.” See what we observed on this passage in the preceding introduction, no. 25. Quesnellus’s note 8 may also be consulted.], that no one should be free to pass from one church to another, whether from the rank of the presbyterate [Col. 0596B], or from the order of the diaconate, or from a subsequent clerical office [Note: [Col. 0596D] Three Vatican manuscripts read: “neither in the diaconate nor in the subsequent order of clerics.” Four others have “in the order of clerics” instead of “in the office of clerics.” The Lucca codex omits “nor in the subsequent office.”]:

we admonish you to restore this discipline in full, so that each person may persevere where he was ordained, not enticed by ambition, not led astray by desire, not corrupted by human persuasion [Note: [Col. 0596D] The Vatican manuscript, collection 24, reads “there, where he was ordained.”].

Thus, if anyone, seeking his own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, neglects to return to his own people [Note: [Col. 0596D] The Vatican Regius reads “and to his own church.” Sichardus deletes “his own people and.”] and church, let him be regarded as a stranger both to the privilege of honor and to the bond of communion [Col. 0597A].

Your Dilection should not doubt that, if—which we do not think will happen—the measures we decree for the safeguarding of the canons and the integrity of the faith are neglected, we shall be moved with even greater severity; for [Note: [Col. 0597B] Distinction 86, “The faults of inferiors,” chapter 1.]

> THE FAULTS OF SUBORDINATE ORDERS

must be referred to no one more than to sluggish and negligent rulers, who often nourish a great plague while they pretend not to apply the harsher medicine.

594. LETTER II  
[Note: [Col. 0597B] Another numbering: 7. What was formerly Letter 2 is now Letter 167. Written around the year 442.]

TO SEPTIMUS, BISHOP OF ALTINUM.

[Note: [Col. 0597B] We have written *Septimus*, not *Septimius*, as in the printed editions; see annotation 3 (Col. 593, c) on the preceding letter. Many, including ancient, manuscripts omit the name of the city; but it is read in manuscripts of collections 12, 23, and 24, and especially in the very ancient collection 8. The printed editions had *Altinum*, from the manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, but this is the name of the city itself. *Altinatem* ought to have been written on the authority of reputable authors; but from the Vallicellian manuscript of collection 8 and the Ottobonian manuscript of collection 23 we have restored *Altinensem*. Thus the bishops of this city are generally called in the councils. See the Council of Aquileia of 381. We found this letter in the manuscripts of nine collections listed in the introduction to the preceding letter, nos. 5 and 7. From these we defended the authenticity of these letters in no. 11 and refuted the difficulties raised by Quesnellus in no. 14.]

[Note: [Col. 0597C] In the index of manuscripts of collection 5, this title appears as chapter 83: “To Septimus the bishop, concerning the titles written above.” The titles of the preceding letter are meant, and this letter is consistently placed immediately after it in all the collections; hence it may be confirmed that they were written at the same time.]

SYNOPSIS

I. Pelagians are to be received only with the renunciation of their error.  
II. Every cleric must remain in the church in which he was ordained.

LEO, BISHOP, TO SEPTIMUS, BISHOP, GREETING.

CHAPTER I

[Col. 0597B]

Having read the letter of your Brotherhood, we have recognized the vigor of your faith, which we had formerly known [Note: [Col. 0598B] The printed editions read *quam* (“which”). We have emended the text on the authority of the Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1; Vatican 5845, collection 8; and Florence, Saint Mark’s, collection 13. The same reading is found in chapter 1 of Letter 18 to Januarius, which was copied from this letter.], congratulating you that you vigilantly carry out pastoral care for the protection of Christ’s flocks, lest wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep (Matthew 7:15) tear apart the simple with bestial savagery [Note: [Col. 0598C] Five manuscripts of different collections read “the savagery of beasts.”], and lest they not only themselves make no progress through correction but also corrupt what is sound [Note: [Col. 0598C] Four authoritative manuscripts read “what is holy.”].

Lest the serpentine deceit be able to accomplish this, we have sent a written communication to the metropolitan bishop of the province of Venetia [Col. 0598A], so that he might recognize that it concerns the danger to his office if anyone coming from the company of the Pelagians and Coelestians should be held in Catholic communion without a legitimate profession of satisfaction.

For it is most salutary and full of the benefit of spiritual medicine that presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any other order who wish to appear corrected should acknowledge without ambiguity that they condemn their own error and the authors of that error, so that no opportunity for hope [Note: [Col. 0598C] Quesnellus reads *spirandi* (“of breathing”), and relegated the common reading *sperandi* (“of hoping”) to the margin. Yet all our manuscripts support the latter reading, as does the letter to Januarius, which repeats this same sentence in the same words.] may remain for perverse and long-disposed-of opinions, and so that no member of the Church may be violated by association with such people, since their own profession will have begun to oppose them in every respect.

CHAPTER II

With regard to these people also, we order that the canonical constitution be observed, so that they may not be permitted to depart from the churches to which they properly belong or to transfer themselves at their own discretion to places not assigned to them.

Since this is rightly not permitted to the innocent, it should be permitted still less to the suspect [Note: [Col. 0598C] This reading, supported by two manuscripts of the highest quality—the Vatican collection 8 and the Florentine manuscript—and also by the letter to Januarius, seemed preferable. Another reading: “ought to be.”].

Accordingly, let your Dilection, whose devotion gives us joy, join your care to our directives, and together with the aforementioned metropolitan take care that those measures which have been prudently proposed for the safety of the whole Church and laudably [Note: [Col. 0598C] Another reading: “have been carried out.”] and salutarily ordered are fulfilled carefully and promptly.

INTRODUCTION

On a fragment of a letter of Saint Cyril of Alexandria concerning Easter in the year 444, addressed to Saint Leo, which will also contribute greatly to clarifying the following letter of Paschasinus. (G)

[Col. 0597]

1. That Saint Leo wrote at least two letters concerning the question of Easter in the year 444—one to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and the other to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum—is evident from Paschasinus’s letter. Both, however, perished through the injustice of time. It was believed that only Paschasinus’s reply survived, and for that reason Quesnellus published only it.

Yet we believe that a considerable fragment of Cyril’s letter, which Paschasinus himself testifies that Cyril delivered to Leo, has also been transmitted to us. To establish this, several matters must be observed.

2. The letter of Cyril concerning Easter that had been delivered to the Fathers of the African council, which Dionysius Exiguus had inserted in full in his collection under no. 135, was first published from Sirmondus’s papers by Petavius in volume II of *On the Doctrine of the Times*, at the end, and afterward by Bucherius in his commentary on Victor’s Paschal Canon, chapter 1, page 72.

Two parts must be distinguished in the text published by Petavius and Bucherius: namely, Cyril’s actual letter to the Africans, which is read in a more correct form in Dionysius; and its addition, which belongs to another letter of the same Cyril.

When an ignorant person discovered these two separate letters of Cyril discussing Easter, he believed that both concerned the same Easter. Therefore, after first copying from Dionysius the letter to the Africans and altering a few words according to his own judgment, he appended and inserted the other letter—which was still read in full in Bede’s time—while omitting its opening.

Since this second letter announces the date of Easter in the year 444, the copyist adapted the date designated in the earlier letter to the Africans to that same day, namely, 9 Kalends of May. Thus Bucherius regarded the entire document as one letter rather than two and believed that it concerned only Easter in the year 444.

### 3.

But if the first part of this text is compared with Cyril’s letter to the Africans, which Dionysius preserved, the same words are found, apart from a few expressions that the copyist altered. There can therefore be no doubt that this first part concerns Easter of the year 420. Indeed, since it is there correctly said to have been addressed to Aurelius and Valentinus, and also to the entire holy assembly gathered at the Council of Carthage, and since Cyril states that he is sending copies of the Council of Nicaea—which points to the Council of Carthage in 419—it is plainly erroneous, where Easter is being discussed, to add that it was to be celebrated on 9 Kalends of May. For this chronological notation indicates Easter in 444, the only year during Cyril’s entire episcopate at Alexandria in which Easter fell on that date. Consequently, this letter would have been written in 443, which is entirely incompatible with the Council of Carthage that requested copies of the Council of Nicaea from Cyril, and also with the age of Aurelius, who had died long before 443 after presiding over that council.

Petavius therefore rightly reported that this letter was written in 419 and concerned Easter of the year 420; accordingly, instead of “9 Kalends of May,” one should read “14 Kalends of May,” the day on which Easter was celebrated in 420.

### 4.

In Dionysius, however, “17 Kalends of May” is read, and Easter fell on that date in 423. But apart from the fact that the date of Easter for the following year was more frequently requested, and that of Easter several years later only rarely, Cyril’s own letter—which announces the Easter of the forthcoming indiction, that is, of the following year—is said to have been transmitted by Dionysius to Boniface together with another letter of Atticus after the consulship of Honorius XII and Theodosius VIII, that is, in 419. It would have been easy for the numeral XIV, through a copyist’s error, to be changed into XVII by the joining of two units.

Nor should one object that the Greek text from what is called the African Church manuscript reads the same numeral as the ordinary text of Dionysius. The Greek text of the African manuscript is not Cyril’s original, but an ancient Greek translation of Dionysius’ Latin text; it derives from a corrupt text of Dionysius and confirms that this copyist’s error is ancient.

It is therefore clear that the true reading in Sirmond’s manuscript was corrupted by the antiquarian who, after attaching the second part to this letter and joining two letters into one, thought that the date of Easter designated in the latter part, which is discussed at greater length, ought also to be transferred to the former part. Through the same liberty, the heading of this same letter of Cyril says that it was given to the Council gathered at Carthage on 5 Kalends of December, whereas in Dionysius no such notation occurs in the heading; rather, Dionysius records in the title the date “6 Kalends of December,” on which the letter was sent by the Africans to Pope Boniface.

So much concerning the letter to the Council of Carthage.

### 5.

Now concerning the addition, or rather the other letter of Cyril, which properly belongs to our present purpose. This letter concerns the celebration of Easter in 444. It says that among the Alexandrians Easter was to be celebrated on 9 Kalends of May because of the intercalary character of the year, while the Latins were considering celebrating it on 7 Kalends of April, on the twenty-second day of the moon, thereby treating an intercalary year as an ordinary year.

All these indications agree only with Easter of 444. The same indications are also found later in Paschasinus’ letter, which is about to follow; consequently this letter of Cyril, like Paschasinus’ letter, belongs to the year 443.

### 6.

In his notes on this addition, volume II of *On the Doctrine of the Times*, Petavius asserts that Easter in the year 607 is indicated here, and consequently concludes that this is not Cyril’s letter but that of an author who lived nearly two centuries later. His entire argument, however, rests on a fictitious nineteen-year cycle that he wrongly attributes to the Romans, because he was unaware of the eighty-four-year cycle then in use among the Latins. His argument must therefore be regarded as worthless.

Pagius, under the year 419, no. 28, after observing that all the indications agree with Easter of 444 and that both all the manuscripts and all the writers attribute this letter to Cyril, withdrew from Petavius’ opinion. He nevertheless believed that Cyril had addressed it to certain monks, arguing as follows: it was written not to one person but to several; and the words “I command you not to do this,” etc., imply that they were inferior and subject to Cyril. That monks are intended, he thought, is suggested by the example of the monk Pachomius, which is inserted in the same letter.

But since the letter was written to Latins who wished to celebrate Easter on 7 Kalends of April, it cannot be said to have been addressed to Cyril’s inferiors and subjects. Just as, by a copyist’s discretion, the letter to the Africans was made to read *we command you*, where Dionysius has *we announce*, so in this letter we should believe that *I command you* was written by the same discretion, whereas something more modest was found in the original and its translation.

The example of a monk cited to support the proposed interpretation proves nothing, so that the letter may be judged to have been addressed to monks—especially since it is not even conceivable that Latin monks questioned Cyril about Easter in 444.

### 7.

Whether, finally, it was written to one person or to several may be questioned. Tillemont, in his *Life of Cyril*, article 147, thinks that it was given to certain Western bishops. If he inferred this from the words “which we desire, dearest brothers,” he did not notice that these words belong to the conclusion of the letter that was transmitted to the Africans.

If, however, he inferred it from the words inserted into this later fragment, “my dearest lords, bear in mind,” which appear more likely to be Cyril’s words than Pachomius’, the evidence is stronger, though not entirely conclusive. For it is possible that the person who attached this letter to the earlier one addressed to the Africans presented these passages in the plural so that they would agree with what preceded, just as we know that he altered other passages according to his own invention.

### 8.

Joannes Vander Haagen, author of a work entitled *Observations on the Prologues and Paschal Letters of the Ancient Fathers and Pontiffs*, Amsterdam, 1734, p. 97, argues that this is Cyril’s letter and that it was transmitted to Pope Leo.

He bases this chiefly on the following considerations. On the one hand, Paschasinus makes it certain that Saint Cyril replied by letter to Leo, who had questioned him about Easter in 444. On the other hand, Bede attributes the text found in this fragment to Cyril’s letter to Saint Leo; and the fragment itself does indeed deal with the question of Easter in 444, concerning which Paschasinus reported that Cyril had replied to Leo.

The same author cites three testimonies of Bede: two in which the letter is attributed to Cyril, namely from the book *On the Reckoning of Time* and from the letter to Wichred; and a third from the short work *On the Phases of the Moon*, where it is said to have been written to Leo, according to Petavius and Bucherius, although Vander Haagen admits that he was unable to find the passage.

Certainly, in the Cologne edition of 1688, volume I, p. 151, we find the following in that treatise *On the Phases of the Moon*:

> Thus it is read in the letter that blessed Cyril wrote to Pope Leo: “For I shall indicate to you what Bachumius [read: Pachomius], the monk, …”

These words are found in the fragment that will shortly be quoted. The fragment also contains the passages that Bede quotes from the same letter of Cyril both in chapter 41 of *On the Reckoning of Time*, volume II of the same edition, p. 83, and in his letter to Wichred, volume II, p. 230.

This testimony of Bede is indeed weighty. Since he declares that the letter was transmitted not to the Africans but to Leo, it appears that he found it not improperly attached to the letter to the Africans, but separate and addressed to Leo; consequently, it lacked the words by which it is presented as having been given to several persons.

We have no doubt, however, that in the genuine letter to Leo Cyril used those formulas of honor and respect toward the Apostolic See that are found in his other letters to the Roman pontiffs. We must therefore believe that all these formulas were altered by the person who added this fragment of the letter to the Fathers of the Council of Carthage.

This very interpolation, however, persuaded us not to insert the fragment absolutely into this work, in which we thought that only wholly genuine letters ought to be printed. Since the interpolation appears to be confined to the words, while the fragment as a whole agrees with the characteristics of Easter in 444 found in Paschasinus’ certain letters, as well as with Cyril’s own opinions contained in his other paschal works, we judged that it should not be entirely omitted. Instead, it should be placed after this warning and illustrated with several notes.

## 601. FRAGMENT OF A LETTER OF SAINT CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA TO SAINT LEO. (C, G)

[Col. 0601A] **[lacuna]**

… Let us celebrate Easter together [Note: [Col. 0601A] He is speaking of Easter in 444, according to the Alexandrian nineteen-year cycle, in which this year was the eighth year of the *ogdoas* and was intercalary, as will become clear from Paschasinus’ letter. For this reason, namely the intercalary character of the Alexandrian year, the Alexandrians maintained that Easter was to be celebrated this year on 9 Kalends of May, not with the Latins on 7 Kalends of April, as though the year were not intercalary but ordinary. This was the entire, or at least the principal, basis of the disagreement between the Alexandrians and the Romans concerning Easter in 444.

To make the matter clear to everyone, it should be understood that lunar years are of two kinds: ordinary and intercalary. Ordinary years are those consisting of twelve lunar months and 354 days. Lunar months are counted alternately as twenty-nine and thirty days. Intercalary years are those in which, after twelve lunar months, another lunar month of twenty-nine days is added—whether it is called the thirteenth month or the second twelfth month—so that an intercalary year consists of 383 days.

This intercalation is inserted into the lunar year from time to time, so that by this addition the deficiency of other lunar years may be corrected in relation to the solar year, and lunar years may thereby be brought into some correspondence with solar years. This was necessary for determining the paschal moon of the first month, which depends greatly upon the solar equinox.

For this reason intercalary years were accepted both among the Alexandrians and among the Romans, but by different methods, according to the differing cycles used by each. In the Alexandrian nineteen-year cycle, the third, sixth, eighth, eleventh, fourteenth, and nineteenth years were intercalary; the remaining years were ordinary. Thus, among them, one intercalary year followed two ordinary years, except in the eighth and nineteenth years, which followed only one ordinary year.

In the Roman eighty-four-year cycle, intercalary years were placed after every two ordinary years without exception. Since, moreover, in this Roman cycle the sixty-third year, into which the common year 444 fell, was ordinary, while in the Alexandrian cycle the eighth year corresponding to 444 was intercalary, it is evident that the first paschal month among the Romans, in the Alexandrians’ reckoning because of the intercalation, was the thirteenth—or second twelfth—month of the preceding lunar year. It therefore could not suit Easter; and chiefly for this reason the two groups differed by an entire month in determining the date of Easter for that year.

We have said that this was the entire, or principal, basis of the disagreement. The Latins had another difficulty that prevented them from adopting the Alexandrian position, namely, their different paschal limits, as will be explained in note 17, column 608, no. k, on Paschasinus’ letter.] on 9 Kalends of May because of the intercalary character of the year.

[Col. 0601D–0602A] But if you celebrate it on 7 Kalends of April, on the twenty-second day of the moon, as you have already prepared to do, you make an ordinary year out of an intercalary year, while you observe the moon illuminated on the third day before the Nones of March according to the rule of the Latins concerning the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 0601D] The subject is Easter according to the Latin cycle, in which, as we have said, this year was ordinary. Since their paschal new moon was on 5 March, Easter fell on Sunday, 7 Kalends of April, the twenty-second day of the moon, as Paschasinus also noted and as will be explained in the following annotation.]

[Note: [Col. 0601D] The Latins recorded in their cycle the weekday of the Kalends of January and the age of the moon, as is clear from Victor’s cycle, from the anonymous cycle appended to the *Fasti* and edited by our Cardinal Norisius, and also from the cycle found in Muratori’s *Latin Anecdotes*, volume III. From the age of the moon, the January new moon and consequently also the March new moon were determined. For the fixed rule of the Latins was: “Whatever the moon is in January, such also is it in March.” From the weekday it was easy to determine the Sunday of Easter.

In this year, 444, the Latin cycle marked the Kalends of January as Saturday and the age of the moon as twenty-seven, as we shall show in the following annotation. The new moon of January and March was therefore on the fifth day; consequently Easter Sunday was 26 March, the twenty-second day of the moon.

Since the year was leap year, Sunday initially fell on 19 March, the fifteenth day of the moon. But since Easter was not to be celebrated before the equinox, and the Latin rule forbade its celebration before the sixteenth day of the moon, it had to be deferred to the following Sunday, 26 March, the twenty-second day of the moon.]

[Note: [Col. 0602B] It should read *Saturday*, not *Sunday*, as is clear from all the Latin cycles. Whether this error is attributed to the copyist or, as some suspect, to Cyril makes no difference. In the anonymous cycle published by Norisius, for cycle-year 63, into which the year of Christ 444 fell, and also in the old cycle published by Muratori, volume III of the *Latin Anecdotes*, pp. 204 ff., for year 62—which through the author’s error corresponds to year 63, as can be seen in Joannes Vander Haagen, author of *Observations on the Anonymous Cycle Published by Muratori*, p. 278—the Kalends of January are marked “Sat.,” that is, the day of Saturn or Saturday, or the seventh weekday. The age of the moon, however, is XXVIII, not XXVII.

These Latin cycles of eighty-four years were constructed at a time when a lunar leap was admitted every twelfth year. From the beginning of the cycle through year 63, this produced five lunar leaps. In the time of Leo, however, when Prosper corrected the system, it was introduced that a lunar leap should be admitted every fourteenth year, as the aforementioned Vander Haagen proved in pp. 217 ff. of his *Observations on Prosper’s Chronicle*. Hence only four lunar leaps occurred from the beginning of the cycle through year 63.

Each lunar leap adds one day to the age of the moon. Therefore, in those cycles that posited five leaps, one day was added to the age of the moon through year 63 above the cycle that, following Prosper’s correction, admitted only four leaps. Thus in those cycles the age of the moon at the Kalends of January in year 63 was XXVIII; in the cycle received in Leo’s time, XXVII.

The very illuminated moon, or paschal new moon, which the author places this year on the third day before the Nones of March, requires an age of the moon of XXVII both at the Kalends of March and at those of January. It should be noted, however, that Cardinal Norisius, in his diagram of the eighty-four-year cycle, where he marked the age of the moon at the Kalends of January for year 63 as XXVIII from the *Fasti*, incorrectly assigned the paschal new moon of that same year to 5 March, or the third day before the Nones. On the hypothesis of an age of XXVIII in the old style entered in the *Fasti*, the new moon would have fallen on 4 March, or the fourth day before the Nones.

He adopted this position because, on the one hand, reliable witnesses testified to the date of Easter in 444 and, on the other, he relied on the cycle appended to his *Fasti*, which he presumed to have been in use in that same year. To reconcile the two, he introduced an arbitrary system of full moons, which he likewise would have rejected had he suspected that the cycle had been corrected before that year, as he later came to suspect because of Easter in 454.] Sunday, the twenty-seventh day of the moon. And it must not be observed in this year for the reasons that we stated above.

[Note: [Col. 0603B] These words indicate that a considerable portion is missing at the beginning.]

For just as the Easter that we mentioned must be avoided in this year, so care must be taken not to make the Easter of an intercalary year fall in an ordinary year, or that of an ordinary year in an intercalary one. For we must investigate the lunar epacts in the months of the whole year, so that we may celebrate Easter on the moon of the first month, at the beginning of the year after the beginning of spring.

[Note: [Col. 0603B] What the Alexandrians called an *epact* was called by the Latins the age of the moon. Lunar epacts are named according to the months of the whole year—that is, they are not annual but monthly—because their investigation is necessary for determining the proper time of Easter.]

[Note: [Col. 0603B–0603C] John Vander Haagen explains this rule, which must be observed above all for determining Easter, with great precision on p. 105 of his *Observations on Cyril’s Letter*. The first month of the sacred Jewish lunar year is intended: it begins at the start of the natural tropical solar year, which begins with the spring equinox after the beginning of spring; the latter is fixed shortly afterward as 12 Kalends of April. This agrees with Cyril’s prologue, where the spring equinox and the beginning of spring are likewise placed on 12 Kalends of April, that is, 21 March, or 25 Pharmuthi.

This date must be especially observed in the computation of Easter. When Easter is said to be celebrated after the beginning of spring, this indicates, according to the Alexandrian rules, that it could not be celebrated on the very day of the spring equinox. Since Easter may not be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, but must be celebrated on the Sunday immediately following that fourteenth day, Easter, when required to fall after the beginning of spring or after the equinox, could among the Alexandrians fall as early as the fifteenth day of the moon if that day were a Sunday, and on the twenty-fourth day of the moon if it coincided with the day of the equinox.]

For the sun itself is enclosed each day equally by land and sea at the end of the day and opened at the beginning of the day. The sun completes the course of the whole year on 12 Kalends of April; and the fullness or diminution of the lunar orb can be foreseen to some extent by the movement of the fingers, the guidance of reason, and calculation, so that we may count only twelve moons according to the legal reckoning of the Hebrews in an ordinary year, and thirteen in an intercalary year according to the computation of days.

[Note: [Col. 0603C–0603D] The Hebrews are meant, since they use the lunar year and lunar months to define the first paschal month according to the commandment of the Law: “Keep the first month.” A reckoning according to days is added, so that when an intercalary month must be inserted before the paschal month—as the Alexandrians maintained had to be done in 444—thirteen lunar months are counted in an intercalary year, comprising 384 days, whereas in an ordinary year twelve lunar months are counted as comprising 354 days.]

This letter was published in full, in Jerome’s translation, by Holstenius after Pachomius’ rule. But since it contains nothing like what is read in this fragment, Cyril appears to be referring to another letter of Pachomius that has perished.

The distinguished Pachomius, outstanding in apostolic grace and founder of the Egyptian communities, sent to the monastery called in the language of the Egyptians Panum a letter that he had received at the angel’s dictation, so that they would not fall into error in calculating the paschal feast and would know the moon of the first month in an ordinary and an intercalary year.

[Note: [Col. 0604C] Bucherius calls this monastery Bonum. Some prefer to read Baum, otherwise Bau or Pabau, which was the principal among Pachomius’ monasteries. My dearest lords, bear in mind what was first ordained concerning Easter in Egypt, as a reminder, so that the children of Israel might eat the lamb as a type of the true Lamb on the moon of the first month.

A later Easter was instituted in remembrance of the occasion when manna descended; this showed that the shadowy lamb would pass away when the true Manna had descended.

Our Lord Jesus Christ joined the Jewish lamb and the true Manna on a single day, when He blessed the bread and wine, saying, “This is my body, and this is my blood,” on the moon of the first month, at the beginning of the year.

Therefore, let us remember and be mindful to offer what Jesus offered for us in the first month. For the Lord Jesus said: “Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance and memorial of me.”

And examine most carefully what the Council of Nicaea ordained:

[Note: [Col. 0604C–0605C] Shortly afterward it is said that the Council of Nicaea “wrote” the lunar cycle of the first month. Unless an error has entered the word *had written* through a copyist’s discretion or an interpreter’s less exactness, Cyril too understood that the nineteen-year cycle had been prescribed by that council, as Ambrose transmitted in his letter to the bishops of Aemilia, writing about Easter in 387, and Proterius, Cyril’s successor, in his letter to Saint Leo concerning Easter in 455.

Some maintain that the same cycle was established by the Council of Nicaea. But it is clear that it had been published earlier by Anatolius and had long before been in use in the Alexandrian Church, as Eusebius shows in book VII, chapter 32. The Fathers of Nicaea therefore could only have approved and prescribed it.

Although no ancient historians mention this, it can nevertheless be understood reasonably in the following way. Since those Fathers decreed that Easter should be celebrated by everyone everywhere on the same Sunday, this could not be achieved unless all used one and the same cycle.

Since, moreover, for this purpose they decreed that the Church of Alexandria, which used the aforesaid cycle and was distinguished for its skill in computation, should communicate the date of Easter to the Roman bishop according to the standard of that same cycle, so that through apostolic authority the universal Church throughout the world might know the appointed date of Easter without dispute, as Cyril himself relates in his paschal prologue, they may reasonably be said by this decree to have approved that cycle and in a certain sense prescribed it.

It should be noted, however, that this Nicene decree instructed not the Roman but the Alexandrian bishop to write to the Roman pontiff according to the aforesaid method, thereby eliciting his agreement and authority, so that Easter might be celebrated on the same day by the whole Christian world without dispute.

Since this Nicene approval of the nineteen-year cycle was highly implicit and obscure and was expressed in no canon, it is not surprising that the Roman pontiffs, although they otherwise held the Council of Nicaea in the highest reverence, did not abandon their own eighty-four-year cycle, which in the earliest period did not differ from the nineteen-year cycle in determining Easter—even though, when paschal controversies later began to arise, they adopted the Alexandrian cycle only after some delay.]

the fourteenth days of the moon of all years according to the nineteen-year cycle, so that we might not be deceived concerning the fourteenth day of the moon with the Jews and the heretics called the *tessares koedecatitae* (“Fourteenth-day observers”). It was established in all synods, except the Synod of Gangra and the Synod of Caesarea, that no Church, city, or entire region should act contrary to what had been established concerning Easter at the Council of Nicaea.

Believe me: if the Council of Nicaea had not written the lunar cycle of the first month, the cycle of the Silenite stone in Persia would have sufficed as an example of the paschal reckoning, since its inner whiteness increases and decreases with the moon of the first month.
