Concerning this spotless lamb the command was given most truly: “You shall not kill a lamb in its mother’s milk”—that is, in the approaching Easter of its conception in its mother’s womb.

Therefore, lest Mary, as though she were a violated and adulterous woman, be stoned to death, Joseph secretly wished to divorce her.

But lest the lamb be killed in its mother’s milk, at the Easter nearest to its birth Joseph fled to Egypt, at the command of the angel, in the month of March, when the year came round—the month in which Cain led righteous Abel into the field to kill him, as a type of Christ led to the praetorium of Pilate on the sixth day of the week. For on that same day He was conceived in the womb and died on the cross, while on the sixth day of the week Adam died in his soul through sin in paradise and on the same day died in his body.

The answer has been given, as I think, to all of you who questioned me.

## 607. LETTER III OF PASCHASINUS, BISHOP OF LILYBAEUM, TO POPE LEO

[Note: [Col. 0606C] Alternatively, after Letter 2. What was 3 is now 4. Written in 443.]

Concerning Easter of the year 444. (G)

### SYNOPSIS

After prefacing a few remarks about the calamity of Sicily, Paschasinus, consulted by Leo concerning the paschal cycle, proves that the Alexandrian computation should be retained in preference to the Roman, both from the calculation of the Hebrews and from a miracle that occurred in the time of Pope Zosimus.

To the truly holy, most blessed, and apostolic lord, and to me, after the Lord, greatly revered Pope Leo: Paschasinus, bishop.

It appears that the property of Churches was for some time assigned by the barbarians to the treasury, as may be inferred from a papyrus of the Church of Ravenna written shortly after 444 and published by Marquis Maffei in *Historia diplomatica*, p. 132. Paschasinus explicitly mentions the octad here and asserts that it began with the consulship of Aetius for the second time and Sigisvultus, namely in 437, from which the Alexandrian nineteen-year cycle then in progress began. Since 444 was the last year of this octad, he adds that it “is closed by the year” in which the question appears to have arisen; the dispute concerned the Easter of that year.], with the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius for the second time and Sigisvultus, 609 which is closed by the year concerning which the question appears to have arisen [Note: [Col. 0607D] Our manuscript has *Segisvultus*, “which is concluded.” Quesnellus, in the margin: elsewhere, *Sigismundus*.]. The reckoning is as follows [Note: [Col. 0607D] Vatican manuscript: “The first two years are common, the third intercalary; likewise the fourth and fifth are common.” This belongs to the Alexandrian reckoning; how the Romans differed from the Alexandrians in determining common and intercalary years, we explained in note 1 on the fragment of Cyril’s letter.]: the first two are common years, the third an intercalary year, the fourth and fifth common years, the sixth an intercalary year, the seventh a common year, and the eighth an intercalary year. Your apostolic prudence clearly sees [Note: [Col. 0608B] Since the year 444, the eighth year of the octad according to the Alexandrian cycle, was intercalary, the intercalation required that Easter not be celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, which belonged to the intercalary month, or last month of the sacred year, rather than the first month, which the Paschal month had to be. See note 1 (Col. 601, n. a) on the aforementioned fragment.] that the eighth year of the octad cannot be otherwise than if we retain the intercalation. [Note: [Col. 0608B] Vatican manuscript: “For if we should wish to celebrate on the seventh day before the Kalends of April what we said above, the first occurrence”—corruptly.]. But if we wish to celebrate on the seventh day before the Kalends of April what we mentioned above—that is, the Easter that occurs first—we shall make it a common year, and from that point onward the reckoning of all the succeeding years will begin to waver.

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 0608A]

And lest what [Note: [Col. 0608C] Thus, better from the cited manuscript, as later also in the plural, “we set forth.” The printed editions read: “I have explained.”] we have explained should bring any obscurity to Your Blessedness, we point out that among the Hebrews common years have only twelve moons, that is, 354 days, whereas intercalary years have thirteen moons, that is, 384 days. Necessity therefore compels us, because of the intercalation, to maintain the date that is later [Note: [Col. 0608C] Easter, namely, must be kept on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, not on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, since the intercalation requires this, as we noted in note 14 above. It is consequently clear that the intercalary month immediately precedes the month of Easter and postpones Easter itself by one month.], lest we appear to depart from the truth. Nor should the fact that the day of the Passion falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May make this seem to us either new or erroneous [Note: [Col. 0608C] Marianus has *erroneous*. To the Romans, postponing Easter to the ninth day before the Kalends of May—that is, 23 April—seemed aberrant. Indeed, under Zosimus they inclined to celebrate Easter on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, or 22 April. Their final limit for Paschal Sundays, however, was the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, or 21 April. Paschasinus answers this objection by saying that although the Paschal Sunday exceeded the Latins’ final limit of 21 April, the day of the Passion did not pass beyond that limit; this could suffice because Easter, as the Greeks hold, received its name from the Passion. Ambrose in his letter to the bishops of Aemilia and Cyril in his Paschal Prologue likewise indicated a similar answer, though by “the day of the Passion” they understood the fourteenth day of the moon, on which legal Passover fell and which was a type of Christ’s Passion. This reasoning of Paschasinus nevertheless persuaded Leo; hence the Easter of 444 was celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, as Prosper testifies in his *Chronicle*: “Nor was there an error, because the day of the Passion was on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.” Leo himself adopted the same reasoning in chapter 2 of Letter 121 to Marcian, written in 453.], from which—as the Greeks think—Easter received its name. Although interpreters of the Hebrew language state that *Pascha* means “passage,” this is nevertheless confirmed by the statement of the evangelist John, who, speaking of the Passion, says: “When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13:1).

Therefore, let us not be alarmed by a date placed one day later, 610 lest, while avoiding it, we fall into error, as happened in the time of Zosimus, of blessed memory, my lord and predecessor in your apostolate, in the eleventh consulship of the emperor Honorius and the second of Constantius. At that time, when people avoided keeping Easter on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, it was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April—that is, [Note: [Col. 0608D] The same Vatican manuscript has *it must be celebrated*, which should be read as *it was celebrated*.] the common year was retained instead of the intercalary year [Note: [Col. 0609C] The printed editions read *a common year was recorded*. The reading of the Vatican manuscript is preferable and is supported by Marianus’s copy, especially since the verb *teneo*, “to retain,” is familiar to Paschasinus: “Let us retain the intercalation” in chapter 1; likewise here, “a common year was retained.”], and a very serious error arose, so much so that this truth was demonstrated by a certain mystery [Note: [Col. 0609C] Marianus has *ministry*.] administered through the gift of the Holy Spirit. I have therefore thought it right to explain this, because the place itself is also well known to my holy and venerable brother, the deacon Libanius [Note: [Col. 0609C] Bucherius has *Bollianus*. The Vatican manuscript has *Libanius*. Quesnellus suspects that perhaps *Silanus* should be read, the person mentioned at the beginning of the letter.]. The miracle of this mystery was as follows.

## CHAPTER III

There is a very insignificant estate called Meltinas, situated among steep mountains and dense forests; there, too, a very small church of humble construction has been built. In its baptistery, on the most holy Paschal night, at the hour appointed for baptism, although there was no channel, no pipe, and no water anywhere nearby, a spring filled itself. After the few had been consecrated, since it had no outlet, the water departed of itself, just as it had come [Note: [Col. 0609C] Quesnellus, in the margin: elsewhere, *descends*. The Vatican manuscript has *discends*.].

At that time, therefore, as we said above, under my former lord, of holy memory, the most blessed pope Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0609C] Marianus adds “in the ninth year of Honorius,” and shortly afterward has “Easterners” instead of “Westerners.” “Westerners” must be read, since the eighty-four-year cycle from which the error arose prevailed only among the Westerners.], when an error had arisen among the Westerners, after the customary readings had been completed on the holy night [Note: [Col. 0609C] Quesnellus, in the margin: elsewhere, “on the holy night.” Shortly afterward we have restored *when the readings had been completed* from the Vatican manuscript; previously *when they had been examined* was read.], and when the presbyter, according to custom, was awaiting the hour for baptizing, the water did not come until daylight, and those who were to be baptized departed without having been consecrated. To relate the matter briefly: on that night which was dawning into Sunday, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, the sacred spring was filled at the proper hour. The evident miracle therefore made clear that the error belonged to the Western regions.

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0609D] What follows to the end, restored from Marianus Scotus and Bucherius’s edition with the help of manuscripts, was added by Quesnellus to his edition. It is also found in our Vatican manuscript, except for the final words, “Pray for me.”]

As far as I could, or as the brevity of a letter allowed, I have written this in obedience to your apostolate. I fall prostrate and beseech you to deign to pray for my insignificance—or rather, for the condition of the whole world—so that, at last freed from so many necessities, we may know that he is our God, who alone works wonders. May he no longer hand over to beasts the souls that confess him, nor allow us to be tested beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation provide a merciful outcome [Note: [Col. 0609D] Marianus Scotus has *of mercy*.] through his goodness, so that we may endure. Pray for me.

## LETTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0609D] Elsewhere numbered 3; what was 4 is now 6. Written on 10 October 443.] [Note: [Col. 0609D] This letter is found in fifteen collections: 2, 5, Dionysiana 6, Hadrian 7 and 8, Hisp. 9, Isid. 10, 11, 12, 13, and 20 through 24. Among these, only three collections are of different origin: the second, Corbeiensis; the fifth, Quesnelliana; and the sixth, Dionysiana. The remaining collections copied this letter from the last of these. In correcting it, we used manuscripts from twelve different collections, among which the principal ones are Vindobonensis 39, collection 5, and the Vatican manuscript of Dionysius, together with two manuscripts of collection 9, the Hispanic collection—one Vindobonensis and the other Vatican.] TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT CAMPANIA, PICENUM, TUSCIA, AND ALL THE PROVINCES.

[Note: [Col. 0610C] In the manuscripts of collection 5, the synopsis of this letter is given in the preceding table, no. 76, as follows: “To all the bishops of Campania, Picenum, and Tuscia, that slaves, *originarii*, or persons bound to any condition whatsoever be barred from ecclesiastical offices, and concerning those clerics who practice lending in order to receive interest.”]

## SYNOPSIS

(From Dionysius Exiguus.)

I. No bishop may promote another person’s slave to clerical office [Note: [Col. 0610C] The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has *promote*; in Dionysius’s table apud Tustellus, *advance*. But in the title prefixed to the chapter, it has *presume to promote*.].

II. Anyone promoted to the priesthood who is the husband of a widow or who has had several marriages [Note: [Col. 0610C] Quesnellus has “who have had.”] is to be excluded from ecclesiastical offices.

III. Not only clerics but also lay Christians [Note: [Col. 0610C] We restored the word “Christians,” omitted by Quesnellus, from the printed editions and the better manuscripts.] must not exact interest.

IV. A cleric must not practice lending at interest either in his own name or in another’s.

V. If any priest acts contrary to the prohibitions, he is to be removed from his office [Note: [Col. 0610C] Elsewhere, “he is to be removed from his own office.”].

LEO, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greeting in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscia, and all the provinces [Note: [Col. 0610C] The words “greeting in the Lord,” omitted by Quesnellus, have been restored from earlier editions, our manuscripts, and Cresconius. Some codices omit the proper names Campania, Picenum, and Tuscia.].

Just as the condition of the Churches, arranged by sound administration, gives us cause for rejoicing, so we are distressed by no slight sorrow whenever we learn that something has been attempted or done contrary to the canonical decrees and ecclesiastical discipline [Note: [Col. 0610D] Two manuscripts and the older editions have “statutes.” Shortly afterward, two Vercelli manuscripts of the Hadrian collection have “either committed or despised” instead of “or committed.”]. If we do not cut away such things with the vigilance we ought [Note: [Col. 0610D] The Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 has “cut off.” Then, in one Vatican manuscript, “be excused.”], we cannot excuse ourselves before the one who wished us to be watchmen (Ezekiel 3:17), since we allow the sound body of the Church, which we must keep pure from every stain, to be defiled by the wicked contagion of those who surround it [Col. 0610C], when the structure of its members itself does not hold together through mutual dissimilarity [Note: [Col. 0610D] The Corbeiensis manuscript of collection 2, apud Quesnellus, has “through wicked thought.”]. [Note: [Col. 0610D] We have retained this correction by Quesnellus, which the sense appears to require, since it is confirmed by our better manuscripts. Hence, in the printed editions, where *through dissimulation* is read, the margin notes *through dissimilarity*. If this was not derived from manuscripts but, as seems likely, from conjecture, the correction was judged to be demanded by the sense. See Quesnellus’s note 1.]

## CHAPTER I

### The ordination of another person’s slave is unlawful

[Note: [Col. 0611B] Distinction 54, “They are admitted,” chapter 21.]

People are indiscriminately admitted to sacred orders who possess no dignity of birth and no dignity of character; and those who have been unable to obtain freedom from their masters are advanced to the height of the priesthood, as though servile baseness could receive this honor [Note: [Col. 0611B] Vatican manuscript 544, collection 24: “servile status may receive the honor.” Two Vercelli manuscripts have “may receive.” Before Quesnellus, the printed editions prefixed *by right* to *may receive*, but the word is absent from all our manuscripts, from Quesnellus’s manuscripts, and from Tustellus.]. It is believed that someone can be approved by God who has not yet been able to approve himself to his master.

There is therefore a double offense in this matter: both the sacred ministry is polluted by the baseness of such an associate, and the rights of masters are violated, insofar as this concerns the recklessness of unlawful usurpation. [Note: [Col. 0611B] Manuscripts Thuaneus 1 and Corbeiensis of Quesnellus begin chapter 1 with these words.]

Let all the priests of your provinces, therefore, dearest brothers, abstain from such men [Note: [Col. 0611B] Distinction 54, “No priest,” chapter 1]; and not only from them, but also from others who are bound by their birth-status or by some condition [Note: [Col. 0611B] This reading is taken from the pure Vatican copy of Dionysius and other Hadrian manuscripts, as well as Vatican 1347 and the edition of Cresconius, chapter 195. It agrees with the Herovallian collection appended by Petit to Theodore’s *Penitential*, where we read: “And from others also who are bound by birth-status or by any condition.” Two Hispanic manuscripts and the Vatican manuscript of Isidore, together with another manuscript of collection 11, add *or* before *birth-status*. Merlinus, with the manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, has “from those also who are bound by birth-status.” Two other Vatican manuscripts, together with the editions before Quesnellus, have “from those also who are bound either by birth-status.” Quesnellus, with four of his manuscripts and our Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, has “from those also who are bound either by their origin”; in note 2 he attempts to defend and prefer the reading *origin*. Yet the reading *birth-status* could not be abandoned, since it appears in all our manuscripts except Vindobonensis, especially in the pure Dionysian manuscript. Nor do we see why *origin* should fit the condition and sense better than *birth-status*, as Quesnellus asserts. *Of origin* would be more satisfactory than *to origin*. By those bound by *birth-status*, or by the condition of origin, are understood the *coloni originales* mentioned in law 14, *On Grain and Tribute*, and in the single law *On Tenants*, and in book 1 of the Justinian Code, *On Farmers and the Slaves of Masters*—hence *originalis inquilinatus* in Sidonius, book 5, letter 19. Those called *originarii* in Valentinian’s Novel 12, and by Gelasius in letter 9, chapter 14, are those who, by the right of origin—as the aforementioned novel says—or, as Augustine explains in *The City of God*, book 10, chapter 1, owe their condition to their native soil because of agriculture under the control of landowners. In fact, by the cause of their origin or by the lot of their birth, they had to cultivate the estates of landowners and were bound to them. These men, bound by the condition of origin, Saint Leo distinguishes from slaves, just as they are likewise distinguished in numerous laws noted by Gothofredus in his *Paratitlon* on fugitive tenant-farmers. They were attached to estates, not to persons as slaves were, and were regarded as a kind of part or member of the estates [Col. 0612B]. When the holy pontiff distinguishes from these *originarii* others who were bound to some condition, he may mean either tenants attached to estates not by right of origin but by thirty years’ possession, concerning whom the aforementioned Novel 12 speaks, or those who bound themselves and their labor to some craft, whence various craft-workers bound by condition—that is, bound by their status to perform certain work—are called *conditionales* by Tertullian in *On Idolatry*, chapter 12. Quesnellus interpreted this passage very well in note 2.], unless perhaps the petition or consent of those who claim some authority over them has been given. For the person who is to be enrolled in divine service must be free from others [Note: [Col. 0612B] Vatican manuscript of Dionysius: “be withdrawn from no worldly necessity.” Vatican manuscript of collection 11: “from the bonds of no necessity.” The Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 has “be withdrawn.”], so that he may not be drawn away by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, to which his name is enrolled.

## CHAPTER II

### The husband of a widow, and a man who has had more than one wife, must be barred from sacred ministry

[Note: [Col. 0612C] This reading, introduced by Quesnellus from the manuscripts cited in his note 3, is also approved by our better witnesses: the pure Vatican Dionysian manuscript, one Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, another of the Hispanic collection, the Vatican manuscript of collection 24, and the copy of the Herovallian collection edited by Petit. The reading of the printed editions is: “What dignity of birth and character each person who is to be associated with the ministry of the sacred altar ought to possess, etc.” It is preferred in the Vatican manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorean collections and in three other Vatican manuscripts, one of which alone has *to be associated*. The omission of the two words “when it has been established,” together with the addition of the words “who and is,” corrupts the reading. In two Vercelli manuscripts of the Hadrian collection, the text omits only the verb “has been established”; in Tustellus’s collection, “has been established” is present, but the following word is missing.]

But when it has been established what dignity of birth and character the person who is to be associated with the ministry of the sacred altar ought to possess, we have learned this both from the Apostle’s teaching (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6), from divine instruction (Leviticus 21:14), and from the rules of the canons, from which we find that many of our brothers have departed and entirely strayed. [Note: [Col. 0612C] After *we find*, the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 adds *we admonish*, or rather *we are admonished*. [Col. 0612D] The following words, “For it is clear,” begin chapter 2 in the Corbeiensis and Thuaneus 1 manuscripts, according to Quesnellus’s postscript.]

For it is clear that husbands of widows [Note: [Col. 0612D] See Quesnellus’s note 4. Shortly afterward, “and also certain men” occurs in the Vercelli manuscripts. The Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 omits *also*.] have attained the priesthood, and that even some men who have had several marriages, and whose lives have been freely open to every indulgence, have been admitted indiscriminately to sacred orders, contrary to the saying of the blessed Apostle, in which he cries out against such men, saying: “The husband of one wife” (1 Timothy 3:2); and contrary to the command of the ancient law, [Note: [Col. 0612D] The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, together with two others, have “in which it is prescribed.”] in which it is said and prescribed: “Let the priest take a virgin as wife, not a widow, not one who has been repudiated” (Leviticus 21:14). Therefore, by the authority of the apostolic see, we order that all such men who have been admitted be excluded from ecclesiastical offices and from the name of priest. For they will not be able to claim for themselves what they were not capable of possessing, since what stood in their way prevented them from possessing it [Note: [Col. 0612D] Quesnellus, in the margin: elsewhere, “because they had become such.” The Corbeiensis and Thuaneus 1 manuscripts have this reading.]. We claim for ourselves especially the responsibility of investigating this matter [Note: [Col. 0612D] See Quesnellus’s note 6 together with our observations.], so that whatever offenses may perhaps have been committed by such men may be corrected [Note: [Col. 0613C] Vatican manuscript of collection 24: “so that it may not be permitted.” Shortly afterward, one Vatican manuscript has “so that no excuse of ignorance may arise.”], that no further offense may be permitted, and that no excuse based on ignorance may arise. Yet it has never been permissible for a priest to be ignorant of what has been defined by the rules of the canons [Note: [Col. 0613C] Two Vatican manuscripts have “for a priest.” Shortly afterward, “what the canons have” occurs in two Vindobonensis manuscripts.].

We have therefore sent this letter to your provinces through Innocentius, Legitimus, and Segetius [Note: [Col. 0613C] Two Vercelli manuscripts have *Sigentius*. Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has “are known to have sprung up.”], our brothers and fellow bishops, so that what is known to have sprung up improperly may be uprooted from the roots, and no weeds may corrupt the Lord’s harvest [Note: [Col. 0613C] The Corbeiensis and Thuaneus 1 manuscripts of Quesnellus have “let no one corrupt it with weeds.”]. For the sound things will indeed yield abundant fruit if those things that habitually destroy the growing crop are cut away more diligently [Note: [Col. 0613C] The same manuscripts of Quesnellus have “defile.” Two Vindobonensis manuscripts have “kill.”].

## CHAPTER III

### Interest forbidden to laymen and clerics

[Note: [Col. 0613C] Distinction 14, question 4, “Nor must this be passed over,” chapter 7.]

We have also decided that this must not be passed over: some men, seized by a shameful desire for profit [Note: [Col. 0613C] See Quesnellus’s note 7.], practice lending at interest and wish to grow rich by usury [Col. 0613B]. We grieve that this occurs not only among those established in clerical office, but also among laymen who wish to be called Christians [Note: [Col. 0613C] We have added the particle *also* from the Vatican Dionysian manuscript, Vindobonensis collection 5, Cresconius, the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, and three other codices.]. We decree that this must be punished more severely in those who have been convicted [Note: [Col. 0613C] Quesnellus has “in them.” We preferred the reading of all our manuscripts and Cresconius. Vatican manuscript of collection 24 has “in those who have been proved guilty.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Dionysian manuscript and two Vercelli manuscripts have *we decreed* instead of *we decree*.], so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed.

## CHAPTER IV

### A cleric must not practice lending at interest either in his own name or in another’s

[Note: [Col. 0613C] In the Corbeiensis and Thuaneus 1 manuscripts of Quesnellus, this chapter forms part of the preceding chapter [Col. 0613D].]

We have also thought it right to give this warning: just as no cleric may practice lending at interest in his own name, so no cleric should attempt to practice it in another’s name [Note: [Col. 0613D] Distinction 46, “Not in his own name,” chapter 10.]. For it is an unbecoming crime to devote one’s own guilt to another’s advantage. We ought to regard and practice lending at interest only in this respect: that what we mercifully grant here, we may receive from the Lord, who will repay it multiplied and enduring forever [Note: [Col. 0613D] Five manuscripts have “from the Lord.”].

## CHAPTER V

### A bishop who violates the canons is to be deposed

This admonition of ours therefore declares that if any of our brothers attempts to act against these decrees [Note: [Col. 0613D] Distinction 19, chapter 1, “If the Roman pontiff,” section “To whom these matters pertain.”] and dares to admit what has been prohibited, he must know that he is to be removed from his office [Note: [Col. 0613D] The editions before Quesnellus, together with the Vatican manuscript of collection 24, have “has come or attempted to come.” Vindobonensis collection 5 has “has wished to come.”], and that he will not share in our communion—he who has refused to share in discipline. But lest anything should perhaps be thought to have been omitted by us, we command that all the decretal constitutions, both those of Innocentius of blessed memory and those of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons [Note: [Col. 0613D] The editions before Quesnellus, together only with the manuscripts of collection 24, have “which have been arranged concerning ecclesiastical ordinations and the disciplines of the canons.” See Quesnellus’s note 8 and our observation. Shortly afterward, these same editions, together with Vindobonensis and the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and five other codices, read: “we command that you must preserve your affection in this way.” But the Vatican Dionysian manuscript, Vindobonensis collection 5, the Hadrian manuscripts, and the Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark defend Quesnellus’s reading.], be observed by your affection, so that if anyone commits an offense against them [Note: [Col. 0613D] These same editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, have “despises them.”], he may know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him [Col. 0614B]. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Maximus for the second time and Paterius [Note: [Col. 0614C] All the printed editions, together with most manuscripts, have *Paternus*, relegating *Paterius* to the margin, although the latter reading appeared in Merlinus’s edition; we found it in the Vatican manuscript, the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, and another Vatican manuscript of collection 11. Pagius proves that this reading must certainly be retained in his notes on the year 443, no. 1 and 11, and Georgius confirms it in his notes on Pagius appended to the latest Lucca edition. The matter is placed beyond all doubt by a contemporary papyrus document of the Church of Ravenna, accurately reprinted by Marquis Maffei in *Historia diplomatica*, p. 132, and donated by him to the Vatican Library; in it, the consulship of that year is designated by the name of Paterius, not Paternus. Another annotator in the same Lucca edition infers from this papyrus monument that Maximus held the consulship not for the second but for the third time, because it there reads “the third consulship of Maximus and the consulship of Paterius.” But since all our manuscripts and all the monuments cited by Pagius and Georgius call Maximus, in nearly full form, consul for the second time, twice, or again, while the others use the numeral II, it is clear that the papyrus must not be read *ter* but *iter.*, that is, *iterum*, “again.” The letter *i* is to be taken from the final letter of the preceding word *Maximi*, since in such monuments it often happens that an initial letter is omitted when the preceding word ends with the same letter. This is even more strongly indicated by the scribe’s practice, who in the words *Paterius* and *Theodosius* avoids writing the double *i*.].

617 [Note: [Col. 0614D] Written on 12 January 444.]

## LETTER V

[Note: [Col. 0614D] This letter is among those collected for the Church of Thessalonica, and was first published in Luke Holstenius’s Roman collection. We have usefully reexamined it against the Barberini manuscript 3386, collection 16, from which Holstenius’s edition was produced, since it is a manuscript of the single Thessalonian collection. This letter should be placed before the following one to Anastasius, since, although both were written on the same day, the following letter already refers to it as having been composed in chapter 6.]

TO THE METROPOLITAN BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT ILLYRICUM.

## SYNOPSIS

I. Unlawful attempts contrary to the canons are prudently forestalled by admonitions.

II. He entrusts his authority throughout Illyricum to Anastasius of Thessalonica, following the custom of his predecessors.

III. He orders that bigamists, husbands of widows, and husbands of repudiated women be barred from the priesthood according to the canons.

IV. Just as provincial bishops are subject to metropolitans, so metropolitans are subject to the exarch or vicar.

V. It belongs to those same exarchs or vicars to ordain metropolitan bishops and to report the condition of the provinces to the apostolic see.

VI. More serious cases and appeals from Illyricum are reserved to the apostolic see.

To the most beloved brothers, the metropolitan bishops established throughout Illyricum, LEO.

## CHAPTER I

Every salutary admonition, which we believe comes to pass with the Lord’s inspiration, benefits both the one who admonishes and the one who is admonished; and for that reason we gladly undertake this task, since we hasten to please our God not only through our own actions but also through those of all our brothers and fellow priests. It returns to our credit if the Churches are governed in such a way that no opening is left for complaints.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let the instruction which you recognize as proceeding from the authority of the apostolic see, while preserving the grace of charity, be sweet and welcome to your affection. Do not think that any of your rights are diminished if you see precautions being taken, for present as well as future circumstances, so that no opening may be given to unlawful presumption. It is wiser to resist usurpations cautiously before they are attempted than to punish what has already been usurped.

## CHAPTER II

Since our care extends throughout all the Churches, as the Lord requires of us—he who entrusted the primacy of apostolic dignity to the blessed Apostle Peter as a reward for his faith [Note: [Col. 0615D] In Holstenius’s edition, through a typographical error, “of his faith.” The emendation discussed by Quesnellus in note 1 is supported by the Barberini manuscript.]—establishing the universal Church upon the solidity of that foundation [Note: [Col. 0615D] See Quesnellus’s note 2, who prefers the reading “of this one,” and our observation.], we share the necessity of vigilance that we bear with those joined to us by the fellowship of the episcopal college.

We have therefore entrusted our authority to our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, following the example of those whose memory we rightly venerate, 618 and have instructed him to stand watch, lest anyone presume anything unlawful [Col. 0615C]. We admonish you to obey him in matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline. For you will not so much be obeying him as us, since he is known to have been entrusted with this responsibility throughout those provinces because of our pastoral concern.

## CHAPTER III
We wish such men to be made priests for the Lord as possess all the qualifications defined by the ecclesiastical canons: [Note: [Col. 0615D] The Barberini manuscript has “that bishop, presbyter, and deacon.”] bishops, presbyters, and deacons must be husbands of one wife, according to the judgment of the blessed Apostle (1 Tim. 3:2), and must have received her as a virgin, in accordance with the precepts of the Law [Note: [Col. 0615D] Holstenius and the manuscript read “receive.” See Quesnellus’s note 3 for his reason for emending it.], not a widow or a divorced woman, as the wording of the Law testifies (Lev. 21:13–14; Ezek. 44:22). Nor may anyone think that he can attain the priesthood if, after the wife he had died, he married another after having been renewed through the grace of baptism, since baptism blots out sins, but does not abolish the number of wives. Indeed, he will not be able to put this forward as an excuse for himself, since he cannot deny that he is the father of the children whom he fathered before baptism. For the wife whom he takes in accordance with the precept of the Law cannot be counted among the sins washed away in baptism.

## CHAPTER IV

Whoever is summoned to a synod must attend and must not refuse the assembly in which he knows that matters relating to God are to be examined [Note: [Col. 0615D] We have added the points to indicate a line and a half left blank in the Barberini manuscript. This signifies that something had been damaged in the older manuscript from which the Barberini was copied and could not be read by the scribe.] [lacuna]. Whatever disputes, as commonly happens, arise among fellow priests must be reserved for the examination of the man to whom we have entrusted our authority, so that, with him presiding in the fear of God, every ambiguity may be brought to an end. No one is to presume to injure either him or us by acting against these provisions of ours. If anything must be referred to us, let it become known to us through his report. For we wish you to belong to him in the same way that the priests of your provinces belong to you. Therefore, those who wish to exercise the right due to them should not try, through their contumacy, to diminish the authority granted by the Apostolic See.

## CHAPTER V

Just as the ordering of the priests of your province is entrusted to your affection, so we wish you to consult our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius concerning the appointment of a bishop. We have reserved to him the consecration of metropolitan bishops, so that, with him as investigator and guardian, when a definite limit is placed upon permission, the order of ecclesiastical discipline may be preserved in every respect. Your affection should recognize that he himself has been admonished in our letters, according to the canons’ definitions, to make us periodically better informed by his report about the condition of your Churches [Note: [Col. 0615D] See Quesnellus’s note 4. The words “in our letters” seem to indicate another earlier letter, distinct from the one that follows, which had been written to Anastasius. In it Leo had advised him, as he says, to make us subsequently better informed by his report about the condition of your Churches. This instruction is not found in the following letter; rather, in chapter 1, the words “in these letters, in which we have been informed about the condition of the Churches” seem to refer to Anastasius’s letter reporting to Leo about the Churches of Illyricum in order to comply with the admonition mentioned above. That gave occasion for writing the following letter.]. He should know that, if anyone acts rashly against what we have ordained, he will be held accountable for it by us.

## CHAPTER VI

But if more serious cases or appeals arise, we have decreed that they must be sent to us together with his report, so that they may be concluded by our judgment according to ecclesiastical custom [Note: [Col. 0616D] This decree is found in chapter 5 of the following letter, which was sent to Illyricum together with this one.]. As for the matters that we have sent in writing through my son, the presbyter Nicholas, reply by return letter so that we may know that you have received them. Given on the day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Albinus.

# LETTER VI [Note: [Col. 0616D] Formerly Letter 4; what was 6 is now 1. Written 12 January 444.]

## TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

[Note: [Col. 0616D] This letter too was taken from the same Barberini manuscript of the sixteenth Thessalonian collection and published in Holstenius’s Roman collection, from which the preceding letter was also taken. Compare the first annotation on that letter. Leo Allatius had published some testimonies to this letter in *The Harmony of the Eastern and Western Church*, p. 1370, from a very ancient Vatican manuscript that cannot be found at present. On the authority of Allatius, we shall also give variants from the manuscript from which the Barberini was derived.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He gladly allows himself to be compelled by letters, as a good shepherd, to care for his fellow bishops.—II. He entrusts Anastasius with his authority throughout Illyricum, following the example of Siricius.—III. He commends observance of the canons, especially in ordinations; bigamists and husbands of widows are excluded.—IV. Provincial bishops are to be ordained by the metropolitan with the knowledge of the exarch; metropolitans by the exarch himself.—V. All are to attend synods; their usefulness and authority.—VI. Presbyters and deacons, as well as bishops, are to be consecrated only on Sundays.

To his most beloved brother Anastasius, Leo.

## CHAPTER I

The love of our fraternal college makes us reread the letters of all priests with grateful affection, since through spiritual grace we embrace as present those with whom we are joined by the exchange of letters and conversation. But we perceive a greater affection in those letters [Note: [Col. 0617D] We have restored the pronoun “to us,” omitted by Quesnellus, from the same manuscript and Holstenius’s edition.] by which, having been informed about the condition of the Churches, we are compelled by consideration of our office to exercise vigilant care [Note: [Col. 0617D] The Barberini manuscript reads *alterni*, corruptly.]. Thus, stationed as watchmen, as the Lord wished [Note: [Col. 0617D] The same manuscript and the Vulgate read “God.”], we may give our assent, according to our desire, to affairs proceeding properly, and may correct by remedies of discipline whatever we see being corrupted by some usurpation: hoping that the seed we have sown will return a rich harvest to us, if we do not allow what has begun to sprout to the detriment of the Lord’s harvest to grow.

## CHAPTER II

Accordingly, after the request of your affection became known to us through our son, the presbyter Nicholas—that authority might be granted to you also, as it was to your predecessors, throughout Illyricum, together with our authority, for the protection of the rules [Note: [Col. 0617D] See Quesnellus’s notes 1 and 2.]—we give our assent and, by our exhortation, urge you to ensure that no concealment and no negligence arise in the government of the Churches situated throughout Illyricum. We entrust these Churches to your affection in our place, following the example of Siricius, who, recognizing the merits of your predecessor Anysius before the Apostolic See and approving his subsequent conduct, first entrusted this responsibility to him according to a definite arrangement [Note: [Col. 0617D] The Vatican manuscript cited by Allatius reads “through concealment.”]. He was to assist the Churches situated in that province, which Siricius wished to be held to discipline.

Glorious examples must be followed with greater zeal, so that, since we wish to use their privileges, we may prove ourselves like them in every respect. We wish you to be an imitator both of your predecessor and of your immediate predecessor, who is known to have both deserved and carried out this responsibility in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0617D] By “predecessor” he means Anysius, mentioned shortly before, who lived until the papacy of Innocent; by “immediate predecessor” he means Rufus, who was elected under Innocent and immediately preceded Anastasius.], so that we may rejoice in the progress of the Churches that we entrust to you in our place [Note: [Col. 0618D] The Vatican manuscript cited by Allatius reads “which we entrusted”; above, however, the text reads “which we entrust.”]. For just as an entrusted responsibility advances the honor of one who acts well and carries out more diligently what is suited to priestly authority, so it is recognized as a burden to one who, having been entrusted with power, does not use it with the moderation required.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore, dearest brother, keep vigilant watch over the helm entrusted to you, and direct the eyes of your mind everywhere throughout the matters committed to your care, guarding what will contribute to your reward and resisting those who try to weaken the discipline of the canons [Note: [Col. 0618D] The same Vatican manuscript reads “those things.”]. Let the venerable sanction of divine law, and especially the decrees of the canons, be observed. Throughout the provinces entrusted to you, let such priests be consecrated for the Lord as are supported by nothing but the merits of their life and clerical order [Note: [Col. 0618D] Thus in the same manuscript, *suffragentur*, “are supported.”]. Permit nothing to personal favor, nothing to ambition, and nothing to purchased support. Those who are to be ordained must be examined more carefully and instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines through the long course of their lives.

Provided, however, that they meet all the requirements established by the holy Fathers and preserve what we read that the blessed Apostle Paul commanded concerning such men: that he be the husband of one wife and have received her as a virgin, as the authority of divine law requires. We wish this to be guarded so carefully that we remove every opportunity for excuses, lest anyone believe that he can attain the priesthood if, after taking a wife before receiving the grace of Christ, he joined himself to another after the first had died. For that first wife cannot be denied, nor can the number of the earlier marriage be abolished; and he is likewise the father of the children whom he fathered by her before baptism, just as he is the father of those whom he is known to have fathered by the other after baptism [Note: [Col. 0618D] We have added “likewise” from both manuscripts; from them we have also restored *is known* in place of *is recognized*.]. For just as sins and things known to be unlawful are abolished through the washing of baptism, so things permitted or lawful by the precept of the Law are not erased [Note: [Col. 0618D] See Quesnellus’s note 4, where he supplied the two necessary words “just as” and emended “will be abolished” to “are abolished.”].

## CHAPTER IV

No bishop is to be ordained throughout those Churches without consulting you. In this way mature judgments will be made concerning those to be chosen, since the examination of your affection will be respected. Whoever, then, is ordained by metropolitan bishops contrary to our instruction and without your knowledge must know that his position has no stability before us, and that those who presume to do this will be required to give an account of their usurpation [Note: [Col. 0618D] Here Quesnellus introduced a necessary emendation; see his note 5. Previously the reading was incorrect: “But whoever among the metropolitan bishops …”].

Just as this power is entrusted to each metropolitan, so that they have the right to ordain within their own provinces, so we wish those metropolitans to be ordained by you, though with mature and well-considered judgment [Note: [Col. 0619C] The Barberini manuscript and the Vulgate read “honorable”; Leo Allatius read “decorous.”]. Although it is fitting that all bishops who have been tested and are pleasing to God should be consecrated, we nevertheless wish those to excel whom we know will preside over the fellow priests subject to them. We admonish your affection to carry this out more carefully and cautiously, so that you may be approved as guarding the apostolic injunction written in Scripture: “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Tim. 5:22).

## CHAPTER V

Whoever of the brethren is summoned to a synod must attend and must not refuse the holy assembly. In it, above all, he must know that whatever can pertain to ecclesiastical discipline is to be established [Note: [Col. 0619C] The Barberini manuscript reads “to be guarded.” Holstenius emended this by conjecture, since decrees are established in synods.]. Every fault will be avoided more effectively if consultation among the priests of the Lord is held more frequently [Note: [Col. 0619C] We restored “every” from the Barberini manuscript and Holstenius’s edition, where Quesnellus had omitted it.], and united fellowship contributes greatly both to correction and to charity.

If any cases arise there, they can, with the Lord’s help, be settled in such a way that no dispute remains, but only charity among the brethren grows firm [Note: [Col. 0619C] We have emended this from the manuscript. The printed editions read “solid,” following Holstenius’s conjecture, though it is not compelled.]. But if a more serious case arises which cannot be decided there while your fraternity presides, let your report be sent to consult us. Then, with the Lord revealing what we profess to owe to his mercy—that is, whatever he inspires us to do—we shall send our reply, so that, in accordance with the tradition of the ancient institution and the due reverence owed to the Apostolic See, we may vindicate through our judgment what comes before our examination.

For just as we wish you to exercise our authority in our place [Note: [Col. 0619C] Thus the manuscript and Holstenius. Quesnellus conjecturally inserted “our.”], so we reserve to ourselves whatever cannot be settled there, and whoever has raised the voice of appeal [Note: [Col. 0619C] See Quesnellus’s note 6 and our observation.].

## CHAPTER VI

You shall therefore make these matters known to all the brethren, so that thereafter no one may find an opportunity to excuse himself through ignorance in observing what we have commanded [Note: [Col. 0619C] Allatius reads “through ignorance,” followed by “and then, the things we command.”]. We have also sent our letters to the metropolitan bishops of each province, in order to admonish them, so that they may know that apostolic judgments must be obeyed and that they obey us when, in accordance with our delegation, they begin to obey your fraternity [Col. 0620A] according to what we have written.

We have learned something that we could not pass over in silence: certain brethren ordain bishops only on Sundays, but allow presbyters and deacons, whose consecration ought to be equivalent [Note: [Col. 0619D] See Quesnellus’s note 7.], to receive the dignity of the priestly office indiscriminately on any day. This usurpation must be corrected, contrary as it is to the canons and the tradition of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0619D] See Quesnellus’s note 8.], since the custom handed down to them concerning all sacred orders must be observed in every respect. Thus, over the long course of time, whoever is to be ordained priest or Levite must advance through all the orders of the clerical office, so that he may learn over a prolonged period the office of which he himself will one day be the teacher.

Given on the day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Theodosius XVIII and Albinus.

# LETTER VII [Note: [Col. 0619D] Formerly Letter 8; what was 7 is now 2. Written 30 January 444.]

## TO THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT ITALY

[Note: [Col. 0619D] This letter is found in thirteen collections: 2, 5, Dionysiana 6, Hadriana 7, Hispana 9, Isidoriana 10, and also collections 11, 12, 13, 21, and the remaining collections through 24. In the index prefixed to collection 5, chapter 73, it is entitled: “General Letter concerning the Manichaeans.”]

[Col. 0620B]

[Note: [Col. 0619D] In Dionysius this title reads: “That very many Manichaeans (or: of the Manichaeans) were detected in the city of Rome through the vigilance of Pope Leo.”]

## SYNOPSIS

He warns that very many Manichaeans have been detected in the city of Rome through his vigilance and that they must be investigated with equal care by the bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0619D] We have preferred this inscription from the pure Vatican manuscript of Dionysius, other Hadrianic manuscripts, and the Viennese Hispana. The Vatican Hispana and Isidorian manuscripts, together with other manuscripts of collection 11, read “Churches” instead of “bishops.” The Corbie manuscript of collection 2 and the manuscripts of collection 5 read: “To all bishops established throughout the various provinces.” The Florentine manuscript of collection 13 reads: “Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to all bishops established throughout Italy.” See Quesnellus’s note.]

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings in the Lord to all bishops established throughout the provinces of Italy.

## CHAPTER I

We call you into partnership in our concern [Note: [Col. 0620C] The manuscripts of the Hispana and Isidoriana collections, together with four others derived from them, add “dearest brothers.”], so that, with pastoral vigilance, you may take more careful thought for the flocks entrusted to you, lest the devil’s cunning be able to do them any harm [Note: [Col. 0620C] The Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of collection 12, reads: “lest the cunning of diabolical fraud be able to do any harm.” The reading introduced by Quesnellus is also confirmed by our manuscripts, except for two later Vatican manuscripts, which read: “lest the cunning of a diabolical thing be able to do any harm.”].

The disease which, through the revelation of the Lord’s mercy, has been driven away from our sheep through our care must not, while you remain uninformed of our warning and ignorant of what is happening, spread through your Churches [Note: [Col. 0620D] Quesnellus, in the margin, reads from Dionysius: “continue through the Churches of your see,” incorrectly. This reading is found in Justellus, but not in our Dionysian manuscripts or in the Hadrianic manuscripts.], nor find a hiding place in the secret tunnels of its lairs [Note: [Col. 0620D] The Corbie manuscript and the first Thuanus manuscript, as cited by Quesnellus, read: “and find the hiding place of their secret tunnels.”]. Thus what is being extinguished by us in the City may not be planted among you with dark roots [Note: [Col. 0620D] The Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with the Vercelli manuscript and Justellus, reads “lest some” incorrectly.].

Our investigation discovered very many followers and teachers of Manichaean impiety in the City; our vigilance exposed them, and authority and discipline restrained them. Those whom we were able to correct, we corrected. We compelled them publicly in the Church, by a formal declaration and by the signature of their own hands, to condemn Manichaeus together with his teachings and practices [Note: [Col. 0620D] Thus the Vulgate manuscripts before Quesnellus, and “with his disciples” in the manuscripts. Shortly afterward, two Vatican manuscripts and the Viennese Hispana collection read “confession” instead of “profession.”]. Having thus confessed their impiety, we lifted them from its abyss by granting them penance.

But some had plunged themselves so deeply that no remedy capable of assisting them could come to their aid [Note: [Col. 0621C] Quesnellus and two of our inferior manuscripts read: “they plunged themselves so deeply that no remedy of assistance could help them.” We followed the older reading found in the manuscripts of the Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispana, and Isidorian collections, as well as collections 12 and 24 and Justellus. The Viennese manuscript of collection 5 reads: “they plunged themselves so deeply that no remedy of assistance could come to their aid.”]. Subjected to the laws, according to the enactments of Christian emperors, they were sent into perpetual exile by public judges, lest they pollute the holy flock by their contagion.

We set before the eyes of the Christian people, with definite disclosure, everything profane or shameful that they possess both in the Scriptures and in their secret traditions, so that the people might know what to reject or avoid [Note: [Col. 0621C] Four manuscripts add “what.”]. Indeed, their alleged bishop himself was detained by us and exposed the disgraceful secrets that he held in his mystical practices [Note: [Col. 0621C] Vatican manuscript 543 of collection 21 reads: “who was called the bishop of the bishops.” In Sermon 16, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month* 5, he is called “the bishop of those who ordained the detestable crime.”], as the record of the proceedings will be able to show you [Note: [Col. 0621C] Most of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, together with the pure Dionysian manuscript and the Viennese manuscript of collection 5, read “in their mystical practices.” The Vulgate, together with the Hispana, Isidorian, and four other manuscripts of the same origin, reads “in their mysteries.” Other manuscripts mentioned by Quesnellus in the margin read “in their mystical mysteries, which they held.”].

For your instruction we have also sent the proceedings themselves, and when you have read them you will be able to know everything that we discovered [Note: [Col. 0621C] Quesnellus, together with certain manuscripts, reads “you can know.” The examples of the Vatican Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispana, and Isidorian manuscripts, together with the earlier printed editions, read “you will be able to know.” A little earlier, the same printed editions together with one Vatican manuscript read “reproved” instead of “discovered.”].

## CHAPTER II

Since we have learned that some of those whom a more severe guilt had ensnared here, lest they be acquitted, have fled [Note: [Col. 0621D] Thus the Quesnellian reading, the Viennese manuscript of collection 5, and two Vatican manuscripts. The others, together with the Vulgate, read “whom they would not absolve.” The same Viennese manuscript reads “more strictly” instead of “a more severe.”], we have sent this letter to your affection through our acolyte [Note: [Col. 0621D] The words “through our acolyte” are absent from the Vatican Dionysian manuscript and from the published Hadrianic manuscripts, but are found in our other manuscripts. Quesnellus reads “through that acolyte.” We have nowhere been able to find that person. Perhaps the letters *ill.*—customarily used in ancient formulas in place of a proper name—stood in one of his manuscripts.], so that, once informed, your holiness, dearest brothers [Note: [Col. 0621D] The words “dearest brothers” are absent from the Hadrianic, Viennese Hispana, and Justellus manuscripts, from two other Vatican manuscripts, and from the editions printed before Quesnellus.], may deign to act more diligently and cautiously, lest people of Manichaean perversity anywhere find an opportunity to harm your peoples or be able to find teachers of this sacrilege.

For we cannot govern those entrusted to us in any other way than by pursuing with zeal for the Lord’s faith those who are destroyers and destroyed, and cutting them off from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread more widely [Note: [Col. 0622C] The Vatican manuscript of collection 11, together with the Viennese Hispana, reads “them.” Shortly afterward, Vatican manuscript 24 reads “lest the plague spread more boldly.”].

Therefore I exhort, beseech, and admonish your affection to keep watch with the concern that you ought to have and can exercise in investigating them, lest they anywhere find an opportunity to conceal themselves [Note: [Col. 0622C] The Viennese manuscript of collection 5 omits “you ought to have and.”]. For just as the one who more diligently carries out whatever benefits the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God the reward of a worthy recompense [Note: [Col. 0622C] The editions before Quesnellus, together with Vatican manuscript 24, read “a great reward of recompense.” Vatican manuscript 11 omits “great” and “worthy.” Quesnellus gives “worthy” in the margin. Shortly afterward, the Viennese Hispana reads: “will not be able to excuse himself before the Lord’s tribunal for the guilt of his negligence.”], so whoever is unwilling to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself before the Lord’s tribunal for the guilt of his negligence.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of Theodosius Augustus XVIII and Albinus, illustrious men.

# LETTER VIII, OR THE CONSTITUTION OF VALENTINIAN III [Note: [Col. 0622C] 19 June 445.]

## CONCERNING THE MANICHAEANS (G)

[Note: [Col. 0622C] Quesnellus reads “to Albinus, prefect of the praetorium and patrician.” After “prefect of the praetorium” we have added “II,” from the printed and manuscript books of the *Novellae*, where the Wurzburg manuscript has “Albinus, prefect of the praetorium” twice. Albinus was evidently first prefect of the praetorium in 426, as may be inferred from book 7, *On Legitimate Heirs*. We have removed “and patrician,” for although he bears that title in laws of 446, he does not bear it in those of 445.]

The emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, Augusti,

to Albinus, prefect of the praetorium II.

Pagan superstition, which has also been condemned by the emperors of former times, as hostile to public discipline and an enemy of the Christian faith, has not unjustly moved our clemency to destroy it. We speak of the Manichaeans, whom the enactments of all earlier emperors have judged execrable and fit to be expelled from the whole world. Nor do the crimes recently discovered permit concealment [Note: [Col. 0622D] They were discovered, evidently, in 443 through the efforts of Saint Leo, according to Prosper’s *Chronicle*. Compare our preceding admonition to the first letter, §23, and Quesnellus’s first dissertation on the life and deeds of Saint Leo in the year 443.].

For what things, and how obscene to say and hear, were revealed by their own open confession in the judgment of the most blessed Pope Leo, before the most distinguished senate? [Note: [Col. 0622D] Leo himself says in Letter 15 to Turibius, chapter 16: “In our judgment, which was attended not only by a very large presence of priests but also by the dignity of distinguished men and by a certain part of the senate and the people, the crimes of those who committed every offense were disclosed by their own mouths.”] Indeed, the one who was called their bishop both exposed them in his own voice and wrote down all the secrets of their crimes [Note: [Col. 0622D] Compare note 13 above, in the preceding letter.].

This could not remain hidden from our knowledge, since it is not safe for us to neglect so detestable an injury to the Divinity or to leave unpunished a crime by which not only the bodies of the deceived but also their souls are polluted beyond expiation. Therefore, dearest parent Albinus [Note: [Col. 0623B] In the editions before Quesnellus, the letters “A. A.” were joined without punctuation; since joined in this way they signify “Augusti,” Brissonius, book III, *On Formulas*, §63, maintained that they should be interpreted as “of the Augusti.” He thought that some scribes, not knowing their meaning, had rendered the sigla in certain manuscripts as “and most affectionately.” Hence Quesnellus inserted Brissonius’s interpretation, “of the Augusti,” into the text rather than the sigla, and noted that the Oxford manuscript reads “dearest and most affectionate father.” In most manuscripts, however, the same sigla appear with punctuation: P. K. A. A. Ritterius observed in his note on the first novella appended to the Theodosian Code that three manuscripts—Wurzburg, Ottobonian, and one Sichardian—read P. K. A. A., with the same punctuation in two Gotha manuscripts, while another Sichardian reads P. A. A. This agrees with the interpretation found in other manuscripts: “dearest and most affectionate parent.” That this was a formula customary at the time is clear from Theodosius’s Novella 17, *On Divorces*, where Florentius is expressly called “dearest and most affectionate parent,” and from letters 20, 23, and 25 in the *Appendix to Symmachus*, where Symmachus, prefect of the City, is similarly addressed by Honorius. In Spartianus’s *Life of Antoninus Geta*, chapter 2, Juvenalis, prefect of the praetorium, is called “most affectionate parent.” Nowhere, however, have we found the formula “dearest parent of the Augusti” written out. In the same book III, chapter 63, Brissonius interprets the sigla Fr. A. in other laws as “most affectionate brother.” Shortly afterward the Oxford manuscript, according to Quesnellus, reads: “your illustrious and splendid magnificence.”], let your illustrious and magnificent authority know that by this law, destined to endure forever, we have enacted that, by published edicts, it be brought to the knowledge of all the provinces [Note: [Col. 0623D] The words “by published edicts” are absent from the Oxford manuscript.].

Wherever in the world any Manichaean is discovered, let him suffer the penalties that the laws have established for sacrilegious persons, imposed by the authority of public severity. Let it be a public crime, and let anyone who wishes have the right to accuse such persons without risk of prosecution. Nor shall it be lawful or safe for anyone either to conceal such people or to connive at them [Note: [Col. 0623D] The Gothic manuscript and Sichard’s edition read “to live with them.” Some manuscripts, together with the Leipzig edition, read *conhibere*, “to restrain,” but Ritterius noted that scribes confused *connivere*, “to connive,” with *conhibere*.].

Since all the enactments of earlier emperors concerning them have been confirmed by us [Note: [Col. 0623D] The Gothic manuscript and all printed books, together with Quesnellus, read “enactments.” We followed Ritterius’s emendation, since the laws against the Manichaeans in the preceding letter, chapter 1, are called the enactments of the emperors. The phrase “imperial constitutions” is expressed somewhat differently. See the *Paratitlon* on imperial constitutions.], let everyone know, once this edictal law has been published, that Manichaeans are to be deprived of military rank and of residence in the cities [Note: [Col. 0624B] The Oxford manuscript reads: “military service, rank, and residence in cities.”], so that no innocent person may be ensnared by association or companionship with such people [Note: [Col. 0624B] The words enclosed in parentheses are absent from the same manuscript.]. They shall neither receive nor leave inheritances [Note: [Col. 0624B] These words enclosed in parentheses are likewise absent there. Shortly afterward, the Wurzburg manuscript reads “nor shall these” instead of “nor shall they.”], but these shall be added to the resources of our treasury. Nor shall anyone seek by fraud what we openly forbid them. Let them lack the right to bring actions for injuries, and let them have no children born of lawful unions [Note: [Col. 0624B] The text in parentheses is absent from the same manuscript.].

Let a fine of ten pounds of gold strike the chief officer of each military or administrative service [Note: [Col. 0624C] The words enclosed in parentheses are likewise omitted in the Oxford manuscript: “or office, to be exacted through your staff.”] if he permits anyone polluted by this superstition to serve in the army [Note: [Col. 0624C] The same manuscript reads “if they knowingly allow any of them to serve in the army.”]. For nothing excessive seems capable of being decreed against people whose incestuous perversity, under the name of religion, commits acts unknown even to brothels, or shameful acts [Note: [Col. 0624C] The Oxford manuscript deletes “or shameful.”].

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July at Rome, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus VI and Nomo, a man of distinguished rank [Note: [Col. 0624C] The Wurzburg manuscript reads “Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July.” The Ottobonian manuscript and editions before Quesnellus incorrectly read “Valentinian VII” instead of VI. The printed editions had “Numo.” We corrected it from the Wurzburg manuscript. In several other documents he is called Nомus, not Numus; he held the consulship with Valentinian in 445.].

# LETTER IX [Note: [Col. 0624C] Formerly Letter 11. What was 9 is now in the appendix. Written 21 June 445.]

[Note: [Col. 0624C] This letter is found in the manuscripts of collections 3, 8, Hispana 9, Isidoriana 10, 12, 18, and 20, in the remaining collections through 24, and in Sichardus. Quesnellus correctly determined, in note 1, that this letter, which lacks a date, should be assigned to the year 445.]

## TO DIOSCORUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

[Note: [Col. 0624C] The editions before Quesnellus prefixed the following headings from the manuscripts of the later collections, taken from the Hispana collection: “I. Concerning the ordination of a presbyter or deacon, to be celebrated on Holy Saturday, that is, on Sunday. II. Concerning festivals: if one celebration [the Vulgate adds, by way of explanation, ‘that is, the celebration of Mass’] is insufficient for the people, there should be no doubt about repeating the sacrifice.” Since this synopsis is less suitable, Quesnellus substituted another.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. Concerning the ordination of bishops, presbyters, and deacons: it is to be celebrated after the Sabbath, either around the beginning of the night immediately following, or on the morning of the Sunday itself.—II. Concerning the repetition of the sacrifice: it ought to be repeated on the same festive day when the basilica is too small to contain the whole people at once and a great multitude of the faithful gathers.

Leo, bishop, sends greetings to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria.

## CHAPTER I  
### On the day on which the priestly or Levitical blessing ought to be celebrated

[Col. 0625B]

[Note: [Col. 0625C] Distinction 75, “What Was Preserved by the Fathers,” chapter 4.] Therefore, we desire that what we know to have been preserved by our fathers with especially careful attention be preserved by you also [Note: [Col. 0625C] Quesnellus has “this” (*hoc*) in place of “also” (*quoque*), as certain manuscripts of lesser authority also read. In Merlinus and Sichardus both words are omitted. We have followed not so much the other editions as our more numerous and superior manuscripts [Col. 0625D].], so that priestly or levitical ordination may not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but that the beginnings of that night which dawns into the first day of the week, after the Sabbath day, be selected [Note: [Col. 0625D] After the word “selected,” the Vulgate and Quesnellus insert this gloss from manuscript collection 21: “that they may be substituted under the law of the divine office.” Quesnellus rightly removed this gloss from his manuscripts cited in note 2, and our other manuscripts support him. Only the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, with different punctuation, reads: “so that priestly or levitical ordination may not be celebrated indiscriminately on every day, but that the beginnings of that night which dawns into the first day of the week may be selected for the consecration of those who are to be consecrated.” The same appears in Isidore’s Vatican manuscript and the Hispanic Vindobonensis, except for the final words “the beginnings for the consecration may be selected,” in place of which they read, as in the text, “the beginnings may be selected.”], during which those who are to be consecrated are fasting [Note: [Col. 0625D] Two of our Hispanic manuscripts remove “and.” Shortly afterward, the same practice appears in the Hispanic Vindobonensis.], and sacred blessing is conferred by those who are fasting.

The same observance will be maintained if the rite is celebrated early on the Sunday itself [Note: [Col. 0625D] See Quesnellus’s note 3 and his dissertation on the Sabbath fast [Col. 0626C].], with the Sabbath fast continued, since the beginnings of the preceding night do not cease to belong to the day of the Resurrection, as is also clearly shown in the Lord’s Passover. For, apart from the authority of custom, which we know comes from apostolic teaching, [Note: [Col. 0626C] The Hispanic Vatican manuscript reads: “we also have sacred Scripture in the example that, when the apostles…”] sacred Scripture likewise makes this clear [Col. 0625C] (Acts 13): when the apostles were sending Paul and Barnabas, at the command of the Holy Spirit, to preach the Gospel to the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0626C] The word “Gentiles” is lacking in the Hispanic Vindobonensis and in Sichardus.], they laid hands on them while fasting and praying. Thus we may understand how great must be the devotion of both those who give and those who receive, lest the sacrament of so great a blessing appear to have been carried out negligently.

Therefore, you will have acted piously and commendably in accordance with apostolic institutions if you too observe this form of ordaining priests throughout the churches over which the Lord has willed you to preside: that those who are to be consecrated never receive a blessing except on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, whose beginning is acknowledged to be reckoned from the evening of the Sabbath, and which has been consecrated by such great mysteries of divine dispositions [Note: [Col. 0626C] The editions before Quesnellus, together with the Hispanic Vatican manuscript, Isidore, and manuscripts of collection 21, read “dispensations.” Quesnellus’s emendation, based on the Grimanic and Victorine manuscripts and on the editions of Merlinus, Nicolinus, Surius, and Sichardus, is confirmed by all our remaining manuscripts, including the Hispanic Vindobonensis.], that whatever has been established by the Lord as especially remarkable has been accomplished in the dignity of this day.

On this day the world received its beginning. On this day, through Christ’s Resurrection, death received its end and [Note: [Col. 0626C] Vatican Codex 1342, collection 3, reads “life received its eternal beginning.” Three manuscripts of collection 8 read “life received an eternal beginning.” Certain manuscripts of collection 21 and the Hispanic Vindobonensis read “life received its beginning.”] life received its beginning. On this day the apostles receive from the Lord the trumpet of the Gospel to be preached to all the nations (John 20:21), and receive the sacrament of regeneration to be brought to the whole world.

On this day, as the blessed evangelist John bears witness, when the disciples had gathered together and the doors were shut, the Lord entered among them, breathed on them, and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose you retain, they are retained” (ibid., 22). [Note: [Col. 0626D] The very ancient Vatican manuscript 5845 and the Hispanic Vindobonensis read: “whose sins you retain, they are retained.” The Hispanic Vatican manuscript reads: “they will be retained.”]

Finally, on this day the Holy Spirit promised by the Lord came upon the apostles (Acts 2:1; John 14:16; 16:7). Thus we know that, by a certain heavenly rule, it has been indicated and handed down that the mysteries of priestly blessings are to be celebrated on that day on which all the gifts of grace were bestowed [Note: [Col. 0626D] The editions read “on which.” We corrected the text on the authority of the aforesaid very ancient Vatican manuscript, two Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and the Vallicellian manuscript of collection 8.].

## CHAPTER II. On repeating the sacrifice of the Mass so as to satisfy the people who arrive afterward

[Col. 0626C]

So that our observance may agree in every respect, we also wish the following to be maintained: whenever each more solemn festival summons a larger gathering of the people [Note: [Col. 0626D] The word “each” is absent from the editions before Quesnellus, from five of our manuscripts, and from Sichardus.] and such a multitude of the faithful gathers for it [Note: [Col. 0626D] The Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and collection 21 read “and for it the multitude of the faithful.” Merlinus reads “and for it the faithful,” and so forth. The editions before Quesnellus, together with collection 24, read “and for it so great a multitude of the faithful.” Sichardus likewise omits only “of the faithful.” Quesnellus proposed in the margin: “and for it the offering of such a great sacrifice repeated,” but this reading is found nowhere.], that the basilica cannot contain them all at once, the offering of the sacrifice must unquestionably be repeated. Otherwise, if only those who arrived first were admitted to this devotion, those who subsequently came together might appear to have been [Note: [Col. 0627B] Copies of collection 21 read “not received.”] excluded, whereas it is wholly fitting, both from piety and reason, that whenever the presence of a new people has filled the basilica in which the rite is being performed, the succeeding sacrifice should be offered each time. [Note: [Col. 0627B] On Consecration, distinction 1, “It Is Necessary,” chapter 51.]

Some part of the people must necessarily be deprived of its devotion if, with the practice of only one Mass observed, they cannot offer the sacrifice unless they have assembled during the first part of the day [Note: [Col. 0627B] The Hispanic manuscripts and Isidore omit “who.”].

We therefore earnestly and familiarly admonish your Belovedness [Note: [Col. 0627B] See Quesnellus’s note 5 and our discussion.] that what has taken root in our custom from the form of our fathers’ tradition should not be neglected by your care either [Note: [Col. 0627B] Another reading, with collection 24 and Sichardus: “so that in all things we may correspond with one another in faith and actions.”], so that in every respect we may correspond with one another in faith and in actions.

For this reason we have given this letter to our son Possidonius, the presbyter, on his return, to carry to your Fraternity [Note: [Col. 0627B] See Quesnellus’s note 6.]. He frequently took part in our processions and ordinations, and, having been sent to us so many times, recognized what authority of the apostolic see we maintained in all matters [Note: [Col. 0627C] Quesnellus emended the text on the basis of the manuscripts and editions listed in his seventh note. Our better and older manuscripts of collections 3, 8, 23, and 24 also support this emendation. The common Leonine editions, together with certain manuscripts of collection 21, read “of the authority of the apostolic see.” Vatican 541 of that collection reads “by the authority of the apostolic see.” The Hispanic Vatican manuscript, Isidore, and manuscripts of collections 12 and 22 read “by the authorities of the apostolic see.”].

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] In the manuscripts of collection 3, in the Hispanic Vatican manuscript and Isidore, and in three manuscripts of collection 21, “given” is omitted. The Hispanic Vindobonensis reads “the tenth day before the Kalends of July.” The editions before Quesnellus, following Merlinus, manuscripts of collection 24, and Sichardus, read “the Kalends of July.” The very ancient Vatican manuscript 5845 of collection 8 reads “the eleventh day before the Kalends of June.” Only the ancient Vallicellian A 5 and Vercelli manuscripts, together with Vatican 3791, have “the eleventh day before the Kalends of July.” Since the Vallicellian and Vercelli manuscripts belong to the same collection 8 as Vatican 5845, one might hesitate over which reading to prefer. The agreement of the other manuscripts concerning the word “July,” however, seems to resolve the doubt; for this reason we have retained the final reading introduced by Quesnellus.]

[Note: [Col. 0628B] Around the time of the following letter, in the year 445.]

# LETTER X

[Note: [Col. 0628B] Manuscript copies of this letter are exceedingly rare, as Quesnellus observed in note 1. So far as we know, it exists only in the Corbie manuscript of the very ancient collection 2, arranged in Gaul during the age of Vigilius, and in the manuscripts of collections 12 and 24. Father Sirmondus saw another ancient copy, which, from the superscription of this letter—varying considerably from those of the cited manuscripts, as will appear in the following note—reveals a different origin. We were able to find and collate only copies of the later collections, namely Vatican 1340 and Venice 569 of collection 12, Vatican 544 of collection 24, and Vatican 541, to which this letter appears to have been added at the end from the same source as collection 12. Since these manuscripts transmit more recent collections, they should not be compared on equal terms with the ancient collection, especially the Corbie manuscript, which, being of Gallican origin, must be believed to have received the letter itself from an older and more accurate copy found among the Gauls, addressed to the bishops of the province of Vienne.
