Quesnellus, and before him Father Sirmondus, setting aside the printed editions derived from Merlinus—that is, from collection 12—relied heavily on the Corbie manuscript in reprinting this letter. We have therefore judged that its readings should not readily be abandoned or altered. Although none of the manuscripts gives the consulship in which this letter was written, it can nevertheless be inferred sufficiently from the following constitution, which was sent to Gaul at approximately the same time. Since that constitution, through correction of the chronological indication with the help of our manuscripts, was written after the letter to Dioscorus in the year 445, we have placed this letter here, since it should not be separated from that constitution.]

## To the bishops established throughout the province of Vienne

On the case of Hilary, bishop of Arles.

[Col. 0628A]

## Synopsis

I. The Church, established by Christ’s institution upon Peter’s solidity, from which no one must depart. Whoever attempts to diminish its authority violates this foundation.

II. He accuses Hilary of disturbing the condition and concord of the churches.

III. He explains that Celidonius, deposed by Hilary, was restored to his see after the judgment had been reconsidered.

IV. Bishop Projectus, in whose illness Hilary had substituted another in his place, was fully restored.

V. The ordination of a provincial bishop is to be reserved to the metropolitan.

VI. No one is to be ordained without the consent of the clergy and people, or outside the lawful day.

VII. Hilary was deprived of metropolitan dignity and authority over the province of Vienne.

VIII. No one is to be expelled from communion for a trivial reason.

IX. No council of another province is to be summoned without the consent of Leontius, the senior bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0628D] Jacobus Sirmondus cited by the sigla “VV. CC.” not an old sheet, as Quesnellus wrongly interpreted it in note 2, but old manuscripts—or at least one ancient copy—in which this letter is prefaced by: “Leo, to his most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Maxima Sequanorum and Vienne.” Quesnellus disliked the addition of Maxima Sequanorum because he did not wish Celidonius to have been bishop of Vesontio, which is the metropolis of Maxima Sequanorum. We shall defend the Vesontine bishopric in the observations on Quesnellus’s fifth dissertation, part 1, chapter 2, where we shall also discuss this superscription further.]

To our most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout the province of Vienne, Leo, bishop of Rome.

## CHAPTER I

The worship of divine religion, which the grace of God willed to shine throughout all peoples and nations, was instituted by our Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the human race, in such a way that the truth, previously contained in the proclamation of the Law and the Prophets, might go forth through the apostolic trumpet for the salvation of all, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18:5). [Note: [Col. 0629C] Quesnellus reads “will go out” and noted in the margin: “Thus the manuscript copies read, a form also familiar to the ancient Fathers.” Sirmondus, however, together with all our manuscripts and the earlier printed editions, reads “has gone out,” as do several Fathers cited by Father Sabatier. Some of these have “went out,” as does the very ancient manuscript Psalter of the chapter of Verona and the Saint-Germain manuscript cited by the same scholar; no Fathers cited by him support “will go out.” If the original text had “will go forth,” then “will go out” might stand. Perhaps “will go out” was printed in Quesnellus’s edition through a typographical error for “will go forth.”]

But the Lord willed this sacramental office to belong to the charge of all the apostles in such a way that he placed it principally in the blessed Peter, chief of all the apostles [Note: [Col. 0629D] The Corbie and Thuan manuscripts cited by Quesnellus in note 3, which should be compared with our discussion, read “might place and might will his gifts to flow from him, as from a kind of head, into the whole body.” Other editions, together with our manuscripts, read “might place, so that from him, as from a kind of head, he might spread his gifts as into a body.”]. He willed his gifts to flow from him, as from a kind of head, into the whole body, so that anyone who dared to depart from Peter’s solidity would understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery.

For he willed the one whom he had taken into a share in indivisible unity to be called what he himself was, saying: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18). Thus, by the wondrous gift of God’s grace, the building of the eternal temple was to stand upon Peter’s solidity. He strengthened his Church with this firmness, so that neither human rashness could assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it.

Yet whoever attempts, with excessively impious presumption, to violate this most sacred firmness of the rock—constructed, as we have said, by God as its builder—attempts to diminish its authority by indulging his desires and refusing to follow what he received from the ancients. He acts as though subject to no law and constrained by no rule of the Lord’s institution, departing from your custom and ours through the ambition of a new usurpation, presuming upon what is unlawful and neglecting what he ought to preserve.

## CHAPTER II

But with God, as we believe, inspiring us, we strive to correct these matters among you while preserving the grace of our charity—the grace which, as you remember, the apostolic see has always extended to your Holiness—and to regulate the condition of your churches through labor shared with you: not establishing new things, but renewing the old. Thus we may continue in the observance of the condition handed down to us by our fathers and please our God through the ministry of good works, once the scandals of disturbances have been removed.

Let your Fraternity recognize with us that, because of its reverence, the apostolic see has, out of reverence for it, been consulted by the priests of your province through countless reports, and that, in accordance with ancient custom, judgments have been either reconsidered or confirmed through appeals in various cases. In this way, while the unity of the Spirit was preserved in the bond of peace, what was done in holiness advanced perpetual charity as letters traveled back and forth. [Note: [Col. 0629D] The editions before Quesnellus, together with only the manuscripts of collection 24 and Sirmondus, read “which.”] For our concern, seeking not its own interests but those of Christ, did not abolish the dignity divinely bestowed either from the churches or from the priests of the churches.

But Hilary has departed from this path, always both well maintained and beneficially preserved among our predecessors, intending to disturb the condition of the churches and the concord of the priests by new presumptions. He desires to subject you to his authority in such a way that he does not allow himself to be subject to the blessed apostle Peter, claiming for himself the ordinations of all the churches throughout Gaul [Note: [Col. 0630C] See Quesnellus’s sixth note and our discussion.], and transferring to his own dignity what is due to metropolitan priests [Note: [Col. 0630C] Sirmondus, together with the editions before Quesnellus, reads “transferring the dignity to his own right.” Our manuscripts read “to transfer the dignity to his own right,” which, with different punctuation, refers it back to the participle “desiring.” Quesnellus preferred the reading of the manuscripts of collection 2.].

He also diminishes the reverence due to the blessed Peter himself by words of excessive arrogance. Although the power of binding and loosing was entrusted to him above the others (Matthew 16), the care of feeding the sheep was nevertheless entrusted to him in a more particular way (John 12). Whoever thinks that his primacy may be denied can in no way diminish that man’s dignity; but, puffed up by the spirit of his own pride, he plunges himself into the depths below.

## CHAPTER III

The order of events recorded in the documents shows what was done and concluded among us in the case of Bishop Celidonius, and what Hilary said when he was heard together with that man, in the presence of the aforesaid bishop.

After Hilary had no reasonable answer that he could give in the council of holy priests [Note: [Col. 0630D] Three of our manuscripts read “he did not have.”], they turned to those hidden matters of his heart [Note: [Col. 0630D] Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Saint Paul, 1 Corinthians 14:25: ‘The secrets of his heart become manifest.’”] which no layman could state and no priest could hear.

I confess, brothers, that we grieved, and we attempted to heal this swelling of his mind with the remedies of our patience. For we did not wish to aggravate those wounds that he was repeatedly inflicting upon his own soul by insolent speeches. We strove to soothe him, whom we had received as a brother, rather than to distress him by our interventions, although he himself was entangling himself in his own replies. [Note: [Col. 0630D] Our manuscripts read “to soothe him more—although he was inviting it by his own replies, perhaps ‘inciting it’—than to distress him,” and so forth. Sirmondus has the same reading, with the one exception that he reads “was entangling” instead of “was inviting.” We nevertheless did not wish to alter the reading of the earlier editions, including Quesnellus’s, who noted in the margin, for “was entangling”: “Alternatively, ‘was ensnaring’ or ‘involving.’”]

Bishop Celidonius was acquitted, because he had shown through the clear testimony of witnesses, even in Hilary’s presence, that he had been unjustly deprived of the priesthood. Thus Hilary had no answer to the charge he could have brought while sitting with us.

The judgment that had been issued in this case was therefore removed: namely, the judgment that a man who had been the husband of a widow could not hold the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0631C] Compare Quesnellus’s eighth note.]. We indeed wished the legal enactments to be preserved and observed more carefully, not only concerning priests but also concerning clergy of lower rank, so that those who had contracted such a marriage would not be permitted to enter the sacred service, nor those who were shown to have been husbands of more than one wife contrary to apostolic discipline.

But just as we decree that those whose conduct cannot be excused are either not to be admitted or, if they have been admitted [Note: [Col. 0631C] Sirmondus adds “if they have been admitted,” although the words, omitted also in our manuscripts, are understood.], are to be removed, so those against whom this is falsely alleged must be cleared after the necessary examination [Note: [Col. 0631C] The editions before Sirmondus and Quesnellus, together with certain manuscripts, read “wrongly, from it it is necessary.”], and we must not allow them to lose their office.

[Note: [Col. 0631C] That Celidonius was bishop of Vesontio will become clear from the arguments that will be made against Quesnellus in the observations on his fifth dissertation, chapter 1. The bishop of Arles therefore possessed no jurisdiction over him. Consequently, when Saint Leo wrote, “The sentence issued against him would have remained if the truth of the charges had existed,” this should not be understood as though the holy pontiff acknowledged any proper jurisdiction of Hilary over Celidonius. Valentinian, in the constitution that follows, which was written and published in accordance with Leo’s mind, declares concerning Hilary that he “removed others incompetently,” which refers to Celidonius’s deposition; the word “incompetently” plainly indicates that Hilary lacked jurisdiction over Celidonius. Saint Leo therefore asserted that the sentence of deposition would have remained not by virtue of Hilary’s jurisdiction, but either by the jurisdiction of the other bishops of Celidonius’s province, whom the author of Hilary’s Life indicates had assembled, or at least by the fact that, according to the legal institutions, the holy pontiff himself would likewise have judged a husband of a widow to be barred from the sacred altars. Hence he prefaced the statement: “What we, preserving the legal enactments, wished to be observed more carefully, not only concerning priests but also concerning clergy of lower rank.” For this reason we believe that the postscript Quesnellus attached to this passage should be removed: “Saint Leo does not challenge Hilary’s authority over the province of Vienne, since he presumes that Celidonius was falsely deposed by Hilary’s right, as Leo admits.”]

For the sentence issued against him would have remained if the truth of the charges had existed. Thus our fellow bishop Celidonius was restored to his own Church and to the dignity he ought not to have lost, as the sequence of the proceedings and the judgment issued by us after the inquiry had been completed testify.

## CHAPTER IV

When this matter had been concluded, the complaint of our brother and fellow bishop Projectus followed. A tearful and grievous letter concerning the bishop who had been placed over him was sent to us. A letter from his citizens was also presented, supported by the numerous subscriptions of individuals, and filled with highly hostile complaints against Hilary: namely, that Projectus, their bishop, had not been free to be ill; that his priesthood had been transferred to another without his knowledge; and that, as though he were an estate lying vacant, Hilary the usurper had installed an heir while its possessor was still alive.

We should like to hear what your Fraternity thinks about this. Yet our judgment ought not to doubt what is in your minds, since you see a brother lying on his sickbed afflicted not so much by bodily illness as tormented by another grief. What hope of life remains to a man who is made to despair of his priesthood when another is substituted for him?

It is evident how gentle-hearted Hilary is, since he thought that the delay of a brother’s death would obstruct his presumption. For, insofar as it lay within his power, he took away the light and removed the life of the man in whose place he installed another, inflicting this grief upon him and leaving him no recourse to recovery.

Even if the customary departure of human beings had come upon our brother swiftly [Note: [Col. 0632C] The sense appears to require “swiftly.” The editions before Sirmondus read “the brief departure of the human condition may have found the brother,” or “the customary departure of the human condition may have been found.” Quesnellus, together with two of our manuscripts, wrongly reads “condition.”], what business does Hilary have in another province? Why does he usurp what none of his predecessors before Patroclus possessed [Note: [Col. 0632C] Quesnellus and certain of our manuscripts read this way. Another reading is: “Why does he usurp it?” The older editions before Sirmondus and Quesnellus read “or Patroclus possessed,” incorrectly. The words “before Patroclus” are found in our manuscripts and in those of Sirmondus and Quesnellus, especially the Corbie manuscript, and the context clearly requires them.]—especially since what appeared to have been temporarily granted to Patroclus by the apostolic see was afterward taken away by a better judgment [Note: [Col. 0632C] This refers to the decree of Pope Boniface I, confirmed by Celestine, by which Narbonensis Prima, previously granted to Patroclus by the decree of Zosimus, was taken from him and restored to the bishop of Narbonne. Zosimus had favored Patroclus because Patroclus established by certain arguments that his predecessors had always possessed that province, arguments to which the bishop of Narbonne was then unable to respond. Under Boniface I, however, when the same bishop of Narbonne had regained his strength and demonstrated the contrary with documents that were so much stronger than those produced by the bishop of Arles that later pontiffs approved them as entirely conclusive, Leo therefore asserts that the province was taken from the bishop of Arles by the better judgment.].

Certainly the wishes of the citizens, the testimony of the people, the judgment of the leading men, and the election of the clergy should have been awaited. These are normally observed in the ordinations of priests by those who know the rules of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0632D] Sirmondus reads “who know.” The rules of the Fathers appear to be the canons of the Fathers of Sardica, whose fifth canon commands that the bishop who is sought by the people be ordained. On this matter Julius I, Innocent, and Celestine issued more explicit regulations, requiring not so much the vote of the people as that of the clergy.], so that the norm of apostolic authority might be observed in everything. It prescribes that a priest who is to preside over a Church be supported not only by the testimony of the faithful but also by the testimony of those who are outside (1 Timothy 3:7), and that no occasion for scandal be left, when, through peace and concord pleasing to God and with the united efforts of all, the man who is to become a teacher of peace is ordained.

## CHAPTER V

But he came unexpectedly upon those who knew nothing of it and departed without warning, traveling rapidly, as we have learned, and covering many journeys. He hurried through distant provinces with such haste [Note: [Col. 0633C] Quesnellus noted in the margin: “Perhaps ‘with maturity,’” but this reading is supported neither by the manuscripts nor, apparently, by the sense.] that he seems to have sought glory more through clownish speed than through priestly moderation.

These are the words of the citizens’ letter sent to us: “He departed before we knew that he had come. This is not returning but fleeing; it is not providing the healing care of a shepherd but inflicting the violence of a thief and robber.” For the Lord says: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door but climbs in by another way is a thief and a robber” (John 10:1). [Note: [Col. 0633C] Our manuscripts read “into the enclosure.” Some printed editions have “into the chort,” others “into the cohort.” But *cors, cortis* is the same as *cohors* and properly signifies a place enclosed by walls, in which something is kept [Col. 0633D].]

Hilary therefore did not so much strive to consecrate a bishop as to kill the man who was ill, and, by wrongly ordaining the man whom he set over him, to deceive that very man.

Nevertheless, having taken counsel for all our brothers together in a matter which, with God as judge, we believe will please you, we have decreed both that the wrongly ordained man should be removed and that Bishop Projectus should remain in his priesthood. We establish this rule: if any one of our brothers dies in any province [Note: [Col. 0633D] Sirmondus adds “from this life.”], the right to ordain a priest belongs to the man who is established as metropolitan of that province.

Two cases, as we see, have been settled, though in them many things appear to have been committed contrary to ecclesiastical reason and ought to await the censure of a just judgment [Col. 0633C]. But we cannot remain here longer, since we are summoned to other matters that must be discussed more carefully with your Holiness.

## CHAPTER VI

An armed force, as we have learned, follows the priest through the provinces, and, supported by the presumption of armed protection, serves to invade tumultuously the churches that have lost their own priests. Candidates for ordination are dragged forward for this office, unknown to the cities over which they are to be placed. Just as a man who is known and approved is sought through peace, so by force it is necessary that an unknown man who is brought in should be imposed.

I appeal and entreat you, and I charge you under the invocation of God: prevent such things, brothers, and remove every source of dissension from your provinces. Certainly, before God we absolve ourselves, since we have charged you not to permit these things to happen any longer.

Let those who are to become priests be requested through peace and quiet. Let the subscription of the clergy, the testimony of the leading men, the agreement of the order, and that of the people be maintained. Let the man who is to preside over all be chosen by all.

As we have already said, let each metropolitan, together with those who surpass the others in the antiquity of their priesthood, defend for himself the right of his own province, restored to him by us. Let no one dare to claim another’s right for himself. Let each man be content with his own boundaries and limits [Col. 0634B] [Note: [Col. 0633D] He is referring to several metropolitans. Those meant appear to be the ones whose provinces included Celidonius and Projectus, since they may have transferred their own right in some manner to Hilary by allowing him to exercise judgments and ordinations in their provinces. Moreover, Hilary the pope testifies in Letter 4 that Ingenuus, metropolitan of the Maritime Alps, was censured by Leo for an unlawful surrender of his jurisdiction. It is uncertain whether this censure of Ingenuus is to be referred to this letter of Leo or to other letters that have been lost. See the fuller discussion in the dissertation on the lost letters, no. 97.], and let him know that he is not permitted to transfer to another the privilege due to himself.

But if anyone, neglecting the apostolic sanctions and giving greater favor to a personal relationship, wishes to become a deserter of his own dignity, believing that he may transfer his privilege to another, it is not the man to whom he has yielded it, but the priest who within the province is senior to the others in episcopal antiquity, who shall claim for himself the power to ordain.

Let ordination be celebrated not indiscriminately but on the lawful day. Let no one consider his status secure if he has not been ordained on the evening of the Sabbath, which dawns into the first day of the week, or on the Sunday itself. For our predecessors judged only the day of the Lord’s Resurrection worthy of this honor, so that priests who are chosen might be especially appointed on that day.

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0634C]

Each province should be content with its own councils, and Hilary should no longer dare to convene synodal assemblies or, by intruding himself, disturb the judgments of the priests of the Lord.

[Note: Thus Sirmondus, in agreement with the editions previously published and with three of our manuscripts. Quesnellus, however, following manuscript collection 24: “who nevertheless should know himself not only [to have been removed] from another’s jurisdiction.”]

He should know that he has not merely been expelled from another’s jurisdiction, but has also been deprived of the authority of the province of Vienne, which he had wrongfully usurped.

[Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Perhaps, which he had misused.” He wrote this solely because, in his judgment—which we shall challenge in the observations to Dissertation 5—Hilary had usurped no jurisdiction that did not belong to him.]

For it is worthy, brothers, that the statutes of antiquity be restored, since the man who claimed for himself the ordination of a province not belonging to him has now also been proved to have been such a man:

[Note: The editions before Sirmondus and Quesnellus, together with inferior manuscripts, omit *exstitisse*, “to have been.” It was an established discipline that a metropolitan who had failed in some respect against the rules of the canons should retain only the priesthood of his own Church, out of consideration for the Apostolic See, while being deprived of the right to ordain bishops, as may be seen in Pope Hilary’s Letter 8, to the Gauls, §1. Compare also Leo’s Letter 12, ch. 9.]

when he repeatedly sought a sentence of condemnation against himself by his reckless and insolent words, our order, out of consideration for the Apostolic See, preserved for him only the priesthood of his own city.

[Note: “The passage has been corrected from Sirmondus’s manuscripts and our own,” Quesnellus says in a marginal postscript. Previously it read: “Therefore let him not have ordination who, conscious of his own merit, when he was sought for accusation, withdrew by a shameful flight,” etc. It appears more corruptly in our manuscript collections 12 and 24: “Therefore let him not have ordination; let him not ordain who, conscious of his merit,” etc.]

Therefore let him have no part in any ordination; let him not ordain—the man who, conscious of his own deserts, when he was sought for the case, thought it necessary to withdraw by a shameful flight,

[Note: Some wrongly interpret this passage as referring to the excommunication by which Saint Leo separated Hilary from his communion. The following makes it clear that Hilary is said to be excluded from apostolic communion because, unexpectedly fleeing from Rome during the sacred rites, he refused, as the pontiff adds, to become a participant in our communion. Hilary, according to the author of his Life, ch. 17, had complained to Leo that some men condemned by public sentence among the Gauls were taking part at the sacred altars in Rome and were being joined to the communion of Celidonius, whom he had condemned together with such eminent men. Since he refused to communicate at Rome with the man whom he perceived ought to be absolved, he withdrew, and in this way withdrew himself from apostolic communion.]

excluded from apostolic communion, of which he did not deserve to be a participant. For God, as we believe, brought this about: although we were unaware of it, He both drew him before our judgments and, amid the examinations that were being conducted, caused him secretly to depart so that he would not become a participant in our communion.

## CHAPTER VIII

Communion should not readily be denied to any Christian; nor should it be left to the arbitrary decision of an indignant priest to impose what the mind of a judge ought, as a punishment for grave guilt, to inflict only reluctantly and with sorrow.

[Note: Thus Quesnellus, with two of our manuscripts. Others read “of one who exacts punishment.”]

For we have learned that some have been excluded from the grace of communion for offenses and words of little importance, and that the soul for which Christ’s blood was shed has been wounded by the imposition of so severe a punishment and, as it were, left defenseless, stripped of every protection, and exposed to the attacks of the devil, so that it could easily be seized.

[Note: Sirmondus reads “attacks.”]

Certainly, if a case should ever arise such that the character of the crime committed justly requires someone to be deprived of communion, only the person whom guilt implicates should be subjected to the penalty; nor should one be made a participant in the punishment who is not shown to have been an accomplice in the offense.

[Note: Four of our manuscripts read: “if any such case should arise.”]

But what wonder is it that he should behave in this way toward laymen, when he is accustomed to rejoice at the condemnation of priests?

## CHAPTER IX

Therefore, since our intention plainly appears to be quite different—for we desire the condition of all the Churches and the concord of the priests to be preserved—we exhort and earnestly entreat you, binding you together in the bond of charity, and we admonish you with fitting affection, to preserve, for the sake of your peace and dignity, those decisions which, with God’s inspiration and with the blessed Apostle Peter, we have now reached after examining and evaluating all the cases.

Be assured that what we are known to have decreed in this matter benefits not so much our honor as your own. We are not defending the ordinations of your provinces for ourselves—something Hilary may perhaps falsely claim, according to his custom, in order to corrupt the minds of your holiness—but by our vigilance we are vindicating them for you, so that novelty may no longer be permitted anything, and so that no opportunity may remain for a presumptuous man to annul your privileges.

[Note: Thus Quesnellus and our manuscripts. Others read “for our rejoicing.” Shortly afterward, Sirmondus reads “concord” instead of “protection.”]

We declare that our rejoicing is increased only if the diligence of the Apostolic See remains unimpaired among you, and if, through the preservation of priestly discipline, we do not allow what belongs to your honor to be destroyed by wicked usurpations.

[Note: Quesnellus reads this way with Sirmondus. Earlier editions, together with Vatican collection 24, read “for new things.” The reading “new things” is better in three other of our manuscripts.]

And since antiquity must always be honored, we wish our brother and fellow bishop Leontius, a commendable priest, to be adorned with this dignity, if it pleases you: without his consent, let no council of another province be summoned by your holiness; and let him be honored by all of you, as his antiquity and probity require, while the dignity of the metropolitan privilege is preserved.

[Note: To Leontius, concerning whom see our observation in Quesnellus’s note 11, only the prerogative of convening synods of different provinces—the prerogative Hilary had possessed—is granted here. That the metropolitan jurisdiction itself, however, was taken away from Hilary and transferred to the bishop of Vienne by another letter of Leo, now lost, is clear from Letter 66, ch. 2. See also what will be said more fully on this matter in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, part 3.]

For it is equitable, and appears to injure none of the brethren, that in their own provinces the other priests should defer, according to the merit of their age, to those who precede them in the antiquity of their priesthood.

[Note: Quesnellus omitted the word “his.” It is restored from all our manuscripts and from the other editions.]

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers.

642

[Note: Written on 8 July 445.]

## LETTER XI, OR

[Note: In his second edition Quesnellus added various readings from the Thuaneus manuscript of Colbert. We have collated it with Vatican manuscript 3833 of the canonical collection of Cardinal Deusdedit, who inserted this law into his collection, Book I, p. 48, taking it from an older exemplar. From the Ottobonian Vatican manuscript we later obtained the reading of the chronological note alone.]

## THE CONSTITUTION OF VALENTINIAN III AUGUSTUS,

[Note: What follows was added by Father Sirmondus and thereafter by Quesnellus. It is highly probable that Leo’s decretal was sent to the Gauls together with this law, so that no impediment would be placed in the way of its execution.]

sent to the Gauls together with the preceding letter of Pope Leo concerning the same matter. On the ordination of bishops. (G)

[Note: The Thuaneus and Vatican manuscripts give this heading: “The Emperor Valentinian Augustus to all those living under the rule of the eternal city of Rome throughout the world.” Although this law was indeed issued on the occasion of the Gallic controversy arising from certain acts of Hilary of Arles, it is nevertheless clear that it was enacted not for the Gauls alone but for all the provinces of the empire, from these words: “Let neither the Gallic bishops nor those of the other provinces be permitted to attempt anything contrary to ancient custom without the authority of the venerable bishop of the eternal City”; and: “Let this be law for them all,” etc. Accordingly, the general heading found in these manuscripts seems appropriate to a general law. In these codices, the details relating specifically to Aetius, master of both services in Gaul, are omitted; only those provisions are read by which the general law is expressed, ending with the words “have conferred upon the Roman Church.” The heading inserted into the text and found in other codices suits the same law as it was sent to the Gauls, where it was especially necessary, and where it was directed to Aetius—who exercised greater authority in Gaul—by means of a particular addition expressed at the end, so that it might be enforced there. It may perhaps also be believed that it was transmitted in a similar way to other prefects or governors of other provinces, as is known to have happened with other laws of the same kind.]

The emperors Theodosius and Valentinian, Augusti, to Aetius, illustrious man, count and master of both services, and patrician.

It is certain both to us and to our empire that our one defense lies in the favor of the heavenly Divinity, which Christian faith and the religion we venerate especially support us in winning.

[Note: The praised manuscripts read “the faith of Christians.”]

Since, therefore, the primacy of the Apostolic See, founded upon the merit of Saint Peter, who is the prince of the episcopal crown, together with the dignity of the city of Rome, has also been confirmed by the authority of a sacred council,

[Note: The same manuscripts read “has confirmed.”]

let no presumption attempt anything unlawful apart from the authority of that See. For then at last the peace of the Churches will be preserved everywhere, if the whole Church recognizes its ruler.

Although these matters have hitherto been preserved inviolate, we have learned from the faithful report of the venerable Leo, Roman pope, that Hilary of Arles has attempted certain unlawful acts with obstinate audacity by presuming to do what should not be presumed. Hence an abominable disturbance has invaded the Churches beyond the Alps, as the recent example most clearly shows.

For Hilary, who is called bishop of Arles, without consulting the pontiff of the Church of the city of Rome, has rashly usurped and encroached upon judgments or episcopal ordinations.

[Note: In both editions Quesnellus added “of the city,” a word unknown to the Vatican manuscript and to all the printed editions. We cannot imagine how he inserted it even in his first edition, when he had not yet seen the Thuaneus manuscript.]

643

[Note: The editions, including Quesnellus’s, previously read: “unlawful ordinations of bishops, without consulting the pontiff.” The reading of both manuscripts is more correct and more consistent with the context. What follows—“he removed some incompetently”—refers to the judgments concerning Celidonius, whom Hilary had deposed from the episcopate, and especially on whose account Leo’s decretal and the imperial law were issued. The other clause—“he indecorously ordained others against the will and opposition of the citizens”—refers to the ordinations by which Hilary supplied successors after removing Celidonius, during the illness of Projectus, or after the deaths of other bishops, as is related in the preceding letter, chapter 6.]

For he removed some incompetently and ordained others indecorously, against the will and opposition of the citizens.

[Note: The Thuaneus manuscript reads: “For he ordained some against the will and opposition of the citizens,” with the rest deleted.]

And since those who had not elected them did not readily receive them, he gathered an armed force for himself, and either surrounded the gates of the walls in the manner of an enemy by laying siege to them, or forced them open by assault; and he led to the seat of peace men who were to preach peace by means of warfare.

After such acts, committed both against the majesty of the empire and against the reverence due to the Apostolic See, had been examined in due order by the judgment of the religious man, the pope of the City, a definite sentence was issued against him and against those whom he had wrongly ordained.

[Note: The Thuaneus and Vatican manuscripts omit “of the religious man.”]

Indeed, that sentence would have been valid throughout Gaul even without an imperial sanction. For what would not be permitted in the Churches by the authority of so great a pontiff?

[Note: Quesnellus corrected the text in his second edition from the Thuaneus manuscript, and the Vatican manuscript likewise supports it. Earlier editions read “in the Churches.”]

But this consideration has also led us to issue our command: henceforth neither Hilary—whom the humanity of the gentle bishop permits still to be called a bishop—nor anyone else shall be permitted to mix arms into ecclesiastical affairs or to oppose the commands of the Roman bishop. For by such attempts the faith and reverence owed to our empire are violated.

644

Nor do we remove only this, which is a very grave offense; rather, lest even a slight disturbance arise among the Churches or the discipline of religion appear to be diminished in any respect, we decree by this perpetual sanction that neither the Gallic bishops nor those of the other provinces may attempt anything contrary to ancient custom without the authority of the venerable bishop of the eternal City.

[Note: From both manuscripts we have written “we decree” in place of “we decide.” “To decree” is more frequently used in laws than “to decide,” as may be seen from the legal glossary to the Theodosian Code.]

But let this be law for them and for everyone: whatever the authority of the Apostolic See has decreed or shall decree. Thus, whoever among the bishops, summoned to the judgment of the Roman bishop, neglects to come, shall be compelled to appear through the governor of that province. In all respects, the provisions shall be preserved which our deified parents have conferred upon the Roman Church,

[Note: Both manuscripts read “have entrusted.” Here the general law ends in those manuscripts, immediately followed by the chronological notation: “Issued on 8 July at Rome, Valentinian Augustus.” The remaining provisions concerning Aetius were added to the imperial letter sent to Gaul, as we noted in note 3 (Col. 636).]

and your illustrious and splendid Magnificence shall, by the authority of the present edictal law, cause the provisions set forth above to be observed, with a fine of ten pounds of gold immediately exacted from every judge who has allowed our commands to be violated.

And in the divine hand: “May the Divinity preserve you for many years, dearest father.”

[Note: The editions read: “Issued on 8 June at Rome, in the sixth consulship of Valentinian Augustus.” We have corrected the month from the two manuscripts mentioned above and from the Ottobonian manuscript, now Vatican, which also supplied the complete consular notation, as it is read in the preceding Constitution of this year above, Letter 8, and in other Novels of the same year.]

Issued on 8 July at Rome, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the sixth time and of Nomo, illustrious man.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

[Col. 0639]

1. Since the three notable forms in which the following letter is usually found in manuscript codices, and from which it appeared in three corresponding forms in the printed editions, introduce considerable difficulty, Quesnellus’s discussion, inserted in his notes and observations, increases the difficulty still further. He sought to retain and defend one form while rejecting the other two and dismissing a large part of the letter as an addition fabricated by some impostor. Without a new codex that might properly reconcile the entire matter, it seems impossible to determine and publish anything with certainty.

2. The first form of the letter, published by Merlinus and Sichardus, and also to be published by us in second place, extends the letter only as far as the middle of chapter 9 and ends with the words of that chapter, “let us punish with just vengeance hereafter.”

This same form is found in the manuscripts of collection 5 published by Quesnellus. He mentions two of them, the Thuaneus and Trecopithoeanus; we can add two from the Imperial Library, marked numbers 39 and 42. It is also found in the manuscripts of Isidore’s collection 10 and collection 12, to which the codex used by Merlinus belongs, as well as the Herovallianus cited by Quesnellus. It occurs in the codices of collection 24, the only one among the later collections to exhibit this form of the letter; and among such codices must also be counted the Victorinus, Regniacensis, and Saint-Martin of Auxerre manuscripts, which, according to the same annotator, contain collection 24 with the letter in this form.

In his second edition Quesnellus added two further codices, whose descriptions he received from Rome after the first printing: namely, Barberinianus 77 and 2888. The first of these was also examined and collated by us. It is approximately of the twelfth century and contains various works of a later period as well; from Leo, however, it presents this one letter alone. The other, extremely ancient and written in capital letters, contains the old collection 3, for which we found another similar manuscript in the very ancient Vatican 1342.

We have also found this same form of the abridged letter—as we shall call it—in three other collections: namely, in the Vatican manuscript of the Queen’s collection 1; in an old codex of the Lucca collection 4, similar to Colbert 784, which Coustant cites in the preface to the Roman Pontiffs’ Letters, §89; and in the manuscripts of the Hispanic collection 9, Vatican 1341, and Vindobonensis Imperial 41, leaving aside several other written copies of collections 10, 12, and 24, which we listed in the preface to the letters.

Thus eight collections—1, 3, 4, 5, 9, 10, 12, and 24—and the special codex Barberinianus 77 exhibit this first form of the letter.

3. The second form of the same letter was first published by Wendelinus, then by Pithaeus, and finally by Voellus and Justellus in the collection of Dionysius Exiguus.

This form omits three complete chapters—6, 7, and 8—which are presented in the first, abridged form. After the final words of that first form, “let us punish with just vengeance hereafter,” it adds the remaining material, which is presented through the end of the complete letter.

This form is found in all the manuscript codices of the collection called Dionysian, though more properly to be called Hadrianian, since all these codices truly belong to Hadrian’s collection 7—namely, the collection that Pope Hadrian I gave to Charlemagne for the use of the Western Churches, enlarged by several additions beyond the Dionysian collection. Accordingly, numerous copies of this collection are found everywhere that preserve this form of the letter.

Quesnellus cited only two Gallic Thuaneus codices, but Father Coustant, in the preface cited above, §128, mentions many more dispersed throughout Gaul, including one from the year 805. We ourselves have also seen many ancient ones at Rome, which we named in the preface to the letters, §16. To these may also be added the codices of collection 8, listed under number 17, which present the Hadrianian collection at the beginning.

4. The third form, produced by combining the two preceding forms—which we shall call the mixed edition—is found differently in manuscripts and in printed editions.

In the codices we have seen, chapters 6, 7, and 8 and half of chapter 9 are omitted, and the entire Hadrianian edition is first presented, generally with the chronological notation: “Issued on 10 August.” Then the omitted chapters, taken from the first abridged edition, are appended through its end, so that the words “Since, therefore, all things,” etc., are repeated. In the abridged edition these words close the letter; in the Hadrianian edition they had appeared in their proper place in chapter 9.

Quesnellus found this reading in two Thuaneus manuscripts and in one Cambridge manuscript. We found it in the manuscripts of four collections—11, 20, 21, and 23—and have no doubt that the three codices cited by Quesnellus belong to them. Collection 11, from which the other collections seem to have derived this form of the edition, deserves particular consideration, since it is older than the time of Hincmar, as we proved in the preface to the letters, §23.

In only one codex, Venetian Saint Mark’s 79 of collection 22, did we find this third form without the repetition of the final chapter beginning “Since, therefore, all things,” etc. Thus only the three omitted chapters are appended to the Hadrianian reading from the abridged edition, continuing through the words “or to have lost the body.”

In the printed editions of Leo prior to Quesnellus’s and in the published editions of the Councils, which derived from codices displaying this third reading, the editors, finding this form inconsistent—both because the chronological note stood before the three chapters 6, 7, and 8 and because of the intrusive repetition of the sentence “Since, therefore, all things”—gave, without the authority of any codex, the Hadrianian edition first, except for the final sentence. They ended it with the words “might receive those who were being consecrated.” They then added from the abridged edition the three chapters 6, 7, and 8, omitting the repeated sentence “Since, therefore, all things.” Finally, after the words of chapter 8, they placed the sentence “But if there are any other causes,” etc., together with the chronological note, thereby concluding the letter.

5. It is therefore not surprising that Quesnellus, concerned to correct from the evidence of the manuscripts the errors of the commonly printed edition of Saint Leo, rejected this printed edition, which rests on no manuscripts.

When he perceived such great variation in the manuscripts themselves and was unable to find a single codex that suggested a suitable way of reconciling everything, he thought that the first form of the edition, which he had seen preserved in the more ancient collections and manuscripts, should be retained and defended.

He rejected the second, Hadrianian form of the edition all the more readily because it contains certain prerogatives of the Roman See. Since he was not well disposed toward these, he thought he saw in that edition an open interpolation and several degrees of forgery, as he calls them, in its additions, and he set these out at great length in his notes.

6. Those who were not equally hostile to the privileges of the Roman pontiffs, although imbued with Gallican principles, reconsidered Quesnellus’s notes. They judged that the abridged edition, the first form, should indeed be approved, but they did not for that reason believe that the additions of the Hadrianian edition should be rejected, nor did they consider Quesnellus’s arguments against them effective or convincing.

Among these was Stephen Baluzius, who, after weighing Quesnellus’s arguments in volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1249, declared:

> “I see nothing contrary to the discipline then received in the Roman Church.”

Although Quesnellus, in his second edition, treated this observation of Baluzius as weak and unworthy of a response—because Baluzius, having dealt with the matter only incidentally there, had not thought it necessary to present his proofs more fully in the form of a dissertation—it will become clear from our observations on Quesnellus’s notes how sound and firm his assertion ought to be regarded.

Coustant, who read both Quesnellus’s first and second editions and whose expertise and critical judgment are known to all learned men from his celebrated edition of the Letters of the Roman Pontiffs, not only regarded as genuine the fragment of the Hadrianian edition rejected by Quesnellus, but also undertook, at the beginning of the second volume—which he had prepared for publication—to defend that same fragment against Quesnellus’s censures.

This is testified by Father Simon Mopinot in his letter *On the New Edition of the Letters of the Supreme Pontiffs*, printed in 1724. After listing the chapters on which Coustant chiefly worked in the second volume, he writes the following concerning Leo’s letters:

> “Certain letters will be restored to that same pope which have been rashly relegated to the class of spurious writings. Among them, by no means the least important, is that outstanding fragment concerning the appeal of Bishop Lupicinus to the Apostolic See, a fragment of the first letter—our Letter 12 to the Africans—which appears, as it seems, to have been inserted there improperly.”

This is the fragment of the letter contained in the Hadrianian edition, which Quesnellus deletes.

7. From Father Mopinot’s words it is plainly evident that Coustant intended to defend this fragment. Yet he seems to have thought that it should not be inserted into the letter itself, but appended to it as an addition. This is also suggested by the following words of Coustant himself, volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 969, note a. When he was about to cite this Leonine fragment as genuine, as he intended to publish it in the second volume, he used these words: “In the additions to Leo’s first letter.”

This arose because he had found no codex presenting the complete and genuine reading and form of this letter, in which that fragment would have its proper place.

That good fortune has now fallen to us. Father Reader Philip Maria Sereno of the Order of Preachers kindly communicated to us a copy of this letter, transcribed with the greatest care from a special Florentine codex of collection 13, marked number 182 and dating from the twelfth century. We have said enough in the preface, §29, about its older and principal provenance with respect to Leo’s letters.

In this copy, all the words of both the abridged and Hadrianian editions that occur in so many ancient codices—and that are shown by the Leonine style to be genuine—are properly joined together in one natural context, so that nothing is excluded and nothing is perverted.

8. The codices supporting the abridged edition—whether produced by Quesnellus or discovered by us—on which his argument chiefly rests prove only that this part of the letter is genuine; they do not demonstrate that the complete letter is represented.

If this should seem strange to anyone, let him consider other similarly abridged texts in the same manuscripts and collections.

Thus the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and also the manuscripts of the Works and Letters of Saint Leo in collection 24, which present this letter in abridged form, likewise present in abridged form the letter of Saint Peter Chrysologus to Eutyches, omitting even half of it. Yet that letter is read in full in all the Greek and Latin codices of the Council of Chalcedon in collection 17.

In all the Latin collections and manuscripts, the Council of Sardica is also presented in mutilated form, without the three final canons that are contained in the Greek exemplars.

In Vatican 1341 and in three other Gallic manuscripts cited by Coustant—volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 772—which contain the Hispanic collection of Innocent I, the letter to the bishops of the Council of Toledo is abridged, since numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 8, as well as part of number 1, are absent.

In the manuscripts of the Hadrianian collection, only the beginning of Hormisdas’s letter to the priests, deacons, and archimandrites of Second Syria is copied; the outstanding manuscript of collection 14 preserves it in full.

And, to omit other examples of the same kind, in Quesnellus’s collection 5, number 51, the letter of Gelasius to the Easterners is cited with a chapter missing.

Why, then, could Leo’s letter to the Africans not likewise have been transmitted in mutilated form?

9. Let us grant that the copy of this letter which is read in the Hadrianian collection without the three chapters of the abridged edition, and with another longer addition, was not inserted by Dionysius into his collection, as Quesnellus correctly conjectured in his notes; and let us even grant that it was added to that collection around the time of Gregory II, as he supposed—that is, around the beginning of the eighth century. Even so, it cannot for that reason be proved interpolated or spurious.

For in all the documents found inserted in the Hadrianian collection, nothing apocryphal or interpolated is detected. Since the style of this letter and its entire context are wholly consistent with Leo, while the arguments advanced by Quesnellus prove nothing, as will be evident from our observations on his notes, one may doubt the authenticity and genuineness of this single document only rashly.

10. Nor should the absence of the three chapters—6, 7, and 8—cause difficulty, since they exist in the abridged edition and are known to be genuine from the most ancient manuscripts and collections.

The examples of similar omissions that we pointed out shortly before in documents of other distinguished collections show that such omissions are not uncommon.

We found the celebrated Letter 14 of Leo, to Anastasius, which is complete in several collections, copied in two ancient manuscripts, Vatican 1347 and Vatican Palatine 579, with chapters 3 and 4 omitted. If other codices or collections had taken it from them, they would have transmitted the same omission; yet the letter could not on that account be called into question.

Are not some letters of Gelasius also shorter in certain collections than they were published in the Councils?

His celebrated letter to the Dardanians is a well-known example. Not only in Quesnellus’s collection 5, chapter 50, but also in nearly all the manuscripts of the other ancient collections, it lacks three longer and nine shorter sections. These are nevertheless found in the manuscripts of the outstanding collection 14 and consequently in the Roman edition of the Letters of the Pontiffs, as well as in the published volumes of the Councils. There can be no doubt that Facundus of Hermiane made use of this fuller example.

Just as, in the manuscripts of Innocent I’s letter to the Toletans mentioned shortly before, only the general decrees were retained while the rest, relating to particular cases and persons, was omitted, so the author of the Hadrianian collection appears to have preferred the same arrangement in this letter of Leo: for the three omitted chapters concern particular persons and cases.

11. Moreover, what Quesnellus thought is not true: namely, that this edition of the letter was added to the Dionysian codex in the time of Gregory II because the more recent document in the Hadrianian codex concerns that Gregory.

Among the Vatican codices we found one marked number 5845, containing the pure collection of Dionysius, which Coustant praised as extremely rare and which ends with the letters of Anastasius II.

In this codex, which is extremely ancient, Dionysius’s letter to the presbyter Julian—found in this one manuscript and published from it—is placed before the Decretals. After the pure collection of Dionysius has been copied, an appendix in the same ancient script follows. First it presents three councils of Pope Symmachus: one from the year 501, another from 502, and a third from 499. Then it gives the headings of six decretals of Pope Hilary, two of Simplicius, and one of Felix; after the headings, the decretals themselves are recited. All these were later inserted into the Hadrianian collection in their proper chronological order.

After Felix’s decretal, on page 155, Leo’s letter is copied with the following title:

> “In the case of Bishop Lupicinus: Leo to all the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauretania.”

“Since [we have heard] concerning ordinations,” and the remainder follow in the same form and with the same reading as the Hadrianian edition.

This letter of Leo is followed, on page 157, by Zosimus’s letter addressed to the presbyters of Ravenna:

> “Zosimus’s admonition to the presbyters and deacons who are in Ravenna. From the report,” etc.,

which is also read in the same Hadrianian codex.

Finally, after this letter, as though it were a new addition, comes the table of 79 chapters, and the documents themselves are appended after the table. We shall discuss these more fully elsewhere. For now, it is enough to mention the first five documents, which are presented as follows:

Page 159. I. Justin Augustus to Hormisdas: “As we have always been,” etc.

Page 160. II. Copy of the petition of the Antiochene and Jerusalemite clergy and monks, etc., to Justin: “Draw water with joy,” etc.

Page 161. III. Hormisdas to Justin: “Meanwhile, the matters that concern the unity of the Church,” etc.

Page 164. IV. Hormisdas to the presbyters, deacons, and archimandrites of Second Syria: “After reading the letter,” etc.

On the same page: “Here begin the enactments of Pope Gregory the Younger: In the name of the Lord,” etc.

These documents, neither more nor fewer, are those found in the Hadrianic manuscripts added to the Dionysian Collection and inserted in their proper place in chronological order. From the different manner in which they are appended in this codex to the pure Dionysian Collection, it is evident that they were not all added at one and the same time, but at least at two different times: first, the documents placed before the table of the seventy-nine chapters; then, the first five chapters of that table. These latter documents, which end with Gregory II, could have been added during the age of that pontiff or shortly afterward. The same, however, cannot be thought concerning the documents placed before this table, which belong to much earlier pontiffs and were perhaps added shortly after the death of Symmachus, since he is the last among the pontiffs whose decrees are recounted in that first appendix. Indeed, the councils of Symmachus are listed first, because this pontiff was of more recent memory; hence perhaps he is called “of holy memory” by a particular formula in the title of the council of the year 502. This also seems to indicate that the addition was attached in the city of Rome itself. For if these documents placed before the table of the seventy-nine chapters had been added after the death of Hormisdas, the collector would not have separated the records of that pontiff from the documents of Symmachus, his immediate predecessor, nor would he have left them to be appended by the collector of the second appendix.

**12.** If these observations and conjectures are judged probable—as they certainly seem to us—then the insertion of Leo’s letter to the Africans, added later to the Hadrianic Collection together with the disputed fragment, is brought approximately to the time of Dionysius, since this latter also flourished at Rome after Symmachus, during the pontificate of Hormisdas. Thus it becomes true that this letter entered the Dionysian Collection about fifty years after Leo, so that it would seem exceedingly rash—we use Quesnellus’s words in the notes at the beginning of this letter—to suspect that, while writing and collecting in the city of Rome itself, he lacked authentic codices. For just as there can be no doubt about the addition of Zosimus’s letter or about the councils of Symmachus, so there should be no doubt about this letter of Leo, which was added at the same time by the same author.

From this, moreover, the origin of the Hadrianic Collection is revealed. Nothing else was done in it except that, while preserving chronological order, certain documents were inserted into the Dionysian Collection which, in two additions and at two different times, had already been appended to that collection—though in disordered sequence—long before the pontificate of Hadrian.

**13.** Furthermore, the distinguished Florentine codex of Saint Mark, Collection 13, presents the complete letter from the abridged and Hadrianic edition. It should not be surprising that this letter is found complete in a single codex, or collection, while in all the other ancient collections it is read in variously mutilated or incomplete form. For the aforementioned letter of Gelasius to the Dardanians is likewise shorter in several—and those ancient—codices and collections, and is found in longer form only in Collection 14.

This Florentine codex, moreover, represents the portions of the abridged and Hadrianic editions properly placed in their appropriate location. First, it presents the entire abridged edition, including the three chapters—6, 7, and 8—that were omitted in the Hadrianic edition. Then, at the final words of that same abridged edition, it conveniently and most appropriately for the context appends the words “for stirring them more particularly” (*in eos specialius commovendi*) and the remainder of the fragment, which is supplied in the Hadrianic edition through its conclusion.

Add also that this Florentine codex not only contains this Hadrianic fragment, which Quesnellus incorrectly believes to be spurious, but generally also exhibits Hadrianic readings in those chapters that are common to the abridged and Hadrianic editions. Quesnellus, who rejects the Hadrianic form and praises the codices of the abridged edition, preferred Hadrianic readings to the readings of the abridged edition in quite a few places, which is not very consistent with his hypothesis.

For the two forms differ in some places not merely in a word or two, but in entire clauses and sentences. This gives us the strongest suspicion that two copies of this letter were found among Leo’s own writings, from which such a divergence arose. Variants in one word or another can indeed be attributed to the carelessness or discretion of copyists, especially when they damage the sense or style. But such great variation in words and sentences—although sometimes extended over several words—which nevertheless everywhere reflects the style of the same author, especially if it is found not in all or many works but in only one or two, seems attributable not to copyists but to the author himself. He may have written the same work once in his own hand and, intending to correct it in a second revision or even to expand it in places, written it again with different words and sentences.

**14.** P. Coustant believed that the difference we mentioned in Gelasius’s letter to the Dardanians—shorter in some codices and longer in others—depended on the fact that the same letter had been issued by Gelasius himself in two forms. He likewise thought that the same thing later happened to Hormisdas and Gregory, and earlier to our Leo. He confirms this by reading *Vindiciae veterum codicum*, chapter 13, page 713.

From what was observed above, it seems to us highly probable that this happened to the present letter. Saint Leo apparently wrote the letter in his first draft in the form found in the manuscripts of the abridged edition; and from this copy, once published or discovered, the authors of the collections of that edition took the letter. Later, in a second revision, when something new had perhaps arisen—for example, the case of Bishop Restitutus, whom the holy pontiff now presents in chapter 10 as having lodged a complaint after the matters reported by Potentius—he explained some things in other words and added certain points in response to the new circumstances.

We shall show in the admonition that Letters 30 and 31, which are found in distinct and very ancient collections, partly in the same words and partly in different words, yet concerning the same matter addressed to Pulcheria, are two copies of one and the same letter. In the letter addressed to the Africans, however, the long fragment read in the Hadrianic Collection appears to have been added in a second revision, because of certain information that arose after Potentius’s report—perhaps reported by Bishop David, who is mentioned in that fragment, or by others who had migrated from Africa to Rome, as is indicated by the Hadrianic reading, “the report of those traveling might convey.”

For this reason the holy pontiff inserted into the first reading of the abridged edition, chapter 9, “Since, therefore, concerning all things,” in a second revision the short passage “almost,” which is read in the Hadrianic edition, because certain matters had arisen that needed to be added to what had previously been written.

Nor should the reference to virgins violated by barbarian violence cause difficulty because it is repeated in chapters 8 and 11. In chapter 8 he teaches what the virgins themselves ought to think about their condition; in chapter 11 he determines what the bishops must do concerning them. Indeed, this double mention of such virgins sufficiently suggests that the fragment of the Hadrianic edition belongs not to some other letter of Leo, which may perhaps have perished, as some have supposed, but to this same Letter 12, as it is presented in the Florentine manuscript. This is confirmed still more strongly by the words inserted in chapter 11 of that same codex when the mention of the virgins is repeated, as was stated above.

**15.** In the edition of the complete letter, which we shall present first, we preferred the Hadrianic readings to the readings of the codices of the abridged letter, not only because the Florentine codex follows the Hadrianic readings—the codex through which the complete letter, as it was written by Leo, has come down to us—but also because readings of this kind seem to have been more pleasing to the same author when he revised and corrected the letter.

Indeed, they are so appropriate that Quesnellus himself preferred nearly the same readings to those of the codices containing the abridged letter. Yet so that no one may be deprived of the readings of either the complete or the abridged edition, after publishing the complete letter from the readings of the Florentine and Hadrianic manuscripts, together with their variants, we shall append the same letter in abridged form, especially according to the exemplar of the very ancient book Barb. 2888 and another similar one, Vat. 1342. Montfaucon calls the latter, in volume 1 of the *Bibliotheca*, page 131, “a most elegant and very ancient codex.” We shall also record the variants of the other codices that likewise preserve the same letter in abridged form.

Whoever compares this abridged edition—which no one has hitherto reproduced exactly—with the complete one—we ask that no one be unwilling to make the comparison—will, we hope, lend us his approval and acknowledge that this edition was corrected and expanded by the author himself.

**16.** As for the date of this letter, Quesnellus correctly determined in the notes that it was written before the year 455, in which Valentinian III was killed. Since it is known to have been written while the Moors were still subject to the Roman emperor, who was Catholic, and while many people from Africa consequently made their way to Rome from time to time, after Valentinian’s death those same people would have been subjected to the Arian Vandals, persecutors of the Catholics. The Roman pontiff would therefore no longer have been able so readily to provide for that province in the matters expressed in this letter.

Since Quesnellus could not establish its precise year, he thought it should be published first, not so much to compensate for the lack of letters written by Leo at the beginning of his pontificate as to avoid interrupting the order of the other surviving letters that bear definite chronological indications. In a marginal note he merely indicates that it was written around the beginning of Leo’s pontificate, and in the notes he places it around the year 443.

The war that raged in Africa between the emperor Valentinian and Genseric, king of the Vandals, plainly seems to have impeded correspondence of this kind. That war continued until the year 442, when Prosper records in his *Chronicle*: “Peace with Genseric was confirmed by Valentinian Augustus, and Africa was divided between the two in specified portions.””

From Novel 23, book II, it is clear that in the year 445 envoys came to Rome from the African provinces left to Valentinian, and that a law was enacted allowing appeal to the prefect of the City. On this occasion of appeals, perhaps the report of certain abuses unlawfully committed among the Moors reached the holy pontiff through those who were traveling there.

Therefore, this letter should more probably and cautiously be placed between the year 445 and the year 455. Moreover, in chapter 1 Leo indicates that he learned from travelers arriving from Africa what had been wrongly done in various cities of Mauretania on account of the opportunity provided by a time of disorder—that is, during the war. It is credible that he learned these things from them after peace had been established, preferably in the year 445, when more people probably traveled to Rome on the occasion of the appeals than at a later time. To allow suitable time for the journey and for Potentius’s report, upon receiving which Leo wrote this letter, it appears to have been issued around the year 446.

**657 — LETTER XII. TO THE AFRICAN BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF CAESAREAN MAURETANIA**  
[Note: Another reading: formerly 12, now 14. Written 10 August 446.]

Now published for the first time in full from the Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark.

[Note: There are no titles in the Florentine manuscript from which we have taken this letter in full. In the Hadrianic Collection, however, there is a single title: “In the case of Bishop Lupicinus,” which nevertheless pertains only to chapter 12. In the table of titles prefixed to that collection, this title appears as number 49: “Leo to the Moorish bishops. Concerning the preservation and discipline of the canons, so that no one may presume to enter the clergy improperly and disorderly.”]

### Synopsis

I. He censures ordinations carried out in tumult.  
II. What it means to lay hands upon someone hastily.  
III. Only husbands of one wife may be deacons, priests, and bishops.  
IV. The inexperienced and newly converted must not be ordained.  
V. Leo tolerates those ordained from among the laity, but not bigamists.  
VI. Concerning Donatus, converted from the Novatians, and Maximus, from the Donatists.  
VII. Concerning Aggarus and Tyberianus, ordained from among the laity and in a tumultuous manner.  
VIII. Virgins violated by force must not compare themselves with the undefiled.  
IX. He exhorts them to obedience and threatens penalties for the disobedient.  
X. In what places bishops ought to be ordained, and concerning the petition of Bishop Restitutus.  
XI. What must be done concerning the virgins mentioned above who were violated by barbarian violence.  
**658 XII. Concerning the case of Bishop Lupicinus.**  
XIII. Concerning the airing of ecclesiastical cases and their referral to the apostolic see.

[Note: The Florentine manuscript and the published editions of the Hadrianic Collection omit the words “Bishop of the city of Rome, and greetings in the Lord”; but other letters copied by Dionysius himself frequently preserve both expressions.]

**LEO, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME, TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT CAESAREAN MAURETANIA, GREETINGS IN THE LORD.**

### CHAPTER I

Since reports more frequently brought to us by those traveling from your region conveyed that certain matters concerning the ordination of priests had been unlawfully usurped among you, the reasonableness of piety required us to seek to ascertain the truth of these matters, in proportion to the concern that, by divine institution, we owe to the universal Church.

[Note: In the Hadrianic Vercelli manuscript the reading is “through the solicitude”; shortly afterward three codices have “we bestow” (*impendimus*) instead of “we owe” (*dependimus*).]

We therefore entrusted the responsibility of our care to our brother and fellow priest Potentius,

[Note: Justellus reads “fellow brother”; the manuscript of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, of the mixed recension, reads “co-bishop” instead of “fellow priest.”]

who, in accordance with the letters that we sent to you through him, was to investigate what the truth was concerning the bishops whose culpable election was being reported and to disclose everything faithfully to us.

Since he has now fully laid everything open to our knowledge and, with an honest report, has made clear to us under what sort of rulers and in what condition certain peoples of Christ are being maintained in the regions of the province of Caesarea, it was necessary for us, by letters now sent also to Your Charity, to express the grief of our heart, with which we burn on account of the dangers threatening the Lord’s flocks.

[Note: The Vercelli manuscript reads “we burn for the Lord’s flock.”]

[Note: Distinction 61, chapter 5, “We are astonished.”]

We are astonished that among you either the presumption of ambitious men or popular tumult has prevailed on the occasion of a time of disorder,

[Note: The same codex reads “through the action of a time of disorder”; shortly afterward two Vatican codices read “of peoples” instead of “popular.”]

**659** so that the pastoral dignity and governance of the Church have been given to persons unworthy and far removed from priestly merit.

This is not to care for the peoples but to harm them; it is not to provide governance but to increase danger. For the integrity of those who preside is the salvation of those subject to them, and where obedience is safe, there the form of doctrine is sound.

[Note: 1, question 1, chapter 25, “Principatus.”]

But a rule that either sedition has bestowed or ambition has seized, even if it does not offend by its morals and actions, is nevertheless harmful because of the example of its very beginning; and it is difficult for matters begun from a bad foundation to reach a good conclusion.

### CHAPTER II

If, then, in every rank of the Church it must be carefully and intelligently ensured that nothing in the house of the Lord is disordered or misplaced, how much more diligently must we work to avoid error in the election of the one who is placed above all the ranks? For the condition and order of the entire household of the Lord will waver if what is required in the body is not found in the head.

[Note: The Vercelli manuscript, with two other codices, reads: “if it is not found in the head.” A little later, the manuscript of the Holy Cross reads: “through the Holy Spirit.”]

Where is that command of the blessed apostle Paul, issued through the Spirit of God, by which, in the person of Timothy, the entire number of Christ’s priests is instructed, and it is said to each one of us: “Lay hands hastily on no one, neither share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22)?

[Note: Quesnellus, following the common editions, reads: “and consequently to each one of us.” The word “consequently” is absent from all the Hadrianic manuscripts and from the Florentine codex, and occurs only in codices of the abridged or mixed recension. Four of these read “and therefore.”]

[Note: Distinction 72, chapter 3, “What does it mean?”]

What is it to lay hands hastily except to bestow priestly honor upon those who have not been tested—before the age of maturity, before the time of examination, before the merit of obedience, before the experience of discipline?

[Note: This is the reading of all the Hadrianic manuscripts and of the Florentine codex. Quesnellus, with the manuscripts and printed editions of the abridged and mixed recensions, reads “before the merit of labor.” Justellus printed both readings: “before the merit of obedience and labor.”] And what is it to share in the sins of others except also to become the kind of ordainer as is the one who has not deserved to be ordained?

For just as the person who preserves sound judgment in choosing a priest gains for himself the fruit of a good work, so the person who takes an unworthy man into his own college inflicts serious harm upon himself.

[Note: The Florentine codex reads “preserves”; the other witnesses of the Hadrianic Collection read “holds.”]

[Note: Thus reads the Florentine manuscript, together with all the printed and manuscript Hadrianic witnesses: “takes an unworthy man into his own college.” Quesnellus’s reading, “elevates an unworthy man to the fellowship of his dignity,” is that of the manuscripts of the abridged and mixed recensions. The words that follow, “For what is contained in the general statutes …,” belong to the manuscripts of the abridged and mixed recensions. Shortly afterward, the Florentine manuscript of Santa Croce, as well as some Hadrianic witnesses, reads “in established matters” instead of “in institutions.”]

Therefore, what is contained in the general statutes must not be disregarded in the case of anyone, nor should that honor be considered legitimate which has been conferred contrary to the commands of divine law.

### CHAPTER III

[Note: The particle “that” (*ut*) is absent from the Vercelli, Florentine, and Angelica codices.]

For when the Apostle says that, among the other rules of election, that bishop should be ordained who is known to have been—or to be—the husband of one wife (1 Timothy 3:2),

[Note: The words “or to be” are absent from the Florentine codex. Shortly afterward, all the Hadrianic manuscripts and printed editions, as well as the Florentine codex, read “so sacred” (*tam sacrata*) instead of “so sacred a thing” (*tam sacra*).]

this command has always been regarded as so sacred that the same requirement was understood to be observed also regarding the woman chosen as the priest’s wife: lest, before she entered into his marriage—he who had had no other wife—she might have experienced the marriage of another man.

[Note: The oldest Vatican manuscript and the Vercelli manuscript read: “before she entered into his fellowship.” Four other codices of the mixed edition likewise read this way. We have nevertheless retained the common reading, which is preferred in the Florentine manuscript, by Justellus, and in other Hadrianic codices.]

[Note: All printed editions and Hadrianic manuscripts of the abridged recension read, “Who then would dare to ignore [it]?” The Florentine codex has both readings: “Who, therefore, would dare either to ignore or to tolerate [it]?”]

Who, then, would dare tolerate an offense against so great a sacrament, when even the statutes of divine law have not been lacking for this great and venerable mystery? Those statutes plainly define that the priest must take a virgin as his wife (Leviticus 21:13–14; Ezekiel 44:22), and that she who is to become the priest’s wife must know nothing of another husband’s bed.

[Note: The word “wife,” which Quesnellus added in his second edition from the manuscripts and Dionysius Exiguus, was likewise found by us in the Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark and also in several Hadrianic collections. It is absent, however, from Vatican 5845 and Vercelli, and likewise from Hadrianic witnesses.]

[Note: The same Florentine codex, together with all the Hadrianic manuscripts, the manuscript of the Holy Cross, and four other codices of the mixed edition, reads this way. The codices of the abridged edition, with Quesnellus, read “of the pontiff.” The following sentence, beginning “For already then” and ending “does not join,” is absent from Vatican 5845 and two Hadrianic manuscripts, Vercelli, and Vatican 1337. It is found, however, in many other codices of the Hadrianic Collection—including the ancient Vatican 4979, Vatican Regina 1021 and 1043—and also in the Florentine manuscript.]
