For already then the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church was represented in the marriages of priests: because, since “the man is the head of the woman” (Ephesians 5:23; 1 Corinthians 11:3), the Bride of the Word should learn to know no other man than Christ, who rightly chooses one, loves one, and does not join another to himself in partnership besides that one.

[Note: The Florentine codex has this distinctive reading: “So that, just as the man is the head of the woman, so Christ is the head of the Church; let the Bride of the Word learn.” The name “Word” was also found in editions before Quesnellus, is read by Justellus, and occurs in the manuscripts of the Hadrianic Collection. It is also found in all the collections of the abridged edition that we were able to consult—1, 3, 4, 5, Hisp., 9, Isid., 10, 12, and 24—as well as in Barberini 77, in Sichardus’s exemplar, and in the codices of Collection 11 of the mixed edition. Only the codices of Collections 20, 21, 22, and 23 of the mixed edition read “Christ.” We do not know why Quesnellus preferred that reading and transferred it from the margin of the editions into the text.]

Therefore, if this form of priestly marriages was observed even in the Old Testament, how much more, established under the grace of the Gospel, ought we to obey the apostolic commands? No matter how much a man may be found to possess good morals and to be adorned with holy works, he must nevertheless not ascend to the rank of deacon, the honor of the presbyterate, or the summit of the episcopate if it has not been established either that he himself was the husband of one wife or that his wife had been the wife of one man alone.

[Note: We restored “it has been shown” from the Florentine and Hadrianic codices; Vatican 544 of Collection 24 and the exemplar of Sichardus also agree, although they belong to the abridged edition. Quesnellus, with other manuscripts, reads “it has been established.” In the Angelican codex of Collection 21, the reading is: “or that she herself had not been the wife of one man.”]

### CHAPTER IV

When the Apostle admonishes and says, “And let these also first be tested, and so let them minister” (1 Timothy 3:10), what else should we understand except that, in these promotions, we must consider not only marital chastity but also the merits of labor? Otherwise, pastoral office might be entrusted either to those newly emerged from baptism or to those suddenly converted from secular life; for throughout all the ranks of Christian service, it must be judged from the progress of their advancement whether greater responsibilities can be entrusted to anyone.

[Note: Quesnellus prefixed the words “we think” in this passage. We removed them on the authority of the manuscripts of the Hadrianic Collection and the Florentine codex, as well as the better codices of the abridged Collection 3, 4, 5, Vindobonensis, Hisp., and 12, together with Barberini 77 and Sichardus. Quesnellus is supported by the manuscripts of Collection 1, Vatican Hisp., Isid., and Collection 24 of the abridged edition, as well as by all the other mixed manuscripts from which the printed editions were produced.]

[Note: The Hadrianic and Florentine codices read this way. The others, together with the printed editions, read “those inexperienced from baptism.”]

[Note: Quesnellus reads “since every rank,” a reading that we found only in the manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24 and in the printed editions with Sichardus and Merlinus. A little later, two codices have “advancements” instead of “progress”; three, as well as Justellus, read “they ought” instead of “he ought.”]

The venerable decrees of the blessed Fathers rightly judged such men suitable for sacred ministries when they spoke of the election of priests—

[Note: The Florentine manuscript, together with all the codices and printed Hadrianic editions, reads this way. In the manuscripts of the abridged edition, this passage is presented with considerable variation as follows: “Whose entire life, from childhood onward to more advanced years, had run its course through the services of ecclesiastical discipline, so that his former life might provide testimony for each one; and no doubt could be entertained concerning the advancement of one to whom, for many labors, chaste morals, and energetic actions, the reward of a higher place was owed. For if …” It cannot be denied that this reading reflects Leo’s style no less than the one inserted into the text, nor can such striking variation be attributed to the carelessness or discretion of copyists.

It should further be observed that the reading “from childhood onward” in the abridged edition agrees with the discipline of the Roman Church and with the decrees of Siricius and Zosimus. In these, while the promotion of laymen by a leap from one rank to another is prohibited, it is provided that no one be advanced to the higher ranks of the Church unless he had been initiated into the clergy from childhood and had conducted himself lawfully in the lower ranks.

They permit only those adults to be received into the clergy who, having been baptized at an advanced age, immediately after baptism devoted themselves to the clergy. See Siricius’s letter to Himerius, chapter 9, and Zosimus’s letter to Hesychius, chapter 3.

At the same time, we observe that the Hadrianic reading inserted into the text does not contradict this discipline. It equally requires what is most important: a probation of long duration through each individual rank, as the cited decrees require. Saint Leo here simply leaves aside the question whether this probation must begin in childhood—which is not the principal point—just as we sometimes find that his predecessors, Celestine in his letter to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonensis, chapter 3, and Innocent I in his letter to Felix of Nuceria, chapter 3, passed over that requirement.

Moreover, although probation from childhood was maintained at Rome and in some other places, it was not observed everywhere or always. In Africa, especially at this time, when the Church had been disturbed for many years by the tumult of war and the clergy had been gravely afflicted, it had not been observed—or could not have been observed—with precision. Thus some older men had been, or appeared likely to be, received into the clergy even though they could provide suitable evidence of their fitness through their successive ranks.

Perhaps for this reason Saint Leo judged that the matter should be handled more leniently in these circumstances and that, following the example of the aforementioned predecessors, he should refrain from insisting upon the condition of childhood. Accordingly, altering the text of the first draft, he impressed upon them only the canonical probation through the successive ranks, which is the more important requirement.

Finally, Leo here appeals to the sanctions of the blessed Fathers. By the name “blessed Fathers” he generally means not the decrees of Roman pontiffs but the canons of councils. Thus, in this very letter, in chapter 5, by the words “the rules of the blessed Fathers” he indicates the Nicene canons, and in chapter 10, by “the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers,” the canons of Sardica.

He calls the decrees of pontiffs “decrees of the apostolic see” or “decrees of his predecessors,” as when, in that same chapter 5, he distinguishes “the statutes of the apostolic see” from “the rules of the blessed Fathers.” Likewise, Zosimus, in his letter to Hesychius, chapter 1, writing about this matter of probation, says: “The commands of the Fathers are on your side; the authority of the apostolic see is on your side.” By “the apostolic see” he means his predecessors, and by “the Fathers” he means the Fathers of Sardica.

Now, although these Fathers prescribe in canon 13 that the life of those to be chosen be tested through each rank and over a long period, and although they indicate the apostolic testimony cited by Leo, they do not command that a person pass through every age, from childhood to advanced years, in the services of ecclesiastical discipline. On the contrary, they permit adults from the marketplace and from civil administration to be received into the clergy and advanced after the prescribed period of probation.

Therefore, when Saint Leo invokes the sanctions of these Fathers, he could not have insisted upon anything other than what is contained in the reading inserted into the text. Likewise, Innocent I, in his letter to Felix of Nuceria, chapter 3, explicitly indicating the statutes of the Sardican canons, affirms in chapter 5—without mentioning childhood—that laymen are not prohibited from entering the clergy:

“Provided, of course, that the periods established by our predecessors be observed. Let no one quickly become a lector, quickly an acolyte, quickly a deacon, quickly a priest; for if they remain for a long time in the lesser offices, and both their life and their service are tested, they may later come to the priesthood after the merits of their service have been completed, and they may not seize in advance what a proven life deserves to receive.”

Celestine, too, in his letter to the Viennese, chapter 3, calling the Sardican canons the decrees of the Fathers, says:

“We have learned that certain men were ordained bishops who had not been established in any ecclesiastical orders before being raised to so great a dignity, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers … For one ought to arrive at the episcopate through those ranks concerning which provision has been made most frequently, so that those initiated into the lesser offices may advance to the greater.”

You see, then, that Saint Leo both had regard to the Sardican canons in the reading inserted into the text and did not depart from the examples of his predecessors. From this it is further understood how improperly Quesnellus transferred this reading into his notes as though it had been stitched into the manuscript codices by some impostor to accommodate a more recent discipline, and as though it were an evident corruption.]

who had advanced for a long time through each rank of service and had given credible proof of themselves, so that the account of each one’s life and actions might bear witness on his behalf.

[Col. 0651A] For if it is disgraceful to attain even the honors of the world without the support of time and without the merit of labor, and if those are customarily marked as ambitious whose claims are not supported by proofs of integrity, how careful and prudent must be the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities?

[Note: Vatican 5845 and Vercelli read “without the support of approval.”]

[Note: Distinction 61, chapter 8, “We decree that in no respect.”]

This is necessary so that the apostolic and canonical decrees may not be violated in any respect, and so that the Church of the Lord may not be entrusted to those who, ignorant of lawful institutions and unaware of all humility, do not wish to rise from the lowest ranks but seek to begin from the highest. For it is profoundly unjust and absurd that the inexperienced should be preferred to teachers, the new to the ancient, and the untrained to those proven by service.

In a great house, as the Apostle explains (2 Timothy 2:20), there must necessarily be different vessels: some of gold and silver, but others of wood and clay. Their service, however, is distinguished according to the quality of their material.

[Note: The Florentine codex, together with Justellus, reads: “and the use of the precious is not the same as that of the common.” We have preferred the reading of the oldest Vatican manuscript, Vercelli, and other Hadrianic collections, which is also supported by three codices of the abridged edition. Vatican Collection 11 reads: “nor is the use of the precious the same as that of the common.”]

The use of precious vessels is not the same as that of common ones. For everything will be disordered if clay vessels are preferred to golden ones and wooden vessels to silver ones.

Just as wooden and clay vessels represent those people who as yet possess no virtues on which to rely, so without doubt the golden and silver vessels signify those who, refined by the fire of long instruction and purified in the furnace of prolonged labor, have deserved to be genuine gold and pure silver.

If these receive no reward corresponding to their devotion, all ecclesiastical discipline is dissolved and the entire order is disturbed, when in the Church those who have undergone no ministry at all obtain, through the perverse judgment of their electors, an authority to which they are not entitled.

### CHAPTER V

[Col. 0651C]

Since, then, the support of the populace or the ambitions of the proud have had such influence among you that we recognize not only laymen but also men who have married a second wife, or husbands of widows, as having been advanced to pastoral office, do not the circumstances most clearly require that the churches in which such things have been committed be cleansed by a stricter judgment, and that appropriate punishment be imposed not only upon such bishops but also upon those who ordained them? [Note: [Col. 0651C] Several manuscripts: “the zeal of the peoples.”] [Note: [Col. 0651C] Alternatively, “most fitting.”] [Note: [Col. 0651C] 1, question 7, chapter 17, “They require.”]

But on one side the gentleness of mercy surrounds us, and on the other the severity of justice. [Note: [Col. 0651C] In the Vercellian manuscript and in Justellus: “And because, compelled by the piety of the universal Apostolic See, we ought thus to temper our sentence”; after *universae* there appears a gap containing the words “the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” We have supplied these from the Florentine manuscript and very many others. Vatican manuscript 5843 omits *cogimur* (“we are compelled”) and instead has: “we ought thus to temper our sentence.”]

And because mercy and truth belong to every way of the Lord, we are compelled, in accordance with the piety of the Apostolic See, to temper our sentence in such a way that, after weighing the gravity of the offenses—for they are certainly not all of one measure—we judge some to be tolerable to some extent, but others to be cut away entirely. [Note: [Col. 0651D] This is the reading of the Hadrianic manuscripts together with the Florentine manuscript. Quesnellus’s reading, “which are evidently not all of one measure,” belongs to the abridged edition. Shortly afterward, the Hadrianic manuscripts and Justellus give *credamus* (“we judge”), which we have adopted; the Florentine manuscript has *definiamus* (“we determine”), as does the abridged edition.]

For neither apostolic nor legal authority permits those who have entered a second marriage or joined themselves in marriage to widows to obtain the priesthood; [Note: [Col. 0651D] The Vercellian manuscript with Justellus has *obtinere* (“to obtain”). Before “in your judgment” we have supplied *in* from the Florentine and Hadrianic manuscripts.] and still more, if he is refuted in your judgment, that man who, as has been reported to us, is simultaneously the husband of two wives, or the man who is said to have taken another wife after being dismissed by his wife. [Note: In Quesnellus there is added: “we decree that he is to be deprived of his dignity”; these words are absent from all manuscripts and printed copies of the Hadrianic edition and from the Florentine manuscript. They are found, however, in the manuscripts of the abridged edition, except in the manuscripts of collection 24, and in Merlinus and Sichardus. They are not really necessary, since everything is governed by what precedes: “Neither apostolic nor legal authority permits him to obtain the priesthood.”]

As for the others, whose advancement incurs only this criticism—that they were chosen from among the laity for episcopal office—and who cannot be blamed on the ground that they have wives, we permit them to retain the priesthood they have undertaken, [Note: [Col. 0652C] This is the reading of nearly all books of the Hadrianic edition, together with the Florentine manuscript and two manuscripts of the abridged edition. Alternatively, “have.”] [Note: Quesnellus, following the reading of the manuscripts of the abridged edition, has: “without prejudicing the statutes of the Apostolic See, nor dissolving the regulations of the blessed Fathers and our own decrees, by which…” He had seen the reading inserted in the text and confirmed by all our Hadrianic manuscripts and by the Florentine manuscript; he had also seen it in the commonly circulated Dionysius and in two Thuanean manuscripts, and nevertheless—strangely—carried this passage over into his notes, no. 9, as though it were corrupt, although the alternative reading accepted by him may rather be judged corrupt, insofar as “the decrees of our predecessors and our decrees” and “the statutes of the Apostolic See” are one and the same. Therefore Saint Leo perhaps corrected the earlier wording and substituted at the end: “nor dissolving the regulations of the blessed Fathers,” referring to the canons of the Fathers of Sardica, whose fourth canon he had mentioned. Thus the reading of the text agrees perfectly with that same chapter 4: “lest the apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in anything”; there “apostolic” indicates the statutes of the Apostolic See, while “canonical” indicates the regulations of the blessed Fathers. Shortly afterward, some copies have *statutum* (“established”) instead of *constitutum*.]

without prejudicing the statutes of the Apostolic See or dissolving the regulations of the blessed Fathers, by which it has been salutarily established that no layman, supported by any votes whatsoever, should ascend to the first, second, or third rank in the Church before he has attained the requisite qualification through legitimate stages of advancement.

For what we now tolerate to some extent as pardonable cannot afterward remain unpunished if anyone usurps what we altogether forbid. [Note: This is found substantially in all the Hadrianic manuscripts together with Justellus. The Florentine manuscript and the manuscripts of the abridged edition have: “if he should presume to usurp.”] For remission of sin does not grant permission to sin, nor will what could once be conceded for some reason any longer be lawfully committed with impunity.

## CHAPTER VI

As for Donatus, who, as we have learned, was converted from the Novatians at Salicinus together with his own congregation, we wish him to preside over the Lord’s flock in such a way that he remember to send us a statement of his faith, in which he both condemns the error of Novatian teaching and confesses the Catholic truth in the fullest manner. [Note: 1, question 7, chapter 20, “Donatus.”] [Note: This is the reading of the commonly circulated copies together with manuscripts of collections 1 and 5, Vindobonensis, Hispanicus, and with collections 12 and 21, as well as Sichardus. The Barberinian manuscript of collection 3 has “Sajensis from Novatian.” In the Carthaginian collation of the year 411, no. 128, Donatus, bishop of the people of Sajensis, is mentioned. The Lucensian manuscript of collection 4 has “Sajacinensis.” The Barberinian manuscript 77 and Quesnellus in the margin have “Sajacensis from Novatian.” The Florentine manuscript has “Sajaciensis from Novatian.” Other erroneous variants of inferior manuscripts are omitted.]

We likewise do not exclude Maximus, although improperly ordained from the laity, from the episcopal dignity which he has acquired in some fashion, provided that he is no longer a Donatist and is alien from the spirit of schismatic perversity; but he too must make clear, by issuing a statement to us, that he is a Catholic. [Note: [Col. 0653C] 1, question 7, chapter 19, “Maximus.”] [Note: Manuscript Vatican collection 12 omits “although.” Then, in that same manuscript, as well as in the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, *tamen* (“nevertheless”) is lacking.]

## CHAPTER VII

As for Aggarus and Tyberianus, whose case differs in this respect from that of the others who were ordained from the laity, namely, that violent disturbances and savage riots are said to have accompanied their ordination, we have entrusted everything to your judgment, so that, once we have learned the facts of the inquiry conducted among you, we may know what ought to be decided concerning the persons mentioned above. [Note: We supplied the word “indeed” from the Florentine manuscript and five other manuscripts of excellent quality.]

## CHAPTER VIII

Those servants of God who have lost the integrity of their chastity through barbarian violence will be more praiseworthy in their humility and modesty if they do not dare to compare themselves with undefiled virgins. [Note: [Col. 0653D] We have added “their own” from the same Florentine manuscript and three other excellent manuscripts.] [Note: 32, question 5, chapter 14, “Those servants of God.”]

For although every sin arises from the will, and the mind, unconquered, could remain unpolluted by the corruption of the flesh, this will nevertheless harm them less if they grieve that what they were able not to lose in spirit they have lost, at least, in the body. [Note: The reading was *invita* (“unwilling” or “against her will”). Quesnellus noted in the margin: “Perhaps *invicta* (‘unconquered’),” and we have restored this reading from the Florentine manuscript. Shortly afterward, from the same manuscript and another Barberinian manuscript of collection 3, we have written “to them” instead of “for them.”]

## CHAPTER IX

Since, therefore, you have been fully informed through our brother and fellow bishop David concerning nearly everything contained in the report of our brother Potentius—David having been approved by us both for the merit of his priesthood and for his character—it remains, brothers, that, as I have exhorted you, you receive these salutary instructions with united accord; that you do nothing through contention, but, unanimous in every effort of devotion, obey the divine and apostolic constitutions; and that you allow the most provident decrees of the canons to be violated in nothing. [Note: [Col. 0654C] This is the reading of all the Hadrianic manuscripts and editions, and of most manuscripts of the mixed edition. Those manuscripts repeat this text twice, following the Hadrianic reading first; Merlinus does likewise, and Quesnellus cites seven other manuscripts with the same reading in note 4. The Florentine manuscript instead has “with harmonious obedience,” as do the manuscripts of the abridged edition.] [Note: [Col. 0654D] Angelica collection 21 has “institutions.” The Florentine manuscript and most manuscripts of the abridged edition have “serve”; most Hadrianic manuscripts have “obey,” and some of these subsequently omit “now.”] [Note: The adverb “nearly” has been restored not so much from the printed editions of Leo as from the Hadrianic manuscripts. Collections 21 and 24, together with Sichardus, likewise prefer it. Quesnellus wrote in a postscript: “The commonly circulated copies add *fere* (‘nearly’) contrary to the testimony of the manuscript copies.” We do not deny, however, that this particle is omitted in the manuscripts of our other collections of the abridged or mixed edition, and also in the Florentine manuscript. We explained in the admonition, no. 14, to what extent this phrase was inserted by Leo in a second revision of the complete letter, as it appears in the Hadrianic copies.]

For what we have now relaxed after careful consideration of particular circumstances must henceforth be guarded according to the ancient regulations, lest we later punish with deserved retribution what we have granted for a time in pious leniency, [Note: The Vercellian manuscript and the edition of Justellus have, apparently incorrectly, “with just petition.” Perhaps the reading is “with deserved retribution.” Moreover, the abridged edition ends with the word “punish,” and what follows has been taken from the Hadrianic collection, the Florentine manuscript, and manuscripts of the mixed edition.]

especially those who have neglected the statutes of the holy Fathers when bishops were being ordained and have consecrated men whom they ought to have rejected. [Note: Some copies have “neglected,” and shortly afterward “consecrated.”] Therefore, if any bishops have consecrated as priest a man who was not permitted to be one, even if they have in some way escaped damage to their own honor, they shall nevertheless have no further right of ordination, nor shall they ever take part in that sacrament which, after disregarding the divine judgment, they unwarrantedly conferred. [Note: Manuscript of Holy Cross collection 20 has “of the consecration.” Three other manuscripts have: “they will nevertheless have no further permission for his ordination.”] [Note: 1, question 1, and 15, question 2, “If any bishops.”]

## CHAPTER X

[Note: [Col. 0654D] Distinction 80, chapter 1, “That indeed.”]

With regard, in particular, to what pertains to priestly dignity, we wish all the statutes of the canons to be observed: bishops are not to be consecrated in just any places, nor in whatever fortified towns, nor where they have not previously existed. [Note: [Col. 0654D] Alternatively, “in just any places.”] Where the peoples are smaller and the assemblies fewer, the care of presbyters is sufficient; episcopal governance, however, ought to preside only over larger populations and more populous cities. Otherwise, what the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers have forbidden would be granted to villages and estates, or to obscure and isolated townships: the priestly dignity would be bestowed there, and the honor that ought to be entrusted to superior communities would be cheapened by sheer multiplication. [Note: [Col. 0654D] Alternatively, “had forbidden.”]

Bishop Restitutus complained that this had now been done in his diocese, and he reasonably requested that, if the bishops of those places in which they ought not to have been ordained should die by the course of nature, those places themselves should return to the jurisdiction of the same bishop to whom they had once properly belonged or been contiguous. [Note: We have corrected the text from the Florentine manuscript. Other copies have: “should be restored to the jurisdiction of the bishop whose they had previously been.” Justellus has: “should return to the jurisdiction of the bishop whose they had previously been.” Some manuscripts have *propria* (“proper”) instead of *priora* (“former”). Vatican manuscript 5845 has: “should return to the jurisdiction of the bishop; for it is useless…”] And it is useless for priestly dignity to be diminished by the thoughtless ease of the ordainer through unnecessary multiplication.

## CHAPTER XI

Concerning those women who, as stated above, had been established in the sacred vocation of virginity and had suffered barbarian violence, losing the integrity of their chastity not in mind but in body, it seems to us that the following moderation should be observed: [Note: We added “as stated above” from the Florentine manuscript, which, although it preserves the complete text of this letter, does not omit the eighth chapter, as the other Hadrianic manuscripts do; that chapter had dealt in another manner with the same virgins who had been violated by force.]

they should neither be cast down into the rank of widows nor be counted among sacred virgins who have persevered in their state; [Note: Virgins corrupted through their own fault used to be called widows before marriage. Thus Cyprian, in his book *On the Dress of Virgins*, says: “While virgins wish to adorn themselves more elaborately and to roam about more freely, they cease to be virgins, corrupted by secret disgrace—widows before marriage, adulteresses not of a husband but of Christ.” Saint Jerome likewise, in his letter to Eustochium *On the Preservation of Virginity*, says: “You may see many widows before marriage covering an unhappy conscience with merely counterfeit clothing.” This makes clear why Saint Leo orders that those virgins who were corrupted solely by barbarian violence, through no fault of their own, should not be cast down into the rank of widows. Shortly afterward, in place of the words “nor among sacred,” the Vatican manuscript 5845 and the Vercellian manuscript have the opposite sense, “but among sacred.” This is incorrect: apart from the fact that the preceding *neque* (“nor”) requires another corresponding *nec* (“nor”), not *sed* (“but”), the very moderation that the holy pontiff proposes seems to require that they be counted neither among widows nor among sacred and undefiled virgins, rather than that they be admitted among sacred virgins as though they had not been violated. If he had decided the latter, there would have been no need to add that communion should not be denied them if they persevered in their vocation. This moderation in the decree also agrees with the intention he previously expressed concerning these virgins in chapter 8, where he declares that they will be more praiseworthy if they do not dare to compare themselves with undefiled virgins.]

yet, if they persevere in virginal conduct and preserve the firmness of chastity in their minds, communion in the sacraments must not be denied them, [Note: [Col. 0655D] The printed editions of Leo have “in all virginal observances”; Justellus and most manuscripts have only “in all virginal matters.” The correct reading is supplied by the Florentine and Fiesolan manuscripts.] [Note: The word “sacraments” is absent from the Florentine manuscript. Leo most wisely decreed that communion should not be denied to virgins violated without any fault of their own because a long penance was imposed upon virgins corrupted through their own fault, by which they were kept from communion for a longer time, as is clear from Cyprian’s Letter 66 to Pomponius, from Letter 10 of Siricius in the edition of Coustant, no. 4, and from Letter 15 and 16 of Innocent I to Victricius. Shortly afterward, Justellus has “has lost” instead of “lost.” Some copies have “them” instead of “those women.”]

because it is unjust that they should be blamed or reproached for what their will did not lose, but hostile force seized from them.

## CHAPTER XII

We likewise order that the case of Bishop Lupicinus be heard there. We restored communion to him when he had repeatedly and earnestly requested it, for this reason: when he had appealed to our judgment, we saw that he had been unjustly suspended from communion while the matter was pending. [Note: Two manuscripts and Justellus have “we are restored.” Shortly afterward, the Florentine manuscript has “had often summoned,” instead of “had appealed.”]

It has also been added that the man who is known to have been rashly placed over him ought not to have been ordained before Lupicinus, while still present, had either been refuted or at least confessed and could therefore be subjected to a just sentence; thus the man who was being consecrated could receive the vacant place, as ecclesiastical discipline requires. [Note: The Vatican manuscript 5845 and the Vercellian manuscript have “confounded.”] [Note: This reading is found in six manuscripts and in Justellus. The printed editions have “should take over.”]

## CHAPTER XIII

If any other cases should arise that concern the condition of the Church and the harmony of the priests, we wish them to be examined there under the fear of the Lord, and a full report concerning all matters both settled and to be settled to be sent to us, so that whatever has been determined justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical custom may also be confirmed by our judgment. [Note: The Florentine manuscript lacks “we wish.” Justellus has “we wish them to be examined by judgment.”]

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of August. [Note: Most manuscripts, including the older ones, and the printed editions have this reading. Four other copies have “Given on the third day before the Ides.”]

## THE SAME LETTER

[Note: Which manuscripts belong to the abridged edition was stated in the admonition, no. 2. In the Hispanic and Isidorian copies the following titles are prefixed, from which the commonly circulated titles derive: I. That unlawful persons should not be promoted to the episcopate. II. Concerning Donatus, bishop of the Novatians, and Maximus from the Donatists. III. Concerning Aggarus and Tyberianus, who were ordained from the laity. IV. Concerning sacred virgins who suffered barbarian violence. V. Concerning the preservation of the statutes of the canons. In the table of Quesnellus’s collection 5 this title is recorded as no. 84: “To the bishops of Mauritania concerning unlawful ordinations and the women who lost their virginity through barbarian violence.”]

From the manuscripts of the abridged edition.

[Note: This heading is taken from the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and is also found in collection 24. The older collections of the abridged edition omit the heading and have only: “Letter of Pope Leo to the bishops of Mauritania”; these words indicate that the heading mentioned the province of Mauritania. Quesnellus retained the commonly circulated heading, which we have found nowhere: “Leo, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauritania in Africa.”]

Leo sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Africa.

## CHAPTER I

Since repeated report was saying that certain things had been unlawfully usurped among you in the ordinations of priests, the consideration of piety required that, out of the concern which by divine institution we owe to the universal Church, we should strive to learn the truth of these matters. Therefore, as a substitute for our own care, we delegated to our brother and fellow priest Potentius the task of investigating what the truth was concerning the bishops whose election was reported to be blameworthy and of reporting everything faithfully to us. [Note: Quesnellus, in his first edition, following the commonly circulated reading, had written “concerning ordinations,” as it is read not only in the manuscripts and printed copies of the Hadrianic collection but also in certain manuscripts of the abridged edition. In his second edition he corrected it to “in the ordinations,” perhaps because he found this reading in Barberinian manuscripts 77 and 2888, whose variants he had received after his first edition. In most, and the better, manuscripts of the abridged edition the same reading is found.] [Note: The manuscripts of collections 3 and 5, Vindobonensis, Hispanicus, collection 24, Barberinian 77, and Fesulanus, together with Merlinus and Sichardus, have this reading. The Vatican manuscript has “more widely known report had told us”; the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, “more widely known report among us had told us”; the Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, “more frequent report had brought word to us”; the Lucensian manuscript of collection 4, “more frequent report had reached us.” All are manuscripts of the abridged edition. Quesnellus, together with the commonly circulated copies, presented the Hadrianic reading: “a more frequent report of those coming to us had conveyed.”] [Note: The words “sent by us,” which are read in the Hadrianic edition and were retained by Quesnellus with the printed copies and inserted here, have been removed from this abridged edition on the authority of the most distinguished manuscripts of this edition: the Vatican, the Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, the Lucensian manuscript of collection 4, the Vindobonensian manuscript of collection 5, the Hispanic Vindobonensian, Barberinian 77, and one Fesulanus.] [Note: The printed copies before Quesnellus have “charging him,” together with the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, Barberinian 77, the manuscripts of collection 24, Merlinus, and Sichardus; and in the margin: “Alternatively, delegating.” Quesnellus preferred this reading from four manuscripts of Dionysius, which nevertheless represent not this abridged edition but the Hadrianic edition. In his second edition he added Barberinian manuscript of collection 3; we join to it the manuscripts of collections 1, 4, and 5, whose reading, belonging to the older collections, seemed preferable. Shortly afterward, Quesnellus has: “who, according to the letters which we sent through him to you, concerning the bishops, etc.” Those words belong to the Hadrianic edition and to inferior manuscripts of the abridged edition. We have preferred the older collections and manuscripts: Vatican Reginensis collection 1, Barberinian collection 3, Lucensian collection 4, Vindobonensian collection 5, another Vindobonensian collection 9, Hispanic, Barberinian 77, and one Fesulanus.]

Since he fully disclosed everything and, in a sincere report, made clear to us under what and what sort of rulers certain congregations of Christ in the territory of the province of Caesarea were being held, it was necessary for us, [Note: [Col. 0657D] Quesnellus inserted, with certain of our manuscripts, “to our knowledge”; we have deleted it on the authority of the manuscripts named at the end of the preceding note, except the Fiesolan manuscript.] by sending a letter, to give expression to the grief of our heart, in which we burn with concern for the dangers threatening the Lord’s flocks. [Note: Quesnellus adopted the Hadrianic reading, which appeared in the commonly circulated copies: “Now also, by letters sent to your affection.” We followed the manuscripts of the abridged edition—collections 1, 3, 4, and 5, Vindobonensis, and Hispanicus—together with Merlinus and Sichardus. The Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts have: “Now, by a letter sent to you.” Since the words “according to the letters which we sent through him to you,” discussed in note 6 above, have been removed, the words “now also to your affection,” which presuppose a mention of earlier letters, likewise had to be removed here. When Leo revised this letter a second time, he inserted the initial words and added these as well.]

We marvel that, under the pretext of unsettled times, either the presumption of ambitious men or popular tumult has had such power among you that the pastoral dignity and governance of the Church have been entrusted to persons who are unworthy and far removed from priestly merit. [Note: [Col. 0658C] The Lucensian, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, and Barberinian 77, together with Sichardus and Merlinus, have “was entrusted.”] [Note: 61, “We marvel greatly,” chapter 5.] This is not to provide for the peoples but to harm them; it is not to furnish governance but to increase danger. For the integrity of those who preside is the safety of those subject to them; and where obedience is secure, there the form of doctrine is sound. [Note: 1, question 1, “The principate,” chapter 25.]

But a principate which sedition has extorted or ambition has seized, even if it does not offend in morals and actions, is nevertheless harmful because of the example of its very beginning; and it is difficult for things begun with an evil beginning to be brought to a good end. [Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and printed copies of the abridged edition. Quesnellus, together with other commonly circulated copies and the Hadrianic reading, has “conferred.”]

## CHAPTER II

And if, in every rank of the Church, care must prudently and wisely be taken that nothing disorderly or improper exist in the house of the Lord, how much more must effort be expended to avoid error in the election of him who is placed above all the ranks? For the condition and order of the entire household will totter [Note: [Col. 0658C] Quesnellus inserted “of the Lord” here, or rather retained it with the commonly circulated copies; it has been deleted on the authority of the manuscripts of collections 3, 4, and 5, the Vindobonensian and Hispanic manuscripts, and Barberinian 77 of the abridged edition. Some manuscripts of the mixed edition read “the condition will go astray,” omitting “and order.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts have “is not found” for “is not found.”] if what is required in the body is not found in the head. Where is that command of the blessed Apostle Paul, uttered through the Spirit of God, by which, in the person of Timothy, the whole number of Christ’s priests is instructed, and therefore each of us is told: “Do not lay hands hastily on anyone, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Timothy 5:22)? [Note: 78, “What does ‘hands’ mean?” chapter 3.]

What does it mean to lay hands hastily, except to confer priestly honor upon those not yet tested—before the age of maturity, before the time of examination, before the merit of labor, before experience in discipline? [Note: The Vatican Reginensis manuscript, collection 1, the Vindobonensian manuscript of collection 5, another Vindobonensian, the Hispanic manuscript, and Barberinian 77, together with the Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark, have: “What does it mean to lay hands hastily on anyone?”]

And what does it mean to share in the sins of others, except to become the sort of ordainer that the man is who did not deserve to be ordained? For just as the man who preserves sound judgment in choosing a priest acquires for himself the fruit of a good work, so he inflicts serious harm upon himself who elevates an unworthy man into the company of his own dignity. [Note: The same manuscripts have this reading. The manuscripts of collection 24, together with Sichardus, have “pursues.” Quesnellus retained “holds.”]

For what is contained in the general regulations must not be set aside in anyone’s case; nor is that honor to be considered legitimate which has been conferred in violation of the commands of divine law. [Note: We restored the reading of the copies circulated before Quesnellus, found in all manuscripts of the abridged edition except the two Vatican manuscripts, Hispanic and Isidorian, which present the Hadrianic reading: “conferred contrary to the commands of divine law.” The Hispanic Vindobonensian, which derives from the pure sources of the Hispanic collection, has, like the other manuscripts of the abridged edition, “conferred through transgression.” It is strange that Quesnellus abandoned this reading, although in note 2 he admitted that it appears in two Trecopithian and Thuanean manuscripts of collection 5, in order to introduce the reading of the Hadrianic edition from Dionysius—that is, from the Hadrianic collection—and from five other manuscripts mentioned in the same note. Two of these he calls Dionysian, or more accurately Hadrianic, in note 1; the other three are recognized from his description as manuscripts of the mixed edition. Shortly afterward, at the beginning of chapter 3, the Hispanic Vindobonensian manuscript omits “otherwise.” The Vindobonensian manuscript of collection 5 has “it has been established,” as do the always sacred texts.]

## CHAPTER III

For the Apostle says that, among the other rules of election, a bishop is to be ordained who has been or is the husband of one wife (1 Timothy 3:2). This command has always been held so sacred that the same condition was understood to be observed even with regard to the wife of the man chosen as priest: she must not previously have experienced the marriage of another man before marrying him who had had no other wife.

Who, then, would dare to overlook the insult inflicted upon so great a sacrament, when even the statutes of the Law have not been lacking with respect to this great and venerable mystery? They clearly define that a priest is to take a virgin and know no other husband’s bed, she who is to become the wife of the pontiff (Leviticus 21:13–14; Ezekiel 44:22). [Note: The manuscripts of all the older collections of the abridged edition—1, 3, 4, and 5—and the Hispanic Vindobonensian, together with Sichardus, have this reading. Quesnellus, together with the commonly circulated copies and following the Hadrianic reading, has: “so that not even the statutes of divine law…”] [Note: The Vindobonensian manuscript of collection 5 and Barberinian 77 add “wife,” a word likewise inserted by Quesnellus in his second edition from manuscripts, as we believe, of collection 5 and from Hadrianic copies. We have removed it because it is omitted in the other collections of the abridged edition and by Merlinus and Sichardus. Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 and Barberinian 77 have *conjugii* (“of marriage”) instead of *conjugis* (“of a spouse”).]

Even then, the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church was prefigured in priests; [Note: The particle *et* (“and”) instead of *ut* (“so that”) is found in the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts. The word “Word,” instead of “Christ,” which Quesnellus had inserted from the margin of the printed copies, has been restored from the manuscripts, especially those of the abridged edition, which we listed in note 19 (column 648, note o) on this complete letter.] so that, because the husband is the head of the wife (Ephesians 5:23; 1 Corinthians 11:3), the bride of the Word might learn to know no other husband than Christ, who rightly chose one and loves one, and does not join another to himself in companionship apart from her. [Note: The Hispanic Vindobonensian manuscript has “than the bridegroom”; for he who chose one. Shortly afterward, “he did not join” is absent from the Barberinian manuscript of collection 3 and from two manuscripts of the mixed edition.]

If, then, this form of priestly marriage was observed even in the Old Testament, how much more ought we, established now under revealed grace, to obey the apostolic commands: no matter how exemplary in morals a man may be found, and no matter how adorned with holy works, he must in no way ascend either to the rank of deacon, the honor of presbyter, or the height of the episcopate if it is established either that he himself has not been the husband of one wife or that his wife has not been the wife of one man?

## CHAPTER IV
True, the Apostle admonishing and saying: “Let these also first be tested, and then let them serve” (1 Tim. 3:10)—what else, we think, is to be understood by this than that in these promotions we should consider not only the privileges of marriages but also the merits of labors? [Note: Compare note 22 (col. 649, n. b) on this entire epistle.] [Note: Quesnellus reads *castimoniam* (“chastity”), as in the Hadrianic edition. In the margin he noted that two codices have *privilegia*. This indeed is read in our manuscripts of the abridged edition, except Vatican Spanish and Isidorian, which sometimes adopted Hadrianic readings; for the pure and genuine Spanish Vindobonensis has *privilegia*, as does Sichardus.] [Note: In place of *vero* (“truly,” “but”) the manuscript Vat. Reg. collection 1 has *ergo* (“therefore”).] Thus we should not entrust pastoral office either to those inexperienced from baptism or to those suddenly converted from secular life, when it ought to be assessed, through all the stages of Christian service, by the growth of their progress whether greater responsibilities can be entrusted to anyone. [Note: Thus read the manuscripts of collections 1, 3, and 5, the Spanish Vindobonensis, and Barberinus 77. The printed editions, with the manuscripts of collection 4 and Vatican Spanish and Isidorian, as well as collections 12 and 24, read *credatur* (“should be entrusted”). Shortly afterward the printed editions read *cum omnis gradus erat* (“when every rank was”). We corrected from all codices of the abridged edition, from which only the manuscripts of collections 1 and 3 differ.] [Note: See Distinction 61, “Miramur,” chapter 5, section “Merito.”]

The venerable decrees of the holy Fathers therefore rightly judged that only those were qualified for sacred administration whose whole life, from childhood onward into more advanced years, had run its course through the disciplines of ecclesiastical service, so that their former life might provide testimony for each one; nor could there be doubt about the promotion of one to whom, for many labors, chaste conduct, and energetic deeds, the reward of a higher position was owed. [Note: The manuscript Vat. Reg. collection 1 reads “for the sacred ranks.”]

For if it is disgraceful to attain worldly honors without the support of time and without the merit of labor, and those whom evidence of uprightness does not assist are commonly marked as ambitious, how careful and prudent must be the administration of divine gifts and heavenly dignities, [Note: See Distinction 61, “Statuimus ne in aliquo,” chapter 8.] lest the apostolic and canonical decrees be violated in any respect, [Note: The Codex Vat. Reg. reads “and to them.” Shortly afterward, the manuscript from Fiesole has *exordium* (“beginning”) instead of *incrementum* (“advancement”).] and the Church of God be entrusted to those who are ignorant of legitimate institutions and unaware of all humility—those who do not wish to advance from the lowest ranks but desire to have their beginning at the highest—when it is exceedingly unjust and absurd that the inexperienced should be preferred to teachers, the new to the old, and the untrained to those who have completed their service?

In a great house, as the Apostle explains (2 Tim. 2:20), there must be different vessels: some golden and silver, others wooden and earthen. But their service is apportioned according to the quality of the material, and the vessel that belongs to the precious class does not have the same use as one of the inferior class. [Note: Quesnellus, along with the printed editions, reads *discernitur* (“is distinguished”), as found in the manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection and in our Vatican Regina manuscript, as well as in another Vatican manuscript of collection 24 of the abridged edition. We have preferred the reading of all the other collections of this abridged edition; it is also supported by a Florentine manuscript of the complete edition. Shortly afterward, *idem usus est vilium* (“has the same use as the inferior”) occurs with *et* omitted in manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 and in the Spanish Vindobonensis, as well as in Merlinus and Sichardus.] Everything will be disorderly if earthen vessels are preferred to golden ones, and wooden vessels to silver ones.

Just as the kinds of people who as yet possess no virtues are represented by the wooden and earthen vessels, so without doubt those are represented by the golden and silver vessels who, refined through the fire of prolonged learning and purified in the furnace of enduring labor, have deserved to be genuine gold and pure silver. [Note: The Codex Lucensis, two Vindobonenses, and Barberinus 77 delete “wooden and.” Shortly afterward, *per longum eruditionis ignem* (“through the fire of prolonged learning”) is found in the Spanish Vindobonensis and Vatican collection 24, together with Sichardus.] If a reward is not given to these according to their devotion, all obedience is dissolved and all order is thrown into confusion, while in the Church those who have undertaken no ministry at all obtain, through the perverse judgment of their electors, an authority to which they are not entitled. [Note: Thus read the better manuscripts of the abridged edition, namely collections 1, 4, and 5, the Spanish Vindobonensis, Barberinus 77, and one Fiesolanus. Otherwise: “all ecclesiastical discipline is undone,” as in the Hadrianic edition. Shortly afterward, two Barberini manuscripts and Vindobonensis collection 5 read *subierint* (“have undertaken”) instead of *subire* (“to undertake”).]

## CHAPTER V

Since popular favor or the ambition of the proud has had such power among you that we know not only laymen but also husbands of second wives and husbands of widows to have been promoted to pastoral office, do not the circumstances most clearly demand [Note: 1, Question 7, “Exigunt,” chapter 17.] that we cleanse, by a stricter judgment, the Churches in which such things have been committed, and that we be moved by a punishment worthy not only of such bishops but also of those who ordained them? [Note: Quesnellus, with the common texts, reads *ultio competens proferatur* (“a fitting punishment be imposed”). But the more excellent manuscripts of the abridged edition cited in the preceding note supplied the reading inserted in the text. Four other codices of the mixed edition agree with them. The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts have *digna districtio moveatur* (“a worthy severity be applied”); two others have *digna districtione moveantur* (“that they be moved by worthy severity”). Shortly afterward, Vatican Reg. collection 1 and Vindobonensis collection 5 read *circumstat*; then Barberinus 77 reads *inde censura* (“then judgment”).] [Note: We have inserted the reading of the manuscripts of collections 1, 3, 4, and 5, the Spanish Vindobonensis, and Barberinus 77. Quesnellus retained the common reading, “that the Churches . . . be purified,” which is supported only by the inferior manuscripts of the abridged edition.]

But on one side the gentleness of mercy surrounds us, and on the other the strictness of justice; and because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 24:10), we are compelled, in accordance with the piety of the apostolic see, to temper our judgment in such a way that, after weighing the measure of the offenses—which plainly are not all of one kind—we may define some as tolerable to some extent, but cut others off entirely.

For we do not permit those who have entered into a second marriage or joined themselves in marriage to widows to remain in the priesthood; [Note: Thus read all the manuscripts of the abridged edition except the manuscripts of collection 24. The manuscript of Santa Croce from the mixed edition agrees. The Vatican manuscript 3791 of mixed collection 11 reads: “we do not permit him to remain in the dignity of the priestly office.” Quesnellus followed the Hadrianic reading of the printed editions.] and even more, we decree that the man who is simultaneously the husband of two wives, or the man who, having been dismissed by his first wife, is reported to have married another, must be deprived of his honor. [Note: This reading is preferred by five manuscripts of the older collections—1, 3, 4, and 5, the Spanish Vindobonensis—and by Barberinus 77. Quesnellus reads: “if, in your judgment, he has been convicted—the man who, as has been reported to us, is simultaneously the husband of two wives, or the man who is said to have married another after being dismissed by his wife—we decree that he be deprived of his honor”; and in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘the man who, after dismissing his first wife . . .’; the common text, ‘who was dismissed by his first wife.’” See notes 36 and 37 (cols. 651 k, 652 l) in the complete epistle.]

But we permit the others, whose promotion incurred only this reproach—that they were chosen from among the laity for episcopal office—to retain the priesthood they have undertaken, since they cannot be guilty merely because they have wives. [Note: The Spanish Vindobonensis and Barberinus 77 read “chosen”; Vatican 3791 reads “promoted.” Shortly afterward, two Vindobonenses have *habeant* (“may have”) instead of *habet* (“has”).] In doing so we do not prejudice the statutes of the apostolic see, nor the decrees of our predecessors or of ourselves, by which it was salutarily established [Note: Two Vindobonenses read “it has been established.” Shortly afterward, *aut tertium* (“or the third”) is absent from Vindobonensis collection 5.] that no layman, however strongly supported by influence, should ascend in the Church to the first, second, or third rank before reaching the requisite merit through legitimate advancement.

For what is now, to some extent, pardonable cannot afterward remain unpunished if anyone dares to usurp what we absolutely forbid, since remission of sin does not grant permission to sin; nor shall we permit with impunity any longer what could in some way be conceded. [Note: Thus read the same manuscripts of the abridged edition, except Barberinus 77, which has: “we shall suffer it to be committed with impunity any longer.” Quesnellus has: “it will not be permissible for it to be committed with impunity any longer,” as in the earlier edition.]

## CHAPTER VI

As for Donatus of Salicina, who, as we have learned, was converted from the Novatians together with his people, we wish him to preside over the Lord’s flock in such a way that he remember to send us a statement of his faith, by which he may condemn the error of Novatian doctrine and confess the Catholic truth in its fullness. [Note: 1, Question 7, “Donatum,” chapter 20. Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘of Sajacina, from the Novatian.’” See note 41 (col. 653 n. b) in this same epistle in the complete edition.]

Likewise, although Maximus was reprehensibly ordained from the laity, nevertheless, if he is no longer a Donatist and is alien to the spirit of schismatic depravity, we do not remove him from the episcopal dignity which he acquired by whatever means; provided that he too make himself known to us by a statement that he is a Catholic. [Note: 1, Question 7, “Maximum,” chapter 19.]

## CHAPTER VII

But concerning Aggarus and Tiberianus, whose case differs from that of the others who were ordained from the laity in this respect: fierce disturbances and savage seditions are said to have accompanied their ordination. We have entrusted everything to your judgment, so that, once we have learned the outcome of the inquiry conducted among you, we may know what ought to be decided concerning the men mentioned above. [Note: The common editions omit *vero* (“but”), which we have added from our better manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER VIII

Those servants of God who lost the integrity of their chastity through barbarous violence will be more praiseworthy in their humility and modesty if they do not dare to compare themselves with undefiled virgins. [Note: See note 44 (col. 653 n. f) in the complete edition of the epistle.] Although every sin arises from the will, and an unconquered mind could, through correction of the flesh, have remained unpolluted, [Note: See note 45 (col. 653 n. h) in this same epistle in the complete edition.] it will nevertheless harm them less if they grieve that what they were able not to lose in spirit they have nevertheless lost in body.

## CHAPTER IX

Since, therefore, you have been fully informed concerning everything contained in the report of our brother Potentius, [Note: Quesnellus retained the common reading, which, taken from the Hadrianic edition, adds the words: “through David, our brother and fellow bishop, who has been approved by us both for the merit of his priesthood and for his conduct.” These words are omitted from all manuscripts of the abridged edition—collections 1, 3, 4, and 5, the Spanish collection, the Isidorian collection, Vatican 1340 collection 12, and Barberinus 77. They occur only in the manuscripts of collection 24 and in Merlinus and Sichardus. Some manuscripts of the mixed edition, which repeat this sentence twice, display the words at the first occurrence, taken from the Hadrianic edition, but omit them at the second occurrence, taken from the manuscripts of the abridged edition. Thus the manuscript of Santa Croce, collection 20, and the manuscripts of collection 21.] it remains, brothers, [Note: Thus read all the manuscripts of the abridged edition, including collection 24, as well as Sichardus and the previously cited manuscripts of the mixed edition in their second occurrence. Quesnellus introduced the Hadrianic reading *ut concorditer* (“that you harmoniously”). Compare note 48 (col. 65, n. k) on the complete epistle. Next, five manuscripts of the abridged edition read *per concertationem* (“through rivalry”) in place of *per contentionem* (“through contention”).] that you receive our exhortation with harmonious obedience, serve the divine and apostolic constitutions with one mind in every effort of devotion, doing nothing through contention, and suffer the pious decrees of the canons to be violated in nothing. [Note: Quesnellus, with the Hadrianic reading, has *providentissima* (“most prudent”). We restore *pia* (“pious”) from the cited codices and editions of the abridged form.] [Note: Thus read almost all the manuscripts, and the best of the abridged form. Quesnellus, with others, has “obey.”] For what we have now relaxed after careful consideration of particular cases must henceforth be guarded according to the ancient rules, lest what we have conceded for a time in pious leniency we later punish with deserved retribution. [Note: This reading of the best manuscripts seemed preferable to that of the others, which, together with the printed editions, have “after these things.”]

---

*Written 6 January 446.* [Note: Epistle 13.]  

# EPISTLE XIII

## TO THE METROPOLITAN BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT THE PROVINCES OF ILLYRICUM

[Note: It was published in Luca Holstenius’s Roman collection from a single Barberini manuscript, no. 3386, of Thessalonian collection 16, with which we have usefully reread it.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He congratulates the metropolitans of Illyricum on submitting to the authority entrusted to Anastasius, especially in the more important cases.

II. He exhorts them not to refuse to come when summoned to a council by Anastasius.

III. No one is to be ordained bishop without the consent of the people.

IV. No bishop is to claim another bishop’s cleric against his will.

To our most beloved brothers Senecio, Carosus, Theodulus, Luke, Antiochus, and Vigilantius, metropolitans established throughout the provinces of Illyricum, Leo.

[Note: The printed editions, including the Barberini manuscript itself, read “through the province of Achaia,” but this is entirely erroneous. Achaia, which was a single province, could not have contained several metropolitans named in the same inscription; nor is the metropolitan of Achaia included among the names of the metropolitans to whom these letters are addressed, although the third chapter speaks against him. We have therefore corrected the text with complete confidence and necessity. For an epistle was also sent to the metropolitans established throughout Illyricum—Epistle 5, cited in chapter 1—and Holstenius correctly identified the provinces of the three metropolitans to whom this epistle is addressed; all belong to Illyricum. See Quesnellus’s note. Holstenius also suspects that *Antiochus* should be read *Atticus*, who was metropolitan of Nicopolis in Old Epirus. We do not agree. For, as the following epistle will show, the metropolitan of Nicopolis submitted under compulsion to the authority transferred to the vicar of Thessalonica, not voluntarily, as did those to whom this epistle was sent.]

## CHAPTER I

The language of the letter returning to us has testified, with grateful acknowledgment, that you received our letters with affection. [Note: These are thought to be Epistles 5 and 6, which we gave above. But if the words “the letters sent by us and received by your affection” indicate that several letters were delivered to the bishops of Illyricum—as is not true of Epistle 6, which was addressed only to Anastasius—then at least one other lost epistle to the same bishops must be supposed to have been written after Epistle 5. It is especially unlikely that they delayed replying for nearly two years to Leo’s earlier epistle, which had demanded a prompt response, until the pontiff returned these letters as his reply. In fact, when Leo sent the fifth epistle to the Illyrians, he sent the sixth epistle to Anastasius. That Anastasius had replied to Leo before this time, and that several other letters had been sent and received back and forth, will become clear from note 1 (col. 666 m) on the following epistle. It is therefore most probable that the Illyrians too replied to the fifth epistle sooner, with the same concern as Anastasius; and that they subsequently received several other letters from Leo, to which the plural expression here refers. The plural alone, however, would not compel this conclusion. For Leo uses the plural in Epistle 102, chapter 1, referring to the single letter of the Gauls, Epistle 99: “We have gratefully received the long-awaited letters.” Similarly, in Epistle 107, concerning Julian’s single letter, he says: “In reply, then, to your letters”; and in Epistle 117, chapter 1, concerning his single letter to Anatolius: “I have sent letters to the bishop of Constantinople.” Shortly afterward the Barberini manuscript has “from your affection”; and a little later “in their provinces,” or rather “in your province”; and in chapter 2, “let your affection know”—expressions suggesting that this epistle was given to an equal. But the plural formula in chapter 4 sufficiently justified Holstenius’s correction in these three witnesses, unless one should instead think that the words of chapter 4 ought to be corrected and expressed in the singular. We note, however, that in Epistle 150, which was given to several metropolitans by an equal, the manuscript of the Grimani collection sometimes has the singular *tua* (“your”) and sometimes the plural *vestra* (“your”).]

We sent them because, concerned for the condition and peace of the Churches, we wished nothing novel to introduce error. We are known to have desired that the things which the authority of the apostolic see has repeatedly established should be guarded by the priests of the Lord; namely, that the Churches established throughout Illyricum should belong to the care of our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius, bishop of the city of Thessalonica. [Note: This refers to the earlier pontiffs and to Leo’s letters concerning the apostolic vicariate of the bishop of Thessalonica.]

Thus, if there are more important cases among the bishops which cannot be settled in their own provinces, they are to be referred to his knowledge and resolved by the same judgment under the fear of divine judgment. [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 1 and our own observation.] Let this order, beneficial to priestly concord, be preserved, so that the Churches of the Lord may be built, as we desire, through harmonious counsel, and that dissension—which, if the devil lies in wait, can always find an entrance—may have no opportunity to scatter what we desire to bind together with great care in a spirit of moderation.

## CHAPTER II

When brothers are invited to settle the greatest cases, cases that cannot be concluded within their own provinces, they should not, unless they are detained by some grave necessity, refuse their fraternal cooperation for the benefit of the Church. [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 2. Shortly afterward, we have judged that *finiri* (“to be concluded”) should be corrected to *finire* (“to conclude”).] This is especially so since our moderation has provided that the need to assemble should not arise frequently or for trivial causes; [Note: Quesnellus’s marginal note indicates that the following epistle to Anastasius, chapter 10, is meant here, as though it had been written earlier; yet we shall show that it was composed later. Other letters of Leo to the same Anastasius are therefore indicated, written before the following epistle and now lost; see note 1 below on the following epistle. Nor is it strange if the same matter is discussed in the following epistle, chapter 10. Leo often repeated similar statements in several letters.] and that it is sufficient for two or three bishops from each province to be present, so that what would be burdensome to many may be light for a few. In this way, through the diligence of charity, the priestly assembly may establish, with the Holy Spirit revealing it, whatever may pertain to ecclesiastical discipline.

Your affection should know that we have determined to correct the disobedience of certain persons with appropriate coercion: whoever, with a proud spirit, when detained by no bodily necessity or necessity of the case, repeatedly wishes to avoid the fraternal assembly should know that he is to be judged. [Note: The manuscript has “and . . . us or bishops.” Holstenius supplied the missing words, as we think with sufficient safety, since in the following epistle, chapter 10, the holy pontiff orders two bishops from each province to travel to Thessalonica. That number, established later, does not prevent Leo, when he wrote this epistle, from having written more broadly “two or three.” In the missing letter to Anastasius, as we indicated in the preceding note, he may likewise have used this broader formula.]

## CHAPTER III

Since we have learned from the careful report of our aforementioned brother that the metropolitan of the province of Achaia has often performed illicit ordinations, forbidden by the established authorities of the Fathers and by our own, and has added this to his acts of presumption: that, against the will and opposition of the people of Thespiae, he consecrated an unknown bishop, one never seen there before, [Note: Holstenius changed the manuscript reading without compulsion to: “we absolutely do not permit that metropolitan to do this.” By the abuse of the metropolitan of Achaia, the holy pontiff is evidently setting forth not a special command for that man but a general law established for all and to be violated by none; the general decree proposed in the following epistle, chapter 5, agrees with this.] we absolutely permit no metropolitan to ordain anyone as a priest according to his own judgment alone, without the consent of the clergy and the people. Rather, he must place over the Church of God the man whom the consensus of the whole city has chosen.

Just as we are not negligent in warning what must be guarded and what must be avoided, so we do not permit anyone to be negligent in carrying out and observing those things. For praise of the highest kind accompanies one who observes such matters, and, as we hope, a richer reward from the Lord will follow. [Note: The manuscript and Holstenius read this way. Quesnellus’s edition has *talis* (“such”) through a typographical error.] But the man who strays and forgets the apostolic constitution will be subject to both ecclesiastical and divine judgment. [Note: *Subsequatur* (“will follow”) seems to require correction; we do not find *obsequor* used with the meaning “to follow” among reliable writers.]

## CHAPTER IV

We also wish all to preserve, with equal observance, this bond of priestly concord: no bishop should dare to claim for himself another bishop’s cleric without the cession of the bishop to whom the cleric belongs; and even that cession must be contained in an explicit written document. [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 3.] For this has been defined by the authority of the canons, and the very principle of preserving unity teaches it, lest the entire ecclesiastical order become unstable through such license.

Therefore, dearest brothers, let what you see decreed by us with pious affection descend more deeply into your hearts. We earnestly desire to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, so that we may receive the fruit of our command and rejoice in the works of your affection. For we wish that what is established through the grace of charity may belong as much to you as to us, and that no trick of the plotting devil may violate it. [Note: The manuscript reads this way; Quesnellus, with Holstenius, has “of pious affection.”]

You ought to observe more fully the things which we wrote to our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius as matters to be avoided. We wish that they reach your knowledge through his letters, and we do not wish your fraternity to depart from them, so that, by guarding the sanction of the Fathers, we may preserve the Lord’s charity. [Note: Quesnellus’s note 1 on the following epistle understands this passage as referring to that same epistle. But in the letters discussed here, St. Leo ordered Anastasius to communicate to the Illyrians by letter what he had decreed; that part of the command is not found anywhere in the following epistle. Likewise, in Epistle 6, when Leo gave Anastasius other instructions and ordered him to make them known to all the brothers, he expressly commanded this in chapter 6. Thus this passage designates another letter to Anastasius, now lost.]

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius for the third time and Symmachus.

---

# EPISTLE XIV

[Note: Alternatively, 12. What was formerly Epistle 14 is now Epistle 18. It was written after the preceding epistle.] [Note: Quesnellus’s note 1 argues that this epistle, which lacks chronological information in all the manuscripts, was written before the preceding epistle, in 445, and should be placed before it. He based this on a certain similarity of statements in the two epistles and thought that this was the epistle referred to in the final chapter of the preceding one, in the words: “You ought to observe more fully the things which we wrote to our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius as matters to be avoided.” Since, however, Leo regularly repeated similar statements and decrees in different letters—and something quite similar occurs in Epistle 6—this similarity proves nothing. We have stronger reasons for considering this epistle distinct and later. In chapter 1 of the preceding epistle, St. Leo not only says that he wrote to Anastasius what was to be avoided, but adds: “We wish that they reach your knowledge through his letters.” We observed in note 16 (col. 666 k) on the preceding epistle that this part of the command is not found in the present letter. Moreover, in chapter 10 of this letter, while limiting Anastasius’s authority to summon bishops to a synod, he establishes that two bishops from each province are sufficient and that they are to be chosen by the metropolitans and delayed no longer than fifteen days. If Leo had intended in the preceding letter to inform the Illyrians of the moderation imposed on the bishop of Thessalonica, he would not have omitted any of these matters; nor would he have indicated vaguely that two or three bishops were sufficient if he had already established that two alone were enough. Add that chapter 3 of the letter to the Illyrians reports that Anastasius had sent a report concerning the bishop of Corinth, metropolitan of Achaia. St. Leo would have replied to Anastasius about this matter in the present letter if it had been written either on the same day as, or shortly before, the letter to the Illyrians. Furthermore, chapter 1 indicates that Leo had sent or received several letters from Anastasius: “For you have an abundance of writings containing our admonitions, by which we have often instructed you concerning the moderation of all actions.” Other letters written before this one therefore seem to have anticipated the matters indicated in the earlier letter to the Illyrians, so that this epistle should be regarded not as earlier but as later—that is, as written after 6 January 446. The event involving Atticus, metropolitan of Epirus, who was brought to Thessalonica under Anastasius’s direction and whose treatment occasioned this letter, occurred in winter, as chapter 1 shows. It could be questioned whether this refers to the winter at the end of 445 or the beginning of 446, or instead to the following winter. But the concern shown by Anastasius makes it difficult to postpone the event until the latter winter: he does not appear to have tolerated a long delay in calling the metropolitans of Illyricum to their duty, even though Atticus alleged only the impediment of illness as a reason not to come to Thessalonica. See what we have added on this matter in the dissertation on the lost epistles, no. 14. If Atticus’s journey is assigned to the winter at the end of 445 or the beginning of 446, allowing time for his journey to Rome, where he complained of violence committed against him, and for the journey of the deacon Anastasius, who was sent with his letters, then this epistle must be said to have been written in 446, somewhat after January. This epistle is found in the manuscripts of collections 2, 3, and 5 through 13, and in collections 20 through 24. It is also found in Vatican Regina 849, and, with chapters 3 and 4 omitted by a leap, in Vatican 1347 and Palatine 579. In the table of titles prefixed to collection 5 in the Thuaneus manuscript, the following appears as no. 72: “To Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, a rebuke of the excessive arrogance of the vicariate of the apostolic see, with six decrees appended.” The six decrees or chapters that follow the long preface of the epistle are indicated. The first chapter begins with chapter 3 of our edition; the second with the words in chapter 6, “When the metropolitan has died”; the third with chapter 7; the fourth with chapter 8; the fifth with chapter 9; and the sixth with chapter 10 and continues to the end of the epistle. We have restored the synopsis prefixed from Dionysius to the pure Dionysian Vatican manuscript 5845.]

## TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA

[Col. 0666C]

## SYNOPSIS

*(From Dionysius Exiguus)*

I. That the bishops of Thessalonica have always fulfilled the functions of the apostolic see.

II. That the metropolitans’ rights are to be preserved.

III. That bishops are to be ordained by the metropolitans only if they are neither laymen, nor bigamists, nor husbands of widows, but irreproachable.

IV. That carnal marriage is to be denied to subdeacons.

V. That no bishop is to be ordained against the will of the people.

VI. That the metropolitan of Epirus is to refer to the bishop of Thessalonica the elected man whom he is about to ordain bishop; and that the provincial bishops are likewise to act concerning an elected metropolitan. [Note: The editions before Quesnellus omit “of Epirus.” The text itself states a general law concerning all the metropolitans of Illyricum. But Dionysius, from whom the titles were taken, wrote “of Epirus.”]

VII. That two provincial councils are to be held each year; and if a difficult matter arises which cannot be settled by the judgment of the bishop of Thessalonica—or, in another version and in the Spanish collection, which has not been settled by his judgment—it is to be referred to the Roman bishop.

VIII. That if a bishop abandons his own city and seeks a greater see out of ambition, he will not only be unable to obtain that Church but must also lose his own. [Alternative, also in the Spanish collection: “nor will he be able to obtain that one, and he must lose his own.”]

IX. That no one presume to solicit or retain another’s cleric unless his own bishop gives consent.

X. That moderation be maintained by the bishop of Thessalonica when summoning provincial bishops. [The Spanish collection adds: “lest under this pretext priestly honor be subjected to insults; and no more than two bishops from each province, approved by the metropolitans, are to be sent.”]

XI. That the bishops not remain away more than fifteen days beyond the time fixed by the council. [The Spanish collection adds: “If a dispute about a matter should arise among them, let everything be disclosed to the Roman pontiff with a report of the proceedings, so that he may arrange whatever is pleasing to God.”]

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.
