If you would truly perceive and weigh in a just examination how much has been entrusted to your fraternity by the authority of the blessed Apostle Peter, and what responsibilities have also been committed to you through our favor, we could greatly rejoice in the devotion with which you discharge the solicitude imposed upon you. [Note: The Spanish Vindobonensis deletes the preposition *a* (“by”). Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of collections 3, 5, and 24, as well as Vatican Regina 849, read *sede* (“see”) instead of *auctoritate* (“authority”). Sichardus has “by the most blessed Apostle Peter.” See Quesnellus’s note 2.]

## CHAPTER I  
### On the Vicariate of Thessalonica and the Case of Atticus, Bishop of Nicopolis
Since my predecessors delegated authority to your predecessors, so I too, following the example of those before me, entrusted to your devotion the responsibilities of my office, so that, as an imitator of our gentleness, you might assist the care which, by divine institution, we chiefly owe to all the churches [Col. 0668B], and might in a certain manner extend the presence of our visitation to provinces distant from us:

[Note: [Col. 0668D] The Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and manuscripts of collection 21 together with Ratramnus in his work against the Greeks (vol. I of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, p. 110), as well as editions before Quesnel, add “in effect” (*effectus*). Shortly afterward, manuscripts of collection 24, together with Sichardus and earlier editions, read “from the apostolic see” instead of “from us.” See Quesnel’s note 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0668D] The Dionysian and Hadrianic codices read “and” in place of “since” (*siquidem*). The printed editions, with manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus, read “because [it was done] immediately” (*quia de continenti*). In the margin, the Thuanus and Cambridge manuscripts read: “If indeed, with fitting [oversight].”]

since, with continuous and timely oversight, it were readily possible for you to recognize what matters you should settle by your own diligence and what you should reserve for our judgment [Col. 0669A]. For since it was within your freedom to suspend greater affairs and more difficult outcomes of cases while awaiting our decision,

[Note: [Col. 0669C] The manuscripts of Thuanus and Cambridge read “greater cases.”]

you had neither reason nor necessity to depart into anything exceeding your measure. For you have an abundance of our written admonitions,

[Note: [Col. 0669C] Manuscript collections 24 and Sichardus read “documents.” Since only one letter of Anastasius to Leo from that period survives—Letter 6—we recognize that the others, which are said to have been frequently sent and to have abounded, are now missing.]

by which we have often instructed you concerning moderation in every undertaking: that, through an exhortation of charity, you might urge the churches of Christ [684] entrusted to you toward the health of obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0669C] Dionysius, Hadrianus, and two Thuanus manuscripts read “hearing.” Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensis collection 5, the Vaticanus Hispanicus and Isidorus, as well as two Hadrianic manuscripts at Vercelli and Justellus, read “exist.”]

For although among negligent or sluggish brothers there are often matters that ought to be dealt with by greater authority,

[Note: [Col. 0669C] The same Vaticanus, Hispanicus, and Isidorian manuscripts read “which ought to be dealt with.” Then, instead of “authority,” three manuscripts cited by Quesnel read “severity.”]

correction must nevertheless be administered in such a way that affection is always preserved. Hence the blessed apostle Paul, instructing Timothy in ecclesiastical governance, says: “Do not rebuke an older man, but exhort him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters, in all purity” (1 Tim. 5:1).

If this moderation, according to apostolic instruction, is owed to any inferior members, how much more must it be rendered without offense to our brothers and fellow bishops?

[Note: [Col. 0669C] The Vindobonensis collection 5 omits “our.”]

Thus, although things sometimes occur that must be censured in priestly persons, benevolence should nevertheless accomplish more toward those being corrected than severity, exhortation more than agitation, and charity more than power.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] This reading, corrected by Quesnel from the manuscripts cited in his note 4, is confirmed by nearly all our manuscripts, certainly the better ones. For the common reading, “But those who seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ, are easily distinguished from this rule,” manuscript collection 24 and the copy of Sichardus prefer: “easily depart from this rule, and, while they prefer to rule.”]

But those who seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), easily depart from this rule; and while they prefer to dominate rather than to advise their subjects,

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Ratramnus, in the passage cited, and the editions of the Councils add: “they seek what pleases their subjects”; the manuscripts of Vaticanus Hispanicus and Isidorus read: “honor pleases, pride inflates.”]

honor inflates pride, and what was provided for concord tends toward harm. That we must say this does not proceed from a small grief of heart.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] The most ancient Vaticanus 1342, collection 3, reads: “Which indeed we must have, thus we say.” Other Vatican manuscripts read: “Which, as we must say, we have”; we would insert this in the text if it were supported by other manuscripts of good authority. Justellus likewise reads *habemus*, “we have.”]

For I feel myself in a certain sense implicated in the fault when I learn that you have departed immoderately from the rules entrusted to you.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] Other manuscripts read, “I feel myself at fault.” Shortly afterward, the Vulgate before Quesnel, together with manuscript collection 24 and Sichardus, reads “to have gone astray” instead of “to have departed.” The Vindobonensis collection 5 and the Vercelli Hadrianic manuscripts read “to have defected.”]

If you were insufficiently concerned for your own reputation, you should at least have spared my reputation, lest what was done solely at your own instigation [Col. 0670A] should appear to have been done by our judgment. Let your Fraternity reread our letters, and run through all the writings sent to your predecessors, the bishops of the apostolic see; and it will find nothing prescribed either by me or by my predecessors that we have learned you presumed to do.

[Note: [Col. 0669D] The Vaticanus Hispanicus and Isidorian manuscripts, together with Ratramnus, Justellus, and the Vulgate before Quesnel, read “you will find,” rather than “you will find ordered.” For it could not be found in the letters of Leo or his predecessors that something was ordered which Saint Leo complains Anastasius presumed. The reading *inveniat* has the force of both pressing and denying.]

685

For our brother Atticus, metropolitan bishop of Old Epirus,

[Note: [Col. 0670C] This is the reading of the manuscripts. Some printed editions, following Crabbus, read “Nicopolitan.” See Quesnel’s note 5.]

came to us with the bishops of his province and complained before your attending deacons, in a tearful account, of the most undeserved affliction he had suffered.

[Note: [Col. 0670C] Quesnel preferred *astrictione*, “constraint,” a reading which he himself found in one manuscript cited in note 6, Victorinus, and which we found in both Vaticanus 544 of collection 24 and in Sichardus. We have judged that the reading found in all the other editions and manuscripts should be restored.]

Your deacons, by offering no reply to his sorrowful complaints,

[Note: [Col. 0670D] The Corbeiensis manuscript of collection 2, cited by Quesnel in the margin, reads “with complaining tears.” Shortly afterward, Ratramnus, together with the Vaticanus Hispanicus and Isidorus, reads “those same deacons of mine.” In the Vindobonensis collection 5 and in the Vaticanus of Dionysius, as in the printed editions before Quesnel, *tui*, “your,” is absent.]

showed that the matters brought before us were not without credibility. It was also read in your letters, which those same deacons brought, that Brother Atticus had come to Thessalonica and had certified his consent by a written declaration,

[Note: [Col. 0670D] The Vindobonensis collection 5 inserts *sua*, “his own,” and shortly afterward reads “may be able” instead of “might be able,” “had been” instead of “to have been,” and “he has written” instead of “he had written.”]

so that we could understand nothing else about his coming and his having written a document promising obedience than that it had been an act of his own judgment and spontaneous devotion. Yet in the mention of that document there appeared a sign of insult.

[Note: [Col. 0670D] The Vaticanus Hispanicus, together with two other manuscripts of collection 21, reads “the insult was proved.”]

There had been no need to bind in writing one who had already demonstrated his obedience by the very service of his voluntary arrival. Therefore your letter provided testimony to the lamentations of the aforesaid man; and by what was not kept silent, what had been covered in silence was exposed—namely, that the prefecture of Illyricum had been approached and that the highest power among worldly offices

[Note: [Col. 0670D] Manuscripts of collection 24, together with editions before Quesnel and Sichardus, read *adhibitam*, “employed.” Our other manuscripts read as in the text. Vindobonensis collection 5 alone reads *aditam*, “approached,” in the first hand, corrected to *adhibitam* in the second.]

[Note: [Col. 0670D] See Quesnel’s note 7.]

had been stirred up for the production of an innocent bishop, so that, once a terrifying enforcement had been dispatched—one that would bring all public offices to bear in carrying out the command—a priest would be dragged from the sacred entrances of the Church, accused of no crime—not even a false one. No respite was granted him on account of the burden of illness,

[Note: [Col. 0670D] The Vaticanus of collection 24, together with Sichardus, reads “notwithstanding winter”; shortly afterward, “through impassable crags.”]

nor because of the severity of winter; instead, he was compelled to undertake a harsh and perilous journey through impassable snows [Col. 0671A]. The labor and danger were so great that some of those who accompanied the bishop are said to have collapsed.

686

I am greatly astonished, dearest brother, and also deeply grieved, that you were able to become so fiercely and violently agitated against a man concerning whom you had indicated nothing beyond the fact that, summoned to appear, he was delaying his arrival and pleading illness—especially since, even if he had deserved such treatment, you ought to have awaited what I would write in response to your inquiries.

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Editions before Quesnel, together with Ratramnus and the Vindobonensis, Hispanicus, and other manuscripts of collection 21, read “had been.” The last of these shortly afterward prefers “what we should write in response to your questions.”]

But, as I see, you formed a good opinion of my character and very accurately foresaw how civilly I would respond for the preservation of priestly concord.

[Note: [Col. 0671C] See Quesnel’s note 8.]

For that reason you hastened to carry out your impulses without concealment,

[Note: [Col. 0671C] This is the reading of Dionysius, three Thuanus manuscripts, and one Corbeiensis cited by Quesnel in the margin, as well as most and the better of our manuscripts, except the Hispanicus, Isidorus, and other manuscripts of collection 24, which, with Ratramnus, Sichardus, and earlier editions, read “without delay.” Shortly afterward, Vaticanus collection 24 and Sichardus read “of one who makes other arrangements.”]

lest, after receiving letters that arranged something else according to our moderation [Col. 0671B], you should no longer have the liberty to do what was done. Or had some crime become known to you, and did the weight of a new charge press upon you against a metropolitan bishop?

[Note: [Col. 0671C] Ratramnus, manuscript collection 24, Sichardus, and the Vulgate add “of a brother.” Shortly afterward, we have restored “metropolitan,” which appeared in editions before Quesnel, from most of our manuscripts of various collections, especially Vaticanus 1342, collection 3, and another pure Vatican Dionysian manuscript. In two Vindobonensis manuscripts, one of collection 5 and the other Hispanicus, “Nicopolitan” is read; Quesnel adopted it without any difference in meaning, since the metropolitan of Epirus mentioned here was the bishop of Nicopolis. Then, “the weight of the charge accused you” is found in the Vaticanus Hispanicus and Isidorus, as well as in Vaticanus collection 3 and collection 21. Vindobonensis collection 5 has only “accused.” The Vindobonensis Hispanicus, the Vatican manuscripts of collection 24, and earlier printed editions read “the weight of the charge pressed upon you.”]

Yet you yourself confirm that this was foreign to him by bringing no accusation against him.

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Four manuscripts read “you had confirmed.” The margin of Labbé’s edition reads “you are recognized to have confirmed.” Shortly afterward, editions before Quesnel, together with manuscript collection 24, read “had done”; the other manuscripts read “would commit.”]

But even if he had committed something serious and intolerable, our judgment ought to have been awaited, so that you would decide nothing before learning what pleased us.

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Justellus reads “than what you knew would please us.”]

For we entrusted our responsibilities to your devotion in such a way that you were called to share the care, not to possess the fullness of power. Therefore, just as the things you have piously managed greatly rejoice us, so the things wrongly done distress us exceedingly. After the experience of so many cases, it is necessary to look ahead more anxiously and take precautions more carefully, so that through the spirit of charity and peace every source of scandal may be removed from the churches of the Lord that we have entrusted to you,

[Note: [Col. 0671D] Distinction 25, question 2, “Therefore,” chapter 5.]

with the eminence of your episcopate indeed prevailing in those provinces [Col. 0672A], but with every excess of usurpation cut away.

687

## CHAPTER II. On preserving the rights of the metropolitans residing under the Thessalonian vicar

Therefore, according to the canons of the holy Fathers, composed by the Spirit of God and consecrated by the reverence of the whole world, we decree that the metropolitan bishops of the individual provinces, whose care is assigned to your Fraternity by our delegation, shall possess unimpaired the right of the dignity anciently entrusted to them, so that they depart from the established regulations neither through negligence nor through presumption.

## CHAPTER III. Who must be excluded from the priesthood

In cities whose governors have died, the following rule shall be observed concerning the appointment of replacement bishops: the man who is to be ordained, even if he has a reputation for good conduct,

[Note: [Col. 0672C] This is the reading of the most ancient Vaticanus collection 3 and Vindobonensis collection 5, together with the manuscripts of collection 24 and the copy of Sichardus, as well as Dionysius. Other collections, with the remaining printed editions, read “be supported by testimony.”]

must not be a layman, a novice, or the husband of a second wife,

[Note: [Col. 0672C] On the necessary correction of this passage, which most of our ancient manuscripts prefer, see Quesnel’s note 9. Certain manuscripts of collection 21 alone give the common reading: “or one who has or has had even one wife, but not one who has joined to himself a widow.” Others of the same collection, together with both Hispanic manuscripts and the Vaticanus Isidorus, read: “or one who has or has had one wife, but not one whom he has joined to himself as a widow”; in Vaticanus Isidorus the particle “not” is marked for deletion by a line beneath it. Vaticanus collection 3 reads: “but one whom he has not joined to himself as a widow.”]

nor one who has or has had one wife, provided that he has married a widow. For the election of priests is so exalted that practices which are not counted as blameworthy in other members of the Church are nevertheless held unlawful in them.

[Note: [Col. 0672C] Distinction 32, “Of all priests,” chapter 1.]

## CHAPTER IV. On the continence of subdeacons

For although those outside the clerical order are free to pursue marriage and the procreation of children,

[Note: [Col. 0672C] See Quesnel’s note 10.]

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Without indicating it, Quesnel added “free choice” (*liberum arbitrium*) after *liberum*. This substantive occurs in Dionysius, the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and other later collections. But the reading of earlier editions, which omits it with manuscripts of collections 3, 5, and 24, Merlinus, and Sichardus, appeared more authentically Leonine.]

for the sake of displaying perfect purity of continence, even subdeacons are not permitted carnal marriage,

[Note: [Col. 0672D] See Quesnel’s note 11.]

so that those who have wives may be as though they did not have them (1 Cor. 7:29), and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried. If this is worthy of being guarded in this order, which is fourth from the highest, how much more must it be guarded in the first, second, or third [688],

[Note: [Col. 0672D] The Vaticanus of Dionysius and Justellus read “or second or third.” Shortly afterward, the phrase “in the Levitical ministry” appears in manuscripts of collection 24 and editions before Quesnel; these also must be corrected, since Quesnel noted in a marginal annotation that the word “ministry” was added in the editions and should be deleted in all manuscript copies. We would insert it into the text as especially appropriate if it were supported by manuscripts of another, older collection.]

so that no one may be judged suitable for Levitical, priestly, or episcopal honor [Col. 0673A] if he is found not yet to have restrained himself from the pleasure of a wife.

[Note: [Col. 0673D] The note appears at the foot of column 673, but the callout letter (j) has not been printed in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0673D] See Quesnel’s note 16. Justellus reads “from the pleasure of a wife.” The Hispanic, Isidorian, and collection 21 manuscripts read “from the pleasure of lust.”]

## CHAPTER V. On the petition and consent of clergy and people in the election of bishops

[Note: [Col. 0673C] Distinction 63, “If by chance,” chapter 36; Ivo, *Decretum*, book III.]

When, therefore, the election of the chief priest is being considered, the man whom the unanimous consent of clergy and people has requested shall be preferred to all others;

[Note: [Col. 0673C] See Quesnel’s note 13.]

if their votes should happen to be divided among different candidates, the metropolitan’s judgment shall prefer to the other the one who is supported by greater zeal and greater merits. Only let no one be ordained against the will or without the request of the people,

[Note: [Col. 0673C] Editions before Quesnel, together with the Hispanic, Isidorian, and collection 21 manuscripts, read: “lest the unwilling people reject a bishop.” At the end of the chapter some copies read “he may have wished” instead of “he wished.”]

lest the city despise or hate a bishop whom it did not desire, and become less religious than it ought to be because it was not permitted to have the man it wanted.

## CHAPTER VI. On reporting to the Thessalonian bishop within his vicariate concerning the bishop to be consecrated

[Note: [Col. 0673C] Distinction 65, “Concerning the person,” chapter 4.]

Concerning the person to be consecrated as bishop, and concerning the consent of clergy and people, the metropolitan bishop shall report to your Fraternity; and he shall inform you of what has been approved in the province, so that your authority also may confirm that the ordination is to be properly celebrated. These arrangements, being rightly made, must create neither delay nor difficulty, lest the Lord’s flocks be deprived of the care of their shepherds for too long.

[Note: [Col. 0673C] Distinction 63, “To the metropolitan,” chapter 19; and distinction 77, “At the beginning.”]

When a metropolitan has died and another must be substituted in his place, the provincial bishops shall convene in the metropolitan city, so that, after the will of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined, the best man from among the presbyters

[Note: [Col. 0673D] See Quesnel’s note 14, and, concerning the words “from among the deacons,” his note 15.]

of that same church, or from among the deacons, may be chosen. Concerning his name the provincial priests shall report to you, fulfilling the wishes of those who have made the request,

[Note: [Col. 0673D] The Vulgate before Quesnel, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, reads “if what.”]

once they learn that what pleased them has also pleased you. For just as we do not wish legitimate elections to be wearied by any delays, so we permit nothing to be presumed without your knowledge.

689

## CHAPTER VII. On holding provincial councils frequently

Concerning episcopal councils, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers salutarily ordained:

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Distinction 18, “Concerning councils,” chapter 3; and Ivo, *Decretum*, book IV.]

namely, that two assemblies be held each year, in which judgment may be given concerning all the complaints that usually arise among the various orders of the Church [Col. 0674A]. But if a case should arise among the rulers themselves concerning greater sins—which God forbid—

[Note: [Col. 0673D] The Vaticanus Dionysian and the manuscripts of collection 24, together with Merlinus and Sichardus, read “arise.” At the end of the chapter the Vindobonensis Hispanicus reads “be referred” instead of “be transferred.”]

and it cannot be settled by provincial examination, the metropolitan shall take care to inform your Fraternity of the nature of the entire matter, so that, if the affair is not resolved by your judgment when the parties have appeared before you, whatever it may be may be transferred to our examination.

## CHAPTER VIII. On abolishing the transfer of bishops

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Distinction 7, question 1, “If any bishop,” chapter 1.]

If any bishop, despising the modesty of his own city, seeks the administration of a more renowned place and transfers himself to a larger people by any means whatsoever,

[Note: [Col. 0673D] Vaticanus collection 3, Vindobonensis collection 5, and the manuscripts of collection 24, together with editions before Quesnel, read “opportunity”; the other manuscripts and all those cited by Quesnel in the margin read “method.” Shortly afterward, the Dionysian, Hadrianic, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts read *pellatur*, “let him be expelled,” instead of *pelletur*, “he shall be expelled.”]

he shall indeed be expelled from the alien see, but shall also lose his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he coveted through greed nor over those whom he despised through pride. Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries, and let no one seek to increase himself beyond the measure of his right.

## CHAPTER IX. On fugitive clerics

[Note: [Col. 0674C] See Quesnel’s note 18. Shortly afterward, editions before Quesnel, together with the Vaticanus Dionysian, two Hadrianic manuscripts, and the Vindobonensis Hispanicus, read “let him agree.”]

[Note: [Col. 0674C] Distinction 19, question 2, “Another’s cleric,” chapter 1.]

Let no one receive or entice another bishop’s cleric against that bishop’s will, unless perhaps, by an agreement of charity, this has been arranged between the giver and the recipient.

690

For he is guilty of serious injury who dares either to entice or to retain from a brother’s church what is more useful or more precious.

[Note: [Col. 0674C] Quesnel writes in the margin: “Thus read the editions of Nicolinus, Merlinus, the Roman edition, and all later editions, as well as three manuscript copies.” Four others, with Dionysius, Cresconius, Sichardus, and Canisius, read “to cast out,” and this is incorrect. Nearly all our manuscripts read “to entice”; the Vaticanus Dionysian reads *illicere*, equally good. Our edition of Sichardus also reads “to entice.” Only the Vaticanus Hispanicus and Isidorian manuscripts read “to cast out.” The Vindobonensis, which preserves a purer Hispanic text, reads “to entice.” Shortly afterward, “if the matter is being dealt with” in the older editions, manuscript collection 24, Sichardus, and Vindobonensis collection 5 is read instead of “is dealt with.” A little later the Vaticanus Dionysian and Vindobonensis Hispanicus read “he recalls” instead of “he shall recall”; older editions and the manuscripts of collection 24 read “he proceeded” instead of “he withdrew.”]

Therefore, if the matter is being dealt with within the province, the metropolitan shall compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. But if he has withdrawn farther away, he shall be recalled by the authority of your command, so that no opportunity is left either for greed or for ambition.

## CHAPTER X. On the summoning of bishops by the metropolitan

In summoning bishops to you, however, we wish you to be extremely moderate, lest you appear to boast of fraternal injuries under the guise of greater diligence. Therefore, if some greater cause should arise for which it is reasonable and necessary to summon a fraternal assembly,

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Quesnel added “reasonable” from the manuscripts. These words are also found in our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, Vaticanus collection 3 reads “will have sufficed” instead of “may suffice.”]

it should suffice for two bishops from each province, whom the metropolitans judge should be sent, to come to your Fraternity, so that those who have assembled may not be detained beyond fifteen days from the appointed time.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] Here Dionysius begins chapter 11, “Exig.”]

## CHAPTER XI. When the other bishops disagree with the Thessalonian bishop, Rome is to be consulted

[Col. 0675A]

But if, in what you judge should be discussed or decided with the brothers, their opinion differs from your own, let everything be referred to us with the testimony of the proceedings,

[Note: [Col. 0675B] This is the reading of most manuscript copies and of the editions together with Dionysius. Quesnel reads “shall be referred.”]

so that, once ambiguities have been removed, what pleases God may be determined. To this end we direct all our concern and care: that whatever pertains to the unity of concord and whatever pertains to the preservation of discipline may be violated by no disagreement and neglected by no indolence.

And so I exhort and admonish you, dearest brother, and those brothers of ours who are offended by your excesses—although the grounds of all their complaints are not alike—not to disturb by any dispute what has been piously ordered and salutarily arranged.

[Col. 0675B]

Let no one seek what is his own, but what belongs to another (Phil. 2:4, 21), as the Apostle says: “Let each of you please his neighbor for his good, for edification” (Rom. 15:2).

[Note: [Col. 0675B] The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and the manuscripts of collection 21 omit “each of you.” Shortly afterward, the editions before Quesnel, together with the Vindobonensis collection 5, read “for good” instead of “for the good”; the latter also reads above, “as the Apostle.”]

For the structure of our unity cannot be firm unless the bond of charity binds us into inseparable solidity. For just as in one body we have many members, but all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another (Rom. 12:5; 1 Cor. 12:12).

[Note: [Col. 0675B] The Vindobonensis collection 5 reads: “This connection.”]

The connection of the whole body produces one health and one beauty; and this connection of the whole body indeed requires unanimity, but above all demands concord among priests.

[Note: [Col. 0675B] There can be no doubt about Dionysius’s reading, as Quesnel doubted in note 19. The most ancient Vaticanus, a pure Dionysian manuscript, reads: “Although their dignity is not common, nevertheless their order is general.” The Vaticanus Hispanicus and Isidorian manuscripts agree, as do all the Hadrianic manuscripts, the Florentine collection 13, the special Vaticanus 1347, and the manuscripts of collection 21. From his own manuscripts of collections 2 and 5—namely, the Corbeiensis, the Trecopithoeanus, and four other Thuanus manuscripts—Quesnel inserted this alternative reading into the text: “Although their dignity is common, nevertheless their order is not general.” We found this in one Vindobonensis Hispanicus. A clearer reading, and one less open to dispute, as he says in the cited note, is found in the Victorinus manuscript and in the editions of Surius, Merlinus, and Nicolinus: “Although their dignity is common, nevertheless their order is not general.” The entire change consists in replacing *etsi*, “although,” with *cum*, “since”; the particle *tamen*, “nevertheless,” is also not infrequently placed after it by reputable writers. We prefer our reading, since it is found in Vaticanus collection 3, Vindobonensis collection 5, Vaticanus collection 24, Vaticanus Reginensis 849, and, besides the copy of Merlinus’s collection 12, the copy of Sichardus. Nevertheless, both readings reduce to the same meaning. Thus this reading is supported by the authority of more collections; three of them, even if they do not surpass the age of Dionysius, certainly equal it, and cannot be said to derive from the same source. The context seems to require this reading. In such propositions, which consist of two clauses, the final clause, marked by *tamen*, is the one being established. The proofs that Leo adds, which distinguish among bishops, require not the affirmative proposition found in Dionysius—“nevertheless their order is general,” that is, without distinction—but the negative reading adopted by us: “nevertheless their order is not general.” Moreover, since Saint Leo admits in what follows that, as formerly among the apostles, so afterward among bishops, power was diverse, he does not understand the dignity which he affirms to be common to bishops as power and jurisdiction, but as the honor or character of the episcopate, which is indeed the same in all. The order which, by denying it to be general among bishops, he indicates to be diverse, he does not take as the sacred episcopal order, as we customarily call it, but as the hierarchical order, which, because it requires greater authority and jurisdiction in some and less in others, is certainly not general—that is, not identical in all without distinction of jurisdiction. Hence, following the pattern of the apostles, by which the pontiff indicates here, and declares more openly elsewhere, that Peter was placed over the others in authority and jurisdiction, he teaches that the distinction among bishops arose so that not all would claim everything equally for themselves. Rather, some in each province would have the first judgment, like metropolitans; while others, established in greater cities, would assume broader care, namely, not so much over bishops as over the metropolitans themselves, from whom they would demand obedience, like exarchs or patriarchs, and like the bishop of Thessalonica himself, whom Leo and his predecessors had placed over all Illyricum as vicar of the apostolic see with special rights. He declares that these arrangements were instituted so that through them the care of the universal Church might converge upon the one see of Peter, and so that nothing anywhere might disagree with its head. By this he declares the supreme authority and primacy of jurisdiction of the Roman pontiff, directed toward preserving the unity of the Church. Thus he establishes, as it were, four hierarchical orders or grades among bishops: episcopal, metropolitan, exarchal or apostolic-vicarial, and pontifical. Although he affirms that these share the dignity of episcopal honor or character, he nevertheless teaches that the general hierarchical order is not common to all, since they are distinguished in authority and power according to the diversity of their hierarchical grade. Those who apply this testimony to the equal right of all bishops, interpreting the words “dignity” and “order” in a later sense utterly foreign to Leo’s thought and contrary to the context, attempt to deceive the uninstructed.]

Since their dignity is common, their order is not general; for even among the most blessed apostles, though they were alike in honor, there was a certain distinction of power. Although the election of all was equal, one was nevertheless given precedence over the others. From this pattern also arose the distinction among bishops, and by a great ordering provision was made that not all should claim everything for themselves. Rather, there should be individual bishops in each province whose judgment would have first place among the brothers; and again, some established in greater cities should assume broader care, through whom the care of the universal Church would converge upon the one see of Peter, and nothing anywhere would disagree with its head.

[Note: [Col. 0676D] Distinction 2, question 6, “He who knows himself,” chapter 14.]

Therefore, whoever knows that he has been placed over some people should not be displeased that someone has been placed over him; rather, he should himself render the obedience that he demands. And just as he does not wish to bear the burden of a heavy load, so he should not dare to impose an unbearable weight upon another (Matt. 23:4).

[Col. 0677A]

For we are disciples of the humble and gentle teacher who says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29). But how shall we experience this unless we also put into practice what the same Lord says? “The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 20:26; Mark 10:43; Luke 22:26; Luke 14:11).

693

[Note: [Col. 0677B] Written on July 21, 447.]

# LETTER XV

[Note: [Col. 0677B] This letter appears in manuscript collections 1, 2, 3, 5, and 8; in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections 11, 12, 18, and 20 through 24. We have reread it in manuscripts of every collection except collections 2 and 18, which Quesnel used. Particularly noteworthy are Vaticanus Reginensis collection 1, Vaticanus collection 3, Vindobonensis collection 5, and Vaticanus 5845, which in its additions contains collection 8; these surpass the others in remarkable antiquity and rarity. See Quesnel’s note 1 for the various ways Turribius’s name is written in the manuscripts.]

## TO TURRIBIUS, BISHOP OF ASTORGA

[Note: [Col. 0677C] Compare Augustine, *On Heresies* 70, and the canons of the First Council of Braga.]

On the errors of the Priscillianists.

[Note: [Col. 0677C] We have brought the common titles, which derive from the Hispanic collection, back into conformity with the manuscript reading. In the table of collection 5, number 71, which Quesnel published from a Thuanus manuscript, the following titles are found: “Constitution to Turribius, bishop of Astorga, responding in eighteen chapters to the sixteen questions concerning the blasphemies of the Priscillianists”; namely:]

I. That they assert the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one person.

II. Concerning the processions of certain powers from God, which they claim began to exist and which, by their own essence, proceeded from him.

III. That the Son of God is called “only-begotten” because he alone was born from a virgin.

IV. That they pretend to honor the nativity of Christ.

V. That they assert the human soul to be of divine substance.

VI. That the devil was never good and that his nature is not God’s workmanship.

[Col. 0677D]

VII. That they condemn marriage and shrink from the procreation of those who are born.

VIII. That human bodies are fashioned in women’s wombs at the conception of seed through the work of demons.

IX. That the children of the promises, although born from women, are conceived from the Holy Spirit.

X. That human souls, before they were placed in human bodies, existed in a body and sinned in a heavenly dwelling.

XI. That they bind both human souls and bodies to the fatal stars.

XII. That, under some powers, there are parts of the soul, and under others, the members of the body.

XIII. That the entire body of the canonical Scriptures is to be understood under the names of the patriarchs.

XIV. That the condition of the body is held under the power of the stars and constellations according to earthly quality.

XV. That, through the devilish presumption of detestable faithlessness, they have falsely titled many books “canonical” under the pretense of truth; and that whatever is found outside the canonical Scriptures ought to be burned by fire.

XVI. Concerning the rejection of the writings of Dictinius.

XVII. Concerning those priests who do not resist those who err.

XVIII. Whether, when Christ descended to the underworld, his flesh rested in the tomb.

## SYNOPSIS

(From the Hispanic collection.)

## I. Against the Priscillianists, who distinguish the holy Trinity not by persons but only by names.—II. Against their belief that the Son of God was later than the Father [Col. 0677B].—III. Against their assertion that Christ is called “only-begotten” because he alone was born of a virgin.—IV. Concerning the Lord’s Nativity: that the Priscillianists observe fasts on it.—V. Against their assertion that the human soul is from the divine substance.—VI. Against their claim that the devil is from himself or from chaos, and has a proper nature [Quesnellus and one of our manuscripts add: “not”].—VII. Against their assertion that marriage and the procreation of children are sinful.—VIII. Against their claim that human bodies are the devil’s fabrications and are formed by demons in the womb [Col. 0678A].—IX. Against their claim that the children of promise were conceived from the Holy Spirit.—X. Against their belief that souls sin in heaven [Another version: “say that they sin in heaven”] and, according to the quality of their sin, receive in this world either a good or an evil lot.—XI. Against their claim that human souls are bound by the fatal stars.—XII. Against their description of the parts of the soul as subject to certain powers and the members of the body to others.—XIII. [Note: Since this title was absent in the printed editions, Quesnellus supplied it by conjecture as follows: “Against their overturning the knowledge of the Scriptures.” We have reproduced the title of the Hispanic collection itself from the manuscripts.] Against their arranging [Another version: “describing”] the names of the patriarchs among the individual members of the body.—XIV. Against their distribution throughout the body of the twelve signs observed by mathematicians.—XV. Concerning the apocryphal writings of those same Priscillianists.—XVI. [Note: Thus one of our manuscripts agrees with the printed editions. The others incorrectly read: “To be emended from the book of Bishop Turribius.” The Vienna Hispanic manuscript has “holy bishop” instead of “bishop.”] Concerning the book of Dictinius [Another version: Dicticinius].

**Leo, bishop, to Turribius, bishop: greetings** [Note: The Vienna manuscript of collection 5 adds “of Asturia”; this should be read “of Asturica.” It omits *salutem*, “greetings.”]

How commendably you are moved by concern for the truth of the catholic faith [Col. 0678B], and how earnestly you devote the diligence of pastoral office to the Lord’s flock, is demonstrated by the letter of your brotherhood delivered to us through [Note: Quesnellus observes in the margin that this person is called Pervincus by Hydatius in his *Chronicle*. In the Vienna Hispanic manuscript, the sign of a proper name is distinguished.] your deacon. In it you have taken care to inform us [695] what kind of outbreak of the disease of error from the remnants of the ancient pestilence has flared up in your regions [Note: Two manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus read “from ancient things.” Shortly afterward, in the Hispanic Vatican manuscript, “error or the disease” occurs instead of “the disease of errors.”]. For both the language of your letter, the sequence of your memorandum, and the text of your little book make clear [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 2. Shortly afterward he printed *eloquitur* from the manuscripts, whereas previously *demonstrant* had been read from only the manuscripts of collection 24.] that the foulest sewer of the Priscillianists has again grown hot among you [Col. 0679A] [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 3. Shortly afterward, some copies read *foedissimam* (“most vile”) instead of *fetidissimam* (“most foul”). Many of our manuscripts of collections 1, 3, and 8, as well as the Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorean manuscripts, have *sententiam* (“opinion”) instead of *sentina* (“sewer”), while the manuscripts of collection 21, together with the Corbie manuscript of collection 2 and the Grimani manuscript of collection 18 cited by Quesnellus in the same note 3, agree with them. Nevertheless, the reading *sentina* is preferred not only by all the printed editions but also by our manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 12, and 24, and by the Grimani manuscript of collection 18 in its first hand, as Quesnellus himself acknowledges; especially by the Vienna manuscript containing the pure Hispanic collection, which should be thought to have drawn this letter, sent into Spain, from a purer source. We therefore judged that this common reading should not be abandoned, particularly since the adjective *fetidissimam* and the following context suit *sentina* better than *sententia*.]

For there is no filth in the minds of any impious persons that has not flowed together into this doctrine. From the mud of every earthly opinion they have mixed for themselves a manifold sediment [Note: Another reading: “they have mixed together a mass of dregs.” Quesnellus gives this in the margin], so that they alone might drink in its entirety whatever others had tasted only in part.

Finally, if all the heresies that arose before Priscillian’s time are carefully reconsidered [Note: The Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads, “then no error will be found.” The reading “will be found to have been more pleasing” is found in seven of our better manuscripts. Elsewhere: “is found.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, but not the purer Vienna Hispanic manuscript or the others, read: “it plunged itself so deeply into the darkness of paganism through the profane secrets of magical arts and the empty falsehoods of mathematicians” [Col. 0679D].], scarcely any error will be found from which this impiety did not draw contagion. Not content to accept the falsehoods of those who deviated from the Gospel under Christ’s name, it also plunged itself into the darkness of paganism, so that through the profane secrets of magical arts and the empty lies of mathematicians they might place the faith of religion and the ordering of morals under the power of demons and the influence of the stars [Note: This is found in all our manuscripts and in the editions before Quesnellus, who preferred *affectu* (“inclination”) from only two manuscripts, those of Thuaneus and Grimani. Shortly afterward, some copies have *debetur* (“is owed”) instead of *debebitur* (“will be owed”). The Vienna Hispanic manuscript has *omniumque* (“and of all”) here.].

If this may both be believed [Col. 0679B] and taught, neither reward will be owed to virtues nor punishment to vices; and all the decrees not only of human laws but also of divine ordinances will be dissolved. For there can be no judgment concerning good or evil actions if fatal necessity drives the movement of the mind in either direction, and whatever human beings do belongs not to human beings but to the stars.

To this madness belongs that monstrous division of the whole human body according to the twelve signs of heaven [696], so that different powers preside over different parts, and the creature whom God made in his own image is placed under as great an obligation to the stars as there is connection among its members.

Our fathers, in whose times this unspeakable heresy burst forth, rightly and persistently acted throughout the world so that the impious [Col. 0679C] frenzy might be expelled from the whole Church. Even the rulers of the world so detested this sacrilegious insanity [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 4. Shortly afterward, instead of “with most of his disciples,” some manuscripts read “and most of his disciples.” Then the Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads: “For they saw … the whole of marriage …,” with the remainder omitted.] that they struck down its author and most of his disciples with the sword of the public laws.

They saw that every concern for moral integrity would be removed, every marital bond dissolved, and divine [Col. 0680A] and human law alike overthrown, if such people were anywhere permitted to live while professing these things.

For a long time this ecclesiastical discipline benefited [Note: These words are absent for a long time in the Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1. Shortly afterward, the Vatican Hispanic, Isidorean, and manuscripts of collection 21 read “shrank from seeking vengeance, yet of Christians.” In the Vienna Hispanic manuscript: “you seek to be vengeance,” corruptly. From this the origin of the variant becomes clear: *ultione esse quaeris* was wrongly written for *ultiones, severis* (“severe punishments”). Then, instead of *ad speratum*, the cited Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts and those of collection 21 have *ad spiritale* (“toward the spiritual”).] the mildness of the Church, which, although content with priestly judgment and reluctant to resort to bloody punishments, is nevertheless aided by the severe enactments of Christian rulers, since those who fear bodily punishment sometimes have recourse to a spiritual remedy.

But after hostile invasion occupied many provinces, and the storms of war blocked the enforcement of the laws [Note: Quesnellus omitted the conjunction, although it fits the sentence better; we restored it on the authority of the Vatican manuscript of collection 3, the Vienna manuscript, collection 5, the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, and another Vatican manuscript of collection 24. Some of these have the plural *exsecutiones*. Shortly afterward, the editions before Quesnellus read *interdixere* (“forbade”) instead of *interclusere* (“blocked”). The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts have “difficult passage,” followed by “for the overthrow of many nations” [Col. 0680D].], and after travel among God’s priests became difficult and assemblies rare, secret perfidy found liberty amid the public disorder and was stirred up toward the overthrow of many minds by the very evils by which it ought to have been corrected.

But what part, and how large a part, of the peoples there is free from the contagion of this pestilence [Note: The Vienna manuscript of collection 5, the Hispanic manuscripts, and the Vatican manuscripts of collections 11, 21, and 24 omit “from the contagion.” Shortly afterward, two manuscripts and the older editions have “your charity” instead of “your affection.”], when, as your affection indicates, the hearts even of certain priests have been corrupted by this deadly disease [697]! Those through whom falsehood was thought to be suppressed and truth defended [Note: The Vatican manuscript of collection 24 reads *fuerat* (“had been”). Shortly afterward, “the doctrine of Priscillian” occurs in the Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, the Vienna Hispanic manuscript, and two manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, as well as in the editions before Quesnellus.] have subjected the Gospel of Christ to Priscillian’s doctrine. Thus, after the piety of the sacred books has been distorted into profane meanings, what the Holy Spirit taught is not preached under the names of the prophets and apostles, but what the devil’s minister inserted.

Therefore, since your affection has gathered, with as much faithful diligence as possible, the opinions once condemned into sixteen chapters [Note: All our manuscripts read this, except the Vatican manuscripts of collections 8 and 24, which have “seventeen chapters,” apparently counting the final chapter of this letter, although it does not belong to the sixteen chapters proposed by Turribius and rejected by Leo in the same number of chapters. Shortly afterward, the editions before Quesnellus, together with six inferior manuscripts, read “let us reconsider.”], we too shall briefly review everything, lest any of these blasphemies should appear either tolerable or doubtful.

## Chapter I. How impiously the Priscillianists think about the persons of the Trinity in God

[Col. 0680C]

In the first chapter it is therefore shown how impiously they think about the divine Trinity: they assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person, as though the same God were now called Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit. They deny that one is he who begot, another he who was begotten, and another he who proceeded from both [Col. 0681A] [Note: The Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts read “or he who…”. Shortly afterward, Theodulf’s *Book on the Holy Spirit* has *procedit* (“proceeds”) instead of *processit* (“proceeded”).]. Rather, they understand a singular unity expressed in three names but not [Note: We inserted *in tribus* (“in three persons”) from the Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, the Vatican and Vercelli manuscripts of collection 8, and the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts. The Vienna Hispanic manuscript has “and not in three,” omitting *sed*. Shortly afterward, six manuscripts read “not undeservedly called Patripassians.” Then the Vienna Hispanic manuscript has “the Son endured obedience to the Father.”] to be present in three persons.

They took this kind of blasphemy from the opinion of Sabellius. His disciples are rightly called Patripassians, because if the Son is himself also the Father, the Son’s cross is the Father’s suffering; and whatever the Son endured in the form of a servant while obeying the Father, the Father himself endured in its entirety.

This is unquestionably contrary to the catholic faith, which confesses the Trinity of the Godhead as *homoousios*—“of one substance”—in such a way that it believes the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be undivided without confusion, eternal without time, and equal without distinction [Note: Quesnellus retained “the Trinity of Unity,” as in the earlier editions and the Grimani manuscript, although he noted in the margin that “the Trinity of the Godhead” occurs in nine of his manuscripts, to which several of ours may be added. Among them, the Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1 and the Vienna Hispanic manuscript alone have “the Trinity of Divinity” instead of “of the Godhead.” This reading must be preferred, as is proved by a similar reading in chapter 17 of this letter, where the preceding matter is repeated in summary. One Barberini manuscript has “the unity of the Trinity.”]. For unity in the Trinity is fulfilled not by the same person but by the same essence.

## Chapter II. Concerning the powers which they falsely claim to proceed from God

[Col. 0681B]

In the second chapter their foolish and empty invention concerning the processions of certain powers from God is exposed: they say that God began to possess these powers and that he himself preceded them in his essence [Note: The Vatican manuscript of collection 8 reads “concerning procession.” Shortly afterward, the Vulgate has “in his own essence.” Quesnellus corrected the text on the basis of all his manuscripts, supported also by ours except one, which reads “and through which his own essence.”].

In this they also support the error of the Arians [Note: We inserted *quoque* (“also”) from the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, the Hispanic collection, Isidore, and other manuscripts. This is quite appropriate, since it indicates that the Priscillianists support not only the Sabellians, discussed in the preceding chapter, but also the Arians, although the latter’s error is opposed to that of the Sabellians. Shortly afterward, one manuscript has *generavit* (“generated”), and two have *generarit* (“may have generated”), instead of *genuerit* (“begot”). Then the Vienna Hispanic manuscript has *essentiale* instead of *essentiae*.], who say that the Father is prior to the Son because at some time he existed without the Son and began to be Father when he begot the Son.

But just as the catholic Church detests the Arians, so also it detests these people, who think that what belongs to God’s own essence was ever lacking in God. Just as it is impious to call him mutable, so it is impious to call him capable of progress. For what is diminished is changed, and what is increased is likewise changed.

## Chapter III. Why the Son of God is called “only-begotten” among them

[Col. 0682D]

The discourse of the third chapter indicates that these same impious people assert that the Son of God is called “only-begotten” because he alone was born of a virgin [Note: Two Vienna manuscripts, one of collection 5 and the Hispanic manuscript, read “In the third chapter” or “In the third chapter, however.” At one point the same manuscript of collection 5, together with the older Vulgate editions, reads “begotten from the highest Father.” Then the Vatican Hispanic manuscript has “if Christ our Lord,” and Isidore has “the Lord Jesus.”].

They would certainly not dare to say this unless they had drunk the poison of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, who said that our Lord Jesus Christ did not exist before he was born of the virgin Mary.

But if they wish something else to be understood from their own opinion, and do not grant Christ a beginning from his mother, they must assert that the Son of God is not one, but that others too were begotten from the supreme Father, of whom this one alone was born from a woman and is therefore called “only-begotten,” because none of the other sons of God assumed this condition of birth.

Whichever way they turn, therefore, they rush into the precipice of great impiety: either they want Christ the Lord to have his beginning from his mother, or they deny that he is the only-begotten Son of God. Yet the one born from his mother was God the Word, and no one was begotten from the Father except the Word.

## Chapter IV. That they fast on the Lord’s Nativity and on Sunday

The fourth chapter contains the charge that they do not truly honor Christ’s Nativity, which the catholic Church venerates according to his assumption of true humanity, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Rather, they pretend to honor it, fasting on that day just as they do on Sunday, which is the day of Christ’s resurrection.

They do this because they do not believe that Christ the Lord was born in a true human nature. Instead, they wish it to appear that what was not real was displayed through a kind of illusion [Note: The Vienna Hispanic manuscript and the Vatican manuscript of collection 11 read “because it was true.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts have “as though true.” Shortly afterward, the Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with some manuscripts, reads “the doctrine of Cerdo,” and “agreeing” instead of “consonant.”].

They follow the doctrines of Cerdo and Marcion and agree in every respect with their kinsmen, the Manichaeans. When exposed and convicted in our examination, these people require the Lord’s Day, which the resurrection of our Savior consecrated for us, to be spent in the sorrow of fasting. They devote this abstinence, as is reported, solely to the reverence of the sun, so that in every respect they may be opposed to the unity of our faith, and the day which we hold in joy may be spent by them in affliction.

Therefore it is fitting that the enemies of Christ’s cross and resurrection should receive the sentence corresponding to the doctrine they chose.

## Chapter V. That they assert the human soul to be of the divine substance

The fifth chapter reports that they assert the human soul to be of the divine substance and that the nature of our condition does not differ from the nature of its Creator.

The catholic faith condemns this impiety, which flows from the opinion of certain philosophers and of the Manichaeans. It knows that no created thing is so exalted and pre-eminent that God himself is its nature. For what is from God himself is what he himself is, and is nothing other than the Son and the Holy Spirit [Note: Another reading: “that same thing.” Certain Vatican manuscripts together with the Vienna Hispanic manuscript read “this is what he himself is, and it is not something else.”].

Apart from this one consubstantial, eternal, and immutable Godhead of the supreme Trinity, there is nothing among all created things that was not created from nothing at its beginning. Nor is everything that rises above other creatures God; nor, if something is great and marvelous, is it therefore what he is who alone does great wonders (Psalm 135:4).

No human being is truth, no human being is wisdom, no human being is justice; rather, many participate in truth, wisdom, and justice. God alone is in need of no participation. Whatever is worthily understood of him in any way is not a quality but an essence.

Nothing is added to the immutable, and nothing is taken away [Note: Six of our manuscripts read “nothing happens to it”; thereafter the Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with certain inferior manuscripts, reads “it receives nothing.”]; for what is eternal is always proper to him. Remaining in himself, therefore, he renews all things and receives nothing that he himself has not given.

They are exceedingly proud and exceedingly blind [Note: The Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1 and the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts read “all who say.” The Vienna manuscript of collection 5 reads “who, when they say.” Then “the nature or soul of it” is found in the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts and three others.] when, while saying that the human soul is of the divine substance, they do not understand that they are saying nothing other than that God is mutable and that he himself suffers whatever can be inflicted upon his nature.

## Chapter VI. That they say the devil was never good and is not God’s work, but emerged from chaos and darkness

The sixth statement indicates that they say the devil was never good, that his nature is not God’s handiwork, but that he emerged from chaos and darkness. Thus, evidently, he has no author of his being but is himself the beginning and substance of every evil [Note: The Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, together with one manuscript of Thuaneus cited by Quesnellus, reads “of all evils.” Another of our manuscripts reads “of every evil.” See Quesnellus’s note 6. Shortly afterward, six of our manuscripts read “although that faith which is…”].

But the true faith, which is catholic, confesses the substance of all creatures, whether spiritual or bodily, to be good, and denies that evil has any nature. God, who is the Creator of the universe, made nothing that was not good. Hence the devil too would have been good if he had remained in what he was made.

But because he used his natural excellence badly and did not stand in the truth (John 8:44), he did not pass into another substance; rather, he departed from the highest good, to which he ought to have adhered; he did not pass into a contrary substance. So too those who assert such things rush from truth into falsehood, and accuse nature in the very matter in which they willingly sin and are condemned for their voluntary perversity.

The evil in them will therefore be evil, but evil itself will not be a substance; it will be the punishment of a substance [Note: The Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, two Vienna manuscripts of collection 5, the Hispanic manuscript, and two other Vatican manuscripts omit the preposition *in*. Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript 5845 and the Grimani manuscript omit “but the punishment of a substance.”].

## Chapter VII. They condemn marriage and marital intercourse

Next comes the assertion that they condemn marriage and shrink from the procreation of those who are born. In this, as in almost everything, they agree with the profanation of the Manichaeans. As their practices demonstrate, they detest conjugal intercourse [Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts and three others read: “for there is freedom for disgrace where the modesty of marriage and offspring is not preserved.” The editions before Quesnellus follow the reading of the text except for the words “and offspring,” for which they have “and the hope of offspring.”], because there is no freedom for disgrace where the modesty of marriage and offspring is preserved.

## Chapter VIII. They say that human bodies are formed by the devil and deny their resurrection

Their eighth teaching is that the formation of human bodies is the devil’s fabrication and that the seeds of conception are formed in women’s wombs by the work of demons [Note: The Vienna manuscript of collection 5 reads “to say that it is the devil’s fabrication.” The Vatican manuscript of collection 3, together with the earlier Vulgate, reads “to say that it is the devil’s fabrication.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1 has “by the operation of demons.” The Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts have “by demons.” In the older Vienna Hispanic manuscript, *per daemonum* is corrupt; it appears to have been written from *ex opere* or *opera*, as in other manuscripts.].

For this reason they say that the resurrection of the flesh must not be believed, because the bodily composition is not suited to the dignity of the soul [Note: This reading is found in the seven manuscripts cited by Quesnellus in the margin, and in many more of ours, together with the editions of Surius and Nicolinus. Another reading: “concretion.” Shortly afterward, the Grimani and Thuaneus manuscripts of Quesnellus delete “to the dignity.”].

This falsehood is undoubtedly the devil’s work, and such monstrous opinions are fabrications of demons. They do not form human beings in women’s wombs; rather, they manufacture such errors in the hearts of heretics.

The most filthy poison proceeding especially from the source of Manichaean impiety was long ago detected and condemned by the catholic faith.

## Chapter IX. They say that the children of promise were conceived through the Holy Spirit

The ninth statement plainly says that they claim the children of promise, although born from women, were conceived from the Holy Spirit. Their purpose is that offspring born from the seed of the flesh should not appear to belong to God’s creation [Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, together with three others, read “to that condition.” Shortly afterward, from the Vienna manuscript of collection 5 and the Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorean manuscripts, we restored the reading of the editions before Quesnellus, *substantia* (“substance”), in place of Quesnellus’s *substantiam* (“substance” in the accusative), which he wrote in the margin as “another reading: subsistence.” Then the Vatican manuscript 5845 reads “while it indeed remains in him.”].

This is opposed and contrary to the catholic faith, which confesses that every human being, in the substance of body and soul, is formed and animated within the mother’s womb by the Creator of the universe. The contagion of sin and mortality, which passes from the first parent into the offspring, indeed remains; but the sacrament of regeneration comes to its aid, through which the children of promise are reborn by the Holy Spirit, not in the womb of the flesh but in the power [Col. 0684C] of baptism [Note: Quesnellus printed “from the Holy Spirit.” We restored the common reading, confirmed by the excellent Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, and the Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts together with three other Vatican manuscripts.].

Thus David, who certainly was a child of promise, says to God: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Psalm 118:73; Job 10:8). And the Lord says to Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5).

## Chapter X. They affirm that souls sinning in heaven are thrust into bodies as punishment for sin

The tenth chapter reports that they assert that the souls inserted into human bodies existed without bodies [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with most of the ancient manuscripts, read “in a body,” but incorrectly, as Quesnellus rightly established in note 7. We confirm his emendation, which he found in only three manuscripts—the Thuaneus and Trecopith manuscripts of collection 5 and the Herovall manuscript of Isidore’s collection 12—with the Vatican manuscript of collection 3, the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, the Vercelli and Vatican manuscripts of collection 8, another Vatican manuscript and the Venetian manuscript of St Mark’s collection 12, and the Vatican Ottobonian manuscript 297 of collection 23. Shortly afterward, “on account of this” is absent from the Vatican manuscript of collection 24. Then the Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorean manuscripts, together with three others, read “to have fallen under rulers of their own quality, and through aerial and sidereal powers to have been enclosed, some in different bodies” [Col. 0685D]. The Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “in their own quality … in reversed bodies”; the remainder agrees with the preceding reading.] and sinned in a heavenly dwelling. For this reason, having fallen from the heights to lower regions, they came under rulers of differing qualities and, through aerial and sidereal powers—some harsher, others milder—were enclosed in bodies, by a diverse lot and unequal condition, so that whatever occurs variously and unequally in this life may seem to happen because of preceding causes.

They wove this impious fable from the errors of many people. But the catholic faith has cut all of them off from the body of its unity, steadfastly and truthfully proclaiming that human souls did not exist before they were breathed into their bodies [Note: The Vatican Reginensis manuscript reads “are inspired into them.”], and that they are incorporated by no one except God the Maker, who is both their Creator and the Creator of their bodies.

And because the whole human race has been corrupted through the transgression of the first human being, no one can be freed from the condition of the old human being except through the sacrament of Christ’s baptism. In it there is no distinction among those reborn, as the Apostle says: “For all of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:27).

What, then, do the courses of the stars accomplish here? What do the inventions of fate accomplish? What of the mutable condition and restless diversity of worldly things? Behold, the grace of God makes so many unequal people equal. Among all the hardships of this life, if they remain faithful, they cannot be miserable [Note: The Vatican manuscript of collection 24 reads “What do they do?” Shortly afterward, the Vienna manuscript of collection 5 has “mutable conditions.” Then the Vienna Hispanic manuscript and two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “made equal.”].

They say with the Apostle in every temptation: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or anguish? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? As it is written: ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we conquer through him who loved us” (Romans 8:35).

Therefore the Church, which is Christ’s body, fears none of the inequalities of the world, because it desires none of the world’s temporal goods. Nor does it fear being burdened by the empty clamor of fate, since it knows that it is strengthened by patience in tribulations [Note: The Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorean manuscripts, together with three others, prefer this reading after a punctuation mark: “What the apostolic saying teaches [another reading: ‘warns’] in every temptation, saying: ‘Who will…’” The same manuscripts and the Vienna Hispanic manuscript read “we are put to death” instead of “we are afflicted unto death.”].

## Chapter XI. They impose fatal necessity upon human beings

Their eleventh blasphemy is that they think both human souls and bodies are bound by fatal stars [Note: The Vienna Hispanic manuscript has “fatally.” Then, in the Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorean manuscripts and three others, “so that human beings” occurs. The Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “so that for human beings,” from which the later reading was corrected in the cited manuscripts.]. Through this madness they must be entangled in all the errors of the pagans, worshiping the stars that they think favorable to themselves and striving to appease those that are hostile.

But there is no place in the catholic Church for those who pursue such things [Note: The Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, together with the Vatican manuscript of collection 24, read “there is a place.” Shortly afterward, five of our inferior manuscripts have “because whoever is devoted to such persuasions…”.]; for whoever gives himself over to such beliefs has wholly departed from the body of Christ.

## Chapter XII. They subject souls to certain powers and the members of the body to others

Among these teachings the twelfth is that they describe the parts of the soul as subject to some powers and the members of the body to others. They establish the qualities of the inner rulers under the names of the patriarchs, and oppose to them, as their counterparts, the signs of the stars, to whose power bodies are subjected [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “and different signs.” Shortly afterward, two Vienna manuscripts read “to which they are subjected.”].

In all these matters they entangle themselves in an inextricable error, refusing to hear the Apostle who says: “See that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. For in him the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power” (Colossians 2:8).

And again: “Let no one deceive you by delighting in humility and worship of angels, intruding into things he has not seen, vainly puffed up by the sense of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and constructed through its bonds and joints, grows with the increase of God” (ibid., 18) [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “glory.” In the following text, both Hispanic manuscripts and the Vatican Isidorean manuscript read “the whole body, compacted and supplied by conjunction.”].

Why, then, should one admit into the heart what the Law did not teach, what prophecy did not sing, what the truth of the Gospel did not preach, and what apostolic teaching did not transmit?

But these things suit the minds of those about whom the Apostle says: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound teaching, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching to hear what pleases their ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but will turn to fables” (2 Timothy 4:3–4) [Note: All the manuscripts agree with Quesnellus and ours, except the Vatican manuscript of collection 24, which, together with the earlier printed editions, reads “these things are covered.” Shortly afterward, “about whom the Apostle speaks, saying” is found in the Vatican Reginensis manuscript of collection 1, the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, the Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, and three others.].

Therefore let those who dare either to teach or to believe such things have nothing in common with us [Note: The Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “with you.” Shortly afterward, the Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts have *communicabunt* (“they will share”) instead of *commune habeant* (“let them have in common”); these manuscripts soon omit “or believe.” The Vienna Hispanic manuscript deletes “or believe.”]. In every way they strive to establish that the substance of the flesh is alien to the hope of resurrection, and thus they dissolve the whole sacrament of Christ’s Incarnation: for it was unworthy to assume a complete human being if it was unworthy to free a complete human being [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 and Justellus’s manuscript cited by Labbe read: “because just as it was fitting to assume a complete human being, so it was fitting to free a complete human being.” The same reading occurs in the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, except that through error they first read “just as it was unworthy.”].

## Chapter XIII. What kind of knowledge of the Scriptures do they assert?

In the thirteenth place it is stated that they say the whole body of the canonical Scriptures must be understood under the names of the patriarchs. For the twelve powers that effect the reformation of the inner human being are indicated by these names [Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts read “are dedicated”; the Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “are said.”], without which knowledge no soul can attain to being reformed into the substance from which it proceeded.

But Christian wisdom despises this impious vanity. It knows that the nature of the true Godhead is inviolable and immutable, whereas the soul, whether living in a body or separated from a body, is subject to many sufferings.

Certainly, if it were of the divine essence, nothing adverse could befall it [Note: This reading, *si de divina esset essentia* (“if it were of the divine essence”), is found in Quesnellus and our manuscripts. Another reading, *si divinae esset essentiae*: “if it were of the divine essence.” Shortly afterward, most of our manuscripts, together with the earlier printed editions, have “ineffably” instead of the reading “incomparably” accepted by Quesnellus. We did not dare to exclude the more suitable reading, which is preferred by the very ancient Vatican manuscript 5845. Then the Vercelli manuscript reads “the Creator is one thing.” Two Vatican manuscripts, together with the editions before Quesnellus, read “the Creator is one thing, the creature another.” At the end of the chapter, the very ancient Vatican manuscript of collection 8 and another Vatican manuscript of collection 24, together with the older editions, read “given” instead of “granted.”].

Therefore the Creator and the creature are incomparably different. He is always the same and is changed by no variation; the creature, however, is mutable even when it has not changed, because its not being changed is something it may have received, not something proper to it.

## Chapter XIV. They subject the human being to the power of the stars and signs
Under the fourteenth chapter, they are said to hold this view concerning the condition of the body: that, according to its earthly quality, it is kept under the power of the stars and signs. Hence many things are found in the holy books that pertain to the outward man, so that in the Scriptures themselves [Note: The Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore read: “between the divine, or earthly and human nature.” After several words, the Vatican manuscript 5845 has *seruntur* (“are sown”) instead of *disseruntur* (“are discussed”).] there is said to be a certain mutual opposition between the divine and earthly nature; and that one thing is claimed by the rulers of souls, another by the creators of the body. These fables are advanced so that the soul may be affirmed to be of divine substance and the flesh believed to be of an evil nature. For they also profess that the world itself, with its elements, is not the work of a good God but the creation of an evil author. And in order to cover these sacrileges of their lies with honorable titles, they have violated almost all the divine utterances by introducing wicked interpretations.

## CHAPTER XV. They corrupt the true Scriptures and introduce false ones.

[Col. 0688A]

The fifteenth chapter’s discussion complains about this matter and rightly detests the devilish presumption. For [Note: The Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, reads “by the testimony of our truthful witnesses.” Another Vindobonese Spanish manuscript and one Vatican manuscript have *testimonium* (“testimony”) instead of *testium* (“witnesses”). Thereafter, the Vatican manuscripts, collections 21 and 24, together with the older editions, read *titulantur* (“are entitled”) instead of *titularentur* (“might be entitled”).] we have learned this through the report of truthful witnesses, and have found many of their utterly corrupted books that were entitled canonical. How could they deceive the simple unless they first smeared their poisoned cups with a kind of honey, so that the unpleasantness of what would prove deadly might not be perceived everywhere? Care must therefore be taken, and provision made especially with priestly diligence, that falsified books, discordant from sincere truth, be used in no reading whatever.

But the apocryphal writings, which under the names of the apostles contain much seed [Note: The Vatican manuscript, collection 3, and the decree on the Apocrypha—which was taken from this passage and will be given in the appendix—read *semina* (“seeds”). The Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1, and the Spanish Vindobonese manuscript read *seminaria* (“seed-beds” or “nurseries”). Thereafter, the manuscripts of Grimani and Victor, as well as Quesnel’s edition, read *intercidendae* (“to be destroyed”) instead of *interdicendae* (“to be prohibited”).] of falsehoods, must not only be prohibited but also utterly [Col. 0688B] removed and burned in the fire. For although there are some things in them that may seem to bear the appearance of piety, they are nevertheless never free from poisons; [Note: The Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore read “and through fables.” The Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, reads “and through servants.” Shortly afterward, three Vatican manuscripts have *narrationibus* (“narrations”) instead of *narratione* (“narration”).
