The Vatican manuscript 5845 reads: “so that those deceived by snares may be entangled in error.” Three manuscripts in the decree on the Apocrypha read: “so that those deceived by snares of whatever error may be entangled.”] and through the allurements of fables they secretly work to ensnare those whom the narration of marvels has seduced in the snares of every kind of error.

Therefore, if any bishop does not forbid apocryphal books from being kept in private houses [Note: In manuscripts of collection 21 and in the decree on the Apocrypha, *per domos* (“in private houses”) is absent. Thereafter, the Spanish manuscript, Isidore, four other manuscripts, and the editions before Quesnel read *corrupti* (“corrupted”) instead of *vitiati* (“tainted”).], or permits books in the Church to be read under the name of canonical books when they have been tainted by the adulterine revision of Priscillian [Note: *707*], let him know that he must be judged a heretic; for **whoever does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error**.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the writings of Dictinius.

[Note: The Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore read: “After this, a just complaint brought forth.” Shortly afterward, Quesnel has *Dicticinii* in the margin instead of *Dictinii*. Concerning Dictinius and his treatises, see Quesnel’s note 8 and the observations that we shall append to it. Thereafter, the Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore have *qui si aliquid* (“who, if they think anything”) instead of *cum si aliquid* (“although they think anything”).]

Finally, this chapter brought forth a just complaint: that the treatises of Dictinius, which he wrote according to Priscillian’s doctrine, were read by many with veneration, although, if they think that anything should be attributed to Dictinius’s memory, they ought rather to love his restoration than his fall. They are therefore not reading Dictinius but Priscillian, and they approve what he taught while he was in error, not what he chose after he had been corrected. [Note: Dictinius’s correction is appended to the First Council of Toledo, and we shall defend it in the observations on Quesnel’s note 8. Shortly afterward, the Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore read *imponere* (“to impose”) instead of *impune laudati* (“praised with impunity”). Thereafter, some manuscripts have *scripturis* (“writings”) instead of *scriptis* (“written works”).]

But no one should presume to do this with impunity, nor should anyone be counted among Catholics who uses writings condemned not only by the Catholic Church but also by their own author. [Note: The same manuscripts read “Let it not be,” and afterward “lest under the guise.” They omit *cordis* (“of heart”), and shortly afterward, instead of *dum se nostros* (“while they pretend themselves to be ours”), they have, with the Spanish Vindobonese manuscript, *dum sensus nostros* (“while [they pretend] our views”).]

Let it not be permitted to the perverse to pretend together what they fabricate, nor, under the guise of the Christian name, to evade the statutes of imperial decrees. For this reason they come together with the Catholic Church with such great diversity of heart, so that they may make as many as they can their own, and, while pretending to be our people, evade the severity of the laws. The Priscillianists do this, and so do the Manichaeans. Their hearts are so closely allied with these people that, distinguished only by their names, they are found united in their sacrileges. For although the Manichaeans reject the Old Testament, which these men pretend to accept, the intention of both nevertheless tends toward one and the same end: what [Note: Thus according to the Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1; the Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5; both Spanish manuscripts; the Vatican manuscript; Isidore; and three other manuscripts. Quesnel reads *isti* (“these men”), as we find in other manuscripts. Other editions read: “These men corrupt it by accepting it; those men attack it by rejecting it.” Merlin has: “These men attack it by rejecting it; those men corrupt it by accepting it.” We have preferred the reading of the better manuscripts, by which the Priscillianists are understood as the ones accepting the Old Testament; concerning them Leo wrote shortly before: “These men pretend to accept it.” The word “those” refers to the Manichaeans.] the latter attack by rejecting, the former corrupt by accepting.

But in their execrable mysteries, which, the more impure they are, the more carefully they are concealed [Note: Alternatively, “hidden”—], there is altogether one abomination, one obscenity, and a similar disgrace. Although we are ashamed to speak of it, we nevertheless investigated it with the greatest diligence and, after it had been disclosed by the confession of the Manichaeans who had been arrested, caused it to reach public knowledge. Thus it could in no way appear doubtful that the matter had been revealed in our judgment, which was attended not only by a very large number of priests but also by the dignity of distinguished men, by a portion of the senate, and by some of the people—revealed by the mouths of those who had perpetrated the entire crime. This is shown by the proceedings that we have now sent to your Belovedness. [Note: Thus the oldest manuscripts—the Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1; another Vatican manuscript, collection 3; two Vindobonese manuscripts, collection 5; the Spanish manuscript; and the editions before Quesnel—and this agrees with other similar passages in this letter. Quesnel reads *vestram* (“your”), as other manuscripts show here. Shortly afterward, the Vercelli manuscript, collection 8, has *ineptissima* (“most senseless”) instead of *incestissima* (“most incestuous”).]

What was once discovered and widely publicized concerning the most shameful crime of the Manichaeans has also been discovered and widely publicized concerning the most incestuous practice of the Priscillianists. [Note: The Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1; both Spanish manuscripts; the Vatican manuscript; Isidore; and “those who are equal in every respect in the impiety of their ideas.” The Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, omits *enim* (“for”).] For those who are equal in the impiety of their ideas in every respect cannot be unlike in their sacred rites.

[Note: The Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore, together with three other manuscripts, read *Discussis* (“Having examined”)—.]

Having gone through everything contained in the sequence of the little book, which does not differ from the form of the memorandum, we have, as I think, sufficiently shown what judgment we hold concerning the matters that your Fraternity reported to us, and how intolerable it is if even the hearts of certain priests consent to such profane errors—or, to put it more mildly, do not resist them. **By what conscience** [Note: The Spanish Vindobonese manuscript reads “who claim for themselves the honor bestowed on the priesthood.” The Spanish Vatican manuscript reads “who claim for themselves the honor of bishops.” The common editions have *debitum* (“owed”) instead of *praestitum* (“bestowed”).] do they claim for themselves the honor bestowed on them, when they do not labor for the souls entrusted to them? Beasts rush in, and they do not close the sheepfolds. [Note: The Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore, and in the margin of Labbe’s edition, read: “Wild beasts lie in wait.”] Thieves lie in wait, and they do not set out guards. Diseases multiply, and they provide no remedies. But when they also add that they refuse to agree with those who act more diligently, and conceal the fact that they anathematize in their subscriptions the impieties once condemned throughout the whole world, what are they to be understood as saying about themselves except that they belong not to the number of brothers but to the party of enemies? [Note: The same manuscripts and the Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, omit *autem* (“but”). The Grimani manuscript and three of Quesnel’s Thuan manuscripts delete *subscriptionibus suis* (“in their subscriptions”). Shortly afterward, *se* (“themselves”) is absent from the Vatican Regius manuscript, both Spanish manuscripts, Isidore, and three other manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XVII. Whether Christ’s flesh truly rested in the tomb.

[Note: We have added the preposition *in* on the authority of the Vatican Regius manuscript, two Vindobonese manuscripts, and three other Vatican manuscripts. Labbe, from Justellus’s manuscript, reads: “Now then, what [you placed] in the final . . .”]

In the final part of your familiar letter you wrote something at which I marvel: that the understanding of any Catholic should be troubled as though it were uncertain whether, when Christ descended to the underworld, his flesh rested in the tomb. For just as it truly died and was buried, so it was truly raised on the third day. The Lord himself had foretold this when he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The evangelist adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (ibid., 21). The prophet David had also foretold the truth of this matter, speaking in the person of the Lord and Savior and saying: “Moreover, my flesh shall rest in hope. For you will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you permit your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15:9). [Note: The Vatican Regius manuscript reads *requiescit* (“rests”), and the same manuscript together with the Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, omits *non derelinquis* (“you will not abandon”).] These words plainly show that the Lord’s flesh truly rested in the tomb after burial and did not undergo corruption. For, being quickly brought to life by the return of the soul, it rose again. [Note: The same Vindobonese manuscript reads “that the flesh of Christ”; the Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore read “that the flesh of Christ also rested in the tomb.”] To refuse to believe this is sufficiently impious and undoubtedly belongs to the teaching of Manichaeus and Priscillian, who, while pretending in sacrilegious understanding to confess Christ, remove the reality of his incarnation, death, and resurrection.

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript, the Spanish manuscript, Isidore, another Vatican manuscript, collection 11, and the manuscript volume cited by Labbe, the text reads: “Let there be therefore among you letters and a council, and let them come together in that place,” etc. Another reading is “in one place.” The Spanish Vindobonese manuscript has only “Let there be.” From this, later copyists of the same collection may perhaps have changed *episcopale* (“episcopal”) to *epistolae* (“letters”), etc.]

Let an episcopal council therefore be held among you, and let the priests of the neighboring provinces come together at a place convenient for all, so that, in accordance with what we have answered to your inquiries, it may be investigated with the fullest examination whether there are any among the bishops who are polluted by the contagion of this heresy. They must without doubt be separated from communion if they refuse to condemn the most wicked sect in all its perverse doctrines. For it is in no way tolerable that one who has undertaken the office of preaching the faith should dare to dispute against the Gospel of Christ, against apostolic teaching, and against the Creed of the universal Church.

What sort of disciples will there be where such teachers instruct? **What religion of the people, what salvation of the populace, will there be where, contrary to human society,** [Note: Thus Quesnel, with seven of his manuscripts and with the editions of Nicolini and Surius, to which most of our manuscripts agree. Only two must be excepted: Vatican manuscript 5845, which has “the modesty of holiness is removed,” and Vatican manuscript, collection 24, which, with the Grimani manuscripts and the editions before Quesnel, prefers: “the shamefastness of rightful modesty is taken away, the bonds of marriages are removed.”] the sanctity of modesty is removed, the bond of marriage is taken away, the propagation of offspring is hindered, and the nature of the flesh is condemned? And where, against the true worship of the true God, the Trinity of the Godhead is denied, the distinct property of the Persons is confused, [Note: The Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore read: “the worship of the true God is forbidden; the Trinity of the Godhead . . .” Three manuscripts seen by Quesnel, two of our Vatican manuscripts, and another cited by Labbe, with the marginal editions, read: “the true worship of God is forbidden,” etc. The Spanish Vindobonese manuscript reads: “Against the true worship of God,” etc. Another Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, reads: “the Trinity of the Godhead, with the distinct property of the Persons denied, is confused.”] [Note: The same Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5; two Vatican manuscripts; the Spanish manuscript and Isidore; one Vercelli manuscript; three other manuscripts; and four manuscripts noted by Quesnel in the margin read: “divine essence is given to human souls.”] the human soul is proclaimed to be of divine substance, and the same soul is enclosed in flesh at the devil’s will; the Son of God is proclaimed the Only-Begotten through what was born of the Virgin, not through what was born of the Father; and he is asserted to be neither the true offspring of God nor the true child of the Virgin—so that, through a false passion and an unreal death, even a deceptive resurrection of the flesh taken back from the tomb may be held?

They use the Catholic name in vain who do not resist these impieties. Those who can patiently hear such things can believe them. We have therefore sent letters to our brothers and fellow bishops, the Tarraconensians, Carthaginians, Lusitanians, and Galicians [Note: It is clear from what Quesnel adduces in note 9 that the bishops of Gallaecia are meant here. He would prefer *Gallicios* or *Gallaecos*; but *Gallicos* for *Gallicios* is frequently found in manuscripts, as Coustantius observed in note c, p. 738, on the letter of Siricius to Himerius. It is surprising that the Baetici are omitted, since the synod convened against the Priscillianists at Leo’s command consisted of bishops from Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Lusitania, and Baetica, as is clear from the Rule of Faith appended to the First Council of Toledo, which was composed at Leo’s direction. If the Gallaecians, whom Leo here ordered to meet with the others, are not mentioned in this synod, some obstacle must have prevented them from joining the other Spaniards; hence, because they were absent, the Rule of Faith was sent from that synod to Balconius, metropolitan of Gallaecia. We shall also note below, in observation 83 (inferior, h), another distinct synod held shortly afterward by the Gallaecians.] and have announced to them a council of a general synod. It will be your Belovedness’s responsibility to ensure that the authority of our decree [Note: Papal letters have been called *authorities* in a special sense because, by reason of the primacy, they possess chief authority in the whole Church. Thus Zosimus says in Letter 1 to the bishops of Gaul, no. 1: “It is clear that we have sent this authority everywhere.” Hence in the ancient Vatican Palatine manuscript 574, which contains an old Gallican collection, the constitutions of the Roman pontiffs are entitled as follows: “Authority of Pope Innocent,” “Authority of Pope Zosimus,” and so forth. Compare Leo’s Letter 19, chapter 1.] be conveyed to the bishops of the aforementioned provinces.

But if anything should intervene—which God forbid—to prevent a general council from being held, [Note: The Spanish Vindobonese manuscript reads: “if any should oppose it—which God forbid.” This means some obstacle, whether from different rulers or, more probably, from war and the public disorder of Spanish affairs. Because of these circumstances, travel among the priests of God became difficult and their meetings rare, as Leo himself relates in the preface to this letter.] let at least the priests of Gallaecia come together in one place. [Note: Thus the manuscripts, both Quesnel’s and ours. Another reading is *congregatis* (“when assembled”). The Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, omits both readings, writing: “for whom our brothers Aedacius . . .” The Spanish Vindobonese manuscript reads *Dacius*.] Our brothers Idacius and Ceponius will oversee their assembly, with your zeal joined to theirs, so that a remedy may as soon as possible be brought to such great wounds by a provincial gathering. [Note: Quesnel added the chronological note from the Corbie, Barb. 1, Trecopith, Chiflet, and three Thuan manuscripts, as well as Surius’s edition. Most of our manuscripts confirm it. In this letter the name is usually written *Calipio*, which is related to *Callypio* in the common editions of Valentinian’s Novels. But the Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1, and the Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, have *Calepio*. The name is written this way not only in the Latin fasti of Prosper, Idatius, Marcellinus, and Cassiodorus, and in the older and more accurate copies of the Novels cited by Riterius—Ottobonian and Würzburg manuscripts, Novel 5, *On Sepulchres*, and Novel 3, *On the Palatine Offices*—but also in the inscription of the Basilica of Saint Paul, no. 201. We have therefore adopted this reading.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of the illustrious men Calepio and Ardabur.

# THE LETTER OF SAINT TURRIBIUS OF ASTURICA

Concerning the rejection of apocryphal writings as authoritative for the faith, and concerning the sect of the Priscillianists. (C, G)

[Col. 0693A]

To the holy and most blessed bishops IDACIUS and CEPONIUS, worthy of all veneration: TURRIBIUS.

## CHAPTER I

A journey is always burdensome and unpleasant when harsh labors and tearful cares of necessity afflict it [Alternative: “produce them”]. Yet it has something helpful, since, as we approach unknown places or learn what was previously unknown, we are enlarged by a certain progress of mind. Often we come to recognize that things which seemed excellent among us are perverse and utterly bad, once the reasoning of better things has been made known to us.

This happened to me. As I traveled through different provinces, I found in all the churches that remain in communion with unity, with every sect of error condemned, that one and the same understanding of the Catholic faith was held, coming from the purest fountain of truth: a faith not split into divergent channels by many little streams and discharged across the level fields into muddy chasms that obstruct the straight path of faith. But those whom the poison of perverse doctrines has infected are either compelled, once corrected, to be restored to the bosom of their pious mother, or, if obstinately defiant, are expelled from the fellowship of the holy inheritance like aborted offspring and illegitimate children.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, after a long span of years, when I returned to my homeland, it seemed sufficiently grievous to me that I found nothing at all diminished of those traditions that the Catholic Church once condemned and that I had believed long ago to have been abolished. Indeed, I recognize that, according to each person’s zeal and perverse will, the evil doctrines sprout like many-headed serpents. Some have added to the ancient error further blasphemies; others still retain it intact; while others, whom contemplation of the truth has led in some measure to regard it, remain bound by retaining certain of its ideas and by the rest.

This has grown more freely because of the evils of our time, since assemblies of synods and their decrees have ceased; and, most impiously—which is worse than everything else—people come together at one altar with different understandings of the faith.

## CHAPTER III

I confess that my daring to speak of these things arises rather from pious love for my homeland than from rash presumption. Otherwise, since I am full of every sin and guilty of grave crimes, with what audacity would I write these things to you, remembering the Lord’s saying: “You see the speck in another’s eye, but you do not consider the beam in your own” (Matthew 7:3)?

Further, I am conscious of the sentence that admonished us, saying: “God said to the sinner: Why do you proclaim my righteousnesses and take up my covenant through [lacuna] yours?” (Psalm 49:16).

But again I consider what is written below: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (ibid., 18). For not only are those acts thefts that are committed by plundering the property of others, nor only those acts adulteries that we commit by violating the affections of the marriage bed. Rather, when what is true is taken away, the assertion of perverse doctrine makes thieves of us with respect to the Catholic faith; and, contrary to the truth of God’s word, seeds of weeds are sown through the adultery of evil teachings.

Should I speak, then, or remain silent? I do not know, because I fear both. But lest your Holiness perhaps remain unaware of what evils and how great blasphemies are contained in the apocryphal books that these local heretics of ours read in place of the holy Gospels, I believe myself guilty of a very great crime if I keep silent. Therefore, what follows is not an exhortation claiming any authority but rather an instructional proposal.

## CHAPTER IV

The first thing, then, is that I disclose what I have learned to exist in the faith—or rather, the infidelity—of many. Although these doctrines are taught by many almost with public authority, whenever some Catholic resists their assertion with a little greater firmness, in order to destroy it, they immediately deny it and conceal infidelity with infidelity.

Let them no longer do this, and let them no longer prefer the apocryphal writings to the canonical books as though they were secret and hidden books—writings that they receive with the greatest veneration. From the traditions they read in them and from the sayings of their own authors, they teach that certain things criticized in those writings are true. Yet some doctrines found in their teaching are not found in the apocryphal books that I have been able to read.

I therefore do not know from where they have produced them, unless perhaps something is indicated inwardly where it is written through those quibbles by which they falsely claim that the holy apostles speak—something that should be argued rather than read. Or perhaps there are other books that are kept more secretly and hidden, open, as they themselves say, only to the perfect.

## CHAPTER V

But in particular, among those Acts that are said to be the Acts of Saint Thomas, the following must be noted and execrated above all else: that it says he does not baptize with water, as the Lord’s preaching teaches, but with oil alone. Our people do not accept this [Perhaps read: “are beginning to accept it”], but the Manichaeans follow it.

This heresy, which uses the same books and pursues the same doctrines—and doctrines even worse—must be condemned as execrable by all throughout the world at the first confession of its profession, without further investigation. For it is clear that through its authors, or through its supreme leader Manes and his disciples, all the apocryphal books were either composed or infected.

In particular, this applies to the Acts called those of Saint Andrew; to those called the Acts of Saint John, which Leucius wrote with sacrilegious speech; to those called the Acts of Saint Thomas; and to similar works. From these works the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, or whatever sect is kindred to them, strive to confirm their entire heresy—especially from that most blasphemous book called the *Memorial of the Apostles*. In it they falsely attribute to the Lord, for the great authority of their perversity, a teaching that destroys the entire law of the Old Testament and everything divinely revealed to Saint Moses concerning the various creatures and their Maker, besides the remaining blasphemies of the same book, which I am weary of recounting.

## CHAPTER VI

Just as there is no doubt that those marvels and miracles written in the apocryphal books either are or could have been those of the holy apostles, so it is established that those arguments and assertions of evil interpretations were inserted by heretics. From these writings I arranged under their respective titles various testimonies full of every kind of blasphemy, and I responded to them as far as I was able, according to the quality of my understanding.

## CHAPTER VII

I considered it necessary to explain these matters somewhat more fully to your ears so that, hereafter, no one may say, as though ignorant of the facts, that he simply possesses or reads books of this kind. It will rightly belong to your judgment and assessment to weigh everything and, together with your other brothers—whoever zeal for the Catholic religion or pious devotion joins to you—to cut off that excuse with spiritual joy, and to restrain with the fiery power of the divine word those things that you see to be unambiguously contrary to truth and faith.

# LETTER XVI

[Note: Written on 21 October in the year 447.]

[Note: This letter is included in all the ancient collections up to collection 13, except collections 2 and 4, as well as in the later collections from 21 through 24; Cresconius also preserves it almost in full from Dionysius. Among the principal manuscripts against which we compared it, the most noteworthy are the older Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1; another Vatican manuscript, collection 3; the Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5; another Vatican manuscript, no. 5845, a pure Dionysian witness; and the very ancient Veronese manuscript, no. 60, of Cresconius. We shall cite the remaining manuscripts of the other collections in the notes.]

## TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SICILY

[Col. 0695B]

[Note: We restored the titles taken from Dionysius according to the authority of the manuscripts, from which we supplied the fifth title that Quesnel had omitted. In the table of collection 5, no. 78, this brief title is read: “To the bishops of Sicily, that they should not administer baptism on the day of Epiphany.”]

## SYNOPSIS

*(From Dionysius Exiguus.)*

I. That the celebration of baptism on the day of Epiphany is prohibited.

II. That all the sacraments of salvation have been arranged for us in the order of events through the incarnation of our Lord.

III. That in baptism death comes through the killing of sin; that the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial; and that the lifting up from the waters is like a resurrection from the tomb.

IV. That blessed Peter baptized three thousand men on the day of Pentecost.

V. That only two times, namely Easter and Pentecost, have been appointed by the Roman pontiffs for baptism.

VI. That at every time those who are pressed by the necessity of death [Alternative addition: “that is, by illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck”] ought to be baptized.

VII. That every three years three bishops from Sicily [Alternative: “from among the bishops, on the third day before the Kalends of October”] should come to Rome and attend the synod without concealment. [Col. 0695C]

LEO, bishop, sends greeting in the Lord to all the bishops established throughout Sicily. [Note: The words “greeting in the Lord” are absent from the Vatican Regius manuscript and another Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: Twenty-five, question 1, “Divine Commands,” chapter 2.]

We are urged by divine commands and apostolic admonitions [Note: Thus, together with the earlier editions, all our manuscripts except the Spanish Vatican manuscript and Isidore, which, with Quesnel, read “we are formed”—] to watch over the condition of all the Churches with unremitting concern and, if anything anywhere is found liable to reproach, to recall it promptly either from ignorant lack of knowledge or from presumptuous usurpation. [Col. 0696A] [Note: Alternatively, “while he admonishes” or “while he exhorts.” The Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, reads “while the Lord’s command remains,” omitting *enim* (“for”).]

For the command of the Lord’s voice remains, by which the most blessed apostle Peter is instructed through the threefold repetition of a mystical injunction to feed Christ’s sheep, whoever loves Christ. The reverence of the very see over which, through the abundance of divine grace, we preside [Note: Alternatively, “we exhort,” supported by two manuscripts of the inferior collections] constrains us to avoid, as far as we can, the danger of negligence, lest the profession of the chief Apostle, by which he testified that he was a lover of the Lord, should not be found in us—those who, by feeding the flock entrusted to us so negligently, are convicted of not loving the chief Shepherd. [Note: Manuscripts of collection 21 and the Veronese manuscript of Cresconius read *promissio* (“promise”). Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript, collection 3, and another Vatican manuscript, collection 24, have *qui* (“who”) instead of *qua* (“by which”). The editions before Quesnel, contrary to all our manuscripts, read *vana* (“empty”)—.]

## CHAPTER I. Baptism is to be celebrated not on Epiphany but at Easter.

Since, then, through the brotherly affection with which I am concerned about the affairs of your Charity, reliable indications have made it known to me that you differ from the custom of apostolic institution in what is the chief of the Church’s sacraments, so that you celebrate the sacrament of baptism more abundantly on the day of Epiphany than during the Easter season [Note: The manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection, together with Justellus; the manuscripts of collection 11; and Cresconius read *celebretur* (“is celebrated”), while the Spanish Vindobonese manuscript reads *celebratur* (“it is celebrated”).], I am astonished that you or your predecessors could have presumed upon so unreasonable an innovation as to believe that, by confusing the times of the two mysteries, there was no difference between the day on which Christ was adored by the Magi and the day on which Christ rose from the dead. [Note: Cresconius reads “with the times of the two mysteries confused.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican Regius manuscript and the Vatican manuscript, collection 3, together with the manuscripts of collection 24 and the editions before Quesnel, omit *Christus* (“Christ”) before “from the dead.”]

You could in no way have fallen into this fault if, from the source where you receive the consecration of your honor, you had taken the rule of the whole observance, and if the see of the blessed apostle Peter, which is the priestly mother of your dignity, had been the teacher of ecclesiastical discipline. [Note: See Quesnel’s note 1 and our observation.] Your departure from whose rules could have been tolerated with less equanimity [Note: The editions preceding Quesnel, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, read “with less equanimity.” Thereafter, those same editions read: “if no rebuke of our agitation had preceded,” a reading that would be preferable if *majore* or *magis* (“greater” or “more”) had been written earlier. The manuscripts of collection 24 read: “if no page of our admonition had preceded.” The Vatican manuscript, collection 3, and the Vindobonese manuscript, collection 5, in a second hand, read: “if no impatience at our agitation had preceded.”] if some rebuke of our admonition had preceded.

But now, because correction is not despaired of, gentleness must be maintained. And although an excuse that pleads ignorance is scarcely tolerable in priests [Note: The same common editions have *inscitiam* (“ignorance”), together with one Vatican Regius manuscript, collection 1, which shortly afterward prefers *rationibus* (“reasons”) instead of *ratione* (“reason”). The Vercelli manuscript and Cresconius read: “Nevertheless, we preferred—”], we nevertheless prefer both to temper the necessary censure and to instruct you by the clearest reasoning of truth.

## CHAPTER II. The distinction between times and mysteries is to be maintained.

The restoration of the human race, indeed, remained immutably preordained in God’s eternal plan; but the temporal order in which all things were to be accomplished through Jesus Christ our Lord took its beginning with the Incarnation of the Word. Hence there is one period when, at the announcement of the angel (Luke 1:26), the blessed Virgin Mary believed that she would conceive through the Holy Spirit and conceived; another when, with her virginal integrity preserved, the child who had been born was announced to the shepherds amid the joyful rejoicing of the heavenly ministers (Luke 2:7); another when the infant was circumcised (ibid., 21); another when the legally prescribed sacrificial victim was offered on his behalf; another when three Magi, stirred by the radiance of the new star, arrived from the East at Bethlehem (Matt. 2:1), and venerated the child whom they adored by presenting mystical gifts.

Nor are the days the same on which he was withdrawn from the impious Herod by the divinely ordered transfer to Egypt (ibid., 15), or on which, after the persecutor’s death, he was recalled from Egypt to Galilee (ibid., 20). Amid these various stages of the divine dispensation, [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “follow.”] bodily growth also advances: the Lord grows, as the Evangelist testifies, in the progress of age and grace (Luke 2:52); during the days of Passover he comes with his parents into the temple at Jerusalem (ibid., 41); and when he has remained behind from the company of those returning, he is found sitting among the elders and disputing with the teachers, who marvel at him. Giving the reason for his remaining behind, [Note: The Vindobonensis Spanish manuscript reads *mansionis* (“remaining”). A little later, Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1 and the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 read “Did you not know” for “Did you not know.”] he says: “Why is it that you were seeking me?” Did you not know [Col. 0697C] that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” (ibid., 49)—signifying that he was the Son of him whose temple it also was.

But when, in his more mature years, he sought the baptism of his forerunner John in order to be more openly revealed, what uncertainty remained concerning his divinity, when, after the Lord Jesus had been baptized, the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained, while the Father’s voice was heard from heaven saying: “You are my beloved Son; [Note: The first hand of the Vindobonensis manuscript and one more recent Vatican manuscript read: “in whom I have been well pleased.” Another Vatican manuscript has the same reading, but “well” has been deleted.] in you I have been well pleased” (Matt. 3:17; Luke 3:22; 9:35)?

We have touched upon all these matters as briefly as we could, so that your Affection may know that all the days of Christ were consecrated by innumerable virtues, and that the mysteries of the sacraments shone forth in all his actions; but [Note: Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, the pure Dionysian Vatican manuscript, and Veronese Cresconius, with the editions before Quesnell, read *quoque* (“also”); Justellus reads *quid quod*. Manuscripts of collection 24 omit this word.] that each matter is proclaimed in one way by signs and fulfilled in another way by events. Nor can everything that is counted among the works of the Savior [Note: The word *posse* (“can”) is absent from Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1, Vatican manuscript of collection 24, and the editions preceding Quesnell. The Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts of the collection, and the Veronese Cresconius manuscript, read *potest* (“can”). Shortly afterward, “let us recall” follows in the Vatican Regina manuscript and, in a second hand, in the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5. Perhaps the other manuscripts descend from older exemplars in which the letters *re* were omitted because of the sequence of similar letters at the end of the preceding word, *honore* (“honor”).] be assigned indiscriminately to the time of baptism. For if we were to honor without distinction even those things that we know were done by the Lord after the baptism of blessed John, all times would have to be devoted to continuous feasts, because all are full of miracles.

Yet because the Spirit of wisdom and understanding so instructed the apostles and the teachers of the whole Church that, in Christian observance, he allowed nothing disordered and nothing confused, the reasons for the solemnities must be distinguished, and in all the institutions of our Fathers and leaders a reasonable distinction must be maintained. [Note: The pure Dionysian Vatican manuscript, another Cresconius manuscript, 1347, and the manuscripts of collection 24, together with the editions preceding Quesnell, read: “a distinction must be maintained.” Some manuscripts read: “strictness.”] For we are one flock and one shepherd only if, as the Apostle teaches, “we all say the same thing”; and if “we are perfect in the same understanding and in the same judgment” (1 Cor. 1:10). [Note: This is the Apostle’s text, as found in most of our manuscripts. Vatican manuscript of collection 24 and three others cited by Quesnell in the margin read *scientia* (“knowledge”) instead. Justellus, Cresconius, and another Thuanus manuscript read *sapientia* (“wisdom”). In the earlier hand of the Veronese Cresconius manuscript the reading is *sapientia*; in the later hand, *scientia*.]

## Chapter III. Why Baptism Is Celebrated Only at the Solemnities of Easter and Pentecost

Although the things that pertain to Christ’s humility and those that pertain to his glory come together in one and the same person, and everything in him that belongs to divine power and human weakness tends toward the effecting of our restoration, [Note: Alternatively, “that which is in him.”] [Note: *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “Properly in the death,” chapter 13.] nevertheless it is particularly in the death of the crucified one and in the resurrection [Note: The editions preceding Quesnell, together with the Vatican, Spanish, and Isidorian manuscripts, read “from the dead.” Shortly afterward, those same editions, together with Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1, the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, and Justellus, place the name “Paul” before the word “Apostle.”] of the one who died that the power of baptism creates the new creature from the old, so that both the death and the life of Christ may operate in those who are reborn. As the blessed Apostle says:

“Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death? We have therefore [Note: We have restored the particle *enim* (“for”), deleted by Quesnell, from manuscripts of the Dionysian collection 4, the Hadrianic, Spanish, and Isidorian collections, and others. The Vindobonensis Spanish manuscript reads “in death.”] been buried with him through baptism [Col. 0698C] into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too may walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be [in the likeness] of his resurrection” (Rom. 6:3, 5);

and the other things that the teacher of the nations discussed at greater length in commendation of the sacrament of baptism. Thus it would be evident, from the spirit of this teaching, that for the regeneration of the children of human beings and their adoption as children of God, that day and that time [Note: The Vindobonensis Spanish and Veronese Cresconius manuscripts, with Justellus, delete *esse* (“to be”). It was also lacking in the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, but was supplied by an ancient hand.] were chosen in which, through the likeness and form of the mystery, the things accomplished in the members would correspond to those accomplished in the head himself: while, according to the rule of baptism, death occurs through the killing of sin; the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial; and the raising from the waters resembles the one rising from the tomb.

The very character of the rite therefore teaches that the proper day for celebrating grace generally is the day on which both the power of the gift and the form of the action arose. In confirmation of this, it is of great importance that the Lord Jesus Christ himself, after he had risen from the dead, gave his disciples—in whom all the rulers of the Churches were being instructed—both the form and the authority for baptizing, saying: “Go, [Note: Vatican Regina manuscript adds *ergo* (“therefore”). The editions preceding Quesnell, together with the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 and the manuscripts of collection 24, read “therefore now.”] teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

He could certainly have instructed them about this even before his Passion, unless he had specifically wished it to be understood that the grace of regeneration began with his resurrection. To this observance is also added the solemnity of Pentecost, consecrated by the coming of the Holy Spirit, which depends upon the celebration of Easter. And although other feasts belong to other days, this one always falls in relation to the day distinguished by the Lord’s resurrection, extending, as it were, the hand of assisting grace and inviting those whom illness, the length of the journey, or the difficulty of navigation kept away from the day of Easter, so that, impeded by whatever necessities, they may obtain through the gift of the Holy Spirit the fulfillment of their desire. [Note: The same editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, corruptly read: “extending, as it were, the hand of assisting grace, so that those whom illness or the length of the journey kept unwillingly shut out from the day of Easter, or whom any necessities had hindered, may obtain the fulfillment of their desire,” and so forth. Quesnell corrected the passage on the basis of his manuscripts, which are supported by the others in our collection.]

For the only-begotten Son of God did not wish there to be any difference between himself and the Holy Spirit in the faith of believers or in the power of works, because there is no difference in nature. He says: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever: [Note: The Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, both Spanish manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and Veronese Cresconius, together with Merlin, Justellus, and other earlier editions, place a comma before “Spirit of truth.” Shortly afterward some manuscripts and Justellus read “my Father will send”; Vatican Regina reads “He himself will guide you.” The Vindobonensis Spanish manuscript inserts “of the Lord”; shortly afterward it deletes “I.”] the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16). Again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything and remind you of everything that I have said to you” (ibid., 26). And again: “When that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). Since, then, Christ is the truth, and the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of truth, and the name “Paraclete” is proper to both, the feast is not dissimilar where there is one sacrament.

## Chapter IV. From the Apostolic Example, Baptism Is Celebrated at Pentecost

[Note: *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “Properly in the death,” § “But this,” chapter 13.]

We demonstrate that we maintain this observance not on the basis of our own persuasion but on apostolic authority, by a sufficiently appropriate example: we follow blessed Peter the Apostle, who on the very day when the promised coming of the Holy Spirit filled the entire number of believers consecrated, through his preaching, three thousand [Note: Not a few manuscripts read *populorum* (“of peoples”).] people who had been converted by the bath of baptism. The Holy Scripture, which contains the Acts of the Apostles, teaches this through a faithful account, saying:

“When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart and said to Peter and the other apostles: ‘What shall we do, men and brothers?’ But Peter said to them: ‘Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins; and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. For [Note: Manuscripts of collection 21 read “this promise.” A little later the words “on that day” are added in both Vindobonensis manuscripts of collection 5 and Spanish manuscripts, in the Vercellese Hadrianic manuscript, in Veronese Cresconius, and in Justellus.] the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far away, whoever the Lord our God shall call.’”

He also testified and exhorted them with many other words, saying: “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” Therefore those who received his word were baptized, and about three thousand souls were added on that day (Acts 2:37–41).

## Chapter V. In Cases of Necessity, Baptism Must Be Administered at Any Time

Since it is therefore most clearly evident that the two times about which we have spoken are the proper times for baptizing the elect in the Church, we admonish your Affection not to mix any other days into this observance. For, [Ed.: Chapter VI.] [Note: We have restored the particle *etsi* (“although”) in place of *si* (“if”), although the following *tamen* (“nevertheless”) seems to require it, on the authority of Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1, the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 in a second hand, and other Vatican manuscripts of collections 21 and 24. The Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts omit both *etsi* and *si* here.] although there are also other feasts to which great reverence is owed in honor of God, we must nevertheless preserve the principal and greatest sacrament’s [Note: Quesnell, who reports various readings of this passage in note 2, preferred *mystica et rationabilis exemplatio* (“mystical and reasonable exemplification”), chiefly because he believed the reading printed by Justellus to belong to Dionysius and Cresconius. We have instead inserted into the text the reading of the pure Dionysian Vatican manuscript 5845, which is further confirmed not only by the ancient Cresconian Vatican manuscript 1347, but also by Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1, Vatican manuscript of collection 3, and another Dionysian manuscript cited by Harduin. The Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 also has this reading in its first hand; in the second hand only the word *rationabilis* (“reasonable”) was corrected in place of *rationalis* (“rational”). The Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, which plainly derive from the pure Dionysian text, have, like the Thuanus manuscript and the Trecopithoean collection 5, *mystice* or *mysticae rationalis exceptio* (“mystically” or “a mystical and rational exception”). This approaches our reading, but differs greatly from the one preferred by Quesnell. We found the latter in several manuscripts of the Hadrianic collection, which Justellus followed. The editions before Quesnell, together with Merlinus and several manuscripts, read *mysticae rationis exceptio* (“an exception of mystical reasoning”). One Vercellese manuscript and the Veronese Cresconius manuscript read *mystica et rationalis exemptio* (“a mystical and rational exemption”). Here *exceptio* or *exemptio* signifies that, apart from Easter and Pentecost—which feasts were assigned for the administration of baptism for a mystical and rational reason—the other feast days were exempted from that ministry by a mystical and rational exception, since they do not possess the same reason; and therefore this exception must be preserved unless necessity in some particular case requires otherwise, as is added below.] mystical and rational exception. [Note: *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “If anyone out of necessity,” chapter 16.]

This does not prohibit the permission by which assistance is provided at baptism, at whatever time, to those in danger. Thus we defer the free vows of the sound and those living in the security of peace to these two festivals, joined and related to each other, so that, in danger of death, in the peril of siege, amid the distress of persecution, or in fear of shipwreck, we may at no time deny anyone this singular aid of true salvation. [Note: The editions preceding Quesnell, together with only our manuscripts of collection 24, read “this remedy.”]

## Chapter VI. The Mystery of Christ Approaching the Baptism of John

[Note: *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “But if anyone [regarding] Epiphany”; and in the *Decretum*, IV, book I.]

If anyone thinks that the feast of Epiphany, which must be venerated in its proper order with due honor, [Note: A Vatican Dionysian exemplar, with the Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts and two Cresconius manuscripts, reads “thinks.”] has the privilege of baptism because [Note: See Quesnell, note 3.] some people believe that on that same day the Lord approached the baptism of Saint John, let him know that the grace and the purpose of that baptism were different, and that it did not belong to the same power by which those who are spoken of as “not [Note: One Vercellese manuscript and Vatican manuscript of collection 11, with the editions before Quesnell, read “of bloods.” Shortly afterward Veronese Cresconius and Vatican manuscript of collection 24 read “from the desire of the flesh.”] born of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” are reborn through the Holy Spirit (John 1:13). For the Lord, needing no forgiveness of sin and seeking no remedy of rebirth, wished to be baptized just as [Note: We have inserted *et* (“also”) from Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1, the pure Dionysian Vatican manuscript, and the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5; both Spanish manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and two Cresconius manuscripts agree. Merlin and Vatican manuscript of collection 24 read “just as he wished to be circumcised.” A little later some manuscripts and the earlier editions read “but to fulfill.”] he also wished to be circumcised, and to have a sacrifice of purification offered for himself (Matt. 3:15): so that he who had been made from a woman, as the Apostle says, might also become subject to the law (Gal. 4:4)—the law that he had not come to abolish but to fulfill (Matt. 5:17), and, by fulfilling it, to bring to completion, as the blessed Apostle proclaims: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4). [Note: The Vatican, Spanish, and Isidorian manuscripts and the Veronese Cresconius manuscript, together with Justellus, read “and as.” The Vindobonensis Spanish manuscript reads “as the Apostle says, saying.”]

He established in himself the sacrament of his baptism, because, holding primacy in all things (Col. 1:18), he taught that he was the beginning. And he sanctioned the power of regeneration when blood of redemption and water of baptism flowed from his side (John 19:34).

Just as, therefore, the Old Testament was a testimony to the New, and the law was given through Moses, while grace and truth came through Jesus Christ (John 1:17), [Note: The editions preceding Quesnell read “thus differently.” Shortly afterward, they read *praeformarunt* (“prefigured”), which Quesnell would gladly have retained had he not thought it necessary, on the authority of Dionysius, Cresconius, and five manuscripts, to substitute *reformarunt* (“reformed”), as he noted in note 4. We have restored the reading from the most excellent manuscripts: Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1, another Vatican manuscript of collection 3, and several others from collections 11, 21, and 24. It is also supported by the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, in which the first hand indeed had *reformarunt*, but an ancient copyist who compared the codex with another older one corrected it to *performaverunt* (“gave full form to”). Shortly afterward, some manuscripts read “the sins of the world.”] just as different sacrifices prefigured one victim, and the slaughter of many lambs came to an end in the immolation of the one of whom it is said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), so John was not Christ but Christ’s forerunner; not the bridegroom but the bridegroom’s friend. He was so faithful, seeking not his own interests but those of Jesus Christ, that he declared himself unworthy to untie the sandals of his feet (Matt. 3:11; Luke 3:16). For John baptized with water for repentance, but Christ was to baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire (ibid.), by a twofold power both restoring life and consuming sins.

Since there are therefore, dearest brothers, so many and such great testimonies by which, with every ambiguity removed, you clearly recognize that, for the elect who are to be baptized—who, according to apostolic [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “teaching.” See Quesnell, note 5.] rule, must be examined by exorcisms, sanctified by fasts, and instructed by frequent preachings [Note: See Quesnell, note 6.]—only two times are to be observed, namely Easter and Pentecost, [Note: *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “Two times,” chapter 12.] we announce this to your Affection, so that you may not thereafter depart in any way from the apostolic institutions. [Note: *De Consecratione*, distinction 4, “This to your,” chapter 10.] For after this it cannot remain unpunished if anyone should believe that the apostolic rules may be neglected in any respect.

## Chapter VII. On the Council to Be Held Annually at Rome

Therefore, first of all, for the preservation of the most harmonious unity, we require this: since it has been most beneficially established by the holy Fathers that there ought to be two gatherings of bishops every year, let three of you always, on the third day before the Kalends of October, come to Rome to be joined in fraternal council, without fail. [Note: Quesnell, in the margin at “the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October,” follows two manuscripts, which we infer to be the Thuanus and Trecopithoean manuscripts of collection 5, from our Vindobonensis manuscript of the same collection, the only one that similarly gives this reading. We have not altered the following text because of the authority of Dionysius, whom all the Hadrianic, Spanish, Isidorian, and later collections follow. The three most ancient collections, however, contain an addition, though with somewhat differing readings. Quesnell’s two manuscripts, the Thuanus and Trecopithoean manuscripts of collection 5, add after *indissimulanter occurrant* (“come without fail”), according to Quesnell, “and let this custom be maintained by you.” Our Vindobonensis manuscript of the same collection reads: “Let them come without fail to the fraternal council at Rome, and through you let this custom be maintained.” Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1 has the same reading, with the words *occurrant et per* (“let them come, and through”) omitted merely through the copyist’s carelessness. Vatican manuscript of collection 3 reads somewhat differently: “Let them come to the fraternal council at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October, and let this custom be maintained without fail by you.” The editions before Quesnell, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, read: “Let them come, joined to the fraternal council at Rome, and let this custom be maintained without fail by you.” Nicolini’s edition in the text, and several others in the margin, though we do not know from which manuscript, read *indissimulanter concurrant* (“let them assemble without fail”), adding: “This is not difficult if this custom is maintained among you in turn.” The Vercellese manuscript and Justellus, adopting the Dionysian reading, have *concurrant* (“let them assemble”).]

For, with the grace of God assisting, it will more easily be possible to ensure that no scandals arise and no errors are born in the Churches of Christ, when, in the presence of the most blessed Apostle Peter, it is always jointly discussed, so that all his constitutions and the decrees of the canons may remain inviolable among all the priests of the Lord. [Note: This reading is better supported by the more authoritative and most of our manuscripts than Quesnell’s *tractandam fuerit* (“will have to be discussed”), or the reading *tractatum fuerit* (“will have been discussed”) found in other editions on the basis of manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, where *in communione* (“in communion”) is also wrongly read for *in commune* (“jointly”). Shortly afterward, the older Vulgate, together with some manuscripts, reads “all the institutions” instead of “all his constitutions.”]

We wish these matters, which we have believed should be brought to your attention at the Lord’s prompting, to reach your knowledge through our brothers and fellow bishops, Baccillus and Paschasinus. [Note: Vatican Regina reads *Bacyllum*. Vatican manuscript of collection 3, together with another Vatican manuscript of collection 21, reads *Bacellum et Paschasium*. The Spanish Vatican manuscript, together with the manuscripts of collections 11 and some of collection 21, reads *Vacillum*, or *Vachillum et Paschasium*. One Vercellese manuscript reads *Vacillium*; another, *Bacillum et Paschasium*. Shortly afterward, Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1 and the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 read “the statutes of the Apostolic See.”] Through their report we shall learn how reverently the institutions of the Apostolic See are observed by you.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Calepio and Ardabur. [Note: We have corrected this on the basis of Vatican Regina manuscript of collection 1. Compare annotation 85 to the preceding letter. Some manuscripts lack the chronological notice. Others read *Calepodio* or *Calapodio* instead of *Calepio*. The printed editions read *Alipio*.]

# Admonition on the Following Letter (G)

1. Quesnell, who readily indulged in conjectures, attempted to cast suspicion upon the following letter through several conjectures, to the point that it might be considered either spurious, fabricated for the purpose of reclaiming for a Church certain properties wrongly alienated, or attributed to another Leo of a later age. The reason that inclined him more strongly toward this latter opinion was that, although he could find no manuscript copy of it—which chiefly moved him to doubt—he nevertheless says in his notes that “a passage from it is read in Gratian 12, q. 2, chapter 52,” where it is attributed to Leo and is inscribed as sent “to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.” But whether it belongs to Leo the first or Leo the second is disclosed neither by the ancient editions of Gratian nor by the more recent ones.

Tillemont, in note 9 of volume XV, p. 894, examined each of Quesnell’s conjectures concerning Leo and showed them to be foolish; but he said not a word about the manuscripts. We, however, who shall refute his stronger arguments in the annotations to be appended to the letter itself, have found excellent and ancient manuscripts that will indisputably vindicate these writings for our Leo, beyond the reach of every conjecture.

2. This letter has been preserved for us in manuscripts of collection 8, of which we mention four: the most ancient, Vatican 5845; Vallicellianus A. S. of the ninth century; one sufficiently ancient Vercellese manuscript; and Vatican 1353, which was copied from a very ancient Bergomate manuscript. The author of this collection, who added many very rare documents to those of Dionysius, used another collection unknown to us, which ended with Gelasius and had been compiled in the sixth century. For documents are added down to Gelasius in a sufficiently consistent chronological order, an indication that an ancient collection had been extended to that point. More will be said about this in the treatise on the ancient Collections of Canons and Constitutions, volume III.

In these manuscripts the same letter is securely asserted to belong to Leo the Great—not only from the consulate, which falls within Leo’s pontificate, but also because it is copied among fifteen other genuine letters of the same pontiff. Thus it would be rash to continue raising doubts about this one without any sufficiently certain argument.

3. This same letter is also found in the tenth-century manuscript Vatican 1343, which belonged to the Church of Pavia, and in Vatican Ottobonianus 297, collection 23. Two authors older than Gratian also incorporated several passages from the same letter into their collections: namely, Cardinal Deusdedit, book III, chapter 34, in Vatican manuscript 3833; and Saint Anselm, book V, chapter 69, and book VI, chapter 189, in several Vatican manuscripts. Finally, to omit other testimonies, Gerhoh, provost of Reichersberg, at the beginning of the twelfth century transcribed the entire letter from a German manuscript in his work *On the Building of God*, chapter 60, edited by P. Pez in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume II, part II. Thus a copy of this letter was also found in Germany.

4. Finally, it should be noted that Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, who was the first of all to print this letter in the appendix to the Mainz edition of the works of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus in the year 1604, used Cardinal Sirlet’s manuscript. From the collection of the other documents that he states he published from the same manuscript, as well as from the distinctive title that he prefixed to this letter from that manuscript, we infer that the manuscript was similar to the aforementioned Vatican Ottobonianus manuscript of collection 23. The superior authority of the other manuscripts we have cited lends greater credibility to the letter.

## Letter XVII

[Note: Written on 21 October 447.]

### To All the Bishops Established Throughout Sicily

[Note: In Vatican Ottobonianus 297, collection 23, and in the similar manuscript of Cardinal Sirlet, from which Vossius published this letter, the title reads: “Edict of Saint Leo, pope and bishop of the city of Rome, to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.” In Vallicellianus manuscript of collection 8: “Here begin the decrees of Saint Leo, pope of the city of Rome. Pope Leo to all the bishops established throughout Sicily.”]

### Synopsis

By a perpetual constitution he prohibits what was improperly done in two Sicilian Churches and unjustly undertaken there by the bishops, who had unlawfully alienated the goods of their Churches; and he decrees that violators of this enactment are to be deprived of office and communion.

Leo, pope, to all the bishops established throughout Sicily. [Note: The Vulgate editions add: “greetings in the Lord.” We have deleted this on the basis of the manuscripts of collection 8.]

The occasion of specific complaints imposes upon us the care of general oversight, so that what has been improperly done and unjustly presumed in two churches of your province may be cut off by a perpetual constitution from the usurpation of all bishops. [Note: We preferred *omnium* (“all”) on the authority of the better two Vatican manuscripts and one Vallicellian manuscript of collection 8; alternatively, *omni* (“every”). The same two Vatican manuscripts subsequently read *Tauromenitanis*.] [Note: The Vallicellian manuscript reads “has imposed.” Deusdedit reads: “what has been improperly done in two churches in two provinces”; Gerhoh reads: “what has been improperly done in two churches of our province.”] For the clerics of Tauromenium were lamenting the destitution of their church, because the bishop was dissipating all its estates by selling, giving away, and alienating them in various ways. Likewise, the clerics of Panormus, to whom a bishop had recently been ordained, brought a similar complaint before the holy synod over which we presided concerning the usurpation of the former bishop. [Note: The printed editions, as well as some manuscripts, read “they brought forward a similar cause of complaints.” The reading of the Vallicellian and Gerhoh is preferable and is confirmed by Vatican manuscript 5845, which omits *causam* and therefore requires the accusative *querimoniam*. Vossius, following the Ottobonian manuscripts and Vatican manuscript 1353, which we were obliged to supervise, inserted *cui praeesse debebamus* into the text, but noted in the margin the reading found in all the other manuscripts, *cui praesidebamus*. Moreover, two manuscripts read *de usurpationibus* rather than *de usurpatione*. We believe that the synod mentioned here was held on the third day before the Kalends of October, and that it was the synod to which three bishops from Sicily were required to come, as is clear from chapter 7 of the preceding letter.]

Although we have already arranged how the interests of both churches are to be safeguarded, [Note: The word *iam* (“already”) must be added from the superior manuscripts Vatican 5845 and Vallicellian, and from Gerhoh; it indicates that a decree had already been issued in the Roman synod. This special decree of Leo for the churches of Tauromenium and Panormus is wanting, as are many other more celebrated letters of Leo; only this general decree addressed to all Sicilians was preserved for us by the author of collection 8. This should have been noted in order to show the weakness of a certain Quesnellian objection.] nevertheless, so that this pernicious example of the most wicked plundering may henceforth become imitable by no one, we wish this form of our command to remain perpetual among you: that, without exception, we decree that no bishop dare either give away, exchange, or sell anything belonging to his church, unless perhaps he does one of these things in such a way that he foresees something better, and chooses, with the deliberation and consent of the entire clergy, what is clearly going to benefit the church. [Note: Chapter “Without exception,” in canon 12, question 2. Two manuscripts, together with Gerhoh, read *sine exspectatione* (“without expectation”).]

[Note: Among the canons attributed in the Hispanic collection, and thence in the printed collections, to the Fourth Council of Carthage, this is canon 32: “A bishop’s gift, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property without the concurrence and subscription of the clerics shall be void.” Although these canons probably are not of the Council of Carthage, they are ancient and occur in the oldest manuscript collections—Corbie 2, Barberini 3, and other Gallican collections of differing origin—under the title *Statuta Ecclesiae antiqua* (“Ancient Statutes of the Church”); in another order this canon is the fiftieth. This shows that the discipline requiring the consent and subscriptions of the clergy for alienation of church property was not from a later and more lax age, as Quesnellus objected, as though this decree could not suit Leo the Great. Those ancient statutes, from the antiquity of the collections themselves, in which “ancient,” that is, earlier than the collections, statutes are prefixed, reach at least to Leo’s age. If Pope Hilary, Leo’s immediate successor, later required the approval of a council for such alienations, that rather favors us: Leo’s precaution could easily have proved insufficient over time, so that Hilary judged a greater precaution necessary. It is therefore unsurprising that the subsequent pontiffs cited by Quesnellus, no. 5, renewed this later and stricter precaution; yet when that later practice became obsolete, Leo’s earlier precaution returned.]

For priests, deacons, or clerics of whatever order who have joined in bringing loss upon the church must know that they are to be deprived both of their rank and of communion. [Note: Quesnellus says that this twofold punishment was not inflicted in Leo’s time except perhaps, as some think, for the gravest crimes, and therefore declares the author of the letter much later. But how does he prove that the easy alienation of church property could not be counted among the gravest crimes, when enormous harm to the church resulted from it?] For it is fully just, dearest brothers, that not only by the efforts of bishops but also of the entire clergy the increase of ecclesiastical benefit should be preserved, and that the gifts of those who, for the salvation of their souls, have bestowed their own property upon the churches should remain unimpaired. [Note: The Vallicellian manuscript and Gerhoh read *ecclesiastica utilitas intemerata servetur* (“ecclesiastical benefit be preserved unblemished”); *intemerata* stands in place of *incrementa* in two other manuscripts.] [Note: The preceding word *eorum* requires *qui*, not *quae*, as found in the Vulgate and in some manuscripts: “which the faithful contributed from their own substance to the churches for the salvation of their souls.” From Vatican manuscript 5845 and Gerhoh we have removed *fideles de* and written *propriam substantiam*; the latter reading is also found in the Vercelli manuscript.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Calepius, illustrious man. [Note: The printed editions give “the eleventh day before the Kalends of November,” without support from any of our manuscripts; indeed, Vossius’s edition contradicts them and, following the manuscripts, reads “the twelfth day before the Kalends of November.” In two older manuscripts, instead of *Data* (“Given”), we find *Danda* (“To be given”) on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November. Whether this formula may indicate that this general decree of Leo was likewise established in the synod convened on the third day before the Kalends of October, at which the particular decree for the churches of Tauromenium and Panormus was issued—so that *Danda* was appended to indicate a date to be added later when the letter was sent—we leave to the judgment of others. Most manuscripts, like the printed editions, have *Calipio*, but we have preferred the reading of the Vatican Ottobonian manuscript, *Calepio*, which we proved more genuine in note 85 (692, [Note: We have fully defended this letter in the preliminary notice to the first letter, where the manuscript and printed collections containing it are also indicated.]) to letter 15. Nor is it surprising that only one consul, Calepius, is named without his colleague Ardabur, who is joined with him in the other letters of this year. It was quite customary to call Calepius alone the Western consul. We possess several laws of Valentinian issued in this year, and although both consuls are named in most of them, Calepius alone is noted in Novel 27, *On Merchants*, and Novel 3, *On the Palatini*. The same practice is evident from other documents of Leo. Thus, of the two letters of the following year, 19 and 20, the former is addressed only to Dorus Posthumianus, consul of the West, whereas the latter joins Posthumianus and Zeno. Nor should it cause difficulty that this letter is said to have been given on the same day to the same Sicilians as the preceding letter. For letters 41 and 42 to Ravennius, 136 and 137 to Marcian, and 164 and 165 to Leo Augustus show that our pontiff repeatedly wrote two letters on the same day to the same person when distinct subjects were available.]

# LETTER XVIII

[Note: Alternatively 14. What was formerly 18 is now 19. Written on 30 December 447.] [Note: We have thoroughly defended this letter in the preliminary notice to the first letter, where you will also find the manuscripts and printed collections in which it occurs. We collated it with several excellent manuscripts, to be cited in the notes. We could not collate Vatican exemplar 5845 of the pure Dionysian collection, because, owing to a defect in the manuscript, not only is this letter absent from it, but also the final chapter of the preceding letter—our letter 16—to the Sicilians. All manuscripts address it to Januarius. The editions before Quesnellus, following Merlinus, title it “To Julian,” and in the margin “To Januarius,” but this is plainly an error: the manuscripts of collection 12 themselves, from which Merlinus derived his edition, read “To Januarius.” See Quesnellus, note 1.]

## To Januarius, Bishop of Aquileia

[Note: In the table of collection 5, number 75, this title is recorded: “To Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, concerning clerics who have fallen into heresy or any schism and are not at all to be promoted.”]

### Synopsis

(From Dionysius Exiguus)

Any cleric of whatever order who, abandoning the Catholic faith, has joined a heretical communion must remain, if he returns to the church, in the rank in which he was, without promotion. [Note: Five manuscripts read “without promotion.”] [The Cresconian text reads: “in the rank in which he had been.”]

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia. [Note: The words “of the city of Rome” are omitted in the Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5.]

Having read the letter of your brotherhood, we have recognized the vigor of your faith, which we formerly knew, and we congratulate you because you diligently carry out pastoral care for the guarding of Christ’s flock. [Note: The same Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5 and manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, together with the older editions, read “the flocks of Christ.”] Thus wolves who have entered under the appearance of sheep (Matthew 7:15) may not tear the simple apart with bestial savagery, and may neither themselves improve through correction nor corrupt what is sound.

To prevent this serpentine deceit from prevailing, we have judged it necessary to admonish your affection, making clear that it endangers the soul if anyone who has fallen from us into the sect of heretics or schismatics, and has in some way stained himself by the contagion of heretical communion, is received, upon coming to his senses, into the Catholic communion without a proper declaration of satisfaction. [Note: Canon “If anyone of heretical communion,” chapter 42, in question 1. The mention of schismatics, and shortly afterward the condition “provided they have not been polluted by a repeated baptism,” appear to indicate Donatists or Novatians discovered in the province of Aquileia; see Quesnellus, note 3. But a general rule is stated here, common to all heretics and schismatics returning to the church, although it is proposed on the occasion of a particular case in the province of Aquileia. No schismatic or heretic returning to Catholic unity could be received without a proper profession of satisfaction; and even if he was a cleric, he was restored to his rank only on condition that he had not been defiled by a second baptism. Those infected by this crime were not received into the clergy but were subjected to public penance. Compare the preliminary notice to letter 1, §4, and note 25 to letter 159. It is therefore unnecessary to suppose that Leo is speaking here of Donatists or Novatians in Aquileia, for there is no other evidence of them in that province. We have shortly afterward added the word *est* from the Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5.]

For it is most salutary and completely filled with the usefulness of spiritual medicine that priests, deacons, subdeacons, or clerics of any order who wish to appear corrected and seek to return once more to the Catholic faith, which they formerly lost, should first openly acknowledge that their errors and the very authors of their errors have been condemned by them. [Note: The Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5 reads: “that their error and the authors of the error themselves be condemned.” Justellus, together with two manuscripts, has only “the authors of the error.” Another manuscript reads “condemned” instead of “be condemned.”] Thus, once their perverse dispositions have also been destroyed, no opportunity for hope should remain, and no member should be capable of being violated through association with such people, since in every respect their own profession has begun to confront them. [Note: The Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5 reads “with their perverse and long-since destroyed opinions.” The word *sperandi* (“of hoping”) appears in all manuscripts and printed editions; Quesnellus confessed in a marginal note that it was found in the postscript, but wrote, “I suspect that *spirandi* should be read.” Five of our manuscripts have *desperandi* (“of despairing”), while the others have *sperandi*.]

With regard to them also, we command that the canonical constitution be observed, so that they may regard it as a great benefit if, after every hope of promotion has been taken away, they remain in the rank in which they are found, in perpetual stability; provided they have not been defiled by a repeated baptism. [Note: The Vatican manuscript of collection 11 reads “the canonical constitution.” In the preliminary notice to letter 1, number 18, we explained which canonical enactment is understood here. See also Quesnellus, note 2. The Vindobonian manuscripts of collection 5 read “may remain in perpetual stability”; the same manuscript subsequently reads “by the sacrilege of repeated washing.”]

Anyone who has judged that one of such men should be promoted to the sacred orders incurs no slight offense before the Lord. [Note: The Dionysian printed editions and the other collections derived from Dionysius read: *ad sacros promovendos ordines judicarit*, “who has judged that someone should be promoted to the sacred orders.” The reading of the Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5, which has a different origin from Dionysius, seemed more suitable: *ad sacros ordines promovendum aliquem judicarit*, “who has judged that someone should be promoted to the sacred orders.”] If promotion is granted to the blameless only after a severe examination, much less ought it to be permitted to the suspect.

Therefore, let your affection, whose devotion gives us joy, join its care to our dispositions and see to it that the measures proposed and salutarily arranged for the safety of the whole church are carried out carefully and swiftly. [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of collection 21, read “have been arranged.”] Let your affection not doubt that, if—which we do not believe—what we decree for the guarding of the canons and the integrity of the faith should be neglected, we shall be moved with greater severity. [Note: Distinction 86, “The faults of inferiors,” chapter 1.] For the faults of those in lower orders are to be referred to no one more than to negligent and careless rulers, who often nourish great pestilence while they pretend not to apply the necessary medicine.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Calepius and Ardabur, illustrious men. [Note: Two ancient collections of different origins seem to have transmitted this letter to later collections, namely the Dionysian collection and the fifth collection.
