In the Dionysian collection, and in Cresconius, its copyist, including the very ancient Veronese manuscript, the date is given as the third day before the Kalends of January. In manuscripts of collection 5, however, two manuscripts, Thuanus and Trecopithoeanus, according to Quesnellus’s note 4, have either the Kalends or the third day before the Kalends of July. Two of our Vindobonian manuscripts of the same collection 5 differ: one, numbered 39, which we used as the more authoritative in the variants, gives the fourth day before the Nones of January; the other, numbered 42, the fourth day before the Kalends of July. Manuscripts of the other collections—Vatican, Hispanic, Isidorian, Hadrianic, and later collections—agree with Dionysius in the month and generally also in the day. Three manuscripts give only the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January; one Vercelli manuscript gives the fourth day before the Kalends. The Vindobonian manuscript of the Hispanic collection, and the editions before Quesnellus based on manuscripts of collection 24 and on Merlinus, differ both in month and day: the first gives the third day before the Kalends of July, while the others give the day before, or the second day before, the Kalends of July. In this variety we have preferred the authority of Dionysius. Since one manuscript of collection 5 agrees with him in the month, and in the day at least one copy of the same collection 5 cited by Quesnellus, as well as two of our Vindobonian manuscripts—Hispanic and Vatican collection 24—also agree with him, we have placed this letter after the letters to Turibius and to the Sicilians. It would have had to precede them if, on the basis of the other readings, it were to be assigned to June. As for the consular note, the editions, together with most manuscripts, give “in the consulship of Alipius and Ardabur, illustrious men.” Quesnellus wrote in the margin: “Alternatively, Calipius or Calepius.” We found *Calipio* in two Vindobonian manuscripts of collection 5 and in the Venetian collection 12; we printed *Calepio* for the reasons given in note 85 (692, [Note: The printed editions of Leo, after inserting a point, corruptly read *Miror, quis fieret* (“I wonder what would happen”), together with Vatican manuscripts of collections 21 and 24. Then the manuscripts of collection 21 have *furoris* (“of fury”) instead of *elationis* (“of arrogance”). The Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5, the Vatican manuscript of collection 11, the Venetian manuscript of Saint Mark’s collection 12, and the Vatican manuscript of collection 24 prefer *fortioris* (“of the stronger”). In the manuscript of Holy Cross collection 20 and in two others, Cambridge and Thuanus, cited by Quesnellus, we find “the vice of fury might overcome”; and in Vatican collection 11, “the vice of fury might be rejected.” Labbeus noted in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘he might begin to become greater, while in him not the virtue of humility but the vice of fury was strengthened.’” In the text we retained Quesnellus’s reading from Merlinus and the editions of the councils, because the word *elationis*, also confirmed in the Leonine editions, is opposed to humility and fits the whole context better than *furoris* or *fortioris*.]) in letter 15.]

# LETTER XIX

[Note: Alternatively 18. What was formerly 19 is now 20. Written on 8 March 448.] [Note: It survives in manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 12, 13, and 20 through 24. The manuscripts of Holy Cross in Jerusalem, collection 20, and Vatican Ottobonian 332, address it to Theodore. In the tables of the Beneventan church, however, he is called Dorus, as in the other manuscripts. Only in manuscripts of collection 21 is *Doroleus* written by error, the two words *Doro Leo*, which appear in the superscription of the letter, having been joined together.]

## To Dorus, Bishop of Beneventum

[Note: In the table of collection 5, at the final chapter, this title appears: “To Dorus, bishop of Beneventum, a letter of rebuke.” In the manuscripts of Holy Cross: “Concerning a priest promoted to the injury of others, and concerning those who asked that he be placed over them.”]

### Synopsis

I. He rebukes Dorus for disturbing the order of the presbytery and for the senior presbyters’ surrendering their own rights.

II. He vindicates each person’s rank according to the time of ordination, while relegating the senior men who had yielded to the lowest place.

To his dearest brother Dorus, Leo, bishop.

We grieve that the judgment we had formed concerning you has been disappointed, since we see that you have committed acts that would disgrace every rule of ecclesiastical sanction by their culpable novelty. [Note: Two of Quesnellus’s manuscripts and our Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5 add “our judgment.” The Holy Cross manuscript reads *nollemus* (“we would not wish”) instead of *dolemus* (“we grieve”). Some infer from the text that Dorus appears to have been consecrated bishop of Beneventum by Leo himself, and that Leo therefore complains that the judgment or hope he had formed concerning him—when he appointed him bishop of the Beneventans—had been frustrated. The phrases “since you know fully” and “you, whom it was fitting to know as most observant of the authority of the apostolic see” also seem to indicate that he had been drawn from the Roman clergy.]

For you know very well with what concern we wish the precepts of the fathers’ canons to be observed throughout all the churches of the Lord, and that this is especially the care of the priests of all peoples, so that the rules of the holy constitutions may not be corrupted by any excesses. Therefore we are astonished that you, whom it was fitting to know as most observant of the authorities of the apostolic see [Note: “The authorities of the apostolic see” are the constitutions of the Roman pontiffs. See note 81 (691f) on letter 15.], acted so negligently, or rather insolently, that you became not the guardian but the transgressor of the laws entrusted to you.

For from the petition of your priest Paul, which is included below, we have learned that the order of the presbytery was disturbed among you by a novel and disgraceful intrigue. [Note: This is the reading of several of our manuscripts and of Quesnellus’s manuscripts of better quality. Alternatively, *colluvio* (“pollution” or “mire”).] Thus the hasty and premature advancement of one man became the downfall of certain others whose age commended their honor and no fault diminished it. [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, read “whom age commended.” The Holy Cross manuscript reads “whom age also commended.” Quesnellus’s edition reads “whose age commended their rank.” The reading of the Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5 seemed more equitable. The honor of the priesthood is understood, hence also the expression below, “in priestly honor.”]

But if the ambition of the aspirant, or the ignorant zeal of his supporters, demanded what custom had never permitted—that a beginner and newcomer be preferred to the experienced and the old—it was your diligence and instruction that should have restrained the unjust desires of the petitioners by reasonable authority, lest, by hastily advancing anyone to priestly honor, he should begin to be an injury to those with whom he was associated. [Note: Quesnellus has this reading. Earlier editions place the preposition *in* before *sacerdotali*. The Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5 reads “whom you were hastily advancing in the priesthood to their injury.” The Holy Cross manuscript reads “whom you were hastily advancing into priestly honor.” Quesnellus noted in the margin, from one of his manuscripts, “lest you advance anyone to the priesthood.”]

He would make himself lesser, while in him the vice not of humility but of arrogance was strengthened. [Note: The Leonine editions, after inserting a point, corruptly read *Miror, quis fieret* (“I wonder what would happen”), together with Vatican manuscripts of collections 21 and 24. The manuscripts of collection 21 then have *furoris* (“of fury”) instead of *elationis* (“of arrogance”). The Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5, the Vatican manuscript of collection 11, the Venetian manuscript of Saint Mark’s collection 12, and the Vatican manuscript of collection 24 prefer *fortioris* (“of the stronger”). The Holy Cross manuscript of collection 20 and two others cited by Quesnellus, Cambridge and Thuanus, read “the vice of fury might overcome”; Vatican collection 11 reads “the vice of fury might be rejected.” Labbeus noted in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘he might begin to become greater, while in him not the virtue of humility but the vice of fury was strengthened.’” We retained Quesnellus’s reading from Merlinus and the editions of the councils because *elationis*, also confirmed by the Leonine editions, is opposed to humility and agrees better with the whole context than *furoris* or *fortioris*.]

Nor were you unaware that the Lord had said: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted, but whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11; 18:14). He also said: “But you seek to grow from a little one and to become lesser from a greater one.” [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with one Vatican manuscript of collection 21, read: “Nor were you unaware that the Lord had said that whoever humbles himself will be exalted, but whoever exalts himself will be humbled; and that he had also said: ‘Whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant, and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave. But you seek to grow from a little one and to become greater in honor.’” The Leonine manuscript used by Hincmarus, *On the Law of Metropolitans*, chapter 17, likewise has this reading. All the other manuscripts we used—fourteen manuscripts, as well as five examined by Quesnellus—omit the text beginning “Whoever wishes,” and ending “shall be your slave.” These same manuscripts, except the single Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5, immediately follow the words “and that he had also said” with “But you seek to grow from a little one.” Quesnellus, together with the cited Vindobonian manuscript, transferred the words “and that he had also said” to before “but whoever exalts himself.” The words “But you seek,” as cited in our text, were printed by Quesnellus not in the italic type used for Christ’s words but in ordinary type, as though they were Leo’s text. Furthermore, “to become lesser from the greater” is found not only in five of Quesnellus’s manuscripts but also in our Vindobonian manuscript of collection 5, Vatican collection 11, the Vatican and Venetian manuscripts of collection 12, Holy Cross collection 20, Venetian collection 22, Vatican Regina 139 collection 24, and one Fiesolan manuscript. Manuscripts of collections 21 and 23, one Vatican manuscript 544 of collection 24, read “to become greater in honor.” After Quesnellus’s first edition, Richard Simon, in *New Observations on the Text and Versions of the New Testament*, chapter 21, page 458, argued that the words “But you seek,” etc., had been taken by Leo from a copy of the Gospel according to Matthew, chapter 20, where they were likewise inserted, as they are found in the Cambridge manuscript and four other manuscript copies. He then contended that the reading should not be “to become lesser from the greater” but “to become greater from the lesser.” In his second edition, note 3, Quesnellus effectively refuted Richard’s reading. For the words that Leo adds—“For both are disordered, both are contrary to proper order”—show that two things opposed to one another had preceded. “To grow from a little one” is not opposed to “to become greater from the lesser”; rather, it is plainly opposed to “to grow from a little one” and “to become lesser from the greater.” Leo intended to censure both Epicarpius, who rose from the lowest place to the first, and those two presbyters who, withdrawing from the highest ranks in Epicarpius’s favor, agreed to become lesser. Most and better manuscripts of Leo favor the reading “to become lesser from the greater,” accepted by Quesnellus and by us. Indeed, the Latin Gospel copies mentioned by Richard also favor it, as he admits. The very ancient Vercelli Gospel book, recently edited by Father Joseph Blanchini in a work entitled *The Fourfold Gospel*, agrees with it, as may be seen at Matthew 20, after verse 28. Other ancient and excellent copies favoring the same reading are cited by Father Peter Sabatier in his notes on Matthew 20, page 120, where he discusses this addition at greater length. Richard mentions only two Gospel manuscripts supporting his reading; to these must be added our ancient Veronese exemplar, also edited by Blanchini. From the many ancient Gospel copies now published, some of which are believed to predate Leo himself, it is clear that the words “But you seek,” etc., were once inserted in Matthew’s Gospel text and read as Christ’s words between verses 28 and 29 of the Vulgate edition, although the reading in the second clause differs somewhat. Whatever one may think about which reading better suits the Gospel context, since it is certain from what has been said that the reading we have accepted suits Leo’s mind and context—and since it is found not only in more and better manuscripts of Leo but also in most of the oldest Gospel books—there is absolutely no doubt that the holy pontiff took this text from a similar copy of Matthew. Since it is also clear from this that Leo recited the text “But you seek,” etc., as Christ’s words in Matthew, while he took the preceding words from Luke, it follows that the words “and that he had also said” are rightly and properly placed before “But you seek” in almost all collections and Leonine manuscripts, so as to indicate another testimony of Christ taken from another evangelist. In the other manuscripts and in Quesnellus, those words have been improperly detached from this position and transferred earlier, so that they interrupt one continuous Lucan text and divide it into two.]

“For both are disordered, both are contrary to proper order. Every fruit of labor is taken away, and every measure of merit is emptied, if someone attains as much dignity as he has obtained flattery, so that the desire for eminence diminishes not only the proud man but also the one who connives at it.

“But if, as is asserted, the first and second presbyters showed such deference to Epicarpius [Note: Three of Quesnellus’s manuscripts read *Epicandium*; two of ours, “Epicandium the presbyter.” Shortly afterward the Holy Cross manuscript deletes *huic* (“to him”), perhaps more suitably, since it appears superfluous.]—who was to be placed over them—that they asked, to their own disgrace, that he be honored, even this should not have been granted to them when they were casting themselves down by their own judgment. For it was more fitting for you to oppose such a wretched desire than to yield to it. [Note: The printed editions read *cui tam miserae* (“to so wretched a desire”). The reading of the Holy Cross manuscript seemed preferable; it is supported by those witnesses which read *qui* (“who”).]

“Yet that shameful and cowardly submission could not, for those conscious of their own integrity and not making God’s grace void, prejudice them, so that, by transferring their primacies to one another through some sort of exchange, they should diminish the dignity of those who followed them and, because they had placed the last before themselves, make him pre-eminent over the others.” [Note: Two manuscripts read *non poterit* (“will not be able”) and, shortly afterward, *minuerint* and *anteposuerint*. The Holy Cross manuscript reads: “because they had placed the last before themselves, so that he might be pre-eminent over the rest.” The editions before Quesnellus, together with several manuscripts, read “and him whom they had placed last,” etc.]

## Chapter II

The aforesaid presbyters, therefore, who declared themselves unworthy of the order of their own honor, although they would even deserve to be deprived of the priesthood, shall nevertheless, out of the mercy of the apostolic see toward them, be counted last among all the church’s presbyters. And, so that they may bear the sentence of their own judgment, they shall be lower even than the man whom, by their own sentence, they preferred to themselves; while all the other presbyters remain in the rank assigned to each by the time of his ordination. [Note: Three manuscripts read “assigns.”]

No one except the aforesaid two shall suffer the injury of diminished dignity. Rather, this disgrace shall fall only upon their status—upon those who chose to become inferior to one newly and prematurely ordained—so that they may recognize as applying to themselves that evangelical sentence: “With the judgment you judge, you will be judged; and with the measure you measure, it will be measured out to you” (Matthew 7:2; Mark 4:24; Luke 6:38). [Note: Some manuscripts omit “the same.”]

But the priest Paul shall retain his own rank, from which he did not withdraw with commendable steadfastness. Nor shall anything further be presumed to the injury of anyone. Thus your affection, upon which the resentment of this entire affair not undeservedly presses, should hasten to cure itself at least by this remedy: that these decisions of ours be carried into effect without delay. [Note: This is the reading of the Holy Cross manuscript, which seemed more suitable to the context than the common reading and that of other manuscripts, “without concealment.”] For if a just appeal should again come to us, it will be necessary for us to be moved more severely, since, once what has been badly done has been corrected, we prefer to restore discipline rather than increase punishment.

You should know that we have entrusted the execution of our commands to our brother and fellow bishop Julius [Note: The manuscripts of Holy Cross collection 20 and Vatican collection 11 read “Julian.” Some think that Julius of Puteoli is meant, whom Leo sent as a legate to the Ephesian synod in the following year.], so that everything may immediately be strengthened as we have determined. [Note: The text formerly read *illi* (“to him”). Quesnellus suspected in the margin that *illic* (“there”) should be restored. The Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark’s collection 13 supplied the correct reading.]

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of Posthumianus, illustrious man. [Note: Some manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus read “on the Ides of March”; but the older and better witnesses read “the eighth day before the Ides,” or lack the chronological notice.]

# LETTER XX

[Note: Alternatively 19. What was formerly 20 is now 23. Written on 1 June 448.] [Note: Just as this letter is contained in manuscripts of collections 3, 8 Hispanic, Isidorian 11 and 12, 17, 21, 23, and 24, and in Sichardus, so we have consulted the more authoritative manuscripts of all these collections. We have added the Greek version from the Greek manuscripts of collection 17 of the Chalcedonian collection.]

## To Eutyches, Constantinopolitan Abbot

[Col. 0713]

[Note: The manuscripts of the Hispanic collection give this brief title: “To Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, against the Nestorian heresy.”]

### Synopsis

He replies that, having been informed by Eutyches’s letter of the resurgence of the Nestorian heresy, he approved Eutyches’s zeal.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

737. **[Note: [Col. 0713C] The Latin codices of the Chalcedonian collection, among them the eighth-century Veronese manuscript, agree more closely with the Greek text in reading “to the most desired son”; but they omit “presbyter,” although this title is not absent from the Greek.]**

**To the most beloved son Eutyches, presbyter, Leo, bishop.**

You have reported to our knowledge through the letter of your affection that the Nestorian heresy was again flourishing through the efforts of certain persons. We reply that your concern in this matter has pleased us, since the message we received is an indication of your mind. Hence you should not doubt that the Lord, author of the Catholic faith, will be present with you in all things. **[Note: [Col. 0714C] Editions before Quesnell, with several manuscripts, read “we do not doubt”; Quesnell, with other codices, especially Chalcedonian Collection 17, reads “you do not doubt.” We prefer the reading of the very ancient Vatican 5845 and Vallicellian A. S. manuscript of Collection 8, with which the Greek translation also agrees.]** But when, with the Lord’s help, we have been able to learn more fully [Col. 0713B] through whose wickedness this is happening, we must take precautions, so that the impious poison, long ago condemned, may be extinguished at the root. **[Note: [Col. 0714C] Manuscripts of Collection 21 read “importunity”; those of Collection 8, better, read “wickedness.”]**

**[Note: [Col. 0713D] Most of our codices, especially those of the Chalcedonian collection, read “letters.” Nevertheless, we have retained “letter,” on the authority especially of the oldest codices of Collections 3 and 8. We now add Quesnell’s highly pertinent observation: “We point out that this letter was written by Eutyches before the publication of his error, because we understand that some have failed to notice this; they may perhaps have been led into error because it was placed at the beginning of the Acts of Chalcedon, as though it belonged to that same synod. I say, before the publication of his error, which occurred at Constantinople in Flavian’s synod, but not, as far as can be inferred, before Domnus, bishop of Antioch, had discovered the seeds of the infamous doctrine. For before Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, brought him before episcopal judgment, Domnus’s accusation that the Apollinarian heresy was being revived through Eutyches’ efforts and devices had already been brought before the emperor Theodosius. We have a reliable witness to this in Facundus, Book VIII, chapter 5; we shall cite his words in the dissertation on the case of Eutyches, together with Domnus’s synodical letter. From these words we also learn who those people were whom Eutyches denounced to Saint Leo as followers and patrons of Nestorius: for it is clear that Domnus, Theodoret, and others of this kind are meant, since they had complained to Theodosius about Diodore and Theodore, whom Eutyches had anathematized.” Thus far Quesnell.]**

May God preserve you safe and sound, most beloved son.

**[Note: [Col. 0714C] The Chalcedonian-collection copies read: “May God keep you safe, most desired son.”]**

Given on the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Postumianus and Zeno.

**[Note: [Col. 0714C] The codices of Chalcedonian Collections 17 and 21 preserve this chronological notation.]**

---

738. **To the most desired son Eutyches, presbyter, Leo, bishop.**

You have brought to our knowledge through the letters of your affection that the Nestorian heresy is again flourishing through the efforts of certain persons. We reply that your zeal in this matter has pleased us, since the message we received is an indication of your mind. Therefore, do not doubt that the Lord, the author of the Catholic faith, will be present with you in all things. But when, with the Lord’s help, we are able to learn more fully [Col. 0714B] through whose shamelessness this is happening, it is necessary for us to take forethought, until the impious poison, long ago condemned, can be extinguished at the root. [Translator’s note: The Greek prints the corrupt verb *σεβεσθῆναι*, here read as *σβεσθῆναι* (“be extinguished”).] May God preserve you healthy, most beloved son.

---

739. **LETTER XXI [Note: [Col. 0714C] This letter was formerly numbered 21 and is now 24. It was written after 22 November 448.] FROM EUTYCHES TO SAINT LEO**

Now inserted for the first time among Leo’s letters. (G)



## SYNOPSIS

**[Note: [Col. 0714D] This letter is an ancient translation of a Greek text that is no longer extant. It is found appended to a collection of ancient documents concerning Nestorianism, edited first from a Cassinese manuscript by Christian Lupus and subsequently by Étienne Baluze. In that collection it appears as chapter 222, and three other chapters are added to it: chapter 223, a fragment of a profession of faith issued by the same heretic; chapter 224, a testimony taken from a letter attributed to Pope Julius; and chapter 225, an anonymous letter refuting Eutyches’ own letter to Leo. In the second edition of Saint Leo’s works, Quesnell printed only Eutyches’ letter in the appendix to Dissertation 7, entitled *On the Case of Eutyches*. Since the letter was delivered to Leo, however, our editorial method required that it be inserted among Leo’s letters, especially because it occasioned Letters 23 and 24. Nor should the two following chapters, which the same Eutyches appended to the letter, be separated from it. The anonymous letter, since it was neither addressed to Leo nor necessarily connected with Eutyches’ letter, is not reproduced here. Nevertheless, lest readers be deprived of this document, we have relegated it to the appendix. This letter was written by Eutyches after Saint Flavian condemned him in the Constantinopolitan synod on 22 November 448. The title is the same as that found in the Cassinese manuscript. At the beginning of the letter we have added the words “and in faith,” omitted in earlier printed editions, as suggested by Vatican codex 1319, used by Father Cacciari.]**

**Letter of Eutyches the heretic:** in it, writing to Leo, pope of the city of Rome, he denies that there are two natures in Christ, namely, divinity and humanity.

## CHAPTER I

Trusting in my hope and faith in the Lord and God of all, Christ, [Col. 0715A] God the Word himself is above all my witness, recognizing in such convictions the proof of truth. I invoke your holiness as witness to my heart, to the reasoning of my thoughts, and to my words.

But the worst devil bewitched this zeal and purpose of ours, through which his power ought to have been destroyed. Stirring up every force at his disposal, he turned Bishop Eusebius of the town of Dorylaeum against me [read: *he turned*], and he presented a written accusation to the holy bishop Flavian of the Church of Constantinople and to certain others [p. 740] who were present in that same city and had assembled for various reasons of their own.

**[Note: [Col. 0715C] This libellus against Eutyches, presented to Flavian and the other Fathers of the Constantinopolitan synod, is extant in Act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon, volume IV of the Councils, Venetian edition, p. 930.]**

[Note: [Col. 0715C] The printed editions incorrectly read *evenerant* (“had happened”) instead of *convenerant* (“had assembled”). Shortly afterward, Vatican codex 1319 reads *ad accusationem motus* (“moved to make the accusation”) instead of *accusationem movens* (“bringing an accusation”).]

He addressed me as a heretic, not bringing forward a truthful accusation but plotting my destruction and disturbance for the Churches of God.

[Col. 0715B] I was summoned by their holiness to answer the accusation. But, held back by severe illness in addition to my advanced age, I appeared to make my defense, knowing that a conspiracy had been devised against my safety.

Indeed, I immediately presented written petitions, adding my signature to them, and displayed my profession concerning the holy faith.

**[Note: [Col. 0715C] He means the libellus of appeal bearing his signature, which he complains that he offered to Flavian and the Fathers of the Constantinopolitan synod, together with his written profession of faith, before the sentence, but that it was not received. Leo calls it a libellus of appeal in Letter 23; see note 10 on that letter (col. 732, n. q). Just as these letters of Eutyches to Leo bear only Leo’s name in the address—whence also the anonymous author, in the letter reproduced in the appendix, says that they were written to Leo, the most blessed pope of the apostolic see—so the libellus of appeal appended to these letters must be understood to have expressed an appeal to Leo alone. But the account of the libellus being offered is false. For it is clear from the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod mentioned above, and much more clearly from the rereading of those acts at the Constantinopolitan meeting held on 13 April 449, that before the sentence Eutyches offered only the written profession of faith, not a libellus of appeal. All these materials are included in the first act of the Council of Chalcedon. After the sentence, when a disturbance had arisen and the meeting had dissolved, the same proceedings show that he silently indicated something about an appeal to the patrician Florentius, so that no one else heard him. See volume IV of the Councils, p. 1086. Flavian did not wish to receive the profession of faith that was offered, but ordered Eutyches to read it himself. Hence, when Eutyches later claimed at the trial that he had given libelli of appeal both to us and to the holy council assembled here, and that he had appealed to your holiness in his letter to Leo, Flavian declared that he was lying in Letter 26.]**

But when the holy archbishop Flavian neither accepted the libellus nor ordered it to be read, although he heard me and answered me in these very words, [Col. 0716A] I was required to confess two natures and to anathematize those who denied this: the faith set forth at Nicaea by the holy synod and confirmed at Ephesus.

**[Note: [Col. 0716B] We have added “this” from Vatican codex 1319. The reason why Eutyches and his disciples thereafter put forward only the Nicene faith will be explained in note 6 on Letter 54 (col. 855, n. g).]**

But, fearing the decree of the synod,

**[Note: [Col. 0716C] He means the Synod of Ephesus, which forbade any other faith besides the Nicene faith. This prohibition was directed against the Nestorians, who had produced another exposition of the faith filled with corrupt doctrines. Eutyches, however, did not wish to be compelled by this wording to profess two natures in Christ, as though this Catholic profession were a new faith forbidden by the Ephesian council. Eutyches proposed the same reasoning in the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, volume IV of the Councils, p. 919, col. D: “But I, fearing to transgress the definition issued by the holy synod which, by God’s will, had first assembled here, and the matters concerning the faith defined by the holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea, asked, etc.” See also p. 911, col. C.]**

—namely, that no word should be taken away or added against the faith set forth by the holy Synod of Nicaea—and knowing that our holy and blessed fathers Julius, Felix, Athanasius, and Gregory, most holy bishops, [p. 741] rejected the expression “two natures,” and not daring to discuss the nature of God the Word, who came in the flesh in the last days into the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, becoming man immutably, in truth and not in appearance, or to anathematize the fathers mentioned above, I asked that these matters be made known to your holiness and [Col. 0716B] that you judge what seemed right to you, professing in every respect that I would follow what you approved.

**[Note: [Col. 0716C] The only testimony attributed to Pope Julius, which Eutyches appended to his letter and which was preserved for us in the Cassinese manuscript, will be given after this letter. It is certain, however, that the Acephali, in a conference held in 533, opposed the testimonies of the same Fathers—Julius, Felix, Athanasius, and Gregory Thaumaturgus—as though they favored the Eutychian position; Catholics replied that these testimonies had formerly been fabricated by the Apollinarists. Certainly the testimony attributed to Pope Julius was taken from a letter of Apollinaris; the Apollinarists gave it the name of Pope Julius in order to create authority for it. See shortly below, note 17 (col. 718, n. h).]**

[Note: [Col. 0716D] These words seem to refer to what Basil, bishop of Seleucia, alone testified at the rereading of the acts on 13 April 449: “I know that the religious archimandrite Eutyches said: If the Roman and Alexandrian Fathers command me, I say this very thing.” He said this not as appealing, but saying: “I did not dare to say it because of the Fathers.” A little later, at the beginning of the next chapter, we have added seven words, *ante cognitionem parabant, in tantum adversum me* (“they were preparing [it] before the hearing; so greatly against me”), on the authority of the aforesaid Vatican manuscript 1319. They had been skipped because of the repetition of *adversum me* (“against me”).]

## CHAPTER II

But without hearing any of what I was saying, they abruptly dissolved the synod and published a sentence of deposition which they had prepared against me before the hearing. They armed themselves against me with such a conspiracy of slander that my life itself would have been endangered, had not God’s work, through the prayers of your holiness, quickly [Col. 0717A] rescued me from the attack of the military force.

Then they began compelling the leaders of other monasteries to sign my deposition.

**[Note: [Col. 0717C] These may perhaps be the twenty-three abbots whose signatures are found on the Constantinopolitan synod’s condemnation of Eutyches.]**

Something that had never happened, not even against those who had professed themselves heretics, nor even against Nestorius himself.

**[Note: [Col. 0717C] This had never happened, because never before had abbots been found who introduced heresy and stirred monasteries against bishops.]**

When I proposed to the people confessions of my faith in order to satisfy them, they not only prevented these from being heard, but those who had been plotting the conspiracy mentioned above against me also seized them,

**[Note: [Col. 0717C] The libellus contained not only a profession of faith but also complaints filled with accusations of injuries and abuse; it had been publicly posted at Constantinople, as Flavian relates in Letter 26. Its removal is indicated here.]**

so that thereafter I might be regarded by everyone as a heretic.

## CHAPTER III

I therefore flee to you, defenders of religion and haters of such conspiracies, introducing nothing new even now against the faith handed down to us from the beginning. Rather, I anathematize Apollinaris, Valentinus, Manes, and Nestorius; those who say that [Col. 0717B] the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior descended from heaven and not from the Holy Spirit and the holy Virgin Mary; and all heresies down to the magician Simon.

Nevertheless, I am endangered in my life as though I were a heretic. I beg you, without allowing any prejudice against me to arise from the things carried out against me by treachery, to pronounce whatever judgment on the faith seems right to you, and henceforth to allow no slander by conspirators to proceed against me. [p. 742] Do not remove and exclude from the number of the orthodox a man who has spent seventy years of his life in self-restraint and complete chastity, only to suffer shipwreck at the very end of his life.

I have appended to this letter of mine both libelli: the one presented by my accuser to the synod, and the one which I did indeed submit but which was not accepted; [Col. 0717C] as well as my published profession of faith and the decrees concerning the two natures issued by our holy fathers.

**[Note: [Col. 0717C–D] Eutyches distinguishes four documents appended by him to the letter. First, the libellus of accusation presented against him by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, at the Constantinopolitan synod. Second, the libellus of appeal, which Eutyches falsely claimed to have offered before the sentence of condemnation. Third, his profession of faith publicly presented at Constantinople. Fourth, the testimonies of certain Fathers. Both libelli were omitted from the Cassinese manuscript. Only a fragment of the profession of faith and one testimony attributed to Pope Julius are reproduced. Since the contemporary anonymous author, when asked to give his judgment on Eutyches’ letter to Leo, thought that the letter itself and only these two fragments required an answer, we believe that these alone were appended to the letter in the Cassinese codex, together with the anonymous refutation, while the other documents omitted by the anonymous author were also omitted.]**

[Note: [Col. 0717D–0718C] “The publication of my faith” names the libellus of Eutyches’ profession of faith, because it had been publicly displayed at Constantinople, as Eutyches himself indicated shortly before by the words “so that I might set forth confessions of faith to satisfy the people.” Compare note 12 (col. 733, n. b) on Letter 23.]

### The words of Eutyches

**[Note: [Col. 0718C] This is a fragment of the profession of faith issued by Eutyches. It agrees with the libellus that Eutyches presented to the pseudo-synod of Ephesus and that is found in the first act of the Council of Chalcedon. Shortly afterward, the printed editions read “which it preserved,” whereas the corrected reading is “which it confirmed.” The correction introduced from Vatican codex 1319 is supported by the wording “the faith which was set forth at Nicaea by the holy synod, and confirmed at Ephesus.”]**

I call you to witness before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who before Pontius Pilate bore witness to [Col. 0718A] that excellent confession: do not act out of favor toward anyone.

For I have always held this same faith as it was handed down by my forebears, and from my childhood I have been enlightened in the manner in which the holy synod of three hundred and eighteen most blessed bishops, assembled from the whole world at Nicaea, established the faith; and I continue to hold only that faith which the holy synod assembled at Ephesus again confirmed and defined. I have never thought otherwise than as the right and only true orthodox faith commands.

I assent to everything concerning this same faith that was established by that same holy synod at Ephesus. Its leader and chief was the bishop Cyril of Alexandria, of blessed and holy memory, together with Gregory the Great, the preacher and teacher of the faith of the holy and elect of God, and likewise Gregory, Basil, Athanasius, [Col. 0718B] Atticus, and Proclus, his associates and companions. I have regarded him and all of them as orthodox and faithful, honored them as saints, and considered them my teachers.

But I anathematize Nestorius, Apollinaris, and all heretics down to Simon, as well as those who say that the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ descended from heaven.

For he who is the Word of God descended from heaven without flesh, and became flesh in the womb of the holy Virgin, from the flesh of the Virgin herself, [p. 743] immutably and unchangeably, just as he himself knew and willed. He who is eternally perfect God before the ages also became perfect man at the end of the days, for us and for our salvation.

Therefore, let your holiness accept this my complete profession.

**[Note: [Col. 0718D] The verb *habeat* (“may have/receive”), which was missing and left the sense incomplete, has been supplied from the aforementioned Vatican codex 1319. Immediately after the profession of faith, a statement addressed to the people followed in the same continuous text; see note 12 on Letter 23 (col. 733, n. b).]**

I, Eutyches, presbyter and archimandrite, [Col. 0718C] have subscribed this document with my own hand.

---

**[Note: [Col. 0718D] This title is corrupt. Father Constantius, in the appendix to volume I of *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, p. 69, thinks it should read: “A copy of the letter of Julius … written to Dionysius.” Baluze’s correction seems better: “From a letter of Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, which Eutyches asserted was written to Dionysius.” For the whole letter is not reproduced here, but only a fragment. The complete letter was published in Greek by Muratori in his *Greek Anecdotes*; the fragment reproduced here, from an ancient translation, ends about the middle of chapter 4. Father Coustantius, among others, has demonstrated most clearly in the warning prefixed to this letter at the cited place that it was falsely attributed to Pope Julius, while it is actually the work of Apollinaris, submitted under Julius’s name by the Apollinarists.]**

**Excerpt from a letter of Julius, bishop of the city of Rome, which Eutyches claims was written to Bishop Dionysius and whose meaning led Eutyches himself into error**

[Col. 0719A] I am astonished when I hear that some people confess our Lord in the flesh but fall into the division wrongly introduced by the followers of Paul.

For those who followed Paul of Samosata understand one as having descended from heaven and confess him to be God, but say that another is an earthly man: the former uncreated, the latter lord, another a servant—impious whether they worship him whom they call servant and created, or do not worship him who redeemed us with his blood. [Note: [Col. 0719C] On the evidence of the Greek, read *impii* (“impious,” plural), or *impie agentes* (“acting impiously”), instead of the printed *impium* (“impious,” singular accusative).]

But those who confess that God descended from heaven and became flesh from the Virgin, and that he is one with the flesh, needlessly raise disturbances, going beyond them into words of impiety. [Note: [Col. 0719C] Read *factum* (“became [flesh],” referring to God), rather than *factam* (“made,” agreeing with flesh). The Greek also requires *conturbant* (“they disturb”) or *turbas concitant* (“they raise disturbances”), in place of *conturbantur* (“they are disturbed”).] For they too, as I hear, say that there are two natures.

John clearly proves that our Lord is one when he says, “The Word became flesh”; and the apostle Paul likewise when he says, [Col. 0719B] “One Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things exist.”

For if Jesus, born of the Virgin, is called Jesus, and he himself is the one through whom all things were made, then there is plainly one nature, since, possessing one person, he is not divided into two; nor is there a proper nature of the body and a proper nature of divinity according to the flesh. **[Note: [Col. 0720C] Delete *facta* (“made”) on the evidence of the Greek; likewise correct the following from the Greek: “and, possessing one person, he is not divided into two, since neither …”.]** But just as man is one nature, so also Christ, who was made in the likeness of man, is one nature. [p. 744] If they do not recognize that what is one through union is one, they can also divide the one into many parts and speak of many natures, since the human body consists of bones, nerves, veins, flesh, skin, blood, and spirit. All these are different from one another, yet their nature is one: the nature of man.

**[Note: [Col. 0720C] From the Greek: “the nature of man.”]**

Thus the nature of divinity is also one with the body, and it is not divided into two natures.

**[Note: [Col. 0720C] Lupus printed *haec* (“these things”) in both places. Baluze’s correction is not supported by the Greek text.]**

[Col. 0720A] For the Son could not have been wholly called the Son of Man if he had descended from the heavens, and again the Son of God if he had been born from a woman, if division into two natures were possible. Rather, that which descended from heaven would be called the Son of Man, not the Son of God. This is the division of the Paulinians.

But divine Scripture teaches us to think of our one Lord both when he descended from heaven and when he was born on earth. Those who think in this way do not depart [from] those who think discordantly and contrarily, [Note: [Col. 0720C] The source prints *non excedunt (ab)*: the parenthesized *ab* (“from”) is supplied to the text.] so that, while agreeing in mind with the divine commandments, they differ in their words.

For if they understand two natures, they must worship one and not adore the other; they would be baptized into the divine nature but not baptized into the human nature.

**[Note: [Col. 0720C] Read “say” from the same Greek text.]**

But if we are baptized into the death of the Lord, we confess one nature: [Col. 0720B] that of impassible divinity and passible flesh. Thus our baptism is received both into God and into the death of the Lord.

Nor do we fear the slanderers who divide the Lord into two persons. When we preach the evangelical and apostolic unity, let them not tear us apart as though we were saying that the flesh is heavenly, since, on the contrary, we read the divine Scriptures saying that the Son is not from heaven.



Nor, when we say that the Son of God was created from a woman, can we be criticized as though we were saying that the Word was from earth and not from heaven. We say both: wholly from heaven on account of his divinity, and wholly from a woman on account of his flesh, without acknowledging division of the one person.

---

[Col. 0719] # EDITORIAL NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)



1. Quesnell, because of his preconceived opinions, was greatly concerned to defend himself against the eminent Baronius by maintaining that Saint Flavian had written nothing to Pope Saint Leo about the condemnation of Eutyches until after he had been prompted by Leo’s letters. Therefore, in Dissertation 1 on the year 449, section 1 and following, he reversed the order of Flavian’s two letters to Leo. He presented our Letter 26, which Flavian wrote around April 449 after receiving Leo’s letters, as the first; and he placed the following letter as the second, sent later. Anthony Pagi himself adopted the same view and consequently thought that Baronius should be corrected under the year 448, section 8.

Quesnell’s principal—or rather, his only—argument, repeated also by Pagi, rests on these words of Flavian in Letter 26. After indicating that Eutyches had been condemned, Flavian adds: “As your Holiness will learn from everything that was done concerning him, which we have sent along with this letter of ours.”

Quesnell comments: “You see that Leo had received from Flavian no letter or acts of the synod before this letter. And when Flavian later mentions Leo’s letters delivered to him by Pansophius”—this is Letter 23—“by which he had learned that Eutyches had sent letters to Leo full of every kind of deceit and cunning, it is likewise clear,” Quesnell continues, “that Flavian did not think of writing to Leo about these matters until he learned that the pontiff had been deceived by wicked methods and had formed a false opinion about the proceedings at Constantinople.”

2. If Letter 23 is read attentively, one finds Leo not deceived but cautious, requesting and awaiting the necessary documents. As for the argument itself, even in Letter 22, after explaining the errors of Eutyches—things that had long before been done against him—Flavian is said to have sent these matters to Leo in chapter 4. There Flavian uses the same Greek verb, ἀπεστείλαμεν, “we sent,” that he uses in Letter 26.

If the word “we sent” seems problematic here, see note 17 on Letter 22. Since, therefore, Flavian wrote to Leo twice about the same condemnation and twice sent him the proceedings—once with Letter 22 and again with Letter 26—nothing can be inferred from this single point in favor of one letter’s priority over the other.

3. If judgment is based on the context of both letters, Tillemont, although he supported Quesnell on many other matters, could not agree with him here. Thus, in article 16 on Leo, he had no hesitation in assigning first place to Letter 22:

“I believe that, with only a little reflection, it will easily be recognized that it [the letter now numbered 22] was written very shortly after the council held against Eutyches, and that it was the first which Flavian wrote to Rome concerning this affair, as Baronius believed.”

The words translated from the Greek, “Such as Eutyches has now most recently appeared to us,” indicate the very recent revelation and condemnation of the heretic. The words near the end, in which Flavian asks that what had happened concerning Eutyches be brought to the knowledge of the Western bishops—[Col. 0721] so that, knowing what Eutyches thought, no one might address him by letter or through any association as though he were orthodox—show that this letter was written at the beginning of the affair.

It would have been inappropriate to ask Leo to promulgate Eutyches’ condemnation at a time when it was already widely known, namely, after Letter 26, when a general council was already being publicly announced for this very reason.

4. Let us produce a still clearer argument. Saint Leo states that he received two letters from Flavian together with the proceedings. First, in Letter 28, written to Flavian himself on the Ides of June 449, he says in chapter 1:

“After reading the letters of your affection, which we are astonished to find were so late, and after reviewing the order of the episcopal proceedings, we finally learned what scandal concerning the integrity of the faith had arisen among you.”

Leo indicates that he had already received this same letter from Flavian when he wrote Letter 27, dated 21 May of that year. If the letter from Flavian received by that date was very late, it must therefore have been written much earlier. These words unquestionably refer to Flavian’s first letter.

Again, in Letter 36 to the same Flavian, dated either the twelfth or fifteenth day before the Kalends of July of that year, Leo mentions another letter received at that time together with the proceedings:

“I received the letter of your affection together with the proceedings conducted among you concerning the question of the faith.”

This refers to Flavian’s second letter, to which the proceedings against Eutyches had been appended just as they had been to the first.

That Letter 36 refers to Flavian’s Letter 26 is clear from the fact that in Letter 26, chapter 2, Flavian says that he hoped the synod which was being announced as forthcoming would be cancelled; whereas Leo, replying to this point in Letter 36, indicates that the council could not be prevented.

Therefore, Flavian’s Letter 26 is the second, and Letter 22 is the first. Letter 22 was sent shortly after the Constantinopolitan synod, at the end of 448 or, at the latest, early in 449.

There is nothing surprising in Eutyches’ letter having arrived sooner, together with the emperor’s letters written on his behalf. We do not know what caused the longer delay in the delivery of Flavian’s letter, whose lateness astonished Leo.

Thus Letter 22 described the earlier events that had occurred up to the Constantinopolitan synod, while Letter 26 added the later events provoked by Eutyches after that synod. The acts of the synod were again appended to this second letter because, from Leo’s letters, Flavian feared that the earlier letter might have been lost together with its acts.

If Letter 26 makes no mention of Letter 22, which we have shown was sent earlier, this presents no difficulty. Letter 22 likewise makes no mention of another letter written previously, although Quesnell considers it the later one.

5. Let it therefore remain established that Letter 22 was sent first and that it is the letter Leo recalls in Letter 28, upon which the whole of Leo’s celebrated doctrinal definition rests.

We believe that this explains why, in the ancient Latin collections 2, 3, and 8, as well as in the Hispanic, Isidorian, and other later collections deriving from those ancient sources, only Flavian’s Letter 22 precedes Letter 28, Leo’s letter to Flavian.

Since this letter was delivered to Leo first, immediately translated into Latin, and disseminated throughout the West, we think that this is why it was inserted in so many distinct and ancient collections. This will be confirmed by what is said at the end of note 5 on Letter 67 (col. 886, n. g).

The same did not happen with Letter 26. Since it was written later, when the matter was already well known through the earlier letter, it was not equally likely to be circulated publicly. Hence it is found only in the manuscripts of Collection 17 of Chalcedon, where a very large number of documents concerning Eutyches were collected with particular care. There it appears after Letter 22, as can be seen in Baluze, volume IV of the Councils, Venetian edition, p. 1981. This arrangement itself confirms that the former was earlier and the latter later.

6. From this it may likewise be inferred that the translation of Letter 22 beginning “Nothing is of the devil,” which appears in the ancient collections mentioned above—and in some manuscripts is also found together with the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches appended to that same letter—is the first translation, promulgated immediately and subsequently received into the collections.

The other translation, beginning “Nothing is,” is found only in the ancient Latin Chalcedonian collection. From that collection it was later transferred into the subsequent Collection 22 along with the other Chalcedonian documents.

That older translation, prepared at the outset, was available to Leo before he wrote his doctrinal letter to Flavian. It is likewise certain that the translation of the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches was available to him, since it was published together in Collections 3 and 8 with the older translation of Letter 22 and is found there as part of the collection. From this translation of the acts he quotes several passages word for word in chapter 6 of the same doctrinal letter.

7. All these considerations make clear how vainly Quesnell labored against Cardinal Baronius to persuade readers that Letter 22 was written after Letter 26—as though Flavian, after writing to Domnus and to other bishops of the East following Eutyches’ condemnation, had neglected to warn the bishops of the West, and especially the Roman pontiff, about so great a heresy.

Immediately after Eutyches’ condemnation, Flavian had been sufficiently warned by Florentius. When the meeting had been dissolved and Flavian went up to the upper part of the house, Florentius told him that Eutyches had appealed to the Roman, Alexandrian, and Jerusalem bishops. Flavian therefore had reason to fear that, if he did not write to Leo immediately, Eutyches might reach the pontiff first.

But there is no need to add more in order to refute Quesnell’s prejudice—or, rather, his fabrication.

## 8.

Of the two Latin versions of the following letter that we mentioned, although the version that begins *Nothing restrains* is the first and older, while the other begins *There is nothing*, it was nevertheless rendered into Latin by a less skilled or not especially careful translator and therefore corresponds less exactly to the Greek original. The other version, however, which is presented in the Chalcedonian collection, was produced by a more skilled and careful translator and comes closer to the Greek text. We have therefore decided to place this later, though sufficiently ancient, version before the former and to print it alongside the Greek text. Afterwards we shall append the older version. In addition to the difficulties arising from the translator’s lesser accuracy, this version has acquired others from the copyists, who, differing remarkably in their readings, have made the text of the original version more obscure and uncertain.

Quesnellus published this older version beside the Greek original, as it is presented in the editions of the Councils, with not a few—and repeatedly longer—readings written in the margin. These may appear to be variants taken from manuscripts, but in fact they are readings taken from the Greek by the Roman first editors of the Greek text and added because the old version seemed less suitable. Indeed, they also altered several passages from the Greek within the text of the version itself, just as they had repeatedly done in the ancient version of the Chalcedonian material. Nevertheless, although Quesnellus possessed several manuscripts of this translation, as well as earlier editions of Leo in which it was read differently, he transcribed the Roman reading in such a way that, making no use either of the manuscripts or of the other printed editions, he failed to restore the ancient version. Yet those who publish ancient versions ought not to present what agrees better with the original, but what was rendered by the ancient translator.

The other, more accurate version, which we shall give first together with the Greek text, was first published by Quesnellus from the Thuaneus manuscript of collection 17 of the Chalcedonian materials. Baluzius later reprinted it from the same manuscript and from two others of the same collection—the Corbeiensis and Divionensis—in his *Ancient Version of the Council of Chalcedon, Corrected by Rusticus*, chapter 5. We too have collated it with four manuscripts of the collection in question: the most ancient Veronensis, two Vatican manuscripts, and the Chigianus, as well as with the Venetian manuscript of the collection of Saint Mark, no. 22. We collated the Greek original, preserved for us by the Greek collection of the Council of Chalcedon, with two Venetian manuscripts of Saint Mark.

# LETTER XXII, THE FIRST LETTER OF FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO POPE LEO (G)

[Note: [Col. 0723C] Elsewhere numbered after letter 23. What was formerly letter 22 is now letter 27. Written at the end of 448 or the beginning of 449.]

[Col. 0723]

## Synopsis

I. On the snares of the devil, which the person who adheres to the teaching of the holy Fathers avoids.  
II. On the cunning of heretics, by which they deceive the unwary.  
III. Eutyches’ attempt to renew the doctrines of Valentinus and Apollinaris.  
IV. On his entirely just deposition and excommunication, which Flavian asks Leo to make known to the Westerners.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**752** [Note: We have supplied this superscription, omitted by Quesnellus, from all our manuscripts and also from Baluzius’s manuscripts.]

To the most holy and God-loving father and fellow priest Leo, Flavian sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0723A]

## Chapter I

There is nothing that can restrain the devil’s wickedness, that uncontrollable evil full of deadly poison (James 3:8). He roams up and down, seeking whom he may strike, whom he may disturb, and whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8).

[Note: All our manuscripts except the Chigianus read in this way. The Chigianus, together with Baluzius, has: “whom he may trouble, whom he may devour.” Quesnellus has: “whom he may disturb, whom he may devour.”]

Therefore we have learned from holy Scripture both to keep watch and to be sober for prayer, to draw near to God, to reject foolish questions, to follow the Fathers, and not to transgress the ancient boundaries.

[Note: Our manuscripts and those of Baluzius supplied the preposition *ex*, omitted by Quesnellus. Later, *Deponens* was corrected from the Corbeiensis and Divionensis manuscripts belonging to Baluzius. The other manuscripts, together with Quesnellus, incorrectly read *Deponentes*.]

Thus, laying aside the burden of grief and the abundance of tears—for one of the clergy under my authority has been seized, and I have been unable to save him or snatch him from the wolf, although I had been ready to lay down my life for him—since he was carried away, since he leapt away, hating the voice of the one calling him and running headlong toward destruction, while also avoiding the memorials of the Fathers and utterly abhorring their paths, I proceed with my account.

## Chapter II

There are some who are in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves (Matthew 7:15); we recognize them by their fruits.

[Note: All the manuscripts, both Baluzius’s and ours, read this way. Quesnellus has *in vestimentis*, “in garments.” A little later, we read *agnoscimus* on the authority of four manuscripts, one Vatican, another Venetian, and also the Corbeiensis and Divionensis. Three of our other manuscripts read *cognoscimus*. Quesnellus, with his Thuaneus manuscript, has *agnoscemus*.]

At first these people seem to be from among us, but they are not from among us; for if they had been from among us, they would certainly have remained with us (1 John 2:19).

[Note: Our manuscripts agree with Baluzius. Quesnellus reads: “But when at some time they have vomited forth their own …”]

But when they have vomited forth their impiety, bursting open the deception that is within them, and have seized the weaker—those whose understanding of the divine utterances is untrained—they drag them along with themselves to destruction (2 Peter 3:16), overturning and insulting the teachings of the Fathers, as well as the holy Scriptures, to their own destruction.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript, together with Baluzius, reads *contrahunt*, “draw along”; elsewhere the reading is *pertrahunt*, “drag along.”]

[Note: Quesnellus alone has *inferiores*, “the lower.”]

We must be forewarned about them and beware, lest some, deceived by their wickedness, be cut off from their own steadfastness. For they have sharpened their tongues like serpents; the poison of asps is under their lips, as the prophet cried out concerning them (Psalm 139:4).

## Chapter III

Such a man has now appeared among us: Eutyches, formerly a presbyter and archimandrite. He seemed to hold our views and to possess the true faith, resisting the impiety of Nestorius and pretending to fight against him. Yet he attempted to overthrow the exposition on the faith composed by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, and the letter of Cyril of holy memory written to Nestorius, and likewise his letter to the Easterners, to which all had assented, renewing the ancient evil doctrines of the impious Valentinus and Apollinaris.

[Note: The Veronensis manuscript reads *revocare*, “to restore,” in place of *renovare*, “to renew.”]

[Note: Quesnellus’s note attached to this passage must be reproduced here in its entirety:

“Flavianus knowingly and accurately mentions only the two letters of Saint Cyril: one to Nestorius and the other to the Easterners, to which all had assented. This latter letter is the letter on peace, beginning *Let the heavens rejoice*, and it was accepted by the Easterners. The former, addressed to Nestorius and beginning *I have learned that certain persons are detracting from my reputation*, etc., is found in Part I of the Acts of Ephesus, chapter 8; it was read in the first session and approved by the individual votes of the Fathers, since it alone contains and explains the Nicene confession of faith. The other letter of Cyril, containing the twelve anathemas, is neither mentioned here by Flavian nor shown in the Acts to have been approved by the Synod of Ephesus, although it was read there; nor did Cyril request that it be approved, nor did the Fathers make any statement concerning it. This gives rise to some suspicion that the Acts of the Synod have been abridged in this respect.

“The Council of Chalcedon likewise did not approve this letter by itself, but approved both of those letters, just as the Synod of Constantinople under Flavian had done previously. Hypatius of Ephesus in the Constantinopolitan conference and Rusticus in his discussion with the Acephali explicitly note this distinction.

“Moreover, the mention of two hypostases, which Cyril seemed to introduce, was the reason why the Synod restrained itself from approving the anathemas. Since the admonition of Pope Celestine to Nestorius had been inserted into Cyril’s letters and transmitted together with Cyril’s letter to that same Nestorius, the Synod of Ephesus therefore asked Bishop Flavian, who was speaking as though there were several letters, whether such letters had been delivered to Nestorius.

“Our Leo likewise cites only one of Cyril’s letters in letters 51, 52, 54, and 88—now 67, 69, 70, and 117. Certainly, the letter of Cyril containing the twelve inserted anathemas was unknown to the Latins until approximately the year 500, as Dionysius Exiguus testifies in his letter to Bishop Peter, which he placed before the letter of Cyril that he then translated into Latin.”]

Several points should be noted concerning Quesnellus’s remarks about Cyril’s letter containing the twelve anathemas. It was not only read in the first session of the Council of Ephesus; it was also inserted into the Acts at the command of Flavian, bishop of Philippi, without any censure. This is an indication of approval, as is clear from the formula by which the letter of the Carthaginian bishop was similarly inserted into the same session; concerning that letter it was said, on page 1078 of volume III of the *Councils*: “Since it contains a clear judgment, let it be inserted among the records of the faith.”

The judges at the end of the first session of the Council of Chalcedon did indeed assert that two canonical letters of Cyril had been published and confirmed by the Council of Ephesus, and both had certainly been written to Nestorius—for the letter to the Easterners was written after the Council. Vigilius made the same assertion concerning the letter containing the anathemas in his letters against Rusticus and Sebastianus, inserted in the seventh conference of the Fifth Council.

The Latins were so firmly persuaded that the anathemas themselves, together with Cyril’s letter, had been approved at the Council of Ephesus that in the ancient manuscripts of collections 3 and 8 they are reported among the acts of that Council, with the subscriptions of the Fathers of the Council itself. More will be said about this in volume III.

Furthermore, the Council of Chalcedon sufficiently approved the same letter of Cyril when, in its Definition, it approved universally everything concerning the faith that had been enacted by the Council of Ephesus, and when it inserted several honorable testimonies concerning Cyril into the Acts. It merely did not consider it opportune to approve that letter by name, because, having been issued against the heresy opposed to that of Eutyches, it contained certain formulas not entirely consistent with those which the Fathers of Chalcedon thought should be used against Eutyches’ error.

Finally, Quesnellus places too much confidence in Dionysius when he says that this letter was unknown to the Latins before Dionysius himself rendered it into Latin. For before Dionysius, Marius Mercator, who had attended the Council of Ephesus, translated it into Latin, and his translation circulated among the Latins; it is therefore found inserted in the Hispanic collection. There is also an ancient version of the same letter prefixed to the ancient translation of the Council of Ephesus. It appears to be older than Dionysius, although it was unknown to him, just as the translation of Marius Mercator was also unknown to him.]

Nor did he fear the command of the true King, who says: “Whoever causes one of these very little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18:6).

[Note: The Chigianus manuscript has “around the neck”; the Corbeiensis and Divionensis manuscripts belonging to Baluzius also have “neck.”]

[Note: Baluzius aptly observed: “This reading is certain and consistent in the ancient copies.” But since the sense seemed incomplete, Quesnellus corrected the passage from another version and restored it as follows: “But casting away all shame.” This is how it is read in the older version that we shall present later. The more ancient translator had before him a corrected Greek manuscript in which αἰδώς, “shame,” was written, as in the received text. The other translator, the author of the version presented here, used a Greek manuscript that preferred the corrupt reading found in the Venetian manuscripts and also noted in the margins of the printed editions, ἀναιδῶς, “shamelessly.”]

But acting shamelessly and casting everything aside, and shaking off the skin that covered him, he openly asserted before our holy Synod, saying:

[Note: Baluzius’s manuscripts and some of ours, through a scribal error, read *vestra*, “your,” in place of *nostra*, “our.” Shortly afterwards the Veronensis manuscript has *humanationem*, “humanization,” in place of *inhumanationem*, “incarnation.”] “We ought not to recognize our Lord Jesus Christ, after the Incarnation, as being from two natures, in one subsistence and one person; nor does the Lord’s flesh exist consubstantial with us, as having been taken from us and united to God the Word according to subsistence.”

[Note: Some manuscripts, together with Baluzius, read *consubsistentiam*, “consubstantial existence.”]

But he said that the Virgin who bore him was consubstantial with us according to the flesh, while the Lord himself had not taken from her flesh consubstantial with us; rather, although the Lord’s body was not the body of a human being, it was a human body, that which came from the Virgin, contrary to all the expositions of the holy Fathers.

[Note: Quesnellus inserted the word *esse*, “was,” between brackets for clarity; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

## Chapter IV

But lest, by recounting everything, I make the letter excessively long, we have already sent to Your Holiness the records concerning him that were drawn up some time ago.

[Note: This makes clear that the Greek adverb πάλαι, “formerly” or “long ago,” refers to the records of the Constantinopolitan Synod, at which Eutyches had previously been condemned. They are contained in the final session of that same Synod, which was immediately translated into Latin and inserted into several ancient collections, especially collection 5 of Quesnellus, chapter 42.

“The Latin translators use the past tense *direximus*, ‘we sent,’ for the Greek aorist ἀπεστείλαμεν. Here it is understood of a present or soon-to-be-completed action, according to a usage not uncommon among the Greeks. Thus Eutyches, in letter 21 to Leo—whose Greek original has perished—says near the end: ‘I have appended both petitions to this letter of mine,’ although the letter to which both petitions were to be attached had not yet been completed. Flavian likewise, in letter 26 to Leo, uses the same aorist ἀπεστείλαμεν of the same records sent again concerning Eutyches: ‘Which we have sent with this letter of ours,’ although the reference is not to letters already delivered, but to those whose writing he was undertaking.

“Leo himself, in letter 75, chapter 2, speaking of the same letter that he was writing, did not hesitate to say: ‘We wish this letter of ours, which we send to Your Love’; and in letter 78 he says: ‘Through our legates we have sent written communications,’ although he is speaking of legates whom, as he says in letter 81, he would send after the venerable day.”]

In them we stripped him of the priesthood, as one convicted in matters of this kind, and deprived him of the administration of the monastery and of communion with us.

[Note: Since the word *captum*, “convicted,” was absent from the manuscript used by Quesnellus, he judged the sense incomplete, as Baluzius reports, removed this entire clause, and printed: “In them we also, as it were, forbade him the priesthood and the monastery,” etc. We restored the true reading from all our manuscripts and those of Baluzius.]

Thus, when Your Holiness has learned what concerns him, may you make his impiety known to all the bishops who are under your reverence and love God, lest, being unaware of what he believes and of the matters in which he has plainly been convicted, they should happen to write to him as to a fellow believer or otherwise make confessions to him.

[Note: The word *ejus*, “his,” is absent from Quesnellus. It has been supplied from our manuscripts and those of Baluzius. Later, the adverb *aperte*, “plainly,” is missing in the Veronensis manuscript.]

I and those who are with me greet most warmly all the brotherhood in Christ that is with Your Blessedness. May you be safe in the Lord, and, praying for us, may you be granted to us, most God-loving Father.

---

**751** To the most holy and God-loving father and fellow minister Leo, Flavian, in the Lord, sends greetings.

[Col. 0724A]

Nothing restrains the devil’s wickedness: the uncontrollable evil, full of deadly poison. For he roams up and down, seeking whom he may strike, whom he may tear apart, and whom he may devour. Therefore we have learned from the divine Scriptures to keep watch, to be sober for prayer, to draw near to God, to reject foolish inquiries, to follow the Fathers, and not to move the eternal boundaries.

Thus, laying aside the burden of grief and the abundance of tears—for one of the clergy under my authority has been seized as prey, and I have been unable to rescue him or snatch him from the wolf, although I was ready to lay down my life for him—how he was carried away, how he leapt away, hating the voice of the one calling him and running especially toward the one who destroys, perhaps also avoiding the memorials of the Fathers and loathing their paths, I shall now proceed with my account.

There are some in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravenous wolves; we recognize them by their fruits. These people seem to be sheep from among us, but they are not from among us; for if they had been from among us, they would have remained with us.

[Note: In the margin of the Roman edition: πρῶτα, “at first.”]

**753** But when they vomit forth their own impiety, bursting open the deception within them, they seize the weaker and those whose faculties are untrained with respect to the divine utterances, and thrust them along with themselves into destruction, distorting and deriding the teachings of the Fathers, as well as the remaining Scriptures, to their own destruction. We must recognize them beforehand and beware, lest some, led astray by their cunning, fall away from their own steadfastness.

“For they have sharpened their tongue like a serpent; the poison of asps is under their lips.” Concerning such people the prophet cried out.

[Note: The printed editions note: perhaps ἁγίας, “holy.” The reading is uncertain.]

Such a man has now appeared among us: Eutyches, formerly a presbyter and archimandrite. He pretended to hold our views and to possess the true faith, resisting the impiety of Nestorius and making a pretense of fighting against him, while attempting to overthrow the exposition on the faith composed by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers, the letter of Cyril of divine memory written to Nestorius, and likewise his letter to the Easterners, to which all had assented, renewing the ancient evil doctrine of the impious Valentinus and Apollinaris.

[Note: In the margin of the Roman edition: ἀναιδῶς, “shamelessly”; this reading also occurs in our Venetian manuscripts of Saint Mark, and from this corrupt reading the author of the version printed alongside the Greek translated the word as “imprudently.”]

And he did not fear the decree of the true King, which says: “Whoever causes one of these very little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the sea.”

Casting away all shame and shaking off the skin of error that he had worn, he asserted openly before our holy Synod, saying that our Lord Jesus Christ ought not to be recognized by us after the Incarnation as being from two natures, in one hypostasis and one person; nor, indeed, should the Lord’s flesh be considered consubstantial with us, as having been taken from us and united to God the Word according to hypostasis.

[Note: The two words καὶ ἑνωθεῖσαν, “and having been united,” have been supplied from the Venetian manuscripts.]

But he said that the Virgin who bore him was consubstantial with us according to the flesh, while the Lord himself had not taken from her flesh consubstantial with us; rather, although the Lord’s body was not the body of a human being, it was a human body, that which came from the Virgin—thus contradicting all the expositions of the holy Fathers.

[Note: In the margin of the Roman edition, ὁμολογεῖν, “to confess,” is supplied. That word must indeed be supplied after δεῖν, “ought.”]

But lest I make the letter lengthy by listing everything, we have already sent to Your Holiness the proceedings that were formerly drawn up concerning him. In them we stripped him of the priesthood, as one convicted in such matters, and deprived him of the charge of the monastery and of our communion. Thus, when Your Holiness has learned what concerns him, may you make his impiety manifest to all the most God-loving bishops who are under your reverence, so that, through ignorance of what he has believed and of the matters in which he was clearly convicted, they may not often be found addressing him as one of the same faith, either by letter or in any other way.

I and those who are with me offer our warmest greetings to all the brotherhood in Christ that is with Your God-lovingness. Being strong in the Lord and praying earnestly for us, may you be granted to us, most God-loving Father.

---

# THE OTHER, OLDER VERSION OF THE SAME LETTER OF FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO POPE LEO (G)

[Note: We have collated this version with the Vatican manuscript of collection 3, another Vatican manuscript no. 5845, the Vallicellian and Vercellian manuscripts of collection 8, the Vindobonensis and Vatican Hispanic manuscripts, another Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and other manuscripts of collections 11, 21, and 24, as well as with Sichardus’s copy.

“The manuscripts of this version repeatedly prefer readings less consistent with the Greek original, which the Roman editors of the Councils sometimes altered to conform to the Greek text, contrary to the testimony of the manuscripts. Here, however, the task is to publish the ancient version as it exists in the manuscripts, not to emend it. See section 8 of the preface.”]

## Synopsis  
*(from the Hispanic collection)*

I. On the snares of the deceitful enemy.  
II. On the fraud and subtlety of heretics.  
III. On the blasphemies of Eutyches.  
IV. On his entirely just excommunication.

[Note: Most of our manuscripts, together with the earlier editions of Leo, read as follows. The manuscripts of collection 8 have: “To the Lord and most beloved, and God-worthy and lovable holy father Leo, eternal salvation in God—or, in the Lord.” The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has: “To the most blessed Lord and beloved father Leo, Flavian sends greetings in the Lord.” Quesnellus, from the editions of the Councils, has: “To the most blessed and most God-loving father”—adding in the margin, “and fellow minister”—“Leo, etc.”]

To the most blessed Lord and God-loving Father Leo, Flavian sends eternal greetings in the Lord.

## Chapter I

No thing restrains the devil’s poisons, nor contains his deadly arrows. For he flies up and down, seeking whom he may kill, whom he may overcome, and whom he may devour.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript of collection 8 has *rapere*, “to seize.” The Vallicellian and Vercellian manuscripts incorrectly have *reparare*, perhaps for *separare*, “to separate,” as it is read in the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript and in other Vatican manuscripts of collections 11 and 21.
