“Shortly afterwards, in place of *Propter quam rem*, ‘For this reason,’ the Vatican manuscript of collection 3 has *Quamobrem*, ‘Wherefore.’ The manuscripts of collection 8 have: ‘Wherefore we must keep watch in prayers and devote ourselves to God, so that,’ etc. The Vindobonensis Hispanic and Vatican manuscript of collection 11 have: ‘For this reason we must keep watch in prayers and devote ourselves to God, so that,’ etc. The manuscripts of collection 24, together with Sichardus, have: ‘We must keep watch in prayers and undertake this, so that,’ etc.”]

For this reason we must keep watch and obtain from God through prayers that we may be able to avoid foolish inquiries.

[Note: The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, together with other manuscripts and Sichardus, has *autem*, “however.” Shortly afterwards Quesnellus, following the reading of the Councils, gives a reading found in no manuscript: “And we have learned from the divine Scriptures not to change the ancient boundaries. Therefore, having laid aside,” etc.

“The earlier editions of Leo, before Quesnellus, have: ‘Nor to change their perpetual definition, whose rule we have learned to be according to the holy Scriptures.’ The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, together with manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, Merlinus, and Sichardus, have: ‘Nor to change their perpetual definition, whose rule according to the holy Scriptures we have learned.’ We preferred the reading of the most ancient Vatican manuscript of collection 3 and the Vallicellian manuscript, together with the other manuscripts of collection 8.”]

For it is fitting that we follow our Fathers and not change their perpetual definition, which we have learned to have been established according to the sacred Scriptures.

Therefore, laying aside the tears and weeping that I pour out without ceasing—for a member of the clergy under my authority has been attacked by a savage demon, and I have been unable to free him or remove him from such a wolf, although I was ready to lay down my life for him—I shall now begin to relate how he was carried away, how he recoiled from the divine purpose and ran to the one accustomed to destroy, abandoning the precepts of the Fathers and despising their ordinances.

[Note: The next three words are absent from the Vercellian manuscript of collection 8 and from the Hispanic collection and the others derived from it. Shortly afterwards the manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus have: “because a cleric living in the highest rank was attacked.”]

## Chapter II

There are some who signify sheep by their clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves; we ought to recognize them by their fruits.

[Note: The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, together with manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, the editions of Leo before Quesnellus, and Sichardus, add *enim*, “for.” Shortly afterwards, some manuscripts have *lupi raptores*, “rapacious wolves,” instead of *lupi rapaces*, “ravenous wolves.”]

At first sight these people appear to belong to our number, but they do not belong to our number. For if they had belonged to our number, they would have remained with us.

[Note: Many manuscripts and the editions of Leo before Quesnellus have *essent*, “they were.” Shortly afterwards Quesnellus, from the editions of the Councils, has *evomere*, “to vomit forth,” instead of *assumere*, “to take up.” We restored the latter from the earlier editions of Leo and the manuscripts.]

When they begin to take up impiety, what was previously concealed in them is revealed, and every deception becomes manifest to all.

[Note: We restored the conjunction *et*, “and,” which was deleted in the Councils and by Quesnellus, from our manuscripts and the editions of Leo.]

They find people weak in faith and ignorant of the divine readings, and hurl them with themselves into destruction, scattering and insulting the teachings of the Fathers and abandoning the holy Scriptures to their own destruction.

[Note: Quesnellus and the edition of the Councils have *contorquentes et vituperantes*, “twisting and insulting.” We restored the reading of all the manuscripts and the editions of Leo.]

[Note: This is the reading of the most ancient manuscripts of collections 3 and 8. Quesnellus, together with the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and collection 21, has *et relinquunt*, “and they abandon.” The other printed editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus, have *et reliquas*, “and the remaining.”]

We must foresee these people and be very much on our guard against them, lest some, ensnared in their wickedness, fall from their own steadfastness.

[Note: The better manuscripts and the printed editions of Leo have: “whom we ought to foresee and from whom we must beware greatly.” Quesnellus, together with the edition of the Councils, has: “whom we ought to foresee and from whom we must beware greatly.”]

For they have sharpened their tongue like serpents, and they have poison on their lips like asps. Concerning these things the prophet cried out.

[Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and two other manuscripts have: “For they have sharpened their tongues like asps; concerning them the prophet cries out: ‘They have sharpened their tongues like serpents,’ and so forth. Such is the man,” etc. The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has “They sharpened”—so written. “Concerning them the prophet cried out. Such is the man,” etc.]

## Chapter III

Such an Eutyches has arisen among us, formerly a presbyter and archimandrite. He seemed to hold the teaching of our religion and preferred it. He affirmed the impiety of Nestorius and girded himself to fight on Nestorius’s behalf in the struggle prepared against Nestorius.

[Note: Most manuscripts read this way. Others have *inter nos*, “among us.”]

But he attempted to overthrow the exposition on the faith composed by the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers and the letter of Cyril of holy memory written to Nestorius, or to those like him, to which all had assented, restoring the ancient sect of the impious Valentinus and Apollinaris.

[Note: The Vercellian manuscript has: “he seemed to hold the doctrines of our religion,” omitting *et hanc praeferebat*, “and preferred it.” Some manuscripts have *capiebat*, “he grasped,” instead of *sapiebat*, “he held.”]

[Note: We restored the reading of the editions of Leo, supported by our manuscripts. Quesnellus, from the editors of the Councils, has: “and likewise his letter to the Easterners, to which all had assented.” Shortly afterwards, the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts have *temptat evellere*, “he attempts to tear out.”]

And he did not fear the command of the true King, who says: “Whoever causes one of these very little ones to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be tied to his neck and that he be plunged into the depth of the sea.”

[Note: The word *minimis*, “very little,” is absent from several—but not our oldest—manuscripts and from the editions before Quesnellus.]

He cast away all shame because of his deception and, shaking off the skin of unbelief that he wore, asserted in our holy Synod, insisting that our Lord Jesus Christ ought not to be confessed as being from two natures after the human assumption, since he is recognized by us as being of one substance and one person.

[Note: All our manuscripts and the Leonine editions before Quesnellus read *substantiae*, “substance.” Quesnellus, together with the printed editions of the Councils, has *subsistentiae*, “subsistence.” He likewise wrote *secundum subsistentiam*, “according to subsistence,” shortly afterwards. We restored *secundum substantiam*, “according to substance,” from all the manuscripts and printed editions. It is otherwise well established that among the ancient Latins *substantia* and *subsistentia* were used interchangeably.]

Nor should the Lord’s flesh subsist as coessential with us, as having been taken from us and united to God the Word according to substance. But he said that the Virgin who begot him according to the flesh was consubstantial with us, while the Lord himself had not taken from her flesh consubstantial with us; rather, the Lord’s body was not indeed the body of a human being, but was a human body, that which came from the Virgin, and he held opinions contrary to the expositions of all the Fathers.

[Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, together with another Vatican manuscript of collection 11, have *consubstantivam*, “consubstantial.” Another Vatican manuscript of collection 3 has *coessentialem*, “coessential,” both here and again shortly afterwards.]

[Note: The Vallicellian and Vercellian manuscripts of collection 8, the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, and the manuscripts of collection 24, together with Sichardus, have this reading. The printed editions have: “and the body.”]

## Chapter IV

But lest I make the letter long by saying many things, whatever we did formerly we have sent to Your Blessedness: in these letters we explained that he had been stripped of the presbyterate because he had been convicted in such matters; we ordered that he have no concern with monasteries and excluded him from our communion.

[Note: The manuscripts of this version read in this way; some have *egerimus* instead of *egimus*. From the same manuscripts we wrote *quibus litteris*, “in which letters.” The editions of Leo before Quesnellus agree and have only *litteras*, “letters,” rather than “in which letters we explained.” Quesnellus, together with the edition of the Councils, has: “We sent to Your Blessedness letters concerning what we had done long ago, in which we explained,” etc. No manuscript supports this reading. Since the ancient version was erroneous here, it was corrected according to the Greek text. See note 17 on the preceding version, at 727b.]

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus and most manuscripts have this reading. Quesnellus, together with the edition of the Councils, has: “because he was convicted in such matters.”]

Thus, when Your Holiness has learned what was done concerning him, may you deign to make his impiety known to all the bishops living under Your Blessedness, lest, being unaware of what he has believed, they should address him as an orthodox man, either by letter or through some form of association.

[Note: Some have *agentibus*, “acting” or “conducting themselves,” instead of *degentibus*, “living.”]

[Note: The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has *communicationem*, “communication.” Shortly afterwards, instead of *loquantur*, “they should speak,” some have *loquerentur*, “they would speak.”]

[Note: Here all the manuscripts of this version and the editions of Leo before Quesnellus end the letter. The Roman editors of the Councils, together with Quesnellus, supplied the conclusion from the Greek, adding:

“[I and those who are with me] greet most warmly the entire brotherhood in Christ that lives with Your Piety. Being safe in the Lord and praying for us, may you be granted to us, most religious Father.”

“In a more recent Vatican manuscript no. 546 of collection 21, the words ‘Given on the third day before the Kalends of February’ are added after *loquantur*, ‘they should speak.’ Since these words are absent from the other older manuscripts of the same collection that we examined, it is unclear from what source they were added.”]

# LETTER XXIII

[Note: Also numbered 20. What was formerly letter 23 is now letter 54. Written on 18 February 449.]

## To Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople

[Note: This letter is found in the manuscripts of collections 3, 8, the Hispanic collection, the Isidorian collection, and collections 17, 18, 19, 21, and 24, as well as in Sichardus. The Greek version is supplied by the Chalcedonian collection.]

[Col. 0731]

[Note: In the Hispanic collection the following title appears: “Letter of Pope Leo to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, in which he asks why Eutyches, holding opinions against the Catholic faith, was separated by him from communion with the Church.”]

## Synopsis

I. Having received Eutyches’ complaints, Leo complains that he was deprived of communion by Flavian.  
II. He asks to be informed of the case and especially wishes charity to be preserved in defending the truth.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To his most beloved brother Flavian, bishop, Leo the bishop.

## Chapter I
The most Christian and most clement emperor, concerned in his holy and praiseworthy faith for the peace of the catholic Church, has sent us a letter concerning the matters that have stirred up the tumult of disturbance among you. We marvel that your Fraternity could have kept silent about whatever that scandal was and did not rather arrange for us to be informed at the outset by the disclosure of your report, so that we might not be left uncertain about the truth of what had occurred. [Note: The Ratisbon collection, column 0732B, deletes “of the catholic [Church].”]

[Note: This letter of the emperor Theodosius, which is also mentioned below and has been lost, seems to have been sent together with Eutyches’ Letter 21 to Leo. For the emperor had undertaken Eutyches’ defense through the agency of Chrysaphius. (Column 0732C)]

For we have received a petition from Eutyches the presbyter, who complains that, although Bishop Eusebius was accusing him, he was deprived of communion unjustly—especially since he asserts that, when summoned, he was present and did not deny his own presence. [Note: All manuscripts and printed editions read this. Quesnellus alone asks what the reading means.] He says that, at the very trial, he presented a petition of appeal, yet that it was not received.

[Note: The Vatican-Hispanic manuscript, Isidore, and Collections 17 and 21, together with the editions before Quesnellus, add “more,” which the manuscripts of the other collections more properly omit.]

[Note: The “petition” understood here is Eutyches’ Letter 21 to Leo, for the matters that Saint Leo reports at this point are contained in it. It may be called a petition of complaint and supplication; in the following letter it is called a petition of distress.]

[Note: Most manuscripts, together with the Vulgate editions, read “did not deny his presence.” The Vindobonensis Hispanicus and one Vatican manuscript read “had not denied it.” Quesnellus reads “had not denied his presence.” We have retained the reading of the outstanding Ratisbon manuscript.]

[Note: In Manuscript Collection 24 and in Sichardus, the reading is “his own” rather than “of appeal.” Both readings have been inserted in the printed editions. We have followed the other, more numerous and better, copies. Since Eutyches’ Letter 21 to Leo mentions a petition offered at the trial and not accepted, but makes no mention of an appeal, some have suspected that Eutyches indicated in other lost letters that he had offered a petition of appeal but that it had not been accepted. But there is no need to conjecture—or rather invent—other letters. For since the petition which Eutyches falsely claimed in the aforesaid letter had been offered and not accepted was sent to Leo together with that same letter, the Roman pontiff could learn from reading the petition itself about the appeal, which unquestionably was contained in it.]

For this reason he was compelled to post petitions of protest in the city of Constantinople.

[Note: Eutyches indicated this in these words of Letter 21: “So that I might set forth before the people, for their satisfaction, a confession of my faith.” More clearly Liberatus, chapter 11: “Eutyches posted edicts at Constantinople and called the people to witness that he had suffered injustice.” The petition of protest, therefore, posted at Constantinople, also contained a profession of faith, as Eutyches himself testifies. Perhaps this was connected with what Eutyches calls, near the end of the aforesaid Letter 21, “the edition of my faith.” A profession of faith was rightly to be prefixed by someone accused of heresy who wished to indicate that his protest was just. The fragment from the Casinensis manuscript that we have appended to that same letter displays only the profession of faith; but there can be no doubt that, in the missing portion, the protest itself, which Leo and Liberatus mention, was expressly given, so that Leo learned from it about the petition of protest.]

In view of these circumstances, we do not yet understand by what justice he was separated from the communion of the Church. But, attending to the case, we wish to know the reasoning behind your action, and we wish everything to be referred to our knowledge. For we, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, can determine nothing to the prejudice of either party while the facts remain unknown, before we have heard truthfully all that was done.

[Col. 0731B]

### 765 — Chapter II

Therefore your Fraternity should inform us, through a person especially suitable and well qualified, in a most complete report, what novelty has arisen against the ancient faith, such that it deserved to be punished by a more severe sentence. For both ecclesiastical discipline and the faith of the most devout prince impose upon us great concern for Christian peace.

[Note: The Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and Collection 24 read “of the Church.” Immediately afterward the Vindobonensis Hispanicus reads “the faith of the most religious prince.” (Column 0734C)]

[Note: Some manuscripts read “bring upon us.”]

The aim is that, once dissensions have been cut away, the catholic faith may be preserved inviolate, and that those who defend what is perverse, after being recalled from error, may be fortified by our authority—those whose faith shall have been found sound.

Nor can any difficulty be raised on this account, since the aforesaid presbyter has confessed in his own petition that he is ready to correct anything found in him that deserves reprehension.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “received.” We have restored the reading of the other editors, confirmed by nearly all the manuscripts. Eutyches’ Letter 21 also agrees, in which he complains that the petition he offered to Flavian was not received. For the extent to which Eutyches lied in this matter, see the note on that same Letter 21.]

For in such cases this must above all be provided for: that, without the tumult of disputes, charity be preserved and truth defended.

[Note: On the authority of the best Ratisbon manuscript and the manuscripts of the excellent Collection 17, we do not dare to insert the words “dearest brother,” which Quesnellus deleted, although they are found in other manuscripts of the other collections and in the Greek text.]

And therefore, since your Love sees that we are necessarily concerned about so great a matter, let it hasten to disclose to us, as fully and clearly as possible—and as it ought already to have done—everything that occurred, lest we be deceived by some ambiguity amid the assertions of the parties, and lest the dissension, which ought to be abolished at its beginnings, be nourished.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 5845, Collection 8, adds “from that point.”]

For, with God inspiring us, this remains in our heart as a matter to be observed: that the constitutions of the venerable Fathers, strengthened by divine authority and pertaining to the stability of the faith, not be violated by anyone’s perverse interpretation.

[Note: Quesnellus excluded the following six words, perhaps on the authority of the Grimanic manuscript of Collection 18. They are indeed absent from our Ratisbon manuscript. Nevertheless, because of the authority of other manuscripts and collections, including Collection 18 of Chalcedon, we have restored them.]

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

[Note: This chronological notation is absent from all the manuscripts of the collections that we have seen, with the exception of three: Chalcedon 17, Ratisbon 19, and 21. Some manuscripts of the latter collection, 21, together with the editions before Quesnellus, incorrectly read “the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.” These letters were received at Constantinople in April, as is clear from Seleucus’s interlocution at the Constantinopolitan assembly on the Ides of April, where mention is made of Eutyches’ appeal recorded in these letters. See volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, page 1067. Other manuscripts of the same collection, and the much better Ratisbon and Chalcedon manuscripts, prefer the day and month inserted in the text. We have printed “Asturius” rather than “Asterius” here and in the following letters of this year, as it is read in the Ratisbon manuscript, in the very ancient Veronese manuscript 57, and in other Chalcedonian manuscripts. Indeed, Quesnellus himself confessed to Norisius in a letter, which he mentions in the Pisan Cenotaphs, dissertation 4, chapter 2, section 1, volume III, page 691, that it is consistently read thus in the Grimanic manuscript as well. In the Leodiensis Diptych, edited by Alexander Vilthemius, “Astyrius” is found. But it is well known that the ancients more than once used y for u, but not for e. Prosper and Idatius, contemporary authors, present “Asturius” in most manuscripts and “Astyrius” in some.]

### Greek version

To the most beloved brother Flavian, bishop.

[Col. 0732A]

Whenever the most Christian and most humane emperor, concerned in holy and praiseworthy faith for the peace of the catholic Church, sent letters to us concerning those matters which produced among you a tumult of disturbance, we marvel at your Fraternity: whatever scandal occurred there, you were able to remain silent about it before us and did not rather take care, above all, to teach us through the report of your account, so that we might not be able to doubt the truth of what had happened.

[Col. 0732B]

[Note: The manuscript of Saint Mark’s in Venice reads “you have been able.”]

For we received a petition from Eutyches the presbyter, who complains that, although Bishop Eusebius was accusing him, he was deprived of communion undeservedly. He especially testified that, when summoned, he came and did not deny his own presence, to such an extent that at the very trial he had handed in a petition of appeal. For this reason he was compelled to post petitions of protest in Constantinople.

[Col. 0734A]

Although these events occurred, we still do not understand by what justice he was separated from the communion of the Church. But, attending to the case, we wish to learn the reasoning behind your action and to have everything referred to our knowledge, since we, who wish the judgments of the priests of the Lord to be just, cannot, while the facts remain undetermined, pronounce a prior judgment to the prejudice of either party before we hear truthfully what was done.

[Note: We have added “with truth” from the same Venetian manuscripts. Thus the Latin autograph also reads, “before we hear truthfully what was done.”]

### 766

For this reason your Fraternity shall make known to us, through a person especially suitable and appropriate, in a most complete report, what novelty has arisen against the ancient faith—something that became worthy of being punished by a severe sentence.

For both ecclesiastical administration and the faith of the most God-loving emperor have cast upon us great concern for the peace of Christians, so that, once dissensions have been removed, the catholic faith may be preserved undefiled, and those who defend what is evil, after being recalled from error, may be fortified by our authority, provided their faith has been approved.

Nor should any difficulty be introduced on this account, since the aforesaid presbyter confessed in his own petition that he was ready for correction if anything were found in him worthy of blame.

[Note: The same manuscripts read “worthy of reproach.”]

For in such cases one must take particular care that, outside tumult and contentiousness, charity be preserved and truth defended, dearest and most honored brother.

And therefore, since your Love sees that we are necessarily concerned about so great a matter, it should hasten to make known to us, as fully and as clearly as possible—and as it ought already to have done—everything, so that we may not be deceived by some ambiguity between the accounts of the parties, and so that dissension may not be nourished, since it ought to be erased at its beginnings.

[Note: The cited manuscripts read *emphrontidas* (ἐμφροντίδας), and we have no doubt that the translator wrote this word—or at least *emphrontidas*—to express the Latin *sollicitos* (“concerned”) in one word. Although this Greek word does not appear in our lexicons, it should not be rejected: it remarkably reflects the character of Greek, as may be seen in ἔμπονος, ἔνσποδος, and similar words. The standard editions read ἐν φροντίδι (“in concern”).]

For we must carefully guard this, with God inspiring us: that the formulations of the worshipful Fathers, which possess their authority from God and pertain to the perfection of the faith, not be defiled by anyone’s faulty interpretation.

[Col. 0736A]

[Note: We have added the article “the” from the Venetian manuscripts.]

May God preserve you in good health, most honored brother.

### 767 — Letter XXIV

[Note: Formerly Letter 21; now 28. Written on 18 February 449.]

[Note: Quesnellus found this letter only in the Grimanic manuscript of Collection 18. We found it in the outstanding Ratisbon Collection 19 and in the manuscripts of Collections 12 and 24, as well as in Sichardus, and compared it with these witnesses. In the manuscripts of Collection 12 it is addressed either to Pulcheria or to Theodosius.]

## To Theodosius Augustus

[Col. 0735A]

### Synopsis

I. After praising the emperor’s faith, he sets forth Eutyches’ complaint.  
II. He censures Flavian’s silence and asks to be informed.

Leo, bishop, to Theodosius Augustus.

### Chapter I

How great a support the Lord has prepared for his Church in the faith of your Clemency is shown also by the letter that you sent me, so that we may rejoice that you possess not only a royal but also a priestly spirit. For, beyond imperial and public concerns, you exercise the most devout care for the Christian religion, lest schisms, heresies, or any scandals grow strong among the people of God.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “you possess.”]

For the condition of your kingdom is then at its best when the eternal and unchangeable Trinity is served in the confession of one Divinity.

[Note: We have emended the text on the authority of the Ratisbon manuscript. Elsewhere, with the preposition omitted, the reading is “the confession of one Godhead.” After the word “served,” Quesnellus added “most gloriously,” which our manuscripts, especially the Ratisbon manuscript, do not contain.]

But what disturbance occurred in the Church of Constantinople that could move my brother and fellow bishop Flavian so greatly that he deprived the presbyter Eutyches of communion, I have not yet been able to understand clearly.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “disturbance.” Subsequently it reads “my fellow bishop,” rather than “our fellow bishop,” and consistently, “I have not yet been able clearly to recognize,” rather than “we have not yet been able clearly to understand.” We have preferred these readings from our manuscripts of Collection 24 and especially from the Ratisbon manuscript. The verb “I have been able” is also found in Sichardus.]

Although the aforesaid presbyter sent to the apostolic See, by a petition, a complaint about his distress, he nevertheless briefly stated certain points in advance, asserting that, while observing the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, he had been accused without cause of diversity in the faith.

[Note: The petition by which Eutyches sent his complaint of distress to the apostolic See is Eutyches’ Letter 21 to Leo. See note 7, column 732, in the preceding letter.]

### Chapter II

The petition of Bishop Eusebius, his accuser, a copy of which the aforesaid presbyter sent to us, contained nothing concerning the clarity of the charges.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “the aforesaid” rather than “the mentioned.”]

[Note: See Quesnellus’s note 1.]

Although it brought against the presbyter the accusation of heresy, it did not clearly express what understanding it was accusing him of holding. The bishop himself, moreover, professed that he adhered to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea; for this reason we had no basis on which to learn anything more fully.

[Note: This reading is better and comes from the same manuscript. Quesnellus reads “professed that he adhered to them” from the Grimanic manuscript. Other printed editions read “professed that in this matter he adhered to the decrees.” The Vatican manuscript of Collection 24, although preferring the same reading, omits “himself.” The phrase “in this matter he adhered” appears to have been written through a scribal error in place of “adhered.”]

And since the merits of the case, the consideration due to the faith, and your piety’s praiseworthy concern require it, there must now be no room for clandestine representations. First we must be informed about the matters on which he is judged to deserve accusation, so that a proper judgment may be made concerning facts that are well known.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with the Ratisbon manuscript, the manuscripts of Collection 24, and Sichardus’s copy, read “has required.” The understood completion is “so that I may pass judgment on this case,” as is clear from what follows.]

I have therefore sent a letter to the aforesaid bishop, so that he might recognize that I was displeased that he continued to keep silent about what had been done in so important a case, although he ought first to have taken pains to disclose everything to us.

[Note: Some editions before Quesnellus read “that he still kept silent even through excessive silence”; others, “that he still kept silent even now.” The Vatican manuscript of Collection 24 reads “kept hidden.” The reading of the text is preferred by the Grimanic and Ratisbon manuscripts.]

We believe that, even after this admonition, he will report everything to our knowledge, so that, once those matters that still seem hidden have been brought to light, judgment may be rendered in accordance with evangelical and apostolic teaching.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

[Note: We have emended the date from the Ratisbon manuscript, with which the Venetian manuscript of Collection 12 agrees. This letter was evidently written on the same day as the preceding one, and both were sent together to Constantinople; hence the preceding letter is mentioned here in chapter 2. Quesnellus, following the Grimanic manuscript and other printed editions of Leo, reads “given on the day of the Kalends of March,” or “toward the Kalends of March”; in the printed editions of the Councils, “toward the Kalends of May.”]

## Notice concerning the following epistle (G)

[Col. 0737]

1. Two Latin editions of letters from Saint Peter Chrysologus to Eutyches have appeared. One contains only a single, or first, chapter; the other contains two chapters. Since Quesnellus possessed this longer epistle and regarded it as the genuine edition, he declared in his notes that he could not determine why the shortened version, rather than this complete one, had been inserted into the standard editions of Saint Leo.

But among the manuscripts that generally preserve the shortened version, considerable doubt arose among scholars as to whether the second chapter was genuine or spurious. Every difficulty disappears, however, if we uncover the origin of both editions. We learned this from examining a great many manuscripts and from the differences among the collections that we carefully investigated.

2. The shortened edition, which alone is found in Leo’s manuscripts and in most collections, derives from the Hispanic collection. For from the Hispanic collection this mutilated edition—which ends with the words, “To all these things I have replied, brother, in your letters”—passed into the Isidorian collection; from the Isidorian collection, which was more widespread and accessible, it passed into Collections 11, 12, 21, and 23.

Since the authors of these collections transcribed all the letters of Leo that they found in the Isidorian collection, they also transcribed Saint Peter Chrysologus’s epistle, just as it had been inserted among Leo’s letters in that collection and likewise in the Hispanic collection.

Therefore, although many manuscripts and many collections preserve the shortened edition of this epistle, they all have a single origin: namely, the author of the Hispanic collection. That only the first chapter of the epistle reached his hands will become clear if we show that the complete edition derives from a source superior in antiquity and authority.

3. Certainly older than the Hispanic collection and of greater authority is the collection of letters concerning the case of Eutyches, which are read before or inserted into the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, both in Latin and in Greek copies.

This is the collection of letters that we called the seventeenth in the preface. It was compiled in Latin at least before the middle of the sixth century, when Rusticus, a deacon of the Roman Church, devoted particular attention to it by comparing outstanding Greek manuscripts.

The same collection was much older in Greek among the Greeks, who had brought together the Latin letters concerning the case of Eutyches, translated into Greek, with other Greek letters relating to the same case, forming them into a single corpus.

Indeed, we demonstrated in the preface to the letters, number 34, that this Greek collection of letters was assembled between the years 453 and 455. No one can fail to see how much this contributes to the authority of the Greek collection, and consequently also to the Latin collection that derives from the Greek, and how much this collection therefore surpasses the Hispanic collection.

Among the letters of the aforesaid Chalcedonian collection, both in Latin and in Greek manuscripts, the epistle of Saint Peter Chrysologus to Eutyches is copied in full, inserted by a contemporary compiler. For this reason, from the antiquity and excellence of this collection, received both among Greeks and Latins, there can be no doubt about the authenticity of the complete epistle.

When Agnellus of Ravenna, edited by Bacchinius and Muratori, gave a summary of the final chapter of this epistle in the Life of Saint Peter Chrysologus, if he did not find the complete epistle in the ancient records of the Church of Ravenna, he certainly had before his eyes some ancient copy of this type of Chalcedonian collection.

Since these copies were rarer and did not produce as many items from Leo as are found in the fairly common Isidorian collection, it is not surprising that later compilers of Leo’s letters gave this epistle not in full but in mutilated form, as it was found in Isidore, who derived his collection from the Hispanic one.

It should not be omitted here that Quesnellus assumed that two Vatican manuscripts of Leo’s letters, mentioned by Vossius, contained this epistle in full. Vossius himself, however, warned in his note that they contain the shortened version. They are manuscripts of later collections that derive from the Isidorian collection.

4. One question remains: whether this epistle, which we possess complete in the manuscripts of the Latin collection just mentioned, is original, or whether it was rendered into Latin from an ancient Greek version.

In the preface mentioned above, we proved clearly enough that the ancient author who added to the old version of the Council of Chalcedon the letters of the Latins contained in the Greek collection inserted the original Latin whenever he was able to find it. At times, however, when no copy of the Latin original was available, he was forced to translate certain Latin documents back into Latin from the Greek version.

This happened with some letters of Valentinian, Placidia, and Eudoxia, as well as with the letter of the deacon Hilary and also with letters of Saint Leo, as we shall note in their proper places.

As an indication of this process, and almost as a general rule, we proposed in the said preface that whenever the chronological notation is universally omitted in the Greek manuscripts of the same collection, it is also found to be absent in the Latin manuscripts. For whenever the original Latin was discovered by the Latin translator and inserted into the collection, the chronological notation is found to have been supplied.

A difference of style, where it can be detected by comparison with other works of the same author, is another indication of translation. Hence we seem to discern some evidence of translation in the complete Latin epistle of Peter Chrysologus. The chronological notation is absent, and some difference of style becomes apparent between the first and second chapters.

The first chapter, which is also preserved in the Hispanic collection, is sufficiently polished and coherent and resembles the style of Peter Chrysologus’s other works, so much so that almost some of the words of this same chapter are repeated in Sermon 145 of Chrysologus.

Since the author of the Hispanic collection did not take this epistle from the Chalcedonian collection, he undoubtedly used a copy of Latin origin.

The second chapter, however, is very intricate and unlike the first; it has the character of a translation from Greek. If you compare the Latin text of both chapters with the Greek, you will discover an original in the first and a translation in the second.

Thus, in the first chapter all the sentences are explained coherently, whereas in the Greek they are recognized as having been rendered less exactly. Among other matters that anyone can observe for himself, Chrysologus’s original wording in Latin is “Origen, investigator of first principles,” referring to his work *On First Principles*. In Greek, however, the term “of first principles” (*τῶν ἀρχῶν*) was rendered as “of ancient things” (*τῶν παλαιῶν*), showing that the translator understood Chrysologus’s meaning less well.

Conversely, in the second chapter, although the Greek version introduces difficulty in some places, it is nevertheless much clearer than the Latin text, to such an extent that the latter appears to have been rendered from Greek that was wrongly written or read. At times it must be explained from the Greek, as will be noted in the annotations. This is certainly an indication not of an original Latin text but of a translation.

5. This second chapter, which directly answers Eutyches’ letter, is especially important. It would be incredible that Chrysologus responded to Eutyches, who was complaining about Flavian’s judgment and seeking his assistance, with only the first chapter, which contains general statements and lacks even a concluding formula.

We think it probable that a manuscript copy of the more carefully composed first chapter remained with Chrysologus, as happens with writings that we produce with greater care. From this copy other versions were subsequently transcribed, which came into the hands of the Latin translator of the Council of Chalcedon and of the author of the Hispanic collection.

The second chapter, written specifically for Eutyches with less care, as is commonly the case in familiar letters, may have been added by Chrysologus only to the autograph letter sent to Eutyches. Thus no copy of it may have existed with the author himself or among the Latins, and it could have been given Latin form only from the Greek translation made immediately afterward in the East.

Whatever may seem more probable in this matter, certainly this second chapter of the epistle—which is of the greatest importance and necessity in the case of Eutyches and is attested by both such an ancient Greek and such an ancient Latin version—cannot be suspected of being spurious.

6. It remains to determine the date. Almost everyone since Quesnellus has judged that this epistle was written after May of the year 449, since they think that the words in Chapter 2, “that you may obediently attend to what has been written by the most blessed pope of the Roman city,” refer to Leo’s famous Epistle 28 to Flavian, sent on the Ides of June of that same year, by which the entire case of Eutyches was decided.

We too adopted this view in Book II of the *Observations* on the works of Cardinal Noris, chapter 7, number 2.

Now we are compelled to adopt another opinion. On the one hand, everyone agrees that Saint Peter Chrysologus was responding in this letter to Eutyches’ epistle, and that, at the same time as Eutyches wrote to Leo, he also sent a letter to Chrysologus, so that he might quickly forestall him as well against Flavian’s judgment.

On the other hand, it is certain that Leo received Eutyches’ letter in February of the year 449 and, for this reason, replied in the same month with Epistles 23 and 24. There is no need, with Quesnellus, to seek out many conjectures to explain a longer delay before Chrysologus’s response.

Indeed, it is sufficiently credible from the very context that Chrysologus replied at the first opportunity. He reveals that he had received no information about the case from anywhere except Eutyches’ letter, and even that information was so scanty that he seems to have feared Nestorianism rather than Eutychianism, and in the first chapter he puts forward precisely those arguments that he most clearly develops against the Nestorian heresy, the opposite of Eutychianism, in Sermon 145.

This would not have happened if, as Quesnellus conjectured in his notes, he had delayed his response in order first to become more accurately informed about the whole matter.

For if Saint Peter had not written the epistle until after the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod had reached Rome—proceedings in which the Eutychian error had been so clearly exposed and Eutyches himself condemned as obstinate—and until after Leo’s letter confirming the judgment of Constantinople had become known to him, how could he have claimed that he did not know the opinion of the Fathers of Constantinople: “What they understood, we do not know because of their silence”?

How could he have treated Eutyches so impartially that he judged him neither innocent nor guilty? How could he, after so solemn a condemnation confirmed even by the Roman pontiff, have called him “most beloved son,” “most honored,” and “a presbyter worthy of honor”?

These features show that he replied immediately, while he was not yet informed about the matter.

Nor do the words, “that you may obediently attend to what has been written by the most blessed pope of the Roman city,” contradict this. For Eutyches seems to have mentioned in his letter the epistle that he had sent to Pope Leo together with certain documents. By these words Chrysologus intended to indicate the letters that he presumed Leo, once better informed, had given, or would shortly give, in a fuller reply.

Indeed, if Chrysologus had read Leo’s dogmatic letter, he would apparently not have written: “We cannot hear—or, according to the Greek, know or judge—cases of faith apart from the agreement of the bishop of the Roman city.” These words declare that the opinion of the Roman bishop was not yet known to him.

Therefore this epistle of Chrysologus seems to have been sent at approximately the same time that Leo wrote Epistles 23 and 24, that is, around February of the year 449.

Perhaps the same man who brought the letters of Theodosius and Eutyches to Saint Leo also traveled to Ravenna with the letter of that same Theodosius to Valentinian, and on this occasion delivered Eutyches’ letter to Chrysologus. As he was returning to Constantinople and carrying Valentinian’s reply, Chrysologus handed him this epistle to Eutyches so that it might be delivered more quickly and safely.

Certainly Chrysologus did not write after learning of the proceedings against Eutyches or after Leo’s definitive letter, as must be assumed according to Quesnellus’s view.

## Letter XXV, of Peter Chrysologus, Bishop of Ravenna, to Eutyches the Presbyter (C, G)

[Note: Formerly Letter 25; now 35. Written around February 449.]

[Note: The manuscripts of the Hispanic collection that preserve the shortened version of this epistle add, in place of a synopsis: “Against his errors, to which he replied with a fitting example.”]

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Synopsis

I. He teaches that the Incarnation of the Word was prescribed long ago against errors attacking it, and that it is not to be debated but believed with honor and fear.

II. He advises Eutyches to attend obediently to the writings of the Roman pontiff, because Peter, directing the rulers of his see, provides guidance to those who seek the truth of the faith.

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts deriving from the Hispanic collection. The Latin copies of the Chalcedonian collection read: “To the most beloved and honorable son Eutyches the presbyter, Peter, bishop of Ravenna.”]

To his most beloved and deservedly honored son, the presbyter Eutyches, Peter, bishop of Ravenna.

### Chapter I

*The supplied source ends here.*
I read your gloomy letters gloomily, and went through your mournful writings with the sorrow they deserved; for just as the peace of the Churches, the concord of priests, and the tranquility of the people make us rejoice with heavenly joy, so fraternal dissension afflicts and casts us down—especially when it arises from such causes.

[Note: Some manuscripts have “I hurried through” (*percucurri*); others, “I ran through” (*cucurri*). The figurative expression *moesta moerore* (“mournful writings with sorrow”), familiar to Chrysologus, which the Greek translator did not render adequately, indicates that the Latin is the original.]

[Note: Thus in all manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection. The common reading, “makes heavenly joy audible,” is found in the other manuscripts deriving from the Isidorian and the less-correct Hispanic collections, as in Vatican manuscript 1341 of that Hispanic collection. The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, which presents a purer Hispanic collection, approaches our reading and that of the Chalcedonian copies: it has “makes [us] rejoice with heavenly joy.” Later scribes, failing to notice that the word *audere* lacked only the letter *g*, thought it should be corrected to “makes heavenly joy audible.”]

For thirty years human laws remove human lawsuits, yet Christ’s generation—written in the divine law as ineffable (Isaiah 53:8)—is after so many ages subjected to reckless disputation.

[Note: Chrysologus says similarly in Sermon 145: “Human laws within thirty years put an end to all contentious questions; but Christ, for nearly five hundred years, provides the causes of his birth, suffers disputes about his origin, and endures questions about his status.” The individual statements that follow are repeated in the same sermon against the error of Nestorius. Quesnellus noted *decem* (“ten”) in the margin instead of *triginta* (“thirty”), but we have found this reading in no manuscript.]

What Origen, investigator of beginnings, suffered, and how Nestorius went astray while discussing natures, is not unknown to your prudence.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection and the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript. Quesnellus, from the less-correct manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, has “went astray.”]

The Magi confess Jesus to be God in swaddling clothes by their mystical gifts (Matthew 2); and the priests, by a sorrowful inquiry, ask who he is who was born through a virginal birth from the Holy Spirit.

[Note: Quesnellus noted in the margin, “Perhaps, deceitful,” but no manuscript supports this. Only in the cited sermon of Chrysologus against the Nestorians does one read: “And you, deceitful investigator, now ask who Jesus is?” Shortly afterward the Chalcedonian-collection manuscripts have *vagitus* (“crying”).]

[Note: The Greek text has “Christ” (*τὸν Χριστόν*, *Christum*), and likewise thereafter “Christ” (*ὁ Χριστός*), where the Latin has “Jesus.” This is found not only in the manuscripts deriving from the Hispanic collection but also in all the Chalcedonian manuscripts that we have seen or that Baluzius consulted. It is therefore clear that this chapter, even in the Chalcedonian manuscripts, was derived from the original Latin, as in the Hispanic collection, and not translated into Latin from the Greek.]

[Note: Chrysologus makes similar assertions in Sermon 145, against the Nestorians who denied that Christ was born as God. Since here likewise he repeatedly insists on the word “God” and on other expressions, without anywhere suggesting anything Eutychian, he seems to have thought that the matter concerned the Nestorian heresy and not to have detected the contrary error of Eutyches. Similarly, Saint Leo, in Letter 34, admits that from Eutyches’ letters alone he could learn nothing about his errors or understand where his complaint was tending, namely, his complaint about the supposed revival of the Nestorian heresy. This became known only from the records transmitted by Flavian.]

When Jesus gave a cry in the cradle, the heavenly host proclaimed: “Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:14). And now, when at the name of Jesus every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Philippians 2:10)—the question of his origin is stirred up.

[Note: Some manuscripts of the collection have *gloriam* (“glory”). The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will, heavenly …,” and so forth.]

[Note: Thus all our Chalcedonian manuscripts, including those consulted by Baluzius, as well as the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and those derived from it. Quesnellus, following only our Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, has *movetur* (“is moved”). Shortly afterward the Chalcedonian manuscripts read: “We, dearest brother, together with the Apostle,” etc.]

We, brother, say with the Apostle: “Although we have known Jesus according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

Nor can we make an insulting investigation of him whom we are commanded to honor, to render fear, and to await, not to scrutinize, while we confess him to be the Judge.

[Note: Thus in the Hispanic manuscripts and the others derived from the same collection. The Chalcedonian manuscripts have “to scrutinize insultingly.” One of these, the Colbertinus consulted by Baluzius, has, with the addition of a single letter, “to scrutinize what is insulting”; Surius and others after him noted *injuriose* (“insultingly”) in the margin. In Labbe’s Councils the reading is “to scrutinize curiously.”]

[Note: We have retained the reading of the Hispanic and other collections that copied this letter from the Hispanic collection. The Greek version agrees. In the Chalcedonian Latin manuscripts, however, the conjunction *et* (“and”) is omitted, and the text reads: “to render fear and await, while we confess that the Judge must not be scrutinized.”]

## Chapter II

[Note: In the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and the others, together with Quesnellus, the reading is: “I have replied to all this, brother, in your letters”; with these words the abbreviated edition in the same manuscripts also ends. The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has: “I have replied to this in all respects.” We have preferred the reading of the Chalcedonian manuscripts as the better one and the one more appropriate to the complete letter.]

I have replied briefly to these matters, brother, in your letters; I would have written more if our brother and fellow bishop Flavian had sent me something in writing about this matter.

For if you are displeased because, as you write, “a judgment was chosen,” how can we judge concerning men whom we neither see because of their absence nor know what they understood, since we are ignorant of it through their silence?

[Note: The ancient translator, who—as we showed in the introductory notice—translated this chapter from the Greek, read, as in the printed editions, *ᾑρῆσθαι τὴν ἀκρόασιν* (“the hearing was chosen”), and therefore translated “the judgment was chosen.” Because the sense was obscure and uncertain, this gave rise to a lengthy controversy. Quesnellus noted *neglectum* (“neglected”) in the margin, but this is equally difficult and has not been found in any of our manuscripts or in those of Baluzius. We believe beyond doubt that the Greek originally read *ἀνῃρῆσθαι τὴν ἀκρόασιν* (“the hearing was taken away”), with *ἀν* having fallen out through an ancient scribal error. It should therefore be rendered from the Greek: “as you write, the hearing was taken away from yourself.” The whole passage is then clear, and it agrees with Letter 21 to Leo, in which Eutyches complained that his petition had not been received at the Constantinopolitan council. We have no doubt that he advanced a similar complaint before Peter of Ravenna, writing that a hearing had been denied him.]

A just mediator is not one who hears one party in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other party.

[Note: Quesnellus noted “judge” in the margin.]

In every respect, however, we urge you, honorable brother, to attend obediently to what has been written by the most blessed pope of the city of Rome; for blessed Peter, who both lives and presides in his own seat, provides the truth of the faith to those who seek it.

[Note: From our manuscripts and those of Baluzius we have added the conjunction *et* (“and”). Since Peter Chrysologus wrote this before Leo’s celebrated Letter 28, issued against the errors of Eutyches, as we demonstrated in the introductory notice, the words here are not peculiar to that letter, as though Peter already knew and approved it. Rather, they express a general principle and a conviction then commonly held with certainty: that Peter, still living in his successors, provides the truth of the faith to those who seek it. For this reason the dogmatic decrees of the Roman pontiffs are to be obeyed.]

For, in our zeal for peace and the faith, we cannot hear or judge matters of faith apart from the agreement of the bishop of the city of Rome.

[Note: The force of the Greek verb is “to know” or “to judge.” To prevent this principle asserted by Peter from appearing singular or incredible, the Egyptians at the Council of Chalcedon, in Act 4, testified that a similar custom existed in Egypt: nothing was done by any subordinate bishop without the Alexandrian bishop. They derived this from a canon of Nicaea and called Anatolius himself, formerly a deacon or priest of the Alexandrian Church, as a witness to the custom. The Egyptians abused this discipline at Chalcedon: by such an excuse they withdrew from signing Leo’s letter and from obeying the council, arguing that they ought to await the election and judgment of the Alexandrian bishop. But the discipline itself cannot be denied on account of this abuse. If it prevailed among bishops subject to the Alexandrian bishop, it is not surprising that it likewise applied to bishops who were subject, by a special title, to the Roman primate of the whole Church.]

May the Lord deem it worthy to preserve your devotion in health for the longest possible time, dearest and most honored son.

## Greek version

To the beloved and deservedly honored son Eutyches, Peter, bishop of Ravenna.

[Col. 0740A]

I read your gloomy letters gloomily, and went through your gloomy writings with the sorrow they deserved; for just as the peace of the Churches, the concord of priests, and the tranquility of the people make us rejoice with heavenly joy, so fraternal dissension torments and casts us down—especially when it springs from such causes.

For thirty years human laws overturn human inquiries, while Christ’s birth—which is written in the divine law as ineffable—after so many ages is examined with deranged reasoning.

What Origen, the investigator of beginnings, endured, and how Nestorius slipped while reasoning about natures, is not hidden from your understanding.

[Note: In the margin of the Roman edition: “ineffably.”]

[Note: In the same place, *ἀρχῶν* (“of beginnings”).]

The Magi acknowledged Christ as God in swaddling clothes through mystical gifts; and the priests, with painful inquiry, investigate who he is who was born by a virginal birth from the Holy Spirit.

[Note: In the same place, the Roman edition’s margin has the incomplete reading *λυπητέᾳ ἐρευ…* (“with painful inquiry …”).]

When Christ gave a cry in the swaddling clothes, the heavenly host cried aloud: “Glory to God in the highest.” And now, when at the name of Jesus Christ every knee bows—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—the question of his ancient origin is stirred up.

But we, brother, say with the Apostle: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him.”

Nor can we examine him insultingly, since we are commanded to give honor, render fear, and await, not investigate, the Judge whom we confess.

[Note: In the same place, manuscript L has *περιέργως* (“with excessive curiosity”).]

[Note: In the same place, manuscript L has *ὅν* (“whom”).]

I have replied briefly to these things, brother, in your writings; I was intending to write more if our brother and fellow bishop Flavian had sent me some written communication about this matter.

For if you are displeased because, as you write, the hearing was chosen for yourself, how can we judge concerning these men whom we neither see because of their absence nor know what they understood, since we are ignorant of it through their silence? A just mediator is not one who hears one party in such a way as to reserve nothing for the other party.

In every respect we urge you, most honorable brother, to attend obediently to the writings sent by the most blessed pope of the city of Rome; for blessed Peter, who both lives and presides in his own seat, gives the truth of the faith to those who seek it.

For we, in our zeal for peace and the faith, cannot judge matters of faith apart from the agreement of the bishop of Rome.

[Note: Printed editions have *σύνεσις* (“understanding”); in the margin, by conjecture, *συναίνεσις* (“agreement”). Our Venetian manuscripts support the emendation. The Latin text agrees: “apart from the agreement.”]

May the Lord deem it worthy to preserve your devotion in health for the longest time, most beloved and most honored son.

[Note: This should be read as in the Venetian manuscripts; the Latin exemplar has “for the longest possible time.” The common text has “for a long time.”]

## Letter XXVI

[Note: Formerly numbered 26, now 29. Written around March 449.]

### Flavian’s second letter to Saint Leo the Pope

[Note: This letter, which we showed in the introductory notice to Letter 22 to have been written after Letter 22, is Flavian’s reply to Letter 23 of Saint Leo the Pope. At the meeting held at Constantinople on 13 April 449, Bishop Selencus said that Leo’s Letter 23 had been communicated to him only a few days earlier. Flavian replied that this had occurred while the forthcoming general council was being announced—the council that had been convened for 30 March. We therefore think that Flavian wrote this letter around March of the same year, before the summons to the council had become certain, and while it could still be prevented, as he hints at the end of the letter. John Cotelerius published the Greek letter in volume 1 of the *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, page 50, from Royal manuscripts 1026 and 2610, and added an exact translation from the Greek. Quesnellus, who in his first edition had given only the ancient version, inserted the Greek text with Cotelerius’s translation in the second edition. We have found two other Greek manuscripts in Rome: Vatican Greek 1455 and another much older manuscript of the monks of Saint Basil, numbered 19; and one further Venetian manuscript, number 165 of the Library of Saint Mark.]

(G)

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## Letter of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, written to Leo, archbishop of Old Rome

To the most holy and most blessed Father and fellow minister, Leo, Flavian sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0743A]

[Col. 0743B] As you know, most beloved of God, nothing is more precious to priests than piety and the right division of the word of truth. For all our hope and salvation, and the repayment of the promised blessings, depend upon this. Therefore everything must be done by us, and every labor undertaken, for the true faith and for the teachings set forth and handed down as dogmas by the holy Fathers, so that in every respect and amid every circumstance these things may be preserved and guarded whole and inviolate.

It was therefore necessary for us even now, seeing that the orthodox faith was being injured and that the heresy of Apollinaris and Valentinus was being renewed by the impious monk Eutyches, not to disregard the matter but to expose the error openly for the protection of the peoples.

For this Eutyches—this Eutyches—retaining within himself the hidden disease of a false opinion, and attacking our gentleness, dared shamelessly and insolently to proclaim his own impiety to many, saying that before the incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ there were two natures, divinity and humanity, but that after the union there had come to be one nature; ignorant of what he was saying and of what he was affirming.

For the union of the two natures that came together in Christ, as your piety also knows, does not confuse their properties in the union; rather, the properties of the two natures remain whole even in the union.

He added another impiety, saying that the body of the Lord which was born from Mary was not of our substance, nor of human material; he calls it human, certainly, but not consubstantial with us, nor with her who bore him according to the flesh.

Yet the acts performed at Ephesus by the holy and ecumenical synod, in the letter written to the impious and deposed Nestorius, expressly state: “The natures that came together for true unity are different, but one Christ and Son is from both—not as though the distinction of the natures had been removed through the union, but rather because the same natures, divinity and humanity, through an ineffable and incomprehensible coming together into unity, perfected for us one Lord Jesus Christ.”

This is not unknown to your holiness, since you have certainly read the acts conducted at Ephesus.

Making nothing of these things, the same Eutyches thinks that he will not suffer the penalty defined by that holy and ecumenical synod.

Therefore, since many of the simpler people were being harmed in the teaching of the faith by his disputation, he was accused by the most religious bishop Eusebius. He appeared before the holy council and, by his own voice, disclosed to the Fathers of the synod what he himself believed. Since he was alien to the right faith, we deposed him, as all the records concerning him will teach your holiness; we have sent them together with this letter.

It is also right, in my judgment, that you should be informed of this: after the same Eutyches had been subjected to a just and canonical deposition, he ought at least to have repaired his former offenses by his later conduct, to appease God through thorough repentance and many tears, and to heal by true repentance our heart, deeply saddened by his fall. But he not only failed to do this; he also made every effort to disturb the most holy Church here, publicly displaying tablets full of insults and curses. In addition, he presented petitions to our most pious and Christ-loving emperor, petitions filled with arrogance and insolence, attempting in every respect to trample upon the divine canons.

When these matters had thus taken place, letters from your holiness were delivered to us through the count Pansophius, worthy of all admiration. From them we learned that the same Eutyches had sent you petitions full of every kind of deceit and trickery, saying that at the time of the trial he had delivered petitions of appeal to us and to the holy synod then assembled, and that he had appealed to your holiness. He did nothing of the sort; in this respect too he deceived you, like the father of lies, thinking that he would steal his way into your ears.

Therefore, most holy Father, moved by all that he has dared to do and by what has been done and is being done against us and against the most holy Church, use your customary confidence, as befits the priesthood. Make the common cause and the settlement of the holy Churches your own, and deign by your own letters to support the canonical deposition pronounced against him; and confirm also the faith of our most pious and Christ-loving emperor.

The matter needs only an impulse and assistance from you, which through your prudence will immediately bring everything to tranquility and peace. Thus both the heresy that has arisen and the tumult aroused because of it will easily cease, with God cooperating, through your sacred letters. The synod that is being publicly announced as future will also be prevented, so that the most holy Churches throughout the world may not be disturbed.

I and all who are with me salute all the brotherhood who are with you. May you be well in the Lord and pray for us; may you be gracious to us, most beloved of God and most holy Father.

[Note: The Basilian manuscript has: “Letter of Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople, to Leo, archbishop of Rome, against Eutyches, before the Council of Chalcedon.” The Venetian manuscript has: “Of the blessed Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople, concerning Leo, the most holy pope of Rome.”]

## Greek version

Letter of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, written to Leo, archbishop of Old Rome.

To the most holy and most blessed Father and fellow minister, Leo, Flavian sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0744B] Of piety and the right division of the word of truth, nothing is more precious to priests, as you know, most beloved of God. For all our hope and salvation, and the repayment of the promised blessings, depend upon this.

Therefore, for this reason, everything must be done by us and every labor undertaken for the true faith and for the things set forth and established as dogmas by the holy Fathers, so that in every circumstance these things may be preserved and guarded whole and unharmed.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “more valuable to God’s priests.” The Basilian and Venetian manuscripts read *ποιητέον ἡμῖν καὶ πονητέον* (“we must do and we must labor”); the Venetian manuscript also has “to be preserved and guarded.” The words “and now” are added from the Basilian and Venetian manuscripts (the latter lacks “was”), and occur also in the ancient version; Cotelerius’s margin notes them as another reading.]

It was therefore necessary for us even now, seeing that the orthodox faith was being harmed and that the heresy of Apollinaris and Valentinus was being renewed by Eutyches the monk, not to overlook it but to bring it into the open for the protection of the peoples.

For this Eutyches—this Eutyches—holding within himself the hidden disease of false doctrine, attacking our gentleness, dared shamelessly and insolently to bring his own impiety before many, saying that before the incarnation of our Savior Jesus Christ there were two natures, of divinity and humanity, but that after the union one nature had come to be; not knowing what he was saying or concerning whom he was making his assertions.

For the union of the two natures that came together in Christ, as your godly reverence also knows, did not confuse their properties in the union; rather, the properties of the two natures remain whole even in the union.

He added another impiety, saying that the body of the Lord which came into being from Mary was not of our substance nor of human material. He calls it human, but not consubstantial with us, nor with the woman who bore him according to the flesh.

And although the proceedings conducted at Ephesus by the holy and ecumenical synod, in the letter written to the impious and deposed Nestorius, expressly say the following—“The natures that were brought together into true unity are different, but one Christ and Son from both; not as though the distinction of the natures had been abolished through the union, but rather because divinity and humanity, through an ineffable and incomprehensible coming together into unity, made for us one Lord Jesus Christ”—this is not hidden from your holiness, since you have certainly read the records of what was done at Ephesus.

[Note: The Basilian manuscript reads “to overlook this”; Cotelerius noted in the margin: “Another reading: to overlook it now.”]

[Note: In the margin of Cotelerius’s edition: “Another reading: of Apollinaris.”]

[Note: The Basilian and Venetian manuscripts read “of Eutyches the monk.” The common text has “of impious Eutyches,” and Cotelerius noted “another reading: the monk.” This reading, which expresses Eutyches’ condition and manner of life, is confirmed by the ancient version.]

[Note: The Basilian manuscript has “for this is Eutyches himself.” Cotelerius noted in the margin: “Another reading: for this is the one himself.”]

[Note: The Venetian manuscript has “holding within himself a doctrine.”]

[Note: In Cotelerius’s margin: “Another reading: to set forth.”]

[Note: The Venetian manuscript has “called it.”]

[Note: The common text is corrupt, reading *συνηχθεῖσαι*. Cotelerius conjectured *συναχθεῖσαι* or *συνενεχθεῖσαι*. The Basilian manuscript confirms the latter as the correct reading: “brought together.”]

[Note: The Basilian manuscript lacks the word “rather.”]

[Note: The wording is more elegant in the same Basilian manuscript, which adds *τέ* (“and”), absent from the printed editions.]

[Note: For Greek ears this reading in the Basilian and Venetian manuscripts will, we think, be preferable to the common text, “and this did not escape notice.”]

Making no account of these things, the same Eutyches thinks that he will not suffer the punishment decreed by that holy and ecumenical synod.

Therefore, because many of the more simple-minded were being harmed in the teaching of the faith by the discussion he had conducted, he was accused by the most reverent bishop Eusebius, appeared before the holy synod, and disclosed in his own voice his personal belief. Since he was alien to the right faith, we deposed him, as all the records concerning him will show your holiness; we have sent them together with this letter.

[Note: The Basilian manuscript has “because of such things.” In the Venetian manuscript the preposition before “by him” is absent.]

[Note: Previously the text read, “disclosing his own opinion to them.” The word *αὐτοῖς* (“to them”) is absent from the Basilian and Venetian manuscripts and ought to be absent, since there is no antecedent to which it can refer. The ancient Latin version also does not recognize it: “disclosing his own sect by his voice.” In his translation, Cotelerius rendered the word as “not to them, but to the Fathers of the synod,” in order to explain the sense, although the Fathers are not named in the Greek.]

[Note: The Basilian manuscript has “of our orthodox faith.”]

[Note: The Venetian manuscript has “all the records concerning him.”]

It is also right, as I think, that you should be informed that the same Eutyches, after undergoing a just and canonical deposition, ought at least to have healed his former offenses by his later conduct, to appease God through thorough repentance and many tears, and to heal by true remorse our heart, deeply grieved at his fall. But he not only failed to do this; rather, he made every effort to disturb the most holy Church here, publicly displaying notices filled with insult and abuse. In addition, he submitted petitions to our most pious and Christ-loving emperor, and these too were filled with arrogance and insolence, attempting in every way to trample upon the divine canons.

[Note: The Basilian manuscript has “deeply grieved.” Shortly afterward, the same manuscript has “through repentance” instead of “through remorse.”]

[Note: The Basilian manuscript has “to disturb”; later, it has *προθείς* (“having set forth”) instead of *προτιθείς* (“setting forth”), and “in addition to this” instead of “in addition to these things.”]

[Note: In Cotelerius’s margin: “Another reading: trampling upon”; and shortly afterward: “Another reading: trampling upon every truth.” A trace of this reading appears in the Basilian manuscript: “attempting to trample upon the divine canons and to attack every truth.”]

When these things had thus occurred, letters from your holiness were delivered to us through the most admirable Count Pansophius. Through them we learned that the same Eutyches had sent you petitions filled with every kind of deceit and trickery, saying that at the time of the trial he had delivered petitions of appeal to us and to the holy synod assembled here, and had appealed to your holiness. This was in no way done by him; in this respect too he lied, being indeed the father of lies, thinking that he could seize your ears.

[Note: From the Basilian manuscript we have added the emphatic particle *δή* (“indeed”), a particle frequent in Greek, especially since Cotelerius found the same word in one manuscript and therefore noted in the margin: “Another reading: being indeed the father of lies.” Shortly afterward he observed that the word *ὢν* (“being”) is absent elsewhere.]

[Note: Thus the Basilian manuscript reads. We do not know why Cotelerius preferred *γενόμενά τε καὶ γινόμενα* (“what has been done and what is being done”) and relegated to the margin the reading we adopted, which was also found by him in another manuscript; the preceding discussion concerned past events: “because of everything dared by him.” Nevertheless, we cannot deny that the reading adopted by Cotelerius is supported by the ancient version: “what has been done and is being done.” In the Venetian manuscript, shortly afterward, the text has “to speak openly, as is customary and as befits …”]

Moved, therefore, most holy Father, by all that he has dared and by what has been done and is being said against us and against the most holy Church, speak openly with your customary confidence, as befits the priesthood. Make the common cause and the order of the holy Churches your own, and deign by your own letters to approve the canonical deposition pronounced against him, while also strengthening the faith of our most pious and Christ-loving emperor.

[Note: The Basilian manuscript omits *πρᾶγμα* (“matter”). Shortly afterward the same manuscript has “by the canonical deposition.”]

[Note: The Basilian manuscript has “and this too I think is right.” The Venetian manuscript omits only the word “as.”]

For the matter needs only the impulse and support that come from you, which, through your own agreement, ought to bring everything immediately into tranquility and peace.

[Note: The common text has *σύνεσις* (“understanding”). The Venetian manuscript and another manuscript noted by Cotelerius in the margin have the better reading *συναίνεσις* (“agreement”), which the ancient translator expressed as “by your own agreement.” The Basilian manuscript likewise has a faulty form, *συνερέσεως*, for *συναινέσεως*.]

[Note: This excellent and most genuine reading should be credited to the Basilian and Venetian manuscripts. We do not see what useful sense can be extracted from the other printed reading, *παρ᾽ αὐτὰ μετασκευάσαι*. The ancient version agrees with the correction: “to bring everything to completion.” Cotelerius’s edition also notes in the margin: “Another reading: everything.”]

Thus both the heresy that has arisen and the disturbance caused by it will easily be brought to an end, with God cooperating, through your sacred letters. The synod that is being publicly announced as about to take place will also be prevented, so that the most holy Churches everywhere may not be disturbed.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript has “to take place.” Shortly afterward it has *ἁπανταχοῦ* (“everywhere”) instead of *ἁπανταχόσε* (“to every place”).]

I, and those who are with me, salute all the brotherhood who are with you.

May you be strong in the Lord and, praying earnestly for us, be gracious to us, most beloved of God and most honored Father.

[Note: This must be read exactly so, with the Basilian and Venetian manuscripts. The ancient version has “may you be gracious to us”; the reading in the printed editions, *χαριτωθῇ ἡμῖν*, should be rejected. Cotelerius’s edition also records our reading in the margin from another manuscript. Shortly afterward, “and most worthy” is absent from the Basilian manuscript and from another of Cotelerius’s manuscripts, which notes in the margin: “Perhaps, most holy.”]

## The ancient version of the same letter of Flavian

[Note: This version is found in manuscript 17 of the Chalcedonian collection and thence passed into the manuscripts of collection 22, to whose letter it was added.]

(G)

### Synopsis

I. He explains the duties of a bishop and sets forth Eutyches’ error.  
II. What proceedings were conducted against him in the synod.  
III. Concerning Eutyches’ fabricated appeal to the apostolic see. He asks for confirmation of his condemnation.

To the most holy and most blessed father and fellow priest, Leo, Flavian sends greetings in the Lord.

## Chapter I

As you know, most beloved of God, nothing is more honorable to priests than piety and the right proclamation of the word of truth. For all our hope and salvation, and the repayment of the promised blessings, lie in these things.

Therefore everything must be done by us, and we must labor, for the true faith and for the expositions and dogmas of the holy Fathers, so that in every respect and amid every upheaval of affairs these things may be preserved and guarded whole and inviolate.

It was therefore necessary now, when we saw that the orthodox faith was being harmed and that the heresies of Apollinaris and Valentinus were being renewed by the monk Eutyches, not to disregard this but to reveal it openly for the people’s protection.

For this Eutyches—this Eutyches—holding within himself the hidden disease of an evil sect, attacking our gentleness, shamelessly and impudently presumed to inflict his own impiety upon many, saying:

“Before the inhumanization of our Savior Jesus Christ there were two natures, divinity and humanity; but after the union one nature was made.”

He understood neither what he was saying nor concerning whom he was making his assertions.

For the union of the two natures that came together in Christ, as your religious devotion knows, did not confuse their properties in the union; rather, the properties of the natures remain perfect in the union.
