[Note: All manuscripts have this reading. In the margin of the printed editions is “after the union.” In any case, *unitas* (“unity”) is frequently used for *unitio* (“union”), which is what the Greek signifies.]

He added another impiety, saying:

“The body of the Lord, which was made from Mary, is not of our substance nor of human mixture; he calls it human, certainly, but not consubstantial with us or with his mother according to the flesh.”

[Note: Thus all the old manuscripts. The printed editions, by editorial choice, read: “The body of the Lord, which was made from Mary, is not,” etc., and shortly afterward have *conspersionis* (“mixture”). We have not wished to alter the ancient reading.]

## Chapter II

He said these things although the proceedings conducted at Ephesus by the holy and universal council, in the letter written to the impious and condemned Nestorius, expressly state:

“Different natures came together for true unity; but one Christ and Son came from both—not as though the difference of the natures had been destroyed because of the unity, but rather because the coming together of divinity and humanity into unity, ineffable and incomprehensible, made for us one Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Note: This is the reading of the very ancient Veronese manuscript of collection 17, to which the Greek text corresponds. Other manuscripts with Quesnellus have “from both, Christ, God’s Son”; the editions of the Councils have “from both, Christ, God’s Son.”]

[Note: Quesnellus correctly emended this passage from the Thuane manuscript, since it previously made no sense, reading “as one thing the properties.” The emendation is confirmed not only by the manuscripts of Baluzius and our own but also by the Greek text. Later, the Chigi manuscript has “perfect in the unity.”]

This also is not hidden from your holiness, since you have certainly read the proceedings conducted at Ephesus.

Making nothing of these things, the same Eutyches thinks that he will not suffer the punishment prescribed by that holy and universal council, although through his words many of the simpler people are harmed in the teaching of the faith.

We condemned him, after he had been accused by the most reverend Eusebius, appeared before the holy council, and disclosed by his own voice his own sect, since he was alien to the right faith. All the proceedings concerning him, which we have sent with this letter, will make this known to your holiness.

It is also right, as I think, that this should be communicated to you: the same Eutyches, having suffered a just and canonical condemnation, ought to have saved his former offenses by his later conduct, to appease God through perfect repentance and many tears, and to heal through true repentance our heart, greatly saddened by his fall.

He not only failed to do this; he also hastened in every way to disturb the holy Church here, publicly displaying statements filled with insults and curses. In addition, he presented petitions to our most pious and Christ-loving emperor, petitions filled with arrogance and insolence, attempting in every respect to trample upon the divine laws.

[Note: The Veronese manuscript reads “and most Christian” in place of “and Christ-loving.”]

## Chapter III

After these events, letters from your holiness were delivered to us through the admirable Count Pansophius.

[Note: Quesnellus and the editions of the Councils read *gestis* (“having taken place”); all our manuscripts and those of Baluzius read *secutis* (“having followed”), which we have retained.] Through them we learned that the same Eutyches had sent you petitions full of every kind of deceit and craft, saying that at the time of the trial he had delivered petitions of appeal to us and to the holy council assembled here, and had appealed to your holiness.

This was in no way done by him; in this matter too he lied, thinking that through the deceit of falsehood he could insinuate himself into your holy ears.

[Note: The translator read *οἷα δι᾽ ἀπάτης τοῦ ψεύδους* (“as though through the deceit of falsehood”), whereas the text has *οἷα δὴ πατὴρ ὢν τοῦ ψεύδους* (“being indeed the father of lies”). Cotelerius notes this.]

Therefore, most holy Father, moved by all that he has presumed to do and by what has been done and is being done against us and against the most holy Church, act with your customary confidence, as befits the priesthood. Make the common cause and the discipline of the holy Churches your own, and deign by your own writings to concur in the condemnation regularly pronounced against him; strengthen also the faith of our most pious and Christ-loving emperor.

[Note: All manuscripts have this reading. Quesnellus, together with the printed editions of the Councils, has “act confidently,” instead of “with customary confidence.”]

[Note: The Chigi manuscript and the margin of the editions of the Councils have “in the condemnation regularly made against him.” The editions of the Councils have “the condemnation,” without the preposition *in*.]

For the matter requires only your consolation and defense, by which you ought, through your own agreement, to bring everything to tranquility and peace.

Thus the heresy that has arisen, and the disturbances that have occurred because of it, will very easily be destroyed, with God cooperating through your most sacred letters. The council that is being publicly announced as forthcoming will also be removed, so that the most holy Churches everywhere may in no way be disturbed.

[Note: The printed editions and most manuscripts have “because of him.” We have corrected this from the oldest Veronese manuscript, with which the Greek text agrees.]

I and those who are with me salute all the brotherhood who are with you.

May you be well in the Lord and pray for us; may you be gracious to us, most religious and holy Father.

## Letter XXVII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 22. Formerly numbered 27, now 31. Written on 21 May 449.]

### To Flavian, bishop of Constantinople

[Note: Quesnellus published this letter from the Grimanic manuscript. We have been unable to find it anywhere in our manuscripts.]

### Synopsis

He informs Flavian that his letter has been received; praises the proceedings he conducted against Eutyches; and pledges his own concern.

Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

The letters of your beloved have reached us [Note: Col. 0752B: He means Letter 22, which, as we showed in the prefatory notice first written for Flavian, was sent by Flavian.]; we announce this as soon as we found an appropriate opportunity through the arrival of our son, the honorable Rodanus. They informed us of the cause which, as we grieve, has been stirred up among you by a perverse error. For the man who until recently seemed to be of religious purpose held an opinion concerning the faith other than was proper; he ought not to have deviated from the Catholic tradition, but to have remained in the same belief held by all.

But concerning this matter [Note: Col. 0752B: Namely, in the following Letter 28. Quesnellus reads *patiemur* after a few words; but the Grimanicus manuscript, the sole source from which we possess this letter, reads *patimur*, according to P. Cacciari.] we are writing more fully through the one who brought us the letters of Your Holiness, so that we may instruct Your Fraternity what ought to be decided regarding the whole affair. For we do not tolerate either that he should persist in the perversity of his conviction, or that Your Holiness, who with zeal for the faith resists a perverse and foolish error, should be disturbed by the prolonged attack of the opposing party.

We wish you to receive with the affection he deserves the aforementioned son of ours, through whom we have delivered these letters, and to write back to us when he returns. Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes.

## Admonition concerning the following letter (G)

### 1

Among all the decrees of the Roman pontiffs concerning the faith, the following letter of Saint Leo to Flavian is the most celebrated. In it the entire controversy concerning the Incarnation is precisely examined and defined; the contrary errors of Nestorius and Eutyches are condemned; and Catholic doctrine is so accurately declared not only in its propositions but also in its wording that everything written in it is demonstrably drawn from apostolic and evangelical teaching (Letter 152).

Saint Flavian, whose knowledge of the authority of the Apostolic See was well established, had already warned that this matter—Eutyches having stirred up disturbances after the judgment at Constantinople—needed only a pontifical impulse and support by which everything might immediately be brought to tranquillity and peace (Letter 26).

Indeed, as soon as this letter was transmitted to the East and published after the Ephesian Robbery, where it had been suppressed by fraud and force so that it would not be read, it was immediately accepted and signed by everyone, so that it was universally regarded as a rule of faith and as a Lydian stone by which Catholics might be distinguished from heretics.

It subsequently became evident that a pontifical definition was sufficient and that a general council was unnecessary, as Flavian had also indicated (Letter 26), since the entire Church accepted it even without a council and before the Synod of Chalcedon was held. The bishops appended their signatures to it not in order to add force or authority to it, but to demonstrate that they were Catholics and to avoid being regarded as heretics if they refused. For it had already become widely known what all the most reverend bishops later proclaimed at Chalcedon, session 4, p. 1403: “Whoever does not agree with the letter of the most holy Bishop Leo is a heretic.”

At that same council, where the proceedings of the Ephesian Robbery were to be annulled, the letter was received with the highest praise in sessions 2 and 4 and was held in such honor as though it had been issued by Peter himself. Even before it was published, Peter Chrysologus, thoroughly knowledgeable concerning apostolic authority, had declared that it must be observed and upheld (Letter 25). Nothing is more illustrious for the authority of apostolic definitions than this testimony of the whole Church and of the general council, which recognizes Peter living and speaking in his successors.

At the Roman synod under Gelasius, an anathema was pronounced: “If anyone disputes even one iota of the text of this letter and does not receive it reverently in every respect” (Tom. V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 387). Saint Gregory likewise says, Book VI, Letter 2: “If anyone ever presumes to say anything against the faith of these four councils, and against the tome and definition of Pope Leo of holy memory, let him be anathema.”

### 2

For this reason, in professions of faith nothing is more common than to profess the doctrine of this letter after the general councils. Among the Easterners, where the heresy of Eutyches had stirred up disturbances, this practice was first introduced, as is clear, among other evidence, from several letters of Hormisdas, from the letter of Peter the Deacon to Fulgentius, and from the Council of Apamea in the year 535.

The same custom also passed to the Westerners and continued there for a long time. See the profession of Adalbert, Bishop of Morinum, to Hincmar of Reims, published by Sirmond in volume X of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1388; and the pledge of the bishops of the province of Aquileia to Paulinus, the patriarch, published from Vatican manuscript 1322 by Father Bernard de Rubeis in *Monumenta Ecclesiae Aquileiensis*, under the year 801, p. 380.

When Saint Amatus the abbot, already near death, wished to issue a profession of faith, he ordered this letter to be brought to him and read aloud, because it contains within itself the fullest exposition of the Catholic faith, as the author of his Life reports, no. 24, volume II, *Saecula Benedictina* II, p. 126.

### 3

Among the divine offices of the Roman Church, this letter was formerly read publicly during Advent. Hence we find it copied in the Lectionaries that were used by the Vatican basilica, as well as in another very ancient one belonging to the basilica of Saints Philip and James.

Accordingly, in Roman Order XI, in Mabillon (*Tom. II, Musaeum Italicum*, p. 123), which was written in the twelfth century by Benedict, a canon of the basilica of Saint Peter, the following is found for the Third Sunday of Advent: “Then the bishops read the fourth and fifth lessons from the letter of Saint Leo the pope, sent to Bishop Flavian concerning the Incarnation of the Lord against Eutyches the heretic.”

We have learned from numerous manuscript Lectionaries of other cities that the same practice was accepted in other Churches of Italy, which present the same letter on different days during the same season of Advent.

From a manuscript of the Royal Library, Quesnell collected evidence (*Dissertation 1 on the year 449*, no. 9) that the same practice was formerly followed in the Churches of Gaul. This can be confirmed by the Lectionary of Saint Benignus of Dijon, which Chifflet used when he published the same letter at the end of the works of Vigilius of Thapsus, as well as by Gallican sources cited by Father Martène in *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, Book III, chapter 2.

From Lectionaries of this kind, the letter was transferred into several collections of the Sermons of Saint Leo, which originated from Lectionaries.

### 4

When Gennadius, chapter 70, listed Leo among ecclesiastical writers, he mentioned only this letter, because it was by far the most widely circulated of all his works. For this reason he undoubtedly considered him its certain author.

The commonly circulated editions of Miraeus, Fabricius, and Vallarsi, however, in chapter 84 of Prosper, read: “There are also letters of Pope Leo against Eutyches concerning the true Incarnation of Christ, sent to various persons and said to have been dictated by him.” Quesnellus argues that this is a corrupt reading and a deception, and that it should read: “dictated by him,” that is, dictated by Leo himself for Prosper, since Ado wrote in his *Chronicle* that Prosper was Leo’s notary.

But the more accurate editions and the manuscripts do not prefer *et* (“and”) or *ei* (“for him”), but read only: “believed to have been dictated by him,” as Antelmius declares in Letter 2, nos. 28 and 30.

In a very ancient manuscript of the chapter-library of Verona, marked no. 46, we read: “Believed to have been dictated by him, as Marcellinus reported from Gennadius in his *Chronicle*.”

Yet Gennadius reported this not from his own judgment but from the opinion of the Gauls, among whom he lived. It commonly happens that things circulated as popular opinion are enlarged or even altered.

### 5

Indeed, the style clearly demonstrates that this letter and the other letters against Eutyches belong to Leo, not to Prosper: their style resembles Leo’s other works and differs unmistakably from the style of Prosper’s works.

Nor can Prosper be asserted to be the author of these letters without making him at the same time the author of all the other works of Leo, so that from the beginning to the end of Leo’s pontificate he would have written all of Leo’s works—not merely his letters but also his sermons—in a style differing from that of his own works. This is plainly incredible. Neither Gennadius’s text nor the opinion commonly held among the Gauls reported such a thing; indeed, Antelmius himself did not dare to affirm it concerning the sermons, as is evident from the same Letter 2, no. 40.

It can only be said that Saint Prosper contributed some diligence and assistance to these letters against Eutyches, which required particular care with Scripture and wording. From this, some believed that they had been dictated by him and spread that claim among the Gauls to the glory of a Gallican writer.

### 6

The importance of publishing so celebrated a dogmatic letter in as accurate a form as possible is sufficiently clear in itself, but it is demonstrated even more clearly by the letter of the three bishops of Gaul to Leo, Letter 67, chapter 2:

“Therefore, if you graciously permit it, we beg Your Holiness to examine a work which we have taken care to commit to writing on sheets for the benefit of both the present and future generations, and, if anything is lacking through the error of the copyists, to correct it.”

For this purpose we examined more than thirty manuscripts, including six of the greatest antiquity, reaching a thousand years of age.

This letter is found in all the collections that we listed in the preface, except Collections 4, 6, 7, 14, 15, and 16. We then reread it in the principal manuscript books of each collection, among which the oldest are Vatican-Reginensis Collection 1; Vatican 1342, Collection 3; Vienna Collection 5; Vatican 5845, Collection 8; Vatican Ottobonianus 93, similar to it; and Vatican 3791, Collection 11. The latter two present the same letter twice, from different sources. We also consulted Vatican 1322 and Verona 57, Collection 17, and Regensburg Collection 19.

We shall mention the other manuscripts of later date in the annotations wherever necessary. Among the Lectionaries we reread the very ancient Vatican 3836.

Two further manuscripts a thousand years old must be added: Verona 8, in which this letter of Leo is copied after the canonical letters, and another Veronese manuscript, no. 58, which presents this letter before certain documents of the Synod of Chalcedon.

When we cite the first edition of this letter, we mean the first edition of the Sermons of Saint Leo, in which this letter is inserted before the sermons on the Nativity, from a manuscript of the third collection of those sermons.

Finally, besides Quesnellus’s manuscripts, four others used by Baluzius will be included: Colbertinus 2574, and the Parisian, Divionese, and Corbeiensis manuscripts. The last three contain Collection 17, the Chalcedonian collection.

### 7

The most ancient Greek version, which was read and inserted in session 2 of the Synod of Chalcedon, was first published by Johannes Leunclavius from the library of Sambucus at Basel in 1578. Later it was published from other manuscripts by Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, at the end of the works of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus in 1604; then by the Roman editors of the Councils in 1608, and by later Roman collectors of the Councils.

We examined the Greek text against the very ancient manuscript no. 19 of the monks of Saint Basil in Rome, to which the Coislinianus 211 appears to be contemporary (*Bibliotheca Coisliniana*, p. 269), cited by Montfaucon. From these manuscripts we learn that this is the only letter of a Roman pontiff inserted into the Greek collection of Canons—a fact that testifies to the letter’s special renown among the Greeks.

We also compared it with the Venetian manuscript of Saint Mark, no. 164, entirely similar to manuscript 555, which contains the Greek Chalcedonian collection, and with another Venetian manuscript, no. 165, which contains certain portions of the same collection.

To distinguish them, we shall call manuscript 164 the First Venetian Manuscript and manuscript 165 the Second.

Since this letter is read twice in these Venetian manuscripts—first among the letters before the proceedings, and then in the proceedings of the council at which it was read—we have sometimes compared both texts of the same manuscript. Accordingly, we shall cite variant readings as presented in the first or second position.

### 8

On this occasion something must be said about the testimonies of the Fathers that are found appended, in the published Greek and Latin Acts of the Councils, session 2, to this Letter 28 to Flavian.

The Roman editors prefixed this note to the testimonies:

“Most of these testimonies of the holy Fathers were added by Saint Leo to his own Letter 97, now 165, to Leo Augustus; but in certain Greek manuscripts of this council they are also inserted here, namely after the aforementioned letter to Flavian.”

Understanding this, Stephanus Baluzius wrote the following concerning the second session:

“These testimonies are not found in the manuscript codices or in the ancient editions. Nevertheless, although in certain Greek manuscripts, as the Roman editors state, they are inserted here, I think that they were not read at the synod and were therefore copied into these Acts in vain, since there is no mention of any of these testimonies, but only of the letter.”

The entire difficulty was removed by an examination of the three Greek Chalcedonian manuscripts from the Venetian library of Saint Mark mentioned above.

Since the aforementioned letter to Flavian appears in them twice, as we indicated—before the proceedings and within the proceedings themselves—the testimonies of the Fathers are not appended to the copy of the letter inserted in the proceedings, as they were published by the Romans. Rather, they are copied after the letter presented before the proceedings.

We have no doubt that in the Greek manuscripts of the Roman editors—which likewise placed this letter before the proceedings, as is clear from the title they supplied before the proceedings themselves, chapter 7 (*Tom. IV of the Councils*, p. 782)—the same testimonies were similarly read after the letter copied before the proceedings.

They merely judged that this letter should be omitted from the documents before the proceedings, so as not to repeat it again in the proceedings themselves; and they therefore thought that the testimonies should be appended to the letter inserted in the proceedings. Since they did not warn their readers of this, they gave rise to the difficulty raised by Baluzius.

The deacon Rusticus acted more cautiously. He omitted this letter before the proceedings because, as he says, it had been inserted in the proceedings (*Tom. IV of the Councils*, p. 1982). He also omitted the testimonies appended to it, rather than placing them after the letter inserted in the proceedings.

Consequently, these testimonies are not found before the proceedings in the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection derived from Rusticus; nor are they present in the proceedings, since they have no place there.

### 9

Moreover, there is no doubt that the same testimonies found in the Greek manuscripts after the following letter have Saint Leo as their author, no less than those that will be presented after Letter 165 to Leo Augustus.

Not only are they the same in both places, apart from a few minor exceptions, but it is also clear from Letter 71 that they were collected after the pseudo-synod of Ephesus and handed over by the pontiff himself to the bishops Abundius and Asterius and to the presbyters Basil and Senator, who had been sent to Constantinople, so that they might confirm the doctrine of the letter to Flavian by the authority of Greek and Latin Fathers.

It is also clear from Letter 88 that these testimonies, together with the letters themselves, were produced by the legates at the Constantinopolitan assembly before the Synod of Chalcedon.

It is therefore unsurprising that these testimonies were appended to the aforementioned letter in the Greek documents before the Chalcedonian proceedings, even though the first copy of the letter lacked them. For this reason they should not be appended to it by us either.

Since no Latin copy has so far been found in which these testimonies are copied after the letter to Flavian, but they appear separately published and inserted in certain ancient Latin collections—namely in Quesnell’s Collection 5, chapter 41, where they will be found in volume 3; in the manuscripts of Collection 3, chapter 82; and in Veronese manuscript 38, chapter 37—it is sufficiently probable that only the Greeks, who had received them as having been brought forward and cited together at the Constantinopolitan assembly, copied exemplars in which the letter was read together with the testimonies, and that they subsequently transferred both together into the Greek codices before the Chalcedonian proceedings.

From this it is evident how wrongly Father Garnerius attributed the collection of these testimonies to Theodoret. More will be said about this in the observations on Quesnellus’s final note.

Among the testimonies collected by Leo, the first place is occupied by three fairly lengthy excerpts taken from Hilary. We believe that this Latin writer, previously unknown to the Greeks, was cited with particular honor at the Synod of Chalcedon by Cecropius, Bishop of Sebastopolis, on the basis of Leo’s testimonies, among the Fathers who affirm the Catholic faith (Act 2, volume IV of the Councils, p. 1207).

## Letter XXVIII

*Alternatively no. 24. Formerly no. 28, now no. 32. Written on 13 June 449.*

### To Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, against the perfidy and heresy of Eutyches

*Most codices call this “Leo’s rescript to Flavian.” In the table of Collection 5, no. 69: “His letter to Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople, concerning the condemnation of the Eutychian heresy.”*

## Synopsis

From the Hispanic collection:

- How ignorance of the Holy Scriptures made Eutyches a heretic.
- Against those who attempt to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons.
- Against those who dare to assert that the Divinity of the only-begotten Son of God was subject to suffering.
- Against those who argue for a blending or confusion of the two natures of Christ.
- Against those who madly assert that the form of the servant, which he assumed from us, was heavenly or belonged to some other substance.
- Against those who deliriously claim that the Lord had two natures before the union but fabricate one after the union.

[The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

## Leo, bishop, to his most beloved brother Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople

*In several very ancient manuscripts this superscription is found: “Leo to his most beloved brother Flavian.”*

### Chapter I. Eutyches’s presumption and ignorance drove him into error

After reading the letters of Your Holiness—which we are surprised were so long delayed—and after reviewing the sequence of the episcopal proceedings, we finally recognized what scandal had arisen among you against the integrity of the faith; and what previously seemed hidden has now been laid open and become clear to us.

Eutyches, who had appeared honorable under the name of presbyter, is shown to have been exceedingly imprudent and utterly ignorant, so that even of him it may be said through the prophet: “He refused to understand, so that he might act rightly; he devised iniquity upon his bed” (Psalm 35:4).

What, indeed, is more unjust than to hold impious opinions and not yield to those wiser and more learned? Yet those who, when some obscure obstacle prevents them from recognizing the truth, turn not to the prophetic utterances, not to the apostolic writings, and not to the evangelical authorities, but to themselves, fall into this folly. Thus they become teachers of error, because they were not disciples of the truth.

For what learning did he acquire from the sacred pages of the New and Old Testament, since he does not even grasp the beginning of the Creed? And what is proclaimed by the voice of all those throughout the world who are regenerated is still not understood by this old man’s heart.

### Chapter II. Concerning the two births and the nature of Christ

Since, therefore, he did not know what he ought to believe concerning the Incarnation of the Word of God, and was unwilling to labor through the breadth of the Holy Scriptures in order to earn the light of understanding, he ought at least to have received by attentive hearing that common and undivided confession which the whole body of the faithful professes:

“To believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”

By these three statements the machinery of nearly all heretics is destroyed.

For since God is believed to be almighty and Father, the Son is shown to be coeternal with him, differing in nothing from the Father: God from God, almighty from almighty, born coeternal from the eternal; not later in time, not inferior in power, not unlike in glory, not divided in essence.

The same eternal Only-begotten of the eternal Begetter was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. This temporal birth diminished nothing from that divine and eternal birth and added nothing to it, but devoted his entire being to restoring humanity, which had been deceived, so that he might conquer death and destroy by his power the devil, who held dominion over death.

For we could not overcome the author of sin and death unless he assumed our nature and made it his own—him whom neither sin could stain nor death hold captive.

He was conceived, therefore, of the Holy Spirit within the womb of his Virgin Mother, who, preserving her virginity, brought him forth just as, preserving her virginity, she had conceived him.

### Editorial notes and textual apparatus

[Col. 0755A: The letter is numbered 24 in some reckonings; what was formerly Letter 28 is now Letter 32, written 13 June 449. Most manuscripts call it Leo’s reply to Flavian. In the table of Collection 5, no. 69: “The same author to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, on the condemnation of the Eutychian heresy.”]

[Col. 0755: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0755A, at no. 801: In several and very ancient manuscripts this superscription is read: “Leo to his most beloved brother Flavian.”]

[Col. 0755A, at “letters”: Vienna, Collection 5, and Vatican Collection 11 in its first position, together with the first edition, read *epistolis* (“letters”). Shortly afterwards Vatican Hispanicus and another Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 in its second position read *sed gestorum* (“but of the proceedings”); Vatican Isidorianus likewise, but with *et gestorum* (“and of the proceedings”).]

[Col. 0755A–0756A, at “what scandal”: Editions before Quesnellus read: “what scandal has occurred among you, and [what has arisen] against the integrity,” etc. Quesnellus deleted *contigerit* (“has occurred”) and *atque* (“and”), since, as he says in note 2, they are superfluous and absent both from the Greek version and from all manuscript codices. Baluzius nevertheless found them in the Corbie manuscript, in ancient exemplars of the Fifth Council, and in the Colbertinus; we found them additionally in the very ancient Verona 57, Vatican 1322, another Vatican 1323, and Chigi 483 of the Chalcedonian collection; likewise in Vatican Collection 3, manuscripts of Collection 8, the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and others derived from them. They are absent, however, from Verona 8, Vatican Reginensis Collection 1, Vienna Collection 5, Regensburg, the very ancient Vatican Lectionary 3836, the exemplar of the first edition, and other exemplars deriving from Lectionaries; and, to pass over the manuscripts of the three later collections and Sichard, they are also absent from Baluzius’s two manuscripts, Parisian and Divionese, of the Chalcedonian collection. Therefore we thought Quesnellus’s reading should not be altered. In the very ancient Verona 58 the text reads: “We have learned that a scandal has occurred among you, arising against the integrity of the faith.”]

[Col. 0756A–0757C, at “exceedingly imprudent”: Verona 8 reads *impudens* (“shameless”); see Quesnellus’s note 3. Shortly afterwards Vatican Reginensis Collection 1 reads *nimium imperitus* (“excessively ignorant”).]

[Col. 0757C, at “even of him”: Two of Baluzius’s manuscripts and five of ours from the Chalcedonian collection read *praedictum sit* (“it may have been said beforehand”). Verona 58 reads *de eo praedictum sit* (“it may have been said beforehand concerning him”).]

[Col. 0757C, at no. 803: Gratian, 24, question 3, “But what is more unjust,” chapter 30.]

[Col. 0757C, at “impious opinions”: The Regensburg codex reads *iniqua* (“unjust things”). Shortly afterwards it, together with Verona 8 and 57, the manuscripts of Collection 8, and *doctoribus* (“to the learned”), reads *non credere* (“not to believe”). Five other manuscripts of ours from diverse collections, with Baluzius’s two and the editions before Quesnellus, read *doctioribusque non credere* (“not to believe those wiser and more learned”). The rest read as in the text. Compare Quesnellus’s note 4.]

[Col. 0757C, at “recognizing”: Six codices read *ad agnoscendam* (“for recognizing”). Thereafter four of our manuscripts read *obstaculo* (“obstacle”) for *obscuro* (“obscure”); the first edition reads *obscuro obstaculo* (“by an obscure obstacle”). See Quesnellus’s note 5.]

[Col. 0757C, at “since”: Several manuscripts of good quality, with the editions before Quesnellus, read *qui nec* (“who does not even”); Vatican 1322 reads *si nec* (“if he does not even”). A little later those editions read *regenaratorum* for *regenerandorum* (“of those to be regenerated”). Quesnellus corrected the reading from all his manuscripts, which ours also support; see his note 6.]

[Col. 0757C–0757D, at “attentive hearing”: Editions before Quesnellus, with manuscripts of Collection 24 and Sichard, read *apprehendisset* (“had apprehended”); see Quesnellus’s note 7. Shortly afterwards *quam fidelium* (“which [the] faithful”) occurs in all manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, both ours and Baluzius’s, and in certain others. Then the more common editions and five of our exemplars read *ex Maria* (“from Mary”) for *et Maria* (“and Mary”); the same reading occurs somewhat later in some manuscripts. All the others, including the better ones, support Quesnellus’s reading; compare his note 8. A little later the first edition reads *dissolvuntur* (“are dissolved”) for *destruuntur* (“are destroyed”).]

[Col. 0757C–0758C, at “almighty and Father”: Printed editions read *et aeternus creditur Pater* (“and the Father is believed eternal”). Although Quesnellus saw that *aeternus* (“eternal”) was absent from most and best of his manuscripts, he nevertheless thought it should be retained because the context seemed to require it; see his note 9. Yet scarcely two of our codices contain the word. We did not think that the many and most excellent exemplars omitting it should be abandoned, especially because Saint Leo here plainly refers back and almost repeats that first clause of the Creed by which, as he said shortly before, the faithful profess belief in God the Father almighty, where “eternal” is not expressed. We note that the four outstanding codices Verona 57 and 58, Vatican 1322, and Regensburg also omit *et* before *Pater*; three other equally notable witnesses—Verona 8, Vatican 3836, and Vatican Isidorianus—delete the same particle before *omnipotens* (“almighty”). We followed Vatican Reginensis Collection 1, Vercelli Collection 8, Vatican Collection 11 in its first position, Chigi, Baluzius’s four manuscripts, and the exemplar of the first edition, with which the Greek translation agrees. Vatican Collection 24, Merlin, and Sichard read: “and [he is] believed almighty, and Father”; Hispanicus and the codices of Collection 21: “and [he is] almighty, and the Father is believed everlasting; the same Son is shown”; Vienna Collection 5: “and [he is] almighty, and the Father is believed [to be], and the Son is shown co-everlasting.”]

[Col. 0759B–0759C, at “devoted his entire being”: Most and indeed the oldest codices read *totum* (“the whole [thing]”), namely the three Verona manuscripts, Vatican Collection 3, Vatican Hispanicus and Isidorianus, another Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 in its second position, Regensburg Collection 19, and all manuscripts of the Latin Chalcedonian collection, both ours and Baluzius’s, except the Divionese, in which *totam* (“the whole [feminine]”) had nevertheless been written by the first hand and *totum* by the second. We retained the received reading *totam* (“wholly,” agreeing with the implied divine person), since it is supported not only by our manuscripts of Collections 1, 5, and 8, Vienna, Hispanicus, Vatican Collection 11 in its first position, manuscripts of Collections 21 and 24, and the very ancient Roman Church Lectionary Vatican 3836, together with the exemplars of the first edition, Merlin, and Sichard, but also by the Greek translation read at the Council of Chalcedon. A little later the first edition and Vossius in the margin read *et jus diaboli* (“and the devil’s right”); then certain codices and the same edition add *nos* (“us”) before or after *superare* (“to overcome”).]

[Col. 0759B] But if he could not draw pure and sincere understanding from this most pure fountain of the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0759C] Ratisbon has “the purest and most sincere understanding.” The reading in the second place of the Vatican collection 11, “the purest and most sincere understanding,” is better. Later, Verona 58 has *sibimet propria* (“peculiar to himself”), and Verona 57 and Vindobonensis Hispanus have *tenebrabat* (“had darkened”).], because by a blindness peculiar to himself he had darkened the radiance of evident truth, he should have submitted himself to evangelical teaching. [Note: [Col. 0759C] We have added “And,” and altered the punctuation, which produces the better sense, on the authority of Vindobonensis collection 5, Ratisbon [Col. 0759D], and Vatican collection 11, in the first place; the Greek version is related to these. This particle could easily fall out because the same letters occur together at the end of the preceding word, a common occurrence among ancient scribes. Shortly afterward, the same Vatican collection 11, in the second place, has *instrumentum* (“resource”) instead of *instructum* (“instruction”). See Quesnel’s note 10.] And when Matthew says, “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), he should also have sought the instruction of apostolic preaching. And, reading the Epistle to the Romans, “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:1), he should have devoted pious attention [809] to the prophetic pages. [Note: [Col. 0759D] Quesnel, following Leo’s printed editions and several manuscripts, inserted *quoque* (“also”). We removed it on the authority of the majority and better of our copies, especially the three most ancient manuscripts from Verona, one Vindobonensis collection 5, and Ratisbon. The manuscripts of Baluze and the printed editions of the councils likewise omit it. Shortly afterward, certain manuscripts cited by Quesnel in note 11 have *pia sollicitudine se contulisset* (“had applied himself with pious diligence”). Then the Vatican manuscript 1322, together with the first edition, has *et inveniret* (“and should find”), in place of which, with the letter *t* omitted, Verona 58 has *et invenire* (“and to find”). [Col. 0760B] The editions printed before Quesnel, together with manuscripts of collections 24 and 21, have *et invenisset* (“and should have found”).]

[Col. 0761A] And finding God’s promise to Abraham, who said, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3; 22:18), [Note: [Col. 0761B] All printed editions, together with most manuscripts, attach a full stop after *gentes* (“nations”) and then read, “And not.” On this arrangement, however, the nominative *inveniens* (“finding”) would remain suspended. Hence in some manuscripts it was previously emended to *inveniret* (“should find”) or *invenisset* (“should have found”). Since almost all the ancient copies have *inveniens*, this passage required correction; we derived it from Verona 8 and Ratisbon, in which the particle *et* (“and”) is absent. It likewise does not appear in the oldest and most carefully corrected manuscript of the Greek version, the Basilian codex.], he would not have doubted the particular identity of this seed had he followed the Apostle, who says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, but as though referring to one: “And to your seed,” which is Christ (Galatians 3:8). He would also have grasped Isaiah’s prophecy with inward hearing when he says: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). And he would have faithfully read the words of the same prophet: “A child is born to us, [Note: [Col. 0761C] The manuscripts Verona 57, Ratisbon, and two of our Chalcedonian collections, as well as four of Baluze’s manuscripts, the printed editions of the Councils, and the first edition, have *et filius* (“and a son”). Immediately afterward, these same manuscripts, together with two other Vatican and two Vindobonensis manuscripts, read *super humeros* (“upon his shoulders”), as do certain manuscripts cited by Quesnel in note 15. Shortly afterward, two of our manuscripts and the editions printed before Quesnel have *et vocabitur* (“and he shall be called”); see his note 16.], a son is given to us, whose authority is upon his shoulder, and they shall call his name, ‘Angel of great counsel,’ [Note: [Col. 0761D] The words “Wonderful” and “Counselor” are absent from Verona 8, Ratisbon, Vindobonensis collection 5, and two Vatican manuscripts. Baluze likewise noted that they are absent from a Paris manuscript and had formerly been absent from the Divionensis, where they were later added above the line. They are also lacking in the Greek version. Conversely, Verona 58 adds two further words, as follows: “Wonderful, Counselor, Son of God, Mighty God.”], “Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come” (Isaiah 9:6). Nor, speaking deceitfully, would he say that the Word became flesh in such a way that Christ, born from a virgin’s womb, possessed the appearance of a human being but not the reality of a body received from his mother. [Note: [Col. 0761D] Four of Quesnel’s manuscripts, cited in his note 17, have *frustratoria eloquens* (“speaking in a futile manner”). The first edition has *frustratorie ita loquens* (“speaking thus futilely”). The word is *Verbum* (“Word”).]

Or perhaps [811] did he think that the Lord [Note: [Col. 0761D] Verona 57, Vindobonensis collection 5, and Ratisbon omit *nostrum* (“our”). Shortly afterward, four of our ancient copies have *nostrae non esse naturae* (“not to be of our nature”). Then Verona 58, together with the first edition, has *ad beatam virginem Mariam* (“to the blessed virgin Mary”). Two other Verona manuscripts, two Vindobonensis manuscripts, Ratisbon, and four Vatican manuscripts, together with the printed editions of the Councils and the Greek version, omit the words *semper virginem* (“ever-virgin”).] Jesus Christ was not of our nature because, when the angel was sent to the blessed Mary, ever-virgin, he said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you”; and therefore “the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35)? Did he therefore think that, because the virgin’s conception was a work of divine agency, the flesh conceived did not derive from the nature of the one who conceived it? [Note: [Col. 0762B] Two Verona manuscripts, one Vindobonensis collection 5, Ratisbon, and one Vatican manuscript delete *et* (“and”).]

But that singularly marvelous and marvelously singular generation must not be understood in this way, as though by the novelty of the creation the particular reality of the nature were removed. [Note: [Col. 0762C] Quesnel, following Leo’s printed editions, has *nobis intelligenda* (“to be understood by us”), as we found in several manuscripts. But following the first edition and the editions of the Councils, we deleted *nobis* (“by us”) on the authority of the better copies—namely, three Verona manuscripts, Vindobonensis collection 5, Vatican collection 11 in the first place, Ratisbon, and all the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collections; the Greek version supports this reading. Shortly afterward Quesnel has *mota sit generis* (“the nature of the race may have been altered”). We restored the previously common reading from our manuscripts. Only Vindobonensis collection 5 has *semota* (“removed”). Shortly afterward, the manuscripts Verona 8, Ratisbon, and Vindobonensis collection 5 omit *enim* (“for”).] For the Holy Spirit gave fecundity to the virgin, but the reality of the body was taken from a body; and when Wisdom was building a house for herself (Proverbs 9:1), the Word became flesh and dwelt in us (John 1:14)—that is, in the flesh which [Note: [Col. 0763C] Vindobonensis Hispanus and Isidore have *suscepit* (“received”); Ratisbon and Vindobonensis collection 5, together with two Vatican manuscripts and the printed editions of the Councils, have *sumpsit* (“took”). Quesnel, following earlier editions of Leo and most manuscripts, has *spiritus vitae* (“spirit of life”). But in note 18 he observed that the editions of the Councils and the Victorinus manuscript read *spiritu vitae* (“with the spirit of life”), “and perhaps this is better,” he says; the Greek likewise has this wording. This reading is confirmed by the two oldest Verona manuscripts, 8 and 57, as well as Vatican 5845, collection 8, Vindobonensis Hispanus, and copies of the first edition and Sichardus; we have therefore adopted it as the better reading.] he took from a human being and animated with the spirit of rational life.

## Chapter III. The faith and God’s plan concerning the incarnation of the Word are explained.

[Col. 0763A]

[Note: [Col. 0763C] Nearly the same words occur in Sermon 21, or the first sermon on the Nativity, chapter 2.]

Thus, while the distinctive reality of each nature [Note: [Col. 0763C] We have retained the words *et substantiae* (“and of substance”), inserted by Quesnel from six manuscripts cited by him in note 19, because they are also found in four of our oldest manuscripts: Vatican collection 3, Vindobonensis collection 5, Vatican collection 8, and the Vatican Lectionary 3836; they also occur in Vercelli, Vatican collection 11 in the first place, and the copy of the first edition. They are absent, however, from our other manuscripts, as also from the Greek version. In Sermon 21, chapter 2, from which these words were taken, *substantiae* is present, but *naturae* (“of nature”) is omitted. Shortly afterward, Verona 57 and 58 have *una coeunte persona* (“with one person coming together”); Verona 8 and Vindobonensis Hispanus, together with some of Baluze’s manuscripts, have *in una coeunte persona* (“in one person coming together”). The reading in the text is also preferred by the cited Sermon 21, chapter 2.] and substance was preserved, and the two came together in one [813] person, humility was assumed by majesty, weakness by power, mortality by eternity; [Col. 0763B] and, in order to discharge the debt imposed by our condition, an inviolable nature was united to a passible nature, so that—as suited our healing—the one and same mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, could die by virtue of one nature and could not die by virtue of the other. [Note: [Col. 0763D] Vatican Hispanus and another manuscript of collection 11, in the second place, have *divinis remediis* (“by divine remedies”). Then four ancient manuscripts have “so that he could die from one and could not die from the other.” The first edition instead reads, “and could rise again,” as in the cited sermon, chapter 2.]

Therefore, in the complete and perfect nature of a true human being, the true God was born, wholly present in what was his own and wholly present in what was ours. By “ours” we mean what the Creator established in us from the beginning and what he assumed in order to restore it. But the things that the deceiver introduced, and that deceived humanity admitted, left no trace in the Savior. [Note: [Col. 0764C] Five ancient manuscripts have *amisit* (“lost”), incorrectly. One, with a double *m*, has *ammisit*, a spelling not uncommon among the ancients, among whom *ammoveo* is written for *admoveo*. From this, after one *m* was deleted, the error in those manuscripts arose.] Nor, because he entered into communion with human weaknesses, did he therefore share in our sins. He assumed the form of a servant without the stain of sin, increasing what was human without diminishing what was divine. For that self-emptying by which the invisible One presented himself as visible, and the Creator and Lord of all things chose to become one among mortals, was an inclination of mercy, not a failure of power.

Therefore, he who, while remaining in the form of God, made the human being, himself became human in the form of a servant. [Note: [Col. 0765C] Three Verona manuscripts and Ratisbon omit *idem* (“the same”).] Each nature [815] retains its own distinctive reality without defect: [Note: [Col. 0765C] Vatican Hispanus and Isidore, together with three other manuscripts, have: “And just as the form of God does not take away the form of a servant, so the form of a servant does not diminish the form of God.”] and just as the form of God does not take away the form of a servant, so the form of a servant does not diminish the form of God. [Note: [Col. 0765C] The remaining lines of this chapter are also found in Sermon 22, or the second sermon on the Nativity, chapter 1.]

For, because the devil gloried that the human being, deceived by his fraud, had been deprived of divine gifts and stripped of the endowment of immortality, had undergone the harsh sentence of death, and that he himself had found some consolation in sharing the transgressor’s evils, he also claimed that God, compelled by the demands of justice, had changed his own decision toward the human being whom he had created in such great honor. [Note: [Col. 0765C] Five of our manuscripts and five of Quesnel’s, identified by him in note 20, have *de praevaricationis* (“from the transgression”). But Sermon 22, chapter 1, from which this passage is taken, has *de praevaricatoris* (“from the transgressor”), as do other manuscripts of this epistle. Shortly afterward, the manuscript Verona 58 has *dura … sententia* (“harsh … sentence”).] It was therefore necessary that, through the dispensation of a hidden plan, the unchangeable God—whose will cannot be deprived of its benevolence—should complete his original disposition of mercy toward us through a more secret sacramental plan; and that the human being, driven into guilt by the devil’s wicked cunning, should not perish contrary to God’s purpose. [Note: [Col. 0765C] The editions printed before Quesnel, together with most manuscripts, have *dispensationem* (“dispensation”). He judged *dispositionem* (“disposition” or “plan”) preferable, on the basis of four manuscripts cited in his note 21. Although only six of our ancient books join these—Verona 8, Vatican Royal collection 1, another Vatican collection 3, Vindobonensis collection 5, Vatican collection 11 in the first place, and Ratisbon—we have nevertheless retained this reading chiefly because Sermon 22, chapter 1, has the same wording.]

## Chapter IV. The distinctive features of Christ’s two births and of his natures are examined.

[Col. 0765B]

[Note: [Col. 0765D] The same appears in Sermon 22, chapter 2.]

Thus the Son of God enters the lowest regions of this world [Note: [Col. 0765D] Verona 8, Vindobonensis, Vindobonensis Hispanus, Ratisbon, two Vatican manuscripts—1322 and 3791, in the first place—together with two of Baluze’s manuscripts and the printed editions of the Councils, have *infirma* (“lowly” or “weak”). The other manuscripts have *infima* (“lowest”), and the Greek translator likewise reads this.] descending from his heavenly seat, [817] yet not departing from the Father’s glory, generated in a new order and by a new birth. In a new order, because, invisible in what was his own, he became visible in what was ours; the incomprehensible One willed to be comprehended; he who existed before time began to exist in time; the Lord of the universe assumed the form of a servant, the immensity of his majesty being veiled; and God, incapable of suffering, did not disdain to become a human being capable of suffering and to submit to the laws of death. He was generated by a new birth because an inviolate virginity, which knew no desire, supplied the material of the flesh. [Note: [Col. 0767C] Three of our manuscripts and one of Baluze’s have *Virgo* (“the Virgin”). Then Vindobonensis Hispanus and Isidore, together with four other manuscripts, have *et carnis materiam* (“and supplied the material of the flesh”); Vatican collection 11 in the first place has *sed carnis materiam* (“but supplied the material of the flesh”); two manuscripts of collection 21 have *inviolata virginitas, quae concupiscentiam nescivit, carnis materiam ministravit* (“inviolate virginity, which knew no desire, supplied the material of the flesh”).] Nature, not guilt, was assumed from the Lord’s Mother. Nor, in the Lord Jesus Christ, born from a virgin’s womb, because his birth is marvelous, is his nature therefore unlike ours. [Note: [Col. 0767C] The more common editions, together with Vindobonensis Hispanus, Isidore, Verona 58, Vatican 1322, and three other manuscripts, have “is unlike our nature.” The other manuscripts and the first edition confirm the reading introduced by Quesnel. See his note 23.] For he who is true God [Note: [Col. 0767C] Three Verona manuscripts and Ratisbon delete *est* (“is”). Shortly afterward, Verona 57, Ratisbon, and two Chalcedonian manuscripts have *dum in invicem* (“while in one another”).] is also true human being, and there is no falsehood in this union, since in it there are both the humility of humanity and the loftiness of divinity. For just as God is not changed by mercy, so the human being is not consumed by [819] dignity. [Note: [Col. 0767C] The same words occur in Sermon 54, chapter 2.]

Each form acts in communion with the other in what belongs properly to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh. One of these shines forth in miracles; the other submits to insults. And just as the Word does not depart from equality with the Father’s glory, [Note: [Col. 0767D] Verona 58 has *non recidit … non reliquit* (“does not fall away … does not abandon”). The editions printed before Quesnel, together with manuscripts of collection 24, have *non recessit … non reliquit* (“did not depart … did not abandon”). Quesnel’s reading, discussed in his note 24, is supported by the rest of our manuscripts.] so the flesh does not abandon the nature of our race.

For the one and the same person is, as must often be said, truly the Son of God and truly the son of a human being. He is God because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1); he is human because “the Word became flesh and dwelt in us” (ibid., 14). He is God because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (ibid., 3); he is human because he “was made from a woman, made under the law” (Galatians 4:4). [Note: [Col. 0767D] Vindobonensis Hispanus has “made from a woman, made under the law,” and connects the phrase with the Word, as in the preceding passage: “the Word became flesh.”]

The birth of the flesh is a manifestation of human nature; the virgin’s delivery is an indication of divine power. The infancy of the little child is shown by the humility of the cradle (Luke 2:7); the greatness of the Most High is declared by the voices of the angels (Luke 2:13). He is like human beings in the beginnings of life, whom the impious Herod attempts to kill (Matthew 2:16); but he is Lord of all, whom [821] [Note: [Col. 0769C] The editions of the Councils, together with Vatican, Vindobonensis Hispanus, Isidorian, and collection 21 manuscripts, have “the rejoicing Magi come humbly to worship.” But the purer Vindobonensis Hispanus manuscript has “the rejoicing Magi humbly to worship.” The later copyists of the same collection seem, through ingenuity, to have supplied the verb *veniunt* (“come”) from the nominative *gaudentes* (“rejoicing”), which arose from an error for *gaudent* (“they rejoice”). Shortly afterward, Verona 58 and Vatican 1322, together with Baluze’s Paris and Colbert manuscripts, have “when he came to his precursor.” Verona 57 deletes *sui* (“his”). Then the editions of Leo printed before Quesnel have *veniret* (“would come”) instead of *venit* (“came”), though none of our manuscripts supports this.] the Magi rejoice humbly to worship.

When he came to the baptism of his precursor John (Matthew 3:13), so that it might not remain hidden that divinity was concealed beneath the veil of flesh, the Father’s voice thundered from heaven and said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (ibid., 17). Thus, just as diabolical cunning tempts him as a human being, so angelic services minister to him as God (Matthew 4:1, 11). To hunger, thirst, grow weary, and sleep is plainly human. But to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves (John 6:5), [Note: [Col. 0769D] Vatican manuscript 5845 has “with five loaves.” The editions of Leo printed before Quesnel, together with Vatican collection 11 in the first place and collection 24, have “and with five loaves.” Shortly afterward, Verona 8 and Vatican collection 3 have *saturare* (“to satisfy”) instead of *satiare*.] and to give the Samaritan living water (John 4:10), a draught of which grants the drinker that he may thirst no longer, [Note: [Col. 0769D] Three Verona manuscripts and two other manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collections have *praestitit* (“granted”). The editions printed before Quesnel, together with manuscripts of collections 11, 21, and 25, have *praestat* (“grants”).] to walk upon the surface of the sea with feet that do not sink [Note: [Col. 0769D] The editions preceding Quesnel, together with manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, have *subsidentibus* (“sinking”). The other manuscripts have *desidentibus*, with a few exceptions that preserve related but corrupt readings: *desitientibus*, *desinentibus*, *desudantibus*, or *desistentibus*. See Quesnel’s note 25.], and, when the storm is rebuked, to lay low the swelling waves (Matthew 14:25; Luke 8:24), is unambiguously divine.

Therefore, to pass over many examples, just as it is not of the same nature to weep for a dead friend out of compassionate feeling (John 11:35) [Note: [Col. 0769D] Verona 58, Vatican 1342 collection 3, Vatican 1322, the Chalcedonian collection 2, Vercelli collection 8, and manuscripts of collection 21, together with the first edition, add *Lazarum* (“Lazarus”).] and, after removing the barrier of a four-day [823] burial, to raise that same person alive at a command (ibid., 43); or to hang upon the wood and, with daylight changed into night, make all the elements tremble; or to be pierced with nails and open the gates of paradise to the faith of a thief (Matthew 27:35), [Note: [Col. 0769D] We deleted the particle *et* (“and”), inserted in some editions and by Quesnel, as superfluous, on the authority of three Verona manuscripts, Vindobonensis collection 5, both Hispanus manuscripts, Isidore, Ratisbon, and other copies. It is also absent from the Greek version and from the manuscripts used by Baluze. Shortly afterward, Vatican collection 3, another Vatican manuscript 5845 collection 8, Vindobonensis Hispanus, Isidore, and manuscripts of collection 21 read *in cruce* (“upon the cross”) instead of *in ligno* (“upon the wood”). Then Verona 57 and 58, three of our manuscripts, and two of Baluze’s Chalcedonian manuscripts have *paradisi januas* (“the gates of paradise”). Rusticus noted that some of his manuscripts had *portas* (“doors”), which we find in the remaining manuscripts and which Baluze has in two Chalcedonian copies.] so it is likewise not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and to say, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Although, therefore, in the Lord Jesus Christ there is one person of God and of the human being, [Col. 0771A] yet one thing is the source of the insult common to both, and another the source of the glory common to both. [Note: [Col. 0771C] This reading seemed better, and is preferred not only by the first edition and the editions of the Councils, but also by three Verona manuscripts, Vatican Royal collection 1, another Vatican collection 3, another collection 11 in the second place, Ratisbon, three of our Chalcedonian collections, and Baluze’s manuscripts. Another reading is: “whence the insult is common in both, another whence,” and so on.] From us he has the humanity that is lower than the Father; from the Father he has the divinity that is equal with the Father.

## Chapter V. The reality of Christ’s flesh is proved from Scripture.

[Col. 0771A]

Because of this [Note: It is peculiar that Leo took this passage from Augustine’s book *Against the Sermon of the Arians*, chapter 8, and thought it appropriate to use sometimes the same words and sometimes others. For there it reads as follows: “And therefore, in order that this unity of person in both natures might be understood, the Son of Man is also said to have descended from heaven, although he was assumed from the Virgin who had been on earth; and the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he suffered these things not in the Divinity itself, by which he is the Only-Begotten, coeternal with the Father, but in the weakness of human nature . . . . Moreover, we all confess in the Creed that the Only-Begotten Son of God was crucified and buried. Hence also comes the Apostle’s statement: ‘For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.’” This redounds greatly to Augustine’s glory and also commends Leo’s care and diligence. Two manuscripts of Verona and three Chalcedonian collections have *enim* (“for”) instead of *ergo* (“therefore”). The editions of the Councils omit both.]

in order, therefore, that this unity of person in both natures might be understood, the Son of Man is read as having descended from heaven, although the Son of God assumed flesh from that Virgin from whom he was born. [Note: Two very ancient Vatican manuscripts, 1342, collection 3, and 5845, collection 8, read *dicitur* (“is said”), as in the quoted text of Augustine. Shortly afterward the first edition has *assumpsit* (“assumed”) instead of *assumpserit* (“has assumed”). Then *crucifixus* (“crucified”) is read in Verona 57.] And again the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although he suffered these things not in the Divinity itself, by which he is the Only-Begotten, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, but in the weakness of human nature. [Col. 0771B] 825 Hence we all confess in the Creed also that the Only-Begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty” (II Cor. II, 8). [Note: All the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collections, both Spanish collections, as well as Isidore and Vat. 5845, together with the editions of the Councils, have “that saying of the Apostle.” Shortly afterward, *Dominum gloriae crucifixissent* (“they would have crucified the Lord of glory”) is found in the Ratisbon manuscript, as also in Augustine.]

When our Lord and Savior himself was instructing the faith of his disciples [Note: Vatican manuscript, collection 24, and Sichard add *suorum* (“his own”). In editions of Leo before Quesnel, *suorum suis interrogationibus audiret* (“he heard his own [disciples] by his questions”) is mistakenly printed. See Quesnel’s note 26.] by his questions, he asked: “Who do men say that I, the Son of Man, am?” [Note: We have added *me* (“me”) from three very ancient manuscripts of Verona, from Vat. Reg. collection 1, Vienna Spanish, Vat. collection 11 in both places, Ratisbon, the Roman Lectionary, the Vatican manuscript, and finally Vat. 1322, Chalcedonian collection, together with four others cited by Baluze. Only two of the manuscripts mentioned, Verona 8 and 58, have: “Who, he says, do they say that I am?” Then: “But you,” he says, “who do you say that I am?” is found in two manuscripts of Verona and in Ratisbon. In another Verona manuscript: “But you, what do you say that I am?” *Ait* (“he says”) is absent in the Vienna Spanish manuscript, while in one Vatican manuscript it is lacking.] And when they had recounted the various opinions of others, he said: “But you, who do you say that I am?”—me, that is, who am the Son of Man, and whom you behold in the form of a servant and in the reality of flesh: who do you say that I am?

Then blessed Peter, divinely inspired and destined by his confession to benefit all nations, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). [Note: The Ratisbon manuscript and Vat. collection 11, second position, omit *Christus* (“Christ”).] And rightly was he pronounced blessed by the Lord, and from the principal Rock he drew both firmness of virtue and of name, because by the Father’s revelation he confessed him to be both God’s Son and Christ. [Note: Verona 58 adds *Deum* (“God”). Shortly afterward, the first edition and Vat. 546, collection 21, have *sine altero* (“without the other”) instead of *sine alio* (“without the other”). A little later, the commonly printed editions before Quesnel have *sed aequalis* (“but equal”), with no support from any of our manuscripts or from the example of the first edition.] For accepting one of these without the other did not bring salvation; and it was an equal danger to believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was God without man, or man alone without God.

After the Lord’s resurrection—which was certainly a resurrection of the true body, since it was not another who was raised than he who had been crucified and died—what else was accomplished during the delay of forty days than that the integrity of our faith might be cleansed from every obscurity? [Note: The first edition and manuscripts of collections 21 and 24 have *hominis fuit* (“was of a man”). Other copies, as in the text, have the present reading. See Quesnel’s note 27. Shortly afterward, the common editions of Leo before Quesnel have *quia aliter non est resuscitatus* (“because he was not raised otherwise”), which Quesnel, together with the first edition, the printed editions of the Councils, and his own manuscripts, adopted as the reading of the text; all our ancient books likewise approve it.]

For he conversed with his disciples [Note: *Suis* (“his own”) is absent from Verona 57, the Vienna Spanish manuscript, and another Vatican manuscript.], lived with them, ate with them (Acts 1:4), and permitted those whom doubt had afflicted to handle him with careful and inquisitive touch. [Note: Verona 8 has “whom he perceived to have doubted.” Shortly afterward, Vat. Spanish has *assensum adhibens* (“giving assent”) instead of *admittens* (“permitting”); the Vatican manuscript of Isidore has *assensum admittens* (“accepting assent”); and Vat. 546, collection 21, has *assensum praebuit* (“gave assent”).] Therefore he also entered to his disciples through closed doors, [Note: Two manuscripts of Verona, 57 and 58, together with the Parisian and Corbie manuscripts of Baluze, have “to the disciples with the doors closed”; Colbert has “he entered to the disciples with the doors closed.”] and by his breath gave the Holy Spirit (John 20:22), and, having bestowed the light of understanding, opened the hidden things of the holy Scriptures. And again [Note: Quesnel expunged this word, which is absent from the printed editions of the Councils and some of our manuscripts. We have restored it on the authority of several and better copies: three manuscripts of Verona, Vat. collection 3, Ratisbon, another Vatican manuscript of collection 11 in the second position, two Chalcedonian collections, four of Baluze, as well as manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, with which the Greek translation agrees: ὁ αὐτός, “the same.”] he showed the same wound in his side, the marks of the nails, and all the most recent signs of his passion, saying: “See my hands and [Note: The copy of the first edition and the Vatican manuscript have *pedes meos* (“my feet”). Shortly afterward, *non habent* (“do not have”) is found in Vat. 1322.] my feet, because I am he. Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39). Thus it might be recognized that in him the distinctiveness of the divine and human nature continued indivisible; and so we might know that the Word is not the same as the flesh, in order that we might confess one Son of God and Word, and flesh.

This Eutyches, so highly esteemed, is devoid of this sacrament of faith, [Note: Verona 58 has *quia naturam* (“because [he did not recognize] the nature”). Shortly afterward, the first edition and five manuscripts have *qui solvit Jesum Christum* (“who dissolves Jesus Christ”).] since he recognized neither our nature in the Only-Begotten of God through the humility of mortality nor through the glory of resurrection. Nor did he fear the sentence of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, who says: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the Antichrist” (1 John 4:1). But what is it to dissolve Jesus except to separate the human nature from him and to empty, by the most shameless fictions, the sacrament through which we have been saved as one?  [Note: Manuscripts of collection 24, together with the more common printed editions, have *et sacramentum fidei, per quod salvati sumus* (“and the sacrament of faith, by which we have been saved”). All our manuscripts, together with the first edition, confirm the reading inserted by Quesnel into the text, except two in which *unum* (“alone/one”) is omitted. See his note 29.]

But if he is confused about the nature of Christ’s body, he must also rave in the same blindness concerning his passion. For [Note: The Vatican Spanish manuscript and Isidore have *qui crucem* (“who [believes] the cross”).] if he does not regard the Lord’s cross as false, and does not doubt that the punishment undertaken for the world’s salvation was real, let him acknowledge the flesh whose death he believes; and let him not deny the man of our body whom he recognizes to have been capable of suffering, since denial of true flesh is also denial of bodily suffering.

If, therefore, he embraces the Christian faith and does not turn his hearing away from the preaching of the Gospel, let him see what nature was pierced by nails and hung upon the wood of the cross. And, when the side of the crucified man was opened by the soldier’s lance, let him understand from where the blood and water flowed, so that the Church of God might be watered both by the washing [Note: Only the Vienna Spanish manuscript has *regeneretur* (“might be regenerated”). Shortly afterward, the Vienna collection 5 manuscript, Ratisbon, manuscripts of collection 24, and Baluze’s manuscripts omit *et* (“and”) before *beatum*. Later, *fiat sanguinis Jesu Christi* (“might become the blood of Jesus Christ”) is found in the Vatican Spanish, Isidore, Verona 58, and Vat. 1322.] and by the cup.

Let him also hear the blessed apostle Peter preaching that the sanctification of the Spirit takes place through the sprinkling of Christ’s blood. Nor should he read casually the words of the same apostle: “Knowing that you were redeemed from your futile manner of life inherited from your fathers, not with perishable silver and gold, but with precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:18).

Nor should he resist the testimony of the blessed apostle John, who says: “And the blood of Jesus [Note: Both Vienna manuscripts add *Christi* (“Christ”) after *Jesu* (“Jesus”).] the Son of God cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7). And again: “This is the victory that [Note: Two manuscripts of Verona and Ratisbon have *vicit* (“conquered”) both here and shortly afterward, instead of *vincit* (“conquers”). We have written *fides nostra* (“our faith”) on the basis of most and better manuscripts, together with the first edition, the editions of the Councils, and the Greek interpretation, instead of *fides vestra* (“your faith”). Verona 8, Vienna collection 5, and Ratisbon omit the conjunction *et* (“and”). In John, the following verses—“Who is it?” and so forth—immediately follow the preceding verse. Shortly afterward, the same manuscripts of Verona and Ratisbon have *quia Jesus est Filius Dei* (“because Jesus is the Son of God”).] conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 5:4). And: “Who is it that conquers the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ—not in water only, but in water and blood. And the Spirit is the one who testifies, because [Note: The editions before Quesnel, together with the Vienna Spanish manuscripts and Vat. collections 11, 21, and 24, have: “Christ is the truth”; the same reading is found in the Vienna collection 5, written by a second hand. Accordingly, Quesnel’s assertion in note 31 that the reading inserted into the text occurs in all manuscripts must be restricted and understood as referring to his own copies. Later, both manuscripts of Verona, both Vienna manuscripts, the Chigian manuscript, and Ratisbon have *et aqua* (“and water”). Verona 57, Vat. collection 3, together with another Vatican manuscript, have “These three are one.” The editions before Quesnel, together with some manuscripts, have “and these three.”] the Spirit is truth. For there are three who give testimony: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and these three are one.”

The Spirit, certainly, of sanctification; the blood, of redemption; and the water, of baptism. These three are one and remain indivisible, and none of them is separated from its own connection, because the Catholic Church lives by this faith and advances by it, [Note: We have restored *hac* (“by this”) from the first edition and five older and excellent manuscripts. Shortly afterward, the words *in Christo Jesu* (“in Christ Jesus”) are absent from ten manuscripts and from the Greek version. The first edition and the Vienna Spanish manuscript have *in Domino Jesu Christo* (“in the Lord Jesus Christ”).] so that in Christ Jesus humanity is believed neither without true Divinity nor Divinity without true humanity.

## Chapter VI. Eutyches’ wicked and deceitful confession; how, if he comes to his senses, he is to be restored to communion; legates are sent to the East.

[Col. 0777A]

When Eutyches answered the statement of your examination, saying, “I confess that our Lord existed from two natures before the union, but after the union I confess one nature,” I am astonished that so absurd and perverse a profession was not rebuked by any censure from the judges, and that a speech so foolish [Note: The words *nimisque blasphemum* (“and excessively blasphemous”) are omitted in two manuscripts of Verona, Vat. 1322, the Vienna Spanish manuscript, Ratisbon, and two manuscripts of Thuanus mentioned by Quesnel in note 33, as well as in Facundus.] and excessively blasphemous was passed over as though nothing offensive had been heard. For it is just as impious to say that the Only-Begotten Son of God existed from two natures before the Incarnation as it is wicked to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there is in him a singular nature. [Note: See Quesnel’s note 34, where he presents the variant reading of the Corbie manuscript and of Facundus; in the latter, shortly afterward, *ante adunationem* (“before the union”) is read instead of *ante incarnationem* (“before the Incarnation”), as Quesnel observes in note 35.]

And lest Eutyches suppose that he has spoken either correctly or tolerably merely because no sentence of yours has refuted him, [Note: Verona 58 has *confutatus* (“refuted”). Shortly afterward, most of the older manuscripts, together with the printed editions of the Councils, the Greek version, and five manuscripts cited by Quesnel in note 36, have *dilectionis tuae diligentiam* (“the diligence of your affection”), rather than the reading of Leo’s editions. Some of these add *igitur* (“therefore”) after *dilectionis tuae*. Nevertheless, the reading of Leo’s editions, confirmed by other manuscripts—especially Vienna collection 5, Ratisbon, and the Roman Church Lectionary Vat. 3836—is so appropriate that it should not be excluded. The first edition has *sollicitudinis tuae diligentiam commonentes* (“reminding the diligence of your concern”).] we remind the diligence of your concern, dearest brother, that if, through the inspiration of God’s mercy, the matter is brought to satisfaction, the stain of even an unlearned man’s folly may be cleansed. [Note: Verona 58 has *per te* (“through you”), incorrectly, instead of *peste* (“plague”). The Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, as well as Vat. collections 3, 11, 21, and 24, together with the editions before Quesnel, have *macula per te purgetur* (“the stain may be cleansed through you”). This reading seems to have arisen from the correction of an ancient scribe who, finding the words *per te* in a manuscript like the Verona copy cited, and seeing that the sense was incomplete, added *macula* from his own conjecture. The Vercelli manuscript, collection 8, has *pravitate purgetur* (“may be cleansed of wickedness”). The remaining copies approve the reading introduced by Quesnel. See his note 37.]

Indeed, as the order of events made clear, he had begun well to withdraw from his own persuasion when, constrained by your sentence, he professed that he was saying what he had not said before and assented to the faith from which he had previously been alien. But when he refused to give his consent by anathematizing the impious doctrine, your fraternity understood that he remained in his own perfidy and was worthy to receive the judgment of condemnation.

If he grieves over this faithfully and beneficially, and recognizes, even late, how rightly episcopal authority was moved; or if, for the fullness of satisfaction, he condemns aloud and by a present subscription everything that he has wrongly understood, then no degree of compassion toward one who has been corrected will be reprehensible. For our Lord, the true and good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:11), and who came to save human lives, not to destroy them (Luke 9:56), wishes us to be imitators of his mercy: so that justice may indeed restrain sinners, but mercy may not reject those who have turned back.

Only then is the true faith most fruitfully defended, when even by its own adherents a false opinion is condemned.

But, in order to carry out the whole matter piously and faithfully, we have sent our brothers Julius, bishop, and Renatus, presbyter, [Note: Quesnel says in note 40 that he found the words *tituli sancti Clementis* (“of the title of Saint Clement”) in all his manuscripts except one Barberini manuscript.
