Accordingly, they are found among others in the Corbie manuscript, collection 2, the Trecopith and Thuan collections, collection 5, the Grimanic collection 18, and others used by him. We, having collated several manuscripts especially for this passage, found these words absent from the manuscripts of eight collections—3, 9, Spanish 13, 17, 19, 21, 22, and 23—as well as from the Greek version and two particular manuscripts of Verona, 8 and 58. Conversely, we found them in manuscripts of five letter collections—5, 8, 10, 12, and 24—which, if Quesnel’s Corbie collection 2 and Grimanic collection 18 are added, gives seven collections supporting the words. The Lectionaries and sermon manuscripts in which this letter is inserted also support them, as does Sichard’s copy. In Ottobonianus 93 and Vat. 3791, collection 11, the letter is copied twice: in the first place the same words appear, while in the second they are absent. We have said nothing about Vat. Reginae, collection 1, because in it the letter ends with the preceding words, “a false opinion is condemned,” just as it ends in two Lectionaries, Basel Vat. 105 and 107. Amid such divergent evidence on both sides, the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection and the Greek interpretation, which was read at the Council of Chalcedon, should be given greatest weight for the negative judgment. For the affirmative judgment, the Lectionaries have the greatest authority, especially the very ancient Vatican manuscript 3836, which was used by the Roman Church in the basilica of Saints Philip and James. Nevertheless, it may seem difficult that Leo, who in so many letters named other presbyters of the Roman Church, and this same Renatus, without ever designating a title, should in this letter alone have attached to him the title of Saint Clement. Whether this title was once written in the margin by someone who knew Renatus’s title and later entered the text, we leave to others to judge. Shortly afterward, some manuscripts and the first edition have Hilary, or Ilary, the deacon.] of the title of Saint Clement, and also my son Hilary the deacon in our place.

We have joined to them our notary Dulcitius, whose fidelity has been proved to us, [Note: The manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collections, Vat. collection 3, Verona 8, Florence collection 13, copies of collection 21, together with the first edition and the editions of the Councils, add *saepe* (“often”). See Quesnel’s note 41.] trusting that divine assistance will be present, so that the one who had gone astray, after condemning the perversity of his understanding, may be saved.

[Note: The following six words are absent from two manuscripts of Verona, Vat. collection 3, both Vienna manuscripts of collection 5, the Spanish manuscripts, Vat. collection 8, Ratisbon, Florence, Vat. 1322, and manuscripts of collection 24, together with the first edition. They were rightly restored on the authority of other manuscripts, especially the Chalcedonian collection and the Greek interpretation. See Quesnel’s note 42.]

May God keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the distinguished men Asturius and Protogenes. [Note: Both Spanish manuscripts, the Isidorian copies, and other books descending from the Spanish or Isidorian tradition record the Spanish chronological era 486. This is a chronological notation peculiar to the Spanish people, added by the Spaniards. It should read era 487, corresponding to the year 449. See Quesnel’s note 44. In one Divion manuscript of Bohier’s Chalcedonian collection, the following distinctive words are added: “Tiburtius the notary, by order of my lord, the venerable Pope Leo, published this.” It cannot be conjectured from what source the scribe of Bohier’s manuscript took this notation, which is omitted not only from all our other Latin manuscripts and those of Baluze belonging to the same Chalcedonian collection, but also from the Greek interpretation. It plainly reveals an ancient origin. Quesnel asserts in note 43 that the word *domni* (“lord”) is foreign to the age of Leo I. Yet we find it prefixed to Leo in the very ancient Vatican Lectionary 3835, which was used by the basilica of Saints Philip and James. Thus it reads there, on page 176: “Here end two sermons of our lord Pope Leo on the Ascension of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Baluze attacks Quesnel’s notation in his notes on this letter, but with arguments that are not convincing.]

802 [Note: The Basel manuscript has: “To the most holy brother and fellow minister Flavian, Leo.”]

To the beloved Flavian, Leo.

Having read the letter of your affection—which we are astonished to find was produced so very late [Note: The Basel manuscript has *καὶ τῇ πράξει τῶν ὑπομνημάτων* (“and in the execution of the records”) in the margin; the Roman edition likewise has *πράξει* (“execution”).]—and having bent over the order of the records concerning what was done among the bishops, we have only with difficulty come to know what scandal had arisen among you against the sound faith. [Note: We have adopted this reading from the Venetian and Basel manuscripts. Its correctness is made entirely clear by the article *τὸ* that precedes it. The editions have *σκάνδαλον ἀνεφύη* (“a scandal arose”).] And what previously seemed to have been concealed has now become clear to us through the events by which Eutyches, who had been judged worthy of the title and honor of presbyter, [Note: Previously the common editions of the Councils had in the text: “having been judged worthy of the title and honor of presbyter,” while the Roman edition had in the margin: “having been judged worthy that the title of presbyter should be an honor.” In another Venetian manuscript—which, to distinguish it from the other already cited, we shall call the second, and in which this letter occurs twice—the first occurrence reads: “having been judged worthy that honor should belong to the title of presbyter”; the second: “having been judged worthy of the honor and dignity of the title of presbyter.” We corrected the text from Greek Vatican manuscript 1341.] proves to be extremely foolish and very ignorant [Note: *Λίαν* (“very”) is absent from the Basel manuscript.], so that what the prophet said about him seems applicable: “He was unwilling to understand how to do good; he practiced wickedness upon his bed.” For what could be more unjust than to think impious thoughts, to yield to those who do not think rightly, and to submit to the wiser?

Those who, being hindered in some way by an obstacle of obscurity, are prevented from knowing the truth fall into this folly; yet instead of turning to the prophetic words, [Note: All these words—“not to the writings of the Apostles”—are absent from the first Venetian manuscript.] to the writings of the Apostles, and to the authority of the Gospels, they turn back upon themselves. And for this reason they are revealed as teachers of error, because they have not become disciples of the truth.

For what instruction from the divine books of the Old and New Testament did he receive, when he did not even grasp the beginning of the Creed? [Note: The first Venetian and Basel manuscripts have *τοῦ προοιμίου* (“of the preface/beginning”).] And what is proclaimed aloud throughout the whole world by the voice of all who are being regenerated is not even understood in the mind of this old man.

[Col. 0758B]

Since, then, he does not know what one ought to think concerning the Incarnation of the Word of God, and does not wish to labor through the divine Scriptures in their breadth, so that he might become worthy of the light of knowledge that comes from them, he ought at least to have embraced, with attentive hearing, that common and undivided confession which the whole multitude of believers confesses: to believe [Note: The first Venetian manuscript has *ἑαυτόν* (“himself”), while the second Venetian manuscript, in both places, has *αὐτόν* (“him”). The Basel manuscript supports both readings, for nothing prevents this from being understood of Eutyches himself. Nevertheless, we alter nothing, since *ἑαυτό* (“itself”) may equally well refer to the multitude of believers mentioned immediately before.] in God the Father almighty, and in Christ Jesus [Note: The Basel manuscript adds: “his only-begotten Son.”] his only-begotten Son, our Lord; who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

By these three declarations nearly all the devices of the heretics are overthrown. For whenever God, almighty, and Father is believed, the Son is shown to be coeternal with him and in no respect different from the Father, since he is God from God, almighty from almighty, and, being begotten from the eternal one, coeternal, [Note: The Basel manuscript has *ἀΐδιος* (“eternal”) instead of *συναΐδιος* (“coeternal”).] not later in time, not lesser in power, not unlike in glory, and not separated in substance. [Note: Previously the text had *οὔτε μεταγενέστερος* (“neither later”), which may not satisfy everyone. The reading adopted here, from the Basel manuscript, *οὐ μεταγενέστερος* (“not later”), is certainly better. Read the entire passage together with the Latin text.]

The same Only-Begotten of the eternal Father was born eternally of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. This birth in time neither diminished anything from his divine and eternal generation [Note: The Basel manuscript has *ἀϊδίου φύσεως* (“of the eternal nature”), a reading we would gladly have adopted if the Latin text did not stand in the way. Shortly afterward, the same manuscript reads: “but he emptied his whole self in order to save the wandering man.” This reading is not without value. In the margin of the Roman edition, beside *ἐκένωσεν* (“emptied”), *ἐνέδωκεν* (“gave himself over”) is noted—a very good reading, and one that corresponds especially closely to the Latin, though its source is uncertain.] nor added anything to it; rather, he emptied his whole self in order to save the wandering man, so that he might conquer death and by his own power overthrow the Devil, who held the power of death.

For we could not have conquered sin and the author of death unless he himself had assumed our nature and made it his own—he whom neither sin could defile nor death could seize. [Note: The first Venetian manuscript has *ἐδυνήθη* (“was able”), which is Attic; the form in the text is common. We have made no change.]

He was therefore, plainly, conceived by the Holy Spirit in the womb of the Virgin Mary his mother. [Note: *Μητρός* (“his mother”) is absent from all the Venetian manuscripts and from the Basel manuscript. The word is not strictly necessary, but it should not be omitted if the Latin text is taken into account.] She gave birth to him while her virginity was thus preserved, just as she had conceived him while her virginity remained undefiled. [Note: We have restored this from all the Venetian manuscripts, for *ἀμεραίου*, found in the Venetian edition, is wholly unknown in Greek.]

But if from this most holy source of the Christian faith he could not draw a pure understanding [Note: We have taken this reading, which is the correct one, from the Basel manuscript and from both Venetian manuscripts in both places. The Roman editors also saw that it should be read so, as appears from a marginal annotation. The editions have *ἐκ ταύτης τινὰ καὶ τῆς ἐν τῇ πίστει* (“some from this and from that which is in the faith”).] because, through the darkness of his own blindness, he himself obscured the radiance of the far-shining truth, he ought at least to have submitted himself to the teaching of the Gospels. And when Matthew says, “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,” and when he read the apostolic proclamation, he ought to have sought its explanation. [Note: The Basel manuscript has *εἰσήγησιν ἐπεζήτησεν* (“he sought an exposition”).] Reading in the Letter to the Romans: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures, concerning his Son, who was made from the seed of David according to the flesh,” [Note: The Basel manuscript omits *τὸ* (“the”).] he ought thus to have directed his devout attention to the prophetic books, and, finding the promise of God to Abraham, who says, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed,” [Note: The Basel manuscript has *εὐλογηθήσονται* (“shall be blessed”).] so that he might not doubt the authority of this seed, he ought also to have followed the Apostle, who says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed.” He did not say, “and to his seeds,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “And to your seed,” [Note: The first and second Venetian manuscripts, in the first occurrence, have *ἐν ἑνί* (“as referring to one”).] which is Christ. [Note: The Basel manuscript adds: “that is, Christ.”]

He ought also to have listened with inward attention to the proclamation of Isaiah, who says: “Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” [Note: The first Venetian manuscript has *ἐν γαστρὶ ἕξει* (“shall have in the womb”).] which, translated, means “God with us.” [Note: The Basel manuscript has: “which means, ‘God with us.’”]

He ought also faithfully to have read the words of the same prophet: “A child has been born for us, a son has been given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder; [Note: The second Venetian manuscript has *οὗ ἡ ἀρχή* (“whose rule”).] and his name shall be called the Angel of Great Counsel, Mighty God, Ruler, Prince of Peace, Father of the Age to Come.” [Note: The second Venetian manuscript has: “Angel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God.”]

Nor would the Word, speaking vainly, have said that he became flesh, if the one born from the Virgin, Christ, had the appearance of a man but did not possess the reality of a body from his mother. [Note: The Basel manuscript has *τοῦ ἡμετέρου σώματος* (“of our body”).] Or perhaps for this reason he thought that the Lord Christ was not of our nature, because the angel sent to blessed Mary said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one born from you [Note: *Ἐκ σοῦ* (“from you”) is absent from the first Venetian manuscript. In the Basel manuscript, immediately afterward, *ἅγιος* (“holy”) occurs instead of *ἅγιον*, namely: “the holy one shall be called.”] shall be called the Son of God.”

How could it be that, since the Virgin’s conception was the work of divine creation, the flesh of the one conceived did not come from the nature of the one who conceived him? But that birth must not be understood in this way. It is uniquely wondrous, and wondrously unique, so that through the new character of the birth the authority of the race might be excluded. For the Holy Spirit supplied fertility to the Virgin, while the reality of the body was assumed from a body. And when Wisdom was building a house for itself, the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—that is, in this body, which he took from a human being [Note: The Basel manuscript adds: “and animated with a spirit of rational life.”] and which he animated with a spirit of rational life.

[Col. 0764A] Since, then, the distinctiveness of each nature is preserved, and the two come together in one person, [814] humility was assumed by the divinity, weakness by the power, mortality by the immortal; and, in order that the debt owed by our nature might be paid, the divine nature was united to the passible nature, so that this same one, existing as the mediator of God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, might be able to die by virtue of one nature and yet not be able to die by virtue of the other.

[Note: [Col. 0764C] In this passage you find ὑπό three times; this is the correct reading, and we have accepted it from the second Venetian manuscript, at the second occurrence. The printed editions have ἀπό, less appropriately. In the same manuscript the entire passage reads as follows: at the first place, “Humility was assumed from the divinity, weakness from the power, mortality from the immortal”; at the second, “Humility was assumed by the divinity, weakness by the power, mortality by the immortal.”]

[Note: [Col. 0764C] The words ἐκτιθῆναι are absent from the Basel manuscript, but incorrectly. In the first and second Venetian manuscripts, at the first occurrence, we find ἐκτισθῆναι; this reading is also found noted in the margin of the Roman edition.]

Thus, in the complete truth and perfect nature of a human being, true God was born: wholly in what belongs to him and wholly in what belongs to us.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] The Basel manuscript has “wholly in what belongs to him and wholly in what belongs to us.”]

By “ours,” however, we mean those things which the Creator originally placed within us, and which he again accepted in order to renew them. For those things which the deceiver introduced, and in which the deceived human being sinned, have left no trace whatsoever upon the Savior.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] In the second Venetian manuscript, ἐν is absent in both places, and can properly be absent.]

[Note: [Col. 0764D] The Roman edition notes in the margin παρεδέξατο, “accepted”; this is, we think, only a conjecture. For if this reading rested on the authority of any ancient manuscript, it ought certainly to have been adopted, since it adheres more closely to the text.]

Nor, because he entered into participation in human weakness, did he therefore become a participant in our sins.

[Note: [Col. 0764D] The Basel manuscript has τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, “with human beings.”]

For he assumed the form of a slave without any stain of sin, increasing what was human and not diminishing what was divine. Since that self-emptying by which the invisible made himself visible, and the Creator and Lord of all willed to become one of human beings, was an act of compassionate condescension, not weakness of power.

[Col. 0766A] Therefore, he who, remaining in the form of God, made the human being, himself became human in the form of a slave.

[Note: [Col. 0765D] The Basel manuscript has “as remaining.”]

For each nature preserves unfailingly its own distinctiveness; and just as the form of God does not abolish the form of a slave, so the form of a slave did not diminish the form of God.

[Note: [Col. 0766C] The second Venetian manuscript, at the first occurrence, has “so also the form of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0766C] The Basel manuscript supplied this as the correct reading; it was also noted in the margin by the Roman editors. The common text has μορφωσις οὐκ ἐμείωσεν, “the form did not diminish.” In the text: “the form did not diminish.”]

Since the devil had boasted over the human being who had been deceived, that through his own error he had been deprived of the divine gifts and stripped of the blessings of incorruption and had come under the harsh sentence of death, he found in his own evils a certain consolation through the fellowship of the one who had become a traitor.

[Note: [Col. 0766C] The Basel manuscript has “and he boasted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0766C] The Basel manuscript has “from his own deception” instead of “from his deception”; this is also noted in the margin of the Roman edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0766C] We have chosen to remove ἐστερημένον, which stood in the printed edition, and to substitute ἐστερῆσθαι, as found in the Basel manuscript. This agrees better with the Latin text, “to have been without the divine gifts.”]

[Note: [Col. 0766C] The Basel manuscript has “to have been stripped bare, and under the …” This is a reading not to be dismissed.]

Thus he found a certain consolation, as though God, because his own justice required it, would alter his own sentence concerning the human being whom he had fashioned in such great honor.

[Note: [Col. 0766C] The Basel manuscript has “and to have found himself a certain consolation in his own evils, since he had become a companion of the one who had become a traitor.” For προδότου, “traitor,” perhaps παραβάτου, “transgressor,” should be read, as the Roman editors also noted in the margin.]

The administration of the ineffable mystery therefore became necessary, so that the unchangeable God, who cannot be deprived of any part of his innate goodness, might fulfill, through the ineffable mystery of his own piety, the first arrangement made concerning us; and so that the human being, driven toward sin by the wickedness of the devil’s malice, might not perish from God against his will.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] The Basel manuscript has “the need for the administration,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0766D] In the second Venetian manuscript τήν is absent in both places.]

[Note: [Col. 0766D] The Roman edition notes in the margin φιλανθρωπίας ἀπό ῥ, “of benevolence,” derived from the Latin.]

[Col. 0766B] Therefore the Son of God approaches this lowly world, descending from the heavenly throne and not departing from the glory of the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0766D] The Basel manuscript has “not being separated.”]

[Note: [Col. 0766D] Earlier editions read καινῇ μὲν τῇ τάξει, “new in order.” We have deleted μὲν as unnecessary, on the authority of the Basel and first Venetian manuscripts. The latter reads καινῇ τινι τάξει, “in a certain new order.”]

He is born in a new order and by a new birth: new in order, because although invisible in what belongs to him, he became visible in what belongs to us; although incomprehensible, he willed to be apprehended; although pre-eternal, he began to exist in time; although Lord of all, he assumed the form of a slave, veiling the greatness of his own divinity; and the impassible God did not disdain to be a passible human being, nor the immortal to be subject to the laws of death.

[Note: [Col. 0768C] The Basel manuscript has “and, being immortal, to be subject to death.”]

But he was born by a new birth, since the undefiled virginity knew nothing of desire, yet supplied the material of the flesh. And the nature of the Lord was assumed from the mother, not sin.

[Note: [Col. 0768C] In the printed editions stood “from the mother the nature of the Lord,” with the article ἡ before “the nature of the Lord.” This made the genitive “of the Lord” appear to modify “nature,” not “mother,” and was not without the suspicion and danger of error, since it must refer to “mother.” The two Venetian manuscripts inserted in the acts of Chalcedon also have this faulty form; but the same manuscripts, in the letter prefixed to the acts, as well as another Venetian manuscript, number 165, supply the true reading in both places: they omit the article ἡ, and in addition place a comma after “of the Lord” in three places. Gerardus Vossius likewise read it in his manuscript, as is clear from his Mainz edition.]

Nevertheless, because the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ, born from the womb of the virgin, is wondrous, our nature is not therefore unlike his; for he who is true God is himself also true human being.

[Note: [Col. 0768C] We have chosen to write this form with the Basel and second Venetian manuscripts in both places. The editions have οὐχὶ φύσις, “not nature.” The article ἡ makes the meaning clearer.]

Nothing false, therefore, exists in this union, so far as both are one with each other: the lowliness of the human being and the greatness of the divinity. For just as God does not undergo change by showing mercy, so the human being is not consumed by the greatness of divine dignity.

[Note: [Col. 0768C] The Basel manuscript has: “and the lowliness of the human being and the greatness of the divinity; for just as God does not undergo change, so also the human being,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0768B] For each form acts in communion with the other what properly belongs to it: the Word accomplishing what belongs to the Word, and the body carrying out what belongs to the body. One of them shines forth in miracles, while the other submits to insults.

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The first Venetian manuscript has “in sufferings”; the margin of the Roman edition likewise has “in sufferings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The Basel manuscript has “that which is the Word’s.”]

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The margin of the Roman edition has ἅπερ, “the things which”; the second Venetian manuscript also has this at the first occurrence.]

And just as the Word is inseparable from the equality of the Father’s glory, so the body has not abandoned the nature of our race. For one and the same truly is both Son of God and truly son of a human being: God in this respect, that “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; human being in this respect, that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The Basel manuscript lacks the words “and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”]

And he is God in this respect, that all things came to be through him, and without him not even one thing came to be; human being in this respect, that he came to be from a woman and came to be under the law.

[Note: [Col. 0768D] The Basel manuscript has “and he came to be under the law.”]

[Col. 0770A] The birth of the incarnation is an indication of human nature, but the virgin’s childbirth is a sign of divine power.

[Note: [Col. 0770C] The margin of the Roman edition has “the birth of the flesh,” derived from the Latin.]

[Note: [Col. 0770C] The Basel manuscript has “is a demonstration of divine power.”]

The infant’s infancy is recognized through the lowliness of the swaddling clothes, but the greatness of his majesty is demonstrated through angelic voices. He is made like newly born human beings—he whom Herod impiously intends to kill—but he is Lord of all, whom the magi rejoice to worship in supplication.

[Note: [Col. 0770C] The second Venetian manuscript has βουλεύεται, “intends,” in both places.]

[Note: [Col. 0770C] The Basel manuscript has “worship in supplication.”]

When he comes to the baptism of his forerunner John, lest it remain concealed that the divinity was hidden beneath the veil of the flesh, the Father’s voice cries out from heaven and says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

[Note: [Col. 0770C] The Basel and second Venetian manuscripts, at the first occurrence, have ηὐδόκησα, “I was well pleased.”]

Therefore, the cunning of the devil tempts him as a human being, while the order of angels ministers to him as God.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Basel manuscript has “but the order of angels ministers to this one as God.”]

For to hunger and thirst, to toil and sleep, plainly belong to a human being; but to satisfy five thousand human beings with five loaves, and to give the Samaritan woman living water, from which she drew so that she would no longer thirst, belong unmistakably to God.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Basel manuscript has “to satisfy five thousand people with five loaves …”]

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Basel manuscript has “living water.”]

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Basel manuscript has “so that she no longer had to thirst.” The Venetian manuscript has ὑπῆρξε, “there was,” in both places.]

And to walk upon the back of the sea, with his feet not being submerged, and to calm the swelling waves by rebuking the storm, unmistakably belongs to God.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Basel manuscript has “to go along.”]

Thus, to pass over much, it is not of the same nature to weep, out of a disposition of pity, for a deceased friend, and to raise that same person, already four days buried, at the command of a voice, once the decay has been dispersed; nor is it of the same nature to be hung upon wood and, when day has been changed into night, to shake all the elements; nor to be pierced by nails and to open the gates of paradise to the faith of the thief.

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Basel and first and second Venetian manuscripts, in both places, have μεταβληθέντα, referring to “the elements,” but incorrectly.]

[Note: [Col. 0770D] The Basel manuscript has “to raise him, who had already been buried in a four-day burial, at the command of the voice.” This arrangement of the words pleases us more. In this same place, the second Venetian manuscript, at the second occurrence, reads “of the final burial” instead of “of the four-day burial.”]

[Col. 0772A] Thus, it is not of the same nature to say, “I and the Father are one,” and to say, “My Father is greater than I.” For although in the Lord Jesus Christ the person of God and of the human being is one, nevertheless one is the source from which the humiliation is common to both, and another the source from which the glory is common. From us comes to him the humanity that is lower than the Father; from the Father comes to him the divinity equal to the Father.

[Note: [Col. 0772C] The Venetian manuscript has “and it is another,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0772A] Because of this union of person, which ought to be understood in each nature, we read that the son of a human being came down from heaven, when the Son of God assumed the body from that very Virgin from whom he was born. Again, the Son of God is said to have been crucified and buried, although these things were endured not in the divinity itself, in which he is the Only-Begotten, coeternal, and of one substance with the Father, but in the weakness of the human nature.

[Note: [Col. 0772C] The Basel manuscript and both Venetian manuscripts have “and, being of one substance with …” in both places.]

Therefore, we all confess in the Creed that the Only-Begotten Son of God was crucified and buried, in accordance with that apostolic saying: “For if they had known, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.”

[Note: [Col. 0772C] This is how the Basel and both Venetian manuscripts read, in accordance with the Latin text, “the Only-Begotten Son of God crucified and buried,” except that the Basel manuscript adds “and risen.” The editions incorrectly have “the Only-Begotten Son of this one crucified,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0772D] The first Venetian manuscript has “we all confess in the Creed.”]

When our Lord and Savior himself was instructing the faith of the disciples through questions of his own, he asked: “Who do people say that I, the Son of a human being, am?” When they answered that different people held different opinions, he said: “But you, who do you say that I am?”—that is, me, the Son of a human being, and the one whom you see in the form of a slave and in the reality of a body: who do you say that I am?

[Note: [Col. 0772D] The Basel manuscript has “that is, to be.”]

[Note: [Col. 0772D] The Basel manuscript has “Whom, he says, do they say that I am?”]

[Note: [Col. 0772D] We have added εἶναι, “to be,” from the Basel manuscript, since it is also present in the Latin text: “Whom do you say that I am?” The common text has only “Whom do you say that I am?”]

There the blessed Peter, inspired by God and destined, through his own confession, to become the salvation of all the nations, says: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” He was rightly declared blessed by the Lord, and from the original rock he drew the solidity both of virtue and of the title: he who, through the revelation of the Father, confessed the same one to be both Son of God and Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0772D] The margin of the Roman edition has στεῤρόν, “firm.”]

For, when one of these is taken apart from the other, it proved useless for salvation; and the same danger was involved in believing the Lord Jesus Christ to be either God alone without a human being, or a human being alone without God.

[Note: [Col. 0774C] The printed editions had κατά, “according to”; we have changed it to μετά, “after,” on the authority of the Basel and both Venetian manuscripts. The Latin text likewise requires no other reading: “But after the resurrection.”]

But after the Lord’s resurrection—which was, of course, a resurrection of his true body, since no one other than the one who had been crucified and died rose—what else was accomplished during the forty days of his life among them than that the things belonging to our faith might be cleansed of every mist? For he conversed with his disciples, stayed with them, and shared their meals, allowing himself to be touched more carefully and inquisitively by those whom doubt afflicted.

[Note: [Col. 0774C] The Basel manuscript has “since it was not another who rose.”]

[Note: [Col. 0774C] Both Venetian manuscripts have “his forty-day life among them.”]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] Both Venetian manuscripts have “with his own disciples.”]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The margin of the Roman edition has συναυλιζόμενος, “dwelling together.”]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The Basel manuscript has “more precisely.”]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The second Venetian manuscript, at the second occurrence, has ἀνεδίδου, “was yielding,” or “was giving back.”]

For this reason he also entered to the disciples while the doors were shut, and by his own breath bestowed the Holy Spirit upon them; and, granting the light of knowledge, he revealed the hidden things of the divine Scriptures. Again, the same one displayed the wounds in his side, the piercings of the nails, and all the marks of his recent suffering, saying: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have,” so that the distinctiveness of both the divine and human nature might be recognized as remaining in him, undivided.

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The Basel manuscript has “so that it might be known to have remained in him.”]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The Basel manuscript has “undividedly.”]

Thus let us learn that the Word is not the same as what the flesh is, but let us confess one Son of God, both the Word and the flesh. Eutyches, being light-minded and unacquainted with the faith of this mystery, must be regarded as one who neither understands nor possesses it: he did not recognize our nature in the Only-Begotten Son of God either through the humility of humanity or through the glory of the resurrection.

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The Basel manuscript has “who did not recognize our nature.”]

Nor did he fear the sentence of the blessed apostle and evangelist John, who says: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that divides Jesus Christ is not from God; and this is the Antichrist.”

[Note: [Col. 0774D] The word ὅτι, “that,” is absent from the Basel and second Venetian manuscripts in both places.]

[Note: [Col. 0774D] We have added Ἰησοῦν, “Jesus,” from the Basel and both Venetian manuscripts. The Latin text agrees: “Jesus Christ in the flesh.” The common text has Χριστόν without Ἰησοῦν.]

What is it to divide Jesus, if not to separate the human nature from him and to attempt, through shameless fabrications, to produce in vain the mystery through which alone we were saved? Whoever sustains this obscurity concerning the nature of Christ’s body necessarily raves with similar blindness concerning his suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0776C] The Basel manuscript has “for he regarded the Lord’s cross as false,” and so forth.]

For if he has not considered the Lord’s cross false, he must acknowledge that the suffering undertaken for the salvation of the world truly occurred, and must not doubt it at all.

[Note: [Col. 0776C] The Basel and Venetian manuscripts have “the suffering that was displayed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0776C] The Basel and first Venetian manuscripts indicate that this should be read as ἀμφιβάλλει, “he doubts.” The printed editions incorrectly have ἀμφιβάλλοι, “he might doubt.” Since above he used νενόμικε in the indicative, he should likewise use ἀμφιβάλλει here.]

If, then, he recognizes the death, let him also recognize the flesh; and let him not deny that the one whom he knew to have become passible was a human being of our flesh. For the denial of the true body is also a denial of the body’s suffering.

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The Basel manuscript has “let him recognize the flesh also,” in accordance with the Latin text; the printed editions do not have καί.]

[Col. 0776B] If, therefore, he accepts Christian faith and does not turn his own hearing away from the preaching of the Gospel, let him consider what nature was hanging, pierced by nails, upon the wood of the cross; and, when the side had been opened and a spear had been driven into the one fastened to the cross by the soldier, let him understand from where the blood and the water flowed, so that the Church of God might be watered both by the bath and by the drink.

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The Basel manuscript has “he was hanging upon the wood of the cross”; the final word is also found in the second Venetian manuscript at the second occurrence, while at the first it has “was hanging.”]

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The Basel and second Venetian manuscripts have νυγείσης, “having been pierced”; the first Venetian manuscript has ἀνυγείσης, which is certainly corrupt from νυγείσης. This reading should not be dismissed, since it derives from νύσσω, “I pierce.”]

Let him also hear the blessed apostle Peter proclaiming that the purification of the Spirit takes place through the sprinkling of the blood of Christ; and let him not read casually the words of that same apostle, who says: “Knowing that you were ransomed from your futile ancestral way of life, not with perishable things, silver or gold, but with precious blood, as of a holy and spotless Lamb, Christ Jesus.”

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The Basel manuscript has “the purification of God.”]

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The Basel manuscript has “you were not ransomed with perishable silver or gold.” The second Venetian manuscript has “not with perishable things” in both places.]

[Note: [Col. 0776D] The Basel manuscript has “Jesus Christ.”]

Nor let him resist the testimony of the blessed apostle John, who says: “The blood of Jesus, the Son of God, cleanses us from every sin”; and again: “This is the victory that has conquered the world, our faith.” And who is the one who conquered the world, if not the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God? This is Jesus Christ, the one who came through water and blood—not in water only, but in water and blood. And it is the Spirit who bears witness, because the Spirit is the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0778C] The Basel manuscript has “Who is the one who conquered the world?”]

[Note: [Col. 0778C] The Basel manuscript has “Jesus is the one who comes through water.” The first Venetian manuscript does not have “Jesus.”]

For there are three who bear witness: the Spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three are one—that is, the Spirit of sanctification, the blood of redemption, and the water of baptism. These three are one and remain undivided, and none of them is separated from their mutual connection, since the catholic Church lives in this unity and advances in faith.

[Note: [Col. 0778C] The second Venetian manuscript, at the first occurrence, has “and the three are one.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778C] The first Venetian manuscript lacks αὐτῶν, “of them.” The Basel manuscript has αὐτοῦ, “of it,” which seems to us a better reading, except that we would prefer αὑτοῦ. The second Venetian manuscript has ἑαυτῶν, “of themselves,” in both places; this too is not to be dismissed.]

Thus neither should humanity be recognized apart from true divinity, nor should divinity be believed apart from true humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0778C] The Basel manuscript has “so that the humanity may be recognized.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778C] The Basel manuscript has “so that the divinity may be believed to exist.”]

[Col. 0778A] To the question put to your hearing Eutyches answered, saying:

[Note: [Col. 0778C] The Basel and second Venetian manuscripts, in both places, have “as Eutyches answered.”] “I confess that our Lord came to be from two natures before the union; but after the union I confess one nature.”

[Note: [Col. 0778C] Both the Basel and second Venetian manuscripts have “after the union,” which we scarcely doubt is the correct reading.]

I marvel that such a bizarre and so distorted confession was not judged objectionable by any of the judges’ censure, and that so foolish a statement, made in passing, offended none of those who heard it.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The Basel manuscript has, corruptly, “as of those who heard, when in the same manner.”] For in the same way it is impious to say that, before the incarnation, the Only-Begotten Son of God existed from two natures, as it is unlawful to assert that, after the Word became flesh, there is one nature in him.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The Basel manuscript has “the Only-Begotten is unlawful,” evidently because the copyist had fallen asleep.]

Lest Eutyches suppose that this was said rightly—or even tolerably—since it has been imposed by no decision of ours, we remind your belovedness, dearest brother, of the need for exactness, so that, if by God’s mercies the affair comes to a full explanation, the ignorance of the unlearned man may be cleansed through you from this corruption of his own understanding.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The Basel manuscript has “or acceptable.” The margin of the Roman edition has εἴτ᾽ οὖν, “whether therefore.” The second Venetian manuscript likewise has this in both places, written continuously as εἴτουν.]

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The margin of the Roman edition has πληροφορίαν, “assurance.”]

[Note: [Col. 0778D] The second Venetian manuscript has “of this corruption of the corruption,” and so forth.]

[Col. 0780A] Accordingly, as the sequence of events makes clear, he had begun to withdraw properly from his own position when, constrained by your sentence, he admitted that he was saying what he had not previously said and professed to rest in the faith from which he had previously been alien.

[Note: [Col. 0780C] The Basel manuscript has “which he had previously said.”]

But when he was unwilling to agree with the impious doctrine that deserved anathema, your brotherhood recognized that he remained in his own false belief and was worthy to receive the judgment of deposition. If he grieves over this faithfully and beneficially, and if, although late, he nevertheless recognizes why the authority of the bishops was exercised against him, or if he looks toward a complete defense, so that everything wrongly thought by him may be condemned by a clear and present statement and by his own written signature, then he will not be unworthy of whatever mercy may be shown to one who has been corrected.

[Note: [Col. 0780C] The Basel manuscript has “if indeed toward perfection,” while the first Venetian manuscript has a reading beginning ἴη εἰ; the second has only εἰ.]

[Note: [Col. 0780C] This correct reading was taken from the second Venetian manuscript, at the first occurrence, which has πόσος οὖν, “how much then,” with the initial syllable ὁ omitted through a copyist’s error. The common text has ὁπωσοῦν, incorrectly.]

For our true and good Lord, the shepherd who laid down his soul for his sheep, and who came to save human souls, not to destroy them, wishes us to be imitators of his goodness: so that justice may discipline those who sin, while the compassion of pity may in no way reject those who turn back.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] We have added αὐτοῦ, “his,” on the authority of the Basel manuscript, in accordance with the Latin text, “his soul.” The common text has “the one who laid down the soul.”]

[Note: [Col. 0780D] The Basel manuscript has “his sheep.”]

[Note: [Col. 0780D] We preferred this reading from the Basel manuscript, as it is less involved, over the common text: “but may the pity of compassion in no way reject those who have turned back.” The first Venetian manuscript has “those who have returned.”]

Then, truly then, the truth of the faith is vindicated together with a good fruit, when even by the leaders of those who cling to impiety their own false belief is condemned.

[Note: [Col. 0780D] The margin of the Roman edition has “of those who cling to it.”]

[Note: [Col. 0780D] At this word, καταδικάζεται, “is condemned,” the second-place copies of Venetian manuscripts 164 and 555, as well as both copies of another Venetian manuscript, number 165, end. The last continues with “It was given on the Ides of June.” The Basel manuscript has καταδικάσθηται, “may be condemned,” and continues, “and furthermore.”]

[Col. 0780D] In order that the entire matter may be completed piously and faithfully, we have sent our brothers Julius the bishop, Renatus the presbyter, and also my son Hilarus the deacon, to our place.

[Note: [Col. 0782C] The two Venetian manuscripts 164 and 555, in the letter at the first occurrence, alone preserve this passage, as noted above. The printed editions incorrectly have “Julian.” See note 81 ([Col. 0779], n. b) on the Latin text of the preceding letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0782C] The Basel manuscript has “my son Hilarus,” and so forth.]

We have joined to them Dulcitius, our notary, whose fidelity we have tested, trusting that God’s help will be present, so that the one who was led astray, having condemned the perversity of his own opinion, may be saved.

[Note: [Col. 0782C] The Basel manuscript has “Dulcitius, my notary, to whom I entrusted the faith of those things,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0782C] The Basel manuscript has “the divine help.”]

May God preserve you in strength, dearest brother.

[Note: [Col. 0782C] The Basel manuscript has “May he preserve you, dearest brother who loves God.” The words that follow, “It was given,” and so forth, are absent from that manuscript.]

Given on the Ides of June.

[Note: [Col. 0782D] The printed editions add: “in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes, most illustrious consuls”; but our manuscripts omit these words, and we do not doubt that the Roman editors supplied them from the Latin text.]

# LETTER XXIX

[Note: [Col. 0781D] Otherwise 26. What was previously 29 is now 23. Written on 13 June in the year 449.]

[Note: [Col. 0782B] This letter is found in the manuscripts of collections 2, 5, 11, 12, 13, 17, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, as well as in Sichard’s copy. We consulted eleven manuscripts, to which three others of Baluzius must be added. In collection 5 the title reads, chapter 89: “To the emperor Theodosius concerning the synod to be held at Ephesus.”]

## TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS

[Col. 0781]

### SUMMARY

He sends legates in his place to the Synod of Ephesus, summoned on account of Eutyches. He hopes for better things concerning him.

[Note: [Col. 0782] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0782] To the most glorious and most benevolent Theodosius Augustus, Leo, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0782B] Only the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection 17, to which belongs the Thuaneus manuscript mentioned by Quesnellus in note 1, preserve this heading: “To the most glorious and most clement Theodosius Augustus, Leo the bishop.” The other collections have the customary heading, except the Regensburg collection 19, in which abbreviated headings are presented: “Leo the bishop to Theodosius Augustus.” In the Florentine manuscript of collection 13 there is a slight variation: “To Caesar Theodosius, most religious and most devout Augustus, Leo, bishop of the catholic Church, sends greetings in the Lord.”]

To Caesar Theodosius, most religious and most devout Augustus, Leo, pope of the catholic Church of the city of Rome.

[Col. 0781A]

How greatly divine providence deigns to care for human affairs is shown by the concern of your Clemency, moved by the Spirit of God, which desires that nothing troubled and nothing discordant exist in the catholic Church; for the faith, which is one alone, cannot in any respect be unlike itself.

[Col. 0781B] Hence, although Eutyches has been shown, as the sequence of the episcopal proceedings revealed, to have gone astray through ignorance and imprudence, and ought to have withdrawn from his own opinion, which is rightly rejected, nevertheless, since your piety, which most devoutly loves catholic truth in honor of God, has established a synodal judgment at Ephesus so that the truth about which that ignorant old man is most deeply mistaken might be made known to him, I have sent my brothers Julius the bishop, Renatus the presbyter, and my son Hilarus the deacon, who could adequately serve in my place according to the nature of the affair.

[Note: [Col. 0782C] This is taken from the Regensburg manuscript and all our manuscripts and those of Baluzius in the Chalcedonian collection. The printed editions, with certain other manuscripts, have “from his own deservedly reprehensible persuasion.” Shortly afterward, “because” is found instead of “since” in the manuscripts of Verona 57 and Regensburg.]

[Note: [Col. 0783B] The words “at Ephesus” are absent from the Regensburg manuscript and from the Greek version.]

[Note: [Col. 0783B] The editions before Quesnellus, together with several manuscripts, including some from older collections, have “council.” We have retained the reading introduced by Quesnellus on the authority of the Grimani manuscript and one Thuaneus manuscript cited by him in note 2, since our Regensburg manuscript and all the manuscripts of the finest Chalcedonian collection, as well as the Greek version, confirm the same reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0783C] The manuscript of Vienna collection 5, several manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, and the Colbertinus of Baluzius, together with the editions before Quesnellus, have “Julian.” The other manuscripts correctly have “Julius,” as can be seen from note 81 ([Col. 0779], n. b) on the preceding letter. Likewise, certain manuscripts and old editions of Leo shortly afterward incorrectly have “Hilarius” instead of “Hilarus.”]

[Col. 0783C] They would also carry with them the disposition toward justice and kindness, so that, since the integrity of the Christian confession cannot be doubted, the perversity of every error might be condemned; and if the one who had gone astray should come to his senses and seek pardon, priestly benevolence might assist him. For in the memorandum he sent us he at least preserved this as a means of obtaining pardon: he promised that he would correct whatever our judgment rejected concerning the matters about which he had thought wrongly.

[Note: [Col. 0783C] Two manuscripts cited by Quesnellus in the margin have “and would carry with him … affection.”]

[Note: [Col. 0784B] The manuscripts of Corbie and Dijon belonging to Baluzius have “But what does the catholic Church …”; that is, as Baluzius interprets it, “What does the Roman catholic Church …?”]

What the catholic Church universally believes and teaches concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation is contained more fully in the writings that I sent to my brother and fellow bishop Flavian.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

[Col. 0782]

To the most illustrious and most benevolent Theodosius Augustus, Leo the bishop.

[Col. 0782A]

The concern of your benevolence, moved by the Spirit of God, shows how greatly divine providence deigns to care for human affairs according to its power. It is fitting that this concern should wish there to be no disagreement concerning the catholic Church, but peace.

[Note: [Col. 0782D] The margin of the Roman edition has: “The concern of your benevolence, moved by the Spirit of God, shows how greatly divine providence deigns to care for human affairs; it does not wish …”]

[Note: [Col. 0782D] The Venetian manuscript has “by a command.”]

Although the faith is one, it ought not to be unlike itself. Therefore, even though Eutyches has been shown, as the sequence of the episcopal records made clear, to have gone astray through ignorance and lack of understanding, and ought to have recovered from his own opinion, which is deservedly rejected, nevertheless, since your piety, which loves the most devout catholic truth in honor of God, has established a synodal tribunal so that the truth concerning which that ignorant old man has most seriously erred might be brought to light, I have sent my brothers Julius the bishop, Renatus the presbyter, and my son Hilarus the deacon, who are able to serve in my place according to the nature of the affair and to bring him over to a disposition toward what is just and good.

[Note: [Col. 0784B] The Venetian manuscript has ἀγαπᾷ, “loves,” an excellent reading that agrees exactly with the Latin text, if ἡ above is read as ἥ.]

[Col. 0782B] So that what the integrity of the Christians’ confession is may be made clear beyond doubt, and the wickedness of every error condemned; and, if the one who has gone astray should recover and plead for pardon, so that the assistance of the bishops may aid him.

[Note: [Col. 0784C] The margin of the Roman edition has “and thus having a disposition toward both justice and kindness, so that …”]

[Note: [Col. 0784C] The Venetian manuscript has “what sort of thing.”]

[Note: [Col. 0784C] We write this on the authority of the Venetian manuscript. The printed editions incorrectly have εἰ ἀνανήψειν, “if he will recover.”]

For in the memorandum of his that was sent to us he also preserved this as a means of being deemed worthy of pardon, promising that he would correct whatever our judgment might reject concerning those things about which he had thought wrongly.

[Note: [Col. 0784C] The margin of the Roman edition has “if this,” derived from the Latin.]

[Note: [Col. 0784C] This must unquestionably be read on the authority of the Venetian manuscript. The printed editions incorrectly have ἀποδοκιμάσειν, “to reject.”]

What the catholic Church as a whole believes and teaches concerning the divine mystery of the Lord’s incarnation is contained more clearly in the writings sent to our brother and fellow bishop Flavian.

# ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING LETTERS XXX AND XXXI (G)

[Col. 0783]

1. Although the two letters found to have been written to Pulcheria on the same day and concerning the same matter are plainly similar in some passages—not so much in their arguments as in their wording—they nevertheless differ from one another in many respects, and one is much longer because of the insertions added to it. The character of the style and the authority of the ancient manuscripts and collections by which both are supported absolutely do not allow either of them to be attributed to anyone other than Leo.

The Latin and Greek copies of the most ancient collection, collection 17 of Chalcedon, and Regensburg collection 19, in addition to collections 12 and 22, sufficiently vindicate the first letter. The manuscripts of collections 2, 5, 11, 12, 13, 18, 20, 21, 22, 23, and 24, together with Sichard’s copy and the special Vatican manuscript Regina 293, support the second. Why two such letters were delivered to Pulcheria on the same day, and which should be considered to have been written first or later, may be investigated with greater curiosity than it can be determined by any sufficiently secure method.

2. In his first edition (vol. II of the first edition, p. 850), Quesnellus thought that letter 30 had first been written by the pontiff and sent to Pulcheria through the legates, while some hope still remained that the synod might be changed into a simple assembly at Constantinople. For this reason, he thinks, the following words were written near the end of that letter: “But better provision will be made for the one who is in error if, in the very place where he went astray, he comes to his senses, and where he deserved condemnation, there he obtains indulgence.”

When obstacles arose and this letter was not delivered to Pulcheria, Leo sent her a copy of it again after the Ephesian pseudo-synod, as is clear from letter 45. On this occasion, he thought, Leo himself expanded the letter, with a few omissions and some alterations, producing letter 31. But if, after the Ephesian Robber Council, when the same letter was sent again to Pulcheria, anything had been altered that no longer suited the time and circumstances, that addition would certainly not have been made by which the holy pontiff more earnestly excuses himself from attending the Ephesian synod.

3. Quesnellus himself abandoned this first opinion in his second edition. Moving entirely to the contrary view, he taught that the longer letter 31 had been written by Leo and sent to Pulcheria immediately after the letters of Theodosius had been received—that is, shortly after the third day before the Ides of May. He supposed that the chronological notice marking the Ides of June, which is absent from several manuscripts, had been taken from the shorter letter 30 and transferred to it incorrectly.

That the shorter letter 30 was sent through the legates on the Ides of June, however, is clear.

4. Yet this opinion can neither be approved nor defended. For since Leo received the emperor’s letter on the third day before the Ides of May, if he had immediately written to Pulcheria, he would also have written back to the emperor. It is clear, however, that after receiving the emperor’s letter on the third day before the Ides of May, and receiving at approximately the same time Flavian’s letters together with the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches, he soon wrote to that same Flavian the very brief letter 27, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June. In it he informed him that he had received the proceedings, and also mentioned that a fuller letter would be sent as soon as possible, once judgment had been given concerning the controversy.

Occupied with this undertaking, and also with choosing and instructing the legates who would attend the council already summoned in his place, he postponed the letters intended for several recipients until the time when the legates would cross over with the doctrinal letter. Hence several letters are read as having been given on the same Ides of June on which the doctrinal letter 28 to Flavian was dated; in all of them the legates are named, and the same letter to Flavian is mentioned as having already been delivered to them.

All this is also explicitly mentioned in the longer letter 31 to Pulcheria: the legates in these words of chapter 4, “In these brothers of mine, whom I sent in my place”; and the doctrinal letter written on the Ides of June in the final chapter: “Let your Clemency also know that I wrote to the holy bishop Flavian.” The same words are likewise inserted in letter 30, which was unquestionably written on those same Ides of June.

How, then, can letter 31 be said to have been composed and sent some time before the month of June?

### 5

What, then, should be said? Leaving uncertainties aside, since the shorter Letter 30 is found in the Greek and Latin collection of Chalcedon and distinctly gives the names of the legates, it cannot be denied that this letter to Pulcheria, like the other letters that were delivered to the same legates together with the letter to Flavian, was sent to her, eventually delivered to her, published in the East, and from there rendered into Greek.

The longer Letter 31, although absent from the Greek collection, nevertheless exists in several ancient Latin collections that lack the shorter letter and everywhere preserve the Leonine account; it therefore cannot be rejected as a letter of Leo. It must be said to have been dated on the same day, the Ides of June, as those collections also indicate which lack Letter 30. For the authors of these collections could not have copied such a chronological notation, as Quesnell conjectured, from the shorter letter, which they did not know. Without some more certain evidence, however, it is not permissible either to affirm or to conjecture anything else.

The only probable conclusion is that Leo composed two copies of the same letter, one longer and the other shorter: he sent the shorter one to the East, where it was translated into Greek, while he kept the longer one with him; this longer version was eventually circulated in the West and passed into most of the Latin collections.

### 6

The longer letter differs chiefly from the shorter in that, from chapter 2 through the middle of chapter 3, it establishes Catholic doctrine by several proofs, which are omitted from the shorter version. Perhaps, after writing Letter 28 to Flavian, in which the same doctrine is set forth more fully with similar proofs, Leo judged that those proofs should be removed from the letter to Pulcheria. On that occasion he also omitted the passage in which he excused himself from attending the synod, and altered or added a few other things in his usual manner—passages that are found in the shorter letter.

After the shorter letter had been sent to the East, the longer letter, because of its fuller doctrinal exposition, was especially valued by Westerners; for that reason it was chiefly this version that circulated among the Latins.

### 7

Someone might suspect that Letter 31 to Pulcheria, since it contains several sentences resembling those in Letter 37 to Theodosius, dated 20 June, was written and sent on the same day and for the same reason. After receiving the imperial letters inviting him to the synod, Leo may indeed seem to have written twice to Theodosius and likewise twice to Pulcheria. First, on the Ides of June, he wrote to both through the legates: Letter 29 to Theodosius and Letter 30 to Pulcheria.

Then, when he sent Letter 37 to the emperor again on 20 June—perhaps because he feared that, in the short time allotted for the synod, the legates might be compelled to hurry to Ephesus and therefore be unable to deliver Letter 29 to the emperor—it may reasonably be judged that on the same occasion and for the same reason he also wrote Letter 31 to Pulcheria.

Yet we were unable to adopt this opinion against the testimony of those collections that give the chronological notation “the Ides of June,” which they could not have taken from Letter 30. We were even less able to do so for another reason, which will increasingly confirm the conjecture proposed in the preceding section.

“If the letter,” Leo says in Letter 45, “which was sent to Your Piety through our clerics had reached you, it is certain that you could have provided a remedy for these things done against the faith ….” This refers to Letter 30, sent through the legates, which did not reach the Augusta because they had gone on to Ephesus. He therefore assumes that he did not send her another, fuller letter on the same matter on a later occasion after the legates’ departure. Otherwise, since that letter would have been conveyed in a manner no less effective than the earlier one, it would have produced a much greater effect, and there would have been no need to send her another copy of Letter 30 together with Letter 45.

Therefore Letter 31 was not sent to Pulcheria. Leo retained it with him, while only Letter 30 was first sent to her through the legates and then sent again with Letter 45. Hence only Letter 30 was translated into Greek, as we conjectured in section 6. Since this shorter letter was certainly sent to Pulcheria, we shall present it first.

[Note: Written 13 June 449.]

## LETTER XXX. TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

[Col. 0785]

### SUMMARY

I. Christ is a man of our race. The errors of Nestorius and Eutyches.  
II. When the reality of Christ’s flesh is attacked, the whole faith is shaken.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**847** [Note: In the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, the inscription is lacking; only this title is found: “Letter of Leo, archbishop of Rome, to Pulcheria Augusta.” From the ancient version found in the Greek Chalcedonian manuscripts, the inscription may be rendered into Latin as: “To the most glorious and most humane daughter Pulcheria, Leo the bishop.” We have retained the customary inscription found in our other Latin manuscripts.]

**LEO**, bishop, to **PULCHERIA**, Augusta.

### CHAPTER I

By many proofs we have often shown how much confidence the Church of God ought to place in the faith of Your Clemency, since, as you have learned under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, you subject your authority in all things to him by whose gift and protection you reign.

Therefore, since I learned from the report of my brother and fellow bishop Flavian that, through the agency of Eutyches, a certain dissension had arisen against the integrity of the Christian faith in the Church of Constantinople, so that the whole character of the case was revealed by the text of the synodal proceedings, it is worthy of Your Glory that an error born more from ignorance than from cunning should be removed before it acquires any strength through the agreement and stubborn depravity of the imprudent.

For just as Nestorius fell away from the truth when he asserted that the Lord Jesus Christ was born from the virgin mother as man alone, so this man too has departed from the Catholic path by refusing to believe that the one born from that same virgin belongs to our nature. Thus, although he bore the form of a servant and was like and conformed to us, he would make him merely an image of our flesh, not its reality.

It is of no benefit to call our Lord the son of the blessed virgin Mary a man if he is not believed to be a man of that race and stock which is proclaimed at the very beginning of the Gospel. Hence I grieve greatly and am deeply sorrowful that this man, who previously seemed praiseworthy for his purpose of humility, now dares to assert, against our one hope and that of our fathers, things vain and exceedingly perverse.

When he saw that the meaning of his folly displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have withdrawn from his opinion and not so stirred the rulers of the Church that he incurred a sentence of condemnation. If he wishes to remain in his present conviction, no one will be able to release him from that sentence. For the moderation of the Apostolic See preserves this balance: it acts more severely toward the obstinate, yet desires to grant pardon to those who correct themselves.

[Note: The manuscripts of Regensburg and Verona 57, together with the Greek version, omit “of Mary.”]

[Note: This reading in the Regensburg manuscript seemed better than the common reading and that of the other manuscripts, since it avoids suggesting that the rulers of the Church were moved in such a way; the same reading is preferred in the following letter, where this passage is repeated in exactly the same words.]

### CHAPTER II

Because I have great confidence in the entirely sincere faith of Your Piety, I beseech Your Most Glorious Clemency to favor now also the freedom of the Catholic proclamation, just as your holy zeal has always assisted it.

For no small portion of our faith, one that has been less clearly explained, is being attacked. Rather, ignorant resistance dares to assail what the Lord did not wish anyone in his Church to ignore.

Therefore, according to the custom of Your Piety, deign to labor so that what blasphemous folly has uttered against the unique mystery of human salvation may be driven from the minds of all.

And if he who has fallen into this temptation comes to his senses, so that he condemns by his own voice and signature what he wrongly thought, let the communion of his own order be restored to him. Let Your Clemency know that I have written this also to my brother and fellow bishop Flavian, and that I have instructed those whom we sent that pardon should be granted if the error is abolished.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “glorious.” Shortly afterward we have corrected “your” in place of “your” from the Regensburg manuscript and five others, since it agrees better with the preceding “of your piety” and with the following “your zeal,” which are incorporated into the same period.]

[Note: Printed editions of the Councils add from the Greek version: “most illustrious and most glorious daughter.”]

[Note: The editions of Leo read: “so that he may be removed as something blasphemous against the unique mystery of human salvation,” etc. We preferred the reading of the Regensburg manuscript, supported by the printed editions of the Councils.]

[Note: In the erroneous printed editions of Leo: “in this temptation.”]

[Note: Five of our manuscripts read “he is better advised.”]

Lest it seem that I was absent from the disposition of the most pious prince by which he wished an episcopal council to be convened, I sent my brothers Julius, the bishop, Renatus, the presbyter, and my son Hilarus, the deacon, who would be sufficient to fulfill the role of my presence.

[Note: Quesnell noted in a marginal annotation: “A council convened by imperial arrangement.” In a second note he observed that the word “arrangement” signifies a princely edict. But in Letter 33 to the Council of Ephesus, Saint Leo remarks, in the very letters of Theodosius that have been lost, that the authority of the Apostolic See had been requested by divine institution so that this imperial arrangement might achieve its effect. He says in chapter 1: “The religious faith of the most merciful prince … rendered this reverence to the divine institutions, that it should apply the authority of the Apostolic See for the accomplishment of the holy arrangement.”]

[Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “Julian,” and shortly afterward the Verona manuscript reads “Hilary.” The others have “Julius and Hilary.” Compare note 81, column 779, note b, on Letter 28.]

But the man in error will be better served if he comes to his senses in the very place where he went astray and receives indulgence where he deserved condemnation.

**Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.**

---

**848** To the most glorious and most humane daughter **Pulcheria**, Leo the bishop.

[Col. 0786]

How much confidence the Church of God ought to place in the faith of Your Humanity, we have often shown by many teachings.

[Note: In the margin of the Roman edition: “we have recognized.” From the Latin.]

You have learned this under the instruction of the Holy Spirit; you have subjected your authority to him; through this gift and protection you reign.

[Note: In the Venetian manuscript: “reigning.”]

Therefore, since I learned through the report of my brother and fellow bishop Flavian that, while Eutyches was exercising authority, a certain dissension had arisen against the undefiled faith of the Christians in the Church at Constantinople, just as the character of the whole matter is shown by the records of the synod, it is worthy of Your Glory that the error—entering through ignorance rather than ill will—should be removed before the stubbornness of depravity acquires any strength from the agreement of the ignorant.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads “from consent.”]

And just as much as Nestorius, who fell away from the true faith, went astray by claiming that the Lord Jesus Christ had been born from the virgin Mary as man alone, so this man too has deviated from the Catholic way. He has believed that the one born from that same virgin is not of our nature, wishing him to be understood as belonging to the Godhead alone; so that although he bore the form of a servant, became like us, and possessed the same form, he is merely some image of our body, and not its reality.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “And just as Nestorius fell away from the true ….”]

Our Lord’s being called a man, the Son of the blessed Virgin, is of no benefit if he is not believed to be a man of her race and root—the one of whom the Gospel proclaims at its very beginning.

[Note: Venetian manuscript: “is believed.”]

Hence I suffer greatly and am sorrowful, because this man, who was previously praised for his intention of humility, dares to utter vain and very perverse things against the hope of our Only-Begotten and of our fathers.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads “the hope of the race,” or perhaps “of the Only-Begotten.”]

When he saw that the perception of his folly displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have recalled himself from his own supposition and not stirred those who remain in the Churches while awaiting the sentence of condemnation.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads “awaiting.”]

For it is clear that, if he should wish to remain in the same conviction, no one will be able to release him. For the moderation of the Apostolic Throne preserves this proportionate restraint: it acts more harshly against those who persist and deems those worthy of pardon who acknowledge correction.

Since, therefore, I have great confidence in the faith of Your Most Blessed Piety, I beseech Your Humanity, most illustrious and most pious daughter, that, just as through divine zeal you have come to the aid of freedom in the Catholic dignity of the Church, so now also you may be a helper to that same freedom.

[Note: In the margin of the Roman edition, perhaps: “that, just as through your divine zeal you have always aided the Catholic proclamation, so now also you may cooperate in its freedom.”]

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “so that, just as through your divine zeal you have always aided the Catholic proclamation, so now also you may cooperate in its freedom.”]

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads: “for the dignity of the Catholic Church.” The Roman edition’s margin reads: “for that of the Catholic ….”]

For no part of our faith that is not clear is being contrived. Rather, ignorant resistance dares to disturb what our Lord absolutely did not wish to remain unknown in his own Church.

Therefore, according to the custom of Your Piety, deign to labor over this.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “so that this ….”]

Let what it has brought forth in a blasphemous folly against the religion of the Only-Begotten, concerning human salvation, be removed from everyone’s mind.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “of the Only-Begotten.”]

And let the man who has fallen into this temptation come to his senses, so that he condemns by his own voice and signature what he has wrongly conceived and restores himself to the communion of his own order.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin, from the Latin, supplies: “and, if he should recover his senses, condemning by his own voice and signature what he wrongly conceived, let him be restored to the communion of his own order.”]

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “conceived.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript reads “and by his signature he shall condemn the common [error].” The Roman edition’s margin likewise notes the word “common.”]

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “let the communion of his own order be restored to him.”]

Let Your Humanity know that I have written this also to my brother and fellow bishop Flavian, and that I have instructed those whom we sent to deem him worthy of pardon if the matters of his error are corrected.

[Note: These words, “Your Humanity,” are absent from the Venetian manuscript.]

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin, from the Latin, supplies: “to deem him worthy,” etc.]

But lest the absence of my presence seem attributable to the intention of the most pious emperor, who wished the council of bishops to assemble, I have sent my brothers Julius the bishop, Renatus the presbyter, and my son Hilarus the deacon, who are sufficient to take the place of my presence.

[Note: In the Venetian manuscript: “wishing in his mind that the council of bishops should assemble according to whatever seemed good.”]

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads “Julian.”]

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin, from the Latin, reads: “But it would be better for the man who has gone astray to come to his senses where he went mad and to receive pardon where he justly underwent condemnation.”]

But it is better for this man who has gone astray to recover his senses where he went mad, and there, where he endured condemnation, he will also be deemed worthy of the honor of pardon.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “to enter together.”]

### LETTER XXXI. TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

[Note: Formerly numbered 27; now 34. Written 13 June 449.]

[Note: See the introductory note to the preceding letter, where the eleven collections containing this letter are also listed. In table 5 of the collections this title appears in chapter 79: “To Pulcheria concerning the condemnation of the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies.”]

[Col. 0789B]

### SUMMARY

I. He solicits Pulcheria’s zeal against Eutyches.  
II. It concerns human salvation that Christ be not merely man but a man of the same race as ourselves.  
III. The generation of Christians flows from Christ’s generation. Eutyches’ obstinacy. The moderation of the Apostolic See.  
IV. Custom, the circumstances of the time, and affection for his fellow citizens prevent Leo from attending the council. The Apostles’ Creed is shaken by the new heresy.

[Note: The Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark’s collection 13 reads: “Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Pulcheria Augusta.” In the editions before Quesnell: “Leo, bishop of the Catholic Roman Church, to the most pious Pulcheria Augusta.” We have retained the inscription prefixed by Quesnell and confirmed by several of our manuscripts. The older manuscripts omit the inscription.]

**LEO** to **PULCHERIA**, Augusta.

[Col. 0789C]

### CHAPTER I

By many proofs we have often shown how much protection the Lord has prepared for his Church in Your Clemency. Whatever priestly diligence has obtained in our times against the enemies of Catholic truth has redounded chiefly to your glory, since, as you have learned under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, you subject your authority in all things to him by whose gift and protection you reign.

Therefore, since I learned from the report of my brother and fellow bishop Flavian that, through the agency of Eutyches, a certain dissension had arisen against the integrity of the Christian faith in the Church of Constantinople, so that the character of the whole case was revealed by the text of the synodal proceedings, it is worthy of Your Glory that an error—which, as I think, was born more from ignorance than from cunning—should be removed before it acquires any strength for itself through the agreement of the imprudent and the stubbornness of depravity.

[Note: The manuscripts of the Vatican Regina collection 293, the Vienna collection 5, and the Vatican collection 11 read “showed.” Shortly afterward, we restored “worthy of your glory,” which occurred in earlier editions of Leo, from those manuscripts and two others. Quesnell and the editions of the Councils, together with the manuscripts of collection 21, read “worthy of your glory.”]

[Note: We deleted the conjunction “and,” inserted by Quesnell, which is absent from all our manuscripts except two.]

For ignorance too sometimes leads to serious falls, and unwary simplicity often rushes into the devil’s pit. Through this, I understand, the spirit of falsehood slipped into the man mentioned above, so that, while he thought he was displaying a more reverent understanding of the majesty of the Son of God by refusing to say that the reality of our nature was present in him, he judged that the whole which the Word became flesh was of one and the same substance.

[Note: We supplied the preposition “into” from the Vatican Regina manuscript, and shortly afterward preferred “the pit,” rather than “the pits,” from the same manuscript and Vatican collection 11.]

[Note: The Vatican Regina manuscript omits “so that” and, after the word “to perceive,” continues with a full stop: “For if the reality of our nature ….” The editions before Quesnell, together with manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichard, have “let him say” and “let him think,” rather than “he would not say” and “he judged.”]
