[Note: In Catholic usage, the whole that is made from the nature of the Word and the nature of man united together is nothing other than Christ, who in one person embraces whatever belongs to both natures. Hence Leo, Letter 124 to the Palestinians, chapter 7: “It makes no difference from which substance Christ is named, since, with the unity of the person remaining inseparable, he is wholly the Son of man because of the flesh and wholly the Son of God because of the one Godhead he shares with the Father.” But Eutyches, supposing that what was made by the incarnation of the Word was of one and the same substance, that is, nature, asserted only the divine nature; and for this reason he thought that he was understanding the majesty of the Son more reverently, as though the reality of the human nature united to him brought disgrace upon him. The Eutychians abused the word “whole,” which the ancients used to indicate the person, in order to confuse the natures. Thus Catholic theologians, following Leo, spoke of “whole” with respect to the natures and “wholly” with respect to the person.]

Just as Nestorius fell away from the truth when he asserted that Christ was born from his mother as man alone, so this man too deviates from the Catholic path, because he does not believe that the substance born from that same virgin is ours, wishing it to be understood as the substance of the Godhead alone. Thus, although he bore the form of a servant and was like and conformed to us, he would make him merely an image of our nature, not its reality.

[Note: Earlier editions before Quesnell, with several later collection manuscripts, read “asserted.” Shortly afterward, manuscripts of collection 21 read “deviated,” as in the preceding letter; hence the erroneous readings “may have deviated” or “might deviate” in others. Collection 11 reads “believed” for “believes”; the same reading stood in the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, but was corrected by a second hand to “believes.”]

[Note: In the Vienna manuscript of collection 5: “so that what bore the form”; in Vatican collection 24 and in Sichard: “so that what was in the form.” Other variants of this passage may be found in Quesnell’s note 1.]

### CHAPTER II

It is of no benefit to call our Lord, the son of the blessed Virgin Mary, a true and perfect man if he is not believed to be a man of that race which is proclaimed in the Gospel.

For Matthew says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). He follows the order of human descent in such a way that he traces the lines of the generations down to Joseph, to whom the Lord’s mother was betrothed.

Luke, on the other hand, reading backward through the stages of succession, returns to the very originator of the human race (Luke 3:23), so as to show that the first Adam and the last Adam are of the same nature.

[Note: Vatican collection 11 reads “was able.”]

For the omnipotence of the Son of God could have appeared for the instruction and justification of human beings in the same way in which he appeared to the patriarchs and prophets in the likeness of flesh, whether he entered into a wrestling match (Genesis 32:24), engaged in conversation, declined no act of hospitality, or even ate food that was set before him (Genesis 18).

[Note: The manuscripts of collection 24 omit “and for justification.”]

[Note: See Quesnell’s note 2.]

But those appearances were indications of this man; mystical signs announced that his reality was to be taken from the stock of the preceding fathers.

[Note: The manuscripts of collection 24, together with the editions before Quesnell, read “indications.”]

Therefore, although the mystery of our reconciliation had been ordained before eternal ages, no figures could fulfill it, because the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon the Virgin, nor had the power of the Most High overshadowed her, so that, within her undefiled womb, Wisdom building a house for herself (Proverbs 9:1), the Word might become flesh (John 1:14); and so that the form of God and the form of a servant, coming together in one person, the creator of times might be born in time; and that he through whom all things were made might himself be born among all things.

[Note: The Vienna manuscript reads “and so that within.” The common editions have “and also within”; the other manuscripts, however, omit “and.”]

[Note: Similar wording is found in Letter 28, chapter 2.]

[Note: The Grimanic manuscript deletes “himself” from “himself among all things,” as Quesnell noted in the margin.]

For unless the new man, made in the likeness of sinful flesh, had assumed our old condition; unless he, consubstantial with the Father, had deigned also to be consubstantial with his mother; and unless, being alone free from sin, he had united our nature to himself, human captivity would universally remain under the yoke of the devil, nor could we otherwise possess the victory of the triumphant Victor, if he had not been joined to our nature.

[Note: The editions of the Councils read “nor otherwise,” as do the older editions of Leo together with the manuscripts of collection 24: “nor could we otherwise possess the victory of the triumphant one.” Quesnell emended the text on the basis of his manuscripts, which our codices also support. The editions, together with most of our manuscripts and one Theodorician manuscript of Quesnell, read “completed” instead of “joined”; Quesnell introduced this word on the authority of other copies of his, as may be seen in note 3. Our Vienna manuscript of collection 5 also confirms this reading.]

### CHAPTER III

Through this wondrous participation the sacrament of our regeneration has shone upon us, so that, through the same Spirit through whom Christ was both conceived and born, we too—who have been begotten through the concupiscence of the flesh—might be born again through a spiritual origin.

For this reason the Evangelist says of believers: “They were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:13).

[Note: We restored “wondrous,” found in the editions of the Councils and accepted by Quesnell in the margin, because all our manuscripts support it except Vatican collection 24, which, together with the Leonine editions and Quesnell, reads “wondrously.” Shortly afterward, the common editions before Quesnell and several of our manuscripts read “bestowed” instead of “shone,” while two of ours and three of Quesnell’s, together with Canisius’s edition, read “introduced.” Compare his note 4.]

Whoever does not share in this ineffable grace cannot be counted among the adoption of the children of God, since he excludes from his faith what principally saves us.

[Note: The editions before Quesnell, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, read: “nor can anyone attain the adoption of the children of God.” The other manuscripts support the reading introduced by Quesnell. See his note 5.]

Therefore I grieve greatly and am deeply sorrowful that this man, who previously seemed praiseworthy for his purpose of humility, dares to assert, against our one hope and that of our fathers, things vain and exceedingly foolish.

[Note: The Vatican Regina manuscript reads “foolish.”]

When he saw that the meaning of his folly displeased Catholic ears, he ought to have withdrawn from his opinion and not stirred the rulers of the Church in such a way as to incur a sentence of condemnation. If he wishes to remain in his conviction, no one will be able to release him from that sentence. For the moderation of the Apostolic See preserves this balance: it acts more severely against the obstinate, yet desires to grant pardon to those who correct themselves.

[Note: The reading is better supported by the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, Vatican collection 11, two manuscripts of collection 21, and the Vatican Regina manuscript, as in the preceding letter, chapter 1. Earlier editions and other manuscripts read “when he saw.”]

[Note: Quesnell’s marginal reference: “24, question 2, chapter 5, ‘The sentence of condemnation.’”]

Since, therefore, I have great confidence in the exalted faith of Your Piety, I beseech Your Glorious Clemency to favor now also the freedom of the Catholic proclamation, just as your holy zeal has always assisted it. Perhaps the Lord permitted it to be attacked by this temptation so that it might become known what sort of people were hidden within the Church.

[Note: All our manuscripts except Vatican collection 24 read “exalted.” In that manuscript, together with the common editions before Quesnell, the reading is “most sincere.” The Vatican Regina manuscript and three of Quesnell’s manuscripts add “and most steadfast.” Shortly afterward, “glorious” is absent from four manuscripts. Earlier editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, read “the glory of your clemency.”]

[Note: The Leonine editions, together with Vatican collection 24, read “that they lie hidden, so that they may be recognized.” Vatican collection 11, together with the edition of the Councils, reads “that they might lie hidden, so that they might be recognized.” The manuscripts of collection 21 read “what sort they are within the Church, so that they may be recognized.” The Vienna manuscript of collection 5 reads “they might lie hidden, so that they may be recognized.”]

Their healing must certainly not be neglected, lest their loss also grieve us.

[Note: Three manuscripts, together with the editions of the Councils, read “lest their own loss.”]

### CHAPTER IV

The most august and Christian emperor, desiring that the disturbances be settled as quickly as possible, assigned an exceedingly brief and restricted period for the episcopal council which he wishes to be held at Ephesus, fixing the first day of August for the assembly. Since most of the time remaining after the third day before the Ides of May—the day on which we received the letter written by His Serenity—must be consumed, it is possible to arrange the departure of the priests sufficient for the matter.

[Note: The Vienna manuscript of collection 5 reads: “from the third day before the Ides of May, on which ….”]

[Note: The letters of Theodosius are meant here, by which Leo had been invited to the Council of Ephesus. Julius, the legate, testified in the Ephesine council, inserted into the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, after the imperial letters addressed to Dioscorus of Alexandria and dated the third day before the Kalends of April had been read, that the letters sent to Leo had not been written in the same but in a similar form, as the more accurate manuscripts and the Greek text prefer. Some difference in the form of address to Leo is indeed indicated by Hilary in the same session: “The most glorious and Christian emperors … sent venerable letters and earnestly requested our most blessed bishop Leo, the ruler of the Apostolic See, to attend this venerable and holy council.” This meticulous form of writing does not appear in the surviving letter to Dioscorus.]

For although His Piety believed that I too ought to attend the council—even if some earlier precedent were required—this cannot now be fulfilled in any way, because the condition of present affairs is too uncertain to allow me to be absent from so great a city. The peoples in turmoil would be driven into a kind of despair if I appeared, under the pretext of an ecclesiastical matter, to wish to abandon my country and the Apostolic See.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript of collection 11 omits “also.” Shortly afterward it reads “believed,” and the common editions before Quesnell, together with some manuscripts, read “on the occasion.”]

Since, therefore, you understand that it has served the public welfare that, with Your Clemency’s pardon, I should not refuse the affection and prayers of my fellow citizens, consider me present in these brothers whom I have sent in my place, together with the others who will be present. I have clearly and fully shown them, in accordance with the case as sufficiently revealed to me by the sequence of the proceedings and by the confession of the man in question, what must be preserved.

[Note: The Grimanic manuscript deletes “and fully.”]

For the question concerns no small portion of our faith, one that has been less clearly declared; rather, the most foolish resistance dares to assail what our Lord did not wish anyone of either sex to ignore in his Church.

[Note: The editions of Leo before Quesnell, together with Vatican collection 24, read “which shines less clearly.”]

[Note: The editions of the Councils read “the most foolish insult”; the earlier common editions before Quesnell read “the most foolish insult.” Vatican collections 11 and 21 read “the most foolish resistance dares to assert.” The Vatican Regina manuscript reads “the most foolish.” The Vienna manuscript of collection 5 reads “Most foolishly,” and inserts “and to introduce.”]

For the concise and perfect confession of the Catholic Creed itself, which is marked by the corresponding statements of the twelve apostles, is so fortified by heavenly protection that all the opinions of heretics can be cut down by its sword alone.

[Note: Quesnell’s marginal note: “Concerning this Creed, see Jerome, Letter 61 to Pammachius; Rufinus, Preface to the Exposition of the Creed; Saint Augustine, Sermon 115, On Time; the dissertations of Vossius; and our own Dissertation 14, which we shall publish in volume three.”]

If Eutyches had been willing to receive the fullness of this Creed with a pure and simple heart, he would in no respect have deviated from the decrees of the most holy Council of Nicaea. He would have understood that the holy Fathers established this principle: against the apostolic faith, which is one alone, no intellect and no eloquence should raise itself.

Therefore, according to the custom of Your Piety, deign to labor so that what blasphemous folly has uttered against the unique mystery of human salvation may be driven from the minds of all. And if he who has fallen into this temptation comes to his senses, so that by a written satisfaction he condemns his own error, let the communion of his order not be denied him.

[Note: Two manuscripts read “the folly of blasphemy.” Two others shortly afterward read “But if he himself ….”]

Let Your Clemency know that I have written this also to the holy bishop Flavian, so that affection may not be neglected if the error is abolished.

[Note: Quesnell, together with the common Leonine text and three of our manuscripts, reads “may not be denied.” To avoid repeating that word twice shortly before, contrary to Leo’s style, we preferred the reading of the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, the Florentine collection 13, several manuscripts of collection 21, and the Vatican Regina manuscript; the editions of the Councils also prefer this reading. Shortly afterward, one Vatican manuscript reads “if the error is renounced.”]

[Note: This chronological notation is found in manuscripts of collections 21, 22, and 23. It is absent from all the others, as it is also absent from the manuscripts cited by Quesnell in note 7. Since, among the manuscripts lacking this notation, the most ancient Corbie manuscript of collection 2—which Quesnell used in correcting this letter—is not mentioned, we suspect that the chronological notation is also found there; this would add considerably to its authority.]

**Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.**

## LETTER XXXII. TO FAUSTUS, MARTINUS, AND THE OTHER ARCHIMANDRITES OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Note: Formerly numbered 28; now 36. Written 13 June 449.]

[Note: This letter is found in four manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collections: 17, the Grimanic collection 18, the Regensburg collection 19, and the Venetian collection 22.]

[Col. 0795]

### SUMMARY

He condemns Eutyches’ opinion, desires that he return to a sounder mind, and thus be restored to communion.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**859** To his most beloved sons **FAUSTUS**, **MARTINUS**, and the other archimandrites, **LEO**, bishop.

[Note: In the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection: “to Marcianus and the other archimandrites of Constantinople.” The Regensburg manuscript reads: “and to Martinus the presbyter and the other archimandrites.” In the Greek version, καὶ Μαρκελλίνῳ (“and Marcellinus”) or Μαρκελλιανῷ (“and Marcellianus”) appears incorrectly. Martinus is named not only in the more accurate Latin manuscripts but also in the inscription of another Greek letter, Letter 53, which was given to the same archimandrites, and in his Greek subscription to the Constantinopolitan synod under Flavian, printed in volume 4 of the Venetian edition of the Councils, page 1024.]

Because Eutyches attempted to disturb the cause of the faith, I considered it appropriate that, since I had sent men from my side who would support the defense of the truth, I should also send a written communication to Your Belovedness. I know for certain that you are so devoted to piety that you cannot possibly hear blasphemous and impious words with equanimity, since the apostolic teaching remains in your hearts, where it says: “If anyone evangelizes you contrary to what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9).

As for the opinion of the aforesaid man—which, as we learned from reading the proceedings, was rightly rejected—we likewise decree that it must be detested. Thus, if the foolish advocate wishes to persist in his perversity, let him share the lot of those whose error he followed. For he will most justly be outside the Church of Christ who denies that Christ possesses a human nature, that is, ours.

But if, corrected by the mercy of the Spirit of God, the same man recognizes the impiety of his error and condemns with full satisfaction what Catholics abhor, we wish mercy not to be denied him, so that the Church of the Lord may suffer no loss: for the penitent may be received, and only the error ought to be excluded.

Concerning the sacrament of the great mystery of piety, in which through the incarnation of the Word of God we possess justification and redemption, what our judgment is according to the tradition of the Fathers has now, as I think, been sufficiently explained in the letters that I sent to my brother Flavian, the bishop. Thus, through the communication of your bishop, you may know what we desire to remain firmly established in the hearts of all the faithful according to the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

**Note [Col. 0795D].** It is false that Quesnellus asserted in note 1 that Leo was the first of all the Roman pontiffs to mention legates sent *a latere*. The name “legates” is found neither here nor in Letter 34, chapter 2; only those are mentioned whom he calls “sent from the pope’s side,” among whom was also Dulcitius, certainly not properly called a legate, but a notary. Moreover, before Leo, Boniface wrote that he had sent Severus, a notary of the Apostolic See, “from our own side” (Letter 13, to Rufus of Thessalonica, no. 5). Before him also, the author—whoever he may have been—of the letter to the Easterners inserted by Hilary among the Fragments, no. 4, mentions three priests of the Roman Church sent from the side of Pope Alexander to Alexandria. Those who adhered to the pope were called “from the pope’s side,” a formula adopted from the usage of the emperors; such were the priest Renatus, the deacon Hilary, and the notary Dulcitius, as well as those at the Roman council, to whom Julius, bishop of Puteoli, belonged. At the Council of Sardica, canon 7, the Fathers likewise requested that a priest be sent by the Roman bishop “from his side.”

**Note [Col. 0796C].** Leo knew this at least from the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches, in which he had seen these archimandrites signing.

**Note [Col. 0796D].** We have deleted the words of Eutyches inserted here in all printed editions, chiefly on the authority of our copies of the Chalcedonian collection and of Baluzius, as well as the Regensburg manuscript, with which the Greek version agrees.

**Note [Col. 0797C].** Earlier editions of Leo before Quesnellus omit the words “in the letters that I sent to my brother Flavian, the bishop.” Quesnellus supplied the omission from his manuscripts and the Greek version, as do all our manuscripts and the printed editions of the Councils. He alone has “in these letters, and now I have sent,” sufficiently. We have preferred the reading of our and Baluzius’s manuscripts.

**Note [Col. 0797C].** Codex Verona 57 of the Chalcedonian collection reads: “in the hearts of all the faithful.”

**Note [Col. 0797C].** The Greek version adds: “May God keep you safe, dearly beloved sons.”

## Greek version

**Note [Col. 0798D].** Perhaps: δεχθέν (*having been received*).

To the beloved sons Faustus and Martin and the other archimandrites, Leo the bishop.

Because of the cause of the faith, which Eutyches attempted to disturb, we therefore sent men who would support the truth. I considered it appropriate also to send a letter to Your Belovedness. I know clearly that you are so devoted to piety that you cannot even admit blasphemous and impious words to your ears, since the apostolic tradition remains in your hearts, in which it is said: “If anyone evangelizes you contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.”

As for the opinion of the aforesaid man, whom, as we learned from reading the proceedings, was rightly deposed, we too have judged that it must be cast out. If the foolish advocate should wish to remain in his own perversity, let him have his share with those whose error he followed. Most justly would he be outside the Church of God who denies that Christ possesses the human nature, that is, ours.

But if the same man, corrected by the mercy of the Spirit of God, should recognize his own error and wish with all his soul to anathematize what those of the Catholic Church anathematize, we wish him to receive mercy, so that the Church of the Lord may suffer no loss; for the penitent can be received, and only the error ought to be forgiven.

Concerning the holiness of the great faith, in which through the embodiment of the Word of God we possess justification and redemption, what we think according to the tradition of the Fathers has now, as I believe, been sufficiently stated in the letters that I have sent to my brother Flavian, the bishop. Thus, when your own president makes it known to you, you may learn what, having been spoken according to the Gospel of our Lord, we desire to remain firm in the souls of all the faithful.

May God guard you, beloved sons.

**Notes on the Greek version [Cols. 0798D–0800D].** In the margin of the Roman edition: *αὐτοῦ* (“his”); shortly afterwards *βλαστός* (“shoot, growth”) was printed for *πλαστός* (“formed”), on the authority of three Greek Vatican manuscripts, 1278 and 1455, and Vatican Ottobonianus 29. The reading *ὅτε λέγοντι τῷ Κυρίῳ* (“when the Lord was speaking”) is to be read with the Venetian manuscript, as the Roman editors also recognized; the vulgate has *ὅτε γὰρ λέγοντι*. In the margin: *σύ, ὅστις εἶ ἀληθῶς* (“you, who truly are”). The vulgate reads *ἑκάτερθεν* (“on both sides”); this was corrected to *ἑκάτερον* (“each [of the two]”) from the cited Roman manuscripts and the Venetian manuscript. We preferred *εἴγε Εὐτυχής* (“if indeed Eutyches”) with the Venetian manuscript to the vulgate *εἴ τι Εὐτυχής*; the margin of the Roman edition likewise records *εἴγε*. The Venetian manuscript has *πεπιστεύκει* and, shortly afterwards, *ἀπὸ τῆς εὐθείας πίστεως* (“from the straight faith”).

# Letter XXXIII

**Note [Col. 0797C].** Formerly Letter 29. What was previously numbered 33 is now 37. Written on the Ides of June in the year 449.

**Note [Col. 0797C].** This letter is preferred by thirteen collections: Hispanic Collection 5; Isidorean Collections 11, 12, 13, 17, 18, and 19; and Collections 21 through 24.

## To the Second Synod of Ephesus

**Note [Col. 0797C–D].** In the Hispanic collection and the others derived from it, the following title is given: “Letter of Pope Leo to the Synod of Ephesus, in which he urges the assembled bishops to condemn the blasphemies of Eutyches.” In the table of Collection 5, chapter 85: “On condemning the Eutychian heresy.” In the Greek Chalcedonian manuscripts: “Letter of the same Leo, archbishop of Rome, to the Second Synod at Ephesus, which was indeed submitted but was concealed because the impious Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, did not permit it to be published to the bishops.” In the Latin manuscripts, chapter 13: “Letter of the most holy Leo, archbishop of Rome, written to the Second Council of Ephesus against Eutyches, which was indeed produced but concealed because Dioscorus did not permit it to be published to the bishops.”

## Synopsis

I. The faith of the incarnation is proved from Peter’s confession.  
II. The council is convened to abolish error and restore those who have gone astray.

**Note [Col. 0798].** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

Leo, bishop of the holy synod assembled at Ephesus.

## Chapter I

The devout faith of the most clement emperor, knowing that it contributes greatly to his glory if no seed of error should arise within the Catholic Church, showed this reverence toward the divine ordinances: for the fulfillment of the holy disposition he applied the authority of the Apostolic See, as though he desired it to be declared by blessed Peter himself what was praised in his confession, when the Lord said: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matthew 16:13).

The disciples indeed reported various opinions of different people. But when they were asked what they themselves believed, the leader of the apostles, encompassing the fullness of faith in a brief statement, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” That is: You who truly are the Son of Man are likewise truly the Son of the living God; you are, I say, true in divinity, true in flesh, and, while the distinctive property of each nature is preserved, one in both.

If Eutyches believed this intelligently and fervently, he would in no way have departed from the path of this faith. For this reason the Lord answered him: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you, you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:17).

But he is utterly foreign to the structure of this building who neither grasps the confession of blessed Peter nor contradicts Christ’s Gospel. He shows that he has never applied himself to knowing the truth and that he was needlessly judged worthy of honor—an old man who adorned the gray hair of old age with no maturity of heart.

## Chapter II

Yet because the treatment even of such people must not be neglected, and because the most Christian emperor wished, piously and religiously, that an episcopal council be held so that every error might be abolished by fuller judgment, I sent our brothers Julius the bishop, Renatus the presbyter, and my son Hilary the deacon, together with Dulcitius, a notary of approved faith. They are to attend your holy assembly in my place and, together with you, establish by common judgment what is pleasing to the Lord.

That is, after the destructive error has first been condemned, the question of restoring the man who fell into error through ignorance is also to be considered—provided that, embracing the doctrine of truth, he has condemned fully and openly, in his own voice and by his signature, the heretical opinions in which his ignorance had become entangled. He also professed this in the statement that he sent to us, promising that in every respect he would follow our judgment.

After receiving the letter of our brother and fellow bishop Flavian, we replied to him more fully concerning what he appeared to have reported to us, so that, once this error—which seemed to have been newly born—had been abolished, there might be throughout the world one faith and one identical confession, and that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

**Note [Col. 0798C].** Codex Florence adds *true*. The wording indicates the emperor’s edict for convening a synod, as is clear from Letter 30, chapter 2; compare our note 8 (Col. 789, note b).

**Note [Col. 0798C].** The oldest Verona manuscript 57 of Collection 17 reads “has been declared.” Shortly afterwards, the Regensburg manuscript reads “the Lord speaking.”

**Note [Col. 0798C].** The Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “is asked.”

**Note [Col. 0798C].** The Vatican Hispanic manuscript and Isidore, as well as the printed editions in the margin, read “of the twofold [nature].” The editions read “on both sides”; from all our manuscripts of the various collections and from Baluzius’s we emended this to “each [of the two].”

**Note [Col. 0798C].** Vatican manuscript 546 of Collection 21 reads: “Certainly he would not have departed from the path of this faith; but the Lord would rightly have answered him.”

**Note [Col. 0799C].** The Vienna manuscript of Collection 5 reads “shows.”

**Note [Col. 0799C].** The editions before Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of Collection 24, read “authority.” One Chalcedonian manuscript and the margin of the printed Councils read *ordained* for *adorned*. Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 reads *was adorning*.

**Note [Col. 0799C–D].** The Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “our brother.” Editions before Quesnellus, together with the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, Isidore, and related witnesses, wrongly read *Julian*. See note 81 (Col. 779, note b) to Letter 28. Both Vienna manuscripts, of Collection 5 and the Hispanic collection, as well as Regensburg and the Chalcedonian manuscripts—including Verona 57—correctly read *Julius*, in agreement with the Greek version. They subsequently read “and Renatus”; later the Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “my son.”

**Note [Col. 0799D].** Codex Grimanicus reads “of piety,” and shortly afterwards “the opinions of the heretics.”

**Note [Col. 0799D].** This is the reading of nine of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, eleven of ours, and Baluzius’s. Vatican manuscript 546 of Collection 21 alone, together with editions before Quesnellus, has “with which [he] was polluted,” wrongly.

**Note [Col. 0799D–0800C].** The Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection add: “May God preserve you safe, dearest,” or “most beloved brothers.” Quesnellus appended to the date, without naming a manuscript or edition: “Alternatively, the Ides of May, or the Ides of January.” We find neither anywhere in our manuscripts. These variants are erroneous, since Letter 28 to Flavian, cited here, was given in the same year on the Ides of June.

## Greek version

Leo, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to the holy synod assembled at Ephesus, to the beloved brothers.

The most pious faith of the most gentle emperor, knowing above all that it greatly concerns his glory that no growth of error should arise within the Catholic Church, paid this reverence to the divine decrees: for the fulfillment of the divine ordinance it applied the authority of the Apostolic See, wishing that what was praised in the confession of blessed Peter might be made clear by Peter himself, when the Lord was speaking: “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?”

The disciples said that the opinions of various people were different. But when he asked them what they themselves believed, the leader of the apostles, encompassing the fullness of faith in a brief statement, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” That is: You are the one who truly is the Son of Man; you are the same one who truly is the Son of the living God; you are true in divinity and true in flesh; and, while the distinctive property existing in the twofold nature is preserved, you are one in both.

If Eutyches had believed this intelligently and earnestly, he would never have departed from the straight path of such faith. Because of this, the Lord himself gives him, the apostle, this answer: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father in heaven. And I also say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it.”

He is therefore exceedingly alien to the harmony of such a building who neither accepts the confession of blessed Peter nor contradicts the Gospel of Christ. He shows that he has never had any zeal to know the truth and that he was seen as worthy of honor in vain—one who adorned the gray hair of old age with none of the vigor of his heart.

But since, most honored brothers, the care of such people must not be neglected, and since the pious and Christ-loving emperor, acting with piety and reverence, desired that a synod of bishops be assembled so that every error might be erased by a more complete judgment, we sent our brothers Julius the bishop, Renatus the presbyter, my son Hilary the deacon, and with them Dulcitius, my notary, whose faith had been tested by us.

They will attend your holy synod in my place and, together with you, decide what is pleasing to God. That is, after his destructive error has first been condemned, the restoration of the man who wandered through ignorance is to be considered—provided that, accepting the teaching of the truth, he is willing fully and clearly to condemn, by his own voice and signature, the heretical opinion into which his false teaching had entangled him.

He promised to do this also in the statement that he sent to us, undertaking in every respect to follow our decisions. After receiving the letters of our bishop and fellow brother Flavian, we wrote back to him more fully concerning the matters which he seemed to have reported to us, so that, once the error newly arisen had been erased, there might be one faith throughout the whole world, for the praise and glory of God, and one identical confession; and so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee might bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

Amen.

**Notes on the Greek version [Cols. 0798D–0800D].** In the margin of the Roman edition: *αὐτοῦ* (“his”); shortly afterwards *βλαστός* (“shoot, growth”) was printed for *πλαστός* (“formed”), on the authority of Greek Vatican manuscripts 1278 and 1455 and Vatican Ottobonianus 29. Read *ὅτε λέγοντι τῷ Κυρίῳ* (“when the Lord was speaking”) with the Venetian manuscript, as the Roman editors also noted; the vulgate has *ὅτε γὰρ λέγοντι*. In the margin: *σύ, ὅστις εἶ ἀληθῶς* (“you, who truly are”). The vulgate has *ἑκάτερθεν* (“on both sides”); it was corrected to *ἑκάτερον* (“each [of the two]”) from the Roman and Venetian manuscripts. We preferred *εἴγε Εὐτυχής* (“if indeed Eutyches”) with the Venetian manuscript rather than the vulgate *εἴ τι Εὐτυχής*; the Roman margin also records *εἴγε*. The Venetian manuscript has *πεπιστεύκει* and, shortly afterwards, *ἀπὸ τῆς εὐθείας πίστεως* (“from the straight faith”). The Roman margin reads *Ἰουλιανόν* for *Ἰούλιον*; it also suggests *καὶ τῇ*. For the passage concerning condemnation and restoration, the margin gives: *πλάνης καταδικασθείσης, μετὰ ταῦτα καὶ περὶ τῆς ἀποκαταστάσεως αὐτοῦ τοῦ ἀμαθῶς πλανηθέντος σκοπηθῆναι* (“once his destructive error has been condemned, thereafter to consider the restoration of the one who wandered ignorantly”). The Venetian manuscript reads *εἶθ᾽ οὕτως* (“and then thus”), though it would be better if it also indicated how the rest could be remedied; it also reads *εἴγε ὅμως* (“provided, however”). The Roman margin reads *ᾧπερ* (“in which”) and, later, *ἀκολουθήσειν* (“to follow”); the Venetian manuscript reads *εἰς πλήρης* instead of *εἰς πλῆρες*. Finally, the Roman margin suggests *δεξάμενοι* (“having received”).

# Letter XXXIV

**Note [Col. 0801B].** Formerly Letter 31. What was previously numbered 34 is now 38. Written on the Ides of June in the year 449.

**Note [Col. 0801B].** This letter has so far been found only in manuscripts of Collections 12, 18, and 19.

## To Julian, Bishop of Cos

## Synopsis

I. Leo grieves that Eutyches has fallen away from the unity of the faith.  
II. He sends legates from his side to the synod.

Leo, bishop, to Julian, most beloved brother and bishop.

**Note [Col. 0801B].** The Regensburg manuscript reads: “To Julian, bishop of the Coans.”

## Chapter I

The letter of Your Belovedness, recently delivered to me, shows how vigorously you flourish in spiritual love of the Catholic faith. It gives me great joy that pious hearts converge upon the same judgment, so that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in us according to the teaching of the Holy Spirit: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfected in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians 1:10).

Eutyches has made himself exceedingly foreign to this unity if he grows old in his perversity and still does not understand by what bonds he is bound by the devil; and he thinks that some priest of the Lord can be found who will agree with his ignorance and madness.

**Notes [Cols. 0801B–0802B].** The printed editions read “in the same judgment”; the reading of the Regensburg manuscript was preferred. The same editions read “makes himself foreign,” while the Vatican and Venetian manuscripts of Collection 12 read “has made himself foreign”; the Regensburg exemplar was preferred. Earlier printed editions wrongly read “by the Lord” for “by the devil.”

For a long time it was uncertain among us what Catholics found objectionable in him. Since we received no letter from our brother Flavian, while Eutyches himself complained in his writings that the Nestorian heresy was springing up again, we could not fully learn where this deceitful complaint arose or toward what it tended. But after the documents of the episcopal proceedings had been brought to us, it became clear how detestable were all those matters concealed beneath the covering of false complaints.

## Chapter II

Since the most clement emperor, out of the benevolence and piety of his mind, wished that the condition of this man—previously considered honorable—be examined more carefully, and for this reason judged that an episcopal council should be convened, I sent through our brothers Julius the bishop and Renatus the presbyter, as well as my son Hilary the deacon, whom I sent from my side in my place, a sufficiently detailed letter to our brother Flavian. Through it both Your Belovedness and the whole Church may learn what we hold as divinely handed down and what we proclaim unchangeably concerning the ancient and singular faith attacked by this unlearned assailant.

Nevertheless, because we must not omit the role of compassion, we believed it consistent with priestly moderation that, if the condemned presbyter should correct himself through full satisfaction, the sentence by which he is bound should be released. But if he should choose to lie in the same mire of his folly, let the decrees remain in force, and let him share the lot of those whose error he followed.

**Notes [Cols. 0802B–C].** The same earlier editions and the manuscripts of Collection 12 read *Julian*; see note 81 on Letter 28. Regensburg reads “immutably.” The Grimanicus manuscript, Quesnellus’s copies, and ours read *credidimus* (“we believed”); Regensburg prefers *credimus* (“we believe”) and later omits *presbyter*, perhaps more correctly. Earlier editions read: “we believed it should be established by fitting moderation that, if …”

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

---

# Notice on the Following Letter

1. The words in chapters 1 and 4, “we sent” and “we shall have sent,” by which it seems to be indicated that the legates sent from Rome and the letter to Flavian said to have been given on the Ides of June had already been dispatched, appear to show that the following letter was written after the celebrated letter to Flavian, indeed even after the departure of the legates. They are said to have set out in Letter 38, given on July 23, and also in Letter 36, given on June 20, as we shall show more probably in note 3 on that letter. This, however, has no bearing on the present matter.

In the same Letter 38 the arrival of the deacon Basil is mentioned; after the legates had already departed, he had brought Flavian’s letter to Leo. If this was the same Basil who is said also to have brought Julian’s letter, it would be much clearer that this letter must have been written after the Ides of June, when the legates had not yet departed from Rome. Thus, of the two letters to Julian that seem difficult to believe were written on the same day concerning the same matter, only the preceding letter would have been given on the Ides of June, while the following one would have to be assigned to a later date. But all the manuscripts resist this conclusion, and although several different collections contain the following letter, all nevertheless mark it as given on the Ides of June.

2. To reconcile these matters, Quesnellus observes in note 8 that in some letters which now bear the date of the Ides of June there is no mention of the already announced synod of Ephesus. He conjectured that, after receiving Flavian’s first letters together with the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod, Leo resolved to send four legates to the East to settle the entire matter at Constantinople.

He believes that several letters now read as dated June 13 were first written solely for this purpose. He names only two: Letter 28 to Flavian and Letter 32 to the Constantinopolitan archimandrites, in which there is in fact no mention of a synod, but only of the matter of the faith, to be handled through the legates.

He adds: “But before the legates had departed, Leo received Theodosius’s letter informing him of the synod that had been summoned. Immediately the same legates, who had been assigned to deal with the matter of the faith with Flavian, were sent to the synod; and their departure was delayed so that time might be given for writing new letters or expanding the earlier ones, in which the council is mentioned.” He therefore suggests that, for this reason, both the earlier and the later letters received the same chronological notation, the Ides of June.

3. Yet these considerations cannot satisfy anyone. First, Quesnellus assumes, without any foundation and indeed contrary to the evidence of the documents, that Leo received Flavian’s letters together with the proceedings of the Constantinopolitan synod before Theodosius’s letter concerning the summoned council was delivered.

Leo stated only in Letter 27, given on May 21, that he had received Flavian’s earlier letters together with the Constantinopolitan proceedings against Eutyches, whereas in Letter 31 he testifies that Theodosius’s letter was delivered to him on May 13. Moreover, the celebrated Letter 28 to Flavian is presumed to have been written before May 13, and the legates had already been appointed.

Yet on May 21, the date of Letter 27, Leo says that he was occupied with writing Letter 28 and had not yet thought of entrusting it to the legates. He says: “Concerning this matter we shall write back more fully through the man who brought to us the letter of Your Belovedness.”

Letter 31, moreover, asserts that after receiving Theodosius’s letter only a very short time remained for arranging the departure of the legates: “Since from the third day before the Ides of May,” it says, “when we received his serene Majesty’s letter, the greater part of the remaining time must be taken up so that the departure of priests adequate to the matter may be arranged.”

Second, even if these matters could somehow be reconciled according to Quesnellus’s opinion, another difficulty would still remain: the date of the Ides of June assigned to this letter, if it must be said to have been written after the legates had already departed, as we noted at the beginning.

4. What, then, are we to do? We consider it wrong to abandon the authority of so many ancient and distinguished collections, which consistently give the date as the Ides of June without variation. We therefore believe that Leo gave two letters to the same Julian, bishop of Cos, on the same day: one brief letter to be carried by the legates, and another, longer one, to be carried by the deacon Basil, who was different from the legates and who, after they had departed, brought Flavian’s letter.

The words referring to the past—“we sent” and “we shall have sent”—will cause no difficulty if one considers what we observed in note 17 on Letter 22, where we cited similar examples of Leo’s use of a past-tense expression for a present or immediately future action. Nor is it contrary to Leo’s custom to give two letters on the same day to the same recipients, as is clear from the examples cited in the notice on Letter 17.

5. One point remains to be noted concerning the Greek version of this letter. Since the editions of the Councils sometimes contain punctuation indicating lacunae, we initially suspected that the beginning had been displaced in the copy used by the Roman editors. But when we compared the Greek text with Vatican manuscript 1455, which is of a different origin from the copy used by the Roman editors, and also with two Venetian manuscripts of St. Mark’s Library, numbers 164 and 555, we discovered that they contain neither such points nor any displacement, but that everything is clearly written in a single continuous context. Nevertheless, they do not supply what is absent from the Greek editions.

We therefore infer, not implausibly, that the ancient Greek translator deliberately omitted in the Greek version the passages that are missing. Perhaps Julian, who seems to have translated Leo’s Letter 93 to the Council of Nicaea into Greek—as we shall observe in an unpublished action of the Council of Chalcedon, which we shall publish in an appendix—immediately rendered this letter into Greek when it was sent to him. Since great disturbances were then raging, he may have thought it best deliberately to omit what is absent from the Greek.

Julian had also indicated to Leo that the Greeks allowed themselves some freedom in concealing matters in another letter of Leo to the Council of Chalcedon, as can be gathered from Letter 127, chapter 3. To identify what has been omitted from the Greek version, we shall enclose those passages in the Latin text in brackets.

# Letter XXXV

**Note [Col. 0803B].** Formerly Letter 25. What was previously numbered 35 is now 39. Written on the Ides of June in the year 449.

**Note [Col. 0803B].** This letter is found in manuscript collections 2, 5, 11, 12, 13, and 17 through 24, as well as in the special Vatican manuscript Regina 293. In the table of Collection 5 the title reads, chapter 88: “To Bishop Julian on the condemnation of the Eutychian heresy.”

## To Julian, Bishop of Cos

## Synopsis

I. Eutyches destroys Christian hope and the truth of all the mysteries.  
II. The properties of both natures are preserved in Christ.  
III. Christ’s soul did not preexist his body, nor was his body created from nothing; rather, both possess the same nature as ours.

**Note [Col. 0803].** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Julian, his most beloved brother and bishop.

## Chapter I

Although through our representatives whom we sent from Rome for the cause of the faith we have sent to our brother Flavian a very full letter against the error of excessive impiety, nevertheless, because through our son Basil the deacon we received a letter from Your Belovedness, which greatly pleased us because of its fervor in Catholic understanding, we have added this page, corresponding to that letter, so that you may resist unanimously and steadfastly those who desire to corrupt the Gospel of Christ. For the Holy Spirit’s instruction in us and in you is one, and its teaching is the same. Whoever does not accept it is not a member of Christ’s body and cannot glory in the Head in whom he asserts that his own nature is not present.

But what benefit is there for a most foolish old man in attacking, under the name of the Nestorian heresy, the opinions of those whose most pious faith he cannot overthrow? For just as Nestorius departed from the truth by separating the divinity of the Word from the substance of the man assumed, so this man also departs from the right path when he proclaims that the Only-Begotten Son of God was born from the womb of the blessed Virgin in such a way that he bore the appearance of a human body, but that the reality of human flesh was not united to the Word.

Who would not see what monstrous opinions arise from this prodigy of falsehood? For whoever denies the true man Jesus Christ must necessarily be filled with many impieties; Apollinaris must claim him for himself, or Valentinus appropriate him, or Manichaeus possess him. None of them believed in the reality of human flesh in Christ.

If this reality is not accepted, not only is the one who, while remaining in the form of God, was born as a man in the form of a servant denied according to flesh and rational soul; it is also denied that he was crucified, died, and was buried, that he rose on the third day, and that, seated at the right hand of the Father, he will come to judge the living and the dead in the same body in which he was judged. For these mysteries of our redemption are emptied of their meaning if Christ is not believed to have assumed the true and complete nature of a true human being.

**Note [Col. 0803B].** The Chalcedonian manuscripts read: “Leo to his most beloved brother Julian.” In the otherwise very correct Regensburg manuscript occurs the erroneous superscription: “To Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem.”

**Note [Col. 0803B].** Manuscripts of Collection 21 read “through those of ours for [the cause].” Shortly afterwards, editions of Leo before Quesnellus, together with the Florentine manuscript, read “from Rome.” The phrase *from Rome* is omitted only in the Chigi manuscript of the Chalcedonian collection.

**Note [Col. 0803B–0804B].** The words *for the cause of the faith* are absent from seven manuscripts of Quesnellus listed in the margin and from two of ours, Vatican Collection 11 and Florence Collection 13. Quesnellus, note 8, likewise considers them to be deleted as words which, he says, crept from the Greek version into the Latin text, a version that has far more divergences from the original text. Incorrectly: they occur in thirteen of our manuscripts, including the Vienna manuscript of Collection 5 and the Regensburg manuscript, which do not depend on the Greek; the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection are so far from deriving from the Greek version that they lack some additions found in the Greek text and preserve three clauses absent from it. Thus the Latin text of that collection derives from Leo’s original.

**Note [Col. 0804B].** Most of our manuscripts, like earlier editions, omit *our*, which Quesnellus inserted; but it is present in the Vienna manuscript of Collection 5, the Florentine manuscript of Collection 13, and the Greek version.

**Note [Col. 0804B].** The Greek version, as Quesnellus also observes in note 1, adds: “for the truth of Christ’s humanity.” A little later, in place of “in us and in you,” it has, as Quesnellus observes in note 2, “in the whole Catholic Church.”

**Note [Col. 0804B–C].** Verona 57, Vienna Collection 5, Vatican Collection 11, and Regensburg read “whoever” or “whosoever does not receive”; shortly afterwards the manuscripts of Collection 21 read: “and cannot be a member of Christ’s body, nor glory in the Head.”

**Note [Col. 0805D].** The Greek version, as Quesnellus observes in note 3, adds: “and from the very conception of the Virgin.” Some manuscripts then read *departs* for *falls away*.

**Note [Col. 0805D].** We judged this reading preferable; it is supported by the Regensburg manuscript, four of ours, and four Chalcedonian manuscripts of Baluzius’s collection, and agrees with the Greek version. Quesnellus, with his Thuan, Grimaldian, Corbie, and Victor manuscripts and Surius, reads: “For whoever denies the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ…” Other editions, with the Vienna manuscript of Collection 5, Collections 21 and 24, and Sichard’s copy, read: “For the denier of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, must necessarily…” Vatican Collection 11 reads: “For, once the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, has been denied, it is necessary…” Quesnellus records in the margin *become entangled* for *be fulfilled*.

**Note [Col. 0805D].** Editions before Quesnellus add “from the dead”; manuscripts, including Quesnellus’s and Baluzius’s, and the Greek version omit it.

**Note [Col. 0805D–0806D].** Regensburg reads *sits* and then “and to judge.” Editions before Quesnellus add “unto death”; the manuscripts and Greek translation do not know it.

## Chapter II

Because the divine signs were manifest, are the bodily evidences to be called false? Shall the testimonies of both natures be valid so that the Creator may be understood, but not valid so that the creature may be saved? The flesh does not diminish what belongs to divinity; divinity does not destroy what belongs to flesh.

The same one is eternal from the Father and temporal from his mother; inviolable in his own power and capable of suffering in our weakness; in the divinity of the Trinity, of one and the same nature with the Father and the Holy Spirit; but in the assumption of humanity, not of one substance, but of one and the same person:

[so that the same one might be rich in poverty, omnipotent in abasement, incapable of suffering in punishment, and immortal in death.]

For the Word was not changed into flesh, nor into soul, in any part of himself. The simple and unchangeable nature of divinity always remains wholly in its own essence, receiving neither loss nor increase. Thus it blesses the nature it assumed, so that the assumed nature remains glorified in the one who glorifies it.

[Why, then, should it seem incongruous or impossible that the Word, flesh, and soul should be one Jesus Christ, and that he should be one Son of God and of man, when flesh and soul, though of dissimilar natures, form one person even without the incarnation of the Word? It is much easier for divine power to establish this unity of itself with humanity than for the weakness of humanity alone to maintain it within its substances.]

Therefore neither was the Word changed into flesh, nor flesh into the Word; rather, both remain in one, and one is in both—not divided by difference, not confused by mixture. Nor is one from the Father and another from the mother; rather, the same one is from the Father in one way before all beginning, and from his mother in another way at the end of the ages.

Thus he might be “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), in whom “the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). For it belongs to the advancement of the one assumed, not of the one who assumes, that God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:9–11).

**Note [Col. 0807D].** The Regensburg manuscript deletes *its own*.

**Note [Col. 0807D].** The same manuscript deletes *all*.

**Note [Col. 0807D].** Two manuscripts omit the name *Christ*.

## Chapter III

[The supplied source ends here.]

[In the matter, however, that Eutyches dared to say in the episcopal hearing that before the incarnation there had been two natures in Christ, but after the incarnation one, it was necessary that he be pressed by the judges’ repeated and careful questions to give an account of his confession, lest something empty should pass away as though insignificant—something that appeared to have been poured out only from a draught of poisoned doctrines. [Note: [Col. 0807D] Thus all our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnel; Quesnel has *affusum*, and in the margin of his edition *effusum*.] For I think that one who speaks in this way is persuaded that the soul which the Savior assumed had previously dwelt in heaven before being born from the Virgin Mary, and that the Word joined it to himself in the womb. [Note: [Col. 0807D] Ratisbon, together with collected manuscripts 21 and the earlier printed editions of Leo before Quesnel, reads *copularit*.] But Catholic minds and ears do not tolerate this, because the Lord, coming from heaven, brought with him nothing belonging to our condition: he assumed neither a soul that had previously existed nor flesh that was not from a mother’s body. For our nature was not assumed in such a way that, having been created earlier, it was assumed later; rather, it was created by the very act of assumption. [Note: [Col. 0807D] Quesnel in the margin: alternatively, *creata sumeretur* (“having been created, it was assumed”).] Hence what was rightly condemned in Origen—who asserted that souls, before being inserted into bodies, had not only life but also various activities—must also be punished in this man, unless he prefers to renounce his opinion. [Note: [Col. 0807D] Verona 57 reads *in corporibus*. Immediately afterward, instead of *insererentur*, Quesnel notes in the margin *misceantur*. Then the printed editions and certain manuscripts read *non solum vitas*. Quesnel’s emendation is approved by our Vindobonese collected manuscript 5 and all the Chalcedonian collections.]

For the Lord’s birth according to the flesh, [Col. 0809A] although it has certain features of its own by which it surpasses the beginnings of human existence—whether because he alone was conceived and born from an inviolate Virgin without the desire of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0809B] All the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection and the Greek version, as well as Sichardus with collected manuscript 24 and the editions before Quesnel, add *ex Spiritu sancto* (“from the Holy Spirit”). The remaining manuscripts of ours and the nine cited by Quesnel in note 5 do not contain these words. Immediately afterward, *sine concupiscentia carnis* (“without desire of the flesh”) occurs in collected manuscripts 11 and 21 and in the editions before Quesnel; he more correctly deleted the word *carnis* in the other manuscripts of ours and in Baluze’s manuscripts on the authority of his own codices.] or because he was brought forth from his mother’s womb in such a way that fertility gave birth while virginity remained—yet his flesh was not of another nature than ours. [Note: [Col. 0809B] Thus from Ratisbon, three manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, and Vatican collected manuscript 11. Elsewhere: *nostra* (“ours”).] Nor was a soul breathed into him by another origin than that given to other human beings, a soul that excelled not by difference of kind but by the sublimity of its virtue. For he had nothing in his flesh opposed to him, [Note: [Col. 0809B] One of our manuscripts, together with the printed editions of the councils, reads: “nor did the conflict of wills produce discord among desires.” [Col. 0809C] The Ratisbon manuscript reads: “Nor did discord among desires produce conflict among wills”; either *discordia* was wrongly written for *discordiam*, or *compugnantia* for *compugnantiam*.] and discord among desires did not produce conflict among wills.

His bodily senses were vigorous [Note: [Col. 0809C] The Corbie manuscript of Quesnel reads *sine sorde peccati* (“without the stain of sin”).] without the law of sin, and the truth of his affections was under the governance of deity and mind; he was neither tested by enticements nor overcome by injuries. True man was truly united to God; he was not brought down from heaven according to a soul that had previously existed, [Note: [Col. 0809C] The Ratisbon manuscript reads *ex alto* (“from on high”). Certain manuscripts read *deductus e coelo*, omitting *est*.] nor, according to the flesh, created from nothing; [Note: [Col. 0809C] The Greek version, as Quesnel observes in note 7, reads: “But possessing the same person in divinity and humanity.”] rather, he bore the same person in the deity of the Word and possessed, in body and soul, the nature common to us. For he would not be the mediator of God and human beings (1 Tim. II, 5) unless the same one were both God and man, and in both were one and true. [Note: [Col. 0809C] The Ratisbon manuscript reads: “For he stirs us up.” The Chigi manuscript of the Chalcedonian collection: “But indeed he stirs us up.” The Greek version adds: “Most honorable brother.”]

The greatness of the subject does indeed urge us toward a broader exposition; but before your learning there is no need for a lengthy treatment. [Note: [Col. 0809C] This reading of the Florentine manuscript seemed better than that of the others and the printed editions: *copia laborandum* (“one must labor with abundance”).] Especially since we have already sent, through our men, sufficient letters to our brother Flavian, to strengthen the minds not only of priests but also of laypeople. The mercy of God, as we believe, will ensure that, without harm to anyone’s soul, what is sound may be defended against the devil’s snares and what has been wounded may be healed. [Note: [Col. 0809C] The Greek version adds: “May God preserve you unharmed, most honorable brother.”]

Given on the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

## 876. To the beloved brother Julian, Leo the bishop.

[Col. 0804A]

Although through our men whom we sent from the city concerning the matter of the faith we have dispatched most complete letters to our brother Flavian against the great error of impiety, nevertheless, since through our son Basil we received the letters of your affection—which greatly pleased us, as they were fervent with zeal for Catholic conviction—we have now added this letter also, which does not differ from those letters. Thus we exhort you to oppose these men unanimously and firmly on behalf of the truth of Christ’s becoming human, men who desire to corrupt the Lord’s Gospel. [Note: [Col. 0804C] In the margin of the Roman edition: perhaps *ἀντιτεῖναι* (“to oppose”).] For the Holy Spirit’s instruction is one throughout the whole Catholic Church, and its teaching is the same. Whoever does not accept it is not a member of Christ’s body, nor can he glory in that head in whom he asserts that his own nature is not contained. [Col. 0806A]

What benefit is there for that ignorant old man in attacking, under the name of the Nestorian heresy, the doctrine of those whose most devout faith he is unable to destroy? When Nestorius departed so far from the truth by separating the Word’s deity from the substance of the man who had been assumed, and from the very conception of the Virgin, how far does this man then run wild from the straight path? He thinks that the Only-Begotten of God was born from the womb of the blessed Virgin in such a way that he had the appearance of a human body but had not assumed the reality of human flesh. [Note: [Col. 0806D] In the margin of the Roman edition: *ἀφ᾽ οὗ* (“from whom”).] [Note: [Col. 0806D] We have restored this passage in accordance with the Latin text, “by separating it from the substance of the assumed man,” with the help of the Venetian and Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read: “separating it from the assumed man.”]

Who could fail to see what monstrous absurdities of blasphemies arise from this falsehood? For one who denies the true man of the Lord Jesus Christ is necessarily filled with countless mockeries of the devil. Apollinaris regards this man as his own; Valentinus claims him for himself; Manichaeus holds him. None of them believed that the truth of human flesh was present in our Savior. If that flesh was not truly assumed, he falls not only into a denial of the fact that the one who, remaining in the form of God, was born as a human being in the form of a servant according to flesh and rational soul, but also into a denial that he was crucified, died, and was buried, and rose again on the third day. [Note: [Col. 0806D] In the margin of the Roman edition: perhaps *τοῦ* (“of the”).] [Note: [Col. 0806D] The Venetian manuscript reads: “God was in the form of God.”] Nor does he confess that, seated at the right hand of the Father, he will come in this body to judge the living and the dead—in the very body in which he had been condemned. [Note: [Col. 0806D] The Venetian manuscript lacks *καθεζόμενος* (“seated”).]

For all these mysteries of our redemption are rendered void if the true Son of God is not believed to have assumed the whole nature of the true man. [Note: [Col. 0806D] In the margin of the Roman edition: “or.”] [Note: [Col. 0806D] The Venetian manuscript corruptly reads: “He had assumed my nature of the true man.” The Vatican manuscript likewise has *ἐμήν* (“my”).] And since the divine signs truly occurred, the things demonstrated through the body are said to be false, so that the Savior may be understood to possess the testimonies of both natures, but not to possess those from which our race is destined to be saved. [Note: [Col. 0806D] The Roman edition notes in the margin: “so that he may be understood as an artificer, not to possess”—it should read: “to possess”—“the fabrication from which it is destined to be saved.” In the Venetian and Vatican manuscripts the final words appear, very corruptly, as: “from which even the mother, who is to become [something], may be saved.”]

What belongs to deity the flesh did not diminish; what belongs to flesh the deity did not corrupt. For he is the same one, both eternal from the Father and, in time, from his mother; in respect of his own power, imperishable, but in respect of our weakness, subject to suffering; in the Trinity, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, of one and the same divine nature; but in the mystery of the man who was assumed, not of one substance but of one person, and the same person. [Note: [Col. 0806D] The Venetian manuscript reads: “But he is one.”] [Col. 0808A] [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Venetian and Vatican manuscripts read: “of the man, one person.”]

For the Word was not changed, in any part of himself, into a body or into a soul, since the nature of deity is simple and unchangeable, always wholly existing in its own substance, accepting neither diminution nor addition. And likewise, in such a way did he perfect the blessed nature that had been assumed, so that the nature glorified might remain in the one who glorified it. [Note: [Col. 0808D] This should apparently be read thus from the Vatican manuscript. The Venetian manuscript also seems to support it, reading *ἀποτελέσασαν*. The printed editions wrongly have *ἀποτελέσας*.]

Therefore the Word was not changed into a body, as we have said, nor was the body changed into the Word; rather, each remains in the one, and the one is in both. [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Venetian manuscript reads *ἐν ἀμφοτέραις* (“in both”), and the Roman edition notes the same reading in the margin.] He was not divided by distinction nor confused by mixture. Thus one was from the Father and another from the mother—but rather the same one was from the Father in one way, before every beginning, and from the mother in another way, at the end of days. [Col. 0808A] He became the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, in whom the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily. [Col. 0808B] For the advancement belongs to the one who was assumed, not to the one who assumed him. As the Apostle says: “God highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.”

Therefore the Lord’s birth according to the flesh, although it has certain particular features by which it surpasses the beginnings of the human passage into life—whether because he alone was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit, from an incorrupt virgin, without desire, or because he was brought forth from his mother’s womb in such a way that fertility gave birth and virginity remained—nevertheless, his flesh was not of a different nature from ours. Nor was a soul breathed into him according to another origin than that given to other human beings, a soul that excelled not by difference of kind but by the superiority of its powers.

For he had nothing opposed to him from the desire of the flesh. His bodily senses were vigorous without any law of sin, and the truth of his movements was under the helm of deity and understanding; he was neither affected by enticements nor yielded to sufferings.

Thus true God was born a man. [Note: [Col. 0808D] In the margin of the Roman edition: “the true God, true man,” from the Latin.] He was neither brought down from heaven according to a pre-existing soul, [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Venetian and Vatican manuscripts read *καταχθείς* (“having been brought down”).] nor, according to the flesh, assumed or born from some element or from nothing. Rather, he possessed the same person in deity and humanity and maintained our common nature in body and soul. [Note: [Col. 0808D] The Venetian and Vatican manuscripts read very badly: “having the same thing as us.”]

For he would not have been the mediator of God and human beings unless the same one were both God and man, and in the same person were one and true. [Note: [Col. 0808D] The printed editions omit *ἄν* (“would”); it must nevertheless be supplied from the Vatican manuscript so that the force of the verb may be expressed as it is in the Latin text.] [Note: [Col. 0808D] *καί* (“and”) is absent, but wrongly, from the Venetian manuscript.]

The greatness of the subject moves us, most honorable brother, toward a fuller discussion; but for your affection there is no need to labor at greater length, especially since, as has been said, we have already sent sufficient letters through our men to our brother Flavian, so that not only the thoughts of the priests but also those of the laypeople might be more firmly strengthened. [Note: [Col. 0810D] *ἡμετέρων* (“our men”) is absent, but wrongly, from the Venetian manuscript.] May the mercy of God, as we believe, grant that, without any soul suffering harm, what is sound may be preserved against the devil’s arrows and what has been wounded may be healed. [Note: [Col. 0810D] The Venetian manuscript has *ἀλλὰ γὰρ καὶ τούς* (“but also those”), which is the reading noted there.]

May God preserve you in health, most honorable brother. [Note: [Col. 0810D] Thus from the Vatican manuscript, more coherently. The printed editions read *φυλάξει* (“will preserve”).]

## 885. Letter XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0809C] Alternatively 32. What was formerly 36 is now 40. Written on 20 June 449.]  
[Note: [Col. 0809D] This letter was published by Merlin from manuscripts of collection 12. Quesnel found the same letter in the Grimani manuscript of collection 18. We were able to collate only the manuscripts of collection 12. In this letter Leo replies to Flavian’s letter 26.]

### To Flavian, bishop of Constantinople

#### Synopsis

He states that he has received the letter and the acts of the synod against Eutyches.

To Flavian, his most beloved brother, Leo the pope.

I have received the letter of your affection together with the acts drawn up among you [Col. 0810B] concerning the question of the faith. And because the most merciful emperor, concerned for the peace of the Church, wished a synod to be convened, although it is clearly evident that the matter at issue in no way requires synodal deliberation, nevertheless, most beloved brother, I signify that those whom it pleased him to appoint for this matter have followed. [Note: [Col. 0810B] Thus the earlier editions with our manuscripts of collection 12, the Vatican, and the Venetian. Quesnel thought that *subsecuturos* (“will follow”) should be emended from the Grimani manuscript, since he judged that the legates had not yet departed, as he inferred from the future tense *portabunt* (“they will carry”) in this letter and from letter 38, dated 23 July, where the legates are said to have departed. He indicated this briefly in a marginal note: “But it is clear from this letter, and from 34, now 38, that the legates had not yet departed.” Yet these points prove nothing. *Portabunt* could be said of legates who had already departed but had not yet reached Constantinople. The legates are said to have departed in letter 38 when Basil brought Flavian’s letters; this is true even if they are thought to have left before 20 July. This seems sufficiently probable both from the date of the Ides of June, on which the preceding letters transmitted by the legates appear to have been signed shortly before their departure, and from the first of August, the date fixed for the Ephesian council, which scarcely allowed the legates to remain longer in the city. These considerations seem sufficient to prefer *subsecutos*. Hence letter 39 frequently says that letters were written to Flavian on suitable occasions, indicating clearly that letter 38 was sent through the legates then transmitted, while this letter and letter 38 were sent on other occasions after the legates’ departure. If Flavian’s letters received by Leo together with the Constantinopolitan acts against Eutyches—the letters mentioned here and undoubtedly the second of Flavian’s letters, since Leo had received the first before 27 May in letter 27—are, as Quesnel assumed, the same as the writing of Flavian to Leo mentioned in letter 38 (see note 2 on letter 38), and if Leo received these writings through Basil after the legates had departed, then the reading *subsecutos* is demonstrated even more clearly. Quesnel could not consistently insert *subsecuturos* into the hypothesis he proposed. On this matter, however, compare what we shall observe in the cited note 2 below. [Col. 0812C] Quesnel called this writing in a marginal note Flavian’s second letter to Leo; he repeats this in Dissertation 1 on the year 449, no. 3. Thus letter 26 would be indicated, which we proved in the notice on letter 22 to have been sent a second time by Flavian together with the Constantinopolitan acts against Eutyches. But we do not see how Leo could here have said of letter 26—or, if one prefers, of letter 22, which Quesnel considered the second—that Flavian had included little about the matter, nor how letter 39, concerning Basil the deacon who brought these letters, could say: “We sent Basil back to you, as you had wished.” This indicates that something had been inserted in those same letters about sending Basil back quickly, although there is no mention of him either in letter 26 or in letter 22. He would also seem to have been sent back much later if Flavian’s second letter, together with the Constantinopolitan acts, had been delivered through him before 20 June, as letter 27 indicates; he would then have been sent back only shortly before 23 July. We therefore think it more probable that the third letter of Flavian, which is missing, and which Basil brought in July, is indicated here.]

Nor was it now necessary to write anything more, since, with God’s favor, you will be more fully instructed about what we believe belongs to the case through the documents that they themselves will bring.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

## 886. Letter XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0811C] Alternatively 33. What was formerly 37 is now 43. Written on 20 June 449.]  
[Note: [Col. 0811C] This letter survives in the manuscripts of collections 12, 18, and 19. We believe that Leo is replying here to the same imperial summons to the Ephesian synod to which he had earlier replied through the legates in letter 29. It is incredible that Theodosius sent Leo two summonses, each receiving a separate reply. In the confusion of affairs and the pressure of the time appointed for the synod, the Holy Pontiff perhaps feared that the legates, hurrying to Ephesus rather than Constantinople, would deliver the earlier letter to Theodosius first; he therefore decided to write this new letter to the same emperor at Constantinople on another occasion.]

### To Theodosius Augustus

#### Synopsis

The unity of faith and confession must be preserved. Legates have been sent to the Ephesian synod, but necessity does not permit him to go there himself.

Leo to Theodosius Augustus.

After receiving the letters of Your Clemency, I perceived that the universal Church had much cause for rejoicing: you wish the Christian faith—which honors and worships the divine Trinity—to be in no respect different and in no respect discordant. [Note: [Col. 0811D] Thus the Ratisbon collection 19 with the Grimani and Herovall manuscripts of Quesnel. Other editions, with the Venetian manuscript of collection 12, read: “the deity is honored,” and later: “he wishes it to be in nothing.”]

For what could more effectively support human affairs in seeking God’s mercy than for one thanksgiving and the sacrifice of one confession to be offered to his majesty by all? [Note: [Col. 0811D] Thus from our manuscripts of collections 12 and 19, with the editions before Quesnel, which has *in qua* (“in which”).] The full devotion of priests and all the faithful will be present in this matter only if, concerning what was accomplished for our redemption through the one Son of God, the Word, nothing other is thought than what he himself commanded to be proclaimed and believed concerning himself. [Note: [Col. 0811D] This reading of Quesnel is approved by the Venetian manuscript of collection 12. Ratisbon omits the first *et*. Other editions read: “he himself commanded to be proclaimed concerning himself.”]

Therefore, although no consideration permits me to arrive on the day that Your Piety has appointed for the episcopal council, [Note: [Col. 0811D] We have preferred the reading of the Ratisbon manuscript. Elsewhere: “on the day of the episcopal council which your piety…”] since no precedent has come before from this side, and temporal necessity does not allow me to abandon the city—especially since the case of the faith is so clear that it would have been more reasonable to refrain from convening a synod—[Note: [Col. 0812B] Thus our manuscripts with two of Quesnel’s. Other printed editions read *rationabilibus causis* (“for reasonable reasons”).
