Later, Ratisbon reads *abstentum* for *abstinendum*.] nevertheless, insofar as the Lord deigns to help, I have contributed my efforts so that Your Clemency’s decrees might be obeyed to some extent. I have appointed my brothers here, who are sufficient to cut off scandals in accordance with the nature of the case and who may fulfill the role of my presence, because no question has arisen concerning which one either could or should doubt. [Note: [Col. 0812C] Thus our manuscripts with the Grimani manuscript; others read *unde* (“from which”) instead of *de qua* (“about which”). Ratisbon omits the first *aut*.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes. [Note: [Col. 0812C] This is better from the Grimani manuscript. Quesnel emended the reading to this date, whereas the editions from manuscripts of collection 12 read *XV kal.*; by a scribal slip, the two units could easily have become V. The following letter to Theodosius was likewise dated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, and Leo seems to have sent this letter to Flavian immediately on that occasion.]

## Letter XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 0812C] 34. What was formerly 38 is now 42. Written on 23 July 449.]  
[Note: [Col. 0812C] This letter is contained in the manuscripts of collection 12 and in the Ratisbon manuscript of collection 19.]

### To Flavian, bishop of Constantinople

#### Synopsis

He informs him that he has received his letters; praises him for defending the faith; and urges mercy if the heretic repents.

Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

Our men, whom we sent to you concerning the matter of the faith, having already departed, we received through our son Basil the deacon the writings of your affection. [Note: [Col. 0812C] Quesnel called these writings in a marginal note Flavian’s second letter to Leo; he repeats this in Dissertation 1 on the year 449, no. 3. See the extensive note above under letter XXXVI.]

In them you had rightly included little concerning the matter of our common concern, [Note: [Col. 0812D] The manuscripts of collection 12 and the editions before Quesnel read *indidisses* (“you had included”); the margin has *indidisti* (“you included”), as in our Ratisbon manuscript.] since the acts previously delivered [Note: [Col. 0812D] The acts indicated are those first delivered before Basil’s arrival with letter 22 and then with letter 26.] had sufficiently instructed us about everything, and the aforesaid spokesman, suitable for a private conversation, was available. Through him we now return our greetings and, trusting in the grace of our God, [Note: [Col. 0812D] Thus from our Ratisbon and collection-12 manuscripts and the editions before Quesnel; Quesnel reads *in quo* (“in which”).] exhort your affection, using the Apostle’s words: “In no respect be terrified by your adversaries; this is for them a cause of destruction, but for you of salvation” (Phil. I, 28). [Col. 0812D]

For what is more destructive than, by denying the reality of Christ’s incarnation, to wish to dissolve every hope of human salvation and to oppose the Apostle, who plainly says: “Great is the mystery of piety, which was manifested in the flesh” (1 Tim. III, 16)? [Note: [Col. 0813C] Ratisbon reads: “And what is so…” Immediately afterward, the cited manuscripts of collection 12 lack the words *nativitatis et* (“of the birth and”).]

What is more glorious than to fight for the evangelical faith against the enemies of Christ’s birth and cross? Concerning the most pure light and unconquered power of this matter, we have already made known in letters sent to your affection what was in our heart, so that there might appear to be no ambiguity between us concerning what we have learned and teach according to Catholic doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0813C] Thus the Ratisbon manuscript. Elsewhere: *de illis* (“about those matters”). Later, in the same manuscript, *videri posset* (“might appear”).]

Since the testimonies of the truth are so clear and so powerful that anyone who does not immediately shake himself free from the darkness of falsehood at the flashing forth of light and reason must be considered exceedingly blind and hardened, we also wish you to apply the medicine of patience to the madness of the uninstructed. Thus, through fatherly rebukes, those who in the old age of their flesh are children in mind may learn to obey their elders. If they lay aside the vanity of their ignorance, repent, condemn every error, and embrace the true and singular faith, episcopal mercy and benevolence must not be denied them. [Note: [Col. 0813C] Thus our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnel, who preferred *misericordiae* (“of mercy”) to *benevolentia* (“benevolence”).] The judgment that has already been passed must, however, remain in force if impiety, rightly condemned, persists in its perversity.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

## 889. Letter XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 0813C] Alternatively 35. What was formerly 39 is now 43. Written on 11 August 449.]  
[Note: [Col. 0813C] We found this letter only in the manuscripts of collection 12, of which we collated Vatican 1340 and Venetian 169.]

### To the same Flavian, bishop of Constantinople

#### Synopsis

He complains about Flavian’s silence; at that time Leo did not yet know the reason for the Ephesian plunder.

Leo the bishop to Flavian the bishop.

Your silence increases our anxiety, since for a long time we have received no writing from your affection, although, sharing your cares and concerned for the defense of the faith, we have frequently sent letters to your affection on suitable occasions, so that we might assist you with the consolation of our exhortations and so that you would not yield to the goading of your adversaries in defending the faith, knowing that we share your labor.

We believe that our men reached your fraternity long ago; through them you retain fuller instruction from our written commands, and we sent Basil back to you, as you had wished. Now, lest you think that we had omitted any suitable opportunity, we have given this letter through our son, a man honorable and dear to us, Eupsychius. [Note: [Col. 0813C] The editions before Quesnel, with Merlin, read *Exitium*. Our manuscripts read *Esychium*. Quesnel, perhaps from another manuscript, possibly the Grimani, reads *Eupsychium*.] We ask that you reply to our writings with all speed, and that thereafter you make us informed about your actions and about those of our men, and about the resolution of the entire case. [Note: [Col. 0813D] The editions before Quesnel, with our manuscripts, read *actibus* (“actions”). Concerning the words “make us informed about the resolution of the entire case,” Quesnel added this marginal note: “The resolution of cases belongs to councils. This is not Leo’s meaning. Did the council at Ephesus, to which Leo is referring here, resolve the entire case, or rather entangle it through Eutyches’ acquittal and the condemnation of Saint Flavian—or rather overthrow it, when it ought to have been resolved if Leo’s letters had not been concealed but read and carried out by the Fathers, as happened in the earlier Council of Ephesus, where the Fathers followed Celestine’s judgment in the case of Nestorius? Anyone familiar with what happened in both places will easily understand.”] Thus we may lighten the anxiety that we now bear for the defense of the faith with more favorable reports. [Note: [Col. 0814C] Quesnel reads *nuntiatis* (“with reports having been announced”). We have restored the reading of our manuscripts, which seems more consistent with Leo’s style.]

Given on the third day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

## 890. Letter XL

[Note: [Col. 0814C] Alternatively 36. What was formerly 40 is now 44. Written on 22 August 449.]  
[Note: [Col. 0814C] It survives in a single Arles collection, 15. Baronius first published it from an ancient manuscript of the Church of Arles; we also usefully reread a copy transmitted from Gaul and contained in the Vallicellian manuscript G, 99. We shall also use Sirmond’s edition, who examined other copies of this collection in Gaul.]

### To the bishops established throughout the province of Gaul through Arles

#### Synopsis

He rejoices in Ravennius’s good and peaceful election and desires that Ravennius justify the favorable opinion formed about him.

To the most beloved brothers Constantine, Audentius, Rusticus, Auspicius, Nicetas, Nectarius, Florus, Asclepius, Justus, Augustalis, Ynantius, and Chrysaphius, Leo the pope.

[Note: [Col. 0814C] Quesnel reads *Ynantius* with Sirmond. Other printed editions, with Baronius and the Vallicellian manuscript, read *Hymnatius*; yet that manuscript has *Unantius* in another letter, 65, with V easily changed into Y. In the Arles council under Ravennius, published by Sirmond from a manuscript of the Church of Lyons in volume V of the Councils, page 23 of the Venetian edition, the name is written *Ynantius*.]

[Note: [Col. 0814D] Quesnel notes in the margin: alternatively *Chrisatio*, although he had seen no manuscript other than the Arles manuscript mentioned in note 1, which reads *Chrysaphio*. He could have gathered this variant from the previously cited Arles synod, where the name is nevertheless *Chrysantius*, as also in the Council of Carthage in 525, in which a document of that same Arles synod was inserted. Whether the same man is meant here or another who is named in Leo’s letter cannot be determined without examining other manuscripts. Certainly, in letters 99 and 102, *Chrisaphius* is counted among the Gallic bishops.]

We have just and reasonable cause for rejoicing when we learn from the Lord’s priests of actions that accord both with the rules of the ancestral canons and with apostolic institutions. For the whole body of the Church must grow with healthy increase if its ruling members excel both in the strength of authority and in the tranquility of moderation.

Therefore, because, after the death of Hilary of holy memory, you unanimously consecrated our brother Ravennius—a man also approved by us—in accordance with the wishes of the clergy, the distinguished citizens, and the people of Arles, we confirm by our judgment this good work of your fraternity. [Note: [Col. 0815C] The Vallicellian manuscript reads *Qui* (“who”); if this reading were accepted, different punctuation would be required.]

For we believe that an election peaceful and harmonious, lacking neither merit of character nor civic support, was indeed a human petition but a divine inspiration. Therefore, most beloved brothers, let the aforesaid bishop make use of God’s gift, and, in accordance with the united wishes of all the orders, let him understand what devotion is expected from him: that, as a diligent and temperate administrator of the charge entrusted to him, he may be no less worthy according to your testimony and in every respect more deserving of our favor.

May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved brothers.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Asturius and Protogenes. [Note: [Col. 0815C] Quesnel, with Rainaud, wrote *II kal.* (“the second day before the Kalends”) instead of *XI kal.* (“the eleventh day before the Kalends”), apparently taking the Roman numeral II for the Arabic number 11. In the margin he noted 22 August, which corresponds to the eleventh day before the Kalends of September. The date would wrongly be the second day before the Kalends, since letter 42, dated the seventh day before the Kalends of the same month, is later than this letter. Sirmond also dated this letter to the seventh day before the Kalends of September. We have followed the Vallicellian manuscript.]

## Letter XLI

[Note: [Col. 0815C] Alternatively 37. What was formerly 41 is now 45. Written at approximately the same time as the preceding letter.]  
[Note: [Col. 0815D] It is found in the manuscripts of collections 12 and 24 and in Vatican 541.]

### To Ravennius, bishop of Arles

#### Synopsis

He congratulates Ravennius, elected bishop; commends episcopal virtues; and urges him to write to Leo more frequently.

[Note: [Col. 0815D] Quesnel, with the printed editions of Leo and certain manuscripts, reads *Domino fratri* (“to the lord brother”). We have corrected the unusual title from Vatican 541; the editions of the councils after Sirmond and the inscription of the following letter support this correction. Quesnel’s marginal note “Observe *Domino*” should therefore be removed.]

To the most beloved brother Ravennius, Leo.

Know that the advancement of your affection, which has attained the dignity of the highest priesthood, pleases us so greatly that we rejoice not only with you over the increase of your honor but also with the Church of Arles, over which the Lord has placed you. For it redounds to the honor and benefit of all the faithful when such a bishop is appointed, one by whose protection many are helped and by whose example they are encouraged.

Since you are not unaware of what we have perceived concerning the sincerity of your mind according to our prior knowledge, you rightly understand that we require you to prove what we presume about you, most beloved brother. [Note: [Col. 0815D] Thus it should be read with the Thuane manuscript, not *praesentem* (“present”), as the printed editions and most manuscripts have. Quesnel correctly established this in note 1, and Sirmond’s reading supports it.] [Note: [Col. 0815D] The printed editions of Leo read *agnoscitis* (“you recognize”), which does not agree with the preceding *non ignoras* (“you are not unaware”). We have corrected it from our two manuscripts, Vatican 541 and Venetian 169. Sirmond also supports this reading.]

Let authority therefore not be lacking in your modesty; let gentleness commend your firmness; let leniency temper your justice; let patience restrain your freedom; and, with pride avoided—for pride is close to falling—let humility be loved, since it is always destined to grow. Your affection is not ignorant of ecclesiastical laws, so that you may contain all the rights of your power within their rules and measures.

The law is said not to have been established for the just (1 Tim. I, 9) because he fulfills the standard of the command by the judgment of his will, when true love of what is right does not possess within itself both apostolic authorities and canonical decrees. [Note: [Col. 0816C] Thus with Quesnel and Sirmond, our manuscripts of collection 24 and Vatican 541. Other manuscripts and printed editions read: “But it is said for the just.”] [Note: [Col. 0816C] The editions before Quesnel read *in semetipso habeat* (“has within himself”). Quesnel, with two manuscripts and Hincmar, supported by three of our manuscripts, printed *in semetipso habet* (“has within himself”), but admitted in note 3 that this reading also lacks the true sense. For although, as he says, true love of what is right subjects the human mind to God’s law and inspires obedience even to human precepts, it can never, by itself, impart knowledge of apostolic authorities or canonical decrees, which are positive laws, as they say. The difficulty is removed by adding the negative particle *non* (“does not”), supplied by Vatican 1348 of collection 12.]

As a devoted follower and diligent executor of these, you will undoubtedly rejoice in the company of those who deserved to hear, concerning the profits of the talents entrusted to them: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. XXV, 23; Luke XIX, 17).

So that you may have no doubt about the confidence of our affection for you, let us more frequently know about the progress of your actions, since, mindful of our judgment, we wish always to glory in your progress in the Lord.

May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved brother. [Note: [Col. 0816D] Although this letter lacks a chronological note, it was written at approximately the same time as the preceding letter, as Quesnel properly demonstrated in note 4.]

## Letter XLII

[Note: [Col. 0816D] Alternatively 38. What was formerly 42 is now 49. Written on 26 August 449.]  
[Note: [Col. 0816D] Baronius also published this letter from the aforementioned Arles manuscript, a copy of which we have seen in the Vallicellian manuscript G, 99.]

### To the same Ravennius, bishop of Arles

#### Synopsis

He warns him about a wandering man named Petronianus who falsely claims to be Leo’s deacon, and asks that he be expelled from communion with all the churches.

To the most beloved brother Ravennius, Leo the pope.

[Col. 0816C] We want you to be watchful and attentive, lest presumption—which deserves punishment—claim some pretext for itself; for when it has found an entrance through false deception, it extends itself to still greater boldness under the name of an assumed dignity. We have learned from the report of certain of your clergy [Col. 0816D]—that is, those who had brought to Leo the letters of Ravennius and his provincial bishops concerning Ravennius’s promotion—that a certain Petronianus, a vagrant and perpetually wandering man, has boasted throughout Gaul that he is our deacon and, under cover of this honor, has gone about the various churches of that province. We wish your Love, dearest brother, to oppose such utterly wicked audacity in this way: after also warning all the bishops of the province, expel him, once his falsehood has been exposed, from communion with all the Churches, so that he may not usurp this position any further. May the Lord keep you safe, dearest brother. Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

[Col. 0817]

1. The two following letters, 43 and 44, concerning the same matter and, as the heading states, written on the same day to the same emperor Theodosius, present almost the same things—if one considers the Latin text—not merely in their ideas but also, for the most part, in their wording. This has aroused suspicion that one may have been interpolated. Moreover, Letter 43 plainly suffers from two serious defects. First, it contains a definite error contrary to historical fact in these words of chapter 1: “This has become known to us . . . from the most reverend bishops themselves who were sent by us.” For only Julius, bishop of Puteoli, was sent as legate to the synod; and, in addition, one deacon, Hilary, who fled from the false synod of Ephesus, is said to have reported the proceedings personally to the pontiff. No mention of Julius is ever made in Letters 44 and 45. Then, in the same chapter 1, an obvious lacuna is revealed. Since the words “according to the will of the aforesaid priest” refer to Dioscorus, they imply that Dioscorus had already been mentioned, as he is mentioned earlier in Letter 44; yet no such mention appears in Letter 43. Therefore this letter has seemed to some, among them Tillemont in note 31 on Leo’s life, to be rejectable as spurious.

2. We, however, are prevented from suspecting that this letter was interpolated or false by the authority of the Greek Chalcedonian collection, in which this letter is copied no less than Letter 44. For although the Latin Chalcedonian collection is sufficient to vindicate the letter—the collection was compiled before the middle of the sixth century and contains it—the Greek collection should remove every suspicion much more clearly, since it was assembled while Leo himself was still alive, between the years 453 and 455, as we demonstrated in the preface to the letters, no. 34. At that time, therefore, a Latin autograph of this letter existed among the Greeks, from which the Greek translation was made. No greater or more ancient testimony to its authenticity can be desired. Nothing now appearing in the letter—neither the lacuna nor the error—can be called into question on that account. Otherwise, other documents that have come down to us with errors or lacunae, even if otherwise wholly certain, could likewise be rejected or viewed with suspicion.

3. Since such authority establishes that Letter 43 is not spurious, we may nevertheless conjecture, though not with equal certainty, something concerning the matters that cause difficulty. First it must be stated that it has hitherto been presumed that Letter 43, as it was published in Latin from the Latin Chalcedonian collection, was itself the original Latin text of Saint Leo, which the ancient collector had found and inserted into his collection, as happened with most of Leo’s other letters, and especially with Letter 44, whose Latin original was likewise found by him and inserted into the Latin collection. This may seem to be confirmed by the chronological note attached to the Latin letter. Since that note would, according to the custom of the Greek translator, have been omitted in the Greek version, it appears to derive from a discovered Latin original.

We have, however, plainly shown that this presumption is false: the Latin text we possess of Letter 43 is neither the original nor a copy of the original Latin. For since the Greek version of this letter contains the not inconsiderable lacuna mentioned shortly before, if the compiler of the Chalcedonian Latin collection had obtained a Latin copy to insert, the lacuna would have been supplied in the Latin text of the letter, just as four lacunae found in the Greek translation of Letter 33 to Julian are known to have been supplied from the Latin copy that he found. Although those lacunae do not damage the sense of that letter as severely as the single lacuna especially damages the sense of Letter 43, the point remains the same. The collector therefore did not supply the lacuna in the Latin text of the Greek version because he did not find either the Latin original or a Latin copy of this letter. Furthermore, if he had found a Latin copy, he would not only have supplied the lacuna but also corrected the error contrary to historical truth. It is entirely incredible that the Latin copy he found was as erroneous and mutilated as the Greek version. We shall speak shortly afterward about the chronological note prefixed to the Latin text.

4. Since, therefore, the Latin collector lacked the original or a Latin copy of this letter and had before his eyes only the Greek version, we think that he constructed the Latin text he gave in the following manner. He found a Latin copy of Letter 44 alone, which contains several sentences resembling those of Letter 43. Wherever he detected similar or nearly similar passages in the two letters, he refrained from translating the Greek text of this letter—which had to serve in place of the original—and transcribed Latin words and complete periods from the Latin original of Letter 44, adapting them to Letter 43. Where he saw different sentences, which do not occur in Letter 44—as happened especially at the beginning of the letter—he was compelled to translate from the Greek.

Evidence of this translation appears in several passages of the first chapter, which differ considerably from Leo’s manner of writing, and also in the imperial title inserted at the beginning of chapter 2, “most tranquil of rulers.” Since this expression is alien to Leo’s formulas and comes closer to the Greek wording, Tillemont likewise recognized this at the place cited. The title “most reverend,” also given in the first chapter to the episcopal legates, is foreign to Leo’s usage and is evidently derived from the Greek; for the Greek εὐλαβέστατος is rendered in the ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon as “most reverend.”

5. If the Latin text was thus arbitrarily composed by the author of the Latin Chalcedonian collection, it is neither a Leonine original nor capable of being treated as one. The entire inquiry must therefore concern not the Latin text but the Greek text, which derives from an original sent to the East and, where the Latin original is lacking, must take the place of the original.

Those who examine the Greek text will plainly see that not only does the opening of the letter differ from the opening of Letter 44, but the entire letters differ, so that although similar sentences generally occur in both, they nevertheless differ in many, even minor, respects. These differences must be attributed not to a different translation of the same letter but to dissimilar Latin originals. For some sentences expressed more briefly in the Greek of Letter 43 and explained more fully in Letter 44 omit certain clauses that a translator would not have passed over; others are presented in a different form altogether. For example: “And let those whose cause is more serious either acquiesce in the counsels or be cut off from the one Church.” The same sentence is expressed differently in Letter 44: “And let those whose cause is more difficult, if they acquiesce in better counsels, not fall away from the unity of the Church.” This twofold manner of expressing the same sentence plainly depends not on a different Greek translation of the same letter but on a different Latin copy.

From this it is beyond doubt that Letter 43, which is known from comparison with the Greek text to differ from Letter 44 in so many chapters, is a different letter. It was therefore necessary to provide a Latin translation of the Greek text, which takes the place of the original—not only so that the obvious difference might be accessible to those less familiar with Greek, but also so that this letter, which survives only in Greek, might exist in Latin. The Latin text we possess is neither the original nor a complete translation, as we have seen; for the most part it presents Letter 44 rather than Letter 43.

6. It must be acknowledged that, besides the lacuna and the historical error mentioned at the beginning, the Greek text contains other passages that are either displaced and corrupted or certainly obscure and confused. We shall observe in note 5 that the historical error can easily be corrected in the Greek text by changing two letters, but cannot be corrected at all in the old Latin translation; it is therefore to be attributed to an ancient copyist rather than to the Greek translator. It cannot be determined whether the lacuna evident in the first chapter arose from a leap by the translator or from a copyist’s omission.

The remaining displaced, confused, and entangled passages derive partly perhaps from a copyist and partly from the incompetent translator himself. This, however, is common to other Greek versions inserted in this collection. Again and again the Greek translator, because of his imperfect knowledge of Latin, failed to grasp the author’s meaning with sufficient accuracy and rendered certain passages incorrectly—passages that those who understand Latin well recognize, by comparison with the surviving originals, ought to be translated otherwise.

The meaning of these obscure and confused passages in Leo’s mind can indeed be gathered from the Latin original of Letter 44, which presents similar sentences. But the same words must not be transferred from that letter into Letter 43, as the Latin collector did. Although Leo sometimes revised the same letter and carried not only the same ideas but nearly the same words into a later copy, as is clear from Letters 30 and 31 to Pulcheria, he also customarily added, removed, or altered certain things. It is therefore uncertain whether something of that sort occurred in the passages under discussion. In the notes it will be possible only to indicate the words that seem either to require supplementation or to clarify Leo’s meaning, without being able to affirm that Leo himself inserted them into this letter. Thus all, or at least the principal, difficulties raised against this letter have been resolved, so that even on this ground there need be no doubt about its authenticity.

7. In asking why two such similar letters were sent to the same emperor, Quesnellus conjectured that Letter 43 might perhaps be a copy of Letter 44, which Saint Leo sent to the Augusta Pulcheria after making certain changes. For in Letter 45, written to the same woman, he states that he is sending her such a copy.

This may appear ingenious if both letters had the same chronological notation, but it is not probable. It is most likely that Leo sent Pulcheria a copy corresponding to the original delivered to Theodosius. The hypothesis that the date marked on both letters was the same depends on the Latin text; but we have already shown that this date is not proper to this letter and was taken from Letter 44.

Once that hypothesis has been rejected, the matter may be conjectured to have happened as follows. The holy pontiff first wrote Letter 43. This is consistently placed first, before Letter 44, in all the Greek manuscripts, both Venetian and Vatican, and also in those seen by the ancient Latin translator, or Rusticus; this indicates an earlier date. After several days, when those to whom Letter 43 had been entrusted had already departed, Saint Leo revised it with certain changes and many additions and entrusted it to others to carry, so that they might offer this version to Theodosius, having recalled or suppressed the earlier one if possible. He also attached a copy of it to the letter written to Pulcheria. Thus both letters reached the East and were found and inserted by the author of the Greek Chalcedonian collection.

8. Finally, something must be said about the canon. Although in printed editions of the councils it is appended to the Greek version of Letter 44, because that letter was printed first at the editors’ discretion, in the manuscripts it is attached to Letter 43, which, as we have already said, is placed first in them.

Since the holy pontiff, in Letter 44, mentions below the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea, he seems to have appended not one canon but several—namely, those enacted at the Council of Sardica concerning appeals, which, according to the ancient custom of the Latin and especially the Roman Church, had been added to the Nicene canons and circulated under the name of the Nicene canons.

Since the same pontiff habitually uses the plural—for example, “letter,” “copies,” and so forth—to signify one letter or one copy, as we saw in note 3 on Letter 13 (Col. 664, i) and note 7 on Letter 45 (Col. 833 e), he must here likewise be understood, by the plural words cited, to indicate one canon, the fourth canon of the same Council of Sardica. The ancient Greek translator rendered this one canon, as all the Greek manuscripts show. Similarly, when Galla Placidia in Letter 56 cited “the definitions of the Council of Nicaea” in the plural, she indicated one canon, the fifth of Sardica, as is noted in the margin of the printed editions.

In editions of the councils, this title is prefixed to the canon from a certain Roman manuscript, but it is not found in three Venetian manuscripts:

> A copy of the council at the place of Novae, where they spoke.

In Greek:

> Ἀντίτυπον συνεδρίου ἐν τῷ τόπῳ τῶν Καινῶν, ἐν οἷς διελάλησαν.

The canon itself, according to the Venetian manuscripts, reads as follows:

> Bishop Gaudentius said: If it is agreeable that this be added to the sentence which you have delivered as fully holy: whenever another bishop has been deposed by the judgment of bishops and has appealed for the matter to be brought before the city of Novae, while another bishop in that same see, after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, cannot have the matter definitively established in another place, unless he receives the decision from the judges there.

The Greek text is:

> Γαυδέντιος ἐπίσκοπος εἶπεν· Εἰ ἀρέσκει προστεθῆναι ταύτῃ τῇ ἀποφάσει, ἥν τινα πλήρη ἁγιότητος προσενέγκατε, ὁπηνίκα ἄλλος ἐπίσκοπος καθρρέθη κρίσει ἐπισκόπων καὶ διεμαρτύρατο ἐν πόλει τῶν Καινῶν κινηθῆναι τὰ τοῦ πράγματος, ὁ δὲ ἕτερος ἐπίσκοπος ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ καθέδρᾳ μετὰ τὴν αἴτησιν τοῦ φαινομένου καθῃρῆσθαι, παντελῶς ἐν ἑτέρῳ τόπῳ τυπωθῆναι τὰ τοῦ πράγματος μὴ δύνασθαι, εἰ μὴ παρὰ τῶν ἐκεῖσε κριτῶν δέξηται τὸν ὅρον.

The very corrupt interpretation of this Latin canon appended by Saint Leo to his letter is demonstrated by the genuine Latin canon of Sardica. We give it from those most ancient manuscripts and canonical collections in which, since the Sardican canons are counted among the Nicene canons according to the custom of the Roman Church, it seems beyond doubt that the reading was taken from the form appended by Leo to his letters:

> Bishop Gaudentius said: If it is agreeable, this must be added to the sentence which you have delivered as full of holiness: when someone has been deposed by the judgment of those bishops who dwell in the neighboring places and has appealed that his case be heard in the city of Rome, another bishop must not at all be ordained in his see—or, in some manuscripts, “in his place”—after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined in the judgment of the Roman bishop.

Now, if this genuine canon is compared with the Greek version we have given, one will detect the omission of the words “who dwell in the neighboring places” and, at the end, an extremely confused sentence. Consequently, the words “in the city of Rome” were wrongly rendered as “in the city of Novae,” ἐν πόλει τῶν Καινῶν; and the words “in the judgment of the Roman bishop” were rendered as “from the judges there,” παρὰ τῶν ἐκεῖσε κριτῶν, so that no mention whatever remains of the city of Rome or of the bishop. Whether this happened accidentally or deliberately, let others judge.

The Roman editors therefore rightly noted:

> The translator of that period rendered this canon together with the letter into Greek in a sufficiently corrupt and mutilated form, just as he did the other letters of the blessed Leo inserted in this Council of Chalcedon.

We shall now first present the Greek interpretation together with its Latin translation; afterward we shall append the ancient Latin edition that came from the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, although it cannot be treated as the original letter of Leo.

## LETTER XLIII

[Note: [Col. 0821C] Alternatively, 39. What was formerly 43 is now 47. Written shortly before 13 October 449.]

### TO THE AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS

[Col. 0821]  
[Note: [Col. 0821] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0821A] 902 Letter of Leo to Theodosius, of blessed memory, in which he requested that a special synod be held in Italy and nowhere else, because the Second Synod of Ephesus is contrary to the canons.

To the most glorious and serene Emperor THEODOSIUS, Leo, bishop.

From long ago and from the beginning, in the synods that have been held, we have received such confidence from the most holy Peter, chief of the apostles, that we possess authority both to defend the truth for the sake of our peace and to prevent anyone from disturbing it, since it is so securely protected and injury is removed without delay.

Since, therefore, the council of bishops which you ordered to be held in the city of Ephesus on account of Flavianus both injures the faith itself and wounds all the Churches . . . [lacuna] . . .

[Col. 0821B] We did not learn these things from an uncertain messenger but from the very men whom we sent: the most devout bishop and our most faithful deacon Hilary, who reported to us what had been done. What happened has this cause: those who assembled did not pronounce judgment concerning the faith and concerning those who had been deceived with a pure conscience and upright judgment according to custom. For we learn that not all who ought to have assembled came to the council, but that some were expelled and others admitted; these, through the deception of the aforesaid bishop, were caught into impious subscriptions. For he issued such a judgment that through him injury was inflicted on all the Churches. Those who had seen this utterly impious deed, contrary to the faith, and had been sent by us, reported it to us.

Therefore, most serene emperor, deign, through your pious conscience, to avert the danger to the faith, and do not allow human presumption to do violence to the Gospel of Christ.

I, most Christian and venerable emperor, together with the bishops who are with me, sincerely desire above all that you please God, before whom the whole Church unanimously pours forth prayers for your imperial power. I advise you to act lest we perhaps pay the penalty before the tribunal of Christ if we envelop such a matter in silence.

I therefore beseech you, before the inseparable Trinity of the one Godhead—which is injured by the things wrongly done and which guards your empire—and before the holy angels of Christ, to order that everything remain untouched, just as it existed before the judgment. Let them await the greater tribunal of the council, in which the entire number of bishops from the whole world will assemble. Do not allow yourselves to bear the burden of another’s sin; and, to state this more clearly, we are compelled by fear of pressing necessity.

But set before your eyes the glory of the most blessed Peter, and the crowns shared with him by all the apostles, and the joys of the martyrs, for whom there was no other cause of suffering than the confession of the true Godhead and perfect continuance in Christ. [Note: [Col. 0823D] Read “perfect” or “true humanity.” See note 3 below on the Greek text.]

Since this confession is now impiously being injured by a few, all the Churches of our regions and all the priests earnestly beseech your Clemency with tears, on account of the appeal contained in the petition of Bishop Flavianus, to order that a special council be held in the regions of Italy, so that every conflict may be removed or moderated, and nothing divergent or doubtful remain concerning the faith. Let bishops from all the Eastern provinces also assemble; and if any of them have strayed from the path of truth, let them be restored completely by salutary remedies. Let those whose cause is more serious either acquiesce in the counsels or be cut off from the one Church. Thus it is necessary also to preserve the things prescribed by the Nicene canon and by the decree of the bishops of the whole world, according to the custom of the Catholic Church and the free faith of our Fathers, through which your Serenity is established.

When those who injure the Church have been expelled, your provinces possess what is justly theirs, and vengeance has been exercised against the heretics, your empire also will be defended by the right hand of Christ.

[Col. 0822A]

901 [Note: [Col. 0821C] We have restored this title according to the Venetian manuscripts. In the printed editions, after Λέοντος, “of Rome,” is added, and τὸν τῆς θείας μνήμης, “of blessed memory,” is omitted. The same manuscripts also add another title: “Letter of Leo, bishop of Rome, to the Emperor Theodosius concerning the holding of the synod in the regions of Italy.”]

> Letter of Leo sent to Theodosius, of blessed memory, in which he requested that a special synod be held in the regions of Italy and nowhere else, because the Second Synod held at Ephesus is contrary to the canons.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] From Vatican Greek manuscript 1455, which supplied a genuine and complete text. The printed editions have διὰ τὸ τοῦτο ὑπεναντίον εἶναι τῶν κανόνων, “because this is contrary to the canons.”]

To the most glorious and most serene Emperor Theodosius, Leo, bishop.

From above and from the beginning, in the synods that have taken place, we have received such freedom of speech from the most holy Peter, chief of the apostles, that we possess authority to defend the truth for the sake of our peace, and that no one can disturb what is so firmly established, while the injury is immediately removed. Since, therefore, the assembly of bishops which you ordered to take place in the city of the Ephesians on account of Flavianus both injures the faith itself and wounds all the Churches . . . [lacuna] . . . and these things have become known to us not from some uncertain messenger but from those themselves who were sent by us, the most reverend bishop and our most faithful deacon Hilary, who reported to us what had been done.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] The manuscript lacks καί, “and.”]

[Note: [Col. 0821D] The printed editions have ὑμῶν, “of you.” The Roman editors placed in the margin ἴσως ἡμῶν, “perhaps of us,” and the old translator, who rendered the opening of this chapter from the Greek as we showed in the notice, read it likewise. We have therefore corrected the text without hesitation.]

The cause of what happened is that those who assembled did not pronounce judgment concerning the faith and concerning those who had gone astray with a pure conscience and upright judgment according to custom. For we learned that not all who ought to have assembled came together in the assembly, but that some were expelled and others admitted; these were captured by impious written subscriptions through the influence of the aforesaid bishop. For the judgment issued by him was such that through it all the Churches were injured. Those sent by us, who saw that this was exceedingly impious and hostile to the faith, reported it to us.

[Note: [Col. 0821D] In the printed editions, πολεμεῖ Φλαυιανῷ, “wars against Flavianus,” appears incorrectly. The Roman editors corrected it in the margin; we have inserted the correction into the text because the context requires it and because the ancient translator reads it this way in the text.]

[Note: [Col. 0822C] Here the suspended sense indicates a lacuna, which had to be marked with dots, although it does not appear in the manuscripts. Some mention of Dioscorus must have been inserted here. Presiding over the Ephesian outrage, he was responsible for the fact that the false synod both injured the faith and wounded all the Churches. I say “undoubtedly,” because the following words, τοῦ προλεχθέντος, “of the aforesaid bishop,” refer to him, not to Flavianus.]

[Note: [Col. 0822D] Thus from the Venetian manuscripts, with a clearer syntax than in the printed editions, which have παρ’ αὐτῶν, παρ’ ἡμῶν. Shortly afterward the same codex incorrectly has Ἱλαρίου instead of Ἱλάρου.]

Therefore, most serene emperor, deign through your pious conscience to avert the danger to the faith, and do not allow human presumption to do violence to the Gospel of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0822D] The printed editions and most manuscripts have the plural εὐλαβεστάτων ἐπισκόπων, “most reverend bishops.” Since the error is evident—for only one bishop, Julius, was sent—we have restored the passage by a certain correction. The copyists’ mistake, writing ων for ου, is easily corrected by the slightest change of two letters.]

I, most Christian and worshipful emperor, together with the bishops who are with me, sincerely desire that you please God above all things. The whole Church unanimously offers prayers to him for your imperial power. I advise you, lest we pay the penalty before the tribunal of Christ for having passed such a matter over in silence.

I beseech you, therefore, before the Trinity of the one Godhead, inseparable, injured by the things wrongly done and serving as guardian of your empire, and before the holy angels of Christ, that all things remain unbroken, as they existed before the judgment. Let them await the greater tribunal of the council, in which the whole number of bishops from the entire inhabited world will be gathered.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] The Roman editors placed in the margin ἴσως ἁρπαγῆ, “perhaps seizure.”]

Do not allow us to bear the burden of the fault of others. To state this more clearly, we are held fast by fear, pressed by urgent necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] The same editors suggested in the margin ὑμᾶς, “you”; that is the reading required.]

But set before your eyes the glory of the most blessed Peter, the common crowns of all the apostles together with him, and the joys of the martyrs, for whom there was no other cause of suffering than the confession of the true Godhead and the perfect continuance in Christ.

[Col. 0824B] [Note: [Col. 0824D] The Roman editors placed in the margin καὶ τῆς ἀληθοῦς ἐν Χριστῷ ἀνθρωπότητος, “and of the true humanity in Christ,” which Eutyches denied.]

Since this confession is now impiously being injured by a few, all the Churches of our regions and all the priests beseech your gentleness with tears, in accordance with the petition of the libellus of Bishop Flavianus, that you order a special council to be held in the regions of Italy, so that every opposition may be removed or softened and nothing superfluous or doubtful remain concerning the faith. Let bishops from all the Eastern provinces also assemble; and if any of them have incurred reproach on the path of truth, let them be restored to wholeness by salutary remedies. Let those whose cause is more serious either be quiet through counsel or be cut off from the one Church.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Thus the Vatican Greek manuscript 1455 and the Ottobonian manuscript 29. The printed editions had οἵ τινες ὕβρεις, “who have suffered insults.”]

It is therefore necessary also to preserve the things that the canon at Nicaea commands, and the decree of the bishops from the entire inhabited world, according to the custom of the Catholic Church and the free faith of our Fathers, through which your Serenity is established.

[Note: [Col. 0824D] Something confused appears here, and perhaps there is a lacuna. Leo’s meaning is clearer in Letter 44.]

When those who injure the Church have been expelled, your provinces enjoy what is justly theirs, vengeance against the heretics has been carried out, and may your kingdom also be sheltered by the right hand of Christ.

## THE SAME LETTER

[Note: [Col. 0823D] Although the Latin text of this letter, which we present here, is contained in manuscripts of the Latin Chalcedonian collection, in which Leo’s originals are generally copied, we showed in the notice that it is not the original text but partly a translation from the Greek and partly a transcript from the following Letter 44. This letter is also found in the Grimanic manuscript of collection 18 and in the Venetian manuscript of collection 22, which received many materials from the Chalcedonian collection.]

### TO THE AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS

As it appears from the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection.

[Col. 0823]

[Note: [Col. 0823D] In the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection this title reads: “Letter of the most holy archbishop of Rome, Leo, to the Emperor Theodosius, in which he requested that a special council be held in Italy and not in any other place, because the Second Synod of Ephesus is contrary to the canons.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He complains to the emperor about the Ephesian outrage.

II. He requests that matters remain in the condition in which they were before the false synod.

III. He begs the emperor to order that a council be held within Italy.

[Col. 0823D] To the most glorious and most merciful Augustus THEODOSIUS, Leo, bishop.

### CHAPTER I

Formerly and from the beginning, in the councils that have been held, we received such confidence from blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, that we possess authority to defend the truth for the sake of our peace, so that no one may disturb it in any way when it is so firmly protected and injury is suddenly removed.

[Col. 0824C] [Note: [Col. 0824D] Thus several of our manuscripts and those of Baluze. Others read “most blessed.”]

Since, therefore, the council of bishops which you ordered to be held on account of Flavianus in the city of Ephesus is shown to oppose the faith itself and to wound all the Churches—[Note: [Col. 0824D] Concerning the lacuna at this point, see note 5 on the Greek text of this letter below ([Col. 0824D] “Something confused appears here, and perhaps there is a lacuna. Leo’s meaning is clearer in Letter 44”).] . . . And these things have become known to us not through an uncertain messenger but from the very [Col. 0825A] most reverend bishops who were sent by us and from our deacon Hilary, the most faithful narrator of what happened.

[Note: [Col. 0825C] Compare note 2 (Col. 822, 8) on the same Greek text. There we exposed the error in this passage, contrary to historical truth. The ancient Latin translator of this passage, further placing after the words “who were sent by us” the words that precede them in the Greek text, confirmed and obscured the error so thoroughly that, although it can easily be detected and corrected in the Greek, it cannot at all be corrected in this Latin version. It should also be noted that Leo never gives bishops the title “most reverend”; it belongs to the translator, who rendered the Greek εὐλαβεστάτων in this way, although elsewhere it is also rendered “most devout.”]

This fault therefore proceeded from the fact that those who had assembled did not, with a pure conscience and upright judgment according to custom, pronounce judgment concerning the faith and concerning those who were in error.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Crabbus and the Antwerp edition of 1583 read “errors.” The same reading appears in a second hand in Verona manuscript 57. Labbe’s edition has “those who had erred.”]

We learned that not all who had assembled were present at the judgment itself. For we learned that some were rejected and others admitted, and that these, at the will of the aforesaid priest, gave captive hands to impious subscriptions.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] That is, of Dioscorus of Alexandria, who was undoubtedly named in the lacuna indicated in note 5 above, just as he is named in the following letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Quesnellus, following earlier printed editions, reads “they gave,” which would be harmful to the sense. We judged the reading of our manuscripts and those of Baluze preferable; it is also supported by the following letter.]

They knew that this would harm their status unless they did what was commanded. He issued such a judgment that through it violence was done to all the Churches. Our representatives, sent from the apostolic see, saw that it was so impious and contrary to the Catholic faith and reported it to us.

### CHAPTER II

[Col. 0825B]

Therefore, most tranquil of rulers, we ask you to remove from the conscience of your Piety the danger to religion and the faith, so that human presumption may not do violence to the Gospel of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0825D] Thus the better manuscripts and the Greek text, from which these few words of the chapter were translated. Quesnellus, following Leo’s printed editions and some manuscripts, reads “most tranquil.”]

[Note: [Col. 0825D] We have retained the common reading, although no manuscript supports it. The reading in the manuscripts—“These things I,” or “These things therefore,” “That man I,” or “That man therefore”—does not fit the Latin context of this letter in any way, whereas “Behold, I” fits the Greek text. Moreover, it is certain that the Latin collector excerpted this passage from Letter 44, where “Behold, I” is read.]

Behold, I, most Christian and venerable emperor, together with my fellow priests, fulfilling toward your revered Clemency the duty of sincere love and desiring that you please God in all things, to whom the Church offers supplication for you, beseech you lest we be judged guilty of silence before the tribunal of the Lord. We beseech you before the inseparable Trinity of the one Godhead, which is injured by such an act and which itself guards and establishes your imperial power, and before the holy angels of Christ, to order that everything remain in the condition in which it was before any judgment, until a greater number of priests from the whole world has assembled. Do not allow yourselves to be burdened by another’s sin; for, since it is necessary for us to speak, we fear that the religion of the one whose faith is being scattered may be provoked to anger.

Keep before your eyes and reverently contemplate with the full concentration of your mind the glory of blessed Peter, the common crowns of all the apostles with him, and the palms of all the martyrs, for whom there was no other cause of suffering than the confession of the true Divinity and the true humanity in Christ.

### CHAPTER III

Since a few thoughtless people are now impiously opposing this sacrament, all the Churches of our regions and all the priests beseech your gentleness with groans and tears. Since our representatives faithfully protested and Bishop Flavianus presented them with a petition of appeal, order that a general synod be held within Italy, so that it may either remove or soften all offenses and ensure that nothing further remains doubtful in the faith or divided in charity.

Let the bishops of the Eastern provinces assemble; and if any of them have strayed from the path of truth because they were overcome by threats and injuries, let them be restored completely by salutary remedies. Let those whose cause is more difficult, if they acquiesce in better counsels, not fall away from the unity of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0826C] The Council edition reads: “if they acquiesce in better counsels, so that they may not fall away from the unity of the Church.”]

That this must necessarily be requested after an appeal has been lodged is testified by the decrees of the canons enacted at Nicaea, which were established by the priests of the whole world. Favor the Catholics, according to your own custom and that of your ancestors; grant freedom for the defense of the faith.

For while we plead the cause of the Churches, we are also pleading for your kingdom and salvation, so that you may possess your provinces in tranquil right.

[Note: [Col. 0826C] Thus most manuscripts, as also in the following letter. Quesnellus reads “while we conduct the case”; other editions of Leo read: “because we conduct the cause and the stability of your kingdom and salvation.”]

Defend the Church’s unshaken condition against the heretics, so that your empire also may be defended by the right hand of Christ.

[Col. 0826C]

Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

[Note: [Col. 0826D] In the notice above we demonstrated that this chronological notation is not proper to this letter but was transferred by the Latin collector, along with many other things, from the following letter.]

## LETTER XLIV

[Note: [Col. 0826D] Alternatively, 40. What was formerly 44 is now 48. Written 13 October 449.]

### TO THE SAME AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS

[Note: [Col. 0826D] This letter is extant in the manuscripts of collection 5, in the Hispanic collection, in Isidore’s collections 13, 17, and 19 through 24, and in Sichardus.]

[Col. 0825]

[Note: [Col. 0826D] In Table of Collection 5, chapter 86, this title appears: “To the Emperor Theodosius, that, once the Ephesian synod has been annulled, a council should be held in Italy with his consent.” In the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, and thereafter in printed editions before Quesnellus: “Concerning the Second Synod of Ephesus, in which the heresy of Eutyches was aided by the perverse understanding of certain bishops; hence he urges the same Augustus that the constitution of the ancient faith not be violated by them, but that the priests of the whole world be assembled.” Finally, in the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection, generally accompanied by the Greek text: “Another letter of the most holy archbishop of Rome, Leo, to the Emperor Theodosius, censuring the Ephesian council, which was held against the most holy Flavian, and requesting that another council be held in the regions of Italy.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. The pseudo-synod of Ephesus, while favoring private hatreds, disturbed everything in the Church; the writings of the Apostolic See were rejected by it; everything was done by force; Hilary alone barely escaped among the legates who opposed it; this synod could never be received by the Apostolic See. — II. He asks Theodosius, together with all the Westerners, to keep everything in the same condition until a greater synod. — III. He requests a general synod to be held within Italy.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0827A] ## Leo, bishop, and the holy SYNOD assembled in the city of Rome, to THEODOSIUS Augustus

[Note: The commonly printed editions add “always”; we have removed it from all our manuscripts. In the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection this superscription stands at the beginning: “To the most glorious and merciful Theodosius Augustus, Leo, bishop, and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome.” In the Florentine manuscript of Collection 13: “Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, and all the bishops assembled in that same city for the sake of holy religion, to Theodosius Augustus.” Leo indicates that several bishops had assembled in Letter 61, chapter 1, where he says of this synod: “which had assembled with a full attendance.”]

### CHAPTER I

From the letters of Your Clemency, which some time ago you sent to the See of the blessed apostle Peter out of love for the Catholic faith, we gained such confidence in your defense of truth and peace that, [p. 911] in so simple and so well-secured a matter, we thought that nothing harmful could arise—especially since those sent to the episcopal council which you ordered to be held at Ephesus had been so well instructed that, if the bishop of Alexandria had permitted the writings which they brought either to the holy synod or to Bishop Flavian to be made public to the ears of the bishops, then, through the clearest manifestation of the pure faith—which we have received as divinely inspired and which we hold—all the uproar of disputation would have fallen silent, [Col. 0827B] so that neither ignorance would continue to rave nor rivalry find an opportunity to do harm.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, with manuscripts of Collection 24, read “assemblies” (*congressionum*); the margin has “contenders” (*concertantium*).]

[Note: Quesnellus reads “they have been instructed.” We have restored the reading of the earlier editions, confirmed by several of our better manuscripts, as the preferable one.]

But while private causes were being pursued under the pretext of religion, through the impiety of a few something was done that would wound the whole Church. For we have learned—not through an uncertain report, but through the most trustworthy narrator of what took place, our deacon Hilary, who barely escaped being forced to subscribe—that very many priests had assembled at the synod. Their number would certainly have benefited deliberation and judgment if the man who claimed for himself the leading place had been willing to preserve episcopal moderation.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, with Merlin, read “conference” (*collationi*). The Hispanic and Isidorian codices read “consolation” (*consolationi*).]

[Note: The Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts read “narrating” (*narrante*).]

Then, as is customary, when the opinions of all had been freely expressed, a tranquil and impartial examination would have established what agreed with the faith and helped those who were in error. [Col. 0827C] But we have learned that not all who had assembled were present at the actual judgment. Some were rejected; others, we learned, were admitted—[p. 913] men who, according to the will of the aforesaid priest, gave their hands captive to impious subscriptions.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript and manuscripts of Collection 21 omit “for.”]

[Note: The Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts read “and would harm”; the Council edition and codices of Collection 21 read “which would harm.”]

They knew that these subscriptions would harm their holy rank unless they did what had been commanded. [Col. 0829A] And a sentence was pronounced by that man such that, while one man was being attacked, the whole Church seemed to be assailed.

[Note: The earlier printed editions of Leo, together with manuscripts of Collection 21, read “seemed to rage.”]

Our representatives sent from the Apostolic See saw this to be so impious and contrary to the Catholic faith that no oppression could force them to consent. With steadfastness, as was fitting, they declared in that same synod that the Apostolic See would in no way receive what was being decreed. For truly the whole mystery of the Christian faith is being destroyed—may this be far from the times of Your Piety—unless this most wicked deed, which surpasses every sacrilege, is abolished.

[Note: The Council edition, together with the same manuscripts, reads “is excluded.” A little later certain manuscripts have “is abolished.”]

### CHAPTER II

Since the devil’s wickedness subtly deceives the simple and, through an appearance of piety, mocks the imprudence of certain people, persuading them that harmful things are beneficial, [Col. 0829B] we ask you to remove from the conscience of Your Piety the danger threatening religion and faith. Grant, in the treatment of divine matters, what the equity of your laws permits in secular affairs, so that human presumption may not use force against the Gospel of Christ.

Behold, most Christian and venerable Emperor: together with my fellow priests I fulfill, toward the reverence due to Your Clemency, the duty of sincere love, and [p. 915] I desire that you please God in all things, to whom the Church prays on your behalf.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “the duty of sincerity.”]

Let us not be judged guilty of silence before the tribunal of Christ the Lord.

[Note: The manuscripts of Verona 57, both Vienna manuscripts, and the Ratisbon manuscript omit “of Christ.”]

We beseech you before the inseparable Trinity of the one Godhead, which is offended by such an act, although it is itself the guardian and author of your imperial power, and before the holy angels of Christ, to order that everything remain in the condition in which it was before any judgment, [Col. 0829C] until a greater number of priests from the whole world has assembled.

[Note: Earlier editions of Leo, together with manuscripts of Collection 24, read “the originator”; thereafter they say “that you order it to remain in that condition.”]

Do not allow yourselves to be burdened by another’s sin. For we fear that—what we must say—the indignation of the one whose religion is being destroyed may be provoked.

[Note: The Vatican, Hispanic, Isidorian, and Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 read: “lest, if this religion is scattered, indignation be provoked against you.”]

Keep before your eyes, and look upon with reverence and the full attention of your mind, the glory of the blessed Peter, the crowns shared with him by all the apostles, and the palms of all the martyrs. They had no other reason for suffering than their confession of true divinity and true humanity in Christ.

### CHAPTER III

Because this mystery is now impiously opposed by a few imprudent men, all the churches of our regions and all the priests implore Your Gentleness with groans and tears. Since our representatives faithfully protested, and Bishop Flavian himself submitted a petition of appeal, [Col. 0829D] order that a general synod be assembled within Italy.

[Note: Quesnellus appended the following note to these words of Leo: “Learned men rightly suspect that the Nicene canons which Leo cites at the end of this letter, and says are appended below, are none other than the Sardican canons. It is certain that the right of appeals to the Roman pontiffs was first and chiefly asserted on the authority of the first and most important of them, and that they were very often adorned with the name of Nicene canons. This is confirmed by the Greek acts of the Council of Chalcedon, which at the end of this letter contain the fourth Sardican canon, which we include in Dissertation 8, where we discuss Flavian’s appeal at length.” This is excellent insofar as he points out that by the name “Nicene canons” the Sardican canons are understood here. In several very ancient Latin collections they were placed below the Nicene canons without any distinction, and were treated and called Nicene; we shall demonstrate this elsewhere. Compare the preliminary note to the preceding letter, no. 8, where we show that the fourth Sardican canon is appended in the Greek manuscripts not to this letter but to the preceding one. But it is false that he adds that the first and chief right of appeals to Roman pontiffs was asserted from the authority of the Sardican canons; for, insofar as this right proceeds from the primacy established by divine institution, we shall demonstrate it in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, part I, chapter 7.”]

This synod should either remove or heal all offenses in such a way that thereafter [Col. 0831A] nothing remains doubtful concerning the faith or divided in charity. The bishops of the Eastern provinces should assemble; and if any of them, overcome by threats and insults, have strayed from the path of truth, [p. 917] let them be recalled wholly by salutary remedies.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 and three manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection read “or insults.” Soon afterward, three of our manuscripts and two of Baluze’s manuscripts of the same collection read “by salutary remedies.”]

Let those whose case is more difficult, if they accept better counsel, not fall away from the unity of the Church.

[Note: The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “let them accept better counsel … let them not depart.” Manuscripts of Collection 24 read “let them not withdraw.” Vatican manuscript 546 of Collection 21 reads: “Let them thus accept better counsel that they may not depart from the unity of the Church.”]

That this should necessarily be demanded after an appeal has been lodged is attested by the decrees of the canons held at Nicaea, which were established by priests from the whole world and are appended below.

[Note: The long note by Quesnellus concerning the identification of these “Nicene” canons with the Sardican canons is translated above.]

Show favor to the Catholics in accordance with your custom and that of your parents. Give freedom to the defense of the faith, which—without detriment to the reverence due to Your Clemency—no force and no worldly terror can take away.

For when we act on behalf of the causes of the Church, we act also on behalf of your kingdom and your salvation, [Col. 0831B] so that you may possess your provinces in peaceful right.

[Note: The Council edition, with our better manuscripts, reads “the causes.” Quesnellus, with the Vienna manuscript of Collection 5, reads “the cause.” The Vienna Hispanic manuscript incorrectly has “the cause, the established condition of your kingdom.” This error was corrected in the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts to “the cause, the condition of your kingdom,” a reading received by the older editions of Leo. Those editions then read “we act.”]

Defend the unshaken state of the Church against heretics, so that the power of your empire may also be defended by the right hand of Christ.

Given on the third day before the ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

[Note: Quesnellus, with the Vienna manuscript of Collection 5, both of our Hispanic manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and other manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21, reads “on the ides of October,” but incorrectly. Since Leo sent a copy of this letter to Pulcheria together with the following letter, written on the third day before the ides of October, this letter cannot have been sent two days later. Three manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection and Quesnellus in the margin read “the fourth day before the ides of October.” We have preferred the reading of the earlier editors, confirmed by other manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection, the Ratisbon and Florentine manuscripts of Saint Mark, manuscripts of Collection 24, and Sichard’s copy: “the third day before the ides of October.” The other letters written and sent to the East on this occasion are dated the third day before the ides; moreover, Leo was accustomed, when several letters were sent through the same person, to date them all on the same day. In addition, the date “the third day before the ides” found in an old copy of the preceding letter was taken from this letter, as we demonstrated in the preliminary note. Hence this chronological note is recognized as having been added to this letter by an ancient Latin collector.]

To the most humane and tranquil Theodosius Augustus, Leo, bishop, and the holy synod assembled in the city of the Romans.

Having read the letters of Your Humanity, which you recently sent to the seat of the most blessed apostle Peter out of longing for the Catholic faith, we received such boldness for the vindication of the truth through you and of peace that, [p. 912] in a matter so simple and secure, we thought that nothing could be contrived to cause harm.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “so as to think that in a matter so simple and well-fortified nothing could be capable of bringing harm, especially since to …”]

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin suggests “perhaps, ‘for the vindication.’”]

Especially since those sent to the episcopal tribunal which you ordered to be assembled at Ephesus were so well secured that, if the bishop of Alexandria had allowed the letters which we sent to the synod and also to Bishop Flavian to be made public to the ears of the bishops, then, [Col. 0828B] through the clarity of the pure faith which we received and preserve as divinely inspired, every dispute and disturbance would have fallen silent.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “the private matters.” The Roman edition’s margin likewise notes this reading.]

Thus neither ignorance would have raved further nor folly found an opportunity for harm.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin suggests: “so that neither ignorance would rave further nor jealousy find an opportunity for harm.”]

But when private matters were being pursued under the pretext of religion, through the impiety of a few something was dared that wounded the Churches everywhere.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “But now, under a pretext of piety, when private affairs were being stirred up, it was done through the impiety of a few …”]

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “impiety”; the Roman edition also notes this reading in the margin and adds: “But why this is so, we plainly do not see.”]

For we learned, not through an obscure report but through a reliable announcement by our deacon Hilary—who barely escaped so as not to be forced to subscribe by violence—that very many bishops had assembled at the synod.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin suggests “barely escaped.”]

They could have contributed to counsel and judgment through their useful and related prudence, if the one who had claimed for himself the place of ruler had been willing to preserve episcopal fairness.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “whose number would certainly have contributed to deliberation and judgment, if that man …”]

[Note: The Venetian manuscript is corrupt here. The Roman edition’s margin suggests: “so that, as is customary, when the judgments of all had been freely offered, that decision might be established.”]

Then, as is customary, [Col. 0828C] when the decisions of all had been freely presented, a tranquil and just examination would have established what agreed with the faith and benefited those who were wandering.

But we learned that not all those who had assembled were admitted to the judgment. Some were expelled; others were admitted—[Col. 0830A] men who, according to the will of the aforesaid bishop, [p. 914] gave their hands captive to impious subscriptions.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin suggests: “We have learned that not all who had assembled were present; for we learned that some were expelled and others admitted, who …”]

For they knew that their holy rank would be harmed unless they did what had been commanded. And he pronounced such a judgment that, while one man was unjustly accused, he might rage against the whole Church.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin suggests “perhaps, ‘judgment.’”]

Our representatives, sent from the Apostolic See, saw this to be so impious and contrary to the Catholic faith that no mistreatment could force them to consent.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads: “They saw it to be so impious and contrary to the Catholic faith that no coercion could force them to consent.”]

Therefore they protested openly in the synod itself that what had been decreed by them could in no way be received by the Apostolic See. For truly the whole mystery of the Catholic faith—which, far be it from the times of Your Piety—is being divided unless this most grievous deed, which surpasses every impiety, is erased.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript and the Roman edition’s margin read “subjects to punishment,” rather than “surpasses.”]

[Col. 0830B] But since the devil’s wickedness, subtly deceiving the simpler-minded, has attempted in this way to deceive ignorance by an imitation of piety, so that it might recommend harmful things instead of healthy ones, remove, we ask, from the conscience of Your Piety the danger threatening religion and faith.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript and the Roman edition’s margin suggest “above” rather than “instead of.”]

And what is permitted in secular affairs through the equity of your laws, provide, after consideration, also in divine decrees, so that human rashness may not use violence against the Gospel of Christ.

[Note: We have corrected *ἐπενέγκῃ* (“may inflict”) with the Vatican Greek manuscript 1455 and Ottobonian manuscript 29, in place of the form found in the printed editions, *ἐπενέγκεται*.]

Behold, Christian and reverend Emperor: together with my fellow minister I perform, with pure affection, the service due to the reverence of Your Piety.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads “together with my fellow ministers.”]

[p. 916] Desiring that you please God in all things, to whom the Churches pray on your behalf, let us not be judged guilty of silence [Col. 0830C] before the tribunal of the Lord.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript has “I perform.” The common editions have a scribal error, “I shall make.”]

We beseech you before the indivisible Trinity of the one Godhead, which is your guardian and the sovereign of your kingdom, and before the angels of God, to order that everything remain in the same condition in which it was before any judgment, until a greater number of bishops from the whole world has assembled.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin suggests: “which is dishonored by what has now occurred, and is the guardian.”]

Do not allow yourselves to be burdened by another’s sin. For, since it is necessary for us to speak, we fear that indignation may follow from the one whose religion is being harmed.

Keep before your eyes, and reverently attend with the sharpness of your heart, to the glory of the blessed Peter, the common crowns of all the apostles who are with him, and the victories of all the martyrs. They had no other reason for suffering than [Col. 0830D] the confession of Christ’s true divinity and true incarnation.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin reads “behold” (*θεάσασθε*) rather than “attend” (*προσέχετε*).]

[Col. 0832A] Since a few foolish men are now impiously opposing this mystery, all the Churches of all our regions implore Your Humanity through the bishops. Since our representatives faithfully protested and Bishop Flavian himself submitted a petition of appeal, order a general synod to assemble in Italy.

Let it remove and calm all offenses in such a way that thereafter nothing is found doubtful concerning the faith or divided in charity. Let the bishops of the Eastern provinces assemble, so that those who, worn down by threats and insults, have turned aside from the path of truth [p. 918] may be recalled wholly by the consolation of salvation.

[Note: We supplied “of the” from the Venetian manuscript; it fell out of the common editions through a serious error.]

And let those whose sentence is most severe, if they follow better counsels, not withdraw in any way from the unity of the Church.

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin suggests: “if their accusations are more serious, let them …”]

[Col. 0832B] For the votes of the canons held at Nicaea testify that we necessarily make this request after an appeal; those canons were established by bishops from every part of the world, as we have appended below.

Show favor to the Catholics in accordance with your ancestral custom, and grant freedom for the defense of the faith. [Col. 0831] While the reverence due to Your Piety is preserved, no force and no worldly threat will be able to take it away.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “while your reverence is preserved.”]

For when we deal with the doctrines of the Church, we are concerned with Your Piety and with your salvation, so that you may enjoy your provinces in peaceful right.

[Note: The Venetian manuscript reads “may enjoy.”]

Defend against heretics the unshaken constitution of the Church, so that the power of your kingdom may also be defended by the right hand of Christ.

## LETTER XLV

[Note: Formerly numbered 41; previously numbered 45, it is now 50. Written on 13 October in the year 449.]

[Note: This letter is contained in the same collections as the preceding one. We have the Greek version only from Cotelerius, volume I of *Monuments of the Greek Church*, page 54; we were unable to find it in any of our Greek manuscripts.]

### TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

[Note: In Table of Collection 5, chapter 87, only a title concerning the same subject as in the preceding letter is prefixed. In the Hispanic collection, however: “Against the same Second Synod of Ephesus, that its errors may be retracted in another synod.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He sends a copy of the letter he had written to her before the synod. — II. He deplores the disastrous proceedings of the pseudo-synod. He sends a copy of the letter written to Theodosius and requests a council in Italy. — III. He entrusts Pulcheria with the apostolic embassy to Theodosius.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0833A] ## Leo, bishop, and the holy SYNOD assembled in the city of Rome, to Pulcheria Augusta

[Note: The manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection read: “To the most glorious and merciful daughter, Pulcheria Augusta, Leo, bishop, and the holy council assembled at Rome.” The Florentine manuscript of Collection 13 reads: “Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, and all the brothers assembled there for divine religion, to Pulcheria Augusta.”]

### CHAPTER I

[p. 919] If the letters concerning the faith which were sent through our clerics had reached Your Piety, it is certain that, with the Lord assisting you, you could have provided an effective remedy for these things done against the faith.

[Note: This common reading is supported not only by manuscripts of Collection 21 but also by the Vienna manuscript of the collection, the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, and the Isidorian manuscript.
