The other manuscripts, with only a slight change in word order, read: “If the letters which were sent concerning the faith to Your Piety had reached you through our clerics.” The letter understood is Letter 30, which the legates, compelled by lack of time to turn aside toward the Ephesian council, could not carry to Constantinople or transmit through others. Compare the note below.]

For when have you ever failed priests, or the Christian religion, or the faith?

[Note: The Greek has been mistranslated: “you have withdrawn from the faith.”]

But since those who were sent were unable to reach Your Gentleness, so that scarcely one of them—our deacon Hilary—returned to us in flight, we thought that the letters should be sent again.

[Note: This is the reading of the better manuscripts. Another reading is: “our deacon Hilary, fleeing from them.”]

And so that our prayers might deserve to be stronger, we have appended copies of the very writings which did not reach Your Clemency.

[Note: The editions of Leo, together with the Vienna manuscript of Collection 5 and another Hispanic collection, read “a copy.” We have nevertheless preferred the reading of the Council editions, which is favored by our other manuscripts, especially the Ratisbon manuscript and the Chalcedonian Collection, as well as the copies of Merlin and Sichard. Although Saint Leo indicates here only one letter, Letter 30, which, as shown in the preliminary note to this letter, he alone sent to Pulcheria, he sometimes calls a single letter “letters” in the plural, as several examples show. Thus here, at the beginning of the chapter, he could call one and the same letter “letters” in the plural and now “copies of those writings.” Similarly, in Letter 61, chapter 2, Saint Leo calls the copies of the same writings “a copy” of one letter, Letter 51.]

[Col. 0833B] We implore you with greater entreaties [p. 921] to oppose, on behalf of the royal faith, matters that have become so much more bitter, and to care for the religion in which you excel with proportionately greater glory.

[Note: The manuscripts of Collection 24, from which the edition before Quesnellus was produced, read “on behalf of the royal see.” The Greek version would require “on behalf of the Roman faith.” Quesnellus argues in his notes that this accords with Leo’s meaning, since Leo urges Pulcheria to resist new errors on behalf of the faith—that is, according to the faith she possesses or through the strength of that faith. Baluze, relying on an ancient Greek version, suspects that the Latin original had “on behalf of the Roman faith.” He conjectures that the reading of the Latin copies arose because the first autograph may have contained “pro fide R.” Some manuscripts use this abbreviation in Letter 29; scribes who did not understand it may have expanded it as “royal” instead of “Roman.” The Greek translator evidently had before him a copy reading either “Roman” or the abbreviation R., which he rendered as “Roman”; otherwise he would have interpreted “royal” differently.]

Take care that the integrity of the Catholic faith not be violated by any occasion of human contention. For what was believed would be accomplished through the synod assembled at Ephesus as a remedy for calming and healing peace proceeded not only to a greater loss of peace but—what is most grievous—even to the destruction of the faith itself by which we are Christians.

[Note: The Verona manuscript of the Chalcedonian Collection reads “remedies for calming and healing peace.”]

### CHAPTER II

Those who were sent—and one of them, fleeing the violence of the bishop of Alexandria, who claimed everything for himself, faithfully reported to us the sequence of what had been done—protested in the synod, as was proper, against the judgment, or rather the fury, of one man.

[Note: The Hispanic Vienna manuscript reads “and that same one of them”; the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “one of whom.” Quesnellus notes in the margin that another reading is “his plots” instead of “force.”]

[Col. 0833C] They declared that proceedings carried out through force and fear could not prejudice the sacraments of the Church or [Col. 0835A] the Creed itself established by the apostles, nor could any insult separate them from the faith which they had brought fully expounded and arranged from the See of the blessed apostle Peter to the holy synod.

[Note: The Greek reads “against the rights.”]

When the bishops requested that this faith be read, its reading was not admitted. Thus, if that faith which crowned patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs were removed, the birth of Jesus Christ our Lord according to the flesh, and [p. 923] the confession of his true death and resurrection would be dissolved—which we shudder to say.

[Note: The Greek has “from the regeneration,” referring to the word “birth” in the preceding line. The Greek version also adds: “most splendid and merciful lady, daughter Augusta.”]

We wrote concerning this matter to the most glorious ruler, and, what is most important, to a Christian ruler, and appended a copy of that letter, so that he would not permit the faith in which, reborn by God’s grace, he reigns to be corrupted by any novelty.

[Note: Several better manuscripts, Sichard, and the Council editions read “a copy.” Two manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection read “we shall append a copy”; two others read “and we appended a copy.” The reference is to a copy of Letter 44.]

[Col. 0835B] For Bishop Flavian remains in the communion of us all, and no reason permits what has been done without consideration of justice and contrary to the entire discipline of the canons to be treated as valid.

Since the Ephesian synod did not remove the scandal of dissension but increased it, let a council be held within Italy, and let a place and time be established, with all complaints and prejudgments of both parties suspended.

[Note: The Verona manuscript says that the Ephesian synod “did not remove but increased” the scandal.]

Then everything that caused offense may be more carefully reconsidered, and, without a wound to the faith or an insult to religion, those priests who were compelled by immoderate power to subscribe may return to the peace of Christ, while the errors alone are removed.

[Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin: “The Cambridge manuscript reads ‘through power,’ corresponding to the Greek version.” But “impotence” can be used by writers of the highest authority for “immoderate power.”]

### CHAPTER III

To obtain this, may your piety—whose proven faith has always aided the labors of the Church—[Col. 0835C] deign to assert our supplication before the most merciful ruler, since an embassy has been specially entrusted to you by the most blessed apostle Peter.

[Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts add “truth.” The Ratisbon manuscript reads “and the labors which …”; the editions before Quesnellus, together with the Greek version and manuscripts of Collection 21, read “aids” instead of “aided,” incorrectly.]

Before this civil and destructive war grows strong within the Church, may he grant, with God’s help, the opportunity to restore unity, [p. 925] knowing that whatever is bestowed upon Catholic freedom by his kindly decision will benefit the strength of his empire.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “for the restoration of unity.” The earlier editions read “opportunity and means, with God’s help.”]

Given on the third day before the ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

[Col. 0834A] To the most glorious and most merciful daughter, Pulcheria, ever Augusta, Leo, bishop, and the holy synod assembled at Rome.

[p. 920] If the letters concerning the faith sent to Your Piety through the clergy had been delivered, it would have been clear that, with God assisting you, you could provide help and healing for these affairs being carried on against the faith.

For when have you ever turned your back on priests, or on the religion of Christians, or on the faith? [Note: [Col. 0834A] The editor proposes *τῆς* (“of the,” feminine genitive) in place of the printed *τοῖς* (“to the,” plural dative), before “the religion of Christians.”]

[Note: Perhaps “of the Christian religion.”]

But since those who were sent were unable to come before Your Humanity, so that scarcely one of them, a deacon named Hilary, returned to us in flight, we thought that the letters should be sent again.

And so that our petitions might prove strong, [Col. 0834B] we have appended here copies of the very writings addressed to Your Humanity, [Note: [Col. 0834B] The editor proposes *τῇδε τὰ ἀντίγραφα* (“here the copies”) for the printed *τάδε τῇ ἀντιγραφῇ* (“these things to/in the copy”).] entreating you with greater protests that, the more grievous the things have become, the greater glory you should show in opposing them [p. 992, as printed] on behalf of the Roman faith and should take care of the religion in which you excel.

[Note: [Col. 0834B] The Greek is corrupt here. The supplied conjecture is *μείζονι δόξῃ φροντίς τῆς θρησκείας ᾗ κατυπερ…*, approximately “with greater glory, care for the religion in which you excel…”; the proposed reading itself is abbreviated. The printed forms include *δοξῆ* and *πιλονεικίας*, the latter apparently for *φιλονεικίας* (“contention”).]

Let no occasion of human contention injure the wholeness of the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0834B] In the ensuing sentence about the synod, the editor proposes *αὐτή* (“it itself,” nominative, referring to the synod) for the printed *ταύτην* (“this,” feminine accusative).] For the synod assembled at Ephesus, believed to be capable of being calmed through the healing of peace, proceeded not only to greater losses for peace but—what is worthy of grief and indignation—even to the destruction and overthrow of the faith itself among Christians.

And these were the men who were sent. One of them, having escaped the violence of the bishop of Alexandria, who claimed everything for himself, [Col. 0834C] faithfully reported to us the order of what had been done.

[Col. 0836A] They resisted in the synod, as was proper, the judgment—not so much the judgment as the madness—of one man. They protested that what was being done through force and fear could not prejudice the rights of the Church or the Creed itself introduced by the apostles, nor could they, because of anyone’s injustice, withdraw from the faith which they had brought fully expounded and formulated from the throne of the most blessed apostle Peter to the holy synod.

[Note: The Greek text is corrupt at this point. It contains the phrase *(ἀπὸ) τῶν ἀποστόλων εἰσηγηθέντι*, “introduced by the apostles,” with the preposition “from” supplied or bracketed. The verb *ἤνεγκαν* (“they brought”) is supplied in parentheses in the source.]

The reading of this faith was not admitted, although the bishops requested it. Thus, once the faith that crowned patriarchs, [and prophets], apostles, and martyrs had been removed, [Note: [Col. 0836A] The source puts *καὶ προφήτας* (“and prophets”) in parentheses as a supplement.] the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh, his true death, and the confession of his regeneration (*ἀναγέννησις*, “rebirth”) would be dissolved—[p. 924] which is dreadful even to say.

[Col. 0836B] Most illustrious and most merciful lady, daughter Augusta, we wrote concerning this matter, as best we could, to the most glorious king and, what is [most important], to a Christian; [Note: [Col. 0836B] *μέγιστον* (“most important”) is supplied in parentheses.] we appended a copy of that letter so that he would not permit the faith through which, reborn by God’s grace, he reigns to be corrupted by any innovation.

For Bishop Flavian has remained in the communion of us all. And since what has occurred without justice and contrary to the knowledge of all the canons must not be permitted to stand as valid, and since the Ephesian synod did not remove but rather increased the scandal of discord, let a council be held in Italy, and let both its place and time be determined, with all complaints and prejudgments of either side suspended.

[Col. 0836C] Then everything that caused offense may be carefully reconsidered, and, without a wound [to the faith] or an insult to religion, [Note: [Col. 0836C] *τῆς πίστεως* (“of/to the faith”) is supplied in parentheses.] the priests compelled by power to subscribe may return to the peace of God, while error alone is removed.

To make this prevail, may [Your] Piety, whose proven faith has always shared in the labors of the Church, [Note: [Col. 0836C] *σή* (“your”) is supplied in parentheses.] deign to make our petition clear to the most merciful emperor, since this embassy has been specially entrusted to you as if from the most blessed apostle Peter.

May he grant, with God’s help, the abundance needed to renew unity before this war, both military and destructive, grows strong within the Church, [p. 926] knowing that whatever is contributed to Catholic freedom through his benevolent decree will benefit the strength of his empire.

## LETTER XLVI

[Note: Formerly placed after Letter 47; previously numbered 46, it is now 59. It was written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

### HILARY, THEN DEACON OF THE ROMAN CHURCH AND LATER BISHOP, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

[Note: This letter survives in the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection, from which it was translated into manuscripts of Collection 22. It is absent from most Greek manuscripts of the same Chalcedonian Collection, but Cotelerius found it in two royal manuscripts and published it in volume I of *Monuments of the Greek Church*, page 60. We believe the original Latin of this letter has perished. The surviving Latin text appears to be an old translation from the Greek rather than the original; hence the chronological note is absent from both the Greek and Latin texts, whereas the Latin collector always supplied it when he found the original Latin. For this reason we have given first place to the Greek text, which serves in place of the original, and second place to the Latin. We place this letter after the preceding one not only because it is written in that order in chapter 17 of the Chalcedonian Collection, but especially because Hilary, who is said in Letters 44 and 45 to have returned to Rome, writes at the end of this letter: “What I reported with constant and courageous authority on behalf of the faith … you will be able to learn from the letters of the most blessed pope.” He is evidently referring to Leo’s preceding letters, with which this letter too was sent.]

## SYNOPSIS

I. Through Dioscorus’s wicked audacity, he was unable to approach her or deliver the letters of Saint Leo. — II. Having escaped Dioscorus’s plots, he came to Rome; the pseudo-synod of Ephesus is rejected by Leo.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0837A] ## Hilary, deacon, to the most glorious and most pious Pulcheria Augusta

[Note: All manuscripts and the Council edition read “most glorious and most pious.” Quesnellus alone reads “most glorious and most merciful.” The Greek text has “most merciful,” or “most humane,” for “most glorious,” but here reads “most pious.”]

### CHAPTER I

I need not say that I was eager to arrive at Constantinople after the synod, since there was an obvious necessity compelling me to deliver the letters of the most blessed pope addressed to Your Clemency, so that I might at the same time fulfill toward Your Piety and toward the invincible and most Christian emperor the duty of reverence that I owed.

But an impediment arose against this appropriate intention of mine—an impediment that is the enemy of all good things and which Christian feeling mourns: namely, the bishop of Alexandria, who is exceedingly powerful in condemning innocent men.

For, [p. 928] after I was unable to share in his unjust will and judgment, [Col. 0837B] he attempted to summon me by threats and plots to another council.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “counsel,” as the context seems to require. We have no doubt that this was the original reading. But since the Greek translator, rendering *σύνοδος*, read “council,” the Latin translator ought likewise to have rendered it “council”; and “council” is found in the Latin manuscripts no less than in the Council editions. The reading therefore should not be changed.]

He intended either—God forbid—through deception to make me consent to the condemnation of the most holy Bishop Flavian, or to detain me if I resisted, so that I would have no opportunity to hasten to Your Piety at Constantinople or to return to the Roman Church.

### CHAPTER II

Nevertheless, trusting in the help of Christ our God, I preserved myself innocent and uncorrupted from the condemnation of that most reverend and holy man.

[Note: Quesnellus, together with the Council editions, reads “with the help of Christ, as concerns the condemnation of the most reverend man,” and so forth. We have followed the reading of the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian Collection and of Venetian manuscript 79 of Collection 22, a reading confirmed as preferable by the Greek text. Only Vatican manuscript 4166 and the cited Venetian manuscript omit “of Christ our Lord.”]

No scourges or tortures could make me consent to his sentence. But, abandoning everything, I departed from there, came to Rome through unknown and trackless places, and presented myself to the most reverend pope as a competent reporter of everything that had taken place at Ephesus.

[Note: All five of our manuscripts have this reading. Only the Verona manuscript reads “reporter” instead of “announcer.” The printed editions read “so that I might prove a suitable reporter to the most reverend pope.”]

[Col. 0837C] Let Your Venerable Clemency therefore know that the aforesaid pope, together with the entire Western council, rejected everything that Bishop Dioscorus did at Ephesus against the canons [Col. 0839A] amid tumult and worldly hatreds.

[Note: All our manuscripts here read “to be rejected,” better than the printed editions. The Greek text likewise uses the past tense, so the passage should be rendered: “Let Your Venerable Clemency know that he, together with the entire Western synod, rejected everything …”]

There is no way that these acts can be accepted in these regions, since they were committed through the power of the aforesaid man, not without injury to the faith and prejudice against the most holy and innocent man.

I believe it unnecessary to recount what I reported on behalf of the faith with constant and courageous authority; for you will be able to learn these things from the letters of the most blessed pope.

[Note: This formula is characteristic of the Greeks and comes from the Greek. It is therefore found in the Greek version of the preceding letter but not in the Latin original. Compare the note to that letter.]

Therefore, most splendid lady and most merciful Augusta, [p. 930] your reverent Piety should not abandon what it willingly began, but should preserve it with steadfast religious zeal for the faith.

[Note: The Verona manuscript reads “preserve it.”]

[Col. 0838A] To the most merciful and most pious Pulcheria Augusta, Hilary, deacon.

I ought not to say that I made it my concern, after the council, to come to Constantinople, since the necessity was obvious: it compelled me to hand over to the courier the letters of the most blessed Pope addressed to Your Philanthropy, so that at the same time I might clearly discharge toward Your Piety and the unconquered, most Christian Emperor the duty which I owed in matters of religion.

But that enemy of all good things—whose disposition Christians lament—the bishop of Alexandria, powerful in condemning the innocent, obstructed my purpose, sacred as it was. For, since I could not share his unjust opinion and decision, he drove me to another council, summoning me with threats and plots, so that I might either—far be the thought—through deception [perhaps: “by deceptions”] consent to the condemnation of the most holy bishop Flavian, or, if I resisted, be detained, in order that I might be granted no opportunity either to hasten to Your Piety and to Constantinople or to return to the Church of Rome.

Nevertheless, with Christ our God assisting me, I have taken courage that He would preserve me innocent and unharmed from the condemnation of the most devout and holy man. For no whip or torture could make me consent to their unjust decision. Rather, leaving everything behind, I withdrew from there and proceeded to Rome through unknown and untrodden regions. I have adequately reported to the most devout Pope all that was done at Ephesus [perhaps: “I have become an adequate informant”].

Let Your worshipful Philanthropy learn that, together with the whole Western synod, he has rejected everything done at Ephesus against the canons, amid tumult and worldly hatred, by Dioscorus the bishop; and that it is in no way possible for these things to be accepted in these regions, since they were perpetrated through the power of the aforesaid man, not without injury to the faith and to the prejudice of that holy and innocent man [perhaps: “were wrongly perpetrated”]. I consider it unnecessary to recount what I reported concerning the faith with steadfast and vigorous authority; for you will learn these things from the letters of the most devout Pope.

Therefore, most illustrious and most philanthropic Augusta, may Your worshipful Piety, which ought not to abandon the undertaking it has assumed, lend its support with devout zeal for the undefiled faith and steadfast purpose.

## Epistle XLVII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 43. The letter formerly numbered 47 is now 51. Written 13 October 449.]

## To Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica

[Note: We found this letter in manuscript collection 12 alone.]

### Synopsis

I. He congratulates him on not having attended the pseudo-synod.  
II. He urges him to preserve the faith, adhere to Flavian, and strengthen the brethren.

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to his most beloved brother Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

### Chapter I

As we have learned from the report of our deacon Hilary, a great crime has been committed at the instigation or through the agency of the bishop of Alexandria, so that, while ancient rivalries and private hatreds raged against our brother Flavian, neither the innocence of a priest of proven character nor the Christian faith was spared.

Therefore we greatly congratulate Your Love that, although you wished to go to that synod, the divine hand held you back by timely obstacles. Thus, since you would undoubtedly have abstained from so great a crime, you would not have been subjected to undeserved insults [and, as we have learned, you would not have been able to resist the impious fury supported by soldiers and weapons].

Since the treachery that had been concealed has therefore burst into the open [Note: Two manuscripts of the cited collection 12, Vatican 1340 and Venice, St Mark’s 169, omit “into the open.”], and they have passed over into the most abominable heresy of a single most ignorant old man’s followers, we must recognize that the time of our testing has arrived and, relying on heavenly defenses against the assaults of our adversaries, prepare the steadfastness of an unchanging spirit.

We know, dearest brother, that divine protection will be present through the sacrament of His great mercy.

### Chapter II

If, therefore, anything concerning the impious decrees should have been pressed upon Your Fraternity, we jointly protest and admonish you not to mingle the consent of your heart either in the condemnation of an innocent brother or in the acceptance of an abominable doctrine [Note: The manuscripts of the same collection read this more correctly than the printed editions, which, following Merlinus, had “indeed in the condemnation,” but later “in the reception.” Quesnel has “in the condemnation and in the reception.”].

For greater is He who is in us than he who is against us (1 John 4:4). Rather, strive, insofar as the One who assumed and glorified our nature assists you, to strengthen the hearts of all our brethren.

For, since we in no way depart from the Gospel concerning the birth, death, and resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: We have added “our” from the Grimani manuscript, whose exact copy Father Cacciarius used in the Roman edition], it is absolutely certain to us that those who attempt to tear down the ancient foundations of the Catholic faith will not belong to the number of those in our communion.

Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

## Epistle XLVIII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 44. The letter formerly numbered 48 is now 60. Written 13 October 449.]

[Note: This letter too was found in the manuscripts of collection 12 alone.]

## To Julian, Bishop of Cos

### Synopsis

He consoles him after the disaster at Ephesus and urges him to hold fast to the faith.

Leo to Julian, brother and fellow bishop, greetings.

Having learned what was done at Ephesus through the presumption of one man, we have indeed been afflicted with great sorrow over the things committed impiously and furiously. But, directing our minds toward our Lord [Note: Thus according to our manuscripts and editions before Quesnel; Quesnel’s reading is materially uncertain in the supplied note], we derive great confidence from the very truth which we follow, while not neglecting to do everything which, with God’s grace assisting, we believe will be beneficial.

We must therefore hold what we hold; and while the storm of a single whirlwind rages [Note: This is the reading of the same manuscripts and editions preceding Quesnel; Quesnel reads “the storm of a single turbid cloud.”], we must embrace the serene tranquility of the faith, until the truth spreads its rays throughout all things and consumes the darkness of unbelief.

You will learn from the messenger’s account what has been arranged [Note: This reading seemed preferable, as found in the Venetian manuscript 109 and Quesnel’s first edition. Alternatively: “what has been ordered.”].

Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

## Epistle XLIX

[Note: Alternatively numbered 42. The letter formerly numbered 49 is now 61. Written 13 October 449.]

[Note: We discovered this letter in manuscripts of collections 12 and 23.]

## To Flavian, Bishop of Constantinople

### Synopsis

He consoles Flavian, against whom Dioscorus had raged savagely, and promises him assistance.

Leo to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople.

Through the deacon who secretly escaped from Ephesus we have learned what and how much Your Love is suffering in defense of the Catholic faith. Although we glorify God, who strengthens you by the power of His grace, we must nevertheless grieve over the ruin of those through whom the truth is attacked and the very foundations of the whole Church are shaken.

Since, however, God’s providence always grants necessary assistance to His own, Your Fraternity should know that, for the common cause, we are omitting none of the things that must be done, so that first of all we may deserve to attain what benefits the entire community of the faithful [Note: Thus our manuscripts agree with Quesnel. Other printed editions read: “if only Your Love endures courageously for the time being.”].

It remains for Your Love meanwhile to endure courageously what you do not doubt will contribute to your eternal glory. The bearer of this brief letter will certainly be able to explain faithfully whatever it is toward which, with the Lord’s assistance, we are directing our zeal for faith and charity.

Given on the third day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes [Note: Editions preceding Quesnel, following Merlinus, who used a manuscript of collection 12, have “the third day before the Kalends of October.” Two of our manuscripts of the same collection support Quesnel’s correction. The Ottobonian manuscript 297 of collection 23 comes close, reading “on the Ides of October”; but “the third day before the Ides” is preferable, since other letters are dated on this same day and it is highly probable that Saint Leo wrote to Flavian at the earliest opportunity in order to console him more quickly.].

## Epistle L

[Note: Alternatively numbered 45. The letter formerly numbered 50 is now 66. Written 15 October 449.]

[Note: This letter survives in manuscripts of collections 12, 17, 18, 19, 22, and 23. Its Greek version was published by Cotelerius in volume I of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 57. From Epistle 59, chapter 1, we learn that this letter was sent through Epiphanius and Dionysius.]

## To the Constantinopolitans, through Epiphanius and Dionysius, notaries of the Roman Church

### Synopsis

I. After the pseudo-synod at Ephesus, he urges the Constantinopolitans to adhere to the faith and to Flavian.  
II. He consoles them concerning Flavian’s unjust deposition.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Leo the bishop and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome send greetings in the Lord to their most beloved sons, the clergy, the dignitaries, and the people residing in Constantinople [Note: We have added the five words “most beloved sons, greetings in the Lord” from all the manuscripts, both ours and Baluze’s collection 17 of Chalcedon, as well as from the Venetian manuscript of collection 22. The Greek version also agrees.].

### Chapter I

When what was done at Ephesus contrary to everyone’s expectation was brought to our knowledge, we confess that our spirit was overwhelmed with great grief. We could hardly have believed that iniquity had been permitted to such an extent, had not our son Hilary the deacon—who had been sent by us, in our place, with others to attend the synod—returned by flight, avoiding participation in an unjust sentence [Note: We have deleted here the words “to us,” inserted by Quesnel, on the authority of the Regensburg manuscript, the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, and the Greek translation. The latter incorrectly offers Ἰλαρίων for Hilary, as do two of our Latin manuscripts.].

For although a voice of opposition had been raised there by our representatives, the bishop of Alexandria, who alone claimed everything for himself through the immoderate power of his position [Note: Thus the majority and the more authoritative of our manuscripts, and all of Baluze’s. “Impotentia” is understood as “immoderate power.” The printed editions read “his power”], contemptuously refused to hear it. He dragged unwilling priests into participation in his own purpose, so that by force they might be compelled to sign, although they had found no adequate cause for condemnation [Note: This is better in the Regensburg manuscript, the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, and the Venetian manuscript of collection 22 than in the printed editions, which read “drawing them out.”].

But we trust that such audacity will in no way please a pious and Christian emperor [Note: The printed editions read “most Christian.” We have followed the excellent Regensburg and Chalcedonian manuscripts, supported by the Greek version.].

Now that we have learned that your Church has been scattered by this action, we have judged that you must be consoled and exhorted by our letters, so that you may resist the wickedness of the faithless in defense of the Catholic faith [Note: Nearly all our manuscripts and the editions preceding Quesnel read this way; Quesnel has “we believe.” Next, on the basis of the Greek, “by this action” should be read in place of “for this reason.”].

For we do not wish Your Love to be weighed down by this grief, since greater glory will follow your steadfastness, if no threats and no fear tear you away from your approved priest [Note: The Ottobonian manuscript of collection 23 reads “since your steadfastness will be followed by greater glory.”] [Note: “Will have torn you away” is more correctly read in the Regensburg manuscript and other Chalcedonian manuscripts than in the printed editions, which read “will have divided you.”].

For whoever, while your bishop Flavian is safe and alive, dares to invade his priesthood will never be held in our communion and will not be counted among the bishops.

For just as we anathematized Nestorius in his perversion [Note: The Ottobonian manuscript reads “we anathematize”], so we condemn with equal execration those who deny the truth of our flesh in the Lord Jesus Christ.

### Chapter II

Stand, therefore, in the spirit of Catholic truth, and receive the apostolic exhortation through the ministry of our mouth: “For it has been granted to you, for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in Him but also to suffer for Him” (Philippians 1:29).

Do not suppose, most beloved, that divine protection is lacking, or will ever be lacking, from His holy Church. The purity of the faith shines forth when the filth of errors is separated from it.

Therefore, again and again, before the sight of the Lord, we jointly implore and admonish you not to be moved by plots or by anyone’s persuasions [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “persuasion”] from the faith in which you have been founded and in which we know the most Christian emperor to remain. Rather, keep before the eyes of your hearts, in the person of your bishop, the one for whom he himself does not fear to suffer all that has been inflicted [Note: The Ottobonian manuscript adds “your.” Immediately afterward, in place of “the same,” the Verona manuscript 57 reads “indeed.”] [Note: This reading is found in several of our better manuscripts. Otherwise: “whatever things were inflicted.”].

We wish you to be imitators of him in every respect, so that you may share with him the reward of faith.

Given on the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes [Note: The Regensburg and Dijon manuscripts of Baluze, as in the preceding letters, especially 44 and 45, which are similarly inscribed in the name of the Roman synod, read “the third day before the Ides of October.” This may be better, as appears from Epistle 59: these letters were delivered to Epiphanius the tribune, to whom Epistle 44 to Theodosius, dated on the third day before the Ides of October, was likewise delivered according to Epistle 54. Hence all the letters inscribed in the name of the synod, including the following one, are dated on the same day in the cited Regensburg and Dijon manuscripts.].

### Greek version

Leo the bishop and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome send greetings in the Lord to the most beloved sons—the clergy, the dignitaries, and all the people residing in Constantinople.

When what was done at Ephesus contrary to everyone’s expectation came to our knowledge, we confess that our soul was overwhelmed with great grief. We could not easily believe that lawlessness had been permitted to such an extent, had not our son Hilary the deacon, who had been sent in our place with others to attend the synod, returned by flight, avoiding participation in the injustice.

Although, to be sure, a voice of opposition had been raised there by our representatives, the bishop of Alexandria—who claimed everything for himself through his immoderate power—spurned hearing it, dragging the bishops unwillingly into participation in his own purpose, so that by violence they might be compelled to sign, although they had been unable to find even one sufficient ground for deposition [Col. 0842C].

But we believe that this audacity can in no way please the pious and Christian emperor.

Now, since we have learned that your Church has been scattered by this action, we believe that you must be consoled and exhorted through our letters, so that you may oppose the lawlessness of the faithless in defense of the Catholic faith [Col. 0844A].

For we do not wish Your Love to be weighed down by this grief, when greater glory follows your steadfastness, so that no threat and no fear may be able to tear you away from your approved bishop [Note: The Greek text has “your steadfastness,” though the Latin manuscripts read “your bishop.”].

For if anyone, while Flavian your bishop is healthy and alive, dares to take over his high-priesthood, he will never enter our communion and will not be counted among the bishops.

For just as we anathematized Nestorius in his perversion, so we condemn with equal detestation those who deny the truth of our flesh in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Stand, therefore, in the spirit of [Catholic] truth, and receive the apostolic exhortation through the ministry of our mouth: since it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in Him but also to suffer for Him.

Do not wish to suppose, beloved, that divine protection will ever be abandoned or lacking to His holy Church [perhaps: “divine vindication”]. For the purity of the faith shines forth when the filth of error is separated from it.

Therefore, again and again, before the Lord, we jointly testify and remind you not to be moved by ambushes or by any deceptions from the faith in which you have been founded and in which we know the most Christian emperor to remain. Rather, keep Him before your eyes in the person of your bishop, for whose sake he himself did not fear to suffer all that was inflicted.

We desire that you become imitators of him in every respect, so that you may be able to receive with him the crown of faith.

## Epistle LI

[Note: Alternatively numbered 47. The letter formerly numbered 51 is now 67. Written 15 October 449.]

[Note: This letter is found in the same collections as the preceding one. We owe its Greek translation also to Cotelerius, who published it from royal manuscripts in volume I of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 64.]

## To Faustus and the other Constantinopolitan archimandrites

### Synopsis

He exhorts them to steadfastness in every good thing, especially faith and charity, and denounces the proceedings of the second council of Ephesus.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

Leo and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome send greetings in the Lord to their most beloved sons, Faustus, Martin, Peter, and Emmanuel, priests and archimandrites of the Constantinopolitan monasteries [Note: The manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection read: “Leo the bishop and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome, to Faustus, Martin, Peter, Magnus, Elias, and Emmanuel, priests and archimandrites of the monasteries of Constantinople, most beloved sons in the Lord, greetings.” The printed editions are not very different, and Quesnel followed them. In his second edition alone, after the name Elias, he added “and Emmanuel,” who appears in the Greek version, and appended the following note:

“Cotelerius, in his notes on the Greek version, suspects that Manuel was formed from Magnus and Elias. With the greatest respect for that learned man, the opposite seems more probable to me. For Emmanuel is always named among the Constantinopolitan archimandrites, both in Leo’s Epistle 53, now 71, and in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, session 4, where these same men are ordered to enter the synod and their petition to Marcian Augustus is reported. Magnus and Elias, however, are nowhere read. Therefore, through a scribal error, Magnus and Elias were put in place of Emmanuel; or else it must be said that both died after this letter was written or joined Eutyches, and for that reason were omitted.”

For this reason we preferred the reading of the Regensburg manuscript, which omits Magnus and Elias but gives Emmanuel. The ancient Greek version also confirms it and demonstrates as highly probable Quesnel’s conjecture that Magnus and Elias have erroneously intruded in place of Manuel.].

Although what we wrote to the Constantinopolitan Church could not have remained unknown to your devoted concern, nevertheless we have thought it appropriate to exhort Your Love also by a special letter, so that, remembering your holy profession, which consists especially in faith and charity [Note: The Grimani and Ottobonian manuscripts read “promise.” In the Regensburg manuscript “holy” is absent], you may drive from your hearts all the scandals that have arisen against the peace of the Church, retaining in devout thought the saying of the blessed Apostle: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Galatians 1:9).

And preserve unanimity with our brother Flavian the bishop, whom the Lord permitted for a time to be tested by the faction of the impious, so that He might make His approved priest more illustrious through the merit of perseverance [Note: The common editions read “unity.” The authority of the Regensburg and Chalcedonian manuscripts, as well as the Venetian manuscript of collection 22, prevailed. The Ottobonian manuscript of collection 23 supports the reading “unanimity with our brother and fellow bishop Flavian.”].

These disturbances must, with the help of God’s grace, quickly be destroyed [Note: Thus most manuscripts and editions. Quesnel reads “so that everything may be destroyed.” Two Vatican manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection read “so that whatever is rejected may be…”], and everything that is rejected must be cast away from the purity of the Church, which receives neither stain nor wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27).

This is especially necessary since insane ignorance has advanced so far that, against the sacrament of human salvation, the truth of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ is denied, and the herald and defender of the ancient faith is subjected to insults because he did not assent to the blasphemies which our holy Fathers long ago condemned in many heretics. In him, indeed, the reverence due to all the Lord’s priests is struck, and all the members of Christ’s body are assaulted.

But since it is glorious for us to endure for the sake of the truth whatever God may wish us to suffer, we call you into fellowship in our endurance through paternal exhortations, so that, through your love, what we have written may become known to all who serve God; and, resisting the enemies of the Gospel, you may abandon neither love for your shepherd nor the unity of the Catholic faith [Note: Quesnel notes in the margin: “Alternatively, unanimity.” The Ottobonian manuscript reads “truth.”].

For the things recently done at Ephesus against justice and the discipline of the canons through the immoderate power of one man do not permit any principle of the Catholic faith to be regarded as valid [Note: The printed editions read “through shamelessness.” The Regensburg manuscript reads “through impatience”; the Chalcedonian and Venetian manuscripts read “through power.” Baluze’s Dijon manuscript alone has “through impotence,” but with dots placed beneath the letters indicating that they should be deleted. The meaning of *impotentia* as “immoderate power” is familiar to Leo in the preceding letters, where he speaks of Dioscorus. It seems to have been unknown to those who either marked the letters for deletion or altered *impotentia* to *impudentia* or *impatientia*. The Greek interpreter also read *impotentia*, from whose version Cotelerius rendered “immoderate power.”].

Given on the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes [Note: This is the reading of Quesnel’s manuscripts, two of Baluze’s, four of our Chalcedonian manuscripts, the Venetian manuscript of collection 22, and the Ottobonian manuscript of collection 23. Baluze’s Dijon manuscripts and our Regensburg manuscript read “the third day before the Ides of October,” perhaps more correctly, as appears from note 15 in the preceding letter. Editions preceding Quesnel read “the eighth day before the Ides of October.”].

### Greek version

Leo the bishop and the holy synod assembled in the city of Rome, to Faustinus, Martinus, Peter, Manuel, priests and archimandrites of the Constantinopolitan monasteries.

Although the things that we wrote to the Constantinopolitan Church could not have escaped the concern of Your Love, nevertheless we thought it fitting to exhort Your Love also by a personal letter, so that, remembering your holy [promise], which consists specifically in faith and love, you may cast away from your heart all the scandals stirred up against the Church, holding fast with devout intention to the declarations of the blessed Apostle:

“If anyone evangelizes you contrary to what you received, let him be anathema.”

And preserve unanimity with our brother Flavian the bishop, whom the Lord permitted for a time to be tested by the machinations of the impious, so that He might make His own approved high priest more illustrious through perseverance.

For these disturbances must quickly be dissolved with the help of God’s grace, and everything rejected must be cast away from the purity of the Church, which receives neither stain nor wrinkle. This is especially so because, through a mad cause [perhaps: “ignorance”], they have advanced so far that, against the mystery of human salvation, the truth of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ is denied; and the herald and defender of the ancient faith, because he did not agree with the blasphemies which our holy Fathers long ago condemned in many heretics, is subjected to insults. In this way the honor of all the Lord’s priests is struck, and all the members of Christ’s body are assaulted.

But since it is glorious for us, if God should wish us to suffer anything, to endure it for the truth [the Greek includes “and”], we are summoned into fellowship in endurance by paternal exhortations, so that through your love what we have written may be made known to all who serve God. Standing against the enemies of the Gospel, do not abandon either the love of your shepherd [Greek: “your shepherd’s love”] or the unity of the Catholic faith.

Since the things recently done at Ephesus against the truth and the knowledge of the canons through the immoderate power of one man do not permit any conformity with the Catholic faith to be accepted, [the letter ends here in the supplied text].

## Epistle LII

[Note: Alternatively placed after Epistle 47. The letter formerly numbered 52 is now 69. Written toward the end of 449.]

[Note: This letter was taken from Theodoret’s edition. It was written after his deposition at the pseudo-synod at Ephesus. When he learned that the legates had opposed his deposition and, after receiving Leo’s famous letter to Flavian, discovered that his own doctrine was confirmed by it and alien to the doctrine of that pseudo-synod, he sent this letter to the same pontiff to commend his case to him. It was therefore written shortly after the pseudo-synod, especially since he had not yet received the council’s proceedings, at least not in their entirety: he believed that Renatus, a Roman presbyter, had attended it, although Renatus had died on the journey before the synod. It was therefore probably written toward the end of 449. In the letter itself, chapter 4, he states that he had governed the Church for twenty-six years; and in another letter, 116, he mentions the same number of years of his episcopate when he was deposed at Ephesus on 10 August 449. He therefore wrote this letter in the same year in which he was deposed.

At the same time he wrote two other letters: one, Epistle 116, to Renatus, whom he presumed to be alive; the other, Epistle 118, to the archdeacon of the Roman Church, asking them to assist him with Leo. Since these matters are contained more fully in the letter to Leo, we judged it superfluous to insert those letters among Leo’s letters. Hence Quesnel also added only the letter to Leo to his edition.]

## Theodoret, Bishop of Cyrrhus, to the holy Pope Leo

### Synopsis

I. He rightly hastens to the apostolic see, which excels the others by so many prerogatives.  
II. He launches into praise of Saint Leo and commends his zeal against the Manichaeans and his letter to Flavian.  
III. He complains how unjustly he was deposed, without being summoned to trial.  
IV. He enumerates the labors he has undertaken for the Church.  
V. He asks not to be rejected when appealing to the apostolic see; he wishes his faith to be proved from his writings, which he identifies.  
VI. He wishes Leo to instruct him what he ought to do concerning the sentence of Ephesus.  
VII. He commends his legates and himself to Leo’s prayers and concern; imperial letters are detaining him and others so that they cannot come to the pontiff.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### To Leo, Bishop of Rome

### Chapter I

If Paul, the herald of truth, the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, hastened to the great Peter in order to bring back from him an explanation for those at Antioch who were disputing concerning life according to the Law, how much more should we, humble and insignificant as we are, hasten to your apostolic see, so that we may receive from you a remedy for the wounds of the Churches.

For it is fitting that you should hold primacy in all things. Your see is adorned with many prerogatives. Other cities are adorned by their size, beauty, or abundance of inhabitants; some that lack these things are nevertheless illumined by certain spiritual gifts. But to your city the giver of good things has granted an abundance of blessings.

It is the greatest and most illustrious of all, presiding over the inhabited world and overflowing with a multitude of inhabitants. In addition, it gave birth to the empire that now rules the world and bestowed its own name upon its subjects.

Above all, faith adorns it, and the divine Apostle is a trustworthy witness, crying out: “Your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world” (Romans 1:8). If, immediately after receiving the seeds of the saving proclamation, it produced these admirable fruits in such abundance, what discourse could be adequate to praise the piety now flourishing in it?

It also possesses the tombs of the common fathers and teachers of truth, Peter and Paul, which illumine the souls of the faithful. That most blessed and divine pair arose in the East and sent forth their rays in every direction; but in the West they willingly underwent the setting of life, and from there they now illuminate the whole world.

They made your see most noble; this is the summit of your blessings. But their God has now also illumined their see, establishing Your Holiness in it, pouring forth the rays of orthodox faith.

### Greek version

To Leo, bishop of Rome.

If Paul, the herald of truth, the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, ran to the great Peter in order to bring from him a solution for those at Antioch who disputed concerning life according to the Law, how much more do we, insignificant and small, run to your apostolic throne, so that we may receive from you healing for the wounds of the Churches.

For it is fitting that you should have primacy in all things. Your throne is adorned with many advantages. Other cities are adorned by their size, beauty, or the multitude of their inhabitants; some deprived of these are illumined by certain spiritual gifts. But to your city the provider of good things has given an abundance of blessings.

For it is itself the greatest and most brilliant of all, presiding over the inhabited world and surging with the multitude of its inhabitants. In addition, it has produced the empire that now rules and has shared its own designation with those under its rule.

Faith especially adorns it, and the divine Apostle is a trustworthy witness, crying out that “your faith is proclaimed throughout the whole world.”

If, immediately after receiving the seeds of the saving proclamation, it became rich in such admirable fruits, what discourse would suffice to celebrate the piety now practiced in it?

It also has the tombs of the common fathers and teachers of truth, Peter and Paul, illuminating the souls of the faithful.

Their thrice-blessed and divine pair arose in the East and sent their rays everywhere. But in the West they willingly received the setting of life, and from there they now illumine the inhabited world.

They made your most illustrious throne renowned. This is the summit of your blessings. But the God of those men has now also glorified their throne, establishing Your Holiness in it and making it send forth the rays of orthodoxy.

### Chapter II

Since there are many other proofs of this matter readily available, your zeal against the infamous Manichaeans is sufficient—zeal which Your Holiness recently displayed [Note: Namely, in the year 444, when Epistle 7 against the Manichaeans was published] and by which you revealed the love you bear toward God through your devotion to divine things.

What you have now written is also sufficient to demonstrate your apostolic character. For we encountered what Your Holiness wrote concerning the incarnation of God and our Savior, and we admired the exactness and care of the work [Note: This refers to Epistle 28, to Flavian].

Both writings declared the same thing: the eternal divinity of the Only-begotten from the eternal Father, and his humanity from the seed of Abraham and David; and that the nature assumed was like ours in every respect, differing in this one regard, that it remained free from sin, since sin arises not from nature but from free choice.

The letters also contained this: that there is one Only-begotten Son of God, and that his divinity is incapable of suffering, incapable of being changed or altered, just as are the Father who begot him and the Holy Spirit.

For this reason he assumed a passible nature, because the divine nature did not receive suffering, so that through the suffering of his own flesh he might bestow impassibility upon those who believe in him.

These things and others related to them were contained in the letters. We, for our part, admired your spiritual wisdom and praised the grace of the Holy Spirit who spoke through you. We ask, entreat, implore, and humbly beseech Your Holiness to extend assistance to the Churches of God tossed by the storm.

### Chapter III

For while we hoped, through those whom Your Holiness sent to Ephesus, for an end to the storm, we fell into a more grievous tempest [Note: In Baronius under the year 449, numbers 116 and following, this letter is transcribed in Latin from the translation of Federicus Metius, highly skilled in both languages, as is clear from number 124. Taking the neuter expression διὰ τῶν ἀποσταλέντων as referring to the letters sent by Your Holiness, he rendered it “through what was written by Your Holiness to Ephesus.” In that sense it would refer to the letter to the Ephesian synod, namely Epistle 33, which Theodoret received together with Epistle 28 to Flavian, as we stated from his Epistle 121 to Anatolius.].

For the most righteous bishop of Alexandria was not content with the unjust and most unjust deposition of the most holy and God-beloved Lord Flavian, bishop of Constantinople; nor was his soul satisfied by the similar slaughter of the other bishops. He also slaughtered me with his pen while I was absent, without summoning me to trial, without accusing me in person, and without questioning me about my belief concerning the incarnation of God and our Savior.

Judges do not condemn murderers, tomb-breakers, or invaders of other men’s marriages before they have either confirmed the crimes charged against them by their own confession or clearly convicted them through others.

But he condemned me, nurtured here in the divine laws, from a distance of thirty-five stages, as he pleased [Note: Quesnel reads “thirty stages.” We have supplied “five” from the Greek].

Nor was this the only time he did so. Even in the preceding year, when two men infected with the Apollinarian disease had gone to him and fabricated accusations against us, he rose up in the Church and fastened an anathema upon us, doing so after I had written to him and explained my beliefs in letters.

### Chapter IV

As for me, I mourn the Church’s storm, but I seek tranquility. For after governing for twenty-six years, with the aid of your prayers, the Church entrusted to me by the God of all, I endured not the slightest reproach either under the most blessed bishop Theodotus of the East or under those who succeeded him in the see of Antioch.

With divine grace cooperating with me, I freed more than a thousand souls from the disease of Marcion and brought many others from the parties of Arius and Eunomius to Christ the Lord.

I also received pastoral care of eight hundred Churches—for Cyrus has that many parishes—in which, with the aid of your prayers, no tares have been left, but our flock has been rescued from every heretical error.

He who sees all things knows how many stones thrown by unspeakable heretics I have received, and how many struggles I have had in the cities of the East against pagans, Jews, and every heretical error.

And after so many sweats and labors I have been condemned without being summoned to trial.

### Chapter V

But I await the judgment of your apostolic see, and I pray and beseech Your Holiness to extend the aid of your upright and just tribunal to me, who am appealing [Note: The Greek text has ἐπικαλουμένῳ. The verb ἐπικαλέομαι frequently means “to appeal” to a higher judge. Thus Acts 25:11: Καίσαρα ἐπικαλοῦμαι, “I appeal to Caesar”; and John Chrysostom, in his letter to Pope Innocent preserved in Constantius, Epistle 4, p. 778: ἡμῶν σύνοδον ἐπικαλουμένων, “when we appeal to the synod.” Three other examples from Plutarch may be found in Robert Constantine’s lexicon. Hence Metius’s translation, in the passage cited by Baronius, expresses the sense of one appealing rather than one invoking: “I supplicate and beseech you that your just and upright judgment may assist me as I appeal,” etc. On Theodoret’s appeal, see our observations in Quesnel’s Dissertation 10.].

Order me to come to you and demonstrate that my doctrine follows in the footsteps of the Apostles.

For I possess writings composed partly twenty years ago, partly eighteen, partly fifteen, and partly twelve years ago: some against Arians and Eunomians, some against Jews and pagans, some against the magicians who are in Persia, others concerning universal providence, and still others concerning theology and the divine incarnation.

By divine grace I have also expounded both the apostolic writings and the prophetic oracles.

From these it is easy to determine whether I have preserved a steadfast rule of faith or departed from its rectitude.

But I beseech you not to reject my supplications, nor to despise my miserable old age, treated insultingly after so many labors.

### Chapter VI

Above all, I ask to be taught by you whether I ought to acquiesce in this unjust deposition or not, for I await your judgment.

If you order me to remain among those condemned, I shall remain and will not thereafter trouble any human being; rather, I shall await the just judgment of God and our Savior.

As the Lord God is my witness, concern for honor and glory does not touch me; what troubles me is the scandal that has been created. For many of the simpler people, especially those who have emerged from various heresies through our efforts, will look at the see of those who condemned us and perhaps think us heretics, since they cannot perceive the perfection of the doctrine.

After having held the episcopate for so many years, I acquired neither a house, nor a field, nor an obol, nor a tomb. Instead, I embraced voluntary poverty and, immediately after the death of my parents, distributed what had come to us from them, as all who live in the East know.

### Chapter VII

Above all, I beseech your sacred head, beloved of God, to extend aid and assistance to me through your prayers.

Through the most reverend and God-beloved priests Hypatius and Abramius, chorepiscopi, and Alypius, the leader of the monks who are with us, I have presented these matters to Your Holiness.

For royal letters detained me, as they did others, so that I could not hasten to you.

I ask Your Holiness to receive them with paternal affection, to lend them your sincere and kindly ears, and, through your care and providence, to deem worthy of consideration my old age, harassed by accusations and attacked without cause.

Above all, may Your Holiness devote the greatest possible care to the faith that has been assailed by plots and preserve the paternal inheritance intact for the Churches, so that for these things Your Holiness may also receive the rewards prepared by the munificent and generous Lord.

There are many other proofs of this as well; but your zeal against the ill-named Manichaeans is sufficient—a zeal which your Holiness recently exercised, demonstrating your devotion to divine things. What you have now written is also enough to reveal your apostolic character. For we have read what your Holiness wrote concerning the incarnation of your God and Savior, and we have admired the precision of what was written.

For you made both points clear at once: the eternal divinity of the Only-begotten from the eternal Father, and his humanity from the seed of Abraham and David. You also showed that the nature assumed resembled ours in every respect, differing only in remaining untouched by every sin, since sin springs not from nature but from the will. Your writings also contained this: that the Only-begotten Son of God is one, while his divinity is impassible, immutable, and unchangeable, just as are the Father who begot him and the all-holy Spirit. For this reason he assumed a passible nature, since the divine nature could not receive suffering, so that through the suffering of his own flesh he might grant impassibility to those who believe in him.

These things, and whatever is related to them, were contained in the writings. We, having marveled at your spiritual wisdom, have praised the grace of the Holy Spirit who spoke through you; and we beseech, entreat, implore, and supplicate your Holiness to come to the aid of the churches of God that are being storm-tossed. [Col. 0850A–B]

For, expecting that the storm would be calmed through those whom your Holiness sent to Ephesus, we have fallen into a more violent tempest. The most just president of Alexandria was not satisfied with the unlawful and most unjust deposition of the most holy and God-beloved Flavian, bishop of the Constantinopolitan Church of the Lord; nor was his anger filled by the similar slaughter of the other bishops. Rather, he slaughtered me also, though absent, with the pen in the same way: he neither summoned me before a tribunal nor judged me when present, nor asked what I believed concerning the incarnation of our God and Savior.

Judges do not condemn murderers, grave-robbers, or those who have violated the marriages of others before the accused themselves confirm the charges by their confessions or are clearly convicted by others. Yet he who was brought up on the divine laws condemned me, absent by thirty-five stations, as he pleased. And he did not do this only now. Last year also, when two men who had embraced the disease of Apollinaris had gone there and woven slanders against me, he rose against us in the churches and anathematized me. I had written to him and explained in letters what I believed. [Col. 0850C]

I grieve over the Church’s storm, but I welcome quiet. For twenty-six years, by your prayers, I have directed the Church entrusted to me by the whole body of the Church. Neither under the most blessed Theodotus, president of the East, nor under those who succeeded him on the throne of Antioch did I incur any reproach of consequence. With divine grace assisting me, I freed more than a thousand souls from the disease of Marcion, and brought many others from the faction of Arius and Eunomius to the Lord Christ. [Col. 0850D]

I was allotted the care of eight hundred churches, for Cyrus has that many parishes; and in them, through your prayers, not even one tare has remained. Our flock has been freed from every heretical error. He who sees all things knows how many stones I received from the ill-named heretics sent against me, and how many struggles I endured in most of the cities of the East against Greeks, Jews, and every heretical error. Yet, after so many labors and sufferings, I have been condemned without trial. [Col. 0852A]

I await the judgment of your apostolic see. I entreat and implore your Holiness to come to the aid of me, who appeal to your upright and just tribunal; to command me to come to you and demonstrate that my teaching follows the apostolic footsteps.

I have works written twenty years ago, others eighteen years ago, others fifteen years ago, and others twelve years ago: some against Arians and Eunomians, others against Jews and Greeks, others against the Magi in Persia, some concerning universal providence, and others concerning theology and the divine incarnation. By divine grace I have interpreted the apostolic writings and the prophetic oracles. From these it is easy to learn whether I have preserved the rule of faith unwaveringly or departed from its straightness. [Col. 0852B]

I beseech you, therefore, do not reject my supplication, nor overlook my wretched gray hairs, insulted after many labors.

Above all, I implore you to let me know whether I must submit to this unjust deposition or not. I await your judgment. If you command me to remain subject to those who voted against me, I shall remain so, and shall trouble no human being any further; but I shall await the unwavering tribunal of our God and Savior. [Col. 0852C]

As the Lord and Master, God, bears witness, I care neither for honor nor glory, but only for the scandal that has occurred. For many of the simpler people—especially those whom we have rescued from various heresies—may, by looking to the throne of those who condemned us, perhaps conclude that we are heretics, being unable to discern the precision of the doctrine. Although I have served as bishop for so long, I acquired neither a house, nor a field, nor an obol, nor a tomb. I possessed only the poverty that came of itself, and immediately distributed whatever came to us from the Fathers after their death, as all who inhabit the East know.

[Col. 0852D] Above all, I entreat your sacred head, beloved of God, to grant me the assistance of your prayers. I have made these matters known to your Holiness through the most reverent and God-beloved presbyters Hypatius and Abramios, chorepiscopi, and Alypius, exarch of the monks among us. For the bonds of the imperial letters prevented me from traveling to you, just as they prevented the others. [951]

I ask your Holiness to receive them paternally, to grant them a favorable hearing with your unbending ears, to deem my slandered and needlessly persecuted old age worthy of your protection, and above all to care with all your strength for the faith that is being plotted against and to preserve intact for the churches the inheritance of the Fathers, so that your Holiness may receive from the generous Lord the recompense for these things. [Col. 0854A]

## ADMONITION ON THE FRAGMENT OF THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

[Col. 0853]

1. The notable fragment of Anatolius’s letter which we place below, from which we learn that he was ordained after the death of Flavian, was edited by Cotelerius from Codex Regius 940 in volume I, page 66, of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*. Quesnell inserted it into his second edition of Leo, placing it before Letters 69, 70, and 71, written in July of the year 450, in which Anatolius’s ordination is discussed. In his observations on this fragment, however, he asserts that Flavian died around the time of those letters of Leo; that Anatolius was therefore appointed in his place; and that around the same time he sent to the same Leo the letter from which this fragment was excerpted.

We do not agree. Prosper testifies in his *Chronicle* that Flavian passed gloriously to Christ in the year 449, shortly after the Ephesian robbery held in August of that year, while he was in the hands of those who were leading him into exile. The *History of the Eutychianists* agrees, stating that he died on the journey itself, at Epipus, a city of Lydia, while being transported into exile.

This death could indeed have been concealed for some time by Flavian’s enemies, because the people of Constantinople were especially favorable to him. Thus the archimandrites, clergy, and people of Constantinople who sent letters to Leo rather early, around October of 449—as may be gathered from the admonition to Letter 59—were unaware of that bishop’s death. Nevertheless, Theodore the Reader makes it clear that Anatolius was ordained before the end of 449. In fragments of Theodore collected by Valesius, after mentioning Anatolius’s ordination and some circumstances surrounding it, he says: “These things were taking place during the consulship of Protogenes and Asterius.” Accordingly, this letter to Leo appears to have been written toward the end of that year, as was another letter concerning his ordination, mentioned in Letter 71; for letters of this kind were written immediately after an ordination.

2. At about the same time, Theodosius and Pulcheria also sent letters to Leo concerning the same matter, and all these letters appear to have been transmitted together. They had not yet reached Rome in March of 450, when Leo wrote Letters 60 and 61, in which he still presumes Flavian to be alive. The pope may have received them in April or May; we do not know what caused the delay. Since they proposed a difficult matter requiring more mature consultation, Leo may perhaps have held the deliberation for which, as he writes in Letter 67 to Ravennius, he detained the Gallicans Petronius and Regulus for a long time; see note 2 (885d) on that letter.

The matter of Anatolius caused the pope such great trouble that he believed it necessary to choose, instruct, and send four legates to Constantinople—something that required no small delay in responding. Hence it is not surprising that Letters 69, 70, and 71, in which he responds concerning this ordination, were written in July of 450.

Meanwhile, since this fragment, excerpted from Anatolius’s letter, was written immediately after his ordination and before the end of 449, but the exact day and month are unknown, we have judged that it should precede Leo’s letter to Theodosius, which is dated 25 December.

## LETTER LIII, OR FRAGMENT OF A LETTER OF ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO SAINT LEO

[Note: [Col. 0853B] Alternatively placed after Letter 51. What was Letter 53 is now Letter 71. Written toward the end of the year 449.]

Concerning his ordination (G)

[Col. 0853]  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### From the letter of Anatolius of Constantinople to Leo of Rome

[Col. 0853B]

For our most pious and Christ-loving emperor Theodosius, who places everything else after matters relating to God, took the greatest care over this matter when the most holy Church of Constantinople was deprived of its shepherd and ought to receive one capable of governing it.

At first he instructed the most reverent clergy of that city to select, after examination, those most suitable for its administration, reserving to himself the choice of the most distinguished of all. Then, when excessive disagreement arose among these men and all were divided into various factions concerning many candidates, the emperor ordered that clerics residing in the imperial city, including those from other cities who happened to be there on various business—as commonly occurs—should be sought out, so that the most excellent among them might be promoted to episcopal dignity without any partiality. [Col. 0853C; 956]

When this had been done, those who hold authority over everything subsequently decided that the clergy should be permitted to choose the chief bishop. And behold, the vote fell upon me, the least of all—not because of my righteousness, but so that Christ Jesus might display in me all his patience, according to the Apostle (1 Timothy 1:16). Therefore the holy synod of bishops residing in Constantinople was charged to proceed without delay to my ordination.

### Greek version

[953] From the letter of Anatolius of Constantinople to Leo of Rome: [Col. 0854B]

For our most pious and Christ-loving emperor Theodosius, who considers all other things secondary to divine matters, took the greatest care over this matter when the most holy Church in Constantinople was widowed of its shepherd and ought to obtain one capable of directing it.

First he entrusted the most reverent clergy belonging to that church with voting, after examination, for those more suitable to preside, reserving to himself the selection of the most distinguished of all. Then, when excessive dissension arose among them and everyone consequently divided his opinion among many candidates, he ordered that clerics residing in the imperial city, and also those from other cities who happened to be there for various business, as commonly occurs, should be sought out, so that the better of them might be advanced to the episcopate without any partiality. [Col. 0854C; 955]

When this had happened, those who control all things decided that the clergy should be permitted to choose the chief bishop. And behold, the vote reached me, the least of all—not according to my own righteousness, but so that Christ Jesus might altogether display in me his complete patience, according to the Apostle. Therefore the holy synod residing in the city was charged to proceed without delay to my ordination. [Col. 0856A]

## LETTER LIV

[Note: Formerly Letter 23. What was formerly Letter 54 is now Letter 70. Written 25 December 449.]

[Note: This letter has been reread against the Vatican and Venetian manuscripts of Collection 12, from which it was published by Merlin, and especially against the excellent Ratisbon manuscript of Collection 19.]

### TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS

[Col. 0855A]

### Synopsis

He writes that he adheres to the Nicene faith; that Eutyches must be condemned no less than Nestorius; and that a council should be held within Italy.

### Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Theodosius, ever Augustus

It is fitting that a most Christian ruler should be solicitous for the integrity of the Catholic faith. I earnestly ask divine mercy that it inspire your heart with what is true and not permit you to be deceived in any matter by the fraud of human rivalries. [Col. 0855B]

What must be defended by me and by all Catholic priests—the piety of the evangelical and apostolic faith—has been set forth fully and clearly in my letters, which I suppose your Clemency already received some time ago through your servant Epiphanius, the tribune, who was sent for this purpose.

There can be no doubt that we believe this with complete purity and affirm it steadfastly: what the venerable Fathers once assembled at Nicaea established, by the most sacred authority, must be believed and confessed according to the faith of the Creed. [Col. 0856A]

[Note: He openly professes the Nicene faith because Eutyches and his supporters, exalting this faith alone—as is clear from Eutyches’ Letter 21 among Leo’s letters—were unwilling to be compelled to confess two natures in Christ, as though this were contrary to the Nicene Creed, to which they claimed nothing could be added. On this account they advertised themselves as Catholics, while accusing Catholics of departing from the Nicene faith. Thus Theodosius, deceived by the Eutychians, often wrote that he would not permit the priests of the Lord to depart from the Nicene synod. See Letter 69, chapter 1. The pope detected this Eutychian strategy and accusation only after the false Ephesian synod, through later reports and through Theodosius’s recent letters, discussed in the dissertation *On the Lost Letters*, no. 38. For that reason, both in this letter and in the subsequent ones, he expressly professes the Nicene faith, while at the same time declaring that the Nestorians—against whom the Eutychians were especially hostile—deviate from this faith no less than the Eutychians themselves. Compare note 5 (col. 886g) on Letter 67.]

For just as we rightly anathematized the perverse doctrine of Nestorius, so also, Glorious One, we justly condemn the impiety of those who deny that the Lord our Jesus Christ assumed the truth of our flesh. [Note: The word “our” has been supplied from the Ratisbon manuscript.] [Col. 0856B]

Therefore, if your Piety deigns to assent to our suggestion and supplication, commanding that an episcopal council be held within Italy, then, with God’s help, all the scandals that have been stirred up to disturb the whole Church can quickly be cut away. Thus, while the integrity of the Catholic faith is preserved throughout your realm, we shall rejoice that Christian peace remains and that your glory before God increases. [Col. 0856B–C]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of the illustrious men Asturius and Protogenes.

[Note: The printed editions had “the eighth day before the Kalends of June.” Quesnell himself suspected this chronological notice and appended a note: “Since Letter 27, now Letter 31, to Pulcheria expressly testifies that Leo received on the third day before the Ides of May the letters announcing the synod summoned by Theodosius, it is surprising that he makes no mention of this same synod to the emperor. Perhaps the pope thought it necessary to conceal the matter so that he could more freely request from Theodosius that a synod be assembled within Italy; or else the number of the day or month is corrupt in one of the two letters.” Moreover, only in letters written after the Ephesian robbery, dated 13 October and thereafter, did Leo indicate that he desired a council in Italy as a remedy for the scandals that had arisen from that robbery. Epiphanius, who is mentioned in this letter, had also left Rome only in October with Letters 44 and 50, as we noted above in note 4. Therefore the reference to June is certainly corrupt, and the reading of the celebrated manuscripts of Collection 12 is likewise erroneous, since they merely anticipate the day by one, giving the ninth day before the Kalends of June. We have emended the text from the excellent Ratisbon manuscript, where an easy scribal error is evident: January has changed into June. This emendation also corrects and reconciles several other matters that otherwise caused great confusion among scholars.]

## ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING IMPERIAL LETTERS (G)

[Col. 0855]

1. Quesnell correctly noted in the brief admonition placed before the following letters why they were inserted among Leo’s letters. His words are:

“It is clear from the series of the appended letters that they were written at the prompting and urging of Saint Leo and of the entire synod, in whose name and from which the preceding letters of the pontiff were sent. Because of the affinity between the two groups, we have therefore judged that these letters should be printed here. They provide us with a clearer knowledge of that synod, revealing its place, time, subject, and other circumstances; and they appear to have been dictated by Leo himself.”
