More about these matters may be found in Dissertation 1 on the life and deeds of Saint Leo, under the year 449. The three imperial letters to Theodosius, and another to Pulcheria, openly attest Leo’s counsel; but nothing indicates that these were dictated by Leo himself. Indeed, some features are wholly inconsistent with Leo’s manner of writing. [Col. 0857]

2. As for the date, since all the letters of the emperors—both those delivered and those returned—displayed in a single Chalcedonian collection lack chronological notation, different scholars have formed different opinions.

First, something must be established concerning the four earlier letters sent to the East. Everything depends on the interpretation of these words of Valentinian in Letter 55:

“When I had come to Rome to appease the Divinity, on the following day I proceeded to the basilica of the Apostle Peter; and there, after the venerable night of the Apostle’s day, I was asked by the Roman bishop and by others gathered with him from different provinces to write to your Mildness.”

From these words it may be gathered that Valentinian came to Rome on the day before the feast of the Apostle Peter; that on the following day—that is, on the feast itself—he proceeded to the basilica of the Apostle Peter; and that there, after the nocturnal service, Leo and the other bishops who had assembled for the same feast persuaded him to write to Theodosius. Other letters of the same women make it clear that Placidia and Eudoxia were asked to write as well.

3. Cardinal Baronius, under the year 449, no. 164, thought that these four letters were written in that same year after the anniversary of the dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter, which is usually celebrated on 18 November. He therefore supposed that the bishops who had attended the Roman synod mentioned in Letters 44 and following were detained in Rome until that date.

But, apart from the improbability that bishops who had assembled in the city on 29 September were kept in Rome for fifty days after the synod had already ended on 13—or, at the latest, 15—October, as is clear from Letter 44 and those following, no ancient document survives proving that under Pope Leo the dedication of the basilica of Saint Peter was celebrated on 18 November.

Moreover, there is no independent evidence that Valentinian was in Rome in 449, while several documents show that he was there in 450.

4. Quesnellus, in Dissertation 1 under the year 450, no. 1, while attacking Baronius’s opinion, adopted another position that is more plainly erroneous, arguing that these letters were written after the feast of Saint Peter on 29 June 450.

The error is clearly exposed by two considerations. First, Valentinian was in Rome in March of that year, when he issued the law included among the Novels under title 7, *On the Remission of the Remains*, and also in April, as appears from title 38, *On the Annual Shipowners*, and other evidence. Therefore the feast of Saint Peter, before which he had arrived in Rome on the preceding day, cannot have been 29 June.

Second, since Theodosius died on 28 July of that same year, if the letters had been written and sent to him after 29 June, they would have reached Constantinople after his death, and he could not have sent the other letters that survive.

Another feast of Saint Peter must therefore be sought, with Tillemont and Pagi, and one earlier than 7 March 450, when the aforementioned law on the remission of the remains was issued. From the ancient Bucherian Calendar, in which the feast days of the Roman Church are recorded, we learn that Rome celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of March a feast marked with this title: “The Nativity of Peter of the Chair.”

Accordingly, in that year Valentinian came to Rome with the Augustuses on the ninth day before the Kalends of March. On the feast itself Leo, together with the bishops, asked them to write to Theodosius.

Furthermore, from Placidia’s Letter 58 to Pulcheria it may be gathered that they wrote before it became known from Pulcheria’s own letters that she favored the good cause; otherwise Placidia would have inserted some mention of this matter in that letter. It became known in Rome before 17 March of that year, when Saint Leo congratulated Pulcheria on the matter in Letter 60.

Thus the four earlier letters were written shortly after 22 February and before 17 March of that year, most probably toward the end of February.

5. Quesnellus placed beneath each letter written by Valentinian or by the Augustuses the letter returned by Theodosius. We have preferred to follow the method and arrangement of the Chalcedonian collection, including its arrangement in time.

To allow a suitable interval for the transmission of the letters, Theodosius’s letters should be assigned to April; we have therefore placed them after Letters 60 and 61, which were written in March.

6. Although we think it more probable that all these letters were written in Latin, just as laws were likewise written in Latin even when issued in the East, we nevertheless believe that the Latin original has perished and that only the Greek version survives. The Latin copies transmitted to us are an ancient translation from the Greek, produced by someone not very skilled in Latin, as will be evident from several highly obscure passages and badly rendered expressions that can in no way correspond to the original of the Augustuses.

For this same reason the date, always omitted by the Greek collector, is likewise absent from the Latin text. It was supplied when the author of the Latin Chalcedonian collection found the Latin originals. See the Preface to the Letters, no. 36.

7. We now present the title prefixed in the Chalcedonian collection to the three imperial letters 55, 56, and 57. In the Greek collection it reads:

“Imperial letter sent, one from our lord Valentinian, another from the divine memory of Placidia, and also from the worshipful Empress Eudoxia, to Theodosius of divine memory, asking that he command a council to be held in the regions of Italy.”

In the Latin manuscripts it is rendered:

“Sacred letters, both from our lord Valentinian and from Placidia of divine memory, and also from Eudoxia Augusta, to Theodosius of divine memory, asking that he command a council to be held in the regions of Italy.”

## LETTER LV

[Note: Formerly after Letter 47; what was formerly Letter 55 is now Letter 74. Written toward the end of February 450.]

### OF THE EMPEROR VALENTINIAN TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS (G)

[Col. 0857]  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To my lord Theodosius, most glorious, victor and triumphant, perpetual emperor and father: Valentinian, glorious, victor and triumphant, ever Augustus and son.

[Col. 0857A]

When I had come to the city of Rome to appease the Divinity, on the following day I proceeded to the basilica of the Apostle Peter. There, after the venerable night of the Apostle’s day, I was asked by the Roman bishop and by others gathered with him from different provinces to write to your Mildness concerning the faith, which, being the guardian of all believing souls, is said to have been disturbed.

We received this faith from our forefathers and must defend it with all fitting devotion, preserving intact in our own times the honor of its proper veneration toward the blessed Apostle Peter. Thus the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome, to whom antiquity has granted the primacy of priesthood over all, may have the place and power to judge concerning faith and priests, most sacred father and venerable emperor.

For this reason, according to the custom of councils, the bishop of Constantinople also appealed to him by a written petition because of the dispute that arose concerning the faith. [Note: The manuscripts read “for this reason.” The note explains that, according to the Greek, this refers to the usage or custom of councils. The plural “councils” indicates not one council but several in which Roman pontiffs, by virtue of their priestly primacy, exercised the power they possess to judge concerning faith and priests—for example, Pope Julius in the Roman synod judged the case of Athanasius, and Innocent judged that of John Chrysostom, who, having been deposed in the East, fled to the apostolic see. The reference may also be to the Council of Sardica, whose explicit canons confirm the custom of appealing to the supreme pontiff.]

I therefore did not refuse to assent to this man, who requested and earnestly pleaded for our common salvation, so that I might present my petition to your Mildness: that the aforementioned priest, after all the other priests from throughout the world had been assembled within Italy and every prejudice had been removed, might investigate from the beginning the entire case at issue with careful examination and pronounce the judgment demanded by faith and the reason of true Divinity.

For in our times the wantonness of mobs must not prevail against religion, while the faith has until now been preserved unshaken. [Note: One manuscript reads “against religion”; another has “against faith and religion.” The printed editions have “and religion,” but the ancient version is retained here.]

For a more complete knowledge of your Divinity, we have also sent the records, through which your Piety may learn both the desires and the acclamations of all. [Note: These proceedings, acclamations, and the mention of the assembled bishops suggest that some kind of synod was held on the feast of Saint Peter itself, 22 February 450. See admonition no. 4 above. One manuscript reads “explanation” instead of “acclamations,” but has “acclamations” in the margin.]

[961] ### Greek version

To Lord Theodosius, glorious, victor and triumphant, eternal emperor and father: Valentinian, victor, glorious, triumphant, ever emperor and son.

[Col. 0858A]

When I had arrived in the city of Rome to make the Divine favorable, on the following day I went forth to the shrine of the Apostle Peter. There, after the venerable night of the Apostle’s day, I was deemed worthy by the bishop of Rome and by others gathered with him from different provinces to write to your Mildness concerning the faith, which, being the guardian of all believing souls, is said to have been disturbed.

We received this faith as handed down from our ancestors and ought, with the appropriate religious devotion, to defend it and preserve intact in our own times the honor of its proper reverence toward the blessed Apostle Peter. Thus the most blessed bishop of the city of the Romans, to whom antiquity granted the priesthood over all, may have the opportunity and means to judge concerning the faith and priests, most holy father and venerable emperor.

For this reason, according to the custom of councils, the bishop of Constantinople also appealed to him by a petition because of the dispute that had arisen concerning the faith. Since this man was requesting and earnestly pleading for our common salvation, I did not refuse to assent and to make my petition acceptable to your Mildness: that the aforesaid priest, after the remaining priests from the whole inhabited world had been assembled within Italy and every prior prejudice had been removed, might investigate from the beginning the case at issue through careful examination and issue the decision demanded by faith and by the reasoning of true divinity. [Col. 0858B–C]

For in our times no innovation in religion ought to be introduced through the tumult of presumption, since the faith has until now been preserved unshaken. For a perfect instruction concerning your Divinity, we have also sent the proceedings, through which your Piety may learn the desires and outcries of all. [Col. 0860B]

## LETTER LVI

[Note: Formerly Letter 56; now Letter 75. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

### GALLA PLACIDIA AUGUSTA TO THEODOSIUS (G)

[Col. 0859]  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To the victorious Lord Theodosius, triumphant, ever Augustus, son: Galla Placidia, most pious and flourishing, perpetual Augusta and mother.

[Col. 0859C]

While, upon our very entrance into the ancient city, we were concerned to render worship to the most blessed Apostle Peter, at the very altar of the martyr, the most reverend bishop Leo, delaying a little after prayer, lamented before us on account of the Catholic faith. Taking that same chief of the Apostles, whom we had recently approached, as witness, and surrounded by a multitude of bishops whom he had gathered from innumerable cities of Italy according to the authority or dignity of their respective places, he mingled tears with his words and called forth our own sighs to share in his lamentation.

For it is no small loss that, as a result of what has occurred, the faith which had been regularly guarded through ancient times by our most sacred father Constantine, the first Christian to shine in imperial power, should recently have been disturbed at the will of one man. This man is said to have exercised hatred and contention rather than justice in the synod of the city of Ephesus, assaulting the bishop of Constantinople, Flavian, with the presence and threat of soldiers, because he had sent a petition to the apostolic see and to all the bishops of these regions through those who had been sent to the council by the most reverend bishop of Rome, who, according to the definitions of the Council of Nicaea, are accustomed to attend councils.

[Note: The reference appears to be to canon 7 of Sardica according to Dionysius, but canon 5 in the Greek version, concerning the pontiff’s legates, who act in councils in his name and by his authority. The Sardican canons were elsewhere shown to have been counted among the Nicene canons, especially according to the ancient custom of the Roman Church, and were called Nicene.]

Therefore let your Mildness, resisting such great disturbances, command that the truth of the Catholic faith be preserved undefiled. Let the matter be referred, according to the form and definition of the apostolic see—which we likewise venerate as pre-eminent—while Flavian remains in every respect unharmed in the priestly office, to the judgment of a council and of the apostolic see, in which that first man who was deemed worthy to receive the keys of heaven established the primacy of the episcopate. [Col. 0861B]

It is fitting that we preserve reverence in every respect toward this greatest city, which is mistress of all the lands. Take even more careful thought in this matter, lest what our generation guarded in former times appear to be diminished under us, and lest the present example produce schisms among bishops and holy churches.

[965] ### Greek version

To the victorious Lord Theodosius, ever triumphant emperor and son: Galla Placidia, most pious and flourishing, eternal empress and mother.

[Col. 0860C]

When, at our very entrance into the ancient city, we were concerned to render worship to the most blessed Apostle Peter, at the very worshipful altar of the martyr, the most reverent bishop Leo, pausing briefly after prayer, lamented before us because of the Catholic faith. Taking as witness the chief of the Apostles himself, whom we had recently approached, he was surrounded by a multitude of bishops whom he had gathered in Italy from innumerable cities according to the authority of their own place and their dignity. Joining tears to his words, he summoned our cries also into fellowship with his own lamentations.

For the loss resulting from what has happened is not small: the faith of the Catholic rule, guarded for so many ages from our most divine father Constantine, who was the first Christian to shine in imperial power, has recently been disturbed according to the opinion of one man. This man is said to have exercised hatred and contentious quarrelling rather than justice in the synod of the city of the Ephesians, striking terror into Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, by the presence and fear of soldiers because he had sent a petition to the apostolic throne and to all the bishops of these regions through those sent to the council by the most reverent bishop of Rome. These men, according to the regulations of the Council of Nicaea, are accustomed to assemble, most pure and worshipful lord, son and emperor.

For this reason let your Mildness, setting itself against such great disturbances, command that the truth be kept undefiled and the faith of the Catholic religion preserved. Let the case be referred, according to the form and definition of the apostolic throne—which we likewise venerate as pre-eminent—to the council of the apostolic throne, while Flavian remains unharmed in the priestly office. In that throne the first man, deemed worthy to receive the keys of heaven, adorned the episcopate of the high priesthood.

It is fitting that we preserve reverence in every respect toward this greatest city, which is mistress of all the lands. Take more careful thought in this matter, so that what our generation preserved in earlier times may not appear to be defiled under us, and so that through this example schisms may not arise among bishops and the most holy churches. [Col. 0862C]

## LETTER LVII

[Note: Formerly Letter 57; now Letter 72. Written at the same time as the preceding.]

### LICINIA EUDOXIA AUGUSTA TO THE SAME THEODOSIUS

Concerning the disturbance of the Catholic Church (G)

[Col. 0861]  
[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: This is the heading of the ancient Latin version. In the printed editions, from the Greek, “triumphant” appears instead of “illustrious,” and “flourishing” is added before “perpetual.”]

To the illustrious Lord Theodosius, ever Augustus and father: Licinia Eudoxia, most pious and perpetual Augusta, daughter.

[Col. 0861C]

It is known to all that your Mildness has care and concern for Christians and for the Catholic faith, to such an extent that you command that nothing at all be done to its injury.

When, therefore, we had happily entered Rome and had arrived at the threshold of the basilica of the most holy Apostle Peter, Leo, the most blessed bishop of the city of Rome, together with many other bishops, presented a petition to us, saying that the entire doctrine of the religion had been disturbed throughout the East and that this had happened in such a way that the whole faith of Christians had been brought into complete confusion.

For he lamented that Flavian, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, had been expelled because of the enmities of the bishop of Alexandria. Together with the other bishops he requested that we write to your Clemency about this matter, most holy father and worshipful emperor, calling as witnesses both the worship of those venerable places and the safety of our Mildness.

I therefore ask, while offering my greetings, that your Tranquility deign to take care over these letters and command that what was badly done be corrected, until, after everything already decided has been revoked, the case of the faith and Christian religion that has been disturbed may be investigated anew in a council assembled in the regions of Italy.

For it is written that all the contention was stirred up so that Bishop Flavian could be removed from human affairs. [Col. 0863B]



### Greek version

To the triumphant Lord Theodosius, ever emperor and father: Licinia Eudoxia, most pious and flourishing, eternal empress and daughter.

[Col. 0862C]

[The supplied source ends here, with the Greek version’s heading and no further surviving Greek text.]

## Supplementary Editorial Apparatus

The paid translation already places eighteen translated notes inline. The following thirty-eight omitted notes are restored in canonical source order. Each source-note index, column, and lemma anchor fixes its actual location in the parallel Latin/Greek text.

- **Source note 5 — [Col. 0855C], at *neque falli vos in aliquo … humanarum aemulationum fraude patiatur*.** The older printed editions read *humanarum calliditatum aemulatione patiatur*—‘allow [you] to suffer through the rivalry of human cunning.’ Our manuscripts also support Quesnel’s reading, *humanarum aemulationum fraude patiatur*—‘allow [you] to suffer through the deceit of human rivalries.’
- **Source note 6 — [Col. 0855C], at *quae evangelicae … atque apostolicae fidei pietas defendatur*.** We added the words *atque apostolicae*—‘and apostolic’—from the Ratisbon manuscript already mentioned. Immediately afterward, the editions before Quesnel read *defendat*—‘may defend’—but our manuscripts do not.
- **Source note 7 — [Col. 0855C], at *satis plene ac lucide … litteris meis*.** He means Letter 44. We infer that it was entrusted to the tribune Epiphanius because Letter 50 to the people of Constantinople was sent through Epiphanius. Since Letter 50 was written at the same time as Letter 44 to the emperor, Letter 44 appears to have been given to Epiphanius especially for transmission. Compare Letter 59, chapter 2.
- **Source note 8 — [Col. 0855C], at *arbitror accepisse … reseratum est*.** The editions before Quesnel, together with the manuscripts of Collection 12, read *ratum est*—‘it has been ratified’—a corrupt reading. Our Ratisbon manuscript confirms Quesnel’s emendation *reseratum est*—‘it has been disclosed.’
- **Source note 14 — [Col. 0857A–0858A], at *Domino meo Theodosio, gloriosissimo*.** In closer agreement with the Greek, the printed editions omit *meo*—‘my’—and then have *glorioso*—‘glorious.’ We print the reading of the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, both ours and Baluze’s: *Domino meo … gloriosissimo*—‘To my lord … most glorious.’
- **Source note 15 — [Col. 0859C], at *domine sacratissime pater … Hac enim gratia*.** Thus in the same manuscripts. The printed editions read *sanctissime pater … Hujus enim rei gratia*—‘most holy father … For the sake of this matter.’ Although that reading expresses the force of the Greek better, it should not have been inserted when publishing the ancient Latin translation.
- **Source note 18 — [Col. 0859D], at *contra religionem turbarum petulantia praevalere … dum*.** Thus the manuscript books, with *dum*—‘while.’ The printed editions have the better Latin *cum*—also ‘while’—but we reproduce the ancient version.
- **Source note 19 — [Col. 0859D], at *Ad perfectiorem vero agnitionem vestrae divinitatis*.** The ancient codices more correctly read *divinitatis*—‘Divinity’—rather than the printed editions’ *dignitatis*—‘dignity.’
- **Source note 21 — [Col. 0860D], at *τῆς ἰδίας εὐλαβείας τὴν ἀξίαν τῷ μακαρίῳ ἀποστόλῳ Πέτρῳ*.** The margin of the Roman edition reads *μακαριωτάτῳ*—‘most blessed’; the Venetian codex instead has *μακαρίῳ τε*—‘and to the blessed [apostle Peter].’
- **Source note 22 — [Col. 0860D], at *ἕνεκα τῆς ἀνακυψάσης φιλονεικίας περὶ τῆς πίστεως*.** The margin of the Roman edition reads *περικυψάσης* in place of *ἀνακυψάσης*. The printed text means ‘because of the dispute that arose concerning the faith’; the marginal form is unusual and may suggest a dispute that ‘bent or peered around,’ so its uncertainty is retained rather than normalized.
- **Source note 23 — [Col. 0860D], at *ἀνακυψάσης φιλονεικίας περὶ τῆς πίστεως … Τοῦτο οὖν αἰτοῦντι*.** The margin of the Roman edition reads *τούτῳ*—‘to this man’—with the siglum L, instead of the text’s *Τοῦτο*—‘this [thing].’
- **Source note 24 — [Col. 0860D], at *τὰς ἐπιθυμίας, καὶ τὰς ἐκβοήσεις πάντων … ἡ ὑμετέρα εὐσέβεια*.** Thus the Venetian manuscript, as the Latin *pietas vestra*—‘your Piety’—also requires: *ἡ ὑμετέρα εὐσέβεια*, ‘your Piety.’ The printed editions wrongly read *ἡ ἡμετέρα εὐσέβεια*—‘our Piety.’
- **Source note 27 — [Col. 0860D], at *piissima et florens, perpetua Augusta et mater … Dum*.** The printed editions have the better Latin *Cum*—‘when.’ But when an ancient translation is being presented, the question is not what is better but what the old translator rendered; the ancient version preserved in the manuscripts reads *Dum*—‘while/when.’
- **Source note 28 — [Col. 0861C], at *summum apostolorum, quem nuper … adieramus*.** All the codices, and Quesnel in the margin, read *adieramus*—‘we had approached/visited.’ The printed editions wrongly read *audieramus*—‘we had heard.’
- **Source note 29 — [Col. 0861C], at *adieramus, testem objiciens, episcoporum multitudine circumseptus*.** The editions give in the margin *quos in unum e mirabilibus*. Literally this is ‘whom into one from among the marvelous [ones]’; the transmitted marginal phrase is fragmentary or corrupt, and that uncertainty is retained.
- **Source note 30 — [Col. 0861C], at *Constantino, qui primus imperio splenduit Christianus … nuper turbata sit*.** Thus three of our codices and the same number of Baluze’s. Two Vatican manuscripts omit the adverb *nuper*—‘recently.’ The printed editions read *perturbata sit*—‘has been disturbed’; then the Chigi manuscript has *arbitrio*—‘at the discretion/judgment.’
- **Source note 31 — [Col. 0861D], at *militum praesentia et metu … appetens Constantinopolitanae civitatis episcopum Flavianum*.** Thus the old books, with *appetens*—‘assailing/attacking.’ The printed editions read *impetens*—likewise ‘attacking’ or ‘rushing upon.’
- **Source note 32 — [Col. 0861D], at *per eos qui … directi fuerant in concilio*.** The printed editions more correctly read *directi fuerunt ad concilium*—‘were sent to the council.’ But we did not emend the ancient translation, *directi fuerant in concilio*—‘had been sent in the council’—which all our manuscripts and Baluze’s exhibit.
- **Source note 34 — [Col. 0861D–0862C], at *Flaviano … ad concilii et apostolicae sedis judicium transmittatur*.** Thus, though badly, the ancient translation in all our codices and Baluze’s. The printed editions emend it from the Greek to *Ad concilium apostolicae sedis judicium transmittatur*—‘Let the judgment be referred to a council of the apostolic see,’ where *judicium* is nominative. We shall observe a similar barbarous rendering by the Latin translator in Letter 58, note at column 865g.
- **Source note 35 — [Col. 0862C], at *principatum episcopatus … ordinavit*.** The printed editions place *ornavit*—‘adorned’—in the margin as a variant for *ordinavit*—‘established/ordered.’
- **Source note 36 — [Col. 0862C–0862D], at *maximae civitati, quae domina omnium est … terrarum*.** Thus the Verona and Colbertine manuscripts, in agreement with the Greek, and Quesnel in the margin: *terrarum*—‘of the lands/earth.’ The Dijon manuscript likewise has this reading, except that its margin gives the alternative *tuarum*—‘of your [lands/things]’; this is also the reading of the Corbie exemplar, as Baluze noted. The printed editions with other codices read *civitatum*—‘of the cities.’
- **Source note 37 — [Col. 0862D], at *Diligentius autem etiam in hoc … providete*.** The printed editions, together with one Vatican manuscript, read *providere*—‘to provide/take care’—instead of *providete*—‘take care’ (plural imperative).
- **Source note 38 — [Col. 0862D], at *quod priscis temporibus nostra generatio custodivit … sub nos*.** Thus all the codices, with the ungrammatical *sub nos*—literally ‘under us.’ The editors emended it to *sub nobis*—‘under us/in our time.’
- **Source note 39 — [Col. 0860D], at *Γάλλα Πλακιδία ἡ εὐσεβεστάτη, καὶ ἀνθοῦσα αἰωνία βασιλὶς*.** The Venetian manuscript reads *ἀεὶ βασιλίς*—‘ever empress’—in place of the text’s *ἀνθοῦσα αἰωνία βασιλὶς*—‘flourishing, eternal empress.’
- **Source note 40 — [Col. 0862D], at *τὸν κορυφαῖον τῶν ἀποστόλων, ᾧ καὶ ἔναγχος … προσείημεν*.** The Venetian manuscript, and likewise the margin of the edition, read *προσείη*—‘he/she might approach’—instead of *προσείημεν*—‘we might approach.’
- **Source note 41 — [Col. 0862D], at *τὸν ἐπίσκοπον τῆς … Κωνσταντινουπόλεως Φλαυιανὸν*.** The Venetian manuscript reads *Κωνσταντινοπολιτῶν*—‘of the Constantinopolitans’—instead of *Κωνσταντινουπόλεως*—‘of Constantinople.’
- **Source note 42 — [Col. 0862D], at *δέσποτα … ἁγνότατε υἱὲ βασιλεῦ προσκυνητέ*.** The margin of the Roman edition reads *ἴσως, ἁγιώτατε*—‘perhaps; most holy’—instead of the text’s *ἁγνότατε*—‘most pure/most chaste.’
- **Source note 43 — [Col. 0862D], at *Φλαυιανοῦ … ἐν τῇ συνόδῳ τοῦ ἀποστολικοῦ θρόνου*.** One should read *εἰς τὴν σύνοδον*—‘to the council’—instead of *ἐν τῇ συνόδῳ*—‘in the council.’
- **Source note 44 — [Col. 0862D], at *δεσποινα πασῶν ὑπάρχει τῶν … γεῶν*.** The margin of the Roman edition gives the alternative *γαιῶν*—‘lands/earth’—for the text’s *γεῶν*, which has the same meaning.
- **Source note 45 — [Col. 0862D], at *ἐφ’ ἡμῶν δόξῃ … μιαίνεσθαι*.** The margin of the Roman edition reads *μειοῦσθαι*—‘to be diminished’—corresponding to the Latin; the text has *μιαίνεσθαι*—‘to be defiled.’
- **Source note 49 — [Col. 0863C], at *Cum igitur feliciter … Romae fuissemus ingressae, et in liminibus*.** The printed editions read *Romam et ad limina*—‘into Rome and to the threshold.’ We retain the reading of the old exemplars that preserve the ancient version, *Romae … in liminibus*—‘at Rome … at the threshold’—although it mistranslates the Greek; errors of this less-skilled translator confirm that it is an ancient translation and exclude an original Latin composition.
- **Source note 50 — [Col. 0863C–0863D], at *postulationem nobis … obtulit*.** Baluze’s Corbie manuscript reads *attulit*—‘brought [a petition] to us.’ The Dijon codex and the printed editions’ margin have the same reading, instead of *obtulit*—‘presented/offered.’
- **Source note 51 — [Col. 0863D], at *ad confusionem … omnem perduceretur*.** The printed editions give *omnino*—‘altogether/completely’—in the margin.
- **Source note 52 — [Col. 0863D], at *ad tuam clementiam ex hac … causa meas litteras destinarem*.** The same printed editions give in the margin *regione has*—‘from this region these [letters]’—or *eas litteras*—‘those letters.’
- **Source note 53 — [Col. 0863D], at *Salutans igitur justa posco, quatenus … his litteris curam*.** The printed editions likewise give *his rebus*—‘to these matters’—in the margin, instead of *his litteris*—‘to these letters.’
- **Source note 54 — [Col. 0863D], at *donec omnibus quae … jam definita sunt revocatis … perquiratur*.** The Chigi codex reads *etiam definita*—‘also defined.’ The same codex and the printed editions’ margin then have *perquiratis*—‘you should investigate’—instead of *perquiratur*—‘it should be investigated.’
- **Source note 55 — [Col. 0863D], at *Scriptum est enim … hic omnem contentionem motam*.** Thus all our codices and the Greek text, with *hic*—‘here.’ The printed editions read *hinc*—‘hence/from here.’
- **Source note 56 — [Col. 0863D–0864C], at *Flavianus episcopus … ex humanis rebus potuisset auferri*.** The printed editions read *ex ecclesiasticis rebus*—‘from ecclesiastical affairs.’ All our exemplars and Baluze’s, agreeing here and below in Letter 63 with the Greek, read *ex humanis rebus*—‘from human affairs’: as Baluze correctly explains, removed from human fellowship and expelled from the administration of human affairs. At this time Rome had not yet heard of Flavian’s death. In Theodosius’s Letter 64 to Placidia, however, both Greek and Latin say that Flavian was expelled from ecclesiastical affairs. The two formulas therefore come to the same thing.

All know that you make concern and care for Christians and for the catholic faith your business to such an extent that you permit absolutely nothing to be done in insult to it. When, therefore, we had fortunately entered Rome and reached the doors of the shrine of the most holy apostle Peter, Leo, the most blessed bishop of the city of the Romans, together with many other bishops, brought a petition before us, declaring that the entire doctrine of religion had been thrown into turmoil in the East. This had happened in such a way as to plunge the whole faith of Christians into confusion; for he lamented that Flavian, bishop of the Church of Constantinople, had been expelled from human affairs because of the hostility of the bishop of Alexandria. Together with the other bishops, he requested this, calling as witnesses both their veneration of the holy places and the preservation of your gentleness.

Therefore, most pure master and father, worshipful emperor, let my letter from this quarter be sent to your philanthropy. Addressing you, accordingly, I make a just request: may your serenity permit a remedy to be provided for these affairs and command that what has been badly done be corrected, until, after all the measures already enacted have been recalled, the matter now agitating the whole faith and religion of Christians may be examined by a council assembled in the regions of Italy. For it was written here that the whole contention had been stirred up, so that Flavian, the bishop, might be removed from human affairs.

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the Venetian manuscript reads τῆς Χριστιανῶν, “of the Christians.”]

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the Roman marginal edition reads συμβεβηκέναι, “to have happened,” instead of συμβέβηκεν, “this has happened,” as in L. Hard.]

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the Venetian manuscript rightly reads τοῖς οὐδοῖς, “at the doors”; the common editions wrongly read ταῖς οὐδοῖς.]

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the Roman marginal edition reads ἡμετέρας, “our,” instead of ὑμετέρας, “your.”]

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the Roman marginal edition reads ἴσως, ἁγιώτατε, “perhaps, most holy,” instead of the reading printed here.]

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the same margin reads ἐντεῦθεν, “from here,” instead of ἑνταῦθα, “here.”]

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the Roman marginal edition reads παρακελεύσοι, “would command,” instead of κελεύσοι, “would command,” in the printed text.]

[Note: At Col. 0864D, the same margin reads ἐκκλησιαστικῶν, “ecclesiastical,” instead of ἀνθρωπίνων, “human.”]

## LETTER LVIII. GALLA PLACIDIA TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA, IN WHICH SHE CONDEMS THE SECOND COUNCIL OF EPHESUS (G)

[Note: This was formerly Letter 58 and is now Letter 78. It was written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: The Latin translation of this letter had been published solely from Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection before Cotelerius published the Greek version as well in volume I of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 62.]

972 Galla Placidia, ever most devout Augusta, to Aelia Pulcheria, ever most devout Augusta, daughter.

[Col. 0863C]

Although we desire to visit Rome with frequent journeys, the reason for our embracing religion requires that we present ourselves at the boundaries of the saints, who, having certainly been established in the heavens according to their virtue, do not disdain the things below. We therefore believe it sacrilegious if we refuse the customary order.

[Note: The manuscripts read desideremus, “we desire”; the common editions read desideraremus, “we might desire.”]

When, then, we had presented ourselves to the blessed apostle Peter, the most reverend Pope Leo, surrounded there by a multitude of priests, approached us first, in accordance with the dignity of his office. Because of the grief interposed by his sighs, he could scarcely express his desire in words. Nevertheless, the steadfastness of the priest’s wisdom prevailed, so that he restrained his tears for a little while and, as the defender of the violated faith, set forth the matter in plain speech.

[Note: The Verona manuscript 57 reads sacrilegium, “sacrilege,” instead of the reading printed in the text.]

[Note: The manuscripts and Quesnellus’s second edition read pene, “scarcely”; other editions read plene, “fully,” placing pene in the margin.]

In that speech we learned that in our own times the catholic faith had been disturbed—the faith which, from our divine father Constantine down to the present, the ancestors of our lineage have preserved.

[Note: Read ἧν, “which,” for the printed τὴν, “the.”] For, it is said, at someone’s bidding something wicked had been stirred up against the bishop of Constantinople.

[Note: The manuscripts of Baluzius read exercitatum, “stirred up”; Cotelerius reads actum, “carried out.”]

We therefore learned that at the council held at Ephesus, where no order or measure of the priesthood was observed, everything had been done without regard for the Divinity, so that presumption and injustice are said to have prevailed even for the condemnation of certain persons—things which appear dreadful in our times.

The faith must therefore have its proper force, most holy and venerable daughter Augusta. Accordingly, may your Clemency, in accordance with the catholic faith, as she has always done together with us, now likewise deign to join her will with ours, so that whatever was enacted in that tumultuous and most wretched council may be removed with every possible force; and, while all things remain intact, let the episcopal cause be sent to the apostolic see, in which the blessed Peter, first of the apostles, having received the keys of the heavenly kingdoms, held the primacy of the priesthood.

[Note: The Chigi manuscript reads in illo, “in that”; two others read in illorum, “in those.” Two manuscripts read luctuoso, “mournful,” for tumultuoso, “tumultuous.”]

[Note: Our manuscripts and those of Baluzius read submoveatur, “be removed”; the editions read removeatur, “be removed,” followed by ut omnibus, “so that to all.”]

[Note: The Dijon manuscript and Quesnellus’s margin read episcoporum causa, “the cause of the bishops,” instead of episcopatus causa, “the episcopal cause.”]

[Note: Some manuscripts omit vim, “force.”]

[Note: The Latin text has a lacuna after “to the apostolic see.” The Greek reads “let the matter be referred to the apostolic throne.” Quesnellus supplied the sense from the Greek; the old translator apparently left a gap after the words “to the apostolic see.”]

We ought in all things to grant precedence to the immortal city, which by the dominion of its own virtue has embraced the whole world and entrusted the world to our imperial rule to govern and preserve.

971 Galla Placidia, most devout and most illustrious ever-Augusta, to Aelia Pulcheria, most devout ever-Augusta, daughter.

[Col. 0864C]

Although we likewise greatly desire to behold Rome amid continual journeys, the subject of religion is an excellent reason for this, so that we may present our presence at the boundaries of the saints, whom it is true, having been established in the heavens according to their virtue, do not disdain the things below.

We therefore are thought to commit a kind of sacrilege if we refuse the customary order. When, then, we had presented our presence to the most blessed apostle Peter, the most reverent Pope Leo, surrounded by a multitude of priests, first put himself forward according to the dignity of his office. Yet, because of the grief interposed by his sighing, he could scarcely express his desire in words.

Nevertheless, the steadfastness of the priest’s mind conquered his tears for a little while, and, as the avenger of the violated faith, he set forth the matter in clear speech. In that speech we recognized that in our own times the catholic faith had been disturbed—the faith which, from our divine father Constantine until today, the ancestors of our race have preserved.

At someone’s bidding, it is said, something wicked was exposed against the priest of Constantinople.

[Note: The printed text has ἐκγυμνᾶσαι, “to expose”; the editor proposes ἐκγυμνᾶσθαι, “to be exposed.”]

973 We therefore learned that at the council held at Ephesus, which preserved no order of the priesthood and no measure, everything had been done without attention to the Divinity, so that presumption and injustice were said to have prevailed even for the condemnation of certain persons—things that seem dreadful in our times.

The faith must therefore prevail in its own right, most holy and worshipful lady, daughter Augusta. Accordingly, may your philanthropy, in accordance with the catholic faith, as she has always done together with us, now likewise deign to breathe with us in harmony, so that everything enacted in that disturbed and wretched council may be removed with all force; and, while all things remain uncorrupted, let the matter be referred to the apostolic throne, in which the most blessed Peter, first of the apostles, having received the keys of heaven, adorned the high priesthood.

[Note: The printed Greek after this has the corrupt words τοῦ ἐπὶ ὑπόθεσις; the editor proposes κληρωσαμένῃ (reading uncertain).]

For we ought in all things to grant the primacy to the immortal city, which by its own virtue has taken possession of the world and, exercising dominion over it, entrusted its circuit to our empire to govern and preserve.

## LETTER LIX

[Note: Also numbered 46. What was formerly Letter 59 is now Letter 79. Written about the middle of March in the year 450.]

[Note: This letter is extant in manuscripts of Collections 2, 5, 12, 13, and 18 through 24, and in the copy of Sichardus.]

### TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF THE CITY OF CONSTANTINOPLE

[Col. 0865]

[Note: In the table of Collection 5 this title appears as chapter 80: “To the Constantinopolitans, an exhortation concerning the steadfastness of their faith.”]

### Synopsis

I. He congratulates them because they remain ever attached to Flavian and resist error.  
II. The reality of Christ’s flesh is proved from the mystery of the Eucharist.  
III. It is also proved from his exaltation over all things and from his bodily actions and sufferings.  
IV. From the necessity of the incarnation for cleansing Adam’s guilt, and from the prophecies announcing it beforehand.  
V. Various errors against the faith of the incarnation.

Leo, bishop, to the clergy, those honored, and the people residing in Constantinople.

[Note: Editions before Quesnellus, together with later manuscripts of Collections 20, 21, 23, and 24, add “and the holy synod that met in the city of Rome.” Quesnellus rightly removed these words on the authority of older collections and manuscripts: Corbie Collection 2, the Trecopith and Thuan Collections 5, and the Griman Collection 18. Our Vindobon Collection 5 and the Florentine Collection 13 of San Marco agree with them. The latter reads: “Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to the Constantinopolitans.” Vatican Collection 11 and the copy of Sichardus likewise contain no mention of a synod. The error arose because this letter was marked as dated on the Ides of October of the preceding year, a chronological notation found in another letter, Letter 50, written to the same Constantinopolitans at a Roman synod; hence it was thought that both letters had been issued at the same synod. Below, in the final note, we shall show that this chronological notation was attached to this letter by mistake.]

### Chapter I

Although we are greatly grieved by the events recently reported as having taken place at the council of priests at Ephesus—for, as consistent rumor has spread and the actual outcome of events itself shows, neither moderation in justice nor reverence for the faith was preserved there—yet we rejoice in the piety of your devotion, and in the acclamations of the holy people, examples of which have been conveyed to us, we have recognized the affection of you all.

[Note: The preposition de, “concerning,” is deleted in Vindobon Collection 5, in manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24, and in the copy of Sichardus. The Corbie manuscript reads bonitate, “goodness,” for pietate, “piety”; for the words on the people’s acclamations, see Quesnellus’s note 2.]

For among good sons the just love of an excellent father lives and remains, and you do not allow the instruction of catholic doctrine to be corrupted in any part.

[Note: The Vindobon Collection 5, together with editions before Quesnellus, reads “and lives and remains.” A similar reading occurs in manuscripts of Collection 21.]

[Note: The Griman manuscript reads “and catholic doctrine in no part.” Quesnellus inserted “his” before “doctrine”; this has been deleted on the authority of all our manuscripts and earlier editions.]

For, as the Holy Spirit has plainly revealed to you, they have joined themselves to the error of the Manichaeans, who deny that the only-begotten Son of God assumed a true human being of our nature and wish all his bodily actions to have been those of a phantom masquerading as reality.

[Note: Vatican Collection 11 omits “to you.”]

[Note: The particle et, “and,” deleted by Quesnellus, has been restored from all our manuscripts and editions.]

[Note: Four manuscripts of Quesnellus read sanctiones, “decrees,” instead of actiones, “actions.”]

So that you might not give any assent to this impiety, we have already sent to your charity, through my son Epiphanius and Dionysius, notary of the Roman Church, letters of exhortation. In them we freely supplied the confirmation that you requested, so that you may not doubt that we are extending fatherly care to you and laboring by every means to ensure that, with the mercy of God assisting us, all the scandals stirred up by the inexperienced and foolish may be destroyed.

[Note: Quesnellus likewise has “lest anyone.” We have restored the reading of the earlier editors, confirmed by all our manuscripts except Vindebon Collection 5, which erroneously has “lest anything.”]

[Note: Vatican Collection 11 wrongly adds ter, “three times,” for Leo had already freely given what later letters show the Constantinopolitans had requested.

We have retained notarium, “notary,” singular, with Quesnellus, as it is read in most of our manuscripts, including Vindebon Collection 5, and in earlier editions. Epiphanius is honored with the title “son” in the singular, and in Letter 54 is called a tribune, which does not seem appropriate to a notary of the Roman Church. The writings said to have already been sent by Leo through Epiphanius and Dionysius to the Constantinopolitans are Letter 50, dated on the third day before the Ides or on the Ides of October of the preceding year.]

Nor may anyone dare to flatter himself on the ground of priestly honor if he can be convicted of the impiety of an accursed opinion.

[Note: Distinction 28, “If among the laity,” chapter 3.]

For if ignorance seems scarcely tolerable in laymen, how much less is it deserving of excuse or pardon in those who preside—especially when they even presume to defend the inventions of perverse opinions and, by terror or favor, draw the unstable into their own agreement?

[Note: Vindebon Collection 5 deletes in, “in.” Vatican Collection 11 has “by the impiety of his work.”]

[Note: Editions before Quesnellus and several manuscripts incorrectly read insanabiles, “incurable,” instead of instabiles, “unstable.”]

### Chapter II

[Note: Nine manuscripts of Quesnellus and six of ours read spernantur, “let them be rejected”; others, with earlier editions, read separentur, “let them be separated.”]

Let such persons be rejected by the holy members of Christ’s body, and let catholic freedom refuse to suffer the yoke of unbelievers to be imposed upon it.

For outside the gift of divine grace and outside the sacrament of human salvation must be reckoned those who, by denying the nature of our flesh in Christ, contradict the Gospel and resist the Creed. They do not perceive that, through their blindness, they are being led into such a precipice that they stand neither in the truth of the Lord’s passion nor in that of his resurrection. For both are made void in the Savior if it is not believed that in him there is flesh of our race.

[Note: On Consecration, distinction 2, “In which things,” chapter 38.]

In what darkness of ignorance have these men lain, and in what torpor of negligence until now, that they have neither learned by hearing nor recognized by reading what is so harmonious in the mouth of everyone in the Church of God that the truth of Christ’s body and blood is not silent even amid the sacraments of communion from the tongues of infants?

[Note: All our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus read “in which darkness of ignorance these men are”; Quesnellus has “in which these are the darknesses of ignorance.”]

[Note: The Corbie manuscript deletes the next three words, as Quesnellus noted in the margin.]

[Note: We have found nowhere in our manuscripts the erroneous reading of the editions of Leo before Quesnellus, “among the sacraments of the common faith.” Manuscripts of Collections 12 and 24 and the copy of Sichardus have the reading of the edition of the Councils, “let it be silent among the sacraments of the common faith.” Three other manuscripts—Vatican 541, Collection 21; Venice 79, Collection 22; and Ottobonianus 297, Collection 23—read “let it be silent in the sacrament of communion.” Seven superior manuscripts have the reading printed in the text, which we retain with Quesnellus because it is confirmed by six other manuscripts of his. See his note 2.]

For in that mystical distribution of spiritual nourishment, this is imparted and this is received, so that, receiving the power of heavenly food, we may pass into the flesh of him who became our flesh.

Accordingly, in confirmation of your charity, which with praiseworthy faith resists the enemies of truth, I shall appropriately and opportunely use the words and affection of the Apostle, and say:

“Therefore I also, hearing of your faith, which is in the Lord Jesus, and of your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making mention of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, the eyes of your heart having been enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, and what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power in us who have believed, according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead and setting him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. And he subjected all things beneath his feet and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and his fullness, who is fulfilled in all things” (Ephesians 1:15–23).

[Note: Some manuscripts, together with earlier editions, have “which is in Christ Jesus.”]

[Note: The words “Jesus Christ” are absent from the copy of Sichardus and from manuscripts of Collection 24.]

[Note: Vindebon Collection 5 deletes the conjunction et, “and.”]

[Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Elsewhere, ‘in us.’” The Griman manuscript has “in you who believed”; three of our manuscripts have “in us who believe.”]

[Note: Vindebon deletes illum, “him.”]

[Note: Vindebon Collection 5 and other manuscripts of Collection 21, as well as four of Quesnellus’s manuscripts together with earlier editions, have in the margin “above all things of the Church.”]

### Chapter III

[Note: Several manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus read hi adversarii, “these adversaries.”]

Let the adversaries of the truth say when the almighty Father exalted his Son over all things, or according to what nature, or to what substance he subjected all things.

For the Divinity of the Word is equal in all things and consubstantial with the Father, and the power of the Begetter and the Begotten is eternally and timelessly one and the same. Since he is the Creator of all natures, because all things were made through him and without him nothing was made (John 1:3), he is superior to all that he created; nor were the things he established ever not subject to their Creator.

To him it is proper and eternal neither to be from anywhere other than the Father nor to be anything other than what the Father is. If power was added to him, dignity illumined, sublimity exalted, then he was lesser than the one who advanced him, and he did not possess the riches of the nature whose generosity he required.

But anyone who thinks such things is seized by Arius into his fellowship. This impiety greatly supports his perversity, denying that the Word of God possesses human nature, so that, while he disdains humility in the majesty of God, he either asserts that the bodily image in Christ was false or says that all his bodily actions and sufferings belonged rather to the Divinity than to the flesh.

Whichever of these he dares to defend is utterly insane, because neither the piety of faith nor the reason of the sacrament accepts that the Divinity suffered anything or that the truth was in any respect false.

The Son of God, therefore, is impassible; with the Father and the Holy Spirit he possesses, in the one essence of the unchangeable Trinity, the perpetual quality of being. Yet, in that fullness of time which had been appointed by the eternal plan and promised by the prophetic significance of words and deeds, he became the Son of Man—not by a change of his substance, but by the assumption of our nature—and came to seek and save what had perished (Luke 19:10).

He came neither by a local approach nor by bodily movement, as though he were to be present from a place where he had been absent or to depart from the place from which he had come. Rather, he came by making himself manifest through what was visible and common to human sight: namely, by taking human flesh and a soul in the womb of the Virgin Mother.

Thus, while remaining in the form of God, he united to himself the form of a servant and the likeness of sinful flesh, through which he did not diminish divine things by human things but increased human things by divine things.

[Note: Manuscripts of Collection 21 read “that he might assume the form of a servant and unite to God the likeness of sinful flesh.”]

[Note: Some manuscripts, together with Vindebon Collection 5 and other editions, add Deus, “God,” after “the Son of God.”]

[Note: Manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24, together with Sichardus, have “is above all things”; manuscripts of Collection 21 have “is superior in all things.”]

[Note: Quesnellus reads this as printed. Our manuscripts, together with earlier editions, have falsatam, “falsified,” instead of falsam, “false.”]

### Chapter IV

The condition of all mortals, drawn from our first parents, was such that, with original sin passing down through their descendants, no one would escape the punishment of condemnation unless the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14)—in that very nature which would be both of our blood and of our race.

Therefore the Apostle says: “As through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of righteousness justification of life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were constituted sinners, so through the obedience of one man the many will be constituted righteous” (Romans 5:18–19).

And again: “For since death came through a man, resurrection of the dead also came through a man. And just as all die in Adam, so all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:2).

These “all” are those who, although born in Adam, are nevertheless found reborn in Christ, possessing the testimony of faith, both concerning justification by grace and concerning communion in nature.

Whoever denies that this nature was assumed by the only-begotten Son of God in the womb of the virgin daughter of David is alien from the whole sacrament of the Christian religion. Since he recognizes neither the bridegroom nor understands the bride, he cannot take part in the wedding feast.

For Christ’s flesh is the veil of the Word, with which everyone who confesses him completely is clothed. But whoever is ashamed of it and rejects it as though it were unworthy will receive no adornment from it. Even if he intrudes into the royal feast and thrusts himself uninvited among the sacred banquets, the wicked guest will not be able to deceive the king’s judgment. Rather, as the Lord himself testified, he will be taken away, bound hand and foot, and cast into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth (Matthew 22:13).

[Note: The same manuscripts read “there he will be,” instead of “where there will be.”]

Therefore, whoever does not confess a human body in Christ should know that he is unworthy of the mystery of the incarnation and has no share in that sacrament which the Apostle proclaims, saying:

“We are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” And, explaining what this signified, he added: “This is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5:30–32).

From the very beginning of the human race, therefore, Christ was announced to all human beings as coming in the flesh. In that flesh, as it was said, “the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). The two are, of course, God and man, Christ and the Church, which came forth from the Bridegroom’s flesh when, from the side of the Crucified, blood and water flowed and she received the sacrament of redemption and regeneration.

For this is the condition of the new nature: in baptism it is stripped not of the clothing of true flesh but of the contagion of condemned antiquity, so that the human being may become the body of Christ, because Christ too is the body of man.

[Note: Earlier editions and five of our manuscripts have nova, “new,” instead of the reading adopted by Quesnellus.]

[Note: Vatican Collection 24 and editions have “of Christ” in the margin.]

[Note: Earlier editions, together with the copy of Sichardus, read “with which Christ is completely clothed.” Quesnellus’s emendation is supported by our manuscripts. Only two manuscripts of Collection 21 have induetur, “will be clothed.”]

[Note: The same editions, together with manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21, have inferat, “introduces himself,” instead of inserat, “inserts himself.”]

[Note: Earlier editions, together with manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24, delete vitae, “of life.” Shortly afterward, Vatican Collection 11 reads constituuntur, “are constituted,” instead of constituentur, “will be constituted.”]

[Note: The Vindebon manuscript reads invenientur, “will be found.” Vatican Collection 11 soon afterward has fidei testamentum, “the testimony of faith.”]

[Note: The copy of Sichardus reads significetur, “might be signified.”]

[Note: Earlier editions before Quesnellus delete omnibus, “all.” Manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24 delete hominibus, “human beings.” Sichardus deletes both.]

[Note: Sichardus reads: “In this, just as it was said.”]

### Chapter V

Therefore we do not say that Christ is God alone, as the heretics called Manichaeans do; nor man alone, as the Photinian heretics do; nor man in such a way that anything is lacking in him which is certainly part of human nature, whether soul, rational mind, or flesh.

We do not say that the flesh was not taken from a woman but was made from the Word changed and transformed into flesh. These three false and empty propositions were advanced in three different forms by the three groups of heretics called Apollinarians.

[Note: Earlier editions, together with Vatican Collection 24, read: “which he did not take from a woman, but which was made from the Word,” and so forth.]

[Note: See Quesnellus’s note 5 and our note 7 in Letter 109. Shortly afterward, editions before Quesnellus and manuscript Collection 24 variously present the reading.]

Nor do we say that the blessed Virgin Mary conceived a man without Divinity, who was later created by the Holy Spirit and then assumed by the Word—as Nestorius preached, whom we rightly and justly condemned.

Rather, we say that Christ the Son of God, true God, was born from God the Father without any beginning in time, and that the same Christ, true man, was born from a human mother in the fullness of the appointed time. Nor does his humanity, by which the Father is greater, diminish anything of that nature by which he is equal to the Father.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts of Collection 21 have “to that nature.”]

This one person is Christ, who most truly said, with respect to God: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and, with respect to man: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

Hold fast, therefore, most beloved, and steadfastly maintain this true and indissoluble faith, which alone makes true Christians and which, as we understand and approve, you defend with devout zeal and praiseworthy love.

And since, after divine assistance, you ought also to obtain the favor of the catholic rulers, humbly and wisely ask that the most merciful emperor deign to assent to the request by which we have sought that a full synod be summoned.

[Note: See Quesnellus’s note 4.]

[Note: Several of our manuscripts, including Vindebon Collection 5, together with earlier editions and the copy of Sichardus, read postulamus, “we request.” This appears to refer to letters written to Theodosius and Pulcheria in the preceding year, in which Leo had requested a council.]

So that the sooner, with the mercy of God assisting, strength may be increased in the healthy, and medicine may be supplied to the sick, if they are willing to be healed.

[Note: The common editions attach the chronological note in this form: “Given on the Ides of October, in the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes, illustrious men.” Although this date is found in our manuscripts of Collections 20, 21, 22, and 23—the last three of which derive from the same source with respect to this letter—it is absent from the other older and better collections, 5, 11, 12, 13, 18, and 24, and from the copy of Sichardus. We do not know whether it occurs in the Corbie manuscript of Collection 2. See Quesnellus’s note 6, where he considers it an addition.

This letter cannot have been written on the Ides of October in the year 449, since Chapter I mentions other letters already sent to the same Constantinopolitans through Epiphanius and Dionysius. The reference is to Letter 50, dated on the third day before the Ides or on the Ides of October of that same year 449. We infer from Letter 54 that Leo entrusted Epiphanius and Dionysius with this and other letters written at about the same time for delivery to Constantinople. In Letter 54, another letter, Letter 44 to Theodosius, dated on the third day before the Ides of October and sent through the same Epiphanius, is reported.

Letter 50, therefore, was written and sent first, and this Letter 59 afterward. Several considerations from Letter 61, written on 17 March of the same year to the Constantinopolitan archimandrites Martin and Faustus, suggest that this took place about the middle of March 450. Letter 51 had been sent to these men together with Letter 50 through Epiphanius and Dionysius.

From Letter 61 it is clear that Leo had received their letters and had learned from them that through Letter 51, written at the synod, he had already granted what they were requesting. This is indicated by the words at the beginning of that letter: “Although, amid the distant spaces of separated regions, our hearts took one decision, so that what you desired from us might have reached you at the time when your letters were being sent—provided that our writings could have been delivered to your charity—which were sent not only by the authority of the apostolic see but also by the unanimity of the holy synod . . .”

The same messenger who brought the letters of these archimandrites to Leo should be thought to have brought at the same time the letter of the clergy and people of Constantinople. Hence, in the present Letter 59, Chapter I, Leo writes similarly to his words in Letter 61: “What you requested, we freely supplied.”

The archimandrites, as well as the clergy and people of Constantinople, had evidently sent letters to Leo together, in one agreement, requesting the same thing. They sent them at approximately the time when Leo sent Letters 50 and 51 to them. When Leo received both sets of letters together, he likewise replied that he had already freely granted what they requested through Letters 50 and 51, sent in October of the preceding year, and at the same time at which their letters were being dispatched.

Thus both this Letter 59 and Letter 61 were written in reply at about the same time. This one, however, was written first, for we think that the words of Letter 61 refer to it: “Although we have written fully about what has always been and is the position of the catholic faithful”—especially in Letter 28 to Flavian, where he discusses catholic doctrine at great length—“yet now also, for the strengthening of everyone’s minds, we have added no small exhortation.”

A very substantial exhortation is contained in this Letter 59, which must be said to have been written now—that is, shortly before Letter 61, perhaps on the same day—and sent to Constantinople on the same occasion.]

## LETTER LX

[Note: Also numbered 48. What was formerly Letter 60 is now Letter 89. Written on 17 March 450.]

### TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

[Col. 0873A]

### Synopsis

Eutyches is shaking the foundations of the faith; Pulcheria is pressing for a general council to be held against him.

982 Leo, bishop, to Pulcheria Augusta.

[Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and another manuscript of Collection 11 add “most glorious and most devout.” Quesnellus noted in the margin: “This opening was adapted by the impostor Isidore for his first false letter of Pope Sixtus II to Gratus.”]

The letters of your Piety have made me rejoice and exult greatly in the Lord. They clearly show how greatly you love the catholic faith and how greatly you detest heretical error.

For that heresy is exceedingly impious and hostile to the truth of the Gospel. It seeks not to injure some portion of the faith but to tear up the very foundations of the Christian religion, denying that the Son of the eternal Father took from the womb of the blessed Virgin Mother true flesh of our nature. It strikes with condemnation those who could not be led away from the evangelical and apostolic faith by any error, and it vainly pretends to hold the faith of the Nicene synod, although it is plainly alien from it, most glorious Augusta.

Since divine protection does not abandon its Church—for the Lord says, “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20)—the Spirit of God, by the same work and at the same time, has kindled both your Clemency’s solicitude and the care of our heart, so that we might both desire the same remedies.

What I previously requested, I now ask still more earnestly, with greater confidence in making my petition, after receiving the support of your reverent exhortation.

[Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and another manuscript of Collection 24 have eadem mente spiritus, “the Spirit with the same mind,” instead of eodemque opere, “by the same work.”]

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21 read petivi, “I requested,” instead of poposci, “I asked.”]

I hope that the mercy of God will be present, so that, with your Clemency cooperating, the disease of this deadly error may be removed; and so that whatever can salutarily be done under his inspiration and assistance may be accomplished to the praise of your faith.

For human affairs cannot otherwise be secure unless royal and priestly authority defend what pertains to the divine confession.

[Col. 0874A]

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and Avienus, most illustrious men.

[Note: The ancient editions deriving from Hispanic manuscripts add: “In the Spanish Era 488.”]

## LETTER LXI

[Note: Also numbered 49. What was formerly Letter 61 is now Letter 89. Written on 17 March 450.]

[Note: This letter is extant in the same collections as the preceding letter.]

### TO THE PRESBYTERS MARTIN AND FAUSTUS

[Note: The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts prefix this title: “Concerning the condemnation of the second council of Ephesus.”]

### Synopsis

I. He reminds them of the letters written to them.  
II. He urges them to assist the cause of the faith and promises them his solicitude.

Leo, bishop, to Martin and Faustus, presbyters and archimandrites.

[Note: Editions before Quesnellus, deriving from the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and others dependent upon them, incorrectly read Martiano, “to Martian.” We have supplied the words “and archimandrites” from the Ratisbon manuscript.]

### Chapter I
It is beyond doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual endeavors: he who stirs minds also assists their actions. This has become clearly apparent to us through present experience. For although our hearts were separated by the long distances of distinct regions, they adopted one purpose, so that what you desired from us might reach you at the time when your letters were being sent—if, indeed, our written communications could be delivered to your affection. These writings were sent not only with the authority of the Apostolic See but also with the unanimous agreement of the holy synod that had frequently assembled before us, so that it might be evident in them how great a concern we have for the whole Church: namely, by exhorting the minds of all the faithful and seeking the support of the most merciful rulers for the defense of the faith. We do not doubt that their pious and catholic minds will offer their assistance and authority to just petitions, so that, with the Lord’s help, the pernicious heresy—long ago condemned by the authority of the holy Fathers, but recently wickedly supported at Ephesus—may be removed more quickly.

[Note: [Col. 0874D] They were sent in the Vatican Collection 11 and in the Ratisbon manuscript, which additionally reads “might come to meet.”]

[Note: [Col. 0874D] He indicates Letter 51. Compare note 48 (Col. 871, n. m) on Letter 59.]

[Note: [Col. 0874D] The Vindobonensis and Hispanic manuscripts incorrectly read *quorum posset catholicos* (an ungrammatical reading, approximately, “of whom [he] might be able [to make] Catholics”). The Vatican Hispanic manuscript has been corrected to *quorum utpote catholicos* (“whose [minds], as being Catholic”); but this reading must be attributed not to Leo but to the corrector.]

## CHAPTER II

Meanwhile, let your affection do everything possible so that it may become known to all the children of the Church what we proclaim against the impious doctrine according to evangelical and apostolic teaching. Although we have written fully what has always been and remains the position of Catholics, nevertheless we have now added no small amount of exhortation in order to strengthen the minds of all.

[Note: [Col. 0874D] The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “we add,” incorrectly; for nothing, or very little indeed, is added here by way of exhortation. We have shown in note 48 (Col. 871, n. m) on the same letter that this refers to Letter 59.]

For I remember that I preside over the Church under the name of the one whose confession was glorified by the Lord Jesus Christ, and whose faith destroys all heresies, but especially attacks the impiety of the present error. I understand that I may do nothing other than devote all my efforts to the cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is under attack.

[Note: [Col. 0875C] In three manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21: “that it is otherwise not permitted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0875C] With these words Quesnell appended the following note: “The pope governs the Church under Peter’s name; hence many Roman bishops also call themselves Peter’s vicars. When the pontiff is said to govern the Church in Peter’s name, he is understood to govern it with the same power and authority which, as Leo and the Catholic Church teach, passed entirely, together with the primacy as it existed in Peter, to his successors. Thus the name ‘vicar of Peter’ does not indicate a delegate but a successor, who succeeded to Peter’s place with the same authority. If this were a matter for discussion, it would be possible to demonstrate this with many examples from the best authors. Whoever wishes may read note 12 on Treatise 15 of St. Zeno, Book II, p. 191 of our Verona edition, and in our *Patrologia*, vol. XI, col. 439.”]

But lest our writings have been unable to reach you through some occasion of negligence, we have now thought it necessary to send copies of them, so that the proclamation of the faith which we defend may in no way be withheld from your knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0875C] The Ratisbon manuscript adds *et in significatione*, apparently also in the sense of an adverb. Although he uses the plural “copies,” he means a copy of Letter 51, about which he wrote in Chapter I: “if our writings could be delivered to your affection.”]

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Shortly afterward the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, together with manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21, read “we believe.”]

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, under the consuls Valentinian Augustus, for the seventh time, and Avienus, a man of clarissimus rank.

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Quesnell placed the following note at the end: “In the preceding letter the compiler of the old pontifical letters made unrestrained use of material from the letters of Anicetus to the bishops of Gaul; in the first letter of Felix I to Paternus; in the second to the bishops of Gaul; in the letter of Sixtus II to Gratus; and in that of Callistus I to Benedict.”]

## LETTER LXII

[Note: [Col. 0875D] Formerly Letter 47. What was previously numbered 62 is now 82. Written around April 450.]

[Note: [Col. 0875D] This letter and the two following letters survive only in the Chalcedonian collection and in Venetian manuscript 79 of Collection 22, to which several letters from the Chalcedonian collection were added. For the date, around April 450, see the preliminary notice to Letter 55, no. 5.]

### THEODOSIUS THE EMPEROR TO VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS, IN REPLY TO LETTER LV (G)

[Note: [Col. 0875] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To my lord Valentinian Augustus, Theodosius.

[Note: [Col. 0876C] The printed editions, together with the Greek version, always add “your”; but the Latin version presented here from the manuscripts omits it.]

## [Col. 0875A]

[Note: [Col. 0876C] Thus read all the manuscripts, both ours and Baluzius’s, for the same reason that shortly below they have “return in the city of Rome,” and Letter 57 has “we had entered Rome”; these readings show the rendering of an unskilled translator from the Greek. The printed editions corrected this to “to Rome,” as was rightly to be translated. But here we have undertaken to publish the old version, whatever it may have been.]

That your gentleness had arrived in Rome, and that a petition had been presented by Leo, the most reverend patriarch, has been indicated by your Majesty in the very text of the letter.

[Note: [Col. 0876C] After Crabbe, the printed editions read “at the very beginning of the letter from your Majesty.” “Something was undoubtedly missing here,” says Baluzius, “in the manuscript used by Crabbe; and when he saw that the sense was incomplete, he added the word ‘beginning,’ guessing incorrectly. For the reading should be ‘in the very text of the letter,’ as the ancient copies show.” Our manuscripts have the same reading, and the Greek version confirms it. Quesnellus writes in the margin: “in the same context of the letter.”]

We accordingly render fitting thanks to the divine Majesty for your safe return in the city of Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Thus read all the manuscripts. The printed editions have “to the city of Rome.” See note 3 (above, n. d).]

Most holy lord, beloved son, and venerable emperor, concerning what the aforementioned most reverend man said, it has been explained to him more fully and at greater length, as we judged appropriate, and he has recognized that we have in no respect departed from our ancestral religion or from the tradition of our forefathers.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] The printed editions read “more broadly and most fully, as we suppose.” We have adopted the manuscript reading.]

For we desire nothing else than that the ancestral sacraments handed down to us by succession be preserved inviolate.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Some manuscripts read “to guard.” The Greek version of other manuscripts supports the printed reading.]

[Note: [Col. 0876D] We have supplied from all the manuscripts the word “since” (*quoniam*), omitted in the printed editions.]

For this reason, then, since we learned that certain persons were disturbing the most holy Churches by a harmful innovation, we decreed that a synod should be held at Ephesus. In the presence of the most reverend bishops, with complete freedom and entire truthfulness, those unworthy of the priesthood were removed, and those judged worthy were received.

We have therefore recognized that nothing contrary to the rule of faith or to justice was done by them.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] Only the Dijon manuscript of Baluzius, and Quesnellus in the margin, add “against the true faith” or “was unjustly done.”]

Thus every dispute was examined by sacred judgment. Flavian, however, who was found guilty of harmful innovation, received what was due to him.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] This is the reading of all manuscripts and of all editions of the Councils before the Roman edition, in which the reading adopted by Quesnellus and others was introduced: “he received his due punishment.”]

After his removal, every peace and concord reigns in the Churches, and nothing but the truth prevails.

### Greek Version

To my lord Valentinian, eternal Augustus, Theodosius.

And it has been declared by your Majesty in the very text of the letter that your gentleness arrived in Rome and that a petition was presented by Leo, the most reverend patriarch. Concerning your safe return to Rome, we have rendered fitting thanks to the divine Majesty, most pure lord, son, and venerable emperor. Concerning the matters mentioned by the aforementioned most reverend man, it has been declared to him more fully and completely, as we suppose, and he has recognized that we have in no respect departed from our ancestral religion or from the tradition of our forefathers.

[Note: [Col. 0876D] We have adopted, with the Venetian manuscript, the conjunction *kai* (“and”), which makes the sentence remarkably clearer and more straightforward. The printed editions read “and most fully, as we suppose.”]

For we desire—or pray for—nothing else than that the ancestral mysteries handed down to us by succession be preserved immovable. For this reason, then, since we learned that certain persons were disturbing the most holy Churches by a harmful innovation, we decreed that a synod should take place at Ephesus. Namely, in the presence of the most reverend bishops, with great freedom and complete truth, the unworthy were removed from the priesthood, and those judged worthy were received.

We have therefore recognized that nothing contrary to the rule of faith or to justice was done by them. Thus every dispute was examined by divine judgment.
