Flavian, who was found responsible for the harmful innovation, received the honor due to him; and after his removal, every peace and concord reigns in the Churches, and nothing else prevails except pure truth.

## LETTER LXIII

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Formerly Letter 63; now 83.]

### THE SAME THEODOSIUS TO GALLA PLACIDIA AUGUSTA, IN REPLY TO LETTER LVI (G)

[Note: [Col. 0877] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To my lady Placidia, venerable Augusta, Theodosius.

## [Col. 0877A]

From the letters of your gentleness our eternity has learned what the most reverend patriarch Leo requested from your eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] This is the reading of both our manuscripts and those of Baluzius, as well as of the printed editions in the margin. In the text, however, they read “serenity,” and shortly afterward “from your serenity.”]

In these letters, therefore, we indicate that concerning the matters stated by the most reverend bishop it has repeatedly been written more fully and more clearly. From these writings it is undoubtedly evident that we have neither defined, decreed, nor understood anything contrary to the ancestral faith, the divine doctrines, or the decrees of the most reverend bishops who were assembled both under Constantine of divine memory in the city of Nicaea and, not long ago, at Ephesus by our command.

Rather, we ordered only this to be established at Ephesus: that all who had disturbed the holy Churches by harmful injury should be removed in a fitting manner. These are the measures decreed by the most reverend Fathers, not for opposition but for concord and the pure bond of the religion that must be worshiped.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] The printed editions incorrectly read “presbyters,” and afterward add “who is called.” We have given the manuscript reading.]

Flavian, the leader of this contention, was expelled from ecclesiastical affairs by sacred judgment. Knowing this, therefore, let your gentleness, most sacred lady, mother, and venerable Augusta, neither suspect nor imagine that we have ever held anything contrary to the faith handed down, as certain people say.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] The Roman editors of the Councils were the first to publish this reading. Previously the text read as restored here from all the manuscripts: with excellent sense, though in barbarous Latin.]

### Greek Version

To my lady Placidia, venerable Augusta, Theodosius.

From the letters of your gentleness our eternity has learned what the most reverend patriarch Leo requested from your eternity. In these letters, therefore, we declare that concerning the matters stated by the most reverend bishop it has often been written more fully and more clearly. From these writings it is manifest beyond doubt that we have neither defined, decreed, nor understood anything contrary to the ancestral faith, the divine doctrines, or the decrees of the most reverend bishops who were assembled, on the one hand, under Constantine of divine memory in the city of Nicaea and, on the other, not long ago at Ephesus by our command.

[Note: [Col. 0878D] The Venetian manuscript reads “under the one of divine memory,” and so forth.]

[Note: [Col. 0878D] In the margin of the Roman edition: “perhaps again.”]

Rather, we ordered only this to be established at Ephesus: that all who had disturbed the most holy Churches by harmful innovation should be removed in a fitting manner. These are the things decreed by the most reverend Fathers, not for overthrow but for concord and the pure bond of the religion that must be worshiped. The so-called Flavian, the leader of such contention, was expelled from ecclesiastical affairs by divine judgment. Knowing this, therefore, let your gentleness, most pure lady, mother, and venerable Augusta, neither suppose nor imagine that we have ever conceived anything contrary to the faith handed down, as certain people have said.

## LETTER LXIV

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Formerly Letter 64; now 84.]

### THE SAME THEODOSIUS TO LICINIA EUDOXIA, IN REPLY TO LETTER LVII (G)

[Note: [Col. 0877] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To my lady Eudoxia, venerable Augusta, Theodosius.

## [Col. 0877C]

We are always delighted by letters expressing your longing, and we embrace them with complete gladness of soul. We have been accustomed to grant all your petitions gladly, lady, most sacred daughter, venerable Augusta. But concerning the present matter—that is, Flavian, who was bishop—and what followed in this affair, our gentleness has fully informed the most reverend archbishop Leo.

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Quesnellus, together with the printed editions of the Councils, reads in the margin “of your affection.”]

[Note: [Col. 0878D] Quesnellus, with the same editions of the Councils, reads “with all the sweetness of the soul.” The Chigi manuscript reads “with all the sincerity of the soul.” We have followed the reading of four other manuscripts of ours, which is also supported by the manuscripts of Baluzius.]

We have approved communicating only this to your sweetness: that the aforementioned Flavian has been removed from human affairs by sacred judgment, so that the entire dispute of uncertainty might be taken away from the holy Churches; and after this nothing further can be decided, since these matters have already been settled once and for all.

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Quesnellus reads in the margin “by divine [judgment].”]

[Note: [Col. 0879C] This is the reading of all our manuscripts and those of Baluzius. The Greek text also agrees. The printed editions read “from ecclesiastical affairs,” as in the preceding letter, both in the Greek and Latin texts. But Theodosius, replying in this letter to Eudoxia’s Letter 57, uses the same formula that she had used there: “could have been removed from human affairs.” There he certainly could not have been announcing Flavian’s death, of which Eudoxia had not yet received word; rather, he meant his deposition, as we explained in note 9 (Col. 863, n. h) on that Letter 57. Theodosius therefore understood the formula here in the same sense. Quesnellus must accordingly be corrected, since he interpreted this text as referring to Flavian’s death in the final note on our Letter 59, as though his death—which had in fact already occurred—were being announced by Theodosius here.]

[Note: [Col. 0879C] We have restored “and” from the manuscripts, as it stood in Crabbe.]

### Greek Version

To my lady Eudoxia, the venerable empress, Theodosius.

We are always delighted by the letters of your longing, and we gladly embrace them with our whole soul. We have been accustomed to assent with great joy to all your petitions, most pure lady, daughter, venerable empress. But concerning the present matter—that is, concerning Flavian, who was formerly bishop—the matters that followed in this affair our gentleness has fully indicated to the most reverend archbishop Leo. [The Greek prints *κατεσήμασεν* for *κατεσήμηνεν* (“has signified”).]

[Col. 0880A]

To your sweetness we have approved making known only this: that the aforementioned Flavian was removed from human affairs by divine judgment, so that every contentious dispute of uncertainty might be removed from the holy Churches, and that henceforth nothing further can be decided concerning matters already once established.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] In the same margin: “ecclesiastical.” L.]

## LETTER LXV

[Note: [Col. 0879C] Formerly after Letter 49. What was previously numbered 65 is now 85.]

[Note: [Col. 0879D] Written long before May 450. This letter survives in a single collection, the Arelatensian Collection 15. Quesnellus defends its authenticity in the observations prefixed to his notes. We compared it with Vallicellian manuscript G. 99, a copy of an older manuscript of the Church of Arles, from which Baronius published it. Since it has no chronological note, its exact date is unknown. It can only be affirmed that it was written before 5 May 450, when Leo replied to these letters in the following epistle, and indeed some time before that date. For these Gallican petitions were sent to Leo through Petronius and Regulus, as is clear from Chapter I of the following letter; and since the holy pontiff says in Letter 67, dated on that same day, 5 May, that he had kept them with him for a long time, it follows that these petitions had been sent long before May. In this uncertainty concerning the date, we have placed them before the following letter of Leo, in which he replies to the same petitions.]

### PETITION SENT BY ALL THE FELLOW-PROVINCIAL BISHOPS OF THE METROPOLITAN CHURCH OF ARLES TO SAINT LEO THE POPE (G)

[Note: [Col. 0880C] In the aforementioned Vallicellian manuscript: “Petition sent by all the bishops of Gaul to Pope Leo.” But the word “of Gaul” was erased by a line drawn over it. Whether the same word was absent in the ancient Arelatensian manuscript from which this copy was sent to Baronius, or whether it was marked with the same erasure, we do not know. Baronius and Sirmondus omit “fellow-provincial.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. After prefatory remarks about Ravennius’s election and character, they ask Leo to restore the ancient privileges of the Church of Arles.

II. They confirm these privileges from various prerogatives of this Church, especially from the arrival of Saint Trophimus in Gaul.

III. They recall the civil rights and privileges granted to the Arlesians by the emperors.

IV. They flatter Leo with various expressions of respect.

## CHAPTER I

Mindful of how much honor and reverence has always been, and must always be, owed to the most blessed Apostolic See, over which our Lord Jesus Christ wished you to preside because of the merits of your holiness, we promptly took care to inform your apostolate by letter of the ordination whereby our holy brother and fellow-bishop Ravennius, after the passing of blessed memory Hilary, bishop of the city of Arles, was advanced, with the unanimous consent of all, to the highest pontificate, with the Lord’s favor.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Letters 40 and 41 of the preceding year are indicated.]

We give immense thanks that your blessedness replied with such great condescension and charity, although we cannot return thanks as fully as we ought. It may already have been made known to us that our holy brother and fellow-bishop had especially earned the favor of your crown by the gentleness and holiness of his character.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] See Quesnellus’s note 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] This is the reading of Sirmondus together with Quesnellus, who consulted the Arelatensian manuscript. Baronius, with the Vallicellian manuscript, reads: “by the grace of his character he deserved the gentleness and holiness of your crown.”]

Yet, now that we have received the letters of your blessedness, we have clearly recognized with what affection you embrace him. Therefore, after rendering the services that are rightly owed to your apostolate, we do not doubt that your crown will willingly hear our petition, which serves the cause of justice: for we desire not that anything new be instituted by you, but that ancient and long-standing things be restored.

Nor is it just that the honor of one whom, as we have learned, you love with such devotion should be diminished by the action through which another offended your piety.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] Namely, Ravennius, whom Leo presented as approved by him in Letter 40. Compare also Letter 41.]

[Note: [Col. 0880C] This is the reading of the Vallicellian manuscript together with Quesnellus. Other editions read “which previously offended your piety.” The reference is to Hilary’s action in the case of Celidonius, on account of which Leo deprived him of metropolitan authority, as is clear from Letter 10. From this it is understood that Hilary’s punishment was personal; consequently, the privileges of the Church of Arles are soon said to have been diminished only temporarily.]

Indeed, it is evident that the Church of Arles enjoys the favor of divine grace, since it has been granted such a priest through whom it might rejoice that the privileges of its ancient dignity—which it grieved had been diminished for a time—have been permanently restored by the more recent authorities of the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] Namely, under Hilary, who had been deprived of metropolitan authority by Letter 10. We shall show in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, vol. II, that this punishment was temporary and lasted only as long as Hilary lived.]

## CHAPTER II

For it is known throughout all the regions of Gaul—and it is not unknown even to the holy Roman Church—that Arles was the first city within Gaul deemed worthy to receive as its bishop the holy Trophimus, sent by the most blessed Apostle Peter. From that time the benefit of faith and religion was gradually infused into the other regions of Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] The letters of Zosimus to the bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces are being referred to. In them the privileges and rights of the See of Arles were established, and from them they became known throughout all the regions of Gaul. These petitions of the Gauls rely so heavily on Zosimus’s letters that they sometimes reproduce almost their exact words.]

[Note: [Col. 0881C] This is the reading of the Vallicellian manuscript, together with Baronius and Sirmondus. Quesnellus reads “the gift of faith.” What is said here about Saint Trophimus’s mission has been taken from the letters of Zosimus. On this matter, see the fuller discussion in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, Part II, Chapter 2.]

It is clear that other places received a priest from this stream of faith, which the currents of apostolic teaching sent to us, before the city of Vienne, which now shamelessly and conspicuously demands primacies that do not belong to it. For that city has always rightly and deservedly held the summit of sacred dignity which first received, in the person of Saint Trophimus, the first fruits of our religion, and afterward spread throughout Gaul, through diligent instruction, what it had obtained as a divine gift.

By reason of this honor, all our predecessors and forefathers have always honored the Church of Arles as a mother with the honor that was due to her, and, preserving the tradition received from her, have requested bishops for their cities from this See.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] Quesnellus writes in the margin: “Perhaps, *notam* (‘known’).”]

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The editions of Baronius and Sirmondus incorrectly read “of the city.”]

It is established that both our predecessors and we ourselves were consecrated to the highest priesthood by a priest of this Church, through the Lord’s gift.

Following this antiquity, the predecessors of your blessedness confirmed by published authorities—just as the archives of the Apostolic See undoubtedly also contain—the institution that ancient tradition had established concerning the privileges of the Church of Arles. They judged it entirely reasonable and just that, just as the holy Roman Church, through the most blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, held primacy over all the Churches of the whole world, so also within Gaul the Church of Arles, which had been deemed worthy to possess Saint Trophimus, a priest sent by the Apostles, should claim the right of ordaining bishops.

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The published letters of Zosimus in favor of the See of Arles are indicated. This also confirms that the authoritative letters of the Roman bishops were called “authorities.”]

In accordance with religious duty, the said Church exercises these privileges.

## CHAPTER III

Moreover, there are many reasons why, according to the institutions of the emperors, it should be preferred to all the cities within our regions. It was honored so especially by Constantine of most glorious memory that, in addition to its proper name, by which it is called Arles, it received from him the name Constantina.

The most faithful emperors Valentinian and Honorius, of most merciful memory, adorned it with special privileges and, to use their own expression, called it “the Mother of all Gaul.”

[Note: [Col. 0881C] The printed editions before Quesnellus and Sirmondus, together with our Vallicellian manuscript, incorrectly read “the marriage of Gaul.” In his constitution addressed to Agricola in 418, Honorius calls Arles “the metropolitan city.” That constitution contains much of what is reported in this chapter concerning the civil privileges of the city of Arles. Valentinian’s constitution is missing. We shall explain in the cited observations, Part II, Chapter 4, nos. 2 and 3, how these constitutions and the title “Mother of all Gaul” should be understood.]

In this city, whoever within Gaul wished, from the time of the aforesaid emperors, to display the insignia of dignity both received and conferred the consulship.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] See Quesnellus’s note 2.]

The highest prefecture always dwells here, as do the other authorities, treating it as a common homeland for all. From every city people come here for many public purposes. Clearly, by divine providence, as we believe, everything has so agreed with the privileges of the Church and city mentioned above that, just as the Church of Arles has always possessed primacy within Gaul in the priesthood by the merit of antiquity, so the city itself has also possessed primacy in secular affairs by reason of its usefulness.

Consequently, not only the administration of the province of Vienne but also that of the three provinces has, in consideration of Saint Trophimus, been entrusted to the care and solicitude of the priest of the Church of Arles, as the authority of your holy predecessors also testifies.

[Note: [Col. 0881D] Sirmondus reads “made manifest.”]

[Note: [Col. 0882D] Since the authority of your predecessors in what follows refers to the letters of Zosimus, in which only three provinces—Vienne and the two provinces of Narbonensis—are mentioned as assigned to Arles, a question arises whether the same three provinces alone are meant here by “the three provinces,” with Vienne included among them. Yet the formula “not only the province of Vienne, but also the three provinces” appears to distinguish those three from Vienne. Moreover, since the first province of Narbonensis had already been restored by Boniface, the successor of Zosimus, to the bishop of Narbonne, these bishops do not seem to have intended to recall that province to the See of Arles—especially since Saint Leo, in Letter 10, praising Boniface’s judgment, declared that this province lay outside the jurisdiction of Arles, as will become clear in the observations on Dissertation 5, Part II, Chapter 2, no. 7. The bishops of the three provinces were from Vienne, Narbonensis Secunda, and the Maritime Alps. This is inferred from the names of the bishops prefixed to Leo’s subsequent reply. Although their sees are not stated there, other documents that identify bishops of this period and their sees make it sufficiently probable that Constantine was bishop of Die and Fonteius of Vaison in the province of Vienne; that Maximus was bishop of Riez, Asclepius of Apt, Armentarius of Antibes, and Theodore of Fréjus in Narbonensis Secunda; and that Valerian of Cimiez, Ursus of Senez, Nectarius of Digne, and Ingenuus of Embrun belonged to the Maritime Alps. These three provinces, therefore, seem to be the only ones these bishops asked Leo to preserve for the See of Arles, unless someone supposes that among the otherwise unknown episcopal names there was a bishop of Tarentaise in the Graian Alps, and that the bishops mentioned also included that province—so that, besides Vienne, they indicated three provinces: Narbonensis Secunda, the Maritime Alps, and the Graian Alps. That they also included the Graian Alps is confirmed by Leo’s judgment, since among the four towns not granted to Arles but adjudicated to Vienne he lists Tarentaise, which all sources place in the Graian Alps.]

He was granted this further honor and dignity: not only was he to govern these provinces by his own authority, but he was also to keep all Gaul, entrusted to him in place of the Apostolic See, under the entire ecclesiastical rule.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] This indicates a kind of apostolic delegation granted to the bishop of Arles by the letters of Zosimus, when Zosimus ordered that anyone traveling to Rome or elsewhere from any part of Gaul should receive from that bishop the appropriate letters of authorization. The right to convene a synod even from other provinces of Gaul was also apparently granted by Zosimus to the same bishop; this makes the delegated representation still more evident. Compare what we shall say on this matter in the observations on Dissertation 5, Part II, Chapter 6, no. 8.]

## CHAPTER IV

Having communicated all these matters and faithfully brought them to the knowledge of your blessedness, we ask and beseech the crown of your holiness, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has chosen in you justice, patience, tranquility, and all the good qualities of holiness and perfection, and by the most blessed Apostle Peter, whom we believe has been restored to us by the divine gift through your life and conduct, that your authority, which will endure forever, command the priest of that Church to reclaim for his own pontificate everything that the Church of Arles, as we indicated above, either received from antiquity or afterward claimed by the authority of the Apostolic See.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] These words refer to Saint Trophimus, mentioned above in note 10 (Col. 881, n. a). We discussed in the preceding note what follows, namely, the authority afterward conferred on the bishop of Arles in place of the Apostolic See.]

We ourselves would have presented ourselves before your holiness, either because of our duties or on account of this embassy, had illness not held some of us back and the scarcity of the present year others from fulfilling this desire of our vows. But we trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, who has granted our prayers and desires the result of your most prompt kindness: those who are now deprived of the duty of an embassy will afterward discharge in person the duty of returning thanks.

## LETTER LXVI

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Formerly Letter 66; now 86. Written on 5 May 450.]

[Note: [Col. 0883C] It is found in Arelatensian Collection 15, in which the preceding letter also appears.]

### SAINT LEO THE POPE’S REPLY TO THE PETITION ABOVE OF THE FELLOW-PROVINCIAL BISHOPS OF THE METROPOLITAN CHURCH OF ARLES

## [Col. 0884A]

### SYNOPSIS

Saint Leo gives his judgment concerning the ancient controversy between the Churches of Arles and Vienne and assigns each its proper boundaries.

To our most beloved brothers Constantine, Armentarius, Audentius, Severianus, Valerian, Ursus, Stephanus, Nectarius, Constantius, Maximus, Asclepius, Theodore, Justus, Ingenuus, Augustalis, Superventor, Ynantius, Fonteius, Palladius: Leo, pope.

[Note: [Col. 0883C] Baronius, following a correction in the ancient hand indicated in Vallicellian manuscript G. 99, published the name as “Armatarius,” whereas the first hand read, as in Quesnellus, “Armantarius.” We preferred Sirmondus’s reading, which is also found in the subscriptions of Letters 99 and 102.]

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Baronius, with the Vallicellian manuscript, reads “Unantius.” In manuscripts, V and Y are easily confused; “Ynantius” is read in both of the cited Letters 99 and 102.]

## CHAPTER I

Having read your letters, which our sons Petronius the presbyter and Regulus the deacon delivered to us, we clearly recognized how benevolent an affection you show toward our brother and fellow-bishop Ravennius: for you ask that what his predecessor had deservedly lost through excessive presumption be restored to him.

[Note: [Col. 0886B] The Vallicellian manuscript reads “Regulinus.” But in the following letter the name is “Regulus.”]

But the bishop of Vienne, by sending letters and legates, had anticipated your fraternal petition with his own representation, complaining that the bishop of Arles had usurped for himself the ordination of the bishop of Vaison.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] Some manuscripts incorrectly read “of the bishop of Vence,” as Quesnellus noted in the margin.]

Since we must preserve both the reverence due to our paternal sanctions and the goodwill of all of you, so that we allow nothing to be torn away or diminished from the privileges of the Churches, it followed that, in order to preserve peace within the province of Vienne, a moderation of justice should be applied that would neglect neither the practice of antiquity nor your desires.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] The printed editions, together with the manuscripts of Baronius and Sirmondus, read “within the provinces of Vienne and Arles.” Quesnellus corrected this from his manuscript: “For at that time there was only one province called Vienne.” He does not indicate in the note which manuscript this was, but it can be inferred from another note attached to this letter that it was the Thuaneus manuscript. He writes: “The rescript above of Leo was first brought to light by the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, together with the petition itself and the other letters concerning the affairs of the Church of Arles; he testifies that he received them from an Arelatensian manuscript. I believe that we have come upon the same manuscript, which is preserved in the Thuaneus library. Although certain marks of difference appear, they are nevertheless too slight to make us believe it is a different manuscript from Baronius’s, since it agrees with it in all other respects, such as in the addition appended to the preceding letter concerning Leo’s decree confirmed by Pope Symmachus.” This, however, is not the same manuscript from which Baronius published this letter, as the variant readings themselves, however minor, demonstrate. Both the manuscript of Baronius and that of Quesnellus belonged to the same Arelatensian collection, as did all the others belonging to that collection; hence it is not surprising that they agree in most respects and that all exhibit the addition appended at the end. But their differing readings in some places—including this reading, which is not altogether insignificant—show that they are different copies of the same collection. P. Coustantius mentions two manuscripts of this collection in the Colbertine Library, to which the Thuaneus manuscripts passed, in the preface to volume I of the *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 161. One of these was formerly Arelatensian; its text was carefully copied and sent by Faber to Baronius, and the published reading “within the provinces of Vienne and Arles” is now found in Vallicellian G. 99. The other, a Thuaneus manuscript different from Baronius’s, must be the one that suggested Quesnellus’s correction. We accept that correction because Leo in this letter always mentions a single province, not two, as will be evident from Chapter II: “within your province,” “the remaining cities of the same province.” Compare the following note.]

## CHAPTER II
Considering, therefore, the allegations of both parties’ clerics, we find that the illustrious cities of Vienne and Arles have always belonged within your province [Note: [Col. 0884D] He names one province in the singular, namely the previously mentioned province of Vienne, within which he includes the cities of Vienne and Arles. He calls it “your province,” although the nineteen bishops whose names appear in the letter belonged to at least three provinces: Vienne, Second Narbonensis, and the Maritime Alps, as we showed in note 16 (Col. 881, n. g) on the preceding letter. Did he understand by “the province of Vienne” not a civil but an ecclesiastical province, which comprised several civil provinces? Or did he intend to set aside those provinces which, by Boniface’s decree to Hilary of Narbonne, were each to have their own metropolitan, as we shall discuss at greater length in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, part II, [Col. 0885C] chapter 6, no. 5 and following? Perhaps, however, the holy pontiff wished in this letter to judge only the dispute that had arisen between the bishops of Vienne and Arles and had been brought before him, and in which alone allegations had been produced by both sides; so that for this reason he passed over even the matter concerning the privileges of the see of Arles, which the bishops had requested in the letters mentioned above. The question concerned only the province of Vienne because of the ordination of the bishop of the city of Vasio, which lies in that province; allegations were produced on this matter and envoys were sent by both sides.]—both Vienne and Arles being distinguished cities—so that, by an alternating arrangement in certain matters, now the one, now the other took precedence in ecclesiastical privileges, although it was reported that they had once shared the same right among the nations. Therefore we cannot permit the city of Vienne to be wholly dishonored as regards ecclesiastical justice, especially since, concerning the reception of its privilege, it already enjoys the authority of our decision; and we have judged that the power taken away from Bishop Hilary should be assigned to the bishop of Vienne. So that he may not suddenly appear to have been made inferior, he shall preside over the four neighboring towns, namely Valence, Tarentaise, Geneva, and Grenoble, so that Vienne itself may be fifth among them [Note: [Col. 0885C] Thus Quesnell and Sirmond, *conjuncta*. The Vallicellian codex has *juncta* instead of “fifth.”], and the care of all the churches mentioned may belong to its bishop. But the remaining cities of the same province [Col. 0885B] shall remain under the authority and ordination of the bishop of Arles; and because of the moderation of his character, we believe that he will henceforth be so devoted to charity and peace that he will never consider taken from himself what he sees granted to his brother. Given on the third day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and Avienus, vir clarissimus.

1000 At the end of this letter, the following words are found in the Arles and Vallicellian codices: [Col. 0886A] “This decree of the Lord Leo was confirmed by the apostolic see, with Pope Symmachus presiding, in the consulship of Probus, vir clarissimus.”

# LETTER LXVII [Note: [Col. 0885C] Elsewhere numbered 51. The letter formerly numbered 67 is now 87. Written on 5 May in the year 450.] TO RAVENNIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

[Note: [Col. 0885C] This letter is found only in the codices of Collection 15 of Arles.]

## Synopsis

He sends Ravennius his celebrated letter to Flavian on the incarnation of the Word of God against Eutyches, so that, in defense of the faith, either this letter or Cyril of Alexandria’s letter may through him become faithfully known to all the bishops of Gaul. He also indicates the confidential instructions entrusted to the envoys.

To his most beloved brother Ravennius, Leo, pope.

For a long time we kept our sons Petronius the presbyter and Regulus the deacon in the City, both because they deserved this favor from us and because the condition of the faith, which is now being assailed by the error of certain persons [Col. 0886B], demanded it [Note: [Col. 0885C] Thus the Thuaneus codex cited by Quesnell, and likewise in Sirmond. Elsewhere, following Baronius, it has been emended, although in the Vallicellian manuscript G 99, which Baronius used, *incessit* is read—plainly a scribal error for *incessitur*.]. For we wished them to take part in our deliberation [Note: [Col. 0885D] Someone might suppose that this refers to a conference held by Leo and many bishops when Valentinian, Placidia, and Eudoxia came to Rome in February; see note 7 (Col. 860, n. f) on Letter 55. But because that conference seems to have concluded in February, Petronius and Regulus could not have been detained until 5 May on its account. It is therefore more probable that a later conference is meant. We conjecture that the reference is to the conference concerning Anatolius: when letters concerning his ordination, which was causing very great difficulty, were received around April, a longer consultation was necessary in order to devise useful counsel amid the grave danger of affairs and to give appropriate instructions to the envoys. See Letter 69, chapter 2. This will become clearer from note 5 (below, n. g).], and that everything we desire through you should reach the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow priests, most dear brother. We specially entrust this to your affection: by the vigilance of your care, let our letter, which we sent to the East in defense of the faith [1001] [Note: [Col. 0886B] We have restored the word *charissime* from the Vallicellian codex and Sirmond, where it also occurs in the printed editions, although Quesnell removed it.] [Note: [Col. 0886B] In our Leonine manuscripts *vel* is sometimes used for *et*, as may be seen in note 22 (Col. 893, n. i) on Letter 80. Certainly, in Letter 113, chapter 3, Leo wrote that, when Proterius had been ordained bishop of Alexandria, he had sent letters to the bishop, *vel* to his ordainers, *seu* to the clergy; he used *vel* and *seu* for *et*. For he gave separate letters, according to custom, to each of those who had written separately; these letters have perished, just as we possess his separate Letters 171, 172, and 173 concerning the ordination of Timothy of Alexandria, Proterius’s successor. A clearer example is available in Letter 131, chapter 1: “The appended copies of the letters which I have sent to the most clement emperor, *vel* to the bishop of the city of Alexandria himself, will show.” Since copies of two letters are indicated—Letter 129 to Proterius of Alexandria and Letter 130 to the Augustus Marcian, both still extant—it is clear that *vel* here too is used for *et*. In the present case it is evident that *vel* is used for *et*, because Saint Leo does not commend Cyril’s letter to the Gallic bishops in such a way that, if it becomes known to them through Ravennius’s agency, he permits his own letter to Flavian, which he transmitted especially for acceptance and subscription, to be suppressed; this is gathered from Letter 99. Compare note 8 (Col. 893, n. i) on Letter 70. The letter of Cyril indicated is his second letter to Nestorius, which Saint Leo used against Eutyches, as is clear from its longer fragment appended to Letter 165 to the Augustus Leo. This is the first mention in Leo’s letters of this letter of Cyril, as it is subsequently in Letters 69 and 70, written in Anatolius’s case; and in these letters—an especially noteworthy fact—the same letter of Cyril and Leo’s celebrated Letter 28 to Flavian are joined and commended to the Easterners with equal solicitude, just as here to the Gallic bishops. Thus it is most strongly confirmed from this passage that Petronius and Regulus had long been detained at Rome for deliberation in Anatolius’s case and instructed in the whole affair. Why, however, among the many testimonies of the Fathers diligently collected at this time and delivered to the envoys sent to the East on this matter, and later appended to Letter 165 (see the prefatory admonition to Letter 28, final number), why, I say, this one letter of Cyril should be especially urged by Leo here and elsewhere, and joined with such solicitude to Letter 28 to Flavian, is sufficiently gathered from Letters 69 and 70. The Eutychians, namely, exalted and pressed the Nicene faith alone; while claiming adherence to it, they asserted that Catholics, enemies of their errors, had departed from it. Compare note 6 (Col. 855, n. g) on Letter 54. Moreover, since they were most hostile to the Nestorians, they especially extolled the letters of Cyril, who had overthrown the Nestorian heresy. Therefore, to remove every suspicion that the Nicene faith had been injured by the Catholic doctrine he had defended in his letter to Flavian, Leo judged Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius most useful; in it Cyril, expounding the Nicene faith, delivered the same teaching as in Leo’s Letter 28. He therefore joined the two together, so that comparison of them might show that their doctrine was one and the same, opposed to the Eutychians; and so that it might also be clear how wrongly the latter vaunted the Nicene faith, from which, as Cyril himself interpreted it, they differed most greatly. From what Leo says here, moreover, it is known that this letter of Cyril was sent into Gaul; and perhaps for that reason it is inserted, from the translation which Leo sent there and used among the testimonies appended to Letter 165, in the very ancient Collection 5 and in the later Collection 12, which we shall elsewhere show were compiled in Gaul. From this letter, further, we learn that Saint Leo sent Ravennius both his Letter 28 to Flavian and Saint Cyril’s letter to Nestorius. From Idatius of Spain, a contemporary writer, we further gather that Flavian’s own letter to Leo was also transmitted, together with other documents concerning the Eutychian heresy. In accordance with Leo’s command, the aforesaid Ravennius sent all these not only to the Gallic but also to the Spanish bishops. “From Gaul,” Idatius says in his Chronicle at Olympiad 130, “letters are conveyed: those of Bishop Flavian sent to Bishop Leo, with the writings of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to Nestorius of Constantinople, concerning Eutyches the Ebionite heretic, and the replies of Bishop Leo to the same; these, with the records (perhaps of the synod of Constantinople against the same Eutyches) and writings of other bishops, are sent to the churches.” Hence Flavian’s Letter 22, beginning *Nulla res*, was inserted into several Latin collections, and especially into the Spanish collection.], or that of Cyril of holy memory, which entirely agrees with our understanding [Col. 0887A], become known to all the brothers, so that, having been made more certain against those who by perverse arguments judge the Lord’s incarnation to be violated, they may fortify themselves beforehand with spiritual strength [Note: [Col. 0887D] The Vallicellian codex adds *charissime* and, after *praemuniant*, adds *frater*.].

You have a favorable opportunity by which you can commend the beginnings of your episcopate to all the churches and to our God, if you carry out these things, most dear brother, just as we believe and have instructed. But whatever was not to be entrusted to writing [Note: [Col. 0887D] Since the emperor Theodosius, who supported Eutyches, had written concerning Anatolius’s case, certain complaints or precautions regarding that emperor were not to be committed to writing. For the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, by which Theodosius maintained that the whole matter had been settled, refused any other council; see Letter 64. The pontiff wished to oppose it not only with the synod held at Rome but also with the signatures of the Gallicans appended to his letter to Flavian; these signatures, though later, were transmitted in Letter 99. Indeed, from chapter 4 of Letter 99 it is clear that Leo intended the Gallicans themselves to write to the same emperor; but the writers there state that, because circumstances soon changed through Theodosius’s death, this was no longer necessary. From these facts it is sufficiently clear what confidential instructions were given to the Gallican envoys; and at the same time it is evident how contrived and false is Quesnell’s interpretation of this passage, offered at the end of Dissertation 5, part II, chapter 9.] you will learn through the message of our aforesaid sons, relying on the Lord’s help; you will execute them energetically and, as we have said, commendably. May God keep you safe, most dear brother. Given on the third day before the Nones of May, in the consulship of the most glorious Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and Avienus, vir clarissimus.

# LETTER LXVIII [Note: [Col. 0888C] Elsewhere placed after Letter 76. The letter formerly numbered 68 is now 88. Written some time after May of the year 450.] CERETIUS, SALONIUS, AND VERANUS, BISHOPS OF GAUL, TO HOLY POPE LEO (G)

[Note: [Col. 0888C] In the table of Collection 5, chapter 65, this title is found: “Ceretus, Salonius, and Veranus, bishops of Gaul, to Pope Leo, giving thanks for his teaching.”]

## Synopsis

I. They give thanks for his letter to Flavian, which they affirm is being celebrated throughout all the churches. — II. They send a copy transcribed by themselves, for Leo to correct and return.

To the holy Lord, most blessed father, and most worthy pope of the apostolic see [Col. 0888A] Leo, Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus.

## Chapter I

Having reviewed Your Blessedness’s letter, which you sent to the bishop of Constantinople as an instruction concerning the faith, we judged it fitting that, enriched by the abundance of so great a teaching [Note: [Col. 0888D] The same codex has *tanta*, “so great.”], we should at least discharge our due thanks by offering the service of a letter. Approving your paternal solicitude toward us, we confess ourselves all the more bound to you by your anticipation of the cure, because we have come to know the benefits of remedies before experiencing the illnesses. For knowing that remedies applied to wounds already inflicted are almost too late, you admonish us, through the voices of your provident piety [Note: [Col. 0888D] Two codices of Collection 12, the Vatican 1340, and the Venetian 169, with different punctuation, read: “Having been forewarned, we recognize,” and so forth. We retained the common reading found in the Vindobonensis of Collection 5, which seems to refer to Leo’s instruction in the preceding letter that Ravennius should send his letter 28 to all the bishops, “so that, having been made more certain against those who by perverse arguments judge the Lord’s incarnation to be violated, they may fortify themselves beforehand with spiritual servitude.” Later codices have *transmiseris*, “you may have sent.”], to clothe ourselves in those apostolic defenses.

We plainly recognize, most blessed pope, what you have conveyed to us from the inner chambers of your heart with particular affection: you come to the aid of the safety of others by curing them; and while you draw forth the poisons of the ancient serpent infused into the hearts of others [1004], as though stationed upon a watchtower of charity, you raise that apostolic cry of care and solicitude [Note: [Col. 0888D] The manuscripts of Collection 12 omit these words.], lest the unexpected enemy come upon the unsuspecting, lest careless security provide a place for the wound—holy lord, most blessed father, and most worthy pope of the apostolic see [Col. 0889A].

Moreover, our particular joy grows great and ineffable because that special page of your teaching is celebrated throughout the assemblies of all the churches, so that the unanimous judgment of all is truly declared to be harmonious, and it is rightly proclaimed that the primacy of the apostolic see was established there from which the oracles of the apostolic spirit are still disclosed.

## Chapter II

Therefore, if you graciously permit it, we beseech you to review a work destined to benefit both the present and future ages, which, in our zeal to preserve it, we have committed to leaves; and, if anything is lacking through a copyist’s error [Note: [Col. 0889C] From the letter to Flavian, which Leo had sent to Ravennius to be disseminated throughout Gaul, many copies were transcribed. In the copy sent to Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus, they implore Leo to correct anything that may be lacking through the copyist’s error. That Leo corrected this copy with the greatest care is clear from the fact that he later instructed the bishops of the province of Milan to obtain a copy of the same letter from Ceretius. See Letter 97, chapter 2.], may Your Holiness deign to correct it; or, if by some addition of your diligence you have enlarged the page beneficial to all who read it, command in your careful piety that the same addition be made to this little book. Thus not only may many of our holy brother bishops throughout Gaul, but also many of your sons among the laity, who greatly desire this letter for the manifestation of the truth, deserve to copy, read, and retain it after it has been returned to us and corrected by your holy hand. If you deem it worthwhile, we desire that those sent on this business return to us at once, so that, since your safety is our joy and salvation, the joys of your health may return to us more swiftly through the welcome report of your well-being.

And in another hand:

May Christ the Lord preserve your crown, mindful of our humility, through a long life, O holy lord, most blessed father, and most worthy pope of the apostolic see.

[Col. 0889C] Ceretius, your servant, salutes your apostolate and commends himself to your prayers.

1005 Salonius, your venerating servant, salutes your apostolate in the Lord and asks for the help of your prayers.

[Col. 0890A] Veranus, devoted to your apostolate, salutes Your Blessedness and asks that you pray for me.

# LETTER LXIX [Note: [Col. 0889D] Elsewhere numbered 52. The letter formerly numbered 69 is now 89. Written on 16 July in the year 450.] TO THE AUGUSTUS THEODOSIUS

[Note: [Col. 0889D] This letter is extant in the manuscripts of the Hispanic Collection, numbers 11, 12, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, and in Sichard’s copy.]

[Note: [Col. 0889D] In the Hispanic Collection this title is found: “Likewise, Pope Leo to the Augustus Theodosius, in which he writes that he should acknowledge what is preached concerning the incarnation of the Son of God by Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, and that a universal council should be held in Italy.”]

## Synopsis

I. He suspends his consent to the ordination of Anatolius of Constantinople and demands a profession of faith. — II. He requests that Anatolius renounce communion with heretics and subscribe to the common faith. He sends envoys. He asks that a synod be held within Italy.

Leo, bishop, to Theodosius, always Augustus [Note: [Col. 0889D] The word *semper* is always absent from the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript. In some others *Augusto* is also omitted.].

## Chapter I

In all the letters of Your Piety, amid those anxieties which we suffer for the faith, you have given us the greatest hope of security by commending the Council of Nicaea; so much so that, as you have often written already, you do not permit the priests of the Lord [Col. 0890B] to depart from it [Note: [Col. 0890C] Manuscript Collection 21 reads, “through all the letters of Your Piety.” The several letters of Theodosius sent to the West in defense of the Council of Nicaea, indicated here, are two letters to Leo: one written shortly after the Ephesian outrage, to which Leo replied in Letter 54; the other written when he informed the same pontiff about Anatolius’s ordination, to which Leo now replies. There is also Imperial Letter 63 to the Augusta Placidia. We explained why the emperor, who favored Eutyches, nevertheless insisted upon the Council of Nicaea in note 6 (Col. 855, n. g) on Letter 54.].

But lest I appear to have done anything prejudicial to the defense of Catholic truth, I have so far thought it inappropriate to write back in either direction concerning the ordination of the man who has begun to preside over the Church of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0890C] The printed editions of Leo add *tibi*, “to you.” Quesnell accepted this word but rashly removed it, and further replaced *rescribendum* with *scribendum*. Manuscript Collection 21 omits *tibi* and *temere*. The Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts omit only *temere* but retain *rescribendum*. The Hispanic Vindobonensis lacks *tibi* and, through a scribal error, reads *terre scribendum*. We preferred the reading of the Ratisbon codex, supported by the Grimani codex, manuscripts of Collection 24, Sichard’s copy, and the editions of the Councils. In the following letter it is said of Anatolius alone: “I have so far delayed writing to him, not denying affection, but awaiting the manifestation of Catholic truth.”]. I have not denied affection, but have awaited the manifestation of Catholic truth. May Your Clemency bear this patiently [1006], so that when he has proved himself toward the Catholic faith to be as we desire, we may rejoice in his sincerity both more fully and more securely [Note: [Col. 0890D] We have added *et* from the excellent Ratisbon codex.].

But lest some unfavorable suspicion of our disposition trouble him, I remove the entire occasion of difficulty and demand nothing that seems either arduous or doubtful [Note: [Col. 0890D] The earlier printed editions of Leo, before Quesnell, read *ambiguum*, “ambiguous.”]; instead, I invite him to what no Catholic can reject. Those who before us have shone throughout the world in proclaiming Catholic truth, whether in the Greek or Latin language [Col. 0890C], are known and manifest; and to their knowledge and teaching certain men of our own age also contribute, from whose writings an equal and abundant instruction is produced. Just as this instruction destroyed the Nestorian heresy, so it has cut off the error that is now sprouting again [Col. 0891A] [Note: [Col. 0891C] The earlier printed editions of Leo before Quesnell read incorrectly: “the error of communion.” Sichard likewise has the incorrect reading. Shortly afterward, the Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts read *et apostolicae sedi*, “and to the apostolic see.”].

Let him therefore carefully reread what faith concerning the Lord’s incarnation was guarded and always proclaimed in the same manner by the holy Fathers; and when he has seen that the letter of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, of holy memory [Note: [Col. 0891C] The reference is to Cyril’s second letter to Nestorius. See note 5 (Col. 886, n. g) on Letter 67.], is consonant with the understanding of those who preceded us—a letter in which Cyril sought to correct and heal Nestorius, reproving his perverse proclamations and setting forth more clearly the faith of the Nicene definition, and which, after being sent by him, was received into the archives of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0891C] It is clear from Letter 8, in Coustant, p. 1091, that Cyril’s letter was sent to Saint Celestine. It is known from Letter 11, p. 1102, that the same pontiff approved it. Hence the archives of the apostolic see received it.], let him also review the acts of the Council of Ephesus, in which, against the impiety of Nestorius, Catholic testimonies of priests concerning the Lord’s incarnation were inserted and cited by Cyril of holy memory. Let him not disdain to review my letter as well, which he will find to agree in every respect with the piety of the Fathers [Col. 0891B].

And when he recognizes that what is beneficial to him has been sought and desired from him, let him consent with all his heart to the judgments of Catholics [1007], so that he may declare, before all the clergy and the entire people, a sincere profession of the common faith by an unreserved subscription [Note: [Col. 0891C] The editions before Quesnell and Sichard incorrectly read *communionis fidei*, “of the faith of communion.” Shortly afterward, the Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts have *et apostolicae sedi*, “and to the apostolic see.”], to be published to the apostolic see, to all the priests of the Lord, and to the churches. Thus, when the world has been brought to peace through one faith, we may all say what the angels sang when the Savior was born of the Virgin Mary: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14) [Note: [Col. 0891C] The Ratisbon manuscript reads *possint*, “may be able.”].

## Chapter II

Since both we and our blessed Fathers, whose teaching we venerate and follow, are united in the harmony of one faith, as the bishops of all the provinces testify, let Your Clemency’s most devout faith ensure that the writings of the bishop of Constantinople—such as those befitting an approved and Catholic priest—reach us as soon as possible [Note: [Col. 0891C] The Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts read *debentur*, “are owed.”], openly and clearly declaring [Col. 0892A] that, if anyone believes or asserts anything concerning the incarnation of the Word of God other than what the profession of all Catholics and my own profession declare, he should separate that person from his communion [Note: [Col. 0891C] Thus, more correctly, with the earlier printed editions and the Vindobonensis Hispanic, Ratisbon, the manuscripts of Collection 24, and Sichard’s copy. Quesnell and Merlin read *lucide*, “clearly”; the Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts read *lucide protestantis*, “of one clearly declaring.”], so that we may rightly extend to him brotherly love in Christ [Note: [Col. 0891D] The Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts read: “so that we may rightly direct toward him brotherly love in Christ.” The indefinite verb *intendere* also appears in the Hispanic Vindobonensis.].

But so that, with the Lord’s help, a swifter and fuller effect may be provided for these salutary concerns through the faith of Your Clemency [Note: [Col. 0891D] Manuscript Collection 21 reads *dispositionibus*, “arrangements.”], I have sent to Your Piety my brothers and fellow bishops, Abundius and Asterius, and also Basil and Senator, presbyters whose devotion has been tested [Note: [Col. 0891D] The editions printed before Quesnell read *nostros*, “our men.” Soon afterward, the Hispanic Vatican has *Sabundium*, and the Isidorian *Sabuldium*, instead of *Abundium*—incorrectly, as is clear from the other letters. The Grimani codex has *Etherium* instead of *Asterium*, both here and in the two following letters. The Ratisbon codex here prefers *Eterium*, but in the following letter has *Aterium*.]. Through them you may graciously recognize the form of our faith, once the instructions we have sent have been made known [Note: [Col. 0891D] The Grimani codex reads *quae nostra fides*, “which is our faith.” What is added, “with the instructions we have sent made known,” certainly included a sufficient exposition of the authority of the Fathers, which is transmitted in Letter 71 to Theodosius. See note 9 there (Col. 896, n. k).], so that, if the bishop of Constantinople consents to the same confession with all his heart, we may rejoice, as is fitting, in ecclesiastical peace with confidence, and nothing ambiguous may appear to remain [1008] from which we might perhaps suffer through unnecessary suspicions [Col. 0892B] [Note: [Col. 0892C] The editions before Quesnell, together with most manuscripts, including the Hispanic Vindobonensis and Sichard’s copy, read “so that we may suffer from superfluous suspicions.” Quesnell’s reading is confirmed by the Ratisbon codex.].

But if any persons disagree with the purity of our faith and with the authority of the Fathers, may Your Clemency grant that a universal council be held within Italy, as the synod that had assembled at Rome for this very reason requested of me [Note: [Col. 0892C] This had been done in Leo’s Letter 44, issued in the name of the Roman synod on 13 October of the preceding year.], so that, when all those who have fallen either through ignorance or through terror [Note: [Col. 0892C] The Ratisbon manuscript, together with the Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts, reads *errore*, “through error,” where perhaps the initial letter *t* was omitted because of the same letter at the end of the preceding word. The error refers to the ignorance expressed in the preceding word. Here, however, the violence inflicted at the Ephesian outrage is indicated, to which some yielded after being struck with terror. See Letter 44, chapter 1. We therefore retained, with the printed Leonine editions, the word *terrore*, “terror,” which is related to *timore*, “fear,” found in the editions of the Councils after Merlin and in Sichard’s copy. Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 reads *ne cuiquam*, “lest anyone.”], provision may be made through remedies of correction, and no one may henceforth be free to make such mention of the Council of Nicaea that he is found to be opposed to its faith [Note: [Col. 0892D] See note 6 (Col. 855, n. g) on Letter 54.]. For it will benefit both the universal Church and your rule if one God, one faith [Note: [Col. 0892D] The conjunction *et*, “and,” is omitted by the Hispanic Vindobonensis, the Vatican Collection 11, and the Ratisbon codex, which shortly afterward reads *una totius mundi confessio teneatur*, “one confession of the whole world be maintained.”], and one sacrament of human salvation are maintained in one confession throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 0892D] The Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts and the manuscripts of Collection 24 omit *hoc*, “this.”].

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Valentinian for the seventh time and Avienus, vir clarissimus [Note: [Col. 0892D] We judged that this date, which appears in the older printed editions and in Sichard, as well as in the Hispanic Vatican and manuscripts of Collections 21, 23, and 24, especially the Ratisbon codex, should be restored. Quesnell preferred the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, a chronological notation found in the Hispanic Vindobonensis, the Isidorian Vatican, another Vatican manuscript of Collection 11, and Merlin’s copy of Collection 12.].

# LETTER LXX [Note: [Col. 0893C] Elsewhere numbered 54. The letter formerly numbered 70 is now 91. Written on 16 July in the year 450.] TO THE AUGUSTA PULCHERIA

[Col. 0893A]

[Note: [Col. 0893C] In the Hispanic Collection this title is found: “Concerning the matters requested above from the Augustus Theodosius.”]

## Synopsis

He is awaiting Anatolius’s profession of faith. He has sent envoys from himself to the East. All scandals must be removed through a general council.

Leo, bishop, to Pulcheria Augusta.

I rejoice at the fact that you graciously devote your religious zeal to renewing ecclesiastical peace, which appears to have been disturbed by the dissensions of certain persons. For this is especially owed to your glory: that, once all the scandals which the enemy had stirred up against the catholic faith have been removed, there may be one and the same confession of the truth throughout the whole world. This will be restored more readily and more securely if no seeds or traces of perverse opinions are left behind.

Yet I must not pass over what belongs to my responsibility: namely, to learn what the bishop of Constantinople maintains concerning the incarnation of the Son of God—especially since harsh matters preceded his ordination, and he ought therefore to have sent us writings of such a kind as would clearly show him to be free from the contagion of the error which has recently emerged.

Accordingly, desiring to have secure concord with him and to extend to him the grace of brotherly charity, I postponed writing to him for the time being—not denying affection, but awaiting a manifestation of catholic truth. For what I ask is simple and unqualified: that, once the labor of lengthy disputations has been set aside, he should accept the letter of Cyril, of holy memory, bishop of Alexandria, which he himself sent to Nestorius. In it Cyril both refuted Nestorius’s error and expounded the faith of the Nicene definition; or that he should assent to my letter which was addressed to Flavian, bishop of holy memory.

After carefully examining these writings, let the bishop of Constantinople unhesitatingly acknowledge that he must reject what unskilled folly dared to define against the pure and singular faith. For my confession concerning the incarnation of the Lord and that of the holy Fathers agree in every respect and are one. If anyone should think that this confession ought not to be followed, he has himself severed himself from the structure of catholic unity, although we desire that everything be restored to its proper condition.

For the more rapid attainment of these salutary arrangements, I have sent my brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, as well as Basil and Senator, most proven presbyters, who should present to your Clemency the form of the faith which we preach according to the teaching of the venerable Fathers. They should also show, without the circumlocutions by which truth is usually obscured, what has been defended concerning the incarnation of the Son of God by the approved priests of the whole world. After divine grace, they ought to be aided by the holy assistance of your piety, lest an imprudent contention proceed to the disturbance of the whole Church; for, once correction has been applied, everyone ought to return to the harmony of one confession.

If perhaps some persons disagree from it, let a universal council of priests be held within Italy, with your Clemency’s support, so that, when every deceptive artifice has been removed, it may at last become clear, after deeper deliberation, what ought either to be restrained or healed.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and of Avienus, a most illustrious man.

[Note: [Col. 0893C] Thus all our codices of the various collections, together with Sichardus and Merlinus, except the Hispanic Vatican and Isidore, in which it reads *videatur* (“may appear”), and the Hispanic Vindobonensis and the manuscripts of collection 21, which, together with the printed editions and Quesnellus, have *videbatur* (“appeared”).]

[Note: [Col. 0893C] Thus in the printed editions, the Grimani codex, the Vindobonensis, the Hispanic codex, manuscript collection 24, and Sichardus. The Ratisponensis has *exciverat* (“had driven out”); the Hispanic Vatican, Isidore, and other codices of the other collections have *exstruxerat* (“had constructed”), as do the three Thuaneian manuscripts cited by Quesnellus in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0893C] Quesnellus introduced this reading from the Grimani manuscript; it is confirmed by the excellent Ratisponensis codex. The Hispanic Vindobonensis and manuscript collection 24 come closer to it, and among these is the Victorinus cited by Quesnellus; they read, as do Merlinus and Sichardus, “since harsh matters had preceded his ordination.” Our remaining manuscripts and Quesnellus’s three Thuaneian manuscripts, together with the other printed editions, read, “since several matters had preceded his ordination.” See Quesnellus’s note 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0893D] The Hispanic Vatican and Isidore have “I desire.”]

[Note: [Col. 0893D] Two of Quesnellus’s codices, one Thuaneian and the Grimani, together with two of our manuscripts, the Ratisponensis and Vatican collection 11, read *dispositionum* (“arrangements”). See Quesnellus’s note 2. Immediately afterward, for “the bishop of Alexandria,” the Hispanic Vatican and Isidore have “the bishop of the Alexandrian Church.”]

[Note: [Col. 0893D] Thus the Grimani and Cambridge manuscripts of Quesnellus; our manuscript books, the Ratisponensis, both Hispanic codices, the Vatican, Isidore, another Vatican collection 11, and two manuscripts of collection 21 also have this reading. The older printed editions, together with Sichardus, have “and my letter.” Quesnellus thinks in note 3 that Anatolius was given the choice of subscribing either to Cyril’s letter or to Leo’s, and therefore judged *vel* (“or”) preferable to *et* (“and”). But we believe *vel* is used for *et*, or in the sense of “also.” Compare annotation 5 (Col. 886, n. g) on letter 67. Indeed, in the preceding letter to Theodosius, who favored Eutyches, Leo does not indicate this as an option but says of Anatolius, absolutely, though modestly, after mentioning Cyril’s letter: “Let him not disdain also to review my letter.” He repeatedly insists elsewhere that subscription to this letter is necessary. It is clear from letter 99 that the Gauls, to whom through letter 67 he wished Cyril’s letter to be made known together with his own letters to Flavian, accepted at the synod only the letter to Flavian, as Leo had demanded. Anatolius himself was not received until the following year, after subscribing to the same letter, as letters 78, 79, and 80 prove.]

[Note: [Col. 0894C] The Hispanic Vatican and Isidore, together with the manuscripts of collection 21, have “carefully.”]

[Note: [Col. 0894C] The printed editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, incorrectly read “what he dared.” Quesnellus’s correction, adopted from the Grimani codex, is confirmed by our Ratisponensis and the Hispanic Vindobonensis. The Hispanic Vatican and Isidore, as well as the manuscripts of collections 11 and 21, have a related reading: “what she dared to define must be rejected by him.” See Quesnellus’s note 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The manuscripts vary. The Ratisponensis has *abscidet* (“will cut off”); the manuscripts of collection 21, together with the editions preceding Quesnellus, have *abscindet* (“will sever”). We have retained the past tense introduced by Quesnellus from his own codices; it is also found in both Hispanic codices, in the Vatican Isidore, and in another manuscript of collection 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The Ratisponensis has “unity”; immediately afterward it has “and should be made to differ.”]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] Three Vatican codices, the Hispanic codex, Isidore, and another manuscript of collection 11 have *Sabundium*; the Grimani, instead of *Asterium*, has *Etherium*; the Ratisponensis has *Aterium*.]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] In the Ratisponensis codex, *urbis* (“of the city”) appears; it seems that the letter *u* mistakenly entered in place of *o*.]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The editions preceding Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus, have *contentio* (“contention”).]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The Ratisponensis has *unitatem* (“unity”); immediately afterward, *discreparetur* (“there should be disagreement”).]

[Note: [Col. 0894D] The earlier editions of Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, have *annuente* (“with the consent of”).]

[Note: [Col. 0895B] We preferred this chronological note, supplied by the Ratisponensis codex as consistent with the preceding letter, to the reading of the Vulgate and other codices, “the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.” For all the letters concerning the same matter, which were to be transmitted by the same legates, were ordinarily signed by Leo on the same day, as is clear from other examples. Perhaps in these codices, whose leaves had become separated, the numeral sign V was incorrectly written XIII instead of XVI before the Kalends, as several manuscripts prefer in the preceding letter and all do in the following letter. Nevertheless, we did not wish to abandon the excellent Ratisponensis.]

# LETTER LXXI

[Note: [Col. 0895C] Otherwise 53. What was formerly 71 is now 92. Written on 17 July in the year 450.]

[Note: [Col. 0895C] It is found in the same collections as the two preceding letters, except collection 19 of the Ratisponensis. Quesnellus added *a pari* (“equally”), which none of our codices supports; the plural number of the context establishes that this letter was addressed to all of them together.]

## To the Constantinopolitan Archimandrites

### Synopsis

He complains about the silence of Anatolius and those who ordained him concerning their renunciation of the errors. He informs them about the legates sent on behalf of the faith.

Leo, bishop, to Faustus, Martinus, Peter, Manuel, Job, Antiochus, Abraham, Theodore, Pientius, Eusebius, Helpidius, Paul, Asterius, and Charosus, presbyters and archimandrites, and to Jacobus, deacon and archimandrite.

[Note: [Col. 0895C] The earlier printed editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 21, have “Martianus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0895C] The printed editions insert “Vivantiacus.” We have removed it not only on the authority of both Hispanic codices, the Vatican Isidore, and the codices of collections 11 and 24, but also because, whereas the other names occur in the subscriptions of the Constantinopolitan synod under Flavian, Vivantiacus alone does not appear. Moreover, in the codices of collection 21, which lack the names Job and Antiochus, *Vivantiaco* is recognizable as having been mistakenly written from these words; the editions derived both forms from different manuscripts.]

The cause of the faith, in which Christian salvation consists, compels me to labor with great anxiety, fearing lest the wickedness which ought to have been cut off at its beginnings should, with the passage of time, become more stubborn and more widespread. For when the most merciful emperor sent us letters demonstrating his concern for the peace of the universal Church, the bishop of Constantinople himself, and those who consecrated him, indicated nothing to us about the errors that had been suppressed or renounced, beyond what concerned the ordination of the new bishop. It was as though no scandal or offense had arisen in that Church, or as though the merit of the one ordained would not be chiefly demonstrated by this: that he had shown himself to be alien to doctrines opposed to catholic understanding.

Therefore, lest the examination of the truth should, as often happens between distant regions, extend into excessive delays, we sent our brothers and fellow bishops Abundius and Asterius, as well as Basil and Senator, presbyters and most proven men, to the most pious prince, with a sufficient presentation of the authorities of the Fathers.

We earnestly desire, dearest brothers, that they be assisted in every respect by your diligence and concern, so that the impiety which, through blind acts of audacity, has advanced into destructive precipices may no longer have power to deceive the simple. At the same time, we desire that those who have fallen either through ignorance or because they were led astray by fear be aided by the remedies of correction through a more suitable medicine.

And therefore, since you are justified by faith, because you love catholic truth and have been instructed by the Holy Spirit concerning the singular sacrament of human salvation, work together with us and strive with all the devotion you can, so that, falsehood having been destroyed and the solidity of the faith defended, we may enjoy God’s secure peace throughout the whole world.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and of Avienus, a most illustrious man.

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The earlier printed editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, have “the wickedness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The same editions have “more destructive.” Immediately afterward, the Hispanic Vatican and Isidore have *altior* (“higher”) instead of *latior* (“broader”).]

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The same printed editions, together with our manuscripts, have “the examinations of the truth should extend.” We judged Quesnellus’s better reading not to be abandoned.]

[Note: [Col. 0895D] The Hispanic Vatican, Isidore, and another manuscript of collection 11 have “Sabundius.” Immediately afterward, the Grimani codex consistently has *Etherium* instead of *Asterium*, as in the two preceding letters.]

[Note: [Col. 0896D] The “authorities” are the testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the incarnation of Christ. See annotation 9 (928, n. j) on letter 88 and the preliminary notice to letter 28. From this passage we learn that Leo carefully collected these testimonies on this occasion and sent them to the emperor; hence in letter 69, chapter 1, he urges him to reread such authorities of both Greek and Latin Fathers. Compare annotations 8 (Col. 890, n. k) and 19 (Col. 891, n. k) on the same letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0896C] The manuscripts of collection 21 have “we desire to assist your diligence and concern.” A Vatican codex, shortly afterward, has “with criminal acts of audacity.” Then, instead of *exitialia* (“destructive things”), Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Otherwise, *exitiabilia*.” Later, both Hispanic manuscripts and the Vatican Isidore have “the simple also,” and the Hispanic Vindobonensis and the manuscripts of collections 21 and 24 have *altiore* (“higher”) instead of *aptiore* (“more suitable”).]

[Note: [Col. 0896C] The older printed editions, together with certain manuscripts, have “or through error.” We preferred Quesnellus’s emendation, which is found in our other codices and agrees with the sounder reading of letter 69; see annotation 23 (Col. 892, n. o) there.]

[Note: [Col. 0896C] The editions preceding Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus, have “who love catholic truth.” The Vatican manuscript of collection 11 has “by which catholic truth.” Quesnellus’s reading is supported by both Hispanic codices, the Vatican, Isidore, and several manuscripts of collection 21.]

[Note: [Col. 0896D] The same printed editions, together with the same manuscripts of collection 24, Sichardus, and the Hispanic Vindobonensis, have “do this.”]

[Note: [Col. 0896D] The Hispanic Vatican has “may you enjoy.”]

[Note: [Col. 0896D] We would gladly assign this letter also to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October, for the reason given in annotation 17 (above, n. a) on the preceding letter, if we had the authority of any codex to support us, and if this letter were not lacking in the Ratisponensis manuscript, whose authority enabled us to correct the date published for the preceding letter.]

# NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

1. Quesnellus placed the following letter, without a chronological note, first among the letters of the year 451, after letter 75, written to the same Faustus on the sixth day before the Ides of November in the year 450. But letter 75 was written when, by the Lord’s favor, the freedom of the catholics had greatly increased—namely, after the death of Theodosius, who had supported the Eutychians. The letter now to be presented, however, was written when some human consideration or fear could restrain someone from an open defense of the truth. Hence the pontiff sharpens Faustus’s spirit, saying: “I exhort your Blessedness not to be ashamed of the Gospel of the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ,” which presupposes that Theodosius was still alive. Thus the following letter appears to have been given before the death of Theodosius, which occurred at the end of July 450, or at least before news of his death reached Leo—news that had arrived before Leo wrote letter 75 on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

2. In the Chalcedonian collection, from which alone we possess this letter, it is described in chapter 6 after Flavian’s letter, among Leo’s letters numbered 22, and before letter 28, given on the Ides of June in the year 449; from this it may appear to have been written around that time. But since the author of the Chalcedonian collection did not everywhere preserve the exact chronological order, as is clear from other documents, the place assigned to this letter in that collection ought not to compel us—especially since its opening words, “It is always a pleasure for me to address your Charity,” indicate that correspondence had already long existed between Leo and Faustus, and this appears to have begun at the outset of the Eutychian controversy.

Among the letters that have reached us, the first to Faustus and the other archimandrites is letter 32, given on the Ides of June in the year 449. Next came another to the same persons, letter 51, written from the Roman synod on the Ides of October of that year; and this was the first after the Ephesian Robbery, when, with Theodosius supporting them, the force and arrogance of the Eutychians became known. After this came letter 61, to Faustus and Martinus, written on 17 March in the year 450.

Since in that letter Leo mentions their letter sent to him at the same time that he himself had sent letter 51, as we observed in annotation 48 (Col. 871, n. m) on letter 59, it seems certain that Faustus’s and Martinus’s letter then received was the first after the Ephesian Robbery, and that letter 61 was the first letter he sent to them after letter 51. Therefore, fearing that letter 51 might perhaps have reached them, he attached a copy of it to letter 61 at the first opportunity.

Hence the following letter, number 72, in which the holy pontiff responds to another later letter of Faustus sent through Parthenius, ought not to be placed before letter 61. Since, moreover, from what has been said it was delivered while Theodosius was alive or before news of his death, but the exact day and month are unknown, we have placed it at the end of the letters given while Theodosius was alive, though we can assert only that it was written between March and November of the year 450.

3. We believe that the Latin original of this letter is lacking. For the Latin text which we possess from the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection appears to be a translation from the Greek interpretation. Hence, besides certain features foreign to Leo’s style, it lacks a chronological note, just as it is absent from all the letters in that collection which were rendered from Greek. We therefore give first place to the Greek interpretation, which supplies the place of the original.

# LETTER LXXII

[Note: [Col. 0897B] Otherwise 57. What was formerly 72 is now 93. Written between March and November in the year 450.]

## To Faustus the Presbyter

### Synopsis

He praises his faith and urges him to vigilance.

[Note: [Col. 0897] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

To his most beloved Faustus, presbyter, Leo, bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0897B] Quesnellus, together with the Roman editors, adds “son,” although this word is absent from the earlier editions of Leo, the Greek version, and all the Latin codices.]

It is always a pleasure for me to address your Charity and to discharge the affection of a greeting, since I know that you are approved and a guardian of the most sincere faith, one who is not carried about by every wind of doctrine but stands firmly upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles, which is Christ. Thus, when the Son of Man comes in his Divinity for the purification of the whole world, may you be found among the chosen grain of eternity, worthy to be stored in the granaries.

Having therefore received the letter through my son Parthenius, I return a reciprocal greeting and exhort your Blessedness, dearest son, not to be ashamed of the Gospel of the birth of the Lord Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham according to the flesh. For this faith conquers the world when someone believes that Christ Jesus is the Son of God.

If any questions of faith should arise, we remind you to write to us more fully about matters that concern the common good; we shall gladly receive those who convey them.

[Note: [Col. 0897B] The editions of Leo have “I know that you are both approved.” We followed the reading of the Council edition, which is also the reading of all the codices.]

[Note: [Col. 0897B] From this point to the end of the sentence the passage reveals not Leo but the translator, who did not render the Greek text very well. A more suitable rendering from the Greek would be: “May you be found among the chosen grain of eternity, worthy to be stored in the granaries.”]
