[Note: [Col. 0897C] Thus all codices and editions before the Roman edition; in the latter, following the Greek, it reads “your perfection.” In any case, the title “Blessedness,” applied by Leo to presbyters, is never found in his original letters. In letter 74, addressed to Martinus, an archimandrite and presbyter like Faustus, he uses the words “of your affection.” The translation is further confirmed by the practice of the person who habitually called monk-presbyters “Blessedness.”]

[Note: [Col. 0898B] Some codices omit the word “Jesus,” and below “Christ,” as these words are also lacking in the Greek.]

To the beloved son Faustus, presbyter, Leo, bishop.

It is always a pleasure for me to address your Love, and I take the greatest delight in returning your greeting. For I do not fail to recognize that you are a proven guardian of the holy faith, not carried about by every wind of doctrine, but remaining firm upon the foundation of the prophets and apostles, who is Christ. Thus, whenever the Son of Man comes in his Divinity for the purification of the whole world, may you be found among the chosen grain of eternity, worthy to be stored in the granaries.

When, therefore, the letter was delivered through my son Parthenius, I return a similar greeting and exhort your Perfection, beloved son, not to be ashamed of the Gospel of the birth of the Lord Christ, son of David and son of Abraham according to the flesh. For this faith has conquered the world, if anyone believes that Jesus is the Son of God.

If any inventions concerning the faith should be found, we remind you to write to us more fully, since we shall gladly receive those who convey these matters.

[Note: [Col. 0898C] In the Venetian manuscript: “of sound faith.” Perhaps this is more correct.]

[Note: [Col. 0898C] In the margin of the Roman edition: “perhaps, these things.”]

# LETTER LXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0899C] Otherwise after letter 57. What was formerly 73 is now 90. Written at the end of August or the beginning of September in the year 450.]

[Note: [Col. 0899C] This letter of the emperor Marcian is found only in the Chalcedonian collection and in the Venetian manuscript of collection 22, which received additions from the Chalcedonian collection. We have no doubt that the Greek text is original, on account of the dating and consular notation, which would have been omitted in a Greek translation, as is consistently observed in the other letters rendered into Greek. Whether the Latin text too is original, or a translation from the Greek, may be investigated. It is certain that the emperor Marcian wrote some things in Latin and Greek, just as he is reported to have addressed the Council of Chalcedon in both Latin and Greek in action 6, page 1472. See Baluzius’s note o. We shall likewise see another letter of the same emperor, letter 100 to Leo, written in both Latin and Greek. We could produce more examples of the same kind if necessary. The gravity and dignity of the Latin expression in the present letter favor a Latin author rather than the translator, who in the other letters was very humble and less skilled in rendering the Greek.]

## Of Valentinian and Marcian to Leo, Archbishop of Rome

On their election and on the celebration of a council. (G)

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Thus the Latin codices and the Greek text, as well as the Council edition. Quesnellus alone has “to the bishop.”]

The victorious Valentinian and Marcian, glorious triumphators, always Augusti, to Leo, most reverend archbishop of the glorious city of Rome.

By the providence of God and the election of the most excellent senate and the entire army, we have come to this supreme imperial power. Therefore, for the sake of the revered and catholic religion of the faith of Christians, whose assistance we trust will direct the strength of our power, we have thought it right first to address your Holiness, who possesses primacy in the episcopate and holds the divine faith, through sacred letters: inviting and entreating you that, for the stability and preservation of our empire, your Holiness may pray to the eternal Divinity, so that we may have such a purpose and desire that, once every impious error has been removed through the celebration of a synod under your leadership, the greatest peace may be established among all the bishops of the catholic faith, remaining pure and undefiled by every crime.

Done at Constantinople, in the seventh consulship of our lord Valentinian Augustus and the consulship of Avienus, a most illustrious man.

[Note: [Col. 0899D] The Divionensis codex has “it happened that we came.” Baluzius’s other codices have “I came.”]

[Note: [Col. 0899D] The Veronese manuscript 57 has “out of reverence.”]

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Quesnellus, together with the Greek, has “bishop.” We restored the common reading of the Council editions from the Latin codices.]

[Note: [Col. 0899D] Thus excellently according to the same Veronese manuscript, to which our other codices come close; only three of Baluzius’s codices incorrectly have “Avienianus,” “Abienus,” or “Avenienus VI” instead of “Avienus, a most illustrious man.” The day and month are absent from the codices and from the Greek. Since, however, Marcian in this letter gives notice of his accession, it was written shortly after his election. Some, following Baronius, believed that Marcian assumed the empire before August of this year, because in the Justinian Code a law of the same emperor against the Eutychians is dated the Kalends of August, with Valentinian VII and Avienus as consuls. But it is clear from the Chalcedonian and Hispanic collections, among others, that Trebonianus incorrectly attached this chronological note to the law *On Apostates*, since the law is transmitted there in full with the date the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August at Constantinople, under Sporatius, a most illustrious man, and the consuls who are announced—namely, 18 July in the year 452. Marcian, moreover, ascended to the empire on 24 August 450, as can be gathered from the Paschal Chronicle. Therefore this letter was written in that year, either at the end of August or at the beginning of September.]

Victorious Valentinian and Marcian, glorious, triumph-bearing, ever kings, to Leo, most reverend bishop of the glorious city of Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] The Venetian manuscript has “we came.”]

We came to this greatest kingdom by the providence of God and by the choice of the extraordinary senate and of the entire army. Therefore, concerning the revered and catholic religion of the faith of the Christians, whose assistance we trust directs the power of our empire, we considered it right first to address your Holiness, who presides as bishop and rules the divine faith, in sacred writings; urging and entreating you that, for the stability and security of our kingdom, your holiness may beseech the eternal Divinity. For our purpose and desire are such that, once every impious error has been removed through the synod that has been convened under your authority, the greatest peace may be established among all the bishops of the catholic faith, having become pure and undefiled by every pollution.

It was done at Constantinople, in the seventh consulship of our lord Valentinian, eternal Augustus, and the consulship of Avienus.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] Thus according to the Greek codices Vatican 1178 and Ottobonianus 29, instead of *agnosynēn*, the reading of the printed edition.]

[Note: [Col. 0900D] The Venetian manuscript has “may you beseech.”]

[Note: [Col. 0900D] In the margin of Cotelier’s edition: “of the synod that will be convened.”]

# LETTER LXXIV

[Note: [Col. 0900C] Otherwise 55. What was formerly 74 is now 94. Written on 13 September in the year 450.]

[Note: [Col. 0900C] It is found in the Grimani manuscript of collection 18 and in our Vatican and Venetian codices of collection 12; the latter incorrectly address this letter to Martianus. Quesnellus notes in a marginal postscript: “It is clear from the context of the letter that Leo did not address this letter to Martinus alone, but equally to his other colleagues.” But at the beginning he writes only to Martinus, as the words “your affection” indicate; shortly afterward he addresses the catholic brotherhood, that is, all the Constantinopolitans, and especially the monks who held catholic opinions.]

## To Martinus the Presbyter

### Synopsis

How good it is to suffer for the truth, whose unity is not divided by distances between places. Mention of the legates.

Leo, bishop, to Martinus the presbyter.

We give thanks to God and receive great confidence in pious rejoicing when we learn that your affection and the catholic brotherhood are flourishing in the spirit of faith, so that no heretical temptation can inflict any weakness upon your hearts. As you know, our concern for destroying it by divine power has neither been lacking nor will be lacking until the right hand of almighty God shatters all the weapons of the devil. He is permitted to attempt something for this reason: so that he may be overcome by Christ’s faithful with greater glory.

If any difficulties or delays arise, they must be endured with equanimity, dearest brothers; for where truth is the teacher, divine consolations are never absent. Although great distances of place divide us, we are nevertheless with you in the unity of faith, confessing with all our heart Jesus Christ our Lord as true God and true man. We suffer no loss in you when we rejoice in the concord of your confession—provided only that, with the Lord’s help, your steadfastness perseveres, as the Apostle says: “For to you it has been granted for Christ, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29).

To strengthen the courage of holy minds in this matter, we believe that our brothers and legates, whom we sent on behalf of the freedom of the apostolic faith and whom we trust have been with you for some time, will be of great benefit. Once you have learned the purpose of all our action, join your concern and counsel to this pious work. It is not necessary to write more fully about this matter now, since we have already sent sufficient letters through the persons mentioned above, by which the entire catholic brotherhood may be most abundantly instructed.

It will be the work of divine power and grace that the Son of God, who made the nature of the human race his own, may assert more fully than we see or understand the great sacrament of his compassion (1 Timothy 3:16). Impious presumption has indeed robbed itself of this mystery, but it could not take it away from upright hearts.

Given on the Ides of September, in the consulship of Valentinian and Avienus, most illustrious men.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] Thus from two of our manuscripts of collection 12, as the context itself requires, not as in the printed editions, which have “we received.”]

[Note: [Col. 0901C] Thus the manuscripts and Quesnellus. The other editions have “it has been granted.”]

[Note: [Col. 0901C] Leo wrote this while he had not yet received news of the death of Theodosius, who favored the Eutychians; hence he presupposes that the catholics were still being harassed.]

[Note: [Col. 0901C] The manuscripts of collection 12, together with the editions preceding Quesnellus, omit *pio* (“pious”). In the margin he gives *operi* (“work”) instead of *opere* (“to the work”).]

[Note: [Col. 0901C] That is, letter 71.]

[Note: [Col. 0901D] Thus our manuscripts, together with the editions preceding Quesnellus; in Quesnellus, “which we foresee.”]

[Note: [Col. 0901D] This date, month, and consular notation are absent from the Grimani manuscript. They are read, however, in our manuscripts and in the printed editions. Only “Augustus” should be supplied after “Valentinian,” making “Valentinian Augustus VII.” Both codices of collection 12 immediately add after the consular note: “through Carterius and Asclepiades, deacons, to Constantinople,” but corruptly. Since letter 80, chapter 1, mentions Casterius—elsewhere Carterius—the presbyter, and Asclepiades, the Constantinopolitan deacon, we believe the reading should be: “through Carterius, or Casterius, the presbyter, and Asclepiades, the Constantinopolitan deacon.” Since the same manuscripts place letter 78 after this letter, and that letter was sent to Constantinople through Casterius and Asclepiades in the following year, on the Ides of April, we judge this notation to belong to letter 78 rather than to the present letter. There is no indication or probability that these clerics were sent twice, both in this year and in the following one.]

# LETTER LXXV

[Note: [Col. 0902C] Otherwise 56. What was formerly 75 is now 95. On 8 or 9 November in the year 450.]

[Note: [Col. 0902C] Published by Quesnellus from the Grimani manuscript of collection 18. We have compared it with the Ratisponensis manuscript of collection 19.]

## To Faustus and Martinus, Presbyters

### Synopsis

I. He writes that what was done at Ephesus against the faith is intolerable to the bishops of the West.  
II. He says that both Nestorius and Eutyches serve Antichrist; against them the Church professes that it worships not one nature but one person.

Leo to Faustus and Martinus, presbyters and archimandrites. Through Maximinus the count.

[Note: [Col. 0902C] We added the words “and archimandrites” from the Ratisponensis codex. Quesnellus added *a pari* (“equally”), which our codex lacks and which the plural context excludes.]

## Chapter I

Welcoming every opportunity for writing, I do not cease to address your affection with priestly love, so that from the very frequency of my letters you may recognize how great a concern we have for the universal Church. Since its most devout faith must be defended with the utmost zeal, your devotion too ought to share in our labors.

For, through our brothers, the bishops and presbyters whom we sent on behalf of the condition of the Christian religion and whom we trust have been with you for some time, you were able to perceive fully from all the instruction we gave them how intolerable it is considered among all the priests of our region that the profane folly of certain persons attempted to introduce something contrary to the sacrament of human redemption.

And now, through our son Maximinus the count, we continually exhort you in our addresses: since, by the favor of the Lord, the freedom of the catholics has greatly increased, assume spiritual courage against the forerunners of Antichrist. Blessed John says: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God; and every spirit that dissolves Jesus Christ is not from God; and this is the Antichrist” (1 John 4:2–3).

[Note: [Col. 0902D] The Ratisponensis has “God.” The freedom of the catholics is said to have increased greatly because Marcian, the new emperor, favored the catholics. This is the first indication of Marcian’s election; it is quite credible that Maximinus the count, an official of that same emperor, brought news of it so that Valentinian might approve it.]

[Note: [Col. 0902D] Quesnellus, from the Grimani codex, has “you may take up.” We preferred the reading of the Ratisponensis.]

[Note: [Col. 0902D] The Ratisponensis omits “spirit” and, at the second occurrence, “Christ.”]

## Chapter II

Nestorius and Eutyches wished to serve under different forms of error but under the same spirit of falsehood. The catholic faith, instructed by apostolic and evangelical doctrines, detests and condemns both of them. From the time when the Word, coeternal with the Father, became flesh (John 1:14), the one whom it believes to be the Son of God it also confesses to be the Son of Man. In the one true God and true man, the Lord Jesus Christ, it professes that it worships not one nature but one person.

United with us inseparably and without distinction in this faith, stand and act steadfastly and manfully. If there are any delays concerning the arrangements we request, nevertheless inform us by letters from your affection on every occasion which divine grace may faithfully provide. For it is a great consolation when the accomplishment of the things desired is reported to anxious minds.

We wish these letters of ours, which we have sent to your affection, to be made known also to the other catholics, so that they may understand that they too are being stirred by these exhortations of ours to defend the faith.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the seventh time and of Avienus.

[Note: [Col. 0902D] The same codex has “the fifth day before the Ides.”]

[Note: [Col. 0902D] The Grimani manuscript and Quesnellus have “act confidently.” The Ratisponensis reading is better.]

[Note: [Col. 0902D] The same codex lacks the words “and evangelical.”]

[Note: [Col. 0902D] Our Ratisponensis has this reading; Quesnellus, from the Grimani codex, has “the coeternal Word of the Father.”]

[Note: [Col. 0902D] The Grimani manuscript and Quesnellus have “act confidently.” The Ratisponensis reading is better.]

[Note: [Col. 0903C] The Ratisponensis has *iisdem* (“these same [exhortations]”).]

# LETTER LXXVI

[Note: [Col. 0903C] Otherwise after letter 71. What was formerly 76 is now 96. Written on 22 November in the year 450.]

[Note: [Col. 0903C] It is found in manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collections 17 and 22, in which the address “to the archbishop” is read, as also in the Greek title; not “to the bishop,” as in Quesnellus’s edition.]

## Of the Emperor Marcian to Leo, Archbishop of Rome

[Note: [Col. 0903] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0903A] [Note: [Col. 0903C] No summary of this letter is prefixed in the Latin manuscripts; but one is read in the Greek manuscripts, from which the Roman editors published the Greek text and from whose Greek summary they made this Latin version. They improperly corrected only “December,” which is read in the Greek, to “September” [Col. 0903D], because they believed, on the basis of an erroneous consulship of a certain law of Marcian, that he had assumed the imperial power before 24 August and that this letter had been written shortly after his accession. Letter 74 was indeed dated immediately after he assumed the empire, to which he was elevated on 24 August, as Antonius Pagius demonstrated from the Paschal Chronicle. But this letter was written after the arrival of the envoys, which, as we learn from this letter, fell in the month of November.]

On 22 November, at Constantinople, in the consulship of our lord Valentinian, our most pious emperor, for the seventh time, and of Avienus, men of the highest rank, a sacred letter was sent by our lord Marcian, perpetual emperor, to the most holy bishop Leo, stating that those who had been sent by that most reverend man had been received with joy. Therefore, may he deign to come there with all eagerness and celebrate a synod; or, if this should seem burdensome to him, may he inform us by his own letter, so that, after the bishops have been summoned by sacred letters, whatever accords with the faith may be decreed in whatever city he approves.

1025 To Leo, most reverend bishop of the Church of the most glorious city of Rome, Marcian.

[Note: [Col. 0904C] Thus our five manuscripts. The commonly printed editions have “glorious.” The Divion manuscript and Quesnellus in the margin have “most reverend.”]

[Col. 0903B]

Your Holiness is not unaware of our zeal and prayer, since we desire the true religion of Christians and the apostolic faith to remain firm and to be preserved by every people with devout mind. [Note: [Col. 0904C] The commonly printed editions likewise add in the margin, from the Greek, “for indeed.” Shortly afterward, in place of “security,” certain manuscripts have “solicitude.”] Indeed, we do not doubt that the security of our power rests upon right religion and the favor of our Savior.

Therefore, we gladly and with grateful mind, as was fitting, received the most reverend men whom Your Holiness sent to our piety. It remains that, if it pleases Your Blessedness to come to these regions and celebrate a synod, you should deign to do so out of religious devotion. Your Holiness will certainly satisfy our desires and determine what is useful for sacred religion.

[Col. 0903C] But if it is burdensome for you to come to these regions, let Your Holiness make this known to us by your own letter, so that our sacred letters may be sent throughout the whole East, and into Thrace itself and Illyricum, in order that all the most holy bishops may assemble at a definite place, wherever we approve, and, as Your Holiness has determined according to the ecclesiastical rules, may by their own decision declare what benefits Christian religion and the Catholic faith. [Col. 0905A] [Note: [Col. 0905C] Thus our manuscripts and those of Baluzius, agreeing with the Greek text. This reading indicates that what benefits religion and the faith was to be declared in a general council, just as Leo had previously determined, especially in his letter to Flavian. The following letter of Pulcheria also expresses a similar view, affirming that the council’s Fathers were to decree the Catholic confession under your direction. This was in fact done by the solemn reception of Leo’s letter to Flavian at Chalcedon.] [Note: [Col. 0905C] The date of this letter, namely 22 November 450, has been preserved for us by the heading that we prefixed from the Greek manuscripts in place of the summary.]

[Col. 0904A]

On the tenth day before the Kalends of December, at Constantinople, in the consulship of our lord Valentinian, our most devout emperor, [Note: [Col. 0904C] Read “the seventh.”] for the eighth time, and of Avienus, men of the highest rank, divine letters were sent by our lord, the eternal emperor Marcian, to the most holy bishop Leo, stating that those sent by that same most reverent man had been gladly received. Therefore, may he deign to come to these regions with all eagerness and complete the synod; or, if this should seem burdensome to him, may he declare it by his own letters, so that, after the bishops have been summoned by divine letters, whatever accords with the faith may be decreed in whatever city he approves.

1026 To Leo, most devout bishop of the Church of the glorious city of Rome, Marcian.

[Note: [Col. 0904D] The word ἐκκλησίας (“Church”) does not appear in the printed editions; we have added it chiefly from the Venice manuscript and from the Latin text.]

[Col. 0904B]

Your Holiness is not in doubt concerning our zeal and prayer: for we wish the true religion of Christians and the apostolic faith to remain firm and to be preserved by all peoples with devout mind. Indeed, there can be no doubt that the tranquility and strength of our empire rest upon right religion and the favor of your Savior.

Therefore, the most reverent men whom Your Holiness sent to our piety we received gladly and, as was proper, with a grateful mind. [Note: [Col. 0904D] Venice manuscript: ἡδέως, “gladly.”] It remains that, if it pleases Your Holiness to come to these regions and complete the synod, you should deign to do so out of love for religion. Your Holiness will satisfy our desires and set forth what is useful for sacred religion.

But if it is burdensome for you to come to these regions, let Your Holiness make this very thing known to us in a private letter, so that divine proclamations may be sent throughout the whole East, Thrace, and Illyricum, [Note: [Col. 0904D] Roman edition, in the margin: ἀποσταλήσοιται; probably read ἀποσταλήσωνται, “may be sent.”] in order that all the most holy bishops may come together at a definite place, wherever we approve, and that what is beneficial to the peace of Christian religion and to the Catholic faith, as Your Holiness has formulated according to the ecclesiastical canons, may be established.

EPISTOLA LXXVII. [Note: [Col. 0905C] Formerly placed after Letter 58. What was previously Letter 77 is now Letter 102. It was written at approximately the same time as the preceding letter.] OF PULCHERIA AUGUSTA TO LEO, MOST HOLY ARCHBISHOP OF ROME. (G)

[Note: [Col. 0905] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0905A]

1028 [Note: [Col. 0905C] This summary is found in the manuscripts of the Latin Chalcedonian collection that contain the complete and finished edition of Rusticus, such as the three manuscripts of Baluzius and our Chigianus 483. It is absent from Vatican manuscripts 1323 and 4166, which preserve some portions of Rusticus and omit others. In the very old Verona manuscript 57 and Venice, St. Mark’s 79, the following summary, expressed in different words, is prefixed: “Here begins the letter of Pulcheria Augusta to the same most holy archbishop of Rome, Leo. It states that the most reverend Anatolius of Constantinople, having abandoned error, was confirmed as bishop, chiefly by subscribing to his dogmatic letter sent to Saint Flavian; it also states that Flavian’s body was brought back to his see and deposited in the Basilica of the Apostles, and reports other matters demonstrated by the contents of his sacred letters.”]

Divine words were also sent by the divinely remembered Pulcheria to the same most holy man, announcing that Anatolius, the God-beloved archbishop of Constantinople, after every error had been set aside, had without any delay subscribed to the letter recently sent to Flavian, of holy memory, and that a synod was now to be held in the regions of the East. [Note: [Col. 0906C] Thus the manuscripts of the same Rusticus; the printed editions read sustinere, “to maintain.”] [Note: [Col. 0906C] Thus the Chigianus manuscript of the Chalcedonian collection, from the complete edition of Rusticus, and likewise the Greek. The printed editions have “sacred letters.”]

They also announced that the body of Flavian, of holy memory, had been brought to Constantinople, to be buried in the Basilica of the Apostles. The bishops who had been united with Flavian, of holy memory, and had been sent into exile were likewise to be recalled, so that they might await the decision of the synod for the recovery of their own churches. [Note: [Col. 0906C] The conjunction “and,” necessary here, is absent from the manuscripts of Baluzius. We found it in the Chigianus manuscript, and it was also present in the manuscript from which the editors of the Councils published their text.]

[Col. 0905B]

1030 To Leo, most reverend bishop of the Church of the glorious city of Rome, Pulcheria, most venerable Augusta.

We received the letters of Your Blessedness with all due episcopal reverence; [Note: [Col. 0906C] The printed editions read “with all fitting reverence for every bishop,” unsupported by any of our or Baluzius’s manuscripts. Baluzius’s Dijon manuscript reads “with fitting reverence for every bishop.” We preferred the reading of our five manuscripts and two others of Baluzius.] through them we recognized your faith as pure and such as ought, together with holiness, to be offered to the sacred temple. I, however, as well as my lord, the most tranquil emperor, my husband, have always remained and continue to remain in the same faith, avoiding every depravity, pollution, and evil practice.

Therefore, Anatolius, the most holy bishop of glorious Constantinople, has remained in the same faith and religion, and embraces the apostolic confession of your letters, after that error which has now arisen among certain persons has been removed. Your Holiness will be able to recognize this more clearly from his own letters also. [Note: [Col. 0906C] Since it is our purpose to present the old version from the Greek, whatever its form may be, we have retained “of the letter,” although “of the Catholic faith” would have been expected from the Greek and is also required by the context. Immediately afterward we have added from the manuscripts the particle “for,” which the editors omitted as unsuitable.]

For he has likewise subscribed, without any delay, to the letter of the Catholic faith which Your Blessedness sent to Flavian, bishop of holy memory. [Col. 0905C] [Col. 0907A] Therefore, may Your Reverence deign to make known, in whatever way you see fit, so that all the bishops of the entire East, of Thrace, and of Illyricum may quickly be able to assemble from the eastern regions in one city, just as it has also pleased our most pious lord, my husband the emperor. Once a council has been held there, let them decree, under your authority, both concerning the Catholic confession and concerning those bishops who had previously been separated, as faith and Christian piety require.

Moreover, let Your Holiness know that, by order of our lord and most tranquil prince, my husband, the body of Flavian, of holy memory, was brought to the glorious city of Constantinople and was suitably placed in the Basilica of the Apostles, where the bishops who preceded him were accustomed to be buried. Likewise, he ordered by his pragmatic decree that those bishops who, for the same reason—because they had joined the most holy Flavian in agreement with the Catholic faith—had been carried into exile should return, so that, by the approval of the synod and the judgment of all the bishops assembling, they might be decreed worthy to recover their episcopate and their own churches. [Note: [Col. 0907C] The printed editions insert “ought,” but the manuscripts do not.] [Note: [Col. 0907C] The printed editions add “together” in the margin.]

[Note: [Col. 0907C] Since Leo replied to this and the preceding letter on the same day, in Letters 78 and 79, this indicates that they were sent together and received by the pontiff at the same time. Accordingly, both contain similar statements concerning the convening of a council from the bishops of the East, Thrace, and Illyricum. Thus, just as Marcian’s preceding letter was written on 22 November 450, this letter of Pulcheria must also have been written then. One point appears to stand in the way: Marcian says nothing about Anatolius’s action, which is reported in Pulcheria’s letter. If it had preceded the emperor’s letter, he would apparently not have omitted, while mentioning the honorable reception of the envoys, so favorable an event, which was the principal object of the embassy and was especially desired by the pontiff. Yet since the purpose of Marcian’s letter was to disclose his plan for convening a council, he could have passed over the other matters after mentioning only the reception of the envoys, knowing that Leo would learn them from other letters and from the acts sent at the same time. If Pulcheria’s letter is therefore considered later, it nevertheless should not be regarded as much later. Since the envoys had been received before 22 November, there is no reason to doubt that they immediately applied themselves diligently to their task and, with Pulcheria and Marcian favorable to them, easily brought the matter to completion. Thus, after everything had been settled within a few days and immediately sent to Rome with Pulcheria’s letter, the holy pontiff could have replied to Marcian and Pulcheria on the same day. On this view, too, the Augusta’s letter should be considered to have been written not long after 22 November and before the end of 450.]

[Col. 0906A]

1027 Divine words were sent by the divinely remembered Pulcheria to the same most holy man, announcing that Anatolius, the most God-beloved archbishop of Constantinople, [Note: [Col. 0906D] Venice manuscript: ἀρχιεπίσκοπον τῆς Κωνσταντινουπόλεως, “archbishop of Constantinople.”] after error had been separated from him, had without any delay subscribed to the letter recently sent to Flavian, of holy memory, and that a synod was already to be held in the regions of the East. [Note: [Col. 0906D] In the margin of the Roman edition: “were sent” [read: “were sent,” plural].] And that the remains of Flavian, of holy memory, had been brought to Constantinople, to be deposited in the Basilica of the Apostles; and that the bishops who had agreed with Flavian, of holy memory, and had been sent into exile were to be recalled, [Note: [Col. 0906D] Venice manuscript: οὕς, “whom.”] in order to recover their own churches while awaiting the decision of the synod. [Note: [Col. 0906D] In the margin of the Roman edition: “who,” “because it.”] [Note: [Col. 0906D] We have corrected this passage by following the reading of the Venice manuscript, which has “he has subscribed,” adding one diphthong and reading “to have subscribed,” as the Roman editors also conjectured in the margin. The commonly printed text incorrectly has “we have subscribed.”]

[Col. 0906B]

1029 To Leo, most devout bishop of the Church of the glorious city of Rome, from our lady Pulcheria, most venerable empress.

We received the letters of Your Blessedness with the reverence due to every bishop. Through them we recognized your faith as pure and such as ought, together with holiness, to be offered to the divine temple.

I, as well as my lord, the most tranquil emperor, my husband, have always remained and continue to remain in the same faith, avoiding every wickedness, pollution, and evil practice. [Note: [Col. 0906D] In the Venice manuscript: “remained.”]

Therefore, Anatolius, the most holy bishop of glorious Constantinople, remained in the same faith and religion, and embraces the apostolic confession of your letters, after that error which has now arisen among certain persons has been cast aside. Your Holiness can recognize this still more clearly from his own letters: for he has likewise subscribed, without any delay, to the letter of the Catholic faith which Your Blessedness sent to Flavian, bishop of holy memory. [Col. 0906C] [Col. 0908A]

For this reason, may Your Reverence deign to make it known in whatever manner seems appropriate, so that all the bishops of the entire East, of Thrace, and of Illyricum may quickly come from the eastern regions into one city, as has also pleased our lord, the most pious emperor, my husband. Once a council has been held there, let them decree, under your authority, concerning the Catholic confession and concerning those bishops who had previously been separated, as faith and Christian piety demand.

Moreover, let Your Holiness know that, by order of our lord and most tranquil emperor, my husband, the body of Flavian, of holy memory, was brought to the glorious city of Constantinople and placed, with the honor due to it, in the Basilica of the Apostles, where the bishops who had previously served were accustomed to be buried. [Note: [Col. 0908D] In the margin of the Roman edition: “is deposited.”]

He likewise ordered by his own pragmatic decree that those bishops who, for the same reason—because they had joined the most holy Flavian in agreement with the Catholic faith—had been subjected to exile should return, so that, through the examination of the synod and the decision of all the bishops assembled, they might be judged worthy to recover their episcopate and their own churches. [Note: [Col. 0908D] “And” is absent from the Venice manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0908D] In the Venice manuscript: “and the decision.”]

1033 EPISTOLA LXXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0908C] Formerly Letter 58. What was previously Letter 78 is now Letter 104. Written 13 April 451.] TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN. He gives thanks for the letters sent and for the defense of the faith.

[Col. 0907B]

Leo, bishop, to Marcian, ever Augustus.

[Note: [Col. 0908C] Letter 76 appears to be indicated here. We believe without doubt that Leo had previously replied to Letter 73 of the same emperor with special congratulations on his accession. It is highly probable that Letter 73 was sent by the emperor through Count Maximinus, who brought news of his accession to Rome. Just as Leo sent Letter 75 through him to Faustus and Martin, the Constantinopolitan clerics, dated 8 November 450, in which the first indication of his election appears, as we observed in Note 3 [Col. 0908D] (Col. 902, note j), so it is likewise beyond doubt that he sent congratulatory letters to the emperor through the same man.]

I rejoice that I have received the letters of Your Piety, and I recognize that they relate to the announcement of every prosperity, [Col. 0908B] since the opening of your letter makes us secure concerning the integrity of the faith. [Note: [Col. 0908D] The older printed editions have “since your speeches make you secure concerning the faith.” The same reading occurs in our manuscripts of Collection 12, which merely improve “you” to “us.” Quesnellus, following the Grimani manuscript, has “since your communications make us secure concerning the integrity of the faith.” We preferred the reading of the excellent Ratisbon manuscript, in which the words “your communication” suggest the beginning of Letter 76, by which Marcian first wrote to the pontiff concerning the affair of the faith; in Letter 73 he had given only a simple account of his accession.]

Therefore, recognize from your benefits to the Church, rather than from our words, how great is the gratitude we owe to your clemency. You do not doubt what sort of rewarder you have in all things, for whose religion you are so devoutly concerned; [Note: [Col. 0909B] The same printed editions and the manuscripts of Collection 12 read tam pia (“so pious”); Quesnellus’s emendation tam pie (“so devoutly”) is supported by the Ratisbon manuscript.] and he who, as the matter itself shows, chose you so gloriously that the Catholic faith might be defended against the ambushes of its enemies. [Note: [Col. 0909B] “Most gloriously,” introduced by Quesnellus, is confirmed by the same Ratisbon manuscript.]

May Your Piety graciously accept that I have now written this briefly through the clerics of my brother Anatolius. [Note: [Col. 0909B] Thus all our manuscripts. Quesnellus has “to have written.” In earlier printed editions both “written” and “to have written” were absent.] We have sent fuller information concerning everything belonging to my care for the condition of the Churches and their concord through our envoys. [Note: [Col. 0909B] This and the three following letters were dated 13 April and sent through the Constantinopolitan clerics. When the holy pontiff wrote these letters, he was also planning to send the envoys together with other fuller letters and instructions. Thus, just as he writes of the Constantinopolitan clerics in Letter 80, chapter 1, “After the venerable day of Easter we sent them back,” so he says of the envoys in Letter 81, “We shall send ours after the venerable day.” It must therefore be said that certain circumstances subsequently arose which postponed the dispatch of these envoys until a later time, namely June, when he sent Letters 83–86 to Constantinople through Lucentius, bishop, and Basilius, presbyter, envoys of the Apostolic See, dated 9 June. That these are the envoys mentioned in the letters delivered on 13 April is clear from Letter 83, chapter 1, where he says that he is sending envoys “as I indicated in my preceding letters,” and from Letter 84, chapter 1, “which I had indicated in other letters that I would do.” We suppose that the delay was caused by the late return of the earlier envoys, whom he thought should be awaited before new envoys were sent to Constantinople. When he wrote these letters, he hoped that they would arrive shortly, perhaps because he had learned either from Anatolius’s clerics or from the envoys’ own letters that, when the clerics departed Constantinople, the envoys were also about to follow them. Hence he indicated that new envoys were to be sent after Easter together with those clerics returning to Constantinople. But when he saw that the return of the former was delayed, he sent the clerics with these letters on 13 April, while postponing the new embassy until June, when they returned to Rome. Thus, concerning new envoys who had not yet been sent, Saint Leo says here “we have sent,” just as, concerning the Constantinopolitan clerics who had not yet departed Rome when he wrote, he says in Letter 80, chapter 1, “We sent them back with our letters,” since they were about to return to Constantinople. Likewise, in Letter 75, chapter 2, he writes concerning the same embassy, which was soon to be sent: “We wish these letters of ours, which we have sent to Your Affection,” and in Letter 83, concerning the envoys to whom he entrusted its delivery: “I have sent my brothers.” It was familiar to Leo to use the past tense of things or actions that were still future when he wrote, but that, from the standpoint of the time when the letters would be read, would already have occurred. Thus the apparently contradictory formulas are reconciled: concerning the same envoys whom he was planning to send shortly, he now uses the past tense in Letters 79 and 80, “whom we sent,” and now the future in Letter 81, “we shall send ours.” The former refers, in Leo’s intention, to the time when the letters were to be read; the latter to the time when they were written. We further observe that neither in this letter nor in the following does he reply to the council requested in the letters of the emperor and his wife Pulcheria. Leo evidently postponed that reply to the fuller writings that he mentions as being sent through the envoys, as is clear from Letter 82, chapter 2, to the same Marcian: “To your most pious concern, which you deign to have regarding the convocation of a synod, whatever I judge relevant to the usefulness of the case will be more fully and appropriately communicated through the embassy that, God willing, will soon reach Your Clemency.” This was done deliberately because circumstances had changed after Theodosius’s death: the new emperor was supporting the orthodox faith, Eutyches and his supporters had been restrained, the Catholic bishops deposed at Ephesus had been recalled from exile, and many who had already been deceived were daily returning to sound understanding. Leo therefore no longer considered a general council as necessary as he had previously judged it; or at least he did not think it should be held in the East, but in Italy. Since war had meanwhile broken out there, he thought the council should be postponed, as is related in Letters 83, 90, and 94. He considered these and similar matters better and more fully treated orally through envoys than in letters.]

Dated 13 April, in the consulship of Adelfius, a man of the highest rank. [Note: [Col. 0910C] The printed editions have “Adelphius.” But the Ratisbon manuscript consistently has “Adelfius,” as do the ancient Vatican manuscript 1322, both Spanish manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and other old books in the other letters. Prosper and Marcellinus likewise have this form, both in the printed editions and in the manuscripts. The same is confirmed by an inscription in Aringhius, vol. II, p. 419: “ADELFO.”]

EPISTOLA LXXIX. [Note: [Col. 0910D] Formerly Letter 59. What was previously Letter 79 is now Letter 105. Written 13 April 451.] TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.

[Col. 0909A]

[Note: [Col. 0910D] In the Spanish collection the following summary is read: “Leo’s letter to Pulcheria Augusta, in which he gives thanks because she destroyed the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies by defending the faith.”]

SUMMARY.

I. He gives thanks for the suppression, by her authority, of Nestorius and Eutyches. — II. Concerning the envoys who were assisted; the priests restored to their sees; the relics of Flavian brought back to the city; and the fallen to be received if they subscribe to the faith. — III. Concerning Eusebius enjoying communion with the Apostolic See, and Julian of Cos; and concerning the clerics of Constantinople who favored Flavian.

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Pulcheria Augusta.

CHAPTER I.

What we have always presumed concerning the holy mind of Your Piety, we have now learned by fullest experience: that the Christian faith, although attacked by the varied plots of the wicked, cannot be disturbed while you are present and prepared by the Lord for its defense. For God does not abandon either the sacrament of his mercy or the merit of your labor, by which you recently drove the treacherous enemy of holy religion from the very entrails of the Church. [Note: [Col. 0910D] The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts read depulisti, “you drove out.”] [Note: [Col. 0910D] The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts, together with manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21, and four manuscripts of Quesnellus, have “the sacrament of faith.”] Nestorian impiety could not defend its heresy, because it did not deceive the servant and disciple of truth, however much poison might be poured into the simple through the colored lies of that talkative man.

From this struggle of virtues it came about that, through your vigilance, those things which the devil contrived through Eutyches did not remain hidden, [Col. 0911A] and that those who had chosen for themselves the separate parts of a twofold impiety fell by the one power of the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0910D] The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts have “the things that the devil, who was perishing, [contrived].”]

Therefore, this is your second victory over the destroyed error of Eutyches. If he had possessed any soundness of heart, he could long ago have avoided it, since it had already been struck down in its authors and had long lain prostrate, lest he attempt to stir up renewed fires from buried ashes and pass into the company of those whose example he had followed, most glorious Augusta. [Note: [Col. 0911B] Quesnellus reads: “who, if he had possessed any soundness of heart, would long ago have avoided the error,” etc. We have restored the reading of the earlier editions, supported by all our nine manuscripts and sufficiently appropriate.]

Therefore, I gladly exult and offer to God worthy prayers for the prosperity of Your Clemency, for he has already bestowed upon you throughout all the regions of the world where the Gospel of the Lord is preached both the palm of a double glory and a crown. [Note: [Col. 0911C] The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts have “he bestowed the palm of a double glory.”]

CHAPTER II.

Let Your Clemency know that the whole Roman Church greatly rejoices over all the works of your faith, whether because you assisted our embassy in every way with devout affection, or because you restored the Catholic priests who had been expelled from their churches by an unjust sentence, or because you caused the remains of Flavian, of holy memory, an innocent and Catholic priest, to be recalled with due honor to the Church over which he had rightly presided. [Note: [Col. 0911C] Some manuscripts omit cum, “with.”] [Note: [Col. 0911C] Thus according to most and better of our manuscripts. The commonly printed editions, together with the manuscripts of Collection 21, have “had been.”] In all these matters your glory is surely increased, since you both venerate the saints according to their merits and wish thorns and thistles to be removed from the Lord’s field. [Note: [Col. 0911C] Thus according to the Ratisbon manuscript, the Sichard copy, and the manuscripts of Collection 24, as it stood in the editions before Quesnellus, who has “to take away.” Immediately afterward, in place of “indeed,” certain manuscripts and older printed editions have “truly.”]

We have learned from the report of our men, rather than from that of my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, whom you deign to commend, [Note: [Col. 0912C] Vatican Isidorian manuscript: nostri, “our”; the Vatican Spanish manuscript has vestri, “your,” through a copyist’s error.] that certain bishops who appear to have given consent to impious acts are asking for reconciliation and desire communion with the Catholics. [Note: [Col. 0912C] Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts read affectum, “affection,” in place of effectum, “effect.”] [Note: [Col. 0911C] The envoys whom Leo sent to Constantinople on Anatolius’s account in 450 are meant here. See Letters 69 and following. We shall see in Note 4 (Col. 919, note e) to Letter 83 that these envoys departed from Constantinople after Anatolius’s clerics had been sent to Rome. The clerics gave Leo an account of what had taken place, which was delivered to the pontiff together with Anatolius’s letters. From both sources he learned that certain bishops were asking for reconciliation and desiring Catholic communion. Since Leo presumed that the same envoys had by then left Constantinople, he decided to send a new embassy to complete this reconciliation. The following words refer to that embassy: “Through the care of our men whom we sent,” etc. These two embassies must be distinguished, lest great confusion arise. Thus in the following letter, chapter 2, the words “What was established in the presence and through the action of our men, we approve” refer to the first embassy; the words that follow, “But with our envoys whom we sent,” refer to the second embassy, which he intended to send together with these letters but postponed until June, as we explained in Note 7 (Col. 909, note d) to Letter 78. It should also be noted that the words of the aforementioned Letter 80, chapter 2, “what was established in the presence and through the action of our men,” seem to indicate what the envoys of the first embassy did while they were present at Constantinople. The same is suggested by the words in chapter 3, “Your Affection ought to preserve what our men, who were established there, said,” as if they were no longer present there; these words confirm their departure. Hence in chapter 1 Saint Leo writes of them: “We learn from the report of our brothers whom we had sent to Constantinople,” where attention must be paid to the tense “we had sent.” See Note 5 (Col. 913, note c) to the following letter.]

We therefore grant effect to their desires, provided that, after correcting their conduct and condemning by their own subscription the things wrongly done, they are granted peace through the care of our men whom we sent, together with the aforesaid bishop. For both belong to Christian devotion: that truth should justly restrain the obstinate, and charity should not reject those who have been converted.

CHAPTER III.

Since we know how much Your Mildness deigns to devote pious concern to Catholic priests, we have taken care to inform you that my brother and fellow bishop Eusebius is living with us and shares our communion. [Note: [Col. 0912C] Vienna Spanish manuscript: nostram, “our.”] We commend his Church, which, it is said, is being devastated by the man who is alleged to have been unjustly appointed in his place. [Note: [Col. 0912C] This, at least, was generally reported at Rome at that time. Liberatus, in his Brief Account, chapter 12, does not state that anyone was appointed in Eusebius of Dorylaeum’s place, as Quesnellus observed in a marginal note.]

We also ask Your Piety for this—which we do not doubt that you will do of your own accord—that you favor both my brother and fellow bishop Julian and the Constantinopolitan clerics who adhered to Flavian, of holy memory, through faithful service, with the favor that you ought to show them. [Note: [Col. 0912D] The printed editions and several manuscripts incorrectly read faveatis, “that you favor”; we corrected this from the Ratisbon, Vatican Spanish, and Vatican Isidorian manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0912C] Thus according to the Ratisbon manuscript, both Spanish manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, other manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24, and the Sichard copy. The printed editions, together with the manuscripts of Collection 21, have “by your piety.” Immediately afterward, the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian manuscripts have “to do” in place of “that you will do.”] We have instructed Your Piety through our men concerning everything that ought to be done or arranged. [Note: [Col. 0912D] The envoys believed to be sent with this letter are meant; but they were not sent until June, as we explained in Note 7 (above, note f) to the present letter. Compare also Note 11 (above, note f) to this letter. Shortly afterward, in place of “to be arranged,” the editions before Quesnellus have “to be avoided.” Quesnellus’s correction, based on the Grimani manuscript and three others, is supported by all our ancient books.]

Dated 13 April, in the consulship of Adelfius, a man of the highest rank.

1038 EPISTOLA LXXX. [Note: [Col. 0912D] Formerly Letter 60. What was previously Letter 80 is now Letter 106. Written 13 April 451.] TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE. [Note: [Col. 0912D] Grimani manuscript, as Quesnellus notes in the margin.] First, concerning peace.

SUMMARY (from the Spanish collection).

I. Concerning his faith, approved by the letters sent. [Col. 0913A] — II. Concerning those who fell into heresy through fear, so that, if they are converted, they may be received. — III. Concerning the names of heretics not being recited at the sacred altar. — IV. Concerning the commendation [formerly: commemoration] of Bishop Julian, or of those clerics who adhered in faith to Bishop Flavian.

Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop.

CHAPTER I.

[Note: [Col. 0913C] The Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Gaudeamus, together with the copy of the first edition and with manuscript collection 24, as well as one Vatican manuscript of collection 21, in which after a short interval they have gloriemur.] We rejoice in the Lord and glory in the gift of his grace, [Note: [Col. 0913C] Three codices have quia; the editions before Quesnellus have quia . . . ostendis.] who, as we have learned from the letters of your affection [Note: [Col. 0913C] This distinction between Anatolius’s letters and the report of the legates may seem to indicate that the legates reported orally, rather than by letters, what is mentioned in this letter, as though they had already reached Rome. But Leo used the term “report” in the preceding letter, ch. 2, when speaking of Anatolius, who certainly reported by letter; moreover, annotation 4 (Col. 919, note e) on Epistle 83 will show that those legates entered the City later.] and from the report of our brothers whom we had sent to Constantinople, has shown you to be a follower of evangelical teaching. Thus, on the strength of a priest’s credible faith, we may rightly presume that the whole Church entrusted to him will have neither the wrinkle of anyone’s error nor any stain, as the Apostle says: “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

For the Church is the virgin, the bride of one husband, Christ, and she does not allow herself to be corrupted by any error, so that throughout the world there may be for us the integrity of one chaste communion. In this communion we embrace your affection; and we approve the sequence of the proceedings that we have received, furnished, as was proper, with the necessary subscriptions. [Note: [Col. 0913C] The surviving fragment of these proceedings, from the *Life of Saint Abundius*, who served as an apostolic legate, will be published in the appendix.]

Therefore, so that your affection might in turn be strengthened through conversation with ours, we have sent our sons, the presbyter Casterius, and the deacons Patricius and Asclepiades [Note: [Col. 0913C] Vallicellian codex A, 5, collection 8, and the copy of the first edition have *Caterium*. Vatican 5845 of the same collection 8 has *Carnerium*. Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Otherwise, Castorius or Carterius”; the latter we find in manuscripts of collection 21.], who brought us your letters [Note: [Col. 0913D] One Vatican manuscript has *detulerant* (“had brought”). The first edition has “who brought your letters.”], together with our letters, after the venerable feast of Easter. [Note: [Col. 0913D] The copy of the first edition has “the festal day of Easter.” The Grimani codex has “we sent them after Easter Day.” Since these letters were delivered to the Constantinopolitan clergy mentioned here, Leo’s use of the past tense is understood as referring to the time that had elapsed, as explained in note 7 above, at col. 909, note d, on Epistle 78.] We have informed them that, as we said above, we rejoice in the peace of the Church of Constantinople, for whose security we have always cared, not wishing it to be violated by any deception of the heretics.

## Chapter II

[Col. 0913C]

As for the brothers whom, both from your letters and from the report of our legates, we have learned to be desirous of our communion [Note: [Col. 0913C] The first edition has “inflamed with desire.” After a short interval, the Vindobonensis Hispanicus and Vatican collection 11 have “against powerlessness,” that is, excessive power.]—because they grieve that, against power and against threats, they did not maintain [Col. 0914A] their steadfastness, [Note: [Col. 0914C] The Hispanic Vatican manuscript has “judgment.” Immediately afterward, when Merlinus printed “to maintain steadfastness toward another’s crime” without any intervening particle, the editions had previously inserted *sed* (“but”) before *alieno* (“another’s”); this is found in the Vindobonensis Hispanicus, in Vatican collection 3, and in two manuscripts of collection 8. The other nine codices of various collections prefer *et* (“and”).] but gave consent to another’s crime, since fear so unsettled them that, in the condemnation of a Catholic and innocent bishop and in the acceptance of detestable depravity, they served with trembling obedience—we approve what was established in the presence and through the agency of our representatives, namely, that meanwhile they should be content with the communion of their own churches. [Note: [Col. 0914C] See annotation 11 (Col. 911, note f) on the preceding letter, where we showed that “our representatives who had previously been sent to Constantinople” are indicated here, and then other representatives who were to be sent. On the words “that meanwhile they should be content with the communion of their own churches,” see Quesnellus’s note 1.] But, with our legates whom we have sent, and with you sharing the concern, we wish it to be arranged that those who condemn their evil deeds with full satisfaction, and who choose rather to accuse themselves than to defend themselves, may rejoice in the unity of our peace and communion; provided that what was accepted against the Catholic faith is first condemned with a fitting anathema.

For otherwise, in the Church of God [Note: [Col. 0914C] *In Ecclesia Dei qua corpus*, 1 question 1, ch. 68.], which is the body of Christ, neither are priestly offices valid [Note: [Col. 0914C] Codices of collection 8, together with the Grimani manuscript of collection 18 and the Barberini manuscript of collection 3, have *sacrata sunt* (“are consecrated”). The first edition has *sacra* (“sacred”).] nor are true sacrifices offered, unless the true High Priest reconciles us in the reality of our nature, and the true blood of the spotless Lamb cleanses us. Although he is seated at the right hand of the Father, in that same flesh which he assumed from the Virgin he nevertheless carries out the sacrament of propitiation, as the Apostle says: “Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Rom. 8:34). [Note: [Col. 0914D] One Vatican codex has “at the right hand.” Immediately afterward, the Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian codices have “For it cannot.”]

Our kindness cannot rightly be criticized when we receive those who, as we grieved, were deceived, provided that they offer satisfaction. Therefore, the grace of our communion must neither be harshly denied nor recklessly granted, because, just as it is wholly an act of piety to restore the Lord’s charity to the oppressed, so it is just that everything be attributed to the authors of the disturbance. [Note: [Col. 0914D] The Vatican and Isidorian codices, together with another manuscript of collection 11, two Thuane manuscripts, and one Cambridge manuscript, have: “it is just that the authority of those who disturb everything be removed.”]

## Chapter III

As for the names of Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius being recited at the sacred altar, [Note: [Col. 0914D] See Quesnellus’s note 2.] your affection ought to observe what our representatives stationed there said should be done, and what does not conflict with honoring the memory of Saint Flavian, nor turn the minds of the Christian people away from your grace. [Note: [Col. 0914D] The editions, together with both Hispanic manuscripts and certain later collections, insert *non* (“not”). We have removed it on the authority of the more reliable and older collections: Vatican collection 3, two manuscripts of collection 8, and the outstanding Ratisbon collection 19; the copies of the first edition and Sichardus agree with them. Anatolius, however, seems to have been uncertain on this point, although the legates, while they were in Constantinople, had declared that Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius were not to be recited from the diptychs because they were regarded as leaders of the Ephesian impiety. The reason Saint Leo gives here approves the legates’ judgment. Accordingly, from Vatican 5845 of collection 8, Ratisbon, and the manuscripts of collection 24, as well as the first edition and Sichardus, we have preferred *dixerunt* (“they said”) to the commonly printed *dixerint* (“they may have said”).]

For it is exceedingly unjust and incongruous that those who harassed the innocent and Catholic by their persecution should be mingled indiscriminately [Note: [Col. 0915C] The Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts, together with three codices cited by Quesnellus, have “enemy.”] among the names of the saints, when they themselves, by not abandoning the condemned impiety, condemn themselves through their own depravity. [Note: [Col. 0915C] The copy of the first edition has: “they are condemned by their own depravity.”] They ought either to be struck down for their perfidy or to labor for pardon.

## Chapter IV

As for our brother and fellow bishop Julian, and the clerics who faithfully served the blessed Flavian, we wish them also to adhere to your affection. [Note: [Col. 0915D] The Ratisbon codex omits “our brother”; it then has *vel clericos* (“or the clerics”), taking *vel* in place of *et* (“and”). The same reading occurs in the Vindobonensis Hispanicus and here and in the title of this chapter in manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, as well as in Sichardus’s and the first edition’s copies.] Thus he whom we know, through the merits of his faith, to live before our God may recognize himself as present to them in you. [Note: [Col. 0915D] The Barberini manuscript of collection 3, Vatican 5845 of collection 8, the Grimani manuscript, and the first edition have “through the sacraments of their faith.”]

We also wish your affection to know that our brother and fellow bishop Eusebius, who endured many dangers and hardships for the sake of the faith, is meanwhile staying with us and continuing now in our communion. We wish his Church to be defended through your care, so that nothing may perish in his absence and no one may presume to prejudice him in any respect, until he reaches you with the delivery of our letters. [Note: [Col. 0915D] The Grimani codex lacks the following six words. Some codices have “and nothing.” The Ratisbon manuscript has “so that nothing,” and then suppresses *ei* (“for him”).]

And so that a greater affection, either ours or that of the whole Christian people, may be awakened toward you, we wish what we have written to your affection to come to everyone’s knowledge, so that those who serve our God may rejoice in the peace of the apostolic see confirmed by you. [Note: [Col. 0915D] The same copy has: “As for the remaining causes of the dispute and of the perversion, your affection . . .”]

Concerning the other causes and persons, your affection will be instructed more fully by the letter which you will receive through our representatives. [Note: [Col. 0915D] This refers to Epistle 85. See note 7 above, at col. 909, note d, on Epistle 78.]

Given on the Ides of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelfius.

---

# Letter 81

[Note: [Col. 0915D] Otherwise 61. Formerly 81, now 107. Written 13 April 451.]  
[Note: [Col. 0916C] This letter is found in the manuscripts of collections 12, 18, and 19.]

## To Julian, Bishop

### Synopsis

Julian, long harassed by the wickedness of Dioscorus, is warned that those who have fallen must not be received into communion unless their perfidy and its authors have been condemned.

Leo, bishop, to Julian, bishop.

I have received a letter from your brotherhood through our sons, the Constantinopolitan clerics, announcing your safety. In it you indicate that you have been burdened with great tribulations, although there was certainly no lack of material for anxiety and toil, which might weary a mind clinging to the truth amid the brazen adversaries of the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0916C] Two codices of collection 12 have *idque, ut scribis, fuerit animi* (“and this, as you write, was a matter of the mind”). The Ratisbon manuscript has *idque, sed animus* (“and this, but the mind”).]

And, as you write, this was your intention: to present yourself, through the occasion of necessity, both to us and to your homeland. I had truly hoped that this would happen, so that through your own mouth I might recognize more openly the devious ways of all the heretics. [Note: [Col. 0916C] Thus according to the manuscripts mentioned in the preceding note. The common editions, deriving from one codex, have *cognoscerem* (“I might know”), omitting *re* because of the similarity of the letters at the end of the preceding word.]

But thanks be to God, because both your safety and the cause of the Church have advanced in such a way that meanwhile you have been free to live among those whose credible agreement has become known to us, as the writings of our brother Anatolius profess and the proceedings conducted in his presence before our representatives demonstrate, dearest brother.

Therefore, as the aforesaid men return, I return the exchange of greetings, and I confidently exhort you to maintain steadfast diligence against the stratagems of falsehood, since both your own mind and our authority support you in this. For although better things have been reported concerning many—namely, that they grieve that they were deceived and, with their perfidy and its authors condemned, seek the grace of our communion, which we have accepted with the greatest willingness and will restore to them when they have fulfilled what they promised [Note: [Col. 0916C] The Ratisbon manuscript has “what they have stated beforehand.”]—we have nevertheless learned that some persist in their obstinacy. These must be restrained more strictly if they cannot be healed by kindness.

For this purpose we will send our representatives after the venerable day of Easter, [Note: [Col. 0916C] The word “Easter,” absent from our manuscripts and editions, was inserted by Quesnellus from the Grimani codex and retained because, similarly, in the preceding letter, chapter I, the Constantinopolitan clerics are said to have been sent—or rather, to be sent—back to Anatolius after the venerable day of the feast of Easter. Saint Leo had already decided to send his own legates with them, as noted above in note 7 at col. 909, note d, on Epistle 78. Quesnellus added this marginal note: “The Grimani manuscript adds ‘Easter,’ perhaps understanding this as the octave of Easter, which was 8 April. He thought so because he believed that this letter had been written on the very Ides of April on which it is dated. But it is more probable that all these letters dated on the Ides of April were written before Easter, when Leo was considering joining his legates to the Constantinopolitan clerics on their return, but were dated at the time when, after changing his plan, he postponed the legation and sent only the Constantinopolitan clerics. In this way the difficulties in these letters are reconciled. There is therefore no need here to understand the octave of Easter instead of Easter Day.”] and, sharing counsel with you, they will carry out whatever we have determined.

Given on the Ides of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelfius.

---

# Letter 82

[Note: [Col. 0917C] Otherwise 62. Formerly 82, now 103. Written 13 April 451.]  
[Note: [Col. 0917C] Found in the manuscripts of the Hispanic collection, Isidore 11, 12, 18, and 21 through 24, and in the copy of Sichardus.]

## To Marcian Augustus

[Note: [Col. 0917C] In the Hispanic collection: “Of the same Leo to Marcian Augustus, where he congratulates him concerning the preservation of the Catholic faith.”]

### Synopsis

I. He congratulates him on preserving the Catholic faith, in return for which peace is granted to the empire.  
II. Action must be taken only against those who have gone astray, not against the faith or the Scriptures, which it is impious to interpret otherwise than the holy Fathers did.

Leo, bishop, to Marcian Augustus.

## Chapter I

Although I previously wrote to your piety through the Constantinopolitan clerics, [Note: [Col. 0917C] The copy of Sichardus has “Although through the Constantinopolitan clerics.” Shortly afterward, the editions before Quesnellus, with manuscripts of collection 24, have “to your piety.”] [Note: [Col. 0917C] This refers to Epistle 78.] nevertheless, having received letters of your clemency through the illustrious Tatianus, prefect of the city and my son, I received great cause for congratulation. [Note: [Col. 0917C] These letters of Marcian, delivered by Tatianus, differ from the preceding letters 73 and 76. The latter of those was given on 22 November 450. Tatianus, however, had not yet departed Constantinople on 18 December of that year, as is clear from book 2 of the Justinian Code, title “On the Office of the Praetorian Prefects,” which is addressed to Tatianus and dated 18 December at Constantinople, in the consulship of Valentinian VII and Avienus. There he is incorrectly called prefect of the praetorium, since both Leo and other documents of 451 and 452 consistently call him prefect of the city. Tatianus evidently arrived in Rome after delivering Epistle 78 to the Constantinopolitan clerics, which was dated 13 April, and handed the imperial letters to Leo; this is indicated here quite clearly. These letters of Marcian, to which Leo is responding, have been lost.]

For I have learned that you are most devoted to ecclesiastical peace. [Note: [Col. 0917D] Quesnellus has “divine.” We have restored the reading of the earlier editions, since all our manuscripts and the copy of Sichardus support it.] To this holy desire a fitting justice is granted: whatever religious condition you wish to have, the same you may have in your kingdom. For when Christian rulers are united by the Spirit of God, confidence throughout the world is strengthened twofold. The advancement of charity and faith makes the power of both kinds of arms invincible, so that, when God has been appeased by one confession, both heretical falsehood and barbarian hostility are destroyed together, most glorious emperor.

Therefore, with hope of heavenly assistance increased through imperial friendship, I dare more confidently to urge your piety, for the sacrament of human salvation, not to allow anyone’s brazen and shameless cunning [Note: [Col. 0917D] The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts have “imprudent and shameless.”] to make people inquire as though it were uncertain what ought to be followed. And since it is not permitted to depart by even one word from evangelical and apostolic teaching [Note: [Col. 0917D] Both Hispanic manuscripts and the Vatican Isidorian manuscript have “not even in one.” Two other codices with Sichardus have “not one.” Shortly afterward, manuscripts of collection 21 have *deviare* (“to depart”) for *dissidere* (“to dissent”), and the Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts have *habere* (“to hold”) for *sapere* (“to think”).], nor to think about the divine Scriptures otherwise than the blessed apostles and our Fathers learned and taught, now those undisciplined and impious questions are again being stirred up—questions which, as soon as the devil aroused them through hearts suited to him, the Holy Spirit extinguished through the disciples of truth. [Note: [Col. 0918C] The editions, with some manuscripts, have *moveantur* (“may be stirred up”). Since otherwise the sense would remain suspended, *moventur* (“are stirred up”), from the Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, seemed preferable. Immediately afterward, Vatican collection 11 has “suggestions” instead of “questions.”]

## Chapter II

It is exceedingly unjust [Note: [Col. 0918C] The Hispanic Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts have “hostile.”] that, through the folly of a few, we should be recalled to conjectures of opinion and to the battles of carnal disputation, as though the controversy had been reopened and it were necessary to consider whether Eutyches thought impiously and whether Dioscorus judged perversely—he who struck himself down in the condemnation of the blessed Flavian and drove the more simple-minded into the same ruin. [Note: [Col. 0918C] The Grimani codex skips the next five words by a scribal leap, from the first *utrum* (“whether”) to the second, perversely. The editions, with the manuscripts of collection 24, have “impiously” instead of “perversely.” It should be noted that Leo did not wish to reopen discussion either of the faith he himself had defined against Eutyches or of Dioscorus’s judgment, that is, the pseudo-Ephesian judgment against Saint Flavian, which he had already declared invalid. He believed that action should concern only those who had fallen and were seeking reconciliation, so that it might be clear whose petitions should be granted and how. For this purpose he sent legates to Constantinople on 9 June.]

Since, as we have learned, many of these people have already turned to the remedies of satisfaction and are asking pardon for their wavering fear, the issue is not what kind of faith must be held, [Note: [Col. 0918D] The copy of Sichardus and the manuscripts of collection 24 omit “must be held.”] but whose petitions should be granted and in what manner. [Note: [Col. 0918D] The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and those of collections 11 and 21 have: “but how the petitions of those who are related to them should be granted.” This agrees with the editions before Quesnellus and with the copy of Sichardus, in which only *sit* (“should be”) is deleted.]

Accordingly, through the legation which, with God’s approval, will promptly reach your clemency, everything that I believe relevant to the benefit of the case will be set forth more fully and suitably to your most pious concern, which you deign to have regarding the convocation of a synod. [Note: [Col. 0918D] In the Vindobonensis Hispanicus *Deo* (“God”) is wrongly omitted. The author of the Hispanic Vatican collection supplied this defect by writing “with Christ’s approval,” whence this reading passed into the Vatican Isidorian and similar codices.] [Note: [Col. 0918D] The same codices have “regarding the gathering of the synod.” The reason why he deferred a response concerning the synod to the instructions of the legates was explained above in note 7 at col. 909, note d, on Epistle 78.]

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelfius. [Note: [Col. 0918D] Thus, together with the editions, all our codices. Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Otherwise, the eighth day before the Kalends.”]

---

# Letter 83

[Note: [Col. 0919C] Otherwise 63. Formerly 83, now 108. Written 9 June 451.]  
[Note: [Col. 0919C] Found in the manuscripts of the Hispanic collection, Isidore 11, 12, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, and in the copy of Sichardus.]

## To the Same Marcian

[Col. 0919A]

[Note: [Col. 0919C] In the Hispanic collection this title appears, together with the editions before Quesnellus: “Where, among other matters, he congratulates him on the defense of the Catholic faith.”]

### Synopsis

I. He congratulates him on Anatolius’s faith having been revealed, Eutyches having been restrained, the bishops having been recalled, and the relics of Saint Flavian having been restored to the city.  
II. He is sending legates to reconcile the bishops who have fallen. The present time is unsuitable for convening a council.

1046 Leo, bishop, to Marcian Augustus.

## Chapter I

Both your letter, which I received with reverence, and the return of my fellow bishops from Constantinople have given me great confidence [Note: [Col. 0919C] Quesnellus has “of replying,” as do our manuscripts of collection 21. From the Ratisbon manuscript, both Hispanic manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and other codices, we have restored the reading of the earlier editions.] in writing to your clemency. They have demonstrated—not merely by verbal assertion but by the actual results of their deeds already accomplished [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Ratisbon manuscript deletes *operum* (“of deeds”).]—that divine protection is active in you for the defense of the Catholic faith. [Note: [Col. 0919C] Since these legates of Leo, returning from Constantinople to Rome, brought him new imperial letters to which he is now replying, they are known to have arrived in Rome shortly before this time.]

Through this protection not only the condition of the Church but also the strength of your empire is fortified, so that you may rightly expect the protection of the one whose truth you honor, most glorious emperor. For your virtue and piety have brought about both the prompt manifestation of my brother Anatolius’s integrity and the exclusion from Christ’s Church of the revived advocate of an error long condemned; the recall from unjust exile of the Catholic bishops whom the persecution of the heretics recently could not corrupt; and the worthy reception of the relics of the blessed Flavian, so that his condemner might recognize his own impiety as condemned. [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts have: “so that the revived advocate of error might find no place,” and “so that the condemned one might recognize his impiety.”]

I trust that the insignia of other victories will also be added, so that, just as the Church of Constantinople rejoices after recovering the freedom of apostolic faith, all the provinces of your kingdom may likewise glory in having been cleansed from the contagion of diabolical doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Vindobonensis Hispanicus deletes *se* (“themselves”). Ratisbon and Sichardus delete *esse* (“to be”). Immediately afterward, six of our codices have *contagione* (“from contagion”).]

As I indicated in my preceding letters, [Note: [Col. 0919D] Epistles 78 and 82 are meant.] I have sent my brothers, the bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basilius, who can carry out the duties of my concern. [Note: [Col. 0919D] The Ratisbon manuscript has *Lucensium* here, and *Lucensem* in the next three letters. Both Hispanic manuscripts, the Isidorian Vatican manuscript, another Vatican manuscript of collection 11, and the copy of Sichardus likewise prefer *Lucensium* in this letter; in the other letters they have *Lucentium*.] I commend them to your piety’s favor in everything that must be done.
