For, together with the writings of my brother Anatolius and the report of our representatives, I have learned that many of those who, compelled by the faction of Dioscorus at Ephesus, gave a regrettable consent to detestable decrees are asking pardon for their inconstancy and seeking Catholic communion through the satisfaction of correction. [Note: [Col. 0920C] The earlier editions have “gave consent, repenting.” Quesnellus corrected this from the Grimani manuscript and three other codices, to which eight of our manuscripts and the copy of Sichardus may be added.] The conversion of such people was not to be neglected, since they are known to have fallen into these things not by their own judgment but at the prompting of an evil usurper, [Note: [Col. 0920C] Earlier editions before Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, have “of an impious usurper.”] in circumstances in which they had not possessed free judgment.

## Chapter II

Therefore, so that either the desires of those who repent might not be wearied by excessive delay or careless leniency might not rashly and indiscriminately receive certain people, the apostolic see has instructed the representatives it sent that, with the bishop of the city of Constantinople added to their deliberations, neither the contagions of the plague should be admitted nor the remedies of health denied. [Note: [Col. 0920D] The manuscripts of collection 21 omit “of their.” From Ratisbon and two other codices, we preferred “with the bishop of Constantinople added” to the common reading “with the bishop of Constantinople summoned”; this indicates that the bishop of Constantinople was to be joined to the legates. The Vindobonensis Hispanicus has “with the bishop of the Constantinopolitan Church”; this was corrected in the Hispanic and Isidorian Vatican manuscripts to “with the Constantinopolitan bishop.”]

This policy, aided by the Lord, will quickly achieve its effect in correcting all the things wickedly done if your piety deigns to add its assistance to the restoration of ecclesiastical peace. Thus, while you reign on earth, may you deserve also to have the kingdom of God within you; may no falsehood violate the Catholic faith, no heresy disturb it; and may no one be permitted to abandon evangelical doctrine while enjoying sacerdotal honor. [Note: [Col. 0920D] The editions before Quesnellus, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, have “while you reign on earth.”]

As for a synod, your clemency remembers that we ourselves also requested that one be held. But the present necessity in no way permits the priests of all the provinces to assemble, since the provinces from which those who must chiefly be summoned are to come, being troubled by war, do not allow them to depart from their churches. [Note: [Col. 0920D] The older editions, together with the Hispanic and Isidorian Vatican manuscripts, the manuscripts of collections 11, 21, and 24, and Sichardus, have “disturbed by war.” Quesnellus, with our Vindobonensis Hispanicus, has “disturbed by wars.” We have preferred the reading of the Ratisbon manuscript. The war stirred up by Attila against Valentinian in this year is indicated; the provinces of the West were consequently thrown into disorder.]

Therefore let your clemency reserve this matter for a more suitable time, when security, with the Lord’s favor, has been restored more firmly. Concerning this, among other matters, those whom I have sent will be able to explain more fully to your piety.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelfius. [Note: [Col. 0921D] We have retained the date of the editions before Quesnellus, since it appears not only in the copy of Sichardus and in the manuscripts of collections 12 and 24 but also in the outstanding Ratisbon manuscript and in the Vindobonensis Hispanicus. Quesnellus, from the Grimani manuscript and our Vatican manuscript of collection 11, has “the seventh day before the Ides.” The Hispanic and Isidorian Vatican manuscripts have “the sixth day before the Ides.” Two manuscripts of collection 21 have simply “the Ides,” the numeral having been omitted through an error of the collector or scribe.]

---

# Letter 84

[Note: [Col. 0921D] Otherwise 64. Formerly 84, now 111. Written 9 June 451.]  
[Note: [Col. 0921D] Found in the manuscripts of collections 12, 18, and 19.]

## To Pulcheria Augusta

### Synopsis

I. He sends legates to deal with those who have fallen, with the greatest prudence and moderation.  
II. Whoever denies our nature in Christ is outside the unity.  
III. He asks that Eutyches be transferred farther away and that a Catholic be placed over his monastery.

Leo, bishop, to Pulcheria Augusta.

## Chapter I

I dare, through more frequent communications, to encourage the religious concern of your piety, by which, with God inspiring you, you provide for the whole world, so that the necessary perfection may follow the progress of your works. [Note: [Col. 0921D] The Ratisbon codex has “of our works.”] And just as we rejoice over the condition of the Church of Constantinople, whose priest and people are now known to hold the faith of Catholic purity, so may the confession of others concerning the incarnation of the Word be in agreement with ours.

Accordingly, I have hastened to send my brothers, the bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basilius, as I had indicated I would do in other letters. [Note: [Col. 0921D] The editions before Quesnellus incorrectly have “I have prepared.”] Joined to the devotion of my brother Anatolius, they will carry out my arrangements according to the instructions they have received, most glorious Augusta. For, as has been disclosed by the writings of the aforesaid bishop and by the representations of his clerics, there are many matters requiring more indulgent care and many requiring more just restraint. [Note: [Col. 0921D] The Grimani codex has “many matters requiring investigation.”] Thus, in a case of such great disturbance, discipline must not be too harsh, nor leniency insufficiently cautious, since one treatment is owed to those who offer satisfaction and another to the obstinate.

## Chapter II

A worthy occasion is therefore offered to your piety, by which it may exercise the care of a holy heart pleasing to the Lord and multiply the crowns of former merits through the abolition of the present error. For, just as Nestorian impiety, so also Eutychian blasphemy must be removed from the fellowship of all Catholics. [Note: [Col. 0921D] The Ratisbon manuscript likewise has “must be removed from the fellowship of all Catholics.”]

For it is equally impious to deny that the divinity of the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, was also brought forth bodily from the womb of the Virgin Mother, and to affirm one nature in the Son of God after the mystery of the incarnation—so that either his humanity or his divinity is rejected. For through the union of both essences, neither was one changed into the other nor was what was assumed dissolved into the one who assumed it; rather, the unchangeability of the Word and the reality of flesh and soul remain inseparably in the unity of the person. [Note: [Col. 0921D] The same codex has “through the union.”]

Those who do not believe this, although the Law testifies to it, the patriarchs believe it, the prophets announce it, the Gospel proclaims it, the apostles teach it, and the whole world confesses it, are outside the sacrament of Christ’s body and outside the unity of the Christian name. [Note: [Col. 0922D] The common editions have “although the prophets assent”; the better reading of three of our codices is “although the prophets announce.”]

## Chapter III

Just as we grieve over their ruin, so we detest their perfidy. But so that impartial judgment may everywhere be maintained concerning such persons, and different treatment be given to those who have corrected themselves and to those who remain obstinate, may your piety deign to support our representatives sent from the apostolic see and assist all the actions we have entrusted to them. Thus, with the Lord’s help, they may more quickly and easily carry out what advances your glory and the peace of the whole Church.

As for Eutyches, the author of all the scandal and depravity, let your clemency order that he be transferred farther away from the place that is too near the city of Constantinople, so that he may not enjoy more frequent support from those whom he drew into his impiety. Command also that a Catholic abbot be placed over his monastery, which he presided over perniciously and unworthily, so that he may both free that congregation of God’s servants from its corrupt doctrine and instruct it in the institutions of truth.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelfius. [Note: [Col. 0922D] Quesnellus, from the Grimani manuscript, has “the seventh day before the Ides.” The other editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 12, have “the Ides.” We follow the Ratisbon manuscript, which consistently gives the same date in the four letters sent through these legates, in accordance with Leo’s usual practice.]

---

# Letter 85

[Note: [Col. 0922D] Otherwise 65. Formerly 85, now 112. Written 19 June 451.]  
[Note: [Col. 0922D] This letter is found in the same manuscripts as the preceding Letter 83.]

## To Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople

[Col. 0922C]

[Note: [Col. 0922D] In the Hispanic collection this title reads: “Concerning those who are entangled in heretical errors through fear, not by choice, so that they may be received into the Church through satisfaction, and so that the names of heretics may not be recited at the altar.”]

### Synopsis

I. Those who have been entangled in heretical errors through fear, not by choice, should be received through satisfaction and an unequivocal profession.  
II. He reserves the leaders of the heretics for his own examination and meanwhile forbids their names to be recited at the altar.  
III. He responds to Anatolius concerning his memorandum, urges him to diligence, and asks that everything be reported to him.

Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop.

## Chapter I
Although I hope that your Love is devoted to every good work, nevertheless, so that your diligence may become more effective, it was necessary and fitting to send, as we promised, my brothers Bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basilius.

[Note: This is found in Ratramnus, Book IV *Against the Greeks*, vol. I of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, p. 109; it was also fitting.]

Your Love is to be associated with them, so that in nothing pertaining to the condition of the universal Church may anything be undertaken doubtfully or sluggishly, while you are present, to whom we have entrusted the execution of our arrangement. Everything should be conducted with such moderation that neither the claims of benevolence nor those of justice are neglected, but that divine judgment is kept in mind in all things, without respect of persons.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript, both Hispanic Vatican manuscripts, Isidore, Ratramnus, Sichardus, and our other ancient books agree with the earlier printed editions in reading “while you are present,” except for two manuscripts of collection 21, which omit “you.” Quesnellus, from the Grimani manuscript, reads “while these men are present.” He also cites Trecopithius and two Thuanean manuscripts, two of which belong to collection 5. Yet this letter is not found in that collection; if it exists in those two manuscripts, it is certainly an addition not belonging to that collection. Thus it does not appear in the table of the Thuanean manuscript itself, published by Quesnellus, which lists all documents of that collection. In a marginal note, moreover, Quesnellus rejects our reading “while you are present,” saying: “As though Leo of Rome had enjoined the execution of his arrangement upon the bishop of Constantinople.” But the words stated shortly before, “Your Love is to be associated with them,” show that Anatolius was delegated in this matter, or specially joined to the legates; compare Letter 83, chapter 2: “It has been enjoined upon those sent by the Apostolic See that, having admitted the bishop of the city of Constantinople to partnership in their deliberation,” etc. The following words of chapter 3 show that execution of the pontiff’s arrangement was enjoined upon him: “Strive, therefore, that you may carry [it] out faithfully and effectively.” A little later Ratramnus and three manuscripts read: “that all these things may be conducted with moderation.”]

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads: “That this may be able to be preserved by proper observance.” The Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, and manuscripts of collection 11, read: “That they may be able to preserve this by proper observance.”]

To ensure that this proper observance is maintained, the integrity of the Catholic faith must first of all be preserved. Since the way that leads to life is narrow and difficult in every respect (Matthew 7:14), one must not deviate from its path either to the left or to the right.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript, together with two others, and the Vatican manuscript read “to the right.”]

And since evangelical and apostolic faith overthrows every error, casting down Nestorius on one side and Eutyches and his associates on the other, remember that this rule must be observed: whoever in that synod—which, as we have learned from your Love’s report, neither can nor deserves to bear the name of a synod—where Dioscorus displayed his ill will and Juvenalis his incompetence,

[Note: The Vienna-Hispanic manuscripts read “inertia” (“inactivity”); the Vatican-Hispanic manuscript, “moestitia” (“sorrow”); Ratramnus, together with the Vatican, Isidorian, and another manuscript of collection 11, reads “industriam” (“zeal” or “energy”).]

lament that they were overcome by fear and overwhelmed by terror, and were compelled to consent to that most criminal judgment, and desire to obtain Catholic communion, let fraternal peace be granted to their satisfaction, provided that in an unequivocal profession they condemn Eutyches, together with his doctrine and his associates, by the curse of anathema.

## Chapter II

But as for those who sinned more gravely in this matter and therefore claimed for themselves a higher position in that same unhappy synod, in order to burden the simplicity of their humbler brothers with the prejudices of their own arrogance,

[Note: The Vatican-Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, together with Ratramnus and manuscripts of collections 11 and 21, read “of their humble brothers.”]

if they come to their senses, and, ceasing to defend their action, turn to condemning their own error, their case should be reserved for the more mature deliberations of the Apostolic See, if a submission of such a kind is offered that it does not appear liable to rejection. After all matters have been examined and weighed, it should then be judged what decision ought to be made concerning their own actions.

[Note: The Vatican and Isidorian manuscripts read “and abandoning the defense of their deed.” Ratramnus later reads “if submission is added.”]

Nor, in the Church over which the Lord has willed you to preside, should the name of any such person be recited at the altar—as we have already written to you—

[Note: The Vatican-Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “as we have already written to you,” namely, in Letter 80.]

until the course of events shows what decision ought to be made concerning them.

## Chapter III

As for the memorandum delivered to us by the clerics of your Love, it was not necessary to include in our letter what seemed appropriate, since it was sufficient to entrust everything to the legates, from whose account you will be more fully instructed about all matters.

Strive, therefore, dearest brother, to carry out faithfully and effectively, together with these brothers whom we have chosen as suitable agents for so important a matter,

[Note: We have restored the reading of the editions preceding Quesnellus on the authority of the Ratisbon manuscript, the Sichardian exemplar, and manuscripts of collections 12 and 24. The Vienna-Hispanic manuscript also has this reading, though through a consistent scribal error it has *ei* (“to him”) instead of *quos* (“whom”), so that the phrase reads “whom we have chosen suitable for so great a matter.” In the Vatican-Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts the wording has been altered by the first scribe to “whom we have consistently chosen as suitable.” In the Vatican-Hispanic manuscript dots are placed after *constanter*, indicating that the word should be deleted. Quesnellus, together with one of our Vatican manuscripts of collection 21, reads “whom we have chosen as suitable for so great a concern.”]

whatever accords with the Church of God. Especially since the very nature of the case and the hope of divine assistance encourage you,

[Note: The Ratisbon, Vatican-Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts add “and.” A little later the Vienna-Hispanic manuscript reads “may encourage.”]

and since the faith of the most merciful rulers is so holy and their devotion so religious that in them we experience not only Christian affection but also priestly affection.

[Note: The Vatican-Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “effect” rather than “affection.”]

In accordance with that piety by which they glory in being servants of God, they will graciously receive all your suggestions that may benefit the Catholic faith, so that through their action also Christian peace may be restored and impious error abolished.

[Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Alternatively, *ope*, ‘through the aid.’”]

And if further deliberation is required concerning any persons, let a report be sent to us quickly, so that, after the character of the cases has been considered, our concern may determine what ought to be observed.

[Note: The Vatican-Hispanic, Isidorian, and manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 read “after the character of these cases has been considered, our concern.”]

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Adelfius, a man of the highest distinction.

[Note: Thus the Ratisbon manuscript and manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, together with Sichardus. Quesnellus reads “the seventh day before the Ides”; the Vienna manuscript, “the sixth day before the Ides.” The Vatican-Hispanic manuscript and another manuscript of collection 11 erroneously read “the sixth day before the Ides of January”; manuscripts of collection 21, “the Ides of June.”]

## Letter LXXXVI

[Note: Alternatively numbered 66. What was formerly Letter 86 is now 113. Written 9 June 451.]

[Note: Published by Quesnellus from the Grimani manuscript of collection 18. We have collated it with the Ratisbon manuscript of collection 19.]

### To Julian, Bishop of Coense

### Summary

For the common bond of friendship and the good of the Church, he asks Julian to join his concern to the care of his legates, in order to extinguish the remaining heretics.

Leo, bishop, to Julian, bishop.

How agreeable it always is to me to receive letters from your Love, so it is also fitting that letters from us should be conveyed to you, especially since we are doing this not merely for the sake of our common friendship, but much more for the condition of the universal Church.

Therefore, through our brothers Bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basilius, whom we had indicated that we would send to Constantinople,

[Note: Namely, in Letter 81.]

I discharge the obligation of conversation and ask you to join the same men in every respect with the zeal of your diligence,

[Note: This reading is better in the Ratisbon manuscript than in Quesnellus’s Grimani manuscript, which reads “with the same men.” The Ratisbon manuscript nevertheless omits *tuae*, “of your.”]

so that, if any remnants of scandal still remain, they may be carefully removed.

Although the light of the Catholic faith now shines everywhere and, most powerfully of all, the hearts of the Christian rulers submit to divine authority, certain matters were nevertheless so confused by that Ephesian tempest that one must act with great restraint, lest the evils of dissension that arose from it persist.

You will learn from their own account what has been entrusted and assigned to our legates. Show me and them such devoted affection that, with the zeal and concern of your Love joined to everything entrusted to them, and with the Lord’s help,

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “with God’s help.”]

they may attain the result we desire.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of Adelfius, a man of the highest distinction.

[Note: Thus the Ratisbon manuscript, as in the three immediately preceding letters, which were transmitted together and dated on the same day in Leo’s manner. Quesnellus, from the Grimani manuscript, reads “the sixth day before the Ides.”]

## Letter LXXXVII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 67. What was formerly Letter 87 is now 114. Written 19 June 451.]

[Note: This letter is found in manuscripts of collections 12 and 18 and in the excellent Vatican manuscript 1322, whose millennium of age enabled us to correct several readings.]

### To Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople

### Summary

He commends to him the presbyters Basilius and John, who, accused of heresy, had come to Rome to give an account of their faith.

Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, his fellow bishop of Constantinople.

To avoid the stain of error by which Nestorian impiety or Eutychian madness has shaken certain persons, our sons, the presbyters Basilius and John, have shown commendable concern for their reputation, so that amid conflicting doctrines of falsehood they might rejoice in the true peace of the Catholic faith.

Having undertaken the labor of a distant journey,

[Note: The printed editions read “of a long journey.” We have corrected the text from the cited Vatican manuscript.]

they disclosed the convictions of their hearts at the Apostolic See,

[Note: This is the better reading of the manuscripts of collection 12 and the earlier printed editions. Quesnellus reads “they may have disclosed.”]

condemning both heresies mentioned above and accepting concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ nothing other than what, under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, we have learned and teach.

Through these men, therefore, dearest brother, as they return to their own country with our testimony, we have sent our letter to your Love, confidently urging you to ensure that those who are adorned with the grace of apostolic communion may rejoice in being assisted in every respect by your favor.

[Note: The Grimani manuscript and the most ancient Vatican manuscript both read “confidently urging that those who…” Quesnellus, following the printed editions and manuscripts of collection 12, reads “praying that those who…” In the Grimani manuscript, however, *quia* (“because”) appears instead of *qui* (“who”).]

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Adelfius, a man of the highest distinction.

[Note: The cited Vatican manuscript reads “the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June.” We suspect that the scribe mistakenly wrote *Junias* for *Julias*, since in Letter 89 the same manuscript likewise unmistakably writes *Junias* for *Julias*. The date itself cannot as easily be attributed to the same error: scribes more readily err by omitting a V than by inserting one. Nevertheless, we have not thought it appropriate to disregard the authority of the manuscripts of collections 12 and 18.]

## Notice concerning the following letter and the others printed below, which concern Easter of the year 455

1. A question that had long before been debated concerning Easter in the year 444 caused Leo concern, so that he might write earlier about the date of Easter in the year 455, in which he knew that the Roman and Alexandrian cycles differed. Hence, from the year 451 onward, when the following letter was written, he devoted his efforts to establishing this date by unanimous agreement.

We possess nine further letters of this pontiff, written in subsequent years on the same matter, besides several others that are missing, and one letter from Proterius of Alexandria to the same pontiff. We shall give these in their proper places.

2. According to the Alexandrian Easter table of Theophilus covering one hundred years, which consisted of five nineteen-year cycles and five additional years, Easter in the year 455 was assigned to the eighth day before the Kalends of May. According to the Latin eighty-four-year cycle, however, it was assigned to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of the same month, and therefore there was a difference of eight days.

This difference arose from the lunar saltuses, which the Latins admitted more frequently and the Alexandrians more rarely. The Alexandrians, following their nineteen-year cycle, assigned the lunar saltus—by which one day is added to the moon’s age at each saltus—once every nineteen years. The Latins, following their eighty-four-year cycle, admitted these saltuses every twelfth year until the correction of Prosper, and after Prosper’s correction every fourteen years.

Thus, because the saltuses were more frequent among the Romans than among the Alexandrians, the moon’s age from which the date of Easter is determined increased by three days in the year 455 among the Romans. Consequently, on the day that was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, a Sunday, and on which the moon was fourteen according to the Alexandrian reckoning, the moon was seventeen according to the Roman reckoning.

Since Easter cannot be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon, lest it coincide with the Jews, the Alexandrians were compelled to postpone Easter to the following Sunday, the eighth day before the Kalends of May. Among the Latins, however, since on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May the moon was seventeen, nothing prevented them from celebrating Easter on that day; and several considerations prevented them from transferring the feast to the eighth day before the Kalends of May with the Alexandrians.

3. First, on that date the moon was twenty-four, and if they had celebrated Easter then, they would have exceeded by two days the final limit of the moon’s age, which among them was twenty-two. Moreover, they would have exceeded by three days the ultimate limit of the Sundays on which Easter could be celebrated, which among them was the eleventh day before the Kalends of May.

As regards these limits for the Sundays of Easter, the matter had been settled in the year 444, because Leo had been persuaded that it was sufficient if the day of the Passion did not exceed the limit of the eleventh day before the Kalends of May. As a result, once this limit was observed, and the day of the Passion fell upon it, Easter was also celebrated by the Latins who followed the Alexandrian calculation two days later, that is, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May.

But this method of reconciliation was of no use in the question of Easter in the year 455, when the day of the Passion would pass that final limit not merely by two days but by three, once Easter had been postponed. The Latins finally thought that Easter would be celebrated according to the Alexandrian reckoning in the second month, although by law it ought to be celebrated in the first month. For they seem to have calculated the first month from the day of the equinox, 21 March, to 21 April.

4. The Alexandrians brought forward many arguments against these objections of the Latins. But they always argued on the assumption that the eighth day before the Kalends of May was the fourteenth day of the moon. At least in the surviving records, they never demonstrated the Latins to be in error when the Latins assigned a different age to the moon on that day, nor did they address the different lunar saltuses from which the differing lunar ages arose.

Had they convinced the Latins on this point, they would undoubtedly have obtained their agreement. The Latins were forbidden by their own rules to celebrate Easter not only when the moon was fourteen but also when it was fifteen. It is therefore unsurprising that Saint Leo declared himself unconvinced by the Alexandrians’ arguments and, solely out of a desire for unity and peace, ordered Easter to be celebrated according to their opinion.

This brief preliminary explanation should suffice to make intelligible what is indicated in the letters presented below concerning this controversy. Other matters will be added in the notes where necessary. We have prefixed this notice to the following letter because it is the first to provide evidence concerning this Easter controversy.

## Letter LXXXVIII

[Note: Alternatively numbered 68. What was formerly Letter 88 is now 117. Written 24 June 452.]

[Note: We collated this letter, which Quesnellus published from the Grimani manuscript of collection 18, with the Ratisbon manuscript of collection 19.]

### To Paschasinus, Bishop of Lilybaeum

### Summary

1. He sends Paschasinus his well-known letter to Flavianus of Constantinople, by which he was to be instructed as a future legate at the synod.

2. Against Eutyches, he asserts two natures in Christ.

3. He sends testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the Lord’s incarnation and announces that the bishops of the Eastern diocese have subscribed to the same letter to Flavianus.

He asks that Easter in the year 455 be investigated more carefully.

[Note: We have taken this heading from the Ratisbon manuscript. Quesnellus, from the Grimani manuscript, reads: “Leo, bishop, to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum.”]

Leo, bishop, to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum.

### Chapter I

Although I do not doubt that your Fraternity is fully acquainted with the whole origin of the scandals that have arisen in the Eastern Churches concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, nevertheless, lest something should perhaps have escaped your concern, I have sent you for more careful reading and examination our letter that we sent on this matter to Flavianus of holy memory, a letter of the fullest exposition, which the universal Church embraces.

Thus, understanding with what completeness the impiety of this entire error has been destroyed, with God’s help,

[Note: The words “with God’s help” are absent from the Ratisbon manuscript.]

you too may receive the same spirit because of your love for God, and may know that those who, according to the impiety and madness of Eutyches, have dared to say that there are not two natures in our Lord, the only-begotten Son of God, who assumed in himself the restoration of human salvation, are to be utterly detested—that is, two natures of perfect Divinity and perfect humanity.

They think that they can deceive our diligence when they say that they believe in one incarnate nature of the Word,

[Note: The Eutychians thought they could deceive Catholics by pressing this formula, which they claimed had also been used by Cyril. Cyril, however, spoke of one incarnate nature of the Word in such a way that in many passages he confessed the distinction of the divine and human natures and asserted their hypostatic union in the incarnation against the Nestorians, as Petavius extensively demonstrates in Book IV of *On the Incarnation*, chapters 7 and following. In this Catholic sense the expression was received by certain Catholics and by the Fifth Synod. The Eutychians, however, said that there was one incarnate nature of the Word in such a way as to remove the distinction between the two natures and to teach that the human nature had been absorbed by the divine. In this way they emptied the truth of the human flesh in Christ our Lord by denying it. Leo exposes and reproves this heretical meaning in the following chapter.]

whereas, in the Word of God, there is one nature in the Divinity of the Father, of the Son himself, and of the Holy Spirit; but, once the truth of our flesh had been assumed, our nature too was united to that immutable substance. For incarnation could not be spoken of unless flesh were assumed by the Word.

This assumption and union are so great and so complete that no division of the Divinity is to be believed to have occurred from the ensouled flesh, not only in the birth of the blessed Virgin but also in the conception, because in the unity of the person Divinity and humanity came together both in the Virgin’s conception and in her childbirth.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads: “The Word of God in the Divinity”; thereafter, “the Divinity is to be believed”; and shortly afterward, “Divinity and humanity,” with the same wording in the passages that follow.]

### Chapter II

The impiety in Eutyches must therefore be abominated.

[Note: The Ratisbon reading is *in Eutyche impietas* (“the impiety in Eutyches”) and agrees with the following words, “in the earlier heretics.” Quesnellus’s Grimani manuscript reads *Eutychis impietas* (“the impiety of Eutyches”).]

It was condemned and destroyed long ago by the Fathers in the earlier heretics,

[Note: We have supplied the verb *est* (“is”) from the Ratisbon manuscript.]

and that ought to have benefited this most foolish man: so that, when he could not grasp the matter by his understanding, he might at least have guarded against it by the example of those who preceded him,

[Note: Quesnellus reads: “he might have guarded against it by the preceding example; and the singular mystery of our salvation…” The reading of the Ratisbon manuscript seemed preferable. *Vel* (“or”) is frequently used in the sense of “at least.”]

lest, by denying the reality of human flesh in Christ our Lord, he should empty the singular mystery of our salvation.

For if the nature of humanity in him is not true and perfect, then our assumption is nonexistent, and everything that we believe and teach is, according to his impiety, vanity and falsehood.

But because Truth does not lie and Divinity is not subject to suffering, both substances remain in the Word of God in one person. Thus the Church confesses her Savior, acknowledging him as impassible in his Divinity and passible in his flesh, as the Apostle says: “Though he was crucified through our weakness, yet he lives through the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

### Chapter III

But so that your Love might be more fully instructed in every respect, I have sent you certain writings of our holy Fathers concerning what they thought and preached to the Churches about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, so that you might recognize this clearly.

[Note: This refers to testimonies of the holy Fathers that are found, in Greek copies of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, appended before the proceedings to Letter 28 of Leo to Flavianus. More will be said about this matter at the end of the notice concerning that same Letter 28. “Our men” here means the legates who had been sent to Constantinople in the case of Anatolius and had already returned.]

Our men also cited these writings at Constantinople together with my letter.

[Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Perhaps *cui* or *ei*; something appears to be missing.”]

You should know that the whole Church of Constantinople, together with all its monasteries and many bishops, gave its assent and, by their subscriptions, anathematized Nestorius and Eutyches together with their doctrines.

You should also know that I recently received a letter from the bishop of Constantinople reporting that the bishop of Antioch, having sent circular letters through his provinces to all the bishops, [had obtained] their assent to my letter and their condemnation of Nestorius and Eutyches by the same subscription.

[Note: Quesnellus likewise notes in the margin: “Perhaps ‘to everyone,’ or something else appears to be missing.” On this matter, at the Council of Chalcedon, in the session concerning Photius of Tyre, Eustathius of Berytus said: “When only a few had assembled at Constantinople” — toward the end of 450 — “a letter of the holy archbishop Leo was sent to all the metropolitans everywhere, and it was subscribed.” Compare another testimony of Leo at the end of Letter 91.]

### Chapter IV

We believe that this too should be entrusted to your care: since you are not ignorant of the method of calculating the Easter feast, investigate there more carefully, and examine with those who are skilled in this calculation and rule, what we find in the table of Theophilus and what troubles us, namely, how the day of the Lord’s resurrection in the fourth coming year is to be observed.

[Note: The Theophilian annotation is the same as the one-hundred-year Easter table compiled by him; see note 8 to Letter 121. The Ratisbon manuscript reads *inquiras illic* (“investigate there”); Quesnellus reads *requiras* (“investigate”).]

For since, by God’s favor, the coming Easter is to be observed on the tenth day before the Kalends of April,

[Note: In the year 452, on 23 March.]

and the following year on the day before the Ides of April,

[Note: In the year 453, on 12 April.]

and the third year on the day before the Nones of April,

[Note: In the year 454, on 4 April.]

the fourth year the blessed Theophilus establishes it on the Kalends of May,

[Note: Easter in the year 455: 24 April according to the Alexandrian reckoning, 17 April according to the Roman reckoning.]

which we find to be wholly foreign to ecclesiastical rule,

[Note: That is, foreign to the Latin Easter rules discussed in the preceding notice, section 3.]

while in our Easter cycles, as you know well, it is written that Easter in that same year must be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Note: It is clear that the Latins had not one but several eighty-four-year Easter cycles. Easter in the year 455 was assigned to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May in all of them: both in the older cycles, which admitted the lunar saltus every twelve years, and in those adopted in Leo’s time, which postponed the same saltus to every fourteen years, as we shall explain more fully in note 14 to Letter 121. Shortly afterward the Ratisbon manuscript reads “the Easter of that year.”]

Therefore, so that every ambiguity may be removed from us, let your concern examine this matter more carefully with all who are skilled in it, so that we may avoid such an error in the future.

[Note: This reading, “therefore, so that,” is better in the Ratisbon manuscript than Quesnellus’s Grimani manuscript, which reads “in every possible way.”]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Adelfius, a man of the highest distinction.

## Letter LXXXIX

[Note: Alternatively numbered 76. What was formerly Letter 89 is now 115. Written 24 June 451.]

[Note: It is found in manuscripts of collection 12 and in the most ancient Vatican manuscript 1322.]

### To the Emperor Marcian

### Summary

Concerning the legates sent to the general council to act in his place, where everything is to be restored to the unity of faith and peace.

Leo, bishop, to Marcian, ever Augustus.

We believed that your Clemency could grant our request by ordering that, in view of the present necessity, the priestly synod be postponed to a more suitable time, so that, with priests summoned from every province, it might truly be a universal council.

[Note: This is the reading of two of our manuscripts, those of collection 12 and Vatican 1322. The editions read *posset*, “might be able to be”; our reading is *possit*, “may be able to be.”]

But since, out of love for the Catholic faith, you have now wished the assembly to take place,

[Note: Saint Leo had not known on 9 June, when he sent Lucentius and Basilius to Constantinople concerning the reception of those who had fallen, that the decree convoking the council had been issued on 17 May. Hence, in other letters now missing, he added these men to the legates already being sent, as is reported in Letter 94. After 9 June, therefore, knowledge of this decree reached Leo; and after considering for several days the instruction and dispatch of legates to the council, insofar as the shortness of time allowed, he finally mentioned the convoked council on 24 June.]

I did not wish to seem opposed to your devoted decision. I have therefore sent my brother and fellow bishop Paschasinus, summoned from the province that appears to be safer, so that he might fulfill the role of my presence.

I have associated with him Boniface, my brother and fellow presbyter, and added to them those whom we had sent earlier; we have also added as their companion my brother Julian, the bishop.

[Note: The letter by which Leo sent Paschasinus as his legate to the council is missing. For nothing expressly concerning such a delegation is found in the preceding letter, signed on the same day and sent to him through Boniface, his fellow legate. The letter of delegation to Paschasinus therefore seems to have been written a few days before the preceding letter, whose first chapter presents him as already sufficiently instructed and supplies an additional instruction.]

With the Lord’s help, we believe that they will conduct all matters with such moderation that whatever has fallen into complaint and disturbance may, once all dissension has been suppressed, be restored to the unity of peace and faith. No trace of either Nestorian or Eutychian impiety should remain in the hearts of any priests.

For the Catholic faith, which under the instruction of God’s Spirit we have learned and teach through the holy Fathers from the blessed Apostles, does not permit either error to insinuate itself,

[Note: This is the better reading of our manuscripts. The editions read “will not permit.” Vatican manuscript 1322 has “to be mingled with it” instead of “to insinuate itself.” The words “most glorious emperor,” added by Quesnellus, are absent from that Vatican manuscript but are found in others. Although the authority of the most ancient Vatican manuscript might suggest that they should be removed, this does not mean that the letter was addressed to Pulcheria rather than to Marcian, as Tillemont suspects in note 41 of his *Life of Saint Leo*, volume 15, page 914. All manuscripts bear the heading naming Marcian, and the words “you should order” and “you have wished” suit Marcian: Leo had asked him in Letter 83, chapter 2, to order that the council be postponed, and Marcian himself then wished it to take place by the decree of convocation mentioned in note 3. The letter to Pulcheria, which Leo undoubtedly wrote on this same matter, is so far missing, as are many others. The difficulty that moved Tillemont arose from the chronological note prefixed in the editions to this letter and to the following letter to Marcian, both assigned to the same day; but that difficulty disappears once the chronological note is corrected.]

most glorious emperor.

If there are any diseases or wounds that can be healed by sincere correction, we desire that they be restored to genuine health. This will certainly not be doubtful or henceforth harmful to anyone’s simplicity if no one wishes to conceal it beneath excuses, since sin obtains abolition only through true confession.

But since certain brothers—we say this without pain—have not been able to maintain Catholic steadfastness against the storms of falsehood, it is fitting that the aforementioned brother and fellow bishop of mine preside over the synod in my place.

[Note: The editions read, “which now certainly will not be doubtful.” We preferred the reading of our manuscripts, in which *quae* refers to the correction. The editions preceding Quesnellus, together with the Venetian manuscript of collection 12, read *nullus*, “no one,” instead of *nullis*, “no.”]

[Note: Our manuscripts of collection 12 add “our brothers.” Quesnellus remarks in a note attached to this passage: “Observe why Leo wishes his legate to preside over the universal synod.” This gives a highly ambiguous meaning, less consistent with papal prerogatives. Just as the pontiff is the first and head of the whole Church, so by right he is entitled to preside over councils. Thus the Fathers of Chalcedon, in the Synodical Letter to Leo printed below as Letter 98, chapter 1, declared: “You presided over them as the head over members.” Marcian himself had sufficiently acknowledged this right in Letter 73, when he indicated that a general synod was to be celebrated on Leo’s authority; Pulcheria likewise acknowledged it in Letter 77.

Leo here suggested that this right, which belonged to him, also belonged to his legates, in the words “in my place,” which both delegate his authority to them and indicate the same right of presidency. The Council of Chalcedon itself records below, in Letter 98, chapter 3, that Leo presided through his legates. Paschasinus said at the beginning of the third session, in volume 4 of the Venetian edition of the Councils, page 1350: “He ordered our humble person to preside over this holy council in his place.”

Leo used the word “fitting” out of modesty. He also wished to add and state more expressly another reason, one that stood out more clearly, drawn from the Ephesian Robber Synod. There, because the legates of the Apostolic See had not presided, the repeated efforts of Dioscorus, the impious presider, prevailed over many who were unable to maintain Catholic steadfastness. This reason neither restricts nor excludes papal right.

At the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, Lucentius, Leo’s legate, indicated this right when he rebuked the aforementioned Dioscorus for arrogating to himself the role of presider at Ephesus, although he did not possess it, conducting everything according to his own judgment, disregarding the Apostolic legates, and daring to hold a synod without the authority of the Apostolic See—something that had never been permitted and had never been done.

The presidency that Leo modestly suggests in this letter he wanted his legates to exercise fully. Hence Paschasinus said at the same council, at the beginning of the third session: “He ordered our humble person to preside over this holy council in his place.”]

For I am certain that those to whom we have entrusted this task are laboring there without hatred or favoritism, so that, with heretical impiety alone destroyed, truth and charity may reign in all the Churches of God.

[Note: All our manuscripts omit the words *sum enim*, “for I am.” Since the first edition of this letter by Merlin was taken from a manuscript of collection 12, if these words are absent from all manuscripts of that collection, as they are absent from the two we have seen and from Vatican manuscript 1322, which has a different origin, they were probably supplied to complete the sense. It would nevertheless have been more suitable to supply *sum autem*, “but I am,” since *enim*, “for,” which gives the reason for the preceding sentence, fits less well: the preceding period concerns Paschasinus alone, whereas here the subject is all the legates. Someone might also think that, at this corrupted point before the word “certain,” something is missing indicating that the legates had been joined to Paschasinus, after which the following sense, common to all of them, would connect better. In that case the addition “for I am” or “but I am” would not be needed.]

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Adelfius, a man of the highest distinction.

1063 **LETTER XC** [Note: Also 73. The letter formerly numbered 90 is now 116. Written 26 June 451.] [Note: It is read in the Hispanic collection manuscripts, Isidore 11, 12, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, and in Sichard’s copy.] **TO THE SAME EMPEROR MARCIAN AUGUSTUS** [Note: Quesnellus correctly prefixed this title; see his note 1. In the Hispanic version the title reads: “On the direct execution of his legation to Constantinople for holding the Council of Chalcedon.”] **Concerning the council first summoned to Nicaea and afterward transferred to Chalcedon, through the presbyter Boniface.**

[Col. 0932A]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He agrees to the convocation of a general council, although he would have preferred that it be postponed because of the troubled circumstances. — II. The faith is not to be treated there as doubtful, nor is anyone to depart from the Nicene faith.

**Leo, bishop, to Marcian Augustus.**

### Chapter I

I had indeed asked your most glorious Clemency to order that the synod which you, at our request also, judge necessary for restoring peace to the Eastern Church [Note: The Vatican Hispanic manuscript, Isidore, and manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 read: “for restoring the peace of the Eastern Church.”] be postponed for a while to a more suitable time [Note: The same manuscripts, together with collection 24 and Sichard’s copy, read “you judged.” The reading introduced by Quesnellus is confirmed by our Vienna Hispanic and Regensburg manuscripts.], so that, with minds freer from every disturbance, those bishops also whom fear of hostilities detains might assemble.

But because, in your pious zeal, you place divine affairs before human concerns, and reasonably and religiously believe that the strength of your reign will benefit if there is no discord among the minds of priests and no disagreement in the preaching of the Gospel, I too do not resist your arrangements, wishing that the catholic faith—which can only be one—may be established in the hearts of all.

From its integrity both Nestorius formerly and Eutyches now have departed, by different paths indeed, but with an equal impiety: utterly detestable in their convictions, which they drew from the muddy pools of devilish falsehood against the pure fountain of the true light.

Therefore the earlier synod of Ephesus rightly and justly condemned Nestorius together with his doctrine; and whoever persists in that error [Col. 0933B] cannot hope for any remedy [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with one Vatican manuscript, read “cannot attain.”].

But the subsequent gathering in the aforesaid city [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “we cannot call it”; the Vienna Hispanic manuscript and Vatican collection 24 read “I cannot call it.” This agrees with the statement of Cecropius, bishop of Sebastopolis, at the Council of Chalcedon, session 10: “We ought not to call that [the Ephesian gathering] a council.”] cannot be called a council, since it is clear that it was conducted for the overthrow of the faith; and since your Clemency, out of love for the truth and in support of the Catholics, by establishing something else [Note: The editions before Quesnellus read *cassabit* (“will annul”), together with the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, Isidore, and manuscripts of collections 11, 12, 21, 22, and 23; these collections, however, all derive this letter from the Isidorian collection. Quesnellus introduced *cassavit* (“annulled”) from the Grimani and Victor manuscripts, and this reading is also preferred by the Vienna, Hispanic, and Regensburg manuscripts and by manuscript collection 24. The copies of Sichard and Merlin have *quassavit* (“shattered”), which is close to it. At least four superior collections of different origins favor this reading, namely Hispanic collections 18, 19, and 24. Since the other copies that prefer *cassabit* derive, as noted, from Isidore, while Isidore took it from a less pure Hispanic manuscript resembling Vatican 1341, whose first scribe often departed from the purer Hispanic source—as comparison of many passages has shown—we have therefore retained *cassavit*, which is found in the purer Vienna Hispanic manuscript, in other collections, and especially in the Regensburg manuscript. If Marcian’s law issued on the day before the Nones of July in 452 were to be considered—the law by which Theodosius’s constitution concerning the Ephesian robbery was annulled, as Leo’s legates and the other Fathers requested at session 10 of the Council of Chalcedon—*cassabit* would be preferable. But since, at the very beginning of Marcian’s reign, he supported the Catholics driven into exile because of the Ephesian pseudo-council, recalled them by the authority of his pragmatic sanction, as related in Letter 77, ordered the body of Saint Flavian to be transferred to Constantinople with honor, and performed other acts by which he repudiated the proceedings of that pseudo-synod, it is more likely that Leo had these actions in mind.] annulled it, most glorious Emperor.

### Chapter II

Therefore, by our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is the author and ruler of your reign, I implore and entreat your Clemency not to allow the faith which our blessed Fathers preached as handed down to them by the apostles [Note: The Vatican Hispanic manuscript, together with another manuscript of collection 11, reads: “Our Fathers the apostles preached as handed down to them.” The Vatican Isidorian manuscript reads: “Our Fathers the apostles preached,” omitting “handed down to them.”] to be reconsidered in the present synod as though it were doubtful; nor permit what was once condemned by the authority of our ancestors to be revived by renewed attempts.

Rather, order that the decrees of the ancient Council of Nicaea remain in force, with heretical interpretation removed [Note: This is the reading of our manuscripts and of the editions before Quesnellus, who, together with only our Vienna Hispanic manuscript, reads “remain.”].

Nor should you think that I am absent from that council, as your Clemency wished, since my presence must be regarded as present in the persons of the brothers whom I have sent: the bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, the presbyters Boniface and Basil, and also my brother Julian, whom I wished to share in their mission [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 2 and our observations appended to it.].

I trust that, with Christ’s help, they will act so that decisions pleasing to our Lord may be reached, with the support of your piety, which may benefit peace, religion, and the guardianship of the truth [Note: The common text reads: “which may benefit religious peace and the guardianship of the truth.” The two Hispanic manuscripts and the Vatican Isidorian manuscript read: “which may benefit peace, and the guardianship of religion,” or “the guardianship of the truth.” Vatican collection 24 reads: “which may benefit peace, and the religion of the guardianship of truth.” Sichard reads: “and may be the guardianship of the truth.” Merlin reads: “and may be the guardianship of religion.” The Regensburg manuscript supplies the true reading.].

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius.

---

**LETTER XCI** [Note: Also 70. The letter formerly numbered 91 is now 118. Written 26 June 451.] [Note: We compared this letter, edited by Quesnellus from the Grimani manuscript, with the Regensburg manuscript.] **TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE**

## SYNOPSIS

Although a shorter period had been allotted for convening the council, he nevertheless sends legates who will discharge his responsibility.

**Leo to Anatolius, bishop.**

When we learned from the letters which the most merciful Emperor sent us of his intention [Note: On p. 837 of volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils are Greek letters of Marcian addressed to Anatolius, inviting him to the synod. In the Greek manuscripts of the Imperial Library cited by Lambecius, vol. VIII, p. 495, however, the same letters are addressed to Λέοντι καὶ Ἀνατολίῳ, “Leo and Anatolius.” Their ancient translation, at p. 1985 of vol. IV of the Councils, bears the general encyclical title: “Sacred letters of the same most pious emperors, everywhere to the bishops beloved of God.” Since the letters themselves say of Leo, “As the letter of the most religious bishop of the glorious city of Rome also shows,” words which in a letter to that pontiff himself would have had to be omitted or expressed differently, if a copy not accompanied by a particular letter had been sent to Leo, it cannot be asserted that we possess the letter addressed to him. In Greek these letters are dated XVI Kalends of June; in the Latin copies of Quesnellus’s collection 5 and of Rusticus, X Kalends of June. For the council, as then announced, to be held at Nicaea, the Kalends of September were appointed.] we were surprised that so short a time had been allotted for assembling the synod. Even if there were no hostile emergency, the small number of intervening days would not allow us to summon the necessary priests from distant provinces. For when could we send messengers through widely separated and distant provinces so that a truly universal council might be held? [Note: He rightly says “truly,” or “properly,” since a genuinely universal council requires bishops to be summoned from the entire catholic world. Nevertheless, the Councils of Chalcedon and the First of Ephesus were treated as ecumenical, although sufficient time for such a general summons was lacking. This must be attributed to the approval of the Apostolic See; after it eventually received the First Council of Constantinople, which had been held without the knowledge of the Roman pontiff, that council began to be counted among the general councils.]

But because we embrace the will of the most merciful Emperor with such devotion that we did not wish to oppose his arrangement—especially since you yourself urgently requested this of us—we have sent our brother and fellow bishop Paschasinus, a man approved by us, by sea from a safer province. We have joined to him our brother and fellow presbyter Boniface from the City. We have also associated with them those who had previously been appointed, so that, with our brother and fellow bishop Julian sharing in all the proceedings [Note: Five Regensburg manuscripts read “in the proceedings.”], they may act in our place at the future council.

For we do not believe that they will have to struggle there with the difficulties of contentious disputes, since you yourself have deigned to report that all the priests of the East have subscribed to the acceptance of the catholic faith and to the condemnation of Eutyches and Nestorius.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius.

---

**LETTER XCII** [Note: Also 71. The letter formerly numbered 92 is now 119. Written 26 June 451.] [Note: We reread this letter, edited by Quesnellus from the Grimani manuscript, against the Regensburg manuscript.] **TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COS**

## SYNOPSIS

The pontiff instructs Julian, as a legate sent to the general council, to join his care and counsel to theirs.

**Leo to Julian, bishop.**

You have often learned what we think of your affection; for many earlier events have led us to form this expectation. Since, therefore, by the will of the most Christian Emperor, a priestly synod is to be held in the city of Nicaea [Note: The synod subsequently held at Chalcedon, which had first been summoned to Nicaea.], so that the uproar of all scandals may be removed, we necessarily impose upon your Fraternity a duty beneficial to the whole Church: join your care and action in all things with our brothers and fellow bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, and with our brothers and fellow presbyters Boniface and Basil, whom we command to go in our place to the aforesaid assembly [Col. 0936B], using the authority of our instruction.

For we know that you have greater knowledge than our legates of everything conducted there [Note: Quesnellus’s edition reads *auctorum*, perhaps through a typographical error. We corrected it from the Regensburg manuscript.]. Thus, when you associate your care and counsel with theirs, they will not be deceived in any respect; but, with God’s help, everything which you judge consistent with the faith and peace will be brought to completion.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius.

---

**LETTER XCIII** [Note: Also 72. The letter formerly numbered 93 is now 120. Written 26 June 451.] [Note: It survives in Hispanic collection 5; Isidore 11, 12, 13, and 18 through 24; in Sichard’s copy; and in Vatican manuscript 1322. In Chalcedonian collection 18 the Greek manuscripts, but not the Latin ones, contain it. This indicates that the Greek manuscript used by the Latin translator lacked this letter. It was published in Greek among the letters preceding the Acts. We also found it in two Venetian Greek manuscripts, St Mark’s 164 and 555: both among the letters preceding the Acts, as it was found by the Roman editors, and inserted into the council itself, as it appears in excerpts of Theodorus the Reader, where it is quoted in session 16, which has not yet been published and will be printed in the appendix.] **TO THE SYNOD FIRST SUMMONED TO NICAEA AND AFTERWARD ASSEMBLED AT CHALCEDON**

[Col. 0935]

[Note: In the table of collection 5, chapter 92, the title reads: “To the Council of Chalcedon concerning the restoration to their own sees of bishops who had formerly been expelled for the catholic faith, and concerning the validity of the First Synod of Ephesus.” In the Hispanic collection it reads: “To the Council of Chalcedon, where, through his legates, he exhorts the priests of God to arrange everything according to the Scriptures.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. The urgency of the time and established custom prevent him from attending the synod; nevertheless, through the legates he sends, he will be present. — II. The audacity of disputing against the faith must be restrained. — III. Bishops expelled for the faith must be restored, while the decrees issued against Nestorius at Ephesus remain in force.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

**Leo, bishop, to the holy synod established at Nicaea.** [Note: This wording is taken from the Regensburg manuscript and is more accurate than the alternative, “at Chalcedon.” When Leo gave this letter, the synod had been summoned to Nicaea, not Chalcedon. Theodorus the Reader testifies in his *Excerpts* that Leo wrote a remarkable letter to the synod which was expected to assemble at Nicaea; Evagrius likewise says this, as Quesnellus cited in note 1. Only after the council’s location had subsequently been changed was this same letter read at Chalcedon, in the unpublished session 16, with the inscription altered to suit that council: the city’s name was changed. For this reason the cited Greek manuscripts of St Mark give Nicaea before the Acts but Chalcedon in session 16. The Latin manuscripts were likewise corrected, since the council was in fact held at Chalcedon, not Nicaea. We deleted the words “of the city of Rome,” printed after “bishop,” because they are omitted in our more authoritative manuscripts and in the ancient Greek version. Conversely, we added “greeting to the beloved brothers in the Lord” from Vienna collection 5 and Florentine St Mark collection 13, since these words occur in the same Greek version.]

Greeting in the Lord to the beloved brothers.

### Chapter I

I had indeed wished, beloved, in keeping with the affection owed to our fellowship [Col. 0937A] [Note: This is the reading of five manuscripts used by Quesnellus and eleven of ours. The editions of Leo before Quesnellus, together with one manuscript of collection 21, read “your affection.”], that all the priests of the Lord should persevere in one devotion to the catholic faith [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “stand firm.” Shortly afterward, Vatican Hispanic, Isidore, and another Vatican manuscript of collection 11 read “of the priests” instead of “of the powers.” Ratramnus omits both readings in book IV *Against the Greeks*, volume I of Acher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 110.], and that no one should be corrupted by favor or fear of secular powers [Col. 0937C] [Note: Three of the cited manuscripts, together with Ratramnus, read “or depart from the way of truth.” In the same manuscripts and in the Vienna Hispanic manuscript, *saepe* (“often”) is absent.], so as to depart from the way of truth.

But because many things often occur that can produce repentance, and because God’s mercy surpasses the offenses of sinners, punishment is therefore suspended so that correction may have an opportunity, the profoundly religious counsel of the most merciful Emperor must be embraced. By it he wished your holy fraternity to assemble for the destruction of the devil’s snares and the restoration of ecclesiastical peace [Note: The same three manuscripts read “he preferred.” Shortly afterward the Regensburg manuscript and Vatican collection 24 omit “the apostle”; the same Regensburg manuscript reads “with honor preserved,” and shortly afterward “and venerable.”], while preserving the right and honor of the blessed apostle Peter. Indeed, he even invited me by his letters to offer my presence to the venerable synod.

This, however, neither the urgency of the time nor any established custom could permit [Note: Vienna collection 5 reads “could.” Leo gave the same reason in Letter 31, chapter 4, for not traveling to the Council of Ephesus; Paschasinus likewise used it at Chalcedon, session 3, volume IV, p. 1250: “For neither did ancient custom maintain this, nor did the general necessity of the time appear to permit it.”].

Nevertheless, in these brothers—namely the bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius and the presbyters Boniface and Basil—who have been sent from the Apostolic See, let your Fraternity consider me presiding over the synod [Note: We added “that is” from the oldest Vatican manuscript 1322, Vienna collection 5, the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, Isidore, and Ratramnus, in agreement with the Greek version. The Regensburg manuscript has “that is”; it shortly afterward, together with Vienna collection 5, reads “Lucentius” as “Lucensis.”], my presence not being separated from you [Note: This is the reading of our better manuscripts and of Quesnellus’s manuscripts. The Vatican Hispanic manuscript and Isidore read: “my presence, not separated from you,” and in collection 21 *aestimet* (“let him consider”) is added; earlier, *confidat* (“let him trust”) appears instead of *aestimet*. The older editions of Leo read: “let him trust that my presence is not separated from you.”], since I am now present in my representatives and have long not been absent from the preaching of the catholic faith [Note: We added the preposition *in*, omitted by Leo’s editions, from Vatican manuscript 1322, the Vienna Hispanic manuscript, and another Vatican manuscript of collection 11, together with the common editions of the councils.].

Thus, since you cannot be unaware of what we believe from the ancient tradition [Note: The Vienna manuscript of collection 5, another Hispanic manuscript, the Regensburg manuscript, Vatican collection 24, and Sichard read: “what we desire.”], you cannot doubt what we desire.

### Chapter II

Therefore, dearest brothers, once every audacity of disputing against the faith divinely inspired has been utterly rejected, let the vain unbelief of the erring fall silent; and let no one be permitted to defend what is not permitted to be believed.

For, according to the authority of the Gospels [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “according to evangelical authority,” a reading supported by the Greek version.], according to the prophetic utterances and the apostolic teaching, it has been declared most fully and clearly, in the letter which we sent to Flavian, bishop of blessed memory, what the devout and sincere confession is concerning the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### Chapter III

Since we are not unaware that the condition of many Churches has been disturbed by wicked rivalries, and that many bishops, because they would not accept heresy, have been driven from their sees, carried into exile, and replaced in the places of those still living [Note: The Vienna Hispanic manuscript incorrectly reads “and many spirits.” In the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, and from it in Isidore, this was corrected by an ancient scribe’s conjecture to “and many brothers.” Shortly afterward Ratramnus and manuscripts of collection 21, together with the editions before Quesnellus, read “have received,” or “may have received.” The Regensburg manuscript reads “the expelled.”], the medicine of justice must first be applied to these wounds [Note: We restored the ancient reading from our manuscripts. Only Vatican manuscript 1322 reads “so that no one,” omitting *ita*. Vienna collection 5 reads “so that no one in this way,” and so forth. The Vienna Hispanic manuscript deletes *ita* alone. Nowhere did we find Quesnellus’s reading, “so that no one be deprived of his own,” or “another use what belongs to others.”].

No one should be so deprived of his own possessions [Col. 0939C] [Note: We restored the ancient reading likewise from our manuscripts.], that another may use what belongs to someone else. If, as we desire, all abandon error [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “leave it.” Shortly afterward Vienna collection 5 reads “in no one.” The older editions, together with manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, omit *suus* (“his own”) and afterward *suo* (“his own”). Quesnellus inserted *suus*, which is also found in our manuscripts Vatican 1322, Vienna collection 5, the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, and Isidore. We likewise inserted *suo* after “privilege,” on the authority of Vatican 1322, Vienna collection 5, another Hispanic manuscript, Vatican collection 11, and the excellent Regensburg manuscript.], no one’s honor ought to perish; rather, those who have suffered for the faith must have their own right restored to them with all their privileges.

But the decrees specifically issued against Nestorius by the First Synod of Ephesus, over which Bishop Cyril of holy memory then presided [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 2. It should be noted that in the Acts of Ephesus Saint Cyril consistently presents himself as acting in the place of Pope Celestine, since that pontiff had delegated to him the authority of the Apostolic See in the matter of Nestorius.], must remain in force, lest the impiety condemned then [Note: The Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “the same thing to itself.” This error was corrected in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and consequently in Isidore, manuscripts of collections 11 and 21, and Ratramnus to “finally flatter itself in something,” followed by “in which Eutyches…”] flatter itself in some respect merely because Eutyches has been struck down by a just anathema.

For the purity of faith and doctrine which we proclaim in the same Spirit as our holy Fathers condemns and persecutes alike the depravity of Nestorius and of Eutyches, together with their authors.

Farewell in the Lord, dearest brothers. [Note: These six words are absent from Leo’s editions but are found in the editions of the councils. We restored them not only because they occur in Vienna collection 5 and Florentine St Mark collection 13, but also because they are present in the oldest Greek translation, which was taken from Leo’s original and read at the Council of Chalcedon, session 16.]

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [26 June], in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius. [Note: All editions, together with manuscripts of collection 24, read “the fifth day before the Kalends of July”; the Greek text, both in the editions and in our manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection preceding the Acts, supports that reading. The manuscripts of Vienna collection 5 and Florence, St Mark collection 13, read “the fifth day before the Kalends of June,” clearly an error in the month, as is evident from note 11 (932, note e) on Letter 89. We preferred the sixth day before the Kalends of July, which agrees with the preceding letters and is supported by Vatican 1322, both Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, Regensburg, and manuscripts of collections 11 and 21.]

[Col. 0936B]

## Greek version

**Leo, bishop, to the holy synod at Nicaea: greeting to the beloved brothers in the Lord.** [Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “to the synod at Chalcedon” in the Acts.]

I had indeed wished, beloved, in accordance with the affection owed to our fellowship [Col. 0938A] [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “relationship.”], to establish all the priests of the Lord in one zeal [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “in one zeal”] for the catholic faith, and that no one, taking up evil through favor or fear of worldly power, should turn aside from the way of truth.

But since many things often occur that can bring about repentance, and since God’s mercy conquers the offenses of those who sin, punishment is therefore held in suspension so that correction may find room, it is right to embrace the wholly pious will of the most tranquil Emperor. Through it he desired your holy fraternity to assemble for the overthrow of the devil’s plots [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read: “for the overthrow of the plotting devil and for the restoration of ecclesiastical peace”], while the rights and honor of the most blessed apostle Peter were preserved, to such an extent that he himself prompted us through his own letters to offer our presence to the holy synod [Note: The same manuscripts read: “so that we might gladly provide our own presence to the holy synod.”].

This, however, was impossible, and neither the necessity of the time nor established custom allowed it [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read: “which was impossible, and neither the necessity … permitted it.”].

Nevertheless, in these brothers—namely Paschasinus and Lucentius, the bishops, and Boniface and Basil, the presbyters—who were sent by the throne of the apostles [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “from the Apostolic See”—literally, “from the throne”], let your Fraternity consider me presiding over the synod [Note: We corrected this from both Venetian manuscripts, with the Latin text supporting it: “my presence not being separated from you.” The common text reads “you not being separated,” while the margin of the Roman edition apparently notes *κεχωρισμένης* (“being separated”).], my presence not being separated from you.

I am present with you through my representatives, and I am not absent through the preaching of the catholic faith; so that you, who cannot be ignorant of what we believe concerning the ancient tradition [Note: We added the article *τοὺς*, which is absent—improperly—from the common editions, on the authority of the Venetian manuscripts. In the Acts both manuscripts read: “so that you also, who cannot be ignorant”; before the Acts one reads: “so that you, who cannot be ignorant,” making it clear that *τοῦ* there is an error for *τοὺς*. The addition of this article plainly improves the clarity of the sentence.], cannot doubt what desire has been established in us [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read: “cannot doubt what our desire is.”].

Therefore, dearest brothers, let every audacious discussion against the faith inspired by God be utterly silenced, and let the vain unbelief of those who have gone astray keep quiet. Let no one defend what it is not lawful to believe. For, according to the authority of the Gospels, the utterances of the prophets, and the teaching of the apostles, it has already been declared most fully and clearly, through the letters which we sent to Flavian, bishop of holy memory [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “of blessed memory”], what the devout and pure confession concerning the mystery of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ is.

Since we have recognized that the condition of many Churches has been disturbed by certain wicked oppositions, and that many bishops who did not accept the things of the heretics have been expelled from their own sees [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “from their own places”], handed over to exile, and others installed in the places of those who still survive [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “in the place of.” We have changed nothing, although the Latin text reads “in the place.”], let the treatment of justice first be applied to these wounds.

No one should be so deprived of what belongs to him that another may make use of what belongs to someone else [Note: This is correct; both Venetian manuscripts have it in both the Acts and before the Acts. The common editions incorrectly read “to the others.” The word *ἄλλον* never has, and does not here have, the meaning “another” in the sense of “someone else” as those editions suppose.].

If, as we earnestly desire, everyone abandons error, no one’s honor ought to perish [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “the honor of no one perishes.”]; rather, the right of those who have labored for the faith ought to be restored to them, together with all their own privileges [Note: The margin of the Roman edition reads “with every privilege he ought to have.”].

But the decrees specifically issued against Nestorius by the earlier synod at Ephesus, over which Cyril of holy memory then presided [Note: We add *then*, absent from the common editions, on the authority of the Venetian manuscripts and the Latin text, which reads “then presided.” In the cited manuscripts the whole passage appears as follows: “And indeed, let the decrees of the earlier synod at Ephesus, over which Cyril of holy memory then presided, issued specifically against Nestorius, remain in force.”], must remain in force, lest the impiety condemned then deceive itself in any respect merely because Eutyches has been rightly struck down and cast out by an anathema.

For the purity of the faith and of the teaching which we proclaim in the same Spirit as our holy Fathers [Note: We correct this by following the reading of the Venetian manuscripts, which exactly corresponds to the Latin text, “in the same Spirit as our holy Fathers.” The common text reads “which [is] in the Holy Spirit.” We nevertheless point out that shortly afterward *ᾥπερ* should be read instead of *ὥσπερ*.] condemns [Note: The Venetian manuscripts read “is condemned.”] and persecutes equally the false doctrine of Nestorius and Eutyches, together with their authors [Note: The preposition *μετά* (“together with”), which has wrongly dropped out of the common text, is supplied from the Venetian manuscripts and from the Latin text, which reads “with their authors.”].

Farewell in the Lord, dearest brothers. [Note: These words are absent from the Venetian manuscripts in their second occurrence, namely in the unpublished Chalcedonian session. We will publish that session in the appendix. Before the Acts, where the same letter is likewise transmitted as it was subsequently published by the Roman editors, the Venetian manuscripts contain the following note: “It was ordered that the synod summoned by Marcian’s letters be held at Nicaea. For Pulcheria herself similarly wrote concerning the same synod, then convened at Nicaea, in her letter to Strategius, the consular governor of Bithynia: ‘According to our sanction, the most reverend bishops assembled.’ The initiative in convening the synod was shared by Marcian and his wife, to whom he owed the Empire, although the woman’s name was omitted from the imperial sanction because such an inscription was contrary to the customary form of those sanctions.”]

It was issued on the fifth day before the Kalends of July [27 June]. [Note: The Greek date is corrupt or incomplete as transmitted.]

---
