**LETTER XCIV** [Note: Also 74. The letter formerly numbered 94 is now 121. Written 20 July 451.] [Note: This letter is found in manuscripts of collections 12, 18, 19, and 24, in Vatican manuscript 1322, and in Sichard’s copy.] **TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS**

[Col. 0941A]

## SYNOPSIS

He commends to the Emperor the legates whom he is sending to the synod and asks that no discussion of the faith be reopened there.

**Leo, bishop, to Marcian Augustus.**

I received with such pleasure the holy zeal of your Clemency, by which you wished to hold a synod for the restoration of ecclesiastical peace, that although I had asked that it be held within Italy [Note: See Letter 83.] and had wished for a more suitable time to be awaited, so that many bishops might also be summoned from more distant provinces [Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of collection 24, read “from distant regions,”], nevertheless, as soon as the letters of your piety had been delivered to me [Note: Compare note 2 (Col. 934, note m) on Letter 91], I sent Boniface, one of my fellow presbyters, from the City, and had my brother Paschasinus, one of the bishops, sail from Sicily [Col. 0941B]. They would adequately fulfill my role.

I also sent letters through them to those who had previously undertaken the legation, so that they too might join the aforesaid men in fulfilling the duties of my presence, most glorious Emperor [Note: The letters to Lucentius, bishop, and Basil, presbyter, are missing.].

Therefore, although an exceedingly short day has been appointed for the synod, I nevertheless hope that the help of almighty God will be present, enabling all to arrive by the appointed time and, with the agreement of the holy fraternity, unanimously define what is suitable for the universal Church.

When the agitation and depravity of the few have been restrained or removed, an approved concord will easily be established, if all hearts unite in the faith which, having been declared by evangelical and apostolic preaching, we received and hold through our holy Fathers [Note: The editions before Quesnellus and the manuscripts of collection 24 read “through the ancient Fathers.”], with absolutely no discussion reopening the matter. Otherwise, through empty and deceptive cleverness, things founded from the beginning on that cornerstone which is Christ the Lord (Ephesians 2:20) might appear weak or doubtful [Note: The common editions and manuscripts read: “which are founded upon Christ himself, the cornerstone, and will remain forever.” Quesnellus’s emendation from the Grimani manuscript is supported by our Regensburg and Vatican 1322 manuscripts.], although they are destined to remain forever.

This is our constant prayer: that no one be found alienated from the mystery of the unique faith, but that, with the impiety of heresy condemned, the catholic Church may suffer no loss through anyone’s destruction.

What I requested of your piety in the letters which I sent through my representatives [Note: The same manuscripts and editions read “concerning those through whom I sent my letters.” The reading introduced by Quesnellus from the Grimani manuscript is also preferred by Vatican 1322 and Regensburg, which alone in the latter place reads “through them” instead of “through my representatives.”], I now ask with similar confidence: deign to regard those who will act in my place as commended to you in every respect, so that what has been arranged through the excellent zeal of your faith may more easily and diligently be brought to a salutary result.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [20 July], in the consulship of the most illustrious man Adelphius. [Note: Our Regensburg and Vatican 1322 manuscripts, and Quesnellus in the margin, presumably from the Grimani manuscript, agree with the chronological notice of the following letter. The common editions and manuscripts of collections 12 and 24 read: “Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.”]

---

**LETTER XCV** [Note: Also 75. The letter formerly numbered 95 is now 122. Written 20 July 451.] [Note: It is found in manuscripts of collections 12, 18, 19, and 24, and in Sichard’s copy.] **TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA** [Note: These words are found only in manuscripts of collection 12. The *magistriani* were *agentes in rebus*, so called because they were subordinate to the *magister officiorum*. On these officials, see Gothofredus’s commentary on book 3 of the Theodosian Code, *De agentibus in rebus*, where among their duties he lists the delivery of imperial letters.] **Through Theoctistus, a magistrianus.**
[Col. 0942B]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He explains that he sent legates to the council, although he had wished it to be convened in Italy.—II. That moderation must be maintained in ecclesiastical cases, a moderation wholly absent from the Ephesian robbery.—III. That he has never refused forgiveness to those who corrected their error.—IV. That even heresiarchs who ask for indulgence should not be rejected, although they should not be received rashly.

## LEO, bishop, to PULCHERIA Augusta

### CHAPTER I

I recognize in every respect the religious concern of your clemency, which you continually devote to the Catholic faith; and I give thanks to God that I see you exercising such care for the universal Church that I may confidently communicate what I judge to accord both with justice and with benevolence, so that what, with Christ’s favor, has thus far been irreproachably accomplished through the zeal of your piety may more swiftly attain a result worthy of rejoicing, most glorious Augusta.

Therefore, when your clemency ordered that a synod be held at Nicaea,

[Note: [Col. 0942C] We have added “and” from the Regensburg manuscript.]

although your gentleness retains my request that it be held in Italy, so that all the bishops of our region, once summoned, might assemble if the security of the times permitted it, I nevertheless received the decision far from disdainfully. I appointed two of my co-bishops and fellow priests who would be sufficient to discharge my office,

[Note: [Col. 0943C] In the Venetian manuscript, St. Mark’s collection 12, and in the Regensburg manuscript, “also” is omitted.]

and I gave them suitable written instructions for the venerable synod, by which the invited brotherhood might learn what procedure it ought to observe in this judgment, so that no rashness might oppose either the rules of faith, the decrees of the canons, or the remedies of kindness.

### CHAPTER II

For, as I have very frequently written from the beginning of this case,

[Note: [Col. 0943C] Namely, in Letters 28 and following, written on the Ides of June in the year 449, where he advised that, if Eutyches should repent and issue a profession of faith together with a condemnation of his error, his rank should be restored to him; and likewise in Letter 14, chapter 3, where he promised forgiveness even to all the authors of the scandals who had acted treacherously at Ephesus, if they accepted better counsels. After a few words, the editions preceding Quesnell, together with manuscripts of collection 11 and Sichardus, read: “The powers of the devil’s works are destroyed.”]

I wished this moderation to be preserved amid conflicting opinions and fleshly rivalries: nothing should be permitted to be torn away from the integrity of the faith, and nothing added to it; but for those returning to unity and peace, the remedy of forgiveness should be provided. For then the works of the devil are destroyed more powerfully, when human hearts are recalled to love of God and of their neighbor.

But it would take too long to explain how contrary to these admonitions and entreaties of mine their actions then were; nor is there any need for an epistolary page to encompass everything that could be perpetrated in that Ephesian event—not a judgment but a robbery—

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The same editions, together with manuscripts of collections 12 and 24 and Sichardus, place a period before this: “There the leading men.”]

where the leaders of the synod spared neither the brothers who resisted them

[Note: [Col. 0943D] The Regensburg manuscript omits “nor those who consented.” The reference is to Domnus of Antioch. Although through weakness of spirit he had consented in the first session to Flavian’s condemnation and Eutyches’ acquittal, he was nevertheless deposed shortly afterward in the same pseudo-synod, with Maximus substituted in his place.]

nor those who consented: in order to break down the Catholic faith and strengthen an execrable heresy, they stripped some of the privilege of honor and infected others through fellowship in impiety. They were plainly more savage toward those whom they separated from innocence by persuasion than toward those whom, by persecuting them, they made blessed confessors.

### CHAPTER III

Nevertheless, because such men have harmed themselves most grievously by their own wickedness, and more serious wounds require more diligent medicine, I have never declared in any letter that forgiveness should be denied even to such persons if they repented.

And although we detest as utterly and immutably hostile to the Christian religion the heresy itself, we do not judge the persons themselves, if they are unquestionably corrected and cleanse themselves by worthy satisfaction, to be excluded from the ineffable mercy of God. Rather, we groan with those who groan and weep with those who weep; and we use the justice of disciplinary indignation in such a way that we do not lose the remedies of charity.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] Quesnell reads “that we should not omit.” We have restored the reading of the earlier editions, confirmed by all our manuscripts, including the Regensburg manuscript. Shortly afterward, the Venetian manuscript, collection 12, reads “we promise.”]

As your piety recognizes, this is promised not only in words but also demonstrated by deeds. For nearly all who had either been led or compelled into agreement with those presiding,

[Note: [Col. 0944C] In the Regensburg manuscript “nearly” is lacking; but it is necessary, since at this time certain persons had not yet obtained the grace of apostolic peace, neither having rescinded what they had decreed nor condemned what they had written.]

[Note: [Col. 0944C] Sichardus reads: “by resisting that which had been decreed by them, and by condemning,” etc. The same is found in manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, which omit only “it.” The editions before Quesnell read: “by rescinding that which had been decreed by them.” The Regensburg manuscript likewise prefers Quesnell’s reading from the Grimani manuscript.]

by rescinding what they had decreed and condemning what they had written, have obtained perpetual abolition of their guilt and the grace of apostolic peace.

### CHAPTER IV

Therefore, if your clemency deigns to consider my purpose,

[Note: [Col. 0944C] The copy of Sichardus, together with the old editions; our reading.]

it will approve that I conducted everything with the intention that, without harm to anyone’s soul, only the extinction of the heresy might be achieved. For this reason I somewhat reduced the customary severity toward the authors of the most savage storms, so that their slowness might be stirred by some compunction to ask for indulgence.

[Note: [Col. 0944C] The Regensburg manuscript reads “might be able.” These words seem to refer to Leo’s decree that the names of the authors of the Ephesian robbery should not be recited at the altar, as the same pontiff wrote in his reply to Anatolius, Letter 80, chapter 4. Although some might perhaps have thought that this should be postponed according to custom until they were deposed, Leo nevertheless judged it necessary to lessen the custom in this matter: since, after their impious crime, they had so far suffered none of the punishment they deserved and still possessed their episcopal sees, this at least might serve as a spur to rouse them to seek indulgence.]

Although, after that judgment, as impious as it was unjust, they are no longer as honorable to the Catholic brotherhood as they had been,

[Note: [Col. 0944D] We have restored from all our manuscripts and Sichardus the particle “thus,” omitted by Quesnell. The other editions read: “thus honorable as they had been.”]

they still retain their sees and enjoy the honor of their episcopates. They will either recover the peace of the whole Church through true and necessary satisfaction,

[Note: [Col. 0944D] Our manuscripts support the word “whole,” which Quesnell added.]

or, if—God forbid—they defend the heresy,

[Note: [Col. 0944D] Manuscripts of collections 12 and 24 and the copy of Sichardus, together with the editions before Quesnell, read “they will defend.” The better reading is found in the Grimani and Regensburg manuscripts. Shortly afterward, in the cited collections and in Sichardus, “Aelpidio” is incorrectly printed for “Adelfio.”]

they will be judged according to the merit of their profession.

[Col. 0944C] Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Adelfius, illustrious man.

---

## LETTER XCVI

[Note: [Col. 0945C] Formerly numbered 76. What was previously 96 is now 123. Written around July of the year 451.]

### TO RAVENNIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

On the Easter solemnity of the following year, 452.

## SYNOPSIS

Unity must be especially maintained in celebrating Easter; it belongs to the Roman pontiff to announce that solemnity.

To his most beloved brother Ravennius, bishop: Leo, bishop.

It belongs to the principal sacrament of our religion that there be no diversity anywhere in the world on the feast of Easter. And because divine institution and paternal tradition have wished this matter to belong to our concern, we solemnly admonish your Brotherhood to recognize that the Lord’s Pascha is to be celebrated by us on the tenth day before the Kalends of April. Clear reasoning has disclosed that this is the proper day for the sacred observance;

[Col. 0945B] and we have wished its date to be announced to everyone through your love also, dearest brother, so that those whose confession of faith is one may likewise have one devotion in this solemnity.

---

## LETTER XCVII: SYNODICAL LETTER OF EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN, TO SAINT LEO THE POPE

[Note: [Col. 0945C] Formerly numbered 77. What was previously 97 is now 124. Written in August or September of the year 451.]

[Note: [Col. 0945C] This synodical letter survives in manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 21, 22, and 23.]

[Note: [Col. 0945C] In the table of collection 5, chapter 56, and somewhat differently in manuscripts of other collections and in the printed editions, the following is added in place of the synopsis: “By this letter, affirming it together with the other bishops, he agreed with and subscribed to the faith which Leo had sent to the East.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He rejoices at the return of his brothers from the East.—II. The letter to Flavian was read and approved at the synod of Milan.—III. He declares that he and his colleagues subscribe to the condemnation of the Eutychians.

To the holy and most blessed Father Leo, Eusebius, bishop of Milan.

### CHAPTER I

When, by the Lord’s favor, our brothers had returned,

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Namely, Abundius, bishop of Como—called Abundantius in this letter and in the subscriptions—and the presbyter Senator. They had been sent to the East in July of the year 450 and returned to Rome in June of 451, according to Letter 83, chapter 1. To allow a reasonable amount of time for their stay in Rome, their journey to Milan, and the gathering of the synod—which Abundius, or Abundantius, of Como subscribed to also in the name of Asimon of Chur—and to allow time for Abundius to revisit Como and on that occasion to see Asinio, the neighboring bishop who entrusted his representation to him, this letter appears to have been written in August or September.]

our brothers whom your watchful and provident blessedness had carefully sent to the East on account of the faith, and when the letters that your holiness had sent through them had been read, I was lifted up with every kind of rejoicing in Christ, because your letter indicated that they had brought back the result of the mission entrusted to them.

Nor is it surprising that our Lord Jesus Christ granted the Catholic faith which we hold the protection and guardianship of his majesty’s grace: for he placed you, a worthy defender of his worship, as bishop in the seat of his apostle,

[Note: [Col. 0946C] Quesnell deleted the word “faith,” having found it absent from two Thuanean manuscripts and one Cambridge manuscript, because he thought Eusebius was speaking about the Church rather than the faith. Although we likewise found the word omitted in Vatican collection 11, we nevertheless found it in other manuscripts, especially in the oldest manuscript of the Vindobonensis collection 5, to which the two Thuanean manuscripts and the Trecopithoean manuscript cited by Quesnell in note 1 belong. We therefore judged that it should be restored, especially since what follows demonstrates that the subject is the faith of the incarnation.]

who are able both to think rightly about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and to preserve the same things more rightly.

[Note: [Col. 0946C] Thus Quesnell and our manuscripts of the Vindobonensis collection 5 and Vatican collection 11. The other editions, together with manuscripts of collection 21, read “true.”]

### CHAPTER II

Therefore, after admonishing my brothers and fellow bishops and holding a meeting, we followed the form of your letters. For, when the letter of your blessedness had been read aloud in the council of the Lord’s priests—the holy brother and our fellow bishop Abundantius and my fellow presbyter Senator had brought it—and their account had been acknowledged, the letter was requested and reread in continuous order according to the sequence of events, just as your written instructions had indicated.

[Note: [Col. 0946C] The printed editions read “reviewing the letter,” leaving the nominative without a governing construction. The necessary correction is supplied by the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5.]

[Note: [Col. 0946D] See Quesnell’s note 2.]

It was the letter that your holiness had formerly sent to the East, fully arranged as an affirmation of the faith, and which reached us through the agency of our holy brother and fellow bishop Ceretius,

[Note: [Col. 0946D] The editions preceding Quesnell, together with one manuscript of collection 21, read “Cyriacus.” Vatican collection 11 reads “Ceritius”; the other manuscripts read “Ceretius.” See Quesnell’s note 3. Shortly afterward, the old editions read “full,” without the support of any of our manuscripts.]

at your direction, with our holy brother and fellow bishop Ceretius lending it.

It became clear that the letter shone with the complete simplicity of faith, radiating with a certain brilliance of light and truth through the assertions of the prophets, the authority of the Gospels, and the testimonies of apostolic teaching, and agreeing in every respect with the doctrines that blessed Ambrose, inspired by the Holy Spirit, inserted in his books concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0946D] See Quesnell’s note 4. Shortly afterward, in the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, the word “mystery” was first written by another hand as “sacrament.”]

### CHAPTER III

And because everything agrees in complete purity with the faith of our ancestors handed down to us from ancient times, holy and most blessed Lord and Father, it pleased all those whose names the subscription appended below can disclose that those who think impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation—although by the perversity of their understanding they have withdrawn from the truth of the Catholic faith and made themselves worthy of rejection—should, by their own consent also, and with the judgment of your authority preceding, be pursued by an appropriate condemnation.

Accordingly, following the form of your letters, we have shown through the letters sent by our brother and fellow bishop Cyriacus that we have observed the procedure prescribed by your decree.

[Note: [Col. 0947C] The editions read “my [brother],” with one manuscript of collection 21. We follow not so much the manuscripts of that collection as those of collections 5 and 11.]

[Note: [Col. 0947C] The editions preceding Quesnell, with a corrupt reading, have: “It remains for you, with the Lord’s approval, to show that, while you continually retain this victory, you leave it memorable for future ages, so that from the present time the insolence of the impious sect, having been extinguished, may appear to have been overthrown by new purifications and lie prostrate forever.” The same wording appears in some manuscripts of collection 21, with the words transposed as “so that, having been extinguished from this present time.” Other manuscripts of that collection, together with Ottobonian collection 23, read: “It remains … that, with the insolence of the impious sect extinguished from this present time—or, in another reading, of the present time—…” The editions of the Councils replace the passage as in the printed text and have only at the end of the sentence: “So that, with the insolence of the impious sect extinguished from this present time, it may appear to have been overthrown, so that, with you as its defenders, it may appear prostrate forever.” Quesnell’s emendation, drawn from the Thuanean and Trecopithoean manuscripts of the oldest collection 5, seemed better and more appropriate; we likewise found it in the excellent Vindobonensis manuscript of the same collection, along with Vatican Ottobonian manuscript 93 and Vatican manuscript 3791 of the ancient collection 11. In these, “having existed” alone was mistakenly written “having been extinguished.” We have retained this reading, and from the aforementioned Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 we have written “defenders” for what Quesnell printed as “fighters.”]

It remains for you, with the Lord’s approval, to retain in peaceful perpetuity the palm of faith and the crown of the completed struggle, and to leave this memorable for future ages: namely, that the insolence of the impious sect existed for this present time so that, with you as its defenders, it might be overthrown and lie prostrate forever.

And in another hand:

May the supreme Divinity protect and guard your blessedness unharmed, holy and most blessed lord and father.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] The editions of Leo, together with manuscripts of collection 21, read “may adorn.”]

Eusebius, bishop of the Church of Milan, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] See Quesnell’s note 6. Since he arranged the order of the bishops differently from the printed Leonine editions on the basis of his manuscripts, our manuscripts also support him.]

I, Faventius, bishop of the Church of Reggio, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Majorianus, bishop of the Church of Piacenza, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Cyprian, bishop of the Church of Brixilliana,

[Note: [Col. 0947D] Thus the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, supported by manuscripts of collections 11 and 21. The common editions read “Brixellensis.”]

have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Col. 0948A] I, Quintus, bishop of the Church of Tortona,

[Note: [Col. 0947D] Some editions read “Quintinus.”]

have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Crispinus, bishop of the Church of Pavia, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Floreius, presbyter, ordered by the holy Bishop Eulogius, my bishop of the Church of Eporedia,

[Note: [Col. 0947D] In the editions preceding Quesnell, this subscription follows the subscription of Maximus, and the continuation differs: “Because he was unable to subscribe on account of illness, I agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who…” Only the Trecopithoean manuscript of collection 5 reads “Florentius” instead of “Floreius.” Vatican collection 11 has “Eporae” instead of “Eporedia,” and in Labbe’s edition the margin reads “Eporegiae.”]

because he himself is unable to subscribe on account of illness, have subscribed to everything written above with his consent, and he anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Col. 0948B] I, Maximus, bishop of the Church of Turin, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Gratus, presbyter, sent by my bishop Euthasius of the Church of Augusta,

[Note: [Col. 0948C] He is called “Gradus” in Vatican collection 11 and in the editions preceding Quesnell; “Gerardus” appears in the margin of the Councils. Instead of “Euthasius,” the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, Vatican collection 11, and the margin of the Councils read “Eustasius.”]

have agreed and subscribed in his place to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Cyriacus, bishop of the Church of Laodicea,

[Note: [Col. 0948C] The editions read “Laodicean.” We have corrected this from Vatican collection 11.]

have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Abundantius, bishop of the Church of Como, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, both for myself and for my absent holy brother Asinio, bishop of the Church of Chur, in the First Rhaetia,

[Note: [Col. 0948C] This subscription is unique in all our manuscripts and in Quesnell; in the earlier editions it was divided into two subscriptions, one by Abundantius on his own behalf and another on behalf of Asimo—as he calls him. Quesnell suspects that this Abundantius of Como was different from Abundius, who carried out the mission of the Apostolic See in the East with Senator and, returning from the mission, brought Leo’s letter to Eusebius. Thus, he thinks, it is unnecessary to call Abundius bishop of Como or to suppose that he attended the Council of Milan. His entire argument rests on the fact that Leo’s legate is called Abundius in all the documents, whereas here, in every manuscript he examined and likewise in our manuscripts, the subscriber is called Abundantius. But Abundantius is not named only in this subscription: he is also named in the text of the letter, where the discussion is plainly about Leo’s legate who returned from the East with Senator, as Quesnell himself does not deny. This Abundantius is therefore recognized as the same person who is called Abundius in Leo’s letters and who is joined with Senator as the other legate. Since chapter 1 says that these men returned from the eastern mission, just as Senator was a presbyter of the Church of Milan, Abundius or Abundantius must be recognized as a bishop of the province of Milan. The Church of Como venerates him under the name Abundius. That he attended the Council of Milan is shown by the words of chapter 2: “and their account having been acknowledged,” which indicate that he was present.]

anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Paschasius, bishop of the Church of Genoa, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Col. 0949A] I, Pastor, bishop of the Church of Asti, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Simplicianus, bishop of the Church of Novara, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0949B] The editions read “Simplicius.” We have corrected this from all our manuscripts, as well as from the three manuscripts mentioned by Quesnell in his notes.]

I, John, bishop of the Church of Cremona, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

I, Optatianus, bishop of the Church of Brescia, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0949B] The editions before Quesnell read “Octavianus”; the Vindobonensis manuscript reads “Obtinianus.” In the sermon of Rampertus, bishop of Brescia, on the translation of Saint Philastrius, where his successors are listed, he is called “Optatianus.”]

I, Justianus, bishop of the Church of Vercelli, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0949B] Thus our old books, except for one manuscript of Vatican collection 21, which, together with some printed editions, reads “Justinianus.” Ferrerius may have cited the same manuscript under the name Justinianus in his book on the bishops of Vercelli.]

I, Quintius, bishop of the Church of Albenga, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0950B] The printed editions, together with the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 and the manuscripts of collection 21 and Vatican collection 11, read “Quintus.” One of Quesnell’s Thuanean manuscripts reads “Quintianus,” and another Cambridge manuscript reads “Quintinus.”]

I, Praestantius, bishop of the Church of Bergamo, have agreed and subscribed to everything written above, anathematizing those who have thought impiously about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 0950B] The Cambridge manuscript of Quesnell reads “Pristinus”; the margin of the Councils reads “Praestius.”]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

[Col. 0949]

1. Quesnell was the first to insert among Leo’s works the excellent letter, or report, of the Council of Chalcedon to Saint Leo, in Greek and Latin, as it appears in the editions of the Councils; yet he used no Greek or Latin manuscript. We have collated the Greek text, which is the original, with two Venetian manuscripts of Saint Mark’s, numbers 164 and 555.

As for the Latin, there are two Latin versions of this report. Quesnell printed the one first published by Crabbe, which passed into the other editions of the Councils. But another, older translation also exists, written shortly after the Council of Chalcedon itself; Pope Vigilius cited testimony from it in his Constitutum. Baluzius was the first to publish it. It has so far been found in only three manuscripts: a Parisian manuscript, one in the Vatican Library of the Queen of Sweden, and another Vatican manuscript, number 1322.

This last manuscript, once belonging to the Church of Verona, is superior in that it preserved for us numerous subscriptions of the Fathers that are absent from the original Greek. Since we judged that this version should not be omitted, it was certainly useful for us to reread that manuscript more carefully.

2. The more recent version has Rusticus, a deacon of the Roman Church, as its author. He prefixed the following annotation, which is read in the pure manuscripts of Rusticus and in Crabbe’s edition:

“I myself translated the reports of the holy synod from the Greek Acumitan manuscript into Latin.”

At the end of the report itself the same annotation of his is added:

“I wrote this on the day before the Kalends of April, Tuesday, in the thirteenth indiction.”

If this indiction is to be referred to the time when Rusticus was staying in the East, it agrees only with the year 550, regardless of the question of the day or weekday, concerning which difficulties arise here no less than elsewhere.

The Roman editors of the Councils removed these annotations, which Crabbe had published, because they did not know that they belonged to Rusticus. They may be excused on this point, since they found no pure and complete manuscript of Rusticus displaying Rusticus’ own annotations.

For we, who carefully examined the Latin manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection in Rome, found no pure manuscript of Rusticus among the five Vatican manuscripts—1321, 1322, 1323, 4166, and 5405—that the Roman editors were able to consult. Only the Chigian manuscript 483 is pure and complete, although it came into the possession of the Chigi Library only after the Roman edition under Pope Alexander VII.

In correcting Rusticus’ version itself, Baluzius used two manuscripts of Rusticus, the Corbie and Dijon manuscripts. We used three other copies: the Chigian manuscript just mentioned, Vatican manuscript 1323, and the very old manuscript of the Verona chapter-house marked number 57.

We shall print this translation, since it agrees more closely with the Greek, alongside the Greek original; afterward we shall append the older version with the subscriptions.

3. It should be noted beforehand that the Roman editors, and Quesnell following them, attached to Rusticus’ translation in the margin several readings more accurately rendered from the Greek. We shall not omit these in our annotations. They also sometimes added other readings which, when we discovered that they were taken from the older version of Vatican manuscript 1322, we judged should be omitted; for they can be sufficiently derived from the ancient version that will be appended.

4. A few words should be said concerning the date of this report, which is absent from all the Greek and Latin manuscripts. Since the final session of the council was held on the Kalends of November in the year 451, this report to Leo was written on that same day or shortly afterward, before the Fathers of the synod were dismissed.

---

## LETTER XCVIII OF THE HOLY SYNOD OF CHALCEDON TO THE MOST HOLY POPE LEO OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

Concerning the proceedings of the synod. (G)

[Col. 0951]

## SYNOPSIS

I. The synod praises Leo as the interpreter appointed for all of the voice of blessed Peter, and declares that he presided through his legates.—II. Concerning the tyranny and impious proceedings of Dioscorus of Alexandria.—III. What was done concerning him, and concerning the definition of the faith.—IV. It explains the reason for issuing the canon concerning the prerogative of the See of Constantinople and asks for confirmation.

[Note: [Col. 0951] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0951A] 1088. [Note: [Col. 0951C] Translated by Rusticus the deacon.]

The holy, great, and universal SYNOD, gathered by the grace of God and by the decree of our most pious and Christ-loving emperors in the metropolis of Chalcedon in the province of Bithynia, to the most holy and most blessed Leo, archbishop of the Romans.

### CHAPTER I

“Our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Psalm 125:2). Grace has adapted this as though it were a prophecy belonging to us, through whom the restoration of piety has been confirmed.

[Note: [Col. 0951C] The Roman editors, from the Greek: “Piety has been confirmed by an excellent work.”]

For what is more exalted than faith for rejoicing? What is more festive for crowns than the recognition of the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0951C] Likewise from the Greek: “for dancing.”]

which the Savior himself once handed down to us for salvation, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit; teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20)?

This chain, as though woven of gold,

[Note: [Col. 0951C] From the Greek: “chain.” Shortly afterward the printed editions read: “from the garment of Christ and the command of the lawgiver.” We have removed the words “from the garment of Christ,” which were inserted improperly and are alien to the Greek original, on the authority of the excellent Verona manuscript 57. Baluzius noted that the Corbie and Dijon manuscripts read “from the garment, a golden chain, from the command.” He believes that the error in the other manuscripts and editions arose because they did not notice that χρυσυῆν σειρᾶν are Greek words meaning “a golden chain,” corresponding to “a chain woven of gold.”]

coming from the command of the lawgiver and reaching all the way to us, you yourself have preserved, having been appointed interpreter for all of the voice of blessed Peter,

[Note: [Col. 0951D] We have added the conjunction “and” from our manuscripts and those of Baluzius.]

and bringing the blessedness of his faith to all above everyone else.

Therefore we, using you as the initiator of good things for the common benefit,

[Note: [Col. 0951D] From the Greek: “Using you as a good guide and originator for the common benefit.”]

have shown the children of the Church the inheritance and portion of truth—not each one teaching doctrine secretly and individually,

[Note: [Col. 0951D] Likewise from the Greek: “each one teaching in secret.”]

but declaring the confession of faith with one spirit, one accord, and one harmony. We were gathered in a common crown of joy, as though feasting at imperial banquets and dining on spiritual delights, which Christ had prepared through your letters for those who had been invited; and we seemed to see the heavenly Bridegroom dwelling among us.

For if he declared that “where two or three are gathered in his name” (Matthew 18:20),

[Note: [Col. 0952C] Baluzius’ manuscripts read “he himself in the midst.”]

he would be in their midst,

[Col. 0951C] how great a special favor could he show to the priests who placed the knowledge of their confession above both country and toil?

[Note: [Col. 0952C] Thus all manuscripts of this version, both ours and Baluzius’, as well as the editions preceding the Roman edition. In the Roman edition, “about five hundred and twenty priests” was supplied from the Greek and the older version.]

You indeed presided over them, as the head over its members, among those who held your place,

[Note: [Col. 0952C] From the Greek: “who represented you.”]

showing benevolence.

The faithful emperors presided with the greatest propriety for the adornment of the Church,

[Note: [Col. 0952C] The word “faithful” is absent from two manuscripts of Baluzius and from our Chigian manuscript, which contains Rusticus’ complete edition. It is found, however, in Verona manuscript 57 and Vatican manuscript 1323, which are certainly manuscripts of Rusticus but omit his annotations, and also in several others that differ in their order. Shortly afterward, instead of “for adorning”—which we have restored from the manuscripts and editions preceding the Roman edition—these and the following manuscripts read “for ordering.”]

just as Zerubbabel and Jesus did,

[Note: [Col. 0953C] All manuscripts read thus. The printed editions read “Zerubbabel and Joshua.”]

inviting the renewal of the building of the Church, as of Jerusalem, around matters of doctrine.

[Note: [Col. 0953C] The printed editions read “striving.” We follow the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER II
And the adversary had indeed been like a beast roaring by itself outside the folds, unable to seize anyone unless the man who had once been bishop of the Alexandrians had thrown himself to him as prey. After previously committing many exceedingly wicked deeds, he surpassed the former ones by the later ones.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts. The editions after the Roman edition, handling the passage most badly, made the earlier deeds subordinate to the later ones. In the earlier editions: “Having acted very badly, he overcame; he surpassed the former deeds by the later ones.” There “surpassed” is a gloss that entered the text, as Baluzius correctly observed.]

For he deposed and condemned that blessed shepherd Flavian, numbered among the saints of Constantinople, who professed the apostolic faith, and the bishop Eusebius, most beloved of God, contrary to every canonical order.

[Note: Thus the older books. The editions read “the bishop most beloved by God.”]

[Note: We have retained the conjunction *and*, absent from Baluzius’s manuscripts, the Chigi manuscript, and the ancient editions, because it is found in the Veronese and Vatican manuscripts, as also in the Greek.]

And he declared Eutyches, condemned for impiety, innocent by the decrees of his tyranny; and he restored the dignity that had been taken from him by your holiness—for he was unworthy of that grace—and, in sum, like a solitary savage beast rushing upon a vineyard, he overturned the finest plantation he found (Ps. 79:14).

[Note: The older editions read “the finest plantation he found.” Quesnellus, following the Roman edition, reads “the finest planting,” and in the margin “plant”; we preferred the reading from the manuscripts.]

But what had been uprooted as fruitless he brought back; he cut off those who understood the things belonging to shepherds, and set over the sheep those who had been shown to be wolves.

[Note: The common editions read “which, truly fruitless.” We added the words “as fruitless” from the manuscripts.]

[Note: The Roman editors, from the Greek, read “were plainly shown.”]

After all this, he extended his madness even against the one to whom the Savior had entrusted the guardianship of the vineyard—that is, against your holiness—and he plotted excommunication against you, who hasten to unite the body of the Church.

[Note: The editions have “apostolic” instead of “we say,” but we follow the manuscripts.]

Although he ought rather to have repented of such deeds and ought to have sought mercy with tears, he exulted as though over honorable deeds, rejecting the letter of your holiness and opposing every doctrine of the truth.

[Note: The editions read “he exulted, soberly ill concerning good things.” Two manuscripts of Baluzius and two of ours read “he exulted, with sober defects”; where, without doubt, “deeds” should be read instead of “defects.” The Vatican manuscript 1323 has “over his own deeds.”]

## CHAPTER III

He ought indeed immediately to have remained among those whose party he had chosen.

[Note: Two manuscripts of Baluzius and one of ours read “among whose party”; the older editions, “in whose party”; Vatican 1323, “from whose party.” The Veronese manuscript agrees with the text.]

But since we profess to be disciples of the Savior, who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4),

[Note: Thus the codices and the ancient editions. The Roman editions have “and to come to the recognition.”]

we hastened to confirm this mercy toward him in deed, and with brotherly gentleness we summoned him to judgment, not as though attempting to cut him off, but granting him an opportunity for defense in order that he might be saved.

[Note: The Roman editors, from the Greek, add in the margin: “Granting him an opportunity to heal him”; and “we hoped that he might prove superior to those who accused him of various crimes.” They continue in the text: “So that, dismissing the council with festive and celebrated joy, we might in no respect be overcome by Satan.” We have adopted the reading of the codices.]

We prayed that he might be declared victorious over those who were charging him with various accusations, so that, bringing the council to a close amid festive and celebrated joy, we might in no respect be overcome by Satan.

But he, bearing within himself the conviction inscribed by conscience, assented to the accusations by refusing judgment and rejected the three lawful summonses issued to him.

[Note: From the Greek: “Convicted within himself by a vehement rebuke of conscience, he assented to the accusations by refusing judgment,” and so forth.]

Therefore we confirmed, as far as we were able by moderating it, the sentence that he himself had pronounced against himself by sinning, stripping the wolf of the pastoral skin with which he had previously been exposed as such only in appearance.

[Note: The common editions add “or in appearance.” It is synonymous with what precedes and is not found in the manuscripts.]

Up to this point our sorrowful circumstances ceased, and the grace of good things immediately shone forth; and, having torn out one tare, we filled the whole world with pure wheat, with delight.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts and editions before the Royal Paris edition, with which Quesnellus has “tare.”]

And, as though receiving authority to uproot and plant, we lamented only the cutting off of one, but carefully planted an abundance of good things.

[Note: Thus the Veronese and Vatican manuscripts, the Chigi manuscript, two manuscripts of Baluzius, and the ancient editions: “we lamented the cutting off.” The editions after the Roman edition read more elegantly, but not according to Rusticus’s translation: “we narrowed the cutting off to one person alone, and carefully planted an abundance of good things.”]

For God was at work, and the victorious Euphemia, adorned with the beauty of victory, crowned the council for her Bridegroom. Receiving from us the definition of the faith as her own confession, she presented it to her Bridegroom through the most devout emperor and the Christ-loving Augusta; she quieted all the disturbance of the opposing party, strengthened the confession of the truth, and, as a friend, had it subscribed by the decisions of all, with hand and tongue, as a demonstration.

[Note: Thus the codices and the ancient editions. Quesnellus, with other common editions, reads *thalamo* (“for the bridal chamber”) instead of *sponso* (“for the bridegroom”). From the Greek, “the victorious Euphemia crowned [the council].” This passage, previously obscure, and from which the story told by Zonaras and certain later Greeks in Baronius under the year 451, no. 119, is believed to have arisen, will be found explained in Letter 101, now published for the first time. See there note 14 (Col. 979, n. c).]

[Note: From the Greek, “subscribing so that all might be made manifest.” From the codices and ancient editions we have restored “having it subscribed,” whereas the other common editions read “subscribing.”]

These are the things we accomplished with you, who were present in spirit, who resolved to approve them as a brother, and who seemed almost visibly present to us through the wisdom of your representatives.

## CHAPTER IV

We also inform you that we have established certain other measures for the orderly settlement of affairs and for the firm establishment of ecclesiastical statutes, knowing that your holiness, once informed, will approve and confirm them.

[Note: The editions read “other things,” which is better; but we give Rusticus’s version from the codices.]

For we have now confirmed by synodal decree the longstanding custom that the holy Church of God of the Constantinopolitans has maintained for ordaining the metropolitans of the provinces of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace—not so much conferring something upon the see of Constantinople as providing appropriate peace for the metropolitan cities.

[Note: From the Greek: “which has prevailed.”]

[Note: The editions add “and of Thrace.”]

[Note: Thus the older books. The common editions read: “not so much conferring something upon the see of Constantinople as providing,” and so forth.]

For, when bishops frequently die, many disturbances arise, with clergy and peoples remaining without a ruler in those cities and throwing the ecclesiastical order into confusion.

[Note: The manuscripts of Baluzius read “seeing appropriate.” The ancient editions read “it seemed appropriate.” Our codices agree with the later common editions.]

[Note: The Roman editors, for the sake of elegance, inverted Rusticus’s reading as follows: “Tumults arise, with clergy and peoples who are in those cities remaining without a ruler and confusing the ecclesiastical order.”]

This has not escaped your holiness, especially because of the Ephesians, on whose account certain persons have often troubled you.

[Note: From the Greek: “on whose account you have often suffered trouble.” This indicates the controversy concerning the episcopate of Ephesus between Bassianus and Stephanus, which seems to have occasioned the intrusion of the prerogative of the see of Constantinople and subsequently the formulation of the canon concerning it. From this passage we infer that, before the Council of Chalcedon, letters were often written to Leo concerning this matter. We also learn that the pontiff himself wrote a letter on the subject, now missing, from the eleventh act of the same council.]

We have also confirmed the canon of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who assembled at Constantinople under the emperor of blessed memory, the great Theodosius.

[Note: The common editions insert “the canon” here; from the codices we have placed it in its proper position.]

It decrees that, after your most holy and apostolic see, Constantinople—constituted second in rank—should have the honor.

[Note: The manuscripts of Baluzius read “while it remains with you.”]

We are confident that, while the apostolic ray shines from you and you customarily extend your care even to the Church of Constantinople, you will often expand this care, since you are accustomed, without envy, to enrich those belonging to you by sharing your own blessings.

[Note: Thus all the codices. The Vatican alone has “from the helm” instead of “for governing.” The editions read “governing, spreading him abroad and expanding him more often.”]

[Note: From the Greek: “joined in sincere love.” Later the Roman editors placed the verb “we determined” after the noun “ordination”; the ancient editions exhibit it in both places.]

Therefore deign to embrace, as things belonging to you, friendly, and most suitable for good order, what we have determined for the destruction of all confusion and the confirmation of ecclesiastical order, most holy and most blessed father.

For the most holy bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, who occupy the place of your holiness, and the most reverend presbyter Boniface who is with them, attempted vehemently to resist these arrangements, undoubtedly wishing this good to begin from your providence, so that, just as the achievement of the faith is attributed to you, so also the achievement of good order might be assigned to you.

We, therefore, taking into account both the most devout and Christ-loving emperors, who rejoice at this, and the illustrious senate and the entire imperial city, so to speak, judged it appropriate that the confirmation of this honor should be celebrated by the universal council. Since these measures seemed to have begun from your holiness, we strengthened them, trusting that whatever is rightly done by children returns to their parents, and making it their own.

[Note: From the Greek: “Obeying not only the most devout and Christian emperors, for whom this was pleasing, but also the illustrious senate and the whole, so to speak, imperial city, we judged it opportune,” and so forth.]

[Note: Also from the Greek: “We dared to strengthen it, knowing that whatever is rightly done by children returns to their own parents.”]

We therefore ask you to honor our judgment with your decrees. Just as we have added harmony in good things to the head, so may your eminence complete for your children what is fitting.

[Note: From the Greek: “we have offered”; and immediately afterward, “it will be pleasing to the devout rulers.”]

Thus the devout rulers also will be pleased, for they have confirmed the judgment of your holiness as though it were a law; and the see of Constantinople will receive its reward, since it has always fulfilled for you every effort on behalf of piety and has joined itself to you in the same zeal for concord.

But so that you may know that we have done nothing by favoring anyone or by opposing anyone out of hostility, but have disclosed to you the whole force of what was done under divine direction, as proof of our sincerity and for the firmness and agreement of what we have done,

[Note: Thus all the codices. The common editions read “by giving anything to anyone.”]

[Note: Thus, together with the editions, the Veronese and Vatican codices. Two manuscripts of Baluzius and our Chigi manuscript read: “but as though governed by a sign.”]

[Note: From the Greek: “for confirmation and agreement.”]

we have made everything known to you.

[Col. 0952A] The holy, great, and universal synod, assembled by the grace of God and by the decree of our most devout and Christ-loving emperors in the metropolis of Chalcedon, in the province of Bithynia, to the most holy and most blessed archbishop of the Romans, Leo.

Our mouth has been filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation; grace has applied this prophecy to us as something belonging to us, for whom the achievement of piety has been confirmed. For what is higher than faith for producing joy? What is brighter than the knowledge of the Lord for producing exultation—the knowledge that the Savior himself, from above, handed down to us for salvation, saying:

“Go, teach all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you.”

You preserved this command for us as though it were a golden chain drawn down to us by the one who gave the command, serving as an interpreter of the voice of blessed Peter for all and drawing blessedness for all from his faith.

[Note: From two Venetian manuscripts, namely 555 and 164, we have recovered this important supplement. The common editions are mutilated: “being established; whence,” and so forth.]

Therefore, using you as the originator of this good for our benefit, we showed the inheritance of the truth to the children of the Church, not teaching each person separately in secret, but making known the confession of the faith in a common spirit, with one accord and harmony.

And we were in common exultation over spiritual things, as at imperial banquets, delighting in foods that Christ had prepared for those feasting through your letters, and we seemed to behold the heavenly Bridegroom dwelling among us.

For if he said that where two or three are gathered in his name, there he is in the midst of them, how much familiarity did he show toward five hundred and twenty priests, who put knowledge of their confession concerning him before both homeland and toil?

You, as a head over members, presided among those who held the order, displaying goodwill.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “good counsel.”]

The faithful rulers presided for the sake of good order, like Zerubbabel and Jesus [for] the Church, as it were Jerusalem, hastening to renew the building of doctrine [the syntax is corrupt].

[Col. 0954A]

And the adversary had been like a beast roaring by itself outside the folds, unable to seize anyone unless the man who had once been bishop of the Alexandrians had thrown himself to him as prey. After previously committing many exceedingly wicked deeds, he concealed the former ones by the later ones.

For he deposed and condemned that blessed shepherd Flavian, numbered among the saints of Constantinople, who professed the apostolic faith, and the bishop Eusebius, beloved of God, contrary to every canonical order;

[Note: The first Venetian manuscript reads “and numbered among the saints.”] and he declared Eutyches, condemned for impiety, innocent by the decrees of his tyranny; and he restored the dignity that had been taken from your holiness—for he was unworthy of that grace.

[Note: We have preferred this reading with both Venetian manuscripts, in exact agreement with the Latin version, which has “since he was unworthy of that grace.” The common editions read “as though he were unworthy.”]

And, like a solitary savage beast rushing upon a vineyard, he overturned the finest plantation he found, but what had been uprooted as fruitless he brought back; he cut off those who understood the things belonging to shepherds, and set over the sheep those who had been shown to be wolves.

After all this, he extended his madness even against the one to whom the Savior had entrusted the guardianship of the vineyard—that is, against your holiness—and he plotted excommunication against you, who hasten to unite the body of the Church.

Although he ought rather to have repented of such deeds and ought to have sought mercy with tears, he exulted as though over honorable deeds, rejecting the letter of your holiness and opposing every doctrine of the truth.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “rejecting the letter,” and so forth.]

## CHAPTER III

He ought indeed immediately to have remained among those whose party he had chosen. But since we profess to be disciples of the Savior, who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts incorrectly read *ἐπαγγελλόμενος* (“professing,” singular participle) in place of *ἐπαγγελλόμεθα* (“we profess”).]

we hastened to confirm this mercy toward him in deed and summoned him fraternally to judgment, not as though attempting to cut him off, but granting him an opportunity for defense in order that he might be healed.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “for a summons.”]

We prayed that he might be declared superior to those who had charged him with various accusations, so that, dismissing the assembly in bright and festive celebration, we might in no way be overcome by Satan.

[Note: We have corrected this from both Venetian manuscripts, in agreement with the Latin version, which reads “bearing within himself the conviction inscribed by conscience.” The common editions have “having within himself an unmixed conviction of conscience.” In the margin of the Roman edition, beside “unmixed,” appears “inscribed.”]

But he, bearing within himself the conviction inscribed by conscience, assented to the accusations by refusing judgment and rejected the three lawful summonses issued to him.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “the rejection of judgment.”]

Therefore we confirmed, as far as we were able by moderating it, the sentence that he himself had pronounced against himself by his offenses, stripping the wolf of the pastoral skin with which he had previously been exposed as such while clothed in it.

Up to this point our sorrowful circumstances ceased, and the grace of good things immediately shone forth; and, having torn out one tare, we filled the whole world with pure wheat, with delight.

And, as though receiving authority to uproot and plant, we narrowed the cutting off to one alone, but carefully planted the fruitfulness of good things.

[Note: We have supplied *men* (“on the one hand”) from both Venetian manuscripts; the particle is recognized by the Latin interpreter, who translates “the cutting off, indeed.” The common editions have “the cutting.”]

For God was at work, and the victorious Euphemia crowned the council for the bridal chamber.

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Both Venetian manuscripts support *τὸν σύλλογον* (“the council”), with the masculine article; the common editions incorrectly print *τὸ σύλλογον*, using the neuter article, apparently through a printer’s error. The Greek here has *τῷ νυμφῶνι* (“for the bridal chamber”); the Latin version above has *sponso* (“for the bridegroom”).] Receiving from us the definition of the faith as her own confession, she presented it to her Bridegroom through the most devout emperor and the Christ-loving Augusta; she calmed all the disturbance of the opposing party, strengthened the confession of the truth as a friend, and, with hand and tongue, had it confirmed by the decisions of all for public demonstration.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “having sealed it,” a word which, in view of what follows—“for demonstration”—sounds better than “having confirmed it by vote.”]

These are the things we accomplished with you, who were present in spirit, who had resolved to approve them as brothers, and who seemed almost visibly present to us through the wisdom of your representatives.

## CHAPTER IV

We also inform you that we have established certain other measures for the orderly settlement of affairs and for the firm establishment of ecclesiastical statutes, confident that your holiness, once informed, will approve and confirm them.

For the longstanding custom that the holy Church of God of the Constantinopolitans has maintained for ordaining the metropolitans of the dioceses of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace, we have now confirmed by synodal decision—not so much conferring something upon the see of Constantinople as providing appropriate peace for the metropolitan cities.

For, when bishops frequently die, many disturbances arise, with the clergy and laity in those cities remaining without a ruler and throwing the ecclesiastical order into confusion.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts omit the article before “the clergy.”]

[Note: The Roman edition’s margin and one Venetian manuscript read *λαῶν* (“peoples/the people”) instead of *λαϊκῶν* (“lay people”).]

This has not escaped your holiness, especially because of the Ephesians, on whose account you have often been troubled.

[Note: Thus, with greater elegance, we have written from both Venetian manuscripts. The common editions read “it escaped.”]

We have also confirmed the canon of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who assembled at Constantinople in the time of the emperor of blessed memory, the great Theodosius. It declares that, after your most holy and apostolic see, the see of Constantinople should possess the prerogatives of honor, being ordered second in rank.

[Note: The first Venetian manuscript reads “of the Fathers assembled.”]

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts lack the word “canon” here.]

[Note: We add “see,” which is certainly necessary, from both Venetian manuscripts. The common editions have only “apostolic”; the Roman edition notes in the margin: “the see.”]

[Note: The words “ordered second” are not necessary, but since the Latin interpreter read them, as appears from his words “which is ordered second,” we have also included them, following the authority of both Venetian manuscripts. The common editions read “to take possession,” and so forth.]

We are confident that, while the ray of your apostolic see prevails and you customarily care for the Church in Constantinople, you have often extended this care, since you are accustomed, without envy, to share your own blessings with those who are genuine members of your household.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “the Church of Constantinople.”]

Therefore deign to embrace, as things belonging to you, friendly, and most suitable for good order, what we have established for removing all confusion and confirming ecclesiastical order, most holy and most blessed father.

For the most holy bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, who occupy the place of your holiness, and the most reverend presbyter Boniface who is with them, attempted vehemently to resist these arrangements, undoubtedly wishing this good to begin from your providence, so that, just as the achievement of the faith is attributed to you, so also the achievement of good order might be assigned to you.

We, while satisfying the most devout and Christ-loving rulers, who rejoice at this matter, as well as the illustrious senate and the entire imperial city, judged it appropriate that its honor should be confirmed by the universal synod. Since it seemed to have taken its beginning from your holiness, we confidently strengthened it through those whom you have always hastened to support, knowing that every good accomplished by children returns to their own parents.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “we judged it opportune that the confirmation of the honor concerning it,” and so forth. This respectable reading may also be inferred from the Latin interpreter, whose version here has “we judged it opportune.”]

[Note: Thus it should be read from both Venetian manuscripts and the Latin version. The Roman edition also notes in the margin “from.” The common editions have “concerning.”]

We therefore ask you also to honor our judgment with your decisions. Just as we have brought agreement in good things to the head, so may the head complete for the children what is fitting.

Thus the most devout rulers also will be pleased, since they have affirmed the judgment of your holiness as a law; and the see of Constantinople will receive its recompense, for it has always displayed toward you every effort on behalf of piety and has joined itself to you in zeal for concord.

But so that you may know that we have done nothing by favoring anyone or by opposing anyone out of hostility, but have acted under divine direction, we have disclosed to you the whole force of what was done, for the establishment of our sincerity and for the confirmation and arrangement of the acts performed by us.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “and of the acts performed by us,” in agreement with the Latin interpreter, who translates “of the things done by us.” The common editions have only “and of the things performed.”]

## THE SAME LETTER. ANOTHER, EARLIER VERSION

Copy of the report of the archetype of the holy, great, and universal synod assembled at the metropolis of Chalcedon, addressed to Pope Leo of holy memory. (G)

[Col. 0959B] The holy, great, and universal synod, assembled at Chalcedon, the metropolis of the province of Bithynia, according to the grace of God and the decree of our most devout and Christ-loving rulers, to the most holy and most blessed Leo.

## CHAPTER I

Our mouth has been filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation (Ps. 125:2), because grace has applied this prophecy to us as something belonging to us, for whom the achievement of piety has been confirmed. For what is higher than faith for producing joy? What is brighter than the knowledge of the Lord for producing exultation—the knowledge that the Savior himself, from above, handed down to us for salvation, saying:

“Go and teach all the nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I have commanded you.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript 1322 reads “that I entrusted to you.”]

You preserved this command for us as though it were a golden chain drawn down to us by the one who gave the command, serving as an interpreter of the voice of blessed Peter for all and drawing blessedness for all from his faith.

Therefore, using you as the originator of this good for our benefit, we showed the inheritance of the truth to the children of the Church—not teaching each person separately in secret, but making known the confession of the faith in a common spirit, with one accord and harmony.

And we were in common exultation over spiritual things, as at imperial banquets, delighting in foods that Christ had prepared for those feasting through your letters. And we seemed to behold the heavenly Bridegroom feasting among us.

[Note: The editions read “we seemed to see.” We have corrected this from the cited manuscript.]

For if he said that where two or three are gathered in his name, there he is in the midst of them (Matt. 18:20), how much familiarity did he show toward five hundred and twenty priests, who put knowledge of their confession concerning him before both homeland and toil?

[Note: The same manuscript reads “he showed.”]

You, as a head over members, presided over them through those who held your place, demonstrating sound counsel.

The faithful rulers presided for the sake of good order, like Zerubbabel and Jesus for the Church, just as for Jerusalem (1 Esdras 3:2), hastening to renew the building of doctrine.

[Note: The same Vatican manuscript, together with the editions, has “like Zerubbabel and Jesus for the Church,” not, as Baluzius noted in the margin, “and God Jesus.”]

## CHAPTER II

And the adversary was like a beast outside the fences, growling by himself, having no one whom he could seize unless the man who had once become bishop of the city of Alexandria had offered himself to him as prey. After first committing many evils, he concealed the former deeds by the later ones.

For he deposed the blessed Flavian, that shepherd of Constantinople numbered among the saints, who professed the apostolic faith, and Eusebius, the bishop beloved of God, contrary to every canonical discipline; and he restored Eutyches, condemned for impiety, by his tyrannical decrees; and he restored the dignity which your holiness had taken away, since he was unworthy of that grace.

And, like a solitary savage beast rushing upon the vineyard, he overturned the good plantation he found (Ps. 79:14), but introduced what was fruitless and abandoned; he cut off those who possessed pastoral wisdom and introduced wolves, plainly revealed as such, among the sheep.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “abandoned.”]

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads “plainly revealed.”]

In addition to all this, he extended his fury even against the one who had received from the Savior the guardianship of the vineyard—that is, against your holiness—and plotted excommunication against the one who hastened to unite the body of the Church.

[Note: Thus from the Vatican manuscript. The Council edition has “to unite,” perhaps through a typographical error.]

Although he ought to have repented of these things and ought to have sought mercy with tears, he rejoiced as though over honorable deeds, scorning the letter of your holiness and resisting all the doctrines of the truth.

## CHAPTER III

He ought indeed immediately to have withdrawn from the party in which he had placed himself.

But since we profess the discipline of the Savior, who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4), we hastened to establish this mercy toward him in deed. We summoned him fraternally to judgment, not as though trying to cut him off, but providing him with an opportunity for satisfaction and healing.

[Note: The Regina manuscript reads “we summoned him.”]

We prayed that he might prove superior to the various accusations written against him, so that, dismissing the assembly in bright and festive celebration, we might in no way be injured by Satan.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “to prevail.”]

But he, having within himself the testimony of conscience inscribed against him, assented to the accusations by refusing judgment and rejected the three lawful summonses issued against him.

[Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript. Baluzius reads “inscribed.”]

Therefore we confirmed, as far as possible and with due moderation, the sentence that he himself had pronounced against his own offenses, stripping the wolf of his pastoral skin, by which he had previously been exposed as such while clothed in it.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “stripping.”]

Up to this point our sorrow remained; then the grace of good things immediately shone forth. Having uprooted one tare, we filled the whole world with pure wheat, with delight.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “with goodwill.”]

And, as though receiving authority to uproot and plant, we restricted the cutting off to one alone, while carefully planting the fertility of good things.

For God was at work, and the venerable Euphemia, who crowned the assembly of the bridal chamber, received from us the definition of the faith as her own confession and presented it to her Bridegroom through the most devout emperor and the God-loving empress. She calmed all the disturbance of the adversaries, confirmed the confession of the truth as a friend, and assigned it for public demonstration by the decision of all, with hand and tongue.

[Note: The same manuscript reads “the unique confession.” From the same manuscript, “confirming” seemed preferable to “strengthening,” as the editions read.]

These are the things we accomplished with you, present in spirit and knowing how to favor us as brothers, who appeared almost visibly to us through the wisdom of your representatives.

## CHAPTER IV

We make known that we have also established certain other matters for the good order of affairs and the stability of ecclesiastical regulations, confident that your holiness, once informed, will approve and confirm them.

For the longstanding custom that the holy Church of God of Constantinople has maintained for ordaining the metropolitans of the dioceses of Asia, Pontus, and Thrace, we have now confirmed by synodal decision—not so much granting something to the see of Constantinople as providing tranquillity for the metropolitan cities.

For when many bishops frequently die, disturbances arise while the clergy and peoples in those cities remain without governance and throw the ecclesiastical order into confusion.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “the clergy.”]

This has not escaped your holiness, especially on account of the Ephesians, who have often caused you trouble.

We have also confirmed the canon of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who assembled at Constantinople in the time of the emperor of blessed memory, the great Theodosius. It declares that, after your most holy and apostolic see, Constantinople should possess the primacy, being ordered second in rank.

We are confident that, while the ray of your apostolic see prevails, you have often extended your protection to the Church of Constantinople in the customary manner, since you are accustomed, without envy, to share your blessings with those who belong to you.

[Note: This is the better reading of the Vatican manuscript. The editions read “power.”]

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “extending.”]

Therefore deign to embrace what we have established for removing all confusion and confirming ecclesiastical discipline—as things belonging to you, friendly, and suitable for good order—most holy and most blessed father.

For the most holy bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, who occupy the place of your holiness, and the most reverend presbyter Boniface who is with them, attempted vehemently to resist these arrangements, undoubtedly wishing this good to begin from your providence, so that, just as the achievement of the faith is attributed to you, so also the restoration of order might be credited to you.

We, while satisfying the most devout and Christ-loving rulers, who rejoice at this matter, as well as the illustrious senate and the entire imperial city, judged it fitting that its honor should be confirmed by the universal synod. Since it seemed to have taken its beginning from your holiness, we confidently strengthened it through those whom you have always hastened to support, knowing that every good accomplished by children returns to their own parents.

[Note: Both Venetian manuscripts read “we judged it opportune that the honor concerning it,” and so forth. This respectable reading may also be inferred from the Latin interpreter, whose version here has “we judged it opportune.”]

We therefore ask you also to honor our judgment with your decisions. Just as we have brought agreement in good things to the head, so may the head complete for the children what is fitting.

Thus the most devout rulers also will be cared for, since they have affirmed the judgment of your holiness as a law; and the see of Constantinople will receive its recompense, for it has always displayed toward you every effort on behalf of piety and has joined itself to you in zeal for concord.

But so that you may know that we have done nothing for the sake of favor or offense, but have acted under divine direction, we have disclosed to you the whole force of what was done, for the establishment of our sincerity and for the confirmation and arrangement of the acts performed by us.

[Note: Baluzius reads “governing.” The Vatican reading, “governed,” is better.]

[Note: The editions omit “the whole force,” which we have supplied from the Vatican manuscript. Pope Vigilius quotes this passage in this form in the *Constitutum*, volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1355: “We took care to make known to you the whole force of what was done, for our establishment and for the confirmation and arrangement of what was done by us.” The editions read “deposition” instead of “arrangement.”]

## SUBSCRIPTIONS

ANATOLIUS, bishop of Constantinople.

[Note: Labbeus found the first three subscriptions in a manuscript formerly belonging to Joly and now belonging to the Paris chapter; they are printed in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1781, throughout as: “I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.” Baluzius likewise printed the first subscription in this form; in the next two he printed “I pray that I may fare well in the Lord,” noting “pray” in the margin from the Vatican manuscript. In the remaining subscriptions, transmitted to us by one Vatican manuscript, he followed that reading and printed “Pray that I may fare well.” We have judged that the Vatican manuscript should be followed consistently throughout. Nevertheless, we do not deny that the original wording was more probably: “I pray that you may fare well in the Lord.”]
