## 1107 LETTER XCIX

[Note: [Col. 0965C] Alternatively, after Letter 76. What was formerly numbered 99 is now 126. Written around December of the year 451.]

### Synodical Letter of Ravennius and the Other Bishops of Gaul to Saint Pope Leo

[Note: [Col. 0965D] Manuscript collection 5, and others derived from it, add the following in place of the synopsis: “To praise his faith, which he sent to the East.”]

[Col. 0966A]

### Synopsis

I. They excuse their delay in replying. — II. Everyone in Gaul received Leo’s letter to Flavian as a statement of faith. — III. In that letter the mystery of the Incarnation is disclosed to believers and unbelievers. — IV. Because of reports brought from the East, they refrained from writing to the emperor. — V. They congratulate the Church that Leo the pontiff was given to it by God.

To the truly holy Lord, deservedly most blessed in Christ, and venerable in apostolic honor, Pope LEO: RAVENNIUS, RUSTICUS, VENERIUS. [Note: [Col. 0965D] Quesnellus has “Constantinus.” We preferred Rainaudus’s reading, since it is approved by our Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 and by another Thuanian manuscript cited by Quesnellus; especially since the Regensburg manuscript supports the same reading in Leo’s reply, Letter 102.] CONSTANTIANUS, MAXIMUS, [Note: [Col. 0965D] Two Thuanian manuscripts have “Armaturus”; manuscripts of collections 11 and 24 have “Armatarus”; the Trecopith manuscript has “Armatharius”; the Regensburg manuscript in Letter 102 has “Armazorius.”] ARMENTARIUS, FLORUS, SABINUS, [Note: [Col. 0965D] Thus our manuscripts, especially collection 5, agree with Sirmondus and with the editions published before Quesnellus. Letter 102 of Leo and the subscriptions appended to it likewise agree, giving Valerianus first and then Valerius. In Quesnellus the order is different: first Valerius, then Valerianus.] VALERIANUS, CONSTANTIUS, [Note: [Col. 0966C] Some inferior manuscripts have “Nestorius”; others, better ones, have “Nectarius,” as in Letter 102.] NECTARIUS, MAXIMUS, ASCLEPIUS, likewise MAXIMUS, URSUS, INGENUUS, JUSTUS, VALERIUS, SUPERVENTOR, CHRYSAPHIUS, FONTEIUS, PETRONIUS, IDATIUS, AETHERIUS, EULALIUS. [Note: [Col. 0966C] Thus Quesnellus and our manuscripts of collections 5 and 21. In Vatican collection 11, “Eustasius”; in another Vatican collection, 24, “Eustasius”; Sirmondus has “Eustachius.” The printed editions of Leo have “Eutychius,” as does the Regensburg manuscript in Letter 102.] EUSTATHIUS, [Col. 0966B] FRATERNUS, VICTURUS, EUGENIUS, [Note: [Col. 0966C] The printed editions of Leo before Quesnellus, together with Vatican collection 11 and four other manuscripts of Letter 102, have “Hilarius.”] HILARUS, VERUS, AMANDUS, GERONTIUS, [Note: [Col. 0966D] “Proculianus” in manuscripts of collections 11 and 24.] PROCULEIANUS, JULIANUS, HELLADIUS, ARMENTARIUS, HONORATUS, [Note: [Col. 0966D] The printed editions of Leo before Quesnellus have “Hypartius”; Sirmondus has “Epatius” in the margin; the Regensburg manuscript in Letter 102 has “Apartius”; the old Thuanian manuscript has “Ebartius.”] EPARCHIUS, ANEMIUS, DYNAMIUS, MAXIMINUS, [Note: [Col. 0966D] Manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, as well as Sirmondus in the margin, have “Inzantius.”] YNANTIUS, and PALLADIUS.

### CHAPTER I

When your Blessedness’s letter reached us [Note: [Col. 0966D] Letter 67, to which they are replying.], the one that you sent to the East in defense of the catholic faith, we would have wished immediately to return thanks to your Apostolate for so immense a gift, had not the difficulty of our being unable to assemble quickly in one place, or the great distances over which we are scattered, or the unseasonable violence of the winds in our regions, brought about this delay. Let your Apostolate therefore pardon our tardiness, which arose not from idleness or dissimulation but from definite necessity; and although it took away from us the grace of speed, it could not take away the occasion for rejoicing.

[Col. 0966C]

### CHAPTER II

Accordingly, with Christ graciously assisting us, we rejoiced when we read the letters of your Blessedness, and, once every instruction had been disclosed, we immediately caused all who are settled throughout Gaul to rejoice as well; at the same time grieving with you for those who, having abandoned the light of the catholic faith, have fallen into the darkness of error. Your Apostolate’s writing was so inscribed, like a statement of faith, upon the tablets of the heart by everyone who does not disregard the mysteries of redemption, and was entrusted to a tenacious memory so that it might be ready to confound heretical errors. [Note: [Col. 0967C] Manuscripts of collection 21 delete “so.” Shortly afterward, Vatican collection 24 has “ascribed” for “ascribes.”]

Many, therefore, rejoicing and exulting in it, recognized the conviction of their faith and rightly rejoice that they have always held it through their ancestral tradition, just as your Apostolate explained. Others, becoming more concerned after receiving the admonition of your Blessedness, congratulate themselves on having been instructed in every way, and rejoice that they have been given an opportunity to speak freely and confidently, with the authority of the Apostolic See also supporting them, so that each person may express and affirm what he believes.

### CHAPTER III

[Col. 0967B]

Who could judge that adequate thanks can be offered to your Apostolate for so great a gift, by which you have adorned not only Gaul but the whole world as though with certain most precious gems? The faithful person owes it to your teaching, after God, that he should steadfastly hold what he believed; the unbeliever owes it to you that, recognizing the truth, he should withdraw from his faithlessness, leave behind the darkness of his error after being illumined by the light of apostolic instruction, and follow and believe more what our Lord Jesus Christ teaches through your mouth concerning the mystery of his Incarnation than what the devil, the enemy of human salvation and truth, instills. [Note: [Col. 0967D] Three manuscripts of Quesnellus and five of our own have “distills.”]

### CHAPTER IV

We would also have wished to send letters to your son, the most glorious and faithful prince, concerning the same matter [Col. 0967C], in which, while congratulating him on his faith, we might also have made known the concern of our humility by which we follow you in Christ, had we not considered it no longer necessary after news had reached us from the eastern regions. [Note: [Col. 0967D] They understand “news” to mean news of the changed situation after the death of Theodosius and of Leo’s letter having already been received throughout the East; for that reason they no longer considered it necessary to write to the new emperor, as Leo had requested while Theodosius was alive, according to annotation 7 (Col. 887, note b) on Letter 67. Some manuscripts lack the word “regions.”] Some manuscripts lack the word “regions.” We would have considered this entirely unnecessary once the report had arrived.

Through the merits of your Apostolate, the pious Lord has brought it about that a heresy secretly nourished for a long time should reveal itself in your days. It belongs to the praise of your vigilance that the error of the wicked could not remain hidden; it redounds to the glory of the faith that the evil persuasion either found no adherents or lost those whom it had found. [Col. 0968A] May the merciful Lord therefore, we pray, look upon your Apostolate and preserve it, and preserve his Church spread throughout the whole world; for while you keep watch in this way, those who care for their souls are made more diligent in the faith, and those who are somewhat negligent are kindled to diligence by so great an example.

### CHAPTER V

Keeping this always before our eyes, [Note: [Col. 0967D] Vindobonensis collection 5 has “we do not cease.”] we shall not cease to give thanks and to offer supplication together to our Lord and God, rejoicing that he has given to the Apostolic See, from which, with Christ’s favor, the fountain and source of our religion has flowed, a prelate of such holiness, such faith, and such apostolic learning. We also ask that he preserve the gift of your pontificate, given and granted to you, for a very long life, for the building up of his Churches. Although unequal in merit, yet equal in faith, if anything—God forbid—should be attempted against the catholic Church by profane assault, we are prepared, with the Lord strengthening us, to lay down our souls with your Blessedness for the truth of the faith, and to devote this life to the author of our salvation and giver of eternity.

And in another hand: Pray for me, my lord, deservedly most blessed and venerable in apostolic honor, O pope.

[Note: [Col. 0967D] In the ancient editions and in manuscripts of collections 12, 21, and 24, only the first three subscriptions were read; in manuscripts of collection 11, only Rusticus’s first subscription. They are found complete in the manuscripts of collection 5, and were first published by Sirmondus from the manuscript of Nicolaus Faber, which later passed into the Thuanian library. It is remarkable that Ravennius’s subscription is omitted, although he is named first in the title. Yet the words written in another hand before Rusticus’s subscription seem to belong to Ravennius: “Pray for me, Lord.” Harduinus attached this note to the subscriptions. The subscriptions are complete as they appear in the manuscript formerly Thuanian, now Colbertine: Ravennius, bishop of Arles; Venerius, bishop of Narbonne; Maximus, bishop of Riez; and so on. Rusticus, however, is bishop of Narbonne, while Venetius is bishop of Marseille. Constantianus should have been placed before Maximus. Moreover, the names of the cities do not appear in the printed editions, although Sirmondus took these subscriptions from the manuscript formerly Thuanian. Thus Harduinus did not present the subscriptions themselves as they appeared in the manuscript, but only with that note. In the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5, which we found to be exactly like the Thuanian manuscript, the subscriptions resemble the printed versions, and Ravennius’s name is likewise absent.]

## LETTER C

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Alternatively, after Letter 77. What was formerly numbered 100 is now 127. Written on 18 December 451.]

[Note: [Col. 0969D] Holstenius published this letter in the Roman collection from the Barberini manuscript 3386, collection 16 of Thessalonica, with which we have collated it. Tillemont, in article 135 of his Life of Leo, appears to regard the Latin text of this letter as original. The words near the end, together with the following salutation written in another hand and apparently added by the emperor himself, seem to suggest this. It may also be inferred that this formula was expressed in Latin because the Thessalonian collection does not say that it was written in Greek, as it does of Anatolius’s subscription to Letter 132 below; concerning that subscription it reads: “And the subscription in Greek letters.” If the emperor’s salutation was originally written in Latin, the same should be thought of the letter itself. The Latin syntax is also quite coherent and differs greatly from the customary method of translation of that period, which is evident in other documents rendered into Latin. Finally, the Greek text that we shall append is in some places fuller by several clauses, while lacking the words “and in another hand”; therefore the Latin text cannot be said to have been translated from the Greek. Whether this letter was written in both Latin and Greek, as the aforementioned Letter 132 of Anatolius appears to have been written not so much in Latin as in Greek, we leave for others to judge. The difference in the clauses does indeed seem to suggest that the Greek text too was original. It is well known that Marcian was skilled in both languages, from the Council of Chalcedon, session 6, where he is reported to have addressed the assembly in Latin and Greek.] OF THE EMPEROR MARCIAN TO POPE LEO.

### Synopsis

I. He congratulates Leo on the faith strengthened at Chalcedon and on peace restored to the Church. — II. The faith was expounded by the synod in accordance with Saint Leo’s letter. — III. He asks that the See of Constantinople be granted second place, in accordance with the decrees of the second and fourth synods. — IV. Through Lucianus and Basilius he requests Leo’s agreement on the same matter.

The victorious VALENTINIANUS and MARCIANUS, illustrious, triumphant, ever Augusti, to the holy father, deservedly venerable, LEO, bishop. [Note: [Col. 0970D] In the Barberini manuscript and in Holstenius these words are added, serving in place of the synopsis: “That the Church of Constantinople ought to become a second see, which was not granted.”]

### CHAPTER I

Divine and human writings agree that the Divinity must first of all be venerated, and that almighty God is propitious where religion is rightly practiced. We have therefore found what we were seeking, and our vows have attained their fulfillment. Religious devotion has found the faith of religion; and there is no doubt that, with God as its author, what was being sought concerning his majesty has been defined. Since the contention and discord that envy, the enemy of the faith, had raised have therefore been expelled, everyone acknowledges God with one mind. We no longer accuse the faithless, nor are we ungrateful. [Col. 0970D] [Note: The words “the faithless” and “nor are we” were omitted by Holstenius but are necessary to the sense; we supplied them from the same manuscript.]

[Col. 0971A] The enemies of religion have brought it about that we seek God more earnestly and find him more clearly. For a light seems greater when it has shone after darkness; drink is sweeter to the thirsty, and rest to the weary. Let your Holiness therefore rejoice in the victory of the faith, whose laurel must be referred to almighty Christ, who triumphed over the faithless. For that reason we hastened to attend the holy synod ourselves, although military expeditions and public necessities detained us in other places.

### CHAPTER II

Accordingly, everything that accords with the vows and prayer of your religion has been ordered by God’s authority. When the most reverend bishops from the whole world subject to our empire had been summoned to Chalcedon and the matter had been debated, the true faith prevailed after many conflicts, and all agreed to the exposition according to your Holiness’s letters, as truth required. We do not doubt that the joy over this matter is shared by us and your Holiness, and that those rejoice together who plainly desired the truth together. It remains for your Holiness, now that everything has been arranged according to the catholic faith and truth and peace has been restored to the Churches, to call upon the divine majesty with everyone’s prayers for the destruction of the enemies—something we are entirely certain you were doing even before our letters.

### CHAPTER III

Since it has also been decreed that the decisions made by the one hundred and fifty most holy bishops under the deified Theodosius the Great [Note: [Col. 0971D] We also supplied the word “deified” from the same manuscript and Holstenius’s edition. The Greek text has “under the deified Theodosius of blessed memory.”] concerning the honor of the venerable Church of Constantinople, as well as what has now been decreed by the holy synod concerning the same matter, should remain firm—namely, that after the Apostolic See the bishop of the city of Constantinople should hold second place, since that most splendid city is now called New Rome—may your Holiness deign to give this side your own agreement as well, although the most reverend bishops who came to the holy synod as representatives of your religion opposed it. For they vehemently prohibited the synod from making any decree concerning this venerable Church.

### CHAPTER IV

We hope that, with the priests of the whole world in agreement, divine favor will deign to provide what will benefit the Roman state. Concerning this matter, we judged that everything ought to be fully reported through Lucianus, a devout bishop, and Basilius, a deacon, the bearers of these letters. We ask that your religion also command that what the holy synod has decreed be observed forever.

And in another hand: May the Divinity preserve you for many years, holy and most religious Father.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, at Constantinople, in the consulship of Our Lord Marcianus Augustus and whoever shall have been named consul.

## THE SAME LETTER: Greek Text with a New Latin Translation

[Note: [Col. 0971] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

1116 Letter of the most pious emperor Marcian to the most blessed archbishop of Rome, Leo.

The victorious VALENTINIANUS and MARCIANUS, glorious, triumphant Augusti, to the most holy and truly venerable father, Archbishop LEO.

### CHAPTER I

[Col. 0971C]

Divine and human writings agree that the Divinity must first of all be worshiped, and that almighty God is gracious there where the faith is rightly practiced. We have therefore found and attained what we were seeking through our prayers. For faithful devotion has found the faith of religion, and there is no doubt that, with God’s help, what was sought concerning his power has been established. Since all contention and discord that the envious demon had cast into the faith have been expelled, everyone acknowledges God with one mind. Moreover, we do not accuse the unbelievers; indeed, we give thanks even to the enemies of religion, for they have enabled us to seek God most earnestly and to recognize him openly. A light appearing after darkness seems greater; drink is sweet to the thirsty, and rest to the weary. [Col. 0973A] Let your Holiness therefore rejoice over the victory of the faith, whose crown must be offered to almighty Christ; for he gave the victory over the unbelievers. And for this reason we ourselves hastened to attend the holy synod, although military expeditions and public necessities detained us in other places.

### CHAPTER II

Thus everything has been defined according to the vows of your Holiness that accord with the faith. When the most pious bishops from the whole world under our empire had been summoned to Chalcedon and deliberation had taken place, the true faith prevailed after many contentions, and all agreed to the exposition according to your Holiness’s letters, as truth required. We have no doubt that the grace of this event is shared by us and your Holiness, and that those rejoice equally who plainly love the truth with equal zeal. [Col. 0973B] It remains, now that everything has been arranged according to the catholic faith and truth and peace has been restored to the Churches, for your Holiness to summon divine power, with everyone’s prayers, against the destruction of the enemies—a thing which it is acknowledged you were doing even before our letters.

### CHAPTER III

Since it has also been established that the decisions made by the one hundred and fifty bishops under the deified Theodosius the Great, in honor of the venerable Church of Constantinople, and those now decreed by the holy synod concerning the same matter, should remain firm—namely, that immediately after the Apostolic See the bishop of Constantinople should hold second place, since that most splendid city is called New Rome—may your Holiness deign to grant agreement to this side as well, although the most reverend bishops who came to the holy synod in place of your love for God opposed it. [Col. 0973C] For they most vehemently prohibited anything from being decreed in the synod concerning this same venerable Church.

We hope that, with the priests of the whole world in agreement, divine providence will deign to provide what is useful to Roman affairs. Therefore we decided that everything should be made known to you through Lucianus, the most God-loving bishop, and Basilius, the deacon; and we ask that your piety toward God command that what has been established by the holy synod be observed forever. May divine providence preserve you for many years, most holy and most God-loving father.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, at Constantinople, in the consulship of our lord Marcianus, ever Augustus, and of the one who shall be announced.

1115 [Note: [Col. 0971D] This letter was published in 1685 by Andreas Arnoldus in the Syntagma of Athanasius, from a Baroccian manuscript transferred to the Bodleian Library, and was subsequently included by Quesnellus in his second edition. We collated and corrected the Greek text from Vatican Greek manuscript 1455; Quesnellus reprinted Arnoldus’s Latin translation, but because of the significant corrections to the Greek text we thought it necessary to provide a new translation.]

### Letter of the Most Pious Emperor Marcian

to the Most Blessed Archbishop of Rome, Leo

Victorious VALENTINIANUS and MARCIANUS, glorious, triumphant Augusti, to the most holy and truly venerable father, Archbishop LEO. [Note: [Col. 0971D] Thus also the Vatican manuscript. But, as Arnoldus likewise observed, instead of “to the patriarch bishop” one should perhaps read “to the father, archbishop.” [Col. 0972D] See Marcian’s own Letter 110.]

[Col. 0972C] Divine and human writings agree that the Divine must first of all be worshiped, and that almighty God is gracious where the faith is rightly practiced. [Note: [Col. 0972D] We added “rightly,” which was absent from the common text, on the authority of the Vatican manuscript. The Latin text likewise agrees, having “rightly.”] Therefore we have found and attained through our prayers the very thing that we were seeking. [Note: [Col. 0972D] The Vatican manuscript has “we are zealous”; read “we were seeking.”] For faithful devotion has found the faith of religion, and there is no doubt that, with God’s cooperation, what was being sought concerning his power has been established. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Thus the Vatican manuscript. The common text is not satisfactory: “there is no doubt through cooperation,” and so forth.]

When all contention and discord that the envious demon had cast into the faith had been expelled, everyone knows God with one mind. [Note: [Col. 0972D] The Vatican manuscript has “had cast in.” Perhaps it should be read “had previously cast in.”] Finally, we do not accuse the unbelievers, but we also acknowledge gratitude toward the enemies of religion; for they enabled us to seek God most earnestly and to recognize him openly. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Supply from the old Latin text and read “with one mind.”]

A light seems greater when it appears after darkness; drink is sweet to the thirsty, and rest to the weary. [Col. 0974A] Let your Holiness therefore rejoice at the victory of the faith, [Note: [Col. 0973D] The Vatican manuscript likewise has this, but ἧς τινος (“of which”) should be read in place of οὗτινος (“of whom”).] whose crown must be offered to almighty Christ; for he gave victory over the unbelievers. [Note: [Col. 0973D] We read this with the Vatican manuscript. The common text incorrectly has “victory from the unbelievers.”] And for this reason we ourselves hastened to attend the holy synod, [Note: [Col. 0973D] The Vatican manuscript likewise has this, but ἠπείχθημεν (“we hastened”) should be read.] although military expeditions and public necessities detained us in other places.

Therefore everything has been established according to the prayers of your Holiness, which accord with the faith. [Note: [Col. 0973D] The Vatican manuscript clearly has this. The common text incorrectly reads “to have been formed,” although the margin notes: “Read, has been formed.”] When the most devout bishops from the whole world under our reign had been summoned to Chalcedon and deliberation had taken place, the true faith prevailed after many contentions, and everyone agreed to the exposition according to the writings of your Holiness, as truth required. We have no doubt that the grace of this matter is shared by us and your Holiness, and that those rejoice equally who plainly love the truth alike. [Note: [Col. 0974D] Thus also the Vatican manuscript, but ἐρᾶσθαι (“to love”) should perhaps be read in place of εἰρῆσθαι.]

It remains, when everything has been arranged according to the catholic faith and truth and peace has been restored to the Churches, for your Holiness, with everyone’s prayers, to summon divine power for the destruction of the enemies; it is acknowledged that you were doing this even before our [Note: [Col. 0974D] Here supply from the old Latin text and read “our letters.”] letters.

Since it has also been established that the decisions made by the one hundred and fifty bishops under the divine Theodosius the Great, for the sake of honoring the venerable Church of the Constantinopolitans, and those now established by the holy synod concerning the same matter, should be preserved firm— [Note: [Col. 0974D] The Vatican manuscript here supplies the true reading. The common text is corrupt, reading “of the later one”; in the margin it says: “Perhaps, of the earlier one.”] namely, that immediately after the Apostolic Throne the bishop of Constantinople should hold second place, [Note: [Col. 0974D] The common text has “should hold.”] since that most splendid city is proclaimed New Rome—may your Holiness deign also to agree to this side. [Note: [Col. 0974D] Perhaps “may grant.”] Although the most devout bishops who assembled at the holy synod in place of your devotion toward God opposed it, [Col. 0974C] for they most vehemently prevented anything from being established in the synod concerning this same venerable Church.

We hope that, with the priests of the whole world in agreement, divine providence will deign to provide what is advantageous to Roman affairs. Therefore, through Lucianus, the most God-loving bishop, and Basilius, the deacon, we decreed that everything should be made known to you, and we ask that your piety command that the decisions established by the holy synod be guarded forever. May divine providence preserve you for many years, most holy and most God-loving father. Given fifteen days before the Kalends of January, at Constantinople, in the consulship of our lord Marcianus, the eternal Augustus, and of the one who shall be announced.

## LETTER CI

[Note: [Col. 0975B] What was formerly numbered 101 is now 128. Written at the same time as the preceding letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0975B] We now publish this letter for the first time from Vatican Greek manuscript 1455, in which we also found the preceding Greek letter of Marcian. Since both letters concern the same matter and were sent through the same envoys, Lucianus the bishop and Basilius the deacon, this letter too is known to have been written by Anatolius at the same time as the preceding one. Thus, just as Leo replied to Marcian’s preceding letter in Letter 104, given on 22 May, so he replied to this letter of Anatolius on the same day in Letter 106.]

### Of Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople, to Saint Leo, Archbishop of Rome

[Col. 0975]

Now published for the first time from a Vatican manuscript. (G)

### Synopsis

I. Leo’s zeal against the heretics whom he overthrew. Concerning the acts brought from Chalcedon to Rome. — II. Anatolius’s legates sent to Rome with the other acts. Concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus. — III. Concerning Leo’s letter, received by everyone, and the definition of the faith issued at the Synod of Chalcedon. — IV. Concerning the other proceedings at Chalcedon after the definition of the faith: first regarding the canons, then regarding particular ecclesiastical cases. Finally, concerning the privilege of the Church of Constantinople. — V. The opposition of Leo’s legates to this privilege. Its confirmation is requested.

[Note: [Col. 0975] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

1122 To the most holy and most blessed father and fellow minister, Leo, archbishop of ancient Rome: Anatolius sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0975A]

### CHAPTER I
The zeal of your Holiness for piety, and your concern for the orthodox faith—dear and pleasing to God, the Savior of all—have rightly become an object of universal admiration. For it is your custom, as befits one so great, to rise to the performance of righteous deeds and to make your own praiseworthy efforts a proof for the Churches of Christ. Therefore your Holiness did not disregard the true faith, undermined by profane assaults; rather, abhorring the evil workers, you struck them down vigorously with the unrelenting weapons of opposition to wickedness.

Since, then, our most devout and Christ-loving emperors, displaying the finest zeal for piety and anxious to cut out every bitter root that was springing up, lest they themselves be polluted by it—for they were elevated to the kingdom above all so that they might bring aid to the faith of the Fathers, which had been subjected to tyranny [Note: This was plainly the condition when Marcian was raised to the imperial office, while Dioscorus was dominant.]—ordered priests to be gathered from almost every place beneath the sun, so that, by common judgment, they might confirm the faith of the blessed and venerable Fathers, together with your Holiness’s letter, which agrees with it, and disperse every innovation of foreign sophistries that injures the understanding of piety.

And since everything that had taken place necessarily had to be reported to your Holiness, we write again to make these matters known, sending from here our most God-loving brother and fellow bishop Lucian, and the most religious deacon Basil.

[Note: Observe the necessity of referring to the Apostolic See; shortly afterward it is again stated that matters which must necessarily come to your knowledge are to be reported.]

Already, indeed, our most God-loving brother and fellow bishop Lucentius, together with your most devout presbyter Boniface and the most religious deacon Marcian, has departed from this imperial city after receiving documents openly setting forth what was done at the holy and ecumenical council.

[Note: Anatolius had written another letter to Leo when Lucentius and Boniface had returned after the council. This may, however, be the very Letter 98, sent to Leo in the name of the entire council, to which Anatolius subscribed first, as is clear from the ancient version. Shortly afterward, however, this letter refers to Letter 98 as having been written by the council. It may therefore be inferred that Lucentius and Boniface had already departed before this time with the acts and report of that synod, and consequently shortly after the beginning of November, when the council’s final session was held.]

[Note: In the Greek, Λουκιανός, Lucianus, is read. But since the presbyter Boniface is joined to him, and Boniface departed together with the council’s acts, it is clear that the reading should be Lucentius, who returned to Rome with Boniface after serving as a legate of the Apostolic See. The following passages confirm this more clearly: after these men are named as those who carried the council’s documents, other documents are said to be sent through “our men.” It follows that these men were Westerners, distinct from “our men”; the latter are Lucianus and Basil, sent from Constantinople to Rome and likewise mentioned in the preceding letter from Marcian. Among the Westerners, therefore, not Boniface alone but also Lucentius must be understood. Nor should it be objected that Paschasinus is omitted, although he was the first among the legates of the Roman See. Just as Saint Leo sent Paschasinus to the council not from the City, as Boniface, but from Sicily, as Letters 89, 91, and especially 94 indicate, so perhaps Anatolius mentions only Lucentius and Boniface because they alone were going to Rome, whereas Paschasinus had departed to return to Sicily. We do not know who the deacon Marcian was who departed with these Western legates, because the evidence is lacking.]

## II

Since it was fitting that after those men the remaining documents, which necessarily had to come to your attention, should also be sent through our people—for certain matters had been dealt with specifically by us—for this reason we selected the aforesaid most devout bishop, a man richly endowed with piety, intelligence, and complete integrity in the faith, and sent him, together with the aforementioned deacon, as a legate to your great Rome. Thus, after making some matters known by letters and others in person, they may return to us joyfully with a response suitable and worthy of you, while we, together with everyone, celebrate the love and kindness with which your paternal solicitude for the blessedness of your office is accustomed to treat the see of this imperial city.

[Note: These documents are said to contain certain matters specifically enacted by us. At the end of the letter sent to Leo, a definition concerning the see of Constantinople is mentioned; since it was drafted after the conclusion of the proceedings, on 31 October, in the absence of the legates, the specific acts concerning this matter, likewise performed in their absence, appear to refer to the interests of that see.]

The manner in which the holy and universal synod, after carefully investigating the storm that had arisen against the common peace, found its author—namely Dioscorus, formerly bishop of the Alexandrians, who was deprived of the priesthood—is set forth in detail in what was written by the holy and ecumenical council.

[Note: This refers to the report of the synod to Leo, which was given above as Letter 98.]

For it was necessary—indeed, necessary—that the wicked man who had filled the whole world with storms and tempests should be removed from their midst. Since these matters have been settled most satisfactorily, we are confident that your Holiness too will agree, because of your innate hatred of wickedness.

[Note: Observe that the Roman pontiffs’ assent to the council’s acts is requested, and is entirely free.]

## III

After the judgment against him, however—for this was the principal reason why the devout emperor most diligently convened the holy synod—it was necessary that everyone’s understanding should converge upon the meaning of your orthodox faith.

[Note: Observe the assertion by Anatolius that agreement with the faith of the Roman pontiff was necessary. By “the faith” he means Letter 28, to Flavian, which was read aloud in the council before the definition of faith. Since some bishops, not fully understanding Leo’s meaning, raised difficulties about accepting it, the council dealt with those difficulties so that everyone’s understanding might agree with the correct sense of your faith. Observe also that these proceedings took place after the judgment against him, that is, against Dioscorus.]

With prayer and tears, and with your Holiness present with us in spirit and cooperating through the most God-loving men whom you sent from there, and with the most holy and beautiful martyr Euphemia as our protector, we all devoted ourselves entirely to this salutary work, setting aside every other concern.

[Note: This refers to the removal of difficulties and the persuasion of the bishops who, because they understood the letter to Flavian less accurately, assembled before Anatolius at the beginning of the council, in the second session, so that after discussion they might lay aside every doubt. This successfully occurred, as is reported in the fourth session, volume IV of the Councils, pages 1382–1383.]

When the time required all the assembled most holy bishops to issue a harmonious definition for the explanation and clearer understanding of the confession concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord God, who is found and appears to those who do not seek him, and appears even to those who do not question him, nevertheless manifested his truth, although some initially attempted contentiously to resist, and ordained that a written statement should be published by all with one mind and without contradiction. It would both strengthen the minds of those who stood firm and invite to the way of truth all who were straying from the truth.

[Note: Opposition arose to the new definition of faith; this is indicated in the same, fifth, session.]

And when we who had assembled in the gathering of our universal synod at the shrine of that same most holy and victorious martyr Euphemia had subscribed to such a document with unanimous consent, and when, with prayer, joy, and gladness from our most devout and Christ-loving emperor Marcian and our most devout and wholly faithful empress and Augusta, our daughter Pulcheria, we had placed upon the holy altar the written definition of the faith of our Fathers, composed for its confirmation according to that sacred letter of yours, we handed it over to their piety, at their own request, so that they might receive it. Having received it, they gave glory with us to Christ the Lord, who drove away the darkness of erroneous opinion and made the word of truth shine forth by complete agreement. Thus, by the grace of the Savior, everything that concerns ecclesiastical peace and the harmony of the priests in pure faith took place.

[Note: This refers to the sixth session of Chalcedon, although not all the circumstances mentioned here appear in the surviving acts. These details explain and correctly clarify the very obscure passage in Letter 98 of the same council to Leo, where it is said that Saint Euphemia, receiving the definition of faith as her own confession, offered it to us, her bridegroom, through the most devout emperor and the Christ-loving Augusta. The present letter makes clear what this was. It also more clearly refutes the later inventions introduced by certain Greeks; see Baronius, year 451, numbers 118–119. We likewise learn that Augusta Pulcheria attended the sixth session together with Marcian, contrary to Baluzius, volume IV of the Councils, page 1470, note 11; Pagius, year 451, number 31; and Tillemont, “Leo,” article 119 and note 51. It is true that Pulcheria’s name is found neither in the Greek acts of this session that have come down to us nor in the complete Latin translation of those acts. Nevertheless, her presence at the session should not for that reason be denied: Anatolius testifies to it as explicitly as does the report of Chalcedon itself, which, agreeing with Anatolius’s text, signifies her presence in the words quoted. There can be no doubt that Pulcheria’s name was included in the original acts of the council. Before the complete acts of the council were translated into Latin—which we believe occurred considerably later, around the time of Hormisdas, as will be established against Quesnellus in the observations on his note 3 to Letter 86, here numbered 113—the principal sections of the council were translated into Latin immediately from the Greek acts. Thus the oldest manuscript collections in Latin contain a few chapters of this council in a translation entirely different from that of all the acts of the same synod. The antiquity of these collections, together with the roughness of their less accurate translation, indicates that the first version of these chapters was prepared while Leo was still alive from the Greek acts then available. In the manuscripts of Quesnellus’s collection, commonly called the fifth, and also in the very ancient Vatican manuscript 1322, where the beginning of the sixth session is translated from the Greek, Pulcheria’s name occurs. It also occurs in another extremely ancient version inserted in the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, as may be seen in volume IV of the Councils, page 2051. The Greek copies used by the first and oldest translators therefore contained Pulcheria’s name. Accordingly, Sirmondus cannot be accused of falsification, nor can the author of the Brief History of the Eutychianists—whom we shall probably show to have been Gelasius in the observations on Quesnellus’s notes to Letter 28—when he wrote of the synod first summoned at Nicaea and then transferred to Chalcedon: “In it both the emperor and Pulcheria took their seats.” Nor can it be doubted that the letter to Strategius, consul of Bithynia, belongs to Pulcheria, since it bears her name in all Greek and Latin manuscripts and promises that she will be present at the council. Indeed, this testimony further makes her presence at the synod highly credible. The difficulty arising from the council’s indiction, which that letter attributes to Pulcheria, is sufficiently resolved by note 5, column 942, n. p., to Letter 95.]

## IV

[Note: This order should be observed. After the definition of faith was issued in Session 6, the twenty-seven canons were first enacted; then ecclesiastical cases were handled, namely those of Maximus of Antioch, Juvenal of Jerusalem, Theodoret, Ibas, and others. The canons should therefore be placed in Session 7, not, as in the printed editions, in Session 15. This will be discussed further in volume II, note 18 to Quesnellus’s first dissertation on the year 451.]

Since it was also necessary for us to consider other matters, so that such a great synod might appear to have done everything without omitting anything that required correction or approval, care was taken both in canonical matters and in ecclesiastical cases by those who govern everything, by the most magnificent and glorious judges, by the illustrious and glorious senate, by the entire clergy, and by the people, that the most holy see of this imperial city, Constantinople, should receive some addition of honor through the agreement of this holy synod concerning the canon of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who had assembled under the great Theodosius of pious memory, emperor of Constantinople, when Nectarius was presiding at Constantinople, Timothy at Alexandria, Meletius at Antioch, Helladius at Caesarea in Cappadocia, Cyril at Jerusalem, and the others.

[Note: The five bishops are expressly named as the principal Fathers of the Constantinopolitan council. Photius, in his book On Synods, calls the presidents of that council Timothy of Alexandria, Meletius of Antioch, Cyril of Jerusalem, and Nectarius of Constantinople, whom he nevertheless says held the first place. But Meletius died before Nectarius’s ordination, and therefore could neither attend nor preside at this council together with Nectarius. Since ancient Latin catalogues derived from the Greek list among the bishops who attended this council both Meletius and Nectarius, together with the others, we believe that Anatolius and Photius used a similar Greek catalogue in which the names of the two Constantinopolitan councils of the same year, 381, had been confused in very early times. At the first, Meletius but not Nectarius was present; at the second—the one under discussion here—Nectarius, newly ordained, but not Meletius, who had already died, was present and presided. If, with Tillemont in the Life of Saint Gregory Nazianzen, we believe that only one council was held at Constantinople that year and that it lasted several months, so that Meletius presided at first and, after his death, Nectarius, ordained there, presided, then the testimony of Anatolius and Photius will be understood in a more proper and precise sense.]

We undertook this action confidently, believing that your Blessedness would rightly regard it as an honor belonging to the see of Constantinople, since your apostolic throne has long shown care and concord toward it and has generously supplied it in every respect with the assistance it needed.

For there is no doubt that your Blessedness rejoices greatly that the assembly celebrated by them has received greater honor.

[Note: For clarity, supply the nominative: “the Synod of Chalcedon.”]

Accordingly, the holy synod proceeded willingly to confirm the canon of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers, who decreed that the bishop of Constantinople should have the honor and precedence after the most holy see of Rome, because Constantinople is also a new Rome. It also decreed that he should ordain the metropolitans of the Pontic, Asian, and Thracian dioceses, while the bishops subject to those metropolitans were to receive ordination from their own metropolitans.

[Note: The Greek manuscript lacks τῶν ἐπισκόπων, “of the bishops.” But since the name is required by the very canon issued at Chalcedon in the sixteenth session, to which this passage refers, we have necessarily supplied it as an accidental omission by the copyist. The bishop of Constantinople was there granted the ordination of the metropolitans of the three dioceses—Pontus, Asia, and Thrace. The ordination of the bishops of those dioceses, which the bishops of Constantinople had claimed for themselves for sixty or seventy years, was taken away from them and restored to the proper metropolitans.]

Thus, rather, the ordinations of the many bishops that the see of Constantinople had been accustomed to perform for sixty or seventy years would be removed from that throne.

## V

When everything had therefore proceeded well and ended in rejoicing, the most devout bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, together with the most reverend presbyter Boniface, although they had often been instructed by us concerning this very matter, and were ignorant of the intention that your Holiness has toward the most holy Church of Constantinople, after the holy synod had formulated and confirmed by subscription such a definition, rejected the synod, disturbed it, and filled the assembly with confusion, treating this see as worthless and doing everything that brought insult both to me and to the most holy Church of Constantinople.

These things too were established by the command of our most devout emperors, while the most magnificent and glorious judges were present at the council and declared that the definition of the holy synod was firm. They themselves strongly insisted and desired that those matters pertaining to the honor of the see should be carried out, as we have said. Of these many matters we have made only a few known to you, lest we seem to burden them while wearying your ears.

[Note: This refers to the pontiff’s legates, as do the following words; we are said to have honored them with respect and gifts.]

For both before and after their arrival we attended in every respect to what concerned your glory and the honor due to you—God is our witness, and the deeds themselves make it clear—namely, how we honored them with respect and the reverence expressed through gifts. And because of the honor with which we regard you, the holy synod also referred such a decree to your Holiness, and we beseech you that we may obtain your approval and confirmation.

[Note: What Anatolius subsequently wrote to Leo in Letter 132, chapter 4, agrees with this: “Although the whole force and confirmation of the proceedings has in this way been reserved for the authority of your Blessedness.”]

We beseech you, most holy ones, to bring this about through your own action as well. For the see of Constantinople regards your apostolic throne as its father and joins itself to you in a special and excellent manner, so that, from your solicitude toward it, everyone may understand that you have long sincerely cared for its interests and that even now you continue to have the same concern for it.

And just as you will deem it right to ratify everything that has taken place and been properly enacted in the most holy and universal synod as beneficial to the ecclesiastical order—

[Note: The Greek reads καταξιώσατε, “deign.” But syntax and sense show that καταξιώσετε, “you will deign,” should be read, since the matter concerns Leo’s approval and confirmation of the acts.]

—we have taken care to send your Holiness the aforesaid definition concerning the see of Constantinople, so that you may know how everything was accomplished through divine wisdom in answer to your prayers. We earnestly beseech you that each proposal may receive an appropriate response, while the most God-loving bishop Lucian teaches you everything. He himself was present at the holy council and, with the utmost prudence, contributed all that he could to our struggle for the faith. We selected him to undertake, well and successfully, the duties of our service toward you. He is a perfect man and has long been a friend of our most devout and Christ-loving emperors. May you deign to send him back to us rejoicing in your kindness.

I, together with those who are with me, offer the fullest greeting in Christ to the entire brotherhood united with your Blessedness. Remain safe in the Lord, pray for us, and may you be granted to us, most God-loving and most blessed Father.

---

## Greek Version

To the most holy and most blessed father, fellow minister, and archbishop of elder Rome, Leo: Anatolius sends greetings in the Lord.

[Col. 0976A]

The zeal of your Holiness for piety, and your concern for the orthodox faith—dear and pleasing to God, the Savior of all—have rightly become an object of universal admiration. For it is your custom, as befits those who are so great, to distinguish yourselves in worthy deeds and to make your own praiseworthy efforts a proof for the Churches of Christ.

[Note: Perhaps the reading should be τοῖς οὕτω μεγάλοις, “for those who are so great.”]

Therefore your Holiness did not overlook the true faith, being undermined by profane assaults; rather, abhorring the evil workers, you wounded them vigorously with the weapon of hatred for wickedness.

[Note: Perhaps the reading should be κατέστρωσεν, “he struck them down.”]

Since, then, our most devout and Christ-loving emperors, being excellent zealots for piety, were anxious to cut out every bitter root that was springing up, lest they be polluted through it—for they were advanced to the kingdom especially so that they might defend the faith of the Fathers, which was being tyrannically oppressed—they decreed that the ministers of God should be gathered from almost every place beneath the sun, so that, confirming by common judgment the faith of the blessed and celebrated Fathers, and your Holiness’s letter agreeing with it, they might scatter every innovation of imported sophistries that injures the understanding of piety.

Everything that had followed necessarily had to be reported to your Holiness. Therefore, sending there, by selection, our most God-loving brother and fellow bishop Lucian and the most devout deacon Basil, we write again to make these things known: our most God-loving brother and fellow bishop Lucian has already departed from this imperial city, having received, together with our most God-fearing presbyter Boniface and Marcian the most devout deacon, documents openly containing what was done at the holy and ecumenical synod.

[Note: The manuscript reads Λουκίντιον, “Lucentius.”]

[Note: The manuscript reads ὑμῶν, “your.”]

Since it was fitting that after those men the remaining documents, which necessarily had to come to our knowledge, should also be sent through our men—for certain matters had been dealt with specifically by us—for this reason we selected the aforesaid most God-fearing bishop, a man richly endowed with piety, intelligence, and integrity concerning the faith, and sent him, together with the aforementioned deacon, to your great Rome. Thus, after making some matters clear through the documents and others through themselves, they may return to us joyfully with a response suitable and worthy of you, while we, together with everyone, celebrate the love and kindness customarily shown toward the throne of this imperial city by the paternal care of your Blessedness.

The manner in which the holy and ecumenical synod, after investigating the storm that had arisen against the common peace, found its author—I mean Dioscorus, formerly bishop of the Alexandrians, and cut him off from the priesthood—is made clear by what was written in greater detail by the holy and ecumenical synod. For it was necessary—indeed, necessary—that the wicked man who had filled the whole inhabited world with storm and tempest should be removed from their midst.

Although these matters have been properly settled, we are confident that your Holiness will agree because of your innate hatred of wickedness.

[Note: The manuscript reads συντίθεσθαι, “to agree.”]

After the judgment against him, it was necessary—for this was the principal reason why the devout emperor earnestly assembled the holy synod—that everyone’s understanding should converge upon the meaning of your orthodox faith. With prayer and tears, and with your Holiness present with us in spirit and cooperating through the most God-loving men whom you sent from there, and with the most holy and beautiful martyr Euphemia defending us, we all devoted ourselves entirely to this salutary work.

When the time required all the assembled most holy bishops to issue a harmonious definition for the clear and fullest understanding of the confession concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord God was found and appeared to those who did not seek him, and appeared even to those who did not question him. Although some initially attempted to dispute, he nevertheless manifested his own truth and arranged that a harmonious and unopposed written statement should be proclaimed by all: strengthening the souls of those who stood firm and summoning to the way of truth all who were turning aside from it.

[Note: The manuscript reads ἀναντίλεκτον, “unopposed.”]

After subscribing unanimously to such a document, we who had come to the assembly of our universal synod at the shrine of that same most holy and victorious martyr Euphemia placed upon the holy altar the written definition of the faith of our Fathers, composed for its confirmation according to that sacred letter of yours. This was done amid the prayer, joy, and gladness of our most devout and Christ-loving emperor Marcian and of our most devout and wholly faithful empress and Augusta, our daughter Pulcheria. We handed it over to their piety when they requested that they might receive it. Having received it, they gave glory with us to the Lord Christ, who drove away all the darkness of erroneous opinion and made the word of truth clear through complete agreement. Thus, by the grace of the Savior, everything concerning ecclesiastical peace and the concord of the priests in the holy faith came to pass.

Since we also had to examine other matters, so that such a great synod might appear to have done everything without omission, both what required correction and what required confirmation, in canonical and in other ecclesiastical matters, care was taken by those who govern everything, by the most magnificent and glorious rulers, by the illustrious and glorious senate, by the entire clergy, and by the people, that the most holy throne of this imperial Constantinople should receive some addition of honor through the consent of this holy synod concerning the canon of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who had assembled under the great Theodosius of pious memory, who became emperor in Constantinople.

At that time Nectarius presided at Constantinople, Timothy at Alexandria, Meletius at Antioch, Helladius at Caesarea and Cappadocia, Cyril at Jerusalem, and the others.

We undertook this action confidently, rightly trusting that your Blessedness would make the honor of the throne of Constantinople your own, since your apostolic throne has from ancient times shown care and concord toward it and has generously shared with it in every respect the assistance it needed.

Since there was no doubt that your Blessedness would rejoice at the honor given to the Church being assembled by them, the synod proceeded willingly to confirm the same canon of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers, who decreed that the bishop of Constantinople should possess the honor and precedence after the most holy throne of Rome, because Constantinople too is a new Rome. It also decreed that he should perform the ordinations of the metropolitans of the Pontic, Asian, and Thracian dioceses, while the bishops subject to them were to be ordained by their own metropolitans. Thus the ordinations of the many bishops that the throne of Constantinople had been accustomed to perform for sixty or seventy years would rather be removed from it.

When everything had proceeded well and ended in gladness, the most devout bishops who were present, Paschasinus and Lucentius, together with the most devout presbyter Boniface, although they had often been instructed by us concerning this very matter, but were ignorant of the intention that your Holiness has toward the most holy Church of Constantinople, after the holy synod had formulated and confirmed by subscription such a definition, stirred up the synod, disturbed it, and filled the assembly with confusion, despising this throne and doing everything that caused insult both to me and to the most holy Church of Constantinople.

These things too were established by the command of our most devout emperors, who were present, together with the most magnificent and glorious rulers, at the assembly. They declared that the definition issued by the holy synod was firm, and themselves eagerly sought the matters contributing to the honor of the throne, as we have said. Of these many matters we have made only a few known to you, lest we seem to burden them while annoying your ears.

For we, both before their arrival and after their arrival, carried out in every respect what concerned your glory and the honor due to you; God is witness, and the deeds themselves make it clear. We honored them with reverence and with the respect expressed through protection, because of our regard for you. The holy synod referred such a decree to your Holiness, and we likewise did so, asking to receive from you approval and confirmation. We beseech you, most holy ones, to bring this about through your own action as well.

For the throne of Constantinople has your apostolic throne as its father, joining itself to you in a special way, so that through your care for it everyone may be persuaded that, since you have long sincerely watched over its interests, you continue even now to have the same concern for it.

[Note: Read ὑμῖν, “to you,” rather than the printed ἡμῖν, “to us.”]

And since all the things enacted in writing in the most holy and ecumenical synod are beneficial to the ecclesiastical order, deign to ratify them all, and we have taken care to send your Holiness the aforesaid definition concerning the throne of Constantinople, so that you may know that everything has been arranged with divine wisdom through your prayers.

[Note: The manuscript reads καταξιώσατε or κατηξιώσατε, “deign.”]

We earnestly beseech you that each matter may receive an appropriate response, while the most God-loving bishop Lucian teaches you everything. He himself was present at the holy synod and, prudently contributing all that he could to our struggle concerning the faith, was selected by us to serve beneficially in the ministry we undertake toward you. He is a perfect man and has long been a friend of our most devout and Christ-loving emperors. Deign to send him back to us rejoicing after he has enjoyed your kindness.

I, together with those who are with me, offer the fullest greeting in Christ to the entire brotherhood united with your Blessedness. Remain strong in the Lord, pray for us, and may you be granted to us, most God-loving and most blessed Father.

---

# Letter CII

[Note: Also numbered 77. The letter formerly numbered 102 is now 131. Written on 27 January 452.]

[Note: It survives in manuscript collections 12, 18, 19, and 24, and in Vatican manuscript 541, which received additions from collection 24. It is the response to Letter 99.]

## To the Bishops of Gaul

On the condemnation of the heretics.

## Synopsis

I. He announces that he has received the letter of the Gallic bishops, full of heavenly doctrine.

II. On the ecumenical synod. Human reasoning about the faith must have no place.

III. The dogmas of Nestorius and Eutyches must likewise be shunned.

IV. The synod agreed with Leo’s letter and proscribed Dioscorus.

V. God must be thanked for all these things; prayer must be offered for the return of the legates; the victory of the faith must be announced to the Spaniards through the Gauls.

Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Ravennius, Rusticus, Venerius, Constantianus, Maximus, Armentarius, Florus, Sabinus, Valerianus, Constantius, Maximus, Asclepius, Nectarius, Maximus, Ursus, Ingenuus, Justus, Valerius, Superventor, Chrysaphius, Fonteius, Petronius, Hydatius, Aetherius, Eulalius, Eustatius, Fraternus, Victurus, Eugenius, Hilary, Verus, Amandus, Gerontius, Proculeianus, Julianus, Helladius, Armentarius, Honoratus, Eparchius, Anemius, Dynamus, Maximinus, Ynantius, and Palladius, bishops established throughout Gaul.

[Notes: The manuscript of Ratisbon reads Constantinus, rather than Constantianus.

The same manuscript reads Armazorius, rather than Armentarius.

Our manuscripts read Savinus, rather than Sabinus.

All our manuscripts read Valerianus, followed later by Valerius. See note 6, column 965, i, to Letter 99. Other copies have Valerius first and Valerianus afterward.

The Ratisbon manuscript reads Eutychius. Vatican collections 12 and 24, together with Vatican 541, read Euticius. We have corrected Victurus from the Ratisbon manuscript, agreeing with Letter 99. The printed editions read Venturus.

The same manuscripts read Hilary.

The Ratisbon manuscript reads Aparcius; Vatican collection 12 reads Epartius; Vatican 541 reads Epatrius.]

## I

We had indeed wished to receive your Fraternity’s letter at the time you promised it, so that the profession of your judgment might be joined to that of our brothers departing for the East, whom we sent to the holy synod in our place for the defense of the catholic faith.

But since many obstacles caused you an unexpected delay, we have gratefully received, through our brother and fellow bishop Ingenuus, the letters that were late and long awaited. As we read them with joy, we approved them, trusting—as we had expected—that through the instruction of the Holy Spirit heavenly doctrine flourishes among you. In the Eastern Churches the cunning of the ancient enemy, through those whom he found to be followers of his falsehood, has attempted to wear it down.

[Note: The printed editions, with manuscripts of collection 24, read: “through those whom he found followers of his own falsehood, and falsehood has attempted”; Vatican collection 12 and another Vatican manuscript, 541, omit the conjunction *-que*. We have corrected the text from the Ratisbon manuscript.]

Yet the catholic faith, which is unchangeable in every part of itself, is always made both stronger and clearer by the very exercises of its adversaries. The grace of God brings this about, so that those who perhaps were less prepared and less attentive to evade the enemy’s subtle arrows may, after receiving the weapons of truth, become stronger against the lies of the impious.

Therefore, because you have faithfully and obediently increased—as the cause required—the confidence that we have in you in the Lord, we rejoice with great exultation.

## II

And rightly we recognize that we made known to our Eastern brothers and fellow bishops that, according to evangelical and apostolic tradition, there is one undivided confession among all of us concerning the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. No disputations of heretics can detain us so as to make us understand anything concerning the truth of this supreme and saving mystery otherwise than we have learned and teach from the preaching of the holy Fathers and from the authority of the unchangeable Creed.

[Note: This reading, “be detained by the disputations,” is better from the Ratisbon manuscript than the readings of the printed editions and other manuscripts.]

The universal Church has condemned both Eutyches now and Nestorius previously. If anyone chooses to cling to their intolerable impieties, he will cut himself off from the body of Christian unity.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript has “will cut himself off.” Earlier editions before Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, read “he has cut himself off”; Quesnellus reads “he cuts himself off.”]

For no further refuge of excuse is now granted to anyone on the grounds of ignorance or inability to understand.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “through ignorance’s lack of knowledge.” The editions of Leo, with Vatican collection 12 and Vatican 541, read “through ignorance and lack of knowledge”; the common editions of the Councils, with manuscripts of collection 24, read “through ignorance and lack of understanding”; the Ratisbon manuscript reads “through the lack of knowledge of ignorance.”]

For this very reason a synod of nearly six hundred of our brothers and fellow bishops was assembled for this very purpose, and it did not permit any art of reasoning or any eloquence of disputation to breathe against the divinely founded faith.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript, like our Grimani manuscript, supports “for this very purpose.” Sirmondus reads “these very things”; the editions of Leo read “this very thing”; the Victor manuscript and three of ours read “by this very thing.”]

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “to breathe,” although shortly afterward it has “to inspire,” with dots beneath the letters indicating that they should be deleted. Earlier editions, together with Vatican 541, read “to inspire against the foundation of the faith.” Vatican collection 12 reads “to breathe.” Quesnellus, with the manuscripts of collection 24, reads “to permit anything divinely inspired against the foundation of the faith,” although in note 1 he admits that all his manuscripts, including the Grimani manuscript, read “to inspire.”]

For, with our brothers and vicars assisting through the help of God’s grace, whose devotion in every session was complete, and with the conjunction supported by our Ratisbon manuscript, it became fully and plainly evident not only to the priests of Christ but also to Christian rulers and authorities, and to all the orders of clergy and people, that this truly is the apostolic faith flowing from the fountain of divine mercy.

[Note: The common editions and most manuscripts read “to all clergy, peoples, and orders.” We have preferred the Ratisbon reading.]

We received it as pure and free from every stain of error, and we preach it as such; now that the whole world agrees, we defend it. Throughout the world the dogmas have been extinguished that either the earlier heretic dared to introduce or the later one, with a different falsehood but an impiety not unequal.

[Note: The printed editions read “invention.” Quesnellus notes in the margin “falsehood,” which we have adopted on the authority of all our manuscripts, especially Ratisbon. From that manuscript we have also substituted “not unequal” for the common reading “equal.”]

## III

For just as Nestorius was not tolerated when he asserted that blessed Mary was merely the mother of a man who was afterward received by the Divinity of the Word, with two distinct and divided persons, so that the son of man was not the Son of God, and that there was not one Christ in both natures but one eternal Christ from the Father and another temporal one from the mother—the authority of the Gospel proclaims the Word to have become flesh (John 1:14) in such a way that it does not present two Christs or two sons, but in the one Lord Jesus Christ it discloses the reality of both God and man. Thus, although the properties of both substances—that is, of the one who saves and of the one who is saved—cannot be confused, neither can the person be doubled.

[Note: The Ratisbon reading is better than that of the other manuscripts and editions: “received from the Divinity of the Word.”]

[Note: Earlier editions and some manuscripts read “with distinct natures and persons, so that he himself was not the Son.” Quesnellus’s correction is confirmed by the Grimani and Ratisbon manuscripts.]

[Note: We have added the word “was” from the Ratisbon manuscript, which shortly afterward deletes *and* before the name Eutyches; later, in place of “was cut away,” it reads “was severed.”]

Therefore, just as Nestorius was execrable in his dogma, so Eutyches, following an error long ago condemned and blaspheming with another profanation, was cut away from the structure of catholic firmness. For he attempted to persuade certain unlearned and excessively simple people that the Word of God became flesh in such a way that he did not take true flesh from his mother; that he did not possess a body of our race; and that there was one nature of his divinity and flesh, or that our one Lord Jesus Christ was both a false man and a passible God.

[Note: Quesnellus, with the Grimani and our Ratisbon manuscript, reads “from the womb of the Virgin”; other copies read “from his mother.”]

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “for the assumption of humanity.”]

Neither the piety of the faith nor the reasoning of the mystery accepts this: either that the Divinity was passible in its own nature or that truth was false in the assumption of humanity.

## IV

The holy synod, agreeing in religious unanimity with the writings of our humility, strengthened by the authority and merit of my lord, the most blessed apostle Peter, has now cut away from the Church of God this abominable reproach.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript reads “as an abomination.” The printed editions read “cut away from the Church of God as an object of abhorrence.” They also read “and Dioscorus of Alexandria, who remained in his impiety, lest that Church….” Quesnellus agrees with our correction, retaining only “as an abomination” rather than “abhorring.”]

Dioscorus of Alexandria too was condemned in his impiety, lest that Church—which from the very beginnings of the Gospel had Saint Mark, the disciple of the most blessed Apostle Peter, as its founder, entirely consonant with the teaching of his master, and which in more recent times has had as its most approved bishops Athanasius, Theophilus, and most recently Cyril—should suffer an unworthy captivity under the domination of a heretic.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript agrees with the Grimani manuscript. Quesnellus’s manuscripts omit the word “teachings,” which earlier editions, together with the Vatican manuscripts of collections 12 and 24 and manuscript 541, inserted.]

Therefore, according to the great mercy of God, know that all the efforts of the devil by which he attempted to disturb the Church of God have been destroyed.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript and two of ours read “the Church of God”; other copies read “the Church of the Lord.”]

## V

[Col. 0987C]

[The supplied source ends here, with Chapter V incomplete.]

[Note: [Col. 0987C] The older printed editions read: “Therefore, dearest brothers, give thanks to God, and offer a worthy thanksgiving, and pray.” Quesnellus: “Therefore, dearest brothers, give God a worthy thanksgiving, [Col. 0987D] and pray.” The reading of the Regensburg manuscript seems more genuine.]

Since a worthy thanksgiving has been offered to God, therefore, dearest brothers, let your affection pray with us, so that we may rejoice that our brothers, whom our expectation longs for, have returned safe as soon as possible, and that, with the Lord’s help, we may be able to instruct you more fully concerning all that has been accomplished. For we did not wish Brother Ingenuus [Note: [Col. 0987D] So the same Regensburg manuscript and two other codices. Elsewhere: “we do not wish.”] to be delayed by this expectation; 1140 rather, for this very reason he ought to have returned more quickly [Note: [Col. 0987D] So the same Regensburg manuscript. Another copy reads: “he ought to have returned, lest the whole substance of our common joys remain unknown to you for longer.”], lest the substance of our common joys remain unknown to you for longer. We wish this also, through the care of your affection, to reach our brother bishops in Spain [Note: [Col. 0987D] See Quesnellus, note 4.], so that what God has accomplished may be unknown to no one. [Note: [Col. 0987D] We have preferred the chronological notation of the day in the most carefully corrected Regensburg manuscript. Other codices and printed editions read: “Given on the Kalends of February”; in those copies the numeral VI could more easily have dropped out than have been added at the discretion of the Regensburg copyist.] Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculanus.

## LETTER CIII

[Note: [Col. 0987D] Elsewhere numbered 82. The letter formerly numbered 103 is now 129. Written around February 452.]

[Note: [Col. 0987D] Merlini published it from manuscript collection 12, of which we have reread two copies, Vatican 1340 and Venetian 169. Sirmondus found two more distinguished codices, the Corbie manuscript of collection 2 and the Pithoean manuscript. As to its date: this letter announces the arrival of the legates of the Apostolic See, whose coming is said in the preceding letters, dated 27 January, to be awaited in chapter 5. Since Letter 101 establishes that they had departed from Constantinople before 18 December of the preceding year, and more probably shortly after the Council of Chalcedon in November, as we observed there in note 4 (Col. 975, note e), they reached Rome in February or March, and certainly some time before the holy pontiff wrote the following four letters. For these were replies to letters dated 18 December and brought by Lucian and Basil, who, having been sent from Constantinople after the departure of the legates, reached the City around April and, their embassy now completed, returned to Constantinople with the following letters shortly before 22 May.]

### TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL

#### Synopsis

When the legates had returned from the Council of Chalcedon and its proceedings had been received, together with the sentence pronounced against Eutyches and Dioscorus, he sends a copy of it to the bishops of Gaul.

To the most beloved brothers Rusticus, Ravennius, Venerius, and the other bishops established throughout Gaul, Leo.

[Note: [Col. 0988C] Rusticus of Narbonne is placed before Ravennius of Arles in this letter, whereas in the preceding letter he is placed after him. The reason for the difference is clear. In the preceding letter Leo replies to the synodical letter of the bishops, Letter 99, in which, since Ravennius preceded Rusticus, he thought that the same order should be followed. But in that synodical letter Ravennius preceded Rusticus because it was written at the Synod of Arles; at synods, however, the metropolitan of the province customarily occupies the first place, even when metropolitans of other provinces who are older or more famous are present. Thus, in the subscriptions of the Council of Aquileia in 381, Valerian of Aquileia, metropolitan of that province, precedes Ambrose of Milan, although Saint Ambrose, famous for so many reasons, presided over the same synod and is placed before Valerian in other documents. In the present letter, however, Leo is not replying to any synodical letter from Gaul; consequently, taking seniority into account, he places Rusticus before Ravennius.]

When, through the mercy of God, our common prayers have been fulfilled, it is fitting that your brotherhood should share in holy joys. For I announce what my brothers, who presided in my place over the Eastern synod, have reported: the Catholic faith has been confirmed and the triumph of apostolic preaching glorified. Even those who had been led astray or driven into deviation rejoice now that the light of truth has been received. Indeed, all the priests of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0988D] Elsewhere: “in one judgment.”] agreed in one judgment, with the Holy Spirit as their teacher; and concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, in which the understanding of many had been darkened, the darkness of error was removed so completely that, in our one Lord, true Son both of God and of man, there is no uncertainty either about the reality of his humanity or about the essence of his divinity.

The copies that we have sent will make known what sentence was pronounced against the impious authors of this unspeakable error, who, judging themselves unworthy of God’s grace, refused to make use of the remedies of correction [Note: [Col. 0989B] From the plural form, Sirmondus inferred that copies of other sentences as well had been sent—for example, against Eutyches and others, or on behalf of those who, after the false Synod of Ephesus, had been corrected and obtained peace at Chalcedon. But Leo speaks of copies of a single sentence, and in the Corbie and Pithoean codices a copy of only one sentence follows this letter of Leo. Just as Leo used the plural “letters” for a single letter from the Gauls in the preceding letters, chapter 1, so here he may have written “copies” for a copy of one sentence. Unless perhaps he sent several copies of the same sentence for distribution among many people, since he was writing this letter to bishops who had not been gathered at the synod but were residing in their own sees.], so that your affection, dearest brothers, may recognize that divine judgment was not absent from the holy tribunal: punishment was assigned to the obstinate, and peace was granted to those who had been corrected. May the Lord keep you safe, dearest brothers.

1142 **Copy of the sentence** [Note: [Col. 0989C] This sentence, absent from the ancient editions of Leo and from manuscript collection 12, had already been published by Crabbe in the older editions of the Councils, at the end of the acts of Chalcedon. Sirmondus was the first to append it to this letter of Leo, having found it attached to the letter in the Corbie and Pithoean codices. Leo himself testifies that it was sent to Gaul together with the letter, in these words: “The copies that we have sent will make known what sentence was pronounced” (“we have sent” is used by the holy pontiff in his customary manner for “we send”). [Col. 0989D] There is therefore no doubt that this copy attached to the letter in Gallic manuscripts is the one Leo transmitted to Gaul. The same sentence, pronounced by the pontifical legates, is read inserted in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, act 3, volume IV of the Councils, p. 1303, Venetian edition. Although the text presented here agrees in substance with the Greek text and with the ancient version of the same council, it differs considerably in wording. That ancient translation of the entire council is later than Leo. We have shown in note 14 (Col. 979, note c) to Letter 101 that immediately after the council certain principal documents of it were translated into Latin. Whether this Latin copy of the sentence, transmitted by Leo to the Gauls, is a translation from the Greek text inserted in the acts of the council—which differs greatly in wording from this Latin sentence—or whether it is the original Latin text, undoubtedly issued in Latin by the legates and brought with them to Rome, which was rendered into Greek at the synod either by Paschasinus, who knew Greek, or by others, is left to the judgment of others.
