It is remarkable that Quesnellus, in his observations on this letter, asserted that it was superfluous to extract this document from the manuscript codices because Crabbe had published it long before. Since, however, it had been published separately from Leo’s letters at the end of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon, where it was incorrectly called a letter, it was necessary to reprint it from the manuscripts in its proper place after Leo’s letter and under its proper title, “sentence.” Quesnellus disliked this title. “The title is misleading,” he says, “because it calls it a sentence, whereas it is only a vote preliminary to a sentence.” Incorrectly: for the acts of the council themselves make clear that, at the insistence of the Fathers, the legates pronounced and promulgated a sentence, to which other bishops subsequently adhered in their speeches and subscriptions. Paschasinus asked the synod not about a vote but about a sentence to be pronounced against Dioscorus, saying: “Does your holiness command that we employ an ecclesiastical sentence against him?” The holy synod said: “We agree.” And Julian, bishop of Hypaepa, addressing the legates, added among other things: “We ask your holiness—or rather, you who hold the place of the most holy Pope Leo—to promulgate against him and to pronounce against him the sentence implanted in the canons. For all, and the entire universal synod, are made one in agreement with the sentence of your holiness.” Maximus of Antioch said: “Whatever seems good to your holiness, we too agree.” [Col. 0990D] After this, all the legates together, in the name of Leo, who possesses the authority of blessed Peter, deposed and condemned Dioscorus in words that most clearly express a sentence properly so called. Evagrius likewise, in book II, chapter 4, where he relates the history of the Council of Chalcedon, and in chapter 18, where he summarizes its acts, plainly reports the words of the legates of the Apostolic See not as a mere speech but as a true sentence. Quesnellus himself, in note 2 to Letter 86, now 113, admits that Leo transmitted to the Gauls a copy of the sentence against both Eutyches and Dioscorus; these words refer to this letter of Leo and to this sentence.]

Bishop Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, [Note: [Col. 0990D] Sirmondus, from his codices: “of Lucentium.”] Bishop Lucentius of Asculum, and Boniface, priest of the Church of the great city of Rome, vicars of the most holy and blessed Pope Leo, bishop of the Apostolic See, pronounced:

It is evident what Dioscorus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, committed against the discipline of the canons and the ecclesiastical rules by his unlawful presumption, as the record of the past proceedings and the present statement have shown [Note: [Col. 0990D] The ancient version expresses this more clearly from the Greek, in act 3 of the Council of Chalcedon, volume IV, p. 1303, as follows: “Both from what was examined earlier in the former session”—that is, act 1—“and from what has been done today.”].

For, to pass over many matters, he is known to have received Eutyches, his accomplice in impiety, who had been lawfully condemned by his own bishop, Flavian of holy memory, into communion, before he sat with the bishops who had assembled in the city of Ephesus. To those men, indeed, the Apostolic See granted pardon, because it is judged that what they had done was contrary to their intention; and to this day they remain attached both to the most blessed Pope and to the universal and holy council. For this reason they obtained the remedy of sacred communion.

But the aforesaid man, who thinks that he is adorned by persevering in evils, although he ought with lowered face to bow to the ground with a groan, as is fitting—since he did not even permit the letter of the most blessed pope, written to Flavian of venerable memory, bishop of Christ, to be read [Col. 0990B]—when those who had brought it asked him to allow it to be read, refused to fulfill, under oath, what he had promised. Thus the impiety of a depraved doctrine might be increased, and an occasion of injury or scandal might be generated for all the churches.

Nevertheless, after these deeds, we wished to overlook these crimes and graciously extend to him the pardon granted to the other bishops, since they were not found to have displayed a like audacity in judging [Note: [Col. 0991C] Sirmondus has *reperiatur* in the text and Quesnellus in the margin. We preferred *reperiantur*, because in the Greek this refers to the other bishops, to whom pardon was granted because they did not have a judicial case similar to Dioscorus’s.] [Note: [Col. 0991C] The sense of the Greek and of the ancient version requires *accessit* to be corrected; but without manuscript evidence we did not wish to alter the text. Moreover, after *fiduciam* and before *adjecit*, or *accessit*, words are known to have dropped out from the same Greek text. We append them here from the ancient version: “But because by his subsequent offenses he has far surpassed his former iniquity—for he also presumed to dictate excommunication against the most holy and blessed archbishop of great Rome, Leo.” It is then added that written accusations had been presented against Dioscorus, to which the following refers: “There was also added the petition of the accusers, filled with various charges.”].

The petition of the accusers, filled with various charges, was also added; and when summoned a third time by our most reverend brothers and fellow bishops through canonical admonition, he refused to come, held back by the secret of his conscience. He also unlawfully received bishops who had been justly condemned by the provincial synod to which they were subject, and by this wrongful usurpation provoked the sentence of condemnation against himself, repeatedly trampling on the statutes of the ancient Fathers.

Therefore the holy and most blessed Pope Leo, head of the universal Church, through us his vicars, with the holy synod consenting, endowed with the dignity of the apostle Peter—who is called the foundation [Note: [Col. 0991D] Elsewhere: “the foundation stone.”] and rock of the Church and the keeper of the heavenly kingdom—stripped him of episcopal dignity and excluded him from every priestly function. It remains for the venerable synod, once assembled, to pronounce against the aforesaid Dioscorus the canonical sentence demanded by justice.

## LETTER CIV

[Note: [Col. 0991D] Elsewhere numbered 88. The letter formerly numbered 104 is now 130. Written 22 May 452.]

[Note: [Col. 0991D] It is found in manuscripts of collections 5 Hispanic, 16 and 18 of Isidore, and the following through 24, as well as in Sichardus’s copy. It replies to Letter 100. The Greek version is here printed for the first time from Vatican Greek manuscript 1455.]

### TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

[Note: [Col. 0991D] This title is found in manuscripts of collection 5, chapter 90. In the Hispanic version it reads: “In which he congratulates him on his faith, [Col. 0992C] concerning what was accomplished at the Council of Chalcedon; and concerning Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, who at that same council wished, through intrigue and contrary to the decrees, to subject the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch to himself.”]

Concerning the ambition of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople. Through Bishop Lucian and the deacon Basil.

#### Synopsis

I. Concerning the victory of the faith and the usefulness of errors in the Church.  
II. Many evils arise from Anatolius’s ambition.  
III. The see of Constantinople, which is imperial, not apostolic, cannot be exalted by the humiliation of other sees.  
IV. He asks Marcian to restrain Anatolius’s ambition.  
V. Anatolius has drawn courage from his earlier excesses.

[Note: [Col. 0992] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: [Col. 0992C] In Leo’s editions after the Canisian edition and before Quesnellus, this heading is found: “Leo, bishop of Rome and of the universal Church, to the Emperor Marcian.” The Greek version reads: “To the most glorious and most humane son Marcian, Leo, archbishop of Rome.”]

Leo, bishop, to the Emperor Marcian.

### Chapter I

By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the whole Catholic Church have been multiplied, when the most destructive error was extinguished through the holy and glorious zeal of your clemency [Note: [Col. 0992C] The Regensburg codex reads: “and our labor has reached . . . its fulfillment.” It omits *vester* shortly afterward, as does the Vienna Hispanic manuscript and the Greek version.]; so that our labor might more quickly reach the desired outcome, which your principate, serving God, assisted both by faith and by authority.

For although, through the power of the Holy Spirit, amid whatever dissensions, the freedom of the Gospel had to be defended through the service of the Apostolic See, nevertheless the grace of God appeared more clearly, granting the world that, in the victory of truth, only the authors of violated faith should perish [Note: [Col. 0992D] So the Regensburg manuscript and both Vienna manuscripts of collection 5 and the Hispanic manuscript, together with other codices and the editions before Quesnellus, who reads “should be destroyed.”], and that its integrity should be restored to the Church.

The war that the enemy of our peace had stirred up [Note: [Col. 0992D] The same Regensburg manuscript reads “had provoked.” Later, *confractum est* appears in place of *confectum est* in both Vienna manuscripts and in manuscripts of collection 21.] was therefore brought to such a happy conclusion, with the Lord’s right hand fighting, that, with Christ triumphant, there was one victory for all the priests, and, as the light of truth shone forth, only the darkness of error with its advocates was driven away.

For just as, at the very resurrection of the Lord, much security was added for strengthening the beginnings of faith when certain apostles doubted the bodily reality of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0993C] So all our codices with Sichardus, except Vatican collection 24, manuscript 544, which, with the printed editions, reads “concerning the body of the Lord.”], and, by examining through sight and touch the impressions of the nails [Note: [Col. 0993C] The Vienna Hispanic manuscript reads “and by examining the wound”; the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and Isidore read “and by examining the wounds.”] and the wound of the lance, removed the uncertainty of all while they themselves doubted, so now also, while the unbelief of some is refuted, the hearts of all who were hesitant have been strengthened. What brought blindness to some has served the illumination of all [Note: [Col. 0993C] The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “the hearts of all who were hesitant have been confirmed.” Shortly afterward we have printed *proficit* rather than *profecit*, on the authority of the Regensburg manuscript, the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, and Vatican collection 11, since it fits better with *nunc quoque*.].

In this work your clemency rightly and justly rejoices [Note: [Col. 0993D] Another copy reads “may rejoice”; and shortly afterward, instead of “properly and truly,” another reads “piously.”], for it faithfully and properly took care that the Eastern Churches should not be harmed by the devil’s snares, but that everywhere more effective holocausts should be offered to appease God [Note: [Col. 0993D] In his first edition Quesnellus, with Raynaudus, read “should be offered up to the end.” The reading of his second edition is supported by the other printed editions and our codices.]: when, through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, the confession of the peoples, of the priests, and of the kings was one and the same, most glorious and most clement son, Emperor Augustus [Note: [Col. 0993D] The following five words are omitted by the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, the Regensburg manuscript, manuscripts of collection 24, and Sichardus. The Grimani and Thuane codices have only “Most glorious emperor.” The Greek version reads: “Most clement son and Emperor Augustus.”].

### Chapter II

When the matters for which so great an assembly of priests had taken place had been settled with a good and desirable outcome [Note: [Col. 0993D] Some copies read “having been completed,” in manuscripts of collections 11 and 21. Shortly afterward the Regensburg manuscript omits “by God.”], I am amazed and grieved that the peace of the universal Church, reformed by divine action, is again disturbed by the spirit of ambition.

Although my brother Anatolius appears to have acted for his own advantage in abandoning the error of those who ordained him and passing, through a salutary correction, into agreement with the Catholic faith, he ought nevertheless to have taken care that he not disturb, through any corrupt ambition [Note: [Col. 0994D] Some editions of Leo, together with manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus’s copy, read “through the desire for any wickedness.”], what he is known to have obtained through your favor [Note: [Col. 0994C] Editions of Leo before Quesnellus, together with the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, read “our favor.” Other codices cited by Quesnellus in note 2 read “your favor.” Only the Regensburg codex has “through a true benefit.” Shortly afterward, in chapter 3, it is said: “Through the aid of your piety and the consent of my favor he obtained the episcopate of so great a city.”].

For, keeping our eyes upon your faith and intervention, and since the beginnings of his consecration were wavering in accordance with those who ordained him, we wished to be more lenient toward him than strict, so that we might soothe through applied remedies all the disturbances that had been stirred up by the devil’s activity. These remedies ought to have made him moderate rather than immoderate.

Even if he had been lawfully and solemnly ordained on the basis of exceptional merits and the best judgment, he could nevertheless receive no support from any endorsements contrary to the reverence due to the paternal canons, contrary to the statutes of the Holy Spirit, and contrary to the examples of antiquity. I speak to a Christian, truly religious, and genuinely orthodox ruler: Bishop Anatolius greatly diminishes his own merit if he desires to increase by unlawful advancement.

1149 ### Chapter III

May the city of Constantinople possess, as we desire, its glory, and, under the protection of God’s right hand, enjoy the long continuance of your merciful rule. Yet the order of secular matters is one thing, and that of divine matters another; and no structure can be stable except upon that rock which the Lord placed as its foundation (Matthew 16:18) [Note: [Col. 0995D] Quesnellus inserted the adverb “of all”; we removed it on the authority of all our codices and also of the other editions. Likewise we removed from Quesnellus the adverb “but” placed before “its own,” since it is absent not only from the earlier printed editions but also from the better codices, the Regensburg manuscript, both Vienna manuscripts of collection 5 and the Hispanic manuscript, Vatican collection 24, and the Greek version.].

He loses what is his own who covets what is not owed to him. Let it be enough for the aforesaid man that, through the aid of your piety and the consent of my favor, he obtained the episcopate of so great a city. Let him not disdain the imperial city, which he cannot make an apostolic see; nor let him hope in any way that it can be increased through the offenses of others [Note: [Col. 0995D] Gratian, 25, question 2, chapter 2, cites this passage, with some alterations; before him it was cited by Anselm, book IV, chapter 2, and Deusdedit, book III, chapter 35, as we observed in Vatican manuscripts. It is generally applied to privileges granted not so much to churches as to monasteries, whereas Saint Leo speaks only of the privileges of churches decreed by the Fathers of Nicaea in canon 6.].

For the privileges of the Churches, established by the canons of the holy Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable Council of Nicaea, cannot be overthrown by any wickedness or altered by any novelty [Note: [Col. 0995D] So all our codices and the printed editions, except Quesnellus, who has “violated.”].

In faithfully carrying out this work, with Christ’s help, it is necessary for me to show persevering service; for an administration has been entrusted to me, and it tends toward my own condemnation if the rules of the paternal ordinances, which were established at the Council of Nicaea for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of God’s Spirit, should be violated while I, God forbid, look on passively; and if, in my judgment, the will of one brother should be greater than the common welfare of the entire household of the Lord.

### Chapter IV

Therefore, knowing that your glorious clemency is devoted to ecclesiastical harmony and offers most piously its consent to those things that promote peaceful unity, I ask and earnestly beseech you to withhold from your whole pious approval any shameless attempts contrary to Christian unity and peace, and to restrain with salutary firmness my brother Anatolius’s ambition—harmful to him if he persists [Col. 0995C]—so that, desiring what is hostile to your glory and to your times, he may not wish to be greater than those who came before him.

Let him be free to shine with as many virtues as he can; he will share in them only if he wishes to be adorned more by charity than stretched out by ambition.

He ought never to have received this conception of shameless desire within the secrecy of his heart. But when my brothers and fellow bishops, who were present in my place, opposed him [Note: [Col. 0996D] The Hispanic Vienna manuscript adds “also.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts add “dearest.”], he ought at least to have withdrawn from his unlawful desire in consequence of their salutary opposition [Note: [Col. 0996D] The Regensburg manuscript omits “at least” and has “saving” instead of “salutary.” Both Vienna codices omit “salutary.” Vatican collection 11 omits both “at least” and “salutary.”].

For both the written communications of your piety and his own letters show that, as was proper, they resisted the legates of the Apostolic See with the most just opposition [Note: [Col. 0996D] The printed editions insert “to him”; we removed it on the authority of the Regensburg manuscript, the Vienna manuscript of collection 5, three other codices, Sichardus, and the Greek version.], so that the presumption would be all the less excusable because it did not restrain itself even after being rebuked [Note: [Col. 0997C] Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “would restrain itself.”].

### Chapter V

Therefore, since it accords with your faith [Note: [Col. 0997C] We restored the particle *vel*, omitted by Quesnellus, from all our codices and Sichardus. The Greek has “and with your glory.”] and glory that, just as heresy has been destroyed through God acting by you, so also every ambition should be blunted, do what is both Christianly upright and royal: let the aforesaid bishop obey the Fathers, consult the peace, and not think that he was permitted what he presumed to do without any precedent against the established rules, namely, to ordain a bishop for the Church of Antioch [Note: [Col. 0997D] We have added this from the same codices and the Greek text.]. We have not ceased to reconsider this out of love for the restoration of faith and zeal for peace.

Let him therefore abstain from injuring ecclesiastical rules and avoid unlawful transgressions, lest, while he attempts things hostile to peace, he sever himself from the universal Church [Note: [Col. 0997D] Another copy reads “depart.”]. I would rather love him acting irreproachably than see him persist in this presumption, which may separate him from everyone.

My brother and fellow bishop Lucian, who brought me the letters of your clemency together with my son Basil, the deacon, fulfilled with complete devotion the embassy entrusted to them [Note: [Col. 0997D] The Regensburg codex reads: “who must not be judged to have been absent from the matter, whom the cause abandoned.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read: “whom we know not to have been absent from the matter, whom rather the cause abandoned.”], for he must not be thought to have failed in the matter whom the cause itself rather abandoned.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious Herculanus. [Note: [Col. 0997D] Only the Vienna manuscript of collection 5 has “the twelfth day before the Kalends of June.”]

### Greek version

To the most glorious and most humane son Marcian, Leo, archbishop of Rome.

By the great gift of God’s mercy [Note: [Col. 0992D] Read: *ἐλεημοσύνης* (“mercy”).], the joy of the whole Catholic Church has been multiplied, when the most destructive error was extinguished through the zeal of your holy and most glorious humanity, so that our labor might quickly come to fulfillment, a labor which you, serving God through your imperial authority and faith, assisted [Note: [Col. 0992D] This passage is not entirely corrupt, but does not correspond to Leo’s text.].

For although, through the power of the Holy Spirit, amid dissensions, liberty had to be defended through the Apostolic See, nevertheless the grace of God appeared more brightly, and the Church received back its own purity.

The war which the enemy of our peace had stirred up was brought to so fortunate an end, while the Lord’s right hand fought, that, with Christ triumphant, the victory of all the holy ones was one; and, as the light of truth shone forth, only the errors of darkness were expelled together with their teachers [Note: [Col. 0992D] The reading should be “with Christ triumphing.”].

At the resurrection, great assurance came for the confirmation of the beginnings of faith—for certain apostles doubted the bodily reality of the sovereign Christ, and, by examining through sight and touch the marks of the nails and the wound of the lance, removed the doubt from all while they doubted—so now likewise, when the unbelief of some is refuted, the hearts of all who are doubtful have been firmly established, and what brought blindness upon some has served the illumination of all [Note: [Col. 0992D] The passage is mutilated and badly transmitted. It could be corrected as follows: “For as at the resurrection of the Lord . . . it came about, because certain apostles . . .”].

In this work your majesty rightly and justly exults, for you faithfully and deliberately took care that the Eastern Churches should not be harmed by the devil’s plot, but that acceptable holocausts might everywhere be offered to appease God; when, through the mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, the confession of the peoples was one, and that of the priests was one [Note: [Col. 0994D] The passage is defective; one might supply: “and that of the kings would likewise be one.”], and that of the kings was also one, most tranquil son and Emperor Augustus.

But when these matters had reached such a successful outcome and the synod had been brought to a good and desirable conclusion [Note: [Col. 0994D] The passage is extremely corrupt. It may be repaired as follows: “But concerning these things, on account of which so great a synod . . .”], I marvel and suffer because ambition’s renewed assault disturbs the peace of the Catholic Church, founded by God.

For although my brother Anatolius appears to have acted most usefully for himself by abandoning the error of those who ordained him and passing into understanding of the Catholic Church through a saving correction [Note: [Col. 0994D] Read “him.”], he nevertheless ought to have taken care that he not disturb by any base desire what he is seen to have obtained through your grace [Note: [Col. 0994D] At first, from Vatican Greek manuscript 1455, we transcribed “our grace” and noted that perhaps “your grace” should be read, so that it would correspond to the Latin. We later inserted this reading into the text on the authority of Vatican manuscript Ottobonianus 29.].

For we, keeping in view your faith and intervention, when the beginnings of his own ordination were faltering according to the authority of those who ordained him [Note: [Col. 0994D] Read “according to the authority of . . .”], wished to be good toward him rather than merely just, so that, by applying remedies, we might calm all the disturbances that had been stirred up by the devil’s activity. These ought to have made him gentle rather than immoderate.

Even if he had been lawfully and customarily ordained on the basis of certain exceptional deeds and the finest judgment, he ought nevertheless not to have been supported in any way against the paternal canons, against the patterns of the Holy Spirit, or against the examples of antiquity. I speak to a Christian, truly devout and orthodox emperor: Archbishop Anatolius greatly diminishes his own worth if he hopes to increase through unlawful advancement.

May Constantinople possess, as we wish, its own glory, and, while God’s right hand watches over it, enjoy your long-reigning empire [Note: [Col. 0996D] Perhaps “may it enjoy.”]. But the order of secular affairs is one thing and that of divine affairs another, and no structure whatsoever can be strong apart from that rock which the Lord placed as its foundation [Note: [Col. 0996D] Read “will be.”].

He destroys what is his own who desires what is not owed to him.

[Note: [Col. 0996D] Perhaps: *ἀρκέσῃ*.]

Let it suffice the aforesaid man that, through the help of your piety and the zeal of my agreement, he obtained the episcopate of so great a city. Let him not disdain to possess an imperial city which he cannot make an apostolic see; nor let him hope in any way that it can be increased through offending others [Note: [Col. 0996D] Read: “nor let him hope in any way that what can be increased through offending others . . .,” or, “nor let him hope in any way that it can be increased through offending others.”].

For the privileges of the holy Churches, established by the canons of the Fathers and fixed by the decrees of the venerable council at Nicaea, can be torn away by no shamelessness, nor altered by any novelty.

In this work, which Christ assists and which is to be faithfully carried through, it is necessary for me to apply persevering zeal. For an administration has been entrusted to me, and it tends toward my condemnation if the canons of the paternal decrees, which at the Council of Nicaea were established for the governance of the whole Church under the instruction of the Spirit of God, should be shaken while I, God forbid, acquiesce. May the opinion of one brother never be greater in my eyes than the common welfare of the entire household of the Lord.

And therefore, knowing that your glorious serenity is devoted to ecclesiastical harmony and offers devout consent to what accords with peaceful unity, I beg and earnestly entreat you to reject from the whole approval of your piety the shameless enterprises opposed to Christian unity and peace [Note: [Col. 0996D] Read “approval.”], and to restrain in a salutary manner my brother Anatolius’s desire, harmful to himself if he persists, so that, desiring things hostile to your glory and to your times, he may not wish to be greater than those who are already first.

Let him be free to shine with whatever virtues he wishes; he will be a participant in them only if he wishes to be adorned by disposition rather than extended by ambition [Note: [Col. 0996D] Perhaps “will be.”].

He ought never to have held this shameless desire in his soul. But when my brothers and fellow bishops, acting in my place, opposed him, he ought at least to have ceased from his unlawful boldness because of their opposition.

For both the syllables of your piety and his own letters indicate that, as was proper, they resisted the envoys of the Apostolic See with the most just opposition, so that the enterprise could not have an excuse—an enterprise that, even when established, did not restrain itself.

Therefore, since it accords with our faith and glory that, just as heresies have been destroyed through you, with God acting, so also every ambition should be cut away [Note: [Col. 0998D] Something is missing here, perhaps “has been destroyed” or something similar], do what is both a credit to Christians and royal.

And let the aforesaid bishop spare the Fathers and take thought for peace [Note: [Col. 0998D] The passage is wholly corrupt. To restore some sense, one should read: “let him spare the Fathers and take thought for peace.” Do not be surprised that the translator renders *φειδέσθω τῶν πατέρων* as “let him obey the Fathers,” for, as we suppose, he read *parcat Patribus* instead of the text’s *pareat Patribus*.], and let him not assume that everything is permitted to him.

For he dared to ordain a bishop for the Church of Antioch without any precedent and contrary to the canons; this we have undertaken to reconsider out of love for the renewal of faith and zeal for peace [Note: [Col. 0998D] Perhaps “we ceased.”].

Let him therefore abstain from insulting the ecclesiastical canons and avoid unlawful transgressions, lest, while he attempts what is hostile to peace, he sever himself from the Catholic Church. We pray that we may love him acting without reproach rather than see him persist in this boldness, which can separate him from everyone.

My brother and fellow bishop Lucian, who carried to me the letters of your serenity together with my son Basil the deacon, fulfilled with complete devotion the embassy entrusted to them. He cannot be considered to have failed in the matter whom the matter itself rather abandoned.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious Herculanus.

## LETTER CV

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Elsewhere numbered 79. The letter formerly numbered 105 is now 134. Written 22 May 452.]

[Note: [Col. 0997D] Found in manuscripts of collections 12, 18, 19, and 24, and in Sichardus’s copy.]

### TO THE AUGUSTA PULCHERIA

Concerning the ambition of Anatolius.

#### Synopsis

I. The victory of the faith is complete, in which both those who fell and those who stood have prevailed.  
II. Nothing can prevail against the Nicene canons, which alone suffice to secure peace.  
III. Flavian ought to be an example to Anatolius; and whatever is contrary to the Council of Nicaea collapses of itself.  
IV. He exhorts her herself to recall Anatolius from his purpose.

Leo, bishop, to the Augusta Pulcheria.

### Chapter I

We rejoice ineffably with your piety over the holy and God-pleasing efforts of your clemency, through which the Catholic faith was defended against the heretics and peace was restored to the universal Church. We give thanks to the merciful and almighty God [Note: [Col. 0997D] Editions before Quesnellus, together with manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, read “to the mercy of almighty God.”], because, except for those who loved darkness more than light (John 3:19), he allowed no one to be deprived of the truth of the Gospel.

Thus, when the fog of error had been wiped away, the purest light arose in all hearts [Note: [Col. 0998C] The Venetian manuscript of collection 12 reads “lest that enemy should exult over the weakness”; the Regensburg manuscript reads “and lest that dark enemy should exult over the infirmity”—perhaps “of the weakened” hearts of some.], and that dark enemy did not exult over the weakness of anyone’s spirit. He was overcome not only by those who stood unharmed but also by those whom he had made change [Note: [Col. 0998D] We have added “those” from the Regensburg manuscript.].

Thus, error having been abolished, true faith might reign throughout the world, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:11) [Note: [Col. 0998D] The same Regensburg manuscript reads “because the Lord Jesus is in glory.”].

Now that the whole world has been confirmed in the unity of the Gospel and the hearts of all the priests have been directed toward the same understanding [Note: [Col. 0998D] This is better according to the same Regensburg manuscript. Quesnellus has “directed toward the same meaning.” Other editions read “in the same spirit.”], it would have been best that, beyond the matters for which the holy synod was assembled and which, according to the zeal of your piety, have been concluded with an admirable result, nothing contrary to so great a good should be introduced, nor, under the pretext of an episcopal council, should something be rashly sought which was not lawful to desire.

### Chapter II
For my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, having given little thought to how great a benefit of your piety, and how great an assent of my favor, had secured for him the priesthood of the Church of Constantinople, was kindled not so much by joy at what he had attained as by an excessive desire for what exceeded the measure of his rank. He believed that this immoderate ambition could be advanced by the coerced signature which, it is said, certain men had given him with their consent.

[Note: Quesnellus added the word “his”; our manuscripts also confirm it. In Sichardus: “to advance the consent of certain persons, which is said to have been offered him.”]

Yet, as his efforts were soon to be destroyed, the opposition of my brothers and fellow bishops, who faithfully and commendably acted in my place, stood in his way.

[Note: Thus the Ratisbon manuscript, with Quesnellus; before him it read “acting in my place.” Soon afterward the Ratisbon manuscript has “would have opposed.”]

For no one is permitted to dare anything against the provisions of the fathers’ canons, founded long ago in the city of Nicaea by spiritual decrees, so that, if anyone wishes to decree something different, he diminishes himself rather than corrupting them. If these provisions are preserved inviolate by all bishops, as they ought to be, there will be peaceful tranquility and firm concord throughout all the Churches: there will be no disagreements concerning the measure of honors,

[Note: The commonly printed editions, together with manuscript collection 24, read “concerning the measure of these honors.” Quesnellus’s reading is supported by our Ratisbon and Venetian manuscripts.]

no disputes concerning ordinations, no uncertainties concerning privileges, and no conflicts concerning the usurpation of what belongs to another.

[Note: The same commonly printed editions read “concerning another’s [property].” All our manuscripts and Sichardus confirm Quesnellus’s correction.]

Rather, with the equal law of charity, the proper order of conduct and duties shall be preserved; and he will truly be great who is free from every ambition. For the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your minister; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant: just as the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20:26; Mark 10:43).

[Note: Earlier editions, before Quesnellus, together with Sichardus, read: “But that observance also promises that his mind will be joined to him, and that the love of the Apostolic See, which we have always shown to the Church of Constantinople, will not be violated by any change.” The Victor manuscript, cited by Quesnellus in his notes, and one of our Fesulan manuscripts prefer the same reading, merely omitting the final word, “unanimity.” The same appears in Vatican Regina manuscript 139, collection 24, which has only at the end: “and the measure of duties shall be preserved.” We have followed the reading of the better manuscripts, the Grimanic collection 18 and the Ratisbon collection 19, and the Vatican and Venetian collection 12. We do not know why Quesnellus abandoned this sufficiently good and clear reading in order to substitute another apparently composed by him from all the variants: “But the order which is reasonable by the law of charity, and of conduct and duties, shall be preserved.”]

Yet these things were being suggested at that time to those who wished to grow from a small beginning and pass from the lowest rank to the highest.

But what more does the bishop of the Church of Constantinople desire than what he has attained? Or what will satisfy him if the magnificence and renown of so great a city are not enough? It is excessively proud and immoderate to reach beyond one’s own boundaries, to trample on antiquity, and to wish to seize another’s right; and, in order that the dignity of one man may increase, to attack the primacies of so many metropolitans, and to bring the war of a new disturbance upon provinces that are at peace and were long ago arranged by the moderation of the holy synod of Nicaea; and, so that the decrees of the venerable Fathers may be dissolved, to produce the consent of certain bishops, whom the long succession of so many years denied any effective result.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript has “and so that,” both here and shortly afterward.]

For it is said that nearly sixty years have passed since this connivance,

[Note: The older printed editions, together with Sichardus, read “of this boastfulness.”]

by which the aforesaid bishop thinks himself assisted, vainly desiring that what no one, even if he dared to wish it, could obtain, should benefit him.

## CHAPTER III

Let him recognize the man whom he succeeded, and, rejecting every spirit of pride, imitate the faith, the modesty, and the humility of Flavian, which raised him even to the glory of a confessor.

[Note: The excellent Ratisbon manuscript suggested adding the words “the faith of Flavian.”]

If he wishes to shine by Flavian’s virtues, he will be praiseworthy and will acquire abundant affection everywhere—not by pursuing human advantages, but by earning divine favor.

By this observance I also promise that my mind will be joined to his, and that the love of the Apostolic See, which it has always bestowed upon the Church of Constantinople, will not be violated by any change.

[Note: This is the reading of the Grimanic, Ratisbon, and Venetian manuscripts, with Quesnellus. The older printed editions of Leo, together with Sichardus, read: “But this observance promises that each person’s mind will be joined to him,” and so forth. The Vatican manuscript, collection 24, has the same reading, except that it reads “my” for “him.” The edition of the Councils reads: “But this observance promises that the mind of each person will be joined to him,” and so forth, as in those editions of Leo.]

For even if bishops who are immoderate sometimes fall into certain faults, the integrity of Christ’s Churches nevertheless endures.

[Note: The printed editions read “complete grace.” We have inserted the excellent reading from the Ratisbon manuscript.]

But the agreements of bishops that conflict with the rules of the holy canons established at Nicaea, with the united devotion of your faith and ours, we annul, and by the authority of blessed Peter the Apostle we cancel them by an entirely general decision, obeying in all ecclesiastical matters the laws which the Holy Spirit established for the peaceful observance of all bishops through the three hundred and eighteen prelates;

[Note: See our observations in note 2 of Quesnellus. Shortly afterward, the editions before Quesnellus lacked the word “matters,” which is also found in our manuscripts. The Ratisbon manuscript lacks the word “these.”]

so that even if many more should decree something different from what those men established,

[Note: Before Quesnellus, the printed editions read: “if others should decree something different from what those men established,” or, as in the Venetian manuscript, “should wish to decree.”]

nothing contrary to the constitution of the aforesaid Fathers is to be held in any reverence.

## CHAPTER IV

I therefore ask that your piety graciously receive the length of my letter, in which I have necessarily explained my judgment, through my brother and fellow bishop Lucian, who, insofar as it depended on him, faithfully carried out the responsibility of the embassy he undertook, and through my son Basil, the deacon.

And because it is your custom to labor for the peace and unity of the Church, beneficially restrain my brother Bishop Anatolius, whom your communication has made dear to me, from those things that would be advantageous to him:

[Note: Quesnellus inserted the word “to me”; it is also found in the Ratisbon manuscript.]

so that the glory of your clemency may be proclaimed as much for ambition restrained as it is magnified for faith restored.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the illustrious man Herculanus.

# LETTER CVI

[Note: Also numbered 80. What was formerly 106 is now 135. Written on 22 May 452.]

## TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He rebukes him for ambition.

[Note: It survives in manuscript collections 5 of the Spanish collection, 11, 12, 16, and 18 through 24, as well as in Vallicellian manuscript 18, title 398, and in Sichardus’s copy. We also found a Greek version in Vatican Greek manuscript 1455, from which we now publish it for the first time. In this letter Leo replies to Anatolius’s Letter 101. In the aforementioned Vallicellian manuscript the following title is prefixed: “Letter of Saint Leo the Pope to Anatolius, who was ordained in place of Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, after Saint Flavian had been sent into exile.” It should have added: “and had died on the way.”]

[Col. 1001]

## SUMMARY

[Note: In the table of collection 5, chapter 91, this synopsis is found: “To Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople: a rebuke concerning his ambition, and concerning the ancient honor of the Alexandrian and Antiochene sees, which is given precedence.” In the Spanish collection it reads: “First he praises the same bishop for his faith at the Council of Chalcedon; then he rebukes him because he had wished to subject the Churches of Alexandria and Antioch to himself against the Council of Nicaea.”]

I. Anatolius’s faith is to be praised, but his ambition condemned.  
II. The prerogative of the Council of Nicaea, which Anatolius’s ambition seeks.  
III. His abuse of the Council of Chalcedon, which was convened solely for the matter of faith.  
IV. He will never consent to unlawful attempts prejudicial to the Council of Nicaea.  
V. The canons of the Council of Constantinople were never sent to the Roman See and provide Anatolius with no valid support.  
VI. It is better for him to lay aside ambition and pursue charity.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: From the Greek: “To the most beloved brother Anatolius, archbishop of Constantinople. Leo, archbishop of Rome.”]

## LEO, BISHOP, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP

## CHAPTER I

When, as we desired, the light of evangelical truth has been made manifest through the grace of God, and the night of the most destructive error has been driven away from the universal Church, we rejoice unspeakably in the Lord that the labor of the stewardship entrusted to us has reached its desired result, as the wording of your letter also declares: so that, according to apostolic teaching, we may all say the same thing, and there may be no divisions among us, but that we may be perfect in the same understanding and in the same knowledge (1 Corinthians 1:10).

[Note: The phrase “of evangelical truth” is absent from the Vindebon collection 5 and the Vallicellian manuscript.]

In devotion to this work we rejoice that your affection is our partner, so that your diligence might benefit those who needed correction and that you might cleanse yourself from all participation with those who deviate.

[Note: The Vindebon collection 5, Ratisbon manuscript, and manuscript collections 11 and 24, together with the older printed editions and Sichardus, have this better reading; the Greek translation agrees. Quesnellus reads “from everyone.” After the word “participation,” the older editions and Sichardus add “and faction.” Five of Quesnellus’s manuscripts and eleven of ours, as well as the Greek version, omit it.]

For when your predecessor, Flavian of blessed memory, was expelled because of his defense of the catholic faith, it was not without reason believed that those who ordained you, contrary to the provisions of the holy canons, appeared to have consecrated one like themselves.

But God’s mercy intervened, guiding and strengthening you for this purpose, so that you might use your bad beginnings well and show that you had advanced not by human judgment but by God’s kindness. This must truly be understood in that way if you do not lose the grace of this divine gift through another offense.

[Note: Distinction 47, “The Catholic Man,” chapter 6.]

For a catholic man, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought no more to be entangled in any error than to be corrupted by any desire.

For Holy Scripture says: “Do not follow your desires, and restrain yourself from your will” (Ecclesiasticus 18:30).

[Note: The Barb. collection 16 and Vatican collection 24 read “do not follow them.” Shortly afterward, the Vindebon, Spanish, Ratisbon, and Vallicellian manuscripts, and two collection-21 manuscripts together with the editions before Quesnellus, read “to turn away,” instead of “to restrain”; Quesnellus introduced the latter from four of his manuscripts, and six others of ours together with Sichardus support it.]

One must resist the many allurements of this world and its many vanities, so that the integrity of true self-control may be attained. Its first stain is pride, the beginning of transgression and the source of sin.

For a mind greedy for power knows neither how to abstain from what is forbidden nor how to rejoice in what is permitted. As it advances in a disordered and wicked course, the excesses of unpunished transgressions increase, and the faults multiply—faults that were tolerated for the sake of restoring the faith and out of love for concord.

## CHAPTER II

After those beginnings of your ordination that were not without blame,

[Note: The beginnings are called blameworthy because of Dioscorus, who had deposed Saint Flavian and received Eutyches. See more in Quesnellus’s note 1.]

and after the ordination of the bishop of Antioch, which you claimed for yourself against canonical rule,

[Note: Anatolius had ordained Maximus to the Antiochene see. Since that see did not belong to the bishop of Constantinople, such an ordination was contrary to canonical rule. By “canonical rule” one may understand either the canons of Nicaea, which command that the privileges of each province be preserved, or any other canons, or the custom of the Churches, as Quesnellus discusses in note 2; the point is essentially the same. Shortly afterward the Vindebon collection 5 and the Vallicellian manuscript read “advanced” instead of “fell.” The same Vallicellian manuscript then has “you try,” perhaps “you may try.”]

I grieve that in this matter also your affection has fallen, so that you attempted to violate the most sacred constitutions of the canons of Nicaea, as though this were an opportune time for you, when the Alexandrian see had lost the privilege of second honor and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of third rank;

[Note: The Vindebon and Spanish manuscripts read “according to the privilege of second honor.” The Vatican Spanish manuscript and another Vatican manuscript of collection 11 read “by the privilege of its honor.” The Vatican Isidorean manuscript reads “by the privilege of its second honor.”]

so that, with these places subjected to your jurisdiction, all metropolitan bishops would be deprived of their proper honor.

You are so carried away by these unheard-of and previously unattempted excesses that you drag the holy synod, convened through the zeal of the most Christian emperor solely to extinguish heresy and confirm the catholic faith, into an opportunity for ambition, and press it to surrender its acquiescence to you;

[Note: The printed editions of Leo and Sichardus, together with manuscript collections 5 and 24, read “give.” We preferred the common reading of the Councils, found in the Ratisbon manuscript, both Spanish manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorean manuscript, and manuscript collections 11 and 21. Earlier, the Ratisbon, Grimanic, and some other manuscripts read “restraint” instead of “acquiescence”; the Vallicellian manuscript and Facundus read “restriction.” Shortly afterward, two manuscripts of Vatican collection 21 read “he wished” instead of “he will have wished.”]

as though what the multitude may have unlawfully wished could not be rejected, and as though the arrangement established by the Holy Spirit through the canons of Nicaea could truly be dissolved in any part by anyone.

[Note: The Vatican collection 11 omits “truly.” Shortly afterward, the older editions, together with five of our manuscripts, read “ever” instead of “for anyone.” The better books—the two Vindebon manuscripts, the Vallicellian, Ratisbon, Grimanic, and manuscripts of collection 24—have “for anyone,” with Quesnellus and Sichardus. Then, for “soluble,” both Spanish manuscripts, the Isidorean, and the Barbian read “dissoluble.”]

Let no synodal councils flatter themselves because of the multiplication of their assemblies, nor let any number of priests, however large, dare to compare or prefer itself to those three hundred and eighteen bishops. The Council of Nicaea was consecrated by such a divine privilege that, whether ecclesiastical judgments are held by fewer or by more persons, everything that differs from the constitution of those Fathers is entirely devoid of authority.

## CHAPTER III

These things, therefore, are exceedingly wicked and exceedingly wrong, because they are found to oppose the most sacred canons. This proud arrogance tends toward the disturbance of the whole Church. It wished to abuse the synodal council in such a way as either to corrupt the brothers, summoned solely for the matter of faith and having completed the definition of the case that had to be settled, into consenting to itself, or to compel them by intimidation.

[Note: The Grimanic manuscript, cited by Quesnellus in note 3, reads “having completed the definition of the case to be settled.” In Pelagius’s letter to Helias and the other bishops of Istria: “drawn into the matter of the definition that had to be settled.” All seventeen of our manuscripts from various collections prefer the common reading, which Quesnellus also found in other manuscripts of his. The passage is omitted in Sichardus’s copy. Shortly afterward the Vindebon Spanish manuscript omits “for himself.”]

For from there our brothers, sent from the Apostolic See, who presided over the synod in my place, commendably and steadfastly resisted unlawful attempts, openly protesting that no presumptuous innovation contrary to the constitutions of the Council of Nicaea should arise.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript omits “attempts.” Shortly afterward the same manuscript, together with the Vindebon collection 5 and the Vallicellian manuscript, reads “against the constitutions of Nicaea.” Manuscripts of collection 24, with Sichardus, read “against the institutions of Nicaea.” The Vindebon Spanish manuscript has “against the institutions of Nicaea,” corruptly written for “Nicaean,” though this may perhaps be the more correct reading.]

Nor can there be any doubt about their opposition, since in your letter you yourself complain about them, saying that they wished to obstruct your efforts. In this respect, by writing these things, you greatly commend them to me; but you accuse yourself because you did not wish to obey them, while undertaking unlawful actions, needlessly desiring what ought not to be granted and harmfully coveting what is contrary to you.

[Note: The Grimanic manuscript reads “you seek, and unwisely desire what is contrary.” Six of our manuscripts, together with the Greek text, similarly omit “for yourself.”]

These things will never be able to obtain the consent of any of us. Far be it from my conscience that such a wicked desire should be aided by my efforts, rather than being overthrown by the work both of myself and of all who do not set their minds on lofty things but agree with the humble.

## CHAPTER IV

Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after condemning the sacrilegious Arius together with his impiety in the city of Nicaea, established laws of ecclesiastical canons that would endure to the end of the world, live among us and throughout the whole world in their constitutions. If anything is ever presumed differently from what they established, it is canceled without hesitation,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “ever” instead of “anywhere.”]

so that what was established generally for perpetual usefulness may not be changed by any alteration,

[Note: Chapter 25, question 1: “Those things that are for perpetual [benefit].”]

nor may what was established for the common good be drawn into private advantage. While the boundaries established by the Fathers remain, let no one encroach upon another’s right;

[Note: Vatican collection 24 reads: “Let no one invade another’s right.” Sichardus and Merlinus have the same, except that they read “let him not” instead of “let no one.” The Vatican Spanish manuscript reads: “Let no one condemn another’s right.” In the Vatican Isidorean manuscript both readings are joined: “Let no one extend himself into another’s right and condemn it.”]

but within his own proper and legitimate limits, let each person exercise himself in the breadth of charity as far as he is able. The bishop of Constantinople can acquire very abundant fruits of this charity if he strives more through the virtue of humility than if he is inflated by the spirit of ambition.

[Note: The Vindebon Spanish manuscript reads “is filled.” This was corrected in the Vatican Spanish and Isidorean manuscripts to “may be filled.”]

## CHAPTER V

Do not think lofty thoughts, brother, but be afraid (Romans 11:20), and cease disturbing the most pious ears of the Christian emperors with wicked petitions. I am certain that you will please them more by modesty than by arrogance.

For the written document produced by certain bishops nearly sixty years ago, as you boast,

[Note: Anatolius says in Letter 101, chapter 4: “through sixty and seventy years.” More accurately, Lucentius, legate of the Apostolic See, reckoned eighty years in act 16 of the Council of Chalcedon: “It adds to the matter,” he says, “that, having set aside the constitutions of the three hundred and eighteen, they are known to have mentioned only the one hundred and fifty, who are not found in the synodal canons, saying that these had been established nearly eighty years earlier.”]

provides no support whatsoever for your persuasion. It was never sent by your predecessors to the knowledge of the Apostolic See,

[Note: There is extraordinary manuscript variation in this passage. The Ratisbon manuscript reads: “and information was never sent by your predecessors to the Apostolic See.” The Vindebon Spanish manuscript: “and never, because information was sent by your predecessors to the Apostolic See.” The Vatican Spanish and Isidorean manuscripts: “and never now—for ‘because’—information was sent to the Apostolic See.” The Grimanic manuscript, corruptly in Quesnellus’s note 4, has “with whom by your predecessors,” and so forth. One Thuane manuscript reads: “when you heard from your predecessors, long ago, and to the Apostolic See.” Two other Thuane manuscripts give the final words as: “information sent to the Apostolic See.” The Vindebon collection 5 reads: “lest, when from your predecessors,” and so forth. Two manuscripts of collection 21 read: “with some information sent by your predecessors to the Apostolic See.” Nevertheless, the words that follow in the context confirm the printed reading, supported by the other manuscripts, especially the Vallicellian and the Greek version: “For the document, already decayed and long since fallen into ruin, concerning the decree of the Fathers of Constantinople for the see of Constantinople is understood; it had in fact been unknown to the Roman See before this time, as we shall show elsewhere.”]

To this document, already rickety from its inception and long since collapsed, you wished now, late and uselessly, to add supports, eliciting from the brothers an appearance of consent which their exhausted sense of shame might offer you to their own injury.

Remember what the Lord threatens the one who causes one of these little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6; Mark 9:41), and understand wisely what judgment of God you will have to face, since you do not fear bringing scandal upon so many Churches and so many priests.

For I confess that I am bound by love for the whole brotherhood in such a way that I will absolutely agree with no one in matters that he seeks against himself. You can clearly recognize that I oppose your affection with a benevolent mind, so that by sounder counsel you may restrain yourself from disturbing the universal Church.

The rights of provincial primacies must not be overturned,

[Note: All manuscripts have this reading except Sichardus’s, which has “primacy.”]

nor may metropolitan bishops be deprived of privileges established in antiquity. Let nothing of the dignity that the Alexandrian See merited through Saint Mark the Evangelist, the blessed Peter’s disciple, perish; nor, with Dioscorus having fallen through the obstinacy of his impiety, let the splendor of so great a Church be obscured by foreign darkness.

Let the Church of Antioch also, in which, when blessed Peter the Apostle first preached, the Christian name arose,

[Note: The Vindebon collection 5 and the Vallicellian manuscript read “of Christians,” perhaps more correctly. The reference is to Acts 11:26, where it is said that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch; the passage, however, attributes this to the preaching of Paul and Barnabas, not Peter. Saint Leo himself explained his meaning sufficiently in Sermon 82, chapter 5, where, speaking of Peter who founded the Antiochene See, he says: “You had already founded the Church of Antioch, where the dignity of the Christian name first arose.”]

remain in the order of the constitution of the Fathers, and, placed in the third rank, never become inferior to itself.

[Note: The Vatican Spanish and Isidorean manuscripts omit “itself.” Shortly afterward the Ratisbon manuscript reads “weaker” instead of “inferior.”]

For the sees are one thing and those who preside over them another, and each person’s integrity is a great honor. Since integrity does not lose its proper distinction in any place, how much more glorious can it be in the magnificence of the city of Constantinople, if, through your observance of the canons and your defense of the ancestral canon, many priests may have an example of probity?

[Note: The Grimanic manuscript, cited by Quesnellus in note 6, and manuscripts of collection 24, together with the printed editions of the Councils, read: “and an example of probity for the defense of the ancestral canon.” We preferred the reading of the other manuscripts and editions, which seems to mean that through Anatolius’s observance there will be both a defense of the ancestral canons—that is, the Nicaean canons—and an example of probity for many priests. The Greek translation also has “ancestral canons.”]

## CHAPTER VI

Writing these things to you, brother, I exhort and admonish you in the Lord that, laying aside the desire for ambition, you should rather burn with the spirit of charity and be profitably adorned with its virtues according to apostolic teaching. For charity is patient and kind; it is not jealous, does not act wrongly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, and does not seek what belongs to itself (1 Corinthians 13:4).

Therefore, if charity does not seek what belongs to itself, how greatly does he sin who covets what belongs to another? I want you to abstain entirely from such things, and to remember the saying that declares: “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown” (Revelation 3:11).

For if you seek what has not been granted, you will deprive yourself, by your own action and judgment, of the peace of the universal Church.

My brother and fellow bishop Lucian, and my son Basil the deacon, insofar as it depended on them, diligently carried out what you had entrusted to them; but justice denied their action its result.

[Note: Only the Vindebon collection 5 reads “the twelfth day before the Kalends,” just as it alone gives the same day in Letter 104.]

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the illustrious man Herculanus.

## Greek Address

To the beloved brother Anatolius, archbishop of Constantinople, Leo, archbishop of Rome.

[Col. 1002A]

[Note: This conjunction is superfluous.]

When, as we prayed, the light of the evangelical truth had been made manifest through the grace of God, and the darkness of the most deadly error had been driven from the catholic Church, we rejoice unspeakably in the Lord that the labor of the stewardship entrusted to us has reached the desired result, as the form of your letter also indicates: so that, according to apostolic teaching, all may say the same thing, and there may be no divisions among you, but that we may be perfect in the same mind and in the same knowledge.

We rejoice that your affection is a fellow worker in this achievement, so that your diligence might benefit those who ought to be corrected, and that you might cleanse yourself from every fellowship with those who go astray.

For when your predecessor, Flavian of blessed memory, had been expelled for defending the catholic faith, it was not without reason believed that those who ordained you, contrary to the holy canons, appeared to have ordained you as one like themselves.

[Note: The word “as” is superfluous; read “of themselves.”]

[Note: This pronoun is superfluous and should therefore be deleted.]

But God’s mercy came first, bringing and strengthening you for this purpose, so that you might use your evil beginnings well and appear to have been ordained not by human judgment but by God’s goodness. This must truly be accepted in that way, if you do not lose the grace of this divine gift through another offense. For a catholic man, and especially a priest of the Lord, ought no more to be entangled in any error than to be corrupted by any desire.

[Note: Perhaps read: “For the divine Scripture cries out,” or something similar.]

The divine Scripture cries out: “Restrain your desires from your own will.” One must resist the many allurements of this world and its great vanity, so that the purity of true self-control may be attained. Its first destruction is pride, the beginning of transgression and the source of sins.

[Note: Delete this particle as redundant; then supply “the mind” or something similar.]

Since a mind desirous of power knows neither how to abstain from what is forbidden nor how to rejoice in what is permitted,

[Note: Something is missing here: either ὅταν (“when”) or something similar.]

in the consequent and wicked advance the paths of unpunished transgressions increase, and the sins grow dark—sins that were borne out of love for the renewal of the faith and concord.

After those blameworthy beginnings connected with your ordination, and after the ordination of the bishop of Antioch, which you claimed for yourself against the canonical regulations, I grieve that your affection has also slipped in this matter, so that you attempted to dissolve the divine enactments of the canons established at Nicaea; as though a suitable opportunity had been presented to you, when the Alexandrian throne had lost the privilege of second honor and the Church of Antioch had lost the prerogative of third rank,

[Note: Perhaps read “for which.”]

[Note: Perhaps read “might lose.”]

so that, with these places subjected to your jurisdiction, all the metropolitan bishops would be deprived of their own honor.

You have so advanced these unheard-of and never-before-attempted violations that you sought to draw the holy synod, assembled through the zeal of the most Christian emperor solely to extinguish heresy and confirm the catholic faith, into an opportunity for ambition, and to force it to combine with you, as though the multitude’s unlawful decision could not be overturned and as though the enactment of the canons established at Nicaea through the truly Holy Spirit could be dissolved in any part by anyone.

[Note: Read “itself.”]

Let no synodal council deceive itself because of the assembled multitude, nor let any number of priests dare either to compare itself with the three hundred and eighteen bishops or to prefer itself to them. The Council of Nicaea was assembled by such great grace of God that, whether ecclesiastical tribunals are constituted by fewer or by more persons, everything written against their enactment is deprived of all authority.

The things that oppose the divine canons are therefore exceedingly shameless and exceedingly wicked. This arrogance tends toward the disturbance of the whole Church. It wished to use the synod in such a way that it would lead the brothers summoned solely for the sake of the faith, and who had completed what had to be considered for that purpose, either into consenting to its deception or drive them by fear.

[Note: Read “its own deception.”]

For from there our brothers, sent by the Apostolic See, who represented me in the synod, commendably and bravely resisted the unlawful attempts, openly crying out that no shameless undertaking against the canons of Nicaea should arise.

Nor can there be any doubt that they resisted, since in your own writings you reproach them because they wished to oppose your attempts. By writing these things, you greatly commend them to me; but you accuse yourself because you did not endure obeying them while undertaking unlawful actions, needlessly seizing what was not permitted and unlawfully desiring those things that will never be able, through any deception, to obtain our consent.

[Note: Read “and unlawfully.”]

Far be it from our conscience that such a wicked desire should be assisted by my efforts, rather than being buried through the zeal both of myself and of all who do not think lofty thoughts but humble ones.

[Note: Supply “not.”]

Those holy and venerable Fathers who, after the sacrilegious Arius had been condemned together with his impiety in the city of Nicaea, established enduring laws of ecclesiastical canons live among us and throughout the whole world in their own enactments. If anything should ever be attempted otherwise than they decreed, it is abolished without hesitation.

[Note: This conjunction is redundant and should therefore be removed.]

And so that the things generally established for perpetual usefulness may not be violated by any alteration,

[Note: Read “usefulness.”]

nor be drawn into a private right when they were established for common benefit; while the boundaries fixed by the Fathers remain, let no one encroach upon another’s right. Rather, within his own proper and lawful boundaries, let each person exercise himself in the breadth of charity as far as he can. The bishop of Constantinople can obtain its flourishing fruits if he strives more through the virtue of humility than if he were inflated by the spirit of ambition.

Do not, brother, wish to think lofty thoughts, but be reverent, and cease troubling the pious ears of the Christian emperors with shameless petitions. We openly know that you will please them more by gentleness than by arrogance.

For the written document produced by certain bishops nearly sixty years ago, as you say, contributes nothing to your opinion, and it was never sent by your predecessors for the knowledge of the Apostolic See. You wished now to add supports to a beginning that was baseless and unstable, late and useless, eliciting from my brothers an appearance of consent which, to your injury,

[Note: Read “which,” or “your own.”]

[Note: Read “harassed.”]

their harassed modesty is understood to have offered you.

[Note: Perhaps read “is recognized.”]

Remember what the Lord threatens the one who causes one of these little ones to stumble, and understand wisely what sort of judgment of God you will enter, since you did not fear to place a stumbling block before so many Churches and so many priests.

For I confess that I am so held by love for the entire brotherhood that I agree absolutely with no one of them in those matters that they seek against themselves.

You will be able to recognize more clearly that I oppose your affection with a benevolent soul, so that you may restrain yourself from every ecclesiastical disturbance by sound reasoning.

Let the rights of the provincials not be displaced; let metropolitan bishops not be deprived of the privileges established from the beginning. Let nothing of the honor of the Alexandrian throne be lost—an honor that it was deemed worthy to receive through Saint Mark the Evangelist, the disciple of Saint Peter. Nor, because of Dioscorus, who fell through the insolence of his own impiety, should the light of so great a Church be dimmed by foreign darkness.

Let the Church of Antioch likewise remain in the enactment of the Fathers. In it, when the most blessed Apostle Peter first taught, the name of Christ began to be proclaimed.

[Note: Perhaps read “the name of Christians.”]

And, established in the third rank, let it never become less than itself.

[Note: This was rendered by the translator, but poorly. See Leo’s Latin text.]

For a throne is one thing and a presiding office another, and each person’s own purity is a great honor. Since this purity does not lose its proper place in whatever places it may be, how much more illustrious can its magnificence be in the city of Constantinople?

[Note: This too is incorrect; it should have been translated: “How much more illustrious can it be in the magnificence of the city of Constantinople?”]

[Note: Read “if.”]

If, through your vigilance and defense, the ancestral canons and many priests may have an example of goodness.

[Note: Perhaps read “might have.”]

I write these things to you, brother, exhorting you in our Lord, and I admonish you that, abandoning the desire for ambition, you should rather burn with the spirit of goodwill and be profitably adorned with its virtues according to apostolic teaching. It is patient and kind, not contentious, does not act in vain, is not puffed up, does not pursue ambition, and does not seek what belongs to itself.

[Note: Read “if.”]

Therefore, if charity does not seek what belongs to itself, how greatly does he sin who desires what belongs to another? I wish you to abstain entirely from such things and to keep in mind this saying: “Hold fast what you have, lest another receive your crown.”

[Note: Read rather: “what is not permitted.”]

For even if you seek what has not been granted, you will deprive yourself by your own deed and judgment of the peace of the entire Church.

Our brother and fellow bishop Lucian, and my son Basil the deacon, insofar as it depended on them, carried out most diligently what had been entrusted to them; but their undertaking was denied its just result.

It was given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious Herculanus.

# LETTER CVII

[Note: Also numbered 81. What was formerly 107 is now 136. Written on 22 May 452.]

[Note: Gerardus Vossius first published this letter at the end of the works of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus, Mainz, 1604, from the manuscript book of Cardinal Sirletus. From the collection of other letters subsequently published, we infer that this was manuscript collection 23, such as Vatican Ottobonian manuscript 297. Quesnellus found the same letter in the Grimanic manuscript; besides the Vatican manuscript mentioned above, we also found it in the Ratisbon manuscript.]

## TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COS

## SUMMARY

I. How highly the authority of the Council of Nicaea must be esteemed.  
II. He rebukes Julian because he favors Anatolius of Constantinople.  
III. Against the order of the universal Church, neither of them may, without guilt, grant anything to himself or obtain anything for the other.

Leo the Pope to Julian, bishop of Cos.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] Quesnellus extracted this complete and genuine reading from the Grimanic manuscript, and we likewise found it in the Ratisponensian and in Vat. Ottob. The earlier editions after Vossius, however, omitting the first four words and inserting two others not found in the text, began as follows: “Your Belovedness does not fail to know how steadfastly,” etc. Nevertheless, we believe that Vossius’s codex, similar to Ottobonianus, preserved the genuine reading. But since he had read *quem* (“whom”) for *cum* (“since”), he added the first four words to the title in this form: “Pope Leo to Julian, bishop, whom he had proved by frequent experience”; and, beginning the letter with the words “Your Belovedness,” he added *non ignorat* (“does not fail to know”) in order to complete the sense. Later editors deleted the words of the title, “whom he had proved by frequent experience.”]

Since your Belovedness has demonstrated by frequent experience how steadfastly and firmly you are resolved to preserve the decrees of the holy [Note: [Col. 1010C] Ratisponensian: *sacrorum* (“holy”).] canons of Nicaea, judging that all ecclesiastical regulations would be dissolved if anything were violated from that most sacred constitution of the Fathers, I am astonished that you could have sent such a letter through our brother and fellow bishop Lucian, in which [Col. 1009C] you so greatly intervene in favor of a desire for a new [Note: [Col. 1010C] The older editions, from Sirlet’s codex, read in the text *litterarum gressionis*, and in the margin *Al.*, *transgressionis* (“transgression”); Quesnellus inserted the latter reading from the Grimanic manuscript, and we have retained it with the Ratisponensian. Vat. Ottob. prefers the reading of Sirlet’s codex, so much so that it was evidently from the same collection.] transgression that you think something special ought to be granted to you if I consent to those things that are illicitly desired. [Note: [Col. 1010D] In the same older editions: “which are illicitly desired.” Grimanic, Ratisponensian, and Vat. Ottob. read as in the text; the abbreviation *q* and *concupiscunt* alone in a Vatican manuscript similar to Cardinal Sirlet’s codex seem to have caused the error.] Although I embrace you with as much affection as possible, you will nevertheless be unable in any way to obtain that you should drive me, whether by persuasion or by entreaty, into the destruction of the ecclesiastical [Col. 1010B] order.

For our brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, if he wisely understands the divine benefits and the assent of my favor, has [Note: [Col. 1010D] The older editions read *suffecerit* (“will have been sufficient”); Vat. Ottob. reads *sufficeret* (“would be sufficient”).] enough in having obtained that the supreme bishop gives thanks to God for the honor of his episcopate and restrains himself from the desire for illicit things; and all who love him in a special way ought to strengthen him with such counsel, so that he does not seek things altogether impossible and does not harm himself by desiring such things. For [Note: [Col. 1010D] Sirlet’s codex and Vat. Ottob., together with the older editions, read *nullus* (“no one”).] no patronage will be able to assist him with me in such a way that I should consent to what he requests, with the constitution of the Fathers trampled underfoot.

In reply, therefore, to your letters, with that affection with which I love you, I admonish you that the condition of the universal Church, fortified long ago by a most salutary and true [Col. 1010C] ordinance, should have greater weight with you than that, for the sake of anyone’s favor, you should wish to request from me those things which, without guilt on the part of either of us, neither may I grant nor may you obtain. [Note: [Col. 1010D] The Ratisponensian omits *ut* (“so that”), as does *a me* (“from me”); it adds *ea*, a word which we have judged should be inserted.] Dated eleven days before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculanus.
