## Letter 108

[Note: [Col. 1011C] Formerly number 83; what was previously number 108 is now 137. Written on 11 June 432.]

[Note: [Col. 1011C] This letter is found in manuscript collections 5 and 8 of the Hispanic Isidorean collection, twice in Vat. 3791 of collection 11, and likewise in codices of collections 12 through 24. It is also found in two particular manuscripts, Vat. 1343 and Vat. Reg. 612. In the manuscripts of the ancient collection 8, and likewise in Ottobon. 297 of collection 23, this title is found: “St. Pope Leo’s letter on penance to Theodore, bishop of the Gauls, from the city of Forum Julii.”]

### To Theodore, Bishop of Forum Julii

[Col. 1011A]

[Note: [Col. 1011C] In the table of contents of collection 5, chapter 70: “Constitution to Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii, concerning the state of penance.” In the Hispanic collection: “That penance and communion not be denied to those who are at the point of death.”]

### Synopsis

I. Each bishop ought, in doubtful matters, to have recourse to the metropolitan.  
II. There are two remedies for sin, and what the order of reconciliation ought to be.  
III. A penitent who dies before reconciliation cannot be reconciled after death.  
IV. Reconciliation must not be denied to anyone at the point of death who asks for it.  
V. How dangerous it is to reserve penance until the end. It must not be denied to anyone who asks for it by signs, while the canonical rules concerning apostates are observed.  
VI. He is to share the responses to the consultation with the metropolitan.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] In the manuscripts of collection 8: “Pope Leo to Theodore, Gallic bishop of Forum Julii.” Vat. 5845 of the same collection adds “greetings.” In the Vindobonensian manuscript of collection 5: “Leo, bishop, to his most beloved brother Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii.”]

**Leo, bishop, to Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii.**

### Chapter I

The proper order of your concern [Note: [Col. 1011D] Vat. Hisp. and Isid. read *iste ordo* (“this order”). Editions before Quesnellus, with Vat. collection 11, read *is ordo* (“that order”).] ought to have been that you first confer with your metropolitan about what appeared to require inquiry, and, if he himself did not know what your Belovedness did not know, that you should both seek instruction together. [Note: [Col. 1011D] The two Hispanic manuscripts, together with the Vat. Isidorean, delete *etiam* (“also”). In the Vallicellian manuscript of collection 8, dated to the fifth year, *etiam ipse* (“he himself also”) appears: “he himself also said that he did not know.”] For in matters that pertain to the general observance [Note: [Col. 1011D] Three of Quesnellus’s codices, both of our Hispanic manuscripts, and four other manuscripts omit the words *omnium Domini sacerdotum* (“of all the priests of the Lord”). Shortly afterward, four manuscripts of collection 8 read *sine primate suo* (“without its primate”); perhaps this is better.] of all the priests of the Lord, nothing ought to be investigated without the primates. 1174 [Note: [Col. 1011D] Vat. collection 11, in two examples of different origin, reads: “But so that the uncertainty of the one consulting may somehow be instructed, or what …” The two Hispanic manuscripts and Vat. Isidorean both have *quoquo modo* (“in whatever way”).] But so that the uncertainty of the one consulting may in any event be instructed, I shall not keep silent about what ecclesiastical rule holds concerning the condition of penitents.

### Chapter II

[Note: [Col. 1011D] *De Poenitentia*, distinction 1, *Multiplex*, chapter 49.]

The manifold mercy of God so comes to the aid of human falls that hope of eternal life is restored not only through the grace of baptism but also through the remedy of penance; [Note: [Col. 1012C] Vindobon. collection 5, the two Hispanic manuscripts, and Vercellensis collection 8, together with Merlinus’s collection 12, read *et qui* (“and those who”). Shortly afterward, Vat. collection 11 and the editions before Quesnellus read *donum* (“gift”).] so that those who have violated the gifts of regeneration, condemning themselves by their own judgment, may attain the remission of sins. The safeguards of divine [Note: [Col. 1012C] The two Hispanic manuscripts and Vat. Isidorean, together with three other manuscripts, read *voluntatis* (“of the will”).] goodness are thus arranged that God’s indulgence cannot be obtained except through the supplications of priests.

For the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, entrusted this power to the leaders of the Church, so that they might both impose the act of penance upon those who confess [Note: [Col. 1012C] The same five codices read *poenitentiae sanctionem darent* (“they should impose the sanction of penance”). This seems to derive from an arbitrary correction of the corrupt reading *agatio* for *actio* in the Vindobonensian and Hispanic manuscripts. Shortly afterward, two manuscripts of Vat. collection 21 read *et eadem salubri sanctificatione* (“and with the same salutary sanctification”).] and admit those who have been cleansed by salutary satisfaction to communion in the sacraments through the door of reconciliation.

The Savior himself is continually present in this work [Note: [Col. 1012C] The word *incessabiliter* (“unceasingly”) is missing in Vindobonensis collection 5. Sirmondus notes in the margin: “Another reading: *incessanter* (‘continually’). Shortly afterward, the Vindobonensian and Hispanic manuscripts omit *quae ministris suis exsequenda commisit dicens* (“which he entrusted to his ministers to carry out, saying”); in Vat. Hisp., Vat. Isid., and three others deriving from them, the following was written to complete the sense: “Nor is he ever absent from those to whom he said: ‘Behold, I am with you,’ etc.”] and is never absent from those things which he entrusted to his ministers to carry out, saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Thus, if anything is accomplished through our ministry in good order and with a rejoicing effect [Note: [Col. 1012C] Both Hispanic codices, Vat. Isidorean, three other manuscripts, and Sirmondus in the margin read *grato impletur affectu* (“is accomplished with grateful affection”); [Col. 1012D] and in the same codices *nobis* (“for us”) is added before *fuisse* (“to have been”).] we should not doubt that it was granted through the Holy Spirit.

### Chapter III

But if any of those for whom we beseech the Lord, hindered by whatever obstacle, should fall away from the present gift of indulgence [Note: [Col. 1012D] In the same manuscripts, except the Vindobonensian Hispanic, another reading is *excesserit* (“should depart”). Later, both Vindobonensian manuscripts and others deriving from the Hispanic collection read *perveniret* (“should reach”).] and, before reaching the appointed remedies, should end this temporal [Col. 1012B] life by the condition of human existence, he will not be able, once stripped of the flesh, to obtain what he did not receive while remaining in the body. [Note: [Col. 1012D] The older editions, together with Vat. collection 11, at the first position read *non receperit* (“has not received”).]

Nor is it necessary for us to examine the merits and actions of those who have died in this way, since our Lord God, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved to his justice what [Note: [Col. 1012D] Five codices read *sacerdotum* (“of the priests”); and in four of these, *implere ministerium non sinit* (“does not permit the ministry to be fulfilled”). In the Vindobonensian Hispanic manuscript: *non sinebit* (“will not permit”).] could not be accomplished by the priestly ministry. He wished his power to be feared in such a way that this [Note: [Col. 1012D] Quesnellus, together with our Vindobonensian Hispanic manuscript, reads *error* (“error”). We have restored the older reading from nine of our manuscripts in collections 5, 8, 11, and 21, and from Vat. Hisp. and Vat. Isidorean.] terror might benefit everyone, and that no one might fail to fear what happens to certain lukewarm or negligent persons. For it is very useful and necessary that the guilt of sins be loosed before the last day through priestly supplication.

### Chapter IV

[Note: [Col. 1012D] *De Poenitentia*, distinction 1, *Multiplex*, chapter 49; and 26, question 6, *His qui tempore*, chapter 10.]

But to those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger, implore the aid of penance and immediately of reconciliation, neither satisfaction must be forbidden nor reconciliation denied; [Col. 1013A] for we can neither impose measures upon God’s mercy nor set times for it. With him true conversion permits no delay in pardon. [Note: [Col. 1013C] The Vindobonensian Hispanic manuscript, together with four other manuscripts of the same origin, omits *vera* (“true”). Vat. collection 11, in both examples, and Quesnellus in the margin read *vera confessio* (“true confession”).]

As the Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved” (Isaiah 30:15, according to the Septuagint). And elsewhere: “You first declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified” (Isaiah 43:26, according to the Septuagint). And again: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption” (Psalm 129:7).

In distributing God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be difficult, nor neglect the tears and groans of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent [Note: [Col. 1013C] The Vat. and Vallicellian manuscripts of collection 8 read *poenitentiae affectionem* (“the disposition toward penance”). Vat. collection 24, together with the editions before Quesnellus, reads *ipsam poenitentiam ex Dei* (“penance itself from God,” etc.). The other manuscripts and all of Quesnellus’s codices agree with the text.] is conceived through God’s inspiration. The Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will” (2 Timothy 2:25). [Note: [Col. 1013C] Vindobonensis collection 5 and Quesnellus in the margin read *capti* (“held captive”). Shortly afterward, Vindobonensis Hispanic has *in ipsius voluntate* (“in his will”); Vat. Hisp. and Vat. Isid. have *in ipsius voluntatem* (“for his will”).]

### Chapter V

[Col. 1013B]

Therefore each Christian ought to possess the judgment of his own conscience [Note: [Col. 1013C] Both Hispanic manuscripts and Vat. Isidorean delete *Christianum* (“Christian”).] so that he does not postpone turning to God from day to day or set the time of his satisfaction at the end of his life. 1176 [Note: [Col. 1013C] The Vindobonensian Hispanic manuscript has the corrupt reading: “Whom human ignorance dangerously confines in this way, so that he reserves himself uncertain for a few hours.” The editions before Quesnellus accepted the same reading, merely omitting *se* (“himself”) at the first occurrence. Quesnellus’s emendation is supported by our manuscripts of collections 5, 8, and 24, and by Vat. collection 11 at the second position.] For human frailty and ignorance dangerously confine themselves under this condition, that a person reserves himself for only a few uncertain hours; and although he could merit indulgence through fuller satisfaction, he chooses the narrow limits of that time [Note: [Col. 1013C] Vindobonensis collection 5 and Vallicellensis collection 8 read *in quo* (“in which”).] in which scarcely enough space may be found either for the penitent’s confession or for the priest’s reconciliation.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Vindobonensis Hispanic reads: “Therefore the need of such persons must also be assisted.” Vat. collection 11 at the first position: “Therefore the needs of such persons must be assisted.” Vat. Hisp., Vat. Isid., and two manuscripts of collection 21: “Therefore the need must be assisted.”] Yet, as I have said, the need even of such persons must be assisted in such a way [Note: [Col. 1013D] The editions before Quesnellus read: “So that neither the act of penance nor the grace of communion be denied them, if, even though they have lost the use of speech, they are shown to seek it by an indication of sound understanding.” A somewhat different reading is found in both Hispanic manuscripts, in Vat. Isidorean, in another manuscript of collection 11 at the first position, and in the manuscripts of collection 21. The final words, “they are shown to seek it by an indication of sound understanding,” are also found in Merlinus’s example of collection 12 and in Vat. collection 24. The manuscripts of collection 8 and Vat. collection 11 at the second position prefer the reading of the text; Vindobonensis collection 5 agrees with them.] that the act of penance and the grace of communion not be denied to them if, even after losing the use of speech, they request it by signs of sound understanding.

But if [Note: [Col. 1013D] Quesnellus, together with certain manuscripts, reads *aliqua aegritudine* (“by some illness”). [Col. 1014C] The reading of the older editions seemed better; it is presented by the ancient codices Vindobonensis collection 5, Vat. and Vallicellensis collection 8, and Vat. collection 24.] they have been so weakened by some force of illness [Col. 1014A] that they cannot indicate, in the presence of the priest, what they had requested shortly before, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them, so that they may receive together both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation—while nevertheless the rule of the Fathers’ canons is preserved concerning those [Note: [Col. 1014C] Vindobonensis Hispanic and two manuscripts of Vat. collection 21 read: “who sinned against the Lord by departing from the faith.” Shortly before this, both Hispanic manuscripts omit *paternorum* (“of the Fathers”).] who sinned against God by departing from the faith.

### Chapter VI

But these matters, brother, I have answered in response to your Belovedness’s inquiry so that nothing contrary might be done under the pretext of ignorance. [Note: [Col. 1014C] Manuscripts of collection 8 read *generetur* (“might arise”). Subsequently, Vindobonensis Hispanic has *innotescant* (“may become known”) instead of *instruantur* (“may be instructed”).] You will therefore bring them to the attention of your metropolitan, so that if any of the brethren should previously have thought that there was uncertainty about these matters, they may be instructed by him concerning everything that has been written to you.

[Note: [Col. 1014C] Vindobonensis collection 5 and Merlinus’s example of collection 12 omit the chronological note. Vat. and Vallicellensis collection 8 read “the third day before the Ides of January,” where *Jan.* may easily have slipped in for *Jun.* Vindobonensis Hispanic reads “the third day of July,” without mention of the Ides. This defect seems to have been corrected arbitrarily in Vat. Hisp., Vat. Isid., and other codices deriving from them by writing “the third day before the Kalends of July.” The editions, together with Vat. 3791 at the second position and another manuscript of Vat. collection 24, read “the fourth day before the Ides of June.” We have preferred “the third day” and “June,” since most of the manuscripts and the more important collections agree on these. We have rejected “the Kalends,” because the notation of the Kalends seems to have been supplied arbitrarily by an ancient scribe in the manuscripts deriving from the Hispanic collection. [Col. 1014D] After the consular notation, Vat. 3791 at the second position adds the following: “For then more people can be called to penance if the penitent’s conscience is not made public to the ears of the people. Dated the second day before the Nones of March.” These words are taken from the end of Letter 168 to the Campanians.]

Dated the third day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Herculanus.

---

## Letter 109

[Note: [Col. 1014D] Formerly number 109; now number 138. Written on 25 November 452.]

### To Julian, Bishop of Coos

First published from the Ratisponensian manuscript.

[Col. 1014B]

### Synopsis

I. He complains about the disturbances and acts of violence of the Palestinian monks, by which they harassed Catholics and extorted assent to the Eutychian heresy.  
II. They are to be restrained by the emperor, and the obstinate are to be driven into exile.  
III. He sends them the letter of St. Athanasius to Epictetus to be set against them.  
IV. Concerning Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, driven out by the same men, and another appointed in his place.

**Pope Leo to Julian, bishop.**

### Chapter I

The grave events which your Brotherhood reports to have been perpetrated by the mobs of false monks are matters to be mourned with no small sorrow. [Note: [Col. 1014D] He is speaking about the Palestinian monks who, under the leadership of Theodosius, immediately after returning to his own people following the Council of Chalcedon, first stirred up enormous disturbances at Jerusalem and then throughout Palestine. See the letters of the emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria written on this matter, which are appended to the acts of that same council, and Evagrius, Book II, chapter 5.] The impious Eutyches is waging war through the frenzy of the deceived against the evangelical and apostolic preaching; may this rebound upon his own destruction and that of his associates. This is delayed by the patience of God so that it may become evident how greatly the enemies of the cross of Christ serve the devil.

While heretical depravity, exceeding the ancient veil of its pretence, can no longer contain itself within the limits of its hypocrisy, it has poured out all the poison that it had long concealed—not only [Note: [Col. 1015C] In his letter to the Palestinian synod, Marcian says of Theodosius, the author of the disturbances: “He devised and composed certain letters which only the devil could have fabricated; and through them he did not cease to slander the holy synod held at Chalcedon.”] raging with words against the disciples of the truth, but also [Note: [Col. 1015C] The same Marcian, writing to the archimandrites and monks of Aelia, says: “You, moreover, by swords and other acts of cruelty, insults, and tortures against honorable and noble women, did not hesitate to impose necessity upon many, so that they should consent to perverse doctrines,” etc.] with physical violence, so as to extort consent forcibly either from uneducated simplicity or from fearful faith.

But the children of light ought not to fear the children of darkness to such an extent that the sound should yield to the raging or think that any reverence ought to be shown to such men. If they prefer to perish rather than come to their senses, care must be taken that they do not cause wider harm through their impunity and, while tolerated for too long, rise up to the destruction of many.

### Chapter II

I do not fail to recognize what charity and favor are owed to our holy and true sons, the monks who do not abandon the modesty of their profession and carry out in their conduct what they have vowed in their purpose. But the proud and restless, who glory in contempt and insults toward priests, must be regarded not as servants of Christ but as soldiers of Antichrist; and they must especially be humbled by their superiors, since they stir up an ignorant multitude to defend their perversity.

Therefore, since the most merciful prince loves the catholic faith with the whole affection of a religious heart, and, as has become widely known everywhere, is greatly offended by this audacity of rebellious heretics, action must be taken with his clemency so that the instigators of these seditions may be separated from the insane gatherings. Not only Eutyches and Dioscorus, but also all who zealously assist this mad depravity, should be placed in regions where they can have no association with their companions in blasphemy.

For perhaps the simplicity of some will be healed by this remedy and they will be recalled more easily to soundness of mind if they are freed from the instigations of pestilential teachers.

### Chapter III

But so that the instruction necessary for strengthening the minds of the devout and refuting the heretics might neither be lacking nor remain hidden, I have sent [Note: [Col. 1015C] A fragment of this letter was appended by Leo to Letter 165. This entire letter, from the same ancient version used by Leo, is found not only in collection 5, chapter 52, but also after Leo’s letters in the manuscripts of collection 12. It should further be noted that in the same collections these letters of Athanasius are followed by St. Cyril’s letter to John of Antioch, in which Cyril discusses Athanasius’s letter and sent him a corrected copy of it. Since Cyril had sent a copy of this letter to John, together with the other acts of the peace established with him, to Pope Xystus, perhaps the genuine letter of Athanasius to Epictetus was also among them; and perhaps everything had been translated into Latin, just as he had earlier sent to his predecessor Celestine similar writings composed in Greek in the matter of Nestorius, as is clear from Cyril’s Letter 8 among Celestine’s letters in Coustant, number 9. Certainly, it may be inferred from Xystus’s Letter 5 that all these documents sent by Cyril to Xystus—surely translated into Latin—were read in the Roman synod. Just as the documents sent to Celestine, and, as we have seen, translated into Latin, were received into the apostolic archives, as Leo testifies in Letter 69, chapter 1, so the same must be believed concerning the acts sent to Xystus; and therefore, from their translation preserved in the archives, they became known to Leo and passed from there into the collections mentioned.] the letter of the bishop Athanasius, of holy memory, to the bishop Epictetus [Col. 1016B]. St. Cyril, of holy memory, used its testimonies at the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius, because it established the incarnation of the Word so clearly and carefully that it had already defeated Nestorius and Eutyches as heretics of that time.

Let the followers of Eutyches and Dioscorus dare to accuse this man of such great authority of ignorance or depravity, they who assert that our preaching deviates from the doctrine and understanding of the Fathers. It ought to benefit the strengthening of the convictions of all the priests of the Lord, whom the heretics formerly recognized and condemned in their own authors, that they have now begun more openly to assert the dogma of their impiety, lest, while the matter remained hidden in silence, it should seem doubtful whether the threefold error of Apollinaris [Note: [Col. 1016C] Above, in Letter 59 to the Constantinopolitans, chapter 5, Leo wrote: “Nor do we speak of Christ as man in such a way that he lacks anything certainly belonging to human nature, whether a soul, a rational mind, or flesh—which he did not take from a woman, but which was made from the Word turned and changed into flesh.” These three heads of Apollinarian error—soul, rational mind, and flesh—are thus described by Augustine, from whom Leo seems to have drawn, in *On Heresies*, chapter 55. First, they said that the Word assumed flesh without a soul; Leo gives their reason in Sermon 4 on the Nativity, chapter 5: the Divinity itself fulfilled the soul’s role. Second, softening their earlier opinion, they taught that Christ did not lack the whole human soul, but its rational part, or mind, so that the Word was in Christ in place of the mind. Third, finally, they asserted that flesh and the Word are of one substance, and in this especially all agreed. Leo, however, attributing this third Apollinarian tenet only to Eutyches in Letters 124, chapter 2, and 165, chapter 2, presents it more fully: Eutyches, he says, chose Apollinaris’s third doctrine, so that, denying the reality of human flesh and soul, he asserted that our whole Lord Jesus Christ was of one nature, as though the Godhead of the Word itself had been changed into flesh and soul, and that being conceived and born, nourished and growing, crucified and dying … belonged to the divine essence alone.] and the insane [Note: [Col. 1017C] Leo also attributes the error of the Manichaeans to the Eutychians in the aforementioned Letter 124, chapter 2, in this sense: if, while avoiding the error of the Apollinarists, they deny that Christ was born, suffered, and so forth in divinity, and nevertheless refuse to confess him as truly human, they are forced to affirm with the Manichaeans that Jesus Christ did everything merely in appearance, and that he had not a human body but a phantasmal bodily appearance visible to the eyes of those who saw him. He attacks this Manichaean error at greater length in Sermon 4 on the Epiphany, chapter 4.] opinion of the Manichaeans were truly present in them.

For since they no longer strive to hide themselves but boldly rise up against the Churches of Christ, ought we not to take care that the strength of all their efforts be taken away, while preserving, as I have said, such a measure of strictness that the incorrigible are separated from the more peaceable?

“Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15:33); and “When the pestilent person has been punished, the wise man will be wiser” (Proverbs 21:11). Thus, by whatever means the society of the reprobate is scattered, some vessels may be snatched away from the devil. For we must not be so offended by their insults and empty talk that we take no concern for their correction.

### Chapter IV

As for Bishop Juvenal, whose injuries are to be mourned, he had rashly joined himself to the blasphemies of the heretics [Note: [Col. 1017D] Namely, when, in the false synod of Ephesus, he joined Dioscorus in absolving Eutyches, something which he later corrected with sounder counsel at the Council of Chalcedon.]; and while he embraced Eutyches and Dioscorus [Col. 1018A] [Note: [Col. 1017D] Read “welcomed” or “supported.”], he drove many ignorant people headlong by his example, although afterward he corrected himself with wiser counsel.

Nevertheless, those who drank more eagerly of the poison of impiety became adversaries of the man whose disciples they had previously been, so that he himself had to suffer the consequences of the nourishment he had given them. It is to be hoped that they may imitate the same correction which he chose, if they may come to their senses even through the testimony of the holy places in which they live.

But what sort of man he is who intruded himself into the place of a living bishop [Note: [Col. 1017D] This is the same Theodosius who was the author of the disturbances in Palestine. See Marcian’s letters and Evagrius in the places cited in note 1 (Col. 1014, n. o).] cannot be doubted from the very nature of the deed; nor should there be any doubt that he is perverse whom the enemies of the faith loved.

Meanwhile, may your Brotherhood continue its care with pious solicitude, so that you may let me know through more frequent letters how matters are progressing. Dated the seventh day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Herculanus.

## Letter 110

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Formerly placed after Letter 88. What was previously number 110 is now number 130. Written on 15 February 453.]

[Note: [Col. 1018C] Published by Andrea Arnoldo from the Bodleian codex and inserted by Quesnellus into his second edition. We compared the Greek with Vat. Greek manuscript 1455, which suggested several corrections. We shall add a new Latin translation, carefully revised in accordance with the likewise corrected Greek text, and much clearer as a result. To this letter of Augustus, the holy pontiff replies in Letter 115.]

### Marcian Augustus to Pope Leo (G)

[Col. 1017]

### Synopsis

He asks the pontiff for confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon as necessary. He praises his steadfastness in defending the canons and restraining innovation.

[Note: [Col. 1017] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

1182 Letter of the most devout emperor Marcian to Leo, archbishop of Rome.

[Col. 1017B]

The victorious Valentinian and Marcian, glorious triumphators, ever Augusti, to the most holy and truly venerable Leo, archbishop.

We most earnestly pray in the words of our serenity that your Blessedness may be in good health, asking that you grant us the favor of almighty God through the intercession of your prayers, so that his merciful and peace-making magnificence may deign to bestow upon our realm everything favorable and desirable.

We are exceedingly astonished that, after the Council of Chalcedon and the letters of the venerable bishops sent to your Holiness, in which they reported everything done at that council, no letters of this kind have been sent at all by your Clemency—letters which, when read in the most holy Churches, ought plainly to have come to the knowledge of everyone. [Note: [Col. 1018C] Letter 98.] [Note: [Col. 1018C] These were therefore letters of the Apostolic See by which general councils were confirmed; they were to be read in the Churches of the East, and this confirmation was to be made known to everyone [Col. 1018D], so that no one, remaining doubtful about it, could resist the decrees of the council. Here, therefore, is the clearest testimony to the necessity of pontifical confirmation.]

This has introduced great uncertainty into the minds of some who even now follow the evil opinion and perversity of Eutyches: whether your Blessedness has confirmed what was decreed at the holy council. For this reason your Piety will deign to send letters [Col. 1019A] 1184 through which it may be made clear to all Churches and peoples that what was accomplished at the holy council is regarded as ratified by your Blessedness.

That which was especially fitting for a bishop of the Apostolic See, your Holiness has most excellently provided: by preserving the ecclesiastical canons, you have allowed nothing of the ancient custom and established order, constituted long ago and observed inviolate down to this day, to be changed. [Note: [Col. 1019C] Here he commends Leo’s steadfastness: insisting that the privileges of the Churches be preserved intact according to the canons of Nicaea, Leo vigorously resisted the canon issued for the see of Constantinople at Chalcedon, in Letters 104, 105, 106, and 107, written on 22 May of the preceding year. This is especially noteworthy: the emperor commends him even though he had previously sent the same Leo effective letters in support of confirming this canon, as described above in Letter 100. Pope Gelasius had already made this observation long before in his letter to the Dardanians, preserved in expanded form in the excellent Avellana collection 14 and printed in volume V of the Council editions, Venice, p. 333. There, alluding to these letters of Marcian, the pontiff says: “Let them hear Marcian, that same ruler of the city, who, after approaching as an intercessor for the enlargement of that city, was unable to obtain anything contrary to the rules, and then praised Pope Leo of holy memory with the highest commendations because he had in no way permitted the rules of the canons to be violated.”]

As for the letters of your Blessedness, what and how great things have been done by certain persons, your Holiness will be able to learn most clearly from those to whom we did not wish to be opposed. [Note: [Col. 1019D] The adverb “not yet” had to be supplied in the Latin, as also the Greek *οὔπω* or something similar; the following words call for an open and public confirmation and response to the synod, which had not yet been sent.] [Note: [Col. 1019C] He is referring especially to Letter 106 to Anatolius, which, although it had sufficiently confirmed the decree of faith issued at Chalcedon, simultaneously contradicted the canon concerning the see of Constantinople and therefore was not made public, as Leo reports in Letters 144, 115, 116, and 117. Hence, when a rumor was spread among the people that the pontiff had written against the Council of Chalcedon, so that for this reason his letters had not been published, the Eutychians stirred up disturbances and seized the opportunity to cast doubt upon the very definition of faith issued at Chalcedon. For, as the same pontiff says in Letter 117, they wished, on the pretext of concealing their perfidy, to make the council’s decrees appear weak or doubtful because they had not been strengthened by the agreement of his judgment.]

Your charity toward God has not yet affirmed that the Council of Chalcedon, with all the bishops in agreement, has followed the catholic faith and true orthodoxy. [Note: [Col. 1019D] Leo learned this from Julian, bishop of Coos, as is clear from Letter 115, chapter 2; from that letter it is also evident [Col. 1020C] that the monks of Palestine were the ones who stirred up the disturbances. As for the addition “to whom we did not wish to be opposed,” since the pontifical and public confirmation of the Chalcedonian definition was lacking—the confirmation required to remove every doubt—it is to be understood as referring to resistance by force and secular authority. It is certain from the same Letter 115, chapter 2, that in letters sent to those same monks the emperor sought both to restrain and to instruct them.] For this reason, let your venerable Dignity issue a decree as quickly as possible, by which it may show most clearly that it confirms the Council of Chalcedon itself, so that those who seek byways impassable may have no suspicion whatever concerning the judgment of your Holiness.

Dated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March, at Constantinople.

---

1181 **Letter of the most devout emperor Marcian to Leo, archbishop of Rome.**

[Col. 1018B]

The victorious Valentinian and Marcian, glorious, triumph-bearing, ever Augusti, to the most holy Father and truly venerable Leo, archbishop.

We wish your Blessedness, in the letters of our Serenity, the very best of health, earnestly requesting that, through the mediation of your prayers for us, the zeal of almighty God may grant that his gracious and peace-making majesty may deem it worthy to provide our empire with every favorable and desirable blessing.

[Note: “ὅπως ἄν” (“so that somehow”). Thus the Vatican manuscript. The Vulgate incorrectly has “ὅτι ἂν” (“whatever”).]

[Note: “Παράσχοις” (“you may provide”). The Vatican manuscript has “παράσχοι” (“may provide”), not entirely incorrectly; for it refers to “μακαριότητα” (“Blessedness”), which precedes.]

[Note: “Καταξιώσῃ” (“may deem worthy”). In the Vatican manuscript, “καταξιώσει” (“will deem worthy”); but perhaps “καταξιῶσαι” (“to deem worthy”) should be read, as Arnoldus also noted in the margin of his edition.]

We are exceedingly astonished that, after the synod at Chalcedon and the letters of the venerable bishops sent to your God-belovedness, through which they reported everything that had been done at that synod, no such letters have at all been sent by your Holiness—[Col. 1018C] letters which, when read in the most holy churches, ought to have come to everyone’s knowledge. This has cast great doubt into the minds of certain people who still pursue the evil doctrine and perversity of Eutyches: whether your Blessedness has confirmed what was enacted at the holy synod. [Col. 1020A]

[Note: “Τοῖς δήμοις” (“and to the peoples”). We add the article from the Vatican manuscript.]

[Note: Perhaps “φανερόν” (“manifest”).]

For this reason your Reverence will deign to send letters 1183 through which it will become clear to all the churches and peoples that the proceedings of the holy synod have been confirmed by your Blessedness; namely, that your Holiness acted with the distinction proper to a bishop of the apostolic see, in that, while observing the ecclesiastical canons, you did not permit anything to be innovated against the ancient custom and order once established and remaining unshaken down to the present day.

[Note: “Διαμεινάσης” (“having remained”). You owe this excellent reading to the Vatican manuscript; “διαμενούσης,” the reading of the printed editions, should be rejected.]

From the letters of your Holiness, both what and how much has been done by certain persons, your Holiness will be able to learn with the utmost clarity from others—things which we would not have wished to oppose—[Note: Something must necessarily be supplied here, such as “οὔπω” (“not yet”), or something similar, so that one reads “οὔπω διαβεβαιουμένης,” “your God-belovedness not yet affirming,” etc.] since your God-belovedness has not yet affirmed that the synod at Chalcedon, with all the bishops agreeing, has followed the catholic and truly orthodox faith. Therefore your Venerability will send decrees as quickly as possible, through which you will most clearly demonstrate that you confirm the synod at Chalcedon, so that those who desire trackless byways may be unable to entertain any suspicion concerning the judgment of your Holiness.

[Note: “Τῶν ἀνοδιῶν” (“of the trackless ways”). So too the Vatican manuscript, except that it lacks the article “τῶν.” Moreover, if this word is derived from the nominative “ἀνοδία,” as we have done in the translation, it should not be written “ἀνοδιῶν” but “ἀνοδίων.”]

Given fifteen days before the Kalends of March, at Constantinople.

[Note: “At Constantinople.” The Vatican manuscript has “from Constantinople,” but incorrectly. If “from” is retained, one must write “from Constantinople” in the genitive.]

1185

## LETTER CXI

[Note: Otherwise 84. What was formerly 111 is now 140. Written on 10 March 453.]

[Note: It survives in manuscripts of collections 12, 18, and 24, and in Sichard’s copy.]

### TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS

Concerning Aetius and Andrew.

### SYNOPSIS

I. The suspicion concerning Anatolius’s ordination was removed through his profession of faith.  
II. He improperly removed Aetius from the office of archdeacon.  
III. Leo asks Marcian to restrain Anatolius from unlawful actions and to favor Julian.

**LEO, bishop, to MARCIAN AUGUSTUS**

### CHAPTER I

The whole world recognizes how the Christian faith was recently restored to its integrity through your outstanding piety and glorious zeal for clemency, and that through you the Lord restored the unique safeguard of its salvation.

[Note: So Quesnellus, with Sichardus and all our manuscripts. Other editions, perhaps more correctly, have: “But if anything…”]

And if anything contrary to the completion of so great a work appears to arise from an opposing spirit, it is necessary that it be referred to the assistance of your piety, which divine providence prepared for the safeguarding of catholic truth. Since it lies within your power to cut off scandals arising even in distant places, how much more must you not allow those which dare to arise before your own eyes to increase.

As the knowledge of God is my witness, the authors of Bishop Anatolius’s consecration had made me regard his ordination as suspect—as must be admitted—and I considered the one elected to be no different from those who had elected him. It followed that, while he was seeking communion with the apostolic see, I long refrained from sending him letters of peace.

[Note: Earlier editions before Quesnellus, together with Sichardus, read: “while he remained alienated from the communion of the apostolic see, I long refrained from sending him letters of peace.” The same reading occurs in the manuscripts of collection 24, in which only “letters of my peace” is found. The reading rightly inserted by Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript—we have also found it in the Vatican manuscript 1340 and in Venetian manuscript 169 of collection 12—has “while” in place of “when.” On letters of peace, compare Quesnellus’s second note.]

But when the testimony of your piety supported him,

[Note: Our manuscripts of collection 12 have this better than the printed editions, which read “when it concerned his faith.”]

and promised everything desirable and pleasing concerning his faith and unanimity, I believed his profession to be so sincere that I nevertheless did not cease to admonish him concerning the conduct he ought to maintain. I earnestly and carefully impressed upon him that he must dare to have no one in his fellowship who had persecuted Flavian of blessed memory, and that he must truly shudder as enemies of Christ at the followers of the heretic Eutyches.

[Note: All editions, not only those agreeing with the manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichardus’s copy, but also the Grimanic manuscript of collection 18, omit several lines, leaping from “Eutyches” to “Eutychian,” thus: “in his fellowship and [as a defender] of the Eutychian heresy”; by this leap the sentence is corrupted and the information necessary for understanding what follows is removed. Only the two manuscripts of collection 12 cited above supplied this notable supplement. To these may be added, from Coustant, confirmed in the *Vindiciae veterum Patrum*, p. 572, the Remigian copy, which we believe belongs to the same collection 12.]

He appeared to receive this so obediently that he declared the deacon Andrew, a defender of the Eutychian heresy, to have been removed by him. It then followed that he wrote to me concerning what had been defined in the synodal council on behalf of the catholic faith in terms such as it was fitting for a catholic priest to write.

### CHAPTER II

Since these things had preceded in order to commend his beginnings, I do not know what cause or occasion has emerged—

[Note: Leo’s printed editions omit the word “nescio” (“I do not know”), which we supplied from the manuscripts of collection 12; they instead prefer “emerserit” (“may have emerged”), while Quesnellus alone has “emersit” (“has emerged”). The editions of the Councils have “miror” (“I wonder”) instead of “nescio.”]

—for him to degrade, under the pretext of promotion, a man of the catholic faith who was steadfastly opposed even to the Nestorian and Eutychian heretics,

[Note: Thus all our manuscripts agree with the common editions. Quesnellus, with a different arrangement and punctuation that alter the meaning, has “steadfastly opposed even the archdeacon”; in the margin, for “even,” he suggested that perhaps “Aetius” should be read. With the corrected reading, this is unnecessary.]

namely the archdeacon,

[Note: The manuscripts of collection 24, together with the editions before Quesnellus, have “sententiae” (“judgment”).]

and suddenly transfer the administration of the entire ecclesiastical case and responsibility to Andrew the Eutychianist—

[Note: See Quesnellus’s third note.]

so disturbed by excessive agitation that he inflicted upon him, on Saturday, the consecration he was granting as an injury,

[Note: Compare Letter 9, chapter 1, and Quesnellus’s second note on it.]

whether ignorant or forgetful of apostolic tradition—

[Col. 1021C]

as though the fault of that ordination concerned a bishop more than a presbyter. Finding nothing in his faith to censure and nothing in his morals to condemn, he carried out the removal of an innocent man under the appearance of advancement, adding this insult in his judgment: that, by assigning him to a cemetery, he condemned him to a certain exile.

[Note: The Grimanic manuscript has “to be assigned.” Immediately afterward, the cited editions, together with the same manuscripts, have “condemned” in place of “damned for a certain [exile].” The reading introduced by Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript is also supported by our manuscripts of collection 12. See Quesnellus’s fourth note.]

Nevertheless, I presume to commend him to your piety, so that he may not be further burdened by any harmful plots—

[Note: Sichardus has “or by intrigues.”]

—he whom, as I have learned, the Lord has placed under your protection.

1187

### CHAPTER III

I add this further entreaty: deign necessarily to rebuke the aforesaid bishop, who is discordant with his own profession and has forgotten too much of your testimony and favor.

[Note: Thus our manuscripts agree with the ancient editions. Quesnellus has “too much”; immediately afterward, the Venetian manuscript has “our” instead of “your,” but incorrectly, since the emperor had given testimony on Anatolius’s behalf.]

Let him cease persecuting Catholics; let him cease crushing those who pleased Flavian of holy memory, and choosing the fellowship of those whom he rejected.

For we shall not otherwise be able to extend brotherly affection to him than by requiring him to show that he abominates the enemies of the catholic faith and to cut off from himself the fellowship of the man whom he rightly cast away.

[Note: The editions and Sichardus’s copy formerly had: “And let him cut off from himself their fellowship and association.” Quesnellus emended this from the Grimanic manuscript, correctly; for the subject here is Andrew the Eutychianist, whom Anatolius himself had long ago professed to have rejected, as the following letter shows. The same reading is supported by our manuscripts of collection 12 and by the ancient editions of the Councils. From these we have restored “let him cut off” in place of “let him withdraw,” which Quesnellus wrote from the Grimanic manuscript. The manuscripts of collection 24 have: “and let him cut off from himself his fellowship and association.”]

Even if he had been cleansed by a great satisfaction, nevertheless, after returning to his doubtful error, he ought to have been placed below catholic deacons, not above them.

I also ask the benevolence of your Clemency to hold my brother Julian, your devoted admirer, in your affection, as you deign to do; through whose services an image of my presence is restored to you. For, trusting in the sincerity of his faith, I have delegated my representation to him against the heretics of our time, and, for the safeguarding of the Churches and of peace, I required that he not be absent from your retinue.

[Note: See Quesnellus’s sixth note.]

Deign to hear his suggestions, which he offers on behalf of catholic unity, as though they were mine—pleasing God, who, in addition to a royal crown, may also confer upon you the palm of the priesthood.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

## LETTER CXII

[Note: Otherwise 85. What was formerly 112 is now 142. Written on 10 March 453.]

[Note: We reread this with the manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, as well as with Vatican manuscript 541 and Sichardus’s copy; only in these did we find this letter.]

### TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

Concerning Aetius and Andrew.

### SYNOPSIS

I. He complains that Andrew was placed in charge of ecclesiastical affairs after Aetius was removed.  
II. He requests that everything be restored to its former condition.

**LEO, bishop, to PULCHERIA AUGUSTA**

### CHAPTER I

Since there are many documents by which your piety’s affection for the Church of God is shown,

[Note: Some have “in affection.”]

your assistance is rightly desired whenever any scandal arises, so that the faith which, with your support, was defended against the devices of heretics may possess the lasting firmness of secure peace.

For what benefit is it that the adversaries of truth have been overthrown outside, if we have them revived within the Lord’s enclosure?

What I have learned to have been done concerning my son Aetius causes me excessive anxiety and compels me, for sound reason, to fear that I may have cause to regret having agreed, at your urging, to think better of the bishop of Constantinople, who had been ordained by the enemies of the faith, since he was being assisted by so great a testimony of your piety, lest the weakness of his ordination burden him where your intervention was present.

Accordingly, I had begun to rejoice that he was said to honor the memory of blessed Flavian

[Note: Some have “to honor.”]

and resist the efforts of heretics. But I grieve that he has changed for the worse, as the lamentable complaint mentioned above demonstrates, and that he has now appointed as archdeacon one whom he himself professed to have rejected, who had revealed himself among us as a defender of the Eutychian heresy.

[Note: Andrew had done this either in his absence, through a letter written to Leo, or in person by his words—if indeed one should infer from this passage, as some think, that he had come to Rome.]

Since he has now placed this man in charge of ecclesiastical affairs, he is shown to be granting his favor to him on account of his heretical perversity; and even if he could have earned pardon through great satisfaction, he ought by no means to have been preferred to those who had remained steadfast in the faith.

1189

### CHAPTER II

Since it is not hidden from your Clemency how much danger is being nourished either by shameful negligence or by deceitful wickedness, deign by the authority of your Clemency to recall the bishop to the profession of his faith.

[Note: Our manuscripts and Sichardus have: “Let him not, lest he … nor let him damage his reputation.” The common editions before Quesnellus have: “And let him not, lest he … nor let him damage his reputation.”]

Let him not impose these stains upon himself, nor despise the reputation he acquired through your favor; let him cut off the fellowship of the heretic whom he formerly removed from himself,

[Note: The following eight words were supplied by Quesnellus; the editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 12 and Sichardus’s copy, omit them.]

and let him cease persecuting the man whom he ought to have held dearer.

I rejoice that you stood by his innocence in such a way that your piety came to his grief with worthy consolation.

With regard to my brother Julian, your devoted admirer, and bishop, estimate how greatly your favor toward him ought to increase according to the judgment of the apostolic see. In the cause of the faith, to which your glory is devoted, I have delegated my representation to him to the extent that, without departing from the respect owed to you, he may never cease presenting me to your piety; carrying out my concern in the guardianship of the faith and in ecclesiastical discipline in every respect, and conveying through timely suggestions whatever may benefit the universal Church.

[Note: Two manuscripts of collection 12 and Vatican manuscript 541, together with all the common editions before Quesnellus, delete “my.”]

Thus, through him, neither may your protection be lacking to Catholics whom we wish to be assisted,

[Note: Some have “to assist.”]

nor my service to you.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

## LETTER CXIII

[Note: Otherwise 86. What was formerly 113 is now 141. Written on 11 March 453.]

[Note: It survives in manuscripts of collections 12, 18, and 24, and also in Sichardus’s copy.]

### TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COS

Concerning Aetius and Andrew.

### SYNOPSIS

I. He thanks Julian for sympathizing with him in his many sufferings, while at the same time protesting against Aetius’s removal.  
II. He wants Julian to keep watch at Constantinople for the cause of the faith. He rebukes Anatolius through the emperor.  
III. Concerning the disturbance of the Egyptian and Palestinian monks.  
IV. Concerning his own letter and the translation of the acts of the Council of Chalcedon into Latin.

1190

**LEO, bishop of Rome, to JULIAN, bishop of Cos**

### CHAPTER I

I recognized in your letter the affection of fraternal charity: that you sympathize with us in pious grief over the evils, many and savage, which we have endured.

[Note: Earlier editions before Quesnellus, together with Vatican manuscript 1340, Venetian manuscript 169 of collection 12, Vatican manuscript 544, Vatican manuscript 139 of collection 24, and Sichardus, add “many.” The evils here indicated as many and savage refer to Attila’s invasion of Italy.]

Would that what the Lord either permitted or willed us to suffer might contribute to the correction of those who are saved,

[Note: Thus the Grimanic manuscript. Some have “of many.”]

and that adversities might cease and offenses come to an end. Both will be the result of God’s great mercy, if he removes the scourges and turns the hearts of his own people back to himself.

Just as the hostility that raged among us grieved your Fraternity,

[Note: Thus from the same Grimanic manuscript. Some have “that raged.”]

so what your letters indicate concerning the Church at Constantinople makes me anxious: the snares of heretics do not rest, and, through carefully contrived opportunities,

[Note: The ancient common editions and Sichardus have “having sought opportunities.”]

those who were defenders of the catholic faith are harassed.

For while Aetius is removed from the office of archdeacon under the pretext of promotion, and Andrew, who had been rejected because of his fellowship with heretics, is appointed in his place; while honor is bestowed upon the accusers of Flavian of blessed memory, and the companions or disciples of the most devout confessor are crushed,

[Note: Thus Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript. The other editions and manuscripts have “are worn down.”]

what pleases the bishop of that Church is shown all too openly.

I defer being moved against him according to the merits of the case, and I await what he himself will do with me through his letters, which our son Aetius has announced that he will send. I am giving opportunity for voluntary correction, by which I wish my grief to be relieved.

Nevertheless, I have written to the most merciful emperor and the most devout Augusta concerning matters pertaining to the safeguarding of ecclesiastical peace. I do not doubt that, through their devotion to the faith, they will take care that, contrary to the glory of their own work, the condemned heresy may not be able to sprout again.

[Note: Some have “may be able.”]

### CHAPTER II

Therefore, dearest brother, let your affection devote a pious and necessary concern to the solicitude of the apostolic see. Since you were nourished there, it entrusts to you, by maternal right, the catholic cause against the heretics Nestorians and Eutychians. Supported by divine aid, do not cease keeping watch over the situation of the city of Constantinople,

[Note: Editions before Quesnellus have: “so that the impious disturbance of the aforesaid doctrines may never arise.”]

lest the impious disturbance of those doctrines arise anywhere.

And since the faith of the glorious emperors is so great that you can confidently suggest to them what needs to be conveyed, use their piety for the benefit of the universal Church.

[Note: Thus the editions before Quesnellus, better than Quesnellus’s reading: “while your affection is advising.”]

When your affection consults me concerning matters about which you think there may be doubt, your reports will not lack the guidance of my reply:

[Note: The common editions before Quesnellus have incorrectly: “so that, their activity and the cases which ought to be settled in each Church by the knowledge of its bishops being set aside, you may use this special care, acting in my place, lest heresy…” Quesnellus’s emendation from the Grimanic manuscript is confirmed by our manuscripts of collection 24, except for the final words, for which they have equally well: “use this special care, acting in my place.”]

so that, setting aside the handling of those cases which ought to be settled in each Church by the knowledge of its own bishops, you may assume this special care, acting in my place, lest Nestorian or Eutychian heresy revive in any part.

For there is no catholic vigor in the bishop of Constantinople, nor is he very concerned either for the sacrament of human salvation or for his own reputation. If he possessed any spiritual diligence, he ought to consider both by whom he was ordained and whose successor he became, so that he might follow blessed Flavian rather than the authors of his own honor.

And therefore, when the most devout emperors deign, in accordance with my entreaty, to rebuke our brother Anatolius concerning matters that rightly give rise to complaint,

[Note: Some have “in accordance with my entreaties.” These words seem to refer to the request Leo made in Letters 104 to Marcian and 105 to Pulcheria, whom he asked in chapter 4 to restrain Anatolius’s desire concerning the prerogative of the see of Constantinople.]

let your affection join its diligence to theirs, so that, with the fullest correction applied, all scandals may be cut away and he may cease injuring our son Aetius.

For in the case of a catholic bishop, even if there seemed to be some reason for anger against the archdeacon, it ought to have been passed over out of reverence for the faith, rather than that a most wicked heretic should occupy the place of a Catholic.

[Note: Quesnellus restored this passage with the aid of the Grimanic manuscript. The others, together with the editions, have: “even if there was in some way a priestly dignity, the archdeacon ought, out of reverence for the faith, to have been placed before the priest, rather than…”]

When I learn what follows, I shall judge more clearly what ought to be done.

For the present, restraining my grief,

[Note: Sichardus’s copy has the preferable reading.]

I have preferred to yield to patience, so that there might be room for pardon.

1192

### CHAPTER III

Concerning the Palestinian monks, who are said to have been in the turmoil of dissension for some time, I do not know with what disposition they are still agitated. Nor has anyone’s account made clear to me what causes they appear to put forward in support of the aforementioned discord: whether, that is, they serve Eutychian perversity with such madness, or whether they are implacably grieved that their bishop could have been led into this impiety—

[Note: From Letter 109 to the same Julian, which we published from the Regensburg manuscript, it is clear that Leo regarded these monks, who had stirred up so many disturbances in Palestine, as Eutychians. In other respects also he is shown to have been well informed from the beginning. What subsequently occurred, leading him to doubt the mind of those same monks and to desire fuller information, we do not know. Perhaps reports had reached Rome that the monks who, after Juvenal was expelled and Theodosius intruded, supported Theodosius openly condemned Eutyches by an anathema, as they had professed in their petition to Pulcheria. See volume IV of the Councils, Venetian edition, collection 1799. From this Leo may have begun to doubt whether these monks, hostile to Bishop Juvenal, were truly Eutychians, as he had previously thought, or whether they were Catholics who, carried away by excessive zeal for right faith, considered Juvenal unworthy of the episcopate because he had formerly favored Eutyches, even though he had corrected himself. In this matter, therefore, Julian could have been asked to inform him more precisely.]

because, contrary to the testimony of those holy places by which the whole world is instructed, he departed from the truth of the Lord’s incarnation, and because they think that what was judged fit to be healed by indulgence in others is not pardonable in him.

Accordingly, I wish to be more fully informed about these matters, so that suitable attention may also be given to correcting such people. For it is one thing impiously to arm oneself against the faith, and another to be moved beyond measure on behalf of the faith.

[Note: The common editions before Quesnellus have “to be detained in some error”; Quesnellus emended this from the Grimanic manuscript, together with other manuscripts and Sichardus’s copy, to “to detain someone in error.”]

You should also know that the documents which the presbyter Aetius previously indicated had been sent, and the *Brief Summary of the Faith* which you say you sent, have not yet reached me.

[Note: See our observations in Quesnellus’s second note, where we believe we have discovered what this *Brief Summary* was.]

Therefore, if an opportunity arises for a more expeditious courier,

[Note: Our manuscripts, together with the ancient common editions, have “a more convenient opportunity.”]

I shall be glad if, should there be any useful information, it is sent to me as soon as possible.

I desire to know how peaceful the Egyptian monks are, or of what faith they are, and what true reports reach you concerning the peace of the Alexandrian Church.

[Note: There had been a great dissension among the Egyptians over the ordination of Proterius, who had been substituted in the place of Dioscorus after his deposition. See Evagrius, Book II, chapter 5, and Liberatus, *Brief Summary*, chapter 14.]

I wished you to know, by copies being sent, what sort of letters I directed to its bishop, or to those who ordained him, or to the clergy.

[Note: These letters to Proterius, the new bishop of Alexandria, are missing. In them Leo seems to have requested from him a fuller and clearer exposition of the faith, as may be inferred from Letter 127, where he states that he had been satisfied, and also from Letter 129, in which he replies after receiving fuller letters from Proterius. See also Letters 134 and 131, chapter 1.]

The copies sent will also make fully clear what my present message is to the most merciful emperor and the most devout Augusta.

[Note: Quesnellus has this from the Grimanic manuscript. The other editions and manuscripts have: “the copies sent.”]

### CHAPTER IV

I wish to know whether my letter concerning the faith of the Lord’s incarnation, which, while Flavian of holy memory was still alive, I sent to your affection through the deacon Basil, was delivered to your Fraternity, since I suspect that you have never given any indication concerning its text.

[Note: Letter 35 is indicated.]

The acts of the synod, which were composed throughout all the days of the council in the city of Chalcedon, are insufficiently clear among us because of the diversity of language.

[Note: From this passage we think it may be inferred that complete Greek acts of the Council of Chalcedon existed among the Romans at this time; but because of the difference of the Greek language, which these men scarcely understood, their knowledge of those acts was not very clear. They knew only the principal points of that same council, rendered in Latin before a complete translation of all the acts; we shall list those principal points in our observations on Quesnellus’s third note to this letter. Since what had been translated into Latin before Leo wrote this letter constituted only a very small portion of the acts of Chalcedon, Leo asked Julian to have all these acts rendered into Latin in a most complete translation. We shall show in the observations cited that Julian did not do this.]

Therefore I specifically charge your Fraternity to have everything gathered into a single codex, translated, of course, into the Latin language in a fully complete rendering, so that we may have no doubt about any part of the proceedings and so that nothing can in any way remain ambiguous once, through your diligence, it has been brought to full understanding.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of the most illustrious man Opilio.

## LETTER CXIV

[Note: Otherwise 87. What was formerly 114 is now 143. Written on 21 March 453.]

[Note: It survives in manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 12, 17, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, in Sichardus’s copy, and in the excellent Vatican manuscript 1322. We now publish for the first time the Greek translation drawn from Vatican Greek manuscript 1455.]

### ADDRESSED TO THE BISHOPS WHO WERE ASSEMBLED IN THE HOLY SYNOD OF CHALCEDON

[Col. 1027]

[Note: In the table of collection 5, chapter 92, this title is found: “To the Council of Chalcedon, so that only what was decreed concerning the faith against Eutyches may have force; the rest is to be rejected.” In the complete manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection 17, from Rusticus’s edition, he prefixed this heading: “Letter of the most holy, most blessed, and apostolic Leo, pope, full in all things by the grace of God, confirming all the proceedings of the holy Council of Chalcedon, and invalidating only those things which, through the ambition of the Constantinopolitans, were enacted there against the decrees of the Council of Nicaea.” This letter responds to the report of the holy synod written above, which he had previously sent; we have given it as Letter 98.]

### SYNOPSIS

I. He agrees with what was established at Chalcedon concerning the faith.  
II. He will never regard as ratified what was enacted there against the Nicene canons.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: From the Greek version: “Leo, archbishop of Rome.” In editions of Leo before Quesnellus, and in Sichardus, the first heading is prefixed as follows: “Letter addressed to Juvenal and the other bishops who were assembled in the holy synod of Chalcedon”; but the inscription is presented as in the text. The manuscripts of collection 24 omit Juvenal’s name from the first heading. Most other manuscripts give only the inscription.]

**LEO, bishop, to the holy SYNOD held at Chalcedon**

[Col. 1027B]

### CHAPTER I
I do not doubt that your entire brotherhood knows that I embraced with all my heart the definition of the holy synod celebrated at Chalcedon for the confirmation of the faith [Note: The manuscripts of the Chalcedonian, Regensburg, and Vatican 11 collections read “definitions,” as does the following letter, chapter 1. Immediately afterward, Vatican 1322 has “of the holy faith.”], since no consideration allowed that I, who grieved that the unity of the catholic faith had been disturbed by heretics, should not rejoice exultantly that it had been restored. You could have recognized this not only from the actual result of that most blessed agreement [Note: This reading, discussed by Quesnellus in note 2, is also supported by our manuscripts. Some editions have *affectu*, perhaps through typographical error: “by affection.”], but also from my letters, which I sent after the return of my representatives to the bishop of Constantinople [Col. 1029A], if you had wished to disclose the response of the apostolic see [Note: In the manuscripts of Rusticus the following is added: “But since in those same letters I had criticized what had been wrongly attempted on the occasion of the synod, the aforesaid bishop preferred to conceal my congratulation rather than publish his own ambition. Therefore, lest …” We examined five manuscripts of Rusticus: Chigi 483, Vatican manuscripts 1323, 4166, and 5405, and the very ancient Verona 57; in all of them we found this addition. Baluzius also cites two other manuscripts of the same Rusticus, Corbie and Dijon, with the same addition, although he admits that these words, though written consecutively, are separated from the text of the letter in the ancient copies. They therefore seem to have been added by Rusticus as a marginal note and subsequently entered the text. He took them from the following letter, 115, which his collection does not place here. In all manuscripts of the various collections these words are absent; they are also omitted in the Greek version, which derives from the original sent to the East, as well as in the very ancient Vatican manuscript 1322. Although that manuscript presents the Chalcedonian synod from Rusticus’s edition, it does not present the whole synod; nor did it receive this letter from Rusticus. The letter occurs at the beginning of the manuscript, written in another hand and having nothing in common with Rusticus’s edition. See Quesnellus, note 3.]. [Note: This passage is quoted by Pope Pelagius II in Letter 2 to the bishops of Istria.]

Therefore, lest it should seem doubtful, through malicious interpreters, whether I approve what was established at the Council of Chalcedon by your unanimous agreement concerning the faith [Note: In Pelagius II, Letter 2 to the bishops of Istria: “whether I approved it.”], I sent the following letter to all our brothers and fellow bishops who had taken part in the aforesaid council. The most glorious and merciful emperor, as I requested [Note: Thus, together with Pelagius II, all our manuscripts except Vatican 1322, which, like the editions preceding Quesnellus, reads “he demanded.” Compare his note 4.], will graciously arrange for it to be brought to your attention, out of love for the catholic faith. In this way both the brotherhood as a whole and the hearts of all the faithful may know that I united my judgment with yours not only through the brothers who acted in my place [Note: The manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection 17, both ours and those cited by Baluzius, read “who carried out my responsibilities.”], but also through my approval of the synodal proceedings [Note: Together with the Grimanic manuscript, the Regensburg manuscript and the manuscripts of Rusticus read “to have united with you.” Other copies have *iniisse*, “to have entered into,” as do the editions of Rome and those published before Labbeus. The same reading occurs in Pelagius’s Letter 3, where the same testimony of Leo is inserted. Baronius, who first published this letter of Pelagius from the manuscript of Nicolaus Faber, and Labbeus, who restored the older reading, rendered the passage as it appears in that manuscript, later Colbert 4064, where, according to Baluzius, it reads *vobiscum munisse*, “to fortify with you.” A related reading appears in Leo’s letter itself as preserved in Vatican 1322: *vobis communisse*. There the final syllable, combined with *vobiscum*, which had wrongly been changed to *com*, produced *communisse*. Once this error is corrected, the true reading of the cited manuscripts is revealed: *vobiscum unisse*, “to unite with you.” The Greek translation confirms it as well.].

That is, solely for the sake of the faith [Col. 1029B]—a point that must often be stated—which was the reason why the general council was convened, both at the command of Christian emperors and with the agreement of the apostolic see [Note: The Regensburg manuscript, together with Pelagius II, reads “of the most Christian emperors.”]; so that, once the heretics who had refused correction had been condemned, no doubt at all might remain concerning the true incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: Editions preceding Quesnellus, having deleted *ut*, read: “with the heretics condemned, who, if they had wished to be corrected …” Quesnellus’s emendation is supported by the Grimanic manuscript, the Chalcedonian and Regensburg collections, Vatican 1322, and another Vatican manuscript of collection 11. The Vienna collection 5 likewise supports it, adding only *sic* before *corrigi*, “to be corrected.”]. Therefore, if anyone should ever dare either to uphold the perfidy of Nestorius or to defend the impious doctrine of Eutyches and Dioscorus, let him be cut off from the communion of Catholics [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads *usquam*, “anywhere.” Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection, both ours and Baluzius’s, read *secernetur* rather than *resecetur*, “shall be separated” rather than “shall be cut off.”]; nor let him share in the body whose reality he denies [Note: In the older printed editions of Leo, as also in the manuscripts of collection 24, the words “dearest brothers” were absent. Other manuscripts and editions include them, as does the Greek translation.], dearest brothers.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning the preservation also of the statutes of the holy Fathers, which were fixed by inviolable decrees at the Council of Nicaea, I urge your holiness to observe them, so that the rights of the Churches may remain ordered as they were established by those 318 Fathers, inspired by God [Col. 1031A] [Note: The same older editions of Leo, together with the Vienna collection 5 and the manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, read “were inspired and ordered.” Quesnellus adopted the reading from the Councils, supported by the Grimanic manuscript, the Chalcedonian manuscripts, Facundus, the Regensburg manuscript, and the Greek version.].

Let no shameless ambition covet anything alien [Note: Facundus reads “wickedly desire.”], nor let anyone seek his own increase through another’s diminution. For however much the arrogant elevation of vanity may fortify itself with coerced assent [Note: Vatican 1322 reads: “however much it may arm itself with assents extorted by flatteries.” The older editions of Leo, followed by the manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, have *sese* instead of *sic*. Shortly afterward, the Regensburg manuscript reads *appetitus*, “desire.” In other letters the expression is “extorted agreement,” especially Letter 105, chapter 2: “He is said to have given his agreement to the consent of certain men, with his signature extorted.” Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Isidore of Seville: ‘with assents extorted.’”], and may judge that its desires are to be strengthened by the name of councils, whatever differs from the canons of the aforesaid Fathers will be weak and invalid [Note: Vatican manuscripts 1322 and 3971 read “would differ.”].

Your holiness can learn from reading my writings—by which I repelled the efforts of the bishop of Constantinople—how reverently the apostolic see uses their rules [Note: Letter 106.], and that, with the Lord’s help, I am a guardian of the catholic faith and of the paternal constitutions [Note: Quesnellus adopts this reading from the Grimanic, Barberinian, and Victorine manuscripts and from Facundus; the editions of the Councils likewise support it, as do all our manuscripts and the Greek version, where the canons are named and the adjectives are translated as “of the paternal faith and of the catholic canons.” Other editions of Leo read “of paternal traditions.”].

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Opilio.

### Greek version

Leo, archbishop of Rome, to the holy synod held at Chalcedon.

I do not doubt that your entire brotherhood knows that I embraced with all my soul the decrees of the holy synod held in the city of Chalcedon for the confirmation of the faith; since no reason allowed that I, who suffered because the unity of the catholic faith had been disturbed by heretics, should not rejoice that it had been restored to health [Note: The particle *δέ* is extremely awkward here and should either be deleted or changed to *δή*.]. You could learn this not only from the actual result of the blessed agreement but also from my letters, which I sent after the return of those who had represented me to the bishop of Constantinople [Note: Read either “of the Constantinopolitans” or “of Constantinople.”], if I had wished to disclose the response of the apostolic throne [Note: Read *ἐβουλήθην*, “I wished.”].

Therefore, lest it should seem doubtful through malicious interpreters whether I confirm what was established at the synod held at Chalcedon by our unanimous agreement concerning the faith [Note: The passage is mutilated and corrupt. It may be restored as follows: “I confirm what was established at the synod held at Chalcedon, through your unanimity, concerning the faith; these things …”], I sent a letter to all our brothers and fellow bishops who had been present at the aforesaid synod. The illustrious and most humane emperor, as I requested, will graciously send it for your information, out of love for the catholic faith, so that both all the brothers and the souls of all unbelievers may learn that I united my own judgment with yours not only through my deacons, who acted in my place, but also through my agreement with the synodal records [Col. 1030B].

That is, solely for the sake of the faith—a point that must often be stated—which was the reason why the general council was convened, both at the command of Christian emperors and with the consent of the apostolic throne; so that, once the heretics who had refused to be corrected had been condemned, no doubt might remain concerning the true incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. Therefore, if anyone should ever dare to uphold the unbelief of Nestorius or to defend the impious doctrine of Eutyches or Dioscorus, let him be cut off from the communion of Catholics; nor let him share in the body whose truth he has denied, most honored brothers.

Concerning the preservation likewise of the canons of the holy Fathers, which were established at the Council of Nicaea by unalterable decrees, I remind your holiness to observe them, so that the rights of the Churches may remain as they were established by those 318 Fathers, inspired by God. Let shameless ambition desire nothing, nor let anyone wish to obtain any increase for himself through another’s diminution [Note: Read, with the Latin, “let anyone wish to obtain for himself.”].

For however much, after assents had been torn away, the pride of vanity may have fortified itself, and may think its own undertakings made more secure by the name of councils, everything whatsoever that departs from the canons mentioned above will be weak and invalid [Note: This passage is so entangled and corrupt that everyone can see the difficulty. It may be restored as follows: “Your holiness will be able to learn from my writings how reverently the apostolic throne has used the instructions of those Fathers, through which I repelled the efforts of the bishop of Constantinople …” The word corresponding to *τῶν* shortly afterward should be read as *καὶ ἐμέ*, “and me,” rather than *ἐμέ*.].

Your holiness will be able to learn by reading my writings how reverently the apostolic throne has used them, writings by which I repelled the efforts of the bishop of Constantinople: that I am, with the help of your God, a guardian of the paternal faith and of the catholic canons.

# LETTER CXV

[Note: Otherwise Letter 89. The letter formerly numbered 115 is now 145. Written on 21 March 453.]  
[Note: It survives in the manuscripts of the Spanish collection, Isidore 11, 12, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, and in Sichardus’s copy. The Greek translation has been recovered from Vatican Greek manuscript 1455.]

## TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

[Col. 1031]

[Note: In the Spanish collection the title reads: “In which he gives thanks that peace has been restored to the catholic Church through the Council of Chalcedon.”]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He gives thanks for the peace restored to the Church, the remnants of the heretics being suppressed, and Anatolius rebuked.  
II. Concerning the monks restrained by Marcian, and the approval of the Council of Chalcedon sent by Leo himself to the bishops.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: From the Greek version: “To the most glorious and most humane son, the Emperor Marcian Augustus, Leo, archbishop of Rome.”]

Leo, bishop, to Marcian Augustus.

## CHAPTER I

I have many reasons for rejoicing in all the letters of Your Clemency [Note: Namely, Letter 110.], since by the great mercy of divine providence I perceive that what has been granted to human affairs is that you graciously deign, with the most devout zeal, to assist ecclesiastical peace, which is preserved only through the unity of evangelical preaching.
