Thus the glory of your faith may increase not only through the benefit of the state but also through the advancement of religion, most glorious Augustus [Note: The older editions have “most glorious emperor.” The Greek version reads: “Most glorious and most merciful son and emperor Augustus.” The Regensburg manuscript omits all these words.].

Therefore I give ineffable thanks to God, who, at the time when he foresaw the scandals of the heretics that were about to arise, placed you upon the imperial throne, so that, for the salvation of the whole world, both royal power and priestly diligence might be active [Col. 1033A]. For since it was chiefly through your work that, by means of the synodal council, the defenders of an impious doctrine were condemned and sacrilegious error lost all its strength, it belongs to the victory of that same devotion that the evil which has been suppressed in its leaders should also be destroyed in whatever remnants remain.

Your Clemency judges that this can be accomplished more readily if it is taught throughout all the Churches that the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon have pleased the apostolic see [Note: The older printed editions, together with Sichardus, read “judges.”]. There was indeed no reason for doubt about this, since the agreement of all who subscribed to that faith had been added to the faith which I had issued according to the form of apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers [Note: The Spanish manuscript of Vienna, together with Vatican manuscript of collection 24, incorrectly reads *subscribendum*, “to be subscribed.” In the Spanish Vatican manuscript, which derives from a Gallican source, this error was corrected less accurately by reading *subscribendo*, “by subscribing”; that reading was adopted by Isidore and by other manuscripts descended from it and passed into the editions preceding Quesnellus. The true reading is supplied by the Grimanic and Regensburg manuscripts, which agree with the Greek version. In the older printed editions, the words *quae ad me*—“which came to me”—are incorrectly inserted, for the subject is the faith issued by Leo in Letter 28 to Flavian and accepted by the subscriptions of all the bishops. Quesnellus’s emendation, based on the Grimanic manuscript, is confirmed by the Spanish Vienna and Regensburg manuscripts, Vatican collection 24, and the Greek translation. See Quesnellus, note 2.]. I also sent, through my brother Bishop Lucian [Note: The Regensburg manuscript omits *talia* and, together with the Spanish Vienna manuscript, reads *antistitem*, “bishop,” instead of *episcopum*. On Lucian, see Quesnellus, note 3.], letters of such a kind both to Your Glory and to the bishop of Constantinople [Note: Letters 104 and 106.] that they clearly showed my approval of what had been defined concerning the catholic faith at the aforesaid synod [Col. 1033B].

But because in those same letters I had criticized what had been wrongly attempted on the occasion of the synod [Note: The Spanish Vienna manuscript and Isidore read “and because.”], the aforesaid bishop preferred to conceal my congratulation rather than make his own ambition public.

I have received great confidence, however, through God’s action in you, because you indicated in the words of your piety that you approved my observance in guarding the canons of the Fathers [Note: All our manuscripts and editions have this reading. Quesnellus alone reads *indicatis*, “you indicated,” and refers to annotation 3 on Col. 1019 in Letter 110. Shortly afterward, the Greek version reads: “I recognize that it pleases you, most glorious emperor.”]. And my joy is rightly doubled when I recognize that it greatly pleases you that the Nicene faith should retain its firmness and that the privileges of the Churches should remain unimpaired [Note: Although Marcian’s Letter 110, to which Leo is responding, contains no explicit mention of the Nicene faith, this should not lead anyone to suspect that something is missing from that letter. The Nicene faith is referred to in those passages of Letter 110 in which the emperor showed concern for the confirmation of the catholic faith defined at Chalcedon against the Eutychians. This was the same faith as the Nicene faith, stated more precisely as the circumstances required in opposition to the new heresy and commonly described in that way. See the Chalcedonian Definition, action 5. Perhaps the holy pontiff also alludes here to Marcian’s letter to the Palestinian monks, which he received from Julian of Cos together with the emperor’s letter; in it, the Nicene faith, confirmed and explained by the Fathers of Chalcedon, is presented. Compare volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1803.].

## CHAPTER II

Although Your Piety said nothing to me about your distinguished work for the faith, nevertheless, through the venerable Bishop Julian, my brother, who is especially close to me [Note: Quesnellus omitted the words *una mecum*, “together with me”; we restored them from our manuscripts, especially the Spanish Vienna manuscript and the Greek version, supported also by the Regensburg manuscript.], I learned how piously you deigned, by your reply, both to restrain and to instruct the minds of ignorant monks [Note: We have added *et*, “and,” from the Regensburg manuscript and the Greek version. The reference is to the imperial letter issued against the rioting monks of Palestine, which is appended to the proceedings of Chalcedon, volume IV, p. 1798.], so that, if divine mercy has not wholly abandoned them, they may recognize that they have learned what they should believe and come to know what they should fear [Col. 1035A] [Note: Thus the Regensburg manuscript and the manuscripts of collections 11 and 21. Other copies read “mercy.” The Spanish Vatican manuscript, Isidore, and manuscripts derived from them read “compassion,” “so that they may know and have learned.”].

Since in every way we must obey the most religious will of Your Piety [Note: The same Spanish Vatican and Isidorean manuscripts and others derived from them, together with the editions preceding Quesnellus, read: “the will of Your Piety and most religious purpose.” The Spanish Vienna and Grimanic manuscripts and the Regensburg manuscript, together with the Greek version, have the reading printed in the text.], I gladly added my judgment to the synodal constitutions which pleased me concerning the confirmation of the catholic faith and the condemnation of the heretics [Col. 1035C] [Note: See Quesnellus, note 4.]. Your Clemency will graciously order that this judgment be brought to the knowledge of all priests and Churches.

I believe and hope that the grace of God will be present, enabling the most holy concern of so great a ruler to attain the fullest fruit of its desire, so that, when every opportunity for dissent has been cut off, peace and truth may reign everywhere through apostolic teaching [Note: These words seem, in my view, to come from the translator, but they are entirely faulty. He should have translated them in this or a similar manner: “so that, when every disagreement has been cut away, peace and truth may prevail everywhere through apostolic teaching.”].

Let Your Clemency know that I have personally entrusted my brother Bishop Julian with this task: whatever he proves to concern the preservation of the faith there, he is to report confidently, in my name, to Your Piety. For I am certain that, with God’s help, you are sufficient both to correct and to defend all these matters [Note: The Grimanic and Thuan manuscripts cited by Quesnellus, and one of our manuscripts of collection 21, read “to cleanse.” Shortly afterward, the Regensburg manuscript omits “with God’s help.”].

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Opilio.

### Greek version

To the most glorious and most humane son, Marcian Augustus, Leo, archbishop of Rome.

I have great cause for joy in all the letters of Your Mildness. For I find that, through the great humanity of divine providence, you have been appointed for human affairs [Note: The pronoun *σε*, “you,” would more appropriately be absent here.], since you graciously deign to assist ecclesiastical peace and unity, preserved according to evangelical proclamation, with devout zeal [Note: The passage is corrupt. It may be remedied as follows: “which is preserved in no other way except through the unity of evangelical proclamation …”]. Thus the glory of your faith may increase not only through the administration of public affairs but also through ecclesiastical works [Note: In the first collation, following Vatican Greek manuscript 1455, we wrote *αὐξηνθείη*, “may be increased.” We have preferred the reading of Vatican Ottobonian manuscript 29, which we received later.], most glorious and most humane son, Emperor Augustus.

Therefore I confess ineffable thanks to God, who, at the time when he foresaw that the scandals of the heretics would arise, established you in the empire, so that, for the salvation of the whole world, both royal power and priestly zeal might flourish. For since it came about through your exceptional work that, once those who defended the impious doctrine had been condemned by the synod, sacrilegious error would lose all its forces, it belongs to the victory of that same disposition [Note: Alternatively, *προθέσεως*, “purpose.”] that the evil which is found among its own leaders should also be wiped out among any others [Note: Either something such as “having been overthrown” is missing after *is found*, or the translator read the passage very differently from us.]. Your Serenity considers this easier to accomplish [Note: Perhaps read “which is to be fulfilled.”] if it is taught throughout all the Churches that the decrees of the holy synod held at Chalcedon pleased the apostolic throne.

There was no suspicion of doubt about this, since, when everyone had subscribed to this faith, the agreement [Note: Read *συναίνεσις*, “agreement.”] had been added [Note: Read *προστέθειται*, “had been added.”] to the faith which I had sent forth according to the form of apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers [Col. 1034B]. Through my brother Bishop Lucian, letters of such a kind were also sent both to Your Glory and to the bishop of Constantinople, and through them it is shown most clearly that I adhere to what had been defined concerning the catholic faith at the aforesaid synod.

But since in those same letters I had criticized what had been wrongly attempted on the occasion of the synod [Note: Read *διεβεβλήκειν*, “I had criticized.”], the aforesaid bishop preferred to silence my thanksgiving rather than publish his own ambition [Note: Read “his own.”]. Through God, who granted it through you, great frankness was also conveyed to me, because you indicated in the letters of Your Piety that you approved my firm observance of the paternal canons.

And my joy is rightly doubled when I know that it pleases you, most glorious emperor, that the faith of Nicaea should retain its own strength [Note: Perhaps read “its strength,” rather than “its own faith.”], and that the privileges of the Churches should remain unshaken.

Although Your Piety said nothing to me concerning the distinguished work of your faith, nevertheless, through the man who reveres you, I indicate that it was made known to me personally, together with my brother and fellow bishop Julian, how piously you deigned, by your reply, both to restrain and to teach the souls of ignorant monks [Col. 1036A] [Note: Read *κατηξιώσατε*, “you deigned.”], so that, if divine compassion had not entirely abandoned them [Note: Read “if it has not.”], they might perceive and learn what they believe and know what they ought to fear.

Since we must obey with all our strength the devout purpose of Your Piety, I gladly added my own judgment to the decrees of the synod which pleased me concerning the confirmation of the catholic faith and the condemnation of the heretics [Col. 1036B] [Note: “I have added.”]. In order that it might come to the knowledge of all the priests and the Churches, Your Mildness will graciously order it to be published [Note: Read “your command.”].

I hope and believe that the grace of God will be present and will enable the holy concern of so great an emperor to attain the fruit of its own desire, so that, once every disagreement has been cut away, peace and truth may prevail everywhere through apostolic teaching [Note: The preceding wording is evidently faulty and perhaps comes from the translator. It should be rendered approximately as follows: “so that, when every disagreement has been cut away, peace and truth may prevail everywhere through apostolic teaching.”].

Let Your Serenity know that I have personally ordered this concerning my brother Bishop Julian: whatever he judges to pertain there to the preservation of the faith, he is to submit it confidently, in my name, to Your Piety [Note: Read *ὑποβάλλοι* or *ὑποβάλλῃ*, “let him submit.”]. For I know with certainty that, with God granting it, you are sufficient for the correction and defense of all these matters [Note: Read *ἐπαρκεῖν*, “to be sufficient.”].

# LETTER CXVI

[Note: Otherwise Letter 90. The letter formerly numbered 116 is now 146. Written on 21 March 453.]  
[Note: We have collated this letter with the Regensburg manuscript of collection 19 and the Venetian manuscript of Saint Mark, collection 12; it was found only in these collections.]

## TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA

[Col. 1035B]

## SYNOPSIS

I. He gives thanks for the vigor of the faith and for the decrees issued against rebellious monks.  
II. He says that he sent letters to the bishops of Chalcedon as witnesses to his agreement.

Leo, bishop, to Pulcheria Augusta.

## CHAPTER I

Although I have received no letter from Your Piety, when the most glorious emperor wrote, I rejoiced in his graciousness no otherwise than if the greetings of Your Serenity had also been delivered to me. Therefore it was necessary that the customary duty owed by me should be observed, so that I might show that I rejoiced in the well-being of Your Clemency and continually ask God in prayer to preserve you in every prosperity, both for the Roman state and for the catholic Church.

Concerning the vigor of your faith, by which you unceasingly offer the Lord a sacrifice of praise, I cannot say how great my thanks to God are [Col. 1036B], since we recognize that the rulers of our time possess not only royal power but also priestly teaching [Note: Marcian and Pulcheria, in the letters issued against the Palestinian monks, which are printed in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, pp. 1798 and 1819, admirably defend the catholic faith. If copies of those same letters, here referred to, had been rendered into Latin for Leo’s easier understanding, they may perhaps have used the version prefixed by Epiphanius Scholasticus to the Codex encyclius, as indicated in volume V of the Councils, p. 33.].

For, as my brother Bishop Julian has reported, salutary decrees contained in copies of your commands have reached us. In them you deigned to chastise the insane ignorance of the monks by showing mercy and to punish it by teaching, so that, if divine mercy should turn them toward repentance, they might wash away with many tears both their participation in wicked violence and the blasphemies of the heretics.

## CHAPTER II

As for the fact that the most devout emperor wished me to send written communications to all the bishops who had taken part in the Council of Chalcedon [Note: Letter 114], in which I would confirm what had been defined there concerning the rule of faith, I gladly fulfilled his wish. I did so lest anyone’s deceptive pretense should wish my judgment to be regarded as uncertain, since, through the bishop of Constantinople, to whom I had abundantly expressed my joy, it could have become known to everyone that I had written [Note: Letter 106.]—unless he had preferred to conceal my joy rather than publish the rejection of his ambition [Col. 1037A].

I ask Your Piety to deign to grant my brother and fellow bishop Julian, to whom I have entrusted my concern in the matter of the faith, such confidence that he may report to Your Piety whatever will benefit the universal Church.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Opilio.

# LETTER CXVII

[Note: Otherwise Letter 88. The letter formerly numbered 117 is now 136. Written on 21 March 453.]  
[Note: We have collated this letter, edited by Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript, with the Regensburg manuscript.]

## TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COS

## SYNOPSIS

I. In order to satisfy the emperor and remove an opportunity from the heretics, he sent letters to the bishops of Chalcedon concerning his agreement.  
II. Concerning the monks restrained by Marcian’s edict, and the archimandrites rebuked by Pulcheria’s reply.  
III. Concerning Eudocia, whom Leo admonished at the emperor’s confidential command.  
IV. That the deposition of Aetius must be endured patiently, lest, by meddling in the governance of other Churches, he seem to exceed his proper measure.  
V. That Anatolius wished to elicit from the Illyrian bishops a subscription in support of his ambition. Concerning the letter sent to the bishops of Chalcedon.

[Col. 1037B]

Leo to Julian, bishop.

## CHAPTER I

How watchfully and devotedly your brotherhood keeps vigil for the catholic faith is shown by the text of your letters, whose explanations greatly relieve my concern [Note: The Regensburg manuscript has this reading. Quesnellus, from the Grimanic manuscript, reads “by which my concern is greatly relieved, with the intervention …”]. Added to this is the most religious piety of the devout emperor, which is clearly seen to have been prepared by the Lord for the strengthening of the universal Church, so that, while Christian rulers act with holy zeal for the faith, the priests of the Lord may confidently pray for their reign.

[Note: The words enclosed in brackets are quoted in Pope Pelagius II’s letter to Elias, chapter 6.]

What the most merciful emperor therefore considered necessary, I gladly fulfilled: I sent a letter to all the brothers who had taken part in the Council of Chalcedon, demonstrating that I approved what our holy brothers had confirmed concerning the rule of faith. I did this especially on account of those who, as an opportunity for concealing their perfidy, wish the council’s decrees to appear weak or doubtful because they were not strengthened by my judgment and agreement. Yet after the return of the brothers whom I had sent in my place, I had written letters to the bishop of Constantinople, so that, if he had wished to publish them, it could have been abundantly recognized from them how greatly I approved what the synod had decreed concerning the faith [Note: Quesnellus, together with the Grimanic manuscript, reads “had decreed concerning the faith.” The Regensburg manuscript supplied the supplement and emendation.].

But because those same letters contained the kind of answer that ambition would receive, he wished it to remain unknown what I thought about the constitutions of the brothers [Col. 1038A], lest it be discovered at the same time what I had written in defense of the inviolable authority of the Nicene canons.

Therefore let Your Affection take care to remind the most devout emperor through frequent representations that, with his own words added, he should order the writings of the apostolic see to be delivered to the priests of each province, so that no enemy of the truth may thereafter presume to excuse himself on the grounds of my silence.

## CHAPTER II

I wish you to know how greatly I rejoice both at the edict of the most Christian emperor, by which he showed what the ignorant madness of certain monks deserved, and at the reply of the most devout Augusta, by which she rebuked the heads of the monasteries [Note: Pulcheria’s letter is called a reply because it was issued in response to the monks’ petition. See Quesnellus, note 4, and annotation 4 on Col. 1036 in the preceding letter.].

I do not fail to recognize that this fervor for the faith has been bestowed upon them by divine inspiration, so that it may become evident to everyone that their excellence belongs not only to the royal summit but also to priestly holiness [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “their entire excellence.”]. Since I have sought both now and previously to make this confidence more familiar to your brotherhood, I trust in their benevolence and believe that they will not reluctantly grant requests that are necessary.

## CHAPTER III

Since the most merciful emperor deigned to command me more privately, through our son Paul, that I should admonish our most merciful daughter, the Augusta Eudocia [Note: The Regensburg manuscript correctly writes this name, as do other manuscripts of ours and the title of Letter 123, whose composition was prompted by this passage. The reference is to Eudocia, wife of Theodosius the Younger, who, while living in Palestine, supported the rioting monks for some time. Quesnellus printed “Eudoxia,” as well as “Eudoxia” in the title of Letter 123, from the Grimanic manuscript; this is incorrect. Eudoxia, wife of Valentinian III, was the daughter of this Eudocia by Theodosius. In a marginal note Quesnellus writes: “Observe from this sole document how Eudoxia [read: Eudocia], having been changed for the better, began to favor the catholic faith.” Rather, this passage shows that she favored the Eutychians, so that for this reason the emperor judged that she should be admonished by Leo. In fact, she only came to her senses in 456, after hearing of Valentinian’s murder and the captivity of her daughter Eudoxia, as we learn from the Life of Saint Euthymius in the Greek Analecta edited by the Benedictine Fathers.].

I did what he wished: I wrote so that she might understand how beneficial it would be for her to support the catholic faith, and I obtained that she should also be admonished concerning this by letters from the most merciful emperor, her son [Note: Valentinian is meant, to whom Eudoxia, the daughter of Eudocia, was married.]. I do not doubt that she too will labor with devout zeal so that the authors of the seditions may recognize the purpose of their profession, and, if they do not understand the preaching of those who teach, may at least fear the power of those who punish.

I therefore wish to learn at once from a letter of your Affection what result this concern of ours has achieved, and whether at last rebellious ignorance has subsided. If it thinks our teaching doubtful, let it at least not reject the writings of blessed memory—Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril, bishops of Alexandria. Our formulation of the faith agrees with theirs so completely that the person who professes agreement with them differs from us in nothing.

## CHAPTER IV

We sympathize with our son, the presbyter Aetius, in his grief. Since someone judged worthy of rejection has been appointed to his office in his place, there is no doubt that this change is an injury to Catholics [Col. 1039A]. For the present, however, these things must be endured patiently, lest we seem to exceed the measure of our customary moderation [Note: The Regensburg manuscript has this reading. Quesnellus, from the Grimanic manuscript, incorrectly reads “the measure of consolidation.”]. For the time being it may be sufficient for the aforesaid man that he is protected by the favor of the most merciful emperors. In my recent letters I commended him to them in such a way [Note: Letters 111 and 112] that I do not doubt his favor will be increased in the eyes of their most religious minds.

## CHAPTER V

We also want you to know that after our admonition Bishop Anatolius persists so recklessly in the audacity of his presumption that he summoned the Illyrian bishops in order that they might subscribe on his behalf. This was reported to us by the bishop who was sent from Thessalonica as the messenger of the ordination [Note: This concerns Euxithaeus, the bishop of Thessalonica who was substituted for Anastasius; Leo sent Letter 150 to him. The fact and date of his ordination can be established from this passage.].

For this reason we did not wish to write to him, although you yourself had requested that it should be done, because we saw that he did not wish to be corrected [Note: The following words refer to Anatolius.].

I prepared two identical letters to the synod: to one I appended copies of my letter to Bishop Anatolius; the other had no copies appended. I leave it to your judgment that you deliver whichever you think should be given to the most merciful emperor, retaining the other yourself.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Opilio.

# LETTER CXVIII

[Note: Otherwise Letter 91. The letter formerly numbered 118 is now 149. Written on 2 April 453.]  
[Note: It is found in the manuscripts of collections 12, 18, and 24, and in Sichardus’s copy.]

## TO THE SAME JULIAN, BISHOP OF COS

## SYNOPSIS

I. That he had omitted nothing on behalf of the faith and the Church.  
II. That the duty of preaching belongs to priests alone, not to monks; the emperor’s zeal must be aroused against the Alexandrian parricides.

Leo, bishop, to Julian, bishop of Cos.

## CHAPTER I
Letters of your affection, which you sent through my son [Col. 1039C], the illustrious man Esychius [Note: [Col. 1039D] Editions before Quesnellus read Isichium; Sichardus, Isicium.], I received at the time when I had already replied to your more recent letters [Note: [Col. 1039D] Letters 113 and 117.] on a repeated occasion. Since in this communication also you complained, with justified grief, of the same most impious heretics, it was appropriate, now that an opportunity for writing had arisen, not to remain silent.

Therefore, in the cause of the faith, whatever could and can be done on behalf of our office [Note: [Col. 1039D] Elsewhere, according to the manuscripts of collection 24, “it was fitting” (oportuit); Sichardus, “it was fitting and we can” (opurtuit ac possumus).]—with the Lord’s help—we carry out both diligently and willingly, so that we may serve Christ’s Gospel irreproachably, lest through our negligence any part of the Catholic Church appear to be neglected. For this reason, as everyone knows, I have not ceased to labor so that, once the truth of the Lord’s incarnation had been made manifest and defended, the whole brotherhood might recognize what, everywhere in accordance with apostolic teaching, ought both to be held and to be taught; and so that, through the divinely inspired zeal of the most glorious emperors, when a synod had been assembled in the city of Chalcedon [Col. 1039D–1040A] 1211, heretical impiety might be condemned, so that neither any follower of Nestorius nor any disciple of Eutyches might be able to enjoy free association with Catholics, since, in what concerns the authority of the holy council, no disagreement remained anywhere.

But if some, blinded by their own obstinacy, have passed into the madness of a rejected mind to such an extent that they prefer to rage rather than to be healed, it belongs to the imperial power to suppress more rigorously those who disturb ecclesiastical peace and the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 1040D] Thus Quesnellus. Elsewhere: enemies of the peace of the Church and of the commonwealth.], which rightly glories in Christian rulers.

## CHAPTER II

But just as, as we have said, it belongs to imperial authority to restrain public disturbances and sacrilegious seditions with greater severity, so it belongs to sacerdotal authority not to allow monks any freedom to preach against the faith [Col. 1040B], and to resist with every strength, lest they dare to claim for themselves what belongs to priests.

Hence we are astonished that Bishop Thalassius [Note: [Col. 1040D] This appears to be that Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, who, although he was among the leaders of the pseudo-Ephesian synod, nevertheless repented of his conduct and was received at Chalcedon.] should have permitted some opportunity for writing or preaching to a certain George who, by presuming to do unlawful things, lost both the purpose and the name of a monk. If it seems good to your affection, we shall send the bishop an appropriate letter on this matter [Note: [Col. 1040D] Thus Quesnellus correctly. Previously, incorrectly: let us send.].

Let your brotherhood therefore act through suitable representations, so that the most merciful emperor may command what will please the Lord, and order the instigators of bloody seditions to be restrained more appropriately. Thus neither those whose hands committed the crimes nor those who make use of such madness may remain unpunished [Note: [Col. 1040D] Quesnellus omitted this word; it has been restored from our manuscripts.]. But if judicial inquiry and the confession of the guilty reach those persons by whose counsel or instigation such great evils were committed, no consolations of favor are to be provided for them. For the more highly they were believed to be good, the more detestable they are, since their impiety, which had been concealed under hypocrisy, is now exposed.

Therefore let the most Christian and most devout emperor do what he understands will benefit ecclesiastical peace. I trust that, through heavenly inspiration, he will be instructed in such a way that he will command the disorderly to be recalled through discipline [Note: [Col. 1040D] Editions before Quesnellus read, incorrectly: to recall.], while ordering that their blood be spared, although those who dared to resist both divine and human constitutions deserve to undergo every punishment. [Note: [Col. 1040D] This chronological note was added by Quesnellus from the Grimani manuscript of collection 18; it is absent from the manuscripts of the other collections.]

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the consulship of the illustrious man Opilio.

## LETTER [Note: [Col. 1040D] Elsewhere numbered 92. The letter formerly numbered 119 is now 150. Written on 11 June in the year 453.] CXIX [Note: [Col. 1040D] Found in manuscripts of collections 3, 8, 12, 18, 19, and 23, and in Vatican manuscript 541, among the letters appended to collection 21, and finally in a copy of the first edition of the sermons of Saint Leo.]

### TO MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH, through Marianus the presbyter and Olympius the deacon.

[Col. 1040D]

### SUMMARY

I. The faith lies midway between two extremes. [Col. 1041A]  
II. Maximus ought to keep watch over the purity of the faith in the Eastern Churches.  
III. The privileges of the Churches ought to remain undisturbed.  
IV. Anatolius’s attempts, contrary to the canons of Nicaea, will be void.  
V. If the legates approved anything at the synod apart from the matter of the faith, it must be rescinded.  
VI. The office of preaching must be granted to no one except bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1041C] In editions circulated after Canisius and before Quesnellus: “Leo, bishop of the Catholic Church, to Maximus, his most beloved brother and bishop of Antioch.” None of our manuscripts has this heading. See Quesnellus’s first note.]

LEO TO MAXIMUS OF ANTIOCH.

## CHAPTER I

The text of your letters shows how greatly your affection values the most sacred unity of the common faith and the peaceful harmony of ecclesiastical peace. Our sons, the presbyter Marianus and the deacon Olympius, brought them to me; they were all the more welcome to us because through them we exchange mutual communications, and the grace of God becomes increasingly known [Note: [Col. 1041D] Thus, together with the editions of the Councils. The common editions of Leo read, “might become known.” The Ratisbon manuscript reads, “so that it might become increasingly known.” A little later, “openly” is found in editions before Quesnellus and in the copy of the first edition.]—the grace by which throughout the whole world people rejoice in the revealed light of Catholic truth [Col. 1041B].

Although, as we deeply regret, some still love their own darkness, as the report of the messengers indicates, and, although the splendor of day has risen everywhere, still delight in the gloom of their blindness; having lost the faith, they remain Christians only in an empty and meaningless name [Col. 1041B–1041C] 1213, possessing no understanding by which to distinguish error from error or to separate the blasphemy of Nestorius from the impiety of Eutyches.

Nor can any of their falsehood be considered excusable because they are themselves opposed to one another in their perversity. For although the disciples of Eutyches detest Nestorius and the followers of Nestorius anathematize Eutyches, nevertheless, by the judgment of Catholics, both sides are condemned, and both heresies together are cut away from the body of the Church, since neither falsehood can have concord with us. [Col. 1041C]

It makes no difference by what sacrilege they dissent from the truth of the Lord’s incarnation, since neither the authority of the Gospel nor the logic of the sacrament accepts what they think most perversely [Note: [Col. 1041D] The first edition reads: “neither has the authority of the Gospel nor the meaning of the sacrament.” Later, we have preferred “receive” to “accept,” on the basis of the Ratisbon manuscript.].

## CHAPTER II

And therefore, dearest brother, your affection ought to perceive with all its heart under whose governance of the Church the Lord has wished you to preside [Col. 1042A], and to remember the teaching which the chief and most blessed of all the apostles, Peter, founded throughout the whole world by a uniform preaching, but with a particular ministry [Note: [Col. 1041D] The Barberini manuscript of collection 3 reads, “ministry.” Immediately before the word “Roman,” the Ratisbon manuscript and the first edition repeat “in.”] in the cities of Antioch and Rome.

Thus you should understand that he who is pre-eminent in the dwelling-place of his glorification demands that the institutions he handed down be maintained, just as he received them from the very truth that he confessed. Nor should you in any way allow the Gospel to be assailed by wicked heretics in the Eastern Churches, and especially in those which the canons of the most sacred Fathers at Nicaea assigned to the see of Antioch [Note: [Col. 1042C] The same first edition reads, “in the Churches of the East.” Quesnellus rightly proves in note 2 that this expression is to be taken broadly, not strictly as referring only to the Churches subject to the bishop of Antioch. Compare our observations to be appended to the same note.], or allow the doctrine of either Nestorius or Eutyches to be defended by anyone.

For, as I have said, the rock of the Catholic faith, whose name the blessed apostle Peter received from the Lord, admits no trace of either impiety [Note: [Col. 1042C] The Vallicella manuscript and the first edition read, “of either impiety.”]. It clearly and plainly anathematizes Nestorius, who separated the nature of the Word from the nature of flesh in the conception of the blessed Virgin [Note: [Col. 1042C] The common editions read, most erroneously, “union.” Quesnellus’s correction, based on the Grimani manuscript and one Barberini manuscript, is also confirmed by our Vatican manuscripts of collection 3, three manuscripts of collection 8, the Ratisbon manuscript of collection 19, and the copy of the first edition. Quesnellus rightly noted that this passage is to be understood of the active conception by which the Virgin conceived the Son of God. A little later, the addition of the words “according to true flesh,” introduced by Quesnellus, is supported by these same manuscripts and by the first edition.], dividing the one Christ into two and wishing there to be one person of the Godhead and another of the humanity.

Yet the one and the same person was born, according to eternal deity, timelessly from the Father, and, according to true flesh, was born in time from his mother. Likewise, it execrates Eutyches, who, emptying out the reality of human flesh in the Lord Jesus Christ, asserts that the Word itself was transformed into flesh [Note: [Col. 1042D] The Ratisbon manuscript and the Vatican manuscript of collection 8, together with the first edition, read, “asserted”], so that birth, nourishment, growth, suffering, death, burial, and resurrection on the third day would have belonged to deity alone, which did not assume the reality of a servant’s form but only its appearance.

## CHAPTER III

Therefore it is fitting that you be guarded with the utmost vigilance, lest heretical perversity dare to claim anything for itself. It is appropriate that you resist these things with sacerdotal authority, while you frequently inform us through your reports about the progress of the Churches and what is taking place.

For it is worthy that you share in the concern of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 1042D] Editions before Quesnellus read, “and to increase confidence.” Two manuscripts of collection 8 read, “and to increase confidence.” A little later, Quesnellus introduced “the third privileges” in place of “the privileges of the third see.” We have restored the old reading from all our manuscripts and from the first edition.] and recognize, for the confidence to act, the privileges of the third see, which no one’s ambition will diminish [Col. 1042D–1043A] [Note: [Col. 1042D] Thus in Quesnellus, the Ratisbon manuscript, and the manuscripts of collection 3. The editions read, “so that they are diminished by no one’s ambition.” The copy of the first edition reads, “which see is found to have exceeded nothing through anyone’s ambition.” The same appears in Vatican manuscript 5845 of collection 8, which omits only “to have exceeded.”]

For I hold the canons of Nicaea in such great reverence that I have neither permitted nor will I permit what was established by the holy Fathers to be violated by any innovation [Note: [Col. 1043B] The same Vatican manuscript, together with the first edition, reads, “nor will I permit it to be confused or violated by any innovation.”]. Although the merits of prelates are sometimes different, the rights of the sees nevertheless remain [Note: [Col. 1043B] The first edition reads, “the rights of the Churches.”]. Rivals may perhaps bring some disturbance against them, but they cannot diminish their dignity.

Therefore, whenever your affection believes that something must be done on behalf of the privileges of the Church of Antioch, take care to explain it in a letter of your own [Note: [Col. 1043B] The same edition reads, “let it strive to explain it through its own messengers.” Here the more probable reference is to the cession of the three Palestinian provinces to the prejudice of the see of Antioch; this will be demonstrated in the observations on Quesnellus’s dissertation 9.], so that we may respond to your consultation clearly and appropriately.

## CHAPTER IV

For the present, it is sufficient to declare generally concerning all matters [Note: [Col. 1043B] The Ratisbon manuscript adds “me”; a little later, three Vatican, Vallicella, and Ratisbon manuscripts read “arisen” in place of “extorted.”] that if anything has been attempted by anyone against the statutes of the canons of Nicaea in any synod, or appears for a time to have been extorted, it can inflict no prejudice upon inviolable decrees [Col. 1044A]. It will be easier to dissolve agreements of any kind than to corrupt in any respect the regulations of the aforesaid canons.

For ambition does not neglect opportunities for stealth [Note: [Col. 1043B] Editions before Quesnellus read, “of creeping in.”], and whenever a general assembly of priests has been held because of circumstances that have arisen, it is difficult for the desire of wicked men not to contrive and seek something beyond measure [Note: [Col. 1043B] The first edition reads, “it is difficult for the desire of the wicked not to contrive and seek something beyond measure.” The Ratisbon manuscript reads, “beyond its own measure.”]. Thus, even at the synod of Ephesus, which struck down the impious Nestorius together with his doctrine, Bishop Juvenal believed that he could advance and establish his audacious designs through forged letters, in order to obtain the primacy of the province of Palestine [Note: [Col. 1043C] Thus according to all the manuscripts of collection 8, the Ratisbon manuscript, and the first edition. Elsewhere, “to suffice.” The note that Quesnellus appended to this testimony in his second edition must not be omitted:

“Observe,” he says, “that in these same words Leo speaks only of the primacy of Palestine, and that Juvenal at that time was thinking only of obtaining that primacy, if we give Leo’s words the credit they deserve. Nevertheless, the suspicion of John of Antioch and his colleagues, which the Reverend Father Lupus considers and condemns as defamatory, should not on that account be judged defamatory. In their first protestation issued from Chalcedon against Cyril and the other Fathers of the Ephesian synod, they mock Juvenal as one who was attempting to subject to himself both Phoenician provinces and Arabia:

‘Formerly, indeed,’ they say, ‘when certain things had been presumed by Juvenal, once most reverend bishop of Jerusalem, we kept quiet, while we saw that we ought to contend for the regulations. At that time we were by no means unaware of his suchlike rash actions and fantasies against both Phoenicia and Arabia.’

These are the words of that protestation, not from the version inserted into the acts of the First Synod of Ephesus, but from the Ephesian records published by Christian Lupus and reprinted by Baluzius. When these are examined, it is as clear as midday that this undertaking of Juvenal is different from the one alleged by John, and from that for which our Leo reproaches him. For when the protestation of the Easterners was issued, the Ephesian synod had not yet been dissolved; nevertheless, it discusses something previously presumed by Juvenal, as the words ‘formerly’ and ‘at that time’ indicate. Our Leo, however, speaks of something attempted at the time of the Ephesian council.”

Thus far Quesnellus. Whether Leo wished here to indicate only what Juvenal was satisfied with at this time—namely, that at Chalcedon he had agreed that only the primacy of Palestine should be attributed to him—or whether he wished to assert that at the Ephesian council also Juvenal had coveted only Palestine and not Arabia and Phoenicia as well, cannot be determined. That he not only coveted these provinces but possessed them at the time of the Council of Chalcedon is evident from the proceedings of that synod, which we shall reproduce and defend in our observations on Quesnellus’s dissertation 9, from the very ancient Vatican manuscript 1322 edited by Baluzius but not sufficiently observed. For in the sentence of the legates recorded in those proceedings, it is indicated that Juvenal restored these provinces in the following words:

‘We have decreed, with the consent of the holy synod, that the first or second Phoenicia together with Arabia, which the see of Antioch had recently lost, be recalled to its former jurisdiction.’

A little later, “through commendatory letters” is found in the Vallicella manuscript and in the first edition.]

The blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, rightly horrified by this, informed me in his letters what the aforementioned ambition had dared [Col. 1044B–1045A]. He earnestly begged that no assent be given to unlawful attempts [Note: [Col. 1045C] The first edition reads, “he took care that no…”].

For the copies of the letter of the blessed Cyril which you sent to us: you should know that, having sought it in our archive, we found it to be authentic. But this is the distinctive principle of my judgment: however large the number of priests who, through someone’s stealth, may decree something that is found to be contrary to the constitutions of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, it must be annulled in consideration of justice [Note: [Col. 1045C] Quesnellus, together with some of our manuscripts, reads “defense.” The reading of the earlier editions seemed better; we restored it from the Ratisbon and Vallicella manuscripts and from Hincmarus. A little later, “by whose subscription he might distinguish it” is found in the manuscripts of collection 8 and in the first edition.], since the tranquility of universal peace cannot otherwise be preserved unless reverence for the canons remains inviolate.

## CHAPTER V

If, indeed, anything is reported to have been done by those brothers whom I sent in my place to the holy synod, beyond what pertained to the matter of the faith [Note: [Col. 1045C] The Ratisbon manuscript reads, “is asserted.” This indicates the assent by which the legates of the apostolic see approved the cession of the three Palestinian provinces to Juvenal of Jerusalem, to the prejudice of the see of Antioch.], it will have absolutely no validity. For they were sent by the apostolic see for this one purpose: that, once the heresies had been cut away, they should be defenders of the Catholic faith.

Whatever is brought before episcopal judgment apart from the specific matters of synodal councils may have some basis for adjudication, provided that nothing concerning it has been defined by the holy Fathers at Nicaea [Note: [Col. 1045C] The copy of the first edition reads, “has been defined.”]. For whatever disagrees with their regulations and constitution can never obtain the consent of the apostolic see.

You will be instructed how carefully this is guarded by us through copies of the letter [Note: [Col. 1045C] Letter 106.] that we sent to the bishop of Constantinople, restraining his ambition. Cause them to come to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow priests, so that they may know that ecclesiastical peace must be preserved through concord pleasing to God.

## CHAPTER VI

Your affection must also take care to prevent anyone except those who are the Lord’s priests [Note: [Col. 1045C] The same matter is touched upon in the preceding letter, chapter 2, and in the following letter, chapter 6. Compare Quesnellus’s note 5.] from daring to claim for himself the right to teach and preach [Col. 1046A], whether he is a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of some learning [Note: [Col. 1045C] The occasion of this decree may be inferred from the following letter, chapter 6, namely from Theodoret’s complaints, which the legates returning from the Council of Chalcedon reported to the pontiff concerning certain Eastern monks who arrogated to themselves the office of preaching. Barsumas the abbot and his followers may perhaps be indicated; how much he favored Eutyches is clearer not from the pseudo-synod of Ephesus than from the fourth session at Chalcedon, where he is said to have stirred up all Syria. For the distinction made here between monks and laymen, see Quesnellus’s note 6.].

For although it is desirable that all the sons of the Church should think what is right and sound, nevertheless no one established outside the priestly order may be permitted to assume for himself the rank of preacher [Note: [Col. 1045D] The Vallicella manuscript of collection 8 and the first edition read, “outside the order of priests”; immediately afterward, the same manuscript together with the Vatican manuscript of that collection reads, “assume the preaching.”], since it is appropriate that everything in the Church of God be ordered, so that in the one body of Christ the more excellent members may fulfill their office and the inferior members may not resist the superior.

Given on the third day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the illustrious man Opilio [Note: [Col. 1045D] Thus, together with editions before Quesnellus, our Barberini and Vatican manuscripts of collection 3, the Vatican and Vallicella manuscripts of collection 8, the Ratisbon manuscript of collection 19, the copy of the first edition, and the very ancient Veronese manuscript 55, which contains the final chapter of this letter. Quesnellus has “the fourth day before the Ides” in his text, but in the margin: “Elsewhere, the third day before the Ides.”].

## LETTER [Note: [Col. 1046C] Elsewhere numbered 93. The letter formerly numbered 120 is now 152. Written on 11 June in the year 453.] CXX [Note: [Col. 1046C] Found in manuscripts of collections 11, 12, 18, and 21 through 24, and in a copy of Sichardus. Quesnellus also cites the Thuan and Trecopithoean manuscripts, which belong to collection 5. But in those manuscripts this letter is an addition to the collection and in no way belongs to it, as we noted concerning another addition in note 4 (Col. 923, note a) to letter 85. We learn that copies of this letter were once very rare and insufficiently circulated from the fact that Facundus of Hermiane and others who defended Theodoret in the affair of the Three Chapters do not mention it, although, among the other documents, it would have been highly honorable to Theodoret. Hence it is not found in the older collections. Furthermore, we observe two peculiar features in this letter. First, the style of the second and third chapters is somewhat obscure and differs slightly from Leo’s customary style, as will be evident to anyone who compares them. Second, at the end of the letter there is a formula, written in another hand and characteristic of those letters, displaying a different character in the closing; it is found in no other letter of Leo. Let others judge what may be inferred from these facts.] TO THEODORITUS, BISHOP OF CYRUS. On perseverance in the faith.

### SUMMARY

I. Heresies, having arisen not without benefit to the Church, are to be suppressed by an irrevocable judgment. [Col. 1046B]  
II. The victory that the Church gains over the heretics belongs to Christ.  
III. Dioscorus’s obstinacy, raging even against Leo.  
IV. Those who write about matters of faith must weigh their words.  
V. Theodoret has been shown to be free from every stain of heresy by invincible truth.  
VI. Vigilance must be maintained even after victory. No one, whether monk or layman, ought to arrogate to himself the office of preaching apart from priests.

To THEODORITUS, his most beloved brother and bishop, LEO, bishop.

## CHAPTER I
When the brethren and our fellow priests whom the see of blessed Peter had sent to the holy council returned to us, we learned that, with heavenly assistance, your Charity had stood victorious with us both against the Nestorian impiety and against the madness of Eutyches. Therefore we glory in the Lord, singing with the prophet:

[Col. 1046C] “Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 123:8);

for he did not permit us to suffer any loss in our brethren, but confirmed by the irreversible assent of the entire brotherhood what our ministry had previously defined:

[Note: [Col. 1046D] The manuscripts of Thuanus and Trecopithus, cited by Quesnell, read: “Our former ministry had defined it; the irreversible assent of the entire brotherhood confirmed it.” Quesnell appended this note: “By the irreversible assent of the ecumenical council, even the judgments of the first see are confirmed,” a view which he frequently presses elsewhere in his notes. But Leo’s words do not convey that meaning, as though the judgments of the Roman see, being insufficiently firm in themselves, required the assent and confirmation of an ecumenical council. The verb “confirmed” does not refer to the judgments of the first see themselves, but to those matters which had previously been defined by the judgment of that see, so that the council’s assent is irreversible when it confirms what had first been defined by the apostolic see. Elsewhere we have already seen Leo recognize as sufficiently firm and irreversible in itself his definition published in Letter 28 to Flavian, which is indicated here, so that he acknowledged no necessity for a council and did not want a question of faith raised in the council, as though the doctrine he had defined in that letter were doubtful and uncertain. See Letters 82, 90, and 93, chapter 2, and Letter 94. If, under Theodosius, he requested a council, he did so not because of uncertainty about the doctrine already defined—which he did not wish to retract—but to remove scandals and more easily establish peace; we shall demonstrate this at length in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 8. Conversely, when the Chalcedonian Fathers themselves, and afterward the emperor Marcian, requested from the pontiff confirmation of the Chalcedonian definition, lest there be doubt about what had been defined in the council (see, among others, Letters 98 and 110), they professed that the judgments of the council, in order to be irreversible, required confirmation by the first see. After several passages, this is shown in the Vatican Collection 24 and in Sichardus.]

so that he might truly show that what had first been formulated by the see first of all had proceeded from him, when it had received the judgment of the whole Christian world:

[Note: [Col. 1047C] Four Thuan manuscripts read: “by the faith and see first of all”; a related reading occurs in Barberini manuscript 57: “by the see first of all faithfully.” Immediately afterward, two Vatican manuscripts, one from Collection 11 and the other from Collection 21, read “confirmed” instead of “formulated.” When the judges sought a definition from the Fathers of Chalcedon, Bishop Cecropius, indicating that this was unnecessary, said in Session 2, p. 1267: “The matters concerning Eutyches were brought forward; and concerning them a FORM was given by the most holy archbishop of the city of Rome; we follow him, and we have all subscribed to the letter [28, to Flavian].” Nor did Cecropius alone think thus, but the whole council also; for it follows: “The most reverend bishops cried out: ‘We all say these things; what has been set forth is sufficient; it is not permitted to make another exposition.’”]

[Note: [Col. 1047C] In the report of the Council of Chalcedon to Leo, that is, Letter 98, chapter 1, where they say that you presided over the members as their head.]

so that in this matter also the members might agree with the head.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Elsewhere: “our joy becomes greater … and all the more.” The Vatican Collection 24 and Sichardus read: “Our reason for rejoicing becomes greater in this matter, the more so,” and so forth.]

In this our reason for rejoicing increases, since the enemy struck himself all the more severely the more savagely he rose against the ministers of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] The Vatican Collections 11 and 21 read: “even against the ministers of Christ.”]

For, lest the agreement of the other sees with the one which the Lord established to preside over all the others seem to be mere consent prompted by flattery,

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Three manuscripts, Vatican Collections 11 and 21, read: “which he established.”]

or lest some other adverse suspicion creep in, there were first found those who doubted our judgments.

[Note: [Col. 1047D] The Illyrians and Palestinians are meant. When Letter 28 to Flavian was read in Session 2, they raised doubts at three points, which Aetius and Theodoret immediately attempted to remove. See volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1238. The Illyrians, who still had some doubts and requested a delay, were granted five days; they learned what, because of the difference of language, they had not correctly understood in Leo’s letter. The Palestinians likewise did so, as reported in Session 4, pp. 1382 and 1393.]

And while some, stirred up by the author of dissension, rushed into battles of contradiction,

[Note: [Col. 1048A] Editions before Quesnell read: “stirred up by the author of dissensions, they rush into battles of contradiction.” Three manuscripts of Quesnell, as well as three of ours and the edition of Surius, read “forced” instead of “stirred up.” Sichardus reads: “stirred up toward dissensions by the author of contradiction, they rushed into insane battles.”]

we reached a greater good through the evil itself, under the direction of him who dispenses all goodness.

[Note: [Col. 1048B] We corrected this from the Vatican Collection 21 and four other manuscripts cited by Quesnell in note 1, one of them being the Grimani manuscript. This reading is preferable to the one retained by Quesnell, “its evil”; for the nominative cannot be used with the impersonal passive expression “it was reached.” “Its evil” could be accepted if the reading were “it advanced,” but no manuscripts support that emendation. Sichardus reads: “its evil is turned into a result” (perhaps “into advancement”).]

For the gifts of divine grace come more sweetly whenever they are acquired not without great exertions; and peace maintained through leisure usually seems less valuable than peace restored through labors.

Truth itself also shines more clearly and is held more firmly when later examination has confirmed what the faith had previously taught.

Finally, the merit of priestly office shines brightly when the authority of the highest authorities is preserved in such a way

[Note: [Col. 1048B] In the printed editions and in the Grimani manuscript alone, Quesnell found the following seven words: “so that the freedom of those below may not be thought diminished at all.” We also found them in manuscripts of Collections 12 and 24 and in Sichardus’s copy. They are absent, however, from the other manuscripts of our Collections 11 and 21, as well as from the seven manuscripts cited by Quesnell in note 2. In one manuscript of Thuanus, in the Cambridge manuscript, and in Trecopithus, the text proceeds abruptly: “so that it may be for the greater glory of God.” Our copies of Collection 11 read “with the utmost care” instead of “of the highest”; the seven manuscripts cited by Quesnell read either “with the utmost care” or “of the utmost importance,” showing that all derive from the same source.]

that the freedom of those below may not be thought diminished at all.

[Note: [Col. 1048C] The freedom of examination usefully exercised by the Fathers of Chalcedon is indicated here. Some bishops who doubted Leo’s definition presented their difficulties in the council; through discussion and examination of Catholic doctrine, their doubts were answered, and they were instructed in the Catholic meaning which they had understood less fully and were confirmed in the faith. Thus truth itself shines more clearly and is held more firmly when later examination confirms what the pontiffs had previously taught; and the outcome of the examination advances the greater glory of God when confidence is taken up for the purpose of exercising—or, in another manuscript, “exerting”—itself so that opposition may be conquered, namely, the opposition of those who resisted what had been defined. Since this freedom and examination have only this end in view—that bishops confirm what the supreme pontiffs have defined, instruct those who oppose it, and remove them from error—it is readily understood how the authority of the highest is preserved in such a way that the freedom of those below is not thought diminished at all. Those are greatly mistaken who infer from these words that Leo thought the bishops at the Council of Chalcedon were free and permitted to submit his definition, set forth in Letter 28 to Flavian, to examination in such a way that they might dissent from it and pronounce a judgment contrary to it. The words “what the faith had previously taught” and likewise those stated shortly before—“what God had previously defined through our ministry”—refer to that definition and letter. Is anyone permitted to depart, through any examination whatsoever, from what the faith has taught and what God has defined? Moreover, at the time of the Council of Chalcedon, the issue concerned not only the definition of the first and apostolic see, which Leo from the beginning believed must be held so firmly that he declared those who thought otherwise to be heretics, and whose subscription he therefore required as entirely obligatory; it also concerned the definition accepted by the subscriptions of the bishops and by the entire Church, as reported in Letter 88, chapters 1 and 3, and Letter 91. Who, even within the freer system adopted by some, would think it lawful to hold or pronounce an opinion contrary to such a definition? That Leo did not think so is shown by Letters 90 and 93, chapter 2, where he entirely forbade the faith already defined in that letter to be retracted in the council and brought into debate as though it were uncertain and doubtful. He agreed that a council should be convened and that discussion should take place in it so that those who had been deceived might be recalled to the unity of peace and faith, with all dissension suppressed. See Letter 89 and the fuller discussion in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 8. We shall add one further point. After the Council of Chalcedon itself, when a new examination was instituted at the request of the emperor Leo to suppress or refute the unjust complaints of the Eutychians against the definition of that council, and the judgments of the bishops of the whole world were issued in the Encyclical Codex, no freedom was or could be granted to the bishops in that new examination except that the new examination should confirm what the council had defined. Consequently, the authority of the Council of Chalcedon suffered no harm; and those who abused that freedom by rejecting the Chalcedonian definition were regarded as heretics. A similar freedom is to be understood here also.]

And the outcome of the examination advances the greater glory of God when confidence is taken up for the purpose of exercising itself, so that opposition may be conquered, lest what is proved reprobate in itself seem to have been suppressed by the prejudice of silence.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore rejoice, dearest brother,

[Note: [Col. 1049D] We restored the conjunction “and,” omitted by Quesnell, on the authority of manuscripts of Collections 11 and 12. The manuscripts of Collection 11 read “for itself” instead of “on behalf of itself”; the manuscripts of Collections 21 and 24 and Sichardus omit both. Later, the printed editions of Leo before Quesnell incorrectly read “we live” instead of “we have conquered.”]

and rejoice as a victor in the only-begotten Son of God. He conquered through us for himself, whose fleshly reality was being denied. He conquered through us and for us, for whom we have conquered.

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Most editions before Quesnell, together with the manuscripts of Collection 21, read: “through whom the second victory is ours.”]

This is the second festival for the world after the Lord’s coming. With the plunderer overthrown, the mystery of the divine incarnation has been restored to the age: the enemy of the human race, because he could not remove it in reality, obscured it with accusations.

Indeed, the immortal mystery had perished from the hearts of unbelievers, because such great salvation benefits unbelievers nothing, while Truth itself says to his disciples: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

[Note: [Col. 1050B] In the margin of the Council, from manuscripts of Collection 21: “The ray of the Sun of righteousness, glowing through the East.” This error arose from an arbitrary correction of a corrupt reading found in the Vatican manuscript of Collection 11, “of the sun of righteousness, glowing through the East”; yet the reading inserted into the text stands out clearly.]

The radiance of the Sun of righteousness, obstructed by the dense clouds of Nestorius and Eutyches throughout the East, shone forth purely from the West,

[Note: [Col. 1050C] The ancient printed editions of Leo, together with the manuscripts of Collection 24 and Sichardus, read “where there is commerce among the apostles.” Binius reads “where there is the holy summit.” Quesnell, from the Grimani manuscript and together with the Roman edition, reads “where he placed his own summit.” We preferred the reading of six other manuscripts cited by Quesnell, as well as our manuscripts of Collections 11, 12, and 21 and the edition of Surius: “where he placed the highest summit in the apostles and teachers.” Labbe reads “where the summit is in the apostles,” with “the highest” in the margin. The highest summit, or prerogative, of the Roman Church over the other principal churches is indicated, on account of the apostles Peter and Paul. For, as Leo says in Sermon 82, chapter 1, “these are the ones who raised you to this glory, so that … through the sacred see of blessed Peter, having become the head of the world, you might preside more widely through divine religion than through earthly dominion.”]

where he placed the highest summit principally in the apostles and teachers.

Although even there he must never be thought to have been without those whom he reserved as outstanding confessors, so that when the ancient enemy again attempted,

[Note: [Col. 1050C] Collections 11 and 21 read: “through the unrepentant heart of the succeeding Pharaoh.” The Egyptian Dioscorus is indicated; during the Robber Council at Ephesus he used force in many ways against Catholics in order to impose the Eutychian heresy. Those who, overcome by terror, yielded to him later returned to sound understanding and to the Church.]

through the unrepentant heart of a second Pharaoh, to extinguish the seed of Abraham’s faith and the son of promise, by God’s mercy he could do nothing except harm himself.

The Almighty also accomplished this more wonderfully, because he did not drown with the author of the tyranny those whom he had summoned as his associates to the slaughter of the people of Israel,

[Note: [Col. 1050D] The Vatican manuscript of Collection 24 reads “those who knew with him.” Later, another Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 reads “he had associated in the slaughter.”]

but gathered them together with his own people; and, as the source of mercy knew was truly worthy and possible to him alone, he made those defeated by us to be victors with us.

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Quesnell notes in the margin: “The Cambridge and Barberini manuscripts read: ‘He made us, the victors, to be victors with us.’” The older editions of Leo read “those who will live” instead of “victors.”]

For since the spirit of falsehood alone is truly the enemy of the human race, there is no doubt that all those whom truth has claimed for itself now triumph over him.

Now the divine authority of those words of our Redeemer becomes entirely clear, since they fit so appropriately against the enemies of the faith that there can be no doubt that they were spoken about them: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to carry out the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks falsehood,

[Note: [Col. 1050D] The same manuscript reads “from his own.” The manuscripts of Collections 12, 21, and 24, together with Sichardus’s copy and the editions before Quesnell, read “he speaks from his own things.” Binius reads “from his own things.”]

he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and its father” (John 8:44).

## CHAPTER III

There is therefore nothing surprising in the fact that those who believed the falsehood concerning our nature in the truth of God agree with their father also in these matters. Whatever was seen, whatever was heard, whatever finally, as the Gospel testifies, was touched and handled in the only-begotten Son of God, they assert to have belonged not to the one whose reality was proved, but to the substance coeternal and consubstantial with the Father—as though either the nature of the Godhead

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Quesnell omitted the nominative “nature”; we restored it from all the other printed editions and all the manuscripts. Two manuscripts of Collection 21 subsequently read “might grow with age.” Later, most editions before Quesnell, together with the Vatican manuscript of Collection 24, read “by the Spirit of God.”]

had been pierced by the wood of the cross,

[Col. 1051A]

or unchangeable Wisdom could have grown with age and eternal Wisdom could have advanced in wisdom,

or God the Spirit, who is Spirit, could subsequently have been filled.

In this too the bitter madness reveals from what author it has proceeded, since it attempted, so far as it could, to harm everyone. For the one who afflicted you by persecuting you corrupted the others by driving them toward agreement in crime.

[Note: [Col. 1051C] The editions of Leo before Quesnell and Labbe, together with the manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24 and Sichardus, read “us.” We retained “you,” supported by other manuscripts and by Binius; here Leo is addressing Theodoret, whom Dioscorus afflicted by persecuting him.]

Yet although he wounded us in each of our brethren, because they are our members, he did not exclude us from particular grief, since he attempted to inflict upon his own head an injury previously unheard of and incredibly audacious.

[Note: [Col. 1051C] Our manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21 prefer the word “previously,” restored by Quesnell. The excommunication pronounced by Dioscorus against his own head, the Roman pontiff, is indicated. The Council of Chalcedon called this an unprecedented and unbelievable act of audacity in its Letter 98 to Leo, chapter 2. See Quesnell’s note 3. Some manuscripts later omit “would that.”]

Would that, after so many abominable deeds, he had at least come to his senses and not also saddened us by the ruin of his eternal damnation.

What measure of crime did he leave untouched, when this was not enough for him: that, sparing neither the living nor the dead, he had already stained his hands even with the blood of an innocent and Catholic priest, after rejecting truth and approving falsehood?

[Note: [Col. 1051C] See Quesnell’s note 4 for what Leo is referring to here. Shortly afterward Quesnell printed “attached” instead of “rejected,” adding in the margin: “So read all the manuscripts.” We do find this reading in the manuscripts of Collection 21. But the other manuscripts of Collections 11, 12, and 24, together with Sichardus’s copy and the earlier editions, read “rejected.”]

And since it is written, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15), he completed by his deeds what he had already committed through hatred, as though he had heard neither this nor what the Lord said: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29–30).

[Note: [Col. 1051D] The manuscripts of Collection 11 delete “is.” Later, the ancient printed editions of Leo and Labbe, together with the manuscripts of Collection 24 and Sichardus, read “because it is read as ‘as though.’”]

The Egyptian devastator was found worthy of being the diabolical preacher of error: like a most savage tyrant of the Church, he imposed unspeakable blasphemies upon our venerable brethren through the violent mob of seditious men and the bloodstained hands of soldiers.

And since the voice of our Redeemer has established that the same one is the author both of murder and of falsehood (John 8:44), he completed both alike, as though the things the Son of God had commanded for salvation had been written not to be avoided but to be perpetrated, and he dragged them along to increase his own destruction.

He also passed by with an exceedingly deaf ear what the same Lord said: “I speak what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have seen with your father” (ibid., 38).

[Note: [Col. 1052C] The manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24, together with Sichardus and Binius, add “therefore.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, while he plotted to take away the life of blessed Flavian in the present age, he deprived himself of the light of true life.

[Note: [Col. 1052C] The Barberini manuscript reads “he deprived himself, with truth as his guide.” The Vatican Collection 24 and Sichardus read “he deprived himself of the light of serene life.”]

While he attempted to drive you from your churches, he separated himself from the fellowship of Christians. While he dragged many along and drove them to assent to error,

[Note: [Col. 1052C] The Vatican Collection 11 and two manuscripts of Collection 21 read “he handed over.” Later, the same manuscript of Collection 11 reads “alone guilty beyond all and on behalf of all.”]

he wounded his own soul with many wounds: alone guilty beyond all, and through all, and on behalf of all, because he was the cause of guilt for everyone.

Although your Fraternity, strengthened by solid food, seems in no way to need these admonitions, nevertheless, so that we may fulfill what belongs to our office concerning the Apostle’s words, “In addition to external things, my daily burden is the anxiety of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (2 Cor. 11:28–29), we believe that this especially ought to be brought to your attention on the present occasion, dearest brother.

Whenever, by the administration of divine grace, we either immerse or cleanse those who are outside in the fountain of instruction,

[Note: [Col. 1052C] The catechetical instruction is indicated by which those approaching baptism were taught, or by which those returning to the unity of the Church were cleansed from heresy or schism.]

let us in no respect depart from the rules of faith which the divinity of the Holy Spirit set forth in the Council of Chalcedon. Between the two enemies of newly arisen unbelief,

[Note: [Col. 1052C] That is, between the Eutychians and the Nestorians, who, attacking the Catholic faith with opposing errors, required the greatest care in speaking, as the holy pontiff explains in the following chapter. Shortly afterward, some editions, together with the Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 and Sichardus, read “let us free” instead of “let us weigh.”]

let us weigh our speech with every precaution—not, God forbid, as though we were debating doubtful matters, but asserting with the highest authority what has been rightly defined;

[Note: [Col. 1052D] So Quesnell reads from the manuscripts of Trecopithus and Thuanus, with which two of our manuscripts of Collection 21 agree. The older printed editions, together with two manuscripts of Quesnell and our Vatican Collection 24 and Sichardus, read differently. After the words “in the letter of the apostolic see,” the Vatican Collections 11 and 21 and six manuscripts cited by Quesnell in note 5—some belonging to those same collections and others descending from a similar source—skip several sentences and proceed abruptly to the following chapter’s words: “But blessed is our God.” In place of the omitted material they insert: “And he immediately carries on the other matters which we set out above in order. But blessed is God.” The formula “and the rest” itself indicates an omission. The complete text is supplied by the manuscripts of Collections 12, 18, and 24 and Sichardus’s copy.]

for in the letter of the apostolic see, confirmed by the assent of the universal holy synod, we know that so many testimonies of divine authority have been gathered that no one can doubt any longer, unless he has chosen to bring upon himself the darkness of error,

[Note: [Col. 1053C] The editions before Quesnell, together with the manuscripts of Collections 12 and 24, read “with the synodal acts,” and afterward “so great is.” Quesnell’s correction, perhaps derived from the Grimani manuscript, is required by the context.]

whether he considers the acts of the synod, or those in which the definition of faith is first said to have been formulated,

[Note: [Col. 1053C] The definition of faith was formulated in the fifth session of Chalcedon, whereas Leo’s letter to Flavian was defended in the preceding second and fourth sessions and accepted with the assent of the entire synod. Therefore “first” cannot be understood chronologically, or Leo did not follow the exact chronological order.]

or those in which the aforesaid letter of the apostolic see was defended through the zeal of your Fraternity,

[Note: [Col. 1053C] When Leo’s Letter 28 was read in the second session, and the Illyrians and Palestinians raised difficulties against one statement in that letter, Theodoret brought forward a similar testimony of Cyril and defended it. See volume IV of the Councils, p. 1238.]

and especially the address of the entire council to the most pious emperors,

[Note: [Col. 1053C] “Especially,” he says, because in the council’s address many testimonies of the Fathers were recited.]

[Note: [Col. 1053D] Part III of the Council of Chalcedon, no. 1.]

all so strengthened by the testimonies of the Fathers who preceded them that they can persuade any mind, however imprudent and obstinate, provided it has not already been condemned with the devil on account of its impiety.

[Col. 1053D]

## CHAPTER V

Therefore it is also fitting that we take proper precautions against the enemies of the Church, so that, as far as we are concerned, we leave them no opportunity whatsoever for slander. Nor, whenever we act against the Nestorians or the Eutychians, should we ever seem to turn our backs on either of them; rather, we must avoid and condemn both enemies of Christ with equal measure.

Thus, whenever the benefit of those listening, however great or small, requires it, we must strike both them and their doctrines with a worthy anathema, most readily and most clearly, so that, if this should appear to be done by us either too obscurely or too slowly, it may not be thought to have been done unwillingly.

Although the matter itself should be sufficient to admonish your prudence,

[Note: [Col. 1053D] So our manuscripts, together with Sichardus and the editions before Quesnell, read; Quesnell has “the circumstances themselves are sufficient to admonish.” The addition “experience has taught” alludes to what happened to Theodoret at Ephesus and Chalcedon.]

experience has already taught this as well.

But blessed is our God, whose invincible truth has shown you to be pure from every stain of heresy, according to the judgment of the apostolic see.

[Note: [Col. 1053D] This judgment of the apostolic see appears in Session 1 of Chalcedon, where the judges said, p. 874: “Let the most reverend bishop Theodoret enter, so that he may take part in the synod, since the most holy archbishop Leo restored his episcopate to him”; and in Session 8, p. 1523, where the same judges requested the council’s judgment in favor of Theodoret, just as the most holy archbishop Leo had judged. The entire council agreed, saying: “After God, Leo judged”; and the pontiff’s legates said, p. 1526: “The most holy and most blessed bishop of the universal Church, Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, previously received Theodoret into communion, just as the letters he sent to our humility attest.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 reads “you may repay.”]

You will repay him with fitting gratitude for so many labors if you preserve yourself, for the defense of the universal Church, as the person whom we have proved and continue to prove you to be.
