For since God dissolves the deceits of all slanderers, we recognize the greatest care of blessed Peter for us all. After he confirmed the judgment of his see in the definition of the faith, he permitted nothing blameworthy to appear concerning any one of you who labored with us for the Catholic faith,

[Note: [Col. 1054C] So our manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21 read, together with Quesnell and Binius. Elsewhere: “who suffered.” Shortly afterward, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 reads “to see.” In place of “to go out,” some editions read “to exist.”]

because, with the Holy Spirit judging, none of those whose faith had already conquered could fail to depart as a victor.

[Col. 1054D]

## CHAPTER VI

For what remains, we exhort you: since we have learned that some remnants of Eutychian and Nestorian error still remain there, now also assist the apostolic see.

For the victory which Christ our Lord granted to his Church, as long as we live in this world, although it gives greater confidence, does not entirely remove anxiety. It was not granted so that we might sleep, but so that we might labor more peacefully.

Therefore we wish to be assisted also by the concern of your vigilance, so that, as your report proceeds, you may hasten to inform the apostolic see what the Lord’s teaching is accomplishing in those regions,

[Note: [Col. 1054D] The older editions, together with the manuscripts of Collections 11, 12, and 24 and Sichardus’s copy, read: “what the doctrine of religion accomplishes among them”; and afterward, “the priests of that religion.” The true reading received by Quesnell is supported by the manuscripts of Collection 21. One Vatican manuscript of Collection 21 later reads: “for whatever uses necessity may require.”]

so that we may assist the priests of that region whenever necessity requires.

As for the matters attempted there in the often-mentioned council by an unlawful presumption against the venerable canons of Nicaea,

[Note: [Col. 1054D] Alternatively, “in the aforementioned council.” The canon concerning the prerogative of the see of Constantinople is meant. Compare the preceding letter to Maximus, which is indicated here; there also the misconduct of certain monks is censured. See the note there, Col. 1045, n. g).]

we have written to our brother and fellow bishop, the bishop of the see of Antioch,

[Note: [Col. 1054D] Letter 119.]

adding also what you instructed us by word, through our representatives, because of the misconduct of certain monks in your region. We expressly established this as well: that, apart from the Lord’s priests, no one may dare to preach, whether he is a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of any learning.

[Note: [Col. 1054D] 16, question 1. We add this as chapter 19.]

Nevertheless, for the benefit of the universal Church, we wished these letters to reach the knowledge of everyone through the aforesaid brother and our fellow bishop Maximus.

[Note: [Col. 1054D] Alternatively, “we wish.”]

For this reason we did not wish to attach a copy of them here, because we have no doubt that what we entrusted to the aforesaid brother and fellow bishop will be carried out.

And in another hand:

May God keep you safe, dearest brother.

Given on the third day before the Ides of June, in the consulship of the illustrious man Opilio.

[Note: [Col. 1055B] The editions before Quesnell, together with our manuscripts of Collections 11, 12, 21, and 24 and Sichardus’s copy, read “the fourth day before the Ides.” Quesnell alone, from the Grimani manuscript, reads “the third day before the Ides.” We did not alter this, because Letter 119 to Maximus is dated on this same day; it is to be believed that the two letters were sent together on the same occasion and, following Leo’s practice, dated on the same day. Otherwise the letter to Maximus, which is presumed to have been written here, would have been composed on the following day. It was easy for copyists to write “the fourth day before the Ides” from “the third day before the Ides” by joining two units.]

# LETTER CXXI

[Note: [Col. 1055C] Elsewhere numbered 94. The letter formerly numbered 121 is now 153. Written on 15 June in the year 453.]

[Note: [Col. 1055C] It survives in manuscripts of Collections 12, 18, 19, and 24, and in Vatican manuscript 541.]

## TO AUGUSTUS MARCIANUS

Concerning Easter

## SYNOPSIS

I. The care of the Paschal cycle was formerly entrusted to the bishop of Alexandria. — II. What difficulty arose from it. — III. He requests that an investigation into this difficulty be ordered.

[Note: [Col. 1055C] The Regensburg manuscript reads: “Pope Leo.”]

LEO, bishop, to Augustus Marcianus.

## CHAPTER I
[Note: Also in many manuscripts, the Laurentian Florentine and Fesulan manuscripts. Now in many copies of Vatican manuscript 1340, in which shortly afterward *geratur* occurs instead of *generatur*.]

Your piety’s faith has become known throughout all the Churches of Christ by so many proofs that, if any concern arises regarding the common religion, your assistance is rightly sought. And because, mindful of the administration entrusted to me, I must anticipate my cares even in matters that lie ahead, I rightly desire to be assisted by the efforts of your Clemency, so that in an observance which is always varied according to a fixed calculation no error may be incurred.

For although the feast of Easter, which chiefly contains the sacrament of human salvation, must always be celebrated in the first month, it is nevertheless so changeable because of the nature of the lunar cycle that the choice of the most sacred day [Col. 1056A] often proves uncertain. Hence it frequently happens—something that must not happen—that the whole Church does not observe simultaneously what ought to be one and the same observance.

The holy Fathers therefore endeavored to remove the occasion of this error, entrusting the entire matter to the bishop of Alexandria—since among the Egyptians expertise in this calculation appeared to have been handed down from ancient times—so that through him the date of the aforesaid feast might each year be communicated to the apostolic see, and from his written notices a general determination might reach the more distant Churches.

[Note: The first edition of Quesnel, together with the earlier printed editions, reads *currat*. This was emended in the second edition, in accordance with our better manuscripts.]

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “to the bishop.” The reference is to the Fathers of Nicaea. Cyril, agreeing with Leo, had written in the Paschal Prologue in the year 437: “By the agreement of the synod of the saints throughout the whole world it was decreed that, since such a Church had been found at Alexandria, one distinguished in knowledge of the date on which Easter ought to be celebrated according to the day of the calendar or the ides and the day of the moon, the date should be announced each year to the Roman Church by letter, so that, by apostolic authority, the universal Church throughout the whole world might know without dispute the determined day of Easter.”]

[Note: We judged the reading of the very ancient Regensburg manuscript preferable, since it is both better and clearer and agrees especially well with Cyril’s testimony, set out in the preceding note, from which Leo perhaps took the expression. In the older printed editions of Leo the text was corruptly read: “Through whom, although the day of the aforesaid solemnity occurred in each year, it should be reported to the Apostolic See, so that the judgment of this writing might extend generally to the more distant Churches.” The same is read in the common editions of the Councils with Merlin, from manuscript collection 12, except that *qui annis* stands for *quamvis*. Accepting this last reading, Quesnel added two emendations: “by whose writings” for “so that the judgment of this writing,” and “notice” for “judgment,” as we find in our other manuscripts.]

## II

But Theophilus, of holy memory, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, when he had compiled a hundred years of this observance, determined that the Easter feast of the seventy-sixth year was to be kept very differently from what the others had decreed.

[Note: Here the *Paschal Table* of Theophilus is indicated, extending over one hundred years and beginning in the year 380. Thus the seventy-sixth year of this Table fell in the year 455, concerning whose Easter the present question was being debated. This Table must be distinguished from the paschal period or cycle of the same Theophilus extending over 418 years, expressly mentioned by Cyril in the Paschal Prologue—not, as Quesnel wrote in note 1 to this letter, 437 years. Nor did the Table, as Quesnel asserted in the same note, present one hundred years extracted from the aforementioned period. For Joannes Vander Haagen has demonstrated very well, in his dissertation on Theophilus’s 418-year Paschal Cycle, § 8, that the 418-year period began with the year of Christ 475, after the completion of five nineteen-year cycles, which Theophilus had published in the Table and which were completed in the ninety-sixth year of that Table.]

[Note: The particle *nam* is absent from the editions before Quesnel, as it is from our manuscripts except the Regensburg manuscript, which contains it. See Quesnel’s note 2.]

For, setting down the succession of the sacred observance beginning with the first consulship of Theodosius the Elder, of august memory,

[Note: In the year 380.]

[Note: Thus Quesnel, as does the same Regensburg manuscript. Other printed editions, together with our other manuscripts, read “the orders of the sacred observance succeeding one another.”]

[Note: Three successive Easters marked in Theophilus’s Table are indicated: Easter 453, assigned in Theophilus’s computation or Table to its seventy-fourth year, on the day before the ides of April; Easter 454, assigned to the seventy-fifth year of the Table, on the day before the nones of April—on neither of which was there disagreement with the Latins; and finally Easter 455, marked in the seventy-sixth year of the Table on the eighth day before the kalends of May. On this Easter the Latins disagreed with the Alexandrians.]

so that the reckoning of a longer period might be preserved in his written records, the seventy-fourth year of this compilation is the year in which we celebrated holy Easter on the day before the ides of April. In the following year, on the day before the nones of April, the same feast, God being propitious, will likewise have to be celebrated, as the regular order of the hundred-year record declares.

[Note: The word “regularly” indicates that the paschal dates for the years 453 and 454 recorded in Theophilus’s Table did not differ from the rule, or cycle, of the Latins’ eighty-four years, which the Roman Church was then using. If the Latin cycle, like Theophilus’s Table, designated the day before the nones of April as the paschal day in 454, it evidently follows that the Romans were then using an eighty-four-year cycle in which the lunar leap was admitted in the fourteenth year of the cycle; for in the eighty-four-year cycle, which accepted the lunar leap in the twelfth year, Easter was marked on the fifth day before the kalends of April. It is therefore clear that the correction of the Latin cycle had already been adopted, by which the lunar leap was postponed from year 12 to year 14.

Another text worthy of notice occurs in Letter 88, to Paschasinus, chapter 4. There, speaking of the Easter of the year 455, which the Romans assigned to the fifteenth day before the kalends of May, the holy pontiff writes: “In our Paschal Cycles, as you know well, it is written that Easter of that same year must be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the kalends of May.” Since he indicates not one but several Latin cycles, and affirms that Easter was marked on that day in all of them, he unquestionably designates at least two cycles, one of which admitted the lunar leap every twelve years and the other every fourteen years. Consequently, even from this testimony the latter cycle is recognized as already adopted; otherwise Saint Leo would have mentioned only one cycle, asserting that it admitted the lunar leap every twelfth year.

The holy pontiff indicated both cycles for the Easter of the year 455 because, although they disagreed in determining the Easter of 454, they all agreed regarding the Easter of 455.

The common editions, together with some manuscripts, read “the order of the hundred-year reckoning.” Quesnel’s emendation is confirmed by the Regensburg manuscript.]

[Note: We have emended this from the Regensburg manuscript and Vatican manuscript collection 24. The printed editions incorrectly read “in which.” Shortly afterward the Regensburg manuscript reads “the holy Paschal feast.”]

But in the year that will be the seventy-sixth, the date of Easter is found entered as one which, since the Lord’s Passion, has the authority of no precedent and no ecclesiastical regulation.

[Note: From the same Regensburg manuscript we supplied the word “is.” Some printed editions, with one manuscript, read “will be found.” The date of Easter indicated is the eighth day before the kalends of May, that is, 24 April, which was recorded in Theophilus’s Table only for the year 455, since the Table began with the year 380. What Leo adds—that “the authority of no precedent and no regulation admits it”—must be understood of the Romans, not of the Alexandrians. The Alexandrians, having always used a nineteen-year cycle, had likewise celebrated Easter on that date in the year 371. Saint Leo may have been unaware of this, since he knew only Theophilus’s Table beginning with the later year 380.]

For we know that he has fixed the eighth day before the kalends of May, a date which greatly exceeds the limit of the ancient regulation.

[Note: Earlier printed editions, together with most manuscripts, incorrectly read “which exceeds the limit of the anciently established year.” The reading restored by Quesnel is supported by the Regensburg manuscript. Leo asserted that the eighth day before the kalends of May—24 April, the date assigned by the Alexandrians to Easter 455—exceeded by too much the ultimate limit anciently established, namely, by the Latins. Among those Latins the latest limit was the eleventh day before the kalends of May—21 April—so the date exceeded it by three days. Accordingly, “the others,” that is, the same Latins, had assigned Easter according to their eighty-four-year cycle to the fifteenth day before the kalends of May—17 April. The dispute between the Latins and Alexandrians therefore concerned this difference of eight days.]

Whereas others have assigned the fifteenth day before the kalends of May to this feast.

For a legitimate interval has been fixed from the eleventh day before the kalends of April to the eleventh day before the kalends of May, within which the necessity of all variations must be contained, so that the Lord’s Easter may be neither earlier nor later than this.

[Note: The eleventh day before the kalends of April—22 March—was among the Romans the earliest limit of the paschal Sundays, just as the eleventh day before the kalends of May—21 April—was the latest limit. Shortly afterward, Quesnel wrote *praefixum* in the margin; elsewhere, *praefinitum*.]

For although the feast is sometimes defended as having reached the tenth or ninth day before the kalends of May, the reason given is this:

[Note: Here Saint Leo refers to the Easter of the year 444, which he had celebrated on the ninth day before the kalends of May on the basis of the calculations of Paschasinus and Cyril, as well as to the Easter of the year 417, which from Paschasinus’s letter he had learned was to be celebrated with the Alexandrians on the tenth day before the kalends of May, beyond the latest Roman limit, which he had said extended as late as the eleventh day before the kalends of May.

For Easter in the year 455 the pontiff resolves this objection by saying that, although in those earlier years the tenth and ninth days before the kalends of May had gone beyond the aforesaid final limit, the day of the Passion had not exceeded that limit. This consideration had formerly persuaded Leo to agree with Paschasinus regarding the date of Easter in 444. See note 18 (Col. 608, n. 1) on Letter 3.

But because the eighth day before the kalends of May did not admit this explanation or reconciliation—since in that case not only the day of the Resurrection but also the day of the Passion would pass beyond the limit—Leo declares that he cannot agree with the Alexandrians.]

For even if the day of the Resurrection appears to have gone beyond the limit, the day of the Passion will nevertheless not be found to have exceeded the appointed boundary. But to extend the paschal observance to the eighth day before the kalends of May is a most unusual and manifest transgression.

## III

Since, therefore, as I have said, in that hundred-year reckoning of Theophilus the seventy-sixth year is shown to have fixed the day of Easter contrary to ecclesiastical custom, and since it is no slight offense if, at the beginning of the sacrament, the truth and unity are not maintained by the universal Church, I beseech your Clemency to deign to lend your efforts, so that the Egyptians—or any others who appear to possess reliable knowledge of this calculation—may relieve the difficulty of this anxiety, and so that the general observance may be directed to a day which neither abandons the standard of the constitutions of the Fathers nor wanders beyond the prescribed limits.

Whatever your piety discovers concerning this inquiry, command that it be promptly brought to my notice, so that no fault of discord may arise in the divine mysteries.

[Note: Thus the ancient and most carefully corrected Regensburg manuscript, as also in the two following letters transmitted on the same occasion. The printed editions, together with other manuscripts, read “the sixteenth day before the kalends of July.”]

Given on the seventeenth day before the kalends of July, in the consulship of Opilio, a man of most illustrious rank.

# LETTER 122

[Note: Formerly 95. The letter formerly numbered 122 is now 148. Written on 15 June in the year 453.]

## CXXII

[Note: It survives in the same collections and manuscripts as the preceding letter. In the common editions it was entitled “To Eudochia Augusta,” and thereafter “To Eudochia Augusta.” The error is sufficiently indicated by the formula “your Fraternity,” for which “your Serenity” was inserted in the printed editions contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts. Our Regensburg manuscript confirms the emendation introduced by Quesnel from the Grimani manuscript. See his note 1.]

## TO JULIAN, BISHOP

### Synopsis

He asks him to investigate more carefully the controversy concerning the Easter of the following year and to write back.

LEO, bishop, to Julian.

[Note: The words “Concerning the observance of Easter,” which Quesnel placed as a title, begin the letter according to the authority of the Regensburg manuscript.]

Concerning the observance of Easter, Theophilus, of holy memory, writing to the emperor Theodosius the Elder, arranged the sequence of the feast for one hundred years beginning with the first consulship of that emperor. The seventy-fourth year of this reckoning is now passing; in that year, during the consulship of Opilio, the sacred feast was celebrated on the day before the ides of April. Accordingly, in the following year, on the day before the nones of April, the same feast will reasonably follow.

[Note: Three manuscripts, together with the editions before Quesnel, read *consequitur*. But since this was written in the year 453 and the passage concerns the Easter of 454, the correction supported by the better manuscripts is preferable.]

But the year that will be the seventy-sixth is known to contain an entry of the aforementioned bishop which disagrees very plainly with the example of all antiquity and with the authority of all the Fathers. For if he transfers the Lord’s Easter to the eighth day before the kalends of May, thereby exceeding the limits established from ancient times far too clearly,

[Note: Some manuscripts read “of antiquity.”]

[Note: The printed editions, together with several manuscripts, read *audenter*, “boldly.” The reading of the Regensburg manuscript seems preferable and more consistent with the position expressed in the other letters. See note 16 (Col. 1057, n. b) on the preceding letter.]

although he could have entered the paschal feast on the fifteenth day before the kalends of May, as the others established,

[Note: That is, the Latins. See the same note.]

I have therefore directed a letter to the most Christian and merciful emperor, because considerable anxiety is arising in me lest this opinion be strengthened among the Egyptians.

[Note: The older common editions, together with most manuscripts of inferior authority, read *probaretur*, “be approved.” The Grimani and Regensburg manuscripts agree in the correction.]

In that letter I carefully explained the cause of my concern and earnestly requested that he graciously devote his efforts, as he is accustomed to do, to the service of religion: that he command those who appear to possess complete knowledge of this calculation to assemble and investigate carefully, lest perhaps this determination be maintained, and lest this deviation, which appears to conflict with earlier times, be attributed to our connivance or negligence, so that in our days something may be presumed which had never previously been attempted.

[Note: He is referring especially to the Alexandrians, as is clear from chapters 2 and 3 of the preceding letter, and as the following words also indicate.]

[Note: Why the editions before Quesnel here prefer “your Serenity” has been explained in note 1 (Col. 1058, n. h).]

Since it is fitting that your Fraternity share this concern with me and take precautions lest anything of this kind occur, deign to urge the most religious and faithful emperor repeatedly,

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript omits “the most religious and.”]

[Note: Thus from the Regensburg manuscript. Elsewhere: “that he command the Egyptians to be admonished.”]

so that he may command the Egyptians to be admonished without concealment, lest on the day of the most solemn feast there be any offense either through disagreement or through transgression.

[Note: Thus the Regensburg manuscript. Other manuscripts and the printed editions read “given on the sixteenth day before the kalends of July.”]

[Note: The older printed editions, with several manuscripts, read: “what your concern, more diligently investigating, may be able to discover.” Quesnel’s reading, found in the Grimani manuscript, is confirmed by our Regensburg manuscript.]

Whatever your more diligent concern discovers regarding this matter, may the glorious emperor command that it be quickly brought to my notice, because it pertains both to his salvation and to that of all that the worship of God not be harmed by any error.

Given on the seventeenth day before the kalends of July, in the consulship of Opilio, a man of most illustrious rank.

# LETTER 123

[Note: Formerly 96. The letter formerly numbered 123 is now 154. Written on 15 June in the year 453.]

## CXXIII

[Note: It survives in manuscript collections 12, 18, 19, and 24, and in the copy of Sichard. The common editions of Leo title it “To Licinia Eudocia”; Quesnel, “To Licinia Eudoxia,” noting that *Eudoxiam* is read in the Grimani manuscript. This is incorrect. The name Licinia Eudoxia belongs not to the wife of Theodosius the Younger, to whom Leo is writing here, but to the wife of Valentinian, who was her daughter. The Regensburg manuscript has *Eudochiam* here, but in Letter 117 it prefers *Eudociam*, as this name is written in other manuscripts and in the printed conciliar editions. See note 6 on Letter 117 (Col. 1037, n. h), from which we learn the occasion or impetus of this letter.]

## TO EUDOCIA, AUGUSTA

### Concerning the Palestinian Monks

### Synopsis

I. He asks her to devote her care to restoring the Palestinian monks to faith and peace.  
II. Having accepted the Council of Chalcedon, they must execrate both Eutyches and Nestorius if they wish to be regarded as Catholics. He wishes to be informed by her letter of what her exhortation has accomplished.

LEO, bishop, to Eudocia, Augusta.

## I

I do not doubt that your piety knows how great my concern is for the Catholic faith, and with what vigilance, insofar as the Lord assists, I must take care lest the Gospel of truth ever be resisted by the ignorant or the impious.

[Note: The common editions, together with manuscript collections 12 and 24 and Sichard, read *debeat praecaveri*, “it must be guarded against.” The emendation drawn from the Grimani manuscript is confirmed by our Regensburg manuscript. Shortly afterward, the manuscripts of collection 12 and the older printed editions read “and to the impious”; Sichard has “and to the enemies of truth.”]

And therefore, together with the duty of greeting by which your Clemency, always worthy of my honor, is addressed, I beseech the Lord to gladden me with your safety and to cause the cause of the faith—on account of which the hearts of certain monks within the province of Palestine had been troubled—to receive ever greater assistance through you, so that, insofar as this can be accomplished by the zeal of your piety, every confidence may be removed from heretical perversity.

[Note: The same common editions, together with the same manuscripts and Sichard, corruptly read: “I beseech the Lord that, in the matter of the faith, he may increasingly make me assist your safety …” The Regensburg and Grimani manuscripts consistently support the present reading.]

For those whom neither the reasoning of the sacraments, nor the authority of the Scriptures, nor even the testimony of the holy places moved—what could be feared for them except precipitous danger?

[Note: Thus the Regensburg manuscript, better than the common editions and also than the other manuscripts of Quesnel, which read *Scriptorum*, “of the writings.” Shortly afterward, the Regensburg manuscript and the manuscripts of collection 12 read *commonebant*, “were reminding.”]

May it therefore benefit the Churches, as it has benefited them by God’s favor, and may it benefit the human race itself, that in the incarnation of the Word of God you chose to make the dwelling-place of your residence there where the signs of wonders and the proofs of sufferings speak to you of our Lord Jesus Christ as true God and equally true man, in the unity of one person.

[Note: The printed editions read “and it benefits, and may it benefit the human race.” The reading of the Regensburg manuscript is better. Since Leo wrote other letters to this Augusta in which he sought to recall her from the support of the Eutychians and move her to favor the Catholics, as we saw in note 7 on Letter 117 (Col. 1038, n. i), he assumes that these letters had produced an effect, so that he could more easily urge her on the basis of the confidence presumed regarding her. It may also be said that the verb *prodest*, “it benefits,” refers to other pious works of the same Augusta, through which she built and richly endowed several churches, hospices, and monasteries in Palestine, as Evagrius relates in Book I, chapters 21 and 22, and the author of the Life of Saint Euthymius.

The same Regensburg manuscript also confirms the emendation introduced by Quesnel, whereas the earlier common editions and the manuscripts of the other collections read: “In the words of God, where your will is that our Lord Jesus Christ be spoken of to you as the true God,” and so forth.]

## II

Therefore, if the aforesaid men venerate and love the Catholic name and wish to be counted among the members of the Lord’s body, let them detest, let them detest, the wicked errors which they rashly admitted, and let them repent of their impious blasphemies and bloodstained deeds.

[Note: The older editions, together with manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, read “if they wish to be named members among the Lord’s body.” Quesnel, on the basis of the Grimani manuscript, reads “if they wish to be counted within the Lord’s body.” The reading of the Regensburg manuscript was preferred.]

Let them submit, for the salvation of their souls, to the synodal decrees confirmed at the city of Chalcedon. And because no one reaches an understanding of the sacrament of human salvation except through true faith and tranquil humility, let them believe what they read in the Gospel and confess in the Creed, and let them not mingle with impious doctrines.

For the Catholic faith, just as it condemns Nestorius, who dared to preach two persons in our one Lord Jesus Christ, so it also condemns Eutyches together with Dioscorus, who deny that true human flesh was assumed in the womb of the Virgin Mother by God the Only-Begotten Word.

[Note: The common editions read *negat*, “denies.” We have emended it from all our manuscripts, as well as Sichard and Binius.]

If your exhortation has achieved anything regarding the conversion of the aforesaid men—something that will secure eternal glory for you—I ask that you report it to me in a letter from your Clemency, so that I may rejoice both that you have received the fruit of a good work and that they have not perished from the mercy of the Lord.

[Note: Thus, with the Grimani manuscript, our Regensburg manuscript. Other manuscripts, together with the editions before Quesnel, read: “so that I may rejoice both that the fruit of a good work has been gained in you, and that the mercy of the Lord has not perished in them.”]

[Note: All printed editions read “on the seventh day before the kalends.” We have corrected this from the excellent Regensburg manuscript; thus this letter is dated on the same day as the two preceding letters, as is Leo’s practice when all appear to have been sent together on the same occasion.]

Given on the seventeenth day before the kalends of July, in the consulship of Opilio, a man of most illustrious rank.

# LETTER 124

[Note: Formerly 97. The letter formerly numbered 124 is now 155. Written at approximately the same time as the preceding letter.]

## CXXIV

[Note: This letter is found in manuscript collections 5, 11, 12, 13, and 20 through 24, and in the copy of Sichard. Although the letter lacks a chronological notation, it was certainly written in this year and was probably sent to Palestine together with the preceding letter. Leo first heard of the disturbances among the Palestinian monks before 25 November of the year 452, from Letter 109, but he did not know their state of mind; hence in Letter 113, chapter 3, he requested fuller information. Shortly afterward he received this information, when Julian sent him the writings of Marcian and Pulcheria to the same monks, in which their audacity and disturbances are described, as is clear from Letters 115, 116, and 117, dated 21 March of the year 453.

Just as he had sent the preceding letter to Eudocia, who was living in Palestine and was the patroness of those monks, so it is highly probable that he also wrote this letter to the monks themselves. Since Leo learned from Letters 126 and 127, before 9 January of the following year, that the disturbance of these monks had already been quieted, this letter to the Palestinians cannot possibly have been delayed until the following year.]

## TO THE PALESTINIAN MONKS

[Note: In the table of collection 5 this title is found as chapter 81: “Correction addressed to the Palestinians concerning their instability of faith, through which they fell into the Eutychian heresy.”]

### Synopsis

I. The Palestinians were led astray by a perverse interpretation of Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian.  
II. Both Eutyches, who confuses the natures in Christ, and Nestorius, who multiplies the persons, must be detested.  
III. Whoever does not confess our nature in Christ has no share in Christ.  
IV. Only those are cleansed by Christ’s blood in whose body he was offered, suffered, and died in triumph.  
V. The properties of each of his natures are made clear by the character of his works.  
VI. Both natures come together without confusion in one person.  
VII. Nothing new was added to the Son of God except in the form of a servant.  
VIII. He reproaches the same monks concerning the scandals arising from their fury.  
IX. He exhorts them to come to their senses and embrace the common faith.

LEO, bishop, to all the monks established throughout Palestine.

[Note: The editions before Quesnel, together with manuscripts of collections 13 and 21, incorrectly read “to the bishops,” whereas the letter was written, as the context shows, to the monks causing disturbances in Palestine. Quesnel therefore rightly followed Binius in substituting “to the monks” for “to the bishops.” See his note 1.

Manuscripts of collections 5, 11, and 12 lack an inscription and carry only the title “Letter of Pope Leo to the Palestinians,” or “to the Palestinian.” The manuscripts of collection 24 give this inscription: “Leo, bishop, to the Palestinians.”]

## I

Through the reports of many people it has been made clear to my concern—which I owe to the universal Church and to all her children—that something offensive has been brought into the hearts of your affection, because either inexperienced interpreters, as appears likely, or malicious ones have caused you to understand certain things differently from the way I preached them, being unable to transfer Latin appropriately and accurately into Greek. For when subtle and difficult matters are being explained, scarcely any disputant is sufficient even in his own language.

[Note: The Vatican collection 11 reads *proficit*, “it benefits.” In the margin of the conciliar edition is *profuit*, “it benefited.” Later the editors noted in the margin, on the basis of manuscripts of collection 24 and Sichard, “even Eutyches himself detests this.”]

Yet this has benefited me to the extent that, since you condemn what the Catholic faith rejects, we understand that you are closer to the truth than to falsehood, and that you rightly repudiate what I too detest on the basis of the teaching handed down from ancient times.

Although my letter to Flavian, bishop of holy memory, is itself fully sufficient to manifest its meaning and in no respect requires either defense or exposition,

[Note: We have restored the conjunction *et*, used in the sense of “also,” which Quesnel deleted, on the basis of the Vienna collection 5, Vatican collections 11 and 24, and the copy of Sichard.]

nevertheless other writings of mine agree with it, in which the meaning of my teaching is likewise evident. For because I had to argue against the heretics who had troubled many peoples of Christ, I made clear to the most merciful emperors, to the holy synodal council, and to the Church of Constantinople what we ought to know and believe concerning the incarnation of the Word according to evangelical and apostolic teaching. I departed in no respect from the confession of the holy Fathers, because the Catholic faith is one, true, unique,

[Note: The editions before Quesnel, together with Sichard, add “perfect, inviolable.” These words are absent from eleven of Quesnel’s manuscripts and from our collections 5, 11, 21, and 24. Later, “nothing has been diminished” is read in the manuscripts of collections 11, 21, and 24.]

and nothing can be added to or subtracted from it. First Nestorius and now Eutyches have attempted to attack it with different assertions but similar impiety, and they have tried to introduce into the Church of God two heresies opposed to each other, so that each would rightly be condemned by the disciples of truth. For what they both believed in their varied falsehood was exceedingly insane and sacrilegious.

## II

Let Nestorius, therefore, be anathematized. He believed that the blessed Virgin Mary was merely the mother of a man, so that he made one person of the flesh and another of the Godhead,

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “lest there be one.” Shortly afterward, Vatican collection 11 reads “from the Word of God.” Then, in the same manuscripts of collection 21, “separated and set apart.” Later, *incommutabili* is read in Letter 165, chapter 2.]

and did not recognize one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but preached one Son of God and another son of man, separately and apart. Yet while that unchangeable essence of the Word remained—an essence which is timeless and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit—the Word became flesh within the Virgin’s womb in such a way that, through one conception and one birth, the same Virgin, according to the union of both substances, was both the Lord’s handmaid and his mother.

Elizabeth also understood and said this, as the evangelist Luke declares: “And from where is this granted to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43).

[Note: Manuscripts of collection 21 read: “Elizabeth, as the evangelist Luke declares, understood this when he says.”]

Let Eutyches likewise be struck by the same anathema. Having been tossed about through the impious errors of the ancient heretics, he chose the third doctrine of Apollinaris, asserting that our whole Lord Jesus Christ is of one nature, after denying the reality of human flesh and soul—as though the Godhead of the Word itself had been converted into flesh and soul.

Thus the Word, he says, would have conceived and been born, been nourished and grown, been crucified and died, been buried and risen again, ascended into heaven, and sat at the Father’s right hand, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead—all as belonging only to that essence which cannot receive any of these things in itself without the reality of flesh.

[Note: The common editions add “divine” and read *considere*, “to sit.” We followed the Vienna collection 5, Vatican collections 11, 21, and 24, and Sichard. Quesnel likewise, although he retained the word “divine,” noted in the margin that the word is absent from four of his manuscripts.]

For the nature of the Only-Begotten is the nature of the Father; it is the nature of the Holy Spirit; and at the same time it is impassible and unchangeable—the undivided unity and consubstantial equality of the eternal Trinity.

Therefore, if this heretic departs from the perversity of Apollinaris so as not to be convicted of believing the Godhead to be passible and mortal, yet if he dares to declare one nature of the incarnate Word—that is, of the Word and the flesh—he unquestionably passes into the madness of Manichaeus and Marcion. He believes that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, performed everything only in appearance, and that there was not a human body in him, but that the eyes of those who saw him encountered merely a phantastic appearance of a body.

## III

Since the Catholic faith has long detested these impious falsehoods, and since the sacrileges of such men have been condemned by the unanimous judgments of the blessed Fathers throughout the whole world, let all those who are so blinded and alienated from the light of truth that they deny that the Word of God has possessed a human nature—that is, our nature—from the time of the incarnation show in what sense they claim for themselves the Christian name and how they agree with the Gospel of truth: whether, through the birth of the blessed Virgin, flesh arose without Godhead, or Godhead arose without flesh.

[Note: The Vienna collection 5 and Vatican collection 11 read “if the birth of the blessed Virgin.” The reading in two Vatican collections, 21 and 24, is better: “if by the birth of the blessed Virgin,” and the same reading occurs in Letter 165, chapter 4.]

For just as it cannot be denied that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), so it cannot be denied that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

What reconciliation could there be by which God might be reconciled to the human race unless the mediator between God and human beings undertook the cause of all?

[Note: Thus the earlier editions, together with our Vienna collection 5, Vatican collection 24, and Sichard, better than Quesnel, who follows manuscripts of collection 21 and reads “of human beings.” For in Letter 165, chapter 4, “of all” is likewise read.]

And how could he fulfill the truth of his mediatorship unless he who was equal to the Father in the form of God also shared our condition in the form of a servant, so that through one new human being the renewal of our old condition might take place, and the bond of death contracted through one transgression might be loosed by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death?

[Note: These words also occur in Letter 165, as stated, and in Sermon 64, chapter 3.]

For the shedding of the blood of the righteous on behalf of the unrighteous was so powerful in securing privilege and so rich as a price that, if the whole multitude of captives believed in their redeemer, no one would remain held by tyrannical chains. For, as the Apostle says, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

And although those born under the sentence of sin have received the power to be reborn to righteousness, the gift of freedom has thereby become stronger than the debt of servitude.

## IV
What hope, then, do those retain for themselves in the protection of this sacrament who deny the reality of human substance in the body of our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed. Who is it that “gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5:2)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh? Although “the death of many saints was precious in the sight of the Lord” (Psalm 115:15), nevertheless the killing of no innocent person was the propitiation of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the courage of the faithful arose examples of patience, not gifts of righteousness. For their deaths were individual, each belonging to the person who died, and no one paid another’s debt by his own end. Among the sons of men, our Lord Jesus Christ alone appeared in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised. Concerning these things he himself said: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

[Note: Vindobonensis Collection 5 and Vatican Collection 24, together with Sichardus, omit “from the earth.”]

For true faith, which justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, having been drawn into a share in his humanity, obtains salvation in him in whom alone the human being finds himself innocent. By God’s grace, humanity is free to glory in the power of the one who, having engaged the proud enemy in the lowliness of our flesh, grants his victory to those in whose body he triumphed.

## CHAPTER V

Although, therefore, in our one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and true Son of man, there is one person of the Word and flesh, and although both natures have actions in common, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood. With the contemplation of sincere faith it must be discerned toward what the lowliness of weakness is raised and toward what the height of power inclines: what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither have conceived nor given birth (Luke 1:31); and without the reality of flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not have lain there (Luke 2:7). Without the power of the Word, the magi would not have worshiped the child revealed by the new star (Matthew 2:11); and without the reality of flesh, the child would not have been ordered to be taken into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution. Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not have said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17); and without the reality of flesh, John would not have proclaimed, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Without the power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the giving of life to the dead would not occur; and without the reality of flesh, neither food would be necessary for the one fasting nor sleep for the one wearied. Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not have declared himself equal to the Father; and without the reality of flesh, that same one would not have said that the Father was greater than he.

[Note: The manuscripts of Collection 21 add “well”: “in whom I am well pleased.”]

[Note: The pronoun “himself” is absent in Vindobonensis Collection 5, Vatican Collection 24, and Sichardus.]

The catholic faith accepts and defends both realities. According to the proper character of the divine and human substance, it believes the one Son of God to be both man and Word.

## CHAPTER VI

[Note: These words are found in Sermon 65, chapter 1.]

Although, therefore, from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb (John 1:14), there has never been any division between the divine and human substance, and although throughout all bodily stages of growth the actions of the entire time belonged to one person, nevertheless we do not confuse those very things that were done inseparably by any mixture. Rather, from the quality of the actions we perceive what belongs to each form.

For the divine things do not prejudice the human, nor the human the divine, since both converge into one in such a way that neither the distinct character of the natures is destroyed nor the person divided into two.

[Note: These words are likewise found in Sermon 65, chapter 4.]

Let these phantasmal Christians say, then, what substance of the Savior was fastened to the wood; what substance lay in the tomb; and, when the stone of the monument had been rolled away, what flesh rose on the third day. Or what sort of body did Jesus bring before the eyes of his disciples when he entered to them while the doors were shut? For, to drive away the disbelief of those who saw him, he required that the still-open marks of the nails be examined with the eyes and handled with the fingers, as well as the recent wound in his pierced side (John 20).

[Note: One manuscript of Vatican Collection 21 reads “required”; another, “required from the disciples themselves.” Immediately afterward, “as if” is found in Vindobonensis Collection 5, Vatican Collection 24, and Sichardus.]

But if, amid so great a light of truth, heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness, let them show from where they promise themselves the hope of eternal life, to which no one can come except through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus. “For there is no other name given among human beings under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12); nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him “who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6).

[Note: The manuscripts of Collection 21 add “and he who.”]

As the blessed apostle proclaims:

> Although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ the Lord is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:6–11).

## CHAPTER VII

Although, therefore, the Lord Jesus Christ is one, and although in him there is altogether one and the same person of true deity and true humanity, and although the solidity of this union cannot be separated by any division,

[Note: Quesnellus writes in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘of the union.’”]

we nevertheless understand the exaltation with which God exalted him, and bestowed on him the name surpassing every name, as pertaining to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification.

For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten there was no distinction in essence and no diversity in majesty. Nor had anything departed from the Word through the mystery of the incarnation that would be restored to him by the Father’s gift.

[Note: The manuscripts of Collection 21 read “of God the Father.”]

The form of a servant, through which the impassible deity fulfilled the sacrament of great piety, is the human lowliness that was raised into the glory of divine power. From the very conception in the Virgin, deity and humanity were joined in such unity that neither divine things were done without the human nor human things without God.

Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who is equal from eternity to God is said to have been exalted.

[Note: The same manuscripts add “to God the Father.”]

It makes no difference from which substance Christ is named, since, while the unity of the person remains inseparable, the same one is wholly the Son of man because of the flesh and wholly the Son of God because of the one deity he shares with the Father.

Whatever Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which those things that it did not have were conferred.

[Note: The copy of Sichardus, which did not have *confertur* (“is conferred”), supplies it. In Epistle 165, chapter 8, some manuscripts read *conferrentur* (“would be conferred”); others nevertheless read *conferuntur* (“are conferred”).]

For according to the power of the Word, the Son also possesses without distinction everything that the Father possesses; and whatever he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of the Father.

[Note: Vindobonensis Collection 5 reads: “And the same one is both rich”; Sichardus has a related reading, omitting only “is.” Epistle 165, chapter 8, agrees.]

The same one is both rich and poor (2 Corinthians 8:9). Rich, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3). Poor, however, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 1:14).

What, then, is his emptying, and what is his poverty, except the taking of the form of a servant, through which, with the majesty of the Word veiled, the dispensation of human redemption was fulfilled?

For since the original bonds of our captivity could not be undone,

[Note: The older printed editions, together with Sichardus’s copy, add: “and released from the power of the enemy.” This is absent both from our manuscripts and from Quesnellus’s manuscripts, as well as from Epistle 165, chapter 9.]

unless there existed a human being of our race and nature whom the prejudgments of the old debt did not hold, and who would erase the deadly bond with his spotless blood (Colossians 2:14), so, as had been divinely ordained from the beginning,

[Note: The same printed editions and Sichardus add: “and foretold by the prophetic oracles.” The manuscripts do not contain this addition.]

it was accomplished in the fullness of the appointed time, so that the promise, signified in many ways, might come to the long-awaited fulfillment; and what had continually been announced by repeated testimonies could not remain doubtful.

[Note: One manuscript of Vatican Collection 21, together with the same printed editions, reads “by repeated signs.”]

## CHAPTER VIII

Since so many heresies have therefore been destroyed—heresies which were cut off from the body of catholic unity through the holy devotion of the presiding Fathers, and thereby deserved to be exiled from Christ because they made the incarnation of the Word, which is the unique salvation of those who rightly believe, for themselves “a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense” (1 Peter 2:8)—I am astonished that your affection struggles to discern the light of truth.

Although it has been made clear by many disclosures how rightly the Christian faith condemned both Nestorius and Eutyches together with Dioscorus, and although no one who assents to the impiety of either the former or the latter can be called a Christian, I grieve that, as I hear, you are resisting the evangelical and apostolic teaching: stirring up cities by seditions, disturbing churches, and inflicting not only injuries but even killings upon presbyters and bishops, so that through fury and savagery you are forgetful of your purpose and profession.

[Note: These words indicate that the sermon was addressed to monks. Quesnellus, in note 1, understands the leaders of the monks to be Carosus and Dorotheus. But these men were Constantinopolitans, not Palestinians. Saint Leo is referring to the Palestinian monks who, under the leadership of Theodosius, disturbed all Palestine by warfare and killings, as Marcianus relates at greater length in his letter appended to the Acts of Chalcedon, and Evagrius in Book II, chapter 5. Compare note 1 in Epistle 109.]

Where is the rule of gentleness and quiet? Where is the patience of long-suffering? Where is the tranquility of peace? Where is the foundation of love and the strength of endurance? What persuasion led you away from Christ’s Gospel, or what persecution separated you from it? Or what deceitful cunning was so great that, forgetting the prophets and apostles, forgetting the saving creed and the confession that you pronounced before many witnesses when you received the sacrament of baptism, you submitted yourselves to diabolical illusions?

What would claws and savage tortures have accomplished against you, if empty inventions of heretics had been able to do so much toward overthrowing the integrity of your faith? You believe that you are acting on behalf of the faith, yet you attack the faith. You arm yourselves in the name of the Church, yet you fight against the Church. Is this what you learned from the prophets, from the evangelists, from the apostles? Do you deny the true flesh of Christ and subject the very essence of the Word to passion and death, thereby making our nature alien to its restorer, and believing that everything the cross inflicted, everything the lance wounded, and everything the stone of the tomb received and gave back was solely the work of divine power and not also of human lowliness?

[Note: Two manuscripts of Vatican Collection 21 read: “you believe that it alone was the work.”]

For this reason the Apostle says, “I am not ashamed of the Gospel” (Romans 1:16), because he knew what reproach the enemies would cast upon Christians. Therefore the Lord also declared, saying, “Whoever acknowledges me before human beings, I too will acknowledge before my Father” (Matthew 10:32).

For those to whom the flesh of Christ is now a cause of shame will not be worthy of the confession of the Son and the Father. They will prove that they have drawn no power from the sign of the cross, since they are ashamed to profess with their lips what they received to bear upon their foreheads.

## CHAPTER IX

Turn away, children; turn away from these diabolical persuasions. Nothing violates the truth of God, but the Truth does not save us except in our flesh. For, as the prophet says, “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12). Thus the Virgin Mary conceived the Word in such a way that she supplied from her own substance the flesh to be united to him, neither with the addition of another person nor with the emptying of the nature.

For he who was in the form of God so took the form of a servant that one and the same Christ exists in both forms: God inclining himself down to the lowest things of humanity, and humanity advancing upward to the highest things of deity. As the Apostle says:

> Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen (Romans 9:5).

## LETTER CXXV

[Note: Formerly Letter 98. What was previously numbered 125 is now 156. Written on June 25, 453.]

[Note: It survives in the manuscripts of Collections 12, 18, and 24, and in Sichardus’s copy.]

### TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COE

By Count R[.....]danus. He gently reproves Julian for his silence and wishes to be informed about everything.

LEO, bishop, to JULIAN, bishop.

[Col. 1068D]

I have very frequently urged your affection by my letters to undertake this care and diligence, so that you might continually inform me of my concern regarding what is happening in matters of faith.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus read “Very frequently,” and in the margin “Most frequently.”]

Although I never cease writing on every occasion, I have received no reply to certain letters of mine,

[Note: Epistle 117 or 118.]

sent, that is, through our son the *subadiuva* Rodanus, a member of the household of our son, the illustrious man Asparacius,

[Note: Sichardus’s copy deletes “that is.” The word *subadiuva* was added by Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript. As Quesnellus noted in his postscript, it signifies “a subordinate from the class of those who assist the assistants.” See Synesius, Epistle 144, and Panciroli’s Commentary on the *Notitia Dignitatum*, chapter 16.]

as though the lapse of time had not allowed you to indicate what had occurred after my letters.

Therefore, through my son Count Rodanus,

[Note: The printed editions, together with the manuscripts of Collections 12 and 24 and Sichardus, omit “count.” Quesnellus added it from the Grimanic manuscript. See Pancirolo, on the office of the *comes*.]

I greet you by this letter, and I admonish you not to neglect any opportunity for writing, so that the heat of my concern may be relieved.

[Note: The editions, together with the same manuscripts, read: “and I admonish you not to neglect any opportunity for writing, in which the burden of my concern is relieved.” Quesnellus emended the text from the same Grimanic manuscript.]

Since the Constantinopolitans have in you a certain share of me, it is fitting, both for our common friendship and for the love of the whole Church, that you watch with unceasing vigor so that nothing concerning the state of the faith may remain hidden from me.

Whatever I have written through the aforementioned persons, either to the most glorious emperor or to your affection, strive by timely representations to have delivered into effect with the greatest speed.

[Note: If letters written earlier are referred to here, “through the aforementioned person,” that is, through the *subadiuva* Rodanus, should apparently be read. Rodanus the official had not yet departed with the letters, and what is now written through him to Julian contains nothing particular that needed to be put into effect. More probably, the reference is to Epistles 115 to Marcian and 117 to Julian, in which serious matters concerning the peace of the faith and the observance of the canons had been proposed. Epistles 121 to Marcian and 122 to Julian cannot be intended, since they contain nothing relating to the faith and the canons. Otherwise, letters that have been lost would be indicated.]

And whatever, with God’s help, has been arranged, let me know, so that, once those things that have been reasonably ordered have been brought into effect, peace in the faith and observance of the canons may everywhere be both more secure and stronger.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Opilio, a man of illustrious rank.

## LETTER CXXVI

[Note: Formerly Letter 99. What was previously numbered 126 is now 157. Written on January 9, 454.]

[Note: Quesnellus published this from the Grimanic manuscript of Collection 18. We have collated it with the Ratisbon manuscript of Collection 19.]

### TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS

#### SUMMARY

He gives thanks for the calming of the disturbances in Palestine and for Juvenal of Jerusalem’s restoration to his own see; he also censures Dioscorus and his Egyptian followers.

LEO to MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.

Having been gladdened by the two addresses of your clemency, I reply with the appropriate expression of thanks,

[Note: Thus the Ratisbon manuscript. Quesnellus, from the Grimanic manuscript, reads “I write.” The two letters of Marcian to which Leo is now replying have not survived.]

rejoicing in the mercy of God, who, in the virtues of your providence and for the benefit of the Roman state and the peace of the catholic Church,

[Note: We supplied the conjunction “and” from the same Ratisbon manuscript.]

has established so glorious a protection.

Therefore I trust that this most salutary care of your piety will be so divinely assisted that complete tranquility may be granted both to the Christian religion and to your empire.

[Note: Thus our manuscript; Quesnellus reads “had settled” (*resedit*).]

That the peoples of the Palestinian provinces have been recalled to unity of faith, and that, once the movements of those in error had been suppressed, the hearts of all have been directed—as you deign to report—toward evangelical and apostolic teaching; and that my brother and fellow bishop Juvenal has at last been permitted to return to the seat of his priesthood,

[Note: From the same Ratisbon manuscript we added “his own.” The reference is to the Jerusalem see, which Juvenal had been forced to abandon after the Council of Chalcedon because of the disturbances of the Palestinian monks. Once those disturbances had been suppressed by the emperor, and Theodosius, the monks’ leader who had been intruded into that see, had fled, the bishop was able to reclaim it.]

with the people no longer resisting but desiring his return—this is the work of your faith and the fruit of your piety.

For its increase, unanimous prayer is multiplied throughout all the Churches of Christ, so that, if any darkness still remains in Egypt that has not yet received the rays of truth, it may receive remedies of illumination through the prayers of the whole world, and may no longer be burdened by the execrable contagions of Dioscorus. Nor may the Lord’s sheep there, through an imprudent attachment,

[Note: Quesnellus, from the Grimanic manuscript, reads “through the fault of imprudence.” Our Ratisbon manuscript is better. The reference is to the affection with which the Egyptians followed Dioscorus, although he had been deposed at Chalcedon and driven into exile. They were so reluctant to proceed to the election of a new bishop that, after Proterius was finally elected, many stirred up dissensions out of love for Dioscorus. See Liberatus, chapter 14, and Evagrius, Book II, chapters 5 and following.]

love the pastoral person whom they have experienced to be most savage, a devastator of morals and faith.

Therefore let your clemency persevere in its holy and admirable zeal, so that if anything anywhere is found sick or disturbed, it may be restored both to health and to peace. For it is fitting that you should preside over human affairs in such a way that you rejoice to serve the divine sacraments.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius, men of illustrious rank.

## LETTER CXXVII

[Note: Formerly Letter 100. What was previously numbered 127 is now 158. Written on January 9, 454.]

[Note: It survives in the manuscripts of Collections 12, 18, 19, and 24, and in Sichardus’s copy.]

### TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COE

[Col. 1070C]

#### SUMMARY

I. On the restoration of the bishop of Jerusalem, the conversion of the Palestinian monks, and the reception of Proterius’s letters.  
II. He wishes the date of Easter in the year 455 to be investigated more carefully.  
III. On his letter to the bishops of Chalcedon, read at Constantinople after Aetius’s inquiry, and on various letters written back and forth.

LEO, bishop of the city of Rome, to JULIAN, bishop.

### CHAPTER I

We have often demonstrated the faith of the most Christian emperor by the clearest evidence, and I give thanks to our God, who in his piety has deemed it right to grant such a ruler to human affairs: one who would guard both the causes of the faith and the commonwealth with the utmost vigilance,

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with most later manuscripts, read “with the zeal of supreme vigilance.” The Ratisbon manuscript supports Quesnellus’s reading.]

always resisting the attempts of heretics and permitting nothing of their madness against the catholic faith.

After God, it is owing to his benefactions that the bishop of Jerusalem has been restored and that, by august authority, he recalled to health the monks whom the perfidy of heretical falsehood had invaded.

As soon as I received your letters containing these matters, I hastened to reply not only on the same day but nearly at the same hour, so that you might be made more certain about everything you had written.

I rejoice that my brother Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, has sent us letters containing a full satisfaction concerning his faith, and has indicated more clearly what he holds.

[Note: Thus from the Grimanic manuscript; Quesnellus and our Ratisbon manuscript likewise read this. Alternatively, “openly.” It is clearer because Proterius, having been raised to the Alexandrian see, had indeed sent Leo letters concerning his faith, to which Leo replied, as he also did to those who ordained him and to the clergy, as may be gathered from Epistle 113, chapter 3. But since the holy pontiff desired a fuller exposition of the faith, here he indicates that he has now received letters containing such a full exposition; he replied to them in Epistle 129.]

I must therefore grant him due favor for the sincerity of his faith, so that he may in no respect lose the honor of his Church, but may possess the privileges of his see, following the example of the ancient Fathers, with their rights unimpaired according to the canons.

[Note: Vatican manuscript Collection 12 reads “and of the see.” In Vatican 541, which contains additions from Collection 24, both “but” and “and” are omitted.]

[Note: In the Ratisbon manuscript *rights* is absent. The sense shows that something is missing. Later copyists, recognizing this, inserted *rights* after *unimpaired*, although *unimpaired* seems more properly to refer not to rights but to privileges. Leo is asserting that the privileges of the Alexandrian Church should remain unimpaired according to the canonical sanctions or rules established at Nicaea, against the prerogative granted to the bishop of Constantinople at the Council of Chalcedon to the prejudice of the Alexandrian see.]

### CHAPTER II

There could be no doubt for us concerning Easter in the present year,

[Note: He is speaking of Easter in the year 454, which was marked both in the Alexandrian Paschal Table of Theophilus and in the Roman cycle for the day before the Nones of April. See note 14 in Epistle 121.]

but we asked about the future date, which Theophilus, bishop of the city of Alexandria, believed should be assigned to the eighth day before the Kalends of May—a date on which it had never been celebrated since the time of the Lord’s resurrection.

[Note: The subject is Easter in the year 455, over which the Romans and Alexandrians disagreed. The Leonine printed editions before Quesnellus incorrectly read “on the ninth.” See his note 1, and compare note 15 in Epistle 121, as well as the other notes there, through which the following becomes clear. We emended *day* from *the day* on the basis of the Ratisbon manuscript.]

Therefore it is appropriate that this be investigated with greater care, so that every opportunity for error may be removed.

For in our annals the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May is read as having been most clearly both established and celebrated by our Fathers.

[Note: In the editions before Quesnellus and in inferior manuscripts, the reading was “on the day of the Kalends of May, most suitably by the Fathers,” and so forth. Raynaudus emended *day* to *days*; Labbeus in the margin and Quesnellus in the text supplied “the fifteenth,” retaining *day*. The Ratisbon manuscript provides the true reading.

As for the term “annals,” in which the dates of Easter were recorded, it should also be noted that such annals existed among the Church of Constantinople. When Hormisdas, because of uncertainty about the date of Easter in 520, asked John, bishop of Constantinople, whether the Easterners agreed with the Westerners on it, John replied, in volume 5 of the Councils, page 654: “We declare that the number of the approaching Lord’s Passion, which is contained in your letters, is correct according to the Paschal Annals preserved among us.”

Saint Leo himself, in Epistle 137, chapter 1, speaking of Easter in 455, mentions several such annals among the Romans, writing: “Since in all our annals the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May is read as having been assigned from the Lord’s Passion.”

Since the dispute between the Alexandrians and Romans concerning Easter in 455 consisted in this: the former maintained that Easter should be celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, while the latter maintained that it should be celebrated on the fifteenth, Leo reports that Easter was indeed assigned to the fifteenth day in all the Latin annals, but not to the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

By the term “annals” he understands both the Paschal cycles of eighty-four years, in which Easter had been assigned to the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May in the first, eleventh, twenty-second, and other years of the same cycle—and it had indeed been celebrated in the years 382, 393, 404, and so forth, corresponding to those years of the cycle—and also other Latin ecclesiastical records in which the dates on which Easter was celebrated each year were customarily noted. Nowhere, however, was the eighth day before the Kalends of May recorded.

That “annals” was used more broadly for any public records is clear from the Roman synod of Boniface II in 531. After the petition of Stephen, bishop of Larissa, had been read, the pontiff said: “Let what has been read be entered in the ecclesiastical annals.” It is also clear from the Theodosian Code, Book II, title 30, Law 65, *On Appeals*: “The appeal of litigants shall be entered in the annals.”

Furthermore, the word *established* seems to fit the eighty-four-year cycles, in which for a long time the date of Easter to be celebrated in each year of the cycle had been assigned, as may be seen in the ancient eighty-four-year cycle published by Muratori in volume 3 of the *Latin Anecdota*. Referring to these cycles in Epistle 88 to Paschasinus, chapter 4, Saint Leo says: “In our Paschal cycles it is written that Easter in that year (455) is to be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

The word *celebrated* appears to refer to ecclesiastical records, in which Easter was recorded as having been celebrated in accordance with what had been prescribed in the aforementioned cycles.]

So that no difference may arise from this matter either among us or among the Easterners, may your affection deign to pursue this matter more insistently in my name with the most Christian emperor, although the most merciful emperor himself has deigned to indicate in his letters that he has entrusted this concern to the Egyptians after the most careful investigation.

### CHAPTER III

You reported in your letters that my letter to the Council of Chalcedon had been read in the presence of your bishops and clergy, but only as far as that chapter in which my agreement appears to have confirmed what had been done concerning the faith.

[Note: This is Epistle 114. Only its first chapter was read, by which the papal assent was added to the decrees of the synod concerning the matter of faith; not the second chapter, in which Saint Leo resisted the prerogative granted to the bishop of Constantinople at Chalcedon, insisting on the observance of the Nicene canons. Nevertheless, the whole letter was translated into Greek and at some time published. We have therefore printed its translation from the Greek manuscript of the Vatican.]

I was therefore astonished that the rest of what followed had not likewise been brought to the knowledge of those to whom the letter had been read, since it ought especially to have been made known to all that we had marked an improper ambition and opposed new usurpations, so that the ancient order established by the canons might remain inviolable, as we have always written.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript, agreeing with the Grimanic manuscript, supports Quesnellus’s emendation. The printed editions erroneously read: “It ought to have been made known that improper ambition had been marked by you, so that what had been established by new usurpations might remain inviolable, as we have always written.”]

We rejoice, however, that the presbyter Aetius, whom you say was investigated, was completely cleared after the inquiry had been conducted.

[Note: Epistle 126.]

You should also know that I sent a letter to the most Christian emperor, in which I thanked him because he had deigned to indicate his concern to me, both for the matter of the faith and for the security of the commonwealth.

He also sent another letter to us, intervening on behalf of Bishop Anatolius, so that our favor might be extended to him, since he promises his correction and pledges that he will satisfy in every respect what pertains to the observance of the faith.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius, men of illustrious rank.

## LETTER CXXVIII

[Note: Formerly Letter 101. What was previously numbered 128 is now 163. Written on March 9, 454.]

[Note: Until now it had been found only in the Grimanic manuscript of Collection 18 and was published by Quesnellus.]

### TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS

#### SUMMARY

Having praised the emperor’s faith and religious devotion, he declares that he will gladly receive Anatolius again into his favor, provided that Anatolius satisfies the canons and does not overturn the rights of priests.

LEO to MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.

If the bishop of the city of Constantinople wished to be as devoted to preserving the ecclesiastical rules as your clemency is concerned for the integrity of evangelical faith, everything would already have returned to its proper state once the scandals of dissension had been suppressed. Nor would the perversity of those who do not allow a remedy to be applied to them still claim anything for itself, while you are established in imperial power, defend everything just, and oppose errors.

But this palm is reserved for your gentleness: that the health of all who are recalled or return to Christ our Lord through the catholic faith may be owed to you.

Therefore, just as we glory in you, so we grieve over those for whom we see you, though they are preoccupied by carnal rivalry, so concerned for the state of the Churches and the peace of all priests with a spirit at once Christian and royal that you grant the favor of your interventions on behalf of those whom you know to be straying, encouraging me through your letters to restore my fellow bishop Anatolius to my favor through fraternal charity.

I bestowed this favor on him affectionately, as you remember, and I always desire to extend it, provided that, as I previously urged, he withdraw from the ambition that has weighed him down and no longer keep in his company those who were obscuring him.

[Note: We corrected this from the Grimanic manuscript, whose copy was used by Father Cacciarius.]

[Note: Compare Epistle 111, chapter 3.]

But he has so far been unwilling to reply to the letters sent to him with pious affection. And since, regarding the person of Aetius or of Andrew, who had been substituted for him, matters followed that ought to be condemned, it is not irrelevant that he is silent about what most needed to be addressed.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “and Andrew.” We have preferred the reading of the Grimanic manuscript, as noted by Father Cacciarius, where *or* is used for *and*, as in other examples of Leo noted in note 5 to Epistle 67.]

I had therefore wished to obey the instruction of your piety and write to the bishop mentioned above, if I had perceived that my earlier letters to him had made any progress either through the effect of events or through his own writings.

[Note: Leo had already received these letters from Marcian on the fifth day before the Ides of January, as is clear from the preceding letter, chapter 3.]

But since he has been unwilling to profess any repentance for his ambition and has taken no care to respond to what I wrote, I have suspended my conversations with him, but I have not changed the disposition by which I desire him to be corrected and improved.

Therefore, if it pleases your clemency—or rather, since I know that it pleases you—let him satisfy the canons, let him reply that he will preserve the favor of all priests through peaceful humility, and let him declare that he has cast off his blameworthy ambition.

I promise that I will receive him again into such favor that I will embrace his fellowship in everything that is pleasing to the Lord, since that will be true peace and firm charity in which we shall strive together to preserve both the catholic faith and the decrees of the Nicene canons.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of March, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius, men of illustrious rank.

# NOTICE ON THE THREE FOLLOWING LETTERS (G)

[Col. 1073]

1. A few words should be said about why, in publishing the following three letters, we have followed an order different from Quesnellus’s. Quesnellus first published the letter numbered 131 in this edition, addressed to Julian, dated 9 March; then Letter 129, addressed to Proterius, dated 10 March; and finally, after inserting Proterius’s Letter 133 to Leo, he appended Letter 130 to Marcian, dated 11 March, relegating 10 March to the margin. These differing dates required this order. But in Letter 131 to Julian, chapter 1, the holy pontiff states that he is sending him copies of the letters that he had sent to the most merciful emperor and to the bishop of the city of Alexandria—that is, Proterius—thus referring to the two letters delivered to Marcian and Proterius. Since these were therefore already written before he drafted the letter to Julian, it is clear that the chronological notes preferred by Quesnellus contain an error, which led him to establish that order. We have therefore more correctly emended the chronological notes from our Regensburg manuscript, from which it is gathered that all these letters were dated on the same day, 10 March.

2. As for the order itself, the testimony of Letter 131 makes it clear that the holy pontiff wrote to Marcian and Proterius before writing to Julian.
