Moreover, from the beginning of chapter 2 of Letter 130 to Marcian, where Leo states that he had written back to Proterius, it is evident that the letter to Proterius preceded the letter to Marcian. Thus, although all these letters bear the same date, their own sequence shows that Leo wrote first to Proterius, then to Marcian, and finally to Julian; and we shall preserve this order in the edition.

## LETTER CXXIX

[Col. 1075C] Formerly 103. What was previously numbered 129 is now 159. Written 10 March 454.

[Col. 1075C] We found this letter, edited by Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript, in the Regensburg manuscript, and emended it from that source.

### TO PROTERIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

[Col. 1075A]

### Synopsis

I. It is the duty of bishops to keep watch lest the unity of the faith be violated, which can happen even through the alteration of a small letter.  
II. He asserts that, following the tradition of the holy Fathers, his own letter is catholic and that the people must be instructed.  
III. He declares that the faith, discipline, and privileges of the Churches must be preserved according to the standard of antiquity.

## LEO TO PROTERIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA

### Chapter I

[Col. 1075C] Bede inserted a fragment of this letter in chapter 42 of *On the Reckoning of Time*. He was mistaken, however, in thinking that Leo was replying in this letter to Proterius’s letter concerning Easter, which Leo received later, as will be shown in Letter 137. See Quesnellus’s note 1. This letter was instead a reply to earlier letters of Proterius, which are now missing. Proterius had first written to the pontiff about his faith when he had been elevated to the Alexandrian see, and Leo replied to that letter, as well as to those who had ordained him and to the people, as indicated in Letter 113, chapter 3. Leo later desired from him a fuller declaration of faith, as indicated in Letter 127, chapter 1. He is now replying to that fuller declaration.

The letter of your affection, which our brother and fellow bishop Nestorius [Col. 1075D] delivered in his pious service, has gladdened me. For it was fitting that such a letter should be sent from the bishop of the Church of Alexandria to the apostolic see—a letter showing that, through the teaching of the most blessed Apostle Peter, the Egyptians had learned from the beginning through his blessed disciple Mark what the Romans are known to have believed: “For there is no other name given to human beings under heaven, by which we must be saved, except that of the Lord Jesus Christ” (Acts 4:12).

[Col. 1076C] Bede reports the beginning of this letter up to these words. [Col. 1076C] We have supplied the words from the Regensburg manuscript.

But since faith does not belong to everyone, and that treacherous tempter takes pleasure in wounding human hearts with no wounds more grievous than those by which he infects unwary minds with errors hostile to evangelical truth, we must strive with the great instruction of the Holy Spirit to ensure that Christian understanding cannot be violated by diabolical falsehoods. Against this danger the rulers of the Churches must above all keep watch, and must turn away from the minds of the simple people lies disguised under a certain appearance of probability.

[Col. 1076C] He is alluding to the deceit of the Eutychians, who, lying in wait for everyone in both words and syllables, claimed that Letter 28 to Flavian conformed to the Nestorian interpretation, as is reported in chapter 2 and more explicitly in the following letter, chapter 3: “The crafty wickedness of certain heretics is said to have falsified my letter ... in order to assert, by changing certain words or syllables, that I was a supporter of the Nestorian error.” Hence, shortly afterward, he warns that the force of the sentences must not be corrupted either by addition or by alteration.

For narrow and difficult is the way that leads to life (Matt. 7:14). Nor are there as many snares in the observance of actions as lie amid the dangers of meanings, when the force of a statement is corrupted by the briefest addition or alteration, and a confession that was bringing salvation sometimes turns, by a subtle transition, toward death.

[Col. 1075C] The number 1254 appears in the printed edition.

Since the Apostle says, “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19), every time the impiety of opposing interpretations reveals itself, it contributes to the benefit of the whole Church. Thus harmful things are not hidden and do not injure the safety of others—others who might not be recalled to salvation. Therefore those who preferred, through imprudent obstinacy, to remain in their guilt rather than accept the remedy offered should attribute their ruin and blindness to themselves. Your Fraternity rightly finds their stubbornness displeasing, and commendably embraces that teaching which has come down to us from the blessed apostles and holy Fathers.

### Chapter II

My letter, in which I replied to the report of holy memory Flavian concerning Eutyches and the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, is not a proclamation of some new teaching. In no respect does it depart from that rule of faith which has been clearly defended by our ancestors and yours. If Dioscorus had wished to follow and imitate them, he would have remained in the body of Christ. He could have been instructed by the writings of blessed memory Athanasius and could have found in the sermons of holy memory Theophilus and Cyril grounds for nobly opposing the dogma once condemned, rather than choosing fellowship with Eutychian impiety.

I therefore admonish you, dearest brother, out of concern for the common faith: since the enemies of the cross of Christ lie in wait for all our words and syllables, let us give them no opportunity, however slight, to pretend that we agree with the Nestorian interpretation.

[Col. 1076D] Saint Thomas uses this passage up to the following sentence in *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 11, article 2, reply to objection 2.

Your diligence must exhort the people, the clergy, and the whole brotherhood toward the advancement of the faith in such a way that you show yourself to be teaching nothing new, but impressing upon all hearts what the Fathers of venerable memory taught in harmonious proclamation, with whom our letter agrees in every respect. This must be demonstrated not only by your own words but also by the recitation of the preceding expositions.

[Col. 1077C] Quesnellus reads “by exposition and recitation.” We have preferred the reading of the Regensburg manuscript, “the preceding expositions.” These signify the testimonies of the Fathers mentioned shortly before, who held the Alexandrian see; somewhat later Leo orders that they be read in the Church. The following letter repeats the same instruction in chapter 3.

Thus the people of God may know that what is being impressed upon them by the present teaching is what the Fathers received from their predecessors and handed down to posterity. Therefore, after the assertions of the aforementioned bishops have first been read, let my writings also be recited, so that the ears of the faithful may recognize that we preach nothing other than what we received from our ancestors.

[Col. 1077C] See Quesnellus’s note. [Col. 1077C] The Regensburg manuscript reads “we receive”; Quesnellus reads “we received.”

And because they possess senses insufficiently trained to distinguish these matters, let them learn at least from the writings of the Fathers how ancient is this evil which is now condemned by us both in Nestorius and in Eutyches, who were ashamed to preach the Gospel of Christ according to the teaching of the Lord himself.

[Col. 1077C] The Regensburg manuscript omits “by us,” but has it later in the sentence “we condemned.”

### Chapter III

In every respect, therefore, let the standard of antiquity be preserved both in the rule of faith and in the observance of discipline, and let your affection exercise the constancy of a prudent ruler. Thus it will benefit the Church of Alexandria that I have conscientiously opposed the improper ambition of certain people while preserving the right of the ancient privileges, and that I have wished the dignity of all the metropolitans to remain inviolate.

[Col. 1077C] Quesnellus reads “of the true privileges.” We have emended it from the Regensburg manuscript.

[Col. 1077C] By “the metropolitans” he includes the bishop of the Church of Alexandria and appears to be referring to the sixth canon of Nicaea, in which only the designation “metropolitans” is found. Hence, shortly afterward, he calls all the bishops of Egypt “provincial bishops,” since the whole of Egypt was regarded as one province.

You will recognize this from the tenor of my letters, which I sent to the holy synod, to the most Christian ruler, or to the bishop of Constantinople.

[Col. 1077D] Quesnellus reads “and of the letters.” The correction is supplied by the Regensburg manuscript, which shortly afterward omits “my.” It then reads “but also the bishop of Constantinople,” and later “to my concern,” followed by “so that there may be no deviation from the faith in the Churches of the Lord,” and so forth.

You will clearly perceive that this is the particular object of my concern: that there be no deviation from the rule of faith in the Churches of the Lord, and that nothing be diminished from anyone’s privileges through another’s misconduct.

Since this is so, let your Fraternity follow the custom of your predecessors and exercise fitting authority over your fellow-provincial bishops, who by ancient constitution are subject to the see of Alexandria.

[Col. 1077C] The wording is suggested by the same Regensburg manuscript.

Let them not resist ecclesiastical custom, but let them not delay coming to your affection, either at the appointed times or whenever the circumstances of a matter require it.

[Col. 1077D] The same manuscript reads “coming”; other copies read “to come.”

And if there is something beneficial to the interests of the Church that must be considered by common deliberation, let the brotherhood gather together and make a unanimous decision. For no reason should recall them from this obedience, since your Fraternity is known to us as so faithful in belief and conduct that we will not permit anything to be diminished from the authority of your predecessors, nor permit you to be disregarded with impunity.

[Col. 1078A] The number 1256 appears in the printed edition.

Given 10 March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studio.

## LETTER CXXX

[Col. 1077D] Formerly 104. What was previously numbered 130 is now 160. Written 10 March 454.

[Col. 1078C] It exists in the Hispanic collections, Isidore 11, 12, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, and in Sichardus’s copy.

### TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS

[Col. 1078C] In the Hispanic collection this heading reads: “I. Concerning Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, that he should preserve the decrees of his predecessors. II. Where he asks the emperor to send to the Church of Alexandria a Greek translation of the letter that he had sent to Flavian of Constantinople.”

### Synopsis

I. He rejoices in the faith of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria.  
II. The Alexandrians are to be instructed by him according to the tradition of their Church.  
III. Leo’s letter to Flavian, falsified by heretics, is to be newly translated into Greek and publicly recited to the Alexandrians.

## LEO, BISHOP, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS

### Chapter I

[Col. 1078B]

You have demonstrated, also through the letter delivered by my brother and fellow bishop Nestorius, the purity of Christian faith with which your Clemency shines forth, showing the most just favor toward my brother Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, by which he has become in every respect more acceptable to me.

[Col. 1078C] The common text, along with Hispanic collection manuscripts 24 and Sichardus, incorrectly reads “Nestorian.” See note 3 (Col. 1075, n. d) on the preceding letter.

For anyone to whom your piety deigns to offer testimony would unquestionably be worthy of approval even if he were silent.

[Col. 1078C] The Regensburg manuscript reads “to offer.”

But this adds to his favor: he is recognized through his own speech, and his profession makes clear how sincere he is as a preacher of catholic doctrine.

[Col. 1078D] Earlier editions before Quesnellus, together with Hispanic collection manuscripts 11 and 21, read “may be recognized,” and then “may become clear.” The Regensburg manuscript reads “therefore” rather than “whence.”

Accordingly, I embrace with the fullest affection the love of my orthodox brother, and I give thanks to God that, after removing the man who wished to oppose the Gospel of Christ and to disagree with the understanding of the holy Fathers, he has provided the Church of Alexandria with such a priest, one who agrees with its preceding rulers both in faith and in life.

[Col. 1078D] The Codex Grimanicus reads “the one condemned.” Ancient copies, together with Hispanic collection 24 and Sichardus, read “to disagree” rather than “to dissent.”

For when he professes with his whole heart that he embraces my letter, which I sent to Flavian of blessed memory against the impious Eutyches, what else does he show himself to be than a disciple of the apostles?

[Col. 1078D] The same manuscripts read: “which I sent, while he professes with his whole heart that it is impious; what else ...?”

[Col. 1078D] The older editions omit the verb “to be,” as do the Regensburg and Vatican manuscripts, Hispanic collection 24, and Sichardus.

For the doctrine of truth remains in its own light, and what is one and undivided cannot be different.

[Col. 1078D] The editions before Quesnellus, together with the Vienna and Hispanic manuscripts, the Regensburg manuscript, Hispanic collection 24, and Sichardus, add “and divine.” The emendation of Quesnellus, introduced from the Grimanic manuscript and Barberinian collection 11, is confirmed by our other manuscripts.

### Chapter II

[Col. 1079A]

I therefore wrote back to the aforesaid brother as I ought, and admonished him to persevere in his holy endeavor.

[Col. 1079B] The Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts and Isidore read “so that he may persevere in his holy endeavor.” The Regensburg manuscript reads “so that he might persevere.”

He will undoubtedly be more steadfast if he is also strengthened by the exhortations of your Clemency. Nor should the uninstructed disagreement of certain people frighten him—people whom ignorance makes subject to the instigations of a few heretics.

[Col. 1079B] Another manuscript reads “has made” for “makes.”

What they cannot attain through their own diligence should therefore be opportunely brought to their hearing.

[Col. 1079C] The ancient Vulgate together with the Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and other copies derived from them, read “negligence.” The Grimanic, Regensburg, Vienna, and Hispanic manuscripts, together with Vatican collection 24 and Sichardus, read “diligence.”

And so that the aforementioned man may not appear to introduce something new or assert something of his own, let the writings of the venerable Fathers who presided over that same Church be read aloud.

[Col. 1079C] The Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and another manuscript of collection 11 read “let them be read.” This testimony of Leo seems to have influenced the emperor Marcian, who, in his letter to the Alexandrian monks published in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1794, and also in the law addressed chiefly concerning the Egyptians to Palladius, prefect of the praetorium, in 455, p. 1832, declared the faith of Chalcedon consistent with the teaching of Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril.

Let them examine what blessed Athanasius, what Theophilus, what Cyril, and what the other Eastern teachers thought about the incarnation of the Lord.

[Col. 1079C] We have added “the others” from the Regensburg manuscript, both Hispanic manuscripts, the Vatican manuscripts, Isidore, and another copy of collection 11. In a postscript Quesnellus explains this as meaning the chief bishops of the Eastern diocese of Antioch, or bishops from that diocese, such as Theodoret. It can be inferred from Letter 119, chapter 2, however, that “Eastern” is used here broadly, not strictly of the bishops of Antioch or of those subject to Antioch; see note 10 (Col. 1042, n. k) on that letter. Indeed, among the testimonies of the Fathers appended to Letter 165 to Leo Augustus, besides the three Alexandrian bishops mentioned, the only Eastern figures praised are John Chrysostom, Basil, and Gregory of Nazianzus, none of whom belongs to the diocese of Antioch.

And let them not be deceived by errors that are beginning to sprout again, errors once overthrown by the power of the evangelical word.

[Col. 1079D] The Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and another copy of collection 11 read “lest they be deceived by errors beginning to sprout again.”

For nearly all the heresies that have arisen at different times have deviated from the Gospel because they did not understand the mystery of Christ’s bodily birth, passion, and resurrection.

And we could labor less in repelling heretics if those falsehoods destroyed by antiquity did not disturb inexperienced minds.

[Col. 1079D] The same manuscripts read “they could.” Vatican collection 24, Sichardus, and Merlinus read “we can.” Two manuscripts of Vatican collection 21 read “they can.”

But now, as I have said, the best method of teaching is that the lines of the Fathers’ understanding be made known to the ears of the Alexandrian people and clergy.

[Col. 1079D] Thus both Hispanic manuscripts with Isidore, the Regensburg manuscript, and Vatican collection 11; elsewhere, “the people themselves.” Shortly afterward the Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and one copy of Vatican collection 11 omit “now.”

And if there are some who despise our writings, let them at least yield to those who agree with us in apostolic understanding.

[Col. 1079D] The Vulgate reads “let the line ... become known.” We have preferred the reading of the Regensburg manuscript. Shortly afterward both Hispanic copies with Isidore and manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 read “of the clergy” rather than “of the clergy” in the alternate form.

In this work I shall greatly rejoice in the devotion of my fellow priest, and I shall always rejoice in his unanimity, because fraternal peace is preserved only in one confession of faith.

[Col. 1080B] The Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 read “our.” [Col. 1080B] We have supplied the particle “only” from the Regensburg manuscript.

### Chapter III

Since, however, the crafty wickedness of certain heretics is said to have falsified my letter, which I delivered to Flavian of blessed memory, in order to disturb the simplicity of our people, and, by changing certain words or syllables, to assert that I was a supporter of the Nestorian error—

[Col. 1080B] Thus according to the excellent Regensburg manuscript. The Vienna and Hispanic manuscripts add “of ours.” This error was corrected by a diligent copyist of the Hispanic collection of Gallican origin, who arbitrarily substituted “of the saints,” as it is read in the Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and manuscripts of collections 11 and 21. The common text from collections 12 and 24, together with Sichardus, reads “of others.” By “our people” Leo means Catholics. For what he indicates here concerning the falsified Greek version of his Letter 28 to Flavian, compare what will be said in note 6 (Col. 1123, n. b) on Letter 152, and especially the third observation in Quesnellus’s first dissertation on the year 454.

—I ask your venerable Clemency to command that this same letter be translated fully and carefully into the Greek language by my brother, Bishop Julian, or by those whom your piety chooses as suitable for this task, and that it be conveyed by a reliable courier under the impression of your seal.

[Col. 1080C] Another reading is “bearer.”

It is to be delivered to the Alexandrian judges, who shall have it recited to the clergy and people of that city together with the preaching of the aforementioned bishops, with whom my writings agree.

[Col. 1080C] The ancient Vulgate, together with manuscript 24 of collection 24, reads “who also agree with my writing.” Quesnellus’s reading from the Grimanic manuscript is approved by our other copies. We have added “also” from the Regensburg manuscript, which Quesnellus omitted.

Thus they may recognize that they must no longer be deceived by the fraud of deceitful men, and may be shown to be sincere disciples of the apostolic see.

[Col. 1080C] This reading of the ancient editions is confirmed by our Regensburg manuscripts, Vatican collections 12 and 24, and Sichardus’s copy. The Vienna and Hispanic manuscript has “sincerity” erroneously in place of “to be sincere”; this error was corrected in the Vatican and Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and the other copies of the same origin, which read without the error. Quesnellus, relying only on the Grimanic manuscript, reads: “and let the sincerity of the apostolic see be proved, at which ...” His observation in the postscript—that the common reading conflicts with the meaning—is correct if the sentence is understood to be governed by the particle “so that”; it is not correct if the clause is joined to the preceding sentence: “let them have it recited ... and let them be proved to be sincere disciples of the apostolic see, while they follow the faith of that see.” Leo explains this particular prerogative of the Alexandrian Church more fully in Letter 9 at its beginning.

For neither Eutyches nor Nestorius has any place at that see, since the universal Church has condemned both of them, just as it has condemned other heretics.

Given 10 March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studio.

[Col. 1080D] All our manuscripts, Sichardus, and Binius read this way. Quesnellus, together with other common editions, reads “11 March,” with “10 March” in the margin as an alternative.

## LETTER CXXXI

[Col. 1081C] Formerly 102. What was previously numbered 131 is now 161. Written 10 March 454.

[Col. 1081C] We collated this letter, edited from the Grimanic manuscript, with the Regensburg manuscript.

### TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COS

[Col. 1081A]

### Synopsis

I. He informs Julian of the letters received from Proterius of Alexandria; he wishes and commands that his letter to Flavian be translated by Julian from Latin into Greek and, having been sent under the seal of Augustus, recited in the church to the Alexandrian people.  
II. He asks that a reply be sent concerning Easter of the following year.

## LEO TO JULIAN, BISHOP

### Chapter I

[Col. 1081A]

Having received the letter of our brother and fellow bishop Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, I learned without doubt that he is devoted to catholic teaching and opposes heretics with an upright heart, so that we may rightly hope that he will benefit the Church over which he presides, both by the example of his conduct and by the instruction of the faith.

But because the Eutychian factions stir up no small amount of trouble for him, and are said to thrust my letter to Flavian of blessed memory, which was corrupted by a deceitful interpretation, upon simple or uneducated people in such a way that certain passages appear to agree with the Nestorian error, I assign this task to your Fraternity, so that this malignity may not be able to boast of having disturbed the faithful.

I ask that you deign to translate this same letter of mine carefully from Latin into Greek. The examples of our predecessors attest that it agrees in every respect with apostolic teaching. The most glorious and faithful ruler is to send it, as I requested, under the impression of his seal to the Alexandrian judges, so that it may be recited in the church to the Christian people together with the preaching of the holy men who presided over that Church.

[Col. 1081C] Letter 130.

[Col. 1081C] The Regensburg manuscript omits “ignorantly.”

Thus those who are said to be wavering through ignorance may, once they have learned the truth, no longer be led astray by corrupt persuasions. And so that nothing concerning the kind of letters I sent to the most merciful emperor or to the bishop of the city of Alexandria may escape your Fraternity, the copies appended to this letter will show it.

### Chapter II

[Col. 1082A]

As I have often already written, be concerned about the coming Easter, and communicate it at the appropriate time in my name to my most merciful ruler, so that he may inform us what reply has been made to him. For the days are approaching when we shall be able to know which day we ought to enter in the *Formatae*, and when every uncertainty on this matter may be more clearly resolved.

Given 10 March, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aetius and Studio.

[Col. 1081C] Thus according to the same Regensburg manuscript, as in the two preceding letters. Quesnellus, from the Grimanic manuscript, reads “7 March.”

## LETTER CXXXII

[Col. 1081C] Formerly placed after Letter 105. What was previously numbered 132 is now 162. Written around April 454.

[Col. 1081C] It is found in a single Thessalonian collection, number 16. We collated it with Barberinian manuscript 3336, from which Holstenius published it. Before him Allatius had published the same letter in *Harmony of the Western Church* from a Vatican manuscript, which we sought in vain. As for its date: when Leo wrote Letter 128 on 8 March of the present year, 454, he had not yet received the letter from Anatolius that he was awaiting; there he therefore asked the emperor to make the same bishop send a reply containing what is found in this letter. Marcian did so, as is clear from chapter 1 of the present letter. In Letter 136, dated 29 May, chapter 1, Leo states that he has now received this letter of Anatolius together with a letter from the same emperor; he therefore immediately replied to both in Letters 135 and 136. To allow sufficient time for the transmission of the letters and for the response, we place this letter of Anatolius after March and before May, that is, around April.

Since the conclusion says, “And the subscription in Greek letters,” this undoubtedly indicates Anatolius’s autograph subscription. Since he did not know Latin writing, he used Greek letters. It also indicates that the copy of this letter sent to Leo was written in Latin, and that only Anatolius’s subscription was in Greek. There is no doubt that Anatolius composed this letter in Greek, just as he wrote Letter 101, which we have now published for the first time, in Greek. But just as Saint Cyril, to make the reading of certain documents written in Greek more prompt and easy for Pope Celestine, first had them translated into Latin and sent them to the same pontiff in Latin—as is clear from his eighth letter among Celestine’s letters in Father Coustant, no. 9—so Anatolius likewise seems to have sent Leo this letter, written by himself in Greek, but rendered into Latin by others and signed by himself in Greek letters. Hence this Latin text should be regarded as the original subscribed by Anatolius’s own hand.

### OF ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO POPE LEO (G)

### Synopsis

I. He friendly complains about the interruption of their correspondence and displays his due obedience to the pontiff.  
II. He writes that Aetius has been restored and Andrew deposed.  
III. He greatly desires to be refreshed by a letter from the holy pontiff.  
IV. He removes from himself the charge of ambition and attributes it to the zeal of his clergy and of the Eastern bishops. He reports that confirmation of the acts of Chalcedon has been reserved to the authority of the pontiff.

## ANATOLIUS TO THE MOST HOLY AND BLESSED FELLOW BISHOP, POPE LEO: GREETINGS IN THE LORD

### Chapter I

Hoping that every consolation and assistance demanded by a life surrounded by toil and cares had been placed in your blessedness, I had rightly believed that the entire burden of my anxiety would thereby become lighter. But now a sharper anxiety than all the others has weighed upon me, produced by the prolonged interruption of letters from your Holiness, which is not your usual practice—especially since letters written by you to others were shown to me. These increased the grief that made me desire more frequently to obtain your words, so that I might fulfill, by obeying you, whatever appeared in every respect pleasing to your most perfect understanding.

For far be it from me to oppose in any way whatever instructions had been given to me in writing. Yet since the most pious and most Christian ruler, who by the benefit of his most prudent foresight governs all human affairs and everywhere possesses the philosophy of divine virtues, does not cease to rival the Church in piety—

[Col. 1083C] Allatius reads “the Church does not cease in piety”; the Barberinian manuscript reads “does not cease in zeal for piety.” Because the passage is corrupt, we have not altered the common reading.

—and since he orders the human race in such a way as to make it more attentive through devotion to God, he read me the letter of your blessedness. I immediately fulfilled what it contained as being pleasing to you.

[Col. 1083C] The Barberinian manuscript, together with Allatius, reads “he fulfilled for us.” Holstenius’s emendation is required by the sense.

I did so both because the common good of peace and because what was fitting urged me to do so.

### Chapter II

The most reverend presbyter Aetius of our most holy Church has indeed been restored to us to his former place and ecclesiastical rank, having given a modest response concerning everything that belongs to his episcopate.

[Col. 1083C] Perhaps “of his episcopate.” The precise meaning of this corrupt and very obscure passage can be inferred from Letter 127, chapter 3: “We rejoice that the presbyter Aetius, whom you assert had been investigated, has, after inquiry, been found clear in every respect.” He had been archdeacon and perhaps had incurred some accusation concerning the administration of property.

Andrew, however, who had not been promoted by us but had been honored with the dignity of archdeacon by advancement through the ranks, has been separated from the Church together with those who had acted against our father and bishop Flavian of holy memory. These men had previously belonged to the utterly faithless party of Eutyches. Although, through many excuses and their own subscriptions appended to your letter of holiness, they now seemed to have made satisfaction for their past offenses, this remains so only until what is pleasing to you concerning them has been decreed.

[Col. 1083D] Allatius reads “while they survive.”

[Col. 1083C] The printed editions and the manuscript read this way, not as Tillemont believes it should be read in article 62 of his *Life of Leo*: “he was separated from the clergy.” Leo indicates only in Letters 135, chapter 2, and 136, chapter 3, that Andrew was removed from the ministry of archdeacon. Since this letter was rendered into Latin from Greek, as we saw in note 1 (Col. 1081, n. g), perhaps the less competent translator rendered the phrase somewhat inexactly as “separated from the Church,” intending to indicate that Andrew had been deprived of every ecclesiastical rank and office until Leo should reply with his judgment concerning what ought to be done with him.

### Chapter III

Your blessedness should consider how pleasing to the Lord Christ himself, who is our peace, our union in love will be; how greatly the spirit of the most faithful ruler will rejoice; and how all the people of God and the Churches of Christ will alike remain free from every discord.

May your blessedness deign to gladden us with a letter by which we may be enabled to attain that affection which we already know in abundance to flourish in your most prudent hearts. Then, having joyfully received the letters of your holiness, we may give thanks to our Lord God Christ, who has broken the bonds of every difficulty, and may offer solemn prayers to him for your blessedness.

### Chapter IV

Concerning what was decreed through the favor of the see of Constantinople at the recent universal synod of Chalcedon, let your blessedness know with certainty that there is no fault in me, a man who have always loved leisure and quiet, keeping myself in humility, from the beginning of my life. Rather, it was the most reverend clergy of the Church of Constantinople who pursued this course, together with the most religious bishops of these regions, who agreed in this matter and assisted one another.

[Col. 1083D] Gelasius praises this testimony in his letter to the Dardani, in the fuller edition drawn from the outstanding collection 14 of Avellanus, printed in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 333: “Let them hear,” he says, “Anatolius, bishop of that see, confessing that the Constantinopolitan clergy rather than himself attempted such things, and declaring that the whole matter had been placed in the power of the apostolic bishop.”

The entire force and confirmation of the proceedings was nevertheless reserved to the authority of your blessedness. Let your holiness therefore know this clearly: nothing in this affair was done through me, since I have always believed that I must avoid every frivolity of boasting and every desire to seek what belongs to another.

We, both I myself and my people, greet most warmly in Christ the whole brotherhood that is with your holiness.

And the subscription is in Greek letters.

# LETTER

[Note: Formerly after Letter 103. Formerly numbered 133, now 164. Written shortly after 4 April 454.]

## CXXXIII

[Note: Two Latin translations exist of this letter, which Proterius wrote in Greek. One, older, was translated in Leo’s time by an interpreter less skilled in Latin; a fragment of it is quoted by Hadrian I in Letter 97 to the bishops of Spain and is presented by Quesnell in his notes. The other is this version. That it is by Dionysius Exiguus, whom Sigebert mentions in *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 27—and indeed Dionysius himself confirms this in the preface to the Paschal Cycle, where he testifies that he translated it and attached it to that work—is clearly proved by the fact that it is found attached to that Cycle in manuscripts. Petavius published it from the Sirmond manuscript in the appendix to volume II of his work *On the Doctrine of Time*; Aegidius Bucherius in his commentary on Victor’s Paschal Canon, p. 82; and P. Labbe more accurately in the *Councils*. Quesnell collated it anew with the Oxford manuscript. Finally, Joannes Guillelmus Janus reprinted a more corrected text from three manuscripts of Dionysius—the Bodleian, Cottonian, and Digby manuscripts—in his *History of the Dionysian Cycle*, Wittenberg edition, 1718, p. 95, and we have benefited greatly from them. This letter concerns the date of Easter in the year 455 and was written after Easter of 454, in the seventh indiction. For in chapter 3 the Easter in question is called a future solemnity, and in chapter 1 the eighth indiction of that Easter is called future. It was therefore written after 4 April of the seventh indiction, on which Easter of 454 fell. Since he had already received it by 29 May, as Letter 136, chapter 1, shows, it is evident that it was written between 4 April and 29 May 454; and, allowing suitable time for its transmission from Egypt to Rome, shortly after 4 April.]

**SAINT PROTERIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO THE MOST BLESSED POPE LEO, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME. On the Paschal Computation. (G)**

To my most beloved lord, brother and fellow priest, Leo: Proterius sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

Our most pious and faithful emperor Marcian recently addressed us in a venerable letter [Note: Janus reads, “recently to us”; shortly afterward, “with the Lord’s help.”], in which he stated that some people did not carefully assign the date of the Paschal feast, which, with God’s help, is to be celebrated in the coming eighth indiction. Yet he did not indicate this as though he had been personally moved by the matter, but because he had received a letter from your holiness [Note: The Oxford manuscript reads “of your brotherhood”; later, “should retain” instead of “should contain.”], and he commanded us to investigate the matter carefully, applying the most exact scrutiny and devoting very great diligence and attention to it.

Therefore I could not neglect to examine the matter at once. From the time when I received the memorandum of your veneration [Note: This memorandum from Leo to Proterius concerning Easter in 455 is missing.], I had taken the greatest care over this question, now consulting the legal books [Note: By “legal books” he seems to mean the books of the law of Moses, in which the first Passover was commanded and assigned to the first month, which is also called the Month of the New Things.], now examining the institutions of ancient learned men [Note: The Cotton manuscript reads “the stated institutions”; the Oxford manuscript more correctly reads “the learned institutions.” He seems to mean the older Paschal cycles and records prior to the hundred-year calendar of Theophilus, or the course of reckoning concerning which he soon testifies: “which entirely agrees with the pages of the ancients.”], from which it is possible to investigate such a computation with greater skill.

I also took up the hundred-year Paschal cycle drawn up by our most blessed father and bishop Theophilus [Note: Janus reads “our fellow bishop Theophilus,” and adds “and, running through the whole.”], and, having reviewed it completely, I found it so carefully and perfectly constructed that no one, whoever he may be, can in any way challenge or disparage the authority of this document [Note: The words “and disparage” are omitted in the Oxford manuscripts.]. For it would have been unreasonable to suppose that a man so watchful and so dear to God, enriched also with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, could have gone wrong in so great and necessary a matter by neglecting painstaking care.

But perhaps, as your holiness writes [Note: The Cotton and Digby manuscripts read “wrote.”], it is an error of a faulty manuscript or a copyist [Note: The printed editions read “or of a writer-copyist.” Quesnell noted that all these words are absent from the Oxford manuscript. On the authority of Janus’s three manuscripts, we have deleted only the superfluous word “writer.”], and for that reason we ought to transfer the day of that holy festival [Note: The Cotton and Digby manuscripts read “we must.” In the calendar of Theophilus and in the Alexandrian computation, Easter in 455 was set for 24 April; according to Leo’s view, who believed an error had entered that calendar, Easter had to be transferred to 17 April, as it seemed to the Latins.]—which God forbid [Note: The printed editions, from the Sirmond papers, read “which has passed away.” Quesnell corrected the text from the Oxford manuscript and Janus from his three manuscripts.]—but rather let it be celebrated as the hundred-year cycle of that same most blessed father and our bishop Theophilus prescribes [Note: The reading should be “let it be celebrated,” from Janus and the Cotton manuscript, rather than “is celebrated,” found in the other printed editions. Janus’s edition reads “our fellow bishop.”], a cycle that entirely agrees with the pages of the ancients: namely, on the twenty-ninth day of the month Pharmuthi according to the Egyptians, which is 24 April. We, and the whole Egyptian region, and all the East likewise, shall celebrate that day in this way, with God’s help [Note: The Digby manuscript reads, “Thus we shall celebrate the authority of that very day.”].

## CHAPTER II

[Col. 1086A]

But so that we may not be thought [Note: “We may be thought” (*arbitremur*) is used passively here in the sense of “we may be considered,” as also by Caelius in Priscian, book VIII, and by Ulpian, *Digest* II.7.12.] simply to write or wish to establish whatever seems good to us, we have also inserted into this letter the reasons by which your holiness may perhaps judge that you ought not to criticize the truth of the Church of the Egyptians, which was the mother of this kind of labor [Note: The particle “also” is supplied from Janus’s edition and the manuscripts. Shortly afterward, “perhaps” is absent from the Oxford manuscript, which reads “to despise” instead of “to criticize.”], and recorded it carefully.

Long ago the Lord indicated the time of Passover through Moses, saying: “Observe the month of new things” (Deut. 16:1), declaring this to be the first month, as he says again: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year” (Exod. 12:2); and: “You shall make the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month” (Lev. 23:5; Num. 28:16).

But the Lord who spoke these things through Moses, being the fullness of the law, when he deigned to become human, on the fifth day of the week [Note: So the Oxford manuscript and Janus’s three manuscripts, instead of “Thursday,” as the printed editions had it.] ate the Passover with his disciples in the upper room, on the fourteenth day of the first month. Shortly afterward he was betrayed by Judas and crucified on the following day, the fifteenth day of the moon, that is, on the sixth day of the week [Note: The words “on the following day” are absent from the Oxford manuscript.]. Descending to the underworld and completing the dispensations of our salvation, he rose from the dead as the Sabbath evening dawned into the Lord’s Day [Note: Labbe wrongly reads “the Lord” instead of “the Lord’s Day.” The reference is to the Gospel: “On the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the week was dawning,” that is, Sunday, on which Christ rose.]. On that day, it is clear, the moon was the seventeenth of the first month according to the Hebrews.

We Christians therefore seek at Easter not only the fourteenth day of the moon—for the Jews do this without the festival—but also the day of the Resurrection of our Redeemer, which is the seventeenth day of the moon of the aforesaid first month of new things, and we observe it with greater care.

If the full moon always occurred on the fifth day of the week, when the Savior ate the Passover with his disciples, every ambiguity would be removed. But because the lunar cycle is unequal to the course of the sun, and the fourteenth day of the Paschal moon often falls on Sunday, it is not possible to celebrate the feast then, nor is it possible to release the fast on the preceding day, Saturday, when the moon is thirteen; the fast must be deferred to the following week [Note: Proterius gives two reasons why, when the fourteenth day of the moon falls on Sunday, Easter cannot be celebrated on that Sunday, but must be deferred to the following Sunday: first, that the Paschal feast cannot then be celebrated; second, that the fast cannot be ended on the preceding Saturday, when the moon is thirteen. Proterius again presses these same reasons in chapter 5 for the same purpose in a similar controversy. Ambrose had already advanced them in a letter to the bishops established throughout Emilia, and Theophilus of Alexandria in his Paschal Preface concerning Easter of 387. From their testimonies it follows that the entire force of these reasons concerns the fast: the Paschal feast cannot be celebrated on Sunday when the moon is fourteen because one may neither fast on that Sunday, when the moon is fourteen, nor release or terminate the pre-Paschal fast on the thirteenth day of the moon. If the Paschal feast were celebrated on the fourteenth day when it fell on Sunday, the fast would have to be observed on that same day and released only in the evening, as the law prescribed; thus one would have to fast on Sunday, which must absolutely not be done, lest we agree with the Manichaeans, who fast on Sunday. If, to avoid this resemblance to the Manichaeans, we do not fast on that Sunday, when the moon is fourteen and we think Easter should be celebrated, we would be forced to release or terminate the pre-Paschal fast on the preceding Saturday, when the moon is thirteen. Yet according to the command of the ancient law, it cannot be released or terminated before the fourteenth moon, on which the Paschal lamb was to be eaten. See chapter 5 of this letter. Thus, to avoid both alternatives, the Paschal feast must be postponed to the following Sunday.].

This is especially so because within that week we have the fifteenth day of the moon, when, as the Apostle wrote, “Christ our Passover was sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). For on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, according to the Hebrews, as stated above, Jesus ate the typological Passover; but on the following day, Friday, the fifteenth day of the moon, he was fastened to the cross for us like a sheep led to slaughter [Note: We have added the particle “but” and thereby made the sense clearer, with the help of the Cotton and Digby manuscripts.], and as the Sabbath evening dawned into the Lord’s Day [Note: The word “Lord’s Day” is absent from the Oxford manuscript. See note 20 above.], on the seventeenth day of the moon he rose from the dead.

## CHAPTER III

Since, therefore, in the coming Paschal solemnity, during the eighth indiction, the fourteenth day of the moon falls on Sunday, the twenty-second day of the month Pharmuthi of the month of new things, which is 17 April [Note: Before Janus, the printed editions insert the word “Sunday,” which is absent from the Cotton and Digby manuscripts and is superfluous.], it is appropriate to defer it to the following week.

For within that week we have the three-day mystery: the fifteenth day of the moon, when Christ was crucified, joined to the fourteenth, as well as the sixteenth and the following seventeenth. On the twenty-eighth day of the month Pharmuthi, which is 23 April, we shall release the fast in the evening of the Sabbath; then, as the Sunday dawns, on the twenty-ninth day of that month Pharmuthi, which is 24 April, we shall celebrate the festival with complete sincerity [Note: We have restored this reading from Janus in place of “will have occurred,” as the context also requires. During the eighth indiction in 455, the fourteenth day of the moon fell on 17 April according to the Alexandrian computation, but not according to the Romans, who had the seventeenth day of the moon on that date. This considerable difference between Alexandrians and Romans arose from their different cycles and their differently arranged lunar intercalations. The Alexandrians, following their nineteen-year cycle, inserted a lunar intercalation every nineteenth year, whereas the Romans, following an eighty-four-year cycle, formerly inserted it every twelfth year and later every fourteenth year. In time this caused the age of the moon in 455 to differ by three days: for the Romans, 17 April was the seventeenth day of the moon, while for the Alexandrians it was the fourteenth. Thus that day was suitable for Easter for the Romans; but if it had been the fourteenth day for them, as it was for the Alexandrians, it could not have been a Paschal day according to either the Alexandrian or the Roman rules. It is surprising that Proterius failed to notice this difference in the lunar age among the Romans, which Saint Cyril had sufficiently indicated in his Paschal Preface. Had Proterius observed it as well, he would have seen that his argument, resting solely on the fourteenth day of the moon, was unstable, unless he had declared the Romans mistaken in assigning another lunar age.].

## CHAPTER IV

In ancient times also, whenever the fourteenth day of the moon was found on Sunday, the festival was deferred to the following week, as is proved by the eighty-ninth and ninety-third years from the reign of Diocletian [Note: The Alexandrians used the Diocletian era, which began in 284 of the common era. Thus Diocletian’s year 89 was 373 of the common era, and Diocletian’s year 93 was 377. Saint Ambrose had brought forward these two examples for the same purpose, to establish the date of Easter in 387, which was Diocletian’s year 103. Although he was a Latin and bishop of the Latin Church of Milan, he used not the Roman but the Alexandrian cycle, months, and era, as is clear from his letter to the bishops of Emilia.]. Thus our most blessed fathers are shown to have acted at that time also.

In Diocletian’s eighty-ninth year, while our father of blessed memory and bishop Athanasius was still alive, when the Paschal fourteenth day of the moon had fallen on the twenty-eighth day of the month Phamenoth—that is, 24 March [Note: The printed editions read “Phaminoth” instead of “Phamenoth.” The Oxford manuscript reads “Pharmuthi.”]—which was Sunday [Note: The same manuscript reads: “Easter was transferred to the following Sunday, so that it was celebrated on the day before the Kalends of April”; and shortly afterward, “to the following Sunday” instead of “to the following week.” Quesnell.], Easter was transferred to the following week, so that the Lord’s Pascha was celebrated on the fifth day of the month Pharmuthi, that is, on 31 March.

In Diocletian’s ninety-third year, when the Paschal fourteenth day of the moon had fallen on the fourteenth day of Pharmuthi, which is 9 April, and this too was Sunday, it was likewise deferred to the following week, so that the Lord’s Pascha was solemnly celebrated on the twenty-first day of Pharmuthi, which is 16 April.

In the one hundred and third year of the aforesaid Diocletian, when the Paschal fourteenth day of the moon was going to fall on the twenty-third day of Pharmuthi, which is 18 April, and that day was Sunday, the following week was again sought, and the Lord’s Pascha is known to have been celebrated on the thirtieth day of that month Pharmuthi, which is 25 April, because the pressure of the approaching date was urgent [Note: These words, and in the following chapter “because the urgency was pressing,” indicate that if the fourteenth day of the moon falls as late as 17 or 18 April on Sunday, and Easter cannot be celebrated at that lunar age but must be deferred to the following Sunday, the final Paschal limit of the Latins, fixed at 21 April, cannot be maintained because of such urgency and necessity; Easter must be transferred to 24 or 25 April.].

Likewise, in Diocletian’s one hundred and sixtieth year, when the Paschal fourteenth day of the moon fell on the twenty-third day of Pharmuthi, which is 18 April [Note: The Bodleian and Digby manuscripts read “fell.” The subject is Easter of 444, which occasioned the earlier controversy under Pope Leo.], on Tuesday of the week, we remember that we celebrated it on the twenty-eighth day of that month Pharmuthi, which is 23 April [Note: We have preferred “then” from Janus. Saint Leo also, accepting Paschasinus’s letter, celebrated Easter on the same day, as we learn from Prosper’s complete Chronicle.].

## CHAPTER V

It is therefore necessary also, in Diocletian’s one hundred and seventy-first year, during the future Paschal feast of the eighth indiction, when the fourteenth day of the moon falls on Sunday, the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi, which is 17 April [Note: The printed editions, from Sirmond’s copy and the Cotton manuscript, read “in the two-hundred-and-fifty-fifth year.” The Oxford and Bodleian manuscripts read “in the one-hundred-and-sixty-fifth year,” and the Digby manuscript “in the two-hundred-and-sixty-fifth year.” This variation indicates a manuscript error, which becomes evident from the question of Easter in 455, discussed here. For the year 455 of the common era is Diocletian’s year 171; hence we corrected the text without hesitation, as all learned scholars recognized that it required correction.], to extend it appropriately to the next week according to the preceding pattern, so that we may celebrate the Lord’s Pascha on the twenty-ninth day of Pharmuthi, which is 24 April, because the urgency is again pressing, just as our fathers did when they deferred the fourteenth days of the moon that fell on Sunday.

For if we celebrate Easter on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi, which is 17 April, when, as I have repeatedly said, the fourteenth day of the moon falls on Sunday, we shall be found on the preceding day, that is, on Saturday, the twenty-first day of the same month, which is 16 April, with the thirteenth day of the moon then present, to release the fast improperly. For Easter is not eaten on the thirteenth day of the moon [Note: The number 1270 is the printed page number.].

Since, therefore, the fourteenth day of the moon falls on Sunday, the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi, which is 17 April, and it is not fitting to fast on Sunday, because that is characteristic of the Manichaeans, it follows that we must proceed to the following week. Within it, as we have said, we have both the fifteenth day of the moon, when the Lord was crucified [Note: We have supplied “the Lord” from Janus’s edition and manuscripts.], and the sixteenth and also the seventeenth, when he rose from the dead. Thus, on the twenty-eighth day of Pharmuthi, which is 23 April, we shall release the fast in the evening of the Sabbath according to custom, and on the following Sunday, the twenty-ninth day of that month, which is 24 April, we shall celebrate the Paschal feast.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1090B]

We must also necessarily inform you that in the future, in Diocletian’s one hundred and ninety-eighth year [Note: The printed editions, following Sirmond, read “the two-hundred-and-sixty-fifth year.” The Oxford and Bodleian manuscripts read “the two-hundred-and-sixty-seventh year.” Another manuscript of Saint Augendus, cited by Bucherius in his corrections, reads “the two-hundred-and-fifty-eighth year.” We corrected the text on the same grounds indicated in note 35 above, since the author is speaking of Easter in 482, which corresponds to Diocletian’s year 198. Janus perhaps omitted the particle “and” before “in the future” from his manuscripts.], when the fourteenth day of the moon again falls on the twenty-third day of Pharmuthi, which is 18 April, the Lord’s Pascha will, with God’s help, be celebrated on the thirtieth day of that month, which is 25 April [Note: The printed editions and manuscripts read “on the twenty-eighth day of Pharmuthi,” incorrectly; for that day corresponds to 23 April, as Proterius himself attests in the preceding chapter. The correction is therefore entirely secure, though some have more cautiously judged it a marginal correction.].

## CHAPTER VII

But some, perhaps ignorant of the subtlety of the Paschal computation [Note: From this and what follows concerning the Jews, it seems that the Jewish computation favored the Romans, although the author declares that the Romans were equally mistaken.], and led astray by Jewish fables, will judge that we withdraw into the second month if we extend the festival so far [Note: The same objection was made against the Alexandrians by the Romans in 387, when the Alexandrians likewise placed Easter a full week after the Latins, as is clear from Ambrose’s letter to the bishops of Emilia and from Theophilus’s Paschal Preface. Cyril also mentions the same objection in his Preface. Proterius indicates in the following chapter in what sense the Latins claimed that the Alexandrians celebrated Easter in the second month; see note 47 below.].

I truly do not know where they get this assertion [Note: Perhaps “they assert” (*asserant*) should be read, or something is missing. Shortly afterward, the words “of the month Pharmuthi” are wrongly absent from the Oxford manuscript.]. For when the fourteenth day of the moon of that month falls on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi, which is 17 April, how shall we endure the complaint that we celebrate Easter in the second month? [Note: This follows Janus’s edition; other copies read “because.” In what follows he turns the objection back against the Latins, as though they themselves celebrated Easter not in the second but in the twelfth month, whenever they celebrated Easter in the month that was embolismic for the Alexandrians; this will be explained in the following note.]

For the Jews, not knowing the Lord, are ignorant also of the time of Passover. Consequently, they often depart from the first month and are thought by some to celebrate Easter in the twelfth month [Note: We have deleted the pronoun “themselves,” found in most manuscripts and all printed editions except Petavius, on the authority of the Cotton manuscript and because the sense requires it. The verb “are thought” is not active here but passive, as above in chapter 2. See note 16. For the Jews never thought that they were celebrating Easter in the twelfth month; rather, they were believed by others to celebrate it in that way to some degree. This happened when the Jews made their year a common year, which was embolismic for the Alexandrians. At that time the Jews celebrated Easter in what was, for them, the first month, but for the Alexandrians—who more correctly admitted the intercalary month—it was the last month. In the Alexandrians’ view, therefore, they departed from the first month established by the law. The embolismic month, although it preceded the first month and had been added at the end of the preceding year’s twelve months, was in reality a thirteenth month. Nevertheless, the Jews counted it as the twelfth month and called it in Hebrew by the same name as the twelfth month, so that it was regarded to some extent as another twelfth month.].

But our most blessed fathers, more accurately establishing the nineteen-year cycle [Note: The words “more accurately establishing” imply that the Christian fathers arranged the nineteen-year cycle better than the Jews. They therefore seem to attribute to the Jews the same cycle, in which they had marked the intercalations and Paschal fourteenth days differently and less carefully, being led by ignorant calculations and deceived by the feigned and false wisdom of outsiders—that is, of the pagan Greeks, who also used a nineteen-year cycle. Shortly afterward, the words “it is impossible to violate” are absent from the Oxford manuscript. Later, Janus omits the word “same.”], which it is impossible to violate as a threshold, foundation, and rule, established this same nineteen-year computation—not according to the Jews’ present ignorant and foolish practices [Note: Bucherius suggests that “calculations” may be missing. Later, the Bodleian manuscript reads “but by the grace of the Holy Spirit.”], nor according to the supposed and fabricated wisdom of outsiders, but instructed according to the grace of the Holy Spirit. In the revolution of the often-mentioned nineteen-year cycle, they marked the Paschal fourteenth days of the moon with greater care [Note: He indicates that only the fourteenth day of the Paschal moon was marked in the Alexandrian nineteen-year cycle for each year. Although the Sundays of Easter could easily be derived from the Paschal moon, they were not designated in that cycle, because during the nineteen-year revolution the Paschal Sundays did not return to the beginning of the cycle as the fourteenth days of the moon did. This did occur in the Roman eighty-four-year cycle, which was therefore a cycle of Paschal Sundays, whereas the Alexandrian cycle was a cycle of Paschal fourteenth moons.].

## CHAPTER VIII

Having established these points, we must also attend to the fact that those who entirely determine the beginning of the first month’s lunar course from the twenty-fifth day of the month Phamenoth, which is 21 March, are greatly mistaken [Note: Proterius here attempts to answer the objection proposed in the preceding chapter: the Romans argued that the Alexandrians, according to their cycle, postponed Easter in 455 into the second month because they celebrated the feast after 21 April, which was the Romans’ final limit for Paschal Sundays—as though the final limit of Paschal Sundays were the last day of the first month. He infers that on this reasoning they began the first month on 21 March, that is, on the date of the vernal equinox. He proves this erroneous because the beginning of the first month, which is lunar and must be calculated according to the course of the moon, cannot be taken from a fixed day of the vernal equinox. The moon completes both its annual and monthly course more quickly than the sun, and therefore the beginning of the first month cannot be attached to a fixed day of the solar year; it must vary from year to year within the nineteen-year cycle. Since, according to the Alexandrian computation, the fourteenth day of the first month in this year fell on 17 April, it followed that the Paschal new moon, and therefore the beginning of the first month, fell on 31 March. Hence 24 April, the day to which they assigned Easter, was the twenty-first day of the moon, or the twenty-first day of the first month; thus they could not be accused of transferring the festival into the second month.

Proterius nowhere proves that the fourteenth day of the moon fell on 17 April, as we noted above in note 27, but simply assumes it as certain from the nineteen-year cycle. It should further be noted that Victor of Aquitaine, in his Paschal Preface, establishes the beginning of the first month differently according to the Latin view. “The Latins,” he says, “have been accustomed to observe especially the period from 5 March to 5 April, namely twenty-nine days, so that whichever of those days the moon is born constitutes the beginning of the first month.” Therefore they did not take the beginning of the first month from the vernal equinox, as Proterius attributes to them; rather, Proterius inferred this, along with the Alexandrians, from the Latins’ objections and reasoning. Indeed, it cannot be understood how the Alexandrians, by rejecting Easter of 455 from 17 April, as the Romans wanted, and transferring it to 24 April—that is, from 17 April to 24 April—would have passed into the second month according to the Roman view, if in Leo’s time they had begun the first month, as Victor later explained, from the Paschal new moon. For since that new moon had fallen on 1 April among the Romans, 24 April, the date to which the Alexandrians postponed Easter, did exceed the Romans’ limit for Paschal Sundays; but since it was Monday and the twenty-fourth day of the moon among the Latins, it did not pass beyond the limits of the first month, so that it did not enter the second month, which would begin with the following new moon.

Therefore, at this time the Romans seem to have begun the second month not from the new moon of the Paschal moon but after the final limit of Paschal Sundays. It may consequently be considered that Proterius did not reason badly when he argued that they began the first month from the vernal equinox. In the fuller manuscript of Prosper’s Chronicle cited by Bucherius on p. 89, the following words are found under the year 455, although they are absent from Labbe’s edition: “In this”—namely, in celebrating Easter with the Latins on 17 April—“there would have been no error either in the calculation of the full moon or in the limit of the first month”; here the author seems to take “the limit of the first month” as the limit of Paschal Sundays.]

For according to the course of the sun, it is indeed recognized that the equinox occurs on the twenty-fifth day of Phamenoth, which is 21 March; but the beginning of the first month must not therefore be fixed absolutely from that equinox according to the course of the moon. Otherwise, the moon’s course ought in every respect to correspond with the sun’s cycle.

But since it is certain to all who possess understanding that the moon’s exceedingly swift motion does not at all keep pace with the sun’s course, let us now, briefly and with God’s help, instruct those who are uncertain that we cannot in any way pass into the second month.

If the beginning of the month were established at the equinox—that is, on the twenty-fifth day of Phamenoth, which is 21 March—according to the lunar course, it would be reasonable to suppose that some might claim that we could pass into the second month. But since, in the coming eighth indiction, the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month is found on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi, which is 17 April, it is certain that the beginning of that first month, according to the lunar course, occurs on the ninth day of Pharmuthi, which is 31 March.

Since, therefore, the fourteenth day of the moon is found on the twenty-second day of Pharmuthi, which is 17 April, and we celebrate the Lord’s Pascha on the twenty-ninth day of that month Pharmuthi, which is 24 April, we do not at all pass into the second month, since we then certainly have the twenty-first day of the moon [Note: Janus’s edition reads “indubitably.”].

How, then, shall we pass into the second month, when the beginning of the first month according to the lunar course is, as stated shortly before, on the ninth day of Pharmuthi, which is 31 March, and the fourteenth day of the moon occurs on the twenty-second day of that month, namely 17 April [Note: Janus’s edition omits “day.”]? Once this has been demonstrated, it is certain that we do not in any way pass into the second month when we celebrate the Lord’s Pascha on the twenty-ninth day of Pharmuthi, which is 24 April.

## CHAPTER IX

Let those who in those regions are uncertain know through your holiness that we shall celebrate Easter legitimately during the eighth indiction [Note: We have corrected this from the Digby manuscript. Other copies read “we celebrate.” Shortly afterward, the same manuscript reads “I have written” instead of “I wrote.”].

For this reason I wrote, following in this matter the ecclesiastical formulas of the Fathers and drawing from them the grounds for this question. For so also our predecessors [Note: Janus, with the Bodleian and Digby manuscripts, reads “predecessors,” with which the Oxford manuscript agrees. Other printed editions read “forerunners.” The Bodleian manuscript reads “my” instead of “our.”], whenever doubt arose, hastened to announce the date beforehand, so that the sacred festival might everywhere be celebrated in harmony [Note: Janus reads “holy.”].

Even now, according to the ancient custom, we believe that the following should be proclaimed in the churches in the Lord: that one faith, one baptism, and one most sacred Paschal solemnity should be celebrated everywhere by all Christians in Christ Jesus our Lord, because “in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28) [Note: Janus reads this from his manuscripts, as we believe; the other older printed editions agree with him, merely omitting the conjunction “and” before “one solemnity.” In Quesnell’s text: “We ought to proclaim in the Lord in the churches that, just as there is one faith and one baptism, so one most sacred Paschal solemnity ought to be celebrated by all Christians everywhere.” The words “ought to be celebrated” do not fit well with the verb “we ought to proclaim.”].

We judged that transferring this letter into the eloquence of the Latin language was not entirely safe, lest those among us who prefer Greek, and who are no longer able to express these matters accurately, should harm the truth through inelegant and unsuitable diction, and lest it should perhaps not be translated with the ardor and skill that the matter required. Greet the brotherhood that is with you. The brotherhood that is with us greets you in the Lord. And, in another hand: “I beg you, most beloved and most desired brother, to remain well and to remember us.”

> **Note:** The final word, which Quesnell and Janus add from their manuscripts, was omitted by Petavius, Bucherius, and Labbeus.

# LETTER CXXXIV

> **Note:** Otherwise Letter 105. The letter formerly numbered 134 is now 165. Written 15 April 454.

## TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN

> **Note:** It survives in the manuscripts of the Hispanic collection, Isidorian collection, 11, 12, 18, and 21 through 24, as well as in Sichard’s copy.

### Summary

1. After praising Marcian, he promises Anatolius his favor if he repents.
2. He asks that Eutyches, who is spreading his poison in exile, be transferred to more remote and secluded places.
3. He gives thanks for the inquiry concerning the date of Easter and asks that Marcian favor the Catholics.

**Leo, bishop, to the emperor Marcian.**

## Chapter I

> **Column 1094B**

What repeated experience has already taught us very often is that your holy devotion toward the Christian religion perseveres and increases through glorious growth. This confidence in your clemency consoles and strengthens not only me but all the priests of the Lord, since we experience in a most Christian ruler a priestly disposition.

> **Note:** Manuscripts of collection 21: “expresses affection.”

If the priests of the Eastern regions strive to imitate this, neither peace nor the Christian faith will suffer any scandal.

> **Note:** Thus all the printed editions, with manuscripts of collections 12, 18, and 24, and the Vindobonensis Hispanicus manuscript. In the latter, “no scandal” is erroneously read. This error was corrected arbitrarily in Vatican Hispanicus, Isidorianus, and manuscripts derived from them, which read “no scandal.” Therefore, since the bishop of Constantinople is shown by the example of your present clemency to be advancing toward every form of devotion, if he faithfully submits to your exhortations, he possesses in me a disposition of sincere favor—provided only that he fulfills what he promises in words.

> **Note:** Vindobonensis Hispanicus and Vatican collection 24 read *antistes* (“bishop”). Shortly afterward, most later manuscripts read *provectum praesentis* in place of *profectum praesenti*.

> **Note:** With Merlinus, Sichardus, and Quesnellus, Vatican collection 24 reads *habet* (“he has”); Vindobonensis Hispanicus reads *desideretur* (“may he be desired”). Vatican Hispanicus, Isidorianus, and the others supplied *habebit* (“he will have”), which is also found in the editions before Quesnellus.

> **Note:** We preferred this reading of Janus, supported by his manuscripts and by Petavius’s edition, to the reading of Bucherius and Quesnellus, *apud vos* (“among you”). The matter concerns those who were “Greekizing” before Proterius; since he feared that he could not accurately express them in Latin speech, he did not wish to render this letter into Latin. Later, Labbeus and Quesnellus place in parentheses, “for we are no longer able to express these matters carefully”; other printed editions have “for they are no longer able,” and so forth—readings that disturb the sense. We preferred to follow Janus.

But if he deliberately chooses what displeases God and your piety, then, with due regard for your gentleness, I shall employ, with and for everyone—and with your own support—a freer firmness against his arrogance. For, as I have often said, most glorious emperor, I would rather embrace him in brotherly love because of holy actions.

> **Note:** Quesnellus reported that his manuscripts read *liberiore conscientia* (“with freer conscience”), because—“as must often be said”—what sprouts badly ought to be cut away by brotherly charity, most glorious emperor. Our Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, with collections 11 and 21, likewise have this reading. We nevertheless preferred the reading of the editions from Merlinus, found in Vindobonensis Hispanicus, Vatican collection 24, and Sichardus. We restored *mallem* (“I would rather”) for *malim* (“I prefer”), which was read only in Quesnellus. Leo’s words, “as must often be said,” appear to refer to what he had written concerning Anatolius in earlier letters to Marcian, Letter 78, and similarly in chapter 5 of this letter: “Whom I prefer to love while acting without reproach rather than to endure him persisting in this presumption . . . .”

> **Note:** On the authority of several of our manuscripts, we deleted *corde* (“in heart”), which printed editions, following Merlinus together with Sichardus and the manuscripts of collection 24, place before *perficiat* (“fulfill”).

## Chapter II

Since you willingly receive my suggestions concerning the tranquillity of the Catholic faith, learn from the statement of my brother and fellow bishop Julian that Eutyches is indeed suffering exile for his own merits,

> **Note:** Vatican Hispanicus, Isidorianus, and collections 11 and 21 read: “Learn from the statement of Julian, the brother whom you received most devoutly, that this has been reported to me.” We retained the reading introduced by Quesnellus, since it is confirmed by Vindobonensis Hispanicus, Vatican collection 24, and the copies of Merlinus and Sichardus. Only *esse* (“to be”) is absent in our manuscripts and in Sichardus; editions before Quesnellus print both readings together. but that even in the very place of his condemnation he is pouring out, with increasing desperation, many poisonous blasphemies against Catholic integrity, and is vomiting forth with still greater shamelessness what the whole world shuddered at and condemned in him, so that he may deceive the innocent.

> **Note:** Thus Vindobonensis Hispanicus and Vatican collection 11, together with the printed editions of the Councils. Elsewhere: “was horrified.”

I therefore consider it entirely reasonable that your clemency order him to be transferred to more distant and secluded places.

> **Note:** Merlinus, Sichardus, and Quesnellus, together with Vindobonensis Hispanicus and Vatican collection 24, read “to more distant places.” Earlier editions read “to more remote places.” Quesnellus notes that most of his manuscripts have “to safer places,” which we found in Vatican Hispanicus and in the manuscripts of collections 11 and 21; Vatican Isidorianus alone has “to safer places for him.” Quesnellus added the preposition *de*, which we deleted on the authority not only of earlier editions but also of several of our manuscripts. Two manuscripts add: “This will be salutary, I think, if …”

As for his monastery established at Constantinople, where the monks dwelling there must be strengthened more frequently and more fully by evangelical and apostolic teaching, I believe it would be beneficial if the man said to be in charge of that monastery did not withdraw from the company of your worshiper, Bishop Julian, whom I appointed to be there as a watchman on behalf of the faith. Through his constant visitation, the progress of the servants of God dwelling there could be increased.

## Chapter III

I rejoice that my request concerning the celebration of Easter was received by your piety in such a way that you immediately sent the *agent in rebus* to Alexandria to investigate the error

> **Note:** The editions from Merlinus and our Vindobonensis Hispanicus and Vatican collection 24 manuscripts, with Sichardus, read: “But I have learned that my request concerning the feast of the Paschal joy was thus received by your piety.” Vatican Hispanicus and Isidorianus, with manuscripts derived from them, read the same, beginning *Petitionem autem* (“But my request”). that the constitution of Theophilus of holy memory appears to have introduced.

> **Note:** Earlier printed editions, together with one manuscript of collection 21, add “Nectarius,” which other manuscripts do not contain and which Quesnellus rightly deleted. Nectarius, an *agent in rebus*, had been sent to Rome with letters from Marcian and Anatolius, as will be clear from the title of the following letter. Vindobonensis Hispanicus then has “to send” and “concerning removing the error.” An ancient copyist corrected these errors, as it is read in Vatican Hispanicus, Isidorianus, and other manuscripts of the same origin as the earlier editions: *mitteret* (“he should send”) instead of *mitteretis* (“you should send”), and *de errore removendo* (“concerning removing the error”). Sichardus and the manuscripts of collection 24, which do not derive from the Hispanic Gallican collection, likewise read *removendo*. We nevertheless retained the reading introduced by Quesnellus from the Grimani manuscript, *admonendo* (“concerning warning”), because what follows indicates not a complete correction of the error but a warning concerning the error that seemed to be present in Theophilus’s register. Thus Leo asks that he be informed of whatever the Alexandrians may reply on this matter.

As you are pleased to write, order me to learn whatever may be brought to your piety’s attention concerning this matter, so that the universal Church may know what ought especially to be observed concerning a practice that must not differ.

I also ask what I know to be fitting for your clemency: protect above all from every ambush those whom you know to be pleasing to me and to your gentleness because of their love of the faith, so that the bishop of Constantinople may not have the power to harm them.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius, men of illustrious rank.

# LETTER CXXXV

> **Note:** Otherwise Letter 106. The letter formerly numbered 135 is now 166. Written 29 May 454.

## TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP

> **Note:** It survives in manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 12, 13, 16, 18, and 21 through 24.

**Through Nectarius, an *agent in rebus*.**

> **Note:** In the table of collection 5, chapter 86, this title appears: “To Anatolius, bishop, concerning the reception of Andrew the archdeacon and Euphratas, and concerning the rejection of the pursuit of the honor of the see of Constantinople.”

### Summary

1. He explains the reason for interrupting their exchange of letters.
2. He praises the deposition of Andrew the archdeacon and the restoration of others in the Church of Constantinople.
3. He desires greater sincerity in acknowledging guilt.

**Leo, bishop, to Anatolius, bishop.**

## Chapter I

If your love had maintained the care of our common favor with a firm and unchanging purpose, nothing at all would have arisen to cause you anxiety. Reason did not permit me to despise the affection of one whom, out of love for peace and zeal for restoring the Catholic faith, I had assisted from the very beginning of his episcopate, hoping to have in him such a colleague in ecclesiastical affairs that I would feel I lacked neither the spiritual and abundant teaching of John, nor the authority of Atticus, nor the diligence of Proclus, nor the faith of blessed Flavian among your holy predecessors.

> **Note:** The manuscripts of Vatican collections 11 and 24, and Hincmarus, *Opusculum* 1, chapter 23, Paris edition of 1615, read “predecessors.” See Quesnellus’s notes 1, 2, and 3.

I wished to make such use of your zeal that no one would dare either to resist the Catholic faith or to oppose the venerable rules of the Fathers at Nicaea. But since, as you acknowledge, actions were attempted against the canons that would generate the greatest scandal for all the Churches, what could I have done more appropriately and moderately than first to admonish you, in a brotherly spirit, by sending letters so that you might withdraw from this intention?
