> **Note:** Thus our manuscripts of collections 5, 11, and 24, and Hincmarus’s copy; the printed editions read *tentata sunt* (“were attempted”). See Quesnellus’s note 4 and our observations upon it.

> **Note:** Letter 106.

When you did not reply to them, you yourself separated yourself from sharing my conversation. Finally, from that time I remained silent toward you, but I did not cease, through frequent letters of petition, to suggest to the most merciful ruler, guardian of the faith, what ought to be done for the peace of the Churches—a peace that you recognize to be especially beneficial to you—so that what has now been done by your affection might be accomplished.

I give him immeasurable thanks because, in accordance with the instruction of the Holy Spirit, whose power fills him completely, he deigns to cultivate priestly concord, knowing that the prayers of those who supplicate will benefit him more abundantly if the servants of the one Lord are in no respect divided from the unity of true peace.

> **Note:** Some manuscripts have *dignetur* (“may he deign”).

## Chapter II

You indicate, then, that certain matters in the offices of the clergy of the Church of Constantinople have been corrected: that you have restored the presbyter Aetius to your favor and affection, and that you have removed Andrew from the office of archdeacon. I reply that this has pleased us, because it greatly raises and commends your reputation, as I had wished.

And rightly, after correction, what appeared liable to censure is consigned to oblivion, since you had been burdened by the promotion of heretics and by the injury done to the disciples of Flavian of holy memory. These matters have now simultaneously ceased to cause every offense, together with your praise, as I wished, because what had been disturbed has returned to its proper order.

As for Andrew, who was reasonably deprived of the office of archdeacon, and Euphratas, who, as I have learned, was a wicked accuser of Flavian of holy memory: if, in fully written professions of faith, they condemn the Eutychian heresy no less than the execrable Nestorian dogma, you shall ordain them presbyters, since pardon must be granted to those who have corrected themselves.

> **Note:** We restored the word *haeresim* (“heresy”), omitted by Quesnellus, from earlier editions and our manuscripts.

Thus they may recognize that they have benefited from a remedy for the Catholic faith. First, however, choose and approve one who can fulfill the office of archdeacon—namely, one whom no report has ever stained with the reputation of either of the impieties mentioned above.

As for the others who were involved in equal guilt, if they seek pardon through a similar profession of faith and with satisfaction, let them be restored to their own orders. Let only those be admitted to the chief offices who are shown to have been free from every error.

## Chapter III

But you would have washed away more effectively and sincerely that fault which, as you assert, you incurred through another’s urging in your desire to increase your power, if you had not transferred to the councils of the clergy alone what could not have been attempted without your will.

For just as one sins through evil persuasion, so also one sins through evil consent.

> **Note:** Quesnellus, following the Grimani manuscript, printed *confessione* (“confession”), and marked as erroneous in the margin the reading of the printed editions, *consensione* (“consent”), which we restored from our manuscripts and Hincmarus. Yet the latter reading is better and more accurate: it means that Anatolius consented to the councils of the clergy, about which Leo had said shortly before, “What could not have been attempted without your will.”

But I am grateful, dearest brother, that your affection professes its displeasure at what ought not to have pleased you even then. Your profession of affection, together with the testimony of the Christian ruler, is sufficient for your return to our common favor. Nor does a correction seem delayed when such a venerable advocate has joined it.

Let the pursuit of an unlawful right, which had caused dissension, be entirely rejected. Let the boundaries established by the most provident decrees of the holy Fathers be sufficient, so that the dignity of all priests may remain secure in accordance with its merits and ancient privileges.

Let the affection of the Lord’s charity be renewed and remain in you—the affection to which I have often exhorted you together with our brother and fellow bishop Julian, who has always desired our common favor. Through his diligence and concern your burdens will be relieved, and the Catholic faith will be fortified.

Above all, I exhort and admonish you in brotherly love to preserve those matters that pertain to the glory and protection of the priestly office: the decrees of the canons of Nicaea that maintain the peace of the universal Church. For charity will remain inviolate among the priests of the Lord if what was established by the holy Fathers is preserved with equal zeal.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius, men of illustrious rank.

> **Note:** Quesnellus notes in the margin that the Barb. manuscript of collection 11 has “the fourth day before the Nones of July,” but incorrectly: Vatican 3791 of the same collection, together with the manuscripts of the other collections, reads “the fourth day before the Kalends of June.” The same date is recorded in the following letter, which was written and sent at the same time.

# LETTER CXXXVI

> **Note:** Otherwise Letter 107. The letter formerly numbered 136 is now 168. Written 29 May 454.

> **Note:** This letter was first published by Lucas Holstenius from Barb. manuscript 3336, collection 16. Quesnellus corrected it from the Grimani manuscript, collection 18. We found it in the Ratisbon collection, 19, from which we restored not a few readings.

## TO THE EMPEROR MARCIAN  
### Concerning the correction of Anatolius

### Summary

1. Why he ceased writing to Anatolius.
2. Under what conditions he will be reconciled with him.
3. Concerning Andrew’s removal from the archdeaconate and Julian’s commendation.
4. That the monk Carosus be restrained.

**Leo, bishop, to the emperor Marcian.**

## Chapter I

The manifold favor expressed in your letters has been received by me with the reverence due to it, and I have joyfully recognized how piously, as is your custom, you care for the Christian religion, since you wish to establish among the priests of the Lord a concord suited both to the universal Church and to divine worship.

That peace is truly worthy of approval, and that charity is genuine, which the blessed Apostle proclaims most fully when he says: “Charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).

Accordingly, obedient and gladly assenting to the holy exhortations of your piety, I have replied, as I ought, to the writings of my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius with a corresponding response. He ought to have attributed the interruption of my conversation to his own silence, since he neglected to reply further to my letters, in which I had admonished him with brotherly charity to withdraw from reprehensible ambition.

> **Note:** The manuscripts of Barb. and Ratisbon, together with Holstenius, read *potuit* (“he could have attributed”).

I, however, though I remained silent toward him, did not cease, out of my concern, to suggest to your clemency what might benefit the peace of the universal Church. For your gentleness received my suggestion so willingly that you always deigned to reply and acted in such a way that the matters now corrected must be credited to your glory: you sent letters in which he asserted that the notable fault of ambition should be attributed to others rather than to himself.

> **Note:** From the Barb. manuscript and Holstenius, *tam* (“so”) is added, as the following *ut* (“that”) seems to require; likewise, *semper* (“always”) was added from the same sources.

> **Note:** Thus Holstenius and the Ratisbon manuscript. Quesnellus has *qui tales* (“who sent such men”), incorrectly; the context refers not to the emperor but to Anatolius’s letter 132.

## Chapter II

Let the aforesaid bishop, therefore, venerable emperor, acknowledge how much more one grows through humility than through exaltation. Mindful of the limits established by the Fathers, let him observe henceforth, as he ought, the salutary canons established for the peace of the universal Church.

Let him also watch unceasingly over the defense of the Catholic faith and maintain diligent vigils for the protection of the Lord’s flock. Let him employ in all things the most devoted assistance of your piety, and if anything anywhere lies hidden under the Catholic name as an enemy’s fraud, let him urgently investigate it so that it may be exposed.

> **Note:** With Quesnellus, our Ratisbon manuscript and the Barb. manuscript read *indiget*; Holstenius emended it conjecturally to *indicet* (“let him disclose”).

You expelled sacrilegious error even from the more distant provinces and recalled the darkened hearts of the Palestinians to the light of truth. How, then, will you allow it to breathe beneath the rays of your faith, when, with God assisting you in all things, we all believe that the remnants of every evil doctrine must soon be extinguished throughout Egypt as well?

> **Note:** Holstenius, with the Barb. manuscript, reads *sperare* (“to hope”), and notes in the margin: “Perhaps *spirare*” (“to breathe”). Quesnellus adopted the latter from the Grimani manuscript, supported by our Ratisbon manuscript. Barb. reads *patiamini*, Quesnellus *patimini*, and Ratisbon *patemini*; Holstenius’s *patiemini* (“you will allow”) is better.

For you act kindly toward those from whom you take away the freedom to pursue execrable error.

## Chapter III

I therefore rejoice, glorious emperor, that what had been disturbed has been settled: the memory of blessed Flavian is honored as a consolation to his disciples; Andrew is removed from the ministry of archdeacon; finally, injury to the holy Fathers is avoided and violation of the canons is renounced. Thus may your kingdom, with Christ reigning, be tranquil and, with Christ defending it, strong.

> **Note:** The Ratisbon manuscript deletes *Christo* (“with Christ”).

Since I am pleased to obey your clemency in all things, I receive my brother Anatolius’s affection with my whole heart. Let him show himself loving and faithful, and let him henceforth separate himself by no change from the charity that I promise him, sincerely joining to himself those whom we have approved as defenders of the Catholic faith.

In all things he has the example of your piety to follow, especially since he is assisted by your kindness. I ask that you hear more favorably, as you do, the suggestions of my brother and fellow bishop Julian, whom I commend to your piety.

This will also benefit my brother Anatolius, if you graciously honor the man whom I wished to be there on behalf of the Catholic doctrine.

## Chapter IV

I also ask that, for the welfare of the Church of Constantinople, the monk Carosus—exceedingly ignorant and exceedingly perverse, who, as I have learned, has subverted the hearts of many—no longer employ his poisons, through the favor of your piety.

Otherwise, where the zeal of your holy gentleness has almost entirely extinguished every effort of the heretics, the glory of your faith and the authority of the synod may be violated by a vile and rejected defender of condemned perfidy.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius, men of illustrious rank.

# LETTER CXXXVII

> **Note:** Otherwise Letter 108. The letter formerly numbered 137 is now 169. Written 29 May 454.

> **Note:** Quesnellus published this letter from the Grimani manuscript; it has nowhere else been found.

## TO THE SAME MARCIAN

> **Column 1100B**

### Summary

1. He gives thanks for the completed inquiry concerning the date of Easter, and says that he has received Proterius’s letter concerning it.
2. The accounts of the Church’s stewards are to be examined not by judges but by priests.

**Leo to the emperor Marcian.**

## Chapter I

I rejoice that my concern regarding the observance of Easter has been resolved, in accordance with my petition, by the holy zeal of your clemency. You ordered a careful inquiry to be made in the Church of Alexandria as to whether, contrary to the ancient observance, the future celebration of Easter could rightly be held on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, according to the determination of Bishop Theophilus, although in all our annals the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May is recorded as the date of the Lord’s Passion.

But since the Egyptians favor a different calculation, I granted my consent so that no disagreement might arise among the provinces concerning the observance of so venerable a feast: the great sacrament of the Lord’s resurrection should nowhere be celebrated on another day, and among the priests of the Lord nothing should differ in so great a solemnity, but throughout all the Churches prayer should alike be offered to our God for the prosperity or reign of your piety.

I signify that I have received the letters of my brother and fellow bishop Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, in which I replied to your piety concerning my consent: not because clear reasoning had demonstrated this, but because concern for unity—which we guard above all—had persuaded me.

> **Note:** From this it is inferred that Leo consented to the celebration of Easter on the eighth day before the Kalends of May solely for the sake of peace, not because he was altogether convinced by the calculations of the Alexandrians, as we indicated in the note to Letter 88. Prosper seems especially to allude to this in the complete Labbean Chronicle under the year 455: “In that year the Lord’s Easter was celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May through the obstinate determination of the Alexandrian bishop, whom all the Easterners thought they ought to follow, although Saint Pope Leo maintained that it should rather be observed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May. Letters of that same pope to the most merciful ruler Marcian survive, in which the grounds of the truth under discussion are clearly disclosed. From them the Catholic Church can learn that this agreement was tolerated for the sake of unity and peace rather than approved, and that it should not be imitated thereafter, since it brought a destructive offense and ought permanently to lose all authority.” Compare Letter 142, chapter 1. Although in later years the Latins retained their eighty-four-year cycle for some time, after Victor introduced a new correction two years later and extended the lunar leap from the fourteenth year to the sixteenth, in the following century they abandoned it after Dionysius Exiguus presented the Alexandrian cycle to the Latins, together with rules adapted to his ninety-five-year cycle and supported by calculations and proofs.

## Chapter II

I also thought it reasonable to append this to the letter: concerning what I requested from your piety in earlier letters, I beg you not to permit the stewards of the Church of Constantinople—especially in the time of your piety—to be heard by public judges in a new and unprecedented manner. Remove this injury also from the sacred orders, and order the Church’s accounts to be investigated according to established custom by priestly examination.

> **Note:** This seems to refer to the case of Aetius, whom Leo says he learned from Julian had been completely cleared after an inquiry, in Letter 127, chapter 3. Perhaps this archdeacon of the Church of Constantinople had been accused of misconduct in administering property and had been summoned before public or secular judges so that the matter might be examined carefully. Since this entirely novel procedure displeased the holy Pontiff, he sent the letter to Marcian mentioned—and now lost—here, probably around the time when he learned of Aetius’s judgment, namely shortly after Letter 127 was written.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Aetius and Studius, men of illustrious rank.

# LETTER CXXXVIII

> **Note:** Otherwise Letter 109. The letter formerly numbered 138 is now 170. Written 28 July 454.

> **Note:** Quesnellus established this letter from the Grimani manuscript. We found it in the manuscripts of collection 12, to which the Venetian manuscript 169 belongs, and compared it with that manuscript.

## TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL AND SPAIN  
### Concerning Easter

### Summary

He sends this calendar of the date of Easter to the Gallican bishops, to be transmitted through them to the Churches of Spain; the state of the controversy is also explained.

**To all our most beloved brothers, the Catholic bishops established throughout Gaul and Spain: Leo, bishop of Rome.**

Since priestly observance ought to be harmonious in carrying out all the rules of the divine commandments, we must take particular care lest, through ignorance or presumption, the sin of disagreement be incurred concerning the day of the Easter feast.

> **Note:** The Venetian manuscript reads, “and this must principally be provided for by us.”

Therefore, since the time of the most sacred solemnity has its boundaries so arranged that the saving sacrament must be celebrated sometimes earlier and sometimes later, the concern of the Apostolic See does not cease to take precautions lest ecclesiastical devotion be disturbed by any uncertainty.

But when, in certain records of the Fathers, the coming Easter of the Lord was found marked by some for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May and by others for the eighth day before those same Kalends, this disagreement moved me so greatly that I disclosed my concern about the matter to the most merciful emperor Marcian. I asked that, at his command, the calculation be examined there more carefully by those skilled in this reckoning, and that it be determined on which day the venerable solemnity could more correctly be celebrated.

> **Note:** “The records of the Fathers” refers, on the Latin side, to the eighty-four-year cycle, according to which Easter in the year 455 had been marked for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, and, on the Alexandrian side, to the Register of Theophilus, which had marked the same Easter for the eighth day before the Kalends of May. The Venetian manuscript omits *proxime* (“the coming”).

When he replied, the date was fixed as the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

> **Note:** This alludes to the letter of Marcian to which Saint Leo replied in the preceding letter. From this it is inferred, as also from Prosper’s text quoted in note 2 to the preceding letter, that Marcian informed Leo not merely of the Alexandrians’ agreement but of that of all the Easterners in establishing Easter for the coming year on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

Since, therefore, for the sake of unity and peace I preferred to acquiesce in the Eastern definition rather than disagree concerning the observance of so great a feast, let your brotherhood know that all are to celebrate the Lord’s resurrection on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, and that you are to make this known through yourselves to the other brothers. Thus, just as we are joined by one faith, so may we be made one in the celebration of one solemnity through the fellowship of divine peace.

> **Note:** Quesnellus states that the following material through the end was added from the Grimani manuscript. Nevertheless it also appears in Labbeus’s edition of the Councils, except for the Easter dating placed after the end of the letter. That dating cannot belong to Leo, since, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August in the year 453, when he wrote the letter, he could not have known the consuls of the coming year, especially the Eastern consul. In the year 455 itself, in the two surviving letters, he names no consul other than Valentinian VIII. This dating is nevertheless found in the Venetian manuscript, from which we published it in a more accurate form than in Quesnellus, where it reads: “Easter, in the consulship of Valentinian III and Anthemius, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.”

May God keep you safe, dearest brothers.

Given after the consulship of Opilio, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August.

In the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius: Easter on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

# LETTER CXXXIX

> **Note:** Otherwise Letter 110. The letter formerly numbered 139 is now 171. Written 4 September 454.

> **Note:** It is found in the manuscripts of collections 2, 3, 5, 8, 11, 12, 18, 19, and 21 through 24, in Sichardus’s copy, and in the special Vatican manuscript Regina 293. Since in this last manuscript and in another similar one used by Quesnellus several notable variants occur that do not seem attributable to scribal error or arbitrary alteration, and that bear the character and style of Leo, there is reason to suspect that the letter contained in these manuscripts was its first form, later revised in some places. Thus the fuller letter published from other manuscripts is probably the authentic copy sent to Juvenal, from which its Greek translation derives. We found this Greek translation, now published for the first time, in Vatican Greek manuscript 1455. Some passages are rendered incorrectly and favor an Eutychian sense; this shows how easily a heretical meaning could be introduced into the Greek interpretation by changing certain words or syllables, as Leo complained in Letter 130, chapter 3, when speaking of his letters to Flavian. For this reason he requested an exact translation of them from Julian in Letter 131. We had written this while we were able to use only Vatican Greek manuscript 1455. But after the Roman edition of Father Cacciari brought to our attention two other Greek manuscripts, Vatican 720 and Vatican Ottobonianus 29, we shall correct several passages from them; see what will be said concerning the present matter in notes h and o (column 1106, note 3, and column 1108, note 4).

## TO JUVENAL, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM

> **Column 1101**

### Summary

1. He rejoices that Juvenal has been restored to his see, without concealing his earlier evasion.
2. He instructs him concerning the very places of the mysteries.
3. From the reality of the crucifixion he defends the reality of our flesh in Christ.
4. He instructs those who err concerning the Lord’s incarnation from the pages of both Testaments.

> **Note:** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

**Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem.**

> **Note:** The words “of the city of Rome” were added by Quesnellus from the Barb. manuscript of collection 3 and others. Several of our manuscripts also agree. The Greek version reads: “Leo, archbishop of Rome, to his beloved brother Juvenal.”

## Chapter I

> **Column 1103A**
Having received your letter, which our sons Andrew the presbyter and Peter the deacon brought to me [Note: Codex Vaticanus 1342, collection 3; another codex, collection 8; and another, collection 21: “my sons.”], I was indeed glad that you had been permitted to return to the seat of your episcopate. But when all the circumstances that came to mind—circumstances which caused you to suffer through certain excesses—converged in my recollection, I grieved that you yourself had become the cause of your own adversities and had lost the steadfastness to resist the heretics, since they think that you are no longer free to dare rebuke those whom you have professed to approve in their own error. For what else was the condemnation of Flavian, of blessed memory, and the reception of the most impious Eutyches than a denial of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh? [Note: Three of Quesnellus’s codices and our Codex Reginae 293 read: “What else was it than a denial of the flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ?”] This denial he himself, in his great mercy, caused to be undone, when he overthrew that detestable judgment of the Council of Ephesus through the authority of the holy Council of Chalcedon, so that he might exclude none of those who had fallen into error from the remedy of correction. Therefore, since in this time of indulgence you chose repentance rather than obstinacy, I rejoice that you have sought heavenly medicine, so that at last you may be able to become a defender of the faith attacked by heretics. For although no priest is permitted to be ignorant of what he proclaims [Note: The same two codices of Quesnellus and Codex Reginae read: “what he proclaims.” In editions before Quesnellus, following Vatican codices collections 12, 21, and 24, these words are followed by: “for he who is ignorant will himself be ignored.” These words are absent from our other codices and from five of Quesnellus’s codices, and were taken from 1 Corinthians 14.], nevertheless any Christian living in Jerusalem is more inexcusable than all the ignorant, since, for learning the power of the Gospel, he is instructed not only by the words of the written pages but also by the testimony of the very places [Note: Vatican codex 5845, collection 8, reads “by testimony.” Immediately afterward, Ratisponensis reads “is taught” instead of “is instructed.”]. And what elsewhere may not be believed cannot fail to be seen there. What difficulty remains for the understanding where sight itself is the teacher? And why should what has been read or heard be doubtful where all the mysteries of human salvation present themselves fully both to sight and to touch [Note: We supplied “to touch” from the manuscripts Vindobonensis collection 5, Ratisponensis, and two Vatican codices collection 21, as well as from the ancient Greek version.]? It is as though the Lord were still using a bodily voice with each person who hesitates and saying: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, for I myself am he. Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:38–39).

## Chapter II

Therefore, dearest brother, make use of the unconquerable proofs of the Catholic faith, and defend the preaching of the evangelists by the testimony of the holy places in which you dwell. With you is Bethlehem, where the saving birth of the Davidic Virgin shone forth; wrapped in swaddling clothes amid the narrowness of the lodging, it was received by a manger. With you is the infancy of the Savior, announced by angels, worshiped by the Magi, and sought by Herod through the deaths of many infants [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 1. In Codex Reginae this passage is expressed more briefly: “With you is the conception and birth of the Davidic Virgin. With you is the manifestation,” and so forth. The codices Vindobonensis collection 5 and Vatican collection 24, together with editions before Quesnellus, read “enveloped” instead of “wrapped.”]. With you is the place where his childhood grew, where his youth matured, and where, through bodily development [Note: Vindobonensis collection 5, two Vatican codices collection 21, and Sichardus read “through every stage of growth.” Immediately afterward, Vatican collection 11 reads “of the body” instead of “bodily.”], the nature of a true human being advanced into a perfect man—not without the food of hunger [Note: Vindobonensis collection 5 reads “and hunger.” Immediately afterward, Ratisponensis omits “not without the sleep of rest.” After the word “fear,” Codex Reginae continues as follows: “In many miracles he manifested the power of his might, and in the submission of humility he endured the violence of suffering. The true generation of Christ,” and so forth, as in chapter 3.], not without the sleep of rest, not without the weeping of compassion, nor without the dread of fear. For one and the same person is he who, in the form of God, performed great miracles of power, and, in the form of a servant, endured the violence of suffering [Note: Ratisponensis reads “the sentence” instead of “the violence.”]. The cross itself speaks this to you continually; the stone of the tomb cries it out, in which the Lord lay according to human condition and from which he rose again by divine power. And when you approach the Mount of Olives, to venerate the place of his ascension, does not that angelic voice resound in your hearing, the voice spoken to those who marveled at the Lord’s elevation: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven [Note: The words “into heaven” are absent from Vatican collections 11 and 24, from Ratisponensis, and from Sichardus’s copy.], will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11)?

## Chapter III

The true cross, therefore, confirms the true generation of Christ, because the same one who is born in our flesh is crucified in our flesh. That flesh, since no sin intervened, could not have been mortal unless it belonged to our race [Note: See Quesnellus’s note 2.]. But in order to restore the life of all, he accepted the cause of all and rendered void, by paying on behalf of all, the force of the former bond, which he alone among all did not owe (Colossians 2:14). Thus, just as through the guilt of one all had become sinners, so through the innocence of one all might become innocent (Romans 5:18), righteousness flowing from there into human beings, where human nature had been assumed. For in no way is he outside the truth of our body [Note: Vatican collection 11 reads “outside the truth of the human body.”], concerning which the evangelist, beginning his proclamation, says: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1). The teaching of the blessed apostle Paul agrees with this when he says: “Their fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Romans 9:5). Likewise, to Timothy: “Remember,” he says, “Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David” [Note: The same editions and manuscripts add “according to the flesh,” as do Vindobonensis collection 5, Vatican collections 11 and 21, and Sichardus. In the Apostle the reading is “according to my Gospel.”] (2 Timothy 2:8).

## Chapter IV

You clearly recognize how greatly this truth is declared by the authorities of both the New and the Old Testament [Note: The manuscripts Vatican Reginae, Corbeiensis, Saint-Thierry’s, and one Thuanus read: “It is a lengthy task to explain how it is declared, since the tradition of the Fathers and my writings,” and so forth. The antiquity of Juvenal’s priesthood refers to his episcopate, to which he had been elevated around the year 424.], in a manner appropriate to the antiquity of your priesthood, when the faith of the Fathers and my writings addressed to Flavian of holy memory, which you yourself mentioned, together with the confirmation added by the universal council [Note: Ratisponensis reads “confirmation.” The Greek version has “into the confirmation of the universal council.” Immediately afterward, the same Ratisponensis reads “And therefore to foresee”], are sufficient. Therefore your affection must take care that no one murmur against the ineffable mystery of our redemption and hope [Note: Vindobonensis collection 5 and two Vatican codices collection 21 read: “so that no one may murmur against …”].

But if there are some who are still darkened either by ignorance or who disagree through perversity, let them be instructed by the authorities of those whose apostolic and clear teaching was present in the Church of God [Note: The editions insert “is.” We deleted it with Vindobonensis collection 5, Ratisponensis, and Vatican collections 11 and 24. Immediately afterward, the same Vindobonensis reads “and concerning the incarnation.”], so that they may recognize that, concerning the incarnation of the Word of God, we must believe what those men believed; and let them not, through their own hardness, place themselves outside the body of Christ, in which we died and rose again together. For neither the piety of faith nor the reason of the sacrament permits the Godhead to have been passible in its own essence, or the truth to have been false in the assumption of our nature [Note: Older editions, together with three of Quesnellus’s manuscripts, our Codex Reginae, and all the codices of collections 12, 21, and 24, as well as Sichardus’s copy, add: “I have reverently received a fragment of the Lord’s cross together with the tokens of your affection.” This addition is absent from the superior codices collections 3, 5, 8, and 11, from Grimani and Ratisponensis, and especially from the Greek version. This indicates that, if the sentence was present in Leo’s first copy, of which we spoke in note 1 [Col. 1102, n. j], it was omitted from the copy sent to Juvenal in Palestine. Codex Reginae lacks the addition. See Quesnellus’s note 3.].

Given on the day before the Nones of September, in the consulship of the illustrious men Aetius and Studius.

## Greek Version

To the beloved brother Juvenal, Leo, archbishop of Rome.

Having received the letter of your affection, which our children Andrew the presbyter and Peter the deacon brought [Note: Codex Vaticanus Graecus 1455 reads “we rejoiced.” We corrected this from the other manuscripts, Vaticanus Graecus 720 and Ottobonianus 29, followed by P. Cacciarius.], I rejoiced that you had been permitted to return to the throne of your episcopate. But when all your circumstances flowed together into my recollection—circumstances which caused you to suffer through certain deviations—I grieved that you had become the cause of so many misfortunes to yourself and had lost your steadfastness in resisting the heretics, since they think that you no longer dare to rebuke them openly, those whom you acknowledged to please you in their own error [Note: In our first edition we followed Vaticanus Graecus 1455: “who think that you no longer dare to rebuke them with frankness.” We have now corrected the text from the other cited Greek Vatican manuscripts.].

For what was it to condemn Flavian of holy memory and receive the most impious Eutyches, if not a denial of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh? This denial he himself caused to be undone by his great mercies, when he overthrew that detestable judgment of the synod at Ephesus through the authority of the holy synod at Chalcedon, so that he might exclude none of those who had turned toward what was worse from correction through healing. Therefore, since during the time of pardon you preferred recovery to persistence [Note: Perhaps “rather than persistence.”], I rejoice that you have sought heavenly healing, so that at last you may be able to appear as a defender of the faith attacked by heretics. For although it is especially forbidden to any bishop to be ignorant of what he proclaims, that man has much less excuse than all the ignorant—any Christian whatsoever who happens to live in Jerusalem [Note: This expression appears excessive.], who, in order to know the power of the Gospels, is instructed not only by the sayings written in them but also by the testimony of the places; and what elsewhere is not permitted to be disbelieved cannot there fail to be seen [Note: Supply, “what is not permitted elsewhere.”].

For what work is there for the mind where sight is present as teacher? And why should what comes from reading and hearing be doubtful where all the mysteries of human salvation visibly present themselves to sight and touch? It is as though the Lord were still using a bodily voice with all who hesitate and saying: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts rise into your hearts? Look at my hands and my feet, for I myself am he. Touch me and see that a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.”

Therefore use affectionately the unconquerable teachings of the Catholic Church [Note: Read “make use, dearest brother, of the teachings,” and so forth.], and vindicate the preaching of the evangelists by the testimony of the places in which you dwell. With you is Bethlehem, where the saving birth of the Davidic Virgin appeared; the manger received him, wrapped in swaddling clothes because of the narrowness of the lodging. With you he was manifested by an angel, worshiped by Magi, and, through the death of most infants, the infancy of our Savior was sought by Herod [Note: Codex Vaticanus Graecus 1455 reads: “the infancy of our Savior, sought by Herod through the death of most infants.” This is less satisfactory. The correction which we expressed conjecturally in the notes in our first edition is now inserted into the text on the authority of Vaticanus Graecus 720 and Ottobonianus 29, which Cacciarius consulted.]. With you it has been established where his childhood grew; where his youth matured; and where, through bodily development into a perfect man, the truly human nature advanced [Note: Codex Vaticanus Graecus 1455, which we were initially able to collate, reads: “κατὰ πρόφασιν σώματος εἰς ἄνδρα τέλειον ἡ ἀληθῶς αὐτοῦ φύσις” (“under a pretext of body, into a perfect man, his truly nature”). This is a corrupt reading, on account of which we wrote in the note: “Here a strong suspicion arises that this passage was interpolated by some Eutychian. For what do those words κατὰ πρόφασιν σώματος (‘under a pretext of body’) mean? And likewise those words ἡ ἀληθῶς αὐτοῦ φύσις (‘his truly nature’), which are silent about the truth of humanity while, on the contrary, speaking only of an appearance of body and fiction. This is perhaps a copyist’s error, not that of the first translator. For the other two aforementioned Greek codices supplied the true reading of the translator, which we inserted in the text.”]—not without nourishment from hunger [Note: This particle “from” appears superfluous.], not without the sleep of rest, not without the lamentation associated with compassion, and not without fear associated with anguish. For he is the same and one person who exists in the form of God and performs the great miracles of power, and who, in the form of a servant, endured the severity of sufferings.

The cross itself speaks this to you without ceasing. The stone of the tomb cries it out, in which the Lord lay according to human condition and from which he rose by divine power. And when you ascend the Mount of Olives, intending to worship the place of his ascension, does not that voice of the angels seem to resound in your ears—the voice that says to those who marvel at the Lord’s elevation: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you, will come again in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” [Note: Vaticanus Graecus 1455 reads “because.” On the authority of the other manuscripts we have written “when.”]?

The true cross, therefore, confirms the true birth of Christ, because the same one who is born in our body is crucified in our flesh. That flesh, since sin existed in no respect within it, could not have been mortal unless it belonged to our race. And in order to renew the life of all, he accepted the common condition of all and, by paying on behalf of all, rendered powerless the force of the former bond, which he alone among all had not incurred. Thus, just as through one who became liable all became sinners, so through one who was without liability all might become without liability [Note: Perhaps “from there.”], with righteousness spreading among human beings where the things of human nature had been assumed [Note: In our first edition, following Greek manuscript Vaticanus 1455, we inserted the word “was manifested,” noting that it suggested Eutychianism, and conjectured that “was assumed” should be read. The other two codices lack both words, and we have therefore removed the word from the text.].

For in no way is he outside the truth of our body, concerning which the evangelist, beginning his proclamation, said: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham.” The teaching of the blessed apostle Paul agrees with this when he says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.” Likewise, in writing to Timothy: “Remember,” he says, “Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David.”

You clearly recognize how this truth is marked out by how many authorities of both the Old and New Covenants, in a way appropriate to the antiquity of your episcopate, when the faith of the Fathers and my writings addressed to Flavian of holy memory—which you yourself mentioned—are sufficient, with the confirmation added to them by the universal council [Note: Here the translator appears to have read something different from the present Latin text, namely: “the writings of Leo to Flavian being added into the confirmation of the universal council.” If the present reading is retained, it should be corrected as follows, or similarly: “the confirmation of the ecumenical council having been added.”].

Therefore your disposition must take care that no one mutter against the ineffable mystery of our redemption and hope. But whoever still endures the mist of ignorance, or disagrees through wickedness, should be instructed by the teaching of those who make the apostolic and clear doctrine present in the churches of God, so that they may know that concerning the incarnation of the Word of God we believe what they believed; and through their own hardness they should not make themselves external to the body of Christ, with which we died and rose together. For neither the piety of faith nor the reasoning of the mystery tolerates the Godhead being passible in its own essence, or the truth being false in the nature that was assumed from us.

## Letter 140

[Note: Formerly numbered 111. The letter formerly numbered 140 is now 172. Written 6 December 454.]  
To Julian, Bishop of Cos.

[Note: It has been found thus far only in a single manuscript, from which Quesnellus published it.]

### Synopsis

He says that correction of those in error will henceforth be easier after Dioscorus has been removed, whose death Julian had reported to Leo. He urges him to write concerning the condition of the Alexandrian Church.

### Leo to Julian, Bishop

I reply that I received the letter of your affection through our son Gerontius [Note: We added “our” on the authority of the same codex whose copy P. Cacciarius used.], and that it was most welcome to me, because you did not neglect the opportunity for familiar conversation, which ought to be frequently practiced between us on every occasion, so that in matters pertaining to our care for the condition of the Church we may have nothing unknown and nothing uncertain.

In this state of concern, divine assistance is never lacking. It prevents the pretenses of hypocrites from accomplishing anything and exposes their hidden wickedness through manifest destruction. Although all the machinations of the heretics were broken long ago and the right hand of truth removed all their strength, now, as you have written, with Dioscorus dying, they have fallen into deeper depths; and with the instigator of their perfidy removed, certain unstable and foolish souls have something to fear but nothing to follow [Note: He means the Eutychian monks, who, while displaying zeal against the Nestorians, favored the Eutychian error under the pretext of defending the faith of Nicaea and the Council of Ephesus.].

Therefore, with the mercy of God assisting, we may more readily hope for the correction of those in error, and the preaching of the Gospel will be more effective once the defender of falsehood has been extinguished. The piety of the most Christian prince cooperates in this remedy; his devotion for all the advances of the Catholic faith always maintains holy vigilance.

And so I exhort and admonish your fraternity to make wise use of the favor and kindness of the emperor, and not to delay offering timely suggestions concerning everything you believe will be beneficial. For we have proved by many experiences that the faith of the most glorious Augustus is such that he considers himself to be caring most especially for his kingdom when he has particularly labored for the integrity of the Church.

If you have learned anything concerning the advancement of the Alexandrian people, let us know, so that just as we rejoice over the peace of the Eastern peoples, we may likewise rejoice over the advancement of this people.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of December, in the consulship of the illustrious men Aetius and Studius.

## Letter 141

[Note: Formerly numbered 113. The letter formerly numbered 141 is now 173. Written 11 March 455.]  
[Note: This letter too is found only in the Grimani manuscript.]  
To the same Julian.

### Synopsis

1. Concerning the correction of the monk Carosus and the mission of John the decurion to Egypt.
2. Concerning Maximus, bishop of Antioch, accused of some crime, and what happened; he asks Julian to write back.

### Leo to Julian, Bishop of Cos

#### Chapter I

Through my son Gerontius I received a letter from your fraternity in which, with your customary devotion, you report what you rightly judge to pertain to our care for the cause of the faith: namely, that Carosus has been corrected in his confession of faith, but continues in some unknown hostility against our brother Anatolius, so that even now, because of his disagreement, he withdraws from communion [Note: This Carosus, who is said to have been corrected, must be distinguished from the monk Carosus who, together with Dorotheus, is said to have been driven into exile because of the Eutychian heresy; see the following letter.].

As for John, an eminent man and commendable in the sincerity of his faith, he was sent to Egypt on behalf of the faith. When he returns, let me know how much he has contributed to peace and correction. I do not doubt that you will do this even without my reminder [Note: Concerning this John, sent to Alexandria, see Marcian’s letter to the Alexandrian monks, volume IV of the Councils, Venetian edition, p. 1794. Since that imperial letter lacks a chronological notice, we learn from the date of this letter that it was issued near the end of the preceding year or at the beginning of the present year.].

#### Chapter II

As for the condition of the bishop of Antioch [Note: He means Maximus, who was substituted for Domnus. Concerning his case, which was discussed at the synod, see Quesnellus’s dissertation 1 on the year 455 and our note there.], I am deeply distressed if—God forbid—the charges brought against him by his accusers are true. But beyond the priestly diligence, which I do not doubt will have concern for the common good, I have the greatest confidence in the justice and benevolence of the most glorious prince. I am certain that he will take every possible precaution so that deceit may prevail in no direction. When this case has reached its conclusion, you will kindly inform me when the opportunity arises.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the eighth consulship of Augustus Valentinianus [Note: Since the two following letters were given on the third day before the Ides, and since Leo customarily dated letters sent to one province on the same day together, we believe this letter too was dated on the third day before the Ides of March. We do not doubt that, if either Ratisponensis or another corrected codex had preserved this letter, that date would appear there and the Grimani copy would have to be emended, just as the date of the following letter will be corrected or supplied. Since no codex assists us, we have not wished to alter the date printed from the single Grimani manuscript.].

## Letter 142

[Note: Formerly numbered 112. Written 13 March 455.]  
[Note: Published by Quesnellus from Grimani, collection 18. We reread it against the excellent Ratisponensis, collection 19.]  
To Augustus Marcian.

### Synopsis

1. Having praised the emperor’s faith, he again informs him of his agreement concerning the celebration of the feast day.
2. He gives thanks for removing Carosus and Dorotheus from their monasteries.

### Leo to Augustus Marcian

#### Chapter I

The love of God in your clemency—God whom you serve by ruling and whom you serve through ruling—is shown by the dignity of your most religious speech. It inflames my whole heart with such affection that I shall never cease offering prayers and supplications for the safety of your glory, since by your safety divine providence greatly cares both for the holy Church and for the Roman commonwealth.

Therefore, on the same occasion when I reverently received the letters of your piety, I fulfill the obligations of due greeting and offer inadequate thanks because your piety, with priestly concern, reminded me of the most sacred day of Easter [Note: Ratisponensis reads this way. Quesnellus has “inadequate,” without sufficient support.]. Although I had long ago professed my assent to this rule of observance [Note: Letter 137.], and had announced to all the priests of the Western regions the same day which the instruction of the bishop of Alexandria declared—namely, that in the present year Easter should be celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May—I did so, setting aside every scruple, out of zeal for unity and peace [Note: Quesnellus reads “for the sake of zeal for unity and peace.” We preferred the reading of Ratisponensis, which Prosper also gives in the complete Chronicle. See note 2 [Col. 1100, n. i] on letter 137.].

#### Chapter II

Concerning Carosus and Dorotheus, who, because of heretical perversity, defended condemned errors to the destruction of many, I rejoice that your piety, as my venerable brother Julian, your bishop, has informed me, most beneficially ordered that, after being removed from their monasteries, they should be commanded to live among people whom they could not harm [Note: Ratisponensis reads “whom they might not be able to harm.”]. This, I hope, will be a remedy for many whom you have liberated from perverse teachers, while all the merits of your glory increase in love for the Christian faith [Note: Ratisponensis reads “in love.” Quesnellus has “into love.”], for whose sake the just and merciful God grants that, just as divine things are dear to you, so worldly things are subject to you.

Given on the third day before the Ides of March, in the eighth consulship of Augustus Valentinianus [Note: The Grimani manuscript reads: “Given on the third day before the Ides of August, in the eighth consulship of Valentinianus.” Quesnellus observed in his notes that “the third day before the Ides of August” cannot be correct, since this letter cannot be extended into August; he printed “Given on the third day before the Ides, in the consulship of Augustus Valentinianus,” and, thinking the month had been omitted, suggested in a marginal note that January or February should be added, since he considered the Carosus mentioned here to be the same Carosus reported as corrected in the preceding letter. Codex Ratisponensis removes the whole difficulty: from it we learn the true month and recognize that the Carosus mentioned here is different from the other corrected Carosus.].

## Letter 143

[Note: Formerly numbered 114. Written 13 March 455.]  
[Note: This letter too was published from Grimani; we compared it with our Ratisponensis.]  
To Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople. That the remnants of the heretics, hiding in the city, should not be fostered and grow strong through excessive leniency.

### Leo to Bishop Anatolius

I gladly receive the duties of affection expressed by your love, and I exhort you to make use of them more frequently, since it contributes to the benefit of the whole Church when we recognize what is being done. You undoubtedly understand how watchful your affection must be in this concern, because you recognize that some remnants of wicked men have remained among you [Note: Ratisponensis reads “who have remained.”]. We desire you to devote yourself earnestly to suppressing them—or rather, insofar as the Lord assists, to abolishing them—lest, God forbid, under some negligence of leniency, what has been destroyed too slowly should grow strong again [Note: Quesnellus reads “under another leniency.” Ratisponensis is better.].

Given on the third day before the Ides of March, in the eighth consulship of Augustus Valentinianus.

## Letter 144

[Note: Written on 1 June 457.]  
To Julian, Bishop of Cos.

First published from the Ratisponensis manuscript.

### Synopsis

He praises Julian’s diligence. The efforts of the Eutychians after Marcian’s death. Their disturbances at Alexandria.

### Pope Leo to Bishop Julian

Thanks be to God that in everything pertaining to the condition of the Church and the mystery of the faith your diligence has in no way disappointed me. I understand that you are watchfully taking care lest the snares of the heretics gain any advantage against evangelical and apostolic teaching. For, as you have deigned to report, the things which the Eutychianists attempted to stir up after the death of the emperor Marcian, of venerable memory, have been destroyed through your effectiveness and through the action of those whom the Spirit of God stirred up with you, with truth itself defending its cause [Note: These Eutychian movements, stirred up immediately after Marcian’s death and quickly suppressed through the efforts of Julian and other Catholics, concern Constantinople. The events that had taken place at Alexandria were not yet fully known to Leo, and remedies for them were secured in the following letters. Epiphanius Scholasticus, in the preface to the encyclial codex, volume V of the Councils, p. 34, after recounting Marcian’s death and the election of the new emperor, says: “But those Eutychians who rejected the universal council, believing that they had license to do whatever they wished, suddenly devised paths of disturbance. Some of them came to the royal city of Constantine and demanded that what had been rightly established at Chalcedon be broken by imperial command.” He then adds the account of the Alexandrian disturbances. For what the new Augustus Leo immediately did to suppress those earlier disturbances, see the following letter, chapter 2, note 2 [Col. 1113, n. c].].

For truly, both to your fraternity and to all the faithful of Christ, and especially to the glorious and Catholic Augustus, as we have found, nothing is more fruitful for eternal blessedness than that what was founded by the author of our hope should not be violated by the wickedness of perverse men, but should remain in secure peace for the perpetual tranquillity of the Church. Therefore let what has been piously and beneficially arranged with the Lord’s assistance be fortified by persevering effort.

For certain reports concerning the actions of the Alexandrian people have been brought to us [Note: This refers to Timothy the Cat, an Eutychian who had been a supporter of the earlier seditions and had been deposed by the bishop Proterius. After hearing of Emperor Marcian’s death, he stirred up a new revolt against that bishop. While Proterius was still alive, Timothy was promoted to the Alexandrian see, and on 28 March his seditious followers killed Proterius in the baptistery and committed other dreadful and horrifying acts, which are described at length by Evagrius, Liberatus, and many other ecclesiastical sources.]. We cannot yet report them more fully because we have not learned in their entirety what is said to have happened. But you must labor for the universal Church to ensure that, if the reported events are true, they cannot prejudice the holy Council of Chalcedon, so that what was defined by the instruction of the Holy Spirit for the salvation of the whole world may remain inviolate.

Given on the Kalends of June, in the consulship of Constantius and Rufus.

## Letter 145

[Note: Formerly numbered 115. Written 11 July 457.]  
[Note: It survives in manuscripts of collections 3, 8, 12, 19, and 23, and in a copy of the first edition of Saint Leo’s sermons.]  
To Augustus Leo.

### Synopsis

1. He asks him to assist the disturbed Alexandrian Church.
2. He says that what has been correctly defined in matters of faith must not be debated again, and asks that a Catholic bishop be placed over the Alexandrian Church.

Leo, bishop of Rome, to Leo, ever Augustus.

#### Chapter I

After fulfilling the duties pertaining to congratulating you on your empire, I have also added this letter of necessary supplication, by which I ask your protection for the favor divinely prepared for the Catholic faith [Note: Three codices—Vatican 5845, Vallicellanus, and Vercellensis collection 8—together with a copy of the first edition of the Sermons, read “labor” instead of “favor.”].

For I learned from the report of my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius that such things had been perpetrated in the Alexandrian Church that the whole Christian religion feels itself attacked and violated unless provision is made universally through the devotion of your faith [Note: The first edition reads “hindered.”], and unless Christian freedom is restored to the aforesaid Church, which was formerly distinguished by Catholic leaders [Note: The common text, together with Vatican collection 3, Ratisponensis, and a copy of the first edition, reads “when the attacks of the heretics have ceased”; followed by “the evangelical doctrine.”]. When the attacks of the heretics have ceased, the evangelical doctrine which flourished there before Dioscorus should be restored in unity with the peace of the whole Church.

This undertaking, worthy of your virtues and glory, will have a swift and God-pleasing outcome if you do not permit anything established at the holy Council of Chalcedon concerning the incarnation of the Lord Christ to be disturbed by any reconsideration [Note: Quesnellus reads “if the holy Council of Chalcedon is firmly established,” less suitably. We restored the reading of the earlier common editions, approved by the manuscripts Ratisponensis and Vallicellanus and by a copy of the first edition. Facundus, book 12, chapter 2, reports that the emperor wished to convene a new council. In this passage Saint Leo endeavors to dissuade him from that plan, lest matters established at Chalcedon be treated as uncertain and reconsidered. Immediately afterward, “because also in that council” is found in the Vallicellanus codex and the first edition.]. For in that council, assembled through the Holy Spirit, everything was established by definitions so full and perfect that nothing can either be added to or taken away from the rule which was brought forth by divine inspiration, most glorious emperor [Note: Quesnellus deleted “either.” We restored it from Vatican collection 3, Vallicellanus collection 8, Ratisponensis collection 19, and a copy of the first edition. Immediately afterward, some codices, together with the ancient editions, omit “most glorious emperor.”].

#### Chapter II
This also, we do not doubt, is clearly evident to the knowledge of Your Clemency: since, as we have learned from the report of many before us, the machinations of the heretics that were attempting to rise up against the authority of the aforesaid synod have been permitted by you to venture nothing further. Therefore, what you of your own accord saw must be denied them, it is glorious for you, at my supplication, to grant to the universal Church, and immutably and perpetually to ensure that those things which, according to the Gospel of Christ and the truth of the apostolic preaching, have been strengthened throughout all past ages by one faith and one understanding, may no longer be overthrown by any further action.

Accordingly, as the mercy of God, through the counsel of his Spirit, shall have instructed the mind of Your Piety, first provide for the restoration of peace to the holy Church of Alexandria, and command that a bishop be appointed through Catholic priests such that nothing reprehensible can be found either in his conduct or in his profession of faith; so that, once everything has been duly arranged, the preaching of the truth may everywhere remain the same. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Constantine and Rufus.

# LETTER CXLVI

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 116. Written 11 July 457.]

[Note: We have collated the edition published from the Grimanic manuscript with the Ratisbon manuscript.]

## TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

### SYNOPSIS

I. The violence perpetrated by the heretics at Alexandria is shown to have aimed at the destruction of the Council of Chalcedon, taking advantage of the death of the emperor Marcian.  
II. He writes to the Emperor Leo to preserve the decrees of the council.

LEO TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP.

## CHAPTER I

Your report, which we received, makes sufficiently clear what a pious and commendable concern you recently showed for the grief of all the churches, by informing us what you had learned had been done at Alexandria to the disgrace of the Christian religion, so that the glorious and most clement emperor might be urged, even by my prayers, to provide remedies. His faith, indeed, is so praiseworthy and his devotion so prompt that, as you yourself indicate, he spontaneously granted whatever was consistent with ecclesiastical peace, without anyone’s intercession, repelling all the plots of the heretics, who thought that they had found an opportune moment in which to annul the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon.

## CHAPTER II

But thanks be to God, who, after the departure of Marcian, of holy and venerable memory, provided by the choice of all with such a ruler that both the Roman state and the Christian religion could rejoice in his virtues. Therefore, following the exhortation of Your Affection, I supplicated the glorious emperor, as was my duty, not to allow heretical audacity to claim anything further for itself through the invasion of the Alexandrian Church, but, by placing a salutary end upon its impious attempts, to safeguard both ecclesiastical liberty and peace.

It remains for Your Fraternity also, taking advantage of the presence of the most faithful emperor, to strive more earnestly to entreat him concerning the preservation, without any reconsideration, of the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon, since those things decreed with God’s inspiration do not permit themselves to be corrupted by any alteration. You must inform me by frequent letters of the progress made by this pious concern, so that we may likewise glory in the Lord over the holy endeavors of the most clement emperor. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

# LETTER CXLVII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 117. Written 11 July 457.]

[Note: We have likewise collated this letter, published from the Grimanic manuscript, with the Ratisbon manuscript.]

## TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COOS, AND THE PRESBYTER AETIUS

[Col. 1116A]

### SYNOPSIS

I. Complaining of his silence, he entrusts the care of the Church to him.  
II. He urges that the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon remain unshaken and that a Catholic bishop be chosen for Alexandria.

LEO TO JULIAN, BISHOP, AND TO AETIUS, PRESBYTER. Likewise.

[Note: The Ratisbon manuscript omits “and to Aetius,” as well as “likewise.” Only Julian’s letter, received some time earlier, is indicated at the beginning; Leo replied to it in Letter 144. This cannot apply to Aetius, nor do the words concerning a neglected opportunity to reply seem applicable to him; for Leo’s exchange of letters was not so frequent with Aetius as with Julian, his legate. Hence we have serious doubts about this reading of the Grimanic manuscript. Certainly another letter to Aetius concerning this same affair, perhaps written at the same time, is missing; we shall quote two fragments of it in the dissertation on lost letters, from the letters of Pelagius II.]

## CHAPTER I

Although I received a letter from Your Affection some time ago, I nevertheless wonder that you allowed to pass in silence the opportunity for replying which our brother Anatolius necessarily used, since, given the circumstances of the time and the causes involved, conversations ought to be more frequent. I, for my part, having been more fully informed by the letters of the aforesaid brother about what heretical rashness had done at Alexandria, wrote to the most clement emperor and, as was necessary, supplicated him on behalf of the condition of the Church, so that he might devote his pious concern to matters that had been excessively disturbed.

Therefore, just as I exhorted our brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, so also I do not cease to admonish Your Affection to surround the faith of the most clement emperor with as many prayers as circumstances permit. We have learned that he has already spontaneously granted certain things for the protection of the Catholic religion, so that it should not be difficult to make a request of one whose voluntary solicitude anticipates us.

## CHAPTER II

Therefore, by unceasing appeals, obtain what is primary in the cause of faith: that the statutes of the holy Council of Chalcedon be assailed by no plots of the heretics, and that nothing be torn away from that definition which, having been inspired by God, unquestionably agrees in every respect with the evangelical and apostolic teachings. Then with all persistence request this also: that the condition of the Alexandrian Church, after the heretics’ blindness has been rejected and driven away, be restored to the liberty of the ancient faith through the provision of Catholic priests; that, in place of Proterius, of holy memory, a bishop of the highest proven character, whose faith cannot be doubted, be appointed. To him, with the security of concord, let the communion of the apostolic See be granted.

For it will be sufficiently glorious for the religious emperor if, through his arrangements, not only the whole state but also the Church of God is at peace. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

# LETTER CXLVIII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 122. Written 1 September 457.]

[Note: It was formerly published from manuscript collection 12. We found the same letter in the Ratisbon manuscript.]

## TO THE EMPEROR LEO

[Col. 1117A]

### SYNOPSIS

He rejoices that the Emperor is the guardian of the Council of Chalcedon and asks that by him the obstinate and treacherous contention of the heretics be restrained.

LEO, BISHOP OF ROME, TO LEO, EVER-AUGUSTUS.

Although recently I sent two writings to Your Clemency—one to fulfill the duty of greeting, the other to make a supplication for the condition of the Church—nevertheless, on the occasion which God’s providence has now provided, it is fitting to repeat both, most glorious emperor.

Accordingly, in keeping with the confidence which, through God’s inspiration, you have displayed toward the universal Church, by establishing, before anyone’s prayers, what all had most earnestly desired, we do not cease to give thanks and to bless God’s providence in the fervor of your faith. Through the holy and Catholic spirit which, as I learned from the report of my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius, you possess, you resisted the impudence of the heretics so firmly that you professed yourselves guardians of the Council of Chalcedon for the peace of the whole world.

Since this has been most salutarily defined according to the judgment of your faith, how much more zealously ought it to be bestowed upon the universal Church, so that the tranquility of the Christian faith may also benefit your empire and heretical wickedness may not in any respect boast of its undertaking! Its obstinate and treacherous contention immediately falls silent if it is restrained by imperial power. Given on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Constantine and Rufus.

# ADMONITION ON THE TWO FOLLOWING LETTERS (G)

[Col. 1117]

1. In the Grimanic manuscript Quesnellus found the following two letters distinguished as separate: one addressed to Basil of Antioch, the other to Euxitheus of Thessalonica and Juvenal of Jerusalem. In the Ratisbon manuscript, however, only one is produced, with the heading: “Leo, bishop, to Basil, Juvenal, Euxitheus, Peter, and Luke, bishops.” The last two, as we learn from the encyclial manuscript, are Peter of Corinth and Luke of Dyrrachium; we recognize that the same letter was addressed to them as well.

After the first period, which belongs exclusively to Basil of Antioch, the same manuscript notes: “Up to this point, to Basil.” From this we are warned that what follows—“Having learned what has happened at Alexandria,” and so forth—was written equally to Basil and to the others named in the heading. This heading and annotation of the Ratisbon manuscript agree especially well with what St. Leo writes in Letter 153: “It has also pleased us to send general letters to the metropolitan bishops, which may strengthen and confirm their minds ... Of these letters you will send one to the Antiochene, another to the Jerusalemite ... We have already sent similar writings to the bishops of Illyricum.”

Here three copies of a similar letter are indicated: one to Basil of Antioch, one to Juvenal of Jerusalem, and one to the bishops of Illyricum—that is, to Euxitheus of Thessalonica, Peter of Corinth, and Luke of Dyrrachium, who are named more precisely in the heading of our Ratisbon manuscript.

From the Grimanic manuscript we have further established that, in the copy of Letter 150 addressed to Euxitheus and the other metropolitans of Illyricum, the words “through Illyricum” were inserted in the final period. Since these words cannot at all apply to Juvenal of Jerusalem, they were certainly absent from the letter addressed to him; and for that reason we judged that Juvenal’s name should be deleted from the heading of that letter.

2. Pagi considered these two letters to be of doubtful authenticity in his note on the year 457, no. 7, as he likewise did Letter 153, because it requested the assistance of the patrician Aspar. He treated the two names, placed separately in Letters 149 and 150, as referring to two persons—the first the son, the second the father—although they signify one Aspar, who was honored with the rank of patrician; hence in Letter 153 he is called “the patrician Aspar.”

Since Aspar was an Arian, Pagi thought it incredible that the holy pontiff should have sought aid from an Arian against the Eutychians and against Timothy the Cat, whose patronage Aspar had undertaken. But since the Emperor Leo owed his empire to the patrician Aspar, it was necessary to have recourse to the man who possessed the greatest authority with the emperor, so that he might either give support or refrain from opposition.

Moreover, since Aspar had once favored the Catholics against the Eutychians—so much so that he interceded with Marcian on behalf of Theodoret, who thanked him in Letter 139—the holy pontiff may perhaps, writing to him at the suggestion of Anatolius or Aetius, have thought that he could hope for some assistance. Timothy’s patronage had not yet been detected at the beginning, or at least there was hope that he might be moved by Leo’s letters and services, just as St. Leo wrote to the Emperor Theodosius with the same hope, although he knew that Theodosius supported both Eutyches and the Ephesian Robber Council.

The style and entire composition of the matter certainly belong to Leo, as Pagi himself could not deny. The third letter of Pelagius II to Elias and the other bishops of Istria, in which he quotes two testimonies from the following letter, likewise leaves no room for doubt about its authenticity.

The authority of two such distinguished manuscripts of different origins, the Grimanic and the Ratisbon, so firmly vindicates the names of Patricius and Aspar that it is plainly fictitious to suppose that these names were inserted into the letters in place of the names of other eminent men, as the aforementioned Pagi conjectured at the end of his annotation—especially since the name Patricius is similarly found in another letter, Letter 151, which we shall publish from the Ratisbon manuscript.

3. The date of these letters, marked by Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript, is manifestly erroneous. Since, in the passage quoted from Letter 153, Leo entrusted Aetius with sending the letter to Basil of Antioch, this letter was undoubtedly transmitted together with the letter itself to Aetius and therefore dated on the same day, according to Leo’s practice—namely, on the Kalends of September.

Furthermore, from the same letter to Aetius we learn that other letters were sent at the same time to the emperor, to Aspar, and to others. We possess Letter 148 to the Emperor Leo, Letter 151 to Anatolius, and Letter 152 to Julian; and since all these are dated on the Kalends of September, there can be no doubt that the two following letters were also dated on the same day, as indeed we have corrected them from the Ratisbon manuscript.

# LETTER CXLIX

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 118. Written 1 September 457.]

## TO BASIL, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH

[Col. 1119A]

### SYNOPSIS

I. After complaining that no messenger had been sent to announce his ordination, he urges Basil to resist the fury of the Eutychians, who, after killing Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, demanded that a new synod be established, with the Council of Chalcedon set aside.  
II. After praising the Emperor Leo, he asserts that everything depends upon the steadfastness of the bishops, so that no new discussions may be undertaken.

LEO TO BASIL, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH.

## CHAPTER I

We ought, according to ecclesiastical custom, to have learned of Your Affection’s ordination through your own report or that of our provincial brother bishops. But since there were causes that could have hindered this diligence, and the emperor Marcian, of holy memory, made your consecration known to us by his own writings, and since we cannot doubt your merit, whom we know, we now admonish Your Affection, as we have admonished certain other brothers, because of the present necessity.

For, having learned what was perpetrated at Alexandria in the fury of the Eutychians, and what I do not doubt has become known to Your Fraternity, I have sent this letter out of the concern which I owe to all the Churches of God. Through it I wished to admonish Your Affection to resist the criminal attempts with holy steadfastness, lest our common faith be found in any respect either fearful or lukewarm. For, by the favor of the Lord, who does not abandon his Church in any tribulation, we possess so religious and Catholic a disposition in the most pious emperor that we must believe of him nothing other than what we proved concerning Marcian, of august memory.

## CHAPTER II

Indeed, while our action was still delayed, the most faithful emperor so abhorred the parricidal crime that he granted no access to the action of the heretics. After the enormity of the crime had been committed, they thought it possible for them to have an episcopal council summoned to other deliberations, once the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon had been dissolved.

But because this, dearest brother, is utterly hostile to the Christian faith, and because it is demanded with such wickedness for no other reason than that the preaching of the Gospel and the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation may be overthrown, I beseech Your Affection not to relax your resolve in anything concerning the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon, and not to permit those things composed through divine inspiration to be violated by any novelty.

For I am certain that the most clement emperor and the magnificent man Patricius, together with the entire assembly of illustrious officials, will not allow the heretics to obtain anything to the disturbance of the Church, if they see that pastoral minds are wavering in no respect.

But so that this exhortation may reach the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops, let the care of Your Diligence see to it, because—as must often be said—the whole Christian religion is disturbed if anything is torn away from what was established at Chalcedon. Given on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

# LETTER CL

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 119. Written 1 September 457.]

[Note: Quesnellus added from the Grimanic manuscript only “and Juvenal of Jerusalem.” We recovered the two other bishops from the Ratisbon manuscript. See the Admonition prefixed to the preceding letter, no. 1, where we also noted that in the Ratisbon manuscript this letter is not separated from the preceding one, as it was in the Grimanic manuscript, because it is wholly contained in the preceding letter. Only the two words “through Illyricum” are inserted in the final period of this letter; they are absent from the preceding letter. From these words we recognize that this was a copy of the letter sent to the Illyrians, not to Juvenal, to whom Illyricum has no connection. Accordingly, we removed his name from the heading supplied by Quesnellus.]

## TO EUXITHEUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA, AND, LIKEWISE, TO JUVENAL OF JERUSALEM, PETER OF CORINTH, AND LUKE OF DYRRACHIUM

### SYNOPSIS

He urges them vigorously to resist the criminal attempts of the Eutychians, who had killed Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, and not to permit another synod to be assembled, but to uphold the firmness of the Council of Chalcedon.

LEO TO EUXITHEUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA.

Having learned what was perpetrated at Alexandria in the fury of the Eutychians, and what I do not doubt has become known to Your Fraternity, I have sent this letter out of the concern which I owe to all the Churches of God. Through it I wished to admonish Your Affection to resist the criminal attempts with holy steadfastness, lest our common faith be found in any respect either fearful or lukewarm. For, by the favor of the Lord, who does not abandon his Church in any tribulation, we possess so religious and Catholic a disposition in the most pious emperor that we must believe of him nothing other than what we proved concerning Marcian, of august memory.

Indeed, while our action was still delayed, the most faithful emperor so abhorred the parricidal crime that he granted no access to the action of the heretics. After the enormity of the crime had been committed, they thought it possible for an episcopal council to be summoned to other deliberations once the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon had been dissolved.

But because this, dearest brother, is utterly hostile to the Christian faith, and because it is demanded with such wickedness for no other reason than that the preaching of the Gospel and the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation may be overthrown, I beseech Your Affection not to relax your resolve in anything concerning the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon, and not to permit those things composed through divine inspiration to be violated by any novelty.
