For I am certain that the most clement emperor and the magnificent man Patricius, together with the entire assembly of illustrious officials, will not allow the heretics to obtain anything to the disturbance of the Church, if they see that pastoral minds are wavering in no respect.

But so that this exhortation may reach the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow bishops throughout Illyricum, let the care of Your Diligence see to it, because—as must often be said—the whole Christian religion is disturbed if anything is torn away from what was established at Chalcedon. Given on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

# LETTER CLI

[Note: Written 1 September 457.]

[Note: Now published for the first time from the Ratisbon manuscript; it is indicated in Letters 157, chapter 4, and 163, where the case of Atticus is discussed.]

## TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

Now published for the first time from the Ratisbon manuscript.

### SYNOPSIS

He praises Anatolius and urges him to purge the Church of Constantinople from heresy. Concerning the investigation of the presbyter Atticus.

LEO, BISHOP, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP.

We gratefully acknowledge the faith and steadfastness of Your Affection, by which you resisted the plots of the heretics; and for that reason we exhort you with more secure confidence to stand steadfastly by the matters you have also defended. For our writings testify to the religious purpose of your charity both before the most clement emperor and before the magnificent man Patricius; through them we have made clear that your diligence has informed us fully.

Therefore, first let Your Fraternity act so that the Church of Constantinople may be purified from every stain of the heretics, and so that Catholic purity—which must also be preserved among the laity—may be found especially unharmed among the clergy, dearest brother.

Although we do not rashly believe reports carried by rumor, nevertheless, because wherever the cause of souls is at stake we strive to block the way to the devil’s deceits, we forewarn Your Affection that you should first investigate privately the presbyter Atticus, who is reported to be fostering the error of the Eutychians through open discussions within the Church. If you find any mixture of heretical poison in his heart, either make him Catholic by correction or drive him from the Church with necessary severity, lest, while one person is spared through useless leniency, many should be harmed by error left unpunished. Given on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

# LETTER CLII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 120. Written 1 September 457.]

[Note: We have collated the edition published from the Grimanic manuscript with the Ratisbon manuscript.]

## TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COOS

### SYNOPSIS

He advises that the preceding letters, written to the metropolitans, be delivered to each by the care of Julian or Aetius; that episcopal steadfastness is required above all; and that there is nothing new, obscure, or doubtful in his letter.

LEO TO JULIAN, BISHOP.

Since the return to Constantinople of our son Gerontius provided an occasion, it was fitting to send writings to Your Affection, by which we might encourage your zeal in ecclesiastical affairs and in matters pertaining to the faith, so that you may steadfastly resist the efforts of the heretics, trusting that God’s mercy will ensure that their criminal attempts receive their due even in this present time.

Let Your Affection know that we have sent letters to certain of our metropolitan brothers and fellow bishops. Your diligence, or that of our son Aetius the presbyter, must see to it that they promptly reach each of them.

For if episcopal steadfastness does not depart from the definition of the holy Council of Chalcedon, I am certain that the most clement and Christian emperor will gladly defend his judgment, which he declared in the letters issued at the beginning of his reign; and what he has already granted spontaneously, he will accomplish much more readily when asked, so that what was well concluded and arranged may not be violated by any novelty.

I am truly amazed that anything still seems obscure to the vanity of those who bring accusations in my letter, which pleased the whole world, so that they think it ought to be explained more clearly, since its assertion of that preaching is so plain and solid that it admits no novelty either in meaning or in wording. For whatever was then written by us is proved to have been taken from apostolic and evangelical teaching. Given on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

# LETTER CLIII

[Note: Elsewhere numbered 121. Written 1 September 457.]

[Note: Quesnellus published it from the Grimanic manuscript; we found it in the Ratisbon manuscript.]

## TO AETIUS, PRESBYTER OF CONSTANTINOPLE

### SYNOPSIS

I. He asks him to send the letters written to the East to each recipient.  
II. He says that he has likewise sent letters from the Gauls and Italians that were written to him. Also concerning other matters.

LEO TO AETIUS, PRESBYTER.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1123B]

We have received a letter from Your Affection which bore witness to your diligence in the cause of the Church. For the present, we briefly exhort you to persist vigilantly in what you have begun, lest the perversity of the heretics obtain anything by which the Church of the Lord might be disturbed.

For our part, in accordance with our diligence, we have sent necessary writings in the cause of the faith both to the most clement emperor and to the magnificent man, the patrician Aspar. Without doubt they will be able to achieve an appropriate result if your care also remains watchful.

It has also pleased us to send general letters to the metropolitan bishops, which may strengthen and confirm their minds, so that they may know that they must strive with equal zeal and harmonious unity to defend the Council of Chalcedon. Of these letters, you will send one to the Antiochene and another to the Jerusalemite, if this seems fitting to you all in common. We have already sent similar writings to the bishops of Illyricum.

### SUPPLEMENTARY EDITORIAL NOTES AND APPARATUS

[Note: Col. 1113D. The Ratisbon manuscript deletes *autem* (“however”).]

[Note: Col. 1113D. Ratisbon reads *cognovimus* (“we have learned”); Vercelli, *comperi* (“I have learned”). On the machinations indicated here, see note 2 (Col. 1114C [Col. 1112, n. n]) on the preceding letter.]

[Note: Col. 1114C–D. That is, the Eutychians, on account of the change of emperor, thought that they had found, as Leo says in the following letter, an opportune time in which to annul the decrees of the holy Synod of Chalcedon. Accordingly, as Epiphanius Scholasticus relates in the preface to the *codex encyclius*, they came to the imperial city of Constantine and demanded that what had been well established at Chalcedon should be broken by an imperial order. The Augustus nevertheless rendered this attempt futile. For at the very beginning of his reign he sent letters to all metropolitans, confirming the laws of his predecessors, especially those issued by Marcian in support of the Synod of Chalcedon, as the Catholic Egyptian bishops relate in their petition to the same emperor, printed in vol. IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 1837. From the letter of the bishops of Second Syria to the same Augustus, vol. IV of the Councils, p. 1864, we learn that all the metropolitans replied to these imperial letters with the subscriptions of the bishops of their provinces, affirming that the Synod of Chalcedon, equally with the earlier councils, was to be held ratified.]

[Note: Col. 1114D. Some old printed editions read “evangelical” (*evangelicae*) in place of “apostolic” (*apostolicae*).]

[Note: Col. 1114D. Two manuscripts of collection 8 and the exemplar of the first edition read: “may be overthrown by the accusation of any other party” (*alterius ... accusatione*).]

[Note: Col. 1114D. Leo had learned of the death of Bishop Proterius and of the whole course of the Alexandrian disturbances from Anatolius’s report.]

[Note: Col. 1114D. Our manuscripts—Vatican collection 3, Vallicellian collection 8, Ratisbon, and the exemplar of the first edition—read, with the old editions, “in integrity of conduct” (*in actuum probitate*). Quesnellus reads *in actus* (“into acts”), instead of *in actuum* (“in [the integrity] of acts”). Three of our manuscripts read *perfectione* (“perfection”) in place of *professione* (“profession”), thus “in perfection of faith.”]

[Note: Col. 1114D–1115D. Quesnellus reads “the fifth day before the Ides of June”; the margin gives another reading, “the sixth.” Tillemont, note 68 on Leo, detected an error in the month. Since Leo learned of the Alexandrian disturbances from Anatolius’s report, he must be believed to have written at the same time both to the emperor and to Anatolius: thus either both letters were dated in June or both in July. Tillemont preferred July because Letter 147 to Julian, sent at the same time, is likewise dated the fifth day before the Ides of July. But he lacked manuscripts preferring July in this letter. Our manuscripts resolve the difficulty. Only manuscripts of collection 12, with editions derived from them, give the fifth day before the Ides of June. Manuscripts of collections 3 and 8, Ratisbon collection 19, Vatican Ottobonian collection 23, and the exemplar of the first edition give July. Vatican 1342, collection 3, alone reads “on the Ides of July” in place of “the fifth day before the Ides.” Some of these manuscripts have Constans in place of Constantine, but wrongly; the consul of this year is called Constantine in inscriptions and other documents.]

[Note: Col. 1115D. Compare note 2 (Col. 1113, n. c) on Letter 145.]

[Note: Col. 1115D. From Ratisbon we have also added “also” (*etiam*).]

[Note: Col. 1116D. Another reading is “advancement” (*provectum*) in place of “progress” (*profectum*).]

[Note: Col. 1116D. Ratisbon reads *de illa* (“from that”); other editions read *ex illa* (“from that”), using a different preposition.]

[Note: Col. 1118B. The same Ratisbon manuscript reads *etiam hac tamen occasione* (“nevertheless also on this occasion”).]

[Note: Col. 1117B–1118B. The two recent writings were presumably the congratulatory letter on Leo’s accession, now missing, and Letter 145, dated the fifth day before the Ides of July. Ratisbon adds: “and the other.”]

[Note: Col. 1118B. See note 11 (Col. 1114, n. l) on Letter 145.]

[Note: Col. 1118B. The Venetian manuscript of St Mark, collection 12, and Ratisbon read: “that you professed yourselves guardians of the Council of Chalcedon for the peace of the whole world”; other editions have *ad totius ... custodem*, with *ad* (“toward/for”) and *custodem* (“guardian,” singular).]

[Note: Col. 1118B. The same manuscripts read “falls silent” (*conquiescit*); other editions read “will fall silent” (*conquiescet*).]

[Note: Col. 1119C. Ratisbon reads *debueram* (“I ought to have [learned]”) rather than *debueramus* (“we ought to have [learned]”). It was the custom of the Eastern Churches to report by letters to the Roman pontiff the ordination of bishops of the greater sees, both by the ordained man and by his ordainers, as is evident, among other evidence, from Anatolius’s Letter 53 to Leo, Letters 71 and 86, chapter 3, and Letter 171, chapter 2, where this is said to have been done necessarily and by custom. See also Letters 172 and 173. This Basil had succeeded Maximus while Marcian was still alive. If the words “whom we know” show that Basil was already known to Leo, perhaps he is the Basil the deacon who brought the letters of Emperor Marcian and Anatolius to the pontiff in 452. See Letters 104 and 106.]

[Note: Col. 1119C. Ratisbon reads *fraternitati vestrae* (“to Your Fraternity,” plural form of address), more consistently with what follows: “Your Affection,” “your diligence,” and so on; Quesnellus, from Grimanic, reads *tuae* (“your,” singular form).]

[Note: Col. 1119C. Pelagius II, Letter 3 to the bishops of Istria, chapter 5, quoting this testimony of Leo, reads “our” (*nostra*) in place of “the common.”]

[Note: Col. 1119C–D. Both Ratisbon and Grimanic, according to Cacciari’s testimony, read “an episcopal council”; Quesnellus arbitrarily printed “judgment.” At first the emperor wished for a new council, as Facundus testifies, book XII, chapter 2, hoping to bring the Eutychians back by this means. From this passage we also learn that the Eutychians pressed for it. But Pope Leo worked and succeeded in preventing it.]

[Note: Col. 1119D. Pelagius II quotes what follows. At the cited passage Pelagius reads “your” and, shortly afterward, “resolve.”]

[Note: Col. 1119D. Ratisbon reads “the eminent Patricius.” This is Patricius Aspar, discussed in the Admonition, no. 2. Perhaps he was called “eminent” to distinguish Aspar, who then possessed the greatest influence with the Augustus, from the other patricians by this common title.]

[Note: Col. 1120C. This passage is cited by Pelagius and Vigilius. The former note likewise quotes it. Vigilius, in the *Constitutum* given on the day before the Ides of May 553, mistakenly reports this letter as written to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, rather than Basil of Antioch; after “may be overthrown” he adds, as though in one continuous passage, “and do not permit things composed by divine inspiration to be violated by any novelty.” Those words occur above. The quotation prints *ulla* (“any”), which the editor corrects to *nulla* (“no”). Both pontiffs read *exhortatio* (“exhortation”); Ratisbon reads *cohortatio* (“exhortation/encouragement”).]

[Note: Col. 1120C. Quesnellus’s margin, from Vigilius, reads “let the diligent care of Your Fraternity accomplish it.” But in the edition of the Councils, vol. V, p. 1356, Vigilius reads “let the care of your diligence accomplish it”; Pelagius reads “let the care of your fraternity diligently see to it.” Shortly afterward Ratisbon reads “is overthrown” (*convellitur*).]

[Note: Col. 1120C. Ratisbon correctly gives “on the Kalends of September.” The common text, from Grimanic, wrongly gives “the tenth day before the Kalends of September”; see the Admonition, no. 3.]

[Note: Col. 1121D. Quesnellus reads “your”; for the reason for preferring the Ratisbon reading here also, see note 2 (Col. 1119, n. c) on the preceding letter.]

[Note: Col. 1121D. Grimanic reads “council,” not “judgment,” which Quesnellus printed arbitrarily. Compare note 4 (Col. 1119, n. e) on the preceding letter.]

[Note: Col. 1121D. Quesnellus gives “the tenth day before the Kalends of September”; we have corrected this from Ratisbon. See the Admonition, no. 3.]

[Note: Col. 1121D. There is a letter to the emperor, Letter 148. But the letter sent to Patricius Aspar is missing.]

[Note: Col. 1121D–1122D. These words imply letters from Anatolius, by which he had informed Leo concerning the movements of the Alexandrian Eutychians; these too are missing.]

[Note: Col. 1122D. This shows both St Leo’s prudence and moderation in Atticus’s case, and how much he deferred to Anatolius. In Letter 163 Leo says that he entrusted to Anatolius the examination of the matters reported to him—namely, in this Letter 151.]

[Note: Col. 1122D. The preposition “in” has been added from Ratisbon.]

[Note: Col. 1122D. Letters 149 and 150.]

[Note: Col. 1122D. Ratisbon reads *debebit* (“will have to”) rather than *debet* (“must”).]

[Note: Col. 1122D. That is, the judgment which the emperor declared in letters published at the beginning of his reign; see note 11 (Col. 1114, n. l) on Letter 145.]

[Note: Col. 1123C–D. The best Ratisbon manuscript reads “more plainly” (*apertius*); other editions read “more fittingly” (*aptius*). Quesnellus reads *plena* (“full”); Ratisbon’s *plana* (“plain”) is better. These words show that Leo had discovered that the objections raised against his letter did not arise from a less satisfactory Greek translation of it, about which he had previously been concerned in Letters 130 and 131, but from the captious perversity of opponents who, under the pretext of obscurity, refused to assent to the truth. He therefore requested that the emperor restrain their audacity.]

[Note: Col. 1123D. Ratisbon reads “lest the Church of the Lord be disturbed”; Quesnellus reads “which disturbs the Church of the Lord.”]

[Note: Col. 1123D. The text reads *pro diligentia nostri* (“in accordance with the diligence of our ...”); perhaps *nostra* (“our [diligence]”) should be read, or *officii* (“office”) or something similar supplied. On the letters mentioned here, see note 2 (Col. 1121, n. f) on Letter 151.]

[Note: Col. 1123D. Compare the Admonition on Letter 149, no. 1. Ratisbon adds “and that they may know.”]

## CHAPTER II
Concerning the sacrament of the Catholic faith, we now have no need for further disputation, since nothing can be investigated more diligently or defined more truly. We have also sent copies of the letters which the bishops of Gaul and Italy sent to us in harmonious agreement of faith, so that it might not remain unknown how one their faith is with ours. Moreover, we wish the letters which we sent both to the most gracious emperor and to the persons of distinction—namely, Anatolius, Julian, and Aspar—through our son Gerontius to be presented either by your Belovedness, or by our son Storatius, if he is still with you, and to be supported by such speech as is appropriate. So that you may know what we have written, we have sent copies, in order that you may be informed about everything. Given on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

[Note: [Col. 1123D] The same manuscript reads “copies,” namely, copies of the letters. From this we learn that Leo sent his letter to Flavian only to the Gauls and Italians—that is, to the bishops of the province of Milan—so that they might receive it with a solemn subscription. For if he had requested the same thing from the bishops of the other provinces of the West, then, when he had received their replies, he would likewise have sent copies of them. He wrote to the Gauls and Italians on this matter because an opportunity for writing had arisen in their case, but not likewise in the case of the others.]

[Note: [Col. 1124C] Letters 97 and 99.]

[Note: [Col. 1124C] Quesnellus reads “either to your Belovedness or to our son Sporatius,” and in the margin: “Perhaps, through your Belovedness, or through our son, etc.” We have emended the text from Ratisponensis. The reading “Storatius” removes the uncertainty whether Sporatius, who was consul in the East in 452, is named here. Nor do we think that Storatius is meant who was prefect of the City in 443; men of that rank are ordinarily addressed by some honorific title.]

## LETTER CLIV

[Note: [Col. 1124D] Otherwise 123. Written 11 October 457.]

[Note: [Col. 1124D] Thus far found only in the Grimanic manuscript, from which Quesnellus edited it.]

### To the Catholic Bishops of Egypt

#### Synopsis

He consoles the Egyptian bishops, exiles for the sake of the faith, and urges them patiently to endure adversity for the mystery of the Incarnation.

### Leo to the Catholic bishops from Egypt residing at Constantinople

[Col. 1124B]

Although I sympathize with all my heart with the labors which your Belovedness has undertaken for the observance of the Catholic faith, and accept what has been inflicted upon you by the heretics no differently than if I myself had suffered it, I nevertheless understand that what has occurred is more a cause for joy than for sorrow: with the Lord Jesus Christ strengthening you in evangelical and apostolic teaching, you have remained unconquered.

And when the enemies of the Christian faith tore you away from the seats of your churches, you preferred to suffer the hardship of exile rather than be defiled by any contagion of their impiety. Therefore, when writing to our most Christian emperor, I gave thanks for his piety, because, as we have been informed, he received you with the charity which was fitting.

[Note: [Col. 1124D] Since Letter 148 contains no indication of these Egyptian bishops, other letters to Leo Augustus are evidently referred to here; they have perished.]

From his benevolence, I have no doubt that such confidence has been granted to you that you may steadfastly carry out what must be done for the condition of the universal Church. For his clemency burns with priestly zeal in defending the decrees of the holy Council of Chalcedon, and nothing more salutary or blessed can be offered to the whole world than that the mystery ordained before the ages may be preserved inviolate in every respect in ecclesiastical peace and royal authority.

[Note: [Col. 1125C] Perhaps one should read “authority.” Quesnellus.]

Therefore, with brotherly and fatherly affection I exhort each of you—whom the same spirit and the same cause of faith have united, and whom, scorning the persecution of the heretics, an unwearied ardor of faith has led from Egypt—to endure these trials with an even and courageous spirit. Recognize that you have not lost what was your own, but have earned greater things. Through the brief hardship by which one reaches the crowns of confessors, God’s providence is so making use of you that, through your patience, the devotion of many may be strengthened and, with the glory of the revered emperor, the Alexandrian Church, once the heretics have been driven away, may recover its ancient dignity.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

## LETTER CLV

[Note: [Col. 1125C] Otherwise 124. Written 11 October 457.]

[Note: [Col. 1125C] It survives in manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 12, 21, and 24, and in Sichardus’s copy. Quesnellus prefixed to this letter the title “Concerning the report against Timothy of Alexandria.” But since nothing of this kind is found in the letter itself, we believe that the title was attached to it by mistake; it more appropriately belongs to Letter 137. Quesnellus himself reports, in Dissertation 1 on the year 437, no. 5, that this title was read in his manuscript, that is, in the Grimanic manuscript. From that manuscript, however, he published the aforementioned Letter 157, in which Saint Leo replies to the report against Timothy transmitted by Anatolius. Letter 155 is certainly not found in the Grimanic manuscript.]

### To Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople

[Col. 1125B]

[Note: [Col. 1125D] In the table of Collection 5, chapter 95, this title is found: “To Anatolius the bishop, concerning the exhortation to overthrow the Eutychian heresy, and concerning his reception of certain men expelled from Egypt for the Catholic faith.”]

#### Synopsis

I. He incites him to vigilance against the efforts of the heretics. — II. He rebukes the connivance of the clergy of Constantinople, regarding whom he desires Anatolius to exercise pastoral firmness.

### Leo to Anatolius the bishop

#### Chapter I

We approve the diligent and necessary concern which your Fraternity displays in sending letters to us, and, having received your pages through our son Olympius, we perceive that priestly care is vigorous in you. We too, insofar as the Lord grants us ability, do not fail in this care, entreating your Belovedness that, since we have entered a time of labor, you persevere in holy vigilance until the right hand of the Lord accomplishes might (Psalm 117:16), and crushes the tempter beneath the feet of his Church.

[Note: [Col. 1125D] The Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with later manuscripts, reads “gives ability.” Then, instead of “entreating,” the Cambridge manuscripts of Quesnellus and our Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 read “exhorting.”]

For the faith of our most gracious emperor, prepared in every respect by divine providence, consoles us; I have again addressed and exhorted him, as was fitting,

[Note: [Col. 1126C] Here a letter to the emperor is indicated; it is said to have been sent through the Olympius mentioned above and is preserved as Letter 158. It was therefore transmitted together with this letter to Anatolius.]

so that, with more stringent constancy, he may cause the efforts of the most impious brigands to be opposed—

[Note: [Col. 1126D] Collections 11 and 21 read “to resist.”]

men who must not presume so greatly upon his favor that they dare even to rage at Constantinople. Yet they are permitted to do this by the design of divine providence so that it may become increasingly clear by what spirit they are driven, and so that no one may doubt into what audacity they would burst if, after the condemnation of their most impious heresy, they were granted power to dispute against the faith. Thus, as far as lies within them, they would spread more widely the fury which our brothers and fellow bishops who recently fled to you from the regions of Egypt lament that they have endured.

I would not doubt that consolations of piety have been offered to them both by our most Christian emperor and by the God-pleasing charity of your Fraternity, even if you had not written yourself.

[Note: [Col. 1126D] Manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24, together with Sichardus, read “by the charity of your Fraternity”; this may be preferable.]

I thought it appropriate, however, to send written words to them also,

[Note: [Col. 1126D] Letter 154.]

which could strengthen them in their resolve regarding the common faith,

[Note: [Col. 1126D] Two manuscripts of Collection 21 read “could strengthen.”]

and enable them to recognize what they merit through heavenly reward for their patience. As the blessed Apostle teaches when he says: “Receive them therefore with all joy in the Lord, and hold such men in honor, because they came near to death for the faith of Christ” (Philippians 2:29).

[Note: [Col. 1126D] The Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with Sichardus, omits “with all.”]

#### Chapter II

[Note: [Col. 1126D] 24, question 2, “But this truly,” chapter 34.]

I make known that I am greatly displeased by the report that among the clergy of your Belovedness there are certain men who connive at the perversity of the opponents, and that vessels of wrath are being mixed with vessels of mercy.

[Note: [Col. 1126D] This concerns Atticus, about whom he had written to Anatolius on the Kalends of September in Letter 151.]

Your diligence must vigilantly devote itself to investigating and restraining them with appropriate severity, so that those whom correction cannot benefit may not be spared excision. For we must remember the evangelical commandment, prescribed by Truth itself: if an eye, or a foot, or a right hand causes us scandal, it must be removed from the structure of the body, since it is better to be without such members in the Church than to go with them into eternal punishment (Matthew 18:8; Mark 9:42).

[Note: [Col. 1126D] Quesnellus and our Vienna manuscript of Collection 5 read: “to be without these members’ offices in the Church.” We have restored the reading of earlier editors, confirmed by the other manuscripts and by Sichardus’s copy, as more suitable.]

For it is useless for us to resist those placed outside the Church if we are wounded by those who are inside, through the very people whom they deceive. This poisonous patience must be entirely removed from priestly vigor—a patience which, by sparing the sins of others, does not spare itself.

Thus, once the priest Eli tolerated the sins of his sons, he deserved to experience with them the sentence of divine justice (1 Samuel 2:27), because through sluggish indulgence he neglected to punish sinners.

Therefore, as the opportunity of your office invites, let your Belovedness strive to visit the most religious emperor frequently, and persist in entreating my prayers—not only his royal mind but also his priestly mind—that, mindful of the common faith which we have received under the teaching of the Holy Spirit, he may shatter all the machinations of the heretics and suffer nothing to be permitted to them in the Churches of Christ. Otherwise the divine mysteries would come under their power, although, on account of the enormity of their crimes, they have neither the right to dwell nor the right to pray in the house of God.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of October, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Constantine and Rufus.

[Note: [Col. 1127A] Earlier Vulgate manuscripts, together with Vatican manuscript of Collection 24 and Sichardus, read “on the day before the Ides,” and in the margin “on the fifth day before the Ides.” This chronological note is more accurate than the reading preferred by Quesnellus’s manuscripts, including our superior manuscripts of Collections 5, 11, and 21. It agrees with the date given in the preceding letter, which is referred to in chapter 1 of this letter and is known to have been transmitted together with it. It was easy for a copyist to transform the letter V, written with separated strokes, into two units and thus write “the second day before the Ides,” as in the manuscripts of Collection 24; not, however, as in the printed editions, “the day before the Ides.”]

## ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

[Col. 1127]

1. The following letter was published by Merlinus from a manuscript of Collection 12. Quesnellus reread it with the Grimanic manuscript of Collection 18. Since this same letter was inserted into the encyclial manuscript, which was written in Greek while Leo was still alive, we would have possessed this letter of Saint Leo in Greek had that manuscript not perished. Its Latin translation, however, survives; Epiphanius Scholasticus laboriously prepared it. When he obtained a Latin copy of Leo’s letter, he inserted it into his own translation. For this reason, from this manuscript—which Baluzius edited from Surius’s edition and compared with two manuscripts, the Beauvais and Corbie copies—several variant readings are available which have been useful to us.

2. This letter was occasioned by the letters of the emperor Leo, which he delivered to all the metropolitans on account of the disturbances at Alexandria. In the aforementioned encyclial manuscript, whose order, as it appears in the manuscripts, is reproduced from Baluzius in volume V of the Venetian edition of the Councils, pages 33 and following, chapter 6 describes the emperor’s letter to Anatolius of Constantinople. Then, in chapter 11, the names of the other bishops to whom similar letters were sent are added; among these, the letters are said first to have been given to Leo, the most reverend pontiff of the City of Rome.

The imperial letter to Anatolius contains certain matters peculiar to that bishop of Constantinople, as well as other matters proper to Pope Leo which had been inserted in it (see note 1 [below, n. b]); it omits these latter matters. Therefore, it cannot be said to have been transmitted in exactly the same form to Leo the pontiff, and for that reason it has not been inserted in this edition. Nevertheless, it is sufficiently clear from it what the emperor’s letter likewise sought from Pope Leo.

After Timothy Aelurus had been advanced by the Eutychians to the see of Alexandria, Saint Proterius had been killed, and a great disturbance had arisen between the Eutychians and the Catholic Egyptians, both parties fled to the emperor with petitions. Leo Augustus sent both petitions, together with his own letter, to all the metropolitans, and especially to the Roman pontiff, asking them to convene a council and there, concerning the aforesaid Timothy and the Council of Chalcedon, to make known to his piety “what you think in common, without any human fear and without favor or hatred toward anyone whatsoever . . . with all speed.”

Pope Leo was the first of all to send the following reply, as Evagrius testifies in Book II, chapter 10. In the encyclial manuscript it is described immediately after the names of the bishops just mentioned, in first place, in chapter 12.

3. From this it is also evident that Pagius was mistaken when, under the year 457, no. 11, he denied that these letters of the pontiff were replies to the emperor’s encyclical. Since the pontiff’s letters are inserted in the encyclial manuscript, we recognize them as replies to the imperial encyclical no less than the other letters of the bishops contained in that manuscript.

Hence, in chapter 4 there is also mention of copies of the petitions of the Catholics and the Eutychians, which, together with the imperial letters, are displayed in the same encyclial manuscript in chapters 7 and 9.

The emperor’s letter was sent with the greatest speed around October of 457 through the magistriani to all the metropolitans. Hence two bishops, Agapitus of Rhodes (page 1892) and Lucas of Dyrrachium (page 1927), indicate that they received these letters in winter. If Marcellinus Comes, in his Chronicle under the year 458, mentions both the letters of Augustus and the replies of the bishops, this happened because, although the imperial encyclical was sent in 457, most of the replies did not arrive until 458; consequently, the letter of the monk Varadatus (page 1934) is dated 27 August. Thus there is no reason to doubt that the following letter of Leo was a reply to the imperial encyclical.

## LETTER CLVI

[Note: [Col. 1127C] Otherwise 125. Written 1 December 457.]

### To Leo Augustus

[Col. 1127B]

#### Synopsis

I. After the Council of Chalcedon, nothing concerning the faith is to be reconsidered. — II. He is Antichrist who re-examines the truth declared by the Church. — III. It is unlawful for the murderers of the Alexandrian bishop to preside over the Church. — IV. The petitions presented to Leo Augustus by Catholics and heretics, and the difference between them. — V. All the offices and mysteries of the Christian religion have been interrupted at Alexandria. — VI. He promises more extensive writings concerning the faith, censures Anatolius’s negligence, and commends the Catholics.

### Leo the bishop to Leo Augustus

#### Chapter I

I reverently received the letters of your Clemency, full of the power of God and the light of truth. I would have wished to obey them even in the matter for which your piety considers my presence necessary, so that I might obtain greater benefit from beholding your splendor.

[Note: [Col. 1127C] These words, which are not found in the letter to Anatolius indicated in the Admonition, were doubtless contained in the emperor’s particular letter to Leo.]

But I judge that what reason has shown must be chosen will please you more. For since, with holy and spiritual zeal, you are fortifying the peace of the Church throughout the world, and since nothing is more suitable for defending the faith than to cling to what has been irreproachably defined in every respect under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, we would seem to be overturning well-established decisions, weakening at the demand of heretical petition the authorities which the universal Church has embraced, and thus placing no limit on the collision of Churches, but, by granting license to rebel, widening rather than calming the conflicts.

[Note: [Col. 1128C] Thus the Grimanic manuscript and our manuscripts, together with Facundus, read “colliding.” The ancient editions of Leo read “correcting”; the encyclial manuscript, “gathering.”]

[Note: [Col. 1127C] Thus the Grimanic manuscript, our manuscripts, the edition of the encyclial manuscript, and Facundus. Earlier editions of Leo read: “how will we seem to wish to overturn the decrees?”]

Therefore, since after the impieties of the Ephesian synod—by which, through the crime of Dioscorus, the Catholic faith was rejected and Eutychian perversity embraced—nothing [Note: [Col. 1128C] Another reading, with the manuscripts of Collection 12: “for confirmation.”] could have been arranged more usefully for preserving the Christian faith than that the holy Council of Chalcedon should abolish the aforesaid crime; and since such care for heavenly doctrine was exercised there that nothing should remain in anyone’s opinion discordant with either the prophetic or apostolic preaching, while this moderation was preserved, that pardon would be denied to no one who had been corrected, but only the rebellious and obstinate would be rejected from the unity of the Church: what could your piety decree that is more reasonable or more religious than that no one should henceforth be permitted to attack what has been established not so much by human as by divine decrees? Otherwise those who have dared to doubt the truth of God himself would truly deserve to lose so great a gift.

#### Chapter II

Since, therefore, the universal Church has become a rock through the building of that principal Rock, and the most blessed Peter, first of the apostles, heard from the voice of the Lord saying,

[Col. 1129B]

[Note: [Col. 1129D] We supplied “the voice saying” from two of our manuscripts of Collection 12 and from the encyclial manuscript.]

“You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my Church,” who is it, unless he is Antichrist or the devil, who would dare to assail its unconquerable firmness?

[Note: [Col. 1129D] Leo’s printed editions before Quesnellus, with no support from any of our manuscripts, read “the truth,” rather than “unconquerable firmness.”]

Who, persisting unchangeably in his wickedness, through vessels of wrath suited to his deceit, under the false name of diligence, while pretending that he is seeking the truth, desires to sow lies? His unrestrained fury and blind impiety have rightly prescribed for themselves contempt and avoidance, so that, while they rage against the holy Alexandrian Church at the devil’s prompting, it might be learned what sort of men those are who desire the Council of Chalcedon to be reconsidered.

[Note: [Col. 1129D] Two manuscripts of Collection 12 read “in despising.” Two manuscripts of Baluzius’s encyclial codex read: “he wrote down as to be despised and avoided.”]

In that council it could in no way be accepted that we should be thought to hold an opinion contrary to the holy Council of Nicaea, as the heretics falsely claim—men who pretend that they hold the faith of the Council of Nicaea. In that council our holy and venerable Fathers, assembled against Arius, affirmed not that the Lord’s flesh, but that the Son’s deity, is homoousios, “of one substance,” with the Father. In the Council of Chalcedon, however, against Eutychian impiety it was defined that the Lord Jesus Christ took from the substance of the virgin mother the reality of our body.

#### Chapter III

Therefore, in addressing the most Christian emperor, who deserves to be numbered among the preachers of Christ, I use the freedom of the Catholic faith, and confidently exhort you, as a companion of the apostles and prophets: steadfastly despise and reject those who have deprived themselves of the Christian name, and do not permit impious murderers, under sacrilegious pretense, to deal with the faith—men who clearly wish to empty the faith.

[Note: [Col. 1129D] The Vulgate, with the manuscripts of Collection 12 and Surius’s copy, omits “themselves” (*ipsi*). Quesnellus added it from his manuscript; Baluzius’s copies support the addition.]

[Note: [Col. 1129D] The ancient editions of Leo read “to deviate from the faith.”]

Since the Lord has enriched your Clemency with so great an illumination of his mystery, you must observe without hesitation that royal power has been bestowed upon you not only for the government of the world, but especially for the protection of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 1129D] Thus our manuscripts of Collection 12 and Baluzius’s manuscripts. Another reading is: “not only for the government of the world.”]

Thus, by suppressing wicked assaults, you may defend what has been rightly established and restore true peace to what has been disturbed, driving out those who have invaded another’s right and restoring to the Alexandrian Church the seat of its ancient faith. In this way, with God’s anger softened by your corrections, may he not repay the previously religious city for what was committed, but forgive it.

[Note: [Col. 1129D] The earlier printed editions of Leo and the edition of the encyclial manuscript read: “may he not repay the royal city for what was previously committed.” Quesnellus’s emendation is supported by our copies and those of Baluzius.]

Set before the eyes of your heart, venerable emperor, all the priests of the Lord throughout the world, who beseech you on behalf of that faith in which the redemption of the whole world consists.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] The Vulgate reads “who.” We have corrected the text from both of Baluzius’s manuscripts.]

In that faith they especially implore you because followers of the apostolic faith presided over the Alexandrian Church, pleading before your piety that you not allow heretical men, deservedly condemned for their perversity, to make use of their usurpation.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] The same Vulgate reading is “through their persuasion.” The Beauvais manuscript reads “through their perversion.” We have followed the better reading in Baluzius’s Corbie manuscript.]

For whether you consider the impiety of their error or attend to the deed of madness they committed, they cannot merely be admitted to the honor of the priesthood; they deserve to be cut off even from the Christian name.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] Another reading: “to be cut off.”]

For, asking pardon from your piety as I speak, they darken the splendor of your serenity by a kind of contagion, most glorious emperor, when sacrilegious murderers dare to seek what even the innocent are not permitted to obtain.

#### Chapter IV

Petitions were presented to your piety, copies of which you appended to your letters.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] Copies of these petitions, both Catholic and heretical, are found in the encyclial manuscript, volume IV of the Councils, pages 1837 and 1848. Fourteen bishops, four presbyters, and two deacons subscribed the Catholic petition.]

But in the petition of the Catholics, who are lamenting, a subscription is included; and because their cause is defensible, the names of each individual, or the dignity of his office, is openly stated with confidence.

In the other petition, which heretical deception did not fear to present to an orthodox emperor, under the uncertain designation of a confused “whole body,” the definite name is withheld, lest not only the smallness of the number of persons but also their worthlessness should be exposed.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] The ancient editions of Leo, together with the manuscripts of Collection 12, read “unity.” The petition of the heretics in the aforementioned encyclial manuscript lacks subscriptions.]

They consider it useful for the quantity of those whose quality has been revealed to remain hidden; and not without reason they are afraid to disclose from what place they come, since they have deserved condemnation.

[Note: [Col. 1130D] Baluzius’s manuscripts read “they are afraid.”]

Thus, one petition contains the supplication of the Catholics; the other lays bare the fabrications of the heretics. In the first, the overthrow of the Lord’s priests, of the entire Christian people, and of the monasteries is lamented; in the other, the continuation of monstrous crimes is displayed—so that what was not permitted to be heard might be permitted to spread.

#### Chapter V

Is it not clear whom your piety ought to assist and whom it ought to oppose, lest the Alexandrian Church, which has always been a house of prayer, should now be a den of thieves?

[Note: [Col. 1131C] 1, question 1, “It is manifest that the cruelty,” chapter 69.]

It is manifest that, through the most cruel and insane savagery, every light of the heavenly mysteries has been extinguished there.

[Note: [Col. 1131C] The edition of the encyclial manuscript reads “through the most inhuman and insane madness.” Baluzius’s manuscripts read “through the most insane madness.”]

The offering of the sacrifice has been interrupted, the sanctification of the chrism has failed, and all the mysteries have withdrawn from the murderous hands of the impious.

Nor can there be any doubt what must be decreed concerning those who, after unspeakable sacrileges, after the blood of a most approved priest was shed and the ashes of his burned body were scattered to insult the air and heaven, dare to claim for themselves the right of the dignity they have usurped and to summon the inviolable faith of apostolic teaching before councils.

[Note: [Col. 1131C] The same manuscripts read “what must be said,” and then “of the most sacred priest”; afterward, “in insult.”]

It is therefore a great thing for you if, in addition to your diadem, the crown of faith is also added to you by the hand of the Lord, and if you triumph over the enemies of the Church. For if it is praiseworthy for you to crush the arms of hostile nations, how great will be the glory of freeing the Alexandrian Church from a most insane tyrant, in whose destruction lies an injury to all Christians?

#### Chapter VI

So that my letters might offer your piety a conversation as though I were present, I understood that whatever I was about to suggest concerning the common faith should be conveyed in the writing that follows.

And lest the page of this letter be extended to excessive length, I have included in another letter matters appropriate to the defense of the Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Letter 165, otherwise 134.]

Although what has been proclaimed by the apostolic see would have been sufficient, these additions nevertheless expose the plots of the heretics.

For your piety’s priestly and apostolic spirit ought also to be stirred to the justice of punishment by this evil: it criminally obscures the purity of the Church of Constantinople, in which certain clergy are found agreeing with the heretics’ view and, by their assertions, assisting the heretics within the very heart of the Catholics.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Other ancient editions of Leo read “assisting the faction of the heretics.” He means the presbyter Atticus, concerning whom the following letter is written.]

If my brother Anatolius is found to be too slack in removing them because he spares them with excessive kindness, may you, in accordance with your faith, deign to provide this medicine also for the Church, so that such men may be expelled not only from the clerical order but also from residence in the city. Thus the holy people of God will no longer be polluted by the contagion of perverse men.

I commend to you, at my request, Bishop Julian and the presbyter Aetius, who are devoted to your piety, so that you may graciously hear their representations in defense of the Catholic faith. For they are truly such men that they can be found entirely useful to your faith.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] The same editions, together with the manuscripts of Collection 12, read “Eutychius,” incorrectly. The Grimanic manuscript, the editions of the encyclial manuscript, and the manuscripts read “Aetius.”]

Given on the Kalends of December, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Constantine and Rufus.

[Note: [Col. 1131D] The same editions of Leo, together with the same manuscripts of Collection 12, read “on the Kalends of November.” The reading of the encyclial manuscript, followed by Quesnellus, is preferable, since the two following letters appear to have been transmitted on the same occasion; one of them is dated on the Kalends of December.]

## LETTER CLVII

[Note: [Col. 1131D] Otherwise 126. On the same day as the preceding letter.]

[Note: [Col. 1131D] In addition to the petition presented to the emperor, mentioned in the Admonition prefixed to the preceding letter, the Catholic bishops presented another petition to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople; it is found in chapter 8 of the encyclial manuscript. In it they asked the same bishop to make their groans known to the most holy pontiff of the Roman Church, Leo, through synodical letters. That he did write to the pontiff is confirmed by his letter to the emperor, recited in chapter 13 of the same manuscript. Epiphanius Scholasticus says in chapter 10 that Anatolius’s letter to Saint Leo was transmitted together with the emperor’s letters. Therefore, this letter of the pontiff, written in reply to Anatolius’s letter, was issued according to Leo’s custom at the same time as the preceding letter to the emperor, namely on the Kalends of December in the year 457; Quesnellus establishes this date by other arguments in his notes. We were unable to find it in any other manuscript besides the Grimanic manuscript, from which it was edited.]

### To Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople

#### Synopsis

I. He urges him to act vigorously before the emperor, whom he praises, for restraining the heretics; and to ensure that the Council of Chalcedon remains firm and that peace is restored to the Alexandrian Church. — II. The murderers must be expelled from it, and the afflicted bishops of Egypt must be assisted. — III. Aid must be given to the bishops who have fled from Egypt; the opponents of the council must be resisted steadfastly. — IV. Concerning the presbyter Atticus and Andrew: they must either be corrected or expelled from the Church.

### Leo to Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople

#### Chapter I

Once again, upon receiving letters from your Belovedness, I learned with great sorrow all that has been done at Alexandria in the most insane manner—if indeed any page of letters could explain such atrocious crimes.

[Note: [Col. 1132D] “Again,” he says, because he had previously received another letter from Anatolius concerning the disturbances of the Egyptians, to which he replied in Letter 155.]

But we must no longer linger in lamenting adversities, since it is more useful to provide for what may help and may finally drive the fury of the heretics away from the peace of the Church.

Since divine providence has given us such an emperor that his faith almost surpasses the concern of the priests, the energetic action of your Belovedness is especially expected: do not cease to entreat the most reverend emperor on behalf of the universal Church, and to ask through frequent representations that the Alexandrian Church be freed as soon as possible from those who have invaded it.

For my part, I have entreated the most devout emperor as much as I could,

[Note: [Col. 1132D] Letter 156.]

so that he might command the statutes of the holy Council of Chalcedon to remain inviolate, recognize that the assertions of the heretics are sinking into the blindness of great ignorance, and understand that what the sacrilegious murderers committed by usurping the priesthood cannot be tolerated by any dissimulation.

Nor can the entire matter be brought to an end in any other way than if the constitutions of the aforesaid council receive the strength of perpetual validity, the utterly insane usurpers are expelled from another’s see, and the Alexandrian people finally become a people of quiet and peace. Otherwise, through the will of a few heretics, they will be plunged into harm to the Church and offense against God.

#### Chapter II

I received great consolation from the fact that, among the entire number of bishops presiding over the Egyptian dioceses, only four of those long ago condemned could be found who were joined to Timothy both in the impiety of heresy and in the brigandage of his crime. They could in no way be admitted to seek a council, even if they were accused only of heretical error.

But since they perpetrated an unheard-of crime both by seizing the episcopate and by killing a bishop, what place is there for them in the Church, even if they accept the Catholic truth?

Therefore, aid and remedy must be provided to all the priests of the Lord within Egypt, whether more recent occupants or residents established there by ancient constitution, so that they may be freed from such unworthy persecutions; this evil, which has intruded into the inner chambers of so great a city, must be expelled by salutary authority; and the Christian people, previously devoted in faith and works, must be able peacefully to serve according to the constitutions of the Fathers.

#### Chapter III

I have not ceased to commend our brothers who came from the Egyptian region to Constantinople to the emperor in my letters. But I also remind you of your humanity, so that you may deign to apply as much effort as you can to the consolation of their exile. Their presence can greatly assist your Belovedness with the most gracious emperor, so that he may not consent to the petition of the heretics for a new council, which is hostile to the universal Church.

Although the apostolic see is founded upon such faith and stability that it will in no way accept assent to this novelty, nevertheless, if anyone believes that the schemes of the opponents should be indulged, he will himself separate from communion with the Catholic Church. For, according to God’s inspiration, the universal Church has one judgment both concerning the faith of Christ’s Incarnation and concerning the preservation of the Council of Chalcedon.

And especially in our regions evangelical teaching is held so firmly that it is considered a great sacrilege to depart even in the smallest matter from apostolic tradition.

#### Chapter IV
[Note: Epistles 152, 156.] I recall having written to Your Charity some time ago, so that you would not allow anyone in the clergy of your Church to consent to the Eutychian heresy, since the danger to the head is involved if anything diseased is found in the members. But since this has still not been cleansed by any correction, and I learn that your presbyter Atticus has advanced to such insolence [Col. 1134A] that in the Church he dares to argue against the Catholic faith and the Council of Chalcedon, I am compelled to complain more vigorously about your dissimulation. For what you ought to have done without being admonished, I am astonished to find neglected even after our explicit letters. Therefore I warn you more sharply and protest that this must no longer be concealed, if you should think that the pestilential man is to be retained any longer in your communion. We would prefer that he be corrected rather than perish, if that is possible: namely, if he wishes to appear corrected and to remain in ecclesiastical fellowship, then, from that place where he argued at length against the Catholic faith, let him now openly appear as a preacher of that very faith, and let him condemn before the Christian people, by an open declaration of his belief, every point of Eutychian doctrine without exception. [Col. 1134B] Otherwise, as I have said, let this dissimulation stain you greatly, if neither this man, so guilty, nor Andrew, his partner in impiety, is corrected or rejected.

## Epistle CLVIII

[Note: Formerly 127. Written 1 December 457.]  
[Note: This epistle, published from the Grimani manuscript, has so far been found in no other codex.]

### To the Catholic Bishops of Egypt Residing at Constantinople

### Summary

He consoles the bishops who are exiles for the sake of the faith and exhorts them to patience by setting before them the hope of heavenly recompense, while reporting his promised action with the emperor.

**Leo to the Catholic bishops of Egypt residing at Constantinople.**

In former times, reports of the crimes committed at Alexandria saddened me and wounded my spirit by the enormity of the deed itself, so that I do not know with what tears or lamentation it should be mourned; and rightly I proclaim in the prophetic words: “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” Yet, anticipating the complaints of Your Charity, I entreated the most merciful and Christian emperor concerning remedies for such great evils. Through our sons Gerontius and Olympius, serving as assistant envoys at different times, I also repeatedly requested that he order the Church of that city—where so many Catholic teachers flourished—to be cleansed of the condemned heresy, and that he allow nothing to be obtained from his clemency by the murderous minds whom neither reverence for the place nor respect for the time could deter from the blood of their own ruler.

[Note: Proterius, evidently, was killed in the baptistery on the day of the Lord’s Supper.]

[Note: The letter sent through Gerontius is Epistle 148, written on the Kalends of September of this same year, 457; for Epistles 152 and 153, which were sent through Gerontius, were given on the same day. The letter sent through Olympius is missing. See note 4 at Col. 1126, at the end, in Epistle 155.]

This is especially urgent since they desire the Council of Chalcedon to be reopened for the overthrow of the faith. Therefore the same cause that drove Your Charity from your own sees ought also to console your endurance: for it is certain that troubled minds, and those who suffer adversity for His name, are never abandoned by the Lord’s protection.

[Col. 1134D] Bear it, then, with great courage, and, keeping in mind that homeland which is truly yours, rejoice in your present exile. Let the grief of banishment be far from you; let there be no sorrow in you on account of this hardship, since you know that the Apostle also gloried in many dangers for the Lord’s faith. You have as the witness of this struggle Him who has prepared the rewards of recompense. Let no one flee from this labor, whose reward is either to reign or to live forever.

[Note: So reads the Grimani manuscript, the sole source from which this epistle was published. See the edition of P. Cacciari. Quesnell changed *vel* (“or”) to *et* (“and”) by the same arbitrary judgment by which, in Epistle 149, he changed *concilium* (“council”) to *judicium* (“judgment”), and in Epistle 128 changed a similar particle, *vel*, to *et*. This example confirms what we have noted elsewhere: Leo repeatedly uses *vel* for *et*.]

Let the feet of all who fight be planted in the courts of Jerusalem. Through hope of that recompense they will be able to fear neither the enemy’s camp nor the battles. Victory is never arduous, nor the palm difficult, over the remnants of a cast-down enemy, struck down together by the whole body—especially when you already see the leaders of those remnants prostrate.

[Note: Eutyches and Dioscorus, condemned and driven into exile.]

Therefore, with constant prayers—as he himself has not ceased to do—seek the favor of the most Christian emperor, which, with God’s gracious help, is readily available. Thus, in accordance with the letters I have sent,

[Note: Epistle 156.]

may he strengthen the cause of the common faith with that devotion of mind which we have found in him; and, in his piety, may he arrange for Your Charity’s return, once all the prejudices generated by the fury of the heretics have been removed; and may he cause every province and every Church, together with its priests, to rejoice in the unshaken peace of Christ.

Given on the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Constantine and Rufus.

## Epistle CLIX

[Note: Formerly 129. Written 21 March 458.]  
[Note: We found this epistle in manuscripts of Collections 1, 3, and 5; in Dionysius, Hadrian, Hispana, Isidore 11, 12, and 13; in Collections 21 through 24; and in a copy of Sichardus. We also compared it with Verona 60 and with Cresconius, and in some places with the Herovallian copy published by Petit. In the latter it is addressed to Niceta.]

### To Nicetas, Bishop of Aquileia

[Note: In the manuscripts of Collection 5 this epistle is divided into four chapters. The first contains the first four chapters published from Dionysius; the second corresponds to the fifth, the third to the sixth, and the fourth to the seventh. The table prefixed to the collection gives these titles under chapter 74: “Response to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, concerning four questions of titles,” namely:

I. Concerning women who, while their husbands were led into captivity during a hostile invasion, joined themselves to other men.  
II. Concerning Christians who, compelled by captivity, were defiled by sacrificial foods.  
III. Concerning those who appeared to have repeated baptism, whether through fear of the enemy or through error.  
IV. Concerning those who first received baptism from heretics, although they had not previously been baptized.]

### Summary  
(From Dionysius Exiguus)

I. Women who had married other men are to be reunited with their former husbands when those husbands return from captivity, so that each may recover what belongs to him.  
II. A man is not to be judged culpable if he appears to have taken in marriage the wife of a captive.  
III. If husbands returning from captivity are not offended by their wives’ conduct and wish to take them back in marriage, they are to have complete freedom to do so.  
IV. If women refuse to return to their former husbands, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as impious.  
V. Captives compelled by terror [Alternative reading: error] or hunger, rather than by reverence, to eat sacrificial foods are to be granted penance.  
VI. Those who, compelled by force or error [Alternative reading: fear], inclined their minds toward a repetition of baptism are to be relieved by a remedy, with careful consideration being given to old age, dangers, illnesses, and other necessities.  
VII. Those baptized by heretics are to be strengthened solely by invocation of the Holy Spirit.

**Leo, bishop, sends greetings to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.**

My son Adeodatus, deacon of our see, who has returned to us,

[Note: The Vatican, Hispana, and Isidore manuscripts omit “of our see.” Later, the words following this are absent from the Vatican and Reginensis manuscripts, Collection 5 of the Vindobonensis, the Florentine manuscript, Collection 13 of Saint Mark’s, and Justellus.]

reported that Your Charity had requested from us the authority of the Apostolic See concerning matters that appear to present considerable difficulty of judgment. But, in view of the circumstances of the times, care must be applied so that wounds inflicted by the adversity of war may be healed especially through religious consideration.

### Chapter I. Concerning women who married others because their husbands were taken captive

Since, therefore, you say that, through the disaster of war and the gravest assaults of hostility, certain marriages were so divided that, when the husbands had been led into captivity, their wives were left without support,

[Note: Vatican Reginensis Collection 1 reads *diversa* (“different”) for *divisa* (“divided”).]

[Note: The disaster inflicted by Attila upon Italy in 452 is indicated; Aquileia was devastated above all.]

and since, believing their own husbands either to have been killed or never to be freed from the power of their captors, they went over, compelled by their isolation, to the marriage of other men, and since now, with the condition of affairs turned for the better by the Lord’s help, some of those who were thought to have perished have returned, Your Charity rightly seems uncertain what we should decree concerning the women who have been joined to other men.

But because we know that it is written, “A woman is joined to a man by God” (Proverbs 19:14), and because we recognize the command that “what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6), we must believe that the bonds of lawful marriage are to be restored.

[Note: Vatican Dionysius 5845 and Verona Cresconius delete *quod* (“what”) and read *a Domino* (“by the Lord”).] When the evils brought by hostility have been removed, what each person lawfully possessed must be restored to that person.

[Note: The particle *quod* (“what”), found with the ancient printed editions, manuscripts of the Vindobonensis Collection 5, both Hispana manuscripts, Vatican manuscripts, Isidore, others of Collection 21, and the copies of Justellus, Merlinus, and Sichardus, is retained. The same printed editions shortly afterward read *putarint* (“they may have thought”) and *crediderint* (“they may have believed”) and *et ad aliorum conjugium* (“and to the marriage of others”). Six manuscripts of different collections, although agreeing with Justellus in reading *putarent* (“they thought”) and *crederent* (“they believed”), nevertheless have *in aliorum* (“into that of others”). The Vindobonensis Hispana has *sed in aliorum* (“but into that of others”); the Vatican Hispana, *et aliorum* (“and of others”); and Vindobonensis Collection 5, *sed et in aliorum* (“but also into that of others”). Later, for *solitudine* (“isolation”), both Hispana manuscripts, together with the Vatican Isidore and related copies, read *sollicitudine* (“anxiety”). Quesnell gives in the margin the alternative: “to the embrace of other husbands, compelled by anxiety.”]

[Note: Vatican Collection 3, Vindobonensis Collection 5, both Hispana manuscripts, Cresconius, Isidore, and Justellus read *id quod* (“that which”) for *hoc quod* (“what”).]

Every effort must therefore be made so that each person receives what is his own.

[Note: The Vindobonensis Hispana has “and of all.”]

### Chapter II. Whether the man who took the place of the captive husband is culpable

Nor is the man to be judged culpable or regarded as an invader of another’s right if he took the place of a husband who was already believed not to exist.

In this way many things belonging to those who had been led into captivity could pass into another’s possession; nevertheless, it is entirely just that, when those people return, their property should be restored to them. If this is rightly observed with slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be done in the restoration of marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored by the remedy of peace?

### Chapter III. That the wife is to be restored to her first husband

Therefore, if husbands returning after a long captivity remain so devoted to their wives that they wish them to return to their partnership, what necessity brought about must be set aside and judged blameless, while what fidelity demands must be restored.

[Note: The ancient printed editions, together with Vatican Reginensis Collection 1 and Vindobonensis Collection 5, read *perseverant* (“remain steadfast”). Later, in place of *omittendum* (“must be set aside”), Vatican Collection 3 reads *admittendum est* (“must be admitted”). Vindobonensis Collection 5 and Justellus read *restituendum est* (“must be restored”).]

### Chapter IV. Women unwilling to return to their first husbands are to be excommunicated

[Col. 1137B]

But if some women have been so captivated by love of their later husbands that they prefer to remain with them rather than return to their lawful union, they are deservedly to be censured, even to the point of being deprived of ecclesiastical communion. They have chosen the contamination of crime in a matter that could be excused, thereby showing that, through their lack of self-restraint, they preferred what a just forgiveness could have expiated.

[Note: Quesnell omitted *his* (“with them”); we have restored it from all our manuscripts and the earlier printed editions.]

[Note: The ancient printed editions, together with the Vatican Collection 24 manuscript and Sichardus, read: “because they inexcusably chose the contamination of crime, and so forth.” The correction introduced by Quesnell from his two manuscripts, Cresconius and Dionysius, is approved by our other seventeen copies.]

[Note: Vatican Collection 3 reads *sibimetipsis* (“to themselves”). It then reads *potuit* (“could”) for *poterat* (“could”); the ancient printed editions, with Vindobonensis Collection 5 and Sichardus, have the latter reading.]

Let marriages therefore return to their proper condition through voluntary restoration, and let what necessity extorted in no way be dragged into the reproach of evil will. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands are to be regarded as impious,

[Note: The Vatican Dionysius, with Justellus, reads *noluerint* (“should refuse”); Vercelli Hadrianus, with Cresconius, reads *noluerunt* (“have refused”).]

so those who return to the affection established by God are deservedly to be praised.

[Note: The manuscripts of the three oldest collections, 1, 3, and 5, read “are to be judged praiseworthy.”]

### Chapter V. Concerning those who, while captive, ate sacrificial food under compulsion of hunger or fear

[Col. 1138A]

Concerning those Christians who, among the people by whom they had been taken captive, are said to have been defiled by sacrificial foods, we have believed that this also must be answered to Your Charity’s inquiry:

[Note: Vatican Collection 3, both Vatican Hispana manuscripts, Isidore, Merlinus, and Sichardus read *credimus* (“we believe”) for *credidimus* (“we have believed”).]

they are to be cleansed by the satisfaction of penance, which is to be measured not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart.

[Note: The Verona manuscript of Cresconius and its edition read: “But these Christians.” The Vatican Dionysius then has: “had been led into captivity, assert that they were defiled by sacrificial foods.”]

Whether terror extorted this from them or hunger persuaded them, it must not be doubted that the matter is to be abolished, since such food was taken because of fear or necessity, not out of reverence for religion.

[Note: The pure Vatican Dionysius, together with one Vercelli Hadrianus and Justellus, reads *error* (“error”).]

### Chapter VI. Concerning those who were rebaptized through fear or error

[Note: Vercelli Hadrianus, together with Justellus and the edition of Cresconius, reads *Hi vero* (“But these”), incorrectly.]

Concerning those whom Your Charity likewise believed should be consulted by us—those who were compelled by fear or led astray by error to repeat baptism, and who now recognize that they acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—we must maintain such moderation that they are received into our fellowship and the unity of communion only through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

[Note: Vatican Collection 24 and Sichardus read *ratio* (“method” or “principle”).]

The periods of their penance are to be established by your judgment, with due moderation, according to how devoted you perceive the minds of those who have turned back to be.

[Note: Canon 26, question 7, “The periods of penance,” chapter 2.]

At the same time, you must take account of old age and consider the needs arising from every kind of danger or illness.

[Note: Justellus, together with the Vercelli Hadrianus manuscripts, both Hispana manuscripts, the Vatican Isidore, and other manuscripts of Collection 21, reads *habentes* (“having”) and shortly afterward *respicientes* (“considering”); these readings are incorrect. The Vatican Reginensis manuscripts, both Vindobonensis Collection 5 manuscripts, the Hispana, and the Verona Cresconius, together with Justellus, read “or illnesses.”]

If anyone is so gravely afflicted in these matters that, while still doing penance, his salvation is despaired of, priestly concern must come to his aid with the grace of communion.

### Chapter VII. Concerning those who were baptized only once, but by heretics

Those who received baptism from heretics, although they had not previously been baptized,

[Note: Canon 1, question 1, “Those who have baptism,” chapter 71.]

are to be strengthened solely by the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, because they received only the form of baptism without the power of sanctification.

[Note: The Vindobonensis Hispana reads “had not been previously baptized.” Concerning the statement that those baptized by heretics are to be confirmed through the laying on of hands by the sole invocation of the Holy Spirit, Quesnell noted in a marginal annotation that the sacrament of confirmation is indicated. Likewise, shortly afterward, at the words “so that they may obtain from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics,” he understood the sacrament of confirmation and added this further note: “Confirmation cannot validly be conferred by heretics.” He also inserted this interpretation in the index, assigning this meaning to the word *confirmentur* (“let them be confirmed”).

But in two other letters concerning the same heretics returning to the Catholic Church, the holy pontiff repeats the same position concerning the laying on of hands, yet does not use the word “to confirm.” In Epistle 166, to Neon: “Let only that which was lacking there be supplied, so that through the laying on of the bishop’s hand they may receive the power of the Holy Spirit.” And in Epistle 167, to Rusticus, chapter 18: “Through the laying on of hands, with the power of the Holy Spirit invoked—the power which they could not receive from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics.”

It is clear that the laying on of hands is indicated here, not the sacrament of confirmation, which was always administered to people already reborn and justified, but the rite by which those deprived of the grace of the Holy Spirit through heresy and separated from the Church received that grace and were admitted into the Church’s unity. This laying on of hands was a rite of penance. Thus Saint Stephen, in the decree concerning the reception of heretics, prescribed that hands be laid upon them for penance—a formula that in no way suits the sacrament of confirmation. Likewise Crescens of Cirta, at the Third Council of Carthage in the time of Cyprian, prescribed that they be reconciled to the Church through the laying on of hands for penance. Innocent I, too, in Epistle 24 to Alexander, says: “We receive their [the heretics’] laypeople under the appearance of penance and the invocation of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands.” And Saint Cyprian, in Epistle 71, says: “[lacuna] to lay a hand for penance.” These words, “for penance,” remove every suspicion that the sacrament of confirmation is intended.

Quesnell himself clearly saw this when he wrote notes on the letter to Rusticus. In the passage cited shortly before from that letter, note 19, he wrote: “When the laying on of hands is mentioned by itself, it signifies no sacrament, much less confirmation, but only prayers and supplications joined to the laying on of hands.” If Leo used the word “to confirm” in this letter, that ought not to cause any difficulty. For since here and in the letter to Rusticus he is speaking of the same heretics—they all concern the same invasion by Attila and the same period—if the sacrament of confirmation is neither to be introduced nor understood in the letter to Rusticus, where the verb “to confirm” is not read, neither is it to be introduced or understood in this letter to Nicetas, nor in the other letter to Neon of Ravenna, where the same heretics are discussed.

When Saint Leo indicated the sacrament of confirmation in Sermon 4 on the Nativity, chapter 5, he said: “The reborn receive through water and the Holy Spirit the chrism of salvation and the seal of eternal life.” The laying on of hands mentioned in the letters cited, which is applied not to the reborn and justified but to sinful heretics returning to the Church, is not confirmation but a rite of penance.

I will bring forward another clear argument on this subject from Leo himself. In many places he speaks of heretical clerics who, on returning to unity, were received in their own rank; he never indicates that hands should be laid upon them, but is content with a profession of faith alone. See Epistle 1 to the bishop of Aquileia, where the reception of Celestian clerics is discussed; Epistle 12 to the bishops of Mauritania, concerning Donatus, bishop of the Novatians, and Maximus, a former Donatist bishop; and Epistle 18 to Januarius, in which he speaks of other heretical clerics and requires from them only a profession of faith. Likewise, in other letters, when he permits Eutychian clerics to be received in their own rank, he requires that they make a completely sincere profession of faith.

This discipline was consistently observed in the Church: when clerics returned from heresy to the Church, if they had not been defiled by rebaptism, they were received by a profession of faith alone and remained in their own rank; hands were never laid upon them. This could be demonstrated by almost innumerable examples. Hence Innocent I, in the passage quoted shortly before, states that only laypeople were received through the laying on of hands. If the sacrament of confirmation had been indicated by this laying on of hands, there would have been no reason for it to be applied only to laypeople and not to clerics converted from heresy who had not been defiled by rebaptism.

Why, then, was there this distinction between laypeople and clerics? Clearly because this laying on of hands was a rite of penance, appropriate to laypeople alone and not to clerics who were to be received in their own rank. The only clerics excepted by Leo were those who had been baptized again, since rebaptism excluded a person from every clerical rank. Therefore, when these men were received into the Church, they too were subjected to penance like the other laypeople, and for that same reason could not be admitted to the clergy. See Epistle 24 of Innocent I to Rufus, section 4, which should be compared with Epistle 2, section 11, where those who have been rebaptized are said to be admitted after prolonged penitential satisfaction.

This concerns the discipline by which, as Vigilius says in Epistle 2 to Profuturus, section 4, the reconciliation of those rebaptized occurs “not through that laying on of hands which operates through invocation of the Holy Spirit, but through that by which the fruit of penance is acquired and restoration to holy communion is accomplished.” The first form of reconciliation, which was completed by the laying on of hands alone without requiring additional penance, was used with laypeople alone, because unrebaptized clerics were received in their own rank. The second was used with all who had been rebaptized, whether laypeople or clerics, since, on account of their repeated baptism, they could not be received into the clergy.

Saint Leo expressly affirms in the same letter to Rusticus, chapter 2, that the first laying on of hands—which, although it did not subject them to arduous penitential works, nevertheless, as we have seen from Innocent I, bore the appearance of penance—was unsuitable for clerics being restored to their own rank. He appeals there both to ecclesiastical custom and to apostolic tradition. We shall discuss this matter further in the observations on Quesnell’s notes.]

And this rule, as you know, we proclaim is to be observed in all the Churches: the washing once begun must not be violated by repetition, since the Apostle says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism.”

[Note: The Vatican Hispana, Isidore, Verona Cresconius, and Justellus read “one God.”]

Its cleansing must not be profaned by repetition; rather, as we have said, only the sanctification of the Holy Spirit is to be invoked,

[Note: The Vindobonensis Hispana and Cresconius omit *est* (“is to be”).]

so that they may obtain from Catholic priests what no one receives from heretics.

[Note: Vatican Reginensis Collection 1 reads *accepit* (“has received”).]

You shall cause this letter of ours, which we have issued in response to your brotherly inquiry, to reach all the brethren and your fellow-provincial bishops,
