[Note: The cited Vatican Reginensis manuscript and Vindobonensis Collection 1 omit *et* (“and”).]

so that the authority given may benefit the observance of all.

[Note: The Vatican Isidore and another Vatican manuscript of Collection 11 read “so that it may benefit observance in every respect.” The Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark’s Collection 13 reads “so that it may benefit all observance.” The Vindobonensis Hispana reads “so that it may be for the observance of all.” We have preferred the reading of Vatican Reginensis Collection 1, Vatican Dionysius, other manuscripts of Collections 12 and 24, and Sichardus.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the Emperor Majorian.

[Note: The day and month are recorded in the Vatican Dionysius, Hadrianus, the Florentine Collection 13 of Saint Mark’s, and one Vatican manuscript of Collection 21. The Vatican Reginensis Collection 1 reads: “Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April,” where it was easy for the double unit, written with two joined strokes, to be changed into a V. Vindobonensis Collection 5 reads: “Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April.”

The consulship of Majorian is recorded in all witnesses except Vatican Dionysius, where by error it is written: “In the consulship of Tarianus Augustus.” Vindobonensis Collection 5 reads: “With Majorian Augustus as first consul,” as in the editions before Quesnell, who corrected the name to “Majorian” but retained “first consul.” This expression is absent not only from the other codices but also conflicts with ancient usage. The Vatican Reginensis manuscript places the siglum “GL. P.” before Majorian’s name, as does the Florentine Saint Mark’s manuscript before the same name in Epistle 163. Whether this should be read as *gloriosi* or *gloriosissimi principis*—“of the glorious” or “most glorious emperor”—may be left to the judgment of others.]

## Epistle CLX

[Note: Formerly 130. Written 21 March 458.]  
[Note: Quesnell published this epistle from the Grimani codex.]

### To the Catholic Bishops and Clergy from Egypt Residing at Constantinople

### Summary

I. He consoles the exiled bishops and clergy of Egypt and informs them that, with the emperor’s approval, he is sending his own envoys to the East.  
II. He urges them to remove every new discussion concerning the faith, since the authority of the Council is sufficient.

To the most beloved brothers Nestorius, Athanasius, Paul, Peter, Theonas, Isaiah, Apollonius, Harpocrates, Isidore, Isaac, Apollonius, Maximus, Marion, Poemenius, and Helpidius, bishops and Catholic clergy from Egypt residing at Constantinople: Leo.

[Note: Fifteen bishops are named here. In the petition submitted to the emperor by these same Egyptians, and transmitted to Pope Leo together with the emperor’s letter—the petition is reproduced in the *Encyclical* in volume IV of the Councils, p. 1843—only fourteen are subscribed. Not only is the order different, but the names of two bishops, Pulsaminon, or rather Pulsamon, and another Athanasius, appear there although they are not listed in this epistle’s inscription. Conversely, this inscription names three bishops absent from those subscriptions: Isidore, Elpidius, and one Apollonius. The other Apollonius appears to be the same person who is called Apollo in the subscriptions.

Elpidius and an Apollonius distinct from Apollo are also read in other subscriptions of the Constantinopolitan synod under Gennadius, in volume V of the Councils, p. 51, where the names of the bishops Theonas and Marion may likewise be found. From a comparison of both sets of subscriptions, the sees of the individual bishops can be determined, with the exception of Isidore, who appears in neither.]

### Chapter I

Believe confidently that the tribulation inflicted upon Your Charity by the spirit of diabolical temptation is to be relieved by Him for whose sake you suffer such things. Assume that you are to be consoled by the help of Him for whose love you endure what you endure. Although He permits adverse things to occur temporarily, He does not wish the constancy of faith to be shaken but tested.

Bearing the hope of the promised blessedness, apply long-suffering patience to your minds. “For God is faithful, and He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear, but with the temptation He will also provide the way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13). Nor should the apparent peace of sinners dislodge your feet, which you ought to keep fixed upon that rock against which, as you read, the gates of hell cannot prevail (Matthew 16:18).

Since, then, dearest brothers, the most Christian emperor has again sent us a letter,

[Note: The emperor’s letter to which Saint Leo responds in Epistle 162 is meant.]

in which he urges us to send someone from our regions—and although your instruction there, capable of opposing the obstinacy of the heretics, is not lacking, he nevertheless wishes someone to be sent by us who can uphold the faith before those who condemn it and, in a diabolical spirit, do not receive it as though it were still doubtful—a faith which is preached as necessary and received willingly—

I warn Your Charity that, by saying the same thing, you should all avoid the competition of empty glory through the power of unanimity.

You know what palm belongs to you in this contest. He who watches it is also its judge and helper; He Himself is sufficient to give strength for victory, and He has already prepared a reward for those who love Him.

Let no one complain that he is an exile from his own seat, or lament that he has been driven from his ancestral borders. None of you is an exile from God, and you may confidently trust that He will help you everywhere. Bear everything patiently, and, with a strengthened heart, faithfully await the Lord.

The tribulation imposed by time is brief. Nor should the things you know that you are enduring from the Lord’s enemies appear new to your confession. For they also persecuted the prophets who came before you (Matthew 5:12).

### Chapter II

[Note: From this point to the end, the passage is quoted by Facundus Hermianus, Book XII, chapter 2, p. 533.]

Therefore, with every effort and labor of Your Charity, you must strive to prevent any debate by those lying in wait from being admitted, and to prevent the heretics from obtaining what is manifestly an attack upon the evangelical faith.

For nothing ought to be debated concerning matters defined by the authority of so great a council or of the most Christian emperor, and confirmed by the assent of the Apostolic See, lest anything seem to be infringed contrary to divine law.

Much is taken away from faith and priestly steadfastness if a contest of superfluous and deeply harmful disputation is held with those who are filled with murder and fury, who wish to overturn the Gospel of Christ, and who are proved by their crime to hate it.

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the Emperors Leo and Majorian.

## Epistle CLXI

[Note: Formerly 131. Written 21 March 458.]  
[Note: Published by Quesnell from the cardinal Grimani codex.]

### To the Presbyters, Deacons, and Clergy of the Church of Constantinople

### Summary

I. He exhorts them to remain steadfast in the faith and separate from the fellowship of the heretics.  
II. He urges that no new judgment be instituted, and that Atticus and Andrew be deprived of the honor of their rank unless they profess, by voice and writing, their adherence to the faith of Chalcedon.

**Leo to the presbyters, deacons, and clergy of the Church of Constantinople.**

### Chapter I

I have been greatly gladdened and exceedingly delighted that the steadfastness of your faith has been made known to me—a faith in which I glory in the Lord. I understand that in every respect you are most devoted disciples of evangelical teaching and that you think absolutely nothing different from the apostolic preaching that flowed from the same source.

For the Catholic faith, which is true and one, does not permit itself to be violated by any diversity. Therefore I do not cease to exhort and admonish Your Charity that, instructed by the Holy Spirit, you should all perseveringly say the same thing, and that there be no schisms among you.

“Be perfect in the same understanding and in the same judgment” (1 Corinthians 1:10). Drive far from your fellowship the errors of those who were long ago condemned, as you have begun to do, remaining steadfast in the faith. Do not allow anyone infected with Nestorian or Eutychian perversity to associate with you, as though the error into which each of these men led the hearts of certain foolish people and inflamed them toward the crimes of diabolical fury were something trivial or tolerable.

[Note: Perhaps the reading should be “the error into which each of the two led certain foolish hearts.”]

### Chapter II

[Note: Quoted by Facundus Hermianus, Book XII, chapter 2, p. 533.]

By God’s favor we possess the great assistance divinely prepared through the most Christian emperor. In my letters I entreated him, as the cause required,

[Note: The printed edition from the Grimani manuscript reads *exstitit* (“has arisen” or “has existed”). We have preferred the reading of Facundus, which Quesnell placed in the margin.]

not to grant any assent of his clemency to the wicked petitions of murderers, and not to allow the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon—which truly proceeded from heavenly decrees—to be violated as though they required reconsideration.

For it is evident that the ambushes of the impious are creeping forward for this purpose: to make decisions consonant with evangelical preaching and the traditions of the Fathers invalid through a new judgment, and, once debate is admitted, to remove authority.

[Note: In Facundus: “with the plotters against the earlier decisions.” Facundus quotes as far as this point.]

As I hope, divine protection will be present through its inspirations and will grant the holy emperor the ability to prevent in every way what he recognizes to be opposed to human salvation.

But Atticus and Andrew—their names I indicated to my brother and fellow bishop Anatolius in letters sent previously,

[Note: Epistle 157, chapter 4.]

men whom I have learned dissent from your praiseworthy faith and most openly connive at the perfidy of the Eutychians—are to be deprived of the honor of their rank unless they first condemn the hostile doctrines by their own voice and signature, and, in the presence of the Christian people in the Church, profess that they will follow the faith strengthened by the Council of Chalcedon.

[Col. 1143B] This is so that the levity of wolves may not be mingled any longer with the simplicity of the Lord’s sheep.

[Note: Perhaps “the cruelty” or “the depravity” of wolves. Quesnell gives the alternatives in the margin.]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the Emperors Leo and Majorian.

## 1339 LETTER CLXII

[Note: Formerly 132. Written 21 March 458.]

**TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** Through Philoxenus, an imperial agent (*agens in rebus*).

[Note: This letter appears in the manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 12, 18, 19, and 21 through 24.]

### SUMMARY

[Note: In the table of collection 5, this summary appears as chapter 94: “On urging the cutting off of the Eutychian heresy and confirming the council.”]

I. He must not allow a faith once defined to be brought back for examination.  
II. He can neither associate with heretics in communion nor dissent from what the synod has defined.  
III. He is sending representatives, not to debate but to instruct.  
IV. Heretics must be avoided; he indicates that punishment also awaits them.

**LEO, bishop, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.**

[Note: The codex of the Venetian collection of Saint Mark, 22, reads: “My mind rejoices with great joy.”]

My mind exults with great joy in the Lord, and I have abundant reason for rejoicing when I recognize that the outstanding faith of Your Clemency is increasing in every respect through the gifts of heavenly grace; and, as your diligence grows, I experience in you the devotion of a priestly spirit. For in the addresses of Your Piety it is plainly evident what the Holy Spirit is accomplishing through you for the salvation of the entire Church, and how much all the prayers of the faithful ought to desire that your rule be extended to every glory, most glorious emperor. You steadfastly devote yourself, beyond the administration of temporal affairs, to the service of religious providence and to divine and eternal dispositions.

[Note: Quesnellus, we believe from the Grimanic manuscript alone, reads “reason for congratulation”; all our manuscripts of the other collections, including Vindobonensis collection 5 and Regensburg collection 19, together with the editions before Quesnellus, read “reason for rejoicing.” We have not wished to remove Quesnellus’s reading as the more suitable one. All our manuscripts and the editions before Quesnellus read “through the gifts” (*donis*); Quesnellus has *dono*. Manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 and the Regensburg manuscript read “by how great [prayers]” (*quantis*) in place of “how much.”]

Thus the catholic faith—which alone gives life to the human race and alone sanctifies it—may remain in one confession, and the dissensions arising from the variety of earthly opinions may be driven away from the solidity of that rock upon which the city of God is built.

[Note: “Most glorious emperor” was added by Quesnellus from the Grimanic codex and is absent from the others. Only the Regensburg manuscript places the abbreviation GL before it.]

These gifts of God will be divinely bestowed upon us only if we are not found ungrateful for what has been granted, desiring instead, as though we had obtained nothing, things contrary to it. For to seek what has been revealed, to reconsider what has been completed, and to tear down what has been defined—[Note: The Grimanic manuscript reads “finished” (*finita*).] what else is this than to fail to give thanks for what we have received and to stretch the wicked desires of deadly covetousness toward the fruit of the forbidden tree?

Since, therefore, you deign to look with particularly vigilant concern toward the peace of the universal Church and the preservation of the catholic faith, you clearly recognize what is being attempted through the great plots of heretics: namely, that a more diligent investigation should be undertaken between the followers of Eutyches and Dioscorus and the one whom the apostolic see has sent, as though nothing had previously been defined; and that what the priests of the entire catholic world approved and rejoiced to see established at the holy council of Chalcedon should be made invalid, even to the injury of the most sacred council of Nicaea.

[Note: We have restored the word “diligent,” which Quesnellus removed on the basis of our manuscripts. Shortly afterward, “by the holy Council of Chalcedon” is found in the Regensburg manuscript and in Vatican collection 11.]

For what was established in our time at Chalcedon concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ was also defined at Nicaea by that mystical number of the Fathers, so that the confession of Catholics should neither believe the only-begotten Son of God in any respect unequal to the Father, nor believe that the same Son, when he became the Son of Man, did not possess the true nature of our flesh and soul.

### CHAPTER II

We must therefore continually detest and avoid what heretical fraud strives to obtain. [Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads, “nor are [such matters] to be recalled in any debate.”] Matters that have been piously and fully defined must not be recalled for debate, lest we seem, at the desire of the condemned, to doubt those things that are manifestly consonant in every respect with prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic authorities.

Therefore, if there are any who dissent from what has been established from heaven, let them be left to their own opinions and depart from the unity of the Church with the perversity they have chosen. For it is in no way possible that those who dare to contradict the divine mysteries should be joined with us in any communion.

Let them boast in the vanity of their speech and glory in the subtlety of their arguments, which is hostile to faith. [Note: The same Regensburg manuscript and Vatican collections 11 and 24 read, “Let it please [us] to obey the apostolic commands, which say”; the editions before Quesnellus, with the manuscripts of collection 21, read, “It pleases [us] to obey the apostolic commands, which say.”] We are pleased to obey the Apostle’s commands, who says: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit of human beings” (Colossians 2:8).

For, according to the same Apostle, “If I rebuild the things I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor” (Galatians 2:18), and I subject myself to those conditions of punishment which not only the authority of the blessed emperor Marcian but I myself also confirmed by my assent.

[Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Others have *defensione* or *confessione* [‘defense’ or ‘confession’].” We found neither reading in any of our manuscripts.]

For, as you have said holily and truly, perfection does not admit increase, nor fullness addition. Since I know, venerable prince, that you are imbued with the purest light of truth, that you waver in no part of the faith, but by holy and perfect judgment distinguish what is right from what is corrupt and separate what must be embraced from what must be rejected, I beg you not to regard my humility as deserving blame for distrust. My caution serves not only the universal Church but also your glory, lest during your reign the wickedness of heretics appear to have increased and the security of Catholics to have been disturbed.

### CHAPTER III

Although I trust in every respect in the heart of Your Piety and perceive that, through the Spirit of God dwelling in you, you are sufficiently instructed, so that no error could deceive your faith, I shall nevertheless strive to obey your command by sending some of my brothers.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “I strive” (*adnitor*). The earlier editions, with our manuscripts and especially the Regensburg manuscript, read “I shall strive to obey” (*adnitar obedire*); the subject is the legates whom Leo sent only in the following August, as letter 164 shows.] They will represent my presence before you and demonstrate—although, as I have said, it is already well known to you—what the rule of apostolic faith is, making clear and proving in every respect that those who do not follow the definitions of the venerable Council of Nicaea or the canons of the holy Council of Chalcedon must not be counted among Catholics.

For it is evident that the holy decrees of both councils proceed from an evangelical and apostolic source, and that whatever does not come from the irrigation of Christ is the cup of a viper.

[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, with the Regensburg manuscript and Vatican collection 12, read “Your Piety”; this is the reading adopted here.]

[Note: Quesnellus deleted “and apostolic.” We have retained it with the earlier editions, which are supported by our Regensburg manuscript and other codices, except for Vindobonensis collection 5.]

Let Your Piety, therefore, venerable emperor, know in advance that the men whom I promise to send will proceed from the apostolic see not to fight against the enemies of the faith or to contend against anyone. Concerning the matters defined at Nicaea and Chalcedon, as God willed, we dare to undertake no discussion—as though those things established by such great authority through the Holy Spirit were doubtful or insecure.

### CHAPTER IV

We do not refuse the support of our ministry to our little ones who, after the nourishment of milk, desire to be satisfied with more solid food.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “solid [food]” and, shortly afterward, “but just as.” The older editions and the Regensburg manuscript and certain other codices read “the Lord’s command, saying.”] And just as we do not despise the simple, so we abstain from rebellious heretics, mindful of the Lord’s command: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7:6).

For it is exceedingly unworthy and unjust that those whom the Holy Spirit signifies through the prophet should be admitted to the freedom of debate, saying: “Foreign children have lied to me” (Psalm 17:46).

[Note: The ancient Vulgate manuscripts, together with codices of collection 12, add: “Foreign children, grown old.”]

Even if they did not resist the Gospel, they would nevertheless show themselves to belong to those of whom it is written: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). The blood of righteous Abel still cries out against wicked Cain, who, rebuked by the Lord (Genesis 4:10), did not become quiet in repentance but burned with a desire for slaughter.

[Note: The older editions, together with certain codices, read: “did not rest.”]

We wish his punishment to be reserved for the Lord’s judgment, so that the wicked plunderer and cruel murderer may fall back upon himself and not hold us.

Nor should you allow the grievous captivity of the holy Church of Alexandria to be prolonged any further. Its freedom must be restored through the support of your faith and justice, so that throughout all the cities of Egypt the dignity of the Fathers and the priestly right may be restored.

[Note: Quesnellus, with other older editions, reads “the eleventh day before the Kalends”; in the margin he gives “the twelfth day before the Kalends.” We have preferred the latter because it is supported by the majority and the better manuscripts—Vindobonensis collection 5, Vatican collection 11, and manuscripts of collections 21 and 24—and because it agrees with the date indicated in the two preceding letters sent through the same Philoxenus to Constantinople. In manuscripts of collections 11, 21, and 24, Leo’s name is omitted from the consular formula. Two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21 read “with the glorious Augustus Majorianus as consul.” Another Vatican manuscript of collection 24 reads “Calipius” for “Glorious.” This seems to have arisen from the abbreviation GLP, which we observed prefixed to Majorianus’s name in certain manuscripts; see note 31, column 1140, note g, in letter 159. The compiler of collection 24, or some copyist, incorrectly interpreted it as “Calipius.”]

Given on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Leo and Majorian, Augusti.

---

## LETTER CLXIII

[Note: Formerly 128. Written 28 March 458.]

[Note: It appears in the manuscripts of collections 5, 11, 12, 13, and 20 through 24.]

**TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** Through Patritius the deacon.

[Note: In the table of manuscript collection 5, this title appears as chapter 95: “To Anatolius the bishop concerning Atticus the presbyter, that the presbyter be compelled to exclude from himself the acceptance of Eutychian error.”]

### SUMMARY

He complains that his admonitions had displeased Anatolius and warns him that, if Atticus the presbyter wishes to appear catholic, he must publicly condemn the Eutychian error in a subscription of his own.

**LEO, bishop, TO ANATOLIUS, bishop.**

After reading the letter of Your Affection, which you sent through our son Patritius the deacon, I understood that you were displeased with the zeal of my concern. In accordance with the Lord’s charity—which you have approved by many proofs to have been shown by me toward you—I warned you to beware of those who were said to be adversaries of the common faith.

[Note: Vatican collection 11 reads: “who were said to be adversaries of the common faith.”]

This was so that it might not be attributed to the negligence of a ruler if anyone in the catholic Church presumed to preach doctrines agreeing with the opinions of heretics.

[Note: See letter 157, chapter 4.]

I entrusted to your judgment the inquiry into whether rumor was making this claim truthfully. Nor did I in any way injure your dignity, to which I entrusted the examination of what had been reported to me.

[Note: See letter 151.]

[Note: The same codex reads: “the matters requiring examination.”]

Thus Atticus the presbyter, whom I had learned to be daring such things, was to be excluded from the grace of communion unless he cleared himself by complete satisfaction and condemned heretics not only by voice but also by a subscription in his own hand.

By sending writings expressing doubtful faith and uncertain profession, he confirmed rather than dispelled whatever rumor had brought to us concerning him.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 546 of collection 21 reads: “he confirms.”]

If he had wished to prove his conscience sincere, he ought to have confessed not merely that Eutyches was hateful to him, but that he rejected and condemned Eutyches’ impiety. For human quarrels even among Catholics are one thing; the devil’s errors, which the catholic faith condemns, are another.

Therefore, dearest brother, you must not doubt our affection in any respect if you follow the example of the prophet and say: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and do I not waste away because of your enemies?” (Psalm 138:21).

[Note: Vindobonensis collection 5 reads “those.” All our manuscripts and editions before Quesnellus have *tabescebam* (“I wasted away”); Quesnellus has *tabescane*, perhaps through a copyist’s or printer’s error.]

You must be entirely certain that, just as I desire my reputation to remain unharmed, so I also wish you to be found blameless in every respect.

[Note: The same Vindobonensis manuscript, with manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, omits “Atticus.”]

The aforementioned Atticus, therefore, must plainly show what he anathematizes and condemns in Eutyches, so that he may appear free from every contrary suspicion; and, with all doubt removed, he must subscribe to the condemnation of the explicitly stated error. He must profess that he will observe in every respect the definition concerning the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, to which Your Affection also gave assent by subscribing and which the authority of the apostolic see confirmed.

[Note: Most editions before Quesnellus read “the symbol.” This is incorrect: the Fathers of Chalcedon did not compose a new creed but issued a definition of faith against the errors of Eutyches. Our codices read “of the synod,” as do two manuscripts cited by Quesnellus, the Barberinian and Trecopithan, as well as Pelagius II, letter 3 to Elias and the other bishops of Istria, chapter 3, where he quotes testimony from this letter. The formula of this profession is given in collection 5, chapter 55, which we shall publish in volume three. From manuscripts of collection 8, we learn that it particularly concerned the Church of Constantinople. In those manuscripts the same formula bears the title 125: “Confession of the presbyters or deacons of the Church of Constantinople,” and begins: “I, that Constantinopolitan deacon or presbyter, by this writing…” This formula, composed according to Leo’s mind, was either sent from Rome to Constantinople or transmitted from Constantinople to Leo, approved by him, translated into Latin, and incorporated into the cited collections.]

He must add a subscription in his own hand, to be read in the Church in the presence of the Christian people, so that neither we may be regarded as negligent concerning the catholic faith nor he thereafter remain under suspicion.

[Note: Vatican manuscript 546 of collection 21 reads: “which the authority of the apostolic see confirmed.”]

But if he persists in the same perversity and refuses to obey salutary commands, let him receive the sentence of the Council of Chalcedon, against whose definitions he rebels.

[Note: The Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark, collection 13, reads “by a salutary command.” The Cambridge manuscript reads “let him incur” instead of “let him receive.”]

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Leo and Majorian, Augusti.

[Note: Vatican manuscripts, together with manuscripts of collections 12, 21, and 24, read “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.” We have preferred the reading supported by the more authoritative codices—Vindobonensis collection 5, Vatican collection 11, and Florentine collection 13—and by three others cited by Quesnellus in the margin. In manuscripts of collections 11, 13, 21, and 24, Leo’s name is omitted and only Majorian’s consulship is mentioned. The other codices, especially Vindobonensis collection 5, name both consuls, as is likewise noted in all the letters sent to the East in this year. Only the two letters sent to the West, 159 and 166, mention Majorian alone as consul.]

---

## LETTER CLXIV

[Note: Formerly 133. Written 17 August 458.]

[Note: This celebrated letter, of which certain fragments survived in Vigilius, Pelagius, and Facundus, and nearly half of which Prudentius of Troyes transcribed in his book *On Predestination*, was published in full by Quesnellus from the Grimanic manuscript. We found the same letter in our Regensburg manuscript. See Quesnellus’s note.]

**TO LEO AUGUSTUS.**

### SUMMARY

I. He sends representatives to act on behalf of the freedom of the Church and asks that what has been correctly defined not be recalled for a new discussion.  
II. There will always be room for debate if the mysteries are permitted to be examined by human reasoning and the loquacity of rhetoricians.  
III. He explains how hostile to the Gospel and to human salvation is the Eutychian doctrine condemned by the synod; nothing must be taken away from it by debate.  
IV. The Alexandrian murderers are unworthy of every indulgence; nevertheless, if they repent, hope of mercy must not be denied them.  
V. He commends the representatives he is sending—not to debate but to plead—and indicates what must be done for the peace of the Church: penitence must not be denied to those who correct themselves, but the obstinate, who remain under the synodal sentence, must remain condemned.

**LEO, bishop, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.**

[Note: We have added “bishop” from the Regensburg manuscript; Prudentius also confirms it.]

### CHAPTER I

Rejoicing that by many clear proofs it has been demonstrated to me how greatly you care for the universal Church, I did not delay obeying Your Piety’s commands as soon as it was possible. I sent Domitian and Geminian, my brothers and fellow bishops, [Note: The Regensburg manuscript and Prudentius read “Donatian.” We retain “Domitian,” because letter 170 repeats these legates’ names.] so that, carrying out before you the pleas of my concern, [Note: Quesnellus notes in the margin, “Perhaps one should read ‘offices’”; but the Regensburg manuscript also has “pleas.”] they might supplicate you for the peace of evangelical teaching and obtain freedom for the faith, in which you yourself excel above all according to the instruction of the Holy Spirit.

May the enemies of Christ be driven far away. Even if they had wished to conceal their fury, they could not remain hidden, for the holy simplicity of the Lord’s flock is one thing, and the pretense of beasts concealed beneath sheep’s clothing is another. Those whose madness has been exposed with such great violence can no longer creep in through hypocrisy.

[Note: Facundus has the following passage, page 87. The Regensburg manuscript omits “of such great”; shortly afterward it omits “august and.”]

Recognize, therefore, august and venerable emperor, to what extent divine providence has prepared you as a protection for the whole world, and understand how much assistance you owe your mother the Church, which especially glories in you as her son.

[Note: “Do not allow” is read in Vigilius’s *Constitutum* and in Pelagius II’s letter to Elias of Aquileia, where this passage is quoted. In both authors, shortly afterward, “to arise” is read instead of “to rise up.”]

Do not allow struggles that have been extinguished to rise again through renewed disturbances against the triumphs of the right hand of the Almighty—especially since such a thing is entirely forbidden to the condemned attempts of heretics long ago. The fruit of pious labors should be that the entire fullness of the Church remains secure in the solidity of its unity and that nothing whatsoever is reconsidered of what has been properly arranged.

[Note: Vigilius reads “of what has been established.” Immediately afterward, Vigilius and Prudentius read: “because to wish to disturb legitimate and divinely inspired constitutions is not…”]

For to wish to contend after legitimate and divinely inspired constitutions have been established is not the disposition of a peacemaker but of a rebel, as the Apostle says: “Quarreling over words is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (2 Timothy 2:24).

[Note: Pelagius reads “of a human being.”]

### CHAPTER II

For if it is always permitted to debate through human persuasions, there will never be a shortage of people who dare to resist the truth and place confidence in the loquacity of worldly wisdom.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “human wisdom.” We have preferred “worldly,” with the Regensburg manuscript; Vigilius and Facundus likewise have this reading.]

Yet faith and Christian wisdom recognize from the very teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ how greatly this most harmful vanity must be avoided. When he was about to call all nations to the illumination of faith, he did not choose philosophers or orators to serve in preaching the Gospel; rather, he took up humble men and fishermen, through whom he might reveal himself, lest heavenly teaching, which was full of powers, appear to need the assistance of words.

[Note: Prudentius deletes “and wisdom.” Shortly afterward, “our” is absent in the Regensburg manuscript.]

Therefore the Apostle protests and says: “For Christ did not send me to baptize but to evangelize, not in the wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power. For the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God. For it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the intelligent.’ Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe? Where is the investigator of this age? Has God not made the wisdom of this world foolish?” (1 Corinthians 1:17–20).

[Note: Facundus ends here.]

For rhetorical arguments and the subtle techniques of disputation established by human beings especially glory in this: that, amid uncertain matters and the confusion of differing opinions, they draw the judgment of their hearers toward whatever each person has chosen to defend by his ingenuity and eloquence.

[Note: Quesnellus, with Prudentius, reads “confused”; in the margin he records that the Grimanic manuscript has “relying [upon them],” less correctly. The Regensburg manuscript agrees with Prudentius.] Thus what is defended with greater fluency comes to be considered more true.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript and Prudentius support “rhetorical arguments.” Quesnellus, following the Grimanic manuscript, reads “the institutions of rhetoric.”]

But the Gospel of Christ has no need of this art. In it the teaching of truth has been manifested by its own light, and one does not ask what pleases the ears where it is sufficient for true faith to know who is teaching.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “manifest.” Shortly afterward it has “nor does it follow,” rather than the corrupt reading in the Grimanic manuscript. Quesnellus’s correction, based on Prudentius, is confirmed by the Regensburg manuscript. Later, Prudentius and the Regensburg manuscript prefer “who may teach”; the Grimanic manuscript has the corrupt reading “what may teach.”]

### CHAPTER III

Nothing separates those who are deceived by their own inventions more greatly from the evangelical light than their belief that the truth of the Lord’s incarnation does not belong to human nature—that is, to our nature. It is as though it were unworthy of God’s glory that the majesty of the impassible Word should assume the reality of mortal flesh, although human beings could not otherwise be restored to salvation unless the one who is in the form of God deigned to assume the form of a servant.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “the divine incarnation”; shortly afterward, “would have been unworthy of glory.”]

Therefore, when the holy Council of Chalcedon—which was celebrated by all the provinces of the Roman world with the consent of the whole world and is undivided from the decrees of the most sacred Council of Nicaea—cut off all the impiety of Eutyches’ doctrine from the body of catholic communion, how can any of the fallen have access again to ecclesiastical peace unless he has been cleansed through complete satisfaction?

[Note: Quesnellus attached the following comment: “Two characteristics of an ecumenical council: first, representation from all provinces; second, the consent of the whole world.” Leo here intended to touch upon the prerogatives of the Council of Chalcedon, which had been received by the whole Church, in order to show it all the more irretractable; he did not intend to propose these as characteristics necessary to a general synod, as Quesnellus’s note seems to imply. A general convocation is indeed required so that, as our author says in letter 89, a council can truly be universal when priests have been summoned from all provinces. “Truly,” he says—that is, strictly general. Nevertheless, if, after a general convocation has been announced, not all those from every province attend or are able to attend—as happened at the Council of Chalcedon, to which, because of the shortness of the appointed time, scarcely even the legates of the apostolic see could be sent from the whole West—does it follow that the council cannot be general? On the contrary, the practice of the Church shows that councils have been regarded as general when Eastern bishops met with some Western bishops, especially those sent by the Roman see. What chiefly asserted for these synods the prerogative of general councils—namely, binding force—was confirmation and assent by the Roman see. The Fathers of Chalcedon themselves asked this of Leo as necessary; if they had judged the assent of the other bishops of the world equally necessary, they would have sought that as well. See the letter of that synod among Leo’s letters, no. 98, and also Anatolius’s letter 101 and Emperor Marcian’s letter 110.]

For what license of discussion can be granted to those who deserved condemnation by a just and holy judgment? They should rightly receive the sentence of the blessed Apostle John, by which, at the very beginning of the nascent Church, he struck down the enemies of the cross of Christ, saying: “Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God; and this is the spirit of Antichrist” (1 John 4:2).

[Note: Vigilius and Pelagius have this passage; Pelagius attributes it to the letter to Basil.]

With this teaching of the Holy Spirit going before us, we must use it piously and steadfastly, lest, while discussion of such persons is admitted, authority be taken away from what has been divinely defined.

[Note: The reading “with the teaching of the Holy Spirit going before” is from the Regensburg manuscript. Quesnellus, with the Grimanic manuscript, has the less correct “passing through.” Vigilius reads “what must be seen,” “what must be lived,” or “what must be avoided.” Shortly afterward Vigilius, together with Pelagius and the Regensburg manuscript, reads “discussion” instead of “debate”; Pelagius alone has “their authority.”]

Since, throughout all the regions of your kingdom and in every part of the earth, the faith established at Chalcedon is preserved in the deepest peace, no one who cuts himself off from the fellowship of our unity is worthy of the Christian name.

[Note: Quesnellus reads “the fellowship of the truth”; we have corrected this from the Regensburg manuscript to “the fellowship of our unity.”]

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript adds the abbreviation GL, which elsewhere in the same manuscript is rendered in other codices as “most glorious emperor.” Shortly afterward we have followed that manuscript in reading “since throughout,” which is better than Quesnellus’s “while.”]

Concerning such a person the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretical person after one and a second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverted and condemned by his own judgment” (Titus 3:10).

### CHAPTER IV

What the wicked murderer committed in the invasion of the holy Church and in the most cruel slaughter of its bishop cannot be expiated

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “persuasion,” but “invasion” (*pervasione*) must be read; it then reads “most cruel slaughter.”]

by human remissions by human remissions unless he is entreated who alone can worthily punish such deeds and alone, through ineffable mercy, can forgive them.

We, however, do not desire vengeance, but we cannot in any respect associate with the ministers of the devil.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads: “But if they depart from those who have persuaded them…”]

If we learn that they have departed from the perverse, recovered from error, and turned from the weapons of discord to the lamentations of repentance, we too can pray for them, so that they may not perish forever. Thus we may imitate the Lord’s mercy, for he prayed for his persecutors while nailed to the wood of the cross, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:24).

[Note: The following passage is found in Vigilius and Pelagius; the latter attributes it to the letter to Basil.]

But so that Christian charity may fruitfully act on behalf of its enemies, let the wicked cease from attacking the ever-religious and ever-devoted Church of God. Nor should they dare to disturb the minds of the simple people with heretical deceit, so that where the sincerest faith flourished throughout all former times, evangelical and apostolic teaching may now also flourish.

[Note: We have supplied the verb “to attack” from the Regensburg manuscript. Consequently, the explanatory note added by Quesnellus in the margin is unnecessary: “That is, the Alexandrian Church which they had invaded.” The reference is instead to the insults of the Eutychians and Timothy against the Council of Chalcedon, Leo’s letter, and the Catholics whom they misrepresented as Nestorians. Shortly afterward, the Regensburg manuscript reads “the minds of the simple people.”]

For, imitating divine mercy insofar as we are able, we desire that no one be punished by justice but that all be freed through mercy.

### CHAPTER V

[Note: This passage is found in Prudentius.]

I beg Your Clemency to make use of the petitions of my aforementioned brothers, whom, as I already stated in the preceding letter, I have sent to you not to debate with the condemned but to plead with you solely for the stability of the catholic faith.

[Note: Letter 162. The Regensburg manuscript reads “not to debate with the condemned.”]

Above all, may Your Piety, for the sake of your faith and in contemplation of the divine majesty, grant this: that, after the contentions of the heretics have been entirely removed, you deign to extend merciful care to those who have unhappily fallen; and that, once the freedom of the Alexandrian Church has been restored to its former condition, a bishop may be ordained there who observes the statutes of the Council of Chalcedon, agrees with evangelical discipline, and is able to restore peace to the disturbed people.

[Note: The same codex reads “to calm”; shortly afterward, “of Your Piety.”]

Let those bishops and clerics whom the wicked murderer expelled from their churches also be recalled at Your Piety’s command. Let the others whom similar wickedness made exiles from their own homes likewise be restored to their former condition, so that, without the noise of further disputes, we may rejoice fully and perfectly in God’s grace and in the merit of your faith.

For if anyone has so forgotten Christian hope and his own salvation that he dares by debate to violate the evangelical and apostolic decree of the holy Council of Chalcedon, thereby attacking the most sacred Council of Nicaea, we condemn him with the same anathema and equal execration as all the heretics who held impious and detestable opinions concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Thus the remedy of repentance will not be denied to those corrected by proper satisfaction, while the synodal sentence, which is full of truth, will remain upon those who resist.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “the Kalends of September.” Quesnellus’s reading from the Grimanic manuscript is preferable: the following letter was given on the same day, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, and appears to have been sent long previously promised through the same representatives who carried this one.]

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Leo and Majorian, Augusti.

---

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

### (G)

1. Among all Leo’s letters, two are found to be especially famous among both Latins and Greeks: letter 28, to Flavian, and the following letter, to Leo Augustus. They explain and defend the catholic doctrine against the Eutychian heresy more fully than the others.

Hence, when Leo’s letters published in defense of the faith are praised, these two in particular are explicitly mentioned. Just as letter 28 to Flavian was called the first volume, so this letter to Leo Augustus was called the second volume by Martin I at the Lateran Council, in these words: “From the second volume of blessed Leo, Roman pontiff, sent to the emperor Leo.”

Accordingly, in professions of faith the teaching of both letters is sometimes declared to have been received equally with the teaching of the councils. Pope Simplicius wrote of this letter in letter 5 to Acacius:

“For they recognize the letter that my predecessor Leo, of blessed memory, wrote in response to the consultation of the emperor Leo of august memory, a letter known to and celebrated by all the authorities there; and they acknowledge how reverently it was received.”

For this reason this letter too is found inserted in ancient lectionaries, as can be seen in Vallicellian codex XXVI. It is also found transcribed in the manuscripts of collection 2 of Saint Leo’s sermons, which derives its material from lectionaries. Compare Vatican Basilica manuscript 210 and Barberinian manuscript 88.

A Greek translation of the same letter is also preserved in several Greek codices. We shall publish it from the *Miscellanies* of Gerard Vossius, provost of Tongeren, who had used the Greek codex formerly belonging to Cardinal Sirlet and later to Cardinal Colonna. We have taken certain corrections, made in a second revision, from Greek Vatican codex 1341, which Father Cacciarius used in the latest Roman edition.

Nor should it be surprising if the letter is not found in the Chalcedonian collection. That collection, as we demonstrated in the preface, was compiled while Valentinian was alive—that is, before this letter was written.

Saint Ephraemius of Antioch used this letter with distinguished praise in Photius, codex 228.

### 2

In order to establish the date—which some call into question—the occasion for writing the letter must be recalled. In the year 457, the Emperor Leo, seeking to blunt the audacity of the Eutychians, who, stirring up disturbances and doubts against the Definition of Chalcedon, had thrown all Egypt into turmoil and were demanding a new examination and a new judgment, requested in an encyclical letter addressed to all the metropolitans, and especially to Saint Leo, among other things, that each of them, having convened a synod of his own province, should explain by letter what they thought about the Council of Chalcedon.

The holy Pontiff replied immediately—that is, on the Kalends of December of the same year—in Letter 156, and at the same time promised a fuller letter in chapter 6, in these words:

> And lest the page of this letter be extended to excessive length, I have included in another letter matters corresponding to the affirmation of the Catholic faith, so that, although what has been proclaimed by the Apostolic See would be sufficient, nevertheless these additions might also expose the plots of the heretics.

That he fulfilled this promise in the following letter is clear from its opening. Tillemont, in note 70 on Leo, inclines to the view that this letter was sent either on the same Kalends of December in the year 457 on which Letter 156 was sent, or shortly thereafter. For he considers it unlikely that the Pontiff postponed for eight months or more a letter which, in the testimony just quoted, he indicated as already prepared. Hence he thinks that the chronological notice attached to this letter should be rejected; he confirms this especially by the fact that the chronological notice is absent from most manuscripts.

Moreover, since he believes that what Leo wrote in Letter 157 to Anatolius, chapter 1, should be referred to this letter—

> I have earnestly entreated the most pious emperor, as far as I could, that he might recognize that the assertions of the heretics were sinking into the great blindness of ignorance—

he more confidently maintains that this letter, together with Letter 156, was delivered on the Kalends of December. Yet the words, “I remember that I promised,” plainly show that the promise had been made long before, and therefore that the letter was sent neither together with Letter 156 nor shortly afterward.

Nor should the use of the past-tense verb *comprehendi*—which in the testimony of Letter 156 seems to indicate that this letter was already prepared and written—prevent us from believing that the fulfillment of the promise was delayed for so long. For we have shown elsewhere, by other examples, that it was customary for Leo to use the past tense of something believed to be about to happen soon, even when it was later postponed for a longer period.

The words in chapter 1 of this letter, “I fulfill it on a faithful occasion,” likewise indicate some occasion that arose after the promise made on the Kalends of December. The first such occasion after those Kalends occurred on 21 March of the year 458, when, through Philoxenus, the *agens in rebus*, Leo sent Letters 160, 161, and 162. He could have attached this letter to them as well. But when the emperor, through the same Philoxenus, requested that Saint Leo send some of his brethren who were thoroughly instructed—whom he promises to send in Letter 162, chapter 3—Leo judged that the transmission of this letter should be postponed until that time. Domitian and Geminianus were the legates; they are the “faithful occasion” which he mentions at the beginning of the letter.

Since these legates departed with the preceding letters, sealed on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, we rightly recognize this same day as assigned also to the present letter, in accordance with Leo’s practice. Of the two possible dates, the thirteenth or the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, the former is found in two manuscripts, those of Troyes and Oxford, in Quesnel’s edition and in the editions of Josias Simler, Surius, and others; the latter is found in Quesnel’s Theodoric manuscript and in our outstanding Regensburg manuscript. We preferred the latter because it agrees with the preceding letters. It would have been easy, through a scribal error, to transform the notation VI into III by separating the strokes, and thus to write XIII instead of XVI before the Kalends of September.

Nor should it be considered an obstacle that most manuscripts and collections lack any chronological notice. For other important letters lack a chronological notice in all manuscripts; yet if one were found in a particular manuscript, no one would therefore think it should be deleted—unless, perhaps, it contradicted the historical evidence. In the present letter, however, apart from the testimony of several manuscripts of different origins, among which the Regensburg manuscript is especially authoritative, not only is there no contradiction, but everything rather agrees with what has been said above.

### 3

Something must finally be said here by way of preliminary notice concerning the testimonies appended to this letter. Saint Leo had first collected these after the false synod of Ephesus and sent them to the East through legates, in order to show that the teaching of his Letter 28 to Flavian was consistent with the teaching of the Latin and Greek Fathers.

The testimonies that he sent at that time, although written by Leo in Latin, survive only in a Greek translation, which is printed in the editions of the Councils beneath the letter to Flavian in act 2 of the Council of Chalcedon. We have discussed this more fully at the end of the note on Letter 28.

He appended the same testimonies again to the present letter. Written in Latin, they are found both in printed editions and in Leo’s manuscripts after the same letter to the Emperor Leo Augustus. They are also found separately inserted in the most ancient collections 3 and 5, as well as in manuscript 58 of the Chapter of Verona.

Among these testimonies are several that are by no means read in act 2 of the editions of the Councils. We believe that this arose because, when the holy Pontiff was writing to the Emperor Leo Augustus, he exercised greater care, sought out new testimonies, and added them.

It is especially important to observe that, among the Latin Fathers, only three are cited—Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine—and that their testimonies were taken from the original Latin sources. There are more testimonies from the Greek Fathers, and these were derived from translations that had appeared in Leo’s time.

Thus Athanasius’s testimony is plainly taken from that translation of the Letter to Epictetus in which the complete letter is presented in collection 5, chapter 52, and in the manuscripts of collection 12. The testimonies of Theophilus plainly display Jerome’s translation of two Paschal letters. Cyril’s testimony is transcribed in the same words from the Letter to Nestorius in the aforementioned collection 5, chapter 56, and among Leo’s letters in collection 12.

## LETTER CLXV  
[Col. 1155C] Elsewhere numbered 134. Written 17 August 458.

[Note: It is found in manuscript collections 2, 3, 5, 8, the Hispanic-Isidorian collections 11, 12, 13, and 18 through 24; in the separate Vatican codex Regina 293; and in a copy of the first Roman edition of the Sermons of Saint Leo.]

### TO LEO AUGUSTUS

[Col. 1155]

## SYNOPSIS

[Col. 1155C] In the Hispanic collection this letter is divided into three chapters, from which the divisions passed into the editions preceding Quesnel:

1. On the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches, and their deserved anathema.
2. That in the one person of the Lord Jesus Christ the twofold nature of deity and humanity must be affirmed.
3. On the chapters of faith collected from the books of the holy Fathers.

In the table prefixed to collection 5, chapter 67, the following title alone is found:

> On the one person of our Lord Jesus Christ and the two natures, of God and man, together with the appended testimonies of the Fathers.

I. He indicates that he is sending the fuller letter previously promised against the doctrine of Eutyches.  
II. The doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches are set forth; the latter imitated Apollinaris, Valentinus, and Mani.  
III. All these monstrous heresies are pierced through by the Nicene Creed.  
IV. The reconciliation of humanity depends upon the incarnation, without which Christ fulfills neither the office of mediator nor that of redeemer.  
V. By Christ’s sacrifice alone the world was reconciled to God and sinners were justified.  
VI. The properties of each nature in Christ are revealed through his various actions.  
VII. The reality of Christ’s flesh is proved by the reality of his death, burial, and resurrection.  
VIII. Christ’s exaltation could not be accomplished except in the true nature of man.  
IX. Under the pretext of honoring the deity, it is inflicted with the greatest insult when it is asserted to have lain hidden under the false appearance of a phantom.  
X. Catholic faith is firmly established by the tradition of the holy Fathers—a faith which it is especially worthy of an emperor to defend.  
XI. Testimonies of the holy Fathers, both Greek and Latin, in support of the reality of Christ’s flesh.

[Col. 1155A] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

## LEO, bishop, TO LEO AUGUSTUS

[Col. 1155]

[Note: In the Vulgate editions of Leo before Quesnel: “Leo, bishop of Rome and of the universal Catholic Church, to Leo, ever Augustus.” This wording is not found in our manuscripts or in the ancient editions of the Councils. In the copy of the first edition: “Pope Leo sends greetings in the Lord to the Emperor Leo.” Codex Florentinus, Saint Mark’s, collection 13: “Leo, bishop of the city of Rome, to Marcian”—corrected to “Leo”—“emperor and perpetual Augustus.” From the Greek version: “Leo the bishop to the most glorious and most merciful son, Leo Augustus.”]

## CHAPTER I

[Note: In Letter 156, otherwise 125, chapter 6.]

I remember, venerable emperor, that I promised, in the matter of the faith—concerning which I know that Your Clemency is piously concerned—that a fuller discourse of my humility should be sent. With the Lord’s help, I now fulfill that promise on a faithful occasion, so that instruction useful, as I believe, to the holy zeal of your piety may not be lacking.

[Note: Quesnel’s Grimani manuscript of collection 18 reads “a more extended.”]

[Note: The copy of the first edition of the Sermons reads “holy”; then “of Your Piety” in Vatican manuscript collection 11, and shortly afterward “Your Clemency” in the same manuscript and in the Vindobonensis Hispanicus.]

Although I know that Your Clemency has no need of human instruction, and has drawn the purest teaching from the abundance of the Holy Spirit, it is nevertheless my duty both to disclose what you understand and to proclaim what you believe, so that that fire which the Lord, when he came, sent upon the earth (Luke 12:49), stirred by the movement of frequent meditation, may grow warm until it burns, and may be so inflamed that it shines.

[Note: Vatican 1342, collection 3; Vatican 5845, collection 8; the Regensburg manuscript; and the first edition read “may become warm” (*incalescat*). Three of Quesnel’s manuscripts—the Barberini, two Bodleian, and the Cambridge manuscript—together with our Vatican Regina 293 and three manuscripts of collection 21, read “may grow strong” (*convalescat*).]

[Note: Vatican collection 11, together with four other manuscripts of Quesnel, reads *Magna enim caligine se Eutychiana*, etc. (“For the Eutychian [heresy] ... with great darkness, etc.”), rather than the reading printed here.]

For the Eutychian heresy has attempted to bring great darkness upon the regions of the East and has tried to turn the eyes of the ignorant away from that light which, as the Gospel says, shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it (John 1:5). And when it has fallen back into its own blindness, what failed in its author now grows virulent again in his disciples.

[Note: The Vindobonensis collection 5, the Regensburg manuscript, and the Vatican Regina manuscript omit “now.”]

## CHAPTER II

For within no long interval the Catholic faith, which is one and true and to which nothing can be added or taken away, was attacked by two enemies. The first of these was Nestorius; Eutyches arose as the second. They wished to introduce into the Church of God two heresies opposed to each other, so that both might rightly be condemned by the preachers of the truth, since what both men held in their various falsehoods was exceedingly insane and sacrilegious.

[Note: This is the reading of the Vindobonensis collection 5, the Regensburg manuscript, and the copy of the first edition. Other witnesses read *nihilve* or *nihilque* (“nor anything”). In the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, *ab opus* was mistakenly written for *a duobus* (“by two”); in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and thence in Isidore it was arbitrarily corrected to *ob hoc* (“on this account”). Three manuscripts read *sibimetipsis* (“to themselves”).]

[Note: The wording from this point through chapter 9, “But in the great…,” is the same as in Letter 124, otherwise 97, to the Palestinians, from chapter 2 through chapter 8, with a few exceptions.]

Therefore let Nestorius be anathematized, who believed that the blessed Virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a man, so as to make one person of the flesh and another of the deity; and who did not acknowledge one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but separately and apart proclaimed one Son of God and another son of man.

[Note: Vatican manuscript collection 11, together with the Vatican Regina manuscript, reads “not one” (*ne unum*). The first edition reads “separate and divided” (*separatum atque sejunctum*).]

[Note: Against Nestorius Saint Leo argues so clearly and precisely that Saint Ephraem of Antioch, in Photius, codex 228, especially praises this testimony. Leo expressly condemns Nestorius’s heresy because Timothy the Cat, in a booklet sent to the emperor, represented the Catholics who defended the faith of Chalcedon, and especially Leo himself, as infected with Nestorian heresy, as Gennadius reports in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 72.]

While the unchangeable essence of the Word—which is timeless and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit—remained, the Word became flesh within the virgin womb, so that, through an ineffable sacrament, in one conception and one birth, the same virgin, both the handmaid of the Lord and his mother, was, according to the truth of both natures.

[Note: The Vindobonensis collection 5, the Regensburg manuscript, and two Vatican manuscripts of collection 21, together with the copy of the first edition, read “unchangeable” (*incommutabilis*). The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript reads “unchangeable true essence”; this was corrected in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, thence in Isidore, and in another Vatican manuscript of collection 11 to the same wording. The Vindobonensis Hispanicus reads “through that which is ineffable”; the Vatican Historicus reads “through that which is ineffable is.” The Vatican Isidorianus reads “through that which was made.” Later, for “timeless,” the Corbeiensis manuscript of collection 2 reads “incorporeal”; for “virgin,” Vatican collection 8 and the first edition read “of the Virgin.”]

Elizabeth also understood this, as the Evangelist Luke makes clear, and said: “And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke 1:43).

Let Eutyches likewise be struck by the same anathema. Having been rolled about in the impious errors of the ancient heretics, he chose the third doctrine of Apollinaris:

[Note: The copy of the first edition reads: “He defended the foul doctrine of Apollinaris.”]

He denied the reality of human flesh and soul and asserted that our entire Lord Jesus Christ was of one nature, as though the deity of the Word itself had been converted into flesh and soul. Thus, he claimed, it was the divine essence alone that conceived and was born, was nourished and grew, was crucified and died, was buried and rose again, ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

[Note: Quesnel, with most manuscripts, reads “at the right hand of the Father.” We have restored the reading found in the Vindobonensis collection 5, the Regensburg manuscript, the Vatican Regina manuscript, and Vatican collection 24, since it is also read in Letter 124, chapter 2.]

This, he held, belonged solely to the divine essence, which receives none of these things in itself without the reality of flesh. For the nature of the Only-Begotten is the nature of the Father and the nature of the Holy Spirit; it is at once impassible and unchangeable, the undivided unity and consubstantial equality of the eternal Trinity.

[Note: The reading printed here, with Letter 124, is that of the Vindobonensis collection 5, another Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, the Regensburg manuscript, Vatican collections 11 and 24, the Vatican Regina manuscript, and the copy of the first edition. The common text reads “everlasting” (*sempiterna*). The pseudo-letter of Pope Agapetus reads “the equality of one will.”]

Therefore, if some Eutychian departs from the perversity of Apollinaris so as not to be convicted of believing the deity to be passible and mortal, yet dares to proclaim that the incarnate Word—that is, the Word and the flesh—has one nature, he plainly passes into the madness of Valentinus and Mani.

[Note: The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript mistakenly reads “will hear” (*audiet*). This was arbitrarily corrected in the Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and other manuscripts of collections 11 and 21, and in witnesses derived from them, to “has dared” (*ausus fuerit*). Likewise, when the conjunction *et* (“and”) before “the mediator” was omitted in the Vindobonensis Hispanicus, the Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and another Vatican manuscript of collection 11 substituted “who [is] the mediator.”] He believes that the mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ, performed everything only in appearance, and that no human body was in him, but that what appeared to the eyes of those who saw him was merely a phantom-like bodily form.

[Note: Vatican collection 21, together with the copy of the first edition, reads “departed”; in the first edition shortly afterward, “to say” appears instead of “to believe.”]

[Note: Quesnel, with a number of respectable manuscripts derived from the Hispanic tradition, reads “nor was there truth in him.” We have restored the reading preceding the common text, since it is found not only in the outstanding Corbeiensis manuscript of collection 2, in the Grimani manuscript, and in one of Quesnel’s Thuane manuscripts, but also in our better manuscripts—Vatican collection 3, Vindobonensis collection 5, Vatican collection 8, the Regensburg manuscript, the Vatican Regina manuscript, and others—and is confirmed by the reading in Letter 124 and by the ancient Greek translation. Shortly afterward the Vindobonensis Hispanicus and Merlinus read “phantom-like”; the Vatican Hispanicus, the Isidorianus, and related manuscripts read “of a phantom-like body.”]

## CHAPTER III

Since the Catholic faith has long detested these impious falsehoods, and since the sacrileges of such assertions were long ago condemned throughout the world by the unanimous judgments of the blessed Fathers, there can be no doubt that we proclaim and defend the faith which the holy Synod of Nicaea confirmed, saying:

[Note: Three excellent manuscripts—the Vindobonensis collection 5, the Regensburg manuscript, and the Vatican Regina manuscript—read “confirmed” (*firmavit*). In his celebrated Letter 28 to Flavian, chapter 2, Leo used only the Apostles’ Creed, which he believed was handed down before baptism among both Easterners and Westerners. Hence in chapter 1 of that letter he reproves Eutyches for not even grasping the opening of the Creed, which is uttered throughout the world by all who are to be regenerated. The words of the Creed quoted in chapter 2 are: “that he believes in God the Father almighty and in Jesus Christ his only Son, our Lord,” etc. The Eutychians, as Vigilius of Thapsus testifies in book IV against Eutyches, p. 730 of volume VIII of the *Library of the Fathers*, maliciously objected to this chapter of Leo because he had not said “in one God the Father and in one Jesus Christ his Son,” in accordance with the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. The Nicene Creed is meant, which Easterners used at baptism; hence the Eutychians continually pressed this Creed, in which they had been baptized. Vigilius, who eloquently defends Leo’s letter, answers the objection thus: “But at Rome, both before the Nicene synod assembled and from the times of the apostles until now, and under Coelestine of blessed memory, to whom this man [Leo] bore testimony of right faith, the Creed is handed down to the faithful in this way.” We explained in note 24 (col. 892, new pagination) to Letter 69 why the Eutychians pressed the Nicene Creed so insistently. To overthrow this objection, which Leo had learned only after writing Letter 28, he sets forth the Nicene Creed in the present letter and shows that the Eutychian heresy is likewise condemned in it.]

[Note: The Vulgate editions before Quesnel, together with manuscripts of collections 12 and 24, read “of others.” Vatican collection 8 and the Hispanic manuscripts, together with those derived from them, read “of others.”]

> We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten from the Father as the Only-Begotten—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father (which the Greeks call *homoousion*, “consubstantial”), through whom all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven, was incarnate, and became man; he suffered and rose again on the third day. He ascended into heaven and will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit.

[Note: The Vulgate editions before Quesnel and the Vindobonensis collection 5 add “of all things.” Later, the Vatican Hispanicus and Isidorianus, together with another Vatican manuscript of collection 11, omit “Only-Begotten.”]

[Note: Four of our manuscripts repeat “for us.” Then, “he came down from the heavens and was incarnate” appears in the Vulgate editions before Quesnel, as the Greek translator also read it. Vatican collection 3, Vatican collection 8, both Hispanic Vatican manuscripts, the Isidorianus, and manuscripts derived from them read “from heaven, and was incarnate”; one Vercellensis reads “from heaven and was incarnate”; the Regensburg manuscript reads “he came down and was incarnate.”]

[Note: Quesnel reads “into heaven,” with Vatican collection 3, the Vatican Hispanicus, and manuscripts derived from them. Other editions read “to the heavens.” We preferred “into the heavens,” with the better manuscripts—the Vindobonensis collection 5, the Vatican and Vercellensis manuscripts of collection 8, the Vindobonensis Hispanicus, and the Regensburg manuscript—to which the Greek translation also agrees. Four manuscripts add “and he ascended.” Shortly afterward Vatican collections 3 and 21 read “from where he will come”; the Vulgate editions before Quesnel read “from there he will come.”]

This profession of faith contains with the greatest clarity what we too confess and believe concerning the Lord’s incarnation: that, for the restoration of the human race to salvation, he did not bring with him from heaven the true flesh of our frailty, but assumed it in the womb of the Virgin mother.

[Note: The Vatican Hispanicus and Isidorianus read “from the womb.”]

## CHAPTER IV

Therefore, let all who are so blinded and estranged from the light of truth that they deny the reality of human flesh to the Word of God from the time of the incarnation show in what respect they claim for themselves the Christian name, and how they agree with the Gospel of truth—if, through the birth of the blessed Virgin, either flesh arose without deity or deity arose without flesh.

[Note: The word “human” is absent from the Regensburg manuscript and Vatican manuscript 11. Ancient editions read “if through the birth of the blessed Virgin,” as in Letter 124, chapter 3; Vatican manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 read “if through the Virgin’s birth”; Quesnel, with ten manuscripts, reads “if by the Virgin’s birth.” We have added “blessed” from two Vindobonensis manuscripts of collections 5 and Hispanic, from the Regensburg manuscript, the Vatican Regina manuscript, another Vatican manuscript of collection 24, and the first edition. The Greek version confirms this addition.]

For just as it cannot be denied, since the Evangelist says that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), so it cannot be denied, since the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

What sort of reconciliation could there be by which God might be reconciled to humanity, unless the mediator between God and humanity assumed the cause of all?

[Note: The ancient editions and most of our manuscripts read “could there be,” as in Letter 124. The Vindobonensis collection 5 reads “can there be,” and Quesnel “could there be,” a reading supported by some manuscripts. Shortly afterward, three manuscripts and the ancient printed editions read “might be propitiated.”]

[Note: Two of Quesnel’s manuscripts, the Thuane and Troyes manuscripts, our Vindobonensis collection 5, and the first edition read: “unless the mediator between God and humanity assumed flesh for the sake of all”; the only difference in the first edition is *suscepisset*, “had assumed,” instead of *susciperet*, “should assume.”]

And in what way would he fulfill the truth of the mediator unless he who is equal to the Father in the form of God became a participant in us in the form of a servant, so that the bond of death contracted through one person’s transgression might be dissolved by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death?

[Note: Vatican collection 3 and the copy of the first edition read “through the death of one.”]

For the shedding of Christ’s blood on behalf of the unjust was so rich in value that, if the whole multitude of captives were to believe in their redeemer, no one would remain held by the bonds of the devil; for, as the Apostle says, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). And since those born under the sentence of sin have received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom has proved stronger than the debt of slavery.

[Note: This wording is found in eleven of Quesnel’s manuscripts, cited by him in note 2, and in twelve of our manuscripts, and these are the better ones. The Vatican Hispanicus and Isidorianus read: “For the shedding of the righteous blood of Christ…” The copy of the first edition reads: “For the shedding of the righteous blood was so rich…” Vatican collection 24 reads: “For the shedding of the righteous blood on behalf of the unjust was so powerful as a privilege, so rich…” as in Letter 124. The editions before Quesnel, adopting this last reading, inserted “of Christ” after “righteous.”]

## CHAPTER V

What hope, then, do those who deny the reality of the human body in our Savior leave for themselves in the protection of this sacrament? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed.

[Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript of collection 2 reads “were reborn.”]

Who is he, as the Apostle says, “who delivered himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant odor” (Ephesians 5:2)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal High Priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh?

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “from the altar”; the first edition reads “upon the altar.”]

[Note: Because the words “Although the deaths of many saints…” were omitted by scribal leap in the Vindobonensis Hispanicus, another reading was introduced arbitrarily into the Vatican Hispanicus and consequently into the Isidorianus: “In the sight of the Lord the death of the righteous was precious”; nevertheless the following words, “yet no one’s,” presuppose “although” or something similar. Vatican collection 8 reads “yet no redemption was found in the killing of a saint.”]

Although the death of many saints was precious in the sight of the Lord (Psalm 115:14), the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the courage of the faithful arose examples of patience, not gifts of justification.

[Note: The Grimani manuscript reads “individual deaths.”]

For each individual had his own death, and no one paid another’s debt by his own end. Among the children of humanity there was one Lord Jesus Christ alone, who truly was the immaculate Lamb, in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised.

[Note: Vatican collection 8 and the first edition read “existed.”]

[Note: The Corbeiensis, Grimani, and Thuane manuscripts of Quesnel, together with our Regensburg manuscript and the first edition, read “may be.” Shortly afterward Vatican collection 8 and the first edition read “even he himself.”]

Of these he himself said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32).

[Note: Both Hispanic manuscripts, together with the Isidorianus and the other manuscripts derived from them, as well as the older printed editions, read “to myself.”]

For true faith, which justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, draws the person who shares in Christ’s humanity into participation with it and obtains salvation in him, in whom alone a human being finds himself innocent. By God’s grace he is free to glory in the power of him who confronted the enemy of the human race in the humility of our flesh and grants his victory to those in whose body he triumphed.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “in the flesh of our humility.”]

## CHAPTER VI

Although, therefore, in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and man, there is one person of the Word and flesh, which possesses inseparably and indivisibly the actions common to both, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood. Through sincere contemplation of the faith it must be discerned to what the humility of the flesh is exalted and toward what the majesty of the deity inclines: what the flesh does not do without the Word, and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads “sincere.” The Vindobonensis Hispanicus reads: “so truly, by contemplating the Son of God.” This was corrected in the Vatican Hispanicus and in manuscripts derived from it, including two manuscripts cited by Quesnel—the Cambridge and Thuane manuscripts—to: “by contemplating the true faith.” This reading is found in the pseudo-letter of Agapetus, which clearly derives from the Isidorian collection.]

For without the power of the Word the Virgin would neither conceive nor give birth, and without the reality of flesh infancy would not lie wrapped in swaddling clothes. Without the power of the Word the Magi would not adore the child, proclaimed by the guiding star; and without the reality of flesh the child would not be ordered to be carried into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution.
