Without the power of the Word the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not say, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17); and without the reality of flesh John would not testify, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

[Note: The Vindobonensis collection 5 and the first edition omit “well,” as in Letter 124. Shortly afterward the Vindobonensis Hispanicus and the manuscripts of collection 24 read: “in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” Vatican collection 11, together with the editions before Quesnel, likewise includes the addition “listen to him.”]

[Note: The Regensburg and Vatican Regina manuscripts read “sin,” singular. Shortly afterward the Grimani manuscript reads “resurrection” instead of “giving life.”]

Without the power of the Word there would be no restoration of the weak or giving of life to the dead; and without the reality of flesh, food would not be necessary for one who is fasting, nor sleep for one who is weary.

Finally, without the power of the Word the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father; and without the reality of flesh he would not say that the Father was greater than he (John 14:28). Catholic faith accepts and defends both, believing, according to the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, that the one Christ, the Son of the living God (Matthew 16:16), is both man and Word.

Although, therefore, from the beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb (John 1:14), there was never any division between the two forms, and throughout all the bodily stages of growth the actions of the entire period belonged to one person, nevertheless we do not confuse by any mixture the very things that were done inseparably; rather, we discern from the character of the actions what belongs to each form.

[Note: The Vindobonensis Hispanicus reads: “For those very things were done at will which are separated.” This was corrected in the Vatican Hispanicus, the Isidorianus, and the other manuscripts of the same origin to: “For those very things, so to speak, were done inseparably.” In manuscripts of collection 21: “Yet those very things, so to speak, were done inseparably.” The compiler of this collection combined both the genuine and the corrected readings. Shortly afterward the Vulgate editions before Quesnel, together with the Hispanic, Isidorianus, and related manuscripts, read “by mixture.”]

[Note: The three manuscripts of Quesnel—the Barberini, Bodleian, and Cambridge manuscripts—together with our Vatican Hispanicus and Isidorianus and another manuscript of collection 11, read “of each form.” This reading originated in Hispanic and Gallican manuscripts.]

[Note: The Vulgate editions add: “For neither do divine things prejudice human things, nor human things divine things, since both converge into the same reality in such a way that neither is the distinctiveness of either destroyed nor the person doubled.” Although these words are found in Letter 124 and Sermon 65, chapter 1, and cannot be doubted to be Leonine, we have omitted them here because they are absent not only from all of Quesnel’s manuscripts and from our manuscripts of the various collections and from the copy of the first edition, but also from the editions of Merlin, Crabbe, Nicolinus, and Binius, as well as from the most ancient Greek translation, which was taken from the copy of Leo’s letter sent to the East.]

## CHAPTER VII

[Note: Vatican collection 8 and the first edition add “now”; the first edition also reads “blindness of mind” (*caeci mentis*).]

Let these hypocrites, then, who refuse to receive the light of truth with blind minds, say in which form Christ, the Lord of majesty, was fastened to the wood of the cross; what lay in the tomb; and in what form the flesh rose again on the third day when the stone of the tomb had been rolled away; and in what form, after his resurrection, he rebuked certain disciples who did not believe and refuted the hesitation of those who doubted, saying:

> “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39);

and to the Apostle Thomas:

> “Put your hand into my side, and see my hands and my feet, and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John 20:27).

[Note: Vatican collection 3 and the first edition add “my.”]

By this manifestation of his body he was already destroying the lies of the heretics, so that the whole Church, which was to be instructed in Christ’s teachings, might have no doubt that it must believe what the apostles had received to preach.

[Note: Seven manuscripts, including the Regensburg manuscript and the Vindobonensis collection 5, read “But if.”]

But if heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness in so great a light of truth, let them show from where they promise themselves the hope of eternal life, which cannot be attained except through the mediator between God and humanity, the man Jesus Christ.

For, as the blessed Apostle Peter says, “There is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Nor is there any redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him “who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6), and who, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, “although he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God to be robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross.”

Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed upon him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:6–11).

[Note: The Regensburg manuscript reads: “because the Lord Jesus is in the glory.”]

Source/review notes: All Latin and Greek textual apparatus and the Hilary testimony variants were checked directly against the canonical restored source; printed Greek readings are distinguished from editorial conjectures.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 1167B] Since, then, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and in him the true Deity and true humanity are altogether one and the same person, we understand the exaltation by which God exalted him, as the teacher of the nations says, and bestowed on him the name that surpasses every name, to belong to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glory. [Note, Col. 1167D: The Regensburg manuscript likewise reads *ad eamdem*, “to that same form.” Quesnell adds *ex* (“from”) before *cum* (“with”), following several of our manuscripts. We deleted it on the authority of the better Regensburg manuscripts, both Vindobonensis manuscripts of Collection 5, the Hispanic Vatican Regina manuscript, and four other Vatican manuscripts of Collections 11, 21, and 24. It is likewise absent from Letter 124.]

For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father, and between the Begetter and the Only-begotten there was no distinction in essence, no difference in majesty; nor, through the mystery of the incarnation, had anything departed from the Word that had to be restored to him as a gift from the Father. [Note, Col. 1167D: The Vatican manuscript of Collection 8, together with the Vatican Regina manuscript and the first edition, reads *Dei Patris*, “of God the Father.”]

The form of a servant, through which the impassible Deity fulfilled the mystery of profound devotion, is human lowliness. This, raised into the glory of divine power, was joined to Deity and humanity in such unity from the very conception in the Virgin that neither divine things were done without the human, nor human things without God. [Note, Cols. 1167D–1168D: Quesnell prints *in tantam unitatem*, “into such unity,” with the editions of the Councils, the better and most of our manuscripts, and Letter 124. Another reading is *in tanta unitate*, “in so great a unity.” The first edition reads *Deitas et humanitas conserta est*, “Deity and humanity were joined.”]

Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who from eternity is equal to God is said to have been exalted: because, with the unity of person remaining inseparable, one and the same person is wholly Son of Man because of the flesh and wholly Son of God because of the one Deity he shares with the Father.

[Col. 1167C] Whatever, then, Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which what it did not possess was conferred. [Note, Col. 1168D: Leo’s Vulgate before Quesnell and Labbe, following the Hispanic, Isidorean, and related manuscripts, adds *enim*, “for”: “For whatever Christ received in time.”] For according to the power of Deity, everything that the Father has the Son also has without distinction; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of God. [Note, Col. 1168D: Seven of Quesnell’s manuscripts, our Vindobonensis manuscript of Collection 5, three Regensburg manuscripts of Collection 21, and Letter 124 read *conferuntur*, “are conferred.” The other witnesses, more correctly, have the printed *conferrentur*, “were to be conferred”: the Vatican manuscript of Collection 3, the Vatican and Vercelli manuscripts of Collection 8, both Hispanic manuscripts, and the other collections derived from them. The agreeing Greek translation in the Vatican Regina manuscript reads: “Whatever Christ receives in time, he receives according to his humanity, to which what it did not possess is conferred”; and shortly afterward, “he receives from the Father.”]

According to the form of God, he and the Father are one (John 10:30); according to the form of a servant, “He did not come to do his own will, but the will of him who sent him” (John 5:30). According to the form of God, “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (ibid., [Col. 1167D] 26); according to the form of a servant, “His soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). [Note, Col. 1168D: The Vindobonensis Hispanic and Vatican Regina manuscripts add *mea*, “my”: “My soul is sorrowful.”] And he is the very same person, as the Apostle proclaims, both rich and poor.

Rich, because, as the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3). Poor, however, because “for our sake the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 14). What, then, is his emptying, and what is his poverty, except the taking of the form of a servant? Through this form, while the majesty of the Word was veiled, the dispensation of human redemption was fulfilled.

## CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1169B] Since the original bonds of our captivity could not be loosed unless there existed a man of our race and of our nature, whom the sentence of sin did not hold and who might wipe away the deadly bond with his spotless blood, what had been divinely ordained from the beginning was accomplished when the appointed time was fulfilled. [Note, Col. 1169C: The Vatican Regina manuscript reads *peccata*, “the original sins of our captivity,” instead of *vincula*, “the original bonds.” The Vatican manuscript of Collection 8 reads *carnis naturae*, “of our fleshly nature,” instead of *nostrae naturae*, “of our nature.”] Thus the promise, signified in many ways, came to the long-awaited fulfillment, and what had continually been announced by repeated testimonies could not remain uncertain. [Note, Col. 1169C: The Regensburg manuscript reads *saepe fuerat nuntiatum*, “had often been announced,” instead of *semper fuerat nuntiatum*, “had continually been announced.”]

The impiety of the heretics reveals itself to be engaged in a great sacrilege when, under the pretext of honoring Deity, they deny the truth of human flesh in Christ; and they think it pious to believe that what saves is not true in our Savior, although, according to the promise extending through all the ages, the world has been reconciled to God in Christ, so that unless the Word had deigned to become flesh, no flesh could be saved. [Note, Cols. 1169C–D: The Regina manuscript reads “the impiety of the heretics is shown to be at variance”; two Regensburg manuscripts and the Vindobonensis manuscript of Collection 5 read “to be at variance”; two manuscripts of Collection 21 read *improbitas*, “depravity.” For *percurrentem*, “extending through,” the Regensburg manuscript and first edition read *praecurrentem*, “running before,” while Vossius notes *praeter currentem*, “running past,” in the margin.]

For the entire mystery of the Christian faith is, as the heretics wish, disfigured by profound darkness if the light of truth is thought to have lain hidden beneath a deceptive apparition. [Note: The lengthy editorial note explains that the parenthesis “as the heretics wish” is present in the ancient position in all the manuscripts and in the old Greek translation. Quesnell moved it and read “the mystery is greatly disfigured by darkness, if, as the heretics wish, the light of truth…” The editor argues that Quesnell’s arrangement produces a false sense. The “mystery of Christian faith” here refers not to Deity but to the incarnation: the heretics, while pretending to honor Deity, wished to obscure the true incarnation by turning it into a phantom. The ancient position of the parenthesis therefore should be retained.]

Let no Christian, then, think it shameful that Christ possesses the truth of our body. [Note: The first edition reads: “Let no one, therefore, think it shameful for Christians that Christ received the truth of a body from our body.” A related reading in the Vatican manuscript of Collection 3 is: “that in Christ he received the truth of a body from our body.”] For all the apostles and the disciples of the apostles, and all the renowned teachers of the churches who were deemed worthy to attain the crown of martyrdom or the glory of confession, shone in the light of this faith, proclaiming everywhere with harmonious judgments that in the Lord Jesus Christ one person must be confessed as both Deity and flesh. [Note: The Regina manuscript reads “the successors of the apostles.”]

By what similarity of reasoning, or by what passage of the divine books, does heretical impiety think itself supported when it denies the truth of Christ’s body, although neither the Law has ceased to testify to it, nor prophecy to foretell it, nor the Gospels to teach it, nor Christ himself to display it? Let them search through the entire sequence of the Scriptures for where they may flee their darkness, not for where they may obscure the true light; and throughout all the ages they will find the truth shining forth so brightly that they will see this great and wondrous mystery believed from the beginning and fulfilled at the end.

Although no part of the sacred writings is silent about this, it is enough to set forth certain harmonious signs of the truth, by which the diligence of faith may be directed into the most radiant breadth and, in the purest light of understanding, may perceive that Christians ought not to be ashamed but to glory most steadfastly in the Son of God, who unceasingly confesses himself to be the Son of Man and a man. [Note, Col. 1171C: Four of Quesnell’s manuscripts, the Corbie and Grimani manuscripts, two Thuanus manuscripts, and three of our manuscripts—the Vatican Regina, Regensburg, and Vindobonensis manuscript of Collection 5—together with the first edition and Vossius, read *consonae*, “harmonious.” For *posuisse*, “to have placed,” the Vindobonensis Hispanic and Vatican manuscript of Collection 24 read *patuisse*, “to have lain open.” Leo’s Vulgate before Quesnell, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 24, and the first edition read *splendidissima latitudine*, “in a most radiant breadth,” rather than *in splendidissimam latitudinem*, “into a most radiant breadth.” The Regensburg manuscript reads *ut sincera*, “so that in the pure light,” rather than *et sincera*, “and in the pure light.”]

## CHAPTER X

So that your reverence may know that we agree with the preaching of the venerable Fathers, I have thought that some of their statements should be appended to this discourse. If you deign to read them, you will find that we proclaim nothing other than what our holy Fathers taught throughout the world, and that no one disagrees with them except the most impious heretics. [Note, Cols. 1171C–D: Quesnell prints *Quibus si dignaveris recensitis*, “if you deign to review these,” following the Grimani, Corbie, and Victor manuscripts, two Thuanus manuscripts, and several of ours. Some may suspect that *v* was written for *b*, as often happens in manuscripts. Collection 21 reads *si digneris* or *si dignaris*, “if you deign.” The Vatican Regina manuscript reads *Quas si dignaveris recensere*, “if you deign to review them”; the first edition, *quas cum dignaberis recensere*, “when you deign to review them”; Leo’s Vulgate before Quesnell, *Quibus, si dignaveris attendere, recensitis*, “when these, if you deign to attend to them, have been reviewed,” a reading found nowhere in the manuscripts; and Quesnell’s Theodoric manuscript, *Quas si dignatus fueris recensere*, “if you have deigned to review them.”]

Having touched on these matters as briefly as I could, most glorious and venerable Emperor, you will recognize that our preaching is united with the faith divinely inspired in you, and that in no respect do we differ from evangelical or apostolic teaching, or from the creed of the Catholic confession. [Note, Col. 1171D: The Vatican manuscript of Collection 3, the Vindobonensis manuscript of Collection 5, and the first edition read *munitam*, “fortified,” instead of *unitam*, “united.” Leo’s Vulgate before Quesnell, with manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24, reads *cognosce*, “recognize”; the Vatican Regina, Vindobonensis Collection 5, Regensburg, and Vatican Collection 3 manuscripts read *cognoscis*, “you recognize”; the others read *cognosces*, “you will recognize.”]

For, as the blessed Apostle Paul teaches, “Great is the mystery of devotion: it was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). [Note, Cols. 1171D–1172C: Quesnell deleted the word *Paulus*, “Paul”; we restored it from seven of our manuscripts and from the Greek. The editions before Quesnell, with our Vindobonensis Collection 5, Regensburg, and Vatican manuscripts of Collections 11 and 21, omit *in* before *gentibus*, giving “preached [to] nations”; the other manuscripts and the Greek translation retain it, “preached among the nations.” The Vatican Collection 3, Vindobonensis Collection 5, both Hispanic, Isidorean, and related manuscripts read *in hoc mundo*, “in this world.”]

What, then, could be more useful for your salvation, or more suited to your authority, than that you should provide for the peace of the churches of God by your decrees, defend the gifts of God among all your subjects, and in no way allow the devil’s agents, through his envy, to rage to the destruction of anyone? Thus, while you rule in a temporal kingdom in this age, you may be found worthy to reign with Christ forever. [Note, Cols. 1172C–1173B: We add *est*, “is,” in “what is more useful,” from the Vindobonensis manuscript of Collection 5 and the Regensburg and Vatican manuscripts of Collection 21. The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript has the corrupt *qui constitutione*, “who by an ordinance,” for *tua constitutione*, “by your ordinance”; a scribe conjecturally corrected this in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and thence in Isidore and related witnesses to *aequa constitutione*, “by an equitable ordinance.” Two of Quesnell’s manuscripts and our Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts and their derivatives read: “you who temporarily rule human beings.”]

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the Augusti Leo and Majorian.

[Note: The Greek version adds: “May Almighty God protect and preserve your kingdom and salvation for a long time, most glorious, most gentle, and august Emperor.” This formula of greeting was undoubtedly present in the original sent to the Emperor. The Greek version omits the chronological note, as do most manuscripts and collections. Quesnell appended the date “Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September” from two manuscripts and printed editions; in the margin he gave “the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September” from another manuscript, agreeing with the Regensburg manuscript. The reason for preferring the latter date is explained in the preliminary notice, no. 2.]

## Letter of Leo, Bishop of Rome, to the Emperor Leo

To the most glorious and most tranquil son, Leo Augustus, Leo the bishop.

[Col. 1156A]

I remember, most devout Emperor, having promised that, in the matter of the faith—which I know your serenity devotes itself most earnestly and piously to caring for—I would send you a discourse as complete as the brevity of my ability permitted. Since the present occasion, with the Lord’s assistance, supplies me with a trustworthy opportunity, I now fulfill that promise. Thus I offer your most devout zeal an exposition that I believe cannot fail to be useful.

For although we have recognized that your serenity has no need of human instruction and has drawn the purest learning from the abundance of the Holy Spirit, it is nevertheless proper to me to make clear what is understood and to proclaim what is believed. In this way that fire which the Lord, when he came, cast upon the earth, driven onward by the frequent movements of meditation, may be so warmed that it also burns, and may be drawn up into a flame so that it also shines.

[Col. 1156B]

For the heresy of Eutyches has contrived to bring the greatest mist upon the regions of the East. It attempted to turn the eyes of the ignorant away from that light which, as the Gospel says, shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it. When it fell through its disciples into its own blindness, it appeared more savagely in them than it had faltered in its teacher.

Within no long period of time the universal faith—which is both one and only, and true, and to which nothing can be added or taken away—received the assault of two enemies. The first of these was Nestorius, and the second Eutyches. They wished to introduce into the Church of God two heresies opposed to one another, so that each was justly condemned by those who proclaimed the truth, since what both held from their varied falsehood was exceedingly insane and impious.

Let Nestorius, therefore, be accursed: he believed that the blessed Virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a man, so that he might make one person for the flesh and another for the Deity. He did not understand the one Christ both in the Word of God and in the body, but proclaimed separately and distinctly one Son of God and another who was from man.

While the essence of the unchangeable Word remained—the essence that was timeless and eternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit—the Word nevertheless became flesh within the Virgin’s womb, so that, according to the ineffable mystery, in one conception and one birth, according to the truth of both natures, the same Virgin might be both the Lord’s servant and his mother. [Note: In Vossius the conjunction “and” is missing; it has been supplied from the Vatican manuscript 1341.]

Elizabeth also understood and said this, as the Evangelist Luke made clear: “Why is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”

Let Eutyches likewise be struck with the anathema. Rolling in the impious errors of the earlier heretics, he chose a third doctrine of Apollinaris, with the result that, after denying human flesh and the truth of the soul, he maintained that our Lord Jesus Christ was wholly of one nature. [Note, Col. 1158D: The same Vatican manuscript reads *πλάναις* (*planais*), “errors”; Vossius prints *πλάγαις* (*plagais*), “blows” or “strokes.”]

It was as though the Deity of the Word itself had changed itself into flesh and soul, and had undergone conception, birth, nourishment, growth, crucifixion, death, burial, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and enthronement at the Father’s right hand, from where he will come to judge the living and the dead.

This would mean that there existed only the divine essence, which could receive none of these things into itself without the truth of the body. For the nature of the Only-begotten is the nature of the Father, and it is also the nature of the Holy Spirit. [Note, Col. 1158D: The mutilated text of this passage was supplied from the Vatican manuscript cited above.] [Col. 1160A] At once impassible and unchangeable, the indivisible unity of the eternal Trinity and its equality existing together according to essence remain so.

Therefore, if some Eutychian, abandoning the distortion of Apollinaris so as not to be exposed as believing in a passible and mortal Deity, nevertheless dares to declare one nature of the incarnate Word—that is, of both the Word and the flesh—he plainly passes over into the madness of Valentinus and Manichaeus. He pretends to believe that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, did everything merely in appearance, and that a human body was not present in him, but that what was visible to the eyes of those who saw him was only an imaginary appearance of a body.

This is a falsehood of impiety, since the Catholic faith has long abhorred it, and the impious teachings of such people have already been condemned by the unanimous judgments of the most blessed Fathers throughout the whole world. It is therefore beyond doubt that we must defend and proclaim the faith which the holy Council of Nicaea confirmed, saying:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible.

“And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Only-begotten, begotten from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God;

“begotten, not made, of one substance with the Father—which in Greek is called *homoousios*—through whom all things came to be, both those in heaven and those on earth;

“who for us and for our salvation came down from the heavens, became incarnate, and was made human, suffered, was crucified, was buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into the heavens; and he is coming to judge the living and the dead.

“And in the Holy Spirit.”

This explicit confession contains what we too confess and believe concerning the Lord’s incarnation: in order to restore the salvation of the human race, he did not adorn himself with true flesh of our frailty brought from heaven, but assumed it in the womb of the Virgin Mother.

Whoever, then, these people are who are so blind and estranged from the light of truth that, from the time of the incarnation, they deny to the Word of God the truth of human flesh—let them show how they seize for themselves the name of Christians, and by what reasoning they agree with the Gospel of truth. For if, in the birth of the blessed Virgin, either flesh without Deity or Deity without a body arose or was born—[Note: “Or was born.” These two words are superfluous and appear to be a mere gloss.]—

just as it is impossible to deny the Evangelist’s statement, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” so it is impossible to deny the proclamation of the blessed Apostle Paul that “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.”

What reconciliation could there be through which God became gracious to the human race unless the mediator between God and human beings took upon himself the cause of all? By what reasoning could he fulfill the truth of the mediator unless he who was equal to the Father in the form of God shared with us in the form of a servant, so that the bond of death which the transgression of one had brought upon us might be dissolved by the death of one—the one who alone owed nothing to death?

For the outpouring of Christ’s blood on behalf of sinners became so rich in its price that, if the entire multitude of captives believed in their Redeemer, no one would remain held by the devil’s bonds. For, as the Apostle says, “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.” And those born under the sentence of sin, receiving the power to be reborn into righteousness, found the gift of freedom stronger than the debt of slavery.

What hope of assistance, then, do those who deny the truth of the human body in our Savior leave for themselves from such a mystery? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled; let them say by what blood they were redeemed. Who is the one who, as the Apostle says, “gave himself for us to God as an offering and sacrifice of sweet fragrance”?

Was any sacrifice ever more suitable for priestly service than that which the true and eternal high priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the sacrifice of his own flesh? [Note, Col. 1164D: The printed Greek has the article *τῆς* (*tēs*), “the,” before “suitable for priestly service”; it appears redundant here and should therefore be deleted.] Although the death of many saints has been precious in the sight of the Lord, the slaughter of none of these innocent people has become the redemption of the world.

The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. The endurance of the faithful is an example of perseverance, not a payment for righteousness. For each of them, clearly, death was an individual death, and no one paid another’s debt by being brought to completion through his own death. [Textual correction: the printed Greek has *αὐτὸς* (*autos*), “he himself,” but the editor proposes *αὐτόν* (*auton*), “him,” so that the construction means “through his being brought to completion.”]

Among the sons of human beings there is one Lord Jesus Christ alone, the only truly spotless Lamb, through whom all have been crucified, all have died, all have been buried, and all have been raised.

Concerning these he himself said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all people to myself.”

For true faith, which justifies the ungodly and gives birth to the righteous, having been drawn toward him who shares in our humanity, obtains salvation in him. In him alone a person finds himself not liable, boldly glorying through the grace of God in that one’s power—he who, having engaged the enemy of the human race in the lowliness of our flesh, bestowed his victory upon those whom he conquered in the body.

Therefore, although in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and man, there is one person of both the Word and the flesh, and although that person inseparably and indivisibly possesses the actions common to both, we must nevertheless understand the qualities of those actions. With the understanding of sincere faith we must discern toward which actions the lowliness of the flesh advances, toward which the height of Deity inclines, what the flesh does not do apart from the Word, and what the Word does not perform without the flesh.

For apart from the power of the Word the Virgin would neither have conceived nor given birth; but apart from the truth of the flesh, infancy would not have lain hidden in swaddling cloths. Apart from the power of the Word, the Magi would not have worshiped the child made known by the indicating star; but apart from the truth of the flesh, the child would not have been commanded to be carried into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution.

Apart from the power of the Word, the voice of the Father, sent forth from heaven, would not have said, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased”; but apart from the truth of the body, John would not have borne witness: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.”

Apart from the power of the Word, there would have been neither the strengthening of the weak nor the raising of the dead to life; but apart from the truth of the flesh, there would have been neither food for the one who fasted nor the necessary sleep for the one who labored.

And, finally, apart from the power of the Word, the Lord would not have confessed himself to be equal to the Father; but apart from the truth of the body, the same person would not have said that the Father was greater than he. The Catholic faith accepts and defends both, for, according to the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, it believes that the one Christ, the Son of the living God, is both man and Word.

Therefore, although from that beginning when the Word became flesh in the Virgin’s womb there was no division between the two forms, and although throughout every bodily growth the actions of the whole time proceeded from one person, nevertheless we do not confuse these inseparably accomplished acts through any intermixture. Rather, from the quality of the actions we perceive what belongs to which form.

[Col. 1166B]

Let these hypocrites, then, who refuse to receive the light of truth with their blind minds, say in what form Christ, the Lord of glory, was fastened to the wood of the cross. What lay in the tomb? When the stone had been rolled away from the tomb, what flesh rose again on the third day? And why, after his resurrection, did he rebuke some of the disciples who did not believe and overturn the doubt of those who hesitated, saying:

“Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have”?

And to the Apostle Thomas:

“Put your hand into my side, and see my hands and my feet; and do not become unbelieving, but believing.”

By this manifestation of his body he was already overturning the false words of the heretics, so that the whole Church of Christ, remembering his teachings, could have no doubt that it ought to believe what the Apostles had received in order to proclaim.

If, then, in so great a light of truth, the persistence of the heretics does not permit their darkness to depart, let them show from where they promise themselves hope of eternal life, to which it is impossible to arrive except through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ.

For, as the blessed Apostle Peter says, “There is no other name given to human beings under heaven by which we must be saved”; nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him “who gave himself as a ransom for all.”

And he, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, “existing in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus Christ every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

Since, then, there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and in him the true Deity and true humanity are altogether one and the same person, nevertheless we understand the exaltation by which God exalted him, as the teacher of the nations says, and bestowed on him the name above every name, to belong to that form which was destined to be enriched by such an increase of glory.

For, being in the form of God, the Son was equal to the Father; between the Father and the Only-begotten there was no separation according to essence and no difference according to Deity. Nor, through the mystery of becoming human, was anything diminished from the Word that had to be restored to him by the Father’s grace.

The form of a servant, through which the impassible Deity fulfilled the mystery of devotion, is human lowliness. This advanced into the glory of divine power and, from the very conception in the Virgin, Deity and humanity were joined in such unity that divine things were not done without his being human, nor human things without his being God.

Therefore, just as the one crucified is called the Lord of glory, so he who is equal to God in Deity is called exalted. For, while the unity of person remains inseparable, one and the same person is wholly Son of Man because of the flesh and wholly Son of God because of the one Deity he shares with the Father.

Whatever Christ receives in time, he receives according to his humanity, to which those things that it did not possess are assigned. For according to the power of Deity, everything that the Father has the Son also has without distinction; and what he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed while existing in the form of God.

According to the form of God, he and the Father are one; according to the form of a servant, he did not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him. According to the form of God, “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son also to have life in himself”; according to the form of a servant, “His soul is deeply sorrowful unto death.”

And he is the same person, as the Apostle proclaims, both rich and poor. Rich, as the Evangelist says:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things came to be through him, and without him nothing came to be.”

Poor, because for our sake the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

What, then, is his emptying, or what is his poverty, except the taking of the form of a servant? Through this form, which, in the printed Greek, became “a veil for the Deity of the servant,” the dispensation of human redemption was fulfilled. [Note, Col. 1170D: The printed words *τῇ τοῦ δούλου* (*tē tou doulou*), “for the [Deity] of the servant,” greatly disturb the sense and should be deleted; or, if they are retained, *λόγου* (*logou*), “of the Word,” should be read instead of *δούλου* (*doulou*), “of the servant,” yielding “a veil for the Deity of the Word.”]

For since the bonds of our ancestral captivity could not be dissolved unless a man of our race and of our nature came into existence—one not held by the sentence of sins, and one who might wash away the deadly bond with his spotless blood—what had been divinely prefigured from the beginning was accomplished in the fullness of the appointed times. Thus the promise announced in many ways came to the long-awaited fulfillment, and what had continually been made known by frequent testimonies could not remain uncertain.

The impiety of the heretics has revealed itself to be engaged in the greatest lawlessness when, under the pretext of honoring Deity, they deny the truth of human flesh in Christ. They think it pious to believe that what saves is not true in our Savior, although, according to the promise made before all ages, the world has been reconciled to God in Christ, so that, unless the Word had deigned to become flesh, no flesh could have been saved.

Indeed, the whole mystery of Christian faith is, as the heretics wish, obscured by the greatest darkness if the light of truth is thought to lie hidden beneath a deceptive apparition.

Let no Christian, therefore, consider it shameful that Christ possesses the truth of our body. For all the apostles, the disciples of the apostles, and all the illustrious teachers of the churches who were deemed worthy to attain the crown of martyrdom or the glory of confession shone in the light of this faith, proclaiming everywhere with harmonious judgments that in the Lord Jesus Christ one person of both Deity and flesh must be confessed. [Note, Cols. 1172C–D: The Latin text has *intonantes*, “proclaiming,” which could be rendered *κηρύττοντες* (*kēruttontes*). Since the Greek translator instead has *ἔκδηλοι γενόμενοι* (*ekdēloi genomenoi*), “having become manifest,” which contributes nothing to the sense here, the translator apparently read a different verb. The following Greek has both *ὡς* (*hōs*), “as,” and *ὅτι* (*hoti*), “that”; one of the two is redundant.]

But by what comparable reasoning, or by what passage of Scripture, does the impiety of the heretics think it supported—the impiety that denies the truth of Christ’s body—when neither the Law testifies to this, nor prophecy foretells it, nor the Gospels teach it, nor Christ himself has ceased to demonstrate it?

Let them search through all the arrangements of the Scriptures to find where, turning, they may flee their own darkness, not where, bending the truth, they may cast darkness over the light. Throughout all the ages they will find the truth shining forth, so that they may see this great and wondrous mystery believed from the beginning and fulfilled at the end. [Note, Col. 1172D: The Greek translator’s printed *ἵνα τὸ μέγα ... ἴδωσι τοῦτο μυστήριον* means approximately “in order that they may see this great ... mystery,” but the translator did not grasp the author’s construction; it should have been rendered *ὥστε τὸ μέγα καὶ θαυμαστὸν εἰδεῖν τοῦτο μυστήριον*, “so as to see this great and wondrous mystery.”]

Although no part of the sacred Scriptures has been silent about it, it is nevertheless enough to insert certain signs of the truth agreeing with these things, through which the diligence of faith may be directed into the most radiant breadth and may behold, in the purest light of knowledge, this: that in the Son of God, who continually confesses himself to be the Son of Man and a man, Christians ought not to blush, but ought steadfastly to glory. [Note, Col. 1172D: At the opening, the printed Greek *Περὶ οὗ καὶ*, “concerning which also,” is uncertain; perhaps read *εἰ καὶ*, “although.” Later, *Τοῦθ’ ὅπερ ἐν τῷ υἱῷ*, “this which in the Son,” is also a poor rendering; the translator should have written *Ὅτι ἐν τῷ υἱῷ*, “that in the Son.”]

So that your reverence may know that we agree with the proclamations of the venerable Fathers, I have decided to append to this present discourse some of their statements. [Alternative: “I have believed that some statements of theirs should be appended to this present discourse.”] If you deign to read them, you will find that we proclaim nothing other than what our holy Fathers taught throughout the whole world, and that no one disagrees with them except the most impious heretics. [Note: The Greek word translated “if you deign” is considered redundant.]

Having touched on these matters, most glorious and venerable Emperor, as briefly as possible, you will recognize, together with the faith divinely inspired in you, that what we proclaim agrees with it and that in no respect do we differ from the teaching of the Gospels and the Apostles, or from the creed of the Catholic confession. [Note: The Greek has a reading meaning “you will recognize,” which the Latin editor recommends.]

For, as the blessed Apostle Paul teaches, “Great is the mystery of devotion: it was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, and was taken up in glory.”

What, then, could be more beneficial to your salvation, or more suitable to your authority, than that you should provide for the peace of the churches of God by your decrees, defend the gifts of God among all your subjects, and in no way allow the devil’s servants, through the devil’s malice, to rage against anyone to that person’s destruction? Thus, while you excel in temporal royal power in this life, you may be deemed worthy also of the eternal kingdom with Christ.

May Almighty God, protecting your kingdom and salvation, preserve them for a long time, most glorious and most gentle august Emperor. [Note: These words are absent from the Latin.]

[Note: This title, published by Quesnell from a Hispanic collection, passed into later collections. In the manuscripts of Collection 8, the chapters begin that were directed—or, alternatively, excerpted—in the synod of the 318 Fathers, together with Pope Leo’s letter to Leo Augustus. The same heading appears in manuscripts of Collection 3, chapter 83, where the same testimonies are presented separately from Leo’s letter. Why these materials collected by Leo are called “directed,” or rather “excerpted,” in the synod of the 318 Fathers is unknown; some error, although common to all the manuscripts examined, has evidently entered the text.

Leo demonstrates in chapter 3 that his faith agrees with the creed of the 318 Fathers; here he strengthens and confirms the same faith with testimonies of the Fathers. Another heading appears in the ancient Verona manuscript 58, no. 37: “Here begin the Catholic testimonies of the most blessed Fathers concerning the incarnation of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, which were confirmed in the holy and venerable Council of Chalcedon against the Nestorians, Eutychians, and heretics.” The compiler of this manuscript had prefixed other testimonies of the Fathers, confirmed in the Council of Ephesus, act 1. He then copied testimonies from the address of the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon to Marcian.

In all these testimonies the compiler used the ancient translation of both councils, which Baluzius published with great accuracy. Since the testimonies collected by Leo do not appear in the ancient translation of the Council of Chalcedon, and since in reality they were neither read nor inserted in that council—as was shown in the preliminary notice to Letter 28—the compiler seems to have placed the Chalcedonian confirmation in the heading by the same editorial liberty by which, without any indication of addition, he appended many other testimonies from Augustine, which Leo certainly did not collect.

The testimonies follow the customary order from the Hispanic collection and others of the same origin, with the exception of one passage from Augustine, which Quesnell added from the Grimani manuscript. In the manuscripts of Collection 5 the testimonies occur twice: first separately in chapter 41, and then among Leo’s letters after the letter to Leo Augustus, chapter 67.

In that collection the order differs from the Hispanic collection, and some testimonies are missing. See volume III, where we will publish Collection 5 itself. Since Quesnell, when editing this collection, gave only the testimonies of chapter 41 and omitted Leo’s letters, it could be questioned whether those testimonies belonged separately to Leo’s letter. All doubt is removed by this notice, since the same testimonies occur in both places with the same numbering and order.

The Verona manuscript 58 gives the same testimonies in the same order as Collection 5, with only two differences. First, it omits Cyril’s testimony from the letter to Nestorius, which in Collection 5 is separated from Cyril’s other testimonies and placed last, after Basil’s text. Second, it moves Augustine’s testimonies to the final position because the copyist added, at the end, other very lengthy testimonies from the same teacher on his own initiative.

The manuscripts of Collections 3 and 8 include all the testimonies found in the Hispanic collection, but with the order somewhat changed. They present first Hilary’s testimonies, then Ambrose’s, then Chrysostom’s, the last of which is from the sermon on the Cross and the Thief; then Gregory of Nazianzus, Theophilus, Augustine, Basil, and Cyril, whose testimony, first in the printed editions, becomes last; finally they conclude with Athanasius’s testimony.

The difference between Collections 3 and 8 is that in Collection 3 these testimonies are copied separately in chapter 83, whereas in Collection 8 they are appended directly to Leo’s letter. We do not give the Greek version of these testimonies. The Greek passages published by Vossius after this letter of Leo in the edition of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus belong to the testimonies Leo sent to the East after the Robber Council of Ephesus, not to those appended here to the letter to Leo Augustus. Although the earlier testimonies are included here, these are much fuller and differ from them not only in number but also in order.]

What follows are TESTIMONIES excerpted from the books of Catholic Fathers concerning the subject written above, collected by Pope LEO and directed to the Emperor LEO. (G) [Note, Col. 1174D: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, though not the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, omit the last three Latin words, *Leonique imperatori directa*, “and directed to the Emperor Leo.”]

[Col. 1173]

## From the second book *On the Faith* of Saint Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers and Confessor, among other passages (No. 23)

[Note, Col. 1174D: The work cited here is commonly called *On the Trinity*. See the recension of Saint Hilary presented in volumes IX and X of our *Patrologia*. —Editor.]

### CHAPTER III

This one thing, therefore, is the immovable foundation; this is the one blessed rock of faith confessed by Peter’s mouth: “You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). [Note, Col. 1174D: The manuscripts of the Hispanic collection and others derived from it delete *est*, “is,” in the opening phrase *hoc est immobile fundamentum*, leaving “this immovable foundation.”] It sustains within itself as many arguments of truth as there will be questions of perversity and accusations of unbelief. [Note, Col. 1174D: The Vatican manuscript of Collection 8 reads *moventur*, “are raised,” instead of *movebuntur*, “will be raised.”]

In the remaining matters there is the dispensation of the Father’s will: the Virgin, the birth, and the body; afterward the cross, death, and the underworld—our salvation. [Note, Col. 1174D: Three of Quesnell’s manuscripts and three of ours—one of Collection 11 and two of Collection 21—together with the first edition, read: *veritatis paternae sit. Ergo*, “let it be the dispensation of the Father’s truth. Therefore.” The Vatican manuscript of Collection 3 reads *sit: Virgo*, “let it be: the Virgin,” instead of the printed *est: virgo*, “is: the Virgin.”]

For the sake of the human race the Son of God was born of the Virgin and the Holy Spirit, the Spirit himself serving him in this work, while his own power—that is, God’s power—overshadowed him. He sowed for himself the beginnings of a body and established the origins of flesh, so that, having become man from the Virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh, and through this union the body of the whole human race, sanctified in him, might exist. [Note, Col. 1175C: Collection 5, Vatican manuscript 58, and the Regensburg manuscript begin the excerpt here. The manuscripts of Collections 3, the Hispanic collection, and Isidore add *est*, “was,” after “born of the Virgin.” For *famulante*, “serving,” the Vatican manuscript of Collection 3 and another of Collection 8 read *alibi consorte participe, et sua*, “elsewhere as companion, participant, and his own”; Collection 5 reads *consorte, et sua*, “as companion, and his own”; the Grimani manuscript reads *participe, et sua*, “as participant, and his own.” For *consevit*, “sowed together,” the Vatican manuscripts of Collections 3 and 8 read *conseruit*, “joined together,” while the first edition reads *conscivit*, “decreed.” Collection 5, chapter 41, reads *assumptionis*, “assumption”; in the testimonies appended to Leo’s letter in chapter 67 it reads the printed *admixtionis*, “mingling.” A little later Quesnell notes *humanum corpus*, “a human body,” in the margin from two manuscripts.]

Thus, just as all were constituted in him through his willing himself to be bodily, so in turn he might be imparted to all through that which is invisible in him. [Note, Col. 1175D: Both Hispanic manuscripts and others of the same origin read *et quemadmodum*, “and just as,” rather than the printed *ut quemadmodum*, “so that, just as.”] Therefore the invisible image of God did not refuse the lowliness of human origin; through conception, birth, crying, and the cradle he passed through all the humiliations of our nature. [Note, Col. 1175D: The Vindobonensis manuscript of Collection 5, chapter 67, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 24, and Hilary’s edition read the spelling *transcucurrit* for the printed *transcurrit*, both meaning “passed through.”]

What, then, shall be given back by us that is worthy of so great an act of condescension? The one Only-begotten God, whose origin from God cannot be expressed, is inserted into the womb of the holy Virgin in the form of a tiny human body and grows. He who contains all things, and within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human birth. At whose voice archangels and angels tremble, the elements of heaven, earth, and all this world are dissolved, and the cry of infancy is heard. [Note, Col. 1175D: Hilary’s edition, both occurrences in our manuscripts of Collection 5, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 3, both Hispanic manuscripts, related manuscripts, and editions before Quesnell have the printed “heaven and earth and all the elements of this world”; Quesnell reads “earth, sea, and all things.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts read *resolvuntur*, “are dissolved,” rather than *resolventur*, “will be dissolved.” Both occurrences in Collection 5, the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, and the Vatican manuscript of Collection 3 put *infantiae vagitus auditur*, “the cry of infancy is heard,” in that word order.]

He who is invisible and incomprehensible is now wrapped in a cradle and encompassed by the sight, perception, and touch of mortals. [Note, Cols. 1175D–1176C: The Vulgate before Quesnell, Hilary’s edition, the manuscripts of Collection 5, the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, and related witnesses read *non visu, sensu tactuque moderandus*, “not to be circumscribed by sight, perception, and touch,” instead of the printed *nunc visu, sensu, tactuque mortalium cunis est obvolutus*, “is now wrapped in a cradle by the sight, perception, and touch of mortals.” The reading introduced by Quesnell from the Grimani manuscript is also found in manuscripts of Collections 3 and 8 and the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript.]

If anyone recalls these things as unworthy of God, he will confess himself subject to a greater benefit precisely because these things are less suited to God’s majesty. He did not need to become man, through whom humanity was made; but we needed God to become flesh and dwell among us—that is, by assuming one flesh, to dwell within the whole of flesh. [Note, Col. 1176C: The Vulgate before Quesnell, supported only by the first edition, reads *membra*, “members,” instead of *interna*, “inner parts”: “by assuming one flesh, he might inhabit the members of all flesh.”]

His humility is our nobility; his humiliation is our honor. What he, God, is while abiding in the flesh, we in turn are renewed into God from the flesh. [Note, Col. 1176C: Quesnell, with the Vatican manuscript of Collection 8, reads *in Deo ex carne renati*, “reborn from flesh in God.” The Vatican manuscript of Collection 3 and two manuscripts of Hilary also read *renati*, “reborn.” We restored the older reading *in Deum ex carne renovati*, “renewed from flesh into God,” as the truer reading from our other manuscripts. See Father Coustant’s note on this passage of Hilary.]

## From the ninth book of the same author, among other passages (No. 3)

Clearly, the one who does not know Christ Jesus as true God and likewise as true man does not know his own life. It is the same danger to deny Christ Jesus, whether as the Spirit who is God or as the flesh of our body.

“Therefore,” he says, “everyone who acknowledges me before human beings, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before human beings, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 10:32). [Note, Cols. 1176C–D: The word *inquit*, “he says,” found in Hilary’s manuscripts used by Coustant is also read by our manuscripts of Collection 5, chapter 67, the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, and the Vatican manuscripts of Collections 11 and 24.]

The Word made flesh was speaking these words, and the man Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, was teaching them. He himself was established as mediator for the salvation of the Church; and, through that very mystery of mediation between God and human beings, he exists as one who is both, while, from natures united into one, he is the same reality of both natures—yet in such a way that neither nature was lacking in the other. [Note, Col. 1176D: One Barberini manuscript of Collection 3 lacks the words that follow through *Haec itaque*, “This, therefore.” For *neutro*, “neither of the two,” another reading is *neutra*, “neither [nature],” which Quesnell gives in the margin.]

Otherwise, God might cease to be God in being born man, and man in turn might not be God while remaining man. This, therefore, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess the Word and the flesh; neither to be ignorant that God is man, nor to fail to recognize that the flesh is the Word. [Note: The Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript and another manuscript of Collection 5, chapter 67, add “and that he is man.”]

## From the same author, in the same book, among other passages (No. 5)

The Only-begotten God, therefore, born from the Virgin as man, and destined, in the fullness of time, to advance humanity in himself into God, maintained throughout the whole pattern of the Gospel discourse this practice: he taught himself to be believed the Son of God and instructed that he be proclaimed the Son of Man. As man, he spoke and performed all that belongs to God; then, as God, he spoke and performed all that belongs to man—yet in that very discourse concerning both kinds he never spoke except with the indication that he was both man and God. [Note, Col. 1176D: The Vulgate before Quesnell, with the Vatican Hispanic, Isidorean, and other manuscripts of Collections 8 and 11, reads *loquens et gerens*, “speaking and acting,” instead of the printed *locutus et gerens*, “having spoken and acting.” Shortly afterward the Vindobonensis manuscript of Collection 5, chapter 67, and Hilary’s edition read *sicut etiam in ipso illo*, “just as also in that very [discourse],” instead of *ut in ipso illo*, “so that in that very [discourse].”]

## From another passage in the same book, among other passages (Nos. 5–7)

Here, then, the heretics find an opportunity to deceive the simple and ignorant: they falsely claim that what he said according to his humanity was spoken because of weakness in the divine nature. And because the speaker is one and the same, they maintain that everything he said about himself was spoken by him in every respect. [Note, Col. 1176D: The Vatican manuscript of Collection 3 and another Vatican manuscript of Collection 8 read *loquitur*, “he speaks,” for the printed *loquebatur*, “he was speaking.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts, like the Vulgate before Quesnell, read *de semetipso*, “about himself,” instead of *de se ipso*, the same phrase written separately.]

We do not, of course, deny that the whole of that speech belongs to the nature that remains his own. But if Jesus Christ is both man and God, neither becoming God for the first time when he is man, nor ceasing also to be God when he is man, nor, after becoming man, failing to be whole man in God and whole God, then the mystery of his utterances must be one and the same according to the distinction of kind. [Note, Col. 1177C: Manuscripts of Collections 3, 11, and 24, the Vindobonensis Hispanic manuscript, and the first edition delete *est*, “is,” after “Jesus Christ is both man and God”; Hilary’s printed editions read *sit*, “may be.” The Vatican Hispanic, Isidorean, and another Collection 11 manuscript read *cum homo sit*, “when he is man.” The same manuscripts, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 24, and the first edition read *neque tum cum et homo*, “nor then when also man,” a reading Coustant preferred. The Vatican manuscript of Collection 3 reads *neque tunc etiam cum homo*, “nor even then when man.”]

When in time you distinguish man from God in him, distinguish also the speech of God and of man. When in time you confess God and man, judge likewise in time what was said by God and by man. But when from man and God you again understand the time of the whole man and now of the whole God, adapt whatever was said to the manifestation of that time. [Note, Col. 1177C: The Vulgate editions read *aliud*, “another thing.” We corrected this to the printed *illud*, “that thing,” with manuscripts of Collection 3, both Vatican Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, another manuscript of Collection 11, the Vatican manuscript of Collection 24, two of Quesnell’s manuscripts, and Hilary’s printed editions.]

Thus, before humanity, God is one thing; humanity and God together are another; and after humanity, the whole man and the whole God are another. Do not confuse the mystery of the dispensation according to times and kinds, since according to the quality of the kinds and natures his speech in the mystery of humanity had necessarily to be one before birth, another while he was still destined to die, and another once he was eternal.

Jesus Christ, therefore, remaining for our sake and born as man of our body, spoke according to the custom of our nature; yet he did not cease to possess what belongs to his nature as God. For although in birth, passion, and death he performed the things belonging to our nature, he nevertheless performed all those things through the power of his own nature; and so forth. [Note, Col. 1177C: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorean manuscripts and another manuscript of Collection 11 read *agens*, “doing,” instead of *manens*, “remaining”; manuscripts of Collection 11 and the first edition read *gerens*, “performing.”]

## From another passage in the same book, among other passages (No. 11)

[Col. 1177C] Do you see how God and man are proclaimed in such a way that death is attributed to the man, but the raising of the flesh to God? [Note: The words enclosed in brackets are lacking in the manuscripts Grim. Barb. 1, Thuan. 1, and in Quesnel’s Thuan. and Oxford manuscripts, as well as in our Vatican collection 3, in a similar Barb. 1, in both places in Vindeb. collection 5, and in Vatican collection 8. They are also absent from the Greek version inserted in the Acts of the second session of the Council of Chalcedon.] (Yet not in such a way that one is he who died and another is he through whom the dead man rises. [Note: Quesnel reads, “For, when the flesh had been stripped away,” together with the first edition and the Vatican Hispanic manuscript, Isidore, and others derived from them; but this is erroneous. Hilary did not understand Christ—or the person of the Word—as stripped of or separated from the flesh. We have restored the reading of the earlier editions, which is supported by Vindebonensis Hispanicus, the Vatican collection, collection 24, and Hilary’s editions. Only Vindebonensis Hispanicus has “the flesh having been stripped off.”] For Christ died with the flesh stripped away, and, again, the same Christ raises Christ from the dead, stripping himself of the flesh.) Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of man in death. And although both things were accomplished according to their respective natures, remember nevertheless that the one who is both is one Christ Jesus.

### 1388. Again, shortly afterward (No. 14)

These points, then, had to be demonstrated briefly by me, so that we might remember that the form of both natures is to be treated in the Lord Jesus Christ. [Note: The manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 in both places, as well as Vatican collection 24, read “person,” although Coustantius notes that, from the context, the word “person” is understood to mean not so much subsistence as the condition and properties of both natures.] For he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant. [Note: The Vulgate, together with the Hispanic manuscripts and Isidore, reads: “because he who, remaining in the form of God, took the form of a servant, did not in any way lose his divinity.” P. Coustantius considered these final four words—which occur in none of Hilary’s manuscripts and ought not to occur there—to have been probably taken by Leonine from the Vulgate, since the Leonine compiler believed them to have been summarized by Leo and later demonstrated more fully by Hilary. But this is not so. We have learned that these words must be rejected and deleted from Leo on the authority of the better collections 3 and 5 in both places, and 8, especially since they are also absent from the Greek version of these testimonies inserted in the second session of the Council of Chalcedon. Vatican collection 24 agrees, likewise omitting the words and reading only: “Because, remaining in the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant.” Hilary’s editions read: “because he who remained in the form of God.”]

## Saint Athanasius, bishop and confessor of the Church of Alexandria, to Epictetus, bishop of the Corinthians

### Chapter IV

How, then, did those who are called Christians dare to doubt whether the Lord, who proceeded from Mary, [Note: Vindebonensis Hispanicus and the manuscripts of collection 21, together with the first edition, add “the Virgin.” Shortly afterward, “God indeed is from the substance and nature of God” occurs in Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore. The manuscripts of collection 21 and the first edition read “is of God’s substance.” Vatican collections 11 and 24 read “the Son indeed is of the substance of God’s nature.” We have preferred the reading of the earlier editions, on the authority of Vindebonensis Hispanicus and another collection 5, chapter 67, because this reading agrees with the complete epistle published in the same collection, chapter 52. In chapter 41 of that collection: “The Son indeed is, by nature, of God’s substance.” Later, “and from the flesh” occurs in Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore and in the manuscripts of collections 11 and 21.] is indeed the Son by the substance and nature of God, while, according to the flesh, he is from the seed of David and the flesh of holy Mary?

## Saint Ambrose, bishop and confessor of the Church of Milan, from the books he sent to the emperor Gratian

[Note: See Ambrose’s work addressed to Gratian in volume XVII of our Patrology. Editor.]

In the second book On the Faith, among other passages (chapter 7, no. 58).

### Chapter V

Hence, when we read that the Lord of majesty was crucified, let us not think that he was crucified as though in his own majesty; rather, because the same one is God and the same one is man—God through divinity, man through the assumption of flesh—Christ Jesus is called the Lord of majesty crucified, because, being participant in both natures, that is, the human and the divine, he underwent suffering in the nature of man. Thus the Lord of majesty who suffered may be spoken of without distinction, as may the Son of Man who, as it is written, descended from heaven (John 3:13). [Col. 1178C]

### 1389. Again, elsewhere in the same book, among other passages (chapter 9, no. 77)

[Col. 1179A]

Let empty questions about words therefore be silent. [Note: Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore, together with another collection 11, read “empty questions of idle dissension.” Quesnel’s Thuan manuscript reads “empty questions of idle disputation.” The first edition, together with the manuscripts of collection 21, reads “empty questions of idle dissension about words.” Shortly afterward, Ambrose’s editions read “in both.” Not only do all our manuscripts, together with Leo’s Vulgate witnesses, have “in both,” but the ancient copies of the Council of Ephesus, supported also by the Greek text in session 1, as well as Marius Mercator, Rusticus, and Ambrose’s Colbert manuscript, agree. See Baluzius, volume IV of the Councils, p. 67, note g.] For the kingdom of God, as it is written, is not in persuasive speech but in the demonstration of power (1 Corinthians 2:4; 4:20). Let us preserve the distinction between divinity and flesh. The Son of God, one in both, speaks because both natures are in the same one. And although the same one speaks, he does not always speak in the same manner. Observe [Note: Vindebonensis collection 5, chapter 67, Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and other manuscripts derived from them read “in him.”] in him now the glory of God, now the sufferings of man. As God, he speaks the things that are divine, because he is the Word; as man, he says the things that are human, because he spoke in that substance. [Note: Quesnel reads “he speaks in my substance.” We have followed the earlier editions, since “in that” is found in the manuscripts of collection 3, Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and other manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, while all the manuscripts support “he was speaking.” Ambrose’s edition reads “he was speaking in my substance.” The copies of the ancient version of the Council of Ephesus and Marius Mercator agree; the Greek interpreter of Ephesus likewise reads this way. But since the Greek version of Leo’s testimonies inserted in the second session of the Council of Chalcedon prefers “he was speaking in that substance,” we believe that Leo wrote this and that it was read in Ambrose.]

Again, in the same author’s book On the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: Vatican collection 3 reads “against Apollinaris.”] against the Apollinarists (chapter 6, no. 49).

[Col. 1179B]

But while we refute these men, others arise who say that the Lord’s flesh and divinity are of one nature. What underworld has spewed forth such sacrilege? The Arians are now more tolerable, since through these men the strength of their treachery grows, so that they may assert with greater insistence that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not of one substance, because these men have attempted to say that the Lord’s divinity and flesh are of one substance. [Note: Vindebonensis collection 5 deletes “are” in both places.] [Note: Quesnel’s Oxford manuscript reads “with less contention.” Shortly afterward, the same manuscript reads “than those who,” instead of “because these men.”]

Again below (chapter 6, no. 52).

These men frequently remind me that they hold to the teaching of the Council of Nicaea. [Note: Quesnel noted in the margin, from the Thuan manuscript, “to expound the treatise.” Vindebonensis collection 5, chapter 67, reads “to retain the treatise.” Shortly afterward, Vindebonensis Hispanicus and Vatican collection 11 delete “of God.”] But in that treatise our Fathers said not that the flesh, but that the Word of God, is of one substance with the Father. They confessed that the Word proceeded from the substance of the Father, but that the flesh was from the Virgin. How, then, is the name of the Council of Nicaea brought forward as a pretext, and new teachings introduced that our forefathers never held? And so forth.

### 1390. Again, in the same author, to Sabinus, bishop, among other passages (nos. 6 and 7)

[Note: See the complete letter among the other works of Ambrose, no. 46, in volume XVII of our collection. Editor.]

Hence the Apostle beautifully used a repetition of the same expression when speaking of the Lord Jesus Christ: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant.” [Note: Vatican collection 11, the first edition, and Ambrose’s Vulgate read: “Although he was in the form.”] What is “in the form of God” except in the fullness of divinity, in that expression of divine perfection? Therefore, although he was in the fullness of divinity [Note: This reading follows Vatican collection 3 and Vindebonensis Hispanicus, with Ambrose’s Vulgate; elsewhere “divinity” is omitted.], he emptied himself (Philippians 2:6), and received the fullness of human nature and perfection. Just as nothing was lacking to God, so nothing was lacking to the perfection of man, so that he might be perfect in both forms. Hence David also says: “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3).

The Apollinarist is trapped and has nowhere to turn; he is enclosed in his own nets. For he himself said, “He took the form of a servant,” not “the servant spoke.” [Note: The Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore manuscripts, as well as another collection 11 together with Ambrose’s edition, read “he had said,” followed by “He answers.” In the same edition of Ambrose, “was read” occurs instead of “spoke.” Then “as he said” occurs in the same Vatican collection 11 and in the exemplar of the first edition.] Again, then, I ask: What is “in the form of God”? He answered, “in the nature of God.” For, says the Apostle, there are those who are not gods by nature (Galatians 4:8). I ask what “taking the form of a servant” means. Without doubt, it means the perfection of human nature and condition, as I have said, so that he might be in the likeness of human beings. And beautifully he said not “the likeness of flesh” but “the likeness of human beings,” because the same nature is in the flesh. But because he alone was without sin, while every human being is in sin, he appeared in human form. Hence the prophet also says: “And he is a man, and who knows him?” (Jeremiah 17:19).

A man according to the flesh, but beyond man according to divine operation. [Note: Both Hispanic manuscripts, together with Vatican collection 11, read “and beyond man through divine operation.” The Vulgate before Quesnel, together with the manuscripts of collections 21 and 24, reads “but beyond man through divine operation.” Vatican collection 3 reads “through divine operation.” Later, “and beyond man” occurs in both Hispanic manuscripts, Vatican Isidore, and another collection 11.] Finally, when he touched the leper, he appeared to be a man, but he was beyond man when he cleansed him. And when he wept for Lazarus, who was dead, he wept as a man over the dead; but he was beyond man when he commanded the dead man to come out with his feet bound. [Note: The manuscripts of Vatican collections 3 and 24 read “bound.” Vindebonensis Hispanicus has the erroneous “to conquer”; this was arbitrarily emended in Vatican Hispanicus and other manuscripts derived from it to “this man.” Later, “and beyond man” occurs in Vindebonensis Hispanicus.] He appeared to be a man when he hung upon the cross; but he was beyond man when, after the tombs had been opened, he raised the dead.

## 1391. Saint Augustine, bishop of the Church of Hippo Regius, to Dardanus, among other passages (no. 10)

[Note: Both Vindobonensis manuscripts, together with Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and another collection 11, read this way; others have “of Hippo.” Shortly afterward, in the last three manuscripts, “from where he will also come” occurs.]

[Note: See the letter to Dardanus, among Augustine’s other letters, no. 187, in volume XXXIII of our Library. Editor.]

### Chapter VI

Do not therefore doubt that the man Christ is now there from which he will come; and recall by heart and hold faithfully the Christian confession: that he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of the Father; and that he will come from there to judge the living and the dead. [Note: The Vulgate, together with some manuscripts, reads “from there he will come to judge the living and the dead.” We have followed the syntax of the other, outstanding manuscripts, which agrees with Augustine’s editions.] He will come in this manner, as that angelic voice testifies: “As you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:11)—that is, in the same form and substance of flesh, to which he certainly gave immortality without removing its nature.

Again, in the same author’s letter to Volusianus, among other passages (no. 9).

Now, indeed, he appeared as mediator between God and human beings, joining both natures in the unity of one person: he exalted the customary through the uncustomary, and tempered the uncustomary with the customary.

Again, in the same author’s Exposition of the Gospel according to John, among other passages (Tractate 78, no. 2).

[Note: That is, tractate 78 on the Gospel of John, found in volume XXXV of our Patrology.]

[Col. 1181B]

What then, heretic? Since Christ is God and man, he speaks as man, and you slander God? He commends the human nature in himself; do you dare to deform the divine nature in him?

And again below (no. 3).

Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, by which he is equal to the Father; the human, by which the Father is greater than he. Yet taken together, these are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. For just as one human being consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man; and therefore Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all these things, Christ in each one of them. Who is he through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant. [Note: In the manuscripts of collections 3, 5, and 8 in both places, and in Veronensis 58, the following words are omitted through the end. The Vulgate before Quesnel, together with our other manuscripts, presents them as a separate testimony: “Again, the same author as above: Who was not abandoned,” and so forth. This seems to indicate a new addition. We have not excluded Quesnel’s reading, taken from the Grimani manuscript, since it agrees with Augustine’s edition; from that edition we have preferred “Again” to “The same,” which Quesnel had.] Again, concerning the individual elements of which a human being consists: Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ Jesus, but in the soul alone. Who, destined to rise, lay for three days in the tomb? Christ Jesus, but in the flesh alone. Thus Christ is spoken of in each of these particulars. Yet in all these things there are not two or three Christs, but one Christ. Therefore he said: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father” (John 14:28). For human nature ought to rejoice, because it was so assumed by the only-begotten Word that it was established immortal in heaven, and thus earth was exalted, so that incorruptible dust might sit at the right hand of the Father.

Again, from the same author’s book The Assertion of Faith.

[Note: Quesnel published this testimony, taken from Leporius’s little book of faith, from the Grimani manuscript. Although we were unable to find it anywhere in the other manuscripts, there can be no doubt that it was excerpted by Leo, since it is found among the testimonies inserted in the second session of the Council of Chalcedon. It is certain that Leo had collected these testimonies long before and sent them separately to the East; for he appended all of them, together with many others, to this epistle. We are surprised only that this testimony is also absent from Veronensis 58, in which the diligent collector added several other lengthy passages to Augustine’s four preceding testimonies at no. 38. See Quesnel’s note Qam.]

For it is ours to believe, but his to know; and thus, just as God the Word himself, receiving all that belongs to man, is man, so the man who was assumed, receiving all that belongs to God, can be nothing other than God.
