Yet because he is called incarnate and mingled, this must not be understood as a diminution of his substance. For God knows how to mingle without corruption of himself, and yet to mingle truly. He knows how to receive into himself in such a way that nothing is added to him, who knows how to pour himself wholly into another without suffering any loss.

Let us not therefore, in order to understand our weakness, form an inference from visible examples of created things entering one another, and suppose that God and man were mingled and that, through such a confusion of flesh and Word, some sort of body was produced. Far be it from us to believe that the two natures were reduced into one substance through some kind of fused composition. For such mingling is the corruption of both parts. God, who is capable of containing but cannot be contained, who penetrates but cannot be penetrated, who fills but cannot be filled, who is wholly everywhere at once and diffused everywhere through the infusion of his power, was mercifully mingled with human nature; human nature was not mingled with the divine.

## 1393. Saint John, bishop and confessor of Constantinople, in the homily On the Cross and the Thief

### Chapter VII

But why do we see him come with the cross? [Note: Vatican collection 11 and the first edition read “he will come,” omitting the verb “let us see.”] Clearly, so that those who crucified him may experience the blindness of their madness; and therefore the sign of their shamelessness is carried. [Note: The manuscripts of collections 3 and 8, the Hispanic manuscripts, and the others of the same origin also have “madness” here. Later, the Hispanic manuscripts and Isidore delete “all.”] Hence the prophet says: “Then all the tribes of the earth will lament” (Zechariah 12:10), seeing their accuser and recognizing their sin.

And what is surprising if he will come bearing the cross, when he himself also displays the wounds of his body? For he says: “Then they will see him whom they pierced” (the same passage; John 19:37). And just as, after the resurrection, he wished to refute Thomas’s disbelief, and showed him the places of the nails, and made known the wounds of his side, and said: “Put your hand here and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (John 20:27; Luke 24:39), so then also he will show the wounds and display the cross, to demonstrate that he is the one who had been crucified. [Note: The two Hispanic manuscripts have “of the dead” instead of “of Thomas,” and afterward “and those things” instead of “and to him.” In the same manuscripts and in the first edition, together with the manuscripts of collection 21, “strengthen” occurs instead of “refute.”] [Note: Vindebonensis Hispanicus erroneously reads “in the side”; this was corrected in Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore to “in his side.”]

Again, in the same author’s homily On the Ascension of the Lord.

For just as, when two people separated by a quarrel have a mediator placed between them, he dissolves the dispute and disagreement of those who are contending, so Christ also did. God was rightly angry with us, and we despised him in his anger, turning away from the merciful Lord; Christ interposed himself and joined the two natures, and himself endured the punishment that threatened us. [Note: The Vulgate inserts “for us.” We have deleted it on the authority of the better manuscripts of collections 5, Hispanicus, Isidore, and others.] [Note: Both Hispanic manuscripts, together with Isidore and Vatican collection 11, read “both things” and “for us.” Shortly afterward, Quesnel reads “the punishment imposed by the Father.” We have deleted “from the Father” on the authority of the manuscripts of collection 3, Vindebonensis collection 5 in both places, Vindebonensis Hispanicus, Vatican collections 11, 21, and 24, and the editions before Quesnel.]

Again, in the same author’s homily, among other passages.

[Col. 1183A]

Christ, then, offered the first fruits of our nature to the Father, and the Father marveled at the gift that was offered, both because such dignity offered it and because what was offered was defiled by no stain. For he received the offering with his own hands, made it share in his own seat, and, what is more, placed it at the side of his right hand. Let us recognize who it is who heard: “Sit at my right hand” (Psalm 109:1; Matthew 22:44); what nature it is to which he said: “Be a sharer in my seat.” That nature is the one which heard: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Genesis 3:19). [Note: Vindebonensis collection 5, chapter 67, reads “who he is who.” Shortly afterward, “What is that nature which heard, ‘You are earth,’” occurs in Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore. Both Vindobonensis manuscripts of collection 5, the Hispanic manuscripts, and Vatican collection 24 delete only the word “is” after “nature.”]

Again, in the same author’s homily, among other passages.

I cannot find what speech to use or with what words to express it. A fragile nature, a despised nature, a nature shown to be inferior to all things, conquered all things, surpassed all things, and today merited to be found higher than all things. [Note: Some manuscripts delete “and.” Vatican collection 3 reads “and today merited to be found higher than all the angels.” Shortly afterward, Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and the manuscripts of collection 11 read “they received what they had long desired.” Vindebonensis collection 5 and Vatican collection 24 have “they received,” with the rest as in the text.] Today the angels received the long-desired fulfillment of their hopes; today the archangels were able to behold what they had desired for so long; they saw our nature shining with immortal glory in the Lord’s seat. [Note: The Vulgate inserts “themselves.” We have deleted it with the manuscripts of collections 3, 5, and 8, the Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and others.]

## Saint Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, from the Paschal Letter that he sent throughout Egypt

[Note: From Jerome’s translation, among his works, Letter 98, no. 4, in volume XXII of this Library. Editor.]

### Chapter VIII

The witness to this is the one who says: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Psalm 13:3). And the prophets, imploring the help of Christ: “Lord, bend your heavens and descend” (Psalm 143:5). [Note: Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore, together with the manuscripts of collection 21 and the example of the first edition, read: “The prophet, imploring the help of Christ.” Later, both Vindobonensis manuscripts and Vatican collection 3 delete “your.” Afterward, these manuscripts, Vatican collection 24, and Jerome’s edition have “places” instead of “place.”]

Not that he might change the place in which all things are, but that, for the sake of our salvation, he might assume flesh of human frailty, as the Apostle Paul likewise declares: “Although he was rich, he became poor, so that we might become rich through his poverty” (2 Corinthians 8:9). [Note: Some manuscripts omit “Paul”; others, together with Jerome’s edition, delete “the Apostle.” Later, the Vulgate before Quesnel, together with Vatican collection 24 and Jerome’s edition, reads “poor for us.” Later still, the same Vulgate witnesses, together with both Hispanic manuscripts and Vatican Isidore, read “we might be enriched.”]

[Note: This reading, “into the lands,” is found in the manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 in both places, both Hispanic manuscripts, the manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, and Jerome’s edition; elsewhere it reads “into the earth.”]

And he came into the lands, and, having become man, emerged from the virginal womb that he had sanctified, confirming through his dispensation the interpretation of his name, Emmanuel—that is, “God with us” (Matthew 1:25). In a wondrous manner he began to be what we are, and did not cease to be what he was, assuming our nature in such a way that he did not lose what he himself was. [Note: The manuscripts of collections 3 and 8, together with Jerome’s edition, read “what he had been.” Shortly afterward, the Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and Vatican collection 11 read “thus he assumed.” Later, Jerome’s edition has “human nature” instead of “our nature.”]

For although John writes: “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14) [Note: The Vulgate, from the Hispanic manuscripts and others derived from them, reads: “that is, in other words, God became man; nevertheless the Word was not changed into flesh.” We have preferred the reading of the manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 in both places, confirmed by Jerome’s edition.], that is, “in other words, man,” yet the one who never ceased to be God was not changed into flesh. To him [Note: Editions before Quesnel, together with the Hispanic manuscripts and others of the same origin, read “the Holy Spirit speaks.” Quesnel, with the manuscripts of collection 5, reads “the Holy One speaks.” We have followed the manuscripts of collection 8, with which Jerome’s edition agrees.] holy David also says: “But you are the same” (Psalm 101:28). And the Father testifies from heaven and says: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” [Note: Vindebonensis Hispanicus, together with the manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, reads “I was pleased.”] (Matthew 3:17; Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22), so that, although he became man, he may be said, according to our confession, to remain [Note: Quesnel inserted “this.” We have deleted it with the earlier editions, supported by most and the better manuscripts and by Jerome’s edition.] what he was before he became man. Paul proclaims the same thing with us: “Jesus Christ, himself, yesterday and today, and forever” (Hebrews 13:8). [Note: The Vulgate reads “the same himself.” We have removed “the same,” on the authority of the same manuscripts, with Jerome’s edition and the context that follows agreeing.]

For by saying “himself,” he shows that he did not change his former nature or diminish the riches of his divinity, because, having become poor for our sake, he had assumed the complete likeness of our condition. [Note: Jerome’s edition reads “who.”]

Again, in another Paschal Letter of the same author against Origen, among other passages.

[Note: Letter 96, no. 3, among Jerome’s works in volume XXII of our collection. Editor.]

[Col. 1185A]

The Father’s one Son and our mediator neither lost his equality with him nor was separated from our fellowship: invisible God and visible man, concealed in the form of a servant, and acknowledged by the confession of believers as the Lord of glory. [Note: Jerome’s Vulgate, together with Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore, adds “is.”] For the Father did not deprive him of the title belonging to his nature after he became man and poor for our sake, nor, when he was baptized in the Jordan River, did he call him by another name, but called him the only-begotten Son: “You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17; Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22). [Note: The same Vulgate witnesses delete “well.” Shortly afterward, “I am well pleased” occurs in the Hispanic manuscripts, Isidore, and the other manuscripts derived from them.] Nor was our likeness changed into the nature of divinity, nor was divinity changed into the likeness of our nature.

## Saint Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus, in the homily On the Epiphany, among other passages

### Chapter IX

When, therefore, God had proceeded from the Virgin, existing as one out of two mutually contrary things—flesh and spirit—one was assumed into God, while the other bestowed the grace of divinity. [Note: The manuscripts of collection 5 in both places delete “for himself.” Shortly afterward, Vatican collection 21 and the first edition read “one into God, two.”]

Again below.

He was indeed sent, but as man. For there were two natures in him. Hence, finally, he both grew weary from the journey, and hungered, and thirsted, and was saddened, and wept according to the law of the human body.

## Saint Basil, bishop of Cappadocia

[Note: Vatican Hispanicus manuscript 1341, of Gallican origin, and Vatican 630, Isidore, together with Vatican 3791 of collection 11 and other manuscripts of the same kind, which derived this letter from Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts of Gallican origin, have “Saint Sabinus, bishop” instead of “Saint Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.” In Vatican manuscript 543 of collection 21 both are found: “Saint Basil of Cappadocia, bishop Sabinus.” It is clear that this was introduced by a diligent copyist who, while writing a Hispanic collection of Gallican origin, arbitrarily corrected several passages (see the preface, section 10). For in the very ancient Vindobonensis 41 of the same, pure Hispanic collection, as in the other ancient manuscripts and collections, the name is not Sabinus but Saint Basil.]

### Chapter X

When, therefore, we see certain things in Christ so human that they seem to differ in nothing from the common frailty of mortals, and others so divine [Note: “So that they belong to no one” in Vatican collection 21 and the first edition.] that they suit no other nature than that ineffable nature of divinity, the narrowness of the human intellect clings fast and, struck by the stupor of such great wonder, does not know where to turn, what to hold, or where to direct itself. [Note: Quesnel, in chapter 41 of collection 5, from the Oxford manuscript, adds: “If he thinks him God, he contemplates him crucified.” But these words are omitted both from all our and Quesnel’s Leonine manuscripts and from the Vindobonensis manuscript of collection 5 in both places, as well as from Quesnel’s Thuan manuscript, which is much better than the Oxford manuscript.]

If he thinks him a man, he sees him returning from the dead, having overcome the realm of death with its spoils. Therefore he must be contemplated with every fear and reverence, so that, in one and the same person, the truth of both natures may be demonstrated in such a way that neither anything unworthy or unfitting is thought about that divine and ineffable substance, nor, on the other hand, are the things accomplished humanly judged to be deceptive images. [Note: The manuscripts of Vatican Hispanicus and Isidore and another collection 11 read “with excessive fear.” Later, the same manuscripts, together with Vindebonensis Hispanicus, collection 3, Vindebonensis collection 5 in both places, and Vatican collection 24, delete “humanly.”]

## Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria

[Note: Oration 2, On Right Faith, addressed to the queens, chapter 9.]

### Chapter XI

He was named man, although by nature he is God, the Word of God the Father, because he likewise shared with us in blood and flesh. Thus he appeared on earth, not abandoning what he was, but assuming human nature perfect in its own constitution. [Note: Only Vindebonensis Hispanicus reads “was born.” Shortly afterward, the same manuscript, Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and another collection 11 delete “God.” Later, Vindebonensis collection 5 in both places reads “appeared in earthly things.”]

### 1397. Again, from the same author’s book called Scholia on the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten

[Col. 1186B]

He is therefore one: both the true God before the incarnation and the one who, in humanity, remained what he was, is, and will be. We must not therefore distinguish one Lord Jesus Christ as a separate man and, separately, as God; rather, we say that Jesus Christ is one and the same, not ignoring the differences of the natures but preserving them distinct and unconfused from one another. [Note: Vatican Hispanicus, Isidore, and another collection 11 read “preserving them among themselves.” Vindebonensis collection 5, chapter 41, reads “retaining them among themselves.” The better reading is found in Vatican collection 3 and the first edition: “preserving them among themselves.”]

Again, from the same author.

[Note: The Vulgate before Quesnel, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, reads “For it is said, as though.” Quesnel omitted “as though”; we have added it from both Hispanic manuscripts, Vatican Isidore, and the other manuscripts derived from them, as well as from the Greek text. Shortly afterward, Quesnel added “or an exchange,” words which these same manuscripts and the first edition contain.]

For it is certainly understood as though one thing dwells in another—that is, the divine nature, without undergoing mingling or exchange in humanity, so that it might become what it was not. For whatever is said to dwell in another does not itself become such as that in which it dwells is, but is rather understood as one thing in another. [Note: Quesnel alone reads “in him.” Shortly afterward, the earlier editions, together with Vatican collection 24 alone, read “person” instead of “nature,” incorrectly.]

But in the case of the nature of the Word and of humanity, their difference signifies for us only the distinction of the natures. For one Christ is understood from both. Therefore, without confusion, as I said before, he says that the Word dwelt in us. [Note: This reading agrees with the editions and with the manuscripts of collection 24. Both Hispanic manuscripts, together with others derived from them, read “he says that he dwelt in confession,” erroneously for “in an unconfused manner,” as I had said before. From the Greek original inserted in the second session of Chalcedon, he carefully says “the Word dwelt in us” in order to exclude confusion.] For he knows that there is one only-begotten Son, made flesh and man.

Again, from the same author, to Nestorius.

The holy and great synod therefore says that he who was naturally born from God the Father—the only-begotten Son, true God from true God, light from light, through whom and with whom the Father made all things—descended, was incarnate, became man, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended once more into heaven. We must follow these words and obey these doctrines, considering what it means for the Word of God to be incarnate and to have become man. For we do not say that God’s nature was changed or altered into flesh, nor that it was transformed wholly into a man composed of soul and body; rather, we say that the Word substantially united to himself flesh endowed with a rational soul, and that, incomprehensibly and ineffably, he became man and was also called the Son of Man—not by bare will alone, nor by the assumption of a person alone, but because natures truly different came together into one, while nevertheless one Christ and Son proceeded from both. The distinction of the natures was neither emptied nor removed by the union; rather, Divinity and humanity together made for us one Lord, Christ, and Son through that mysterious and ineffable union into one.

[Note: [Col. 1187C] We have added “and incomprehensibly” from Corb. ms. collection 2, cited by Quesnell in the margin, and from our Vatican collection 8. Vindob. collection 5 likewise has it in both places, reading *indeprehensibiliter* (“incomprehensibly”) where the other has *incomprehensibiliter*; and another ancient version inserted into the Council of Ephesus reads *inintelligibiliter* (“inconceivably”). The Vulgate, together with collection 3 and others derived from the Spanish tradition, incorrectly reads *et inreprehensibiliter* (“and irreproachably”), which Quesnell, not understanding it, deleted; but in collection 5, chapter 41, he printed *indeprehensibiliter*. Shortly afterward Vindob. collection 5 also deletes the word.]

[Note: [Col. 1187D] The Vulgate of Leo before Quesnell, together with Vatican collection 24, reads *copulationis adunationem* (“the uniting of the union”). Vatican collection 8 reads *copulationem adunatam* (“a union made one”); in this manuscript, as also in Vatican collection 3 shortly afterward, *creditur* (“is believed”) occurs in place of *dicitur* (“is said”). Then, after *procreatus* (“begotten”), the printed editions add *in tempore* (“in time”); we have deleted it, following the better manuscripts and the Greek text.]

Accordingly, he who was born from the Father before all ages is also said to have been physically begotten from a woman.

[Col. 1187C] This is not because his divine nature took its beginning from the holy Virgin, nor because he himself needed to be born a second time after the birth which he had from the Father—for it is absurd and foolish to say that he who is coeternal with the Father before all ages needed a second generation in order to begin to exist—but because, for our sake and for our salvation, he united to himself a human nature and proceeded from a woman; for this reason he is said to have been born physically.

Nor was an ordinary man first born from the holy Virgin, and only afterward did the Word dwell in him; rather, in the very virginal womb and uterus he united flesh to himself and underwent a physical generation, making the birth of his flesh his own.

[Note: [Col. 1187D] Some copies have *primum* or *primitus* (“first” or “at first”). In Vatican collection 3, the reading is *secum carnem conjunxit* (“he united flesh to himself”).]

Thus we say that he also suffered and rose again—not because God the Word in his own nature suffered blows, the piercing of nails, or other wounds (for God, being incorporeal, is beyond suffering),

[Note: [Col. 1187D] The Vulgate adds *susceperit* (“received” or “underwent”). We have deleted it, following the manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 in both places, together with Vindob. and Spanish manuscripts and Vatican collection 24. The other versions and the Greek text likewise lack this verb.]

but because that body which became his own suffered; therefore all these things are said to have been suffered by him for our sake. God, who could not suffer, was present in that body which was suffering.

We understand his death in the same way. The Word of God is naturally immortal and incorruptible, life itself, and life-giving. But because his own body, by the grace of God, as Paul says, tasted death for everyone (Hebrews 2:9),

[Col. 1188B] therefore he himself is said to have suffered death for us.

[Note: [Col. 1188C] The printed editions read *in se* (“in himself”). We have followed the reading of the better manuscripts of collections 3 and 5 in both places, supported by the ancient Ephesian translation and especially by the original Greek. Later, collection 5 manuscripts read *vera caro ipsius* (“his true flesh”). Some time afterward, Vindob. collection 5, chapter 11, both Spanish copies, Isidore, and Vatican collection 24 read *ceciderat* (“had fallen”). Shortly afterward the editions before Quesnell, together with collection 21 manuscripts, have *quod absit* (“far be it”).]

This does not mean that he himself experienced death insofar as his own nature is concerned—for it is madness either to think or to say this—but, as we said above, that his flesh tasted death. Likewise, when the flesh rose again, we speak of his resurrection—not because it had fallen into corruption, God forbid, but because his body rose again.

Thus we confess one Christ and one Lord, not worshiping a man together with the Word, as though some form of division were thereby introduced, but worshiping one and the same person; for his body is not alien to the Word, since it also sits with him at the Father’s side.

[Note: [Col. 1188D] Vindob. collection 5 reads here *ipse* (“he himself”). In place of *impossibilem* (“impossible”), the Vatican and Spanish copies and Isidore have *impassibilem* (“incapable of suffering”), incorrectly. Perhaps from this was corrected the reading *passibilem* (“capable of suffering”) in Vatican collection 24, which passed into the editions before Quesnell. The same copies shortly afterward have *voluerimus* (“we shall have wished”) instead of *noluerimus* (“we shall not have wished”). They also read *incidemus* (“we fall into”) here, as do the Spanish copies, Isidore, and another collection 11.]

Nor do we say this as though two sons were sitting there, but one Son with the flesh, through unity. For if we refuse to accept that such a substantial union took place, regarding it as either impossible or somehow unbecoming, we necessarily fall into saying that there are two sons:

[Col. 1188C] for we must distinguish and say that the man was separately honored merely by the title of Son, while the Word who is from God was Son of God both in name and in reality.

[Note: [Col. 1188D] Only Vindob. collection 5, chapter 41, reads *nec enim debemus discernere* (“for we ought not to distinguish”); in chapter 67 it reads *nec enim discernere*. Thuanus and Quesnell’s copy of the same collection, chapter 41, have *nec enim discernere fas est* (“for it is not lawful to distinguish”). We have retained the common reading, supported by the other manuscripts and consistent with the original Greek; Cyril teaches this as a consequence of Nestorius’s doctrine.]

But we must not divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons. Nor does this help the correct rule of faith, although some people assert some sort of union of persons.

[Note: [Col. 1189A] In Vindob. Spanish, *copulationem* (“union”) is omitted. Vatican Spanish and Isidore arbitrarily emend it to *personarum distinctionem* (“a distinction of persons”); Vatican collection 24 has *divisionem personarum* (“a division of persons”).]

[Col. 1189A] For Scripture did not say that the Word of God assumed to himself the person of a man, but that he became flesh (John 1:14).

This means that the Word of God, like us, shared in flesh and blood, made our body properly his own, and proceeded as a man from a woman—not abandoning or laying aside his Godhead or that generation which he had from the Father, but remaining God even in the assumption of flesh, as he was.

[Note: [Col. 1189A] Vatican collection 3, the Spanish manuscripts, and another Vindob. collection 5 read *participatum* (“shared in”) in both places. The Vatican and Spanish copies and Isidore read *participium* (“participation”).]

The rule of right faith everywhere bears witness to this. We find that the holy Fathers held this sense. For this reason they did not hesitate to call the holy Virgin *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος, “God-bearer” or “Mother of God”)—not because the nature and Godhead of the Word took their beginning from the holy Virgin,

[Note: [Col. 1189B] Since *in* was absent from Vindob. and a similar Spanish copy, the Vatican and Spanish copies, Isidore, and others derived from them supplied *de* (“from”).]

but because that sacred body, animated by a rational soul and substantially united to the Word of God, was born from her, and the Word is said to have been physically born.

[Note: [Col. 1189B] In the manuscripts of collections 3 and 8, two additional testimonies are inserted. They do not pertain to Leo’s case and do not have Leo as their author. They are as follows:

“Likewise, the faith of Saint Hilary. For, following in the footsteps of the Fathers, instructed by the words of Scripture, we teach and preach in the churches and confess that the uncreated and eternal Trinity is of one substance in three substances [read: subsistences], and we worship one Godhead. Likewise, the faith of Saint Augustine. We believe in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. These are eternal and unchangeable: one God, one substance, and an eternal Trinity. God, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, in whom all things are. For we know his source, from which all things exist; his image, through whom all things are formed; and his holiness, in whom all things are ordered.”

Finally, this conclusion is added: “The testimonies extracted from the books of the holy Fathers have been completed. They show that Christ was begotten of two substances—that is, of the true and perfect natures of both Godhead and humanity—and that there is one person of Christ.” In the manuscripts of collection 3, *gigantem esse* (“to be a giant”) is erroneously written instead of *geminae substantiae gignitum esse* (“to have been begotten of two substances”).]

ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

[Col. 1189]

1. The superscription of the letter itself presents no small difficulty. We find it in manuscripts of nine collections: namely, the Spanish, Isidorian, collections 11, 12, and 20 through 24, and in Sichard’s copy. The superscription varies in these manuscripts both in the bishop’s name and in the name of the episcopal see. For the Vatican Spanish and Isidorian copies, together with manuscripts of collections 12 and 20–23, present Leo as bishop of Ravenna—*Ravennatem*, *Ravennensem*, or *Ravennatensem*. But the manuscripts of collections 11 and 24, together with the copies of Merlin and Sichard, give Neon, Neonium, or Neoniam, likewise of Ravenna. The three manuscripts cited by Quesnell in note 1, in which *Neonae* or *Neoniae* is read, we have determined to belong to collection 24. Isidore’s edition, cited by the same author, points to Merlin’s copy, which in this letter, as in several others, approaches the readings of collection 24.

Since the manuscripts known thus far were similar to those which agree in naming the see of Ravenna, only the bishop’s name could be in doubt. We have, however, found two old Vindobonese books in which Leo’s name is retained but the episcopal see differs substantially. The Vindobonese copy which, as we have said elsewhere, contains the purer Spanish collection gives Leo as bishop of Arbon in the title, and in the superscription reads: “Leo sends greetings to Leo, bishop of Arbon.” Another Vindobonese copy, marked collection 5, number 42, into which several letters from the Spanish collection were inserted, gives this title: “To Leo, bishop of Narbonne.”

2. To make the solution easier amid such variety of manuscripts and collections, we observe that this letter derives from two separate sources: first, the Spanish collection, from which the authors of the Isidorian collection and of collections 12 and 20–23 derived it; and second, another copy from which the author of collection 24, Merlin, and Sichard took it. The variants which we find when rereading the letter in these same manuscripts reveal this twofold origin.

Since, however, with regard to the name of the episcopal see, several manuscripts of the first origin which name Ravenna agree with all the manuscripts of the other source, there can be no doubt that the see was Ravenna. This is confirmed above all by the fact that the two Vindobonese manuscripts which disagree contain an evident error. The bishopric of Arbon, which is read in the Spanish Vindobonese manuscript, is unknown; and at this time Narbonne was not held by Leo but by Rusticus, to whom we shall see that another, later letter was addressed.

Nor should the fact that the first Vindobonese manuscript contains the purer Spanish collection influence us. Although it is purer insofar as it did not receive the corrections introduced into Gallican manuscripts, it is nevertheless extremely corrupt, and it sufficiently reveals its error in the same superscription, in the bishopric of Arbon, which no one will find.

This error is demonstrated even more clearly by the older and more carefully corrected Spanish manuscripts used by the author of the *Breviary of the Canons of the Spanish Church*, edited by Cardinal de Aguirre. We have found a manuscript copy of this *Breviary* among the Vatican manuscripts, number 4887. This work, written at the end of the seventh century—as P. Coustantius also proved in the preface to his *Epistles of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 150—is a breviary of the Spanish collection, which its Spanish author certainly took from Spanish manuscripts.

In book IV, titles 30 and 35, it cites two titles from the following letter. In both places the letter is cited in these words: “Letter of Leo to Leo of Ravenna,” title 1 or 2, beginning at chapter 73; in that chapter the following letter is recorded in the Spanish collection. Therefore, concerning the name of the see of Ravenna, in which the purer and older Spanish manuscripts and those derived from them agree with the other manuscripts descended from a different source, there can be no uncertainty.

3. Since the Ravenna bishopric is thus established, the name Neon must be accepted, as the catalogues of Ravenna demonstrate; for during this period no Leo is found among the bishops of that see.

Here, however, the ancient catalogues of the bishops of the Church of Ravenna create a difficulty—ancient catalogues, I mean, which can be read in Agnellus, first published by Bacchinius. Although the more recent catalogues in Rubeus and Ughellus do not impede the present argument, they abandoned the ancient order arbitrarily in order to reconcile certain later-discovered monuments with various preconceptions.

In those ancient catalogues no Leo, certainly, is found as bishop of this period; yet Neo appears before Saint Peter Chrysologus, whereas from this letter he ought to be later. To remove this difficulty, two things must be distinguished in these catalogues: the order of the bishops, and the time and deeds attributed to them.

The order of the ancient catalogues, insofar as the bishops of the earlier centuries are concerned, was derived from the most ancient diptychs, which had long been preserved in each church. Unless something altogether evident compels us otherwise, that order must be retained.

The dates and deeds assigned to individual bishops, however, could not have been taken from diptychs, in which only the bishops’ names were recorded. They therefore depend on the discretion of medieval authors, or even on certain widespread preconceptions, which should count for very little in ancient matters.

Hence such catalogues sometimes contain numerous fables, rejected by the calculations of learned scholars; and other uncertain or contradictory details are repeatedly exposed when more reliable ancient monuments come to light. We have shown this to be established in the catalogues of other churches, and particularly evident in those of Ravenna, in book II of the *Observations on the Sacred Works of Cardinal Noris*, chapter 7, no. 3, volume IV, page 915. There we also showed that when the order of the bishops conflicts with the deeds and dates attributed to them, it is better to suspect an error in the wrongly assigned deeds and dates than in the order of the bishops.

4. The order of the bishops of Ravenna in this period, as given by Agnellus and the other ancient writers of the Church of Ravenna, is as follows: Ursus, Peter, Neo, Exuperantius, John, Peter.

Since they attribute Valentinian III’s privilege to John, they assign to the second Peter the facts that are certain about Saint Peter Chrysologus. Three monuments published later oppose this: first, Leo’s letter to Neon, which suits the bishop who succeeded Peter Chrysologus; second, Pope Simplicius’s letter to John, bishop of Ravenna, who held that see after Peter and Neo; and third, the Roman synod under Symmachus, in which another Peter of Ravenna is found subscribed.

Observing this, P. Bacchinius resorted to two measures in order to resolve the threefold difficulty. First, he suspected that Leo’s letter was sent not to Neon of Ravenna but to Ravennius of Arles, to whom other letters of the same pontiff were sent during this period, since it is established that the Gauls were devastated by Attila and that captives were taken from there and later returned to their homeland, as this letter relates.

Then, in order to accommodate the other two monuments, he thought that two bishops should be added to the catalogues just mentioned: another John, who lived under Simplicius, and a third Peter, who lived under Symmachus—as though Agnellus and the other writers of the ancient catalogues had confused two Johns and two Peters under John Angeloptus and Peter the second.

Anyone who does not suspect errors in the wrongly assigned facts and dates is necessarily driven to introduce all these wholly arbitrary suppositions.

5. To place Ravennius of Arles in the superscription of Leo’s letter is contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts. It was not Gaul alone that Attila devastated: he reached Italy itself, as far as the Po, beyond which the province of Ravenna—and even part of its diocese—extended.

Moreover, this letter appears from its context to be an encyclical addressed to several persons, so that no special argument need be sought on behalf of Ravenna. The addition of the two bishops, John and Peter, would be plausible if there were no other means of reconciling everything.

But when an error in a catalogue is certain and can be corrected simply by revising facts and dates that were added at the discretion of its authors or established by their preconceptions, the order of the bishops—which originated in the most ancient diptychs—should not be abandoned or disturbed by additions.

By this sufficiently clear rule, which will be found extremely useful in the catalogues of other churches, you will discover that in the present case the entire difficulty and confusion introduced by the catalogues arise from the fact that what should have been assigned to the first of the two Peters of Ravenna was assigned to the second. In this way they gave an earlier age to Neo and the others.

But if this error is corrected, and Saint Peter Chrysologus is understood to be the first Peter rather than the second, everything is immediately restored and found to fit perfectly. He will be the one who wrote the celebrated letter to Eutyches. Neo then succeeded him, and to Neo the Holy Pontiff wrote the following letter. Afterward, following Exuperantius, Neo’s successor, came John under Simplicius, and finally another Peter under Symmachus.

If Agnellus and the authors of the ancient catalogues had seen these monuments, we have no doubt that, while preserving the order of the bishops, they would have reconciled the same monuments in the manner of Rubeus and Ughellus; and thus the true date of Neon would have been confirmed by them. The fact that the monuments were unknown at that time cannot prejudice the certain testimony of the manuscripts, which address this letter to Neon of Ravenna.

1405 LETTER [Note: [Col. 1191B] Also numbered 135. Written 24 October 458.] CLXVI. TO NEON, BISHOP OF RAVENNA. Concerning those who return from captivity and are uncertain whether they received baptism before their captivity.

[Col. 1191A]

SYNOPSIS (From the Spanish collection)

I. Concerning children who fell into captivity and do not remember the grace of baptism.—II. That one baptized by heretics should receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands.

LEO, bishop, sends greetings to NEON, bishop of Ravenna.

Often, with the Spirit of God instructing us, we have strengthened the wavering hearts of our brothers amid the uncertainty of various questions, gathering the form of our response either from the disciplines of the holy Scriptures or from the rules of the Fathers;

[Note: [Col. 1191B] The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian copies, together with manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 and the other manuscripts of the same origin, read *ambiguis* (“uncertain” or “ambiguous”).]

but recently, in a synod, a new and previously unheard-of kind of consultation has arisen.

[Note: [Col. 1191B] Thus the Vulgate, together with manuscripts of collection 24 and the copies of Merlin and Sichard. Vindob. Spanish reads *nunc per in synodouum*, a corrupt reading corrected by the author of the Gallican manuscripts of Spanish origin as *nunc periculosum novum* (“now a dangerous new [matter]”). This arbitrary and false correction is found in the Vatican Spanish, Isidorian, and other manuscripts of collections 11 and 21 and those derived from them; the two manuscripts cited by Quesnell in the margin should be assigned to these.]

For we have learned from the report of certain brothers that some captives, returning freely to their own places—namely, those who had fallen into captivity at an age when they could have retained no reliable knowledge of anything—seek the remedy of baptism;

[Note: [Col. 1191B] The Vulgate before Quesnell, together with manuscripts of collection 24 and Merlin, reads *libertatemque redeuntes* (“returning to freedom”), and shortly afterward *pervenerint* (“had arrived”).]

but, because of the ignorance of infancy, cannot remember whether they received the mystery and sacrament of baptism; and therefore, amid the uncertainty of this hidden memory, they put their souls in danger, while, under the appearance of caution, grace is denied them because it is thought to have already been given.

[Note: [Col. 1192B] We preferred this reading from the manuscripts of collection 24. Vindob. Spanish also approaches it, though corruptly, reading *forma poterit* (“the form will be able”). The Vulgate before Quesnell, together with Merlin, reads *firmam poterat* (“could have had a firm [knowledge]”). Quesnell reads *ferme poterat* (“could scarcely have had”), with our Vatican Spanish, Isidorian, and other manuscripts of the same origin; these shortly afterward have *implorant* (“they seek”) instead of *implorare* (“to seek”).]

Since some brothers’ fear quite reasonably hesitated to confer on such people the sacraments of the Lord’s mystery,

[Note: [Col. 1193B] Thus the old Vulgate editions and most manuscripts. Quesnell, with the Vatican Spanish, reads *titubaret* (“hesitated” or “wavered”).]

we received in the synodal assembly, as we have said, a consultation of this kind. Examining it more carefully, we wished it to be treated with thoughtful concern according to the understanding of each person, so that, with the knowledge of many applied, we might arrive more certainly at the truth.

[Note: [Col. 1193B] Likewise the Vulgate, together with Vatican collection 24 and Sichard’s copy, reads *discuti* (“to be examined”), followed by *pro uniuscujusque* (“according to each person’s”).]

Accordingly, the same conclusions that came into our minds through divine inspiration were also confirmed by the frequent agreement of the brothers.

[Note: [Col. 1193C] The Vatican Spanish and Isidorian copies, together with Vatican collections 11 and 21, read: *in somnis mihi divina inspiratione* (“in dreams, through divine inspiration, came to me”).]

We must therefore first take care lest, while we maintain a certain appearance of caution, we incur the loss of souls who ought to be regenerated.

[Note: [Col. 1193C] Both Spanish manuscripts and the Vatican Isidorian copy read *causationis* (“of excuse”), less correctly, perhaps because shortly before the text had said *sub specie cautionis* (“under the appearance of caution”). Shortly afterward, two of Quesnell’s manuscripts read *regendarum* instead of *regenerandarum*. Vindob. Spanish has *suspicionibus* (“suspicions”).]

For who is so devoted to his suspicions that he would define as true what he suspects from an ambiguous opinion, when all revelation is absent?

[Col. 1193B]

[Note: [Col. 1193C] Both Spanish copies, the Vatican Isidorian copy, and another collection 11 read *Domini manifestatione* (“by the Lord’s manifestation”). Three manuscripts read *est suspicatus* (“has suspected”) instead of *suspicator* (“he suspects”).]

[Note: [Col. 1193C] On Consecration, distinction 4, “Cum itaque baptismi,” chapter 112.]

Since, therefore, the person who desires regeneration does not himself remember having been baptized, nor can another testify concerning him who does not know whether he was consecrated, there is nothing in which sin can insinuate itself, since in this matter of conscience neither the person who is baptized nor the person who baptizes is guilty.

[Note: [Col. 1193C] Quesnell, with two of his manuscripts and also with Ivo and Gratian, reads: *Cum itaque baptismi sui nihil recordetur* (“Since, therefore, he remembers nothing of his baptism”). We have restored the reading of the earlier editions as the better one; it is supported by manuscripts of collection 24 and the copies of Merlin and Sichard. Vindob. Spanish has the corrupt reading *Cum itaque baptismatum se nihil recordetur*, in which *baptismatum* was written for *baptizatum*, and *se nihil* for *se nec ille* by error. The author of the Gallican manuscripts of Spanish origin corrected this error by conjecture, as Quesnell printed it from manuscripts derived from the Gallican Spanish source, including our Vatican Spanish, Isidorian, and Vatican collections 11 and 21. The following words *nec alter* (“nor another”) more appropriately require *nec ille* (“nor he”) than *nihil* (“nothing”).]

We know that it is an inexpiable crime whenever, in accordance with the institutions of heretics condemned by the holy Fathers, someone is compelled to undergo twice the washing that was granted once for those who are to be regenerated, the apostolic teaching protesting that there is one Godhead in the Trinity, one confession of faith, and one sacrament in baptism (Ephesians 4:5).

[Note: [Col. 1194C] Thus the old Vulgate, together with the manuscripts of collection 24 and the copies of Merlin and Sichard. The error in Vindob. Spanish approaches this reading: *juxta haereticorum doctrina a sanctis Patribus instituta*, where *doctrina* (“doctrine”) was erroneously written for *damnata* (“condemned”). The reading adopted by Quesnell—*juxta haereticorum dogma, contra sanctorum Patrum instituta* (“according to the heretics’ dogma, contrary to the institutions of the holy Fathers”)—was found by him in the Thuan and Cambridge manuscripts and was likewise found by us in the Vatican Spanish, Isidorian, and similar copies derived from a Gallican manuscript of Spanish origin, where arbitrary corrections have prevailed, as we have seen from many examples. When the scribe of this manuscript detected an error in *doctrina* but did not think of substituting *damnata*, he altered several words, as above. Manuscripts of collection 21 corruptly read: *juxta haereticorum dogma a sanctis Patribus institutum* (“according to the heretics’ dogma instituted by the holy Fathers”). See Quesnell’s notes 2 and 3.]

[Col. 1194A]

But in the present case there is no comparable danger to fear, since what is altogether unknown to have happened cannot be charged as a crime of repetition.

Therefore, whenever such a person comes before you, investigate the matter first with careful examination. Unless perhaps the end of life is at hand, inquire over a long period whether there is absolutely no one who can assist the ignorance of the uninformed person with his testimony.

When it has been established that the person who needs the sacrament of baptism is being prevented solely by an empty suspicion, let him approach fearlessly to obtain the grace of which he knows there is no trace in himself.

[Col. 1194B] [Note: [Col. 1194D] See Quesnell’s note 4.]

Nor should we fear opening to him the gate of salvation, which he is never shown to have entered before.

CHAPTER II

If it is established that someone was baptized by heretics, the sacrament of regeneration must in no way be repeated for him. Only what was lacking there should be supplied, so that through the episcopal laying on of hands he may receive the power of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] Thus the ancient editions, together with both Spanish copies, the Vatican Isidorian copy, and the copies of Merlin and Sichard. Others read *episcopatis* (“of the episcopate”). See Quesnell’s note 5, together with annotation 25 (Col. 1138, note q) on letter 159.]

For this reason, dearest brother, we wish this to come to the knowledge of all of you generally, lest, while excessive fear is entertained, God’s mercy be denied to those who desire to be saved.

[Note: [Col. 1194D] We have restored *vestrum* (“of you”)—deleted by Quesnell—from the manuscripts of Vatican collection 24 and the copies of Merlin and Sichard. Shortly afterward we likewise restored *metuitur* (“is feared”) from the same manuscripts and from the Vatican Spanish, Isidorian, and another collection 11. Quesnell, with other manuscripts, reads *metuimus* (“we fear”).]

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of November,

[Col. 1196A]

[Note: [Col. 1195A] The printed editions, together with the manuscripts of collection 24, Sichard, Merlin, and some manuscripts of collection 21, read *consulatu Marciani Augusti* (“in the consulship of Augustus Marcian”). Quesnell, note 1, correctly perceived that an error lay in this consular notation and that *Majoriani* (“of Majorian”) should be substituted for *Marciani*. But since the manuscripts, which generally omit the chronological note, did not help, he assigned the letter to this year while retaining the printed reading *Marciani* and noted in a postscript that *Majoriani* should be read. We have not hesitated to insert the consulship of Majorian, because that consulship is recorded in the Vindobonese Spanish manuscript as follows: *Dat. VIII kal. Novemb. consulatu Majuriani Augusti* (“Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Augustus Majorian”). In dating a document, ancient scribes more easily omit a unit than add one. As for what Quesnell says in note 3—that Leo never used the consular notation *consulatu*, but only *consule* or *consulibus*—this is not entirely clear. For in letter 159, to Nicetas, we find the same formula in the Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark, collection 13; and since the abbreviation *Cons.* precedes the genitive *Tariani* (to be read *Majoriani*) Augusti in the Vatican manuscript of Dionysius, and similarly precedes it in other Hadrianic manuscripts, it must plainly be understood as *consulatu*. To signify the consul, one would have had to write *Majoriano Augusto consule* (“with Augustus Majorian as consul”).]

in the consulship of Augustus Majorian.

ADMONITION ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER (G)

[Col. 1195]

1. On the very weak arguments of Tillemont, Quesnell dated the following letter to approximately the years 442, 443, or 444. Since Sirmond and Baluze assigned it to the year 452, though they produced no evidence, Quesnell conjectured that they held this view because they thought that the letter’s reference to those who had been captured by enemies in childhood pointed to the devastation which the Huns inflicted in Gaul in 451.

He argued, however, that this letter should not be referred to the Hunnic invasion but to the persecution of the Vandals, who, after gaining control of Africa under Genseric, attacked the Catholics. For in inquiry 18 the following heading is found: “Concerning those who came from Africa or Mauretania and do not know in which sect they were baptized.” After describing the Vandal persecution inflicted on Christians in Africa after 439, he supposes that on this occasion some people withdrew to Gaul, and that the same letter speaks about them. For this reason he believes that it was written around the indicated years 442, 443, or 444, when that persecution was raging.

2. First, however, we produce clear evidence demonstrating that this letter is later than the year 445 itself. Hermes, who brought Rusticus’s letter to Leo, is called a deacon in the inscription of the Church of Narbonne reproduced by Quesnell in his notes. Quesnell himself, with Pagi’s support, interprets this inscription very well against Baluze at the year 445, numbers 24 and 25, and correctly proves that it was engraved in 445.

The same Hermes, moreover, is called archdeacon at the beginning of Leo’s letter to Rusticus. This letter, therefore, was written after that inscription—that is, after the year 445—since Hermes had advanced from the diaconate to the archdiaconate.

3. Furthermore, although the African persecution of the Vandals grew fierce after 439, Mauretania remained under Roman control until Valentinian’s death, which occurred in 455. Therefore, if those who came from Mauretania to Gaul did so because of persecution, as Quesnell supposes, this must be placed after 455.

### 4.

But to dispel Quesnellus’s conjecture and establish the true date of this letter, clearer and more compelling evidence is supplied by Rusticus’s own Inquiries. For not only does Inquiry 18 speak of those who came from Africa or Mauretania, but Inquiry 17 also concerns those who, having been captured as children by enemies, later came into Roman territory; and Inquiry 19 concerns those who, having been captured as children by pagans, later came into Roman territory while still young.

Let us suppose that Inquiry 18 concerns those who for some reason withdrew from Africa into Gaul during the time of the Vandal persecution. Nevertheless, the cases in Inquiries 17 and 19 cannot belong to the same circumstances. For there it is stated that certain people, captured as children by enemies—and those enemies pagans—and carried outside the Roman Empire, eventually returned while still young into Roman territory, and that some of them came into the province of Narbonensis; it was on their account that Rusticus submitted these inquiries.

The matter, therefore, does not concern African exiles or refugees fleeing because of persecution, nor Vandals, who were not pagans but Arians. We must accordingly understand the pagans to have been the Huns and other barbarians, likewise enemies of the Romans, who, after devastating Gaul, carried children away captive with them. Their invasion of Gaul, and of the province of Narbonensis itself, is famous; Jerome mentions it in his letter to Ageruchia in the year 409.

If the question had concerned children captured at that time, Rusticus, as it seems, would not have written around the year 442 in Inquiry 19 that they had come into Roman territory while still young. The Huns likewise fought against the Goths in Gaul in the years 437 and 439. But on that occasion they were auxiliaries of the Romans, not enemies. Rusticus, however, speaks of pagan enemies and of captives who returned from their enemies into Roman territory while still young.

The invasion of the Huns into Gaul in the year 451 is therefore more suitably understood, when they fought against Aetius, the Roman commander, not as auxiliaries but as enemies. If Rusticus’s inquiries are thought to concern children captured in that war, then, allowing sufficient time for those children, captured by pagans, to return to their homeland as young people, this letter cannot be assigned to the year 452.

### 5.

It appears more probably that it should be placed around the year 458. First, in two letters from the year 458—one, Letter 159, to Nicetas of Aquileia, chapter 5, and the other, Letter 166, to Neon of Ravenna, chapter 1—there is mention of Romans returning to their own country from captivity among unbelievers. Some of them had raised doubts about baptism, others about food sacrificed to idols, just as we read in the letter to Rusticus of Narbonne.

Since all these letters correspond to captives who had been taken when Attila, king of the Huns, was devastating Italy and Gaul, the letter to Rusticus, no less than the other two, is most reasonably recognized as having been written around the same year, 458.

### 6.

Then, in Letter 166 to Neon, chapter 1, Leo says:

> Recently, in a synod, a kind of consultation arose that had previously been new and unheard of. For, through the representation of certain brothers, we learned that some captives were returning freely to their own sees—captives who had evidently fallen into captivity at an age when they could scarcely have had knowledge of anything—and were seeking the remedy of baptism, but could not, through the ignorance of infancy, remember whether they had received the mystery and sacraments of baptism.

This is the same question as that which Rusticus of Narbonne submitted. But how could Leo, in the year 458, have asserted in Letter 166 to Neon that this was a new and previously unheard-of kind of consultation, if Rusticus had already presented the same question to him long before? How could he have added in the same Letter 166 that a longer and more careful discussion had been necessary for its solution, if he had already solved it in the letter to Rusticus in the same manner?

It is therefore clear that Neon—or rather, someone else who gave occasion for the letter to Neon—wrote to Leo about this question before Rusticus did. Consequently, this letter to Rusticus is known to have been written after 24 October 458, the date on which the letter to Neon was delivered. We therefore place this letter after the letter to Neon, since we have no doubt that it is later. We do not, however, wish to assert that it was written in that same year, 458, since it may have been written somewhat later.

Nevertheless, it must be said to have been written not long afterward. For Hermes, who is called archdeacon in this letter, was appointed bishop of the people of Béziers while Rusticus was still alive. Since they did not accept him, he returned to Narbonne, and Rusticus and Hermes sent letters to Leo concerning this matter, as may be inferred from Letter 8 of Pope Hilary.

To allow sufficient time for these events, Hermes seems to have been promoted to the see of Béziers before Leo’s death, which occurred in 461, probably around the year 460. This letter, however, was written while Hermes was still serving at Rome as archdeacon; it should therefore be dated as late as the year 459.

### 7.

Once the date of this letter has been established, it becomes clear how empty are the two conjectures of Quesnellus. Having observed that several of the doubts submitted by Rusticus had been settled in the First Council of Orange, the First Council of Vaison, and the Second Council of Arles, he concludes in Note 1 that one of two alternatives must be accepted:

> Either Rusticus wrote to Leo before those difficult questions had been discussed and disentangled in the councils mentioned above—for it would seem superfluous and contrary to Gallican custom to hold another consultation about the same matters after doubts had been resolved in several provincial councils, or even in greater synods—or, if Rusticus’s letter did not precede those synods, it should not be thought to have been very distant from them in time. Perhaps Rusticus thought that he was not obliged to abide by their decrees, either because a harsher discipline appeared in many matters, or because some hostility existed between himself and Hilary, bishop of Arles, through whose authority and presidency the canons had been established. Hilary’s authority over the Gallican Churches was so great that it overshadowed the dignity of the metropolitan of Narbonne and of the other metropolitan bishops.

The first alternative—namely, that Rusticus wrote to Leo before the aforementioned councils—is plainly false with respect to the First Councils of Orange and Vaison, in view of the date established for this letter.

As for the Second Council of Arles, which lacks every chronological indication, it is wrongly believed to have been held during the lifetime of Rusticus. For it places before itself a collection of the canons of earlier synods, arranged according to the practice proper to Caesarius of Arles. Father Sbaraglia therefore rightly proved that this council was held by Caesarius. We can confirm this from the Gallican manuscript collections that we examined in the Vatican and Verona libraries, where this synod immediately precedes the Councils of Agde and the Second Council of Orange, both convened by Caesarius at the beginning of the sixth century.

We shall speak shortly of the explanation proposed by Quesnellus. His other conjecture, concerning hostility between Rusticus and Hilary, is likewise clearly fictitious. At the time when Rusticus wrote to Leo, no hostility between Rusticus and Hilary could have existed, since Hilary had died long before. Moreover, by Leo’s decree the boundaries of the ecclesiastical provinces were already settled, and the rights of each metropolitan were already peacefully observed.

The true reason, therefore, why Rusticus wrote to Leo even about doubts that had been settled in Gallican synods was that he wished a more certain determination to be supplied by the authority of the Apostolic See. It is also clear from this that it was not contrary to the custom of the bishops of Gaul to consult the Roman See after doubts had been resolved in Gallican councils. From the tradition of their forebears they had learned how greatly the authority and judgment of that See prevailed, and how much certainty it produced in matters of doubt.

### 8.

The date established for this letter also exposes as false the two arguments that Quesnellus thought could support the year he proposed.

First, we understand that the proceedings mentioned at the beginning of the letter as having been conducted in the examination of bishops and persons of rank on account of the presbyters Sabinianus and Leo do not belong to the First Council of Orange in 441, nor to the First Council of Vaison in 442. Quesnellus himself observed that Rusticus, the bishop of those presbyters, did not attend either council. Rather, the proceedings belong to another gathering, perhaps at Narbonne, held shortly before this letter to Rusticus—that is, around the year 458.

Baluzius therefore rightly established a Council of Narbonne in which the case of those presbyters was heard, although he wrongly assigned it to the year 452.

Furthermore, since this letter was written to Rusticus so late, the depression of spirit that led that bishop, troubled by scandals, to tell Leo that he greatly desired release from the burdens of the episcopate did not fall at the beginning of his episcopate or in his youth, as Quesnellus thought, but in his old age, when, weighed down by years, he was approaching death.

### 9.

Something remains to be said about the manuscripts. We found this letter in seventeen manuscript collections: namely, Collections 1, 3, and the others through 13, as well as Collections 18 and 21 through 24. It is also found in the especially ancient manuscript of the Chapter of Verona, no. 58.

In such collections it is presented in two ways. In all the collections later than Dionysius, Rusticus’s Inquiries themselves are lacking. Dionysius, omitting the inquiries, prefixed to the letter, in their place, a set of headings. He sometimes joined two of Leo’s responses together in an unsuitable way, as we shall note in its proper place.

We have found these same headings alone in the manuscripts of the other later collections—the Hispanic, Hadrianic, and others—which are known to have received this letter from Dionysius. We shall present these headings, together with Quesnellus, in the synopsis above.

Sirmondus was the first to publish the Inquiries, without which Leo’s responses generally cannot be understood. We found them in four manuscript collections older than Dionysius: Vatican Regina Collection 1; Vatican and Barberini Collection 3; Lucan Collection 4; and Vienna Collection 5. Finally, they are also found in the special manuscript Verona 58.

Thus, apart from the manuscripts of the later collections, which lack the Inquiries, we had available six excellent copies containing them and representing different origins. Quesnellus was able to find only two copies of one collection, Collection 5.

## 1415 — LETTER CLXVII

*[Note: [Col. 1197A] Alternatively, 2. Written in 458 or 459.]*

### TO RUSTICUS, BISHOP OF NARBONNE

With the responses appended below to his inquiries.

*[Note: In Verona 58 and Vatican Regina Collection 1, instead of “responses” the reading is “responding”; in Lucan Collection 4, “you have responded”; in Vienna Collection 5, “they respond,” perhaps to be read as “responding.” In the table of headings prefixed to Collection 5, chapter 72, it reads: “With the responses appended below to the nineteen chapters of inquiries.”]*

*[Col. 1197A]*

## SYNOPSIS  
### (From Dionysius Exiguus)

**I.** That those are not to be regarded as bishops whom neither the clergy elected, nor the people sought, nor the provincial bishops consecrated. Nevertheless, if clerics are ordained by such pseudo-bishops, their ordination can be regarded as valid.

*[Note: So read the manuscripts. Quesnellus has: “that such an ordination is to be considered valid.”]*

**II.** That presbyters or deacons, if they are detected in some crime, cannot obtain the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands.

*[Note: So read the manuscripts and Justellus in the headings prefixed to the collection. Quesnellus, together with the heading inserted by Justellus into the body of the canons, has “who have fallen.”]*

**III.** That deacons, like bishops and presbyters, must cease from conjugal relations, but must not repudiate their marriages.

**IV.** That a wife is one thing and a concubine another; and that anyone who gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has had a concubine does not err.

*[Note: We have retained the reading of Dionysius’s headings, although Quesnellus, following the heading inserted by Justellus into the body of the canons, printed a reading more coherent with Leo’s text: “who had a concubine as a wife.”]*

**V.** That there is no repetition of marriage when, after a slave woman has been rejected, a wife is taken.

*[Note: Alternatively, “after the wife has been abandoned.”]*

**VI.** Concerning those who are deprived of communion and die in that condition.

*[Note: So read the manuscripts from Dionysius’s headings. Quesnellus, following the heading inserted by Justellus into the body of the canons, has: “Concerning those deprived of communion and dying in that condition.”]*

**VII.** Concerning those who postpone doing penance.

**VIII.** That anyone who seeks forgiveness for unlawful acts must also abstain from lawful acts.

*[Note: So reads Dionysius. Elsewhere: “from many lawful acts,” or “from acts lawful to many.”]*

**IX.** That it is not appropriate for a penitent to engage in commercial profits.

**X.** That after penance one should not return to secular military service.

**XI.** That if a young man has performed penance because of some pressing danger and does not remain continent, he may be sustained by the remedy of a wife.

**XII.** That if anyone abandons the monastic way of life, he must be cleansed through the satisfaction of public penance.

*[Note: Alternatively, “he must be cleansed through public satisfaction.”]*

**XIII.** That girls who, not under compulsion but of their own will, have undertaken a resolve of virginity sin if they marry, even though they have not yet been consecrated.

*[Note: The Hispanic Collection manuscripts, together with the others derived from them and with Leo’s editions before Quesnellus, add another heading: “Concerning those who have already been consecrated, if afterward they marry.” More will be said about this addition in Note 76 below, column 1207, note k.]*

**XIV.** Concerning those who doubt whether they have been baptized: it is necessary that they be baptized.

*[Note: We preferred the heading of the Dionysian table. Elsewhere: “Concerning those about whom it is doubtful whether they have received baptism: they must be reborn.”]*

**XV.** That those who acknowledge that they have been baptized but do not know in what profession of faith should be received through the imposition of hands.

*[Note: Elsewhere: “in what faith,” or “in what profession of faith”; shortly afterward, “they should be received” instead of “it is appropriate that they be received.”]*

**XVI.** Concerning those who have partaken of a banquet of pagans and of sacrificial foods.

*[Note: Some manuscripts have: “Concerning the baptized who…”]*

## LEO, BISHOP, TO RUSTICUS, BISHOP OF NARBONNE

I gladly received the letters of your brotherhood, which your archdeacon Hermes delivered.

*[Note: Concerning this Hermes, see what we indicated in Notes 2 and 6 of the preliminary notice, and Quesnellus’s Note 2. Shortly afterward, the word “your” is absent from the Florentine manuscript of Collection 13 and from Justellus’s edition.]*

They contain a multiplicity of different matters joined together, but they are not so burdensome to the reader’s patience that something among the concerns pressing upon us from every side has been overlooked.

*[Note: The Vatican Hispanic manuscripts, together with others derived from them—but not the more accurate Vienna Hispanic manuscript—add “of the provinces.” Shortly afterward, two Vatican manuscripts have “with anxiety intervening everywhere.”]*

Accordingly, after taking in the whole substance of your discourse and reviewing the proceedings conducted in the examination of bishops and persons of rank,

*[Note: The earlier Vulgate editions before Quesnellus have “having learned,” a reading that we found in a manuscript of the Vercelli Hadrianic Collection. Concerning the proceedings mentioned below, see preliminary notice 7.]*

we understood that confidence was lacking in your action concerning the presbyters Sabinianus and Leo,

*[Note: Quesnellus corrected the text on the authority of five of his manuscripts—Grimani, Barberini, and three Thuane manuscripts—whereas previously it read “of his own action.” The latter reading may appear more suitable because the subject is a judicial action, which was undertaken not by Rusticus but by the presbyters Sabinianus and Leo against certain adulterers out of zeal for chastity. Tillemont also preferred this reading in his brief note on the Life of Rusticus, p. 404, provided that the reasonably fair sense of Quesnellus’s reading is not adopted.

We have observed that the earlier common reading, before Quesnellus, derives from manuscripts of the Hispanic Collection of Gallican origin, in which arbitrary corrections have occurred, as we have noted elsewhere with many examples. This reading is found in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript of that origin, in the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and in others derived from the same source.

But the reading of Quesnellus is consistently presented not only by the manuscript copies of the oldest collections of different origin—Collections 1, 3, 4, and 5—and by Verona 58, which contains this entire letter with the Inquiries, but also by the manuscripts of the Dionysian and Hadrianic Collections, by Justellus’s copy, by Grimani Collection 18, Vatican Collection 24, and, most significantly, by the more accurate Vienna Hispanic manuscript. From this manuscript the arbitrary correction introduced into the Gallican manuscripts of the same collection appears to be confirmed.

We therefore judged that the reading of Quesnellus, supported by such authority, should not be abandoned, although the opinion underlying it remains obscure through ignorance of the facts and circumstances. Perhaps the crime of adultery was privately known to Rusticus no less than to Sabinianus and Leo. Hence they hoped that Rusticus, although acting as judge in the assembly of bishops and persons of rank, would also support their action against the adulterers, or show favor to the accusers.

But since they lacked sufficiently suitable evidence, and voluntarily withdrew from the proceedings they had begun, Rusticus not only could not favor them but judged, according to the laws, that they deserved correction. On this point the holy pontiff replies that he should act toward them with greater mildness.]*

nor that those who had voluntarily withdrawn from the proceedings they had begun had any just complaint remaining.

*[Note: We restored this reading with Sirmondus from manuscripts of Hispanic-Isidorian Collections 4 and 5, one Vercelli manuscript, and five other manuscripts, among them the very ancient Verona 58. Three manuscripts of the Hadrianic Collection and one of Quesnellus’s Corbie manuscripts, together with Justellus, have “withdrew.” The Vatican Dionysian manuscript, with Merlinus and the editions of Leo before Quesnellus, has “they will withdraw.” Quesnellus, with certain manuscripts, has “they withdrew.”]*

As to what form and measure of justice you ought to maintain toward them, I leave that to your judgment. Nevertheless, I urge you, in the spirit of charity, to apply spiritual medicine to the sick; and since Scripture says, “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17), deal more mildly with those who appear, in their zeal for chastity, to have exceeded the proper measure of punishment.

*[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have “act”; shortly afterward, “of the adulterers” instead of “of adultery.”]*

Do not let the devil, who deceived the adulterers, exult over those who avenge adultery…

I am astonished that your affection should be so disturbed by the adversity of scandals arising on every occasion

*[Note: Justellus, together with one of Quesnellus’s Thuane manuscripts and with the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, has “to falter.”]*

that you say you prefer release from the labors of the episcopate, and would rather spend your life in silence and leisure than remain in the duties entrusted to you.

*[Note: Verona adds “your.” See Quesnellus’s Note 4. Shortly afterward, instead of “to spend life,” the same manuscript has “to direct life”; and instead of “have been entrusted,” it has “have been permitted,” indicating the matters that had been permitted to Rusticus amid the difficulties of which he complained.]*

But since the Lord says, “Blessed is the one who perseveres to the end” (Matthew 24:13), whence does blessed perseverance arise if not from the virtue of patience? For, according to apostolic preaching, “All who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12).

This must not be reckoned only as what is inflicted against Christian devotion by sword or fire

*[Note: Five excellent manuscripts—Vatican Regina Collection 1, Barberini Collection 3, Vienna Collection 5, Grimani Collection 18, and Verona 58—have “is stirred up.” Shortly afterward, the Verona manuscript supplies “the persecution of the world.” Then, instead of “of the disobedient,” Quesnellus’s Victor manuscript and our Verona manuscript have “of disobedience.”]*

or by punishments of any kind. For the savagery of persecutions is also supplemented by differences of character, by the obstinacy of the disobedient, and by the weapons of malicious tongues.

These conflicts continually strike all the members of the Church,

*[Note: The Vulgate before Quesnellus, together with Lucan Collection 4 and Vatican Collection 24, adds “of the Church.” Shortly afterward, Justellus, together with the Vatican Dionysian manuscript, both Vatican Hispanic manuscripts, the Isidorian manuscript, many of our other manuscripts, and four of Quesnellus’s Thuane manuscripts, has “in the conflict” instead of “in the temptation.” Vatican Collection 24 adds here, before “from temptation,” the words “in temptation.”]*

and no part of the devout is free from temptation. Thus, since neither leisure nor labor is without danger, who will steer the ship amid the waves of the sea if the helmsman departs? Who will guard the sheep from the ambushes of wolves if the shepherd’s care does not keep watch (John 10:12)?

*[Note: The Vatican Dionysian manuscript and Justellus have “of shepherds.” Shortly afterward, we corrected “lead toward” to “lead away” on the basis of more accurate manuscripts.]*

Finally, who will resist robbers and thieves if love of repose draws the watchman stationed at his lookout away from his vigilant purpose?

One must therefore remain at the work entrusted to one and at the labor undertaken. Justice must be held firmly, and mercy must be offered kindly.

*[Note: Distinction 86, “Let sins be hated,” chapter 2.]*

Let sins be hated, not people.

*[Note: Vatican Collection 24 has: “Let the arrogant sometimes be corrected; let the weak sometimes be tolerated.” One Vercelli manuscript, through error, has “not” in both places instead of “sometimes.” Shortly afterward, the Barberini Collection 3 and Vienna Collection 5 manuscripts have “in those who sin” instead of “in sins.” Both readings are deleted in the Vatican Dionysian manuscript, Verona 58, the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, but not in the more accurate Vienna Hispanic manuscript.]*

Let the arrogant be corrected, let the weak be tolerated; and whatever in sins must be punished more severely must be punished not with the spirit of one who rages but of one who heals.

*[Note: The printed editions have “But if.” The reading of the Vatican Regina, Verona, and both Vienna Collection 5 and Hispanic manuscripts seemed better. Shortly afterward, Quesnellus has “as though to anyone”; we found this in only two manuscripts. We restored the reading found before the printed editions, which is preserved by the other manuscripts of better quality. The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts omit the words “to anyone” and “to him.”

Shortly afterward, the editions before Quesnellus, together with Vatican Collection 24, read “one must resist with one’s own strength.” We would gladly have inserted this reading into the text, had all the other manuscripts not supported Quesnellus’s correction.]*

And if more severe tribulation should press upon us, let us not be so terrified as though we had to resist that adversity by our own strength, since Christ is both our counsel and our strength,

*[Note: The editions of Leo before Quesnellus, together with Merlinus and Vatican Collection 24, have “without whom.” In the Vienna Hispanic manuscript, “and” is omitted through error; or at least “so that” was corrected in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and thence in the Isidorian and other manuscripts of the same origin: “without whom we can do nothing, but through him we can do all things.” Justellus, retaining the reading of the text, has “we can do all things.”]*

and without him we can do nothing, but through him we can do all things.

He who strengthens the preachers of the Gospel and ministers of the sacraments says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (John 15:5).

And again he says: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me” (Matthew 28:20).

*[Note: The earlier printed editions, before Quesnellus, together with Vatican Collection 24, have “But in the world.” Shortly afterward, instead of “be of good courage,” the Vatican Dionysian manuscript, together with the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and several others, has “have confidence.” Then, with the pronoun “I” omitted, “because I conquered” appears in the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts.]*

“In this world you will have tribulation; but be of good courage, because I have conquered the world” (John 16:33).

Since these promises are unquestionably clear, we must not be weakened by any scandals, lest we appear ungrateful toward God’s election, whose aids are as powerful as his promises are true.

As for the inquiries of your affection, which your archdeacon delivered separately,

*[Note: “Your” is absent from the Vatican Dionysian manuscript. The words “concerning each matter,” inserted by Quesnellus, are found not only in the manuscripts of the later collections but also in the oldest manuscripts—Vatican Regina Collection 1, Barberini Collection 3, and Vienna Collection 5. They are absent from Lucan Collection 4, Verona 58, the Vatican Dionysian manuscript, both Hispanic manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, and another Vatican Collection 24 manuscript. Shortly afterward, instead of “if the opportunity for a copy should arise,” both Hispanic manuscripts and the Isidorian manuscript have “if an opportunity should arise.”]*

it would be more convenient to inquire into each one in person, if we had the opportunity of your presence. For since some of the questions appear to exceed the proper bounds of careful inquiry,
