*[Note: The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, together with three others and Justellus, have “appear to exceed the manner of inquiry.” The Vienna Hispanic manuscript, together with the Vatican Dionysian manuscript, omits only the word “careful.”]*

I understand that they are more suitable for conversation than for writing.

For, just as there are certain things that cannot be overturned by any reasoning,

*[Note: Distinction 14, “As certain things,” chapter 2.]*

so there are many matters that must be moderated either in consideration of people’s ages or according to the necessities of circumstances.

*[Note: The Grimani and Vatican Collection 24 manuscripts have “tradition.” Elsewhere, instead of “according to the necessities of circumstances,” the editions of Leo before Quesnellus have “there was according to the necessities of circumstances.” In the margin of Sirmondus’s edition, “of times” appears instead of “of circumstances,” and “consideration” instead of “condition.”]*

This condition must always be preserved: in matters that are doubtful or obscure, we must know to follow what is found to be neither contrary to the evangelical commandments nor opposed to the decrees of the holy Fathers.

*[Note: Sirmondus likewise relegated the word “contrary” to the margin and placed “different” in the text, but we find the latter nowhere.]*

## 1420

*[Note: Dionysius preserved this heading, although he omitted the Inquiries. In the manuscripts of Collection 5 the same heading is found, with only the word “begin” omitted. In the Barberini and Vatican manuscripts of Collection 3 and in Verona 58, this letter and the Inquiries with their responses are written under separate numbers. In Verona, the preceding letter is numbered 50, and the Inquiries with their responses are numbered 51. In the manuscripts of Collection 3, the letter is numbered 55, and the Inquiries and responses 56. In these manuscripts the heading reads: “The Inquiries begin,” or “The Inquiries and Responses.”]*

The responses appended below to the inquiries of the same bishop begin.

*[Col. 1203A]*

## INQUIRY I

*[Note: The Vatican Collection 3 manuscript gives Dionysius’s heading only for this first inquiry, which does not appear attributable to the compiler of the collection. In Verona: “Concerning presbyters or deacons who…”; likewise, the following inquiries use the plural number.]*

Concerning a presbyter or deacon who falsely claimed to be a bishop, and concerning those whom he ordained as clerics.

### RESPONSE

*[Note: Distinction 62, “No reason,” chapter 1.]*

No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the judgment of the metropolitan.

*[Note: See Quesnellus’s Note 5. Justellus has “by the neighboring bishops” in the edition of the Dionysian and Cresconian collections.]*

Since a question about improperly received honor often arises, who could doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred must in no way be attributed to such men?

*[Note: Six manuscripts of the best quality, together with Justellus, have “is not shown.”]*

But if clerics were ordained by such pseudo-bishops in churches that belonged to their proper bishops, and their ordination was performed with the consent and judgment of the bishops presiding there, it may be regarded as valid, so that they may remain in those churches.

*[Note: See Quesnellus’s Note 6. Shortly afterward, the Vienna Hispanic manuscript deletes “to such men,” and, together with Verona, omits “to them.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, with Merlinus, have “in their churches.” Then, instead of “which belonged to their own,” the editions before Quesnellus have “which,” so that the relative pronoun refers to the churches. But the relative pronoun “who,” preserved by most manuscripts, refers to the clerics.]*

Otherwise, the ordination must be regarded as void, since it is founded neither upon the proper place nor supported by authority.

*[Note: So read the Grimani manuscripts, two of Quesnellus’s Thuane manuscripts, and our Vatican Regina Collection 1, Vienna Collection 5, Vatican Dionysian, Verona 58, another Verona manuscript, no. 60 of Cresconius, and several others. The manuscripts of Collection 3, both Hispanic manuscripts, the Vatican Isidorian manuscript, one Vercelli manuscript, and four other Vatican manuscripts, together with Justellus and the Cambridge manuscript, and finally the second hand of Verona 60, have “consecration.” The editions before Quesnellus, together with Vatican Collection 24, have “ordination.”]*

## 1421 — INQUIRY II

Concerning a presbyter or deacon who, after recognizing his crime, asks for public penance: should it be granted to him through the imposition of hands?

### RESPONSE

*[Note: Distinction 50, “It is foreign to custom,” chapter 67.]*

It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those who have been consecrated to the honor of the presbyterate or to the rank of the diaconate should, on account of some crime of theirs, receive the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands.

*[Note: See Quesnellus’s Note 7. Shortly afterward: “Those who have attained the honor of presbyter or the rank of deacon” in Vatican Collection 24.]*

This undoubtedly derives from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?” (Leviticus 5, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, for such fallen persons to obtain the mercy of God, private withdrawal must be sought, where, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.

*[Note: The Vatican Collection 3 manuscript has “a withdrawal must be awaited, so that it may be for them.” Verona 60 of Cresconius has “as it is in them.”]*

## INQUIRY III

Concerning those who minister at the altar and have wives: may they lawfully have relations with them?

### RESPONSE

*[Note: Distinction 31, “The law of continence,” chapter 10.]*

The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. While they were laymen or lectors, they could lawfully marry and beget children.

*[Note: See Quesnellus’s Note 8.]*

But when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had previously been lawful for them began to be forbidden.

*[Note: The editions before Quesnellus, together with the Vienna Hispanic and Vatican Collection 11 manuscripts, have “when they have reached.”]*

Therefore, so that a carnal marriage may become spiritual, they must neither dismiss their wives nor live as though they did not have them. In this way the charity of marriage is preserved, while the activity of married relations ceases.

*[Note: Elsewhere, “of marriages.” Shortly afterward, Vatican Collection 11, together with the editions preceding Quesnellus, has “let the works cease.” Justellus, together with the Vatican Dionysian and other Hadrianic manuscripts, has “let the activity cease.”]*

## 1422 — INQUIRY IV

Concerning a presbyter or deacon who gives his virgin daughter in marriage to a man

*[Note: Verona 58 has “has joined in marriage.”]*

who already had a woman joined to him, from whom he had also fathered children.

### RESPONSE
[Note: [Col. 1204D] Distinction 32, question 2, “Not every woman,” chapter 12.] “Not every woman” [Note: [Col. 1204D] Two Vatican collections 21 read “is by right the man’s wife.”] joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. The bonds of marriage, moreover, are legitimate between freeborn persons and between equals; [Note: [Col. 1204D] Justellus, with four of our manuscripts, adds the conjunction “and.” Then, one manuscript of Vatican collection 11 reads *exstiterit* instead of *existeret*.] the Lord established this much earlier (Genesis 2:24) than the beginning of Roman law came into existence. Thus a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another. For this reason the Apostle too, to make clear the distinction between these persons, adduces testimony from Genesis, where it is said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Galatians 4:30; Genesis 21:10). [Note: [Col. 1204D] The Vindobonensis Hispanic and Vatican collection 11 manuscripts, with the printed editions before Quesnellus, read “with the son of the free woman.” Therefore, etc. Distinction 27, question 2, “When the partnership,” chapter 17; and *Decretum* IV, book VI.]

Therefore, since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it contained within itself the sacrament of Christ and the Church (Ephesians 5:32), [Note: [Col. 1204D] See Quesnellus’s note 10. Then, “in which it is not taught that there was a nuptial mystery” is the reading in Vatican collection 11 and the older printed editions; the Vatican, Hispanic, and Isidorian manuscripts, which follow the reading of the text, have *ministerium* (“ministry”) instead of *mysterium* (“mystery”).] there is no doubt that a woman does not belong to marriage if it is taught that there was no nuptial mystery in the union.

[Note: [Col. 1205C] The Lucensis collection 4 manuscript, omitting the words “Therefore a cleric of any place,” begins the sentence as follows: “If therefore anyone gives his daughter …”] Therefore, if a cleric of any place gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as though he had given her to a married man—unless perhaps that woman appears to have been made free, lawfully endowed with a dowry, and honored by a public wedding. [Note: [Col. 1205C] Veronese manuscript 58 reads: “that woman, having been made free … may appear honorable.” Another Veronese manuscript, Cresconius 60, has *honesta* in the first hand and *honestata* in the second.]

## INQUIRY V

[Note: [Col. 1205C] Six of our manuscripts that preserve the inquiries distinguish this section from the preceding one, whereas in other copies, which lack the inquiries, it is joined to the preceding section from Dionysius; but incorrectly, as may be seen in Quesnellus’s note 11. The Lucensis collection 4 and Vindobonensis collection 5 manuscripts omit *viris* (“to men”) within the inquiry itself.] Concerning girls who marry men who have concubines.

### RESPONSE

Girls joined to men by their fathers’ decision are without guilt, if the women whom those men kept were not married to them. [Note: [Col. 1205C] The Vatican Regina manuscript reads “had not been.” Moreover, in all editions and in the manuscripts that omit the inquiries, as well as in collection 5, although it preserves the inquiries, the following words are added after “were not”: “for a married woman is one thing, and a concubine another.” On the authority of the other manuscripts preserving the inquiries, we have rejected these words from this place and transferred them to the beginning of the following response, to which they clearly belong from the context.]

## 1423 INQUIRY VI

Concerning those who abandon the women by whom they have had children and take wives.

### RESPONSE

[Col. 1205B]

Since a married woman is one thing and a concubine another, [Note: [Col. 1205D] Distinction 31, question 2, “To cast the slave woman from the bed,” chapter 11.] to cast a slave woman from one’s bed and take a wife of unquestionably free birth is not a duplication of marriage but an advance in honor. [Note: [Col. 1205D] Cresconius also reads in the Veronese manuscript: “to cast away the slave woman after accepting a married woman.”]

## INQUIRY VII

Concerning those who receive penance during illness and, when they recover, do not perform it.

### RESPONSE

The negligence of such people is to be censured, [Note: [Col. 1205D] See Quesnellus’s note 12. The Vatican manuscript of Dionysius, with Cresconius and one Vercellese manuscript, reads: “The negligence of such people should certainly be censured, but they should not be utterly despaired of.” The same reading occurs in another Vercellese manuscript, in Hadrianus and Vindobonensis Hispanicus, and in the pre-Quesnellian printed editions of Leo, except that they have *est* (“is”) instead of *sit* (“should be”). Justellus’s Dionysius and Sirmondus, following the reading of the text—which occurs in most of the better manuscripts, both ours and Quesnellus’s—add *sane* (“certainly”) after “is to be censured.”] but they are not to be utterly abandoned, so that, stirred by frequent exhortations, they may faithfully carry out what they necessarily sought. [Note: [Col. 1206C] On Penance, distinction 7, “No one is to be despaired of,” chapter 1.] For no one is to be despaired of while he remains in this body, because what is sometimes postponed through distrust of one’s age is accomplished through more mature counsel.

## 1424 INQUIRY VIII

[Note: [Col. 1206C] Distinction 24, question 2, “Concerning communion for the private,” chapter 1.] [Note: [Col. 1206C] Sirmondus and Quesnellus insert *animo* (“in intention”); we have deleted it on the authority of our manuscripts.] Concerning those who receive penance when they are already dying and die before communion.

### RESPONSE

Their case must be reserved for God’s judgment, [Note: [Col. 1206C] Compare Quesnellus’s note 13. One Vercellese manuscript reads *differatur* (“may be postponed”); another Vercellese manuscript and the second hand in Veronese Cresconius 60 read *non differretur* (“would not be postponed”); Justellus reads *non differatur* (“may not be postponed”). A little later, Veronese manuscript 58 reads *non communicamus* (“we do not communicate”).] in whose hand it lay whether the death of such people would be postponed until the remedy of communion. [Col. 1205C] But we, who did not communicate with them while they were alive, cannot communicate with them after their death.

## INQUIRY IX

Concerning those who, when excessive pain presses upon them, ask that penance be given to them, but when the priest comes to give what they requested, if the pain has abated somewhat, make excuses and refuse to accept what is offered. [Note: [Col. 1206C] The Lucensis collection 4 and Veronese manuscript 58 read “when the pain presses too severely.” The same Veronese manuscript reads “if the pain has been slight” instead of “if it has abated somewhat.”]

### RESPONSE

This dissimulation may arise not from contempt for the remedy but from fear of committing a more serious offense. Therefore, [Note: [Col. 1206C] On Penance, distinction 1, “Penance which,” chapter 62.] when delayed penance has been requested with greater earnestness, it should not be refused, so that the wounded soul may somehow reach the medicine of pardon.

## INQUIRY X

Concerning those who have professed penance, if they begin to litigate in the courts.

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1206D] On Penance, distinction 1, “One thing indeed is,” chapter 65; and distinction 11, question 1, chapter 34.] One thing is to demand what is justly owed, [Note: [Col. 1206D] The Vatican Regina collection 1 reads “to demand what is justly owed.”] and another is, out of love of perfection, to disdain one’s own possessions. But one who asks pardon for unlawful acts ought to abstain even from many lawful things, [Col. 1206B] as the Apostle says: “Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is beneficial” (1 Corinthians 6:12). [Note: [Col. 1206D] Six reputable manuscripts and Cresconius omit “for me.” One Vercellese manuscript, with Justellus, reads: “if penitents have a case … they ought not.”] Therefore, if a penitent has a case that perhaps ought not to be neglected, it is better for him to seek an ecclesiastical judgment than a secular one. [Note: [Col. 1206D] Veronese manuscript 58 reads “let him seek.” The Vatican manuscript of Dionysius, with Cresconius, the Veronese manuscript, and two other Vatican manuscripts, reads “someone seeks.” Another Vatican manuscript, with Barbatianus, Victorinus, and the second hand of Vindobonensis collection 5, reads “demands” instead of “seeks.” See Quesnellus’s note 14.]

## INQUIRY XI

Concerning those who engage in business during penance or after penance.

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1206D] On Penance, distinction 5, “The quality of profit.”] The nature of the profit either excuses or condemns the person conducting business, since there is both honorable gain and disgraceful gain. Nevertheless, it is more useful for a penitent to suffer losses than to be entangled in the dangers of business, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the dealings of buyer and seller.

## 1425 INQUIRY XII

[Col. 1206C]

Concerning those who return to military service after penance.

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1206D] On Penance, distinction 5, “The contrary,” chapter 3.] It is wholly contrary to ecclesiastical regulations to return to secular military service after performing penance, since the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs” (2 Timothy 2:4). [Note: [Col. 1207B] Vatican collection 11 adds: “so that he may please the one to whom he has presented himself.” Later, five manuscripts and the older printed editions of Leo read “worldly military service.”] Therefore, the person who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the devil’s snares.

## INQUIRY XIII

Concerning those who take wives after penance [Note: [Col. 1207B] See Quesnellus’s note 15. A little later, the Veronese manuscript 58 and the Vatican Regina manuscript of Leo’s response omit “of death.”] or join concubines to themselves.

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1207B] Distinction 33, question 3, “In adolescence,” chapter 14.] If a man in adolescence performed penance because of pressing fear of death or danger of captivity, and afterward, fearing a fall into youthful incontinence, chose marital intercourse so as not to incur the sin of fornication, he appears to have done something pardonable, provided that he knew no woman at all besides his wife. [Note: [Col. 1207C] Quesnellus, with some manuscripts, reads “incur.” We have preferred the reading of the earlier editors, since it is supported by more and older manuscripts of ours. Shortly afterward, the Veronese manuscript 58 reads *jubenalem* instead of *venialem* (“pardonable”); the Vatican Regina manuscript reads *juvenalem*, perhaps meaning *juvenilem* (“youthful”). Then, after “no woman at all,” Sirmondus adds “another.”] Nevertheless, we do not establish a rule in this matter; we judge only what is more tolerable. For according to true understanding, nothing is more fitting for one who has performed penance than persevering chastity of both mind and body.

## 1426 INQUIRY XIV

Concerning monks who either begin military service or take wives. [Note: [Col. 1207C] The Vatican Regina and Lucensis manuscripts read “take wives.”]

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1207C] Distinction 20, question 3, “The resolve,” chapter 1.] The monastic commitment undertaken by one’s own decision or will cannot be abandoned without sin. For what one has vowed to God, one must also repay (Deuteronomy 23:21; Psalm 49:14). Therefore, anyone who, having abandoned his profession of singleness, has turned to military service or marriage must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance, because, although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the choice of better things is a transgression. [Note: [Col. 1207C] Vindobonensis collection 5 adds *sit* (“may be”). Then, after “choice,” Sirmondus, with the earlier printed editions, adds “nevertheless.” Shortly afterward, one Vercellese manuscript, with Justellus, reads “the better thing” instead of “the better things.”]

## INQUIRY XV

Concerning girls who for some time wore religious dress but were not consecrated, if they later marry.

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1207C] Distinction 20, question 1, “The girls,” chapter 8.] Girls who, not compelled by parental command but by spontaneous judgment, have undertaken a purpose and habit of virginity, if they later choose marriage, commit a violation, even if consecration did not follow; [Note: [Col. 1207C] See Quesnellus’s note 16. Then, “even if consecration did not follow” is the reading of all manuscripts that prefix the inquiries, as well as Vatican collection 24. The others, which follow the Dionysian reading, have: “Even if the grace of consecration has not yet come to them.”] they would certainly not be deprived of its gift if they persevered in their purpose. [Note: [Col. 1207D] The pre-Quesnellian printed editions add a chapter with the title “Concerning those who have already been consecrated, if they later marry.” Its wording is as follows: “There can be no doubt that a great crime is committed where both the purpose is abandoned and consecration violated. For if human agreements [elsewhere, ‘deeds’] cannot be trampled with impunity, what will await those who have violated the divine bonds of the sacrament?” Quesnellus removed all this, judging, on the arguments found in his note 17, that it had entered the text from a marginal note, whether by Gratian or another scholar. These words are found inserted in the text in the oldest manuscripts of Vindobonensis Hispanicus and Vatican Hispanic collection, in all Isidorian manuscripts deriving from the Hispanic tradition, and in other collections that flow from the same source. It is therefore surprising that they are absent from Merlin’s edition, which published the Isidorian collection with many additions, apparently from a manuscript of collection 12; we found the same words in that manuscript, Vatican 1340. Indeed, these words are likewise written in the margin, added by a later but ancient hand, of the very old Vatican manuscript 5845, which presents the pure Dionysian collection. Since, however, they are absent from all manuscripts preserving the inquiries—which are the best of all—as well as from the text of the manuscripts of the Dionysian and Hadrianic collections, the Grimanic manuscript, and the manuscripts of collection 24, we have not inserted them into the Leonine text. It is impossible to guess where the author of the excellent Hispanic collection—which was compiled shortly before the middle of the seventh century and contains nothing apocryphal—obtained this addition, since elsewhere he received all the letters of the Dionysian collection without any addition. In some manuscripts of later collections this section is joined to the response to the preceding inquiry, as also in Sirmondus’s edition. In his annotation, however, he indicated uncertainty on the basis of manuscripts that present the inquiries without this chapter.]

## 1427 INQUIRY XVI

[Note: [Col. 1208C] Veronese manuscript 58 presents this inquiry as follows: “Concerning those who were abandoned as little children by their parents, and it is unknown whether they were baptized.” The Lucensis manuscript omits only the word “Christian.”] Concerning those who were abandoned as little children by Christian parents, and it cannot be discovered whether they were baptized: should they be baptized?

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1208D] On Consecration, distinction 4, “If no indications exist,” chapter 113; and *Decretum* V, book I.] If no indications exist among relatives [Col. 1208B] [Note: [Col. 1208D] Quesnellus reads “and household members … and neighbors.” We have preferred the reading of the earlier editors, which is supported by the better manuscripts.] or household members, nor among clergy or neighbors, by whom it can be shown that those in question were baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn: lest those perish manifestly in whom reason does not permit what is not shown to have been done to be regarded as repeated.

## INQUIRY XVII

Concerning those who, as little children, were captured by enemies and do not know themselves to have been baptized, [Note: [Col. 1208D] Veronese manuscript 58 reads “but they suppose so,” and shortly afterward “when they come to the Roman province.” Moreover, *Romania*, meaning the Roman Empire, is used by Possidius in *Life of Augustine*, chapter 30, and by Orosius, book VII, chapter 4, from which the common expression is also derived. In the pre-Quesnellian printed editions and in the Dionysian, Hispanic, Isidorian, and other manuscripts of the same origin, this section is joined to the preceding one, and they generally read: “But those who can remember,” adding the particle “but.”] but know that their parents brought them to church several times: may they or should they be baptized when they come to Roman territory?

### RESPONSE

Those who can remember that they went to church with their parents can recall whether they received what was given to their parents. [Note: [Col. 1209C] The cited Veronese manuscript reads “even if this too.” Shortly afterward, Sirmondus and the older editions read “from their memory.”] But if even this is beyond their memory, it appears that what is not known to have been conferred should be conferred upon them, because there is no rash presumption where there is diligent piety.

## INQUIRY XVIII

Concerning those who came from Africa or Mauretania and do not know in which sect they were baptized: what is to be observed regarding them?

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1209C] The older manuscripts that lack the inquiries read as follows: “But these people about whom you have written do not know that they were baptized” (or “If these people …”). Other, more recent manuscripts read: “But if those about whom you have written do not know that they were baptized” (the pre-Quesnellian editions: “who know that they were baptized”), “but profess that they do not know of what faith those who baptized them were; since in any event …” Shortly afterward, *invocata* (“having invoked”) is found in the Lucensis collection 4, Veronese manuscript 58, both Hispanic collections, the Isidorian collection, and Justellus’s edition. Compare Quesnellus’s note 18.] These people do not fail to know that they were baptized, [Note: [Col. 1209D] On Consecration, distinction 4, “These people about whom,” chapter 38; and *Decretum* IV, book I.] but profess that they do not know of what faith those who baptized them were. Therefore, since they received the form of baptism in some manner, they are not to be baptized; but through the laying on of hands, after invoking the power of the Holy Spirit—which they could not receive from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics.

## INQUIRY XIX

[Col. 1209B]

[Note: [Col. 1209D] The manuscripts of collection 3 divide this final inquiry and the response that follows into two, so that there are twenty inquiries and responses, as follows: Inquiry XIX, “Concerning gentiles who have eaten sacrificial foods.” Response: “If they have used only the banquet …” Inquiry XX, “Concerning those who have worshiped idols or been defiled by murder or fornication.” Response: “But if they have either worshiped idols …”] Concerning those who, having been baptized as little children, were captured by gentiles and lived with them as gentiles; if, while still young, they come to Roman territory [Note: [Col. 1209D] The Veronese manuscript reads “to the Roman province.” Compare annotation 79 (Col. 1208, n. o).] and ask for communion, what is to be observed?

### RESPONSE

[Note: [Col. 1209D] Both Hispanic Vatican manuscripts, the Isidorian manuscript, and another manuscript of collection 24, together with the editions before Quesnellus, read: “If they have used only the banquet …”] If they have used only the banquet of gentiles and sacrificial foods, [Note: [Col. 1210C] Compare Quesnellus’s note 19.] they can be cleansed through fasts and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from things sacrificed to idols, they may be able to share in Christ’s sacraments. But if they have either worshiped idols or been defiled by murders or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

# 1429 LETTER CLXVIII

[Note: [Col. 1210C] Elsewhere numbered 136. Written on 6 March 459.] [Note: [Col. 1210C] Found in manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections 11, 12, and 20 through 24, and in Sichardus’s copy.] TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT CAMPANIA, SAMNIUM, AND PICENUM

## SUMMARY

From the Hispanic collection.

I. Baptismal rebirth is not to be administered at every time, but only at Easter and Pentecost, unless dangerous illness has overtaken someone.

II. Concerning the penance of the faithful: their confession is not to be made public.

LEO TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT CAMPANIA, SAMNIUM, AND PICENUM

## CHAPTER I

I am deeply moved with indignation and afflicted with great sorrow because I have discovered that some of you have become so forgetful of apostolic tradition and so intent upon pursuing their own error that, apart from the paschal feast—to which only the solemnity of Pentecost is comparable—[Note: [Col. 1210C] The pre-Quesnellian printed editions, with Vatican collection 24 and Sichardus, read “the feast of Easter.”] they dare to claim for themselves the right of baptism, not compelled by any necessity of human weakness but solely by the freedom of an undisciplined will, [Note: [Col. 1210C] Vatican collection 11 reads *in natalitiis martyrum* (“on the birthdays of the martyrs”).] and to celebrate the mysteries of rebirth on the birthdays of the martyrs, whose end must be honored in a manner different from the day of the Lord’s Passion. [Note: [Col. 1210C] Vindobonensis Hispanicus adds “and.” Since this conjunction does not fit the sense, it was changed in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript and others of the same origin to “on that day,” but incorrectly.]

They hand on the sacrament to the ignorant and inexperienced without any spiritual [1430] instruction or preparation, so that, regarding those who are to be renewed, neither the teaching of the Church, nor anything in the exorcisms, nor the laying on of hands, nor the fasts themselves—by which the old person is destroyed—has any effect; nor, in so great a mystery of human salvation, [Note: [Col. 1210D] Vindobonensis Hispanicus and other manuscripts deriving from it read *in tot mysteriis* (“in so many mysteries”); the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, through scribal error, read *ministeriis* (“ministries”). Only the manuscripts of collection 24 and the copies of Merlin and Sichardus read as in the text.] [Col. 1210B] is any exception made for that day, [Note: [Col. 1210D] Vindobonensis Hispanicus reads “because in that very gift”; the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and another manuscript of collection 11 read “because in that gift.” Shortly afterward, the pre-Quesnellian editions, with Merlin and Sichardus, read “for those being reborn.”] on which the very gift of rebirth was established.

Therefore we admonish and, not without danger to the condition of those who do this, declare that this presumption must cease, and that you must confer this supreme and most powerful grace of God only on those who desire and believe on the days of Easter and Pentecost. [Note: [Col. 1210D] The pre-Quesnellian editions, with Vatican collection 24 and Sichardus, read “consideration of serious necessities.”] At every other time, consideration must nevertheless be given to the more serious necessities and dangers, according to which it is right to provide assistance, lest weakness constrained by mortal circumstances be deprived of the necessary means of deliverance. For, while preserving—as we have stated—the reverence due to only these two feasts, one must beware, because of the many dangers, lest rebirth through the Lord’s priest be denied to anyone in desperate illness, during an enemy attack, or in fear of shipwreck.

But if, after this prohibition, anyone is discovered to have continued this same usurpation, he will suffer a punishment worthy of his obstinacy, because he has shown that he pursued disgraceful gain rather than the worship of religion.

## CHAPTER II

I also decree that, by every means, that presumption contrary to apostolic rule be removed which I have recently learned is being committed by certain people through unlawful usurpation. [Note: [Col. 1210D] The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts, with other collections 21, read “which we now see being committed by some through unlawful usurpation.” Shortly afterward, those same Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts read “we establish.”]

[Note: [Col. 1211B] Thus our manuscripts of various collections consistently present the text, as do the copies of Merlin and Sichardus. The oldest author of the collection of the Herovallian manuscript, published by Jacques Petit after Theodore’s *Penitential*, chapter 68, page 237, reads likewise. All editions before Quesnellus also read this, using “namely” instead of “that is,” and adding “thus” before “which is requested by the faithful,” as is also added in the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and in two manuscripts of collection 21. Quesnellus removed the words “namely, concerning the penance which is requested by the faithful,” judging in his marginal note that the manuscripts indicate them to have been the title or a marginal annotation. We do not know which manuscripts he means or why he inferred from them that a title or marginal annotation was indicated. Our copies, although very old and of diverse origin, place these words in the text, which excludes the possibility that they are an annotation or title. For material that has entered the text from the margin in some place, if it is found inserted equally in several manuscript books, will almost always, if one may not say always, belong to the same collection; or, if the manuscripts belong to different collections, they will all derive from another, older source. Thus the same additions, as well as the same omissions and the same arbitrary readings, that occur in the Vatican Hispanic manuscript of Gallican origin are found not only in all Hispano-Gallican manuscripts but also in the Isidorian manuscripts and in the manuscripts of collections 11, 21, and others deriving from the Hispanic-Gallican source; yet they are not found in other copies of different origin. In the present case, at least two different sources exist from which this letter was derived: one is the Hispanic collection, while the other is the source from which the author of collection 24 took the same letter. Hence the chronological note found in the other manuscripts deriving from the Hispanic collection is absent from the manuscripts of this latter collection. Since, therefore, the same words are read in copies of both origins, we cannot suspect that they were inserted from elsewhere. Indeed, when properly considered, these words are not superfluous. The presumption that Leo orders to be removed concerned penance, when the faithful requested it; for some pastors, exceeding proper bounds, required the public disclosure of sins among the works of penance. In this sense, “namely, concerning penance” means the same as “with regard to penance”; and when the particle “thus” is excluded, it has the force of a prohibition, so that the sentence is perfectly coherent. After removing the quoted words, Quesnellus continues: “That is, lest the sins of individuals …,” although “that is” is supported by no manuscript of ours. Then Merlin and Sichardus, with the Vindobonensis Hispanicus manuscript, read *libellis* (“in written booklets”); the Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts and other manuscripts of collection 21 read *libelli* (“the booklets”). Later, Quesnellus has “be published” instead of “be publicly recited,” a reading not found in our manuscripts. Merlin deletes “only” and, with Sichardus and Vatican collection 24, prefers “to indicate.” From this text it is plainly gathered that, even in public penance itself, confession of sins was kept private, so that the causes of penance remained concealed; at least not all the sins of the penitents were brought into public view by their own disclosure.]

[1431] Namely, concerning the penance requested by the faithful: a written declaration of each kind of sin must not be publicly recited, since it is sufficient for the guilt of consciences to be disclosed to priests alone through secret confession.

[Note: [Col. 1212B] On Penance, distinction 1, “Although fullness,” chapter 89.] For although the fullness of faith appears praiseworthy when, through fear of God, it is not ashamed before human beings, nevertheless, because the sins of all people are not of such a kind that those who seek penance are unafraid to make them public, this highly blameworthy custom must be removed. [Note: [Col. 1212C] The Vindobonensis Hispanicus manuscript reads “are not afraid.” Sichardus reads: “because not all sins of this kind are such that they wish to make them public as public penance requires.”] Otherwise many will be kept from the remedies of penance because they are either ashamed or afraid that their actions will be disclosed to their enemies, by whom they may be punished under the provisions of the law. [Note: [Col. 1212C] Elsewhere: “revealed.”]

For that confession is sufficient which is first offered to God [Col. 1211B] [Note: [Col. 1212C] Sichardus reads: “then also to the priest, who approaches as intercessor for the sins of the penitents.” Some manuscripts add “may approach.” The Vatican Hispanic and Isidorian manuscripts delete “finally.”] and then also to the priest, who approaches as intercessor for the sins of the penitents. Then more people will be able to be drawn to penance, if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people. [Note: [Col. 1212C] Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Alternatively, ‘of the penitent.’]

Given on the day before the Nones of March, during the consulship of Recimer.

# LETTER CLXIX

[Note: [Col. 1212C] Elsewhere numbered 137. Written on 17 June 460.] [Note: [Col. 1212C] The following five letters are found in one collection, which we called the Avellana collection in the preface. Quesnellus found no manuscript and therefore corrected some passages by conjecture, relegating the printed reading to the margin. We were able to consult several additional copies, which we found in the Vatican, Angelica, and Venetian libraries of Saint Mark.] TO LEO AUGUSTUS

## SUMMARY

I. Concerning Timothy Aelurus, expelled from the Church of Alexandria, and the election of a Catholic bishop in his place.

II. That both integrity of faith and moral uprightness are required in a priest.

III. That the impious Aelurus cannot be restored, even if his faith should perhaps be sound.

LEO, BISHOP, TO LEO AUGUSTUS

## CHAPTER I

If we wished to pursue with praise as great as the greatness of the matter demands [1432] the glorious purpose of your piety in defending the faith, we would prove unequal to the task of giving thanks if we celebrated the joy of the universal Church only within the narrow limits of our own speech. But recompense from Him will more worthily be reserved for your actions and merits, in whose cause you excel both in particular devotion and in the desired outcome of glorious renown. [Note: [Col. 1212D] The printed editions read “as great.” The correction was suggested by manuscript S. III, 9 of the library of the Augustinian Hermits of Saint Augustine in Rome.] [Note: [Col. 1212D] The printed editions of Leo had *servabatur* (“was preserved”), as do two manuscripts of Saint Mark and Vatican 3787. Quesnellus corrected it by conjecture to *servatur* (“is preserved”). We have preferred the reading received in the editions of the Councils from the very old Vatican 4961 and the Angelica manuscript.]

Let your Clemency know that all the Churches of God rejoice and are glad together with praise for you, because the wicked parricide has been driven from the yoke of the Alexandrian Church, and the people of God, upon whom the criminal predator had pressed, have been restored to their ancient freedom of faith. They can now be recalled to the way of salvation through the preaching of faithful priests, since they see that the entire seedbed of poisons has been cast down along with its author.

Now, therefore, since you have accomplished this with steadfast purpose and great resolve, add this to the work of faith brought to completion: decide what is pleasing to God concerning a Catholic bishop for that city, one infected by no stain of the impiety so often condemned. Otherwise perhaps a hidden wound will grow beneath the appearance of a scar, and the Christian people, openly freed from the perversity of heretics through your efforts, will again be exposed to deadly poisons.

## CHAPTER II

You see, venerable emperor, and clearly recognize that, in the person whose removal is under discussion, not merely the integrity of faith must be considered. Even if it could be cleansed by various corrections and professions and restored completely under any conditions, nevertheless what has been committed wickedly and bloodily cannot be erased by declarations expressed in plausible words. For in a pontiff, a priest of God and especially of so great a Church, the sound of the tongue and speech of the lips are not sufficient; it gains nothing if God is proclaimed by voice while the mind is convicted of impiety. [Note: [Col. 1213C] In the pre-Quesnellian editions of Leo and in the manuscripts, corruptly, *de hac maxime* (“especially concerning this,” feminine). In the editions of the Councils, *de hoc maxime* (“especially concerning this,” masculine). We have retained Quesnellus’s sufficiently reasonable correction.]

Concerning such people the Holy Spirit speaks through the Apostle: “Having the appearance [1433] of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:5); and again elsewhere: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). Therefore, since in every member of the Church both the truth of sound faith and the fullness of good works are sought, how much more ought both to excel in the supreme pontiff, since one without the other cannot have cohesion with the body of Christ! [Note: [Col. 1213D] The editions of the Councils omit *in* (“in”). Quesnellus notes in the margin: “Perhaps, ‘of impiety.’] [Note: [Col. 1213D] Thus in the manuscripts that support Rainaudus’s correction. The older editions had only *compagem* (“cohesion”). Binius corrected it to *compagem facere* (“to make cohesion”). The editions of the Councils and Quesnellus read *compaginari* (“to be joined together”).]

## CHAPTER III

Nor is it necessary now to recount everything that makes Timothy detestable, since what was done by and on account of him has spread abundantly and openly throughout the knowledge of the whole world. If anything has been perpetrated by the disorderly mob against justice, everything converges upon the head of the one whose desires the hands of the frenzied served. Therefore, even if in his profession of faith he neglects and deceives in nothing, it is entirely suited to your glory to exclude him from this aspiration, because in the bishop of so great a city the whole Church ought to rejoice with holy exultation, so that the true peace of the Lord may be glorified not only by the preaching of faith but also by the example of morals. [Note: [Col. 1213D] We restored the reading of the codices and the editions before Quesnellus, who preferred to print “even if.”] [Col. 1214A] [Note: [Col. 1213D] The manuscript from which the first edition of this letter was produced had *universa Ecclesiae*, and it was noted that *membra* (“members”) seemed to be missing. That annotation improperly entered the text of several editions. Labbeus and Quesnellus printed only “all the members of the Church.” The noun *membra* is absent from all manuscripts. The Angelica manuscript supplies the true reading.]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius. [Note: [Col. 1214C] In the manuscripts the month appears as the abbreviation R\; but July is correctly supplied, as is clear from the following letter, which was written on the same day and concerning the same matter.] Through Philoxenus, agent in public affairs.

# LETTER CLXX

[Note: [Col. 1214C] Elsewhere numbered 138. Written on 17 June 460.] TO GENNADIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE

## SUMMARY

It is complained that Timothy has been permitted to come to Constantinople; that no hope of restoration should be left to him; and that care must be taken lest he involve himself in public or private conversations.

LEO, BISHOP, TO GENNADIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

From the letter of Your Dilection, and from the report of our brothers and fellow bishops Domitian and Geminian, I learned [Col. 1214B] that, after Timothy was expelled from the city of the Alexandrian Church, he was permitted to come to Constantinople through the efforts of certain opponents of the faith. The apparent purpose was that, so far as can be understood, constrained by the judgments of all the Lord’s priests, he might at least unwillingly convert to the catholic doctrine and, as though he had been expelled for this one reason alone,

[Note: At [Col. 1214D], the Angelica codex reads *qui*. A little later the older editions read *ut tamquam*. The codices confirm Quesnellus’s emendation.]

[Note: The printed editions, with the Venetian manuscripts, read *culpam* (“fault”). We have preferred the reading of the older manuscripts.]

might, after the error of heretical perversity had been condemned, consent to apostolic teaching and return to Alexandria; although, even if he were proved catholic, this would still be a very serious obstacle to him: while the bishop is alive, he is an invader of so great a see, and he has shown himself the author of an act of unheard-of cruelty.

[Note: The Vatican and Venetian codices read *et cum auctor*. The Angelica codex has the better reading, *et quod auctor*.]

Therefore Your Dilection must strive and labor with the diligence in which you excel

[Note: So the Angelica codex; others have *clareas*, while the printed editions read *claret*.]

to ensure that no private or public conversation takes place with so wicked a man, and that, under the pretext of correcting him, no occasion is offered for a gathering of certain persons; nor should he be given complete freedom to return, since the most Christian prince has already judged him by his edicts.

[Note: Others read *indicavit* (“declared” or “made known”).]

Strive, therefore, with every effort and vigilant prudence, for the benefit of ecclesiastical unity, dearest brother, so that his supporters may be deprived of hope and that, from the Alexandrian clergy, a catholic bishop may be consecrated for the Alexandrians according to ancient custom by orthodox Egyptians.

[Note: The printed editions read *episcopos* (“bishops”). We have inserted the reading of the codices. By prescribing the observance of the canons and ancient custom, Leo wished to prevent a bishop of another province from consecrating the new Alexandrian bishop in the manner in which Anatolius of Constantinople consecrated Maximus of Antioch—a proceeding Leo himself rejected in Letter 106, chapter 2.]

For that parricide is not abandoned by his own defenders unless the Alexandrian Church—which must be restored to the honor of the Fathers and to its own liberty—has obtained a ruler of proven excellence for healing all that has been wrongly done.

[Note: The Angelica codex reads *deseretur* (“will be abandoned”).]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius. Through Philoxenus, *agentes in rebus*.

## Letter 171 [Col. 1215D]

[Note: Formerly Letter 139. Written 18 August 460.]

### To Timothy, Bishop of Alexandria

### Synopsis

1. He congratulates him on his election and commends charity.  
2. He urges him to watch over matters of faith and to write to him frequently.

Leo, bishop, to Timothy, catholic bishop of the Alexandrian Church.

[Note: This is Timothy Solofaciolus, the catholic, who was substituted for Timothy Aelurus, the heretic and usurper. He is believed to be the Timothy, priest and steward of the Alexandrian Church, who, when he and other Catholics were expelled from Egypt in 457, presented the emperor with a petition against Aelurus. See the *encyclical dossier*, chapter 7, volume IV of the Councils, col. 1843.]

### Chapter 1 [Col. 1215A]

It is clearly shown, under the splendor of the apostolic judgment, that “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28), and that, by the dispensation of divine mercy, where adversity is received, prosperity is also bestowed.

The experiences of the Alexandrian Church demonstrate this. In it, the modesty and endurance of the humble have gathered many treasures of patience for itself:

[Note: So the codices. The Vulgate has *humilitas*, “humility.”]

“For the Lord is near to those who are brokenhearted, and he will save the humble in spirit” (Psalm 33:19).

The faith of the illustrious prince has been glorified in all things; through him “the right hand of the Lord has done valiantly” (Psalm 117:16), so that the disgrace of Antichrist might no longer sit upon the throne of the blessed Fathers. His impiety harmed no one more than himself: for although he drove some into partnership in his crime, he nevertheless stained himself with blood beyond expiation.

[Note: The printed editions read *se tantum denique inexpiabiliter* (“himself alone, finally, beyond expiation”). We have preferred the reading of all our manuscripts, which have *sed* alone in place of *se*.]

[Note: Four of the better codices read this way. The printed editions have *in fraternitatem tuam*, “against your brotherhood.”]

Therefore, concerning the election which, moved by the prompting of faith, the clergy, people, and all the faithful carried out in your brotherhood, I write that the whole Church of the Lord rejoices with me; and I desire that divine mercy may confirm this with multiplied grace.

May your devotion serve it—that divine mercy—in all things, so that you may earnestly bring even those who have in some measure resisted the truth to reconciliation with God through the prayers of the Church, and may you carefully join them to the sacrament of the catholic faith,

[Note: The printed editions have *sacramenta*. We have corrected the text from the codices.]

whose solidity admits no division. Imitate the true and good shepherd who “laid down his life for his sheep” (John 10:11), and who did not restrain the one wandering sheep with blows, but carried it back to its own fold on his shoulders (Luke 15:5).

### Chapter 2 [Col. 1215C]

Let Your Dilection, therefore, dearest brother, act so that no trace of either Nestorian doctrine or Eutychian error can be found among God’s people. For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 3:11); and he would not reconcile the whole world to God the Father unless, through the rebirth of faith, he assumed all people in the reality of our flesh.

Whenever opportunities for writing arise for your Brotherhood to use, just as you rightly and customarily did when you sent us, through our sons Daniel the priest and Timothy the deacon, a written account of your ordination, so persevere in this duty at all times.

[Note: So the codices. The printed editions read *ut*.]

[Note: Quesnellus explains in a marginal note that this means “unceasingly,” as noted elsewhere. But the reference should properly be understood as the duty of major sees to report the ordination of bishops to the Roman pontiff, as we showed in note 1 to Letter 149.]

Let reports concerning the progress of peace be sent to our concern as often as possible, so that through reciprocal communication we may perceive that the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Romans 5:5). [Col. 1216A]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius.

## Letter 172 [Col. 1216D]

[Note: Formerly Letter 140. Written 18 August 460.]

### To the Priests and Deacons of the Alexandrian Church

### Synopsis

He invites them to preserve and increase concord in the Alexandrian Church, and to summon those who have been led astray by heretics to the remedy of repentance.

Leo, bishop, to the priests and deacons of the Alexandrian Church, his most beloved sons in the Lord: greeting.

I rejoice exultantly in the Lord over the most devout affection that exists among you; for, as your letters reveal, both shepherd and flock are shown to love one another. Therefore, being concerned for one another, as the Apostle says, “to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:3), hasten to attain the fruit of true patience.

[Note: The printed editions add in the margin *ut possitis*, “so that you may be able,” but the codices do not contain it. The Venetian copies have *vestrae*, “of your,” instead of *verae*, “of true.”]

For what more worthy thing could you wish or do than, with God’s grace assisting, to use the faith of the most glorious prince for the advancement of the most solid peace, having removed far away that beast which, as the prophetic Psalm sings, was devastating the vineyard of the Lord’s planting with singular ferocity (Psalm 79:14)?

Since, therefore, neither the ambushes of thieves nor the attacks of robbers are now feared in the Lord’s sheepfold, let your whole community return to concord, and let that unity in all things be sought under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, for the sake of which the Apostle says: “Not seeking what is useful for me, but what is useful for many, so that they may be saved” (1 Corinthians 10:33).

Let all say and think the same thing; let there be no conflicts of opinions or disputes. What the disciples of truth learned and taught in the Alexandrian Church down to its catholic bishops, let all the faithful proclaim with the same confession, for truth—which is simple and one—admits no VARIETY. [Col. 1216C]

If the impious lies of heretics have disturbed Christians of any rank, summon them to the remedies of satisfaction, and correct them in a spirit of gentleness and with kindness. For, as the blessed apostle Peter says, “the Lord is not slow concerning his promise, but acts patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish, but all to turn to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). [Col. 1216D]

We must therefore act lest the difficulty of obtaining pardon make the cure more delayed. [Col. 1217A]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius.

## Letter 173 [Col. 1217B]

[Note: Formerly Letter 141. Written 18 August 460.]

### To Certain Egyptian Bishops

### Synopsis

He congratulates them on the election of Timothy the catholic in place of Timothy Aelurus; commends unity; and invites them to join their concern with his in restoring those who have gone astray.

Leo, bishop, to Theophilus, John, Athanasius, Abraham, Daniel, Johae,

[Note: So the manuscripts. The Vulgate has *Iohaae*. Later, Vatican manuscript 4961 has *Panulino* instead of *Panulvio*.]

Paphnutius, Musaeus, Panulvius, and Peter, bishops of Egypt.

I rejoice to have learned from the letter of your Brotherhood, which our sons Daniel the priest and Timothy the deacon brought to me, that the faith of the glorious and venerable prince, united with prophetic and evangelical teachings, has reached the holy and God-pleasing fulfillment of its purposes. [Col. 1217B]

The most bloodthirsty invader of the Alexandrian Church has been expelled and transferred to a more distant place, and the election has deserved a ruler worthy to govern the whole city. No ambition drew you to his consecration, no sedition drove you, and no injustice incited you; but, with the sanctity of his merits established in the midst, you did not hesitate to place him before all—the one whom the whole community desired to preside over it.

Therefore, rejoicing that God’s peace has been restored to Christian peoples, we commend to each of you the worthiness of your mutual work, so that the bishop, lawfully appointed in all respects, may experience the support of your fraternal assent,

[Note: So the Vatican and Venetian codices. The Angelica manuscript has *se incitari*. The printed editions read *se vivere*.]

and may rejoice to be aided by your cooperation in abolishing the scandals that heretical error had aroused.

[Note: The Vulgate has *Excluso*. We have followed the reading of all the codices.]

For, once he who was the devil’s imitator and “did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44) has been expelled, having wrongly used the appearance of the office and title he had usurped, it is fitting that the Alexandrian Church should venerate and love the man whom it has proved worthy of so great a priesthood both by uprightness of conduct and by the integrity of catholic faith. [Col. 1218A]

To him we offer the full affection of our mutual charity. We exhort and confidently require you, dearest brothers, to preserve in the preaching of the word and in the teaching of the commandment that pattern of charity without which no virtues can be beneficial.

You know that we wrote to our brother and fellow bishop Timothy concerning the recall of those who, having strayed from the path of truth, acted too rashly and fiercely. Let Your Dilection understand that this too belongs to your care: since that pestilential illness has spread widely, the same medicine must everywhere be applied to all its wounds.

Thus, through pastoral diligence, the Lord’s sheepfold may be restored in all the churches, and through the care of charity and teaching all Christ’s sheep may know that they have one shepherd. [Col. 1218B]

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Magnus and Apollonius.

# On the Lost Letters

Both those of Saint Leo to others and those of others to Saint Leo, together with other documents relating to the letters, arranged in chronological order (G). [Col. 1217]

## Dissertation

In which three fragments that survive from Leo are also inserted.

Quesnellus, at the end of the second volume, provided a catalogue of these letters and documents, but it was so incomplete and disordered—without preserving chronological order and with some documents repeated twice—that it is of little use. We have therefore thought it worthwhile to present here a clearer and more accurate account.

We shall provide information only about those documents whose distinctive indications have come down to us; yet there can be no doubt that many others existed of which no mention survives. [Col. 1217C]

## In the Year 431

### 1

Before Saint Leo’s pontificate, one letter of Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, to Leo, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, is mentioned in Letter 119, chapter 4. Its subject is explained as follows:

“At the Council of Ephesus, which struck down the impious Nestorius together with his doctrine, Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, believed that he could suffice to obtain primacy over the province of Palestine, and dared to reinforce his insolent claims through fabricated writings. Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, rightly recoiling from this, informed me in his letters of what the aforesaid ambition had dared to attempt, and earnestly pleaded that no assent be given to unlawful efforts.” [Col. 1217D–1218C]

See note 24 ([Col. 1013, n. h]) to the aforementioned letter.

## Around the Year 442

### 2

Septimus, bishop of Altinum, sent Leo a report, which Leo appended to his first letter. In it Septimus indicated—as the pontiff himself testifies in that first letter—that certain priests and deacons, together with clerics of various ranks, who had been entangled in the Pelagian or Coelestian heresy, had returned to catholic communion in your province, Aquileia, without any condemnation of their own error being required of them.

This report of Septimus is the same as the letter from him to Leo that the holy pontiff says he read in Letter 42. Photius mentions this letter of Septimus in *Codex* 54, in these words:

“When, as time went on, the members of this sect had been restored to the Church, the evil was renewed by them. But Bishop Septimus checked the course of the reborn plague by sending a letter to Leo, who at that time held the apostolic see; and Leo fought against the impious with fervent zeal”—namely, in Letters 1 and 2. [Col. 1218D–1219A]

## Around the Year 443

### 3

At about this time, or somewhat later in 443, Leo sent a letter to Cyril. When Cyril had replied, the holy pontiff delivered another letter to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, to which he appended Cyril’s reply. See the note to Letter 3.

All these letters concerned uncertainty about the date of Easter in the year 444. Only Paschasinus’s reply and a fragment of the letter of Saint Cyril of Alexandria survive; we have published them in their proper places.

### 4

Toward the end of 443, when the holy pontiff was about to expose and publicly convict the Manichaeans at Rome, he prepared a record of the proceedings through the most careful investigations, in a very large assembly attended, besides priests, by some members of the senate, other distinguished men, and many of the people. See Sermon 16, chapter 4; Letter 7, chapter 1; and Letter 15, chapter 16.

These proceedings, in which the perverse doctrine and corrupt morals of the Manichaeans were revealed by their own confessions, were sent on 30 January 444 together with Letter 7, addressed to the bishops of Italy, and later, in 447, to Turibius of Astorga together with Letter 15, from chapter 16 onward. [Col. 1219A–B]

### 5

Before Letter 6, written at the beginning of 444, Leo had sent another letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica, in which he admonished him to keep informing us from time to time, by his reports, about the condition of “your churches” in Illyricum, as he writes in Letter 5, chapter 5.

This admonition, as we observed in note 8 ([Col. 615, n. g]) to Letter 5, is by no means found in the sixth letter to Anastasius that survives. Perhaps, after his accession, Saint Leo commended this responsibility to Anastasius in a careful admonition when writing to the bishop of Thessalonica.

### 6

To comply with this admonition, Anastasius sent the priest Nicolaus to Leo with a letter informing Leo about the condition of the churches. On this occasion he asked that the authority of the apostolic vicariate over Illyricum, once granted by the Roman pontiffs to his predecessors and conferred upon him by Xystus, be confirmed.

See Letter 6, chapters 1 and 2. Since Leo returned it to him on the day before the Ides of January in 444, this letter of Anastasius belongs to the year 443. [Col. 1219C]

## In the Year 445

### 7

After Bishop Hilary of Arles had deposed Celidonius, a Roman council was held with both parties present. Its proceedings are mentioned in Letter 10, chapter 3:

“What proceedings were conducted and recorded among us in the case of Celidonius, bishop, and what Hilary said when he was heard together with him in the presence of the aforesaid bishop, the order of events set down in writing demonstrates.” [Col. 1219C]

### 8

The letter of Projectus, bishop, and another letter from his fellow citizens to Leo against Hilary—who had appointed another bishop over him while he was ill—are mentioned in the same Letter 10, chapter 4.

### 9

Leo’s letter stating that he had removed metropolitan jurisdiction from Hilary of Arles and transferred it to the bishop of Vienne, mentioned in Letter 66, chapter 2, has not come down to us.

Since this was not done in the letter that we rejected as spurious and placed in the appendix, it must be attributed to another lost letter. [Col. 1219D]

### 10

A letter to the bishops of Mauretania, in which the holy pontiff informed them that he had delegated his authority to Bishop Potentius, who was traveling to Africa, so that he might investigate what the truth was concerning bishops whose election was reported to be blameworthy and faithfully report everything to Leo, is inferred from Letter 12, chapter 1.

### 11

Potentius’s report, by which he fulfilled the delegation, laid everything open to Leo’s fullest knowledge and sincerely revealed under what sort of rulers certain Christian communities in parts of the province of Caesarea were living. This report is indicated in the same Letter 12, chapter 1.

### 12

A letter from the Illyrian metropolitans replying to Leo’s letter, by which he had subjected the churches of Illyricum to the bishop of Thessalonica, endowed with apostolic authority, is explicitly mentioned in Letter 13, chapter 1.

It is uncertain, however, whether Leo’s letter to which the Illyrians replied was Letter 5 or another letter that has perished. See note 3 ([Col. 664, n. i]) to Letter 13.

Since Letter 13 was written on 6 January 446, the letter of the Illyrians to which Leo replied in that letter appears to belong to the year 445. [Col. 1219D–1220A]

### 13

In Letter 13, chapter 3, mention is made of a report from Anastasius of Thessalonica, from which Leo learned that the metropolitan of Achaea had repeatedly performed ordinations forbidden by the enactments of the Fathers and by the authorities of the Roman pontiffs, and had added to these acts the consecration, against the will and opposition of the people of Thespiae, of an unknown bishop never previously seen there.

This report appears to have been sent to Rome together with the letter of the Illyrians; consequently, this document too is assigned to the year 445. [Col. 1220B]

## In the Year 446

### 14

There is no doubt that Leo replied to these two letters, that of the Illyrians and that of Anastasius. His reply to the Illyrian letter is contained in Letter 13; but the letter to Anastasius concerning the affair of the metropolitan of Achaea is lost.

Several of Leo’s letters to Anastasius, written before Letter 14, have indeed perished. For in Letter 14, chapter 1, we read:

“For you have an abundance of writings containing our admonitions, by which we have frequently instructed you . . .”

The words “abundance” and “frequently” cannot refer only to the surviving Letter 6 addressed to him.

In one of the missing letters, moreover, Leo had provided that no frequent necessity of meeting should be imposed for trivial causes, and that it would be sufficient for two or three bishops from each province to attend, as reported in Letter 13, chapter 2.

This cannot, with Quesnellus, be referred to Letter 14, which we have shown in note 1 ([Col. 666, n. m]) to Letter 14 to have been written after Letter 13. Furthermore, in Letter 14 Leo commands only two bishops from each province to attend, not two or three; this must therefore refer to another lost letter.

That provision was probably contained in the letter in which Leo issued his ruling concerning the metropolitan of Achaea. In that same letter he also seems to have proposed the decrees mentioned in Letter 13, chapter 4:

“They must more fully observe the provisions which we wrote to be safeguarded in our letter to our brother and fellow bishop Anastasius; and we wish these matters to come to your knowledge through his letter.” [Col. 1220C]

### 15

Two letters of Anastasius to Leo concerning Atticus, metropolitan of Old Epirus, are mentioned in Letter 14, chapter 1.

The first is represented by these words:

“Concerning Atticus, you had indicated nothing more than that, although summoned, he had delayed in appearing and had offered an excuse of illness.”

The second is represented by these:

“It was also read in your letters, which those same deacons of yours brought, that our brother Atticus had come to Thessalonica and had confirmed his consent by a written declaration.”

The first piece of information may have been inserted into the report that Anastasius gave concerning the metropolitan of Achaea, to which we indicated that Leo replied on 6 January 446.

But since, in Letter 14, chapter 1, the pontiff complains that Anastasius, without waiting for the reply to his earlier letter—which had advised that Atticus be treated moderately—had arranged for Atticus to be brought by force to Thessalonica in winter, it is confirmed that this happened in the winter at the end of 445 or the beginning of 446, as we have already established in note 1 ([Col. 666, n. m]) to Letter 14.

Consequently, the second letter of Anastasius concerning Atticus must be assigned to the year 446. [Col. 1220D]

### 16

Three writings of Turibius, bishop of Astorga, sent to Leo concerning the Priscillianist heresy then raging in Spain, are praised in the preface to Letter 15:

“The language of your letter, your memorandum, and the text of your treatise makes this clear.”

Leo calls the first writing a personal letter in chapter 17. The memorandum, divided into sixteen chapters, contained the same number of opinions formerly condemned as Priscillianist. Finally, Turibius’s carefully composed treatise contained, likewise in sixteen chapters, a refutation of those opinions.

He himself testifies to this in his letter to Idatius and Ceponius, chapter 6; more will be said about it in the note to that letter, which is to be inserted in the appendix.

We assign sixteen chapters both to the memorandum and to the treatise because Saint Leo testifies in the preface to Letter 15 that Turibius refuted the errors of the Priscillianists in sixteen chapters. In chapter 16, moreover, he gives the same form to both the memorandum and the treatise, indicating that each was divided into the same number of chapters.

Bishop Montanus of Toledo included this treatise and memorandum under the name of “books” in his letter to the people of Palencia appended to the Second Council of Toledo. Writing about the Priscillianist heresy, he praises “the books of Bishop Theoribius, issued to Saint Leo, pope of the city of Rome, in which he explained and exposed this filthy heresy and brought into the open what had been hidden in its darkness and veiled in the cloud of its treachery. For from those very books the devout reader will find how he may beware and what he may answer against the sacrilegious.”

Montanus’s statement that these books of Bishop Theoribius were issued to Saint Leo should not be understood as though the treatise, just like the memorandum, had been written by Turibius after he became bishop. We shall show in the same appendix that the treatise was probably written before his episcopate. Rather, the statement is to be understood in the sense that the treatise and memorandum were sent to Leo together with Turibius’s letter, and that Montanus found them together.

Idatius reports that all these writings were sent to Leo through the deacon Pervincus in the year 446. [Col. 1221A–B]

## In the Year 447

### 17

When Saint Leo replied to Turibius in Letter 15 on 21 July 447, he also sent another letter to the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Galicia. In it he summoned a council of a general synod, so that, in accordance with his reply to Turibius’s questions, a full investigation might determine whether any bishops were contaminated by this heresy and should unquestionably be separated from communion if they refused to condemn the most abominable sect in all its perverse teachings.

See Letter 15, chapter 17. [Col. 1221C]

### 18

In Letter 15 to Turibius, chapter 17, Leo provided that, if this general council could not be convened because of some impediment, at least the bishops of Galicia, among whom the error was spreading, should assemble without fail.

Later, when he learned that the bishops of other provinces—those of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica, but not the Galician bishops—were to assemble at the Council of Toledo, he is believed to have sent another letter to those bishops, ordering them to issue a decree of faith and send it to Balconius, metropolitan of Galicia.

Some inferred this from the reading published after Merlin in several editions of the Councils, where the heading of the rule of faith appended to the First Council of Toledo is given as follows:

“Here begins the rule of the catholic faith against all heresies, especially against the Priscillianists, which the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica composed at the command of Pope Leo of the City and sent to Balconius, bishop of Galicia.”

Only the codices of the Hispanic collection of Gallican origin, which Isidore copied, prefer this reading and punctuation; in them we have often observed alterations made by arbitrary judgment.

The codices of the purer Hispanic collection read as follows:

“Here begin the rules of faith . . . which the bishops of Tarragona, and so forth, composed and sent, together with the command of Pope Leo of the City, to Balconius, bishop of Galicia.”

In the letter to the Spaniards mentioned in the preceding item, Leo had ordered all the Spaniards to convene a general synod against the Priscillianist heresy; and if anything prevented that general synod, he had commanded in Letter 15 to Turibius that at least the priests of Galicia should meet together.

Therefore, when, in accordance with Leo’s command, the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica had held a synod in which they composed a rule of faith, they sent this rule, together with the aforementioned command and Leo’s letter addressed also to the Galicians—and perhaps also with the letter to Turibius, in which a council of Galicia was especially desired—to Balconius, metropolitan of that province, so that he might thereby be stirred to convene a synod.

This is also a convenient interpretation of what Lucretius, bishop of Braga, said at the Second Council of Braga (volume 6 of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 517):

“By whose command also the bishops of Tarragona and Carthage, and likewise those of Lusitania and Baetica, having held a council among themselves, composed a rule of faith against the Priscillianist heresy with certain chapters and sent it to Balconius, then bishop of this Church of Braga.” [Col. 1221D–1222A]

### 19

The same Lucretius further testifies that Saint Leo sent his writings to the council of Galicia against the impious sect of Priscillian through Turibius, notary of his see.

This was the letter to the bishops of Galicia that has perished. In the oldest codex, number 59, of the Veronese chapter, which contains a *Breviarium* of the canons and decretals of the Roman pontiffs, the following is found both in the preceding table and in the work itself under number 30:

“From a letter of Pope Leo to Balconius.”

No fragment or chapter of the letter itself follows.

It is unknown whether this was a special letter to Balconius or a general letter sent to him and the other bishops of Galicia through Turibius, the notary. Leo’s letter to the council of Galicia seems to have been written after he learned that the bishops of that province had not attended the general synod, and he sent Turibius, the notary of the Roman see, with the same letter in order to urge them more forcefully to convene a council of their own province.

Thus these letters may belong to the year 448. [Col. 1222B]

### 20

From chapter 7 of Letter 17, written to the Sicilians on 21 October 447, it is clear that a council was held annually at Rome, to which three representatives from Sicily were always required to come.

No records survive from any of these synods. Letter 17 alone indicates that, because of a complaint brought by the clergy of the churches of Tauromenium and Palermo against bishops who had alienated ecclesiastical property, a decree was issued at a Roman synod for those churches. In it Leo prescribed how the interests of both churches were to be protected.

See note 6 ([Col. 705, n. a]) to Letter 17. [Col. 1222C]

### 21

Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, wrote a letter to Leo in which he explained that Pelagians of his province had been recalled to sound judgment and to the Church. Some of the clerics among them, he said, had been cautiously restored to their rank, while others had been promoted to a higher rank.

Leo replied to him on this matter in Letter 18, dated 30 December 447.

In his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, John Trithemius lists, among the minor works of Leo copied in his manuscript, the following in fourth place:

“Book 1, On the Questions of Januarius the Bishop,” beginning: “No reason permits that . . .”

In tenth place he lists:

“Book 1, To Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne,” beginning: “With the appended answers . . .”

These words, however, do not belong to the beginning of the letter but to its inscription or title.

From Trithemius’s distinction between the letter to Rusticus and the questions of Januarius, some may suspect that another letter of Januarius of Aquileia is missing, in which he posed several questions to Saint Leo, and that another letter of Saint Leo is likewise missing, in which he answered Januarius’s questions.

But the beginning “No reason permits that” agrees with the pontiff’s replies to Rusticus’s questions. Since these replies are copied in some collections under a separate number after the letter itself, perhaps in Trithemius’s exemplar a scribal error separated them from the letter to Rusticus and attached them to the shorter letter to Januarius. This led him to attribute to Januarius what must be attributed to Rusticus. [Col. 1222D]

## In the Year 448

### 22

Two older Beneventan priests had yielded first place to Epicharpius, who had been ordained more recently, to the prejudice of the others. Paul the priest, distressed by this, went to Rome and presented Leo with a petition of complaint concerning the matter. It was appended to Letter 19 to Dorus, bishop, from chapter 1 onward, but it has not come down to us. [Col. 1223A]

### 23

Since, in this case, Leo vindicated each person’s rank according to the time of ordination, relegating those who had yielded to the lowest position, he entrusted the execution of this command to Bishop Julius in a letter that has been lost.

See chapter 2 of the aforementioned Letter 19.

### 24

During the disturbances in the Church of Ephesus concerning Bishop Bassianus, Leo issued a letter mentioned at the Council of Chalcedon, in volume 4 of the Councils, pages 1610a and 1614c. In it he wrote that Bassianus ought not to be bishop, since he had been ordained contrary to the rules.

See our notes to Quesnellus’s first dissertation, under the year 447, number 4.

### 25

Before Eutyches was condemned at the Constantinopolitan synod by Saint Flavian, he sent a letter to Saint Leo reporting that the Nestorian heresy was again being nourished by the efforts of certain persons.

See the pontiff’s reply in Letter 20. [Col. 1223B]

### 26

After his condemnation, the same heretic sent another letter to Leo, preserved from a Casinensis manuscript and read as Letter 21. To it he appended four documents.

Among these, the petition of accusation of Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, produced at the Constantinopolitan synod, is nevertheless copied among the proceedings of that synod inserted at Chalcedon, although it is omitted in that manuscript.

Another petition of appeal to Leo is missing. Eutyches falsely claimed that it had been presented at that synod but not received.

Of the third document, the first part survives, containing Eutyches’s profession of faith; the second part, containing his protest addressed to the people of Constantinople, is missing.
