The fourth document bore the spurious testimonies of Julius, Felix, Athanasius, and Gregory Thaumaturgus. In the same manuscript, the testimonies of the last three Fathers, as produced by Eutyches, are omitted. [Col. 1223C]

### 27

At this same time Eutyches sent another letter of complaint to Saint Peter Chrysologus, as appears from Letter 25.

### 28

In a letter to Leo, the emperor Theodosius, favoring Eutyches, complained about the disturbances raised against him at Constantinople and declared himself concerned lest schisms, heresies, or any scandals should grow strong among God’s people, as may be inferred from Letters 23 and 24.

These imperial letters, together with Eutyches’s preceding letter, were probably sent toward the end of 448. [Col. 1223D]

## In the Year 449

### 29

Theodosius sent Leo another letter inviting him to the Council of Ephesus; Leo received it on 13 May 449, as appears from Letter 31, chapter 4.

Julius, Leo’s legate at the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, declared that these letters had been written in similar terms when the emperor’s letter to Dioscorus was read at that same synod, session 1.

We observed that there was some difference between them in note 29 ([Col. 793, n. j]) to Letter 31. Hence the legate Julius used the expression *τῷ ὁμοίῳ*—“in similar wording”—rather than *τῷ αὐτῷ*—“in the same wording.”

30. A letter of Julian, bishop of Cos, written at Constantinople and sent to Leo through the deacon Basil, in which he declared the Catholic doctrine against the Eutychian heresy. The holy pontiff replied to it in two letters, 34 and 35, one sent through legates and the other through the same Basil.

31. A third letter of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, sent to Leo through a deacon named Basil, different from the one who had brought Julian’s letter, after the other two letters that survive. It expressed his longing for Leo. [Note: [Col. 1223D] See the introductory note to letter 35, no. 4.] It was brief, because a fuller instruction had been entrusted to Basil. The pontiff replied to it in letter 38. Compare note 2 (Col. 812, n. o).

[Col. 1224A] 32. A letter of the Gallic bishops who, after Hilary’s death, had ordained Ravennius bishop of Arles, together with another letter of Ravennius himself. In accordance with the ancient discipline, both the ordainers and the ordained wrote to the Roman pontiff concerning that ordination. Leo replied to them in letters 40 and 41, issued on 22 August 449.

33. A petition of appeal to Leo, given by Saint Flavian of Constantinople to the legates 1447 at the false synod of Ephesus, is mentioned in letter 44, chapter 3. On this, see our observations in Quesnell’s Dissertation 8.

34. In the matter of the Ephesian robbery, the acts of the Roman synod in whose name Leo wrote letters 44, 45, 50, and 51 to the East, dated 13 October 449.

35. Copies of the acclamations of the Constantinopolitan populace on behalf of Bishop Flavian and against the Ephesian robbery, which were sent to Leo together with the letter of the clergy and people of Constantinople, to which the pontiff replied in letter 59. See chapter 1. These letters [Col. 1224B] were sent before Flavian’s death had been heard of, around the same time at which Leo wrote letters 50 and 51, that is, around the Ides of October of this year, 449. Compare note 4 (Col. 886, n. l) on letter 59.

36. At the same time as the clergy and people of Constantinople, the archimandrites Martin and Faustus also wrote in the same sense; Leo replied to them in letter 61.

37. On the same occasion, letters of the Augusta Pulcheria were very probably sent to the same pontiff. In them she clearly showed how greatly she loved the Catholic faith and how intensely she detested heretical error. See the reply in letter 60.

38. Toward the end of 449, just as Anatolius was ordained bishop of Constantinople and sent Leo a letter concerning his ordination, as we have shown in the introductory note to letter 53, so too the emperor Theodosius, the Augusta Pulcheria, and the ordainers [Col. 1224C] of the same man wrote letters to the same pontiff concerning that ordination. Only a fragment of Anatolius’s letter survives. The other letters are lost. Leo replied to Theodosius in letter 69 and to Pulcheria in letter 70. The letter of the ordainers is mentioned in letter 71.

Here, however, we point out that in letters 62, 63, and 64, which he delivered to Valentinian and the Augusti, Theodosius asserts that he had already written to the same pontiff more fully, at greater length, more clearly, most fully, and repeatedly concerning the matters Leo had mentioned—namely, Flavian and the proceedings of the Ephesian robbery. The adverb *saepius* (“repeatedly”), which is read in letter 63, indicates not merely one but several letters written by the same emperor to Leo on this subject. A similar adverb, *saepe* (“often”), which Leo likewise uses in letter 69, chapter 1, concerning Theodosius’s letters, agrees with this. From both letters, 63 and 69, it is also clear that in those same letters to Leo the emperor had always presented himself as concerned for the preservation of the Nicene synod.

It is possible that something of this kind was touched upon in the letters that the same Theodosius wrote to our pontiff on the occasion of Anatolius’s ordination. [Col. 1224D] But since the same emperor wrote more than one letter for this reason, at least one earlier letter, sent to Leo not long after the Ephesian robbery, must be posited. In it, the fuller account of the Ephesian proceedings would have been contained, since it suited Eutyches’ patron to forestall the pontiff as quickly as possible.

This letter was delivered to Leo in December and provided the occasion for his writing to the same Augustus letter 54, in which, while discussing the preservation of the Nicene faith, he refrained in other matters from pressing the emperor’s mind too sharply and referred him back to the letters previously written to him on 11 October.

## YEAR 450

39. The acts of another Roman synod, convened in February 450 for the same reason—the Ephesian robbery—from countless bishops of all Italy. At their request, the emperor Valentinian, together with his mother and wife, sent letters 55, 56, 57, and 58 to Theodosius and Pulcheria. The acts of this synod are said to have been sent in letter 55. For the date indicated, see the introductory note to letter 55.

40. The bishop of Vienne sent a letter to Leo with legates, complaining that the bishop of Arles had usurped the ordination of the bishop of Vaison, as reported in letter 66, chapter 1. The allegations of both parties are also presented in chapter 2.

41. A letter of Faustus, the Constantinopolitan archimandrite, sent to Leo through Parthenius, in which he made known his steadfastness in the faith. Leo replied to it in letter 72. See the introductory note to that letter, no. 2.

42. Martin the presbyter also seems to have sent a letter expressing a similar steadfastness, to whom Leo replied in letter 74.

43. We have shown in note 2 (Col. 908, n. i) on letter 78 that Leo’s letter to the emperor Marcian, sent through the count Maximinus, in which he congratulated him on his accession to the imperial power, was a reply to an imperial [Col. 1225B] letter 73.

44. Since the earlier letter of Anatolius of Constantinople, written to Leo after his ordination—of which we gave a fragment in letter 53—had indicated nothing concerning suppressed or renounced errors beyond what pertained to the ordination of the new bishop, as Leo says in letter 71, the pontiff awaited an explicit profession of faith in order to confirm that ordination.

For this purpose, after 16 July 450, four legates were sent to Constantinople: the bishops Abundius and Asterius, and the presbyters Basil and Senator, who appear to have been sent by the Roman synod. See *Acta sanctorum*, 2 April, p. 92. The acts of this synod are lost.

45. When the legates had arrived in the imperial city, a synod convened. There the dogmatic letter 28 of Leo to Flavian was read, together with the testimonies of the Fathers that Leo had sent through the legates and that are appended to the same letter [Col. 1225C] in the edition of the Council of Chalcedon, act 2. Anatolius and all the bishops, archimandrites, presbyters, and deacons signed the celebrated letter and pronounced an anathema against Nestorius, Eutyches, and their teaching.

These proceedings, which are praised in letter 80, chapters 1 and 2, were sent to Leo through the clerics Casterius, Patricius, and Asclepiades, together with the report of the legates from letter 79 and two letters to the same pontiff, one from Anatolius and the other from Julian of Cos. See letters 77, 80, and 81.

A memorandum 1449 of the celebrated Anatolius is also said to have been entrusted to the same clerics and presented to the pontiff, as stated in letter 85, chapter 3. Of all this, however, nothing survives except a single fragment of the proceedings, which will be published in the appendix.

Perhaps the profession mentioned in letter 112, chapter 1, was contained in Anatolius’s letter, in these words: “He [namely, Andrew, as an Eutychian] himself professed that he had been rejected by him.” Otherwise, a new and later letter of Anatolius would be missing.

Just as the Constantinopolitan proceedings in which Anatolius signed Leo’s letter are more probably [Col. 1225D] assigned to the end of 450, as may be gathered from note 13 (Col. 907, n. f) on letter 77, so there can be no doubt that Anatolius’s memorandum, the report of the legates, and the letters mentioned above were also sent around the same time.

Some believe that on this same occasion, through the same Constantinopolitan clerics, another lost letter of Marcian to Leo was transmitted together with letter 77 of the Augusta Pulcheria. In it, he is thought to have borne witness that Anatolius’s faith had been approved by the proceedings just mentioned. For Leo indicates in letters 104, chapter 2, and 111, chapter 1, that he approved Anatolius’s ordination on the basis of the emperor’s testimony; yet no such testimony is found in letter 76 of the same Augustus, which we think was delivered at this time.

But since Leo’s letter 78, which was delivered through the aforementioned clerics returning from Constantinople in reply to Marcian’s letter written at this time, says nothing about Anatolius, there is likewise no indication that the emperor wrote anything about him in [Col. 1226A] his letter. Otherwise, just as in the Augusta Pulcheria’s letter 77, which testified concerning Anatolius and was certainly sent to Leo on this occasion, the pontiff replied about Anatolius in letter 79, so he would have acted similarly in the praised reply to Marcian, which he returned through the same clerics on the same day, if he had found in Marcian’s letter any mention of Anatolius and any imperial testimony.

Accordingly, this reply of the pontiff, namely letter 78, appears to have been delivered in response to Marcian’s letter 76, with which it certainly agrees. Leo could have gathered the same emperor’s testimony concerning Anatolius’s faith from Pulcheria’s letter 77 itself, or more clearly from the report of the legates. Thus there is no need to posit another letter of Marcian testifying concerning Anatolius, to which the pontiff’s reply does not correspond.

## YEAR 451

46. A letter of Marcian sent through Tatian, prefect of the city of Constantinople, reached Leo [Col. 1226B] after the return of Anatolius’s legates to the imperial city—that is, after 13 April 451 and before 23 April, as is clear from note 5 (Col. 917, n. f) on letter 82. Since Tatian, a man honored with so high a dignity, made the journey rapidly, the letter appears to have been written in the year 451 itself.

In it the emperor, most devoted to ecclesiastical peace, again urged the pontiff with even greater concern that a general synod be convened. From Leo’s reply in letter 82, chapter 2, it may be gathered that he requested that everything be discussed anew, 1450 so that matters might more easily be brought to unity.

47. Another letter of the same emperor was brought to Leo by the pontifical legates returning from Constantinople to Rome before 9 June 451. In it, the same plan of convoking an ecumenical synod was again proposed, as appears from letter 83.

48. The bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basil were sent by Leo to Constantinople on 9 June 451 for the purpose of receiving back those who had lapsed. The fullest possible instruction [Col. 1226C] was entrusted to them, although at that time the matter concerned only the convocation of a synod. See letters 83, 84, 85, and 86.

49. Meanwhile the emperor’s letters, dated 17 May—others say 23 May—in which a synod had been summoned at Nicaea for the Kalends of September, reached Leo. We have shown in note 2 (Col. 934, n. m) on letter 91 that special letters, now lost, were sent to him, since the same letters are mentioned there.

On this occasion, perhaps, a letter of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, was sent to the same pontiff. In it he had indicated that, in accepting the Catholic faith and condemning Eutyches and Nestorius, all the Eastern priests had signed, as may be gathered from Leo’s reply in letter 91.

Hence in letter 88 to Paschasinus, chapter 3, the same pontiff also states that he had recently received a letter from the bishop of Constantinople reporting that the bishop of Antioch, having sent circular letters through his provinces, had obtained the consent of all the bishops to Leo’s letter and had condemned Nestorius and Eutyches by a common subscription. The adverb *proxime* (“recently”) deserves particular [Col. 1226D] notice.

50. Leo received the celebrated summons of the synod after 9 June, when the legates mentioned above had already departed. In these circumstances he chose Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, as legate to the council. We have proved that the letter concerning this delegation is lost in note 4 (Col. 930, n. p) on letter 89.

51. Leo sent the presbyter Boniface from Rome as another legate and added him to the aforementioned Paschasinus and the two legates already dispatched, Lucentius and Basil, so that they might preside over the council in his place. He gave Boniface a letter to the same Lucentius and Basil explaining this delegation, as is clear from letter 94.

52. He also entrusted Boniface with a memorandum, a fragment of which, produced by the presbyter himself in act 16 of the Council of Chalcedon, we append here, emended from the manuscripts of Baluze and especially from the very ancient Vatican manuscript 1322.

1451 **Fragment of the Memorandum**

[Col. 1227A]

“Boniface, presbyter and representative of the Apostolic See, said: ‘The most blessed and apostolic man, the pope, among other things commanded us this.’ And he read from a document:

“‘Do not suffer the constitution of the holy Fathers to be violated or diminished by any rashness. In every way preserve the dignity of our person in you, whom we have sent in our place; and if anyone, relying perhaps on the splendor of his own cities, should attempt to usurp something for himself, repel this with the firmness that is fitting.’”

Perhaps this memorandum also contained the command that Paschasinus stated in act 1 of the Council of Chalcedon, in these words, according to volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 863:

“We have in our hands the commands of the most blessed and apostolic man, the pope of the city of Rome, who is the head of all the Churches. In them his Apostolate has deigned to command that Dioscorus not sit in the council, but be admitted to be heard. This, therefore, we must observe. If, then, Your Magnificence commands it, either let him leave, or we shall leave.”

53. Leo’s letter to the same legates concerning Theodoret is mentioned in act 8 of the same council, volume IV of the Councils, p. 1525, d:

“Paschasinus and Lucentius, most reverend bishops, and Boniface, most reverend presbyter, together with Julian, most reverend bishop of Cos”—the last was added to the other legates—“holding the place of the Apostolic See, said:

“‘The most holy and blessed bishop of the universal Church, the city of Rome, received the most holy and venerable bishop Theodoret into communion some time ago, just as the letter sent by him to our lowliness testifies.’”

Since the same holy pontiff also received Maximus of Antioch into communion, and since for this reason Maximus was received at the Council of Chalcedon, as appears from the tenth action, it is unknown whether the fact of that communion was established from Leo’s letter to the legates or from his letter to Maximus himself.

54. Leo’s letter to Eusebius, bishop of Milan, was sent before August 451 [Col. 1227C] through Abundius and Senator. In it, after mentioning the successful outcome of the Constantinopolitan embassy, he instructed him to convene a council of the province, to have his letter 28 to Flavian read there, and to subject the followers of the Eutychian heresy to anathema, as we learn from letter 97.

55. Certain special proceedings, perhaps concerning the privilege of the see of Constantinople, are indicated in letter 101, chapter 2, as having been sent by Anatolius to Leo during the time of the Council of Chalcedon. See note 6 (Col. 977, n. a).

56. A letter of Julian of Cos to Leo, in which he intervened on behalf of what he called the “appetite for a new transgression,” is mentioned in letter 107—namely, on behalf of the prerogative granted to the see of Constantinople at Chalcedon. 1452 This letter, concerning the desire for a new transgression—namely, the prerogative granted to the see of Constantinople at Chalcedon—was brought by the bishop Lucian together with letters 100 and 101, written on the same matter, in December 451.

## YEAR 452

57. A letter of Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii in Gaul, containing certain questions concerning the reconciliation [Col. 1227D] of penitents, to which Leo replied on 11 June 452 in letter 108.

58. A letter of Julian concerning the disturbances and acts of violence of the Palestinian monks, by which they harassed the Catholics and favored the Eutychians. Leo replied in letter 109.

## YEAR 453

59. The words of Leo’s letter 112, chapter 1—“the aforementioned Aetius’s grievous lament”—imply a letter of Aetius himself to Leo, in which he complained of the injury inflicted upon him by Anatolius: he had been promoted to the presbyterate under the appearance of honor, deprived of the archdeaconate, and placed in charge of a cemetery, having in a certain sense been condemned to exile.

He also indicated that Anatolius intended to send letters to the pontiff, which, however, Leo testifies that he did not receive in letter 113, chapter 1. He further stated that documents had previously been sent to Rome, which likewise, as is reported in chapter 3, did not arrive there.

It may be gathered that this letter of Aetius was sent around the beginning of 453 [Col. 1228A] from letters 111 and 112, written on this subject to Marcian and Pulcheria on 10 March of the same year.

60. For the same reason and at the same time, Julian wrote to Leo. He also expressed sorrow there for the evils inflicted upon Italy by Attila’s war. He indicated that a brief statement of faith had previously been sent. Leo replied to this letter in letter 113, dated 11 March 453.

61. Three letters to Leo concerning the ordination of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, may be gathered from three replies addressed to each of them: one from Proterius himself, another from his ordainers, and a third from his clergy. The same pontiff sent copies of these replies to Julian with letter 113, chapter 3.

In his letter to Proterius, he seems to have requested a fuller and clearer exposition of the faith, as appears from letter 127, chapter 1. All six of these letters have perished.

62. At about this same time, other letters of Euxitheus of Thessalonica concerning his own ordination and that of his ordainers—and, as was customary, also letters from the clergy and people—were sent to Saint Leo through a bishop who is reported in letter 117, chapter 5, dated 21 March 453, to have been entrusted by Euxitheus with the announcement [Col. 1228B] of his ordination.

There is no doubt that the pontiff replied to these with an equal number of letters, but none of them survives.

63. Together with Marcian’s letter 110, written on 15 February 453, Leo received a letter from Julian. In it, commending the distinguished actions of the same emperor and of Pulcheria, Julian sent the same pontiff copies of the enactments of both rulers concerning the suppression and instruction of the Palestinian monks.

These enactments survive in volume IV of the Councils, pp. 1798 and 1819. An ancient translation of them also survives, which we believe, not implausibly, Julian transmitted. See note 4 (Col. 1036, n. j) on letter 116. Julian’s letter itself, however, has been lost.

64. Two letters to Eudocia, urging her not to favor the Palestinian monks, are lost. One was written by Leo at the prompting of the emperor Marcian, who secretly conveyed this wish to Leo through Paul, as appears from letter 117, [Col. 1228C] chapter 3. The other was sent by the Augustus Valentinian at Leo’s urging, according to the same letter.

65. Another letter of Julian concerning the disturbances of the Palestinian monks, sent through Esychius, is indicated in letter 118, chapter 7.

66. When at the Council of Chalcedon a cession of the three Palestines had been made to Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, contrary to the Nicene canons and to the prejudice of the see of Antioch, Maximus, bishop of Antioch, sent Leo a letter in which he complained about this cession. See Leo’s reply in letter 119 and our observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 9.

67. Two letters of Marcian to Saint Leo, to which Leo replied on 9 January 454 in letter 126, were written in 453. In one he had written about the Palestinian disturbances being suppressed and Juvenal being restored to his see. In the other he had interceded on behalf of Bishop Anatolius, as is clear from letter 127, chapter 3.

In one or the other of these letters he had also indicated that he had entrusted the most diligent investigation of the date [Col. 1228D] of Easter in 455 to the Alexandrians. See chapter 2 of the same letter.

68. Together with these letters of Marcian, Leo was given a letter from Julian of Cos. Besides reporting the same events communicated by Marcian, Julian stated that Leo’s letter 114 to the Council of Chalcedon had been read at Constantinople in the presence of the bishops and clergy in an abbreviated form: the final section had been suppressed, namely, the section in which Saint Leo complained about Anatolius’s ambition and about the canon enacted for the see of Constantinople.

He also added that the presbyter Aetius, after an investigation had been held, had been examined and completely cleared. See letter 127, chapter 3.

69. Proterius of Alexandria’s letter to Leo, in which he sent a fuller exposition of his faith, is reported in letter 127 to have been received through Bishop Nestor, and since that letter was written on 9 January 454, Proterius’s letter is known to have been written in 453. The holy pontiff replied to it on 10 March 454.

## YEAR 454

[Col. 1229A]

70. A lost letter of Leo to Marcian is mentioned in letter 137, chapter 2, in these words:

“In my earlier letters I asked that you not allow the stewards of the Church of Constantinople, by a novel precedent, and especially in the time of Your Piety, to be heard by public judges, and that you remove this injury from the sacred orders; but that you order the Church’s accounts to be investigated according to the established custom by a sacerdotal examination.”

We have plausibly conjectured in note 3 (Col. 1101, n. a) on letter 137 that this was written shortly after letter 127, dated 9 January 454, and concerned the affair of Aetius.

71. In this year Julian wrote to Leo that the exiled Eutyches was pouring forth many poisonous blasphemies against Catholic integrity, and that what the whole world had shuddered at and condemned he was vomiting forth with even greater shamelessness, so that he might deceive the innocent. See letter 134, dated 15 April, chapter 2.

72. A letter of Marcian in which he had informed Leo that, in order to comply with Leo’s wishes, he had sent an *agentes in rebus* to Alexandria concerning the question of Easter [Col. 1229B] in 455, and that he would immediately transmit to the pontiff’s knowledge whatever reply was brought from there. See letter 134, chapter 3.

73. Two other letters of the emperor Marcian to Saint Leo, sent in April 454. In one, after receiving the Alexandrian reply concerning Easter in 455, he stated that the date of Easter had been fixed among the Easterners for 24 April, and he simultaneously sent Leo Proterius’s letter 133 concerning the same question. See letters 137, chapter 1, and 138.

In the other he explained everything he had done with Anatolius in order to reconcile him to Leo. He enclosed Anatolius’s letter 132, in which Anatolius sought to satisfy the pontiff, and urged Leo to write to him. See letter 136, chapter 1.

74. Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, sent Leo a letter through the presbyter Andrew and the deacon Peter, announcing that he had been restored to his see. Leo replied to him in letter 139, on 4 September [Col. 1229C] 454.

75. Julian announced Dioscorus’s death to Leo in a letter to which Leo replied in letter 140, on 6 December 454.

## YEAR 455

76. Other letters of Julian to Leo, to which Leo replied in letter 141 on 11 March 455, appear to have been written at the beginning of this same year. In them Julian had indicated that the monk Carosus had been corrected in his confession of the faith, but that he nevertheless remained in some unexplained hostility toward his brother Anatolius, so that because of this disagreement he still separated himself from communion.

He also stated that John the decurion had been sent to Egypt for the sake of the faith, to promote peace and correction. He added that certain accusations had been brought against Maximus of Antioch, who was therefore in danger of losing his episcopate.

Moreover, it is clear from letter 142, chapter 2, that Saint Leo had likewise learned from Julian that the emperor had ordered that another Carosus and Dorotheus, who defended condemned errors, should be removed from their monasteries and live among people whom they could not harm. [Col. 1229D]

77. Another letter of Marcian, in which he earnestly reminded Leo about the date of Easter and to which Leo replied in letter 142 on 13 March 1455 455, is inferred to have been written in this same year.

78. A letter of Anatolius to Leo concerning the remnants of the heretics hiding in Constantinople appears to be indicated by letter 143, signed on the same day and in the same year.

## YEAR 456

79. A letter of the emperor Marcian informing Leo of the ordination of Basil of Antioch is mentioned in letter 149, chapter 1. Maximus, his predecessor, had been accused in 445. Nicephorus states that he was deposed, but others hold that he died.

Whatever the truth may be, just as Basil’s consecration, which took place while Marcian was still alive, must be assigned to around 456, so too the emperor’s letter concerning that ordination must be placed at that time.

## YEAR 457

[Col. 1230A]

80. Julian of Cos reported in a letter to which Leo replied in letter 144, written on 1 June 457, the disturbances stirred up by the Eutychians at Constantinople after Marcian’s death, and what he and the other Catholics had done with the new emperor Leo to suppress them.

81. From letter 145 to the Augustus Leo, dated 11 July, it is clear that Saint Leo had previously given him other letters in which he congratulated him on his elevation to the imperial power.

82. It is clear from the celebrated letter 145 and from letter 146, both written on the same day, that shortly beforehand Anatolius had reported to the pontiff the death of Proterius and the disturbances at Alexandria.

83. Other later letters of the same Anatolius, in which he reported the Alexandrian disturbances, may perhaps be inferred from letter 151, to which Leo replied on 1 September of this year, 457.

But [Col. 1230B] there is a reason why we cannot assert this with certainty. Just as the holy pontiff, on two occasions, wrote to the emperor Leo about the same Alexandrian disturbances—first on 11 July in letter 145 and then on 1 September in letter 148—so he may likewise have sent two letters to Anatolius on the same days on the basis of his earlier report, without having received a new letter from him concerning that matter.

84. A letter of Aetius, presbyter of Constantinople, to Leo concerning the same Alexandrian disturbances is lost. It bore witness to Aetius’s diligence in the affairs of the Church, and the pontiff replied to it in letter 153, dated 1 September.

Perhaps in this letter Aetius also warned Leo about Atticus, a presbyter of Constantinople, so that on the basis of this information Leo wrote to Anatolius in letter 151, composed on the same day. Atticus is said to have fomented the Eutychian error through open disputes within the Church.

1456 85. When, during the Alexandrian disturbances, the Eutychians demanded a new examination of the matters defined at Chalcedon [Col. 1230C], Saint Leo firmly resisted in several letters written in 457 and 458.

During this period, a letter of the same holy pontiff to the presbyter Aetius was sent, of which two notable fragments survive, displaying the same steadfastness. We have plausibly assigned it to 457 in note 2 (Col. 1116, n. h) on letter 147, although it cannot be stated with certainty that it was written later.

We insert the aforementioned fragments here from letter 7 of Pelagius II to Elias of Aquileia and the other bishops of Istria, chapter 6. Paul the Deacon testifies, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 10, alternatively chapter 20, that this letter was written by Saint Gregory I while he was still a deacon, in the name of Pope Pelagius. These passages are found in volume VI of the Venetian edition of the Councils, p. 264.

**Two fragments of a letter to Aetius**

“Among the final words of the often-mentioned Leo to the presbyter Aetius, you also cite this testimony, in which he says:

“‘Let him not suffer the contest over matters that have been laid to rest to be brought [Col. 1230D] forward; whoever reopens them is found to be nothing but a sacrilegious person.’

“He himself makes clear what matters he is asserting this about, when writing to the same Aetius and saying:

“‘I shall never be able to think anything different from the Apostolic See, nor myself deviate from my own judgment, so as to change by any variation what I confessed through the revelation of the Holy Spirit and what I made known while the whole synod, together with me, proclaimed it; for it would be easier for me to be removed from this world by any punishments whatsoever than to be changed from the confession which I have embraced universally [perhaps, “which I have published”].’”

86. Leo’s letter to Patricius Aspar, together with letter 148 to the emperor Leo, was sent through Gerontius on 1 September 457 and is mentioned in letters 151 and 153.

In it Leo commended to Patricius, who enjoyed great influence with the emperor, not only through favor but also through authority, the same measures that he requested from the emperor in letter 148—namely, the suppression of the obstinacy of the heretics who called the definitions already made a new matter for examination. [Col. 1231A]

87. Anatolius sent other letters to Leo through Olympius, to which Leo replied in letter 155 on 11 October 457. In them Leo explained how greatly he had benefited the Catholic bishops of Egypt who had fled to Constantinople to the emperor for the sake of the faith.

88. Saint Leo also wrote another letter to the Augustus Leo on the same day and sent it through the same Olympius [Note: [Col. 1231D] See note 4 (Col. 1126, n. f) on letter 155 and note 2 (Col. 1133, n. d) on letter 158.], together with letters 154 and 155. According to letter 154, he thanked the emperor for receiving the Egyptian bishops with the charity that was fitting. According to letter 157, chapter 3, he commended them to him again and again.

Furthermore, according to letter 155, he urged the same Augustus to confront with sterner firmness the acts of the most impious robbers—that is, the Eutychians, the followers of Timothy Aelurus—who were daring to presume so greatly upon his favor that they even ventured to rage at Constantinople.

[Col. 1231B] 89. After Catholic and Eutychian petitions had been presented to the emperor by those who had fled from Egypt to him, the same Augustus sent both petitions, together with his own letters, to all the metropolitans and especially to Pope Leo. He indicated that Leo’s presence was necessary to suppress these disturbances.

See the introductory note to letter 156, in which the holy pontiff replied to the imperial letters on the Kalends of December of this year, 457. Only the two petitions mentioned have been published, in the *encyclical* code, volume IV of the Councils, pp. 1837 and 1848.

90. Another letter of Anatolius, written at the request of the Egyptian Catholics, was likewise sent to Leo together with another petition of those Catholics. Leo replied to it in letter 157. See note 1 (Col. 1131, n. j) on this letter.

## YEAR 458

91. Since the emperor had not obtained from the pontiff, in the letters mentioned in no. 86, that Leo himself come to Constantinople, he wrote to him again, asking him to send some of his brothers in his place.

This imperial letter is indicated in letter 160, chapter 1, and Leo [Col. 1231C] replied to it in letter 162, dated 21 March 458. Hence it is known that these letters of the Augustus were written at the beginning of this year.

From this letter the holy pontiff quotes the following words in the aforementioned letter 162, chapter 2: “Perfection does not admit increase, and fullness does not admit addition.”

92. Around the same time Anatolius likewise wrote to Leo in reply to letter 157, and showed his displeasure at what Leo had written about Atticus. See Leo’s reply in letter 163, written on 28 March 458.

93. The letter of Atticus himself is mentioned in this letter; with it, writings of doubtful reliability and uncertain profession were sent to Leo.

94. The proceedings of the Roman synod of 458, in which a new and previously unheard-of kind of consultation arose—namely, concerning those who had been captured by barbarians in childhood and, after returning to their own people, did not know whether they had been baptized—are found in letter 166, written on 24 October 458.

95. A letter of Rusticus of Narbonne, sent to Leo shortly before that time through the archdeacon Hermetes [Col. 1231D] concerned the case of the presbyters Sabinianus and Leo, together with the proceedings drawn up during the examination of the bishops and other distinguished persons.

In it Rusticus also wrote that he preferred release from the labors of the episcopate and would rather spend his life in silence and leisure than remain in the duties entrusted to him. Separately he added 1458 consultations containing nineteen questions, which are inserted in the letter 167 in Rusticus’s own words.

## YEARS 459 AND 460

96. Since the aforementioned Hermes, appointed bishop of Béziers, had not been accepted by the people there, Hermes himself and Rusticus appear to have sent letters concerning this matter to Leo, as appears from letter 8 of Pope Hilary. There, after mentioning the cities of Narbonne and Béziers, which had been disturbed for this reason, he adds:

“Formerly, therefore, the governors of the aforementioned cities brought grief to my predecessor of holy memory no less [Col. 1232A] than to us, by daring to pursue with unlawful petitions what could scarcely be softened in the face of our patience except by the mere lamentation of their necessities.”

Perhaps Rusticus insisted that Hermes renounce the episcopate. These events took place shortly before Leo’s death, around the year 460.

### 97.

From another letter of the same Pope Hilary we gather two further documents: first, a report—apparently by Veranus, bishop of Vence, and by other provincial bishops of the Maritime Alps—to our Leo concerning the two episcopal sees of the city of Cimiez and the castle of Nice; second, Leo’s reply, in which he ordered that both places be governed by one bishop alone. The aforesaid pontiff Hilary confirmed this decree after annulling the contrary privilege that had been extorted from him by deception.

Since, moreover, in the letter just mentioned Hilary adds that Ingenuus, metropolitan of the Maritime Alps at Embrun, had previously been censured by the same Leo for the unlawful surrender of his province, it is uncertain whether this reproach was contained on this occasion in the aforementioned reply, or rather in another letter written to Ingenuus himself; or whether the expression “previously” indicates an earlier reproach, namely that by which St. Leo, in Letter 10, chapter 6, charged several metropolitans with transferring to another—that is, to the bishop of Arles—the right that belonged to them.

The first possibility seems more probable. For since Ingenuus, even after Letter 10 had been published, presented himself to Leo as a suffragan of the see of Arles in his petition for the privileges of that see, Letter 65, while at the beginning of Hilary’s pontificate he represented himself as a metropolitan, we cannot understand how so great a change could have occurred in him unless St. Leo later censured him individually and expressly, rather than generally and indistinctly together with the others, as had been done in Letter 10. This particular correction may have moved him to claim for himself the right over the province of the Maritime Alps.

That, perhaps, happened on the occasion of the report mentioned above. For since it was not Ingenuus but Veranus, together with other provincial bishops, who wrote to Leo, St. Leo may consequently have learned that Ingenuus was not exercising his metropolitan right. In addition to replying to Veranus and the other provincial bishops, he therefore also wrote to Ingenuus, in which letter, censuring his unlawful surrender of his own right, he caused him thereafter to assert that right for himself.

These matters will be understood more fully from what we shall discuss at greater length in volume II, in the observations on Quesnellus’s dissertation 5, part II, chapter 6. Since, however, Ingenuus carried the letter of the Gallican bishops to Leo at Rome toward the end of the year 451 or at the beginning of 452, as is clear from Letter 102, chapter 1, if anyone should prefer to believe that it was on this occasion that he was censured by the pontiff and stirred up to seize his own right, we shall not delay over the matter.

### 98.

A letter of Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, by which he informed Leo that Timothy the Cat, after he had been expelled from the Church of Alexandria, had been permitted to come to Constantinople, certain opponents of the faith having brought this about. The pontiff replied in Letter 170, chapter 1, dated 17 June 460.

### 99.

Three letters: the first from Timothy Salophaciolus, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria; the second from those who ordained him; and the third from the clergy of Alexandria, to Leo concerning Timothy’s ordination. Leo replied to them in Letters 171, 172, and 173, dated 18 August 460.

### 100.

Among the fragments of Leo’s lost letters, Quesnellus first transcribed two from Letter 7 of Pope Pelagius to Elias of Aquileia and the other bishops of Istria, where the following is read in chapter 6:

> “Moreover,” says Pelagius, “you insert in your writings a testimony from the letter of the same blessed Leo, which he addresses to Basil:
>
> “ ‘We must act with piety and constancy; [Note: In Letter 162, more correctly, “we must avoid.”] lest, while a discussion of such matters is admitted, the authority of what has been divinely defined be diminished. And below:
>
> “ ‘For matters fully defined must not be recalled for debate, [Note: In Letter 162, more correctly, “nor must they be piously and fully recalled for any debate.”] lest we seem to doubt, at the will of the condemned, those things which plainly agree in every respect with prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic authorities.’ ”

He then added this admonition:

> “We have the first fragment not in the letter to Basil, but in chapter 3 of the letter to the Emperor Leo, which we are now publishing for the first time from the manuscript codex of Cardinal Grimani; it is numbered 133 (now 164). The second, however, I found neither in this letter, nor in that one, nor in any other letter to Basil, although nearly the same words occur in Letter 132 (now 162) to the same Emperor Leo, chapter 2.
>
> “Thus one of three conclusions must be drawn: either these words, which are read in the letter to the Emperor Leo, were repeated by our Leo in another letter to Basil that has not yet emerged from the darkness; or the letter to Leo is mutilated and the part containing the fragment reported by Pelagius has perished; or, finally, Pelagius suffered a lapse of memory when he indicated that the second fragment had been taken from the same letter from which the first had been taken.
>
> “I would scarcely believe that the last alternative occurred. For Pelagius alone would not have fallen into this error; the bishops of Istria would likewise have fallen into it, since both fragments had been copied from their letter in that manner. If they had cited them otherwise, Pelagius would not have failed to point this out, since he did not neglect even to criticize the order of the letters cited by those bishops.
>
> “There is nothing whatever from which one could even slightly conjecture that the new letter to Leo is mutilated, for everything coheres perfectly. We must therefore have recourse to the first answer: namely, that Leo wrote another letter to Basil besides the one we published as number 118 (now 149), unless one should adopt a fourth conjecture and say that all the printed copies of this letter of Pope Pelagius are corrupt.”

We have reproduced this passage at length from Quesnellus because we intended to include everything he wrote. Yet such an admonition and so many conjectures were unnecessary. The matter is easily resolved if we say that the bishops of Istria, from whose letter Pelagius transcribed both fragments, made an error here in the heading of the letter to Basil instead of the letter to the Emperor Leo, just as Vigilius erred in the Constitutum, volume V of the Councils, page 1356, when he cited another passage from a letter which he reported as having been addressed to Anatolius of Constantinople, although it had in fact been delivered to Basil, as we observed in note 7 (column 1120, note j) on Letter 149.

Those fragments are found word for word in Letters 162 and 164 to the Emperor Leo. When Vigilius recited the same fragments in his Constitutum, he cited letters to that emperor, not to Basil. They therefore ought not to be inserted among Leo’s lost letters to Basil.

## Decrees Attributed to Pope Leo

[Column 1233D] Three decrees are attributed to our Leo in the commonly circulated Pontifical Book.

### I.

He established that, within the action of the sacrifice, the following should be said: “The holy sacrifice, the spotless offering.” This first decree is not found in the Paris edition of Fabrotti, the Roman edition of Francesco Bianchini, or Muratori’s Milanese edition, nor is it found in the ancient copies used by those scholars. Yet, besides being preserved in other codices, it was also written in the exemplar from which the ninth-century author Walafrid Strabo excerpted the same words in his book *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22.

An older testimony to this decree is supplied by the shorter and more ancient Pontifical Book preserved in the Veronese manuscript, whose first author, ending with Conon, flourished in the seventh century. See this Pontifical Book, edited by P. Joseph Bianchini in volume IV of Anastasius, page 6.

The ancient author of the books *On the Sacraments*, which are included among the works of Ambrose, reciting at the end of the sixth book the prayer of the canon that begins “Upon which things, O gracious Lord,” concludes with the words “Your priest Melchizedek,” and lacks the words “the holy sacrifice, the spotless offering.” These words therefore seem to have been absent before Leo.

### II.

He also established that a nun should not receive the blessing of the head-covering unless she had been tested in virginity for sixty years; but other codices and the aforementioned Veronese Pontifical Book more correctly read “forty years.” There exists a law of the Emperor Majorian from the year 458 that requires a probation of forty years. Perhaps St. Leo was the author of Majorian’s promulgation of this law, and for this reason the decree is attributed to Leo.

### III.

He also established and added to the tomb of the apostles guards from the Roman clergy, who are called *cubicularii*, or chamberlains.

The decree concerning apocryphal books will be given in the appendix.

Quesnellus indicated in the margin, in their proper places, the decrees inscribed in Gratian under Leo’s name that were excerpted from letters of our pontiff. We have noted those that were taken from his sermons. The remainder, which do not belong to our Author, should not be listed among the decrees certainly attributed to Leo I. A simple heading “Pope Leo” cannot establish that they were attributed to our Leo rather than to another pontiff of the same name.

Six decrees of this kind, with no sermon or letter cited by Gratian, have other authors. Canon 1 of Distinction 72 is Canon 18 of the Roman council held under Eugenius II and confirmed by Leo IV. Canon 16 of Cause 3, Question 9, seems to be attributed to Leo III or IV. Canon 4 of Cause 16 accords especially with Leo IV. Canon 4 of Cause 30, Question 5, is Canon 8 of the Council of Troslejanum of 909. Canon 1 of Cause 31, Question 1, belongs to the Council of Tribur of 895, canon 51. Finally, Canon 101 of *On Consecration*, Distinction 4, perhaps belongs to the Council of Soissons of 853.

Charles Sebastian Berard will discuss these matters more fully in his distinguished work entitled *Gratian’s Genuine Canons Distinguished from the Apocryphal*, part II, volume I.

Two other decrees taken from two letters are likewise read in Gratian, but they are not by our Leo. The first, Distinction 68, canon 4, comes from a letter to the bishops of Germany and Gaul, which we shall list in the appendix as Letter 2. The second, Cause 33, Question 2, canon 13, comes from a letter to Gallerus, bishop of Tripoli, which Pithoeus found attributed to Leo IV in his codex. It can be gathered even from its style that it does not belong to our Leo. It is enough to have indicated these matters.

[Column 1233]

# First Appendix to the Second Part of the Works of St. Leo the Great

## Preface

[Column 1233]

### 1.

This appendix will comprise three kinds of documents.

First, letters falsely attributed to Leo, together with the sentence concerning apocryphal writings, which has been partly transcribed from Leo’s letter to Turibius.

Next, two letters added by Quesnellus to the Leonine collection: one from Turibius to the bishops Idatius and Ceponius, the other from Julian of Cos to the Emperor Leo.

We shall then append a third, published from a Cassinese codex by Christian Lupus and Baluze, in which an anonymous contemporary author refutes the twenty-first letter of Eutyches written to Leo.

Finally, we shall include two monuments relating to Leo’s letters: namely, a fragment of the acts of the Council of Constantinople, published from the Life of St. Abundius of Como, in which Leo’s Letter 28 to Flavian was received; and an unpublished act of the Council of Chalcedon, in which Leo’s Letter 93, first intended for the synod summoned at Nicaea and later held at Chalcedon, is known to have been recited in Latin and Greek.

### 2.

In the series of letters wrongly attributed to Leo, we have not included the letter to Demetrias, because it is a longer treatise that should not be separated from the two books *On the Calling of All Nations*, which are reserved for the second volume.

It seemed more appropriate to insert here the brief fragment of anathemas against the errors of the Manichaeans and Priscillianists, which Ludovico Muratori published from a very ancient manuscript of the Ambrosian Library in volume II of his *Anecdota Latina*, page 112. Since St. Leo condemned the errors of these heretics, Muratori suspected him of being the author of the same anathemas. Hence P. Mansius reprinted this fragment under Leo’s name in volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, page 118.

But since nothing certain can be affirmed about Leo, so much so that Muratori himself wrote on page 119, “Whether the one who anciently proposed these anathemas was Leo the Great or someone else, I do not wish to guess,” it is enough to mention this fragment, lest we seem to enlarge the appendix on the basis of a mere suspicion—which cannot justify calling it Leo’s when the codex itself gives no support.

### 3.

Among the documents relating to Leo’s letters, one could also have presented the fourth book of Vigilius of Thapsus against the Eutychians, published in volume VIII of the *Library of the Fathers*, page 730, as well as the passages that Photius excerpted in Codex 228 from books of St. Ephrem of Antioch and of Eulogius of Alexandria against the Severians and Acephalites. In these works a brilliant defense of Leo’s Letter 28 to Flavian is constructed.

But lest the edition be enlarged excessively, we have decided to place in this appendix only documents of this kind that were contemporary with Leo.

# Admonition Concerning the First Letter

[Column 1235]

### 1.

Quesnellus brought the following letter of Leo to the Gallican bishops of the province of Vienne under suspicion on no slight grounds. Nevertheless, he tried to explain and soften those grounds by appealing to the sense of others rather than his own, so that, although he regarded the letter as of suspect authenticity, he did not believe that it should be entirely removed from the Leonine collection. Moreover, in dissertation 5, part I, chapter 8, he used it as though it were an unquestioned work of Leo.

Let us first set down his entire observation, inserted in his notes:

> “This letter, which has emerged from the library of Fleury, scarcely deserved to occupy a place among the Leonine letters, since it displays very many marks of forgery.
>
> “First, it departs altogether from the polish of Leonine diction and can scarcely be understood in several places.
>
> “Second, the heading of the letter, ‘To the bishops throughout Gaul and the province of Vienne,’ is foolish. As though Vienne were situated outside Gaul!
>
> “Third, although St. Leo gave his powers to certain men—namely, to the bishops of Thessalonica—he never called them his vicars, nor did he use that term anywhere. The forger likewise uses it here as though he had many vicars throughout different regions, whereas at that time the sole Thessalonian bishop exercised his powers. The vicariate of Arles belongs to a later age.
>
> “Fourth, the title ‘archbishop’ points to another, and indeed a more recent, period. Although it was already in use among the Greeks, it was by no means so among the Latins.
>
> “Fifth, the consular notation in no way agrees with the year in which the dispute arose between Leo and Hilary and the sentence was issued against Hilary. Indeed, it agrees with no year. When Valentinian Augustus held his fourth consulship, namely in 435, he had not Avienus but Theodosius Augustus as his colleague, and Leo had not yet obtained the pontificate. When Avienus was consul, in the year 450, Valentinian was holding his seventh consulship, and Hilary had already died.
>
> “Finally, this shorter letter was quite unnecessary, since Leo wrote the longer letter that follows to the bishops of the same province in the same year and with the same purpose.
>
> “Anyone wishing nevertheless to defend the authenticity (*auctoritas*) of this letter could reply that the title ‘archbishop’ was substituted for ‘bishop’ through a scribal error, since the scribes had before their eyes the usage of their own age; that the writing of IV instead of VI in Valentinian’s consulship should likewise be attributed to their carelessness; and that Avienus was written instead of Nomo, since one name could easily be taken for another in manuscript codices.
>
> “Finally, the less polished style may be explained by the fact that, as soon as Hilary had departed from the city, Leo, having completed the judgment that had been begun, immediately wrote these very brief letters to Gaul in haste, to anticipate Hilary’s arrival and account. He intended afterward to write a longer letter at leisure.
>
> “For this reason, they will say, the letter does not seem altogether useless; indeed, it was necessary, since almost six months intervened between the two letters, and one appears to have been written in January, the other in June. The author of Hilary’s Life relates that he departed from Gaul in winter. Thus St. Leo could have written in January to the Gallican bishops. When he learned that they were nevertheless inclined toward Hilary and had not relaxed anything of their favor and attentions toward him, Leo then wrote the longer letter, and took care to fortify it with Valentinian’s edict, so that the Gallican bishops would be compelled to obey.
>
> “In the same library of Fleury, among the ancient documents concerning the affairs of Vienne, there is a letter of Pope Hadrian I to Berteric, archbishop of Vienne, in which the pontiff testifies that after the Council of Chalcedon St. Leo distinguished for each metropolitan the cities subject to him. This is true only of the sees of Arles and Vienne, and indeed it occurred before the Council of Chalcedon.”

### 2.

Since the objections that Quesnellus advanced in his own name and from his own reasoning are sufficiently serious, everyone will recognize how weak are those that he supplied from the arguments of others.

Although the error in the consular notation could easily be attributed to a copyist’s carelessness in writing the numeral IV instead of VI in Valentinian’s consulship, the writing of Avienus instead of Nomo cannot be blamed on the same lapse; nor will anyone easily prove that one such name could have been substituted for the other in manuscript codices.

Nor can it be true that this letter was given on 6 January 445, approximately six months before the other, which we have shown was written not in June but in July. The beginning of this letter states that Hilary had departed from Rome, and from chapter 16 of Hilary’s Life it is clear that he traveled on foot through the Alps to Rome during the winter and, after remaining there for some time, fled from it in winter as well. This seems to refer at least to the end of January, if not to the beginning of February.

It is therefore highly probable that the pontiff had not yet issued anything against Hilary, at least in public letters, when Hilary returned to Arles and, wishing to appease him, sent first the presbyter Ravennius and then the bishops Nectarius and Constantius to Rome, while the Prefect Auxiliaris, replying to Hilary, recommended a milder policy.

If, in order to reconcile these facts with Tillemont, anyone should suspect that in Leo’s letter “the eighth day before the Ides of January” ought to be read as “the eighth day before the Ides of June,” as had been printed in Valentinian’s novella included among Leo’s letters as Letter 11, this method of reconciliation cannot stand, since we shall show that the novella was dated the eighth day before the Ides of July, not June.

### 3.

Finally, one further argument for forgery must be added, which in our judgment is the strongest.

This letter emerged in the library of Fleury from the archive of the Church of Vienne, from which other decretal letters introducing the prerogatives and privileges of that church were likewise published. Since all the other letters of the ancient pontiffs that were disseminated from that book are apocryphal and fictitious—as can be seen in P. Coustant, volume I of *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, who therefore rejected them into an appendix of spurious letters with appropriate admonitions—who would fail to recognize that this letter too, especially since it is marked by several indications of falsity, was fabricated by the same imposture?

P. Sirmondus correctly declared it spurious in his posthumous notes in volume IV of the Councils, page 697, especially because of the manifest error in its chronological notation. He warned that no effort should be spent excusing this defect and attributing it to the scribes, since in the other letters of the pontiffs to the bishops of Vienne contained in that volume there are many other matters so plainly false that they rightly undermine confidence even in what is probable.

### 4.

Nor should the remarkable agreement with the events of this period, or the very simple candor of antiquity discovered in the letter, move us.

The impostor, in order to conceal the fraud beneath the appearance of antiquity and simplicity, excerpted several passages from ancient documents. This can be observed especially in the letter of Silvester concerning the Church of Vienne, which was copied almost word for word from the genuine letters of Zosimus concerning the Church of Arles.

This decretal of Leo, in turn, received certain sentences from his genuine and fuller letter to the bishops of Vienne. Among the particular additions found there is the following:

> “Let the ancient privilege and right of the archbishop of Vienne be restored, which apostolic benevolence transferred in part to the city of Arles.”

The words “in part” presuppose that the province of Vienne had previously obtained from apostolic authority a division into two parts—the division that Leo himself established by a later decree—so that this sentence appears to have been derived from Leo’s Letter 66 to the bishops of the province of Arles. The consular notation of Valentinian and Avienus was likewise copied from that letter. This confirms and demonstrates the forgery even more clearly.

# Letter I

[Note: In Quesnellus, among the Leonine letters, no. 9.]

## To the Gallican Bishops of the Province of Vienne

[Column 1237A]

Leo, bishop, to his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Gaul and the province of Vienne.

Your holy fraternity is not unaware with what obstinacy Hilary, bishop of Arles, evaded our judgment. We therefore see that it is just that, since the bishop of Arles did not await the great moderation in judgment that the prince of the apostles always displays in the exercise of authority through his vicars, he should be removed from the privilege of his city and learn in a lowly position what he refused to retain as a great gift freely granted by our predecessors.

Let the privilege and ancient right of the archbishop of Vienne be restored, which apostolic benevolence transferred in part to the city of Arles, so that Hilary, restrained by such severity, may learn not rashly to transgress the ancient boundaries established by canonical decree.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of January [or, according to another reading, the third day before the Ides], in the fourth consulship of Valentinian Augustus and the consulship of Avienus.

# Letter II

[Note: Formerly among the Leonine letters, no. 88.]

## To All the Bishops of the Regions of Germany and Gaul: On the Privilege of Chorepiscopi or Presbyters

Leo, bishop of the Roman Church and the apostolic see, sends greetings to all the bishops of the regions of Germany and Gaul.

When, in the name of God, we had held in the Roman Church a synod assembled from bishops, or from the other fellow priests and faithful of Christ, see the remainder in volume II, in Quesnellus’s dissertation 11.

[Note: This letter, which in the editions published before Quesnellus was Letter 88, is attributed to our Leo in the codices of Collection 11 and thereafter in manuscript Collections 12 and 20 through 24. Yet it cannot be attributed to Isidore, since it is not found in Vatican Codex 630, which contains the pure Isidorian collection. Since Quesnellus inserted it in dissertation 11 while marking it as an evident forgery, we refer readers there, so as not to repeat the same document twice.]

# Admonition Concerning the Third Letter

[Column 1237]

Since the following letter is presented in the old circulated editions as Letter 96 of Leo, Victor, and Eustochius, and is listed among the Leonine letters in the codices of Collection 12, it was published together with Leo’s letters by Merlin and passed from him into the editions that preceded Quesnellus.

Hincmar of Rheims twice cited it as though it were by our Leo and concerned a synod held at Rome: first in the *Quaternio to King Charles*, *Opusculum* 1, volume X of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 1243, and then at the beginning of *Opusculum* 2, column 868. Its ancient misattribution is therefore evident.

Several scholars detected the forgery, but the chief authority is P. James Sirmondus in his posthumous notes, volume IV of the Councils, page 667:

> “Leo’s name,” he says, “has until now led almost everyone to attribute this letter to Pope Leo and to place it among his letters as number 96. In reality it belongs to Leo of Bourges, who wrote it together with Victurius of Le Mans and Eustochius of Tours to the bishops and presbyters of the province not of Thrace, as it has been commonly printed among Leo’s letters, but of the Third Province, by which name the province of Tours is designated, namely the Third Lyonnaise.
>
> “At the end of the letter, after the subscriptions of the three bishops, the following was then found in the codex of St. Remigius of Rheims: ‘and the other bishops who were present subscribed.’ From this it appears that the letter was issued by several bishops, perhaps in some synod, after the Council of Angers (453), which Chariato too had attended together with these three, and who is here numbered among the bishops of the same Third Province.
>
> “Accordingly, this letter was written during the lifetime of our St. Leo. The aforementioned Sirmondus corrected certain errors of the printed editions from the Remigian codex of Collection 12, and the manuscripts of our own copy of that collection likewise support him. Hence only the errors of the printed editions will be indicated in the notes.”

# Letter III

[Note: Formerly among the Leonine letters, no. 96.]

## Leo of Bourges, Victurius of Le Mans, and Eustochius of Tours to the Bishops and Presbyters Established within the Third Province

[Column 1239A]

Leo, Victurius, and Eustochius, bishops, to their lords, most blessed in merit and venerable in Christ: Sarmatio, Chariato, and Desiderius, bishops, and to the presbyters of all the churches established within the province of the Third.

[Note: The printed editions read “Samartio” and “Charatio.”]

[Note: Another reading has “Victurius”; shortly afterward the printed editions have “Eustachius.”]

[Note: The same printed editions read “Thrace.”]

The powers of this world prevailed with such reverence toward the priestly order that even those whom divine power commanded to rule the earth under the imperial name permitted holy bishops, in accordance with the imperial constitutions, to exercise the right of deciding contentious matters.

[Note: The particle *ut*, wrongly transposed, appears to belong before *etiam*. Later, for *distringendorum* (“contentious”), the printed editions read *distinguendorum* (“distinguishable”).]

Although this has frequently been confirmed both by the formulas of ancient law and, still more often, by enacted laws, we nevertheless find that in the present age it has been trampled upon by many.

[Note: The printed editions read *illibatis* (“unimpaired”).] For, bypassing priestly judgment, they have commonly proceeded to secular examination.

[Note: In the same printed editions, “therefore” is added.]

For this reason it seemed to us that this insult to the sacred law and to our order should both be punished at once by full severity and be regulated by a rule to be observed in the future.

[Note: The editions read “we decree.”]

We therefore decreed that whoever, bypassing the priest of his church, comes to a secular tribunal shall be expelled from the sacred thresholds and excluded from the heavenly altar. After this definition, which has been established by common judgment, no one shall attempt to claim for himself anything beyond what has been prescribed.

Thus those who previously went astray will correct themselves by suitable amendment, and anyone who is proved, under clerical discipline, to serve the heavenly office shall know that he is to be expelled from the clergy if, bypassing the judgment of the priests, he has approached secular authority.

[Note: The words “shall know himself” were missing from the printed editions.]

We wished every individual and all alike to recognize this, so that what has been established with the full order of justice and law may receive the force of complete validity in all matters concerning the clergy.

Certainly, if a layman brings a charge against a cleric, he should first ask to be heard by the bishop. Then, if he sees that the cleric opposes his petition, he may, with the permission of his bishop, engage in dispute before the ruler of the secular sphere.

[Note: The printed editions reverse the sense and contradict the context, reading “a cleric brings a charge against a layman.” A little later they read “by the bishops.”]

I, Leo, bishop, have subscribed.

[Note: The printed edition reads “writes.”]

I, Victurius, bishop, have subscribed.

I, Eustochius, bishop, have subscribed.

# Admonition Concerning the Following Sentence

[Column 1239]

In two Vallicellian manuscripts, XVIII and B. 58, as well as in the much older Vatican Palatine manuscript 277, there is presented a *Sentence of Pope Leo Concerning Apocryphal Scriptures*.

James Petit published this sentence, attributing it to Leo, from a codex of the Herovallian collection after Theodore’s *Penitential*. Later our fellow citizen P. Joseph Bianchini published it from the aforementioned Palatine manuscript in volume I of the *Vindications of the Canonical Scriptures*, page 405; on page 295 he also provided a specimen of its script, which belongs approximately to the eighth century.

The first chapter of this sentence is indeed taken from Leo’s Letter 15 to Turibius, chapter 15. Leo, however, is not the author of the second chapter.

The diversity of this second chapter in the manuscripts mentioned above is remarkable. The older Palatine codex contains several passages lacking in the other three manuscripts. In the latter, the form of a general sanction introduced in the first chapter prohibits the reading in church of books corrupted by heretics; the shorter second chapter decrees that the books of orthodox Fathers are to be read.

In the Palatine manuscript, however, the first chapter, taken more accurately from Leo, forbids the reading, under the name of canonical books, of books corrupted by Priscillian. The second chapter sets out the order in which the canonical books are to be read according to the rite of the Basilica of St. Peter; this appears to have been taken from some very ancient Roman Order.

The Order found in Burchard, book III, chapter 222, and in Gratian, Distinction 15, chapter 3, section 82, is placed after the decree of Gelasius concerning apocryphal books. Although it agrees in many respects with the Palatine text, it is fuller and more recent.

The Palatine manuscript also contains a few additions concerning the reading of the books of the holy Fathers, and these differ somewhat from the text of the other codices.

We shall present the reading of the older Palatine codex; the variants of the others will be indicated in the notes.

# Letter IV, or the Sentence of Pope Leo

[Note: This title is found in Vatican Palatine manuscript 277, Vallicellian manuscript B. 58, and in the Herovallian manuscript published by Petit. In another Vallicellian manuscript, of the eleventh century, the title is “Concerning Apocryphal Scriptures from Pope Leo.”]

## Concerning Apocryphal Scriptures

[Column 1239C]

Care must therefore be taken, and above all provision must be made with priestly diligence, that false codices, discordant with sincere truth, be used in no way for reading.

[Note: This agrees with the Palatine codex and with Letter 15 of Leo to Turibius, chapter 15. Another reading has *providentia* (“forethought”). A little later, *falsati* (“falsified”) is better than *falsi*, since corrupt codices of the Priscillianists are meant. Other manuscripts, omitting certain words, continue as follows: “Because they contain seeds of falsehood. But not only are these things to be prohibited, they must also be entirely removed and burned with fire” (read “burned,” feminine, agreeing with *Scripturae*). “For although there are in them,” etc.]

Apocryphal Scriptures, which under the names of the apostles contain many seeds of falsehood, are not only to be prohibited but also to be entirely removed and burned with fire.

For although there are in them certain things that seem to possess an appearance of piety, they are never free of poisons;

[Note: Two Vallicellian manuscripts read *videntur* (“appear”).] and through the enticements of stories they secretly work in such a way that those seduced by the narration of marvels are ensnared in the traps of every kind of error.

[Note: We have followed the older Palatine codex, since it agrees more closely with Leo’s letter. From that letter we corrected only two errors in the same codex: “seduced by narrations” and “they ensnare.” The copyists of the other codices, correcting the first error according to their own judgment, altered other things as well. In the Herovallian manuscript: “So that, seduced by the narration of marvels and by admiration, they may be entangled in the snares of every kind of error.” In Vallicellian manuscript B. 58: “So that, seduced by the narration of marvels, they may be entangled in the snares of every kind of error.” In another Vallicellian manuscript: “They speak what is hoped for, so that even the simple, seduced by the narration of marvels, may be entangled in the snares of every kind of error.”]

Therefore, if any bishop either fails to prohibit apocryphal writings from being possessed or permits books to be read in the church under the name of canonical codices which have been corrupted by the adulterating revision of Priscillian, he must know that he is to be judged a heretic.

[Note: Some codices omit “either”; shortly afterward they incorrectly read “to possess.”]

For whoever does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error.

[Note: Two codices read “another.”]

[Note: Up to this point the passage is taken from Leo’s Letter 15 to Turibius.]

## CHAPTER II

**[Note: The following material, up to the words “But the treatises,” is found only in the Palatine manuscript and appears to preserve the oldest surviving order of the sacred readings of the Roman Church. The other manuscripts, continuing the form of the decree, immediately add the following: “But the treatises of Saint Jerome, Ambrose (the Herovall manuscript adds ‘and Augustine’), and the other holy Fathers, together with expositions of the Old and New Testament composed by the most renowned orthodox teachers (one Vallicellian manuscript reads ‘orthodox Fathers’), are to be read in the Church as the order requires.” This clause agrees with that of the Palatine manuscript, with the words “and expositions,” etc., inserted in the middle, up to “composed”; these words appear to have been taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict and can likewise be restored from it to give a more satisfactory reading. For there it reads, in chapter 9: “Books of both the Old Testament and the New, of divine authority, are to be read at the Vigils; and also expositions of them composed by the most renowned orthodox and catholic teachers.”]**

The whole of the divine Scripture of the holy Canon is read in the Church of Saint Peter from the beginning of the year to its end, in the following order.

In springtime—that is, from seven days before the beginning of Lent until the eighth day before Easter—the five books of Moses are read, together with Joshua son of Nun and Judges. Seven days before Easter, the book of the prophet Isaiah is read, from the passage where he comes to the Passion of Christ [so the manuscript reads], together with the Lamentations of Jeremiah.

During the days of Easter, the Epistles of the Apostles, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse are read until Pentecost.

In summertime, the books of Kings and Chronicles are read until mid-autumn, that is, until the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November. Then the book [read: books] of Solomon, and of Women, and of the Maccabees, and the book of Tobit are read until the Kalends of December.

Before the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Daniel are read until Epiphany. After that, Ezekiel, the Minor Prophets, and Job are read until the Ides of February.

The Psalms are read at all times. The Gospel and the Apostle [read: Apostles] likewise. But the treatises of Saint Jerome, Ambrose, and the other Fathers are read as the order requires.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 1241]

Turribius of Astorga’s letter to the bishops Idatius and Ceponius, which Quesnellus published among the Leonine letters after Leo’s letter to Turribius, is regarded as suspect by Stephen Baluzius (see vol. 4 of the Councils, p. 731) and several others. Its antiquity, however, is sufficiently vindicated by the manuscript of Saint Emilianus, from which it was first published by Ambrosius Morales, as we shall demonstrate more fully in the observations on Quesnellus’s note 8 to Saint Leo’s Letter 15 to Turribius.

The other objections that might be brought forward are easily dispelled if we believe that this letter, no less than the treatise against the Priscillianists—which is acknowledged to have been sent together with this letter to the bishops Idatius and Ceponius—was written by Turribius before his episcopate. Hence Idatius and Ceponius must be regarded as bishops senior to Turribius; accordingly, Idatius names himself before Turribius in the year 445.

The same treatise, together with the letter prefixed to it, seems afterward to have been sent to Leo, so that the holy pontiff, learning from this letter the antiquity and merit of Idatius and Ceponius, considered them, at the end of Letter 15, especially suitable to lend more effective assistance to the younger bishop Turribius, so that a synod of Galicia might be convened against the Priscillianists.

## LETTER V OF SAINT TURRIBIUS OF ASTORGA

[Col. 1241C]

**On apocryphal Scriptures not to be admitted as authoritative for the faith, and on the sect of the Priscillianists**

To the holy, most blessed, and in every respect venerable bishops Idatius and Ceponius, Turribius sends greetings.

A journey abroad is always burdensome and unpleasant.

[Col. 1242C] Here the whole letter of Turribius ought to have been inserted. But since it was printed after Leo’s Letter 15, addressed to the same Turribius, in column 711, and since we found it appended there in the Quesnellian edition that we used, we refer readers to that location so that it may not be repeated twice.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 1241]

### 1

Regarding the letter of Julian, bishop of Cos, to the emperor Leo, Quesnellus prefaced it with the following remarks:

“We append to the letters of Leo the Great the sole surviving letter of Julian, bishop of Cos, not merely to fill an otherwise blank page, but also because of the close relationship that existed between the two pontiffs. This relationship was displayed especially in the matter of the faith, which one of them defended against Eutychian impiety from the watchtower of the apostolic see, particularly in the Western regions, while the other defended it in the East as a deputy of apostolic concern.

“Liberatus the Deacon gives the subject of the letter in chapter 15 of his *Breviary*, where he relates that the emperor Leo, in order to restrain the heretics who were importunately demanding that a new synod be assembled, wrote to the bishops of the individual cities, consulting them about both matters—what ought to be done concerning the ordination of Timothy and concerning the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon . . . They replied that the Council of Chalcedon must be defended even to the shedding of blood, because it held no other faith than that established by the Council of Nicaea. As for Timothy, they declared that he should not merely be counted among the bishops but should even be deprived of the Christian name. This entire judgment is contained in Julian’s single letter, which ought by no means to be separated from the eighteen—now twenty—letters that Leo wrote to him.”

### 2

Moreover, Quesnellus, in Dissertation 1, on the year 457, section 7, supposes that this letter was written by Julian from Cos. From it he infers that Julian returned to his own Church, and he believes that Julian no longer remained in Constantinople after Marcian’s death.

These conclusions, however, are false, as is shown by Letter 144, now published for the first time, addressed to Julian himself, and also by Letters 147 and 152, written under the emperor Leo in the year 457. In these letters it is plainly assumed that Julian was still in Constantinople and that he had also sent letters to Saint Leo concerning the disturbances that arose in Constantinople after the accession of the new emperor; Saint Leo replied to these in Letter 144.

It is unbelievable that Julian abandoned, without the pontiff’s consent, the office and care entrusted to him by that same pontiff, especially since other difficult circumstances required his diligence. Nor can Aetius be thought to have been substituted for Julian as though Julian had already departed from Constantinople and relinquished the office committed to him. For Letters 152 and 153 of Leo survive, written to Julian and Aetius on the same Kalends of September in the year 457; in them both men are urged to care for the good of the faith.

Nor should the superscription of Letter 147 to Julian be an obstacle. Since in the Grimani manuscript it is addressed also to the presbyter Aetius, as though to an equal, it is believed to have been sent to Aetius as well in the same copy, because the pontiff was uncertain whether Julian was residing in Constantinople. We suspect that both that superscription and the words “also to the presbyter Aetius,” which are omitted in the Regensburg manuscript, should be deleted; and we conjectured that another letter was delivered to Aetius, perhaps on the same day, in note 2 (Col. 1116, note h) on Letter 147.
