If, in this letter, the holy pontiff complains that Julian did not write on the occasion when Anatolius sent letters to the same pontiff, this rather presupposes that Julian was still in Constantinople. He may have omitted writing because he had written shortly before about virtually the same matter and knew that Anatolius had supplied a fuller report.

There is nowhere any indication that Aetius was delegated or substituted in Julian’s place. The fact that no other letters to Julian have been found in the following years, although several others are certainly known to have been written, is a weak argument for believing that Julian left Constantinople and abandoned his office, which was still required for the sake of the faith.

Since, moreover, Julian is read as having subscribed to the Constantinopolitan synod under Gennadius, the successor of Anatolius, around the year 459 (vol. 5 of the Councils, p. 51), it seems sufficiently probable that he remained in that city until that time.

### 3

Among those to whom the emperor Leo sent the encyclical discussed in the notice on Letter 156 was Julian. Although Julian was residing in Constantinople, the encyclical could have been addressed to him, just as it is also found inscribed to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople.

Since all the others to whom the same imperial letter was sent were at least metropolitans, Julian alone, as the simple bishop of Cos, lacked this rank. This demonstrates his special esteem on account of his distinguished actions against the Eutychians.

This letter was preserved for us in the encyclial codex by Epiphanius the Scholastic. Besides Leo’s autograph letter, which an Occidental easily found and inserted, Epiphanius translated the other letters from Greek. Accordingly, this letter of Julian is not the original itself but a translation from Greek; for the entire encyclial codex was produced in Greek.

Baluzius published this codex, collated with several manuscripts, after Surius, and its variant readings have been useful to us.

## LETTER VI OF JULIAN, BISHOP OF COS, TO THE EMPEROR LEO

[Col. 1243A]

To the most devout and most faithful, victorious and triumphant Leo, prince and ever-August emperor, Julian, humble bishop of Cos.

I, my lord, emperor beloved of Christ, taking to heart that most wise admonition in which it is said, “Know yourself,” wished to remain silent and submit to the judgment of my elders [Note: Baluzius’s older books read *malorum*, “of evils”]. For equality of summons does not preserve an equal effect in affairs; but when a person is compelled and the summons agrees with the compulsion, then the similarity of the names also possesses an unalterable correspondence with the realities.

Nevertheless, since your tranquillity has commanded us to offer counsel on each of the matters contained in the petitions of the God-beloved fellow priests of the Egyptian diocese [Note: Thus the same manuscripts; the Vulgate reads “to consult”], I make known the disposition of my insignificance, mourning and watered by torrents of tears, not knowing what I should say, grieving both the captivity and destruction of piety and the unexpected death of the pontiff [Note: Saint Proterius of Alexandria].

For the things committed in the city of Alexandria, as the account itself makes clear, reveal the passion of the mind and appeal solely to your equity for the punishment of so great a crime. Since you have been appointed to govern the whole world, you hasten with the greatest zeal to heal the sickness of indiscipline that is leading to destruction—not unsheathing the sword for slaughter, but bringing the undisciplined, by the word of threat, in due order to the will of obedience.

The sentence that the impious Timothy imposed upon himself has been more clearly explained by the holy canons [Note: The Vulgate reads “sanctions . . . which”; we have preferred the reading of the manuscripts]. He repeatedly rejected them through his tyranny, confounding ecclesiastical discipline and inflicting injuries, becoming, somehow, an enemy of all Christianity. Since he has been caught in such acts, he ought to experience only your justice; for, in proportion to the magnitude of his offenses, as the petitions state, the authority of ecclesiastical sanctions is insufficient [Note: The manuscripts omit “in”].

I openly declare to your power what I am recognized as thinking concerning the holy Council of Chalcedon. For it in no respect disagrees with the truth: it confirmed, with harmonious agreement and by divine inspiration, the faith handed down by the holy and blessed three hundred and eighteen Fathers; it introduced no other dogma, no other creed, no vain exposition, no duality of the only-begotten Son of God, nor did it celebrate any novelty. Rather, it agrees in every respect with the sacred council of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers and likewise with the Council of Ephesus, presided over by the thrice-blessed and most holy Fathers Celestine, pontiff of the Roman city, and Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

We therefore beseech your power to preserve inviolably the things that have rightly been established by Christ, through Christ, concerning Christ. For where so great a multitude of pontiffs had gathered, together with the presence of the holy Gospels and frequent prayer, there we believe that the maker of all creation was present by invisible power.

At that time there was no terror of imperial authority, because Marcian, of holy and devout memory, crowned with the diadem of divine love and undertaking spiritual care as well, hastened to have the doctrines of the Apostles confirmed by the bishops of the Church, inflamed by his desire for the orthodox faith. When your piety imitates him, you both gain victory over the barbarians and destroy the enemies of the truth.

Julian, humble bishop, have stated this as my definition.

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LETTER

[Col. 1243]

Eutyches’ letter to Saint Leo, numbered 21 among the Leonine letters, together with the other documents appended to it, was sent after the death of Flavian, or after the year 449, by a certain nobleman to some scholar whose identity I do not know, asking him to explain what he thought about these matters.

What this scholar judged should be refuted was added, together with the refutation itself, as an appendix to documents concerning the Nestorian heresy, which Lupus and Baluzius printed from the Casinensis manuscript and which are found reprinted in volume 4 of the Councils, p. 490.

We have already presented Eutyches’ letter and the other fragments that the anonymous writer subjects to examination in Letter 21. We now publish the refutation itself. Since it makes no mention of the Council of Chalcedon, it appears to have been written before that Council, probably around the year 450.

We present the title itself from the same Casinensis manuscript.

## LETTER VII

**Written anonymously to a certain old man wishing to know what Eutyches thought contrary to the catholic faith** (C)

[Col. 1245A]

Your nobility sent me a copy of Eutyches’ treatise on the exposition of the new faith, which he set forth in writing to the most blessed pope Leo of the apostolic see. You also deigned to write that, if I had any opinion about it, I should indicate it in a letter from my humility.

You graciously imposed this upon me out of zeal for the holy cause; but, since my mind is hesitant and my heart filled with fear, it seems dangerous to undertake this question, especially at the command of the teacher and enlightener of the nations, the Apostle Paul, who gives the general admonition: “Avoid foolish and ignorant questions, controversies, and disputes about the law. They are useless and vain.”

Nevertheless, relying on the prayers of that most blessed Apostle Paul, with the help of the Lord and God Jesus Christ, I shall undertake what my rustic speech and limited understanding can manage—not as the greatness and majesty of the faith require, but as the weakness of my humility permits.

When, therefore, I read through the aforementioned copy of Eutyches’ letter or treatise on the faith, among other things I found in the text of his words that he complained that the holy council of bishops demanded that he confess two natures in Christ.

If, out of regard for the integrity and ancient chastity that he had preserved in himself, he had wished to confess this, he would never have been exposed to danger concerning his judgment of the faith. But because he refused to confess two natures in Christ in the one person of Christ, according to the tradition of the Apostles, the Prophets, and the Gospels, at the very harbor of his departure he not only suffered shipwreck in the labors of his disciplined life, but also disturbed the faith of the Churches throughout the world, which had long been well founded. To complete the measure of his perfidy, he killed the blessed bishop Flavian, a worshiper of Christ and faithful preacher of the true faith.

Flavian, receiving the crown of martyrdom in peaceful times, when no public persecution existed, now rejoices with his blessed teacher, the Apostle Paul, and says:

“I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness remains for me, which the Lord, the just Judge, will give me on that day—not only to me, but also to all who love his appearing.”

Since he rejoices with all the saints in the Lord, it is necessary for us, if we deserve to follow his footsteps and the tradition of the faith through which he merited such a glorious departure, to hold with all the strength of faith and even unto death that in the one person of Christ there are two natures: of divinity and humanity, of the Creator and the created, of the one assuming and the one assumed.

These substances or natures, however, are not confused but united, inseparably in one and the same person, while always remaining in their own properties. Therefore the proper characteristics of each substance and nature must be appropriately assigned to it: weakness belongs to the humanity, which was created, but not changeability to the divinity, which created.

For these two natures are so united and joined together in the one person of Christ that the same Jesus Christ, Son of God, God and man, sometimes does or speaks human things and sometimes divine things.

Thus, to display in himself the substances of the two natures—that is, of divinity and humanity—he sleeps in a boat while sailing, as man, and commands the storm, the high wind, and the sea as God, saying, “Be silent; be still.” After fasting forty days and nights, he hungers as man, and in the wilderness he feeds five thousand men, apart from children and women, with five loaves and two fish, as God.

And why say more? Crucified by the Jews and pierced in the side with a lance, he dies as man, and as God he raises Lazarus, four days dead, from the tomb, saying with divine authority, “Lazarus, come out.”

Therefore, my lord, the tradition of these two natures in Christ must be guarded with firmness, lest, by confusing them into one with Eutyches or those who agree with him, we adopt a new path of uncertain faith.

You rightly despise them, because everything that is known to be confused is obscure and uncertain. For, as can be understood, they seem, through imprudent reasoning, to confuse the proper natures of divinity and humanity into one, so that, by failing to separate the substance of humanity from the nature of Christ’s divinity, they declare with their very words that God is passible.

Indeed, the letter that Eutyches says belonged to Julius, formerly bishop of the city of Rome—which, I do not know why, he produced, perhaps falsely, as a support for his perfidy, and by whose perverse meaning he is evidently led—at the very end of its text professes the following:

“Those, therefore, who think in this way do not depart from those who think contrary and discordant things, so that while in mind they agree with the divine commandments, they differ in their words. For when they understand two natures, they must worship one and not worship the other; they must be baptized into the divine nature but not baptized into the human nature.”

You see, then, how those who attack and confuse the substance of the two natures attempt, in their perverse understanding, to declare God passible.

But we, who hold to the straight path of the catholic faith, setting aside this confusion of the two natures, are baptized into the Lord’s flesh and therefore worship it, because it has been assumed by the divinity and so united to it that we confess not one God and another, but one and the same God and man, the Son of God.

For if Eutyches or those who agree with him separate the man from Christ God, we never worship or serve that man. Or if one of us were to find a purple robe or a royal diadem lying on the ground, would he attempt to worship them? But as soon as the king has put them on, he incurs the danger of death if he refuses to worship them together with the king.

So too, if anyone refuses to worship the perfect humanity of Christ our Lord—not as something solitary and bare, but united to his divinity—as the one and same Son of God, true God and true man, he will suffer eternal death.

Julius likewise, whose meaning Eutyches follows, says:

“If, however, we are baptized into the death of the Lord, we confess one nature, that of the impassible divinity and the passible flesh.”

I would like to know more fully what they mean when they speak of “flesh.” If this flesh is without a soul, what is that flesh but earth without sensation, which could neither give thanks nor feel the sufferings of the cross? That flesh without a soul cannot feel is evident to all.

If, as they think, the divinity took the place of the soul in that Lord’s flesh, then they subject the divinity to sufferings. But if, as the most faithful truth of the Scriptures teaches, he assumed a human soul together with the flesh, then perfect God assumed the perfect nature of man, showing that together with human flesh he also assumed a human soul—that is, a perfect man.

For he says: “The good shepherd lays down his soul for his sheep”; and, “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it again.” At the very moment of his Passion he says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death”; and, “Now my soul is troubled.”

God is never troubled. It was that man who hungered, thirsted, slept, grew weary, and wept. The flesh alone could not feel any of these things without the movements of a soul, unless it was that perfect man whom perfect God assumed, as the prophet Jeremiah says:

“This is our God; no other shall be accounted beside him. He found the whole way of discipline and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he was seen on earth and lived among men.”

In what form he was seen and lived on earth, the most holy of the prophets, Isaiah, explains fully and more clearly:

“Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced him before his face as a child, like a root in thirsty ground. He has no appearance or glory. We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his appearance was without honor and rejected above all men. A man placed in suffering, knowing how to bear infirmities.

“Because his appearance was despised, he was dishonored and esteemed as nothing. He bears our sins and suffers for us. We considered him to be in pain, under punishment, and in affliction. But he was wounded for our sins and weakened for our iniquities. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruises we were healed.

“All we like sheep have gone astray, and all men have strayed from their own way. The Lord delivered him over for our sins. He, being grievously afflicted, restrained his lips; like a sheep he was led to the slaughter. And as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth.

“In his humiliation judgment was taken away from him. But who will declare his generation? For his life will be taken from the earth, and he was led to death because of the iniquities of my people. And I will give the ungodly for his burial and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth.

“And the Lord willed to cleanse him from his wound. If you give your souls for sin, you will see offspring of long life, and the Lord will desire to consume his soul, to show him light, to form understanding, to justify the just one who serves many well. And he himself bore their sins.

“Therefore he himself will possess many as an inheritance and will divide the spoils of the strong. Because his soul was handed over to death and he was reckoned among the wicked. And he himself takes away the sins of many, and he was handed over for our iniquities.”

Consider carefully, then, my lord, in accordance with the concern of your holy mind, how the aforementioned prophets Jeremiah and Isaiah, agreeing with one another, affirm that perfect God descended from heaven for the salvation of the human race and assumed a man; and how Isaiah, as stated above, assigns to both natures the sufferings of that man assumed in Christ.

Could God, who is invisible, be comprehended in an incomprehensible manner, be handed over to enemies, be reckoned among the wicked, die, or have his life removed from the earth? It was that man, as we have already said, who hungered, thirsted, grew weary, slept, and wept. He also, while hanging on the cross of his Passion, saw the God dwelling in him departing from his body and cried out after him in a voice of lamentation, saying in the Hebrew language:

**“Heli, Heli lamasabactani”**—that is, **“My God, why have you forsaken me?”**

Although he was going to raise him on the third day, it was nevertheless necessary that what Jesus had already foretold in the Gospel should be fulfilled when he said to his disciples:

“I proceeded from God; I came forth from the Father and came into this world; and again I leave this world and go to the Father.”

For even in the Passion itself, although that perfect man, assumed by perfect God, suffered the impious punishment of dying on the cross, nevertheless the impassible God himself, in that perfect man whom he had assumed, did not endure the Passion but did suffer the insult.

Just as someone who tears a garment insults the person wearing it, so those who crucified his flesh inflicted an insult upon his divinity. All the elements, seeing this insult to the divinity, were therefore terrified.

The earth trembled, the rocks were split, the sun fled into night, the moon was darkened with a blood-red color, and, as though the world were already oppressed by everlasting condemnation, the stars were torn from their heavenly places and fell; the order of the elements was confused, the tombs were opened, and bodies long since buried received back their souls.

For this reason the most faithful catholic teachers of the Churches throughout the world, in accordance with the authority of the Scriptures, proclaim two natures in Christ: divinity and humanity [“May Eutyches have considered this!”]. If only Eutyches, after so many years of disciplined labor, had not plunged himself into this error with open eyes, nor brought impious disturbance upon the Churches of the East by confusing the substances of the two natures and declaring God passible.

But since the Apostle Paul’s statement is fulfilled in this matter when he says, “For in the last times some shall depart from the faith,” he nevertheless warns us earnestly:

“Give heed to seducing spirits, in the hypocrisy of liars whose conscience is seared.”

If, according to the Apostle’s saying, he had not possessed a seared and uncertain conscience concerning his faith, he would never, by stirring up such confusion in the Churches of God, have made the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, as well as Cyril, Athanasius, Felix, Gregory, and Proclus, holy bishops, partners in his perfidy.

These men are numbered among the saints and elect of God and in the book of life—not by following his perfidy, but by teaching the faith that I have expounded above in my humility.

But in order to deceive the simple and unlearned, and to draw their minds to himself and unite them with his own, he pretends that the aforementioned men, authors and preachers of the catholic faith, are partners in his new and most recent perfidy.

In Eutyches, the Apostle’s sentence has truly been fulfilled:

“Such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light. Therefore it is no great thing if his ministers also transform themselves as ministers of righteousness; their end shall be according to their works.”

According to this sentence of the Apostle, since Eutyches is a minister of perfidy, he pretends to be a companion of the ministers of righteousness. He did [not] hold the aforementioned doctrine of our faith received from these men, but set forth a system taught by himself.

Among their disciples and most beloved faithful children of the faith, I desire that your nobility also be enrolled together with me, so that, if we are worthy, by following the footsteps of their faith we may merit to obtain mercy at the future judgment through the prayers of the united and triple majesty of the divine compassion—that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## LETTER VIII, OR FRAGMENT

**[Note: The acts of this synod, sent to the holy pontiff, are praised in Letter 80. Only this fragment survives, inserted into the Life of Saint Abundius of Como. Abundius was one of the four legates sent by Saint Leo to establish peace with the Easterners on the condition that they receive Leo’s letter to Flavian and subscribe to it. Although the author of this Life was neither contemporary nor very ancient, he found the acts of the synod themselves and therefore deserves complete trust in this part. Accordingly, Cardinal Baronius rightly inserted the fragment into his *Annals* under the year 450, section 29, and it was subsequently reproduced in editions of the Councils. We promised to publish it in an appendix in note 6 (Col. 913, note d) on Letter 80.]**

## ACTS OF THE CONSTANTINOPOLITAN SYNOD HELD IN THE YEAR 450

In which Saint Leo’s Letter 28 to Flavian was read and received, from the Life of Saint Abundius, bishop of Como

[Col. 1248C]

Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, New Rome, having received the letter of Saint Leo the pope for the confirmation of the catholic faith against the madness of the heretics, gathered a council of all the bishops, archimandrites, presbyters, and deacons.

In the presence of all, the letter of Saint Leo the pope was read, which the blessed Abundius presented before everyone [Note: This account, derived by the author of the Life from the acts of the synod, agrees completely with Leo’s words inserted in Letter 88, chapter 3, to Paschasinus].

With the testimonies of the Roman and Greek Fathers agreeing, Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, with full devotion consented and subscribed to this letter of Saint Leo the pope, which contained the truth of the catholic faith; the testimonies also agreed of the Fathers whose decrees had been issued by that same apostolic see [read: “sent”; read also: “of those who had issued them”]. He pronounced an anathema against Eutyches and Nestorius, against their doctrine, and against their followers.

All the bishops, presbyters, archimandrites, and deacons who were present did the same.

**[Note: Here the fragment of the acts begins.]**

Immediately Saint Abundius and Asterius, bishops, and Basil and Senator, presbyters, said:

“Thanks be to almighty God, because we have learned that the professions of the venerable bishops, presbyters, archimandrites, deacons, and the entire clergy confess the true faith handed down by the Fathers, as their subscription inserted into these acts plainly declares.

“Therefore we also, since we have discovered that all demand and expect this, in accordance with the declaration of the venerable Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, and the judgment of Flavian, bishop of holy memory, or with the assent of Pope Leo, who sent us from Rome to make the catholic faith known to all, pronounce an anathema against Eutyches and against all who follow his perfidy and say that in Christ there were two natures before the Incarnation but only one nature after the Incarnation.

“For the catholic faith confesses that before the Incarnation there was only one nature of the Word, but after the Incarnation there are two, namely, the natures of the Word and of the perfect man, remaining in one person with their properties unconfused.

“We also pronounce an anathema against Nestorius, who long ago spread his insane doctrine [as it is read], saying that the Lord Jesus Christ was born of the Virgin Mary as man only and not also as God, and against his followers who persist in this perversity.

“Therefore, in confirmation of our subscription, it is fitting that the holy brotherhood present here should likewise pronounce an anathema against these men and against all who follow their teaching.”

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING, HITHERTO UNPUBLISHED, ACTION OF THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON

[Col. 1249]

### 1

The Greek codices of the Council of Chalcedon in the Library of Saint Mark at Venice, numbers 164 and 555, are fuller than those used by the Roman editors.

The lacunae marked by dots in the Greek at the beginning of Action 4 are supplied in these manuscripts, so that in the third lacuna noted on p. 1357 of volume 4 of the Venetian edition of the Councils, two complete pages are filled with the names of bishops, which are missing from the ancient Latin version placed alongside them.

The names of the bishops at the beginning of Action 6 are likewise supplied. They are absent from the common Greek text and occur only in the ancient Latin translation. For that reason the words **καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ὁσιωτάτων καὶ εὐσεβεστάτων ἐπισκόπων**—“and the other most holy and most devout bishops”—are omitted, since they have no place after the complete catalogue of the bishops has been recited.

In Action 14, concerning Sabinianus, bishop of Perrha, which is Action 15 in the Venetian manuscripts, the edited Greek text gives only certain names that are entirely absent from the ancient version. The same manuscripts, however, add more names, and only some intermediate names were omitted through the negligence of the ancient copyist, who skipped over them.

The same thing occurs in the action numbered 16 in the common editions but 17 in these manuscripts. The names displayed in the ancient translation but absent from the common Greek can be drawn from the manuscripts mentioned above, as can other names that will become evident to those who compare the texts.

## 2.

What is found here above all is **Action 16**, hitherto unknown, in which Leo’s Letter 93 was read. This most especially confirms the conclusion that not all the actions were collected in the Greek manuscripts of the Council of Chalcedon, and that an action cannot be rejected merely because it is absent from one or more Greek manuscripts. Thus the action concerning Domnus is not read in our Greek manuscripts or in the Roman ones, and it was also absent from the exemplar from which the ancient version was produced; but it was found in the manuscript of Patricia Julia discovered by Rusticus. The action concerning Photius, bishop of Tyre, which was absent from the exemplars of the ancient translator and of Rusticus, is found in the Roman Greek manuscripts and in ours at the end of the other actions, just as it was in the manuscript praised by Balsamon. Likewise, the known Greek manuscripts of the Council of Ephesus lack several actions which, since they survive in the ancient version, were found in an ancient Greek manuscript. Baluzius explains the reason for this very well in the preface to the ancient version of the Synod of Chalcedon, nos. 40 and 41.

That this unpublished action, which only the Venetian manuscripts supplied, cannot be called a later interpolation is clear, apart from the authority of the manuscripts, from the fact that, according to the practice of all councils, letters of the supreme pontiff were always read before the council. This action, therefore, which concerns our Saint Leo most directly, will close the appendix.

## 3.

Since mention has here arisen of the usefulness of the Greek manuscripts of Saint Mark’s Library, we think that another observation, which may prove welcome, should be added. We have drawn it from another Greek manuscript of the same Venetian library, marked no. 165.

This manuscript, which contains part of the Acts of Chalcedon, has the twenty-seven canons of that council written in it, each canon being assigned a number—1, 2, 3, and so on up to 27—because these canons were enacted in one and the same action. After the final canon, a line is drawn to indicate the end of the canons; after a certain interval, three other additional canons are appended without any numerical designation. These are transmitted together with the others only in the Greek collections of canons, and all thirty together constitute the canons as they have been published from the Greek collections and collectors of canons, *Councils*, vol. IV, p. 1691.

The first canon, which in the commonly printed editions is numbered 28, determines the privileges of the see of Constantinople. It is expressed in the same words as in the printed editions and is taken from the final action.

The other two canons, however, are fuller than in the printed editions. The canon numbered 29 in the printed editions, excerpted from the action concerning Photius, metropolitan of Tyre, begins with the words of that action on p. 1440: “The most magnificent and most illustrious officials said: ‘Concerning the bishops …’” and continues to the words “to the holy synod,” by which the petition of the judges, necessary for understanding the canon, is expressed. Then the interventions of the legates of the Apostolic See and of Anatolius are appended, from which the printed canon was compiled. Finally, the synod’s approval is taken from the same action, p. 1449C.

The canon numbered 30 in the printed editions, badly arranged from Action 4, begins in our manuscript with the intervention of the judges and senate, p. 1407D. After the intervention of Paschasinus, legate of the Apostolic See, the judgment of those same judges and the senate concludes the canon, continuing to p. 1410A.

The same account of these canons is found in the Greek collection of canons contained in the ancient manuscript XIX of the monks of Saint Basil at Rome, p. 54. From this it is clearly understood what these three additional canons are and whence they derive.

# LETTER IX, OR ACTION XVI OF CHALCEDON

[Col. 1249]

[Note: In the cited Venetian manuscripts, the Chalcedonian canons assigned in the printed editions to Action 15 are most appropriately placed in Action 7; more will be said about this elsewhere. This action is therefore placed after the action concerning Sabinianus, bishop of Perrha, held on the same day, 31 October. In the printed editions that action is Action 14, but in the same manuscripts it is Action 15.]

Now published for the first time from the Greek manuscripts of the Library of Saint Mark at Venice, nos. 555, of the twelfth century, and 164, of the fourteenth century, in which Letter 93 of Saint Leo to the synod itself was read.

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1249B] In the consulship of our lord Marcian, ever Augustus, and of the consul who is to be announced, on the day before the Kalends of November, at Chalcedon, in accordance with the command of our most divine and most pious lord Marcian, ever Augustus, the assembly having gathered in the most holy church of Saint Euphemia, the holy martyr,

[Col. 1251A] in the presence of the most magnificent and most illustrious master of the soldiers, former consul and Patrician Anatolius; the most magnificent and most illustrious prefect of the sacred praetoria, Palladius; and the most magnificent and most illustrious master of the divine offices, Vincomalus;

and with the most reverend bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, and the most reverend presbyter Boniface, representing the most holy senior archbishop of Rome, Leo; and Anatolius, most reverend archbishop of Constantinople, the great city; and Maximus, most reverend bishop of Antioch in Syria; and Juvenal, most reverend bishop of Jerusalem; and Quintillus, most reverend bishop of Heraclea in Macedonia, representing the most holy archbishop Anastasius of Thessalonica; and Thalassius, most reverend bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia; and Stephen, most reverend bishop of Ephesus; and Lucian, most reverend bishop of Byza, representing the God-beloved Cyriacus, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace; and Eusebius, most reverend bishop of Ancyra in Galatia; and Diogenes, most reverend bishop of Cyzicus; and Peter, most reverend bishop of Corinth; and Florentius, most reverend bishop of Sardis; and Eunomius, most reverend bishop of Nicomedia; and Anastasius, most reverend bishop of Nicaea; and Julian, most reverend bishop of Cos, himself also representing the Apostolic See of Rome; and Eleutherius, most reverend bishop of Chalcedon; and Basil, most reverend bishop of Seleucia in Isauria; and Meletius, most reverend bishop of Larissa, representing Domnus, most reverend bishop of Apamea in Syria;

[Col. 1251B] and Amphilochius, most reverend bishop of Side; and Theodore, most reverend bishop of Tarsus; and Cyrus, most reverend bishop of Anazarbus; and Constantine, most reverend bishop of Bostra; and Photius, most reverend bishop of Tyre; and Theodore, most reverend bishop of Damascus; and Stephen, most reverend bishop of Hierapolis; and Symeon, most reverend bishop of Amida; and Epiphanius, most reverend bishop representing Olympius, most reverend bishop of Constantia; and John, most reverend bishop of Sebasteia; and Seleucus, most reverend bishop of Amaseia; and Constantine, most reverend bishop of Melitene; and Patricius, most reverend bishop of Tyana; and Peter, most reverend bishop of Gangra; and Eustathius, most reverend bishop of Berytus; and Apragmonius, most reverend bishop representing Calogerus, most reverend bishop of Claudiopolis; and Atarbius, most reverend bishop of Trebizond, representing Dorotheus, most reverend bishop of Neocaesarea; and Photinus the archdeacon, representing Theoctistus, most reverend bishop of Pessinus;

The most illustrious officials said:

“Let the letter of Leo, the most reverend archbishop of Rome, be read.”

[Note: Julian’s competence in both languages, Latin and Greek, is very well known. By origin he was Italian and therefore possessed the Latin language; but, as prefect of the Greek Church, he could not have been ignorant of Greek. Hence Leo desired, according to Letter 131, that Julian should produce the interpretation of Letter 28 to Flavian. Why, then, did Julian, rather than Boniface, who had just requested that this letter be read, present it together with its Greek interpretation? No more probable reason seems available than that Julian himself was the author of this interpretation. The Latin original is reported to have been presented together with the Greek version because, as Philip, presbyter and legate of the Apostolic See, testified in Action 2 of the Synod of Ephesus: “It was customary that the letters of the Apostolic See should first be read in Latin.” In the Greek Acts, however, only the Greek versions are found transcribed.]

[Note: See annotation 3 (Col. 936, n. k) on Letter 93, where we have inserted the complete version of this letter into this action.]

‘Farewell in the Lord, most beloved brothers.’”

# SECOND APPENDIX TO THE SECOND PART OF THE WORKS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT

[Col. 1255]

## NOTICE

After the publication of the first volume of our edition, in which, in addition to the Sermons, the Letters of Saint Leo were also collated chiefly against Roman manuscripts and corrected, that part of the works of the same holy teacher which contains his Letters, revised against nearly the same manuscripts, was published from the Roman press of Joseph Collini.

Concerning these manuscripts, which were useful both to our edition and to the Roman edition, we must offer one necessary warning, lest anyone perhaps doubt our reliability in citing the same manuscript exemplars. In the preface to the Roman edition, p. 53, the following notice is found:

“In this our edition, the learned reader will encounter the lists of manuscript witnesses, which are lacking in all other editions. We did this for the purpose of removing from the reader’s mind every suspicion that we had indulged in conjectures rather than conscientiously adhered to the readings and authorities of those same manuscript codices. Therefore, in future, anyone who doubts our reliability will find it entirely easy to appeal to the sources we have indicated and to ascertain in due course whether the variant readings, either those which we have noted at the end of each letter or document or those which we have introduced into the text, truly and faithfully correspond to the sources from which we have indicated that they were drawn.”

When we compared the Vatican codices indicated in this edition in the margin of each letter with those cited by us in our edition, we discovered that the Roman edition sometimes states that a particular Letter of Leo is found in certain Roman manuscripts which certainly lack it. We had prepared an exact catalogue of the letters transcribed in each codex on separate pages, so that confusion could not enter; and we are completely certain that no more and no fewer Letters of Leo are found in the individual codices or manuscript collections than those listed by us either in the preface or in the notes, as will also be evident to anyone who compares the codices themselves. The Roman edition, however, not infrequently assigns to letters codices in which those letters are absent; and from the same edition we can demonstrate that this must certainly be attributed to error.

In the catalogue of the manuscripts of the Vatican Library appended to the preface of that edition, p. 66, Vatican Codex 1341 is said to contain forty-one Letters of Leo. It should read “one of forty,” for that codex belongs to the Spanish collection, which contains only the thirty-nine Letters of Leo that we carefully listed in the preface to the Letters, §10, pp. 522–523.

In the edition of the Letters, however, not only is the citation of this codex omitted for the ten letters that it contains, but the number of the codex, Vat. 1341, is attached to forty-five letters, sixteen of which are absent from the same codex—namely, Letters 24, 34, 35, 36, 39, 46, 48, 58, 68, 98, and 99, together with one letter of Valentinian to Theodosius, one of Marcian to Leo, and letters of Pulcheria, Ceretius, and Salonius, as well as the letter of the Synod of Chalcedon to the same pontiff. In our edition these are Letters 54, 37, 38, 39, 42, 50, 51, 72, 67, 123, 124, 55, 73, 77, 68, and 98.

In the same catalogue of manuscripts, p. 65, sixteen Letters of Saint Leo are assigned to Vatican manuscript 1342 of the third collection—precisely the number that we found in it. In the body of the edition, however, the number of that codex, 1342, is noted for twenty-one letters. Thus, although its citation is omitted for six letters that it does contain, the same number is wrongly added to eleven letters that one will by no means find in it: namely, that edition’s Letters 3, 7, 8, 14, 15, 73, 81, 91, 95, and 139, together with the synodical letter of Ravennius and the other Gauls to Leo. In our edition these are Letters 3, 2, 7, 18, 15, 93, 106, 115, 120, 166, and 99.

Similar lapses occur in the citation of several other codices. For example, Letter 24—in our edition, Letter 54—is assigned in the margin to Vatican Codices 1340, 1341, 1343, 1353, and 3791, although that letter is found only in manuscript 1340 and is absent from the others.

Letter 39—in our edition, Letter 42—which exists only in the Arles collection, from which we were able to locate a single Vallicellian codex, G 99, is assigned in the margin to Vatican Codices 541, 542, 1340, and 1341, which belong to other collections lacking that letter.

We shall refrain from reporting the same matter concerning other letters, since what has been indicated thus far is sufficient. These errors seem attributable partly to the carelessness of the printers and partly to confusion among the annotations in the working copies, which did not place a separate description of each codex before the notes.

Whether a similar error may also lie hidden in certain readings assigned in the same edition to one codex or another, we have not had the opportunity to investigate. Certainly, on p. 1, note a, where it is stated that all the older and more distinguished Vatican codices, except the Vatican Royal Codex 1997, contain the words “In the case of Lupicinus the bishop,” there is an obvious error. For the older and more distinguished codices cited in the margin, Vat. 1341 and 1342, not only lack those words, but in the body of the first letter itself—in our edition, Letter 12—they omit the section concerning the case of Lupicinus.

On p. 62, note e, concerning Letter 15 to Turribius, Codex Vat. Reg. 1997 is said to read *sentinam*, although we read *sententiam* there.

On p. 194, notes b and f, concerning Letter 47—in our edition, Letter 59—readings are cited from Vatican Codices 3787 and 4961, although, since they belong to the Avellana collection, they do not contain that letter. We found those readings in manuscripts of Collection 21, to which Vatican Manuscripts 542 and 543 belong; these are cited in the margin of the same edition together with the two aforementioned manuscripts of the Avellana collection.

We omit other observations that are not necessary for defending our edition.

Moreover, in the same Roman edition, in which the distinguished author devoted very much work and labor to the undertaking and also arranged for the Greek codices to be examined, we found three previously unpublished Greek fragments, which we thought should be reprinted in this Appendix.

The first was taken from Vatican Greek Manuscript 720, said to be of the tenth century. This codex contains many short works or fragments of the Greek Fathers. Among them is part of a letter of Saint Leo to the Emperor Theodosius. Nothing could be inferred from its style, since it is a Greek translation. Its substance, however, contains nothing contradictory, for it presents the same right faith and doctrine that Leo taught.

The author of the Roman edition believes that this fragment belongs to the letter which Leo identifies as Letter 24—in our edition, Letter 54—to the same emperor, in these words:

“But what defense of the piety of the evangelical faith is maintained by me and by all Catholic priests has been sufficiently fully and clearly disclosed in my letter, which I believe Your Clemency received through your servant Epiphanius, the tribune who was sent for this purpose.”

He formed this opinion because he was misled by the erroneous chronological notice of that letter, which in the printed editions was marked as dated on the eighth day before the Kalends of June—that is, before our Letter 44 to the same emperor. Hence the words just quoted seemed to refer to another letter, written by a synod of priests and subsequently lost.

But once that chronological notice is corrected from our excellent Ratisbon manuscript to read “the eighth day before the Kalends of January,” that is, 25 December of the year 449, it immediately becomes clear that the words refer to Letter 44 itself, which had been sent by the synod long before the aforementioned Letter 54, namely on the third day before the Ides—or, according to another reckoning, on the Ides—of October of that same year.

What, then? If this fragment, taken from a Greek miscellany, is to be trusted at all, it is much more credible that Leo is referring here to Letter 69, when he writes to the same emperor in chapter 2:

“You may graciously recognize what the form of our faith is from the instructions that we have sent.”

For this purpose Leo sent to the East, to be delivered to Theodosius, testimonies of the Fathers, by which he could prove that in his dogmatic Letter 28 he had taught no doctrine other than that handed down by the holy Latin and Greek Fathers. See Letter 71.

But from this fragment, if it is genuine, it seems that another written declaration, addressed to the emperor himself, was sent at the same time. It should be regarded as having been added to the testimonies of the Fathers and to the instructions of the legates.

Since, however, only Letter 28 is famous, and the testimonies of the Fathers were attached to that letter alone in the ancient Greek manuscripts of the Chalcedonian collection before the Acts of the council, and since no mention anywhere is made, apart from it, of another Leonine declaration or sort of formula of faith addressed to the Emperor Theodosius—which might seem superfluous after the publication of the dogmatic Letter 28—some suspicion concerning this kind of fragment necessarily arises, and it is not altogether slight.

Whatever the truth may be, we shall present the fragment in this Appendix just as it was published.

The second is a fragment of a libellus of Saint Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, addressed to Saint Leo, supplied by Vatican Greek Manuscript 451. In this fragment several matters of somewhat greater difficulty occur.

Two parts must be distinguished in it. The first proposes a certain libellus of faith; the second describes what happened concerning John and Gregory.

In the first part, that is, in the libellus of faith, Leo’s dogmatic Letter 28 is praised, in which two natures and one person are declared to exist in Christ:

“For into one person,” he says, “as Your Holiness also teaches [in Letter 28], two natures converge.”

This Letter 28 of Leo was delivered to Flavian not at Constantinople but at Ephesus, where Flavian had gone to the council. The pontiff’s legates, who had received the same letter for delivery, were compelled by the time appointed for the council to travel not to Constantinople but to Ephesus.

The events narrated in the second part, however, took place at Constantinople. The condemnation of John and Gregory by Flavian, and the disturbance of the people against them, belongs not to Ephesus or to the time of the Ephesian Robber Council, when the Eutychian faction prevailed, but to Constantinople before that Robber Council, when Flavian, after condemning Eutyches, was freely defending the Catholic faith and the people were supporting him.

Nor can it be placed after that Robber Council, for at that time Flavian did not return to Constantinople but was driven into exile and died on the journey itself. See our notice on Letter 53.

Since the first part of this fragment, in which Leo’s letter is mentioned, contains the libellus of faith which is said to have been read before the events at Constantinople concerning John and Gregory—“When the libellus had contained these things, after it had been read …”—the libellus itself must also have been written at Constantinople before Flavian went to Ephesus.

How, then, could Leo’s Letter 28 have been praised in it, when Flavian received that letter only at Ephesus? Moreover, when this libellus was read at Constantinople, Eutyches had already been deposed. How could Flavian have called a man whom he himself had already deposed and deprived of the dignity of archimandrite “archimandrite” in that very libellus?

Since the complete document from which this fragment was excerpted is lacking, nothing certain can be affirmed. Yet, so that it should not be branded as a forgery, one may conjecture that this fragment belongs to Flavian’s libellus of appeal, which was written at Ephesus and delivered to Leo’s legates.

The libellus of faith that had been read at Constantinople should then be understood as inserted into it, together with the account of what happened concerning John and Gregory. The words praising Leo’s Letter 28 were added to that libellus when it was copied at Ephesus. Flavian then called Eutyches “archimandrite” because, after being restored at the pseudo-synod, he conducted himself as an archimandrite.

The third fragment, taken from Vatican Greek Manuscript 1455, is merely a paraphrase of chapter 8 of Leo’s Letter 14 to Anastasius.

# FRAGMENT I

From Vatican Greek Codex 720.

## OF POPE LEO TO THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS, CONCERNING THE INCARNATION OF THE DIVINE WORD

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1257A] A copy of the interpretation of part of a letter written by Leo, bishop of Rome, to the Emperor Theodosius concerning the divine incarnation and against those who believe the detestable doctrines of the heresiarchs Photinus and Apollinaris and their like.

We believe that the Son of God, who exists eternally and without an external beginning with the Father and the Holy Spirit, in the last ages took from Mary, ever-virgin, a perfect man of our nature; and that the Word became flesh by assuming a man, without changing the Divinity and without the Holy Spirit, as some impiously supposed, having served in place of seed. Rather, by the power and wisdom of the Creator of the nations, we confess Christ to be one person of the Son, but two perfect and complete substances, of Divinity and humanity, the latter consisting of soul and body.

We pronounce an anathema against Photinus, who asserts that Christ was a mere and naked man; likewise against Apollinaris and his followers, who say that the Son of God assumed something less than human nature, whether in flesh, soul, mind, or in the assumption of man, and that in what was assumed he was unlike us. We believe that this man, except for the sole stain of sin—which is not a physical substance—was made in every respect of the same form as we are.

We also execrate the blasphemy of those who, by a novel invention, attempt to say that from the time the flesh was assumed all things belonging to the divine nature were changed into the human, and all things belonging to the human nature into the divine—a claim that no heresy has ever dared to make. For by such a confession they assert that both the nature of Divinity and that of humanity were changed into something else, and they do not confess the Son to be, in truth, either perfect God or perfect man.

We, however, say that our nature was assumed by the Son of God while the Divinity remained impassible. For the Son of God suffered not in appearance but in reality everything that Scripture testifies to: hunger, thirst, weariness, labor, death, and other things of this kind. He suffered according to that which was capable of suffering—that is, not according to the one who assumed, but according to the nature that was assumed.

For the Son of God himself, according to his Divinity, is impassible, just as the Father is invisible, just as the Father cannot be touched, and just as the Father is immutable. The proper person of the Son, God the Word, assumed a passible man and dwelt in him, yet suffered nothing, just as the Father and the Holy Spirit suffered nothing. For we must confess the Trinity to be altogether impassible.

When, therefore, the Son of God had died according to the Scriptures, insofar as he was able to die, he rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God, while the substance of his flesh remains—the flesh in which he was born, suffered, and rose again. For the substance of humanity was neither dissolved nor changed, but, remaining in the Divinity, it was glorified forever.

[Col. 1258A] A copy of the interpretation of part of a letter of Leo, bishop of Rome, which he wrote to the Emperor Theodosius concerning the divine incarnation and against those who believe the detestable doctrines of the heresiarchs Photinus and Apollinaris and their like.

We believe that the Son of God, who exists eternally and without beginning with the Father and the Holy Spirit, took in the last ages a perfect man of our nature from Mary, ever-virgin. And that the Word became flesh by assuming a man, without changing the Divinity and without the Holy Spirit, as some vilely supposed, having become seed in place of seed; rather, by the power and wisdom of the Creator, we confess Christ to be one person of the Son, but two perfect and complete substances, of Divinity and humanity, the latter consisting of soul and body.

We anathematize Photinus, who says that Christ was a mere and naked man. Likewise Apollinaris and his followers, who say that the Son of God assumed something less than human nature, whether in flesh, soul, or mind, in the assumption of man, and that he became unlike us in what was assumed. We believe that this man, except for the sole stain of sin—which is not a physical substance—was made in every respect of the same form as we are.

We likewise anathematize the blasphemy of those who, by a strange conception, attempt to say that from the time the flesh was assumed everything belonging to the Divinity was changed into the man, and everything belonging to humanity into God—something no heresy has ever dared to say. For by such a confession they suppose that each nature, both of Divinity and of humanity, was changed into something else. They do not confess the Son, according to truth, to be either perfect God or perfect man.

But we say that our nature was assumed by the Son of God while the Divinity remained impassible. For the Son of God suffered not in appearance but in truth everything that Scripture testifies to—that is, hunger, thirst, weariness, labor, death, and the rest of such things. He suffered according to that which he was capable of suffering—that is, not according to the nature that assumed, but according to the nature that was assumed.

For the Son of God himself, according to his Divinity, is impassible, as the Father is invisible, as the Father is beyond touch, and as the Father is immutable. For God the Word, the proper person of the Son, assumed a passible man and dwelt in him, yet suffered nothing, just as the Father and the Holy Spirit. For it is altogether necessary to confess the Trinity to be impassible.

Therefore, when the Son of God had died according to the Scriptures, insofar as he was able to die, he rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God, while the substance of the flesh itself remains—the flesh in which he was born, suffered, and rose again. For the substance of humanity was neither dissolved nor changed, but, remaining in the Divinity, it has been glorified forever.

# FRAGMENT II

From Vatican Greek Codex 451.

## OF FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO SAINT LEO, POPE

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1259B] Of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, from the libellus that he wrote to Leo, Roman pontiff, concerning the dispensation of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God.

The Word, he says, became flesh and dwelt among us. But the dwelling is one thing, and the one who dwells another. I do not say [Col. 1259C] “one and another,” as referring to two persons, but “different and different,” as referring to two natures. For every evangelical and apostolic exhortation and testimony concerning Emmanuel is divided in two ways: sometimes signifying his single person, and sometimes clearly declaring his two natures. For the one and only Son and Christ was, and is, twofold, and the account concerning him is twofold—not before the union, but after the inexplicable union: the same one perfect both in divinity and in humanity.

For if he were simple, how could he suffer and die? How could he be scourged, nailed with nails, and struck with blows, except in a passible body and an earthly nature? Just as, being consubstantial with God the Father, he is perfect, perfect God from perfect God, so also, possessing the same nature as we do, he exists as perfect man. For he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant for our sake. The form of God signifies the substance of God, just as the form of man declares human nature [Col. 1259D].

The wounds, therefore, the cross, and death belong to the man in whom the Lord God the Word is; but glory and power belong to the Lord, in whom is the servant—that is, the man. If, then, what cannot suffer belongs to divinity, while suffering belongs to humanity, how could any person of sound judgment call the two natures in him one? But if it is one, then either God, being half-divine, became incarnate, and a man of half-nature was assumed. Yet the ordinance of piety does not teach this; Eutyches the archimandrite rejected it by proclaiming one nature of the uncreated divinity and of Christ’s humanity, which is the same as ours.

The entire choir of the saints, however, confesses that Christ has a twofold substance—or nature—but not a twofold subsistence—or person. For the two natures came together in one person, as your Holiness also teaches; and we confess that they are preserved in Christ both unchangeably and indivisibly. [Col. 1261A] For there is one and only-begotten Son and Word of God—not because his two natures are divided into a duality of subsistences, but because the ineffable Word united the two natures in one subsistence: inwardly, the most holy body being adorned through the divine Word, and outwardly guarded by the Spirit, so that through both he might display the distinctness of the natures.

Thus we say that he eats—not only before the Passion, but also after he rose again—and we believe in the nature of his body. If, then, the body concerning which the heretics raise doubts is called a nature and a substance, it is consequently evident that both natures—namely, the divine and the human—are preserved in the one Christ. In the divine nature he received what belongs properly to God, while in our nature he again uttered human and lowly things. He has no admixture, confusion, or division concerning the natures, but exists as one Son, Christ, Lord, and Savior for those who wish to believe piously in him.

When the treatise contained these things and had been read, both John and Gregory expressed disgust at what was written in it, rejected it, and struck it with anathema [Col. 1261B]. After they had cursed and anathematized it, we brought forward the books of the holy Fathers, from which all the testimonies contained in the treatise had been taken. We had those books there at hand [Col. 1262B], prepared, together with explicit refutations from each citation. When we demonstrated from their own books that it was not Flavian but the holy Fathers whom they had cursed and anathematized, the common rabble rose up in extreme contempt and almost wished to overwhelm them with stones. This was the triumph and disgrace publicly suffered by John and his associates.

[Col. 1260B] From Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, from the treatise that he wrote to Leo, pope of Rome, concerning the incarnational dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ, our true God.

The Word, he says, became flesh and dwelt among us. The tent, however, is one thing, and the one who dwells in it another. I do not say [Col. 1260C] “one and another,” as referring to two persons, but “different and different,” as referring to two natures. For every evangelical and apostolic exhortation and testimony concerning Emmanuel is divided in two ways: in one respect indicating his single person, and in another clearly bearing witness to his two natures.

For the one and only Son and Christ was, and is, twofold, and the account concerning him is twofold—not before the union, but after the ineffable union. The same one is perfect both in divinity and in humanity. For if he were simple, how could he suffer and die? How could he be struck, nailed, and slapped, except in the passible and earthly nature of the body? Just as, being consubstantial with God and the Father, he is perfect, perfect God from perfect God, so also, being consubstantial with us, he is fully a perfect man.

For he who was in the form of God took the form of a servant for our sake. The form of God signifies the substance of God, just as the form of man declares human nature. The wounds, therefore, the cross, and death belong to the man in whom the Lord God the Word is; [Col. 1260D] but glory and might belong to the Lord, around whom is the servant—that is, the man.

If, then, the impassible belongs to the divine, while the sufferings belong to the human, how could any person of sound judgment call his two natures one? But if there is one nature, then God became incarnate as a half-divine being, and a man of half-nature was assumed. Yet the ordinance of piety does not teach this. Eutyches the archimandrite rejected it by proclaiming one nature of the uncreated divinity and of Christ’s humanity, which is like ours.

The whole choir of the saints confesses Christ to have a twofold substance, or nature, but not a twofold subsistence, or person. For the two natures came together in one person, as your Holiness also teaches, and we confess that they are preserved in Christ without alteration and without division.

For there is one and only-begotten Son and Word of God. His two natures are not cut apart into a duality of subsistences; rather, the ineffable Word united the two natures in one subsistence [Col. 1262A]: inwardly, the most holy body being adorned through the divine Word, and outwardly guarded by the Spirit, so that through both he might display the distinctness of the natures.

Thus we say that he eats—not only before the Passion, but also after the Resurrection—and we believe in the nature of his body. If the body concerning which the heretics raise doubts is called a nature and a substance, it is consequently clear that both natures are preserved in the one Christ, namely, the divine and the human. In the divine nature he received what belongs properly to God, while in our nature he again uttered human and lowly things. He has no mixture, confusion, or division concerning the natures, but exists as one Son, Christ, Lord, and Savior for those who wish to believe piously in him.

When the treatise contained these things and had been read, both John and Gregory expressed disgust at what was written in it, rejected it, and anathematized it. After they had cursed and anathematized it, we brought forward the books of the holy Fathers, from which all the citations contained in the treatise had been taken. We had those books there at hand, prepared, together with the refutation demonstrated from each citation. When we showed from their own books that it was not Flavian but the holy Fathers whom they had cursed and anathematized, the common rabble rose up in utter contempt and almost wished to stone them. This was the triumph and disgrace publicly suffered by John and those with him.

## FRAGMENT III

From Vatican Greek manuscript 1455. Letter of Pope Leo to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

[Note: [Col. 1261] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 1261B] Leo, bishop of Rome, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

If any bishop, scorning the modesty of his own city, should transfer himself to the ministry of a more distinguished place and, through foolish judgment, move himself to a larger people, he shall be expelled from the foreign see and [Col. 1261C] deprived also of his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he sought through greed nor over those whom he despised through arrogance. Let each person, therefore, be content with his own boundaries and not desire that the measure of his power be increased.

Know, dearest brother, that there is one reason for moving from city to city arising from necessity and advantage, and another arising from rashness, personal will, or private pleasure; but that a person is transferred on account of necessity and advantage. For the advantage of the many must be preferred to the advantage or will of one person. To move voluntarily is one thing; to be transferred is another. The former is to advance of one’s own accord, the latter to proceed under compulsion and unwillingly. Therefore such persons do not change cities; rather, they are changed. They do this not voluntarily but under force imposed upon them.

Those who deny that a transfer may take place for the sake of advantage and necessity, whenever common necessity and advantage recommend it, therefore do not understand the ecclesiastical canons.

Leo, bishop of Rome, to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

[Note: Through a copyist’s error, the manuscript reads Ἀθανασίῳ (“to Athanasius”) instead of Ἀναστασίῳ (“to Anastasius”).]

If any bishop should despise the modesty of his own city, undertake the service of a more distinguished place, and through foolish judgment transfer himself to a larger people, he shall be expelled from the foreign see and [Col. 1262C] deprived also of his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he desired through greed nor over those whom he disregarded through arrogance.

Let each person, therefore, be content with his own boundaries and not desire to increase his power beyond its proper measure. Know, dearest brother, that one reason for moving from city to city arises from necessity and advantage, while another arises from rashness, personal will, or private pleasure; but that a person is transferred on account of necessity and advantage. For the advantage of the many must be preferred to the advantage or will of one person.

To move voluntarily is one thing, and to be transferred another. To move voluntarily is one thing; to come under force or compulsion is another. Hence such persons do not change the city; they are changed. They do this not by their own choice but under compulsion.

Those who deny that this can take place for the sake of advantage or necessity, whenever common necessity or advantage persuades it, therefore do not understand the ecclesiastical canons.

## PASCHASIUS QUESNEL’S VARIANT READINGS, NOTES, AND OBSERVATIONS ON THE LETTERS OF SAINT LEO THE GREAT, WITH REFERENCES TO THE NUMBERED ANNOTATIONS BELOW

[Note: [Col. 1263D] In the Ballerini edition, Quesnel’s notes are relegated to the end of the second volume. Therefore, since the typographical arrangement permitted it, we restored them here, so that in the same volume the reader might have both the text and all the annotations on it arranged together. In our second volume we supplied the lacuna with the excellent work of P. Cacciari entitled *Exercises on Saint Leo*. EDITOR.]

[Col. 1263]

### 1279. ON LETTER I IN QUESNEL, VI. To the Bishop of Aquileia

[Col. 1263A]

1. It is by no certain means clear at what time and to which bishop of Aquileia this letter was sent. We must therefore proceed by conjectures. As for the date, it seems to me preferable to assign it to no other year than 444. For since the author of the book *On Promises and Predictions of the Half-Time*, among Prosper’s works, chapter 6, testifies that at the same time when Saint Leo was overthrowing the Manichaeans in Campania, he also crushed the Pelagians there, and especially Julian, and since it is established from Leo’s Letter 8 to the bishops of Italy that the Manichaeans were overthrown by Leo in that same year, scarcely any doubt remains that this letter belongs to that defeat of the Pelagians and was therefore written in 444.

Although from the year 439 the Pelagians had attempted to insinuate themselves into the communion of the Church by a pretended renunciation of their error, Leo must nevertheless already have spent several years in the episcopate when he wrote this letter, since he testifies that he had often issued decrees concerning certain points of ecclesiastical discipline. Nor do I believe that the letter was issued later, in which he indicates that the hypocrisy of the Pelagians had recently been exposed in part: “Now at least,” he says in chapter 2, “after their hypocrisy is exposed in part.” For, as Prosper testifies, the deception of these heretics had already begun to be exposed by Leo from the year 439.

If, then, it is true that this letter was issued in 444, it is likewise certain that it was not written to Nicetas and that his name was erroneously attached to the letter by [p. 1280] an ignorant scribe who had another letter of Leo to Nicetas before his eyes. Indeed, from Letter 129, now 159, written by our Leo to Nicetas in 458, and from Letter 14, now 18, of the same Leo to Januarius, also bishop of Aquileia, it is clear that in 447, when this last letter was written, Nicetas had not yet been raised to the episcopate of that city. Nor is the reliability of the consular date that it bears undermined, since both Dionysius Exiguus, who wrote shortly after Leo’s death, and Cresconius, as well as ancient manuscript codices, transmit it to us with that date.

On the other hand, several ancient printed codices—those of Crabbe, Sicardus, Isidore, and Cologne of 1551—and all the manuscripts that we have seen—the two Barberini, three Thuaneus manuscripts, the Cambridge, Cistercian, and Trecopithoean manuscripts, the manuscript of Saint Marianus of Auxerre, the Herovallian manuscript of Isidore, and others—do not give the name of Nicetas in the letter that we are now considering. They have only: “To the bishop of Aquileia,” with the exception of the Cistercian and Isidorian manuscripts.

In the former it reads: “To the metropolitan bishop of the province of Venetia,” which is found added in the margin of earlier editions, as though it were another title of an encyclical letter written to an equal. Yet the bishop of Aquileia was also the metropolitan of Venetia, and this is the title by which he is designated in the following letter. Thus all the printed and manuscript codices that bear this same title support our opinion.

In the edition of the Councils by Merlin, or the Isidorian collection, and in its manuscript codex, the following appears as the title: “Likewise, from the same to the same,” namely, to Altinus, bishop. This title cannot be genuine, since Leo says that he wrote the letter in response to a report from that same Bishop Altinus.

From what has been said, we must correct the author of *Italia sacra* where he [p. 1281] writes about the bishops of Aquileia and must amend the history of Aquileia itself. First, when he asserts that Januarius succeeded Nicetas—by which I mean the Nicetas to whom Leo wrote in 447—he is plainly mistaken, since he ought rather to have said that Nicetas was substituted for Januarius.

The history of Aquileia, and Baronius, Ughellus, and others who followed it, are likewise convicted of error when Nicetas is numbered immediately after Chromatius. Chromatius, from whom Rufinus professes to have received the seal of faith, was bishop before the year 400; consequently at least one Januarius stood between him and Nicetas. Indeed, Palladius, the writer on Aquileian affairs, places Augustine and Adelphus, also bishops of Aquileia, between Chromatius and Januarius, as H. de Noris testifies in *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 12.

Third, if our conjecture concerning the date of this letter is not groundless, it must have been sent not to Nicetas but rather either to Januarius or to Adelphus. H. de Noris thinks it was addressed to Januarius, and indeed sent in 447, the year in which another letter from Leo to the same Januarius is dated.

I readily agree with him concerning the person of Januarius. For it appears that he was already seated in the chair of Aquileia in 444. This is suggested by the opening words of the letter dated 447: “The vigor [p. 1282] of your faith, which we knew long ago.” These words indicate that he had governed the Church of Aquileia for several years and had maintained some correspondence with Leo.

Nor would it perhaps be rash to suspect that Leo then had in mind the affair concerning the Pelagians, which gave Leo occasion to write to the bishop of Aquileia and to test the vigor of his faith. This conjecture confirms our opinion concerning the year in which the letter was sent and proves that it was written rather around 444 than in 447, as Noris thinks.

He derives support for his opinion from the similarity between Letter 14, now 18, to Januarius and the letter to Septimius of Altinum, supposing that one was a copy of the other and that both were written to the two bishops at the same time. But the difference between the two, which we shall establish in the notes to the following letter, will remove all force from this conjecture.

2. Let them condemn the authors of proud error—namely, those who have been heard, examined, and condemned both in the African and Eastern councils and in the Roman judgment, and in the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, publicly confessing, defending, and disseminating the condemned meaning of their error.

[Note: It was sufficient for Pelagius, who had sprinkled his books with errors, not to submit to judgment in order to be justly condemned by Innocent I; consequently he cannot be said to have been heard and examined. Indeed, since his errors were evident from his own books, the same pontiff thought that he should not be summoned to judgment. “For if he trusts,” he says in his letter to Aurelius and four other African bishops, “and knows that what he says is not deserving of condemnation by us, or that he has already refuted all that he said, he should not be summoned by us; rather, he himself ought to hasten so that he may be acquitted. For if he still thinks in this way, when summoned to our judgment by letters of any kind, knowing that he is going to be condemned, how will he entrust himself to us?”]

Although Pelagius deceived Zosimus, the successor of Innocent, through that letter and profession of faith by which he attempted to conceal his errors, he was nevertheless later condemned by the same pontiff, after the latter had been informed of his errors, even though he was absent. Likewise Coelestius, who had deceived the same pontiff when he was heard, was struck with anathema by him when he withdrew after being summoned to judgment.

Pelagius’s profession of faith concealed his errors so effectively that he could appear to be a Catholic and would have deceived Augustine as well, had Augustine not uncovered it through a more careful examination as ambiguous and deceptive, recognizing his errors from other sources. See the book *On Original Sin*, no. 20.

Thus, although Pelagius could not be said openly to confess, defend, and disseminate the condemned meaning of his error through such a profession, he nevertheless could not escape Zosimus’s condemnation, nor prevent the same pontiff from requiring others, through letters of the *tractoria*, to subscribe to his condemnation.

Those in the province of Aquileia who refused to subscribe to Zosimus’s *tractoria* on the ground that they should not condemn persons who were absent and unheard were the only ones infected with the same heretical stain, and for this reason they were condemned, as we shall see in the following note.

Compare the *Book of Faith* in the appendix to volume X of the works of Saint Augustine, which we have seen to pertain to the province of Aquileia in the admonition to Letter 1, no. 26.]

[Note: When Saint Leo wished professions to be required from Pelagians returning to the Church—professions in which they would explicitly and without any deception condemn both the errors and the authors of the errors—he appealed to synodal decrees that the authority of the Apostolic See had confirmed for the eradication of this heresy. He referred to the decrees of the African synods, which Zosimus confirmed through the celebrated *tractoria* circulated throughout the world. Through it this heresy was eradicated from the universal Church.

Thus Prosper writes in the *Chronicle* under the year 418: “At the council held at Carthage of two hundred and fourteen bishops, synodal decrees were brought to Pope Zosimus; when these had been approved, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the whole world.”

Leo spoke in the same sense as Prosper, his contemporary and intimate associate. Why, then, does Quesnel introduce the Ephesian synod here, concerning which the holy pontiff did not even think in this matter? Did he wish to indicate that no one can be required to condemn either errors or the authors of errors until the judgment of a general council has been given?

Did not the whole Church, before the Council of Ephesus, subscribe to Zosimus’s *tractoria*, by which the Pelagian errors and their authors were punished with anathema? Were not these subscriptions required before that same council? And when Julian and his other accomplices refused to subscribe, were they not, as Marius Mercator reports in his *Commentary*, deposed and deprived of office by imperial laws as well as priestly statutes and expelled from all Italy?]

3. Synodal decrees, especially those of the African [p. 1283] Church, repeatedly assembled at Milevis and Carthage. These decrees were first approved by the Roman pontiffs Innocent, Zosimus, Boniface, and Coelestine; then they were confirmed by an irretractable decree of the ecumenical Council of Ephesus, together with the proceedings conducted by Pope Coelestine for the condemnation of the same heretics.

Thus the Fathers write in their synodal letter to Coelestine: “Moreover, when the records concerning the deposition of the impious Pelagians—Coelestius, Pelagius, Julian, Perfidius, Florus, Marcellinus, Orontius, and the others who held the same opinions—were read in the holy synod, we too judged that what your Piety has decreed must remain solid and firm, and we all hold the same opinion.” See also canons 1 and 4 of the same synod.

[Note: We have refuted at greater length the claim that only the decree of the ecumenical Council of Ephesus is irretractable, as though the judgments of the Apostolic See could be rescinded unless confirmed by a general council, in note 2 (Col. 1046, n. l) on Letter 120.]

[Col. 1265B]

4. “So that in whatever part of the detestable doctrine they may have separated themselves from the solidity of the doctrines to be condemned.”

We have corrected this passage on the basis of the two Barberini manuscripts, the Trecopithoean, the Thuaneus and Cambridge manuscripts, and the edition of Nicolini, although the later codices were not entirely free from errors. The passage had previously been read in printed editions as follows: “So that in whatever part of the detestable doctrine they may have separated themselves from the fellowship of the condemned,” and so forth.

What sense could this have? I do not know. For how could anyone distinguish himself from the fellowship of the condemned through a detestable doctrine? Moreover, there is no doubt that Saint Leo is referring here to the Semi-Pelagians, whom the author of the letter to Demetrias, chapter 11, depicts in almost the same words.
