There he likewise teaches that they are offshoots of the Pelagians and mentions that they preserve the crafty plans and simulated confession of the Pelagians, retaining only one portion of the Pelagian doctrine—one that conceals all its poison.

5. “For ease of insinuating themselves.” Thus the reading appears in Barberini 2, the Trecopithoean, the Thuaneus manuscript, the Roman edition of 1591, and Nicolini’s edition, whereas the common edition has “for such great ease,” and three manuscripts have “for the insinuating ease,” which is also found in several printed editions.

[Col. 1266A]

6. “Therefore every gift of good works is a divine preparation, because no one is justified first by virtue and then by grace, which is given to each person,” and so forth.

We preferred this reading of the passage, which is supplied by the Roman edition in the margin and by the Barberini manuscript, two Cambridge manuscripts, the Trecopithoean, and the three Thuaneus manuscripts, to the reading found in the common Isidorian edition and in the Victor manuscript:

“Therefore every devotion to good works is a divine preparation; no one is justified by his own virtue, since grace is given to each person,” and so forth.

We preferred it because it agrees more closely with the words of the Apostle on which Saint Leo bases his argument. The editions of Canisius and Paris of 1568 have in the margin: “divine operation.” [p. 1284]

Whichever reading one chooses, it makes no difference to Catholic doctrine, for all the readings contain it. But the reading we have retained is especially worthy of acceptance, and Saint Fulgentius expresses it in the same words in *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 35, as something to be held with the firmest faith:

“For that predestination,” he says, “is the preparation of a gratuitous gift by which the Apostle says that we were predestined to adoption as sons of God through Jesus Christ in him” (Eph. 1:5).

Fulgentius followed Augustine. For Augustine writes in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 20: “Predestination is the preparation of grace; grace itself, however, is already the gift.”

7. “To save what had perished.”

After these words, all the editions that I have seen, as well as the Victor manuscript and another manuscript, insert a patchwork sewn together from several passages of Saint Augustine’s *Enchiridion*, namely chapters 45, 46, and 47, except for the first portion of the patch, whose source I have not yet been able to discover.

Since we did not find this patch in several manuscripts, and in codices of much better quality—namely, the three Thuaneus manuscripts, the two Barberini manuscripts, the Cambridge manuscript, and the Trecopithoean—we thought that it should be removed from the text of the letter. Nevertheless, so that no one may complain that it has been taken away from him, we reproduce it here. It is as follows:

> For this reason they also say that if infants depart from this world without baptism, they cannot be condemned and are not held guilty in Adam’s sin, but proceed without hesitation to the kingdom of God or to eternal life, although the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so it passed into all human beings” (Rom. 5:12); for this reason infants too are baptized.

> Although several sins may be understood in that one sin, if the one sin itself is divided, as it were, into its individual members. For pride is present there, because man preferred to be in his own power rather than in God’s power; sacrilege, because he did not believe God; murder, because he plunged himself into death; spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by the serpent’s persuasion; theft, because he appropriated the food that had been forbidden; greed, because he desired more than ought to have sufficed for him; and whatever else may be found in that one offense through careful consideration (Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 45).

> It is not implausibly said that infants are bound not only by the sins of the first human beings but also by the sins of their own parents, from whom they were born. For the sentence “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children” holds them, certainly, before they begin through regeneration to belong to the New Testament. This testament was foretold when it was said through Ezekiel [p. 1285] that children would not bear the sins of their fathers, and that the proverb would no longer exist in Israel: “The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth are set on edge” (Ezek. 18:2, 20; Jer. 31:29).

> For this reason each person is reborn, so that whatever sin there is in him with which he is born may be removed. The sins committed afterward through evil action can be healed through repentance, as we see happening even after baptism. Consequently, regeneration was instituted for no other reason than that generation is defective, to such an extent that even one begotten in a lawful marriage says: “In iniquities I was conceived, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Ps. 50:5). Nor did he say here, “In iniquity” or “in sin,” although that could rightly have been said; rather, he preferred to say “iniquities” and “sins.” For in that one sin which passed into all human beings, and which is so great that by it human nature was changed and turned into the necessity of death—as I discussed above—there are several sins, as well as other sins of the parents. Although the latter cannot change nature in the same way, they nevertheless bind the children by guilt unless gratuitous grace and divine mercy come to their aid (Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 46).

> From the newly born infant to the decrepit old man, whatever bodily age they possess, just as no one should be prevented from baptism, so no one exists who does not die to sin in baptism. Infants die only to original sin; adults die also to all the other sins that they have added through evil living to what they brought with them at birth (Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 43).

8. “It has often been decreed by us.” See our note on chapter 8 of Letter 12, now 14, and consult also chapter 9 of the same letter; if desired, see also the Council of Antioch, canon 3, and the other canons abundantly reported by Cresconius in title 17 of his collection.

## ON LETTER II IN QUESNEL, VII. To Septimius, Bishop of Altinum

[Col. 1267D]

For a long time I was uncertain what judgment to pronounce concerning the authenticity of this letter; nor was I yet certain in which direction I should incline when it was printed in the first edition of our work.

[Note: We removed this letter from the suspicion of forgery in the preliminary admonition to it, nos. 10, 13, 14, and 19.]

We nevertheless immediately detected its spurious character and already explained it in the notes. We did not, however, think that the letter should be moved from its place, lest the order and numbering of the other letters, already fixed, be altered to the reader’s inconvenience. I now turn to the arguments for its spurious character.

First, it is so similar to another [p. 1286] letter of our Leo written to Januarius of Aquileia—which is numbered elsewhere as Letter 3, now 14 [in this edition, Letter 18]—that there can be no doubt that one was copied as a model from the other.

Certainly this was not done by Leo himself. Who could believe that a pontiff of such eloquent and fertile speech had been reduced to such poverty of words that he copied in full a letter once written to one bishop in order to send it to another, especially when both bishops held sees within the same province?

The letter to Januarius is unquestionably a genuine work of Leo, since it was included among Leo’s genuine letters by the ancient collector Dionysius Exiguus, and later by Cresconius, the African bishop. Moreover, we found it in two Thuaneus manuscripts, the Pithoean, the Victor manuscript, and others. The ancient records of the Church of Aquileia also testify, according to Ughellus in *Italia sacra*, that Saint Leo wrote a letter to Januarius of Aquileia.

The other letter must therefore be marked as spurious, even though it exists in some manuscripts, since it was copied from the Isidorian collection.

[Note: We refute this objection in the same preliminary admonition, nos. 19 and 20.]

2. These words inserted into the letter to Septimius—“We sent a written communication to the metropolitan bishop of the province of Venetia”—betray the fraud of the forger. For, unless I am mistaken, before the division of the metropolitan jurisdiction of Aquileia we never read in ecclesiastical writers of “the metropolitan of the province of Venetia”; rather, we repeatedly find “the metropolitan of Istria” and “the bishops of Istria.”

In civil matters the names Venetia and Istria are very often joined; in ecclesiastical matters I do not recall that the province of Venetia is mentioned by itself. Nor do I think that anyone was called metropolitan of Venetia before an episcopal see was established at Venice.

Thus three letters of Pope Pelagius are addressed to Elias, bishop of Aquileia, and all the bishops of Istria; by that designation he undoubtedly means all the bishops of Istria and Venetia. Gregory the Great likewise writes to Peter and Prudentius, bishops of Istria, and also to Firminus, bishop of Istria.

The same pontiff calls the schism the “schism of the Istrians,” and speaks of “Istrian bishops” and “the parts of Istria” in connection with the same affair in Book VII, Letters 94–99, although it is certain that the bishops of Venetia were also involved in that schism.

The emperor Maurice, too, writing to Gregory the Great, calls them “the bishops of Istria or Venetia.” From this it is clear that Venetia was also included under the name Istria.

At the Roman synod, Agatho subscribes as “bishop of the holy Church of Aquileia in the province of Istria,” in the letter to the emperors that was read in act 4 of the Sixth Council. The bishops of Padua, Altinum, and others also subscribed to the same letter; unquestionably they were from the province of Venetia [p. 1287] and consequently must here be understood under the name Istria.

That designation, “metropolitan of the province of Venetia,” therefore belongs to a more recent style. It may have been invented after the ecclesiastical metropolitan province of Venetia was established. It may even have been fabricated for the purpose of deriving from an ancient record some support for establishing it. No one who, with Sabellicus, asserts that the first bishop was appointed at Venice in 772 will believe that this occurred before the ninth century.

3. These words inserted into the letter—“by which he would recognize that it concerned the danger to his status,” and so forth—do not have the flavor either of Saint Leo’s period or of his style.

I do not believe that he used, or was accustomed or willing to use, threats of this kind against metropolitan bishops, still less against the bishop of Aquileia, who at that time did not belong to the Roman synod and was not ordained by the Roman pontiff but by the bishop of Milan.

In the preceding letter to the bishop of Aquileia, Leo does indeed threaten that he would be moved more vehemently if the bishops showed themselves negligent in guarding the canons and preserving the integrity of the faith. But such threats are not directed against a single metropolitan, nor does he threaten to depose him from his see.

For this reason, in the genuine Letter 14, now 18, from which these words were stolen, the pontiff warns the bishop of Aquileia not of danger to his status but of danger to his soul: “We point out,” he says, “that it concerns the danger of the soul.”

4. Although Photius mentions the letter of Septimius to Pope Leo in *Bibliotheca*, Book I, codex 54, he is silent concerning Leo’s reply to Septimius. These are his words:

> “A copy,” he says, “of the proceedings conducted by the Western bishops against the Nestorian doctrines”—by this designation he also means the Pelagian doctrines—“contains the following: When, as time passed, the adherents of this sect had been restored to the Church through their renunciation of their heresy, the evil again took its beginning from them. Thus, when the same plague was re-emerging in the time of Bishop Septimius, it had to be restrained before it spread farther. Letters were therefore sent to Leo, who at that time occupied the Apostolic See at Rome; and Leo fought against the impious with fervent zeal.”

If Saint Leo’s reply to Septimius had existed when Photius wrote, or rather when the proceedings reviewed by Photius and copied from an earlier source were composed, its existence would not have been omitted from the account.

Certainly there was no necessity for him to write a special letter to Septimius, since Septimius could learn Leo’s judgment from the letter written to the bishop of Aquileia.

[Note: This negative argument from the silence of Photius—or rather from the silence of the proceedings that Photius reviewed—can prove nothing against the positive arguments that we presented in the cited preliminary admonition in defense of the authenticity of this letter of Leo. Indeed, since those proceedings, and Photius through them, establish the existence of Septimius’s letter to Saint Leo, who would question that Leo sent him a reply?]

5. An argument for the letter’s spurious character is that [p. 1288] although the two letters were sent at different times and, as we shall prove, against different heretics, they nevertheless contain the same details—details that could scarcely have occurred simultaneously in different affairs.

In both cases Leo received a letter from a bishop reporting the revival of a heresy; the bishop was one in whom the faith was vigorous, and whose vigor Leo had known for a long time; the different heretics were admitted into communion with the Church without a legitimate profession of satisfaction; their clerics left their own churches and transferred themselves to places not assigned to them.

These and other details of the same kind seem to have occurred almost by agreement on different occasions and in connection with different errors, so that one letter could have been sent to both bishops. This is scarcely, if at all, credible.

As for the learned man Henry de Noris, who thinks that the two letters were copies of the same model, sent concerning the same Pelagian affair at the same time to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, and to Septimius, bishop of Altinum, I say, with all respect for this excellent man, that it cannot be true.

If they were copies of a single letter, certain words that seem necessary would not have been cut out of one of them, such as those concerning the fellowship of the Pelagians and Coelestians. Moreover, the letter to Januarius contains certain decrees concerning clerics returning from heresy that do not appear in the other: namely, that they should not be promoted to a higher order but should be permitted to remain in the order they had attained, provided that they had not been defiled by repeated baptism.

Many other things are also omitted in the letter to Septimius—things that would not have been removed from an encyclical letter.

But what is especially worthy of attention, and settles the question, is that the letter speaks of entirely different and distinct heretics in the two cases [Col. 1269D]. The whole of the letter to Septimius concerns the Pelagians and Coelestians; in the other, there is profound silence about them, but rather there is discussion of the Donatists. This is most clearly suggested by the following conditional clause: “provided they have not been defiled by repeated baptism.” For the Pelagians were never said to have rebaptized anyone; indeed, since they did not acknowledge the contagion of original sin, they did not consider it very necessary even to receive baptism once. But it is certain that the Donatists rebaptized people. It is also certain that those who returned to the Catholic Church were permitted to retain their rank. Finally, it is certain that any who had been rebaptized by them were not admitted to the clergy. Nothing, therefore, in that Letter 14 (now 18) does not fit the Donatists; they are still designated by the term “schismatics” inserted here. For they had turned from schism to heresy and openly fought against the unity of the Church.

Since this is so, knowledge of the episcopal see of Septimius remains just as obscure as if this letter had never become known. For the impostor who fabricated the letter assigned Septimius whatever see occurred to him, according as he thought it would better serve the purpose of his fraud. In reality, Ughelli found nothing in the ancient records concerning a bishop of Altinum of this name, since nothing about him is read in *Italia sacra*.

## On Letter III

Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, to Saint Leo, concerning Easter. In Quesnellus, after Letter II.

In earlier editions this letter was truncated [Col. 1270B] and mutilated; we now publish it complete and corrected from Marianus Scotus and from the works of Petavius and Bucherius on the reckoning of time. In those works, Petavius corrected several passages against the manuscripts of Jacques Sirmond, while Bucherius transcribed the whole letter from other manuscripts, making it much fuller and more polished. Ado of Vienne mentions it in his *Chronicle*, as does the venerable Bede in his book *On Times*. Marianus Scotus not only cites the same letter but reproduces it in full in *Chronicle* II, under the year 445, although he improperly divides it into two letters. Marianus also has the same conclusion to the letter that Bucherius added.

Before all of them, Dionysius Exiguus used it in his letter *On the Calculation of Easter* to Boniface, first secretary of the notaries, and Bonus, second secretary, which Bucherius and Petavius brought to light. “Since,” he says, “your Holiness, when the question concerning this matter arose, has now produced writings from the archive of the Roman Church by Paschasinus, the venerable bishop who is known to have presided at the holy Council of Chalcedon as representative of the most blessed Pope Leo, writings sent to that same pope at the same time, and which agree with the holy Fathers by evident reasoning, we have included them in the present work, so that we might also rely upon the testimony of this man, who by a manifest miracle confirms the Easter decrees of the venerable pontiffs.”

This shows how carefully the Roman pontiffs always preserved in the archive of the apostolic see the rescripts of other bishops. That the letter we have in hand is the same one is demonstrated both by the mention of the miracle and by the division of the years into common years and embolismic years; Dionysius devotes himself exclusively to explaining these matters in his letter, which the reader may consult as a kind of commentary in Bucherius, p. 489.

Some reader, however, may be troubled by the words “at the same time,” that is, at the time of the Council of Chalcedon, and may conclude that Dionysius was speaking rather of writings sent to Saint Leo concerning the Easter controversy of the year 455 than of that of the year [Col. 1270D] 444. For it is established that, in the very year in which the synod was summoned, our Leo wrote to Paschasinus concerning Easter and expected an answer from him. We now make the former publicly available; the latter has not yet been brought out of darkness, if indeed it was ever sent.

But, as we have already said, both the miracle and the explanation of the embolismic and common years prove that Dionysius must be understood as referring to no other letter than this very one. Anyone who supposes that Dionysius believed it concerned the difficulty of the year 455 would certainly wrong that learned man, who was most skilled in the whole of this discipline and who was expressly commenting on Paschasinus’s letter [Col. 1271A]. We therefore interpret the words “at the same time” benevolently. Although an interval of a full eight years separates the year 443, when Paschasinus’s letter was sent, from the Council of Chalcedon, it is nevertheless not an unusual manner of speaking for a man writing nearly a hundred years later and indicating the period of Saint Leo by this mode of expression.

The *Ecclesiastical Annals* must therefore be corrected (Baronius, under the year 453, no. 34). Failing to distinguish between the two Easter controversies, they assign this letter to the later one; but Paschasinus’s own words refute this. He writes that the year whose Easter had given rise to the dispute was the sixty-third according to the Roman reckoning, which began with the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius. Their consulship, moreover, fell in the year of Christ 382; if sixty-three years are counted from that point, the calculation ends in the year 444. Hence the earlier editions of this letter must be corrected, and in place of *sixty-fourth* one must read *sixty-third*, as Petavius corrected it from the Sirmondian manuscript, Bucherius from his own, and as Marianus Scotus had also read it in his manuscripts [Col. 1271B].

From this you should also correct Marianus himself, who after the words “from the consulship of Antonius and Syagrius” adds “in the fourth year of Gratian.” One must read “of Theodosius,” whose fourth year it really was; Gratian’s was the sixteenth. Alternatively, the phrase should be deleted altogether.

Furthermore, Paschasinus says that the seventh day before the Kalends of April of that year was a Sunday and the twenty-first day of the moon, and again that the fourth day before the Kalends of May was a Sunday and the nineteenth day of the moon. This can fit no year other than 444. He also adds that the eight-year cycle which had begun under the consulship of Aetius and Sigisvultus ended in that very year about which the inquiry had been made. In the year of Christ 437, when those men held the consulship, the lunar cycle was at its first year, and therefore the beginning of the eight-year cycle; its final year fell in 444, when Theodosius was consul for the eighteenth time and Albinus for the first. We have taken these details from Petavius.

Baronius perhaps took the occasion for his error from Jordanes, who likewise became confused in his *Annals* concerning the two Easter questions when he says that Proterius and Paschasinus wrote to Pope Leo about the Easter of the year 444. This is true of Paschasinus, but entirely false of Proterius, who was ordained bishop of Alexandria only in 452. Jordanes ought to have said Cyril, who died in that same year, in June, and who had previously written to Leo concerning Easter; Paschasinus himself mentions those letters.

Although Baronius and Jordanes share the same error, the error of one is contrary to that of the other. Since one of the letters of Paschasinus and Proterius belongs to the year 444 and the other to the year 455, Jordanes assigned both letters to the earlier year, while Baronius attributed both to the later year.

From this error the same author fell into another (under the year 454, no. 22), when he assigned to the year 454 the devastation of Sicily that Paschasinus records in his letter. He then criticized Ado of Vienne, as though Ado had improperly connected the destruction of Sicily with the capture of Carthage in these words: “The Vandals, after capturing Carthage, also devastated Sicily; Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, mentions this capture in the letter he wrote to Pope Leo concerning the calculation of Easter.”

This is entirely sound and agrees with Prosper, who in the fuller *Chronicle*, under the consulship of Valentinian Augustus for the fifth time and Anatolius—that is, in the year of Christ 440—relates that Sicily was severely afflicted by Genseric, after saying that Carthage had been captured by treachery under the pretext of peace in the preceding year. Ado therefore correctly connected one event with the other. Nor could Baronius have assigned the devastation of Sicily mentioned by Paschasinus to the year 454 except by means of a chronological displacement of thirteen or fourteen years.

We have made many corrections and additions in this letter [Col. 1272A], partly from manuscripts and partly from the editions of Petavius and Bucherius. In their works, where the science of chronology is accurately explained, the reader will find Paschasinus’s letter illuminated.

Anyone who wishes to confirm the miracle related by the same author—namely, that a baptistery was regularly filled and emptied by water sent down from heaven—may consult the *Spiritual Meadow* (whose author is said to be Sophronius), chapters 214 and 215, and Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs* I, chapter 24.

[Note: [Col. 1271D] See note 10 ([Col. 607, n. d]) on Letter 3.]

If anyone is curious to see the Hebrew, or legal, reckoning mentioned by the bishop of Lilybaeum, whose ignorance he says led the Romans into error, he will find it in Bucherius, together with a substantial investigation of this Jewish cycle. Bucherius proves in chapter 6 of his commentary on the Paschal Canon of Victorius of Aquitaine that this cycle was used by the early Christians without any correction, at least until the year of Christ 222. Around that year Hippolytus, bishop of Portus, produced the Paschal Canon, though without fortunate results [Col. 1272B].

Because this canon was easily recognized as inferior to the Jewish one, the legal reckoning was newly revised and restored to use [Note: [Col. 1271D] This Latin cycle of eighty-four years was in use before the year 382, as our Cardinal Norisius proved from the ancient consular fasti, dissertation 1.] around the ordinary year 382. This is the cycle that Paschasinus calls the “Roman reckoning.” Prosper of Aquitaine also mentions it in his fuller *Chronicle*, under the Eusebian year of the world 5583, the year of Christ 382; so does our Leo in Letter 104, now 130, and Letter 150, now 134. During Leo’s lifetime its use continued in the Roman Church and throughout the entire Western Church. Concerning this cycle, which consisted of eighty-four years, see the same Bucherius, *Treatise on the Jewish Paschal Cycle*, chapter 9, and throughout his work.

## On Letter IV

In Quesnellus, III. To the bishops established throughout Campania, Picenum, Tuscany, and all the provinces.

[Col. 1272C]

### 1. “The structure does not agree through dissimilation.”

We thought this should be corrected on the basis of the edition of the Letters of Saint Leo published in Paris in 1568, together with the works of Saint Clement of Rome and the letters of other Roman pontiffs, which are said to have been corrected according to the authority of the Victorine manuscripts. The editions of the Councils by Peter Crabbe, Nicolinus, and Merlin’s edition of Isidore likewise have *dissimilation* in the text, while some more recent editions place it in the margin.

All the manuscripts of this letter that we used—the six Thuanean manuscripts, the Victorine, Corbie, Beauvais, Trecopithoean, Cambridge, and Herovallian manuscripts of Isidore, as well as the collections of Dionysius, Cresconius, and others—consistently read *dissimulation*. The Roman edition has *dissimilitude* in the margin, evidently by conjecture, as I think.

### 2. “Those who are bound either to their origin or to some condition.”

[Note: [Col. 1272D] We established another reading from the better manuscripts in note 16 ([Col. 611, n. f]) on this letter.]

The two Thuanean manuscripts, the Corbie manuscript, and the Trecopithoean manuscript present the reading in this form. It agrees better with the construction and sense than the alternative reading *originali*, which appears in Dionysius and Cresconius and in the copies of the editors generally.

Gratian, *Decree*, distinction 54, chapter 21—“They are admitted indiscriminately”—reads as follows: “But also from other *originarii*, or those who are bound to some condition.” The collector seems to have borrowed this from civil law.

A person was said to be bound to his origin, or an *originarius colonus*, if he was the son of a conditional tenant, since by birth he was subject to the condition of colonage. A conditional tenant—or, as Leo says, one bound to a condition—was someone who, by virtue of his status, received estates or fields to cultivate from his master; both he himself during his lifetime and his sons after him were obliged to perform this service.

Saint Leo may also be understood as referring to slaves assigned to any condition. Concerning such persons, Tertullian, in *On Idolatry*, chapter 12, while pursuing various excuses made by those Christians who, for the sake of earning a living, devoted themselves to occupations serving idolatry, has this to say: “But I was under a condition,” says the craftsman. “No one,” Tertullian replies, “can serve two masters,” and so forth.

If, moreover, *conditionarii* are the same as *ascriptitii*, we leave the matter for jurists to examine more carefully. It must then be said that Justinian, as reported by Gratian, distinction 54, chapter 20, later permitted those whom Saint Leo here and Pope Gelasius in Letter 9 to the bishops established throughout Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily prohibit from ordination to become clerics even against the will of their masters, while remaining on the very estates to which they were attached [Col. 1273A]. This was permitted only on condition that, after becoming clerics, they continued to perform the agricultural labor imposed upon them.

It should further be observed that this law of Saint Leo, removing slaves from the clergy, is the first of all ecclesiastical constitutions—unless my memory deceives me—although it was nevertheless framed on the model of an apostolic constitution. See also the First Council of Orléans, chapter 8.

### 3. “Since the nobility of birth and character that each person possesses must determine what sort of man is to be associated with the ministry of the sacred altar,” and so forth.

The passage in the earlier editions was so corrupt that I think no one understood it. It was read as follows:

“Since we have learned, both from the Apostle who teaches us and from divine instruction and the rules of the canons, what the nobility of birth and character must be in each person who is to be associated with the ministry of the sacred altar…”

Through the omission of two small words, *cum constiterit* (“since it has been established”), and through faulty punctuation, a sense emerges that is both alien to Leo’s intention and entirely false: namely, that an edict declaring slaves ineligible for ordination and declaring nobility of birth necessary for the clergy had been issued by divine, apostolic, and canonical command. Such a position, unless I am mistaken, is found nowhere, nor did our author intend it. He wishes only to teach what further qualities Scripture and the canons require in a churchman whose nobility of birth and integrity of character have already been established.

The manuscript of the Church of Beauvais reads exactly as we have restored it. Cresconius and the printed Isidore—not, however, the manuscript—agree, except for the defective punctuation; most of the other manuscripts likewise follow this reading.

### 4. “Husbands of widows.”

He does not mention Apostolic Canon 18, which suggests that those canons had not yet attained full authority at that time. Nor does he mention the letter of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 8; or the letter of Innocent to Victricius, to Felix of Nuceria, to the bishops of Macedonia, and others; or the letter of Celestine to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, where they exclude the husbands of widows and men married twice from the clergy [Col. 1274A]. He indicates these matters, however, at the end of the letter.

For the rationale of this constitution, see above in Letter 1, now 12, chapter 3, and in Innocent III’s letter to the bishop of Metz. It will also be worthwhile to read the French treatise of D. Leschassier on men married twice, although it departs from the common opinion.

### 5. “Nor will they be able to claim for themselves…”

The printed copies read *pro arbitrio vindicare* (“claim for themselves at will”). This was doubtless added from a more recent custom, under which men married twice generally do not enter the clergy at their own discretion, but nevertheless do so by dispensation and with the permission of the pontiff.

In that golden age, however, no one was permitted either to undertake or to retain ecclesiastical ministry if, after previously marrying, he was not the husband of one wife, or if his wife was not the only wife of one husband, as Innocent III puts it. Saint Leo enforced this so rigorously that, even amid the extreme shortage of ecclesiastical ministers from which the Churches of Caesarean Mauritania were suffering, he did not allow men married twice who had been ordained to enjoy their rank, as is clear from Letter 1, now 12.

Indeed, even toward the end of the twelfth century, Pope Lucius III did not think that a dispensation could be granted to a man married twice who had been ordained, allowing him to remain in the priestly rank—provided that the letter attributed to him, cited under *Super eo*, *On Men Married Twice*, is genuine.

The words in question are therefore rightly omitted from all the manuscript copies, as well as from Dionysius Exiguus and Cresconius. They are found in the printed collection of Isidore, but not in his Herovallian manuscript or in others.

### 6. “Claiming for ourselves the care of this investigation…”

[Note: [Col. 1273C] If Saint Leo had extended the reservation of judgment in cases where some doubt arose, by these letters, not only to the suburbicarian provinces but also to all the provinces, there would be nothing surprising in this. As Roman pontiff, he presides over the entire Church and all the provinces by virtue of his primacy, and therefore can command not only the bishops of the suburbicarian provinces but also those of other provinces, as Leo commanded many things to the Gauls, Spaniards, Africans, and others. Unless, perhaps, it is thought impractical, because of certain inconveniences and difficulties, to extend such a reservation of judgment in factual matters to more distant regions [Col. 1273D]. Nevertheless, P. Coustant’s conjecture in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 47, is not implausible: namely, that Leo’s letter was first addressed only to the bishops throughout Campania, Picenum, and Tuscany, to which provinces the words in chapter 2 seem to refer: “We have therefore sent these instructions concerning your provinces through our brothers and fellow bishops Innocentius, Legitimus, and Segetius.” It was subsequently communicated to the bishops of other provinces, as happened with other decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs sent to particular provinces; in this way it became a general letter, and for that reason the words “and all the provinces” were added to its inscription. Coustant confirms this by other examples.]

Nor is it surprising, since the Churches to which he was writing in the first instance belonged to the Roman synod, being part of the suburbicarian provinces. I would therefore suppose that these decrees originated not from Leo alone but also from the Roman synod. From that synod, and by its decree, the three bishops Innocentius, Legitimus, and Segetius were sent to carry Leo’s letter. The date of the synod and of the letter agrees: the letter was sent on the sixth day before the Ides of October, and Letter 16 shows that the synod ordinarily met at Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October [Col. 1274C].

### 7. “To practice lending at interest.”

[Note: [Col. 1273D] Several points here deserve attention. Apart from the Council of Elvira, the Council of Carthage under Gratus also censured usury among laymen in canon 13, and Basil, in his first canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 14, calls it unjust profit even among laymen [Col. 1274C]. Although there are not very many canons on this subject, it is nevertheless certain that the Fathers of the Church, even in the earliest times, discussed this vice in sermons and catecheses. When they pointed out its injustice—as, among others, we read in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* II, chapter 18; Lactantius, *Institutes* VI, chapter 18; Saint Hilary, on Psalm 14, books II and 15; Saint Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 4 on Ezekiel; Saint Ambrose, *On the Good of Death*, no. 57; and others—they also taught clearly that restitution was owed. For who does not know that what was unjustly received must be restored? It is therefore false that the bishops of those times did not dare openly and publicly to condemn this crime, which Scripture plainly condemns. The same tradition and teaching always flourished. If fewer and less explicit testimonies from those times survive, this results not from any lack in the teaching but from the lack of books or occasions that would have required such writing. For the same reasons, many other testimonies are absent concerning other certain points of doctrine, although we have no doubt that these too were handed down in the earlier centuries.]

Before this statement of Leo, one will scarcely find an ecclesiastical law forbidding usury to laymen, except for canon 20 of the Council of Elvira. Even that canon neither orders the return of profit obtained through lending at interest nor imposes any penalty upon those guilty of usury; it merely prohibits them from practicing it thereafter.

This was not because the Church approved the wicked profit of usury in the early centuries—far from it—but because, as Augustine says, even the laws themselves and the judges ordered interest to be repaid (Letter 54, toward the end). At that time the bishops did not dare openly and publicly to condemn what the laws and rulers of the world sanctioned by their authority; for that reason they speak cautiously.

Yet Augustine, addressing Macedonius, the judge of Caesarea, writes in the letter cited: “These things and things of this kind are certainly possessed unjustly, and I would wish them to be restored; but there is no judge before whom they can be reclaimed.”

Thus Saint Leo laments that this applies not only to those established in clerical office but also to laymen who wish to be called Christians. Nevertheless, even here, although he speaks with greater confidence, he does not condemn lay usurers. Nor did almost anyone before him dare to inflict any penalty upon laymen. The holy Fathers of the First Council of Arles, canon 12; of Nicaea, canon 17; of Laodicea, canon 4; of Carthage I under Aurelius, canon 5; and Leo, Gelasius, and others attempted to deter only clerics, who were more subject to their jurisdiction, from this disgraceful profit by imposing a penalty.

“The first of the emperors,” says Grotius in his commentary on the sixth chapter of Saint Luke, “as Hermenopulus likewise notes, believing that all lending at interest was forbidden to a Christian, sanctioned this by a general law; whereas previously the Churches themselves were accustomed to borrow money at one-third interest.”

### 8. “All the decretal constitutions, both those of blessed memory, Innocent, and those of all our predecessors, which have been promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the disciplines of the canons…”

[Note: [Col. 1275C] Two points in Quesnellus’s following note require observation. First, he says that the decretal constitutions of Leo’s predecessors are called promulgated because they are read as having been inserted into the Code of Canons, which he believes was publicly published as the code of the Roman Church. This rests upon a false hypothesis, whose falsity we shall demonstrate in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 12, concerning the Code of the Roman Church, which will be included in volume III.

They are called promulgated only in the sense that they were publicly issued after being sent to bishops throughout the provinces. Although not a few constitutions were addressed only to particular provinces, copies were subsequently circulated from them to neighboring provinces, so that they became known generally, as P. Coustant properly establishes in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 47.

The second point is that Quesnellus alleges, as though this were the view of Leo and Hincmar, that decretal constitutions promulgated contrary to canonical discipline possess no authority. Yet in the passages of Saint Leo that he cites, the subject is not the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs but the canon of Chalcedon establishing the prerogative of the see of Constantinople. Since that canon conflicted with the canons of Nicaea, the holy pontiff refused to confirm it and instead declared it null and void.

Nor does Hincmar pronounce anything concerning pontifical decretals. He merely presses the testimonies in which Leo and other pontiffs, commanding the guardianship of the sacred canons, branded as criminal those who rashly departed from their observance. Among the many testimonies, he quotes Leo’s words concerning the decree of Chalcedon, in which Leo wished whatever conflicted with the Nicene constitutions to possess no authority.

Although Hincmar praised Innocent’s decree concerning the settlement of cases or disputes among clergy within a province, he immediately added that the reservation of major cases had been confirmed by the same pontiff, saying: “And there, after a little: If any greater cases should arise, they are to be referred to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment, as the synod established”—namely, the Council of Sardica—“and as ancient custom requires.”

Why did Quesnellus transcribe only the first part of Hincmar’s statement? Neither Leo nor Hincmar anywhere says that decretal constitutions promulgated contrary to canonical discipline possess no authority. On such an interpretation, a discipline once established by the canons could never be changed, and no decrees could be issued by anyone’s authority that established different provisions according to changing times and circumstances. Compare what we observed on this matter in the observations on Sermon 4 of Saint Leo, volume I, col. 465, where we examined another passage of Quesnellus.]

The five Thuanean manuscripts, the Herovallian manuscript of Isidore, and the manuscripts of Beauvais, Corbie, Victor, and Cambridge read this way; so do Dionysius Exiguus, Pope Nicholas I, both Hincmars—of Reims and Laon—and the margin of Canisius’s edition, as well as Nicolinus and others. Some editions read *ordinations* for *orders* and *ordained* for *promulgated*. The former reading is certainly preferable. It seems to me that these words indicate a code of decretal constitutions promulgated by the Roman pontiffs, as we have explained more fully in the dissertation on the Roman Code.

Hincmar, bishop of Laon, inserted these same words into his collection of ancient letters of the Roman pontiffs sent to Hincmar, bishop of Reims, in order to prove that no one could refuse obedience to those letters without incurring the charge of temerity. In replying to him, Hincmar of Reims discusses these words at length in chapter 10 and the following chapters of his *Opusculum of 55 Chapters*, treating even more fully the etymology of the word.

He therefore supposes that *promulgo* means something like *promo vulgo*, “I bring forth publicly,” or “I first publish to the people.” Hence, he says, Paul in his *Glosses* writes as follows: “Laws are said to be promulgated when they are published to the people…” Isidore likewise, as Hincmar himself says, explained the word on Cicero’s authority: “A thing is promulgated when it is brought forth, as a law is said to be promulgated; a promulgated thing is one made known to everyone and communicated to the whole populace.”

Hincmar then discusses what Leo intended by these words:

“First, we must know that it is one thing to promulgate sacred orders and the disciplines of the canons, and another to promulgate regulations concerning sacred orders and the disciplines of the canons, just as it is one thing to promulgate laws and another to promulgate regulations concerning laws. To promulgate laws means to establish laws; to promulgate regulations concerning laws means to pass judgments concerning them, to judge according to them, and to make their observance and judgments known to all.

“Thus to promulgate sacred orders means to establish bishops, presbyters, and so forth by the Lord, through the ministry of those whom the Lord has appointed for this purpose [Col. 1276A], while the Lord carries out what belongs to him. To promulgate regulations concerning sacred orders means to establish who and how many persons there are, what sort they are, how and by whom or when they are to be ordained, and how and to what extent each is to minister in the various grades, and so forth.”

Similarly, Hincmar adds shortly afterward [Col. 1276B], “it is one thing to promulgate the sacred canons and another to promulgate decretal regulations established concerning the disciplines of the sacred canons.

“What the canons are, concerning whose disciplines Saint Leo the pope commands that the promulgated regulations be so carefully preserved that anyone who violates them should know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him, is clearly shown by the blessed Innocent, whom Leo mentions, in the discipline decreed from those same sacred canons in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen: ‘If any cases or disputes should arise among clergy of either the higher or the lower order, so that, according to the Council of Nicaea, the dispute may be settled after the bishops of the same province have assembled,’ and so forth.”

Finally, after bringing forward many further testimonies of holy Fathers and pontiffs, Hincmar concludes from them that Leo commands nothing other than observance of the sacred canons. Indeed, by the authority of Leo’s principal predecessors and successors, he shows that decretal constitutions promulgated contrary to canonical discipline possess no authority. Leo writes:

“If anything anywhere is presumed otherwise than those Fathers [of Nicaea] established, it must cease without hesitation” (Leo, Letter 80, now 106, chapter 4).

And elsewhere:

“Whatever differs from their constitution shall be entirely without authority” (ibid., chapter 27).

These excerpts from Hincmar’s fuller treatment both clarify Leo’s intention and show Hincmar’s view concerning the decretal decrees of the pontiffs.

## On Letter V

To the metropolitan bishops throughout Illyricum.

[Col. 1277A]

Holstenius likewise published this letter together with the preceding one, now the following letter. It was necessary in some places to apply the physician’s hand. To avoid appearing to have indulged our own conjectures excessively, we must give the reasons for the corrections here.

### 1. “By the reward of his faith.”

Holstenius read *sui* (“of his own”), which can scarcely have any meaning in the construction of the text.

### 2. “In the solidity of that foundation itself.”

I suspect that *istius* (“of that”) should be read, referring to the faith mentioned previously. [Note: [Col. 1277D] We have shown more fully in the observations on Sermon 2 that Saint Leo explains the rock upon which the Church was built as faith without excluding Peter or in any way diminishing the authority of the apostolic see.] In this way the same pontiff elsewhere interprets the rock upon which Christ built his Church, as in Letter 92, now 119, to Maximus of Antioch, chapter 2; Letter 132, now 162, chapter 1; Letter 10, chapter 1; and Sermon 3, now 4, *On the Anniversary of His Assumption*, chapter 2.

In this he did not depart from the tradition of the other Fathers, who generally interpret Christ’s words from chapter 16 of Saint Matthew—the words that Saint Leo explains—in the same way. If desired, consult the letters of John Launoy, theologian of Paris, part II, his letter to Adrian Vallant, and part IV, letter 1, where he gathers abundant testimony from the holy Fathers on this matter.

### 3. “They have received.”

Holstenius read *accipiant* (“let them receive”). But both the following words and the preceding letter, where nearly the same thought appears in this form—“that he be the husband of one wife, and that he have received her as a virgin, as the authority of divine law prescribes”—show, I say, that the text ought to be corrected in this way.

For the sense conveyed by that necessarily defective reading is proscribed by the authority of the ancient canons and of the Church’s never-interrupted custom; a more appropriate place for discussing it will occur below.

### 4. “But that very person, according to what the canons have defined,” etc.

This entire passage is rather obscure. It nevertheless seems to assert that the right of reference (*jus relationis*) belonging to the apostolic see had been conferred upon it by the authority of the holy councils, out of reverence for the prince of the apostles.

> **[Note: [Col. 1277D]]** Although the right of reference, especially in more important cases, which belongs to the apostolic see, is asserted in the sacred canons, it nevertheless proceeds from the higher right of primacy, which acknowledges a divine origin. Hence, even before any canons were enacted concerning such references, several cases of this kind were brought before the Roman pontiffs, among the few documents surviving from earlier centuries. We have shown in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, part I, chapter 7, that the right of appeal in major cases proceeds from primacy of divine law.

Innocent expressly asserts this in his letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 3; he also traces that right back to ancient custom:

> “If any cases or disputes,” he says, “have arisen among clerics, whether of the higher or the lower order, so that, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea, the quarrel may be settled by the bishops of the same province assembled together, no one is permitted—without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, toward which reverence must be preserved in every case—after abandoning those priests who by divine will govern the Church of God in that province, to rush off to other provinces. But if more important cases have arisen, they are to be referred, after episcopal judgment, to the apostolic see, as the synod has decreed and ancient custom requires.”

Pope Gelasius likewise writes in his *Memorial to Faustus*:

> “The canons themselves are the ones that have wished appeals from the whole Church to be brought before the judgment of this see.”

I scarcely think it can be doubted that Gelasius, Leo, and Innocent, the Roman pontiffs, had the same synod and the same canons in mind.

> **[Col. 1278D]** But which canons those were is disputed among scholars.

> **[Note: [Col. 1278D]]** Since the Sardican canons establish nothing concerning cases involving clerics of the lower order, except in canon 16, where it is permitted to appeal to neighboring bishops, Hincmar’s opinion is more probable. Father Coustant defends it in Innocent’s Letter 1, volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 749, note a (*Patrologia Latina* XX, col. 463).

The entire passage of Pope Innocent just transcribed seems, according to the illustrious Peter de Marca, *Concordia sacerdotii et imperii*, book I, chapter 10, to refer to the Council of Nicaea.

> **[Col. 1278A]**

Hincmar of Rheims formerly understood it otherwise in Letter 9, chapter 12. He considered the first two chapters to belong to the Council of Nicaea, but the final one to belong to the Council of Sardica.

The reasons to be explained below compel me to adopt an opinion different from both. I attribute the whole passage to the Council of Sardica, whose canons in those ancient times were cited by Roman bishops under the name of the Council of Nicaea. Witnesses to this are Innocent himself, Zosimus, and our Leo in Letter 40 (now 44).

The Roman Codex, which we are publishing, makes clear how they fell into this error. Innocent I, I say, seems to cite not the Nicene canons but the Sardican canons under the name of the Council of Nicaea, because he is dealing with clerics of both the higher and lower orders who are disputing among themselves. The Nicene synod says nothing about such persons in chapter 5, which some think Innocent had marked; it speaks only of those who have been excommunicated by their own bishop, whether they belong to the lay order or the clergy. That does not at all apply to clerics of the higher order, who were subject to deposition rather than excommunication, nor does it correspond in any way to the disputes among such clerics of which Innocent speaks.

Innocent’s words, however, correspond most closely to Sardican canon 3, whose title in Dionysius Exiguus reads:

> “That the neighboring bishops of the province hear disputes between rival bishops; but if the condemned party appeals to the Roman pontiff, whatever he decides is to be observed.”

Moreover, concerning those who, abandoning the priests of their own province, rush into other provinces to be judged, there is not a word in the Nicene canon; in the Sardican canons, however, there are several statements on the matter.

Finally, the Nicene Fathers are entirely silent about referring major cases to the apostolic see after episcopal judgment; the Sardican Fathers, on the other hand, deal with this expressly in canons 3, 4, and 7.

Accordingly, taking up the argument of the illustrious Peter de Marca, I confirm the contrary opinion as follows. Innocent’s passage, however extensive it may be, must here be understood of the same synod; but in the later passage the Sardican, not the Nicene, council must be understood. Therefore, in the earlier passages also, Innocent was directing his attention to the Sardican canons.

## To Letter VI in Quesnell: IV  
### To Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica

We owe the recovery of this letter to the most learned and distinguished Lucas Holstenius, canon of the Vatican and of the Basilica, and prefect of the library. He published it at Rome in 1662, inserting it into the Roman collection among the acts of the Roman synod held under Pope Boniface II. The edition, begun by Holstenius, was prepared for publication after his death by the eminent and most learned Cardinal Francesco Barberini.

Leo Allatius had already brought fragments of it to light in 1648 in his work *On the Agreement of the Eastern and Western Churches*, in the additions, p. 1368; but they abound in very numerous errors.

### 1. “Since in our stead,” etc.

To avoid repeating matters already treated learnedly, consult the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius in the appendix to book V of the illustrious Peter de Marca’s *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, chapter 22. There he argues from this letter and others that the vicariate of Thessalonica had been granted to that Church,

> **[Col. 1279A]**

and that it was not merely a personal privilege.

> **[Note: [Col. 1279C]]** Indeed, it seems possible to infer that it was a personal privilege which expired upon the death of each pontiff. Anastasius, although he had previously been appointed by Xystus as vicar of the apostolic see in Illyricum, nevertheless sought from Leo a confirmation of the same prerogative. The holy pontiff granted his request and bestowed the privilege in such a way that he sent an encyclical on the matter to all the metropolitans of Illyricum. This presupposes that they needed to be informed of the new delegation.

See also, if you wish, Franciscus Florens, treatise 6, under the title *On Election and the Power of the Elected*; and Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius in his notes on Vigilius of Thapsus, where he argues against the opinion of Lucas Holstenius.

### 2. “For the safeguarding of the rules”

Just as these are the chief responsibilities of the Roman pontiff, as head of the universal Church—namely, to uphold divine law, defend tradition, guard the canons, and diligently execute the constitutions of the Fathers—so those whom he delegates in his place to various parts of the Christian world are chiefly and exclusively charged with watching over and keeping guard of the rules, or canons:

> “So that no unlawful act,” as Leo says in the following letter (now the preceding one), “may be presumed by anyone against the canons.”

If these rules are properly observed everywhere and by everyone, the delegated authority of vicars in other Churches is almost idle.

The holy Pope Gregory I himself reveals what he thought about his own authority in book VII, Letter 65, to John, bishop of Syracuse.

> **[Note: [Col. 1279D]]** This was not enough for Quesnellus. He thought that the authority of apostolic vicars had to be restricted still further, as though the vicars could be granted no power beyond what pertained to safeguarding the canons. But since the Roman pontiff, in addition to safeguarding the canons, can exercise many other powers throughout the Church by virtue of his primacy under divine law, he can also entrust other powers to certain persons acting in his place within the provinces, as he judges appropriate in view of differing circumstances and times. Thus, even in ancient times, certain responsibilities are recorded as having been entrusted to the bishop of Thessalonica, or to others in other provinces, which were not necessary for safeguarding the canons. Was it necessary for this purpose to reserve to the bishop of Thessalonica the ordination of metropolitans? To grant him the hearing and determination of episcopal cases? To require his agreement or presidency for the summoning of synods? To assign him the right of the *formatae*? Yet these powers are attributed to the bishops of Thessalonica in the letters of Coelestine, Xystus, and Leo.

### 3. “At the proper time he first entrusted it”

In what sense the vicariate of Thessalonica owed its beginnings to Siricius—although Innocent I, Nicholas I, and John III, Roman pontiffs, attribute it to Damasus, as is also clear from the letter of Damasus to Acholius of Thessalonica published by Holstenius in the Roman collection—see Peter de Marca’s appendix to book V, chapter 23.

There the Baluzius cited above rightly distinguishes the first dawn of this dignity, which began to shine under Damasus, from its greater subsequent development, which was first firmly established in a certain way by Siricius, so that the two opinions can easily be reconciled.

### 4. “For just as sins and those things which,” etc.

We supplied the two words *sicut enim* (“for just as”); and, conjecturally, replaced *abolentur* (“are abolished”) with *abolebuntur* (“will be abolished”). I do not regard this conjecture as rash; indeed, the necessity of completing the sense confirms it.

These words, moreover, concerning bigamy remaining even after baptism seem to have been transcribed by Leo from chapter 3 of Innocent I’s letter to Rufus, Eusebius, and the other bishops of Macedonia. Around that time Jerome held the contrary opinion, writing to Oceanus in Letter 83; Augustine seems to criticize him without naming him in book I of *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 18, where he defends the true opinion. I call it an “opinion” because Augustine appears to have had no canon or established rule on the matter before his eyes.

### 5. “But whoever of the metropolitan bishops,” etc.

We judged that Holstenius’s Vatican exemplar should be corrected—

> **[Col. 1280A]**  
> **[Read: Barberinian]**

—which reads, if indeed it reads correctly:

> “But whoever of the metropolitan bishops…”

This is plainly contrary to Leo’s meaning. He is not speaking here of the ordination of metropolitans, which he touches upon a few lines later, but only of provincial bishops who were ordained by metropolitans without consulting the vicar of Illyricum. This is confirmed both by the subsequent letter (now the preceding one), chapter 5, and by Letter 12 (now 14) to the same Anastasius, chapter 6.

He makes a real distinction between the two kinds of ordination. He wishes all metropolitans not merely to be ordained with the vicar of Illyricum’s advice, but to be consecrated by him himself. He orders other provincial bishops to be ordained not by the vicar, but by their own metropolitans, who are to refer the matter of their ordination to the vicar of Illyricum.

Against the latter he does not impose a penalty, because he feared that the metropolitans, offended by threats, might attempt to throw off the yoke of the vicariate, which Leo’s own letters indicate that they had accepted reluctantly.

> **[Note: [Col. 1280C]]** Can the apostolic vicariate be called a “yoke,” which the Roman pontiffs, from the time of Damasus or Siricius onward, established in Illyricum for the safeguarding of discipline and the canons, by virtue of their right over the whole West—a right which they later called patriarchal?

But he declares that bishops ordained without consulting the bishop of Thessalonica will receive no stability whatsoever for their status from him.

### 6. “The word ‘appeal’”

The reason for the qualification is that the provinces of Illyricum, as a portion of the Western regions, belonged to the Roman pontiff by a special right.

> **[Note: [Col. 1280D]]** If appeals from the provinces of Illyricum belonged by a special right to the Roman pontiff, namely as patriarch of the West, because they were a portion of the Western regions, they nevertheless belonged to him by a higher right by virtue of the universal Church, since the whole Church was subject to him as primate by Christ. Hence the Sardican canons established rules concerning appeals to the Roman see not only from the Western regions but also from the Eastern ones. We have proved in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, part I, chapter 6, no. 16, that Quesnellus is wrong to repeat that these canons were unknown to the Easterners at that time.

What Saint Leo writes here about appeals he asserts on the basis of the Sardican canons, as the mention of the ancient institution and reverence owed to the apostolic see demonstrates. At that time those canons were unknown to the Easterners.

### 7. “Concerning whom equal consecration ought to be performed”

Leo is very far from supporting the opinion attributed to Saint Jerome when he grants equal consecration to a presbyter, and even to a deacon, together with a bishop.

These three degrees do indeed agree in many respects, while the prerogative of their dignity is everywhere preserved for bishops and presbyters. What Saint Leo undoubtedly has in mind when he suggests equality among the men of those three orders is the laying on of hands, by which both deacons and priests are consecrated.

Hence the author of the *Commentaries on the Epistles of Paul*, who was a contemporary of Pope Damasus and is called Ambrose, says:

> “The ordination of bishops and presbyters is one and the same”; and the same may be asserted of the deacon.

For this reason Optatus did not hesitate, in book I, to honor deacons with the title of the priesthood. When listing those who had fallen during the persecution, he says:

> “Why should I mention the laymen, who at that time were supported by no dignity in the Church? Why mention the many ministers? Why mention the deacons in the third priesthood? Why mention the presbyters established in the second priesthood? The very highest and chiefs of all were certain bishops,” and so forth.

Epiphanius even suggests, in a certain sense, that a subdeacon is a priest. In book III of *Against Heresies*, in the *Exposition of the Faith*, no. 21, he says that a subdeacon, like the other clerics of the higher orders, abstains from wives, but not a lector:

> “For a lector,” he says, “is not a priest” (*καὶ γὰρ οὐκ ἔστιν ἱερεὺς ὁ ἀναγνώστης*).

Innocent, Pope, says in his letter to Decentius of Eugubium:

> “Although presbyters are priests, they do not possess the summit of the pontificate.”

We are therefore compelled to speak differently about the priesthood from the way in which most people ordinarily speak. They fix their eyes first upon the presbyterate and regard the episcopate as nothing other than a certain extension and enlargement of the presbyterate. Rather, at first sight the episcopate should be viewed as the highest summit of the priesthood, its fullness and, so to speak, its perfect totality. From the pontificate, the remaining degrees are cut off as portions, so to speak, and are circumscribed by certain offices and ministries according to the needs of the Church.

For, as the anonymous commentator already cited says:

> “All the orders are in the bishop, because he is the first priest—that is, he is the chief of priests—and he is a prophet and an evangelist, and possesses the other offices to be fulfilled in the ministry of the faithful. Nevertheless, after churches had been established in all places and the offices ordered, the arrangement became different from what it had been at the beginning.”

That author understands the deacon by “evangelist,” and by “the other offices,” lectors and exorcists.

When these points are properly understood, everyone will likewise understand what the holy pontiff means when he asserts here that presbyters and deacons receive the dignity of priestly office—although he says not “the priesthood” but “priestly office”—and how greatly, at least in his manner of speaking, he differs from the canon said to belong to the Fourth Council of Carthage, which denies that deacons receive the power and consecration of the priesthood:

> “When a deacon is ordained, only the bishop who blesses him places his hand upon his head, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to the ministry.”

### 8. “Against the canons and the tradition of the Fathers”

Saint Leo mentions the apostolic tradition, which Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, had forgotten or did not know when he ordained Aetius priest on the sixth day of the week, in Letter 84 (now 111), chapter 2.

He likewise invokes it in Letter 11 (now 9) to Dioscorus. In neither letter, however, does he mention canons; nor, in fact, do we possess any from before his time that prohibited such ordinations from being celebrated on any day. Perhaps this was because no one had acted against tradition and custom in a way that provided an occasion for the enactment of a canon.

By “the canons,” therefore, I think Leo means nothing other than an ecclesiastical rule established solely by usage and ecclesiastical tradition, a usage he appears to employ very frequently.

## To Letter VII in Quesnell: VIII  
### To the Bishops Established throughout Italy

The seven manuscript codices to which we referred in examining this letter do not agree concerning its title.

Corb. and Thuan. 1 have:

> “To all the bishops established throughout the various provinces.”

Bellovac. has:

> “To all the Churches established throughout the provinces of Italy.”

One Thuaneus has:

> “To all the bishops established throughout Sicily.”

Three Thuanei, Dionysius, Exiguus, and Isidore have:

> “To all the bishops throughout the provinces of Italy.”

The common printed edition has:

> “Throughout Italy.”

Those who know how often great difficulties either arise from titles of this kind or are resolved by them will not be surprised that we have recorded these matters so scrupulously.

It was chiefly from the words of this letter that the spurious letters of Pope Anastasius I to all the bishops of Germany and Burgundy were fabricated. The conclusion of Pope Lucius’s letter to the Gauls and Spaniards, and the rescript of Pope Mark to Anastasius concerning the Nicene canons, were likewise formed from the conclusion of this letter.

## To Letter IX in Quesnell: XI  
### To Dioscorus, Bishop of Alexandria

### 1. “Let the beginnings be chosen”

This letter, which has until now been wandering outside its proper place, seems to me to belong here. It is certain from its very beginning that Saint Leo wrote it to Dioscorus when he was beginning to preside over the Alexandrian Church:

> “We desire to establish your beginnings more firmly.”

Possidonius the presbyter, who was still then staying at Rome, brought news of those beginnings, or of Dioscorus’s ordination.

It is established that Dioscorus was elevated to this see in the year 444, both because his predecessor Cyril departed this life in that year, in either February according to the Latins or June according to the Greeks, and because Dioscorus was deposed from the episcopate in the seventh year of his ordination, as the deacon Liberatus testifies in chapter 13. This occurred in October of the year of the Lord 451, and therefore his ordination falls in the year 444.

The letter could not have been written in the same year in which Dioscorus was created bishop, since several months would have been required for the election and consecration of the bishop of so great a see. Possidonius could not have been sent to the Roman pontiff with the news of the ordination until several further months had passed, nor could he have received letters from the pontiff to carry back to Dioscorus earlier. The letter was therefore written neither earlier nor later than the Kalends of July in the year 445.

The whole ecclesiastical history of the fifth century loudly proclaims what kind of man Dioscorus was, and those heretics are still called by his name to this day.

His election had been supported by the merits of spiritual or special grace, as Leo himself says in the same passage of the preface. The swift report of his reputation, as Theodoret says when writing to Dioscorus himself in Letter 60, had spread in every direction and filled everyone’s ears with his glory; above all, everyone praised the moderation of his character.

> **[Col. 1282C]**

How greatly reputation had deceived them both, the fourth year afterward made clear in the Ephesian Robber Synod.

### 2. “Let the beginnings be chosen”

After these words, the following words somehow entered all the printed copies:

> “That is, let them be substituted under the law of divine office.”

We judged that they should be deleted, both because they are absent from the manuscript codices Grim., Vict., Cantabr., and Thuaneus, and even from Gratian and Isidore, in both printed and manuscript form, and because they overturn the entire meaning of this passage.

The subject is the selection of the day and hour for conferring priestly and Levitical blessing. Saint Leo orders that the beginning of that night which dawns on the first day of the week be chosen for this purpose. He is not speaking of the selection of ministers to be consecrated, as that ignorant glossator understood.

Perhaps he was misled by manuscript codices resembling those of Thuaneus and Cambridge, in which one reads:

> “Let the beginnings of the one to be consecrated be chosen.”

### 3. “From these words and those immediately following”

From these and the adjacent words a twofold difficulty arises for some.

The first is whether Saint Leo designates every Saturday or every Sunday occurring during the year as appointed for the ordination of priests and Levites, or whether he means only Holy Saturday and the annual solemnity of the Lord’s Resurrection.

The second difficulty is whether the night following Saturday was chosen for this consecration as part of the preceding Saturday or as part of the approaching Sunday.

Both problems are easily resolved if Leo’s words are considered somewhat more carefully and the customs and discipline of that period are brought to mind.

So far from the consecration of the Church’s ministers having taken place only on Holy Saturday, it seems rather that it never took place on that day—not merely in Leo’s time but also during the time of many of his successors.

> **[Col. 1283A]**

For this reason we rightly removed the title formerly prefixed to this letter, which asserted that priestly ordination was to be celebrated on Holy Saturday.

> **[Note: [Col. 1281D]]** If this is understood of Easter Day, which begins with the vigil of Holy Saturday, it may perhaps be true of the Roman Church and of many other Churches, but not of all. Certainly, in the Church of Verona, in the age of Saint Zeno, the advancement of ministers took place on Easter Day, or during the Easter vigil—that is, on Holy Saturday—as can be clearly inferred, at least in our judgment, from his treatise 50 of book II. We noted this in annotation 4 to the same sermon, p. 261. This testimony, previously overlooked, contributes greatly to demonstrating the ancient origin of sacred ordinations on Holy Saturday.

The solemnity of baptism makes me believe that this could not have happened. Easter Day had been consecrated to the conferring of baptism, so that the days preceding this holy solemnity were entirely devoted to scrutinies, exorcisms, catechisms, and the other ceremonies preparatory to baptism. The eighth day of Easter itself was called the eighth day of the neophytes.

Hence Pope Gelasius I, writing to the bishops established throughout Lucania and Bruttium, does not mention Holy Saturday, although he carefully lists the four customary seasons of the year. He says:

> “The ordinations of presbyters and deacons must not be performed except at fixed times and on fixed days; that is, they are to be celebrated during the fast of the fourth month, the seventh and the tenth, and also at the beginning of Lent, in the fast of midweek, and in the fast of Saturday, toward evening.”

The Roman synod under Pope Zacharias in the year of the Lord 743, canon 2; the synod of Limoges under Benedict in 1034; and the Council of Clermont under Urban II in 1095, canon 9, likewise remain silent about Holy Saturday while enumerating the other days mentioned.

Even if this were not certain—as it certainly is—it would nevertheless be clear that there is nothing in this passage of Leo concerning ordination on Holy Saturday.

For when he investigates to which day the beginning of the night following Saturday belongs, he concludes that it belongs to the day of the Resurrection, that is, to Sunday. He proves this by adducing the example of Holy Saturday, whose night, because of the solemnity of ecclesiastical worship and the administration of baptism, certainly belongs to Sunday.

Once this has been established, it remains to examine whether certain Sundays were assigned to ordination or whether any Sunday could be chosen for that purpose.

The latter is, in my judgment, entirely certain.

First, our Leo designates no particular Sunday and therefore excludes none, just as we find no such exclusion before his time.

Second, we know from present-day custom that every Sunday was adopted for the consecration of bishops by the authority of ancient custom, apostolic tradition, and the sacred Scriptures, from which Saint Leo argues. If this was true of bishops, it was undoubtedly also true of presbyters and deacons, for Saint Leo makes no distinction between them concerning the day of ordination in the present letter.

Third, this custom prevailed in those golden ages, so that the Church, deprived of her shepherd, might be assisted as quickly as possible through the election of another pontiff. We have likewise seen that this was prescribed by the decree of Chalcedon.

The second question can finally be answered without difficulty. It is sufficiently clear from this letter alone that the night chosen for celebrating ordinations belonged to Sunday.

First, Saint Leo expressly states that Dioscorus must take care that those who are to be consecrated never receive the blessing except on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, which is acknowledged to begin with Saturday evening.

Next, when he lists the more illustrious mysteries that occurred on Sunday by divine appointment,

> **[Note: [Col. 1283D]]** See Dissertation 6, *On the Fast of Saturday*.

he sufficiently indicates that the day of the Lord’s Resurrection must be understood as the day we now call simply Sunday. It was Sunday itself, not Saturday, that was dedicated by apostolic institution to the consecration of priests.

Finally, to omit many other points, Urban II indicates this in the cited Council of Clermont. When ordering that ordinations be celebrated on the Saturday of the Ember seasons, he adds:

> “And then let the fast be prolonged until evening, and, if possible, until the following day, so that it may more clearly appear that ordinations are performed on Sunday.”

Nothing proves more clearly that this most sacred day was appointed for conferring orders than the fact that the holy pontiffs did not wish even then to let the memory of that custom be completely erased, although, as we may reasonably believe, weighty reasons compelled them to change it.

The stages of this change occurred gradually over successive periods. First, there seems to be no doubt that this ceremony was celebrated by the apostles and by the bishops of apostolic times on Sunday itself, during the sacred synaxes, and at the third hour of the day, which had always been assigned to the celebration of the sacred mysteries.

Later, when persecution by the pagans broke out and Christians began holding the same gatherings before dawn, in order to elude the daytime vigilance of the enemies of the faith, it is highly probable that ordinations too were celebrated at that same hour.

This continued after peace had been restored to the Church. Hence the vigils of Saturday were introduced, concerning which our Leo speaks:

- so that the memory of a custom consecrated, as it were, by the blood of the martyrs would not disappear;
- so that honor might be shown at the same hour to the Lord’s Resurrection, which had occurred at the earliest dawn;
- and finally, so that the Saturday fast, if prolonged into a further portion of Sunday, would not overly fatigue either the consecrating bishop or those being consecrated.

I think this was the reason why ordination gradually moved backward: first from Sunday morning to the beginning of the night; then from the beginning of the night to Saturday evening, as is clear from the Gelasius cited above; afterward from evening to midday; and finally from midday to the morning hours, as is done today.

Some say that ordinations were celebrated around the beginning of the night so that the Sunday office would not be interrupted by the solemnity of the ordination occurring at the same time. I do not consider this correct.

For just as on the very day of the Resurrection, and indeed throughout the entire octave of Easter, the whole office of the Church concerned the neophytes, so on the day of ordination there was no other Sunday office and no offering of the sacrifice except what was celebrated on account of the ordination itself.

This is so true that, when the solemnity of ordination was transferred to Saturday, the office of the Mass was also transferred to that same day, and the following Sunday was deprived of its proper office.

> **[Note: [Col. 1283D]]** Since all the codices of the Gregorian Sacramentary display proper prayers for the Mass of the Saturday of ordination, and likewise proper prayers for the Sunday following the Saturday of ordination, it cannot be true that, because ordinations were transferred from Sunday to Saturday, the entire office of the Mass was also transferred to Saturday and Sunday was left without the office of the Mass.
