Who could believe that these Sundays, which were always devoted to divine worship in the Church just as the other Sundays were, lacked the sacrifice? If the same Sacramentaries say that these Sundays were vacant, this must be understood in some other sense than of the sacrifice. In the Ottobonian manuscript Gregorian Sacramentary published by Muratori, which is the oldest of all, antiphons, responsories, the offertory, and the communion—sung by the choir—are listed for every Sunday. Only on the four Sundays following the Saturdays already assigned to the four Ember ordinations are all these items omitted. This seems to indicate that on those four Sundays it was not the Mass, nor the entire office of the Mass, but only the more laborious choral office of antiphons, responsories, and so forth that was omitted, perhaps so that the ministers, relieved by the sacred ordinations from labor and prolonged singing, might be spared. In this sense those Sundays were said to be vacant, namely, vacant of the choral office. For this reason, when they fell during Advent or Lent, when they should have received stations, they were also without station and procession. If the antiphons, responsories, and so forth of these Sundays are nevertheless recorded in the Gregorian Antiphonary published by Cardinal Thomasius, this seems attributable to a later addition, since the Ottobonian codex published by Muratori, which is older, records nothing of the kind for these Sundays. Hence three manuscripts cited by the Maurist monks in volume III of Saint Gregory, p. 672, note h, lack an office for the Second Sunday of Lent and contain only the prayers belonging to the Mass. The same editors noted there: “Perhaps Mass was indeed celebrated on this Sunday, but nothing was sung because of the excessive labor of the preceding Saturday.” It is possible, however, that Quesnellus himself understood by “the office of the Mass” the singing of antiphons, responsories, and the like.

Thus those Sundays which follow the Saturday of ordination have continued to be called “vacant” to this day. Today they do possess their own office, but it is composed from the offices of the preceding days. See the *Micrologus*, chapter 29.

### 4. “So that whenever the presence of a new congregation has filled the basilica in which the service is being conducted, the following sacrifice may be offered,” etc.

Here you should note numerous elements of ancient discipline, both in these words and in those attached to them.

First, we learn that the custom of the Roman Church at that time was that, whenever the gathering of a larger crowd required it, the offering of the sacrifice was repeated. Leo likewise demands that this be observed among the Alexandrians:

> “So that our observance may agree in every respect.”

We read that in the African provinces, during the same period of our Leo, this was done even for less important reasons. In the book *On the Promise and Predestination of God*, part of the time, chapter 6, we read that, after the morning sacrifice had been completed and a girl had been rescued from the power of the demon, an offering was made **again** in thanksgiving for her, and the girl, receiving a portion of the sacrifice, was restored to the ancient practice.

Indeed, it is clear from canon 8 of the Council of Carthage of the year 397, which is canon 41 of the African Code, that the celebration of Mass was repeated and that a sacrifice was also offered in the afternoon for the dead:

> “If a commemoration of some of the dead, whether bishops or others, must be made in the afternoon, let it be done with prayers alone if those who perform it are found already to have eaten. But if they are found fasting, nothing prevents the celebration from taking place even in the afternoon, although it may already have been celebrated in the morning.”

Second, Saint Leo says that the repeated offering of the sacrifice was not a recent custom in the Roman Church but an ancient institution that had taken root in accordance with the form of the tradition of the Fathers.

Third, it follows that this practice was introduced into the Roman Church—or also into the African Church, where we see the repetition of the sacrifice immediately decreed at the pontiff’s discretion and as circumstances required—not by a canon or any ecclesiastical law, but solely by custom.

Fourth, Leo does not extend this permission to every Sunday (which [Note: [Col. 1285D] Some things in what follows are uncertain or difficult for us. What Quesnell asserts here—that at Rome only Sunday was assigned for the celebration of the mysteries—may be conceded if he means that on other weekdays not marked by a particular feast no fixed and solemn Mass had been prescribed. But if he means that the sacrifice of the Mass was not offered on other days, we do not know what foundation can support that claim. For if he inferred it from the Gelasian and Gregorian Sacramentaries, in which Masses are assigned only to Sundays, and not to weekdays except during Lent, does it not follow that in the more ancient Sacramentary, attributed to Leo and published by us in this volume, no proper Masses are found for the Sundays after [Col. 1286C] Easter and Pentecost, although no one would doubt that the sacrifice was celebrated on them? Just as during this period, when Sundays lacked a proper Mass, Masses were taken from the common forms at the celebrant’s discretion, as we observed in the preface to that Sacramentary, so after Masses had been assigned to each Sunday [Col. 1286D], those who celebrated the sacrifice on weekdays repeated Masses either from the preceding Sunday or from the common forms. Nor should one think that the ancient fervor which flourished in the Roman Church and clergy in the age of Jerome and Augustine had entirely died out—namely, that many communicated daily, and therefore that sacrifice was offered to God daily.]) but only to a more solemn feast, and then only in the case and condition that a congregation larger than usual gathered at the basilica.

Fifth, the offering could have been made not merely once and again, [Col. 1286A] but as often as a new congregation filled the basilica in which the service was being held.

I think that from this arose the custom of celebrating twice or three times on certain solemnities, 1311 [Note: [Col. 1286D] The custom of celebrating three times on the Nativity of the Lord seems rather to have arisen because, on that day, three stations and Masses were celebrated at distinct hours in three distinct Roman basilicas: first at Saint Mary Major, then at Saint Anastasia, and finally at Saint Peter’s, as may be inferred from the Gregorian Sacramentary and Antiphonary. Perhaps the same occurred on other solemnities that included different Masses celebrated on the same day at different hours; thus, formerly, on the feast day of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, two Masses were sung in their two churches, one at Saint Peter’s and the other at Saint Paul’s.] such as the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, the Nativity of Saint John, the feast days of the apostles, and so forth, so that the offering of the sacrifice was repeated not only in the same basilica and at the same altar, but also by the same priest. I would nevertheless doubt that this was anciently practiced at Easter, both because I have no ancient witness and because the solemn administration of baptism, together with the lengthy ceremonies surrounding those being baptized and those already baptized, stood in the way of repeating Masses.

A trace, at least, of an ancient custom in England may be found in what was decreed by Stephen Langton, archbishop of Canterbury, at the Council of Oxford in 1222, canon 6: “Moreover, we have judged it necessary to decree, strictly forbidding any priest to celebrate the solemnities of Mass twice in one day, except on the day of the Nativity of the Lord and of the Lord’s Resurrection.” The same is read in the English Constitutions, vol. II of the *Collectio Anglica*, around [Col. 1286B] the year 1237, or in the funeral rites of the dead—namely, when someone’s body was to be buried on that same day. (In the collection of Councils one reads “in the Church,” which is rightly absent from the Canterbury provincial collection.) In that case the first Mass was to be celebrated for the day, and the later one for the deceased. William Lyndwood reports this in the English provincial collection; he also lists other reasons for the same priest’s repeating the sacrifice on the same day, and presents them in these verses:

> One day demands only one Mass:
>
> The deceased, certainly, is excepted, together with the pilgrim,
>
> The sick man, the traveler, the Nativity of the Lord, and the guest,
>
> And the woman marrying, when her appointed time is passing away.

Sixth, it follows that the sacred mysteries were celebrated not only in the morning hours, even on the more solemn feasts, but also in the evening. Since the sacrifice was customarily celebrated at about the third hour—or, in our manner of speaking, at the ninth hour of the morning—and since the rites and prayers interwoven with the sacrifice were lengthy, the mysteries often could not be completed in the morning, but had to be prolonged until evening. To this perhaps belongs the mention of evening Masses found in the Council of Agde, canon 30, and in the Third Council of Orléans, canon 29, although these passages may be understood of days of fasting. Unless the time was changed because of the necessity of offering the sacrifice several times, which does not seem improbable; and this appears to be confirmed by these words of Leo: “If, while the custom of one Mass is preserved, they cannot offer the sacrifice except those who have gathered in the FIRST PART OF THE DAY.” Here it is scarcely possible to understand “the first part of the day” as the third hour, or what is now the ninth hour. Since this seems to conflict with the custom just mentioned, of celebrating at the ninth hour, I think the matter can be reconciled in this way: on ordinary Sundays the sacrifice was celebrated at the third or ninth hour, but on the more solemn feasts of which Leo is speaking here, the sacrifice of the Mass was completed in the first part of the day—that is, very early in the morning. The reason for the distinction is that these solemnities were celebrated with nocturnal vigils. When those were completed, it was entirely fitting that the people, wearied by fasting and vigil, should be dismissed to their homes only after the mysteries had been celebrated and received. Thus, when other groups of the faithful newly filled the basilica, sufficient time was available for the offering to be repeated. This very epistle testifies that the ninth hour was often anticipated by the sacrifice, namely when, on the morning of the Sunday itself—whose beginning reaches back to the opening of the preceding night—the blessing of priestly consecration was bestowed, unquestionably amid the mysteries of the sacred offering.

7. From this we recognize that Saint Leo had sufficient reason for repeating the sacrifice: he considered it completely consistent with piety and reason that the devotion of the people should not be deprived of its vows and expectation.

8. This expression deserves notice: “in which it is being celebrated,” by which the sacrifice of the Mass is signified. For *to celebrate* and *to sacrifice* mean the same thing; hence *actio* also denotes the consecration itself in the canon: “after the consecration,” and *agenda* is often used for the Mass. This occurs in the Second Council of Carthage, in the Lectionary bearing Jerome’s name, in the Rule of Saint Benedict, in Bede, and in the Capitularies of Charlemagne. See further Book I, chapter 3, of the *Liturgical Matters* of the most eminent and learned Cardinal Bona, alas, recently snatched from the Church militant by a premature death, to the profound grief of all good and learned people. But see also the earlier synopsis of this epistle. Although we have substituted another for it because it contained both false and barbarous material, it will nevertheless not be inappropriate to transcribe it here. It reads as follows:

> Concerning the ordination of a presbyter or deacon, that it be celebrated on Holy Saturday, that is, on Sunday I. Concerning feast days: if one *agenda*, that is, one celebration of Mass, has not sufficed for the people, there should be no doubt that the sacrifice may be repeated II.

9. We understand from this that the custom which we have seen practiced in the Roman and African Churches did not at that time prevail in Alexandria. Whether it was adopted there after Leo’s admonition is not clear to me. The fact that an ancient rite was observed there, unlike the Roman practice, is suggested by what learned men report concerning the more recent Greeks, Syrians, and other Eastern peoples. “The Maronite Syrians,” says Morinus (*Preface to the Ordination of the Maronite Syrians*), “generally follow the customs of the Greeks . . . They celebrate Mass in the church only once each day, and without urgent necessity and the bishop’s permission they do not sacrifice twice in one day upon one and the same altar.” I think Morinus took this from a letter of the Maronite Abraham Ecchellensis, which he wrote to him from Rome in 1654. The same Morinus asserts elsewhere that all the Eastern peoples—the Greeks, Muscovites, Ethiopians, and others—have preserved this same custom inviolate down to our own time, and consequently that only a single altar is placed in their churches.

10. Observe that the verb “to offer” is also attributed to laypeople; this could readily be demonstrated by six hundred examples. Indeed, the sacrifice is offered to God by the whole Church, even though it is consecrated by one priest alone. Hence, in the sacred liturgy: “Pray, brethren, that my sacrifice and yours”; and, “of all those standing around who offer to you,” and so forth.

11. From these words, “which one basilica cannot receive all at once,” I seem to be able to infer [Note: [Col. 1287C] From the words, “such a multitude of the faithful will have gathered that one basilica cannot receive them all at once,” it indeed follows that the passage concerns one basilica in which some great feast was celebrated with the greatest concourse of people; but it does not follow that Alexandria had only one basilica in which the offering was made. Thus, even if at Rome a feast were celebrated in a single church with a great attendance, the sacrifice was not for that reason celebrated nowhere else on the same day. This is made clear by Innocent I’s Letter 25 to Decentius, chapter 5, where he says that he sent the *fermentum* to the presbyters of the city’s titular churches on every Sunday, because on that day they could not assemble with us on account of the people entrusted to them. These presbyters, or parish priests, therefore celebrated the sacrifice with their respective congregations on Sundays in their titular churches, and a portion of the sacrifice offered by the bishop in the Lateran Church was sent to them, so that, as he says, “they would not consider themselves separated from our communion especially on that day.” Therefore, just as at Rome, so also at Alexandria a single sacrifice was celebrated in each titular church; and only if, for some feast being celebrated somewhere, such a multitude gathered that the basilica could not contain them all at once, was the sacrifice permitted to be repeated there.]) that there was only one basilica there in which the offering was made. We say nothing here about basilicas, because at some time the learned reader will receive a fuller and more precisely informed treatment of the form and capacity of Eastern basilicas in the extensive work *On Basilicas* by Jean Morin, a priest of the French Oratory. We shall soon publish it, together with his epistle on the same subject to Allatius.

5. “We familiarly admonish.” Our Leo seems to me to distinguish three kinds of letters. The first are those which we call synodical, written from a synod and in the name of a synod; such are Letters 40, 41, 45, and 47 (now 44, 45, 50, and 51), and several others bearing this heading: “Leo and the holy synod,” and so forth. There are others [Note: [Col. 1288C] Quesnell calls “decretal” here the letters of the Roman pontiff sent to the Churches or provinces which he governed with metropolitan or exarchal authority. Those sent to the bishops of other dioceses—that is, of the East—he calls not decretal but familiar letters. What is the basis of this distinction, and of this interpretation of the terms? Let it be granted that this letter to Dioscorus may be called familiar insofar as it was not solemnly drafted in a synod or sent to a synod. Yet because it contains disciplinary rules and commands, indicated by the word “We wish” in chapters 1 and 2, it ought rightly to be regarded as decretal. Even if, in the East, it did not possess the force of a decree by virtue of metropolitan, exarchal, or patriarchal authority, it cannot be denied that by virtue of the primacy it possessed force throughout the whole Church—unless one denies, with the heterodox, that the primacy of divine right belongs to the apostolic See of Peter. The formulas “we familiarly admonish,” “paternal and fraternal conference,” commend Leo’s moderation and gentleness; but they detract nothing from the authority sufficiently indicated by the repeated word “We wish.”] decretal letters, which he also calls decretal constitutions: namely, letters concerning matters of ecclesiastical discipline that he sent to those Churches or provinces which the bishop of Rome governed with metropolitan or exarchal authority, and for whose execution he delegated certain bishops from those same provinces. Such are Letters 2, 3, and 8 (now 167, 4, and 7), and many others. Letters of the third kind are called familiar; they were written to the bishops of other dioceses, either concerning the observance of ecclesiastical discipline, concerning ecclesiastical matters that had arisen, or to express the bond of episcopal relationship. This letter to Dioscorus seems to me to be of that kind: Leo admonishes him earnestly and “familiarly,” and in the preface calls it a paternal and fraternal conference. In the same way he seems to distinguish Turribius of Astorga’s familiar letter from a *commonitorium*, both in the preface and in chapter 17. Finally, one letter of Pope Innocent I to five African bishops is called familiar in the *Code of Canons of the Roman Church* and elsewhere, to distinguish it from the other letters in which he replied from a synod to the synodical letters of the African bishops.

6. “To the presbyter Possidonius.” We sometimes see bishops sent as messengers of ordinations from those principal sees, especially when some of them were seeking a journey to Rome. At other times presbyters, or even clerics of the lower orders, were sent with letters. Sometimes both were omitted, as our Leo complains concerning Basil of Antioch in Letter 118 (now 149). Possidonius the presbyter, moreover, is, I think, the same as that deacon who was once sent to Rome by Cyril, the predecessor of Dioscorus, to Pope Celestine in the year 430, when the Nestorian heresy was arising. For this reason Leo says that he was sent to Rome many times.

7. “Of apostolic authority.” Thus read the manuscripts of Grimani and Victor, as well as the editions of P. Canisius, Nicolinus, Crabbe, [Col. 1289B] Surius, Sichard, the Merlin edition of Isidore, and others. Baronius also reads it this way. Accordingly, the Roman edition and the others which have “of the authority of the apostolic See” ought rightly to be corrected, as should the latest edition of the Councils, which places this interpolated reading in the text and relegates the other to the margin: “The authority of the apostolic See prevails.” For these words do not pertain to the authority of the apostolic See, but to apostolic tradition, or to the custom of the Roman Church derived from the form of paternal tradition, as he says a few lines earlier; or, as in chapter 1, to the authority of the custom which, he says, “we know to come from apostolic teaching.” In the same passage he calls it apostolic institutions.

[Note: [Col. 1289C] Since we rejected Quesnell’s Letter 9 to the Gallican bishops of the province of Vienne and placed it in the appendix to Volume I of the Letters, col. 1469, we inserted Quesnell’s fuller note in the admonition prefixed to it, col. 1465.]

## TO LETTER X. To the Gallican bishops of the province of Vienne

1. It is surprising that this very celebrated and important letter, which many people had an interest in copying and transmitting to posterity, has scarcely been found by us in any of the manuscripts. It lies in the Corbie manuscript of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, which is of respectable antiquity, and in another manuscript of Thuaneus; but the latter is so similar to the Corbie manuscript that I think it was copied from it. It is also found in the Victorine manuscript containing all the Letters and Sermons of Saint Leo, though that codex is not especially ancient. It appears scarcely at all in other manuscripts. It is found in the Isidorian collection. Yves and Gratian preserve a record of it: Gratian, in distinction 19, chapter “Thus the Lord,” transcribes almost the whole of the first chapter of this letter; Yves does so in Part V, chapter 6. Both the style and the entire sequence of the letter show that it truly belongs to Leo.

2. “Through Vienne,” and so forth. James Sirmond says that on an old sheet this letter of Leo is inscribed as having been sent not only to the bishops of the province of Vienne but also to the bishops of Maxima Sequanorum, in the following form: [Note: [Col. 1289C] See note 2 (col. 628, n. n) on this letter, and especially the observations in Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, Part I, chapter 2, no. 4, where we defended this inscription.] “Leo to all the most beloved bishops established throughout the provinces of Maxima Sequanorum and Vienne.” [Col. 1290B] This both makes a plausible conjecture concerning the place of the synod—namely, Vesontio—and confirms that Celidonius was bishop of Vesontio, the metropolis of Maxima Sequanorum. Thus Sirmond. Our view of these matters has already been stated in Dissertation 5. I say only this: that sheet, of uncertain antiquity and reliability, cannot outweigh the testimony of all the manuscripts, whether handwritten or printed. None of all those that have come into our hands presents anything of the sort; moreover, the title appears to have been fabricated by those who placed Celidonius’s see at Vesontio, a claim which we have shown to lack all probability.

3. “May place PRINCIPALLY,” and from him, as from a kind of head, may wish his gifts to flow into the whole body. Thus the Corbie and Thuaneus manuscripts, instead of the former reading: “that he might place them, as from a kind of head, so that from him he might diffuse his gifts, as it were, into the whole body.” Perhaps someone will interpret these words [Note: [Col. 1289C] The sense in which Saint Leo uses the adverb “principally” in chapter 1 is so clear from the context that Quesnell’s explanation seems rather to obscure what is clear than to clarify what is obscure. The holy pontiff is speaking of the preaching of the Gospel throughout the world, which Christ entrusted to the apostles, as it is written: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” He affirms that Christ entrusted this office to all the apostles, but in such a way that he “placed it principally” in Peter, the chief of all the apostles, and wished his gifts to flow from him, as from a kind of head, into the whole body. Thus anyone who dared to depart from Peter’s firmness would understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery. [Col. 1289D] The words calling Peter supreme among all the apostles declare his primacy among the apostles; what follows explains the force and nature of that primacy. He affirms that the very office of preaching, although entrusted to all the apostles, was nevertheless placed principally in Peter by reason of his primacy, as in the head from whom his gifts flow to all. He says this in such a way that anyone who dared to depart from Peter’s firmness would understand himself to be excluded from the divine mystery. Peter’s firmness must, according to Leo’s mind, be understood of Peter’s preaching, or of the faith that Peter preached, as will become clear from the observations on Sermon 3, no. 2. In the same place, no. 3, we showed that the same firmness of faith which the holy pontiff affirmed to be in Peter was, according to his teaching, transmitted to all Peter’s successors and remains equally firm in the Roman Church. [Col. 1290C] Therefore, the person who wishes to depart from the doctrine of the faith of Peter and of the Roman pontiffs—doctrine which was made firm in Peter by Christ and passed with the same firmness to the Roman pontiffs—will depart from Peter’s firmness. When Leo affirms that anyone who departs from Peter’s firmness is excluded from the divine mystery, he indicates the necessity of agreement with the faith and teaching of Peter and his successors. In this sense the preaching of the faith, though entrusted to all the apostles, was entrusted principally to Peter, because it was entrusted to Peter alone in such a way that the same firmness of faith, passing to his successors, imposes upon all Catholics the necessity of agreement. This did not occur with the bishop of any other apostolic see. Therefore Saint Irenaeus wrote not of any other see or Church but of the Roman Church alone, in words Quesnell himself cited shortly before: “It is necessary that every Church should come together with the Roman Church, because of its more powerful principality.” He could not have meant rites and discipline, which could differ among the Churches, especially at that time. The statement must be understood of the doctrine of the faith. Since this must be one in all the Churches, all Catholics must agree with the doctrine of faith of the Roman pontiffs, Peter’s successors, into whom the same firmness of Peter and of his faith passed, lest those who depart from this firmness of Peter be excluded from the divine mystery. Saint Irenaeus attributed this to the Roman Church “because of its more powerful principality,” that is, because of the primacy. Among the many prerogatives of primacy, this is the chief and principal one, since Christ instituted primacy for the purpose not merely of displaying but also of forming and preserving in Peter and his successors the unity of the whole Church, especially the unity of preaching and faith, of which the next observation will speak. This is the straightforward explanation of the Leonine text. It coheres not only with other testimonies of the same pontiff but also with those of other Fathers, and it demonstrates the special force and capacity of pontifical primacy. Those who try to distort Leo’s words in another direction should fear that, while verbally acknowledging the primacy of principal jurisdiction, they may weaken it so greatly that they depart from Leo’s mind no less than those who in reality seem to assert only a primacy differing little or not at all from a mere primacy of rank.]) so as to imagine that the apostolic and priestly dignity was full and perfect in Peter and his successors, but in the other apostles and in their episcopal successors diminished, as it were, rather than equal. But, asks Pope Gelasius, “were not the other holy and blessed apostles also girded with similar power? Who would dare affirm this? Yet, so that the occasion of schism might be removed by establishing a head, and so that the body of Christ might be shown to have one structure . . . there were certainly twelve apostles, supported by equal merits and equal dignity; and although all shone equally with spiritual light, Christ nevertheless wished one of them to be the prince.” (Gelasius I, *Treatise against the Greeks*, in Sirmond’s appendix to the *Theodosian Code*, pp. 184 and 187.)

What, then, does “principally” mean? Not “more completely” or “more perfectly.” First, it can signify what Pope Gelasius means: namely, that Peter, among the other apostles, who were supported by equal merits and equal dignity and who shone equally with spiritual light, was established as their prince. Who would deny this except someone ignorant of antiquity or hostile to unity? Second, “principally” can also mean, so to speak, “originally,” at the very institution and beginning of apostolic and pontifical dignity. In this sense the same Saint Leo says in Letter 93 (now 120) to Theodoret: “He placed the Sun of justice principally in the West, its summit among the apostles and teachers”; and in Letter 12 (now 14) to Anastasius of Thessalonica, chapter 1, that “by divine institution he principally owes care to all the Churches”; and in Sermon 83 (now 85), on Saint Lawrence, that “the courage of the soul was conceived principally from the love of Christ.” In the letter to Demetrias, which we now assert to be his, he says that “our nature was principally instituted in Adam,” that is, at the very beginning of creation.

Cyprian must be understood in the same sense when, in Letter 54, he calls the Roman Church “principal,” immediately explaining that it is the source from which priestly unity arose. So too Irenaeus, when in Book III, chapter 3, he writes: “It is necessary that every Church should come together with the Roman Church because of its more powerful principality,” since among the apostolic Churches—the “mother Churches,” and the “originals of the faith,” as Tertullian calls them—from which the other Churches thereafter borrowed, and still borrow, the offshoot of the faith and the seeds of doctrine in order to become Churches (*On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 20), Rome is more powerful, more fruitful, more ancient among the Western Churches, and, because of the authority and prerogative of the prince of the apostles, from whom the origin of unity begins, the head of all the Churches.

The fact that this is Irenaeus’s sense of “principality,” even if it does not please everyone, is established both by the context of the passage itself and by another passage in Book IV, chapter 75, where he speaks of the origin of all things derived from God. “And thus,” he says, “God will have the principality in all things, since he alone is uncreated, prior to all, and himself the cause of all things that exist.” The word has the same sense in Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 31, when he says: “But I shall return from the digression to the priority of truth and to assigning later origin to falsehood.” In the same sense Facundus of Hermiane, Book IX near the end, asserts that the ancient teachers of the Church said that “God the Word is principally, and according to essence, the only-begotten Son of God”; but the man assumed through the unity of his person received the status that he should always be and be called the only-begotten Son.

Finally, Leo’s words have no other meaning than those of Pope Innocent I in his letter to Victricius of Rouen: “With the help of the holy apostle Peter, through whom both the apostolate and the episcopate in Christ received their beginning, I shall begin.” Nor is there any intention here of detracting from the authority of the Roman pontiff, who undoubtedly holds the principal chair and, by reason of apostolic primacy, far surpasses each bishop of the Christian world in splendor, authority, and jurisdiction.

1319 4. “Taken into the fellowship of indivisible unity.” [Note: [Col. 1291C] Why is so much being amassed here to explain a testimony that is perfectly clear? The holy pontiff, in order to give the reason for his statement that whoever dared to depart from Peter’s firmness would be excluded from the divine mystery, added: “For he wished him, taken into the fellowship of indivisible unity, to be called what he himself was, when he said: ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock [Col. 1291D] I will build my Church’; so that the building of the eternal temple might, by the wondrous gift of God’s grace, stand upon Peter’s firmness. By strengthening his Church with this firmness, he made it such that neither human recklessness could assail it nor the gates of hell prevail against it.” Is it not clear that “the fellowship of indivisible unity” refers to this: just as Christ, for the sake of the unity of the Church, is the rock and foundation to which the whole Church must adhere, so Peter was taken by Christ into the fellowship of this prerogative for the sake of that same unity, when Christ established him in his own place as the rock of the Church—a rock so firm that the gates of hell could not prevail against it? Hence Leo similarly said in Sermon 4, chapter 2: “Although I am the inviolable rock, I the cornerstone who make both one, I the foundation besides which no one can lay another, yet you too are a rock, because you are made firm by my power, so that what belongs to me by authority may be common to you with me by participation. And upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” “Upon this strength,” he says, “I shall build the eternal temple, and the Church’s exaltation into heaven shall rise upon the firmness of this faith.” These words harmonize wonderfully with those quoted from the present epistle and make it clear that Saint Peter, established as the rock of the Church, was endowed by Christ with such firmness and stability of faith that the Church could stand strengthened in it; and this can occur only through unity of faith with Peter. Hence, in the sermon just cited, Sermon 4, chapter 3, after writing, “The Lord takes special care of Peter, and prayer is offered especially for Peter’s faith, so that the condition of the others may become more secure if the mind of the prince has not been overcome,” Leo concludes: “In Peter, therefore, the strength of all is fortified, and the help of divine grace is so ordered that the firmness which is bestowed upon Peter through Christ is conferred through Peter upon the apostles.” Since Saint Peter was taken by Christ into the fellowship of indivisible unity insofar as, for the forming and preserving of the Church’s unity, he was taken into the fellowship of that rock—which is Christ—and established as the rock and foundation of the Church, not less in name than in its firmness, there is nothing surprising if the holy pontiff called anyone who dared to depart from the firmness not so much of Christ as of Peter an outsider to the heavenly mystery, that is, someone outside the unity of the Church. What he teaches here of Peter must equally be understood of Peter’s successors, since, for the same purpose, the same firmness of faith passed to them, as we showed in the preceding observation.]

Whittaker, according to Andrew Rivet, *Sacred Criticism*, Book IV, chapter 22, read “of indivisible Trinity.” I do not know where he got this. I do know that there was nothing in these words that ought to have offended him, so that he might attack them with a dog’s tooth, as though they breathed an overbearing spirit. As though anyone had accused Saint Peter himself of arrogance and ambition, when he proclaims that he and all Christians have become participants in the divine nature.

I am also surprised that Isaac Casaubon, a man of more generous intellect, wrote (*Exercise* 15 on Baronius’s *Ecclesiastical Annals*) that these words greatly require the *anexikakia*—the patient forbearance—of a fair-minded reader. “For if the words are considered,” he says, “every path to a sound interpretation seems to be blocked. For what is it to be taken into the fellowship of indivisible unity except to be enrolled among the persons of the sacred and *hypersousios*—superessential—Trinity?” But whoever wishes may believe that such an opinion, so manifestly impious and blasphemous, ever entered the mind of a holy man; I shall never bring myself even to suspect it of him.

He then interprets Saint Leo’s words as referring to the conjunction of Peter, the shepherd of the Church, with Christ—not insofar as Peter is one of the three persons of the sacred Trinity, but insofar as he too, though in a different manner, is the shepherd of the Church. Casaubon has indeed said this correctly, although far too hesitantly. It should be presented somewhat more fully.

This is Saint Leo’s meaning and purpose. The Lord Christ, he says, wished the worship of God, previously confined within Judea, to be spread among all nations. He determined that this should be accomplished through the preaching of the apostles, whose sound would go out into all the earth. [Col. 1293B] But because all the works of almighty God derive from unity and tend toward unity, he wished the common office of preaching the Gospel to belong to all the apostles in such a way that he would choose one from among them, to whom alone, before all and on behalf of all, he would entrust that office—an office which all would receive in him and toward whom all would converge as toward the beginning of their common dignity. Thus Saint Leo says in Sermon 3 (now 4), *On the Assumption*: “What is announced to all is entrusted to one”; and “This is entrusted uniquely to Peter because the form of Peter is set before all the rulers of the Church.” Or, as Saint Cyprian says in *On the Unity of the Church*: “To manifest unity, by his authority he arranged that the origin of that same unity should begin from one . . . The beginning proceeds from unity, so that the Church may be shown to be one.”

“This is the mystery of unity,” as Saint Cyprian says in the same work, whose beginning and origin, exemplar and end, supreme and indivisible Trinity is the unity of the Trinity. The Church imitates and participates in it, as Christ testifies when addressing the Father concerning Christian unity (John 17): “That they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me, and I in you; that they too may be one in us”; and “that they may be one, as we also are one.” In this mystery of unity, therefore, the bishop is in the Church and the Church is in the bishop.

Again, when Christ established Peter, all the apostles and bishops, and the Church itself, were in Peter. Finally, Peter was with all in Christ, [Col. 1293C] taken into the fellowship of indivisible unity in such a way that Christ wished him to be called what he himself was, saying: “You are Peter,” and so forth; that is, as Saint Leo himself explains in the sermon cited: “Although I am the inviolable rock, I the cornerstone who make both one, I the foundation besides which no one can lay another, yet you too are a rock, because you are made firm by my power, so that what belongs to me by authority may be common to you with me by participation,” and so forth.

Thus the unity both of all pastors among themselves and of the pastors with the Church imitates the indivisible unity both of Christ the Lord with his body and of the same and the other persons of the Trinity with one another. “In the likeness of the Trinity,” says Pope Symmachus (Letter 1 to Aeonius of Arles), “whose power is one and indivisible, the priesthood is one through different bishops.”

If the heterodox did not have eyes obstructed by a spell, they would easily see that Leo’s words contain nothing in which he did not follow Cyprian, the Apostle Peter, and Christ himself as his predecessor and guide. Nor is he more deserving of criticism here than when, in Sermon 3 (now 4), *On the Assumption*, chapter 2, he said: “The divine condescension granted this man [Peter] a great and wondrous fellowship in its power,” and so forth.

### 5. Safely preserved

All the manuscript codices—Corbeiensis, Thuaneus, Victorinus—which alone we were permitted to use, present this reading: “safely preserved,” not, as elsewhere, “safely established.” These two readings differ very substantially.[Col. 1293C] For although the words “safely preserved,” applied to appeals to the Apostolic See, in themselves indicate a custom, nevertheless, since this custom is supported both by the sacred canons and by divine law—as we have demonstrated at length in the Observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, part I, chapters 6 and 7—it cannot be denied that Leo may also have had a certain ecclesiastical and divine right in mind. Indeed, the Roman pontiff elsewhere invoked the Sardican canons under the name of the Nicene canons in support of the right of appeal; and he seems also to have contemplated a certain divine right when he complained that Saint Hilary’s opposition to Celidonius’s appeal was not contained by any rule of the Lord’s institution, and that Hilary was in some measure attacking the power of binding and loosing which Christ had attributed to Peter above all others. See chapters 1 and 2 of Letter 10.[Col. 1293D] The former expression therefore indicates merely a custom, whereas the latter signifies either a divine or an ecclesiastical law; and I would not think that Leo had the latter in mind here.

### 6. Claiming for himself the ordinations of all the Churches throughout Gaul

When Saint Leo reproves Saint Hilary for claiming for himself “the ordinations of all the Churches throughout Gaul,” he takes the words “all the Churches” in a broad sense, because Hilary had extended himself into foreign provinces. For we have established at length, in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, parts I and II, that the ordination of the bishop in Projectus’s place took place in a foreign province, and that Celidonius’s deposition outside Narbonensis itself pertained to Maxima Sequanorum.[Col. 1293D]

If one considers the more usual meaning of the words, nothing occurs to the mind sooner than the supposition that Saint Hilary of Arles wished to claim for himself the consecration of all the Gallican bishops. We have nevertheless proved that Leo’s words must be understood otherwise, in part III, chapter 1, of the Apologetic Dissertation for Saint Hilary. There we interpret them not of the consecration of bishops, but of the administration—whether exarchal or metropolitan—of the Churches; and not of all Gaul, but of those provinces of Gaul that had once formed the ancient province of Narbonensis.

### 7. Although the power of loosing and binding was entrusted to him above all others, the care of feeding the sheep was nevertheless specially assigned to him

No one except a person of disturbed mind or heretical obstinacy would wish to detract from the primacy of Saint Peter and his successors, which we believe was established above all others together with Leo himself. Here, however, I do not think that “above all others” should be read,[Col. 1295A] but rather “for the sake of the others.”

All our manuscripts, both Quesnell’s and our own and Sirmond’s,[Col. 1293D; Col. 1294C] have “above all others.” But when no codices support it, who would think of emending it to “for the sake of the others”? Besides, no emendation is necessary. If one observes what the two members of the sentence refer to, and recognizes the force of the comparative *specially* inserted in the second member, one will derive an excellent sense without any correction.

The passage should therefore be understood as follows. Although Christ specially entrusted Saint Peter, above the others, with the power of binding and loosing when he said to him once, before his Passion, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind…”; nevertheless, the care of feeding the sheep was entrusted to him more specially, since after the Passion Christ commanded him not once—as in the case of conferring the power of the keys—but three times, with a threefold question and intervening response: “Feed my sheep, feed my lambs, feed my sheep.”[Col. 1294D]

If, however, one should at some point discover a codex in which “for the sake of the others” is to be read, it is nevertheless certain that the power of binding and loosing was entrusted to Saint Peter not only for the sake of the others but also above the others: for by virtue of the primacy he was given power over the apostles themselves and over all bishops, the successors of the apostles. No Catholic can deny that, by right of primacy, he presided over them.

The force of the power of binding and loosing did indeed pass to the other apostles and to the bishops. But since the primacy passed to no one except the Roman pontiffs, the successors of Peter, no one else received that power which, as proper to the primacy, extends over the whole Church and over all bishops. Add that, since this power passed to the others through Peter—as Leo and other Fathers teach—the power and jurisdiction of the other bishops themselves are subject to the power and jurisdiction of Peter and his successors. Thus Leo states in Sermon 4, chapter 2, that “Peter himself properly rules all, and the successors of Peter likewise rule and govern.”[Col. 1295D]

The adversative particle *nevertheless*, as grammarians teach, presupposes another adversative particle or an opposed member in the same period.[1323] Thus our Leo writes in Sermon 1, now Sermon 2: “And although it is necessary to tremble concerning merit, nevertheless it is religious to rejoice concerning the gift.” And in Sermon 3, now Sermon 4, chapter 1: “Although what was accomplished is common to all, nevertheless it is religious to rejoice as though over a personal honor”; and in chapter 2: “Although in sharing this office we have great reason for common rejoicing, nevertheless the truer…” In these passages the particle *although* is likewise used adversatively, in the sense of “even though,” just as here.

But in the period under discussion the two members are in no way opposed to one another. For the statements that the power of binding and loosing was entrusted to Peter above the others, and that the care of tending the sheep was committed to him more specially than to the others, do not differ in meaning. They are opposed to one another only to some extent in this respect: Peter received a special care of the sheep, and yet he received the power not for himself alone but also on behalf of the others.

I would therefore propose the following correction, subject to the judgment of more learned men:

> Although the power of loosing and binding was entrusted to him for the sake of the others, the care of feeding the sheep was nevertheless specially assigned to him.

The conjecture is confirmed by Leo himself, who repeatedly teaches that when it was said to Peter, “I will give you the keys,” and “Whatever you bind…” the right of this power also passed to the other apostles, and that the constitution of this decree extended to all the leaders of the Church, so that “what is entrusted to one is announced to all” (Saint Leo, Sermon 3, now Sermon 4, chapter 3).

The scarcity of manuscript copies of this letter does not permit us to establish our conjecture on the authority of any of them; we leave it to the judgment of others.

### 8. That he could not hold the priesthood as the husband of a widow; and that we wished the legal ordinances to be observed with greater care

Leo understands by “legal ordinances” not the canons but, as he says in Letter 5 to the bishops of Illyricum, the precepts of the Law—namely, Leviticus 21:14, which Ezekiel repeats at 44:22. Siricius had previously inserted these same legal precepts into Letter 1 to Himerius, chapter 7. Leo himself cites Leviticus in Letter 4, chapter 2.[Col. 1295D; Col. 1296D]

Both the canons and the Holy Spirit, speaking through the Apostle Paul, everywhere proclaim that bigamists are to be excluded from the priesthood. Hence there was no room for doubt that anyone who had or had had two wives was to be entirely barred from ecclesiastical office.[Col. 1295C]

But that those who had had one wife, yet a widow and not a virgin, should be subjected to the same penalty is decreed neither by the Apostle nor by the canons before our Leo. I except one canon of the Council of Valentia, canon 1, which establishes that a bigamist or the husband of a woman who had remarried could not be ordained a cleric; yet it says nothing about the status of those who had already been ordained, nor does it decree that they should be removed.

There is also Apostolic Canon 17, which explicitly excludes from the clergy the husbands of widows and of women who had been divorced. But I do not think that Leo had either of these in mind. For at that time the Roman Church did not ordinarily make use of the canons of other Churches—unless perhaps the African canons, which it had made its own by approving them. Nor had the Apostolic Canons yet been received by it. Pope Gelasius relegates them among the apocrypha; nor were they prefixed shortly afterward by Dionysius Exiguus to his Collection of Canons except with this caution:

> Since very many have not readily given their assent to these, we have wished you not to be unaware of this, Your Holiness.

Nevertheless, Saint Leo would not have established this rule unless he had been persuaded that what he read had been commanded and observed by his predecessors Celestine, Zosimus, Innocent, and Siricius, and descended from apostolic tradition.[Col. 1295D; Col. 1296A]

Indeed, just as the Easterners had formed the Apostolic Canons from customs and rules handed down and received, as it were, by the apostles and apostolic men, so it is certain that many ecclesiastical rules prevailed in the Roman Church from the earliest times, derived from no other source than ancient custom and the tradition of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. Who, then, would be surprised that these rules agree with certain Apostolic Canons, since all the apostles had one faith and generally one discipline, descending from the school of one teacher?

This explains why certain decrees of the pontiffs appear to have been taken from the very canons, as Dionysius Exiguus says in the preface to the canons, when in fact both the decrees and the Apostolic Canons flowed from the common source of tradition. Nevertheless, I readily admit that Leo may in some way have had the Apostolic Canon in view here. For although in several places he invokes the authority of the Apostle alone in order to remove bigamists from ecclesiastical office, and likewise invokes only the precept of the Law by which the husbands of widows and of women who had remarried are forbidden admission to the clergy—as in Letter 3, now Letter 4, to the bishops of Campania, and in this letter to the Viennese, and in Letter 12, now Letter 14, to Anastasius of Thessalonica—yet in Letter 5, now Letter 5, to the bishops of Illyricum, he seems to remember certain canons, which he calls ecclesiastical.

> “We wish such men to become priests of the Lord as possess everything that has been defined by the ecclesiastical canons: that bishops, presbyters, and deacons be husbands of one wife, according to the judgment of the blessed Apostle; and that they have taken this woman as a virgin, according to the precepts of the Law, not as a widow and not as one who had been repudiated, as the Scripture of the Law bears witness.”

Here, nevertheless, it should be noted that those ecclesiastical canons can be referred only to the first member; and even if Leo had the Apostolic Canons in view, he does not call them “Apostolic.” Otherwise authority would thereby have been added to canons that were doubtful and not yet received.[Col. 1296B–C]

In Letter 1, now Letter 12, to the Africans, chapter 3, our author suggests that this rule concerning the bigamy of priests’ wives is an extension and explanation of the apostolic precept, which had always been understood in this way in the Church:

> “When the Apostle says, ‘the husband of one wife,’ this command was held so sacred that the same condition was understood to be observed even concerning the woman to be chosen as the priest’s wife,” and so forth.

### 9. And supported by the presumption of armed protection, etc.

We have restored this entire passage with the help of the manuscript codices, since it had previously been confused and defective. It now reads as follows:

> “And [one] supported by the presumption of armed men, toward inv. P. [an unexpanded abbreviation in the source]; then the household of the Church, which may have lost its own [object omitted].... Those to be ordained to this office are assigned, unknown, to the cities over which they are to be placed.”[Col. 1296D]

We inserted “cities,” as it appeared in the previously published editions. Sirmondus likewise found it in his manuscripts.

### 10. He who is to preside over all must be elected by all

This is a familiar statement, repeated many times by the holy Fathers. I think that in it they alluded to the common saying found in Pliny’s *Panegyric of Trajan*:

> “He who is to rule all ought to be chosen from among all.”[Col. 1296D]

### 11. Leontius

Leontius of Fréjus had already died around the year 432. Faustus of Riez, in his *Praise of Saint Maximus*, his predecessor as bishop, relates that Maximus, before being promoted to the bishopric of Riez, had been especially sought as bishop by the city nearest the island of Lérins, which embraced him as a native inhabitant of its own territory and boundaries. The city nearest Lérins, whose territory and boundaries then included the island itself, was Forum Julii—Fréjus. Accordingly, Saint Maximus was sought for the bishopric of Fréjus before he ascended the see of Riez.

Since he obtained the latter see in 433, Leontius of Fréjus had already died before that year, so that Saint Maximus could be sought for the see left vacant by his death. But when Maximus declined the bishopric of Fréjus, Theodorus, bishop of Fréjus, is rightly believed to have succeeded Leontius in Maximus’s place. For, having been consecrated bishop for the people of Fréjus in the very year 432 in which Leontius died, he was sufficiently senior in the priesthood to Maximus—who later assumed the bishopric of Riez—to subscribe before him at the councils of Riez in 439 and Orange in 442.[Col. 1297C–D]

Thus Leo indicates another Leontius, whose episcopal see is unknown. The holy pontiff wished the honor of the primacy to be accorded to Leontius in such a way that his consent would be required if a synod were to be summoned from other provinces. Since this right had been taken away from Saint Hilary, Leo thought it should be assigned to Leontius because of his seniority.

Since this was a new arrangement and might displease the metropolitans, who could resent a simple bishop being preferred to them in this matter, Leo did not command it absolutely, as he did the other provisions; rather, he submitted the condition to their approval: “If it pleases you.” The words “not instituting new things but renewing old ones,” described in chapter 2, do not refer to this new institution, nor does the phrase “with the labor shared with you” in the same chapter, as the context itself will show.

Whether the Gallican bishops assented to Leo’s wish is unknown because of the scarcity of records. It is certain, however, that they did not resist the other matters commanded and established by Leo, as we proved in the observations on Dissertation 5, part III, chapter 2. From this it is recognized as false what Quesnell asserts shortly before the end:

> “Gaul remained faithful to its ancient customs, and the right to summon the greater synod and the other prerogatives of the primacy always remained with the Church of Arles.”

Nor did the right to summon synods from other provinces—which had been taken away from Hilary absolutely—remain with the Church of Arles during his lifetime; nor did the other prerogatives of metropolitan jurisdiction remain there, as we demonstrated in the same place.[Col. 1298C–D]

It is highly probable that Leontius was bishop of Fréjus in the second Narbonensis. I mean the famous Leontius whom Hilary of Arles himself praises in his *Life of Saint Honoratus*, his predecessor, who went to the island of Lérins:

> “Apart from the opportunity for solitude, he was delighted by the proximity and bound by the affection of the holy and most blessed man in Christ, Leontius the bishop.”

The Roman pontiffs Boniface and Celestine also wrote to this same Leontius. John Cassian dedicated his *Conferences* to him. Anyone wishing to know more should consult *Gallia Christiana*.

He must nevertheless be distinguished from another Leontius to whom Apollinaris Sidonius wrote in Book VI, Letter 3. The mention there of the toga-wearing advocates pleading, of the legal consultation, and of the privilege of the place suggests that this Leontius was bishop of Arles. Moreover, from the beginning of that letter we learn that Sidonius was already invested with the episcopal dignity when he wrote; consequently, the letter was not written before the year 472, when he was appointed to replace Eparchius, the deceased bishop of Clermont.

It is established—and the distinguished authors of *Gallia Christiana* themselves admit—that Leontius of Fréjus died before the year 455, when Theodorus, his successor, was disputing jurisdiction with Faustus, abbot of Lérins; indeed, he died before 452. For in that year our Leo wrote Letter 83, now Letter 108, to Theodorus. The authors of *Gallia Christiana*, John Savaro, and Cardinal Baronius did not attend sufficiently to this point, since they do not distinguish between the two men.[Col. 1297A–B]

That Saint Leo chose Leontius of Fréjus above the others, in order to confer upon him the honor of primacy over five provinces, was not done without deliberation and great prudence. He knew the character and customs of the Gallican bishops and foresaw that they would be difficult to bring to accept a new discipline, since they clung tenaciously to the ancient one.

For this reason he disavows for himself the hatred and resentment of novelty—“not instituting new things but renewing old ones”—and promises that nothing will be done except through labor shared with them. He renews the memory of the favor that the Apostolic See had always shown to Gaul; he declares that their cause, rather than his own, is at stake; and finally he earnestly asks for their consent: “If it pleases you.”[Col. 1297C]

He hoped that consent would more easily be given if he adorned Leontius, already clearly a primate by age, priestly rank, and moral integrity, with the primacy of honor and authority. The suggestion that antiquity should always be honored gave most of the Gallican bishops hope that they might one day attain this dignity, if the primacy were attached not to the excellence of a see but to seniority in the priesthood.

Finally, the example of the African Church, whose discipline the Gallican Church was emulating, promised an easier outcome. For there, as everyone knows, the honor of primacy followed not the splendor of the see but the seniority of the episcopate, with the exception of the see of Carthage.[Col. 1298A]

The matter turned out otherwise. Gaul remained faithful to its ancient customs, and both the right to summon the greater synod and the other prerogatives of the primacy always remained with the Church of Arles.

This arrangement was in fact more suitable to ecclesiastical affairs: that such power should reside with a fixed see, to which a bishop capable of exercising it would be chosen, rather than wandering from city to city according to the antiquity of each consecration. For since it would fall only to old and decrepit men—whose mental vigor is accustomed to fail no less than the strength of the body—such power would generally have remained inactive and useless, and would more easily have been exposed to the attempts of other powers.

Gregory I, pope, perceived this long after Leo. Writing in Book I, Letter 72, to Gennadius, exarch of Africa, he urges him:

> “To order that a council of Catholic bishops be warned not to appoint a primate according to the rank of the place, setting aside the merits of his life; for before God it is not the more elegant rank but the conduct of the better life that is approved. Let the primate himself not remain here and there, as is customary, in villages, but remain in one city, according to their choice, so that the possibility of resisting the Donatists may be arranged through the better judgment of the person who has attained the dignity.”[Col. 1298B]

## On Letter 12, Letter 1 in Quesnell: To the African Bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis

Before discussing the date, interpolations, and emendation of this letter, it is worthwhile to place it whole before the reader’s eyes, in the form represented by all editions for more than a hundred years, with one exception. In this way our notes and observations will be more easily understood, and no one will be able to complain that anything has been taken from the letter.

For the sake of brevity, however, we omit the first part, or first chapter, since all printed and handwritten codices agree about it, apart from the various readings that can be seen in the margin of the letter itself.[Col. 1298C–D]

### Letter 87

Leo, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauretania in Africa: greeting in the Lord.

#### Chapter I

“Since a more frequent report of those coming to us was bringing word that certain matters concerning the ordination of priests had been unlawfully assumed among you,” and so forth, as found in Volume I, page 195—now above, page 645—up to, but not including, chapter 6 of our edition, page 197—now above, page 653.

#### Chapter II

These words, up to “more specially against them,” enclose the genuine letter.[Col. 1299D]

> Since, therefore, you see that, concerning nearly all the matters contained in the report of our brother Potentius, your Charity has been fully instructed through our brother and fellow bishop David, who has commended himself to us both by the merit of his priesthood and by his character, it remains, brothers, that you receive his salutary admonitions with harmonious obedience [correct to: harmoniously], doing nothing through contentiousness but united in every effort of devotion, and that you obey the divine and apostolic constitutions, suffering the most prudent decrees of the canons to be violated in nothing.
>
> For whatever we have now remitted after consideration of particular cases must henceforth be preserved according to the ancient rules, lest what we have granted for a time in pious gentleness we later punish with just vengeance. We must be moved more specially and more strongly against those who have neglected the statutes of the holy Fathers in the ordination of bishops and have consecrated those whom they ought to have rejected.
>
> Therefore, if any bishops have consecrated a priest of such a kind as may not lawfully exist, even if they have in some way escaped damage to their own honor, they will nevertheless no longer possess the right of ordination, nor will they ever take part in that sacrament which, by neglecting the divine judgment, they conferred undeservedly.

[Note: 1st Question, chapter 1, and 15th Question, chapter 2, “If any.”]

[Note: Distinction 80, “That indeed.”]

> We especially wish this, which pertains to priestly dignity, to be observed among all the statutes of the canons: that bishops not be consecrated in just any places, nor in just any castles, nor where bishops had not previously existed. For where the peoples and assemblies are smaller, the care of presbyters is sufficient; episcopal governance ought to preside only over larger populations and more populous cities. Otherwise the priestly dignity—which the divinely inspired decrees of the holy Fathers had forbidden to be assigned to villages, estates, obscure places, and solitary townships—would become cheap through its very multiplication, and the honor to which more excellent responsibilities should be entrusted would be diminished.
>
> Restitutus the bishop complained that this had now been done in his own diocese, and he reasonably requested that, if the bishops of those places where they ought not to have been ordained should die by human destiny, those places themselves should be restored to the jurisdiction of the bishop to whose authority they had previously belonged. It is useless for priestly dignity to be diminished through the thoughtless ease of the ordainer by excessive multiplication.

[Col. 1299A–D]

> Concerning those women who, having been established in the sacred commitment of virginity, suffered barbarous violence and lost the integrity of their modesty not in mind but in body, we think that this moderation should be observed: they should neither be cast down into the rank of widows nor counted among sacred and persevering virgins.
>
> If they persevere in every respect in their virginal state and preserve the firmness of chastity in mind, communion in the sacraments must not be denied them, because it is unjust that they should be accused or branded for what their will did not lose but hostile force tore away.
>
> We also order the case of Bishop Lupicinus to be heard there. Since he repeatedly and earnestly requested communion, we restored it to him for this reason: when he had appealed to our judgment, we saw that he had been unjustly suspended from communion while the case was pending.
>
> It has also been discovered that someone was rashly superimposed upon him who ought not to have been ordained before Lupicinus, being present and either refuted or at least confessing, could be subjected to a just sentence, so that the person being consecrated might receive the vacant place, as ecclesiastical discipline requires.

The commonly published editions then continue with chapters 3, 4, and 5, which in our edition are chapters 6, 7, and 8. The following words conclude that fifth chapter and the whole letter:

> But if other cases arise that concern the condition of the Churches and the harmony of the priests, we wish them to be examined there under the fear of the Lord, and a full report concerning everything that has been settled and resolved is to be sent to us, so that whatever has been defined justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical custom may also be strengthened by our judgment.
>
> Given on the fourth day before the Ides of August. Thus far the letter.

[Col. 1300C]

I confess that this letter tormented me for a very long time. Since both the printed codices and the manuscripts represented it in various forms, either diminished in certain parts or enlarged by additions, I could scarcely discern until at last which side I should favor amid such confusion.

This much was almost immediately certain: the letter presented to us in the latest published copies was not in the form in which Saint Leo had released it. But how it could be restored to its former integrity I did not at once understand.

On the one hand, I saw that this letter to the Caesarean Moors had been inserted into the Collection of Dionysius Exiguus, who attached the decretal letters, as they are called, of the Roman pontiffs to his book of canons around the fiftieth year after the death of our Leo. It seemed the height of rashness to suspect that this collector, writing in Rome itself and examining all the archives of the Apostolic See, had lacked authentic copies or had preferred more recent examples to them.

Dionysius’s Collection contains the first and second chapters of this letter in the form in which they are read in the recent editions. But it lacks several other portions—namely, the third and fourth chapters and half of the fifth—which concern Donatus, Maximus, Aggarus, Tyberianus, and the sacred virgins violated by barbarian oppression.[1331]

After examining this, who would not immediately declare that these portions should be rejected as additions, while judging all the others genuine and authentic—especially since some manuscript codices support Dionysius? Two Thuanean manuscripts likewise lack what Dionysius lacks. Two other Thuanean manuscripts, together with one Cambridge manuscript, do contain it, but outside the context of the letter, after its ending and conclusion, like an appendix.[Col. 1301A]

On the other hand, six other manuscripts of much better age and quality—the Thuaneus, Trecopithoeanus, Victorinus, Herovallianus, and the two Barberini manuscripts 77 and 2888—contain what is absent from the codices cited above: namely, chapters 3 and 4 and half of chapter 5. They do not, however, contain the second chapter, except for its first nine lines, nor the end of the fifth chapter.

Among printed codices, the Parisian edition of the Councils agrees with these manuscripts. It appeared in folio in 1524 and in octavo in 1535 under the direction of Jacobus Merlinus, a doctor of theology. The acts into which Leo’s letters were inserted are found in that edition, and this letter to the Moors appears in the same form in which it is found in the six aforementioned manuscripts.[Col. 1301B]

Two others join them: one from the monastery of Régny, of the Cistercian order, near Auxerre; the other from Saint-Marien of Auxerre, of the Premonstratensian order. In these, the same material is found as in the six manuscripts mentioned above.

Finally, a third edition was compiled from the two editions just described. This is now in everyone’s hands and, alone, has until now deserved to be accepted by most people as genuine through its repeated impressions.

I am certain, however, that this edition has been interpolated: first, because no handwritten codices represent it to us in this form; and also because of what we are about to say concerning the other two forms, one of which, to the exclusion of the other, I am entirely persuaded should be chosen.

Although strong arguments seem to contend on both sides, we have nevertheless been compelled to yield to the authority of those codices that omit chapter 2 but preserve chapters 3 and 4 and the portion of chapter 5 rejected—or, more correctly, omitted—by the others.[Col. 1301D]

#### 1

Because the manuscript codices that favor the latter portion surpass in number and antiquity those on which the former portion rests.[Col. 1301C]

Of the four Thuanean codices that agree with the reading of Dionysius, two were written by a more recent hand, and they contain the material we reject only outside the context of the letter. The other two are Dionysius’s own Collection and therefore have no greater authority than the printed codices.

As for the Cambridge manuscript, which I was unable to consult in person, the various excerpts transmitted to us from Oxford by the distinguished Edward Bernard demonstrate that it is corrupt in very many places.

What must be said in response to the authority of Dionysius will be explained below.

By contrast, the other codices are of the highest quality: the two Barberini manuscripts, the Victorinus, Trecopithoeanus, Herovallianus, and especially the Thuaneus. The latter contains the letters of Leo that follow the Roman codex; we have had their catalogue printed. The antiquity of this collection of letters is strongly commended by its connection with the book of canons, while the diligence of the scribe is indicated by the agreement of other ancient codices and by the word *contuli*—“I have compared”—which is read at the end of this letter and several others.[Col. 1302A]

[Note: These codices prove only that the material contained in this shortened form of the letter belongs to Leo and that it represents the first form of this letter. They do not prove that the portion defended by the other codices of excellent quality is spurious; in the cited admonition we have shown that it belongs to another complete edition of the same letter.]

#### 2

Since those chapters—the third, fourth, and half of the fifth—fit together extremely well with the beginning of this letter up to the second asterisk of chapter 2 described above, it is reasonable to believe that all these portions belong to the same letter, a belief confirmed by the testimony of the ancient manuscript codices.

For in the very opening it is evident that our Leo is dealing with the African province of Caesarea. The three later chapters likewise suit that province: they discuss the conversion or ordination of several Novatianist and Donatist bishops and barbarian oppression, all of which are entirely appropriate to the condition of the African region during the troubled period in which Leo wrote.

#### 3

By contrast, everything extending from the second asterisk of chapter 2 to the end of that same chapter is understood to be wholly foreign both to the condition in which the African Church then found itself,[Col. 1302B] to Saint Leo’s style, and finally to the customs and practices of the African bishops.

[Note: These arguments, by which he seeks to prove that it was foreign to the state in which the African Church then stood to forbid the consecration of bishops in just any villages where they had not previously existed, rest on a false hypothesis. For not all Africa was then under the barbarians. Mauretania, to which this letter pertains, remained subject to the Romans until the year 455; and Quesnell himself, later, when treating the date of this letter, judges that it was written before this province came under barbarian rule. The argument from Victor of Vita concerns the time when Mauretania was occupied by barbarians and therefore contributes nothing to the present question.][Col. 1301D; Col. 1302D]

How unnecessary it would have been for our pontiff to prohibit the consecration of bishops in just any places or castles in the African region, and in places where bishops had not previously existed, while allowing them only over larger populations and in more populous cities! What reason could Leo have had at that time to fear that the priestly dignity would become cheap among the Africans through its very multiplication, or that it would be diminished by excessive multiplication resulting from the ease of ordination?

Who could believe that these and similar abuses had been attempted in some Churches of that region, as a certain Bishop Restitutus is said to have complained, when during that period the Vandals were occupying the whole of Africa, the barbarian armies were ravaging all the Churches, scarcely any bishops remained in the more important cities, and replacements for those who died could be installed only secretly and clandestinely? It was entirely impossible that anyone should have thought of assigning bishops to obscure villages and solitary townships.[Col. 1302C]

Indeed, in Leo’s time the African Churches suffered such a shortage of ecclesiastical ministers and priests that, when many captives taken by the Vandals had been given as a gift to a certain king of the Moors living in a remote part of the desert, and those captives had brought a great multitude of peoples to knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ, Victor of Vita testifies in Book I of *The Persecution of Africa* that envoys were sent to Rome by way of the extended desert routes, at the request of the new believers, to ask the pontiff to send them a presbyter and ministers. The same source records that this request was fulfilled with joy.

Who, then, could believe that an embassy to the Roman pontiff would have been undertaken with such labor and such expenditure of time and lives unless all the neighboring provinces had been so exhausted of ecclesiastical ministers that they were compelled to seek help from across the sea?

### 4

When we read in this part of the letter: “What Restitutus the bishop complained had now been done in his diocese,” etc., it is easily proved that its author was someone other than Saint Leo. It is certain that in Leo we never find the word *diocese* (*dioecesis*); indeed, in those times it was scarcely established among Roman or Eastern bishops as meaning a provincial parish subject to a particular bishop. I know that this usage was familiar to the Africans; I know also that it was used by the Gauls after Leo’s time, but I do not remember ever finding it used by the Italians.

There is, unless I am mistaken, a single passage in Innocent I, in his letter to Florentius, bishop of Tibur, where he says that “the parish belonging to his diocese.” But in this passage the word *diocese* seems to mean an administration, which is the proper force of the word; in that sense it could generally be used by exarchs, metropolitans, and any other prelates. If you substitute *administration* for this word, nothing objectionable follows in Innocent’s sentence: “the parish belonging to his administration.” In the passage of the letter we are examining, however, it means the actual places subject to the authority of that bishop Restitutus, so that the word *administration* cannot be substituted for it without making the expression obscure and barbarous: “What Restitutus the bishop complained had now been done in his administration,” etc.

> **Note.** The term *diocese* (*dioecesis*) was used to mean a provincial parish not only by the Africans, to whom Leo was writing, but also by Italians and Romans. This can be seen in Hilary, Leo’s successor, as likewise in Gelasius, Vigilius, and others. Coustantius proves, against Quesnellus, that Innocent too uses the same word not for an administration but for a provincial parish, in his note on Innocent’s letter, note L, p. 914.

### 5

What is said there concerning the case of Lupicinus—how contrary it is to the troubled circumstances of the African persecution and to the customs and discipline of that Church! Everyone knows how strongly the Africans opposed appeals across the sea. In the Council of Carthage called the Sixth, and also in the letter of the later council to Pope Celestine, they refused to submit themselves to a discipline that was unknown to them. The memory of that affair was still recent, scarcely thirty years having passed since it occurred.

Moreover, at that time the disturbances of war and the violence of persecution were ravaging all those provinces so completely that there could have been no place either for conducting an episcopal judgment or for assembling a synod. Yet the author of the letter orders the case of Lupicinus to be heard there. I add that I am persuaded that this cannot have been our Leo for the following reason: if he had been that most discerning man, he would either have summoned the case to himself when a bishop appealed to the Roman tribunal, or at least would have sent one of his own men to attend the judgment and, on his authority, examine the whole matter with the others. He would not have been content merely to write that the case should be heard there, without mentioning either the place, the judge, or the legate.

> **Note.** Quesnellus attempts to evade this appeal of Lupicinus in three ways, but all his arguments are weak and empty. As to the first—persecution and the disturbances of the barbarians who were harassing Africa—we excluded Mauritania in the preceding annotation. His second argument, concerning African customs and laws opposed to appeals across the sea, applies to clergy of the lower orders, not to bishops, as we proved at length in our observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, chapter 5, no. 12, and chapter 6, nos. 20 and following. His third argument is insulting to the most holy pontiff, since it portrays him as extremely shrewd and eager to seize opportunities for exercising his jurisdiction.
