He could have summoned the case to himself; he could have sent someone to Africa, or delegated specific judges, as the Council of Sardica itself had decreed. But he was not obliged to do what he could have done, and he preferred to entrust the matter to the provincial bishops. In this, his moderation is shown, since he did not insist upon the highest possible exercise of his authority.

### 6

I infer that the edition of this letter presented by the Dionysian collection is not genuine, whereas the edition found both in Merlin’s edition of the councils and in the six manuscripts cited is authentic: preserving chapters 3 and 4 together with part of chapter 5, they excise almost the whole of chapter 2.

The beginning of chapter 2 is such that it appears rather to be the ending and conclusion of the letter, as it actually is in other manuscripts of better quality. For the author of the letter, speaking as one who is bringing it to a close, testifies that he has dealt with everything contained in Potentius’s report. The phrase commonly read in the printed editions is shown by the manuscript codices to be an addition, and it is to be believed that it was inserted by those who attempted to alter the order of the letter and enlarge it with foreign fragments. The author then says that the only thing remaining is that they should obey his admonitions and the apostolic constitutions in concord. Yet immediately afterward follow decrees of the greatest importance: concerning bishops illicitly ordained or ordaining others; concerning the appointment of no bishops over the same small villages; concerning Restitutus’s complaints; concerning virgins violated by barbarian violence; concerning Lupicinus’s case and appeal to the apostolic see; and concerning another man superimposed in his place.

It is therefore perfectly clear that the opening words of the chapter have no connection whatever with what follows and have been placed outside their original position. Moreover, several things are repeated awkwardly in that part of the letter which had already been written a second and third time in the earlier chapter—for example, the indulgence which he declares that he has shown, and the greater punishment with which he threatens to punish those who henceforth despise the sacred canons.

He also determines in two distinct places of the letter what should be done with virgins oppressed by barbarian violence, and he does not give the same ruling in both. In chapter 8 of our edition he decrees—or rather advises—as follows: “They will be more worthy of praise if they do not dare to compare themselves with virgins who have remained undefiled.” But in the passage which we reject, as though he had written nothing earlier about those virgins, he gives this ruling: “They are neither to be cast down to the rank of widows nor counted among the number of sacred and persevering virgins.” He then decrees that communion is not to be given to them unless they have been approved. Anyone can easily see that these statements, if they are Leo’s, cannot belong to the same letter.

> **Note.** We answered this objection in the admonition, no. 14, where all the points are reconciled from the two copies of this letter. Although Quesnellus defends only the abbreviated edition or form as genuine, he frequently replaces readings excluded from this first edition and form with others taken from the second, Hadrianic edition or form, which he considers interpolated. We have published both distinctly, with the proper readings of each form. From their comparison it will be clear what Leo wrote in his first revision, what he altered or added in his second revision, and what Quesnellus rather confused and corrupted.

### 7

The style of this part seems to me to differ from Leo’s style. I can scarcely persuade myself that our most eloquent bishop would have used expressions such as “to be moved more particularly and more favorably,” “to escape harm to one’s own honor,” “to preside over the episcopal helm,” “while the matter is pending,” and so forth. The last of these, in particular, seems to me to have been familiar only to later pontiffs or canonists.

> **Note.** Since the entire context of this chapter, attested by the best and most ancient manuscripts, displays Leo’s syntax, it is the work of a captious and overly fastidious person to select a few expressions which, while they would offend no reader free from prejudice, could, if necessary, be defended by other certain testimonies of Leo.

### 8

This is a testimony of great importance in the matter of the Isidorian collection, first because of its antiquity—for it appears to be almost nine hundred years older—and secondly because of the agreement of the manuscripts belonging to it. Finally, Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, who is said to have published that collection and perhaps interpolated it—or whoever else among the ancients assembled those letters of the Roman pontiffs and inserted them into the collection—was entirely opposed to shortening this part of the letter, in which the authority of the Roman see shone forth wonderfully through the appeal of Lupicinus, the African bishop. On the contrary, he forged or interpolated so many letters for no other purpose than to support and enlarge the authority of the Roman see.

> **Note.** The author of the Isidorian collection did not fabricate so many decretals with the purpose of supporting or enlarging Roman authority. Rather, he did so in order, as far as possible, to withdraw bishops from the authority of metropolitans and provincial councils. For that reason he supplied this letter in abbreviated form: in copying Leo’s letters, he used the Hispanic collection, which presents the same letter in this abbreviated form. Hence it is not surprising that he did not present it either in full or in the form of the Hadrianic collection, since he did not use that collection in copying Leo’s letters.

Thus he found the letter in the ancient manuscripts which he used in precisely the form in which he presented it in his collection.

### 9

The authority of the manuscript codices that agree with the Dionysian collection is greatly weakened by the fact that in all other places they agree both among themselves and with that collection. It consequently appears that one was copied from another and that they ought therefore to count as a single witness.

The title common to all of them is: “On the case of Lupicinus the bishop.” This title itself causes me either to suspect the entire second chapter of being an insertion or to conclude that it was transferred here from elsewhere. For although this letter is extremely long and contains decrees of far greater importance—which ought to have supplied material for a more expansive title and several chapters—the author directs his attention solely to this chapter, where mention is made of the appeal of some Lupicinus to the apostolic see, while omitting everything else. This rightly gives grounds for suspecting that the letter was deliberately corrupted and interpolated by someone wishing to derive support from it for appeals across the sea.

> **Note.** The similar titles and readings in these codices, though different from those of the abbreviated edition, prove that this second, Hadrianic edition is different from the abbreviated edition; they do not, however, prove that it is corrupt or interpolated. The variants themselves do not come from a copyist or interpolator, but have Leo himself as their author. Leo first composed the abbreviated form; afterward, because of certain new circumstances, he added some material and altered certain passages. This will become clear from our admonition, no. 15, and from the annotations. It is astonishing that Quesnellus adopted certain readings from the edition which he represents as defective and corrupt. The two passages which he proposes as examples of corruption we have fully defended in annotations 27 and 39; in the second case we have shown that Leo himself altered and improved the reading of the earlier form.

I shall omit nearly ten places in which those more recent manuscripts of Thuaneus and the Dionysian edition agree in a faulty and corrupt reading. One or two examples will suffice, from which judgment may be formed about the rest.

All the printed copies and the manuscripts Barberinianus, Thuaneus, Victorinus, Herovallianus, and Trecopithianus have this passage in chapter 1 of the letter (chapter 4 in our edition):

> “All of them had passed from their earliest childhood to more advanced years through the stages of ecclesiastical discipline, so that each person’s former life supplied testimony on his behalf; nor could there be any doubt about the advancement of one who, for his many labors, chaste conduct, and energetic actions, deserved the reward of a higher position.”

There is nothing here that does not breathe Leo’s style, discipline, and genius. In place of this, however, both Dionysius and the two manuscripts agreeing with him read only:

> “Those who, having advanced for a long time through the several grades of office, had given credible proof of themselves, so that for each person the record of his life and actions bore witness.”

Again, at the end of the same chapter 1 (chapter 5 in our edition), the printed editions and the better manuscripts read:

> “Without prejudging the statutes of the apostolic see, or the decrees of our predecessors and of ourselves, by which it was salutarily established that no one should …”

But Dionysius and the two manuscripts agreeing with him read:

> “Without prejudicing the statutes of the apostolic see, or dissolving the rules of the blessed Fathers, by which it was salutarily established that no one should …”

Who does not see that the former passage, especially, was truncated by recent persons and adapted to the practice of a later discipline? And who does not see that so evident a corruption removes all authority from those manuscripts and from the pseudo-Dionysian edition?

> **Note.** He rightly excludes this letter from Dionysius’s collection, because Dionysius Exiguus inserted neither its abbreviated nor its complete form into his collection. In addition to Quesnellus’s arguments, we may add two. First, the Hispanic collection accurately copied every pontifical letter which it found in the Dionysian collection, even adopting their titles. It would therefore have taken this letter from Dionysius as well, had it found it there. Since it presents the abbreviated letter with other titles, it derived it, like much else, from other collections. Secondly, Codex Vaticanus 5845, which presents the pure Dionysian collection, does not contain this letter in that collection but among the additions that were appended later. See the admonition, no. 11.

I call it pseudo-Dionysian because, although almost nothing among writings of this kind is older than the Dionysian collection, and although no authority seems preferable to that collection’s authority, I nevertheless believe that in this matter its testimony must be set aside. I do not hesitate to assert that this complete letter was used to enlarge and strengthen that collection, and I base this on substantial arguments.

1. The first argument comes from the titles of the decrees prefixed together to the entire Dionysian collection. Leo’s decrees are counted and listed as forty-nine. Yet it is clear that the forty-ninth and last was attached to the others by a different and later hand. It differs from them in this respect: the others merely identify the subject of the canon, whereas this one has Leo’s name at the beginning, as follows:

> “Leo to the bishops of the Moors, concerning the preservation and discipline of the canons, and that no one should presume to enter the clergy improperly and disorderly.”

We find that Dionysius did this neither in the titles of Leo’s decrees nor in those of the decrees of other pontiffs. It was all the more unnecessary to add it to this final chapter or decree, since forty-eight titles of the same pontiff had already preceded it and sufficiently indicated the author.

2. The titles of Leo’s forty-eight decrees and of the other pontiffs, collected together at the beginning of the whole collection, agree in every respect with the titles prefixed to the individual decrees in the body of the Dionysian codex. The title of this letter alone differs in the index from the title placed before the letter itself. At the beginning of the letter we read:

> “On the case of Lupicinus the bishop: Leo to all the bishops established throughout Caesarean Mauritania.”

This title is entirely different from the other title which we described above. It is therefore evident that it was not composed by Dionysius but fabricated by someone else.

3. If Dionysius had inserted this letter into his collection, he would not have presented it to us under a single title but would have divided it into several parts, assigning a title to each, as we see him do with all the other letters, even though they were much shorter than this one. This letter, undivided by any titles, occupies five complete columns in the Justellian edition. Yet the letter to Nicetas of Aquileia, which immediately precedes it—to say nothing of the others—does not fill three columns, and nevertheless is divided into eight parts with extensive titles.

4. Dionysius, a Roman abbot writing in Rome, would not have omitted from the titles matters that appeared greatly to enhance the authority and dignity of the Roman pontiff. Such a matter is the appeal of Lupicinus, an African bishop, as the fragment of the letter represents it. This is an entirely exceptional example from the African Church in Leo’s time.

5. But even if these considerations, which we have now weighed, have no force, Cresconius, the African bishop, supplies us with a decisive argument—one worth six hundred such arguments—in two surviving works.

> **Note.** Cresconius’s *Breviary* and *Collection of Canons* are not two works but one and the same. The *Breviary* is nothing other than an index or table of the canons prefixed to the *Collection of Canons*. Since it was published separately from the collection by Justellus, the impression arose that they were two works. More will be said about this in volume III, in the treatise on ancient collections and collectors of canons.

One of these works is called the *Canonical Breviary*. It contains chapters—or rather an index of the chapters—of both synodal canons and pontifical decrees included in the Dionysian collection. The other is called the *Collection*, or *Book of Canons*. In it he copied the complete canons of the councils and the decrees of the pontiffs in the order in which they are cited in the *Breviary*. He did not follow the order of councils and canons, but considered only the subject matter.

What bears upon our question is this: Cresconius followed the collection of Dionysius Exiguus in every respect, except for the numbers assigned to the African canons. He presents the same canons and the same decrees, from the same edition, in the same words and with the same numbers. It is therefore evident that this African bishop undertook to arrange Dionysius’s collection according to subject matter. All learned collectors and students of canonical manuscripts freely acknowledge this.

> **[Col. 1307B]** However carefully you examine and search through Cresconius’s *Breviary* and *Collection*, you will not find even a word excerpted from this letter of Leo to the Caesarean Moors. It is impossible to believe that Cresconius would have omitted it if he had found it in the Dionysian collection toward the end of the seventh century, when he lived. Leo’s authority, the usefulness and importance of the matters treated in the letter, and Leo’s own concern for his fellow Africans would all have commended that rescript to Cresconius. Therefore, in the period when Cresconius lived and wrote, the Dionysian collection of pontifical letters contained neither Leo’s letter to the Africans nor the decrees of Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Symmachus, or Hormisdas. Cresconius lived, as the eminent editors of the libraries of ancient canon law infer from Baronius, around the end of the seventh century, or approximately the year 690.

For this reason I am certain that this letter was not inserted into Dionysius’s collection by Dionysius himself, but was added later by someone else—perhaps by the same unknown author who enlarged that collection with the letters of the Roman pontiffs Hilary, Simplicius, Felix, Symmachus, Hormisdas, and the younger Gregory. Since the last of these was still alive in the thirty-eighth year of the eighth century, and since his decrees enacted at the Roman council around the year 720 are read at the end of this addition, it is possible to suspect that the letter of Leo under discussion was added at approximately the same time.

> **Note.** If this letter was not read in the Dionysian manuscript used by Cresconius, and for that reason was not inserted by Dionysius into his collection, it does not follow that it was added to Dionysius after Cresconius’s time. It appears that the first addition was made to some Dionysian copy shortly after the death of Symmachus. See the admonition, no. 11.

The suspicion concerning the date of this addition is strengthened by the agreement of all the oldest manuscript copies of the Dionysian collection which I have seen, and which appear to be contemporaneous or nearly contemporaneous with Emperor Charlemagne. They all present this letter. It therefore seems certain that the copy which Pope Adrian I gave as a gift to Emperor Charlemagne, and from which perhaps all the copies now preserved in Gallican libraries were made, likewise contained the same letter. Consequently, before it was carried from Rome into Gaul, the letter must have been truncated, interpolated, and inserted into the Dionysian codex sometime between Gregory the Younger and Adrian I—that is, within approximately sixty years.

Several such codices may be seen in the royal library; two in the Thuanean library; two in the Seguerian; one particularly distinguished copy in the celebrated monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris; and, in addition, a codex of venerable antiquity from the monastery of Saint Gall, which we saw through the kindness of the learned Baluzius.

The antiquity of this interpolation is also proved by Hincmar of Reims’s work of fifty-three chapters against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 5. There, from the letter to the Moors, are cited both the case of Lupicinus and—although they are not found in the Dionysian appendix—the cases of Donatus of Salicina, Maximus, Aggarus, and Tyberianus, the bishops.

It should not seem surprising that this letter was corrupted so many years after Dionysius, since Leo himself frequently complained that the letter he wrote to Flavian had been corrupted, even while he was still alive.

> **Note.** Leo at one point believed that the Greek translation of his letter had been corrupted, but he later discovered that this was false; we have shown this more fully in annotation 3 on the year 454. Quesnellus has not yet proved that this letter to the bishops of Mauritania was corrupted. Consequently, the explanation he soon gives of the manner in which this corruption was introduced must be attributed to the emptiest conjecture, and our arguments, by which we establish this part as genuine, decisively refute it.

### 1341

As for the manner in which this corruption occurred, although wishing to conjecture about it may seem the occupation of an idle person, I shall nevertheless state what occurred to me.

That part of the letter which forms chapter 2 was found by some learned person and adorned with Leo’s name. When he wished to place it in his own codex, he attached it either in the margin or at the end of Leo I’s letter to the Moors, whether because of the similarity of subject or because of the similarity of names. Indeed, it is still found at the end of the letter in certain manuscripts preserved in the Thuanean library.

Learned men know how many errors have been caused by the similarity of names. It even resulted in a letter of Leo, bishop of Bourges, being attributed to Pope Leo down to our own age. Those accustomed to handling ancient handwritten codices know how many are found in which monuments of every kind from ecclesiastical antiquity have been collected indiscriminately, with no order preserved except some loose arrangement according to subject.

There are many points of agreement between the genuine letter and that fragment. Both deal with illicit ordinations, and in both cases the pontiff responds to a consultation concerning virgins corrupted after being oppressed by barbarian violence. It was therefore easy for the fragment to pass from the side or end of the letter into the letter itself through the error of an ignorant scribe.

The collection of Gratian almost persuades me that this piece was taken from some collection of canons and decretals. In Gratian’s decree, certain passages from this second chapter are inserted as though they had not been excerpted from the letter to the Moors. Nor are they headed by the name of Leo I; they are simply and absolutely attributed to Leo, in this form: “Likewise Leo the bishop,” or simply, “Likewise Leo.” Other material drawn there from chapters 1, 3, 4, and 5 is expressly said to have been taken from the letter to the Moors.

This distinction is not detected in the later editions of Gratian, in which many things were badly corrected by Roman correctors. It is evident, however, both from the manuscript codices and from the edition published in Paris in 1531 under the supervision of a certain Theodoricus Minimitanus, as well as from the Lyon edition of Hugo a Porta, published in 1548. See Causa 1, question 1, chapter 44; Causa 15, question 11, chapter 24, *Si qui episcopi talem*; Distinction 80, *Illud sane quod ad*, chapter 4; and Causa 32, question 5.

We also read part of this piece in the fourth addition to the capitularies of the emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. But, such is the cunning of these interpolators, it is interwoven with many further additions. Its title is:

> “On the case of Lupicinus the bishop, from Leo the pope’s letter addressed to the African bishops.”

The following chapter then reads:

> “We order that the case of Lupicinus the bishop, BECAUSE THIS HAS PLEASED US, be heard there,”

and so forth, as in Dionysius, until these final words:

> “May our judgment also be confirmed.”

These are not the final words there, as they are in the Dionysian codex, for the following words are added:

> “From these matters we can learn how the others are to be treated, and how we may regret having done nothing contrary to the statutes of our predecessors. Given on the fourth day before the Ides of August.”

From this, reader, you understand how intemperate was the passion for interpolation, and how freely it ran wild in the letter we are examining.

> **Note.** Since all these stages of corruption rest upon a hypothesis which was never proved—and which is in fact disproved by our arguments—it is perfectly clear that they are mere inventions and dreams. The second stage, for example, which counts among the additions and interpolations the words “with concordant obedience” in place of “concordantly,” is so fictitious that all the Hadrianic codices accused of interpolation have *concordantly*, while the codices of the abbreviated edition, which Quesnellus himself regards as genuine, have *with concordant obedience*. See Annotation 48 (column 654, note k) on the complete letter, and Annotation 42 on the abbreviated letter. Quesnellus is troubled especially by the authority of the Roman see in matters of appeal, which is confirmed in this chapter. For that reason, most of these stages are directed toward elevating that authority under the name of interpolation.

The first plan was to enlarge the Dionysian collection with this letter to the Africans, so that the decrees of the Roman pontiff delivered to Africa might derive greater authority from the codex, and so that neither the Gallican Churches nor others could receive the Dionysian collection without at the same time embracing Roman power in matters of appeals and other aspects of this kind of discipline.

But it was not enough that the pontiff’s commands had been transmitted there unless the obligation to obey them and an example of obedience were also made apparent. For that reason these words were inserted at the beginning of chapter 2:

> “It remains, brothers, that with concordant obedience you receive salutary exhortations,”

whereas the manuscripts have only *concordantly*.

What happened next? The response of the African council to Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine—the predecessors of Leo—remained deeply fixed in their minds. That council had firmly maintained that ecclesiastical cases could not be transferred from Africa to the Roman pontiff by a written appeal. It was therefore necessary to present an appeal by an African bishop to Saint Leo, showing those African bishops repentant of their action and yielding to the right of appeal.

Hence the fragment concerning Lupicinus’s case and appeal was sewn on, together with other decrees concerning illicit ordinations and various other matters, both to conceal the plan more effectively and to suggest that the Roman pontiff possessed supreme dominion over the African Church.

Nor was this enough. In order that the pontiff’s full jurisdiction in all cases of the African Church might shine forth more clearly, it was decided that, whenever anything arose concerning the ecclesiastical state or the harmony of the priests, a full report should be sent to the Roman bishop concerning all such matters, whether resolved or still to be resolved, so that by his judgment they might either be overturned or confirmed. These are the very words of the added conclusion.

Nor did the audacity of the interpolators stop there. They wished to establish that, after an appeal had been lodged, the case could not merely be concluded in the African province in which it had arisen by judges appointed, as they say, locally by the pontiff; rather, it had to be transferred to the Roman tribunal. If on some occasion things happened otherwise, that was to be understood as having been permitted by the pontiff’s indulgence and will.

With this aim, later corrupters of the already corrupted letter inserted these words into the sentence, “We order that the case of Lupicinus be heard there”:

> “BECAUSE THIS HAS PLEASED US,”

as though the pontiff’s will ought to have the force of all reasons and all canons. I consider that idea utterly foreign to the mind of the pontiff himself.

Finally, the last addition, which is read in the fourth addition to the capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious and which has been described above, attempts to make the entire conduct of the Roman bishops appear to rest solely upon the statutes of their predecessors.

Far be it from me to think that the most holy bishops of the principal see were either the authors or accomplices of corruptions of this kind. We are persuaded that they attempted nothing of the sort, and with all our heart we profess this against innovators who eagerly seize such opportunities to assail the apostolic see with dreadful insults. All this is the work of flatterers and of men corrupted in mind, deprived of the truth, who believe gain to be piety (1 Timothy 6:5), apostolic tradition, and whatever the Christian religion holds most sacred.

There is one further matter of which I wish to warn the reader: this entire piece, which we have removed from the letter, is found in Merlin’s edition of the letters of Saint Leo, not inserted into this letter but attached to a spurious letter to the bishops of Gaul and Germany concerning chorepiscopi. Truly, the lid is worthy of the pot. Let anyone who delights in such rubbish inquire how or for what purpose this was done.

This certainly demonstrates plainly that the torn piece was once scattered among various places, now attached to one letter and now to another, until at last the impostor decided to fix it in the letter to the Africans.

If the distinguished Baluzius had carefully read and weighed all these matters, he would not have doubted that the piece was an insertion. Nor would he have concealed the irresistible arguments which we have brought from the manuscript codices and from Cresconius’s *Breviary* and *Collection* against the interpolator of Dionysius Exiguus and of the Leonine letter, in addition to the other indications of interpolation that can be drawn from the fragment’s position, titles, and very appearance as it lies in the collector’s work. The other points which he annotates on this subject in the fourth addition to the *Capitularies*, p. 1249, are weak and require no answer.

From the restoration of this letter and the recognition of the interpolation in the later editions, all the observations which John David had built upon it collapse.

> **Note.** Indeed, from the vindication of this chapter—which Quesnellus attempted to attack and accuse of interpolation by nothing but empty conjectures—it is sufficiently clear that the arguments which John David built upon it are firmly established.

For, after the removal of these inserted pieces, David asserted:

1. That the Sardican canons were held in the highest esteem by Saint Leo. No one may deny this, but it is now clear upon how weak a foundation David asserted it.

2. That a large part of this letter was composed from several of those canons.

3. That the third canon in particular, by which appeals are vindicated for the Roman bishop, was cited by the same authority in the case of Lupicinus.

4. That by the authority of the fourth canon it was forbidden for another bishop to be superimposed upon a bishop appealing to the Roman see.

5. That mention was likewise made of the sixth canon, which forbids bishops to be ordained in villages.

6. He is especially eager to insist that this letter, sent to the Africans and composed from the Sardican canons, is a most powerful argument that the entire commotion stirred up at the Sixth Council of Carthage against appeals ultimately subsided to the advantage of the apostolic see. For, he says, we have seen that the successor of Celestine, exercising the same right over which the dispute had then arisen, not only sent legates to Africa but also placed before the Africans the Sardican canons, on account of which the controversy had arisen, as rules of discipline accepted by them.

7. That the pontiff alone had authority to judge the cases of African bishops who appealed.

8. That he alone also had authority to restore African bishops to ecclesiastical communion whenever he judged it expedient, even though they had been excluded from it by a provincial decree.

When that writer asserts these and similar propositions from the fragment of this letter, he can now learn from the preceding observations how unstable and ruinous was the foundation upon which he attempted to build his opinion.

1345

1. As for the year in which this letter was written [Note: See our admonition, no. 16.], we have no certain information. The most eminent Cardinal Baronius, in his *Annals*, and Blondel, in his *Apology for St. Jerome’s opinion concerning presbyters*, assign it to the year of Our Lord 456—the former on the occasion of the embassy sent to the Roman pontiff by Catholic captives for the establishment of a new Church that was arising within the dominion of a certain king of the Moors; the latter following Baronius’ lead incautiously in an obscure matter.

I cannot, however, persuade myself of this. First, it is established that in the preceding year, namely 455, the city of Rome was captured by the Vandals. This disaster and sack so occupied our excellent shepherd Leo that he was compelled to interrupt, to some extent, his care and concern for distant Churches. For this reason we possess no letter written by him between the fifth day before the Ides of May 455 and the fifth day before the Ides of June 457, so that the exchange of letters appears to have been interrupted for a full two years. For, after the Vandal disaster, holy Leo was wholly occupied, as the *Book of the Roman Pontiffs* testifies, with restoring the sacred ministries, repairing the ruin of the city, and making good the losses that the barbarian army had inflicted upon the community.

Moreover, it seems quite clear to me from Victor of Vita’s narrative that Leo could have established or ordered nothing concerning the African Churches either immediately after this disaster or even in the following years. In Book I of *The African Persecution*, he relates that Geiseric, as soon as he had gained possession of the city of Carthage, divided among his army, as he says, by lot of inheritance, each of the African provinces—retaining for himself Byzacena, Abaritana, Getulia, and part of Numidia—and assigning Zeugitana, or Proconsular Africa, to his forces, while the emperor Valentinian still defended the remaining provinces, although they had already been devastated. After Valentinian’s death, which was inflicted by the sword in 455, Geiseric gained possession of the whole extent of Africa. From this it is evident that after Valentinian’s death scarcely any further communication could have existed between the African Churches and Leo, since the Vandals were occupying and ravaging all Africa [Col. 1312A]. Nor could any judicial procedure or order of priestly consecrations have been established there. It is therefore necessary to place the date of this letter within those fifteen years extending from the beginning of St. Leo’s episcopate to Valentinian’s death—that is, from 440 until the beginning of 455.

Indeed, Leo himself calls that period merely “unsettled,” and it appears from this that the letter was written while Valentinian still possessed Mauritania. Although everything there was unsettled because of the neighboring barbarian forces threatening what remained of Africa, and although much disturbance had consequently been introduced into the Churches, the bishops had not yet been deprived of freedom in ordinations. [Note: [Col. 1311D]

The disposition of this ill-minded man, hostile to pontifical authority, is revealed here, as though the appeals of the bishops of Africa and their references to the apostolic see of Peter were something new and contrary to the right of its Primacy, by which, through divine institution, it presides over the whole Church. We have sufficiently restrained and refuted this writer’s bold effort concerning appeals in the observations to Dissertation 5, where he uttered similar things. What was proved there concerning the right of appeal can be proved equally, indeed much more strongly, concerning the right of reference, for which far more documents and examples are available.

Thus, what the holy pontiff undertook, instructed by the reports of travelers concerning the elimination of abuses, he transfers—as Quesnell himself later admits—from the impulse of that concern which, by divine institution, he ought to exercise over the universal Church [Col. 1312D] into an ambition to extend his jurisdiction. He notes that Leo did this voluntarily, without any African bishop inviting him. But if the Africans had been negligent, were so many abuses to be concealed by the one to whom Christ had entrusted the care of the whole Church? Potentius, however, who disclosed these evils in his report, was an African bishop. The bishops Restitutus and David were also Africans: one complained about certain abuses in his province, while the other had been sent to Rome after Potentius and had then returned to Mauritania with Leo’s instructions and letters.

After such an audacious censure, he excuses the holy pontiff in Casaubon’s words. But this very confession by a heterodox man ought to have taught him not to spread suspicion of ambition or of an encroachment upon another’s jurisdiction concerning so holy a pontiff.]

And certainly it seems to me highly consonant with the prudence and ingenuity of our Leo that he seized the opportunity to strengthen the authority of his see over the African Churches. No one is unaware how often and with what great efforts Leo’s predecessors had attempted this, nor how much Boniface and Celestine themselves labored toward that end in Leo’s own time, while the Africans had always stubbornly defended the customs of their Churches. They had to await a more favorable opportunity; and when it presented itself to Leo, that most resolute man did not allow it to escape him.

Together with African liberty, that former vigor of discipline had perished which both St. Cyprian and the councils of those regions display to us. Countless Churches, now deprived of their pastors and ministers, were groaning under Vandal tyranny. Carthage itself—the mother of all the African Churches and the head of the entire region—lay prostrate in pitiable ruin, deprived of its senate, its clergy, and its bishop. For Geiseric ordered Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage, together with a great multitude of clergy, to be placed upon ships with broken timbers and committed to the waves of the sea. God, in the mercy of his goodness, graciously brought them by a prosperous voyage to Naples in Campania [Col. 1312C].

And, so that nothing might be lacking that could aid the pontiff’s plan, the emperor Valentinian was moved according to Leo’s direction and will. How he used that power against the primate of the Gallican Churches in accordance with his wishes is shown by the constitution of that same emperor issued against St. Hilary of Arles in 445.

With matters standing thus, and with the protection of Augustus always ready to serve Leo’s wishes, he seriously considered bringing the affairs of the African Churches to the knowledge and judgment of his own see—not those regions that lay oppressed under Vandal rule, but those that still obeyed Valentinian, among which Caesarean Mauritania was especially important.

Accordingly, he sent Potentius to the bishops of that province as his representative. He also gave him letters to them, so that he might investigate carefully illicit ordinations, violations of the rules of the canons, and other matters of this kind, and report them in full to the apostolic see, whose authority he bore [Col. 1313A]. When St. Leo had been informed by Potentius’ reports, he wrote this second, longer letter to the Africans. In it he maintains the moderation appropriate to the circumstances, while displaying the vigor necessary to abolish abuses and establish his authority.

All this, moreover, was undertaken by Leo on his own initiative, without any African bishop inviting him, as the very beginning of this letter testifies. There he states that he had been informed only by the reports of travelers about illicit usurpations in African ordinations; that he had been moved to send a legate solely because piety required it; and that he had acted under the impulse of that concern which, by divine institution, he was obliged to exercise toward the universal Church.

As I write this, I seem to hear some Catholics murmuring on one side and sectarians applauding with both hands on the other, as though they thought we were accusing the Roman pontiff of evil ambition and of diminishing another’s jurisdiction. I shall satisfy both parties with the words of Casaubon [Col. 1313B], with which neither non-Catholics dare, nor Catholics ought, to disagree in this matter.

Thus that most learned man—would that he had also been Catholic!—writes in Exercise 15 on Cardinal Baronius’ *Ecclesiastical Annals*:

“We do not fail to recognize how great a defender of the sincere faith this Leo was, how many labors he endured for the true faith, and how useful they were to the Church of God. Nor do I doubt that the great zeal which we see him exerting to enlarge the Roman see proceeded from a good principle and was directed toward an excellent end. At that time the most abandoned heretics were devastating the Churches. Like boars entering a vineyard, they inflicted great slaughter daily, and there was no one who could oppose their progress and thereby assist the good cause, except the Roman bishop. No one experienced in the affairs of the Church is unaware that for many centuries God used the work of the Roman pontiffs to preserve intact the doctrine of the true faith.

“Understanding this, and taught by daily experience how much the true faith depended upon having an especially firm refuge always prepared for it in the Roman see, Leo the Great did everything possible to secure that result. This should seem less surprising because, at that time, every good man believed that it was advantageous to the Church of God—and in fact it truly was so in those times.”

I think no one will fail most willingly to subscribe to these words.

The letter was therefore written during the period extending from Leo’s election to Valentinian’s death; but it is difficult to determine the precise year. From what has been said, it is not obscure that it belongs to the beginning of Leo’s episcopate, and for that reason we have thought it should be placed first of all. We possess no earlier certain date than 10 October 443, by which time four years had already passed since the capture of Carthage and the exile overseas of the bishop and clergy of that city.

There is one objection that may be raised against this dating of the letter: namely, that from chapter 5—which in earlier editions forms the final part of the preceding section—it appears that this was not the first of our pontiff’s letters, and that other decrees of his had preceded it. He cites them in these words:

“Without prejudicing the statutes of the apostolic see, nor the decrees of our predecessors and of ourselves, by which it has salutarily been established that no layman, supported by any kind of popular favor, should ascend to the first, second, or third rank in the Church [Col. 1314A] before he has reached that dignity through the lawful stages of advancement…”

These words seem to indicate Letter 12 (now 14) to Anastasius of Thessalonica, where chapter 3 decrees:

“That the man who is to be ordained, even if supported by the testimony of a good life, must not be a layman, a neophyte, or the husband of a second wife.”

This, however, does not harm our opinion. Leo could have issued certain decrees during the first three years of his pontificate by which he established the discipline he mentions. Moreover, the passage does not seem to me to refer to the decree in the letter to Anastasius, since that decree contains no mention of the second or third rank, nor of the various stages by which laymen were to advance to the priesthood.

Even if it should happen that the letter was issued later, its first position has nevertheless been assigned more conveniently, since it fills the otherwise empty three-year period rather than, if reserved for a lower place, interrupting the chronological order of letters whose dates are certain.

What concerns the correction of the remainder of the text, whether variant readings or readings rejected to the margin, you will find either in the margin [Col. 1314B] or briefly noted here.

2. “Against the commands of divine law.” Thus four manuscripts of Thuaneus together with the Cantabrigian, as well as Dionysius Exiguus, Letter 3 of Pope Hadrian II to the Emperor Basil, and Gratian, Distinction 61. In place of these words, both the common editions and the manuscript of Trecopithoeus and one of Thuaneus have: “Concerning transgression.”

1349

3. Gregory of Neocaesarea, in his canonical letter, chapter 1, thinks that a different decision should be made concerning virgins of this kind who have been violated by barbaric force. He believes that judgment should be made from the woman’s previous life: if she had been free from every suspicion, he absolves the violated virgin; but if not, he considers that one should not readily communicate with such a woman in prayers.

4. “With one accord.” Thus it is read in seven manuscript codices and in Dionysius Exiguus. It is also found in the pseudo-Isidorian letters, which have been assembled from fragments of this letter. In later editions, however, instead of “with one accord” [Col. 1314C], we read “with harmonious obedience.” The manuscripts establish that Leo did not write it in that form.

## To Letter XIII

To the metropolitan bishops of Achaia. (Read: of Illyricum.)

The present letter has been restored to us by the Roman collection of Lucas Holstenius. From it we understand that the Illyrian metropolitans replied to St. Leo only after a considerable delay—for a full two years had intervened [Note: We have conjectured that several letters written by both sides during these two years have been lost; see note 3 (Col. 664, no. i) on this letter.]—and we learn at the same time that not a few of them resisted and submitted only reluctantly to the authority which Leo had both confirmed for Anastasius and considerably enlarged by substantial additions.

Lucas Holstenius conjectures that the letter concerns Peter, metropolitan of Corinth, and his illicit ordinations; certainly chapter 3 touches upon him. The same most illustrious scholar asserts that Senecio was bishop of Scodra, Lucas of Dyrrachium, and Vigilantius of Larissa. He further suspects that “Atticus” should be read instead of “Antiochus,” [Note: We do not agree. See our note 2 on the same letter (Col. 663, no. h).] Atticus having been metropolitan of Nicopolis in Old Epirus; concerning him, see Letter 12 (now 14), chapter 1.

[Col. 1314D]

1. “More important cases among the bishops.” He does not reserve such cases for judgment at Rome, but wishes them to be referred to Anastasius—not all of them, however, but those that cannot be settled in the provinces subject to him. Finally, he does not so much command that Anastasius investigate and conclude them as judge, but wishes them to be settled by him as arbitrator, under the fear of divine judgment.

The same arrangement is found more or less in Letter 4 (now 6) to Anastasius and in Letter 5 to the same metropolitans, which were published above from Holstenius, except that in this letter he seems to claim somewhat less for himself than in the preceding letters.

In Letter 12 (now 14), which he wrote to Anastasius concerning Atticus, metropolitan of Old Epirus, Leo does not say that it was necessary for him to suspend more important matters and more difficult conclusions of cases pending the latter’s judgment, but only that it was permitted to him. From this it also follows that judgments in major cases were referred to greater sees not because metropolitan bishops lacked authority, but because of the difficulty of the questions that arose. Since such questions were examined more frequently and by more people, they were finally settled on the advice of the wiser.

Indeed, St. Leo refers at least some of these matters to consultation rather than judgment, as is clear from the following words of the earlier letter, Letter 4 (now 6), to Anastasius, chapter 5:

“If any major case should arise which your Fraternity, presiding there, could not decide, let your report sent to us consult us, so that, with the Lord revealing it—whose mercy we profess to be the source of whatever we can do—we may write back whatever he has inspired us to write.”

[Note: In Letter 6 to Anastasius, chapter 5, Leo reserves two kinds of cases for himself: (1) those that Anastasius could not settle; and (2) those in which an appeal had been made to the apostolic see. Since neither of these kinds of cases is under discussion in the present letter, it is not surprising that St. Leo reserves nothing here for himself. If some cases could not be settled in the provinces but could be settled by the bishop of Thessalonica, it is clear that he had been appointed not merely as arbitrator but also as judge, as appears from Letter 14, chapter 7, where Leo reserves for himself only the more serious case that had not been settled by Anastasius’ judgment.]

2. “The brethren invited in the greatest cases, etc.” From this too you may learn that the greater and greatest cases which could not be settled in the provinces did not depend solely upon the decision of the exarch, but were examined and concluded in a council of bishops summoned from different provinces.

3. “Because the authority of the canons has also defined this, and the very principle of preserving unity.” The reference is evidently to Canon 16 of Nicaea and Canons 18 and 19 of Sardica. Indeed, it seems to me that St. Leo also had regard to Canon 5 of the First Council of Carthage, no less than to those canons. [Note: Whenever Leo cites canons, he always means the Nicene and Sardican canons designated by the name of Nicene, which alone the Roman Church had received down to this pontiff’s time, as we shall see in the treatise on the ancient collections of canons in Volume III. If he adduces a reason found in other canons, this is incidental: several persons can independently devise the same reason.] For the principle of preserving unity that he mentions, and the reference to an agreement committed to writing, belong neither to Nicaea nor to Sardica.

The Council of Nicaea contains neither point. Sardica has something concerning the principle of unity, but the Council of Carthage expressly contains both in these words:

“Bishop Privatus of Vegesela said: I suggest to your Holiness that you establish that it is not lawful for anyone to receive another’s cleric without letters from his own bishop, to retain him, or to take for himself a layman from another’s congregation in order to ordain him without the knowledge of the bishop whose congregation he belongs to.

“Bishop Gratus said: This observance preserves peace, for I also remember that it was established in the most holy Council of Sardica that no one should seize a man belonging to another’s congregation; but if he should happen to be necessary, let him ask his colleague and possess him with consent.”

See also the preceding Letter 12 (now 14) of St. Leo to Anastasius concerning Atticus, chapter 9.

Some are surprised that Gratus cited the Sardican rather than the Nicene Council in confirmation of Privatus’ statement, and they draw from this a strong argument in favor of the authority of that council. But there is no reason to make so much of this, nor is there any hidden mystery here. Gratus, hearing Privatus speak against the seizure of other men’s clerics, first cited what had most readily remained in his memory.

He mentioned the Sardican rather than the Nicene Council because the former was more recent and because he himself had taken part in it with many bishops of the African diocese. Such is human nature: people are more likely to bring forward what happened to them as witnesses, supporters, or participants than what they have learned from the report of others. This was also because the principle of peace and concord, which Gratus had mentioned, had been set forth in the Sardican council, though not likewise in the Nicene.

Finally, the weakness of the argument that this was intended to establish the authority of the Sardican canons and prove their use in Africa is evident from the fact that the actual words of the canons are neither produced nor cited by others, and that they are mentioned only from a possibly recent memory of events that had taken place there, not from the archives of the Church of Carthage. That they were not preserved in those archives is amply testified both by this passage and by the letter of the African Fathers assembled under Aurelius to Pope Celestine.

[Note: Gratus’ mention of the Sardican canons at the Council of Carthage is not such a weak argument for their authority as Quesnell represents it here. Rather, his argument is weak because Gratus does not produce the actual words of the canon but uses the expression “I remember,” since the words of other canons are not ordinarily recited in councils. Osius of Corduba likewise used the expression “I remember” at the Sardican synod, Canon 14, when speaking of the Council of Eliberis, which certainly possessed the highest authority among the Spaniards.

Who, moreover, could believe that the Africans held the canons of the Council of Sardica in little esteem and brought no copy of them with them to Africa, when African bishops who were present had confirmed them and one of the canons had been issued especially for the Africans, apparently at the insistence of Gratus?

If the Africans were ignorant of these canons under Celestine, this seems to have resulted from the fact that, being sufficiently instructed in more recent canons in which the older ones were repeated, they did not spend much time examining the ancient canons kept in the archives.

Certainly, the Council of Carthage under Gratus, where the Sardican Council was praised, was preserved in the archives of the African Church. Its canons were found there not only under Boniface of Carthage in the *Book of Canons*, from which one was inserted into the synod of the year 525, but also under Aurelius and Augustine at the time of the Council of Carthage in 419, in which two of those canons are found repeated. Nevertheless, Augustine was unaware of them when he wrote against the Donatists in 406.

For when they produced against him the Sardican letter to Donatus of Carthage, if he had known Gratus’ canons, he could have offered an easier and more effective response, by which the Donatists’ fraud would have been more clearly exposed: namely, that the Catholic Sardican Council, in which not Donatus but Gratus of Carthage had participated, as is learned from the cited canon, could not have written the alleged letter to Donatus, the pseudo-bishop of Carthage. He could thereby have confirmed much more clearly that the council which, under the name of Sardica, wrote to Donatus was an assembly of Arians, whereas the true Sardican Council communicated with Gratus and the other African Catholics, not with Donatus and the Donatist schismatics.

It must indeed be admitted that, in their letter to Celestine, the Africans indicate that, concerning the two Sardican canons that had been cited as Nicene, they examined not only the Nicene canons existing in their archives but also copies of other synods, and found those canons in none of the Fathers’ councils. It therefore appears that no copy of the Sardican Council existed in their archives.

Yet since it cannot be denied that some copy of the acts of Sardica had been brought to Africa by the Africans, since certain canons had been composed on behalf of the Africans, and since, according to Athanasius, several other Africans had subscribed to those same acts, it must be said that in the time of Celestine the Africans did not exercise all the diligence in examining their archives that Ferrandus of Carthage later applied more effectively. Having found those same canons transcribed from some copy in a particular arrangement, Ferrandus inserted them into his abridgment of the canons.]

TO LETTER XIV. XII IN QUESNEL.

To Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica.

[Col. 1317A]

1. No consular dating is attached to this letter, by means of which its year could be determined [Note: We showed in Note 1 (Col. 666, no. m) that this letter was written after the preceding one.]. Nevertheless, we do not assign it rashly to the year 445. In the preceding year, the responsibilities of the apostolic see for Illyricum and the neighboring provinces were entrusted to Anastasius, and therefore the letter cannot have been written earlier.

The events and measures undertaken by the bishop of Thessalonica through that delegated authority of Leo against Atticus, metropolitan of Old Epirus, the long journey of Atticus and his fellow provincials to Rome, and the examination of their entire case in the Roman court consumed at least a year. The letter therefore could not have been written before the middle of the following year. This is further confirmed by Leo’s words in chapter 1:

“For you have an abundance,” he says, “of writings containing our admonitions, by which we have frequently instructed you concerning the moderation of all your actions,” and so forth.

I also think I can establish with certainty from the following letter—now the preceding one—which was dated 6 January, that this letter was written before 446.

First, it is probable that the entire dispute between Anastasius and the metropolitans of those provinces arose on account of the vicariate granted by Leo, and during the two-year period between Leo’s first letter to them and their agreement, which the later letter—now the preceding one—reports. No other cause for so long a delay appears than that same dispute; once it had been settled, they submitted.

Second, the later letter—now the preceding one, or Letter 13—contains several statements indicating that peace and concord had been restored not long before.

Third, in chapter 2 of that letter he warns the metropolitans not to refuse to attend the councils summoned by Anastasius, and adds:

“Especially since our moderation has taken care that the necessity of assembling should not be announced frequently or for trivial causes, and that the presence of two or three bishops from each province should suffice, so that what would be burdensome to many may be light for a few.”

Who does not see in these words an indication of chapter 10 of this letter, where Leo says:

“In summoning bishops to you, we wish you to be most moderate, lest under the appearance of greater diligence you seem to glory in injuries inflicted upon your brethren. Therefore, if some major cause should arise for which it is necessary to summon a fraternal assembly, two bishops from each province should suffice to come to your Fraternity,” and so forth.

Fourth, what Leo decrees in chapter 5 of this letter—

“That no one is to be ordained against the will and without the request of the people, nor without the consent of the clergy and people”—

was enacted because of the ordination of the bishop of Thespiae, who had been consecrated against the will and opposition of the inhabitants, concerning which Anastasius had reported, as appears from chapter 3 of the later—now the earlier—Letter 13.

Fifth, both letters establish that another’s cleric is not to be received against the will of his own bishop: this letter in chapter 9, and the following—now the preceding—letter in chapter 4.

Sixth, finally, Leo indicates at the end of the subsequent letter that this letter to Anastasius was written either on the same day or shortly before it [Note: We proved in Note 16 on Letter 13 that these words indicate another letter that has been lost. [Col. 1318D]]:

“More fully, however, those things must be observed which we wrote to that brother and our fellow bishop Anastasius concerning what should be guarded; and we wish these matters to reach your knowledge through his own letter.”

So much concerning the year in which the letter was issued.

It is otherwise surprising that, in the dispute that arose in the year 517 between the bishops of Thessalonica and Nicopolis, no mention was made of the present letter, since it would have shed considerable light upon the rights of the Church of Thessalonica.

2. “By authority.” Thus most codices, as well as Dionysius Exiguus. The Corbeiensis, Victorinus, one Thuaneus, and the Trecopithoeanus manuscripts [Col. 1318A], together with the editions, have “by the see” in the margin. There is no difference in meaning.

3. “From us.” Thus five Thuaneus codices, the Corbeiensis, Cantabrigensis, Trecopithoeanus, the Isidorian manuscripts, and Dionysius Exiguus, in place of the reading formerly given: “From the apostolic see.”

4. “But those who seek what is theirs, etc.” We have restored this passage from Dionysius and Cresconius and from the Corbeiensis, Cantabrigensis, Trecopithoeanus, and five Thuaneus manuscripts. We nevertheless give the old reading:

“But those who seek what is theirs, not what is Jesus Christ’s, are easily distinguished from this law; and while they seek rather to dominate than to provide for their subjects, honor pleases them, pride puffs them up,” and so forth.

Who could understand this?

5. “Metropolitan.” Crabbe, Nicolinus, Canisius, Sichardus, and Surius read “Nicopolitan.” It is certain, even from the subscriptions of the Council of Chalcedon, that the bishop of Nicopolis was in fact metropolitan of Old Epirus. Moreover, from the dispute that arose between the bishop of Nicopolis and the bishop of Thessalonica in the time of Pope Hormisdas, it appears that the former metropolitan of Epirus eagerly seized the opportunity to exempt himself from the authority of the bishop of Thessalonica, an opportunity he had gained from the Acacian schism, to which the bishop of Thessalonica at that time adhered.

This had also been attempted before St. Leo’s time, as is testified by the letters of Pope Boniface to Rufus and to the Illyrian bishops in Holstenius, or in volume IV of Labbe’s Councils, p. 1702. From these letters it may be inferred [Note: This is certain concerning some, but not concerning the majority.] that many bishops of those regions had not acquiesced in the statutes of the Roman see issued concerning the Thessalonian vicariate and had endured with great reluctance their subjection to the bishop of Thessalonica.

Hence I suspect that the entire controversy discussed in this letter arose because Atticus either postponed or refused to present himself at the synod of Thessalonica summoned by Anastasius, offering as an excuse, as Anastasius complained, that he was ill.

Among the other privileges of the bishop of Thessalonica, as exercising the office of the apostolic see in those regions, was this. In the words of Innocent to Rufus:

“When some ecclesiastical matter must be discussed or investigated either in your own province or in the provinces mentioned, you may take with you whichever bishops you wish as companions from whatever Churches you choose. With their faith and moderation, you should direct as the best and principal arbitrator whatever necessity or case may require, and, since you have been specially chosen by us, settle it as the chief mediator.”

They often resisted this arrangement, so that Sixtus and Leo were compelled to recommend with particular insistence that no one summoned to the synod of the metropolitans should disdain to come or refuse to attend the holy gathering to which he ought to hasten. See Stephanus Baluzius’ appendix to Book XV of Peter de Marca.

Read also Pope Sixtus’ letter in Holstenius’ Roman collection, or in volume IV of the more recent edition of the Councils, and the following—now preceding—letter of Leo, chapter 2. If you compare it with chapter 1 of this letter, you will judge that it is the letter mentioned above as occasioning the dispute and the case of Atticus.

6. “By constraint.” Thus the editions of Merlini, Crabbe, Nicolinus, and Surius, and the manuscript of Victorinus. Most others read “by affliction,” which fits less well. This word was familiar to the ancients, and Leo himself uses it more than once.

7. “For the production of an innocent bishop.” In civil law, *exhibere*—“to produce”—means to provide the bodily presence of someone. Hence *exhibitio* is, so to speak, the presentation of a person; concerning this, see the *Code*, Book IX, title 3, “Concerning the Production and Transfer of Defendants.”

Our Leo rightly rebukes Anastasius for causing an innocent bishop, accused of no crime or of a false one, to be produced. In the same title, an edict of the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius commands that if someone is to be summoned from a distant place, the accuser must not be granted assent before he has bound himself by the solemn law and, with a trembling pen, exposed himself to the penalty of retaliation.

Anastasius had therefore approached—that is, had summoned by petition—the prefect of Illyricum, so that he might order Atticus to be produced because he refused to obey the summons conveyed by official letters to the synod. For the emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius order that no one be produced in court unless the judge has ruled that he is to be produced.

The prefect sent a terrible execution, as Leo calls it, from Thessalonica to Nicopolis—that is, a troop of public executors or officials whose duty it was to carry commands and judgments into effect. See the law *Exsecutorem*, *Code*, title 61, “Concerning Executors.”

“This execution,” Leo says, “would enlist all the public offices for carrying out the prefect’s command.” By “public offices” he means the officials themselves and the ministers of magistrates and governors, several of whom are named in the same title 61: the compulsor, exactor, admonisher, bearer of the command, *agens in rebus*, *palatinus*, or the apparitors of illustrious authorities, and so forth.

Through the service of these men, Atticus is said to have been dragged from the sacred recesses of the Church—either because, after leaving his own Church, he was compelled by the praetorian command to depart immediately for Thessalonica, or because he was violently dragged from the sanctuary in which the executors had found him.

They granted him no postponement on account of the inconvenience of illness or the severity of winter; Leo adds these particular grounds to the general law. For the emperors Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, in the *Code*, Book IX, title 3, “Concerning Those to Be Produced,” command that persons to be produced be granted a sufficient period of time, but not less than thirty days.

From this it is clear both how explicitly our Leo describes the injury inflicted upon Atticus and how precisely he uses terms drawn from the law itself: *adire praefecturam* (“to approach the prefecture”), *exhibitio* (“production”), *exsecutio* (“execution”), *public offices*, *insimulatus* (“accused”), *induciae* (“postponements”), *civilia* (“civil matters”), and so forth. I considered it worthwhile to note these terms for the benefit of beginners.

8. “Civil.” Among jurists, *civil* is opposed to *praetorian* [Col. 1319C]. Perhaps, therefore, St. Leo, by taking this word from the courts, indicates that he would not approach the authority of the prefecture, as Anastasius had done, but would act and respond by the authority proper to his own see.

In law, those words are also called *civil* which are lawful and mandatory. Papinian, in the *Digest*, Book VII, and frequently elsewhere, uses *civil* in the sense of just, equitable, and lawful; I think Leo too uses it in this sense. Conversely, *incivile* means dishonorable, unlawful, inequitable, and contrary to the order of law.

BRISSONIUS.

### 9. Or one who has or has had a single wife, but has joined himself to a widow.

Those who use the earlier editions must beware lest they fall into the error presented by the defective reading of this Roman edition and of other later editions: “Or one who has or has had even one wife, but neither one who has joined himself to a widow.” For the Church never removed from ecclesiastical offices men of one wife, whether she was still living or had already died, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching. Thus, above all, a correction was necessary; this was supplied to us by the collections of Dionysius and Cresconius, the editions of Surius, Nicolinus, and Merlinus, and the manuscripts Corbeiensis, Cantabrigiensis, Victorinus, Thuaneus, and Trecopithoeanus.

### 10. Of clerics.

He uses the name “clerics” more strictly for those who had been initiated into the higher orders. Readers—for they are usually called clerics of the lower order—could marry and beget children, as Leo himself expressly says in Letter 2 (now 167) to Rusticus of Narbonne, chapter 3.

### 11. Nor is carnal marriage permitted to subdeacons.

This discipline, whose witness and defender Saint Leo is both here and in Letter 2 (now 167) to Rusticus of Narbonne, chapter 3, presents no slight difficulties when compared with the practice of earlier and later times. For he speaks so certainly and unambiguously of a precept of continence prescribed, as it were, everywhere and universally to subdeacons that from it he draws an argument from the lesser to the greater, as they say, in support of the law of continence imposed on the higher grades. Yet in the time of Gregory the Great, who lived one hundred and fifty years after Leo, that law had not yet fully prevailed—at least in the province of Sicily, which belonged to the Roman bishop’s synod or jurisdiction, although it was observed at Rome.

“Three years ago,” he says (*Registrum*, book I, letter 42), “the subdeacons of all the Churches of Sicily had been forbidden, in the manner of the Roman Church, to associate sexually with their wives in any way.” But this seems harsh and inappropriate to me: that one who has not found the practice of that same continence and has not previously promised chastity should be compelled to separate from his wife,” and so forth.

What seemed harsh to Gregory then did not seem so to him when he wrote to Leo, bishop of Catania. There (*Registrum*, book IV, letter 34), he forbids subdeacons to have permission to associate sexually with their wives, but commands that they abstain in imitation of the Apostolic See.

Since, therefore, in provinces not far removed from the city of Rome this law of continence was not yet in force in the time of Gregory I, I am surprised that Saint Leo argues from the continence of subdeacons as though it had been introduced everywhere in his own time.

Meanwhile, it must be acknowledged—something that exposes the ignorance and corruption of more recent Greek writers—that the ancient Greek Church preceded the Latin Church in imposing on subdeacons the obligation of continence and celibacy. Epiphanius is a witness to this. He lived scarcely into the beginning of the fifth century, and he says that the holy Church of God by no means admits to the order of deacon, presbyter, bishop, or hypodeacon a man who still lives in marriage and devotes himself to his children, even if he is the husband of one wife. Rather, it admits only one who has abstained from association with a single wife or has been deprived of her—something done especially in those places where the ecclesiastical canons are carefully observed.

As for the fact that in some places presbyters, deacons, and hypodeacons have children, he asserts that this occurs contrary to the canons, either because of necessity or because of human negligence. The passages of Epiphanius are in book II of *Against Heresies*, against the Cathari, heresy 39 or 59, and in book III of the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, no. 21.

What canons Epiphanius is referring to, however, we do not know. We must either say that he understood by them a custom received by all the Churches and possessing the force of a canon through usage itself, or that those canons have perished and have been condemned to oblivion by the Greeks. Nevertheless, we find some trace of them in canon 14 of the Council of Chalcedon.

### 13. When the consent of the clergy and people has been sought.

See Saint Cyprian’s Letter 68 to the clergy and people of Emerita in Spain. There he asserts that the power either to choose worthy priests or to reject unworthy ones—which the canons and decrees of councils and popes commonly attribute to the people—and the practice that a priest should be chosen in the presence of the people, before the eyes of all, and that his worthiness and suitability should be established by public judgment and testimony, derive from divine authority and tradition and from apostolic observance.

Yet it should not be thought that priests are created by the people. “The election of a bishop,” writes the vigorous defender of the episcopal order, “is not the creation of a bishop, but the beginning of his creation.”

There are readily available many other testimonies and decrees of Celestine, Leo, and other pontiffs concerning the consent of clergy and people; we refrain from listing them.

### 14. Of the same Church.

It was always lawful for the greater sees to depart from this rule. This is established by numerous examples from Rome. Aurelius bears witness concerning Carthage in the Council of Carthage, chapter 55 of the *Code of the Canons of the African Church*. There the bishop Numidius also says:

“This see has always possessed the liberty that, from wherever it wished and from whomever an assembly had agreed upon, it might ordain a bishop according to the desire of each Church.”

The bishop of Arles in our Gaul also seems to have claimed the same prerogative, for in every respect he rivaled the greater sees. Many men from the monastery of Lérins, which was subject to the jurisdiction of the bishop of Fréjus, or from other monasteries in other provinces, were made bishops: Honoratus and Hilary to Arles, Faustus to Riez, another Honoratus—Hilary of Arles’s disciple—to Marseille, and Rusticus to Narbonne.

I think Pope Celestine took offense at this. When he wrote to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, I believe he turned his eyes toward the monastery of Lérins:

“Let no one presume to do anything in another’s province; and let foreigners, outsiders, and those previously unknown not be placed over clergy who have served honorably in their own Churches, to the exclusion of those who have deserved well of the testimony of their fellow citizens, lest it appear that a new institution has been established—a college from which bishops are made.”

Here also observe why the sacred canons decree that clerics should be taken from the bosom of the same Church for the sacred orders.

### 15. Or from among the deacons.

They were accustomed generally to choose deacons, and especially the chief among the deacons, rather than presbyters to replace deceased pontiffs, because it was customary to entrust the administration of the entire ecclesiastical business and care to the archdeacon, as these words of Saint Leo in Letter 84 (now 111) make clear. He was therefore more suitable than anyone else for bearing the burden of the pontificate.

We have an example—so that we do not go beyond Leo’s time—in Hilary the deacon, who succeeded Leo, and in Leo, who succeeded Sixtus. Sixtus, however, was a presbyter when he was elected pontiff. Thus that custom of the Roman Church must either never have prevailed or must then have fallen into disuse.

[Note: This testimony of Photius, taken from Saint Eulogius, a Greek writer of the late sixth century, is to be regarded as worthless. Although he wrote against the Novatians, just as he was mistaken when he relates that Novatian—whom he calls Novatus—was made a presbyter by Saint Cornelius from the rank of archdeacon, although Novatian had already been a presbyter before Cornelius’s election, so too he is mistaken when he reports that it had been established that an archdeacon should succeed the supreme pontiff.]

Photius of Constantinople is a witness to this in book I, codex 182, following Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria. Eulogius, he says, in his book against Novatus on ecclesiastical administration, or the Church’s power in receiving the lapsed (in Greek, *περὶ οἰκονομίας*), relates that Novatian, under Pope Cornelius, had been made archdeacon of the Roman Church. To him, according to the custom of that time, the pontificate itself was transferred when the pontiff died; for it had been established that an archdeacon should succeed the supreme pontiff.

But when Cornelius learned, says Eulogius, that Novatian was afflicted with pride and was threatening Cornelius’s death, he ordained him a presbyter, thereby cutting off all his hopes of attaining the supreme chair.

### 16. The holy Fathers.

He means the Fathers of Nicaea, who in canon 5 establish that one council is to be held before the forty days of Easter (Lent) and another around the time of autumn.

Saint Leo sufficiently indicates that even more serious cases could be discussed and concluded at that council, if it is acceptable to include among such cases the deposition of bishops. For he orders that bishops accused of grave crimes, whose conviction would entail deposition, should be judged there and not transferred to his own jurisdiction, if the case of the bishop of Thessalonica had been settled by judgment. How much less, then, did the cases of the Eastern bishops belong to the Western patriarch by a right equal to that of the vicariate of Thessalonica?

### 17. If any bishop, etc.

Two matters should be noted here. First, our Leo does not condemn every transfer of bishops to other sees, but only those transfers made through ambition or greed. Celestine, Leo’s predecessor, approved the transfer of Proclus, who had been made bishop of Constantinople from bishop of Cyzicus, by letters previously written to Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, and Rufus of Thessalonica. This is reported by Socrates, book VII, chapter 40.

Second, Saint Leo decrees a much more severe punishment against bishops who change their see solely to satisfy their desire for another position: he orders that they be deprived of both sees. This is more severe than what the holy Fathers had decreed before him.

The Council of Nicaea, canon 15, merely provides that if anyone attempts such a thing, the action is to be completely annulled and the man restored to the Church of which he had been bishop.

The Council of Chalcedon, held after this letter was written, seems to have revised Saint Leo’s decree when it decreed in canon 5:

“Concerning bishops or clerics who transfer from city to city, it has been decided that the canons established by the holy Fathers on this matter shall retain their proper force.”

Accordingly, when Hilary, Leo’s successor, complained in Letter 1 to the bishops of the province of Tarragona about a certain bishop Irenaeus, who had been transferred from his own Church to Barcelona, he did not order him, in accordance with Leo’s decree, to be deprived of both sees, but ordered him to be sent back to the first, in accordance with the Nicene statute.

Nevertheless, Leo’s severity has the support of the Fathers of Sardica, who in canons 1 and 2 order that bishops who have transferred from their own city to another be deprived even of lay communion. They prescribe the same punishment at the end of life or at death if the bishops have purchased letters or popular support with money in order to conceal their ambition.

### 18. A foreign cleric, etc.

Here too understand nearly the same exception that we noted above as having been granted to the greater Churches: namely, that they might take a bishop from any Church. Balsamon bears witness to this concerning Constantinople and Carthage, in his commentary on canon 17 of the Sixth Council and on the *Nomocanon* of Photius, title 1, chapter 26.

### 19. Although their dignity is common, their order is not general.

[Note: We present this more accurate reading in annotation 52 (col. 675, new ed., note e), where we also set forth its equitable meaning—one not injurious to the bishops, yet at the same time consonant with the eminent rank and authority of the supreme pontiffs. Consequently, certain things that Quesnellus adds here require correction.]

This passage was formerly corrupted in order to diminish the bishops. Until now it was read in the printed manuscripts as follows:
