“Although their dignity is not common, their order is nevertheless general.”

According to this defective reading, the passage recognizes bishops within the general order of clerics, but denies that all share the same dignity—contrary to the unanimous judgment of the holy Fathers. To use Cyprian’s words, “the episcopate is one and indivisible, spread among the many bishops in harmonious plurality, and each holds his portion of it in full” (*Letter* 52, or the book *On the Unity of the Catholic Church*).

“For among us,” says Saint Jerome (*Letter* 54), “bishops occupy the place of the Apostles.” The same writer says (*Letter* 85, to Evagrius): “All are successors of the Apostles: the Roman bishop of Peter, and the other bishops of the other Apostles.”

Moreover, the other Apostles were what Peter was, endowed with an equal partnership of honor and power (Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church*). “All,” says Jerome (*Book I against the Pelagians*), “receive the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and upon them all equally the strength of the Church is established.”

Our author also acknowledges this here, when he confesses that in all things there is both likeness of honor and equality of election. See also the previously cited Pope Gelasius, in Letter 10.

Therefore, the dignity of all bishops is common, but their order is not general, because Peter is the head of all, and Christ arranged by his authority that the origin of unity should begin from one person, Peter (Cyprian, *On the Unity of the Church). As Saint Leo says in this very passage, “to one was given the role of standing above the others.”

It is useful to illuminate this with the distinguished testimony of Saint Augustine, from chapter 1 of book I of *Against the Letters of the Pelagians*, addressed to Pope Boniface. He speaks to him as follows:

“Since the pastoral watchtower is common to all of us who perform the office of the episcopate—although you yourself stand above it at a loftier height—I do what I can according to my small share of the office.”

The common text wrongly reads *speculae* instead of *specula*. This error, combined with faulty punctuation, disturbs the sense of the passage and obscures the author’s meaning.

We correct Leo’s text on the authority of the manuscripts Corbeiensis, Trecopithoeanus, and four Thuane manuscripts. The codex Victorinus and the editions of Surius, Merlinus, and Nicolinus have a clearer reading, less open to quibbling, as follows:

“Although their dignity is common, their order is nevertheless not general.”

Nevertheless, we acknowledge that the corruption of this passage is ancient. Hincmar of Reims, in the thirty-second of his *Opuscula of Chapters*, chapter 55, addressed to Hincmar of Laon, reads it in the same way, namely in chapter 13, whose title also rests upon this error:

“Chapter 13: Although the order is general for all bishops, dignity is nevertheless not common to all.”

He then quotes Leo’s words in the body of the chapter.

The error was drawn from an even earlier source, namely Dionysius Exiguus, who presents the same reading that we reject. Hincmar derives from that collection of Dionysius everything he cites from papal decrees; this is also clear concerning this very letter from *Opusculum* 45, *On Transfers*, chapter 14. It is therefore unsurprising that the same error is found in both writers; accordingly, they must both be regarded as a single witness.

The authority of Dionysius is indeed great, if it were established that the collection of his that was sent into Gaul was of the same form as the one he himself compiled. On the contrary, we have proved above, in the discussion of Letter 12, from an examination of all the manuscript codices with which the libraries of Gaul abound, that the earliest copies of the Dionysian codex brought there had been enlarged, interpolated, and corrupted in many ways.

For the present I shall assert one thing: in the collection of the letters of Saint Leo found at the end of a Roman codex older than the Dionysian one, our reading is found. I vouch for this concerning the Thuane manuscript; concerning the Oxford manuscript, whose relevant portion I have not had the opportunity to see, the same may be conjectured.

### 20. Lest all should claim everything for themselves.

The various and distinct ranks of priests in the Church converge toward unity.

[Note: Since all the grades of bishops converge toward unity, the center of unity itself was therefore placed in the Roman see and in the successors of Saint Peter, so that through all the grades of bishops the care of the universal Church might flow together toward the one see of Peter, and nothing anywhere might disagree with its head. Saint Leo himself says this in this letter, chapter 11.]

“For this reason one is chosen from among the twelve, so that, once a head has been established, the opportunity for schism may be removed,” says Jerome (*Book I against the Pelagians*). Pope Gelasius transcribed him in his treatise to the Greeks, in Sirmond’s appendix to the *Theodosian Code*, page 184.

Again, speaking of that arrangement, Saint Leo says:

“From it also arose the distinction of bishops, lest all should claim everything for themselves.”

Finally, in ancient times the presbyter was the same as the bishop—these are Jerome’s words, in his commentary on chapter 1 of the Letter to Titus—and before rivalries arose in the Church through the devil’s instigation, the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters.

This does not mean that bishops and presbyters were then equal, but that no presbyter was appointed who was not also adorned with the full and perfect priesthood that exists in bishops. At that time he took more pleasure in the name “presbyter,” which refers to age, than in “bishop,” which is the name of dignity.

## On Letter XV: To Turibius, Bishop of Astorga

### 1. To Turibius, etc.

It is remarkable with what variety the name of this bishop is written. The Grimani codex has *To Toruvius of Asturica*; three Thuane manuscripts and the Trecopithoean, together with Surius, have *To Turbius of Astorga*; the Royal codex has *Tubirio* and *Tuberio of Astorga*; the Corbeiensis and Thuane 1 have *Torebius of Asthoraca*; Isidore Mercator has *Tornulus of Austuriga*; and Montanus, bishop of Toledo, in his letter to the brothers of the territory of Palencia, at the end of the Second Council of Toledo, has *Theoribius*.

Finally, some have *Turibius of Asturia*, as Surius does, or *Turribius of Astorga*, as it is commonly read and as we have retained it. The word is the same as that which modern Spaniards call *Torrez* and we French call *de la Tour*.

It is certain that this Turribius was bishop of Astorga—commonly called Astorga, in the province of Galicia, formerly under the metropolitan authority of Braga and now under the archbishop of Compostela. Ecclesiastical records proclaim him distinguished for piety, learning, and religious zeal; they number him among the saints whose cult has been vindicated, on 16 April. His letters also bear witness to this: he wrote both to our Leo and to the Spanish bishops Idatius and Ceponius. The latter letters are found in Ambrosius Morales, *History of Spain*, book II, chapter 26; Bivarus, in his commentaries on the *Pseudo-Chronicle of Dexter*; and Cardinal Baronius, under the year 447.

We have also placed Leo’s letters to him here, because they are related to those letters and because they were omitted both from García de Loaysa’s edition of the Councils of Spain and from the most recent complete collection of the Councils, as though they had not yet seen the light of publication.

There is a passage in the First Council of Braga, on the occasion of which Baronius and his follower Binius raise a question scarcely worth serious examination. These are the words of Bishop Lucretius, speaking in that synod:

“I believe that your Blessedness knows that, at the time when the most abominable poisons of the Priscillianist sect were spreading through these regions, the most blessed pope of the city of Rome, Leo, who was approximately the fortieth successor of the Apostle Peter, sent his written instructions through Turribius, the notary of his see, to the council of Galicia against the impious sect of the Priscillianist heresy.

“By his command also, the bishops of Tarragona and Carthage, as well as those of Lusitania and Baetica, having held a council among themselves, composed a rule of faith against the Priscillianist heresy, together with certain chapters, and sent it to Balconius, then bishop of this Church of Braga.”

The eminent cardinal therefore wishes there to have been only one Turribius, who was both bishop of Astorga and, at the same time, notary of the Roman see. He ridicules as contrary to the truth the opinion of Ambrosius Morales, who distinguished two Turribii: one to whom Leo wrote, namely the bishop of Astorga; and another through whom Leo wrote to the bishops of Spain, who had been sent from Rome to Spain by Leo to carry his letters.

The author of the *Annals* produces two arguments for his opinion, both of them slight and extremely weak.

“If he had given letters,” he says, “both to Turribius the bishop and to his notary, also called Turribius, for the convocation of a synod, he would certainly have mentioned him in the letter written to the bishop. For this was customary,” and so forth.

Let it be granted that it was customary for the person through whom letters were delivered to be mentioned in every letter—for we grant this from an abundance of legal generosity, although it rests on no foundation. He himself admits that this was indeed done.

But there was no necessity for the same messenger, sent to the synod of the entire province, to be named in the letter written to Turribius. Leo replied to Turribius through the same deacon from whom he had received Turribius’s letter, and he mentions him in his reply. But to that synod, or to that province of Spanish bishops, from whom he had received neither letters nor a messenger, he sent a letter through Turribius, dispatched from his own side.

This is what I assert to be most firmly established: when Roman pontiffs wrote to a synod or to certain bishops concerning an important matter, they did so through one of their own men specially appointed for that purpose, not through an outsider’s cleric. Had Leo done otherwise, the Spanish bishops would undoubtedly have suspected that it arose from some contempt.

Moreover, to turn Baronius’s argument back upon him, it was customary for the name of the person who received the letters for delivery, and actually delivered them, to be written in the letters themselves, whether he was a deacon or a notary—not the name of the person to whom the bearer was commended.

But it cannot be said that Turribius of Astorga delivered these letters of Leo to the Spanish bishops from Rome, nor that he himself received them from Leo’s deacon for delivery. Who would wish to assign such a task to a bishop?

Thus, when Baronius uses as his second argument the fact that Saint Leo entrusted everything that had to be handled in this matter to the care and concern of Bishop Turribius, in order to prove that the letters were carried by that same man to the Spanish bishops, he seems to have forgotten the difference between a bishop occupied with the affairs of the Church through priestly care and a deacon or notary carrying out the bishop’s commands according to instructions and carrying letters here and there like a courier.

I pass over the fact that the word “notary” is never used in ecclesiastical documents with the meaning that this author assigns to it, as though one should call someone a notary who strives to report to the Roman see and make known what is being done in the provinces.

Furthermore, since we are compelled to recognize three entirely distinct letters of Leo—partly from Leo himself and partly from Lucretius of Braga’s speech—we are not likewise compelled to think that they were sent at the same time.

The matter, as I think, was as follows. Having been informed by Saint Turribius of Astorga about the advance of the Priscillianist heresy, which was raging throughout Spain, our Leo immediately began to consider by what remedies such a nefarious plague could be opposed.

Nothing occurred to him more readily than the gathering of a general assembly of the Spanish bishops, who could investigate the condition of affairs and make decisions. Therefore he entrusted a letter to Turribius of Astorga for delivery by his deacon Pervincus, as the Chronicle of Idatius records. In it he urged him to convene a general synod:

“Therefore,” he says, “let an episcopal council be held among you, and let the priests of the neighboring provinces assemble at a place convenient for all.”

But Turribius had no authority to convene such an assembly, since he was not a metropolitan; rather, among the bishops of Galicia belonging to the same province, he was the lowest in rank. It was therefore necessary that the Spanish bishops be informed of the entire matter.

Accordingly Saint Leo wrote to the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Galicia, exhorting them to celebrate properly a council of a general synod. He informed Turribius about these letters, so that through his care they might be delivered to all the bishops and the entire matter brought to its desired conclusion.

But at that time those Spanish provinces lay under different rulers: Rechila, king of the Suevi, occupied Galicia, while the others lived under Gothic rule. Leo’s desire could therefore not be fulfilled, because the bishops of Galicia were not permitted to meet with the bishops of the other provinces.

Saint Leo already anticipated this when he wrote to Turribius:

“But if anything—which God forbid—should prevent a general council from being held, let the priests of Galicia at least assemble together. Our brothers Idatius and Ceponius will take charge of gathering them, with your joined efforts.”

There is no doubt that several months passed after Turribius received Leo’s letter before Leo’s letters were sent to the individual bishops of Spain. During that interval, the primates of those Churches deliberated among themselves about the matter, sought to discover the rulers’ wishes, and attempted to obtain permission for the gathering of a full council.

When they finally saw that their efforts were fruitless because the rulers resisted, the bishops of that province then began to plan the holding of a synod of Galicia.

Saint Leo learned of this, either because Turribius wrote to him again or because the messenger whom he had sent with letters to the bishops of those four provinces returned. He considered it in the Church’s interest to write to the synod that was being prepared, or perhaps had already been convened. These, then, are the writings that Lucretius, speaking at the Council of Braga, says Leo sent through Turribius, the notary of the Roman see, to the Council of Galicia against the impious sect of the Priscillianist heresy.

While the Council of Galicia was being prepared, or after it had already been dissolved, the bishops of the other provinces also held an assembly among themselves, as the same Lucretius testifies, following Leo’s advice in this matter. At that assembly they composed a rule of faith together with certain chapters and sent it to Balconius, then bishop of the Church of Braga.

I mean the rule of faith that is wrongly appended to the First Council of Toledo under the year of Christ 400. In reality it belongs to this council of the four Spanish provinces, as is demonstrated even by the title of the rule and the appended chapters, which contain the same material as Lucretius in his speech, but especially by the First Council of Braga, which attributes both to that Spanish synod, assembled in Leo’s time and at his command.

More will be found concerning this rule of faith in Dissertation 14.

From what has been said it is clear that this letter to our Turribius and the other letter which Lucretius testifies was written to the Council of Galicia were not sent at the same time. For the latter council had not yet been assembled, and in the present argument I believe I can establish with certainty that it was not convened so quickly.

### 1366

Baronius also admits that those two synods—the one of Galicia and the other of the four provinces—were held at nearly the same time, and Lucretius’s speech plainly declares this.

When the latter synod was convened, Balconius was bishop of Braga. It does not, however, appear that he governed the Church of that city when Saint Leo wrote to Turribius and to the other Spanish bishops. It is highly probable that either Idatius or Ceponius occupied that see.

First, this seems to be proved by the letter that Turribius wrote to those two bishops when he first noticed the impious doctrine of the Priscillianist sect spreading. Why would he have addressed his complaints to those bishops alone, omitting the others, unless they stood above the rest by metropolitan authority, and for that reason the responsibility and concern of suppressing this nefarious heresy belonged to them?

[Note: When Saint Leo names Idatius and Ceponius among the bishops of Galicia at the end of this letter, Quesnellus, by an elaborate conjecture, represented these two as the metropolitans of Galicia, Idatius as bishop of Lugo and Ceponius as bishop of Braga. Apart from his erroneous interpretation of the Council of Lugo of the year 569—in which, after the province of Galicia had been divided into two, the right of metropolitan authority is said to have been assigned for the first time to the see of Lugo, although at this period it belonged to Braga alone—it is entirely false that Idatius presided over the Church of Lugo.

The same Idatius, who in the preface to his Chronicle says that he was made bishop around the year 427 or 428 and who calls himself bishop in the year 431, expressly calls Agrestius bishop of Lugo under the year 433, not around the year 430, as Quesnellus marked in this same annotation.

That Ceponius was not bishop of Braga is clear from the First Council of Braga and from the rule of faith sent by the Spanish synod, at Leo’s command, to Balconius. That rule names Balconius, not Ceponius, as bishop of Braga.

If Balconius of Braga, to whom Avitus wrote a letter in the year 416 concerning the relics of Saint Stephen, is not believed to be different from the Balconius who lived under Leo, Quesnellus’s opinion becomes even more untenable, since he thinks that Balconius was succeeded by Ceponius.

Saint Leo therefore named Idatius and Ceponius as the principal men responsible for gathering the bishops of Galicia against the Priscillianists in Letter to Turribius, chapter 17, not because they surpassed the bishops of that province in metropolitan dignity, but because, having learned from Turribius’s letter to them—which the holy pontiff received together with Turribius’s treatise—of their seniority and merit, he judged them especially suitable to assist the younger bishop Turribius in convening the Council of Galicia against the Priscillianists.

See the admonition to Turribius’s letter to Idatius and Ceponius, which we inserted above in the appendix to the letters.

Hence Idatius, who reports that he was captured in the Church of Aquae Flaviae around the year 462, is believed to have been bishop of that same Church, to which he says he returned after three months. Quesnellus denied that this was his episcopal see solely on the basis of an unproved hypothesis by which he presumed him to have been metropolitan of Lugo.

Turribius is recognized as his closest friend and as endowed with the same zeal, since in the year 445 both of them fought together at Astorga against the hidden Manichaeans.]

Second, Saint Leo sufficiently indicates that these same men were metropolitans of the province of Galicia when he asserts that responsibility for gathering the bishops within that province rested with them:

“Our brothers Idatius and Ceponius will take charge of gathering them.”

Third, we read that this same Idatius held episcopal proceedings in the city of Astorga, when, together with the bishop of that city, he directed proceedings of this kind against the hidden Manichaeans—whom they condemned by their judgment—to Antoninus, bishop of Mérida. Idatius himself testifies to this in his *Chronicle* under Olympiad 306.

He could not have exercised such judgment in another Church unless he possessed metropolitan authority in the province of Galicia.

If it is permissible to indulge conjectures in so obscure a matter, I would readily believe that even at that time metropolitan authority in the province of Galicia belonged to two bishops. The reasons for this assertion are as follows.

### 1.

When Turribius wished to warn those whose office and power it was to extinguish such errors in the province of Galicia about the errors of the Priscillianists, revived after their apparent death, he approached not one but two bishops, Idatius and Ceponius, jointly, as though they were equal in dignity and authority. His letter to them bears witness to this.

### 2.

Saint Leo indicates that these same men ought to preside over the convocation of the Council of Galicia. This right undoubtedly signifies metropolitan dignity. For unless each of them had possessed that dignity, and unless Saint Leo had been free to appoint the president of the council at his own discretion, he would not have honored anyone other than Turribius with this office, since he knew his concern and industry.

### 3.

The immense size of this province also supports the argument. Its size led to the Council of Lugo in the year 569, which, at the ruler’s command, divided it into two ecclesiastical provinces and assigned metropolitan rights to the Church of Lugo.

This does not seem to me so much a new institution as a restoration of an earlier one, which had been altered on account of the disturbances of war, despite its antiquity, so that at that time all metropolitan rights had converged upon a single bishop.

### 4.

This is confirmed by the opinion of those who place the Council of Lugo at Celenis, a municipality of the diocese of Lugo, and assign it to this same period. For if this is true, the bishop of Lugo must almost necessarily have possessed metropolitan authority: while the bishop of Braga, as metropolitan of the same province, held a synod at Braga, the other bishop would have convened another synod in that same province by his own authority.

See what is reported in the preface to the First Council of Toledo of the year 400 concerning this Council of Celenis or Lugo. Those materials, although wrongly inserted there, seem to have to be assigned to Leo’s time, although for our present purpose it makes no difference whether that Council of Lugo was convened in this period or in an earlier one.

### 5.

In the preface to the First Council of Braga, which preceded that Council of Lugo in which the province of Galicia is said first to have been divided between two metropolitans, I seem to detect some trace of a division already made earlier. For the Church of Braga is called the metropolitan church of the province of Braga, whereas it ought to have been called the metropolitan church of the province of Galicia if there had been only one ecclesiastical province. Moreover, only eight bishops attended this council, although there were at least fifteen bishops in the province of Galicia; so one may reasonably suspect that only those who were subject to Braga assembled, and not those subject to Lugo. As for the fact that the division is said to have been made first at the Council of Lugo, I readily interpret it in this way: at that time, by synodal decree and royal command, what had already been in use from ancient times, but had perhaps been interrupted for some period through the ambition of the metropolitans of Braga, was restored anew. Finally, in that council an end was put to the dispute which had existed between the two metropolitans 1368, by a peremptory decree that asserted the metropolitan dignity of Lugo.

### 6.

Idatius, in his *Chronicle*, at Olympiad 303, around the year 430, reports that the following occurred:

> At the assembly of Lugo, against the will of Agrestius, bishop of Lugo, Pastor and Syagrius were ordained as bishops.

In these words you see several arguments for the metropolitan dignity of the bishop of Lugo. Why, indeed, do the bishops assemble at Lugo, unless it was a metropolis? Why were episcopal ordinations performed in that city, unless it was the seat of a metropolitan? For it was customary in antiquity for a bishop to be ordained either in the Church over which he was to preside or in the metropolitan city. Finally, why does he note that those bishops were ordained against the will of the bishop of Lugo, unless this involved an evident [Col. 1328B] contempt of the canons, which so often forbid a bishop to be consecrated without the will and knowledge of the metropolitan bishop?

I shall now briefly gather together what I said above. First, that there were two metropolitans in the province of Galicia; second, that one of them was certainly the bishop of Braga; third, that one or the other of the bishops named—namely, Ceponius and Idatius—was metropolitan of Braga; fourth, that Ceponius appears to have governed the Church of Braga in this year, 447, rather than Idatius. For the man who was then in charge of the people of Braga must have died before the synod of Galicia, since at the time of that synod Balconius was governing the Church of Braga. Yet Idatius was still alive at that time, if we may trust the little book on the twelve ecclesiastical writers, which is customarily appended to Isidore and Ildephonsus:

> He died, it says, under the emperor Leo, already almost in extreme old age, as the beginning of his own preface also demonstrates.

This is likewise clear from the *Chronicle* itself, which he extends beyond the time of Pope Leo [Col. 1328C]. Fifth, therefore, Idatius seems to have been the metropolitan of Lugo, although Sigebert makes him bishop of Lemica. But Sigebert appears to confuse two Idatiuses: one who lived in the time of Leo and was the author of the *Chronicle*, and another who was once an accuser of Priscillian and who really was bishop of Lemica. Sigebert was also led into error by the fact that the later Idatius states in the preface to his *Chronicle* that he was born in the city of Lemica. If he had been bishop of that same city, he would not have failed to mention this in the passage where he referred both to Lemica and to his birth there. It would be more accurate to say that he seems to indicate his metropolitan dignity when he says there that he had been made bishop of the highest office (*summi officii praesul*). For among the bishops of a province the office of the metropolitan is the highest; and at the end of that same preface he laments, with such groaning, the disfigured condition of the ecclesiastical order in the province of Galicia that he appears to have had a special responsibility for it, as though he were the head of the province, and to have been obliged by his office to confront and assist against the indiscriminate ordinations which he condemns and against the almost universal decline of religion in divine discipline [Col. 1328D].

Finally, Idatius leaves scarcely any room for doubt 1369 when, at Olympiad 310, he describes the devastation of the province of Galicia and reports that the Suebi were plundered at Lugo. He immediately adds:

> After Bishop Idatius had been captured on the seventh day before the Kalends of August in the Church of Aquae Flaviae, they devastated that same district with great destruction.

It is evident that he is speaking of no one other than himself, and of no assembly other than that of Lugo, whose devastation he had begun to narrate; nor does he indicate any other episcopal see of his than Lugo. For the Church of Aquae Flaviae which he mentions was not an episcopal see, but some local church belonging to the parish of Lugo [Col. 1329A].

Now, because this same Idatius frequently calls one body the “Bracarensian assembly” and another the “Lugensian assembly,” I suspect that by these terms he indicates the division of the province of Galicia. I take the very extensive province to have been divided into two parts, which it pleased them to distinguish by the name “assembly” (*conventus*), assigning to each its own metropolis—Braga to one and Lugo to the other—with metropolitan rights both in civil and in ecclesiastical matters. In much the same manner of speaking, especially in ancient and African documents, each province is called a *council* (*concilium*), which is equivalent to an assembly (*conventus*).

### 2. “The wording of the letter, the sequence of the memorandum, and the text of your little book.”

He clearly distinguishes three things [Col. 1329D]: a letter, a memorandum, and a little book.

[Note: See our dissertation on the lost letters, no. 16, which we published after the letters of Saint Leo.]

He himself calls the letter a personal letter in chapter 17. The memorandum—which we ordinarily call a memorial—is the writing arranged in sixteen chapters, containing the opinions of the Priscillianists formerly condemned, and to each of whose chapters Saint Leo responds in this letter. Finally, the little book, likewise consisting of sixteen chapters, is a different kind of writing from the preceding one: in it Turribius refuted the blasphemies of these heretics, as he himself testifies at the end of his letter to Idatius and Ceponius. The addition to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, cited above, calls these writings “books”; there it is said that the same Priscillianist heresy was detested, refuted, and properly rejected in them.

The same little book seems to be intended by what Montanus, bishop of Toledo, writes in his letter to the people of Palencia, attached to the Second Council of Toledo:

> Whoever reads the published books of the most blessed and religious man Theoribius, bishop, addressed to the holy pope Leo of the city of Rome, will learn more fully what sort of man this Priscillian was. In them he explained and exposed this filthy heresy and brought into the open what had been hidden beneath the darkness of its own deceit and the cloud of its falsehood. For from those very BOOKS the devout reader will learn how he can guard against the sacrilegious and what answer he can make to them [Col. 1329C].

### 1370 3. “That the most fetid cesspool of the Priscillianists has become hot again among you.”

Saint Leo appears to have borrowed this expression from Augustine’s *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, heresy 79. Anyone wishing to know the origins and development of this most shameful sect should consult Sulpicius Severus, *History*, book II, at the end. He should also consult Jerome on Daniel, chapter XL, and *To Ctesiphon against the Pelagians*; the *Chronicle* of Idatius, Olympiad 291; and the First Councils of Toledo and Braga. There is nothing concerning this heresy in Epiphanius, who perhaps did not distinguish it from the sects of the Gnostics, Manichaeans, and others, with which the Priscillianists shared many features. Augustine’s sixth volume also contains the consultation of the Spaniard Orosius addressed to Augustine himself, and Augustine’s reply to Orosius, or rather his book against the Priscillianists and Origenists.

All printed copies and several manuscripts give the earlier reading, “the most fetid cesspool.” Most, however, read: “the cesspool,” namely the two Corbeiensis manuscripts, the Cambridge manuscript, and the first Thuaneus. The Grimanican manuscript also has this reading, but corrected in different ink, although, I think, by the same hand; previously it read *sentina*. For *foedissimam*, the same hand and ink have likewise substituted *foetidissimam*, “most fetid,” which is also found in Corbeiensis 1 and Thuaneus 1.

### 4. “That the rulers of the world might strike down its author, together with most of his disciples, with the sword of the public laws.”

“What shall I say of Priscillian,” Jerome writes to Ctesiphon against Pelagius, “who was condemned both by the sword of the world and by the authority of the entire world?” The same account is found in Sulpicius Severus. But neither he nor Jerome, nor any other of the holy Fathers who lived in the age of Priscillian, approved such bloody measures in this way. Saint Martin, indeed, exerted every effort before Maximus to prevent the shedding of those unfortunate men’s blood, and he did not cease rebuking Idatius for persisting in the prosecution. He declared it a new and unheard-of outrage that a secular judge should judge the cause of the Church; it was more than sufficient that heretics, once judged by an episcopal sentence, should be expelled from the Churches.

Severus himself, who reports these events in book II of his *History*, testifies that the Priscillianists were killed or punished with exile through unsound counsels, obstinate zeal, and a most deplorable example. No one is unaware that for this reason Ithacius was deprived both of communion with his fellow bishops and of his episcopate. This was why Jerome, in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, attributed the death of Priscillian to the faction of Hylatius—perhaps Idatius—and Ithacius.

Yet in that passage, to tell the truth, I strongly suspect that Jerome’s book has been corrupted and interpolated, and that everything it says 1371 about Priscillian was once inserted by one of his followers.

[Note: There is no reason to suspect corruption in this passage of the *Catalogue*, a suspicion for which no manuscripts provide support. The true reason why Jerome wrote differently about Priscillian in that book than in his later works is that he was not then as well informed about Priscillian’s errors and deeds as he was afterwards. [Col. 1329D, 1330D]] For it is scarcely possible to reconcile what Jerome says elsewhere—whether in writing *To Ctesiphon against Pelagius* or in his commentary on Daniel—with what is read about Priscillian in this *Catalogue*. Here he calls Priscillian bishop of Ávila, although he was installed there as bishop by a few of his disciples and was never regarded as a bishop by the Catholics, never called a bishop, and never found to have been accused or condemned as such. Moreover, Jerome attaches no stigma to him and does not call him a heretic. On the contrary, he does not even call his accusers bishops, but rather denounces them as factious men.

Finally, regarding a notorious heresiarch—or rather, the reviver of all the ancient heresies—Jerome is content merely to indicate that some accused him of heresy on the basis of rumors, while asserting that many others defended him, so that the uncertain reader is forced to remain unsure which side to take:

> To this day, he says, he is accused by some of the Gnostic heresy—that is, the heresy of Basilides and Marcion, about whom Irenaeus wrote—while others defend him, claiming that he did not hold the opinions of which he is accused [Col. 1330C].

Thus Jerome wrote in the fourteenth year of Theodosius, that is, in A.D. 392—a man ignorant of nothing that was taking place in the Church—after the Council of Saragossa, after the Council of Bordeaux, after Priscillian had been condemned, as he himself says, by the authority of the whole world, and after the rebuff from Damasus, in whose presence Jerome himself was present: a rebuff such that Priscillian and his companions were not even admitted into the presence of the pontiff when they wished to clear themselves.

Indeed, in the book cited above, *To Ctesiphon*, he calls Priscillian a part of the Manichaean heresy, asserts that he shares in the Gnostic heresy derived from the impiety of Basilides, and there and elsewhere directs his pen sharply against Priscillian’s depravity.

### 5. “Sixteen chapters.”

This is the reading of the manuscripts Barb. 1, four Thuaneus manuscripts, two Corbeiensis manuscripts, Trecopithoeanus, Cambridge, Herovallianus, Isidori Merc., and the editions of Crabbe, Canisius, Sichard, Nicolinus, Surius, and others—and rightly so. For the memorandum and Turribius’s little book really comprised only sixteen chapters, as is clear from the words of chapter 16:

> Since, then, all that the sequence of the little book contains has been traversed, and since its contents do not differ from the form of the memorandum, etc. [Col. 1330D]

In printed editions, however, the common reading is: “in seventeen chapters,” a reading supported by the Grimanican manuscript.

It is also worth noting that the chapters composed by the First Council of Braga for a clearer exposition of Catholic truth were formed not only from the ideas but almost from the very words of these sixteen chapters, or responses, of Leo. For after rereading and approving both the rule of faith and the chapters appended to it, which had formerly been issued by the councils of the provinces of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica, assembled at Leo’s suggestion, the Fathers of the Council of Braga thought it appropriate to propose several additional chapters, so that they might be more readily understood by the less learned as being simpler 1372 and clearer.

They believed that they could accomplish this no more suitably than by placing before themselves Leo’s responses, once addressed to Turribius, and ordering the people to accept them in abridged form under penalty of anathema. This was carried out successfully, as will be perfectly clear to anyone who reads the material. There is scarcely a word that they did not borrow from Leo, and there is scarcely one of Leo’s chapters that they did not incorporate into their own. The first five articles of the council correspond in order to the first five chapters of Leo; the others correspond to one another completely, although neither the same order nor the same numbering is preserved.

There is only one chapter of Leo which they left untouched: chapter nine, in which he refutes the Priscillianist opinion that “the children of promise were indeed born from women, but were conceived by the Holy Spirit.” They omitted this either because they had observed that the Priscillianists of their own time did not hold such an opinion, or because the ambiguous proposition could be defended in a Catholic sense if it were understood solely of the sacrament of regeneration, in which sense those heretics perhaps defended it. For not everything said by heretics is heretical.

### 6. “But that he himself is the beginning and substance of every evil.”

This is the reading of all the manuscripts except one Thuaneus, which has: “that he himself is among all evils,” etc.; and Grimanican and Barb. 1, which read: “But that he himself is the beginning and substance of all things,” etc. The latter reading seems to be confirmed by Saint Augustine, who, in *On Heresies*, addressed to Quodvultdeus, chapter 70, lists among the doctrines of the Priscillianists the claim that this world was made by an evil ruler, and that the work of all flesh is attributable not to the good and true God but to evil angels. Leo likewise testifies in chapter 14 of this letter that they held the same view regarding the creation of the entire world. Let the reader judge and choose.

### 7. “Without a body.”

This is the reading of the one Thuaneus manuscript together with the Trecopithoeanus, which one might say was copied from it, since it agrees with it in every respect. It is also the reading of the manuscript of Herovallianus Isidori Merc. All the others, both handwritten and printed, including those of the Isidorian collection of Merlin, have: “In a body.”

But anyone can understand that the reading we have restored must be preferred to the other, both from the context of the passage—which asserts that the souls were afterward enclosed in bodies by demons—and from Augustine’s words in *On Heresies*, chapter 70. The similarity of both meaning and wording shows that these words were before our author’s eyes:

> They say, he writes, that souls are of the same nature and substance as God, and that they descend by stages through seven heavens and through certain authorities, in order to undergo on earth a kind of voluntary contest; then they encounter the evil ruler, by whom they wish this world to have been made, and by this ruler they are sown through various bodies of flesh [Col. 1332B].

### 1373

#### 8. Dictinius’s Treatises

> **[Note: [Col. 1331B]** Everything Quesnellus argues in this annotation concerning Dictinius’s expulsion rests upon the testimony of Idatius, which was cited in the first edition of Leo but which, in the second, he admits is not found in Idatius. He had evidently been prompted by Tillemont’s letters to indicate where that passage was found in Idatius. Thus he exposed his mistake and testified, solely by way of excuse, that he had not fabricated the passage himself but had transcribed it in good faith from some book whose identity he had forgotten. Although he acknowledges, and indicates plainly enough, that once this testimony is removed everything constructed upon it throughout the annotation collapses, he nevertheless continued, in his usual manner, to heap up many conjectures [Col. 1331C] by which the copies of the professions of faith submitted by Symphosius and Dictinius to the First Council of Toledo, as well as the sentence of that same synod edited by Ambrosius Morales, might be rendered suspect. Since several serious controversies among scholars also concern these documents and certain other matters relating to that Council of Toledo, we—who believe that the manuscripts we have seen can shed some light on the matter and establish the genuineness of these documents—think we shall do something welcome for our readers if we discuss them at some length.

> In recent editions of the councils, twenty canons are published under the name of the First Council of Toledo; these are followed by the rule of faith against the Priscillianists, then by copies of the professions of Symphosius and Dictinius, and finally by the sentence of the same council. The canons are said to have been issued at the Council of Toledo during the consulship of Stilicho, in the Spanish Era 438; these chronological marks correspond to the year 400. The rule of faith, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Lusitania, and Baetica are said to have composed against the Priscillianists at Leo’s command [Col. 1331D], agrees with the council that the same pontiff ordered to be convened in his letter to Turribius, chapter 17. The copies of the professions of Symphosius and Dictinius give the Era as 438, while the sentence of the council presupposes that Saint Simplicianus was alive at Milan and displays other indications; all of these details agree with the year 400, to which Idatius assigns the recantation of Symphosius and Dictinius—that is, the professions of faith just mentioned.

> Yet in the same copies of the professions these bishops, Symphosius and Dictinius, are called “of holy memory,” a formula showing that the document was written after their deaths and therefore after the year 400. These various indications have produced differing judgments among critics. Most have held that the canons, the professions of faith, and the sentence were issued at the Toletan synod of the year 400 or 405, when Stilicho held the consulship, but that the rule of faith belonged to another synod, under Pope Leo, in 447 or shortly afterward.

> Tillemont, volume VIII, note 15, in his *History of the Priscillianists*, p. 796, although he recognized that the professions of Symphosius and Dictinius, as well as the sentence of the synod, were composed at the Council of Toledo in 400, nevertheless maintained that these documents, in their present form, were excerpts from the acts of that same council, and that they had been recited and inserted into another synod under Leo. He further attributed to the latter not only the rule of faith but also the canons, chiefly for this reason: in the preceding title it is asserted, in the same context, concerning the Fathers who composed the rule of faith under Leo, “They also established the aforesaid twenty chapters of canons.” Thus, in the same volume, p. 524, he indicates that all these materials can be referred to the Toletan synod held under Leo.

> Father Coustant, however, in his note to the third letter of Innocent, no. 4, finding it incredible that the canons should be denied to the Council of Toledo convened in 400, took another route toward reconciling the difficulties. He asserted that the rule of faith belonged to the synod under Leo, but held that the remaining materials—which he does not doubt belong to the First Council of Toledo—could be referred to the synod under Leo insofar as, before the rule of faith, the twenty canons enacted at the earlier synod had been reread and confirmed. This, he thought, sufficiently explains the expression “they established.” After the rule, the professions and the sentence, he maintained, were excerpted from the fuller acts of the First Toletan synod.

> Only the manuscripts from which these documents emerged can provide assistance in this controversy. The canons and the rule of faith, first published by Merlin from a manuscript of the Isidorian collection [Col. 1332D], derive from the Hispanic collection, which Pseudo-Isidore transcribed. All copies of this collection, in the first part containing the councils, present the First Council of Toledo with its twenty canons and append only the rule of faith. The canons are preceded throughout by this chronological note: “In the time of Arcadius and Honorius, on the twelfth day before the Ides of September, during the consulship of Stilicho.” These details designate the time of the canons and the council. Several of the same manuscripts add the Spanish Era, with slight variations.

> Joannes Baptista Perezius examined four codices of the purer Hispanic collection, which he lists in Vatican manuscript 4887: that of Vigila at Albelda, the Lucensis, the Hispalensis, and that of Saint Aemilianus. We have compared the same number of manuscripts in this matter: two of the purer Hispanic collection, one Palatine manuscript, no. 755, and the other belonging to the eminent Cardinal Passionei; a third, the very ancient manuscript of the chapter of Verona, no. 59, which contains an abridgment of the canons derived from Hispanic manuscripts older than the Hispanic collection itself; and finally Vatican manuscript 1341, which presents the Hispanic collection in a Gallican and less pure form.

> Of all these manuscripts, three omit the Era: the Hispalensis, the Palatine, and Vatican 1341. The others record it as follows. The Albelda manuscript of Vigila gives Era 435; the excellent Lucensis gives Era 438; and the very old Veronese manuscript likewise has: “From the Toletan synod, Era 438.” The manuscript of Saint Aemilianus agrees with these. Although mutilated in its conciliar material and lacking the First Council of Toledo, it presents elsewhere—as we shall later explain—the most ancient excerpts from the acts of that same Council, and in them Era 438 is recorded. Finally, the manuscript of the Hispanic collection belonging to the eminent Passionei gives Era 439.

> From this diversity, however, it may be concluded that such a synod cannot be assigned to a council under Leo; it requires the Council of Toledo, which agrees with the consulship of Stilicho specified in the same inscription. Since Stilicho held the consulship twice, namely in 400 and 405, and none of the Eras recorded in the manuscripts falls in 405, the second consulship, or the year 405, cannot be intended. Since Era 438, recorded in three of the oldest manuscripts, corresponds to the year 400, it is clear that the other two Eras have been corrupted through scribal error and must be corrected to Era 438. Consequently, the council is indicated as having been held at Toledo in 400, when Stilicho first held the consulship; hence the inscription calls him not “consul for the second time,” as it ordinarily does in his second consulship, but simply “consul.”

> The canons, therefore, and the bishops who subscribed them belong to the Council of Toledo of the year 400. After the canons and the bishops’ subscriptions there follows this clause: “The enactment of the Council of Toledo is concluded.” It is omitted from the printed editions of the councils, but Garzia Loaysa publishes it from Hispanic manuscripts in his edition of the Councils of Spain. This clause shows that the preceding canons, but not the Rule of Faith described afterward, belong to the same synod.

> The matter is even clearer from the different title immediately attached in the manuscripts of the pure Hispanic collection. That title plainly designates another council commanded by Leo in Letter 15, chapter 17:

> “Here begin the rules of Catholic faith against all heresies, and especially against the Priscillianists, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Lusitania, and Baetica composed and sent, in accordance with the command of Pope Leo of the City, to Balconius, bishop of Galicia. They also established the aforesaid twenty chapters of canons at the Council of Toledo.”

> The Rule of Faith itself follows immediately. Let the final words—“They also established the aforesaid [canons]”—cause no difficulty: we shall show below that they are an erroneous insertion.

> Vatican manuscript 1341, of Gallican origin within the Hispanic collection, gives this variant form of the title:

> “Here begins the Rule of Catholic Faith against the Priscillianists, which the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Lusitania, and Baetica composed at the command of Pope Leo of the City and sent to Balconius, bishop of Galicia, etc.”

> According to this reading, since the Rule of Faith is said to have been composed at Leo’s command and sent to Balconius, another letter from Leo to those bishops would have to be posited, containing this command. But manuscripts of the purer Hispanic collection must be preferred to those of Gallican origin. In all of these, the phrase is read with different punctuation: “together with the command.” Baluzius likewise cites three other similar manuscripts, in note 14 to Letter 40 of Saint Cyprian, which similarly read “together with the command.”

> From this reading and punctuation it seems that the bishops mentioned—those who had assembled under Leo—sent to Balconius, metropolitan of Galicia, together with the Rule of Faith they had composed, also Leo’s command, or letter, in which he had ordered that all the bishops of Spain, and especially those of Galicia, should convene a synod against the Priscillianists, who had particularly infected that province. See the dissertation on lost letters, no. 18.

> After this Rule of Faith, the manuscripts mentioned pass to another Council of Toledo, the Second, and not one of them appends copies of the professions of Symphosius and Dictinius or the sentence of the council.

> These documents, together with Turribius’s letter to Idatius and Ceponius, were published by Ambrosius Morales from the manuscript of Saint Aemilianus, which was kept in the royal library of Saint Lawrence at El Escorial. Since he did not give sufficiently exact information about that manuscript, nor indicate where in it the documents were found, it was believed that they were appended there, as in the printed editions, to the First Council of Toledo [Col. 1334B]. Because no other manuscript among the many containing this synod presents these documents, the reliability of that manuscript and of such documents came under suspicion. Some judged them spurious; others thought them interpolated; still others, on the basis of the formula “of holy memory,” proper to the deceased and applied to Symphosius and Dictinius, judged that the documents should be transferred to a council held under Leo.

> But Joannes Baptista Perezius, who saw the manuscript before Ambrosius Morales, removes every difficulty. In 1575, at the command of Gaspar Quiroga, then bishop of Cuenca, he compiled from Hispanic manuscripts a book of canons containing the variants of the councils of Spain already published, together with unpublished material carefully transcribed and various annotations added wherever necessary. This book was sent by the same bishop to Rome to Gregory XIII, who had commissioned the work so that it might assist the edition and correction of Gratian. It is preserved in the Vatican Library under no. 4887.

> Four distinguished manuscripts of the Hispanic collection are praised there, among them the manuscript of Saint Aemilianus, which is described on p. 128 in these words:

> “The manuscript of Saint Aemilianus, brought from the monastery of Saint Aemilianus of La Cogolla, near Nájera, was written, as is stated there, in the year of the Lord 962. It is the fullest of all, for besides the common materials it contains the following, etc.”

> Then, after asserting on p. 143 that the Rule of Faith had been wrongly added to the First Council of Toledo and belonged to a later synod, he adds the following concerning the documents mentioned above:

> “Now, having rejected this appendix to the Council of Toledo, let us substitute another more genuine one, which exists in the same very ancient manuscript of Saint Aemilianus, although it is placed separately and not in this very location among the materials of the First Council of Toledo: namely, the abjuration of the Priscillianist heresy made by the bishops Dictinius and Symphosius, and the sentence of the council concerning whether communion should be restored to certain bishops or denied them.”

> He then appends those monuments, previously unpublished, together with certain annotations. It is therefore clear that these documents are not presented in the manuscript after the Toletan synod, but in a separate location.

> Perezius also implies that the same documents are found among the pontiff’s letters in this codex. Speaking of Turribius’s letter to Idatius and Ceponius, which he says was found in the same manuscript together with the documents mentioned above, he calls the manuscript a “book of pontifical letters” [Col. 1334D]. He does not call it this as though it contained only letters of pontiffs—for he also states that it contains the councils of the Hispanic collection—but because, in the section comprising pontifical letters, those monuments are inserted.

> The remarkable antiquity and singular excellence of this manuscript, which also contains other outstanding documents absent from the rest and universally regarded as genuine, excludes every suspicion of interpolation or fabrication, including with respect to the professions of Symphosius and Dictinius and the sentence of the council. The scribe must be believed to have derived these materials, just as he did the others, from ancient and genuine [Col. 1335A] sources.

> From the separate location in which these documents were copied, we recognize that they were wrongly appended to the First Council of Toledo in the commonly published editions, as though not only the documents themselves but also the introductions prefixed to them were attributed to that council, together with the formula “of holy memory,” which cannot belong to it.

> This separate location likewise indicates a distinct work, separated from the Toletan material, in which someone later excerpted these documents concerning the Priscillianists from the fuller acts of the synod. Hence, finding Era 438 recorded in the acts from which the excerpts were taken, he called Symphosius and Dictinius “of holy memory,” since they were already dead.

> When the compiler of the Hispanic collection stated in the preface to the First Council of Toledo that the Fathers of that council had sent a written sentence against the Priscillians in other acts, he apparently thought it sufficient to allude to that sentence; accordingly, he was not the author of the excerpt containing the sentence. It is not disclosed by any certain indication whether this excerpt was composed at the council held under Leo.

> Since not only this excerpt but also Turribius’s letter to Idatius and Ceponius was inserted in the codex, perhaps Turribius himself was the excerptor. But nothing can be asserted without evidence. This much, however, suffices to dispel every suspicion of fabrication or interpolation that Quesnellus has cast upon the material.

> The excerptor did not transcribe the complete acts themselves. Rather, whatever he thought should be excerpted from the professions and the sentence, he extracted in the very words he found in the fuller acts. Only in the titles or introductions prefixed to the sentence and the professions did he use his own words, thereby indicating the acts and recording from them the Era and the various dates of proceedings connected with the case of the Priscillianists.

> In the manuscripts of the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, the words inserted in the preface to the canons concerning the Fathers of Toledo—who, “in other acts,” issued a written sentence against the followers of Priscillian and against the heresy he had constructed—show that the compiler who wrote this preface intended to copy only the canons from the First Council of Toledo, not its acts against the Priscillians. Hence, after the canons, he added the clause “The work is concluded.”

> Perhaps the compiler of the collection omitted the sentence of the First Council of Toledo because he thought that the Rule of Faith, which seemed more explicit and authoritative against the Priscillian heresy, should be appended after the canons of that council.

> The consulship and the Era sufficiently show that the canons cited belong to the Council of Toledo of the year 400, not to another council—perhaps a Toletan council held under Leo—to which the Rule of Faith certainly belongs. In particular, among the subscriptions at least three bishops agree with the year 400 but not with 447: Ortigius, mentioned in the sentence, and Patruinus and Hilary, named in the letter of Innocent I to the Toletan synod.

> Moreover, Innocent I, in the cited letter, chapter 6, no. 9, when praising the decree of the Council of Toledo establishing that ordinations were to be carried out according to the Nicene canons, plainly refers to the intervention of Patruinus prefixed to the canons, as Father Coustant has most accurately observed. Consequently, this intervention cannot be assigned, together with the same canons, to a time after Innocent.

> Idatius, certainly, in his *Chronicle*, under Abraham’s year 2416, attributes to this council not only disciplinary proceedings against the Priscillians but also the canons. Since Abraham’s year 2416 began on the Kalends of October in the year of Christ 399, the month of September of that same year, to which the acts assign the council, corresponds to September of the Christian year 400.

> Furthermore, the same subscriptions and the concluding clause show that the aforesaid canons cannot be attributed to the council under Leo even in the sense that they were reread and confirmed at that council before the Rule of Faith was established, as Coustant believed. For if they had been taken from the council under Leo, rather than from the First Council of Toledo, and if the Fathers of that council had adopted and established them as their own—as the word “established” indicates—then neither would the subscriptions of the First Council of Toledo have been inserted, nor would the clause “The work is concluded” have been placed after the canons and subscriptions and before the Rule of Faith [Col. 1336A].

> If they had been confirmed by rereading the First Council of Toledo, the text would not have said “they established,” but—as happened in a similar case at Braga in 563—“they reread,” or something comparable. The concluding clause would have been omitted, and the Fathers would have proceeded directly to composing the Rule of Faith.

> What, then, should be thought of the word “established,” which cannot in any way apply to the Fathers of the council under Leo? Only conjecture is possible. Since it is certain that the canons belong to the Council of Toledo of 400, whereas the Rule of Faith belongs to another council under Leo—and since the Rule of Faith alone is attributed to that council in the Braga synod cited above—the words inserted in the title of the Rule of Faith, “They also established the aforesaid twenty chapters of canons at the Council of Toledo,” appear to be an improperly introduced addition. It has no connection whatever either with what precedes or with what follows, and undoubtedly did not exist in the codex from which the Rule itself was taken [Col. 1336B].

> Perhaps it was once a marginal note added by someone to the subscriptions, which later slipped from its proper place into the text of the title immediately preceding the Rule. Without this foreign addition, which the context does not admit, the Rule itself should have followed directly after that title.

> If this explanation is not accepted, the error must be attributed to the Hispanic compiler. In the treatise on ancient collections of canons, which we shall place at the beginning of volume III, further errors will be exposed in the titles and prefaces of the African canons; there we shall prove that their collection is older than the Hispanic collection and was received by the Hispanic compiler. See, among other matters, what will be said about the canons of the Council of Milevis and the Fourth Council of Carthage.

> Just as this ancient compiler erred when, in the titles or prefaces of these councils, he attributed to them canons that do not belong to them—as will be shown at greater length in the treatise cited—so it is not surprising if the later Hispanic compiler, who received this collection of African canons together with the same errors, likewise asserted, when assembling the canons of the Spanish synods, that the canons enacted at the First Council of Toledo belonged to the Fathers of the synod that composed the Rule of Faith under Leo.

> It is also worth noting another error discovered in the preface of the same Council of Toledo. The final bishop listed there is called, in a peculiar form with mention of his see, *Exuperantius de Galletia Lucensis conventus municipii Celenis* (“Exuperantius of Galicia, of the Lucensian district of the municipality of Celenis”); yet in the same preface, in the subscriptions, and in the sentence of that synod, Ortigius is named, whom we know from Idatius to have been bishop of Celenis at the time of the Toletan synod.

> Since in other manuscripts used by Merlin the same Exuperantius is read without mention of his see, and since the order of the bishops is changed and the words are otherwise presented, as follows—“Exuperantius, Serenus, Florus, Leporius, Aurelianus, Lampadius, Leona of Gaul, Lucentius”—some have suspected that another assembly, or the Council of Celenis held under Leo in Galicia, had been confused here with the First Council of Toledo.

> But the whole conjecture disappears if this reading is thought to have originated not with the Hispanic compiler but with the arbitrary intervention of his copyist, who, not understanding the corrupt reading of the manuscript of the pure Hispanic collection, thought it should be corrected in this way.

> That this is so becomes evident from the manuscripts of the pure Hispanic collection, which know nothing of this reading, and from those of Gallican and Isidorian origin, which alone prefer it, like many other arbitrary corrections of the same kind [Col. 1336D].

> The manuscripts of the pure Hispanic collection give the order and reading that we first supplied from Garzia Loaysa’s edition; Perezius confirms it from the Lucensis manuscript, and we likewise find it in our own copies of the pure Hispanic collection.

> Some of these books merely offer the same reading in a greatly corrupted form, as in Vatican Palatine manuscript 575, where we find: *Exuperantius de Callatia Lucentiosis conventus mancipii Celenis* (“Exuperantius of Callatia, of the Lucensian district, of the estate of Celenis”).

> Someone who did not so much copy as correct this collection in manuscripts of Gallican origin within the Hispanic collection encountered a similar error. He not only changed the order of the bishops but also corrected the passage as follows:

> *Exuperantius, Serenus, Florus, Leporius, Eustochius, Aurelianus, Lampius de Gallia, Lucentius. Is conventus municipii Celenis actus est* (“Exuperantius, Serenus, Florus, Leporius, Eustochius, Aurelianus, Lampius of Gaul, Lucentius. This assembly of the municipality of Celenis was held”).

> Thus it appears in Vatican manuscript 1341, of Gallican origin, and similarly in other Isidorian manuscripts that received this council from Hispanic manuscripts of Gallican origin. It is clear there that *de Gallatia Lucentiosis* (“of Galicia, of the Lucensian district”) was corrected to *de Gallia Lucentius* (“of Gaul, Lucentius”). The phrase “was held” was also added in order to complete the sense.

> Once this arbitrary correction has been dismissed as worthless, so that no Celenian assembly or synod may be inferred from it, it becomes evident that the manuscripts of the purer Hispanic collection contain an error committed by the compiler at this point—an error that no one will easily be able to understand or explain.]

They say that Dictinius was bishop of Asturica, and that Turribius himself—whose letter we have in our hands—was appointed in the place of the departing Dictinius. That he had Symphosius, or Symposium, the bishop, as his father is indicated by Dictinius’s own profession of faith [1374], issued at the First Council of Toledo, in these words:

> “I follow the judgment of my lord, my father, my begetter, and my teacher, Symphosius.”

Furthermore, from that same man he imbibed the poison of the Priscillianist heresy, and from him also he received life. Both men were accused of that heresy at the Council of Zaragoza in 381, convened against Priscillian [1375]. Symphosius is said to have evaded its judgment by withdrawing from the sentence of the First Council of Toledo.

Thus, when afterward he asked that peace be restored to him together with the others, he scarcely obtained a hearing unless Saint Ambrose had intervened by his letters [1376], both on behalf of Symphosius the bishop and Dictinius the presbyter, as well as the others accused of the same error. They seem to have gone to Milan to discuss their reconciliation with Saint Ambrose. In his presence and hearing, they are said to have imposed upon themselves certain conditions of peace [1377]. One of these was that Dictinius should retain his position in the presbyterate in the interest of good peace and should not receive an increase of honor; another was that they themselves should condemn what they had wrongly done.

They fulfilled neither condition. For they not only persevered for a long time in their own judgment [1378], but Symphosius also consecrated Dictinius as bishop.

When summoned by the bishops of Spain to the Council of Toledo to give an account of these matters, they refused to appear before it and evaded its judgment [1379], until, having returned to a sounder mind, they presented themselves at the other Council of Toledo in the year 400. There they rejected all their erroneous opinions and voluntarily condemned Priscillian together with his writings.

By the indulgence of that council, each was permitted to remain in his own see. Their communion, however, was suspended and was not to be restored until letters proved that they had been received into the communion of the Roman and Milanese pontiffs; thus they awaited communion from those from whom they had previously received hope of future peace. In the meantime, they were removed from the power to ordain bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

It is clear from what has been said that there were more Toletan synods than has hitherto been believed. Cardinal Baronius, following others, had posited only the one of the year 400 [1380]. In later editions of his *Annals* he recognized and defended a second, assigning it to the year of Christ 405, no. 43.

We now assert a third, earlier than both of those, namely one that must be placed between the Council of Zaragoza of 381 and the Council of Toledo of 400. For in this last synod the heretics are accused of having previously avoided a council summoned in the city of Toledo. “We had summoned them,” the Fathers say, “and we would have heard why they had not fulfilled the conditions that they themselves had imposed in the holy presence and hearing of Ambrose.”

No one can object that only a council announced, and not one actually convened, is intended; for they could not be said to have evaded a council that had not been assembled.

We can also add a fourth council, held in the time of our Leo [1381] by the bishops of Tarraconensis, Carthaginiensis, Lusitania, and Galicia. Leo himself urges that it be convened at the end of this letter, and the First Council of Braga testifies that it was in fact convened; that council also relates that the Rule of Faith was composed by the same bishops. Finally, the title of the Rule of Faith improperly attached to that synod indicates its location.

Concerning Dictinius’s writings or treatises, whose reading Saint Leo forbids in this chapter, see chapter 17 of the First Council of Braga, which forbids anyone to read them under penalty of anathema.

What we have reported about Dictinius from the sentence of the First Council of Toledo—namely, that his see was preserved for him after he had abjured the Priscillianist sect—seems to me scarcely reconcilable with what Idatius, a most trustworthy witness in this matter, reports:

> “Dictinius, bishop of Asturica,” he says, “was expelled, together with other bishops of the same sect, because of the Priscillianist heresy that he professed; Turribius succeeded him.”

I shall not blush to confess and publish the lapse of memory, or hallucination, that I suffered at this point in the first edition. I do not find this account of Dictinius, which I cited and reported in good faith under the name of Idatius, in Idatius; nor can I say in any way whose it is. I can testify and solemnly affirm that I did not fabricate it, but copied it from some book whose identity is now buried in profound forgetfulness.

I had intended to scrape this historical fragment, now deprived of its parent, from this passage, together with everything built upon it. But afterward I abandoned that plan, hoping that what does not now return to my own memory might perhaps someday occur to the eyes of some learned reader during his reading and be communicated to the printer for insertion in this place [Col. 1338B].

For if Dictinius was expelled from his see and Turribius immediately succeeded him, I do not see how Dictinius could have recovered the see of Asturica at the Council of Toledo in 400, since the canonical laws forbade two bishops to govern one Church simultaneously.

Add to this that, if before the year 400 Turribius was bishop of the Asturicenses—as he must have been if both the acts of the Council of Toledo and the account of Idatius are true—he had reached nearly eighty years of age when he wrote this letter to Saint Leo and the other letter to Idatius and Ceponius.

The fact that both letters were written at the same time is made clear by the mention of each in our Leo’s letter, and by the identical complaints that Turribius brought to the Spanish bishops and to the Roman pontiff against the same heresy, which had revived.

He wrote those letters after he had finally returned to his own church following a long and arduous journey, which he had undertaken to visit the churches throughout Spain [Col. 1338C]. As he says, the severe hardships of that journey and the tearful burdens of necessity were wholly unsuitable to such an advanced age. It therefore seems unlikely that Turribius would ever have undertaken it if he had already reached the old age that he must necessarily have attained had he held the bishopric before Dictinius’s repentance [1382].

There is scarcely any path by which we can escape these difficulties. Certainly the account of Dictinius’s restoration must appear suspect to me:

1. First, because although Idatius says that Turribius was appointed in the place of Dictinius, who had been expelled for heresy, he says nothing about Turribius’s resignation or Dictinius’s restoration. Nothing, therefore, should outweigh the testimony of an author of such authority, who flourished at the same time among the bishops of that province and was a close associate of Turribius. With him, as he himself relates, he exposed the Manichaeans hiding in the city of Asturica through episcopal proceedings, brought them to judgment, and published their condemnation throughout Spain. By “Manichaeans” he appears to mean the Priscillianists, as Saints Leo and Jerome also do [Col. 1338D].

2. Although the Fathers of the Toletan synod wished to grant pardon to other bishops who repented after their fall, whatever the cause, there were very serious reasons why Dictinius should be separated from them and excluded from the grace of indulgence [Col. 1339A]. He had not merely adhered to the doctrine of the heretics; he had defended it in books and had thereby drawn many into error. Those writings produced such ruin that their poison continued to destroy many even after their author’s abjuration, as is evident from Turribius’s complaints to Leo and Leo’s reply to Turribius. It is also evident from chapter 17 of the First Council of Braga, held almost a hundred years later, which again proscribed Dictinius’s writings, so widely and deeply had that pestilence spread.

3. The following facts also oppose Dictinius’s restoration: he had been ordained after embracing the heresy; he had been ordained by his father, who had himself fallen into heresy; he had been demanded by the tumultuous people and forcibly elevated to the episcopal see; and this was contrary to Saint Ambrose’s decree, which had determined that he should remain content with presbyteral honor.

All these facts are contained in the cited excerpts from the acts of Toledo [Col. 1339B]. Whoever fears to call their reliability into question must entangle himself in these difficulties. Whoever judges them spurious or adulterated will free himself from all these complications and embrace what is most probable.

I confess that the reliability of those excerpts seems to me highly unstable. They became known to the public only recently through the work of Ambrosius Morales, from a single manuscript; nowhere is there any trace of them in other manuscripts, especially those through which a double edition of the Toletan canons was produced long ago.

Moreover, I suspect, not without reason, that those professions were fabricated by someone favoring the Priscillianist party. First, they call Symphosius and Dictinius “bishops of holy memory,” which, although tolerable elsewhere, seems absurd in a profession by which they renounce heresy.

Next, they scarcely touch upon the errors of Priscillian and his followers. They speak [1383] only of the Son’s being unbegotten, of two principles, and of the soul’s consubstantiality with the Father. These opinions they condemn in such a way that they seem to be practicing deception and reserving for themselves the ability to explain their professions in their own sense.

For from the third chapter of Saint Leo it is clear that they had said, in some sense, that the Son was begotten. From the fifth it is clear that they did not expressly maintain that God and man have one nature—which is the only thing Dictinius condemns in that profession—but rather that the human soul is of divine substance, which appears to be a different claim.

Finally, we do not read that they acknowledged two principles. They attributed the entire creation of flesh and bodies to the devil, while they seem to have imagined that souls were something divine and uncreated.

Thus those professions appear to have been composed wholly for purposes of deception. The remaining features increase this suspicion. When Dictinius condemns his own writings, he does so in highly obscure language:

> “In my earlier apprehension, and in the beginnings of my conversion, whatever I wrote, I reject with all my heart.”

Later he says:

> “Everything that is found to be against the faith.”

By these words he seems to reject not all his writings but only certain ones, and even those only if they are proved to be contrary to the faith.

Similarly, Symphosius does not reject and condemn all the books of Priscillian, but only those in which he is said to have written that the Son was unbegotten. The expression “where it is said,” together with the mere mention of “unbegotten,” reveals, in my judgment, the deceitful mind of the man or writer, as does the statement found in the latter part of the profession:

> “If he composed any books wickedly, I condemn them together with their author.”

In the excerpt of the definitive sentence there are also certain things that weaken its credibility. For it diminishes the fault of both bishops so greatly that one could scarcely say that they had fallen into error. “We find,” say the Fathers, “that Symphosius, deceived and held fast, conducted himself improperly in certain matters for a considerable time, though he was not entangled in any apocryphal books or novel teachings composed by Priscillian; Dictinius, having nearly fallen through several letters, etc.” All this agrees very poorly with what both Idacius and others report about Dictinius and his associates; or at least we leave it to others to reconcile these accounts.

If, however, it is still permissible to attempt another way out and to proceed by conjecture, we shall not posit two Dictiniuses—for although that method of reconciliation is altogether easy and convenient, it is also full of rashness—but perhaps it will not be unreasonable to distinguish two falls of Dictinius. On this supposition, it would have to be said that, rising again from his first fall, Dictinius recovered his see through the indulgence of the First Council of Toledo. But after relapsing some years later, he was deservedly rejected from priestly dignity and yielded his place to Turribius. Anyone wishing to retain the traditionally accepted date of the Council of Toledo, not to reject that portion excerpted from the Acts, and to reconcile both accounts with the 1384 Chronicon of Idacius must necessarily take this course.

Nor is there lacking in that excerpt material by which we can strengthen our conjecture concerning Dictinius’s double fall. His own words in the profession suggest as much: “At my former apprehension, at the beginning of my conversion, whatever I wrote.” From this also perhaps derives the fact that in the excerpt of the sentence Dictinius is said merely to have “nearly fallen”; whereas in the excerpt of the profession he accuses himself of error, condemns his presumption, asks to be corrected, prays that the door not of hell but of heaven be opened to him, strikes with anathema the things he had previously written, and so forth.
