I seem to be able to infer from a letter of Pope Innocent himself to the Synod of Toledo, chapter 3, that Symphosius and Dictinius were at some time restored to their sees—indeed, during the pontificate of Pope Innocent. From that letter it is clear that certain people took the restoration of both bishops badly, arguing that it was contrary to the canons. But if they had been restored only to ecclesiastical communion and not also to their sees, it is unlikely that Bishop John and perhaps others would have been so troubled by it, since the grace of ecclesiastical communion was never denied to anyone returning from heresy or schism.

In any event, these copies of the profession of the repentant bishops and of the definitive sentence of the council appear either to have been taken down by an unskilled person or to have been abridged and interpolated by a heretic, who perhaps presented us with badly stitched-together fragments from different councils. Yet it is not at all difficult to believe that he inserted some genuine material in them in order to make the fraud more effective. Whatever the truth may finally be, we set forth conjectures and leave the whole matter to the judgment of the more learned.

**9. “Tarraconenses, Carthaginenses, Lusitanos, atque Gallicos.”** Thus *Gallicos* is found in the manuscript codices of Grimani, Corbie, Victor, Cambridge, and Thuani; all editions likewise have it, except for the two more recent collections of Councils and Nicolini’s edition, which have *Gallaecos*, or in the margin *Gallicios* or *Gallicianos*. But the difficulty does not lie here, since, in view of the many manuscripts and printed books that present the reading in this form, it would be rash to resist it.

The question is whether this word should be understood of the bishops of Gaul, or rather of those who were established in the Spanish province of Galicia. The former view is supported by the fact that Priscillian and his followers had spread the seeds of their perfidy through the Gallic provinces of Aquitaine, as Sulpicius Severus relates in book II, and had especially corrupted the people of Elusa with their perverse preaching. It is also relevant that Gallic bishops took part in the Council of Zaragoza, assembled against the Priscillianists around the year 381, and that another synod was convened at Bordeaux against the same heretics, at which there is no doubt that Spaniards likewise were present.

It is also certain that in the time of Saint Leo there was extensive intercourse between the Gallic and Spanish Churches. Two letters of our pontiff bear witness to this: one in which he wishes the Spaniards to be informed through the Gallic bishops of events then taking place in the East, especially of the prosperous outcome of the Council of Chalcedon (*Epistle* 77, to the Gallic bishops, chapter 1); the other, which he wrote jointly to the bishops of both provinces concerning Easter.

Idacius’s *Chronicle* accords with the former letter: “From Gaul,” he says, “the letters of Flavian, sent to Bishop Leo, are brought, together with the writings of Cyril of Alexandria to Nestorius of Constantinople concerning Eutyches, the heretical Ebionite, and the replies of Bishop Leo to him; these are circulated throughout the Churches along with the acts and writings of other bishops.”

Add to this that, since the Churches of Spain were then living in great ignorance and confusion, with many of their bishops either infected with error or insufficiently instructed in the Church’s doctrine, it was highly appropriate that their synods should receive strength from the faith and teaching of the Gallic bishops. Leo knew that in them, as he himself puts it, heavenly doctrine flourished through instruction from the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, I more readily accept the other view:

1. Although the Gallic Churches had once suffered from the Priscillianist plague, at that time they were entirely free from it, as is clear from the silence of the synods.

2. I do not remember ever reading the word *Gallicos* used for Gallic bishops, regions, or peoples, at least not in Leo or in ecclesiastical authors of roughly his period. They always use *Galliae*, *Galliarum*, or *Gallicanae regiones*.

3. When Saint Leo wished to convene a general council from all the provinces of Spain, who could believe that the province of Galicia was omitted? It seems to have been the largest and most distinguished of all. Turribius, Idacius, and Ceponius were its bishops; it especially needed the healing hand of a synod, since the Priscillianist disease had broken out there above all; and it was chiefly from its bishops that Saint Leo wished the council to be assembled, even if the bishops of the other provinces could not attend. Who, I ask, could suppose that Saint Leo did not write to the bishops of Galicia?

Lucretius of Toledo names the Baetican bishops in their place in the First Council of Braga, whose words we quoted above. But he had already been speaking of the bishops of Galicia, who had assembled separately in the synod of their own province and had not been permitted by their rulers to attend the council of the other four provinces.

I have thought it worthwhile to say this about a matter that is by no means obscure, since I see that some incline to interpret the word as referring to our Gallic bishops.

## On Epistle XVI

**“To all the bishops established throughout Sicily.”**

**1. “If you receive the consecration of honor from a certain source, you should also take from that source the rule of your entire observance.”**

Among learned men it is disputed whether, in the suburban regions, each province had its own metropolitan bishops by whom the provinces were governed, provincial bishops were consecrated, synods convened, and other metropolitan duties performed. Many affirm this; some deny it.

I think it should be regarded as certain that, if there were metropolitans, they possessed the title without the substance, at least in Leo’s time. For the Roman pontiffs had drawn to themselves all the prerogatives and duties of metropolitan dignity, with the support of the emperors and the acquiescence of the provincial bishops, who considered it a great honor to receive pontifical dignity from the bishop of the first see and the summit of all bishops. The metropolitans themselves did not resist; having received the honor of their priesthood from the pontiffs of the City, they depended entirely upon them.

[**Note:** It cannot be said that the Roman pontiffs drew to themselves the prerogatives and duties of metropolitan dignity in the suburban regions unless it is assumed that each province of those regions had ecclesiastical metropolitans. Yet this is false. When ecclesiastical metropolitan sees began to be established in the West after the age of Constantine, as may be gathered from what we discussed at length concerning the origin of ecclesiastical metropolises in Gaul in the observations on Quesnel’s dissertation 5, part II, chapter 5, the sees of Milan and Aquileia acquired metropolitan dignity toward the end of the fourth century, and Ravenna during Leo’s pontificate. No metropolitan was established in the other provinces, or in the suburban regions, until much later; in those regions the Roman pontiff alone exercised metropolitan jurisdiction, as he had always done before. Thus Saint Leo did not draw this dignity, with its prerogatives and duties, to himself; rather, he continued and persisted in exercising his right over what had belonged from the beginning solely to his see, as did his successors, until they judged it expedient, through the establishment of metropolitans in those regions, to share this rank with other bishops. Hence all that Quesnel discusses in his more extensive note falls away.]

I therefore seem to discern some distinction between the manner of ordaining that the Roman pontiff claimed for himself in the suburban regions and that which the other exarchs or patriarchs exercised. They convened the council of their exarchate in such a way that each metropolitan was free, by his own right and by the canons granted to him, to summon the synod of his province. In the ordination of provincial bishops they interposed their decree in such a way that the metropolitan’s authority came first, and they learned of the clergy’s election and the people’s consent only through his report. They administered their entire exarchate in such a way that the metropolitans’ rights and duties remained intact.

Nothing of this sort existed in the suburban regions. First, we find that the metropolitans were given no power to convene their own provincial council; indeed, no acts of such synods exist, at least, if I am not mistaken, before the tenth or twelfth century, nor is any mention of them celebrated among ecclesiastical authors. On the contrary, even the bishops of the most remote provinces were ordered to present themselves at Rome for synod every year, as is clear from chapter 7 of this very letter. Since Saint Leo testifies that he commands this on the authority of the Nicene canon (Canon 5 of Nicaea), it is evident that he drew to his own see those synods which, according to the intention of the Nicene canons, were to be convened at the metropolitan see of each province.

For the canon just cited deals only with provincial synods: “It has seemed good,” it says, “that in each province councils be held twice a year, so that, with all the bishops of the province gathered together, such questions may be examined jointly by all.”

**2.** [**Note:** See Gregory I, book V, letter 13, to the rector of Sicily, concerning the clergy of Lilybaeum asking permission from the Roman pontiff to elect a bishop for themselves.]

The metropolitans appear to have played no part in the elections and ordinations of bishops. It is reasonable to believe that the clergy and people of each city conducted the election. When they had reported it to the Roman pontiff, he either delegated someone to consecrate the elect or—as happened very often—the person to be consecrated was summoned to Rome, or came there voluntarily.

We infer this from the fact that no letters now appear either from metropolitans to the bishop of the City or from him to the metropolitans containing reports of episcopal elections or anything else concerning the matter of consecration. The pontiffs never complain about improperly ordained bishops or about suburban metropolitans; nor are complaints about those metropolitans ever brought to them by the provincials. Yet there are many letters in which the authority of the Apostolic See is invoked against bishops who had ordained clerics contrary to the canons, and others in which the Roman pontiff rebukes bishops for admitting certain persons into the clergy contrary to canonical regulations.

Finally, he entrusted the execution of his constitutions not to the care and diligence of the metropolitans, but for this purpose selected certain provincial bishops at his discretion—now one, now another—without any mention of the metropolitans.

I omit the authority of Pope Celestine, often cited by others. In a letter written to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, he claims their ordinations for himself. I also omit the testimony of the *Liber Pontificalis*, which records that Roman bishops consecrated more bishops than could plausibly have belonged only to the metropolitan province of Rome. Sixtus III, Leo’s predecessor, is said to have ordained fifty-two bishops during at most eight years of pontificate, and Leo himself created one hundred and eighty-four. If these had all been taken from the single metropolitan province, it would have to be said that the see of each city was vacant at least three times during the course of twenty years—a claim that would scarcely find credence.

**1388 3.** As for the various consultations, reports, and other matters that usually arise in the administration of a province, no trace remains from which it might appear that these were handled by suburban metropolitans. Rather, matters that in other dioceses and exarchates are ordinarily brought to the patriarch through the intervention and report of the metropolitans were brought to the Roman See by the bishops, clergy, or even citizens of the individual cities.

The bishop of Nuceria consulted Innocent I concerning various points of ecclesiastical discipline, without involving a metropolitan. Innocent praises this:

“We cannot but marvel,” he says, “that your charity follows the institutions of the elders and refers to us, as to the head and summit of the episcopate, everything that may admit of some doubt,” and so forth. (*Epistle* 4, to Felix, bishop of Nuceria.)

The same Innocent wrote to Maximus and Severus, bishops established among the Bruttians, after receiving a complaint from a certain Maximilianus, a lay official, concerning unworthy priests. The pontiff does not complain of metropolitan negligence, as is customary when something of this kind is perpetrated contrary to the canons in other provinces.

The same should be observed concerning his letter 6, to Agapitus, Macedonius, and Maurianus, bishops of Apulia. He refers none of these matters to the metropolitans, contrary to the practice customary in other dioceses.

Witness also letter 83, now 108, to Theodore, bishop of Forum Julii in the Gallic province. When he had consulted Saint Leo about certain questions, the holy pontiff rebuked him as follows:

“The order of your concern should indeed have been this: that you first confer with your metropolitan concerning the matter that appeared to require inquiry; and if your affection did not know what he himself also did not know, you should both have asked to be instructed together. For in matters that concern the general observance of all the Lord’s priests, nothing ought to be investigated without the primates.”

Compare this with Innocent’s words to Felix of Nuceria.

Moreover, when Saint Leo wrote in reply to the bishops of the suburban provinces, or wished to address them with his admonitions, he did not send letters to the metropolitan and through him to the other provincials; rather, he delegated another bishop for this purpose. This indicates that such metropolitans exercised scarcely any function at all.

Thus, in the present letter, he wished his instruction to reach all the priests through Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum in the same province of Sicily, and Baccillus, bishop of another city. He ought to have sent it to the bishop of Syracuse, unless he believed that all the metropolitan duties he had taken upon himself could be assigned by him in turn to one bishop and then another.

In the same way, when writing to Dorus of Beneventum, he entrusted the execution of his command not to a metropolitan but to a certain Julius, perhaps bishop of Puteoli.

He acted quite differently when letters had to be sent not only to bishops of more remote dioceses, such as the Gallic, Spanish, and Illyrian dioceses, but also to the Italian dioceses adjoining the City. For the metropolitans of the provinces of this diocese had full power to ordain their own provincial bishops; they convened their synods without the summons of the Roman pontiff; and if any questions arose in such provinces that ought by custom to be referred to the Apostolic and primary see of the West, they were transmitted through the metropolitan’s consultation. In short, whatever could pertain to the administration of each province always remained with the metropolitans.

Examples exist in Saint Leo—outside him, it is not appropriate for us now to range. For the letters that he wrote to the three metropolitans of the Italian diocese—namely, the bishops of Milan, Aquileia, and Ravenna—make the clearest possible mention of the discipline of which we have just spoken.

Septimius, bishop of either Altinum or another city in the province of Istria, informed Saint Leo by letter that remnants of Pelagianism were reviving. Leo immediately urged the metropolitan of the province by letter to watch with pastoral care over the preservation of the decrees of the sacred canons and the protection of the Church against the serpentine deceit of heretics, and he entrusted the entire concern of this matter to him.

Likewise, in the year 458, some years after the disaster of Attila, when Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman See, had returned from the region of Aquileia and reported to Saint Leo—not in writing, but solely by word of mouth—that Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, was experiencing difficulty concerning certain points of discipline arising from the occasion of the war and was asking for the judgment of the Apostolic See, Leo directed letter 129, now 159, to the metropolitan alone, and to the other bishops only through him.

“This letter,” he says, “which we have sent in response to the consultation of your fraternity, you shall cause to reach all your brother and fellow-provincial bishops.”

The case of Ravenna is no less clear. On the same occasion a serious controversy arose concerning the sacrament of baptism: both concerning its administration to those who had been baptized by heretics and concerning infants of whom it was not known whether they had been baptized before the barbarian captivity. The matter was first debated in a Roman council. The Fathers of the council then decided that an encyclical letter should be sent in Leo’s name to all the provinces of Italy that had suffered hostile incursions, so that they might know what ought to be done.

That this letter was directed to the individual metropolitans is attested by the conclusion of Leo’s letter 135, now 166, to Neon or Leo, bishop of Ravenna:

“For this reason, dearest brother, we wish this matter to reach the knowledge of all generally, lest, while more fear than is just is entertained, God’s mercy be denied to those who desire to be saved.”

By these words Saint Leo almost excuses the unusual character of the matter. Since the province of Emilia, whose metropolitan was Neon, did not belong to the council of the suburban diocese, the decrees of that synod were not ordinarily sent to it.

Nor should I omit to note that Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, when replying to the letter of Eutyches, who was imploring his assistance, stated that he could do nothing without the consent of the Roman pontiff, because the matter concerned not the discipline of his own Church or province but the faith:

“For the sake of peace and the faith,” he says, “we cannot hear cases of faith without the consent of the bishop of the Roman city.”

In other matters, however, he did not act so.

The case of Milan is likewise demonstrated by Saint Leo’s letter to Eusebius, bishop of Milan, which we recognize from Eusebius’s reply. It is clear that Eusebius held a special synod of the bishops of his province. That he likewise possessed their ordination, as the bishops of Ravenna and Aquileia possessed that of their provincials, is understood, among other arguments, especially from the solemn expression by which belonging to someone’s council, belonging to his consecration, and belonging to his ordination are treated as precisely equivalent.

From what has been said we conclude that there was a broad distinction between the use of patriarchal jurisdiction claimed by the Roman pontiff over the Churches of the West and that which belonged by right to the other patriarchs. If one considers the Italian diocese and the other transalpine or overseas dioceses, the Roman pontiff neither summoned their bishops to his synod nor ordained them personally or by his decree. If one considers the suburban regions, he both ordained the elect and compelled them to attend his council in such a way that the jurisdiction of the metropolitans in those regions was entirely inert and idle. They were not permitted to summon their provincials either to their own council or to their own consecration; the Roman pontiff alone possessed the entire right.

I have not been reluctant to examine this matter somewhat more fully on the occasion of these words: “If you receive the consecration of honor from a certain source, you should also take from that source the rule of your entire observance,” and so forth. These final words also confirm what we said above. It was the metropolitan’s role to imbue the bishop to whom he had given the honor of consecration first with the laws of ecclesiastical discipline and thereafter to instruct him in questions that arose, when he consulted him, as the principal teacher and master of his province.

The Council of Tarragona, canon 5, strongly supports this custom and rule:

“If anyone has not been ordained bishop in a metropolitan city, after he has received the blessing through the metropolitan’s letters and has obtained the honor of bishop, we decree that it is best that, at the appointed time—namely, after two months have been completed—he should present himself before his metropolitan, so that, instructed by him in ecclesiastical admonitions, he may more fully recognize what he ought to observe.”

This returns to the same point that we quoted above from the letter of our Leo to Theodore of Forum Julii.

The formulas for episcopal promotions inserted by Jacques Sirmond in the *Gallic Councils*, and reprinted by Baluzius in volume II of the *Capitularia*, should also be consulted. The older *Pontificals* should likewise be consulted. From all these sources it is understood with what care those being ordained, or newly ordained, were instructed by their consecrators or metropolitans. They also received in writing a book of ecclesiastical rules, which they called a *decretum*.

**2. “Mystical and rational exemplification.”**

There are almost as many different readings of this passage as there are codices. The Cambridge and Thuani manuscripts have: “A rational exception of mystical tradition.” Another Thuani manuscript and the Trecopithanus have: “An exception that is mystical, or mystically rational.” All editions place in the margin: “Mystical and rational exception.” Isidore Mercator has: “An exception of mystical reason.”

We have retained in the text the reading of Dionysius Exiguus and Cresconius—although Cresconius reads *rationalis*—both because of the certain antiquity and authority of each witness and because this reading seems to me to approach more closely the mind of our author.

Saint Leo calls the mystical and rational exemplification of the principal and greatest sacrament—that is, baptism—“mystical and rational” when it is conferred at Easter because, as he says in chapter 3, that day and season appear to have been chosen for the regeneration of the children of human beings and their adoption as children of God. Through the likeness and form of the mystery, what is performed in the members corresponds to what was performed in the head itself, since in baptism they die with him, are buried with him, and rise again with him.

**3. “Some think that on that same day the Lord came to baptism,” etc.**

You see that even in that century it was not certain on what day the Lord Jesus was baptized, since Saint Leo says that, according to the opinion of some, it was to be assigned to the eighth day before the Ides of January. Epiphanius, however, who was still alive at the beginning of this fifth century, says that he was baptized on the sixth day before the Ides of November, in book II of *Against Heresies*, heresy 5, section 24.

**[Col. 1345D] 4. “Different sacrifices fashioned one victim.”**

I would gladly have retained *prefigured*, which is commonly read, had it not been rejected by the agreement of Dionysius, Cresconius, and the five manuscripts cited above. Our author’s meaning is this: it was not by a single legal sacrifice that the one victim of our sacrifice was prefigured; rather, many different sacrifices had once been instituted, so that the Christian sacrifice might be outlined and prefigured in many forms and in many ways.

In the present passage, therefore, this is the force of the word *reformare*: to form again and again, or to figure and foreshadow.

**5. “According to the apostolic rule.”**

What apostolic rule is this? Is it a rule handed down through tradition from the apostles, prescribing exorcisms, scrutinies, and fasts to be undertaken by those who are to be baptized? Perhaps so, though I do not know whether this is asserted by the holy Fathers.

Augustine, in book II of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, chapter 29 toward the end, calls the ancient tradition of the Church the custom by which infants are exorcised and breathed upon. “The holy Church throughout the whole world does this uniformly with regard to those who are to be baptized,” says our Leo in the chapters once attributed to Celestine. Therefore, according to Saint Augustine’s rule, since this practice is found neither in Scripture nor in the decrees of councils, it must be said to descend from apostolic tradition.

Leo may also have had in mind that apostolic injunction found in 1 Corinthians, chapter 5, which Pope Siricius indicated in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 2. Leo was certainly observing it when he wrote these words about both the time of baptism and the accompanying ceremonies:

“Only those who have given their names forty days or more beforehand, and who have been cleansed by exorcisms, daily prayers, and fasts, are to be chosen for the sacrament of baptism, so that that apostolic injunction may be fulfilled: once the old leaven has been purged, the dough may begin to be new.”

Concerning the fasts and the whole penitence of the catechumens, see, if you wish, the excellent observation of Gabriel Albaspinaeus, bishop of Orléans, which is the first of book II of his *Observations*.

**6. “Only two seasons, Easter and Pentecost.”**

Before Saint Leo, no canon or decree, apart from the Sirician text cited shortly before, fixed a time for the administration of baptism. Siricius appeals only to the authority of his see and to the custom of all the Churches. Saint Leo mentions only the custom of apostolic institution, the apostolic rules, and the practices of his see.

The author of the Gallic work *On Bishops Judged Canonically*, page 78, therefore vainly imagined that Saint Leo had marked out and established certain canons on this subject, in order somehow to defend another dream concerning a code of the canons of the universal Church. For the mention of canons that Saint Leo introduces in the following chapter concerns the general observance of the canons, as anyone who reads even hastily will see.

After Saint Leo, Pope Gelasius likewise decreed concerning Easter and Pentecost, in his letter to the bishops of Lucania, chapter 10, in the year 494; so did the Council of Gerunda in 517; Auxerre, canon 18, in 578; the Second Council of Mâcon, canon 3, in 585; and Pope Gregory II in 723, in his letter to the clergy and people of Thuringia, and elsewhere.

**7. “Let them attend without delay.”**

Thus read Dionysius and all the manuscript codices. They do not have the words that follow in most printed books, “and let this custom be observed by you,” except for one Thuani manuscript and the Trecopithanus, one of which was copied from the other.

Nicolini’s edition in the text, and the editions of Surius, Crabbe, Sichardus, and Canisius in the margin, present the reading as follows: “Let them come together without concealment,” which is certainly not difficult if this custom is mutually observed among you.

## On Epistle XVII

**To the bishops established throughout Sicily**

**1.** [**Note:** We have answered at full length the objections that Quesnel raises here in order to cast doubt upon this letter, in the admonition prefixed to it and especially in the notes appended to it.]

Gerard Vossius, a Catholic doctor, was the first to publish this letter to the bishops of Sicily, of which we have been unable to obtain any manuscript copy. He received it from an ancient manuscript codex of Cardinal Sirlet and, on the basis of the consular note and of the phraseology and diction of Leo, which seemed to him to breathe Leo’s spirit, he not only suspected but plainly and unequivocally asserted that it was the work of Leo the Great.

For my part, I am almost certain that it is not Leo’s, even from an examination of its style alone, which anyone can easily recognize as differing from the Leonine style. Besides, the diction of the entire letter is in every respect barren and exceedingly meager.

**2.** This letter is identified as having been sent to the bishops of Sicily on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, during the consulship of Alypius or Calepius. Yet we have another letter—one certainly genuine and belonging to our Leo—written to the same bishops on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November under the same consul, that is, the day before this letter was supposedly written, if it please God.

Who could persuade himself that Leo wrote two letters at almost the same time to bishops established in a very remote region? If he had needed to write to those same bishops about the alienation of property, he could very easily have done so in the letter that he was sending to Sicily during those days concerning the time for celebrating baptism. Or, if some new complaint had compelled the pontiff to write a second letter, the later letter would contain at least some reference to the earlier one.

**3.** In Leo’s time there was not such great disorder in ecclesiastical discipline that, in a province subject to the Roman See and containing exceedingly vigilant bishops—including Paschasinus of Lilybaeum—one bishop could dissipate all the property of a Church by selling, giving away, and alienating it in various ways. Still less was there such corruption that several persons engaged in this conduct, as the letter expressly asserts.

I therefore think that this kind of depredation must be assigned to later centuries—unless someone refuses to assert that this letter is entirely spurious.

**4.** The same letter mentions a double decree by which Leo had ordered how the interests of both Churches were to be protected against such plunderers of ecclesiastical property. If these decrees had truly been issued by Leo, their memory would not easily have disappeared.

Although many familiar letters of Leo and other pontiffs have either perished altogether or been withdrawn for a time from human knowledge, this could happen much less easily with decretal letters and constitutions relating to the affairs and regulation of several Churches, and still less if they had been addressed to the bishops and Churches of an entire and very extensive province and island. These decrees, if genuine, must have been of that character, as must those to which the letter refers.

But this point should be weighed above all: no letters survive in more numerous handwritten copies than those written to the bishops of Italy and the neighboring provinces. This happened because, since they were more closely connected with the care and concern of the Roman pontiff, they frequently assembled at his synod and depended upon his will and pronouncement. They were therefore also obliged to obey his decrees, which all the bishops and clergy of those Churches had good reason to copy with greater diligence. Indeed, copies of such letters were accustomed to be sent in duplicate—“in equal form,” as they used to say—either by Leo himself or by the metropolitans to the individual bishops of the provinces.

You could scarcely conjecture, therefore, by what means the memory of decrees of such importance could have been lost for so many centuries.

**5.** If these decrees belonged to our Leo, his successors would never have failed to mention them when issuing constitutions concerning the prohibition of the alienation or transfer of ecclesiastical property. Hilary, Leo’s immediate successor, did so when writing to several bishops of Gaul; Symmachus treated the matter in a Roman council; Agapetus wrote to Caesarius of Arles; Gregory the Great wrote to the same bishops of Sicily; and so forth.

Yet the pontiffs just mentioned do not say a word about these decrees. Later writers, indeed, look back to Hilary’s decree and even borrow his words. From this alone it may be determined that no decree earlier than Hilary’s was known concerning the preservation of the property of the Church.

**6.** This letter decrees:

“No bishop shall dare to give away, exchange, or sell anything belonging to his Church, unless perhaps he does one of these things in such a way as to provide something better, and, after deliberation and consent of the entire clergy, chooses what will undoubtedly benefit the Church.”

But this belongs to a more recent and less rigorous discipline, since it permits the alienation of ecclesiastical property to depend upon the will and consent of the clergy of a single Church. Pope Hilary, on the other hand, forbids such property to be transferred into another’s possession unless the reason for the alienation has first been presented before a council, so that what ought to be done may be considered by the common deliberation of all.

**7.** When the author of the letter wishes to deprive transgressors of his decree of rank and communion, he reveals himself as later than our Leo, since in Leo’s time this double penalty was not imposed upon clerics, except perhaps—as some prefer to hold—for the most serious crimes of all.

Having weighed these considerations, I am readily led to the conclusion that this letter is spurious, fabricated namely for the purpose of recovering anew the estates of one of those churches after they had been alienated—something which is known often to have happened, when forged documents, suitably adapted in one way or another to asserting the rights or privileges of churches, were substituted for genuine records; or at least I shall believe that it belongs to a different Leo from ours—perhaps the second, the third, or even a later one. The name of the consul could easily have slipped in, or deliberately have been inserted, especially since both the doubtful reading of Alypius and the omission of any mention of his colleague Ardabur arouse some suspicion of fraud or error.

What nevertheless prevents me from considering the letter forged is that a portion of it is read in Gratian, *Decretum* 12, q. 2, chap. 52, “Without Exception.” There it is attributed to Leo, and is headed as having been sent to all the bishops established throughout Sicily. But whether it belongs to Leo I or Leo II, neither the older nor the more recent editions of Gratian make clear. Gratian also adds certain material as though it were part of the same letter, although it is not found in the letter itself; rather, it is read as canon 31 and canon 32 of the council—whether genuine or forged—which is called the Fourth Council of Carthage:

31. “That a bishop should use the possessions of the Church as entrusted to him, not as his own.”

32. “The donation, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property by bishops without the concurrence and subscription of the clergy shall be invalid.”

Perhaps the canons, written in the margin, had slipped into the text of the manuscript used by Gratian. Let the reader judge from these facts what decision should be reached concerning the whole letter. We have reproduced it, whatever its character may be.

## On Letter XVIII in Quesnell, XIV  
### To Januarius, bishop of Aquileia

**To Januarius.** The printed manuscripts have *Julianus*, but this is contradicted by Dionysius Exiguus, Cresconius, Hincmarus, manuscript codex Barberinus 1, five Thuane manuscripts, the Cambridge manuscript, and the Victorinus manuscript, which read *Januarius*; this reading is also found in the margin of the printed edition. This letter should be compared with Letter 7 (now 2), which is addressed to Septimius, together with the notes concerning its spuriousness.

**1396 2. “If, however, they have not been defiled by repeated baptism.”**  
[Note: Compare our annotation 6 (Col. 707, note e) on Letter 18.]

He perhaps added this exception with the African canons in mind. Canon 27 of the African Collection reads: “Nor should it be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the clerical rank.” See also Felix III, Roman pontiff, in the Roman synod of A.D. 487, both among the acts of the council and in the synodal letter to all the bishops. An exception to that African canon is found in favor of children in canon 47, and another in canon 68, concerning clerics ordained among the Donatists, who were to be received in their own rank.

**[Col. 1349A] 3. “Ordered for the safety of the whole Church.”**  
[Note: Which canons are cited by Leo, and in what sense they should be referred here, although the subject is neither the Donatists nor the Novatians but the Pelagians, we explained in the aforementioned admonition, nos. 18 and 26. Compare also annotation 5 (Col. 707, note c).]

I marvel at the writer’s obtuseness, since he misuses this passage and a similar one in the fourth letter. “The canons,” he says, “concerning the prohibition against promoting to a higher clerical rank those who return from heresy to Catholic communion are shown by these words of Leo to have been enacted for the universal Church everywhere: ‘Let him take care that those things which have been commendably proposed and salutarily ordered for the safety of the whole Church be carried out carefully and promptly.’” Yet, he insists, such canons are found neither among the Nicene canons nor anywhere in Justellus’s collection.

There were therefore, he concludes, besides the Nicene decrees, certain other provisions by which Saint Leo wished Januarius to be bound, and which were in use throughout the Church in the discussion of ecclesiastical matters. What extraordinary carelessness is this, to interpret these words as referring to canons? Is it not clearer than midday to anyone who reads them that the things said to have been “commendably proposed” are to be understood as the letters full of the vigor of faith which Januarius had written to Saint Leo, whereas the things “salutarily ordered” refer to this very reply of Saint Leo, by which he commands that the canonical constitutions be observed? That writer could easily have noticed this, had he not cut away, to obscure the truth, the words immediately preceding the cited passage. “Therefore,” says Saint Leo, “let your affection, whose devotion brings us joy, join its care to OUR ORDINANCES, and let it take care that they be carried out carefully,” and so forth.

As for his further claim that no canon is contained either in the Council of Nicaea or in Justellus’s collection prohibiting clerics from being raised to a higher ecclesiastical ministry when they return from heretical or schismatic communion to the Catholic Church, this is a lapse of memory. For if he had consulted canon 8 of Nicaea, he would have read these words:

“Concerning those who call themselves Cathars, that is, Pure Ones: if at any time they return to the Catholic and Apostolic Church, it has seemed good to the holy and great synod that, after they have received the imposition of hands, THEY SHALL REMAIN IN THE CLERGY. Above all, they must make a written profession that they will consent to and follow the doctrines of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, and so forth. Wherever, whether in villages or cities, they alone are found ordained, those who are found among the clergy SHALL REMAIN IN THE SAME ORDER.”

Thus reads the Council of Nicaea in Justellus’s collection. Nothing, it seems to me, could be clearer: those who are commanded to remain in the clergy and to remain in the same order are unquestionably barred from access to the higher ministries. Since Saint Leo’s words correspond most closely to the language of that canon, I readily persuade myself that the holy pontiff had that canon in mind. Although Nicaea speaks only of the Cathars, nothing prevents those words from being extended to other heretics. Indeed, the very manner in which he speaks here—“concerning whom also we command that the canonical constitution be observed”—seems to me to indicate an extension of the canon.

Saint Leo could all the more justly do this because this letter of Leo does not concern heretics in general but, as I think, the Donatists. First, the mention of schism itself indicates this; for at that time scarcely any other heresy was in existence that had arisen from schism. Second, the addition concerning the repetition of baptism—“if, however, they have not been defiled by repeated baptism”—is significant. It was characteristic of the Donatists to baptize again those who defected from the Catholics to them; it was scarcely practiced by others. Moreover, the Donatists shared a common yoke with the Novatians, or Cathars, as Saint Epiphanius understands and describes the matter: they held the same opinions as them and rebelled for the same reason. “For this reason,” he says, “we did not consider it necessary to treat them separately at greater length; rather, we thought they should be joined with their like” (*Against Heresies*, book II, tome I, Heresy 59, at the end).

It is therefore not surprising if Saint Leo turned against the Donatists the weapons which the Nicene Fathers had wielded against the Cathars. Nor is there anything preventing us from believing that Saint Leo wrote these words against the Novatians themselves, since it is clear from Pope Innocent’s letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 8, that those heretics too repeated baptism for those who defected to them from the Catholics. For when Innocent had decreed that those coming from the Novatians and Montenses should be received merely through the imposition of hands, he adds: “Except those who may perhaps have been rebaptized after passing from us to them.”

This further exposes the writer’s delusion, since he did not hesitate to assert that Saint Leo’s decree was contained in no canons. Now, when Leo adds that these provisions were “both proposed and ordered for the safety of the whole Church,” who could deny that whatever any bishop proposes or establishes against heretics pertains to the safety of the whole body—especially, and above all, whatever is decreed by the Apostolic See against heresies or corruptions of morals and discipline?

**1398 4. “The third day before the Kalends of January.”** Thus read Dionysius Exiguus and Cresconius, whom we followed as the most ancient witnesses, with the support of one Bellovacensis manuscript and three Thuane manuscripts. One Thuane manuscript, the Trecopithoean, and the Victorinus have “on the Kalends” or “the third day before the Kalends of July.” We record this detail so carefully because the resolution of more difficult questions often depends upon such chronological notes.

The opening of the forged rescript of Pope Mark to Athanasius and the other bishops of Egypt, concerning the Nicene chapters, was assembled from the beginning of this letter, as was also the opening of Pelagius II’s letter to Benignus.

## On Letter XIX in Quesnell, XVIII  
### To Doro, bishop of Beneventum

**[Col. 1350C] 1. “And would become lesser than himself.”** Thus read the Thuane manuscripts, three Cambridge manuscripts, the Trecopithoean, and Nicolinus’s edition, which the last edition followed. Previously it read: “I wonder who he would become.” I would gladly read and punctuate the whole passage as follows: “Lest the man whom you were hastily advancing to priestly honor should begin with an injury to those with whom he was associated, and become lesser than himself.”

**2. “But the vice of arrogance would be strengthened.”** Thus read the common printed editions. In their place two Thuane manuscripts, the Victorinus, and the Trecopithoean read: “But the vice of greater strength would be strengthened.” The Cambridge manuscript and another Thuane manuscript read: “But the vice of frenzy would prevail.”

**3. “For you were not unaware that the Lord had said,” and so forth.**  
[Note: We discussed this passage and Simon’s observation sufficiently in annotation 10 (Col. 710, note k) on this letter.]

The earlier editions and Hincmarus, *Opusculum* 44, *On Metropolitan Law*, chapter 17, read the entire passage as follows:

“For you were not unaware that the Lord had said that whoever humbles himself will be exalted, but whoever exalts himself will be humbled; and that he had likewise said: ‘Whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave.’ But you seek to grow from what is little and to become greater from honor.”

Since, however, the later Gospel passage—“Whoever wishes,” and so forth—is absent from all three manuscript codices which I have seen, namely the two Thuane manuscripts, the Cambridge manuscript, and the Victorinus, as well as from the Surian edition, we judged that it should be deleted. We corrected the remainder according to these manuscripts. It should be observed that Saint Leo’s words, “But you seek to grow from what is little,” are opposed to the earlier Gospel saying, “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted”; while the words *de majore minores esse* (“to become lesser from a greater rank”) correspond to the following saying, “but whoever exalts himself will be humbled.” Since this was not noticed by the ancient editors of Saint Leo’s works, they corrupted the text.

For the following words of the author show that these two expressions must be opposed to one another: “For both are disorderly, both are contrary to proper order,” and so forth. This would not be the case if the passage were read, “to grow from what is little and to become greater from honor,” since those expressions are not opposites.

After my first edition of Leo, *New Observations—French—on the Text and Versions of the New Testament* appeared, by R. S. P., that is, Richard Simon the priest. In chapter 21, p. 458, the author criticizes my correction of the Leonine text. First, he argues that these words in the letter to Doro—“But you seek to grow from what is little and to become lesser than the greater”—were taken from the Gospel according to Matthew in a copy which Leo possessed. Nearly the same words are found in the famous Greek manuscript of the Gospels which once belonged to Theodore Beza and is now preserved at the University of Cambridge.

Yet, surprisingly, he complains that I wrongly supplied the reading *de majore minores esse* (“to become lesser from a greater rank”), even though he prefers the corrupt reading *de minore majores esse* (“to become greater from a lesser rank”); nevertheless, he admits that my earlier reading agrees with Beza’s manuscript. Second, he himself cites four other manuscripts that support Beza’s. Third, he cites the Saxon versions, which, he says, were based on ancient copies. Fourth, five manuscript codices—that is, all those available to me for rereading this letter—support my correction. Fifth, Labbeus evidently possessed other manuscripts containing the same reading, since he wrote it in the margin of volume III of the *General Councils*. Sixth, the printed Surian edition reproduces the same reading. Seventh, Juvencus’s metrical version, which Simon himself cites, supports it. Eighth, Simon himself calls this reading “ordinary” three times. Ninth, he corrects Leo’s text by reading *minore* (“lesser”) instead of *honore* (“honor”), without the assistance of any manuscript and against the testimony of all editors. Tenth, Simon admits that the reading I preferred was found in the ancient Vulgate. Eleventh, on the following page he writes that this reading, although ordinary, obscure, and scarcely capable of yielding good sense, ought nevertheless not to be changed. It was therefore rightly restored.

Twelfth, he criticizes certain rash critics for erasing the words *de majore minores esse* (“to become lesser from a greater rank”) and replacing them with *de minore majores esse* (“to become greater from a lesser rank”), an unhappy conjecture which, he says, they derived from the Greek text, whose words do not resemble one another as closely as the Latin words do. Thirteenth, R. Simon likes to believe that this addition existed in the ancient Vulgate and that copies of it remained at Rome while Pope Leo governed the Roman Church. But if the pontiff alluded to it, he could have done so for no other reason than that it was known to most people and extremely widespread because of the abundance of copies. Who could persuade himself that the pontiff had at hand nothing but corrupt manuscripts?

Finally, Simon openly confesses that only one consideration prevents him from retaining our reading, which he calls the ordinary one: Leo himself, he says, explained the passage in Letter 79 (now 105), addressed to the Empress Pulcheria, where he appears to repeat the same addition of the ancient Vulgate in these words: “And yet these things were being suggested to those who wished to grow from what is little and to pass from the lowest things to the highest.”

But I do not know whether anyone could persuade himself, as an educated man, that these final words—“to pass from the lowest things to the highest”—are an explanation of *de minore majores esse* (“to become greater from a lesser rank”). It seems certain to me that they are nothing other than a repetition of the earlier words expressed in different terms. The only aim occupying Leo’s mind in that letter was to condemn Anatolius’s ambition and make him hateful to Pulcheria, by appealing to the authority of the words with which Christ had restrained the ambition of the two apostles. But the apostles did not wish “to become lesser than the greater,” and for that reason Leo refrained from reproducing those words; instead, he repeated the preceding thought under different terms: “and to pass from the lowest things to the highest.”

The pontiff would certainly not have drawn these words from his own resources while rejecting the native wording that appeared in the same place—*de minore majores esse* (“to become greater from a lesser rank”)—if those words had truly been found in the Vulgate at that time. The fact that the pontiff did not use them is, to my mind, certain proof that they were not read in the copy he used, and that the reading was rather “to become lesser than the greater.”

In the letter to Doro, however, Leo not only had no reason to remove or alter these final words; on the contrary, they were so necessary to the pontiff that without them the truth of his own words would not stand. He rebukes two things in the Beneventan Church:

1. The premature promotion of the newest presbyter.

2. The degradation of those whose age commended them to the rank and whose conduct diminished nothing from it:

“Those who demanded that he be honored to their own disgrace”;  
“those who cast themselves down by their own judgment”;  
“those who, transferring their primacies to another by a shameful and sluggish degradation, diminished the dignity of those who followed them”;  
“those who had placed the last before themselves”;  
“those who had professed themselves unworthy of their own rank of honor”;  
“those who chose to become inferior to one newly and prematurely ordained.”

There are Leo’s words, *de majore minores esse* (“to become lesser from a greater rank”), expressed by Leo himself in other terms six times. The bishop is severely reproved by the pontiff for failing to oppose these two kinds of vice; Leo demonstrates that both are contrary to Christ’s words in this way:

“For you were not unaware,” he says, “that the Lord had said: ‘WHOEVER HUMBLES HIMSELF WILL BE EXALTED’; and that he had likewise said: ‘BUT WHOEVER EXALTS HIMSELF WILL BE HUMBLED.’”

Here the pontiff divides the Lord’s very brief saying into two parts, assigning one clause to each vice and showing that both were condemned by Christ. He immediately adds:

“But you seek to grow from what is little and to become lesser than the greater; for both are disorderly, both are contrary to proper order.”

Could Leo have made it clearer that he was reproving two opposed vices in those words—one in “to grow from what is little,” and the other in *de majore minores esse* (“to become lesser from a greater rank”)? If, in place of the latter, one substitutes *de minore majores esse* (“to become greater from a lesser rank”), there are no longer two disorderly and contrary things, but only one; and, finally, Leo’s discourse has no intelligible sense.

Simon, I think, now understands what he had previously despaired that anyone could understand, and he will no longer raise the supposedly insuperable difficulty by which he wrote that he was deterred from accepting our reading. The pontiff reproves Doro for not restraining, with reasonable authority, the unjust desires of those who made the request—preventing the new presbyter from being exalted, and the older men from being humbled, casting themselves down by their own judgment, and becoming lesser from a greater rank. Thus the phrase is readily understood when applied to those distinguished by seniority and age.

Nor, when applied to the new presbyter, does it lack meaning. Leo himself explains it in these words: “Lest the man whom you were hastily advancing to priestly honor should begin with an injury to those with whom he was associated, and become lesser than himself, while in him not the virtue of humility but the vice of arrogance was being strengthened.” In this sense, the one who seeks exaltation seeks to be humbled and to become lesser from a greater rank, while growing from what is little: before God, the person casts himself down who, through the vice of arrogance, wishes to excel and dominate the others.

What Simon again objects concerning Hincmarus of Reims’s reading has no force. First, he gratuitously asserts that Hincmarus’s writings are more ancient than our manuscript codices. Second, Simon himself exposes the corruption of Hincmarus’s reading by rejecting the word *honore* (“honor”), which it contains, and substituting *minore* (“lesser”) on his own authority. Finally, that Hincmarus, or anyone else, corrupted this entire passage of Leo’s letter—moving some words from their proper place and adding others of his own—is evident from a comparison between the reading I cited above and the reading which all the manuscript codices and the sequence of the context itself loudly proclaim to be genuine.

Let the reading therefore remain correctly emended, and, with Simon’s kind permission, it will be retained in this later edition as well.

## On Letter XXII in Quesnell, after Letter XXXIII  
### Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, to Leo

**[Col. 1353A]**

We gave Quesnell’s note in full in annotation 10 (Col. 725, II, note a) on this letter, and there also presented our observations.

## On Letter XXIV in Quesnell, XXI  
### To Theodosius Augustus

**1402 1. “Of Eusebius.”** Saint Leo mentions the same man in the following letter and in several others. He was bishop of Dorylaeum, a city in the province of Salutary Phrygia. The supplicatory memorandum which he presented against Eutyches to the Council of Constantinople, and which our pontiff mentions here, is found in the first session of the Council of Constantinople, and likewise in the first session of the Acts of Chalcedon. So too is another memorandum addressed to the emperors Valentinian and Marcian against the same Eutyches and Dioscorus, by whom he had been deposed at the predatory synod of Ephesus.

This is the singular praise of that distinguished man, scarcely shared by anyone else: he was the first in the Church of Constantinople to rise against the two opposing heresies that emerged in his time. Against the monk Eutyches he presented his memorandum while already a bishop; against the bishop Nestorius he raised the standard while still a layman. For when Nestorius, as Saint Cyril says in book I *Against Nestorius*, was using profane novelties of language in the midst of the church, by which he attacked both the title *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκον, “God-bearer”) and the twofold birth of Christ, “a certain very upright man, who was still among the laity but had nevertheless acquired for himself an admirable education, moved by fervent and religious zeal and crying out in a still more forceful voice, said: ‘The very Word who existed before the ages has also undergone a second generation.’”

**2. “Although the bishop himself professes that he adheres to the decrees of the Nicene synod; for this reason we had no basis for saying anything.”** We corrected this according to the Griman codex, the only one available. Previously it read: “Although he himself, a bishop of the Nicene synod, professes that in this matter he is in accordance with the decrees; for this reason we had no basis for learning anything else.”

**3. “On the first day before the Kalends of March.”**  
[Note: See our emendation in annotation 12 (Col. 736, note n) on this letter.]

Thus read the Grimani codex and all the printed editions. In the first part of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, however, we read “on the Kalends of May,” and in Letter 20 (now 23), “the twelfth day before the Kalends of May.” We believe that in both places “of March” should be read.

From the session held at Constantinople after the deposition of Eutyches, it is certain that Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian had already reached that city when the session took place; that session was held on the fifth day before the Ides of April. Leo’s letter therefore could not have been sent from Rome in May, but rather in March. “A few days ago,” said Bishop Seleucus, “the letter of the most holy Leo, archbishop of the Romans, was made known to us, stating that the most reverend archimandrite Eutyches had lodged a complaint and, at the time of the examination, had appealed to our hearing by submitting a memorandum,” and so forth. The same conclusion must be reached concerning Letter 20 (now 23) to Flavian.

## On Letter XXV  
### Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, to Eutyches the archimandrite  
### In Quesnell, after Letter XXIII

**[Col. 1354A]**

I find three editions of this letter:

[Note: There are only two editions to be distinguished, concerning which we spoke in the admonition to this letter: one is the abridged edition, the other the complete edition. Quesnell called them three because the edition of Vossius and the edition of the Councils, although both present the complete letter, may nevertheless be regarded as different editions, since they derive from different manuscripts. In the cited admonition, while defending the complete edition, we also traced the origin of the abridged edition to the manuscript collections of the Hispanic and Isidorian traditions, without imputing any fraud to the editors.]

The first is found in the later editions of Saint Leo, where the letter is printed from a manuscript codex of the Thuane library. The second was produced by Gerard Vossius, a Catholic doctor, from the Vatican manuscript codices nos. 2574 and 2580 and from the manuscripts of Cardinal Sirletus. The third is the version found in the first part of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, together with its Greek translation.

The first edition contains only the first chapter and lacks the second in its entirety; the other two contain both chapters. I would not dare to assert with certainty how this difference arose. It is nevertheless likely either that the editor happened upon a mutilated manuscript or that the manuscript itself was mutilated by the editor. Being ill-disposed toward the Apostolic See, he evidently thought that Peter Chrysologus had attributed more authority to it than was proper.

As though it would have been a crime for Eutyches to listen obediently to Leo the Great, who so devoutly and so catholicly explained the evangelical and apostolic doctrine of the Lord’s incarnation in his letters sent to the East—or for Peter to urge Eutyches himself to do so! Rather, it was an act of the greatest madness for Eutyches not to obey the holy pontiff’s admonitions, whereas Peter fulfilled his priestly office and charity by attempting to turn away a presbyter who was departing from apostolic doctrine and voluntarily rushing toward destruction.

Now, concerning what Peter of Ravenna asserts—namely, that he cannot hear cases of faith without the consent of the Roman pontiff—one must first carefully note that he is not speaking of all cases, but prudently and cautiously distinguishes cases of faith from other matters that concern ecclesiastical discipline or the administration of his own province.

Second, he is not excusing himself from cases of faith arising in his own province, but from those which might be brought to his see from elsewhere. Since such matters were ordinarily brought forward only by a written appeal, they concerned either the Western synod and its primate, the Roman pontiff, or the exarch of the relevant diocese; nor was it proper for a matter of the common faith to be handled there without the knowledge of the Apostolic See.

[Note: We showed in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 7 that the written appeal in the strict sense was sent by Eutyches to the Roman pontiff, not to the Western synod. We explained there, nos. 9 and 10, why he also wrote to Saint Peter Chrysologus.]

Third, Peter adds something that greatly restricts his statement: “For the sake of peace and faith,” he says, “we cannot.” He says “peace” because he knew that the Roman pontiff, especially Leo, would never permit a case of faith to be handled within Italy without the knowledge of the Roman synod. He says “faith” because Eutyches was supported by such powerful protectors in the East, and the eunuch Chrysaphius had inclined the emperor in his favor, that only the Roman pontiff—who could move Valentinian at will—could usefully take charge of the case.

Nothing, therefore, prevents the complete letter from being that of the bishop of Ravenna. Why it is found abridged in the common editions of Saint Leo I do not understand. They mention a Thuane manuscript from which the editor supposedly drew it. I do not know whether this is so. I do know that, among the catalogued Thuane manuscripts, I found only one containing a letter of Saint Peter Chrysologus, together with several others relating to the Council of Chalcedon; in that manuscript the letter is complete.

If one adds to this the Vatican manuscripts, the codices of Cardinal Sirletus, and the ancient and recent editions of Baronius and the Councils, scarcely any room remains for doubt that the reduction of the letter must be attributed either to that editor’s bad faith—or, if not bad faith, at least his carelessness—or to a defect in the manuscript.

The very learned Henry de Noris, one of the earliest disciples and defenders of Saint Augustine, although chronologically he ought rightly to be numbered among the latest writers, apparently either did not see the complete letter or did not attend to it. In book II, chapter 11, of his *Pelagian History*, he writes:

“In the year 448, that same Chrysologus sent a letter to Eutyches, who was already being heard unfavorably because of his heresy.”

If he had seen the letter, he would have understood from its second chapter—

[Note: We proved in the admonition to this letter, no. 6, that Peter Chrysologus wrote it at approximately the same time that Saint Leo wrote Letters 23 and 24.]

—that the letter sent by the bishop of Ravenna to Eutyches was not written until after he had received from Eutyches complaints concerning the judgment of Constantinople, which was delivered on November 22, A.D. 448; nor could it have been written before the beginning of the following year, 449, indeed not before February 18. On that day Saint Leo’s first letter concerning the Eutychian affair was written. That Peter wrote his letter after Leo’s is shown by these words:

“In all things, however, we urge you, honorable brother, to attend obediently to what has been written by the most blessed pope of the city of Rome.”

If these words are understood of that longer letter to Flavian which Leo sent to the East with seven others on June 13—as they certainly appear to require—then Chrysologus wrote to Eutyches not at the beginning of 449 but when nearly half of that year had already passed. This is why I placed his letter before Leo’s longer letter to Flavian: it is probable that it was sent to the East together with that letter and the other seven.

I have seen only this one letter of Peter of Ravenna. When the prolific writer Philip Labbeus reviewed it in his theological dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he added the following:

“Another letter of the same man is also read among those placed before the Council of Chalcedon.”

Here the learned man was undoubtedly either suffering from a lapse of memory, or he treated the Greek-Latin letter and the Latin fragment of the same letter as two complete and distinct letters. Nor can I agree with him when he writes that this letter of Bishop Peter was sent before Saint Leo’s celebrated letter to Flavian of Constantinople. Chrysologus unquestionably refers to that letter, since the two shorter letters that preceded it decree nothing at all and demand nothing to which Eutyches could have given obedient attention.

**1.** From this letter of Saint Peter of Ravenna we learn that Eutyches did not deposit his complaints only with the Roman pontiff, as we discussed more fully in Dissertation 7; he also complained to other metropolitans of the West concerning the judgment of Constantinople and gave them a written appeal. Perhaps the letters of several other bishops, or other records, are lying hidden in libraries, just as this letter of Peter remained concealed for twelve hundred years. If they came to light, they would make it clear that Eutyches had likewise sought the judgment of other Westerners, just as it is now evident from the letter of the bishop of Ravenna that Eutyches had appealed to his tribunal.

For it is clear from this letter that Eutyches sent a letter to Peter of Ravenna. “Sadly,” he says, “I read your sad letter . . . . . This is the brief reply I have made to your letter,” and so forth.

**2.** It appears that Eutyches complained of the sentence of the Constantinopolitan synod as having been issued by corrupt and ill-disposed judges. “If it displeases you,” says the bishop of Ravenna, “because you wrote of an elected judgment”—that is, of judges who had been hired and influenced—

[Note: We conjectured in annotation 15 (Col. 1354, note d) that this passage is corrupt and requires correction.]

Here he seems to me to be referring to the synod which was *endemousa* (ἐνδημοῦσα), the resident synod from which Eutyches had received his sentence. Strictly speaking, that synod was not canonical, since it was convened neither by the primate of the diocese nor by the metropolitan of a single province, but was composed indiscriminately of bishops from various dioceses who happened at that time to be residing in the city, under the authority of the bishop of Constantinople, an authority strengthened only by recent custom.

**3.** From the same letter it appears certain that Eutyches sought the judgment of the bishop of Ravenna, since Peter repeatedly denies that he can provide it, for several reasons.

The first is that, because Eutyches had received a sentence of condemnation from his own bishop, no metropolitan had the authority to reconsider that judgment, unless perhaps with the agreement and permission of Eutyches’s own bishop. Peter hints at this reason in these words:

“This is the brief reply I have made, brother, to your letter; I would have written more if our brother and fellow bishop Flavian had sent me something concerning this matter.”

The second is that it was contrary to equity either to examine or even to hear one party’s case without hearing the other. “How,” he says, “can we judge these matters when we have not seen them because of the absence of the parties, and do not know what they understood because of their silence? A just mediator [another reading: judge] is not one who hears one party in such a way that he reserves nothing for the other.”

The third reason is that, since Eutyches had sent letters to the Apostolic See and letters had in turn been sent from it to the East, it was better for him to attend obediently to those letters and to hear from blessed Peter, living and presiding in his own see, the truth of the faith which he appeared to have sought from the Roman See.

“In all things,” he says, “we urge you, honorable brother, to attend obediently to what has been written by the most blessed pope of the city of Rome, because blessed Peter, who both lives and presides in his own see, provides the truth of faith to those who seek it.”

The fourth reason was the pursuit of peace and faith. “For the sake of peace and faith,” he says, “we cannot hear cases of faith outside the consent of the bishop of the city of Rome.”

To hear cases arising in some part of the Church belongs either to the bishop of that Church, in which the case arose, or to the one to whom an appeal is made from that bishop. Since, however, an appeal had been made to the bishops of the West, the consent of the Roman bishop, unquestionably the chief of all the others, had to be sought. He was both the head, in a special sense, of the Western synod and the procurator and principal executor of the canons which the ecumenical councils had formerly established against heretics.

[Note: The matters here and below, by which Quesnell attempts to restrict the Roman pontiff’s authority in appeals, are refuted in the observations on Dissertation 7, no. 9.]

**4.** It is therefore evident that Eutyches could not have sought the judgment of the bishop of Ravenna except through an appeal, whether genuine or fictitious, by means of a written petition. This confirms what we asserted above: Eutyches appealed to the Western synod and therefore wrote to several of the principal metropolitans, especially to the Roman pontiff, the head of the entire synod and of all the bishops.

## On Letter XXVIII in Quesnell, XXIV  
### To Flavian, bishop of Constantinople
1. Because this most celebrated letter of the most holy pontiff [Note: [Col. 1356D] See more concerning the fame of this letter and its Latin and Greek manuscripts in the admonition prefixed to it], ought to be published in the most rigorously corrected form, since the interests of Christianity greatly depended upon this, we collated it with the manuscripts with the utmost care: two Barberini manuscripts, seven Thuani, two Regii, the Victorinus, Corbeiensis, Trecopithoeanus, Oratorianus, and Remensis of Saint Remigius; with all the editions, the Greek version, and so forth. To these may be added three other manuscripts of approved quality and venerable antiquity, which Petrus Franciscus Chiffletius testifies in his notes on Vigilius of Thapsus to have been collated by him for this same letter; he arranged for it to be printed at the end of that work and illustrated it with scholia.

The first of these three manuscripts is the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, collected by Rusticus the deacon, from the library of D. Joannes Bouhier of Dijon, a senator; the second is from the Book of Sacred Readings of Saint Benignus of the same city; the third belongs to Chiffletius himself and contains statements of faith excerpted from Ambrose, Augustine, Fulgentius, and various decrees of councils and pontiffs.

To all these it is permissible to add Josias Simlerus of Zürich [Col. 1357B] and Joannes Leunclavius the Calvinist. Their testimony should not be suspected here, since they report manuscripts they themselves examined and reproduce various readings excerpted from them. Simlerus did this in his collection of ancient writers on the two natures in Christ; Leunclavius did it after the embassy of Manuel Comnenus Augustus to the Armenians, where he published the Greek-Latin letter at Basel in 1578.

Since every Catholic is bound, under penalty of anathema, to receive the text of this letter with reverence, down to a single iota, by the authority of the Roman council received by the universal Church under Pope Gelasius, we have not been reluctant to record with the greatest scrupulousness every variant reading found in the manuscripts, lest it be believed that even the slightest thing had been altered by our own judgment.

2. “What scandal has occurred among you, and so forth.” The vulgate editions add two superfluous words in this form: “What scandal has occurred among you and, on the contrary”; they are absent both from the Greek version and from all the manuscripts.

[Col. 1357C] 3. “Imprudent.” Not “impudent,” as some manuscripts have it. The Greek is ἀσύνετος, “without understanding.” It makes little difference which reading one follows, since either is consistent with Eutyches’ character.

4. “To yield.” Thus the Chiffletian manuscript and one of the Thuani; it corresponds to the Greek expression εἴκειν, “to yield.” All the other manuscripts and printed editions have “to believe.”

5. “In obscurity.” Thus two Thuani, three Chiffletiani, the Trecopithoeanus, and the two Regii, as well as Simler’s edition. The Greek reads κατὰ τί μὲν ἐμπόδιον ἀσαφείας, “through some obstacle of obscurity.” Hence it is clear that this reading should be preferred to the other, which occurs in the margin of the vulgate and Surius’s editions and in four Thuani and two Barberini manuscripts, in this form: “They are hindered by some obstacle,” a phrase far removed from the author’s meaning.

6. “Of those who are to be regenerated.” The vulgate has “of the regenerated”; the Greek is ἀναγεινωμένων, “of those who are being regenerated.” The reading that we have substituted for the vulgate is shown to be preferable by all the manuscripts, Merlin’s edition, and the whole context of the passage. From this it is evident that Saint Leo is speaking of catechumens—not of those who are in the first stage of instruction among the hearers, as Tertullian calls them, but of those whom Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and the Council of Agde, canon 13, call the competentes, “those who are seeking admission.” To these the Creed was delivered; they were required to recite it from memory on the Thursday of the final week of Lent, according to the Council of Laodicea, canon 46; the Council of Agde, canon 13; and the Second Council of Braga, canon 1. See also Isidore of Seville, *On the Divine Offices*; Fulgentius, *Letter on Two Questions*; and the Roman Order.

[Col. 1357D] 7. “Had received.” Thus the second Barberini, the Corbeiensis, two Thuani, the Trecopithoeanus, the Remensis, and three others among Chiffletius’s manuscripts; not “had apprehended,” as in the vulgate.

8. “From the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.” Thus the second Barberini, five Thuani, three Chiffletiani, the Victorinus, Remensis, Trecopithoeanus, and the editions of Merlinus, Sichardus, Canisius, and Crabbus. The same wording is also found in Saint Augustine in six hundred passages, in earlier ecclesiastical writers, and in ancient Greek and Latin copies of the Constantinopolitan Creed, as well as, among other sources, in the Breviary of the monastery of Monte Cassino, written nearly six hundred years ago and preserved in the library of the House of the Institution of the Oratory of Jesus at the Parisian suburb of Saint Michael. The Greek version agrees, reading καὶ Μαρίας, “and Mary”; the same wording is also found in more recent copies of the Greek creeds, as is clear from the little work of Gabriel, Metropolitan of Philadelphia, *On the Sacrament of Penance*, printed at the end of Joannes Morinus’s *Commentary on Penance*. The vulgate, however, reads “from the Virgin Mary.” Whether this slight variation produces any difference in meaning I leave to theologians to determine.

9. “The Father is believed to be both almighty and eternal.” I very nearly removed the word “eternal,” as Chiffletius did, since it is absent from two of his manuscripts, the two Barberini, four Thuani, the Trecopithoeanus, Remensis, Victorinus, and also the text of the Greek version. Nevertheless, I thought it should be retained, both because it occurs in other manuscripts—three Thuani, two Regii, the Corbeiensis, and others—in addition to all the printed copies, and because the sequence of the context seems to require it: the eternity of the Son is inferred from the eternity of the Father, and the Son’s perfect equality with the Father in all things is demonstrated.

10. “Instructed.” Thus all the manuscripts. The marginal reading in the edition is “instrument”; the Greek is εἰσήγησιν, “instruction” or “teaching.”

11. “Had bestowed pious concern.” The Corbeiensis and several other manuscripts have: “Had betaken himself with pious concern.”

12. “And finding.” Thus all the manuscripts and the Greek version, εὑρίσκων, “finding”; the vulgate has “and had found.”

13. “He will receive in the womb.” Thus the Barberini, four Thuani, Remensis, Trecopithoeanus, and Victorinus manuscripts. Chiffletius says nothing about his own manuscripts and retains the vulgate reading, “he will conceive.”

14. “They will call.” Thus the manuscripts just cited together with the Chiffletiani, to which the Greek καλέσουσι, “they will call,” agrees. The vulgate has: “And he will be called.”

[Col. 1358C] 15. “Upon the shoulder.” Victorinus, Trecopithoeanus, and some others have “upon the shoulders.”

16. “They will call.” Thus the Remensis, Trecopithoeanus, Victorinus, and four Thuani, as well as the Greek in the margin.

17. “Speaking deceitfully.” The Trecopithoeanus and three Thuani have “speaking a deceitful discourse.”

18. “The Spirit of life.” Surius in the margin, and Canisius, Merlinus, Sicardus, and Crabbus in the text, together with the Victorinus manuscript, read “by the Spirit of life”; and this may indeed be better. The Greek is πνεύματι, “by the Spirit.”

19. “And of substance.” We added these two words from the Barberini, Remensis, Trecopithoeanus, and Corbeiensis manuscripts and two Thuani.

20. “Of the transgressor.” The Remensis and Victorinus manuscripts, one of the Thuani, and two of the Chiffletiani have “of transgression.”

21. “Disposition.” Thus three Thuani together with the Remensis, and the text of the letter published among the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. The Greek version has διοίκησιν, “administration”; the vulgate has “dispensation.”

22. “Therefore it was assumed.” We removed the final word, because it is absent both from all the manuscripts and from the Greek version.

23. “Is unlike our nature.” Thus the three Chiffletian manuscripts, three Thuani, the Remensis, and the Trecopithoeanus. Fulgentius also reports this wording in the more corrected manuscripts of his *Reply to the Second Question of Ferrandus*. The Greek version supports it with ἡμῖν, “to us.” The vulgate has *nostrae est naturae dissimilis*, “is unlike our nature”; elsewhere, *nostrae est natura dissimilis*, a variant inflection/order whose distinction cannot be preserved in English alone.

24. “Withdraws … leaves behind.” Thus most of the manuscripts and the Greek version; formerly: “withdrew … left behind.”

25. “While the feet remain seated.” Thus the first Barberini, Corbeiensis, Remensis, Trecopithoeanus, four Thuani, and two Chiffletiani. The vulgate has “while the feet are sunk down”; the Greek is τῶν ποδῶν οὐ βαπτιζομένων, “while the feet are not immersed.”
