26. “He might instruct the faith of the disciples by his questions.” Thus all the manuscripts. The vulgate has: “He might hear the faith of his disciples through his questions.”

[Col. 1359A] 27. “Of the true body.” Thus in all the manuscripts. The Greek is σώματος, “of the body”; the vulgate has “of the true man.”

28. “It is not another who was raised.” Thus all the manuscripts, with which the Greek agrees. The vulgate has: “He was not raised otherwise.”

29. “The sacrament through which one is saved.” The vulgate has “the sacrament of faith through which one is saved.” All the manuscripts give the former reading, which agrees with the Greek.

30. “Has flowed.” Thus all the manuscripts, instead of the former “have flowed out.”

31. “The Spirit is truth.” Thus all the manuscripts read; Augustine likewise read this in chapter 22 of *On the Gift of Perseverance*, and Fulgentius in Book 10, *Against Fabianus*, and elsewhere. The Greek text both of Saint John’s letter and of Saint Leo has: Τὸ πνεῦμά ἐστιν ἡ ἀλήθεια, “The Spirit is the truth.” The Syriac version of John likewise has it. Therefore there can be no doubt that Saint Leo read it in this way, and not, as in the vulgate, “Christ is truth.”

32. “Exchange of words” or “dialogue.” Thus all the manuscripts together with the Greek version, διαλαλίας. The vulgate has “questioning.”

[Col. 1359B] 33. “And excessively blasphemous.” These words are absent from two Thuani and from Facundus.

34. “So omitted, as though nothing offensive had been heard.” The Corbeiensis manuscript and Facundus, Book 2, chapter 6, have: “So dismissed, as though nothing offensive had been heard.”

35. “Before the incarnation.” Facundus alone has: “Before the union.”

36. “Of your concern.” The Bouhier manuscript, four Thuani, and several editions have: “Of your love.”

37. “May he be cleansed from this plague of his understanding.” Thus all the manuscripts, together with Facundus, and the Greek version agrees with them. Elsewhere the vulgate has: “May he be cleansed by you from this stain of his understanding.”

38. “Our brothers.” Thus most manuscripts and all the printed editions, together with the Greek version; the wording also agrees with the customs of that age, when bishops habitually called presbyters “brothers.” Four manuscripts have “our brother,” a reading presented by Chiffletius, though he makes no statement about his own manuscripts.

39. “Julius.” That this should be read both in this letter and in the others that mention the same legates sent to the Ephesian synod is demonstrated by the manuscripts—the Grimanianus, the two Barberini, two Thuani, the Trecopithoeanus, and others—and by the Greek version of letters 26, 29, 30, and 31 (now 38, 33, 30, and 34), which are found in the first part of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

Only in the Greek version of this letter, Letter 24 (now 28), to Flavian, [Note: [Col. 1359C] Two of our Venetian manuscripts of the Greek version have Ἰουλιόν, “Julius,” not Ἰουλιανόν, “Julian.” The manuscript copies of the Fifth Synod, as Baluzius notes in his collation, also have “Julius.”] does one read Ἰουλιανός, “Julian”; and in the Latin edition of that same version, found in the sixth collation of the Fifth Synod, one reads “Julian.” I conjecture that this should be attributed to the carelessness of scribes, on the evidence of the manuscript of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon from the library of Joannes Bouhier of Dijon, a manuscript which Chiffletius praises as being of good quality and venerable antiquity: in it he read “Julius,” not “Julian.”

“Julius” is likewise found in Evagrius, Book 1, chapter 10; Nicephorus Callistus, Book 14, chapter 47; Prosper’s *Chronicle*; the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* prefixed to Saint Leo’s letters in the Roman edition, and therefore not first edited by Sirmondus; the book *On the Roman Pontiffs*; Marianus Scotus; and others. From the last four of these we learn that Julius was bishop of Puteoli.

It is therefore clear that the very learned Morinus was mistaken when, in Book 1, Exercise 20, he wrote that Julian of Cos was sent by Leo to the Second Synod of Ephesus, as is shown, he says, by Leo’s Letters 15, 18, and 19 (now 15, 19, and 20), and others. Christianus Lupus likewise erred in chapter 5 of his dissertation *On the Ephesian Robber Synod*, when he maintained that the legate whom Leo says in his letters was sent to this synod was Julian, bishop of Cos, and reproached Prosper’s *Chronicle* because, as he said, it wrongly changed Julian of Cos into Julius, bishop of Puteoli.

As though Prosper, who was then living at Rome, most intimate with Leo, and his secretary, counsellor, and correspondent, could have been unaware of who and what sort of man this legate was—so much so that not only these letters, but all the others against Eutyches concerning the true incarnation of Christ, were believed to have been dictated by Prosper himself, as Marcellinus Comes in his *Chronicle* and Gennadius in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men* testify.

Morinus and Lupus were misled both by the similarity of the names and by the fact that the man who acted in Leo’s place at the synod is called “Julian” almost everywhere. But although it seems probable to me that Julian of Cos attended the synod in Leo’s name, it is absolutely certain that Julian of Cos was not the man sent from Rome to the synod and so frequently mentioned with the other legates in Saint Leo’s letters.

The latter point, although already sufficiently established by the authority of numerous manuscripts and writers of that period, is made still clearer by the following two arguments.

1. Julian, bishop of Cos, attended and subscribed both the Council of Constantinople, at which Eutyches was first condemned by Flavian, and the gathering of bishops held in the same city the following year by order of the emperor. Since this gathering was held in April, who could easily believe that the same man was sent from Rome in June of that year, the year in which the pontiff’s letters are dated?

2. Leo wrote Letters 25 and 31 (now 35 and 34) to Julian of Cos while he was residing in the East, on the same day on which he wrote other letters mentioning the legates who had been sent. Indeed, in the later letter he names those same legates, including Julius the bishop. This certainly cannot be reconciled with their opinion.

But that not [Note: [Col. 1359D] Quesnellus is entirely correct in maintaining here that the bishop whom Leo sent as legate to the Ephesian synod was Julius of Puteoli, not Julian of Cos, as some had wrongly thought. But his more extended attempt to prove that Julian of Cos attended the Ephesian synod in place of Julius rests upon a false foundation. He assumes that Renatus, who is reported in the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* to have died on the island of Delos, was still alive, on the basis of Theodoret, who wrote a letter to him after the same synod. Thus, asserting that the author of the *Brief History* had either suffered a lapse of memory or been deceived by unreliable documents, he conjectures that Julius of Puteoli died at Delos, and that Julian of Cos took his place in the Roman legation and sat in the Ephesian council. Hence, in the published Acts, the man who acted there in Leo’s place is called Julian.

This is the whole force of Quesnellus’s reasoning in brief. His other arguments are mere conjectures relying upon Theodoret’s authority and the published Acts, so that if these foundations totter, all the rest must likewise collapse.

Accordingly, that Renatus the presbyter, not Julius the bishop, died before the synod is first sufficiently indicated by Prosper, a contemporary author. Speaking in his *Chronicle* under the year 449 of the Ephesian pseudo-synod, he mentions only Hilary the deacon and Julius, bishop of Puteoli; concerning Renatus he says not a word: “Hilary, deacon of the Roman Church, protested; he had been sent from the apostolic see in place of Saint Leo the pope together with Julius, bishop of Puteoli.”

If Renatus too had been sent, Prosper nevertheless does not mention him because he is speaking of those who reached Ephesus and opposed the proceedings there; nor would he have mentioned Julius in place of Renatus if Renatus, rather than Julius, had sat at the synod.

The Acts of Ephesus themselves, which are read inserted in the first session of the Council of Chalcedon, demonstrate this much more clearly. For although not only the legates are named there, but also Dulcitius, a notary of the Roman Church, Renatus is nowhere mentioned. This would be incredible if he had been present with the others.

Nor should Quesnellus claim that the Ephesian Acts themselves are missing, or declare that what is read at Chalcedon is merely an excerpt from those same Acts. The Chalcedonian Acts plainly refute him: from them it is known that the Ephesian Acts themselves were read in full and without any break up to the session containing the acquittal of Eutyches and the condemnation of Flavian and Eusebius, and that only the legates of the Roman see were present at that session.

Why, then, when Julius the bishop, Hilary the deacon, and Dulcitius the notary are mentioned, is Renatus omitted from these Acts, unless it is because he had died at Delos and therefore, as the *Brief History* reports, was not present at that council? How could he have been omitted if he had challenged and restrained the bold proceedings carried out at Ephesus, as Theodoret states in his letter? He especially ought to have been named in the Acts, and his contradiction would undoubtedly have been inserted in those same Acts.

Since the Acts show that Julius spoke, while Hilary’s protest is supported not so much by the Acts as by Prosper’s *Chronicle*, Theodoret is seen to have been misled by uncertain report and some ambiguity, attributing to Renatus what ought to have been attributed to Hilary—unless one prefers to suppose that the name Renatus accidentally entered the superscription of Theodoret’s letter in place of Hilary’s name. Yet we do not even dare to suspect this.

Rather, we believe that Theodoret, who had learned from Letter 28 to Flavian that three legates had been sent by Leo, and had heard by report that the legates had resisted the proceedings at Ephesus, but had heard nothing about Renatus’s death, wrote to each of them on the same model in order to commend his cause to them; only the letter to Renatus, however, has survived.

The surviving letter of Theodoret to the archdeacon of the Roman Church, which we believe was addressed to the man who held the first place in that Church, though Theodoret did not know his name, cannot have been addressed to Hilary. The power of archdeacons was well known; but since he knew that Hilary had served as a legate, he would have inserted something distinctive concerning that office in the letter.

Moreover, it is absolutely certain that Julius, not Julian, attended the Ephesian synod. The speeches through an interpreter recorded in the Ephesian Acts could provide a sufficiently effective argument for this: they suit Julius, but are foreign to Julian of Cos, who, as bishop of a Greek city, spoke Greek himself through no interpreter, not only at Chalcedon but also at the council held under Flavian at Constantinople before the Ephesian synod. Hence Quesnellus’s bold attempt to evade this argument is futile—namely, his claim that Julian was less skilled in the Greek language at the time of the Ephesian synod.

Still clearer evidence is supplied by the Acts themselves. The manuscripts of the ancient version of the Council of Chalcedon have “Julius,” not “Julian.” We examined six manuscripts of this version: four Vatican manuscripts, 1321, 1323, 4166, and 5405; the Chigianus 483; and the most ancient Veronensis 57.

Of the six occasions on which this legate is named, he is called “Julius” five times in four manuscripts—namely, in the three Vatican manuscripts 1323, 4166, and 5405, and in the Chigianus—and only once, by error, “Julian” in the Chigianus. “Eusebius” likewise occurs once in the same three Vatican manuscripts. In the most ancient Veronensis and in the more corrected Vatican 1321, however, “Julius” is written everywhere without exception.

Baluzius observed the same thing in four of his manuscripts. The Corbeiensis and Colbertinus show “Julian” only once; the Parisian and Divionensis always give “Julius.” Consult Baluzius himself for each passage of the council. Do not consider with Quesnellus only the first text, in which he noted that “Julian” is preferred in two manuscripts; that could mislead certain readers.

From this the erroneous reading of the editors, who everywhere print “Julian,” becomes clear—a reading upon which Quesnellus relied. From this ancient translation, revised by Rusticus, we also learn that the Greek copies used by the ancient translator and Rusticus likewise had “Julius.” Evagrius and Nicephorus, Greek writers, therefore rightly preferred “Julius,” not “Julian”; and in some printed Greek editions of the councils “Julian” is found by error where the man was Julius.

Indeed, in both Greek manuscripts of the Council of Chalcedon in the library of Saint Mark at Venice, numbers 164 and 555, Ἰούλιος, “Julius,” is read everywhere except in the second session of the Acts, where Ἰουλιανός, “Julian,” occurs. That single passage should be corrected on the basis of the five others that prefer Ἰούλιος, “Julius.”

If, then, Julius served as the legate of the Roman see at the Ephesian synod, two consequences follow that overthrow Quesnellus’s system. First, all that he invents about Julian of Cos as legate rests upon empty conjectures; second, the man who died at Delos was not Julius the bishop, but Renatus the presbyter, as the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* reports.

Since Quesnellus dismisses this testimony of the *Brief History* as spurious because it is absent from chapter 43 of Quesnellus’s collection, where the same history is inserted, it is very important to determine the truth of the matter with the help of the most ancient manuscripts.

In the Quesnellian collection and several other ancient collections, this history, prefixed to the documents of the Acacian affair, is described more briefly. It begins with the condemnation of Dioscorus and ends with the proceedings preceding the condemnation of Acacius.

Two additions were subsequently made to this history. One was placed at the beginning, where the history is traced from its origin—namely, from Nestorius and Eutyches. The other was placed at the end, where the same history is carried down to the condemnation of Acacius.

Sirmondus found this history with these additions in the Verdun manuscript, which contains only Acacian documents, under the title *Acts Concerning Acacius*. We found it under the same title in Vatican Regina 1997.

Finally, an addition of several lines was made at the end. With this addition the work had long before been printed in the Roman edition of the letters of the Roman pontiffs, published in 1591, volume 1, part 2, page 142.

We found this complete document in several manuscripts of the excellent Avellana collection. In these, the following beginning, omitted by the Roman editors, occurs:

“Beginning. In the cause of the Christian faith, whose enemies are shown never to have been absent from its origin. In our own age, and so forth.”

Hence Quesnellus noted that this history is two lines shorter in the Roman edition than the version published by Sirmondus.

Liberatus used the history in this complete form, not the reverse, as Pagius wrongly thought under the year 496, number 4.

We now observe that this history is prefixed to the Acacian documents—which end with Gelasius—in the Quesnellian collection, Vatican manuscripts 1342 and 1344, Barberini 2888, Veronensis 46, and the Verdun manuscript; that in Vatican Regina 1997 it follows Gelasius’s letter; and that in the Avellana and similar collections it is placed among Gelasius’s letters. Thus Henricus Valesius was not wrong to conjecture that Gelasius was the author of the history.

The date indicated at the beginning of the work, corresponding to the year 493 or 494, and the conclusion of the history agree with the time of Gelasius.

Moreover, Gelasius had the practice of adding certain matters to his shorter works, as is clear from the letter to the Dardani, which is shorter in the Quesnellian and other collections but is found with several additions in the Avellana manuscript, from which the Roman editors printed it.

We therefore believe that the same thing happened with the history of the Eutychianists, so that the additions subsequently made to it should be attributed to Gelasius.

From this everyone can see how great is the authority of the testimony that Renatus is reported to have died at Delos. Even if someone else rather than Gelasius is considered the author of that addition, he was nevertheless a Roman who, in Gelasius’s time, gave testimony concerning a Roman presbyter. His testimony ought therefore to carry the greatest weight in this matter, especially since it agrees both with Prosper and with the Acts of the Ephesian pseudo-synod.] Julius of Puteoli, but Julian of Cos, attended the Ephesian synod in Leo’s place, although I do not wish to assert this as certain. There are nevertheless many considerations that make it probable.

If this last point is true, I think it happened for the following reason: either Julius died before the pseudo-synod began, [Col. 1363A] or some other obstacle prevented him from reaching Ephesus. Since it was very important that the man who was to represent the Roman pontiff at that council should be distinguished by episcopal dignity, Julian was substituted in Julius’s place, undoubtedly in accordance with the instructions given to the other legates.

The following conjectures lead me to regard this as plausible.

1. Whenever the legate of the apostolic see is mentioned at the Ephesian synod, he is always called “Julian” in the Latin version. In the Greek text he is called “Julian” three times and “Julius” only twice. It is therefore surprising that the distinguished Baluzius wrote in the first volume of his new collection of councils, in the preface to Chalcedon, that he is consistently called “Julius” in all the ancient manuscripts.

This indicates that the person in question was someone other than the man sent from Rome, who is always called Ἰούλιος, “Julius,” in the Greek version of Saint Leo’s letters in the first part of the Council of Chalcedon, with the sole exception of Letter 24 (now 28).

Therefore it was not Julius but Julian who represented the pontiff at the synod, [Col. 1363B] and no one other than Julian, bishop of Cos.

2. Unless Julius had died in the East, some mention of him after the unfortunate synod would be found. Either his return would have been recorded, or his death would have been listed among the wicked acts of that robber assembly. He himself would have written to Pulcheria; he himself would have reported the proceedings of the synod to Leo; Leo would either have reproached him for the agreement he had given or praised him for refusing it. Yet nothing of this sort is found.

3. Leo’s Letter 44 (now 18), written to Julian of Cos on 13 October of that same year, and Letter 61 (now 81), written on 13 April of the following year, testify that Julian of Cos was harassed by many and severe tribulations through the uncontrolled cruelty of Dioscorus. We must believe that this happened for no other reason than that, as the legate of the Roman pontiff, he had steadfastly defended the cause of faith and justice and had openly opposed the impious schemes of Dioscorus.

4. It is clear from the same Letter 61 (now 81) that Julian had in some way represented Saint Leo or exercised his authority even before the Council of Chalcedon. While exhorting him to maintain persistent vigilance against the cunning of falsehood, Leo adds:

“Your spirit and OUR AUTHORITY both support this.”

And later:

“For this purpose, after the venerable day of Easter, we shall send our representatives, who, having taken counsel with you, will carry out whatever we have determined.”

Moreover, in Letter 25 (now 35), written to the same man through the legates sent to the Ephesian synod, Leo testifies that he wrote to him so that, as he says, “you may resist with one mind and steadfastly those who wish to corrupt the Gospel of Christ.”

In Letter 60 (now 80), he also carefully commends Julian to Anatolius of Constantinople and wishes him to remain attached to him. This suggests that Julian had acted on Leo’s side at the synod and that there was therefore reason to fear that the followers of Eutyches might harass him.

5. It is scarcely possible to doubt that Julian of Cos attended the pseudo-synod, since he received Saint Leo’s instructions before the synod for the very purpose of resisting the opponents of the truth with the other legates; the pontiff wrote to him concerning the wrongs committed both before and during the synod; and he also instructed him through more confidential orders concerning his own counsels in the same matter.

Yet the name of Julian of Cos nowhere appears in the Acts of the pseudo-synod, if the Julian or Julius who is said to have represented the pontiff there was someone other than Julian of Cos.

6. The *Brief History of the Eutychianists* relates that one of the legates sent from the Roman see to the Ephesian synod did not reach it, having been overtaken by death on the island of Delos.

“The representatives sent from the apostolic see were also present,” it says, “Julius, bishop of Puteoli, and Hilary the archdeacon, because Renatus the presbyter had been overtaken by death on the island of Delos. Dulcitius the notary was also present,” and so forth.

It says that Julius was present at the council but that Renatus died. I greatly fear, however, that the author of the *Brief History* suffered a lapse of memory or was deceived by uncertain reports or writings; so that it should rather be said that Renatus attended the synod and that Julius was overtaken by death.

When he writes that one man died on the island of Delos, there could scarcely have been room for error. The author did not invent this; but when he says that Julius attended the synod, he could have been deceived by the similarity of the names.

For when he read in Saint Leo’s letter that Julius had been sent to represent the pontiff, and found in the Ephesian Acts that Julian—or Julius—was named as exercising the same authority in Leo’s name, it was easy for him to suppose that the two were one and the same person. Consequently, he understood the statement about the death of one of the three legates as referring to another of them.

It certainly did not refer to Hilary, whose frequent presence is recorded both during and after the synod. Thus he concluded that the statement concerning Renatus was true.

But, I reply, it cannot be true of Renatus, to whom Theodoret wrote after the synod. For when he had been deposed from his see by the sentence of the pseudo-synod, Theodoret brought his complaints both to Saint Leo and to Leo’s legates, Renatus the presbyter and Hilary the deacon.

This adds a double strength to our conjecture. The fact that Theodoret wrote to Renatus indicates an error in the uncertain author who said that Renatus had died before the synod; while the fact that he did not write to Julius provides some support for the view that Julius was no longer alive at that time and had not been present at the synod.

Otherwise, Theodoret ought especially to have approached Julius, who would have held the first place in representing the pontiff at the synod, so that through him he might move Saint Leo and stir him to undertake the defense of the deposed bishop.

The reason Theodoret did not write to Julian of Cos is obvious: Julian remained in the eastern regions and was not in a position to conduct Theodoret’s affairs personally before the Roman pontiff.

If, then, Julius was dead, Julian, bishop of Cos, is unquestionably the man whom we read in the Acts of the Ephesian Robber Synod to have exercised the authority of the Roman pontiff.

Those who arranged for a new edition of the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* argue from its statement concerning the death of Renatus the presbyter that Theodoret’s letter was not written to that presbyter but rather to Hilary.

Yet Theodoret’s letter to Hilary still survives. Moreover, if an error must be acknowledged in one or the other of these authors, it is more reasonable and less troublesome to admit an error on the part of the author of the *Brief History* than on the part of Theodoret.

For what then? Was Theodoret unaware of what had happened to Renatus? No one would say so. Was it a scribal error, with Renatus substituted for Hilary? But scribal carelessness is not usually so learned as to cause one legate to be written in place of another.

Add that the same superscription is consistently found in all the manuscript and printed copies of Theodoret’s works. The superscriptions of letters are not ordinarily composed by anyone other than their authors, whereas this often happens differently with other kinds of writings.

The author of the *Brief History* is unknown, his authority uncertain, his reliability wavering, and its rare manuscript copies were produced a hundred years later. What, then, does he possess with which to contend against Theodoret in this controversy?

If these things are true, the various writers have erred in different ways at this point. Those who asserted that Julius of Puteoli was both sent from Rome and present at the synod were mistaken. Those who maintain that both facts concern Julian of Cos are likewise mistaken.

For Julius was indeed sent so that he might attend the synod, but he did not attend. Julian of Cos was not sent—he was at that time residing in the East—yet he attended in Leo’s place, being substituted, as I have said, for Julius.

Accordingly, correct Evagrius Scholasticus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 1, chapter 10:

Καὶ μὴν καὶ Ἰούλιος (συνῆν) τόπον πληρῶν Λέοντος τοῦ τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ῥώμης ἐπισκόπου

“And indeed Julius also was present, occupying the place of Leo, bishop of ancient Rome.”

Likewise correct Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book 14, chapter 47:

Παρῆσαν δὲ τῇ συνόδῳ . . . πλὴν Λέοντος τοῦ τῆς πρεσβυτέρας Ῥώμης ποιμένος, τούτου γὰρ τὸν τόπον ἐπίσκοπος Ἰούλιος πεμφθεὶς ἀνεπλήρου

“There were present at the council . . . except Leo, shepherd of ancient Rome, whose place was filled by Julius the bishop who had been sent.”

I say that the account of both authors must be corrected because each confuses Julius of Puteoli’s mission from Leo with Julian of Cos’s presence at the synod.

But the text itself should not be corrected in the way proposed by the learned Henricus Valesius in his note on this passage of Evagrius. He thinks that in both authors Ἰούλιος, “Julius,” should be corrected to Ἰουλιανός, “Julian.” It is certain that the authors wrote it in this way, failing to observe the distinction noted above and, like many other writers, believing that the man who had been sent for that purpose had attended the synod in Leo’s name. I also think that this distinction escaped Valesius himself.

The learned men who uphold the contrary opinion—that Julius was present at the synod, while Renatus had already died on the island of Delos—do so with arguments that are not without force. First, Renatus is nowhere mentioned at all in the acts of the Ephesian Robber Synod. From this silence the account of the *Breviculum* is confirmed: its author writes that Renatus had died before he could reach Ephesus. The difficulty is certainly serious, unless one says that there was scarcely any opportunity for the legates to speak at the pseudo-synod, especially for Renatus, since Julian, in virtue of his episcopal dignity, took the floor, while Hilary, in his capacity as archdeacon and special legate of the Roman Church, held the principal role in the embassy. For he always addresses the synod at greater length; he alone asks that Saint Leo’s letter be read once and again; he alone intervenes against the decree of the Robber Synod.

2. They press Prosper’s silence concerning Renatus, together with his testimony that Julius had been sent. We do not deny that Julius was sent, or “designated,” to use Prosper’s studied expression. He is indeed silent about Renatus, but he is equally silent about Dulcitius, whose presence at the synod is clear from the acts, so that nothing can be established from this silence.

3. The account of the *Breviculum* of the Nestorian and Eutychian History seems to possess weighty and irresistible authority. Its author apparently wrote at Rome about forty years after the synod. Yet perhaps someone will reply that the authority of this *Breviculum* is uncertain, since the author is unknown and the work itself may likewise be considered of uncertain reliability. It appears to have been compiled from several patches, sewn together at different times. The oldest of all the patches seems to me to be the one that constitutes chapter 43 of my Roman manuscript, dealing exclusively with events in the Alexandrian Church from the condemnation of Dioscorus to that of Acacius; for the shorter sections are generally the older ones. From this material the deacon Liberatus inserted several passages into his *Breviary*, chapters 15, 16, and 18, as did the unknown author in his *Breviculum*. Indeed, the *Breviculum* itself seems to be nothing other than this shorter work, later enlarged by some writer who, taking up the entire history from its beginning, fashioned the *Breviculum* for his own purposes. In the edition of 1591 it is shorter by two lines at the beginning, but longer at the end by twelve or fifteen others.

Moreover, although in the portion preserved in our Roman manuscript nothing appears that is inconsistent with the truth, the same cannot be said of the passages that constitute the first part of the *Breviculum*: there are many statements that diverge from the truth and from Liberatus’s account. Therefore scarcely any certain confidence can be placed in that little work, since it has no other writer to support it, although its authority should not seem entirely to be rejected, since it agrees with several others in a number of matters.

4. Yet it seems unprecedented, and never otherwise practiced, for one legate to be substituted for another by the other legates. Perhaps this was new and not customary, but necessity demanded it. Since Saint Leo had been invited to the synod unexpectedly, and only a very short time had been granted for selecting and sending bishops, the pontiff was forced to content himself with the legates whom he had designated to be sent to Constantinople. Nothing more suitable occurred to him than to add to the legates Julian of Cos—a bishop indeed from the East, but Roman by birth and brought up in the bosom of the Apostolic See—especially since he had a full understanding of the entire affair of Eutyches and had written to the pontiff about it.

We produce no letters that disclose this plan of Leo’s. Yet this was not the subject of letters, but of more private instructions, which were not to be made public unless necessity required it. In the same way, Pope Celestine had entrusted secretly to a private memorandum the instruction ordering his legates to the First Synod of Ephesus, before reaching Cyril of Alexandria, to turn all their attention to him. I know that the pontiff’s authority was delegated to Cyril by letter, because Celestine evidently foresaw what in fact happened: that the legates would not arrive sufficiently early for the appointed day of the synod. Leo’s situation was not the same, and therefore it was enough for him to leave with the legates a precaution concerning the substitution or addition of a new legate, to be brought forward as circumstances or necessity required.

Meanwhile, from Celestine’s example we infer that it was not without precedent—and a recent one—that the authority of the Roman pontiff was entrusted to a bishop from the Eastern regions. It is quite clear from Letter 61 (now 81), written to this same Julian to repair the disaster of the pseudo-synod, that even then he was carrying the authority of the Apostolic See throughout the Eastern regions. For, after exhorting him to maintain persevering diligence against the devices of falsehood, Leo adds:

> “Since both your own spirit and our authority support you in this matter … for this purpose we shall send our men, who, after taking counsel with you, will carry out what we have determined.”

When, then, had Julian been armed with the authority of the pontiff? Is this not some trace of the authority he had received, by which he would act in the synod in the pontiff’s place?

5. They insist that the bishop who acted as legate at Ephesus always spoke through an interpreter, whereas Julian always spoke in Greek and without an interpreter at the Council of Chalcedon. Perhaps, however, the Latin had not yet mastered Greek sufficiently at the time of the pseudo-synod of Ephesus to speak Greek in so large an assembly of bishops; later, having become more practiced in the language during the intervening two years, he no longer needed an interpreter.

The same consideration of his homeland explains why, when speaking in the synod about Leo, he calls the most holy pope “his own.” This was fitting for a man brought up in the bosom of the Roman Church.

6. They set against this Leo’s words in Letter 39 (now 43):

> “We learned of these Ephesian robberies not through an uncertain report, but from the most reverend bishops themselves who were sent by us, and from Hilary, the most faithful narrator of what was done.”

[Note: [Col. 1365D] See annotation 5 (Col. 825, note a) on Letter 43.]

But the bishop sent from Rome to the synod was no one other than Julius of Puteoli. For my part, if any confidence can be placed in the letter that some regard as a rough draft of the subsequent one, I think it supports rather than opposes the first opinion. Since only Julius was sent from Rome, Leo could not truthfully have written that several men had been sent, unless the meaning is that two men were in fact invested with the office of legate: one sent from Rome for this purpose, the other either added or substituted at Ephesus.

7. The most illustrious Baluzius presses the point concerning the manuscript codices. He asserts that Julius is consistently called Julius in all the ancient manuscript codices of the Ephesian Acts, and that Julian is not mentioned in any of them in the same words. Yet he contradicts himself. In the same preface to the Council of Chalcedon he admits that in some places Julius is read and in others Julian.

In fact, at the first passage of the Ephesian synod, page 115 of Labbe’s edition, he admits that only the Dijon and Paris manuscripts have Julius, while the others have Julian. Among these manuscripts are those of Crabbe, Surius, Nicolinus, and the other printed editions that he claims preserved the old translation; the Greek text itself also belongs to this group. I add Labbe, who carefully excerpted the variant readings of the Dijon manuscript and entered them in the margin: he recorded nothing of the kind, but displayed only the name Julian. Baluzius himself observes nearly the same variation in other passages of the Acts.

It should also be observed that in the Greek exemplar of the letter to Flavian, and in the accompanying Latin version among the Acts of Chalcedon, Julian is found; the same is true of the exemplar of that letter inserted into the sixth session of the Fifth Synod, which derives from the Acts of Chalcedon. I do not wish to determine how this came about, since Julius is read everywhere in the letters of Saint Leo. But what if it was restored by Julian himself, whom learned men think to have been the author of the version of the Acts of Chalcedon, and this is highly probable?

[Note: [Col. 1367D] We shall show this to be false in the observations on Quesnel’s note 3 on Letter 113.]

What if the legates themselves made the change in the exemplar of the letter that was to be presented to the synod? But I set conjectures aside. This much is certain: it was not a recent copyist’s error, since the same reading stood in the Acts of Chalcedon that the Fathers of the Fifth Council used. This proves that the reading really existed in the genuine codices of the Council of Chalcedon, whether Greek or Latin, and therefore in that ancient version which the illustrious collector says was used by the Fathers of the Fifth Council. Perhaps, through a perverse correction, Julius was restored in place of Julian from Leo’s letters. For although it is certain that Julius should be read in the letters outside the Acts of the synod, if the name Julian was anciently written in the letters inserted into the Acts, then the restoration of the good reading was itself erroneous.

As for the authority of Theodoret, who wrote to Renatus, they reply that Theodoret was not sufficiently informed about the affairs of the legates. But this is asserted without evidence, whereas it is not without evidence that Theodoret’s letters to Renatus were written. Indeed, it is not merely unsupported but absurd. For who, thinking seriously, could suppose that Theodoret had not been carefully informed about what had taken place at the synod? I mean Theodoret, on whose word all the bishops of the Eastern diocese depended, and for whose sake he had been ordered to remain within Cyrus and had been compelled by imperial decree to absent himself from the synod by name.

Although absent in body, he was present through his friends, by whose efforts he could easily learn everything. In fact, by the time Theodoret wrote to Leo, Renatus, and the other Romans, he had received Leo’s letter to Flavian. It could have been sent to him only after the pseudo-synod, and by those who had attended the synod, since it had first been brought into the East by the Roman legates.

By then he had also learned that Renatus had been present only at Flavian’s deposition, and that he had left the synod before the same sentence was pronounced against the other bishops. That this information was not drawn from the earliest and most uncertain rumors, but from reliable reports, seems clear from what he writes first about the ardent zeal and righteous freedom with which Renatus had resisted Dioscorus’s wicked machinations:

> “Nor have we alone learned these things,” he adds, “but the sound of your right-mindedness has gone out into the whole world, and everyone celebrates your justice, zeal, freedom, and the threats you directed against iniquity. And your piety did these things after witnessing a single slaughter—that is, a deposition. But if you had also seen the others that were perpetrated after your departure, you might perhaps have imitated Phinehas.”

No one will readily believe that Theodoret bestowed such praises on a man known only by the title of legate, and not through particular knowledge of the things he had done. Surely he would have reserved these praises for Bishop Julius if Julius too had been present at the synod and Theodoret had written to him.

But nothing of this kind is read concerning Renatus in the Acts. That is true. But who now possesses the complete Acts of the pseudo-synod? Only excerpts have been preserved, inserted into the Council of Chalcedon, and from those excerpts the Fathers were given almost exclusively what had to be condemned and annulled. Thus, after the sentence had been pronounced against Flavian and Eusebius, only Hilary’s one word, “He contradicts,” remains in the Acts. The other things that Theodoret and others report about the legates have perished.

The importance and gravity of the matter itself make it clear that Theodoret did not write to the Romans about the Ephesian robbery on the basis of the first uncertain rumors, and consequently that he was well informed about the circumstances of the entire affair and of the persons who had taken part in it. For when the question concerned appealing to a council of the entire West, selecting legates to be sent to Rome, furnishing them with instructions and mandates, and writing several lengthy letters, who could believe that Theodoret and his friends had not deliberated on all these matters carefully and in good time, especially with those whose cause was the same?

In fact, Theodoret’s own letters prove that the legates were not sent immediately. He did not write to the West until after reading Leo’s letter to Flavian, as is certain; yet he did not receive that letter immediately after the Ephesian disaster was announced. When he wrote Letter 19 to the patrician Anatolius, Leo’s letter had not yet reached his hands, although he himself had already been informed about the Ephesian judgment and, as he writes, its report and most righteous decision had already gone out into the whole world, to the ends of the earth.

Indeed, he had learned about each of the bishops of the synod—what fate had befallen each and what their state of mind then was—so thoroughly that he complained to his friend that scarcely any Church existed which had not felt the storm stirred up by the affair. Some had inflicted injury, others had suffered it; those who had neither been injured nor inflicted injury themselves nevertheless grieved with those who had been wronged and mourned for those who had committed the wrong.

Later, after receiving a copy of Saint Leo’s letter, he congratulated himself on agreeing in doctrine with Saint Leo. As Garnerius admits, he could not restrain himself from preparing an apology for himself before his most powerful friend in Letter 121. Garnerius also considers it likely that by then Theodoret possessed a copy of the events at Ephesus, because he seems to have read several letters directed by Leo to the Ephesian Fathers and to have shared them with the patrician Anatolius at that time.

If this is true, it is pointless to object that Theodoret, deceived by uncertain rumors, wrote to Renatus as though he were a witness and participant in the synod because he falsely believed him still to be alive.

Having brought forward the proofs for both opinions, I leave the dispute to the judgment of the learned, intending to adhere to whichever side they determine to rest on firmer foundations. Joannes Garnerius, an erudite man, takes both sides in his *Auctarium Theodoritianum*. For in Dissertation 1 on the History of Theodoret, chapter 9, number 9, he says nothing at all about Julius, but writes that Julian and Renatus went to Ephesus with Hilary. Again, concerning both of them, in number 10:

> “It is uncertain what service Julian performed; Renatus certainly resisted the malignant leader of the synod with the greatest confidence, and thereby earned praise from the supreme pontiff.”

Finally, in chapter 10, number 5:

> “Two eyewitnesses of the Ephesian robbery, Renatus the presbyter and Hilary the archdeacon, both legates of the Apostolic See, both addressed by Theodoret in suppliant letters.”

But in the second dissertation on Letter 116, which is addressed to Renatus, without changing the wording of the first, he writes the opposite and ridicules as fabricated the opinion he had previously made his own, although in the same passage he is forced to admit that the history of Julius is exceedingly perplexing.

## 40. The Titles of Saint Clement

[Note: [Col. 1368D] See our annotation 82 (Col. 779, note c) on this letter.]

So read all the codices, both handwritten and printed, with the single exception of the Barberinian manuscript. The Greek version alone, to which Bouhier’s Latin codex of the Acts of Chalcedon was adapted, omits that annotation.

For this reason I would rather accuse the copyist of this pair of codices of negligence than accuse the most ancient codices of the Christian world of falsity—especially those which their bishops left to our Gauls, corrected by Leo himself, as is clear from the letter of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranius to Saint Leo.

What Chiffletius says—that it was by no means customary before the time of Pope Symmachus for Roman presbyters to be designated in writing by their titles—is asserted without evidence. It is much more reasonable to affirm this than to deny it, since the evidence for the assertion is this very letter of Saint Leo. If it is permissible to call this passage interpolated, then it will also be permissible to attribute the same fault to that Roman synod under Symmachus in which, according to the cited writer, such an annotation was first attached.

Indeed, I am surprised that he does not want such presbyters to have been designated in writing by their titles, since he freely admits that this was customary in usage and in spoken language. Moreover, why does he refuse to admit that it was practiced in Leo’s time when he acknowledges that it was practiced about forty years after Leo, and when so many codices show that it was practiced by Leo?

## 41. “It has been approved”

In the common editions: “It has often been approved.” But the word “often” is absent from the Greek and from nearly all the manuscript codices.

## 42. “May God keep you safe, dearest brother”

The two Barberinian codices, the five Thuanian manuscripts, and the Remensian, Victorine, and Trecopith manuscripts do not contain this closing clause.

## 43.

At the end of this letter, after the consular annotation, Chiffletius adds the following words:

> “Tiburtius the notary, by order of my lord, the venerable Pope Leo, published this.”

We have thought this subscription should be omitted, since it appears only in Bouhier’s single manuscript codex of the Acts of Chalcedon, corrected by Rusticus the deacon; moreover, it is not known which Leo Tiburtius was the notary of—Leo I, Leo II, or someone else.

For I do not think that the word “lord” (*domnus*) was in use in the time of Leo I.

[Note: [Col. 1369C] See annotation 85 (Col. 781, note c).]

Moreover, it is otherwise clear that this letter was published and praised repeatedly on various occasions.

## 44.

We have not thought that the era—whether 483 or 486, as is added at the end of this letter in several codices—should be retained in the text. This method of reckoning time is thought by most scholars to be later than the time of Saint Leo, and to have been attached to this letter only afterward. It was brought in from Spain, where Idatius the Spaniard, who wrote in the age of our Leo, seems to have been the first of all to use this notation—unless a later hand, foreign to his chronicle, added it. I believe that the same hand of Isidore Mercator added it to Saint Leo’s letter.

This is the Spanish era, which precedes the common Christian era by thirty-eight years. Hence an error is found in the addition itself. For when thirty-eight years are added to the year 449 of the common era, in which this letter was issued, the result is not the year 483 or 486, but the year 487 of the Spanish era.

At the end of this letter, in the second session of the Council of Chalcedon, the following are appended:

[Note: [Col. 1369C] In the admonition to this letter, number 8, we showed that in the common editions these testimonies were wrongly inserted into the second session of the Council of Chalcedon after Leo’s letter to Flavian, whereas in the Greek codices they are appended to that same letter before the proceedings are recorded. In the same place, number 9, we proved that this collection of testimonies should be attributed to Leo, which sufficiently disposes of Garnerius’s opinion that the testimonies were collected by Theodoret and added to Leo’s letter. We believe it more probable that Theodoret received certain authorities of the Latin Fathers from Leo. It makes no difference that his dialogues were written in the year 448, before Leo sent these testimonies to Constantinople. For Theodoret could have added some material to testimonies collected earlier when he received Leo’s collection translated into Greek. This consideration strongly supports our view. Leo, when speaking of the Greek Fathers, easily took their testimonies from the Latin versions that were already famous among the Latins, so that he did not derive them from Theodoret’s Greek, as we observed in the admonition to Letter 165, number 3.

Although Theodoret inserted some testimonies of Latin Fathers—namely Damasus and Ambrose—which were known to the Greeks, in his dialogues from the first draft, and which are not found in Leo, other testimonies of Hilary and Augustine must be said to have been taken from Leo and added to the second dialogue. For the works or treatises of these Fathers, especially Augustine’s letter to Volusianus and his exposition of the faith, cannot be said to have been published or known among the Greeks before Leo.

That Theodoret received these from Leo’s collection is confirmed all the more by the fact that all the authorities of the Latin Fathers which are recorded after Leo’s letter and before the proceedings are inserted in the second dialogue of Theodoret in the same words, from the same Greek version, and in the same order. Among them, the clearest indication of this addition is the testimony of Saint Ambrose from Book II of *On the Faith to Gratian*, which begins in Leo: “Let empty questions about words therefore be silent.” The portion of this testimony that begins with the word “let us preserve” had already been brought by Theodoret from a Greek version different from Leo’s. Later he again inserts the same complete text among Leo’s testimonies, from another Greek version, of the kind found in the Greek versions of Leo’s works.

If Theodoret had not taken these texts from Leo’s testimonies rendered into Greek, would he not, when he first cited the text, have presented it complete and in the same version? This repetition in a different version declares that the later addition was taken from Leo. Theodoret wished to add all the authorities proposed by Leo to his earlier testimonies, and perhaps, because the different translation concealed the resemblance, he did not notice that he had already cited the same testimony of Ambrose shortly before, so that there had been no need to repeat it.

If the three testimonies of Saint Cyril in Theodoret are displayed in the same Greek words as in Leo’s testimonies, that is irrelevant, since both Leo’s Greek translator and Theodoret could equally have excerpted them from Cyril’s works written in Greek.]

Testimonies of the holy Fathers, partly Latin and partly Greek, who asserted two natures in Christ. The opinion of Joannes Garnerius, in the latter part of the works of Marius Mercator, near the end of the preface to Saint Cyril’s *Scholia on the Incarnation*, is that these were added to Leo’s letter by Theodoret. He brings forward several arguments; in my judgment, none is sufficient.

“From Saint Cyril’s *Scholia*,” he says, “Theodoret cited three testimonies in the second dialogue of the *Eranistes*, and in exactly the same words in which they are reported at the end of the letter in the second session of Chalcedon.” Granted. But if the Council of Chalcedon took place before Theodoret’s dialogues were written, as Baronius and others maintain, then Theodoret should be considered to have taken them from the acts of the synod, rather than the synod from Theodoret.

Moreover, Theodoret is reported in the second session of Chalcedon to have said that Saint Leo’s letter had been attacked by the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops, citing a testimony of Cyril that is included among those appended. He would not have cited it if it had already been attached to the letter. Nothing prevents a testimony copied by Leo from having been brought forward later by Theodoret; indeed, Leo’s agreement with the Catholic and Cyrillian position was thereby all the more clearly demonstrated by Theodoret, since the same testimony had been cited by both.

In addition, Theodoret cites only a very brief testimony, the middle part of which Leo did not transcribe.

Garnerius adds:

> “That the letter was translated into Greek by Theodoret, or at least by those who favored Theodoret’s party, and indeed corrupted by the translators, is demonstrated by the fact that Leo himself complains of this to the Emperor Marcian.”

I do not recall having read the names of those who assert this opinion.

[Note: [Col. 1371] On this matter see further annotation 3 in Quesnel’s Dissertation 1 on the year 454.]

This alone I assert: as far as can be inferred from his writings, our Leo never suspected anything of the kind concerning Theodoret. Indeed, it is more likely that the letter was translated and corrupted by Theodoret’s adversaries than by his supporters.

The adversaries of Leo’s letter wished to corrupt it for this purpose: having cast him under suspicion of Nestorianism, they wanted him to incur the hatred of the Catholics and for his letter to be rejected as contrary to the faith. Who, moreover, could believe that this was attempted by Theodoret, who wished to erase by every effort and means the suspicion of Nestorianism once cast upon him at the Council of Ephesus, and who loudly proclaimed that he held no other faith than Leo?

How much more reasonable, then, is it to suppose that this corruption of Leo’s letter was introduced by the Alexandrians, with whom Theodoret and the other bishops of the Eastern diocese had carried on such prolonged hostility. Nor is this merely conjecture. Leo’s own Letter 104 1427 (now 130), which Garnerius cites, makes it exceedingly clear.

The entire letter concerns the Alexandrians. In its first chapter it praises the faith of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria. In the second, it advises that a few ignorant men, stirred up by the instigations of heretics, should be instructed from the tradition of the Alexandrian Church itself—namely, from the writings of Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril—by Proterius.

In the third, Leo complains that, through the crafty wickedness of certain heretics, who wished to disturb the simplicity of others, “my letter,” he says, “which I sent to Flavian of blessed memory, is said to have been falsified, so that by changing certain letters or syllables they might represent me as an adherent of the error of Nestorius. I ask your venerable Clemency to order that the same letter, through my brother Julian the bishop, or through those whom your piety chooses as suitable for this work, be translated into Greek completely and carefully, and delivered by a trustworthy messenger under the impression of your seal, to be handed over to the judges of Alexandria. Let them have it read to the clergy and people of that city together with the teaching of the aforementioned bishops, with which my writings agree,” and so forth.

From this it is plainly evident that the entire deception concerning Leo’s writings was constructed by the devices of Alexandrian heretics, and that the translation of the pontiff’s letter should be attributed to Julian rather than to Theodoret.

Theodoret himself had subscribed to Saint Leo’s letter even before the Council of Chalcedon, together with all the other bishops of the Eastern diocese, as Letter 68, chapter 3, relates; and in the synod he subscribed to it again, as the legates of the Apostolic See affirm in session 8. Indeed, he had defended it in the second session against the Illyrian and Palestinian bishops, as Facundus also records. The corruption of the letter, however, was the work of heretics.

Garnerius presses an argument for his conjecture:

> “Throughout the entire letter there is no mention or promise of bringing forward testimonies.”

The answer is at hand. When the letter was written, and even when it was first sent to the East for the Council of Ephesus, the pontiff had no intention of adding testimonies of the holy Fathers by which he might fortify his teaching against the calumnies of the heretics.

But when, at the Ephesian robbery, Dioscorus had savagely attacked the Catholic bishops and the faith of the Church itself, when the defenders of the faith had been expelled, deposed, and beaten, and when the letter of the Roman pontiff had also been rejected, other legates were later sent to the East with the same letter. Since Leo foresaw that it would be attacked by the heretics, he fortified it with the testimonies and authority of the holy Fathers, so that the bishops of all the Churches to whom he had sent it for approval, moved by these proofs, might subscribe to it more readily.

Fortified with these testimonies, the letter was brought to Constantinople by a double embassy in the years 450 and 451 through the legates of the Roman See; it was also sent to Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, who had already been designated for the Council of Chalcedon; and at that synod it was reread and approved.

This selection of testimonies should be understood as the material alluded to, or explicitly mentioned, in Letters 52, 53, 54, 55, and 56 (now 69, 71, 70, 74, and 75), concerning the sufficient instruction supplied from the authorities of the Fathers. A passage in Letter 68 (now 88) to Paschasinus, now published for the first time, will stand for all the others. In chapter 3 Leo says:

> “But so that your Beloved may be more fully instructed in all things, I have sent to your Beloved certain writings of our holy Fathers concerning what they thought about the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and what they preached to the Churches, so that you might recognize it clearly. Our men at Constantinople also cited these, together with my letter.”

The examination of the testimonies themselves also proclaims Leo their author. For there is nothing in the Chalcedonian collection—except the testimony of Leporius—that is not read in exactly the same words and from the same passages in Letter 134 (now 165) to Leo Augustus. It must therefore be considered that both collections were composed by the same person, though the material in Letter 134 (now 165) is fuller, since later writings are usually more extensive than earlier ones.

After the first edition of Leo’s works, Garnerius published Theodoret’s posthumous *Auctarium*. In it, still adhering to his opinion concerning the testimonies, he writes that they were appended to Saint Leo’s letter by Theodoret, and that Theodoret then sent the letter, fortified with these defenses, to the patrician Anatolius and afterward returned it to Pope Leo himself. This is a mere dream. Not a single word of it appears either in Theodoret’s Letter 121 to Anatolius—which Garnerius cites and needlessly strains in chapter 9, number 26, of the *History of Theodoret*—or anywhere else.

In Dissertation 2 on the *Eranistes* of his author, he also severely rebukes me for imprudently following the two Calvinists Albertinus and Blondellus and for expressing the opinion in this controversy according to them. One might think that the dispute concerned some very grave and principal article of the faith, whereas in fact it concerns a very minor matter, incapable of justifying so hostile and discourteous a criticism, especially since he could and should rather have written that I had expressed the opinion of the eminent Baronius.

I shall state the matter as it is. I did not read this opinion on the subject in Albertinus or Blondellus, nor is my opinion identical with theirs as Garnerius reports it. They maintain that the testimonies cited by Theodoret were taken by him from Saint Leo’s letter. I wrote only this:

> “But if the Council of Chalcedon took place before Theodoret’s dialogues were written, as Baronius maintains, then Theodoret should be considered to have taken them from the acts of the synod, rather than the synod from Theodoret.”

I made it sufficiently clear that neither had borrowed from the other, and especially that this was my opinion concerning the testimonies of Cyril, which were at issue, when I wrote that the very brief testimony cited by Theodoret had scarcely half of its substance reproduced by Leo.

Garnerius had referred to the end of the chapter the things he intended to say against me; but, as the editors say, this portion of the dispute was lost, through an unknown accident. Meanwhile he admits that I and the Calvinists whom he attacks were led into error by what Baronius committed to writing in his *Annals*.

In fact, the eminent author believed that the dialogues of the *Eranistes* had been written after the Council of Chalcedon. It is no concern of mine either to affirm or refute this. Even if the composition of the dialogues had preceded Leo’s letter by an entire decade, it would not therefore follow that Leo took his testimonies from them. A little farther on it will become clear which opinion I think should be adopted. But first it is useful to inquire how true and certain Garnerius’s proofs are when he argues that the dialogues were written before the year 445.

The first proof is drawn from Theodoret’s Letter 16 to Irenaeus, which Garnerius admits was written after the announcement of the Ephesian pseudo-synod had first been delivered to the primate of Antioch and then transmitted to the metropolitans of the Euphratesian province, and therefore scarcely before June of the year 449.

But even if we grant Garnerius that this letter mentions the book of the *Eranistes*, why must it follow that this book had been composed four or five years earlier? It rather appears that the composition of this book, whatever its character may have been, was then recent, and that Irenaeus was only then revealing in friendship what he himself thought about it and what others also judged.

But, to bring forward what I think—not for the sake of contradiction, but to illuminate the history—I am convinced that Theodoret was writing to Irenaeus not about the book of the *Eranistes*, but about an entirely different work.

First, he writes about a work in which the question was treated whether it was permissible to call the Virgin Mary simply “Mother of God” (*Theotokos*), or whether it was necessary to add “Mother of Man” (*Anthropotokos*), or at least whether Mary had very often been called simply “Mother of God.” But this does not occur even once in the three dialogues. Everywhere there is profound silence concerning this question and title, and the subject matter really did not require its treatment.

Second, after Theodoret had satisfied the objections of others, he also removed Irenaeus’s scruple:

> “Since you also reproach me,” he says, “as though I had passed over the holy and blessed Fathers Diodore and Theodore in my enumeration of teachers, I considered it necessary to say a little about this as well.”

But Irenaeus would have raised such a complaint against the dialogues of the *Eranistes* to no purpose, and it would have been entirely useless for Theodoret here to do what he considers necessary: to give an account of omitting those two men from his enumeration of teachers, or to demonstrate from his other books the reverence he held for them.

He had already done all this in the first dialogue, satisfying such complaints in advance:

> “I would also present to you the expositions of Diodore and Theodore, those most powerful defenders of the truth, unless I saw that you were hostile toward them and that the hatred and malice of Apollinaris had succeeded against them. For you would see that they too wrote things consonant with the others, drew their streams from the divine fountain, and themselves became channels of the Spirit. But I shall pass over them, because you have undertaken an implacable war against them.”

### 3.

The work about which Irenaeus speaks in this letter was an *Apology* against certain Catholics from whom Theodoret’s faith was being demanded. “This too,” he says, “must be considered: that the person who is accused ought to produce witnesses who are by no means open to doubt, whom none of his accusers could refute.” And afterward: “If, when I was accused, I undertook my defense and brought forward unimpeachable witnesses, why do they blame us to no purpose, when they are unwilling to see anything of these witnesses?”

But the author declares in the preface—and indeed throughout the entire work—that the dialogues were written against heretics. Everywhere, if he does not act the part of a litigant, at least he assumes the role of a Catholic teacher. Thus, at the very beginning, he depicts those whom he has undertaken to refute. After first citing the examples of Alexander the Money-changer, Semei, and Manes, who, since they possessed no distinction deserving praise by birth, learning, or illustrious achievements, nevertheless strove to become remarkable through wicked pursuits, he says:

> “This very thing some people are doing **now**, who, fleeing the glory of virtue that must be sought through the labors preceding it, have acquired for themselves the most disgraceful and wretched reputation. Since they desired to become authors of new doctrines, they begged impiety from many sects and forged **this pernicious heresy**. I shall therefore try to discuss the matter with them briefly,” etc.

Moreover, whoever does not recognize in these words the Eutychian heresy, and Eutyches himself, the heresiarch, portrayed in his native colors, has failed to remember what Flavian of Constantinople transmitted concerning both of them in his two letters to Leo and in his Constantinopolitan synod, and what Leo himself and the Council of Chalcedon set forth in their writings and decrees.

For in the three dialogues, and especially in their titles, the principal doctrines of the Eutychian heresy are attacked, and the very words of Eutyches are often reported. “The rock of the Catholic faith,” says Saint Leo (*Epistle* 92, now 119), “abhors Eutyches, who, emptying the truth of the human flesh in the Lord Jesus Christ, asserts that the Word itself was transformed into flesh, so that birth, nourishment, growth, suffering, death, and so forth belonged to the Divinity alone.”

Here, in a few words, he indicates the subject matter of the three dialogues: they affirm that the unchangeable person of the Word united to himself, without confusion, the true form of a servant, so that Christ’s passion might not be said to have belonged to the Divinity alone. Likewise, the Council of Chalcedon, in its definition of faith, condemns Eutyches and all who, saying that the nature of the flesh and the Divinity was one, asserted through confusion that the Divinity of the Only-Begotten was changeable and passible. It establishes that one and the same Christ, Son and Lord, must be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation.

The Dialogist also agrees with Flavian’s synod. For the Eranist and Eutyches, using precisely the same language, each says that Christ is from two natures; each denies two natures, or that he is in two natures; each maintains that after the union there was one nature; and each refuses to call Christ’s body a human body.

From these statements it is easy to assign the true date of composition of the *Dialogues of the Eranistes*: namely, between November of the year 448, when Eutyches was convicted of heresy and condemned in Flavian’s synod, and April or June of the following year, when news arrived first to the metropolitans of Euphratesia and afterward to Theodoret concerning the convocation of the Second Synod of Ephesus.

As soon as Eutyches, having openly professed his heresy, was expelled from the Church, and had obtained a sect, disciples, and patrons, a man inflamed by extraordinary zeal for the Catholic faith undertook, out of charity and perhaps at the request of Flavian, with whom he was intimate, to convict Eutyches publicly, to instruct his followers, and to draw them back from their precipice.

At approximately the same time, Letter 83 to Dioscorus was written. In it he clearly notes that the heresy of Eutyches had arisen and been made public, in these words:

> “For those who deny the difference between the Lord’s flesh and the Divinity, and who now say that the divine nature has been changed into flesh, but now that the flesh has passed over into the nature of the Divinity, we endeavor to heal with the remedies of those admirable Fathers. For they plainly teach us both the distinction of the two natures—Theophilus and Cyril—and proclaim the unchangeability of the divine nature.”

How astonishing is Garnerius’s subtlety! He wishes Cyril to be mocked both by these words and by the entire work of the *Eranistes*, under the mask of fictitious praise and a fictitious name. Such a course of action would have been not merely imprudent, as Garnerius thinks, but imprudent and insane.

The same words with which he ridicules Gennadius’s account—Gennadius believed that the dialogical work, which Theodoret praised when sending an explanatory letter to Dioscorus, had been written against Dioscorus himself—may be applied to Garnerius, who thinks that the work was written against Cyril and the Cyrillians.

Theodoret would either have been the most shameless of men, if he had urged the prelate ranked second after the bishop of the Roman Church to read a work in which Cyril was ridiculed under a fictitious persona; or the most ill-advised, if he had wished to clear himself before one whom he himself accused in his *Cyril*; or the most insane, if he had sought the friendship of a man whom he mocked.

Someone may reasonably object, however, that the work called *Dialogues* by Gennadius was not this work, but another book *On the Incarnation of the Lord*, which Theodoret himself praises in his letter to Saint Leo and which Garnerius includes among Theodoret’s works. Gennadius writes that in this work the mystery of the Incarnation is defended by reason and testimonies from Scripture, without mentioning the testimonies from the holy Fathers that Theodoret collected abundantly in the *Dialogues*. Hence there is a definite distinction between the two works.

Those words therefore do not concern Cyril or his friends, but Eutyches and certain of his monk-followers in Egypt. Since Dioscorus had not yet openly and publicly undertaken their protection, Theodoret rightly thought that, at that moment, it would be most welcome to the primate that he was writing to him against a new heresy which had already been suppressed, together with its author, by the authority of a synod.

Accordingly, he confidently urges Dioscorus either to treat those who do not hesitate to corrupt the doctrines of the truth with salutary remedies, or, if they refuse treatment, to drive them from the fold as incurable. Cyrillians—or Eutychians? No one except someone asleep could think of the former together with Garnerius.

For the rest, Theodoret was deceived in his expectation. As he writes to Flavian, he thought that he would have as an assistant and ally, against the things being undertaken against the apostolic faith, the very dear-to-God bishop of Alexandria, Lord Dioscorus. Even then, however, Dioscorus had conceived the plan of helping Eutyches and undertaking to defend his party against Flavian.

What Garnerius adds concerning the *Dialogues*, allegedly proscribed and consigned to the flames by two constitutions of the Emperor Theodosius, is pure invention. In the first constitution, Theodoret’s name does not even appear, nor is any work of his mentioned.

As for the second, it does indeed proscribe *Allocutory Sermons*, or *Traditions*. But:

1. These words are no more to be referred to Theodoret than to Nestorius: “The interpretations of Nestorius and Theodoret, or of those called *Allocutory Sermons* or *Traditions*.”

2. It is doubtful whether, instead of *Theodoret* (*Theodoriti*), one should not rather read *Theodore* (*Theodori*). Thus it is read in the Fifth Council, session 5, where Theodosius’s constitution is cited.

3. Everyone who reads these things without a prejudiced mind will clearly recognize that *Allocutions*, as in the Fifth Council, or *Allocutory Sermons*, as elsewhere, are nothing other than sermons delivered orally to the people or to others. This can be proved by six hundred examples.

Thus Cyril of Alexandria calls Theodore of Mopsuestia’s sermons to those preparing for baptism *Allocutions*. So too there is the *Allocution of the Emperor Marcian to the Fourth Synod*. In the Fifth Synod excerpts are produced:

> “From the Allocution of Theodoret delivered against Saint Cyril at Chalcedon,” etc.

And from another allocution delivered in the same city. And later:

> “Again, after the death of blessed Cyril, the same Theodoret, in an Allocution delivered at Antioch in the presence of Domnus,” etc.

Learned men, I think, will agree with me that Theodosius’s words must be understood of such allocutions, whether they concern Theodore or Theodoret. They will reject Garnerius’s interpretation, as well as the untimely diligence and unfortunate affectation with which he attacks Theodoret’s books—especially the Catholic ones—in an attempt to drag most of their passages, by force, toward a heterodox meaning.

It is therefore plainly evident that the arguments by which Garnerius attempted to establish his opinion that Theodoret’s *Dialogues* were written before the year 445 are worthless. At the same time, the testimonies of the holy Fathers appended to the letter to Flavian collapse—testimonies which he vigorously maintains were due to Theodoret’s diligence, not to Saint Leo.

## On Letter XXIX, XXVI in Quesnellus: To the Emperor Theodosius

### 1.

“To the most religious and pious Caesar, the Emperor Theodosius, Leo, pope of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome.”

One manuscript, the Thuaneus, has: “To the most glorious and most clement Emperor Theodosius, Leo, bishop.” The Greek version, which gives the same title, seems to support the view that this was the original and genuine title.

Nevertheless, we have retained the former title, which we found in two Thuanean manuscripts, the Grimanian, Trecopithian, Corbeiensis, and Victorine manuscripts, and in all the Latin editions.

When you read “pope” or “bishop of the Catholic Church,” however, beware of thinking that this means the same as “ecumenical and universal bishop.” Our pontiff never used that title, as Saint Gregory the Great testifies in several places. Indeed, he is very often content with the simple designation “Leo, bishop,” or “Bishop of the city of Rome.”

“What, then,” you may ask, “does that heading mean?” Nothing other than what is written concerning Aurelius of Carthage, Augustine, and Fortunatianus, African bishops, in the Carthaginian conference with the Donatists:

> “Fortunatianus, bishop of the Catholic Church; Aurelius, bishop of the Catholic Church; Augustine, bishop of the Catholic Church, spoke.”

Both Saint Leo and the others intended by this formula to distinguish themselves from the assemblies and communion of heretics.

> **Note:** Although every bishop who belongs to the Catholic communion is and may be called “bishop of the Catholic Church,” the Roman pontiff is nevertheless called by that name in a special sense, just as the Roman Church is specially called Catholic by reason of its primacy. The center and root of communion and Catholic unity is located in the Roman see and in the supreme pontiff precisely because of that primacy. Thus, as Irenaeus testifies, every Church must come together with this Church because of its greater preeminence—that is, all the faithful everywhere. Quesnellus himself, in the Seventh Memorial, p. 137, urged that this testimony of Irenaeus be regarded as highly important, because although Irenaeus was a Western bishop, he was nevertheless an Easterner and brought to us the tradition of all the mother and original Churches of the East. Many further testimonies on this subject could be produced from Leo and other Fathers, and from the Gallican clergy itself, which recognizes the center of Catholic unity as situated in the Roman see; but this is not the place to burden the reader with more detail.

“Bishop of the Catholic Church,” therefore, means “bishop of the Catholic communion,” as Epiphanius says (*Against Heresies* 42).

The Donatists, I believe, first gave occasion for this designation. They confined the Church to one part, whereas the bishops who defended the Catholic Church opposed to them the name of the Church spread throughout the world.

Hence also the Emperor Constantine, in his letter to Anulinus, quoted by Eusebius, Book X, chapter 7:

> “In the province entrusted to you, in the Catholic Church over which Caecilianus presides,” etc.

Thus every particular Church, when it preserves the unity of Catholic communion and faith, is called Catholic.

For this reason, the very learned man who, following Pamelius, takes similar words of Cyprian to Cornelius as peculiar to the Roman Church does not seem to me to have grasped the meaning of Saint Cyprian’s words. The converted Novatians say:

> “We know that Cornelius was elected by God bishop of the most holy Catholic Church.”

It is clear from the sequence of the letter that this also extends to all the other Churches spread throughout the whole world. This, says Optatus in Book II, is the characteristic of the Catholic name.

For just as it belongs to the entire Church—as they strongly insist—to have one God, one Lord, and one Spirit, so what is said there concerning one bishop applies both to the whole Church and to every particular Church:

> “Nor are we ignorant,” they say, “that there is one God and one Christ who is Lord, whom we have confessed; one Holy Spirit; and that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church.”

As for the same author’s claim that the Roman Church is specially called Catholic because it is the root and mother of the Catholic Church, I say, with all respect to so learned a man, that this was not Cyprian’s meaning, nor could it have been.

In reality it was not so. For when Letter 45 to Cornelius contains the words adopted by that author—“We know that we gave an account and urged them to recognize and hold the mother and root of the Catholic Church”—Cyprian’s meaning is that he urged them not to adhere to Novatus’s party and not to pursue schism and division, but to recognize and hold the Catholic unity which he calls the root and mother of the Catholic Church.

There are so many passages in Cyprian confirming this interpretation concerning unity that they readily present themselves to everyone’s notice. Whoever wishes may consult the treatise *On the Unity of the Church*, the letter to Antonianus, and others, where he constantly preaches the unity of the Church, to which everyone ought to be joined by an indivisible unity, like a ray to the sun, a stream to its source, and a branch to its root.

> “Separate the sunbeam from the body,” he says (*On the Unity of the Church*), “and the division of light does not admit unity; break a branch from the tree, and once broken it cannot sprout; cut off a stream from its source, and once cut off it will dry up. So too the Church of the Lord, flooded with light, extends its rays throughout the whole world; it spreads its branches over the whole earth with the abundance of its fruitfulness; it expands its abundantly flowing streams ever more widely. Yet there is one head, one origin, and one mother, rich in the successions of her fruitfulness. From her offspring we are born; with her milk we are nourished; by her spirit we are animated.”

Finally, Saint Cyprian makes perfectly clear what he means by “mother” in Letter 71 to Quintus:
