> “It is established that those who were baptized here—that is, in the Catholic Church—and passed from us to the heretics, if afterward, having recognized their sin and digested their error, they return **to the truth and to the mother**, need only to have a hand laid upon them in penance.”

Thus “to hold the mother” in the letter to Cornelius means the same as for a heretic “to return to the mother” in the letter to Quintus. It means to hold the unity of the Catholic Church, as Letter 71 also says, and to return to it from schism through restoration.

But that the Roman Church could not properly have been called by Cyprian simply “the mother of the Catholic Church” is clear, since this name belongs with greater right to other apostolic Churches that had first been established in the East and Palestine, before the faith and episcopate were brought to the city of Rome.

This applies especially to the Church of Jerusalem, which is in fact called the mother and origin of all the Churches in the letter of the Fathers of the Council of Constantinople to Damasus, Ambrose, and the other bishops assembled at Rome.

The same designation is given to the Roman Church in the letters of Lucius I to the bishops of Gaul and Spain, and of Felix I to Benignus; but everyone knows that these letters are spurious.

In reality, Pope Innocent III, in his letter to Bishop Decentius, when listing the provinces that owed the seeds of the faith and the establishment of Churches to Saint Peter and his successors, names none except Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands.

### 2. “Synodal judgment”

Thus read the Grimanian and Thuanean manuscripts, instead of “synodal council,” which appears in the other two Thuanean manuscripts and others, apart from all the printed editions. I do not know whether there is any distinction between the two expressions.

Someone might say that the former, which we have retained, can refer to any synod, whether provincial or ecumenical; whereas the latter generally refers to a council composed of all the synods, or to an ecumenical council, or at least to one formed from several synods or the bishops of several provinces.

Such were the synods from which Leo forbade Hilary of Arles in his Letter 10, calling them “synodal assemblies,” because bishops from several synods or provinces gathered under the principal metropolitan.

## 1436 — On Letter XXX, Pulcheria Augusta

### 1.

This letter is very similar to Letter 27, now 31, which is likewise addressed to Pulcheria, although it is shorter. The present letter seems to have been sent through legates, while Leo still retained some hope that the synod summoned at Ephesus might be changed into an ordinary assembly at Constantinople, as may be inferred from the end of the letter.

> **Note:** See the admonition prefixed to Letters 30 and 31.

Concerning the other letter, which in the better manuscripts lacks the notation of consuls, day, and month, we said, in the note on Letter 27, now 31:

> “But better provision will be made for the person who is in error if **where** he went astray, there he comes to his senses; and **where** he deserved condemnation, there he receives pardon.”

### 2. “According to the emperor’s disposition”

Saint Leo frequently uses the same expression, as do many other writers. At hand are the Second Synod of Mâcon under Guntram, and Hincmar of Rheims, Letter 6, chapter 26, Mainz edition.

The expression signifies an imperial edict, as can often be seen in the imperial law code. Hence the “archives of dispositions” and the “counts of dispositions” are also mentioned there.

Our pontiff extended the expression to ecclesiastical sanctions in Letters 64 and 65, now 84 and 85, and elsewhere; likewise to divine and eternal decrees, as in Letters 24 and 132, now 28 and 162, and elsewhere.

## On Letter XXXI, XXVII in Quesnellus: To Pulcheria Augusta

### 1. “Since he bore the form of a servant”

The manuscripts vary greatly. One Thuanean manuscript and the Trecopithian read: “Ut in quo formam, etc.” (“That in whom [the] form …”); the Victorine: “Ut quod in forma, etc.” (“That which [was] in [the] form …”); and the Corbeiensis and Grimanian: “Ut quod in formam, etc.” (“That which [was] into [the] form …”). Others read otherwise.

### 2. “He appeared to the patriarchs and prophets in the appearance of flesh”

The holy Fathers before Augustine generally attributed such appearances to the Son. They held that, as the angel, minister, and representative of the Father, he had been sent by him under bodily appearance in the Old Testament, so that, they said, he might learn to converse with human beings and accustom them to his presence.

The Synod of Sirmium, assembled in the year 351 against Photinus, condemned the contrary opinion as erroneous. But because the Arians twisted this opinion in support of their heresy, Augustine judged that another approach should be taken in interpreting the appearances of earlier times. He therefore argued with all his strength, in Books II and III of *On the Trinity* and elsewhere, that these appearances should be attributed to angels.

Most of the Fathers and writers of the following age followed him, so that it is surprising that our Leo departs from him here.

### 3. “Nor could we possess the victory of the triumphant one if it had been achieved outside our nature”

Thus read all the manuscripts and many of the printed copies. The common editions read instead:

> “Nor would we otherwise possess the victory of the triumphant one, if it had been accomplished outside our nature.”

I would have retained the word *accomplished* (*confecta*), found in the Theoderician manuscript, since it suits this passage better, unless the excellent Grimanian, Trecopithian, and Thuanean manuscripts read *conserta* (“joined” or “engaged”).

“Shone forth.” Thus read the Corbeiensis, Theoderician, Barberinian, and one Thuanean manuscript. Three Thuanean manuscripts, as well as Canisius’s edition and others in the margin, read *induxit* (“introduced”); but this reading may easily have arisen through the alteration of a single letter in place of *inluxit* (“shone forth”), which seems necessary for the integrity of the sense. The common editions and the Grimanian manuscript have *indulsit* (“granted” or “showed favor”).

### 5. “Nor can he be reckoned among the adoption of the sons of God”

Thus read five Thuanean manuscripts, as well as the Theoderician, Barberinian, Trecopithian, Corbeiensis, Grimanian, and Bodleian manuscripts. The earlier reading was:

> “Nor can he attain the adoption of the sons of God.”

### 6. “Primarily saves”

On this word, see Note 3 on Letter 10, to the bishops of the province of Vienne.

The Divinity of Christ primarily saves us if we consider the dignity of the price and merits, which comes wholly from the Divinity to the humanity. The humanity primarily saves us because the mysteries of the passion and death, through which we have been reconciled to God, could be accomplished only in human nature; consequently, the beginning and origin of human salvation is the human nature assumed by the Word.

### 7.

The notation of the day, month, and consuls is absent from the Grimanian, Bodleian, Trecopithian, Victorine, Barberinian, and Thuanean manuscripts. It therefore seems to me to have been transferred here by mistake from the shorter Letter 30, which was written to the same Pulcheria on the same day, in the same month, and under the same consuls, and in nearly the same words.

> **Note:** Compare our Note 40, column 795, note b, and the admonition prefixed to Letter 30, where we examined more carefully what should be thought concerning this letter and the preceding one.

We therefore believe that this notation should be erased—not only for that reason, but also because the letter appears to have been written several days, or even weeks, before 13 June. This is clear from the words of chapter 4:

> “Since, from the third day before the Ides of May, when we received his serene Majesty’s letter, most of the remaining time must be consumed in order that the departure of priests sufficient for the matter may be arranged.”

Who could fail to understand from this that the letter was written immediately after the imperial letter had been received—that is, shortly after 16 May, and before the legates had been equipped for their departure?

This letter, therefore, was sent first, in May; then the other, which is an abridgment of this one, was sent through legates in June.

The conjecture of the earlier edition must necessarily give way to this later conclusion—a conjecture in which I had suspected that the first letter was nothing other than an expanded copy of the second, which is known from Letter 41, now 45, to have been sent to Pulcheria. Hilary, who was to carry it, was unable to reach Constantinople because of Dioscorus’s brigandage.

## On Letter XXXII, XXVIII in Quesnellus: To Faustus, Martinus, etc.

We reread this letter in the Grimanian manuscript, in one Thuanean manuscript only, and in the Greek version. From these sources we supplied the two lines that were missing toward the end.

### “From my side”

Saint Leo was the first of all the Roman pontiffs to mention legates sent *a latere*.

> **Note:** This opinion is refuted in Note 3 on this letter (col. 795, at the end). This manner of speaking, which is also found in Letter 31, chapter 2, seems to have been adopted from the style of secular rulers with the following meaning. Some examples may be found in the notes of the very learned Christopher Justellus on the code of the canons of the African Church, or on canon 7 of the Council of Sardica, which is cited at the beginning of that code. There, for the first time, the expression *a latere mitti* (“to be sent from the side”) is transferred to ecclesiastical affairs.

The African Fathers of the council, taking this seriously, did not hesitate to write the following in their letter to Pope Celestine, published at the end of the cited code:

> “For we find no provision established by any synod of the Fathers that some should be sent as if from the side of Your Holiness.”

To be sent “from the side,” says Morinus, means to be selected and deputed for some task as if from the pontiff’s household, from his domestic officials and agents. He treats the matter more fully in *Ecclesiastical Exercises*, Book I, chapter 20, as does Peter de Marca in *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and Empire*, Book V, chapter 4.

In my view, however, both Morinus’s definition of a *legatus a latere* and the distinction between pontifical legates and legates of the Roman council—which he thinks can be derived from these words—are alien to Leo’s meaning.

Julius, bishop of Puteoli, the chief of these legates, was neither a member of Leo’s household nor one of his domestic officials or agents. The same cannot even be said of the presbyter Renatus of the title of Saint Clement. Moreover, Leo speaks indiscriminately of these men and two others, both in the present letter and in Letter 31.

In my judgment, therefore, these words contain no special mystery, at least in the present passage. They mean nothing other than “from here,” as is also established by the Greek version, which has only **ἐντεῦθεν** (*enteuthen*), “from here”—that is, from the city, as Letter 25 has “from these parts.”

It is not plausible that Julian, bishop of Cos, whom we should reasonably regard as the author of this version, and who had lived among the Romans for many years, would have been ignorant of the force and use of the formula if it concealed any other secret meaning.

Indeed, Saint Leo interprets himself when, writing again concerning the same legates in Letter 33 to the Emperor Theodosius, he agrees entirely with the Greek expression and says only:

> “Having appointed **from here** my brothers, who may fulfill the place of my presence.”

If there is nevertheless something distinctive in these words, I would readily believe that the person sent “from the side of the Roman pontiff” was one delegated to some task from the bosom of his own Church, province, or diocese—just as emperors used to send certain persons from their own side or retinue into the provinces, and these were also commonly called *missi dominici* (“lord’s emissaries”).

## On Letter XXXV, XXV in Quesnellus: To Julian, Bishop of Cos

### 1. “We added”

The Greek version adds:

> **Ὤστε ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας τῆς ἐνανθρωπήσεως τοῦ Χριστοῦ**

That is: “So that [we might act] for the truth of Christ’s humanity.”

### 2. “In us and in you”

For these words the Greek version has:

> **Ἐν πάσῃ τῇ καθολικῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ**

That is: “In the whole Catholic Church.”

### 3. “From the substance of the assumed man”

The Greek version adds:

> **Καὶ ἀπὸ αὐτῆς τῆς συλλήψεως τῆς Παρθένου**

That is: “And from the very conception of the Virgin.”

### 4. “For whoever denies the man Jesus Christ, mediator between God and human beings”

Thus read the Thuanean, Grimanian, Corbeiensis, Victorine, and Surian manuscripts, etc. Earlier the reading was:

> “For the denier of the mediator,” etc.

The Greek reads:

> **Ὁ γὰρ ἀρνούμενος τοῦ ἀληθινὸν ἄνθρωπον τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ**

That is: “For whoever denies that the Lord Jesus Christ is a true man.”

### 5. “Or because he alone was conceived of the inviolate Virgin without desire”

Thus read two Barberinian manuscripts, four Thuanean manuscripts, the Cantabrigian, Grimanian, and Trecopithian manuscripts.

In the common editions, however:

> “Or because he alone was conceived from the Holy Spirit by the inviolate Virgin without the desire of the flesh.”

This wording was taken from the Greek version, although that version does not have the word “flesh,” just as the Victorine manuscript and the other manuscripts already cited do not.

### 6. “Nor did discord among the desires produce conflict among the wills”

We have retained this reading from most witnesses. The Grimanian manuscript has:

> “Nor did discords of desires produce conflict of wills.”

The Greek has nothing corresponding to these words. But the adjacent Latin witnesses, as well as Canisius, Sicardus, Nicolinus, and Surius, read:

> “Nor did conflict of wills produce discord of desires.”

This is not inept; nevertheless, in retaining the first reading we have followed the majority of the manuscripts, and it is also the best reading.

### 7. “Bearing the same person in the Divinity of the Word”

The Greek reads:

> **Ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔχων ἐν Θεότητι καὶ ἀνθρωπότητι πρόσωπον**

That is: “But having the same person in Divinity and humanity.”

### 8.

Before the consular notation, the Greek version has:

> “May God keep you safe and sound, most honorable brother.”

> **Note:** We have discussed more fully the date of this letter and its Greek version in the admonition prefixed to it.

Concerning the day and month noted there, however, there is greater difficulty. The letter is read as having been sent on the Ides of June, that is, on the 13th. For this reason we have not dared to separate it from the other letters sent on that same day.

Nevertheless, it plainly appears to have been written several days later, namely together with the letter to Flavian sent on 23 July. Both this letter and that one were written after the letters of each recipient had been received through the deacon Basil.

Basil did not bring Flavian’s letter until the legates had already departed for the synod, only a few days before 23 July, as appears from Letter 34, now 38. Therefore this letter to Julian was also written a second time at that period.

This has the useful consequence that, although two letters to the same person are recorded as having been written on the same day, the earlier one, now placed as Letter 31, now 34, will henceforth be regarded as sent on 13 June, while the later one, now numbered 25, now 35, will be regarded as sent on 23 July.

The latter begins:

> “Although through our men, whom we sent from the city for the sake of the faith,” etc.

We think that the three words “for the sake of the faith” should be deleted on the authority of at least seven manuscripts, since they have entered the Latin text from the Greek version, which differs from the original text in many more respects.

It should also be observed that something similar occurs in Letter 24, now 28, the famous letter to Flavian. Saint Leo writes that the same legates were sent “to carry out every matter piously and faithfully,” without mentioning a synod.

I do not know whether my conjecture concerning the reason is mistaken. When Leo received Flavian’s first letter together with the acts of the Constantinopolitan synod against Eutyches, he recognized that the heretic did not submit to his condemnation or withdraw from his perverse doctrine, but was instead plotting many things against Flavian.

He therefore resolved to send four legates to the East, who might either recall Eutyches to a better mind by the authority of the pontiff or restrain him by the authority of the emperor.

Several letters now read as having been sent on 13 June were first written for this sole purpose, especially the famous Letter 24, now 28, to Flavian. In it there is in fact nothing about a synod, but only about managing the affair of the faith through legates.

The same is true of Letter 28, now 32, to the archimandrites of Constantinople, in which Leo writes that legates had been sent from his side for the sake of the faith.

But before the legates departed, Leo received Theodosius’s letter announcing the convocation of a synod. Immediately the same legates, who had been designated to discuss the matter of the faith with Flavian, were directed to the synod, and their departure was delayed so that time might be given for writing new letters or expanding the earlier ones.

In some of these letters Leo obeys Theodosius’s commands concerning the synod to be convened and summoned, yet returns to his earlier plan and wishes it to be carried out, as in Letter 30:

> “But better provision will be made for the person who is in error if where he went astray, there he comes to his senses; and where he deserved condemnation, there he receives pardon.”

Since Theodosius’s letter concerning the synod had been received long before 13 June—that is, on 16 May—and the legates were already ready to depart, their departure was delayed for almost an entire month, and the date attached to Letter 24, now 28, was altered.

It follows from these statements that Letter 25, now 35, belongs in its original position after Letter 34, now 38.

## On Letter XL, XXXVI in Quesnellus: To the Bishops of the Province of Arles

### “To Constantine,” etc.

If the condition of the province of Vienne in the time of Pope Leo had been what it is displayed as being in Sirmond’s *Notitia*, there could scarcely be any doubt that the twelve bishops of Gaul to whom Leo writes the present letter all—and only they—belonged to the province of Vienne.

For if you add the bishops of Arles and Vienne, who were disputing the primacy, you will find the number that constituted the whole province: namely, fourteen bishops. These are the bishops listed in the *Notitia* and those who assembled for the consecration of Ravennius.

The matter, however, is otherwise. We can derive nothing on this point from the *Notitia*, which we have proved to be later than Leo’s time in Dissertation 5, Part I, chapter 10. Moreover, although the *Notitia* does not count Tarentaise among the cities of the province of Vienne, Leo’s Letter 50, now 66, proves that it then belonged to that province, since it subjects it to the bishop of Vienne.

> **Note:** We have shown in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, Part II, chapter 4, that this *Notitia* describes civil, not ecclesiastical, provinces. In the same place, chapter 5, we proved that the ecclesiastical provinces of Gaul did not at all conform exactly to the civil arrangement.

From the number of bishops presented by this letter, however, we learn two things.

First, as we have already suggested elsewhere, nothing new was introduced into the province of Vienne, even though the decree of Pope Leo and the constitution of Valentinian may have established something new.

> **Note:** You will find it proved in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 5, Part II, chapter 2, no. 4, that insofar as the bishops attached to the see of Arles took part in Ravennius’s ordination, they acted contrary to no decree of Leo.

Rather, following the ancient custom, all the bishops came together to the city of Arles as to the metropolis of the province; all unanimously assembled for the ordination of that bishop; all conferred the primacy upon him; and all removed the bishop of Vienne from it.

We see that he neither bestowed the grace of consecration upon Ravennius nor complained that this consecration had been usurped by another.

The second point that we derive from this is that Rusticus, who is listed in the heading of this letter among Ravennius’s fellow consecrators, is without doubt a different person from the Narbonese Rusticus to whom Saint Leo wrote elsewhere. For a metropolitan of another province, such as the Narbonese Rusticus represented himself to be, would never have intruded, contrary to the canons, into an episcopal ordination in a foreign province—much less in the Viennese province, whose metropolitan either still claimed at that time, or certainly had claimed not long before, that the Narbonese province was subject to him. Rusticus would have given the Arelatensians the greatest support if he had hastened to the ordination of the bishop of Arles as a bishop of that same province. Moreover, the Narbonese Rusticus would not be found written third in this letter, [Col. 1382B] since elsewhere he is found named either immediately after Ravennius—as in the synodal letter of forty-four Gallic bishops to Saint Leo and in the third Council of Arles—or even before Ravennius, as in Saint Leo’s Letter 82 (now 103).

It is therefore preferable to suppose that a Rusticus other than the Narbonese is named in this letter. We believe this all the more willingly because the name Rusticus was very common, and because we in fact read that several men of that name flourished in Gaul around that time. Apollinaris Sidonius mentions some of them in *Letters* II.11, V.9, and VIII.11. Another Rusticus, perhaps distinct from all these, wrote to Eucherius the letter published by J. Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius, *Letters* II.11.

## On Letter XLI, Letter XXXVII in Quesnell. To Ravennius, Bishop of Arles

[Col. 1382C]

1. “According to the preceding notice.” This is how it must be read with the Thuane manuscript, not, as the printed editions have it, “According to the present notice.” Saint Leo is referring to the embassy which Ravennius, then a presbyter, had undertaken in the name of Saint Hilary of Arles, in order to appease Leo. On that occasion Ravennius became known to the pope, and is said to have earned his favor through the gentleness and holiness of his character, as appears in the supplicatory petition of the Gallic bishops to Leo (see Col. 880 of this volume).

1443 2. “Therefore let authority not be lacking in your modesty, and let gentleness commend your steadfastness.” This is the reading of the manuscript codices. Formerly the text was corruptly printed: “Therefore let authority not be lacking in your modesty; let gentleness commend not your steadfastness, but your justice; let leniency temper it,” and so forth.

3. “When true love of what is right possesses within itself …” This is the reading of the manuscript codices Herovallianus and Thuaneus, as well as of the Merlinian edition of Isidore. Some may perhaps prefer the other commonly printed reading: “When true love of what is right possesses within itself [Col. 1382D] both apostolic authorities and canonical sanctions, as has at some time also seemed right to me.” But—something I am compelled to admit after considering the matter more carefully—this reading appears to me so devoid of meaning that, in my judgment, it also lacks a genuine sense. For although true love of what is right subjects the human mind to God’s law and inspires complete obedience even to human precepts, it can never by itself impart knowledge of either apostolic authorities or canonical sanctions, which, as they say, are positive laws.

I confirm the reading we have restored by the authority of Hincmar of Reims and of the manuscript codices he used. For in the *Opusculum of 55 Chapters against Hincmar of Laon*, which appears as number thirty-three in Sirmond, chapter 10 quotes a passage of this letter beginning with the words “For to the just person, therefore …,” and there the very same reading is found.

4. That this letter was written during the consulship of Asterius and Protogenes, that is, in the year 449, is proved by another letter of Leo written to the bishops of the province of Arles in the same year in which Hilary of Arles died and Ravennius was appointed in his place. From this you should correct Philippe Labbe, who, in his dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, states that Hilary of Arles lived until 5 May of the year 454. That statement is disproved by two letters written to Ravennius, Hilary’s successor, and by a third written to the consecrators, all in this year 449; also by four other letters sent to him during the following three years; and by the letter of the Gallic bishops, among whom he is counted, in the year 451.

## On Letter XLIII, Letter XXXIX in Quesnell. To Theodosius Augustus

[Col. 1383B]

What should be thought about the present letter is entirely uncertain.

[Note: [Col. 1383D] To resolve the difficulties raised here, see what we have done in publishing this letter in our preliminary notice prefixed to it.]

The editors of both the Council of Chalcedon and the works of Saint Leo judged it to be more likely a fragment of the following letter than a complete letter. They held that not everything in it cohered and that it had not been found in manuscript codices.

As for the manuscripts, we have found several that contain it, including one Thuane manuscript and another of our Grimanian manuscripts, more than eight hundred years old, as we have said, and of excellent quality. Perhaps it is a copy of the following letter, namely Letter 40 (now 44), which Saint Leo sent to the Augusta Pulcheria with some alterations. For in Letter 41 (now 45), which he writes to the same woman concerning the Ephesian Robber Council, he testifies that he is sending her such a copy. Nevertheless, the two letters differ in many respects.

[Col. 1383C] Saint Leo writes this first letter in his own name alone, whereas he writes the following one in his own name and that of the Roman council. In the former he draws great confidence from his own authority in defending the truth personally; in the latter he derives confidence for the defense of faith and peace from the emperor’s letter. In the latter he says that what happened at Ephesus was reported to him by the deacon Hilary, who alone had escaped. In the former he asserts that these events were reported by the most reverend bishops who had been sent by the apostolic see. This is false, since only one bishop had been sent to the East, namely Julius of Puteoli, whom we even suspect to have died before reaching Ephesus.

Furthermore, one letter has appended to it a copy of the Nicene—or rather Sardican—canons, while the other does not. Finally, there are several features in the former letter that indicate that it was truncated, or had not yet been completed and finished, so that it is more a rough outline of a letter than one to be counted with the others. A manifest gap appears at the place marked by dots. A little farther on we read: “According to the judgment of the aforesaid priest …,” although Dioscorus has not previously been mentioned; these words point to him in the other letter. Whatever the truth may be, we did not wish to remove it from the number of the letters, leaving each person free to form his own judgment about it.

The beginning of this letter was taken by the impostor Pseudo-Isidore in constructing the opening of the forged Letter 2 of Dionysius I, Roman pontiff, to Severus, bishop, and of the forged reply of Pope Liberius to Athanasius of Alexandria and the other bishops of Egypt.

## On Letter XLV, Letter XLI in Quesnell. To Pulcheria Augusta

[Col. 1384A]

Joannes Cotelerius published a Greek version of this letter from manuscript codex Regius 1026. Where the text has the words “For the royal faith,” which we restore from the Grimanian manuscript and others—for previously it read “For the royal see”—the Greek has ὑπὲρ τῆς Ῥωμαϊκης πίστεως, “for the Roman faith.” This is plainly contrary to Leo’s intention, since he urges Pulcheria to resist novel errors on behalf of the faith—that is, according to the faith with which she is endowed, or by the power of that faith.

[Note: [Col. 1383D] Compare our note 8 (Col. 834, n. f) on this letter.]

1445

## On Letter LIII, or on the Fragment of the Letter of Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople, to Saint Leo. After Letter LI in Quesnell

[Col. 1384B]

1. This notable fragment of a letter was extracted by the most learned Joannes Baptista Cotelerius from manuscript codex Regius 940 and published in 1677 in volume I of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, page 66, two years after the first edition of our Leo. In his notes he advises comparison with what Sozomen says in Book VII, chapter 8, concerning the election of Nectarius, likewise bishop of Constantinople.

This portion of the letter ought not to have been omitted from this edition, nor assigned another place, since it is mentioned in the letters that follow and was first received by Leo when the pope was writing Letters 52, 53, and 54 (now 69, 71, and 70), and others, to Theodosius, Pulcheria, and the rest, on 16 July. Some of those letters refer to it; several explicitly recall it. Thus in Letter 53 (now 71), to the archimandrites, we read:

“The bishop of Constantinople himself, and those who consecrated him, apart from what concerned the ordination of the new bishop, reported nothing to us about errors that had been suppressed or renounced.”

[Col. 1384C] From these words, compared with the fragment, we learn: first, that around this time Saint Flavian had passed to the better life;

[Note: [Col. 1384D] On the date of Saint Flavian’s death, Anatolius’s ordination, and the letters written to Saint Leo concerning his ordination, see the preliminary notice prefixed to this fragment.]

second, that before Flavian’s death Anatolius had neither been elected nor ordained, since the ordination followed the election without delay; and third, that not only Anatolius but also his consecrators sent Saint Leo letters announcing the ordination.

## On Letter LIX, Letter XLVI in Quesnell. To the Clergy and People of the City of Constantinople

1. “By the acclamations of the people.” That the people’s votes formerly took part in the elections of bishops is clear from our one Leo alone; that they were likewise admitted in translations is equally certain from the *Miscellaneous History*, Book XX, chapter 23. We learn from these words that they had a role in the deposition of bishops, whether in approving or rejecting it.

This was very often done through the acclamations of the people. When these were seditious and tumultuous, they were rightly rejected; indeed, they were prohibited by the holy Fathers, who wished elections conducted through such acclamations to be annulled, as in the eleventh session of Chalcedon and in Palladius, *Life of Chrysostom*, chapter 13 and following. But when the people acclaim with moderation and out of fervor for faith or justice, then—as Leo did here—the votes expressed in such acclamations were both accepted and formally incorporated into ecclesiastical records.

The transfer of this practice from the pagans to the Christians and from civil affairs to ecclesiastical matters was aptly noted by the most learned Franciscus Florens in his note on title 7, “On the Translation of a Bishop.”

2. “So that the truth of the body and blood of Christ may not be silenced even by the tongues of infants among the sacraments of communion.” This passage must necessarily be restored in this form from the Grimanian, Barberinian, Trecopithian, and three Thuane codices. A fourth Thuane manuscript reads “among the common sacraments.” The commonly printed reading, however, has: “so that it may not … be held among the common sacraments of faith,” which contains a wholly absurd meaning and is far removed from Leo’s intention.

He is alluding to an ancient practice of the Church and to the very words of Ambrose by which that practice is explained to us in *On the Sacraments* IV.4:

“When you receive it, you say, not without reason, AMEN, already confessing in spirit that you receive the body of Christ. The priest says to you, THE BODY OF CHRIST; and you say, AMEN, that is, ‘true.’”

Leo himself says in Sermon 5, *On the Fast of the Tenth Month*:

“This is received by the mouth, and those who argue against what they receive answer AMEN in vain.”

Since both Ambrose and Leo assert that only those receiving Christ’s body customarily answered “Amen,” and since Leo says that infants uttered it amid the mysteries of communion, it seems to me to follow that they too were accustomed to receive and eat Christ’s body. This practice is likewise attested by the letter—or book—of Saint Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, shortly before the end, a passage commented on by Saint Augustine in Letter 23 to Boniface.

But in Letter 107 to Vitalis, when Augustine speaks of those same children receiving or not receiving the Lord’s body and blood, I do not consider it certain whether this should be understood of the infants’ receiving it with their mouths or in some other sense.

3. “Above the whole Church.” This is the reading of the Grimanian, Victorine, Trecopithian, and one Thuane manuscript, together with the Vulgate edition of Paul. But the Corbeian manuscript, three Thuane manuscripts, and the Vulgate edition of Leo in the margin have “above all for the Church,” in accordance with the Greek text, ὑπὲρ πάντα τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ.

4. “The Manichaeans.” This does not mean that they held even a sound belief concerning Christ’s divinity. They contaminated this confession with many fables, asserting, among other things, that Christ was the one whom our Scripture calls the serpent, and so forth, as appears from Augustine, *On Heresies* 46.

5. “The Apollinarists.” What Saint Leo says about them was borrowed from Augustine, *On Heresies* 55, just as Augustine borrowed it from Epiphanius, Book III, *Against Heresies*, volume II, heresy 57, or 77, which is the heresy of the Dimoerites. There Epiphanius transmits at length a letter of Saint Athanasius of Alexandria to Epictetus.

Epiphanius numbers and distinguishes the three divisions of the Apollinarists differently. According to him, the first asserted that Christ had brought his body down from heaven; second, that Christ had not assumed a soul because the divinity itself had fulfilled its function, as our Leo says in Sermon 4, *On the Nativity of the Lord*. There he records only this one opinion of Apollinaris, so that it is plausible that the other doctrines of this heresy were the product of his disciples. Third, they did not hesitate to assert that Christ’s body was consubstantial with the divinity.

[Col. 1385D]

6. Note that the day, month, and consuls under whom the letter was issued are absent from the Grimanian, Barberinian, Trecopithian, and Victorine manuscripts and from some of the Thuane manuscripts, as well as from the editions of Merlin and Crabbe. I am therefore easily persuaded that the date supplied in the Vulgate edition—“on the Ides of October”—is an addition.

Second, another letter to the same people is found as having been issued on those same Ides and under the same consuls, so it is not likely that this letter was issued on the same day. The distinction between them is that the shorter one was written not by Saint Leo alone but also by the Roman synod, which had assembled either on the occasion of the Ephesian Robber Council or, as was customary, on the third day before the Kalends of October, as may be gathered from Letter 16, chapter 6. [Col. 1386A]

But Leo wrote this longer letter in his own name, as is clear from the sequence of the letter. The words “and the holy synod that assembled in the city of Rome” must therefore be rejected from its heading, as we have rejected them on the authority of the Grimanian, Corbeian, Trecopithian, and Thuane manuscripts, in which they are absent.

The letter was certainly written after Letters 39 and 40 (now 43 and 44), in which Leo asks the emperor to summon a council; for at the end of this letter he informs the Constantinopolitans of that request.

Third, the first letter was written immediately after news of the Ephesian turmoil had been received and before the letters and acclamations of the Constantinopolitans had reached Leo. The second was issued only after those letters had been received, as is clear from chapter 1, and therefore some time later.

In fact, no report of Flavian’s death appears to have reached Rome before July of the year 450.

[Note: [Col. 1385D] We conjectured in note 2 of Quesnell’s dissertation 1 on the same year 450 that Saint Leo received news around April not only of Flavian’s death but also of Anatolius’s ordination. There we also gave the reason why the holy pontiff delayed replying on this matter to Theodosius.]

Before 16 July, 1448 when Saint Leo wrote to Theodosius Augustus concerning the recently ordained Anatolius, who had begun to preside over the Church of Constantinople, the surviving letters of that year are rare. In that letter Leo indicates that he had then first been informed either of Flavian’s death or of the ordination of his successor.

From 15 October of the year 449 to 17 March of the following year, only two letters of Leo written to the East appear: one to Pulcheria and one to the presbyters Martin and Faustus. We have no others until 16 July.

[Note: [Col. 1386D] Before the two letters just mentioned there is another Letter 54, written to Theodosius in December of the year 449, as we saw in note 8 (Col. 856, n. i) on Letter 54.]

There is nothing about Flavian’s death in the letter to Pulcheria. It is therefore easy to infer that Pulcheria had likewise written nothing about it. In the other letter Leo testifies that he had not yet been informed that the letter written by the Roman synod on 15 October of the preceding year had been received. This shows that at that time nothing had yet been heard at Rome concerning the new state of the Church of Constantinople.

From this I infer again that Theodosius’s letter to Valentinian and the Augustae had not yet arrived at Rome in March. For from the letter written to Licinia Eudoxia it appears that Flavian had died at that time. The Greek must therefore be translated as follows:

“Flavian mentioned above was removed from human affairs by divine judgment, so that the contention of all uncertainty may be removed from the holy Churches.”

[Note: [Col. 1386D] We explained this passage differently in note 5 (Col. 879, n. b) on this letter.]

It is scarcely credible that Theodosius replied so late, since four full months had elapsed from 15 October to 17 March. In the second letter the first is mentioned as having been written earlier and sent through other messengers. It is therefore clear that the second was not issued on the same day but some time after the Ides of October.

## On Letter LXV, or on the Petition Presented to Saint Pope Leo by the Bishops of the Province of Vienne. After Letter XLIX in Quesnell

The authenticity of this supplicatory petition, which the Gallic bishops sent to Saint Leo on behalf of the privileges of the Church of Arles, is questioned by men of outstanding learning: Jacobus Sirmond, who had it printed in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul* as though it were spurious and in a character different from that of the genuine monuments; Joannes Launoius, in his dissertation *On the Two Dionysiuses*; and several others.

1449 On the other hand, the most learned Henri Valois accepts it as genuine in his notes on Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* II.29, as do other ecclesiastical writers. In my judgment, certainly, there is nothing that deserves to brand it as a forgery, whether one considers its style or the matters that the Gallic bishops set forth in this petition. Nor does any sufficiently valid reason appear for undermining the authenticity of this distinguished ecclesiastical monument.

1. The whole sequence of this little petition coheres extremely well, and nowhere does anything occur in which the intelligence, sincerity, prudence, and diligence of its authors are lacking, as they usually are in fictitious writings. Since undertaking to fabricate such little works is wholly foreign to a sensible person of generous character, such writings generally turn out either to be constructed from scraps sewn together or to be everywhere full of disordered and barbarous expressions, anachronisms, and other similar indications of spuriousness, so that their falsity often becomes obvious even to less perceptive eyes.

2. Writings of this kind are never usually fabricated unless some support is sought from them for a desperate cause. The fabricator of this writing would have acted very imprudently in advising the interests of the Church of Arles if he had persuaded himself that its privileges could be confirmed by a petition presented in the name of those who had undertaken to defend its cause. For who would render a decision against one litigant on the basis of the prejudice of the opposing party?

Certainly, if the advocate of the cause of Arles had anything to fabricate, it should have been promulgated in the name of the person whose judgment was being sought. A decree of some Roman pontiff, in which all the arguments contained in this petition were set out, would have been far more significant than the petition itself, which, apart from the reasons supporting it, presents nothing but the wishes of those making the supplication and possesses no authority of its own.

3. Let those who accuse this writing of forgery say when and in what period they think it was fabricated. During the time of Leo and Ravennius? Why should genuine and authentic petitions not rather be believed to have been presented than others be judged artificially fabricated? [Col. 1387C] Nothing prevents this; indeed, it is established that Gallic bishops sent letters to Leo on this very subject.

Or was it fabricated in the centuries after Leo and Symmachus? But after the decrees of both these pontiffs, by whose authority the whole controversy was settled through the assignment of definite Churches to the sees of Arles and Vienne, the bishop of Arles never again attempted to claim the ordination of the three provinces mentioned in the petition. It would therefore have been entirely pointless to compose petitions that would serve no purpose.

For if disputes later arose between those two bishops, they arose because one or the other invaded Churches that the supreme pontiffs just mentioned had decreed to be subject to the other.

4. Almost nothing occurs throughout this petition that does not breathe antiquity. Its style belongs to the age, and is used repeatedly both in Leo’s letters and in other contemporary monuments of our Gaul. Such are the expressions “apostolate,” “supreme priesthood,” and “supreme pontificate,” the last attributed to any bishop, as Leo himself has it at the beginning of Letter 37 (now 41) to Ravennius; “your crown,” which the three Gallic bishops Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus likewise adopt in their letter to Leo; “priest” for “bishop” everywhere; “authorities of the apostolic see” for “decrees”; “the summit of holy dignity”; “the pontifical right of ordaining”; “primacy” for metropolitan jurisdiction; “powers” for magistrates; “to govern by one’s own authority”; “to hold under every ecclesiastical rule”; and “to recall to one’s pontificate.”

The entire texture of the discourse likewise declares and persuades every attentive reader, free from all mental prejudice, that it is ancient and genuine.

5. Some things in this letter presuppose a more recondite learning than could have been employed by little scholars and recent impostors plotting a fraud. Such is the statement: “He wished to display the insignia of his dignity; he assumed and bestowed the consulship,” about which we shall speak below.

There are also other things that would scarcely have occurred to anyone as inventions and that demonstrate the writer’s good faith and the sincerity of the writing, such as the statement about the scarcity of the present year in which they were writing.

6. It is characteristic of the authors of spurious writings that, because they are chiefly attempting a fraud, they disseminate such writings everywhere with great ostentation, so that no one may fail to see what they eagerly desire everyone to know, even by the worst possible artifice. Hence numerous copies of them are circulated and subsequently appear frequently in library codices.

Nothing of this kind happened with the petition of the province of Arles. On the contrary, it remained hidden down to our own times in the archive of Arles, from which it was recently brought out alone and inserted by the most eminent Cardinal Baronius in his *Annals*.

Finally, all the arguments advanced against this petition by that most learned investigator of antiquity seem to me to be of such a nature that, from what we are about to say, he will, I hope, confess himself fully satisfied—a man more devoted to the truth of an opinion than to his own opinion.

1. “There is no honorable address to the pope to whom the petition is sent,” he says. But what if it was omitted through the carelessness of one scribe? Since this petition was copied from a single exemplar, it is not apparent what may have been done by others; nor is it permissible to decide anything against such a writing on the prejudice arising from a slight omission.

Moreover, a letter to be sent by a courier is arranged differently from a supplicatory petition to be presented by presbyter and deacon legates. Finally, so far is the omission of such splendid addresses from being an argument for forgery that it rather proves the writing’s sincerity, since such titles are usually elaborately embellished and contrived for the purpose of fraud and deception, as the pseudo-Isidorian letters demonstrate. The same writer has more than once shown that titles of this kind were added, through bad counsel, even to genuine letters.

2. “The writing appears without consul and date,” he says, “although these two details confer authority on public documents.”

This too is more appropriate to a letter than to a supplicatory petition. Moreover, there are so many monuments of indisputable authenticity in which this practice is omitted that nothing certain can be established from its absence.

This dating formula was more familiar among Roman bishops than among bishops of other regions. For scarcely anywhere in the letters of Eastern, African, Spanish, Italian, or Gallic bishops does such a formula appear. Where, indeed—to remain within the age of Leo—is the consular dating in the letters of Augustine of Africa, Flavian of Constantinople, Ambrose and Eusebius of Milan, Paschasinus of Sicily, Proterius of Alexandria, Ceretius, Salonius, Veranus, and more than forty other Gallic bishops in their synodal letter to Leo?

[Col. 1388D]

3. “Nothing is found in this petition by which it can be detected that it is addressed to Leo rather than to Anastasius or Symmachus.”

On the contrary, there are many things by which this can be detected, namely the following:

“We have taken care to inform your Apostolate without delay, by sending letters, of the ordination by which our holy brother and fellow bishop Ravennius was advanced, with the agreement of all votes, to the supreme pontificate in the city of Arles after the death of blessed Hilary, bishop, by the favor of the Lord. We give immense thanks that your blessedness has answered with such great kindness and charity.”

And later:

“Although it was already known to us, we nevertheless know that the aforesaid holy brother and fellow bishop of ours earned the favor of your crown especially through the gentleness and holiness of his character.”

From these words, I say, it is clear that this supplicatory petition could have been offered to our Leo. Under which Roman pontiff did Hilary of Arles die and Ravennius receive ordination in his place, if not Leo I? To whom but Leo did the Gallic bishops send news of this ordination? From whom but Leo did those bishops receive a reply about it? To whom did Ravennius demonstrate the gentleness of his character? By whom was he greatly loved? Whose favor did he earn, if not that of our Leo, to whom he had been sent by Bishop Hilary together with Constantius in order to soften the anger of the Roman pontiff, provoked by the deposition of Celidonius, as the author of the *Life of Saint Hilary of Arles* testifies?

Whom, moreover, did Hilary, Ravennius’s predecessor, have as an enemy, if not Saint Leo the Great? Everything, therefore, supports the view that the petition was addressed to Leo.

4. The same most learned man derives an argument against the petition from its own words:

“It is known throughout all the regions of Gaul, and it is not unknown to the holy Roman Church, that, first among the Gallic regions, it merited having as its bishop Saint Trophimus, sent by the most blessed apostle Peter,” and so forth.

“But this,” he says, “is as obscure as anything can be. For there is no Greek or Latin, Gallic or Italian writer who, during the six hundred years from Christ, bears witness to this matter.”

What wonder if something that was perfectly clear in that age became, with the passage of time and an interval of twelve hundred years, as obscure as anything can be? Yet even today the most learned man would readily admit that this is not obscure if he remembered that he himself asserted, on the authority both of the author of the *Life of Saint Saturninus* and of Gregory of Tours, that the first seeds of the Christian faith were sown in the regions of Gaul by Saint Trophimus and his six companions, whom the apostolic see sent there.

It can scarcely be doubted that all of them first arrived at Arles and stayed there, since Arles was prominent among the cities of the Roman province. For not only was it close to the sea, but, as we read in the constitution of the emperors Honorius and Theodosius to Agricola, prefect of Gaul, in which they order that the provincial assembly be held in that city:

“The course of the Rhône and the return of the Tyrrhenian Sea must necessarily make [Col. 1389C] it nearby and almost contiguous, whether because the one flows past it or the other encircles it, so that by sail, oar, vehicle, land, sea, or river, whatever is produced in the several regions may be brought to this city.”

Furthermore, if no author for six hundred years after Christ bore witness to this matter, from whom did the two authors just mentioned derive it—authors whom no one will wish to regard as impostors? Even if neither they nor anyone else had transmitted anything in writing about it, how many things are passed down through the Churches as though by the hand of living speech and transmitted to later generations, even the most remote?

I see what troubles the most diligent investigator of antiquity and the other authors in this portion of the petition. It is this: since Saint Peter is mentioned, the text appears to attribute to the apostle himself the mission of Saint Trophimus, which they consider contrary to the truth.

I, however, think this entirely false. But, in my opinion, the meaning of those words is not what they seem at first glance to convey. It is so customary and familiar among ecclesiastical writers to use the name of the apostle Peter for the apostolic see of Peter that scarcely anything is more obvious to a reader.

Although it should be enough merely to point this out, I shall nevertheless offer some examples, more as illustrations than as proofs. Pope Boniface writes in his letter to Rufus of Thessalonica, as preserved by Holstenius and in the latest collection of the councils:

“Thus blessed Peter the apostle, acting in his place, entrusted everything to the Church of Thessalonica,” and so forth.

The same pope writes in his letter to the bishops established throughout Thessaly:

“You know that blessed Peter can do both things: that is, in gentleness to be mild toward the gentle, and with the rod to rebuke the proud.”

Likewise, in his letter to Rufus and the other bishops of the Thessalonian vicariate, he says that to be separated from “the communion of blessed Peter” is the same as being separated from “the communion of the apostolic see.”

In later centuries Nicholas I writes in Letter 24:

“Let no one presume to contradict the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.”

But, so as not to wander beyond our proper bounds or beyond Leo’s letters, do we not read the following in this same sense in Letter 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne against Saint Hilary of Arles?

“So desiring to subject you to his authority that he does not allow himself to be subject to blessed Peter the apostle.”

And later:

“By diminishing in his more presumptuous words the reverence due to blessed Peter himself.”

Again, in Letter 41 (now 45) to Pulcheria Augusta, chapter 3:

“May your piety deign to defend our petition before the most merciful emperor, a mission specially entrusted to you by the most blessed apostle Peter.”

I pass over six hundred similar testimonies.

These words of the petition, therefore, detract nothing from its authority, nor do they seem in any way to conflict with Gregory of Tours or with the true date of the arrival in Gaul of the first seven bishops, which the most learned men embrace.

## 5.

He presses the following words: “And from that time the gift of faith and religion was gradually infused into other regions of Gaul,” etc.

[Note: Compare the observation in the same chapter 2, in part II, dissertation 5.]

“These statements,” he says, “are incompatible with Pope Innocent, who writes in his letter to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio: ‘Since it is manifest that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one established Churches except those whom the venerable Apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests.’”

These statements certainly cause no difficulty. For who does not see that from words placed together so indistinctly and confusedly nothing certain or clear can be extracted that would contribute to an exact knowledge of history? Who would not admit that Innocent here, somewhat more agitated than usual, gathered together many things in the manner of an orator in defense of Roman privileges?

[Note: Innocent reports the matter as manifest from the fact itself. Why, then, should it be said that this pontiff, somewhat stirred, gathered together many things in the oratorical manner? There is no reason.]

Or who, finally, would not observe that this pontiff’s speech is so constructed that it is meant to be understood distributively and relatively, as people customarily speak? For, while discussing the Churches of six different regions, he did not wish to assert that all of them had been established by Peter alone or by bishops sent by him, but added “or his successors,” thereby indicating that not all of them had been founded by Peter, but that some had been founded by his successors. Among these, the Gallican Churches must undoubtedly be counted, even according to the assertion of that same learned man.

Now, although it may be asserted, without prejudice to the Roman See, that after the Church of Arles had been established through the work of Saint Trophimus, sent by the Roman pontiff, several others within Gaul itself were founded by him, the Gallican bishops do not assert this in their petition. They assert only that from that point onward—that is, from the city of Arles, as the same writer interprets it—the gift of faith and religion was gradually infused into other regions of Gaul. For from that city, and either on Trophimus’ advice or by his command, six other men who had arrived there with him proceeded to the cities of those other regions, after they had examined the opportunities from that metropolis, as if from a kind of watchtower, and had determined what would best serve the Christian religion and the salvation of Gaul, which cities were to be approached, at what time, and which places should first be visited.

For a fuller clarification of this passage, I observe that when the bishops here mention Gaul, this need not necessarily be understood of all the regions of Gaul, but only of the Narbonensis as a whole. This was the region first reduced by the Romans to the status of a province and consequently called the Roman Province; it was also often designated simply by the name “Gaul.” Since we have treated this matter more fully elsewhere, there is no need to linger over it here.

## 6.

They also think that the impostor betrays himself by these other words:

“To the bishop of Arles this honor and dignity were also conferred: not only was he to govern these provinces by his own authority, but he was also to keep all Gaul under the entire ecclesiastical order, entrusted to him in the place of the Apostolic See.”

The cited author says plainly that the writer who stitched together such a petition shows himself to have lived after Caesarius, Auxanius, Aurelian, and the other bishops of Arles, to whom the Roman pontiffs, in the centuries after Leo, entrusted their representatives’ authority in Gaul. For before these men, he says, no such commission is recorded as having been entrusted to the bishops of Arles in the place of the Roman pontiff.

I admit that these words present a somewhat greater difficulty, but not so much that the petition must therefore be rejected. First, since the Gallican bishops were especially anxious to preserve their own rights intact, they flatter the pontiff with courteous words. Supported by imperial power, he had already begun seriously to shake those privileges, and he could be appeased only by humble expressions of deference.

Moreover, when they acknowledge that apostolic authority was once entrusted to the bishops of Arles in the place of the Apostolic See, perhaps they understand this in the same sense in which Saint Leo himself writes that the blessed Apostle Peter entrusted an apostolic legation to the empress Pulcheria in the aforementioned letter 41 (now 45). That is, because they had always been accustomed to direct their letters to the bishop of Arles, as primate of Gaul, both when announcing the date of Easter and in other matters arising within Gaul.

Furthermore, although the letters of the Roman pontiffs in which they expressly wished to entrust their authority to the bishops of Arles are not now extant, it is not, in my view, sufficient grounds for declaring that this never happened, since many ecclesiastical records of this kind have perished through the injury of time.

In a similar matter the learned heterodox scholar Blondel was mistaken, and he reached his judgment too hastily when, in his work on the Primacy, he declared that no traces of the vicariate of Thessalonica existed among the ancients, at least before the time of Pope Leo I.

[Col. 1391C]

There were certainly many such traces, but they lay hidden and eventually came to public light in the Roman collection of Luca Holstenius. The records that still survive could also have been sufficient for the Gallican prelates, who wished to flatter Roman ears and draw Leo, by agreeable language, toward their own desires, to make their claim without incurring the charge of falsehood or fabrication.

For although the Gallican bishops had always governed their Churches in their customary manner, even after Leo’s judgment had been issued against Saint Hilary, they saw that the emperor, dependent upon Leo’s word, had confirmed the pontiff’s decree by his own authority and had assigned its execution to the master of soldiers. They therefore judged it to be in their interest to soothe Leo’s mind and demonstrate to him the justice of their rights and privileges.

They thought that this could scarcely be impressed upon him in any other way than by persuading him that the bishops of Arles had long ago been honored with the authority of the Roman pontiffs, so as to keep Gaul under the whole ecclesiastical discipline. That is, from that metropolis they were to watch carefully that nothing contrary to the canonical regulations was attempted in the Gallican Churches. Such vigilance is properly the concern and solicitude of the Roman pontiff, since he is the primate of all bishops, the executor and vindicator of the canons, and the one to whom, as the Fathers of Chalcedon write to Leo himself, the Savior entrusted the guardianship of the vineyard.

Indeed, as far as the Western dioceses are concerned, Saint Leo observed this practice especially: whenever circumstances required, he sent bishops there to act in his place, or granted this authority to bishops already residing there.

Thus, in Letter 1 (now 12), he entrusted Potentius with responsibility in the African province of Caesarean Mauretania. He delegated the vicariate of Thessalonica to Anastasius. He wished Turribius to join the metropolitans Idatius and Ceponius in Spain against the Priscillianists, in order to convene a synod—to say nothing of the Eastern bishops, including Julian, bishop of Cos, and several others sent to Constantinople in the pontiff’s place.

Saint Leo also attempted something of this kind in the Gallican diocese when he transferred to Leontius the authority, removed from Hilary, to convene the synodal assembly of the Gallican provinces. He would not have assumed this authority unless he had either believed—or wished it to be believed—that the man who stood out among the other metropolitans by reason of his pre-eminent authority was acting in his place. He could therefore preserve or depose him at will.

Nor did the same pontiff undoubtedly think that he was introducing anything novel when he entrusted Ravennius with all the matters that he wished to be undertaken in Gaul against the rising error of Eutyches.

“We desire,” he says in Letter 51 (now 67), “that everything through you should come to the knowledge of all our brothers and fellow priests. We specially entrust this to your affection, so that through the vigilant care of your watchfulness . . . it may become known to all the brothers.”

That this concern also extended to other provinces, over which the bishop of Arles did not claim metropolitan jurisdiction, is clear from the subscriptions to the letter that the Gallican synod sent to Leo.

The same plan of Leo is evident in Letter 38 (now 42) to the same Ravennius. There he warns him about a certain wandering pseudo-deacon named Petronianus and instructs him to have the man excommunicated by all the Churches of Gaul. It is also evident in Letter 76 (now 96), in which he orders that the bishops of Gaul be informed of the date of Easter through Ravennius’ care.

This indicates sufficiently that the practice had been carried out by him from long-standing custom. It was therefore enough to enable the Gallican bishops, who wished to speak words pleasing to Leo, to assert without falsehood that the authority of the Apostolic See had been entrusted to the bishop of Arles.

Pope Celestine, Leo’s predecessor after Sixtus, confirms the same point when he writes to the bishop of Arles about a certain Daniel. Daniel had come from the Eastern regions, where he had stained himself with many crimes, and was reportedly ordained bishop in Gaul. The pontiff wishes him, wherever in Gaul he might be, to be brought by that same bishop of Arles before an episcopal tribunal.

By what authority? By what right? In my opinion, by the right which the Gallican prelates had always traditionally accorded him, but which Celestine wished to appear to have been exercised by virtue of his own delegation. In the same letter he declares that he is delegating to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne the judgment of the bishop of Marseille, who had been accused of rejoicing over the death of his brother and fellow bishop.

No one will deny that the same authority was expressly delegated to the bishop of Arles by Pope Zosimus, unless he wishes to maintain that the letters of this pope relating to the controversy of Arles are spurious. We demonstrate in the apologetic dissertation for Saint Hilary of Arles that such a claim is unfounded, both on the testimony of the most learned men, who regard these letters as genuine, and through several further arguments.

## 7.

He again argues against the petition on the ground that it joins Valentinian and Honorius in the government of the empire as though they had been colleagues.

They are indeed joined together, but not as colleagues—for not even a syllable is said of that relationship—but as predecessor and successor, as father and son, and as the authors and defenders of the same privileges of the city of Arles.

He presses the point: “No privilege granted by Valentinian to the people of Arles is found in which Arles is called the mother of all Gaul.”

But in this matter negative proof is of no importance. How many constitutions of the emperors have emerged from darkness in later centuries, after previously lying buried? Moreover, who does not know the frequent use of that figure by which the plural number is put for the singular, especially when several persons have just been mentioned?

Augustine proves by numerous examples that this is a customary way of speaking even in sacred history. In Book III of *On the Harmony of the Gospels*, chapter 16, he discusses the two thieves who are said to have blasphemed Christ together, although another evangelist reports this only of one of them.

## 8.

He argues against the petition from the words of its third chapter, in which it asserts that “just as the Church of Arles, within Gaul, possessed the primacy in the priesthood by the meritorious right of antiquity, so the city itself also possessed primacy in secular affairs by reason of its advantageous position.”

“Who,” he asks, “from Christ down to Constantine the Great ever called the bishop of the Church of Arles the primate of Gaul? Who, from Constantine down to Honorius and Theodosius, granted the primacy of Gaul to the Church of Arles? Who assigned the primacy of Gaul to the town of Arles in the time of the preceding emperors? These,” he says, “are the dreams of more recent times, which the Gallican bishops would never have dreamed.”

These are certainly not dreams, most learned sir, unless we say that Leo the Great was dreaming when, in Letter 50 (now 66), which settled the controversy that had arisen between the bishops of Vienne and Arles, he said the following—not from his own invention or under the influence of any authority, but, as he puts it, after considering the allegations of both parties’ present clergy:

“We have always found the cities of Vienne and Arles within your province of Vienne to have been so distinguished that, by the alternating circumstances of various cases, now one excelled in ecclesiastical privileges and now the other, although it was reported that they had once possessed a common right from the peoples.”

[Col. 1393B]

Here Saint Leo freely admits what the Gallican bishops assert, after considering the allegations of both sides. If those allegations had come down to us, they would have removed every opportunity for evasion. But it is more than sufficient that even before the light of the Christian faith shone upon Gaul—and therefore before Constantine—it is acknowledged that Vienne and Arles at least possessed a common right.

Saint Leo ought not to profess anything more, since he intended to make the two provinces equal on the basis of their common right, although he clearly showed himself more convinced of the rights of Arles when he assigned a far greater number of Churches to its metropolis.

As for the primacy of the city of Arles, even if what has been said proves that it existed before the birth of Christ, it is sufficient to derive it only from the time when Saint Trophimus began to govern the Church of Arles. It is therefore superfluous to ask who asserted its primacy between the birth of Christ and Constantine.

Finally, the last argument against the supplicatory petition is drawn from the fact that Saint Leo, in his reply to the bishops in whose name the petition was supposed to have been presented—if it is genuine—says nothing at all about the two provinces of Narbonne. He should have spoken of them if he was replying to the petition in question.

I answer that Saint Leo’s judgment was issued only between the bishops of Arles and Vienne. It is clear that their dispute concerned solely the primacy, or metropolitan jurisdiction, over the province of Vienne; for the bishop of Vienne had never claimed anything for himself in the province of Narbonne. Leo therefore had to pronounce only concerning the province of Vienne.

Add to this that after the death of Hilary, who had always vigorously defended the rights of his Church, Ravennius—being, by his character, less inclined toward such disputes and, as the bishops say in the petition, gentle in his morals—defended his right over the other provinces only very tepidly and in a manner resembling concession. He was content to preserve the primacy over Vienne.

This is the entire concern of the petition. It does not mention the three provinces except incidentally and in the course of pursuing another matter, namely, to strengthen its claim over Vienne more and more. These observations will suffice here; the remaining matters relating to the same controversy may be found in apologetic Dissertation 5 for Saint Hilary of Arles.

Once these points have been explained, I think nothing further prevents the supplicatory petition of the Gallic prelates from being regarded as genuine and authentic. It contributes no little authority and strength to the privileges of the Church of Arles.

It remains, if there are other matters in this letter that require clarification, to dispose of them briefly.

### 1. “Your crown.”

The marginal notes of earlier editions show that some people regarded this epithet as belonging exclusively to the pontiff. But it is clear from various sources that it was applied indiscriminately to any bishop.

Augustine, for example, addresses Proculianus, a bishop of the Donatist party, in Letter 147 as follows: “Your people adjure us by our crown; our people adjure you by your crown.”

Jerome likewise addresses Augustine himself: “I beseech your crown.”

Sidonius Apollinaris addresses Leontius of Arles in the same words in Letter 3 of Book VI.

That this form of greeting was familiar to the Gauls is clear both from Sidonius himself and from the subscriptions to the synodal letter of the Gauls to Saint Leo, from the letter of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus, and from that of the Gauls to the same pontiff. It is also clear from this very petition, in which the same expression is used three times.

But where did it come from, and what is its meaning?

Some think that it alludes to the clerical and episcopal tonsure, which resembled a crown, especially according to the form formerly in use. Whatever may be said about this custom—you may consult, if you wish, Gregory of Tours when he speaks of Nicetius, bishop of Trier, and the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 40—I do not think that this is what came to Jerome’s mind. Nor does it seem at all probable that the others intended this.

The expression breathes something loftier and, in my view, signifies the supreme summit of the ecclesiastical order, such as the dignity of the episcopate. In this sense, in the imperial novella concerning the ordination of bishops against Hilary of Arles, the emperor Valentinian calls Saint Peter “the prince of the episcopal crown,” that is, of episcopal dignity.

This formula was adopted indiscriminately. In the synodal letter of the Gauls to Leo, some greet him by his crown, others by his sanctity, others by his blessedness, and others finally by his apostleship.

### 2. “He assumed and bestowed the consulship.”

The learned H. Valesius explains “to bestow the consulship” in his notes on Socrates, Book II, chapter 29, concerning the Circensian Games, which the consuls used to present at the beginning of their consulship.

In the same way he interprets the words of that passage of Socrates, *τὰς συνήθεις ὑπατείας*—“the customary consulships”—as referring to the solemn games customarily presented by the consuls.

## Concerning Letter LXVIII

By Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus to Pope Leo, in Quesnellus after Letter LXXVI.

### 1. Ceretius, etc.

The words of the letter itself clearly proclaim that these three men, who sent the present letter to Saint Leo, were bishops: “Our holy brother bishops throughout Gaul.” For it is characteristic of bishops alone to call bishops “brothers.”

That they were from Gaul is sufficiently indicated by their concern that Leo’s letter should be circulated throughout Gaul.

It is the common opinion of Baronius, Sirmond, and others that two of them, Salonius and Veranus, were brothers and sons of Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, whom the writers of that age frequently celebrate. I regard this opinion as highly probable, indeed almost certain, even from this one letter, which they met together to write.

But in which part of Gaul they exercised the episcopate has hitherto remained unknown.

At one time I suspected that they came from that part of the province of Vienne which, in the division recently made by the decree of Pope Leo, had been assigned to the bishop of Vienne. The reason for my suspicion was that the bishops of the province of Milan had borrowed that doctrinal letter of Leo from one of them, namely Ceretius, apparently for no other reason than proximity.

No Gallican bishops, however, were closer to the Italian diocese than some of the four bishops subject to Vienne. One of those dioceses, Tarentaise, is very near Augusta Praetoria, which even today counts it among its comprovincial sees.

Moreover, there was no reason why these three bishops should not be found among the forty-four Gallican prelates who wrote to Leo about the same letter and to whom Leo replied, or why they should not be read as having participated in the Gallican synod, except that they came from that part of the province of Vienne whose bishops alone refused to subscribe to the rights of the Church of Arles, lest they prejudice the rights of their own metropolitan, the bishop of Vienne.

A different opinion now seems more persuasive to me. I therefore conjecture that these three bishops came from the province of the Maritime Alps, both for other reasons and especially because they were neighbors. I believe that I can establish by firm arguments that one of them, Veranus, came from that province.

First, from Letter 4 of Pope Hilary we learn that the bishop Veranus wrote to Saint Leo in defense of the metropolitan rights of Ingenuus, metropolitan of the Maritime Alps. He did not write alone, but together with the other priests of the province, as Hilary says: “of the province of the Maritime Alps,” which was the subject of the dispute and which he had mentioned in the preceding third line.

But why, I ask, would Veranus have been so concerned for the rights of that metropolitan that, when Ingenuus was voluntarily relinquishing his own rights, Veranus brought complaints to Leo about the diminished authority of the metropolitan? Why would he have written a common letter with the bishops of that province unless he believed that he ought to act for the dignity of the common province of the Alps?

Why would Pope Hilary also write to that same Veranus concerning the case of the city of Cimiez and the fortress of Nice, and join him to Leontius, the leading metropolitan of those regions, unless Veranus belonged to that same province of the Alps?

### 2.

Joannes Savaro asserts in his notes on Letter 15 of Book VII of Sidonius, from an old manuscript of the monastery of Lérins, that Veranus, the son of Eucherius, was bishop of Vence in the province of the Maritime Alps. The manuscript contains the names of the bishops, abbots, and monks who were enrolled among the saints from Lérins:

“Veranus, bishop of Vence.”

Vincentius Baralis likewise confirms this from the martyrology of the Church of Vence in his *Lerinian Chronology*, p. 362:

“In Gaul, in the city of Vence, the burial of blessed Veranus, bishop of Vence, who was a monk of the island of Lérins, a disciple of blessed Hilary, abbot of that island, and afterward bishop of Arles.”

[Col. 1395C]

“This blessed Veranus was buried in the same church of Vence in a marble sarcophagus fixed into the wall. He was renowned for many virtues and miracles, was born of noble lineage, and rested in peace on the fourth day before the Ides of September.”

When the author of the martyrology makes Hilary abbot of the monastery of Lérins, he is mistaken. He is contradicted by the words of Eucherius, who writes that Salonius, the brother of Veranus, was formed by the teaching of the most blessed Hilary. This does not mean that Hilary was an abbot, since Eucherius, on the contrary, calls him there “Hilary, a novice of the island.”

### 3.

This opinion concerning Veranus’ episcopate is made still more probable by the fact that the city of Vence was very close to the island of Lérins. One may therefore easily believe that Veranus was summoned from that monastery to the see of this city because of the reputation for holiness that his proximity had made well known.

Moreover, Cimiez was close to the same city, as was the fortress of Nice. Concerning their union under one bishop, Veranus had once written to Saint Leo with the other bishops of the province, and Pope Hilary afterward wrote to him above all the others.

What moved both Jacobus Sirmond and David Blondel to write that this Veranus had been a prelate of the Church of Lyons, I do not know. Perhaps they formed this opinion from certain lists of the bishops of Lyons, whose reliability scholars reject.

From Veranus’ see I now reasonably infer that his brother Salonius and Ceretius exercised the episcopate in the same vicinity, and therefore that all three held sees near the province of Milan. None are closer than Vence, Glandèves, and Senez, which are very near Albenga, Genoa, Turin, and other cities.

This was why the bishops of the province of Milan borrowed Saint Leo’s letter from one of the three, Ceretius, in accordance with Leo’s own admonition.

These observations concerning the episcopates of Ceretius, Salonius, and Veranus have been occasioned by the letter they sent to the Roman pontiff.

The illustrious archbishop of Auch praised another letter addressed to the same men while pleading his own case at the general assembly of the Gallican clergy in 1665, as I learn from its Acts. I do not know, however, whether that learned prelate became acquainted with the letter through printed editions or through manuscripts.

## Concerning Letter LXX
