In Quesnellus LIV. To the Empress Pulcheria.

### 1. “Since harsh things preceded his ordination.”

I judged that this should be restored from the Grimani manuscript, whose reading is closely approached by the Victorine manuscript: “Since harsh things preceded in his ordination.” Leo uses the word “harsh” here in almost the same sense as above, when he says, “whose cause was the harsher one,” in Letter 40 (now 44).

Nevertheless, three manuscripts of Thuaneus, one Cambridge manuscript, and the common printed editions read: “Since many things preceded in his ordination.”

### 2. “Disputations.”

The Grimani manuscript and one Thuaneus manuscript read *dispositionum*, “arrangements,” instead of *disputationum*, “disputations.” Since the former reading extends to a wider range of matters, Leo may perhaps have used it here, as he did in the same letter.

### 3. “Or my letter.”

This is the reading of the Grimani and Cambridge manuscripts, not “and my letter,” as in the common editions. The difference is slight, but not insignificant.

For if one reads “or,” Anatolius was given the option of subscribing to either letter. Leo anticipated that the bishop would more willingly subscribe to the letter of Saint Cyril, the bishop of the Eastern regions, whose writings had been approved by the First Synod of Ephesus, than to Leo’s own letter, which had not yet been received by the Eastern Churches.

Leo leaves the same option of subscribing to either letter when writing to the Gallican bishops in Letter 51 (now 67) to Ravennius:

“We specially entrust this to your affection, so that through the vigilant care of your watchfulness our letter, which we sent to the East in defense of the faith, or the letter of Cyril of holy memory, which entirely agrees with our convictions, may become known to all the brothers.”

[Note: We refuted this explanation in note 8, col. 893, n. i, on this letter.]

### 4. “Which ignorant folly dared to define.”

This is the excellent reading of the Grimani manuscript. In its place, the printed editions have: “Which he dared to define: ignorant folly,” etc., with a thoroughly false meaning alien to Leo’s intention.

For Anatolius, to whom these words would apply, had defined nothing contrary to the faith, nor had he defined anything at all, either after or before his consecration. He had not taken part in the pseudo-synod of Ephesus while it was being held; rather, at that time he was staying at Constantinople, as the *Brief History of the Eutychianists* expressly observes, serving as Dioscorus’ representative in the retinue.

Add to this that Leo never marked Anatolius with words so harsh that he accused him both of ignorance and folly.

## Concerning Letter LXXX

In Quesnellus LX. To Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople.

### 1. “So that they might be content with the communion of their own Churches.”

This form of abstention comprised four principal points.

When bishops enjoyed communion only with their own Churches:

1. They neither received visits from their colleagues nor did their colleagues receive them from these bishops.

2. They were not permitted to celebrate the sacred offices solemnly in another parish.

3. They were forbidden reciprocal exchange of *litterae formatae*, or formal letters of recommendation.

4. They did not meet together with the others in councils or other ecclesiastical assemblies, and they were deprived of all authority and voting rights in them.

For the first point, see canon 15 of the First Council of Toledo. For the second, see Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 70, where he writes that in the time of Polycarp and Victor the Easterners, separated from the Westerners, received no letters of peace from one another.

The third and fourth points are sufficiently indicated by the expressions used for this kind of excommunication: “to be deprived of the charity of the brethren,” “to be outside the communion of the brethren,” and similar phrases that occur frequently.

Anyone who wishes to investigate the matter further should consult the most learned Jean Morin, *Ecclesiastical Exercises*, Book II, Exercises 17, 18, and 19. See also Saint Augustine, Letter 261.

### 2. “Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius.”

It is well known why he makes particular mention of Dioscorus and Juvenal. The former was the leading figure in the impiety of the Ephesian synod; the latter supported it in every respect, as is clear from Saint Leo’s letter to him and from the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

Eustathius, bishop of Berytus, was one of those who possessed authority and occupied leading positions at the Council of Ephesus, as is stated in Act 4 of Chalcedon.

But why should Saint Leo and Anatolius have singled out Eustathius rather than Thalassius of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Eusebius of Ancyra, and Basil of Seleucia in Isauria, who are likewise counted among them? The following reason occurs to me.

Eustathius, more than the others, seemed to have issued a confession consonant with the Eutychian position at the Ephesian Robber Council, using these words:

“Therefore, one must not understand two natures, but one incarnate nature of God the Word.”

Although this statement was approved at Ephesus, as soon as it was read out at the Council of Chalcedon the bishops, especially the Easterners, cried out: “This is what Eutyches says; this is what Dioscorus says.”

Furthermore, perhaps some remnant of hostility remained between Anatolius and Eustathius because Eustathius had acquitted Ibas, bishop of Edessa, at the council held at Berytus, while Dioscorus was intensely hostile to Ibas.

At that time Anatolius was Dioscorus’ representative. He favored him as much as he could, even after Dioscorus had been condemned by the Council of Chalcedon, since Dioscorus had been the source of Anatolius’ dignity.

[Note: Quesnellus’ conjecture concerning hostility between Anatolius and Eustathius rests on no evidence. Indeed, since Anatolius appears to have doubted whether Eustathius’ name should be read from the diptychs in the sentence of the legates, as we observed in note 19, col. 914, n. r, on this letter, such hostility is rather excluded. Compare note 15, col. 944, n. j, on Letter 95.]

### 3. “Not to be recited at the sacred altar.”

It is clear that the subject here is the sacred diptychs. How highly they were once regarded is evident from the controversies that erupted in the Church on the occasions of Saint John Chrysostom, Acacius, the Eutychians, the Three Chapters, and others.

The reader may consult the letter of Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, to Saint Cyril of Alexandria, in Nicephorus Callistus, Book XIV, chapter 26, as well as Cyril’s reply to him, both at the place cited and among Cyril’s works.

It is useful to transcribe one passage here, both because it is relevant to our subject and because it briefly describes the nature, origin, and use of the diptychs. It occurs in the letter of the Egyptian bishops to Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, against Timothy, the invader of the Church of Alexandria, in Part III of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon:

“They also placed his own name and that of Dioscorus in the venerable diptych, in which are contained the names of the bishops of pious memory who have passed to heaven, and which are reread according to the holy regulations during the time of the holy mysteries,” etc.

## Concerning Letter LXXXVIII

In Quesnellus LXVIII. To Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum.

No one fails to understand how highly this letter to Paschasinus must be valued, both because of the knowledge of those matters that we owe to him alone and especially because it was addressed to Saint Leo’s principal legate, whom Leo was then sending to act in his place at that great synod of Chalcedon on behalf of the faith.

In addition to this memorandum, Leo gave him another, more secret memorandum, as is shown by Act 16 of that synod. From it we excerpted and printed a portion of the mandate in Volume I.

[Note: We inserted a fragment of this memorandum in Dissertation on the Lost Letters, no. 52, which we placed after Leo’s letters. See above, col. 1227.]

Concerning the subscription of all the Easterners against Nestorius and Eutyches, and concerning Anatolius’ letter, from which Saint Leo learned that this had been done, there is another testimony of the pontiff in Letter 70 (now 91), written to Anatolius two days later.

We noted the remaining matters worthy of attention in Dissertation 1, *On the Life and Deeds*, under the year 451.

## Concerning Letter XC

In Quesnellus LXXIII. To the Emperor Marcian.

### 1.

The editors of earlier editions, and even the authors of the manuscript collections, mention the Council of Chalcedon in the title of this letter. Yet the council was transferred from the city of Nicaea, where it had first been convened, to Chalcedon only toward the end of September.

2. But also in my brother Julian, namely the bishop of Cos, whom he testifies in Letter 69 (now 89) to have added as a companion to his legates, and whom in Letter 70 (now 91) he orders to participate in all the proceedings; likewise, in Letter 71 (now 92), written to Julian himself for this reason, he commands him—as he says—“to unite your care and action in all things with the brothers whom, in our place, we command to go to the aforesaid assembly, making use of the authority of our command,” etc. From this it is clear [Note: [Col. 1397D] It cannot be denied that Julian performed some function at the Council of Chalcedon in the legation of St. Leo and the Apostolic See; but it cannot be affirmed that his legation was of the same kind as that of Paschasinus, Lucentius, and the presbyter Boniface. A sufficient distinction is plainly shown by the two principal proceedings, in one of which Dioscorus was condemned and in the other the definition of faith was issued and subscribed. The three legates mentioned jointly established the sentence against Dioscorus and the definition of faith, or signed them before all the others. Julian, although he calls himself a legate, did not approve them together with those men, but after several bishops of the principal sees. If elsewhere he speaks together with the other legates, and if his name is sometimes even placed before that of the presbyter Boniface, nevertheless we do not believe that he would have been separated from the other legates in the principal proceedings, especially those in which the force of the apostolic delegation was most evident, had he exercised equal authority with them. Perhaps because Julian was not listed by Pope Leo with the other legates in Letter 93 to the council, he was not assigned an equal place in the principal acts of the council; nevertheless, his delegation, made known by other letters of Leo, secured for him a higher position than his episcopate would have warranted, above the other bishops and metropolitans. See the annotations of the Deacon Rusticus, vol. IV of the Councils, col. 1306, note f, and col. 2031, note a.] Julian held St. Leo’s place in the council no less than the other legates. We have noted this because the very learned Morinus, in *Exercitation* 20, book II, wrote that the bishop assumed the title of legate when subscribing to the Council of Chalcedon for no other reason than that he believed the title which shortly before he had actually and deservedly used in the pseudo-synod of Ephesus should, as honorable and respected, be taken up again and retained by him. The learned H. Valesius, who rendered outstanding service to ecclesiastical history, suspects that Julian’s legation was general and honorary, not special, such as that of Paschasinus and Lucentius, in his notes on Evagrius, book I, chapter 10; there he also points out the inconsistency of Baronius when speaking of Julian. Moreover, since Julian was not a member of the Western synod, [Note: [Col. 1399D] We have refuted at length in the observations on Dissertation 8, § 3, the claim that the legates of the Apostolic See are being represented here as legates of the Western synod. Paschasinus, Lucentius, and Boniface are never said to have held the place of the Western—or even of the Roman—synod, but always that of St. Leo. That Julian, although an Eastern bishop, could nevertheless perform a genuine legation of the Apostolic See is recognized from St. Cyril, who at the Council of Ephesus held the place and legation of St. Celestine. See note 2 (below, n. c) on Quesnell’s notes to the following letter. The reason is also evident. Whoever received a mandate of delegation from the Roman pontiff was a true legate, whether Western or Eastern.] and since the other legates supplied the representation and presence of that body, I think this is why he did not enjoy precedence of seating among those Western legates; in other respects, I readily believe that there was no distinction between him and them.

## 1466. TO LETTER XCIII, LXXII IN QUESNELL. To the Council of Chalcedon.

1. “Established at Chalcedon.” On account of these words, in addition to this letter written to the Council of Chalcedon, the very learned scholar mentioned in Letter 4 of Part VI of the *Letters*, dedicated to John Brayer, asserts that another letter to the same bishops previously assembled at Nicaea must be sought. The grounds for this suspicion are not merely the words of the title, but also Evagrius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 2, which reads as follows: “For these reasons the council was convened at Chalcedon, and messengers and letter-carriers were sent; priests were summoned from everywhere by letters full of piety, first to Nicaea. Thus, when Leo, bishop of Rome, sent letters to them through Paschasinus, Lucentius, and the others whom he had sent there to take his place, he addressed them in this way: ‘TO THE BISHOPS CONVENED AT NICAEA.’”

[Note: [Col. 1399D] See our note 3 (col. 936, note k) on this letter, where we printed from the Regensburg manuscript the original superscription of the letter, which names Nicaea; afterward, when the location of the synod was changed, this word was changed to Chalcedon.] I am nevertheless certain that no other letter was written. For this very letter, which is now addressed to the Council of Chalcedon, was without doubt directed to the bishops assembled at Nicaea. Since it was written on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, it could not have been addressed to bishops established at Chalcedon, who were not summoned there from Nicaea by imperial letters until before the tenth day before the Kalends of the following October. This is further confirmed by Letter 73 (now 90) of St. Leo to Marcian, written on the same day concerning the same synod. Although its title mentions the Council of Chalcedon, it is nevertheless certain that it concerns the council then summoned to Nicaea, not Chalcedon, both for the reason already given and because, when discussing the decrees of the great Council of Nicaea, it calls it “ancient Nicaea,” in order to distinguish it from the later synod being prepared there. Indeed, in Letter 71 to Julian he explicitly writes that a priestly synod was to be held in the city of Nicaea. Therefore, nothing of importance should be determined from the titles and arguments of letters, since many such additions were composed and altered according to the understanding and judgment of copyists. This is evident from the title of this letter: the Greek version, which undoubtedly follows the Latin text, has τῇ ἐν Νικαίᾳ, “at Nicaea.”

2. “Cyril, bishop, then presided.” [Note: [Col. 1400D] Before the arrival of the Roman legates, St. Cyril presided over the Council of Ephesus because he was exercising the place and legation of Celestine, entrusted to him by that pontiff in earlier letters. Accordingly, at the very beginning of the acts, action 1, after Cyril is named first, it is said that he also held the place of Celestine, most holy and most sacred archbishop of the Roman Church. Moreover, that general synod showed such regard for pontifical authority that, in its very sentence against Nestorius, the Fathers declared that they had been compelled to proceed to his condemnation by the sacred canons and the letter of our most holy father and fellow-minister Celestine, bishop of the Roman Church. See vol. III of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 1078.] Testimonies of so many ancient writers occur everywhere establishing that Cyril presided over the Council of Ephesus that I judge it superfluous to enumerate them. Some of them report that Celestine and Cyril presided, others Cyril and Celestine. The word “then” in Leo’s statement seems to me worth observing. I think the pontiff’s meaning is that he wished to indicate that Cyril was presiding at that time when the particular decrees of the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius were issued and his impiety condemned. In fact, the legates of the Apostolic See did not reach Ephesus until the eighteenth day after the sentence had been pronounced against Nestorius, as both the acts of the synod demonstrate and the learned Jean Garnier recounts in his historical preface to the later part of the works of Marius Mercator. [Col. 1400A]

## TO LETTER XCVII. Of Eusebius, Bishop of Milan, to St. Pope Leo. AFTER LETTER LXXVII IN QUESNELL.

1. “Catholic.” From the manuscripts of Thuaneus, Cambridge, and Trecopith, the only ones we used in revising this letter, one Thuaneus manuscript and the other Trecopith manuscript add *of the faith*, as do the standard printed editions. But Eusebius seems to me not to be speaking of the faith, but of the Church, which ancient writers very often call “Catholic” without an addition; Augustine frequently does so. Take the following single passage, which is at hand, from book III of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapters 10 and 11: “The Novatianists rebaptize those who come over to them from the Catholic Church . . . nor would it be necessary to do this in the Catholic Church . . . but the Catholic Church ought not to repeat it,” etc. Thus either nothing should be added here, or the word “Church” should be added.

2. “Senator.” At that time he was a presbyter of the Church of Milan; afterward he became bishop under Pope Simplicius, around the year 480. Ennodius of Ticinum mentions his legation to the East at the end of an epigram in which he celebrated the praises of that most holy and learned bishop:

> Sent to the secrets of the world’s farthest edge,  
> He diligently cared for what had been torn apart.  
> Then the East, confessing itself conquered by the traveler’s light,  
> Halted before the sight of another lamp.

When Ughellus extends this to a legation to the Council of Chalcedon, he is unquestionably mistaken. A similar error occurs in the summary of this letter, chapter 1, where I would prefer *From the East* to *From the Council of Chalcedon*. Senator is numbered among the saints in the Roman Martyrology on May 28.

3. “Cretio.” The editors of earlier editions printed *Cyriacus*. Because that name occurs below, they thought him to be the same person from whom Eusebius had received Leo’s letter and who had carried Eusebius’s letter to Leo. But all the manuscripts—those of Thuaneus, Cambridge, and Trecopith—testify that they were mistaken, with the eminent Baronius also supporting them. For all of them read *Ceretius*, whom we believe to be the same man who wrote to Leo together with Salonius and Veranus.

4. “Whom blessed Ambrose,” etc. From this you may understand that the following custom existed in the Church: whenever questions of faith arose or some writings were proposed [1469] [Note: [Col. 1400D] Quesnell seems to imply by this note what he stated more explicitly in Dissertation 1 on the year 451, no. 4: that Leo’s dogmatic letter was not only submitted to the examination of the Fathers of the Council of Milan, but was also accepted by them because, after such examination, it was found to agree with the tradition of the Church of Milan. To prevent anyone from falling into error on this point, see our note 8 on Dissertation 1 on the year 451. It cannot indeed be denied that the tradition of the universal Church is formed from the tradition of all the Catholic Churches that agree in the same doctrine. But since true tradition must also be apostolic—that is, since it must derive its origin from the teaching and preaching of the apostles—the tradition of particular Churches, in order to be true, must agree with the doctrine of those Churches which the apostles established and in which they deposited their teaching. Accordingly, Tertullian, in *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 21, wished it to be investigated, in order to distinguish true tradition from false, whether it agreed with the faith and doctrine of the apostolic Churches. “It is established,” he says, “that every doctrine which agrees with those Churches that are the original and mother Churches of the faith is to be attributed to truth, unquestionably holding what the Churches received from the apostles, the apostles from Christ, and Christ from God; but every other doctrine is to be prejudged as false.” Among all the apostolic Churches, however, since the Roman Church holds the first place as the center of Catholic unity and the head of all the Churches, the doctrine and tradition of every Church must be compared above all with it, so that it may be discerned whether it is apostolic and genuine or adulterated. Therefore St. Irenaeus, although Greek by origin and exceptionally well acquainted with the privileges of the Greek Churches, assigns this prerogative above the other apostolic Churches to the tradition and doctrinal faith of the Roman See: because of its more powerful primacy, all the faithful and Churches everywhere must agree with it. After praising the tradition of that Church, which it possesses from the apostles Peter and Paul, and the faith announced to humanity that has come down to us through the succession of bishops, he adds: “For with this Church, because of its more powerful principal authority, every Church must agree—that is, the faithful everywhere—so that from the agreement and uniformity of doctrine with Rome it may rightly be discerned what true tradition is; from the dissimilarity, false tradition or error may be exposed.” Hence the sign and character of true tradition is agreement with Rome. Accordingly, Satyrus, the brother of St. Ambrose, as Ambrose relates in his sermon on his brother’s death, book I, no. 47, when he wished to judge whether the bishop of a certain place possessed sound and Catholic doctrine, thought that he should ask him whether he agreed with the Catholic bishops, that is, with the Roman See. Likewise St. Jerome, book I against Rufinus, says: “What faith does he call his own? Is it that which the Roman Church possesses?” And immediately he inferred from agreement with Rome: “If it is Roman, he will reply, then we are Catholics.” In this sense, therefore, bishops who accept the doctrine of the Roman See as defined in a dogmatic letter may compare it with the tradition and doctrine of their own Churches, so that, if they find the latter in agreement with the former, they may rejoice. The bishops of the province of Milan followed this method, as did the Gallicans. When they found the doctrine of their Churches to agree with Leo’s, they declared their joy and testified to the opportunity granted them—we give the words of the Gauls from Letter 99, chapter 2—“to speak freely and confidently, with the authority of the Apostolic See supporting them, and for each one to affirm what he believes,” since what he believes is recognized as Catholic by its agreement with the Roman faith. Furthermore, if they had found anything in the doctrine of their Churches or bishops that differed from Leo’s letter, there is no doubt that they would immediately have corrected it and recalled themselves and their Churches to the Roman doctrine, with which, according to Irenaeus, all Catholics and all Churches must agree. But if, concerning the Council of Chalcedon itself, in which some people differed from Leo’s doctrine, Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, affirmed in Letter 101, chapter 3, to the same pontiff: “It was necessary that everyone’s understanding should agree with the meaning of your right faith,” who could suppose that at the Milanese synod, which was subject in a special way to the Roman bishop, something was not necessary which had been necessary in a general council? What the tradition of the Milanese Fathers was in this matter may be gathered sufficiently from Ambrose—or from that ancient bishop of the province of Milan who was the author of the books *On the Sacraments*. For, clearly drawing on the tradition of his own people, he wrote in book III, chapter 1: “In all things I desire to follow the Roman Church.” Since this was not true in every respect of rites, it must especially be understood of the doctrine of faith. Many other arguments that we could bring in support of this same position cannot be accommodated within the narrow limits of a note. See more in the note cited above, note 8. (At the place cited above.)] all the bishops, especially those of the principal sees, would have had recourse to the tradition of their own Church. This was done by the bishops of the province of Milan, who testified that St. Leo’s letter agreed in every respect with what blessed Ambrose, under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, had inserted in his books concerning the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation. Thus the Gallicans, in their letter to St. Leo, reviewing his letter to Flavian, recognized the meaning of their faith and testified that they had always held it according to their ancestral tradition. Thus Leo himself, in his letter to the same bishops of Gaul, and elsewhere, condemns Dioscorus of Alexandria on the basis of the tradition of the Church of Alexandria, which he traces from Peter through Mark, the founder of that Church, and through its bishops Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril. In this way the general tradition of the universal Church is formed from the traditions of the individual Churches, and the definitions of faith enacted in councils, together with the agreement of the Churches, must rest upon it. Hence Eusebius and his colleagues approve the definition of the Council of Chalcedon: “Because it agrees in complete purity with everything of the faith of our ancestors handed down to us from ancient times.” [Note: [Col. 1402C] Through a lapse of memory, Quesnell wrote that the definition of the Council of Chalcedon, which had not yet been issued, was approved by the Milanese bishops. They are speaking only of Leo’s definition. [Col. 1402D] He errs still more when he indicates that it was approved for this reason: because it agrees in complete purity with the whole of the faith handed down to us from ancient times. The context assigns this reason elsewhere. Namely, because the tradition of Milan also agreed with Leo’s dogmatic letter, they say: “Therefore, with the judgment of your authority preceding, we recognize that the Eutychians must be condemned; following the form of your letter, we have shown that we observed the procedure prescribed,” etc. By these words they attest their respect for the authority of the apostolic letters and their due obedience to them.]

5. “It remains that,” etc. How much the whole of this passage required the physician’s hand will be made clear by comparing it with the standard printed reading; we have emended it from the Trecopith and Thuaneus manuscripts:

> “It remains that, with the Lord’s approval, you preserve these things perpetually and leave them as a memorial for future ages, so that from the present time onward the insolence of the impious sect may appear extinguished, and, overthrown by new purifications, may remain prostrate forever.”

6. “Eusebius.” Concerning him, as also concerning the other bishops subscribed to in this letter, anyone wishing to know more should consult Ughellus, volume IV of *Sacred Italy*. I shall touch only on matters that he either does not include or reports incorrectly. I do not know from whom he learned that Eusebius was ordained by St. Leo I. I do know that, among the bishops [Note: [Col. 1402D] This is generally false of the metropolitans of every province. For it is clear from Letter 24 of Innocent I to Alexander of Antioch, no. 1, that the bishop of Antioch had the right and custom of ordaining the metropolitans of the provinces in his diocese. The same right belonged to the Thessalonians in the provinces of Illyricum, according to Leo’s Letter 5 to the metropolitans of Illyricum, chapter 5, and Letter 6 to Anastasius, chapter 4. The same was established for the see of Constantinople in the final action of the Council of Chalcedon. As for the Italian provinces, it is certain that after his election the metropolitan of Ravenna customarily had to go to Rome to be consecrated by the supreme pontiff. The metropolitans of Milan and Aquileia, however, appear originally to have been ordained by the Roman bishop. For when distance or the difficulty of the journey made it too burdensome for them to be ordained by the Apostolic See, the practice was introduced that they should ordain one another, as Pelagius relates. P. Bernard de Rubeis proves in his *Dissertation on the Aquileian Schism*, chapter 4, that the consent of the Roman pontiff was required in this later discipline. As for Quesnell’s further claim, that in the year 1059 the Milanese maintained that the Roman pontiff had no power of judging or disposing in that see, this belongs to those most unhappy times when, because of concubinage and other vices, the Milanese refused to heed the Roman See and created something resembling a schism.] of each province, it was then the right and custom to ordain their own metropolitan. The Donatists complained, as St. Augustine testifies in the *Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists*, that Caecilianus had not waited “for a chief to be ordained by a chief.” “For the custom of the Catholic Church,” he says, “is otherwise: the bishop of Carthage is ordained not by the bishops of Numidia but by those who are nearer, just as no metropolitan bishop ordains the bishop of the Roman Church, but the bishop of Ostia, who is nearest.” The same should be said of the other Churches. St. Ambrose was ordained at Milan; and from a letter of Pelagius, book I, part of the Roman Pontiff’s correspondence, in the year 555, we know that the bishop of Milan was customarily ordained by the bishop of Aquileia, as by the first metropolitan of the Italian diocese after him, just as he himself was ordained by the bishop of Milan, as by the head of that same diocese. Indeed, in the year 1059 they even maintained that the Roman pontiff possessed no power of judging or disposing in the see of Milan. The same writer does not indicate where he learned that Eusebius of Milan took part in the Roman council under Pope Hilary in the year of the Lord 465, since its Acts are silent about him. [Col. 1403B]

There exists an epigram of Ennodius of Ticinum concerning this bishop, indicating that he came from the eastern regions:

> Eusebius, a stranger, succeeded in the lands of Liguria,  
> Befriending the regions of an unknown people.  
> He was welcome to his companions, the Sun whom he beholds at its fiery rising  
> Shaking the waters from his burning summit, etc.

The third verse is read as follows in the supplement to the Library of the Fathers:

> The Sun was burdensome to his companion, whom he beholds at its rising;

but I would judge that it should be emended thus:

> He was Greek, whom the Sun beholds at its customary rising.

[1472] It is also clear that the name itself is Greek and familiar among the Greeks. Cardinal Baronius must likewise be corrected when, in his notes on the Martyrology for August 12, the day on which this saint’s memory is celebrated, he states [Col. 1403C] that this synodal letter was sent after the Council of Chalcedon. That is not true: the Council of Milan was held between the return of Abundius and Senator from the East and the celebration of the Council of Chalcedon.

**Faventius.** His subscription is absent from the Cambridge manuscript. Trithemius, writing about Prosper in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, relates that Prosper succeeded him in the episcopate.

**Quintus.** Ughellus calls him Quintianus; he is Quintinus in the Surian edition. He was bishop of the city of Dertona, now commonly called Tortona.

**Crispinus.** “A venerable bishop,” says Ennodius, “unacquainted with favoritism, terrifying by the stubborn severity of his censures, and one whom nothing but a good conscience ever led to mercy.” Concerning his holiness, see the same author’s testimony both in his own poem and in the *Life of St. Epiphanius*, bishop of Ticinum and Crispinus’s successor; see also the Roman Martyrology and Baronius’s notes on January 7.

[Col. 1403D] **Maximus.** This, I think, is the celebrated bishop whose homilies are frequently read in the Church and who is honored among the saints on June 25.

**Eulogius.** Ughellus calls this man Elilegius, bishop of Eporedia, and also thinks him to be the same as Eulalius, who is mentioned in the letter of the Gauls to Leo and in Leo’s letter [Col. 1404A] to the Gauls. This is unquestionably fictitious. Eporea, or Eporedia, a city of the Salassi in Cisalpine Gaul, which formerly belonged to the metropolitan jurisdiction of Milan, is now subject to Turin, even under Pope Innocent III.

**Florejus.** He who subscribed in the name of his bishop is called Florentius in the Trecopith manuscript and Florerius by Ughellus.

**Gratus, or Gradus.** He is called Gyrardus in the Cambridge manuscript and Gerardus by Surius in the margin. Augusta Praetoria, called Osta or Aosta by the Italians, was formerly subject to the metropolitan of Milan, but at that time to the metropolitan of Tarentaise.

[1473] **Cyriacus.** Through him this letter was delivered to St. Leo. He is regarded in the Church of Lodi as distinguished for doctrine and holiness.

**Abundantius** [Note: [Col. 1404D] See our note 21 on this matter (col. 948, note j) in Letter 97.]—which Cardinal Baronius thinks was mistakenly written for Abundius—is believed to be the same as Abundius, who, together with the presbyter Senator, undertook a legation to the East on behalf of St. Leo before the Council of Chalcedon. I dare affirm nothing, since in the preceding letters that mention that legation, in the acts of the legation, and in Theodoret, who wrote to him, *Abundius* is consistently read in all the manuscripts I have seen. But all those manuscripts that I collated for this letter of Eusebius—namely, the two Thuaneus manuscripts, the Trecopith manuscript, and the Cambridge manuscript—agree with the printed books in reading *Abundantius*. Certainly, if someone should say that Abundantius was different from Abundius, that he was not bishop of Como, that he did not attend the Council of Milan, but that after delivering Leo’s letter to Eusebius’s own Church, from which he had long been absent, he immediately returned—both because there was no uncertainty about his opinion concerning St. Leo’s letter and because a council could not have been convened so quickly—if, I say, anyone should argue this, I do not know whether his position could be shown to be false from any ancient writer or document. Ughellus asserts that Abundius was from Thessalonica and was consecrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December in the year 450, but he is mistaken, since it is established that already in the preceding July Abundius had undertaken a legation to the East in Leo’s name and was by then already adorned with episcopal dignity.

For *Asinio*, some manuscripts have *Asymono*. Curia, commonly called Coira, is the principal city of Rhaetia and is today subject to the archbishop of Mainz.

**Pastor.** It seems just as certain that this bishop of Asti was called Pastor, since we read this asserted in all the manuscripts, as it is clear that the Synod of Milan, to whose synodal letter he subscribed, was not convened to confirm the Council of Chalcedon, since the latter occurred later than the Milanese synod. Nevertheless, Ughellus asserts this; and he mocks the former statement as rashly believed, because in the seventh century a Pastor is found among the bishops of Asti—as though two prelates of the same name could not have existed.

**Simplicius.** He is also called Simplicianus both by Ughellus and in the Trecopith, Cambridge, and [Col. 1404D] Thuaneus manuscripts.

**John.** Ughellus calls him Roman and incorrectly says that he was appointed in the year 452.

**Optatianus.** In place of this name, *Octavianus* had until now been written incorrectly, as Baronius and Ughellus rightly observed, with all the manuscript books supporting them. He is numbered [1474] among the saints in the Martyrology on July 14.

**Justinus.** This is what the manuscript books read. Ughellus, the abbot, and Ferrerius, bishop of Vercelli, have this form in their catalogues of predecessors. The common reading is *Justinianus*, who is reckoned among the saints.

**Quintius**, also called Quintus, is read in the two Trecopith and Thuaneus manuscripts as bishop of Albigaunum; Ughellus has *Quiritius*. Sigonius mentions him in book XII of *On the Kingdom of Italy*. The bishop of Albigaunum is subject to the archbishop of Genoa. He is called Quintinus in the Cambridge manuscript and Quintianus in one Thuaneus manuscript.

**Praestantius.** Ughellus calls him Projectitius; the Cambridge manuscript has Pristinus.

## TO LETTER XCIX. Of Forty-Four Gallican Bishops to St. Pope Leo. AFTER LETTER LXXVI IN QUESNELL.

[Col. 1405B] 1. **Ravennius**, bishop of Arles and metropolitan of the province of Vienne, who succeeded St. Hilary immediately; concerning him, see above Letters 36, 37, 38, 50, 51, and 76 (now 40, 41, 42, 66, 67, and 96), as well as the *Petition of the Gallican Bishops* and the *Life of St. Hilary*.

**Rusticus**, bishop of Narbonne in Narbonensis I; concerning him, see the note on Letter 2 (now 167).

**Venerius**, bishop of Marseille, concerning whom see the heading of the Narbonensis letter addressed to the same Rusticus.

**Maximus.** Formerly a monk of Lérins, he became bishop of Riez in Narbonensis II in the year 433. For he succeeded Honoratus in the administration of the monastery of Lérins in 426 and governed it for seven years, as is stated in the homily of Faustus of Riez on this same Maximus, among the homilies called Eusebian or Eucherian. He subscribed to the Council of Riez in 439 and to the First Council of Orange in 441. More about him may be found in the Lérins chronology, in *Gallia Christiana*, and in his life written in Italian by Francesco Fulvio Frugoni [Col. 1405C], which is filled with many fables.

**Constantinus.** This is the reading of the two Thuaneus manuscripts and of Victorinus, as well as of the Thuaneus exemplar of the Roman codex, in whose chapter 57 this letter is found. The standard edition has *Constantianus*. We have learned nothing about him except that he is found subscribing to the Councils of Riez and of Orange I, and that St. Leo writes to him with the other bishops of Gaul in Letters 36 and 50 (now 40 and 66), where he is named first. Since the former letter concerns the consecration of Ravennius, he must, in my view, necessarily have belonged to the province of Vienne. Cardinal Baronius, however, makes the man who attended the two councils mentioned [1475] a bishop of Vaison, in the year 441.

**Armentarius.** Since two men of this name occur here, one of whom is said to have presided over the Church of Le Puy, it is not sufficiently clear of which city this man was bishop, unless perhaps he was from Auch. An Armentarius of that name is recorded in *Gallia Christiana* as having held the episcopate there around this time, on the basis of the cartulary of the Church of Auch. [Col. 1405D] Two Thuaneus manuscripts have *Armaturus*; the Victorinus manuscript, *Armatarus*; the Trecopith manuscript, *Armatharius*. The author of the *Supplement to the Gallican Councils*, on the authority of J. Sirmond and the Savaro codex, makes him a bishop of Antibes in Narbonensis II. Let the credibility of this claim rest with those authorities.

**Valerius**, as the two Thuaneus manuscripts and Victorinus read, or, as the Trecopith and the exemplar of the Thuaneus codex, together with the standard editions and Isidore, read, *Valerianus*, appears to be that bishop of Cimiez in the province of the Maritime Alps who, having become bishop after being a monk of the island of Lérins, attended the Council of Riez in 439 and was summoned by Ravennius to the Third Council of Arles in the year 455, as the very learned Sirmond conjectures. Sirmond also published his homilies, to which Theophilus Raynaudus appended his vindication. His pious memory is recorded in the Lérins calendars on the ninth day before the Kalends of August, as also in the monastic Martyrology of Arnaud, in which he is called not Valerianus but Valerius. St. Leo writes to him with others in Letter 50 (now 66).

**Nectarius.** The distinguished and learned Peter Gassendi reports in his *Description of the Church of Digne*, of which he himself was provost, that Nectarius was bishop of Digne in the province of the Maritime Alps. He drew this both from the work of Dom Polycarp de la Rivière, the Carthusian, and from the very ancient manuscript codex of John Savaro, which supplied, in the subscriptions of this letter, the see assigned to each bishop. He subscribed to the Councils of Riez and Orange and seems to be the same man whom St. Hilary of Arles sent to Rome to St. Leo with Constantius to negotiate the restoration of friendship between them. In place of Nectarius, [Col. 1406B] which is what I read in the Roman Thuaneus codex and the Trecopith manuscript, the two Thuaneus manuscripts, Victorinus, the Cambridge manuscript, and Isidore have *Nestorius*, joined by Surius, who has *Nestarius*. Nevertheless, he is called Nectarius in the *Life of St. Hilary*, which calls him and Constantius leading priests.

**Constantius** is recorded as the first bishop of Uzès or Ucetia in Narbonensis I; he is mentioned as Nectarius’s colleague, as we have said, in the Roman legation; he is named in the heading of St. Leo’s Letter 50 (now 66), and was summoned by Ravennius to the Third Council of Arles. In that letter Hilary wished the authority to ordain bishops in the province of Narbonensis I, which had been taken from Hermes of Narbonne, to be transferred to him as a metropolitan, in accordance with the honor due to a primate. [Note: [Col. 1405D] Since the province of Narbonensis I had its own metropolitan, as we have shown in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 5, Part II, chapter 2, we do not believe that Constantius, who was sent to Rome with Nectarius on behalf of Hilary of Arles, was a bishop of Narbonensis I. Rather, he was some other bishop from the provinces on this side of the Rhône, especially since the matter concerned appeasing Leo because Hilary had disturbed the jurisdiction of other metropolitans; for this purpose, a bishop of another province, if he had shown himself to be an adherent of Hilary, would appear less suitable.]

**Maximus**, bishop of Avignon, according to the already mentioned manuscript of Savaro.

**Asclepius**, bishop of Apt in Narbonensis II, is identified as such in Savaro’s manuscript. He attended the Council of Riez and was one of the bishops to whom St. Leo wrote in Letter 36 (now 40); he was also among those whom Ravennius summoned to the Third Council of Arles in the case of the island of Lérins.

**Maximus**, the third person numbered by this name. I do not dare affirm which see he held. They say that he was bishop of Toulouse in Narbonensis I, and Baronius and Savaro think that he was the man to whom Sidonius Apollinaris wrote in book IV, Letter 24. On this matter anyone may speculate.

**Ursus** was bishop in Senecium in the province of the Maritime Alps, if Savaro’s manuscript is to be trusted; before him no bishop of Sanitium is listed. St. Leo writes to him in Letter 50 (now 66), as does Pope Hilary in Letter 2, in the year 463.

**Ingenuus**, metropolitan of Embrun in the same province, as is plausible, although he is placed after Ursus. This is so both because at that time he had yielded his right, for which he was censured by St. Leo and by Hilary, his successor, and because metropolitans did not enjoy their privilege outside their own province, as may be seen—leaving aside many other arguments—from the First Council of Orange, to which Eucherius of Lyon subscribed after bishops who were not metropolitans. At that time either the order of consecration or a mixed practice was being observed. Ingenuus subscribed to that same council and was summoned to the Third Council of Arles. St. Leo writes to him in Letter 50 (now 66), and Hilary in Letter 2; the latter also vindicated metropolitan rights for him against Auxanius, as is evident from Letter 4 of the same pope. Ingenuus is commended especially for this reason: he was chosen by the Gallican bishops to carry this letter to St. Leo, as is clear from Leo’s reply. [Col. 1407A] He also attended the Roman council in the year 465 under Pope Hilary.

Justus. I found nothing about him, except that he may perhaps be the same man who is recorded as having subscribed to the First Council of Orange, is listed among the Gallican bishops in St. Leo’s Letter 36 (now 10), and was invited by Ravennius to the Third Council of Arles.

1477 Valerius. The manuscript of John Savaron makes him a bishop of Mende in Aquitania Prima. Around this time two other bishops of the same name flourished: one of Couserans in the province of Novempopulania, concerning whom Gregory of Tours, in *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 84, speaks as a man distinguished for holiness; the other was bishop of Antibes, who, according to ancient manuscripts, was crowned with martyrdom under Euric, the Arian king of the Goths, in the year 473.

Superventor. While not yet a bishop, he subscribed to the First Council of Orange in place of his father and bishop Claudius and revised its Acts [Col. 1407B]; he must be thought to have been appointed in his place. But it is not yet known to me over which city either of them presided. St. Leo wrote to him in Letter 50 (now 66).

Verus. I would suppose him to have been bishop of Orange in the province of Vienne. For he is placed in *Gallia Christiana* after St. Eutropius, who is assigned to the end of the fourth century and whose life Verus is said to have written, according to Sigebert in his *Book on Ecclesiastical Writers*, as well as according to Usuard, Ado, and others.

Helladius. Bishop of Lodève, or Luteva, as is thought by the most learned prelate of that see, John de Plantavit de la Pause, in his *Chronology of His Predecessors*, whose series he expanded after Bernard Gui and Catel; Savaron’s manuscript also supports him.

Etherius, bishop of Maguelonne—whose see was transferred to Montpellier—but we have no other witness than the manuscript of John Savaron, already cited several times [Col. 1407C]. We find no mention of him anywhere else; and that city is also absent from Sirmond’s ancient *Notitia*,

[Note: [Col. 1407] We demonstrated that this *Notitia* is older in the observations on Quesnel’s Dissertation 5, part II, chapter 4.]

which is later than Leo.

Anemius is assigned the see of Albi on the authority of the same manuscript of Savaron.

Petronius. He was, as I conjecture, that former presbyter who was sent with the deacon Regulus to St. Leo by the Gallican bishops in the year of our Lord 450, to deliver letters requesting that the rights of the Church of Arles, taken away from Hilary, be restored to Ravennius. He is called bishop of Dées in Savaron’s manuscript.

Fonteius. Fonteius was elected in place of Auspicius, bishop of Vaison, to whom St. Leo was writing in Letter 36 (now 40), on 26 August 449. To Fonteius Leo gave Letter 50 (now 66) on 5 May of the following year, and Pope Hilary gave him Letter 11 in 462. He was still alive in 472. For Sidonius Apollinaris wrote to him at the beginning of his own episcopate, in Letter 7 of Book VI. The illustrious Cardinal Baronius proves that Sidonius assumed the see of Clermont in 472, under that year, no. 12 and following [Col. 1407D]. Fonteius is one of the bishops to whom the presbyter Lucidus is said to have presented his libellus [p. 1478], whether fictitious or genuine.

Idatius. The see of which he was bishop does not appear. He may perhaps be the bishop to whom Pope Hilary, together with others, wrote concerning the case of Mamertus, who had ordained a bishop for Dées.

Hilary—as Sirmond reads it, together with the manuscript codices of Troyes, Victorinus, and two of the Thuani, which agree; or Hilarus, as others read it in the printed editions. It is unknown which Church he administered. A certain Hilary, bishop of Carcassonne, is indeed placed around this time; but since the ancient notices of the Gallic provinces do not number that town among the cities [Col. 1408A], I do not think this testimony should be followed.

Victurus. Pope Hilary wrote to him in Letter 2 concerning the case of Mamertus of Vienne in 463, where he is listed first, and in Letter 4 concerning the case of Ingenuus and Auxanius in 464. At that time there was a Victurius, bishop of Le Mans in the Third Lyonnaise; but I am persuaded that he is not our man, both because of the slight difference in the name and because the bishops listed in this and the following letter do not seem to me to be sought outside the seven provinces.

Eugenius, bishop of Nîmes in Narbonensis Prima, according to the assertion of John Savaron’s manuscript. Apart from this, we know absolutely nothing about him.

Palladius. One of those to whom St. Leo writes in Letter 50; which city he governed is unknown to me.

Fraternus, bishop of Glandèves in the province of the Maritime Alps, as Savaron’s manuscript testifies.

Dynamius. Someone might conjecture, to some extent, that he was bishop of Angoulême in Aquitania Secunda [Col. 1408B], on the grounds that Gregory of Tours, in Book II of his *History*, chapter 13, praising—on the authority of the presbyter Paulinus—a bishop of this name distinguished for faith and religion, lists him among the bishops of Angoulême; *Gallia Christiana* places him after the year 400. If, however, another conjecture may be drawn from the Narbonese inscription which you have in the notes on Letter 2 (now 167), since it records that Bishop Dynamus contributed fifty solidi for the repair of the Church of Narbonne, it is permissible to suspect that he was a bishop in that same province of Narbonensis Prima, and perhaps of Béziers, since this is the only Church remaining in these subscriptions that does not recognize its own bishop. This is a conjecture which I would not have regarded as an assertion.

Julianus. He is listed in *Gallia Christiana* under this year as bishop of Cavaillon, or Cabellio, in the province of Vienne. Savaron’s manuscript has the same. Consider whether this may be Julian Pomerius, author of the work *On the Contemplative Life* [p. 1479], or another Julian to whom that work is dedicated.

[Col. 1408C] Armentarius. Around this time he is counted among the bishops of the Vellavi, or of Le Puy, in Aquitania Prima; David Blondel explicitly asserts this in his *Apology for Jerome’s Opinion*, section 3, p. 132. He thinks that this is the same Armentarius who was deposed by the Council of Riez because he had been ordained bishop at Embrun by only two bishops, contrary to the canons, in the year of our Lord 439. For this reason the fathers of that Gallican synod had determined that he should not thereafter be advanced to the episcopate. Nevertheless, they later made use of a dispensation in his case, so that he might be elected in a province other than the Maritime Alps. He is mentioned in St. Leo’s Letter 50 (now 66) to the Gauls in the year of the Lord 450.

Honoratus is called bishop of Toulon in Savaron’s manuscript. In the *Notitia* of the Gauls and the Seven Provinces, which is later than Leo, the city of Toulon does not appear. From this the manuscript of Savaron is rendered suspect both here and in its designation of the sees of other bishops.

[Col. 1408D] Eparchius, as Sirmond reads him in volume I of the *Gallican Councils*, and as the manuscript of Grimani reads him in the following letter; or Epartius, as he is commonly read; or Ebartius, as in the exemplar of the Thuani manuscript. He occurs nowhere else, nor have we been able to discover what locality’s bishopric he held.

Eustachius, Eustathius, or, as one Thuani manuscript has it, Eustochius. One might readily believe him to have been a bishop of Tours who flourished at that time, if this investigation were permitted to extend beyond the seven provinces. He does not appear in the Roman Thuanean manuscript, nor in Isidore.

Maximinus. This is the reading of the Thuaneus manuscript. Elsewhere it is Maximus, who would be the fourth person of this name mentioned in the inscription of the letter.

Ynantius. He seems to me to have been a bishop in the province of Vienne [Col. 1409A], because St. Leo numbers him among those to whom he writes in Letter 36 (now 40) concerning the election and consecration of Ravennius as bishop of Arles; otherwise he could not have contributed his vote to it.

2. The storm. Idatius, in his *Chronicle* under the twenty-eighth year of the Emperor Valentinian—that is, the year of Christ our Lord 452—testifies that Euphronius, bishop of Autun, sent a letter to Count Agrippinus concerning the signs that appeared in the regions of Gaul [1480]. Among these signs one may reasonably include this one, concerning which the Gallican bishops write: the violent disturbance of the winds.

3. All within Gaul, etc. Although we do not deny that there was considerable communication between the seven provinces of Gaul and the other Gallican provinces—namely, the Lyonnaises, the Belgicae, the Germanias, and so on—as is clear from the journeys of St. Hilary of Arles and St. Germanus of Auxerre, I am nevertheless almost certain [Note: [Col. 1409D] This does not seem so certain as Quesnel thinks. Since St. Leo had been extremely eager to move Theodosius by means of this full synod of Gaul, in which he might show that Letter 28 to Flavian had been received by the subscriptions of the bishops of all the Churches of Gaul, it is quite credible that bishops were summoned from all the provinces of Gaul, and that others came from the neighboring provinces of Lyon and elsewhere.] that the Gauls of whom the Gallican bishops speak here are none other than the seven provinces. I am also nearly certain that the synod which wrote this letter to St. Leo, and to which St. Leo sent the following reply (now 102), was composed only of bishops from those provinces [Col. 1409B].

4. Your apostolate. That this form of address was indiscriminately applied to bishops is known from six hundred testimonies [Note: [Col. 1409D] Although the titles “apostolate” and “pope” are recorded as having once been applied also to other bishops, care must nevertheless be taken lest anyone infer from this the equality of other bishops with the Roman pontiff. For, apart from the fact that most other bishops do not occupy sees founded by the apostles themselves, no other bishop of an apostolic Church is properly the successor of St. Peter except the Roman bishop alone; consequently, the primacy and the rights of primacy of St. Peter passed to the Roman bishop alone.] We shall mention only one example from Sidonius Apollinaris, who, writing both in Gaul and at approximately the same period, addressed Fonteius in almost the same way—Fonteius, I mean, the bishop of Vaison, who subscribed this letter. See Sidonius, Letter 7 of Book VI and Letter 4 of Book VII.

We say the same concerning the word “pope.” Indeed, all bishops are successors of the apostles; all occupy the apostles’ chairs; and just as St. Leo, in Letter 49 (now 61), chapter 2, testifies that he presides over the Church under the name of Peter, so the other prelates of the Church must be considered to preside under the name of the apostles. They could therefore be called apostolic and honored with the title of apostolate without any accusation of envy, although present usage—which possesses the right and norm of speech—wishes the term to be reserved for the Roman pontiff.

See the letter of Clovis, king of the Franks, to the bishops of his kingdom, whom he greets as follows: “To the holy lords, bishops most worthy of the apostolic see, Clovis the king”; and at the end: “Pray for me, holy lords and popes most worthy of the apostolic see.”

1481 TO LETTER CII. QUESNEL’S LXXVII. To the Gallican Bishops.

1. Inspired. All the manuscript codices that I have seen read *inspirare*, as Sirmond also retains it, although it yields no more than an obscure sense. The Grimani codex indeed has *inspirare*; but since *divinitus*—“by divine agency”—is read immediately before it, it is clearer than daylight that *inspiratae*, “inspired,” should be read. Some printed codices also exhibit this reading.

2. With distinct and separate persons, etc.; thus the Grimani codex [Col. 1410A], instead of which the common printed edition has: “with distinct natures and persons, so that he himself was not,” etc.

3. Theophilus. One may wonder that St. Leo counts this man among the most esteemed prelates and considers him worthy to be proposed to Dioscorus as an example. That this should not be restricted merely to sincerity of faith is shown by the fact that the same Leo calls him “of holy memory” in Letter 94 (now 121) to the Emperor Marcian and in Letter 68 (now 88) to Paschasinus of Lilybaeum. His writings are also cited, with praise of his holiness, both in Letter 134 (now 165) to Leo Augustus and in the extracts from the Holy Fathers reread at the Council of Chalcedon.

Nor could St. Leo have been unaware of the impious methods, the dreadful calumnies, and the open violence by which Theophilus persecuted and finally overthrew John Chrysostom, the most holy teacher of the Church. Whoever wishes to inquire whether Theophilus repented before his death of so many crimes should consult Book IX, chapter 5, of the *Life of St. John Chrysostom*, recently written in French with extraordinary diligence, judgment, learning, and elegance [Col. 1410B] by the most learned Godefroy Hermant, doctor of the Sorbonne and canon of the Church of Beauvais.

[Note: [Col. 1409D] Others, considering Theophilus’s learning, distinguished deeds, and virtues, do not deny that he was carried away by excessive zeal, exceeded the limits of moderation, and acted with rash judgment against St. John Chrysostom; but they add that even St. Cyril, at the beginning of his pontificate, persisted for some time in the same opinion of Theophilus, which he regarded as entirely just. Just as these human prejudices did not seem sufficiently serious to St. Innocent I for him to break communion with Theophilus, so they did not prevent our Leo from calling Theophilus a most esteemed man and one of holy memory.]

I would not conclude from these formulas of speech concerning the holiness of bishops that they were necessarily holy, since we see the most depraved men adorned with the same titles even in ecumenical councils. This custom also prevailed in those times: whenever bishops had in no way deviated from the Catholic faith and had died in communion with the Church, they were restored to the sacred diptychs and called men of holy memory.

4. To our brothers in Spain. Here we see that St. Leo was first concerned about the Church of Gaul and then about the Church of Spain, because Spain generally received from the Gauls what was necessary or useful for the beginning, growth, and preservation of the faith. The Spaniard Idatius, in his *Chronicle* under Olympiad 307, has several remarks relevant to this subject and place: “From Gaul letters are brought,” etc., above in the notes on Letter 15, no. 9 [Col. 1410C].

By the same route, and through the ministry of the Gallican bishops, the celebrated letter of our Leo to Flavian was sent to the bishops of the Italian diocese, as we learn from the following letter (now 97) of Eusebius of Milan to St. Leo: “It reached us,” he says, “at your admonition, through the assistance of our holy brother and fellow bishop Ceretius.”

TO LETTER CIII. And the Text of the Sentence Pronounced against Dioscorus. QUESNEL’S LXXXII.

Text of the sentence. James Sirmond thought that this sentence should also be copied here from the Corbie and Pithou manuscripts, in which it was appended to this letter. In meaning it agrees almost entirely with the vote of St. Leo’s legates [Col. 1411A] [Note: [Col. 1410D] Quesnel argues in this annotation that the sentence of St. Leo’s legates against Dioscorus, pronounced by the authority of the pontiff at the Council of Chalcedon, was not properly a sentence but merely a vote which, although delivered after the synod’s mind had been sought, left the matter still wholly in the hands of the Fathers. We proved that it was a true sentence in annotation 6 (Col. 989, note b) on Letter 103. But when the Fathers were later asked by those same legates to add their own votes to the sentence, this was done not because Dioscorus had not been sufficiently deposed by the true sentence of the legates unless the synod’s sentence were added, but so that the unanimous judgment of all the synod’s Fathers in the same deposition might be inserted in the Acts, and Dioscorus might thus be known to have been deposed not only by the pontifical sentence but also by that of the entire synod.] found in Act 3 of Chalcedon.

It is especially worthy of observation that the legates of the Apostolic See were unwilling to cast even their own vote against Dioscorus before they had repeatedly explored the mind and judgment of the entire synod by questioning it. “Therefore,” they ask, “by what [penalty is] one who so despises [to be judged]? Let your holiness make it manifest with your own mouth.” The holy synod said: “With the indignation established by the holy canons against the disobedient.” And below Paschasinus said: “We wish to learn what pleases your holiness.” The holy synod said: “What has been established by the canons.”

Paschasinus then pressed the matter twice: “Does your religiousness command that we use ecclesiastical punishment against him? Do you consent?” [1483] The holy synod said: “We all consent.” And after much else: “We therefore ask your holiness, who occupy the place of the most holy Pope Leo, to pronounce against him and to deliver against him the sentence inserted in the canons.”

After Paschasinus had again asked, “What pleases your blessedness?” and Maximus of Antioch had further assured him of the consent of the entire synod [Col. 1411B], only then did the legate deliver this vote in the name of Leo, whose representatives they were. For they clearly showed that they themselves had left the whole matter undecided when, after delivering their sentence, they added: “It remains for the venerable synod, once assembled, to pronounce against the aforesaid Dioscorus the canonical sentence, as justice demands.”

That text of the sentence, I say, is nothing other than the vote delivered by the legates in Act 3 of Chalcedon, but corrupted—or even interpolated—by an unskilled translator. Nor was it necessary to extract it from manuscript codices, since it had long before been printed in the Crabbe and Nicoline editions of the Councils, at the end of the Acts of Chalcedon. The title is therefore misleading when it calls it a “sentence,” since it is merely the preliminary vote to a sentence; and in both those editions of the Councils it is called a letter.

TO LETTER CIV. QUESNEL’S LXXVIII. To Marcian Augustus.

[Col. 1411C]

1. Leo to Marcian Augustus. In most editions published after the Canisian edition of 1546 and 1547, this letter is prefaced by a title fabricated for pomp and display in the following form: “Leo, bishop of the Roman and universal Church,” etc. But this novel heading is absent from the editions of the Councils by James Merlin, published in 1524 and 1535; the Cologne editions of 1530, 1535, and 1538; the Surian edition of the works of St. Leo, by Sicard at Paris in 1568; Holstenius himself in the Roman collection dedicated to the Roman pontiff by the most eminent Cardinal Barberini; and several manuscript codices of Grimani, Thuaneus, Victorinus, the Troyes-Pithou manuscript, and others.

2. By your favor. Formerly *nostro beneficio*, “by our favor,” was read; but all the manuscript codices—Grimani, Troyes-Pithou, Cambridge, Victorinus, the four Thuani manuscripts—and the editions of Canisius, Merlin, Sicard, Nicolini, and Surius contradict this, as does Baronius under the year 452, no. 14, and in the third part of the *Council of Chalcedon* [Col. 1411D]. It is manifest that *vestro beneficio*, “by your favor,” should be read from the following letter to the Empress Pulcheria. Addressing her, Anatolius says: “Anatolius, giving little consideration to the extent to which the priesthood of the Church of Constantinople was obtained by your pious favor and with the assent of my support,” etc.

3. Which cannot make it an apostolic see. Sees, or apostolic Churches [Col. 1412A], are called apostolic in several senses.

First, the Roman See is called the Apostolic See *αντονομαστικῶς*—“by antonomasia,” or in a distinctive sense—because it was founded by the princes of the apostles and consecrated by the blood of both.

Second, the Alexandrian and Antiochene sees: the latter because, after the preaching of Saints Peter and Paul, the Christian name first arose there; the former because it was founded by St. Mark, Peter’s disciple.

Third, Churches that received the seeds of the faith from other apostles, or were administered by them, as the See of Jerusalem is called apostolic by Theodoret in Book IV, chapter 21.

Fourth, for Tertullian that Church is apostolic which unfolds the order of its bishops through successive generations running continuously from the beginning, so that its first bishop had as founder and predecessor one of the apostles or apostolic men who had persevered with the apostles. In this manner the apostolic Churches present their registers of descent: thus the Church of Smyrna reports that Polycarp was appointed by John (Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 32).

Fifth, in chapter 20 of the same work, those Churches are also reckoned apostolic which are offspring of apostolic Churches and which, having received from Churches founded by the apostles the transmission of faith and the seeds of doctrine, became Churches [Col. 1412B].

Sixth, some think that Augustine, in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8, counts as apostolic those Churches that were worthy to receive apostolic letters, such as Thessalonica, Ephesus, Colossae, and others. But although they are truly apostolic in the sense of Tertullian just explained, Augustine does not call them apostolic in that passage; rather, he sets them against those Churches as distinct.

From the opening of this letter that famous impostor fashioned the opening of the fictitious letter of Pope Eleutherius to the bishops of Gaul.

TO LETTER CV. QUESNEL’S LXXIX. To the Empress Pulcheria.

[Col. 1412C] Only two codices, namely the Grimani and Victorine, were available for rereading this letter and Letters 84 and 86 (now 111 and 113). These letters plainly required a physician’s hand in many places, as will be evident to anyone wishing to compare them.

1. But he who [is] by the law of reasonable charity, and the order of conduct and of duties will be maintained [the text is corrupt]. The passage almost sticks fast, for neither the printed codices nor the manuscripts seem sufficiently corrected to me. The printed editions had: “But the unanimity which is reasonable by the law of charity, of conduct and of duties, will be maintained.” The Victorine codex has almost the same reading, although its final word, *unanimitas*, “unanimity,” is missing. In the Grimani we read: “But by the equal law of reasonable charity the order of conduct and of duties will be maintained.”

Although we chiefly constructed Leo’s text from this reading, with a few alterations, we nevertheless conjecture that another form may be pieced together from all these witnesses: “But the unanimity which is reasonable by the law of charity, and the order of conduct and of duties, will be maintained.”

2. We annul. He uses this same verb in the following letter (now 106), as well as in Letter 73 (now 90), chapter 1, and Letter 99 (now 126). The word does not always have the same meaning. Usually it is equivalent to “to invalidate”; sometimes *cassari* means “to be invalid and devoid of all authority”; at other times *cassare* means “to declare invalid” and “to pronounce void”; and [Note: [Col. 1412D] Two kinds of acts are customarily annulled. Some are performed with legitimate authority and according to legitimate procedure; they are ratified and valid. If a higher power judges that such acts must be annulled, *annul* in this case means “to invalidate.” Others are performed either with illegitimate authority, without legitimate procedure, or with gross iniquity and injustice; and because they possess no force in themselves, whenever a competent authority annuls them, it declares them void. The acts of the Ephesian Robber Council belonged to this second category.

[Col. 1413C] Since the Council of Chalcedon, which established the celebrated canon concerning the See of Constantinople, was an ecumenical council no less than the Council of Nicaea, it could certainly derogate from the Nicene canons in a matter of pure discipline, which is subject to change. Thus that canon must be referred to the first category, and to annul it would be the same as to invalidate it.

Since the force and authority of a general council require the assent of the Roman pontiff, decrees lacking that assent remain suspended until they obtain the assent of the supreme head. Much less should they be regarded as the enactments of a general synod if they have encountered the contradiction and dissent of the Roman pontiff or his legates.

This is recognized as still more true if the decree is contrary to canons enacted by a general council with the assent of the Roman pontiff and received with the supreme veneration of the whole world. Those who in the Council of Chalcedon derogated from the Nicene canon were for the most part from Eastern Churches that did not belong to the West. Hence they represented only the Eastern Church, not the Western Church as well, although representation of both is necessary for a general council.

Therefore the pontifical confirmation of the aforesaid Chalcedonian canon was rightly recognized as necessary to its force. Thus Anatolius of Constantinople says in Letter 101, chapter 5: “The holy synod has also referred such a decree to your holiness, and we do so that we may obtain approval and confirmation from you.” And again in Letter 132, chapter 2: “Since the entire force and confirmation of the proceedings has likewise been reserved to the authority of your blessedness.”

Therefore, just as the authority of the supreme pontiff was necessary for the confirmation of the canon that derogated from the Nicene canons, so, in the absence of that authority, the canon enacted by the Chalcedonians against the Nicene canons possessed no force of a general synod in itself. Hence St. Leo regarded it as invalid, and by annulling it declared it void.

Yet since the canon had acquired some incipient force from the authority of the Fathers of Chalcedon, and apostolic authority had to be added to complete that force, St. Leo can be said, by the word “we annul,” to have rendered whatever force it possessed invalid. From these points we press Quesnel as follows.

Does he think that when the Council of Chalcedon enacted the aforesaid canon it was a general council and possessed the force of a general council, even though the pontifical legates had contradicted that canon and the pontiff’s confirmation had not been added? For on this hypothesis, since it is certain that a general council can introduce a new decree in matters of discipline and derogate from the decree of an earlier general synod—the later general councils being no less capable than the earlier ones—it must likewise be certain that, if the Council of Chalcedon remained a general council and possessed the force of a general synod despite the contradiction of the legates and the absence of the pontiff’s approval, it could validly enact a canon concerning the prerogatives of the See of Constantinople, even though it contradicted the Nicene statutes.

But then, when St. Leo annulled that canon, he would have annulled a valid canon and, exercising his authority over a general council, would have rendered that canon void.

If this opinion is not acceptable, only one thing remains to be said: although the Council of Chalcedon was general because not only Eastern bishops but also Western legates attended it—especially the legates of the Roman pontiff, who is the head not only of the West but of the entire Church—it nevertheless did not possess the force of a general synod in its decrees unless the Western bishops, and especially the Roman pontiff himself or his legates, joined their votes to those of the Eastern bishops.

On this well-known view, the Chalcedonian canon contrary especially to the Nicene decrees, which the legates contradicted, did not possess the force of a general council. Consequently, when Leo annulled it, he must be said to have declared it invalid and null in itself.]

this seems to me to be St. Leo’s meaning here. Indeed, neither the acts of the Ephesian Robber Council nor the final canon of Chalcedon needed to be annulled and invalidated, since no reason allowed the former to be called a council, as Leo himself says, and since the concessions of the Chalcedonian Fathers in favor of Anatolius had to be regarded as null precisely because they had been made contrary to the inviolable decrees of the Nicene Fathers:

“Whether ecclesiastical judgments are conducted by fewer or by more persons, whatever differs from their constitution is entirely devoid of authority.” He expresses the same thing in these words in the same letter: “If anything is presumed anywhere contrary to what they established, it is annulled without hesitation.”

For Leo, therefore, “to be entirely devoid of authority” and “to be annulled without hesitation” mean the same thing; that is, as follows shortly afterward concerning the record of the Constantinopolitan synod, it was “fallen from the beginning of its existence and long since collapsed.”

But what is entirely devoid of authority, what is annulled immediately and without hesitation as soon as it is presumed, what is fallen from the beginning and long since collapsed, does not need to be made void and invalid by a sentence or by any authority; it needs only to be declared and announced as void and invalid. This is what St. Leo does here as guardian and executor of the canons, together with the emperor’s faithful piety. The latter’s authority is rightly joined to the pontifical authority, because the matter concerned the execution and defense of the ancient canons and the rejection of the rashness of novel decrees. The case would be different if acts that had previously possessed some force had needed to be invalidated.

Lest what we have said concerning the meaning of this word seem to have arisen merely from our own ingenuity, the reader should be informed that it is used in the same sense in the decretal attributed to Pope Celestine III, chapter *Cum dilectus*, title *De Electione et electi Potestate*: “Annul them”—that is, says the gloss, “pronounce them to have no force”; and in Innocent III’s decretal, chapter *Accedens*, 1, title *Ut lite non contestata*: “We annulled”—that is, says the glossator, “we declared them void.”

For when a sentence is null, it ought not to be annulled; rather, it ought to be declared void and invalid, because what is nothing cannot be annulled, and everything must be restored to its former state by such a sentence. Our Leo likewise demanded this from the emperor above, when he was dealing with the false synod of Ephesus; and he shows it in the following words of this letter, which establish that he could in no way approve Canon 28 for two reasons.

First, in all ecclesiastical cases he had to obey the laws to which that canon was contrary; consequently, before any sentence concerning it, the canon was already void and invalid.

Second, the authority of the Nicene canons was so great that whatever was decreed against them by even a much larger number of persons was to be held in no regard.

TO LETTER CVI. QUESNEL’S LXXX. To Anatolius, Bishop of Constantinople.

[Col. 1414B]

1. His beginnings were not free from blame. I see that most people have not sufficiently weighed Leo’s words, although he himself chose them with the greatest care. He does not say that Anatolius’s ordination was invalid or defective, or that it had been usurped contrary to the canons, as he soon asserts concerning the ordination of Maximus. He says only that “his beginnings were not free from blame”; and, as he says to Pulcheria in Letter 55 (now 70), that hardship preceded his ordination; as he says to Emperor Marcian in Letter 78 (now 104), that his beginnings had been unstable; and in Letter 84, that his ordination was suspect, because his faith could be called into question, since he had been ordained by defenders of Eutyches. It was not without reason that Leo had said above that Anatolius’s ordainers seemed to have consecrated one like themselves, contrary to the decrees of the holy canons [1488].

In other respects, Anatolius’s situation was not the same as that of Maximus and the others who had been placed over bishops improperly deposed by the Ephesian Robber Council. Anatolius was not consecrated while Flavian was alive; otherwise St. Leo would never have counted him among the bishops, as he wrote repeatedly. Rather, he was consecrated after Flavian’s death, as is also clear from Liberatus’s *Breviary*, chapter 12. Therefore, once the integrity of his faith became evident—an integrity which, unlike the fallen bishops, he had violated by no subscription—there was nothing to prevent his ordination from being regarded as valid.

It was therefore not a dispensation that had to be used in his case, but an inquiry alone, by which the sincerity of his faith concerning the Incarnation might be proved. St. Leo never demanded anything else from him except such testimony. Before it was given, Leo was unwilling to support Anatolius’s ordination by letters of communion, lest he should seem to communicate with a heretical man. He was not denying affection, but awaiting the manifestation of Catholic truth [lacuna].

“I remove,” he says shortly afterward, “the occasion of the entire difficulty, and I demand nothing that might seem arduous or doubtful; rather, I invite him to what no Catholic would reject.” When Anatolius had done what Leo invited him to do, and had cleared himself of participation with all who had deviated, the holy pope most gladly granted him his communion and acknowledged that he had been advanced not by human judgment but by God’s kindness.
