Thus his case did not require the subsequent reconsideration of a council,

[Note: [Col. 1415D] Add: “or the judgment or dispensation of the pontiff.” How powerful Leo’s judgment was in the restoration of Theodore, who had incurred suspicion of Nestorianism, we have shown in the observations on Quesnel’s Dissertation 10. The same pontiff’s dispensation in the case of Maximus of Antioch—that his case did not need the reconsideration and judgment of a council—is clear from the Acts of Chalcedon themselves.]

as the cases of the other bishops did.

2. Contrary to the canonical rule. Since it is clear that this canonical rule is distinguished in the context of St. Leo from the Nicene canons, scarcely any canon appears to which the holy pontiff could have been referring. For among the canons of the other Greek councils, by which nearly the entire ecclesiastical law of that age was governed, indeed not even among the apostolic, Sardican, or African canons, is there any canon that established anything concerning the ordainers of metropolitans, primates, or provincial bishops.

Nevertheless, this had always been observed, first by an ancient custom that possessed the force of a canonical rule and thereafter by the Nicene decrees: provinces were not to be confused, and metropolitans were to receive the grace of consecration from their fellow provincials.

Such is the ancient custom which the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea confirm, and which the Sardican canon 5 presupposes when it establishes the circumstances in which bishops may lawfully ordain bishops in another province. The statements made both by St. Leo and by others concerning a canonical or ecclesiastical rule must be understood as referring to this custom, although it is not found among the canons received in that age.

### 3. “Having dealt with the matter of its cause …”

Pelagius I, in his letter to Elias of Aquileia and the other bishops of Istria—which Paul Warnefridus says was composed by Gregory the Great when he was still a deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book III, chapter 20—quotes this passage as follows: “Having dealt with the definition of its cause, which required attention,” alluding to the *tractoriae* letters, which were sent to summon bishops to a council. The Grimanian manuscript reads: “Having dealt with the definition of the cause requiring attention.”

### [Col. 1415D] 4. A document composed sixty years earlier

It is certain, both from other evidence and from the letter of the emperor Marcian to Saint Leo concerning this same matter, that these words must be understood of the First Council of Constantinople:

“at which the bishops who had assembled decreed that the bishop of the city of Constantinople ought to possess the primatial honor after the bishop of Rome, because it is New Rome.”

Concerning the canons of that council and their reception by the Roman Church, consult the most illustrious Petrus de Marca, in his dissertation *On the Institution of the Patriarchate of Constantinople*, as well as book III, chapter 3, of *The Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, and Stephanus Baluzius, who continued that work in book V, chapter 21.

It is indeed remarkable and worthy of notice that Saint Leo asserts that no such document of the bishops of the Constantinopolitan council had ever been transmitted to the knowledge of the apostolic see by Anatolius’s predecessors, although it was always counted among the principal and ecumenical councils, even by the Roman pontiffs: by Gelasius in the synodal decree concerning apocryphal books, by Gregory I in book I, letter 24, and by others.

[Note: [Col. 1416D] We shall show more fully in volume III that the First Council of Constantinople was not always regarded by the Roman pontiffs as ecumenical, and that it was even unknown to them for a considerable time; consequently, it was not truly ecumenical so long as it had not been acknowledged and received by the Roman Church. There we shall subject Quesnell’s note to a more exact examination.]

Nevertheless, it must also be acknowledged that both of them—Gelasius, namely, in his letter to the Dardani, and Gregory, in book VI, letter 31—testify that its canons had not come to the knowledge of the Roman Church, or had not been received by it.

To reconcile these statements with one another, it is necessary to have recourse to that distinction which does not please certain learned men, and to say that the exposition of faith composed at that council was sent to the Roman see and received by it; but that the canons, which the Fathers of the same synod issued for the ordering and privileges of the Churches, were neither sent by the Eastern bishops nor received by the Westerners, since they appear to have been unknown to the Roman see until the time of Saint Leo.

This distinction is considerably clarified by the letter which the Fathers of the Constantinopolitan council, having assembled again in that city somewhat later, wrote to Pope Damasus, Ambrose of Milan, and the other leaders of the Roman council. For that letter presupposes that the confession of faith promulgated at that ecumenical council had been sent to the Western bishops. When the Easterners were explaining their faith to them, so that they might be instructed in it with fuller knowledge, they refer them to the written statement issued by the Council of Constantinople:

“Concerning these matters,” they say, “you will be able to acquire fuller knowledge in your minds if you are willing to read both the written statement concerning the definition of the faith issued when the council was convened at Antioch, and also the one composed in the previous year by the general council. In these we both explained our faith more fully and formally proclaimed in writing an anathema against the heresies recently devised.”

Such words would have been extremely foolish if they had not either been sending the aforesaid written statement to the Westerners at that time or remembered that it had already been sent long before.

Concerning the other matters that pertained to the rights and privileges of the see of Constantinople, however, they say not a word. Either they did not dare to send such canons, knowing that they would be most unwelcome to the Westerners, or they were convinced that when the Eastern bishops decreed something concerning the ordering of the Eastern Churches, the consent of the Westerners was in no way necessary. It was enough, moreover, that they took care to bring to the Westerners’ knowledge what they had decreed concerning the confession of faith against the heretics.

For since the matter of faith is common not only to all bishops but also to the Catholic laity, and is the proper subject of an ecumenical council, it is necessary that everything relating to it should also become known to everyone, and especially to the head of all the bishops, whose particular duty it is, from the watchtower of the apostolic see, to oversee the custody and purity of the faith.

Although Saint Leo objects that those statutes had never been sent to the apostolic see, he does not press this argument very forcefully. He even conceals the fact that he had any definite knowledge of that ecumenical council, lest he incur hatred on that account from the emperor and from the Eastern Churches, which were exceedingly zealous for the greatness of Constantinople.

He draws the principal force of his argument, instead, both from the permanence and excellence of the Nicene canons, which were being violated by novel constitutions, and from the fact that, despite the decrees of the Constantinopolitan council, the bishop of that city had always remained in his proper rank. It would therefore have been absurd to produce the agreement of certain bishops when so many years had denied it any effect, and to provide late and useless supports, sixty years afterward, for a document that had been unstable from its beginning and long since collapsed, by eliciting from the brethren at the Council of Chalcedon an appearance of consent.

In addition, we must warn the reader here that the most reliable manuscript copies of this letter which have come to our attention present a corrupt reading in this passage, so that one can only suspect that it was once read differently from the way it is now read.

For the Grimanian manuscript, instead of “and never transmitted by Anatolius’s predecessors,” has: “Since that which was transmitted by Anatolius’s predecessors …”

One Thuanus manuscript represents the whole passage thus: “Since, when you had heard from your predecessors that it had long ago been transmitted to the apostolic see …”

Two other Thuanus manuscripts vary the final words as follows: “The information transmitted to the apostolic see.”

We have wished to report these readings, although they will of themselves be useful to no one, so that learned men may be made more attentive if copies of this letter should happen to come into their hands, and may apply a physician’s hand to this passage of the greatest importance.

### 5. The rights of provincial primates

This should be read *provincialium primatuum*, in accordance with the manuscript copies, not *primatum*, as the celebrated Morinus reads it in book I, *Ecclesiastical Exercises*, exercise 8. We must also depart from his interpretation, since he understands these words of the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch. They are more properly spoken of the metropolitans of the dioceses of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace, whose ordination the canon of Chalcedon assigned to the bishop of Constantinople, and concerning which there was a dispute.

Saint Leo was attacking two distinct points in that canon. The first concerned those primary sees, Alexandria and Antioch, which the bishop of Constantinople, usurping the second place, was attempting to deprive of the second and third rank; the following words concern these sees.

The second concerned the metropolitans of the dioceses mentioned above, whose privileges Anatolius was likewise invading when he claimed their ordination for himself. By the authority of the ancient canons, that power had always rested with the synod of each individual province.

For this had always been a fixed and immovable rule: that the bishops of one province should never attempt anything in another province, and that other metropolitans should not encroach upon the rights of any metropolitan. Yet this was what the bishop of Constantinople was doing. By definite stages he had paved himself a road toward monarchy over the Eastern Church.

First, he arranged that only privileges of honor should be decreed to him—namely, the second place after the Roman pontiff—by the canon of Constantinople.

Second, he intruded himself into the ordinations of various dioceses through the voluntary concession of the metropolitans, obtained or extorted by various devices. The most illustrious de Marca reports several examples of this in his extremely careful dissertation *On the Institution of the Patriarchate of Constantinople*, which should be consulted.

Third, he caused what had already been introduced by usage itself to be confirmed by the canon of Chalcedon and also by imperial edicts.

Fourth, when he saw that he had become equal to the bishops of the sees of Alexandria and Antioch through the administration of their extensive dioceses, and superior to them through the second place that he had acquired, he then conceived the plan of usurping the ordination of both primates. When the opportunity presented itself after the Ephesian conciliabulum, in the ordination of Maximus of Antioch, he eagerly seized it, thereby opening the way for such schemes and for constitutions that were later to be devised.

Fifth, the step following the fourth would easily have led to the final stage. For, as that same prelate has most aptly observed in book I, chapter 7, of *The Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, it was a principal feature of the ancient discipline that bishops should present themselves at the synod of the person by whose decision they had been ordained. Hence bishops who depended upon their primates are said indiscriminately and commonly to belong to someone’s council or to his consecration.

If the bishop of Constantinople had ordained the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, he would likewise have summoned them to Constantinople whenever he wished, as belonging to his council, and would have subjected them to himself in every respect.

Sixth, after this he would have climbed the final step of primacy without difficulty. For, once he had subjected Alexandria and Antioch to his ordination, he would eventually have drawn all the other metropolitans subject to those two primates under his own dominion. He would have done in the Eastern regions what we see the Roman pontiff doing in the West: reserving to his authority the institution both of all the metropolitans and of the bishops of the second order subject to them. Leaving the metropolitans only the shadow of their metropolitan title, he would alone have invaded all the duties of that dignity and alone exercised all its rights.

Saint Leo seems to have foreseen this when he wrote the following words above, in chapter 2:

“So that, with those sees”—Alexandria and Antioch—“subject to your authority, all the metropolitan bishops may be deprived of their proper honor.”

For it is scarcely possible to understand otherwise how the subjection of those two sees could result in the overthrow of all the metropolitans, unless the words are understood, in the manner we have explained, of the metropolitans both of the Egyptian and Eastern dioceses and of the Pontic, Asian, and Thracian dioceses.

All these attempts were to be feared unless Saint Leo had firmly resisted the undertaking. At least he achieved this much: that the ambition of that unrestrained bishop did not advance any farther.

[Note: [Col. 1417C] It is remarkable that the effort of the bishop of Constantinople to subject the metropolitans of the three dioceses of Thrace, Asia, and Pontus to his ordination is here compared with the right of the Roman pontiff to reserve to himself the institution of the bishops of the West, as though the position of the two were equal in this matter, and as though the bishop of Constantinople had not extended himself over the whole East in the same way that the Roman see extended that reservation over the whole West.

Who could fail to perceive the broad difference here? The Roman bishop not only occupies a see of apostolic origin, and one which by divine right possesses primacy of jurisdiction over the whole Church; he also holds the mother-see of all the Churches and bishoprics of the West, which received their bishops from her together with the Christian religion, as Innocent I most clearly testifies in the preface to his letter to Decentius, section 2.

What wonder, then, if all the Western Churches and bishoprics have always revered this see, the mother of them all, above all others, and if the institution of bishops could be reserved to the Roman bishops?

Let the fair-minded reader judge whether the case of the see of Constantinople with respect to the Churches of the East was comparable, since it was neither apostolic nor the root and mother of the other Churches, but a simple bishopric like many others. By the protection of the imperial see alone, it sought to be preferred to the apostolic Churches of the East and to subject the ordination of the metropolitans of the three dioceses to itself.

To make the Roman right shine forth more and more, two further points should be added. The illustrious pontiff Saint Innocent, in letter 24 to Alexander of Antioch, chapter 1, not only testifies that the ordinations of the metropolitans of his patriarchate had already been claimed for him by custom; he also recognizes his right in the ordination of the bishops themselves, or at least requires his assent in the case of those who were more distant.

For he says:

“Therefore, dearest brother, we judge that, just as you ordain the metropolitans by your singular authority, so you should permit the others also to be made bishops not without your permission and knowledge. In their case you will properly observe this procedure: that you should direct by letters that those who are far away be ordained by the men who now ordain them solely according to their own judgment; but the neighboring bishops, if you think fit, you should arrange to come to the laying on of hands of your grace. For those over whom the greatest care is expected of you ought especially to deserve your judgment.”

If, in those ancient times, Innocent I granted the bishop of Antioch so much authority over the ordinations of the bishops of his patriarchate, who could call the right of the Roman pontiff to reserve the ordinations or institutions of the bishops of the whole West incompetent or usurped?

Saint Leo claimed a similar right in the ordinations of the bishops of all Illyricum, which was part of the Western diocese, for the bishop of Thessalonica as vicar of the apostolic see, as is clear from letters 5 and 6.

If the pontiff possessed this right over the most remote Churches of the West, so that it could be delegated to the bishop of Thessalonica, are we not compelled to acknowledge that he possessed the same right over the other, nearer Churches of the West as well?]

### 6. “If by your observance …”

Here we have followed the common edition and most of the older copies, together with some manuscript codices. The Grimanian and Victorine manuscripts, however, along with certain editions, such as the Surian edition and the Royal edition of the Councils, read:

“If by your observance and defense of the paternal canon many priests may have an example of probity.”

## On Letter 107, Letter 81 in Quesnell’s edition. To Julianus, bishop of Cos

We now present a brief but vigorous letter, full of apostolic force. It had long ago been published from the manuscript of Cardinal Sirletus, but in a corrupt form; it is now exhibited in a much more accurate state from Cardinal Grimani’s codex.

The first line, which the earlier manuscript lacked, had been supplied by the editor responsible for the publication as follows: “Your affection is not unaware.” We restore it thus: “Since your affection has proved by frequent trials …”

## 1494. On Letter 108, Letter 83 in Quesnell’s edition. To Theodore, bishop of Fréjus

[Col. 1419C]

### 1.

From letter 1 of Pope Pelagius II to Elias and the other bishops of Istria—which Gregory the Great calls a book in book II, letter 36, and which Paul the Deacon testifies was written in Gregory’s style, book III of *The History of the Lombards*—it appears that this letter had become known to the bishops of that province, and that they had produced from it Saint Leo’s testimony in support of their contention that the dead ought in no way to be condemned by human beings.

From Pelagius himself, however, it may be suspected that neither he nor Gregory the Great had ever seen the same letter. He says:

“In the testimonies which you have quoted from the letters of Leo, our predecessor, you prefaced them by saying: ‘It is the teaching of your venerable see, through blessed Leo and his successors, and therefore we have presumed to recall a few passages: The dead ought in no way to be condemned by human beings.’ Yet you added none of his testimonies by which you might establish this opinion.

“For the passages you have appended prohibit a reconsideration of the faith, but do not contradict the condemnation of dead unbelievers. Nor do we remember that blessed Leo, our predecessor, said this anywhere.”

Pope Vigilius, however, who preceded Pelagius by several years, remembers this letter and reports part of it in his *Constitutum*, almost near the end:

“For,” he says, “the most blessed Pope Leo says the following to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus, after other matters:

‘It is not necessary for us to examine [another reading: *discutere*, “discuss”] the merits and actions of those who have departed in this condition, since the Lord our God, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved to his justice the matter of one who was unable to fulfill the priestly mystery’”—or, in another reading, “ministry.”

From these words and from the whole of Vigilius’s *Constitutum*, the bishops of Istria seem to have said what we reported above. They judged that Vigilius’s authority ought to be set aside on this account, since, by assenting to the Fifth Synod, Vigilius himself had deprived his earlier *Constitutum* of all authority.

It should be observed, however, that Theodore had recourse to transalpine deliberations without consulting his metropolitan. For this reason Leo himself censured Theodore at the beginning of his rescript, because he had neglected the metropolitan’s advice.

“Your concern,” he says, “ought to have followed this procedure: first, you should have discussed with the metropolitan what seemed to require investigation,” and so forth.

[Col. 1420B]

Why Theodore refrained from consulting his metropolitan may perhaps be explained as follows. At that time a serious controversy had arisen between Theodore and Faustus, the abbot of Lérins, together with all the monks of that island. The hostility had become so intense that it generated a very grave scandal throughout the Gallican Churches, as is attested in the Acts of the Third Council of Arles, in the case of the island of Lérins, in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*, and in the latest edition of the general councils.

Since this affair had divided the bishops of those regions into opposing parties—some who had been taken from Lérins standing with Faustus, and others who wished to preserve intact the rights of episcopal authority fighting on Theodore’s behalf—it is quite probable that the metropolitan of Second Narbonensis belonged to those who favored Faustus of Lérins, and that communication between him and Theodore had therefore been interrupted at that time.

If anyone does not approve this conjecture, let him accept another.

The bishop of Arles claimed a right, as we noted in connection with letter 10, over the province of Second Narbonensis. A serious dispute had formerly arisen between Leo and Hilary concerning this matter, and Hilary had been repulsed from it by Leo’s decree.

But that decree, although also supported by an imperial rescript, had not been received by the Gauls, who retained their ancient custom and were extremely zealous for the privilege of the see of Arles.

The metropolitans of Aix in Second Narbonensis and of Embrun in the Maritime Alps also appear voluntarily to have surrendered whatever right they possessed; and the latter in particular remained for a long time afterward subject in many matters to the bishop of Arles.

Thus, if Theodore had wished to approach the metropolitan for consultation, he would already have offended the Gallican bishops—and especially the bishop of Arles—by consulting the bishop of Aquae. If, on the other hand, he had consulted the bishop of Arles as metropolitan, he would have offended Leo, by whose decree he had been exempted from that bishop’s ordination.

Moreover, Ravennius, the disciple of Honoratus, successor of Hilary, and a friend of Faustus for the same reason, could not fail to be favorably disposed toward the monks of the island of Lérins, and was therefore suspect to Theodore of Fréjus.

[Note: [Col. 1419D] We have shown in the observations on Quesnell’s dissertation 5, part III, chapter 2, section 3 and following, that it is false that the Gauls did not receive Leo’s decree, or letter 10, issued in the case of Hilary.

Moreover, everything that Quesnell assembles in the preceding and following passages in order to resolve the question why Theodore refrained from consulting his metropolitan is wholly arbitrary.

Certainly, his claim that Theodore did not consult the metropolitan of Arles lest he offend Leo, whose decree had exempted him from that bishop’s ordination, is utterly empty. If Theodore did not fear offending Leo when he wrote to him concerning the right of the see of Arles, to which he professed adherence, as he himself stated in letter 65 to that same pontiff (see note 16 [Col. 881, n. g] on that letter), he had far less reason to fear him if he consulted the metropolitan from whose authority Leo had exempted him—not the bishop of Fréjus, but the four other Churches whom Leo subjected to the see of Vienne in letter 66.]

Certainly, as far as I can judge from an examination of Leo’s letter, his great concern for the rights of primates and metropolitans readily leads me to believe that he then had in mind the controversy which had arisen on the occasion of Hilary concerning the boundaries of the see of Arles. For this reason Theodore was censured for neglecting the metropolitan, since the bishop of Aquae, who by Leo’s decree ought to have enjoyed that dignity, did not appear to be regarded by Theodore as metropolitan.

This little letter is overflowing with so many constitutions of such great importance and displays so many observations concerning the ancient discipline that there would be much to annotate here, were it not that everything has already been observed, discussed, and illustrated by the monuments of the whole of antiquity in the immensely learned commentary of John Morinus on the administration of penance.

Nevertheless, we shall not hesitate to gather ears of grain after the harvest, adding certain points in confirmation of his observations and noting some matters which, hastening toward other subjects, he omitted.

It should first of all be observed that the opening words of the letter repeatedly insist upon the authority of the metropolitan bishops, whom it calls primates, and decree that they must be approached in all ecclesiastical matters whenever necessary. Thus nothing should be brought before the knowledge or tribunal of the holy see without the primates—not even for the purpose of consultation. On this subject, see letter 16 to the Sicilian bishops and the notes we added to it, drawing both on Innocent I and on canon 5 of the Council of Tarragona.

### 2.

By these words—“I shall not be silent about what the ecclesiastical rule teaches concerning the condition of penitents”—it is clear that Leo did not wish to introduce anything new into the practice and observance of penitential discipline, but that he derived everything from the rules of the canons or from the usage of his Church.

I believe that these two things are signified by the ecclesiastical rule that he mentions, since there are certain matters in this letter which at that time seem to have been in use scarcely anywhere except in the Roman Church.

It is also clear that everything discussed throughout the letter concerns those who were performing public penance. Morinus proves this from the following words in book V, chapter 10, of the work cited. In book X, chapter 4 and following, he examines from the same letter the various classes and conditions of penitents, where he discusses at length the action of penance and the reconciliation to be granted immediately to those who are dying, as well as those who depart this life before reconciliation.

### 3.

What Saint Leo adds at the end of this letter concerning those who sinned against God by departing from the faith does not seem sufficiently explained.

For when he determines that those who request penance at the end of life, and who, overcome by the illness itself, are unable even by a gesture to indicate in the presence of a priest what they had requested shortly before, ought nevertheless to receive both the benefit of penance and that of reconciliation, with the testimony of the faithful standing by supplying the sick person’s voice and gesture, he adds these words:

“Nevertheless, the rule of the paternal canons must be observed concerning those persons who have sinned against God by departing from the faith.”

What this rule may be, which he requires to be observed with respect to such persons, may reasonably be questioned.

First, it seems clear that the matter concerns those who, having been placed in the final danger of life, were granted the benefit of penance and reconciliation and afterward recovered—namely, what was to be observed with respect to them after they had returned to their former health.

For concerning those who, overwhelmed by illness, requested penance and reconciliation either by voice or by gestures, it is established by canon 13 of Nicaea that, generally, to anyone placed at the point of death and asking that the grace of communion be granted, the bishop ought reasonably to give it from the offering.

Therefore even apostates are not excluded from this gift of penance and reconciliation.

Will you say that something special was decreed concerning those who had abandoned the faith: either that they should again receive penance, or that they should be compelled to complete the penance imposed upon them when illness threatened?

But penance imposed upon the dying was never imposed upon them a second time after they had recovered their health. Nor was it peculiar to apostates that, once they had recovered, they should undergo the period of public penance imposed upon them.

Indeed, it was always common to everyone that those who were reconciled in that condition, although their arduous penance had been remitted out of reverence for communion, were obliged to complete what remained.

Certainly, scarcely any way of resolving this difficulty is open unless we wish to say that Leo intended the act of penance and the grace of reconciliation to be granted to all sinners placed in extreme danger of life, even if, having lost the use of speech and being overwhelmed by illness, they were unable to signify anything of their desire, provided that others testified that it had previously been signified.

Perhaps, however, he excepted apostates alone from this indulgence, so that they would indeed receive penance, but would not enjoy the grace of communion, in accordance with the ancient and stricter discipline of the canons.

For the final canon of the First Council of Arles is famous:

“Concerning those who apostatize and never present themselves to the Church, nor even seek to perform penance, and who afterward, when seized by illness, request communion, it has been decided that communion is not to be given to them unless they recover and produce worthy fruits of penance.”

[Col. 1422B]

The Gallican bishops seem to have relaxed this harsher discipline only at a later time. Although several canons of subsequent synods exist in which something more lenient is decreed concerning other kinds of sinners who seek pardon when in extreme danger of life, no question is known to have been raised concerning apostates who were on the point of death, deprived of the use of voice, mind, and sense, but who had previously requested penance.

The Gallican bishops may therefore reasonably be believed to have always observed this same discipline concerning them, since they were such strict guardians of the Gallican canons.

This also becomes highly probable from the more frequent complaints in which we read that the bishops of Gaul were harassed by the Roman pontiffs, or from the questions on this matter to which the pontiffs replied when consulted by the Gauls. These show that the discipline of the Gallican Churches concerning penance was stricter than that of Rome.

Thus the First Council of Valence, in the year 374, imposed a more severe law of penance upon those who, after baptism, had polluted themselves with sacrifices to demons or with incestuous ablution, extending their penance until the day of death in canon 3.

Thus also Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, consulted Pope Innocent I and asked him:

“What ought to be observed concerning those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves at all times to the pleasures of unrestrained conduct, and at the very end of their life request both penance and reconciliation with communion?”

Exuperius undoubtedly knew that canon 13 of Nicaea had decreed that, generally, the bishop ought reasonably to give communion to anyone placed at the point of death and asking that the grace of communion be granted. He found an occasion for doubt nowhere except in the different practice of the Gallican Church, which denied communion to some who were placed in that condition.

We learn that the Gallican bishops acted in this way not by conjecture but by certain evidence from chapter 2 of Pope Celestine’s letter to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonensis:

“We have learned,” he says, “that penance is denied to the dying, and that the wishes of those who, at the time of their death, desire to be aided by this remedy for their souls are not granted,” and so forth.

Likewise, in the First Council of Orange in the year 441, canon 3, and in the Second Council of Arles, canon 28, it is clear that the reconciling laying on of hands was not granted to those who, having received penance, departed from the body. Yet Innocent, Celestine, and Leo wished to grant it.

In these circumstances, it is not unreasonable to think that Leo wished to exclude from the general benefit of communion, when placed at the point of death, certain apostates—namely, those who were not in the same circumstances as those about whom Popes Innocent and Celestine had spoken.

This is further confirmed by examining the reasoning which Pope Innocent brought forward and by considering the discipline of the ancient canons.

The earlier and harsher custom prevailed in this way: penance was granted to those who requested it at the end of life, but communion was denied, because the frequent persecutions of those times drove many to deny the faith. It was therefore necessary to take care that the ease with which communion was granted should not make people secure concerning reconciliation and thus fail to deter them from apostasy.

But after God had restored peace to the Church and fear had been removed, it was decided that communion should be given to those who were departing this life. Communion was therefore given to such persons after peace had been restored to the Church, since there was no longer reason to fear that the faithful would be driven by fear of death to renounce the faith.

If such severity was exercised toward these people, how much more reasonable was it that a stricter discipline should be maintained toward others who had not been driven by terror, but had abandoned the faith either through their own lust, through inconstancy of will, or—and this must be especially considered in the present case—in order to evade the discipline of the Church.

There was much greater reason to fear that those who held religion in such low esteem or suffered from such great levity of mind would trample upon the grace of communion once it had been granted to them again.

Nor does this observance contain anything cruel. Otherwise the whole ancient penitential discipline would have to be harassed by the same accusation.

Moreover, the punishment of a few such apostates served greatly to instruct others, lest they allow themselves too easily to be led into denying Christ by hope of pardon.

Finally, such persons were not deprived of every assistance and help, but only of the benefit of reconciliation. For, as the First Council of Orange and the Second Council of Arles say in canon 3, communion was given to them without the reconciling laying on of hands. This was sufficient consolation for the dying, according to the definitions of the Fathers, who appropriately called such communion *viaticum*.

“If they survive,” says the Council of Orange, “let them remain in the order of penitents, and, after displaying the necessary fruits of penance, let them receive legitimate communion with the reconciling laying on of hands.”

Those who do not approve this explanation of Leo’s words may, we think, be satisfied by a single statement: that Leo our pontiff may have required something from apostates who had returned to Christ and recovered from their illness—namely, that they should publicly recite a symbol of the worship of idols or of whatever other superstition they had followed, or should in some other way show that they detested the most atrocious crime.

Finally, our Leo may have had in mind the opinion of his predecessor Siricius, in chapter 3 of his letter to Himerius. There Siricius commands Christians who have apostatized and returned to Christ to perform penance for as long as they live, and grants them the grace of reconciliation only at the very end of life.

Leo therefore wishes that those who have been reconciled in this manner, if they recover, should again be subjected to penance and perform it for as long as they remain alive, whereas others who had been reconciled in this way completed their penance over a definite period, or the Church dealt with them even more indulgently.

See also canons 11 and 12 of Nicaea and the canons of Ancyra.

### 4.

The final point that occurs to us as requiring notice in this letter concerns the form of absolution or reconciliation. Three passages of this letter most clearly demonstrate that in Leo’s time it was supplicatory:

Chapter 2: “Thus the provisions of divine goodness having been arranged, so that God’s indulgence cannot be obtained except through the SUPPLICATIONS of priests.”

Chapter 3: “But if any of those for whom we SUPPLICATE the Lord…”; and afterward: “For it is of great usefulness and necessity that the guilt of sins be loosed before the final day by priestly SUPPLICATION.”

A notable passage of Letter 136 (now 168) agrees with these testimonies: “That confession is sufficient,” he says, “which is first offered to God, and then also to the priest, who approaches as an intercessor for the sins of penitents.” Finally, Letter 139 (now 171), chapter 1: “Earnestly obtain that they be reconciled to God THROUGH THE PRAYERS OF THE CHURCH.”

The matter would require a more extensive discussion, unless it had already long ago been treated by the most diligent investigators of ecclesiastical antiquity: Hugh Menard, a Benedictine ascetic, in his notes on the Gregorian Sacramentary [Col. 1424A], and Jean Morin, a priest of the French Oratory, in Book VIII, chapters 8 and following, of his Commentary on Penance.

I had resolved to insert here a notable testimony to that practice, which I extracted from a manuscript Breviary nearly six hundred years old, formerly written for the use of the monastery of Monte Cassino: namely, the order for giving and receiving penance, in which no form of absolution appears except the supplicatory one; also the order for administering extreme unction and the order for receiving the Eucharist. I trust that all these things would be most welcome to the ecclesiastical reader. But since the bulk of this volume is already becoming too great, I shall for the present refrain from publishing them, while nevertheless taking care that the reader’s curiosity not long be disappointed in this treasure of antiquity.

Meanwhile I present here another, and indeed older, document, which likewise sheds light on penitential discipline. Since it belongs to a Gallican bishop, it may appropriately be appended to the reply given to the inquiry of Theodore, bishop of Fréjus.

## JUDGMENT OF CHRODEBERT, BISHOP OF TOURS

### Concerning an adulterous woman

Now published for the first time from a manuscript codex of the Thuane Library.

[Col. 1424B]

To N., mother of a household, to be sweetly named for her religious devotion and embraced by the bond of charity, Chrodebert H., a sinner, sends perpetual greeting in the Lord.

By your letter you asked my insignificance to seek out the judgment of the canons concerning a woman who, after having been consecrated and having professed that she would preserve chastity for God, committed adultery. Although in the holy Synods of Nicaea, Chalcedon, Ephesus, and Constantinople we have found no chapter concerning this matter—and our country reverently receives and acknowledges only these four synods—[Note: [Col. 1423D] Hincmarus uses similar language in *Opusc. 12 Capitum contra Hincmarum Laudunensem*, chapter 24: “Since this land is full of those very judgments.”] nevertheless, in the Synod of Orléans we have found a judgment prescribed on this matter, [Note: [Col. 1424D] This appears to be canon 16 of the Fifth Council of Orléans, A.D. 549.] which we have sent to you; and on the authority of that same synod we have sent the aforesaid woman the judgment she must observe.

Along with this sentence we have offered counsel drawn from the fountain of the divine Scriptures—living streams of judgments, or immovable trunks of columns. Drinking from their waters and holding fast to their embrace, let her not fear falling again into ruin, nor, because of her past fall, despair of pardon, provided that she keeps the counsels given above.

Let her remember that evangelical sinful woman, Mary Magdalene, who had been filled with seven vices, from whom the Lord cast out seven demons. She washed the Lord’s feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them with lips pressed upon them in burning love, and anointed them with precious ointment [Col. 1424D]. Of her the Lord said: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7:47).

She is also the one who followed the Lord continually, even to the crucifixion and burial; and she was the first after the resurrection—before any of the apostles and before the glorious ever-virgin Mary, the Lord’s Mother—to merit seeing angels and the Lord. She is the sister of Martha and Lazarus, whom the Lord raised after he had been dead for three days.

Our Redeemer said that he had come into this world for sinners and adulterers, not for the just. The Truth himself also says that the healthy do not need a physician [Col. 1425A], but the sick.

The Apostle Paul, persecutor and murderer of Christians, slayer of Saint Stephen, became the teacher of us and of all the nations. What shall I say of Matthew the tax collector, afterward an evangelist? What of Zacchaeus, who, already enlightened in heart, wished to see the Lord from the sycamore tree because of his short stature? What of that publican in the holy Gospel who beat his breast, saying: “I am not worthy to lift my eyes to heaven. Be merciful to me, Lord, a sinner”? He went down more justified than that Pharisee who boasted of his merits and prayed standing.

What more does our Lord and Redeemer say in the Gospel to increase consolation? He completed the glorious likeness of the most merciful Shepherd who, leaving ninety-nine sheep in the mountains [Col. 1425B], diligently searched the desolate places with great labor for the one that had gone astray; he found it, placed it on his shoulders, and brought it safely back to the flock. Thus he both completed the perfect number of one hundred, was master of the perfect flock, and joined us wretched sinners, wandering through the frailty of the body, to the just and innocent. And he said that he rejoiced more over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance.

But, by Christ’s gracious gift, care must be taken for the future so that the fault is not repeated, and the past must be wiped away through many tears, by day and by night, publicly and privately, through fasts, prayers, groans, sighs, labors, obedience and silence, humility and charity [Col. 1425C].

The periods of years required for performing penance are not to be sought out or counted. What matters is the strength of whatever period or moment is given, together with contrition, fear of one’s sin, and love of God from the heart’s whole desire.

The most excellent prophet bears witness to the confirmation of these words. Filled with the Spirit of God, he says: “On whatever day, at whatever hour, a sinner turns and groans, all his sins are consigned to oblivion.”

And that thief who had been crucified beside the Lord, after confessing in a sudden confession, believed with a faith that was full. He did not spend years, months, or days in penance; swift death seized him, and, according to the Lord’s word, he entered before the Apostle Peter.

The people of the city of Nineveh, through a three-day fast, weeping, ashes, sackcloth, lamentation, and united groaning, deserved to escape from the abyss of their destruction and the wrath of God [Col. 1425D].

King and prophet David, filled with the Spirit of God, after the crime of murder and adultery, when the prophet Nathan reproved him, was not ashamed, before the whole multitude [Col. 1426A], to present his face in the dust from the royal throne. At the same time he burst into the most loving utterance of repentance, saying: “I have sinned against the Lord; I have sinned” (2 Samuel 12:13). And the Lord said to him through the prophet: “Your sin is forgiven” (ibid.).

Behold how much humility accomplishes, how much charity obtains. For although our sins are hard—according to the Apostle, like straw, hay, and wood—if we abound in the fire of the love of God, we can more quickly burn away the burdens of sin. In their place, upon the foundation [Col. 1426A] of faith, which is the hope of the spirit, we can build gold, silver, and precious stones; and we can be counted among the true stones as an ornament of the eternal King, our Redeemer, so that the Apostle may say to us: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 4:5).

And again: “Where sin abounded, grace abounded still more” (Romans 5:20). Yet we must listen to that same Apostle Paul in all things and keep intact his counsels, since he possesses the Spirit of God.

He says in his Letter to the Romans: “For just as you presented your members as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness leading to lawlessness, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness leading to sanctification” (Romans 6:19).

For example, whoever kept many hidden and harmful vigils in lust should multiply the occasions on which his body is roused from sleep [Col. 1426B] in the same way, rising and secretly exhausting and afflicting itself in prayers in a corner of the church or monastery. Thus the pains—of whatever quantity and kind—which he remembers having endured for carnal love, should, according to the command of the Apostle Paul, be endured for spiritual love. His body should become no less weakened by vigils than it was in its crimes, when it was shamefully bent down and disgracefully exhausted by various contrivances and distorted entanglements of the limbs.

This is the complete restoration of health and the supreme work of salvation: that by the highest love of God a new love drive out the old love of sin; that the sinner die to his former love; that our human nature be renewed; and that the body of sin be destroyed, so that we may no longer serve sin.

For whoever has died to this world and has been crucified with Christ has been justified from sin. Thus, renewed in conduct and justified from sin, we shall be saved from wrath through him, so that sin may no longer reign in our mortal body. Instead, the reign of the Savior may come through his grace, which the same Apostle Paul invoked with a groan, saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25).

To him belong honor and glory and dominion, majesty and power, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, for endless ages of ages.

I, Chrodebert, an unworthy sinner, servant of the servants of God and bishop, have subscribed.

I give many thanks for the well-woven, seamless, long and broad garment, received with great affection and prepared, as though knowingly, for my body with grace [Col. 1426D].

## Observation on the Judgment of Chrodebert, Bishop of Tours

We found this outstanding little book on penance in a manuscript codex of the Thuane Library, marked number 780. In it we likewise read a privilege granted by Pope Adeodatus to the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours during the lifetime of the same Chrodebert.

Jacques Sirmond, in his notes on this privilege, which he included in volume I of the Councils of Gaul, testifies that he compared it with the Pithaean papers, in which, he says, there is also the letter of that same Chrodebert, bishop of Tours, concerning the judgment of a woman who, after having been consecrated and having professed that she would preserve chastity for God, committed adultery.

Sirmond read this in the same manuscript codex from which we transcribed this judgment. For what reason, then, and with what intention, he begrudged the public the work, is a mystery which I leave to others to investigate [Col. 1427A].

Perhaps two passages of this writing deterred him from publishing it. In one, Chrodebert writes: “Our country reverently receives and acknowledges only these four synods: the Nicene, Constantinopolitan, Ephesian, and Chalcedonian.” In the other, he asserts that Mary Magdalene was the first after the resurrection—before any apostle and before the glorious ever-virgin Mary, the Lord’s Mother—to merit seeing angels and the Lord.

From the first passage it follows that the Fifth Synod, which had condemned the Three Chapters, had still not been received by the Gallican Churches when half of the seventh century had already passed. This is also suggested by Chrodebert’s deliberate restriction, through which he implies that some general synod had been rejected by the Gallican bishops; and no other synod can be meant than the universal Fifth.

Although the memory of these matters is exceedingly obscure in the monuments of Gallican antiquity, it nevertheless appears certain from several sources [Col. 1427B] that the Gallican Church contended on behalf of the Three Chapters. I touch upon this all the more willingly because the most learned H. de Noris, who recently treated this controversy in a very extensive historical dissertation, said much about all the other Churches but nothing about the Gallican Church from which we might learn anything of his opinion in this celebrated dispute.

The matter therefore seems first to be made clear by a letter of Pope Vigilius to Aurelian, bishop of Arles, from whom he had received a letter showing that Vigilius had come under suspicion among the Gallican Churches either of having violated the faith or of having injured the reverence owed to the Council of Chalcedon and to Leo’s decrees.

“It is therefore necessary for us,” says Vigilius, “to relieve, briefly for the present and as far as the circumstances of the time permit, the anxiety of your charity through conversation, so that you may be fully confident that we have done absolutely nothing which could be found—God forbid—to be contrary either to the constitutions of our predecessors or to the faith of the four synods, namely, the Nicene, Constantinopolitan, First Ephesian, and Chalcedonian, which is one and the same holy faith; OR WHICH MIGHT PERTAIN TO AN INJURY TO THE PERSONS who subscribed to the definition of that same holy faith.”

And afterward: “Punishing with a similar penalty those who, in accursed pride, called impious the faith of Blessed Cyril … and of the other Fathers whom the pontiffs of the Apostolic See received and followed.”

You see how displeased our bishops were that Vigilius had admitted—so rumor spread—anything that might constitute an injury to those who had subscribed to the faith of Chalcedon and whom the pontiffs of the Apostolic See had received. These words clearly designate the Three Chapters.

The words of Datius, bishop of Milan, in the letter addressed to the Frankish legates, which is found in Sirmond, volume I of the Councils of Gaul, bear witness to the same thing:

“Behold, I and part of all the priests among whom my Church is established—that is, of Gaul, Burgundy, Spain, Liguria, Emilia, and Venetia—testify that whoever has consented to this edict [of Justinian against the Three Chapters] cannot have the bishops of the provinces written above as communicants,” and so forth.

Below, Anastasius, the legate of Orléans, is mentioned as having promised at Constantinople that he would incline the minds of all the Gallican bishops toward condemning the Chapters. This shows the inclination of the Gauls’ minds in the same matter.

Something concerning their mind and judgment is also found in the fragment concerning the condemnation of Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, carried out by Pope Vigilius, in volume V of the new edition of the Councils, page 335.

That the Gauls persevered in the same position even after the Fifth Synod persuades me is the profound silence concerning that synod in the other Gallican councils and monuments of that age. From this it appears that the Gauls were not pressed to receive the Fifth Council, but were left to their ancient opinion. The same course was followed with many other Churches, which, although they neither condemned the Three Chapters nor received the Fifth Synod, nevertheless did not break the bond of communion with those who condemned the Chapters and supported the Fifth Synod.

That Pelagius used this moderation with the Gauls is shown by his letter to King Childebert, which he wrote to declare that he had done nothing against the faith, having been suspected of this in Gaul because of the condemnation of the Three Chapters. So far was he from trying to drag the Gauls into that condemnation or into acceptance of the Fifth Synod that he carefully avoided even discussing the matter. He writes that, since the death of the blessed empress Theodora, the Church of God, by God’s mercy, feared no questions concerning the faith in the eastern regions, but that certain Chapters outside the faith had been debated, “concerning which it would take too long to speak in a letter.”

He then carefully clears himself of the rumors spread against him, without mixing in a single word about the Fifth Synod, on whose occasion he was nevertheless said to be suspect in Gaul. This was in the year 556, three years after the celebration of the synod.

Not long afterward, in order to obey the king’s command and remove this scandal of suspicion, he sent Childebert a statement of his confession. There he declares that he holds and defends [Col. 1428B] the definitions concerning the same Catholic faith which were established in the four holy councils.

Mention of the other councils prompted him to speak of the Fifth; yet he suppressed it in silence, lest the letter be displeasing to the king, preserving in this matter the *oikonomia*—the prudent accommodation—maintained by Saint Gregory and other pontiffs.

Nothing afterward occurred in Gaul that would have driven the Gallican bishops to another opinion. We are therefore easily persuaded that the Fifth Synod had not been received when Chrodebert sat as bishop at Tours and wrote: “Our country reverently receives and acknowledges only four synods.”

In this he almost followed the example both of Pelagius, who, as we have seen, wrote to Childebert, and of Saint Gregory the Great. When Gregory wrote to Theodolinda, queen of the Lombards, who was opposed to receiving the Fifth Synod, he abstained from mentioning that synod and recalled only four (Book III, Letter 17):

“Therefore we now act as you have desired,” he writes to Constantius of Milan, “so that we should praise only four synods … We have done as you wished, so that we should make no mention whatever of that Fifth Synod.”

Sirmondus therefore trembled with fear where there was no fear, if he thought that Chrodebert’s words provided grounds for condemning this judgment concerning the adulterous woman to darkness.

As for the second point, concerning the first appearance of the risen Christ, I know that Jansenius, in both places, wrote in these words, “He appeared first to Mary Magdalene,” that this does not prevent the Lord from having appeared earlier to his most blessed Mother:

“Piety strongly urges us to believe that the Lord appeared first to his most beloved Mother.”

Maldonado, on Matthew 28, says:

“It is rightly believed by Catholics, although it is not written, that Christ appeared first of all to his Mother.”

And below:

“That he appeared first to his Mother is to be believed—not because the Evangelists say that this happened, but because it was fitting that it should happen. Nor do I approve of the diligence of those who spend much effort refuting this opinion, which has already taken root in the minds of almost all Catholics” [Col. 1428D].

“Who doubts that he appeared to his blessed Mother before all others?” asks Toletus in his commentary on John 20.

There are nevertheless Catholic and pious teachers who doubt this; it is not the present occasion to list them. To defend Chrodebert’s judgment against censure, it will suffice to transcribe here a rule full of wisdom from the annotations on Mark by William Estius, a man of distinguished learning and piety:

“Certain arguments of fittingness are brought forward for this opinion. But concerning such arguments it must be noted above all that attention must be directed to what Scripture or the Church teaches; and, once that is known, arguments of fittingness may be employed to make it more probable. One must not, conversely, establish something from such arguments against what Scripture or the Church says or holds.

“Such would be the attempt, from certain arguments of fittingness, to prove that Christ, returning from the dead, appeared first to his Mother, when Scripture says so clearly that he appeared first to Mary Magdalene [Col. 1429A] and nowhere else suggests anything different.

“If one is to proceed according to such little arguments, it will also be necessary to say that Christ brought his Mother to the Last Supper, placed her in the first place of honor, and distributed his body and blood to her first—as Hesselius argues well.”

## On Letter 111 According to Quesnell, 84

### To the Emperor Marcian

#### 1. “When he was seeking communion with the Apostolic See”

So Grimanus’s codex reads; the common editions instead have: “While he remained alienated from the communion of the Apostolic See,” which gives a completely false meaning.

For it would be unacceptable to suppose that the pontiff, who, addressing Flavian in Letter 20 (now 23), wishes the judgments of priests to be mature, denied Anatolius his communion merely on suspicion. That this truly did not happen is indicated by Letter 54 (now 70) to Pulcheria, where he asserts that he is not denying Anatolius his affection but is awaiting a manifestation of Catholic truth [Col. 1429B]. He therefore merely delayed the signs of communion.

#### 2. “By letters of peace”

The ancients called such letters “peace letters,” or “letters of communion,” because they were signs and attestations of peace, that is, ecclesiastical communion. Augustine discusses them in Letters 62 and 63; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 70; and others.

In the present letter, however, these expressions can be restricted to a narrower meaning, so that they signify specifically those letters sent in reply to a newly ordained bishop, whether by the Roman pontiff or by anyone else. This is how Theodorus Balsamon uses the term for letters customarily sent by a bishop who had recently been consecrated.

#### 3. “Of the whole ecclesiastical cause and care”

From these and other words of the following letter one may understand how great the archdeacon’s authority and duties were. On these matters see also the letter of Isidore of Seville to Ludifredus, or Lantfredus, which is quoted in distinction 25, chapter 1, “After reading.”

There the correction made by the Roman Correctors must itself be corrected. They wish the manuscripts to be read as follows: “He publicly preaches it in the Church.” It should instead be restored as it was previously: “They are publicly preached”—namely, the days of fasts and solemnities. At that time it had not yet been granted to deacons or archdeacons, nor even to priests, to deliver public sermons to the people in the Italian, Gallican, or Spanish regions. Yet the example of Saints John Chrysostom, Augustine, and others teaches us that this custom had already been received in practice in the Eastern and African regions.

See also many other passages in Gratian and others.

#### 4. “Assigned to a cemetery”

In the early ages of the Church it was customary for Christians to celebrate the sacred mysteries in cemeteries, both because of persecution and out of reverence for the martyrs buried and resting there. For this reason, by the edicts of Valerian and other emperors, they were forbidden to visit cemeteries, and those who were discovered performing this work of charity and piety were handed over to death.

After peace had been restored to the Church, priests were assigned to these same cemeteries to perform sacred rites there for God in honor of the martyrs [Col. 1429D].

But as charity cooled with the passage of time, assignment to cemeteries began to seem burdensome to priests, because the cemeteries were farther from the cities and less frequented than the ordinary churches of the faithful [Col. 1430A]. Their care therefore began to be entrusted to priests of a lower rank. Leo complains that this kind of insult had been inflicted upon the archdeacon.

#### 5. “It is necessary to rebuke”

That is: continually, without interruption, without delay or cessation, until the person is brought to correction.

For *necessum* is derived from *cesso*, “to cease,” because one must not cease in this matter, says Donatus in his commentary on Terence.

The word is used in the same sense by our Leo in Letters 20, 71, 78, 86, 90, and 139 (now 23, 92, 104, 113, 116, and 171), and very frequently in his sermons.

#### 6. “So that he might not be absent from your entourage”

Similar expressions occur in the following letters. From them one can discern the origin of the representatives—or, as we now customarily say, [Note: [Col. 1429D] Although the form and origin of apostolic nuncios may perhaps be traced back to this, we have sufficiently established in the observations on Quesnell’s first dissertation, annotation 3, on the year 453, that Julian’s delegation was not organized according to the model of the *apocrisiarii*. Since Julian had been raised in the Roman Church and was especially well known and necessary to Leo, the holy pontiff placed his greatest trust in him. He therefore entrusted him with this apostolic delegation solely on account of the faith, because he had not found in the bishop of Constantinople the firmness of faith demanded by the difficult circumstances of that time.

“To conjecture with Quesnell about other plans of Leo, even from an earlier period, and about secret arrangements, is to guess—or rather to dream—for they cannot be proved by any document. If Julian is found to have been at Constantinople at some time before this, there is nothing remarkable in that: as a bishop of the Greek Church, and one living not far from Constantinople, he could easily and repeatedly have gone there for various reasons, without this requiring us to say that he had existed there in the entourage as the pontiff’s nuncio.

“By this letter alone Leo requires that he not be absent from the entourage. It was only at this time, therefore, that he imposed upon him the office of nuncio. For the other matters which Quesnell presses at this point, see the preliminary notice to Julian’s letter to the Emperor Leo, which you will find inserted above in the appendix to the Letters (Col. 1241).] nuncios of the Apostolic See serving in the imperial entourage [Col. 1430B]. It would not be inappropriate, following learned writers, to compare these men with the *apocrisiarii* of the Eastern patriarchs, provided that certain differences between them are observed.

First, the patriarchs had already been sending *apocrisiarii* to the entourage of the Eastern emperor when the imperial capital was transferred to Byzantium. The Roman pontiffs’ vicars, however, were established after—or shortly before—the Council of Chalcedon, in the person of Julian, bishop of Cos.

Second, the patriarchs’ *apocrisiarii* remained in the entourage not on account of the faith but for the special affairs of a Church or diocese. The Roman nuncios, on the other hand, were ordered to reside there to attend to matters of faith.

Third, the former were generally chosen from the order of deacons or priests for such duties; the latter were sometimes also chosen from the episcopal order, in keeping with the dignity of the Apostolic See, as appears in the case of Julian.

In establishing this vicar, therefore, Saint Leo imitated the custom of the Eastern patriarchs, while nevertheless distinguishing himself from them in many respects by his prerogative, and completing and adorning this office with definite advances and additions. I think it will not be idle, nor out of place here, to examine this more closely.

Saint Leo had seen the Eastern Churches shaken and tossed by dreadful storms through the new heresy of Nestorius, and scarcely, if at all, brought to rest by the definitions of the Council of Ephesus. Since, at the time of that synod, he had served as a deacon under Pope Celestine and, as the pontiff’s assistant, had managed ecclesiastical affairs, he understood how greatly the faith depended upon a Catholic bishop presiding over the Church of Constantinople.

For the most part, those who were elevated to this dignity were men who possessed great influence and favor with the emperor. The result was that, when such men had once allowed themselves to be corrupted by perverse opinions, they inspired the emperor and the administrators of the empire with the same opinions and abused their power to protect their heresy.

He also knew that the bishop of Constantinople, relying upon the canon of the Second Council, was striving with all his strength to enlarge his authority and would not bring his efforts to an end until he had subjected all the greater primates to himself. Once these had been subjected, there was reason to fear that he might eventually think of diminishing the authority of the Roman See as well.

The bishop of Jerusalem imitated the bishop of Constantinople. At the Council of Ephesus he believed that he could establish his claim to the primacy of the province of Palestine and sought to strengthen his insolent ambitions through fabricated writings [Col. 1430D; Col. 1431A].

Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria of blessed memory, rightly shuddered at this. “In his writings,” Saint Leo says, “he informed me of what the aforesaid man’s ambition had dared to do, and earnestly requested that no assent be given to unlawful efforts.”

Having considered these matters, the pontiff judged that it would be best to send someone in his place to the royal city who could observe more closely the mind and plans of the bishop of Constantinople, watch over the common faith and ecclesiastical peace, and report to the Roman See whatever the bishop of Constantinople or anyone else attempted against the faith, the Nicene canons, and ecclesiastical statutes in order to enlarge his own power. In this way the pontiff could more quickly confront the evil as it arose and act with the emperor to restrain efforts contrary to Christian faith and ecclesiastical discipline.

But to undertake this openly would have been dangerous. The Easterners had always been displeased that Westerners did not allow them to conduct their own affairs as they wished. Nor was there any hope that the bishop of Constantinople—puffed up by the splendor of his see, which also reflected upon the empire itself, and supported by the favor of the nobles and of the emperor—would tolerate a measure which its very novelty made especially hateful.

What was the most skillful Saint Leo to do? He chose Julian, bishop of Cos, a man highly experienced in ecclesiastical affairs. Since Julian had been raised in the bosom of the Roman Church, he was entirely formed according to Western and Roman customs and was deeply devoted to the Apostolic See. Moreover, as a bishop of the Greek Church, no one would be more acceptable to the Greeks or more suited to dealing with Greek dispositions.

But Leo also intended to attempt nothing further, except secretly. No one’s residence in the royal city and in the imperial household would be less suspect than that of one of those bishops whose ordination the bishop of Constantinople had drawn to himself and whom he frequently ordered to be present there for the handling of ecclesiastical matters as they arose. Finally, many of these bishops often needed to be present in the entourage to conduct the affairs of their Churches before the emperor [Col. 1431C].

Julian was such a man. I believe that he had lived at Constantinople for several years even before the Council of Chalcedon, by secret command of Leo, so that he might secretly keep watch there over matters of faith and discipline.

He was indeed present in the imperial city in the year of Our Lord 448, when Eutyches was accused of violating the faith and condemned in the Constantinopolitan council under Bishop Flavian. Julian wrote to Saint Leo concerning Eutyches’ condemnation in a letter full of firmness in the faith, and Leo replied to him in Letter 25 (now 35), instructing him at greater length concerning the mystery of the Incarnation and exhorting him more forcefully to resist those who corrupted the Gospel of Christ.

This provides grounds for suspecting that Julian already then possessed secret instructions to inform the Apostolic See carefully about the condition of the faith and of the Eastern Church, although nothing concerning this was permitted to appear in the letters, for the reason mentioned above.

Indeed, Julian seems to have been so concerned with the responsibility entrusted to him that, not content with informing Leo through this first letter about Eutyches’ error and condemnation, he sent another through a different messenger at approximately the same time. In it he informed our pontiff about the same heretic, who was growing old in his perversity.

Leo likewise wrote again to the same bishop of Cos. He informed him about his legates, whom he was sending to the council summoned by the emperor; about the letter he had given to Flavian; and about the entire course which he thought should be followed in this case—namely, that the aspects of mercy should not be omitted. If Eutyches should repent and make satisfaction, he was to be released from the sentence by which he was bound; but if he chose to lie in the mud of his folly, he was to share the lot of those whose error he had followed.

Moreover, as soon as the pontiff had been informed of the Ephesian Robbery, he sent Julian a letter in which he stated that he was omitting nothing that he thought would help restore the affairs of the Churches. He also instructed him, through the more private conversations of the bearer, about everything that had been arranged according to the circumstances of the present time [Col. 1432A].

This suggests that Julian, too, had sent letters to Saint Leo in which he informed him about the wicked treachery of the Ephesian false synod. Both those letters and these show that the Roman pontiff had entrusted Julian with a certain care of the affairs of the Church, to be exercised, if not openly and publicly, at least more secretly, as we have said.

For the same reason, in writing to the Empress Pulcheria on the Ides of April in the year 451, before anything concerning the convoked Council of Chalcedon had been learned at Rome, Leo says:

“We also ask this of your piety—something which we do not hesitate to believe you will do of your own free will—that you favor both my brother and fellow bishop Julian and the clergy of Constantinople who adhered to Flavian of blessed memory with faithful service, with the favor you ought to show.”

He repeats nearly the same words in a letter written at the same time to Anatolius. It can therefore easily be perceived that a secret relationship had already been established between Leo and Julian [Col. 1432B], such as ordinarily exists between a Roman vicar or nuncio and the pontiff of that same city. For Julian was later commended to the emperors in almost the same manner as in the present passage, once his delegation began to become known to everyone.

The legation was explained still further when Saint Leo, sending Lucentius and Basil to the East, did not omit to warn Julian before their departure from the City and to reach an understanding with him through the same men by letter. We have now brought these letters out of obscurity; they show that even then Julian, at Leo’s command, was devoting his attention to the affairs of the Church. “Through our brothers,” he says, “Bishop Lucentius and the presbyter Basil, whom we had announced that we were going to send to Constantinople, I offer the due greeting, admonishing you to deign to join your diligent zeal to these same men.” And afterward: “You will learn through their report what has been enjoined and entrusted to our legates, and you will show toward me and them such affection that whatever has been entrusted to them, joined with the devotion and solicitude of love, may, with the Lord’s help, reach the result we desire.” Leo wrote this when he was sending legates to settle the affairs of the Eastern Churches.

But when he had received the Emperor’s letters concerning the ecumenical council summoned at Nicaea, he immediately adopted the plan of joining Julian as well to the legates whom he was sending to that council. This is attested by several letters written on the matter, but especially by those which he sent to Julian himself and which we are now publishing for the first time. “We entrust to your fraternity,” he says, “something that will benefit the whole Church: join your care and activity to those of our brothers and fellow bishops Paschasinus and Lucentius, and also to those of our brothers and fellow presbyters Boniface and Basil, whom we command to go in our place to the aforesaid assembly, using in everything the authority of our injunction. For we know that you have greater knowledge than our men of all that is being done there; and so, when you have joined your care and counsel to theirs, they may not be deceived in any respect.” [Col. 1432D]

In almost the same words he wrote about this legation to Anatolius of Constantinople in a letter recently made public by us. It strongly supports our opinion, since he declares that Julian’s fidelity had been proved to him by repeated experience: “Let them use, in the future council, our authority in all its proceedings, with our brother and fellow bishop Julian, whose fidelity we have often proved, participating in everything in our place.” These words agree with the following opening words of the already-mentioned Letter 71: “You have often recognized what judgment we form of your affection; for many things have preceded which would lead us to make this assumption.”

That after the completion of the Council of Chalcedon he finally resided at Constantinople, or at the imperial court, 1513 in the place of the Roman pontiff is something noted by others and expressly asserted in Letters 86 and 88 (now 113 and 117) to Julian; 84 and 89 (now 111 and 115) to Marcian; and 85 and 80 (now 112 and 116) to the Empress Pulcheria. It is therefore unnecessary to dwell on it any longer.

We infer that Julian’s legation lasted until the year 457 from the fact that we possess two letters of Leo to him, written in that same year, in July and September. From those same letters, however, it may likewise be inferred that around this time Julian, intending to return to his own Church, had resigned his legation. For after he had been absent for many years from the Church of Cos entrusted to him by divine providence, he perhaps took advantage of Marcian’s death to ask Leo for a successor who would attend upon Marcian’s successor as legate. Indeed, after this present year, 457, Saint Leo makes no further mention of Julian, and no letter to him appears to have been written after September of that year.

In the letter which Saint Leo wrote to him on the Kalends of September, the pontiff complains that Julian had let pass a very opportune occasion for writing. In the other, he calls upon Aetius to take care and make every effort to send his letters to the metropolitans, and joins him with Julian, as though he had foreseen—or perhaps had been warned by earlier letters—that Julian would no longer be found at Constantinople. [Col. 1433B]

Since he also sent a separate letter on the same day to the presbyter Aetius, entrusting to his care and diligence several important matters, I am entirely persuaded that this presbyter succeeded Julian as the representative of Cos, and that Leo likewise selected him as the man to whom he could entrust his own responsibilities in the royal city for the safeguarding of the faith and ecclesiastical peace, and through whose reports he could be informed about everything.

Yet letters sent by Pope Leo to the Emperor Leo on the Kalends of December of that year—three months after these letters—scarcely permit this to remain in doubt. In them he commends the presbyter Aetius to the Emperor in such a way that one may readily suppose that he was first joined to Julian, as legate, in the handling of affairs, and afterward substituted for him. For at the end he writes:

“But I commend to your Piety, at my request, the devotees of your piety, Bishop Julian and the presbyter Aetius, so that you may graciously hear their representations in defense of the Catholic faith; for they are truly such men as may in every respect be found useful to your faith.” (Epistle 125, now 156, chapter 6.) [Col. 1433C]

In this text we have restored “the presbyter Aetius” from the manuscript of Grimani in place of “Eutychius,” which all the printed copies erroneously have, as the sequence of events also demonstrates.

Aetius was especially well suited to such an office. His industry and expertise in the conduct of affairs had shone forth most conspicuously in the office of archdeacon and chief of the notaries of Constantinople, in which he had long been engaged; and likewise at the Council of Chalcedon, whose 1514 Acts mention Aetius very frequently. Moreover, since Anatolius had removed him from the rank of archdeacon under the pretext of promotion, and since for this reason he had often been commended by Leo’s letters to the Emperor, the pontiff had no reason to fear that Aetius would be excessively inclined toward the bishop of Constantinople, or that he would conceal anything which, whether by Anatolius’s initiative or with his connivance, might be attempted against the truth of the faith or the reverence due to the canons. Finally, there was this advantage: nothing concerning Eastern affairs could escape him, since he had long discharged the office of archdeacon, to which all the affairs of the Church were customarily entrusted.

That Saint Leo adorned a presbyter rather than a bishop with his own authority may perhaps have been due, in addition to the reasons mentioned above, to the fact that in those blessed times he would scarcely have found a bishop who would not have bitterly resented prolonged exile from his own Church. Another reason may have been that the bishops of Constantinople would not long have tolerated with equanimity a bishop residing in their city in the name of the Roman pontiff.
