Although Saint Leo had to some extent forestalled their envy or rivalry by entrusting his authority to Julian—and, in Letter 86 (now 113), instructing him to exclude from his activity the hearing of those cases which ought to be settled in each Church by the knowledge of its own bishop—nevertheless a bishop intensely concerned for the extent of his rights and his dignity could not fail to fear that the power of such representatives might gradually increase and, extending beyond its prescribed limits, eventually invade some portion of his jurisdiction.

This ground for fear was in some measure removed, and complete security was thereby obtained for the bishop of Constantinople. Saint Leo’s most wise *oikonomia*—οἰκονομία, that is, his prudent arrangement—was imitated for a long time by his successors. Pelagius, a deacon of the Roman Church and afterward pontiff, served in the name of Pope Agapetus; and Gregory the Great, while still a deacon, served in the name of Pelagius II; several others subsequently performed at Constantinople the office of *apocrisarius*, or envoy, of the Apostolic See, while they were permitted to watch over their own flocks as bishops and nourish them by word and example. [Col. 1434B]

## On Epistle 113, 86 in Quesnell

To Julian, Bishop of Cos.

### 1. “Under the pretext of promotion”

A similar example of this kind of simulated promotion may be found in Gregory the Great’s account of Honoratus, archdeacon of Salona, *Book I of the Register*, Letters 10 and 19, and *Book II*, Letter 16. The power of archdeacons was such that their order was even preferred to that of presbyters. Presbyters and archpresbyters were subject to their jurisdiction, once the dignity of the latter began to be recognized in the Church. I believe the reason for this disciplinary arrangement was 1515 that the archdeacon exercised the bishop’s functions and was the administrator of the whole Church, at least in the Western Church; for the Eastern Church had administrators distinct from archdeacons.

The presbyters, however, bore this subjection with difficulty, since it was in some sense an insult to their order. Consequently, in later centuries archdeacons were invested with presbyteral honor, whereas earlier—so we gather from Leo and Gregory—an archdeacon was considered to be degraded when he was promoted to the presbyterate. [Col. 1434C]

### 2. “A summary of the faith”

James Sirmond published a *Summary of the Faith* written against the Arians, and suspected that this was the very work sent by Julian of Cos, which Saint Leo here complains was not returned to him. Chifflet, Sirmond’s associate, disagrees; in his preface to Ferrandus the deacon he testifies that he found that *Summary of the Faith* attributed to the deacon Alcuin in a manuscript of the Carthusian monastery of Portes.

Certainly, although such a booklet vigorously defends Catholic doctrine, it does not seem so important that it should have been sent from the East all the way to Rome to the learned pontiff Leo—especially since it attacks the Arians, whose cause was not then at issue, more than the Eutychians, with whom the Catholic bishops were actually dealing.

I am almost persuaded that the “Summary of the Faith” sent by Julian was nothing other than the definition itself of the Council of Chalcedon, or the “treatise of faith,” as it is called several times elsewhere.

That definition has two parts in Session 5. The first begins: “Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ,” and so forth. In the Greek-Latin Roman, Binius, and Labbe editions of the Council of Chalcedon, it precedes the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds. The second follows both Creeds in those editions and begins with the words: “It would indeed be sufficient.” The same arrangement is found almost entirely in our Roman manuscript and in Isidore Mercator.

That two-part decree, which was published by Crabbe, Surius, and Nicolinus in four translations, is believed by Severinus Binius, in his annotations on this synod, to constitute a single and complete definition, so that the one part coheres with the other and neither should be separated from the other. In Crabbe, Surius, and Nicolinus, however, it is divided into two definitions—or rather, into the definition of the faith, 1516 which comes first, and the treatise of the faith, which follows the definition.

Thus, in their editions of Acts 5 and 6, they call the latter part, “It would indeed be sufficient,” the treatise of the faith. This seems to be confirmed by Liberatus’s *Brief Summary*, who, in reviewing the individual sessions of the Council of Chalcedon, writes the following about the fifth:

“In the fifth session, this was done: while the bishops and judges were discussing the confirmation of the faith, from the treatise of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, and of all the metropolitan bishops, a Creed was dictated together with a definition of the faith, and it was confirmed.”

The Fathers of the Third Council of Toledo agree with Surius and Liberatus. When proposing for subscription the Catholic faith to the Goths converted from Arian perfidy, they place this treatise after the Nicene faith and the Constantinopolitan Creed. In the confession subscribed by the king and queen, it is called “the treatise of the Council of Chalcedon”; in the confession of the bishops, “the treatise of the faith of the Council of Chalcedon”; or, as another edition of Garcia de Loaysa has it, “the holy faith which the treatise of the Council of Chalcedon expounded.”

In this council’s text, with the first part of the definition omitted—the part beginning “Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ”—the treatise contains only the latter section, “It would indeed be sufficient.” [Col. 1436A]

From what has been said, I suspect not without reason that this is the same treatise of the faith which Leo and Julian called the *Summary of the Faith*. For it is evident from Epistle 77 (now 102), written to the Gauls on the Kalends of February of the preceding year, 452, that Leo had not yet been informed about the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. He had learned nothing else about it except that, through the confirmation and approval of his letter to Flavian, the Eutychian perfidy had been condemned together with Dioscorus, its accomplice.

Before the return of the legates from the synod, he wrote this to the Gallic bishops. After their return, he wrote to the same bishops again and, together with his confirmation of the condemnation of Eutyches and Dioscorus, sent them a copy of the sentence issued against both at the council. But he said not a word about the definition or the treatise of the faith. I therefore rightly believe that even at that time Leo had not yet examined the Acts and documents of that synod.

For this reason he requested the relevant materials from Julian of Cos and urged him to arrange for all of them to be translated accurately, put in order, and sent to him as quickly as possible. 1517 I believe that these materials included both the documents which Aetius had indicated had been sent and the *Summary* which Julian had reported that he had sent but which Saint Leo complained he had not received. [Col. 1436B]

[Note: Since Leo had already approved the definition of the faith, as indicated in Epistle 114, chapter 1, it seems certain that he had received it, perhaps brought by the legates who had already returned and translated into Latin by someone; therefore he could not have understood by the name *Summary* the definition which he says he had not yet received. Moreover, the word *Summary* does not fit a complete document. Let it therefore be called a “Treatise of the Faith,” if it was the Chalcedonian definition. Nevertheless, it should not be called a *Summary of the Faith*. More probably, by this name we understand a Latin abridgment of the third and sixth sessions of Chalcedon, which was preserved for us in a very ancient manuscript once at Verona and now Vatican 1322, published by Baluze and inserted in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 2065. Since the *Summary* of these two sessions makes clear everything that was done concerning the faith, it could properly be called a *Summary of the Faith*. As for the *Summary against the Arians*, which we published in the appendix to volume II of this work, see the notice prefixed to it, column 283 (see our volume II).] [Col. 1435B]

That definition has two parts in Session 5: one beginning “Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ,” and so forth, and the other beginning “It would indeed be sufficient.” The former is placed before the Nicene and Constantinopolitan Creeds in the Greek-Latin Roman, Binius, and Labbe editions of the Council of Chalcedon; the latter follows both Creeds. The same arrangement is found nearly so in our Roman manuscript and in Isidore Mercator.

The two-part decree, published by Crabbe, Surius, and Nicolinus in four different translations, is regarded by Severinus Binius, in his annotations on this synod, as forming one single and complete definition, so that the one part is connected with the other and neither can be separated from the other. In Crabbe, Surius, and Nicolinus, however, it is divided into two definitions—or rather, into the definition of the faith, which is the first, and the treatise of the faith, which is joined to the definition.

Thus, in their editions of Acts 5 and 6, they call the later portion, “It would indeed be sufficient,” the treatise of the faith. This appears to be confirmed by Liberatus’s *Summary*, which, while reviewing the individual sessions of the Council of Chalcedon, writes the following about the fifth:

“In the fifth session this was done: while the bishops and judges were discussing the confirmation of the faith, from the treatise of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, and of all the metropolitan bishops, the Creed of the faith was dictated together with the definition, and it was confirmed.”

The Fathers of the Third Council of Toledo agree with Surius and Liberatus. When proposing that the Catholic faith be subscribed by the Goths converted from Arian perfidy, they place this treatise after the Nicene faith and the Constantinopolitan Creed. In the confession supported by the subscription of the king and queen, it is called “the treatise of the Council of Chalcedon”; in the confession of the bishops, “the treatise of the faith of the Council of Chalcedon”; or, as another edition by García de Loaysa has it, “the holy faith which the treatise of the Council of Chalcedon expounded.”

In this council the first part of the definition, beginning “Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ,” is omitted, and the treatise contains only the latter part, “It would indeed be sufficient.” [Col. 1436A]

From these considerations I suspect, not without reason, that this is the same treatise of the faith which Leo and Julian called the *Summary of the Faith*. It is evident from Epistle 77 (now 102), written to the Gallic bishops on the Kalends of February of the preceding year, 452, that Leo had not yet been informed about the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. He had learned only that, through the confirmation and approval of his letter to Flavian, the Eutychian perfidy had been condemned together with Dioscorus, its accomplice.

Before the legates returned from the synod, he wrote this to the Gallic bishops. After their return he wrote to the same bishops again and, together with confirmation of the condemnation of Eutyches and Dioscorus, sent a copy of the sentence issued against both at the council. But concerning the definition and the treatise of the faith he said not a word. I therefore rightly believe that at that time Leo still had not examined the Acts and records of that synod. This was why he requested them from Julian of Cos and urged him to arrange for all of them to be carefully translated and systematically organized and to send them to him as soon as possible. I believe that among them were both the documents which Aetius had indicated had been sent and the *Summary* which Julian had stated that he had sent but which Saint Leo complained had not reached him. [Col. 1436B]

### 3. “Of the synodal Acts”

From this, if I am not mistaken, it is possible to determine 1518 [Note: In order to judge Quesnell’s third note, it must first be established what material from the Council of Chalcedon had been translated into Latin before Rusticus and what Rusticus himself accomplished.

Only a few portions of the Chalcedonian Acts had been translated into Latin before the complete translation of the Acts. It is uncertain whether the Latin copy of the sentence which Leo sent to the Gauls with Epistle 103 is an original document or a translation from the Greek, as we noted there in annotation 6.

The first certain translation is that of almost the whole of Session 6 preserved in Vatican manuscript 1322, about which we said more in our observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 9 in the case of Domnus. The Chalcedonian definition is inserted in this translation; it is then appended again from another version in the same manuscript, as we observed in the work just mentioned.

Five translations of this definition printed by Baluze are found in volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils: one taken from the Hispanic and Isidorian collections, column 2055d, and four others from different ancient collections, column 2057b. One of these is the same as the second version cited from the Vatican manuscript.

All of them, however, are earlier than the two translations prepared by the ancient translator of all the Chalcedonian Acts, who inserted one in the fifth session and the other in the sixth. We therefore believe that this definition was translated from the Greek into Latin by six translators before the complete translation of all the Acts.

Two versions of the canons also survive which are older than the complete translation of all the Acts. One was transmitted into the Quesnellian and other very ancient collections of different origin—the Vatican Regina, Barberini, Lucense, and Colbertine collections, as well as the Justellian collection—and the other into the Hispanic collection and from there into the Isidorian collection.

We have also presented, in the observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 9 cited above, three sessions concerning Maximus of Antioch which were translated into Latin during Leo’s lifetime.

Finally, apart from certain letters of Marcian promulgated before and after the synod, which appear to have been published in Latin and derived from a Latin original, since similar versions are found in Latin collections of different origin and were immediately available to Romans and Westerners, a Latin abridgment of the two principal sessions, the third and the sixth, was prepared before the complete translation of the Acts. We have said enough about this in the observations on the preceding note.

It is certain that the fuller translation of the Acts, which Leo requested from Julian in Epistle 113 as complete and finished, was made before Rusticus. The first translator, however, used Greek manuscripts in which two sessions were missing—those concerning Photius of Tyre and Carosus and Dorotheus, and two concerning Maximus and Domnus of Antioch—as well as the session in which Leo’s Epistle 93 to the synod was read. On these matters see what we said in annotation 18 of Quesnell’s Dissertation 1, concerning the year 451.

Only two manuscripts of this ancient translation, so far as we know, survive: the Paris manuscript, which Baluze used, and the manuscript of the Queen of the Swedes, of which he received information from Cardinal Casanata.

The fact that this translation cannot be attributed to Julian of Cos, before Rusticus, is chiefly suggested by the following consideration: if the Chalcedonian Acts had been translated into Latin by him immediately after the synod, since he possessed complete copies of the council, his translation would not contain as many omissions in several sessions as those we have indicated.

The following point demonstrates even more clearly that this translation is not Julian’s: it places before the Acts the Chalcedonian canons in the translation of Dionysius Exiguus. Dionysius plainly did not take these canons from the older translation, but translated them from the Greek. Hence this same version also received the titles of the canons which Dionysius composed in his own manner. Likewise, in Act 11, Antiochene canon 16 is reported from the same translation of Dionysius in the Paris manuscript.

Therefore this translation of the Chalcedonian Acts was either prepared by Dionysius Exiguus himself, or produced in the age of Dionysius after the publication of his collection of the canons. We accordingly think that this version was made around the pontificate of Hormisdas, at the beginning of the sixth century.

The first people certainly to use this translation lived under Vigilius, as Baluze clearly demonstrated in his preface to the ancient translation of the Council of Chalcedon, where he confirms this judgment with several arguments.

The material which Baluze published and annotated from three manuscripts of Rusticus plainly shows that Rusticus collated and corrected not merely the first session of the ancient translation, but the whole translation, comparing it with both Greek and Latin manuscripts from Constantinople; he also repeatedly added annotations.

Rusticus was not merely an editor and commentator of the ancient translation. He produced a new translation of Session 7, concerning Maximus and Juvenal, and of the two reports of the synod to Saint Leo and to the Empress Pulcheria. He also added a translation of the session concerning Domnus, which was absent from the ancient translation; he took it from the still older version which we have shown, in our observations on Quesnell’s Dissertation 9, to have been made during Leo’s lifetime.

He also inserted Marcian’s original Latin address to the synod—which the ancient Latin collections had already preserved for us, for example the Quesnellian collection and Vatican manuscript 1322—and several imperial laws promulgated in Latin.

Baluze, volume IV of the Councils, column 2025, after presenting Rusticus’s note, “I myself translated the reports of the holy synod into Latin from a Greek manuscript of the Acoemetes,” adds the following:

“I found this note in ancient copies and in Crabbe’s edition.”

Therefore the items translated by Rusticus are these. Besides the reports, he mentions four laws of Marcian and one of Theodosius, which in the uncorrupted manuscripts of Rusticus are appended to the third session.

Rusticus states that he himself translated only the reports into Latin. Since the laws had been published in Latin, he did not translate them into Latin but inserted them as he found them already published. Two of these laws are read verbatim in the Quesnellian collection, chapters 26 and 27, which is earlier than Rusticus; some are also found in the Hispanic collection, which was not derived from the manuscripts of Rusticus.

This happened because the laws had been published in Latin. Consequently, both these collectors and Rusticus found and inserted them in the same words. It is therefore not surprising that Facundus, *Book XII*, chapter 2, quoted from Marcian’s edict in confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon the same words that are found in Rusticus. We do not attribute to Rusticus the act of giving these laws a Latin form, but rather the act of adding laws already written and published in Latin to the ancient translation.

Rusticus altered the order of the sessions in some places. The session that is Session 3 in the ancient translation he made second on the basis of the Greek manuscripts; the one that had been second he transferred to third place. He removed the canons that had been appended to Session 6 and constituted Session 15 from them.

Baluze correctly assigned this work of Rusticus to the period between the tenth day before the Kalends of March in the year 549 and the third day before the Kalends of April in the year 550, in the preface cited above, section 21. His edition must be observed carefully in order to understand the order in which Rusticus arranged his edition of the Council of Chalcedon. See volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 1980 and following.

On this occasion, since we have spoken about Rusticus’s edition, we offer information not previously explained about certain manuscripts which, although they contain Rusticus’s edition, differ from his uncorrupted copies.

Baluze found only three pure manuscripts of Rusticus: the Divionensis, the Corbeiensis, and the Thuane-Colbertinus, although the last is mutilated and ends in the first session. We found one manuscript, Chigianus 483, entirely similar to them. Peter Crabbe used another manuscript of the same type when he published the complete Acts according to Rusticus’s edition.

We have also encountered more numerous manuscripts which present the same edition of Rusticus but omit all or nearly all of his annotations and sometimes depart from his order as well. Such are all the Vatican manuscripts 1321, 1323, 4166, and 5405, and our very ancient manuscript 57 of the chapter of Verona.

In Vatican 1322, which begins with the second session, the synod’s report to Leo is taken from the ancient translation, although the remainder follows Rusticus.

Since the Roman editors of the councils knew only these manuscripts, which lack Rusticus’s annotations, they should not be blamed for omitting the annotations published by Crabbe. Since those annotations were absent from their manuscripts, they did not know with what authority Crabbe had added them.

At the end of the manuscripts Verona 57 and Vatican 1321, 1323, and 5405, which contain an incomplete edition of Rusticus, there is appended a letter on the Catholic faith in defense of the Three Chapters. It begins, “He warns certain people.” Peter Dacherius published it under the name of Facundus from a copy in the *Spicilegium*, and for this reason it was reprinted among the works of Facundus in the edition of the works of Peter Sirmond.

But apart from the fact that the author’s name is not found in the manuscripts just mentioned, and that this letter is not listed in the outstanding manuscript Verona 61, nearly contemporary with Facundus and containing his works, an equally ancient manuscript, Verona 57, has the following note written by a second hand in the upper margin beside the letter:

“The whole letter, if properly examined, is entirely suspect and plainly infected with the stench of the pestilential heresy of Nestorius and Theodore of Mopsuestia. Its author is not stated here, but is wholly unknown today.”

In Vatican manuscript 1321 this letter, like the others, is appended to the Chalcedonian Acts but is separated from the works of Facundus. For after this letter, copied without an author’s name, there follow other short works which have nothing whatever to do with the Three Chapters. Then, under the name of Facundus, come twelve books on behalf of the Three Chapters and his letter against Mutianus Scholasticus.

Does not this separation of the first letter, which lacks an author’s name, from the certain works of Facundus marked with his name indicate that it was written by a different and unknown author? Since Dacherius does not identify the manuscript from which he took his copy, nor explicitly state that the name of Facundus was prefixed to the letter in it, a substantial doubt arises for us as to whether this letter was copied from some manuscript resembling the aforementioned Chalcedonian manuscripts, in which alone we have happened to find this letter without an author’s name.

It may have been attributed to Facundus because it deals with the defense of the Three Chapters, just as all his other works do, and perhaps also because it was found together with his works, as in the Vatican manuscript mentioned last.

Facundus wrote his works before the Fifth Council, under Vigilius; this letter, however, was written after the council, under Pope Pelagius. Unless its authorship is established more securely, we do not dare affirm that Facundus broke into the open schism revealed by the letter.

Those Africans who did not accept the council were punished with exile. The author of the letter complains about the exiles but does not identify himself as one. This raises the suspicion that he was an Italian who had fomented the schism on account of the Three Chapters. Whether the style differs from that of Facundus may be determined by others through comparison.] [Col. 1435B–D]

From these considerations it follows, unless I am mistaken, that the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon were collected, translated, and arranged in the form in which they now exist by Julian, Bishop of Cos, at the request of Saint Leo; and that those who proclaim the deacon Rusticus their collector should not be heard.

For from the annotation alone 1519 which is appended to the first session it is evident that the Acts had merely been collated, annotated, and distinguished by Rusticus from other copies. This is made still clearer by the Thuane manuscript, which contains part of the first Chalcedonian session with the following title:

“Here end the preliminary proceedings which were set forth above; now begin the proceedings of the first Council of Chalcedon. Rusticus corrected them from Latin and Greek copies, especially from the Acoemete monastery. The first session of the Council of Chalcedon 1520, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, began to be corrected on the tenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twelfth indiction.”

Chifflet also testifies that he read the same statement in a manuscript of the Chalcedonian Acts, with Rusticus the deacon described as the collector—or rather, as I think it should be read, the corrector—in which manuscript of the library of Jean Bohier of Dijon, a senator, Rusticus likewise mentions the manuscripts of the Acoemetes which he had used in correcting the Acts of the council.

Nor does Nicolinus’s Venetian edition of the Councils, 1521, remain silent about the same manuscripts, although it corruptly calls them “Acuminian,” and wished certain passages from them to be inserted in smaller type into the received text.

From an examination and comparison of all these witnesses, I believe that I can draw several conclusions not unworthy of notice.

First, the Latin collection of the Chalcedonian Acts now in everyone’s hands is older than the deacon Rusticus, who around the year of our Lord 550 was residing at Constantinople with Pope Vigilius and working there to correct the aforesaid collection. This is clear both from the edition of Nicolinus already mentioned and especially from the Thuane manuscript, which not only mentions correction but also, while preserving intact the ancient order of the Acts, displays Rusticus’s corrections in the margins, preceded by this notice:

“I have placed the annotation marked with a + outside each individual speech, in such a way that the Greek manuscript of the Acoemetes contains it in Latin.”

### [Col. 1439B] 2.

It may be suspected that Rusticus corrected only the first session; this seems to me to follow from the title which I transcribed above from the Thuane manuscript. Moreover, at the end of the first and only session, all the printed manuscripts which I have seen, and also the manuscripts, mention Rusticus’s collation and correction.

Finally, only the first session contains passages inserted from the Acumete—or rather Acoemete—manuscript in the editions of Nicolinus and Surius.

I would not, however, have these conclusions accepted as certain, just as I would not dare deny that the Acoemete manuscript which Rusticus had begun to examine might afterward have been carried to the West and copied by many people.

If what we say is true, and only part of the Acts was corrected by Rusticus, this may perhaps have happened because, after he had defected from Vigilius when Vigilius descended to the condemnation of the Three Chapters, together with his colleague Sebastian, Rusticus was forced to leave the imperial city and the monastery of the Acoemetes, where, because of the controversy then raging, he had begun to investigate the Chalcedonian materials more carefully. [Col. 1439C]

A third conclusion drawn from what has been said is that the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon were scarcely known in the more remote parts of the West before the Fifth Council, particularly in our Gaul. The Gauls had learned about the outcome of that synod almost exclusively through the letters of Saint Leo written to the Gallic bishops and through the sentence against Dioscorus attached to one of those letters.

A witness to this assertion is canon 1 of the Fifth Council of Orléans. Its bishops, suppressing mention of the Council of Chalcedon, seem to rely solely upon the decree of the Apostolic See against Nestorian and Eutychian doctrine. This occurred in the year 549, at the time when Rusticus was attacking Pope Vigilius.

Later, when the controversy over the Three Chapters had grown more heated, and their condemners were openly and everywhere denounced throughout the provinces as opponents of the Council of Chalcedon—especially when the decrees of the Fifth Council were persistently rejected by Africans, Illyrians, Dalmatians, Insubrians, Istrians, 1522 Gauls, Spaniards, Iberians, and others as having been issued to the prejudice of the preceding council—then copies of the Acts of this Fourth Council began to be eagerly sought everywhere, avidly read, and copied by many.

There is no doubt that Rusticus, who was so hostile to Vigilius and the other opponents of the Three Chapters, and who had been made still more embittered by his own deposition, undertook the task of spreading copies of the synod throughout the provinces, just as he everywhere proclaimed Vigilius a deserter of the Council of Chalcedon.

It is especially likely that our Gauls, who seem either never to have accepted the Fifth Council or to have accepted it only later, received such copies from Rusticus, since they had been warned by him of what he considered Vigilius’s unspeakable betrayal of the holy Council of Chalcedon. This may be understood both from Vigilius’s letter to Aurelian, bishop of Arles, and from the letter of the clergy of Italy to the Gallic legates sent to Constantinople.

This suspicion is strengthened by the fact that we have no edition of the Council of Chalcedon in the West which does not mention Rusticus, as though the first copies of that synod to arrive in Gaul had come from him.

The Roman, Crabbian, Nicolinian, and Surian editions of the Councils all likewise mention Rusticus, as does the manuscript of Bohier cited by Chifflet and in the edition mentioned above. [Col. 1440A]

## On Epistle 114, 87 in Quesnell

To the bishops who had attended the Council of Chalcedon.

### 1. “To the holy synod held at Chalcedon”

After the Council of Chalcedon had been dissolved and the adherents of the Eutychian sect condemned, its opponents thought that they had found one principal objection against the decrees of the synod: namely, that these decrees had not been enacted and received by the unanimous agreement of all, and indeed that the first of all sees—the Roman See—had contradicted them so completely that it had utterly refused to give them its consent.

The heretics had seized upon the fact that Saint Leo’s legates had rejected canon 28 and that Leo himself had disapproved it as an opportunity for spreading the slander that the Council of Chalcedon had been rejected by the Apostolic See.

The Emperor wrote to Leo about this matter and observed that no more effective means of rebutting the slander could be found than to make it known throughout all the Churches that the definitions of the holy Council of Chalcedon were pleasing to the Apostolic See. (Epistle 89, now 115.)

Saint Leo complied and wrote the present letter to all the bishops of the synod, whom he still addresses under the title “the holy synod.” In this letter and in others sent on the same day, he rebuts the slander of the heretics with several arguments.

First, there could be no doubt that he embraced the definition of that synod with his whole heart, since one who had grieved so deeply over the Church’s being torn apart by heretics could not fail to rejoice at the restoration of unity. (Epistle 87, now 114, chapter 1.)

1523

Second, this was evident from the agreement of the legates who had represented him at the synod. (The same letter.)

Third, it was no less clear from the letters which he had written to Anatolius after the legates’ return to the City. (The same letter.)

Fourth, the synod had defined nothing which he himself had not previously written in the letter to which the consent of all who subscribed had been given, since that letter had been issued according to the form of apostolic teaching and the tradition of the Fathers. (Epistle 89, now 115.)

Fifth, he had united his own judgment not only personally with that of the holy Fathers through the persons of his legates, but also through his approval of the synodal Acts—though only in the matter of the faith, on account of which the general council had been convened. (Epistle 87, now 114, chapter 1.)

It is therefore clear that this approval arose solely from the occasion of the calumny, namely, lest someone’s deceitful pretence should make his judgment appear uncertain (Epistle 90, now 116, ch. 2), and lest, through malicious interpreters, it should seem doubtful whether he approved what had been decreed concerning the faith at the Council of Chalcedon (Epistle 87, now 114, ch. 1). He did not therefore write this letter of approval because the sacred decrees lacked [Col. 1441A] force.

[Note: [Col. 1439D] The sacred decrees certainly did not lack force—not because the synod’s decrees, by themselves and without the pontiff’s approval, possessed the force of a general council, but because, in regard to the faith, these decrees had already been sufficiently approved by Leo in earlier letters, and especially in Epistle 106 [Col. 1440D], to Anatolius, as the same pontiff openly testifies in this very Epistle 114 and in the following Epistle 115. Thus, in Epistle 115, to Marcian, he writes: “Through my brother Bishop Lucian I sent to your Glory and to the Bishop of Constantinople such letters as would clearly show that I approved what had been defined concerning the Catholic faith in the aforesaid synod.” Those same Orientals who had introduced doubt concerning the definition of Chalcedon on the ground that Leo had not approved it—the letter of Leo to Anatolius, by which he had approved the synod, having been suppressed—plainly show that the Orientals considered this pontifical approval altogether necessary, so that no doubt could be entertained concerning the council’s definition [Col. 1441D]. Hence Marcian requested not so much its confirmation as its publication in the Churches as something necessary, in Epistle 110; compare our note 2 (Col. 1018, n. h). Other testimonies of Leo and of the Orientals likewise confirm this necessity of confirmation for the force of the council’s decrees. Hence, when Leo declared the council’s definition irretractable, he joined it with the pontiff’s confirmation, Epistle 160, ch. 2: “For concerning matters defined by the authority of so great a synod . . . and confirmed by the assent of the Apostolic See, nothing ought to be questioned.” He repeats the same in Epistle 163, to Anatolius.]

He wrote it rather so that he himself might not be disgraced through contempt for the venerable synod, nor might those who opposed the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon boast that he was their leader; and, finally, lest he should seem to contradict the imperial will, which he openly professed that he himself must obey in every way (Epistle 89, now 115, ch. 2). Anyone who wishes to learn more about this kind of confirmation of the Council of Chalcedon should consult the most learned Jean Launoy, Part II of his *Epistles*, in the letter to the illustrious Jacques Bevilaqua (Boileau), Parisian theologian, now most deserving dean of the metropolitan and primatial Church of Sens and, during the vacancy of the see, appointed to administer justice and govern the diocese.

All earlier editions, except the Roman edition of the decretal letters, give this letter the following heading, addressed to Juvenal: “To Juvenal and the other bishops who were assembled in the holy Synod of Chalcedon.” Juvenal was one of these bishops, and beyond doubt a copy of the letter was sent to him [Col. 1441B]; from that copy it was later transcribed, retaining his name. The heading is absent, however, from the Griman, Victor, and Trecopith manuscripts, from three Thuan manuscripts, from the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, and, as I have said, from the Roman edition of the pontifical letters. Pope Pelagius II and Facundus of Hermiane likewise cite the letter in the same form.

### 2. “With the effect of agreement”

Thus read the manuscript copies, the Roman edition, and Facundus, not “with affection,” as it was formerly read. I believe this must be understood of the agreement of the legates, as he himself explains in these words: “Not only through the brothers who acted in my place, but also through the approval of the synodal acts, I united my own judgment with yours.”

### 3. “He would have wished to make known”

After this, says Baluzius, the following words occur in the manuscripts of Rusticus:

“But because in the same letters I had criticized what had been wrongly attempted on the occasion of the synod, the aforesaid bishop preferred to conceal my congratulation rather than publish his own ambition.”

Baluzius adds:

“It must nevertheless be admitted that, although these words are written consecutively, in the ancient copies they are divided and separated from the text of the letter.”

The style is that of St. Leo, and these are his words. For, treating this very matter in Epistle 60, now 116, to the Empress Pulcheria, he says: “Unless he had preferred to conceal my joy”—that is, my congratulation—“rather than publish the rejection of his ambition.” The editors of St. Leo’s letters did not notice this. Indeed, Baluzius, we did notice it—not in the Divion manuscript, which we were not able to use, but in the third part of the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, p. 881 of Labbe’s edition. Labbe had excerpted the same words from your Divion manuscript before you and relegated them to the margin. The learned man understood that they were indeed Leo’s style and words, but that they had been taken from Epistle 59, now 89, for us 115, ch. 1. This explains why this patch was found separated from the text of Epistle 61, Book VIII, now 87, for us 114: some student had cut it from its original location and sewn it onto this letter for the purpose of illustrating it.

### 4. “I requested”

This is the reading that must be adopted, as we have emended it, not “he requested,” as the Roman edition of 1525 and other editions have it. This is demonstrated by the Victor, Griman, and other manuscripts, as well as by Epistle 89, now 115, ch. 2, where our Leo requests precisely this from the emperor.

### 5. “I united my own judgment with yours”

This is the reading of the Griman manuscript, with which Facundus agrees when he transcribes these words on p. 203 of Book V, ch. 4, although in Book II, ch. 6, he reads: “I communicated my own judgment to you,” which I believe is due to a scribal error. Pelagius II, together with the common text [Col. 1442B], reads: “I entered into my own judgment with you.”

## On Epistle CXV, Epistle LXXXIX in Quesnellus: To the Emperor Marcian

### 1. “Both royal power and priestly diligence”

[Note: [Col. 1441D] Three things must be distinguished in priests, or bishops: order, the power of the keys, and solicitude for the Church. If someone, even a layman, undertakes this last—so far as it lies within his power—which involves vigilance, labors, diligence, and concern for the faith, unity, and discipline of the Church [Col. 1442C], then, as a participant in priestly solicitude, he may obtain the title of priest and bishop. In this sense St. Leo commends in the emperors Marcian and Leo their priestly diligence, mind, spirit, disposition, holiness, and solicitude. They labored greatly for the faith and unity of the Church against the heresy of Eutyches. Since Marcian and Pulcheria issued very learned enactments against the same heretics, in accordance with the teaching of the Church and of the bishops, he professed that a priestly teaching was present in them [Col. 1442D]. Other testimonies concerning other Augusti must be understood in the same sense. Nevertheless, no one can regard a layman, merely because he shares in priestly solicitude, as equally participating either in the priestly order or in the power of the keys, by which spiritual jurisdiction is signified. All Catholics acknowledge that this belongs solely to priests, or bishops, whom the Holy Spirit appointed to govern the Church of God, and to whom Christ entrusted the keys of the Church in Peter. Hence the first Emperor Constantine, who undertook great solicitude for the Church, carefully distinguishing his own authority from that of the bishops, spoke to the bishops as Eusebius reports in *Life of Constantine*, Book IV: “You are bishops over what is within the Church; I am appointed by God as bishop over what takes place outside.”]

A similar expression occurs in Epistle 124, now 155: “To implore not only his royal but also his priestly mind,” etc.; in Epistle 125, now 156, ch. 6, to the Emperor Leo: “For the priestly and apostolic spirit of your Piety,” etc.; and in Epistle 112, now 142, ch. 1: “Your Piety has admonished me with priestly solicitude.” Above, too, in Epistle 84, now 111, ch. 3, to Marcian: “Who grants you, besides the royal crown, also the palm of priesthood”; in Epistle 90, now 116, to Pulcheria: “We recognize that the rulers of our age possess not only royal power but also priestly instruction”; and in Epistle 88, now 117, [Col. 1442C] ch. 2, to Julian: “So that everyone may see their excellence to be not only that of royal majesty but also of priestly holiness.” Either read *omnibus* (“to all”), or, in place of *appareat*, put *intelligant* (“they may understand”). In Epistle 105, now 134: “He expresses a priestly disposition in a most Christian ruler”; and in Epistle 123, now 154: “He burns with priestly affection.”

Truly I would call our pontiff’s spirit royal: he so willingly admits the emperor into fellowship with his priesthood and apostleship, fearing neither that his own dignity will thereby be diminished nor begrudging the increase and splendor of royal eminence. Our most Christian emperors rewarded Leo in his successors by granting them temporal dominion in turn and increasing, through earthly rule, the priestly dignity of the city of Rome, so that, while both powers were joined and as it were intermingled in such close alliance, neither might ever be separated from the other for the peace of the Church and the Empire.

The Fathers of Chalcedon had preceded Leo in this. In Act 6 of the council they acclaimed Marcian: “To the priest-emperor, many years!”—Τῷ ἱερεῖ τῷ βασιλεῖ. Indeed, the bishops of the Constantinopolitan synod under Flavian likewise honored Theodosius with the same encomium, acclaiming: “To the high-priest-emperor”—Τῷ ἀρχιερεῖ τῷ βασιλεῖ—“to the pontiff-emperor.”

In the same sense Fortunatus, Book II, poem 11, praises Childebert, king of the Franks:

> Our Melchizedek, rightly both king and priest,  
> fulfilled as a layman the work of religion.

The basis of this praise, leaving other matters aside, may be read in Justinian, *Novella* 7, ch. 2, where he says: “Since priesthood and imperial power do not differ greatly from one another, nor sacred matters from common and public affairs.” For this reason, long before all these writers, Eusebius praises this emperor in *Life of Constantine*, ch. 44: “Because, taking special care of the Church of God, when certain persons in different provinces were at variance with one another, he, as though appointed by God as the common bishop of all, assembled synods of God’s ministers.” And in Book IV, chs. 22 and 24, Constantine himself says to the bishops: “You are bishops over what is within the Church; I am appointed by God as bishop over what takes place outside.”

### 2. “Since the agreement in the faith of all who subscribe has also been added, [the faith] which was issued by me”

Thus reads the Griman manuscript. In the common editions, however: “Since, by their subscribing, the agreement of all has been added to the faith which was sent to me.” This appears to have been understood of the definitions of the Council of Chalcedon sent to St. Leo, whereas the pontiff most certainly speaks of his own letter written to Flavian and confirmed by the subscriptions of all.

[Col. 1443C]

### 3. “Lucian”

It is probable that this legate was the same Lucian, bishop of Byzia, who participated in the Council of Chalcedon both in his own name and in that of Cyriacus, bishop of Heraclea in Thrace. In Act 16, where the privileges of the See of Constantinople were defined, he subscribed once and again: first on behalf of Cyriacus, and second in his own name, as follows: “Lucian, bishop of Byzia and Arcadiopolis, subscribing to the definition.” It is therefore not surprising that he, already bound by his own signature and zealous for the dignity of the Bishop of Constantinople, to whose ordination he belonged, was chosen to act before St. Leo for the confirmation of the privileges of both Anatolius and the emperor, indeed [Note: [Col. 1443C] Lucian is known to have been sent to Leo in the name of Anatolius and the emperor from Epistles 100 and 101, but not likewise in the name of the synod. Although he is mentioned in Epistle 100 of the emperor and Epistle 101 of Anatolius, he is not named in the synodal report, our Epistle 98. Moreover, in Epistle 101 Anatolius states that the synodal report was delivered to the pontiff not by Lucian but by the Roman legates.] in the name of the entire synod.

### 4. “And concerning the condemnation of the heretics”

These words are absent from Pope Pelagius II’s letter to Elias and the other bishops of Istria in the matter of the Three Chapters. No one will believe that they slipped out accidentally or were deliberately omitted. To suppose the latter either of Pelagius or of Gregory the Great, who is thought to have written the letter while he was still serving as a deacon, would be a grave sacrilege. The subject itself prevents the other assertion: the entire letter investigates only this question—whether the writings of St. Leo composed to confirm the acts of the Council of Chalcedon are produced merely in defense of the unimpaired faith, or also for particular episcopal cases that were discussed at Chalcedon. In that controversy, to have suppressed the words in question would not have been free from the fault of evasion [Col. 1444B]. It is therefore preferable to attribute the omission to the scribes’ negligence, since the words are present in all other printed and manuscript copies, especially in the insufficiently commendable Griman manuscript.

## On Epistle CXIX, Epistle XCII in Quesnellus: To Maximus, Bishop of Antioch

### 1. “Leo to Maximus of Antioch”

Thus reads the Griman manuscript, Barb. 1, and two Thuan manuscripts, with which agree all the earlier editions of Canisius, as in the councils edited at Merlin, Cologne 1530 and 1535. In the common editions after Canisius’s edition: “Leo, bishop of the Catholic Church, to Maximus, his most beloved brother, bishop of Antioch.”

### 2. “In the Eastern Churches”

For the various meanings and divisions of the East that may assist in understanding this passage, consult, if you wish, the illustrious Peter de Marca’s dissertation on the establishment of the Constantinopolitan patriarchate, and Books I, Exercises II and III, of the Oratorian priest Jean Morin’s *Ecclesiastical Exercises*.

I will say only that by the term “Eastern Churches” the passage seems to include both those provinces that at that time lay under the jurisdiction of the Eastern, or Antiochene, patriarch and others that were virtually *autocephalous*—αὐτοκέφαλαι—and subject to their own authority, at least if we consider their original status.

[Note: [Col. 1443C] When St. Leo commends to Maximus’s vigilance that he should in no way permit wicked heretics to assail the Gospel in the Eastern Churches, and especially in those which the Nicene canons of the most sacred Fathers assigned to the See of Antioch, this passage concerns neither the question of the rights of the See of Antioch violated by Juvenal of Jerusalem, of which he speaks later, nor that of the rights of the metropolitans of Thrace, Pontus, and Asia violated by Anatolius, which did not concern Antioch; rather, it most plainly concerns solely the cause of the faith, the perverse doctrines of the heretics, and their efforts in the East. To understand what he means by the provinces of the East, one need not resort to the question of sees’ rights, but must infer it from elsewhere. The following Epistle 120, to Theodoret, dated on the same day and mentioning this letter to Maximus, provides sufficient indication. In Epistle 120, likewise concerned for the cause of faith, the Holy Pontiff commends the same cause to Theodoret in chapter 6: “For the rest, we exhort you, because we know that THERE some remnants of the Eutychian and Nestorian error remain, now also to cooperate with the Apostolic See,” etc. And shortly afterward: “Hasten to inform the Apostolic See what progress the Lord’s teaching is making in THOSE regions, so that we may assist the priests of THAT region . . . .” If the whole letter is read, the expressions THERE, THOSE REGIONS, and so forth cannot be referred to anything but the East in its broad sense, as distinguished from the West. Thus he says in chapter 2: “The radiance of the Sun of righteousness, obstructed by the thick clouds of Nestorius and Eutyches throughout the East, shone forth purely from the West.” The heresy had indeed spread its poison throughout the whole East; and especially at this time, while heretics were causing disturbances in Palestine and Egypt, remnants of error could not be lacking. Leo therefore commended the East broadly understood to Theodoret, that, cooperating with him, he might keep watch, report to the Apostolic See, and so forth. Why should he not have commended the same to Maximus, who had greater authority than Theodoret? Quesnellus’s arguments below to exclude Egypt will prove weak and trivial. For no right over the Churches of Egypt was entrusted to the Bishop of Antioch; but amid the very grave disturbances caused by heretics, in which St. Proterius, recently ordained bishop of Alexandria, had neither a sufficiently secure see nor adequate authority, St. Leo thought the authority of Maximus, bishop of the third see, would be useful.]

Such were the Asian and Pontic dioceses. Because Constantinople had subjected them to its ordination, with the support of the emperors and even by decree of the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon, St. Leo, who wished that decree to be nullified, commends them to the care and solicitude of the Bishop of Antioch—not by patriarchal right, since they did not belong to him, but by the title of charity, which has no limits. Thus, by these Churches we should not understand all those that are distinguished from the Western Churches, but only those distinct dioceses that had been under his authority.

1. Leo intended to criticize and restrain Anatolius’s ambition. Anatolius had certainly not sought to subject all the Eastern Churches in the former sense, but only the Thracian, Pontic, and Asian dioceses.

2. By these words he would have turned the hatred and envy of the Bishop of Alexandria against himself if he had commended to the Bishop of Antioch Churches obedient to Alexandria’s jurisdiction, especially since some hostility had always existed between them.

3. The end of this letter and of the following letter shows that Leo’s solicitude arose chiefly from the presumption of certain monks who were blurting out many things against the faith in their preaching. He therefore warns both Maximus and Theodoret that, to cut off this evil, the ministry of preaching should be forbidden to monks and to others who did not possess the priestly rank.

Moreover, another letter of Leo, addressed to Julian of Cos and dated in April of this year, 453, makes clear that this presumption of the monks was especially prevalent in the Caesarean Church of Cappadocia, the chief church of the Pontic diocese. There, a certain monk named George, supported by Thalassius, bishop of Caesarea, arrogated to himself the office of writing and preaching. Previously, as St. Leo complains, by presuming to do what was unlawful he had forfeited both the proper purpose and the name of a monk.

Thus the occasion seems to have arisen for Leo to write to Maximus and Theodoret about this matter, because he was prevented from warning Anatolius about it both by the interruption of their correspondence and by Anatolius’s ambition to claim the Pontic Churches, an ambition in which he would have supported him.

[Note: [Col. 1445D] This will be shown false from note 30 (Col. 1045, n. g) on this letter.]

When Leo adds, “and especially in those which the canons of the most sacred Fathers of Nicaea assigned to the See of Antioch,” he means those provinces which the Bishop of Antioch administered at the time of the Council of Nicaea. Its sixth decree established that the ancient customs should remain in force both in Egypt and in Antioch, and that their Churches should retain their privileges. By these words Leo also reproves and pierces Juvenal’s ambition. As is stated below, Juvenal had drawn courage and confidence to invade the primacy of the province of Palestine from the dispute that had arisen between Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch at the First Council of Ephesus.

Since Juvenal could not obtain this by ecclesiastical decree against the opposition not only of the Bishop of Antioch but also of the Bishop of Alexandria, he appealed to imperial rescripts. By their authority not only Palestine but also Arabia and Phoenicia were detached from the Antiochene diocese and assigned to the See of Jerusalem. Yet when the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon judged that all pragmatic sanctions and imperial rescripts by which the rights of Churches had been transferred must be set aside, and when the dispute between the two Churches arose again, the litigants eventually settled it in Act 7 on the condition that, while Arabia and Phoenicia remained with Antioch, the Antiochene would yield the three Palestines to Jerusalem.

I do not recount these matters here without purpose. I wish the reader to wonder with me and to ask why our Leo, who resisted with all his strength the efforts of the Bishop of Constantinople because they appeared contrary to the Nicene canons, does not here rise against the Bishop of Jerusalem, who was trampling upon an ancient custom equally confirmed by the Nicene decree when he invaded provinces belonging to another.

Furthermore, why does he speak of Juvenal’s efforts as though they had been fruitless and had achieved nothing, when Juvenal nevertheless held the three Palestines subject to himself?

[Note: [Col. 1445D] The two conjectures that follow, which Quesnellus attributes to the suspicions of others, are entirely foreign to Leo’s mind. He did not resist the privilege of the See of Constantinople because he feared that it might thereby threaten him, but because, out of zeal for discipline, he was exceedingly anxious that the Nicene canons be observed, and detested attempts by which those canons would be nullified. The hypothesis that Leo overlooked Juvenal’s efforts because he thought it useful to diminish the power of the Eastern patriarchs rests on a false premise. Leo did not overlook them in this letter but criticized them; he merely judged that the proper time had to be awaited for acting more forcefully against Juvenal, who at that time, expelled from his see, did not possess the privilege he had obtained, as we explained in the observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation 9, no. 9. If no contradiction is found on this point in Epistle 139, which he sent to Juvenal after Juvenal had been restored to his see, either Maximus had not yet written anything definite, or at this time Leo thought it more useful to concentrate, for the sake of restoring the faith, on this one matter—that is, on the restoration of the faith.]

Someone may think that Leo concealed these matters *κατ’ οἰκονομίαν*—“by a prudent policy”—lest new seeds of disturbance should be sown in such turbulent times. He may have done so all the more readily because the power and increase of the Bishop of Jerusalem were not as alarming to the Roman bishop as those of the Bishop of Constantinople, who rivaled the privileges of the first see in every respect and was advancing with great strides toward a monarchy over the Eastern and perhaps even the Western Churches.

Others may suggest that Leo, who wished to diminish the authority of the bishop of the imperial city because he regarded it as threatening his own, vigorously defended the privileges of the other patriarchs so that Constantinople might not grow; but when those same patriarchs were contending with other men who coveted primacy, he was not unwilling to allow something to be taken from the splendor and strength of the former—not from any wrongful envy of their eminence and glory, but because, in those most difficult times when the errors of Nestorius and Eutyches were invading every province, it was greatly in the interest of religion and the Church that the power of the Eastern bishops be diminished.

I would rather believe that, because Rome at that time had only an insufficient understanding of the synodal acts—the acts completed at Chalcedon on every day of the council, as Leo himself states in Epistle 86, now 113—owing to the diversity of languages, not everything that had been done there came to Leo’s knowledge. Thus he was completely unaware of what had taken place in the seventh act between Maximus and Juvenal.

[Note: [Col. 1446D] St. Leo was not ignorant of the seventh act concerning Maximus and Juvenal, since it was sent to him by Maximus together with two other acts, as we explained in the observations on Dissertation 9, no. 9. The following conjectures of Quesnellus must therefore be evaluated in light of that fact.]

Although the dispute had been settled by the mutual agreement of both parties, and not only the Eastern but also the legates of the Roman See had confirmed the synodal decree by their assent, I believe that St. Leo would never have tolerated such a thing had he known of it. He did not consider it permissible for a bishop to surrender the privileges of his see to another contrary to the statutes of the Council of Nicaea and to a custom strengthened over many centuries. He testified to this when he wrote against Hilary, Bishop of Arles, and rebuked Ingenuus of Embrun because, for Hilary’s benefit, he had not defended his own rights against him. If St. Leo had detected anything about Juvenal’s ambition, he learned it from Maximus’s letters.

For although Maximus, for the sake of peace and in order not to have the emperor as an enemy, had yielded to some extent so that the Bishop of Jerusalem might obtain the three Palestines, there is no doubt that he was deeply distressed at having the most extensive provinces taken from his jurisdiction.

As soon, therefore, as he learned that Leo disapproved of what had been decreed in the final canon of Chalcedon for the enlargement of the See of Constantinople, and that Leo could be induced by no arguments—even when the emperors and one of the legates, Julian, intervened on Anatolius’s behalf—to accept that decree, out of reverence for the Nicene canons by which the privileges of the Churches had been confirmed, Maximus recovered courage and suggested to Leo by letter what rights had been taken from him through Juvenal’s ambition.

He wrote rather obscurely, both about the power adjudicated to Juvenal over the three Palestines and about the assent given by the legates, lest he should be accused before the emperor of having violated the peace and renewed the dissension, and lest he should turn the legates’ goodwill away from himself. Yet he did write this, as I seem to gather clearly enough from Leo’s reply. 1532

First, this is the reason Leo speaks so cautiously when he exhorts Maximus “in no way to permit the Gospel to be assailed by wicked heretics in the Eastern Churches, and especially in those which the canons of the most sacred Fathers of Nicaea assigned to the See of Antioch.” At that time disturbances caused by the wicked efforts of the heretics continued especially in Palestine and Egypt. Egypt did not concern Maximus at all, while Palestine alone lay under his administration by very ancient right.

Second, St. Leo says in chapter 3: “If Your Belovedness believes that anything must be done for the privileges of the Church of Antioch, let him take care to explain it in a personal letter, so that we may be able to answer your consultation clearly and appropriately.” Who does not see that Maximus had written to our pontiff rather obscurely about his own affairs, since Leo requests an explanation in order to answer “clearly and appropriately”?

“Now,” he continues, “it is sufficient to declare generally concerning all matters that, if anything has been attempted by anyone in any synod contrary to the statutes of the Nicene canons, or appears for a time to have arisen, it can inflict no prejudice upon inviolable decrees.”

It seems to me clearer than daylight that these words do not refer to the efforts of Constantinople. A writer who was doubtful and uncertain would not have written: “If anything has been attempted,” and so forth. Nor would Leo have been content to speak generally about this matter, since he had already opposed it openly and consistently in so many letters.

Finally, it is clear from chapter 5 of this letter that another matter is being treated. There Leo cites, as an example of his own observance, what he had written against the efforts of the Bishop of Constantinople, and adds that, “if anything is reported to have been done by those brothers whom I sent to the holy synod in my place beyond what pertained to the case, it will have absolutely no validity, because they were sent for this purpose alone,” and so forth.

Leo certainly knew that his representatives had opposed the decree enacted at the end of the synod in favor of the bishop of the imperial see. He had learned this from their letters and from the emperor’s letters. He would not therefore have spoken hesitantly about their agreement in this matter. The reference must accordingly be to the agreement that, according to Maximus’s letters, had obscurely been indicated as having been given by the legates in the case settled between Maximus and Juvenal.

### 3. “By conception”

Thus read the Griman and Barb manuscripts. In their place, all the editions contain the monstrous error “by conjunction.” Understand *conception* actively, as in the angel’s words to Mary in Luke 1: “Behold, you will conceive in the womb.” A little later, where the common editions read, “And born of the mother,” we have added from Griman: “And according to true flesh he was born of the mother.”

1533

### 4. “As also in the synod of Ephesus, etc.”

David Blondel, in his book *On the Primacy*, p. 546, thought that these words, together with what follows up to “Yet this is proper,” should be rejected as interpolated; or, if they were Leo’s, that they should be attacked with the “dog’s tooth” as the words of an angry man [Col. 1448A].

But they are Leo’s, and they belong especially to a passage in which he displays his full strength. Certainly anyone who does not recognize Leo’s style here is a stranger to his writings; and anyone who, as Blondel did, is carried away by a strange itch for contradiction into mutilating an epistle in its noblest section, despite the unanimous testimony of all printed and manuscript copies, must be suffering from an extraordinary compulsion to contradict.

Leaving aside the other matters—which it would be an abuse of the reader’s leisure to refute—the principal dilemma with which he attacks the authenticity (*αὐθεντία*) of these words is easily blown away. “Either,” he says, “Cyril wrote to Leo as pontiff, or as archdeacon. The former is absurd, since Celestine then occupied the Roman See; but who would say the latter—that Cyril, neglecting the pontiff on whom everything depended, approached his deacon?”

I regret that so learned a man was moved by such petty arguments, if indeed he was moved by them. I say that St. Cyril wrote to Leo as deacon and did not neglect Pope Celestine. Who, after all, would think that a king was being passed over when affairs are referred to the ministers of his kingdom? And who does not know that Leo, as archdeacon, directed the affairs of the Church and served as a confidential adviser to the pontiffs Celestine and Sixtus?

Prosper’s *Chronicle* bears witness to how energetically Leo the deacon assisted Sixtus in repelling the Pelagians, and how, at Leo’s urging, Sixtus vigilantly opposed their plots. John Cassian bears witness to the extent to which Leo the archdeacon watched over the affairs of the Church: he dedicated to him his work on the Incarnation of the Lord, without neglecting the pontiff. The Church owes that work to Leo’s encouragement, around the time of the Council of Ephesus.

Finally, Leo himself bears witness to the ecclesiastical administration that he must then have exercised. In Epistles 74 and 75, now 94 and 95, he states that the archdeacon, whose office he himself held, had been placed in charge of ecclesiastical affairs and that the administration of the entire ecclesiastical case and responsibility had been entrusted to him.

Add also that, even if Cyril’s letter to Celestine is not extant, it cannot therefore be asserted with certainty that it was never written, since so many ecclesiastical records of this kind have perished through the injury of time. If Cyril did not write about this matter to the Roman pontiff, it was not through any injury or contempt toward him, but by deliberate judgment and prudence: namely, so that the matter might be handled more privately, lest Juvenal should thereby seize an opportunity to attack Celestine, which would have caused great harm to the already deeply troubled affairs of the Eastern Church.

Alternatively, Cyril and Celestine may have wished to repel Juvenal’s efforts together, so that the cause of justice might be advanced more effectively while they did not appear to have agreed together on such an opposition. To bring this about, Cyril wrote to Leo so that, through Leo, he might suggest to Celestine what Celestine himself ought not to do directly.

Indeed, if Leo’s words are considered more attentively, they sufficiently indicate that Cyril did not write to him as an arbiter of the matter, but as one who could offer advice and convey a warning. For after saying, “The blessed Cyril indicated to me . . .,” Leo does not add, “And with anxious entreaty he earnestly requested me not to give my assent to unlawful attempts.” Instead he says only: “And with anxious entreaty he earnestly requested that no assent be given to unlawful attempts.”

On this occasion Cyril approached the Roman pontiff by the same route by which Theodoret, deposed by the pseudo-synod of Ephesus, approached St. Leo. Not content to write to Leo, Theodoret also wrote to the archdeacon of the Roman Church, with whom he knew that Celestine shared knowledge and management of all ecclesiastical affairs.

Finally, Blondel’s last argument—that the words now under discussion are placed among others that have an essential connection with one another, so that these words appear to have been inserted by a modern hand—is of little weight. It is clear that the words accused of falsity should be enclosed as a parenthesis, as will be evident to the reader. They belong both to what precedes and to what follows, yet they do not impede the connection and relation between the two. This invariably happens in speech whenever examples are introduced.

### 5. Besides those who are priests of the Lord

It seems clear to me that these words do not take away from presbyters the power of teaching and preaching: first, because it is established that this had long been permitted to them in the Eastern Churches, as is especially confirmed by the example of John Chrysostom in the case of the Antiochene Church, which is under discussion here; and secondly, because he excludes from the office of preaching only those who are outside the priestly order—something Saint Leo would never have said of presbyters, whom elsewhere he calls priests of the second order. Finally, while he expressly bars monks and laymen from that office and says nothing about presbyters, he leaves the latter’s right untouched.

I do not wish to go over again a matter already harassed by many commentaries. Nevertheless, I can scarcely refrain from warning inexperienced investigators of ecclesiastical antiquity not to confuse many things that must be distinguished. Since the practice was not the same everywhere—in every region, Church, or age—one must carefully weigh, while reading, what belonged to each circumstance.

Moreover, several distinct grades must be noted in this office.

1. To exercise it with full right, as the more important part of the apostolic ministry, belongs exclusively to bishops. Upon them rests not only the doctrine of Scripture and the faith, but also the teaching of the faith and responsibility for explaining it.

2. To speak before the people, as Optatus says (Book III, or VII), for the purpose of recommending some particular practice—for example, a fast or a solemnity, though not for expounding the subject, which belongs to bishops—was officially appropriate to a presbyter or deacon. There was also this distinction: they spoke plainly, whereas the episcopal exposition is shown by all to have been clothed in sanctity, with a doubled salutation and so forth. See also Isidore, cited above by us, concerning the office of the archdeacon, and canon 2 of the Second Council of Vaison.

3. It is also clear that preaching or reading the Gospel always belonged to deacons, although neither a deacon nor a presbyter was permitted to expound it, since that belongs to bishops. Thus, when the Second Council of Vaison in Gaul, in 529, canon 2, granted presbyters the power of delivering a discourse, it decreed that, if a presbyter were prevented from doing so, the homilies of the Fathers should be read by deacons—not that they should give a sermon of their own to the people.

4. At no time was either a presbyter or a deacon permitted to preach or do anything else without the bishop’s permission.

5. For a long time a presbyter was not granted the faculty of preaching in the presence of the bishop. Some restrict this to the custom which Augustine, in Letter 77, praises in Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, as having been abolished, and which Jerome criticizes in his letter to Nepotian and elsewhere.

6. Finally, at some point a presbyter was permitted to deliver a sermon to the people whether the bishop was present or absent, both in cities and in parishes, as the Fathers of Vaison, already mentioned, established in Gaul in the year of the Lord 529.

### 6. Or a layman

Here he distinguishes a monk from a layman, as in the following letter: by “monk” understanding one who had been distinguished by some ecclesiastical ministry, and by “layman” a monk possessing no such distinction. It seems to me that the Third Council of Arles, held, as Sirmond thinks, in 455, at approximately the same time, also made this distinction when it distinguished the clerics of Lérins from the lay multitude and congregation of the monastery.

## 1536 — To Letter 120 according to Quesnell, 93. To Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus

### 1. “His evil, with the dispenser of all goodness as its author”

This should be read in accordance with the common editions, although the Grimani, Barberini, and Thuane manuscripts, together with one Cambridge manuscript, read: “His evil,” and so forth.

> **Note:** We preferred *his evil* on the basis of the manuscripts and the context. The words “with the dispenser of all goodness as its author” agree with Augustine, who taught in several places that God knows how to make good use even of evils—namely, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 16; *Tractate on John* 27, section 10; *On Continence*, section 15; Sermon 10, section 5; and *Expositions on the Psalms*, Psalm 104, section 17. Hence that famous and excellent saying of the same teacher in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 27: “For God judged it better to do good with evils than to permit that there be no evils.” See also chapter 96.

In these words, moreover, our Leo wonderfully agrees with Augustine when he writes about God’s ordering of sins, in *On the Predestination of the Saints*, book I, chapter 16, and in the *Confessions*, book I, chapter 10. On the latter passage, consult the corrections and notes of the most celebrated doctor of the Sorbonne, Antoine Arnauld—mentioning whom is itself a form of praise—at the end of the Latin-French edition.

### 2. “So that the freedom of those below may not be thought to have been diminished in anything”

These words are found in the common edition and in the Grimani manuscript alone. They are absent from the Thuane, Barberini, Trecopithian, and Cambridge manuscripts, which also read *summoperum* or *summopere* instead of *summorum*; so too do the Trecopithian and Cambridge manuscripts and one of the Thuane manuscripts, where the text reads: “so that the outcome of the examination may contribute to the greater glory of God,” and so forth.

### 3. “He plotted an injury against his own head”

For Dioscorus excommunicated the lord archbishop Leo, as Anatolius says in the Council of Chalcedon; concerning this there is also the testimony of Theodore, the Alexandrian deacon, in act 3 of that council, and the report of the council itself to Saint Leo. This was perpetrated by Dioscorus at Alexandria, after he had enlisted several bishops for the purpose—not at the Robber Council of Ephesus, but after that gathering had been dissolved.

> **Note:** The Greek text of Theodore, the Alexandrian deacon, which is read in act 3 of Chalcedon, volume IV of the Councils, column 1271—as the Roman editors observed—places the event in the metropolitan city of Nicaea. The ancient translator, however, seems to have read differently in his Greek exemplar. He rendered it not as “in the metropolitan city of Nicaea,” but as “against the Council of Nicaea”; these words mean that Dioscorus, by condemning Saint Flavian and excommunicating Saint Leo, the defenders of Catholic doctrine—which agrees with Nicaea—was fighting against the Council of Nicaea itself.

> Several errors are indeed found in the common Greek text, which must be corrected from the ancient version. If, however, the common Greek text is not believed to be corrupt at this point, since it is incredible that Dioscorus would have dared to do this in the city of Nicaea under Marcian, when everything was stirred up against Dioscorus, it must be said that he pronounced the excommunication against Saint Leo while Theodosius was still alive, relying upon his favor and protection, and while he was staying at Nicaea during various journeys. He may perhaps have learned there that Leo had declared the acts of the Robber Council of Ephesus null and void, and that the same pontiff had sharply rebuked him in Letter 44 to Theodosius.

Liberatus, whom Baronius cites here, says nothing about this excommunication of Leo.

### 4. “Hands polluted long ago”

For he did not begin his career of wickedness at the Robber Council of Ephesus. Rather, according to the testimony of the deacon Liberatus in chapter 10 of his *Breviary*, immediately after he was ordained bishop of Alexandria he oppressed the heirs of Cyril and, by many calumnies, took money from them. Moreover, pamphlets presented against him at the Council of Chalcedon stigmatize him as an Origenist and an Arian, as well as a murderer, arsonist, and scoundrel of the most disgraceful life.

That Dioscorus was a man of extremely turbulent character and great cunning is confirmed by a manuscript fragment of the *Life of Saint Euthymius*, cited from the Royal Society’s library in England by its excerptor, Andreas Arnoldus, in his notes on Marcian’s letter.

### 5. “Since also the letter of the apostolic see …”

These words, together with what follows up to the words at the beginning of the next chapter, “But blessed is our God,” are indeed found in the Grimani and common editions. They are absent, however, from the Barberini, four Thuane, Trecopithian, and Cambridge manuscripts, in which the text reads:

> “Since also in the letter of the apostolic see and in the other matters which we set out above in order he proceeds immediately. But blessed …”

This seems to have been taken from some collection of canons, although it is now also found in other manuscripts.

## To Letter 121 according to Quesnell, 94. To Marcian Augustus

### 1. “When Theophilus had collected one hundred years of this observance”

When Scaliger read these words hastily—and Calvisius followed him—he was astonished that our pontiff should write that Theophilus had defined a period of one hundred years, rather than ninety years, which he thought had been established by that bishop. But I am astonished that Scaliger read in Leo what no one has read there.

> **Note:** See annotation 8 (column 1056, note j) on this letter, from which the errors of Quesnell’s annotation will be exposed.

For not even the slightest trace of a period bounded by exactly one hundred years appears in this or any other letter. We read only that Theophilus arranged a series of one hundred years of this observance. In reality Theophilus had not established a period enclosed within precisely one hundred years; he presented one hundred years excerpted from his period. The entire period consisted of 437 years, during which he had marked down all the Passovers that were to follow from the year of Christ 380 onward. His nephew and successor Cyril, considering this cycle too long, reduced it to a span of ninety-five years, as he himself testifies.

### 2. “From the first consulship of the elder Theodosius”

According to Dionysius, Gennadius, and other authorities, this is the year of Christ 380, in which Theodosius had Gratian as his colleague. According to Bucherius’s calculation, it was the ninety-sixth year of Diocletian.

On this basis Scaliger must be accused of a double error. First, he writes that Theophilus began his cycle with the first year of Diocletian, whose final year was the year of Christ 379, marked by the consulship of Ausonius. Second, he assigns the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius, in the year 381, to the preceding year, that is, 380.

### 3. “If the legitimate interval from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May has been fixed”
