For “the tenth day before the Kalends of May,” as the common editions read, we have restored “the eleventh,” as Petavius and Bucherius long ago conjectured should be done. Their conjecture is confirmed by the authority of our Grimani manuscript and by the following words of Leo:

> “For the fact that the solemnity sometimes seems to have extended to the tenth and ninth days before the Kalends of May occurred because of the day of the Passion, even though the day of the Resurrection had passed beyond it.”

If the ninth and tenth days before the Kalends of May were an extraordinary limit for Easter, it remains that Saint Leo said that the eleventh was the ordinary boundary. Bede likewise reports that, according to the opinion of the Latins, this was the limit of the Paschal feast.

It is not entirely certain whom Saint Leo regarded as the author of these boundaries. Nevertheless, I readily agree with Bucherius that he understood them to be the Fathers of the Council of Caesarea. They seem to have been the first to establish these same Paschal limits when they met at Caesarea in Palestine in the customary year of Christ 196, 166 years after the Passion, as is taught by the letter of Philip, who was still alive at that time and which Bucherius published after Bede in a more corrected form.

“Therefore,” says Philip, “it was established in that synod that Easter should be observed from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April up to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, and that no one should have the power to cross the fixed boundary either before or after it.”

Leo used almost the same words, so that I believe he took them either from that letter or from the very acts of the council, which were probably sent to Pope Victor, since at that same period he was laboring with such anxiety over the Paschal controversy.

Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, reports in Bucherius that the same boundary had been fixed by certain African computists. It is known from Ambrose’s letter to the bishops of Aemilia that the same boundary was used in Italy in his time. It is therefore not surprising that Leo should say so securely and confidently that these boundaries had been established in antiquity and lawfully, according to the rule of the constitutions of the Fathers, while the Alexandrian limits disagreed with the example of all antiquity and with every authority of the Fathers, and had been established against ecclesiastical custom by an excessively insolent and open transgression (*Letter* 104, now 130).

When experience nevertheless showed that these boundaries were somewhat too narrow, the holy Fathers were compelled to admit an interval extended by two days, so that they extended the Paschal period to the tenth and ninth days before the Kalends of May. Leo himself admits this:

> “For the fact that the solemnity sometimes seems to have reached the tenth and ninth days before the Kalends of May is defended in a certain way, because, although the day of the Resurrection seems to have passed beyond the boundary, the day of the Passion will not be found to have crossed the established limit.”

He was evidently responding to the objection of the Alexandrians, who could complain that the boundary praised by Leo had sometimes been violated, even with the support of the Romans:

> “Easter,” he says, “has sometimes passed beyond the appointed boundary of the Resurrection, but never beyond Easter σταυρώσιμον—that is, the crucifixion.”

Thus, from the ambiguous word “Easter,” which signifies Christ’s Passion no less than his Resurrection—together making up one complete solemnity—he proves that the Latins had never passed beyond the Paschal boundary fixed by the Fathers.

From this it is also clear that the Latins took great care to ensure that, before the fourteenth day of the moon, they should celebrate not only the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection but even more especially the day of the Passion. Accordingly, if the fourteenth day of the moon fell on a Saturday, the Paschal feast of the Resurrection was not celebrated on the following Sunday; it was postponed to the twenty-second day of the moon, so that the thirteenth day of the moon would not be treated as the solemn day of the Passion. Victorinus also testifies to this.

## To Letter 122 according to Quesnell, 95. To Julian, bishop of Cos

### 1. “Leo to Julian, bishop”

Thus reads the Grimani manuscript. It was certainly necessary for the removal of the most disgraceful errors that had crept into this title, either through the negligence of scribes or through the misguided diligence of more recent editors. The common edition reads:

> “Leo, bishop of the Roman and universal Church, sends greetings to Eudocia Augusta.”

This letter is likewise addressed to Eudocia in the printed editions of the Councils by J. Merlin, in the editions of 1524, Cologne 1530 and 1535, Crabbe 1538, and Surianus 1567, as well as in the Victorine manuscript. They differ from the more recent editions, however, in omitting that magnificent title and presenting the simpler form:

> “Leo to Eudocia Augusta.”

### 2.

It is not only the Grimani manuscript that indicates that the letter was sent to Julian; the entire context of the letter does so as well. The restrained manner in which Leo was accustomed to write to emperors or empresses in no way suits this text.

### 3.

Even in the corrupted manuscripts, traces of the ancient and genuine reading still survive. Near the end of the letter, the word *fraternitatem* (“brotherhood,” or “your brotherly relationship”)—which certainly does not suit Eudocia or any woman, but does suit a bishop—is found in Merlin’s edition of the Councils of 1524 and 1535, and also in the Victorine manuscript, in this form:

> “Since, however,” he says, “your brotherhood ought to share with me in the care of this matter …”

It is therefore clear as sunlight that the word *serenitatem* (“your serenity”) has been substituted for the other reading in order to make it correspond to the title, which we have corrected on the authority of the Grimani manuscript.

### 4.

Marianus Scotus praises this letter under its proper heading in the year 454. “Saint Leo the pope,” he says, “to Julian, bishop: *On the Paschal Observance*.”

> “Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, of holy memory [the edition deletes “bishop of Alexandria”], writing to the elder Augustus Theodosius, arranged over one hundred years, beginning with the first consulship of the aforesaid prince, the order of the day of the Paschal feast [the edition deletes “of the day … Paschal”]. The seventy-sixth year of this reckoning is now passing; when [edition: “whereby”], in the consulship of Opilio, the sacred Paschal solemnity was celebrated on the second day before the Ides of April. Therefore, in the following year, Easter will reasonably fall on the second day before the Nones of April [edition: “on the day before the Nones”].”

> **Editorial variant:** The edition reads “the same feast” instead of “Easter.”

> “But the year which will be the seventy-eighth”—the edition has “seventy-sixth,” and omits some words here—“seems to disagree, since Easter is assigned to the eighth day before the Kalends of May, whereas it ought to have occurred on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.”

> **Editorial variants:** The edition deletes “the Paschal” in the first sentence, reads “will have transferred” instead of “is assigned,” and differs in the remaining words.

### 5.

Finally, it is certain that at that time there was neither an Eudocia nor an Eudoxia Augusta to whom Saint Leo would have wished to write about these matters. Eudocia, the wife of the younger Theodosius, was already living in Jerusalem after her husband’s death. It was entirely appropriate for Leo to write to her in the following letter about the rebellious Palestinian monks, whom she favored against the Catholic faith; but it would have been highly unnecessary for him to discuss Easter with her and advise her to make suggestions to Marcian so that he might consult the Egyptians on the matter.

Eudoxia, the wife of Valentinian, was then living in Rome, or at least in the Western provinces. The same is certain of the younger Eudoxia, daughter of this elder woman, who was still under her mother’s care. Anyone who wishes to compare the remainder of the text will find the passages we have corrected with the help of manuscript evidence marked in the margin.

## To Letter 124 according to Quesnell, 97. To the Palestinian monks

### To the Palestinian monks

We have substituted “to the Palestinian monks” for “to the Palestinian bishops,” which appears in the common editions. It is clear that this letter was written to monks, both from Surius’s edition and from the manuscripts used by him and by us—namely, the Victorine, Cistercian, Cambridge, Thuane, and Royal manuscripts—and from the character and reading of the letter itself. It is evident that Saint Leo is not dealing with bishops but only with the monks of Palestine.

These men, led by Carosus and Dorotheus, were openly and publicly rising up and fighting against the Council of Chalcedon, stirring up, as our Leo says, seditions in the cities and disturbing the Churches; and they were inflicting not only injuries but also killings upon presbyters and bishops, so that, through the fury and savagery of their undertaking and profession, they were forgetful of both.

> **Note:** It should not have been written “led by Carosus and Dorotheus,” but “led by Theodosius.” The former caused disturbances in Constantinople, not in Palestine. The leader of the Palestinian rioters was Theodosius, as we observed in annotation 26 (column 1067, note f) on this letter.

There is no doubt that by “undertaking and profession” he means the monastic undertaking and profession, and that he is addressing those same men about whom he wrote to Eudoxia and Julian, as well as to Marcian, whom he thanked for the conversion of the Palestinian monks.

In so clear a matter it would be pointless to add more. It is evident from what has been said that the present letter must be assigned to the year of the Lord 453, since in that same year Saint Leo wrote to Eudocia Augusta and to Julian, bishop, about this matter. The present letter is plainly related and contemporary with those letters. Nor can it be postponed to a later year, since the letter to Marcian cited above, dated 9 January in the year of the Lord 454, clearly shows that the rebellious monks in question had by then been converted.

## To Letter 125 according to Quesnell, 98. To Julian, bishop of Cos

### “Subadjutor”

We have supplied this word here from the Grimani manuscript. It occurs again in Saint Leo’s Letter 127, now 158, where there is mention of the *subadjutores* of Gerontius and Olympius, and also in Liberatus’s *Breviary*. It is rarely recorded among Latin writers, although it is Latin. Synesius, in Letter 144, interprets it as follows:

> Ἀποκρατίων τίς ἐστι τοῦ Ἡρακλειανοῦ δορυφόρων, ταξινέχων τῷ βοηθῷ βοηθεῖν, ἡ γὰρ σουβαδιούβα λέξις, τοῦ τὸ ἑρμηνεύειν πιστεύεται.

> “A certain Harpocratio is one of Heraclianus’s attendants, of the class who assist the assistant; for the word *subadjuva* is believed to mean this.”

Thus the *magister officiorum*, who had been assigned an assistant, had assistants under him in turn; these were called *subadjutores*. See the *Notitia dignitatum* of the empire and Guidus Pancirolo’s commentary on it, chapter 16.

## To Letter 127 according to Quesnell, 100. To Julian, bishop of Cos

### 1. “On the eighth day before the Kalends of May”

Thus reads the Grimani manuscript, not “on the ninth day before the Kalends of May,” as the common editions have. This is made clear by Letter 68, now 88, to Paschasinus of Lilybaeum, which we publish publicly, and by Letter 94, now 121, chapter 2, where Saint Leo explicitly asserts that Theophilus designated the eighth day before the Kalends of May and says that, if the solemnity reached the ninth or tenth day, this could be defended in a certain way. Yet here he also asserts that Easter had never been celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of May from the time of the Lord’s Resurrection.

What he says about the ninth and tenth days before the Kalends of May is taken from Paschasinus of Lilybaeum’s letter to him, written in 443, when controversy arose over Easter in the following year. At that time Leo, together with the Westerners, maintained that the feast should not be celebrated on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, as Theophilus had recorded.

### 2. “Established by the canons …”

Compare this entire passage with the earlier editions, which read:

> “It ought to have been made known that the disgraceful ambition among you had been marked out, so that what had been established by new usurpations might remain inviolate, as we have always written.”

## To Letter 129 according to Quesnell, 103. To Proterius, bishop of Alexandria

### 1.

This letter to Saint Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, is the very letter whose loss the eminent Cardinal Baronius deeply lamented when writing under the year of the Lord 453, and which the manuscript of Cardinal Grimani happily restores to us after its memory had been lost for so many centuries. The style itself and the subject of the letter loudly proclaim it to be genuinely our Leo’s, so that it would be superfluous to establish this at greater length.

It is mentioned by the following authorities.

1. Leo himself mentions it in Letter 104, now 130, to Marcian Augustus:

> “I therefore replied to the aforesaid brother [Proterius] as I ought, and admonished him to persevere in his holy devotion,” and so forth.

2. The venerable Bede quotes a brief fragment of the same letter in *The Reckoning of Time*, chapter 42. Speaking there about the Paschal cycle established by Theophilus, he says:

> “Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, giving a clear account of this cycle in response to the inquiry of Saint Leo the pope, deserved to be praised by him in the following terms of a reply: ‘Your letters of affection have gladdened me, which my brother and fellow bishop Nestorius brought in the pious fulfillment of his duty. For it was appropriate that such writings should be sent from the bishop of the Alexandrian Church to the apostolic see—writings that would show that, by the teaching of the blessed apostle Peter, the Egyptians had learned from the beginning through the blessed Mark, his disciple, what the Romans are known to have believed,’” and so forth.

> “If he had added these words,” says Philip Labbe, editor of the final collection of the Councils, “he would have earned the greatest gratitude from all students of ecclesiastical antiquity.”

We therefore earn that gratitude. There is no doubt that these words were taken from the opening of this letter. Yet one cannot help wondering how Bede connects them with Theophilus’s cycle or with the question of Easter, since not even a trace of either appears in the whole letter.

One of two things must certainly be admitted: either Bede possessed only this excerpt and not the entire letter, or sleep overtook that pious and learned man while he was reading. For the whole letter concerns the mystery of the Incarnation. Indeed, not even in that fragment is there anything that can in any way be referred to the Paschal cycle. No one will say that the Egyptians received from the blessed evangelist Mark, or the blessed Mark from the apostle Peter, any teaching about the calculation of Easter that could relate to the controversy raised in Leo’s time.

Let it be granted that the Church received from the apostles themselves the command and practice of celebrating the Paschal feast, as learned men have attempted to prove on the authority of the present letter—an argument suggested to them by Bede’s excerpt. But who would assert that the apostles established or transmitted to posterity any of the stricter limits of this feast?

Furthermore, it is the very opposite of the case that the letters which Saint Proterius wrote to Saint Leo about Easter gladdened him, or that Proterius deserved to be praised in such a reply because of the clarity of the account he had given. Saint Leo, rather, bore with great difficulty the position advocated by the Alexandrian bishop and considered it contrary to the ancient observance. For this sole reason he granted his agreement to the Alexandrians: so that there might be no disagreement among the provinces concerning the observance of so venerable a feast, and so that nothing might be different among the priests of the Lord during so great a solemnity. This is what the letter to Marcian says in Letter 108, now 137, chapter 1.

In that letter, now published for the first time, we also have testimony that Leo had not written to Proterius about this Paschal controversy:

> “I signify that I have received the letters of my brother and fellow bishop Proterius, bishop of the city of Alexandria, in which I replied to Your Piety concerning my agreement.”

Nor had Leo himself previously written to Proterius about this inquiry, as is clear from several of his letters and from the opening of Proterius’s own letter.

Finally, add that Saint Leo had written this letter to Proterius—the one we are publishing—some time before he received Proterius’s letter about Easter, as becomes clear from several writings concerning the matter.

### 3.

Saint Thomas quotes several passages from the same letter in *Summa theologiae*, II-II, question 11, article 2, reply to objection 2:

> “Thus Pope Leo says in a certain letter to Proterius, bishop of Alexandria: ‘The enemies of the cross of Christ lie in wait for all our words and syllables, if we give them even the slightest opportunity to pretend that we agree with the Nestorian position.’”

For Proterius, his collection, and his murder, see Liberatus’s *Breviary*, chapters 14 and 15; Hormisdas, bishop of Rome, Letter 8, to the synod of Old Epirus; Nicephorus, book XV, chapter 16; and our Leo in Letters 100, 102, 104, 117, 118, 125, 126, and 133, now 127, 131, 133, 147, 149, 156, 157, and 164.

It is almost certainly the case that Proterius had been ordained by Dioscorus, archpriest of the Church of Alexandria; that he was later substituted in his place; and that he was finally killed by the faction of the heretics, especially Timothy—either in the baptistery of the Church, as Liberatus says, or among the very altars, as Hormisdas testifies.

As soon as he was placed in charge of the Alexandrian Church, he wrote to Saint Leo, sending letters that testified both to his ordination and to his faith. Our pontiff calls these letters “full of satisfaction.”

> **Note:** The letters of Proterius which Leo testifies were full of satisfaction were not the first letters written immediately after his ordination, but the second. In Letter 127, chapter 1, the pope had requested these from him, with a fuller and clearer exposition of the faith.

He sent them through Nestorius, the bishop whom Bede’s fragment corruptly calls Nectarius, and whom the common edition of Letter 104, now 133, to Marcian calls a Nestorian. Marcian had written to our Leo through the same bishop.

In both places the Grimani manuscript reads “Nestorius.” I think he was the same person as Nestor, bishop of the city of Flagonitorum, who was the first to subscribe the petitions of the Egyptian bishops to Emperor Leo against Proterius’s murderers.

After the assertions of the aforementioned priests have first been read, then my own writings should be read as well. It was an ancient custom, derived from the earliest times of the Church, that the letters and writings of the apostles should be read at the sacred assemblies of the faithful. I do not know, however, whether before the time of our Saint Leo the more recent practice had become established of reading the writings of Fathers or bishops before an assembled people. From this occasion, perhaps, or from a similar one, arose the custom of reciting the homilies of the holy Fathers publicly in church and inserting them into the ecclesiastical office.

## To Letter 133 of Saint Proterius to Saint Leo the pope I, following Quesnell’s Letter 103

### 9. “Athanasius”

This should be read “Athanasius,” not “Anastasius,” as Petavius and Bucherius had already observed in their respective works *On the Doctrine of Time*. The matter is beyond doubt. The authority of the Oxford and Saint-Oyend manuscripts now supports this reading; they have “Athanasius.”

From this Bucherius draws a certain argument concerning the age of Saint Athanasius, maintaining that he did not die before this year, which was the year of Christ 373. Jerome in his *Chronicle* appears to support him, assigning to that same year the ordination of Peter, who succeeded Saint Athanasius.

Others oppose the authority of Rufinus, Saint Cyril of Alexandria, and especially Socrates, who assign Athanasius only forty-six years of episcopate. According to them, he died in the consulship of Gratian and Probus, who held the consulship in the year 371.

When these opposing proofs are compared and weighed against one another, I confess that the authority of Saints Jerome and Proterius carries greater weight with me than that of the others. Their proofs are indirect—for they are derived from the number of years of his episcopate, except in the case of Socrates—and that number can be reconciled with Proterius’s date for his death.

For what if the man who was the first of all to mention those years did not count them with complete accuracy, since there was no particular necessity for him to do so? What if the beginnings of Saint Athanasius’s episcopate are not entirely certain? If they occurred later than is commonly believed, then it may be true both that he held the episcopate for forty-six years and that he did not die before 373.

But Jerome, a careful writer, when he assigns the ordination of Peter, Athanasius’s successor, to this year, could only have written this on the basis of indisputable records. Proterius likewise must be believed to have learned the matter from the archives of his own Church, and there is no legitimate way to twist the testimony of either into another meaning.

As for Socrates, although he wrote in the same period as Proterius, he cannot be compared with Proterius in authority on this point. I mean Proterius, who wrote at Alexandria, where knowledge of this date was clear; who could search the archives of his own Church as he wished; and who, being devoted to a single matter, was less liable to error than Socrates, who, hurrying toward many other subjects, could both be deceived and deceive others.

An unnamed chronicler cited by Scaliger in his *Commentaries on Eusebius* reports that Athanasius died on the seventh day of Pachon in the year of Christ 377.

Pope Adrian I mentions this letter of Proterius and quotes a double fragment from it in his Letter 97 to the bishops of Spain, which appears in volume III of Du Chesne’s *Scriptores Historiae Franciae*:

> “Pay attention, most beloved brothers, to what blessed Proterius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, sent by order of Marcian, the prince of holy memory, to our most blessed predecessor, Pope Leo. After much else he says:

> ‘Formerly the Lord, signifying this through Moses, said: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month among the months of the year,” and so forth: “You shall celebrate the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month.”’

> “A little later he added: ‘If the fourteenth day of the moon should ever fall on the Lord’s Day, the solemnity must be postponed to the following week, just as our ancient Fathers did when they transferred fourteenth-day moons that occurred to another Sunday.’”

Adrian’s translation seems different from the one we inserted into Leo’s letters. Since Sigebert of Gembloux, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 27, and Johannes Trithemius testify that Proterius’s writings on Easter in the year 455 were translated from Greek into Latin by Dionysius Exiguus, the question arises which of these two translations is Dionysius’s work.

Perhaps Adrian’s translation is the same one that, it is scarcely possible to doubt, was made at Saint Leo’s command immediately after the letter had been received from him—by some Greek speaker, I suppose, who knew little Latin. Offended by the barbarous quality of that translation, Dionysius may afterward have prepared another.

## To Letter 135 according to Quesnell, 106. To Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople

### 1. “John’s spiritual and abundant teaching”

Here Saint Leo admirably sketches the characteristic quality of each of Anatolius’s four immediate predecessors, giving us reason to marvel at our pontiff’s exceptional knowledge of the Churches and of the writings of the holy Fathers. Everyone can see how graphically he captures the distinctive character of John Chrysostom in a brief eulogy.

### 2. “The authority of Atticus”

On this subject see Socrates, book VI, chapter 20, and book VII, chapters 2 and 25, and elsewhere. The authority that you see Leo commending in Atticus was won for him by religion, prudence, constant diligence, learning, extraordinary charity, urbane speech most suited to attracting people’s minds, and the defeat of the heretics’ efforts.

“Under his pontificate,” says Socrates, “the Churches also made their greatest progress. For he not only protected those within the faith, but also overwhelmed heretics with admiration for his prudence.”

Pope Celestine I likewise mentions Atticus’s vigilance in purging heresies in his letter to Maximian, bishop of Constantinople, in which he also proposes the example of his predecessors:

> “Follow the examples of the earlier pontiffs by whom you were instructed and nourished: the knowledge of the most blessed John in preaching; the vigilance of Saint Atticus in purging heresies; and the simple purity of your predecessor Sisinnius, whose successor we believe you to be.”

See also Saint Prosper in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*.

### 3. Proclus’s diligence

Socrates testifies that this consisted chiefly in patience and gentleness, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 4. “He tried,” he says, “to bring the heretics back to right faith by this means rather than by force [Col. 1458A] … and preserved the dignity of gentleness unimpaired, restoring it to the Church as a kind of deposit.” And in chapter 45:

“He recalled to unity those who, because of John’s deposition, had separated themselves from the body of the Church, soothing their grief by prudent counsel. With the emperor’s consent, he transported John’s body, which had been buried at Comana, to Constantinople, and, after it had been carried through the city with solemn pomp, deposited it with great honor in the Church of the Apostles.”

Sozomen, book VIII, chapter 2, also has much to say about Atticus, and agrees with Leo’s statement even more explicitly when he says [1547]:

“Moreover, since he was prudent by nature more than by training, he displayed the greatest skill in conducting affairs and was exceedingly clever at devising and avoiding intrigues. In character he was gentle, so that he was agreeable to most people. He is also said to have been discerning and diligent toward those who shared his opinion; but toward those who followed a different sect he was formidable, so that whenever he wished he could instill fear in them; indeed, completely changed, he would appear gentle toward them.”

### 4. “These attempts were made in violation of the canons,” as you recognize

We read nothing of the kind in Anatolius’s letter, which seems to me to have been composed with such skill that it appears fully to satisfy Leo’s complaints, while in reality the Constantinopolitan bishop yields nothing concerning his own rights.

[Note: [Col. 1457D] Since Anatolius, in letter 132, which is indicated here, chapter 4, asserts: “The whole force and confirmation of the proceedings was reserved for the authority of your Blessedness; and he confessed that all the right acquired by these proceedings depended upon apostolic confirmation and authority, so that it might be valid and certain.” If, notwithstanding this confession and in opposition to the pontiff, he and the Easterners did not withdraw from the decree once issued at Chalcedon, then, just as in the case of Marcian, letter 110, constancy must be attributed to Leo because he firmly opposed this ambition, contrary to the Nicene canons; so the Easterners cannot be praised if, against those same canons, they did not desist from Leo’s just criticisms.] 

For he barely mentions, near the end, canon 28 of Chalcedon, and concerning it he wishes only this to be accepted as certain regarding himself: that he was guilty of no fault and had always been very far from seeking what belonged to others.

The Eastern bishops were so firmly resolved never to withdraw from their decree that, when Saint Leo’s letter—by which he confirmed the acts of Chalcedon with his consent—had been read by Julian at the assembly of bishops in Constantinople, mentioned in letter 100, now 127, to Julian, he did not dare read the words in which Leo refused to give his consent to the decree enacted at Chalcedon in favor of the imperial see, as is clear from that same letter.

Indeed, when Anatolius promised correction through Marcian’s letter, he promised only this: “that he would satisfy all requirements relating to the observance of the faith,” as Leo himself reports in the already-mentioned letter 100, now 127, chapter 3.

### 5. “That you have restored the presbyter Aetius to your favor and affection”

He does not say “to his former position and ministry,” as Cardinal Baronius mistakenly thought, *Annals*, year 453, no. 8. For once someone had advanced from the office of archdeacon to the dignity of presbyter, he was never permitted to return to his former ministry.

Hence, in this same letter, Saint Leo reveals his concern about appointing an archdeacon in Andrew’s place, when he says:

“First let one be elected and approved who can fulfill the office of archdeacon—that is, one whom no rumor of any of the aforementioned impieties has ever stained.”

It would have been entirely superfluous to give this warning if Aetius had either recovered or been able to recover his former position. Therefore, what is found written in Anatolius’s letter to Pope Leo—namely, that Aetius was restored to his former ecclesiastical position and honor [1548]—can derive some light, and in my judgment no insignificant light, from Leo’s one reply, since the loss of the Greek text has left the matter obscure.

It is certain from this letter and from the following letter of Leo that letter 106, now 135, answers Anatolius’s letter, and that when the Roman pontiff writes that Aetius had been restored to Anatolius’s favor and affection, he is referring to Anatolius’s own words, in which he had asserted that Aetius was restored to his former ecclesiastical position and honor.

[Col. 1459A] There was therefore nothing in the authentic Anatolian letter indicating that Aetius had been reinstated in the archdiaconate, since nothing of the sort is shown to have been read by Leo in Anatolius’s letter, as this reply makes clear.

Those words of Anatolius must therefore be understood not of the office of archdeacon, but merely of the ecclesiastical rank and honor from which he had been cast down through the envy and hostility of his adversaries when he was assigned to a cemetery, as our author complains in letter 84, now 111, or of his restoration to his former good reputation.

For it is clear that Aetius had been accused of some crime, since we learn from letter 100 that he was examined in an episcopal assembly and, after investigation, was cleared in every respect.

A learned man, from these words of letter 86, otherwise 56, now 113—

“For under a Catholic bishop, even if there was in some degree priestly dignity, the archdeacon ought, out of reverence for the faith, to have been preferred to the priest, rather than that a most wicked heretic should occupy the place of a Catholic”—

words which he openly admits are seriously corrupt, conjectures [Col. 1459B] that, in correcting the error, Anatolius opened the way for Leo to propose that a Catholic presbyter should be permitted to perform the office of archdeacon rather than a heretical deacon.

But how far removed this is from Leo’s meaning and text, which he could read in a much more accurate and entirely unambiguous form in the new edition of Leo already published at that time! From it it becomes clear that Leo was proposing to Anatolius what he ought to have done before Aetius’s consecration as presbyter: that he should pardon Aetius’s lesser errors rather than be compelled to yield his place to a heretic.

## 1549. ON LETTER 139, IN QUESNELLUS 110. To Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem

### 1. “Amid the constraints of the lodging”

These words indicate that Saint Leo was convinced that Christ the Lord was not born in a cave situated outside Bethlehem, as most seem to think, but in a lodging in which, according to the Evangelist, there was no room for him [Col. 1459C]—that is, not in a chamber or bedroom, but only in a stable situated beneath the roof of that lodging.

Saint Ambrose held the same opinion, thinking that the stable was an annex of the lodging. The sacred Gospel text favors both interpretations when it says simply: “She laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the lodging” (Luke 2:7). It contrasts not a stable separated from the lodging, but the lodging’s manger with its chamber or bedroom, which was especially necessary for the woman in labor and for the newborn child.

Similarly, the angel announces to the shepherds that Christ had been born in the city of David and placed in a manger. The shepherds themselves say: “Let us go as far as Bethlehem.” Before returning, they appear to have openly related to everyone who was in the lodging all that they had heard and seen: “And all who heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. And the shepherds returned.”

Finally, when the Magi came to worship the newborn king, “entering the house,” Matthew says, chapter 2, verse 11, “they found the child with Mary his mother.”

This interpretation is almost necessary if the prophecy of Micah is to be said to have been fulfilled literally: “And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come a Leader.”

Nor should Eusebius, Jerome, Paulinus, and others be brought forward against this view. Where the lodging was for the Lord at his birth, only a stable and cave may have remained in the times of those Fathers; and it may even have been outside the city. For the example of Rome, Jerusalem, and other cities makes it sufficiently clear that, through the changes of time, the devastation and destruction caused by wars often result either in the layout of cities being altered, and destroyed cities being rebuilt in more distant places for the sake of convenience, or in certain suburban areas being cut off, leaving other areas separated from the city that had formerly been joined to it [1550].

### 2. “If he had not been of our race, he could not have been mortal”

[Note: [Col. 1459D] Take care rather not to suppose Adam’s immortality in his original state to have been natural to him because of the condition of his body. For immortality, as Saint Augustine clearly taught in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book VI, chapter 25, was granted to him through the tree of life, not through the constitution of his nature. He was separated from that tree when he sinned, so that he could die; had he not sinned, he could have remained undying. He was therefore mortal by the condition of his animal body, but immortal through the beneficence of the Creator. Hence this proposition was also condemned among the so-called Baiian propositions, number 78; let others judge whether Quesnellus alludes to it here: “The immortality of the first man was not a benefit of grace, but a natural condition.”]

Take care not to suppose from these words that death was natural either to Adam and his descendants because of the condition of their bodies, as certain modern writers have thought, or to Christ the Lord because of his maternal origin.

For both Adams, the first and the last, shared the first immortality: the ability not to die, which Saint Augustine explains in *On Rebuke and Grace*, chapter 12; *The City of God*, book XXII, final chapter; and elsewhere.

I say that his flesh could have remained undying, because it was not sinful flesh. But because he was sent “in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order to condemn sin in the flesh,” Christ’s flesh drew mortality from the mortality of his mother’s body, because he found a mortal body in her; but he did not draw the contagion of original sin, because he did not find the lust of sexual intercourse.

If he had received from his mother not even mortality, but only the substance of flesh, then his flesh could have been neither sinful flesh nor the likeness of sinful flesh (Augustine, *Against Julian*, book V, chapter 15).

### 3. “I reverently received a fragment of the Lord’s cross together with the tokens of your affection”

[Note: [Col. 1460D] On these words, see our note 29 (Col. 4408, n. j) on this letter.]

These words conclude the letter and lie in the common printed edition and in the three manuscripts that I saw immediately before the consular note. But since they are absent from the Grimani manuscript, the two Barberini manuscripts, the Cambridge manuscript, the Trecopith manuscript, and three of the Thuane manuscripts, everyone understands that they are an interpolation.

## YEAR 455. ON LETTERS 141, 142, AND 143, IN QUESNELLUS 112, 113, AND 114

[Col. 1460C]

The Grimani manuscript has preserved for us three letters sent by Leo in this year, 455, so that this year would not pass entirely empty for us.

These letters must have preceded the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, since the Roman historians establish that the emperor Valentinian, whose eighth consulship is recorded in them, was killed on that day.

It was therefore easy to correct the copyist’s error: in letter 113, now 141, to Julian, he seems to have read “the fifth Ides of March.” It was also possible to resolve another doubt arising in connection with letter 112, now 142, to Marcian, from the ambiguous reading of an abbreviated character.

For the text there reads: “Given on the third Ides of August, during the eighth consulship of Valentinian.” Although it would be easy to read “the third Ides of August,” since no other month’s name appears [1551], it nevertheless seems preferable to read “during the eighth consulship of the emperor Valentinian,” and to believe that the name of the month was omitted through the copyist’s negligence.

Besides this argument drawn from Valentinian’s death, which prevents the letter from being assigned to August, another argument arises from the subject matter of the letter itself: it concerns the controversy over the date of Easter. Since Easter had already been celebrated three months earlier, it would have been highly inappropriate to mention Leo’s agreement given to the Alexandrians, or the letters he had sent to the Westerners concerning the celebration of that same feast.

A third argument is supplied by letter 113, now 141, to Julian, dated on the fifth Ides of March. Since it mentions the correction of the rebellious monk Carosus—

[Note: [Col. 1461D] This Carosus, who was corrected, is different from the other man whom Marcian expelled from the monastery, as may be gathered from our note 7 (Col. 1111, n. g) on letter 142, where we also corrected the erroneous date of that letter from the excellent Regensburg manuscript.]

—it is clear that letter 112, now 142, to Marcian, had been written earlier. In that letter he thanks Augustus for having ordered that the same man and Dorotheus, his partner in error, be driven from their monasteries. Marcian would certainly not have inflicted this punishment on a monk returning to sound doctrine. Thus the letter to Marcian appears to have been written either in January or in February.

Furthermore, from letter 113, now 141, to Julian of Cos, we clearly learn in what year John Decurio had been sent by Marcian to the Alexandrians: namely, in this year, 455, or toward the end of the preceding year.

Everyone can see that this John, a distinguished man and commendable for the sincerity of his faith, who was sent to Egypt for the sake of the faith, is the same John the decurion to whom the Emperor Marcian entrusted his letters to be delivered to the Alexandrian monks, which are reported in part III of the Council of Chalcedon, no. 8.

Marcian likewise praises this man’s faith and says that he had attended the sacred Council of Chalcedon. Therefore the distinguished author of the *Annals* should be corrected, since he assigned this embassy of John to the year 452.

## ON LETTER 157, IN QUESNELLUS 126. To Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople

Although this new letter bears no indication of year or day, it must have occupied the place we have assigned to it.

For it praises letter 125, now 156, which is said to have been written on November 1—read “December 1”—and mentions another letter by which Leo commended to the emperor the Egyptian bishops living in exile. It is probable that this letter was sent together with that one, perhaps attached to letter 127, now 158, written on December 1.

Finally, after receiving this letter 126, now 157, Anatolius replied somewhat angrily [1552], as is clear from letter 128, now 163, in which our Leo reproves him for his agitation.

Thus, since the latter letter was written around the middle of March, and since approximately two or three months would have been required for letter 126, now 157, to be carried to Constantinople and for Anatolius’s reply to return from there, the new letter 126, now 157, could scarcely have occupied any other place.

[Note: [Col. 1462D] The chronological note of letter 163 reads “the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April.” We corrected it to “the fifth day before the Kalends.” Compare our note 12 (Col. 1148, n. j) on this letter.]

## ON LETTER 159, IN QUESNELLUS 129. To Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia

Nicetas, to whom this letter is said to have been written, is called Nicaeas by others.

Certainly, if he is the same person as the one mentioned in the Roman Martyrology on June 22, by Saint Jerome in letter 42, and by Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, he should be called Nicaeas, not Nicetas; for they consistently call him by that name. Nevertheless, Lucas Holstenius asserts that Nicetas is the reading in what he calls a codex of admirable antiquity of Gennadius preserved at Saint Andrew della Valle, in his *Observations*, or marginal notes, on Baronius’s Roman Martyrology.

[Col. 1461D] I now see no small difficulty in distinguishing several men named Nicetas, or Nicaea, whom I do not think should be confused into one.

Cardinal Baronius distinguishes between Nicetas, bishop in Dacia, and Nicaea of Romatiana—or, as he interprets it, bishop of the city of Aquileia. He lists the former under January 7, but commemorates the latter on June 22.

Lucas Holstenius, in the place cited, asserts that the two are one and the same. I would judge that two, or perhaps even three, persons must be counted.

First, there is the man of whom Saint Paulinus speaks so honorifically in letter 10 to Severus, calling him a venerable and most learned bishop, deservedly admired by the Romans, and also in the poem for the feast of Saint Felix, where he praises him as both his teacher and his father.

Since the feast of Saint Felix, according to Caesar Baronius’s reckoning, falls in the year of Christ 397, it must be maintained that this Nicetas was already a bishop at that time. It is therefore far from possible that he was the same as our Nicetas, to whom Saint Leo writes, who was not yet a bishop in the year of Christ 447, when Januarius was governing the Church of Aquileia.

There is also a difference in their names. It is certain that the man who was a friend of Paulinus was called Nicetas; most manuscripts call the other Nicaea.

Moreover, their homelands were different. It is probable that this man was from Aquileia; I infer that the other came from Dacia [1553] from Paulinus, who accompanies him as he returns to Dacia in these words:

> May that same guide now accompany  
> You on the road along which you hasten back,  
> And bring you safely, Nicetas,  
> To your ancestral threshold.

Finally, the episcopal sees of the two men were as far apart from one another as the Dacians from the people of Aquileia.

The man about whom Gennadius and Honorius of Autun write, I would judge to be none other than Paulinus’s friend, both because it is probable that the works Gennadius mentions were composed by so learned a pontiff as Paulinus calls him, and because the old manuscripts of Gennadius, one of which Holstenius cites, read Nicetas, not Nicaea.

Finally, the title of bishop presents no obstacle.

If anyone insists that he was a different person, I do not object. But I cannot be persuaded to believe that Gennadius’s Nicetas was the same as the Leonine one.

First, the Leonine Nicetas was bishop of Aquileia. But who could believe that Gennadius called Aquileia a Roman city, when we do not find that name bestowed upon it by any ancient writer? Even if an orator or encomiast could have used such a title, certainly not a historian, whose discourse should employ proper and familiar names.

Gennadius himself follows this practice. When he writes of Rufinus on the preceding page, he does not say that Rufinus was Roman or Romatian, but that he was from Aquileia.

Second, since this author preserves chronological order in his catalogue when he lists distinguished men, he places Nicaea long before writers contemporary with Leo—indeed, before Paulinus, Theophilus of Alexandria, Sabbatius, and others who flourished in the fourth century—not after half of the fifth century had already passed, as would be required for Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.

As for the Nicaeas about whom Saint Jerome writes, the only consideration that seems to persuade one that he was the same as the bishop of Aquileia is the name of the city; many other considerations argue against it.

First, Jerome calls that man Nicaeas, while Leo calls this one Nicetas.

Second, since Jerome’s friend Nicaeas had already been a subdeacon of the Church of Aquileia around the year 390, and since it is probable that he had not attained that rank before the age of twenty-five, he would have been about seventy-five or eighty years old when he was raised to the labors of the episcopate.  Yet in 447 he had not yielded his place to another, since Januarius was still in office. This is highly improbable.

The matter is further confirmed by Saint Jerome’s letter 42, which was written when Chromatius was not yet bishop of Aquileia. In it, when Jerome recalls the journeys that he and Nicaeas had made together, he indicates that Nicaeas was almost his contemporary, with whom he was joined by an unusually close relationship.

From this you see that at least three persons arise from the one name Nicetas, or Nicaea:

First, Nicetas, celebrated in Paulinus’s poems, praised by Gennadius, and bishop of the city called Roman or Romatian;

second, the man called Nicaeas [1554], a subdeacon of Aquileia and a friend of Jerome;

third, the bishop of Aquileia after the year 447, to whom Saint Leo writes in the year 458.

As for the episcopate of the first of these, I readily agree that he was placed over the city of Romatiana, which Gennadius calls Roman, the Peutinger Table calls Romesiana, and the *Itinerary of Antoninus* calls Remisiana.

I would gladly accept, therefore, that the two commemorations of Nicetas, or Nicaea, made by Baronius should be referred to one person. But I cannot agree with his claim that by the city of Romatiana Aquileia is meant.

First, because no one—not among the ancients, nor even among more recent writers—is found to have called it by that name, unless one excepts a certain later cosmographer named Leander, cited by Baronius, who asserts that it was called a second Rome. Even if this were true, it would not prove what Baronius intends.

Suppose that someone praising the city had called it by that name, just as Arles in Gaul is said to have been called Rome. Nevertheless, when the city is being discussed, it would not therefore be called simply “the Roman city,” any more than we ever find Arles designated in that way.

Second, it seems to me utterly absurd to interpret the city of Romatiana, which the Martyrology mentions on June 22, as Aquileia. Since it mentions Aquileia nearly ten times under that very name, why would its author, when treating Nicetas, suddenly abandon his customary manner of speaking and, setting aside the proper name known to everyone, use another name that was new and unknown?

Third, even if Aquileia were to be adorned with a name derived from the city of Rome, it would never have been called Romatiana, except perhaps by ignorant and half-barbarous people, but either Romana or Romaniana—especially since there was another city in Dacia called by that name, from which ambiguity would necessarily have arisen.

### 4. The authority of the inscription of the work *On the Eight Beatitudes*

The authority of the inscription of the work *On the Eight Beatitudes*, in which Chromatius is called its author, “a Roman bishop,” should not be highly valued. It is entirely uncertain whether the inscription refers to Chromatius of Aquileia, and it is highly unusual for anyone other than the bishop of the apostolic see to be designated “Roman.”

Let us nevertheless grant that the bishop of Aquileia was genuinely called by that name. I believe, however, that this happened many years later, if it happened at all.

I think I can derive the occasion for it with sufficient plausibility from Paul the Deacon: it arose from the devastation caused by the Lombards. Fleeing from that devastation, the people of Aquileia chose the nearby island of Grado as their dwelling place and subsequently created a bishop for themselves. To distinguish him from the other bishop who continued to be appointed in old Aquileia, they may perhaps have called him “Roman,” either because he was appointed by Romans or because he governed people subject to the Romans.

Hear Paul the Deacon himself bearing witness to this in his own words, book IV of *The History of the Lombards*, chapter 34:

“In those days, after Severus the patriarch had died, John the abbot was ordained patriarch in his place in old Aquileia, with the consent of King Agilulf and Duke Gisulf. At Grado too, Candidianus was ordained bishop, *Romanus* (otherwise *Romanis*). … After Candidianus too had died at Grado, the patriarch Epiphanius (otherwise Epiphanius), who had been chief of the notaries, was ordained by the bishops who were under the Romans. And from that time there began to be two patriarchs.”

[Col. 1463D] You see, reader, that the bishop of Aquileia was at some point called Roman—not for the reason given by Cardinal Baronius in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, namely, that Aquileia was called either a second Rome, or Romatiana, or a Roman city; nor because some bishop of that city was a Roman by birth, as Sixtus of Siena imagined concerning Chromatius; nor finally because he was Catholic and in communion with the Roman Church, as Baronius thinks in his account of the year of Christ 605, where he discusses Candidianus, whom Paul the Deacon called Romanus.

Although other editions do not read in this way—“Romanus Candidianus was ordained bishop”—but rather “Romanis was ordained,” and so forth, I am nevertheless willing to accept the former reading, which is found in the old Paris edition of 1514.

But from the passages we have quoted it is clear that he was called Roman because he had been ordained by Romans—namely, by those inhabitants of old Aquileia who had crossed over to Grado and were subject to the Romans; also because he had been ordained by bishops who were under the Romans, as Paul the Deacon expressly says; and finally because he had been elected by the authority of the exarch in opposition to the other patriarch, who had been ordained at old Aquileia with the support of the Lombard king and was subject to him.

Even if these points are so, the difficulty has not yet been exhausted. What does this have to do with Chromatius, who preceded Candidianus by two hundred years, or with the election of two patriarchs?

It is not necessary, however, that Chromatius have lived at that time in order to receive the title “Roman.” It is enough that the treatise circulating under his name was copied after the beginning of the seventh century [Col. 1464B], after the two Aquileian bishops had been established.

Moreover, it is probable that titles of this sort were the work of copyists alone. When copying the work of an ancient bishop, they may have thought that he ought to be given the title which they knew was commonly applied to the bishops of Aquileia in their own age.

## ON LETTER 164, IN QUESNELLUS 133. To the Emperor Leo

Of all the letters that we publish, none is supported by the authority (*αὐθεντία*) of more numerous or more eminent authorities.

Saint Prudentius, bishop of Troyes, who around the middle of the ninth century vigorously defended the Catholic doctrine concerning predestination and the grace of Christ against the innovators [1556] of his age, transcribes nearly half of this letter in chapter 1 of his notable work *Against John Scotus Erigena*.

“I have decided,” he says, “to set forth the judgment of one Father, so that, with his testimony, the faith of the others may in no way be diminished. LEO, BISHOP, TO LEO AUGUSTUS. Rejoicing that it has been established by many clear and manifest proofs …”

He quotes as far as chapter 3; then, omitting the third chapter together with the fourth, he again reports several passages from the beginning of chapter 5. He also quotes from another letter of the same pontiff to the same emperor, which in our edition precedes this one.

It is surprising that so distinguished a fragment escaped the later collectors of councils and papal letters, among which it deservedly ought to have held a place.

From it we corrected several errors that had been scattered through the Grimani codex. Conversely, with the help of our codex, several passages in Prudentius’s book require correction, both in the edition first produced by Ludovicus Cellotius from a manuscript of the Thuane Library and in the other edition prepared by the distinguished and learned Gilbert Manguinus, volume I of the collection of ancient authors who wrote in the ninth century on predestination and grace.

Several fragments of the same letter are quoted by Vigilius and Pope Pelagius II, who flourished in the sixth century: the former in his *Constitutum*, the latter in a letter to Elias, bishop of Aquileia. You will find the locations of both marked in the margin of the letter.

Finally, Facundus, that famous bishop of Hermiana in Africa and defender of the Three Chapters, reproduces a substantial portion of this letter in book II, chapter 6, page 87 of the edition by Jacques Sirmond. Sirmond, however, took it not as a letter of Pope Leo to the Emperor Leo, but as words spoken by Facundus to the Emperor Justinian.

Pelagius quotes something from chapter 3 as though it came from a letter written by Leo to Basil. If this is correct, then either it must be said that the same material written by Pope Leo to Leo Augustus was also inserted into another letter written to Basil, and that this letter was lost through the injury of time; or else Pelagius, or his copyist, must be admitted to have suffered a lapse of memory.

## ON LETTER 165, IN QUESNELLUS 134. To the Emperor Leo

[Col. 1465A]

### 1.

We corrected this letter on the authority of ten manuscript codices, comparing all the ancient printed exemplars as well, and restored it to its proper place from the editions of Saint Leo by Surianus and Nicolinus, from the collection of ancient writers on the two natures edited by Josias Simler at Zurich in the year 1571, and from the volume of *Miscellanies* of G. Vossius, provost of Tongeren, printed at Mainz in the year 1604 under his supervision.

To these are added the Trecopith manuscript and the Oxford manuscript, all of which [1557] preserve the consular date omitted by the others.

Among the letters of Pope Agapetus there is one said to have been written to Anthimus. The learned Cardinal Baronius long ago proved it false from the difference between its style and Agapetus’s manner of expression.

It would have been easy for anyone comparing it with the present letter of Leo to detect that it was spurious [Col. 1465B], for it has been assembled entirely from fragments sewn together from this letter.

If it matters to know the age of the forgery, I would readily believe it to be a hundred years later than Anthimus, as I infer from the alteration of certain words.

For in chapter 2, where Saint Leo reads “the consubstantial equality,” the fabricator of the pseudo-letter substituted “the equality of one will” in place of these two words. It is therefore beyond doubt that he was acting in support of Sergius, bishop of Constantinople, who desired to produce some testimony of a Roman pontiff in support of his inadequate defense of the doctrine of Christ’s single will.

For such adulterine offspring are not introduced in place of legitimate works without a definite purpose. The entire letter reveals no other desire in the impostor than to support the error of the Monothelites.

Through a similar forgery, chapter 4 and the chapters following it, up to the testimony of Saint Hilary, were transformed into a spurious letter of Pope Caius; and that same excerpt from Saint Hilary was inserted into the first letter of Pope Eutychian, which is addressed to the bishops of the province of Baetica.

### 2. “The outpouring … of Christ’s blood was so rich in payment”

This is the reading of two Barberini manuscripts, four Thuane manuscripts, the Trecopith manuscript, the Corbie manuscript, the Cambridge manuscript, the Bodleian manuscript, the Grimani manuscript, and the pseudo-letter of Agapetus.

In the common printed edition, however, it reads: “The outpouring … of the righteous blood of Christ was so powerful in privilege, so rich in payment.”

But the words that are excessive here have been transferred from letter 97, now 124, to the Palestinian monks.

### 3. “For every sacrament of the Christian faith is greatly disfigured by darkness if—as the heretics wish—the light of truth is thought to have lain hidden beneath the lie of a phantom”

We moved the parenthesis “as the heretics wish” to its proper place [Note: [Col. 1465D] We restored these words to their proper place on the authority of all the manuscripts and the ancient Greek version, and explained the meaning sufficiently in note 71 (Col. 1169, n. f) on this letter 165.]—not because we were led to do so by the authority of any manuscript, as we admit, but solely by conjecture, or rather by the necessity of the sense itself.

The former position of the parenthesis produces a false meaning. It reads:

“For every sacrament of the Christian faith is greatly—as the heretics wish—disfigured by darkness, if the light of truth is thought to have lain hidden beneath the lie of a phantom.”

Did the Manichaeans and other heretics who denied the reality of Christ’s flesh [1558] wish their opinion to be an insult to the divinity? On the contrary, this was utterly foreign to their intention. They argued instead that great injury was inflicted upon the eternal Son of the Father if he were believed to have been clothed in true flesh.

What the heretics wanted was that only an apparent flesh should be attributed to Christ the Lord.

It was nevertheless easy for the parenthesis—perhaps newly added—to have been moved by an ancient copyist to the line above its original position.

### 4. “Then the testimonies follow,” and so forth

The ancient Fathers frequently mention these testimonies. Among them is Vigilius of Tapsus, bishop in Africa, in book V of *Against Eutyches*, section 32:

“Let us bring forward all the teachers of the Church, and, selecting from their many statements a few brief passages, append them to this work. We send the diligent reader to their fuller and more extensive treatments of this confession, which the most blessed Leo gathered together into one collection of testimonies with provident care.”

Most of these testimonies of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 1466D] These testimonies, collected by Leo and sent to the East after the Robber Council of Ephesus, do not belong to the Council of Chalcedon. Although in the common editions they are attached to Leo’s letters and inserted into the second session of Chalcedon, they are not found there in the manuscripts. See the warning in letter 28, nos. 8 and 9.] are found appended to Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, in the second session of the Council of Chalcedon, though not in the same order or in the same number. More are appended to this letter than appear in the Acts of Chalcedon.

I shall not omit what Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, writes concerning this selection of testimonies in his treatise *On the Non-Trinal Deity*, since it contains a remarkable commendation of Leo himself. He dares to assert that our holy pontiff was not inferior in merit to the distinguished lights of the Church—Hilary, Athanasius, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Cyril, and Augustine himself.

“For Leo,” he says, “the pontiff of the holy Catholic and apostolic see, deemed it sufficient, for the confirmation of the Catholic faith, to send to Leo Augustus the few testimonies—great in authority and in the spirit of right faith—of those who preceded him in time, though not in place or merit.”

See more above, in the discussion of letter 24, now 28, to Flavian.

At the end of this collection, the following is appended in one manuscript of the Barberini codex:

“The testimonies extracted from the books of the holy Fathers have been completed. They show that Christ is a giant of two substances—that is, that the true and perfect natures both of divinity and of humanity constitute one person of Christ.”

## 1559. ON THE BOOKLET OF CONFESSION OF LEPORIUS THE MONK, whose author is now asserted to have been Saint Augustine for the first time

[Col. 1466C]

Our present edition displays this letter, or collection of testimonies, enriched by one testimony—and indeed an outstanding one—which has come to us through the favor of our repeatedly praised manuscript of the Grimanic codex. It is placed last among the testimonies excerpted from Augustine and is attributed to him under this title: “Also, the same author, from the book *Assertion of the Faith*.” It begins as follows: “For it is ours to believe,” and so forth.

However carefully one examines Augustine’s works, nowhere will one find such a treatise from which these words were taken, nor any other work bearing a similar title. They are instead the words of that distinguished little book called Leporius’s letter or confession, or the book of correction, or the booklet of satisfaction. Ancient authors who either quoted part of it or at least mentioned it include John Cassian, Book I *On the Incarnation of the Lord*; Pope John II, Letter 3, to Avienus and the other senators; Vigilius of Thapsus, Book XI *On the Trinity*; Facundus of Hermiane, Book I of the *Defense of the Three Chapters*; Gennadius, in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*; and Sigebert.

John Garnerius adds Basil the deacon, Thalassius, and other monks, whose supplicatory booklet to the Emperor Theodosius is preserved in Part I of the Acts of the Council of Ephesus, chapter 30. But it is certainly evident from that booklet that the Leporius mentioned there among the bishops who defended the divinity of Christ was himself a bishop, and not the monk whose confession we are examining.

Basil appears to preserve the chronological order in that enumeration, [Col. 1467A] and therefore seems to be speaking of some Bishop Leporius who flourished before Ambrose of Milan, the entire African synod whom he mentions, John Chrysostom, Severianus, and Atticus of Constantinople, all of whom are named after Leporius.

Moreover, if Basil had intended to speak of our Leporius and of that African synod which supported his confession, he would have placed the two together, and would not have inserted Ambrose between Leporius and the synod. Finally, similarity of name alone is too weak a foundation to support this assertion, since several men bearing this name are found both at the First Council of Toledo and elsewhere.

As for the synod which Basil calls the whole of Africa, who could persuade himself that it was the same synod at which Leporius’s confession was approved, if he examined the letter sent from there to the Gallican bishops and the subscriptions of the Africans? Certainly, if from Basil the deacon’s words we are to understand the universal synod of Africa, I would suppose that he had in mind the one held in the year 397, under the consulship of Atticus and Caesarius, [Col. 1467B] at which the profession and faith of the Council of Nicaea were recited and confirmed, as may be seen in chapter 2 [Note: [Col. 1467D] He calls this the collection of canons which we shall reprint, corrected, in Volume III and shall prove not to be Roman.] of the Roman codex.

The same excerpt from Leporius’s confession appears in the selection of testimonies contained in Action 2 of the Council of Chalcedon, under this title: “Also, a sermon of the same Augustine: *On the Exposition of the Faith*.” But since it appeared disguised until now in words belonging to another—having evidently been translated from Greek—this explains why no one detected Leporius as its author, even though these same words could be read transcribed both in John Cassian and in Vigilius of Thapsus, before the complete work was rescued from obscurity through the care of the learned Sirmond.

Relying on this twofold support, [Note: [Col. 1467D] This testimony of Augustine does not belong to the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, as we noted in annotation 3. The Greek text is an ancient translation of the testimonies that Leo sent to the East; and this very ancient Greek translation, apart from the Grimanic Latin manuscript, confirms the testimony, although it is omitted in other Latin codices [Col. 1468D].] namely, the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon and the gold of the Grimanic manuscript, I do not hesitate to assert that the booklet of Leporius’s correction is truly the offspring of the great Augustine. I do not think it superfluous to strengthen this claim with several considerations, since this booklet gains no small authority from the name of so great a parent, while Augustine himself gains no small glory from the composition of a synodal booklet.

First, therefore, each of these two testimonies seems to me to possess much greater authority because both Saint Leo and the Fathers of that ecumenical synod flourished in Augustine’s time. Ten years had not yet passed since Augustine’s death when our Leo was raised to the Roman see. In the eleventh year of his pontificate, those six hundred Fathers assembled at Chalcedon in an ecumenical synod.

### 2

While Saint Leo was still serving as archdeacon, he spent some time in the Gallican provinces. Leporius had initially begun to infect these provinces with his error, and later restored them through the publication of his correction.

Although we have no testimony from any ancient monument confirming what a more recent writer has reported—namely, that our Leo visited the Gallican provinces more than once before attaining the summit of the pontificate—it is nevertheless certain, on the testimony of Prosper, who was not only a contemporary but also an eyewitness, that our Leo was in Gaul when Pope Sixtus died, at the beginning of approximately the year of the Lord 440 [Note: [Col. 1468D] From our most ancient Sacramentary we have judged it more probable that Sixtus III died on August 11; see our annotation 23 in §33 of the month of October, in this volume, col. 135 (our Volume II).]

It was therefore easy for a man who was an eager investigator of all ecclesiastical affairs to learn from Prosper, or from other inhabitants of that region, precisely what he later wished to make known to the universal synod, to the Emperor Leo, and indeed to all posterity: that the Leporian confession had been written in Augustine’s style.

### 3

Unless Saint Leo had known with absolute certainty, either from public information or from some other source, that this booklet under discussion truly belonged to Augustine, he would never have undertaken to present it to the ecumenical synod under the name of so great a doctor as an authentic witness to Catholic truth [Note: [Col. 1468D] Leo did not send the Fathers’ testimonies to the Council of Chalcedon; he had sent them to the East through legates the year before. See the admonition to Letter 28, at the end.], especially since several bishops from the African Church were present at the Council of Chalcedon and knew all the works of their Augustine thoroughly.

For it is certain that in the sacred ecumenical synods of the Church Catholic doctrine is established only from the definite tradition of the holy Fathers, expressed in their indisputable writings. Anyone who acted otherwise would willingly expose the most holy truth and the Church herself to the contempt and insults of heretical men. Such a thing must be judged less likely of our pontiff than of anyone else.

[Col. 1468B] ### 4

There is no one unaware of the position Augustine occupied in that age, both in the universal Church and especially in Africa. At that time no council was convened in those regions in which Aurelius was not the leader and Augustine the mind—not merely the mind, but also the eye, tongue, and hand.

Since Leporius’s affair was conducted and his confession approved in an African synod—for Pope John II explicitly asserts this in his letter to Avienus and the other senators, and the letter of the African bishops to the Gauls itself indicates it, since it bears the form of a synodal letter—who could doubt that on this occasion, as on others, the synod borrowed Augustine’s style?

### 5

The same argument that just praised letter of the Africans attributes it to Augustine as author—a judgment to which Sirmond subscribes—and also vindicates the booklet for him. The style in both is Augustinian; and not merely the style, but the doctrine and the very ideas [Col. 1468C] unmistakably breathe Augustine, as will readily be apparent to the reader.

Thus, in Letter 3 to Volusianus, Augustine says that “the God-man was mingled with man” and that “the person of Christ is a mixture of God and man.” There he warns the reader, as he does in the excerpt, to withdraw from the analogy of bodies, in which two liquids are ordinarily mixed so that neither preserves its integrity. See also Book IV *On the Trinity*, chapter 20, and the *Enchiridion*, chapters 35 and 36.

The statement likewise found in this same testimony—that God contains, and is not contained—belongs to Augustinian style. Thus Augustine says in his dispute with Pascentius:

“They neither read nor rightly defend the claim that the Father is incapable of being contained. For how is the Father incapable of being contained, when the Son contains him wholly? … How is the Father incapable of being contained, when he is wholly contained by the Son? … He who contains all things, whom no one contains except among human beings—for he is wholly contained by the Son.”

Finally, concerning the manner in which God wholly fills all things, Augustine speaks in identical terms both in this part of Leporius’s confession and in the letter just mentioned to Volusianus.

I deliberately refrain from a more exact and extensive comparison of the two texts. The learned Benedictines of Saint-Germain will adorn this field more elegantly: they are soon to publish the works of Saint Augustine, purged, enlarged, and illustrated through new labors. In the meantime, read the other passages of Augustine that correspond to this confession, as indicated in the notes of the learned John Garnerius, Part I of the Works of Marius Mercator, p. 230.

[Col. 1469A] ### 6

Leporius the monk does not seem to have been endowed with enough learning to be capable of composing a profession of such exceptional faith, especially when the subject was the most abstruse mystery of the Incarnation, which far surpasses the entire capacity of the human mind.

Indeed, I would judge that what Leporius confesses about himself with the deepest humility was stated without compromising the truth. I mean that he himself attributes his error to his own ignorance and accuses his “foolish simplicity,” as he calls it.

But if Leporius was compelled to seek someone’s assistance in setting forth his confession, it should have been no one other than Augustine—both for the reason given above in section 4 and because Leporius had been corrected and recalled to sound faith through Augustine’s efforts. Gennadius and the Liège codex of the Africans’ letter in Sirmond’s first volume of the Councils of Gaul name Augustine, while suppressing the names of the others.

### 7

Finally, Leporius himself, by subscribing his booklet, sufficiently indicates that it had been written by another, since he says that it was dictated according to his own understanding and speaks of it as follows:

“The faith of this letter, the profession of this letter.”

By this wording he seems not to have dared to call it his own, because he knew that it had been dictated by another.

Nor is it of great importance that someone might object, on the basis of the synodal letter of the African bishops, that they testify that the confession was Leporius’s own. It was his, and was called his, for many reasons: it had been dictated according to his understanding and was to be published in his name; it openly proclaimed his faith and correction; and, finally, he himself was sending it to Gaul, copied in his own hand and secured with his own signature.

Certainly, at that time it was very important that it should be believed to have been composed through his own industry and ability, so that the agreement and subscription of those whom he had drawn along with him into his error and taken with him to Africa might be elicited more willingly and readily.

Finally, there are many examples of letters of this kind which are said not to belong to those who composed them, but to those [Col. 1469C] in whose place and name they had been drafted by another. Such is the celebrated letter of Pope Pelagius II to Elias and the other bishops of Istria. There are many such letters in Augustine, Bernard, and others: when they were sent, they were attributed for the stated reason to those by whom they were dispatched, but now they are rightly restored to their genuine authors.

Although this letter or confession is clear and worthy of Augustine, it nevertheless did not possess such authority that Leporius was therefore counted among the Catholic doctors in the East, or that Augustine—who alone of the four subscribers survived in the year 430—was summoned to the Council of Ephesus. Nevertheless, J. Garnerius adds, and these are also his words on page 230, that Volusianus, since he was then living at the court of Theodosius, may reasonably be called the instigator who caused Augustine to be summoned by name before the other Africans.

For Leporius, as we have seen, was not numbered among the doctors in the East; nor did Augustine need this recommendation to be summoned before the synod, since on so many other grounds he was owed not merely this prerogative but every exceptional privilege. See above, p. 43 [Note: [Col. 1469D] Here Quesnellus cites the collection of canons edited by himself at the beginning of Volume II; we shall reprint it in Volume III, and he indicates the end of chapter 16.].

## TO LETTER CLXVI, LETTER CXXXV IN QUESNELLUS. To Neon, Bishop of Ravenna

We have removed this letter of Leo from the place it formerly occupied. Since it was thought to belong to the consulship of the Emperor Marcian, which fell in the year of Christ 451, we now believe that it should instead be assigned to the consulship of the Emperor Majorian, that is, to the year 458.

First, although twenty letters of Leo dated to the year 451 still survive, none of the others is found marked with the consulship of Marcian; all bear the consulship of Adelphius. Who, then, could persuade himself that Leo, so consistent in everything, even in matters of little importance, after so many letters marked with the name of the consul Adelphius, suddenly changed his practice and thought of adding the name of Marcian?

The fact that he does not mention the consulship of this emperor in those letters should not be attributed to a lapse of memory, negligence, or some accident. Rather, it should be supposed that it was not customary at that time to reckon the years by his consulship, even if the reason for omitting it is not apparent.

This should also be regarded as certain: Leo would by no means have omitted the name if usage had required it, especially since all those letters were sent to the East and addressed to Eastern bishops—indeed, to the bishop of Constantinople, Julian of Cos, the Augusta Pulcheria, the Council of Chalcedon, and the Emperor Marcian himself.

In view of this, no one will persuade himself that a single letter, written after all those others and sent to an Italian bishop, was, contrary to custom, marked with the name of Marcian.

### 2

Whenever Leo recorded a single consul in his letters, he named the Western consul, not the Eastern one. He did this not merely in the consulship of this year, where the practice appears nearly twenty times, but also in many other years.

Letter 18 [now 19], in the year 448, is marked only by Postumianus; six letters from the year 452 only by Herculanus; fourteen from the year 453 only by Opilio; the two letters from the year 455, which are the only ones from that year, by Valentinian alone; Letter 129 [now 159], from the year 458, only by Majorian; and Letter 137 [now 169], from the year 459, only by Ricimer.

Here, then, we have the reason why so many letters of the year 451 bear the consulship of Adelphius rather than that of Marcian, including the nine letters addressed to Marcian himself and to his wife Pulcheria. It also explains why the letter under discussion should not have been marked by the sole consulship of Marcian. Evidently, the custom at that time was for Westerners to record the Western consul and Easterners the Eastern consul in public documents.

### 3

It is easy for a reader to see that Leo never wrote the consular designation in this form—“in the consulship of”—but used either “with the consul” or “with the consuls.” Thus everyone can see that the heading of this letter was added by another hand [Note: [Col. 1469D] See our annotation 21 (col. 1195, note a) on this letter.].

### 4
