An examination of this letter shows that it was written by Leo [Note: [Col. 1470D] This letter does not appear to have been written in response to a consultation by the bishops of the province of Ravenna. It seems to be an encyclical addressed to several persons, as we observed in the admonition.] in response to a consultation from the bishops of the province subject to Ravenna. The consultation arose because certain people who had been carried into captivity from those regions several years earlier, after some barbarian incursion, had finally returned to their homes and freedom.

It is certain that Italy enjoyed peace during the time of Pope Leo, at least until the year 451, the year in which some wish to place this letter. The Romans had indeed begun to fear an invasion of the barbarians under Attila. At that time that man, born to terrify humanity, was laying waste to Gaul, and Rome rightly feared so great and so nearby a multitude of barbarians. But he did not enter Italy until the following year, 452. Then, as Paul the Deacon writes, Attila, having immediately recovered his confidence, attacked Italy in bloodshed, utterly destroyed Aquileia after capturing it, and demolished Ticinum and Milan, royal cities.

It is therefore highly probable that the region of Ravenna, one of the most distinguished in Italy, experienced Attila’s fury—although some report that the city itself was saved through the prayers of its bishop—and that at least many people from the territory and diocese of Ravenna were carried into captivity in the year 452.

At that time, because of their immature age, they could not yet possess a firm understanding of anything, as Leo says. After several years—namely, in 457 and 458—they may have attained both freedom and their homeland, begun to doubt their baptism, and sought the grace of regeneration.

This gave the Italians occasion to consult the Roman pontiff, and the Roman pontiff occasion to write this letter to the bishops of that region. In the same way, because of controversies arising from the same barbarian disaster and captivity, he wrote another letter to the bishop of Aquileia during this same consulship of the Emperor Majorian.

Everyone can see how easily, through the error of scribes, the name of Marcian may have slipped in where the name of Majorian belonged—especially since the uncertain and elusive characters of manuscript codices very often force a reader to guess, and since the scarcity of manuscripts compels us to be satisfied with these conjectures, if indeed they are nothing more than conjectures.

There was scarcely a second manuscript available. Nor does the Cambridge manuscript, whose variant readings were sent to us, provide any illumination, except that the very courteous Mr. Gale indicates that the day on which the letter was written is not marked there; it is therefore probable that the consular designation was also absent from that codex.

It was not altogether useless to investigate these matters so carefully, both to establish the order of Saint Leo’s letters with greater security and to prevent ecclesiastical writers from continuing to misuse this date. They commonly consult the consular heading of the letter in order to determine the year of the death of Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna; indeed, they also use it to determine the date of the death of Saint Germanus of Auxerre, who died on the journey during which he was received at Ravenna by Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of that city.

### 1. Neon or Neonia

Thus the Victor manuscript and the Cistercian and Claromontane indexes, together with the Isidorian edition; likewise Ughellus in *Sacred Italy*. Nor is this name unusual. Neon, bishop of Psyllium in Pamphylia, subscribed the Council of Chalcedon. That Neon—or Leo, as others call him—succeeded Peter Chrysologus in the year 450 and died in the third year of his episcopate, as Ughellus reports.

### 2. An unforgivable crime

But compare the meaning of our Leo with Augustine, Letter 203:

“To rebaptize a heretic is altogether a sin; but to rebaptize a Catholic is a most monstrous crime.”

As you see, Augustine places a broad distinction between a Catholic who rebaptizes a heretic and a heretic who rebaptizes a Catholic.

### 3. According to the doctrine of the heretics, contrary to the ordinances of the holy Fathers

[Note: [Col. 1471D] We have restored the common reading. See our annotation 16 (col. 1194, note j) on the present letter.]

Thus the readings of the Thuanus and Cambridge manuscripts; but the common edition reads: “According to the institutions condemned by the heretics and the holy Fathers.”

Saint Leo seems here to indicate either the Donatists, according to Saint Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 69, or perhaps the Novatians and Montanists, concerning whom Innocent I makes the same assertion in his letter to Victricius, chapter 8.

“Judgment.” Thus the Thuanus and Cambridge manuscripts, as well as Gratian and Ivo; the common reading is “doctrine.”

### 4. Nor should we fear opening this door of salvation, and so forth

[Col. 1471D]

The Fathers of the Council of Carthage, which they call the Fifth Council, in the African codex, number 72, Saint Leo in Letter 2 [now 167] to Rusticus of Narbonne, and Gregory III in the eighth century, boldly wished such persons to be baptized even without an accompanying condition. This practice continued almost to the twelfth century, when they began to adopt a new method of supplying baptism.

Pope Alexander III appears to have been the first, after the year 1160, to introduce this formula of baptism administered conditionally:

“If you have been baptized, I do not baptize you; but if you have not been baptized, I baptize you in …”

Scholastic theology, which arose around the same century, derived this formula from him [Col. 1472A].

### 5. He imposed it by the laying on of the bishop’s hand

Read the same discipline affirmed in Letter 2 [now 167] to Rusticus of Narbonne, inquiry 18; and in Letter 129 [now 169] to Nicetas of Aquileia; in canon 8 of the First Council of Arles; canon 7 of the First Council of Constantinople; in Pope Siricius’s letter to Himerius of Tarragona; and in Innocent I’s letters to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, and to Victricius of Rouen [Note: [Col. 1471D] Compare our annotation 25 (col. 1138, note q) on Letter 159.].

Since the last of these decrees that Arians and other heretics of this kind should be received through the laying on of the bishop’s hand, either “under the image” or “with the image” of penance, this learned man seems to have taken a middle course between the older discipline—which subjected heretics returning to the Church to penance and, in Cyprian’s words, to lamentations and acts of satisfaction—and the discipline imposed here by our Leo, which includes nothing beyond the laying on of hands for the reception of the power of the Holy Spirit.

But since Siricius, who was earlier than Innocent, requires nothing more than our Leo does, this distinction cannot be accepted by us. Nor would I think that anything other than the renunciation of the former error is signified by “the image of penance,” expressed through a profession of faith and certain ceremonies indicating a humbled and penitent spirit, which ordinarily preceded the laying on of hands.

## 1567. TO LETTER CLXVII, LETTER II IN QUESNELLUS. To Rusticus, Bishop of Narbonne

### 1

Sirmond, *Councils of Gaul*, Volume I, assigns this letter to Rusticus of Narbonne to the year of Christ 452; other writers subsequently agreed with him. No reason is offered on which this date rests.

I suspect that they had the following considerations in mind. The letter appears to have been written in troubled times, as suggested both by the anxiety of Rusticus—whom the adversity of various scandals had almost driven to renounce his episcopal dignity [Col. 1472C]—and by the various questions that it is natural to believe arose from the barbarian invasion and the devastation of the provinces. These include questions concerning children carried into captivity by barbarians, baptized by heretics, living as pagans, and contaminated by sacrificial food.

The mind immediately turns to that pitiable disaster which the Huns, under Attila, inflicted upon Gaul in this year 452. It was not doubted that our Leo, consulted by Rusticus on the occasion of this calamity, sent him this letter.

But I think that the date of this letter must be established differently [Note: [Col. 1472D] In the admonition prefixed to these letters, we have shown that they were written no earlier than 458; there we believe that we have answered each of Quesnellus’s arguments.].

If the titles of the inquiries are considered—the titles restored by Sirmond from numerous manuscript codices and which we ourselves saw in the two manuscripts, the Thuanus and the Trecopithoeanus—it will not be difficult to conclude that Rusticus of Narbonne sent this consultation to Pope Leo not because of the Gallic disaster inflicted by Attila’s forces, but rather because of the Vandal plunder and persecution by which the African regions had been devastated far and wide [Note: [Col. 1472D] We refuted this in the admonition, sections 3 and 4.].

This is sufficiently indicated by inquiry 18: “Concerning those who have come from Africa or Mauretania and do not know in what sect they were baptized,” and so forth. In addition to the authority of the manuscript codices, this title is supported by the authority of Book II of Auxilius *On the Ordination of Pope Formosus*, where the same wording is found.

When Geiseric had plundered most of Africa and subjected the city of Carthage itself to his power, Victor of Vita relates that this impious and barbarous king placed a great multitude of clergy, together with Quodvultdeus, bishop of Carthage, on ships with their sides broken, and that they reached Naples in Campania after a favorable voyage, naked and stripped of everything.

[Col. 1473A] He first crushed the multitude of senators and distinguished men through cruel exile and then cast them across the sea. Indeed, Geiseric compelled all of them, after losing all their possessions, to sail to Italy, as the same Victor and the Acts of Fulgentius testify.

There is no doubt that many who were fleeing persecution also crossed into Gaul. This is confirmed by the cited title or inquiry 18 and is made likely by the frequent intercourse that always existed between the Gallican and African regions.

Since Geiseric took possession of Carthage at the end of the year 439, Catholics—and even Manichaeans, as Baronius infers from Leo’s own letters—began withdrawing from Africa in the following years, when the tyrant began exercising his fury most violently. Thus the circumstances became known in Gaul because of the arrival of these people, and the bishop of Narbonne wished Saint Leo to give judgment concerning them.

That I should believe this letter was written around the same period—namely, in the years 442, 443, or 444—is also suggested by the fact that some of the questions Rusticus raises [Col. 1473B] were being debated in those same regions at those same times, and that the Fathers of the Gallican councils issued decisions on them, specifically at the First Council of Orange, the First Council of Vaison, and the Second Council of Arles.

The First Council of Orange discusses, in canon 3, penitents who depart from the body; in canon 4, whether penance should be granted to clerics; in canon 12, whether penance should be given to a sick person who suddenly becomes mute; in canons 23 and 24, the continence of deacons; in canons 8, 9, 21, and 25, illicit ordinations; and in canon 28, those who have professed chastity and violate it, so that they may be subjected to penance.

The First Council of Vaison discusses penitents who die suddenly, decreeing that their offerings should be received. The First Council of Arles, which resumes most of the preceding topics, likewise includes and resolves these questions.

From this I think one of two conclusions follows [Note: [Col. 1473D] We showed these two conjectures of Quesnellus to be groundless in the same admonition, section 7]: either Rusticus wrote to Leo before these difficult questions had been debated and resolved in the councils mentioned above [Note: [Col. 1473D] Even on Quesnellus’s view, Rusticus certainly wrote after the First Councils of Orange and Vaison. He therefore considered it neither superfluous nor contrary to Gallican custom to seek apostolic authority after questions had been resolved in provincial or greater synods, so that no uncertainty might remain. See the admonition, section 7. Similarly, Theodore of Fréjus, although a Gaul—and although it is more probable that he was the Theodore who subscribed the First Council of Orange—nevertheless did not hesitate to inquire of Leo concerning several matters defined at that synod, as will become clear from what Quesnellus brings forward shortly afterward.];

for it would seem superfluous and contrary to Gallican custom for another consultation concerning the same matters to be held after they had been resolved in several provincial or even greater synods.

Or, if Rusticus’s letter did not precede those synods, it should nevertheless be thought not to have been written long after them. Rusticus may perhaps have believed that he was not bound by their statutes, both because their discipline appeared harsher in many respects and because there was some disagreement between himself and Hilary, bishop of Arles, who had been the author and president of those canons. Hilary’s supreme authority over the Gallican churches overshadowed the dignity of the metropolitan of Narbonne and of the other metropolitan bishops.

Indeed, a serious dispute had formerly broken out between the bishops of those two cities under the Roman pontiffs Zosimus and Boniface, as is clear from their decrees. It is not reasonable to believe that the bishop of Narbonne ever yielded anything of his rights, especially since a later judgment of Pope Boniface had asserted those rights for the Church of Narbonne.

In fact, Rusticus never attended those synods which Hilary of Arles convened from bishops of several provinces, such as the Council of Riez, the First Council of Orange, the First Council of Vaison, and the Second Council of Arles. He did this so that his metropolitan rights might not suffer any diminution. Nor did he think that he was bound to obey their decrees, lest he acknowledge the jurisdiction of the man under whose presidency they had been chiefly composed and promulgated.

[Note: [Col. 1473D] These things are written not only gratuitously but falsely about Rusticus. Since he attended without difficulty two synods of Ravennius of Arles, he is wrongly thought, for that reason, to have neglected or withheld assent from other synods of Saint Hilary, lest his metropolitan right be diminished in any way, etc. For the same reason he would equally have stayed away from Ravennius’s synods.]

I believe that canon 29 of the First Council of Orange applies to Rusticus—or to some other metropolitan who for this reason neglected to appear at the synod or refused to consent. That canon threatens with punishment those bishops who had not presented themselves at synods either personally or through legates, or who would not subsequently do so.

“We do not pass over,” it says, “those who refuse to be present at the synod, either personally, through their representatives, or through legates sent in their place, so that those who despise the statutes of the Fathers may be pleasing to them above us,” and so forth.

From these words one understands that there were some who wished to take no part in those synods—not only personally or through legates, but not even through their representatives. It is easier to think that this applied to Rusticus than to anyone else, because of the dispute he had raised with the bishop of Arles over the rights of his Church, or—what was our earlier explanation—because of the severity of the discipline, which he hoped Leo’s reply would soften.

Rusticus had once lived at Rome, as Saint Jerome testifies in his letter to him, and had seen that many practices there differed from those followed in Gaul. In fact, the discipline found in this Roman letter of Leo differs in many respects from the Gallican discipline, and it will not be superfluous to examine this somewhat more carefully.

For canon 3 of the Council of Orange forbids the laying on of the hand of reconciliation to be granted to penitents who are departing from the body. Saint Leo, in Letter 83 [now 108] to Theodore, chapter 4, commands that communion not be denied them.

[Col. 1474C]

Canon 12 decrees that penance may be given to someone who suddenly becomes mute if there is testimony of his past will in the words of others, or of his present will in his gesture [Note: [Col. 1474D] Since the same canon, speaking equally of baptism and penance, decrees that a person who has become mute may, according to his condition, be baptized or receive penance if he has manifested his will, and so forth, the word “penance” appears also to include communion, or reconciliation. For just as it is not contradictory to confer the sacrament of baptism upon him, so neither is it contradictory to confer the sacrament of penance—especially since the subject is someone whom penance alone, which he cannot complete in that condition, would assist uselessly without reconciliation.].

But the canon sufficiently indicates by its silence that communion is not to be given, whereas our Leo in the same place decrees that it should be granted.

Canon 4 asserts that penance must not be denied to clerics who desire it. If, however, the term “clerics”—as is usually the case when nothing further is added—includes clerics of every order, then this is contrary to Leo, who says in inquiry 2 that it is foreign to ecclesiastical custom for priests or deacons to receive the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands.

Canons 22, 23, and 24 release all lower clerics, including subdeacons, from the law of continence, imposing it only upon deacons and those above the diaconate.

Saint Leo, in inquiry 3, says:

“The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and priests. While they were laymen, they could lawfully marry and beget children; but when they reached the aforementioned orders, what had been lawful for them ceased to be lawful.”

There can be no doubt that he counts subdeacons among the ministers of the altar and among those who have reached the aforementioned orders, especially since he asserts that marriage is not lawful for clerics beyond the rank of lector. He explains himself clearly enough in the letter sent around the same time to Anastasius of Thessalonica, in chapter 4 of which he expressly affirms that ecclesiastical law forbids marriage to subdeacons.

Canon 25 permits a man who has contracted a second marriage to be promoted to the subdiaconate, although it prohibits him from advancing further. Our Leo, in chapter 3 of Letter 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne, does not permit those who are or have been married to a widow, or who are not shown to have been husbands of only one wife, to enter the sacred service [1571]:

> For our part, he says, observing the legal enactments, we have wished them to be guarded with greater care, not only in the case of priests but also in that of clerics of lesser office.

This is far removed from that Gallican canon.

The First Council of Vaison, canon 2, decrees:

> In the case of those who, after receiving penance, live the course of a good life with satisfactory contrition, but are sometimes overtaken by an unexpected death in the fields or on journeys without communion, their offering is to be received, and their funerals, and thereafter their memory, are to be honored with ecclesiastical affection, etc.

From these words it is clear that the Gallican Churches gave communion after death to penitents who died unexpectedly, even though, while they were alive and still completing the course of penance, they had not admitted them to communion. Saint Leo, on the other hand, replying to Inquiry 8, says:

> Their case must be left to the judgment of God, in whose hands it lay to defer the deaths of such persons until the remedy of communion: but those to whom we did not give communion while they were alive, we cannot give communion when they are dead.

He writes something not very different in Letter 83 (now 108), to Theodore of Fréjus, chapter 3.

I have wished to report and compare these decrees with one another, both so that the variety of discipline in different Churches, even neighboring ones, might become evident, and so that we might at the same time understand what moved Rusticus to consult Pope Leo about these matters [Col. 1475C]. This also contributes greatly to establishing the date of Leo’s letter.

I shall add one or two points that may strengthen our conjectures. [Note: [Col. 1475C] We refute both conjectures in Admonition 8.] First, Leo may be speaking of one of the synods we mentioned when, at the beginning, he discusses the Acts recently reviewed, which had been drawn up in the examination of bishops [1572] and distinguished persons; hence it may be thought that he wrote shortly afterward about one of those synods [Col. 1476A].

The second point is that the dejection and faintheartedness to which Rusticus gave himself on account of the scandals arising everywhere does not seem characteristic of a bishop who had grown old in that dignity, nor does that trembling, in treating the diseases of the Church, seem characteristic of a most experienced physician. Ravennius uses this designation of Rusticus when inviting him to the Third Council of Arles, which, as Sirmond conjectures, was assembled in 455 in the case of the island of Lérins. That year is only three years after 452, the year to which Sirmond assigned this letter; yet its date fits better the beginning of Rusticus’s episcopate, or the years not far removed from its beginning.

For when several years of episcopal administration had disclosed the weight and difficulty of so serious a burden, the man who had been brought up in the peace and quiet of a monastery began to feel himself unequal to so great a responsibility. He began to desire release from the labors of the episcopate and wished to spend the remainder of his life in silence and peace, so that Saint Leo had to strengthen his courage by his exhortations and fortify him against such terrors with the hope of heavenly assistance [Col. 1476B].

There is an excellent letter of Saint Jerome to this Rusticus, in which he instructs him in the monastic life when, as Jerome puts it, Rusticus was then treading the first impulses of adolescence—or rather of puberty—and climbing toward the threshold of mature age. I infer that he was a native of Massilia from the already mentioned letter of Saint Jerome, in which he sends Rusticus, while still living in his mother’s house [1573], to the discipline of Proculus, bishop of Massilia:

> You have there, he says, the holy and most learned bishop Proculus, who by his living and present voice surpasses our little writings and directs your path by his daily instruction.

(Hieronymus, Letter 4, to Rusticus, near the end.) The inscription from Narbonne supports this: it records that Rusticus was the companion of Venerius, bishop of Massilia, in the monastery, and a fellow presbyter of the same Church.

[Note: [Col. 1475C] “In his mother’s house,” says Quesnellus, according to his own view, by which he supposes that Rusticus was not yet a monk when Saint Jerome wrote to him; for he subsequently endeavors, at considerable length, to establish that Rusticus became a monk not in the monastery at Massilia but in one at Toulouse. We do not agree. The inscription which Quesnellus himself later presents, and which testifies that Rusticus was the companion of Bishop Venerius in the monastery—that is, a monk—and his fellow presbyter of Massilia, plainly indicates the monastery at Massilia. Jerome, moreover, in his letter formerly numbered 4 and now numbered 126 in the Veronese edition, signifies both in the inscription that Rusticus was a monk and in the text that he was living near Massilia. Quesnellus attacks this only because he supposes that these letters to Rusticus were written before another letter of Jerome, Letter 11, now 123, to Ageruchia, which he believes was written in 407, when John Cassian had not yet founded the monastery at Massilia. But besides the fact that Quesnellus’s assumption is far from certain—namely, that no other monastery had existed near Massilia before the one John Cassian built after returning to Massilia after 407—Jerome’s letter to Rusticus was certainly written after Rufinus’s death. For Grunius, whose death is mentioned in it in section 18, is none other than Rufinus of Aquileia [Col. 1476C]. He died in 410, and therefore the letter can appropriately be dated to 411, when the monastery at Massilia had already been founded by John Cassian. Rusticus therefore lived the monastic life near Massilia together with Venerius when Saint Jerome wrote to him; and there is no reason to assign him to a monastery at Toulouse. In this way the statements in the same letter of Saint Jerome about Saint Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, are properly understood:

> Follow in his footsteps from nearby;

and those about Proculus of Massilia:

> You have there the holy and most learned bishop Proculus, who by his living and present voice surpasses our little writings [Col. 1476D] and directs your path by his daily instructions.

Do you see the difference in the expressions? Jerome speaks of the bishop of Massilia as present because Rusticus was living in the monastery at Massilia; but he calls Saint Exuperius “nearby” because, although Toulouse was distant from Massilia, it was near in comparison with Palestine, where Jerome was. If Jerome’s letter to Rusticus was written in 411, Quesnellus’s conjectures about Sisinnius, the monk of Toulouse, have no foundation—namely, that Sisinnius was sent to the East by Saint Exuperius in 406, first carried Rusticus’s letter to Jerome, and returned Jerome’s letter to Rusticus in the same year. For in that year Rufinus had not yet died.]

Jerome says that Rusticus had a religious mother, a widow for many years, who nourished and educated him as a child and, after he had completed his studies in Gaul—which were then at their flourishing height—sent him to Rome without sparing expense, sustaining the absence of her son by hope of future rewards. Since Jerome testifies that he had heard this:

> I hear, he says, that you have a religious mother, etc.

(Ibid., near the beginning), it is not unreasonable to suppose that when Rusticus wished to consult Jerome about the ordering of his life, he gave his letter to Sisinnius to carry—namely, to that monk Sisinnius whom Saint Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, sent to the East with a large sum of money intended to support the monks of Palestine [Col. 1477A] and Egypt.

For Sisinnius did not carry to Jerome only a letter from Exuperius, but also letters from other monks of the monastery at Toulouse, Minerius and Alexander, and from the holy presbyters Riparius and Desiderius, who also sent him books of Vigilantius, as well as from many other men and women. Jerome himself says:

> Sisinnius brought me many questions from the holy brothers and sisters of your province.

(Jerome, Letter 152, to Minerius and Alexander.) Among these I count Rusticus, who, while living at Massilia, gave this monk a letter for Jerome as he boarded a ship in the harbor of that city. Jerome’s fame had spread far and wide throughout all the regions of the Christian world, but especially through Gaul; and from the conversations of this messenger he could easily have learned what he reports about Rusticus’s family, studies, and the piety of his mother.

The mention of Exuperius and of his alms carried to Palestine also supports this view. Jerome speaks of them as of a present matter, although Jerome himself shows that the event occurred in the year of Christ 406. Therefore [Col. 1477B] Jerome’s letter to Rusticus must have been written around the same time.

I have investigated these matters with particular care because they shed some light on the monastery of Rusticus, which the inscription from Narbonne mentions. The learned Étienne Baluze had placed him in the monastery at Massilia; but when some difficulty arose in that opinion, he later thought that Rusticus should be assigned to the monastery at Lérins. I do not think that it can easily be proved that Rusticus was a monk either there or at Massilia; rather, I believe that he was a member of the monastery at Toulouse.

For it is certain that Jerome’s letter to Rusticus was written at least some time before the devastation inflicted on Gaul by the army of the barbarians, which Jerome laments in his letter to Ageruchia on monogamy (Jerome, Letter 11, to Ageruchia). When the sword began to devastate, or famine to oppress, the cities of Aquitaine, Narbonensis, and the other provinces on the last day of 406, Jerome would not have omitted mention of them, nor would Exuperius have sent resources and assistance to the regions of Palestine and Egypt, where his own people would then have needed them most.

At that time John Cassian had not yet established his residence at Massilia, nor had he built his monastery. Since he was deeply concerned about the affairs of his excellent teacher John Chrysostom, in whose name he had also carried letters to Innocent, it is not right to believe that he left Rome before the death of that holy bishop, which occurred in 407 and brought his cause to an end.

The monastery at Lérins was scarcely then beginning to rise, nor had it become so famous that its reputation would have drawn Rusticus from a region so remote. Jerome was pointing him instead to the ancient monastery at Toulouse, where the institutions of the monastic life flourished and which was further commended by the presence of Exuperius, a man distinguished by episcopal solicitude, the example of his life, and charity toward the poor. Indeed, we cannot doubt that the monks of Narbonne were under the authority of that holy bishop [Col. 1477D], since we read that Sisinnius was chosen from among them to carry his alms as far as Palestine and Egypt.

2. Since Jerome sent this same Rusticus, who was planning to undertake the monastic life, to the teaching and admonitions of Proculus of Massilia and to the example of Exuperius, no one will readily believe that Rusticus wished to withdraw far from the vicinity of those bishops. How highly he valued Jerome’s advice he sufficiently showed by not hesitating to consult him, although Jerome was living overseas, in regions extremely remote from Gaul and although Rusticus was unknown to him.

3. In this passage the same teacher makes no mention either of the desert of Lérins or of the monastery at Massilia. Rather, he seems to have invited that young man to the monastery at Toulouse in these words:

> Follow in the footsteps of this man (Exuperius) from nearby, and of the others who resemble him in virtue, whom the priesthood makes both humbler and poorer.

[Col. 1478A] 4. Jerome seems to have had an exchange of letters and pious relations with this monastery of Gaul alone. Hence frequent letters were sent from there to him, Exuperius was mentioned more often, and he showed greater affection toward Toulouse. This affection drew tears from him when the city’s destruction came to mind:

> I cannot, he says in writing to Ageruchia, mention Toulouse without tears.

Therefore he should not be thought to have had another monastery in mind when he replied to a man of that province who was consulting him about undertaking the monastic life. He may once have seen this one when he traveled through Gaul. Certainly neither Lérins nor Massilia had yet laid its foundations at that time.

5. I add this also: if Venerius of Massilia and Rusticus of Narbonne had been called from the island of Lérins to the episcopal dignity, it would scarcely be possible that no trace of the matter should remain in the ancient records, since they were among the most celebrated of the Gallican bishops. Hilary, bishop of Arles [Col. 1478B], who at that same time was living at Lérins under the same discipline of Honoratus, would have spoken of them; or the other Honoratus, author of the Life of Hilary and bishop of Massilia. Eucherius would not have been silent about them when, writing instructions to his son Salonius, he recalled those by whose companionship or admonitions Salonius had advanced on the island.

But above all, Sidonius Apollinaris, in his Eucharisticus addressed to Faustus of Riez, where he recalls to Faustus the leading inhabitants of that island—Caprasius, Lupus, Honoratus, Maximus, Eucherius, and Hilary, whose companion Faustus had been—would never have omitted to list either Venerius or Rusticus. Venerius had been so highly esteemed that Rusticus, in that celebrated inscription which he arranged to have engraved for posterity, considered it something of which to boast that he had been Venerius’s fellow student in the monastery; and Pope Celestine, writing to all the bishops of Gaul about Saint Augustine and his writings, thought Rusticus should be named first among the few.

Rusticus himself was extremely renowned [Col. 1478C], distinguished by an episcopate in which he flourished for more than thirty years, according to the testimony of Ravennius, bishop of Arles. Ravennius especially desired his assistance, regarding him as the most experienced of the Gallican bishops, so that a controversy which had arisen between certain bishops of those regions and Faustus, abbot of Lérins, might finally be settled at the Third Council of Arles, as may be understood from the encyclical letter of Ravennius.

Jerome’s own letter to Rusticus was also known in Gaul. The esteem in which the writings of that holy teacher were already held there is shown by canon 4 of the First Council of Vaison in 442, which cites his letter to Nepotianus. Finally, the Lérins Chronology—whose author spared no labor or diligence in gathering everything that could contribute to the honor of that most famous monastery, and who especially listed those who had at some time adorned it by their piety—records absolutely nothing about that distinguished pair of bishops [1576]. We must therefore conclude that he found not even a trace of them in the many ancient records which he examined or reproduced [Col. 1478D].

6. Even if no decisive argument is sought from the location and proximity of the city of Narbonne and the monastery at Toulouse—for both were situated in the same province—it is nevertheless more natural to believe that Rusticus was taken as bishop from the monastery of that diocese in which monastic discipline flourished than from Lérins, which was separated from that city by a considerable distance.

7. When Ravennius invited the bishops to assemble at Arles to settle the case of the island of Lérins, he sent an encyclical letter throughout Gaul. This point, however, deserves particular attention: copies sent to those who had been taken from the island itself contained a special addition, namely these words:

> It is especially fitting that your Beatitude should be present, you whom the island itself, nourishing you as though in a mother’s bosom, brought forth, with the Lord’s prompting, to the grace that is now in you.

It is therefore sufficiently clear that Rusticus was not among their number, since the copy sent to him does not contain those words but substitutes these others at the end of the general letter:

> And especially we first beg your Beatitude to be present, because a more serious illness necessarily requires the most skilled physicians.

Such were the beginnings of Rusticus’s career. He lived in the monastery in such a way that he deserved to become a cleric, as Jerome urged him, and afterward was raised to episcopal dignity. In what year this occurred, however, is difficult to say. The often-mentioned and often-deserving Baluze conjectures that Rusticus’s ordination should be assigned to the year of Christ 430. Whether his conjecture was successful cannot be determined without examining and explaining the celebrated inscription from Narbonne, which he included in his notes on Salvian and in the supplement to Book V of *Concordia sacrae et imperii*. Since it bears on the inquiry into the beginning of Rusticus’s episcopate, it cannot be omitted here.

An ancient inscription preserved at Narbonne in the archiepiscopal palace, on a marble altar. From the *Inscriptions* of Janus Gruterus, p. 1058, and from Étienne Baluze.

[Col. 1479]

### Explanation of the Narbonne inscription

[Col. 1479B]

> By the mercy of God and Christ, this threshold was set in place in the fourth year, when Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time, three days before the Kalends of December, in the nineteenth year of the episcopate of Rusticus . . .
>
> Rusticus, bishop, son of Bishop Bonosus, grandson on his mother’s side of Bishop Arator, companion of Bishop Venerius in the monastery, fellow presbyter of the Church of Massilia; in the fifteenth year of his episcopate, on the fifth day of the year, three days before the Ides of October, together with the presbyter Ursus, the deacon Hermes, and those who followed them, began to remove the wall of the Church, long since burned. On the thirty-seventh day the squared stone began to be laid in the foundation. In the second year, seven days before the Ides of October, the subdeacon Montanus caused the apse to be set in place. Marcellus, prefect of Gaul, a worshiper of God, prevailed upon the bishop by his request to undertake this burden, promising the necessary expenses. During the two years of his administration he provided the craftsmen’s wages: six hundred solidi for the work, and the others one thousand five hundred solidi . . . Hence the offerings of Saint Bishop Venerius, one hundred solidi . . . of Bishop Dynamus, fifty . . . of Oresius, two hundred . . . of Agroecius, one . . . and of Deconia . . . for the welfare . . .

[Col. 1479C]

1578 The chief difficulty concerns the interpretation of the final line of this inscription:

> THIS THRESHOLD WAS SET IN PLACE IN THE FOURTH YEAR, WHEN VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS WAS CONSUL FOR THE SIXTH TIME.

Baluze assigns these words the following meaning: the threshold of the basilica was set in place in the fourth year after the beginning of Valentinian’s sixth consulship, which fell in the year of Christ 445. For, he says, they counted the years from the last consulship as first, second, third, and so forth, until they again assumed the consulship, as is evident from ancient inscriptions. Therefore he thinks that the threshold was set in the year 448, which was the fourth year after 445. Since this was the nineteenth year of Rusticus’s episcopate, it follows that he had been placed over the Church of Narbonne in 430.

The learned man will not take it amiss if we bring this interpretation back to the anvil for reconsideration, so that we may not remain ignorant of the beginnings of Rusticus’s episcopate. I cannot, therefore, persuade myself [Note: [Col. 1479C] During the period of Leo’s episcopate, some examples are indeed found in which the first year after a consulship is counted by the formula *anno*—for example, in the year 449, *post consulatum Zenonis et Posthumiani*, who had been consuls in 448—even though the ordinary consuls of the current year were known. Thus, in the pseudo-synod of Ephesus in 449, on the sixth day before the Ides of August, the cited formula appears both in the Greek original, volume IV of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 889, and in the ancient version revised by Baluze, note a, although Protogenes of the East, the ordinary consul of that same year 449, designated in the Acts of Constantinople inserted with that pseudo-synod, cols. 1027 and 1030, could not have been unknown to the Fathers. Yet no example proves that in this period the second, third, and—as in our document—the fourth year was also designated after a consulship. Still less can any example be produced proving that the formula *ANNO IIII. CS. VALENTINIANO AUGUSTO VI*, that is, “in the fourth year, when Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time,” was used. If the cited formula had been customary in this age for marking the second, third, fourth, and subsequent years, we would read *anno quarto P. C.*, that is, “in the fourth year after the consulship of Valentinian Augustus VI.” Therefore Quesnellus interpreted the matter most accurately: the threshold of the Church was set in the fourth year after the beginning of the construction, while Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time. Baluze’s interpretation, which Quesnellus later reports, collapses for two reasons: first, because it is contrary to the practice of that period to designate the fourth year after a consulship; and second, because the formula “in the fourth year, when he was consul,” was never used to designate the fourth year after a consulship. These observations suffice to defend Quesnellus’s interpretation; consequently, certain points which he discusses at greater length in his own interest, though not with complete accuracy, ought not to trouble us. There is no time to examine every detail.]

that this method of counting years from one imperial consulship to another was in use during that period.

First, Onuphrius, an authoritative witness in controversies of this kind, writes in his commentary on the *Consular Fasti*, Book I, that this method of counting years began long after the time of Rusticus of Narbonne. When Rome was repeatedly besieged, captured, plundered, and at times destroyed and burned during the Gothic War under the emperor Justinian, and when the Gothic kings, who appointed the Western consuls, were occupied by war, the consular title was interrupted in the West and also neglected in the East, so that the East was without a consul for twenty-five years.

At the beginning of the reign of Justin the Younger Augustus, the consular dignity began to be used again, but in a different manner from the ancient practice. Thereafter no private person was ordinary consul. Only the emperors, beginning with Justin the Younger, were created consuls once for a single year, around the beginning of their reign; and after the consulship had ended, they counted the subsequent years of the reign from that consulship in this way: “After the consulship of Emperor N., in the first year”; again, “After the consulship of Emperor N., in the third year”; “After the consulship of Emperor N., in the fourth year,” and so forth. This is what Onuphrius, the father of the *Fasti*, says.

2. Sometimes years are indeed found marked by the formula “after the consulship,” examples of which occur in the African book of canons, where the date of several councils is designated in this way. But this happened for no other reason than that the consuls had not yet been announced to the Africans. For there was a fixed rule that this formula for marking years was then used contrary to the customary practice of consular dating.

As long as the consular dignity continued—which in the West lasted until the time of the emperor Justinian and the Gothic-Italian War—the dates were marked and the years counted by the ordinary consuls of each year. Since Zeno and Posthumianus were the ordinary consuls of 448, as the *Fasti*, two letters of our Leo, and all the chroniclers indicate, it would have been highly unusual for Rusticus to use in a public inscription, which he intended to be useful to posterity, a method of counting that was not customary.

3. Even if he had wished to do so, he would not have written, “In the fourth year, when Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time,” but rather: “After the sixth consulship of Valentinian Augustus, in the fourth year” [Col. 1481B]. The first words can scarcely, or scarcely at all, be drawn into the latter meaning, and I do not think they were ever used in that sense.

4. Nor would Rusticus have taken the trouble to inscribe on the stone the final words we have mentioned, “after the consulship,” and so forth. This method of counting was then used only when ordinary consuls had not been designated, or were not yet known or announced.

> Onuphrius says that the notation P. C. must be interpreted as referring to a year in which there was no ordinary consul, just as if one were to say: “A year without consuls, which was after the consulship of N.”

(Onuphrius, Book I of the *Fasti*, section “On Consuls.”)

Who, then, would say that Posthumianus and Zeno, who were the consuls of 448, had not been designated by the third day before the Kalends of December, when Leo had already dated his letter to Dorus, bishop of Beneventum, by their consulship as early as March 1580? Who would suppose that they were still unknown at that time in the Gallican province—so near, I say, to the province where the praetorian prefect had his seat [Col. 1481C]?

From these considerations it is evident that another method must be adopted for explaining this inscription. I find no more suitable one than to count the fourth year in question not from Valentinian’s sixth consulship but from the laying of the basilica’s foundations.

It was familiar to the ancients to indicate for posterity, in inscriptions of this kind, the time when a public building had begun to be constructed and the time when it had been completed. This practice was always in use and is still employed everywhere today. Rusticus therefore meant that the basilica at Narbonne was built over four years, or that it was completed in the fourth year, beginning with the laying of the squared stone—that is, from the laying of the foundations until the threshold was set in place and the work brought to an end.

A squared stone was customarily laid in the foundation. Hence Livy, in Book VI, writes: “The Capitol was built upon squared stone.” From this, among the ancients, “to lay the squared stone” came to mean “to lay the foundations” and “to place the first stone of a building,” as in this inscription. Likewise, since the threshold was ordinarily set in place only when a house had been completed, among the ancients “for a building to be completed” meant the same as “for the threshold to be set in place,” or for the work to be brought to an end.

Thus Justinian’s *Institutes*, Book I, title 12, says:

> Just as thresholds in a house mark a certain end, so the ancients wished the threshold to be the end of an empire.

Hence *limen*—“threshold”—was so called as being a kind of end and boundary.

Our interpretation is confirmed by the fact that, after generally indicating at the very beginning of the inscription, in an elongated line, that four years had been spent in building the basilica, Rusticus then explains individually in the remaining lines what was done in each year and in what order.

In the first year, the old basilica was demolished and the foundations of the new one were laid. In the second, the apse was set in place, and the entire work of those two years was completed at the expense of the prefect Marcellus. In the other two years, the remaining work was completed from the offerings of the holy bishops and others [Col. 1482A].

“But,” you will say, “from the fifteenth year of Rusticus’s episcopate to the nineteenth there are not four years but five.” It may be answered that from the laying of the squared stone to the setting of the threshold there were four years and approximately ten days—or at most fifteen, if that thirty-seventh day is counted from the day of his ordination, although it seems more properly to be counted from the day when the wall of the burned church began to be removed.

This discrepancy was not so important that the round number of four years had to be increased by mentioning fifteen days. Certainly the days and years that had elapsed from the beginning of the building were not counted with the same precision as the periods and almost the moments of the episcopate, especially since, in the construction of massive stone buildings, many days may have passed without work, and perhaps many days elapsed after the foundations had been laid before work was resumed.

We have explained the word *quad.* in the inscription as referring to the squared stone laid in the foundations; the authority of Livy cited above confirms this [Col. 1482B]. Those who interpret the passage as referring to the thirty-seventh day of Lent depart from its true meaning. No such method of counting is found anywhere, nor is it plausible that work on building the basilica was first begun during the days of Holy Week, which are close to Easter and occupied with sacred solemnities. Finally, from the third day before the Ides of October to the thirty-seventh day of Lent there are nearly six months, which certainly were not necessary for removing the wall of the old church.

Once these matters have been explained, it becomes clear that the basilica at Narbonne was completed in the very year of Valentinian Augustus’s sixth consulship, namely 445. This is the genuine meaning of the words:

> When Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time,

which was the nineteenth year of Rusticus’s episcopate. He must therefore have been ordained in the year of the Lord 427, three years before Baluze’s date.

It may perhaps at some time be worthwhile to have examined these matters somewhat more carefully, both with regard to Rusticus’s monastery and with regard to the beginning of his episcopate [Col. 1482C]. At least, the inquiry is useful for historical truth and for knowledge of the Gallican episcopates, which is extremely obscure and uncertain in those times.

I wish the learned Baluze had weighed more carefully what I wrote above in my first edition before attempting to overthrow my explanation of that portion of the inscription, as he tried to do in his notes on the *Capitularies of Our Kings*, volume II, p. 1252. I shall reply briefly here, after first amicably warning the distinguished man about several points.

First, he must remember that the question between us is not whether the formula “after the consulship” was used before the time of Rusticus of Narbonne—for who could deny that? The question is whether it was used at that time when the consuls of the current year had both been appointed and were known to those who drew up public records.

2. It is useless to heap up a mass of examples in support of the same formula “after the consulship,” since nothing of that kind occurs in the inscription [Col. 1482D].

3. No example can be produced in which, during that period, a year is dated from a consulship that had already ended three years earlier.

4. The method of counting years which the learned man so vigorously defends in the inscription is, by his own admission, unusual and divergent from common practice.

Finally, the dispute about the formula “after the consulship” can easily be settled by the very rule concerning the formula “after Easter” that he himself adduces in his own favor from the Council of Carthage. For since the former formula was used only when the date of Easter was either uncertain or not yet known, it is plainly evident that exactly the same must be said of the formula “after the consulship.” The Council Fathers place the one alongside the other. Their words are:

> Letters of ordination issued by primates, or by any bishops to their own clerics, must contain the date of Easter. But if the date of Easter for that same year is still uncertain, the preceding one is to be added, as is customary for “after the consulship” to be written in public records.

This is canon 106 of the African code, enacted at the Council of Carthage held under the primate Aurelius in the year 407. Therefore the learned man should not have taken it from the Second Council of Milevis; for it has long been established among scholars that the collection of twenty-seven canons circulated under the name of the Second Council of Milevis bears that title most falsely.

But whatever the origin of those words, they offer Baluze no support, since the two formulas “after the consulship” and “in the fourth year, when Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time” differ completely from one another. The inscription has the latter and not the former, and no artifice can reduce one to the meaning of the other.

Furthermore, the canon itself which Baluze invokes in defense of his opinion argues against him. Just as it was necessary to inscribe the date of Easter in letters of ordination whenever it was certain and known, so it was necessary to inscribe the names of the consuls of the current year in public records when they had been designated and were known in the places where the records were drawn up. But who, even in a dream, would say that Zeno and Posthumianus, the ordinary consuls of 448, had not yet been designated or recognized as such in the Roman province—so near to Rome—on the third day before the Kalends of December of that same year, the day on which the threshold of the basilica at Narbonne was set in place and the inscription carved?

He produces and presses the example of the Synod of Ephesus, whose proceedings are prefaced by the formula:

> After the consulship of the emperors Theodosius and Valentinian,

although it is certain that in that same year Bassus and Antiochus were appointed consuls. But this exceptional example had an exceptional reason. Since the ecumenical synod had been convened by the command and under the consulship of the emperors, and since their consulship was to be written above each action at its beginning, where mention had to be made of their decrees, the Greeks granted this honor to the imperial dignity.

If this answer does not satisfy the learned man, there remains the general—and multifaceted—answer: the Ephesian and Narbonne formulas are very different. The former says “after the consulship”; the latter says “in the fourth year, when Valentinian Augustus was consul for the sixth time,” according to Baluze’s interpretation. Moreover, and this is still more important, although it is not uncommon for an occasional year during that period to be dated by the consulship of the immediately preceding year, Baluze has never read anywhere that a year was marked by consuls who had completed that office three or four years earlier. Yet this is precisely the issue in dispute, and he will make no progress until he has found both conditions together in his examples.

### 1583

The learned scholar consequently appeals to Onuphrius—quite properly; I do not reject this judge. Thus Onuphrius, *Commentary on Book II of the Fasti*:

> Since frequent mention will henceforth be made of years without CONSULS, which during this period they called POST-CONSULATE years, it will not be out of place to say a few things about these years.

You see that, for Onuphrius, the subject is years without consuls, and that he says only these were called post-consulate years, not others. The same father of the *Fasti* immediately proves this at length:

> It often happened that, because of civil or foreign wars, the murders of emperors, plagues, or other causes, a year was arranged WITHOUT ORDINARY CONSULS, who ordinarily used to give their name to the year and to the *Fasti*. I think this happened in the present year because of the tyranny of Maxentius, who was ruling in the City, where it was customary for consuls to be designated and to inaugurate their consulship. At that time the two consuls who had held office in the preceding year gave their name to this year.

Finally, if anything more precise and clearer is desired, let Onuphrius continue and let Baluzius listen:

> When it is said, POST-CONSULATE, it means exactly the same as if you said: A YEAR WITHOUT CONSULS, which followed the consulship of Diocletian for the tenth time and Maximian for the seventh time.

Here, then, are the reasons, according to Onuphrius, why years were not designated by ordinary consuls: they were years without consuls. Here is why the year from the foundation of the City 1061, or A.D. 309, was called “post-consulate,” and so forth: because, owing to the tyranny of Maxentius, there were no ordinary consuls. And yet our Baluzius does not hesitate to write:

> Cassiodorus records that the year 309 and the following year were designated post-consulate of Diocletian for the tenth time and Maximian for the seventh time, although, as Onuphrius and Baronius have likewise left recorded, in the year 309 Maxentius and Maximus held the consulship.

“Maxentius,” he says, “and Maximus held the consulship in this year”—and this on the authority of Onuphrius and Baronius? How false this is with respect to Onuphrius is abundantly clear from the words quoted just above:

> I think this happened in the present year because of the tyranny of Maxentius—

that is, I think that it was a year without ordinary consuls.

Onuphrius does indeed report that the book of Damasus, in the *Life of Saint Miltiades*, mentions Maxentius Augustus, consul for the fourth time, and Maximus as consuls appointed for this year. But Onuphrius so far from approving this that he rather overturns it in the whole discussion quoted above in part: by the authority of Cassiodorus, Cuspinianus, the Greek *Fasti*, and the *Book of Prefects*, as well as by that very book of Damasus in the *Life of Saint Marcellus, Pope*.

As for Baronius, he consistently maintains that the ordinary consuls of this year were entered in neither the Latin nor the Greek *Fasti*, either because they were in fact not appointed, or because, on account of Maxentius’ tyranny, his name and consulship were erased from the *Fasti*. Insofar as the consular designation is concerned, these alternatives amount to the same thing: that he was not appointed consul, or that his name and consulship were erased from the *Fasti*. Therefore the year ought to have been marked post-consulate in exactly the same way as if there had been no ordinary consuls.

### 1584

Baluzius adduces another example from A.D. 351. In that year, he says, Magnentius and Gaiso were consuls, as the author of the *Book of Prefects* reports in Onuphrius. Yet the book of Cuspinianus, Cassiodorus, and Socrates, Book II, chapter 26, assign to this very year the designation:

> Post-consulate of Sergius and Nigrinianus, who had held the consulship in the preceding year.

Add also the book of the *Fasti* and Idatius in the *Fasti*, so that we have five writers of the highest authority against whom the anonymous *Book of Prefects* is overwhelmed. Who, after all, would think that the doubtful authority of one unknown writer should be preferred to those five witnesses, so rich in evidence?

Socrates, in the passage cited, says:

> These men assembled at Sirmium after the consulship of Sergius and Nigrinianus. In that year, because of the disturbances and rebellions of war, NO CONSUL was able to perform the customary duties of the consulship.

Socrates undoubtedly drew this from the actual Acts of the Council of Sirmium. He expressly writes that this was a year without consuls and therefore affirms that the Acts of the council were dated post-consulate.

Onuphrius, however, reconciles all these authors, whom Baluzius sets against one another. Namely, in the East the year was designated post-consulate because there were no consuls in the East; in the West, however, the *Book of Prefects* inscribes Magnentius and Gaiso because they held the consulship in the West. Consequently, Baluzius’ entire argument collapses.

I consider the consular dating of the so-called Fifth Council of Carthage—which is said to have been held in the year 398 post-consulate of Attecius and Caesarius—as false and fabricated as the Acts of the synod themselves. Furthermore, even if we assume the Acts of the synod to be genuine, it is Baluzius’ responsibility to prove by solid arguments that the consuls of that year were known to the Africans at the time when the synod was held. With this single reply we destroy the entire force of the argument drawn from the consular datings of other synods.

For until Baluzius proves this, when I read “post-consulate” contrary to the usual practice, with the names of the ordinary consuls omitted, I assert on good grounds that those consuls had not yet been announced in the provinces. I follow the rule mentioned by the Council of Carthage:

> If the day of Easter is still uncertain, the preceding [consulate] is added, just as it is customary for “post-consulate” to be entered in public records when the consuls of the current year have not yet been announced.

Nor will it seem surprising that in May, June, or July the Roman consuls were often uncertain in Africa, since it is certain that formerly even the ordinary consulship was begun by the Romans in September or October. As for substitute consuls, it is clear that at certain periods they did not take up office at the beginning of the year. After the time of Julius Caesar it was extremely common for ordinary consuls not to complete the entire year in their office but to be compelled to yield their place to others substituted for them.

Indeed, Onuphrius does not hesitate to assert that after the reign of Augustus very few are found who were consuls for a complete year. Although at the beginning of his own singular reign he granted an annual consulship for several years according to ancestral custom, after some intervening years he changed it from annual to six-monthly, so that there were two consuls from the Kalends of January to the Kalends of July, and then, after their resignation, two others from the Kalends of July to the end of the year. Tiberius Caesar made the consulship four-monthly; later the emperor Claudius made it two-monthly. Indeed, when offices became purchasable under the emperor Commodus, it is written that in one year as many as twenty-five consuls were sometimes counted.

Although Constantine the Great restored the consulship as an annual office according to the ancient custom, nevertheless, because of the varying turns of events, it often happened either that the ordinary, or senior, consuls were designated later than usual, or that, after they had been removed, other, junior consuls were substituted for them, or that one consul was designated in the East while the Western consul had not yet been designated—or at least had not yet been announced.

This occurred in A.D. 431. In a law of Theodosius issued that year, Antiochus is named consul in the East at the end of March, while on the tenth day before the Kalends of April the Easterners did not yet know the Western consul:

> Antiochus, a man of clarissimus rank, consul, and whoever shall have been announced. Yet at Rome public acts were already being dated by the names of both consuls, as is evident from the letter of Pope Celestine addressed to the bishops and priests traveling to the East. It is read as having been issued on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Bassus and Antiochus.

Amid such uncertainty and doubt, the Africans could have found no more convenient or reliable way of recording dates than to designate the year by the certain consuls of the year immediately preceding, especially if the consul of the Western empire, on whom they depended, had not yet been announced.

I said: by the consuls of the year immediately preceding. For that a year possessing its own designated and announced consuls should nevertheless have been dated by the consulship that had ended three years earlier, after three intervening pairs of consuls who had completed their terms in the usual manner, cannot, so far as I know, be demonstrated by any example of that period; nor does it possess any more basis in reason than in example.

Therefore what the learned scholar argues occurred in that Narbonese inscription is utterly monstrous. He thinks that the year 448 was the fourth year after Valentinian’s sixth consulship. Yet he himself admits, and it is established, that Posthumianus and Zeno were consuls in that year—ordinary consuls, as is made clear partly from the ancient inscription which Onuphrius assigns to the year 423 and partly from other monuments. Consequently their consulship was established on the Kalends of January, as was customary, or at least in March, as is clear from Saint Leo’s letter to Dorus of Beneventum.

I do not think that their consulship could seriously be said to have remained unknown at the end of November in the Roman province of Gaul. But let us grant that this did happen, and that there was some necessity for dating the year by the preceding consuls with the formula “post-consulate.” Certainly, since after Valentinian’s sixth consulship, which fell in the year 445, there were ordinary consuls in the West—namely, Aetius and Symmachus in 446, and Alipius and Ardabur in 447—then, if the year 448 had lacked consuls, it ought to have been designated by the consulship of Alipius and Ardabur, who immediately preceded that year. It ought not to have been necessary to go back to the consulship of three years earlier, passing over three pairs of consuls.

From this point a very broad distinction emerges between all the examples cited by Baluzius and the passage of the inscription, even when understood in Baluzius’ sense. All those years are reckoned from the immediately preceding consulship, whereas Baluzius imagines that his year was designated from the consulship that had ended three full years earlier.

Baluzius therefore proved none of the things that he ought to have proved in order to defend his explanation of that inscription.

In reviewing this letter, we used the manuscript codices of Grimani, Barberini, Corbie, Trecopithoeus, Victorinus, Cambridge, Navarre, and five Thuane manuscripts. We also consulted the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, Cresconius, and others, as well as the corrections of the learned Sirmondus, which he himself published on the basis of manuscript codices in volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*.

We have also inserted into our edition the titles of the inquiries which he prefixed here to the individual chapters, because we too extracted them from manuscript codices and because they contribute considerable light toward understanding the letter. Nevertheless, so that the other titles might not perish altogether—the titles which the Grimani manuscripts and others, as well as Dionysius Exiguus and the printed editions, display at the beginning of the entire letter—we thought that these too could be placed before the letter in a single overview. We have, however, rejected the one that was numbered fourteenth in earlier editions, because it is absent from the Grimani and Barberini manuscripts and from Dionysius, and because we shall show in its proper place that the chapter to which it was attached is an interpolation.

### 2. Hermes

Hermes had long performed the office of archdeacon in the Church of Narbonne. Later he was chosen and ordained bishop of Béziers. But when, as he himself complained, he had been disgracefully excluded by the people of Béziers, he was received by the Church of Narbonne, which at that time had been deprived of its bishop Rusticus. Pope Hilary protested, but eventually yielded after the Gallic bishops Faustus of Riez and Auxanius had acted on Hermes’ behalf before him. On this matter see Hilary’s letters to the Gallic bishops.

The same Hermes is mentioned by the Narbonese inscription, the Roman and Gallican Martyrologies, and the Martyrology of Usuard under the seventh day before the Kalends of November.

### 3. “We have understood that the confidence of Sabinianus and Leo, the presbyters, was lacking in your action”

In the common edition one reads *actionis suae*, “of their action”; in the Grimani and Barberini manuscripts and in three Thuane manuscripts, *actionis tuae*, “of your action.” Dionysius Exiguus agrees with the latter reading, and we have thought that it should be corrected accordingly.

[Note: Why, and in what sense, *tuae* should be read instead of *suae* has been explained in note 18 (column 1199, n. n.) on this letter.]

The word is not to be understood of a human or natural action, but of a judicial action—that is, of a judgment, prosecution, or the authority to prosecute someone for an offense. The word is used in nearly the same sense in Letter 12, now numbered 14, to Anastasius of Thessalonica. There Atticus, metropolitan of Old Epirus, is said to have complained before Leo, in a tearful *action*, of the most disgraceful constraint that he had suffered. Anastasius’ deacons were standing by, and, by offering nothing in reply to his tearful complaints, showed that the charges brought forward were not without credibility. There *actio* means a written complaint or a judicial accusation.

### 4. “That he might obtain relief from the burdens of the episcopate,” etc.

Innocent III was the first to decree that these three matters—the transfer, deposition, or resignation of a bishop—were reserved by divine institution to the Roman pontiff alone (*C. Inter corporalia*, concerning the transfer of a bishop).

There are nevertheless abundant ecclesiastical records of men who either laid down the episcopal burden without consulting anyone, or dealt concerning it with the bishops of their own province. For examples of this kind, if desired, see Peter de Marca, *On the Concord between the Priesthood and the Empire*, Book VI, chapter 8, and Book VII, chapter 26, as well as *The Life of Dom Bartholomew of the Martyrs, Archbishop of Braga*, Book IV, chapter 11, written by the distinguished V. cl. D. Le Maître de Sacy. See also Saint Augustine, Letter 261 to Pope Celestine; Book II *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, chapter 11; Cyril of Alexandria, letter to Domnus of Antioch; and others.

### 1588

“Nor were they elected by the clergy.”

There is scarcely any need to explain that the word *clericus*, “cleric,” does not always signify someone devoted to the lower ministries. This is evident from this single passage, since it is certain that the election of a bishop belonged especially to presbyters and to the other ministers of the higher orders.

Indeed, the word often designates clerics of every order when it occurs without qualification in ancient writers: as once and again in this first inquiry; likewise in inquiry 4; in Letter 10 to the bishops of the province of Vienne, chapter 6; and in Letter 3, now numbered 4, to the bishops of Campania, chapters 3 and 4, where clerics are forbidden to practice usury.

It also often signifies clerics of the higher order alone, as when Siricius, Roman pontiff, says in Letter 1, chapter 14:

> No one of the clerics is permitted to perform penance.

The words that follow indicate that he means those who undertake the instruments of administering the sacraments. The same is true in Saint Leo’s Letter 12, now numbered 14, to Anastasius of Thessalonica, chapter 4.

When lower ministers are meant, the meaning is restricted by some addition, as when in Letter 10 to the people of Vienne he calls them “clerics of a lower office,” and so forth.

### 6. “But if any clerics were ordained by those pseudo-bishops in the Churches to which their own bishops belonged,” etc.

In place of *qui ad proprios*, “who belonged to their own,” as found in the Grimani and Barberini manuscripts, four Thuane manuscripts, the Trecopithoean manuscript, and the Isidorian manuscript in the margin of Canisius and Crabbe, as well as in Gratian, Part I, Question 1, the common editions, Dionysius Exiguus, Hincmar of Rheims, *Opusculum* 33, J. Sirmondus, and volume I of the *Ancient Councils of Gaul* have *quae ad proprios*, “which belonged to their own.”

[Note: If the agreement of nearly all, and certainly of the more important, manuscripts of diverse origin had not preferred *qui*, we would gladly have adopted in our edition the reading *quae*, which better accords with Leo’s usual syntax, especially since the word *eis* seems to demand that reading. But some codices omit *eis*, while others have *eorum*, as we have noted in its proper place. We have therefore dared to change nothing.

As for the meaning of this passage, among the many interpretations produced by its difficulty, the following seems to us the simpler and more probable. When Rusticus asked about a presbyter or deacon who had falsely claimed to be a bishop, he did not mean a presbyter or deacon lacking the episcopal character. Nor did he mean only those who had been promoted from the diaconate or presbyterate to the episcopate by one or two bishops, rather than—as discipline then required—by at least three bishops. Rather, he meant those whose consecration suffered from some canonical defect: namely, those who had not been elected by the clergy, or not requested by the people, or not consecrated by the provincial bishops with the metropolitan’s judgment.

Leo’s reply indicates all these defects. Since Rusticus did not regard such men as true bishops, he called them merely deacons or presbyters who falsely represented themselves as bishops.

Leo, replying that because of the defects mentioned they were not to be counted among the bishops and calling them pseudo-bishops, wished to indicate that they lacked not the episcopal order but only episcopal jurisdiction. For although they had been consecrated by bishops without the legitimate solemnities, they had not acquired legitimate jurisdiction.

He did not doubt that they had been validly marked with the episcopal order. Therefore, in replying to the second question of the inquiry, concerning those whom they had ordained as clerics, he affirmed that their ordination could be held valid if two conditions were present:

1. It had been performed with the consent and judgment of those presiding.
2. The ordinands remained in the Churches in which they had been ordained.

Otherwise it would not be valid, since, through the lack of the consent of those presiding, it would lack an author or legitimate authority; and through departure from the Church in which they had been ordained, it would not be founded in a proper place, since according to the ancient discipline no one was ordained unless he was attached to some Church.

Whatever reading—*qui* or *quae*—is preferred, this explanation fits it sufficiently. If *quae* is preferred, the passage concerns the ordination of a cleric in a Church belonging to another diocese, with the consent of his own bishop. If *qui* is preferred, the passage may concern some Church of that diocese over which someone had been illegitimately placed as bishop. Since he lacked jurisdiction over it, Leo requires the consent and judgment of at least those who presided over that Church and possessed some right to present clerics who were to be promoted by the bishop to an order in that same Church.]

The reading *quae ad proprios*, “which belonged to their own,” is found in the common editions, Dionysius Exiguus, Hincmar of Rheims, *Opusculum* 33, J. Sirmondus, volume I of the *Ancient Councils of Gaul*, and others.

This very slight variation in the reading produces a broad difference in meaning. If the latter reading is retained, the relative pronoun *quae* must refer to the Churches, and the question appears to come down to this: Can a cleric ordained in another Church by such pseudo-bishops remain in the rank in which he was so accepted?

The answer is that such an ordination may be held valid, but only under two conditions:

1. Such ordination must have been performed with the judgment of those presiding.
2. The clerics ordained in this way must remain in the same Churches in which they were ordained.

If these conditions were absent, the ordination was to be regarded as invalid, since it was not founded in a proper place. If the cleric did not remain in the Church in which he had been ordained, he would be a wanderer and, contrary to the canons, a cleric of no place—especially after the pseudo-bishop had been deposed from the Church over which he had wrongly been placed.

Nor would that ordination be supported by a legitimate authority, since it had been attempted against the will and consent of those presiding. In this Leo’s decree agrees with canon 8 of the First Council of Orange, which reads:

> If anyone thinks that a cleric residing elsewhere ought to be ordained, he must first determine that the man will live with him. Even then, he must not presume to ordain him without consulting the bishop with whom the man had previously lived.

Nevertheless, it seems better to me to retain the earlier reading, so that the relative pronoun *qui* refers to the clerics who were ordained and who belonged to those same Churches—Churches which at that time had pseudo-bishops, but which formerly had, and would later have, their own bishops. Thus, in my view, pseudo-bishops and proper bishops are set in opposition.

This reading is supported first by the agreement of all the manuscript codices. Second, the earlier reading assumes that such clerics had been ordained in another Church; otherwise Leo would falsely say that the ordination was not founded in a proper place.

It would also be falsely feared that clerics might dare to migrate elsewhere, and the requirement that they remain in those Churches would be imposed without purpose as a condition of ratification. In the ancient Church it was exceedingly rare for bishops to celebrate ordinations in another Church; it was no less rare for a cleric ordained in his own Church—even by a foreign or false bishop—to consider leaving it. It would therefore have been superfluous to add a condition that, by the common law of all Churches and the authority of the canons, was always understood even when not expressed.

A cleric ordained in his own Church by that Church’s pseudo-bishop could, because of the defect in his ordination, be deposed by his own bishop, who had been substituted in place of the pseudo-bishop, or be treated as not ordained. For Leo says that the ordination *can* be held valid, not that it *must* be. Moreover, even after the ordination had been confirmed, it remained within the power of the proper bishop either to retain such a cleric in the ministry of his Church or to arrange for his transfer to the man by whom he had been ordained, wherever that man might reside. This is expressly decreed by canon 4 of the Council of Riez in the case of Armentarius, bishop of Embrun.

The ordaining bishop was obliged to receive and support the man whom he had ordained. In such a case the cleric would have been a wanderer if he remained in the clerical order; and then the ordination would truly have been neither founded in a proper place nor supported by legitimate authority.

We read *auctore*, “with an author” or “by an author,” with the Grimani, Victorine, Trecopithoean, Thuane, and printed Isidorian manuscripts, not *auctoritate*, “with authority,” as found in Sirmondus, volume I of the *Councils of Gaul*, Dionysius Exiguus, Hincmar of Rheims, the Isidorian manuscript, and the common edition.

From the same manuscripts, in the preceding line, I read *creatio*, “creation” or “appointment,” rather than *ordinatio*, “ordination,” as in the common edition, or *consecratio*, “consecration,” as in Dionysius and three manuscript codices.
