But however the preceding words are read and understood, a serious difficulty arises, in my judgment: how can the ordination of those clerics be held valid who were ordained by men whom, as Leo expressly asserts in the same passage, no consideration permits to be counted among the bishops? Leo declares that they must by no means be granted what they are not taught to have received. Finally, he pronounces them pseudo-bishops because they were neither elected by the clergy, nor requested by the people, nor consecrated by the provincial bishops with the metropolitan’s judgment.

There is no doubt that even the higher clergy are meant here, since the difficulty principally concerned them. It is not reasonable to believe that Leo and Rusticus were concerned about lower-office clerics ordained by pseudo-bishops while taking no account whatsoever of the higher clergy, in whose hands lay both the ministry of the altar and the other more important functions of the Church.

There is an even greater difficulty—one that I confess myself unable to resolve—if Leo is to be understood as speaking of pseudo-bishops who had received no laying-on of hands from any bishop by which they might become bishops. The words of the inquiry may seem to suggest this to some:

> Concerning a presbyter or deacon who falsely claimed to be a bishop.

Yet I can scarcely, if at all, persuade myself that this was Leo’s meaning.

Before explaining this passage—which I am surprised was left entirely untouched by Haller and Morinus when they wrote their commentaries on sacred elections and ordinations—we must recall what we considered above and what is confirmed by this inquiry and response: when Rusticus presented these matters to Leo, he was referring to the canons of the Councils of Riez, First Orange, and Second Arles.

Those canons make it clear that illicit ordinations by two bishops were then common throughout Gaul, and these were the occasion for Rusticus to consult the Roman pontiff on the matter. Although among the Gauls there was a definite rule of discipline, sanctioned by public councils, which required at least three bishops to assemble for the consecration of a bishop, Rusticus evidently thought that the Gallican custom would gain considerable strength if the practice and judgment of the Roman Church—and therefore of the principal Church—gave it support.

Two matters in particular seem to have troubled Rusticus. First, by the authority of canon 3 of the Council of Riez, the pseudo-bishop Armentarius—who had been ordained by only two bishops—had been granted permission to perform certain episcopal functions, such as the confirmation of neophytes. Second, the consecration of clerics ordained by him had not been declared invalid if no stain in the ordinand’s conduct stood in the way, as canon 4 determines.

Therefore light must be shed on Saint Leo’s response from the canon of the Council of Riez. On the basis of that canon, and of the canons of Orange and Arles, it must be said that those whom Saint Leo calls pseudo-bishops had been ordained bishops by episcopal laying-on of hands or anointing. But because they had been consecrated either by only two bishops, contrary to the canons, or by men who were not their fellow provincials, and without the metropolitan’s judgment, they were not counted among the bishops.

That is, in the words of Saint Augustine, Book I *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 1, they had not exercised the episcopate, but nevertheless possessed the sacrament of their ordination. Or, as is said of the bishop of Ephesus in the twelfth act of the Council of Chalcedon, they had been deposed while retaining the honor of the episcopate. Or, to adopt modern terminology, they had been marked with the sacerdotal or pontifical character, which remained after their deposition, but they had been stripped of all jurisdiction, which had been defectively conferred.

For the former, the presence of even a single bishop who consecrates is sufficient; for the latter, according to the Church’s ordinance, it is necessary that two or three assist the consecrating bishop. The reason is that, although there is one episcopate distributed through the concordant multitude of many bishops—as I may use that oft-repeated axiom of Cyprian, Letter 52 to Antonianus—and although each bishop holds a share of that one episcopate in its entirety, it is by no means fitting that, against the will or without the consent of all the bishops, a share of that episcopate, likewise to be held in its entirety, should be entrusted to anyone. Rather, the consent of all should be present; and if all cannot personally be present to celebrate the ordination, the presence of at least two or three should confirm it, with the others giving their assent.

The First Council of Arles even required the presence of seven bishops. Just as all the bishops of a single ecclesiastical province represent all the bishops dispersed throughout the world, so two or three bishops together with the metropolitan act on behalf of all the bishops of that province in the consecration of a fellow bishop. This is so that, as Pope Innocent says in his letter to Victor, chapter 1, it may not appear that a benefit has been conferred clandestinely, or that something contrary to the faith, or to the cause of the faith, has been attempted by one or another person ill-disposed toward it.

These observations are sufficient for one who touches upon the matter without treating it fully.

### 1592

After I had written these things, an excellent work arrived from England by the learned Herbert Thorndike, a man devoted—as his work itself shows—to ecclesiastical unity. It was published in London the previous year, that is, in 1674, under the title *Ecclesiastical Origins, or Exercises on the Right and Power of the Christian Church*.

He solves this knot concerning ordinations performed by pseudo-bishops in another way. He writes in chapter 20:

> In ordination, since it is clear from what has been said that two things are involved—first, the authority and right of the Church in the one who ordains; and second, the solemnity of consecration, by which the Church that is the author of the order conferred publicly registers itself—so much greater is the authority of the Church than the rite of consecration that a consecration performed correctly and according to the custom of the Church nevertheless falls into invalidity if the authority of the Church has been usurped. For although whatever has once been duly consecrated to God is sacred to God forever, nevertheless that which has not been consecrated to God by the lawful authority of the Church ought not to be regarded as duly consecrated to God, even if the rite of the Church has been observed.

And later on the same page:

> Therefore, if there is doubt concerning the authority of the Church, but not concerning the rite of ordination, it is not surprising that, once the authority of the Church has been added, an ordination not performed lawfully should be valid for the purpose for which the authority of the Church that is added wishes it to be valid. There are few examples of this matter in the affairs of the ancient Church; few indeed, but they exist, and they do not permit the matter to remain doubtful.

> At the Council of Riez in Gaul, the ordination of the bishop of Embrun was declared invalid; nevertheless, following the example of canon 8 of Nicaea, he was granted permission to be a chorepiscopus, though under strict limitations, in canons 2 and 3—namely, that as chorepiscopus he could perform only confirmations.

> This did not follow from the force of the invalid ordination, unless the consent of the Church had been added through that synod. Pope Leo I, in his first inquiry to Rusticus of Narbonne, considers the ordinations of clerics performed by certain pseudo-bishops—which it is certain were invalid in themselves—to be valid if they were performed with the consent of the bishops.

> Since nothing greater can be sought in this entire matter than that those things administered to the faithful people by men whose ordination is doubtful should be valid before God, and since it has not been said that the people should judge matters common to the Church, it must be established that those things cannot be harmful to the faithful before God in which they follow the faith of the Church.

I leave this method of explanation, suggested by a theologian laboring outside the Church’s camp, for Catholic doctors to examine, and in advance I subscribe to their judgment.

I do not approve in this writer his saying “the consent of the bishops” instead of “the consent of those presiding.” For the latter is what Leo has, and it has a broader scope: it extends also to the clergy, by whose authority and judgment ordinations are celebrated in the Church when bishops are hindered by some impediment or when the see is vacant.

### 7. “It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom,” etc.

See our most learned Morinus discussing the penance of clerics at length, both in his *Commentary on Penance*, Book IV, chapter 12 and following, and elsewhere throughout, as well as in his *Ecclesiastical Exercises*, Book II. Nevertheless, it will be worthwhile to point out several matters.

### 1593

First, it can be drawn from Saint Leo’s words [Note: From Saint Leo’s having been questioned only about presbyters and deacons, it does not follow that lower clerics—whom he passes over merely because Rusticus did not ask about them—were at least sometimes subject to public penance. Nor do the canons subsequently cited by Quesnell, which grant clerics entangled in certain crimes a foreign or lay communion, signify that they were assigned to public penance. Add that canon 22 of Epaon does not speak of lower clerics but of presbyters and deacons.] that clerics of the lower order, among whom subdeacons were numbered, were not always exempt from the obligation of performing penance.

This is likewise demonstrated by canon 2 of the Fifth Council of Carthage—or rather by the memorandum of the Sixteenth Council of Carthage, dated the Kalends of July in the year 401, in the African Codex, number 62, which agrees with Leo’s decree—and it is expressly asserted in canon 5 of Agde, canon 22 of Epaon, and elsewhere.

## 2. That this discipline

[Note: [Col. 1491A] Saint Leo makes two points in his response to the second inquiry: (1) that it is contrary to ecclesiastical custom for hands to be imposed upon presbyters or deacons for any crime as a form of penance; (2) that this custom derives from apostolic tradition. For the first point to be true, it is not necessary that the custom have always and everywhere prevailed; it is enough to establish a genuine custom if it was introduced and maintained for some time before Leo. Siricius bears witness that this discipline was already customary. Yet, lest he be thought its originator, we learn from Optatus, who flourished before Siricius, that it had prevailed earlier as well. Near the end of his second book, Optatus reproves the Donatists because they imposed hands upon fallen deacons, presbyters, and bishops: “Many know and acknowledge that, during the persecution, certain bishops, through cowardice, fell away from confessing God and offered incense; yet none of those who survived either imposed hands upon the fallen or ordered them to kneel.” These words clearly prove that, during the persecution itself, this discipline had not been introduced by Siricius, who in his letter to Himerius, no. 18, speaks of an already established practice: “Just as it is not permitted to every member of the clergy to perform penance” (public penance is understood, which was joined to the imposition of hands), “so after penance and reconciliation no layman may ever attain clerical rank.” These words establish an ancient custom, sufficient to defend Leo’s position, so that it should not trouble us if, perhaps, at some time and in some place, hands were imposed upon clerics.

There is, however, another important point to be observed in Leo, which explains his judgment much more fully and confirms its general truth. Rusticus’ inquiry concerns deacons and presbyters who voluntarily requested public penance, not those who were compelled by any law or custom to undergo it. “Concerning a presbyter or deacon,” he says, “who, having acknowledged his crime, should request public penance: whether it ought to be given to him through the imposition of hands.” The subject, therefore, is a crime that was not subject to the canons of public penance [Col. 1491D], and that did not by itself remove a cleric from his order; consequently, Leo’s response assumes that he should be left in his rank and order. With respect to such clerics, it was always contrary to the Church’s custom that they should be subjected by the imposition of hands to public penance, which, according to the consistent discipline of all ages, excluded public penitents from the clergy.

Hence, whenever clerics returning from heresy or schism to the unity of the Church seemed, for the sake of peace, to be admissible to their former rank—provided that they had not been baptized a second time—they were received by a suitable satisfaction and guarantee, without any imposition of hands. See annotation 25 (Col. 1138, no. q), on epistle 159. Hence Saint Jerome says in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, no. 13: “A layman baptized outside the Church in the faith is received as a penitent; but a bishop either does not perform penance and remains a bishop, or, if he performs penance, ceases to be a bishop.” No example can certainly be found in which clerics received in their own rank, or not to be deposed from it, were subjected to the imposition of hands or to public penance [Col. 1492A].

Since Saint Leo is speaking of such persons, his proposition is entirely true in general. Moreover, even those who were removed from their rank and clergy were not ordinarily subjected to the imposition of hands or to public penance, lest the same crime, punished by deposition and also by public penance, impose a double penalty. This is reported in the *Apostolic Canons*, chapter 25, and by Saint Basil in his letter to Amphilochius, chapter 3. Thus also, in the Council of Carthage held under Isidore in 401, on the Ides of September, canon 11, repeated in another plenary synod of 419 [Col. 1492B], canon 27 of the African Code, concerning clerics to be removed from their ministry and rank, states:

“It has likewise been confirmed that, whenever presbyters or deacons are convicted of some more serious fault, for which it is necessary to remove them from the ministry, hands are not to be imposed upon them as upon penitents, or as upon faithful laymen.”

Augustine clearly distinguishes these two classes of clerics—those who were received in their rank and those who were excluded from it—in Book I of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 1, and indicates that hands were imposed upon neither. Speaking of those returning to the Church, he says:

“Those who return, having been ordained before they departed, are certainly not ordained again. They either perform the ministry which they previously performed, if the usefulness of the Church requires this” (that is, when they were received in their former rank, upon whom hands were plainly not imposed as penance), “or, if they do not perform it” (that is, when they were not received in their former rank), “they nevertheless possess the sacrament of their ordination, and therefore hands are not imposed upon them among the laity,” since, like laymen, they were not subject to public penance [Col. 1492C].

Accordingly, Augustine’s words in epistle 185 to Boniface, no. 44, where he says that converted heretics were not deprived of clerical or episcopal rank after doing penance for their error, are not to be understood of public penance, which was joined to the imposition of hands, but of secret penance, by which signs of inward contrition and necessary conversion are manifested.

If at some time fallen clerics returning to unity were not only excluded from their rank but also subjected, like laymen, to public penance, as certain testimonies of Saint Cyprian and others suggest, this was a special practice of particular places and times. Yet one will never find clerics who, because of some crime, were not removed from their rank and were not to be removed from it, undergoing public penance. Therefore, when Leo replied to Rusticus’ inquiry concerning such men, he rightly said that it was contrary to ecclesiastical custom for them to receive the remedy of penance through the imposition of hands.

[Col. 1492D] Quesnellus himself admits that this discipline—by which clerics retaining their rank were not punished with public penance—derives from the apostolic tradition according to which clerics must be irreproachable and free from every stain and disgrace, a requirement Saint Paul openly taught.

Two passages from the Council of Nicaea seem capable of being opposed to our assertion that it was always contrary to the discipline of the Church for clerics guilty of some crime to be received by the imposition of hands, or through public penance. The first is the eighth canon of that synod, which decreed that the Cathari, on receiving the imposition of hands, should remain among the clergy. The second is the Nicene synodal letter in Theodoret, which granted that those ordained by Meletius, once confirmed by the imposition of hands, should be received in their rank. Yet, although in these passages the formulas of Greek expression allowed ambiguity, if rightly explained they do not hinder these testimonies at all.

In both cases the imposition of hands is indeed expressed. But the Greek term χειροτονία (*cheirotonia*) is used in a threefold sense, because hands were imposed on three occasions: in chrism, in ordination, and in penance. Where the meaning is multiple, the sense to be chosen in our case is unquestionably that which does not conflict with the common discipline of that age, established by other testimonies. Now, since, as we have seen, it was contrary to practice to receive into the clergy those upon whom hands had been imposed for penance, it follows that the imposition of hands indicated in the cited passages of the Nicene synod cannot possibly be understood in the sense of penance.

Some explain it as the sacrament of confirmation, which Theodoret reports that the Cathari rejected. But apart from the fact that no one before Theodoret reported this, that error cannot be attributed to the Meletians, who were sound in faith and differed only by schism; nor does this interpretation suit the passages themselves. The remaining meaning is ordination. But this too can be understood in two ways: either of ordination already received, or of a new ordination to be received; for the Greek formula admits either sense.

The ancient translator responsible for the version undertaken by Isidore, commonly called the Isidorian, expressed the second sense in canon 8 concerning the Cathari or Novatians: “If any should wish to come to the Catholic Church from among the Novatians, the holy council decreed that they should be ordained and thus remain in the clergy.” The author of the Quesnellian collection adopted this same meaning from the same Isidorian version in his canon 14. Likewise, in the received version of the Nicene synodal letter included in volume II of the *Councils*, the same sense is expressed concerning the Meletians: “But those who were chosen by him [Meletius] for sacred order, once confirmed by a more sacred ordination, are thereafter to be admitted to communion and permitted indeed to enjoy their honors and discharge their sacred duties,” etc.

But this is wholly alien to the meaning of the Nicene Fathers, who, no less than the Catholic Church, believed that sacred orders conferred outside the Church, like baptism, were valid and were not to be repeated. Both testimonies must therefore be understood of ordination already received: that those previously ordained by sacred imposition of hands, whether among the Cathari or among the Meletians, should each be received in his own rank.

Thus canon 8 concerning the Cathari must be rendered literally: “It pleased the holy and great synod that those who have received the imposition of hands should thus remain in the clergy.” Under any other interpretation the statement is utterly absurd. For among the Cathari there were not only clerics previously ordained, but laymen also. Unless our meaning is applied to the canon, one would have to say that the Nicene Fathers decreed generally that all who came from the Cathari to the Church, clerics and laymen alike, upon receiving the imposition of hands—whether for penance, confirmation, or ordination—should thus remain in the clergy. Nothing could be more absurd.

Therefore, in order to restrict the general name “Cathari,” used at the beginning of the canon, to clerics alone, for whose reception some dispensation had to be provided (for there was no difficulty about laymen), the Nicene Fathers used the words χειροθετουμένους αὐτούς, that is, “those who have received the imposition of hands,” or orders. Of these they commanded that they should thus remain in the clergy, requiring no other condition than that, before being so received, they should give a suitable assurance and profession of right faith, as was always customary in receiving heretics.

Rufinus appears to have understood this canon in this sense when, in canon 9, he summarized it thus—as you will find corrected in the latest Veronese edition: “And that Cathari, who among us are Novatians, if perchance they turn penitently to the Church, having confessed the doctrines of the Church, ought to be received as clerics indeed in their own rank, but in the ordination already given.” Do you see that he says “given,” not “to be given”? Similarly, in the version of Philo and Evaristus, sent by Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, to the Africans in Augustine’s time, canon 8 reads: “If the Cathari should at any time come to the Catholic Church, the holy and great synod decreed that, being ordained, they should thus remain in the clergy.” Ferrandus, deacon of Carthage, states the canon still more explicitly in accordance with our explanation in his *Breviary of Canons*, no. 172: “That those called Cathari, when they come to the Church, if they are ordained, should thus remain in the clergy.”

That this interpretation excludes a new ordination and refers only to one already received is demonstrated clearly by the following context of the same canon, which prescribes the manner of receiving the Cathari themselves: “Wherever, then, whether in villages or cities, they alone are found ordained, those found in the clergy shall remain in the same rank. But if some of them come where there is a bishop or presbyter of the Catholic Church, it is clear that the bishop of the Church shall retain the dignity of bishop; while he who among those called Cathari is named bishop shall have the honor of presbyter, unless it pleases the two bishops that he share the honor of the title. But if this does not please him, he shall devise for him the place either of chorepiscopus or of presbyter, so that he may appear to be altogether in the clergy.” This is the translation of Gentian Hervetus from the Greek, and the versions of Philo and Evaristus, Dionysius Exiguus, and the Quesnellian collection, as well as the Greek reading itself, agree with it. It does not say that they should be ordained, but that those found ordained should remain in the same rank if they are alone in that place. Otherwise provision is to be made for them in different ways according to differing circumstances; yet there is no indication whatever that sacred order is to be repeated.

After writing this, we happened to observe William Beveridge’s annotations on Nicene canon 8, vol. II, p. 67. There, while expressing surprise that Christopher Justellus and others had interpreted this canon of the imposition of hands by which heretics were anciently received into the Catholic Church, he remarkably confirms our opinion. “For,” he says, “the Fathers treat throughout this canon not of every kind of Novatian, but only of Novatian clerics, who had previously received canonical ordination; and they decree that, upon conversion to the Church, they should remain in the same clerical rank in which they had stood among the Novatians, as becomes clear from the very words of the canon when properly considered. For this is decreed concerning the Novatians: Ὥστε χειροθετουμένους αὐτοὺς μένειν οὕτως ἐν τῷ κλήρῳ [‘that those who have received imposition of hands should thus remain in the clergy’]. But to what does οὕτως [‘thus’] refer except χειροθετουμένους [‘those who have received imposition of hands’]? And how can it refer to that unless this χειροθεσία [imposition of hands] had preceded? For they cannot thus remain in the clergy unless they had previously been in the clergy; nor could they previously have been in the clergy unless they had received imposition of hands. Consequently, this χειροθεσία of the Novatians must necessarily precede, not follow, their conversion to the Catholic Church.” He adds that Balsamon and Zonaras (add also Aristenus) interpreted the canon in the same sense; and, after quoting Rufinus’s preceding words, observes that Rufinus aptly rendered the Greek word χειροθετουμένους of the canon as “clerics.” This much on the Nicene canon.

The Greek words of the Nicene synodal letter concerning the Meletians, τοὺς δὲ ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ κατασταθέντας μυστικωτέρᾳ χειροτονίᾳ βεβαιωθέντας, κοινωνηθῆναι ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐφ᾽ ᾧ τε ἔχειν μὲν αὐτοὺς τὴν τιμὴν καὶ λειτουργεῖν, we render thus: “But those appointed by him [Meletius] in the Churches, having been confirmed by sacred imposition of hands, are to be received into communion on this condition: that they themselves retain their honor and perform sacred functions.” The words μυστικωτέρᾳ χειροτονίᾳ βεβαιωθέντας (“having been confirmed by sacred imposition of hands”) must be referred to the preceding τοὺς δὲ ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ κατασταθέντας (“those appointed by him”), not to the following words; and they indicate the ordination already received by which clerics had been appointed in the Churches by Meletius. The other interpretations, therefore, which render the imposition of hands in an equivocal or other sense, must be brought back to this meaning.

Thus Innocent I, in epistle 17 to Rufus, after citing Nicene canon 8 concerning the Cathari—“It pleased the holy and great synod that, having received imposition of hands, they should thus remain in the clergy”—expresses the same meaning in other words: that those returning from the Novatians and other heretics should be received in their own order. By this he indicates that the order they had received was valid, and sufficiently excludes a new ordination. Nothing, therefore, in the cited decrees of the Nicene Fathers is opposed to our position. Indeed, these passages agree closely with the constant discipline of the Church: public penitents were excluded from the clergy, while clerics returning to the Church were received with a suitable profession of faith without public penance, indeed without even that imposition of hands which Pope Vigilius, epistle 2 to Profuturus, no. 4, mentions as imposed without requiring a more rigorous penance, and which Innocent I, epistle 24 to Alexander, no. 4, when he calls it an image of penance, shows was employed not for receiving clerics but only laymen.

Saint Gregory aptly describes three rites for receiving heretics in Book XI, epistle 67 to Quiricus: “And indeed we have learned from the ancient institution of the Fathers that all who are baptized among heretics in the name of the Trinity, when they return to the holy Church, are recalled to the bosom of Mother Church either by the anointing of chrism, or by the imposition of hands, or by profession of faith alone.” The holy doctor proposes the third rite, in which profession of faith alone was required, for Nestorian clerics. Discussing their reception with Quiricus, he says: “If they provide a right profession, receive them into your communion, preserving to them their own orders.” Do you see that profession of faith alone is so distinguished from the imposition of hands that no hands whatever were imposed upon those received by profession of faith alone?]

It is characteristic of our Leo that, whenever he speaks of apostolic tradition, he means the tradition which he believed had been handed down from the Apostle Peter to the Roman Church. He thought that practice descended from the tradition of blessed Peter which he found had once been observed and had been established by decrees of the pontiffs of his own Church whose records still survived at that time. It is probable, both from the collection of Dionysius—which gathered, with as much care and diligence as possible, the constitutions of earlier bishops of the Apostolic See and arranged all that he found—and from other evidence, that no decrees of a Roman pontiff earlier than Siricius were preserved in the archives of the Roman Church during the pontificate following Leo’s. I would therefore readily believe that Leo derived this tradition from Siricius.

Indeed, Leo seems to have copied the decree of Siricius which we cited above, and he thought that its form had been established by Siricius according to the constitutions and discipline of his predecessors [Col. 1495B]. But since we find that it had sometimes been used otherwise, even in the Roman Church and also in Africa during the time of Saint Cyprian, when the discipline of the two Churches did not differ in this matter, Saint Leo should be understood more leniently. He plainly asserts that this practice descended from apostolic tradition, but he shows that he relies on no other proof than the custom which he knew had prevailed in his own Church from the time of Siricius down to his own day.

We think that Leo’s words can be reconciled with the testimonies of others only in this way. Other answers, which Morinus calls decisive, do not appear sufficient, if I may say so with due respect for so learned a man. He says that this custom—namely, exempting clerics from the imposition of hands for penance—could not have been observed during times of fierce persecution, and that this explains why clerics are also said to have submitted to public penance during that period. I do not see how this explanation can satisfy anyone [Col. 1495C].

For, on the contrary, if one had to defend the opposite position—namely, that the Church’s discipline was introduced by apostolic tradition so that clerics, no less than laymen, were assigned to public penance, and if it were objected that this had not been observed during the first three centuries—I think one could rightly answer that the custom had been interrupted during the turbulent periods of persecution. When tyrants were raging and all Christians scarcely dared even to whisper, it was much easier to compel fallen clerics, removed from their office, to withdraw privately and perform penance than to subject them, through a solemn imposition of hands, to public penance; to make them, clothed in sackcloth and covered with ashes, prostrate themselves at the feet of all the faithful; and finally to lead them through all the stages of mournful satisfaction [1600].

Certainly, if the explanation of this difficulty is to be sought in the storms of persecution, it would be better to say that the ministers of the Church were then subjected to this mournful and public penance, so that presbyters and deacons would be deterred from apostasy by fear of such a great and extraordinary punishment imposed upon clerics. For, just as the Churches then had the greatest need of their services, so there was everywhere a great shortage of them, and their apostasy was more harmful.

The second answer offered by Morinus is that Leo’s judgment concerns only clerics who had been suspended, and exempts them from the necessity of public penance. But anyone who reads the pontiff’s words with even slight attention will see clearly that his response is entirely general, defined by no condition and no restriction, and embraces absolutely all clerics—all who had committed some crime, whatever their crime. Since he makes no distinction among crimes, we must believe that none is excepted, and that, according to Leo, clerics were never compelled to public penance, whether they had committed offenses punished only by suspension or those punished by deposition. Indeed, public penance was not even granted to those who requested it voluntarily.

For it is manifest that Leo’s response concerns such persons, as the heading of the inquiry shows. The same point is found in canons 4 of the Council of Orange and 29 of the Second Council of Arles, to which we have often noted that Rusticus was referring; and also in Siricius himself, who mentions only the granting of penance, not compulsion to perform it.

What we have said about apostolic tradition must also be said about ecclesiastical custom, which Saint Leo either believed had prevailed everywhere and always, or thought ought to be accepted by all Churches. Thus whatever was done otherwise elsewhere he would count among corruptions of morals and discipline. Yet the matter stood differently, as this single example makes clear. What was never granted at Rome to any cleric of the higher orders who desired penance was done very properly and wisely. But the Gallicans’ view that penance ought not to be denied to clerics who desired it—as is clear from the canons of the First Council of Orange and the Second Council of Arles—was certainly not blameworthy [1601]. For, as Augustine says in epistle 118 to Januarius, “What is imposed neither against the faith nor against good morals is to be regarded as indifferent and observed according to the fellowship of those among whom one lives.”

A third point that must be observed in this chapter is that, when Leo wished to prove that a hand should not be imposed upon a cleric for penance, he brought forward these words: “If a priest sins, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel 2:25). The reason may be either that penitents were said to be released from sins through the supplications of priests, or that hands were never imposed without prayer, whether for confirmation, ordination, or penance.

Since the imposition of hands was in itself an indifferent act, it was at times an honorific one, as in ordination; at other times it was joined to public humiliation and degradation, as in penance, and was directed toward that effect by prayer. For this reason it was removed from Levites and priests, who possessed the right to impose hands upon others, lest it seem that priestly dignity was thereby insulted—and all the more because, during the course of their penance, penitents were made to prostrate themselves not only at the knees of the clergy but also at those of the laity.

## 8. The law of continence is the same for the ministers of the altar

That the subdeacon is counted among the ministers of the altar is clear from epistle 12 (now 14) to Anastasius of Thessalonica, chapter 3, where Siricius discusses his continence more distinctly; we also say something about it there. Here I merely observe that it is rather surprising that Leo says the law of continence was imposed upon the ministers of the altar, especially in the Roman Church, since Pope Siricius holds that bishops and presbyters were always bound to it by divine law, whereas subdeacons were bound to continence only by ecclesiastical law—and by a law that was scarcely then emerging into public view.

For all the canons of councils and decrees of Roman pontiffs promulgated before Saint Leo declare that only presbyters and deacons were subject to the law of continence [Col. 1497B]. See Siricius, letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapters 7 and 9; Innocent I, letter to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 9, and letter to Exuperius of Toulouse, chapter 1.

Indeed, in the Gallican Churches even in Leo’s time no clerics other than presbyters and deacons were commanded to profess continence. The First Council of Orange bears witness to this, canon 22:

“It was further decreed that henceforth married men are not to be ordained deacons unless they have first professed chastity with the intention of conversion.”

And canon 23:

“If anyone, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found to be incontinent with his wife, let him be removed from office.”

Finally, chapter 4 says:

“Concerning those who, having been ordained earlier, fell into this same offense, the judgment of the Council of Turin is to be followed, by which it is ordered that they not be promoted further.”

The Second Council of Arles, canon 42, supports this; its canon 45 also decrees that those who contracted intermarried or second marriages should no longer receive ecclesiastical dignities beyond the subdiaconate. If they have perhaps already done so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office [Col. 1497C].

The Council of Angers likewise, in 452, canon 11, decreeing that digamists or husbands of widows were not to be admitted to the rank of deacon or presbyter, says nothing about subdeacons. It therefore wished them to be regarded among the clerics of the lower offices, who were not bound to continence.

This should also be noted in canon 22 of Orange, which says, “henceforth they are not to be ordained,” as though this arrangement concerning deacons had then been newly established. The same seems to be indicated by canon 24. For, when it decrees that deacons ordained before this constitution who afterward had intercourse with their wives should be punished by the very light penalty of not being promoted further, but that those consecrated thereafter should be removed if they fell into the same offense, this indicates that it had previously been commonly practiced throughout Gaul for deacons not to be bound by the law of continence. Whether this resulted from corruption or was introduced through the indulgence of the Gallican bishops because of the shortage of ministers caused by the calamity of war, it is not clear.

Certainly, the subdeacons of Gaul were so far from being compelled to continence [Col. 1497D] at that time that the deacons themselves submitted to this yoke only with great reluctance. This moved the Gallican bishops frequently to issue complaints about their incontinence and repeatedly to renew the same law in synods, as at the First Council of Tours in 461, canons 1 and 2—which was held when Leo had scarcely been carried from the living—and at Agde in 506, canon 9.

Something similar, though not expressed entirely explicitly, is found in the Council of Vannes in 465, presided over by Perpetuus of Tours, who had also presided over the First Council of Tours. Its canon 11, which is canon 39 in the Council of Agde, states:

“Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and those below them, who are not permitted to marry, must also avoid the banquets of other people’s marriages.”

Yet, just as the discipline concerning this matter varied among different regions of the world, so there was considerable variation even within Gaul itself among its different provinces and Churches [Col. 1498A]. This is shown to us by the brief letter of Saints Lupus, bishop of Troyes, and Euphronius, bishop of Autun, to Talasius, bishop of Angers. In it we see that, at that time, the discipline of clerical continence in the Churches of Gaul was uncertain and fluctuating, at least with respect to the subdiaconate and the lower orders (vol. I of the *Gallican Councils*, under the year 461).

It will not be out of place to examine more closely how precisely and distinctly each matter is explained in this letter. It will be highly useful for reconciling the various and sometimes contradictory decrees of canons and pontiffs, which differ according to the times, regions, and Churches. It is also useful because there is no more authoritative witness to the discipline of the Gallican Churches of this age than Lupus of Troyes: father of fathers, bishop of bishops, another James of his age, who from a watchtower of charity, and not from a lower Jerusalem, looked down upon all the members of the Church of our God; worthy, with good reason, to be consulted by all; the colleague of the Apostle Peter; the first among all pontiffs throughout the whole world over which his authority extended; before whose prerogative the episcopal college itself was subject and before whose judgment even the assembled company of bishops trembled; in comparison with whose gravity the hearts of old men themselves became childlike; the most renowned standard-bearer of the saints of both orders, monastic and episcopal; the rule of morals, the pillar of virtues; a younger rather than a lesser Moses; for more than ten periods of five years preferred not only to priests of equal age but also to ancient priests (Apollinaris, *Synodal Letter*, Book VI, letter 1; Book IX, letter 11) [1603].

It is fitting that we hear so great a man discussing the continence of clerics and distinguishing what was done in his own Church of Troyes, what in that of Autun, and what throughout the whole Church; what was based on custom, what on necessity, and what was established in fact; what he desired, what he praised in others, and finally what he himself did not dare to do. First, the very words of the letter must be set out; then they must be examined section by section.

“Concerning clerics who have married twice,” he says, “the Church permits and tolerates them as far as the doorkeepers; and whatever rule any priest has adopted for the sake of stricter discipline, he will rightly observe. But it entirely excludes exorcists and subdeacons from second marriages.

“It would be better, if it could be done, to prevent the begetting of children by those whom we admit while married. It is better not to admit such men than afterward to dispute about them amid various differences of opinion, since it is better to exclude every cause of controversy. Therefore, whoever does not wish married men to be produced in the clergy should not place married men at the altar.

“These things we have set down in the language of this letter as the custom of our Churches, of which there is one rule. But if anything can be added for the honor of the Lord by way of stricter discipline, even if we cannot imitate it, we shall praise it for the Lord’s honor.

“For we do not now permit those already attached to the services of the Church to pass to a second marriage; and once they have been admitted, we entirely exclude them even from a first marriage—exorcists and subdeacons alone.

“In the Church of Autun, however, even a doorkeeper established in the lowest office, if he takes another wife, is entirely removed from office. Subdeacons ought to approach one another for the peace in the sacristy; but at the altar only when they hand the cloths to the deacon or receive what is brought back. They are not permitted to receive the peace at all.

“If, however, an exorcist, subdeacon, or even a doorkeeper, as mentioned above, should be so insane as to bind himself to a second marriage, he is entirely excluded not only from office but also from communion.”

The first conclusion drawn from this letter, therefore, is that, by the permission and tolerance of the Church, minor clerics, including doorkeepers, could be digamists. That is, men who were or had been married could be admitted to the office of doorkeeper and to the grades of the lowest offices; and clerics established in such offices were permitted both to take a wife and to enter a second marriage, and even to beget children. This is the sense of the letter’s words: “Concerning clerics who have married twice, as far as the doorkeepers, the Church permits and tolerates them.”

[Col. 1499A] 2. The same things were entirely permitted to exorcists and subdeacons, with one exception: they were not allowed to enter a second marriage. For the letter says: “But it entirely excludes exorcists and subdeacons from second marriages.”

3. The bishops were free to follow this permission of the Church, but each could nevertheless introduce stricter discipline into his own Church at his discretion: “Whatever rule,” he says, “any priest has adopted for the sake of stricter discipline, he will rightly observe.”

4. The holy bishops would have wished married men never to be admitted to the office of exorcist or subdeacon, because it was extremely difficult to prevent many controversies from arising in the Church, when the use of marriage could scarcely be confined within fixed limits among those who, having been joined in marriage, were admitted to the offices of the Church.

5. At least, they wished, if it could be done, to prevent the begetting of children by those who were admitted while married. The sense of both parts of this statement is contained in these words:

“It would be better, if it could be done, to prevent the begetting of children by those whom we admit while married. It is better not to admit such men than afterward to dispute about them amid various differences of opinion, since it is better to exclude every cause of controversy; so that whoever does not wish married men to be produced in the clergy should not place married men at the altar.”

6. They assert that these provisions, which they had previously taught were to be observed, had been received in practice in both their churches: that of Autun, that of Lyons I, and that of Troyes in Sens—or Lyons IV. “These things,” they say, “we have woven into the words of this page as the custom of our churches, of which there is one rule.” But, in accordance with the right which he above acknowledged to belong to each bishop in his own church—namely, to adopt whatever rule he wished for the sake of stricter discipline—each of these two bishops testifies that he himself had introduced a stricter and purer discipline into his churches, with some difference between one church and the other, at least in regard to the punishment imposed on those who acted contrary to it.

7. In the church of Troyes, Saint Lupus had enacted that no one initiated into any ministry there should be permitted to involve himself in a second marriage: “For we no longer permit those who have already been enrolled in the service of the Church to pass on to a second marriage.” This is also to be understood of the lower orders, so that at first they were permitted to take a wife; but as regards exorcists and subdeacons, if anyone had been placed in those grades before any marriage, Lupus did not permit them to marry even once: “After they have been appointed, we completely bar them even from a first marriage—exorcists and subdeacons only.”

8. In the church of Autun, however, the discipline sanctioned by Euphronius was stricter in this respect: the punishment of deposition was imposed even on the ostiarius, the lowest of all the orders, if he had taken a second wife; while an exorcist or subdeacon who had done the same was excluded not only from his office but also from communion. “In the church of Autun,” he says, “even an ostiarius, appointed in the lowest office, if he takes another wife, is utterly removed from office. But if someone has been guilty of that madness—whether an exorcist, or a subdeacon, [Col. 1500A] or even, as was mentioned above, an ostiarius—and has bound himself to a second marriage, he is completely excluded not only from office but also from communion.”

But were those whom he here prohibits from either a first or a second marriage nevertheless left free to make use of wives whom they had taken before ordination? I think that this was indeed the case, as is also found in the Venetian and Agde canons cited above. The fathers of those councils, undoubtedly inspired by the example of Saints Lupus and Euphronius, prescribed stricter laws of continence for ministers of the altar and began to draw nearer to the discipline which we see prevailing in the Roman Church in the time of our Leo. Yet they still differed from it in many respects, as may be understood from this letter of Saint Lupus if it is compared with his letter to Rusticus and with those to Anastasius of Thessalonica, to the bishops of Italy, and to the bishops of Vienne. In the last of these, chapter 3, he does not permit even clerics in the minor offices to remain in office if they have been husbands of more than one wife.

[Col. 1500B] Moreover, I would not think that the looser discipline by which, as we have mentioned, subdeacons were permitted to have intercourse with their own wives, nor the corruption which appears to have spread through the Gallican churches before the first Council of Orange and the second Council of Arles—namely, that deacons were sometimes ordained without having previously professed a resolve of conversion or continence—arose merely from moral corruption or the negligence of bishops. Rather, I would attribute it to the canons of the Eastern synods, by which [Note: [Col. 1499D] Quesnellus understands by the name “Gallican code of canons” a code authorized, in his own interpretation, which, as he calls it elsewhere, had been received by the Gallican Church and possessed authority among the Gauls. No such code of canons, however, is known to us. The only similar work is Codex Vaticanus Palatinus 574, like the Morbacensis, which P. Coustantius and others cite. It is a collection compiled in Gaul before the middle of the sixth century, since, apart from the Nicene and Sardican canons, it contains only the canons of councils of Gaul. It knows nothing of the canons of Ancyra or of the other Greek canons. In the council commonly entitled the Second Council of Arles, which is in fact a collection of canons made under Saint Caesarius of Arles at the beginning of the same sixth century, no Greek canons are cited except those of Nicaea. If some codices in Gaul contained a Latin version of other canons of Eastern synods, they were private scholarly compilations, not works possessing public authority. [Col. 1500D] The code of the Roman Church cited by Quesnellus is not Roman; and that the Roman Church formerly received no canons other than those of Nicaea and Sardica, we shall demonstrate in volume III. Quesnellus himself eventually perceived this and confessed it with some clarity when he wrote in Dissertation 11, no. 6: “We have never read of Roman pontiffs citing any canons, whether in the time of Leo or of his equals or predecessors, other than the Nicene canons, or the Sardican canons regarded as Nicene . . . nor do we find the decrees of particular synods—by which, from the context, he means Greek canons—received as authoritative before the Council of Chalcedon among most of the churches of the western regions. Quesnellus’s conjecture is therefore empty, by which he supposes that the looser corruption concerning the continence of deacons in Gaul was derived from the canons of Ancyra inserted into a Gallican code.”] The Gallican code of canons was partly composed of canons among which was Canon 10 of Ancyra. This canon permitted a deacon who had refused, at the time of his ordination, to promise continence to pass on to marriage, and did not deprive him of his rank on that account. Roman discipline, much purer and more conformed to tradition, had always imposed the law of continence upon deacons; nor had it received Canon 10 of Ancyra except by correcting it and adapting it to its own usage, as we stated in the dissertation on our ancient code of the Roman Church.

[Col. 1500C] 9. They must not dismiss their wives. The Apostolic Canon forbids this: “A bishop or presbyter must under no circumstances cast away his own wife under the pretext of religion; but if he casts her away, let him be excommunicated; and if he persists, let him be deposed.” Several Latin constitutions agree with this decree of the Eastern Church. Nevertheless, with more cautious forethought, they provided that a married cleric of a higher order should not live in the same house with his wife unless the sleeping quarters were separated, after the profession—or promise—of religion, as the Council of Agde has it in Canon 16, after both had likewise converted.

10. The sacrament of Christ and the Church. Several reasons are usually offered for why a marriage between a freeborn man and a slave woman or bondwoman is invalid; but I do not know whether sufficient attention is commonly paid to the reason which Saint Leo derives from the meaning of the sacrament itself. Namely, besides the voluntary union of the sexes, it is necessary that marriages should possess the sacrament of Christ and the Church. For just as Christ took a free Church as his bride—or made her free by taking her as his bride and redeeming her—and her children became heirs of God and co-heirs of Christ, incorporated into the fellowship of this divine person and admitted to certain rights of the Only-Begotten, so it is necessary that the woman should be free when she is taken as a wife, or should be made free when she is knowingly taken and redeemed: “Made freeborn, lawfully endowed, and honorably established by public nuptials,” as Leo says elsewhere.

As regards this condition of public nuptials, the holy pontiff seems to require it as necessary for marriages to be ratified and valid. This strongly supports the view of certain very learned experts in canon law who maintain that clandestine marriages were always invalid and null. But since the sacred Council of Trent judged such marriages to have been ratified and true so long as the Church had not rendered them invalid, it is better to understand Leo’s words as referring only to marriages involving bondwomen, which could be honored and vindicated into freedom only through the solemnity of public nuptials. See Saint Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 5, who requires far fewer things for a true marriage, although he speaks with some hesitation.

Moreover, what is said in this chapter about concubines must not be taken in a negative sense, but of those concubines whose use was lawful at that time. They were, as it were, wives, although they had neither dotal instruments nor been solemnly taken nor been made freeborn; rather, they were taken for a time with marital affection, for the purpose of begetting children. To avoid uselessly revisiting a subject treated in many works, one should consult the new commentary of Emanuel Gonzalez, J.C., on the Council of Elvira, chapter 8, appended to the older commentaries of Mendoza, where he refutes this contrary opinion and examines more fully the ways in which such concubinage and marriage either agree or differ.

11. At the father’s discretion, etc. This section is connected with the preceding one not only in the collections of Dionysius Exiguus, chapter 18; Isidore; Gratian, 32, question 2, *Not every woman*; and those of Burchard and Ivo, but also in the manuscript codices Corbeiensis, Grimaniensis, Victorinus, and four of the Thuanean codices. We followed the single Thuanean manuscript together with the Barberinian, Trecopithoean, and Cambridge manuscripts in making it a distinct chapter, as the subject itself requires. The preceding chapter concerns only clerics giving their daughters in marriage; this one concerns any faithful girl who, at her father’s discretion, is given to a man who had previously been united to a concubine. These words—“For a married woman is one thing, and a concubine another”—which conclude the answer to Inquiry 5, begin Inquiry 6 in the Barberinian manuscript, and not with a bad meaning.

12. It is certainly to be censured, etc. Among the same collectors just mentioned, this chapter is immediately joined to the preceding one; the same is true of the corresponding manuscripts, except Thuaneus 1, the Trecopithoean, the Barberinian, and the Cambridge manuscript. The wide difference in subject sufficiently shows that the chapters must be distinguished. Indeed, without a distinct title for the inquiry, this chapter cannot be understood at all.

13. On account of these people, etc. We have already indicated above that this custom of the Roman Church was generally not observed by other churches. The Council of Carthage IV, if it is genuine, bears witness to the Carthaginian practice in Canon 74: “Those penitents who diligently fulfill the laws of penance, if they should happen to die on a journey or at sea, where no assistance can be given them, let their memory be commended by offerings and prayers.” The Gallican practice is attested by Canon 2 of the Council of Vaison I, cited above. The Spanish practice is attested by the Council of Toledo, called the Eleventh, assembled in the year 675, which Pope Innocent calls authentic in his letter to Peter of Compostela. “Concerning those,” says Canon 12, “who, having received penance, have departed this life before being reconciled, although there is a diversity of precepts regarding this matter, it has nevertheless pleased us to follow the judgment of those who, being greater in number, decreed more humanely in such cases: so that the memory of such persons may be commended in the churches and an offering dedicated for their spirits may be accepted.” There the synod [Note: [Col. 1501D] In his letter to Peter of Compostela, Innocent III calls not the Toledan but the Emeretan synod authentic, using the term in the sense of showing it to be genuine, or not spurious. He proved this from the Spanish collection, or from the book of canons received among the Spaniards, which, he says, Pope Alexander approved as authentic by an interlocutory judgment. Since the matter concerned no precepts binding on all, and since the discipline of the churches differed, it is not surprising that the Toledan fathers preferred the discipline of the Carthaginians and Gauls. But one must not infer from this that the Spaniards preferred the authority of these many men to the authority of the Roman pontiffs; numerous documents clearly show that they always held the latter in the highest regard. Nor was this a comparison of authority with authority, but a choice of a milder discipline over a stricter one. For this reason the Toledan fathers cited the examples of many predecessors, lest they should appear to be the first to introduce a relaxation of the ancient rigor.] judges the Carthaginian and Gallican bishops to be preferred to Leo because they were greater in number. Yet in the same canon it follows the position which he defined in his letter to Theodore of Fréjus: reconciliation must not be denied in danger of death. He departs from that position when, in the same letter, he declares that communion must not be given to those who die while still undergoing penance.

14. He prefers an ecclesiastical judgment to a secular one. Since Leo gives penitents this choice in such a way that he approves even more strongly if, abandoning a secular judgment, they flee to an ecclesiastical one for whatever cause, this proves that laws were still in force by which emperors—Constantine, as Sozomen testifies in Book I, chapter 9, and Honorius—had granted bishops the power to judge disputes between Christian litigants, even laymen, including disputes concerning temporal matters.

15. Inquiry 13. On those who take wives after penance or join concubines to themselves. This inquiry appears to have arisen from Canon 21 of the Second Council of Arles, except that here the subject is only second marriages and illicit intercourse, whereas Saint Leo excludes penitents even from first marriages and is in this, as in other matters, less indulgent than our Gauls.

16. The resolve of virginity. Saint Leo clearly distinguishes two things: a resolve joined to a habit, and consecration. The resolve was either solemn, through entry into a monastery, or private, through the reception of the virginal habit in one’s own home, which could be undertaken by a twelve-year-old girl. Leo decreed, however, that consecration should not take place before the fortieth year of age. “Here too,” says the book *On the Roman Pontiffs*, “he established that a nun should not receive the blessing of the head-veil unless she had been tested in virginity for forty years.” The emperor Majorian enacted the same in the year of Christ 458, at the urging, as is reasonable to believe, of Saint Leo; in the same edict he forbade anyone to compel unwilling daughters to receive the sacred veil.

The Council of Agde prescribed the same period of forty years for testing virgins before consecration in Canon 19; it had been preceded by Canon 15 of Chalcedon, which made the same provision concerning deaconesses. Saint Leo does not say what punishment virgins who withdrew from their resolve would suffer. Innocent I writes in his letter to Victricius of Rouen that they should do penance for some time; but a woman who had violated consecration by marrying was to be subjected to penance after her husband’s death. See the Council of Ancyra, Canon 19.

This solemn consecration was to be performed by no one other than a bishop, and only on the greater solemnities. Pope Gelasius, in his letter to the bishops of Sicily, Lucania, and Bruttium, orders that the sacred veil be given only on the days of Epiphany, during the Easter octave, or on the feasts of the apostles. Pope Liberius consecrated Marcellina, the sister of Saint Ambrose, [Col. 1503A] and other virgins to God on the very feast of the Lord’s Nativity, and delivered a sermon to them which Saint Ambrose transcribes in Book III of *On Virgins*.

17. In all published copies this chapter follows, and it is also found in Gratian, 20, question 1.

There can be no doubt that a serious crime is committed where both the resolve is abandoned and consecration violated. For if human agreements cannot be trampled upon with impunity, what fate will await those who have violated the bonds of the divine sacrament?

But this entire section is absent from the manuscript codices Grimaniensis, Barberinianus, Victorinus, Trecopithoeanus, Navarricus, and three Thuanean manuscripts, as well as from Dionysius Exiguus, Burchard, and the edition of Isidore’s collection published at Paris in 1524 and 1535 under the care of Margarinus de la Bigne. It is therefore beyond doubt that these are either Gratian’s words or those of some zealous scholar who, noticing that Leo’s decree dealt only with girls who had made a profession of virginity, inferred what should be established concerning consecrated women and wrote a marginal note, which later entered the text through the ignorance of scribes. Certainly, this passage reveals a man reasoning rather than defining, and it does not appear to have proceeded from a pontiff speaking with authority.

In some copies it is combined with the preceding chapter as a single chapter, as in Gratian and Sirmond, who found no corresponding inquiry. In others it is treated as a separate chapter, as in the common edition and in two Thuanean manuscripts and the Cambridge manuscript. Moreover, the argument drawn from the sacrament of the divine covenant seems to have been taken by the author from the letter of Innocent I to Victricius of Rouen, chapter 13.

[Note: [Col. 1503D] We have shown in note 76 (Col. 1207, note k) on the present letter that this addition is much older than Gratian.]

18. Of what faith those who baptized them were, etc. Our Leo gives the same definition in Letter 135 (now 166), chapter 2, and Letter 129 (now 159), chapter 7. There, although he forbids anyone baptized by any heretic to be baptized again, take care not to suppose that the Paulianists—whose baptism the Nicene Council declared invalid—are to be counted among the competent baptizers recognized by him. For, as Innocent I says, the Paulianists did not baptize at all in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Consequently, their baptism—and likewise that of any others who did not baptize in the name of the Trinity—was not baptism, because they did not use the form of baptism which Leo here assumes to have been received in some manner.

“For who,” says Augustine in Book VI of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, “does not know that it is not the baptism of Christ if the evangelical words, of which the creed consists, are absent?” Saint Leo nevertheless speaks indiscriminately, because other holy Fathers often spoke indiscriminately as well, and because heretics who do not baptize at all are more easily found—something Augustine says in the passage just cited—than those who baptize without using those words.

19. They can be cleansed by fasting and the laying on of hands. Here you see [Note: [Col. 1503D] See our note 25 (Col. 1138, note q) on Letter 159, where Leo’s genuine meaning is explained; from it one may sufficiently learn what in Quesnellus’s subsequent conjectures should be approved.] something intermediate between public penance and the laying on of hands alone, or confirmation. By the latter alone, those who had been baptized as infants by heretics were joined to the Catholics, as is decreed in the preceding chapter. Those who, after having been baptized by Catholics and captured while still children by pagans, had polluted themselves among them through idolatry, homicide, or fornication were subjected to the labors of public penance and were thus admitted to communion.

But if these same people had merely taken part in pagan banquets and eaten sacrificial foods, they were not punished with public penance, since this had been done by young people who had been carried off in infancy, did not know what they were doing, and had been compelled by hunger. Nor were they subjected to the laying on of hands, with an invocation of the power of the Holy Spirit—that is, to confirmation—because, having been baptized by Catholics, they had likewise received from Catholics the sanctification of the Spirit. [Col. 1504A] Rather, they were cleansed by fasting and the laying on of hands. It seems clear to me from the context of the chapter and from the inquiry itself that this laying on of hands is to be understood neither of public penance nor of the sacrament of confirmation.

Our Leo appears to prescribe a somewhat stricter discipline in Letter 129 (now 159) to Nicetas of Aquileia, chapter 5. There he orders those polluted by such sacrificial foods to be cleansed by satisfaction in penance, whether fear had extorted the act or hunger had persuaded them. But the difference lies in the punishment, since those who sinned there were adults and advanced in age. Moreover, Saint Leo does not speak as though on the authority of the canons, but as though from his own judgment: “We have believed,” he says—by which he either does not speak of the satisfaction of public penance or wishes its moderation to be left to the prudence and discretion of the bishop—“that it should be measured not so much by length of time as by contrition of heart, since such food was taken from fear or necessity, not from reverence for religion.”

[Col. 1504B] That he orders those younger people to be cleansed by fasting and the laying on of hands, although the acts they had committed may scarcely seem to belong among the smallest sins, will not surprise anyone who has read Augustine’s *Homily 50, On Penance*: “For daily sins, each person does not cease to offer, according to his strength, the sacrifices of almsgiving, fasting, prayers, and supplications.” Nor should it cause difficulty that he mentions the laying on of hands. By that very fact what we have said is confirmed: when the laying on of hands is mentioned by itself, it signifies no sacrament, and still less confirmation, but only prayers and supplications joined to the laying on of hands, in accordance with Augustine’s statement in Book I of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 10: “The laying on of hands, unlike baptism, can be repeated. For what else is it but prayer over a person?”

Thus, in this very letter of Leo to Rusticus, Inquiry 2, when he wished to prove that clerics ought not to receive public penance through the laying on of hands—the laying on by which that mournful stage customarily began—he adduces these words of Scripture: “If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?” 1 Kings 2:25.

Finally, I shall point out that the intermediate penance, or shadow of penance, which Saint Leo here mentions throws light upon the words of Pope Innocent I, which I see many people twisting to meanings foreign to them. “We receive,” he says, “lay ARIANS who have been converted to the Lord UNDER THE APPEARANCE OF PENANCE and through the sanctification of the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands.” What he here calls the “appearance of penance” seems to me to be precisely what Saint Leo includes under fasting and the laying on of hands. Compared with all those laborious stages of penance which were commonly practiced in the reconciliation of sinners, this penance is rightly called an appearance and shadow of penance rather than penance itself.

Although the hand was presumably laid upon them publicly by priests making supplication, it was not designated by the name of public penance, because it was exempt from that entire discipline of public humiliation. [Col. 1504D] We see this sort of slight and intermediate penance undertaken, first, by adults who were preparing themselves for the sacrament and consecration of baptism. Saint Augustine discusses this in the homily cited above, where he lists three acts of penance, of which this is the first: it “gives birth to the new man” until, through saving baptism, forgiveness of all previous sins is obtained.

Second, it was undertaken by those whom Innocent I says were received from the Arians into the Catholic Church through the sacrament of confirmation. For they prepared themselves for this sanctification of the spirit through fasting and prayers.

Third, it was undertaken by those who returned from captivity, where they had polluted themselves with sacrificial foods, and desired to share in the sacraments of Christ. Communion in them had previously been withheld until they had been cleansed by fasting, priestly prayers, and the laying on of hands.

Moreover, when I read here of the laying on of hands, I can scarcely restrain myself from directing the eyes of my mind toward the rite of private confession and sacramental absolution as it is practiced today. I offer this as a suspicion, but assert nothing.

Before I finish these observations, it is worth noting that certain material from the preface to this letter was transferred to the prologue of the spurious rescript of Pope Mark to Athanasius. Some material from Inquiry 13 was also transferred into the letter of Pope Julius to the Easterners concerning the same case of Athanasius. There may be other material in other of Isidore’s pseudo-letters.

NOTICE.

You will find Quesnellus’s observation on the letter numbered 9 in his edition, to the Gallican bishops of the province of Vienne—which we rejected as spurious—in the admonition prefixed to that letter, volume I, column 1465 (above, column 1235), where we added our observations.

## A
[Col. 1513] Aaron: the order of Aaron and Melchizedek, and the distinction between them, 11, 21. Abraham, an Egyptian bishop and consecrator of Timothy Salophaciolus, 1437. Abraham, a chorepiscopus and envoy of Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, to Leo, 950. What sort of succession was promised to Abraham, 118. Why it was compared with the multitude of the stars, ibid. The promise made to him was also fulfilled, 120. His vision, 121. Abraham’s spiritual offspring, 203, 256.

[Col. 1514] Absolution of sins. See Way. Reconciliation.

Abstinence prepares the way for the Lord and raises the mind toward heavenly things, 58. When one abstains from what is permitted, one resists what is forbidden more easily, 355. Through abstinence, the incentives to vice are cut off, 314. See Fasting.

How the abundance of the earth should be used, 62. In abundance, one should not inquire into the cheapness of the price, 41, 42. See Fertility.

Abundantius, bishop of Como, 1081, 1083. The same as Abundius, Leo’s legate, ibid. note. See Abundius.

Abundius, Leo’s legate to Theodosius, 1007, 1010, 1012. His acts and those of his companions at Constantinople, 1487. They said that the names of Dioscorus, Juvenal, and Eustathius should not be recited at the altar, and Saint Leo approved this, 1040 note. He returned to the West, 1080. He carried Leo’s letters to Eusebius of Milan, 1081. He took part in the synod of Milan, 1083.

Acatholics are not members of the Church, 350.

The vinegar tasted by Christ on the cross is explained mystically, 210.

The quality of an action is assessed from the will, 364.

Adam could merit in the state of innocence, 79. He desired angelic honor, 86. He sinned freely, 98. Comparison of the first and second Adam, 86, 270. No merits of the saints could make satisfaction for Adam’s sin, 248. If Adam had not sinned, the Word would not have become flesh, 309.

Adelphus, the bishop praised by Saint Peter Chrysologus, was bishop of Aquileia, 586.

A salutary admonition benefits the one who admonishes and the one admonished as a reward, 617.

Adeodatus, a deacon of the Roman see, returned from Aquileia to Rome, 1330.

Adversities either correct or test, 40. Not only adversities but also prosperity corrupts many of the faithful, 164.

Leo consoles the Egyptian bishops exiled on account of the faith, 1316, 1328. They were received by Anatolius of Constantinople, 1318. They presented a petition to the emperor, 1319, 1324. The Egyptian Eutychians presented another petition, without any of their names, ibid. The Catholics presented another petition to be sent by Anatolius to Leo, 1326 note. The Egyptian Eutychians requested a new synod, 1327. Leo refused, ibid. Certain Constantinopolitan clerics favored these heretics, 1318, 1325. Egyptian merchants spreading the Eutychian error at Rome were rejected, 372, 373.

Aetherius, a bishop of Gaul, 1111. Another Aetherius, of Smyrna, 1105.

Aetius, archdeacon of Constantinople, was deposed by Bishop Anatolius because he had been ordained a presbyter, 1186, 1188, 1190. He sent documents to Leo, which did not arrive, 1092. He was examined and cleared at the assembly in Constantinople, 1249. His ordination on Friday was rejected by Leo, 1186. Aetius was recalled through Anatolius’s favor, 1262, 1278. The pontiff commended him to Leo the Emperor, 1325. Leo entrusted certain matters to him, 1315.

The ecclesiastical discipline of Caesarea in Mauretania, Africa, was disturbed, 658. Leo entrusted a legation and apostolic authority to Bishop Potentius, who was going there, ibid. The solemnity of the Maccabees was celebrated throughout Africa, 451.

Aggarus, an African bishop, was ordained from the laity and amid a tumult, 665. Leo entrusted the investigation of his ordination to the bishops of Mauretania, reserving his decision to himself, 666.

The Alexandrian Church was founded by Saint Mark, 628, 629, 1139, 1167, 1253. Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril were its most distinguished bishops, 1139. Their teaching was praised, 1254, 1257, 1258. Dioscorus also belonged to it, 628. Timothy Salophaciolus, 1435. The care of calculating Easter was assigned to the bishop of Alexandria, 1228. Through him the date of Easter was to be announced each year to the apostolic see, 1229.

The tumult of the Alexandrian monks at the ordination of Bishop Proterius, 1192 note. Leo’s instruction to restrain them, 1254, 1257. The same tumult increased, and the Alexandrian Church was thrown into far greater disorder by massacres after Marcian’s death, 1299 note, 1300, 1302, 1303, 1304, 1310, 1324, 1327, 1342, 1347. Proterius was killed, 1299. See Proterius. Leo’s concern to suppress these disturbances, ibid. He obtained the expulsion of the usurper, 1432. Timothy, a Catholic bishop, was elected, 1435 ff.

The bishop of Albigaunum, Quintius, 1084.

Property belonging to others, which has come to us in good faith, must be returned to its owners, 1331.

The alienation of Church property is forbidden. See Ecclesiastical property.

Alypius, chief of the monks and Theodoret’s envoy to Leo, 950.

Amandus, a Gallic bishop, 1111.

Ambition in ecclesiastical affairs censured, 673.

Saint Ambrose cited by Leo, 1388. Praised in the synodical letter of Milan, 1081.

The love of God is the love of justice, 370. Earthly attractions are not easily avoided except through the love of God, 352. Direct love toward God ought neither to become proud amid prosperity nor fail amid adversity, 42. The love of God and neighbor is one, 353, 365. From love of God and neighbor arises the fullness of all justice, 337. In the martyrs, love of God shines forth more sublimely and clearly, ibid. No one is justified without love of God and neighbor, 358. See Charity.

The two loves, of God and of the world, from which all wills proceed—so different in quality as they are divided according to their authors—[Col. 1516] 352. Quesnel’s postil on this passage examined, 498. Leo’s opinion explained, 501, 502. Love of the world is incompatible with love of God, 371. A person loves himself when he loves God above himself and his neighbor according to himself, 63. The rational mind cannot exist without love, 352. Without love of the good, no one is good, 349. Love of eternal things, 97. When is it good to pray by loving? 303. The love by which the Lord redeemed us cannot be equaled by anyone’s kindness, 337.

Ananias, sent to Saint Paul, is interpreted as “sheep,” and he changed a wolf into a sheep, 446.

The basilica of Saint Anastasia, in which Saint Leo preached a sermon, 372.

Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, requested and obtained from Leo an apostolic vicariate in Illyricum, 617, 683. He was called to share in the responsibility, not in the fullness of power, 686. Abusing this authority, he used force against the metropolitan of Epirus and was therefore rebuked by Leo, 683 ff. Saint Leo congratulated him because he had not taken part in the false synod of Ephesus, and urged him to adhere to Flavian and strengthen the brethren, 929.

A fragment of the letter of Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, concerning his ordination, 953. This letter was suspect to Leo, and the reasons why, 1185, 1188. For this reason the holy pontiff delayed communicating with him, ibid. and 1005, 1009, 1012. What he demanded of him before granting him communion, 1006, 1007. He improperly claimed for himself the ordination of Maximus, bishop of Antioch, 1161, and ibid. note. He subscribed Leo’s letter to Flavian, 1030. He sent an embassy with letters to Leo, 1039. Suspicion regarding his ordination was removed by his professions of faith, 1186. He was reconciled with Leo, 1038, 1041. Indulgence was granted to him although he had been ordained by heretics, 1147. Through the emperor’s favor and the pontiff’s consent he obtained the episcopate, 1149, 1189.

Leo commended to him Basil and John, presbyters of Constantinople, who had come to Rome, accused of heresy, to give an account of their faith, 1054.

Anatolius of Constantinople subscribed the report of the Council of Chalcedon to Leo and requested confirmation of the privilege of his see, namely, primacy after the Roman see, 1103. He made the same request in private letters, 1130, 1134. He sent legates to Leo for this reason, 1126. Leo’s legates opposed this privilege, 1120, 1103, 1132, 1151. The holy pontiff likewise resisted and charged Anatolius with ambition, 1147, 1149, 1155, 1161 ff., 1171, 1197, 1199. Anatolius solicited the bishops of Illyricum to support him, 1209.
