The emperor intervened for the reconciliation of Leo and Anatolius, 1249. The conditions demanded by the pontiff, ibid., 1275. Anatolius gave satisfaction in a letter, 1261. The extent to which Leo was satisfied, 1277, 1280. Anatolius is praised and urged to eradicate the hidden remnants of heresy, 1298. He informed Leo of the disturbances in the Alexandrian Church, 1302. He demonstrated the obedience owed to the pontiff, 1262.

Anatolius of Constantinople deposed Aetius, a Catholic archdeacon, under the pretext of honoring him, ordained him a presbyter, and promoted Andrew, a deacon suspected of Eutychian heresy, to the archdeaconate, 1186, 1188, 1190. Leo rebuked him, ibid. The emperor did likewise at the pontiff’s request, 1191. Leo warned him of his obligation to investigate his own clerics, some of whom were said to connive with the Eutychians, 1318.

Andrew, a defender of Eutychian heresy, 1186. Anatolius had previously rejected him for this reason, 1186. Later he promoted him to the archdeaconate, ibid., 1190. At Leo’s command he was removed from office, 1262 note, 1278, 1280. If he condemned the Eutychian heresy, Leo ordered that he be promoted to the presbyterate, 1278. He had subscribed Leo’s letter to Flavian, 1262.

Andrew, a presbyter and envoy of Juvenal of Jerusalem to Leo, 1285.

Anemius, a Gallic bishop, 1111.

The soul is created and infused into the body at the same time, 703. The error of the Manichaeans and Priscillianists concerning its nature, 699, 702. The soul becomes more purified as the substance of the flesh is more afflicted, 314. The Christian soul must be purified especially on feast days, 153. Whoever is not afraid to lose the soul for Christ saves it, 194. Without the soul, the flesh desires nothing, 59. It belongs to the soul to restrain external things, ibid. The body ought to be subject to it, ibid., 342. Each faithful person possesses more in the soul than he admires in heaven, 96.

The Roman annals, in which the date of Easter was recorded, 1248 note, 1282.

What sort of years the Hebrews had, 609. The common and intercalary years, 601 note. What the years among the Hebrews were, 609. What they were among the Alexandrians, 601 note. Every part of the year is filled with divine mysteries, 184.

Further material on the Annunciation of the Blessed Mary, 438, 439, 440.

The Church of Antioch, in which the Christian name first arose when the blessed apostle Peter preached, 1167. In it the dignity of the Christian name arose, 324. Founded by the blessed Peter, 1213. It is placed in the third rank, 1167. The Eastern [Col. 1517] Churches assigned to it by the Nicene Fathers, 1213. Its bishops: Theodotus, 948; Maximus, 1212; Basil, 1309.

The ordination of the bishop of Antioch was carried out by the bishop of Constantinople contrary to the canons, 1153. It was nevertheless concealed, ibid.

Antiochus, one of the metropolitans of Illyricum, 677.

Antiquity must be preserved in faith and discipline, 1255.

Anysius of Thessalonica was appointed vicar in Illyricum by Siricius, 620.

The apocryphal books must not merely be prohibited but also burned, 706, 707.

The Apollinarian Games among the Romans, 25. When and how they were celebrated, 26.

The madness and error of Apollinaris, 81, 179, 373, 1238, 1357. His threefold error is distinguished, 1179 note. A spurious letter of Pope Julius, a fragment of which Eutyches appended to his letters to Leo, is attributed to Apollinaris, 743 note.

Apollonius, one of two Egyptian bishops exiled for the faith, 1336.

The apostles did not lack the Holy Spirit before the Lord’s Passion, 302. After they had been filled with the abundance of the Holy Spirit, they began to desire more ardently and to be able more effectively, 304.

The apostles’ fear at the Last Supper, 221. Through Peter, firmness of faith was conferred upon the apostles, 18. Through Peter the power of the keys passed to the apostles, ibid. See Peter.

The poverty of the apostles, 367.

The distinction between apostolic and episcopal dignity, 22.

The apostolic ordinances must be observed, 32, 34.

The authority of apostolic tradition, and how it may be recognized, 316.

On the apostles, formerly fishermen, 442. Pilgrimages to the thresholds of the apostles, ibid.

The appearances of God recorded in Scripture were effected not through angels but by God himself, 85.

Appeals to the apostolic see from Illyricum, 619, 622. From Gaul, 634. Their customary practice, ibid. From Africa, 668. From Thrace concerning Eutyches, 763, 791. From Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, 906, 915, 962, 966. From the East, concerning Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, 947.

The bishop of Aquileia to whom Leo wrote his first letter: who he was, 582. He is called metropolitan of the province of Venetia, 594. Bishops of Aquileia: Adelphus, 586; Augustine, 587; Januarius, 582 ff., 730; Maximus, 586; Nicetas, 1330.

The Pelagian heresy in the province of Aquileia, 587, 589. Leo ordered that its remnants be brought forward for examination, 587, 590, 594, 730 and note.

Archelaus, bishop of Caschara in Mesopotamia, held a public disputation with Manes, 490.

The duties of archdeacons at Constantinople, 1188.

Platforms for preaching, 94, 471.

Arles, a city of Gaul called Constantina, 995. The mother of all Gaul, 996. The bishops attached to the Church of Arles requested that Leo confirm its primacy and privileges within Gaul, 995. Its first bishop, Saint Trophimus, was sent by the blessed Peter, 994. Controversy between the Churches of Arles and Vienne concerning primacy in Gaul, 998, 999 note. Leo settled it by assigning each its own boundaries, 999. Bishops of Arles: Patroclus, see Patroclus; Hilary, see Hilary; and Ravennius, see Ravennius.

The errors of Arius, 81. The source of the Arians’ opportunity for error, 74. They are refuted, 75, 84, 299, 698. Arius was condemned at the Council of Nicaea, 1165.

The weapons of Christians, 146.

Armentarius, a bishop in Gaul, 998, 1110. Another, 1111.

Arpocrates, an Egyptian bishop exiled for the faith, 1336.

Why Christ’s Ascension was delayed until after forty days, 290, 291. It is a cause of joy for us, 294. How much the apostles gained from it, ibid. The effects of the Lord’s Ascension, 424.

Asclepias, a deacon of Constantinople and Anatolius’s envoy to Leo, 1039.

Asclepius, a Gallic bishop, 890, 998, 1110.

Asinius, bishop of Chur in Rhaetia, 1083.

Aspar, an Arian patrician. Why Saint Leo wrote to him to suppress the disturbances of the Alexandrian Eutychians, 1307, 1315.

Pastor, bishop of Asti, 1084.

Asterius, a bishop sent by Leo as legate to the East, 1007, 1010, 1012.

The superstition of astrology is refuted, 336, 695, 704. The empty science of the stars, 217. Superstitious worship, 94.

Athanasius, an Egyptian bishop exiled for the faith, 1336. The same man, or another, who consecrated Timothy Salophaciolus, 1437.

The letter of Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, to Epictetus, which Saint Cyril used at the Council of Ephesus against Nestorius, 1178. In it he also overcame Eutyches among the heretics of that period, ibid. Saint Leo sent it to be set against the Eutychians, ibid. A fragment of it was appended to the letter to Leo the Emperor, ibid. note.

Athanasius’s teaching praised, 1209, 1254, 1257. He was still alive at the time of the Paschal season of the year, 373. According to Proterius of Alexandria, 1268 note. Leo brought forward his testimony against the Eutychians, 1388.

[Col. 1518] Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, is praised, 1277.

Atticus, metropolitan of Old Epirus, went to Leo to complain of the force used against him by Anastasius of Thessalonica, 685.

Atticus, a presbyter of Constantinople infected with Eutychian heresy, was committed to Anatolius for examination, 1313. He disputed against the faith in the Church, 1327. Leo ordered that he be deposed and deprived of communion unless he condemned his error in his own voice and by subscription and publicly professed the faith of Chalcedon in the Church, 1338, 1343. He sent writings of doubtful faith, and Leo demanded from him an explicit profession, 1343. What this profession was, ibid. note.

The invasion of Attila mentioned, 1190 note.

How pernicious greed is, 232. The greedy person is an enemy of justice, 232. He deceives when he claims to be offering a benefit, 53.

The designation “authority” specifically attributed to pontifical constitutions, 711 note. The same designation also given to those constitutions by the Gallic bishops, 995 note.

Audentius, a Gallic bishop, 890, 998.

Augustalis, a Gallic bishop, 890, 998.

Euthasius, bishop of Augsburg, 1083.

Augustine of Aquileia, to whom the petition of the Pelagians was addressed, not to Pope Zosimus, 587. Saint Augustine of Hippo is set against the Eutychians by Leo, 1391. A passage of Saint Augustine transcribed, 824 note. A booklet by Leporius attributed to Augustine, 1392 note. A sermon on the Maccabees vindicated for him, 452. Likewise another sermon on the resurrection, 417.

Auspicius, a Gallic bishop, 890.

God’s help, see God.

B

Baccillus, a bishop in Sicily delegated by Pope Leo, 724.

Baptism, the principal sacrament, 716, 721. When its power was established, 722. Its twofold power, 723. What preparation formerly preceded baptism, 723, 1429. The covenant, profession, and renunciation in baptism, 257. The recitation of the Creed in it, 1242. In certain Churches, the first chapter of the Gospel of Saint John was read to the neophytes, 418.

The effects of baptism, 66, 93. In baptism, people are regenerated by the same Spirit by whom Christ was begotten, 218. The imitation of Christ’s death and resurrection, 246, 274. Justification is not repaid according to merits but is granted solely by the generosity of grace, 186.

The water of baptism is like the Virgin’s womb, 80. By washing, it removes sin, ibid., but not bigamy, 618. Triple immersion in baptism, 274, 719. The distinction between John’s baptism and Christ’s baptism, 722. There is no distinction in the sacrament of baptism, 703. The body of the regenerated person becomes the flesh of the crucified one, 246.

Baptism was solemnly celebrated in Sicily on the day of the Epiphany, 716. It is to be celebrated at Easter, 718, and at Pentecost, 719, following apostolic example, 720. It was administered on Easter night, 418, 610. Leo forbade its celebration on the Epiphany, 716. On the feast of martyrs, 1429. In cases of necessity, baptism is to be administered at any time, 721, 1430.

The great number of those baptized, of every age and from every kind of human society, 186.

What should be done when it is uncertain whether baptism has been administered, 1407, 1427. What should be done when it is unknown by members of which faith it was administered, 1428. What should be done when it is certain that it was administered by heretics, 1334, 1408. How serious a crime its repetition is, 1407. Those infected with this crime were not admitted to the clergy, 731, but were subjected to public penance, 730 note, 1334 note. What is to be said of those rebaptized through error or fear, 1332.

Baptism administered by the Priscillianists with oil alone, 713, 714.

The Basilica of Saint Peter was dedicated to God alone, 94. It faced the setting sun from its entrance, 95 note. Its staircase provided access to the upper platform by thirty-five steps, 475. These steps were divided into five groups, ibid. The steps were ascended on bended knees as an act of devotion, ibid.

The Basilica of Saint Anastasia at Rome, 1032.

The Basilica of the Apostles at Constantinople, 1032.

Basilides, a heretic, 49.

Basil, bishop of Antioch, 372. Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, cited by Leo against the Eutychians, 1395. Basil, a deacon sent to Leo by Julian, bishop of Cos, 875. Basil, a presbyter of Constantinople, fled to Rome with John to give an account of his faith, 1054. Basil, a presbyter, was sent by Leo with three others as legate to Theodosius, 1007, 1010, 1012. He was sent as legate to Constantinople with Lucentius, 1046, 1048, 1052. Likewise to the Council of Chalcedon, 1065, 1069.

The seven Beatitudes explained by Leo, 366 note. Their order varies, 369 note. Blessedness is promised not to the idle but to those who labor, 130. See Heavenly glory.

[Col. 1519] The sacrament of blessing, 629.

The mysteries of priestly blessings, 630.

Benedict XIV, the author and patron of this edition, in the dedicatory letter. He is praised there and at 467.

It is ungrateful to remain silent about God’s benefits, 7. What disposition should be formed from them, 8. How harmful the devil’s benefits are, 276. How much contemplation of God’s benefits profits, 259. See Gifts.

Dorus, bishop of Benevento, 732.

Praestantius, bishop of Bergamo, 1084.

Bigamists are not to be ordained, 614, 618, 621, 636, 671, 687. Leo does not dispense from this rule, even in necessity, 674.

Church property must not be alienated, 728. Leo asks the emperor that judgment concerning the property of the Church of Constantinople belong not to public but to ecclesiastical judges, 1283. The contrary would be an innovation, ibid.

Boniface, a presbyter of the Roman Church and legate to the Council of Chalcedon, 1065, 1066, 1067, 1069, 1098, 1131.

We have been entrusted not so much with possession of temporal goods as with their distribution, 34. Their use, 60. They are provisions for the journey, not the enticements of a dwelling place, 352. One may not rejoice immoderately in the increase of temporal goods, 153. No good person is good for himself alone, 338. Without love of the good, no one is good, 349. Why the good are hated by the wicked, 178.

A brief statement of the faith sent by Julian of Cos to Leo, 1192.

Optatianus, bishop of Brescia, 1084.

Cyprianus, bishop of Brixia, 1082.

The age of the Bucherian list and its author are established, 496.

C
Caiaphas, when he tore his garment, deprived himself of priestly honor, 211. Observance of the canons is a bond of peace, 1155, 1217. Ignorance of the canons in priests is not to be tolerated, 614. The statutes of the canons must be observed, 667, 1280. Leo dispenses with those ordained contrary to the canons, 664, 665. He does not dispense with bigamists, 664. See Dispensation. What reverence for the canons exists at the Apostolic See, 1197. See the Council of Nicaea.

Singing in churches, 434. Singing of psalms, 11. Throughout the universal Church, 21, 33, 353 n. The flesh must continually be chastised, 320. Whence the spirit’s victory over the flesh, ibid. The conflict of flesh with spirit, 351. See Soul.

Carosus, one of the metropolitan bishops of Illyricum, 677. Leo asks Marcian that the monk Carosus, who was overthrowing many people, be restrained, 1281. Who he was, 1297 n. Expelled from his monastery, ibid. Carosus, distinguished from the preceding man, corrected in his confession of faith, but withdrawing from Anatolius’s communion because of their hostility, 1296. See 1295 n.; 1298 n.

Cassian dedicates his books On the Incarnation of Christ to Leo, then a deacon of the Roman Church, in the Testimonies.

Casterius, a priest and legate of Anatolius of Constantinople to Leo, 1039.

Commendation of chastity, 211. See Continence.

The catalogue of the Roman pontiffs edited by Bucherius: by whom it was written, 496. How highly the order of bishops displayed in ancient catalogues is to be valued, 1403. Why the same judgment should not be made concerning the deeds, and especially the dates, recorded in those catalogues, ibid.

The discipline of the catechumenate, 723. See Baptism.

The Chair of Saint Peter. Its solemnity was instituted because of the pontificate received by Peter, 435. Concerning this feast, 431, 498. The chair of ecclesiastical primacy was divinely handed over to Peter in such a way that it is founded upon perpetual stability, 436. See Peter. Two kinds of chairs, good and evil, 436. Who sit in the chair of pestilence, ibid. Christ overturned those same chairs of pestilence, ibid.

More serious or major cases, and appeals in Illyricum, reserved to the Apostolic See, 619, 622. Cases of the bishops of Illyricum that cannot be settled in their own provinces are to be referred to the bishop of Thessalonica, the apostolic vicar, so that he may settle the dispute, 678. In more difficult cases judgment is to be suspended and the pontiff’s decision awaited, 683. If these cases cannot be settled by the bishop of Thessalonica, they are to be referred to the Roman pontiff, 689. The same is to be done if the bishops’ opinions are divided in council, 690.

The case of Bishop Celidonius, brought by appeal before Saint Leo against Hilary of Arles, and his acquittal, 635 n.

Ceponius, a Spanish bishop, 711, 1475.

The error of Cerdo, 699.

Ceretius, a bishop in Gaul, 1003. He communicates Leo’s letter to Flavian to Eusebius, bishop of Milan, 1081.

The Council of Chalcedon. In announcing it, the emperor Marcian sought Leo’s authority and agreement, 1019, 1025. It was assembled at the command of the Christian rulers and with the consent of the Apostolic See, 1197; likewise through the Holy Spirit, 1301; solely on account of the matter of the faith, 1163, 1217. Pope Leo presided over it in his legates as the head over the members, 1090, 1100, 1140, 1141. The emperor Marcian, and also the empress Pulcheria, attended its sixth session, 1127 n. It was compelled to have all the bishops declare what Leo had defined, 1025 n. Leo did not wish what had been defined to be debated as though it were a doubtful matter, 1064, 1071. To what extent examination of Leo’s letter to Flavian was free, while the authority of the Apostolic See remained intact, 1220 n. It was necessary that the understanding of all the Fathers should agree with Leo’s faith, 1126 n. Leo ordered that provision be made for and that those bishops who had not accepted the heresy, but had been driven into exile, be restored, 1071. The council’s agreement in establishing the faith, 1138. After many struggles, the true faith triumphed, 1113. The definition of faith, issued under the guidance of the Holy Spirit for the salvation of the whole world, 1300. The same definition, subscribed by the Fathers, was placed upon the altar of Saint Euphemia and thereafter handed over, in the presence and at the request of the emperors, 1128, 1129. A summary of the proceedings, described by Anatolius, 1126 ff. The proceedings were sent to the pontiff, 1087. Certain parts were reviewed by Leo, 1125. What was established concerning the see of Constantinople, 1095, 1118, 1129. The contradiction of the legates, 1097, 1120, 1132, 1151, 1163. The entire force and confirmation of these proceedings, as Anatolius himself acknowledged, was reserved to Leo’s authority, 1263. This confirmation, or the pontiff’s assent, was required as entirely free by the Fathers, 1197, 1099; by the emperor, 1113, 1120; by Anatolius, 1126 n., 1134. Since for some people the council’s definition itself might be doubtful, an express papal confirmation was requested as necessary, 1182. Leo approved this definition in special letters, together with everything pertaining to the faith, 1195. The authority of the Apostolic See confirmed it, 1343. This confirmation by the pontiff was to be published throughout all the churches, 1182, 1201. The Chalcedonian canon concerning the see of Constantinople was rejected by Leo, 1151, 1155, 1163, 1172, etc. If anything was done apart from the matter of the faith with the assent of Leo’s legates, it was revoked, since they had been directed by the Holy Pontiff solely to the matter of the faith and had not obtained his assent, 1217. Nothing is to be revoked in the definitions of this council concerning the matter of the faith, 1301, 1304, 1306, 1310, 1222, 1338, 2340. To what extent a new examination was instituted under the emperor Leo without prejudice to the authority of the Council of Chalcedon, 1221 n. Saint Leo wished the acts of this council to be collected and rendered into Latin by Julian, 1194. The number of Fathers at this synod, 1100, 1137. See 1089 n. The synod’s report to Leo, with the more extensive subscriptions of the Fathers, 1099. Its definition was accepted by everyone, 1147. Nothing is to be added to or taken away from it, 1301, 1311. The proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon, in Greek and Latin, now published for the first time, 1491.

Charity, the highest of the virtues, 183. It has no limit, ibid. Through charity a human being is distinguished from beasts, 62, 63. Nothing is more effective against the devil, 296. Charity is the mother of all virtues, 142. It extends even to unbelievers and enemies, 73, 129, 142, 155. It makes everything common, 181. Without charity the other virtues contribute nothing to salvation, 182, 296, 317. The connection of charity and faith, such that wherever they are together, they are absent together, 171. In what respect, or in what sense, Saint Leo wrote this is explained, 482. Faith can exist without charity, 31. All the commandments are reduced to faith and charity, 172. Without charity no one is a child of God, 188. Those who find something of the fruits of charity stored within their consciences should not doubt that God dwells in them, 183. Charity toward God and neighbor is the virtue and wisdom of Christian faith, 170. It is the first rule of morals, 60. Charity gives life to faith and the other virtues and makes them useful, 36. Works are weighed on the scales of charity, 32. Charity itself is charity’s greatest reward, 359. All affections must be directed by love of God and neighbor, and according to what rule, 60. The model for loving one’s neighbor is to be taken from the love with which God loves us, 63. God is to be loved with the whole heart, etc., 40, 89. When one’s neighbor is loved, God is loved, 365. In love of God nothing is excessive; in love of the world everything is harmful, 352. To love God is nothing other than to love justice, 370. See Love of God.

The sanctification of chrism, 256, 1324. The sacrament: chrism is the chrism of salvation and the seal of eternal life, 81. Chrism is sanctified by the bishop on Holy Thursday of Holy Week; its sanctification ceased at Alexandria after the killing of Saint Proterius, 1324.

In what sense a Christian is a king and a priest, 15. Whence the dignity of a Christian comes, 90, 203. Christians are members of Christ, 77. All are one body, 155. One Christ, head and members, 244. How they are joined to God, 90. They are God’s fellow workers, ibid. [Col. 1521] Heirs of heavenly glory, ibid., 266. Reborn for future things, 97. They are not Christians unless they imitate Christ, 87. Crucified in Christ’s crucifixion, raised in his resurrection, placed at the Father’s right hand in his ascension, born together with him in his nativity, 88, 286. The weapons of Christians, 146. They have undertaken the warfare of a great name, 203. The life of Christians must correspond to their profession, 257. It is a perpetual cross, 173. What use do heretics make of the Christian name? 1238. One cannot be called a Christian who deviates from the faith, 1242. The delights of Christians, 151, 191. Their desires should tend toward eternal things, 283. What their discipline is, 137, 138. Their principal duties, 87. Certain Christians who turned toward the East when praying were reproved, and why, 94 n. Christians ought to advance from day to day, 148, 168, 190, 229. Compare the observations on this passage, 481. See Christian justice. What Christian liberty is, 348. Christians are reborn into the family of liberty, 203. Some Christians are just, others penitents, and catechumens, as Leo mentions, 170. Christians adopted in place of the Jews, 210. Among Christians, communion in Christ’s name must be an inseparable union with Christ, 285. In what manner they die and rise again with Christ, 246. How few are truly Christians, and why, 185. Few are chosen, ibid. The early Christians rejoiced in possessing nothing of the world and possessing everything with Christ, 268.

The Incarnation of Christ, decreed and necessary for the salvation of humanity, 65, 70, 75, 79, 86, 88, 92, 98, 136, 141, 176, 198, 199, 274, 310, 807, 855, 979, 1375, 1435. If Adam had not sinned, the Word would not have become incarnate, 309. The Incarnation was foretold from the beginning of the world, 67, 76, 248, 980, and promised, 78, 244, 248. The promised time of the Incarnation, 118. Why the Incarnation and redemption were delayed, ibid. and 76, 268. The devil did not know of it, 59. Why, ibid. and 239. The Incarnation is ineffable, 73, 102, 106. It was always believed even by the Fathers of the Old Testament, 76, 1377. They held the same faith as in the New Testament, 204, 244. They believed that what we now believe to have been accomplished would take place, 76, 204, 256, 268. What faith in it accomplishes, 123. It benefited few under the old law, innumerable people under the new, 78. The faith of the Incarnation is proved and explained, 64, 68, 73, 75, 80, 84, 92, 98, 100, 107 ff., 175, 176, 179, 193, 204, 251, 803 ff., 854, 863, 879, 977, 1021, 1058, 1138, 1237 ff., 1289, 1395 ff. How the Word became flesh in the Incarnation, 92. He emptied himself, 75, 84. He descended to earth, ibid., 978. In what sense this is called a sending, 85. The mystery of equity, 64. How excellent it is, 108. Unique, 109. It surpasses all miracles, 76, 79. The Incarnation is both sacrament and example, 86. Its fruits and effects, 66, 71, 75, 84, 93, 110, 407. It benefited even the ancients, 199, 204, 256, 268. Why God provided for human salvation by this way, 67, 69, 78, 98. The Incarnation of the Word could not take place except in a virgin, 64, 69. Why the Son of God, rather than another, became incarnate, 248. Who can attain to an understanding of the Incarnation, 1235. When this mystery is considered, one must follow not reason but faith, 92. God’s wisdom alone, not that of the world, is to be considered, 85, 86. For Christians it is a means of illumination; for heretics, of blindness, 99. What is to be believed concerning the incarnate Christ, 176. Errors concerning the Incarnation, 74, 99, 107, 179, 356, 373, 1179, 1237, 1359. In the Incarnation a complete human being was assumed, 705. Christ’s body was not formed earlier and then assumed by the Word, 98. The new order of the Incarnation, 68. Without the pollution of earthly seed, 80, 85, 86, 89, 93. Without sin, 64, 70, 76, 86, 98, 225, 249, 310, 813, 817, 1239. Christ’s coming is proved against the Jews, 104.

Christ’s Nativity. He was born for all and as the cause of joy, 64, 97. Born of a Virgin, and why, 60, 70. A man without a father, 98. Why in Bethlehem, 112. Born in an inn, 1289. Christ became our flesh by being born, and we become his body by being reborn, 77, 245. Christ’s generation is the origin of the Christian people, 88. It surpasses all generations, 108. The condition of servitude was accepted by Christ as an act of pious purpose, 175. Why circumcision and the offering in the temple were fulfilled in him, 722. His infancy is God’s glory, 105. It is to be honored, ibid.; adored, 122. The virtues of the infant are to be imitated, 114, 138. The adoration of the three Magi, 113, 115, 119, 122, 128, 133, 136, 1289. See Magi. Why he fled into Egypt, 115, 120. Why he received baptism, 722. Why he permitted himself to be tempted, 145, 158, 159. The order of the temptation explained, 159. By what weapons it was overcome, 145. Why he refused to turn stones into bread, 150. The reason why this should make us fearful and render us more cautious, 154. He proved both natures, 150. Christ did not reveal himself as God to the devil, 159. The Transfiguration demonstrated true divinity and humanity in Christ, 193. Why it took place together with the disciples, 194. In it Moses and Elijah signified the Law and the Prophets, 195. The pages of both covenants bear witness to Christ, ibid. His preaching, 366. Why he performed miracles, ibid.

He celebrates Passover on Thursday, the fourteenth day of the moon, 1266. At that time he instituted the sacrament of his body and blood, when the plot for his death was being made, 220. The Passion was not punishment of the Word but of the flesh, 253. [Col. 1522] Whoever believes that Christ became incarnate truly believes that he suffered, 248. Figures of Christ’s Passion, 231. Fulfilled in his death, 204. Betrayed by Judas, 199, 202, 205, 220. Why he was afraid, 205. Concerning his prayer, 213. Why he prayed, 223, 224. Arrested by the Jews, 199. Brought before Pilate, 216, 225. Falsely accused, 234. Condemned, 226. The crime of the Jews and Pilate compared, ibid. Why he carried his own cross, 226, 227. What the transfer of the cross to Simon of Cyrene signifies, 227. Why Christ did not want the women to weep, 235. Why he was crucified outside, and beyond Jerusalem, 227. The crucifixion of Christ is a great mystery, ibid. A new and true sacrifice, 266, 1363. The divinity that was in the suffering Christ was not itself in the suffering, 264. Why Christ was abandoned by the Father, and in what manner, 263. He in a certain sense abandoned himself, 265. Why he cried out on the cross, ibid. His utterances were not complaints but teachings, ibid. During the Passion the severity of the laws was relaxed, 152, 485. Its history is read in the Church, 198, 207, 212, 255, 272. Participation in it makes certain the expectation of blessedness, 177. Christ’s Passion is prolonged to the end of the world, because he himself suffers in his saints who endure adversity for the sake of justice, 275. Concerning Christ’s words “It is finished,” 210. Prayer on the cross for those crucifying him, and the disposition from which many were converted, 240, 1347. There is no one for whom Christ’s prayer is not helpful, 257. On the cross he drew everything to himself, 216, 228. Christ’s Passion is more rightly a cause for rejoicing than for sorrow, 231. Christ reigned from the wood, as had been foretold, 209. What he did on the Cross, 202. See the Cross of Christ.

In Christ’s Passion the work of both natures is present, 199, 200. Christ’s death occurred on Friday, the fifteenth day of the moon, 1266. Why he died at Passover, 218. Christ and the Jews sought the same death for different ends, 273. The mystery of Christ’s death, 266. Christ died for all, 200, 205, 208, 225, 257. Especially for the wicked, 229. Even for those who killed him, Christ’s death would have been beneficial if they had believed, 205. Even for Judas, if he had not hastened to the noose, 247. The power of Christ’s death, 270. Its twofold fruit, 262. Through Christ’s death the transfer from the synagogue to the Church, and from many sacrifices to one victim, became evident, 266. Why the veil of the temple was torn, ibid. and 237. Miracles at Christ’s death, 202. Why Christ is called the firstfruits of those who sleep, 254. In death the divinity abandoned neither his soul nor his body, 282. Christ’s death liberates the faithful and accuses the Jews, 201. His burial was called into question in Spain, at which Leo expressed his amazement, 709. His days were shortened for the sake of the disciples, 282. His descent into hell, 86, 419, 709, 1266. Neither Christ’s soul remained long in hell nor his flesh in the tomb, 282. The Resurrection took place on the evening of the Sabbath at the dawning of Sunday, on the seventeenth day of the moon, 1266. It was proved by many arguments, 282, 283. What transformation took place in Christ’s flesh through the Resurrection, 283. In Christ’s Resurrection the form of the transformation of our flesh preceded, ibid. Why the disciples’ hesitation concerning the Lord’s Resurrection was permitted, 290. We must rise again with Christ, 282. We die and rise together with Christ when we believe in God and renounce the devil, 216. Why on the night of the Lord’s Resurrection the first chapter of the Gospel of Saint John was read in some places, 417. Why he preserved the marks of the nails and the lance, 291. Why he did not wish to be touched by Magdalene, 295. The soldiers guarding the tomb were witnesses of the Resurrection, 422.

Why Christ’s Ascension into heaven was delayed until after forty days, 290, 293. What Christ did during this interval, 291. How greatly the Ascension strengthened the Apostles, 291, 294. We should rejoice on this feast, 293. Our ascension is an advancement, and its benefit, 290, 292, 293, 294. In the Ascension Christ did not abandon us, 287. He began to be more present in divinity when he became more distant in divinity, 294. Christ’s greater miracle was to rise with his body and raise earth into heaven, 423.

Why the order of Christ’s genealogies differs in Matthew and Luke, 111, 854. Two natures in Christ and one person, 65, 70, 92, 99, 101, 124, 150, 175, 179, 193, 204, 252, 274, 811, 1241, 1371. God without a mother, man without a father, 98. Consubstantial with the Mother and the Father, 110. Christ’s flesh and soul are like ours, 883. Why the divine and human substance had to come together, 212, 271. See above, “The necessity of the Incarnation.” The properties of both natures considered, 109, 175, 176, 250, 258, 264, 274, 374, 815, 1305, 1373. The union of both is inseparable, 110. The operations of both natures are distinct, but not the persons, 204, 819. In Christ there are two wills and two affections, 213. True and not feigned human actions, 222. All Christ’s mysteries prove that he possessed true flesh, 253, 254. The truth of his flesh proved from the Scriptures, 823. Christ assumed all infirmities that arise from sin, without sharing in sin, 245. Christ’s priesthood is eternal, 21. Christ is the new and true sacrifice, 227. His final coming: why a multitude of angels will be present then, 295. Christ is the true patriarch of all nations, 246. In what sense he is the way, the truth, and the life, 285. No one has ever received salvation except through Christ, 111, 199. This was so even in the Old Testament, ibid. Christ bestowed more upon us than the devil took away, 202. [Col. 1523] He stripped the devil of his power, 71. In what sense he is less than the Father, 75, 85, 92. Christ’s life is the law of living, 136.

Chrysaphius, a Gallic bishop, 890, 1111.

The nature of all foods is good; with the Manichaeans, no foods are to be condemned. It is excess, not nature, that is vicious, 160. Abstinence and discrimination moderate the use of foods; they do not condemn their nature, ibid.

The Romans, devoted to the circus games, were reproved by Leo, 336.

The keys of Saint Peter, 17, 18. The power of the keys opens the gates of mercy, 186.

Clergy. Who ought not to be admitted into the clergy, 612 ff. See Ordination, where impediments are discussed. They cannot abandon their own church, 593. No one should receive another’s cleric against the will of his bishop, 689. The bishop’s permission must be given in writing, 679. Clerics returning from heresy or schism were, in what circumstances, received back into their rank through indulgence and dispensation, 575. But they were not promoted to a higher rank, 577. In receiving them, the laying on of hands was not used unless they had been rebaptized, and why, 1334 n. They were not subjected to public penance but to private penance, 1421. Ignorance in clerics is not to be tolerated, 976. Priority of ordination within the same rank assigned the earlier place; those who, because of a later ordination, yielded their place to others were reproved, 735. Usury was especially forbidden to clerics, since it is illicit even among laypeople, 615. Clerics ought to shrink from bloodshed, 1211. Clerical continence, 687, 688. See Continence.

Manuscript codices to be used in editions, Preface n. 4. How important it is to distinguish and identify codices of different origins, 513. Which such codices were used in recovering Leo’s sermons, Quesnellian Preface. How many codices of different origins were examined in the edition of the letters, 514 ff. Greek codices useful for this edition, and what peculiar features they contain, 557.

The celestial bodies serve human utility, 95, 96. The heavenly kingdom. See Heavenly glory.

Collects, concerning which Saint Leo delivered several sermons: from what they originated, 23. In which month they occurred and on how many days they were held, ibid. For what purpose they were used, ibid. They were to be brought to the city’s deaconal churches, 38 n.

Collections, partly published and partly unpublished, of diverse origin, containing Leo’s letters, reviewed in this edition, 513 ff.

I. The Vatican–Queen of Sweden collection, 514.  
II. The Corbie collection, ibid.  
III. The Barberini and Vatican collection, 515.  
IV. The Lucca and Colbert collection, ibid.  
V. The Quesnellian collection, ibid. The excellence of the five preceding collections, 518.  
VI. The Dionysian collection, 519. The Cresconian collection agrees with it and was taken from Dionysius, ibid.  
VII. The Hadrianic collection, which added something to Dionysius, ibid.  
VIII. Later, more extensive additions to Dionysius, 521.  
IX. The Hispanic collection, ibid. Two kinds of manuscripts in this collection must be distinguished: one purely Hispanic, the other copied in Gaul from a Hispanic codex. The first was found in the Vindobonensis codex, the second in the Vatican. In the former many corrupt readings were found, but readings that came closer to the genuine text; in the latter, the errors of the purer Hispanic codex were emended more freely, but according to the copyist’s judgment, and thus readings departed from the genuine text, 523. Several examples of this matter are given, 696 n., 701 n., 702 n., 703 n., 709 n., 775 n., 918 n., 922 n., 983 n., 1005 n., 1045 n., 1046 n., 1051 n., 1064 nn., 1065 n., 1072 n., 1074 n., 1165 n., 1166 n., 1174 nn., 1176 n., 1200 n., 1201 n., 1258 n., 1259 n., 1275 nn., 1276 n., 1359 n., 1365 n., 1366 n., 1369 n., 1381 n., 1405 n., 1407 nn., 1416 n., 1418 n., 1429 n., 1444.  
X. The Isidorian collection, which was taken in Leo’s letters from the Hispanic collection of Gallican origin, 525. It is not the same as the collection published by Merlin, ibid.  
XI. The Vatican–Ottobonian collection, fuller than Isidore’s collection, ibid.  
XII. The Merlinian collection, 527. The Sichardian collection, 531.  
XIII. The Florentine collection of Saint Mark’s, 531.  
XIV. The Avellana collection, 533.  
XV. The Arelatensian collection, ibid.  
XVI. The Thessalonican collection, 535.  
XVII. The Chalcedonian collection, 537. In the Greek text it is the oldest of all, and its date is established, 539. Noteworthy features of its Latin text, 541.  
XVIII. The Grimanic collection, 543. Its prerogatives, 546.  
XIX. The Regensburg collection, and its antiquity and excellence, 547. It seems to be the collection that Pope Vigilius sent to the emperor Justinian, ibid.  
XX. The Roman collection of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, 549.  
XXI. A collection of fifty-six letters of Saint Leo, of an origin different from Collection XI, 551.  
XXII. The Venetian collection of Saint Mark’s, ibid.  
XXIII. Another Vatican–Ottobonian collection, 553.  
XXIV. A collection of seventy-one letters, ibid.

Comensis, Bishop Abundantius, who is the same as Abundius, 1083 n.

How the communion of good works takes place, 346. Communion under both kinds, and why, 161. The communion of the sacraments is to be granted by priests to penitents through the door of reconciliation, 1174. Paschal communion, 189. [Col. 1524] The Manichaeans avoided communion of the blood, and why, 161. The Roman and Eastern Paschal calculations differ, 1282. See Passover.

The usefulness of provincial councils, 622, 689, 724. They are to be attended frequently, and what is to be done in them, ibid. The Holy Spirit is present at them as well, 679. It is not lawful to be absent from them without legitimate cause, ibid. A council was held at Rome every year on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, 724. On the day of Saint Leo’s ordination, 6, 9. Yet no law compelled this, 22 n. What harms result from the interruption of councils, 713. A sentence passed against a heretic cannot be relaxed by anyone unless he repents, 856. Which council is truly a general council, 1060, 1065 n. What its proper work is, 1157. The pontiff’s assent was required in its convocation, 1019, 1025, 1197. Its presidency was exercised through legates, 1062 n., 1090, 1100. Its confirmation was required; see Chalcedon.

A council of the province of Aquileia against the Pelagians was ordered by Leo, 590. Chalcedon: see Chalcedon. Constantinople against Eutyches, 739, 740, 756. Another at which Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian was read and received, 1487. Constantinople under Theodosius, 1096, 1113, 1130. Its presidents, 1130 n. Its canons were neither sent to nor received by the Apostolic See, 1165. The First Council of Ephesus is praised, 1064, 1073, 1215. At it Juvenal’s ambition for primacy over Palestine is mentioned, ibid. and n. Saint Cyril presided, 742. In what sense he presided, 1073 n. The Ephesian council that turned into a bandit council: see Ephesus II. A Gallican council, from which a synodical letter was sent to Leo, 1107. The Milanese council, from which another synodical letter was sent, 1080. The First Council of Nicaea against Arius, 1323. A Roman council against the Manichaeans, 50 n., 624, 626, 708. Another concerning the case of Hilary of Arles, 635. Another at which Leo took precautions concerning the affairs of the Church of Palermo, 728. Another against the Ephesian bandit council, 909, 919, 937, 938. Another held on the sacred day of Saint Peter, 962. What day and year this was, 959. Another concerning a certain question about baptism, 1406. Saint Leo requested from Theodosius a council within Italy, after the Ephesian bandit council, as a remedy for the scandals, 906, 915, 923, 957; Valentinian requested it, 964; Placidia, 966; Eudoxia, 970.

The office of preaching belongs exclusively to priests, 1217, 1227. Not to laypeople or monks, ibid., 1211. It is owed by bishops and must not be abandoned, 118, 140, 218, 238, 1287. The custom of episcopal preaching in the Roman Church, 285.

Whether a concubine is a spouse, and what kind of spouse, 1422, 1423.

Concupiscence. See Desires. Many good desires exist in human souls, 361. Who are understood to be bound by the original condition, 613 n.

Confession, and accusation within it, 90, 1174. It frees one from judgment, 190. It is made only to priests and is secret, 1431. Certain pastors who prescribed public disclosure of sins among the works of penance were reproved, 1430 n. Priests impose the act of penance, and penitents, cleansed through the door of reconciliation, are admitted to communion of the sacraments, 1174. Absolution is conferred through the prayers of the priest, ibid., 1431; through the prayers of the Church, 1435. See Reconciliation. Unless confession is true, it does not obtain the abolition of sin, 1062. The crowns of confessors, 1317. The glory of confession, 1377.

The sacrament of confirmation: chrism is the chrism of salvation and the seal of eternal life, 81.

How the conscience is to be examined, 146, 153, 165, 183, 455. Whatever stains the secret conscience must be removed by the most diligent cleansings, 190. The conscience must take delight in good deeds, so that one willingly does what one rejoices to have done, 353.

Those who had been baptized were called the consecrated, 610, 611. Consecrated virgins, 1426. The consecration of a bishop, priest, and deacon, 622.

Constantianus, a Gallic bishop, 1107, 1110, 1136.

The Council of Constantinople: see Council.

Bishops of Constantinople: John Chrysostom, Atticus, Proclus, 1277. Flavian: see Flavian. Anatolius: see Anatolius. Gennadius: see Gennadius.

The city of Constantinople, being an imperial city, cannot become an Apostolic See, 1149. The clergy of Constantinople favored the Eutychians under the emperor Leo, 1318, 1325.

Constantine, a Gallic bishop, 890, 998. Constantine, the first Christian emperor to shine with imperial splendor, 96.

Constantius, a Gallic bishop, 998, 1107, 1110, 1136.

The constitutions of Innocent and of Leo’s predecessors must be observed; those who violate them deserve a particular penalty, 616. The constitutions of the Roman pontiffs are called authoritative enactments, 711 n., 733. This was also said by the Gallic bishops, 995 n. They were also called apostolic decrees, 663 and 665 n.

The law of continence is twofold, of spirit and of body, 355, 363. Praise of continence, 190. It is the mother of virtues, 191. Nothing pertains more properly to the virtue of continence than abstaining from errors, [Col. 1525] 317. Clerical continence, 687, 688. The law of continence imposed upon bishops, priests, and deacons, and what is to be said concerning those who were married before ordination, 1421. It was also prescribed for subdeacons, 687.

Conversion must not be delayed, 1176. How uncertain it is when delayed, ibid.

The quality of human hearts is revealed by their works, 135. In what ways the field of the heart is cultivated and made fertile, 44, 57, 58. The eye of the heart must be cleansed so that God may be seen, 371.

Moral correction is a gift of God, 144. Correction of one’s neighbor is always to be desired, 172, 182. No one is to be despaired of as long as he lives, 1423. Correction is to be omitted when there is no hope, 1209. It must also be undertaken against the perversely impious, 1180. How Christ corrected Judas, 220. Love must be preserved in correction, 684. Correction is to be administered differently according to the differences among persons, ibid. Whoever does not recall others from error through correction demonstrates that he himself is in error, 707. Those for whom correction is of no benefit should not be spared excision, 1318. The moderation of the Apostolic See observes this restraint: it acts more severely with the hardened and desires to grant pardon to those who have been corrected, 849. How greatly prelates are obliged to correct, 1318. How blameworthy their sluggish indulgence is, 1319.

The preaching of creatures is the glory of God, 59. No nature among creatures is evil, 700. How creatures are to be used, 96. A creature is mutable even when it is not changing, 705.

Cremonensis, Bishop John, 1084.

Crispinus, Bishop of Ticinum, 1082.

The Cross of Christ, the sacrament of the true altar, 209. The cause of our hope, 212. The mystery of the Cross, 227. Sacrament and example, 285. Prefigured in ancient times, 204. It is not to be considered shameful, 197, 199. The sign of the Cross is to be borne on the forehead, 1243. How great the Cross’s efficacy is, 228. Its effects, 257. It is the weapon of Christians fighting against the world, 287. The Cross is never absent from the godly, 173. What it means to carry the cross, 288. The cross that the wickedness of the Jews prepared as a punishment was made, by the Redeemer’s power, a step for us toward glory, 208. The Cross is glory for some and punishment for others, 231. The victory of the Cross is denied to no one, 257. In temptation one must have recourse to the Cross, 275. The Cross at Jerusalem in Leo’s time, 1289. Whether Juvenal sent a fragment of the Cross to Leo, 1293 n.

What true worship of God is, 89. Desires serve the devil, 296.

Curiensis, Bishop Asinius in First Rhaetia, 1083.

The nineteen-year cycle of the Alexandrians: which years it counted as embolismic and which as common, 601, 609. Whether the Fathers of Nicaea approved this cycle, 604 n. Its division into the eight-year and eleven-year periods, 608 n. The Latin cycle of eighty-four years, 608 n. In what year it began, ibid. Leo praised the Roman Paschal cycles, 1090. They lasted eighty-four years, but the ancients inserted the lunar correction every twelve years, while later computists did so every fourteen years, ibid. n., 1230 n. Prosper introduced a correction, 602 n., 1055.

Cyprianus, bishop of the Church of Brixilliana, 1082.

Cyriacus, Bishop of Lodi, 1083. He was sent to Leo by the Milanese synod, 1081.

Saint Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, presided over the First Council of Ephesus, 1073. He acted in the place of Pope Celestine, ibid. n. Cyril’s letter preserved in the archive of the Roman Church, 1006, 1216. He wrote to Leo, then a deacon of the Roman Church, concerning Juvenal of Jerusalem’s ambition for primacy over Palestine, 1216. Two of his letters were praised by Saint Flavian, 754. Why, ibid. n. Cyril’s letter to Nestorius was presented to the Gauls by Leo, 1001. Why, ibid. n. His teaching is praised, 1006, 1010, 1139, 1254, 1257, 1258. He wrote to Leo concerning the Passover of the year 444, as Paschasinus testifies, 608 n. A fragment of this letter, 601. That it was addressed to Pope Leo and speaks of the Passover of the year 444 is demonstrated, 595, 599. Testimonies excerpted by Leo from his works, 1396.

## D
### D

Dacianus, persecutor of Saint Vincent the martyr, 248. Daniel, Egyptian bishop and consecrator of Timothy Salophaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, 1437. Daniel the presbyter, sent to Leo concerning the ordination of Timothy Salophaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, 1436, 1437. King David lived a thousand years and more before Christ, 260. How he suffered in Christ, and how Christ was crucified in the flesh in David, ibid. David, African bishop, sent back by Leo with letters, 666. The dedication of a church is called the church’s “birthday” and is celebrated as a feast, 453. Quintus, bishop of Dertona, 1082. Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, who later became Victor III, 473.

God is supremely perfect, 700. All-knowing, 165. [Col. 1526] His description, 67. In God’s justice and mercy, 40. His justice ought not to displease us, 41. God’s foreknowledge, 260. By foreknowing what is to be done, God does not compel it to happen, 261. In God there is an unchangeable order of things, 260. His nature is ineffable, 299. God’s face—that is, his divinity—cannot be seen by bodily eyes; his posterior parts, or humanity, just as it was visible in the world, is likewise visible in heaven, 453. God’s will can be learned even from the elements themselves, 57, 59, 355. Why God is the Father of the faithful, 89. Thanks are to be given to God for everything, 48. Not so much in abundance as in barrenness, 41. What should be offered to him, 90. The true worship of God, 89. How God is to be worshiped, 60. He alone is to be adored, 72. He is honored in the saints, 275. His honor must not be mingled with the rites of unbelievers, 95. God’s grace and will must be served, 90. God is to be imitated, ibid., 171, 370. God loved us first, 39. He works every good thing in us, 20, 40. He gives both the will and the ability, 90. Through God’s gifts we merit reward, 117. God gives what is asked, for he gave the means by which it could be asked, 135. If he is the author of the burden, he is also the helper in its administration, 9. Signs of God’s indwelling in us, 142. What it means that God does not repent, 21. We must glory in God, 22. When God is the teacher, what is taught is learned quickly, 297. He kindles the lamps of our minds and inflames us with the fire of his charity, so that we may love not only him but also whatever he loves, 40. Why God willed there to be rich and poor in the world; see Rich and Poor. God administers the general laws that he established, 48. God has always provided for the human race, 78. God’s kindness denies his mercy to no one, 130. He suspends the sentence of his justice so that repentance may be sought, 165, 189. God’s patience must not be abused, 189. It is an act of his mercy to deny what would harm the petitioner, 213. God is not the author of sin, 261. Help must be sought from God when he commands; see Prayer, God’s Grace. Those who are pure in heart shall see God, 371.

The devil’s cunning and devices, 93, 149, 179, 182, 217, 276, 341, 349. The devil’s instruments: what they are, 133. He uses human beings to deceive others, 94. How the devil is to be overcome, 133, 134. How he is weakened, 146. The devil subjects most of humanity to himself through superstitions, 30. First he was proud, so that he might fall; then envious, so that he might do harm, 31. Formerly, not without justification, he claimed tyrannical rights over human beings, 70. He was deceived at Christ’s birth, 69, 70, 71. His dominion was destroyed by Christ, 232, 249, 269. He was defeated on the cross, 236. By the very means through which he conquered, he was conquered by Christ, 243. His dominion was destroyed not by force of power but by the justice of reason, 248. Why Christ was tempted, 159. He is tormented by our sanctification, 45. He lies in wait especially for those who do good, 45, 49, 149, 179, 186. He rages most fiercely against Christians because they renounced him in baptism, 154. His envy toward us, 182. Those whom he cannot corrupt by evil actions, he overthrows through impious errors, 271. Heretics are ministers of the devil, 49. The devil has as many forms as falsehood has images, 271. If the devil finds justified souls negligent, he ensnares them again with more savage snares, 275. The devil’s benefits are more harmful than his wounds, 276. His new persecution of Christians, 134. The fury of the devil and Herod in laying snares is alike, 133. How he first deceived the human race and deprived them of what they had, 67. Those who imitate the devil’s envy, 182. The mystery of redemption was hidden from the devil, 270. The Priscillianists denied that the devil was God’s work, 700. The ancient dissension between human beings and the devil, 145.

The urban diaconates: which and how many they were, 23. Alms collected were to be brought to the city’s diaconal churches, 38 note. The deacon is the minister of Christ’s blood, 427. The deacon’s twofold office: to administer the sacraments and to distribute the Church’s material goods, 338. According to canon and tradition, a deacon is to be ordained on Sunday, 622. Marriage is forbidden to them, 687, 1421.

Dictinius, bishop in Spain, wrote treatises infected with Priscillian’s doctrines, 707. He withdrew from error, ibid. Sunday is the day of our salvation and joy, 161. The day of the Lord’s resurrection, 630, 699. Whence its preeminence, 630. On this day the world began, ibid. This day was disputed as suitable for ordination, 639. On feast days the clothing is more splendid and the churches more richly adorned, 153. How they are to be celebrated, 434. The soul must be purified above all, 153. Work must cease, 435.

The love of God; see Charity. Letters of release are to be given to clergy in writing, 679. The term “diocese,” entrusted to the governance of bishops, came to have its present common meaning, 1327. Dionysius, notary of the Roman Church, brought Leo’s letter to the Constantinopolitans, 931, 976. Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, is praised and instructed by Leo at the beginning of his episcopate, 628. His evil devices at the Council of Ephesus, 911. He prevented the reading of Leo’s letter to Saint Flavian, ibid. His tyranny and impious deeds, ibid., 921, 926, 929, 933, 946, 1040, 1092, 1222 ff. Destroyer of faith and morals, 1246. With unheard-of and incredible audacity he plotted excommunication against Saint Leo, 1092, 1223 note. His name is not to be recited at the altar, 1040. Condemned at the Council of Chalcedon, 1094, 1126, 1139. The sentence against him, 1142. His death, 1295.

How discipline is to be adapted to circumstances, 1330. Pontifical dispensation from the canons; see Canons. Leo, out of concern to restore faith and peace, dispensed with the canonical rules in the case of Maximus, bishop of Antioch, who had been ordained contrary to the canons, 1153. Dispensation was granted to Andrew of Constantinople so that he might be promoted to the presbyterate, 578. Other dispensations, ibid., 664, 665. Dispensations granted after the fact on grounds of necessity, 664, 665. Dispensation was refused even in cases of necessity to bigamists or to husbands of widows, 674.

Disputes with heretics concerning settled matters, and new treatises, which must be avoided and why, 1301, 1303, 1310, 1322, 1338, 1340, 1345. No rich person was made rich for himself alone, 27, 52, 61. Why God willed the rich to abound, 27, 48. How the rich ought to use their wealth, 35, 38. The rich person is God’s minister and the steward of the poor, 188. He has the poor person’s share, ibid. Neglect of the poor is not a venial matter, 35, 57. Those who do not help the poor are as unjust as those who oppress them, 38. It is not enough for a rich person not to take what belongs to another unless he also gives what belongs to himself, 341. The disposition of a good rich person, 367, 368.

Wealth is good, and to what extent, 34. It is not so much its possession as its distribution that has been entrusted to us, ibid. Wealth that is not properly spent becomes a cause of sin, ibid. Wealth stored up wrongly perishes, 35. To whom it should be entrusted so that it may become eternal, 53. While it is distributed, it increases, ibid. How it may be placed in safety, 338. What use of wealth religion teaches, 339. Pride must be feared in wealth, 367.

Catholic doctrine can have neither a stain of unbelief nor a wrinkle of falsehood, 252. It is not permissible to depart from evangelical doctrine by even a single word, 1044. How masters and subjects ought to conduct themselves toward servants and dependents; see Servants. Domitian, bishop and Leo’s legate to the East, 1344, 1433. The Donatist, characterized by schismatic depravity, 665. Donatus, bishop of Salicina in Africa, converted from Novatianism together with his people, 665. The measure of heavenly gifts does not depend on the quality of our works, 9. God does not wish his gifts to lie idle, 341. God’s gifts must be used justly and wisely, 34. Earthly and bodily gifts come from God’s generosity, 34. See Benefits. Dorotheus, a monk removed from his monastery, 1297. Dorus, bishop of Benevento, 732.

Doubts were frequently brought to Rome, 1405, 1416. They were decided either from Scripture or from the rules of the Fathers, 1405. Leo wished to deal with more difficult matters in a synod, and why, 1406. A matter must not be decided on the basis of ambiguous suspicion, 1407. Certain matters are more suitably settled through discussion than in writing, 1419. What rule is to be observed in doubtful cases, ibid. Even after the decisions of the councils of Gaul, the Gallic bishops brought their doubts to the apostolic see, and why, 1414. Dulcitius, notary of the Roman Church, 837. Leo’s legate to the Second Council of Ephesus, 865. Dynamius, Gallic bishop, 1111.

### E

The Church is founded upon Peter’s faith, 12, 239, 461. It rests upon Peter’s firmness, 634. Whoever attempts to diminish Peter’s authority violates this firmness, ibid. Christ prayed for the whole Church, 289. Nothing can prevail against it, 13. It is ordered in distinct ranks, and its integrity arises from diverse members, 14. See Ecclesiastical Hierarchy. Outside the Church nothing is whole, nothing pure, 317, 491. The Church of Christ is the household of freedom, 203. The unity of the Church requires harmony among the priests, 691. The faith and unity of the Church must be guarded, 1077. The Church had its origin in Christ’s birth, 88. The Church grows amid persecutions, 134. Whence the progress of the whole Church, 58. Its visible unity explained, 155. The one chaste communion of the one Church, 1039. The Church is Christ’s body, 1040. The faults of presiding priests do not prejudice the integrity of the Church, 1157. How advantageous it is to perform works of piety with the whole Church, 345, 348. The unity of these works is most powerful, ibid. Whatever the Church has received into devotional practice as custom derives from apostolic tradition and the teaching of the Holy Spirit, 316 note. Although the Church’s gentleness is contained within priestly judgment and shuns bloody vengeance, it is nevertheless aided by the severe enactments of Christian rulers, 696. The Church fears and desires nothing from this world, 703. The bond of both powers is necessary for the peace of the Church, 983. Those who disturb the Church are to be restrained by royal authority, 1211. [Col. 1528] The Church is adorned with lights, 434. More richly adorned on feast days, 153. See Basilica; Dedication of a Church.

Praises of the Roman Church, 321, 374, 941 ff., 1222. Founded upon the stronghold of the apostolic rock, 14. The churches of the city’s districts, 29, 32. Public collections were brought to them, to be distributed by the leaders for the relief of the needy, 38. How many of these churches were assigned to deacons, 23. The privileges of churches and the foundations on which they rest, 1147. They must not be violated, 1149. Church property must not be alienated, 728. The conditions under which alienation was permitted, ibid.

The “Elect” and “Electae” among the Manichaeans, 50. The elect are few, 185. Why, ibid. All the elect were crucified in Christ and will be crowned in Christ, 271. Ecclesiastical elections ought to be as far removed from flesh and blood as possible, 11.

Almsgiving: its merit and usefulness, 27, 28, 29, 32, 34, 36, 37, 48, 49, 53, 57, 61, 172, 343. It is expended upon Christ, 27, 28, 38. It is a kind of baptism and a second washing from sins, 28, 63. Through its cleansing, sins are washed away, 36, 63, 186, 316. Although not everyone has equal means for it, there ought to be equal piety, 29, 39, 45, 47. In almsgiving it is not wealth but intention that is weighed, ibid., 63, 346. Those whose wealth is unequal may have equal disposition, 346. It must be practiced by all, 30, 45, 169, 346. Even by the poor, 30, 63. Whatever is spent in alms is not diminished but increased, 183, 315. It is pious interest, 53. It aids prayer, 48, 52. It must be joined with fasting, 343. Those who cannot fast should give more abundant alms, ibid. Its omission is a ground for condemnation, 35, 57. To whom it should especially be given, 33. It should also be given to unbelievers, 155. The faithful are to be preferred, ibid., 350. It should be given to the modest in such a way that both poverty and shame are considered, 33. It should be given to the needy before they ask, 411. Whoever gives alms is a minister of divine mercy, 188. The generosity of almsgiving must be so regulated that the poor rejoice in their nourishment while the household’s sufficiency is not strained, 347. It is not enough not to take what belongs to another unless one also gives what belongs to oneself, 341. Whoever does not care for the needs of others differs in nothing from beasts, 62.

Eparchius, Gallic bishop, 1111. The First Council of Ephesus; see Council. The Second Council of Ephesus was summoned by Theodosius, 851, 856, 865. Leo’s authority was required for its summons to take effect, 863. It became a robbery, 1077. What was perpetrated there, 911, 912, 946, 974, 1077, 1322. Leo’s letter was not read, 921. Leo’s legates opposed that robbery, 913, 921, 923, 928, 933. Leo rejected its proceedings, 904, 913, 923, 928. So did every western council, 928. Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, was the evil author of it, 929. It does not deserve the name of synod, 1051, 1064. Its judgment was detestable, 1287.

Epicarpius, presbyter of Benevento, improperly placed over men older than himself, 735. Epiphany is Christ’s manifestation, 112, 115. It was foretold by the prophets, 121. At Epiphany the calling of the nations began, 121. Why this feast was instituted, 128. How it is to be honored, 117. The mystery of Epiphany is still fulfilled in the Church, 132, 140. Some think that on this day the Lord approached John’s baptism, and therefore confer baptism, 722. Epiphanius, sent by Leo with letters to Constantinople, 931, 976. He is called a tribune, 956.

Bishops are high priests, 891. They are placed above all ranks, 671. What their virtues are, ibid. It is their duty to watch lest the unity of the faith be violated, 1253. All were taught in Christ, 719. Faith and doctrine alone do not make a bishop, 1432. Their dignity is common, but not their order, in the sense explained, 691 note.

The election of a bishop must not be long delayed, 688. In the election, the consent of the clergy and people is required, 637, 639, 679, 688, 1420. No bishop should be appointed against the will of the people, 679, 688. If the votes of the parties are divided, the metropolitan’s judgment should prefer the candidate who is supported by greater zeal and greater merits, ibid. Who are to be elected, and by what testing, 659. They must not be ordained from among the laity, 662, 665. The best candidate should be chosen from among the presbyters or deacons, 688. The anointing of bishops, 11, 228. Provincial bishops are to consecrate them together with the metropolitan’s judgment, 1420. They must not be bigamists; see Bigamists. The anniversary solemnity is to be celebrated, 10.

Bishops must not easily be removed from their sees, 690. Translations of bishops are rejected, 689. During wartime bishops ought not to leave their churches, 1047. What is to be thought of bishops who do not work, 708, 709. The pattern of Peter is set before bishops as rulers of the Church, 18. What episcopal gentleness and mildness are, 696. Difficulties and labors must not deter a bishop, 1417. The continence of bishops, 688. Whoever does not recall others from error shows that he himself is in error, 707, 708. Those negligent in feeding their flock are censured, 716. Ignorance in bishops is inexcusable, 614, 717, 1287. [Col. 1529] It is the duty of bishops to preach; see Preaching. The steadfastness of bishops is greatly necessary, 1311, 1314. The four ranks of bishops; see Hierarchy. A bishop’s fall ought not to harm his see, 1167. The greatest concern of bishops is observance of the canons, 733. The judgments of bishops must be mature, 763. Their faults do not prejudice the Church, 1157. They are obliged to correct, 1318. Sluggish indulgence and connivance are especially blameworthy in them, 1319. Bishops exiled for the faith were recalled, 1032, 1046.

Letters of peace, that is, of communion, 1185. Letters is used in the plural for a single letter, 677 note. Papal letters are called authoritative, 711 note. Likewise, apostolic decrees, 663, 665. Those that confirmed a general synod were to be read in the churches of the East, 1182. Those in error are to be instructed from the tradition of the saints, 1257. Errors lend splendor to the truth, 1112.

The Eucharist is participation in Christ’s body and blood, 247. It makes us pass into what we receive, ibid. In it is the truth of Christ’s body and blood, 356, 977. It is set against the error of Eutyches, 356 note. It is a sacrifice, 356. Those receiving it answered, “Amen,” 357. It was given to young children, 977. The Manichaeans avoided communion in the blood, 161. See Communion.

Eudocia Augusta was admonished by Leo at the emperor’s private request, and why, 1209 note. Eudoxia Licinia wrote to Theodosius after the Ephesian robbery concerning the disturbance of the churches, 968. She is different from Eudoxia, who restored Saint Peter’s church at Rome, 453 note. Eugenius, Gallic bishop, 1111. Eulalius, Gallic bishop, 1111. Eulogius, bishop of Yporium, 1083. Eunomius the heretic, 49.

Saint Euphemia. At her shrine the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon placed the definition of the faith upon the altar, 1128 note. Euphratas, accuser of Flavian, bishop of Constantinople: if he gives satisfaction, Leo permits him to be ordained presbyter, 1274. Eupsychius brought Leo’s letter to Flavian, 889. Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, gave Bishop Flavian a written accusation against Eutyches at the Constantinopolitan synod, 739. He approached Leo, 1037. He endured many dangers and labors for the sake of the faith, 1041. Leo commends his church to Anatolius of Constantinople, lest anything deteriorate during his absence, ibid. Eusebius, bishop of Milan, convened the synod of his province at Leo’s command, together with its synodical letter, 1080. Eusthasius, bishop of Augsburg, 1053. The name of Eusthatius, bishop of Berytus, is not to be recited at the altar, 1040. He persecuted innocent and Catholic people, ibid. Eusthatius, Gallic bishop, 1111.

Before the condemnation of his error, Eutyches wrote to Leo accusing certain people of Nestorian heresy, 737 note. He was very imprudent and exceedingly ignorant, 801. Accused by Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, he was condemned at the Constantinopolitan synod, 739, 756, 763, 767, 786. He revealed that he had lodged an appeal at the synod and that it had not been accepted, 740, 741, 742, 763. In this he lied, 786. After his condemnation he wrote to Leo, 739. He sent him a written appeal, 742. He issued a statement of his faith, ibid. note, and directed it to Leo, ibid., 1481. He feigned obedience to Leo, 741, 765, 841, 867. He wrote to Saint Peter Chrysologus, who replied to him, 775. Flavian sent Leo the proceedings held against Eutyches at Constantinople, 755, 786.

Leo granted that Eutyches, if he condemned his error, might be restored to communion and received again in his rank, 835, 841, 851, 858, 861, 867, 870. Leo requested that he be sent to more remote places and that a Catholic be placed over his monastery, 1049. He taught perversely while in exile, and it was requested that he be transferred to more distant and secluded places, 1275, 1276. He defended heresy under the appearance of piety, 854. He was anathematized by the Church of Constantinople, 1059. All the Easterners signed against him before the Council of Chalcedon, 1066.

The error of Eutyches and its rejection, 100, 179, 204, 288, 356, 373, 756, 784, 809, 833, 1049, 1138, 1158, 1214, 1223, 1238, 1357. It is akin to that of the Manichaeans, 976, 1179; to Valentinus and Apollinaris, 756, 782. It favors Arius’s error, 978, and that of Photinus, 980. It had long ago been condemned in other heretics, 373, 1036, 1058. It was spread at Rome by Alexandrian merchants, 373. The Church’s victory in extinguishing this error, 1145. Treatises against the errors of Eutyches, 365 ff.

How the Eutychians tried to deceive Catholics, 1058 note. They claimed to be defenders of the Nicene faith and accused Catholics of abandoning the Nicene faith, 955 note, 1323, 1359 note. They charged Pope Leo with Nestorianism, 1258. They called his letter to Flavian obscure, 1314. Hence Leo initially thought that his letter had been falsified in the Greek [Col. 1530] version, ibid., 1260. Later he discovered that this arose from the perversity of the translators, 1314 note. Crowds of Eutychians after Marcian’s death, both at Constantinople and at Alexandria, 1299 note, 1301 note. Leo wrote to Euxitheus, bishop of Thessalonica, 1311.

The Gospel relates what prophecy foretold, 230. It is not permissible to depart from evangelical doctrine by even a single word, 1044. How far examination of Leo’s letter to Flavian was permissible at Chalcedon while preserving the authority of the apostolic see, 1220 note. Examination of conscience; see Conscience.

Excommunication must not be imposed for trivial matters, 640. Nor at the discretion of an indignant bishop, ibid. Its effects, ibid., 859, 861. One must not communicate with those rejected from the unity of the Church, 374. The excommunication of heretics; see Heretics. Threatening excommunication, 1169.

To provide a good example is to benefit both oneself and others, 130. The fruits of a good example and the harm caused by a bad one, 131. Examples are stronger than words, 338. The use of exorcisms in the Church, 342, 723.

### F

Servants and subjects: what place they are to occupy, 152, 155, 173, 180. Why God wills some to be subject to others, 188. Faventius, bishop of Rhegium, 1082. Faustus, abbot of Constantinople, to whom Leo wrote, 859, 937, 983, 1011, 1015. The fertility of the earth is to be attributed to God, 48. See Abundance. Feast days; see Festal Days.

There were few faithful in the Old Testament and many in the New, 78. See Christian.

Faith: its virtue and merit consist in things not subject to sight, 268, 293. The justice of faith, 21. Faith brings both the impious to justice and the dead back to life, 193. Faith justifies, 1012. Without works it is dead, 36. Charity is the strength of faith, and faith is the strength of charity, 171. The bond of faith and charity; see Charity. Faith can exist without charity, 31. It is not sufficient for salvation, 182. What is believed by faith must necessarily be imitated in action, 136. Faith makes everything precious, 169. Whoever serves desire boasts vainly of the freedom of faith, 135. Faith is the narrow way that leads to life, 83. Without faith there is nothing holy, nothing pure, nothing living, 82. This is explained, 493.

Whence the Catholic faith, 1061. The source and channel of faith, 1075. Its commendation and unity, 82, 839. The Catholic faith, which is true and one, permits itself to be violated by no diversity, 1338. It is the duty of bishops to watch lest faith be violated, 1253. True faith is defended most fruitfully when a false opinion is condemned even by its own adherents, 835. It can be violated by the briefest addition or alteration of letters, 1254. Nothing can be added to or taken away from the faith, 1237. Faith is not subject to contrary reasoning, 1138. It requires humility, 1235. Once defined, matters must not be called into question, 1075. Nor must they be retracted, 1064, 1301, 1303, 1304, 1310, 1322, 1338, 1340, 1345. The noise of quarrels and disputations must be avoided, and the extent to which the faith is to be defended, 765, 1075, 1337, 1345. Nothing is more glorious than to defend the faith, 888. The steadfastness of faith is made more wonderful by the difficulty of believing, 274.

The faith of the Old and New Testaments is the same, 204, 244. The ancients lived and pleased God in faith in Christ, 199, 204, 244, 256, 268. Only by the light of faith can the mystery of Christ as God and man be attained, 140. Faith was increased by the Lord’s ascension and strengthened by the gift of the Holy Spirit, 294. The wondrous effects of this faith, ibid. Faith must be discussed cautiously, 1225. Many come to the faith in Leo’s time, 83. The purity of faith shines forth when the stains of errors are separated from it, 935. Peter’s faith is the foundation of the Church; see Church. The firmness of Peter’s faith is perpetual, 12, 461. The same firmness of faith was transmitted to his successors, 22. The Roman faith was commended by the Apostle and violated by no heresy, 274. It was preached throughout the whole world from the beginning of the Gospel, 14.

The Son of God is the only-begotten Son of the Father, 803. Consubstantial with the Father, 110, 823. Coeternal, 805. True God, 817. Never inferior to the Father, 101. His divinity is equal to the Father’s, 823. The Son of God was begotten by the Father before the ages and is coeternal with the Father in everlasting and consubstantial equality, 83. Differing in nothing from the Father, and why, 805. Remaining in the form of God, he made man, 813. He became man; see Christ. The appearances of the Son of God in the Old Testament, 854.

Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, condemned Eutyches at the synod and sent the proceedings to Leo, 756, 786. Eutyches accused him of refusing to receive the written appeal that Eutyches had submitted, 740, 742. Flavian replied that Eutyches had lied about this, 786. How necessary he considered Leo’s judgment and how highly he valued it, [Col. 1531] 788. Leo’s letters to him in this matter, 767, 792, 801, 885, 887, 889, 931. His zeal is praised, 792, 887, 1036, 1156, 1277. At the Ephesian robbery he gave the legates a written appeal to the apostolic see, 906, 915. At that same council he was perversely condemned, 946, while the legates protested, 928. Dioscorus raged savagely against him, 931. Leo ordered the Constantinopolitans to adhere to Flavian, 933, 937. They did so, 975. He died in exile; the time and place of his death, 952. His body was brought honorably to Constantinople and placed in the Basilica of the Apostles, 1032, 1036, 1046. Flavian’s virtues, which raised him to the glory of a confessor, 1156. Flavian is called “of holy memory,” 1278, 1285, 1293. The memory of blessed Flavian, 1280. He is to be commemorated among the saints, 1090, 1101.

Florejus, presbyter of the Church of Yporium, 1082. Florus, bishop in Gaul, 1110. Usury: how grave an evil it is, 53, 54. It is unjust, ibid. It was also exacted by the rich, 467. It was forbidden to laity and clergy, 615. What kind of interest with God is pious, 53. Fontejus, a Gallic bishop, 998, 1111. He was bishop of Vaison, 996 note.

The “formatae” letters, indicators of the date of Easter, were sent annually by the Roman pontiff, 1079, 1260, 1283, 1297. Solid courage, which is shaken by no disturbance of inequalities, belongs to few, 164. Fraternus, Gallic bishop, 1111.

### G

Galla Placidia; see Placidia. The bishops of Gallaecia are called Gallicii or Gallici, 710 note. Leo ordered them to convene a council, ibid., 711, because of the Priscillianist heresy spreading in Gallaecia, ibid. The religion of the Gallicans came from the apostolic see, 1109. Through innumerable reports the Gallic bishops consult the apostolic see, 634. By custom they bring appeals to the apostolic see, ibid. Saint Leo issued many decisions concerning the Gallic churches, 635 ff. The pope’s judgment was to have force throughout Gaul, 643. The sanction of the emperor Valentinian forbade the Gallic bishops to attempt anything contrary to ancient custom without the pope’s authority, 644. Leo confirmed by his judgment the consecration of Ravennius of Arles, 890. The bishops’ petitions concerning the see of Arles against that of Vienne were sent to Leo, 993. The controversy was settled by him, and boundaries were assigned to each metropolitan see, 998. Leo sent the Gallic bishops his Letter to Flavian together with secret instructions, 1001. What these instructions concerned, ibid. note. How much the Gallicans defer to the Roman pontiff, 1109. They gave thanks for receiving his letter, 1108. They sent him a synodical letter, 1107. Leo sent this to Constantinople, 1315. The doctrine of the Gallic Church was praised by the pontiff, 1137, 1315. Leo instructed the Gallic bishops concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus, 1140. Three Gallic bishops thanked Leo for receiving his letter to Flavian, which they also declared was honored throughout all the churches, 1003. They sent Leo a copy of that letter, transcribed by themselves, to be corrected by him if anything had been omitted through a scribal error and then returned, 1004. It was returned, ibid. note.

Joy; see Gladness. Gelasius’s letter to the Dardani, written by the same pontiff in two copies, 651. Geminianus, bishop and Leo’s legate to Leo Augustus, 1344, 1433. Christ has a twofold genealogy in the Gospels, and why, 854. The Gentiles were called to the faith, 105. The fury of the Gentiles against Christians, especially those of the priestly order, 338. The Gentiles despise what is human in Christ, 212, 213. Paschasius, bishop of Genoa, 1083.

The human race: its root is corrupted, 361. It is born into condemnation, 86. See Original Sin. Georgius, a monk, lost both his purpose and the name of monk by presuming to do what was unlawful, 1211. Gerontius, Gallic bishop, 1107, 1111, 1136. Gerontius, bearer of the letter of Bishop Julian to Leo, 1295, 1296. He was sent back with Leo’s letter, 1328.
