The glory of the heavenly kingdom: its eternal good, 45, 48, 75, 97, 142, 185, 203, 343, 345, 352, 364, 1329. For the hope of eternal things, every temporal loss should be considered light, 194. The way to glory, 271, 288, 341. The glory of Flavian of Constantinople as confessor, 1156.

The glory of God: everything must be referred to God’s glory, 318. We must glory not in ourselves but in the Lord, 22, 142, 318, 1219. Our glory must be recognized in God’s glory, 173. The gifts given to us must be used for the glory of the giver, 60. The vain glory of the world must not be sought, 138, 359, 364. It is more to be feared that one will receive glory than that one will be trampled in humility, 455.

How few among the Latins knew Greek properly and could produce an exact translation from Greek; and likewise how rare among the Greeks were those who perfectly knew Latin and could produce an accurate translation from Latin, 557. Hence Leo doubts the less exact Greek version of his letter to Flavian, 1236. He wishes it to be rendered into Greek by someone skilled in both languages, 1258, 1260. The difficulty of suitably translating into Greek works that treat subtle matters, 1237. The difficulty of translating into Latin, 1274. Many of Leo’s letters were rendered into Greek, and when, as well as the authority of these translations, 558, 559. Certain Greek letters were written and sent to the West from the outset in both Greek and Latin, and both copies are to be regarded as originals, 1112 note, 557. Greek-speakers at Alexandria, 1274.

The various ranks in the Church, 14. See Ecclesiastical Hierarchy. Praise of divine grace, 39. Its necessity, 55, 141, 187, 1207. It was mercifully prepared not according to human merits, but according to the abundance of the riches of God’s wisdom, 261. The contrary error of the Pelagians is condemned, 591. Awakening grace, 181. The help of grace, 211. Christ’s grace not only awakens the mind but also assists action, 983. God justly insists upon the command because he goes before it with help, 265. It belongs to grace to begin and complete; it belongs to the human being to cooperate voluntarily, 181. We are co-workers with God’s grace operating in us, 130. He who gave the will will also give the ability, so that we may be co-workers in his works, 90. God’s strength is sufficient for victory, 1337. A person doing good receives from God both the result of the work and the beginning of the will, 141. Grace works all things in all, 346. Every gift of good works is a divine preparation, 592. God, who granted the will, also gives the ability, 187. How a person cooperates with grace so as to be renewed inwardly, 163. The conversion of the thief is a work of grace, 202. No one is justified by virtue before being justified by grace, which is for each person the beginning of justice and the source and origin of merits, 592. What grace chiefly works in the heart, 47, 48. In what it appears more wonderful, 9. The work of grace in the Magi, 112, 123.

A redeemed and reborn person would be corrupted by carnal desire unless fortified by spiritual help; for just as the occasion of falling is never absent, so the means of standing firm is always present, 55. The same grace was given to the ancient Fathers as is given to us, 76. The human race was always provided for by divine goodness through grace, 78. But especially after the incarnation, ibid. What divine grace conferred on us in the incarnation, 97. No gift of grace is to be denied to any believer, 245. Without God’s help we cannot be strong, 353 note. Things made impossible by our weakness become possible through the power of grace, 352. God’s grace presents the help, and obedience softens the command, 130. Obedience must not be withheld from grace, 163. God’s help must be implored so that, through him without whom we can do nothing, we may accomplish everything, 187. If a person finds anything impossible or difficult in the commandments, let him have recourse to the one who commands, who gives the command precisely to awaken desire and provide help, 163. The command is given so that the help of the one commanding may be sought, 187. Special gifts of grace, 259. Grace that grants victory does not remove the material for struggle, 314. This is a reason for the saints to fear lest, lifted up by their very works of piety, they be abandoned by the aid of grace and remain in the weakness of nature, 141. Through Christ we can do all things, while without him we can do nothing, 1418. His aids are as powerful as his promises are true, 1419.

Thanksgiving owed to God, 7, 20, 41, 48, 52, 62, 66, 72, 115, 121, 247, 986, 1042, 1076, 1109, 1139, 1154, 1172, 1206, 1246, 1256. Leo gives thanks to the Romans for their support in his election to the pontificate, 7. Gratianopolis was subjected by Leo to the bishop of Vienne, 999. Gratus, presbyter, acted in the place of Euthasius, bishop of Augsburg, at the Council of Milan, 1083. Gratitude; see Benefits; Thanksgiving. Leo sets the testimonies of Saint Gregory of Nazianzus against the Eutychians, 1395. The allurements of gluttony, 159, 319. Every vice was infused through the allure of eating, 342. The evil of gluttonous intemperance, 58.

### H
Heresy derives from false religion, 854. It arises from private opinions and the presumption of teaching without knowledge, 106. [Col. 1533] Why it is permitted by God, 856. What evil it produces, 982. Most hostile to the Christian religion, 1078. It must be suppressed before it acquires strength, 854. The first step toward heresy is to listen patiently to heretics, 710. Catalogue of heresies against the Incarnation, 49, 81, 99, 107, 373. Heresies cannot remain hidden, 372. Heretics must be exposed, and those to whom they must be denounced, 33, 51, 161. Those who think heretics should not be exposed are guilty of silence, 51. They have been expelled from the unity of the Church, 374. Heretics are ministers of the devil, 49. Sons and disciples of the devil, 150. They come in sheep’s clothing, 49. They usurp the Christian name, 49, 271, 1212, 1213, 1238. Their deceptive arts, 81, 82, 707. Their intelligence, 1223. They must be avoided, 81. They must not be tolerated, 1178. They must be restrained by the emperors, 1306, 1320. The weapons of faith must be taken up against them, 33, 51. Their leaders in particular must be driven into exile, 161. They have no right to reside or pray in churches, 1320. Prayer must be offered for heretics, 127. Their names must not be recited at the altar, 1040, 1051. Conversations with them must be avoided, 271, 373, 374. Nor should one communicate with them in civil affairs, 50. They anathematize one another, 1213. With what precautions corrected heretics are to be received into communion, 589, 594, 665, 709, 731, 835, 851, 861, 867, 870, 1037, 1040, 1078. Those who fell into heresy through fear, were converted, and were received, 1039. They are to be left in the same order in which they return, 575, 577, 731. Provided that they have not been rebaptized, 730 note, 731. Leo reserves the examination of their leaders to himself, 1051. Faith must not be debated with condemned heretics, 1340. How unhappy an outcome such debates ordinarily have, 1322. Heretics baptize validly, 1334. In what sense those baptized by them, after conversion, were to be confirmed by the imposition of hands, ibid. note.

Helladius, a Gallic bishop, 1111. Helpidius, an Egyptian bishop exiled on account of the faith, 1336.

Herod was a foreigner, 118. His savagery, 113, 120, 128, 140. His blindness, 124. The fury of Herod and the devil in laying ambushes is alike, 133. He announces Christ as born for the world, while attempting to remove him from the world, 115. God orders his malice toward the good of the infants, 113. What Herod signifies mystically, 128.

Hermes, archdeacon of Narbonne, brings to Leo the letters of Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, 1416.

Ecclesiastical hierarchy. Its three ranks are listed: Levites, elders, and priests, 228. The chief prelates; priests of the second order, ministers of the sacraments, 181. Four ranks: episcopal, presbyteral, Levitical or diaconal, and subdiaconal, 687, 688. Four hierarchical ranks among bishops: episcopal, metropolitan, exarchal, and pontifical, 692. In what sense these ranks have dignity but do not constitute a common order, 691 note. On the primacy of the Roman pontiff over the universal Church, see *Primacy of the Roman Pontiff*. Within the same rank, one older by ordination could not yield his place to a junior, 735. Converts from heresy who were received in their own rank are not to be promoted to primacy within that same rank, 1278.

St. Hilary, bishop of Arles, deposes Celidonius, bishop, 635. He irregularly ordains another in place of the sick bishop Projectus, 636, 637. Because of Celidonius’s appeal to the Roman pontiff, he is present at the council in Rome, 635. Afterwards he withdrew, 640. He is deprived of metropolitan authority, 639, 999. Valentinian issues a law on this account, 642. Leo calls him “of holy memory” after his death, 890.

St. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, cited by Leo, 1383.

Hilarus, a Gallic bishop, 1107, 1111. Hilarus, deacon of the Roman Church and Leo’s legate to the Second Council of Ephesus, 837, 841, 851, 865, 870. To avoid being compelled to subscribe to the impious proceedings, he escaped, 911, 921. He made a formal protest, 913. He reported all the proceedings to Leo, 907, 911, 921, 929. He writes to Pulcheria Augusta, 926.

Leo orders a synod of the Spanish bishops against the heresy of Priscillian, 710. This heresy was discovered in Spain by Turribius, 712. The Gallic bishops send to the Spaniards documents received from Leo against Eutyches, 1002 note. Leo entrusts the Gallic bishops with announcing to the Spanish bishops the victory won by the faith at the Council of Chalcedon against the Eutychian heresy, 1140. A *formata* concerning the proclamation of the date of Easter for the year, 455. Sent by Leo to the Spaniards, 1283.

Why man was created in the image of God, 39, 62. If he had remained in the state of innocence, he would not have died, 79, 1291. From the first man, condemnation passed to all together with sin, ibid. The root of the human race was corrupted, 361. The excellence of man, 96. His neediness, 700. Renewed in Christ, 66. Human nature is always mutable and can continually fall back and rise, 148. No one in this life is free from temptation or exempt from guilt, 185. In human beings, the community of nature must be considered, 180, 182, 191, 192. Similarity of character unites human beings, 40. See *Human nature*.

[Col. 1534]

Honoratus, a Gallic bishop, 1111. Leo uses the terms “humility” and “humanity” interchangeably, 83 note. Humility is the whole discipline of Christian life, 137. Christ’s humility is victorious and instructive, 136. Christ taught humility, 114. By remedies of humility he healed the wounds of pride, 86. For the humble and obedient nothing is arduous or difficult, 130. The humility of the Divinity is our advancement, 199.

Hypatius, chorepiscopus and Theodoret’s legate to Leo, 950.

## I

Idatius, a Gallic bishop, 1110. Idatius, a Spanish bishop, 711, 615, 1475.

Eating food sacrificed to idols is unlawful, 1332, 1428.

Leo writes to the metropolitans of Illyricum, 617, 677, 1311. Aetius and Theodoret endeavored to remove the Illyricians’ doubt concerning Leo’s letter to Flavian, 1220 note.

The emperors were raised to the throne chiefly for this reason: that they might bring aid to the faith and the Church, 1122, 1323, 1345. Heretics must be restrained by them, 1306, 1327. It is their duty to cut away scandals against the faith and discipline, 1185, 1188, 1381. In honor of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection they released the guilty, 152, 180, 485.

The imposition of hands understood in various ways, 1334 note. The rites of penance and reconciliation, ibid. It was not used with converted clerics, and why, 1335 note, 1421.

The Incarnation of the Word. God’s purpose in the Incarnation, 811. The dogma of the Incarnation is affirmed, 84, 85, 1019, 1071. See *Christ’s Incarnation*. What constitutes a true worshiper of the Incarnation, 92.

How pleasing infancy is to Christ, 138. Christian infancy, ibid. See *Children*.

Against what the gates of hell cannot prevail, 13. In hell there is no satisfaction, 131. Eternal death, 65. Eternal punishment, 1318. Eternal fire, 36. Eternal torments, 32.

Unbelief is the mother of all evils and is divided into many opinions, 268. It pollutes the person who is fasting, 317. In what sense, 492. Whether St. Leo taught that all works of unbelievers are sins, 491. The unbeliever is excluded from Christ’s mercy, 168. In what sense Leo wrote this, 486.

Ingenuus, a Gallic bishop, 998, 1110, 1136. He was bishop of Embrun, 1458. Sent as a legate to Leo by the Gallic bishops, he is sent back, 1139.

How dangerous ingratitude is, 335. It is characteristic of an ungrateful spirit to conceal benefits, 7.

Enemies are to be loved, and why, 41, 63, 147, 180. They are to be spared, 147, 166, 187.

Innocence. The faithful must strive for perfect innocence and complete purity, 190. The holy Innocents, true martyrs, were brought by Christ into heaven, 113. They shared in Christ’s Passion, 139. In them the pattern of all martyrs went before, 140. Blessed was their ignorance, 116. There were many of them, 1289.

Leo orders that the decrees of St. Innocent I, Roman pontiff, and of his predecessors be observed, 616. Innocentus, a bishop from one of the suburban provinces, carries Leo’s letter into his own province, 615.

The intervals required in ordinations; see *Orders*.

Those who imitate the devil’s envy, 182.

Eulogius, bishop of Iporium, 1083.

The Italian bishops instructed by Leo, 623.

## J

Jacob prophesies about Christ, 118.

Leo praises the vigor of Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, 729. Leo’s first letter to the bishop of Aquileia was not addressed to Januarius, 581.

Fasting accords with both Testaments, 351. The commandment of fasting was not abolished by the grace of the New Law but confirmed, as was also the commandment of love, 46, 52. Although the fast of Christians is shared with the Jews in its timing, it does not agree with them in conduct, and why, 348. The fasts of the Church were instituted by the authority of the Holy Spirit, 313. They were arranged by apostolic decrees, 62. They derive from apostolic tradition, 168, 319. Fasting was practiced immediately by the apostles after they had been filled with the Holy Spirit, 314. Fasting is commanded by authority and recommended by charity, 340. By apostolic institution, the rules of all the virtues are to begin with fasting, 319.

The fast of Lent, 189. See *Lent*. The four-season fast prescribed by the Church throughout the year, 59. Why it was instituted, 43, 48, 52, 62, 266, 315, 320, 365. The fast of the tenth month taken from the Old Testament, 46. Added to the ecclesiastical regulations, 62. [Col. 1535] The fast of the seventh month chosen in accordance with both apostolic and legal institutions, 363. The four-season fast was not commanded and observed everywhere, 56 note. To what extent it could nevertheless be called a prescription from apostolic tradition, 316 note. Why it was ordained after the feasts of Easter and Pentecost, 315, 320.

The praise and usefulness of fasting, 42, 43, 47, 58, 59, 143, 156, 317, 320, 342. Almsgiving must be added to fasting, 43, 47, 63, 147, 151, 168, 183, 343. And prayer, 42, 44, 48, 343. Other virtues as well, 146, 147, 151, 157, 162. Some fasts are lawful, others voluntary, 340. How much is accomplished when sanctioned by law, 347 ff.

Fasting must be observed by everyone, 184. It was observed even by catechumens, 165. What kind of fasting is appropriate for the sick, 168. Whoever cannot fast should make up for it by almsgiving, 343. Fasting was imposed on the well-fed and strong, as well as on the weak and pale, 409. The fast of repentance is necessary, 351. Fasting ought to be cheerful, 347. One must fast from food, but much more from errors, 355.

A twofold fast: of the flesh and of the spirit, 364. What spiritual fasting consists in, ibid. Bodily fasting without spiritual fasting is of no benefit, 60, 364. Holy and spiritual fasting, 174. One must fast from guilt, 191. What sterile fasting is, and in what sense, 343 note. Discernment regarding foods during fasts, 160. Public fasts and other pious works are more effective than private ones, 56 note, 345, 346, 348—especially against the devil’s snares, 56. Through fasting all vices must be driven out, 342. Certain demons were not expelled by exorcisms but by prayer and fasting, ibid. The Israelite people did not please God except through fasting, 344. The fasts of unbelievers; see *Unbelief*.

To what extent a Christian living in Jerusalem is instructed by the mysteries of those places, 1287, 1289.

St. John the Baptist prophesies in his mother’s womb, 108, 128. He indicates the Mother of God, 108. He taught that the true Passover had been fulfilled, 273.

John the Baptist Marus, *Pr. Serm.* § 7.

St. John Chrysostom praised, 1277. Testimonies excerpted by Leo from his works, 1393.

John the decurion sent to Egypt on behalf of the cause of the faith, 1296.

John, bishop of Cremona, 1084. John, the bishop who ordained Timothy Salophaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, 1437. John, a presbyter of Constantinople, appeals to Leo, 1054. Johas, the ordainer of Timothy Salophaciolus, 1437.

The blindness of the Jews, 116, 119, 212, 236, 253. Their impiety, 104, 219, 226, 236, 415. Their blasphemies, 209. Their cruel and feigned clemency toward Christ, 216. Their obduracy, 236, 266. Their punishment, 207, 237. They were servants and hirelings of the devil, 269. What the Jews lost, the Gentiles obtained, 203. Many Jews were converted, 210. Prayer must be offered for the Jews, because through their offense we received the grace of reconciliation, 273. Care must be taken that they repent, and how, 129. The Church’s prayer for them during the Passion, ibid. Nor was the sacrament of salvation denied to them, ibid. Their savagery was turned into an occasion of salvation, 129, 201. The Jews’ barefoot observances, 348 note. How Jews differ from Christians in their understanding of the Scriptures, 104. How the Jews prepared themselves for battle against the Philistines, 143. Christ’s prayer on the cross for the Jews, and the effect of this prayer, 240. How the Jews serve Christians, 119. For the Jews truth is a stumbling block, 129. They are urged toward recognition of Christ, ibid.

Judas was more wicked and wretched than all, 215. He performed miracles, 262. At the Supper he received Christ’s body and blood, 215. Why he was not excluded from this sacrament, 220. Possessed by the devil, and when, 221. Cut off from the body of apostolic unity, ibid. By the privilege of his faithlessness he had obtained leadership in the crime of Christ’s arrest, 213. His repentance was fruitless, and why, 201. His conversion was so perverse that even in repenting he sinned, 214. A man incapable of conversion, 205. He passed into despair before Christ fulfilled the sacrament of universal redemption, 240. He could have obtained a remedy if he had not hastened to the noose, ibid. He would have moved Christ’s mercy if he had not denied his omnipotence, 201. Judas deserved the punishment assigned to him, since no one could be found more savage than he in inflicting punishment upon himself, 262. Even in dying he sinned, 240. His crime had exceeded every measure of vengeance, 205.

The judgments of bishops must be mature, 763. The various degrees of ecclesiastical judgments, 689. The form of the Last Judgment, 31, 172. It will be concerned especially with whether people have shown mercy to the poor, 36, 37. Christ’s authority in judgment, 200. Although the day of judgment is hidden, it is not doubted to be near, 58. Why it has been delayed, 130. This delay deceives sinners, ibid. A multitude of angels will be present at it, and why, 205. Meditation on judgment is useful, 30, 31. Each person holds his own sentence in his hand, 191. Vengeance upon another is judgment upon oneself, 188. Christ will not come to judge until the periods appointed for multiplying the children of the Church have been completed, 294.

[Col. 1536]

Julianus, a Gallic bishop, 1111. Julianus, bishop of Cos and by birth an Italian, 1042. Brought up at Rome, 1190. His friendship with Leo, 1052. Leo’s letters to him, *Alphabetical Catalogue of Letters*, *Dissertation on the Lost Letter*. He is commended to Pulcheria, 1037; and to Anatolius of Constantinople, 1041, 1270. Supported by Leo’s authority, 1042. Leo’s legates were to share their plans with him, 1043, 1052, 1053. Attached to the legates appointed for the general council, 1061, 1065, 1066, 1067. Leo reproves him for intervening on behalf of the privilege of the see of Constantinople, 1172. A legate in the entourage acting in Leo’s place, 1187, 1189, 1190. His office, 1189, 1191, 1205, 1276. He sends Leo a *Brief Summary of the Faith*, 1192. Leo assigns him the collection and translation of all the acts of Chalcedon, 1194. Also the translation of the letter to Flavian, 1260. Leo’s Letter XXXV was rendered into Greek, with several passages abridged, 875. Why, 873. Recommended by Pope Leo to the emperor Leo, 1325.

Julius, bishop of Puteoli, sent by Leo as legate to the Second Synod of Ephesus, 837, 867. The same Julius, or another, to whom Leo entrusted the execution of the letter to Dorus, bishop of Beneventum, 736. The letter of Pope Julius cited by Eutyches is spurious and attributed to Apollinaris, 743 note.

The power of binding and loosing, which was in Peter, remains in his successors, 22. The rights of the sees must not be diminished, 1214, 1267. Roman law, 1422.

Justianus, bishop of Vercelli, 1084.

Justification is gratuitous, 223. It is not granted in return for merits but bestowed solely by the generosity of grace, 186. God is the author of justification, 262.

What is the justice of the truly perfect, 148. To love justice is to love God, 370. The abundance of evangelical justice consists in an abundance of charity, 358. What hunger and thirst for justice are, 370. Justice gives greater delight than iniquity, 362. In what respect Christian justice exceeds Pharisaic justice, 358. It must always be increased, 168, 481. No one should presume upon his own justice, 9. No one ought to fear suffering for justice, 197. What the just have cause to fear, 141. They must never presume themselves perfect, 148. They are subject to the reproaches of the wicked, 164. The justice that leads to life is gentle, 186.

Justus, a Gallic bishop, 890, 1110.

Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, attempted to subject Palestine to himself at the First Synod of Ephesus, 1215. St. Cyril opposed him and wrote to Leo, then archdeacon of the Roman Church, 1216. At the false Synod of Ephesus he joined himself too rashly to the blasphemies of the heretics and embraced Eutyches and Dioscorus, 1180, 1192, 1285. He harassed the innocent and the Catholics, 1040. He displayed ignorance, 1051. His name was not to be recited at the altar, 1040, 1051. Afterwards he corrected himself through wiser counsel, 1180, 1287. Consequently, he was expelled from his see by the heretics, 1180. He was restored to it, 1245, 1246, 1280. He sends two legates with letters to Leo, by which he answers to God, 1285.

## L
## L

The wicked lips and deceitful tongue are described, 49. They are likened to the devil, ibid. Christian joy, 151, 231. God is the true joy of the soul, 360. Joy, or the joy of the world, 185. Harmful joy of heart, 362. The thief guilty even to the cross, and suddenly on the cross a confessor of Christ, 202. His conversion is the work of grace, ibid. How swift was the effect of his faith, 210. The two thieves as figures of the elect and the reprobate, 208. Cyriacus, bishop of Lodi, 1083. Praises are not always genuine, 163. Human praise is the reward of hypocrites, 359. A man is not without praise when he does something for another man precisely as a man, 172. Saint Laurence, overseer of the sanctuary and of the Church treasury, 338. His courage, ibid. His punishment, 339. The fire which burned outwardly was less fierce than that which was kindled within, ibid. Rome is illustrious because of Laurence, ibid. Lectors may marry and beget children, 1422.

Legates of Leo to the Second Council of Ephesus, 837, 867. Others sent to repair the scandals of the Ephesian Robber Council and concerning Anatolius of Constantinople, 1007, 1010, 1012. Others sent for the restoration of those who had fallen, 1046, 1048, 1052. Two further legates were added to these and sent for the council first summoned at Nicaea and later held at Chalcedon, 1061, 1064, 1066, 1069. Two were sent to the East at the request of Leo Augustus, 1344. Julianus was a legate in the retinue; hence the origin of apostolic nuncios; see Julianus.

Legates of the pontiff are present at councils, 1061, 1064. At the councils themselves the pontiff presides, 1062 note, 1090, 1100, 1140, 1141. Legates sent from the pontiff’s side, 859, 870. Hence the formula *de latere*; it predates Leo, 859 note.

[Col. 1537]

The legitimate bishop is the bearer of Leo’s letter in one of the suburbanicarian provinces, 615. The leniency of ecclesiastics—what it is, 696, 1347, 1348.

### Saint Leo the Great

His homeland was Rome, 857. As archdeacon, he moved John Cassian to write books on the Incarnation against the heresy of Nestorius; these books were dedicated to him, *Testim.* Saint Cyril wrote to the same archdeacon, 1216. He was elected bishop of Rome while absent, 7. By unanimous votes, ibid. note. On the day of his consecration he delivered a brief sermon in which he gave thanks for his election, 7. He rejoiced not so much to preside as to serve, 22. He celebrated the anniversary of his consecration, 8 ff.; on that occasion a gathering of bishops was held, 13.

Leo’s zeal against the Pelagians of the province of Aquileia, 589, 594, 730 note. Other Pelagians, especially Julianus, were crushed by Leo, 584; they disappeared from Rome, ibid. Through Leo’s investigation the Manichaeans were discovered at Rome, 50, 80, 127, 624. For this reason he held an assembly and proceedings against them, ibid., 626, 708. At what time, 584. Leo sent these proceedings to the bishops of Italy, 624, and to Turribius in Spain, 708. On account of these heretics having been defeated, Leo’s zeal was also celebrated in the East and praised by Theodoret, 944. Leo condemned the errors of the Priscillianists, 695 ff. What he did in the case of Eutyches: see Eutyches, and below.

Invited by the emperor Theodosius to the Second Council of Ephesus, Leo did not attend, 857. From the same Theodosius he requested a council within Italy as a remedy for the scandals of the Ephesian Robber Council, 906, 915, 923, 957. He held a conference at Rome concerning the ordination of Anatolius, 1000 note. On the feast of Saint Peter he urged Valentinian and the Augustas to seek a council within Italy, 962, 964, 968, 972. What feast this was, 959. Marcian invited him to a synod to be assembled in the East, 1025. Why he did not answer this earlier, 1034 note. He wished the synod to be postponed, 1047. He sent legates to fulfill the role of his presence, 1061, 1064, 1065. What he did concerning the Council of Chalcedon: see Council of Chalcedon.

Because he refused to confirm the Chalcedonian canon granting privilege to the see of Constantinople, Marcian praised Leo’s steadfastness, 1184 note, 1203. How boldly he resisted Anatolius’s ambition, 1172. He begged Marcian to restrain that ambition, 1151. How deeply Leo cared for observance of the canons, 733. His reverence for the Nicene canons, 1149, 1155, 1163, 1165, 1171, 1217. When he believed dispensation could be granted, 1217.

Leo Augustus invited him to the East, 1321. Leo refused to be compelled to convene a new council requested by the Egyptian Eutychians, 1327. He sent legates not to dispute with heretics about matters already defined, but to instruct the sons of the Church, 1341, 1344 ff. Leo’s tireless vigilance, especially when matters of faith were concerned, 1210, and frequently elsewhere. His zeal against heresies and heretics, 1019, 1122. He was praised by the bishops of Gaul, 997, 1109. He followed the tradition of the Fathers, 1012 note, 1059, 1293, 1379. From this tradition he determined the questions submitted to him, 1405. At first he opposed the Eutychians with the Apostles’ Creed, 803; afterward also with the Nicene Creed, and why, 956 note, 1359 note.

Leo altered or expanded some of his sermons and repeated them in that altered form, 66 note, 153 note, 353 note, 328. From his sermons he transferred certain chapters, in the same words, into his letters, 811 ff., 1239 ff. From the letter to the Palestinians he incorporated several chapters into Letter CLXV, to Leo Augustus, 1355. His letters were written in duplicate copies and in some cases altered or expanded, and why, 654, 846, 898, 1285 note, 1293 note, 1294 note. Why several sermons were falsely attributed to Leo in the Lectionaries, 389. How they may be distinguished, 380. There is no contemporary authorial collection of all Leo’s sermons and letters, 509. Later collections of sermons derive from the Lectionaries, Preface. Several letters relating to the Council of Chalcedon and to the Eutychian heresy were translated into Greek during Leo’s lifetime, 509. They were collected in Latin around the time of Vigilius and inserted into the outstanding collection of Regensburg, 547. How authoritative their Greek version is, 558, 559. The profession of faith made by the Greeks concerning Leo’s letters, ibid.

Leo’s Letter XXVIII, to Flavian, was celebrated in all the churches, 1004. It was also highly esteemed by the laypeople of Gaul, ibid. It was received as a confession of faith, 1108. The whole world was enriched by it, ibid. Its privileges and praises, 795, 943, 1081. All the Easterners had subscribed to it before the Council of Chalcedon, 1059 note, 1066. It is included in certain Greek collections of canons, 797. Letter CLXV, to Leo Augustus, was highly celebrated, 1349.

The primacy of Leo, the Roman pontiff, over the universal Church is asserted by Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, 942; by the emperor Valentinian, 642, 962; and by Placidia Augusta, 968, 974. See *Primacy of the Roman pontiff*. Leo is the head of the universal Church, endowed with the dignity of the apostle Peter, 1144. He possesses primacy in the episcopate by divine faith, 1017. By virtue of his primacy in the priesthood he can judge concerning faith and priests, 962.

[Col. 1538]

### Leo’s jurisdiction and pastoral care throughout the universal Church

#### In the suburbanicarian provinces

He reproved Dorum, bishop of Beneventum, 733. He issued a ruling concerning certain Beneventan priests who had renounced their right, 734, 735. He entrusted the execution of the command to Julius, bishop, ibid. He admonished and rebuked the bishops of Campania, Picenum, and Tuscia concerning certain abuses, 612, 616. He reserved to himself the investigation of a certain abuse, 614. He censured the bishops of the same Campania, Samnium, and Picenum for other abuses, prescribed a remedy, and threatened punishment for the disobedient, 1429, 1430.

The Sicilian bishops received the honor of consecration from the apostolic see, 716. Leo reproved and admonished them on account of certain abuses concerning baptism, ibid. He ordered three of them each year to attend the Roman synod, 724. He issued a ruling for the benefit of the churches of Tauromenium and Panormus, 728. He decreed that the goods of the churches were not to be alienated, ibid.

#### In the province subject to the metropolitan of Ravenna

Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, testifies to Eutyches that he could neither hear nor judge cases concerning faith without the consent of the Roman bishop, 779. Leo sent to Neon of Ravenna the decisions defined in the Roman synod, 1405.

#### In the province subject to the metropolitan of Milan

At Leo’s command a synod of the bishops of this province was held. Following the form of Leo’s letters and observing the procedure prescribed for ordination, it condemned the Eutychians with its own consent, while the prior judgment of the apostolic see stood before it, 1081.

#### In the province subject to Aquileia

In this province Septimus of Altinum reported to Leo that certain Pelagians had been wrongly received into communion, 589. Soon afterward the holy pontiff ordered the bishop of Aquileia to convene a synod and prescribed the manner in which they were to be received, 590, 594. He forbade those who had been received to be promoted to a higher rank, 730. Nicetas of Aquileia submitted several questions to Leo, and, seeking a solution, requested the authority of the apostolic see, 1330. In his reply Leo ordered that his letter be communicated to all the bishops of the province, so that the authority granted might be effective in everyone’s observance, 1335.

#### In Gaul

The Gallic bishops consulted the apostolic see through innumerable reports, and judgments in various cases were either confirmed or reconsidered by appeal, 634. Leo reproved many things in Hilary of Arles, 634 ff. He deprived him of metropolitan honor, 635. He acquitted Celidonius, a bishop who had appealed from Hilary’s sentence, after the matter had been examined in a synod, 635. Projectus, a bishop, and his fellow citizens complained to Leo by letter about Hilary’s promotion of another bishop over them, 636. Valentinian’s sanction prohibited the Gallic bishops from attempting anything against ancient custom without the pope’s authority, 644.

The prayers of Ravennius of Arles and other bishops were sent to Leo on behalf of the privileges of the see of Arles against that of Vienne, 993. Leo’s decision in this controversy, and the boundaries assigned by him to each metropolitan see, 998. Theodorus of Fréjus consulted Leo concerning certain doubts, 1174. Leo ordered him to bring the reply to the attention of the metropolitan, so that the other bishops might thereafter be instructed by it, 1176.

He sent the Gallic bishops his letter to Flavian together with confidential instructions, 1001. They returned a synodical letter and excused their delay, 1108. Rusticus of Narbonne sent the archdeacon Hermetes to Leo with several inquiries, so that he might learn what judgment should be held, 1416, 1419. He also inquired about matters that had been defined in certain Gallic synods, so that he might become more certain through apostolic authority, 1413. Saint Leo’s replies, 1420 ff.

The same Rusticus sent Leo the proceedings held in the case of two priests, asking what form and measure of justice he ought to maintain, 1416. Leo left this matter to Rusticus’s moderation and proposed an outstanding rule of moderation, 1417.

#### In Spain

Turribius, bishop of Astorga, informed Leo both in writing and through messengers about the remnants, errors, and books of the Priscillianists in Spain, 694, 695, 707. Saint Leo condemned the errors, 695 ff. He issued regulations concerning corrupted or apocryphal books, 706. He prescribed a general synod of all Spain, 710. He ordered the Galicians at least to convene a provincial synod, 711.

#### In Africa

Leo delegated Potentius, bishop in Caesarean Mauretania, to investigate certain abuses in that province, 658. Potentius sent the pontiff a report about everything, ibid., 666. Leo corrected the abuses, 659 ff. On this one occasion he tolerated certain matters by dispensation, 665. He entrusted the examination and judgment of two bishops to their fellow provincials, with the obligation of reporting after the examination, so that he might know what should be decided concerning them, 666.

A restored bishop complained that bishoprics had been established in his diocese that had not existed before; Leo prohibited such establishments, 667. Lupicinus, a bishop, appealed to Leo’s judgment, and communion was restored to him, 668.

#### In Illyricum

Leo ordered the metropolitans of Illyricum to obey Anastasius, the apostolic vicar of Thessalonica, 617, 618. He congratulated him on his obedience, 677. He prescribed that the metropolitans were not to ordain the bishops of their province without the consent of the apostolic vicar, and that the ordinations of those metropolitans themselves were to be reserved to the same vicar, 618, 621. He decreed that more serious cases and appeals were to be sent through the vicar’s report to the apostolic see, 619, 622, 689, 690. He prescribed other matters to the same metropolitans, 677 ff.

When the bishop of Thessalonica requested the apostolic vicariate in Illyricum through a messenger, Leo granted it and sent instructions, 620. He addressed other instructions to the same bishop, 687. He rebuked him, 683, 684, 686, 690. Atticus, the metropolitan, went to Rome with several of his fellow provincials to complain against the same vicar about violence inflicted upon him, 685. The bishop of Thessalonica sent a bishop to Rome as a messenger of his ordination, 1209.

#### In Thrace

Eutyches, archimandrite of Constantinople, warned Leo about Nestorians springing up, so that he might take precautions, 737. Condemned by his bishop Flavian of Constantinople, he complained to the same Leo, 749. He also appealed to him, 739 note, 742 note, 763, 786. The emperor Theodosius wrote to Leo on behalf of Eutyches, 761, 767. Leo urged Flavian to report the events in a fully detailed account, 765, 768.

Saint Flavian reported to the pontiff concerning Eutyches’ errors and his own judgment, and sent him the proceedings, 754 ff. After being informed of Eutyches’ appeal to Leo, he sent the acts again and acknowledged that the case needed the pontiff’s assistance, 782, 788. Leo’s celebrated judgment in his dogmatic letter to Flavian, 801. He declared that Eutyches’ error, not refuted by the synod of Constantinople, ought to be condemned, and he condemned it, 833, 881.

He mercifully granted that Eutyches, if he repented and corrected himself through full satisfaction, should be received in his own rank, 835, 841, 851, 867, 870, 888. He sent legates to carry out the entire case, 835, 836.

Anatolius of Constantinople, ordained in the place of Saint Flavian, reported his ordination to Leo, 954. The emperor and those who ordained him did likewise, 1012. Leo suspended approval of this ordination, and the reason why, 1185. He indicated the conditions under which he would grant it, 1005, 1010, 1012. He sent legates concerning this matter, 1007, 1010, 1012. After Anatolius had given an adequate satisfaction, Leo received him into communion, 1038.

He arranged the manner in which those who had fallen were to be received, and for this purpose added Anatolius to his legates by a special delegation, 1050 note. Reserving judgment concerning the leaders of the infamous Ephesian synod to the apostolic see, he prohibited Anatolius from having their names recited at the altar in the meantime, 1051.

When Leo rebuked Anatolius for his ambition, Anatolius promised obedience and satisfaction, 1262. How he gave satisfaction, ibid., 1277, 1280. Obeying Leo, he deposed Andrew, a deacon and defender of the Eutychian heresy, 1186. Aetius complained to Leo that Anatolius, the bishop, had deprived him of the archdeaconate of the Constantinopolitan Church, 1188, 1199. At Leo’s command Anatolius restored him to favor, 1262, 1278.

Anatolius suspended Andrew, suspected of Eutychian heresy and promoted to the archdeaconate of Constantinople, in order to satisfy Leo, 1262. He sought Leo’s opinion concerning what should be done with him and with other clerics hostile to Flavian, 1263. Leo replied that Andrew was to be ordained priest after giving the fullest satisfaction, while the others were to be restored to their ranks, 1278.

Basil and John, priests of Constantinople, accused of heresy, went to Rome to give an account of their faith. After being vindicated, they returned and were commended by Leo to Anatolius, the bishop, 1054. The case of Atticus, a priest of Constantinople, was entrusted by Leo to Anatolius for examination, 1313, 1343. Leo ordered Atticus to retract his errors publicly, or else to be deprived of every honor, 1328, 1338. Atticus sent writings of doubtful faith to Rome; Leo rejected them and prescribed an explicit and complete satisfaction, 1343. Leo rebuked and admonished Anatolius concerning his connivance toward his suspect clerics, 1318, 1325.

#### In Asia

Because of the controversy concerning the bishopric of Ephesus, Leo’s authority was repeatedly invoked, almost to the point of harassment, 1096 note.

#### In the East

Leo refrained, for the sake of peace and faith, from rescinding the ordination of Maximus of Antioch, performed by Anatolius of Constantinople, 1153. The same Maximus sent legates to Leo to consult him, 1212, 1214. Leo imposed certain matters upon him for execution, 1217, 1227. Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus, having been deposed, appealed to Leo, 948 note. For this reason Leo sent legates to him, 950.

#### In Egypt

Leo admonished Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning certain customary matters of discipline that he wished to be observed, 629, 631. Saint Proterius, likewise bishop of Alexandria, wrote to Leo concerning his ordination, 1192. To satisfy Leo, he sent him a clearer exposition of his faith, 1247 note, through Nestorius, 1253, 1256, 1259. Saint Leo urged him to vigilance, 1253.

After the Alexandrian Church was thrown into disorder following Marcian’s death, Leo showed concern to suppress the disturbances, exclude the heretical usurper, and elect a Catholic bishop, 1301, 1304, 1323, 1327, 1342, 1347. The usurper was expelled, 1432. Leo insisted that he not be returned to the Alexandrian see even if he made a profession of faith, but that a new Catholic bishop be ordained, ibid. and 1434.

Timothy, the Catholic bishop-elect, sent two legates to Leo with letters from the ordainers and the clergy, 1435, 1436, 1437, 1438. Leo’s authority concerning the general councils—the Second Council of Ephesus and the Council of Chalcedon: see *Second Council of Ephesus* and *Council of Chalcedon*.

Leo used Prosper’s *Chronicle* in historical matters, 259 note, 323 note, 488. Immediately after his election, Leo Augustus voluntarily suppressed the schemes of the Eutychians that had arisen at Constantinople, 1299 note, 1301 note, 1303, 1306. He thought it useful to convene a new council, 1301 note, 1310 note. Pope Leo removed him from that position, ibid.

Leo Augustus wrote to Pope Leo and to all the metropolitans, asking that they set out in writing their judgment concerning Timothy the Cat, the usurper of the Alexandrian Church, and concerning the Council of Chalcedon, 1319. He invited Pope Leo to the East, 1321. Later he requested legates, 1341, 1344. He arranged for Timothy the Cat to be expelled from Alexandria, 1432. He is praised, ibid. He was guardian of the Council of Chalcedon, 1316. He is to be numbered among the preachers of Christ, 1323. His faith almost surpassed the solicitude of the priests, 1326.

Leo, priest of Narbonne, went beyond proper bounds in his zeal for chastity, 1416. A letter of Leo, bishop of Bourges, and of two others was wrongly attributed to Leo the Great, 1471. Leontius, a bishop venerable for his antiquity, was delegated by Leo to convene councils of several provinces of Gaul, 641.

Levites: see *Deacon*.

The Old Law, insofar as it concerns the simple worship of God and rules of conduct, was not destroyed by the New Law but increased, 52, 245, 246, 358. But insofar as it concerns ceremonies, it ceased, 358. What is to be retained from the Old Law, 64. The difference between the Old Law and the Gospel, ibid. The Old Law has figures; the New has the realities themselves, 268. The law of sin must be overcome by the law of God, 362.

Libanius, deacon, 610. Christian freedom does not fulfill the law through fear but through love, 348. True freedom and peace exist for a person when the flesh is governed by the soul as judge, and the soul by God as ruler, 144.

Letters of release are to be issued in writing, 679. *Formatae*—letters given by the pontiff each year to all the bishops of the West for announcing Easter, 1079, 1260, 1283, 1297. The holy places of Palestine were venerated even by the ancients, 1289. How greatly the inhabitants of the holy places are instructed, 1287, 1288.

Lucas, one of the metropolitans of Illyricum, 677, 1307, 1311. Lucentius, bishop of Ascoli, legate of Leo to the East, 1046, 1048, 1052; and for the ecumenical council held at Chalcedon, 1061, 1064, 1066, 1069. He brought the Chalcedonian proceedings to Rome together with the synod’s report, 1124 note.

Lucianus, bishop of Byza, subscribed to the report of the Council of Chalcedon, 1104. He was sent to Rome by the emperor and Anatolius to obtain confirmation of the Chalcedonian canon in favor of the see of Constantinople, 1120, 1136. Leo sent him back, 1153, 1158, 1169, 1201.

Lupicinus, an African bishop, appealed to Leo, who received him into communion and decreed that his case should be judged in Africa, 668.

## M

The error of Macedonius and the Macedonians, 81, 299. The solemn feast of the holy Maccabees was celebrated in Africa, 452, but not at Rome in Leo’s time, ibid. A sermon on the Maccabees attributed to Leo is restored to Augustine, ibid. Their martyrdom is described, 454. How their virtues are to be imitated, 455.

Where the three Magi saw the star, 112. To understand the sign of the star, they could also have been prompted by Balaam’s prophecies, 123. But aided more greatly by grace, they understood, 112, 119, 123, 124, 128. And they sought the child, 112. Whence they came, 132. Why the star appeared to them, 118, 119. Why it led them to Jerusalem, 116. Why they sought the child there, 112, 123. The calling of the Magi represents the beginnings of our calling, 117, 121. The Magi represented the nations, 129, 140. Their gifts, 113; explained mystically, 124. What they signify, 113, 119. How they can be offered by Christians, 133. Why the Magi returned by another road, 120.

Majorianus, bishop of Piacenza, 1082. Why Manes is often called a Manichaean, 304 note. The heresy of Manes, 307, 1238. At what time it became known that he was to be condemned, 305, 487 ff. The Manichaeans believed that the Holy Spirit had appeared in Manes and had not descended earlier, 304, 305. They worshiped Manes under the name of the Holy Spirit, 126. The madness of Manes, or of the Manichaeans, 373. Manes was a teacher of impiety, 126.

The errors of the Manichaeans, 33, 50, 72, 80, 81, 125, 126, 160, 161, 179, 709, 877, 976, 1359. In other heresies something true is found; in the doctrine of the Manichaeans, nothing, 81. The Manichaeans worshiped Christ in the sun and moon, 126. In honor of the sun and moon they fasted on the first and second days of the week, 160, 699, 1270. Therefore they were impious twice over, 161. Their abstinence was perverse and blameworthy, 127, 159. They received Christ’s body with an unworthy mouth, 161, but avoided drinking the blood, ibid. Their sacrifices, 30. Their adorations, 72. Their male and female elect, 50. They disturbed very many regions, ibid. Their number at Rome increased, and why, ibid. note. Their bishop, ibid., 50, 624. They were discovered through Leo’s investigation, 50, 80, 127, 624; when, 584. They were to be denounced to the priests, 33. Leo held an assembly against them, and what was done there, ibid., 626, 708. Their hypocrisy, 127. One must abstain from their company, 50, especially women, 51. Many were brought back to repentance; others were assigned perpetual exile by judges, 624. On account of those who fled Rome, Leo wrote to the bishops of Italy, ibid. Imperial statutes against them already existed, ibid., 626. Valentinian’s constitution after Leo’s judgment, 626. The Priscillianists agree with the Manichaeans, 699, 701, 708. The error of Eutyches is akin to that of the Manichaeans, 976, 1179. Leo sent the proceedings against the Manichaeans to Turribius, 708.

When the emperor Marcian assumed the imperial office, 1019 note. He informed Leo of his election and disclosed his plan to convene a council, 1017. He ordered that the bishops at it should declare what Leo had defined, 1025. At his command the body of Saint Flavian was brought honorably to Constantinople, and the bishops deposed and exiled with Flavian were recalled, 1032.

He summoned the council, 1060, 1063, 1063 note. He attended the council at its sixth session, 1094. Together with his wife Pulcheria, he received the definition of faith given to them, 1128. He sent legates to Leo with letters requesting confirmation of the proceedings, especially concerning the privilege of the see of Constantinople, 1114. He requested explicit confirmation of the Chalcedonian definition as necessary, 1182, 1184 note. He praised the pontiff’s steadfastness because Leo refused to confirm the privilege of the see of Constantinople, 1184 note, 1203. Leo commended Atticus to him, 1186, and advised him to rebuke Anatolius, 1187. Marcian rebuked him, 1191.

He restrained and instructed the Palestinian monks who were rioting against the Chalcedonian definition, 1203 note, 1207 note, 1208, 1245, 1246. In confidence he asked Leo to admonish the Augusta Eudocia, patroness of the monks, 1209. Leo asked Marcian to inquire diligently among the Egyptians or other experts concerning the date of Easter in the year 455, 1231 ff. For this purpose the emperor sent an *agens in rebus* to Alexandria, 1276, 1282.

Following Leo’s example, and intending to suppress the rioting Alexandrian monks, Marcian declared the Chalcedonian faith consistent with the teaching of Athanasius, Theophilus, and Cyril, 1257 note. Leo asked him to have the letter to Flavian carefully translated and, sealed with his own seal, delivered to the Alexandrian judges, 1258, 1260. He ordered that the heretics Carosus and Dorotheus be expelled from their monasteries, 1298. He wrote to Leo concerning the consecration of Basil of Antioch, 1309.

He was most devoted to ecclesiastical peace, 1044. Guardian of the faith, 1277. Full of the power of the Holy Spirit, 1278. Of venerable memory, 1299. Of holy memory, 1309. Of blessed memory, 1340. His benefits to the Church, 1046. Through his zeal nearly every attempt of the heresies was extinguished, 1281.

Marcion, the heretic, 49. His error, 699, 1238. Saint Mark the Evangelist first governed the Alexandrian Church, 628. He was ordained by Saint Peter, 629. He could transmit nothing other than what he had received from the one who ordained him, ibid., 1253.

Saint Mary the Virgin conceived first in her mind and then in her body, 63. Her faith was confirmed by the miracle involving Elizabeth, 65. Her virginity before and during childbirth, ibid., 68, 72, 73, 74, 79, 80, 92, 109, 175, 817; and after childbirth, 69. In the Incarnation of the Word she was only the minister of the bodily substance, 8. She was the branch from the root of Jesse foretold in Isaiah’s prophecy, 78.

Marianus, a priest and legate of Maximus of Antioch to Leo, 1212. Marion, an Egyptian bishop exiled for the faith, 1336. Martinus, archimandrite of Constantinople, adhering to Saint Flavian, 850, 937, 983, 1011, 1019, 1021.

Martyrs are rivals of the apostles in triumphs, 826. Through imitation of love they are as close to Christ as through imitation of his Passion, 337. The number of Christians increased through the punishments of the martyrs, 134, 325. Thousands of blessed martyrs surround and crown Rome, 326. Innumerable thousands of martyrs, 306. Martyrs can be called teachers, not by word but by deed, 338. Miracles through martyrs, 22. Praise of the martyrs, 271. They are honored above others in the churches that they raised by their teachings, 427. The glory of martyrdom, 117, 133. Churches dedicated in honor of the martyrs, 336 note.

Marriage is a sacrament, 1422. It is indissoluble, 1331. It exists only between freeborn and equal persons, 1422. How a legitimate marriage can exist between a free person and a slave, ibid. Whether it is lawful for one who has completed penance, 1331. It is genuine even before baptism, 621. If a woman’s husband has been taken captive and she has joined herself to another, she is to return to the first, 1330. In such a case the second husband is not culpable, 1331. Women who refuse to return to their first husbands are to be excommunicated, 1332.

Maximinus, a count, 1022. Maximinus, a Gallic bishop, 1107, 1136. Three Gallic bishops named Maximus, 1107, 1110, 1136. One of these, or another fourth Maximus, 998. Maximus, an African Donatist bishop ordained from the laity after giving a pledge of conversion, was not rejected by Leo, 665.

Maximus, bishop of Antioch, was ordained by Anatolius of Constantinople against the canons, 1151, 1153, 1161. Through Leo’s *tractoria*—his letter to Flavian, to be subscribed by the bishops of Maximus’s provinces—he obtained the condemnation of Nestorius and Eutyches, 1059. Leo’s letter to the same man, 1212. The Eastern churches were commended to him, 1213. He was accused, and it was ordered that his case be examined, 1296. Maximus, an Egyptian bishop exiled for the faith, 1336. Maximus, bishop of Turin, 1083.

The bishops of the province of Milan, assembled at Leo’s command, sent him a synodical letter, 1081. Leo sent the same synodical letter to Constantinople, 1315. Eusebius, bishop of Milan, 1080.

One must frequently devote oneself to sacred meditation, 59. The order of Melchizedek is explained, 11. Why his parents are not mentioned in Scripture, ibid. His sacrifice was a figure of Christ’s sacrifice, 21. “Meos” [possibly an OCR corruption; context uncertain]—blessed is she who is a guest of earthly beings, 186.

Greater delights were given to the mind than to the flesh, 320. Merit is measured according to the will, 39.

Metropolitans are called primates, 1156, 1173. They are to be chosen with greater care, 622. They ordain their fellow provincials, 621. They have the right of first judgment, 619. From where their prerogative arose, ibid. Their rights are to be preserved, 1167. In doubtful matters the metropolitan is to be consulted by the bishop, 1173. Lesser metropolitans obey greater ones, 685.

Miracles through martyrs occur almost everywhere to manifest their merits, 22.

The mercy of God has never been denied to the human race, 322. It was the cause of our restoration, 39. Its work is the more wondrous because…, 203, 204. It must not be abused, 189; who abuse it, ibid. God’s mercy is held out to us amid adversity, 266. It is to be sought by showing mercy, 37. It is ready for the merciful, 166. No one should despair of it, 9. It surpasses the sins of wrongdoers, 1069. How pleasing mercy toward the poor is to God, 183. Works of mercy save human beings, 32. God wishes us to be merciful, 370. The merciful person is an imitator of God, 166. God’s mercy and truth are to be imitated, and the connection between the two, 171. Commendation of mercy, 211. See *Almsgiving*.

The Mass is a sacrifice, 631. In the same basilica it is to be repeated as often as a new people arrives, ibid. The offering of Christ’s body and blood now stands in place of all the sacrifices of the Old Law, 228.

The meek: who they are and what their reward is, 369. The character of Christian modesty, 157.

Whether monks may abandon their chosen way of life, 1426. Whether they may serve in the army or marry, ibid. Their profession is a commitment to humility, 856. It consists chiefly in faith and charity, 937. Who the true monks are, 1178. The monks’ commitment and profession, 1242. It is not theirs to preach, but the priests’, 1211, 1217, 1227.

Death is the punishment of sin, 71. Death is to be meditated upon, so that it may not be unexpected, 354. How one must die and rise again with Christ, 18. What the life-giving death is, 281.

The rule of conduct in doubtful matters: see *Doubts*. Human conduct must be weighed on the scales of the divine commandments, 187.

### Woman

Through the credulity of one woman all human beings perished, 51. In what sense the serpent’s head is to be crushed by the seed of the woman, 67. Women above all must beware of heretics, 50.

The world was created in the same month in which it was redeemed, 232. The wisdom of the world can know neither God nor the truth, 85, 176. The peace of the world is dangerous, 275. How one should use the things of the world, 96, 295.

Musaeus, the bishop who ordained Timothy of Solofatiolus, 1437. The deceptive melody of music, 349.

## N

Rusticus, bishop of the Church of Narbonne, 1107, 1110, 1136, 1416, 1458. The bishop’s “birthday” means the day of his consecration, 7 note. The Nativity of Christ: see *Christ*. Human nature, inclined toward worse things through the stain of sin, [Col. 1543] 55. Nevertheless it is supported by spiritual assistance, ibid. It was exalted through Christ, 71, 75, 97, 202. God gave human nature more in restoring it than in creating it, 79. See *Human being*.

Nectarius, a Gallic bishop, 890, 998, 1110, 1136. The perilous condition of merchants, 1424. Neo, bishop of Ravenna, 1405. The white garment of the newly baptized, 420. Neophytes are not to be ordained, 662, 687.

The error of Nestorius, 74 note, 100, 288, 356, 847, 854, 1049, 1138, 1213, 1235, 1237, 1355. Nestorius was anathematized by the Church of Constantinople, 1059, and by the First Council of Ephesus, 1064. Those whom Eutyches had denounced as Nestorians, 738 note, 870, 877. Before the Council of Chalcedon the Easterners had subscribed against both Nestorius and Eutyches, 1066.

Nestorius, an Egyptian bishop, brought to Leo the letter of Proterius of Alexandria, 1253, and likewise the letter of the emperor Marcian, 1256. He was exiled for the faith, 1336.

Whether the Council of Nicaea prescribed a nineteen-year cycle, 604 note. The Nicene canons are inviolable and are to be observed reverently, 687, 1155, 1163, 1165, 1171, 1214, 1279. The Nicene Creed set out by Leo, 1359. Why Leo opposed it to the Eutychians, ibid. note.

Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, seeks the judgment and authority of the apostolic see in several doubtful matters, 1330. Nicetas, a Gallic bishop, 89. Nicolaus, a priest and legate of Anastasius of Thessalonica to Pope Leo, 619, 620. Simplicianus, bishop of Novara, 1084. The doctrine of the Novatians, 665. The origin of apostolic nuncios to rulers, 1187. Legitimate marriages, 1422. The Priscillianists, together with the Manichaeans, condemned marriage and its use, 701. See *Marriage*.
