## O

Nothing is difficult for the obedient and humble, 130. God’s grace offers its help, and obedience softens command, 130. The offering of Christ’s body and blood, 228. The term “observances” used for fasting, 159 note. The stewards of the Church are not to be heard by lay judges, 1283. The antiquity of ecclesiastical office demonstrated from Leo, 148 note. See Sacred Scripture. Olympius, deacon and legate of Maximus of Antioch, 1212. Olympius, subassistant and informer concerning Anatolius of Constantinople’s letter to Leo, 1317. He was sent back, 1328. The necessity of good works, 46, 90, 117, 130, 1433. The distinction between heavenly and earthly things, 173. Good works torment the devil, 29. To what extent all good works are to be made common to everyone, 346. The good works of the flock also benefit pastors, 13, 14. The measure of heavenly gifts does not depend upon the quality of our works, 9. Whether, and to what extent, the works of moral virtues in unbelievers are sins, 491.

Optatianus, bishop of Brescia, 1084.

The commendation of prayer, 42, 43. The excellence of common prayer, 56, 57, 345. Prayer is aided by almsgiving, 48, 52. And by fasting, 42, 44, 48. The prayer of one who fasts is terrifying to the devil, 342. Prayer is necessary against the force of temptation, 213. Prayer is to be employed in temptation, 223. God commands that one have recourse to him, 364. The commandment is therefore given so that the help of the one commanding may be sought, 187. If anything in God’s commandments appears impossible or difficult, one must have recourse to the one who commands, 163. The condition of Christian prayer, 177, 187, 191. One may ask for what ought not to be granted, 213. God shows mercy by refusing what would cause harm, ibid. No one prays as he ought without the Holy Spirit, 303. Leo censures the practice of praying facing east, 94 note.

The Lord’s Prayer. How we ask for the coming of God’s kingdom, 353. How we ask that God’s will be done, ibid., 361. How we ask God to forgive us our debts, 177, 187, 190.

Ordination. What it means to lay hands on someone hastily, 619. The punishment of one who ordains improperly, 660. Ordination is a sacrament, ibid. What must be examined in those to be ordained, 621, 662. With thorough examination, 731. Not neophytes, ibid. and 687. Not slaves, 612. Not bound by any original condition unless the consent of those who claim some authority over them has been obtained, 613. Not bigamists, nor husbands of widows, 614, 618, 621, 636, 671, 687. Not laymen, 662, 665. Not one whose life is freer, 614. They are to be instructed in ecclesiastical disciplines from childhood, 673. The discipline of the Roman Church admitted to the orders only those who, either from childhood or, among adults, immediately after baptism, had devoted themselves to the clergy, 662 note. This discipline was not universal, ibid. The merits of labor and other matters are to be weighed, 663. Leo does not dispense with bigamists, 674. Whether an ordination performed by a pseudo-bishop is valid, 1420. Certain unlawful ordinations among the Africans censured, 658. How dangerous a bad ordination is, 659. Ambition, favor, or money must have no place, 621. The required intervals between orders are to be observed, 623, 663. No one is to be ordained by leaping over stages [Col. 1544], 623. The ordination of bishops, presbyters, and deacons is called consecration, 622, 1186. The more sacred anointing of priests, 228. Priestly or Levitical ordination is to be celebrated after the Sabbath, or around the beginning of the following night, or on the morning of the Sunday itself, 629. The fast of both the ordaining bishop and the ordinand must precede it, ibid. The day of ordination is Sunday, 622, 639, 1186. According to apostolic tradition, 1186. The ordination of a presbyter performed by Anatolius of Constantinople on Friday is censured by Leo, 1186. According to apostolic tradition, 1186. The ordination of a presbyter performed by Anatolius of Constantinople on Friday is censured by Leo, 1186. The day of the ordination of pontiffs, or bishops, is called a “birthday,” 7 note.

Origen’s error concerning souls, 881. Origen, investigator of the principles, 775. Why he was so called, 771.

Original sin. See Original Sin.

The dangers of leisure, 134.

## P

Saint Pachomius, founder of the Egyptian coenobia, 603. The disturbances and violence of the Palestinian monks against the Catholics, 1177 notes, 1180, 1192, 1234, 1242. They were to be restrained by the emperor, 1178. The emperor Marcian and the empress Pulcheria sent letters to restrain and instruct them, 1203 note, 1207 note, 1208 note. The empress Eudocia, residing at Jerusalem, favored them, 1209 note. Leo writes to Eudocia so that she may bring them back to sound judgment, 1234. He also writes to the monks themselves, 1236. Through Marcian’s concern these disturbances were brought to an end, 1245, 1246.

Palladius, a Gallic bishop, 998, 1111, 1136. Silanus, deacon of the Church of Palermo, 607. The clergy of Palermo complain to Saint Leo in the Roman synod about their recently deceased bishop, 728. Pansophius, a court official, delivered Leo’s letter to Flavian of Constantinople, 786. Panulvius, the bishop who ordained Timothy Solofaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, 1437. Paphnutius, bishop and ordainer of the same Timothy, 1437.

The eight hundred parishes of the bishopric of Cyrus in the time of Theodoret, 947. Parish priests in the smaller communities, 667. The urban parishes of Rome, to whose presbyters the Manichaeans were to be brought, 33.

The origin of the word “Passover,” 609. The greatest of festivals, 177, 180, 183, 189, 1079, 1282. This alone is to be called the great day, and why, 422. How it is to be celebrated, 274, 276, 287. How evil it is to neglect the Paschal feast, 274. Paschal communion, 189. At Easter, criminals were released by the emperors, 152, 180, 485. Leo appears to have believed that the Passover had been delayed by the Jews at the time of Christ’s Passion, 219. We ought to remain such as it is fitting to be found on the feast day, 156. The Paschal day in the year 417 was revealed by a miracle in the time of Zosimus, 610. Responsibility for calculating the Paschal date was assigned to the bishop of Alexandria, 1228 note, 1248. How important it is not to differ or err on this day, 1233. Leo was concerned with determining the date of Easter; concerning Easter in the year 444 he wrote to Saint Cyril and Paschasinus, who replied in writing, 608. What the controversy concerning Easter in that year consisted in, 601 note. For Easter in the year 445 he wrote to Paschasinus, Marcian, and Julian, 1059, 1228, 1232, 1247, 1260, 1276. Proterius’s reply, 1264. What the controversy was, 1055. Out of a desire for peace, Saint Leo adhered to the Easterners in this year, 1282 note, 1284, 1297. The Paschal day was announced to all Westerners by the Roman pontiff, 1297. Formal letters announcing Easter, 1079, 1260, 1283. The Paschal cycle. See Cycle. What the Paschal day was in the year 452, 1079. What it was in the years 453 and 454, 1232.

Paschasinus, bishop of Lilybaeum, assisted by Leo in his distress caused by the Vandal invasion, 607 note. He replied to Leo concerning the question of Easter in the year 444, ibid. Leo entrusted his decrees for the Sicilians to Paschasinus’s care, 724. He instructed him concerning Eutychian affairs, 1057. He charged him to investigate carefully the date of Easter in the year 455, 1059. He was appointed legate to the Council of Chalcedon, 1061. He was to preside there as the pontiff’s representative, 1062.

Paschasius, bishop of Genoa, 1083.

The Passion of Christ. See Christ.

Pastor, bishop of Asti, 1084.

The holy Fathers as interpreters of the faith and of Scripture, 1044. Leo follows the tradition of the Fathers, 1012 note, 1059, 1293, 1379. From that tradition he determines the questions proposed, 1405. The tradition of the holy Fathers is the rule of faith, 1006. Those who err from it are to be instructed, 1209, 1254, 1255, 1257. Saint Leo confirmed the doctrine defined against the Eutychian heresy by the tradition and testimonies of the Fathers, 1059 note.

The title “patriarch” given to the Roman pontiff by the emperor Theodosius, 985, 989.

Patricius, deacon of Constantinople and Anatolius’s legate to Leo, 1039.

The disciples of Sabellius are rightly called Patripassians, 697.

[Col. 1545] Patroclus, bishop of Arles, received authority from the Apostolic See which no one before him had obtained, 637.

Saint Paul, made a preacher from a persecutor, 443, 445. A partner in Peter’s glory, 323. Joined to Peter under Nero, 325. Father and shepherd of the Romans, 321. In what sense, ibid. note. The special teacher of the nations, 325. In what sense Leo wrote that the election made Saints Peter and Paul equal, without touching Peter’s primacy, 326 note. Paul’s predestination before all ages, 446. Why Paul’s feast was transferred to another day, 445. Paul, an Egyptian bishop exiled for the faith, 1336.

The poor and the rich have one nature, 38. Whether neglect of them is venial, 35. The poor are to be assisted, 48. Especially modest and bashful, 32. What it means to understand the poor, 33. In the poor we feed Christ, ibid. Without mercy toward the poor no virtue is beneficial, 35. The poor are not excluded from giving alms, 30, 63, 158. The poor person needs little, 45. A Christian poor man is always rich, 157. Who are the true and evangelical poor, 368. The poor are to be crowned for their patience, 48. Why God willed there to be poor, ibid. Poverty of spirit, or humility, is the first step toward blessedness, 367. Meekness is the friend of poverty, ibid. The magnanimous poverty of Christ and the apostles, 368.

What peace with God is, 89, 91. What true peace is, 103, 644, 371. Peace arose for us from Christ’s birth, 90. What the peace of the world is, 91. Who are the peacemakers, the children of God, 371. The necessity of fraternal peace, 188.

God makes good use of sin, 1220. Not all sins are equal, 190. The twofold remedy for sin, 1174. After sin one must repent quickly, and why, 284. No one is without sin, 20, 46, 137, 185. No sin is without pleasure, 135. Sins are the cause of calamities, 1190. Sinners are not to be hated, 182. The remission of sins. See Reconciliation.

—Mortal sin, 170.—

—Original sin, 79, 88, 186, 198, 255, 269, 351, 361, 592, 703. It passed from one person into all, 79. Weakness and mortality are the punishment of sin, 286.—

—Lighter sin, and the care with which such sins must be removed, 165, 345.—

The errors of the Pelagians, 591. Their booklet presented to Augustine of Aquileia, 587. They were found in the province of Aquileia, ibid., 589. Leo orders a remedy to be applied to their remnants, 590, 594, 730 note. Other Pelagians, especially Julian, were crushed under Leo and fled Rome, 584.

Pentecost. Why the Holy Spirit was sent fifty days after Easter, 297. This sending of the Holy Spirit was not the beginning of the gift but an addition of generosity, 302, 309. The patriarchs and prophets, and others, were animated by the same Spirit, 302. The Pentecost fast according to apostolic tradition, 300, 308.

Pilgrimages to the thresholds of the apostles, 444.

The true justice of the perfect is that they never presume themselves to be perfect, 148. One must always make progress in this life, ibid., 168, 190. See Christian Justice.

Persecution is to be endured patiently, 1328, 1336. All good people suffer persecution, 271. There was not one cause alone of the persecution of Christians, 178. The first general persecution was under Nero, 325. The eighth persecution, 305, 490. Persecution increases the Church, 325. How much it contributed to faith, 134. It is not absent even in the Church’s peace, 455. What persecution in the Church’s peace is, 1417.

Perseverance in goodness, 281.

The distinction of persons in the Trinity, but unity of essence, 83, 196. Why certain things are attributed to individual persons, 301.

The rock of the Church: what it is, 461. See Saint Peter.

Petronianus, a vagabond, falsely claimed to be Leo’s deacon in Gaul, 893. Petronius, a Gallic bishop, 1111. Petronius, a presbyter and legate of the Gallic bishops to Leo, 998. See Regulus.

Saint Peter, first of all bishops, 13. Prince of the whole Church, 19, 291. Placed by Christ before all the apostles and all the Fathers of the Church for the calling of the nations, 16. First in apostolic dignity, 16, 17. Prince of the apostolic order, 323. He obtained the primacy of the apostleship, 445. Prince of the episcopal crown, 642. The episcopate was principally established in Peter, 633. Peter’s primacy was the reward of his faith, 617. The chair of ecclesiastical primacy was divinely handed over to Peter so that it might be founded upon perpetual stability, 436.

Peter confessed Christ so that, prepared to govern the whole Church, he might first learn what he was to teach, 239. Peter was called “rock” by Christ because he was made solid by Christ’s power, 17. He received the solidity of a rock that would not be shaken by any assaults, 13, 193. Because of the firmness of faith that Peter was to preach, he heard: “You are Peter, and upon this rock…” 239. Apart from that rock which the Lord placed in the foundation, no structure will be stable, 1149. Peter’s surname is the rock of the Catholic faith, 1213. The Church was founded upon Peter’s faith, 12, 193, 461. It was established by Christ in Peter’s firmness, 617, 633, 634. The firmness bestowed upon Peter through Christ was conferred through Peter upon the apostles, 18. Peter’s solidity was transmitted to his heirs, that is, to the Roman pontiffs, 22. Peter, persevering in the strength he had received as a rock, did not abandon the reins of the Church’s government, 12. Why Christ prayed for Peter’s faith, 18. In Peter the strength of all is fortified, ibid. The honor of power in Peter, 325. In Peter’s chair Christ both utterly overturned evil things and strengthened good things with eternal stability, 436. Who would attempt to diminish Peter’s power? 634.

Saint Peter’s privileges, 12. The keys were given to him, 17. The right of this power passed to the apostles and other bishops, but Peter’s form was placed before all, 18. What Peter’s privilege is in this matter, ibid. It is explained, 463. Peter’s confession of faith expounded, 825, 863. Peter’s threefold confession of love, 19. Peter was kindly corrected by Christ, 194. In Christ’s Passion, Peter’s human boldness, 215. Fervent in faith and charity, he drew the sword, 222. In Peter’s fall constancy was lacking, not faith, 233. Why he was permitted to fall, ibid. Peter’s tears possessed the sacred power of baptism, ibid. With what eyes Christ looked upon Peter, who was to be converted, 206, 233. He quickly returned to his firmness, 233. How he was led out of prison, 447.

Saint Peter founded the Church of Antioch, 324, 1167, 1213. By preaching he imbued Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, 324, 325. He came to Rome under Claudius and died under Nero, 324. His two arrivals in Rome must be distinguished, 325 note. Why he was sent to Rome, 325. Peter’s wealth and poverty, 368. Concerning the day of the death of Saints Peter and Paul, 494. Peter’s body is in Rome, 19, 332. The gathering of pilgrims at the thresholds of the apostles, 444.

The feast of Saint Peter’s Chair, 432, 498. On what day it was celebrated at Rome, ibid., 959. Very solemn, 962. Vigils were held for it, ibid.

Peter, an Egyptian bishop exiled for the faith, 1336. Ordainer of Timothy Solofaciolus, 1437. Peter, archimandrite of Constantinople, 937.

Saint Peter Chrysologus, bishop of Ravenna, writes to Eutyches, 775. His complete letter is vindicated, 769. Its date, 773.

Peter, bishop of Corinth, 1307, 1311. Peter, deacon and legate of Juvenal of Jerusalem to Leo, 1285.

Philocalus Furius Dionysius, author at Rome of the Bucherian calendar and other documents of the fourth century, 496.

Photinus’s error, 49, 81, 373. The Photinians, 980.

Christ died through Pilate’s cowardice more than through his power, 207. His crime and judgment, 225. Cruel clemency, 226, 235.

Placentinus, bishop of Majorian, 1082.

The empress Placidia came to Rome on the day before Saint Peter’s feast, 959. At Saint Leo’s request she wrote to the emperor Theodosius, 964, and to the empress Pulcheria, 972.

Poemenius, an Egyptian bishop exiled for the faith, 1336.

Why punishment is delayed by God, 130.

Repentance is not to be postponed, 135, 1176. Everyone needs it, 165. It is necessary even for the just, 167, 170. The order of repentance, 1174. Whether communion is to be given to those dying in repentance, 1174, 1175, 1423. What is to be done concerning those who become mute after seeking repentance, 1176. Whether repentance is later to be granted to those who initially refused it, 1424. Whether penitents may conduct business and bring lawsuits, ibid. Whether they may serve in the army, 1425. Whether it is venial and more tolerable for a young person to marry after repentance, ibid. What penance is required of those who eat sacrificial foods, 1332, 1428. What is required of idolaters, murderers, and fornicators, 1428. In the case of apostates from the faith, the canonical rule is to be observed, 1176. The measure of repentance is contrition of heart, 1332. What penance is to be given to those baptized out of fear, ibid. What is to be given to those baptized by heretics, 1334. The time of repentance is shortened at the bishop’s judgment; he must take account of old age, dangers, and illness, 1333. Care must be taken lest the difficulty of pardon make the cure slower, 1437. See Confession, Imposition of Hands, Reconciliation.

Public penance was not imposed on presbyters and deacons who had fallen, but private penance was imposed according to apostolic tradition, 1421. Nor was it imposed on other clerics, 1334 note.

Polemius, the writer. See Silvius.

The Roman pontiff. See Roman Pontiff.

Possidonius, an Alexandrian presbyter sent to Rome several times, 632 note.

Potentius, an African bishop delegated by Saint Leo, sent a report, 658, 666.

The commandments of the old law. See Old Law.

Why the commandment was given, 163, 187, 364. The most splendid mirror of life, 187. Things impossible because of human weakness become possible through grace, 362, 479. See Grace. In difficult matters one must have recourse to prayer. See Prayer.

Preaching is the priestly office, 140. See the duty of preaching.

Prescription. Human laws remove human claims after thirty years, 775 note.

Praestantius, bishop of Bergamo, 1084.

Presumption is to be avoided, 9. To presume that one can easily resist temptations is a sin, 154.

Presbyters, according to apostolic tradition, are not subject to public penance but to private penance, 1421. The order of consecration must be observed among them, 735. Titular presbyters at Rome, 33. Parish priests in the smaller communities, 667. A parish priest in a rural church, 610.

Rulers ought to restrain those who disturb the Church, 1211. See Emperors.

The true dignity of rulers is to serve Christ, 134.

The sect of the Priscillianists, almost a cesspool of all errors, 695. Sabellians, 697. Arians, 698. It adopted the poison of Paul of Samosata and Photinus, ibid. The poison of Cerdo, Marcion, and Manichaeus, 699. How impiously it understood the Trinity, 697. It introduced a fatal necessity from the stars, 695, 704. Other errors, 697 ff. Bishops infected with this heresy, 697. They baptized with oil, 713, 714. They corrupted the Scriptures, 697. They fabricated apocryphal writings, 714. They were discovered in Spain, 695, 712, 715. When Bishop Turibius reported these errors, Leo condemned them, 695 ff. He ordered Spanish councils to be held, 710, 711.

The privileges of the Churches are to be preserved, 1149, 1214.

Saint Proclus of Constantinople, 1277. His sermon translated into Latin and attributed to Leo, 385. Also another sermon, whose ancient version, previously unpublished, is presented, 438.

Proculeianus, a Gallic bishop, 1111, 1136.

The complaint of Projectus, a Gallic bishop, against Hilary of Arles, 636.

The prophets spoke of future things as though they were past, 260.

Saint Prosper corrected the Latin Paschal cycle, 602 note, 1055. Leo used Prosper’s Chronicle in historical matters, 259 note, 323 note. Prosper produced three or four editions of this Chronicle, 488. When Prosper presented booklets against the Pelagians, those heretics disappeared from Rome, and at what time, 583.

The prosperity of the wicked is a stumbling block to some of the just, 164.

Saint Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, writes to Leo with those who ordained him and with the clergy concerning his ordination, 1192. Leo replies to him, ibid. He demands fuller letters from him, 1247. Leo’s replying letters to the same man, 1253. He congratulates him on his faith, 1256, 1259. Proterius writes to Leo concerning the date of Easter in the year 455, at the emperor’s command, 1282. His death at the hands of the heretics, 1299 note. His body was burned and his ashes scattered as an insult, 1325. He was called “of holy memory,” 1304.

Divine providence. See God.

Who our neighbor is, 40. He is to be loved, and why, ibid., 41.

The singing of the Psalms. See Singing.

The passage of Psalm 95, “The Lord has reigned from the wood,” 209.

We must become children, 138, 139, 190.

The eulogies of the empress Saint Pulcheria, 849, 853, 919, 1009, 1035, 1036, 1048, 1076, 1158, 1188, 1206, 1207. Leo stirred up her zeal against the new heresy of Eutyches, 849, 856, 921. He specifically entrusted her with an apostolic mission to the emperor, 923. The letter of Hilary, a Roman deacon, to the same woman, 926. And to the empress Placidia, 971. Saint Leo rejoiced at Pulcheria’s letters, 982, 983. She informed Leo that Anatolius of Constantinople had subscribed to the letter to Flavian, that Saint Flavian’s body had been honorably transferred to Constantinople, and that the bishops expelled with Flavian had been recalled, 1029, 1031. Leo commended his legates to her and asked that Eutyches be transferred to a more distant place, 1049. She attended the Council of Chalcedon with the emperor Marcian and received from the Fathers, at the confession of Saint Euphemia, the definition of the faith, 1128 note. She instructed and rebuked the turbulent monks in Palestine by letter, 1207 and 1208 note.

## Q

Lent, the greatest and most sacred fast, 184, 156. Why it precedes Easter, 181. Useful and necessary for Christians, 165, 184. It derives from divine and apostolic institution, 156, 168, 177. It was observed throughout the whole world, 149. During this time one must serve God more diligently and live more holily, 144, 149, 153, 157, 167, 173, 176, 183, 186, 191. Whoever does not live more holily during Lent casts reproach upon the Church, 137. It is a time of reconciliation and forgiveness, 155, 180, 183, 187, 188. During this time the clemency of rulers is to be imitated, 152. At this time the devil uses more serious snares, 144. In some places it began on the Sunday of Quinquagesima, 408 note. To what pursuits one should devote oneself during Lent, 173.

Various questions frequently proposed to the Roman pontiff, 1405, 1416. Where they were decided, see Doubts.

Quesnel refuted, 5, 9 note, 14 note, 21 note, 23, 38 note, 95 note, 192 note, 259 note, 279, 326 note, 327, 334, 337 note, 379, 433, 451, 461, 464, 467, 479, 480, 481, 482, 486, 488, 490, 491, 495, 498 ff., 502, 567, 574, 586, [Col. 1548] 626, 633, 636 note, 639 note, 645, 648, 651, 654, 663 note, 665 note, 666 note, 671 note, 678 note, 680 note, 681 note, 725, 727 note, 728 note, 730 note, 734 note, 745, 748, 754 note, 773, 801 note, 838 note, 843, 852 note, 859 note, 871, 875 note, 885 note, 887 note, 889 note, 897, 917 note, 951, 959, 984, 992 note, 1002 note, 1010 note, 1013, 1020 note, 1043 note, 1050 note, 1061 note, 1083 note, 1142 note, 1215 note, 1219 note, 1229 note, 1242 note, 1251, 1257 note, 1298 note, 1304, 1307, 1317 note, 1333 note, 1346 note, 1375 note, 1408 note, 1409, 1411, 1426 note, 1429 note, 1436 note.

Quintius, bishop of Albigaunum, 1084. Quintus, bishop of Tortona, 1082.

## R

Ravennius, bishop of Arles after Saint Hilary, 890, 993. He was also approved by Leo before his own election, 890, 994. Leo approved the election, 890, 891. He asks Ravennius to expel from communion with all the Churches Petronianus the vagabond, who pretended to be a Roman deacon, 892. The prayers of the bishops adhering to the see of Arles were sent to Leo so that he might restore to Ravennius the prerogatives that he had taken from Hilary, 994. The bishop of Vienne complains to Leo that Ravennius ordained the bishop of Vaison, 998. Leo’s response and judgment concerning this controversy, 999. Leo sends Ravennius the letter written to Flavian together with instructions, 1000. He sends him formal letters announcing the Paschal day of the year 452, 1079. After convening a synod at Leo’s command, Ravennius sends him a synodical letter, 1107. Leo admonishes him concerning the proceedings at Chalcedon, 1137 ff. Through him this information was to be transmitted to the Spaniards, 1140. He receives from Leo a copy of the sentence of Chalcedon against Dioscorus, 1111.

The bishops of Ravenna: Saint Peter Chrysologus, 775; Neo, 1405. The ancient catalogues of the Church of Ravenna are to be judged only with respect to the order of the bishops, 1403.

Reconciliation and the remission of sins do not take place without the invocation of the Holy Spirit, 303. Sins are absolved through the supplication of priests, 1174, 1175; through the prayers of the Church, 1435; with the apostolic key unlocking the doors of mercy, 186. See Confession, Imposition of Hands, Penance.

The cause of our redemption was God’s mercy, 39, 255. Why redemption was delayed, 118. The restoration of humanity is more wonderful than creation, 255. No human being could have merited it, ibid. It extends even to all the ages that preceded it, ibid. In our restoration the Trinity divided the work among itself—in what sense, 310.

Faventius, bishop of Reggio, 1082.

The kingdom of God is promised to those who labor, not to the idle, 117.

Regulus, deacon, together with Petronius the presbyter, delivered to Leo the prayers of the bishops of Gaul, 998. Leo wished them to be present at the discussion in Rome, 1000. What this discussion was, ibid. note.

Reports to the Roman See are useful to the whole Church, 1298. The Apostolic See was consulted through innumerable reports, 634. People converge from the whole world upon Peter’s see, 20. It was customary to refer the ordination of bishops of the major sees to the pope by letters from the ordained bishop and from those who had ordained him, 1309 note.

Renatus, a presbyter of the Roman Church of the title of Saint Clement, Leo’s legate to Flavian of Constantinople, 837; and to the Second Council of Ephesus, 841, 851, 865, 870. He died on the journey before the council, 941 note.

Things that have come to us in good faith are to be restored to their owners, 1331.

Restitutus, an African bishop, complains to Leo about bishops ordained where they ought not to have been ordained, 667.

The festival of the Resurrection is common to those below and those above, 419. See Christ’s Resurrection.

Bodies were raised before Christ’s Resurrection, 202.

Rodanus, a court official, 1244. Another subassistant, ibid.

Rome received its name from fratricide, 321. The citadel of the Roman Empire, 323. Enlarged by victories, it extended the right of empire by land and sea, 322. It had served the errors of all nations, ibid., 323. Why Peter’s see was chosen, ibid. Through Peter’s see it became the head of the world and presided more widely through divine religion than through earthly dominion, 322. Peter came to Rome under Claudius, 324. Peter and Paul died at Rome under Nero, ibid., 325. Thousands of martyrs surround Rome, 326. Their tombs, 944. Rome is made illustrious by Saint Laurence, 339. When Rome was occupied and, after its depopulation, emptied by the Vandals, 335. Because of this liberation a thanksgiving feast was celebrated annually, but later neglected, ibid. The Pelagians disappeared from Rome, 583. Manichaeans were discovered at Rome, and their bishop was at Rome. See Manichaeans. Egyptian merchants spread the heresy of Eutyches at Rome, 372, 373. Special collections at Rome. See Collections.

The Roman chair is called Peter’s see, 10. The feast of Saint Peter’s Chair. See Saint Peter’s Chair. People converge upon Peter’s see from the whole world, 20. ## Works of Saint Leo, First Part—Sermons.

## Preface

117. Admonition concerning the two sermons that follow. 137. FIRST SERMON.—St. Leo, elected in his absence, gives thanks for the favor and earnestly requests the prayers of his Church. 141. SERMON II.—I. No one should presume upon his own righteousness or despair of God’s mercy.—II. The assembly of bishops on the anniversary of the consecration of the Roman pontiff, whom the Church receives as Peter, the heir of Peter. 142. SERMON III.—I. The honor of the priesthood must be referred to God. Its figure was prefigured in Melchizedek; the distinction between the two.—II. How unequal human weakness is to so great a burden. Christ always governs the Church. The steadfastness of Peter’s faith remains.—III. The praises of Peter, who even now does not abandon the care of the Church. In what sense he is the rock and foundation.—IV. Peter must be honored in his successors: first among all bishops. The progress of the flock is the shepherd’s praise. 144. SERMON IV.—I. This feast (he is speaking of his own birthday) is common to all Christians, who are both kings and priests.—II. How much was bestowed upon Peter beyond the others: the Church founded in Peter and upon his faith.—III. The power of the keys, which Peter received, passed to the other apostles. Peter’s special privilege: the Lord undertakes his special care, and Christ prayed particularly for his faith, so that the firmness bestowed upon Peter through Christ might be conferred upon the apostles through Peter.—IV. Whatever good is accomplished by his successors is owed to Peter’s prayers and solicitude. 148. SERMON V.—I. Everything must be referred to God.—II. The higher the position someone holds in the Church, the more he must fear.—III. Christ is truly the Priest according to the order of Melchizedek and is always present to his Church.—IV. Peter always cares for the Roman See.—V. Honor is owed above all to him whose See his successors serve. 153. SERMON VI.—After a preliminary commendation of almsgiving, he announces that the Lord’s collection is at hand. 157. SERMON VII.—Almsgiving is a second washing from sins and an act of the greatest charity. 159. SERMON VIII.—The collections were instituted on the occasion of pagan superstitions, from which not even the poor are excluded; almsgiving torments demons; the poor are not strangers to the benefit of the collections. 159. SERMON IX.—I. By the light of the Gospel the darkness of pagan superstition is driven away, from which all crimes proceed.—II. For this reason Christ foretells the coming judgment, so that sins may be redeemed by generous mercy.—III. The collections are of apostolic institution: they were arranged on the occasion of pagan superstition; the especially bashful poor must be assisted.—IV. To expose heretics is especially pleasing to God. The doctrines of the Manichaeans. 160. SERMON X.—I. The faithful are assisted by the custom of collections handed down from the apostles. Wealth has been entrusted by God not so much to be possessed as to be distributed.—II. How wretched are those who spend their wealth only for their own use and not upon the poor.—III. Without mercy toward the poor, the other virtues are of no benefit.—IV. Faith without works is dead [Col. 1554] and is brought to life through charity. What are the benefits of almsgiving and self-restraint? 164. SERMON XI.—I. How greatly the final sentence of our Judge commends works of mercy.—II. From where the custom of collections arose in the Church. 166. SERMON XII.—I. Humanity was created in order to imitate its Creator; and this too is God’s gift.—II. Charity embraces not only God but also one’s neighbor, even one’s enemies; such is the breadth of Christian charity.—III. Everyone must be subject to all God’s judgments and give thanks no less for poverty than for abundance.—IV. All virtues are comprehended in fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. 168. SERMON XIII.—Why the fast of the tenth month was instituted; praise of that fast and of Christian mercy toward the poor. 172. SERMON XIV.—I. How the field of the flesh is to be cultivated.—II. The devil rages most fiercely against the faithful when they are practicing good works. 173. SERMON XV.—I. The threefold remedy of prayer, fasting, and almsgiving against the devil’s temptations and the wounds of sin.—II. The command to fast, like the command to love, has not been abolished by the grace of the new law; works of mercy must be joined to it. 174. SERMON XVI.—I. Let the rich give thanks to God, who bestows wealth upon them, and share it with the poor.—II. Why the fast of the tenth month was instituted. Prayer is effective when supported by almsgiving.—III. Heretics serve the devil under the Christian name in order to corrupt the faithful.—IV. The Manichaean heresy is the cesspool of every pollution. What Leo did against them at Rome.—V. They must both be avoided and exposed.—VI. Through zeal against heretics, prayers, fasts, and almsgiving become more pleasing to God. 176. SERMON XVII.—I. Fasting was transferred from the old law into the new and is owed to God as an expression of gratitude; it also makes prayer more effective.—II. A pious loan is to be practiced with God; but how unjustly and impiously loans are exacted by human beings.—III. Whatever outcome may follow from lending, the lender’s account is always evil.—IV. The abundance of some and the poverty of others have been ordered for this purpose: that the rich may imitate God’s goodness. 180. SERMON XVIII.—I. Although the soul has been regenerated and is inclined by itself toward worse things, it is fortified by God’s goodness with many defenses.—II. Abstinence is prescribed for the whole Church, so that the devil may be overcome both in part and in his entirety.—III. Christ condemned the barren tree in order to commend works of mercy. How the Christian is constantly attacked, and what weapons the devout possess against invisible enemies. 182. SERMON XIX.—I. Abstinence prepares the way for the Lord and raises the mind toward heavenly things.—II. Why the fasts of the Four Seasons were instituted; to them must also be added fasting from vices.—III. Concerning the worship of God and the use of temporal goods. Concerning the twofold fast. 185. SERMON XX.—I. Some things were instituted in the law for a time, while others were to remain also under the new law. What fasting is, and the character of all moral precepts.—II. The fast of the tenth month, prescribed by ecclesiastical regulations, is for giving God thanks for the fruits received from the earth. Let the fertility of the earth be rivaled by the abundance of souls, so that the human being may imitate God.—III. Charity contains all the commandments, and by it humanity is distinguished from the beasts. We must love our neighbor as God loves us. Not even the poor are excluded from works of mercy. 188. SERMON XXI.—I. No one is a stranger to the joy of the Lord’s Nativity, which alone is without the stain of sin.—II. Wonderful is the ordering of this mystery. [Col. 1555]—III. Whoever wishes to put on the new man must lay aside the old. 190. SERMON XXII.—I. Through the Incarnation of the Word the first disposition of God toward humanity was fulfilled, but through a more hidden sacrament.—II. In a new order and through a new birth the Son of God was generated.—III. Why Christ chose to be born of a Virgin.—IV. The devil was deceived through the Incarnation from a Virgin.—V. Christ was therefore born in the flesh so that we might be reborn from the Spirit.—VI. The Manichaeans worship not the rising of the God-man but the rising of a new sun. 193. SERMON XXIII.—I. Both generations of Christ are indescribable, and both natures were brought forth by Mary.—II. From where did Arius’s error arise? The sacrament of the Incarnation is explained.—III. The necessity of the Incarnation, so that the errors and sins of humanity might be removed.—IV. The faith and power of the Incarnation have always been one and the same as they are today.—V. The Lord’s Nativity must be celebrated not with carnal but with spiritual joy. Christ became our flesh by being born, and we become his flesh by being reborn. 199. SERMON XXIV.—I. Through the Incarnation of the Word, figures and promises were completed.—II. Unless God became human, no remedy would remain for human wounds.—III. Christ is true God and true human being, free from original sin; his birth is represented in baptism.—IV. The Manichaeans, who deny that Christ was born bodily, are alien to this faith.—V. Other heretics possess something sound; the Manichaeans possess nothing that is not impious.—VI. We must beware of their feigned piety and cling to the unity of faith, without which nothing is true. 203. SERMON XXV.—I. Leo confesses that he is indebted to the uneducated children of the Church. The narrow way lies not only in observing the commandments but also in the path of faith.—II. The Word, equal and consubstantial with the Father, was made less than the Father in the Incarnation with respect to his human nature.—III. The profound mystery of the Incarnation is examined.—IV. Christ was foretold in the old law and sent in the new; he can be known only through the Spirit of God.—V. Unless the Word had become flesh, death would have reigned from Adam onward. The Son of God became human so that human beings might become sons of God. The power of baptism.—VI. The Incarnation is both a mystery and an example. 208. SERMON XXVI.—I. The mysteries of Christ’s birth and infancy must always be recalled.—II. While venerating Christ’s birth, the Church celebrates her own.—III. What is the peace that Christ, born without seed, bestows?—IV. Whoever is a son of God must imitate God and serve God’s grace and will.—V. The Lord’s birthday is the birthday of peace. What is the character of the peace of the world and of the elect? 212. SERMON XXVII.—I. To deny either nature in Christ involves equal danger.—II. How is “the Word became flesh” to be understood? What were its effects?—III. The devil tests people in different ways according to their various desires and pursuits.—IV. The practice of certain Christians who bow toward the rising sun is superstitious.—V. The heavenly bodies serve human usefulness.—VI. What is the proper use of creatures? Humanity was born for present things and reborn for future things. 216. SERMON XXVIII.—I. With how great a joy the mystery of the birth of Christ must be received.—II. At no moment was the Word absent from Christ’s human flesh and soul.—III. In the destruction of Adam’s voluntary sin, justice was preserved.—IV. Various errors concerning the Lord’s Incarnation.—V. The impious doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches.—VI. The truth of both natures in Christ comes together in the unity of the person.—VII. How the fullness of divinity dwells bodily in Christ and in the Church. 221. SERMON XXIX.—I. What peace was announced by the angels at Christ’s birth?—II. The mysteries passed over only with respect to their bodily dispensation. “The Lord said to my Lord” is examined.—III. We must glory in the mercy of the one who adopts. Christ’s infancy must be honored. 226. SERMON XXX.—I. Both generations of Christ are ineffable.—II. Various errors concerning the Incarnation of the Word.—III. The fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in Christ.—IV. Christ’s conception is unique among all conceptions.—V. The properties of both natures in Christ are examined.—VI. Christ is consubstantial with the Father and with his mother; from both he saves us.—VII. One faith in Christ saves all the faithful of every age. Why Christ’s genealogy differs in Matthew and Luke. 230. SERMON XXXI.—I. Christ, born to be acknowledged by all, gives the sign of a star and at the same time the gift of understanding and seeking.—II. Herod rages against Christ in vain. The Magi proclaim their faith through gifts.—III. Christ directs Herod’s wickedness toward the good of the infants. What virtues we ought to imitate in the infant God. 234. SERMON XXXII.—I. Herod announces Christ’s birth to the world while attempting to remove him from the world. Christ, exiled into Egypt, prepares Egypt for salvation. [Col. 1556]—II. How much we owe God is demonstrated by the blindness of the Jews, who did not acknowledge him, yet crucified him.—III. The ignorance of infants is more fortunate than the knowledge of the Jewish priests. Christ consecrates the infancy of little children through his own infancy.—IV. The calling of the Magi is the beginning of our calling. Everyone ought to imitate their gifts, so that we may cooperate with Christ as he works our salvation. 237. SERMON XXXIII.—I. Christ came to free the world when all were shut up under sin, so that no one might glory in his own merits.—II. Why was he born under Herod, and why was he shown by a star? Grace worked inwardly so that the sign might be understood and Christ sought.—III. How great was the blindness of the Jews at Christ’s birth. The calling of the nations fulfills the promise made to Abraham.—IV. Why did the Magi return by another route after worshiping Christ? Why did Christ wish to be transferred to Egypt?—V. This feast, in which the first fruits of the calling of the nations are present, must be celebrated with thanksgiving. How shall we imitate the star? 240. SERMON XXXIV.—I. The Magi were called from a distant region so that the Christian faith might be strengthened, since it believes Christ to be God and human being.—II. The Magi were instructed by Balaam’s prophecy and confirmed by the Jews’ answer. The latter were deceived by hope of a temporal ruler; Herod was disturbed by fear of a rival.—III. The Magi’s journey and choice of gifts were the work of grace teaching inwardly. Their diligence served our faith.—IV. The impiety of the Manichaeans overturns faith in and the truth of the Incarnation.—V. The Manichaeans must be avoided; their sacrileges have been exposed. It is an institution of the Church to pour out prayers for them and for other heretics. 244. SERMON XXXV.—I. What the star that effectively moved the Magi and persistently drew them onward signifies.—II. Herod still rages in the devil against the children of the Church, while the Jews, blinded, serve Herod and have become bereft of every religion; the nations take their place.—III. We must pray for the Jews. We must cooperate vigorously with God’s grace. Grace provides assistance; obedience makes authority gentle.—IV. God invites everyone through his benefits; if a person does not obey him, an obstinate and ungrateful mind is itself a punishment. Earthly things must be abandoned and heavenly things desired, so that we may be joined to the fellowship of the saints. 249. SERMON XXXVI.—I. The mysteries must always be honored; they both retain their power and continue to be fulfilled in the Church. Grace works inwardly what the star signifies outwardly. How the faithful offer the same gifts.—II. The devil still plays the part of Herod, exercising envy in the Jews, deceit in heretics, and savagery in pagans. Yet Christ triumphs through charity in his members.—III. The Church grew through persecutions. It is the glory of rulers to serve Christ. In the Church’s peace, the persecution of desires must be feared—desires by which the demon is worshiped no less than through sacrifices.—IV. We must repent while there is opportunity for repentance; we must not yield to difficulty but pray to God, who gives the means of asking and grants what is asked. 253. SERMON XXXVII.—I. What is believed by faith must be imitated in action. Christ’s mysteries are both sacraments and examples.—II. Christ’s infancy, which is a law for living, proclaims nothing but the cross and humility.—III. Christ’s entire strength is humility, which is the whole discipline of Christian wisdom and whose teacher is his infancy.—IV. In what Christian infancy consists, to which Christ’s infancy invites us. 725. SERMON XXXVIII.—I. The star represents grace, the Magi all the nations, Herod the pagans, and the infants who were killed the martyrs. This feast is present in every age.—II. The mystery of Christ as God and human being, necessary for humanity’s restoration, can be reached only by the light of faith.—III. The necessity of grace. When a person does good, both the effect of the work and the beginning of the will come from God. The saints must fear lest, lifted up by their very works of devotion, they be abandoned without the aid of grace. By what signs can each person test whether God dwells within him?—IV. We recognize God as the inhabitant of the heart first through charity. How diligently we must labor for charity. 260. SERMON XXXIX.—I. The example of the Hebrews shows that one must fast especially against invisible enemies.—II. The demon lays his snares particularly during Lent.—III. Why Christ wished to be tempted, and how great are the human struggles in this life.—IV. How great is the devil’s envy. What weapons Christians possess.—V. What virtues ought especially to accompany fasting.—VI. True fasting consists especially in works of mercy. 263. SERMON XL.—I. One must always make progress in this life.—II. During Lent one must strive especially toward this, since the devil rages more fiercely.—III. Why Christ, when hungry, did not change stones into bread.—IV. The abstinence of Lent must not be barren.—V. During Lent the mercy and clemency of rulers must be imitated. 267. SERMON XLI.—I. With how great purity of conscience fasting must be celebrated. How should each person examine himself? [Col. 1557]—II. The devil’s boldness in tempting Christ ought to make us more cautious, especially at this time.—III. Fasting is sanctified by compassion. 272. SERMON XLII.—I. Lent was salutarily instituted for cleansing the stains of souls.—II. One must pursue every virtue at this time, and each is weighed according to the will.—III. The devil lays snares through piety itself; the order and method of his temptations against Christ are explained.—IV. Concerning the perverse abstinence of the Manichaeans.—V. They fast in honor of the sun and moon on the Lord’s Day and the second day of the week, abstain from participation in the blood of Christ, and so forth.—VI. How Lent may be sanctified through works of virtue. 274. SERMON XLIII.—I. How a person cooperates with grace so that he may be renewed inwardly, a necessity for everyone.—II. Few are unshaken by adversity or not inflated by prosperity.—III. The necessity of repentance rests upon everyone.—IV. Sins are especially erased through works of mercy. 281. SERMON XLIV.—I. The vices of the old nature must be cleansed especially during Lent, and no one is free from them.—II. Integrity of mind, unity of peace, and generosity in almsgiving, from which no one is excluded, must be joined to fasting.—III. The pursuit of pride and vengeance must be driven out by a spirit of humility and gentleness. 285. SERMON XLV.—I. Everyone—whether righteous, sinful, or a catechumen—must prepare the way for the Lord through Lent.—II. During Lent one must devote oneself to mercy and truth in imitation of God, and to faith and charity.—III. What is provided for Christ is provided for Christ himself.—IV. At this time one must undertake the exercise of every virtue. 288. SERMON XLVI.—I. Not only vices but also errors must be rejected; and Christ’s twofold nature must be acknowledged.—II. In all Christ’s actions varied testimonies of both natures shine forth.—III. What must be believed concerning Christ incarnate.—IV. Fasting and prayer are made fruitful not only by almsgiving but also by forgiving offenses. 291. SERMON XLVII.—I. During the greater, that is, Lenten, fasts, Christians are prepared for the paschal feast through endurance of the cross.—II. Not only moral uprightness but also faith must be preserved, especially faith in Christ’s divinity and humanity.—III. God is especially appeased by mercy and forgiveness of offenses. 294. SERMON XLVIII.—I. Everyone must prepare himself through a forty-day fast for the paschal sacrament, which consecrates all other things. The working of grace and human cooperation.—II. Envy of one’s neighbor’s good, which belongs peculiarly to the devil, must especially be avoided.—III. Without charity the virtues are bare and fruitless; there must be no limit to that virtue.—IV. Each person must earn mercy through mercy.—V. Alms must be distributed abundantly at this time. 297. SERMON XLIX.—I. The great and most sacred fast of Lent is imposed on everyone without exception, because it is necessary for everyone, since no one is free from fault.—II. How few enter the way of salvation, while how many are occupied with temporal things.—III. Just as the devil lays more snares and rages more fiercely during Lent, so Christians must devote themselves more fully to God and their salvation.—IV. To prepare ourselves for the paschal feast, we must carry out God’s commandments, which are given so that God’s grace may be sought and one’s own life seen as in a mirror.—V. The first effect of mercy, namely, forgetfulness of offenses, must both be sought from God and granted to one’s neighbor.—VI. Whoever wishes to be regarded as a son must possess love for his brother and give alms, as a minister of divine mercy. 301. SERMON L.—I. Everyone must prepare for the paschal banquet by examining his conscience and correcting his life.—II. Mercy must be practiced, one must fast from vices, and cling to heavenly things.—III. Everyone is prepared for the paschal sacrament, which was established for the remission of sins, when he imitates it by forgiving offenses. 305. SERMON LI.—I. True faith confesses Christ as both God and human being; this faith was rewarded with great power in Peter.—II. Christ was transfigured especially to prove the truth and power of his flesh.—III. He also did so to remove the scandal of the cross and strengthen the hope of his Church.—IV. The concord of the Old and New Testaments concerning Christ is signified by the appearance of Moses and Elijah.—V. Peter’s desire was not blameworthy but disordered.—VI. “This is my Son,” and so forth, is explained.—VII. “Hear him” is examined.—VIII. By this testimony of the Father, the weakness of all is strengthened. 308. SERMON LII.—I. Salvation comes to humanity through the Incarnation of the Word alone; faith in it was necessary even in the Old Testament and before the law.—II. Salvation is brought about through the power of the Word and the humility of the flesh.—III. The cross and abasement of the one who by a single word struck down the soldiers during his Passion must not be despised.—IV. Christ voluntarily handed himself over to death; he both restrained Peter’s zeal and restored the servant’s ear.—V. We are freed by Christ’s death, while the Jews and Judas are accused; yet they too could have been redeemed by it. 313. SERMON LIII.—I. The conversion of the thief, who was guilty right up to the cross and suddenly became a confessor of Christ, was the work of grace.—II. When all creatures bore witness to Christ on the cross, they pronounced judgment against the Jews.—III. Christians must be conformed to Christ’s humility and patience; there is no other way to eternal life. 317. SERMON LIV.—I. The mystery of the cross and redemption, prefigured from ancient times, requires two natures in Christ.—II. The properties of both natures are distinct, as are the voluntary sufferings of the human nature.—III. How unjustly Judas distrusted the Lord’s goodness, when the Lord had not excluded him from communion in his body and blood.—IV. Our sadness and fear were voluntarily assumed by Christ.—V. Peter’s conversion was the work of Christ’s inward gaze.—VI. How many evils originated from the cries by which the Jews delivered Christ to death. 318. SERMON LV.—I. Concerning Christ’s crucifixion, in which the distinction between the elect and the reprobate is represented through the thieves.—II. The Jews’ blasphemies against Christ were ignorant, since it had been foretold that he would not descend from the cross but would reign from the tree.—III. On the cross, which is the sacrament of the true altar, the record of sin was erased by Christ’s blood, and the thief was wonderfully converted.—IV. Concerning the vinegar he tasted, the words “It is finished,” the inclination of his head, and Christ’s death.—V. Hearts must be prepared through charity and purity to celebrate the paschal feast. 322. SERMON LVI.—I. Our salvation has been placed in the cross, in which Christ contended with justice and power, divinity and humanity.—II. Concerning Christ’s prayer and the conflict of the two wills, which was ordered for our instruction.—III. Concerning Christ’s gentleness toward Judas, Judas’s criminal repentance, and humanity’s redemption through Christ. 325. SERMON LVII.—I. Christ, voluntarily seized, did not wish to be defended.—II. In the same words Christ strikes the consciences of unbelievers and strengthens the hearts of the faithful. When Caiaphas tore his garment, he stripped himself of priestly honor.—III. What blindness possessed the priests, who crucified Christ with their tongues while wishing to appear to withdraw their hands from the killing. Their equally blind superstition concerning Judas’s money.—IV. When Christ was lifted up on the cross, he drew all creatures into communion with his Passion.—V. Christians, redeemed at so great a price, must beware of the devil’s snares, by which he deceives people through the vain science of the stars. 328. SERMON LVIII.—I. Why Christ chose to suffer during the paschal solemnity.—II. The Jews, intent on committing a crime, neglected the things belonging to the law.—III. Christ instituted the sacrament of his body and blood at the time when a plan was being formed for his death; his kindness toward Judas and Judas’s obstinacy.—IV. Judas was physically present at the supper but inwardly intent upon crime. Christ’s discourse after the supper, his prayer in the garden, and his common counsel with the Father concerning his death.—V. Through Christ’s prayer and trembling, our fear is driven away. 331. SERMON LIX.—I. Christ, having cast off the trembling of weakness, allowed himself to be led away willingly for all.—II. By how many prejudices the Jews impelled Pilate to condemn Christ; with what cowardice he yielded to their cries.—III. Pilate’s cruelty toward Christ arose from a certain clemency; the Jews were burdened with the whole crime.—IV. While Christ carried the instrument of punishment, he transformed it into a scepter.—V. Through Simon of Cyrene the nations called to faith in Christ’s cross and sanctified by a new sacrifice were represented.—VI. Christ’s cross must be viewed especially with the inward gaze.—VII. How does Christ, when lifted up, draw all things to himself? What is the excellence of the Christian religion? How great is the power of the cross?—VIII. We must not live for ourselves but for Christ, who died for us. 337. SERMON LX.—I. The mysteries of the new law were foretold in the ancient law and narrated in the Gospel.—II. The paschal feasts, which brought us true redemption, must not be celebrated sadly.—III. The figures are shown to have been fulfilled in Christ’s death, in which the devil was caught by his own fraud.—IV. How greatly greed must be avoided, as shown by Judas’s fall; Peter, who stumbled through fear, rose through charity by Christ’s inward gaze. 341. SERMON LXI.—I. How falsely Christ was accused of seeking an assumed kingdom.—II. Whatever Christ did belonged to divine power, not to an earthly king.—III. Why Christ restrained the women’s tears.—IV. How Christ turned punishments back upon his enemy.—V. The whole creation condemns the Jews who blasphemed Christ; the torn veil shows that they were deprived of all the sacraments of religion. 346 [Col. 1559]. SERMON LXII.—I. How dull the human intellect is for contemplating the mysteries.—II. The faith of the Incarnation is taught through the creed. The steadfastness of Peter’s faith, on account of which he was established as the rock and foundation of the Church.—III. The devil was deceived by his own malice. Christ’s prayer for his enemies brought them to faith through Peter’s preaching.—IV. Since Christ died for all the impious, Judas too could have obtained a remedy if he had not hurried to the noose.—V. Christ’s death was cruel in the mind of the Jews but marvelous in the power of the one who was dying. 349. SERMON LXIII.—I. Christ did not fight by his own power alone but from our humility, so that justice might be preserved.—II. Whatever we possess fulfilled, the ancients possessed in shadow; there is one faith and one hope for all.—III. The union of Christ with both his bodies, the natural and the mystical, is inseparable.—IV. The Christian must strive above all to imitate his head.—V. Only the ceremonial precepts were changed; grace was given for the moral precepts.—VI. Christ begets countless sons for himself through baptism, in which the image of death and resurrection shines forth.—VII. All the Christian’s merit is Christ’s glory; he who feeds them with his flesh also moves and governs those whom he feeds with his spirit. 353. SERMON LXIV.—I. The Lord’s Passion must be contemplated attentively; faith in it depends upon faith in the Incarnation.—II. Why was the Son, who is equal to the Father and alone without sin, incarnate, and not another person?—III. Of what value are Christ’s death and sacrifice on the cross?—IV. While each nature preserves its own properties in Christ, the two have different parts in the mysteries. 357. SERMON LXV.—I. When the Eutychians do not acknowledge true flesh in Christ, they either believe him to be a false human being or believe God to be passible.—II. Christ contained the power of divinity so that by suffering he might both save and strengthen.—III. Christ’s Passion was real; the Jews deny him as God, the Eutychians as human being.—IV. All Christ’s mysteries prove true flesh in Christ, without which he is not the firstfruits of those who sleep.—V. Unless Christ’s flesh is real, divinity cannot dwell bodily in him. 361. SERMON LXVI.—I. The grace of restoration is gratuitous; it was to be expected from no one except Christ, who alone is innocent and, even in the Old Testament, justified only those who believe in him.—II. The same mysteries exist in both Testaments, veiled in one and revealed in the other.—III. Easter is not rightly celebrated except by believers. Everyone must be instructed by the miracles that occurred when Christ died. The marvelous effects of Christ’s death [OCR: “morus”].—IV. Whatever was done by Christ was done for our sake; unbelief alone excludes us from him.—V. Christ’s enemies were destroyed through his grace. 364. SERMON LXVII.—I. How beneficial it is to contemplate God’s benefits, whose prediction establishes faith.—II. Christ’s Passion was decreed by God’s plan in such a way that neither he himself is the author of the crime nor the Jews are excusable.—III. Even Christ’s executioners were not excluded from the gift of redemption.—IV. How detestable Judas’s crime is, and how great the punishment of the crime.—V. Through his voluntary death Christ gave both a remedy and an example.—VI. Christ’s death removes every opportunity for pride and negligence; the commandments cannot be fulfilled except through him.—VII. Christ said, in the person of his members: “Why have you forsaken me?” 367. SERMON LXVIII.—I. The divinity inseparable from Christ could not have abandoned him.—II. Christ’s voluntary death for the world’s salvation is demonstrated by his cry; nor could the voices of those who blasphemed prevent it.—III. Despite the blasphemies, Christ offered his sacrifice; this was also signified by the tearing of the veil.—IV. The devil never ceases to lay snares. What benefit the Lenten fast provides. 372. SERMON LXIX.—I. The height of the mystery of the cross is ineffable. Its faith is as unified as unbelief is varied and uncertain.—II. The figures ceased because the truth has shone forth, though its faith has always been the same.—III. Christ, God and human being, died willingly; the devil was deceived by his cunning.—IV. While killing Christ, the devil gave humanity the opportunity to be freed and to gain complete victory over death and sin.—V. The devil’s snares must be diligently avoided, so that, crucified with Christ through mortification, we may be crowned in him. 375. SERMON LXX.—I. How true faith makes Christ’s Passion present to us, though it is utterly different in the mind of the Crucified One and in the deed of those crucifying.—II. Christ used the Jews’ malice so that by his death he might sacrifice the true Passover, through which even the killers themselves could be saved.—III. The wisdom of the world is confounded in the mystery of the cross, in which both Christ’s power and weakness save us.—IV. The cross must continually be carried, so that what was accomplished mystically in baptism may be completed in action.—V. The Lord’s Passion is completed until the end of the world through the mortification of his members. His bond of friendship must be preferred to the devil’s snare.—VI. The mortification of our vices is Christ’s power and victory. 379. SERMON LXXI.—I. Care must be taken that the fruit of fasting is not nullified, so that those who have died with Christ may also rise with him.—II. The days of burial were shortened for the sake of the disciples.—III. Christ proved his resurrection by many arguments.—IV. What transformation took place in Christ’s flesh through the resurrection.—V. The Christian must despise earthly things and cling in mind to heavenly things.—VI. One must beware of returning to the pleasure of sin after the paschal feast. 385. SERMON LXXII.—I. Christ’s cross is both a sacrament and an example for us.—II. The Word assumed our nature in the Incarnation in order to offer it as a price.—III. We have died and risen together with Christ; Christ strengthens us by remaining with us on earth and invites us to glory while reigning in heaven.—IV. Everywhere the power and example of the cross are present for us, by which we are armed against desires.—V. Through contempt for earthly things we must strive toward heavenly things, while preserving faith in both natures in Christ.—VI. Through Christ’s passage—which occurs only in our nature—a passage for us to heavenly things is prepared.—VII. The Eutychians are excluded from the paschal feast because they suppress our nature in Christ. 390. SERMON LXXIII.—I. Both Christ’s delay on earth after the resurrection and the disciples’ doubt were arranged to confirm faith.—II. How many things Christ accomplished during these days.—III. By the touch of his wounds he confirmed the disciples’ trembling hearts.—IV. Christ’s Ascension brought joy to those whom his death had made fearful and his resurrection had left doubtful. Through Christ, greater things were bestowed than those taken away by the devil. 394. SERMON LXXIV.—I. Through the Ascension our joy is fulfilled and our faith and hope become more wondrous.—II. In order that we might be capable of blessedness, Christ ascended into heaven, where he will remain until the day of judgment.—III. Faith was so strengthened by the Ascension that it could be overcome by no torments, even in young girls.—IV. Through the Ascension Christ became known in a more exalted way, and his divinity became more present. What the angelic conversation signifies.—V. Christ’s Ascension stirs us to despise earthly things as pilgrims and to become rich in charity, without which one does not go to Christ. 397. SERMON LXXV.—I. The Christian Pentecost corresponds to the Mosaic one.—II. How swiftly and wondrously the disciples were taught by the Holy Spirit.—III. The perfect equality of the persons in…

Equality in the Holy Trinity explained. — IV. The error of the Macedonians concerning the Holy Spirit, who is the source and cause of every good thing. — V. All things in the Church are sanctified through the Holy Spirit; even the fasts themselves were instituted by him.

400 **SERMON LXXVI.** — I. The Holy Spirit must be discussed both for the sake of the spiritually mature and for that of neophytes. — II. The persons of the Trinity are perfectly equal in all things, even though certain properties are attributed to each individually. — III. The Holy Spirit was given in the Old Testament. — IV. He was also given to the Apostles before Pentecost, and without him no one prays rightly. — V. What is it that the disciples were not yet able to bear? — VI. How the folly of the Manichaeans is refuted from the Gospel, and when Manes lived. — VII. How foolish it is to say that the Church lacked the Holy Spirit until Manes. — VIII. One must deny that the Holy Spirit was given to the Church if one rejects that Christ truly possessed flesh. — IX. Fasts are numbered among the gifts of the Holy Spirit and are prescribed on the basis of apostolic tradition.

404 **SERMON LXXVII.** — I. The Holy Spirit did not begin his gifts at Pentecost but increased them, since the Trinity works indivisibly. — II. Sin brought it about that the persons of the Trinity divided among themselves the work of our restoration, and how this occurred. — III. That division does not impair the equality and consubstantiality of the persons. — IV. Nothing analogous to created or visible things should be conceived concerning the Trinity, which is wholly equal. — V. Why Christ wishes the disciples to rejoice at his ascension. — VI. The three persons possess one being and perform one work.

411 **SERMON LXXVIII.** — I. Fasts were instituted at the prompting of the Holy Spirit so that Christians might fight more powerfully against their enemies. — II. The devil is unarmed against one who is free from carnal desires. — III. A fast was instituted after the feasts so that their fruits might endure and that negligence concerning them might be punished. — IV. The fast accompanied by mercy possesses the greatest power.

415 **SERMON LXXIX.** — I. The fast of Pentecost, derived from apostolic tradition and instituted by the Holy Spirit. — II. What distinction there is between the fasts of the faithful and the fasts of unbelievers. — III. What kind of fast does not proceed from the Holy Spirit and from which human glory is sought. — IV. The fast must be referred to God, because he is the author of every desire and good work.

418 **SERMON LXXX.** — One must fast in such a way that what is taken away from one’s meals is devoted to charity, which surpasses fasting.

420 **SERMON LXXXI.** — I. Gluttony was the cause of sin; therefore it must be subdued by abstinence. — II. The inner person possesses the greater wisdom the more the outer person restrains itself from the allurements of the senses. — III. After the periods of indulgence, one must return to fasting, so that negligence may either be corrected or not creep in. — IV. Through fasting and good works a person is cleansed from sins. **Ibid. SERMON LXXXII.** — I. How greatly Rome’s glory increased through religion and the ministry of the Apostles. — II. How the Roman Empire served the rule of Christ. — III. Why Rome was established as the principal see of the Church. — IV. How great were the courage and charity of Peter as he entered Rome. — V. Peter’s labors before he came to Rome. — VI. Peter and Paul—Paul associated with Peter—were two illustrious shoots of the divine seed. — VII. How greatly one should rejoice on their feast.

421 **SERMON LXXXIII.** — I. Peter’s confession and excellence. — II. What Christ bestowed upon him. — III. Christ prayed for his faith and granted firmness to that faith. He made him the head of the whole Church.

429 **SERMON LXXXIV.** — I. The Romans, devoted to the Circus games, dangerously forgot God’s benefits. — II. Rome’s deliverance from the barbarians was not the work of the stars but a gift of God, to be recalled with a grateful heart.

433 **SERMON LXXXV.** — I. The difference between Christ’s death and the death of the martyrs. — II. The efficacy of each. — III. The courage of Laurence, who preserved both the resources and the faith of the Church. — IV. Laurence was made invincible by charity.

435 **SERMON LXXXVI.** — I. He commands a fast with authority and urges it out of charity, so that the body may be disciplined and the poor assisted. — II. It is not enough to take nothing belonging to another unless one also gives one’s own to the poor.

437 **SERMON LXXXVII.** — I. The devil must be resisted through self-restraint: he seeks in us, through the enticement of eating, the fruit of the seed first cast into our original parents. — II. Fasting is of the greatest benefit both to the salvation of others and to each person’s own salvation. — III. Those who cannot fast should give more abundant alms. — IV. Wealth is placed in safety and increased when it is distributed to the poor.

438 **SERMON LXXXVIII.** — I. Fasts, without which God’s justice was not appeased for the ancients, are also necessary for us. — II. They are much more powerful when celebrated by all the faithful together. — III. Each person ought sometimes to withdraw from worldly cares in order to devote himself more attentively to his salvation. The power of united prayer. — IV. The agreement of the good has great force before God. In almsgiving, the disposition, not the amount of wealth, is weighed. — V. Each person ought to give alms according to his means, without distrust.

441 **SERMON LXXXIX.** — I. The fast fulfilled by Christians through God’s grace is far superior to the carnal observance of the Jews. — II. The common and public should be preferred to the private, as possessing greater merit and efficacy. — III. The devil has countless weapons, and they are avoided only by one who loves God above all things. — IV. Certain seasons have been appointed so that we may draw breath toward divine things. — V. Almsgiving, especially toward the faithful, must be joined to fasting. — VI. The poor are to be saved by patience, the rich by mercy.

444 **SERMON XC.** — I. Penance is always necessary because of the enemy’s continual snares and the lust of the flesh. — II. Everything impossible through human weakness is possible through divine power. — III. The love of God and of the world. — IV. The love of God is nourished by good works. Why the fast of the seventh month is observed.

447 **SERMON XCI.** — I. God’s will is taught even by the elements themselves, and it commands abstinence both from foods and from worldly wisdom. — II. The heresy of Nestorius and that of Eutyches alike must be detested. — III. The reality of Christ’s flesh is proved by the Eucharistic sacrifice and by the command to give alms.

450 **SERMON XCII.** — I. The moral commandments of the Law have not been abolished; no one has ever been justified without charity; the abundance of evangelical righteousness consists in the abundance of charity. — II. The fasts of the New Law were taken from the Old but must be fulfilled in a different spirit. — III. Each person ought to please God alone: each person’s treasure is of the same character as that to which his heart clings. — IV. The seventh month has been consecrated by fasting, good works, and the number itself.

453 **SERMON XCIII.** — I. The end of the Law is the victory of right love over wrong love. Concerning the evil and the good will. — II. Righteousness gives far greater delight than iniquity, which must be overcome by the law of God. — III. How greatly the fast of the seventh month, instituted by the Law and the Apostles, benefits us.

456 **SERMON XCIV.** — I. Spiritual fasting must be attended to more than bodily fasting. — II. In what spiritual fasting consists [Col. 1562], and by what help it is to be fulfilled. — III. Why the fast of the four seasons was instituted. — IV. God is loved when one’s neighbor is loved and helped.

458 **SERMON XCV.** — I. Through outward healings Christ prepared souls for inward healings, which are accomplished through the gentleness of grace. — II. Humility, which is accessible to everyone, is the first step toward blessedness. — III. The apostles’ poverty, and above all Peter’s, was exceedingly rich and powerful. — IV. What kind of mourning is the road to blessedness? — V. What land was promised to the meek? — VI. Thirst for righteousness is nothing other than love of God. — VII. Mercy makes a person like God. — VIII. The eye of the heart must be cleansed so that God may be seen. — IX. What is the true peace that makes a person a child of God?

460 **SERMON XCVI.** — I. He warns those who cling to the Apostles’ Creed to beware of the Alexandrian negotiators defending at Rome one nature in Christ. — II. Eutyches was formerly condemned in the case of other heretics. One must determine in Christ what belongs to his divinity and what to his humanity. — III. One must not share communion with condemned heretics. Praise of the Roman faith.

466 **APPENDIX TO THE FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF ST. LEO.**

467 **Preface.** Ibid. **SERMONS ATTRIBUTED TO ST. LEO.**

477 **SERMON ONE.** — Treatise against the errors of Eutyches and other heretics. Ibid. **SERMON II.** — On the Nativity of the Lord.

487 **SERMON III.** — On Lent I.

488 **SERMON IV.** — On Lent II.

490 **SERMON V.** — On the Passion of the Lord I.

491 **SERMON VI.** — On the Passion of the Lord II.

492 **SERMON VII.** — On Palm Sunday.

493 **SERMON VIII.** — On the Resurrection of the Lord I.

495 **SERMON IX.** — On the Resurrection of the Lord II.

497 **SERMON X.** — On the Resurrection of the Lord III.

499 **SERMON XI.** — On the Ascension of the Lord. Ibid. **SERMON XII.** — On the Most Holy Trinity.

500 **SERMON XIII.** — On the Feast of St. Vincent the Martyr.

501 **SERMON XIV.** — On the Chair of St. Peter.

505 **SERMON XV.** — On the Annunciation of the Blessed Mother of God and Virgin Mary.

508 **SERMON XVI.** — On the Feast of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

511 **SERMON XVII.** — On the Feast of Blessed Paul the Apostle.

512 **SERMON XVIII.** — On St. Peter: how he was led out of prison.

515 **SERMON XIX.** — On the Feast of the Seven Maccabees.

517 **SERMON XX.** — On the Transfiguration of the Lord.

520 **OBSERVATIONS ON THE SERMONS OF ST. LEO.**

521–551 **SECOND PART OF THE WORKS OF ST. LEO — LETTERS.** Preface.

551 **LETTER ONE, TO THE BISHOP OF AQUILEIA.** — I. Pelagians are wrongly received into communion without renunciation of their error and a profession of faith. — II. He orders a synod to be convened so that a profession of faith may be required from them. — III. What is to be thought concerning the grace of Christ? — IV. Anyone who does not submit to the Church’s decrees concerning grace must be expelled from it. — V. Each person must remain wherever he has been ordained.

593 **LETTER II, TO SEPTIMUS OF ALTINUM.** — I. Pelagians are to be received only after renouncing their error. — II. Every cleric must remain in the Church in which he was ordained.

597 **Fragment of a letter of St. Cyril of Alexandria to St. Leo.**

601 **LETTER III, OF PASCHASINUS, BISHOP OF LILYBAEUM, TO POPE LEO.** — Paschasinus, consulted by Leo about the paschal cycle, after prefacing a brief account of Sicily’s devastation, proves that the Alexandrian computation should be retained in preference to the Roman, both from the calculation of the Hebrews and from the miracle that occurred in the time of Pope Zosimus.

606 **LETTER IV, TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGH CAMPANIA, PICENUM, TUSCIA, AND ALL THE PROVINCES.** — I. No bishop should presume to promote another person’s slave to clerical office. — II. Whoever has been promoted to the priesthood despite being the husband of a widow or having contracted numerous marriages is to be barred from ecclesiastical offices. — III. Not only clerics but also Christian laymen ought not to exact interest. — IV. A cleric must not conduct lending at interest either in his own name or in another’s. — V. If any priest acts against these prohibitions, he is to be removed from his office.

610 **LETTER V, TO THE METROPOLITAN BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGH ILLYRICUM.** — I. Unlawful attempts against the canons should prudently be forestalled by admonitions. — II. He entrusts Anastasius of Thessalonica with his authority throughout Illyricum, following the custom of his predecessors. — III. He orders that bigamists, husbands of widows, and husbands of repudiated women be barred from the priesthood by the canons. — IV. Just as provincial bishops belong to the metropolitans, so the metropolitans belong to the exarch or vicar [Col. 1563]. — V. The metropolitans are responsible for ordaining them and for reporting the condition of the provinces to the apostolic see. — VI. More serious cases and appeals from Illyricum are reserved to the apostolic see.

615 **LETTER VI, TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA.** — I. A good shepherd willingly allows himself to be compelled by letters to attend to his fellow bishops. — II. He entrusts Anastasius with his authority throughout Illyricum, following the example of Siricius. — III. He commends observance of the canons, especially in ordinations; bigamists and husbands of widows are excluded. — IV. The provincial bishops are to be ordained by the metropolitan with the knowledge of the exarch; the metropolitans by the exarch himself. — V. All are to attend synods; their usefulness and authority. — VI. Presbyters and deacons, as well as bishops, are to be consecrated only on Sundays.

617 **LETTER VII, TO THE BISHOPS THROUGHOUT ITALY.** — He warns that very many Manichaeans have been discovered in the city of Rome through his vigilance and are to be sought out with equal diligence.

620 **LETTER VIII, OR THE CONSTITUTION OF VALENTINIAN III.** — Concerning the Manichaeans.

622 **LETTER IX, TO DIOSCORUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA.** — I. The ordination of bishops, presbyters, and deacons is to be celebrated after the Sabbath, either around the beginning of the immediately following night or on the morning of the Sunday itself. — II. The sacrifice should be repeated on the same feast day when the basilica is too small to contain the entire people at once and a great multitude of the faithful has assembled.

624 **LETTER X, TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGH THE PROVINCE OF VIENNE.** — I. The Church, established by Christ upon Peter’s solidity, must not depart from it. Whoever attempts to weaken its authority violates it. — II. He rebukes Hilary for disturbing the condition and harmony of the Churches. — III. Celidonius, deposed by Hilary, was restored to his see after the judgment was rescinded. — IV. Bishop Projectus, in whose place Hilary had appointed another while he was ill, was restored in full. — V. The ordination of a provincial bishop is to be reserved to the metropolitan. — VI. No one is to be ordained without the consent of the clergy and people or outside the lawful day. — VII. Hilary is deprived of metropolitan dignity and authority in the province of Vienne. — VIII.
