No one is to be expelled from communion for a trivial cause. — IX. No council of another province is to be summoned without the consent of Leontius, the senior bishop.

628 **LETTER XI, OR THE CONSTITUTION OF VALENTINIAN III AUGUSTUS.** — Concerning the ordination of bishops.

636 **LETTER XII, TO THE AFRICAN BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF MAURITANIA CAESARIENSIS.** — I. He censures ordinations carried out amid tumult. — II. What it means to lay hands quickly. — III. Deacons, presbyters, and bishops must be men of one wife only. — IV. Inexperienced persons and neophytes ought not to be ordained. — V. Leo tolerates those ordained from the laity, but not bigamists. — VI. Concerning Donatus, converted from the Novatians, and Maximus, converted from the Donatists. — VII. Concerning Aggarus and Tyberianus, ordained from the laity and amid tumult. — VIII. Virgins violated by force ought not to compare themselves with the undefiled. — IX. He urges obedience and threatens punishment to the disobedient. — X. In what places bishops ought to be ordained, and concerning the petition of Bishop Restitutus. — XI. What should be done concerning the virgins mentioned above who were violated by barbarous violence. — XII. Concerning the case of Bishop Lupicinus. — XIII. Ecclesiastical cases are to be debated and referred to the apostolic see.

645 **LETTER XIII, TO THE METROPOLITAN BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGH THE PROVINCES OF ILLYRICUM.** — I. He rejoices that the metropolitans of Illyricum submit to the authority granted to Anastasius, especially in more important cases. — II. He urges those summoned by Anastasius to a council not to refuse to come. — III. No one is to be ordained bishop without the consent of the people. — IV. No bishop may claim another bishop’s cleric against that bishop’s will.

653 **LETTER XIV, TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA.** — I. The bishops of Thessalonica have always fulfilled the duties of the apostolic see. — II. The metropolitans’ rights are to be preserved. — III. The metropolitans are to ordain as bishops neither laymen, nor bigamists, nor husbands of widows, but men who are irreproachable. — IV. Carnal marriage is forbidden to subdeacons. — V. No one is to be ordained bishop against his will. — VI. The metropolitan of Epirus is to report to the bishop of Thessalonica concerning the man he has elected and is about to ordain bishop; the provincial bishops are likewise to report concerning an elected metropolitan. — VII. Two councils of bishops are to be held each year; and if a difficult matter arises that cannot be resolved by the judgment of Thessalonica, it is to be referred to the Roman bishop. — VIII. If any bishop abandons his city and seeks a greater see out of ambition, he will not only be unable to obtain that Church but will also have to lose his own. — IX. No one may solicit or retain another’s cleric without that bishop’s consent. — X. In summoning provincial bishops, the bishop of Thessalonica must maintain moderation, lest under this pretext priestly honor be subjected to insults; and no more than two bishops from each province, approved by the metropolitans, are to be sent. — XI. Bishops are not to remain away more than fifteen days beyond the time fixed by the council.

666 **LETTER XV, TO TURRIBIUS, BISHOP OF ASTORGA.** — Against the Priscillianists, who distinguish the Holy Trinity not by persons but only by names. — II. Against their belief that the Son of God was later than the Father. — III. Against their claim that Christ is called “only-begotten” because he alone was born of a virgin. — IV. Concerning the Nativity of the Lord, on which the Priscillianists observe fasts. — V. Against their claim that the human soul is of divine substance. — VI. Against their claim that the devil is from himself or from chaos and possesses a nature of his own. — VII. Against their assertion that marriages and the procreation of children are sins. — VIII. Against their claim that human bodies are fabrications of the devil and are formed by demons in the womb. — IX. Against their claim that the children of promise are conceived from the Holy Spirit. — X. Against their belief [variant: claim] that souls sin in the heavenly regions and, according to the quality of their sin, receive a good or evil lot in this world. — XI. Against their claim that human souls are bound to fatal stars. — XII. Against their division of the parts of the soul under some powers and the members of the body under others. — XIII. Against their distribution of the names of the patriarchs among the individual members of the body. — XIV. Against their distribution throughout the entire body of the twelve signs observed by astrologers. — XV. Concerning the apocryphal Scriptures of those same Priscillianists. — XVI. Concerning the book of Dictinius.

677 **LETTER OF ST. TURRIBIUS OF ASTORGA.** — Concerning the rejection of apocryphal writings as authorities for the faith, and concerning the sect of the Priscillianists.

693 **LETTER XVI, TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SICILY.** — I. Baptism is prohibited from being celebrated on the day of Epiphany. — II. All the sacraments of salvation have been arranged for us in an ordered sequence through the incarnation of our Lord. — III. In baptism death occurs through the slaying [Hispanic reading: infection] of sin; the threefold immersion imitates the three-day burial, and the raising from the waters is like resurrection from the tomb. — IV. Blessed Peter baptized three thousand men on the day of Pentecost. — V. The Roman pontiffs established only two seasons for baptism, namely Easter and Pentecost. — VI. At all times those pressed by the necessity of death—that is, by illness, siege, persecution, or shipwreck—must be baptized. — VII. Each year three bishops from Sicily are to come to Rome on the third day before the Kalends of October and attend the synod without fail.

695 **LETTER XVII, TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SICILY.** — By a permanent constitution he forbids the bishops to repeat what was wickedly done and unjustly undertaken by the bishops in two Sicilian Churches: they had unlawfully alienated the goods of their Churches. He decrees that violators of this ruling are to be deprived of rank and communion.

703 **LETTER XVIII, TO JANUARIUS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA.** — Any cleric of whatever rank who, abandoning the Catholic Church, joins heretical communion, if he returns to the Church, is to remain without promotion in the rank in which he was [Cresconius: had been].

706 **LETTER XIX, TO DORUS, BISHOP OF BENEVENTUM.** — I. He rebukes Dorus for disturbing the order of the presbytery and for the senior presbyters’ yielding their rights. — II. He vindicates each person’s rank according to the time of ordination, relegating those senior men who had yielded to the lowest place.

709 **LETTER XX, TO EUTYCHES, ABBOT OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He replies that, having been informed by Eutyches’ letter of the revival of the Nestorian heresy, he approved his zeal.

713 **LETTER XXI, EUTYCHES TO ST. LEO.** — Letter of the heretic Eutyches, in which, writing to Leo, pope of the city of Rome, he denies that Christ has two natures, namely divinity and humanity. Ibid. **LETTER XXII, THE FIRST LETTER OF FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO POPE LEO.** — I. The devil’s snares are avoided by one who adheres to the teaching of the Holy Fathers. — II. The cunning of heretics by which they deceive the unwary. — III. Eutyches is reviving the doctrines of Valentinus and Apollinaris. — IV. His deposition and excommunication were entirely just; he asks that Leo make this known to the Westerners.

723 **LETTER XXIII, TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — Having received Eutyches’ complaints, he protests that Eutyches was deprived of communion by Flavian. — II. He asks to be informed of the case and especially wishes charity to be preserved in defending the truth.

731 **LETTER XXIV, TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS.** — I. After praising the emperor’s faith, he sets forth Eutyches’ complaint. — II. He censures Flavian’s silence and asks to be informed of the matter.

735 [Col. 1565] **LETTER XXV, OF PETER CHRYSOLOGUS OF RAVENNA TO EUTYCHES THE PRESBYTER.** — I. He teaches that the incarnation was prescribed long ago against errors attacking the incarnation of the Word; it is not to be debated but believed with honor and fear. — II. He advises Eutyches to attend obediently to the writings of the Roman pontiff, because Peter, directing the rulers of his see, provides guidance to those seeking the truth of the faith.

739 **LETTER XXVI, THE SECOND LETTER OF FLAVIAN TO ST. LEO.**

743 **LETTER XXVII, TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He informs Flavian that he has received his letters; he praises what Flavian did against Eutyches and promises his own concern.

751 **LETTER XXVIII, TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, AGAINST THE PERFIDY AND HERESY OF EUTYCHES.** — I. Eutyches became a heretic through ignorance of the Holy Scriptures. — II. Against those who attempt to divide the mystery of the Lord’s dispensation into two sons. — III. Against those who dare to assert the passibility of the divinity of the only-begotten Son of God. — IV. Against those who argue for a mixture or confusion of Christ’s two natures. — V. Against those who madly assert that the form of a servant, which he assumed from us, is heavenly or of some other substance. — VI. Against those who deliriously claim that the Lord had two natures before the union but one after the union.

756 **LETTER XXIX, TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS.** — He sends legates in his place to the synod at Ephesus, convened on account of Eutyches. He hopes for better things from Eutyches.

781 **LETTER XXX, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. Christ is a human being of our kind. The errors of Nestorius and Eutyches. — II. When the reality of Christ’s flesh is attacked, the entire faith is shaken.

785 **LETTER XXXI, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — He stirs up Pulcheria’s zeal against Eutyches. — II. It is essential to human salvation that Christ be not merely human but human of the same kind as ourselves. — III. The generation of Christians flows from Christ’s generation. Eutyches’ obstinacy. The moderation of the apostolic see. — IV. Leo is prevented from attending the council by custom, the circumstances of the time, and affection for his fellow citizens. The Apostles’ Creed is shaken by a new heresy.

789 **LETTER XXXII, TO FAUSTUS, MARTIN, AND THE OTHER ARCHIMANDRITES OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He curses Eutyches’ opinion, wishes him to return to a sounder mind, and thus to be restored to communion.

795 **LETTER XXXIII, TO THE SECOND SYNOD OF EPHESUS.** — I. The faith of the incarnation is proved by Peter’s confession. — II. The council was convened to abolish error and restore those who had gone astray.

797 **LETTER XXXIV, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COOS.** — I. He grieves that Eutyches has fallen away from the unity of the faith. — II. He sends legates from his own side to the synod.

801 **LETTER XXXV, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COOS.** — I. Eutyches destroys Christian hope and the truth of all the mysteries. — II. The properties of both natures are preserved in Christ. — III. Christ’s soul did not pre-exist his body, nor was his body created from nothing; rather, both are of the same nature as ours.

803 **LETTER XXXVI, TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He informs him that he has received the letters and proceedings of the synod against Eutyches.

809 **LETTER XXXVII, TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS.** — The unity of the faith and confession must be preserved. Legates have been sent to the synod at Ephesus, but necessity does not permit him to go there.

811 **LETTER XXXVIII, TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He informs him that he has received his letters; he praises him for defending the faith and urges mercy if the heretic repents.

812 **LETTER XXXIX, TO THE SAME FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He complains of Flavian’s silence; at that time Leo was unaware of the pillage at Ephesus.

813 **LETTER XL, TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGH THE PROVINCE OF ARLES IN GAUL.** — He rejoices at Ravennius’s good and peaceful election and wishes him to live up to the favorable opinion formed of him.

814 **LETTER XLI, TO RAVENNIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES.** — He congratulates Ravennius on his election as bishop, commends episcopal virtues, and urges him to write to him more often.

815 **LETTER XLII, TO THE SAME RAVENNIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES.** — He warns him about Petronianus, a vagrant who falsely claimed to be Leo’s deacon, and asks that he be expelled from communion with all the Churches.

816 **LETTER XLIII, TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS.** — I. He complains to the emperor about the Robber Council at Ephesus. — II. He asks that matters remain in the condition in which they were before the false synod. — III. He begs the emperor to order a council to be held within Italy.

823 **LETTER XLIV, TO THE SAME THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS.** — I. The false synod at Ephesus, favoring private hatreds, threw everything in the Church into confusion; it rejected the writings of the apostolic see; everything was done by force; Hilary alone barely escaped among the legates who opposed it; this synod must never be received by the apostolic see. — II. He asks Theodosius, together with all the Westerners, to keep everything in the same condition until the greater synod. — III. He requests a general synod within Italy.

825 **LETTER XLV, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. He sends a copy of the letter he had written to her before the synod. — II. He laments the shameful proceedings of the false synod. He sends a copy of the letter written to Theodosius and requests a council in Italy. — III. He entrusts the apostolic legation before Theodosius to Pulcheria.

831 **LETTER XLVI, OF HILARY, THEN DEACON OF THE ROMAN CHURCH AND LATER BISHOP, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. Through Dioscorus’s wicked boldness he was unable to approach her and deliver the letters of St. Leo. — II. Having escaped Dioscorus’s plots, he came to Rome; the false synod at Ephesus was rejected by Leo.

837 **LETTER XLVII, TO ANASTASIUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA.** — I. He congratulates him on not having attended the false synod. — II. He urges him to preserve the faith, adhere to Flavian, and strengthen the brethren.

839 **LETTER XLVIII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COOS.** — After the disaster at Ephesus, he consoles him and urges him to hold fast to the faith.

840 **LETTER XLIX, TO FLAVIAN, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He consoles Flavian, against whom Dioscorus had raged savagely, and promises him assistance.

841 **LETTER L, TO THE CONSTANTINOPOLITANS, THROUGH EPIPHANIUS AND DIONYSIUS, NOTARIES OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.** — I. After the false synod at Ephesus, he urges the Constantinopolitans to adhere to the faith and to Flavian. — II. He consoles them over Flavian’s unjust deposition. Ibid. **LETTER LI, TO FAUSTUS AND THE OTHER ARCHIMANDRITES OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He exhorts them to steadfastness in every good thing, especially faith and charity, and detests the proceedings of the Second Council of Ephesus.

843 **LETTER LII, OF THEODORITUS, BISHOP OF CYRUS, TO POPE ST. LEO.** — I. He rightly hastens to the apostolic see, which stands above the others by so many prerogatives. — II. He launches into praise of St. Leo and commends his zeal against the Manichaeans and his letter to Flavian. — III. He complains how unjustly he himself was deposed without being summoned to court. — IV. He enumerates the labors he has undertaken for the Church. — V. He prays that he not be rejected when appealing to the apostolic see; he wishes his faith to be proved by his writings, which he identifies. — VI. He wishes Leo to instruct him about what he ought to do concerning the judgment at Ephesus. — VII. He commends his legates, himself, and his concerns to Leo’s prayers and solicitude; he says that he and others are being detained by imperial letters so that they cannot go to the pontiff.

845 **LETTER LIII, OR FRAGMENT OF A LETTER OF ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO ST. LEO.** — Concerning his ordination.

853 **LETTER LIV, TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS.** — He writes that he adheres to the Nicene faith; Eutyches must be condemned no less than Nestorius; he asks that a council be held within Italy.

855 **LETTER LV, OF VALENTINIAN TO THEODOSIUS.**

857 **LETTER LVI, OF GALLA PLACIDIA TO THEODOSIUS.**

859 **LETTER LVII, OF LICINIA EUDOXIA AUGUSTA TO THE SAME THEODOSIUS.** — Concerning the disturbance of the Catholic Church.

860 **LETTER LVIII, OF GALLA PLACIDIA TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — She detests the Second Council of Ephesus.

863 **LETTER LIX, TO THE CLERGY AND PEOPLE OF THE CITY OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. He rejoices that they continue to adhere to Flavian and resist error. — II. The reality of Christ’s flesh is proved from the mystery of the Eucharist. — III. It is also proved from his exaltation over all things and from his bodily actions and sufferings. — IV. From the necessity of the incarnation for wiping away Adam’s guilt, and from the prophecies that foretold it. — V. Various errors against the faith of the incarnation.

865 **LETTER LX, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — Through Eutyches the foundations of the faith are shaken; with Pulcheria’s support he wishes a general council to be held against him.

873 **LETTER LXI, TO MARTIN AND FAUSTUS, PRESBYTERS.** — I. He informs them about the letters written to them. — II. He urges them to support the cause of the faith and promises them his concern.

874 **LETTER LXII, OF THE EMPEROR THEODOSIUS TO VALENTINIAN AUGUSTUS.** — He replies to Letter LV.

875 **LETTER LXIII, OF THEODOSIUS TO GALLA PLACIDIA.** — He replies to Letter LVI.

877 [Col. 1567] **LETTER LXIV, OF THE SAME THEODOSIUS TO LICINIA EUDOXIA.** — He replies to Letter LVII. Ibid. **LETTER LXV, OR THE PETITION SENT BY ALL THE PROVINCIAL BISHOPS OF THE METROPOLIS OF ARLES TO POPE ST. LEO.** — I. After prefacing some remarks about Ravennius’s election and character, they ask Leo to restore the ancient privileges of the Church of Arles. — II. They confirm these privileges from various prerogatives of this Church, especially from St. Trophimus’s arrival in Gaul. — III. They recall the civil rights and privileges of the people of Arles granted by the emperors. — IV. They flatter Leo with various testimonies of their devotion.

879 **LETTER LXVI, OF POPE ST. LEO IN REPLY TO THE FOREGOING PETITION OF THE PROVINCIAL BISHOPS OF THE METROPOLIS OF ARLES.** — St. Leo gives his judgment concerning the ancient dispute between the Churches of Arles and Vienne and assigns each its boundaries.

883 **LETTER LXVII, TO RAVENNIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES.** — He sends Ravennius his celebrated letter to Flavian concerning the incarnation of the Word of God against Eutyches, so that through Ravennius this letter, or the letter of Cyril of Alexandria, may be faithfully made known to all the bishops of Gaul. He also indicates the secret instructions entrusted to the legates.

886 **LETTER LXVIII, OF CERETIUS, SALONIUS, AND VERANUS, BISHOPS OF GAUL, TO POPE ST. LEO.** — I. They give thanks for his letter to Flavian, which they assert is celebrated throughout all the Churches. — II. They send him a copy transcribed by them, for Leo to correct and return.

887 **LETTER LXIX, TO THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS.** — I. He suspends his consent to the ordination of Anatolius of Constantinople and demands a profession of faith. — II. He asks that Anatolius likewise renounce communion with heretics and subscribe to the common faith. He sends legates and requests that a synod be held within Italy.

890 **LETTER LXX, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — He awaits Anatolius’s profession of faith. He has sent legates to the East. All scandals must be removed through a general council.

893 **LETTER LXXI, TO THE ARCHIMANDRITES OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He complains about the silence of Anatolius and those ordained by him concerning the renunciation of error. He informs them that legates have been sent on the matter of the faith.

895 **LETTER LXXII, TO FAUSTUS THE PRESBYTER.** — He praises his faith and urges him to vigilance.

897 **LETTER LXXIII, OF VALENTINIAN AND MARCIAN TO LEO, ARCHBISHOP OF ROME.** — Concerning their election and the holding of a council.

899 **LETTER LXXIV, TO MARTIN THE PRESBYTER.** — How good it is to suffer for the truth, whose unity is not divided by distances of place. A mention of the legates. Ibid. **LETTER LXXV, TO FAUSTUS AND MARTIN, PRESBYTERS.** — I. He writes that what was done at Ephesus against the faith is intolerable to the Western bishops. — II. Both Nestorius and Eutyches serve Antichrist; against them the Church professes that it worships not one nature but one person.

901 **LETTER LXXVI, OF THE EMPEROR MARCIAN TO LEO, ARCHBISHOP OF ROME.**

903 **LETTER LXXVII, OF PULCHERIA AUGUSTA TO THE MOST HOLY LEO, ARCHBISHOP OF ROME.**

905 **LETTER LXXVIII, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — He gives thanks for the letters sent and for the defense of the faith.

907 **LETTER LXXIX, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. He gives thanks that, through her authority, Nestorius and Eutyches have been suppressed. — II. Concerning the legates who were assisted, the priests restored to their sees, the relics of Flavian brought back to the city, and the lapsed to be received if they subscribe to the faith. — III. Concerning Eusebius, who enjoys communion with the apostolic see, and Julian…

Of Coensa; and concerning the clergy of Constantinople who supported Flavian. 909

**LETTER LXXX, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. His faith is approved by the writings he sent. — II. Concerning those who fell into heresy through fear, that they should be received if they have been converted. — III. The names of heretics are not to be recited at the holy altar. — IV. Concerning the commendation [Al.: commemoration] of Bishop Julian, and of those clergy who remained faithful to Bishop Flavian. 912

**LETTER LXXXI, TO JULIAN, BISHOP.** — He warns Julian, long harassed by the wickedness of Dioscorus, that those who have fallen must not be admitted to communion unless their perfidy has been condemned together with its authors. 915

**LETTER LXXXII, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. He offers congratulations on the preservation of the Catholic faith, for which the peace of the empire is granted in return. — II. Action should be taken only against those who are in error, not against the faith or the Scriptures, which it is unlawful to interpret otherwise than the holy Fathers did. 917

**LETTER LXXXIII, TO THE SAME MARCIAN.** — I. He congratulates him on Anatolius’s faith having been revealed, Eutyches having been suppressed, the bishops recalled, and the relics of Saint Flavian brought back to the city. — II. He is sending legates for the reconciliation of the bishops who have fallen. The time is not suitable for convening a council. 919

**LETTER LXXXIV, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. He sends legates who are to deal with those who have fallen with the greatest prudence and moderation [Col. 1568]. — II. Anyone who denies our nature in Christ is acting outside unity. — III. He asks that Eutyches be transferred to a more remote place and that a Catholic be placed over his monastery. 921

**LETTER LXXXV, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. Those who became involved in the errors of heretics through fear rather than by choice should be received through satisfaction and an unambiguous profession of faith. — II. He reserves for himself the examination of the leaders of the heretics; meanwhile he forbids their names to be recited at the altar. — III. He replies to his memorandum, urges him to vigilance, and asks that everything be reported to him. 922

**LETTER LXXXVI, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — For the sake of their common friendship and the good of the Church, he asks that Julian’s concern be joined to the care of his legates, so that the remnants of heresy may be destroyed. 924

**LETTER LXXXVII, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He commends to him the presbyters Basil and John, who had come to Rome accused of heresy in order to give an account of their faith. 926

**LETTER LXXXVIII, TO PASCHASINUS, BISHOP OF LILYBAEUM.** — I. He sends Paschasinus his famous letter to Flavian of Constantinople, by which the legate who was to attend the synod might be instructed. — II. He asserts the existence of two natures in Christ against Eutyches. — III. He sends testimonies of the holy Fathers concerning the Lord’s incarnation, and announces that the bishops of the Eastern diocese have subscribed to the same letter to Flavian. — He asks that the question of Easter in the year 435 be investigated more carefully. 927

**LETTER LXXXIX, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — Concerning the legates sent to the general council, who will act in his place; there everything must be restored to the unity of faith and peace. 930

**LETTER XC, TO THE SAME MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. He agrees to the convocation of a general council, although, because of the disturbance of the times, he would have preferred that it be postponed to another occasion. — II. The faith must not be treated there as doubtful, nor must anyone depart from Nicaea. 932

**LETTER XCI, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — Although a shorter interval had been granted for convening the council, he is nevertheless sending legates who will fulfill his role. 934

**LETTER XCII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — The pontiff instructs Julian to join his care and counsel to those of the legates sent to the general council. 936

**LETTER XCIII, TO THE SYNOD FIRST SUMMONED TO NICAEA AND AFTERWARDS ASSEMBLED AT CHALCEDON.** — I. The pressure of time and established custom forbid him to be present at the synod; nevertheless he will be present through the legates whom he is sending. — II. The audacity of disputing against the faith must be restrained. — III. Bishops expelled on account of the faith must be restored, while the decrees enacted at Ephesus against Nestorius remain in force. Ibid.

**LETTER XCIV, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — He commends to Augustus the legates whom he is sending to the synod and asks that no debate about the faith be initiated there. 941

**LETTER XCV, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. He has sent legates to the council, although he would have preferred it to be assembled in Italy. — II. Moderation must be observed in ecclesiastical cases, a moderation far removed from the brigandage of Ephesus. — III. He has never denied pardon to those who have been corrected. — IV. Even heresiarchs who ask for mercy should not be rejected, although they should certainly not be received rashly. 942

**LETTER XCVI, TO RAVENNIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES.** — Unity must above all be preserved in the celebration of Easter; it belongs to the Roman pontiff to announce this solemn observance. 945

**LETTER XCVII, THE SYNODAL LETTER OF EUSEBIUS, BISHOP OF MILAN, TO SAINT POPE LEO.** — I. He rejoices at the return of his brothers from the East. — II. The letter to Flavian was read and approved at the synod of Milan. — III. He declares that he and his clergy subscribe to the condemnation of the Eutychians. Ibid.

**LETTER XCVIII, OF THE HOLY SYNOD OF CHALCEDON TO THE MOST HOLY POPE LEO OF THE ROMAN CHURCH.** — I. The synod praises Leo, established for all as the interpreter of the voice of Blessed Peter, and declares that he presided through his legates. — II. Concerning the tyranny and impious acts of Dioscorus of Alexandria. — III. What was done concerning him, and concerning the definition of the faith. — IV. It explains the reason for issuing the canon concerning the prerogative of the see of Constantinople and asks for its confirmation. 951

**LETTER XCIX, THE SYNODAL LETTER OF RAVENNIUS AND THE OTHER BISHOPS OF GAUL TO SAINT POPE LEO.** — I. They excuse their delay in replying. — II. They state that everyone in Gaul received Leo’s letter to Flavian as the statement of the faith. — III. In that letter the hidden mystery of the incarnation is unveiled to believers and unbelievers alike. — IV. Because of the reports brought from the East, they refrained from writing to the emperor. — V. They congratulate the pontiff Leo, given by God to the Church. 966

**LETTER C, OF THE EMPEROR MARCIAN TO POPE LEO.** — I. He offers congratulations on the faith being strengthened at Chalcedon and the peace of the Church restored. — II. The faith was expounded by the synod in accordance with Saint Leo’s letter. — III. He asks that the see of Constantinople be granted second place, according to the enactments of the second and fourth councils [Col. 1569]. — IV. Through Lucian and Basil he asks for Leo’s agreement on the same matter. 970

**LETTER CI, OF ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO SAINT LEO, ARCHBISHOP OF ROME.** — I. Anatolius praises Leo’s zeal against the heretics whom he overthrew. Concerning the acts brought from Chalcedon to Rome. — II. Anatolius’s legates were sent to Rome with the other acts. Concerning the condemnation of Dioscorus. — III. Concerning Leo’s letter, received by everyone, and the definition of the faith issued at the synod of Chalcedon. — IV. Concerning the other proceedings at Chalcedon after the definition of the faith: first, as regards the canons, and then as regards particular ecclesiastical cases. Finally, concerning the privilege of the Church of Constantinople. — V. Leo’s legates opposed this privilege. Its confirmation is requested. 975

**LETTER CII, TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL.** — I. He announces that he has received the letter of the Gallic bishops, full of heavenly doctrine. — II. Concerning the ecumenical synod. Human arguments about the faith ought to have no place. — III. The doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches must alike be avoided. — IV. The synod agreed with Leo’s letter and proscribed Dioscorus. — V. God must be thanked for all these things; prayer should be offered for the return of the legates; and the victory of the faith should be announced to the Spaniards through the Gauls. 983

**LETTER CIII, TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL.** — After the legates had returned from the synod of Chalcedon and the acts had been received, together with the sentence pronounced against Eutyches and Dioscorus, he sends a copy of it to the Gallic bishops. 987

**LETTER CIV, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. Concerning the victory of the faith and the usefulness of errors in the Church. — II. Many evils arise from Anatolius’s ambition. — III. The see of Constantinople, which is imperial rather than apostolic, cannot be elevated by depressing the others. — IV. He asks Marcian to restrain Anatolius’s desire. — V. Anatolius has been emboldened by his earlier excesses. 991

**LETTER CV, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. The victory of the faith is complete, in that both those who fell and those who stood firm have prevailed. — II. Nothing can prevail against the canons of Nicaea, which alone are sufficient to establish peace. — III. Anatolius ought to take Flavian as an example; whatever is contrary to the Council of Nicaea will collapse of itself. — IV. He urges her herself to recall Anatolius from his purpose. 997

**LETTER CVI, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. Anatolius’s faith deserves praise, but his ambition condemnation. — II. The prerogative of the Council of Nicaea, which Anatolius’s ambition seeks. — III. He abuses the synod of Chalcedon, convened solely for the matter of the faith. — IV. He will never consent to unlawful attempts prejudicial to the Council of Nicaea. — V. The canons of the synod of Constantinople were never sent to the Roman see; Anatolius wrongly invokes them in his support. — VI. It would be better for him to abandon his ambition and pursue charity. 1001

**LETTER CVII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — I. How highly the authority of the Council of Nicaea must be valued. — II. He reproves Julian for favoring Anatolius of Constantinople. — III. Against the order of the universal Church, without guilt on either of their parts, neither may he grant anything nor may Julian obtain anything for him. 1009

**LETTER CVIII, TO THEODORUS, BISHOP OF FORUM JULII.** — I. In doubtful matters each bishop ought to have recourse to his metropolitan. — II. There are two remedies for sin, and he explains what the order of reconciliation should be. — III. A penitent who dies before reconciliation cannot be reconciled after death. — IV. Reconciliation must be denied to no one who, placed at the point of death, asks for it. — V. How dangerous it is to reserve penance until the end. It must be denied to no one who asks for it by signs, while the canonical rules concerning apostates are observed. — VI. He asks that he communicate his replies to the consultation to the metropolitan. 1011

**LETTER CIX, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — I. He complains about the disturbances and violence of the Palestinian monks, by which they harassed Catholics and extorted assent to the Eutychian heresy. — II. They must be restrained by the emperor, and the obstinate must be driven into exile. — III. He sends Saint Athanasius’s letter to Epictetus to be set against them. — IV. Concerning Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, expelled by the same men, and another person substituted for him. 1014

**LETTER CX, OF MARCIAN AUGUSTUS TO POPE LEO.** — He asks the pontiff for confirmation of the synod of Chalcedon as something necessary. He praises his steadfastness in defending the canons and restraining innovation. 1017

**LETTER CXI, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. The suspicion concerning Anatolius’s ordination has been removed by his profession of faith. — II. He wrongfully removed Aetius from the office of archdeacon. — III. He asks Marcian to draw Anatolius away from unlawful actions and to favor Julian. 1019

**LETTER CXII, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. He complains that Andrew has been placed in charge of ecclesiastical affairs after Aetius was removed. — II. He asks that everything be restored to its former condition. 1023

**LETTER CXIII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — I. He gives thanks that Julian has shown sympathy with him in his many sufferings, while also complaining about the deposition of Aetius [Col. 1570]. — II. He wishes Julian to remain vigilant for the cause of the faith. Anatolius has been rebuked by the emperor. — III. Concerning the disturbance caused by the Egyptian and Palestinian monks. — IV. Concerning the translation of his letter and the acts of the Council of Chalcedon into Latin. 1024

**LETTER CXIV, ADDRESSED TO THE BISHOPS WHO WERE ASSEMBLED IN THE HOLY SYNOD OF CHALCEDON.** — I. He agrees with what was decreed at Chalcedon concerning the faith. — II. He can never regard as ratified what was done there against the canons of Nicaea. 1027

**LETTER CXV, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. He gives thanks for the peace restored to the Church, the remnants of the heretics suppressed, and Anatolius rebuked. — II. Concerning the monks restrained by Marcian and the approval of the Council of Chalcedon sent by him personally to the bishops. 1031

**LETTER CXVI, TO PULCHERIA AUGUSTA.** — I. He gives thanks for the vigor of the faith and for the sanctions issued against rebellious monks. — II. He has sent letters to the bishops of Chalcedon as witnesses to his agreement. 1035

**LETTER CXVII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — I. In order to satisfy the emperor and remove an opportunity from the heretics, he sent letters concerning his agreement to the bishops of Chalcedon. — II. Concerning the monks restrained by Marcian’s edict and the archimandrites rebuked in Pulcheria’s reply. — III. Concerning Eudocia, whom Leo warned at the emperor’s secret command. — IV. The deposition of Aetius must be borne patiently, lest, by interfering in the government of other Churches, he appear to exceed his proper measure. — V. Anatolius wished to obtain from the Illyrian bishops a subscription in support of his ambition. Concerning the letter written to the bishops of Chalcedon. 1037

**LETTER CXVIII, TO THE SAME JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — I. He has omitted nothing on behalf of the faith and the Church. — II. The ministry of preaching belongs to priests alone, not to monks; the emperor’s zeal must be aroused against the Alexandrian parricides. 1039

**LETTER CXIX, TO MAXIMUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH.** — I. The faith stands midway between two extremes. — II. Maximus ought to watch over the purity of the faith in the Eastern Churches. — III. The privileges of the Churches must remain unshaken. — IV. Anatolius’s attempts, contrary to the canons of Nicaea, will be null. — V. If the legates should approve anything at the synod apart from the matter of the faith, it must be rescinded. — VI. The ministry of preaching must be granted to no one except bishops. 1040

**LETTER CXX, TO THEODORITUS, BISHOP OF CYRUS.** — I. Heresies, which have arisen not without benefit to the Church, must be suppressed by an irrevocable judgment. — II. The victory which the Church gains over the heretics belongs to Christ. — III. The obstinacy of Dioscorus, raging even against Leo. — IV. Those who write about matters of faith must weigh their words. — V. Invincible truth has shown that Theodoretus is free from every stain of heresy. — VI. Vigilance is necessary even after victory. No one, whether monk or layman, ought to arrogate to himself the ministry of preaching apart from priests. 1045

**LETTER CXXI, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. The care of the Paschal cycle was formerly entrusted to the bishop of Alexandria. — II. What difficulty arose from that arrangement. — III. He asks him to order an investigation of this difficulty. 1055

**LETTER CXXII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP.** — He asks him to investigate more carefully the controversy concerning Easter in the following year and to send a reply. 1058

**LETTER CXXIII, TO EUDOCIA AUGUSTA.** — I. He asks her to devote her care to restoring the Palestinian monks to faith and peace. — II. Once they have accepted the Council of Chalcedon, they must execrate both Eutyches and Nestorius if they wish to appear Catholic. He wishes to be informed by her letter of what her exhortation has accomplished. 1060

**LETTER CXXIV, TO THE PALESTINIAN MONKS.** — I. The Palestinians have been misled by a perverse interpretation of Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian. — II. Both Eutyches, who confuses the natures in Christ, and Nestorius, who multiplies the persons, must be detested. — III. Anyone who does not confess our nature in Christ has no part in Christ. — IV. Only those are cleansed by Christ’s blood in whose body he was offered, suffered, and died in triumph. — V. The properties of each of his natures are declared by the character of his works. — VI. Both natures come together without confusion in one person. — VII. Nothing new has been added to the Son of God except in the form of a servant. — VIII. He reproves these same monks concerning the scandals arising from their fury. — IX. He exhorts them to recover their senses and embrace the common faith. 1061

**LETTER CXXV, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — Through the count Rodanus he amicably reproaches Julian for his silence and wishes to be informed about everything. 1068

**LETTER CXXVI, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — He gives thanks for the disturbances in Palestine being calmed and Juvenal of Jerusalem restored to his see, while also censuring Dioscorus and his Egyptian followers. 1069

**LETTER CXXVII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — I. Concerning the restoration of the bishop of Jerusalem, the conversion of the Palestinian monks, and the receipt of Proterius’s letters. — II. He wishes the matter of Easter in the year 455 to be investigated more carefully. — III. Concerning his letter to the bishops of Chalcedon, read at Constantinople, the examination of Aetius, and the various letters written back and forth. 1070

**LETTER CXXVIII, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — Having praised the prince’s faith and piety, he declares that he will gladly receive Anatolius back into his favor, provided that Anatolius gives satisfaction to the canons and does not overturn the rights of priests. 1073

**LETTER CXXIX, TO PROTERIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA.** — I. It belongs to bishops to watch lest the unity of the faith be violated, which can happen even through the alteration of a small letter. — II. From the tradition of the holy Fathers he asserts both that his own letter is Catholic and that the peoples must be instructed. — III. The faith, discipline, and privileges of the Churches must be preserved according to the standard of antiquity. 1075

**LETTER CXXX, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. He congratulates him on the faith of Proterius, bishop of Alexandria. — II. The Alexandrians must be instructed by him according to the tradition of his Church. — III. He asks that Leo’s letter to Flavian, falsified by the heretics, be translated anew into Greek and publicly recited to the Alexandrians. 1078

**LETTER CXXXI, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — I. He informs Julian of the receipt of Proterius’s letter from Alexandria; he wishes and commands that his letter to Flavian be translated by Julian from Latin into Greek, and, having been sent under the emperor’s seal, publicly recited to the Alexandrian people in the Church. — II. He asks for a reply concerning Easter in the following year. 1081

**LETTER CXXXII, OF ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE, TO POPE LEO.** — I. He amicably complains about the interruption of their correspondence and demonstrates his obedience, which he owes to the pontiff. — II. He writes that Aetius has been restored, while Andrew has been deposed. — III. He greatly desires to be refreshed by the letters of the holy pontiff. — IV. He removes the charge of ambition from himself and attributes it to the zeal of his clergy and the Eastern bishops. The confirmation of the acts of Chalcedon is said to have been reserved to pontifical authority. 1082

**LETTER CXXXIII, OF SAINT PROTERIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO THE MOST BLESSED POPE LEO, BISHOP OF THE CITY OF ROME.** 1084

**LETTER CXXXIV, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. Having praised Marcian, he promises Anatolius his favor if Anatolius comes to his senses. — II. He asks that Eutyches, spreading his poison in exile, be relegated to more remote places. — III. He gives thanks for the investigation of the date of Easter and prays that he favor the Catholics. 1091

**LETTER CXXXV, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP.** — I. He explains the reason for the interruption of their correspondence. — II. He praises the removal of Andrew the archdeacon and the restoration of others in the Church of Constantinople. — III. He desires greater sincerity in acknowledging guilt. 1096

**LETTER CXXXVI, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS: ON THE CORRECTION OF ANATOLIUS.** — I. Why he ceased writing to Anatolius. — II. On the conditions under which he will be reconciled to him. — III. Concerning Andrew, removed from the archdeaconate, and Julian, who is commended. — IV. He asks that the monk Carosus be restrained. 1098

**LETTER CXXXVII, TO THE SAME MARCIAN.** — I. He gives thanks for the thorough investigation of the date of Easter, concerning which he indicates that he has received Proterius’s letter. — II. The accounts of the Church’s stewards must be examined not by judicial judgment but by the scrutiny of priests. 1100

**LETTER CXXXVIII, TO THE BISHOPS OF GAUL AND SPAIN.** — He sends this formal letter announcing the date of Easter to the Gallic bishops, so that through them it may be transmitted to the Churches of Spain; the state of the controversy is also explained. 1101

**LETTER CXXXIX, TO JUVENAL, BISHOP OF JERUSALEM.** — I. He rejoices that Juvenal has been restored to his see, without concealing his earlier evasion. — II. He wishes him to be instructed by the very places of the sacred mysteries. — III. The truth of our flesh in Christ is defended from the truth of the crucifixion. — IV. Those who are in error concerning the Lord’s incarnation must be instructed from the pages of both Testaments. 1102

**LETTER CXL, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — The correction of those in error will henceforth be easier, now that Dioscorus has been removed, whose death Julian had announced to Leo. He also asks Julian to write about the condition of the Church of Alexandria. 1109

**LETTER CXLI, TO THE SAME JULIAN.** — I. Concerning the correction of the monk Carosus and the mission of John the decurion to Egypt. — II. Concerning what happened to Maximus, bishop of Antioch, after he was accused of some crime; he asks Julian to send a reply. 1110

**LETTER CXLII, TO MARCIAN AUGUSTUS.** — I. Having praised Augustus’s faith, he again informs him of the agreement he has given concerning the celebration of the feast day. — II. He gives thanks for Carosus and Dorotheus being removed from their monasteries. 1110

**LETTER CXLIII, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He asks that the remnants of the heretics hiding in the city not be fostered by excessive leniency and regain strength. 1111

**LETTER CXLIV, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — Now published for the first time from the manuscript of Regensburg. He praises Julian’s diligence. The efforts of the Eutychians after Marcian’s death. Their disturbances at Alexandria. 1112

**LETTER CXLV, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** — I. He asks him to aid the troubled Church of Alexandria [Col. 1572]. — II. The faith, once properly defined, must not be debated again; and a Catholic bishop must be appointed over the Church of Alexandria. 1113

**LETTER CXLVI, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. The frenzy of the heretics at Alexandria, perpetrated for destruction, tends toward the overthrow of the Council of Chalcedon, taking advantage of the death of the emperor Marcian. — II. He has written to Leo Augustus on behalf of preserving the decrees of the synod. 1115

**LETTER CXLVII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA, AND AETIUS THE PRESBYTER.** — I. Having complained about Julian’s silence, he entrusts the care of the Church to him. — II. He asks that the decrees of the Council of Chalcedon remain unshaken and that a Catholic bishop be elected for Alexandria. 1116

**LETTER CXLVIII, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** — He rejoices that Augustus is the guardian of the Council of Chalcedon and asks him to restrain the obstinate and treacherous contention of the heretics. 1117

**LETTER CXLIX, TO BASIL, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH.** — I. After first complaining that the announcement of his ordination was not sent, he urges Basil to resist the fury of the Eutychians, who, after murdering Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, demanded that a new synod be established while the Council of Chalcedon was set aside. — II. Having praised the emperor Leo, he asserts that everything depends on the steadfastness of the bishops, so that no new proceedings may be undertaken. 1119

**LETTER CL, TO EUXITHEUS, BISHOP OF THESSALONICA, AND, IN A SIMILAR LETTER, TO JUVENAL OF JERUSALEM, PETER OF CORINTH, AND LUKE OF DYRRACHIUM.** — He urges them vigorously to resist the criminal attempts of the Eutychians, who had killed Proterius, bishop of Alexandria, and not to allow another synod to be convened; rather, they must uphold the firmness of the Council of Chalcedon. 1120

**LETTER CLI, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — Now published for the first time from the manuscript of Regensburg. He praises Anatolius and urges him to purge the Church of Constantinople from heresy. Concerning the examination of the presbyter Atticus. 1121

**LETTER CLII, TO JULIAN, BISHOP OF COENSA.** — He instructs Julian to ensure that the preceding letters written to the metropolitans reach each of them through Julian’s or Aetius’s care. Episcopal steadfastness is required above all. There is nothing new, obscure, or doubtful in his letter. 1122

**LETTER CLIII, TO AETIUS, PRESBYTER OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. He asks him to forward individually the letters written to the East. — II. He likewise sent letters written to him by the Gauls and Italians, and also concerning other matters. 1123

**LETTER CLIV, TO THE BISHOPS OF EGYPT.** — He consoles the Egyptian bishops exiled for the faith and urges them to endure adversity patiently for the sake of the mystery of the incarnation. 1124

**LETTER CLV, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. He rouses him to vigilance against the attempts of the heretics. — II. He reproves the connivance of the clergy of Constantinople and desires pastoral firmness from Anatolius in dealing with them. 1125

**LETTER CLVI, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** — I. Nothing concerning the faith is to be treated again after the Council of Chalcedon. — II. Anyone who reexamines the truth declared by the Church is an Antichrist. — III. It is impious for the Alexandrian parricides to preside over the Church of Alexandria. — IV. The prayers offered to Leo Augustus by Catholics and by heretics, and how they differ. — V. All the offices and mysteries of the Christian religion have been interrupted at Alexandria. — VI. He promises longer writings concerning the faith, censures Anatolius’s negligence, and commends the Catholics. 1127

**LETTER CLVII, TO ANATOLIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. He asks him to act energetically with the emperor, whom he praises, to suppress the heretics; and to ensure that the Council of Chalcedon remain firm and that peace be restored to the Church of Alexandria. — II. He asks that the parricides be expelled from it and that the afflicted Egyptian bishops be assisted. — III. Help must be provided to the bishops who have fled from Egypt; the adversaries of the synod must be resisted steadfastly. — IV. Concerning the presbyter Atticus and Andrew: they must either be corrected or expelled from the Church. 1132

**LETTER CLVIII, TO THE CATHOLIC BISHOPS OF EGYPT RESIDING AT CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He consoles the bishops exiled for the faith and urges them to patience by setting before them the hope of heavenly reward and by promising his action with the emperor. 1134

**LETTER CLIX, TO NICETAS, BISHOP OF AQUILEIA.** — I. What women should do who, after their husbands were captured, married other men: when their former husbands return from captivity, they should be reunited with them, so that each may recover what is his. — II. A man who appears to have married the wife of a captive is not to be judged culpable. — III. If the husbands return from captivity and are not offended by the misconduct of their wives, and wish to receive them again in marriage, they must have the freedom to do so. — IV. If the women refuse to return to their former husbands, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as impious women. — V. Captives who were compelled by terror [Al.: error] or hunger, not by reverence, to eat sacrificial foods are to be granted penance. — VI. Those who were compelled by force or error to consent to a second baptism are to be relieved by a remedy, with careful consideration being given to old age, dangers, illnesses, and other necessities. — VII. Those baptized by heretics are to be confirmed solely through the invocation of the Holy Spirit. 1135

**LETTER CLX, TO THE BISHOPS AND CATHOLIC CLERGY OF EGYPT RESIDING AT CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. He consoles the exiled Egyptian bishops and clergy and informs them that, with the emperor’s approval, he is sending his legates to the East. — II. He urges them to remove every new discussion concerning the faith, since the authority of the synod is sufficient. 1140

**LETTER CLXI, TO THE PRESBYTERS, DEACONS, AND CLERGY OF THE CHURCH OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — I. He urges them to remain steadfast in the faith and separate from the company of heretics. — II. He asks that no new judgment be initiated and that Atticus and Andrew be deprived of the honor of their order unless they profess, orally and in writing, their adherence to the faith of Chalcedon. 1142

**LETTER CLXII, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** — I. He asks that he not permit the faith once defined to be called back for examination. — II. He can neither join the heretics in communion nor dissent from what the synod has defined. — III. He is sending legates, not to dispute, but to instruct. — IV. Heretics must be avoided; he indicates that punishment also awaits them. 1143

**LETTER CLXIII, TO ANATOLIUS OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He complains that his admonitions displeased Anatolius and warns him that, if Atticus the presbyter wishes to appear Catholic, he must publicly condemn the Eutychian error in a subscription of his own, which is to be read aloud. 1146

**LETTER CLXIV, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** — I. He sends legates who will act in his place for the liberty of the Church and asks that what has been properly defined not be recalled for a new discussion. — II. There will always be room for dispute if the mysteries are permitted to be weighed by human reasoning and the loquacity of rhetors. — III. How hostile to the Gospel and to human salvation is the Eutychian doctrine proscribed by the synod; no debate should diminish it. — IV. The Alexandrian parricides are unworthy of every indulgence; nevertheless, if they come to their senses, hope of mercy must not be denied them. — V. He commends the legates whom he is sending, not to debate but to petition concerning what must be done for the peace of the Church. Penance must not be denied to those who are corrected, while the obdurate remain under the synodal sentence. 1148

**LETTER CLXV, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** — I. He indicates that he is sending the writings previously promised against the Eutychian doctrine. — II. The doctrines of Nestorius and Eutyches are set forth; the latter imitated Apollinaris, Valentinus, and Mani. — III. All these monstrous heresies are pierced through by the Nicene Creed. — IV. The reconciliation of humanity depends on the incarnation; without it Christ fulfills neither the office of mediator nor that of redeemer. — V. Through Christ’s sacrifice alone the world has either been reconciled to God or sinners justified. — VI. The properties of Christ’s two natures are made manifest by his different actions. — VII. The truth of Christ’s flesh is proved by the truth of his death, burial, and resurrection. — VIII. Christ’s exaltation could not be accomplished except in a true human nature. — IX. Under the pretext of honoring his divinity, it is subjected to the greatest insult when it is asserted that he lay hidden beneath the falsehood of a phantom. — X. The Catholic faith is firmly established by the tradition of the holy Fathers, and it is especially worthy of an emperor to defend it. — XI. Testimonies of the holy Greek and Latin Fathers asserting the truth of Christ’s flesh. 1155

**LETTER CLXVI, TO NEON, BISHOP OF RAVENNA.** — Concerning those returning from captivity who are uncertain whether they received baptism before their captivity. — I. Concerning children who were taken into captivity and do not remember the grace of baptism. — II. Anyone baptized by heretics is to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. 1191

**LETTER CLXVII, TO RUSTICUS, BISHOP OF NARBONNE.** — I. Those are not to be regarded as bishops whom neither the clergy elected, nor the people sought, nor the provincial bishops consecrated. Nevertheless, if any clergy are ordained by these false bishops, such an ordination may remain valid. — II. Presbyters or deacons who have been discovered guilty of any crime cannot obtain the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands. — III. Deacons, like bishops and presbyters, must abstain from marital relations, but must not repudiate their marriages. — IV. A wife is one thing and a concubine another; no one errs who gives his daughter in marriage to a man who had a concubine. — V. There is no repetition of marriage when, after a female slave has been dismissed, a wife is taken. — VI. Concerning those who are deprived of communion and die in that condition. — VII. Concerning those who delay doing penance. — VIII. Anyone who asks pardon for unlawful acts must also abstain from lawful ones. — IX. It is not fitting for a penitent to engage in commercial profit. — X. After penance he ought not to return to secular military service. — XI. If a young man undertook penance under the pressure of some danger but does not remain continent, he may be supported by the remedy of a wife. — XII. If anyone abandons the monastic vocation, he must be cleansed by the satisfaction of public penance. — XIII. Girls who, not under compulsion but of their own will, have undertaken a vow of virginity sin if they marry, even if they have not yet been consecrated. — XIV. Those who doubt whether they have been baptized must be baptized. — XV. Those who acknowledge that they were baptized but do not know under what profession should appropriately be received through the laying on of hands. — XVI. Concerning those who have taken part in the banquets of pagans and eaten sacrificial foods. 1197

**LETTER CLXVIII, TO ALL THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGH CAMPANIA, SAMNIUM, AND PICENUM.** — I. The regeneration of baptism must not be granted at every time, but only at Easter and Pentecost, unless dangerous illness has overwhelmed someone. — II. Concerning the penance of the faithful: their confession must not be made public. 1209

**LETTER CLXIX, TO LEO AUGUSTUS.** — I. Concerning Timothy the Cat, expelled from the Church of Alexandria, and the election of a Catholic prelate in his place. — II. Both integrity of faith and uprightness of morals are required in a priest. — III. The impious Cat, even if his faith should perhaps be sound, cannot be restored. 1212

**LETTER CLXX, TO GENNADIUS, BISHOP OF CONSTANTINOPLE.** — He complains that Timothy was permitted to come to Constantinople. No hope of restoration must be left to him, and care must be taken that he not involve himself in public or private conversations. 1214

**LETTER CLXXI, TO TIMOTHY, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA.** — I. He congratulates him on his election and commends charity. — II. He asks him to watch over matters of faith and to write to him frequently. 1215

**LETTER CLXXII, TO THE PRESBYTERS AND DEACONS OF THE CHURCH OF ALEXANDRIA.** — He invites them to preserve and increase harmony in the Church of Alexandria and to summon those who have been led astray by heretics to the remedy of penance. 1216

**LETTER CLXXIII, TO CERTAIN BISHOPS OF EGYPT.** — He congratulates them on the election of the Catholic Timothy in place of Timothy the Cat, commends unity, and invites them to join their care to his in restoring those who are in error. 1217

**DISSERTATION** on the lost letters both of Saint Leo to others and of others to Saint Leo, and on other monuments relating to the letters. 1217

**APPENDIX I** to the second part of the works of Saint Leo. — **SPURIOUS LETTERS.** 1233–1255

**APPENDIX II.** — Certain fragments. 1255–1263

**OBSERVATIONS AND NOTES OF QUESNEL** on the Letters of Saint Leo the Great. 1263–1506
**END OF THE FIFTY-FOURTH VOLUME.**
